# Patrologia Latina, volume 179 — English translation

## Volume front matter

**Patrologia Latina, volume 179.**

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library … of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … **Second Series**.

**Volume 179 of the Patrology.** William of Malmesbury, monk; Innocent II, Celestine II, and Lucius II, Roman pontiffs; Anacletus, antipope; Benedict, canon; Hugh Farsitus; Frowin, abbot; Arnulf.

**One volume.**

Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, in the street called d’Amboise, near the gate of Paris commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1855.

## Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, and economical—of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III.**

A chronological reprint of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, most diligently corrected according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; augmented with doubtful and apocryphal works which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; and enriched with two general indexes.

The first is an index of subjects: by consulting it one may see at a glance whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any topic. The second is an index of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily to be preferred to all others if consideration is given to the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of its correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes and its constant uniformity throughout the work, and the low price; above all, to this single methodical and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but now first brought together in our library from works belonging to all ages, places, languages, and forms.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Under the direction of J.-P. Migne, editor of the Library of the Universal Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The 260 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the 300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition includes all the authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

**Volume 179 of the Patrology.**

William of Malmesbury, monk. Innocent II, Celestine II, and Lucius II, Roman pontiffs. Anacletus, antipope. Benedict, canon. Hugh Farsitus. Frowin, abbot. Arnulf.

Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, in the street called d’Amboise, near the gate of Paris commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1855.

## Twelfth century

**The complete works of William, monk of Malmesbury.**

The writings of William which various editors—Henry Savile, Thomas Gale, Henry Warton, and recently Thomas Duffus Hardy—formerly published separately are now, for the first time, brought together and printed in one collection, after the most diligent correction.

Added are the short works, charters, and letters of Innocent II, Celestine II, and Lucius II, Roman pontiffs; Anacletus, antipope; Benedict, canon of the Church of Saint Peter in the city of Rome; Hugh Farsitus; Frowin, abbot of Mount of the Angels among the Swiss; and Arnulf.

Under the direction of J.-P. Migne, editor of the Library of the Universal Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

**One volume. Price: eight French francs.**

Printed and sold by J.-P. Migne, publisher, in the street called d’Amboise, near the gate of Paris commonly called d’Enfer, or Petit-Montrouge. 1855.

# THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1143. INNOCENT II, ROMAN PONTIFF

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0021]

## NOTICE FROM THE ROMAN BULLARIUM

(COCQUELINES, *Bullarum, privileg. ampl. Collect.*, Rome 1739, fol., vol. II, p. 202.)

[Col. 0021A] Gregory, a Roman by nation, monk of the Lateran monastery of Saints John the Baptist, John the Evangelist, and Pancras, likewise abbot of the monastery of Saints Nicholas and Primitivus, of the Order of Saint Benedict, at the place called Gabis, near Burranum [Note: [Col. 0021B] Baronius so reads in the archive of the title of Saint Praxedes.], was soon cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. He was elected Roman pontiff on 15 February 1130, was ordained priest on the following Saturday, and on the next day, namely Sunday the 23rd of the same month, was consecrated pontiff. He sat in the pontificate thirteen years, seven months, and nine days [Note: [Col. 0021B] Excluding the day of death. If anyone wonders why the years of Innocent are here reckoned from the day of his election contrary to custom—for, as I have often said, the years of the papal administration must be reckoned from the day of consecration—let him observe that I ought to follow Innocent himself, who, in the rescript to be printed below, no. 7, though it is dated 22 February 1132, nevertheless has: “Given, etc., 8 Kalends of March 1132, in the third year of the pontificate of Innocent.” Likewise, in the document by which Pope Innocent subjected the monastery of Cheminon, transferred from the order of Saint Nicholas of Arrouaise to the Cistercian order, to the monastery of the Three Fountains, we read: “Given . . . 13 Kalends of March, first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1137, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of our lord Innocent II.” This date, 17 February, falls between Innocent’s election and consecration.], while John Comnenus reigned in the East and Lothair II, then Conrad king of the Romans, in the West. He died on 24 [Note: [Col. 0022B] That this day must be assigned to Innocent’s death is taught us by the letter of his successor Celestine II, by which he informed the Cluniacs of his election and which we report in its place.] [Col. 0021B] September 1143, and was buried in the Lateran basilica; seven years later his body was transferred to the church of Saint Mary in Trastevere, the title of Callistus. The see was vacant for one day.

### Twenty-sixth schism in the Church

On the day after the election of Pope Innocent, Peter, son of Leo, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, [Col. 0022A] a man of sin, who by arms, fire, and money, not by merit of life or virtues, invaded the holy place against the Catholic and canonically elected Catholic [Note: [Col. 0022B] Saint Bernard testifies thus in his letter to the bishops of Aquitaine, no. 126.], took the name Anacletus II. He was consecrated at Saint Peter’s on the day on which Pope Innocent was consecrated at Saint Mary Nova. Rejected by the French at the council of Étampes and excommunicated at Rheims and Pisa, he finally died on 25 January 1138, after the seventh year of the schism. His body was buried in concealment.

### Twenty-seventh schism in the Church

In the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Innocent II, supreme pontiff, in March of the first indiction, [Col. 0022B] that is, in 1138, when Anacletus the antipope had died, his cardinals, having taken counsel, set up Cardinal Gregory as pope and invader for themselves and called him Victor. But two months later Victor laid aside the usurped insignia at the feet of Pope Innocent, and peace was restored to the Church.

[Col. 0023]

## NOTICE FROM MANSI’S COUNCILS

(Vol. XXI, col. 389.)

[Col. 0023A] Innocent II, born at Rome of a noble family and called Gregory before his pontificate, whose life and reputation, as Saint Bernard testifies in his letter to the bishops of Aquitaine, feared no rival, was cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. After a legitimate and canonical election, by the vote of the principal supporting cardinals, he was made successor of Honorius II on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, the very day Honorius died, in the year of the Lord 1130, in the time of Emperor Lothair. One party of a very few cardinals made Peter, son of Leo, a most powerful Roman citizen, cardinal and, as Bernard testifies in letter 127, a man unworthy of authority even over one little village, a schismatic antipope. They gave him the name Anacletus, which, as Saint Bernard says in letter 124, was the name of Antichrist and [Col. 0023B] abomination, and so caused the greatest schism. Since Innocent, Frisingensis says, could not resist because of the violence of Anacletus’s friends in the City and the power of Roger of Sicily, by whose favour he had been intruded into the see, he crossed the Alps and went to France. There he held the councils of Rheims, Clermont, and Pisa, excommunicated the antipope and his supporters, then went, attended by Saint Bernard the abbot, to Liège. Having summoned there a synod of bishops, he invited King Lothair to defend the Roman Church. And although on this occasion Lothair Caesar vainly demanded that investitures, restored to the Church at great loss to the empire, be given back to him, and learned that he could obtain nothing from the pontiff, [Col. 0023C] he promised and brought the aid requested.

For when he had scarcely entered the City, he crushed and put to flight Roger and all the supporters of the schism. Having restored Innocent to the see and the City in the seventh year after the latter had left Rome for Gaul and Germany, he was crowned emperor by him in the church of the Holy Saviour, called the Constantinian, and received the name Augustus.---These facts are from Frisingensis, Viterbiensis, Robert the continuator of Sigebert, and the abbot of Ursperg.

[Col. 0024A] In his time Peter Abelard, the Breton heresiarch and supreme philosopher, taught that there was something external to God and that some third thing must be posited between Creator and creature; that Christ had not assumed flesh in order to free man; and that the fear of the Lord is not chaste in the age to come. Concerning the Trinity he followed Arius, concerning the person of Christ Nestorius, concerning grace Pelagius, and concerning several other heresies several other heretics.---Saint Bernard in his letters, and Peter of Luxembourg.

At the same time Peter of Bruys produced the Sacramentarians, Petrobrusians, and apostolics, deformed by many errors.---Peter the Venerable, second letter and elsewhere; Bernard, letter 241, etc. On returning from Italy after restoring Innocent, Lothair, [Col. 0024B] as Frisingensis says, was seized by illness near Trent, and, as Viterbiensis says, near Verona; in the mountains themselves the most powerful emperor died in a very wretched hut, leaving a miserable reminder of the human condition, in the thirteenth year of his reign. By election of the princes at the assembly held in Mainz, Conrad, duke of Swabia and nephew through the sister of Emperor Henry IV, was designated successor to the kingdom.

At about the same time, in the eighth year after he had invaded the apostolic see, Peter, or Anacletus, the pseudo-pontiff, died struck by God’s judgment, according to Robert the continuator of Sigebert. Pope Innocent decreed that those ordained by him should be degraded and not thereafter promoted to sacred orders; thereupon his party’s cardinals substituted another Victor IV in the [Col. 0024C] schism. But after holding the see for a few months, as Saint Bernard relates—he laboured for seven years to remove this schism—he voluntarily resigned the pontificate. After these things Pope Innocent, of most unimpaired integrity of life and reputation, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Lord 1143, having sat fourteen years, seven months, and eight days. Urspergensis writes in his *Chronicle* that he held the papal see only thirteen years and seven months.

# THREEFOLD LIFE OF POPE INNOCENT II

(MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. III, part I, p. 433.)

[Col. 0025]

## MURATORI’S PREFACE

(Ibid., p. 274.)

[Col. 0025] The Lives of the ancient Roman pontiffs, committed to writing by various authors and circulated under the name of Anastasius the Librarian, end with Adrian II and Stephen VI, or, more correctly, V; the last of them are attributed to William the Librarian. It is reasonable to believe that the Lives of their successors were once written in their own times by librarians of the Holy Roman Church or by other historians. Time, however, has consumed some, and no one has hitherto collected the surviving ones into a single body. I decided to add a portion. The Este library supplied me with an ancient parchment folio codex in which are read Deeds of Popes omitted from chronicles. Its rubric runs: “There follow certain deeds of certain Roman pontiffs which are not found in the common chronicles; because they are worthy of remembrance and serve for the instruction of posterity, they have been collected in the manner written below. First, concerning Pope Leo IX, who began in the year of the Lord 1050.” The codex seems to have been written about the year of Christ 1360, or at least a few years later; for there also appears, in the same hand, a *Little Book on Preservation from Epidemic*, compiled by Master Maynus de Mayneris of Milan, professor of philosophy, medicine, and the arts, in 1360. There are therefore Lives of Leo IX, Stephen IX, Nicholas II, Alexander II, Gregory VII, Paschal II, Gelasius II, Callistus II, Honorius II, Innocent II, Celestine II, Lucius III, Eugenius III, Anastasius IV, Adrian III, Alexander III, and Gregory IX, which I now publish together for the convenience of scholars. A nearly similar codex was available to the great father of the *Annals*, Baronius; from his teaching I learned who had collected these Lives. “The Vatican library,” he writes under the year of Christ 1073, “has the deeds of Pope Gregory VII, separately written by an author of that time, which Nicholas Aragonius, in the commentary he wrote on the Roman pontiffs, beginning with Leo IX, interwove as they stand.” He had also mentioned, under 1055, the earlier *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* collected by Cardinal Nicholas Aragonius. Thus we have the collector of these Lives: Nicholas Rossellius Aragonius, who flourished under Pope Innocent VI and was added to the college of cardinals of the Holy Roman Church in 1356. Baronius further tells us under 1097 that, besides this collection, the Vatican library possesses, together with other commentaries by the same author, a commentary on the fourfold jurisdiction of the Roman Church in the kingdom of Sicily.

Most of these papal Lives were committed to writing by contemporary, or at least near-contemporary, authors, especially librarians of the Holy Roman Church. Baronius often used them in composing his *Annals*, and so did Raynaldus. Yet, apart from the advantage of having together what Baronius presented in excerpts for his purpose, he omitted much which will now be brought to public light. Moreover, the pieces produced from the Vatican codex sometimes differ so greatly from our codex that I once doubted whether the collection of Lives praised by Baronius was really the same as ours. The city of Milan also supplied two ancient codices in which the same Lives are read; the Ambrosian preserves one, the library of the metropolitan chapter the other.

The very rich treasury of the Ambrosian library presents the Lives of certain supreme pontiffs composed by Pandulf of Pisa. The Palatine associates and I judged it most useful to insert these also into the present collection. They begin with Gregory VII and end with Alexander III, and come from an author who was alive in the same period and recorded these matters in writing. We already knew, on the testimony of Felinus, Onuphrius Panvinius, Ludovico a Sancto Carolo, and others, that Pandulf had composed such Lives; and the great illuminator of ecclesiastical history, Baronius, had transferred much from them into his *Annals*. Indeed, in 1638 Constantine Cajetan printed at Rome, with notes, the Life of Gelasius II written by Pandulf; from it we learn that in 1118 this writer was enrolled in the ecclesiastical militia and lived in the Roman curia. Some identify this Pandulf with Pandulf Masca, added by Pope Lucius III to the senate of the purpled Fathers, and extend his life to 1198 and even later. Oldoinus, Cave, and others accepted this opinion; but Pagi rejected it under 1121, no. 9, and rightly, as it seems to me as well. For it is not likely that the historian Pandulf prolonged his life so far as to exceed a hundred years and, even as a centenarian, undertake arduous and distant embassies, as is recorded of Cardinal Pandulf Masca. It is therefore fairer to posit two men, alike in name and country but utterly different in age and person.

Furthermore, the Lives of the Roman pontiffs composed by Bernard Gui will be added to our collection; of these I must now speak. Bernard Gui is an illustrious name among ecclesiastical writers, and his reputation is so widespread in learned books that it would be plainly superfluous to add anything here about his life and writings. Yet I shall select a few points. He was a native of Limoges, born about 1260 in the village of Royère near the rock of the Bee. Having entered the Order of Preachers, he held distinguished offices among them; in 1305 he was appointed inquisitor of heretical depravity against the Albigensians. In 1323 he was made bishop of Tuy in [Col. 0027] Galicia, and in the next year was transferred to the see of Lodève, or Lodovensis, in Narbonese Gaul. Finally, in 1331 he ended his last day and was buried in the church of the Preachers at Limoges. He was a man of great counsel, great experience, proved prudence, and tested religion; modest and sensible, profoundly humble; illustrious in reputation, favour, learning, and eloquence; and further likened to the primitive Fathers in fervour of faith and in zeal and sincerity of religion. These words outline the singular prerogatives of this distinguished man in his anciently written Life prefixed to the *Speculum Sanctorale*—a bulky work likewise composed by him and still unpublished—which Philippe Labbe published in *Nova Bibliotheca manuscriptorum librorum*, vol. II, p. 512, where all other matters concerning his Life are available. He was called not Bernard Guido but Bernard Guidonis, that is, son of Guido, as in *Paulus Warnefridi*, “Paul, son of Warnefrid”, and *Petrus Damiani*, “Peter of Damian”; Peter took his surname from his brother Damian, who had stood in place of a father. Dupin in his *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica* and Cave in his *Historia litteraria*, to omit other admirers of this distinguished writer and bishop, have published a catalogue of the books Bernard left behind. The reader must now be informed that the vast Ambrosian library preserves a very ancient manuscript codex containing various works of Bernard, written with the greatest care and ornamented with pictures and gold. One might say it was written and compiled while the author himself lived, and even at his direction, to be presented to some prince. At least I think it was copied not long after his age by a certain Antonio the Spaniard, who is mentioned at the end. There first occur the *Flowers of Chronicles*, or *Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*. The little book is dedicated to Pope John XXII. The author identifies himself in these words: “Brother Bernard Guidonis, of the Order of Preachers, inquisitor of heretical depravity in the kingdom of France, appointed by the Apostolic See.” An old marginal note in the book stated: “Note: this inquisitor was afterwards bishop of Lodève; I write Lodovensis.” Bernard testifies that he collected these Lives through the sixteenth year of Pope John, that is, 1331. And in fact the narrative is carried down to that year, although the end of his letter to the same pope reads: “Given at Avignon, 7 Ides of August, when exactly four years and not a day more or less had elapsed since the creation of your pontificate, in the year of the Lord 1320.” Thus Bernard wrote this in that year and then, as often happens, added events that occurred from time to time until the day of his death, that is, until 1331 [the supplied text prints 1131 here, evidently for the 1331 stated above].

[Col. 0027]

## FIRST LIFE, BY BERNARD GUI

[Col. 0027A] Innocent II was a Roman by nation, son of John from the region of Trastevere. He began in the year of the Lord 1130, although 1132 is found in a certain chronicle. He sat thirteen years, seven months, and eight days; the bishopric was vacant two days. He was previously called Gregory and was cardinal-deacon of Saint Vincent. He was elected pope, though not unanimously, by the greater part of the cardinals, while Peter, son of Leo, was elected by the smaller part; Gregory took the name Innocent and Peter, son of Leo, that of Anacletus. But while Peter, son of Leo, remained at Saint Peter’s through the power of his relatives, he held the Church itself with an armed hand and by violence; taking the golden crucifix, the hanging crowns, and the whole treasury of gold, silver, and precious stones, [Col. 0027B] he plundered it. He did the same to Saint Mary Major, rich in a great treasury, and to other churches of the City; with that treasury he corrupted almost all the Romans. Innocent, having no support in the City, left Rome with the cardinals, set out for Gaul in two galleys, and was honourably received by the king of France. When the Gallican Church adhered to him, he held councils, first at Rheims and second at Pisa, was confirmed in the papacy, and Peter, son of Leo, was anathematized by all the bishops of Gaul and Germany. Yet Martin’s chronicle and another one say that he held councils first at Clermont, [Col. 0027C] then at Rheims.

When Pope Innocent held the council at Rheims, with the king of France present, on 8 Kalends of November, Louis, son of Louis and brother of Philip the firstborn, who, as has been said, had been suddenly carried off by death, was consecrated king about the year of the Lord 1137 and reigned forty-three years.

In those days the Church, bride of Christ, had a fair and beautiful countenance. Surrounded by a variety of orders and professions, Cluniacs here, Cistercians, Carthusians, Grandmontines, and Premonstratensians there, and elsewhere religious women of diverse habit and profession, women devoted to God and living regularly in poverty, continence, and under the yoke of obedience, challenged one another in religious fervour, and new monasteries were founded in different places in rivalry. [Col. 0028B] The Carthusian monks indeed gradually spread; more continent than the rest, seeing very many labour under the pest of avarice, they set limits by establishing a fixed number of men, animals, and possessions which they may by no means exceed. Since each has his own cell, they chose more perfectly to die to the world and more carefully to live to God than the rest.

In the year of the Lord 1132 Emperor Lothair II prepared expeditions into Italy and, bringing Pope Innocent to Rome with bishops and archbishops against Peter, son of Leo, who had fortified the monastery of Saint Peter, placed him powerfully in the pontifical see in the Lateran *Epompio* [Col. 0028C]; Lothair himself was crowned emperor by Innocent. But a certain new chronicle writes it in this way: “In the year of the Lord 1139, Innocent, returning from Gaul to Italy at Lothair’s urging, [Col. 0029A] came into Italy. Lothair met him with a great army and, with bishops, brought him to Rome. Having overcome Peter, son of Leo, and extirpated all his offspring, he banished them from the City and restored Innocent also to his own see. In the same year Lothair was crowned by Innocent in the Lateran.” This is from the aforesaid chronicle, which reports that the same events occurred, though under another year.

When the aforesaid Pope Innocent was returning to Rome, after making peace between the Genoese and Pisans, he considered the great services they had rendered to himself and to the Church. He therefore made the bishop of Genoa, who had been subject to the archbishop of Milan, an archbishop; likewise he raised the bishop of Pisa to be archbishop of Tuscany and primate of all Sardinia. This is said in the aforesaid new chronicle to have occurred in the year of the Lord 1140. [Col. 0029B]

After Lothar had been crowned emperor, emperor and pope entered Apulia together against Count Roger, king of Sicily, who was rebellious and hostile to Pope Innocent and supported Peter Leo. They drove Roger out of Apulia; and, after the Sicilian Roger had been put to flight, the pope returned to Rome and Emperor Lothar to Germany.

In the year of the Lord 1135 Henry, king of England, died, and his nephew Stephen, by Henry’s sister, succeeded to the kingdom; but, after being greatly weakened, he soon lost all Normandy. Henry’s daughter Matilda, who, as was said above, had married Geoffrey, count of Anjou, attacked Louis, king of France, in the duchy of Normandy [Col. 0029C] and inflicted great troubles and disasters upon him in England itself; she later captured him in war, but released him in exchange for her brother Count Robert, who had been taken from the kingdom. In the following year, 1136, William, count of Poitou and duke of Aquitaine, set out for Saint James and died on Good Friday, 9 April, in the church of Saint James, where he was honourably buried before the altar. As he died, he charged the nobles with him to give his elder daughter Eleanor in marriage to Louis, king of France, with the duchy of Aquitaine. Louis accordingly joined her to himself in marriage in the presence of the leading men of his kingdom, with very solemn wedding celebrations. Louis’s father died at Paris within a month [Col. 0029D] and was buried in the church of Saint Denis before the body of that martyr on 1 August, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign and the year of the Lord 1137.

At this time Count Theobald of Champagne flourished: a father of orphans, guide of widows, eye of the blind, foot of the lame; exceptionally generous in supporting the poor, building monasteries, and showing incomparable liberality to all religious persons. The Lord made him great and enlarged him in noble offspring. For he begot Count Henry, Count Theobald, Count Stephen, William archbishop of Reims, and several daughters. The youngest, named Adela, was later taken as wife by the most devout Louis, king of France, as will appear below; by her he begot Philip, heir to the kingdom. [Col. 0030A] William, count of Nevers, a man distinguished by justice and honour, also flourished; his wonderful devotion later shone out when, from a mighty secular prince, he became in the Charterhouse a most humble poor man of Christ.

At the same time Saint Malachy, archbishop in Ireland, shone forth as a pattern of virtue and an example of every perfection. Among the other signs of his virtues he raised a dead man, through whom faith was renewed and religion spread in Ireland. Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, also shone, a most celebrated teacher and master, greatly trained in the knowledge of the liberal arts and of Holy Scripture and almost incomparably learned. After the great Anselm, he produced a useful gloss, full of sacred delights, on the Psalter [Col. 0030B], Paul’s Epistles, and the Lives of the Saints. In 1138 Pope Innocent II confirmed and fortified by privilege the Cistercian abbey of Blessed Mary of Ardorello in the diocese of Albi, whose first abbot there was then Fulk, in the ninth year of Innocent’s pontificate. Pope Alexander III later repeated that confirmation and strengthened it with a fuller grant in 1165, the sixth year of his pontificate. Its foundress at Montpezat was the devout noblewoman Cecilia, viscountess of Bourges, who lies buried there beside the threshold of the church. The following verses are inscribed on the stone of her tomb: [Col. 0030C]

> Let everyone who does not know learn that true Cecilia rests
> in this sarcophagus, a woman of strength.
> She made this monastery and gave the brothers many goods
> from her other houses, whether cultivated or uncultivated.
> Therefore let those now present and those to come alike pray
> here for the dead woman, by whom all these things were provided.

In 1139 John of the Times died; he had lived 361 years from the time of Charlemagne, whose armour-bearer he had been in 1140. Hugh, canon of Saint Victor at Paris, famous for religious life and learning and second to none of his time in his command of the seven liberal arts, died. He shone with such quickness of intellect and subtlety of spirit that he scarcely had an equal in his time. At the same time, and in the same monastery, Richard, a man distinguished in learning and religion, flourished [Col. 0030D]; he discussed the Trinity with the greatest subtlety.

At the same time a council was held at Sens, with Louis present, of bishops and abbots against Peter Abelard, who was scandalizing the Church by a certain profane novelty of words or opinions. Summoned by them to answer, he feared the judgment of justice and escaped by appealing to a hearing before the apostolic see; not long after, he died at Saint Marcellus near Chalon.

Pope Innocent then fell ill and died after a solemn council had been held in the Lateran; he was buried in the Lateran church in a porphyry sarcophagus in 1144. One chronicle writes 1145, but the former date is preferable.

## Second Life, by Pandulf of Pisa

Innocent, a Roman by nation, son of John, from the Trastevere district, ruled for thirteen years, seven months, and eight days; the see was vacant for two days. He went with a Roman army against Roger, duke of Apulia, but was captured by him with those of his party with whom he had taken flight. He condemned the whole party of Peter Leo together with its ordinations. This Peter, son of Peter Leo, was elected by the smaller number of cardinals and called Anacletus. He caused hostile attacks upon the strongholds of the Frangipani and the places in which Innocent had taken refuge with the cardinals. Since he gained nothing thus, he went with an armed force to the church of Saint Peter the Apostle and violently stripped away the golden crucifix, the hanging crowns of gold and silver, and precious stones. He also destroyed the ciborium which Pope Saint Leo had built. He did the same at Saint Mary Major, rich in treasure, and at the other churches of the City. After corrupting almost all the Romans with this treasure, Pope Innocent, having no support in Rome, crossed with the cardinals to France in two galleys and was honourably received by the king of France, after holding councils at Clermont and Reims.

On his return, after making peace between Genoa and Pisa, he considered the great services they had rendered to himself and to the Church, made the bishop of Genoa—formerly subject to Milan—an archbishop, and made Pisa primate of all Sardinia. Immediately after Lothar was crowned emperor, both entered Apulia together; after Roger of Sicily, who was rebellious against the lord pope, was put to flight, the most Christian Lothar returned to Germany and the pope to Rome. There, after a solemn council, he was buried in the Lateran in a porphyry sarcophagus wonderfully carved.

## Third Life, by Cardinal Aragonio

Innocent II, a Roman by nation, from Trastevere, son of John, also called Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo [Note: A and M read “of the title of Saint Angelo,” etc.], ruled thirteen years, seven months, and eight days. In the same day, amid contention, he was elected with Peter, son of Peter Leo, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Calixtus, on 14 February 1130; from this a great discord arose in Rome, and bishops and cardinals divided into two parties. But the better [Note: A and M: “greater,” etc.] and sounder party adhered to Innocent, who was aided by greater zeal and merits. Those who steadfastly stood with him were William of Palestrina, Matthew of Albano, John of Ostia, and Conrad of Sabina, bishops; also Peter of Saint Martin, John of Saint Chrysogonus of Cremona, Hubert of Saint Clement, Anselm of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, Josselin of Saint Cecilia, Gerard of the Holy Cross, and Peter of Saint Anastasia, cardinal-priests; and the cardinal-deacons Romanus of Saint Mary in Portico, Gregory of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, Aimeric of Saint Mary the New, chancellor of the apostolic see, Albert of Saint Theodore, and Guido of Saint Mary in Via Lata. Three of those who had adhered to the opposing party—Desiderius of Saint Praxedes, Liutfrid [Note: M: *Luccifredus*; A: *Luccafredus*.] of Saint Vitalis, and R. of Saint Sabina—were converted to Pope Innocent.

Peter, son of Peter Leo, with his followers, despised Innocent’s humility. He did not make God his helper, but trusted in the multitude of riches, the power of his kin, and the strength of his fortifications; he caused hostile attacks upon the houses of the Frangipani where Innocent had taken refuge with his brethren. Yet the result was contrary to his expectation: he slightly injured Innocent’s party, while his own followers returned to him with serious loss. Moved to indignation and anger, he rode with a very great multitude to Saint Peter and seized the church itself by violence. He entered the sanctuary and, like a sacrilegious robber, plundered and broke up the golden crucifix, the hanging crowns, and the whole treasure of gold and silver, precious stones and gems which Roman pontiffs and orthodox emperors had devoutly offered to that church. [Note: M reads *minuit*, “diminished,” for *comminuit*, “broke up.”] He also presumed to strip the ciborium which Saint Leo had built over the altar. Having removed everything, he went to the patriarchal church of Blessed Mary [Note: M has a marginal note in the same hand: “He means the church of Blessed Mary of the City.”] and likewise tried to despoil that church, enriched with a far greater treasure. He laid hands besides upon other churches of the City, seizing and carrying off whatever precious thing he found in them. Thus enriched everywhere by such great merchandise [Note: A: *inique*, “wickedly,” for *undique*, “everywhere”.], he endeavoured to buy the greater part of the venal City, corrupting the great and oppressing the small. He also bound the common people so closely to himself that, apart from the fortifications of the Frangipani and Corsi, Pope Innocent had no support in Rome.

Since the pontiff was thus besieged on every side, so that no one could approach him without danger of life, he decided to leave the City and cross to Gaul. He embarked in two galleys with all the brethren who had stood with him, except Conrad, bishop of Sabina, whom he left as his vicar in Rome. Having passed the difficult mouth of the Tiber, he arrived safely, with the Lord’s help, at Pisa. After staying there for some time, he made, with God’s help, a firm truce in the serious war being waged between the Pisans and Genoese. When this was properly accomplished, he entered the sea again and, passing through Genoa, arrived safely at Saint-Gilles. Going on through Viviers and Le Puy, he entered Auvergne and first held a solemn council at Clermont. There, after receiving messengers from Lothar, king of the Germans, and arranging other matters which seemed to concern the condition of the Church, he turned his way toward France. Thus Louis, king of France, received Pope Innocent at Orléans with glory and due honour, and Henry, king of England, did so at Chartres. He afterwards crossed to Lorraine, where the aforesaid King Lothar met him at Liège with bishops and other prelates of the German realm. After gladly receiving the pontiff, the king, having taken counsel with his princes, caused an expedition to Rome to be sworn and promised to restore the pope to Saint Peter’s see in the second year. The pope then returned to France and held a second synod at Reims, in mid-Lent, after calling a general council from five kingdoms. When these things were done, he prepared to return to the City; passing through Saint-Gilles and Montgenèvre, he entered Lombardy and, after celebrating Easter at Asti, came to Piacenza. There he held a third council, having assembled bishops and other prelates of churches from Lombardy, the province of Ravenna, and the regions of the Lower March.

Meanwhile King Lothar, as he had promised, came with an army into Lombardy and held a general conference at Roncaglia with the same pope and the Lombards concerning the state of Church and Empire. The pontiff went before the king and, crossing Tuscany by Mount Bardone, returned to Pisa. There he summoned the Genoese and, after receiving sufficient oaths from both cities that they would obey his command without contradiction concerning the war stirred up between them, ordered both henceforth to preserve firm peace with each other. Considering the filial devotion and the many useful services which those cities had freely rendered to Roman pontiffs in many necessities of the Church, the holy pontiff judged them worthy of honour and special advancement. From the customary liberality of the apostolic see, he granted the Pisan Church primacy over Sardinia, subjecting to it the bishop of Populonia and three other bishops in Corsica: namely those of Aleria and Nebbio . . . . . . . . . . He emancipated the bishop of Genoa from subjection to the archbishop of Milan and newly made him a special metropolitan of the apostolic see, ordering the bishop of Bobbio and the abbot of Pruni, whom he created bishop, to obey him. He also granted him three bishops in Corsica.

While this was happening, King Lothar came into Tuscany and again conferred with the pope at Calcinara in Pisan territory. Agreeing that they should hasten to Rome, the king went by the public road and the pope by the coast road as far as Viterbo. They then proceeded together, conversing, through the territories of Orta, Sabina, and Farfa; approaching Rome, they encamped beside the church of Saint Agnes. The prefect of the City, Theobald, Peter Latro, other Roman nobles, and Trasteverines met them; they entered Rome in 1134. The pope lodged in the Lateran palace, while Lothar pitched tents on the Aventine. Then the Pisans and Genoese came to Rome with a naval force to aid Pope Innocent and subjected to him the old city, the Tower of Pulverio, and all the Marmorata. The king was crowned emperor Augustus by the pope in the Lateran church on 4 June, and both returned joyfully to the Aventine. At that time the greater part of Rome turned to Pope Innocent and Peter Leo’s strength was greatly diminished. Because the summer heat was then imminent and the Germans greatly feared the unhealthy Roman air, the emperor, after arranging in the City what seemed necessary for the pope’s faithful supporters, returned home; the pope again returned, through the Lord’s aid, to Pisa. In that year he held a fourth council in the greater church of Pisa, having summoned all Church prelates from Spain, Gascony, England, France, Burgundy, Germany, Hungary, Lombardy, and Tuscany. Among other matters, the following bishops were deposed: Eustace of Valence, the bishop of Orange, Peter of Tortona, Hubert of Lucca, the bishop of Bergamo, and Bojanus of Arezzo.

Because Count Roger of Sicily had risen against the unity of the Catholic Church and fostered and defended the heresiarch Peter in his error, the most Christian Emperor Lothar, inflamed with zeal for God and the faith, again summoned the forces of the Empire as the Catholic advocate of the Church and undertook to disinherit and expel the count from the whole Empire. Thus, in the fifth year of Innocent’s pontificate, he entered the territory of L’Aquila in force with the pope. The Pisans also roused their strength to aid the pope in expelling the count and, having prepared a great fleet of galleys and other ships, came as far as Salerno, plundering Amalfi and Ravello and other neighbouring fortified places. After Bari had been besieged and conquered and the remaining Apulian cities subdued, Count Roger fled to Sicily; emperor and pope together made Count Raino duke of Apulia. Having won so great a triumph through Saint Peter’s merits, the emperor returned gloriously to Germany and the pope to Rome. A few days later the heresiarch Peter died in his error and was secretly buried. As his followers wasted away and failed among themselves, in order to make peace with Pope Innocent more honourably they set up one of their idols, which the Romans mockingly called Carnecorium [Note: A: *Carnecornium*.]. After a few days, led by repentance, they brought the idol to the pope’s feet and were mercifully received into the Church. Then the whole City turned to Innocent as shepherd and bishop of their souls. A voice of joy was heard throughout the world, because, through God’s aid, there had come to be one flock and one shepherd; through the pope’s zeal and power such peace flourished in Rome as no one remembered from earlier times. In the year of the Incarnation 1138, the tenth of Lord Innocent’s pontificate, he held a great council after summoning patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and other Church prelates from all parts of the world. On its final day, among other things, these decrees were proclaimed:

> “If anyone, at the devil’s persuasion, incurs the guilt of this sacrilege by laying violent hands upon a cleric or monk, he is subject to anathema. No bishop may presume to absolve him, except where danger of death presses, until he is brought before the apostolic presence and receives its command. Moreover, we annul the ordinations made by Peter Leo and other schismatics and heretics, and judge them void.”

### On the severe famine in Rome in the time of Pope Innocent II

In the first year of his pontificate Rome suffered so severe a famine that a sextary of grain was sold for five solidi of Pavia coinage. This blessed pontiff established from his treasury an annual benefice of one hundred pounds in Pavia money for the judges and advocates of the Roman City, and ordered them to take the following oath.

### Oath taken by advocates appointed in Rome by Pope Innocent

> “In the name of the Lord, Amen. I, N., advocate, swear that from this hour forward I shall not maliciously prosecute or defend the pleadings or cases of Romans in which I am advocate or patron; rather, according to the knowledge granted me by God, I shall conduct them according to constitutions, laws, and good customs. When justice in such cases has become known to me, if I am asked, I shall disclose it to the judges and give them my assent in the judgment. I shall accept no payment for this, neither myself nor through a subordinate person, nor permit it to be accepted; if it is accepted, once I know of it, I shall cause it to be returned within fifteen days. I shall not through ill will refuse my advocacy to anyone who has a case, if asked by him, saving the benefices which we have from churches or others, and excepting gifts worth twelve denarii, offered to us freely and without demand. I shall observe all these things in good faith, without deceit or evil intent, so long as Pope Innocent or his successors pay us advocates and judges each year the one hundred pounds, or their value, in Pavia denarii.”

This blessed pontiff completely renewed and built the church of Blessed Mary Mother of God, of the title of Calixtus. He excellently repaired with great beams the roof of the Lateran church which had suddenly fallen. In the church of Saint Paul he strengthened most firmly the title which was falling into ruin, building a wall upon marble columns, and repaired part of that church’s roof with very long beams. He also thoroughly repaired the church of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, shaken by excessive age. In the Lateran palace he built two chambers from the foundations and strengthened the whole *longura sinino* [Note: M: *Summo*; A: *Simuo*.]; he did many other famous things in his time. Near the end of his pontificate the Roman people, lovers of novelty, under the guise of public advantage, set up a senate on the Capitol against his will. He made many ordinations in December and other months: eighteen deacons, twenty priests, and sixty-two bishops in various places. He died in Rome on 24 September and was honourably buried in the Lateran church in a porphyry sarcophagus, wonderfully made.

## Three letters asserting the canonical character of Innocent’s election

*(Mansi, Councils, XXI, 432, from the Udalric codex.)*

### I. The cardinals and bishops of the Holy Roman Church to King Lothar

L., most renowned king of the Romans, radiant with the strictness of justice, by the clemency of God that inspires you: Bishops N. and N. and the Roman cardinals, with their other brethren, send greeting and everlasting victory over your enemies.

No Christian, most excellent king, is ignorant that the Roman Church, by God’s institution, the imitation of the holy Fathers, and the devotion of religious men, is mistress not of the City but of the world. While she stands, all things stand prosperously; when she fails, all things decline. As she excels more highly, so she more easily repels from herself the tyranny of winds and storms; and the more she is shaken by the whirlwind of worldly things, the more brightly she is purified. When Pope H., of blessed memory, departed and entered the way of all the earth, we bishops and cardinals chose G., cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo—a respectable man, restrained in conduct, beloved by God and by those who fear God—as supreme pontiff. We led him to the Lateran church surrounded by crowds of the faithful; seated on the highest throne, he was honoured by us and an innumerable multitude of religious people. We then went up to the palace, performed the customary rites, and gave him all the pontifical insignia of Pope H., Pope Calixtus, Pope Paschal, and their predecessors. When this had been duly done about the third hour, Peter Leo, at the sixth hour—when Judas crucified Christ and the darkness of night covered the world—hurried with his conspirators, kinsmen, and others openly hired for money to the church of Saint Martin, near the towers of the brethren. He indecently put on a red cope and seized the counterfeit insignia of the pontificate. On the next day he attacked Saint Peter’s church with arms, surrounded it with engines, broke roofs and walls, and, after killings and an immense shedding of human blood, entered the gates of the prince of the apostles with the wicked. On the following day he went with an armed force to the Lateran church and violently assaulted it with smoke, fire, and blood. He mounted to the palace, broke the bridges, shattered the papal seats, opened Saint Lawrence’s treasury, plundered what seemed best to him, and withdrew to his own place. Afterwards he attacked the stronghold in which our lord Pope Innocent resided with the Catholic Church. But, having lost many knights and horses, he withdrew shamefully to his house in the confusion of his disgrace.

Those going and returning who hasten to Rome or Jerusalem report how great are the plunderings of churches—especially of Saint Peter’s treasure, which Roman pontiffs and most sacred emperors dedicated to God and Saint Peter in golden lamps, chalices, censers, candlesticks, images, crosses, gems, and other precious vessels, as well as cloths and silken garments woven with gold and gems—the misdirection of ecclesiastical estates, and the despoiling of pilgrims. What other shameful things he and his accomplices do must not be related to royal ears. Yet, by God’s grace, he now lies hidden within the enclosures of the paternal walls; abbots, marquises, princes, and other barons hasten to aid the Catholic and apostolic Church. The Eastern and Western Churches, with equal will, consent, and spirit, condemn the said invader by anathema; they embrace, venerate, and continually visit with messengers the lord Pope Innocent, canonically elected by Catholics and canonically consecrated, as universal father and vicar of Saint Peter. Let your royal prudence, most glorious king, inspired by the Holy Spirit, determine what your Highness ought to do. Therefore gird yourself and hasten, in the accustomed manner, with archbishops, bishops, abbots, religious men, and the princes of the realm to the aid of the prince of the apostles, so that the Church of God may rejoice, Christian religion be exalted, the treachery of schismatics be suppressed, and the King of heaven bless the crown of your head. Our venerable brother G. [Gualter] and God-beloved archbishop of Ravenna will explain to you by word of mouth what is lacking here; we commend him carefully to your Serenity and ask that, for reverence of Saint Peter and the whole Catholic Church, you treat him honourably.

### II. Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, to N., archbishop of Naples or Magdeburg

To the venerable lord N., archbishop of the holy Church of Naples, or Magdeburg: G., servant, though unworthy, of the holy Church of Ravenna, sends greeting and perpetual love in Christ.

We have greatly rejoiced and given thanks in the Lord on seeing your most holy fatherhood’s letter, by which you wished to visit one who is unknown and unwelcome in appearance. Although long spaces of land separate us bodily, we embrace you spiritually, since what joins things divided joins those that are separated; to the best of our ability we are ready to serve you. As to the single point on which you seek our counsel, we reply thus. When the bishop of the most holy Roman see, our father Honorius of blessed memory, died, as we heard and have found true, Innocent, formerly called Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, was canonically raised to govern the holy Roman Church by the election of our venerable brethren and lords, who unanimously came together: William of Palestrina, M. of Albano, John of Ostia, D. of Sabina, bishops, and the other Catholic cardinals. Afterwards Peter Leo, who had long coveted the papacy, tried to usurp and occupy our universal mother, the holy Roman Church, shamefully and simoniacally, by the violence of his relatives, the shedding of blood, the stripping of holy images, and brazen action and conspiracy, putting on a red cope for himself. Since this truth is known, together with the whole Italian Church we unhesitatingly embrace, devoutly honour, and venerate the aforesaid Innocent—sober, prudent, chaste, gentle, humble, and formed by every moral excellence—divinely consecrated by the aforesaid venerable brethren in the Church’s manner, as our universal father, pope, and apostolic. But Peter, truly son of the roaring lion seeking whom he may devour, we condemn and reject: not elected but raised against God and the holy Church; not assumed but intruded; not apostolic but apostate; not Catholic but heretical; not consecrated but accursed, with divine authority opposing him in all things and through all things.

We therefore humbly entreat the prudence of your holiness and, with reciprocal charity, strengthen the constancy of your faith as an immovable column in the Lord: remain firmly in the faith of Saint Peter, obedience to his vicar our most beloved father Innocent, elected by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and love of the holy Roman Church. Moreover, lest Christ’s seamless garment be divided by the treacherous and faithless who cast lots, which may divine mercy avert, and lest Peter’s ship, shaken by sea-waves on every side, be endangered, we earnestly urge you to exhort Lord Lothar, invincible king of the Romans, strongly and without delay to come to the City. Confirm without hesitation in this faith both the brethren and bishops of your diocese and all your fellow provincials, like another Peter once converted, so that peace in the Church may be restored through the lord king and through you; so that the heresy of Jewish perfidy, recently arisen in that Church, may by the Lord’s help be wholly uprooted; and so that you may set yourselves firmly, like an iron wall for the house of the Lord, against everything that exalts itself against unity and truth. Finally, we humbly commend ourselves to your most holy prayers in all things and earnestly ask that what we are called or thought to be before men and by men, we may at some time deserve to be before God through the aid of your merits. May divine mercy preserve your praying holiness in safety for a long time, for the benefit of many and for the honour and usefulness of the holy Church.

### III. Henry, bishop of Lucca, to the same recipient

To the venerable lord N., worthy archbishop of the holy Church of Naples: H., by God’s grace servant and bishop of Lucca, wishes the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

## On the election of the Roman pontiff

Had it pleased you that an account of the election of a Roman pontiff should be made known to you by religious men wiser than I, it would not have been improper to seek it. But since I ought not to fail in my duty toward you, my father and lord, I shall touch briefly on a few points out of many.

When the cardinals had assembled in the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle, they decreed that the election of the pontiff should be entrusted to eight persons: two bishops, G., of Palestrina, and C., of Sabina; three cardinal priests, P. of Pisa, P. Rufus, and Peter Leonis; and three cardinal deacons, Gregory of Sant’Angelo, son of Jonathan, Aimeric the chancellor, and Jonathan. If Pope Honorius, then at the point of death, should depart this life, the person chosen unanimously by them, or by the sounder part of their counsel, was to be received by all as lord and Roman pontiff. The bishop of Palestrina, with the others, further decreed that anyone opposing an election so made should be subject to anathema; anyone attempting to elect another was to have his act treated as void and was never again to hold a place in the Church. Peter Leonis himself confirmed this orally, adding that they need not fear a scandal in the Church on his account: he would rather be drowned in the abyss than occasion one.

It was then decreed that the electors should meet together on the following day. Peter Leonis, however, left them with Jonathan and, like that raven—whether overwhelmed or detained by greed for flesh—scorned to return to his brethren. Gathering separate cabals, he strove to set up an altar of malediction. Had Pope Honorius, whom they believed already dead, not shown himself at the window to the people, the herald of Antichrist, supported by a crowd of relatives, servants hired by gifts and services, would before the appointed time have exalted himself above what is called God.

Those whose hearts God had touched, fearing danger to the Church and the growing storm, therefore acted when Pope Honorius was gathered to his fathers on the sixth day before the beginning of Lent. After funeral rites suited to the emergency of place and time, though not performed in the customary manner, the bishops of Palestrina and Sabina, B. Rufus, Aimeric the chancellor, and Gregory, cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo—the fifth man—elected as supreme pontiff a man unwilling and resisting in every way, in the presence of religious bishops, cardinal priests, deacons, and subdeacons. Peter Leonis, the eighth, P. of Pisa, the sixth, and Jonathan, the seventh, remained apart.

When this became known to those who had conceived deceit in their hearts in order to bring forth iniquity, Peter Leonis—who for a long time, greedy and ambitious, had coveted this very outcome, enticing now one group and now another by three kinds of gifts—was clothed, alas, by those whom they could assemble, with the red cape, in the presence of the bishop of Porto. Much bloodshed, destruction of places in the city, and dreadful stripping of sacred images followed, shameful crime, to pay his soldiers and those obedient to him. Yet Leo, Peter Leonis’s brother, and another Leo, called “the Bread-breaker,” although they gnawed their teeth at each other, had before the pope’s death sworn before the cardinals that neither would make a scandal over the pontifical election, but that they would honor and reverence as lord whomever the Church chose.

We therefore embrace, approve, and follow the judgment and counsel of religious, Catholic, and orthodox men from Tuscany, Lombardy, and regions beyond the Alps. We utterly reject Peter Leonis as a schismatic in this crime and, because he defends his schism, as a heretic; but we hold, receive, reverence, and honor Lord Innocent as father and supreme pontiff. May the Lord of all deign to preserve your fatherhood as it prays for us. I beg you to regard me, in unwavering fidelity, as one of the servants of your holiness.

## Letters of Vulgrin, sixty-second archbishop of Bourges, in the cause of Innocent II

**Editorial note.** Lord Vulgrin, the sixty-second holder of the see, was noble, learned, eloquent, prudent in counsel, and adorned with every virtue. In the third year of his pontificate he blessed Suger, elected at Saint-Denis in France, as abbot there in the presence of King Louis. When Girard, bishop of Angoulême, a factional man and schismatic defending the cause of the antipope Anacletus (formerly Peter Leonis), began a grave persecution of the Catholic Church and presumed to drive resisting bishops from their sees, the other orthodox bishops of Aquitaine resolved to seek advice from their patriarch and primate Vulgrin as an asylum. They knew that his authority could restrain violent schemes and that he would willingly spend himself in charity for the peace and safety of churches subject to his primatial right. Several therefore sent him letters, inserted here as evidence of the events.

### I. V., bishop of Saintes, to Vulgrin

V., bishop of Saintes, sends greeting and obedience to Vulgrin, by God’s grace archbishop of Bourges, his dearest lord. We report that Girard of Angoulême has so disturbed God’s Church in our regions that men now ask one another what profession each holds. Because we and the bishops of the province refused his perverse persuasion, he used our prince’s aid to expel the bishops of Poitiers and Limoges and intrude others; since he could not obtain bishops, he did not consecrate them. By the count’s hand he also drove the abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély from his monastery in our diocese. Because we would not consecrate—indeed, would not execrate—his intruders, he sowed such discord between us and our prince that we and our canons have left our see, city, homes, and possessions for justice’s sake, through fear of the prince’s threats.

By God’s merciful providence, this most wicked forerunner of Antichrist, as he passed one day through our diocese, was captured by our brother-in-law Aimar of Archiac, a valiant knight, and is still held captive. His capture brings the greatest joy and exultation to our Church and all the people. We therefore beg you to send letters to the church of Bordeaux, which chose him archbishop, and to the bishops of Agen, Périgueux, Poitiers, Limoges, and to us, clergy, and people; by obedience forbid and command all to obey him in nothing or honor him in any way. State that you have excommunicated him and order all bishops to excommunicate him. Annul and condemn his election, made by the Bordeaux canons under the count’s violence without the election and consent of all suffragans and against the opposition of Agen; depose Girard permanently. Grant favor and absolution to his captors, excommunicate anyone attempting violence to secure his release, and order the archbishop of Auch, Bordeaux, and their suffragans publicly to excommunicate all who aid the duke of Aquitaine while he continues this disturbance. Command our fellow bishops to help Aimar with money, gifts, and other assistance so that he may defend himself against our prince and the count of Angoulême, who threaten him to procure Girard’s release. Farewell.

### II. G., bishop of Périgueux, to Vulgrin

G., humble servant of the church of Périgueux, sends greeting and due obedience to his most holy and venerable lord Vulgrin, by God’s grace primate of Bourges. Your fatherhood knows the persecution raised in the province of Bordeaux, and even in Bourges, by Girard’s schism, and the great affliction we there endure. We rejoice greatly to hear that you and the king of France steadfastly remain obedient to Pope Innocent. Yet we greatly wonder that you, our primate, have not yet visited or strengthened us by letters. Assure and confirm us and all the Bordeaux suffragans in our proposed obedience, so that whatever turn events take, you will always sustain us and change nothing without us, but with us all reach a settled end. We must answer Girard of Angoulême, who made himself archbishop of Bordeaux without our counsel and challenges our obedience; we must follow you, our primate and head. Cherish and protect us as your sons and members in the bosom of your protection. Obtain letters from the king of France promising and granting his support to us and all the Bordeaux suffragans. Send us your letters and the king’s. If you could come down as far as Cahors and meet us there, it would be praiseworthy. Farewell.

### III. V., bishop of Poitiers, to Vulgrin

V., humble priest of Poitiers and exile for righteousness, sends greeting and blessing to Vulgrin, archbishop by God’s grace, his deservedly beloved lord. Your paternal kindness will readily grant the just petitions of your sons, the suffragans of Bordeaux. They unanimously beg you to excommunicate again Girard of Angoulême, heresiarch, sacrilegious man, and invader of the see of Bordeaux; using the authority given you by God as primate, forbid both suffragans and Bordeaux clergy to receive him as archbishop; and have him, Peter of Château-Aurard, the inflated calf, all their helpers, whose leader is V. Bocherellus, publicly excommunicated on Saint Mary Magdalene’s feast. As far as we are concerned, we have handed such invaders of a shameful sacrilege over to Satan for destruction of the flesh and excluded them from ecclesiastical honors and promotions. Would that you exercised this power of the Holy Spirit also upon V. Bocherellus.

### IV. Vulgrin to the bishops, clergy, and people

Vulgrin, by God’s grace primate of the churches of Aquitaine, sends greeting and blessing to the venerable brothers and Catholic children of holy Mother Church: the bishops of Agen, Poitiers, Périgueux, and Saintes, and clergy and people of the province of Bordeaux.

Remember, dearest brethren, and engrave it firmly upon your minds: this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. Though holy Catholic Church is often shaken by adversities, she remains unconquered and immovable in the unity and truth of faith. Catholic and religious bishops have often been expelled from their sees by heretics’ schemes and princes’ tyranny, yet God’s Church could not be overthrown, because it is built upon the rock and the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. Since the gate of hell is opened in your regions, let all Catholics beware lest they fall through it and go down alive into hell. Those fall and descend who depart from the Roman Church, imagining the Roman Church to be walls or marble. The Catholic bishops and cardinals suffering persecution with Pope Innocent for righteousness are the Roman Church; it is not those persecutors who violate the sacred see by violently holding it, nor those schismatics who feared man more than God. Clinging to Peter Leonis, they have lost the rock of righteousness, which will tread down lion and dragon and soon crush every power of Satan beneath its feet.

Cling firmly, then, to the rock’s foundation upon which you began to build. Despise threats of princes, loss of possessions, and bodily vexations—charity casts fear outside—or rather receive them as discipline, that with the Apostle you may say confidently and rejoicing: “Who shall separate us from Christ’s love? Tribulation, distress, famine, nakedness, persecution, or sword? In all these we conquer; for the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us.” Knowing that all things work together for good to those who love God, do not be terrified if you suffer adversity for righteousness. Divine mercy, which does not permit believers to be tempted beyond their strength, will turn the storm into a breeze and bring its own to their desired haven.

We exhort you to preserve Roman unity and resist Girard of Angoulême with unconquered strength. He makes himself leader and standard-bearer of manifest schism; his fruits show him now, since he indecently expelled from their sees the bishops of Limoges and Poitiers, canonically and Catholicly ordained, set his mouth against heaven, and openly attacks Catholic truth. We proclaim and command the observance of the excommunication which the lord pope has issued against him and his supporters. We disapprove the election made of him, already excommunicated, by the Bordeaux clergy, and forbid anyone to obey him, etc.

### V. Vulgrin to the same

Vulgrin, primate of the churches of Aquitaine, to the venerable and beloved Catholic suffragan bishops of Bordeaux: greeting and blessing. We give thanks to God for you, dearest brothers, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the world. You have become an example of God’s Church and a mirror of virtue and faith; in you the courage of the holy martyrs has been renewed. While others bend their knees to Baal, you fight faithfully for Catholic faith, and by God’s gift are steadfast in faith and effective in action. You believe in faith and confess the truth with your mouths. The tempest of adversity does not break you, nor tribulation or distress separate you from Christ’s love.

We, placed by God in the government of the primatial see, obey Lord Pope Innocent with sincere devotion as bishop of the apostolic see and Catholic pastor of the universal Church, and nothing can move us from his obedience. Patriarchs, primates, countless metropolitans and bishops remain with us in this unity, as do the king of France, king of England, king of the Germans, king of Spain, king of Jerusalem, and dukes and princes of almost the whole world. This is the Catholic and universal Church, shining in the East and appearing even to the West. Girard’s conventicles are empty and harmful; though they deceive women burdened with sins, they cannot harm just and truly Catholic men, “for heresies must occur, so that those approved may become manifest.”

Stand firm, beloved brothers, in defense of Catholic truth. Trust him who says, “In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, for I have overcome the world.” Hope in him who commanded winds and sea and made a great calm; he will give you tranquillity and peace. Be certain of the counsel and aid of your holy mother, the church of Bourges: we willingly stand ready to share your afflictions and bear your burdens in charity. If Girard, who calls himself archbishop through invading Bordeaux, demands obedience, your prudence knows the answer. What subjection or obedience is owed one whom the Catholic Church condemned, excommunicated, and deposed from every ecclesiastical honor for schism at the council of Reims? Clearly, one who is not Catholic is not canonically appointed. Armed with these and other canonical reasons, prudence must wisely resist shameless falsehood, follow Innocent’s innocence, persist without change or hesitation in Catholic unity, and thus, fighting lawfully and persevering to the end, merit eternal salvation and the crown: “no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully,” and “not he who begins, but he who perseveres, shall be saved.” We desire fellowship with you; when God grants opportunity, we shall choose a suitable place and announce it. May your sincerity prosper in Christ, venerable and beloved brothers.

## Roman coronation of Emperor Lothar III (4 June 1133)

**Editorial note.** The sentence against Pope Anacletus pronounced by the princes of the realm is printed from D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, III, 485–86, and Schaten’s *Annals of Paderborn*, 730, which used Baluze’s copy. The oath Lothar gave at his coronation, long ago printed by Baronius, is copied from Cencius’s book of revenues in the Vatican Archive, a manuscript of about 1400, fol. 1331.

### Sentence against Pope Anacletus

Lothar, by God’s grace king of the Romans, sends greeting to kings, archbishops, bishops, princes, and all God’s faithful to whom these letters come. Divine majesty’s dispensation and counsel have appointed us patron and defender of holy Roman Church, and we therefore must labor more earnestly for its liberation. Summoning archbishops, bishops, abbots, princes, dukes, counts, and margraves of our realm, and taking with us bishops, counts, and other Italian barons, we set out for Rome with military force. We repeatedly received envoys of the schismatic Peter Leonis. Pleading justice on his behalf, they publicly asserted that a party prepared to go to law ought not be denied a hearing or troubled by hostile attacks. Moved by their persistent appeals, we communicated this to the bishops and cardinals with Pope Innocent. Since they knew canonical sanctions and ecclesiastical institutions, they replied that God’s whole Church had already pronounced judgment, condemned Peter Leonis and his accomplices, and that what belonged to all ought not become a private matter.

Bearing this patiently, we led our father Pope Innocent gloriously to Rome, restored him to the Lateran chair, and encamped on the Aventine. There Peter Leonis continued, through Peter formerly bishop of Porto and other supporters, to solicit our ears and those of our princes under color of justice. They promised orally and in letters to give sufficient fortresses and hostages for observing judgment. Desiring to restore peace in God’s Church without bloodshed, we personally reported their terms to the brethren with Pope Innocent. Lovers of peace and confident in justice, they freely offered into our hand both themselves and Leo and his sons, Cencius, Peter Frangipani, Peter Leonis, and their fortresses. The opposing side, seeking to gain time, delayed us by fraudulent promises; finally, after repeated warnings, when they refused fulfilment, they were condemned with Peter Leonis and his accomplices as deceitful, perfidious, and guilty against divine and royal majesty, and judged enemies by the princes of our court: Norbert of Magdeburg, our chancellor, and A., archbishop of Bremen [Note: Adalbero was archbishop of Bremen; Dethard, bishop of Osnabrück; Bernard, bishop of Paderborn; and Anselm, bishop of Havelberg.]; D. of Osnabrück, B. of Paderborn, An. of Brandenburg, B. of Parma, R. of Alba, O. of Asti, O. of Cremona, and G. of Ivrea, bishops; the abbots Henry of Fulda, Albero of Neuburg, and [the abbot] of Lüneburg; the magnates Albero and Henry, margraves; the counts Otto, Sigifrid the standard-bearer, Herman, William of Lomello, Goto of Marchuingo, Hildebrand, and Tancred of Prato; and Albert of Castello.

### Coronation oath, 4 June 1133

This is the oath Lord King Lothar gave Pope Innocent during the heresy of Peter Leonis’s son, before the doors of Saint Saviour’s basilica called the Constantinian, on the day Innocent crowned him and before he received the crown; Lord Cencius Frangipani administered it, with Otto his nephew and other Roman nobles present.

“I, King Lothar, promise and swear to you, Lord Pope Innocent, and your successors security of life, limb, and freedom from wrongful capture; I will defend the papacy and your honor, hold in my hand the regalian rights of Saint Peter which you possess, and recover to the best of my ability those which you do not possess.”

## Diplomatic notice on the letters and privileges of Innocent II

(Philipp Jaffé, *Regesta Romanorum Pontificum*, p. 558.)

The bulls of this pontiff use ordinary, Florentine, and Pisan years of the Incarnation. [Note: Ordinary Incarnation years begin 25 December; Florentine years begin three months after Christ’s Nativity; Pisan years nine months before it.] The indictions are sometimes papal and sometimes Constantinopolitan. [Note: The Constantinopolitan indiction begins 1 September; the Caesarean or Constantinopolitan 25 September; the papal or Roman 1 January.] Innocent’s formula is: **“Help us, O God our Saviour,”** in nos. 30, 44, 47, 65, 80, 85, 90, 93, 96, 101, etc.

## Letters and privileges of Pope Innocent II

### I. To King Lothar — Conrad, invader of the realm, is reported excommunicated by Honorius; Cardinal Gerard’s apostolic legation through Germany is confirmed (18 February 1130).

Gregory, formerly cardinal deacon of Sant’Angelo and now, by God’s ordering, elected Roman pontiff; William of Palestrina, Matthew of Albano, John of Ostia, Chuno of Sabina, bishops; and the Catholic cardinals who are in Rome, to Lothar, illustrious and glorious king, defender and special son of holy Catholic Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest father, Pope Honorius of happy memory, with the whole holy Catholic Roman Church, because he hoped the greatest benefit for holy Church from your person, confirmed by apostolic authority what had been done concerning you and pronounced excommunication upon Conrad, invader of the realm. Following his footsteps and relying greatly on the firmness and justice of your faith, we command through our dearest brother Gerard, cardinal priest and legate of the apostolic see, that in the coming winter you come to the apostolic see to receive, by the Lord’s working, the fullness of honor and dignity. Come armed as befits so great a man, so that by divine grace you may establish peace and subdue the enemies of Church and empire. We have committed the case of the bishop of Halberstadt to Gerard; to the archbishop of Cologne, for whom you asked, we grant the episcopal office so that he may be more faithful to you. Given at the Palace [perhaps *Palatium*], 12 days before the Kalends of March.

### II. To the Germans — confirmation of Cardinal Gerard’s legation through Germany (18 February 1130).

Gregory, formerly cardinal deacon and now, by the Lord’s ordering, elected Roman pontiff, to all archbishops, abbots, clergy, and other faithful established in God throughout the German realm: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest father Honorius of happy memory entrusted his duties in the German realm to his beloved son and our brother G., cardinal priest, a religious and prudent man. Following his footsteps with divine mercy’s aid, we have commanded him by Saint Peter’s authority to complete, under God’s guidance, the work entrusted to him. Receive him kindly as legate of the apostolic see for reverence of Saint Peter and holy Roman Church. We also command you unanimously to give aid and counsel to the illustrious King Lothar, whom you chose and raised as king in confidence of his prudence and probity. Since what we have done for him was confirmed by our predecessor Pope Honorius and holy Roman Church, send him in the coming winter to the thresholds of the apostles to receive imperial dignity and the fullness of honor; help him vigorously, as is fitting, so that he may come honorably and powerfully, establish peace, and defend the Church. Given at the Palace, 12 days before the Kalends of March.

### III. To A., prior, and the brothers of Saint Frigdian at Lucca (6 May 1130).

Innocent, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons A. [Atto], prior, and the other brothers of Saint Frigdian: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more fervent we have found you in the love of religion, the fuller confidence we have in you. For Peter Leonis is attempting to oppress the holy Roman Church and subject it to perpetual servitude. We therefore exhort your steadfastness in the Lord: standing firm as Catholic men in the faith of blessed Peter and in love for us, bring Saint Peter’s ship, now tossed amid storms, to the harbour of salvation by abundant prayers to God.

Given at Trastevere, 6 May.

## IV. To King Lothar — Innocent recounts his canonical election and Anacletus’s unlawful election, and announces that he is sending the archbishop of Ravenna (11 May 1130)

*(Mansi, Councils, XXI, 428.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son L., illustrious and glorious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because the excellence of your nobility has always been zealous, fervent, and devoted in fidelity to blessed Peter, the grace of divine goodness has adorned your person with honours and raised you to royal heights for the defense of its Church and the restoration of the condition of the Empire. Our predecessor, Pope H. of happy memory, believing that you would be of great benefit to the Church, confirmed by apostolic authority the election made of you by the archbishops, bishops, and princes of the realm, for the inviolable preservation of the unity of Church and kingdom. Through our beloved son G. [Gerard], cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, he summoned you to the apostolic see to receive the fullness of imperial dignity.

After he was removed from human affairs by the law of human nature, the bishops and Catholic cardinals unanimously elected me, though unwilling and resisting, to be Roman pontiff—something for which I was not worthy. Before God I gave no assent out of ambition for honour or any presumption; but, compelled solely by the obedience of so many and so great religious men, which could not be rejected without grave danger, and trusting besides in the mercy of almighty God, I accepted the office laid upon me for the honour of God and of the Roman Church.

But Peter Leonis, who had long desired the papacy, occupied Saint Peter’s chair by the violence of his relatives, bloodshed, and the stripping of holy images. He never ceases to torture with hunger, thirst, and many kinds of torment pilgrims and all religious people who come devoutly to the thresholds of the apostles, after they have been captured and committed to the filthy misery of prisons and iron chains. Thirsting greedily for our blood and that of those who are with us, he lies in wait for our lives with swords, poison, and many kinds of treachery.

Therefore, to restrain his cruelty and reform for the better the condition of both Church and Empire, we again command Your Excellence through these letters and through our venerable brother G. [Walter], archbishop of Ravenna, a man religious, prudent, and conspicuous in every moral excellence: come next winter to our presence with archbishops and princes of the realm, by the Lord’s help to receive the fullness of imperial dignity.
