Thus, dearest son, let your kingdom aid the heavenly kingdom, so that, after the temporal kingdom—which may the Lord make long-lasting for you—you may reign with him without end. In your days may the Church possess its honour, rejoice in its king, flourish and glory in your glory. May Catholics be exalted and heretics oppressed in your days, so that God may exalt your kingdom and humble your enemies beneath your feet.

Furthermore, we carefully commend to your glory the aforesaid G., our venerable brother and archbishop, asking that for reverence of the apostolic see you receive him kindly and treat him honourably. May almighty God preserve you, dearest son, in safety and grant you faithfully to watch over the concerns of his Church. On our behalf greet devotedly our glorious daughter Queen R. [Richeza], and invite her to come with you to us to receive the fullness of the imperial blessing.

Given at Trastevere, 11 May.

## V. To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and princes established throughout the German realm (20 June 1130)

*(Philipp Jaffé, Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 561, from the codex of the Olomouc chapter.)*

To the venerable brothers, archbishops and bishops, and beloved sons, abbots and princes established throughout the German realm: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not doubt that by divine disposition you unanimously elected our beloved son Lothar, assuredly a Catholic man and worshipper of justice, as king. Our predecessor Pope Honorius of happy memory, for preserving the unity of the Church and reforming the condition of the Empire for the better, confirmed by apostolic authority what you had done concerning him, and summoned him through our beloved son, the bearer of these letters, G. [Gerard], cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, to the apostolic see to receive the fullness of imperial dignity.

After he was taken from human affairs by the law of human nature, the bishops and Catholic cardinals commonly elected me, although I was unworthy, unwilling, and resisting, to be Roman pontiff. Before God I gave no assent from ambition for honour or any presumption; compelled only by the obedience of so many and such great religious men, which could not be disregarded, and trusting in the mercy of almighty God, I accepted the office imposed upon me for the honour of God and the Roman Church. But Peter Leonis, who had long desired the papacy, occupied Saint Peter’s chair by the violence of his relatives, bloodshed, and the destruction of sacred images; he never ceases to torture with hunger, thirst, and many kinds of torment pilgrims and religious persons coming devoutly to the thresholds of the apostles, after they have been captured and consigned to the foul misery of prison and iron chains.

Therefore, by these letters and through our most dear brothers G. [Gerard], cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, and Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, we command your whole body: now, when your mother the holy Roman Church has the greatest need, assist her to the extent of your power; diligently encourage our aforesaid son King Lothar to our honour and service; and bring him to our presence next winter, so that, by the Lord’s help, we may do what must be done. We also carefully commend to your love the aforesaid legates, Gerard the cardinal-priest and Walter, archbishop of Ravenna. For reverence of the apostolic see, receive them kindly and treat them honourably. May almighty God keep you under his protection and grant you the abundance of his blessing both now and in the future.

Given at Pisa, 20 June.

## VI. The monasteries of the Vallombrosan congregation are received under the protection of the apostolic see, with confirmation of other grants and privileges (June 1130)

*(Cocquelines, II, p. 203.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Attho, abbot of Vallombrosa, and his successors forever.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to spread religion pleasing to God. Service is never pleasing to God unless, springing from the root of charity, it is lived in religious purity. Therefore, out of this concern of charity, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Attho, granting your reasonable requests, we receive under the guardianship and protection of the apostolic see the monastery of Vallombrosa, over which by God’s favor you preside, together with all its subject monasteries. We fortify it by this page of our writing and decree that every immunity and every liberty granted to that monastery by our predecessors of happy memory—Victor, Gregory VII, Urban, and Paschal, Roman pontiffs—shall remain firm and unimpaired forever for you, your successors, and the Vallombrosan congregation. No person may rashly seize, retain after seizure, or harass with any vexations the converts or monks of the said monastery or of the whole congregation.

Moreover, we decree that the tithes of your fruits, cultivated anywhere by your own expense and labour, shall be rendered and possessed by your hospice without opposition from bishops, episcopal ministers, or parish priests. You may receive, without anyone’s opposition, clerics fleeing the world and laypersons seeking conversion; and, without prejudice to other churches, receive the offerings of those who have vowed burial in your cemetery and of other faithful persons.

We further add that every possession and every good which the said monastery now justly and lawfully holds, or may hereafter reasonably acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain tranquil and whole for you. We decree that no person at all may rashly disturb this monastery, take away or diminish its subject churches or possessions, or harass them by reckless vexations. Rather, all things are to remain whole and serve in every way the uses for whose support and governance they were granted.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning and without making suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the wrong committed, be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Pisa by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130, the eighth indiction, and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## VII. To Didacus, archbishop of Compostela — thanks for the gifts sent (2 August 1130)

*(Flórez, *España Sagrada*, XX, 511.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Didacus, archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

For the submission and obedience rendered by your brotherhood to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, and for the gifts sent to us by your generosity, we give thanks to your love. We truly love your person in the Lord and gladly honour the Church of Compostela for reverence of blessed James the Apostle and for affection toward you. At this time of our new office, we have partly granted the requests presented to us through the messengers M., archdeacon, and P., priest; where a written instrument was needed, we sent apostolic letters. We carefully commend to your brotherhood the aforesaid priest, chaplain of your Church, who has laboured greatly for the good of the Church of Compostela and for your service.

Given at Genoa, 2 August.

## VIII. To the same — the evil custom abolished by royal decree (2 August 1130)

*(Flórez, as above, p. 510.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Didacus, archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Holy Mother Church, shining brilliantly in spiritual things with the splendour of perpetual unity, without wrinkle, stain, or schism, ought in temporal matters neither to be burdened by any imposition nor troubled by anyone’s compulsory service, nor to endure anything extraordinary. It is fitting that every Church, steadfast in the prerogative of its estate, remain free and immune from such harassment. We therefore rejoice that the wicked practice and unjust custom once observed in the Church of blessed James at Compostela has been condemned by our dearest son King Alfonso and annulled by the authority of a royal decree: after the death of the bishop of Compostela, the revenues of the bishopric were diverted to royal use, and the Church of Compostela, bereft of its pastor, remained vacant for a long time. We praise and confirm by apostolic authority the enacted provision that, when a bishop dies in that Church, the vacancy shall not be prolonged but a free election shall take place.

Given at Genoa, 2 August.

## IX. To the archbishops and bishops established in Spain (2 August 1130)

*(Flórez, as above, p. 511.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops established throughout Spain: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Kings, princes, and other faithful of God have vowed gifts to blessed James for the remission of their sins and the salvation of their souls, and have established that they be paid annually without hindrance. Therefore, that you may share in that benefit, we command your brotherhood by these letters to place no impediment in the way of paying the aforesaid vows, but to permit them to be paid freely and without any molestation according to ancient custom.

Given at Genoa, 2 August.

## X. To P. [Pelagius], archbishop of Braga (2 August 1130)

*(Flórez, as above, p. 509.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother P., archbishop of Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest brother Didacus, archbishop of Compostela, makes a grave complaint against you. He says that you violently retain the villages of blessed James which you received from him as a benefice, on the condition that whenever that archbishop demanded them from you, you would restore them freely and without any trouble—a condition which you are said to have confirmed in writing. By these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to restore without any difficulty to our venerable brother the said Didacus, archbishop, those villages and the other possessions of blessed James received in the manner stated, and no longer retain them against his will. We also command you to allow the vows of the faithful owed to blessed James through your parish to be given and paid without opposition according to ancient custom.

## XI. To P. [Pelagius], archbishop of Braga (2 August 1130)

*(Flórez, as above, p. 510.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother P., archbishop of Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

For the offense and contempt of the holy Roman Church which you committed in the consecration of the bishop of Coimbra, our predecessor Pope Honorius of happy memory summoned your brotherhood by apostolic letters to appear before him and answer on the Sunday just passed on which “I am the good shepherd” is read. But you neither came nor sent representatives to the apostolic see to conduct your case. Because we cannot let so great an offense pass unexamined, we command and order you by these letters to come to our presence at the next Purification of Blessed Mary, prepared to answer concerning these matters.

## XII. Privilege for the Church of Pavia

*(Spelta, *History of Pavia*, p. 289.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bernard, bishop of Pavia, and his successors canonically appointed forever.

The most holy Roman and apostolic Church was established by our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, as head and hinge of all churches. I do not say that the members depart from the head; rather, they obey the head’s eminent reason and heavenly providence. The governing discernment of the head, considering the dutiful assistance of each, distinctly preserves for every one the right and order established by nature, and maintains for its noble members the dignity of their beauty and indivisible social charity. Moved by this reasoning, we wish to preserve the papal honour of the Church of the apostolic see’s own and special daughter. Therefore, venerable brother Bernard, whom we love in full charity in Christ for the Church’s vigour in learning, religion, and honorable conduct, granting your reasonable requests, we too confirm by the authority of this present privilege every dignity granted to your Church by the privileges or authentic writings of our predecessors.

We grant you, during the sacred solemnities of Mass, the use of the pallium; and to you and your successors, in the Palm Sunday and Monday-after-Easter processions, the right to ride a white horse covered with an *udone* and to carry the cross while proceeding. Let the monastery of Saint Mary in Charity and the monastery of Saint Donatus founded at Scovilla, although they lie outside your diocese, be held as they have hitherto been held, with everything belonging to them.

The following text survives only in fragments; its gaps are retained: “Of the other monasteries . . . . . of your diocese, the canonical ordering, and of abbots . . . . . examination, election, and consecration always . . . . . whom indeed, or whose priests, it is expedient to come to you; [at] certain monasteries or chapels . . . . . we wholly forbid a general baptism to be performed . . . . . should be found lawful by the institutions of the canon: clerics, nuns, widows, . . . . . no one may presume in conscience . . . . . to inflict upon their goods, nor upon cemeteries, which . . . . . care or power for you . . . . . person may presume. Nor may any person whatsoever . . . . . under the pretext of hospitality, [act] against the venerable bishop, or in the houses of your priests and all . . . . . without the will . . . . . of you and your successors . . . . . nor in movable or immovable goods . . . . . of whatever condition belonging to your Church, [may] invasion or violence . . . . . be done without lawful . . . . . we permit.”

We decree, therefore, that no one at all may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken . . . . . or harass [them] with reckless vexations; but all things are to remain whole and serve in every way the uses for whose support and governance they were granted, with the privilege of the apostolic see preserved in all things. For the greater [honour] of the Church of Pavia itself . . . . . confirming [this], we decree that in celebrations of synodal assemblies . . . . . you and your successors shall perpetually have, at the left of the Roman [bishop], the first place of seating. If any . . . . . ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third [warning] . . . . . unless that person makes suitable satisfaction, let him or her lose the dignity of power and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the wrong committed . . . . . be cut off from the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ . . . . . and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. Upon all, however, who preserve the rights of that Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of the Church of Sabina, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Equitius, have subscribed. I, Anselm, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence, have subscribed. I, Goselm, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Genoa by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on 7 August, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130 and the first year of Innocent II’s pontificate.

## XIII. The possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saints Gervasius and Protasius at Fos are confirmed (11 September 1130)

*(Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, VI, 192.)*

At that time Abbot William presided over the monastery of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, situated at Fos in the diocese of Arles. When Innocent II was staying at Saint-Gilles that year, William asked him for a privilege of apostolic protection and immunity. Granting his requests, the pope, following the example of his predecessors Sergius IV and Paschal II, fortified the said monastery with the patronage of the apostolic see, confirmed its possessions, and decreed that the monks of that place should be free from every secular service. Thus, diligent in the observance of holy religion, they are subject to no one but the Roman Church.

Given at Saint-Gilles by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on 11 September, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130 and the [first] year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II. [The source ends the dating formula after *anno*; the bracketed ordinal is supplied only from the preceding formula and remains uncertain.]

## XIV. To Berthold, abbot of Saint Blaise — confirmation of Saint Blaise’s liberty from the advocacy of Basel (2 November 1130)

*(Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, III, p. 62.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Berthold, abbot of the monastery of Saint Blaise, situated in the diocese of Constance, in the place called the Black Forest, and to his successors regularly appointed forever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to strive for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s help, beneficially provide for their peace and welfare. It is worthy and becoming that we who have been taken up for the governance of churches should protect them from the malice of wicked people and fortify them with the patronage of blessed Peter and the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Berthold, we graciously grant your petition and strengthen with the aid of the apostolic see the monastery of Saint Blaise, over which by God’s favor you preside, with all its appurtenances. We decree that whatever that monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may in the future justly and canonically acquire by grant of pontiffs, generosity of princes, or offering of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. No person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away or retain its possessions, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, all things are to remain whole and serve in every way the uses for whose support and governance they were granted.

You shall receive consecrations of altars and basilicas, ordinations of monks, chrism, holy oil, and the other things belonging to the episcopal office from the bishop of Constance, in whose diocese you are, provided that he is Catholic, possesses the grace and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to provide them freely and without wrongdoing. Otherwise you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, if, supported by the authority of the apostolic see, he grants what is requested. We decree that burial at the same place shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Nor may the opposition of any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving for conversion laypeople or clerics living in the secular state.

When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one may be placed over it by any trick of clandestine procurement or violence, unless he has been elected by the brothers with common consent or by the sounder part of their counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Furthermore, with due reverence for the bishop of Constance, we confirm for your monastery the cell of Silva Suazzewalt, built by Reginbert, with all possessions, estates, and lands belonging to it.

We also confirm the arrangement concerning your monastery’s liberty and advocacy which Emperor Henry IV of blessed memory made, which our predecessor Calixtus of happy memory strengthened by his privilege, which our beloved son King Lothar fortified by the authority of his command, and which Pope Honorius of holy memory confirmed by the deliberation of bishops and cardinals. Namely: in choosing an advocate, the abbot shall have free power, with his brothers’ counsel, to choose one whom he recognizes as good and useful for defending the monastery’s liberty, and who wishes faithfully to hold and administer that advocacy not for earthly profit but for God’s love, remission of his sins, and the reward of eternal blessing. But if he proves a harasser rather than an advocate, seizes the monastery’s goods, and does not rather defend them, the abbot, with the brethren’s counsel, may appoint for himself another, more useful advocate. Thus, as was determined by judgment of the aforesaid Emperor Henry and the aforesaid King Lothar, the liberty of your monastery shall in every way be free from the jurisdiction of the Church of Basel. As a token of our protection and the liberty granted to your monastery, you shall pay one gold coin annually to the Lateran palace.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning and without making suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the wrong committed, be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, John, bishop of Ostia. I, Guido, bishop of Tivoli. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Equitius. I, Ubert, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Goselm, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at Cluny by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on 2 November, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130 and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II. [Note: Innocent II was elected pope on 15 February 1130. Because of the schism of Peter Leonis, to whom the Romans adhered, he withdrew into Gaul. Before holding the Council of Clermont he stopped at Cluny and dedicated the monastery church there, about 18 October or a few days later, as Pagi argues (*Brief History of the Roman Pontiffs*, II, p. 618); according to Orderic Vitalis he remained there only eleven days, yet before leaving issued this bull on 2 November. Mabillon (*Annals*, VI, p. 186) assigns 25 October to the dedication; the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis* wrongly assigns it to 1131, since in that same year, on 25 October, Innocent consecrated the younger Louis king at Reims.]

## XV. To Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis — confirmation of Honorius II’s decree concerning the monastery of Argenteuil

*(Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, p. 369.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The body of God’s Church is unquestionably kept sound, and the first things are joined to the middle and the middle to the first by a social bond, if the arrangements reasonably established by our predecessors the Roman pontiffs are strengthened by us and our successors with apostolic authority. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Suger, we strengthen by the protection of the apostolic see and decree shall remain unimpaired in future times the monastery of Argenteuil: granted to you and to your monastery by our venerable brother Stephen, bishop of Paris, in the presence of our venerable brothers Matthew, bishop of Albano and then legate of the apostolic see, Rainald, archbishop of Reims, Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Goselin, bishop of Soissons, through the intervention of our dearest son Louis, illustrious and glorious king of the French; and confirmed for the reform of religion there by our predecessor Pope Honorius of happy memory. [Note: Suger obtained this favor and notable privilege from the journey on which, after the Council of Étampes, acting as envoy of King Louis VI, he “delegated to him [Innocent] at Cluny through us the first fruits of reception and service,” as Suger himself says in the *Life of Louis*.]

Given at Cluny, 2 November.

## XVI. Bull for the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (3 November 1130)

*(Bouillard, *History of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, proofs, p. XXXVI.)*

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus, bishop of the city of Paris, and to his successors forever.

Whenever a request is made to us for something that is recognized as consonant with reason, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford appropriate support to the desires of those who petition us. Therefore, out of regard for charity, beloved son in the Lord Hugh, abbot, we receive the monastery of Blessed Germanus, over which by God’s authorship you preside, together with all its appurtenances, under the guardianship and protection of blessed Peter, and fortify it by the patronage of the apostolic see. Accordingly, by the text of this present privilege, we confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity that whatever liberty and whatever dignity has been bestowed upon your monastery by the privilege of blessed Germanus, by the writings of Childebert, Clothar, and other kings of the Franks [Col. 0065D], whatever goods and possessions are known to belong to that monastery through grants of popes, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, and whatever it may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, [Col. 0066A] and be wholly useful for their purposes. Every abbot after you who is elected by the community of the same monastery according to the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff or by whatever Catholic bishop he may prefer. We also command by apostolic authority that none of the bishops deny to them or to their successors oil, chrism, blessings, consecrations, orders, or anything necessary from pontifical ministry.

Accordingly, we prohibit any bishop or cleric of the Church of Paris from celebrating masses, ordinations, or stations in that monastery without the consent of the abbot or community. Nor do we grant them authority there to command anything; nor to place the abbot, monks, priests, or clerics [Col. 0066B] of the churches of that place under interdict or excommunication, or summon them to a synod.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should fail to make proper satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0066C] I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have signed. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano, have signed. I, John, bishop of Ostia, have signed. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have signed. I, Hubert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, have signed. I, [unnamed] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have signed. I, Joslen, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia.

[Col. 0066D] Given at Cluny, through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of November [3 November], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## XVII. He confirms the substitution of monks for nuns in the monastery of Saint Mary at Laon. (4 November 1130.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 374.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DROGO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint John the Baptist in the city of Laon, and to his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The duties of pastoral office have been committed to us by the Lord so that we may labor both to establish religion pleasing to God and, with the greatest diligence, to preserve its stability. For our venerable brethren Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, with the counsel of our brethren Goslin, bishop of Soissons, Simon, bishop of Noyon, Peter, bishop of Beauvais, and Robert, bishop of Arras, and also through the intervention of our most illustrious son Louis, king of the Franks, placed religious men—indeed monks—in the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Mary and Saint John, where certain women [Col. 0067B], under the name of nuns, were leading a depraved and dishonorable life; and they appointed you, beloved son in the Lord Drogo, abbot over that community.

What they have therefore done concerning the aforesaid monastery for the establishment and reform of religion, we confirm by apostolic authority and will to remain firm for all future time. We decree that whatever the aforesaid monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, reasonably acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and for your successors regularly appointed. But if anyone knowingly attempts with rash presumption to oppose this our confirmation, let him know that he will incur the indignation of blessed Peter and Paul [Col. 0067C] and of ourselves.

Given at Rouen, on the second day before the Nones of November [4 November].

## XVIII. Privilege confirming the goods and rights of the priory of Saint Arnulf at Crépy, of the Cluniac order, in the diocese of Senlis.

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 46.]

INNOCENT, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son AYMAR, prior of the monastery of Crépy, and to his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A desire known to concern the profession of religion and the salvation of souls ought, by God’s authorship, to be fulfilled promptly in its effect. Therefore, son Aymar in the Lord, assenting to your petitions [Col. 0067D], we fortify by the authority of this decree the monastery of blessed Arnulf the martyr, over which you preside by appointment of our most beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny. All things known to have been entrusted to Saint Arnulf and your community by the founders of your house—namely Walter, of good memory, count of Amiens, and his wife Adela—we confirm to you and your successors, following the example of our predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory, to remain in the same liberty in which they were granted.

We further decree that all things now appearing to belong to that place shall always remain peacefully and intact for you: namely, the church of Saint Agatha with its appurtenances; [Col. 0068A] the altar of Diogeny with its appurtenances; the altar of Frénicourt; the church of Saint Germanus situated beside the castle of Pontoise, with its appurtenances; the cell called the monastery of Moranum; the estate in the village of Vilet near Mont Désiré; the altar of Villers; the altar of Germigny, which you possess by the charter of Bishop Fulk; the church at Locelles; the church at Bonoculum; the church of Rossolio with all their appurtenances; and the freehold estate of Frasueta.

Whatever else has been bestowed on that place by anyone from his own right, or shall hereafter be bestowed, shall always remain firm and unimpaired, to be possessed, governed, and administered in perpetuity both by you and by those appointed over that place through the abbots of Cluny. We also establish [Col. 0068B] that no bishop, unless perhaps invited by the prior and brethren of your monastery, may celebrate public masses there, lest an occasion for popular gatherings be given in the retreats of the servants of God.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless exactions; but that all things be wholly preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, and be wholly useful for their purposes. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should fail to make proper satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano. I, John, bishop of Ostia. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Col. 0068D] I, Goslin, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0067D] “Rouen” should be read. JAFFÉ.] through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the Nones of November [5 November], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## XIX. Confirmation of all goods and privileges of the monastery of Cuxa. (28 November 1130.)

[COCQUELINES, II, 203, from the cartulary of the monastery of Cuxa.]

[Col. 0069A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GREGORY, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael of Cuxa, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A desire shown to concern the profession of religion and the salvation of souls ought, by God’s authorship, to be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore, beloved son in Christ Gregory, abbot of blessed Michael the archangel, we receive under the protection of the apostolic see the monastery over which by the Lord’s ordering you preside [Col. 0069B], and strengthen it by the text of our writing. We establish that whatever possessions and goods the aforesaid monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, reasonably acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names: namely, the freehold estate surrounding the same monastery with its appurtenances; the estate of Taurinianum; the church of Saint Fructuosus with its appurtenances; and the tithes of the church of Allone.

Whatever has besides been bestowed upon your monastery through grants of our predecessors Sergius, Agapetus, and John, Roman pontiffs, we confirm to you and your successors. Upon your death as abbot of that place, no one shall be placed over it through intrigue or violence, but the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall judge ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. That abbot shall not be compelled to go to the synod of the bishop of that place.

If any penitent person, excluded from the threshold of the Church, should flee there, he shall, as long as he remains there, have permission to go freely to church and to hear every divine office. No bishop shall presume to excommunicate the monastery itself, the churches belonging to it, or the abbot. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or burden it with reckless vexations [Col. 0069D]; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, and be wholly useful for their purposes. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should fail to make proper satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that place [Col. 0070A] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Clermont, through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December [28 November], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## XX. To the bishops of the province of Narbonne. (29 November 1130.)

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XV, p. 370.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren RAYMOND, bishop of Maguelonne; B[ERMUND], bishop of Béziers; P[ETER], bishop of Lodève; J[OHN], bishop of Nîmes; and R[AYMOND], bishop-elect of Agde: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of our sons Peter, abbot, and the monks of Aniane against certain knights, your parishioners—namely Pons of Agonès, R[aymond] of Pimanès, Olivarius of Melgueil, Peter Raimund Malaura, and their accomplices—that they miserably killed one of their men returning from the fair. Therefore, by this present writing we command you diligently to admonish those knights to make satisfaction to the aforesaid abbot and monks for so grave an offense and injury inflicted upon them. If, within [perhaps fifteen or forty] days after they have been admonished by you [Col. 0070C], they disdain to make satisfaction, from then on we bind them by sentence of excommunication, and command you to have it observed throughout the various parishes.

Given at Clermont, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November].

## XXI. To William, bishop of Langres. (3 December 1130.)

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XIV, p. 247.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUILENCO, bishop of Langres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Great care must be taken lest the peace of monks and religious brethren be disturbed [Col. 0070D] on the occasion of some dispute. Therefore, as we enjoined upon you in person, so by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that, having summoned with you our beloved sons S[tephen], abbot of Cîteaux, and B[ernard], abbot of Clairvaux, you bring the controversy being conducted between the Church of Saint Stephen and Saint-Seine to a canonical conclusion, or establish concord and peace. For this purpose we command the canons and monks of the aforesaid churches to observe without reconsideration whatever shall be adjudged by you with the counsel of the aforesaid brethren.

Given at Clermont [Note: [Col. 0069] In the year 1130, when Innocent II held a council at Clermont.] on the third day before the Nones of December [3 December].

## XXII. He confirms the goods of the church of Saint Martin at Nevers. (19 December 1130.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, documents, p. 340.]

[Col. 0071A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son STEPHEN, prior of the church of Saint Martin situated in the suburb of Nevers, and to his brethren both present and future who profess the canonical life there: greeting in the Lord.

Set by the Lord’s ordering upon the eminent watchtower of the apostolic see, we ought to grant assent to religious desires and to defend from the assaults of wicked men both ecclesiastical persons and their places, especially those that shine with the splendor of religion. Moved by this consideration, beloved son in the Lord Stephen [Col. 0071B], prior, graciously assenting to your reasonable petitions and adhering to the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Honorius of blessed memory, we strengthen by the support of the apostolic see the church of blessed Martin at Nevers, over which by God’s authorship you preside.

Accordingly, by the text of this present privilege we establish that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have added the following, recorded by their proper names: namely, the two churches of Luciniac with their appurtenances; the chapel of Baefias; the church of Buciac; the church of Moresca; the church [Col. 0071C] of Coloncello; the church of Bazolis; the church of Spiriac; the church on Mount Rumilion; and the church of Saint Ouen.

We also confirm to you the grant of grain offered at church dedications, bestowed upon your church by Fromond, bishop of Nevers. Further, we strengthen for you the church of Saint Martin of Guiespey with its appurtenances—namely, the church of Saint Germanus of Escay; Saint George of Scadun; Saint Lawrence of Onach; Saint Stephen; the church of Saint Hilary; Saint Symphorian; of Suency; and Saint Desiderius upon the Yonne—granted to you by the same our brother Bishop Fromond; namely, on condition that in that church of blessed Martin at Gispey, just as in your own church, the canonical order according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be preserved inviolably for all future time [Col. 0071D]. Moreover, we likewise confirm to you the church of Saint Leodegarius of Saxeis-Bordin. If anyone hereafter, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Decize, through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December], in the ninth indiction, in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## XXIII. To Vulgrin, archbishop of Bourges. (1131?)

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 489.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother VULGRIN, archbishop of Bourges: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of our beloved Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, against Her., abbot of Clusinum, that he has unjustly taken from him the church of Saint Martial, at Saint-Désirat, and the church of Blessed Marinus at Corciac. Therefore, desiring that justice be preserved for each person, we have commanded the same abbot by apostolic letters to come before you on the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September] to answer our aforesaid son Abbot Suger concerning his complaint, or to send sufficient representatives. Then, having heard the arguments of both parties, let the discretion of your brotherhood impose a due settlement upon the aforesaid controversy, etc.

## XXIV. To Her., abbot of Clusinum. (1131?)

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 489.]

[Col. 0072B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HER., abbot of Clusinum: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, does not cease to complain against you, namely because you have unjustly taken from him the churches of Blessed Martial, at Saint-Désirat, and of Saint Marinus at Corciac. Therefore, by these present writings we command you to appear before our venerable brother the archbishop of Bourges on the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September], or to send sufficient representatives, prepared to make satisfaction to our aforesaid son Abbot Suger [Col. 0072C] according to his judgment; otherwise, you are to come into our presence on the next feast of blessed Luke [18 October] to answer the same complaint, etc.

## XXV. Privilege for the abbey of Fontevraud. (20 January 1131.)

[PAVILLON, *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, p. 626.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ P. [PETRONILLA], abbess of the monastery of Fontevraud, and to the sisters there devoted to divine service, both present and future, in perpetuity.

Since without the worship of true religion neither the unity of charity can endure nor anything pleasing to God be offered, it is fitting for apostolic authority to love religious persons [Col. 0072D] and to foster by the protection of the apostolic see religious places—especially those belonging to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and particularly subject to the Roman Church. Therefore, beloved daughter in the Lord P. [Petronilla], abbess, assenting to your just and reasonable petitions, we fortify and strengthen by the text of our writing, after the example of our predecessors, the monastery of nuns of Fontevraud, placed under the jurisdiction and protection of blessed Peter and over which by God’s authorship you preside. We establish that whatever goods and possessions the monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter reasonably acquire by God’s authorship through grants of princes, generosity of kings or princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and for those who shall regularly succeed you in the same governance.

Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names: namely, the place of Brajerac with its appurtenances, from the gift of Aimeric, prior, and all the brethren of the same place, with the consent of the bishop of Toulouse; the place of Paradise, from the gift of Fortis of Bic and Amauvis of Paradiso, with his wife and sons, with the consent of Raymond, bishop of Agen; the place of Fontanis, from the gift of Count Theobald, with the consent of Burchard, bishop of Meaux; the waste land which the same Burchard, bishop of Meaux, granted to the aforesaid monastery as a gift; the place of Fontanis in the bishopric of Périgueux, from the gift of Bernard of Saint-Austere, Elias Guibert, and Bovis Curti, and also [Col. 0073B] Arnald of Joncelia, Elias of Marollio, Elias of Castellio, and many others, with the consent of William, bishop of Périgueux; the place of Pont-Sage and of Pont-Cainon, from the gift of Fulk, count of Anjou; the place of Eremelia, from the gift of Elias Thysi, Benedict of Mauritania, and Bernard of Parcellian, with the consent of Peter, bishop of Saintes.

The place of Cerasorum, from the gift of Geoffrey, viscount of Thouars, and his wife and sons, with the consent of Aimeric, son of Herbert; likewise the tithes of the crops of the same Viscount Geoffrey, which were his own property. [lacuna] The place of Porcaria, from the gift of John of Beaumont, and the tithes from his mills and cellar, with the consent of his sons; the place of Vallicuae and the land of Villeneuve, from the gift of Ralph Maliclavellus and Idert of Mirebeau, with the consent of William of Pinelles; the place of Capreoli, from the gift of Carbonel of Cheniche; the place of Jarrie, from the gift of William of Mirebeau and Gani, his brother; the place of Ascay, from the gift of Lady Remfredis, Arnald, and Belot of Clairvaux, Ribotellus of La Haye and his brother; the place of Font-Alerie, from the gift of Alexander of Pocenaria and Alexander of Herbergement; the place of Regreperia, from the gift of Mauritil Puellus and Direx of Vallicula; the place of Asini, from the gift of Guy of Poitou and Geoffrey Malumminat, and with the consent of Roland Savaric and his sister, Geoffrey of Poceio, Gilbert of Loudun, Alon his son, and Giraud Berlai.

The place of Saint Karileff, from the gift of Kalon of Blazon, and the things belonging to that place, given [Col. 0073D] to the same monastery of Fontevraud by Geoffrey of Doe, Griscia his mother, and Philip of Blazon; the place of Malta, from the gift of Alberic of Mont-Jean; the wood, land adjoining it, and mill, from the gift of Ogisi and his brother Offred; the place of Valenthay, given by Aimeric of Passavant, Renaud of Senzay, and Peter Blojo; the place of Ramonaria, from the gift of Geoffrey Ursellus, and given and granted to William of Saintes; the place of Colungentiae, from the gift of Aaleth and her son Alberic; and whatever Adam, son of Garin, held in that place, granted to you by his own gift, with the consent of his brother Philip and Viscount Geoffrey, together with his wife and son Peter; and whatever is in the place of Sibrey, from the gift of Amaury of Mextenum; [Col. 0074A] the flat land and *exempla* [uncertain: perhaps “rights/tenures”] from the gift of Nivard of Metlino, his brother, and his mother, with the consent of Nivard of Satollia. [lacuna] From the gift of Henry, illustrious king of the English, sixty marks from his London revenue, from the farm of the city, and forty marks from the farm of the city of Winchester.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, and be wholly useful for their purposes. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second [Col. 0074B] and third time, should fail to make proper satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Étampes in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## XXVI. To Peter, bishop of Beauvais, and the canons—He forbids them to molest the monks of Saint-Lucien on account of the little pies which they demanded from them, and for other reasons, until he himself should come and hear the arguments of both parties. (27 January 1131.)

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XV, p. 371.]

[Col. 0074C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable P[ETER], bishop, and to his beloved sons the canons of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son S[ERLO], abbot of the monastery of Saint-Lucien, coming before us, complained that contrary to the privileges granted to his monastery by Roman pontiffs, kings, and bishops of Beauvais, you harass that place with many and various exactions [Col. 0074D]. Therefore we command your whole body that you leave in peace both the aforesaid Abbot Serlo and the monastery committed to him, until, by the Lord’s provision, we come into your parts. When we are present, having heard the arguments of both sides, we shall establish between you, with grace’s assistance, what is just.

But whenever you receive from the abbot and brethren of the aforesaid monastery a complaint against your parishioners, after they have been admonished by you and have not repented, take due action against them; and, on account of the *pastilli* [Col. 0075A] [Note: [Col. 0075] According to Du Cange, *pastillus* and *pastellus* mean a baked preparation stuffed with meat or other foodstuff—French *pâté*. Here it is understood as a light meal.] which you exact from them, do not inflict any molestation upon them until the matter is settled in our presence.

Given at Provins, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January].

## XXVII. He confirms all the goods of the church of Saint Mary of Bellelocus and receives it under the patronage of the holy apostolic see. (14 February 1131.)

[HUGO, *Annals of the Premonstratensian Order*, I, 254.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ODO, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Bellelocus, situated on the river Aube, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to spread religion pleasing to God. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Odo, abbot, inclined by the prayers of our venerable brother Hatto, bishop of Troyes, we graciously assent to your petitions and fortify by the patronage of the apostolic see the church of Blessed Mary, over which by God’s authorship you preside. We establish that whatever goods and possessions the same church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, through grants of popes, benefactions of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s provision acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names [Col. 0075C]: namely, the territory on which that aforesaid church is built; the watercourse from the village of Gessenna to Juvanzzeum, together with the ban, granted to the aforesaid church by Airard, formerly count of Brienne; and, throughout the whole county of Brienne, according to the ordinance made by the aforesaid Airard and Walter, his son, counts of Brienne, and in the appurtenances of the town of Bellefort, the livestock of the brethren of that place shall have free pasture both in woodland and open fields.

Moreover, we confirm in perpetuity to the same church the chapel built in the forest of Der, given by our son Simon, lord of the castle of Bellefort, and by Amelina, his late mother; rights of use in the forests belonging to that castle, for making fires and other necessities; and Rostera with its appurtenances, given [Col. 0075D] by the knight Guarnier and his brother Mainard; Vendolium; and the lands of Darzeicourt. No one shall presume to exact from the brethren of the aforesaid monastery tithes of the produce which they cultivate at their own expense.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, wholly useful for their purposes, while always preserving the due justice and reverence owed to the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time [Col. 0076A], should fail to make proper satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Châlons, through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy [Col. 0076B] Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March [14 February], in the ninth indiction, in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## XXVIII. To Didacus, archbishop of Compostela. (16 February 1131.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 521.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our predecessors, apostolic men and Roman pontiffs, loved your person and the Church of Compostela, a devoted daughter of blessed Peter and of the holy Roman Church; and we likewise desire to follow in their footsteps and to grant your prayers in those matters which we can and ought to grant. Therefore we have thought fit to inform you, as a Catholic man and a familiar friend of the apostolic see, concerning the condition of the Church and our own position.

After a council had been solemnly celebrated at Clermont on the octave of the recent feast of blessed Martin, our most beloved son Louis, king of the Franks, joyfully met us at Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire and escorted us with glad heart from there to the city of Orléans. Afterwards the illustrious Henry, king of the English, humbly presented himself before us at Chartres and, promising us and our brethren his counsel and assistance for the liberation of the Church, furnished support from his resources [Col. 0076D]. Having completed with the aforesaid kings those matters which we recognized to concern God’s advantage, we are hastening to Liège; for there our glorious son Lothar, king of the Romans, has arranged to deliberate with us, together with the archbishops, bishops, and princes of his land, concerning the peace of the Church and the safety of the realm.

To the archbishop of Braga, who neither came to us nor sent representatives at the term set by us—namely, the Purification of Saint Mary—we have granted a postponement until the next feast of blessed Luke. Let your brotherhood, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, hold commended to you our common sons P., priest and chaplain of the church of blessed James, who has labored greatly for the honor of the Church of Compostela, and G. [Col. 0077A], canon of the same church.

Given at Châlons, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March [16 February].

## XXIX. To P[elagius], archbishop of Braga. (16 February 1131.)

[FLOREZ, as cited above, p. 522.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable P., archbishop of Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

On account of the offence and contempt against the Holy Roman Church which you committed in the consecration of the bishop of Coimbra, we remember that, by apostolic letters, we commanded your brotherhood to come into our presence on the past feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary, there to answer. [Col. 0077B] But you, adding worse things to worse, though summoned both by us and by our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Honorius, neither came nor sent to us anyone to plead your cause. Therefore, by repeated letters, we command and direct you that, on the coming feast of Blessed Luke, you present yourself before us, prepared to answer for such grave offences.

Given at Châlons, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.

### XXX. Privilege for the Hospital of Jerusalem. (A.D. 1130.)

[Bosio, *Dell’istoria della sacra militia di S. Giovani Hierosolym.*, vol. I, p. 108.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable [Col. 0077C] brothers the archbishops and bishops, and to the beloved sons the abbots and priors, and to all prelates of churches to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How pleasing this place is to God, how venerable to humankind, and what a useful and beneficial refuge the Hospital of Jerusalem provides for pilgrims and the poor, is continually recognized by those who, through the various perils of sea and land, visit the holy city of Jerusalem and the Lord’s Sepulchre out of devout devotion. For there the needy and poor are refreshed; the sick receive manifold offices of humane care; and those exhausted by diverse labours and dangers recover their strength and are restored. [Col. 0077D] And so that they may be able to proceed to the most holy places of our Lord Jesus Christ, consecrated by his bodily presence, the brothers of the same house—unafraid to lay down their lives for their brethren—together with servants and mounted men specifically assigned to this duty and retained at their own expense, defend them against the attacks of pagans both on their outward and return journeys.

These are those through whom God frees the Eastern Church from the filth of the pagans and subdues the enemies of the Christian name. And because their own resources do not suffice for carrying out so holy and pious a work, we exhort your charity in the Lord by apostolic letters: supply their need from your abundance, and frequently exhort the people entrusted to you to join their brotherhood and to make collections for the support of the poor and pilgrims, for the remission of their sins. [Col. 0078A] Know that we have received that same house of hospitality, with all that belongs to it, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and have fortified it by the page of our written decree. And whoever assists them from the resources bestowed on him by God, joins himself to this most holy brotherhood as a fellow member, and pays them annual benefactions, we remit to him one seventh of the penance imposed upon him, trusting in the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Moreover, out of reverence for this venerable house, by apostolic authority we decree that, if those who have joined their brotherhood should die while the churches to which they belong happen to be under an interdict from divine services, ecclesiastical burial shall not be denied them—unless they are excommunicated or have been specifically named in an interdict. [Col. 0078B]

We further will that they may carry for burial at the churches of the Hospital those of their confraternity whom the prelates of churches have not permitted to be buried at their own churches—unless they are excommunicated or specifically named in an interdict—and may retain, without prejudice to another’s right, the offerings made both for them and for others who rest in their cemeteries. We add also that the collectors for the same brotherhood or collection shall stand under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, without prejudice to the rights of their lords. [Col. 0078C] Further, if any of the said brothers sent for these brotherhoods or collections arrive in any city, castle, or village, and that place happens to be under an interdict from divine offices, then, at their welcome arrival, the churches shall be opened once a year; the excommunicated having been put out, divine offices shall be celebrated.

Furthermore, for a fuller increase of their reward and yours, we command and direct you to have this our constitution announced by your parish priests through letters of your own. We also command that, if any clerics of your churches, with the permission of their prelate, freely and without payment resolve to serve the brothers of the aforesaid Hospital for one or two years, they shall by no means be hindered, and meanwhile shall not lose their benefices [Col. 0078D] or ecclesiastical revenues.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, John, cardinal bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.

I, Conrad, cardinal bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.

I, William, cardinal bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Brother Matthew, cardinal bishop of Albano, have subscribed.

I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin in the Mountains, have subscribed.

[Col. 0079A] I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed.

I, Joselmus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed.

I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed.

I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.

I, Albert, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore, [Col. 0079B] have subscribed.

> **Note:** [Col. 0079] The chronological clause is corrupt; in place of *Laterani* (“at the Lateran”), I think *Catalauni* (“at Châlons”) should be read. —Jaffé.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Haymeric, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the eighth indiction, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent II.

### XXXI. He assigns the prebends of the secular canons of the church of Saint Mary Magdalene at Châteaudun to regular canons. (A.D. 1131, February 21.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, Documents, p. 326, from the house cartulary.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ARCHEMBALD, abbot of the church of Blessed Mary [Col. 0079C] Magdalene of Châteaudun, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

For this purpose the care of the universal Church, etc. . . . . Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Archembald, inclined by the prayers of our venerable brother Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, we graciously grant your reasonable requests and strengthen by the patronage of the apostolic see the church of Blessed Mary Magdalene, over which, by God’s appointment, you preside; decreeing that whatever possessions, whatever goods, etc. . . . . Moreover, when the secular canons of the same church die, no one except a person professing the canonical life shall be appointed there; and we decree that the prebends of the former canons shall revert to those professed canons, [Col. 0079D] to be of benefit for their use. Therefore let no one, etc. . . . .

Given at Resbac, through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### XXXII. To Stephen, abbot of Saint Memmie—concerning the privileges of the same monastery. (A.D. 1131, February 25.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 398.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son STEPHEN, abbot of the church of Saint Memmie, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

The authority of our office urges us to labour for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s assistance, to provide beneficially for their peace and welfare. For it is judged fitting and honourable that we who have been appointed to their governance should both protect them from the malice of wicked persons and fortify them by the patronage of blessed Peter and the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Stephen, we receive under the protection of the apostolic see the church of Saint Memmie, over which, by the Lord’s appointment, you are known to preside, and fortify it by the page of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods the aforesaid church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings [Col. 0080B] of the faithful, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Indeed, by this privilege of the apostolic see we decree that, after the death of the secular canons, no canon shall be appointed in the aforesaid church of Blessed Memmie unless he has professed the regular life; and that the prebends of deceased canons shall be assigned to the use of the regular brethren. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, no abbot shall be substituted there unless he is a regular canon and lives under the Rule of Blessed Augustine. We therefore decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. [Col. 0080C] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts to act against this page of our constitution, let that person incur the wrath of God and the indignation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and at the last judgment be subject to severe punishment, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Thus signed:

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Jotti, through the hand of Haimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth indiction, in the year [Col. 0080D] 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent II.

Sealed with the red cord of the lead seal.

### XXXIII. Privilege for the church of Saint Peter at Undensdorf, in the diocese of Freising. (A.D. 1131, March 28.)

[Cocquelines, vol. II, p. 204.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RUDPERT, provost of the church of Blessed Peter at Undensdorf, situated in the bishopric of Freising, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

[Col. 0081A] The care of the pastoral office has been entrusted to us by God for this purpose: that we should labour both to establish religion pleasing to God and, with exact diligence, to preserve it once established. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Provost Rudpert, inclined by the prayers of the illustrious Otto, Count Palatine, we graciously grant your requests and strengthen by the patronage of the apostolic see the church of Blessed Peter, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, constructed by that same son of ours Otto, Count Palatine, and offered to blessed Peter. We decree that whatever goods and whatever possessions the aforesaid church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the grants of pontiffs, the gifts of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, [Col. 0081B] shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Upon your death, as provost of that place, no provost shall be chosen there by violence, save the one whom the brethren, according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, have decreed should be appointed. Moreover, for the defence and welfare of the church itself, we grant you full liberty to choose whatever advocate you prefer. We therefore decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with unjust vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the complete benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving, of course, the canonical and due right and reverence owed to the diocesan bishop. As a token [Col. 0081C] of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall each year pay one bezant to our Lateran palace.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly and rashly attempts to contravene this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person recognize himself or herself as answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit [Col. 0081D] of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Liège, through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent II.

### XXXIV. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Lambert at Liège. (Fragment.)

[A.D. 1131, March 28.—See Reiffenberg, *Monuments*, vol. VII, p. 641.]

### XXXV. He confirms the foundation and privileges of the Church of Beuron and receives it under the special protection of the apostolic see. [Note: [Col. 0081D] Suspect.] (A.D. 1131, March 29.)

[Petri, *Suevia ecclesiastica*, p. 214.]

[Col. 0082A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FRIDERIC, provost, and his brethren in the church called that of Blessed Martin, which is to be consecrated in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, at the place called Beuron, between two mountains, on the bank of the River Danube, in the territory of Constance; to those professing the canonical life, and to their successors who shall live canonically for ever.

Just as assent ought to be denied those who ask for unreasonable things, [Col. 0082B] so we ought to respond with kindly assent to your just requests. Therefore, dearest son Frederic in Christ, granting your just petitions, we receive, as our own right and as specially to be cherished under the protection of the apostolic see, the church of Mary, blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin, over which, by the Lord’s appointment, you preside. It was built on his own land by our son Peregrinus and offered to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church as its own freehold. We fortify it against the malice of all, however few, by the authority of this privilege. Accordingly, by the present decree we establish that whatever your church now possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, [Col. 0082C] shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors, always under the protection of the apostolic see.

In addition, we decree that no one among you, once profession has been made, may possess anything as private property; nor may anyone leave the cloister without the permission of you, dearest son Frederic, or of those succeeding you in the same office, or without the common permission of the congregation. If anyone does leave and, when admonished, refuses to return, you and your successors shall have authority to exclude such a person from communion wherever he may be; and no bishop, abbot, or provost shall receive one so excluded. Upon the death of you, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any craft of intrigue or violence, except the one whom the brethren by common consent [Col. 0082D]—or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, in the fear of God—shall provide to be chosen, either from the same congregation or from another of the same profession.

We therefore decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the complete benefit of you, your successors, and the poor, saving the canonical right and reverence of the bishop of Constance, if he is Catholic. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall annually pay to our Lateran palace a gold bezant, or silver of the same value. [Col. 0083A] Moreover, by our favour we command that no one presume to assume the advocacy of that church except one whom the provost of the same church, with the counsel of his brethren, has chosen; he shall be their advocate only so long as, and no longer than, they please.

And so that this authority of our protection may remain firm and unshaken for ever, we have ordered this written document to be made and distinguished by the impression of our seal.
