If, therefore, hereafter any archbishop, bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, advocate, or person of any rank violates the page of our decree or knowingly and rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person recognize himself as guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to severe punishment. [Col. 0083B] But upon all who preserve their rights for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninth indiction, and in the sixth year of the reign of the most serene Lothair, king of the Romans.

Done happily at Liège. Amen.

> **Note:** [Col. 0083D] Below is read: “The messenger and executor of this charter was Brother Henry of Schweindorphe. It pleased us also not to consign to oblivion, by failing to write them down, the names of certain princes whom we knew to have been present at the court at Liège: the archbishop of Mainz, the archbishop of Cologne, the archbishop of Magdeburg, the archbishop of Bremen; the bishop of Bamberg, the bishop of Regensburg, the bishops of Würzburg, Eichstätt, Halberstadt, Hildesheim, Zeitz, Merseburg, Paderborn, Münster, Osnabrück, Constance, Strasbourg, and Worms; those of Utrecht, Metz, Toul, Verdun, Liège, Cambrai, and Cremona. Likewise the royal abbots of Fulda, Hersfeld, Corvey, etc., etc. Moreover, from the kingdom of the Franks, the archbishop of Reims; the bishops of Laon, Chartres, Albano, Ostia, and Tivoli; and twelve cardinals; [Col. 0084D] and, in addition, several bishops whose names and cities we do not know; the abbot of Aurea Vallis. There were also lay princes there: Duke Simon, Duke Paganus, William, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Otto, Count Palatine of Bavaria, Frederic of Saxony; Margrave Thetbald, Margrave Henry, Louis, Landgrave of Thuringia, Count Otto of Reinegge, Count Adalbert of Saxony, Count Sigefrid, the count of Holland and his brother; the count of Namur; Count Gerhard of Guelders; the count of Mauthenou and his brother; the count of Luxembourg; Count Reinold of Munzun and his brother; Count Frederic; Arnold of Luon; Count Arnold of Cleves; Count Hugh; Count Hermann of Salem and his son; the son of Duke Simon; the son of Duke Paganus; William, count of Glizberg. Moreover, many nobles, whom it would take too long to enumerate.”

### XXXVI. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Bonn. (A.D. 1131, March 31.)

[Guenther, *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus*, I, 210.]

[Col. 0083C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GERARD, provost, and GERARD, dean, and the other brethren of the church of Bonn, and to their successors for ever.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized to accord with reason, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and furnish appropriate assistance, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting your just requests, [Col. 0083D] we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and the apostolic see the church of Bonn, in which you devote yourselves to divine service, [Col. 0084A] and fortify it by the page of our writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods it now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter reasonably acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names: namely, two estates at Bonn, with a share of the tithes; the estate and church of Reida, with the entire tithe; the estate of Lomere and its church, with the entire tithe; the estate of Waleuelt; the estate of Dattenuelt and its church, with the entire tithe; the estate of Berenbach and its church, with the entire tithe; the estate of Aldenkirchen and its church, with the chapels and tithes belonging to them; [Col. 0084B] the estate of Wila and its church, with the entire tithe; the estate of Limorstorp and its church, with the entire tithe; the estate of Mecdenheim and its church, with the entire tithe; the estate of Mehtestorp and the church of Lezzenich, with the chapels and tithes belonging to it; the estate of Gudenesberg and the church of Rinmigestorp, with the surrounding chapels and their tithes; the estate of Uckenestorp; the estate of Ruzenthorp; the estate at Saint Paul; the church of Saint Martin at Bonn, with its entire tithe; the church of Mucha, with the entire tithe; the church of Waltprugele, with the entire tithe; the church of Nuenbret, with the entire tithe; the church of Liuuenskeit, with the entire tithe; the church of Hamne, with the entire tithe; the church of Herchlingen, with the entire tithe; the church of Frisenhagen, [Col. 0084C] with a tithe; the church of Moresbach, with a share of the tithe; Winterskeit, a share of the church and a share of the tithe; the church of Ruoprehtrothe, with the entire tithe; the church of Okenrode, with the entire tithe; the church of Stildorp, with the entire tithe; around and below Grasaph, all tithes from sixty-eight villages; one half of the church of Geistingen, with half the tithe of the entire parish; Lesser Wintere, its church with the entire tithe; the church of Uvadenheim, with the entire tithe; the church of Frankin, with tithes; the church of Calewilere, with tithes; the church of Aeverstorp, with the entire tithe; the church of Entenich, with the entire tithe; a share of the church of Rindorp, with a share of the tithe; the church of Wisebenne, with the entire tithe; the chapel of Saint Isidore [Col. 0084D] with a share of the tithe; and also the quarter-share which you possess in [Col. 0085A] the church of Ginesheim, the quarter-share which you possess in the church of Duna, and that which you possess by gift in the church of Ulma—we likewise confirm these to you.

Besides these, we confirm the following estates: Corengouen, Burnheim, Rindorp, Blankenheim, Bobenheim, Dolendorp, Wintere, Halreberg, Stronberch, and Cuorneskeit, belonging to the alms of the brethren; likewise the vineyards which you possess at Bonn as gifts made to your church by Archbishop Frederick; and also the tithe from the forests which you possess beyond the Rhine through your parishes. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm the liberty of the aforesaid church of Bonn—namely, that the churches belonging to it shall be free from every episcopal due—which you are known to have possessed until the present time.

[Col. 0085B] We therefore decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the complete benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly and rashly attempts to act against this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and authority; let that person recognize himself or herself as answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and [Col. 0085C] at the last judgment let that person be subject to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Liège, through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent II.

### XXXVII. At the request of Abbot Henry, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of the Saviour and Saint Boniface at Fulda. (A.D. 1131, April 1.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 383.]

[Col. 0085D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, abbot of the monastery of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, and Saint Boniface, situated beside the bank of the river called Fulda, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

Established by the Lord’s ordering on the lofty watchtower of the apostolic see, we are bound by the office entrusted to us to love religious persons and to defend the places committed to them by the patronage of apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Henry, granting your reasonable petitions, we strengthen by the support of this present writing the monastery of the Saviour [Col. 0086A] our Lord Jesus Christ, over which, by God’s appointment, you preside. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the gifts of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names: namely, the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, called Exaiulum, situated at Rome near the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, called *ad Praesepe* (“at the Manger”), given out of affection by our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Leo, to your predecessor, the religious Abbot Hecbert, together with all [Col. 0086B] dwellings, heated chambers, cells, wine stores, and kitchen; with its courtyard and well; with entry through the principal gate from the public road; and with all things pertaining to the same monastery, situated both within and outside the city, which are known to belong to it justly and rightly. We also confirm for ever to that monastery, by our apostolic authority, the newly cleared land which you bestowed upon it out of devotion.

We forbid every priest of any church to exercise any lordship or authority in your aforesaid monastery of Fulda, apart from our apostolic see—especially the bishop in whose diocese it appears to have been built—so that, unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, he shall not presume even to celebrate there the solemnities of Mass. We confirm to the same monastery, in perpetual security and without opposition from any person, the gifts, offerings, and tithes [Col. 0086C] of the faithful. We also forbid any woman ever to presume to enter there; and we forbid anyone ever to hold a court there or in its other places, or to compel either serfs or tenant-farmers to any service, except one to whom the abbot has given consent for the benefit of his own need.

Upon your death as abbot of that place, no abbot shall be appointed there by violence or intrigue except one whom the brethren, by common consent and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, have decreed should be elected. We further establish that at suitable times information shall be given to our ecclesiastical concern concerning how monastic religion is governed according to regular observance and devoted to fitting concord through ecclesiastical discipline, lest—God forbid!—under cover of this privilege your spirit and steps of uprightness should in any way be turned aside from the norm of justice. [Col. 0086D] We also grant to you, dearest son, authority by our apostolic power to preach the word of God; and we grant that both you and your successors shall possess, before all other abbots of Gaul or Germany, precedence of seating in every place and assembly, by our apostolic authority. We likewise grant, by authority of our permission, to you and your successors the use of the dalmatic and sandals in the solemnities of Mass, according to what is contained in the privileges of our predecessors.

The abbot, moreover, shall be blessed only by our see, by which he ought to be blessed; and if he is accused of any crime, the judgment of that same see alone [Col. 0087A] shall be carried out. We have also judged it fitting to add generally that whatever is established to have been granted to your monastery of Fulda by the authority of our predecessors, kings, or emperors is likewise confirmed by our apostolic authority through this our privilege. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly and rashly attempts to act against this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be cut off from the most sacred body of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and at the last judgment be subject to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action [Col. 0087B] and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

(Personal sign.) I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. (Farewell.)

Given at Liège, through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent II.

### XXXVIII. Privilege for the Premonstratensian Order. (A.D. 1131, April 12.)

[Lepaige, *Bibliotheca Sacri Ordinis Praemonstratensis*, p. 419.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of Prémontré, and his [Col. 0087C] fellow abbots, provosts, priors, and all the brethren of the Premonstratensian Order: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The sacred religious life of your order has, through the excellence of its merits, made you so worthy of favour and grace that we willingly grant you those things which, according to God, we believe will benefit you through the mercy of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the just intervention and requests of our venerable brother Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, and gladly concurring in your reasonable petitions, we receive under the patronage of blessed Peter and the protection of the Apostolic See your persons and the churches to which you are devoted in divine service, together with all the possessions and goods which you now justly and lawfully possess, or may hereafter, by the grant [Col. 0087D] of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or just means, with the Lord's aid, be able to acquire; and we strengthen them by the authority of this present written decree.

We also decree that henceforth none of you or your successors shall presumptuously dare to violate or alter the form of the Rule and the prerogative of religious life observed in the Church of Prémontré. Rather, each person, imploring divine help, shall labour more diligently so that your order may advance from good to better.

No brother who has promised stability and obedience in your churches may depart; nor may anyone dare to retain one who has departed unless he bears letters of recommendation [Col. 0088A]. Further, in order that the integrity of your order may be inviolably maintained among both prelates and subjects, we decree that, if any abbot of your churches departs from the purpose of his order and the custom of the monastery of Prémontré, Father Abbot shall admonish him concerning his correction twice or three times. If he appears incorrigible, the diocesan bishop, in the presence and upon the testimony of Father Abbot and two abbots of the same order, shall without any delay depose the transgressor against his order. The bishop shall send the deposed man back to the church from which he came, and shall immediately appoint another suitable person, elected canonically by the brethren, in his place.

Therefore let no person whatsoever unlawfully disturb your persons or churches, or seize their possessions [Col. 0088B], retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; but let all be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to make suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all those same persons, churches, and your places who preserve their rights, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0088C] Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Laon through the hand of Haimeric, deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the second Ides of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### XXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Martin of Laon. (A.D. 1131, April 12.)

[LEPAIGE, *Bibliotheca Praemonstr.*, p. 448.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUALBERT, abbot, and the canons of the church of Blessed Martin, situated in the suburb of Laon [Col. 0088D], and to their successors there devoted to divine service for ever.

Since without the true worship of religion neither the unity of charity can endure nor service pleasing to God be rendered, it is fitting for apostolic authority to love religious persons and to foster religious places by the protection of the Apostolic See. For whenever something is requested of us which is known to accord with reason, it teaches us to grant it with a willing spirit and to extend suitable support to the desires of petitioners.

Therefore, beloved abbot Walter in the Lord, granting your reasonable requests, we receive under the patronage of blessed Peter and the protection of the Apostolic See the church of Saint Martin, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, and we strengthen it by this page of our decree. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the aforesaid church now justly and lawfully holds, or may hereafter reasonably acquire by grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names: namely, the vineyards which the church itself possesses at Tiriniacum, Jovia, Mount Antelli, Ursellum, Criptis, Mons, and Mount Laon; and the allods and rent-paying lands which it has at Avenis, Verciniacum, Brucis, Makigni, Pomeretum, Morolzis, Vele, Salmunceum, Villa Mariae, and Vorgia. It also possesses the cultivated land [Col. 0089B] called Monstrata, granted to the same church by Godfrey, with the consent of our dearest son Louis, king of the French; the cultivated land of Surmont; the ovens of Moncels and Verciniacum; the mill called Crollet; a mill-site at Chivi; and another mill-site at Parenni.

We further decree that henceforth none of you or your successors shall presumptuously dare to violate or alter the form and manner of the Rule and the prerogative of religious life now observed in the Church of Prémontré. Rather, each person, invoking divine help, shall labour more diligently so that your order may advance from good to better.

No brother who has promised stability and obedience in that place [Col. 0089C] may depart, and no one may dare to retain a departing brother except with letters of recommendation. Further, in order that the integrity of your order may be inviolably maintained among both prelates and subjects, we decree that, if any abbot of the churches subject to the aforesaid church of Blessed Martin departs from the purpose of his order and, after being admonished a third or fourth time by the diocesan bishop, appears incorrigible, he shall be brought back to the same church and a suitable person shall be canonically appointed in his place—while preserving, of course, the due justice and reverence owed to the diocesan bishop.

Therefore let no person whatsoever unlawfully disturb the aforesaid church, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; but let all be preserved entire for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted [Col. 0089D]. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it and, having been admonished a second or third time, fails to amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of honour and power; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0090A] Given at Laon through the hand of Almeric, deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the eleventh [read: second] Ides of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### XL. To William, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He complains of the disobedience of John, Bishop of Glasgow.

[Monasticon Anglicanum, III, p. 147.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See.

Thus should rebels and ingrates be urged by stern penalties. Since John, Bishop of Glasgow [Col. 0090B], has raised his heel against his mother, the holy Roman and York Churches, and has not feared to lead into the error of schism all whom he could, we direct your solicitude to summon that same John sternly, since you exercise our office in those regions, so that he may come to his senses from his errors and return to the due obedience and subjection of the Church of York. But if, within three months after being admonished by you, he scorns to do this, then, until he has made satisfaction, subject him to excommunication together with your suffragans. We have ordered his metropolitan, Thomas, Archbishop of York, to do the same. Farewell.

[Col. 0090C] Given at Paris, 10 Kalends of May [22 April].

### XLI. He adorns the Abbey of Lobbes, of the Order of Saint Benedict, with privileges; and first declares that no one may be buried in the abbey church, because of the honour of the relics of the holy apostle Peter preserved there. (A.D. 1131, April 26.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, vol. II, p. 1161.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LEON, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Peter at Lobbes, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as consistent with reason, it befits us willingly to grant it and to extend suitable [Col. 0090D] support to petitioners’ desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a speedy effect. For service is never pleasing to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in religious purity.

Accordingly, beloved son Leon, abbot in Christ, we graciously grant your reasonable requests; and, after the example of our predecessor of happy memory John, Roman pontiff, we receive the monastery of Blessed Peter at Lobbes, over which by God’s appointment you are known to preside, under the protection of the Apostolic See, and strengthen it by the authority of our decree. We decree that all possessions and goods which that monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s aid, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings and princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means [Col. 0091A], shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, no one shall be installed there through stealth or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the judgment of the sounder part, shall provide to be elected according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, and whom the Bishop of Liège shall set over them.

That bishop shall never lose the gift of the abbey granted to him by the generosity of ancient kings and emperors; accordingly, he shall preserve without disturbance for the monks the things which they now hold or ought to hold, or shall acquire hereafter.

We also confirm to you and your successors the prerogative of liberty granted to your predecessors by our venerable brethren, the bishops of Liège, in the Church of Liège [Col. 0091B].

We wholly forbid public stations to be held in that monastery by the Bishop of Liège, and forbid that bishop ever to come there or, by his arrival, impose any burden, unless he is invited by the abbot and brethren.

Protecting also the right of the Church of Lobbes, we decree that no monastery shall presume, on grounds of conversion or burial, to receive any person from its household without the permission of the Church just mentioned.

We abolish that evil custom which, under the name of “personatus,” had grown up irregularly until the time of our predecessor Pope Urban of good memory [Col. 0091C].

When a priest serving an altar dies, we order that another suitable person be presented to the bishop by you or your successors. With your consent he shall undertake the care of the parish, render account to the bishop for the pastoral care of the people, and show to you and your successors the due subjection with regard to temporal matters belonging to the monastery.

Moreover, because that place is consecrated in honour of blessed Peter, whose office we discharge, and is especially distinguished by his sacred pledges, we have judged it fitting that its precinct, as established by our holy Fathers and hitherto observed, should henceforth not be opened for the burial of any human corpse.

We also decree that the advocacy of that monastery shall henceforth be entirely free [Col. 0091D], so that no advocate shall be appointed there except one whom the abbot and brethren appoint for the benefit of that place. Wherever and whenever he is invited by the brethren, that advocate shall protect the aforesaid place without disturbance.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may unlawfully disturb the aforesaid monastery, seize its possessions or retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but let all be preserved intact and entire, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, while safeguarding the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of diocesan bishops.

[Col. 0092A] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it and, having been admonished a second or third time, fails to amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that monastery may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Paris through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman [Col. 0092B] Church and chancellor, on the sixth Kalends of May [26 April], in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### XLII. Confirmation of the confraternity of the Church of Osma. (A.D. 1131, May 4.)

[LOPERRÁEZ CORVALÁN, *Descripción histórica del obispado de Osma*, vol. III, p. 13.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all God’s faithful established throughout the parishes of Segovia, Osma, Palencia, and Sigüenza: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the other works of virtue and mercy, almsgiving is especially commended [Col. 0092C]; for it is that which frees from sin and does not permit the soul to go into darkness. Of its praise it is said through the Prophet: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3).

And since our venerable brother Beltran, Bishop of Osma, loving the beauty of the house of the Lord, is striving to build up the church committed to him—a work which is known to require many and great expenditures in order to bring it to a happy conclusion—and since his own resources are insufficient, we ask and command your charity by apostolic letters, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that from the goods granted you by God you provide, by God’s grace, the necessary assistance for carrying out so holy and praiseworthy a work [Col. 0092D]. Thus, through the merits of the blessed Mother of God, in whose honour the said church is founded, and through the prayers poured out to God for you by the secular brethren of the same place, may your goods receive a welcome increase in this age; and, in return for transitory and temporal substance expended through your devotion upon pious places, may we deserve, with forgiveness of sins, to attain the joys of eternal life.

Moreover, we confirm by the Lord’s authority and decree to remain valid the confraternity which, as we have learned, our venerable brother Raymond, Archbishop of Toledo, established there for the support of the place and the salvation of your souls.

Given at Monte Furtino, on the fourth Nones of May [4 May].

### XLIII. To Alvisus, Abbot of Anchin.—He commands Alvisus, though refusing, to undertake the care of the Church of Arras. (A.D. 1131, May 5.)

MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 403.

[Col. 0093A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ ALVISUS, Abbot of Anchin: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is clear that the person who, with charity growing cold, stores away in a cloth the talent entrusted to him by the Lord is ungrateful for divine benefits. For one who neglects to provide for a neighbour’s salvation does not fear to bring upon himself the indignation of the gracious and strict Judge.

We have learned that the Church of Arras, deprived of its own shepherd [Col. 0093B], has chosen you with unanimous vote and equal consent as bishop and pastor. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command and direct your affection to undertake without any resistance the work of God to which you have been called, so that the Church of Arras, greatly diminished, because of sins, both spiritually and temporally, may, with divine grace assisting, receive increase through your salutary exhortations and the example of a good life.

Given at Pontoise, on the third Nones of May [5 May].

### XLIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Denis at Paris. (A.D. 1131, May 9.)

[DOUBLET, *Histoire de Saint-Denys*, p. 485.]

[Col. 0093C] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ SUGER, abbot of the venerable monastery situated at Paris in honour of blessed Denis the martyr, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

The beauty of the house of the Lord must be loved, and the place where his glory dwells must be honoured with attentive diligence and reverence. For the Church of God, which makes its temporal pilgrimage on earth not without much sweat and labour, reveres and loves more earnestly religious and honourable places consecrated to God and devoted to his service, because of love and longing for that Church which shall enjoy in heaven the everlasting and unshaken rewards of joys.

For this reason, we, who by the office of apostleship committed to us by God bear the care and administration [Col. 0093D] of all churches, love with paternal affection and defend from the assaults of wicked men the famous and noble monastery of Blessed Denis, enriched by the munificence and liberality of emperors and kings. Therefore, beloved son Suger, abbot in the Lord, whom we have found by certain proofs to be faithful and devoted to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, and through whose industry and diligence we have learned that religion pleasing to God has been reformed in the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Denis, we grant favourable assent to your reasonable requests.

We therefore decree that whatever dignity has been granted to that place by the authentic privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Zachary, Stephen, Leo, Alexander, Paschal, and [Col. 0094A] Calixtus; whatever goods are known to belong to that monastery through the lawful offerings of Catholic kings or other faithful persons; and whatever it may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, acquire through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to name expressly:

In the district of Metz, the cell of Nova, with all its appurtenances, namely Hulsperc, Autminge, Enmelingas, the church of Fulcreia, the saltworks and salt-pans at Marsal; and the monastery of Argenteuil, situated in the district of Paris on the river Seine, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Orléans: the field of Mainerius, Villare, Vendrous, Villammeium, Fejenis, Linus. In addition, we confirm to you and your successors the county of Vexin [Col. 0094B], which belongs by right to Blessed Denis and which our dearest son Louis, king of the French, is known to have received from blessed Denis through you as a benefice and fief; for he possesses it in whose name it is possessed. We likewise confirm to you the vicariate, all jurisdiction, and full liberty around the village of Saint Denis, as it is defined by the following boundaries: namely from the river Seine, from the mill popularly called Bayard, as far as the upper end of the village called Halbervillare. The aforesaid king, acknowledging that this belonged by right to Blessed Denis, restored it to him.

[Col. 0094C] Moreover, by the protection of our confirmation, we confirm to you the full authority, all jurisdiction, and all the customs of the appointed fair, granted to you through the liberality of that king, so that you may possess them peacefully for ever.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may unlawfully disturb the aforesaid monastery, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; but let all be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of deceit or by violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the judgment of the sounder part, have elected according to the fear of God and [Col. 0094D] the Rule of blessed Benedict. The person elected shall be consecrated either by the Roman pontiff or by whatever Catholic bishop he prefers.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of monks or clerics belonging to the same monastery from Catholic bishops, as has been established by the privileges of canonical equity of our predecessors. We forbid public Masses to be celebrated or a station to be held in that monastery apart from the abbot’s will. Nor do we permit bishops or their ministers to interdict, excommunicate, summon to synod, either the abbot or the monks of that place.

Moreover, we grant both you and your successors leave to appeal to the Apostolic See in more serious matters; and let no harm befall appellants before the matter is concluded, so that, with God as author, you may remain peaceful and diligent in the pursuits of holy religion [Col. 0095A].

If anyone in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it and, having been admonished a second or third time, fails to amend by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, William, Bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, John, Bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Guy, Bishop of Tivoli, have subscribed.  
I, Gozelinus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal-priest of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Equitius, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0095C] I, Ubertus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed.  
I, Rusticus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cyriacus, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Albert, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Theodore, have subscribed.  
I, William, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at Rouen through the hand of Almeric, deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the seventh Ides of May [9 May], in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation 1131, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### XLV. He receives under protection and confirms the possessions of the hospital house at Falaise, founded by Geoffrey with the assent of Henry, king of the English. (A.D. 1131, May 9.)

[*Neustria pia*, p. 751.]

[Col. 0095D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GONFRID: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the office of apostleship entrusted to us by God, we ought to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain its effect more swiftly. Therefore, beloved son Gonfrid in the Lord, we graciously grant your requests, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and strengthen by the authority of the Apostolic See the hospital house of Falaise [Col. 0096A], built by you with the consent of our dearest son Henry, glorious king of the English, and confirmed by his written decree.

We decree, therefore, that whatever goods and possessions have been bestowed upon that place, or shall hereafter, with the Lord’s aid, be bestowed by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, no one may dare to seize or diminish them; but let all be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of the poor, for whose governance and support they were granted. If anyone should perhaps rashly attempt to disturb that place or seize or diminish its possessions, let him incur the indignation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and our own; but let those who preserve them obtain remission of sins and the favour of those same apostles.

Given at Rouen, on the seventh Ides of May [9 May].

### XLVI. He summons Didacus, Archbishop of Compostela, to the council to be held at Reims.—He commends Subdeacon G. (A.D. 1131, May 19.)

[FLÓREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, p. 525.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, Archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

For the preservation of the unity of the Church, and for cutting off the schism that has recently sprung up in the holy Church of God [Col. 0096C], we have judged it useful, by the counsel of our brethren the bishops and cardinals, to celebrate, with the Lord’s help, a council at Reims on the coming feast of Saint Luke. We have therefore decided to summon our brethren and sons—the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other religious and wise men—of Germany, Lorraine, France, Normandy, England, and Spain.

Accordingly, by these present letters and through our dearest son G., subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, we command and direct your fraternity to come to our presence at the stated time, all excuse set aside, so that, strengthened by your counsel and that of our other brethren, we may correct errors and, with God’s grace assisting, establish those things that must be ordained for God’s honour.

We also earnestly commend to you, whom we especially love, our aforesaid son [Col. 0096D] G., whom we embrace in the arms of paternal affection; and we ask that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and love for us, you receive him kindly and treat him honourably.

Given at Beauvais, 14 Kalends of June [19 May].

### XLVII. To Peter, Abbot of Cluny.—Concerning one hundred marks given in England by King Henry. (A.D. 1131, May 20.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, p. 407.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, Abbot of Cluny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, for ever.

[Col. 0097A] We wish, by apostolic authority, to confirm the gifts and benefactions granted to holy churches for the support of the brethren by kings, princes, and other lovers of religious law, as things made subject to divine law. Therefore, by this page of our present decree, we strengthen under the patronage of the Apostolic See the donation made by our dearest son Henry, illustrious and glorious king of the English, of one hundred marks of silver to be paid annually to the monastery of Cluny: namely, sixty at the London toll and forty at the Lincoln toll.

This donation was made at Rouen by that same son of ours, King Henry, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, in the ninth indiction, in the month of May, on Sunday, in the presence of ourselves and our brethren [Col. 0097B]: namely, William, Bishop of Palestrina; John of the title of Saint Chrysogonus; Humbert of Saint Clement; Rusticus of Saint Cyriacus; Gozelinus of Saint Cecilia, cardinal-priests; Gregory of Saints Sergius and Bacchus; Aimeric the chancellor; Guy of Saint Mary in Via Lata, cardinal-deacons; Oldegarius, Archbishop of Tarragona; Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen; Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres; John, Bishop of Lisieux; John, Bishop of Sées; Bernard of Clairvaux; Suger of Saint Denis; Boso of Bacho, abbots; William, Count of Warenne; Robert, son of the king himself, Count of Gloucester; Robert de Sigillo; Robert de Laha; Rabel, chamberlain of Tancarville; Nahel, treasurer; and Haalo, prior of Saint Oswald.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may in future disturb the aforesaid monastery regarding that donation, seize it, diminish it, or rashly harass it; but let it be preserved entire for the benefit of those for whose governance and support it was granted [Col. 0097C]. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our confirmation, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, William, Bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, John, Bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Guy, Bishop of Tivoli, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0097D] I, Ubertus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed.  
I, Gozelinus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed.

Given at Beauvais through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the thirteenth Kalends of June [20 May], in indiction XI, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### XLVIII. He commends Alvisus, bishop, to the clergy and people of Arras. (A.D. 1131, June 18.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, II, p. 164.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Arras [Col. 0098A]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received with due charity our venerable brother Alvisus, your bishop, when he came to us, and we have judged it fitting to send him back to you with the favour of the Apostolic See and the support of our letters. Therefore, by these present letters, we command and direct all of you to receive him kindly and treat him honourably; humbly render to him obedience and reverence as to your own shepherd and bishop of your souls; and, like good and devoted sons, give him unanimous assistance in recovering the possessions of the Church which have been alienated, restoring peace, and restraining plunderers.

[Col. 0098B] Given at Compiègne, 14 Kalends of July [18 June].

### XLIX. He commands Walter, Abbot of Saint Vaast, to obey Alvisus, Bishop of Arras. (A.D. 1131, June.)

[BALUZE, *ibid.*, p. 164.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUALTER, Abbot of Saint Vaast: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Placed by the Lord in the seat of justice, we ought, with God as author, to defend our own rights in such a way that each church preserves its rights. According to the ordinances of the paternal canons, it is fitting for us to do not merely what is within our power, but rather to render to each person what the order of reason requires.

For this reason [Col. 0098C], by these present letters, we command and strictly enjoin your affection that, as has been established by the privileges of our predecessors Urban, Paschal, and Calixtus, Roman pontiffs, and later renewed by ourselves, you render canonical subjection and obedience to our venerable brother Alvisus, Bishop of Arras.

### L. To Hugh, Bishop of Rouen.—He requests that financial aid be collected for rebuilding the Church of Noyon, burned with the houses of the bishop and canons in a fire. (A.D. 1131, June 27.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XV, p. 372.]

[Col. 0098D] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY [corrected: HUGH], Archbishop of Rouen, to the bishops, and to his beloved sons the abbots, clerics, barons, and other faithful of God established throughout the province of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

This exchange ought to seem useful and altogether gracious to humankind, in which eternal things are bestowed in return for temporal, and unchangeable for transitory things. For the Lord, giver and rewarder of all good things, under whose jurisdiction and lordship all things are enclosed, does not leave good will unrewarded, but from the fullness of his abundance is accustomed to grant the greatest things for the least and heavenly things for earthly ones [Col. 0099A]. Moreover, we do not believe that your charity is unaware of what recently happened at Noyon, as sins required: how the episcopal and mother church, together with the episcopal residences, was consumed by fire.

[Note: [Col. 0099D] Pseudo-Robert of Monte, edited by Pistorio, says under the year 1131: “Almost the whole church of St. Mary in the bishopric, and almost the entire city of Noyon, was consumed by fire—a just misfortune, it is said—because many had dishonoured the supreme pontiff Innocent with mocking words” [Col. 0100D]. William of Nangis says the same in his Chronicle. Vassorius, however, refutes this calumny very well in the Annals of Noyon; nor does Innocent’s letter permit any such suspicion.]

Therefore, because we ought mercifully to sympathize with so great a calamity and, out of regard for piety, to provide brotherly assistance, we exhort all of you in the Lord by these present letters, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that you send aid from the resources bestowed upon you by God for rebuilding the aforesaid church to the honour and service of the Lord; so that you may be able truly to sing with the Psalmist: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house, and the place where thy glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8), and, through the Lord’s grant, receive an unfading crown in the heavenly homeland [Col. 0099B].

Given at Crépy, the fifth day before the Kalends of July.

LI. To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen.—He exhorts him to restrain various crimes. (A.D. 1131, July 26.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 421.]

INNOCENT, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Archbishop of Rouen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

He who presides in the Church of God and bears the title of bishop should take care that his conduct accords with his title. For if, when able, he does not recall others from error, he shows himself to be in error. Indeed, he seems to consent to one in error who does not intervene to cut off things requiring correction [Col. 0099C]. It is consent when one who could rebuke remains silent or flatters. But what does it profit anyone not to be defiled by his own error, if he gives consent to another’s error? A priest ignorant of the law thereby accuses himself of not being a priest; for it belongs to a priest to know the law and to answer questions from the law. If he knows it, let him recognize that he is not a guardian of the written documents and letters of the law, but of souls. For the servant who stores in a cloth the talent received from the Lord shall be beaten severely.

In the province of Normandy, whose spiritual administration has been entrusted to you by God, dearest brother, many evils, as we have learned, are springing up—evils which elsewhere either have never existed at all or have been obscured by disuse. New cases require a new judgment, and the discerning physician applies a new medicine to new diseases [Col. 0099D]; and if he perceives no benefit from a poultice, he drives them away by incision or cautery, lest the whole frame of the body rot away.

It is certainly wicked and detestable, and deserving of punishment, that in the bishopric of Rouen certain laymen presume to usurp episcopal rights, seize the offerings of altars, and occupy ecclesiastical revenues; and that some even—something monstrous—presume to call themselves archdeacons. For since the canons and sacred laws prohibit laymen, however religious, from administering ecclesiastical property, and do not permit officials or stewards to be appointed in churches unless they are clerics: if anyone has presumed, with sacrilegious audacity, to hold such estates, ecclesiastical possessions, or revenues assigned to divine purposes, he must be struck by a sentence of anathema, so that his spirit may be saved, and separated from the body and blood of the Lord [Col. 0100A].

Indeed, no one ought to be chosen archdeacon unless he has first fulfilled the office of deacon. But if any layman, through greed for ecclesiastical goods, claims that title for himself, he ought to be called not an archdeacon but an archdevil. Furthermore, it is a matter of most certain law that the Churches of God seek no one as successor by hereditary right or according to the flesh, but require for their government and for the administration of their offices persons who are honourable, wise, and religious [Col. 0100B]. For ecclesiastical honour belongs not to blood but to merit. Therefore, if anyone presumes to demand prebends, provostships, chaplaincies, churches, or ecclesiastical offices by right of succession, let him be deprived of the dignities he seeks, and let him be punished severely for such offences.

A man also ought to be ordained priest for a definite title of a church; he should not depart from that church, to whose service he is permanently assigned, unless his prelate transfers him elsewhere for the common good. It is contrary to the sacred canons, and closely akin to the leasing and hiring of secular property, for hired and mercenary priests—like most frivolous, wandering, and fickle deserters—to be bound to ecclesiastical service [Col. 0100C].

Moreover, if a priest, after undertaking the care of souls, is summoned to a synod where he ought to be instructed concerning faith, morals, and the order of penance, and does not go, while striving to excuse himself by some custom: because he withdraws himself from the presence of his pastor and brethren, he himself indicates that there is within him a heap of crimes, from fear of which he is ashamed to present himself before the judge. Only those customs deserve to be observed which contradict neither reason nor the canons. Such priests, then, and such presumptuous men, are to be deprived of the administration of the Church, from whose unity they separate themselves.

Moreover, it is certain that an ecclesiastical benefice ought not to be clandestine; and whoever is promoted to orders without the bishop’s consent furnishes in himself a proved and evident reason why he ought not thereafter to be promoted [Col. 0100D]. Let those, therefore, be admitted to sacred orders whom dignity of birth, morals, and condition supports. For those begotten outside lawful marriage—who according to the laws are called *vulgo concepti*, “conceived promiscuously,” whose father is unknown—or bastards, that is, those called sons without a father, are not admitted to paternal succession unless this has been solemnly granted by imperial permission. The man judged unworthy of his paternal inheritance must be most carefully prevented from being improperly applied, as a minister of God, to ecclesiastical offices [Col. 0101A].

Furthermore, one who has subjected himself to shamefulness and a dishonourable life, contradicting God by his morals, should not approach in order to serve in the camps of the Lord. Those who are bound to public functions, obliged by the duties of the civic curia, and weighed down by the burden of servitude, must by no means be ordained clerics while they remain subject to the aforesaid burdens; for no one can serve two masters. Reason and propriety likewise prohibit the ordination of men ignorant of letters and unacquainted with the divine law, as though they were useless stumps.

Therefore, dearest brother, diligently fulfilling the office of pastor and evangelist, speak these things, exhort, rebuke, entreat, and reprove; so that, by the example of your good life and the word of your preaching, with divine grace assisting, you may be able to present to the Lord with a hundredfold fruit the sheep entrusted to you [Col. 0101B]. Whatever your considered discretion shall canonically determine concerning the restraint of such grave offences, we shall ratify by apostolic authority.

Given at Auxerre, the seventh day before the Kalends of August, 1131.

LII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint-Amator at Auxerre. (A.D. 1131, September 24.)

[Le Beuf, *Ecclesiastical and Civil History of Auxerre*, vol. II, proofs, p. 264.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HURRICUS, prior, and the brethren of the church of Saint-Amator, situated in the suburb of Auxerre, professing the regular life, for ever [Col. 0101C].

The care of pastoral office has been entrusted to us by God for this purpose: that we should labour to establish religion pleasing to God and preserve its stability with exact diligence. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, a lover indeed of religion and of the poor, by whose consenting zeal and diligent concern religious life has been established in your church, we assent to your reasonable requests and strengthen by the support of the apostolic see the church of Saint-Amator, in which you devote yourselves to divine service.

First, we decree that the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine be preserved in that church for all time; and that no one be installed there as a canon unless he has professed canonical life according to the same Rule [Col. 0101D]. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods you now justly and lawfully possess, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s aid, shall remain secure and inviolate to you for ever. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names:

namely, the church of Saint Peter of Canuaninis, and two chapels in the same parish—the chapel of Orgiac and the chapel of Villa-Ferreol—with tithes and meadows; the church of Saint Martin of Lanosiccum with its appurtenances; and whatever rights you possess in the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius [Col. 0102A]; likewise tithes from three enclosed vineyards which our aforesaid brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, is known to possess in your parish. We likewise confirm to you the tithe from the enclosure of Saint Saviour at Castanet.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the reverence and right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to make suitable satisfaction and amendment, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment [Col. 0102B]. But upon all who observe what is just toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Auxerre through the hand of Emeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0102C], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

LIII. He consecrates Odo, abbot of Saint-Médard of Soissons, on the day before the Kalends of October. (A.D. 1131, September 30.)

[Chronicle of Saint-Médard of Soissons, in Achery, *Spicilegium*, II, 489.]

LIV. To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen.—Confirmation of the rights and estates of the Church of Rouen. (A.D. 1131, October 6.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 423.]

[Col. 0102D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Archbishop of Rouen, and his successors canonically appointed, for perpetual remembrance.

The customary kindness and discerning simplicity of the apostolic see, from the fullness of its grace, binds many persons by fruitful success, complete honours, and benefits; and when needed it displays an unfailing abundance of charity toward its household and humble children. Therefore, it is all the more fitting that whenever we have received from anyone a piously offered benefit or service, we should take care to appear far more generous in repaying than in receiving it, responding not in equal measure or equivalence but with abundant bounty [Col. 0103A]. For the vice of ingratitude is wicked and detestable and must be utterly driven from the minds of good people; indeed, the ungrateful person deserves punishment, not favour.

We have not forgotten with what zeal and untiring concern, in this troubled time, you have fearlessly undertaken the cause of your mother, the holy Roman Church; and how, detesting the ambition of Peter Leo the invader—

[Note: [Col. 0103D] Namely, Anacletus.]

—and crushing the fury of Jewish perfidy, you have by frequent exhortations fortified with reason confirmed the hearts of clerics, princes, and others in the Catholic faith and in obedience to us. Therefore, dearest brother Hugh, archbishop, a man surely wise, religious, and tested in adversity, we receive you as a special and personal son of Blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, and retain you in the bosom of our affection with familiar sweetness [Col. 0103B].

Assenting, therefore, to your reasonable requests, we protect by apostolic defence the Church of Rouen, over which by God’s authority you preside, together with its goods; and we strengthen for you and your successors by the authority of this document those things which belong to its right. We decree that the Archbishop of Rouen shall preside by metropolitan right over the bishops of Bayeux, Avranches, Évreux, Lisieux, Coutances, and Sées; they are to receive consecration from him and humbly obey him as their own metropolitan.

We also decree that priests established in the parish of Rouen shall receive from you the administration of churches and care of souls, and, when summoned to synod, shall not delay to come without any objection [Col. 0103C]. Furthermore, we prohibit any layman within the aforesaid bishopric from assuming for himself the office of archdeacon or presuming to claim an ecclesiastical composition. Nor may any archbishop or bishop dare to perform episcopal functions in the parish of Rouen without your consent or that of your successors. Moreover, let no one demand tithes from your crops or animals, since it belongs to bishops to receive tithes from their subjects and to distribute them, according to canonical enactments, for the use of their own table, for the needs of clerics, for repairing church buildings, and for supporting the poor.

Whoever, moreover, is assumed to pastoral office within the bishopric of Rouen, while your episcopal right remains wholly preserved, shall show due reverence without opposition to you and your successors [Col. 0103D]. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods are known justly and canonically to belong to the aforesaid Church, or which you may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through the generosity of kings, grants of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate to you for ever. Among them we have thought fit expressly to name the following:

namely, the town called Andely, with its villages, woods, meadows, waters, jurisdictions, and liberties [Col. 0104A], with its harbour and revenues from ships; and the right that both you and all servants of your household may at all times have free passage for wine, grain, and every other commodity, whether by water or land, at bridge crossings and sea ports. In England, in the bishopric of Winchester, the manor called Bintae-Worda; in Normandy, the town of Gisors, Willam Duvrent, and Daiville, with fields, woods, waters, meadows, mills, and every liberty and jurisdiction; also the meadows above Sotteville on the Seine, and a house there for storing hay; at Rouen, your own house, court, and garden, the orchard outside the walls, and the household tenants from whom you receive rent and jurisdiction; likewise those things held from the fief of the Archbishop of Rouen; the French Vexin [Col. 0104B], except those castles which by ancient custom belong to the king’s right.

We likewise strengthen for you by apostolic authority, as the other possessions, Alba Marla with all that pertains to it, the castle of Teoni, and the castle of Allium near the city of Amiens, situated above the river Somme. We confirm to you the parish boundaries, within which Melun and Pontoise are contained, as they extend from Pontoise to the sea; and, on the other side, as they are distinguished by the ancient boundaries of territories from the castle of Melun, not only by the river Seine but also beyond the Seine, as far as the river Bithle, and thence by the Seine to the sea.

Therefore let no person presume rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions [Col. 0104C], retain those taken away, diminish them, or burden it with any molestations; but let all things be preserved whole, for the benefit of you and of those for whose governance and support they were granted.

LV. To Saint Aybert, monk and recluse. (A.D. 1131, October 21.)

[Cousin, *History of Tournai*, book II, p. 215.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son AYBERT, monk and recluse, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because by trustworthy report I have learned that you received from my most holy predecessors Paschal and Honorius permission to impose penance and grant absolution to those confessing their sins, by the authority of God, of the blessed apostle Peter, and of ourselves, we grant you the same power. I ask your charity to remember us in your prayers. Concerning the rebuilding of your little dwelling, about which you sent word to me, I ask and entreat all whom you send to and ask, for the remission of their sins, to assist you from their alms. Therefore, to all your benefactors we remit one fourth part of their penance, on behalf of God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and ourselves.

We also grant you permission to celebrate Masses with open doors in your oratory, even if the rest of the country has been placed under ban because of some offence committed outside it [Col. 0105A]. We command that all who visit you shall have complete peace both going and returning; against those who lay hands upon them, we wield the sword of excommunication until they repent and make satisfaction to you. Farewell.

Given at Reims, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.

The attached lead seal bears on one side this inscription: INNOCENT POPE II; and on the other, images of the apostles Peter.

This copy corresponds word for word with its original, which is preserved intact to the present day in the archives of our church of Crespin. I testify that this is so, with our seal also attached, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, 1614.—CLAUDE, humble abbot of the same church.

LVI. He receives under protection the church of Saint Deodatus in the valley of Galilee and confirms its possessions and rights. (A.D. 1131, October 24.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, II, proofs, p. CCXCII.]

[Col. 0105B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALBERT, provost of Saint Deodatus, and the brethren there devoted to divine service, and their successors for ever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to labour for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s assistance, to provide beneficially for their welfare and peace. For it is fitting and recognized as becoming that we, who have been appointed to govern churches, should both defend them from the wickedness of evil men and fortify them by the patronage of blessed Peter and the apostolic see [Col. 0105C]. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Provost Albert, assenting to your reasonable petitions and following the example of our predecessors Calixtus and Honorius, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the guardianship and protection of blessed Peter the church of Saint Deodatus, situated in the valley of Galilee, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, together with all its appurtenances; and we strengthen it by this document.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through grants of pontiffs, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord present, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names:

1. The altar of the Holy Cross, which you, son Albert, provost, with the common consent of your brethren, have permanently granted to the same church for its ornaments [Col. 0105D].

2. Your houses also, and whatever else has been acquired through your effort and contributed by you to the common uses of the brethren of that church.

3. Furthermore, whatever your predecessor Rembald granted to the aforesaid church in houses or other things, we likewise confirm to you.

4. The allod of Moriviller and of Ainvilla, given by the noblewoman Hevuseda.

5. The dower of the woman Ida, namely the allod of Mogins [Col. 0106A], together with half of one mill, granted by her to your church.

6. The church on Mount Saint Remigius, as our brother Riquinus, bishop of Toul, of worthy memory, confirmed to you by his document.

7. Likewise, the tenure of your churches in the bishopric of Basel, as you have held it down to our own time and received it confirmed by the document of Rudolf, bishop of Basel, of blessed memory: namely, that in the fourth year the church of Hungrersem shall pay forty solidi of Basel currency for tithes, and the chapel of Mitteguilre five solidi, and that of Nunneguilre likewise five solidi.

8. In these churches, whenever need arises [Col. 0106B], priests shall be appointed according to the decision of the provost and brethren of your church.

9. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one gold coin yearly to the Lateran palace.

Therefore, no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless exactions; but all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit of you and your successors. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to correct the deed by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour [Col. 0106C]; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Reims through the hand of Americ, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the most holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent.

LVII. Privilege for the church of Saint Martin of Tours. (A.D. 1131, October 28.)

[*Defence of the Privileges of Saint-Martin of Tours*, p. 16.]

[Col. 0106D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours, both present and future, for ever.

Although by the authority and benevolence of the apostolic see we are debtors to all churches and ecclesiastical persons, we ought nevertheless to provide with more earnest care for those persons who are known to adhere more especially to the holy Roman Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we have thought fit to fortify with the protection of the apostolic see and strengthen by the patronage of this document the church of Blessed Martin of Tours [Col. 0107A], in which you devote yourselves to divine service, and which is known especially to belong to the right and property of the holy Roman Church.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods now appear to belong justly and lawfully to that church, or which you may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate to you. Among them we append the following, recorded by their proper names: namely, the borough of Saint Peter the Maiden, with its appurtenances, granted to you by our dearest son Louis, illustrious and glorious king of the Franks; the church of Saint Paul of Cormery [Col. 0107B], the church of Saint Mary of Beaumont, and the church of Saint Cosmas with its appurtenances.

Furthermore, let the liberty and immunity, honours and benefices of your church of Blessed Martin, collected in the documents of our predecessors Adeodatus, Leo, Adrian, Sergius, Gregory, Urban, Paschal, Calixtus, and Honorius, Roman pontiffs, or in those of the archbishops of Tours Crodbert, Ivo, and Airard, be preserved whole and unviolated to you. Let your cloister remain wholly free as far as the corners of its walls, as it is known to have remained hitherto. Likewise, let the priests dwelling within the precinct of the church, in your cells and oratories, in the church of Saint Venantius, and in the church of Saint Peter called “of Cardonet,” remain henceforth in the liberty in which they remained in former times [Col. 0107C].

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church of Blessed Martin, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or burden it with any molestations; but let all things be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, and the ordinations of canons to be promoted to sacred orders from the Archbishop of Tours, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to provide these things freely and without improper exaction; otherwise you shall receive them from any Catholic bishop [Col. 0107D]. If one of your canons is also a canon of churches belonging to the archbishop’s right, then, if he renounces that benefice, the archbishop shall have no authority to excommunicate him.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 0108A] and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Reims through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent II, pope.

LVIII. He confirms the discipline instituted by Bishop Otto in the churches of Bamberg. (A.D. 1131, October 28.)

[Canisius, ed. Basnage, *Treasury*, III, II, 50.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother OTTO, bishop of Bamberg, and his successors canonically appointed [Col. 0108B], greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever we are asked for something recognized as consistent with religion and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and provide suitable assistance, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Therefore, venerable brother Otto, bishop, in accordance with the customary gentleness of the apostolic see we graciously assent to the desires of your petition, first decreeing that the form of religious observance instituted by your diligence, with the Lord cooperating, in the churches entrusted to you be firmly preserved in them for all time.

We further decree that no one shall be appointed in those churches through the simoniacal heresy; rather, honourable persons, supported by dignity of morals and condition [Col. 0108C], shall be ordained there. In the monasteries which were either built long ago in your parish, or which you yourself established out of devotion, or which may come into the possession of your church by other just means, or which may hereafter be built by any of the faithful in your diocese through divine inspiration, we decree that the order of sacred religion shall remain. Nor may anyone in any way alter the form of that institution, unless perhaps he should wish, with the Lord’s aid, to advance it to the prerogative of a better state. Nor shall this be entrusted to the individual judgment of any person; rather, we decree that it must be done by the counsel and consent of all the monasteries belonging to the Church of Bamberg, or of their sounder part.

If anyone should rashly attempt to oppose this constitution of ours [Col. 0108D], and, after a second or third warning, fails to correct the deed by worthy satisfaction, let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But those preserving what is just for these places shall obtain the favour of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves.

LIX. To Ulger, bishop of Angers.—Concerning confirmation of the possessions and privileges of the Church of Angers. (A.D. 1131, October 29.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanies*, III, 15.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ULGER, bishop of Angers, and his successors canonically appointed, for ever [Col. 0109A].

Established by the Lord on the lofty watchtower of the apostolic see, we are bound by the office of apostleship entrusted to us by God to love religious men and defend their places by the protection of the holy Roman Church. For it is fair and reasonable that those whom we know to be faithful and devoted toward blessed Peter and ourselves in times of need should both be defended by us against the wickedness of evil men and graciously heard in their petitions.

Therefore, venerable brother Ulger, bishop, a prudent man indeed and a lover of religion, assenting to your just requests, we strengthen by the patronage of this document the Church of Angers [Col. 0109B], over which by God’s authority you are known to preside.
