We decree that whatever possessions and goods are now known justly and canonically to belong to that church, or which it may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, by the gifts of kings, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. Among them we append the following, recorded by their proper names:

namely, the church of Blessed John the Baptist, situated in the suburb of the city of Angers, which the illustrious man Count Geoffrey the Younger restored to you, so that both you and your successors may have the fullest right of lordship and freedom to appoint an abbot and canons there and to dispose both of prebends and of all other things belonging to it [Col. 0109C]. We forbid anyone to give or promise to another the prebend or deanship of that church before the incumbent person has been removed by death. We condemn those detestable expectations and successions, guilty of homicide; nor may any person dare to receive such a gift or promise, nor may the chapter grant one.

We also strictly admonish that no layman shall presume to claim any right in that church or in any prebend of that church, or to demand any part of its revenues. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority the churches and villages of Chureii and Solona with all their appurtenances, as they have been delivered and granted to you and your church by the nobleman Robert of Buzançais [Col. 0109D].

Therefore, no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or burden it with any molestations; but let all things be preserved whole, for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer [Col. 0110A]; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Issued at Reims through the hand of Haymeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

### LX. He takes the monastery of Mallersdorf under protection.  
*(1131, 29 October.)*

[LANG, *Regesta*, I, 134.]

[Col. 0110B]

### LXI. He informs the clergy and people of Hildesheim that Godehard, formerly their bishop, has been enrolled among the saints by the Synod of Reims.  
*(1131, 29 October.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 463.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Hildesheim: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Bernard, your bishop, appearing before us in the plenary synod which, by God’s grace, had assembled at Reims, declared, supported by the testimony of our brother bishops, abbots, and others who had come with him, that Godehard, your bishop of holy memory, had lived praiseworthily in the world and had shone forth by many miracles both during his life and after his death. Therefore, giving thanks to almighty God with our brethren, and having taken their counsel and approval, because we believe that he is crowned in heaven among the saints, we decree that he be honoured among the saints. We command you both to establish a feast for that blessed man in your church and to take care to assemble annually for it.

Given at Reims, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

### LXII. He confirms to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, the place called Prins.  
*(1131, 31 October.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 416.]

[Col. 0110D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, PETER, abbot, and the monks of Cluny, in perpetuity.

In administering the Apostolic See, we desire to correct what is irregular, to bring what has been ordered into a better condition, and, that it may remain secure in its goodness, to strengthen it by ecclesiastical authority. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, we grant, donate, and transfer to you the donation made to us at Reims, in the palace of our venerable brother Rainald, archbishop, by Girinus and his brothers, of the place called Prins with its appurtenances; and we confirm it by the page of this present writing.

Therefore let no person whatsoever presume rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole in perpetuity for the lordship and possession of the monastery of Cluny. But if anyone should attempt, with rash presumption, to oppose this our constitution, etc.

Given at Reims, on the second day before the Kalends of November.

### LXIII. To Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis.  
*(1131, 2 November.)*

[DOUBLET, *Hist. de Saint-Denys*, p. 487.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SUGER [otherwise SUGGER], abbot of Saint-Denis, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Prudent foresight counsels that matters reasonably established, judicially decided, or settled by agreement should be made secure by charter and ink, lest they be obscured through failure to remember them. For we do not wish lawsuits and disputes to be extended without end, but rather to devote care to the peace and tranquillity of the churches.

A controversy, long conducted by our son Lanzo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael on the river Meuse in the territory of Verdun, against you and the monastery of Saint-Denis, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, has been settled in the following manner by our venerable brethren Matthew, bishop of Albano; Rainald, archbishop of Reims; Goslen, bishop of Soissons; and Albero, elect of Trier; and by our beloved sons Tytoin, abbot of Gorze; Master Otto of Metz; and Simon, provost of Amiens. We confirm it by the page of this present writing.

That is: Abbot Larizo and his successors, and the monastery of Saint Michael, shall pay annually, from the village of Salona, five marks of good gold on Mid-Lent Sunday—the Sunday on which *Laetare, Jerusalem* is sung—at Reims, in the monastery of Saint-Remi, to a duly authorized representative of you, your successors, or the monastery of Saint-Denis, or to the abbot or prior of Saint-Remi for your use. Whatever may happen or be done concerning the village of Salona, the aforesaid monastery of Saint Michael, or the abbot of that place, shall always pay the specified amount of silver at the appointed term to a representative of the monastery of Saint-Denis or to your representative.

Accordingly, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Suger, you and the monastery committed to you have abandoned and wholly renounced whatever claim you advanced against the monastery and abbot of Saint Michael. It was also agreed that you and the monastery of Saint-Denis, and the abbot of Saint Michael with his monastery, should mutually confirm this pact, both by the consent of your chapter and by the impression of the seal. Moreover, Abbot Lanzo must obtain and deliver to you the grant of the bishop of Verdun, confirmed by the authority of his seal.

If anyone, knowingly and with rash presumption, should attempt to oppose this our confirmation, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance, unless he correct his presumption by worthy satisfaction. But those who preserve it shall obtain the blessing and grace of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of ourselves. Amen.

Given at Reims, on the fourth day before the Nones of November.

### LXIV. To Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux.  
*(1131, 4 November.)*

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XIV, p. 247.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ STEPHEN, abbot of Cîteaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0112B] Since a troubled and disturbed mind cannot render service worthy of God, it is our duty, with the Lord’s help, to provide more earnestly for the peace and tranquillity of churches and servants of God. We have learned that a controversy is being conducted between our sons Herbert, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon, and Herbert, abbot of Saint-Seine. Therefore, because we know you to be a wise, discerning, and religious man, we command your charity to appoint a date for both parties, hear the case, and decide it canonically. Having heard the arguments of each side, let whatever your discernment determines between them be inviolably observed.

Given at Reims, on the second day before the Nones of November.

### LXV. Bull for the monastery of Saint Satyre.  
*(1131, 5 November.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, Documents, vol. II, p. 52.]

[Col. 0112C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot, and the brethren devoted to divine service in the church of Blessed Satyre, present and future, in perpetuity.

Placed, by the Lord’s ordering, in the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we are bound by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God to love religious men and willingly to labour for the spread of religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, providing beneficially for the peace and welfare of the church of Blessed Satyre, in which you are devoted to divine service, we have judged that it should be fortified by the protection of the Holy Roman Church.

First, we establish that the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be preserved there irrevocably for all time. When the secular canons who are there die, their prebends having been assigned to the use of the regular brethren, no one shall be substituted for them unless he has professed the canonical life. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter obtain, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you in perpetuity.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all be kept whole for the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Upon your death, beloved son Peter, now abbot of the same place, let no one be set over it through deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren of that place, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, shall have provided to be elected for themselves. We also establish that no one may dare to usurp the goods of that church, but that they shall remain under the free disposal of you and those who regularly succeed you, saving, of course, the justice and reverence due to the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to be guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But may peace from the Lord Jesus Christ be granted to all who preserve justice for that place, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the severe Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Reims through the hand of Americ, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of November, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

[Col. 0113C] On the reverse of the charter is written: “Privilege of Pope Innocent concerning the confirmation and establishment of the Order of Saint Augustine in the church of Saint Satyre, and concerning the removal of the secular canons.”

### LXVI. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Fusniac.  
*(1131, 5 November.)*

[*Historia Fusniacensis coenobii*, p. 23, cited by BRÉQUIGNY, *Table chronologique*, II, 57.]

### LXVII. To King Lothair.  
He praises Lothair’s support for him; gives thanks for the gifts sent; and urges him “to hasten to fulfil what he had indicated in his letter, so that he may receive the imperial crown from his hands at Rome.”  
*(1131.)*

[SCHLOSSER and BERCHT, *Archiv*, II, 370.]

### LXVIII. To Peter, archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See.

[PÉRARD, *Recueil de plusieurs pièces curieuses servant à l’histoire de Bourgogne*, p. 105.]

[Col. 0113D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We make known to your brotherhood that we have directed our brother Guillencus, bishop of Langres, by our letters that he is not to permit any harassment to be inflicted on our beloved son Hebert, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon, regarding the church of Saint Michael, either by the priest Humbert or by any other subordinate person. We likewise enjoin this upon your experience, that you shall in every way provide that the same abbot may hold the aforesaid church quietly and peacefully. For we have learned by trustworthy report that the aforesaid Humbert has justly lost that church.

Given at Paris, on the third day before the Nones of November.

### LXIX. To Guillencus, bishop of Langres.  
That he must not allow Hebert, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon, to be harassed by the priest Humbert.  
*(1131, 11 November?)*

[PÉRARD, ibid., p. 105.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUILLENCUS, bishop of Langres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We enjoined you orally that you should love religious men and support them in the office entrusted to you. With this in view, by apostolic letters we command and order you not to permit any harassment or injury to be inflicted upon our beloved son Hebert, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon, regarding the church of Saint Michael, either by the priest Humbert or by any other subordinate person; rather, take every care that the same abbot may henceforth possess that church peacefully.

Given at Paris, on the third day before the Nones of November.

### LXX. At the request of Heloise, prioress, he takes under protection the monastery of the Holy Trinity (the Paraclete) and confirms its goods, on condition that the nuns pay six pennies annually to the Lateran palace.  
*(1131, 28 November.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, document 259.]

[Col. 0114C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, HELOISE, prioress, and the other sisters devoted to divine service in the oratory of the Holy Trinity, situated in the district of Troyes, in the parish of Quincey, above the river Arduçon, present and future, in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us that is known to accord with reason, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and bestow appropriate support upon the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Holy Trinity, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the page of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions or goods you now justly and lawfully possess, or may in future acquire, through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means with the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you in perpetuity.

We grant you, to possess without any opposition, the tithes from your labours which you cultivate at your own expense, or of annual produce. Let no person whatsoever presume to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all these things be preserved whole, for your use in perpetuity. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay six pennies annually to the Lateran palace.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should fail to make suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But those who preserve it, through the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul intervening, shall obtain the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the rewards of eternal felicity. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Auxerre through the hand of Almeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

### LXXI. To John, bishop of Glasgow.  
That he should obey Thomas [Thurstan], archbishop of York.  
*(1131, 29 November.)*

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, 146.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, bishop of Glasgow: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our predecessor Pope Paschal, of blessed memory, imposed upon you the hands of consecration, while preserving the right of the Church of York. Afterwards his successors, the Roman pontiffs Calixtus and Honorius, of holy memory, commanded you by apostolic letters to render obedience and reverence to our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of York, as to your own metropolitan. Although, as he asserts, you promised obedience to him, you have not yet duly fulfilled that promise in effect. Therefore, by these present letters, we command you, removing every delay and evasion, humbly to obey our aforesaid brother Thomas, archbishop; otherwise we cannot fail him in the justice due to him.

Given at Auxerre, on the third day before the Kalends of December.

### LXXII. To all the bishops of Scotland.  
Concerning the obedience to be rendered to their metropolitan, the archbishop of York.  
*(1131, 29 November.)*

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. III, p. 147.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops throughout Scotland, suffragans of the Church of York: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that one who desires to preside over others should not at all be ashamed to be subject to his own prelates. For obedience and humility are guardians of virtues; but the proud and disobedient incur God’s indignation, and, made hateful themselves, drive away the love of their neighbour. Moreover, just as obedient and humble persons are sons to be cherished in the bosom of the Apostolic See, so, conversely, the rebellious and proud deserve the stern severity of justice. By apostolic letters we command and order you to render humbly, without any opposition, obedience and reverence to our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop, as to your own metropolitan; and, as was commanded you by our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Calixtus and Honorius, to obey him irrevocably.

[Col. 0116B] Given at Auxerre, on the third day before the Kalends of December.

### LXXIII. To Stephen, abbot of Réigny.  
He releases the abbots of Réigny from the obedience which they had rendered to the bishop of Autun for the place of Fontenay. [Note: [Col. 0115] Fontemay.]  
*(1131, 13 December.)*

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 373.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son STEPHEN, abbot of Réigny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The principle of equity requires that no one should seize another’s possessions, but that each should be content with his own right and proper dignity. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Stephen, since the abbey of Réigny, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, is undoubtedly situated in the diocese of Auxerre, we release you by apostolic authority from the profession which you made to our venerable brother Stephen of Autun and from the obedience which you promised him.

We command that you, and the abbots to be substituted for you, render humble obedience and reverence to our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, and his successors, as to your own bishop. The place of Fontenay, moreover, with its goods, although it lies in the diocese of Autun, shall nevertheless remain wholly under the right and lordship of the abbey of Réigny.

Given at Auxerre, on the Ides of December.

### LXXIV. To Hildebert, archbishop of Tours.  
Privilege of Fontevraud.  
*(1131, 17 December.)*

[PAVILLON, *Vie de Robert d’Arbrissel*, proofs, p. 626.]

[Col. 0116D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren HILDEBERT, archbishop of Tours, and his suffragans, and also to the venerable bishops of Poitiers and Saintes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more fragile the female sex is, the more diligently it must be provided for with paternal solicitude. Moreover, your fatherhood does not fail to know how tested and renowned is the religious life of the monastery of Fontevraud, and how much gain for the Lord, with his grace cooperating, has arisen from it. Since the sisters serving God there stand greatly in need of others’ aid and alms, we command your brotherhood to exhort the people entrusted to you by God, for the remission of sins, to support and sustain them from the goods given them by God.

Furthermore, if any of the faithful, from devotion, grant them places in which those religious women wish to build an oratory, then, at their request, provide them without molestation, as required by episcopal office, with holy water and the other ecclesiastical sacraments. And, as we have established that they are free from every exaction, so also we decree that their servants may freely devote themselves to their service without disturbance from the priests to whose parishes they are known to belong.

Given at Auxerre, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### LXXV. To Hebert, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon.  
*(1131, 18 December.)*

[PÉRARD, *Recueil de pièces*, etc., p. 104.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HEBERT, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the administration of the office entrusted to us by God, necessity is imposed upon us to strive to establish religion and, once established, to promote it with the utmost diligence. And as ecclesiastical sacraments are more acceptable to the divine majesty, so they ought to be administered more attentively, with devotion and humility, through discerning and suitable persons for the salvation of souls. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we grant and command you that, if it should happen that your churches become vacant, you may freely and without any opposition place in them wise and discerning regular canons, who shall undertake the care of souls and know how to provide for their salvation, saving, of course, the justice and reverence due to the diocesan bishop.

Given at Auxerre, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### LXXVI. To the abbot of Fontenelle.  
That he should receive blessing from his prelate and obey him.  
*(1131, 30 December.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 425.]

[Col. 0117D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbot of Saint Wandrille: greeting and apostolic blessing.

He makes it clear by manifest proofs that he is a companion of tyrants who, guilty of obstinacy and ambition, desires to rule subjects and neglects to fulfil the office of ruler. It has indeed reached our ears, to our great astonishment, that, although you hold the place of abbot, preside over the brethren, and administer at your own discretion the goods of the church of Blessed Wandrille as its prelate, you nevertheless, under the pretext of a certain evil custom which resists sacred authority and reason, disdain to make profession to your archbishop and refuse to receive the divine sacrament which pertains to an abbot.

Therefore, having rejected the sacrament, you are surely an empty vessel and bear the name of abbot vainly and without substance. If you strive to deceive men, you certainly cannot deceive God. Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and order you not to delay receiving the blessing and obeying your prelate without resistance, as the rule of strict law requires. If you evade and defer fulfilment of this command, then, with the Lord’s authority, we shall regard as valid the sentence which our aforesaid brother Hugh, archbishop—a wise and discerning man—shall pronounce or promulgate against you and the monks obedient to you, justice dictating it.

Given at Auxerre, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### LXXVII. To Guillencus, bishop of Langres.  
*(1131, 30 December.)*

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XIV, p. 247.]

[Col. 0118B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUILLENCUS, bishop of Langres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have entrusted for settlement the controversy being conducted between our sons Herbert, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon, and Herbert, abbot of Saint-Seine, to our beloved sons Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and any others whom they may wish to join them. Therefore we command and order your brotherhood to cause to be observed without opposition whatever they shall establish concerning this matter, whether by justice or agreement. If either party should refuse to comply with their judgment, pronounce an appropriate sentence both against the contemnor and against his property.

Given at Auxerre, on the third day before the Kalends of January.

### LXXVIII. To the archbishops and bishops of France, etc.  
He orders that the religious women of Fontevraud, who do not wish to defend their property by red-hot iron or trial by battle, be defended in their possessions by the testimony of two or three suitable witnesses.  
*(1132, 18 January.)*

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XV, p. 373.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses are situated the possessions and goods of the religious women of Fontevraud: greeting and apostolic blessing.

True lovers of religion give lands and possessions to most holy churches with this intention and desire: that, through the prayers poured out to God by the religious persons serving the Lord in them, both they and their predecessors may be released from the bonds of sins and receive eternal things in exchange for temporal things, heavenly things for earthly ones.

But because the world is inclined to evil, and greed increases as charity grows cold, certain persons, as has been reported to us, forgetful of the salvation of their own souls and those of their parents, strive to take away the goods granted through the devotion of God’s faithful to the religious women of Fontevraud. They take for themselves this subtle pretext for rapacity: that these women are undefended persons and do not wish to defend their property by red-hot iron or battle—because this is not canonical and was prohibited by their master Robert, of good memory, founder of the place.

Yet your whole body recognizes how unjust and detestable it is to divert to private use what has become subject to divine right, and to render void the vows of the faithful. Therefore, venerable brethren, we command that you diligently maintain and defend those women, and do not permit any injury or harassment to be inflicted upon them regarding possessions which they can prove, by two or three suitable witnesses, were lawfully granted to them and possessed by them. If anyone should presume to attempt this, perform full justice upon him as the duty of episcopal office requires.

Given at Autun, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

### LXXIX. To Louis VI, king of the Franks.  
He writes that he has arrived safely at Cluny.  
*(1132, 2 February.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 401.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious and glorious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Sound and safe, thanks be to God, we arrived at Cluny on the Kalends of February. There, celebrating solemnly and honourably the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary with our brethren—the bishops, abbots, and other wise and religious men—we received letters of obedience and submission from our brethren William, patriarch of Jerusalem, and A. [Asquitillus], bishop of the city of Bethlehem.

Since we have long known by certain proofs that you uphold with us the cause of the Church with all steadfastness and courage, and rejoice in our prosperity, we have thought fit to send copies of these letters to your serenity, so that those whom the sincerity of your love joins in a bond of fellowship may likewise rejoice in these favourable outcomes. Let the nobility of your valour know that we have neither absolved A. of Montfort nor ordered him to be absolved. We give manifold thanks to our beloved daughter Adelaide, your queen and wife, for the gifts sent to us, and through you greet in the Lord both her, our most beloved son King Louis, and your other sons.

Given at Cluny, on the fourth day before the Nones of February.

### LXXX. Privilege for the church of Saint Stephen at Dießen.  
*(1132, 6 February.)*

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. VIII, p. 161.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved son HARTWIC, provost of the church of Saint Stephen at Dießen, and to his successors canonically appointed: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever a request is made of us that is known to accord with reason and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and bestow appropriate support upon the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Provost Hartwic, we graciously assent to your just and reasonable petitions. Inclined by the prayers of our venerable brethren Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, and Herman, bishop of Augsburg, we receive under the guardianship of Blessed Peter and the protection of the Apostolic See, and secure by the protection of this present writing, the church of Saint Stephen, entrusted by the hand of the nobleman Degenhard to Blessed Peter by Counts Berchtulf and Otto, their wives Sophia and Laurita, and their sons, and over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside.

We establish that whatever possessions or goods this church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter obtain by grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you. We praise and confirm by our apostolic authority your transfer, made with the consent and support of our aforesaid brother Herman, bishop of Augsburg, from the church of Blessed George—where you had previously been devoted to divine service—to the church of Saint Stephen, because that place appeared more suitable both for maintaining religious life and for the use of the brethren.

We also decree that the chapel situated in the place called Werde shall henceforth be subject in every right to the church of Blessed Stephen. Whatever right or dignity it is known to have possessed up to this time shall be transferred wholly to the church of Saint Stephen; provided, however, that you take diligent care to provide for the aforesaid church of Saint George, so that divine office may be continually rendered there to the Lord. Furthermore, we grant in perpetuity to that place the tithes which the aforesaid church of Saint Stephen has hitherto justly held by grants of pontiffs.

If any brother or sister, after making profession there, should, at the devil’s persuasion, flee to other places without leave of the provost of that place, we prohibit and forbid anyone to presume to receive them; rather, as violators of their own vow, they shall be compelled to return to that church. In addition, we establish that the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be maintained in that church in future times. On your death, as present provost of that place, no one shall be placed over it by any crafty deceit or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall have provided to elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

As a token of this protection and liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one gold coin annually to the Lateran palace. Let no person whatsoever presume to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted. We also decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But those who preserve it, through the merits of the apostles Peter and Paul intervening, shall obtain the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the rewards of eternal blessedness. Amen.

Given at Cluny through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of February, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

### LXXXI. To Briccius, bishop of Nantes.  
That he must not injure the monastery of Tournus.  
*(1132, 6 February.)*

[JUENIN, *Histoire de l’abbaye et de la ville de Tournus*, proofs, p. 151.]

[Col. 0121C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B. [BRICCIUS], bishop of Nantes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received a complaint from our beloved son P[eter], abbot of Tournus, against you: namely, that you disturb his monastery with new exactions and customs. Since that place belongs in a special way to the right of Blessed Peter, we command your brotherhood not to introduce new exactions or customs upon its possessions. Remove completely any that you have introduced; and cause the decision in the case of the church of Saint Vitalis, as made in the Roman Curia, likewise to be observed.

[Col. 0121D] Given at Cluny, on the eighth day before the Ides of February.

### LXXXII. To Peter, abbot, and the monks of Saint Benignus of Dijon.  
He confirms by apostolic authority the revenues of the toll of the town of Dijon, concerning which there had been a dispute.  
*(1132, 8 February.)*

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XV, p. 374.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot, and the brethren of Saint Benignus of Dijon, present and future.

The dispute between you and Hugh, Robert, and Charles, who are indeed your men, concerning a share of the toll—that is, the revenues from sales in the town of Dijon—which belong by right to your monastery, has long been litigated. [Col. 0122A] Moreover, when we came to that place with certain of our brethren, we investigated the same case in the presence of both parties, and received the testimony and sworn oath of Josbert, viscount of Dijon, and of the knight Wirric, that these revenues had been adjudged to your monastery. Therefore, because we ought to strengthen by apostolic authority those things which we know to have been lawfully established, acceding to your just requests, we confirm these same revenues to the monastery of Saint Benignus in perpetuity and secure them by the text of this present document. We decree that henceforth no person may assail that monastery in this matter or inflict upon it any trouble or diminution on that account. But if anyone should presumptuously dare to attempt this, [Col. 0122B] let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and be subject to strict vengeance at the Last Judgment. But may those who preserve these provisions obtain the grace of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

Given at Cluny, 8 February, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

LXXXIII. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Cîteaux. (Year 1132, 18 February.)

[MANRIQUE, *Annals of Cîteaux*, I, 234.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son STEPHEN, abbot of Cîteaux, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Those dwelling in the house of God preserve, in the sincerity of charity and with one mind, the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For religion issuing from a pure mind, strengthened by the indissoluble bond of divine love, inclines the countenance of the most merciful Creator by prayers continually poured forth with pure hearts, so that earthly things may be joined to heavenly and the lowly united with the things above. Since, therefore, we have learned that the brethren of the monastery of Cîteaux, free from secular concerns and devoted to divine service, live piously and religiously, we have accordingly judged it right to grant your just petitions, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Stephen.

For we decree that whatever goods or possessions are known at present to belong justly and canonically to that place, [Col. 0122D] or that may hereafter be bestowed upon it, with the Lord’s help, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. And because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom,” so that you may more freely devote yourselves to divine service and, with the sight of your minds purified, apply yourselves to contemplation, we forbid any archbishop or bishop to compel you or your successors, or any abbot of the Cistercian order, to attend a council or synod, except on account of the faith.

And because the monastery of Cîteaux is the origin and beginning of this religious order, it shall deservedly enjoy, by our grant, this prerogative: whenever it is deprived of its own pastor, [Col. 0123A] it may freely elect and obtain, without any opposition, as its head any abbot from among all the abbots of your order, or any monk. But to the other abbeys of your order which have one or more abbeys subject to them and derived from the fruitful abundance of their own body, we grant, when their abbot has departed this life, the free power to elect whomever they prefer from among the abbots subject to them, or any monk from among all Cistercian communities. But an abbey which has no dependent house may freely elect and have as its abbot any monk from among all the communities of the aforesaid religious order.

Furthermore, no archbishop, bishop, or abbot may presume, without your willing permission, to receive or retain one received of your lay brethren (*conversi*), who are not monks, after they have made profession in your monasteries. [Col. 0123B] But since, as we have learned from blessed Gregory instructing Augustine, bishop of the English, what need is there to speak to those living in common life about making distributions, showing hospitality, and fulfilling mercy? For all that remains over must be expended upon pious and religious causes, as the Lord, the teacher of all, says: “Give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). We decree that no one may presume to demand or receive from you tithes from the produce which you and the brethren of your whole congregation cultivate with your own hands and at your own expense, or from your animals. [Col. 0123C]

Therefore let no one, etc. But upon those preserving for that place what belongs to it, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Cluny through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 10 February, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation; [Col. 0123D] in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

LXXXIV. He assigns to Henry, bishop of Toul, the estate of Berchem, adjudged to the monastery of Moyenmoutier. (Year 1132, 11 February.)

[Dom CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, II, proofs, p. 296.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Toul, and to his successors in perpetuity.

It is our desire to establish the peace of God’s Church; and, lest lawsuits be prolonged without end, but rather be brought to rest, whenever a complaint against it arises, to bring it to a fitting conclusion by the judgment of apostolic administration. And since things not always before one’s eyes commonly fall from human memory through the obscuring effect of neglect unless they are frequently recalled, we have judged it right to commit to writing, for the perpetual remembrance of posterity, the suit and controversy between you, brother Henry, bishop of Toul, and Milo, abbot of the monastery of Moyenmoutier, concerning the estate called Bercheim, which was settled in the presence of ourselves and our brethren. [Col. 0124A]

Thus, when you and the aforesaid abbot appeared before us at Cluny on the date appointed by us, you alleged that the estate of Bercheim belonged by right and property to the Church of Toul, asserting that it had been granted to that Church by the glorious Emperor Otto of illustrious memory. You produced for public reading royal charters: one of another Emperor Otto, who, as was contained in his document, restored that same estate to your Church because the excommunicated Lothair had unjustly taken it away; another of Emperor Henry, who granted the market, ban, and coinage in that same estate to Udo, bishop of Toul; and the privilege of our predecessor Pope Leo of blessed memory, who confirmed to the Church of Toul by apostolic authority that estate together with its market, ban, and coinage. [Col. 0124B] This was done.

But Abbot Milo, after many words had been exchanged, moved by repentance because he had inflicted much trouble and disturbance upon you concerning that same estate, acknowledged before all who were present the right of the Church of Toul and freely renounced the aforesaid estate of Bercheim by a certain charter delivered into our hand, in the presence of our brother bishops and cardinals and a multitude of laymen and clerics who were present. [Col. 0124C]

Therefore, after taking counsel with our brother bishops and cardinals and other religious men, by that same charter we restored the estate of Bercheim to you, brother Henry, bishop, and through you to the Church of Toul, over which you preside by God’s authority; and we confirm it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that neither the aforesaid Abbot Milo nor any person whatever may henceforth disturb the Church of Toul in this matter or inflict any trouble or diminution upon it. [Col. 0124D] But if anyone knowingly attempts in rash presumption to oppose this our restoration or confirmation, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the Last Judgment. But may those who observe these provisions, through the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, obtain the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the rewards of blessedness.

Given at Cluny through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 11 February, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation; [Col. 0125A] in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II, in the tenth indiction.

LXXXV. At the request of Bishop Henry, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Toul. (Year 1132, 11 February.)

[*Defence of the Church of Toul*, proofs, p. 14.]

LXXXVI. To Herbert, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon. (Year 1132, 12 February.)

[PÉRARD, *Collection*, p. 104.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HERBERT, abbot of the church of Saint Stephen [Col. 0125B] at Dijon, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Just as we desire that the things established by ourselves should remain firm and inviolate, so we desire that those established by our brethren through reasonable foresight, whether by contrition [perhaps: “controversy”] or by agreement, should remain inviolate. For a controversy concerning two churches, namely Stabulis and Dalreis, had long been litigated between you and Herbert, abbot of Saint-Seine. At last, in the presence of your venerable bishop Guilencus, as we have learned from his writings, the possession of those churches, together with their tithes, was adjudged to you by the decision of Walter, bishop of Chalon, Gerard, abbot of Bèze, Ayrard, dean of Langres, and the two archdeacons Jocelin and Garnerius. [Col. 0125C]

But because the mind of the abbot of Saint-Seine did not desist from seeking to recover the churches, we, desiring to provide for the peace and quiet of both churches, entrusted the settlement of this case to our beloved son Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, on the condition that whatever he should establish through justice or agreement should remain valid by apostolic authority. He, indeed, as a religious man and lover of peace, having heard and carefully considered the arguments both of yours and of the other party, and acting on the counsel of our dearest son Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and of other religious men, settled by agreement the aforesaid controversy concerning the two churches in this manner: namely, that you and your brethren should hold one half of those churches and the church of Saint Stephen the remaining half. [Col. 0125D]

Therefore, because we ought to establish what contributes to peace in the Church of God, we strengthen by apostolic authority the agreement established by our aforesaid son Abbot Stephen, and by this present decree enact that no one may assail your church in this matter. If anyone knowingly attempts to oppose this our constitution, let him be struck by the sentence of anathema.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Cluny through the hands of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 12 February, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

LXXXVII. At the request of Abbot Bernard, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Mary of Clairvaux. (Year 1132, 17 February.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, II, 577.]

[Col. 0126A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity. . . .

Moreover, how steadfastly and perseveringly your zeal for religion and discernment, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Bernard, undertook to defend the cause of blessed Peter and your holy mother, the Roman Church, when the schism of Peter Leonis was inflamed; and how, setting yourself as an impregnable wall before the house of God, you laboured, fortified with frequent arguments and reason, to lead the minds of kings and princes and of other persons, both ecclesiastical and secular, to the unity of the Catholic Church and obedience to blessed Peter and to us—this is made clear by the great benefit which has accrued to the Church of God and to us. [Col. 0126B] Therefore, granting your just requests, we have secured by the protection of the apostolic see the monastery of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, over which you preside by God’s authority, together with everything belonging to it; decreeing that whatever possessions or goods belong to that place, etc., as above.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano. I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in [Col. 0126C] Portico. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Lyon through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 17 February, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

LXXXVIII. Bull for the establishment of regular canons in the monastery of Saint Laud of Coutances. (Year 1132, 2 March.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI, documents, 238.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0126D] brother ALGAR, bishop of Coutances, and to his successors to be canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Then the Church of God is governed in its proper order when its administration is entrusted to a wise and religious person. We rejoice greatly, dearest brother Algar, bishop, because divine providence has called you to the administration of the Church of Coutances. Therefore, providing for you and your Church for the future, we strengthen by the safeguard of our privilege, for you and your successors, the goods and possessions, liberties and immunities which the Church of Coutances is known to have possessed peacefully and lawfully until these times.

Moreover, we grant to you, with the consent of the prince, the church of Saint Laud, situated in the city of Rouen, [Col. 0127A] and Saint Laud in the diocese of Coutances, with their appurtenances and liberties, so that you may bring them into canonical order. For we have heard that secular clerics live there irregularly; provided, however, that as the secular clerics die, their prebends and alms shall pass to the use of regulars. When the prelate dies, no one shall be set over them there by any violence whatever, except one whom the canons, by common assent and according to the fear of God and the statutes of the apostolic see, determine should be elected. If anyone, therefore, should rashly presume to violate the text of this our constitution, etc. . . .

Given at Vienne, 2 March, in the year of the Lord 1132.

LXXXIX. To those who visit the monastery of Cluny on the anniversary of the dedication of the high altar, he remits forty days of their imposed penance. (Year 1132, 2 March.)

[*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1380.]

[Col. 0127B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his prudent son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

It is a praiseworthy kind of generosity that those who devote themselves to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church with humble devotion should obtain a greater prerogative of familiarity and worthier benefits. The Church of God knows, and greatly rejoices, how pleasing a service the monastery of Cluny renders to God and how brilliantly it shines among men through the splendour of religion. [Col. 0127C] Therefore justice requires that this same place should enjoy the privilege of apostolic affection and possess freedom both in head and members.

We ourselves visited that monastery, which belongs in a special manner to the right of blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church. On the same day on which, after the passage of many years, our predecessor Pope Urban of happy memory had consecrated there the high altar, we, with the archbishops and bishops assembled with us and through the cooperation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, solemnly dedicated the same monastery. Moreover, having regard for the devotion and humility of the faithful who gather there on the anniversary of the dedication for the love of God and reverence for that place, we, trusting in the grace of God and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, remitted to them forty days of the penance imposed upon them. [Col. 0127D]

We also decree that the immunity of that same monastery shall be preserved inviolate and entire in future times. If anyone within the bounds of the ban established around Cluny by that same predecessor of ours knowingly presumes to seize or wound persons, or violently take away property of the said monastery, let him be bound by the sentence of excommunication and remain excommunicated until he restores what he took and makes suitable satisfaction to the monks of Cluny for the injury inflicted. Further, we decree that whoever seizes monks of Cluny or their companions, or the things which they carry or transport, shall likewise be subject to excommunication. [Col. 0128A]

But if anyone, in the absence of the monks themselves, has plundered anywhere goods belonging to the food or clothing of the brethren serving God in the monastery of Cluny, then, unless he restores what was taken within ten days, we command that he shall thereby be subject to anathema, and we prohibit the celebration of divine offices in his land. We order that the places to which such persons have fled shall, for as long as they remain present there, cease from divine worship, except for the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying; and none of those offenders shall be absolved except by the Roman pontiff alone.

Furthermore, whoever violently takes from the aforesaid brethren, wherever they may dwell, any other thing besides those listed above, unless he restores what was taken within ten days, shall be subject to excommunication and shall not be absolved until he renders the principal amount and makes suitable satisfaction. [Col. 0128B] We solemnly command archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses these acts have been committed, by the authority of blessed Peter and by our own, that once the complaint reaches their ears or the crime becomes known, they shall, putting aside all slackness, cause the aforesaid sentence of excommunication to be observed.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Vienne through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, in the eleventh indiction, in the third year of our pontificate, on 2 March.

XC. To Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.—Settlement of the controversy between Cluny and the abbot of Saint-Gilles. (Year 1132, 8 March.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 409.]

[Col. 0128C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ PETER, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We willingly desire to establish the things which concern the peace of the Church, and to provide with careful diligence that they be inviolably observed in future times. For you, dearest son in the Lord, Abbot Peter, and the monastery of Cluny had long carried on a suit and controversy against our beloved son Peter, abbot of Saint-Gilles, and his monastery. [Col. 0128D] You challenged them concerning the subjection granted to you and your predecessors by the apostolic see; but he maintained the ancient liberty of his monastery.

At last, in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, the bishop-cardinals, this matter was settled at Bellay in the following manner. Namely, if—may it never happen!—the order of religion in the monastery of Saint-Gilles should be diminished, it shall there be reformed by the command and counsel of you and your successors. If it should happen that you or your successors go to that monastery, you shall be received reverently, and, for as long as you remain there, you and all your company shall be honorably provided for. You shall also have free power, in the presence of the aforesaid abbot or his successors, to sit in that abbot’s seat, to preside over the chapter, and to correct whatever needs correction there. [Col. 0129A]

Nevertheless, upon the death of that abbot, or if he or his successors transfer to another place, the brethren of the monastery of Saint-Gilles shall have the liberty to elect an abbot from their own community without impediment. Yet, for an abbot who has transferred to another monastery, they may take no pastor except from the monastery of Cluny. When that man dies, or is removed from his community, they shall likewise have the power to elect an abbot, subject to the same condition.

Moreover, as recompense for the labours and expenses which you or your predecessors had borne for the monastery of Saint-Gilles, that abbot, with the consent of his brethren, gave to you, and through you to the monastery of Cluny, the obedience called Limantio, [Col. 0129B] with its appurtenances, and transferred it forever into its right and ownership. If anyone should trouble you concerning that obedience, the aforesaid Abbot Peter has made himself and his successors, according to justice, its advocates and defenders.

But you, beloved son Abbot Peter, after taking counsel with your brethren, have renounced in perpetuity every complaint which you had against the monastery of Saint-Gilles, except those matters which have been stated. It was also established that, if the monastery of Cluny holds any privileges concerning the monastery of Saint-Gilles, or the monastery of Saint-Gilles holds any concerning Limantio, they shall be returned on both sides. But if any general privileges exist, they shall have no force in this matter.

Therefore, by the authority of God and our own, we command that the aforesaid agreement shall be observed forever, without objection by anyone. [Col. 0129C] If anyone should presume to oppose the aforesaid concord or this command of our confirmation, let him incur the indignation of the blessed Peter and Paul and of ourselves, and let his undertaking be frustrated.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano, have signed. I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico Noles, have signed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have signed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have signed. I, Luke, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, [Col. 0129D] have signed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George, have signed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have signed.

Given at Valence through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 8 [read: 15] March, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

XCI. To all archbishops and bishops.—Cluniac privileges. (Year 1132, 8 March.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 405.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, archbishops and bishops, to [Col. 0130A] whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is a praiseworthy kind of generosity that those who devote themselves to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church with humble devotion should obtain a greater prerogative of familiarity and worthier benefits. The Church of God knows, and greatly rejoices, how pleasing a service the monastery of Cluny renders to God and how brilliantly it shines among men through the splendour of religion. Therefore justice requires that this same place should enjoy the privilege of apostolic affection and possess freedom both in head and members.

We ourselves visited that monastery, which belongs in a special manner to the right of blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church. And on the day on which, after the passing of many years, our predecessor Pope Urban of happy memory had consecrated the high altar there, we, together with the archbishops and bishops who had assembled with us, through the cooperation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, solemnly dedicated the same monastery. [Col. 0130B] Moreover, having regard for the devotion and humility of the faithful who gather there on the anniversary of the dedication for the love of God and reverence for that place, we, trusting in the grace of God and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, remitted to them forty days of the penance imposed upon them.

We also decree that the immunity of that same monastery shall be preserved inviolate and entire in future times. If anyone within the bounds of the ban established around Cluny by that same predecessor of ours knowingly presumes to seize or wound a person, or take away his property, let him be struck by the sentence of excommunication until he restores what he has taken and makes suitable satisfaction to the abbot and monks for the injury inflicted. [Col. 0130C] Further, we decree that whoever seizes monks of Cluny or their companions, or the things which they carry or transport, shall be subject to excommunication.

But if anyone, in the absence of the monks themselves, has plundered anywhere goods belonging to the food or clothing of the brethren serving the Lord in the monastery of Cluny, then, unless after warning he restores what was taken within forty days, we command that he shall be subject to anathema, and we prohibit the celebration of divine offices in his land. We command that the places to which such persons have fled shall, while they remain present there, cease from divine worship, except for infant baptism and the penances of the dying; and none of those offenders shall be absolved, except in fear of death, by anyone other than the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0130D]

Furthermore, whoever takes from the aforesaid brethren, wherever they may dwell, any other thing besides those enumerated above, unless he restores what was taken within forty days after our warning, shall be subject to excommunication and shall not be absolved until he renders the principal amount and makes suitable satisfaction. If you learn that these acts have been committed, or if a complaint about them reaches your ears, we command you to ensure that the aforesaid sentence of punishment is firmly observed throughout your dioceses.

Given at Valence, 8 March.

XCII. He informs the abbots, clergy, princes, and people of Trier that Albero, whom they had elected, had been consecrated by him and granted the pallium; he directs them to obey him. (Year 1132, 11 March.)

[JAFFÉ, *Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 568. “In the Royal Archive at Berlin. From Pertz’s papers.” Opening: “Our dearest brother.”]

[Col. 0131A]

XCIII. Privilege for the monastery of Tournus. (Year 1132, 16 March.)

[COCQUELINES, vol. II, p. 206.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ PETER, abbot of the monastery of Tournus, and to his successors to be regularly appointed [Col. 0131B] in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is known to accord with reason, it becomes us to grant it willingly and to bestow fitting support upon the wishes of those who ask. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Peter, assenting to your reasonable requests, we protect the monastery of Tournus, over which you preside by God’s authority, by the patronage of the apostolic see, following the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs.

Accordingly, by the text of this present privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever goods and whatever possessions now lawfully belong to that monastery through the benefactions of Catholic emperors or other princes, the grants of bishops, or the offerings of other faithful persons, or which it may justly acquire in future, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. [Col. 0131C] We also confirm by the authority of the apostolic see the settlement, which we have learned from their writings was made by our predecessors of holy memory, Lords Urban and Calixtus, between your monastery and that of blessed Florentius concerning the churches of Holy Cross and Saint Nicholas.

Further, we decree that the same place, where rest the bodies of the blessed martyr Valerian and Saint Philibert the confessor, shall remain forever free from every yoke of secular power. No bishop of whatever diocese may disturb it by excommunication or absolution, or impose crosses or any new exactions upon the borough and other possessions of the monastery. We forbid public masses to be celebrated in that monastery, or stations to be held there by a bishop, against the will of the abbot or brethren. [Col. 0131D]

Moreover, out of reverence for blessed Mary, mother of the Lord, whose name distinguishes your place, we permit the abbot or brethren to pronounce the angelic hymn during the solemnities of Mass on the Annunciation of the Lord. Upon the death of the abbot of that place, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of intrusion or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall determine ought to be elected according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, and who is to be consecrated by the bishop of the apostolic see or his legate.

Therefore let no person whatever be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or oppress it with any vexations. Rather, let all things remain intact, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted. [Col. 0132A] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this text of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment of the wrong committed; and let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject to strict vengeance at the Last Judgment.

But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0132B]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, Luke, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have signed. I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have signed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have signed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George, have signed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have signed.

[Col. 0132C] Given at Valence through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 16 March, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

XCIV. Bull for the monastery of Tiron. (Year 1132, 16 March.)

[MABILLON, *Benedictine Annals*, VI, 636.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, abbot of Tiron, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to have care for all churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide for their peace and welfare. Therefore, beloved [Col. 0132D] son in the Lord, Abbot William, inclined by the prayers of our dearest brother Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, we graciously grant your reasonable requests and have judged that the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Tiron, over which you preside by God’s authority, should be fortified by the protection of the apostolic see.

We decree that whatever possessions or goods are now known to belong justly and canonically to that monastery, or may hereafter be offered to that place, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have added the following, to be specified by their proper names.

In the kingdom of England, in the bishopric of Saint David: the church of Saint Mary of Cathmeis with its appurtenances. [Col. 0133A] In the bishopric of Saint Andrew in Scotland: the abbey of Saint Mary of Roxburgh with its appurtenances; the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul of Ogra with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Giles of Castenariis; the church of Saint Leonard of Ferreries; the church of Saint Mary of Asneriis; the church of Saint Mary of Telio; the church of Saint Lawrence of Brigia; the church of Saint Peter of Audita; the church of Saint Martin of Hildrevilla; the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Jarzia; the church of Saint Mary of Aguille; the church of Saint John the Baptist of Murgeriis; and the church of Saint Andrew of Anglia with its appurtenances.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatever may disturb your monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any troubles; but let all things be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, with due respect nevertheless for the diocesan bishops. [Col. 0133B] We grant you the possession, without any objection, of the tithes from the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, and likewise from your animals.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this text of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects the deed by worthy satisfaction, let him suffer the loss of his power and honour, and let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. But may those who preserve what is just for that place obtain the grace of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Valencia through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent II, pope. [Col. 0133D]

XCV. To William, lord of Montpellier.—He receives his person and all property pertaining to him under the guardianship and protection of the Roman Church, so that no one may dare to take them away, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations. (Year 1132, 24 March.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XV, p. 375.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ WILLIAM, lord of Montpellier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The principle of equity and justice persuades us that those whom we know to be more devoted toward Blessed Peter and ourselves should be embraced in the arms of a closer charity and be cared for more intimately within the very bosom of the holy Roman Church. For it is fitting that a loving mother should show greater kindness toward her humble sons and defend them against the assaults of wicked persons. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord William, we receive you—as our man and faithful servant, and as a special soldier of Blessed Peter—together with your inheritance, namely Montpellier with its marsh, and your goods which you presently possess lawfully, under the guardianship and protection of Blessed Peter; and we secure them by the page of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may henceforth disturb your person, or the aforesaid inheritance, or your goods; take them away; diminish them; or harass them by any vexations. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him not doubt that he will incur the indignation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of ourselves.

Given at Avignon, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the first [third] year of our pontificate.

XCVI. To Peter the Venerable.—A privilege concerning the monastery of Blessed Mary of La Charité above the Loire: it is always to be a priory of the Cluniac order, and an abbot is never to be established there. (Year 1132, 30 March.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 48.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ PETER, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, for ever. [Col. 0134C]

The holy mother, the Apostolic Roman Church, dispenser and provident guardian, having received authority and privilege from our very Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, distributes to individual churches their respective dignities according to a governing rationale. For the Lord said to Blessed Peter: “When once you have turned again, strengthen your brethren”; and: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven”; and: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.” After the resurrection He told him for the third time to feed the Lord’s flock. In accordance with the custom of the ancients in cities where laws were given to peoples by prudent men, Blessed Peter and his successors established bishops, archbishops, and primates, who should instruct the people in divine law. In certain new and religious places, however, abbots were established by the Apostolic See, men who knew how to preside over and benefit a community of brethren. In still other places, for the preservation of true humility—which is the seasoning of all virtues and repels pride and envy, its constant companions—it was likewise established that they should always be subject to obedience and priorate.

Therefore, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, we decree that the church of Saint Mary of La Charité, which from its first foundation was offered to the monastery of Cluny by Geoffrey, bishop of Auxerre, of good memory; William, count of Nevers; Bernard of Cailan; and other faithful persons, to whose right that place belonged both in temporal and spiritual matters, shall remain for all future times your dependent house and priory. We therefore forbid, on the part of Blessed Peter and of ourselves, that any person whatsoever may establish an abbot in that place. Rather, let the brethren serving the Lord there, content with the governance of the abbot of Cluny and their own prior, fulfill what they have professed and render vows pleasing to God. If anyone becomes a transgressor of this our constitution, let him know that he will incur the wrath of God and the indignation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand: “HELP US, O GOD OF OUR SALVATION.”

[Col. 0135B] Given at Vapingum, through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

XCVII. To Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.—He newly invests him with the abbey of Saint-Bertin, commanding its monks to obey him. (Year 1132, 30 March.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 47.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The precepts of the canons instruct us that, in carrying out business, we should undertake nothing too hastily and nothing irregularly. Your belovedness recently requested insistently at Rheims, in the presence of our brethren the archbishops, bishops, and other religious men who had assembled there with us, that we restore to you the abbey of Saint-Bertin, entrusted by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, to the monastery of Cluny and confirmed by their privileges. Yet, after deliberation with the same our brethren, we granted the monks of that place a respite until the recent feast of the Epiphany, so that they might then come into our presence, prepared to answer you concerning your complaints. But when that term had elapsed, they neither came nor sent representatives; rather, through R., archbishop, and N., bishop of Thérouanne, our brethren, and through our beloved son T., the illustrious count of Flanders, they sent two monks asking for a longer truce of peace. Wishing to remove every excuse from them, we waited for them until the recent Mid-Lent; yet even then they neither came nor sent anyone to prosecute their case. Since neither strict law requires, nor equity demands, that we grant them a longer term while they persist in their contumacy, following in the footsteps of our predecessors we have invested you with the aforesaid abbey of Saint-Bertin for the reform of religion. By apostolic letters we command the monks of that monastery humbly to obey you, beloved son in the Lord Peter, abbot, and to elect an abbot in accordance with your direction and counsel. [Cols. 0135C–0136A]

Given at Vapingum, on the third day before the Kalends of April.

XCVIII. To William, lord of Montpellier.—He commends his devotion toward himself and the Roman Church, and exhorts him to persevere in his good purpose. (Year 1132, 13 April.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XV, p. 377.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, the illustrious man WILLIAM of Montpellier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We often recall the love and service which you do not cease to render to Blessed Peter and to us, and for these things we offer manifold thanks, in heart and speech, to your devotion. Since the welcome service of one who serves merits the reward of true love, we embrace your person in the arms of sincere charity, as we have often made known to you. We beseech, by humble prayer, that the mercy of almighty God may deign to preserve it unharmed.
