If anything has been attempted through such audacity, it shall be held wholly void.

Nor may bishops, without your consent, restrain the clerics of your monastery by sentence of suspension or excommunication. Whatever else the aforesaid monastery may hereafter obtain, with the Lord’s help, through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, we confirm to you by this present writing.

Moreover, from the benevolence of the Apostolic See we grant to your person those insignia of dignity which your predecessors are known to have used during the solemnities of Mass: namely, on feast days, in celebrating the offices of Mass, you may be vested in dalmatic, mitre, gloves, and sandals. Furthermore, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid convent, etc., so that it may always rejoice in the defense and protection of the Apostolic See, to which it properly belongs. If hereafter any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince, duke, count, viscount, judge, castald, or ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and after a second or third admonition does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor and know himself guilty before divine judgment, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 0163D]  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. [Col. 0164A]  
I, George, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.  
I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

Given at Nonantola through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1133 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

### CXXI. To Berthold, Abbot of Saint Blaise.—He approves the separation of the church of Burgl from the church of Eggenheim. (A.D. 1132, November 4.)

[D. GERBERT, *History of the Black Forest*, III, p. 66.]

[Col. 0164B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERTHOLD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Blaise, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.

Just as we desire those things which we establish to remain firm and inviolate, so we decree that things performed by our brethren with reasonable care shall be kept uncorrupted. Accordingly, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Berthold, we confirm by authority of the Apostolic See what was established concerning the dependent house of Burgala and the chapel of Saint John, situated in the place called Ekkeneim, by our venerable brethren of blessed memory, Odelric, bishop of Constance, [Col. 0164C] and his successor, likewise Odelric, with the consent of the archpriest and the other priests of that parish:

> [Note: [Col. 0163D] Conrad, monk of Saint Blaise, wrote a chronicle of this dependent house of Burgl; it was published by our Father Rustenus Heer in the anonymous chronicle of Muri, where much material elucidating this bull is found.]

> [Note: [Col. 0163D] The church of Saint John in the village of Eggenheim, at the foot of Mount Burgl, was a parish church and, though its religious status has changed, still remains.]

> [Note: [Col. 0163D] From a charter of Herman, bishop of Constance, of the year 1155, it is clear that Ulrich I, bishop of Constance from Dillingen, who died in 1127, transferred the church of Burglen into the power of the monks by authority of Pope Honorius and Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz. Thus Ulrich I had already begun this business; his successor Ulrich II, bishop of Constance, completed it. His confirmation of the settlement concerning the place Burgulum, assigned to the abbot of Saint Blaise, is found in Father Hergott, *Codex Probat.* vol. II, part I, p. 154, “given at Basel, A.D. 1130, 8 February,” which date falls on the seventh feria, that is, Saturday.]

Namely, the aforesaid dependent house of Burgala and the church of blessed John, which were built with the consent of the aforesaid bishops upon the freehold estate which Quarnerius and Aguipertus, when they came to religious conversion, offered to the monastery of blessed Blaise over which, by God’s grace, you preside, shall forever belong by right to the aforesaid convent together with their appurtenances.

> [Note: [Col. 0164D] These are Wernher of Kattenbach and his brother Wipert, who became monks at Saint Blaise under Abbot Rustenus around the year 1120 and bestowed their property at Burglen, Ekinheim, Kaltinbach, and elsewhere upon the same monastery, as is clear from the cited Burgl Chronicle.]

Yet the brethren of the monastery of Saint Blaise shall freely serve the Lord in the aforesaid dependent house of Burgala without anyone’s opposition, while in the church of blessed John built at the foot of the mountain the people shall receive the divine sacraments; and each shall be content with its own boundaries, as was established by the aforesaid bishops. Therefore, no person may infringe or alter this charter of our confirmation; rather, all things, as set forth above, shall be preserved in their stability for perpetual future times. But if anyone proves a violator of this our constitution, let that person know that he will incur the indignation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Piacenza, on the second day before the Nones of November.

### CXXII. To Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Stephen, bishop of Paris.—That they should endeavor to restore to the subdean of Orléans and his associates the honors and property taken from them. (A.D. 1132, November 5.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 401.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brethren GEOFFREY, bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, and STEPHEN, bishop of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As your brotherhood knows, we placed in your judgment and assessment the restitution of the losses and injuries inflicted upon our beloved sons Archembald, subdean of Orléans, Master G., and their associates, together with the honors taken from them. Since we have learned that this has not at all been carried out, we command and direct your affection to proceed, as you have well begun, in the name of the Lord, and bring the same matter to completion.

Given at Piacenza, on the Nones of November.

### CXXIII. Privilege for the Church of Saint Ursus of Aosta (province of Tarentaise). (A.D. 1132, November 19.)

[*Monuments of National History*, Charters, I, p. 769, from the archive of the collegiate church of Saint Ursus of Aosta (L. C.).]

[Col. 0165C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HERBERT, bishop of Aosta, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

It accords with the governance of the Apostolic See mercifully to assent to the wishes of religious men and to give them aid, so that their undertaking may receive an increase pleasing to God. Therefore, acceding to your petitions, venerable brother Herbert, bishop, we strengthen by this charter the church of Saint Ursus, situated in the suburb of the city of Aosta.

We decree that, according to your wish and the approval and consent of your brethren—namely Boso, provost, Stephen, archdeacon, and the whole chapter—the canonical order shall be preserved inviolably in that church in future times; and when the canons presently known to reside there die, no one shall be substituted for them unless he has professed the canonical life. Moreover, whatever goods or possessions the aforesaid church now justly and lawfully possesses in this tenth indiction, or may hereafter obtain, by God’s favor, through grants of pontiffs, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to the brethren living there according to the Rule.

Therefore, no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain things removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for the perpetual benefit of the regular canons. If anyone should attempt with rash boldness to oppose this our constitution, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of power and honor and subject to the sentence of excommunication. But those who observe it shall obtain the grace of almighty God and the rewards of eternal life.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Piacenza, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1133 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

### CXXIV. To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—The monastery of Saints Facundus and Primitivus in Spain is granted to him. (A.D. 1132, December 13.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 410.]

[Col. 0166B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.

The Lord came to cast fire upon the earth, and he wills that it should burn. Since, therefore, the free gifts of God have illuminated the sacred community of Cluny by the grace of his visitation, kindled in it the fire of charity, and suffused it with the discerning humility of religious life, it is altogether right that what it receives freely it should devoutly expend upon needy brethren; that it should raise up the fallen, awaken the lukewarm, and diffuse far and wide, illuminating the different provinces of the world, the rays of pious religion and the fragrance of a manner of life well pleasing to God. Thus may the love and glory of divine worship, which, thanks be to God, flourish abundantly among you, be multiplied through your administration in a fruitful and God-pleasing abundance of offspring.

Therefore, we entrust to you, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Peter, and to your successors, by the benevolence of the Apostolic See, for the restoration of religious life and the increase of temporal resources, the monastery of the holy martyrs Facundus and Primitivus, situated in the regions of Spain and known to belong specially by right to blessed Peter. It has fallen away, through sins that demand it—to our great sorrow—from the splendor of religious observance and the abundance of temporal goods in which it had flourished in former times. We do this upon mercifully accepting the wishes of our illustrious son Alfonso, king of the Spains, and assenting to your petitions; saving, nevertheless, the annual payment due to blessed Peter and the due right and reverence of the holy Roman Church in all things.

It is therefore for you, dearest sons, by your help, counsel, and earnestness, to restore religious life in that monastery, and, with the Lord’s assistance, to return the place, both inwardly and outwardly, to its former condition and dignity.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 0167A]  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Urban, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed.  
I, Anselm, cardinal priest, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.  
I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Bologna through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of December, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1132 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

### CXXV. To Norbert and his successors, archbishops of Magdeburg, he confirms their possessions and goods, both collectively and individually. (A.D. 1131–1133.)

[LUDEWIG, *Manuscript Remains*, XII, p. 388.]

[Col. 0167B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother NORBERT, bishop of Magdeburg, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

Then the honor of the apostolic see and of the Roman pontiffs is preserved in its entirety when each Church’s own dignity is safeguarded; for we regard the glory of our brethren as our own. Indeed, the customary kindness and discerning humility of the Roman Church, when it finds sons devoted and meek, makes some, [Col. 0167C] by dignities and honors, more especially bound to itself, and exalts others by the prerogative of intimacy and affection. It is certainly reasonable that, since we remember having received the benefits and services of those men, we should take care to respond to their devotion with a willing mind—not in an equal measure or amount, but out of more abundant goodwill.

Moreover, with what firm and persevering constancy, venerable brother Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, the zeal of your religious commitment and the discernment of your prudence undertook to defend the cause of the right of your holy Roman Church during the blazing schism of Peter Leonis; and how, setting yourselves in mutual, inexpressible opposition for the house of God, you labored by frequent arguments fortified with reason to bring the minds of the king, the princes, and other persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, into the unity of the Catholic Church [Col. 0167D] and obedience to blessed Peter and to us; and what great benefit thereby came to the Church of God and to us—all this is manifest. Therefore, dearest brother, whom we love with full charity in the Lord and hold in the familiar bosom of the apostolic see, assenting to the reasonable petitions of our dearest son, the illustrious and glorious King Lothair, and to yours, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to your successors, and through them to the Church of Magdeburg, the possessions and goods which you justly and lawfully possess; and we secure them by the present page of privilege. Among them we have thought fit to note the following by their proper names.

In the diocese of Magdeburg: the abbey of Blessed John the Baptist; the church of Blessed Mary; the church of Blessed John the Evangelist; the church of Saint Nicholas; the church called Grace of God; the abbey of Haldensleben; the provostship of Saint Mary of Galle in the bishopric of Ossenburg; the church of Eugerius in the bishopric of Münster; the abbey of Borchorst in the diocese of Mainz; etc. [Col. 0168A]

Furthermore, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, the holy men John, Benedict, and Leo, Roman pontiffs, we grant you the prerogative of the cross and pallium and metropolitan dignity, as is contained in their privileges; and we likewise confirm these to you over the cities and together with episcopal dignity. Whatever else the aforesaid Church may hereafter be able to acquire, by the generosity of kings, the gifts of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s bounty, shall henceforth remain firm and unimpaired for you. [Col. 0168B]

We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church of Magdeburg, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any exactions; but that all things be preserved intact, to benefit you and your successors forever. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself to be liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be estranged from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0168C]

This present copy was read aloud and carefully collated by me, Otto Coepes, public notary, and it does not differ from its principal letters by a single word; which I attest with my own hand.

### CXXVI. Privilege for the monastery of St Mary of Morrona. (23 January 1133.)

*[Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. III, p. 341, from the original of the bishopric of Volterra.]

[Col. 0168D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GERARD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Morrona, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The more intimately religious men are known to cleave to almighty God, the more zealously ought they to be cherished with paternal affection. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Gerard, we graciously assent to your reasonable petitions; and we receive under the guardianship and protection of the apostolic see the monastery of Blessed Mary, over which, by God’s gift, you are known to preside, with all its appurtenances; and we have judged it should be strengthened by the patronage of blessed Peter, to whom it especially belongs. [Col. 0169A]

For we decree that whatever estates, possessions, or goods have been justly granted to your monastery by Count Uvicio, of noble memory, and his sons Uvolino, Rainerio, Lotherio, and Bolgarino, or by other Catholic men, shall remain firm and unimpaired forever for you and your successors. Among these we have added the following, noted by their proper names: namely, the castle of Vivario, with its *paritario* [uncertain local term] and other appurtenances; the possessions of Morrona; the possessions of the Castle of Sojana; of Negoriana; of Rivoalto; of Massa; and of Montegemule. Whatever goods the aforesaid monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, we confirm to you by the page of this present writing. [Col. 0169B]

We decree, therefore, that no bishop and no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and be of every benefit to the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be estranged from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0169C]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed: **HELP US, O GOD, OUR SAVIOUR.** I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, John, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. [Col. 0169D] I, Martin, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1134 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

I, Marchesius, public judge of the sacred Lateran palace, saw and read the original and subscribed. I, Albert, notary of the apostolic see, saw and read that original and subscribed. I, Albert, notary of the apostolic see, saw and read that original and subscribed. [Col. 0170A] I, Hugh, notary of the apostolic see, saw and read that original and subscribed.

### CXXVII. Privilege for the nunnery of St Mary of Fontaines. (9 February 1133.)

[Duplessis, *History of the Church of Meaux*, II, p. 26.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, the lady prioress of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Fontaines, and to her sisters, present and future, regularly appointed there in perpetuity, etc.

. . . . Decreeing that whatever possessions and goods it now justly and lawfully possesses . . . . shall remain firm and unimpaired for you forever; among these we have added the following items: [Col. 0170B] possessions near Fontaines with their appurtenances; meadows; cultivated holdings, with all appurtenances belonging to them; etc. . . . . At Jambri, houses and lands granted to your monastery by title of donation from the illustrious man Theobald, Count of Blois; etc. . . . .

Given at Pisa by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of February, in the eleventh indiction, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXXVIII. Confirms the Premonstratensian observance and goods of the Church of Upper Zell. (20 February 1133.)

[Hugo, *Annals of the Holy Premonstratensian Order*, vol. I, p. 384.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0170C] son JOHN, provost of the Church of Zell, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

It accords with the governance of the apostolic see to love religious men with due kindness and to strengthen their places through the protection of its patronage. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Provost John, assenting to your reasonable petitions, we have judged that the Church of Blessed Michael the Archangel at Zell—known to have been founded near the city of Würzburg by you and your brother Henry in devotion—should be confirmed by this present privilege.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which, according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, has been established there through the zealous effort of our venerable brother Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, a truly religious and prudent man, shall be preserved inviolably in that church forever. [Col. 0170D] The brethren also who, by the inspiration of divine mercy, come there for conversion shall, after making profession in that place, have no permission to flee to other places. No archbishop, bishop, abbot, or any other person may presume, without the permission of their provost, to receive them or retain them once received; for this is forbidden by the sacred rules and ought to be foreign to ecclesiastical persons.

Further, we confirm by apostolic authority the exchange that was reasonably made between you and our venerable brother Embricus, Bishop of Würzburg, concerning that place, with the consent of his canons and confirmed by the page of his writing. Whatever has further been either purchased by you from that bishop or canonically conferred on the same church through offerings of other faithful persons, or may hereafter be conferred by just means through the Lord’s help, shall remain firm and unimpaired forever for you and your successors, without prejudice, of course, to the right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop. [Col. 0171A]

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly assail that church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any troubles; but that all things be kept intact, to benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person incur the loss of power and honor and be estranged from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer. But upon all who preserve what is just for that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 0171B]

Given at Pisa by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1133 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXXIX. To Didacus, Archbishop of Compostela, Aria, Bishop of León, and P[eter], Bishop of Lugo. (1 March 1133.)

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, p. 529.]

[Col. 0171C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren DIDACUS, Archbishop of Compostela, ARIA, Bishop of León, and P., Bishop of Lugo: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having examined the letters of your brotherhood, we have plainly learned of the madness and disobedience of that man of Oviedo. Since, indeed, he did not fear to add sin to sin, and, contrary to the sentence of interdict first pronounced against him through our legates and afterward confirmed by our authority, attempted to perform the episcopal office, [Col. 0171D] we subject him to excommunication by the authority of the Holy Spirit; and we command your diligence, by way of mandate, that you abstain from him as from an excommunicated person.

Furthermore, rendering you manifold thanks for the love and reverence which you bear toward the holy Roman Church and ourselves, we admonish your prudence by this letter to apply yourselves more earnestly to those matters which you know to be expedient for blessed Peter, and to labor effectively in his service as good and devoted sons.

Given at Pisa, on the Kalends of March.

> **Note:** [Col. 0171D] Innocent, having travelled through Gaul, returned to Italy in the year 1132.

### CXXX. He informs the archbishops, bishops, and abbots established throughout the provinces of Toledo, Braga, and Compostela that A., invader of the Church of Oviedo, has been excommunicated by him. (1 March 1133.)

[Flórez, *ibid.*]

[Col. 0172A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the archbishops, bishops, and abbots established throughout the provinces of Toledo, Braga, and Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not wish your charity to be unaware that we have promulgated a sentence of excommunication against A., the occupier of the Church of Oviedo, because, against the prohibition of our legate, he received consecration [Col. 0172B] and, after the suspension pronounced against him through a messenger of the apostolic see and subsequently confirmed by us, attempted to perform the episcopal office, with the counsel of our brethren having been taken. Therefore we have thought fit to admonish your brotherhood by these letters, that you carefully keep yourselves from him as from an excommunicated person and likewise admonish your subjects to keep themselves from him.

Given at Pisa, on the Kalends of March.

### CXXXI. At Bishop Landulf’s request, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Ferrara. (11 March 1135.)

[Cocquelines, II, p. 209.]

[Col. 0172C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LANDULF, bishop, and to the consuls and people of Ferrara, in perpetuity.

We perceive that, by the Lord’s ordering, we have been set in the chair of the apostolic see so that we may more freely assent to just petitions and take care more closely to cherish in the bosom of that same pious mother those whom we know to be more devoted in obedience to us and more specially attached to the holy Roman Church. Since, therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, you have promised to render every obedience and welcome service to blessed Peter, to us who, though unworthy, act in his place, and to our successors, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of holy memory—Adrian, Benedict, and Paschal, Roman pontiffs—we strengthen the Church of Ferrara, as a special daughter of the apostolic see, by the patronage of the holy Roman Church, and confirm its estates by the page of this present privilege.

Among these we have added the following, noted by their proper names: namely, the *massa* of Babylonia, called Ferrara, with its twelve estates; to it we subject twelve other, lesser *massae* of ours, with all obedience and service: that is, the *massa* and riverbank of Palatiolus with its twelve estates; likewise the *massa* of Quartisiana with its twelve estates; similarly the *massa* of Populare with its twelve estates; also the *massa* of Curulum; the *massa* of Saletum with its twenty-four estates; the *massa* of Sentica and Tastilione, with their estates; and also the *massa* called Firmignana, with all its estates. [Col. 0172D–0173A]

These *massae*, with all their appurtenances, were granted from the lordship, right, and power of the holy apostolic see to the Church of Ferrara by our aforesaid predecessors. We likewise establish them as firm for that Church by the authority of this present decree, so that both you, brother Landulf, bishop, and your successors may have permission in each *massa* to ordain clerics, deacons, and priests, and to consecrate churches.

The boundaries of the county of Ferrara are marked by these limits: on the east, on one side by the River Po, and on the other by our *massa* of Fiscalia and Veteraria; they cross the River Sandalo as far as Bucciletum; through Bucciletum they cross the River Gabiana by way of Ludurium; they encircle the great village of Madraria, reaching as far as Malletum; from Malletum they proceed beside the Anxian embankment, through the marshes and fisheries as far as Vitrica; and, crossing Vitrica, they reach the Burana ditch, and from there enter the Po and go down westward as far as Ulmus Formosa, which is the fixed boundary between Romagna and Lombardy. [Col. 0173B]

On the other side of the river the boundaries are likewise as follows: on the east, the boundary track, which is the boundary with our county of Comacchio; they extend through the marshes and fisheries as far as the ditch of Silvula, and encompass the *massa* of Corneti and Lacinanus, which belong to our county of Ferrara. Descending from there westward through the marshes and fisheries to the River Tartaro, they issue into the River Po. [Col. 0173C]

For the inhabitants of the greater *massa* of Ferrara, we abolish wicked and bad customs, provided nevertheless that, as they have been accustomed to do, every free person gives, through their messenger, one Venetian penny toward the support of the holy Roman Church, according to the ancient custom. Of the revenue from dues, tribute, and tolls at the bank and river, we grant one half, as a blessing, for the common benefit, improvement, or restoration of the aforesaid greater *massa*; but we reserve the other half to ourselves. Likewise, of the market toll we retain one half for ourselves and remit the other half to our aforesaid bishop of Ferrara.

We also reserve the general court in the lordship and power of the holy Roman Church: that is, it shall be held before our messenger, administering justice once a year, and shall be observed by all for three days. We exact no levy or *fodrum*, nor any wrongful or unjust service, payment, or custom; that is, out of fear and love of God, we have spared all the inhabitants of the aforesaid Church of Blessed George in its greater *massa*, and we subject to it the other lesser *massae*, as stated above, with all their services. [Col. 0173D]

Furthermore, assenting to the desire of your devotion, we shall grant the aforesaid county of Ferrara, the general court of the city, and the banks of Comacchio, with every right belonging to the lordship of the holy Roman Church within the city and county, to no one except either the commune of your city or the bishopric of Ferrara; provided, however, that you shall pay to blessed Peter, by just compensation of goods and upon the counsel of prudent and worthy men, whatever we may be able to receive from them on this account. Moreover, placing the fullest confidence in your fidelity and service, we remit to you, through the kindness of the apostolic see, those offenses which you committed against us and our predecessors.

Therefore, in return for such great benefits received from the apostolic see, your whole community shall assist us and our successors, through its own messenger, jointly . . . and you shall faithfully assist us and our successors in recovering, retaining, and defending, in the city and throughout the county of Ferrara, the rights of blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church. [Col. 0174A–B]

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, or presume to diminish the Church of Ferrara in respect of the matters stated above, or take from the holy apostolic see its rights in it, as set forth above, let that person pay to the same holy apostolic see one hundred pounds of the finest gold as a penalty and composition. And unless the wrongful presumptions are amended by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be estranged from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for the aforesaid churches may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0174C]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given in the territory of Volterra by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1133 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXXXII. He adorns Syrus of Genoa, made archbishop from bishop, with the pallium, and subjects to him as suffragans the bishops of Mariana, Nebbio, and Accia. (19 March 1133.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, IV, p. 859.]

[Col. 0174D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother SYRUS, Archbishop of Genoa, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

“The Lord is just and loves justice; his face has beheld equity.” If the Son of God became man for lost humanity and endured an ignominious death for its redemption and salvation, then the Catholic and holy mother Church of God, lest her children be damned, ought continually to bestow her goods with cheerful countenance and joyful mind, [Col. 0175A] since the principle of equity and justice itself demands this.

Accordingly, the most holy apostolic see, providing for the salvation of souls, because incomparable slaughter of men, captivities of Christians, and countless destructions of churches resulted from the discord and war that long ago arose, through the subtle favoring of the enemy of the human race, between the said city of Genoa and Pisa, raises your person—and through you the Church of Genoa—to distinction and exaltation by a glorious prerogative, so that henceforth such detestable quarrel and dissension may cease. That city has been faithful to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, prompt in service, and promises more eagerly to do so in the future.

Therefore, dearest brother Syrus, archbishop, adorning you with the grace of the pallium and endowing you with ampler favor, we promote you to be an archbishop. We subject to you and your successors by metropolitan right three bishoprics in Corsica: namely Mariana, Nebbio, and a third whose see we establish as the Church of Saint Peter of Accia, which shall have one *plebs* [parish district] of Marana and another of Meria, together with Vobza and Brunate, which we now establish as a new bishopric. [Col. 0175B]

Nevertheless, we freely retain in our own hand the bishopric of Genoa and you and your successors, emancipated from every subjection, decreeing that the Archbishop of Genoa shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff alone, in the same manner as the Archbishop of Pisa. But if it should happen that the Archbishop of Pisa is consecrated by his suffragans, then the Archbishop of Genoa likewise shall similarly be consecrated by his own suffragans. Thereafter, however, he shall wear the pallium within the Church, namely on the days of the Lord’s Supper, Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Lawrence, the three feasts of Saint Mary, the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, and the anniversary of your consecration; likewise at the consecrations of bishops and churches and at the ordinations of clerics. [Col. 0175C]

We also entrust to you, venerable brother Syrus, Archbishop, the abbey of Tyre for its improvement, without prejudice to the ownership and consent of the holy Roman Church. If, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be estranged from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who observe these our decrees may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0175D]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, John, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0176A] I, Rudolf, bishop of Orta. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Chrysogonus. I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Martin, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Rainerius, bishop of Siena. I, Roland, bishop of Roselle. I, Ildizo, bishop of Savona. I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of St George at the Velum Aureum. [Col. 0176B] I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Grosseto by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1133 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXXXIII. To Hugh, Duke of Burgundy.—He urges him to protect Abbot Herbert of Dijon against the monks of Saint-Seine, whom he declares excommunicated. (19 May 1133.)

[D. Bouquet, XIV, p. 248.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HUGH, illustrious Duke of Burgundy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The controversy long conducted between our sons Herbert, Abbot [Col. 0176C] of Dijon, and the monks of Saint-Seine has been settled by the prudent judgment of our beloved brother Stephen, Abbot of Cîteaux, a wise man indeed, to whom we committed it to be settled by justice or agreement. But the aforesaid monks, drunk with the spirit of pride, not only failed utterly to observe the agreement established by our said brother; rather, invading a certain village of the church of Saint Stephen, they poured out the wine of the brethren of that place, smashed their wine vessels, and plundered the same village both of animals and other goods. We bear this all the more gravely because we have learned that these acts were committed with your support.

We, therefore, whose particular concern it is to restrain wrongdoers by due sentence, renew the excommunication formerly pronounced against those same monks, and decree that all who gave help and counsel in the same wrongdoing shall be subject to an equal sentence until the aforesaid damages are restored. We command your nobility, therefore, to cause the said agreement, made by so wise and industrious a man, to be observed, and to take care that the aforesaid abbot is not troubled further on this account. Otherwise, you must fear that it will be imputed to you if, being able to prevent evil, you do not prevent it. We greet and bless in the Lord our beloved daughter, the duchess your wife.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.

> **Note:** [Col. 0175] In the year 1133, when Innocent was received by the Romans into the Lateran palace.

### CXXXIV. He receives the Church of St Stephen at Prato into protection and confirms its rights. (21 May 1133.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, III, p. 331.]

[Col. 0177A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ILDEPRAND, provost of the Church of Saint Stephen of Prato, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The order of justice and reason admonishes us, who by divine providence have been raised to the governance of Churches, both to defend them from the attacks of wicked men and to cherish them beneath the pious bosom of the holy Roman Church. Therefore, with this charity in view, beloved son in the Lord, Provost Ildeprand, we have judged it proper to assent to your prayers and receive the Church of Blessed Stephen, protomartyr, over which by God’s gift you preside, under the guardianship of blessed Peter and our protection. [Col. 0177B]

We decree, therefore, that within the parish of that church, against your will or that of your successors or brethren, no person whatsoever may build a church or inflict any injury in this matter, without prejudice to reverence for the apostolic see. We also grant that you may possess, without anyone’s objection, the tithes of those who belong to your church by parochial right. We likewise confirm to you and your church the burial ground of that place for the benefit of those regarded as belonging to your parish. We also decree that no one may dare to promulgate against you a sentence of interdict or excommunication without just and reasonable cause.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics to be advanced to holy orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor of the apostolic see, and is willing to provide these to you freely and without any corrupt dealing. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. Whatever goods the same Church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 0177C]

Therefore, no person whatsoever may lawfully rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; and let all things be preserved intact for the benefit of the uses of you and your successors, without prejudice to reverence for the diocesan bishop. If, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be estranged from the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 0177D–0178A] But upon all who preserve their rights for that Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

C. I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1133 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

### CXXXV. To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—Delivered from various dangers, he requests prayers offered in thanksgiving. (23 May 1133.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, p. 416.]

[Col. 0178B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Peter, abbot, and the brethren of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“God has protected us from the assembly of evildoers and from the multitude of workers of iniquity” (Psalm 63). For long ago, when Jewish fury raged, the right hand of divine power, from the depth of its counsel, led us and our brethren, reserved for its service, out of the City under the protection of its mercy. But now it has looked upon the face of its Church and has restored us safe and sound to our own see. It is fitting, therefore, that for such great benefits bestowed upon us by the heavenly power, you should rejoice with us and render due thanks to the divine majesty, earnestly praying [Col. 0178C] that it may raise ever higher the cause of the Church, hitherto sustained under its protection, and bring better outcomes to its good beginnings.

For we believe that your prayers obtain greater efficacy with God than the secular power of any worldly supporters. We, established in the City with our dearest son Lothair, King of the Romans, give manifold thanks to your devotion for the concern and zeal that you show toward the holy Roman Church; and, thanks be to God, we are beneficially laboring in matters concerning the liberation of the Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CXXXVI. He establishes the monastery of Brugnato as an episcopal see, suffragan to the Church of Genoa. (27 May 1133.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, IV, p. 984.]

[Col. 0178D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ILDEPRAND, bishop-elect of Brugnato, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

As the Apostolic See stands set over all the Churches throughout the world, according to the Lord’s words to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16), so it has always had power to combine two bishoprics into one, to divide one into two when circumstances require, to create new ones, and to adorn abbeys [Col. 0179A] and other venerable places with the highest prerogative of episcopal rank. Therefore, with a view to this dispensation, for the good of peace, the welfare of the Catholic Church, and to support it, we fortify by the present page of writing the monastery of Brugnato, known to have been built in honour of the blessed Apostle Peter and of Saints Lawrence and Columban; and we decree that henceforth it shall be an episcopal see. We establish that the churches lying within its bounds, together with the castles and villages that belong to its jurisdiction, shall be subject to that monastery by parochial right; and that the bishop who at any time holds office there shall possess and administer tithes, offerings, and other revenues, in temporal as well as spiritual matters, as its proper bishop; and that he shall be obedient and subject [Col. 0179B] to the Church of Genoa as his metropolitan.

We have also judged that this provision should be added to our constitution: that all things conferred upon that Church either by grants of pontiffs or offerings of the faithful, or which shall hereafter, with the Lord’s help, be justly and canonically bestowed, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired to it and to its successors, with the justice and reverence due in all things to the Holy Roman Church being preserved. Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain things offered to it, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; rather, all shall be preserved intact and shall wholly benefit the uses for which they were granted—the governance and support of those concerned.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, should attempt to contravene it, then, having been warned a second and a third time, unless he makes fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who observe these our enactments may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Churrard, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Rodulf, bishop of Orte, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Chrysogonus, have subscribed.  
I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross, have subscribed.  
I, Anselm, cardinal priest, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, G., deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.  
I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of St George, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1133, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXXXVII. To Adalbero, Archbishop of Hamburg.—That all bishops of Denmark, Sweden, Norway, etc., are subject to him. (27 May 1133.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*, p. 132.]

[Col. 0180A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable ADALBERO, archbishop of Hamburg, and to his successors, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We are seen to have been placed, by the Lord’s ordering, in the chair of Blessed Peter for this purpose: that we may preserve for each Church and ecclesiastical person its rights, and may diligently make salutary provision that its condition, both temporal and spiritual, may remain unimpaired. [Col. 0180B] For it is fitting and reasonable that, just as the most holy Church of God is the perpetual mother of unity and faith, so its privileges should be kept inviolate and should not be harassed by any vexations or oppressions of petty men.

Our venerable brother Adalbero, archbishop of Hamburg, has frequently complained before our predecessors of happy memory, Calixtus and Honorius, and before us, that Asser of Lund and the other bishops of Denmark refuse him the obedience due to him as their metropolitan, as is contained in the ancient privileges of the Roman pontiffs Gregory, Sergius, Leo, Benedict, Nicholas, and Adrian. The aforesaid predecessors of ours, Calixtus and Honorius, and we ourselves, repeatedly commanded them either to return to obedience to you and to the Church of Hamburg, or, if they believed that they had any just ground in this matter, to come prepared to show it before the Apostolic See. [Col. 0180C] But they, despising obedience to apostolic commands, neither came nor sent representatives.

Since no one ought to profit from his own contumacy, therefore, after deliberate counsel with our brother bishops and cardinals, we restore to you both the bishop of Lund and the other bishops of Denmark. Accordingly, following the form of the privileges of Gregory, Sergius, Leo, Nicholas, Benedict, and Adrian, and moved by the petitions of our dearest son Lothair, king, we confirm to you and through you to the Church of Hamburg, its own [Col. 0180D] metropolitan see, by this page of writing, the bishoprics of Denmark, Sweden, Norway, the Faroes, Greenland, Hälsingland, Iceland, Skridvinia, and the Slavs.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who observe these enactments may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0181A]

Given at Rome, on the Aventine Hill, through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1133, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXXXVIII. To Nicholas, King of the Danes.—On the same subject. (27 May 1133.)

[LAPPENBERG, ibid., p. 133.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ NICHOLAS, illustrious king of the Danes, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our predecessors of happy memory—Gregory, [Col. 0181B] Sergius, Nicholas, Benedict, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs—established the Church of Hamburg as a metropolitan see and subjected to it both the see of Lund and the other bishoprics of Denmark. But our brother Adalbero, archbishop of Hamburg, has complained, both in the time of our predecessors and in ours, that the bishops of those Churches disdain to show him the reverence due to him. Accordingly, the aforesaid predecessors of ours, Calixtus and Honorius, and we ourselves, ordered them in writing to come before the Apostolic See to answer concerning this matter; but they neither came nor sent representatives.

Therefore, wishing to preserve to each his right, and having taken counsel with our brethren, we restore to our aforesaid brother Adalbero, archbishop, [Col. 0181C] both Lund and the other bishoprics of Denmark, as is contained in the ancient privileges of the above-named Roman pontiffs Sergius, Gregory, Leo, Benedict, Nicholas, and Adrian. We therefore command your prudence by apostolic letters, requesting that you humbly obey the same our brother Adalbero, archbishop, as your metropolitan, and diligently endeavour to bring the bishops of your kingdom back to obedience.

Given on the Aventine Hill, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May].

### CXXXIX. To . . . . . King of the Swedes.—On the same subject. (27 May 1133.)

[LAPPENBERG, ibid., p. 134.]

[Col. 0181D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ . . . . . . , king of the Swedes, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Hamburg, having come to the Apostolic See, complained in our presence that, although he presides over the bishops of your kingdom by metropolitan right, as the ancient privileges of our predecessors Gregory, Sergius, Leo, Benedict, Nicholas, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, are known to declare, they presume to deny him the obedience due to him. Since it is our office to correct what has been wrongly done and recall it to the way of rectitude, we command your nobility by request that you humbly obey the aforesaid [Col. 0182A] our brother Adalbero, archbishop of Hamburg, as your metropolitan; and that, to the extent of the capacity God has granted you, you diligently ensure that the bishops of your land return to his obedience.

Given on the Aventine Hill, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May].

### CXL. He orders Asser, Bishop of Lund, to obey his metropolitan A[dalbero]. (27 May 1133.)

[LAPPENBERG, as above, p. 135.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ASSER, bishop of Lund, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0182B] Just as it belongs to natural law not to injure another, so it belongs to our office to assist one who has been injured. Moreover, our venerable brother A., archbishop of Hamburg, complained before Calixtus and Honorius of blessed memory, and now also before us, that you neglect to show him the obedience and reverence due to him as your metropolitan. Although you have often been summoned in this matter, both by them and by us, through letters and messengers, neither you nor your representatives have visited the Apostolic See. Since it belongs to our office to preserve to each person his own right, we earnestly command your fraternity by the present letters to return to his subjection and reverence, and to obey him in all things as your metropolitan.

Given on the Aventine Hill, on the sixth day before the Kalends [Col. 0182C] of June [27 May].

### CXLI. He commands the bishops of Sweden to obey A[dalbero], Archbishop of Hamburg, as their metropolitan. (27 May 1133.)

[Ibid.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, all the bishops of Sweden, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that he who desires to preside over others should not be ashamed humbly to show reverence to his own superiors. Moreover, our venerable brother A., archbishop of Hamburg (the text has *Hamminbergensis*), having come to the Apostolic See, complained gravely that, although he presides over you by metropolitan right, as is also [Col. 0182D] contained in the ancient privileges of the Roman pontiffs Gregory, Sergius, Leo, Benedict, Nicholas, and Adrian, you withdraw the obedience due to him. This is to be corrected by you with all the greater diligence because you are bound to furnish even in this respect examples of good conduct to the people subject to you. Therefore, by the present letters we command your fraternity to render obedience and reverence to our aforesaid brother A., archbishop of Hamburg, as your metropolitan, and henceforth to inflict upon him no trouble in this matter.

Given on the Aventine Hill, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May].

### CXLII. Bull concerning certain bishoprics in Poland and beyond, subject to the Archbishop of Magdeburg. (4 June 1133.)

[BOLLAND., vol. VI for June, p. 48.]

[Col. 0183A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother NORBERT, bishop, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman and Apostolic Church, ever since it received you as its special son, has established by sure evidence the fervour and industry of your devotion in matters concerning its welfare. More recently, when in these days the providence of divine ordering was pleased to call us—although unworthy and less fitted—to the administration of the apostolate, this quality shone forth more and more in your person; and the steadfastness of your faith and religious commitment became manifest not only to neighbouring but also to remote nations. For neither any temporal labour nor threats or blandishments of any kind could prevent you from setting yourself up as an impregnable wall against the tyranny of Peter Leonis, and from effectively labouring to bring the hearts of the king himself and of other princes into the obedience of Blessed Peter [Col. 0184A] [the text reads: “you have performed noble deeds,” perhaps corrupt].

It is fitting, therefore, that the Apostolic See, which rejoices with its whole heart over so devoted a son, should respond with due kindness to your services and labours and should bind you more closely to the performance of its service.

Accordingly, venerable brother archbishop, we have thought that the complaint which you laid before us against the bishops of Poland ought to be committed to writing and ink. You asserted that the bishops of that region were, by ancient institution, subject by metropolitan right to the Church of Magdeburg; and in confirmation of your claim you invoked the authority of our predecessors of blessed memory, John [Note: [Col. 0183B] That is, John XIII, who ratified and confirmed the archbishopric, appointed Adalbert as its first archbishop, granted him the pallium, and, in letters discussed by us, conferred upon him various privileges.], Benedict [Note: [Col. 0183B] This is Benedict VII, concerning whose letters, and especially their title, we have already spoken.] and Leo [Note: [Col. 0183C] This Leo can be none other than the eighth of that name, commonly counted by some among the true pontiffs and by most among the antipopes. Yet I cannot understand what privilege he could have granted to the archiepiscopal Church of Magdeburg, having died before this archbishop was appointed—unless Norbert in his time found some apocryphal document written in Leo’s name, as he did under the name of John XIII.].

You further maintained that, through the intervention of the most pious Emperor Otto, the bishoprics that then appeared to lie beyond the Saale, Elbe, and [Col. 0184B] Oder, or which thereafter, through the co-operation of divine mercy, were to be established there, had been made subject to the Church of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0183C] These assertions were drawn from the letters establishing the archbishopric, issued by Pope John and Emperor Otto.]. The names of those bishoprics are as follows: Elbe and Oder, Stettin [Note: [Col. 0183C] *Stetinum* or *Stetina* in Latin: the chief city of Pomerania, on the left bank of the Oder, not far from the Baltic Sea and the island of Rügen. I do not find that this city itself was a bishop’s see by its proper name. But I find in the Life of St Otto, bishop of Bamberg and apostle of the Pomeranians, that when he was labouring in 1124 for the conversion of that people, and perhaps in that same year or the next was hastening to return to his own see, he could not then establish the Pomeranian bishopric as he wished. Trusting the prudence of Duke Bolesław III of Poland, he entrusted its arrangement to him when at leisure. The duke raised one of his chaplains, named Adalbert, to episcopal rank among that people. Whether he immediately chose a fixed see, or travelled the country town by town in Otto’s manner; and whether Stettin was from the beginning designated as the episcopal see by the Roman pontiff and later superseded by Julin, is unknown to me. Nevertheless, Norbert must at that very time—this cannot be doubted—have had grounds for claiming Stettin as under his jurisdiction, either as an episcopal city or, under that name, as the Pomeranian bishopric, as it is called in ancient lists of churches.] and Lubusz [Note: [Col. 0183D] Commonly now Lübeck, in Latin *Lubeca*, a very well-known trading town in the Lower Saxon Circle, not far [Col. 0184B] from the Baltic Sea, about ten German miles east of Hamburg. It was formerly subject to the bishopric of Oldenburg, founded in the same region by Otto the Great. But when Oldenburg declined and Lübeck emerged, the bishopric gradually began, as these letters show, to be called after Lübeck, and in 1163 was altogether transferred thither together with its bishop.]; beyond the Oder, Pomesania [Note: [Col. 0184C] It is in Prussia beyond the river Vistula, between Elbląg and Toruń; its bishopric was later joined to that of Chełmno.], Potatuan [Note: [Col. 0184C] The Magdeburg Chronicle incorrectly calls it *Pornam*; the Saxon chronicler more correctly calls it Poznań, now Pomania, the first bishopric established in Poland, beyond the Oder and on this side of the Warta River, as stated above.], Gniezno [Note: [Col. 0184C] Gniezno, now a well-known Polish city distinguished by the title of primacy. Yet we judged above that it was not episcopal before the year 999. From the bull of Pope Innocent quoted above, however, it appears that when it was written Gniezno had not yet had an archbishopric lawfully established, still less the primacy of Poland. For how, if the bishop of Gniezno in the time of Norbert and Innocent II had already been recognized by the Roman pontiffs as archbishop and primate of Poland, and had thus been lawfully withdrawn from the metropolitan see of Magdeburg, could Norbert then have claimed Gniezno for his metropolitan see or Innocent have wished to subject it to that see? For the present I leave these things in the state in which they then stood. Here I attempt only, to the extent of my ability, to elucidate the bull.], Cracow [Note: [Col. 0184D] Cracow, likewise too well known a city to require fuller treatment here. We have mentioned above that it was never itself archiepiscopal.], Wrocław [Note: [Col. 0184D] The chief city of the duchy of Wrocław and of all Silesia, on the Oder River, distinguished by a bishopric in the eleventh century. Długosz writes that the bishopric was transferred there from Smogorzów, but this is not sufficiently certain.], Kruszwica [Note: [Col. 0184D] Kruszwica, also called Cruwicia, once an ancient royal city surrounded by the very large Lake Gopło, says Długosz, where an episcopal see was established, later transferred to Włocławek, as he also writes at the beginning of book II. This papal bull establishes, however, that in 1133 the bishopric still retained its original name.], Masania [Col. 0185A] [Note: [Col. 0185D] I believe that *Masovia* or *Mazovia* should be written: it is the name of a duchy in roughly central Poland, and a Mazovian bishopric is found under the archbishop of Gniezno in ancient lists of bishoprics printed by Charles of St Paul and others.], and Lake Lodi [Note: [Col. 0185D] There is no episcopal city in Poland under such a designation. Włocławek on the Vistula and its bishopric must be meant; the same Długosz mentioned above writes that the see was transferred there from Kruszwica.].

Having granted lawful delays, we summoned the bishops of those Churches to appear before us, once and a second time, both by letters and by messengers, so that they might answer you concerning your complaint; but they neither came nor sent us any representatives.

3. Therefore it seemed good to us and to our brethren that they ought not to profit from their contumacy, nor should the Church of Magdeburg be any longer deprived of its own right. Accordingly, dearest brother Norbert, archbishop, by the kindness and justice of the Apostolic See, we have put you in possession of and invested you with the aforesaid bishoprics and territories, which our above-mentioned predecessors are known to have granted to your predecessors and to belong to your Church; [Col. 0185B] and by our letters we command that henceforth the same bishops obey your fraternity. Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors, and through you to the Church of Magdeburg, that they are to possess in perpetual right, without possibility of revocation, not only the bishoprics named above but also those which, with the Lord’s help, may hereafter be established there [the text has *mihi*, better read *inibi*, “there”] [Note: [Col. 0186D] Note the terms in which the pontiff declares that the subjection and obedience of all the bishops mentioned above are due by right to Norbert, and through him to his successors and the Church of Magdeburg. I judge that in this prerogative consists the whole primacy of the Church of Magdeburg, which Norbert requests be confirmed to him, both from the bull and from the discussion given above.].

4. It is therefore your concern, most beloved brother, to persevere in love and obedience toward the Holy Roman Church and to watch with diligent attention over those things which you know concern its honour and advantage. And so that what we have canonically established may remain firm, by apostolic authority, under attestation of the divine judgment, we command that no person, humble or [Col. 0185C] great, nor any of our successors, presume to infringe what we have ordained. Let the violator of this privilege be condemned, with Judas the betrayer, to eternal punishments.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, John, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Chrysogonus.  
I, Gerhard, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross.  
I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John [Col. 0185D] and Paul.  
I, Martin, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.  
[Col. 0186A] I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of June [4 June], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1133, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXLIII. He grants Bernard, Bishop of Paderborn, and his successors the use of the rational. (5 June 1133.)

[SCHATEN, *Annales Paderbornenses*, I, p. 732.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, bishop of Paderborn, [Col. 0186B] and to his successors to be canonically promoted.

Just as every good gift and every perfect present is from above, and, as the authority of Holy Scripture declares, comes down from the Father of lights, so beyond doubt we believe that it will be our glory and joy if our brethren are found worthy of honour and, through their uprightness and learning, deserve to be raised from great ecclesiastical honours and dignities to still higher ones. With this in view, venerable brother Bernard, bishop, because much concerning the zeal of your devotion toward Blessed Peter has been reported to us, and because we have confirmed this same thing by certain proofs, it is fitting that you should be more highly honoured by the Apostolic See for the service rendered, and that henceforth [Col. 0186C] we should bind your fraternity more closely to ourselves, so that, with the Lord’s help, you may receive a welcome benefit in temporal as well as spiritual matters.

And because we believe that divine providence has called you, like Aaron, to the summit of pontifical dignity, and has appointed you in Moses’ place to rule and govern the Christian people, we also appoint you chief in their dignity and grant, by the kindness of the Apostolic See, the use of the rational (*rationale*) to you and your successors. We decree that you may use it on the days set down in this page of writing, but only within your diocese and within the church: namely, on the Lord’s Supper, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, the feasts of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, the solemnities [Col. 0186D] of Blessed Mary and of All Saints, the Nativity of the Lord, and Epiphany; likewise at the consecration of churches within your diocese, at ordinations of clergy, on the anniversary of the dedication of the Church of Paderborn, and on the feast of St Liborius.

It is therefore your concern, most beloved brother, that the effectiveness of your works may commend what you bear in the sight of the Church, and that your charity may always be found worthier of this grace.

[Col. 0187A]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand: “HELP US, O GOD OF OUR SALVATION.”

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of July [7 July], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXLIV. At the request of Abbot Bertoo, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the Monastery of the Saviour and St Boniface at Fulda. (5 June 1133.)

[DRONKE, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 385.]

[Col. 0187B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERTOO, abbot of the monastery of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of St Boniface, situated beside the bank of the river called Fulda, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of our office exhorts us to exercise diligent concern for the Churches of God, both near and far, and, with the Lord’s help, to make salutary provision for their peace and welfare. For it is recognized as fitting and honourable that we who have been taken up to govern the Churches should protect them from the malice of wicked men and strengthen them by the safeguard of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Berthoe, we graciously assent to your reasonable requests and fortify with the privilege of the Holy Roman Church the monastery of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may in future acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, or offerings of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0187] “The lacuna is to be supplied from the privilege of 1 April 1131, above, no. 37.”]—given to your predecessor, the religious Abbot Hecbert, out of affection, etc. [lacuna] are known to belong to it. We further prohibit every . . . in whose diocese it is known to have been built; we decree that, notwithstanding opposition, it shall remain perpetually firm to the same monastery. We forbid [lacuna] [Col. 0187D] that anyone be placed over it by any craft of deceit or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, elect according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict. We decree that at suitable times information be given to our ecclesiastical solicitude concerning the manner in which monastic observance is directed among the brethren entrusted to your rule [lacuna] at the solemnities of Mass, by the kindness of the Apostolic See, we grant to your beloved self according to what is contained in the privileges of our predecessors. And, because of the greater prerogative of familiarity which you have deserved to attain in the Holy Roman Church in our time, we likewise grant to you and your successors permission to use the mitre and ring. But the abbot [lacuna] [Col. 0188A] let this also be confirmed by our apostolic authority through this page of writing.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to disturb rashly the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it by vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact and wholly benefit the uses for which they were granted—the governance and support of those concerned [lacuna] unless he makes amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; and let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God [lacuna] [Col. 0188B] may they find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

(Seal.) I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. (Monogram.)

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of June [5 June], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1133, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent.

### CXLV. To Lothair and Richenza.—He grants the allodial estate of Countess Matilda’s lands. (8 June 1133.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 392.]

INNOCENT II, pope, to LOTHAR, Augustus Emperor, and to RIGET, Empress.

[Col. 0188C] If the sacred authority of pontiffs and imperial power are truly united to one another by the bond of charity, the service due to the Almighty can freely be rendered, and the Christian people will enjoy welcome peace and tranquillity. For in this present age nothing is more illustrious than a pontiff, nothing more exalted than a king; nothing shines with a brighter light than right faith in a prince, and nothing is less subject to decline than true religion. All these things, thanks be to God, shine forth all the more manifestly in your person because from your earliest age you are known to have been a lover of religion and a cultivator of justice; and because lately, sparing neither your person nor your own money, you have borne many labours and immense [Col. 0188D] dangers in the service of Blessed Peter.

Since, therefore, sacred Scripture bears witness that even evil fathers ought to share good gifts with their children, it is certainly fitting that we, who by the Lord’s ordering owe paternal care to all the children of the Catholic Church, should love your person more closely and, as the Church’s most special defender, should increase your imperial power—both in accordance with ecclesiastical office and in temporal matters—in those things known to concern the preservation of the Empire in its strength and the welfare and liberation of the Catholic Church.

With this in view, we entrust and grant to you, by dispensation of the Apostolic See, the allodial estate of Countess Matilda of blessed memory, which is known to have been granted by her to Blessed Peter; and, in the presence of our brother archbishops, bishops, abbots, and also princes and barons, we invest you with it through a ring. This is on the condition that every year you pay one hundred pounds of silver to us and to our successors, and that after your death ownership shall return, whole and undiminished, without hindrance, to the right and lordship of the Holy Roman Church. If we or our successors must come, stay, or pass through that land, we are to be honoured in reception, provisioning, and safe-conduct, as the Apostolic See shall decree [variant: “as befits the Apostolic See”]. Whoever holds the fortresses [variant: “whoever hold them”], or is governor of the land, [Col. 0189B] shall swear fealty to Blessed Peter, to us, and to our successors.
