Furthermore, out of regard for your affection, we grant the same land by apostolic kindness, under the aforesaid payment and stated conditions, to the nobleman Henry, Duke of Bavaria, your son-in-law, and to your daughter, his wife; provided, however, that the same duke shall perform homage and swear fealty to Blessed Peter, to us, and to our successors. After their death, the aforesaid allodial estate of Countess Matilda, together with its right and lordship, shall, as stated above, revert entire and without diminution or any difficulty to the Holy Roman Church—while in all things the right and ownership of that same Holy Roman Church is always preserved.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June].

### CXLVI. Privilege by which the monastery of Prüm in the diocese of Trier, together with all its possessions, is received into the protection of the Apostolic See. (8 June 1133.)

[COCQUELINES, II, p. 214.]

[Col. 0189C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADALBERO, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, situated in honour of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, in the diocese of Trier, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized to accord with reason, it befits us to grant it willingly and to afford appropriate support to the desires of petitioners. For it is fair and reasonable that we, who have been appointed to the governance of the Churches, should both protect them from the wickedness of perverse men and strengthen them by the safeguard of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Adalbero, we graciously assent to your just petitions and confirm by the privilege of the holy Roman Church the monastery of Prüm, dedicated to our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour, over which you preside by God’s authority. We decree that whatever is known to have been granted to that monastery of Prüm by the authority of our predecessors, or of the emperors—namely Pippin and Charles—and of other princes, and confirmed by their charters and protections, shall remain stable and secure to you and your successors.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods [Col. 0190A] the said monastery now justly and lawfully holds, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other reasonable means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you. Indeed, out of the fuller benevolence of the Apostolic See, we decree that, if anyone should presume to invade or retain the possessions and goods of that monastery, and, having been admonished by his bishops, should fail to make satisfaction, authority is granted to your beloved self to place such persons under interdict or excommunicate them. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass them in any other manner; but that all shall be preserved entire for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to make fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0190C] I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aymeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord 1133, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXLVII. Privilege for the Monastery of Vallombrosa. (1133, September 2.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 776.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ATTO, abbot of Vallombrosa, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the author of all things and of every good, in order that [Col. 0190D] we may love religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptable to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore, that, with divine mercy giving aid, religious observance may be established according to the Rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 0191A] and of the monastery of Vallombrosa in the church of Blessed Vigilius, situated in the bishopric of Cremona at the place called Torre Trentina—this church our beloved son Obert, canon of the Church of Brescia, with the consent of his father Richelin and of his brothers Otto, Lanfranc, Beltran, and William, offered through our hands to blessed Peter, under an annual payment of six denarii of Milanese currency to be paid yearly to the Lateran palace—we grant it, with all its appurtenances, to you and your successors and, through us, to your monastery, under the aforesaid census; and we confirm this by the document of the present writing.

It is your concern, dearest son in the Lord, in accordance with the desire of our venerable brother Bernard, bishop of Verona—by whose will and prayers this matter was indeed accomplished—and with the devotion of the aforesaid Obert and his relatives, to establish religious life in the aforesaid church and to labour with all your strength so that services pleasing to the Lord may be rendered there. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the monastery of Vallombrosa now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, acquire by grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, [Col. 0191B] offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you in perpetuity.

We therefore decree, etc., as far as: “for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted.” If anyone therefore, etc., as far as: “may find the rewards of eternal peace.” Saving, however, the reverence due to the diocesan bishop. Upon all, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Ubert, priest cardinal of the title of St Clement, have subscribed. I, Lucas, priest cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Romanus, deacon cardinal of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Guido, deacon cardinal of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.

Given at Siena through the hand of Almeric, deacon cardinal [Col. 0191C] and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of September, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1133 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third [fourth] year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CXLVIII. He rebukes R[ainald], archbishop of Rheims, and B [read: Henry], archbishop of Sens, because they did not more promptly pronounce a sentence of excommunication upon those who killed the prior of St Victor. (1133, November 16.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, III, 493.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers R., archbishop of Rheims, B., archbishop of Sens, and their bishops: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0191D] The dreadful murder of our beloved son Thomas, prior of St Victor, of good memory, has disturbed the hearts of all who hear of it and filled us and our brethren with deep sorrow. For what advantage is there in Gaul’s not being defiled by the horror of monsters or polluted by heretical depravity, if sacred dignity is there stained by the shedding of priestly blood? It is therefore most astonishing that, while our dearest son, the illustrious and glorious Louis, king of the Franks, reigns—by the vigour of whose royal justice murderers, sacrilegious persons, and criminals ought to be restrained by the severest punishment—so atrocious and detestable a crime should in his time have been undertaken by the accursed audacity of certain rash men.

Let the laws therefore arise, since they ought not to be silent in the face of so atrocious a crime; and let both ecclesiastical and [Col. 0192A] secular censure arm itself with its proper swords. What disaster of war, savage hostility, or harshness of the weather could inflict upon the people of God so great a slaughter as would result if priests—who have the care of souls and the divine sacraments entrusted to them, whom it is dangerous not to obey—as well as clerics taken into God’s lot, and monks, were killed? Since crimes committed, if impunity follows, give others boldness to offend, lest the enormity of so great a wickedness and this profane audacity leave a foul example for posterity and produce imitators through its contagion, cast down the accomplices in this crime by the severity of sacred discipline, so that the righteous may rejoice at justice having been declared, and the wicked, hearing of it, may be brought to rest. For if the zeal of your punishment had blazed forth in a similar crime, a doubled outrage would not today have been committed.

Awake, therefore, brethren, to whom power has been entrusted in the administration of the divine law; setting aside all dissimulation, administer just punishment severely against those parricides and all persons cognizant of this crime. For if anything is overlooked or omitted by you, you will know that it concerns the peril of your souls and your office. Whatever your prudence decrees in these matters, moreover, shall be supported by the authority of blessed Peter and ourselves. The decrees of the holy Fathers and both the recent and ancient enactments of councils instruct you what ought to be decided in such a case. Furthermore, we command that the body of the aforesaid good man, who now before the heavenly Judge bears testimony to his justice and innocence, and who, while living under obedience, was killed in the service of his own bishopric, be honourably buried in his church.

Given at Pisa, 21 December [read: the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, i.e. 16 November].

### CXLIX. To Atto, bishop of Pistoia.—Concerning the immunity granted to the Church of Pistoia. (1133, December 21.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 493.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ATTO, bishop of Pistoia, and to his successors canonically promoted in perpetuity.

The Church of Pistoia, through the bounty of the Lord, author of all good things, has from times long past received in the regions of Tuscany this special prerogative: that it should shine forth under the government of wise and discerning pastors and, through their industry, receive growth pleasing to God both in spiritual and temporal matters. We indeed rejoice and exult with due gladness because the providence of the heavenly dispensation has established you, venerable brother Bishop Atto—a wise man, certainly, and proven in religious life—as shepherd of that place, and by divine mercy has called you to govern and instruct your people by the example of doctrine and life.

Therefore, the more religious your life is, and the more devoted to blessed Peter is the aforesaid Church of Pistoia, over which you preside by God’s authority, the more gratefully the necessity imposed upon us by the office of the apostolate [Col. 0193A] obliges us to fortify with apostolic privileges that Church entrusted to you by God and to preserve its rights inviolate and entire. Accordingly, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Urban and Paschal, Roman pontiffs, we decree by the present enactment that all things which the same Church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall be secure to you and your successors and remain inviolate.

We further decree that the bishopric of the diocese of Pistoia, just as its boundaries have been defined by the privileges of our aforesaid predecessors, shall remain in its right and condition to the bishop of Pistoia without anyone’s molestation or disturbance; within these boundaries the following chapels and churches are known to be situated, etc.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, John, priest cardinal of the title of St Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Gottfried, priest cardinal of the title of St Justina, have subscribed. I, Lucas, priest cardinal of the title of Saints Peter, John, and Paul, have subscribed. I, Martin, priest cardinal of the title of St Stephen [Col. 0193C] on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon cardinal of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Guido, deacon cardinal of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Odo, deacon cardinal of St George, have subscribed. I, John, deacon cardinal of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Haiméric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1133 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CL. To Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Stephen, bishop of Paris.—What penance the killers of Archembald, subdeacon of Orléans, must perform in order to make satisfaction and be absolved from excommunication. (1134, January 8.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, III, 493.]

[Col. 0193D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers GEOFFREY, bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, and STEPHEN, bishop of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your belovedness know that Geoffrey of Viconovo, having lately come to us, affirmed under oath in the presence of our brethren that, without prejudice to the fidelity due to our dearest son Louis, king of the Franks, [Col. 0194A] he will perform liege homage to our beloved sons Stephen the subdeacon, S. the provost, and the other relatives and nephews of Archembald, subdeacon of Orléans, of good memory, who are willing to receive it; and that he will swear to them and to all others who had been exiled with the deceased man security for life, limb, and property. The worthier members of his kindred shall swear the same security with him. This is added: that he shall faithfully endeavour to ensure that Henry likewise swears and performs the same, and that each of them shall make satisfaction to the Church of Orléans, which they have grievously injured.

Moreover, Hervé of Viconovo, his nephew Hugh, Theobald of Hervé, and, with him, as many knights as will make up the number of one hundred, together with one hundred and forty of the worthier burgesses of the city of Orléans whom they can find for this purpose, shall perform homage to the aforesaid relatives [Col. 0194B] of Subdeacon Archembald. If Henry refuses to swear this, the aforesaid Geoffrey shall nevertheless ensure its fulfilment on his own.

Thereafter, on the next feast of All Saints, they shall present themselves before us, faithfully to undertake whatever penance we decide to impose upon them, and then to be absolved by us from the bond of excommunication. Finally, the aforesaid S., the subdeacon, and S., the provost, in the presence of our brethren, mercifully forgave Geoffrey the death of the said Archembald of revered memory for God’s sake; and they shall do the same for the other knights who killed the same subdeacon, provided that they make satisfaction to the Church of Orléans and to the relatives of the slain man.

Nevertheless, all these persons shall meanwhile remain outside the Church and in penance; and if any of them should come to the end of life, neither absolution from excommunication nor viaticum shall be denied him. We wish, however, that on account of those who have made satisfaction to the Church, the Church of Orléans shall no longer cease from divine offices. But if any of the same killers withdraw themselves from that satisfaction, then, so long as they remain in land under the special lordship of our glorious son Louis, king of the Franks, within that same bishopric of Orléans, the whole city and the archdeaconry of Stephen of Garlande shall cease from divine offices until they make satisfaction. We therefore command your diligence, since the condition of the territory is better known to you, to take care on our behalf concerning the manner of satisfaction and the absolution of the Church held under interdict.

Given at Pisa, on the sixth day before the Ides of January.

### CLI. Privilege for the monastery of Rebais. (1134, January 12.)

[DUPLESSIS, *History of the Church of Meaux*, II, p. 27.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ NATALIS, abbot of Rebais, and to his successors regularly promoted in perpetuity.

As we have learned from the writings recording ancient deeds, a certain venerable man, named Dado and a Frank by nation, built a monastery, out of devotion, at the place called Rebais, upon the stream of that name in the district of Meaux. He wished it to be called Jerusalem; and, having solemnly consecrated it in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul, he offered it to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church with the counsel and assent of St Faro, bishop of Meaux, many other bishops, and also the kings of France. Our predecessors of good memory, John and Martin, Roman pontiffs, received it into the power, lordship, and protection of the Apostolic See, together with the distinguished abbot Agil and the abbots appointed after him, the fellow-monks and clerics serving the Lord there who had been entrusted to him for governance, and with all things and persons subject or to become subject to the monastery; and they confirmed this by apostolic documents.

[Col. 0195B] We therefore, following in their footsteps, receive you, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Natalis, together with the same monastery over which, thanks be to God, you are known to preside, into the guardianship and patronage of the holy Roman Church and of ourselves, and strengthen you by the document of the present privilege. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names:

namely, the borough itself called Rebais, with all its appurtenances, churches and tithes, male and female serfs, [Col. 0195C] meadows and pastures, the water called Mucra and all its fishing rights, islands and mills, fisheries, bridges and all crossings of that water, and all adjoining cultivated and uncultivated lands; the village of Orly and the village of Montboitron, with the churches, tithes, male and female serfs, meadows and pastures of those villages, and all adjoining cultivated and uncultivated lands; the village called Ulciacus and the village called Septemsortes, with the churches, tithes, male and female serfs, meadows and pastures of those villages, and their appurtenances, cultivated and uncultivated; the port of Fay; half of the village called Brigenium, with its mother church and the tithes belonging to it, male and female serfs, meadows and pastures, and other surrounding cultivated and uncultivated lands; the village called Montigniacus, with church and tithes, and the surrounding meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands; the village called Capella on the Mucra, the village called Cormaiot on the same bank, and the village called Melleraie on the same bank, with the churches, tithes, male and female serfs, mills, fishing rights, meadows, pastures, and all appurtenances of those villages, cultivated and uncultivated; the village called Campus Coellus, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadow, pastures, and all appurtenances, cultivated and uncultivated; the island called Bellus-Locus, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, fishing rights, [Col. 0196A] and all its cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; the village called Herbicia, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and its cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; the village called Agillimansio, with church, tithe, male and female serfs, pastures, meadows, and adjoining cultivated and uncultivated lands; the tithe of the village called Senionia, with the attached land and male and female serfs; the land and tithe of the village called St Lupus, with male and female serfs; the village called Laqueius on the bank of the river Marne, with male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; on the same bank, the holding called Porteion and another called Vernolium; and the church called Capella, with male and female serfs, meadows, pastures, and other cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances; the castle called Brecus in the village called Lesser Brociacus, land with male and female serfs, meadows and pastures, and other cultivated and uncultivated appurtenances, etc. [lacuna]

Moreover, we confirm for you by this present decree the liberty under which the monastery of Rebais is known hitherto to have remained, together with the parish churches adjoining it—namely St John’s, St Nicholas’s, St Denis’s, St Leodegar’s, and St Christopher’s—so that the abbot of that place shall be subject to the judgment, jurisdiction, or admonition of no one save the Roman pontiff alone. The priests of the aforesaid churches likewise shall not be compelled to attend the diocesan bishop’s synod or any other summons of his; but shall rather be subject, with all their parishioners, to the authority and ordering of you and your successors. Nor shall the diocesan bishop or any of his officials, on any pretext, possess jurisdiction or authority of admonition in those parishes; rather, in every matter they are left to the judgment of you and your successors.

And so that the liberty of that monastery may in no way be diminished in future but may instead remain inviolate, we likewise decree that the extorted profession which, beloved son Abbot Natalis, we understand you made to our brother Bulcard, bishop of Meaux, of good memory, for the sake of peace, shall create no impediment for you or your successors. Furthermore, we decree that no one whatsoever shall presume, without the commission or authority of the holy Roman Church, to prohibit that place [Col. 0196D] or the churches where an assembly of parish priests takes place from sacred offices, or that on this account the divine office of the altar be interrupted—unless perhaps, which God forbid, such offence or fault should be unjustly inflicted upon you by wicked men, for which, fortified by our authority and licence, you pronounce against the same evildoers the sentence of anathema according to the canons. By apostolic benevolence we grant you the power, as circumstances require, to bind or loose them—a power which we see [lacuna] have conferred.

Furthermore, in all the churches which you possess, except the aforesaid five, you shall elect priests to be appointed according to custom and shall present them to the diocesan bishops, there to serve the Lord. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars [Col. 0197A] or churches, and the ordinations of monks or clerics to be promoted to holy orders from the diocesan bishop, if he enjoys the favour of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide them to you without malice or exaction. From him likewise you shall freely receive the abbot’s blessing, without an exaction of profession; otherwise, you may approach any Catholic bishop, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay yearly two bezants to us and our successors. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb your monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; but let all be kept entire for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to amend by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the just rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal [Col. 0197C] peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Gerard, priest cardinal, have subscribed. I, Anselm, priest cardinal, have subscribed. I, Lictifrid, priest cardinal, have subscribed. I, Lucas, priest cardinal of the church of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Guido, unworthy priest, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Albert, deacon of the title of St Theodore, have subscribed. [Col. 0197D] I, Guido, deacon cardinal of St Adrian, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aymeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of January, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1134 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CLII. Bull by which the monastery of Frankenthal is confirmed and at the same time received into the protection of the Holy See. (1134, January 23.)

[SCHANNAT, *History of the Bishopric of Worms*, vol. II, p. 66.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 0198A] to his beloved sons GUILBERT, provost of the church of St Mary Magdalene, situated at the place called Frankenthal, and his brethren, in perpetuity.

We ought to make suitable provision, with due consideration, for those choosing the religious life. Therefore, beloved sons, we graciously grant your petitions and receive into the protection of blessed Peter the church of St Mary Magdalene in which you are occupied with divine office. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established there according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed inviolate in that church for all time. We also confirm for you and your successors, under the protection of this document, all goods which now canonically belong to that place or which, with the Lord’s aid, you may hereafter acquire. Among them we have thought fit to record by their proper names:

namely, the church called Omerscheim, consecrated in honour of All Saints, in which religious women are known to serve the Lord. We have likewise thought fit to protect it, together with all its appurtenances, by the support of the holy Roman Church. We decree that all things bestowed upon that place in devotion by the nobleman Erkembert, founder of your church, or by other faithful servants of God, shall remain secure to you in perpetuity. Further, the tithes of all things which you shall possess within your enclosure and immunity, just as they were granted or remitted to you by our venerable brother Burchard, also called Buggo, bishop of Worms, we establish by apostolic authority as belonging to your [Col. 0198C] church in perpetuity. In accordance with the ruling of that same brother of ours, you shall have licence to receive penitents in aid of the bishops of Worms and to visit the sick. We decree that you shall be free from every secular exaction and shall likewise enjoy whatever rights or privileges other monasteries in the bishopric of Worms are reasonably held to possess.

When you, the present provost of that place, or any of your successors die, no one shall be put in charge there by any artifice of intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren of that place, with the consent of all or of the sounder part of the counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, judge ought to be elected. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with vexations; but let all be preserved whole and inviolate for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to make fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself guilty of the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment [Col. 0199A] let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all preserving the rights of that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Guido, bishop of Tivoli. I, Littifrid, priest cardinal of the title of Vestina. I, Lucas, priest cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Stephen, deacon cardinal of the title of St Lucy. I, Odo, deacon cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Americ, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1134 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CLIII. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of St Flora of Arezzo. (1134, March 23.)

[COCQUELINES, vol. II, p. 223.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, abbot of the monastery of St Flora, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized to accord with reason, it befits us to grant it willingly and to afford appropriate support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot John, we graciously grant your petitions and strengthen by the support of the Apostolic See the monastery of St Flora, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. Accordingly, by the document of the present privilege we decree by apostolic authority that whatever goods or possessions that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s aid, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other means, shall be kept secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have added the following, to be recorded by their proper names:

the castle of St Flora, with the chapels known to be situated there: namely, the chapel of St Anastasius, the chapel of St Angel, the chapel of St [Col. 0199D] Apollinaris, the chapel of St Zeno, and what you possess in the chapel of St Mary; the greater monastery of St Peter in the city of Arezzo, with its hospice and all its appurtenances, adding that you may order it according to established custom; the chapel of St Gregory, and the right which you possess in the chapel of St Laurence; the monastery of St Michael of Mount Pinculi, with its chapels and appurtenances; the church of St Peter and St Tiburtius at Gargonsa, with its appurtenances; the parish church of St Martin of Galoniano, with all its appurtenances; two parts of the parish church of St Mustiola, with their appurtenances; the right which you possess in the church of St Vincent at Cortona; the castle of Quarata, with the church of St Andrew and its estate; the castle of Sarna, with the church of St Flora and its estate; and whatever you possess at St Mamma; the castle of Muglano, with the church of St Angel and estate, and what you possess in the church of St Mary at Villa-Alba; the castle of Fontia, with the church of St Peter and its appurtenances; the castle of Rughitino, with its churches and estate; [Col. 0200A] the church of St Leo, with its appurtenances; the church of Lesser St Flora, with half its estate and the estate of Bulgari, together with what you possess in the church of St Laurence and St Sebastian; the church of St Peter at Majano, together with what you possess there; and whatever you possess in Politiano, Pinli, and Vico.

When you, the present abbot of the same place, or any of your successors die, no one shall be put in charge there by any artifice of intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, judge ought to be elected.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever shall be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any molestations; but let all be preserved entire for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, with the canonical right and reverence due to the bishop and Church of Arezzo always reserved. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt [Col. 0200C] to act against it and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Guido, bishop of Tivoli, have subscribed. [Col. 0200D] I, Rudolph, bishop of Orte, have subscribed. I, Anselm, priest cardinal, have subscribed. I, Lictifrod, priest cardinal of the title of Vestina, have subscribed. I, Lucas, priest cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Guido, unworthy priest, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa [through] the hand of Aymeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth [read: thirteenth] indiction, in the year 1135 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth [read: sixth] year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CLIV. To Briccius, bishop of Nantes. (1134, April 22.)

[MORICE, *Memoirs for the History of Brittany*, I, 571.]

[Col. 0201A]

## CLIV. To Briccius, Bishop of Nantes. (22 April 1134.)

[MORICE, *Mémoires pour l’histoire de Bretagne*, I, 571.]

[Col. 0201A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BRICCIUS, bishop of Nantes, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

To settle the disputes of litigants by a swift judgment accords, beyond doubt, both with equity and with firmness. Therefore we have judged that the settlement of the controversy hitherto conducted between you and the monks of Marmoutier concerning the churches, namely, of Holy Cross, Saint Saturninus, Saint Albinus, and Saint Mary, situated within the city of Nantes, ought to be committed to parchment and ink. Thus the illustrious [Col. 0201B] man Conan, count of Brittany, first through our venerable brothers William, bishop of Palestrina, and Guy, then cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, and afterwards repeatedly through his many letters, frequently informed us that the aforesaid churches were, according to the custom of the princes of that land, so fully his own by right that the bishop of the city claimed absolutely nothing in them. And, having long considered their establishment, he declared that by divine inspiration he had been moved to wish to offer them to blessed Peter, and afterwards, by our kindness, to place them in the hands of the monks of Marmoutier, so that religious men might serve the Lord there where clerics of disgraceful life and conduct had until then lived.

Rejoicing indeed in the devotion of the count himself, we warned him in our letters that, since divine mercy had inspired him with so pious a work, he should restore these same churches to their own bishop and entrust their governance and ordering to his care. Although this had often been urged upon him in our letters, he declared that he wished devoutly to comply with our exhortations; but he charged the bishop himself with negligence, because he refused to place religious persons there. Accordingly, we also wrote repeatedly to your brotherhood, and jointly advised you concerning the reception of the aforesaid churches and the establishment of religious observance in them.

Meanwhile, when almost a year had elapsed, the aforesaid count sent his envoys to us and humbly asked that his devotion might be brought to effect through us. And, lest this should be thought to proceed in any way from impulse or levity, through those same envoys we received letters from our venerable brothers Geoffrey of Chartres, legate of the Apostolic See, and Ancelin, bishop of Rennes. These men, praising the good intention of the same count, likewise requested that we grant assent to his petitions. Since, therefore, he pressed us so urgently and was supported by the testimony of such eminent men, and since during this period you had sent no reply to the many exhortatory letters which we had sent you, we at last, though reluctantly, granted the petition of the aforesaid count, judging it better to remove these churches from lay hands on so honourable a ground [Col. 0202A] and place religious men there, than to allow them thus to remain under the count’s power.

Having therefore received the aforesaid churches into the ownership and protection of blessed Peter, at the request of our aforesaid brothers we granted them, by our kindness, to the abbot and brethren of Marmoutier, without prejudice to your right and honour, and confirmed the grant by the text of our document. When, therefore, the aforesaid abbot had repeatedly complained to us through his envoys that he endured various troubles and injuries from your brotherhood concerning this same grant, we commanded by apostolic letters that you should cease harassing those brothers, or should appear before us on the octave of Saint Martin, to answer both us and them concerning contempt and injuries.

But when the day of that term was at hand, although worn out by old age and weighed down by illness, you came into our presence. Having waited for the abbot and monks for some time, at last certain persons sent by them arrived with letters, asserting that they had neither come nor would come; for, just as the injuries inflicted upon them appeared to redound to the Roman Church, so the matter itself principally concerned the lord pope. Yet your brotherhood nevertheless set forth again the calamities and oppressions which you had suffered at their hands. You asserted that the aforesaid churches—which the monks maintained had belonged to the power of the illustrious man Count Conan, and had been granted by him to them, and for the confirmation of which they had obtained a privilege from the Apostolic See—had, before the monks received investiture from that same count in the chapter of Saint Peter of Nantes on the feast of Saint Nicholas and before they were put by him into possession, been relinquished into your hands for the use of the Church of Nantes.

And when the aforesaid count had already been induced, despite your resistance and opposition, to hand over the aforesaid churches to those monks, you, perceiving that the Church entrusted to you was being seriously burdened, publicly appealed to the hearing of the Roman See in the presence of many persons; and you declared that the aforesaid monks had received them despite that appeal. You also stated that they had fraudulently obtained the church of Saint Mary, said to belong to the abbey of Holy Cross of Quimperlé, so that it might be added to their privilege.

Since the monks were absent and had not sent adequate representatives, although worn out [Col. 0202D] by old age and hindered by ill health, you spared not your person but remained at our court until the monks presented themselves before us. When they came before us in mid-Lent and ought to have answered your objections, although warned by us to send persons competent to conduct the business, they maintained that they had neither come nor been sent for that purpose, and they showed that it was not safe for them to submit to judgment concerning matters which appeared to have been granted to them by the same count—especially since that count was absent and had not been summoned in a cause of this kind.

At length, since your side had abundant necessary proofs and you produced witnesses concerning the matters you had alleged, we received their testimony according to the differing nature of the case. First, John and David, priests, testified that by your command and consent, and under your obedience, they had been established in the church of Holy Cross and had there celebrated the divine mysteries. Then, when we sought other witnesses, you presented three priests to us: two from the church of Saint Saturninus, namely Rainerius and Akarius, and one from the church of Saint Albinus, namely Acharias. They asserted the same thing that the earlier witnesses had affirmed concerning the church of Holy Cross.

Concerning also the relinquishment which you asserted had been made by the count, the archdeacon Titio and Norman, subdeacon and canon of your church, testified that they had been present, had seen and heard, when the aforesaid count, beside the river Vicenonia, freely relinquished to you and to the Church of Nantes the claim which he had until then held in the same churches, before they had been granted by Count Conan to the monks in the chapter of Saint Peter of Nantes and before the monks had been placed in possession by the *cuffia* [a ceremonial cap or symbol of investiture], without any mention that they were to be conferred upon Marmoutier.

Moreover Simon, abbot of Saint Gildas of Rhuys, and Guy, chaplain of Saint Mary, testified that, because of the burden which the aforesaid count was laying upon the Church of Nantes in the chapter of Nantes, before the abbot and monks of Marmoutier had received investiture of the aforesaid churches in the chapter of Nantes and before they had been put into possession of them by the aforesaid count, you had publicly appealed to our hearing. All these men swore upon the most holy Gospels that this was true as they had testified.

Therefore, instructed by so many and such weighty reasons, and having taken counsel with our brethren, we adjudged and established you, venerable brother Briccius, as possessor of the churches of Holy Cross, Saint Saturninus, Saint Albinus, and Saint Mary—in which the monks of Quimperlé serve the Lord—which the same monks of Marmoutier had caused to be inserted in a fraudulently obtained privilege; and through you we invested the Church of Nantes fully with their appurtenances by the ring. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly presume to oppose this our determination. But if anyone attempts this and does not make suitable satisfaction, let him know that he is subject to anathema . . .

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church (with many other cardinals who subscribed).

[Col. 0203D] Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1135 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

## CLV. He informs [Didacus], Archbishop of Compostela, that after Emperor Lothair’s departure he remained for some time in Rome with his followers; then, “that his brethren might have safer and easier access to him,” he went to Pisa. He commends Astaldus. (3 May 1134.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 549.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0204A] Having great confidence in your prudence and integrity, we have considered it proper briefly to inform your brotherhood of our condition. After the departure of our dearest son Lothair, august emperor, we, who ought to provide for the sheep subject to us lest they seem to be exposed to slaughter by ravening wolves, trusting more in the shelter of divine protection than in the strength of human aid, remained with them in the City. Thus it came about that our faithful people, strengthened against the enemies of the Church, persevered more steadfastly in their fidelity to blessed Peter and to us.

Finally, after we had defended them for some time by our bodily presence, we left the City and came to Pisa, so that our brethren might have safer and easier access to us and that we might comfort those who labour with appropriate support. [Col. 0204B] There, living with our brethren, we work more earnestly at matters pertaining to the honour of the Church. Yet we are surprised that, after so much time has passed, you have given us no assurance concerning your condition and safety. Therefore, that the devotion of your love toward your mother, the Roman Church, may appear more clearly, strive to demonstrate it by the performance of deeds.

Moreover, we earnestly commend to your affection our son Astaldus, bearer of the present letter, who is exceedingly faithful to the holy Church of God; we ask that, for reverence toward blessed Peter and out of love for us, you receive him kindly and furnish him with assistance where necessary.

Given at Pisa, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].

## CLVI. Privilege for the Abbey of Prémontré. (3 May 1134.)

[LE PAIGE, *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, p. 622.]

[Col. 0204C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, HUGH, abbot of Prémontré, and the co-abbots, provosts, priors, and all brethren of the Premonstratensian order, both present and those to be regularly appointed in the future, in perpetuity.

Your sacred order, planted by divine dispensation in the Lord’s field, deservedly merits to be exalted by apostolic favours; for its professed members, having put away worldly enticements, devote themselves to heavenly contemplation and continually labour for the advancement of souls. Directing, therefore, the attention of apostolic consideration toward the said [Col. 0204D] order—which we have decreed and desire to remain in a lofty, firm, and stable condition—we willingly attend to those matters by which the said professed members may suffer no loss of true peace and the state of religious life may sustain no injury, but may apply themselves more devoutly to divine worship and works of salvation in proportion as their condition is more tranquil and they themselves have been granted greater liberty.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting your petitions, we establish and sanction by the authority of the Apostolic See that the canonical order which is known to be established in the same church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the observance of the brethren of Prémontré shall be observed inviolably for all time in all the churches of your order. We also establish that, according to the ordinance of Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, of good memory, all your abbots and provosts of the Premonstratensian order shall come annually to Prémontré for the common chapter; there, by the common counsel of the brethren, they shall correct what needs correction and, with the Lord’s help, establish what ought to be established.

Furthermore, by this present decree we enact that no ecclesiastical person may presume to demand a palfrey or anything else for the blessing of abbots or the consecration of your churches; nor may any of your abbots presume to give it, even if it is demanded, because the mark and danger of simoniacal depravity threaten both the person demanding and the person giving. No one of your churches shall choose as its pastor a person from another order, nor shall any member of your order be appointed abbot of a monastery of another order, except by authority of the Roman Church.

No archbishop, bishop, or other prelate may place your churches under interdict or excommunicate your persons, since the offences of your members can and ought to be corrected through the common chapter of Prémontré. We also enact that you may receive free and unencumbered persons fleeing from the secular world for conversion, and retain them, without objection, together with their goods and possessions. No one may hinder the sick who in their final disposition have resolved to be transferred to you or buried among you, nor presume to retain their lawful goods, provided always that the lawful portion of the heirs and the canonical rights of those churches [Col. 0205C] from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact.

Likewise we decree that in your courts and granges you may build oratories according to your means and usefulness, so that there you may celebrate the divine offices for the salvation of souls for your community and other faithful persons. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your churches, take away their possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of these same churches and your places may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0206A] I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano. I, Anselm, cardinal-priest. I, Lictifredus, cardinal-priest of the title of Vestina. I, Ubido, unworthy priest. I, John, cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth [Col. 0206B] day before the Nones of May [3 May], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1135 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

## CLVII. Privilege for the Monastery of Sesto. (9 June 1134.)

[*Annales Camaldulenses*, Appendix, vol. III, p. 343, from the original of Saints Bartholomew and Pontianus of Lucca.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, abbot of Saint Benedict above the Po, and his successors regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0206C] Both the necessity of the times urges us and the diminution of persons requires that, whenever monasteries once flourishing in religious life have fallen away from the splendour of their religion, we extend to them a helping hand and, with the Lord’s cooperation, direct all our strength to their restoration. The monastery of Sesto, which spiritually belongs to blessed Peter, is known to have flourished in former times in true religious life and in an abundance of temporal possessions. But because, with iniquity increasing, the charity of many grew cold and human malice became established, the place itself has been very greatly reduced in both temporal and spiritual matters, as we cannot say without sorrow.

Therefore we, who sit in the place of the prince of the apostles and ought to exercise attentive care for all churches, especially those belonging by right to the holy Roman [Col. 0206D] Church, carefully deliberated with our brethren. After prolonged discussions, for the sake of ecclesiastical usefulness and administration, it was at length determined by our judgment that we ought to commit that monastery to you, beloved son in the Lord Henry, abbot, and to your successors. By the present charter of privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that henceforth you shall have the governance of that same monastery of Sesto and diligently devote yourselves to its restoration. Thus, when religious observance has there been reformed through your zeal, whatever needs correction in that place may be corrected through your diligence; and the abbot who is to be appointed there from time to time shall be chosen by your oversight and counsel.

Concerning the novices of the same monastery, we establish this: if it seems useful and suitable to religious life to you or your successors, those novices shall be transferred by the abbot of Sesto to the monastery of Saint Benedict within a year, and others from that cloister shall be received in their place. No person, therefore, may lawfully rashly disturb you concerning this grant or withdraw the aforesaid monastery from your governance and correction. Rather, both the abbot and the brethren of that place shall in future be subject and obedient to your discipline, while, of course, the ownership of blessed Peter and the due reverence of the Apostolic See remain unimpaired.

As a sign that the same church belongs by right to the Apostolic See, you shall pay three bezants each year to us and our successors. [Col. 0207B] If anyone should rashly attempt to act against this our constitution, let him know that he will incur the indignation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. But may those who preserve it obtain the favour of those same apostles. Amen, amen, amen.

**HELP US, O GOD, OUR SAVIOUR.**

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, subscribed. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano, subscribed. I, Hubert, archbishop of the Church of Pisa, subscribed. I, Anselm, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, subscribed. I, Lictifredus, cardinal-priest of the title of Vestina, subscribed. [Col. 0207C] I, Martin, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy priest, subscribed. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, subscribed. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, subscribed. I, Luke, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of June [9 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1135 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

[Col. 0207D] I, Vido, judge of the imperial court of Henry Pepe and notary, saw, read, and faithfully copied the original from which this copy was taken, together with the seal of our lord Pope Innocent II. I, Bonotius, notary of the sacred palace of Gonzaga, saw and read the original, sealed with the seal of our lord Pope Innocent II, from which this copy was taken, and therefore subscribed here. I, Agnellus, notary of the sacred palace from the place of Gonzaga, etc. I, Arlothus, notary of the sacred palace of Gonzaga, etc.

## CLVIII. He grants to Henry, abbot of Polirone, and his successors the church of Saint Caesarius (of Vilzacara), on condition that they pay three bezants annually. (9 June 1134.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 259.]

[Col. 0208A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict above the Po, and to his successors regularly appointed in his place, in perpetuity.

Our heart is moved by the devout inspiration of the Godhead to reform for the better places once established in the observance of ecclesiastical religion and to assist their destitution as our office requires. For this purpose and desire, the faithful also [Col. 0208B] build churches for the honour of God and bestow possessions and estates upon them: namely, that religious persons may be established there to serve the divine majesty humbly and devoutly, and that, through their prayers poured out to God, founders, predecessors, and posterity alike may be freed from the bonds of sins and may deserve to obtain eternal rewards in exchange for temporal benefits.

With this intention, Matilda, illustrious countess of revered memory, enriched with her goods and possessions the church of blessed Caesarius in the territory of Modena, which had been offered to blessed Peter; she endowed it abundantly with books, vessels, and other ecclesiastical ornaments; and she caused brethren who might devote themselves to the service of almighty God according to the Rule of blessed Augustine to be placed there. It has consequently happened that, since the world lies in wickedness and continually declines for the worse, those things which she had offered to God and blessed Peter for the good of religion and the remedy of her soul have been occupied and dissipated by wicked men. Where formerly religious observance and integrity flourished together with an abundance of temporal goods, now, because sins so require, scarcely even traces of spiritual goods can appear on account of the insolence of wicked men.

Having often considered this matter with our brethren, lest so pious a purpose of the aforesaid woman should be frustrated, but rather obtain the desired remedy for her soul, we have judged that the same church, with its appurtenances, should be granted to you, beloved son in the Lord Henry, abbot, and to your successors. Thus, through your diligence and that of your successors, a community of religious brethren may be established in that place according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, and its number determined according to the resources of that church.

We decree, therefore, that no person may rashly disturb you concerning this our constitution, nor remove the aforesaid church from our ordering or correction so long as religious life endures there through the Lord’s cooperation. Rather, both the church itself and the goods belonging to it shall remain under our governance and free ordering, with the ownership and lordship of blessed Peter, and the due reverence owed to us and our successors, of course remaining intact. As a sign that the same church belongs by right to the Apostolic See, you shall pay three bezants annually to us and our successors. [Col. 0209A] If anyone should rashly attempt to act against this our constitution, let him incur the indignation of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. But upon those who preserve it may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Matthew, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Humbert, bishop of the Church of Pisa, have subscribed. I, Anselm, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy priest, have subscribed. [Col. 0209B] I, Lucifredus, cardinal-priest of the title of Vestina, have subscribed. I, Martin, cardinal-priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Luke, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Almeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of June [9 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1135 of the Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

## CLIX. Bull confirming the estates and other possessions of the monks of Quincy. (12 October 1134.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, IV, document 164.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALBERIC, abbot of Quincy, and to his successors regularly appointed.

How great is the joy which your praiseworthy religious community produces in our heart, he surely knows who searches hearts and inward parts. For you, going forth from the monastery of Pontigny like swarms of bees, fill countless hives far and wide with heavenly [Col. 0209D] manna, and refresh the hearts of many who thirst by nourishing them with the saving doctrine of water springing up into eternal life. Therefore we cherish your sacred community with the affection of true charity and strengthen by the support of the Apostolic See the monastery of the blessed Mother of God, in which you devote yourselves to divine service. We establish that whatever goods and possessions you justly and canonically possess in the present twelfth indiction, and whatever you may reasonably acquire in future by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you in perpetuity.

Among these we have thought it necessary specifically to name: the place of Quincy itself; the place of Fontaines; and the place of Bâtery. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may lawfully rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved whole for the beneficial use of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, if he does not amend his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all those who preserve the rights of this place [Col. 0210B] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, Luke, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

[Col. 0210C] Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of October [12 October], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1135 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

## CLX. To Geoffrey, archbishop, and to the suffragan bishops and abbots of the Church of Dol established throughout that province: he invites them to the Council of Pisa. (8 November 1134.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 487.]

The ship of the Church, over which Christ the ruler presides, although it is often tossed by the driving of the waves, is nevertheless never submerged when the Lord rows within it. From the depth of his counsel, the providence of the heavenly sailor [Col. 0210D] stirs up the winds, troubles the sea, and shakes the ship, in order to awaken sleeping ministers, encourage the sluggish, and make the cautious more industrious. Glory therefore be to God in the highest, because your faith has never failed. When schism arose in the Church, you were found proven, and you manifestly illuminate the house of the Lord as true disciples of Christ.

But, so that we may more safely deliberate with you concerning the state of the Church and that the way to us may be easier for you, having appointed a vicar in the City and arranged those things which we recognized to be necessary for our faithful people, we are, thanks be to God, staying at Pisa with our brethren, sound and safe. And, in order that new remedies may more conveniently be applied to new diseases, we have decided, by the Lord’s ordering, to celebrate a general council there at the approaching feast of Pentecost. Therefore, by the authority of the present letter, we command your whole body to present yourselves before us at that time, every excuse set aside, so that, assisted by the grace of the Holy Spirit and relying upon your counsel and help, we may establish those measures by which the Church may rejoice both now and hereafter.

We also earnestly commend to your brotherhood our beloved son John, a monk and our chaplain, asking that for reverence toward blessed Peter you receive him kindly and treat him honourably.

Given at Pisa, on the sixth day before the Ides of November [8 November].

## CLXI. At the request of Bishop John, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Fiesole. (16 November 1134.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 241.]

[Col. 0211B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, bishop of Fiesole, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Placed, by the Lord’s ordering, upon the lofty watchtower of the apostolic see, we ought to love our brother bishops and preserve their rights for the Churches committed to them by God. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, Bishop John, we graciously grant your just requests and strengthen by the privilege of the apostolic see the holy Church of Fiesole, over which, by the Lord’s authority, you are known to preside.

For we decree that whatever possessions or goods this [Col. 0211C] Church now justly and lawfully possesses, or may reasonably acquire in the future, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors. Among these we have added the following, to be recorded by their proper names: the court-estate and city of Fiesole, with the churches, court-estates, and adjoining lands; likewise the castle of Monte Lauri, and Monte Regis; Baiana and the court-estate of Sala; Festiliano and Prato Regis; the church of St Mary at Urbana, with its court-estate, Libiano, and Biviliano; the castle which is known to have been built through your efforts beside the river Fontana, with the court-estate of the stream Ferioli and Palranti; the castle of Ciselo; the court-estate on Monte Acuto; and, in the Ampinana mountain district, that of St Gaudentius, with their mountain pastures and appurtenances, as these were bestowed upon your Church by royal grant; the castle of Agna; [Col. 0211D] the court-estate of Turricola and Castiglione; the castle of Monte Bonelli; the castle of Rofiano; the monastery of St Saviour, situated in the diocese of Pistoia, with the churches of St Potitus and St Martin built at Fugnano in the plain of Novoli, the church of St Martin.

In Capraccia, one half of the church of St Christina; at Ripole, the church of St Saviour; St Michael of Marine; the court-estate of Calenzano; the court-estate of St Donninus; the court-estate of Bagnasca; and whatever the Church of Fiesole possesses in the parish church of St Stephen in Campo and in the parish church of St John at Settimo. At Mengnano, the church of St Peter with its court-estate and all their tithes; the monastery of St Bartholomew, situated at Fiesole, with its dependent churches and tithes; the monastery of St Martin; [Col. 0212A] the monastery of St Gaudentius with their appurtenances; the patrimony of the sons of Hemio; the castle called Flumen; and whatever, by right of the aforesaid Church, the sons of Hugh, the sons of Raimbert, Azo son of Albich, the sons of Hugh of Castaniola, Lombard of Molezzano, the sons of Hugh of Casula, Longobard of Terliano, Longobard of St John Major, and Longobard of Arena hold in the territory of Macello, or whatever any person appears to hold in that place by right belonging to your Church.

Likewise, whatever Hugh son of Rayner gave to the aforesaid Church in Ampinana, Monte Acuto, Lece, Magnale, and Politiano, and one half of the church and court-estate at Quaracla. Moreover: the parish church of St Criscus situated at Albine; the parish church of St Gervasius with its court-estate, situated in [Col. 0212B] Alpiniano; the church of St Minias with its court-estate on Monte Lauro; the parish church of St John; the parish churches of St Babillus and St Ditalis; the parish church of St Leoninus; the parish church of St Mary; the parish church of St Stephen; at Pomino, the parish church of St Jerusalem; at Glaceto, the parish church of St Jerusalem; at Izermano, the parish church of St Gervasius with its court-estate; at Pitiana, the parish church of St Peter; at Cascia, the parish church of St Peter with its court-estate and the castle called Novum; at Sco, the parish church of St Mary with its court-estate; at Capiclia, the parish church of St John; the parish church of St Pancras; the parish church of St Romulus with its court-estate; the church of St Minias with its appurtenances; at Campinione, the church of St Mary with its court-estate; the parish church of St Vitus; at Regitino, the parish church of St Peter; the parish church of St Lawrence with its castle and court-estate; at Robiana, the parish church of St Minias; at Cintoria, the parish church of St Peter with its court-estate; the church of St Justus on [Col. 0212C] Monte Rantuli; at Sillano, the parish church of St Peter; at Novale, the parish church of St Criscus; at Panzano, the parish church of St Leoninus with its court-estate; the church of St Euphrosynus with its court-estate near the castle of Corbulus; the church of St Romulus with the court-estate of Novella; the parish church of St Mary with its court-estate; the church of St Cassian with its court-estate; at Avanano, the church of St Mary and St Peter; the parish church of St Justus with its court-estate; the parish church of St Paul with its court-estate; at Collina, the parish church of St Leoninus; at Monte Milliario, the parish church of St Mary; at Testinula, the parish church of St Martin with its court-estate; at Stagia, the parish church of St Mary.

Whatever your predecessors are known hitherto to have possessed within the parish of the Church of Fiesole or within the parishes of other Churches, we decree shall remain secure and inviolate to you. Therefore let no person presume rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, [Col. 0212D] or take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for your use and for the benefit of the clergy and the poor.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, and, having been warned a second and third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the injustice committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same Church [Col. 0213A] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Gerard, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Lictifred, priest-cardinal of the title of St Vitalis, have subscribed. I, Guido, unworthy priest, have subscribed. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. [Col. 0213B] I, Guido, cardinal of St Adrian, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Alberic, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December [16 November], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1134 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II, etc.

## CLXII. He informs G[regory], bishop of Bergamo, that he has summoned the canons of St Alexander, who had rejected the judges appointed by him, and the canons of St Vincent, for the forthcoming Ascension of the Lord (16 May 1135). (Year 1134, 30 November.)

[LUPUS, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomensis*, II, 985.]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G[REGORY], bishop of Bergamo, greeting [Col. 0213C] and apostolic blessing.

It grieves us that the canons of St Alexander, concerning the controversy being conducted between themselves and the canons of St Vincent, refused to submit to the judgment of our venerable brothers P., bishop of Pavia, and A., cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, to whom we had entrusted the settlement of that case. Nevertheless, because those appointed judges made no progress in the case, and because we do not wish to furnish either party with material for any pretext, we have summoned them to appear before us and have fixed for them the coming Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ as the date, forbidding each side, under peril to its order, to injure the other in goods or persons.

[Col. 0213D] Given at Pisa, on the second day before the Kalends of December [30 November].

## CLXIII. He thanks Diego, archbishop of Compostela, for gifts sent. (Year 1134.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 561.]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACO, archbishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because a dutiful son ought not to forget his mother when she is in need, we have not ceased to wonder why you delayed for so long in providing assistance to the holy Roman Church. Yet since we have learned that you were entangled in various occupations, we pardon, in apostolic gentleness, what was done not from will [Col. 0214A] but from necessity. For we believe that such is the warmth of your affection that, if time and means had been available to you, the Roman Church would assuredly lack nothing which your generosity would not supply.

Therefore, giving more earnest attention to the affection of your charity, we offer thanks for the gifts sent to us by your devotion. For, regarding your will rather than your means, and following in the footsteps of our predecessors, we love your person with true charity in Christ and desire to honour you. And if perhaps any persons should arise—for the world lies in wickedness, and men are perverse—who strive to oppose the honour of St James or your person, we are certainly prepared both to repel by apostolic authority what is hostile to you [Col. 0214B] and to cherish with paternal affection those who love the same shrine of St James. It is therefore your concern to persevere in the service and love of St Peter, and in all things to show yourself his devoted and humble son, so that you may increasingly deserve to be heard and honoured by the apostolic see in your needs.

Given at Pisa.

## CLXIV. To Rainald, archbishop of Reims; Hugh, archbishop of Rouen; Hugh, archbishop of Tours; and their suffragans—concerning the murder of Thomas, prior of St Victor. (Year 1134.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 450.]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0214C] brothers RAINALD, archbishop of Reims, HUGH, archbishop of Rouen, HUGH, archbishop of Tours, and to their suffragan bishops, greeting and apostolic blessing.

More serious crimes must be cleansed by the more bitter tears of grave penitence; and what is committed against sacred orders ought swiftly to be expiated by fitting punishments. For what place is safe, and what person can be assured of security, if clerics of God’s Church, devoted to heavenly service, are violently afflicted by abandoned men with injuries, seizure, or bodily torture—or, what is more detestable, punished with death and the shedding of sacred blood?

Therefore, against so God-hated and so accursed a crime, committed against our beloved sons Thomas, formerly prior [Col. 0214D] of St Victor, and Archembald, subdean of Orléans, let the canons rise up, setting aside slackness and taking on the strength of justice; let the laws be armed; and, if the matter requires it, let a novel crime be crushed by the considered sentence of a new synod. What was recently adjudged by your charity at Jotrum in this matter, we decree, by apostolic authority, to be confirmed.
