[Col. 0241C] We, whose special concern it is to cherish and foster places belonging to the right of the holy Roman Church, have judged that we should graciously assent to your wishes, through the intercession of our beloved son, the fourth Mangold, an illustrious man.

By the page of this present privilege, we decree by Apostolic authority that this monastery, offered to Blessed Peter by its founders themselves, shall remain for all time under the protection of the holy Roman Church; and that the monastic order, established there, as is known, in accordance with the Rule of St Benedict by our already-mentioned beloved predecessor, shall be observed there irrevocably, without diversity or change of sex. We also forbid the diocesan bishop to presume to claim anything for himself in that place, except consecrations of altars or churches, ordinations of monks or also of clerics, provided that he is willing to confer these freely and without exaction or corruption. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, in order to receive from him what pertains to spiritual matters.

[Col. 0241D] We also decree that burial in the place itself shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated, while the right of the mother church is nevertheless preserved.

We therefore decree that absolutely no one may remove from there a portion of the wood of the life-giving Cross believed to be kept in that place, in whose honour your monastery was founded; and that all things which our aforesaid predecessor Leo IX confirmed to that church, which you now possess canonically, or which you may hereafter, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of emperors or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means under the Lord’s provision, acquire, shall be [Col. 0242A] preserved firm and inviolate for you in perpetuity. As a token that your monastery belongs to the right of Blessed Peter, you shall annually pay one gold coin to us and our successors.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and rank; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgement for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgement let that person be subject to strict vengeance.

[Col. 0242B] But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Aymeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of [Col. 0242C] July, in the thirteenth indiction [read: fourteenth], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CXCII. By letter he confirms the judgement rendered in the controversy between the canons of St Alexander and St Vincent at Bergamo. (19 June 1135.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, IV, 453.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, provost, and the brethren of the Church of St Alexander at Bergamo, present and future, in perpetual memory.

The order of justice and reason counsels that, just as we are called Fathers in name, so we should also prove ourselves such in deed. And just as we must especially establish those things which make for the peace of Jerusalem, so likewise, whenever a dispute arises between most holy churches, it is necessary that it should not perhaps be prolonged indefinitely but instead come to rest, and that we should speedily settle it through judicial process.

[Col. 0242D] [Col. 0242D] With this object, while we were formerly in the regions of Lombardy, we often laboured with our brethren to quiet the discord known to be agitated between you and the canons of St Vincent. Among other matters concerning the chaplains of the churches of St Saviour, St Agatha, St John, St Grata, and St Vigilius; the penances of criminals; fealties; and certain other matters which you asserted belonged to your church, [Col. 0243A] you maintained that this custom had prevailed between you from ancient times: whenever the clergy of St Alexander met with those of St Vincent, either in the church of St Vincent or in other churches, for funerals of the dead or at solemnities, the provost was accustomed to hold the first seat on the left side of the choir.

You strove to claim this all the more insistently because you demonstrated by many authorities that your church had been an episcopal see in ancient times and had enjoyed this and various other prerogatives. Conversely, the canons of St Vincent replied that their church had anciently been the mother church, and freely declared that they owed no such duty to you or to your provost. If at any time the provost was seen to have held that same seat, this had proceeded from charity and favour rather than from obligation. What charity had customarily given, they said, ought not to be made compulsory.

After we and our brethren had long been wearied by these and similar disputes, we often wished to put an end to the controversy. Indeed, from each side we received oaths from the older and more mature persons, through whom we might learn the truth of the matter and decide the cause in due order. When therefore we had fully heard the case both through the allegations of the parties and through the oaths received, we postponed deciding it at that time, judging that within that interval such a dispute might be ended by agreement and the case could be more conveniently settled between you and them.

Finally, since the matter could not be ended by agreement either through the judges appointed by us or by others, and since both churches had been severely worn down both by the expenses frequently incurred and by the wars and dissensions arising from this occasion, we—whose special concern it is to provide beneficially for the peace of churches—summoned you, the bishop, and the canons of St Vincent to appear before us at a fixed time. Since, as we have said, the case was already more fully known to us, we promulgated this judgement between you and them:

[Col. 0243C] “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, by the counsel of my brother bishops and cardinals, command that whenever the canons of St Alexander meet with the canons of St Vincent at solemnities and funerals of the dead, whether in the church of St Vincent or elsewhere, the provost of St Alexander shall hold the first place on the left side of the choir. The chaplains of the churches of St Saviour, St Agatha, St John, St Grata, and St Vigilius shall come to the church of St Alexander for the principal masses on Sundays and chief feasts. Offenders from the parish of St Alexander shall receive penance in the presence of the provost or one of the priests of that church. Likewise, we decree that priests who swear fealty to Blessed Vincent shall also swear it to Blessed Alexander. We further command that one of the priests of St Alexander shall carry the reliquary. At the transfer of the church, two priests [Col. 0244A] of St Alexander shall carry the chest together with two priests of St Vincent. They shall assemble, according to customary practice, for the scrutinies, on Maundy Thursday, for baptism, and at other solemnities. When the canons of St Vincent come to the church of St Alexander, they shall be honourably received, both in the ringing of bells and in other matters, as custom requires, and they shall occupy the whole choir as they have been accustomed to do.”

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may henceforth disturb the Church of Blessed Alexander of Bergamo concerning this our constitution, infringe or alter it for any reason; rather, all these things shall be preserved whole for you in perpetuity, as they are known to have been established by the sanction of this present writing. If anyone, with rash [Col. 0244B] boldness, attempts to oppose this our constitution or decision, and, after a second or third warning, does not make suitable amends, let that person suffer the loss of the dignity of office and rank and be subject to excommunication. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Hubert, archbishop of the Church of Pisa, have subscribed. I, Transmundus, bishop of Signa [printed *Sign nus*], have subscribed. I, Theodwin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Guy, bishop of Tivoli, have subscribed. I, Rodulf, bishop of Orte, have subscribed. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, [Col. 0244C] have subscribed. I, Anselm, cardinal priest, have subscribed. I, Intifred, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, have subscribed. I, Luke, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Martin, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen, have subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy priest, have subscribed. I, Azo, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Odo, deacon cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of St Adrian, have subscribed. I, Boethius, deacon cardinal of St Vitus, have subscribed. [Col. 0244D] I, Vassallus, deacon cardinal of St Eustace, have subscribed. I, Ubald, deacon cardinal of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Grisogonus, deacon cardinal of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Aimeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CXCIII. Privilege for the monastery of Blessed Mary at Cagia. (20 June 1135.)

[DUPLESSIS, *History of Meaux*, II, p. 32.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ELIAS, abbot of the church of Blessed Mary of Cagia, [Col. 0245A] situated at Meaux, and to his successors canonically appointed there in accordance with the Rule of Blessed Augustine, in perpetuity, etc. …

We confirm to you all that has been conferred by authentic privileges of our predecessors or by writings of princes or of any bishops, and all that you may hereafter, by God’s generosity, justly and canonically acquire. Among these we have thought fit to record the following by their proper names: namely, the church of Blessed Mary of Cagia itself … and the priesthood of that church, with all things belonging to the priesthood, for which you pay sixty solidi annually to the canons of St Stephen, until, by God’s favour, they receive from you an equivalent value; likewise, the annual revenues of all prebends of the church of St Stephen, however the persons of the canons may change; and the prebend of the priest Isembard at St Stephen, for which your church must provide the service of one priest for one week at the church of St Stephen.

[Col. 0245B] I also confirm to you the choir-service of St Stephen, called the Chaplaincy; likewise the altar of Ulcorra and the church of Cloia, with everything belonging to it, while the episcopal right is preserved; also the tithes possessed by Simon, son of Atto, at Pressi and in the village called Pinus; etc. … likewise, the site of the hermit Gilinus, which our venerable brother Manasses, bishop of Meaux, with the counsel of Theobald, archdeacon of Meaux, granted to you and your church, after the death of that same Gilinus, to hold in perpetuity; etc. …

[Col. 0245C] Therefore no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the complete benefit of the uses for which they were granted, namely, the governance and support of those concerned. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and rank; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgement for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last [Col. 0245D] judgement let that person be subject to strict vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Aimeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent II.

CXCIV. Privilege for the church of St John at Monza. (25 June 1135.)

[FRISI, *Historical Memoirs of Monza*, II, 50.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0246A] son in Christ WILLIAM, archbishop of Monza, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Just as no effect ought to be granted to those who demand what is unjust, so the petition of those who desire what is lawful ought not to be delayed. Therefore, beloved son Archbishop William, we receive under the protection of the apostolic see the church of Saint John the Baptist, over which, by God’s providence, you are known to preside, and we fortify it, together with all that belongs to it, by the patronage of Saint Peter. For that place, built by Queen Theodelinda of noble memory and endowed with extensive honours, possessions, and treasure, is held worthy of veneration and renowned.

Therefore, by the authority of this present privilege, we decree that whatever goods and whatever possessions it presently holds, or may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors. Among these, the following seemed fit to be expressly named: namely, the monastery of Saint Peter of Cremella, with the church of Saint Sisinnius; the churches of Saint John of Bulciaco, Saint George of Colciaco, and Saint John of Castromartis; at Uellate, the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Fidelis; the church of Saint Julian of the parish of Colonia, with its chapels; the church of Saint Eusebius; in Sesto, the churches of Saint Alexander, Saint Michael, and Saint Saviour; the churches of Saint Martin, Saint Peter, Saint Michael, Saint Saviour, Saint Agatha, Saint Donatus, Saint Maurice, Saint George, and the churches of Saint Alexander and Saint Eugenius of Concoretio.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, have licence rashly to disturb your church, to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Certainly, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors those feudal benefices which the venerable brother Jordan, Archbishop of Milan, granted to your church in the aforesaid churches for the common support of the brethren, decreeing that no person whatsoever may henceforth remove, withdraw, or alter them in any way from the common benefit of the brethren. Furthermore, we establish by apostolic authority whatever has been lawfully granted to you by emperors, and likewise strengthen for you the rights and reasonable customs which you possess in the aforesaid church of Saint Peter of Cremella.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person forfeit the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the just rights of this church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, unworthy priest, have subscribed.  
I, Luke, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

[Col. 0247B] Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

## CXCV. Bull confirming the possessions of the monastery of Quadraginta. (Year 1135, 7 November.)

*[Gallia Christiana*, VI, Instrumenta 36.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Rikinus, abbot of the church of Quadraginta, and to his successors regularly appointed, etc.

Accordingly, beloved son in Christ, we graciously grant your petitions and receive under the protection of Saint Peter and of ourselves the church of Quadraginta, over which, by God’s providence, you are known to preside. First, indeed, decreeing that in that church the canonical order according to the Rule of Saint Augustine shall be inviolably observed in times to come, we confirm to you and your successors whatever goods and whatever possessions that church lawfully possesses, by grants of pontiffs and gifts of princes. If, therefore, anyone hereafter, etc.

Innocent II, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
Gerard, cardinal priest of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
Luke, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul.  
Matthew, bishop of Albano, etc.

Given through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 0247D] on the seventh [otherwise, the day before] the Ides of November [7 or 12 November], thirteenth indiction, year of the Incarnation 1136, sixth year of the pontificate.

## CXCVI. He grants Albero, bishop-elect of Liège, the use of the rational. (Year 1135, 29 November.)

*[CHAPEAUVILLE, Acts of the Bishops of Tongeren*, II, 99.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALBERO, bishop-elect of Liège: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Charity, the mistress of all good things, tastes nothing harsh and nothing alien; for its proper good is to show, by the advancement of others and by other evidences, its own loving affection toward neighbours. Although this virtue ought to shine forth in all the faithful, it is known to belong especially and above all to the most holy Roman Church. And just as that same universal and loving mother raises her sons to high rank and appoints some patriarchs, others archbishops, and others bishops, so too, clothed in the splendour of diversity, from the abundance of divine gifts granted to her by God, she mercifully adorns them with the beauty of various insignia.

Since, therefore, venerable brother Albero, bishop-elect of the holy Church of Liège, we believe that your person will be useful, we have judged that you should be honoured by the kindness of the apostolic see and more intimately cherished beneath the gracious bosom of Saint Peter. And since we trust that, like Aaron, you have been called by divine grace to the summit of episcopal dignity, and that, in Moses’ place, you have been established by God’s providence to govern the Christian people, we also make you a participant in their dignity. After you have been consecrated bishop, we grant to your person the use of the rational, decreeing that you may use this sacred ornament within the church only on the days set forth in this document: namely, on the Lord’s Supper, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, the feast of Saint John, the solemnities of the apostles Peter and Paul, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, the feast of Blessed Lambert, All Saints, the Nativity of the Lord, its octave, Epiphany, the Purification of Blessed Mary, dedications of churches within your diocese, ordinations of clerics, and the anniversary day of the dedication of the church of Liège.

Act, then, dearest brother, so that what you wear outwardly in the sight of the Church you may possess inwardly, and so that the effect of your deeds may attest the distinction of so sacred a gift.

Given at Pisa, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November].

## CXCVII. Privilege for the canonry of Saints Peter and Ursus of Aosta. (Year 1135, 30 November.)

*[Monuments of the History of the Fatherland, Charters*, I, p. 776, from the original archive of the Collegiate Church of Saint Ursus of Aosta.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ARNALD, prior, and to the brethren professing the canonical life in the church of Saints Peter and Ursus at Aosta, both present and future, forever.

[Col. 0248D] The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all goods, so that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to spread the religious life pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptably to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved by the purity of religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your reasonable petitions and fortify with the privilege of the apostolic see the church of Saints Peter and Ursus, in which you devote yourselves to divine service. We decree that all things which you now possess justly and canonically, or may in future acquire, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, shall be preserved whole and unimpaired forever to that church.

We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that, without prejudice to the right of the mother church, no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Upon the death of you, the present prior of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Augustine.

We therefore decree that neither the mother church nor any person whatsoever may rashly disturb your church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, demand from you anything beyond what was established of old, or harass you with any troubles whatsoever. Rather, let all things be kept whole for your benefit, to serve the needs of those for whose governance and support they were granted; saving, nevertheless, the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of this church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of December [30 November], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## CXCVIII. To Didacus, Archbishop of Compostela. (Year 1135, 27 December.)

*[FLOREZ, Sacred Spain*, XX, 566.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, Archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your belovedness know that we love your person with brotherly charity and are willing graciously to grant assent to your petitions, with due regard for the honour of the Church. But you should know that, just as the apostolic see does not seek to take away from other churches their rights, so it ought not to lose those rights that are its own. Since, therefore, the sacred canons provide that each suffragan is to be consecrated by his own metropolitan, it is recognized as equitable that this be maintained in due order in the case of the bishop-elect of León. This is especially so because our brother R., Archbishop of Toledo, was suspended from episcopal office because he presumed to consecrate Arias, bishop of León, without the mandate of the Holy Roman Church, of which he was a suffragan; and the man thus consecrated, for the same offence, surrendered the bishopric into our hands by means of the episcopal insignia.

Let your brotherhood therefore bear it patiently if, amid difficulties of this kind, we are unwilling to furnish grounds for diminishing the right of Saint Peter. Moreover, let your kindness keep our son P. Fulco, chaplain of your church, most earnestly commended to you. He has often laboured in the Roman Church for your honour and service and has proved very faithful and devoted to you. We presently wish this proof to be made in the following way: namely, that you cause those revenues of his chaplaincy which the brethren have diminished for him to be restored to him without further delay by equitable compensation, as you and they are said to have promised him. For the benefits which you have conferred upon him, we return thanks to your devotion, and we likewise ask that you bring the benevolence begun toward him to a happy and better conclusion.

Given at Pisa, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January [27 December].

## CXCIX. He confirms to William, Archbishop of Canterbury, and to the Church of Canterbury the church of Saint Martin at Dover, granted by Henry, King of the English. (Year 1130–1136.)

*[Monasticon Anglicanum*, II, 4.]

INNOCENT, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, Archbishop of Canterbury, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

A desire shown to concern the religious purpose and the salvation of souls must be fulfilled without delay; and whenever that which is known to accord with reason is sought from us, it is fitting for us willingly to grant it and to lend suitable support to the vows of those who make just requests. Therefore, brother William, Archbishop of Canterbury, in accordance with the customary kindness of the apostolic see, we graciously grant your reasonable petitions. We confirm forever to you and to the Church of Canterbury—and through you to your successors—the church of Blessed Martin of Dover, granted and very fittingly confirmed to you and to the Church of Canterbury by our dearest son Henry, illustrious and glorious King of the English, together with all that it now justly and lawfully possesses or may hereafter reasonably acquire by the generosity of kings, the gifts of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means.

Accordingly, granting the prayers of our aforesaid son King Henry, we decree that the order of canons according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be established in the aforesaid church of Blessed Martin and inviolably preserved in times to come. Moreover, an abbot who may benefit and preside over the brethren shall be established there in accordance with the same Rule.

If anyone should therefore rashly attempt to oppose this our decree, let him incur the peril of his honour and office and be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction. But those who observe it shall obtain from the Father of mercies and God of all consolation an everlasting crown and the desirable favour of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

## CC. To Adalbero, Archbishop of Trier.—Against the abbot of Saint Maximin; if the accusations against him are true, he judges that he is to be deposed. (Year 1133–1136, 20 January.)

*[HONTHEIM, Diplomatic History of Trier*, I, 524.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ADALBERO, Archbishop of Trier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that your brotherhood is unaware that Gerard, abbot of Saint Maximin, was recently accused before us by certain brethren of his monastery of simony and of wasting ecclesiastical goods. For this reason, we summoned him to appear before us on the next Sunday on which *Misericordia Domini* is sung, prepared to answer and make satisfaction concerning these charges. But he, raging in a spirit of pride, not only despised our letter, but also, as we have learned, deprived of their offices those of his brethren who had come before us on this matter, subjected others to various injuries and assaults, and deprived them of their own benefices according to his will.

If this is true, we remove him from the governance of the abbey; and we command that both the bearer of this letter and the others whom he is said to have deprived be restored and reinstated in full to office and benefice. We enjoin your brotherhood firmly to observe and carry this sentence into effect until he comes into our presence and makes satisfaction for his contempt and the charges brought against him.

Given at Pisa, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January].

## CC bis. Privilege for the monastery of Liesborn. (Year 1132–1143.)

*[NIESERT, Münster Charters*, etc., vol. IV, p. 106, from a fifteenth-century cartulary of Liesborn.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BALDWIN, abbot of Liesborn, and to his successors regularly promoted, forever.

The care of venerable places admonishes us diligently to consider their peace and welfare, so that those who serve in ecclesiastical duties may likewise be cherished under the desired protection of ecclesiastical guardianship. Moreover, just as we wish what we establish to remain firm, so it is fitting that we strengthen by apostolic authority what has been reasonably done by brethren.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Baldwin, granting your desires, we have confirmed by the page of this present document what was done by our brother of good memory Egbert, Bishop of Münster, concerning the church situated in the place called Liesborn, on account of the immoral life of certain nuns who had formerly lived there disgracefully; this was done by the counsel and authority of our predecessor Pope Honorius of holy memory and was confirmed by our brother Werner, Egbert’s successor. We decree that monks of upright life shall henceforth serve there according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict; and that the provisions established by our said brother shall remain forever firm and unimpaired: both those concerning the free and canonical election of the abbot of that place, to be conducted according to the fear of God and the monastic Order, and those concerning the twenty tithes—namely, twenty solidi in Münster coin—to be paid annually to the same monastery within the parish of Disteden, in the places Dullen and Beldinchusen.

Let no person, therefore, presume rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery in this respect or inflict any trouble upon it on that account; rather, let all things, as stated above, be preserved uninjured for you and your successors. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him incur the peril of his power and honour and be subject to excommunication. But those who preserve for that place what is its own shall obtain the grace of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Pisa, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September].

A seal is appended in lead, suspended by silk threads.

## CCI. To Gerard, Abbot of Saint Maximin.—He charges him with simony and dissipation. (Year 1133–1136, 30 October.)

*[HONTHEIM, ibid.*, p. 523.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GERARD, Abbot of Saint Maximin: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as reports of good deeds done by sons gladden us, so adverse reports likewise grieve us. For the bearers of this letter, the priest Henry and Egelolf, coming into our presence, accused you of the Simoniacal heresy. They further alleged that you have stripped the monastery of Blessed Maximin—which was rich in temporal treasures and its ornaments—disregarding the fear and reverence of God, and have reduced it almost to nothing. Since we can neither may nor ought to pass over these matters without examination or punishment, by the authority of this letter we command and order you to present yourself before us, all excuse and evasion set aside, on the next Sunday on which *Misericordia Domini* is sung, prepared to give a sufficient answer concerning all these matters and any others that may be charged against you.

Meanwhile, we forbid and in every way prohibit you from selling or pawning the goods of the monastery, or inflicting any opposition or molestation upon the aforesaid persons or their companions.

Given at Pisa, on the third day before the Kalends of November [30 October].

> **Note:** [Col. 0253D] Novillanius says the following of this Gerard in the *Chronicle of Saint Maximin*: “He presided about the year of the Lord 1135, in the time of Pope Innocent II. He was a Simoniac and a squanderer of the resources of our monastery; he governed most wretchedly, and sold or pawned all valuable things. Therefore his brethren accused him before Pope Innocent II; summoned by the pope, he did not appear. Moreover, he subjected the brethren who accused him to various calamities and injuries. When the pope learned of this, he removed him from the abbacy and appointed the bishop of Trier, namely Adalbero, as executor of the sentence.” Add Innocent II’s letter of 20 January of the following year.

## CCII. To certain abbots.—He commends their assemblies for strengthening the discipline of the Order. (Year 1133–1136, 17 November.)

*[MANSI, Councils*, XXI, 430, from vol. I of Martène’s* Anecdota*.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons: II, of Rebais; R., of Lagny; S., of Chézy; II, of Saint-Theodoric; A., of Saint-Amand; Jo., of Aulnoy; W., of Lessies; SE., of Lobbes; PA., of the Holy Sepulchre of Cambrai; S., of Saint-Lucian of Beauvais; S., of Saint-Éloi of Noyon; B., of Saint-Nicholas of the Wood; assembled together in the name of the Lord; and to the other abbots gathered in the same spirit: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the evangelical teaching testifies that where two or three are gathered in my name, he himself is in their midst. There is added also what the Psalmist sang: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity; it is like ointment upon the head, which runs down upon the beard, Aaron’s beard.” Therefore, we rejoice concerning you in the Lord and are filled with due exultation, because, as disciples of Blessed Benedict, you adhere to the observances of monastic discipline and, desiring daily to advance therein, strive more and more to please almighty God.

> **Note:** [Col. 0253D–0254D] The abbots of the province of Reims mention this approval in their letter to Pope Adrian IV among the letters of Saint Bernard, in these words: “Confirm by your apostolic blessing our association, which Pope Innocent of blessed memory confirmed by a privilege of apostolic authority.” From this Mabillon concludes that the origin of the general chapters of the Order of Saint Benedict should be referred to Pope Innocent. Yet I find that general chapters were held at Marmoutier in the time of Abbot Alberic, about two hundred years before this letter. But only superiors subject to Marmoutier attended those chapters. —Martène.

This indeed pleases us, and we confirm it by apostolic authority: namely, that you have decreed to hold an assembly jointly every year in one of your monasteries. It is also our desire that the ointment of sweetness which descends from the head upon the beard may fill the inner chambers of your hearts and grant you, in the sacred assembly, ability both to speak and to carry out what is right. Nor is there any doubt that in this very matter you will show yourselves imitators of those of whom we read that in the primitive Church they were of one heart and one soul.

Accordingly, whatever your discernment shall establish by your common decree concerning the preservation of the monastic order and the correction of brethren according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict and the rules of the other holy Fathers, we shall, with the Lord as author, hold as ratified. We add that no brother of yours, after making profession in his own monastery, may dare to flee to another place without the permission of his superior and the other brethren; nor may anyone receive or retain him. Finally, offering to your whole body the expression of due greeting and apostolic blessing, we exhort you in the Lord: love the brotherhood, and preserve inviolably among yourselves mutual charity for the honour of God. May almighty God, by his inspiration, go before your actions and mercifully pursue them by his aid. Amen.

Given at Pisa, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December [17 November].

## CCIII. To Bishop B[ernard] of Hildesheim and his successors, forbidding them to alienate Winceburg Castle. (Year 1133–1136, 25 November.)

*[Origins of the Guelphs*, p. 448.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B[ERNARD], Bishop of Hildesheim: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as the Church ought not, from a zeal for rapacity, to usurp the property of others, so it ought not lose its own possessions through anyone’s negligence or favour; nor can there be any doubt that what has once become subject to divine law can by no means be transferred to other uses. Therefore, by apostolic authority we decree and, under anathema, prohibit that you or your successors should have any licence to enfeoff or alienate Wintzenborc Castle from the hand or lordship of the Bishop of Hildesheim. We add further that whoever should presume violently to occupy that castle to the damage of the same church shall remain subject to excommunication until satisfaction is made.

Love and honour our beloved son Tideric, provost of the aforesaid church, so for our reverence; hold him so dear, even dearer than the dear, that he may feel that our prayers on his behalf have profited him with you, and that we may owe thanks to your devotion on his account.

Given at Pisa, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December [25 November].

## CCIV. To Margrave L[eopold], he announces that, having learned from Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg, of Leopold’s devotion, he has received under protection the church of Blessed Augustine. He adds greetings to his wife A[gnes], to Margrave A[dalbert], and to his other sons. (Year 1134–1136, 30 March.)

*[FISCHER, Merkwurd Schnicks v. Klosternenburg* [German title as printed; uncertain], II, 119.]

## CCV. To Albero, Archbishop of Trier.—He commits to him for decision the delayed case of the abbot of Saint Maximin. (Year 1134–1136, 10 April.)

*[MARTÈNE,* Great Collection, I, 723.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother A., Archbishop of Trier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As your brotherhood knows, G., abbot of Saint Maximin, was some time ago accused in our presence of simony and of dispersing ecclesiastical goods. Therefore, on the past Sunday on which *Misericordia Domini* is sung, we summoned him to appear before us to answer the charges made against him. But, because imperial intercessions afterwards intervened, we judged that the case should be postponed until the time of the expedition. Nevertheless, on the appointed date the opposing party appeared before us, ready canonically to prove what it had charged against the aforesaid abbot.

Thus, sparing their labours and expenses through paternal provision, we have committed the same case to your brotherhood for determination. We command your discretion, therefore, to decide the aforesaid matter by a canonical judgment before the time of the expedition. If this cannot be done in the meantime, let the case be reserved for our judgment. But first of all, setting aside delay and sluggishness, restore Godfrey, Henry, Giselbert, Eilolf, Ludewic, Frederick, and Hugh fully to their offices and benefices; diligently ensure that they enjoy peace and quiet in the monastery of Saint Maximin; and labour with utmost zeal for the recovery of the ecclesiastical goods that have been dispersed.

Given at Pisa, on the fourth day before the Ides of April [10 April].

## CCVI. To the clergy and chapter of Saint Deodatus in the valley of Galilee. (Year 1134–1136, 22 April.)

*[Dom CALMET,* History of Lorraine, II, Preface, p. CCCII.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and chapter belonging to the church of Saint Deodatus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0255D] Just as, according to the sanctions of the canons, the life and conduct of clerics and holy laypersons ought to be separate, so likewise ecclesiastical judgments ought properly to be exercised by ecclesiastical persons. Therefore, we command and order your whole body that, if any ecclesiastical cases arise in your place, they shall be decided according to the statutes of the canons and concluded in canonical order, without regard to fear of any secular power. We also forbid and in every way prohibit that benefices and parish churches among you be claimed by anyone through hereditary right or occupied by secular power.

Given at Pisa, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April].

## CCVII. To Guigo, Prior of the Carthusians.—He announces that Saint Hugh of Grenoble has been enrolled among the saints and urges him to write his life. (Year 1134–1136, 22 April.)

*[MANSI, Councils*, XXI, 417.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUIGO, Prior of the Carthusians: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In response to divine benefits, having learned of his life and heard of the miracles performed through the merits of Blessed Hugh, we praised the mercy of the heavenly Majesty. Having taken counsel with the archbishops, bishops, cardinals, and others who were present with us, we ordered that he be honoured among the saints and elect, and that the day of his assumption be solemnly celebrated with joy.

Since, therefore, the life which he led piously in the body and the splendour of miracles by which God makes him shine forth among men are especially well known to your belovedness, we command you by the authority of Saint Peter and our own diligently to write down and transmit to posterity whatever is known to you concerning this matter. Thus God may be honoured in his saint, and clergy reading and people hearing may give thanks to the Lord and deserve, through his intercession, to receive forgiveness of sins. Through you, we greet and bless in the Lord our beloved sons, the Carthusian brethren, who pray for us.

Given at Pisa, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April].

## CCVIII. He receives the monastery of Ahus under protection. (Year 1134–1136, 3 May.)

*[LANG, Regesta*, I, 141.]

## CCIX. He commands A[lbero], Archbishop of Trier, to compel Brunicus and his sons to restore the estate of Filestanges to the monastery of Remiremont. (Year 1134–1136, 7 June.)

*[JAFFÉ, Registers of the Roman Pontiffs*, with this notice: “In the archive at Koblenz. From Pertz’s papers.”]

## CCX. Privilege for the monastery of Ripoll. (Year 1134–1136, 11 June.)

*[MARCA,* Marca Hispanica, appendix, p. 1277.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers O., Archbishop of Tarragona, and the Bishops of Urgell, Vic, Girona, and Elne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The monastery of Ripoll belongs by special right to Saint Peter and is subject to the defence of the Roman Church. Whoever, therefore, loves Saint Peter ought to defend monasteries that belong to his right against the assaults of evil men. Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to maintain the monastery of Ripoll, together with all its possessions and goods; and if any of your parishioners should attempt to harass that place or anything belonging to it, you shall administer canonical justice against him. If you neglect to administer justice against evildoers, you will incur the peril of your rank and office.

Given at Pisa, on the third day before the Ides of June [11 June].

## CCXI. To John, Prior, and the Brethren of Saint Mary in Porto. (Year 1134–1136, 22 June.)

*[UGHELLI,* Sacred Italy, V, 1237.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, prior, and the brethren of Saint Mary in Porto: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our son Marcus Julianus of Venice, from the time of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of good memory, made a vow to build a church in honour of Blessed Mary and to establish regular canons there; the governance of this foundation has been granted to you. But, delaying the fulfilment of his vow, you have not yet begun to govern it. Therefore, lest his undertaking be frustrated, we command you, if it seems expedient, to assume without delay the governance of the aforesaid place; or else freely to relinquish it, so that he may establish other canons there.

Given at Pisa, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July [22 June].

## CCXII. To the clergy of Modena.—He announces that the consuls of Modena have been excommunicated for harassing the monastery of Nonantola. (Year 1134–1136, 24 June.)

*[TIRABOSCHI,* History of the Abbey of Nonantola, vol. II, p. 245.]

[Col. 0257C] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable son B. and beloved sons F., provost, and the clergy of Modena: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your belovedness is not unaware how great evils the people of Modena have inflicted upon the monastery of Nonantola, which belongs to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter. Therefore, by frequent letters we warned the consuls to desist from injuring the aforesaid monastery and to come into our presence to make satisfaction. But they neither desisted from their wrong nor came to us, though summoned so often. Accordingly, after taking counsel with our brethren the bishops and cardinals, we pronounced upon them a sentence of excommunication. Therefore, by these present letters, we command and enjoin upon all of you that [Col. 0257D] you wholly avoid the aforesaid consuls as excommunicated persons and, publicly proclaiming the same sentence throughout the diocese of Modena, cause your parishioners in every way to abstain from them. But if perhaps the aforesaid consuls persist in their obstinacy and do not desist from harassing the said monastery, by the Lord’s authority we shall pronounce a sentence of anathema upon your entire city.

Given at Pisa, 24 June.

CCXIII. To the abbot and monks of Bec. (1134–1136, 7 August.)

[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 421.]

[Col. 0258A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons L., abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Bec: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning those things which are reported to us about your religious devotion and uprightness, we praise almighty God and greatly rejoice in your devotion. It is fitting, therefore, that, the more perilous the times known to be impending, the more earnestly you implore the mercy of the divine Majesty, that He may deign to grant peace to His Church, wearied by long afflictions, and to relieve the faithful and Catholic people from their troubles [Col. 0258B]. For we do not doubt that Christ, sleeping in the ship, will swiftly be awakened by the voices of yourselves and other religious persons, and that after storms and tempests great calm will follow. Know, moreover, that we love your monastery and community with paternal affection, and that, in whatever matters it may be necessary, we wish to support you in accordance with the office committed to us. For the book sent to us by your devotion, we return manifold thanks to you.

Given at Pisa, 7 August.

CCXIV. To Berthold, abbot of St Blaise.—Concerning the maintenance of peace with the monks of Schaffhausen. (1134–1136, 8 August.)

[GERBERT, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. III, p. 67.]

[Col. 0258C] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERTHOLD, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of St Blaise: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those who dwell in the house of the Lord ought to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Therefore, since by divine grace inspiring you, you have rejected worldly desires and professed the monastic life according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, it is fitting that you attend more diligently to your purpose and take care to please almighty God in word and deed. Thus the body of the faithful may be formed for the better by your example and good conduct, and your devotion may deserve, in return for temporal labours, to acquire eternal life.

Moreover, we have received our beloved son Ricc., your brother, with paternal kindness; and concerning the controversy which is being conducted between [Col. 0258D] you and the monks of Schaffhausen, we have judged it proper to write to you as follows: by the Lord’s favour, we shall shortly send our legate into your regions. Having heard the arguments of both parties, he will take care, as justice dictates, to impose a due end upon that dispute. May divine grace, for which you pray for us, preserve you unharmed and render you acceptable in His service.

[Note: What this controversy of the Blasians with the monastery of St Salvator at Schaffhausen was, or how it was settled, the local records do not disclose. It nevertheless appears to have concerned Mount Stouphen; Conrad III, emperor, settled it by a diploma issued in 1150, printed in P. Hergott, vol. II, pt. I, p. 174, by which he adjudges that mountain to St Blaise.]

Given at Pisa, 8 August.

[Note: Innocent II held a council at Pisa on 30 May 1134, at which this bull was issued.]

CCXV. Privilege for the monastery of Hilsenburg. (1136, 2 January.)

[*Neue Mittheilungen aus dem Gebiet historisch-antiquarischer Forschungen*, vol. II, p. 296.]

[Col. 0259A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LAMBERT, abbot of Hilsinneburg, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, in order that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptably to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion [Col. 0259B]. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Lambert, we graciously admit your petitions and strengthen, by the privilege of the apostolic see, the monastery of Hilsinneburg over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever goods and possessions the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s assistance, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have appended the following, to be named expressly: from the gift of Arnold, bishop of Halberstadt of good memory, founder of your monastery: at Berverdiggerode [Col. 0259C], nine *mansi*, with the adjoining wood and the tithe of the same village; at Sutherrode, two *mansi*; at Suthseauno, seven and a half *mansi*, with the tithe of that village; at Bireslevo, eleven *mansi* with the tithe of that village; at Lieren, one *mansus*; at Thiedeziggerode [Thiedorz], seven *mansi* and tithes [“tithes of the same place”]; at Aldenrode, eight *mansi*; at Culisberi [Culesberi], half a *mansus* and the tithes of that place [“and tithes of that place” is absent]; at Geveneslevo [Geveneslove], half a *mansus*; at Beddigge, ten *mansi*; at Isiggerode, three *mansi*; at Warmeresthorpe [Warmerestorphe], six *mansi*; at Thiedesthorpe [Thiedestorphe], two *mansi*; likewise, tithes at Dudiggerode, [Col. 0259D] Winetherode, Brodessende, Luntheriggerode [Lutherigg], Boviggerode, Emmenrode, Geschenrode, Ecarzinggerode [Ecarzigg], Bachenrode, Benesiggerode [Bensigg], and Waliggerode.

Further, the estates which Bishop Burchard, of good memory, is known to have bestowed upon the blessed apostles Peter and Paul at Hilsineburch: namely, at Aderstade, an estate with all its appurtenances; at Aeherslevo [Asch], twelve *mansi*; at Merigge, ten *mansi*; at Domeneslevo, one *mansus*; at Badeslevo, five *mansi*; at Scipenstide [Schipenstede], eight *mansi*; at Bisikentorp [Bisichentorpe], two *mansi*; at Aneslevo, four *mansi*; at Ramereslevo [Ratmersleve], five *mansi*; at Iggelevo, eight *mansi*, with the tithe of the same village; at Abbenrode [Albenrode] [Col. 0260A], fifteen and a half *mansi*; at Bethcenesheim [Bechtenesheim], three *mansi*; at Anderbike, one *mansus*; likewise, tithes at Bareslevo [Balerslene], Roresheim, Thrubiki [Biche], Aldenrode, Thurwardiggerode, Gunderaderode [Gundraderode], Ezerdiggerode, and Vreslevo.

Moreover, the tithes at Daunenstade and Suthlochtenheim, granted to your monastery by Herrand [Bernhard], formerly bishop of Halberstadt, who was also called Stephen. Also tithes from newly cultivated lands in all places where you appear to hold tithes, which Bishop Reinhard, of blessed memory, bestowed upon your monastery [see there]. Also, the estates at Papestorpe and Wochkinstide, paying a rent of eight talents [Col. 0260B], which Bishop Otto bestowed upon your monastery in exchange for Godenhusen and Abrstide.

We prohibit and in every way forbid that it be lawful for you or your successors to dispose of, or in any manner alienate without the common assent and will of the chapter, the goods or possessions of the aforesaid monastery. Moreover, in order that you, our brethren, may be able more freely to devote yourselves to divine service, we likewise confirm to you the immunity reasonably granted to your monastery by our aforesaid brother Bishop Burchard: namely, that you shall never suffer any prejudice, burden, or exaction from the bishops of Halberstadt, from any clerics, or from secular persons, except insofar as you may freely choose to grant something to them for the sake of hospitality.

Upon the death of the present abbot of that place, yourself, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over the monastery by any contrivance of fraud or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common assent or by the sounder part of their counsel, shall determine, according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, to be elected. The person elected, according to the Cluniac, Fructuarian, or Gorze order, shall be consecrated without corruption or any exaction. Meanwhile, in recording, providing for, or administering the affairs of the monastery, the bishop shall in no way interfere, but shall merely invest the elected person with the charge of government by the fitting solemnity of blessing [Col. 0260C].

Especially in consideration of the merit of your praiseworthy integrity and good conduct, for the honour of God and of your Church, by apostolic authority we grant to you and your successors the use of pontifical vestments. Thus, for the reverence of divine worship, in every church, by confirmation of our dispensation, you may take the place of your bishop and act pontifically.

Let no person, therefore, rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things remain intact for the benefit of the uses for which they were granted, namely the governance and support of those concerned—saving, of course, the due reverence owed to the Church of Halberstadt. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution [Col. 0261A], shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve for that place what is its own, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St Adrian, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0261B] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aymericus, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 2 January, the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCXVI. To Fromund, abbot of Vendôme.—Concerning the agreement made between Bishop Ulger of Angers and the monks of Vendôme. (1136, 12 January.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 386, from the archives of the monastery of Vendôme.]

[Col. 0261C]

INNOCENT, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son FROMUND, abbot of Vendôme, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Among our various concerns and manifold anxieties, the one that presses upon us most is when a controversy arises between religious persons concerning spiritual or temporal goods. Every effort must therefore be made that quarrels may not increase, but that, in accordance with charity—the mistress of all good things, which savours nothing alien, harsh, or confused, but by its own equity nourishes concord and joins those who are divided—peace and unanimity may be preserved among the servants of the Lord, who ought not to quarrel [Col. 0261D]. For it is right that those led by the Spirit of God should not be divided by any partition of minds or contrary will, lest discord take its beginning where the bonds of peace ought to receive increase.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Fromund, we have judged that the controversy hitherto conducted between you and our venerable brother Ulger, bishop of Angers, concerning churches, offerings, and other matters, should be brought to an end by agreement, in accordance with the arbitration of our brethren and with the consent both of yourself and of our aforesaid brother. You claimed for the monastery of Vendôme certain dues in certain churches of the diocese of Angers, which our same brother called *gyndragia*; in our presence you renounced both these dues and the offerings of baptismal churches [Col. 0262A]. Thereupon the aforesaid bishop renounced every controversy which he had had against you and the monastery of Vendôme concerning the borough of Briolet and other matters.

He has therefore granted to you in perpetuity, to be held freely, the aforesaid borough and whatever you possessed before the promotion of the same bishop, or before the complaint raised by him, in the church of St Clement with its appurtenances and in the other places written below, as well as whatever you may hereafter justly acquire. We have thought it proper to name these expressly: the church of Atheis; the church of Capella; the church of Cella; the church of St Saturninus; the church of Congreto; the church of Beluli Campus; the church of Pomerolis; the church of Laignio; the church of Avireo; the church [Col. 0262B] of Jallia; the churches of Meduanuillo; the church of St Saturninus on the Loire; the chapel of Braccosacco; the church of St Peter of Maziac; the church of St Medard of Caveriac; the church of St Mary of Broc; the church of St Mary of Castellis; the church of St Symphorian of Porcellis; the church of St Mary of Cosma; the church of St Peter of Villeriis; the church of St Hippolytus; and the church of St German of Arethio.

He has also granted to you and your successors, as you have hitherto held them, the offerings of churchings, weddings, and others, for love of us and affectionate reverence for the holy Roman Church, to whose right and lordship the monastery of Vendôme belongs. Nevertheless, with respect to the tithe of the borough of Briolet, which is known to belong to the chapel of St Maurice [Col. 0262C], you shall provide one *arpent* of vineyards, according to the judgment of good men, for Master Guido the chaplain to hold and enjoy only during his lifetime, and for his successor, one half. You have granted, for love of the same bishop, the income from offerings and first-fruits from Cella to the priest of that place, who is said to be worn out by old age, to hold and retain during his lifetime; that is, he shall receive it from you and acknowledge that he holds it from you. After his death, both the offerings and first-fruits shall freely return to the right and lordship of the monastery of Vendôme.

But if, pressed by the hardship of mortality, the same priest should die before the bishop’s return, the aforesaid bishop, while he lives, shall hold the said income, which after his death shall return to the monastery of Vendôme [Col. 0262D]. Meanwhile, as a token of your right, on five feast days each year you shall receive one candle from the offerings.

Whatever churches or ecclesiastical benefices in the diocese of Angers may be bestowed upon you or your successors for the use of the monastery of Vendôme—excepting abbeys, canonries, and those churches in which the bishop or the canons of St Maurice have all or a named part—are granted by the same bishop to you and your successors, and through us to the monastery of Vendôme. Likewise, the bishop and canons of St Maurice shall not further attempt to acquire churches in which the monastery of Vendôme has all or a part.

Concerning the church of St Nicholas of Craon, it is decreed that the number of prebends and canons shall be reduced to six. You and your successors shall freely give two distinct prebends out of the six, in perpetuity, to two reputable men and their successors. After receiving their benefice from you, they must be presented to the bishop of Angers, free from every vexation of exaction [Col. 0263A]. Upon the death of one or both of them, none of those prebends shall be held in your hand through bad intent; but without futile delay it shall be conferred by you upon a reputable clerk. If the lord of Craon should attempt to oppose your will in this matter and hinder you in the grant of the two prebends, the bishop shall restrain him according to his office and ecclesiastical discipline.

Of the four remaining prebends, the regular canons of Rota shall confer three and the bishop one. The bishop of Angers, unless he retains for himself the prebend which he has in the church of St Nicholas or gives it to the canons of St Maurice, may give it to no one except the monastery of Vendôme. And since the same place of St Nicholas is known to be unsuitable for the residence of religious men, neither the monks of Vendôme nor the canons of Rota shall presume to reside there; rather, as has been determined, six canons shall be established in that place. The condition of the mother church of St Clement, both in baptism and in its own burial ground and in other respects, shall remain unimpaired and intact [Col. 0263B].

The measure of oil which was annually supplied to the church of St Nicholas by the canons of Rota shall no longer be given. The aforesaid matters which require the authority of the bishop of Angers shall be strengthened by his own written instrument and the attestation of the canons of St Maurice, so that neither in his time nor in that of his successors may this peace and agreement established between us be dissolved by any contrivance.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this agreement or overthrow it on any pretext; but all things shall be preserved firm and unimpaired in perpetuity by both parties, as is established above. If anyone should rashly attempt to act against these provisions and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the offence by fitting amendment, let that person know that he will incur a sentence of excommunication [Col. 0263D].

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Willoius, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Ulger, called bishop of Angers, have subscribed.  
I, Littifred, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina.  
I, Rodulphus, bishop of Orta.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of John and Paul.  
I, Guido, unworthy priest, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.  
[Col. 0264A] I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St Adrian.  
I, Vassallius, cardinal deacon of St Eustachius.  
I, Hybaldus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata.  
I, Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Alberic, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 12 January, the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCXVII. He commands Henry, archbishop of Sens, to abstain from episcopal office. (1136, 15 January.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, Instrument 33.]

[Col. 0264B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother H., archbishop of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

No priest of the Lord may be ignorant of the ordinances of the apostolic see and the venerable decrees of the canons. For it belongs to a priest to know the law and to answer questions from the law; and if he is ignorant of the law, he thereby condemns himself as improperly usurping the honour of the priesthood. Nor does ignorance of the canons excuse a bishop. Indeed, the bishop who knowingly violates the canons is judged by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift they were composed. For those who act or presume to speak anything insolently against those same sacred canons, or who willingly consent to persons wishing to do so, seem not inappropriately to blaspheme the Holy Spirit [Col. 0264C].

Evangelical authority also testifies that blessed Peter is Christ’s vicar on earth and master of the whole Church, established by the Lord Himself when He said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” Consequently the apostolic see is the head and hinge, mother and teacher, of all Churches; and assuredly all may freely appeal to it. Once an appeal has been lodged, all things must remain in the same condition, and nothing whatsoever may be altered until the Roman pontiff, if appeal has been made to him, first examines whether the appeal was just or unjust. If he judges that the case must be reheard, or that new judges must be appointed, or finds that the case is such that matters already done should not be reopened, whatever he decrees shall be observed without challenge [Col. 0264D].

Since this is so, we are greatly astonished and afflicted with grave sorrow because, at the recent assembly held at Peveris concerning the marriage between Ar. of Soliac and the daughter of Ra. of Baugenciac, against whom an impediment of kinship was alleged, although you sat as judge, you rashly attempted to make yourself equal to blessed Peter or to set yourself above him. For after Ar. had appealed from you to us—who, though unworthy, exercise Christ’s legation and discharge the office of blessed Peter on earth—you, so far as lay in your power, setting your mouth against heaven and rendering void the keys of that prince of the apostles, presumed to proceed so far in this affair as to receive the sworn testimony of witnesses concerning the alleged kinship [Col. 0265A]. Yet you would by no means have fallen into this fault if the apostolic see, which is the mother of your dignity, had been what it ought to have been, namely the teacher of your reason. Therefore, lest we be accused by the Lord of having left so great an offence unpunished, we suspend you from episcopal office until you make satisfaction to blessed Peter and to us.

Given at Pisa, 15 January.

CCXVIII. To Robert, abbot of St Mary of Rota in the diocese of Angers. (1136, 25 January.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, III, 17.]

[Col. 0265B] INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Robert, abbot of St Mary of Rota, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

We ought readily to give assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Robert, acceding to the petitions of our venerable brother Ulger, bishop of Angers—a religious, prudent, and discerning man, proved by certain tests in the Catholic faith—we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Blessed Mary of the Wood, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. We strengthen it by this present charter of privilege, first decreeing that the canonical order, instituted there by God’s favour according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, shall be preserved inviolate in that place for all time [Col. 0265C].

Further, whatever goods and possessions that same Church now justly and canonically possesses, and whatever it may hereafter be able to acquire, through the Lord’s bounty, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall be preserved firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought it proper to name these expressly: the church of St Mary of Liureio; the church of St Mary of Camazeio, with its chapels, namely St Peter’s and St Leonard’s; the church of the Holy Saviour; the church of St German [Col. 0265D] of Daona; the church of St Peter of Vaus; the church of St Mary of Arisel; the church of St Bomirus of Fonte Cooperto; the church of St Peter of Bremio; the church of St Mary of Roalderia; the church of St German; the church of St Mary of Villeport; the church of St Peter of Chanceio; the chapel of St Mary of Port Sononia; the chapel of St Mary of Peston; the chapel of St John of Long-Alnet; the chapel of the Holy Cross of Cancellis; the chapel of St Mary Magdalene of Breliengaud; the chapel of St Lambert; and the chapel of St Dionysius of the Mill of Blochet.

We also grant you the right to confer three prebends in the church of St Nicholas of Craon upon three reputable clerks. After receiving the benefice from you, these must be presented to the bishop of Angers, free from the burden of exaction. Upon the death of any of them, none of the same prebends shall be held in your hand through bad intent, but without futile delay shall be conferred by you upon a reputable clerk [Col. 0266A]. Since the same place is known to be unsuitable for the residence of religious men, you may not live there; rather, as has been established, six canons shall be appointed in that place. The measure of oil which you used to supply annually to that Church shall no longer be given.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things remain intact for the benefit of the uses for the support of those for whom they were granted, saving, indeed, the due justice and reverence owed to the bishop of Angers [Col. 0266B]. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be subject to excommunication. But those preserving for the same place what is its own shall obtain the grace of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen. Fare well.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0266C] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Ulger, called bishop of Angers, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, cardinal of St Adrian, have subscribed.  
I, Vasallus, cardinal deacon of St Eustachius, have subscribed.  
I, Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed.  
I, Litifredus, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, unworthy priest.  
I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca [Col. 0266D], have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimericus, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 25 January, the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Fossatus. (1136, 20 February.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VII, Instrument 56.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ASCELIN, abbot of the monastery of St Peter of Fossatus, situated in the district of Paris, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 0267A] Whenever a request is made to us which is known to accord with reason, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and provide suitable support for the petitioners’ desires. Accordingly, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Ascelin, giving favourable paternal assent to your reasonable petitions, we strengthen by the privilege of the apostolic see the monastery of Blessed Peter at Fossatus, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions or goods you now justly and canonically possess by grant or confirmation of Roman pontiffs, kings of the Franks, or any bishops, and whatever you may hereafter be able to acquire with the Lord’s aid, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you forever. We have thought it proper to name these expressly [Col. 0267B].

In the archdiocese of Sens: the village called Seia and its church; the priory of Capella and its church; the church of Acheriis; and the church of Colliac.

In the diocese of Chartres: the priory of St Arnulf and its church; the priory of Monasteriis; the church of Long Villari; and the church of St Maurice.

In the diocese of Paris: in the borough of Castrum, the priory of St Clement and its church; the church of Evriac in the castle of Corbeil; the priory of St John the Baptist in the castle of Turnomium; the priory of St Dionysius and its church, with the chapels and property belonging to that priory; the church of the Oratory; the church [Col. 0267C] of Ferreolis; the church of Brucia; the church of St Hilary of Varennes, with the chapel of St Nicholas situated in the town of Fossatus; the church of Boissiac; the church of Mansionibus; the church of Nobiliac; the church of Noisy-le-Sec; further, the priory of St Eligius situated within the city of Paris, and the churches belonging to it: namely, the church of St Martial; the church of St Peter of Arsionibus; the church of the Holy Cross; the church of St Peter of Bobus, situated within the walls of that city; the church of St Bonitus beyond the Great Bridge; and the church of St Paul outside the city, with the lands and property belonging to it. Also, in the archdiocese of Sens, the church of St Hilary in the village called Messia; further, the priory of St Veranus, with the lands and property belonging to it; and the priory of Equata, with all its appurtenances.

We likewise confirm to you one prebend in the Church of Paris belonging to your monastery, and another prebend in the same church belonging to the priory of St Eligius [Col. 0267D].

In the diocese of Meaux: the church of Curte Prothasii. Moreover, by apostolic authority we firmly forbid any bishop or archbishop, except by mandate of the Roman pontiff or unless a legate has been specially sent for that purpose, to presume even to pronounce a sentence of excommunication against you, or against any brother or monk of your community. If such a sentence is pronounced or promulgated in any manner, we decree by apostolic authority that it shall have no force [Col. 0268A].

For the dedication of churches, the consecration of altars, chrism, oil, and similar things, or for the installation of an abbot when he is installed in his new pastoral office, no dean, archdeacon, or prelate of the Church may ever presume to demand or extort anything. Upon the death of the present abbot of that place, yourself, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed there by any fraud or force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of their counsel, shall determine to elect in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict.
