## CCXLI. Privilege for the Monastery of Saint George of Prüfening.  
*(A.D. 1136, 22 October.)*

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. XIII, p. 155.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HERBO, abbot of the monastery of Saint George of Prüfening, situated between Regensburg and the Danube, and to his successors canonically appointed [Col. 0289C] for ever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to love religious persons and places entrusted to their governance and, with the Lord’s aid, to provide beneficially for their peace and welfare. For it is recognized as worthy and consonant with propriety that we, who have been raised to the governance of the Churches, should defend them from the malice of wicked men and fortify them by the protection of blessed Peter and of the holy Roman Church. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Herbo, abbot, we graciously assent to your just petitions and honour by the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of Saint George, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside.

We decree that whatever possessions or goods that same monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, we confirm to you and your successors, and through you to the aforesaid monastery, by this document. Moreover, we confirm by this present writing the tithe granted to you by our venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, which he is known to have obtained from Hartwic, bishop of Regensburg, by an amicable exchange. We also decree that the cell called Aspach, which that same bishop, having acquired it through his own labour and effort, bestowed upon that place out of love for God, shall never be alienated by anyone or taken away in any manner.

We further decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery from ancient times shall be preserved there unimpaired for all time. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, [Col. 0290A] no one shall be set over it by any craft of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren in counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your labour, whether within or outside the monastery enclosure, which you cultivate at your own expense.

We further prohibit any bishop who may for the time being hold office in the Church of Bamberg, or anyone else, from presuming, under pretext of any matter or of advocacy, to burden that monastery with exactions; to give to anyone as a benefice possessions granted to you by the aforesaid bishop, or acquired from any source or bestowed upon you; or to withdraw them from the brethren’s use. Further, whatever goods the monastery may hereafter acquire, through the grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you.

Let no person, therefore, be permitted to disturb that monastery rashly, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit both of you, of your brethren, and of the poor. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, recognize himself or herself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and at the final judgment be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there rest the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0290D] I, Theodwin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed.  
I, Anselm, cardinal priest, have subscribed.  
I, Boethius, cardinal deacon of Saints Vitus and Modestus, have subscribed.  
I, Latrifredus, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Grisogonus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0291A], and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent III.

## CCXLII. To Henry, Bishop of Regensburg.  
*(A.D. 1136, October.)*

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. XIII, p. 152.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Regensburg: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

It is equitable and reasonable that monks and regular canons who ought to live on the alms and beneficence of others should not be compelled to pay tithes on the produce which they cultivate at their own expense and with their own hands. This was indeed confirmed by us with apostolic authority at the Council of Pisa which, by God’s favour, we recently celebrated. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we direct your brotherhood that you shall not in any way harass the brethren of Prüfening, either yourself or through the knight Hoholdus, concerning newly cleared land or other produce which they cultivate at their own expense and with their own hands; nor shall you permit them to be harassed by others. Otherwise, know that we shall by no means leave unpunished contempt of the Apostolic See.

## CCXLIII. Privilege for the Church of Polling.  
*(A.D. 1136, 23 October.)*

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. X, p. 39.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CHUNO, provost, and the brethren professing the regular life in the Church of Polling, present and future, in perpetual remembrance.

In the lofty watchtower of the apostolic see, in which we have been placed by the Lord’s disposal, it is fitting that we take diligent care to love religious houses with paternal affection, and to ensure, by attentive diligence, that they are not harassed by the molestations of wicked men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, yielding to the prayers of our venerable brother Walter, bishop of Augsburg, we graciously assent to your requests and strengthen with the privilege of the apostolic see the church of Saint Saviour, situated in the village called Polling, in which you are devoted to divine service. [Col. 0291D] We decree that the apostolic life and the canonical order established in that same church, divine mercy assisting, be preserved there inviolate for all future time. Whatever goods or possessions you now possess justly and canonically, or may hereafter be able to acquire, God being favourable, by grant of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired to you. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: namely, the village in which the said church has been built, where also, according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, you render divine service to almighty God; the village of Villhaim; the village of Ubingen; the village of Friheim; the village of Rieden; the village of Ascheringen; the village of Hunenwanch; [Col. 0292A] the village of Phafenhoven; and likewise the other possessions which King Secundus formerly restored and conveyed to your said church.

We also decree that, after making profession in that place, no one may transfer to another church without the brethren’s permission. Moreover, we forbid anyone, from wrongful zeal, to receive such a person into his church or monastery, or to dare retain one whom he has received. If such deserters, after a second or third warning from their brethren, scorn to return to the same church, we grant the superior and his brethren leave to pronounce against them a sentence of interdict or anathema. We confirm for you by apostolic authority the tithes which you possess by grant of pontiffs or may hereafter acquire.

[Col. 0292B] You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the ordination of clerics to be advanced to sacred orders, and any other ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is catholic, enjoys the grace and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to administer these things to you without abuse or exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is sought.

[Col. 0292C] Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, or harass it by any molestations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit of your use, for whose governance and support they have been granted. If anyone, knowingly, attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, does not make amends for his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him incur the peril of losing his power and honour, be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But those who preserve for the same place what belongs to it shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. [Col. 0292D] I, Anselm, cardinal priest, have subscribed. I, Insifred, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, have subscribed. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Guido, unworthy priest, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Boethius, cardinal deacon of Saints Vitus and Modestus, have subscribed.

[Col. 0293A] Given at Pisa by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on 23 October [the tenth day before the Kalends of November], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## CCXLIV. Privilege for Schuttern Abbey. (1136, 28 October.)

[WURTVEIN, *Nova Subsidia diplomatica*, vol. VII, p. 92.—From the *vidimus* of the judge of the court of Strasbourg of the year 1391, in the archive of Schuttern Abbey.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son CONRAD, abbot of the monastery of Schuttern, situated in the diocese of Strasbourg, in the place called Mortinaugia, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0293B] The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and endeavour by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptably to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it has been confirmed by the purity of religion. Therefore, with this purpose of charity, beloved son in the Lord Conrad, abbot, assenting to your requests, we receive under the care of blessed Peter and under our protection the monastery of Schuttern, over which, by God’s authorship, you preside, and fortify it by the present page of writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now canonically possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire, the Lord granting it, by concessions of pontiffs, gifts of [Col. 0293C] princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you forever. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names:

Friesenheim with its church.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] Friesenheim belongs to the Margrave of Baden; it is situated in the bailiwick of Mahlberg, where Schuttern Abbey enjoys tithes and the right of patronage.]

Scopheim with its church.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] Oberschopfen belongs to the same margrave, where Schuttern Abbey receives tithes and enjoys the right of patronage.]

Rogenswiler (today Heiligenzell); Zunsvilere (Zuntwyhr) with its church; Odenheim (Ottenheim) with its church; Wagenhurst (Wanhurst); Kippenheim; Kirrechcella (Kirtzel) with its church; Albeswiler (Almansweiler); Ichenheim; the church of Sasbach (Saspach), with its appurtenances; and the possessions which your ministeriales hold in Breisgau, Heimbach, Dirmuntigen; the church of Wopelinesbergen with its appurtenances and with the possessions which your ministeriales hold in that province. In Alsace: Gersheim (Gerstheim), [Col. 0293D] Herbousheim (Herbolsheim), Sigelesheim (Sigolsheim), with their appurtenances and with the possessions which your ministeriales hold in that province; likewise, the serfs which it is known to have in Swabia, Lorraine, and Altdorff (Altorff).

We also forbid any of your successors to alienate the monastery’s possessions or grant them as benefices. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, [Col. 0294A] diminish them, or harass it with any molestations; but that all things shall be kept whole for the benefit of your use, for whose governance and support they have been granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But those preserving for that place what belongs to it shall obtain the grace of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0294B] I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodwin, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Guido, bishop of Tivoli. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Grisogonus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico.

Given at Pisa by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on 28 October [the fifth day before the Kalends of November], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## CCXLV. General privilege for the monastery of Saint Nicasius at Reims. (1136, 10 November.)

[VARM, *Archives administratives de Reims*, I, 288.]

[Col. 0294C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JORAN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Nicasius, and to his successors to be canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

… Whatever possessions and whatever goods the monastery … is known to possess, we confirm to you and your successors by the present page of writing. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names: in the diocese of Reims, the altar [church benefice] of Buxolio on the river Marne; on the river Aisne, the altar of Celto; the altar of Anteniacum with the three [Col. 0294D] chapels of Oggeium, Altovillare, and Fulzeium; the altar of Branzonis Court with the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Sarpeia Court; the altar of Hanonia; the altar of Burcium; the altar of Saint Leodegarius with its church; the hermitage of Azo of Ham; half the jurisdiction in the allod of Saint Leodegarius, with ban and justice, pasture-rights, watercourse, fishery, and other revenues; likewise half the mill with its fishery; a certain allod from Lord Trajan, with the male and female serfs belonging to it, with ban and [Col. 0295A] justice, watercourse, and a mill with fishery.

The altar of Gons; Fulcaud’s *mansus*; Robert of Corbineio’s *mansus*; the village of Singli, with ban, justice, and every seignorial right which Count Hugh of Registeten had held there; half the mill of Coopello with the land belonging to it; Hugh of Cirelio’s allod. The land called Mount Regulus, and all the land and woodland from the stream called Dogthorn, which runs into the valley of Morendi, as far as the archbishop’s wood towards Reims, bestowed upon your monastery by Hugh, formerly Count of Troyes, with ban, justice, watercourse, and all the customary dues which that count had held there. Two parts of the tithe from all lands belonging to Mount Regulus; also the lands called Aceles; Helbert of Halmericurte’s mills with the land belonging to them; an allod beside the same village; forty *journaux* in the diocese of Laon near Ribold’s Mount.

[Col. 0295B] One court with the houses belonging to it and two orchards, and with the cultivated lands nearest that castle; arable land sufficient for one plough-team, and one-third of the meadow adjoining the castle. In the diocese of Châlons: the altar of Saint Hilary of Buxitum, with the chapel belonging to it, which is in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Nicasius; the altar of the village called Cappa; the altar of the village of Saint Basolus; the altar of Lord Martin. In the diocese of Liège: the altar of Morelineis; the altar of Senzelia; the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene of Cymacum with its appurtenances.

[Col. 0295C] We also decree that the cloister and suburb around the monastery and belonging to it shall be free from every exaction, so that no one may dare impose any exactions there. Rather, you and your successors who shall from time to time be in that place, or anyone whom they direct, may freely possess the customary dues which the monastery is known to have held in those places—namely portage, wheelage, toll, market-measure dues, and forage dues—with ban and justice … We forbid … that any monk, after making … profession, may ever leave your monastery or transfer to another place without the free permission of the abbot and brethren. But if, which God forbid, this should occur, and after a second and third warning from his brethren he does not return to his proper place, we grant his abbot and brethren authority to place him under interdict or excommunicate him.

[Col. 0295D] Therefore no person may rashly disturb the said monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it in any manner; but all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, with the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop nevertheless preserved. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, [Col. 0296A] does not make fitting satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the wrong he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, William, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Guido, bishop of Tivoli, have subscribed. [Col. 0296B] I, Anselm, cardinal priest, have subscribed. I, Linfred, cardinal priest, have subscribed. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Grisogonus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa by the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on 8 November [the sixth day before the Ides of November], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## CCXLVI. He confirms the foundation of the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu in the diocese of Reims. (1136, 23 November.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 312.]

[Col. 0296C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved brethren devoted to divine service in the monastery of Saint Mary of Mont-Dieu, present and future, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and endeavour by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever acceptably rendered to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it has been preserved by the purity of [Col. 0296D] religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just desires and fortify by privilege of the apostolic see the monastery of the blessed Mother of God, in which you devote yourselves to divine service. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to the rule and institution of the Carthusian brethren shall there be observed inviolably for all future time. We also decree that no one whatsoever may infringe, diminish, or alter the Carthusian order established in the same monastery; and that your monastery shall likewise possess the freedom which Chartreuse, namely the head of this order, possesses, and that no one may violate it in any way.

[Col. 0297A] Moreover, so that you may be freer to serve almighty God in mind and body, we likewise decree that you shall remain quiet and free from every disturbance concerning any matter or plea, and shall suffer no injury or molestation concerning what has been bestowed upon you in lands, pastures, woods, or cultivation. We have thought fit to state the boundaries of your place in their own terms: from Mont-Dieu itself to the hill beside Setona towards the east, as Nicholas of Burgo and William gave that land; westward as far as the water of Bairon; southward as far as the ancient embankment which runs from the bridge of Bairon [or *Bariorone*, as it stands in Eugenius’s bull] to the castle of Mouzon; northward as far as the beeches at the bottom of the wooded valley belonging to the Count of Registeten, by whose will and grant this gift was made and confirmed.

[Col. 0297B] We further add that no woman may enter your boundaries, unless perhaps this occurs by reason of passage, which travellers must have in common through your lands. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but all things shall be kept intact for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they have been granted, with the due right and reverence of the diocesan bishop nevertheless preserved [in Eugenius’s charter it reads: “with the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical reverence due to the diocesan bishop preserved”].

[Col. 0297C] If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, does not correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the wrong he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all preserving their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0297D] I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, Theodewin, bishop of Rufina. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul.

Given at Pisa by the hand of Armerac, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on 23 November [the ninth day before the Kalends of December], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent, Pope of Rome II.

## CCXLVII. He confirms the immunities of the church of Marsna near Maastricht, belonging to the monastery of Blessed Remigius, in which monks are substituted for canons. (1136, 23 November.)

[COCQUELINES, II, p. 232.]

[Col. 0298A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ODO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

The care of venerable places admonishes us to think diligently of their peace and welfare. Nor is there any doubt that, if we graciously respond to the petitions of God’s servants, we find the Lord merciful toward our own needs. [Col. 0298B] Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Odo, we graciously assent to your reasonable requests, and strengthen by the present page of writing the liberty of the church of Marsna, belonging to the monastery of Blessed Remigius, granted to you by Alexander, formerly bishop of Liège, and approved and confirmed by Herman, his archdeacon, and his brethren. We decree that it shall remain unimpaired for future times: namely, that both in the provostship and in the canonries, monks may be substituted, according to the prudent judgment and disposition of yourself and your successors, in place of suitable clerics who hold the benefices of the aforesaid church.

[Col. 0298C] The provost appointed over that place by you or your successors shall present to the archdeacon of Liège a priest appointed to such a prebend as that provost, with the consent of the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Saint Remigius then in office, shall provide. The archdeacon will entrust the cure of souls to him; and the priest himself shall answer for every episcopal and synodal obligation according to the custom of the diocese of Liège.

Therefore no person may infringe, alter, or by any pretext overthrow this same grant made to the monastery of Blessed Remigius. Rather, all things shall remain intact to you and your successors, as the present sanction of writing and the grant of the aforesaid former bishop Alexander are known to have established. If any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 0298D] person, knowingly, attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and, after a second or third warning, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the wrong he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance.

But upon all preserving this our confirmation may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0299A] I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico.

## CCXLIX. He confirms the order of regular canons of Saint Augustine, recently introduced into the monastery of Steinfeld in the diocese of Cologne. (1136, 10 December.)

[COCQUELINES, vol. II, p. 232.]

[Col. 0299D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons EVERWIN, provost, and the brethren professing the canonical life in the church of Steinfeld, present and future, in perpetuity.

A devout request ought to be fulfilled by the effect that follows it, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the benefit sought may undoubtedly gain strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, willingly assenting to your reasonable requests, we fortify with the privilege of the apostolic see the church of Steinfeld, in which you are devoted to divine service. First, we decree that the canonical order [Col. 0300A] known to have been established there according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed inviolate for all future time.

Moreover, we command that no one of your brethren, after making profession, may leave your church and transfer to another place without the free permission of the provost and brethren; nor may anyone presume to retain him in the provostships established by your brethren. Let your order be maintained according to the Rule of blessed Augustine; and if anything new must be established in the order, let it be established in agreement by the common consent of the prelates at your annual assembly. We likewise decree that the provostships founded by your brethren shall be visited by you for confirmation of the order, and that their provosts shall visit your church every year. Moreover, communities of nuns who subject themselves to the governance of your church’s teaching may not presume to withdraw themselves from it and thereafter subject themselves to another.

[Col. 0300B] So that you may be able to serve almighty God more securely, at the request of our venerable brother Bruno, we decree that the liberty granted to your church by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne of revered memory, and afterwards approved by Bruno, his successor, shall possess every strength in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that same church of Steinfeld now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, the Lord granting it, acquire by grants of pontiffs, liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

[Col. 0300C] If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly, attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and after a second or third warning does not make amends by satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the wrong he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of Jesus Christ our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all preserving their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca.

## CCL. To Stephen, king of the English.—He receives him, unanimously elected and consecrated king, as a special son of Blessed Peter and of the Roman Church. (1136.)

[D. BOUQUET, vol. XV, p. 391.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ STEPHEN, illustrious king of the English, [Col. 0301B] greeting and apostolic blessing.

The King of kings and Lord of lords, in whose hand are all powers and all rights of kingdoms, by the incomprehensible dispensation of supreme providence changes times and transfers kingdoms when he wills. For, as the Prophet testifies: “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he wills” (Dan. 4:14). How much prosperity, how great a tranquillity of joy, and how much enforcement of justice flourished in the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy during the reign of our son, the glorious King Henry, became clearly manifest by direct experience after he was removed from human affairs.

Because he was a lover of religious men, a cultivator of peace and justice, and [Col. 0301C] a kindly consoler of widows and orphans, and a merciful defender of those who could not defend themselves because of weakness, after he was taken away, as we have learned, religion in the kingdom of England was thrown into confusion, no command of peace or justice prevailed through royal assistance, and impunity accompanied the atrocity of so many crimes. But lest dreadful ferocity, continuing to rage, should be able to vent its fury upon the people of God any longer, the merciful compassion of God bent to the prayers of religious men. Powerfully confronting such great crimes, as the letters of our venerable brothers, the archbishops and bishops of those regions, of lovers of the holy Roman Church, of the glorious king of the Franks, and of the illustrious Count Theobald testify, and as the assertion of diligent men has informed us, divine mercy provided that by the common vote and unanimous assent [Col. 0301D] of both magnates and people you should be elected king and consecrated by the bishops of the realm.

[Note: [Col. 0301D] “Stephen, Count of Boulogne,” says Orderic Vitalis (*History*, book XIII, p. 902), “on hearing of his uncle’s death, immediately crossed the sea. Received by William, archbishop of Canterbury, and the other bishops and princes of the land, he ascended the royal throne and, on 15 December [the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January] 1135, was crowned king, the fourth of the Norman line to reign. The Normans, however, meeting his brother Theobald at Neubourg, wished to set him over themselves. But at that assembly they heard from a certain monk, Stephen’s envoy, that all the English had accepted Stephen, wished all to obey him, and desired to appoint him their king. Immediately all, with Theobald’s consent, resolved to serve one lord, because of the honours which the barons possessed in both regions. Theobald, therefore, being the elder, was angry that he had not received the kingdom, hurried to the great affairs pressing upon him in Gaul, and carelessly allowed Normandy to be trampled down for a long time. Meanwhile, the king being occupied in England, Normandy lacked a ruler,” etc., vol. XII, p. 755.]

[Col. 0302A] We, recognizing that the wishes of so many men had, divine grace leading the way, converged upon your person; also that, on the very day of your consecration, you promised blessed Peter obedience and reverence; and that you are known to have drawn your descent from the family of the aforesaid king in a near degree of kinship—

[Note: [Col. 0302D] Stephen was born of Adela, sister of Henry I, king of England, who had formerly bound by oaths the faith of the magnates and of Stephen himself in order to secure the kingdom for his daughter Matilda, formerly empress and then countess of Anjou, and for the children born or to be born from her.]

—holding favourably what has been done concerning you, we receive you with paternal affection as a special son of Blessed Peter and of the holy Roman Church, and we desire most willingly to retain you in the same prerogative of honour and familiarity in which your predecessor Henry, of distinguished memory, was crowned by us.

## CCLI. Bull in favour of the regular canons of Saint John in the suburb of Sens. (1136.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, *Instrumenta*, 359.]

[Col. 0302B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HAIMARD, abbot of the church of Saint John the Evangelist situated in the suburb of Sens, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

The authority of our office exhorts us to concern ourselves with the institutions of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide beneficially for their peace and welfare. For it is known to be fitting and consistent with propriety that we who have been appointed to govern churches should protect them from the malice of wicked men and fortify them by the patronage of blessed Peter and of the apostolic see. [Col. 0302C] Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Raynard, abbot, we graciously accept your petitions and fortify by the privilege of the holy Roman Church the church of Saint John, over which you are known to preside by God’s authorship. We decree that whatever goods and possessions the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God enlarging its estate, be able to acquire by grant of pontiffs, liberality of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have added the following, to be recorded by their proper names: namely, the church of Saint Stephen of Château-Renard with its appurtenances, granted to the aforesaid church of Saint John by our venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Sens, with his chapter’s consent; likewise the church of Saint Saviour, [Col. 0302D] entrusted to you by the chapter and canons of Sens with all its appurtenances, the said Henry our brother, archbishop, giving his consent. We grant, ratify, and approve it by apostolic authority, as it was confirmed by our predecessor Pope Honorius of blessed memory, [Col. 0303A] etc. …

Given in the year of the Lord 1136.

## CCLII. To the canons of the church of Saint Fridianus of Lucca. (About 1136.)

[BALUZ., *Miscellanea*, IV, 591.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Saint Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We grieve all the more deeply over the death of our dearest son, your prior A., of revered memory, because by his removal greater counsels and consolations have been taken away from us and from you. Yet we are consoled no little because his life was praiseworthy before God and men; because, instructed in his sacred disciplines, you unanimously agreed upon the person of our beloved son Jer.; and because, in peace and unity … The remainder is lacking.

CCLIII. He commends Prior Atto and the brethren of the church of St. Fridian to all clerics and laity established throughout the diocese of Lucca. January 5, 1133–1137.

[BALUZ., ibid., p. 589.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all clerics and laypeople dwelling throughout the diocese of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0303C] The church of Blessed Fridian is honoured with the greatest devotion and reverence, both among neighbouring peoples and among foreign nations, because of its religious life and the upright conduct of those who serve the Lord there. Indeed, through his institution, very many people, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, have abandoned worldly pomp and devoted themselves to the service of almighty God; and by the example of their good manner of life they do not cease to train the hearts of the faithful people in the practice of right works. It is fitting, therefore, that the Apostolic See should love the brethren of that place with paternal affection and openly display the effectiveness of its love for them. Therefore we exhort all of you in the Lord that you most devotedly honour your beloved son Atto, prior, and the brethren [Col. 0303D] of the aforesaid church of St. Fridian, and that, both in hospitality and in their other needs, you furnish them aid with cheerful kindness. Whoever denies them hospitality shows that he does not abide in charity. It is therefore your concern, most beloved sons in the Lord, humbly to obey our admonitions, so that, through the interceding merits of the same Blessed Fridian and of the other saints, because of your reception of these brethren and the benefits bestowed upon them, you may deserve to share in the prayers offered to the Lord in that place and, after the course of this life, to receive from God, the rewarder of all good things, the recompense of eternal reward.

Given at Pisa, on the Nones of January.

CCLIV. To Petronilla, abbess of Fontevraud. January 5, 1133–1137.

[PAVILLON, *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, Pr., p. 628.]

[Col. 0304A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved in Christ Petronilla, abbess of Fontevraud: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been made known to us that you greatly seek rest and wish the necks of the flock entrusted to you to rest; and we bear this all the more grievously because in these last days dangerous times are known to be impending. Consider what is said by the Lord’s voice to the prince of the apostles: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” From this it is plainly inferred that, if one who presides over the Lord’s flock by the gift of heavenly grace in order to feed it [Col. 0304B] refuses even to do this, he demonstrates that he does not at all love the supreme Shepherd. But the glorious Blessed Martin, confessor of the Lord, leaving a praiseworthy example to the prelates of the Church, showed himself humbly prepared to undertake labour for the people if he were still necessary to them. Therefore we admonish your love, and command you through obedience, that you leave the flock entrusted to you on no account; but rather, as usual, strive to provide for your sisters in temporal and spiritual matters, so that with them you may deserve to be presented to the Queen of Virgins, there to receive from the Lord, the rewarder of all good things, the robe of immortality in return for your enduring labours.

CCLV. To Hugh, archbishop of Rouen: severe in correcting vices, he exhorts him to gentleness; he promises that, if the abbot of St. Wandrille “shall have scorned to obey him until the next feast of Pentecost, he will hold ratified the reasonable sentence which he may pronounce against him.” He sends him a stole as a gift. January 20, 1133–1137.

[*Neustria pia*, p. 174.]

[Col. 0304C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, archbishop of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The holy Church of God has proved, by the very fruits of your works, the fervour of your charity and constancy of faith which have hitherto shone forth in your person, as the need of the time has required, among both ecclesiastical and secular persons. Therefore, set by divine providence as a watchman over the house of the Lord, you keep careful watch over the flock entrusted to you, after the manner of a good shepherd; and by showing yourself severe in correcting vices, you strive to fulfil the episcopal office in word and example. Now then, dearest brother, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, entreat, rebuke, reprove [2 Tim. 4], yet in all things with charity and gentleness, and with the rule of the holy canons preserved. Nor should you in any way suppose that we wish to invalidate what you have rightly established, or to destroy or root up what you have planted; rather, we wish that whatever you do according to God and justice shall be observed with enduring firmness. But if the abbot of St. Wandrille should scorn to obey your fraternity until [Col. 0305A] the next feast of Pentecost, we shall, by apostolic authority, hold ratified the reasonable sentence which you pronounce against him. Moreover, dearest brother, we have thought it right to admonish you by this letter that you should prepare yourself, so that, when you receive our messenger, you may be able to perform the service of Blessed Peter. As a token of affection, we send to your charity, through our beloved sons R. and G., capable men devoted to you, a stole taken from our own neck, so that you may use it continually for the honour of God, the reverence of Blessed Peter, and remembrance of us.

Given at Pisa, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.

CCLVI–CCLVII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter at Melk. January 3, 1137.

[HUEBER, *Austria illustrata*, p. 8.]

[Col. 0305B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HERCHINFRID, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Melk, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

By the authority of the Apostolic See, over which by the Lord’s disposition we preside, we are bound to love venerable places, especially those belonging to Blessed Peter, and, with God’s help, to take salutary care for their peace and welfare through the holy communities which serve the Lord there. For this reason, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Herchinfrid, granting your reasonable petitions, we fortify by the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Peter, over which you preside by divine providence. It was built at Melk, in the diocese of Passau, by the parents of the illustrious Margrave Leopold; and, having been held under his right of patronage, it was offered to the holy Roman Church. In accordance with the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Paschal and Calixtus, Roman pontiffs, we place it under that Church’s protection for ever. We decree that whatever possessions, estates, or churches with offerings of tithes the aforesaid princes Leopold and his father Leopold, and their other relatives, or other faithful persons have bestowed upon that monastery from their own right, or may happen to bestow in the future, are confirmed by the present page to you and your successors. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one may be put over it by any stratagem of encroachment or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected, moreover, shall come to the Roman pontiff for consecration. Furthermore, you shall not be compelled to submit to the judgment of the surrounding abbots, except perhaps those who belong to the right and property of the Apostolic See, when a cause of ecclesiastical necessity requires it. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the bishop of Passau, [Col. 0306A] provided that he enjoys the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by apostolic authority, shall grant what is requested.

You shall have permission, without the objection of any bishop or provost, to receive into conversion laypeople or clerics living a secular life. We also decree that burial in that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who desire to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Margrave Leopold, or his heir—whoever shall thereafter hold the march—shall remain advocate of that place. Yet neither they nor any person whatsoever may rashly claim anything for themselves in that monastery or its goods, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations. Rather, all that the same monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with God’s help, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall be preserved whole and unimpaired, entirely to benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance they have been granted. As a sign of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay to us and our successors one gold coin each year.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to amend his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he is guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Hunneric, deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of January, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCLVIII. He consoles Agnes, formerly wife of Margrave Leopold, and her sons over Leopold’s death. He commends the monks of Melk. He adds: “In accordance with your requests, when it happens that we see our dearest son Emperor Lothair, we shall gladly and affectionately ask him to preserve your rights for you.” January 8, 1137.

[FISCHER, *Remarkable Fortunes of Klosterneuburg*, II, 132 (SCHRAMB, *Chronicle of Melk*, 71).]

CCLIX. He takes under protection the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Sacargia and confirms its privileges. January 21, 1137.

[*Annals of Camaldoli*, III, 258.]

[Col. 0307A]

CCLX. Privilege for the church of Bonne-Espérance. January 27, 1137.

[HUGO, *Premonstratensian Annals*, I, 301.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ODO, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by its ensuing effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Odo, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, a religious, prudent, and discerning man, we graciously grant your just desires and fortify with the privilege of the Apostolic See the church of Bonne-Espérance, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter reasonably acquire, by the Lord’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly the following: namely, the allod on which the aforesaid church of the Blessed Mother of God stands, at the place called Valleréille; the allod of Ramelgies; the allod of Gays; three mills, two beside the abbey and the third in the valley of Lestines; the allod of Morteri, subject to the annual rent which you owe to pay to the canons of St. John at Valenciennes for it—namely, five measures of oats, two and a half measures of good wheat, two and a half measures of rye, thirteen denarii, and an equal number of chickens. For the entire tithe, both of grain and livestock: ten measures and three solidi. For the tithe of the estate beside the abbey: six denarii, payable to the church of St. Mary of Cambrai. For the tithe of Ramelgies, of grain and livestock: ten solidi to the church of Lobbes. For the tithe of livestock at Gays: five solidi to the church of St. Hubert at Marolles. These aforesaid things have been granted and secured to you by the writings or charters of those through whom you possess them.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary of Bonne-Espérance, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; rather, let all be preserved for it intact, to benefit the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving nevertheless the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, after a second or third warning, should fail to correct his offence by appropriate satisfaction, let him suffer loss of his power and honour, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, Theodwin, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Drogo, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0308B] I, Albert, bishop of Albano. I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Bezifred, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul. I, Martin, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen. I, Guido, unworthy priest. I, G.G., cardinal priest of the title of St. Prisca. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 0308C] I, Guido, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1137 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCLXI. Confirmatory bull concerning the transfer of the abbey from St. Firmin to St. John beside the Selle, and concerning the possessions of that abbey. January 30, 1137.

[HUGO, *Annals of the Premonstratensian Order*, I, 691.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son FULCO, abbot of St. John at Amiens, [Col. 0308D] and to his brethren regularly appointed for ever.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by its ensuing effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Fulco, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, a religious, prudent, and discerning man, we graciously grant your just desires and fortify with the privilege of the Apostolic See the church of St. John, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, [Col. 0309A] or may hereafter reasonably acquire, by the Lord’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly: the altar of St. German, the altar of St. Firmin of the valley, and the altar of St. Marcellus, with the entire tithe of the church; and to the said altar of St. Marcellus belong the village called Marlemont and the hamlet called Bertincourt. Also the mill which the vidame of Pinchegny [Pepigny] gave you. Likewise, the tithes of your livestock and their increase, which the canons of the church of St. Mary at Amiens granted to you at the request of our venerable brothers Rainald, archbishop of Reims, and Guarin, bishop of Amiens. Also the estate situated in the valley of Guy, with the oratory and the land belonging to that valley, together with its tithe. Further, wherever outside the brothers cultivate land in the territory of Mairieu. One third of the tithe of the church’s holding at Wavercourt, given by Robert the cleric. All these things are known to belong to your church.

We therefore decree that no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid church of Blessed John the Baptist, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any visitations; rather, let all be preserved for it intact, to benefit the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving nevertheless the canonical right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to correct his offence by appropriate satisfaction, let him suffer loss of his power and honour, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0309D] I, William, bishop of Palestrina. I, Theodwin, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Drogo, bishop of Ostia. I, Albert, bishop of Albano. I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Lettifred, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Martin, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen. I, Guido, unworthy priest. I, G.G., cardinal priest of the title of St. Prisca. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 0310A] I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of the title of St. Adrian.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Alberic, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1137 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCLXII. Privilege for the monastery of St. Peter at Selincourt. January 30, 1137.

[HUGO, *Annals of the Premonstratensian Order*, II, p. 360.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GALTER, abbot of Saint Peter at Selincourt, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

[Col. 0310B] We ought to fulfil pious requests by their ensuing effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, son Galter, abbot of Saint Peter at Selincourt, we graciously grant your just desires and fortify with the privilege of the Apostolic See the church over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions or goods it now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter reasonably acquire, by the Lord’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these the following are to be stated expressly: namely, the land [Col. 0310C] opposite the church; two parts of the tithe of Selincourt; one third of the tithe of Warsuvio; likewise the tithes of all the animals and gardens of that place, granted by Lord Frumold, prior, and the entire chapter of St. Martin at Amiens; and one third of the tithe of Tancheremaisnil, etc. . . . . All that Bishop Guarin and Archdeacon Simon of the aforesaid church granted, etc. . . .

We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact, to benefit the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving nevertheless the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, after a second or third warning, should fail to correct his offence by appropriate satisfaction, let him suffer the penalty of the loss of his power and honour, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, [Col. 0311A] cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1137 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCLXIII. At the request of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, he confirms the possessions of the monastery of St. Mary of Columba. February 7, 1137.

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, II, 213.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever in the place called Columba, anciently named Caretto, situated in the diocese of Piacenza.

[Col. 0311B] A pious request ought to bring about its fulfilment by its ensuing effect, so that the singularity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, dearest son in the Lord, Abbot Bernard, granting your petitions, we fortify with the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery situated in the place called Columba. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that entire place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the Lord’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain for ever secure and unimpaired for the brethren who shall be there from time to time. Among these [Col. 0311C] we have thought fit to record especially all those lands which the illustrious Marquis Pallavicino,

> [Note: [Col. 0311D] The Marquis Pallavicino, mentioned here as a particular benefactor of the monastery, was Oberto, as appears in the cartulary of the same monastery: “The boundaries which Oberto Pallavicino, marquis, together with his wife and sons, and Conrad Cavalcabò, marquis, together with his wife, granted from lands belonging to their own right, for the salvation of their souls, to the venerable monastery of St. Mary of Columba, with the counsel of their men and other worthy men; and which they set out, and caused to be set out, with their own hands, and confirmed by the guarantee of their subscriptions in the charters which they made for the aforesaid monastery, in the year 1136 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.” This is that Oberto whose family, derived in a long line from the ancient Lombard age, has continued down to our own time. Oberto died in 1147. He is buried in a noble marble tomb near the doors of the monastery of Columba, without any inscription whatever.]

and the noble standard-bearer of the city of Piacenza, or other worthy men, bestowed upon that place out of devotion. We decree that these lands shall remain for ever peacefully and freely, by perpetual right, to the brethren of the same place and exempt from every secular exaction. And because those living the common life ought to live from the alms and beneficence of others, we ordain that no one may dare to demand or receive tithes from the labour which the brethren of that monastery cultivate with their own hands or at their own expense. We further decree that, from the village called Senna as far as Bundium, or within other boundaries specially designated by our venerable brother Arduin, bishop, and by the clergy and people of Piacenza, [Col. 0311D] no church may at any time be built and no secular settlement whatsoever may be made.

Therefore no person may lawfully rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any molestations; rather, let all be preserved whole [Col. 0312A] for the benefit of the brethren serving the Lord there. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our grant, should rashly attempt to act against it and, after a second or third warning, should fail to correct this presumption by appropriate satisfaction, let him suffer loss of his power and honour, be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to severe vengeance. But let those who preserve these provisions obtain the grace of almighty God and of his apostles, Blessed Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. [Col. 0312B] I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Ivo, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1137 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCLXIV. He takes under protection the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem, confirms its goods, and enlarges its privileges. February 8, 1137.

[*Privileges of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem*, p. 85.]

[Col. 0312C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAYMOND, master of the hospital of the holy city of Jerusalem, and to his brethren, present and future, for ever.

The religion of the Christian faith piously believes and truthfully professes that our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, though rich in all things, became poor for our sake. Therefore, promising suitable consolatory rewards to his followers, he says: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of heaven.” Likewise, as father of orphans and refuge of the poor, exhorting us in the Gospel to hospitality and beneficence, he says: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me”; and, in order to demonstrate the surpassing goodness of so great a humanity, he declares that he will render a reward even for a cup of cold water. And so we, upon whom by the office entrusted to us rests the duty of providing with paternal solicitude for those far away and those near at hand, embrace your devotion with due kindness; and, as you have requested, we take under the protection of Blessed Peter the hospital house of the holy city of Jerusalem, and fortify by the privilege of the Apostolic See the persons and property belonging to it. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you for ever.

If deserted places are at any time bestowed upon that venerable house by anyone out of pious devotion, you may build villages there [Col. 0313B] and construct churches and cemeteries for the use of all who dwell there. But when cultivated or uncultivated lands are granted to you by lawful title, you shall have the power and permission to build oratories there and establish cemeteries solely for the use of brethren who eat at your table. We decree, therefore, that the receivers of your fraternities or collections, without prejudice to the right of their lords, shall stand under the protection of Blessed Peter and of us and shall enjoy peace in the lands where they are. Likewise, we decree that any person admitted to your fraternity, if the church to which he belongs should be prohibited from divine offices and it should happen that he dies, shall not be denied ecclesiastical burial, unless he has specifically been bound by the bond of anathema.

Moreover, if any of your brethren, sent by you to receive those fraternities or collections, should arrive in any city, castle, or village [Col. 0313C] and that place should happen to be under an interdict from divine offices, then, in reverence for almighty God, at their arrival the churches shall be opened once in the year and, with excommunicated persons excluded, divine offices shall be celebrated there. Since all your possessions ought to go toward the support of the poor and pilgrims, and for this reason must by no means be applied to other uses, we decree that you shall not be compelled to pay tithes from the labour which you cultivate at your own expense.

Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb you in respect of this our grant, take away your possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any molestations; rather, let all be preserved whole, entirely to benefit your uses and those of the poor. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, after a second or third warning, should fail to correct his offence by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he is guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights in those same places may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, [Col. 0314A] so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [lacuna] Amen.

In place of a seal, the following is written in a circle:

> HELP US, O GOD, OUR SAVIOUR.

And in the centre:

> SAINT PETER, SAINT PAUL, POPE INNOCENT THE SECOND.

Subscribed:

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of Saints John [Col. 0314B] and Paul. I, Brother Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus. Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Drogo, bishop of Ostia. I, Grisogonus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Porto. I, Ubald, cardinal of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Theodemir, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Wido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Guido, cardinal of St. Adrian. I, Vassallus, cardinal deacon of St. Eustace.

[Col. 0314C] Given at Pisa through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year one thousand one hundred and thirty-seven of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCLXV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter near Perugia. February 10, 1137.

[COCQUELINES, II, p. 234.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HIERONYMUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, situated beside the city of Perugia, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

[Col. 0314D] A pious request ought to be brought to fulfilment by a corresponding effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved son Jerome in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, we strengthen with the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of blessed Peter, over which by God’s authority you preside. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that place now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s favour, acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors [Col. 0315A], whether in churches or dependent cells, estates, parish churches, monasteries, lands, and rural holdings. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the parish churches of Saint Constantine, Saint Rufinus, Saint Martin, and Saint John; the parish church of Saint Martyrius; the church of Saint Benedict at Angellione with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Justin with its estate; the churches of Saint Andrew and Saint Angel of Aliano, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary at Petiviano and that of Saint Clement; the estate of Casale, the estate of Petroniano, and that which pertains to you from the estate and church of Saint Donatus of Civitella; likewise the land of Hugh, nephew of Berno, of Monte Negro.

By the protection of the Apostolic See we also confirm to you the churches of Saints [Col. 0315B] Apollinaris, Blaise, and Montanus, with all their appurtenances, saving the annual payment due to the church of Farfa. Moreover, we confirm three estates situated in the county of Perugia: one called Cusulo, another Filontio, and another called Casalina, with churches, vineyards, fields, gardens, mountains, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and all their appurtenances. We likewise confirm the monastery of Saint Angel in the county of Asti, in the place called Limisano, with its cells and chapels and all that pertains to it; the monastery of Saint Saviour at Cathale, with all that pertains to it; and the monastery of Saint Peter at Plojano with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Sylvester at Murcella; the church of Saint Donatus; whatever is known to be of your right [Col. 0315C] at Agello; the church of Saint Mary at Poggio with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Paul at Monticello; and the church of Saint Peter of Petroniano with its estate.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders and of clerics belonging to that monastery, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and is willing to provide these things freely and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration; supported by the authority of the holy Roman Church, he shall grant what you request.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, [Col. 0315D] or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any artifice of deception or by force, except one whom the brothers, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers, shall elect, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. We altogether forbid public masses to be celebrated in that monastery by a bishop, or stations or any ordinations to be held, without the will of the abbot and brothers, lest any occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of the servants of God. Nor may any bishop, apart from the consent of the Roman pontiff, burden, place under interdict, or excommunicate that monastery or its cells, or impose new exactions [Col. 0316A]; nor may any secular magnate extort fodrum (a provisioning levy), or any other service, from that monastery or its appurtenances, saving of course the right and lordship of the holy Roman Church.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, remove its possessions, retain for personal use possessions unjustly taken away, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall hereafter knowingly attempt with rash audacity to contravene this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he is answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Drogo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Theodewimus, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Berard, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross [Col. 0316C] in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Anselm, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Martin, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen, have subscribed. I, Guido, unworthy priest, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Vassalus, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0316D] 1137, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

CCLXVI. Bull for the monastery of Eleemosyna. (Year 1137, February 18.)

[Gallia Christiana, VIII, Instrument 422.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ OLRIC, abbot of the monastery of Eleemosyna, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to labour for the condition of the churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide salutarily for their peace and welfare. For it is recognized as worthy and fitting to honour [Col. 0317A] that we who have been raised to the governance of churches should protect them from the attacks of wicked persons and take care to foster them under the patronage of the Apostolic See of blessed Peter. Therefore, beloved son Olric, abbot in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing the monastery of Eleemosyna, over which you are known to preside by God’s authority. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that place now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, through the generosity of princes, grants of pontiffs, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s bounty, acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

And since monks and other religious men living in community ought to be supported by the alms [Col. 0317B] and beneficence of others, we likewise decree that no one may presume to demand or receive tithes from you from the produce which you cultivate at your own expense, or from your own livestock. Thus, the freer you are from the harassment and claims of ecclesiastical or secular persons, the more earnestly you may devote yourselves to divine service and take care humbly to offer your vows to almighty God in accordance with the observance of your monastic profession.
