### CCCLXII. Privilege for the church of Formbach.  
*(29 March 1139.)*

*[Monumenta Boica, IV, p. 130.]*

[Col. 0415A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DIETRICH, abbot of the church of Formbach, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The effect should follow a devout petition, so that faithful devotion may shine forth worthily and the benefit sought may unquestionably take effect. For this reason, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Dietrich, we graciously assent to your requests; and we receive under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the church of Formbach, freely founded by Counts Eckbert of blessed memory and his kinsman Udalric [Col. 0415B], over which, God being its author, you are known to preside. Confirming by apostolic authority the privileges of liberty granted to it, we establish by the tenor of this present writing that it shall be free from every service due to mortals and subject to the Roman pontiff alone.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting it, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: namely, the parish and market at Neunkirchen, with its tithes; the church [Col. 0415C] at Butten, with its tithes; the church at Antesin, with its tithes; the church at Echolsingen, with its tithes; likewise the market at Neunkirchen, with the mint and every profit that may arise from it; and whatever rights the same church ought to possess by the devotion of the aforesaid Counts Eckbert and Udalric, and of Herman their brother. In particular, we likewise confirm to you timber, pasture, buildings, and every use of the adjoining forest.

Moreover, consecrations of altars or churches and the ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders shall be received from the bishop of Passau, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to confer them upon you without improper dealing [Col. 0415D] and exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, may grant what you request.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraud or violence, except the person whom the brothers of that place by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers, shall elect for themselves according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected, moreover, shall not be invested except by receiving the staff from the altar. In like manner, an advocate from the family of the aforesaid counts, judged more suitable by the common decision and election of the brothers, shall be appointed; and if he proves unserviceable, you shall have authority to remove him and elect another in his place.

As a token [Col. 0416A] of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay to us and our successors one Byzantine coin every year as an annual due. Therefore let no person whatsoever presume rashly to disturb our aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any molestations; but let all things be preserved entire for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted.

If, therefore, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after having been warned a second and third time, and fails to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0416B], and be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But those who observe these provisions shall obtain the grace of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1139 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXIII. Privilege for the Abbey of Walburg.  
*(8 April 1139.)*

*[WURTWEIN, Nova Subsidia, vol. VII, p. 111, from the autograph in the archive of the episcopal seminary of Strasbourg.]*

[Col. 0416C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DITMABO, abbot of the monastery of the holy apostles Philip and James and of St Walpurga, virgin, situated in the diocese of Strasbourg near the Sacred Forest, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Since, by the office of the apostolate laid upon us by the Lord, we ought to have care for churches and ecclesiastical persons, it is fitting that we devote more earnest attention to those churches which belong by right to blessed Peter and are known specially to pertain to him. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Ditmar, we graciously assent to your reasonable requests, and receive under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Sacred Forest, over which, God being its author [Col. 0416D], you are known to preside; and we strengthen it by the privilege of the Apostolic See.

Following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Paschal, Calixtus, and Honorius, we decree that whatever possessions and goods the said monastery now justly and lawfully possesses—bestowed in devout generosity upon the same monastery by the noblemen and princes Duke Frederick and Peter, founders of that place, or by other faithful servants of God from their own right, or reasonably acquired in other ways—or may hereafter acquire, the Lord granting it, through grants of pontiffs, liberality of kings and princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

You shall peacefully possess, without objection from bishops or their ministers, from the brethren of Sals, or from any other persons, the tithes of your crops and animals which you cultivate or gather throughout all the land of the Sacred Forest or in other places by your own labour or expense [Col. 0417A]. Your peasants, however, shall freely render their tithes to the priests of the parishes to which they belong.

Furthermore, we confirm to you and your brothers serving in the same place the use of the Sacred Forest itself, both for building and for heating, at their pleasure; the use of its waters for fishing and for your own advantage; and its meadows for your animals throughout the forest, just as it is established that these were granted to you by the liberality of our aforesaid sons Emperor Henry, Duke Frederick his nephew, and Count Peter [Col. 0417B].

We also grant that burial in this place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. And so that you may serve almighty God more freely and fervently, we establish by the present ordinance that, when the nobleman Duke Frederick—who is now said to be your advocate—has died, no other advocate shall thereafter be appointed there except the one whom you or your successors, with the consent of all the brothers, determine ought to be appointed for the greatest advantage.

You shall receive consecrations of altars or churches and the ordinations of monks or clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See [Col. 0417C] and is willing to confer them freely and without any improper dealing. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, may grant what is requested.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraud or violence, except the person whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder party of the same community, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict; or, if no suitable person is found there—which God forbid—from another religious community.

We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them [Col. 0417D], or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved entire for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, and that the same monastery belongs by right to blessed Peter, you shall pay one Byzantine coin every year to us and our successors.

If, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after being warned a second or third time, and fails to amend the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, recognize himself or herself as guilty before divine judgment for the wrongdoing committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer [Col. 0418A], and be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But may all who preserve what is right for that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

I, Chrysogonus, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1139 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXIV. Bull concerning the immunity of the monastery of Bregenz.  
*(9 April 1139.)*

*[Gallia Christiana, V, Instrumenta, 515.]*

[Col. 0418B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GEBHARD, abbot of the monastery of Bregenz, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Placed, by the Lord’s ordering, upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to exercise attentive concern for the peace and welfare of churches, so that we who have been appointed to govern churches may both protect them from the wickedness of evil men and at the same time strengthen them by the defence of our protection. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Gebhard, with fatherly kindness we grant assent to the just requests of you and your brothers [Col. 0418C]. Following the example of our predecessors of holy memory, Gregory and Urban, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the guardianship and protection of the prince of the apostles himself the monastery of Bregenz, over which, God being its author, you preside, and which was offered to blessed Peter by the nobleman Count Udalric of blessed memory, by his wife Bertha, and by their sons, the founders of that place. By the page of this present privilege we strengthen it with all its appurtenances.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting it, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 0418D]. We decree that burial in the same place shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated, without prejudice to the rights of the mother church.

If, with the consent of bishops, God granting it, you are able to recover from laymen any tithes belonging to churches which you possess or may possess, we decree that they shall be permanently assigned to your use without any objection from bishops. By apostolic authority we prohibit the demanding from you of tithes from lands which you cultivate at your own expense. No objection of any bishop or provost shall prevent you from receiving into conversion laypersons or clerics fleeing the secular life.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors [Col. 0419A], no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraud or violence, except the one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder party of the brothers, shall elect for themselves according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict.

You shall receive consecrations of altars or churches, ordinations of clerics, chrism, holy oil, and the other things which pertain to the episcopal office from the bishop of Constance, in whose diocese you are situated, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide them freely and without improper dealing. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration; supported by our authority, he may grant what you request [Col. 0419B].

The abbot, moreover, together with the brothers, shall freely choose and appoint whatever advocate he wishes; if that advocate should prove unserviceable to the monastery, he shall remove him and appoint another over the same place.

Furthermore, so that the brothers of the aforesaid monastery may be able, without disturbance, more securely and carefully to pursue their purpose and render to almighty God the service of due devotion, we establish and forbid by apostolic authority that no priest, king, duke, count, or any great or small person shall presume to claim at that place any conditions of ownership—whether of hereditary right, advocacy, investiture, or any kind of authority—that may harm the liberty of the monastery; nor to seize, diminish, or alienate the ornaments or possessions of the church [Col. 0419C].

You therefore, beloved sons in Christ, ought to labour more diligently and devoutly in the observance of regular discipline; and the more free you are from secular tumults, the more earnestly you should strive, with all the powers of mind and body, to please the Lord—especially taking care to observe the venerable decrees of the Roman Church, by whose protection you are, the Lord granting it, secured from every yoke imposed by men. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay every year to us and our successors one gold coin, called a Byzantine. But if anyone with rash boldness should presume to do this [lacuna], let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. But those who observe these provisions shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and of the same apostles [Col. 0419D].

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul.  
I, Chrysogonus, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1139 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXV. Bull for the Abbey of Vangadizza.  
*(9 April 1139.)*

*[MITTARELLI, Annals of Camaldoli, III, p. 378.]*

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LITALD, abbot of the monastery of St Mary of Vangadizza, situated in the county of Montagnana upon the old Adige, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity [Col. 0420A].

The authority of the Apostolic See, over which by God’s ordering we preside, exhorts us to concern ourselves with the condition of churches and to establish with more earnest diligence those things arranged for their peace. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Litald, we graciously assent to your reasonable requests. We strengthen by the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Vangadizza, over which, by the Lord’s ordering, you are known to preside; it is established that it was built by Marquis Hugh of revered memory and endowed with liberty by our predecessors of holy memory, the Roman pontiffs Sylvester and Calixtus [Col. 0420B], as belonging by a special prerogative to the right of blessed Peter and the Holy Roman Church.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods the said monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire with the Lord’s help, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors for ever. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the abbey estate upon which the monastery is situated, with the parish church of St John; Vangadizza, with the church of St Michael; the estate called Salvaterra, with the church of St Antoninus; and Cavazzana, with the church of St Lawrence.

Within the city of Verona, the church of St Saviour with all its appurtenances; whatever possessions you have in Ilafe and Pardulino, and in any places whatsoever within the diocese of Verona [Col. 0420C]. In the diocese of Vicenza, the land of Albereto. In the diocese of Padua, the church of St Peter situated at Montagnana, with all its appurtenances; the estate of the valley of Aimeric, with the church of St Andrew. At Este, the churches of St Firminus and St Peter with their appurtenances; at Palso, the church of St Michael; possessions in the court of the estate and elsewhere in the same diocese. In the diocese of Adria, Venete, with the church of St Martin; Broxetum, with the church of St Zeno; at Castinacum, the church of St Sixtus; at Gorgano, the church of St Bartholomew; in the estate of Comeda, the church of St Peter; and whatever other possessions you have in the same diocese or county [Col. 0420D]. Possessions in the diocese of Ferrara; and, in the diocese of Bologna, the church of Saints Simon and Jude of Urbizano, with its appurtenances.

Finally, wishing to observe without any opposition the ordinances of our aforesaid predecessors, we decree that the monastery itself, placed under the protection of Roman pontiffs alone, shall remain entirely free from the lordship of other bishops, together with all the churches which it is now known to possess or shall hereafter justly acquire, and exempt from all synodal exactions. It shall be lawful for you and all your successors to possess peacefully your churches of every kind, with cemeteries, baptisteries, chapters, and synods, and to govern them through priests of your own, without objection from any bishop [Col. 0421A].

We establish with perpetual force that the promotion of your clerics, the consecration of churches, and the confirmation of infants living in your estates shall be performed, in reverence for the Apostolic See, by such Catholic bishops as you choose to invite, with no taint of venality intervening. Furthermore, priests appointed at any time in the parish churches of the monastery are, by the authority of the present privilege, granted permission to impose penances upon the people committed to them for public as well as secret offences [Col. 0421B].

Questions arising concerning marriages shall be subject to their care; and more difficult matters, so that they may be settled according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, shall be referred to you and your successors. It shall furthermore be your concern to receive holy chrism each year through your representatives from whichever Catholic bishop you choose, and to distribute it when received, according to custom, to the baptismal churches.

Indeed, out of regard for piety, we grant to you in full possession the tithe of the abbey estate, together with those of Vangadizza, Salvaterra, and Cavazzana, and also those which you have customarily received from ancient times from the territory of Broxetum. In the other aforesaid places, which have been cultivated at your own expense [Col. 0421C], you shall claim by our authority the tithes of your revenues.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraud or violence except the person whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder party of the brothers, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, whether from their own community or, if no suitable person should be found there—which God forbid—from another religious community. The one elected shall come to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

If, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after having been warned a second or third time [Col. 0421D], and fails to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour, recognize himself or herself as guilty before divine judgment for the wrongdoing committed, be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1139 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXVI. Privilege for the monastery of Baumburg.  
*(10 April 1139.)*

*[Monumenta Boica, II, p. 184.]*

[Col. 0422A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GOTSCHALK, provost of the church of St Margaret of Baumburg, and to his successors regularly promoted in perpetuity.

The character of a devout petition requires that we willingly grant assent to just petitions. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Provost Gotschalk, following the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Paschal and Honorius [Col. 0422B], we strengthen by the page of our writing the church of Blessed Margaret of Baumburg, over which, God being its author, you are known to preside.

We establish that whatever Count Berengar bestowed upon your aforesaid church out of devotion, and whatever possessions and goods the same place now justly and lawfully possesses, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: namely, Megenlingen with its appurtenances; Antwurthe, with its mill and one estate; Hochstet, with one estate; and Windeburch, with its appurtenances. Moreover, whatever it may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall be preserved peacefully and intact for you and your successors, saving the right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop [Col. 0422C].

We decree that no person whatsoever may presume rashly to disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved entire for the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Furthermore, because the church of St Margaret at Baumburg stands under the right and protection of St Peter the Apostle, we decree and permit by apostolic authority that you, beloved provost, and your successors may freely choose advocates. If at any time, led by a ruinous disposition, they prove not defenders or lawful guardians but disturbers of the church, oppressors of the poor, and invaders of your goods, we establish by the authority of blessed Peter and our own that, once they have been expelled and cast out, you may choose others, more worthy persons whom you know to be better suited to you and the Church [Col. 0422D].

As a token of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay one Byzantine coin every year to us and our successors. Upon the death of yourself, the present provost of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraud or violence, except the person whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder party of the brothers, shall canonically provide to be elected according to the fear of God.

Indeed, after making profession, none of you may possess private property or leave the cloister without the permission of the provost or community. By the authority of the Apostolic See, we also permit and confirm to your charity and that of your successors that you may receive ordinations of clerics and other sacraments from good and religious men if your bishop has been infected by simoniacal or another heretical perversity and does not enjoy the favour of the Apostolic See [Col. 0423A].

Moreover, so that you may serve the Lord Jesus Christ freely and exercise your life peacefully and without complaint in divine service, taking every care for your salvation, we decree that your servants, who serve you in your offices and at your court, shall, without any harassment or vexation by that place, hear the word of God and Masses as parishioners in the church, receive the sacraments, and be subject to the other divine laws.

We grant to you and your successors, without objection from episcopal ministers, the right to possess the tithes of your newly cleared lands, so that, through the Lord’s gift, you may remain for ever in peace in the office you have undertaken. Indeed, no cleric or layperson whatsoever shall demand tithes from you on the produce of your labours, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals [Col. 0423B].

If, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after having been warned a second or third time and failing to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour, recognize himself or herself as guilty before divine judgment for the wrongdoing committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But may all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace [Col. 0423C]. Amen.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1139 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXVII. He takes the monastery of Reinhardsborn under protection and confirms its goods.  
*(10 April 1139.)*

*[Thuringia sacra, 210.]*

### CCCLXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of St Lambert in the valley of the Salz, in the diocese of Salzburg, of the Order of St Benedict.  
*(11 April 1139.)*

*[COCQUELINES III, p. 242.]*

[Col. 0423D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUNTHER, abbot of the monastery of St Lambert the martyr, situated in the diocese of Salzburg, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The clemency of the Apostolic See befits the granting of the protection of maternal affection to all who implore its aid. As we have learned from the writings of our predecessor Pope Sylvester of blessed memory, Count Acribo, formerly, for the remedy of his own soul and of those of his parents, built, out of devotion, a monastery in honour of Saint Lampert the martyr upon a place belonging to him, which was once called Burgili but is now called Serva by its inhabitants. For the increase of his salvation and reward, through the intervention of Otto III, Augustus and emperor of glorious memory, he caused that same place, offered to blessed Peter, to be strengthened by an apostolic privilege. Therefore, following in his footsteps, we grant assent to your petitions, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Gunther, and by the text of this present privilege protect the monastery of Saint Lampert; decreeing that whatever possessions and goods it now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favour, acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other reasonable means, shall remain secure to you and your successors. [Col. 0424A]

Moreover, when you, the present abbot of the same place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, provide to preside over them. We further add that no one may usurp the advocacy of that monastery; rather, at your discretion, you may freely choose for yourselves a suitable person as advocate. If he proves unserviceable to your monastery, you shall have leave, without anyone’s objection, to remove him and appoint another in his place.

We therefore decree that no ecclesiastical or secular person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery on account of this our confirmation and grant, or take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any other injuries; but that all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall annually pay twelve denarii to us and our successors. Likewise, according to the ordinance of our aforesaid predecessor, one collect shall be said every day at Mass for the Roman pontiff reigning at the time, and similarly for the dead. [Col. 0424B–C]

We further enact that none of your brethren, after making profession in the same monastery, may transfer to another place without permission of his superior. If anyone departs and, having been canonically warned, refuses to return, you shall nevertheless have authority to exclude him from the divine offices; and no bishop or abbot shall dare receive or retain one so excluded. If anyone in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the Last Judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of this church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0424D–0425A]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1134.

> [Note: Read 1139, so that this year may agree with the other chronological data appended; for it is easier to suppose that, through the copyist’s carelessness, an error crept into this one datum than into all the others. Col. 0425D–0426D.]

In the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXIX. Confirmation of the goods of the monastery of Prüfening, in the diocese of Regensburg.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 11.)*

[COCQUELINES, II, p. 241.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ERBO, abbot of the monastery of Prüfening, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Just as no effect should be granted to those who seek unjust things, so the petition of those who desire lawful things ought not be delayed. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Erbo, we graciously assent to your petitions; we receive the monastery of Prüfening, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, under the protection of the Apostolic See; and we fortify it by the text of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favour, acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit expressly to name the villages or estates which our venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, granted to that monastery: Gebernebach, Munnebach, Malistorff, Stainloch, Ahebach, Oberdorff, Grassolfing, Hemburch, Neunkirchen, Dietpurgerreut, and Vittenreut, with their appurtenances. [Col. 0425B–C] We further forbid the aforesaid bishop, or any of his successors, to alienate or diminish the aforesaid properties already granted, or to be granted hereafter, to the same monastery.

We decree that, since you lead a common life and ought to live upon the alms and beneficence of others, no one may presume to demand or receive tithes from you for those whom you gather at your own expense. We also enact that the monastic order which is known to have been established in that monastery according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and your observance shall be preserved there forever in times to come. We further establish that none of your brethren, after making profession in that monastery, may go to another place without the permission of his superior. [Col. 0425D]

Accordingly, no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away or diminish its possessions, or harass it with any injuries; but all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; and let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. But those who observe these things shall obtain the grace of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen. [Col. 0426A]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints George and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Susanna, have subscribed.  
I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Vassallo, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa, have subscribed. [Col. 0426B]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor, on the third Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130, in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXX. Confirms the rights and possessions of the monastery of Murbach.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 11.)*

[SCHOEPFLIN, *Alsatia diplomatica*, I, p. 219.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERTULF, abbot of Murbach, and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetual remembrance.

The ancient custom and dignity of the most holy Roman Church require it to provide the help of fitting protection to all who implore its aid. Nor is there doubt that, if we yield to the petitions of religious men, we shall without doubt find the Lord gracious toward our own petitions. With this in view, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Bertulf, we grant paternal assent to your desires and fortify the monastery of Murbach, over which by God’s appointment you are known to preside, by the text of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods this venerable place now justly and canonically possesses—whether in colleges, provostships, churches, tithes, or any other properties—which Everard, founder of the monastery, and other faithful men granted to that abbey, and whatever it may hereafter, through God’s providence, acquire by grants of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just titles, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 0426C–D]

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid abbey because of this our confirmation, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last examination let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 0427A–B]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina.  
I, Suido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul.  
I, Chrysogonus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes.  
I, Ivo, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence, of the title of Saint Damasus. [Col. 0427B–C]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXXII. Privilege for the monastery of Kastl.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 11.)*

[*Monumenta Boica*, XXIV, p. 314.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son OTTO, abbot of the monastery of Kastl, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The course of a pious petition requires that we willingly grant assent to just requests. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Otto, we graciously assent to your reasonable petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor, Pope Paschal of holy memory, we fortify by this present privilege the monastery of Kastl, founded on their allodial land by the noble men Berengar, Frederick and his son Otto, together with Countess Siutgarda, and offered by them to blessed Peter. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same place now canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s bounty, justly and canonically acquire through grants of popes, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall be preserved secure and entire to you and your successors. [Col. 0427D–0428A]

When you, the present abbot of the same place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be placed over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect from their own community, if they find someone worthy, or from another community if necessary, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. The abbot, with the brethren, shall appoint for himself the advocate he judges more useful. If that person later proves unserviceable to the monastery and burdensome to the brethren, they shall remove him and appoint another.

The brethren of the same place shall receive holy oil, the consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks to be advanced to holy orders from the bishop in whose diocese they are situated, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these things freely and without corruption. Otherwise, they may approach whichever Catholic bishop they prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration. Supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he shall grant what is requested. [Col. 0428B]

By the dispensation of blessed Peter and with our support, the abbot shall have permission and authority to preach; to receive penitents, care for them, bind and loose them; to visit the sick; to bury in the same place the dead from whatever place they come; and to remit all offences, both for the living and the dead. No one may be placed over the churches granted to the aforesaid monastery—namely Loviterhoven, Phapenhoven, Heswanc, Furhenriet, and any others now existing within the bounds of these churches or to be built in the future—except by the will of the abbot or monks of the same place. [Col. 0428C]

For the consolation of the brethren and their fixed maintenance, we likewise confirm to you the tithes within all the boundaries and districts of these churches, whether from noblemen or poor persons, from all lands, revenues, and newly cleared lands, which you have acquired through the intervention of the aforesaid noblemen and with the assent of Ulrich, bishop of Eichstätt, or may already have acquired or hereafter be able to acquire by the consent of bishops. And, under anathema, we forbid any bishop, cleric, layperson, or any other person to presume to trouble you concerning these matters.

We also forbid anyone whatsoever to impose new exactions, to demand tithes from you for labours which you cultivate at your own expense, rashly to disturb your monastery, to take away or retain its possessions, diminish them, or harass it by any other injuries. Rather, all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted. [Col. 0428D]

None of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, may transfer to another place without permission of his superior. If anyone departs and, after canonical warning, refuses to return, you shall nevertheless have authority to exclude him from the divine offices; and no bishop or abbot shall dare receive or retain one so excluded. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, after each three-year period you shall pay three gold bezants to the Lateran palace. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes amends by fitting satisfaction, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last examination let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 0429A–B]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1109.

> [Note: A striking error, since Innocent II was first raised to the papal dignity in the year 1130.]

In the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXXIV. Privilege for the abbey of Saint Saviour of Carracedo.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 11.)*

[YEPÈS, *Corónica general*, etc., vol. V, p. 450.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son FLORENTIUS, abbot of Saint Saviour of Carracedo, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

A petition of pious will ought to be fulfilled by an answering result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly take effect. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Florentius, we grant paternal assent to your just petitions and fortify by the authority of this present privilege the Church of Saint Saviour of Carracedo, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favour, acquire through grants of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the fodder of your animals. We have specifically thought fit to confirm to you those possessions which Sanctia Germana, sister of the illustrious Alfonso, king of the Spains, held by hereditary right at Carracedo, and which, with all their appurtenances, she granted and confirmed in writing to your church in perpetuity. [Col. 0429D–0430A]

No one who wishes to remain in communion with the holy Roman Church may presume in any manner to impose a forced service (*angaria*), a carriage-service (*parangaria*), or a burden upon your church; to levy an assessment upon it; or to seek from it tribute, fodrum, or any extraordinary service. When you, the present abbot of the same place, die, no abbot shall be chosen there by deception or by the violence of any person. Rather, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the person whom the whole concordant community, or the sounder part of its counsel, chooses shall be put forward once elected and, when presented to the diocesan bishop, shall be consecrated and blessed by him freely and without corruption. [Col. 0430A–B]

Whoever wishes to enter your monastery for the remission of his sins and receives your habit or makes profession shall have full freedom to do so. We also grant to all founders of your church free burial there, without anyone’s objection. You shall receive the ordinations of your brethren and the consecrations of churches or altars from the diocesan bishop, if he enjoys the favour of the Roman Church and is willing to provide them freely and without corruption; otherwise, you may receive authorization from whichever bishop you prefer, provided that he is Catholic.

We decree, therefore, that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any injuries; but that all things shall be preserved entirely for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the judgment. [Col. 0430C–D] But upon all who preserve their rights to that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor, on the third Ides of April, in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aymeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, in the second indiction, in the ninth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXXVI. Receives the monastery of Saint Gall under protection and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 12.)*

[ZAPF, *Monumenta anecdota Germaniae*, vol. I, p. 88.—Original parchment in the archives of the princely abbey of Saint Gall; copy at Zug in the Zur-Laub Library, vol. I of Swiss charters from the seventh century, pp. 552–553, manuscript in folio.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WARNER,

> [Note: The notes of the Necrology of Saint Gall state concerning him: “On the sixth day before the Nones of July died Warner, our abbot. Elected by common suffrages, he began to hold the helm of the monastery in 1135. At first stricter toward his own men, but finally changing austerity into kindness, he himself was not merely a diligent cultivator of virtues, but also promoted, to the extent of his ability, the welfare of the monastery. He founded and endowed the provostship of Saint Leonard in the suburb of Saint Gall. By his authority and generosity there were also founded the monastery, or college, of regular canons of Saint Augustine at Ittingen, and another house of nuns there as well. He died in 1167.” Burkard says much concerning him in *On the Vicissitudes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chap. 9, p. 71, in Goldast, *Writers on Alemannic Affairs*, vol. I, part I, Frankfurt, 1661, folio. Col. 0431D.]

abbot of Saint Gall, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Although, by the office of apostolic ministry imposed upon us by God and by goodwill, we are debtors to all the faithful, we ought nevertheless to give more attentive care to those, and preserve justice for the churches entrusted to them, whom it is evident specially belong to the Apostolic See and are its property. With this in view, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Warner, we graciously assent to your petitions and, following the example of our predecessor Pope John XIII of good memory, protect by this present document the monastery of Saint Gall, over which by God’s appointment you preside. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favour, acquire through gifts of kings, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 0431B–C]

We further add that the liberties and prerogatives which Burkhard, formerly the administrator of that place, obtained from the Apostolic See through the privileges of our predecessors of pious memory shall be kept inviolate for you and your successors.

> [Note: In 968 Abbot Burchard of Saint Gall obtained a bull from John XIII, which bull is still preserved in the archives of that abbey. Col. 0431D.]

That is: no ecclesiastical or secular power, nor any person of whatever condition or order, may presume to enter that monastery against the will of the abbot and brethren; nor dare impose unlawful exactions or customs upon any churches, tithes, estates, or any possessions belonging to that venerable place; nor by any contrivance presume to forbid the divine office in the aforesaid monastery. Rather, as that monastery has remained in its liberty from ancient times up to the present, so may it remain forever under the protection of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0432A]

We also enact that the monastery shall never be compelled to render to anyone the tithes and possessions which the advocate of that place is able to vindicate or confirm for the monastery by sufficient witnesses or by his oath.

> [Note: The advocate of the monastery at this time was Count Ulrich of Gameringa or Gamertinga—now a town near Veringen. When he died there with his son, Abbot Warner recovered the advocacy for the monastery as a pledge, so that thereafter the election of the advocate lay with the abbot, although the monastery was not thereby without an advocate. Later, for better and stronger protection, the same abbot chose Count Rudolph of Psullendorf as his advocate, receiving from him 300 marks of silver. In 1167, intending to go to Jerusalem and to devote himself to divine service at the Lord’s Sepulchre, Rudolph renounced the advocacy. Abbot Warner granted it to Count Rudolph of Habsburg, by authentic letters which still survive in the archives of the abbey of Saint Gall. Col. 0432D.]

We therefore decree that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery on account of this our grant and confirmation, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any other injuries. Rather, all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes fitting satisfaction, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last examination let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to that abbey, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 0432B–C]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II. [Col. 0432D–0433A]

> [Note: On 12 April 1139 the second indiction was current, as was the tenth year of the pontificate of Innocent III, elected in February 1130. This bull is sealed with a hanging lead seal.]

### CCCLXXVII. Confirms certain rights of the monastery of Ursberg.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 12.)*

[LANG, *Regesta*, I, 153.]

### CCCLXXVIII. Privilege for the abbey of Admont.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 13.)*

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, III, 661.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GOTEFRID, abbot of the monastery called Admont, situated in the parish of Salzburg, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Although, by the office of apostolic ministry imposed upon us by God, we are debtors to all churches and ecclesiastical persons, we ought nevertheless to cherish with greater paternal affection those who, setting aside worldly matters, have bound themselves more closely to the service of almighty God. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Gotefrid, we graciously assent to your reasonable petitions; receive under the protection and guardianship of the Apostolic See the monastery of Admont, over which by God’s appointment you preside; and fortify it by the text of this present document. It is known to have been built within his diocese and enriched with many goods by our venerable brother Gebhard, archbishop of Salzburg, of blessed memory. [Col. 0433B]

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods were granted by the aforesaid Archbishop Gebhard, by his successor Archbishop Thiemo, or by other faithful servants of God, whether in tithes or grants of other lands, and whatever may hereafter be offered in lands, vineyards, or any other possessions, or acquired by the same abbey through any grant of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, we confirm to you by the text of this present document. Neither the bishop nor the abbot himself nor anyone else may, without the consent of the better and more discerning brethren, give the goods of that abbey to anyone in fief or benefice, or alienate them in any other way. [Col. 0433C]

We decree that the burial-place of that monastery shall be free, so that no one may oppose the last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. No objection of bishop or provost shall prevent you from receiving laymen or secular clerics for conversion. Furthermore, we strengthen by apostolic privilege for you the hospice built at Friesach by our venerable brother Chunrad and granted to the abbey of Admont, with tithes at Modinizze, both old and new, and with all other appurtenances, whether *patellis* [uncertain], woods, lands, serfs, exchanges, or lawful gifts. [Col. 0433D]

When you, the present abbot of the same place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be put over it through any cunning of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall judge should be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

No one whatsoever may rashly disturb that abbey, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the archbishop of Salzburg. Yet he shall by no means be permitted to impose upon it any vexation or custom injurious to the peace of regulars. [Col. 0434A]

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes fitting satisfaction, let him forfeit the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last examination let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 0434B]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Theodewin, cardinal bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed.  
I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed.  
I, Chrysogonus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed. [Col. 0434C]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Blessed Martin at Muri.  
*(A.D. 1139, April 13.)*

[HERRGOTT, *Genealogia diplomatica Hasburgica*, II, p. 161.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROZELIN, abbot of the monastery of Muri, situated in the diocese of Constance in the district of Aargau and known to be dedicated in honour of blessed Martin, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity. [Col. 0434D]

The pious request of a will ought to be fulfilled by its consequent effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may unquestionably acquire strength. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Rozelin, graciously assenting to your reasonable petitions, we fortify by the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of Muri, over which, by the Lord’s authority, you preside. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or by other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you in perpetuity.

We also confirm to you [Col. 0435A] whatever has been bestowed upon that place by our brother Count Werner of Habsburg [Note: [Col. 0435D] Werner, Count of Habsburg, whom Pope Innocent II calls “our brother,” was bishop of Strasbourg. Stumph asserts that he was descended from the house of Froburg: *Chronicle of Switzerland*, book XII, chapter 25, p. 392. His name recurs in document no. 220.], and by their kinsmen, who are known to have founded that monastery from their own property; and they wholly strengthened it by the bond of apostolic authority, should anyone, in rash audacity, wish to violate what they themselves had done with great devotion.

Moreover, you may appoint an advocate for the benefit and service of your house; and no one shall at any time be appointed there except one whom you, by the common counsel of your brethren, have decided to elect. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the council, according to [Col. 0435B] the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, shall have judged to be elected.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and government they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, duke, margrave, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed [Col. 0435C], and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that place, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Lucas, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. I, Grisogonus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Almeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0435D] 1139, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent II.

### CCCLXXX. He receives the Church of Basel under protection and confirms its property and privileges, at the request of Bishop Orthlieb.  
*(Year 1139, 14 April.)*

[HERRGOTT, cited above, p. 162, from a manuscript diplomatic codex of the Church of Basel, p. 61.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ORTHLIEB, [Note: [Col. 0435D] Orthlieb, bishop of Basel named here, [Col. 0436D] is said by Stumph to have been descended from the house of Froburg: *Chronicle of Switzerland*, book XII, chapter 25, p. 392. His name recurs in document no. 220.] bishop of Basel, [Col. 0436A] and to all his successors canonically entering office, for ever.

By the Lord’s ordering, we have been placed in the seat of equity and justice so that, with God’s aid, we may beneficially provide for the welfare and tranquillity of churches and, lest they be wearied by the vexations of wicked men, may take care to give them the attention of paternal solicitude. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and receive under the protection of Saint Peter and of ourselves your church, over which, God willing, you preside, together with all its appurtenances. We fortify it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future [Col. 0436B] acquire, the Lord granting it, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or by other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these, we have judged the following to be expressly named: the place itself on which the aforesaid church has been built, with all its appurtenances; a fourth part of the tithes in the bishopric of Basel and in the county of Breisgau; all hunting rights and silver mines, whether already discovered or yet to be discovered; the cloister of Salzburg with all its appurtenances; the estate of Haltingen with its church; the estate of Hystein; Winstat; the estate of Chilcoven with its church and daughter churches, namely Stouffen with the whole tithe, Amperingen, Oeristetten, and Offmenningen; the churches [Col. 0436C] of Merdingen with its daughter church; the estate of Opfingen; the estate of Untkilche with its church and daughter churches, namely Gottenheim and the other chapels belonging to it; the church of Leheim; the church of Zeringen; the estate of Bichinsol with its church and daughter church; the estate of Bichocvingen with its church and its daughter church Bergen, and all its other appurtenances; the church of Breisach with its church and daughter church Hostat, and one estate in that same village; the castle of Usenberg with the whole of Augia; Mount Eggehardi; and the church of Achheim with all its appurtenances.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb you or your church on account of this our constitution, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with unlawful vexations; but that all things shall be preserved wholly [Col. 0436D] for your benefit in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of your metropolitan. If anyone in the future, knowing the tenor of this our decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable amendment, let him incur the indignation of God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and be subject to excommunication. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that church, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 0437A] and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Lamerit, [Note: [Col. 0437D] We count Lamerit, the chancellor, among the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, since Roman pontiffs from the time of Leo IX were accustomed in bulls to employ the chancellor’s name with the designation of cardinal deacon or cardinal priest, and sometimes the bare title “chancellor,” beneath which the dignity of cardinal was concealed. Compare Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book II, chapter 13, pp. 125–126.] chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, in the tenth year of the pontificate of lord Innocent.

### CCCLXXXI. He receives the monastery of Saint George in the Black Forest under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Year 1139, 14 April.)*

[GERBERT, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. III, p. 72.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, abbot of the monastery of Saint George, situated in the Black Forest beside the River Brigach, [Col. 0437B] and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetual remembrance.

It accords with the clemency of the Apostolic See to cherish religious and holy places, and with paternal solicitude to provide for their peace and advantage, so that, just as through divine clemency we are called fathers among God’s people, so through God’s grace we may be shown such by our deeds. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot John, we grant apostolic assent to your and your brethren’s desires. Following the example of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban, we receive under the guardianship and protection of the prince of the apostles the monastery of Saint George, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. It was indeed bestowed upon blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by the noblemen Hezelo and Hesso, founders of that house. We strengthen the monastery itself, with everything belonging to it, by the force of this present document.

We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods have been bestowed upon that monastery by the aforesaid men or by other faithful persons, and whatever in the future the same place may justly and canonically acquire by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have judged the following to be expressly named: the village called Stetten; one third of the village of Phiezen; estates in the places called Cambit and Flausingen; the villages of Walda and Eckha, Degernauw, Ingeltingen, and Eystetten; [Col. 0437C–D] the estates of Onningen, Leidringen, Degewingen, Magerben, Wluolingen, Baltrameshoven, Tindenhoven, Gugenwaldt, Achara, Schlatta, Betechoven, Gruningen, Schweningen, Aseheim, Embach, Arnoldesbach, Mulnheim, Drudenheim, Altheim, Endingen, Schopfsheim, Butenheim, Eggeholdesheim, and Steneneswilare; the cell of Luchesheim with its appurtenances; likewise the estate of Megenhelmeswilare, in which is also the cell called Saint John’s; the cell situated on the estate called Fridinwillare, which was exchanged by lawful exchange with the Church of Reichenau; [Col. 0438A] and the cell of Ambtenhusen.

We also permit the church in the place called Vokhenusen to be held permanently under the charge of you, your successors, and the brethren. The tithes of all things proceeding from the forest belonging to that cell, or from neighbouring places otherwise already belonging to it, shall accrue wholly to your and the brethren’s use, as was established by the venerable Bishop Gebehard.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, ordinations, consecrations of altars or churches, and any other sacred rites from the bishop of Constance, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to confer them freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer [Col. 0438B] and receive from him the sacred rites of consecration. We decree that the burial place of the aforesaid monastery and of its cells shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common assent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s council, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. No ecclesiastical or secular person shall have licence in the aforesaid monastery to claim for himself any condition of ownership, hereditary right, advocacy, or usurpation of any authority harmful to the liberty of that place; nor may anyone take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them with unlawful vexations. Rather, all things shall be kept intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose preservation they were granted.

Furthermore, we grant you the entirely free power, by common consent, to appoint an advocate; if he proves useless to the monastery, you may remove him and appoint another suitable person in his place. As a token of this liberty received from the Holy Roman See, you shall pay one Byzantine coin each year to us and our successors. If anyone in the future, knowing the tenor of this our decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable amendment [Col. 0438C–D], let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. But those who preserve these provisions shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aymeric, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s [Col. 0439A] Incarnation 1139, in the second indiction, in the tenth year of the pontificate of lord Innocent II.

### CCCLXXXII. Privilege for the abbey of Saint Stephen of Dijon.  
*(Year 1139, 14 April.)*

[PERARD, *Recueil*, etc., p. 109.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HEBERT, abbot of the church of blessed Stephen, protomartyr, and to his successors regularly appointed, for ever.

Care for venerable places admonishes us to give diligent thought to their peace and tranquillity, so that we who, by the disposing divine clemency, have been raised to the governance of churches may both protect them from the wickedness of evil men and strengthen them by the privilege of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Hebert, with paternal kindness we grant assent to your just desires and strengthen, by the support of this present document, the church of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, together with all its appurtenances.

First, we decree that the canonical order established in that church according to the Rule of blessed Augustine . . . shall be observed there inviolate for all future time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same place now justly and canonically possesses in buildings, lands, churches, chapels, villages, male and female serfs, or other property, or may in future acquire, God being favourable, by grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings [Col. 0439B–C] of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named: namely, the mother church dedicated in honour of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, with the cemetery within the castle wall; the church of Saint Medard with its tithes; the church of Saint Michael, situated outside the wall, with cemetery and tithes; the church of Saint Anianus of Aquaeductus, with cemetery, tithes, and its lands; the church of Saint Martin of Quincey, with cemetery, tithes, and its lands; the church of Saint Maurice of Siliciac, with cemetery, tithes, and its lands; the right which you have in the church of Saint Genesius of Dearilla and in the chapel of Stabiclis, with cemetery and a share of the tithes; [Col. 0439D] the church of Saint Martin of Prato, with the chapel of Fontanis, their cemetery, and appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Gimellis, with the chapel of Picangis, cemetery, lands, and tithes; the church of Saint Florentius of Tylecastro, with the chapel of Saint Mary and their cemetery, tithes, lands, and appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Mirebeau, with its cemetery, tithes, lands, and appurtenances; the tithe of Geac; the tithe of Curey; the site of the chapel between Leuglerium and Saint Fidolium, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Andrew of Ormentiac, with chapels, cemetery, and the share of tithes belonging to the parish priesthood; the site of Puteol; the site of Annin Fountain, with its appurtenances; the site of Galdo Alirey, with [Col. 0440A] its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Archo, with cemetery and its appurtenances; the site of Mount Cyniaco, with its appurtenances; the site of Francis, with its appurtenances; the site of Bonavalle Jurensi, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Germanus of Copiac and the chapel of Saint Andrew of Parriniac, with tithes; the chapel of Saint Mary of Marcennac, with their cemeteries and lands; and your right in the church of Saviniac, with cemetery and one half of the tithes and lands.

By this present decree we also enact that, upon the death of Garnerius, provost of that place, or of the other secular canons, no one except a regular provost or likewise a regular canon shall be substituted for them. Upon the death of you, abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren, or the sounder part of their council, shall judge to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

We also prohibit anyone within the boundaries of the parishes of that church from presuming to construct or consecrate a church, chapel, or cemetery. Further, we enact that the regular canons of the aforesaid church shall freely and without contradiction undertake the care and administration of the parish churches and, with the Lord’s assistance, provide for the salvation of the souls committed to them. No one of your canons may, after having made profession in that church, leave it or transfer to another place without the abbot’s or the brethren’s permission; and no bishop or abbot may presume to receive or retain those who leave. [Col. 0440B–C]

Furthermore, by apostolic authority, according to what we have decreed in general councils, we forbid tithes to be demanded from you from the produce which you gather by your own hands and at your own expense, or from the maintenance of your animals. By this present decree we also enact that you shall freely possess the burial of your parishioners, unless some of them have decided to be buried in other churches.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church on account of this our constitution, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose government and support they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable amendment, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.
