We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, seize its possessions, retain possessions seized, diminish them, or harass it in any manner; rather, all shall be preserved [Col. 0601D] whole and unimpaired for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, indeed, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, after a second or third warning, does not correct his or her offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person suffer loss of authority and office; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0602A] I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Gerard, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October], in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXXXVI. At the request of Abbot Alehotf, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of the Saviour and St Boniface of Fulda. (Year 1142, 15 November.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 391.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALOLF, abbot of the monastery of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of St Boniface, situated [Col. 0602B] beside the bank of the river called Fulda, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Although, by the apostolic office entrusted to us by God, we are indebted to all God’s faithful, we ought nevertheless to apply ourselves with a more devoted zeal of charity to those places and persons known especially to belong to the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Alolf, we mercifully assent to your reasonable petitions and fortify with the privilege of the Holy Roman Church the monastery of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, [Col. 0602C] or may in future, with the Lord’s assistance, acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record by their own names: namely, the monastery of St Andrew the Apostle, called Exaiulum, situated at Rome beside the church of St Mary, ever-Virgin Mother of God, called *ad Praesepe* (“at the Manger”), which Pope Leo, our predecessor of happy memory, granted out of affection to your predecessor, the religious Abbot Hecbert; together with all its chambers, dwellings, cells, wine-stores, and kitchen; vineyards, gardens, and diverse kinds of fruit trees; a court and well; entrance through the principal gate from the public road; and everything generally belonging to that monastery, whether situated within or outside the city, which is known justly and properly to belong to it.

We prohibit every priest of any church from holding any jurisdiction or authority in your aforesaid monastery of Fulda apart from our apostolic see. This prohibition applies particularly to the bishop in whose diocese it is known to be built: unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, he may not presume even to celebrate there the solemnities of Mass. Furthermore, we decree that the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful shall remain perpetually secure to that monastery without opposition from any person. We also forbid any woman ever to presume to enter there, and forbid anyone ever [Col. 0603A] to hold a court there or in its other places, or to compel its slaves or tenants to any service, except one to whom the abbot has granted consent for the benefit of his own need.

On the death of you, now abbot of that place, no one may be set over it through the cunning of any fraudulent scheme or by violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, elect according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. We further decree that at appropriate times notice shall be given to our ecclesiastical solicitude concerning how monastic religion among the brethren entrusted to your governance is being guided by regular observance and devoted to concord through suitable ecclesiastical diligence, lest—God forbid—under the pretext of this privilege the mind and steps of your uprightness should in any way be turned aside from the norm of justice.

[Col. 0603B] We also grant you, dearest son, authority from our apostolic office to preach the word of God; and we grant that both you and your successors shall hold primacy before all other abbots of Gaul or Germany in every place and assembly. We also grant your affection, from the kindness of the apostolic see and in accordance with what is contained in the privileges of our predecessors, the use of the dalmatic and sandals in the solemnities of Mass. Further, because of the greater prerogative of intimacy which you have deserved to attain in the Holy Roman Church in our time, we likewise grant to you and your successors permission to use the mitre and ring. The abbot may be blessed only by our see, by which he ought to be blessed. If he is accused of any crime, the judgment of that Roman see alone shall be carried out.

[Col. 0603C] We have moreover judged it fitting to add generally that whatever is certainly known to have been granted to the monastery of Fulda by the authority of our predecessors, kings, or emperors shall also be confirmed by our apostolic authority through the page of this writing. Therefore no person whatsoever may, etc., as in the privilege of the year 1137 above, through “find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.”

(Seal.) I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. (Bene valete.) I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina. I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina. I, Guido, unworthy priest of the Holy Roman Church. [Col. 0603D] I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Pastor. I, Thomas, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Humbald, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in Carcere. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Agro. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Porticu.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Gerard, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 0604A] on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December [15 November], in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXXXVII. He informs I[erome], prior of the Church of St Frigdianus at Lucca, that he has been elected bishop by the clergy and laity of the Church of Arezzo summoned to Rome. He urges him to assume the episcopate. (Year 1142, 22 November.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, IV, p. 592.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son I., prior of St Frigdianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Church of Arezzo, deprived of a shepherd, laboured for some time over an election because, as commonly happens in such cases, the votes of the factions [Col. 0604B] had divided among different persons and it could not itself agree upon an honourable and religious person. Since, by the apostolic office entrusted to us by God, it is our concern to have care for all churches and to provide for all with paternal solicitude, we summoned before our presence the weightier and more honourable persons of that church—both clergy and laity—acting on behalf of the whole community, and we took care to recall them to unity and concord through ourselves and our brethren. Therefore, inspired by Him from whom comes every good thing and without whom we can do no good, they agreed upon you, beloved son in the Lord; and, in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, the provost, archdeacon, abbots, and other clergy, together with the consuls [Col. 0604C] and judges who had come with them, unanimously and concordantly elected you as their shepherd and bishop.

Therefore, because a servant of Christ ought not to place his own seclusion—*secretum* in the source, marked *sic*—before the advantage of his neighbours, since the Father’s Only-Begotten himself came forth from the bosom of the Father into our public sphere in order to benefit many, we command you by this present writing, and in commanding require you under obedience, to accept, trusting in God’s mercy, the governance of the Church of Arezzo, to which you have been called by the Lord’s disposition, and to endeavour to benefit not yourself alone but also the people entrusted to you by God.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November].

### DXXXVIII. Privilege for the Church of Belley. (Year 1142, 4 December.)

[*Gallia Christiana vetus*, II, p. 361.]

[Col. 0604D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Belley, and to his successors to be canonically appointed in perpetuity.

A petition of pious will ought to be carried through to effective fulfilment, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may assuredly gain force. Therefore, beloved brother in the Lord, Bishop William, we mercifully assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of St John the Baptist at Belley, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and we fortify it with the privilege of this present [Col. 0605A] writing.

First, we decree that, as has been established in the presence of the brethren of Portes by your discretion, brother bishop, with the assent of the stronger and sounder part of the brethren of that church, the same Church of Belley shall be ordered according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Henceforth no one but a regular canon shall be appointed there. The regular canons shall have the use and administration of all the goods of that church, except for three obediences—namely those of Belley, Veron, and the one at Motte. Their revenues shall be divided into twenty-four portions, and each secular shall receive one of them; the rest shall be applied to the uses of the regular canons. When the secular holders of the aforesaid obediences die, the obediences shall revert to the administration of the [Col. 0605B] regular canons; they shall nevertheless pay the customary revenue in common. On the death of you, the present bishop of that city, no one except a bishop of a regular order shall be elected there.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods you presently justly and canonically possess, or may in future acquire by lawful means with God’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors . . . and to that church. Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: episcopal right, namely in the churches of Pont; in the church of Dombalin; of St John; of Avelan; and of Avaut; in the church of St Benignus; of St Albinus; and the estate of Bredoria; of St John of Verel; and of Oncin; and of Boschia; of Aquabella; of Lepin; of Dullin; of Ain; of St [Col. 0605C] Franco; of Palude; of St Andrew; of Festileu; of Pressin; of Romanc; of Chimilino; of Corbelino; of Favergiis; of St Symphorian; of Avolin; of St Martin; of Amonstro; and of Coesin. In the archbishopric of Lyons: the churches of Izernore; lands there; the church of Genriscio; the church of Nato with its appurtenances; and the church of Pulley. In the archbishopric of Besançon: the church of Savineo and that of Sarruniaco.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, seize its possessions, retain possessions seized, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; rather, all shall be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. [Col. 0605D] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, after a second or third warning, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of authority and office; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; [Col. 0606A] and at the last judgment let that person be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[The supplied source ends here.]

I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina; Stephen, bishop of Palestrina; Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil; Aymar, bishop of Tusculum; Guy, unworthy priest of the holy Roman Church; Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus; Thomas, cardinal priest of the title, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the Roman Church, [Col. 0606B] on the day before the Nones of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXXXIX. He adorns Arnulf, second provost of Sonnebec, of the Order of Saint Augustine in the diocese of Thérouanne, with abbatial dignity, and confirms the privileges of his monastery.  
*(1142, December 5.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, II, p. 1163.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ARNULF, abbot of Sonnebec, and his brethren, both present and those to be appointed in the future, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0606C] It befits the clemency of apostolic governance to cherish religious persons and to fortify their places by pious protection. For it is recognized as worthy and consonant with propriety that we, who have been raised to the governance of Churches, should protect them from the malice of wicked men and foster them through the patronage of the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-Virgin, in which you are dedicated to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

We further decree that the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institution of the brethren of Arrouaise shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

[Note: [Col. 0605D] Aridagamantia, now Arouaise, an abbey of regular canons in Artois, was formerly the head of a famous congregation, to which Sonnebec also belonged. The first founder of the abbey of Blessed Mary of Sonnebec, near Ypres, was Fulpold, castellan of Ypres, who established three canons. Thereafter Theobald, his son, not only approved and confirmed the foundation, but increased it from his own resources to seven canons. Lambert, the son of this Theobald, was the first provost of Sonnebec, until later, in the fourth year of his provostship at Sonnebec, he became bishop of Noyon and Tournai and died in 1123.]

We also forbid anyone, after making profession there, to dare leave that cloister without the permission of the abbot and the whole congregation; and no one shall receive a person departing without the common authorization expressed in letters. Upon your death, now abbot of the same place, or upon the death of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of fraud or by violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the judgment and consent of the sounder part, shall, according to God, provide to be elected.

[Col. 0607A] We decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be useful to them in every way, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him or her be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him or her be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 0607C] on the Nones of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXL. Privilege for the monastery of Rott.  
*(1142, December 6.)*

[Monumenta Boica, II, p. 356.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERTRIC, abbot of the monastery of Rott, and his brethren, both present and those in the future professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saints Marinus and Anianus, in which you are dedicated to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

[Col. 0608A] We also ordain that the monastic order according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be preserved there inviolate for all time, and that no brother after making profession may have anything of his own, but shall remain in obedience to his abbot with all humility. Further, no cleric or layman shall presume to demand tithes from you from the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals.

Upon your death, now abbot of the same place, or that of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of fraud or by violence; rather, you may, by common counsel and the counsel of the sounder part, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, elect an abbot without anyone’s opposition. Moreover, no one shall presume to seize or usurp the advocacy of your place, except one whom the abbot and brethren, according to God and the welfare of that monastery, shall provide to be elected there.

[Col. 0608B] We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be useful to them in every way. As a token of the protection received from the apostolic see, moreover, you shall pay yearly to us and to our successors one gold Byzantine coin.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him or her be separated from the most sacred body and blood of Jesus Christ; and let him or her be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who justly preserve their rights at that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy priest of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed. I, Boethius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, [Col. 0608D] have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXLI. To Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg—He entrusts to him the protection of the monastery of Rott against Count Henry of Lechsgemünd.  
*(1142, December 6.)*

[Monumenta Boica, I, p. 358.]

[Col. 0609A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother C[ONRAD], archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Bertric, abbot of Rott, coming into our presence, complained gravely that Count Henry of Lechsgemünd had unjustly occupied the possessions of his monastery and, setting aside reverence for almighty God, had violently taken from his monastery the privilege of the apostolic see. [Col. 0609B] We do not believe that it is unknown to your brotherhood how serious this is and with what severity it ought to be punished. Therefore, by these present letters we command you—and in commanding, direct you—to admonish the same count strictly either to restore to the aforesaid abbot the privilege and possessions of the same monastery, or to render justice in your presence. If he should scorn to fulfill this within forty days after your admonition, restrain him by canonical censure.

Given at the Lateran on the eighth day before the Ides of December.

### DXLII. He receives under protection the monastery of Saint Michael of Lunelac.  
*(1142, December 8.)*

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, I, 335, from the autograph.]

[Col. 0609C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CUONRAD, abbot of Lunelac, and his fellow brethren, both present and those regulars to be appointed in the future, in perpetual remembrance.

It is fitting for us willingly to grant a desire shown to pertain to the religious purpose and salvation of souls, and to afford fitting support to the wishes of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the monastery of Blessed Michael the Archangel, in which you are dedicated to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. [Col. 0609D] We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify expressly: the church of Mansee; the church of Steinenkirchen; the church of Wisilburg; the church of Schönau; the church of Straswalchen; the church of Absdorf; the estate which Conrad of Irembrechtingen and his wife Mechtild gave to the same monastery, namely Irembrechtingen; one manor at Tettingen; one *mansus* holding at Rattveld; and half a *mansus* at Liugane, [Col. 0610A] with [lacuna] belonging to that estate; [lacuna] the court which Engelmar and his sister Benedicta gave you at Direnek; [lacuna] which you, son Cuonrad, abbot, bought at Cremisse.

Upon your death, now abbot of the same place, or that of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of fraud or by violence, except one whom the brethren, by common counsel and consent or by the counsel and consent of the sounder part, shall provide, according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, to be elected.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose governance [Col. 0610B] and support they were granted, to be useful to them in every way, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him or her be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him or her be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, [Col. 0610C] before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Gregory at the Golden Veil. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere. I, Thomas, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina.

Given at the Lateran through the hands of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXLIII. He grants the abbey of Park, of the Premonstratensian Order, apostolic confirmation and protection.  
*(1142, December 17.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, II, preface, p. 310.]

[Col. 0610D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PHILIP, abbot of Park, and his brethren, both present and those to be appointed in the future according to the rule, in perpetual remembrance.

It is fitting for us willingly to grant a desire which pertains to religious purpose and is shown to concern the salvation of souls, and to afford fitting support to the wishes of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of Park, in [Col. 0611A] which you are dedicated to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

We further decree that the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institution of the brethren of Prémontré shall be observed inviolate in that church in future times. No brother, moreover, after making profession, may leave the same cloister without the permission of the abbot and of the entire congregation; and no one shall receive a person departing without the common authorization expressed in letters. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct any who decide to be buried there, unless they are perhaps excommunicated; yet the right of the mother church is preserved.

[Col. 0611B] We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be useful to them in every way, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to reform himself or herself by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him or her be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him or her be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve their rights at that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ; and may they receive here the fruit of good action, so that before the strict Judge they may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina. [Col. 0611D] I, Gregory, deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina. I, Igmar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Guy, unworthy priest of the holy Roman Church. I, Guy, cardinal priest of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Goizo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Thomas, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina.

Given and issued through the hands of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXLIV. He confirms by apostolic authority donations made to the Church of Cambrai. Privilege for the Church of Cambrai.  
*(1142, December 21.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, II, p. 1163.]

[Col. 0612A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother NICHOLAS, bishop of Cambrai, and his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

A devout petition ought to be fulfilled by a corresponding effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved brother Nicholas, bishop in Christ, graciously granting favorable assent to your petition with paternal kindness, [Col. 0612B] we confirm to you and to your successors in perpetuity whatever you now justly and canonically possess through the generosity of princes and offerings of the faithful, or may hereafter, by God’s favor, acquire through reasonable means.

Among these we have thought fit to specify expressly: jurisdiction over the city; the mint; tolls; judicial district; the mills of Salis; the mill at the Water Gate; breweries and householders; all peers and tenants; the castle with its small dwellings. Outside the city: arable lands, meadows, fisheries, Puerorum Villa, with the lands belonging to it, its mill and fishpond; Santollum with its appurtenances; the district of Raillencourt and Bantineiis; Tunium and Dalencourt; Strunium with its lands, [Col. 0612C] woods, meadows, waters, mills, and with the district and fishpond of Navia; the wood of Nereio; Saultoit with its lands, meadows, waters, mills, and two parts of the tithe; the new castle, with jurisdiction, mint, toll, district, passage-toll, ovens, breweries, mills, waters, meadows, woods, and arable lands; Ors with its appurtenances and the household of Ranseries; Saulce with Serires; Wantineies, the portion of Combles; a chapel in the district of Brabant; Melin with church and altar, its other appurtenances, and household.

In the district of Soissons: Tevine with its household. In the district of Boulogne: Villax or Vilra, namely with its household; likewise a meat-market within the same city of Cambrai. [Col. 0612D] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may henceforth rashly disturb you, take away your possessions, retain those taken away, or harass you by presumptuous vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, to benefit both your own use and that of the clerics and poor.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him or her be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him or her be subject to severe vengeance in the end.

But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be [Col. 0613A] the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Guy, unworthy priest of the holy Roman Church. I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Guy, priest and cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas [Col. 0613B] in Carcere. I, Go[izo], cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXLV. Privilege for the monastery of La Roche.  
*(1142, December 23.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, Instrument 113.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GAUFRED, abbot of the monastery of La Roche, and his brethren, both present and those to be appointed in the future according to the rule, in perpetual remembrance.

[Col. 0613C] The religion of a pure mind, strengthened by the indissoluble bond of divine love, continually and more abundantly inclines the countenance of the most merciful Creator through pure prayers, so that earthly things may be joined to heavenly things and the things below united with those above. Since, therefore, we have learned that the brethren of the aforesaid monastery live piously and religiously, free from secular care and dedicated to divine service, we judge it right, beloved son Gaufred, abbot in the Lord, to grant your just petitions.

We decree, therefore, that whatever possessions or goods are now known justly and canonically to belong to the same place, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, come to be granted to it through concessions of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

[Col. 0613D] And because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom,” in order that you may more freely devote yourselves to divine service and, with the eye of the mind cleansed, attend to contemplation, we forbid any archbishop or bishop to harass you or your successors, or any abbot of the Order of Pontigny, with unlawful summonses or to trouble them contrary to the Rule. Moreover, no archbishop or abbot shall presume, without your willing permission, to receive or retain converts—men who are not monks—after they have made profession in your monasteries.

But since, as we have learned from blessed Gregory instructing Augustine, bishop of the English, concerning the portions to be made, hospitality to be offered, and mercy to be fulfilled by those living the common life, what are we to say, when everything remaining over must be spent on pious and religious causes, the Lord, teacher of all, saying: “Give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you”? We decree that no one shall presume to demand or receive tithes from you from the produce which you and the brethren of your entire congregation cultivate with your own hands and at your own expense, or from your animals.

[Col. 0614A] Therefore no person may rashly disturb your monastery, take away its possessions, diminish those taken away, or harass it with any troubles; but all things shall be preserved intact for your use and that of the other poor of Christ. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person incur the loss of power and honor, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon those who preserve for that place what belongs to it may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. [Col. 0614C] I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Stephen, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy priest of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 0614D] and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXLVI. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Pontigny.  
*(1142, December 23.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 1228.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUICHARD, abbot of Pontigny, and his successors appointed according to the rule, in perpetuity.

Those who dwell in the house of God, being of one mind in the sincerity of charity, preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For the religion of a pure mind, strengthened by the indissoluble bond of divine love, continually and more abundantly inclines the most merciful Creator through pure prayers, so that earthly things may be joined to heavenly things [Col. 0615A] and the things below united with those above. Since, therefore, we have learned that the brethren of the monastery of Pontigny live piously and religiously, free from secular care and dedicated to divine service, we have judged it right, beloved son Guichard, abbot in the Lord, to grant your just petitions.

We decree, therefore, that whatever possessions or goods are now known justly and canonically to belong to the same place, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, come to be conferred upon it through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors. We also confirm to you the right of use throughout the whole forest called Otta, as it was reasonably granted to you for your animals, buildings, and all your necessities by Henry, archbishop of Sens, and Atto, bishop of Troyes, and preserved by their written instruments.

[Col. 0615B] And because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom,” in order that you may more freely devote yourselves to divine service and, with the eye of the mind cleansed, attend to contemplation, we forbid any archbishop or bishop to harass you or your successors, or any abbot of the Order of Pontigny, with unlawful vexations or to trouble them contrary to the Rule. Moreover, no archbishop or abbot shall presume, without your willing permission, to receive or retain your converts, who are not monks, after they have made profession in your monasteries.

But since, as we have learned from Blessed Gregory instructing Augustine, bishop of the English, concerning the portions to be made, hospitality to be offered, and mercy to be fulfilled by those living the common life, what are we to say, when everything remaining over must be spent on pious and religious causes, the Lord, teacher of all, saying: “Give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11)? [Col. 0615C] We decree that no one shall presume to demand or receive tithes from you from the produce which you and the brethren of your entire congregation cultivate with your own hands and at your own expense, or from your animals.

Therefore no person may rashly disturb your monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any troubles; but all things shall be preserved intact for your use and that of the other poor of Christ. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person incur the loss of power and honor, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 0615D] But upon those who preserve for that place what belongs to it may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0616A] SAINT PETER. SAINT PAUL. Place of the monogram: INNOCENT POPE II. HELP US, O GOD OUR SAVIOR.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Igmar, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Guy, unworthy priest of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden [Col. 0616B] Veil, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1142 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

### DXLVII. He informs the clergy and people of Arras that Bishop Alvisus has cleared himself of blame before him.  
*(1142, December 27.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, II, 164.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When your venerable bishop Alvisus came to us [Col. 0616C] and excused himself concerning certain unfavorable matters that had been reported to us about him, we received him with due kindness, both on account of our long-standing familiarity with him and because of his religious devotion and integrity, as well as at the prayers of many religious persons; and we restored our favor to him. We therefore send him back to his own see with the favor of the apostolic see and with the support of our letters, and exhort your whole community to receive him kindly, love and honor him, and humbly render to him, as your father and bishop of your souls, the obedience and reverence due to him, without any opposition.

Given at the Lateran on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

### DXLVIII. Bull in favor of Hugh, bishop of Auxerre.  
*(1142, December 30.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, Instrument, p. 112.]

[Col. 0616D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, bishop of Auxerre, and his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

By the office of apostolic ministry entrusted to us by God, it befits us to provide with paternal care for our brethren both near at hand and far away, and to preserve for the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their proper rights, so that, just as we are called fathers in name, we may likewise be proved such in deed. Therefore, venerable brother Hugh, bishop, we graciously grant your just [Col. 0617A] requests, and grant to you and to your successors, and confirm by apostolic authority, episcopal right in respect of the blessing of the abbot of Saint Germanus and the obedience and reverence due from him, and likewise in the other churches belonging to the bishopric of Auxerre, as your church is known hitherto to have possessed it.

We also forbid any secular person to have authority to judge or punish clerics in your bishopric for any crime whatsoever. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and honor; let him or her know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him or her be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him or her be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 0617B] But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Acquiro, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Thomas, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, [Col. 0617C] have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the year 1142, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent II.

### DXLIX. To Henry, bishop of Winchester and legate of the apostolic see in England, and Robert, bishop of Hereford.  
*(1142.)*

[*Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores*, Chronicle of William Thorn, II, p. 1802.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

[Col. 0617D] As your brotherhood can know, a dispute has long been carried on between them on account of the 50 shillings and seven pence which the monks of Saint Augustine customarily paid each year to the Archbishop of Canterbury. For those monks, having heard the prohibition of our venerable brother Alberic, Bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, that no price should be paid for chrism, oil, or other ecclesiastical sacraments, refused to pay those moneys to the aforesaid archbishop, asserting that they had not for a long time paid them for chrism and oil. Consequently, as they later complained to us, very many losses and injuries were inflicted upon them by the archbishop. He was summoned into our presence on these matters; but because, owing to the wars and troubles of that land, he could not come, we extended the term appointed for him and commanded him under injunction that, after the Octave of Saint Martin just past, he should answer the same monks in our presence, either personally or through his messengers.

At length, when both parties had appeared before us, and the monks renewed their complaint concerning the injuries and losses, the archbishop’s representatives said that they ought in no way to answer their complaints unless the money were first restored—money by which, they alleged, the Church of Canterbury had been despoiled without judgment. The monks, on the other hand, replied that that money ought not to be restored because, as has been said, our legate had forbidden money to be given for chrism and oil; and they produced witnesses on this point. Moreover, they said—and this is true—that we had also forbidden [Col. 0618B] those moneys to be given for chrism and oil. To prove this further, the monks adduced as evidence that on the same day, at the same table, chrism and oil were given and the money paid; so that if the money was not paid, chrism and oil were refused.

The archbishop’s legates denied this, maintaining that the money had been given as a rent-charge and for an honourable cause, and affirming that they would prove this through many suitable witnesses in England. Again, the aforesaid monks complained against the same archbishop that both he and his men had inflicted many serious injuries on them and unjustly withheld much belonging by right to their monastery. The archbishop’s legates denied almost all these charges.

Having carefully heard all these matters, and since the principal persons were absent and fuller knowledge of all these things can be had in those regions, after taking counsel with our brethren we have thought fit to commit the determination of the case to your discretion. We therefore command you to summon both parties before you at a suitable place and time, so that, after hearing the arguments on either side and making diligent inquiry, you may, with the Lord’s help, bring it to its due conclusion.

Given at the Lateran, etc.

DL. To the Archbishop of Tours.—That he is to come to the Apostolic See to answer the Bishop of Dol, who complained that he had been despoiled of the bishopric of Alet. (1142.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 886.]

[Col. 0618D]

Our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Dol, appearing before us, complained that in the controversy concerning the subjection which you demand from him, he has often been oppressed. He asserts that in many places—namely Saumur, Vannes, Le Mans, Paris, Tours, and Poitiers—he was prepared to settle this controversy in the presence of our venerable brother G[aufrid], Bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See; and he complains that he has also borne many expenses on this account, and further that he has been deprived, without reason or judgment, of the bishopric of Alet, which he says you hold.

Therefore, lest the Churches of Tours and Dol be further harassed by such procrastinations, by the present letter we command and enjoin you to present yourself before us on the feast of Saint Luke in the following year, prepared to show your church’s right in this matter and to answer concerning the bishopric of Alet, so that then, after hearing the arguments of both sides, we may settle the controversy itself as justice directs.

In Book XI of the Registers of Pope Innocent II, year 12.

DLI. He takes under protection the Church of Saint Crispin at Cavea in the diocese of Soissons. (1142.)

[Gallia Christiana, X, Instruments, 117.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROGER, abbot of Saint Crispin at Cavea, [Col. 0619B] and his brethren, present and future, to be regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

By virtue of the apostolic office entrusted to us by the Lord, it befits us to provide with paternal care for the peace and welfare of religious men, and to preserve their rights to the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord; so that, just as by the Lord’s ordering we are called fathers in name, we may likewise be found such in deed.

For this reason, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, receive under the protection of Saint Peter and of ourselves the church of the blessed martyr Crispin, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by God’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the rent-charge at Cavea itself; the wine-presses; the vineyard called Aignelet, with others; the land of Poilgli, together with the adjoining land of Bellomonte; the estate of Vallerami, with its appurtenant cultivated lands; one third of the entire tithe of Nancel; three mills; the land of Valle-leonis, with an entirely free estate and the whole tithe; the land called Vans or Millencort, with its mill and all its appurtenances; and the rent-charge in the city of Soissons.

We also decree [Col. 0619D] that the canonical order, according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the institution of the brethren of Arida Gamancia, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. We further forbid anyone, after making profession there, to dare depart from that cloister without permission of the abbot and the whole community; and no one shall receive a departing brother without a common letter of authorization.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of fraud or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by the common assent of all or of the sounder part, shall in the Lord provide to be elected. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but all shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly presume to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall fail to make due amends by suitable satisfaction, etc. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

DLII. To Stephen, Bishop of Paris.—That he should absolve the churches of Saint Geneviève from the interdict. (1130–1143.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 402.]

[Col. 0620B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother Stephen, Bishop of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember that we formerly wrote to your brotherhood that you should absolve the churches of Saint Geneviève from the interdict by which you have bound them, without prejudice to the right of the Church of Paris. We marvel all the more that this has not yet been done because the aforesaid church stands under the guardianship and protection of Saint Peter. For this reason, by renewed letters we command your belovedness to absolve those churches from the same interdict. Thereafter, if you believe that you have any right, you shall obtain what is just at a suitable place and time.

We further ask your charity that, if our son La., whom we committed to your care, has left you, you should assist our son Jo., surnamed Piccutus, with provisions and other necessities, and, out of reverence for Saint Peter, keep him under your more diligent protection.

DLIII. To Stephen, Bishop of Paris, the dean, and chapter.—He asks them to grant one prebend in the Church of Paris to the canons of Saint Victor. (1130–1143.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 371.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother STEPHEN, the dean, and chapter of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your belovedness does not doubt that the Church of Blessed [Col. 0620D] Victor is commended both for the religious devotion and honourable conduct of its venerable persons and for its observance of regular order and ecclesiastical discipline; so much so that, by the instruction of its praiseworthy institution, many churches in different regions have already advanced, [thanks be to God]. In these, indeed, praise, honour, and glory are offered to the divine majesty, which looks upon the lowly; and by the example of good life and conduct the people of God are more fully formed for better things.

You should therefore take care that, just as the brethren serving in that place provide spiritual feasts not only to those nearby but also to those far away, they themselves, established among you, are not permitted to lack the support of temporal resources. Therefore, that you may be aided by the devout prayers and intercessions of these brethren, we admonish and exhort your whole body in the Lord by these present letters to grant them one prebend [Note: [Col. 0621D] The canons of Paris feared that the Victorines would be introduced into their church by Bishop Stephen. By letters and an oath the king had bound himself never to allow the Church of Paris to be removed from its ancient status and order, nor that regular canons should possess any prebend or office in that church. Yet by this wise dispensation of the pope, the quarrel which had long agitated the Church of Paris was quieted.] in your church, from which they may obtain the means of life and you may merit the rewards of eternal life in return for temporal goods.

DLIV. To Radulf, Abbot of Lagny.—He rebukes him for contempt of the Apostolic See and for wasting the property of his monastery. (1130–1143.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 763, from a manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to RADULF, Abbot of Lagny [Note: [Col. 0622D] The monastery of Lagny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, on the River Marne in the diocese of Paris, founded by Saint Fursy, still exists under the Congregation of Saint Maur.].

The authority of the holy Fathers teaches that no one has ever been permitted, without peril to his own standing, to oppose apostolic commands and institutions. Had you weighed this with careful consideration, you would never have rushed with rash boldness into so great an injury to Saint Peter. But you, just as you scorned to receive our letter and messenger, also presumed, to the greater injury of Saint Peter and ourselves, violently to take away what we had graciously granted from the kindness of the Apostolic See to our beloved son the provost, and to violate it. You have also unlawfully bestowed houses, lands, and vineyards of the monastery committed to you upon your relatives, and you have not feared, contrary to your Rule and office, to place the brethren of that monastery under arrest.

Since, therefore, we neither wish nor ought to allow such great obstinacy on your part to pass unpunished, nor the other matters reported to us about your person by adverse rumour to remain unexamined, by the present letter we command and strictly enjoin you to appear before us on the next Sunday on which is read, “I am the good shepherd,” prepared to answer concerning all these matters and the other charges brought against you.

DLV. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary of Chartres. (1130–1143.)

[PETIT, *Theodori Poenitentiale*, II, p. 423, from a manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother GAUFRID, Bishop of Chartres, and his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0621D] The discerning and provident administration of the Apostolic See has customarily observed this moderation: that it preserves intact the right and dignity of each person, and binds to itself by the benevolence of closer affection and familiarity those whom it finds more devoted and ready for its service. Therefore, venerable brother Gaufrid, Bishop of the Church of Chartres, because we have perceived through manifest proofs that you revere and love your mother, the holy Roman Church, with all the desire of your heart, and that, amid the arising disorders of persecution, you have laboured manfully for its benefit and service as one proved in religion and steadfast in the Catholic faith, we cherish your person with fuller affection of charity and more willingly honour the church entrusted to you from the height of the pontifical office laid upon us.

Accordingly, dearest brother in Christ, granting favourable assent to your reasonable requests, by the page of this present privilege we confirm to you and your successors, and through you to the Church of Chartres of blessed and glorious Mary the Mother of God, whatever possessions and goods it now justly and canonically holds, etc. We further command that the liberty acquired for the episcopal residence from that predecessor of yours be kept entire and inviolate: [Col. 0622B] namely, that upon the death of bishops no one whatsoever may invade the episcopal residence, seize in any way what is there, or presume anything of those things which are set forth in the privilege of our predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory, etc. We decree that the men of the household of Blessed Mary who belong to your right or to that of the canons shall, as has been granted by our aforesaid son Louis, illustrious King of the Franks, be admitted to every testimony and every proof as free laymen, etc.

DLVI. At the request of blessed Odo, its first abbot, he confirms the Church of the Abbey of Bonne-Espérance, of the Premonstratensian Order, and its temporal goods, and grants certain privileges. (1130–1143.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 331.]

[Col. 0622C]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ODO, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, and his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

To grant assent to just requests and graciously to hear the prayers of religious persons befits apostolic dignity. Nor is there any doubt that, if we kindly respond to the petitions of the servants of God, we find the merciful God favourable in our own needs, so that, just as by divine providence we are called fathers among God’s people, we may also, through the accomplishment of our work, deserve to preside beneficially over the faithful.

Although we ought to provide generally for all ecclesiastical persons, we must nevertheless show more earnest care toward those who are known to strive with greater zeal in the service of almighty God and to shine forth in stricter religious observance and moral integrity.

For this reason, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Odo, we grant with due kindness our assent to the prayers of your devotion, and strengthen by the page of this present privilege the Church of Bonne-Espérance, over which by God’s authority you preside, with all that belongs to it. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with God’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: namely, the estate of Riverolis, subject to a rent-charge of twelve denarii in Valenciennes currency; and the estate of Ramelgies, subject to a rent-charge of ten shillings in the aforesaid currency.

No one may dare to alter your order and purpose of living canonically according to Augustine’s Rule and the institution of the Church of Prémontré, [Col. 0623B] or impose upon you the order of another profession. None of your brethren who have promised stability and obedience may depart without the permission of their own abbot and chapter, and no one may presume to retain a departing brother. If one canonically summoned refuses to return, the abbot shall have authority to pronounce sentence against him. Moreover, your church shall not cease its services because of a general interdict laid upon the parish, provided only that persons known to be interdicted or excommunicated are not admitted.

Likewise, we decree that you shall not be compelled to pay tithes to anyone from the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from your own livestock. And because it especially befits us to provide more and more for your peace, and because we desire you to be assiduous in divine offices, we likewise decree that neither you, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Odo, nor any of your successors may presume to go away, except perhaps when summoned to a synod or on other business.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb you or the aforesaid Church of Bonne-Espérance in respect of this our constitution, take away its goods or possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any injuries; but all shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted.

If anyone, however, with rash boldness presumes to act against this our decree, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and be subject to excommunication. But those who preserve these things shall obtain the grace of God, of our Lord and Redeemer, and of his apostles. Amen.

DLVII. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Saint Omer in Artois, later a cathedral. (1130–1143.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, IV, p. 13, from the legal memorandum of the chapter of Saint Omer, pp. 28 and 50.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the provost and canons of Saint Omer, who profess the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0624A] It befits us to preserve the rights of churches in which men are known to serve the Lord . . . . . We strengthen by the privilege of the Apostolic See the Church of Blessed Omer, in which you devote yourselves to divine service . . . . . decreeing that whatever possessions and goods that venerable place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, with God’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you by perpetual right.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names, for the service and reception of Christ’s poor in the hospital house of the aforesaid Church of Saint Omer . . . . . the land of Rubruc, the land of Staples . . . . .

[Col. 0624B] We also confirm to you by the page of this present document the good and reasonable customs that have flourished in your church up to the present time, and forbid anyone to impose new and improper customs upon you against your will. The dean, as is customary, shall appoint the ministers or officials of the same church after consultation with the brethren; and these, if they ever offend, shall be corrected in the customary manner by those concerned, according to the long-standing custom of your church.

Upon the death of you, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of fraud, except the person whom the brethren by common assent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God and with ecclesiastical propriety, provide to be elected.

We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any other vexations; but all shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly presume to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, shall fail to make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, recognize himself or herself as guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, [Col. 0624D] and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

DLVIII. To the Bishop of Cremona.—The omission of baptism does not harm one who credibly believes himself to have been baptized. (1130–1143.)

[*Corpus Juris Canonici*, vol. II, Decretals of Gregory, book III, title 43, chapter 2.]

You have resolved to consult the Apostolic See . . . And below: Therefore we answer your inquiry as follows: concerning the priest whom you report to have ended his final day without the water of baptism [Col. 0625A], because he persevered in the faith of holy mother Church and in confession of Christ’s name, we affirm without hesitation that he has been freed from original sin and has attained the joy of the heavenly homeland. Read the gloss on the eighth book of Augustine’s *City of God*, where among other things one reads: “Baptism is administered invisibly when it is not contempt for religion but the limit of necessity that excludes it.” Consult also the book of blessed Ambrose, *On the Death of Valentinian*, which affirms the same.

Therefore, putting controversies to rest, hold to the judgments of the learned Fathers, and order continual prayers and sacrificial offerings to be made to God in your church for the priest mentioned.

DLIX. He settles a dispute between the Church of Saint Lawrence at Florence and the monastery of Crispin concerning a hospital house. (1130–1143, 1 May.)

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Church of Florence*, III, p. 1778.]

[Col. 0625B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior, and the brethren of Saint Lawrence: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the dispute that has long been carried on between you and the monks of Crispin over the hospital house situated beside the Church of Saint Lawrence, we summoned both parties before us and carefully heard the arguments and allegations on either side. From an examination of your documents and from the assertion of your party, we learned that this hospital house had been granted by certain citizens, with the consent [Col. 0625C] of Bishop Rainerius and Hubert, prior, to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Bifurco, together with all appurtenances; and had been confirmed by a privilege of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of good memory. Although the opposing party could not deny this, it nevertheless maintained that the brethren of the said monastery had entirely relinquished the house and that it had afterwards been granted by the same patrons to the monastery of Crispin.

But you replied that the aforesaid patrons could have granted nothing in that house to the monastery of Crispin, since they had already long before granted it, with all its rights, to the aforesaid monastery at Bifurco. You further asserted and affirmed by production of a public instrument that the abbot of Bifurco, in the presence and with the consent of our beloved son William, cardinal priest and then legate in those regions . . . . . . had granted the same house to you subject to an annual rent-charge, and had confirmed this by his document.

Therefore, after hearing and carefully examining the arguments of both parties, and after consultation with our brethren, since laymen, once they had granted the same house, as aforesaid, to the monastery at Bifurco, could thereafter grant nothing there either to the monastery of Crispin or to anyone else, we judged that the monks of Crispin should restore the said house with all its appurtenances to you in full and that you should thereafter possess it peacefully. We also ordered you to reimburse them for the reasonable expenses they had incurred in the house. We further ordered them, [Col. 0626A] if any goods of that house had been unlawfully alienated or pledged by them, to restore them to you whole. If anyone knowingly presumes rashly to act against the page of this decision, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be subject to the loss of his order and office and incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen . . . . . .

Given . . . . . . on the Kalends of May.

DLX. To the Archbishop of Genoa. (1130–1143.)

[*Corpus Juris Canonici*, vol. II, Decretals of Saint Gregory, book III, title 28, chapter 3.]

[Col. 0626B] We do not believe that your brotherhood is unaware that graves and cemeteries of the dead have from ancient times been established at those churches and monasteries in which communities of religious brethren are constituted and prayers and solemn Masses are more frequently celebrated both for the living and the dead. Therefore the devotion and last will of those who desire burial at churches of this sort ought not in any way to be opposed.

But those who, abandoning ancient churches and the graves of their fathers and other relatives, transfer themselves to new and less religious places, contrary to the custom of the Fathers of the Old Testament, who are recorded as having been buried with their fathers, seem to act unreasonably and against ancient custom.

Therefore, if P. de Castello has directed anything concerning the burial of his body contrary to ancient and reasonable custom, this does not prejudice right but ought to have no force. Accordingly, we command you to have his body restored to the monks of Saint Stephen and buried with his fathers [variant: brethren].

DLXI. To the Patriarch of Aquileia and the Bishop of Mantua. (1130–1143.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 448.]

We do not believe that it has escaped your prudence how often our brother Adispertinus, Bishop of Todi [variant: Trent], has been accused of simony both in our presence and yours. When his case was finally argued in our presence, accusers and witnesses were produced, accusing him orally and in writing because he had given the Church of Saint Peter at Sajo to the priest Paul in exchange for the delivery of four modii of grain, which he received from that church. But since neither the witnesses nor the accusers could proceed in that case according to the form of the canons of the holy Fathers, after common counsel with our brethren we judge that he must clear himself in your presence of the aforesaid simony by a third hand of his own order and a fourth hand of abbots and religious priests.

The form of the purgation shall be this: the bishop himself shall swear upon the holy Gospels, first, that for the Church of Saint Peter at Pajo, he received no payment from the priest Paul for its grant [*de ada*; variant: *de danda*, “for giving”], whether through an intermediary or, to his knowledge, through anyone else on his behalf. Then the compurgators shall swear upon the holy Gospels that they believe true what he has sworn.

DLXII. He confirms the judgment of Urban and Calixtus, decreeing “that abbots shall not appoint priests in the parish churches which they hold without the counsel of bishops.” (1130–1143.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 436.]

With respect to priests who are appointed in churches to parishes belonging to monasteries, we confirm the judgment of our predecessors of sacred memory, Urban and Calixtus. We decree that abbots shall not appoint priests in the parish churches which they hold without the counsel of bishops; rather, bishops, with the abbots’ consent, shall entrust the care of the parish to a priest, so that such priests may render account to the bishops for the care of the people, while showing the abbot due subjection in temporal matters belonging to the monastery; and thus the rights of each may be preserved.

DLXIII. To Henry, Bishop of Regensburg, that he restore the Church of Blessed Sixtus to the Monastery of Saint Peter (Münchmünster). (1132–1143.)

[LUDEWIG, *Scriptores Rerum Germanicarum*, I, 579.]

INNOCENT, servant of the servants of God, to H[ENRY], Bishop of Regensburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0627C] As your brotherhood knows, it belongs to the episcopal office to support and love religious men and to provide for their necessities with paternal solicitude. Therefore your predecessor of good memory, Bishop Cuno, granted to the monks serving God in the Church of Blessed Peter, in the place called Monasterium, the Church of Blessed Sixtus with the parish adjoining it. But now, as the abbot of that place reports, we have learned that the aforesaid church and parish have been taken away, and that the brethren, for whose support they had been granted, suffer grave harm as a result. Accordingly, by the present letter we command and enjoin you to restore the aforesaid church with its parish to those brethren, and henceforth, as a devout and good shepherd, to make merciful provision for them.

DLXIV. He confirms the discipline and possessions of the Church of Blessed Mary of the Round Church at Auxerre. (1137–1143.)

[HUGO, *Annales Praemonstratenses*, p. 144.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HERVAEUS, prior, and the brethren in the Church of Blessed Mary of the Round Church, professing the regular life, present and future, in perpetuity.

Established by the Lord’s ordering upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought, from the office entrusted to us, to love religious men and protect and foster their places by our own defence.
