Likewise, estates dedicated to the uses of the heavenly mysteries ought to suffer neither the forced services of the powerful

[Col. 0654B] nor any extraordinary burden. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, take under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the safeguard of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, obtain through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. We have judged that these should be expressly named: the hospital situated beside the same church of Saint Lawrence, with all its appurtenances;

[Col. 0654C] the church of Saint Mark, with all its appurtenances; the hill of Saint Lawrence, bounded on one side by the land of Saint John and two running roads, and on the other by Saint Romulus and, thirdly, by Saint Mary; etc. Also, whatever has been granted to you by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and confirmed to your church by their privileges.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it in any way by vexations; rather, all shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they have been granted, without prejudice to the canonical right of the bishop of Florence. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter,

[Col. 0654D] knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, fail to amend by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor, acknowledge himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0655A] I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Alberic, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Stephen, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Humbald, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.  
I, Guido, unworthy priest of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed.  
I, Boethius, least priest of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, priest-cardinal of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed.  
I, Thomas, priest-cardinal of the title of Vestina, have subscribed.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed.

[Col. 0655B] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of May, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1143 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## DXCVII. Privilege for the Monastery of the Holy Apostles of Mont-Cornillon near Liège.  
*(A.D. 1143, May 4.)*

[HUGO, *Annal. Praem.*, I, p. 273.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LUKE, abbot of the church of the Holy Apostles situated on Mont-Cornillon near Liège, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

[Col. 0655C] The care of the Catholic Church has been entrusted to us by God, the supreme shepherd, in order that we may love God’s servants with paternal affection and strive all the more, by every means, to foster their devotion as they are known to adhere more fervently to ecclesiastical discipline and the Rules of the holy Fathers. For apostolic service pleasing to God is then rendered when the wholesome institution, rigor, and order of holy places are preserved by our protection in purity of religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, take under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and of you, and fortify it with the privilege of this present writing. We decree that

[Col. 0655D] whatever possessions and goods it now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, obtain by God’s favor, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. We have judged that these should be expressly named: at Viler, called “of the bishop,” the land of Udelin, Gissebert, and Hillin, with houses, courtyards, and meadows; in the city of Liège, twenty-five solidi which Bishop Obert gave you annually from his toll at the dedication of the church; the house which Lambert of the Meuse gave in the village called Latius, with houses and courtyards; the land which Frederick, steward of Jupille, and his wife Mabilia gave you in the same village of Latius;

[Col. 0656A] also, the land which Gislebert and his wife Richeldis gave you in the village called Hollonia above the Jeker, and in another village called Hactaples, with houses, courtyards, meadows, and a money-rent. Moreover, whatever you possess in the village called Richen: namely, in the church, money-rents, arable land, woods, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands; likewise, whatever you possess in the village called Mercherul, and in the clearing called Collieres, in the place called Heys, or Aufred’s court, and in the village called Gonheris: namely, in the church of Blessed Peter and Saint George, in the tithe, money-rent, arable land, woods, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands; and in the village called Radenchen, namely the hospice with its appurtenances.

[Col. 0656B] Certainly, no cleric or layperson whatsoever shall presume to demand tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the nourishment of your animals. Nor shall anyone dare to alter your order and purpose of canonical life according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institution of the Church of Prémontré, or impose upon you the order of another profession. Nor may any of your brethren, after making profession there, leave that cloister without the permission of his abbot and chapter; and no one shall dare to retain one who has departed. You shall receive oil for the sick, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics from the diocesan bishop, if he enjoys the favor of the apostolic see and is willing to provide these things

[Col. 0656C] freely and without any exaction; otherwise, you may receive them from any Catholic bishop who, supported by our authority, will grant what is requested. Furthermore, we confirm for you by apostolic authority the liberty of your church, defined by the privilege of Bishops Obert and Albero and confirmed by the assent of the Church of Liège.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter,

[Col. 0656D] knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, fail to amend by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor, acknowledge himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0657A] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1143 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## DXCVIII. To P., Prior, and the Brethren of the Church of Saint Fridianus at Lucca.  
*(A.D. 1143, June 26.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscell.* IV, 502.]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons P., prior, and the brethren of Saint Fridianus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The purpose of the regular life has long flourished in your church by God’s grace, and your community has formed many persons to live well by the example of its holy manner of life.

[Col. 0658A] Yet, having left behind the life of little children, which remains in Segor, you have ascended with the Lord to the higher things of the mountain, where you receive the lofty commands of justice as though from his own mouth and laudably fulfill them in the performance of works. We therefore exhort your charity, not to begin, but to persevere manfully in so holy and pious a purpose; and, according to the Apostle, forgetting the things behind, to stretch yourselves day by day, growing in virtues, toward the things before you, with the Lord’s help. We truly love your persons and your place with charity in the Lord, and desire, according to the Lord, to aid and sustain you in all things.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

[Col. 0657]

# VARIOUS LETTERS TO INNOCENT

## I. Reply and Apologia of Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz, and of the Synod of Mainz, excommunicating Gebehard after examination and conviction for proved crimes, and refuting what Gebehard’s friends had alleged to Innocent II by stealth and deception.  
*(A.D. 1130.)*

[HARTZEIM, *Conc. Germ.*, III, 311.]

[Col. 0657B]

To INNOCENT, most holy and universal pope: ADALBERT, by God’s grace humble minister of the holy Church of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see, offers the obedience due to so great an apostolic authority and the most devoted reverence due to so great a Father.

Having received your Holiness’s letters concerning the case of that brother—if indeed he ought to be called a brother—who usurps for himself the bishopric of the holy Church of Würzburg, we have understood that the entire course of the case has become known to your supreme apostolate very differently from the way truth actually stands, since much is commonly done by surreptitious means. For he has lodged complaints against us with your Holiness, saying that he suffers injury from us and is oppressed contrary to justice. Yet in this case, with God and our conscience as witnesses, we have done nothing contrary to canonical rules; nothing for which we ought to be suspect to your Holiness; nothing for which anyone who has examined the case more fully could rebuke us. But whatever we have done in this case, we have done not out of bitter zeal but out of zeal for justice; not prompted by any hatred but with regard to duty; not against the canons of the holy Fathers but according to the canons.

We indeed know, according to the divinely inspired rules of the holy Fathers, that a bishop ought not be deprived of his bishopric

[Col. 0658B] before the outcome of his case is apparent. But your most holy apostolate knows very well that this judgment of the holy Fathers must be understood concerning doubtful cases of bishops, not manifest ones. The most shameless case and certain crime of the man in question admits no appearance of lawful defense or just excuse. For it is clearer than daylight to all that he was elevated to the rank of so great a priesthood by no privileges of merit and with no election preceding it; rather, introduced by tyrannical violence, he entered the Lord’s sheepfold not through the door but broke in elsewhere, through ambition and the heresy of simony, most shamelessly as a thief and robber. And—what we cannot say without great grief and contrition of heart—he usurped for himself the place of the lawful shepherd,

[Col. 0658C] whom the holy Church of Würzburg had chosen from among her own sons, by the common vote and assent of clergy and people and with our approval and consent, to be canonically enthroned: a man noble in birth and character, most thoroughly trained in ecclesiastical discipline, Catholic in faith, prudent by nature, chaste in conduct, sober, humble, affable, learned, instructed in the law of God, keen [the printed reading is *tacitum*, perhaps *acutum*] in the meanings of Scripture, and in every respect most worthy of the name and honor of priesthood.

## II. Letter of Guigo, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse, to Innocent—He consoles the supreme pontiff amid the troubles of the schism.  
*(Written before A.D. 1131, the year in which Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, mentioned in this letter, died.)*

[*Works of Saint Bernard*, ed. Mabillon, II, p. 1055.]

To Lord and Father, most dear and most reverend INNOCENT, supreme pontiff of the apostolic see: the poor servants and sons of the Chartreuse offer that peace which the world cannot give, devoted service to his fatherhood, and obedience, though it is not necessary.

[Col. 0659A] We had intended to offer many prayers to the sacred ears of your apostolate, many supplications for the church of Grenoble, urged thereto by the clerics of that church and especially by our most dear father and bishop Hugh, most worthy of every reverence. He is—what we do not write without tears—worn down by illness and old age, and, so far as the episcopal office is concerned, may be counted among the dead. But, as we believe, through divine mercy it came about that the venerable Hugh, abbot of Pontigny and most devoted to your obedience, visited our lowliness in the meantime. We poured into his ears all that we had conceived, to be brought more effectively and fully to your presence in living speech.

[Col. 0659B] And since once, though we are nothing, we perhaps began to speak to our lord not without danger of presumption, we ask and beseech you—though we are less fit to admonish or exhort—that in all things which the Roman Church suffers or does in your days, you may in no way be terrified, but rather be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, armed with the unconquerable weapons which the blessed Apostle supplies to his fellow soldiers from the resources of the universal Emperor: namely, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which slays not members but errors and vices.

For now it is truly necessary—or has been necessary—to fight not merely against flesh

[Col. 0659C] and blood, which will not inherit the kingdom of God, but against the rulers of darkness and spiritual wickedness. For what but diabolical malice and a viper’s inspiration has so cruelly incited the stony hardness and leonine rage that opposes and exalts itself against the vicar of the prince of the apostles? What but dulling avarice and ambition, stirred by diabolical suggestions, compelled Gerard of Angoulême, inveterate in evil days, to proceed so rashly and stubbornly against Catholic peace and truth? What but serpentine cunning, finding through human changeability an entrance for doing harm, joined to the lamentable authors of so detestable a schism many even from among those in whose knowledge and faith confidence had been placed?

[Col. 0659D] Yet these things ought to disturb and terrify religious minds founded in Catholic truth all the less because they were foretold long before by the Lord himself, more frequently attempted by the ministers of iniquity, and more numerous and more happily overcome by the followers of truth. Who can sufficiently count how often the apostolic faith and constancy, which he who gave it proclaimed—and strengthened by foretelling—not merely would not fail but would also strengthen others? Who, I say, can sufficiently count how often it has been assailed by the cruelties of secular powers and attacked by the snares and deceits of schismatics and heretics? Why have they ever been permitted, by him through whose permission or command all things occur, to have any power, except that the weak might be shaken, the strong exercised, the unlearned instructed, the wise made manifest, and, universally,

[Col. 0660A] the good crowned and the evil condemned?

Now, because perhaps longer than was fitting we have held the attention of your sacred heart, called away from better and more divine concerns, occupied by our trifles, we prostrate ourselves at the feet of your Majesty and offer prayers for all, but especially for the new religious communities—namely Cîteaux and Fontevraud—and also for the whole world. For not one part only, but almost the whole world is your diocese. For just as God is one, the mediator one, the world one, the sun one, and, to mention lesser things, there is one head in all animals, so the vicar of Blessed Peter—that is, the pope—cannot be other than one.

[Col. 0660B] Therefore you owe to the whole world the rigor of discipline, the rectitude of justice, the light of doctrine, and the example of that blameless innocence which you bear even in your name. For as, in this visible world, light is opposed to darkness and heat to cold, so your innocence is opposed to the sins of the whole age, your wisdom to its errors, your temperance to its excesses, your endurance to its adversities, and your justice to its vices; so that, when the one world is conquered by the one man—that is, by the vicar of Blessed Peter—the more the victory has been won without the strength of a multitude, the greater honor and glory may be rendered to God, whose is the whole. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## III. Letter of the Clergy of Trier to Innocent II, Supreme Pontiff, announcing that they have elected Albero as their archbishop.  
*(A.D. 1131.)*

[HONTHEIM, *Hist. Trevir. diplom.*, I, p. 517.]

[Col. 0660C]

To the most blessed pontiff of the Catholic Church, the persons of the Church of Trier offer devoted service of obedience and attendance.

You are not unaware, reverend Father, how the Church of Trier has now for two years been deprived of its own shepherd. You know also that we were unable to retain Lord Bruno, whom we had unanimously elected. But, passing over the labors and evils we endured in the meantime,

[Col. 0660D] we now report to you new distresses and dangers and desire to obtain their end as soon as possible through your fatherly assistance. Indeed, when the king was in our city, together with the Lord Bishop of Albano, the bishops of Metz and Toul, and the barons of our province, an assembly was held to elect a shepherd. We named three persons so that one of them might more easily be chosen by all in agreement. Once they had been named, the barons and all the laymen withdrew from us separately to deliberate; but, returning immediately, they requested not one of those previously named by us or by themselves, but all with one voice demanded that Gebehard of Würzburg be given to them. Although we showed them a just reason for rejecting him, they nevertheless persisted in that demand with shouting and tumult,

[Col. 0661A] so much so that many of our brethren began to concur with them; thus the assembly was dismissed that day without accomplishing its business.

Afterward, we few, not sufficiently trusting in our own strength against so great a multitude, sought counsel from the bishops, namely those of Albano and Metz. At length, we placed ourselves and our cause so entirely in their hands and counsel that whatever person they might recommend—provided that he were acceptable to you, Father, and that the lord king were willing to invest him—we would elect. They spoke at length on this matter to the king. Then, returning to us, they advised us to elect Lord Albero of Metz,

[Note: [Col. 0661C] Albero of Metz, primicerius of the church. Albero, of the Lotharingian family of nobles of Monsterol or Montreil, had already been a canon and archdeacon of the churches of Toul and Verdun before becoming primicerius of Metz. See the obituary of Toul in Ruir, *Antiquities of the Vosges*. Yet Knauff, in *Defensio Prumiensis*, [Col. 0661D] p. 45, and the Chronicle of Novillany of Saint Maximin under Abbot Siger, write that he was abbot of Prüm. He was a man of altogether extraordinary character and great spirit. Baldric, his household officer, says in the *Life*: “This man newly began to be a soldier and, by the marvelous weapons of his intellect and counsel, to be a defender of the holy Church.” Later he calls him “a vigorous man, provident in all things”; soon afterward, “a man unconquerable and undaunted.” Then he compares him to a river which, when confined, though it had previously flowed quietly in a silent current, as though indignant at the opposition of the obstacle, batters the banks with roaring sound and foaming waves and bursts its barriers.], primicerius of the church, and said that this man pleased the lord king and that his favor would be with us in this matter. Strengthened by this confidence, when we assembled to make the election,

[Col. 0661B] the count palatine, advocate of our church, together with the other nobles and the people, as soon as they perceived our purpose, wholly disrupted us by creating a crowd and tumult. Then all requested that Lord Gebehard, provost of our church, who had been first named among the three, be given to them. But because, as stated above, we were bound by our undertaking, we refused to satisfy their request and deferred the election until the departure of the king and barons; for in their presence we did not dare at all to elect the primicerius. As the king departed, he appointed us a day at Mainz, declaring that there he wished to deal with our affair by the judgment of bishops.

Meanwhile,

[Note: [Col. 0661D] “We few,” namely the provost, etc. Baldric in his unpublished *Life of Albero* thus describes those few who consented to Albero’s election: “These were resolute men, tried in tribulation: Godfrey, provost of the greater house; Folmar, dean; Arnulf, archdeacon; Theodoric and Bolso, archdeacons; also Lord Hillin, at that time still a subdeacon, who succeeded the aforesaid Lord Albero next in the archiepiscopal see; and Lord Bruno, then provost of Koblenz and later archbishop of Cologne, brother of Count Adolf of Mont. The people of Trier had unanimously elected him, before they named Lord Albero for archbishop, during the time of that tribulation; but he obtained absolution from Lord Pope Innocent with much effort, putting forward certain hidden reasons. It was said, however, that through ambition for a richer bishopric, although one of lesser dignity, he had refused to accept the honor offered to him. He himself afterward made this sufficiently probable: for, after a short interval, while he was in France for study, the people of Cologne, by common agreement of clergy and people, elected a certain Godfrey, provost of Xanten. On learning this report, Bruno immediately returned, caused that election to be annulled, and received that bishopric himself.”]

we few—namely the provost of the greater house, the dean, two archdeacons, the provost

[Col. 0661C] of Saint Paulinus, the master of the schools, the custodian, and four other canons of the greater house—assembled in our choir and elected Lord Albero, under this condition: that he should be acceptable to you, lord Father, and that the lord king, as the bishops of Albano and Metz had promised us, should be willing to invest him by the gift of his right. For we knew, and still truly know, that the anger and fury of the laity cannot be quieted by any means or contrivance except royal power and favor.

The reason why we did not summon more brethren to the election was fear of our citizens. Had they perhaps learned of it, they would have rushed upon our throats. We had little hope of the assent of certain of our brethren, because we had previously seen them, as we believe, terrified by fear of death and favoring the laity. Yet, at that time, most of them received the election brought to them by us with goodwill in mind and word. But afterward, when we came to Mainz on the appointed day and presented the election made to the lord king, he, altered by the favor of the laity, heard us without the expected kindness and did not uphold our cause. At last, when reminded by the Lord Bishop of Albano of the aforesaid promise, he testified before all the bishops and princes

[Col. 0662B] present that he had never promised the Lord Bishop of Albano or of Metz that he had any favorable intention toward the person to be elected, unless it could be done with the assent and agreement of all, both laity and clergy. Thus confused and frustrated, we departed from him. When we returned home, we found nearly all the clergy, except ourselves who had made the election, in disagreement with us. Whenever we speak to them and try to encourage them, they represent to us the destruction of the cloisters, the plundering of their prebends, and danger to life itself; and they cry out that they can find no remedy for any of these evils.

Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your Majesty, we beseech you through the charity of Jesus Christ quickly to obtain the king’s favor,

[Col. 0662C] which the lords of Albano and Metz promised us. Otherwise, it remains either that you restore to us our first elect,

[Note: [Col. 0662D] Namely Lord Bruno, Count of Mont, of whom we have just spoken. Novillany, in the catalogue of abbots of Saint Maximin under Abbot Gerard, notes: “Bruno was elected archbishop before Albero, but he refused with every effort, especially because of the poverty of the Church of Trier.” And then: “Maximin, three heller poorer.”]

namely Lord Bruno; or else, with due respect for your fatherhood, we are necessarily obliged to elect another person upon whom the wishes of clergy and people may agree. Indeed, it is not so much the evils which we endure or expect to endure that move us, as the continual lamentation and complaint

[Col. 0663A] of our brethren, clerics, monks, nuns, orphans, and widows, who miserably complain that through our fault they have been exposed to every danger.

[Note: [Col. 0663D] Baldric continues the account of the outcome of this petition as follows: “While matters stood thus, it happened that a council was assembled at the city of Reims, over which Lord Pope Innocent II presided. To this council the aforesaid Lord Albero and certain clerics of Trier came with different aims. The latter strove to obtain, through the compulsion of the lord pope, their elect, who resisted them; but Albero labored to be released from this burden and to recover the dignities and ecclesiastical benefices which he had lost through his disobedience. For when the aforesaid Lord Pope Innocent, after Albero had repeatedly refused his command, found that he continued to decline this burden, he suspended him from every ecclesiastical office and benefice. At this council, therefore, the lord pope ordered him to be raised aloft and, clothed in a cope, seated among the archbishops; then, taking him to Vienne, and while he was still laboring for absolution, he consecrated him archbishop.”]

#### IV. Letter of Lord Oldegarius, Bishop of Tarragona, to Innocent. (About the year 1131.)

*[Councils of Spain, vol. III, p. 342, from a manuscript of the Church of Roda.]*

To the most blessed lord and Father, INNOCENT, pontiff of the Apostolic See by divine calling, OLDEGARIUS, unworthy steward of the metropolitan church of Tarragona, due submission of obedience in all things.

Oppressed by many tribulations and by bodily infirmity [Col. 0663B], we have recourse, as is our custom, to the standard of your mercy, as to the singular protection of our hope after the Lord, that we may be enlightened by the counsels of your authority and strengthened by its assistance.

But, to report a few matters out of many, let your prudence know that the canons of Barbastro, by the common vote of clergy and people, chose as their bishop a certain religious monk of the monastery of Tomières. [Note: [Col. 0664D] His name was Peter.] That church, afflicted by the long absence of a shepherd with many troubles, has fallen into such poverty, both through the loss of its possessions and through the capture of its canons, that it can scarcely supply the needs of its children. They presented [Col. 0663C] their elect to us and to the suffragan bishops who had gathered for this purpose, so that, with God’s grace aiding us, we might lay hands upon him [perhaps add: *our hands*]. Finally, when we had already assembled in the church for this purpose, we received through the envoy of the bishop of Huesca letters without your seal, stating that your Holiness had forbidden the divine office in the churches of Barbastro. Having learned this, we judged that we should defer what we had begun until we could receive counsel from your Majesty as to what we ought to do in this matter.

It is certainly established among us, and, I believe, at your court, that by royal commands the Church of Barbastro received the dignity of the bishopric of Roda, which the Roman pontiffs, judging it to be just, confirmed by their privileges. But while Lord Bishop Raymond, supported by these authorities, held the Church of Barbastro peacefully—the church in which he was consecrated—the king of Aragon, who was always hostile to him (for he did not wish to follow him over the Christians), sent Stephen, bishop of Huesca, with an armed force, and had that bishop shamefully expelled from the church and city while he was holding [Col. 0664A] the horn of the altar. We believe that the Roman curia is not unaware that this occurred because excommunications against that same Stephen had been issued by the Roman pontiffs.

At length, after the death of the devout Raymond, bishop of Roda, and after Stephen of Huesca had been killed, the king himself, on hearing that God was working many miracles through that same Raymond, bishop of Roda, summoned bishops and religious men, confessed the wrong he had done, and said before them all:

> “For my sin I expelled that religious man from his see at Barbastro without judgment or reason. But now, fearing God’s judgment, I restore the see of Barbastro to Peter, bishop of Roda; and, according to the ordinances of my father and brother, kings of blessed memory [Col. 0664B], and according to the privileges of the Apostolic See, I confirm it by royal authority to him and to his successors.”

These facts concerning the see of Barbastro, so far as we know them truly, we have briefly communicated to your prudence. It should be the enduring concern of your discernment how the miseries of the Church of Barbastro may be relieved, and what we ought to do concerning the consecration of a bishop there.

#### V. Letter of the Abbots and Clergy of Paris to Innocent.—They report the obstinacy of Theobald, Archdeacon of Paris, toward his bishop. (About the year 1132.)

*[Dom d’Achery, Spicilegium, folio edition, vol. III, p. 491.]*

[Col. 0664C] Lord Stephen, bishop of Paris, summoned us to Paris for his case. For Theobald, his notary and archdeacon, was disputing with him, usurping for himself the right of his bishop. A certain canon of Paris, travelling in his archdeaconry, lost his belongings, which a robber had taken from him; the person of the canon, however, was neither injured nor captured. On the following day the archdeacon placed his archdeaconry under interdict and began to excommunicate the robber, although his bishop was in the same archdeaconry and had not been consulted.

The bishop, distressed by the presumption and contempt of his archdeacon, lifted the interdict and released the man who had been bound by the bond of anathema without any summons. The archdeacon demanded satisfaction from the bishop for this alleged offence, to the astonishment of the abbots and clergy [Col. 0664D] who had come for the case, when rather the archdeacon’s rash imposition of an interdict and unjust excommunication ought to have been punished by the bishop. Nevertheless, having heard his complaint and the bishop’s reply, we abbots and clergy withdrew apart; and, after a judgment had been imposed which set forth the archdeacon’s presumption and the bishop’s office, we returned [Col. 0665A] to pronounce it.

But when the judgment, heard in common, was to be pronounced by a certain deacon, a canon of Blessed Mary of Paris, Theobald appealed to the hearing of the Roman pontiff, saying that he was aggrieved because the man pronouncing the judgment imposed by the judges was at the bishop’s table. Therefore we humbly implore the discernment of your Holiness so to restrain in this man the rashness of such great presumption that other archdeacons may fear, and may not dare, in the presence of and without consulting their bishop, to place his entire bishopric under interdict and close the mouths of all priests. For, though they have already presumed many things, they have dared to do this thing—unheard of and unprecedented—down to your times. May your Holiness prosper.

#### VI. Letter of Stephen, Bishop of Paris, to Innocent.—On the impious murder of Thomas, Prior of St. Victor. (Year 1134.)

*[It is extant among the letters of St. Bernard as no. 159, Patrologia, vol. CLXXXII, col. 319.]*

[Col. 0665B]

#### VII. Letter of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, and A. S. L., to Pope Innocent concerning their proceedings in the matter of the church of Beciano. (Year 1134.)

*[Mansi, Councils, XXI, 493.]*

To the universal pope INNOCENT, his lord and Father, HUGH, priest of Rouen, devoted and due reverence.

At your command we appointed and fixed a place [Col. 0665C] for the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu and the abbot of St. Thibéry to settle the dispute between them concerning the church of Beciano: namely, at Montpellier, on the third day before the Nones of November. But the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu sent us messengers and a letter at Tarascon, declaring that he could not come on the appointed day because he had to hold certain customary chapters with his brethren, and that he could not safely come to the place assigned to him because of Peter of Ribalta, whom, he said, was his enemy.

We replied that, in obedience to you, we had to pass through open enemies and ambushes which Alfonso had openly caused to be laid for us in many places. Finally, after a few days, protected by your blessing, we reached Montpellier [Col. 0665D], to the astonishment of many. There we had with us the venerable archbishops B. of Arles and A. of Narbonne, legates of the Apostolic See, and many bishops and religious men.

The abbot of St. Thibéry appeared before us to seek justice; but the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu neither came himself nor sent an advocate on his behalf, nor put forward any excuse or any . . . . Accordingly, since he was thus in default, we asked the bishop of Agde, in whose diocese the church of Beciano is situated, to show us before God and the Fathers there assembled to which monastery—the Chaise-Dieu or St. Thibéry—the aforesaid church belonged by canonical right. The bishop and his clergy, when questioned, [Col. 0666A] replied that truly, according to what they had received from their predecessors, it belonged to the right and possession of St. Thibéry.

Then documents concerning these matters made by Berengar, bishop of Agde of blessed memory, were produced; and witnesses came forward, men of good reputation and advanced age, who, when examined, proved that they had seen the monastery of St. Thibéry possess the church of Beciano peacefully for many years before the monks of La Chaise-Dieu came into it. We also found, through the attestation of Lord A., bishop of Narbonne, and of authentic witnesses, that Bernard, successor of Berengar as bishop of Agde, who had introduced the monks of La Chaise-Dieu into the church of Beciano, having learned the truth, corrected the deed and adjudged that the church of Beciano should be restored to St. Thibéry.

A. of Narbonne asserted that this had been proved before him on an appointed day between the abbots of St. Thibéry and La Chaise-Dieu by lawful witnesses, and there he adjudged that the monks of St. Thibéry should be reinvested with the church of Beciano—a reinvestiture which Lord Guy, cardinal-deacon and legate of the Apostolic See, ordered to be carried out. This reinvestiture, repeatedly adjudged canonically, we and the Fathers who were with us held valid and ordered to be maintained, on account of the canonical donation formerly made by Berengar, bishop of Agde, and the lawful possession that followed for nearly thirty-three years, as they assert, after Berengar’s episcopal document, which is established as strengthened by the year of the Lord’s Incarnation and competent witnesses.

#### VIII. Letter of Erpo, Dean of Halberstadt, to Pope Innocent II.—On the election of Gerard, Provost of St. John’s, as Bishop of Halberstadt. (Year 1136.)

*[Martène, as above, from a manuscript of St. Germain-des-Prés.]*

To the venerable lord INNOCENT, pontiff of the holy Roman Church, ERPO, dean of Halberstadt, together with the other electors of Lord Gerard, obedience as devoted as it is due, with service and prayer.

God knows with how great sorrow of heart and likewise shame we waste away because we so often burden the gentleness of your fatherhood with the misfortunes of our distress, and so often assail the ears of your lordship with our complaints; and beneath the increasing weight of grief [Col. 0666D] we are now almost failing. Yet, when we consider the greatness of divine goodness toward all who are afflicted, and likewise the paternal affection of your mercy ever shown toward us, encouraged by great hope of recovering salvation, we cast all our care upon its grace and upon the counsel of your fatherhood.

But now, as we are about to set forth our new and unexpected miseries, we invoke God, the author of all truth, as witness upon our souls that, pursuing pure truth as far as the brevity of a letter allows, we seek to make known to you the matter as it occurred. Having received the letters of your most sweet fatherhood—[Note: [Col. 0665D] In these letters the supreme pontiff signified that Otto, bishop of Halberstadt, had been removed from the see of Halberstadt [Col. 0666D] at the synod of Pisa, and set a definite time for the clergy and people to elect.]—in which we greatly rejoiced both at the liberation of our Church and at your pious concern for us [Col. 0667A], and after various causes of delay and impediment had intervened on both sides, and the days prescribed by the command of your authority for electing a bishop had now almost passed, we finally came together in the principal church, as was right.

And having first invoked, as you had instructed us, the grace of the Holy Spirit . . . . . we might elect a bishop worthy of God . . . . and fit to restore our wretched Church, now fallen into ruin both in spiritual and temporal matters. On the first day, indeed, worshipping from morning to evening, we made no progress. But on the second day, when we had again assembled as one under the invocation of the Holy Spirit, greatly fearing transgression of your command and the guilt of disobedience, after many deliberations we at last agreed upon the person [Col. 0667B] of Lord Gerard, [Note: [Col. 0667D] This Gerard is not mentioned in the Chronicle of Halberstadt; but Rudolph is recorded as having succeeded Otto after his deposition in the following year, in these words: “Therefore, in the year of the Lord 1137, in the fourteenth indiction . . . . when the Church of Halberstadt had no shepherd, Emperor Lothair, Gerard, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, Adalbert, archbishop of the see of Mainz, Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim, with many religious bishops, assembled for an election; and, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked [Col. 0668D], Lord Rudolph, a patient and peaceable man . . . . was elected bishop on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday, the sixth day before the Nones of March,” etc. Hence we conjecture either that Gerard died in the same year, or that his election was invalid; the latter seems more probable and is in some measure confirmed by Lothair’s following letter.] provost of St. John’s in Halberstadt, a man sufficiently approved in the Church by life and morals. We, namely the bearers and senders of this letter, canonically elected him bishop to the see of Halberstadt, for no reason whatever except that we were unable to find in the principal church anyone upon whom the consent of all could converge.

Although certain of our fellow brethren opposed this election and wished altogether to prevent it, and among other things alleged an election made of Lord [Note: [Col. 0668D] Martin is likewise not mentioned in the aforesaid Chronicle.] Martin but annulled before your legates, and finally sought by a disorderly appeal to the Apostolic See to deter us from what we had begun, nevertheless, considering the fear of God, the authority of your command, and the shortness of the time, [Col. 0667C] we completed what we had begun with the consent of many clergy and laity.

Now therefore, most reverend Father, amid so great a tempest of our troubles, fleeing to the counsel of your fatherhood and to the customary comfort of your pious compassion shown us, as to the safest harbor of our hope after God, all of us alike, absent and present, cast ourselves at the feet of your Holiness. With all the devotion of heart and urgency of prayer that we can command, we invite and urge the lord chancellor and the whole Roman curia to grieve with us and aid us, so that, according to the wisdom given you by God, you may determine in the present affair whatever justice dictates; and, taking counsel with the Angel of Great Counsel, may you not delay to provide for your honor and our necessity by placing some certain end upon our calamities [Col. 0667D]. For our part, we who are prepared under your obedience to suffer any extremities and to undergo death itself await the consolation of your prudence with unfailing hope, as a weary man awaits shade and a thirsty man a spring.

#### IX. Letter of Emperor Lothair to Pope Innocent II.—On the disputed election of the Bishop of Halberstadt. (Year 1136.)

*[Martène, Amplissima Collectio, I, 753, from a manuscript of St. Germain-des-Prés.]*

[Col. 0668A]

Your fatherhood often warned and requested us, insofar as we could do so without impairing imperial reverence, to relax our severity toward the enemies of the empire and, because of the necessity threatening the Church, to grant them opportunity to obtain our favor. That this might be done more fittingly was the disposition not of ourselves but of God, who, by his mercy, softened and settled all things, just as you wished and requested, for the honor [Col. 0668B] of Church and empire.

Indeed, Frederick at Bamberg, and Conrad at the court most recently held, both overcome by the material and the spiritual sword, came into our favor, both bound to us by oath for the service of the Church. Yet we received them as bound under this caution and condition: that they should obtain the fullness of their absolution only from your fatherhood. Thus, with all things settled as desired, we should have been wholly bound to the liberation of the Church if better provision had been made for the Church of Halberstadt.

Concerning its affair we have often sent you messengers and letters this year, in which, God being witness, we set forth nothing but truth and due order, being wholly intent upon restoring peace and concord to that Church [Col. 0668C]. How they perverted this by their lies and turned you away from our counsel need not be written to you again. Yet we firmly promise you this: in the presence of the Roman Church and before you, while life remains, we have clearly proved that all things stand as we communicated to you through our messenger and letters.

Nevertheless, despite the contempt shown for our counsel, we would not have been less willing, if unity and concord could in any way have been restored; and we would have endured enough if any benefit had resulted from this evil. But it is far otherwise. For when that Church ought, by the holy command of your fatherhood, to have agreed in electing a person suitable both for Church and empire, two parties arose. The canons of the mother [Col. 0668D] church at one time put forward the election made of Martin, the provost; and all except four unanimously affirmed this election, naming only three other persons of the same Church in the alternative, so that if his election were canonically rejected, they might secure one of these.

But the regular clergy, approving none of these, did not give them assent; and so, by the common counsel of both parties, they deferred the election until the following day. Meanwhile, the regular clergy, summoning the four members, as we said, from the principal church, elected Provost Gerard, while the clergy and people of the other party objected and protested and appealed to the Apostolic hearing under the testimony of the canonical rule which commands that no bishop or shepherd be given to unwilling persons.

Since imperial dignity is established in the regions of Saxony, especially in the aforesaid Church, let your fatherhood at least now accede to our request; and, having heard both sides, send them back to us in such a way that, with freedom of election preserved, we may, on the counsel of the archbishop and suffragans and in the presence of religious persons, provide someone beneficial to Church and empire. For such a man must necessarily be elected as has strength and knowledge to carry out those things [Col. 0669B] that belong to God and Caesar.

And that you may know that we desire these things which we have said with a single eye, send your cardinal legate to us, so that, with him present and advising, aid may be brought to the desolate Church. I also wish you to know that we shall celebrate the Nativity of the Lord at Speyer; having summoned the princes, we shall deliberate concerning the Roman expedition. We desire that your legate and letters be sent to that court, through which you may admonish the archbishops and abbots, by whatever threat, to your and our service.

#### X. Letter of Henry I, King of England, to Innocent.—He complains that Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, requires obedience from abbots. (Before the year 1137.)

*[Dom d’Achery, Spicilegium, folio edition, vol. III, p. 484.]*

[Col. 0669C]

To INNOCENT, supreme pontiff by the grace of God and his venerable Father, HENRY, by the same grace king of England and duke of Normandy, greeting and due obedience.

I complain to your fatherhood of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, who has disturbed my person and burdened my duchy of Normandy, and has acted violently and irreverently against me and against the dignities and estate of my duchy, which were held by my father, all my predecessors, and myself down to your last departure from Normandy in peace, and were possessed unimpaired and inviolate in the time [Col. 0669D] of your most blessed predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and of the holy archbishops of Rouen, his predecessors.

That is to say, he has exacted from my abbots of Normandy, outside my duchy and outside his province, blessings and extorted written professions, without consulting me, although complaints concerning this had been presented to you in council; and although, when I last crossed into my kingdom, I left them in peace and sent the archbishop himself amicably to you.

Therefore I earnestly and humbly beg your fatherhood to lay the hand of correction in such manner upon these matters and upon any others which you see tend against the honor, customs, and dignities of my kingdom and duchy, both upon those who have done them and upon those from whom it is demanded that they do them, lest—God forbid!—by unaccustomed innovations and similar burdens you compel me to withdraw from love, fidelity, and service toward you and yours. For I could not hold the land without the honor long possessed and due; nor could I in any way be permitted by my barons and men, without whose counsel and assistance I cannot exist, to hold the land any longer in such abasement and disgrace [Col. 0670A]. They reproach and insult me about this vehemently and repeatedly, as one who in his own time suffers the former honor and the rights of my kingdom, hitherto always preserved so wholly, to be taken from me with such negligence and excessive laxity.

Nor will the barons of the land any longer consent that I and the archbishop himself remain in the same land in peace or friendship unless you and he endeavor to amend these and similar matters [Col. 0670B]. For if that archbishop, while we were at Rouen, had spoken before you on this matter, I would have acquiesced in everything that I knew God willed and that was not contrary to my honor.

Therefore, since I am and always have been ready to obey in matters that pertain to God, to the holy Roman Church, and to the dignity of your person, I ask of you that the honor due to me and hitherto wholly maintained be preserved, and that I be reinvested with respect to the matters mentioned above. May God preserve your apostolate for his honor and for the peace of his Church.

#### XI. Letter of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, to Pope Innocent II.—On the death of Henry, King of England. (Year 1137.)

*[Martène, Amplissima Collectio, IX, 1236.]*

[Col. 0670C]

To his lord and Father, Pope INNOCENT, his servant HUGH, priest of Rouen, the obedience due.

We judged it fitting to notify your pious fatherhood concerning my lord the king, whose memory cannot be recalled without sorrow: overtaken by a sudden illness, he sent envoys with all speed and wished us to be present for the consolations of his illness. We came to him, and spent three days with him full of sorrow. As we spoke to him, he himself confessed his sins with his own mouth, struck his breast with his own hand [Col. 0670D], and renounced his evil will. By God’s counsel, our counsel, and that of the bishops, he promised that he would observe an amendment of his life.

Under this promise, in fulfillment of our office, we absolved him for the third time and throughout three days. He worshipped the cross of the Lord, devoutly received the body and blood of the Lord, and arranged his almsgiving, saying:

> “Let my debts be paid; let the discharges and fixed payments that I owe be rendered; let the rest be distributed to the needy.”

Would that those who held, and hold, his treasures had done so. At last we set before him with care the authority concerning the anointing of the sick, which the Church received from blessed James the apostle; and at his own devout request we anointed him with holy oil. Thus he rested in peace. May God grant him peace, because he loved peace.

#### XII. Letter of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order to Innocent.—It writes on behalf of Humbert, Bishop of Autun, whose jurisdiction the monks of Vézelay did not acknowledge. (About the year 1140.)

*[Martène, Thesaurus, I, 392, from a manuscript of the monastery of Aulne.]*

[Col. 0671A]

To the reverend Father and supreme pontiff, our lord INNOCENT, RAINARD, called abbot of Cîteaux, and the assembled convention of the general chapter of the same order, the fruit of prayer according to the affection of devotion.

We write simply because we are simple. For paternal bowels are moved not by eloquence but by devotion. Certainly, whenever we write to your Holiness, the spirit is filled with joy and the mind with longing; but when speech does not equal what the mind [Col. 0671B] inwardly desires, joy is frustrated, though longing increases. Receive, therefore, holy Father, whatever letters and whatever discourse may come from your servants, but their perfect devotion. Receive our common desire and our common prayers. Receive the common thanks of all of us together, because, most reverend Father, through our fellow abbot Bernard of St. Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0671D] That is, he who afterwards became Pope Eugenius III.], you visited the humility of our littleness with the condescension and paternal greeting of apostolic exaltation.

When was the house of the poor filled with such joy and zeal as when the voice of greeting was made in our ears? We lay before the sight of apostolic majesty, with reverence and humility, one matter. The Church of Autun, of noble and ancient dignity, complains of a thing of which [Col. 0671C] it now mourns itself miserably deprived. Humbert, the noble and venerable bishop of that same Church, also complained in our chapter; so much so that, descending to the humility of supplication, he humbled himself before us concerning the intolerable injury done to the Church of Autun by the abbot of Vézelay.

Now, since it is manifest that the Church of Vézelay has hitherto in every respect been subject, by ecclesiastical law, to the Church and bishop of Autun, Abbot Pons, to the grave and general scandal of that whole region, withdrew himself altogether, not from any necessity or oppression but, as is said, from impatience with subjection alone. Let therefore the prayers of our humility ascend to the ears of your gentleness, so that you may provide, with due compassion [Col. 0671D], for a fitting peace concerning complaints of this kind, as befits your fatherhood. For it is no small scandal in our regions that so great a Church should be deprived of its ancient right, especially since in former times the Church of Autun possessed such dignity among the Gallican Churches that it seems even to have obtained, above the others, the prerogative of apostolic intimacy.

#### XIII. Letter of the Bishops of the Province of Reims to Innocent.—On the condemnation of Abelard at the Council of Sens. (Year 1140.)

*[Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 224.]*

To the most reverend lord and dearest Father, INNOCENT, supreme pontiff by the grace of God [Col. 0672A], SAMSON, archbishop of Reims; JOSCELIN of Soissons; GEOFFREY of Châlons; and ALVISUS of Arras: the willing service of due submission.

With ears occupied by many matters, we make a brief statement concerning a lengthy affair, chiefly because the matter itself is contained more fully and extensively in the letters of the lord of Sens. Peter Abelard strives to empty Christian faith of its merit, while he judges that he can comprehend by human reason all that God is. He ascends even to heaven and descends even to the abyss; nothing is hidden from him, whether it be the depth of hell or the height above. He is great in his own eyes, disputing about faith against faith, walking in things great and wonderful beyond [Col. 0672B] himself, a searcher of majesty, a fabricator of heresies.

Long ago he made a book concerning the Holy Trinity, but it was tested by fire under a legate of the Roman Church, because iniquity was found in it. Cursed is he who rebuilds the ruins of Jericho. That book has risen from the dead, and with it the heresies of many which had slept have risen and appeared to many. Already it spreads its branches to the sea and its shoots even to Rome. This is the boast of that man: that his book has a place in the Roman curia where it may lay its head; thereby his madness has been confirmed and strengthened.

Therefore, when the abbot of Clairvaux, armed with zeal for faith and justice, accused him of these matters in the presence of the bishops, he neither confessed nor denied [Col. 0672C], but appealed from the place and judge whom he himself had chosen, without injury or burden, to the Apostolic See, in order to prolong his iniquity. Yet the bishops who had assembled for this purpose, deferring to your reverence, did nothing against his person, but merely rejected, as a medicinal necessity lest the disease spread, the propositions of his books condemned by the holy Fathers.

But because that man draws a multitude after himself and has a people who believe him, it is necessary that you meet this contagion with a swift remedy.

> Too late is medicine prepared,  
> When evils have grown strong through long delay.

We have proceeded as far in this affair as we dared [Col. 0672D]. It remains for you, most blessed Father, to take care that in your days no stain of heretical depravity defile the beauty of the Church. To you Christ’s bride has been entrusted, friend of the Bridegroom; it is yours at last to present the chaste virgin to Christ as to one husband.

#### XIV. Letter of Albero, Bishop of Verdun, to Pope Innocent.—On the church of St. Paul granted to the Premonstratensians. (Year 1142.)

*[D’Achery, Spicilegium, vol. XII, p. 320.]*

To his most reverend Father and lord INNOCENT, supreme pontiff of the universal Church by the grace of God, ALBERO, unworthy minister of the Church of Verdun, sincere affection with humble obedience.

[Col. 0673A] The grace of God and yours, through the election of your Church, consecrated me bishop, although my merits declared me unworthy, and taught me both afterwards and before how I ought to serve in my office. Among other things, it particularly persuaded me to keep watch over the ordering of the churches entrusted to me.

Therefore, keeping watch according to my small ability over that ordering, which is quite necessary here among us, I found a certain church situated near our city which, through the negligence and irreligion of the few monks living there, had been reduced to such infamy that it was now said to be not a house of God but a brothel. I shall briefly state, as certainly as I can, what I did concerning it.

In that church, consecrated from its first foundation in honor of blessed Paul the apostle, there were first clerics through the times of nineteen bishops; but through their irreligion and negligence it fell into such poverty that what had formerly been ample for many could scarcely suffice for the sustenance of one priest [Col. 0673B]. A predecessor of mine named Wilfrid, a lover of religion, expelled those clerics on this account and placed religious monks there. For a long time they persevered in religious fervor, restored the dispersed goods of the Church, and acquired many more. But those who succeeded them gradually began to decline from that religious observance, and, in declining, continued down to our times wantonly to destroy the goods of the Church.

Grieving over the excessive ruin of that church, which in ancient times had been of great renown [Col. 0673C], I first met its abbot alone, alone; later, with other abbots and religious men. I laid before him many charges which, before your dignity, ought not even to be named, but which were truly reported of him; and I admonished him fatherly to correct himself and his monks in these matters and to restore the ancient religious observance in his church. He promised, for God’s sake and ours, to do whatever I wished. But because:

> “The newly formed vessel, once imbued,  
> Will long retain its scent,”

when he ought to have corrected what he had done amiss, he increased his infamy daily. At last, after frequent vain and useless warnings, the persons of our Church and religious abbots assembled in our presence, denounced those monks as a disgrace to their order [Col. 0673D], and demanded that I expel them and appoint other religious men in their place.

Compelled by their constant requests, I summoned religious men—abbots and clerics—to a chapter, called that incorrigible abbot [Col. 0674A] to answer, and brought many charges against him concerning his evil way of life. He confessed what he could not deny because it was evident: namely, that he had despised the rule of his order and committed many unlawful acts there. Having taken counsel with the religious men, I admonished him under obedience to go to the church of St. Vito in order to do penance among religious men; and, because he could not bear fruit in the church over which he presided, to allow fruitful men to enter. He consented, but immediately, that very day, returning to his vomit, refused to do what he had promised.

When we heard this, on the next day we came to that church with clerics and abbots, and also with two abbots of the Cistercian order—the abbot of Trois-Fontaines and the abbot of La Chalade. Asked why he had not fulfilled the obedience he had undertaken [Col. 0674B], he answered that he would not leave his cloister except by judgment. Then the abbots and clerics, astonished at such impudence—that after undertaking obedience he should seek a judgment—produced, through one of them, namely the abbot of St. Vito, the judgment of Blessed Gregory concerning faithless abbots. When it had been read, all told me that even if he were unwilling I should confine him in the church and provide for the church so long desolate.

Thus he was confined, and the few monks who lived evilly with him were placed among religious men. I earnestly sought monks who would restore the former condition of the church, not only from our own communities or neighboring ones, but also from the Church of Cluny, through our letters, through letters of the lord archbishop of Trier, and indeed through letters of the lord king. When I could not obtain them [Col. 0674C], I placed there the poor of Christ from the Church of Prémontré, living commendably according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

Moved by this, monks who are not religious but who, in a similar matter, fear opponents to their own party, rage daily—not so much at the expulsion of the aforesaid abbot, whose life they themselves openly detest, as complaining of a change of title. Yet in this they speak falsely: for we do not change the title, but restore it in the form of its original foundation. Moreover, the abbot of that place is the bishop’s vicar, an office more suited to the order of clerics than to monks.

Therefore, with suppliant devotion, we beseech your Majesty to deign to confirm by the hand of your authority our act, which is praised by all except monks of this sort [Col. 0674D]. May your life flourish long for the honor of the holy Church.

See the letters of St. Bernard and Peter the Venerable to Innocent among the works of each.

[Col. 0675]

# THE COUNCIL OF POPE INNOCENT II AT REIMS

At which the antipope Anacletus was excommunicated and Louis the Younger, in the presence of his father, was crowned king of France by the pontiff himself, in the year 1131.

(MANSI, *Concilia*, vol. XXI, col. 454.)

## I. ACTS OF THE COUNCIL FROM VARIOUS AUTHORS

[Col. 0675A] The acts of this council have perished, but the following alone concerning it is found in the Life of St. Bernard (book II, chapter 1), by Bernard, abbot of Bonneval: “After traversing France, Pope Innocent summoned a council at Reims. There, after many matters had been arranged for the honor of God, he crowned King Louis king in place of his brother Philip while his father was still living. In all these affairs the lord pope would not allow the abbot—that is, St. Bernard—to be separated from him; instead, he sat with the cardinals in deliberations on public affairs. Moreover, all who had private business consulted the man of God in confidence. He, after hearing them, reported their cases to the curia and offered his advocacy to the oppressed. Therefore, when the council had been dissolved, etc.” That is all that is found there.

St. Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, attended the same council with the others. The author of his [Col. 0675B] Life mentions him [Note: [Col. 0675] Chapter 47. It is printed in the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*, June, vol. I, under June 6] while discussing what was done at that council: “When a council was summoned at Reims, bishops from different nations assembled from every quarter. Father Norbert also came. There they excommunicated that intruder Peter; after approving Innocent’s election, they delivered Peter Leonis, unless he should come to his senses, to the roaring lion. Norbert brought with him the most ancient privileges of his church, which were almost consumed by worms. He had them all renewed and corrected under Roman authority, adding those which he had recovered from the hands of men who had seized them unjustly and violently. He also added another privilege privately, so that, when the opportunity was given, supported by Roman authority he might propagate the order of his religious profession in his episcopal church.” Thus far that work speaks of the matters carried out [Col. 0675C] in the synod of Reims.

At this same council of Reims, at the request of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, the same pontiff Innocent consecrated as king of the Franks and successor to his father the latter’s son, who was likewise named Louis and numbered the seventh of that name. Concerning the consecration of this new king, Abbot Suger of St. Denis, who had recommended it to the elder king, writes as follows: “We, therefore, who were his closest and most intimate associates, feared his sudden death because of the continual infirmity of his weakened body. We advised him to establish his son Louis, a most handsome boy, as king together with himself, crowned with the royal diadem and anointed with the sacred oil, in order to repel any uprising of rivals. He agreed to our counsel and came to Reims with his wife, his son, and the leading men of the kingdom. There, in the full and most distinguished council which the lord Pope Innocent had summoned, he provided the kingdom with a fortunate successor, elevating the boy as king through anointing with the sacred oil and the conferral of the royal crown. For this reason it seemed to many, as though by a certain foretoken, that his power was destined to be enlarged, since he received the abundant blessing [Col. 0676B] of so many and such great and diverse archbishops and bishops—Franks, Germans, Aquitanians, Englishmen, and Spaniards. And while the father returned to Paris, alleviating the pain of the dead son with joy in the living one, the lord pope, after dissolving the council, chose to remain at Auxerre.” These things Suger wrote as one who was present and witnessed them all.

The Chronicle of Ursperg speaks in this way about the causes, date, and acts of this synod of Reims: “In the year of the Lord 1130, Pope Honorius II died, and Innocent II succeeded him by canonical election. But because of the intrusion of Peter Leonis, who had the support of the Roman multitude, he could not retain his see. He therefore went to France, where, after holding a council at Reims with many bishops, he excommunicated the aforesaid Leonis and his supporters; and thus he remained in the regions of Germany until the seventh year. He occupied the see for thirteen years and seven months.” [Col. 0676C] Thus the Ursperg chronicler at the place cited.

Robert, the continuator of Sigebert, adds that at this same synod not only was the election of Pope Innocent approved, but the ordination of the antipope Peter was also condemned with an anathema by all the bishops of Gaul and Germany. A little later he says: “At the council held at Reims in the presence of Louis, king of the Franks, his son Louis was consecrated king by Pope Innocent on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [October 25].” For a few days before this [Col. 0677A] synod was held, the king’s son Philip, recently anointed king, had been killed when he accidentally fell from his horse, to the great grief and sorrow of all, in accordance with St. Bernard’s prophecy. “Pope Innocent presided over the council of Reims,” says Dodechinus in his appendix to Marianus, “on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November [October 19], in the presence of Louis, king of France, whose still very young son he consecrated king.” Thus Dodechinus.

The matter is narrated much more fully in the Chronicle of Morigny in these words: “Accordingly, on Saturday King Louis entered the council with Ralph, count of Vermandois, who was his kinsman and chief officer of the royal household, and with many leading men of the Franks. He mounted the tribunal, kissed the lord pope’s feet, and sat on a chair placed beside him. He spoke a few words about his deceased son [Col. 0677B] [Note: [Col. 0677D] Namely Philip] and moved everyone to tears. The pope then turned his gaze toward the king and began to speak as follows: ‘It is fitting,’ he said, ‘most excellent king, that you, who hold dominion over the most noble nation of the Franks, should raise the eyes of your mind to the majesty of that supreme King through whom kings reign, and should revere his will in all things. For he who created all things governs all things; and because he possesses knowledge of all things, he neither does nor permits anything at all to be done unjustly in the whole order of creation, although many unjust deeds are committed. That most loving Lord is accustomed, good king, both to console his faithful with prosperity and to instruct them through adversity. For, as we read in Holy Scripture—which is his letter sent down from heaven through the Holy Spirit to us who dwell on earth—he himself wounds and heals (Job 5:18), and he scourges every son whom he loves (Heb. 12:6). “I,” he says, “will kill and I will make alive; I will strike and I will heal” (Deut. 32:39). He acts so that man, created in God’s image but cast down by the guilt of transgression into the darkness of this mortality, may not love exile as his homeland, but may hasten to return as quickly as possible to that heavenly city from which he lives as a pilgrim on earth: holy Jerusalem, whose foundations are upon the holy mountains—that is, upon our apostles—which is above and is our mother. For we are strangers and pilgrims, as all our fathers were, and we have here no abiding city, but seek the city that is to come. In it those who here vigorously trample carnal desires underfoot rejoice eternally with God. [Col. 0677D] To that city your son, a boy of simplicity and innocence, has departed. For of such is the kingdom of heaven.

“‘O king, when the son of David—who was a model of virtues for good kings—lay sick, David wept most bitterly; but after he was told that the boy had died, he rose from the ashes and sackcloth in which he lay, changed his clothes, washed his hands, and summoned his household to a feast. For it is impossible that what has been done should not have been done. And that man, filled with God, knew how gravely one sins by opposing divine justice even in desire. Put aside now this sorrow of spirit, which carnal affection has produced in you and which you bear in heart and countenance. For he who has taken one son to reign with himself [Col. 0678A] has left you several others who may reign afterward. You also ought to console us, strangers driven from our own sees, whom you, first of all men, received honorably into your kingdom for love of God and blessed Peter, honored with acts of service, and laden with benefits. May the Lord repay you in kind and with an eternal reward, lord king, in that city of which glorious things are spoken, where there is life without death, eternity without corruption, and joy without end.’

“By the marvelous antidote of this speech the holy apostolic lord soothed the king’s wounded heart. Immediately rising to his feet, and silently reciting the Lord’s Prayer as Christian custom requires, he absolved the soul of the dead boy. Then, under obedience, he instructed the archbishops, bishops, and abbots that on the following day, which was to be Sunday, they should present themselves dressed in the sacred and festal vestments that they wore in the assembly and should take part in the consecration of the new king.

“On that day, then, the sun shone more brightly than usual and seemed joyfully to offer its service to the business at hand. Early in the morning the pope left the bishop’s palace with the members of his curia, the archbishops, bishops, and abbots, and proceeded to the church of St. Remigius, where the king and his son were lodged. There he was received most fittingly, with great devotion and a procession of monks. Clothed in all the insignia of the Roman pontiff and, according to his custom on sacred and great feast days, crowned with the phrygium, he made his way to the cathedral church consecrated in honor of the Blessed Mary. He went with the boy who was to be consecrated, surrounded by a countless multitude from the ecclesiastical and military orders and from the people. [Col. 0678C] Before the doors of the church they were awaited by the king, his leading men, the archbishops, certain bishops, abbots, monks, canons, clergy, and fellow scholars who had streamed to the council from various parts of Gaul and Germany. They entered the church and presented the boy at the altar. With immense rejoicing the lord pope consecrated the child, about ten years old, using the oil that St. Remigius had received from an angelic hand and with which he had anointed Clovis, king of the Franks, as a Christian. Some said that never in France had there occurred either a comparable celebration of a council or a royal consecration performed by the Roman [Col. 0678D] pontiff himself. And so King Louis, receiving consolation after his grief, returned with his wife, his son, and his court to conduct the affairs of the kingdom.

“Moreover, on the following day, while the lord pope was presiding in council, letters from Lothair, king of the Germans, were presented by a certain archbishop of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 0677D] St. Norbert]. In them obedience was again promised, and the king announced that he was preparing for the expedition [Note: [Col. 0678D] Namely the Italian expedition] with all the forces of his realm. Likewise Henry, king of the English, sent both a most ornate letter [Col. 0679A] through Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, and a promise of obedience. The kings also—the elder Alfonso of nearer Spain [Note: [Col. 0679D] That is, Alfonso VI, king of Aragon and Navarre], and the younger Alfonso of inner Spain [Note: [Col. 0679D] That is, Alfonso VII, king of Castile]—sent letters through the bishops of their provinces. They greeted the pope, declared themselves his obedient sons, and humbly begged for assistance against the enemies of the Christian name and the Almoravid invaders of those regions. The letters of the most excellent Carthusian hermits also brought both joy and wonder in connection with this matter. They were carried by a certain venerable abbot of the Cistercian order and read in the council by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres.” The chronicler next gives those letters, in which the most holy men exhort the pontiff not to lose heart in these extremely difficult times.

## II. CANONS OF THE COUNCIL

Now published for the first time from a copy made by our Sirmond, who had transcribed it from an old manuscript codex of Mont-Saint-Michel, together with Sirmond’s own annotation.

### TITLES OF THE CANONS

[Col. 0679B]

I. On simoniacs. II. That bishops and clerics should please God in both their inward and outward bearing. III. That no one plunder the goods of dying clerics. IV. That a subdeacon who is married or keeps a concubine be deprived of office and benefice. V. That no one hear the masses of married priests. VI. That monks or regular canons not study law or medicine for profit. VII. That laymen who possess churches restore them to the bishops. VIII. That no one be appointed archdeacon or dean unless he is a deacon or priest. IX. That every church have its own priest, not a hired one. X. That clerics, monks, pilgrims, merchants, and farmers always be safe. XI. On the days and seasons when the Truce of God is to be observed. XII. That knights not hold markets or fairs. XIII. That no one lay hands upon a cleric or monk. XIV. That no one lay hands upon those who have fled to a church or cemetery. XV. That no one claim prebends or benefices by hereditary right. XVI. That blood relatives not be joined in marriage. XVII. On arsonists.

### CANONS

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Compare canons 1–20 of the Second Lateran Council.]

[Col. 0679D]

#### I. On simoniacs

We decree that if anyone has been ordained through simony, he shall lose the office which he unlawfully usurped. If anyone has acquired prebends, an honor, or any ecclesiastical promotion by means of money, through the intervention of the accursed heat of avarice, he shall be deprived of the honor wickedly acquired, and buyer, seller, and intermediary shall be struck with the mark of infamy.

#### II. That bishops and clerics should strive to please God in both inward and outward bearing

[Col. 0680B]

We also command that bishops and clerics alike strive to please God and men in the state of their minds and the bearing of their bodies. They must not offend the sight of those for whom they ought to be the pattern and example through extravagance or the color of their clothes, but wear what befits their holiness.

#### III. That no one plunder the goods of dying clerics

We also command the inviolable observance of what was established at the holy Council of Chalcedon: namely, that the goods of deceased bishops are not to be plundered by anyone at all, but are to remain freely under the control of the steward and clergy for the use of the church and of the deceased bishop’s successor. Henceforth, therefore, let that [Col. 0680C] detestable and savage rapacity cease. If anyone should presume from now on to attempt this, he shall be subject to excommunication. Anyone who plunders the goods of dying priests or clerics shall be subject to the same sentence.

#### IV. That a subdeacon who is married or keeps a concubine be deprived of office and benefice

We decree that those who, from the subdiaconate upward, have taken wives or have kept concubines shall be deprived of office and ecclesiastical benefice. For since they ought to be and to be called the temple of God, vessels of the Lord, and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, it is unworthy for them to serve beds and uncleanness.

#### V. That no one hear the masses of married priests

Moreover, following in the footsteps of our predecessors Gregory VII, [Col. 0680D] Urban, and Paschal, Roman pontiffs, we command that no one hear the masses of those whom he knows without doubt to have wives or concubines.

#### VI. That monks or regular canons not study law or medicine for profit

As we have learned, an evil and detestable custom has become established: monks and regular [Col. 0681A] canons, after receiving the habit and making profession, spurn the rule of their blessed masters Benedict and Augustine and learn secular law and medicine for the sake of temporal profit.
