Inflamed by the fires of avarice, they make themselves advocates in lawsuits; and although they ought to devote themselves to psalmody and hymns, they trust in the protection of an eloquent voice and, through the diversity of their pleadings, confound justice and injustice, right and wrong. Imperial constitutions testify that it is absurd, indeed disgraceful, for clerics to wish to profess themselves skilled in disputes of the forum. The canons and monks themselves also deserve to be severely punished as violators of this kind [Note: [Col. 0681] Correction from the Lateran text: “We decree by apostolic authority that violators of this kind are to be severely punished. They themselves also,” etc.]; neglecting the care of souls and paying no attention at all to the purpose of their order, they promise health in return for detestable money and make themselves healers [Col. 0681B] of human bodies. And since an immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart, religious men ought not to handle even those matters of which decency blushes to speak. Therefore, so that the monastic and canonical orders, pleasing to God, may be preserved inviolate in their holy purpose, we forbid by apostolic authority that this be presumed in the future. Bishops, abbots, and priors who consent to so great an enormity shall be stripped of their own honors.

#### VII. That laymen who possess churches restore them to the bishops

We command that laymen who possess churches either restore them to the bishops or be subject to excommunication.

#### VIII. That no one be appointed archdeacon or dean unless he is a deacon or priest

[Col. 0681C]

We renew the decree and command that no one be appointed archdeacon or dean unless he is a deacon or priest. Archdeacons, deans, and provosts who have not attained the aforementioned orders shall be deprived of the honor they have received if in disobedience they refuse to be ordained. We also prohibit these honors from being granted to youths or to those below the sacred orders; they are to be granted to men distinguished for prudence and worthiness of life.

#### IX. That every church have its own priest, not a hired one

It has also been determined that churches are not to be entrusted to hired priests, and that every church which has sufficient means [Col. 0681D] should have its own priest.

#### X. That clerics, monks, pilgrims, merchants, and farmers always be safe

We also command that priests, clerics, monks, merchants, countrymen going and returning and remaining at their agricultural work, the animals with which they plow, and their sheep shall be safe at all times.

#### XI. On the days and seasons when the Truce of God is to be observed

We command that the truce be observed inviolably by all from sunset on Wednesday until sunrise on Monday, from the Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany, and from Quinquagesima until the octave of Pentecost. If anyone attempts to break the truce and does not make satisfaction after the third warning, his bishop shall pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him and announce the sentence in writing to the neighboring bishops. No bishop shall receive the excommunicated man into communion; rather, each shall confirm in writing the sentence he has received. If anyone presumes to violate this, he shall imperil his rank. And because a threefold cord is difficult to break, we command that the bishops, looking only to God and to their own salvation, put aside all tepidity and furnish one another mutual counsel and aid for firmly maintaining peace. If anyone is found lukewarm in this work of God, he shall incur the loss of his own dignity. [Col. 0682B]

#### XII. That knights not hold markets or fairs

We altogether forbid the holding of those detestable markets or fairs at which knights are accustomed to assemble by agreement and rashly engage one another in a display of their strength and boldness, from which deaths of men and dangers to souls often result. If any of them dies there, though penance and viaticum are not to be denied him if he requests them, he shall nevertheless lack ecclesiastical burial.

#### XIII. That no one lay violent hands upon a cleric or monk

It has likewise been determined that if anyone, at the devil’s persuasion, incurs the guilt of this sacrilege by laying violent hands upon a cleric or monk, he shall be subject to anathema; [Col. 0682C] and no bishop shall presume to absolve him until he presents himself before the apostolic see and receives its command.

#### XIV. That no one lay hands upon those who have fled to a church or cemetery

We also command that absolutely no one dare lay hands upon those who have fled to a church or cemetery. Whoever does so shall be excommunicated.

#### XV. That no one claim prebends or benefices by hereditary right

It is beyond doubt that ecclesiastical honors belong to merit, not to blood, and that the Church of God does not seek anyone as successor by hereditary right or according to the flesh, but demands upright, wise, and religious persons for its governance and for the administration [Col. 0682D] of its offices. Therefore, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from claiming, or presuming to demand, churches, prebends, provostships, chaplaincies, or any ecclesiastical offices by hereditary right. If any shameless man guilty of ambition presumes to attempt this, he shall be punished with the due penalty and shall be deprived of the things he has requested.

#### XVI. That blood relatives not be joined in marriage

We wholly prohibit unions between blood relatives. For the statutes of the holy Fathers and the sacrosanct Church of God detest incest of this kind, which, at the instigation of the enemy of the human race, has now almost passed into custom. [Col. 0683A] Secular laws also pronounce those born of such a union infamous and exclude them from inheritance.

#### XVII. On arsonists

By the authority of God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we utterly detest and prohibit the most wicked, depopulating, and horrifying evil of arson [the printed text reads “fires,” corrected to “arsonists”]. For this plague, this hostile devastation, surpasses every other form of pillage; no one is ignorant how harmful it is to the people of God and how great an injury it inflicts upon souls and bodies. We must therefore rise up and labor in every way so that, for the salvation of the people, so great a calamity and so great a ruin may be rooted out and destroyed. If, then, after the promulgation of this prohibition of ours, anyone maliciously—whether from hatred or revenge—sets fires, causes them to be set, or knowingly gives counsel or aid to those setting them, he shall be excommunicated. [Col. 0684A] If the arsonist dies, he shall lack Christian burial. He shall not be absolved unless, after first repairing according to his means the damage he caused, he swears that he will set no more fires. As penance, he shall be ordered to remain for a full year in the service of God at Jerusalem or in Spain. If any archbishop or bishop relaxes this sentence, he shall make good the damage and abstain from episcopal office for a year. We do not, however, deny kings and princes the power to execute justice after consulting the archbishops and bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0683B] The collection in the Évreux codex likewise attributes these canons to the Council of Reims. The same canons, however, were all promulgated again afterward at the Lateran Council of the same Innocent. It is probable that these same canons, either all or in part, were also promulgated at the Council of Auvergne, which this same Innocent had held at Clermont in the preceding year. Bernard Gui, in his short work on councils, testifies that at this Council of Clermont the canon prohibiting the laying of violent hands upon clerics was enacted. He says: “In the year of the Lord 1130, in the eighth indiction, in the month of November, a synod was celebrated at Clermont. Pope Innocent II presided there with cardinals, archbishops, bishops, religious men, and a multitude of wise and learned men. At it the Catholic faith, the building up of souls, upright conduct, and the rooting out of evils were discussed; and obedience was gladly promised by all to this same Pope Innocent, who was present. At that same synod a privilege was also granted to clerics; it is found in the Decretals, cause 17, question 4, chapter ‘Si quis suadente.’” Peter of Cluny also mentions Innocent’s councils at Clermont and Reims in book II, chapter 16 of *On Miracles*. —Jacques SIRMOND.

At the Council of Reims, Godehard, bishop of Hildesheim, was granted the honors of the saints. Bernard, bishop of that same city, had requested this from Innocent II at the Council of Liège, as we related under the Council of Liège. According to the anonymous author of the *History of the Canonization and Miracles of St. Godehard*, Innocent had referred the matter to the national council which, the anonymous writer says, “had then been announced for the city of Reims on the feast of St. Luke.” The feast of St. Luke fell on feria I, that is, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [October 18]; but Abbot Dodechinus says that the council was held on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November [October 19], because, according to custom, the first session was convened and the handling of business begun on the next day after the feast of St. Luke, that is, on feria II. Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim, came to the city of Reims with St. Norbert, his metropolitan, when the synod had already been in session for several days, says the same anonymous author, who adds a little later: “The bishop of Tarragona, a religious man trained in literary learning, explained the order in which the translation was to be performed.” This man was blessed Olegarius, bishop of Barcelona and archbishop of Tarragona, and not Michael, as Henschenius maintains in his commentary on the Life of St. Godehard under May 4; Michael was bishop of Tarazona in the kingdom of Aragon, not of Tarragona in the principality of Catalonia, that is, Barcelona. “The assembled synod ended with the canonization of St. Godehard,” says the anonymous author, who immediately reports the letters of Innocent II addressed to the clergy and people of Hildesheim and dated at Reims on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [October 29]. In them he announces that he has enrolled Godehard among the saints, and from them we understand that the synod of Reims ended on October 29. These are the letters of Innocent: “Innocent, bishop, etc.” (See above among Innocent’s letters, no. 61.) Thirteen archbishops and 263 bishops were present at this council, as well as a great multitude of abbots, monks, and clerics. “The king and queen and all the nobility of France came there,” says Orderic, book XIII, p. 893. Baronius, no. 7, seeing Bernard—or, more correctly, Ernald, abbot of Bonneval—write that the Council of Liège was held after the Council of Reims, left it in doubt which of the two had been convened first. Yet even if other testimony were lacking, the anonymous author cited by us, who lived at this time, would by himself certainly teach us that the author of the Life of St. Bernard was mistaken on this point.]

[Col. 0683]

# ADDITION TO THE COUNCIL OF REIMS

Sirmond first published the canons of the Council of Reims, and after him all the compilers did so; learned men never made public any others enacted at that council, nor did they suspect that any others could be made public. I thought the same as they did until chance put into my hands the codex of Udalric of Bamberg. Having obtained it, I immediately encountered the canons of this council at the very beginning of the codex. On comparing them with the published canons, I found that they differed from them in many respects. For the codex both presents certain canons which one seeks in vain among those commonly published and, in canons which agree with the published ones, adds certain things lacking there. Conversely, Udalric lacks certain things that are read in the published canons. There is no available explanation for this difference other than that in one of the two collections certain decrees have been gathered under the single title of the Council of Reims although the same pontiff defined them at other councils—for example, at Clermont and perhaps also at the general Second Lateran Council. Given this discrepancy among the codices, it would not be easy for anyone to decide which canons should be judged genuine canons of Reims and which were adopted from elsewhere. Yet the canons presented by Udalric may perhaps be accepted as the genuine canons of Reims on the ground that he completed his codex around the very years in which the council was held.

[Col. 0685]

# COUNCIL OF POPE INNOCENT II

These are copies of the decrees which were issued by the lord Innocent, apostolic head of the Catholic Church, and unanimously received by the whole synod of Reims.

## I

[Col. 0685A] First, therefore, it was decreed that no buying or selling of an ecclesiastical gift is to take place. Whoever buys one is deprived of what he had received, while the buyer, seller, and intermediary in the purchase are condemned by a sentence of excommunication.

## II

It was also determined by the lord apostolic and the whole council that no one hear the mass of a priest who has a concubine or wife.

## III

It was also confirmed with the consent of all that all clerics from the subdiaconate upward are to be continent, and those who are not continent are to be deposed.

## IV

It was also commanded, with everyone’s acclamation, [Col. 0685B] that no one be appointed archdeacon, dean, or bishop unless he is a deacon or priest.

## V

It was also sanctioned by apostolic authority and that of the whole council that none but the learned be admitted to instruction in divinity, where the secrets of divine mystery are to be examined. This remedy was devised against a disease which has grown very strong. For when the unlearned hear a reading of the divine page and do not understand it, they dispute in the streets before silly women, fall into error, and burst forth into profane words.

## VI

Sentence was also given that ordained clerics who possess ecclesiastical benefices are, wherever they may be, whether at home or at study, to wear clerical dress, with hair tonsured, beard shaved, [Col. 0685C] and garments rounded. This remedy was found for the vice by which certain rich men with ecclesiastical endowments avoid the presence of their prelates so that they may live more freely at their pleasure and spend the alms of the poor on their own extravagances.

## VII

The lord apostolic also commanded, with the voice of all consenting, that when a priest or bishop has died, his goods shall remain freely under the steward’s control until his Catholic successor receives them all intact.

## VIII

The venerable assembly of all the brethren also agreed on this: every church whose endowment is sufficient to support a cleric is to have its own priest, and no wage-earner [Col. 0685D] or hired man is to be admitted.

## IX

[Col. 0686A] It was declared and decreed in the word of the Lord that no one lay hands upon either a cleric or a monk of any order. Whoever violates this shall be kept far from participation in the divine office and from all ecclesiastical communion.

## X

It was ordained that churches, once they have been consecrated, are to be free and released from the hands of laymen.

## XI

It was confirmed under ban that countrymen are to have peace every day in their persons and possessions while they go to or return from their agricultural work, remain at it, or engage in any work of their hands.

## XII

[Col. 0686B] A general law was established for the observance of peace in every place and at every season of the year, from the evening of feria IV [Wednesday] until the morning of feria V [Thursday]. Moreover, it was decreed that what in our common speech is called the “peace of the day” is to be kept inviolably at the times established from of old. Perpetual peace was granted under confirmation of the ban to clerics, monks, and women.

## XIII

Concerning the dissolution of marriages, it was carefully determined that after the public celebration of a marriage neither husband nor wife is permitted to seek a pretext of his or her own choosing for dissolving the marriage. Nor is the oath of persons to be accepted who, prompted by private intimacy, swear that the spouses are related by blood. But if any faithful person, for the love of Christ, reveals some line [Col. 0686C] of blood relationship that prevents the marriage, and proves it by other indications and testimony, the venerable authority of the apostolic see judges that he is to be believed.

## XIV

Nor, by decree of the apostolic see and the whole council, is this pretext to be accepted: that after a man has taken a wife, he accuses himself of incest secretly committed with one of his wife’s female relatives.

At the end, Peter Leonis and Conrad, invaders of the kingdom and the Church, were condemned by a sentence of excommunication together with all their supporters. The archbishops, bishops, and abbots of the whole council inclined their burning candles to extinguish the memory of those men. The cardinals who departed from the unity of holy mother Church were also deposed.

[Note: [Col. 0685D] Canon 1 is canon 1 of Reims, but in place of “the mark of infamy,” Udalric writes “are condemned by a sentence of excommunication.” The canons of Reims of the year 1119, canon 1, and of Girona of the year 1078, canon 2, likewise impose no penalty upon them other than excommunication. It is also contrary to the decree of the Council of Chalcedon, canon 2.

[The source chunk ends here, in the middle of the note.]

Canon 2 is canon 5 in the published Rheims text. Canon 3 is canon 4 in the published text. Canon 4 is canon 8 in the published text; but in the published text nothing is read concerning a bishop except that he is at least to be chosen from among deacons. Urban II nevertheless enacted these provisions concerning a bishop at the Council of Clermont in 1095, chapter 5. Canon 5 is not found in the editions. Canon 6 corresponds to Rheims canon 2, but explains somewhat more concerning the form of vestments. Canon 7 corresponds to published canon 3. Canon 8 corresponds to published canon 9. [Col. 0686D] Canon 9 corresponds to published canon 13; for here to lay a hand upon a cleric is equivalent to inflicting violent hands upon him. Canon 10 corresponds to published canon 7. Canon 11 corresponds to published canons 10 and 11; but among those to whom perpetual peace is granted, women too are expressly included, something lacking in the editions. Yet the ancient canons also expressly included them: Audomar, 1099, canon 3; Narbonne, 1054, canon 15; Clermont, 1095, canon 1. Canon 12 is canon 11 in the editions, but is expressed in other words and differs somewhat from the editions in that the peace or truce of God is prescribed in the editions until sunrise on the second weekday [Monday], whereas here it extends until the evening of the first weekday [Sunday]. For this is how it should be read, as I noted in the annotation in that place. Canon 13 is wholly absent from the editions, but a not dissimilar enactment occurs in canon 16 of the Council of London. The final canon has almost nothing in common with published canon [Col. 0687] 16, but has parallels in the canons of preceding and subsequent councils.—It is worth observing here that the seventeen canons attributed to this council by two manuscript codices, whence they were taken by Sirmond, who first published them, all or nearly all belong to the other Council of Clermont, held by Innocent in the preceding year, which preceded this one. This is established, first, because canon 13, “If anyone at the instigation of the devil,” etc., is listed among the Clermont canons published by Baluze as canon 10, and is likewise ascribed to Clermont by Bernard Gui in his little work *On Councils*, and by Ptolemy of Lucca in Baluze, in the note on this council, to be read in the Venetian Labbe collection above page 449. Secondly, because nearly all those canons attributed to the Council of Rheims are read word for word [Col. 0688] among the Clermont canons; observe this in all the canons except 5, 9, and 14. Conversely, we know that several provisions were enacted at the Council of Rheims which are either not read at all among these canons, as is clear from the summary of the Rheims canons which we gave above from Udalric’s codex; or are otherwise absent. This is also clear from Innocent’s Letter LV, reproduced in the same collection, col. 426, in which the pontiff states that it was commanded by him at the Council of Rheims that bishops should receive the obedience and profession of abbots—a enactment which one searches for in vain among the seventeen canons. I therefore judge that these seventeen canons are a compilation of canons from the two councils held by Innocent in Gaul, Clermont and Rheims, and perhaps also Liège.]

## Appendix to the Privileges and Letters of Innocent II

## Anacletus, Antipope

[Col. 0687]

## Historical Notice

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, “A Chronologico-Historical Attempt toward a Catalogue of the Pontiffs,” in the propylaeum to the *Acta Sanctorum* for May.)

“Peter, a Roman by nation, son of Peter Leo, cardinal of SS. Cosmas and Damian, was elected by the smaller party on 17 February 1130; and on Sunday, the twenty-third, having assumed the name Anacletus, was consecrated. He sat seven years, eleven months, and twenty-two days; he died on the seventh day of February in 1138, and was buried in concealment, without pomp.”

No one explains the occasion of the schism more clearly than Abbot Suger in these words:

“After the supreme pontiff and universal pope Honorius, of venerable memory, had entered upon the way of all flesh, the greater and wiser men of the Roman Church, in order to avert disturbance, agreed that a public election should be held at St. Mark’s and nowhere else, and only collectively, according to Roman custom. But those who, through continual attendance and familiarity, had been closer to the apostolic lord, fearing to assemble there because of the disorderly Romans, before the death of the lord pope was announced chose as supreme pontiff the venerable Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo. Those, however, who favored the party of Peter Leo assembled at St. Mark’s, inviting others there in accordance with their agreement; and, learning of the lord pope’s death later, they elected, by acclamation, that same Peter, cardinal-priest, with the consent of many bishops, cardinals, clergy, and Roman nobles.”

The author of the *Beneventan Chronicle*, however, describes the course of the schism thus:

“After Innocent had been elected, on that very day at the third hour Peter, bishop of Porto, elected Peter, son of Peter Leo, as Anacletus; then, condemning that election of Innocent, they confirmed the election of Anacletus as pontiff. And Leo Frangipane, who followed Innocent’s party, began to exhort the Roman citizens, his adherents, and his friends to favor Innocent with their assistance. Then Leo, brother of the aforesaid Anacletus, having opened the treasury, urged nearly the whole Roman people to defend his brother’s election according to their means; and this was done. Thus a most savage civil war was violently begun by both sides.”

Then, as our Saxon Chronologer writes, “in the year 1131 a general synod was held in Lent at Liège, Pope Innocent presiding, with a numerous multitude of bishops, abbots, and clergy of various orders, and with King Lothair and Queen Richenza present. There Peter Leo, Conrad, and his brother Frederick, with all who favored them, were excommunicated by the apostolic lord himself and by the entire Church assembled there. Afterwards Pope Innocent, again gathering ecclesiastical men and crowds of the faithful, presided for several days over a general synod at the city of Rheims on the feast of St. Luke the Evangelist.”

For the rest pertaining to this matter, read Baronius. Only for chronological proof, take from the aforementioned Chronicle [Col. 0689] that in 1137, according to the Norman style:

“Anacletus, who lived under the name of pontiff, died on the seventh day before the end of January; he sat seven years, eleven months, and twenty-two days.”

When Baronius cites these words, he proves our point: that Anacletus’s election occurred not on 14 February, as he himself says, but on the 17th; and that Innocent’s death was concealed for the entire intervening two days, until the votes of those present in the cardinals’ palace had assembled for choosing a successor. They acted as though the pontiff were still alive, though dying by the hour, in order to conceal the matter from those outside. The Saxon Chronologer recorded Anacletus’s death in these words, under the year already mentioned:

“Peter Leo, who usurped the apostolic see against Pope Innocent, died”; but he makes no mention of a successor elected after him, I suppose because news of him had not crossed the Alps.

[Col. 0689]

## Letters and Privileges of Anacletus, Antipope

### I. To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, and other clergy and laity established throughout Germany and Saxony

(24 February 1130.)

[Eccard, *Corpus historiarum*, II, p. 351, from Udalric’s codex, no. 339.]

[Col. 0689B]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, and all other clergy and laity established throughout Germany and Saxony: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the authority of the blessed Apostle Paul we have learned, and have lately experienced in ourselves, that the judgments of God are truly unsearchable and his ways past finding out. For when my predecessor Pope Honorius died, our brethren the cardinals, deprived of their shepherd’s comfort, elected us to the supreme summit of the pontificate by a marvellous and astonishing unanimity of clergy and people. With what honor, with what concourse of people, and with what joy of all were we then conducted to the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and placed upon his most sacred chair—who could conceive it, who could tell it? Therefore, exhorting you by these present letters, we admonish and beseech you in the Lord to persist in the love and constancy of faith in which you have always stood, and, with the customary and due reverence toward the Roman Church, to strive by God’s grace to do what pertains to our honor and that of the same Church. Know assuredly [Col. 0691B] that you will by no means find us ungrateful for the effects of your good will. If, moreover, you hear any adverse report, do not be greatly surprised; for it belongs to God alone to unite purposes and wills. Nevertheless, consider false whatever may be reported other than what we have said, since you know that our election was celebrated in this manner. May almighty God preserve the fire of his love in your hearts and make you co-heirs of eternal blessedness.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

### II. To Lothair, king of the Romans, and Queen Richenza

(24 February 1130.)

[Eccard, *Corpus historiarum*, II, 351, from Udalric’s codex, no. 340.]

[Col. 0691C]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ LOTHAR, glorious king of the Romans, and likewise to R[ICHENZA], queen, special daughter of blessed Peter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

After, by God’s ordering, we were raised to rule the whole Church, as you will learn from the letters which we have sent to the bishops of your realm, we judged that Your Highness should be addressed by a special letter. Following the example of our predecessor Pope H[onorius], we desire with singular affection to love both you and your honor, and to regard your friends and enemies alike as ours. We ask that, for reverence toward blessed Peter and love for us, you endeavor to love your mother, the Roman Church, and to honor her in all things according to the authority given you by the Lord. Moreover, because Your Serenity petitioned Pope Honorius on behalf of our beloved brother, the archbishop of Cologne, we, upon the counsel of our brethren, graciously granting your prayers, relax our predecessor’s interdict for the sake of our love for you and restore our aforesaid brother to the full exercise of his office. Concerning Halvere, bishop of Stade, we reply briefly that we have decided to send one of our brethren to those regions, [Col. 0692A] who, with the counsel of our legate, the archbishop of Mainz, will, together with you, fulfill by the Lord’s aid what pertains to your honor and that of the realm. Through the same brother whom we shall send, for the sake of you and the entire realm, we have decided that full justice shall be done to our brother A., archbishop of Bremen, and that the privileges of his church shall be confirmed for him.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

### III. He grants Simon, abbot of Rastede, the use of the mitre, gloves, and sandals, at the request of A[dalbero], archbishop of Hamburg

(24 February 1130.)

[Lappenberg, *Hamburgische Urkunden*, I, 132.]

[Col. 0692B]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son S., abbot of the monastery of Rastede: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The nature of the office entrusted to us requires that we grant a gracious assent to our brethren and sons when they request what is just and honorable. Therefore, beloved son Abbot Simon, moved by your prayers, and especially overcome by the request and affection of our most beloved brother A., archbishop of the Church of Bremen, we grant, by the liberality of the apostolic see, to you and to your church a mitre, gloves, and sandals. Thus, by our authority, you may wear these insignia during the solemnities of Mass in councils and on the principal feasts of your monastery and of the Church of Bremen.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

### IV. Privilege for the monastery of St. Paul outside the City

(27 March 1130.)

[Margarini, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 139, from the archive of the sacred monastery of St. Paul outside the City, casket T, no. 3.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his reverend son in Christ ANASTASIUS, abbot of St. Paul the Apostle, and to the brethren regularly serving the Lord there now and in the future, for ever.

The administration of the apostolic see compels us, and the obligation of our office urges us, especially to honor the venerable monastery of blessed Paul the Apostle, made glorious by his most sacred body, and to endeavor to grant it our support, and support to those whom we can assist through the Apostle’s merit; especially since we appear not so much to bestow what is ours as to confirm what belongs to it. Therefore, granting the petitions of you, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Anastasius, and of your brethren, we grant and confirm to the monastery of that Apostle entrusted to you all offerings made by faithful Christians upon its high altar, in which the glorious apostolic body rests, or in the confession and at the other altars of that church, just as our predecessor Pope Alexander and other Roman pontiffs before him granted them to the said monastery. We likewise grant and confirm to you and your successors these possessions belonging to the same monastery at Albano: namely, the cell of St. Nicholas; the cell of St. Mary in the palace, called the Lesser; the church of St. Stephen; the church of the Holy Trinity; the church of St. Leonard; and the entire estate of Anseranum, with everything belonging to the aforementioned churches. In the larger lake of the same city, one fishery; in the smaller lake, called Lurnus, a fourth part; and whatever else the monastery is known to possess in that city. Likewise houses, lands, vineyards, gardens, cultivated and uncultivated places, and whatever we know it possesses in Antra. In the same way, the wood called Lapigium, with the church of St. Proculus, [Col. 0693B] under whatever other names it is called, and the cultivated and uncultivated places belonging to that wood. We grant and confirm to the same venerable monastery the city of Ardea, with everything generally belonging to it; the castle of Patrica; Decimum; Trifusa; the estate called “of the dragon”; the Florian estate, under whatever other names it is called, with lands, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, and all things generally belonging to it.

Likewise we grant and confirm to the same venerable monastery of St. Paul the Apostle the church of St. Anastasius at Fundus; Aquae Salviae, with the church of St. Nicholas and the other churches in the estate called Nemus; likewise that estate itself, with lands, vineyards, gardens, hemp-fields, watermills, fisheries, and everything generally belonging to it; together with the castles belonging to the same church of St. Anastasius. Moreover, we grant and confirm the estate of Paternus, situated outside the gate of St. Lawrence, with lands, marshes, gardens, watermills, cultivated and uncultivated land, and all appurtenances; the court of St. Cecilia de Mega, situated outside the gate of St. Lawrence, bounded as follows: on one side by the river Tiber, on the other by the stream of Mega; it ascends beside that stream as far as the lands of St. Lucy de Renatis, then to the public road, and thence descends to the public well, from which it ascends by small channels to the river Tiber. Also the two adjoining castles, namely Longetia and the castle of Palea, with all their appurtenances. Further, the castle of Osa, the estate of St. Julian and its court, with marshes, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, as they were anciently bounded, together with half of the place of Borranum, bounded as follows: on the first side by the river Tiber; on the second by the stream of Osa, as far as the bridge of Sts. Digna and Merita; on the third side, from the same bridge and along that other boundary as far as the broken pillar, and along that paved way to the stream of Spinetum; the fourth side is bounded by the same stream of Spinetum as far as the stream of Silicinum, and by that stream as far as the river. Further, the castle of Passaranum, with Rocca and all its appurtenances; the castle of Corcurulum; the castle of St. Victorinus, with all its appurtenances; [Col. 0694A] the church of St. Peter de Massa in the territory of Praeneste; also the castle of Formelli with all its appurtenances; the cell of St. Stephen with its castle in the territory of Sutri, with vineyards, lands, woods, gardens, mills, farmsteads, and tenant settlements belonging to it; the castle of St. Severa, with churches, lands, vineyards, woods, gardens, hemp-fields, a harbor and sea fisheries, and everything generally belonging to it; together with the castle of Campagnano, houses, lands, vineyards, and one estate in the territory of Nepi, and one estate at Giuliano; likewise the little town of Colonis and half the city of Stertiliana; Flagianum, Leprinianum, Morlupum, the castle of Vaccaritia, and the castle of Regianum, with all their appurtenances; the estate called Quintum, also called Lubra, with all its appurtenances. Likewise, one villa in Campo Rotondo; the estate called Ulmetium; the monastery of St. Leo situated beneath the Clivus Scauri, at the Seven Ways, with all its appurtenances; the church of Sts. Sergius and Bacchus situated in the Subura, with all its appurtenances; and the church of St. Nicholas by the aqueducts, with its goods.

Moreover, we will that the aforementioned monastery remain free and released from every yoke and jurisdiction of any person, except by the authority of our own and this privilege of the apostolic see; so that it may be subject in no manner to any person or any church other than our apostolic see alone. Therefore, we wholly forbid every priest of any church to exercise jurisdiction by any authority in the aforementioned monastery or in all the churches belonging to it, save by authority of our apostolic see. We further prohibit anyone, unless invited by the head of the same monastery, from presuming in any way to celebrate Mass there. Wherever, or from whatever bishop, the brethren of that place wish to be ordained, to have altars blessed, or to receive chrism, they shall have free power to do so. We also decree that no bishop may dare to excommunicate any monk or cleric established in the various places of the same monastery, or summon him to a synod, [Col. 0694D] without the permission of you or your successors; nor may he place under interdict churches belonging to that monastery. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that monastery, or of any of your successors, no one shall be installed there through any stratagem of intrusion, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict.

By the authority of this present privilege, therefore, we grant and confirm to the frequently mentioned venerable monastery whatever is known to have been granted by blessed Pope Gregory and by our other predecessors, Roman pontiffs of holy memory—Sylvester, Marinus, Leo, Stephen, and Alexander; whatever the aforementioned monastery possesses today through the donation of kings, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of any other faithful persons; and whatever, by the Lord’s bounty, it may acquire in the future. We grant and confirm these things both to you and to your successors hereafter.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be kept intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they have been granted. But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with rash boldness to violate or infringe in any respect this statute of our apostolic see, or should oppose it in any matter, then, by the authority of the holy and undivided Trinity and of Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, in whose place, though unworthy, we act by divine favor, let him be consigned to the bond of anathema, separated from the kingdom of God, and irrevocably joined to the devil and his angels unless, repenting, he makes satisfaction. But whoever, out of reverence, proves to be an observer and defender of this confirmation and grant, may he deserve, through the power of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, to receive from the just Judge, the Lord our God, entrance into the heavenly kingdom, grace and glory, and eternal life, for ever and ever. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 0695C] I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of the Apostles, have subscribed. I, Desiderius, cardinal-priest of the title of Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of St. Susanna the martyr, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Comes, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Sabina, have subscribed. I, Lictefredus, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Vitalis, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Balbina, [Col. 0695D] have subscribed. I, Jonathan, cardinal-priest of the title of Callixtus, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Pastor, have subscribed. I, Silvius, cardinal-deacon of the title of St. Lucy, have subscribed. I, Hermannus, cardinal-deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Saxo, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1130, [Col. 0696A] and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Anacletus II.

### V. He exhorts D[idacus], archbishop of Compostela, to persevere in zeal and faith toward Blessed Peter and to send envoys to him; he recalls the archbishop’s former friendship with his father of blessed memory, Peter Leo

(16 April 1130.)

[Flórez, *España Sagrada*, XX, 512.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You have always aided the common mother, the holy Roman Church, with outstanding zeal, and have diligently endeavored to assist our predecessors in their utmost necessities. Hence our lord and foster-father, Pope Paschal of holy memory, and the Roman pontiffs after him loved your Fraternity above others and adorned it with splendid marks of favor. We therefore, mindful both of your merits and of the former friendship which you especially maintained with my father, Peter Leo of good memory, desire, with the Lord’s help, principally to love and honor, after the Church of the apostles Peter and Paul, your person and the church of the blessed Apostle James entrusted to you. Let your energetic care, therefore, according to its accustomed practice, now gird itself for the service of Blessed Peter, and, persevering in its former love and constancy of faith, strive to love the Roman Church more on our behalf and to assist it more earnestly. Furthermore, we have sent letters to your Fraternity containing an account of our accession and of the scandal perpetrated by false brethren. We ask, therefore, that you have them publicly read before all who are in your regions and send copies to other regions. Moreover, do not delay in any way to send envoys of your Fraternity to us.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

### VI. He writes to the Cluniacs concerning his zeal for their monastery, where he recalls having assumed the monastic habit; he announces that, after Honorius’s death, he was elected in the church of Blessed Mark and consecrated in St. Peter’s basilica

(1 May 1130.)

[Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 1130, no. XXXV.]

[Col. 0696D]

Calling to mind the beginnings of my conversion, I find myself greatly indebted to the monastery of Cluny, because there, under the protecting grace of divine power, I received both the monastic habit and the beginning of a monastic way of life. Although I cannot repay in equal measure all that it has bestowed upon me in pious devotion from the full abundance of its charity, nevertheless, insofar as I can, I place myself under it in most faithful service. Therefore we have judged it fitting to inform your holy love by letters sent to you concerning our condition and those things which, through God’s merciful regard, have been successfully accomplished or are being accomplished in our affairs. For when our lord and predecessor Pope Honorius of pious memory departed this life, [Col. 0697A] the cardinal-priests, cardinal-deacons, and cardinal-subdeacons of the Roman Church, the primicerius with the whole school and orders of the palace, the judges and scriniaries, and all the Roman clergy, at the request of all the people and with the most devoted assent of the nobles, unanimously elected me—though unworthy—as Pope Anacletus in the title-church of Blessed Mark. Our venerable brother Peter, bishop of Porto, together with bishops from diverse regions, most solemnly consecrated the elect in the church of Blessed Peter, our patron.

But certain false brethren—sons of Belial, sons of pestilence, sons of Hagar—seeking the wisdom which is from the earth (Baruch 3), intoxicated by the cup of the wrath of almighty God, appeared with wicked boldness to oppose God’s ordering and the constitution of the Church. Their head is Aimeric, former chancellor, a slave of avarice, a crazed encourager of actors and buffoons, despoiler [variant: plunderer] of churches, wicked exactor from the servants of God, another Gehazi, who through public and private simonies has inherited by hereditary right the leprosy of Naaman (4 Kings 5) and God’s curse. John of Crema, a miserable man and truly a Nicolaitan, formerly condemned among the *biothanati*—those who have sought their own death—by Pope Honorius and the cardinals, plays along with him, induced by empty promises. Concerning Peter, cardinal of St. Anastasia, who proved an insatiable robber of the treasury of Cluny through habitual evasions, and concerning Gozelmus of St. Cecilia, we judged it more fitting to remain silent than to write to you concerning them and their most disgraceful servitude. They lived from Aimeric’s table [Col. 0697C] and, as is well known among us, bound by oath, follow the head of their wickedness in every respect.

> **Note [Col. 0697D]:** See Peter of Cluny, book III, letter 34.

As for certain pseudo-bishops whom the aforesaid man introduced as accomplices of his faction, we have no word and no concern, since nothing concerning the election of a Roman pontiff belongs to them. Moreover, since through God’s grace all things prosper for us, they are unable to harm us in any way and therefore multiply their curses. Most shameless dogs bark against us; with viperous mouth they slander us; and, belching forth their foul drunkenness, they vomit much out of their most evil conscience into God’s Church with most fetid mouth. For, according to the testimony of the wicked, they have made falsehood their hope, keeping their eyes darkened, not knowing that they speak iniquity on high and set their mouth against heaven, so that their tongue passes over [Col. 0697D] the earth. Nor is it surprising if they blaspheme us together with God’s Church, since their fathers called the master of the household, the Lord, Beelzebub (Matthew 10).

Therefore, dearest brethren in Christ, greeting you in paternal speech, we admonish your love in the Lord that, avoiding their deceptions if they should perhaps allure you, you may hold most steadfastly to the unity of the Roman Church. Those brethren of whom we have written, because they attempted to divide God’s Church and to set up an altar of anathema or a title of cursing, have been condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by their own judgment. For when our brethren met with all the Roman clergy, and they had been summoned three and four times but disdained either to give an account or to make satisfaction, they were cut off from the bosom of the Church by a deserved anathema. We delivered them to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme. Because it would be long to write of their intrigues and deceptive inventions, we have entrusted their investigation to the bearer of these letters, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of our see. We ask, therefore, Your Holiness not to withdraw, now that we are established in the governance of the apostolic see, the affection which you seemed to show toward me while I exercised an office of lesser rank. For, considering my weakness, I preferred to decline this burden, lest I should fail in the pastoral governance through an unequal administration, since I could not suffice for the summit of the apostolic see. But because one must not oppose the will of God who ordains, I obediently followed what the merciful hand of the Almighty willed to accomplish through me. May our lords and princes Peter and Paul, to whom you continually minister in the holy place, obtain for you the joys of eternal blessedness as you pray for us.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

### VII. He grants [Girard, bishop of Angoulême] legatine authority from the apostolic see in Aquitaine; commends Cardinal Gregory; and directs him to convene a council

(1 May 1130.)

[Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 1130, no. XLII.]

[Col. 0698C]

Because of your integrity, which the holy mother Roman Church has long experienced, and because she has loved and specially honored you as her most beloved and distinguished son, our lord and foster-father Pope Paschal, and the Roman pontiffs after him, on account of your outstanding virtues entrusted to you their authority for exercise in the regions of Aquitaine. Therefore, mindful of the past affection and care with which you have always loved and more readily heeded your mother, the Roman Church, we also grant the legation of the apostolic see, previously granted you through the liberality of our predecessors. As you are known to have held their authority, so we desire that henceforth you hold ours; and we confirm this freely and with a full regard of charity. To strengthen this our grant, [Col. 0698D] we have sent our beloved son Gregory, cardinal-deacon, whom we wish to remain for some time in those regions. We therefore command your Fraternity to endeavor to convene a council with that our son, in which, trusting in charity as mediator and acting with the counsel of the brethren and the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, you may correct what requires correction and confirm what is worthy of confirmation. Through him we also make you more fully informed concerning our elevation and the scandal which you have heard occurred in the Roman Church, so that your love may reject every falsehood and be able to adhere without hesitation to the testimony of truth.

[Col. 0699A] Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

> **Note [Cols. 0699D, 0700D]:** William of Malmesbury, in *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, mentions this same legation of Gerard in Aquitaine under Paschal. These things concerning the legation believed by the antipope to have been granted to the bishop of Angoulême. For the occasion, see St. Bernard, who treats him extensively in Letter 126 to the bishops of Aquitaine.

### VIII. To certain bishops, he commends Gregory, cardinal-deacon, sent by him to the regions of Aquitaine; he exhorts them to show reverence to Girard of Angoulême, whom, he writes, he has directed to hold a council

(1 May 1130.)

[Baronius, *ibid.*, no. XLI.]

The long-standing custom of our predecessors, and affairs that have recently arisen, compel us to send to you a legate from our side. We therefore dispatch our beloved son Gregory, cardinal-deacon, into the regions of Aquitaine, that you may receive him kindly, with your customary goodwill, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for ourselves [Col. 0699B], and that you may without hesitation lend your ears to him concerning the manner in which the Lord has willed that we preside over the Apostolic See, and concerning the disturbance which, as you have heard, has been caused in the Roman Church by a very few persons. The most holy Roman Church has found his fidelity proven; nor will he relate to you anything other than what truth teaches.

Furthermore, we make known to all of you that, because of the uprightness of his character and the effectiveness of his prudence, just as our foster-father Pope Paschal of blessed memory, and after him other Roman pontiffs our predecessors, did, we have called our venerable brother Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, with the generosity of the Apostolic See assisting him, to share in our concern throughout your provinces. [Col. 0699C] Therefore, by these present letters we command you to take care to show our same brother the reverence due to a legate of the Apostolic See. For we have instructed him and our beloved son that, once the assembly of the brethren has been convened and the grace of the Holy Spirit invoked, they are to correct what needs correction and strengthen what proves worthy of confirmation.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

IX. He recalls to the mind of a certain man’s “noble prudence” the friendship formerly maintained with his father of blessed memory. He explains the pontificate conferred upon himself, etc. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XIII.]

Mindful of our ancient friendship, and especially of that which [Col. 0699D] endured for a long time in steadfast firmness between you and my father of blessed memory, we judged it fitting to visit your noble prudence by letters of the Apostolic See and to renew the bonds of mutual affection by fitting representations. Therefore, the more closely we desire to embrace you in the arms of charity, the more carefully we have taken pains to make known to your affection, in the sequence of our letters, the condition of the Roman Church and the events that have taken place among us.

For when Pope Honorius of pious memory died, our brethren the cardinal-priests and deacons, together with all the Roman clergy, at the people’s request and insistence with untiring voices, and with the consent also, [Col. 0700A] in accordance with the tenor of the canons, of the honoured persons, unanimously chose me—though unwilling and unequal to the task—with devout hearts and united affection. Afterward, when bishops from different regions had assembled, our brother Peter of Porto most solemnly consecrated me, now elected, Roman pontiff at the altar of blessed Peter, before the eyes of all.

But certain brethren, novices in position and time and very few in number, smothered by the flattering cunning of certain traitors, attempted in darkness to set up another altar, introduce the anathema of Jericho into God’s sanctuary, and fashion the idol of Peor from the earrings of foolish women. Yet almighty God, who made foolish the counsel of Ahithophel, has now wonderfully destroyed their wicked designs. [Col. 0700B] For, fleeing by night from the house of Leo Frangipani [variant: Fraiapani, and so elsewhere], upon whose power they seemed chiefly to rely, they crossed the Tiber and, hiding there as though in a prison, are mournfully experiencing through repeated griefs the disgrace of their presumption.

Indeed, the whole Roman clergy adheres to us in indivisible charity. Leo Frangipani, prefect of the City, with his son and Cencius Frangipani, and all the nobles and all the Roman populace, have rendered us their customary fidelity. We too freely exercise, within and outside the City, the duties belonging to our office: we have made appointments of cardinals and, by God’s gift, consecrated bishops. Therefore we ask your nobility that, as we possess the firmest hope in you, you should labour with your customary zeal for the Roman Church [Col. 0700C] and allow us to experience the marks of your affection in manifest deeds. By doing this, you will make both the Roman Church always indebted to you and us hereafter your debtors.

Nor, dearest friend, let the monstrous falsehoods of Haimeric, formerly chancellor, an infamous robber and slave of simony, or of John of Crema, a most disgraceful and uncircumcised man, and a true Nicolaitan, move you; nor let their empty talk or poisonous lies penetrate the wall of your faith. Like Cain fleeing from the face of the Lord (Gen. 4), accursed from the earth, they are compelled to bear upon their prostituted brow the mark of fratricide.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

X. [To Louis, king of the Franks.] He commends his legate Otto, bishop of Todi. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XXVII.]

[Col. 0700D]

It has long been our will and desire to visit your person, dear to us, and the whole Gallican Church through such a legate as would know and be able vigorously and faithfully to promote the honour of God and of the Church, as well as your welfare. But, occupied with many affairs, we have until now delayed our desire. Now that an opportunity has arisen, we do not delay to perform, compelled by the obligation itself, what we perceive we have for a time omitted. [Col. 0701A]

For we place great confidence in the noble and proven constancy of your affection, by which you have loved our person from youth and fostered us with the kindly affection of your sweetness, so that, according to your custom, you may venerate our common mother, the Roman Church, with due honour and personally attend upon us with the abundance of your favour. Therefore we send from our side to your presence our dearest brother Otto, bishop of Todi, one of the principal members of the Church: a man of upright and religious character, and a planting of our lord and predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory. He will inform you concerning our condition and, in the various parts of your kingdom, will in our stead correct and confirm whatever requires correction or confirmation. [Col. 0701B]

By these present letters, therefore, we ask your nobility to receive him reverently and to endeavour to honour him as one bearing our authority. For whatever obedience or honour you show him, we shall count as shown to ourselves. We embrace you more fully in the arms of our goodwill and, the Lord granting, desire effectively to exalt the honour of you and of your son, the glorious King Philip.

Moreover, we have charged this our legate to make known more fully to you and your kingdom our promotion, celebrated by our brethren the cardinals and the suffragan bishops of the Roman Church; the unanimity of clergy and people with us; and likewise the disturbance created by a few false brethren. [Col. 0701C] Therefore we ask you to set yourself as a most strong wall for the Church of God and turn your ears utterly away from their lies and slanders, so that, among the other princes of the Christian people, the whole Church together with us may recognize you, as always, so now also, as a foremost defender of the Catholic faith.

We greet with the apostolic blessing the lady queen, most beloved daughter of blessed Peter. May almighty God, through the merits of His apostles Peter and Paul, preserve your persons and authority, and through temporal rule grant you a share in the eternal kingdom.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

XI. [To Philip, son of Louis, king of the Franks.] He commends his legate Otto; he asks him not to heed the lies of his enemies. (1130.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XXIX.]

[Col. 0701D]

The memory of your noble deeds and the grace of ancient friendships move us to visit your person, dear to us, by means of a legate who knows how vigorously and faithfully to promote the honour of God and of the Church, and your welfare. Accordingly, we send to you from our side our dearest brother Otto, bishop of Todi, one of the principal members of the Roman Church: a wise and religious man, a planting of our lord and predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory. He is to visit you yourself and our brethren and sons, [Col. 0702A] and to report to you orally the manner in which the Lord has willed that we be advanced to this office of honour—and the prosperity that, by God’s grace, has attended us. Further, if there is anything in those regions needing correction or confirmation, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, he is to correct and confirm it in our stead.

By these present letters, therefore, we ask your nobility to receive him reverently and to endeavour to honour him as one bearing the authority of ourselves—indeed, of blessed Peter. But let not the malicious talk and false inventions of certain pseudo-brethren shake the constancy of your affection; for their lies, once exposed, will become more fully known to you and your kingdom through our legate. Moreover, the many offices of generosity bestowed both upon our predecessors and personally upon ourselves [Col. 0702B] cannot, and ought not, to pass from our memory. For these, God granting, we desire to respond with an equal return to you and to your honour.

We therefore ask that, as always, so now you persist more diligently in the service of blessed Peter and in love for us, so that, according to the praiseworthy custom of your goodwill, we and the whole Church with us may find you among other kings and princes a foremost helper.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s.

XII. He commends his legate Otto to certain bishops. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XXX.]

It had long been our desire to send you a suitable messenger [Col. 0702C] from our side; but, being occupied with many affairs, we have until now delayed that desire. Now that an opportunity has arisen, we have judged that our dearest and venerable brother Otto, bishop of Todi, one of the principal members of the Roman Church, should be sent into your regions. He is to visit you more fully on our behalf and inform you concerning our condition; and, should any matters among you require discussion, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, he is to deal with them together with you in our stead.

By these present letters, therefore, we ask all of you to receive him reverently and to endeavour to assist and obey him as our vicar. We also urge that the praiseworthy constancy of your faith not be disturbed by the malicious talk and deceptive inventions of certain persons [Col. 0702D] who, following their own desires, have presumed to erect another altar in God’s Church and to fashion in secret darkness an idol with bloodstained hands.

You should know that what, by God’s ordering, you have heard was done concerning our promotion was celebrated not in a corner or hiding place, but in light and openly, by the whole clergy and people of the City, after the brethren’s deliberate counsel, with common consent and unanimous desire. By God’s grace, we freely exercise throughout the City, inside and outside it, the duties belonging to our office. We have directed that whatever is less fully contained in this letter be reported more completely to you orally and in writing by our same legate. May almighty God encompass you with His blessing and make you fervent in His love.

[Col. 0703A] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

XIII. To certain bishops he commends Otto, bishop of Todi, his legate. He exhorts them to fidelity. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XLII.]

Both the authority of the Apostolic See and the necessity of emergent affairs compel us to visit our brethren dwelling everywhere with more frequent letters and with envoys sent from our side. Above all, we have judged the Gallican Church most worthy of our visitation, since among the other Churches of Christendom it has never yielded to any errors, nor could it at all be stained by the reproach of schismatic perversity. Persevering always in steadfast fidelity to God, it has sought to preserve the peace and unity of the Roman [Col. 0703B] Church and always to exalt it by great demonstrations of service.

Accordingly, we have judged that our dearest brother Otto, bishop of Todi, one of the chief members of the Roman Church, should be sent to you, associating him [perhaps *asciscentes*, “enlisting him”] in our pastoral concern: a man indeed wise . . . . . and religious, trained in the Roman Church from early youth. He is to visit your Church and yourselves on our behalf, bless clergy and people, and inform you more fully concerning the matters which, by God’s grace, have prosperously happened to us. We have also instructed him to hold councils in your regions and, should any affairs arise, [Col. 0703C] to settle them together with you, justice mediating.

We therefore ask your brotherhood to receive him reverently and endeavour to assist and obey him as our vicar. Nor let the constancy of your faith be disturbed by the malicious talk or deceptive inventions of certain persons who, following their own desires, have presumed to erect another altar in God’s Church and fashion an idol in darkness with bloodstained hands. You should know that what, by the Lord’s ordering, you have heard was done concerning us was celebrated not in a corner or hiding place but in light and openly, after the brethren’s deliberate counsel, by the whole clergy and people of the City. By God’s grace we freely exercise, throughout the City, within and outside it, the duties belonging to our office. Whatever is less fully contained in this letter, our same legate [Col. 0703D] will relate more completely to your affection. May almighty God encompass you with His blessing and always make you fervent in His love.

Given at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

XIV. To a certain bishop he commends Otto, his legate. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XXXI.]

You yourself know how great is our confidence in the diligence of your integrity and how fully we embrace you in the ampler arms of our goodwill. We believe that you have already received an account of the manner of our promotion; and now you will be able to learn what prosperity the Lord has bestowed upon us.

[Col. 0704A] For we are sending our legate, the venerable brother Otto, bishop of Todi, one of the principal members of the Roman Church, into the regions of Gaul. He is to visit our dearest and glorious son the king, yourself, and our other brethren and sons, and to inform them concerning our condition. If there is anything in these regions needing correction or confirmation, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, he will correct and confirm it in our stead.

We therefore commit him to your affection and especially commend him to your proven ability, asking that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and affection for ourselves, you assist and support him in everything you recognize to be proper. Do not merely give him dutiful assistance, but, taking care of our cause upon yourself, do not shrink from placing upon your shoulders the laborious burden of solicitude for us, [Col. 0704B] knowing that you will never find us ungrateful for the services of your charity. May the Lord deign to preserve your brotherhood, obedient to our admonitions, unharmed.

Given at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

XV. To a certain bishop. He excuses himself for sending him letters late. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XXXIV.]

Do not wonder, dearest brother, that we wrote to you late concerning our condition and that of the Roman Church, for we too have been occupied by the grievous burden of the unexpected care of the government we have undertaken. Pressed by diverse waves in so great a forest of roaring beasts, we have been tossed by the harsh whirlwinds of storms. Such burdens of thought weigh me down, I am struck by such scourges of affairs, and afflicted by such tempests of a tumultuous life, that my mind can in no way raise itself to things above, and I am compelled rightly to cry: “I came into the depths of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68).

[Col. 0704C] For I consider who I am; and, plainly considering my own weakness, I see that by my own merits I could not attain the summit of the Apostolic See. I preferred to decline this burden, lest I should succumb in the pastoral office through deeds of administration unequal to it. But because one may not resist the decision of God who disposes all things, I obediently followed what the merciful hand of the Almighty willed to accomplish concerning me. Therefore, since the custom of the Church required it and the affection of your blessedness urged us, we have taken care not only to fulfil, in writing, our vows of charity and friendship to your brotherhood, but also to inform you, through the bearer of this letter, our venerable brother Otto, bishop of Todi—ordained by our holy lord and predecessor Pope Paschal—of our promotion, which we believe was welcome to you.

He, indeed, can more truthfully relate to your experience the matters transacted among us and the condition of the City and the Church, inasmuch as he knows them more fully. We believe that through the reports of many persons you have already learned [Col. 0705A] that our election was carried out by unanimous vote and harmonious procedure by our brethren the cardinal-priests, deacons, and subdeacons, by the *primicerius*, by the entire staff of the palace, and by all the Roman clergy, with all the people requesting it and the honourable persons consenting in accordance with the tenor of the canons.

Perhaps you do not fail to know how our consecration was solemnly celebrated at the altar of blessed Peter by our venerable brother Peter, bishop of Porto, together with bishops from different regions; and how, proceeding by the Sacred Way, with the Phrygian cap placed upon our head according to the custom of our predecessors, we came to the Lateran palace. Therefore, placing fuller confidence in the faith and constancy of your most sweet blessedness, we earnestly beseech you to support us with the devout assistance of your prayers before almighty God and to watch with your customary zeal for the Roman Church. But how [Col. 0705B] we ought to trust in the charity of your brotherhood, we infer from the character of the affection which we bear toward you. Nor do we think that you love our person and the Apostolic See otherwise than we ourselves love you.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

XVI. [To a certain Gallic prince.] He seeks to win him to his cause. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XXXIII.]

Your predecessors of noble memory, being wise men and provident in counsel, took care to honour the Holy Roman Church and to exalt it more earnestly in return for the power bestowed upon them by the Lord. As we ourselves saw and testify, [Col. 0705C] they served our predecessors with noble devotion. Hence the Apostolic See embraced them with greater favour among the other princes of Gaul.

Therefore, addressing your affection in paternal words, we earnestly exhort your prudence in the course of this letter: be the noble successor of noble predecessors, remain always united to the Roman Church in indivisible charity, and never decline from its unity. If you wisely rest upon it with untiring devotion, you will be able, God granting, to reign in secure stability. We, placing much confidence in your nobility and in the steadfastness of your faith [variant: “in the immovability and constancy of your faith”], have resolved in every way to honour your person with fitting titles and to enlarge your honour by the affection of paternal love.

Our venerable brother Otto, bishop of Todi, the bearer of this letter and our legate, whom we send to your regions on various affairs, will inform your affection concerning our promotion [Col. 0705D] and the things transacted among us. We therefore earnestly commend him to your excellent integrity and ask that, out of love for blessed Peter and for us, you come to his aid with your customary generosity and support him with your assistance. Thus, with God cooperating, he may effectively carry out the charge committed to him through your customary diligence, and we may experience in him your care.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

XVII. To the bishop of Drivasto he announces that he has been made pontiff. He states that he has sent a legate to the emperor of Constantinople. (1130, 1 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XLVII.]

[Col. 0706A]

The nature of the office we have undertaken urges us to communicate the beginnings of our appointment to brethren both near and far. Let your brotherhood know, therefore, that when our predecessor Pope Honorius died, our brethren the cardinal-priests and deacons of the Holy Roman Church, together with the entire clergy and people of the City, chose us by common vote and desire for the supreme height of the pontificate; and, when elected, we were most solemnly consecrated by our brethren, the suffragan bishops of the Roman Church, at the most holy body of the blessed apostle Peter.

But your labours and persecutions inflicted upon you by the barbarians are grave; accordingly, both the common obligation of charity and the governance of the Apostolic See compel us [Note: [Col. 0705D] The passage is corrupt.] to suffer with the afflictions of all our brethren and give more careful aid to their distress. [Col. 0706B] We regret, however, that you did not make known to us before these days what you are suffering. If [perhaps *nam si*, “for if”] we had heard it earlier, we would more willingly have written on behalf of your peace and aid through the legate whom we sent to our dearest son, the emperor [Note: [Col. 0705D] The emperor whom he names must necessarily be understood as the Eastern emperor, since the Western Empire was still vacant.].

But we exhort your affection to bear all things patiently and to endure with equanimity the oppressions inflicted upon you, so that you may deserve to receive the blessedness [Col. 0706C] which the Lord promises to those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. Let no persecution or oppression ever disturb you so greatly that you abandon your spouse, namely the Church of Drivasto, or in any way depart from the ancient law and tradition of the Fathers. We, however, shall not fail your brotherhood whenever we may render the aid owed and appropriate to you and your Church.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Kalends of May.

XVIII. [To King Lothair.] He regrets that Lothair has neither answered the letters sent to him through [Adalbert], archbishop of Bremen, nor sent envoys. (1130, 15 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XIX.]

[Col. 0706D]

At the very beginning of our promotion, we sent letters to your serenity through our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bremen, setting forth more explicitly both the condition of the Roman Church and the matters which had occurred concerning us. Yet we have so far merited no reply from your clemency, nor, amid the manifold anxieties by which we are oppressed while set over the government of the Apostolic See, have we been relieved by the consolation of your envoys.

When we were established in the administration of a lesser order, we greatly loved your person because of the extraordinary reputation of your virtues, and so far as we then could, we fostered the fortunes of the kingdom you had undertaken. Therefore [Col. 0707A] your experience should know beyond doubt that it is our wish that, the more the Apostolic See is supported by the piety of the kingdom, the more fully we should embrace your honour and kingdom in close arms. For royal power and sacred Roman authority ought mutually to answer one another with reciprocal care.

Indeed, the condition of subjects will then be secure if, in your days, kingdom and Church smile upon one another through their corresponding claims of fellow-feeling; and the governance of your kingdom will extend more broadly to the height of empire if you obtain God’s grace in this matter by devout dedication.

Further, that we may seem to satisfy your wishes, we desire that the matters concerning us become better known to your diligence. By God’s grace and the merits of His apostles Peter and Paul, we are well and prosperous; [Col. 0707B] we freely administer, within and outside the City, the affairs belonging to our office, and all that we possess is at peace. Our brethren the cardinals and bishops, and the whole Roman clergy, adhere to us in indivisible charity. The illustrious men Leo Frangipani, Hugh prefect of the City, his brother, son of Leo Frangipani, and his brother Cencius; Stephen of Peter, Stephen of Theobald, the sons of Henry of Saint Eustace; all the nobles and all the Roman populace; and the captains and counts who are outside the City have sworn us the fidelity due to us. We hold peacefully and securely the basilica of blessed Peter, the Lateran palace, and the other strongholds of the City.

We solemnly excommunicated Conrad, the usurper of the kingdom—although we held his name of very little account—on Maundy Thursday, in the Lateran basilica of the Saviour, before the eyes of the Church, which had gathered in great numbers that day from different [Col. 0707C] parts of the world, and also in the sight of all his own land.

We therefore ask your noble prudence and admonish you in the Lord, that, as we possess good and firm hope in you, you may rejoice at our successes, show royal and pious concern both for us and for the whole Roman Church, and render us effective care. Nor let the wicked empty talk of certain poisoners disturb you. Wishing to poison the whole Church of God, while they intended to establish former exactions and customary trading in the sanctuary of the Lord, they attempted to fashion a clay idol with bloodstained hands; but that cornerstone descending from the mountain of the Lord (Eph. 2) shattered it with a hard blow. [Col. 0707D] May God’s merciful right hand protect you unharmed from all evils and mindful of us.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the days of [the Ides of] May.

XIX. To Queen Richenza. He extols her virtue with praise and exhorts her to strengthen King Lothair’s devotion to the Roman Church. (1130, 15 May.)

[BARON., ibid., no. XXII.]

We have heard, dearest daughter in the Lord, that you shine with truly Christian holiness; that you love churches; and that everywhere you sustain the servants of God with devout aid. Nor indeed are you to be exalted with lesser praises because the governance of the whole kingdom is said to depend especially upon your administration, directed by the rule of justice. Whatever we have heard concerning your blessedness, most illustrious daughter, we believe without hesitation. These and many other good things frequently reported to us about you rejoice us, and in constant prayers we beseech almighty God, through the merits of the apostles Peter and Paul, to grant you to bring the works of holiness you have begun to a devout and better end.

We therefore exhort your noble prudence and admonish you in the Lord: amid the cares of the kingdom, the anxieties of secular affairs, and the glories of the age, always keep your heart directed to the Lord and remember that you too will someday die. Do not seek the world’s praise for pious works, lest, while it delights you to please people outwardly, [Col. 0708B] you displease the eyes of God inwardly.

Urge your husband, our dearest son Lothair, the most Christian king, by earnest counsel, so to preside by human authority over his earthly kingdom that he may always carefully and diligently attend to Him who is above us, through whom kings reign and princes decree what is just (Prov. 8), who transfers kingdoms when He wills, makes kings inglorious, and girds their loins with a cord. Although he embraces the Roman Church with full arms, as we are certain, we nevertheless desire, through your diligence especially, that his love and affection for the Apostolic See and for ourselves—who have long loved it—may increase.

For our part, we love his person with more earnest charity [Col. 0708C] and, the Lord granting, desire to preserve, carefully and effectively enlarge, his honour. Since, because my sins required it, I have been compelled to undertake the governance of the Church and am forced to bear the burden of the apostolate in bitterness of soul, I need the support of holy persons, that by the persistence of their prayers they may always render God favourable to me and increase His grace at all fitting times and in every need. Therefore we earnestly beseech you both to pray more insistently to God for us and more frequently to relieve us by your help and devout counsels.

May almighty God, through the merits of His apostles Peter and Paul, increase your life and years in good works and, after the course of this life, grant you eternal life.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, in the days of [the Ides of] [Col. 0708D] May.

XIX *bis*. To a certain bishop. He reports that he has received homage from the Romans, and complains of the abbot of Farfa as an adversary. (1130, 15 May.)

[MARTENE, *Ampl. Collect.*, I, 698, from a Cassinese codex.]
