At the beginning of our promotion we sent letters to all of you, in which we took care to inform you more fully about what the Roman Church had then done concerning us. But after our consecration, which by God’s grace was solemnly celebrated at the altar of blessed Peter, many favourable and advantageous things have occurred to us. We therefore judged it fitting to visit you with repeated letters [Col. 0709A] and make your brotherhood more certain concerning the matters relating to us.

For we are, by the Lord’s gift, well and prosperous; and, after confuting the enemies of the Catholic Church with fitting rebukes, we effectively perform everywhere in the City, inside and outside it, the duties that appear to belong to our office. Our brethren the cardinals and the Roman clergy are united to us in indivisible charity. Leo Frangipani, with his son and his brother Cencius, most illustrious men, the prefect and all the nobles, and the whole people have rendered us homage and fidelity.

Accordingly, if any ravings of schismatics reach you, if their old wives’ tales and fraudulent lies gain credibility through anyone’s assertion, refute them with prompt diligence. Do not look to vanities and false madness, and, in the Apostle’s words, do not share in unfruitful works, but rather rebuke them. For it is shameful even to speak of what is done in secret. These are the persons who, as the prophet testifies, practised divination for foreign pay, and “our [lacuna] put something into their mouths; they proclaim war against them.” [Note: [Col. 0709D] Here the sentence is mutilated.] [Col. 0709B]

They have set altar against altar in God’s Church; they have been cut off by the canonical sword. Know that the same has happened to the abbot of Farfa. After the death of Pope Honorius of blessed memory, he despised the oath which he had made to the Roman Church, brazenly and rashly seized the regalian rights of blessed Peter, and now does not cease to persecute God’s Church and, aided by fury wherever he can, to harass it. Yet, driven back, struck by the Church’s sling, and condemned by the sentence of excommunication, he can no longer retain accomplices in his iniquity.

We therefore command your brotherhood and admonish you in the Lord, while you persist most steadfastly in fidelity to blessed Peter and to ourselves, diligently to pursue the aforesaid abbot of Farfa—the plant of Antichrist—as a bloodstained beast by every means, and to cut down with axe and adze the horns with which he tosses about the Roman Church. [Col. 0709C]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the Ides of May.

XX. To Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, he commands that he restore what he unjustly took from the archdeacon and appear before him “on the octave of Saint Martin next” (18 November). (1130, 18 May.)

[BARON., *Annals*, for 1131, no. VI.]

[Col. 0709D]

Atticus, the bearer of this letter and archdeacon of your Church, having come to the thresholds of the apostles, stated in our presence and that of our brethren that he had been severely oppressed by your brotherhood. He reported that you had accused him before the brethren of treason, that he had denied it, and that he had answered in chapter that canonical satisfaction had been rendered to you. When, therefore, on the appointed day for proceeding in the same case he came before you and the chapter, and clearly perceived that you were both accuser and judge—which [Col. 0710A] is wholly contrary to reason and justice—he appealed to the Apostolic See and named a date on which he would render you justice before the Roman pontiff.

After this appeal, as he himself asserts, taking occasion from the death of our predecessor Pope Honorius of blessed memory, you despoiled him, when he was coming to us as he had proposed, of his ecclesiastical benefices and other possessions. Let the prudence of your brotherhood consider, then, how grave and inappropriate it is for you to attempt to take from the Apostolic See that privilege which, through divine gift and the ancient tradition of the holy Fathers, it has deserved to possess until now by God’s grace, and which, through the merits of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—for whom Christ Himself prayed that his faith might not fail—it will possess inviolate to the end. [Col. 0710B]

Therefore we command your brotherhood and, by the authority of the Apostolic See, order you to restore in full to that archdeacon what you have taken away and henceforth permit him peacefully to hold all his possessions. On the octave of Saint Martin next, present yourself before us, there to receive full justice concerning him in the presence of ourselves and our brethren. We also command you by these present letters—as our predecessor of blessed memory commanded you—that you no longer presume to prevent our sons, the canons of the Church of Magdeburg, from coming to us, if you wish to retain the favour and affection of blessed Peter.

For we take nothing from you or your honour. Rather, if there is no failure on your part, we desire, with the full affection of all charity, to love both you and the Church entrusted to you and, the Lord granting, to honour it. [Col. 0710C]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, fifteen days before the Kalends of June.

XXI. To certain friends. Concerning his promotion. (1130.)

[MARTENE, *Ampl. Collect.*, I, 699, from a Cassinese manuscript.]

From the very beginning of our elevation, we resolved, in fulfilment of the duty of the Roman pontificate, to send our letters to you as to spiritual brethren and sons of blessed Peter. But since we are occupied with many affairs, we have resolved to visit you by letters of apostolic blessing. Having therefore obtained an opportunity through the bearer of these letters, we have taken care to direct to you a letter of our affection, by which you may more fully learn of our elevation [Col. 0710D] and of the condition of the Roman Church. For when Pope Honorius, our predecessor of good memory, died, our brethren of the Roman Church—the cardinal priests and deacons, the suffragan bishops, together with the primicerius and all the orders of the palace, the abbots, archpriests, and the whole clergy and people of the City—under the obedience of the whole Church, imposed upon me, though unworthy, the most weighty burden of the high-priesthood at the altar of blessed Peter. We give thanks to almighty God, moreover, because from that time we have everywhere, both within and outside the City, carried out the service of the Church in full liberty.

## XXII. He affirms that he has resolved to exalt and honour the city of Jerusalem.  
*(Fragment.—Year 1130.)*

[BARONIUS, under the year 1130, no. XLVIII.]

[Col. 0711A]

Since the holy city of Jerusalem and the most glorious place of the Lord’s burial were, by God’s ordinance, restored to Christians, the Roman Church has never ceased to labour by every means for the protection of its defence. Therefore we, who by divine appointment have been raised to the watchtower of the apostolic see, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and reverencing with due honour that renowned city of Jerusalem and those places where His feet stood, have resolved to exalt and honour them exceedingly by whatever means we can, through the grace of almighty God [Col. 0711B], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0711] From this fragment it is clear that Anacletus sent an envoy with letters to the king of Jerusalem.]

## XXIII. To a certain friend.—He wonders that he has sent him neither letter nor messenger, and urges him to visit him by letter.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 699, from a Cassinese manuscript.]

From almost the very beginnings of our childhood, we have experienced plainly the affection with which you loved us especially; and we too, if you remember rightly, have embraced you with no sluggish charity. Therefore we wonder not a little that, since our elevation, we have deserved no visit from your brotherhood either by letters or by messengers. Whatever the reason may have been, we nevertheless retain the firmest hope of your affection; and therefore, visiting your brotherhood by this present letter, we ask that you cause us to experience the warmth of your love through reciprocal letters. For silent affection represents the affection of one who does not love, and it is an image of hatred not to disclose what one loves. We believe this sufficient for a wise man.

## XXIV. To a certain bishop.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[LUPUS, *Letters of Various Fathers concerning the Council of Ephesus*, vol. I, p. 514.]

Every occasion on which we write to your brotherhood, venerable brother, is welcome to us. For perfect love knows no weariness, nor does it eat bread in idleness [Col. 0711D].

## XXV. To a certain prince.  
*(Year 1130.—LUPUS, ibid.)*

Very many good reports reach us concerning your noble prudence, and the praises of your law-abidingness are proclaimed by widespread renown.

## XXVI. To a certain person.  
*(Year 1130.—LUPUS, ibid.)*

We know that, before we assumed the government of the apostolic see [Col. 0712A], you loved us with especial devotion; and we do not at all doubt that now you ought to love us with still fuller affection.

## XXVII. To a certain prince.  
*(Year 1130.—LUPUS, ibid.)*

The illustrious report of your nobility, dearest son, gladdens us; and although unknown to us in face, the praises of your renown make you most well known to us, etc.

## XXVIII. To a certain kinsman.—He complains that he has not come to him and has caused others to fear his elevation.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 700, from a Cassinese manuscript.]

[Col. 0712B] Concerning your affection, dearest son, we had hoped very differently from what has occurred; for it is plainly evident in you that thorns spring up for us instead of wheat, and briars instead of barley. For when you had learned by certain reports of our elevation—which we hoped would be most welcome to you—you ought, both because of our kinship and because of the common obligation owed to the Church, to have presented yourself to us promptly. Yet not only did you yourself fail to come to us, but by your discouragements you caused the hearts of others to fear. We therefore command your affection, since we desire to see you, to hasten to come to us as quickly as possible.

## XXIX. To a certain bishop adhering to him.—He receives his letters gratefully and has great hopes of him.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, ibid.]

[Col. 0712C]

We have received the letters of your affection, dearest brother in Christ, with the fullest affection of charity. In them we see that the devotion which you are known hitherto to have shown toward your mother, the Roman Church, and toward our honour, now overflows more warmly and more intimately. While we were placed in the administration of a lesser office, we always loved your person with special affection from our earliest years. But now, although unworthy, by the disposing mercy of God, established in the government of the apostolic see by the vote and desire of the whole Roman clergy and people, we desire to embrace you all the more in the arms of charity [Col. 0712D], because we recognize that the Roman Church has very great need of your counsel and aid.

## XXX. To certain bishops.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[LUPUS, *Letters of Various Fathers concerning the Council of Ephesus*, p. 515.]

We give thanks to almighty God and to His apostles Peter and Paul because what we hoped concerning the constancy of your faith, dearest brethren in Christ, is more fully made manifest by the actual performance of your deeds toward us, etc.

## XXXI. To the bishop of Aquileia.—He congratulates him on the care of the Church of Aquileia entrusted to him and promises him great honours.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 701, from a Cassinese manuscript.]

[Col. 0713A]

We greatly rejoice that the Church of Aquileia has been entrusted to your care and protection, being certain that through your zeal and labour it will suffer neither loss in external matters nor harm in those within. Therefore, by this present writing, we admonish your affection not to delay in providing, as wisely as possible and to the extent that lies within you, for the liberty and honour of the Church. Moreover, we especially invite you to the service of blessed Peter and to our own. For among the other faithful princes and sons of the Roman Church, we wish to honour you [Col. 0713B].

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s.

## XXXII. To a certain bishop.—He commends to him the priest Marcuald, whom he permitted to celebrate Mass.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, ibid., from the same manuscript.]

The priest Marcuald, coming to us, set forth his complaint about the injury inflicted upon himself and your Church more by his expression than by speech, and humbly entreated that by our authority he might be permitted to celebrate Mass. Therefore, grieving over the insult inflicted upon him and following the authority of the Council of Nicaea, by canonical judgment and with the counsel of our brethren the bishops and cardinals, we order him to celebrate the solemnities of Mass [Col. 0713C]. And because your brotherhood has asked on his behalf, we commend him to you in the Lord.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s.

## XXXIII. He commands the clergy of [Justinopolis] to come to him on account of the bishop’s most grave offences.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[BARONIUS, *Annals*, under the year 1130, no. LIV.]

Very grave matters concerning your bishop have been reported to us; and, if they are true, we cannot leave them unpunished without compromising our salvation. For we have learned that many laymen and clerics have been mutilated, and many killed through his agency. Therefore, by the present letters we admonish you to come before us before the feast of All Saints [Col. 0713D], so that with your aid and counsel we may be able to provide for the Church of Justinopolis in this matter and in others.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s.

## XXXIV. He confirms the possessions of the Roman church of St Lawrence, consecrated by him on 24 June [VIII Kalends of July].  
*(Year 1130.)*

[BARONIUS, *Annals*, under the year 1130, no. L.]

If we wish to weigh with integrity of mind the obligation of the pastoral office which, by God’s disposal, we have undertaken, we ought to impart more generously the bounty of our liberality to all churches throughout the world, but especially to those of kindly Rome itself. Yet we openly recognize that we are debtors in a greater degree to the churches of the City and to our sons, the Roman clergy, inasmuch as, through their unanimous vote and the integrity of their affection, divine grace cooperating, we have attained the height of the high-priesthood [Col. 0714A]. Therefore, graciously consenting to your petitions, most beloved sons, by the generosity of the apostolic see alone we bestow, grant, and remit to you—and through you to the church of blessed Lawrence, whose venerable altar was solemnly consecrated through God’s grace by our hands, as though by the hands of blessed Peter, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June—all revenues from the estates which you possess to this day in the estate of Vestrano, or in the wood called Proba, situated in that same estate: namely, lands, a village, vineyards, meadows, woods, and brushwood. The peasants who live on those same properties shall likewise remain forever under your lordship [Col. 0714B] and jurisdiction, saving an annual rent of two marabotins, which, as a sign of this our gift, you shall pay each year to the Lateran palace on the anniversary of the aforesaid consecration. Moreover, we confirm to you the church of St Lucy and that of St Hippolytus, which you are to build on the aforesaid properties of that estate, with episcopal right in all matters reserved. We therefore decree that no ecclesiastical or secular person may presume to violate this charter of our constitution. Should anyone presume to do so, let him be deprived of the rank of his authority and honour and be subject at the last judgment to strict punishment. But whoever proves to be its guardian shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God through the merits of His apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0714C] Given at St Peter’s.

## XXXV. To a friend.—That he may persevere in adhering to him.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 701, from a Cassinese manuscript.]

The very ancient remembrance of your religious devotion and the dutiful diligence of your integrity give us great confidence concerning you: that you will pay no heed to the schism of those men and to the empty talk of their barking, but will persevere with your customary steadfastness of faith in the service of blessed Peter and in love for us.

## XXXVI. To a certain bishop.—He praises him for having opposed his adversary and promises him his protection.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, ibid., from the same manuscript.]

[Col. 0714D]

From the very beginning of our appointment, we have found your brotherhood devoted to us and pursuing with diligent prudence the vain falsehoods of those who bark against us. For this reason we now render thanks the more freely, the more effectively you persist in the service of blessed Peter and in love for us, and have already begun manfully to oppose the pride of our enemy. Henceforth we desire to support you with such goodwill that, whether we make peace or undertake some other measure according to the pressure of circumstances, we may attend to the interests of you and your Church as to our own interests and the advancement of the Roman Church.

## XXXVII. To a certain bishop.—Priests ought, in accordance with the canons, to abstain from wives.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, ibid., col. 702, from the same manuscript.]

[Col. 0715A]

We rejoice greatly at your priestly solicitude, venerable brother, because, as we learned from the clear report in the letters which you sent to Pope Honorius, our predecessor of blessed memory, through the bearers of the present letters, you show vigilance and care for the people entrusted to you and for the ministry of the priests. For together with our most beloved son Duke Ubald, you asked what should be done concerning the priests of your parish, who, freely bound by the obligations of wives, serve at the holy altars. To answer you briefly: if we wish to agree with the rules of the holy Fathers, a wife and sacred ministries cannot coexist in priests of this kind [Col. 0715B]. For if, according to the ordinance of blessed Gregory, no one may be ordained subdeacon unless he promises by canonical declaration to live chastely, how much more must this be observed in the priests of God, who make the sacred body of Christ with their own mouths and distribute His sacred flesh to the peoples of the faithful with their own hands. And if, according to blessed Paul, the chief teacher of the Church, lay people must abstain from a wife for a time so that they may devote themselves to prayer, what do you think must be done by Christ’s priests, who, according to the oracle of the divine law, are commanded always to be holy and always ready to pray for God’s people? At the death of Eli the old priesthood is read to have been changed, and in Samuel renewed by a divine transformation. Nevertheless, God granting, we have decided to send to you a prudent and honourable man as legate concerning these and other affairs of the Church [Col. 0715C].

## XXXVIII. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of St Bertin at Sithiu, at the request of Abbot John.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[Mention of this privilege occurs in the Cartulary of Sithiu, *Collection de Cartulaires*, vol. III, p. 302.]

## XXXIX. To Roger, duke of Sicily.—He grants him the royal title.  
*(Year 1130, 27 September.)*

[BARONIUS, *Annals*, under the year 1130, no. LII.]

[Col. 0715D]

… served the Church through innumerable acts of obedience under our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Urban and Paschal of venerable memory; and your mother also, of happy memory, nobly following in her husband’s footsteps, took care, according to the resources given her by the Lord, most dutifully to honour and support that same Church of God with a generous hand of liberality. You also, whom divine providence has distinguished above the other princes of Italy with a greater prerogative of wisdom and power, because you have endeavoured to honour our predecessors more magnificently and serve them more abundantly, have determined [perhaps: *we have determined*] to adorn and exalt your person and that of your heirs with perpetual titles [Col. 0716A] of grace and honour.

We therefore grant, give, and authorize to you, your son Roger, and your other sons, to be established in the kingdom according to your ordinance, and to their heirs, the crown of the kingdom of Sicily, Calabria, Apulia, and all the lands which both we and our predecessors gave and granted to your predecessors, the dukes of Apulia called Robert Guiscard, Robert his son. We grant that kingdom itself to be held, together with the whole royal dignity and royal rights, to be held and ruled by perpetual right forever. And we establish Sicily as the head of the kingdom.

Moreover, we authorize and grant that you and your heirs may be anointed kings and crowned at appointed times by the hands of such archbishops of your land as you wish, according to your will, with such other bishops as you and your heirs may wish attending [Col. 0716B]. Likewise, all grants, gifts, and consents which our predecessors granted, gave, and consented to your predecessors—Robert Guiscard, Robert his son, William, dukes of Apulia—and to you, we give, grant, and consent that you, your sons, and your heirs may hold and possess forever.

We also give and authorize to you and your heirs the principality of Capua with all its holdings, as the prince [variant: *princes*] of Capua have held it both now and in the past; and we grant and confirm the honour of Naples and its appurtenances, and the assistance of the people of Benevento against your enemies. Consenting to your submitted petitions [Col. 0716C], we grant to the archbishop of Palermo, his successors, and the Church of Palermo the consecration of three bishops of Sicily—namely, those of Syracuse, Agrigento, and Mazara, or Catania—on this condition: that the aforesaid churches may suffer no diminution in their dioceses or possessions from the archbishop of Palermo or from the Church of Palermo itself. Concerning the remaining two, however, we reserve the matter for our fuller deliberation.

All the aforesaid matters, through these our grants, we thus grant, convey, and authorize to you and your sons to hold and possess by perpetual right, provided that you, or they, shall have sworn homage and fealty to us and our successors in a suitable and safe place for us and for you. If this should not remain possible on the part of us or our successors, they shall not on that account suffer any diminution of their honour, dignity, or land. But you shall pay the tribute … and your heirs, namely six hundred *schifati*, which you must pay annually to the Roman Church if you are requested. If you are not requested, then, once a demand has been made, you shall pay it, no occasion being taken from sums not paid [Col. 0716D]. … If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter attempts to oppose this our grant or gift, unless restored to obedience by fitting satisfaction, let him be struck with the sword of anathema. But upon all who observe these our terms, grants, and consents, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest. Amen.

[Col. 0717A] I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Matthew, priest of Eudoxia.

The sign of the hand of Peter Leo, consul of the Romans; the sign of the hand of Roger, his brother; the sign of the hand of Peter, son of Uguiccio; the sign of the hand of Cencius … of Guy; the sign of the hand of Peter Leo of Fondi; the sign of the hand of Abucius; the sign of the hand of John Abdiricius; and the sign of the hand of Milo.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Saxo, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1130, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Anacletus II.

[Note: [Col. 0717C] So much for that time. But we are about to state what else he granted to the same Roger. The Beneventan Chronicle, cited above, thus recounts what followed later in the same year: “In that same year, therefore, the aforesaid Anacletus sent one of his cardinals, a count by name, to that duke, whom he crowned king in the city of Palermo on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. Prince Robert of Capua placed the crown upon his head, and he rendered him an unworthy recompense.” So it says there.

But what Anacletus granted Roger together with the title of king, so as to win him over and make him defender of the schism, Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino—who was living at that time and could easily have been present at all these events—relates as follows (*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, ch. 99): “Peter the cardinal, who was also Anacletus, bestowed a crown upon Roger, duke of Apulia; and, confirming to him by privilege the principality of Capua and the duchy of Naples together with Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, and making him king, drew him to himself, commanding that the bishops and abbots dwelling in territory subject to his authority should obey him.”

Here, reader, is what we demonstrated in the preceding volume: the beginning of the Sicilian monarchy was not initiated by Urban II, as some have attempted to infer from forged letters attributed to him, but by the schismatic pseudo-pope Anacletus, as you have heard from Peter the Deacon [Col. 0718C]. Do not be surprised that you do not find these matters in the diploma recited above, which has been repeatedly curtailed, since much is known to be missing from it; or rather, because these assertions reported by Peter the Deacon may have been contained in other letters of the same Anacletus. These are found in the same Cassinese codex, frequently cited above, containing letters from the first year of Anacletus’s pseudo-pontificate. At the end, the following curtailed portion of his letter to Roger is recorded in these words:

“The foresight and benevolence of the apostolic see move us to extend the hand of our generosity to those who love the most holy Roman Church. Therefore, dearest son in Christ Roger, by God’s grace duke of Apulia, deservedly illustrious, because your father Roger, of glorious memory, by much bloodshed and many labours [Col. 0718D], [won] the entire island of Sicily …”

The remainder is missing; and who cannot understand that it was curtailed, as appears, so that it should not be known what Anacletus shamefully conferred upon Roger?]

## XL. He consoles a certain provost concerning injuries inflicted upon him and his Church “by the unlearned man of Rheims.”  
*(Year 1130.)*

[BARONIUS, *Annals*, under the year 1131, no. V.]

[Col. 0717B]

Although the sequence of your letters did not at all bear witness to the ardour of your affection which you are seen to entertain toward us and the Roman Church, we nevertheless read in our heart what we ought to think of your devotion. Therefore, because the unlearned man of Rheims, a useless stump, is known to have acted wickedly and shamelessly against you and your Church, let no sorrow or pain affect you—especially since, against us and the Roman Church, to which he bound himself by oath, he has, like one drunk and heated with wine [Col. 0717C], insolently vomited forth many things in the manner of actors, “setting his mouth against heaven, that his tongue may pass over the earth.” Like another Dioscorus, he has attempted to judge the apostolic see, while in zeal for wickedness—or perhaps “in the heat of zeal”—he strives to nurture a planting in God’s Church, and, like another Babylonian, frenziedly urges all manner of simple people to worship the statue in the plain of Dura (Dan. III). Yet that same statue before which he has prostrated himself will swiftly be cast down, the Lord granting, by a stone cut from the mountain.

Moreover, we judge his barking and follies to be like the barking of dogs [Col. 0718A] and the frenzies of the possessed. For the foundation of God remains immovable; and the chair of Peter and the place of Paul can be shadowed by no deceptions and shaken by no mockeries. For the whole Roman Church has adhered to us with undivided charity from the beginning of our elevation, agrees in all things with the sacred canons, and is one fold of God, with one shepherd; although Esau too wanders through wild and steep places (Gen. XXVII), in order to overthrow the minds of simple people with his customary lies. Yet Jacob dwells simply at home, and, with his mother’s intervention, the guileless man prepares simple food for his father.

To state everything briefly: our glorious son Roger, duke [king] of Apulia, humbly coming to our feet, acknowledged us as pope Catholic and as his legitimate lord, according to the custom of his predecessors. All the archbishops and abbots of Apulia and Calabria, as also the whole Eastern Church—Jerusalem, Antioch, and Constantinople—are with us, and visit and attend us. Know also that, once the council which, God willing, we shall hold at Bari on the fifth day before the Ides of November has been dissolved, we shall hasten to Milan [Col. 0718B]. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, be strengthened in the Lord, perform your office manfully, and do not at all fear the poisonous words or threats of the man of Rheims.

## XLI. Fragment of a letter.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 702.]

[Col. 0718C]

We carry out the heavenly commands more effectively if we share our burdens with our brethren; and thus the affection of our spiritual sons will be present to us. Therefore, by reason of the office entrusted to us, we ought generously to bestow the hand of our kindness upon all who suffer need, so that they may receive abundantly the remedies for which they hope, and that we may be able more fully to perform in them what belongs to our office …

## XLII. He grants Francon, abbot of the monastery of St Sophia at Benevento, permission to construct a mill.  
*(Year 1130, 10 November.)*

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, p. 499.]

[Col. 0719A]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of the Lord, to his beloved son FRANCON, abbot of the monastery of St Sophia, situated within the city of Benevento: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because of the love and affection which we have for the monastery of the virgin St Sophia, and because of the service which you have shown with especial devotion to the Roman Church, we grant to you and your successors that, on the same property at Ponticellum, where you now have two mills, you may, whenever you wish, construct and remove a third without opposition from us [Col. 0719B], our court, or anyone else.

I, Anacletus, bishop. I, Peter of Pisa, cardinal. I, Matthew, cardinal and priest.

Given at Capua, through the hand of Saxo, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, indiction XVIII, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1139, but in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Anacletus II.

## XLIII. He gives the garden at Ponticellum to the monastery of St Sophia at Benevento.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, p. 498.]

[Col. 0719C] ANACLETUS, servant of the servants of the Lord, to his most beloved son in the Lord FRANCON, abbot of the monastery of St Sophia, situated within the city of Benevento, within our sacred palace, and to his successors to be appointed canonically, forever.

The office entrusted to us requires that we too, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, should honour and more willingly provide for the needs of religious places which our predecessors laboured with utmost care to foster and exalt. Therefore, beloved son in Christ Franco, abbot of the monastery of St Sophia, situated in the city of Benevento beside the sacred palace, graciously consenting to your petitions, we grant and give [Col. 0719D] to you, and through you to the monastery of St Sophia, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and to the brethren there serving the Lord and to serve Him forever, namely, one garden which our court is known to possess in the place called Ponticellum. Its boundaries are: on one side the aforesaid Ponticellum; on the second side the mill-ditch of the same monastery; on another side, the road. We grant and donate this aforesaid garden with all its appurtenances to the above-mentioned monastery forever, so that from this hour onward you may have authority to enter, possess, use, or do with it whatever may please you.

If at any time in the future an ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our grant and donation, should presumptuously attempt to act against it [Col. 0720A], and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend the matter by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his authority and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the wrong committed; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict punishment. But upon all who preserve justice for that same monastery may there be the peace and tranquillity of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find and receive the rewards of eternal and everlasting peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic religion. I, Peter, cardinal priest of St Mary and the Virgin Susanna. I, Crescentius, cardinal priest and overseer of St Marcellus. I, Matthew, cardinal and priest. I, Sylvius, cardinal deacon. I, Romanus, cardinal and deacon.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Saxo, priest and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of December, indiction IX. Amen.

## XLIV. Privilege for the church of Giovinazzo.  
*(Year 1130.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VII, 723.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother URSUS, bishop of Giovinazzo, and to his successors to be appointed canonically, forever.

By the office of the apostolic see laid upon us, we are compelled to extend the hand of our protection and defence to our brother bishops and the churches entrusted to them by God [Col. 0720C], and, the Lord granting, to preserve justice for all. Therefore, dearest brother Bishop Ursus, graciously consenting to your reasonable requests, we have judged that the church of St Mary Ever-Virgin at Giovinazzo, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, should be strengthened by the protection of blessed Peter and the charter of this present writing. Therefore, whatever goods and possessions the aforesaid church now justly and lawfully possesses shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. These are expressly named as follows: in the city of Giovinazzo, the monastery of St Mary; the church of St Saviour outside the city; the church of St Leo; the church of St Sylvester; the church of St Eugenia; and the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul with their appurtenances. At the castle of Terlizzi: the church of St Angel; the church of St Mary; the church of St Nicholas; the church of St Lucy; the church of St Julian with their appurtenances; the hamlet of Vrassano with its churches; the hamlet of St Leutius and its churches; and the hamlet of Circitano with its churches [Col. 0720D].

Whatever else, through God’s bounty, you may be able in future to acquire by just means, shall remain secure and entire to you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole [Col. 0721A], to benefit in every way both you and the uses of the clergy and poor. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend the matter by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his authority and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the wrong committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict punishment. But upon all who preserve justice for that same Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal [Col. 0721B] peace.

Place of the sign in which appear the words written below, namely: “THE LORD IS THE STRENGTH OF HIS PEOPLE,” in a circle; and within: “SAINT PETER, SAINT PAUL, POPE ANACLETUS II.”

I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Place of another sign.

Given at Benevento, through the hands of Saxo, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, in the year 1130 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth indiction, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Anacletus II.

## XLV. He establishes the monastery of Cefalù as an episcopal see, suffragan to the archbishop of Messina.  
*(Year 1131, 14 September.)*

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, vol. I, p. 588.]

[Col. 0721C]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons in Christ serving the Lord under a canonical rule in the Church of Cefalù, forever.

Divine providence has promoted us to the administration of the apostolic see so that we may be obliged to provide more carefully for the honour and exaltation of venerable places. Therefore we desire to exalt, so far as we can by the grace of God, the holy Church of Cefalù. Accordingly, with the counsel of our brethren and sons, the cardinals and bishops, we decree, the Lord granting, that the aforesaid Church shall henceforth be an episcopal see, in which we wish a cardinal bishop thereafter to remain, who shall receive the mysteries of consecration at the hands of the archbishop of Messina [Col. 0721D]. Both he and his successors must strive to render due obedience to the Church of Messina as to their metropolitan see. We command that the church of Balnearia, with all its appurtenances, be subject to the see of Cefalù.

We decree, therefore, that whatever the aforesaid Church of Cefalù lawfully possesses in this present ninth indiction, and whatever it may hereafter be able canonically to acquire through the gifts of our glorious son King Roger, grants of pontiffs, or offerings of the faithful, shall always remain secure and unimpaired. No one whatsoever—neither the archbishop of Messina nor any ecclesiastical or secular person—may in any way diminish the aforesaid Church of Cefalù [Col. 0722A] or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, as we have said, let all things be preserved for it forever, secure and unimpaired, with all privileges and grants which the Roman Church has bestowed upon our glorious son King Roger and his sons reserved in every respect.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend the matter by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his authority and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the wrong committed; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict punishment. But upon all who preserve these just provisions may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0722B] Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Crescentius, cardinal priest of SS. Marcellus and Peter, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Pastor, have subscribed. I, Amatus, cardinal priest of the title of St Eusebius, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Eustachius, have subscribed. I, Sylvius, cardinal deacon of St Lucy, have subscribed. I, Raynaldus, cardinal deacon of St Lawrence, have subscribed.

Given at Privernum, through the hands of Saxo, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Anacletus II.

## XLVI. He establishes the monastery of Lipari as an episcopal see, suffragan to the archbishop of Messina.  
*(Year 1131, 14 September.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 777.]

[Col. 0722C]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons in the Lord regularly serving the Lord in the monastery of Lipari, and to those who shall serve Him forever.

The governance of the Apostolic See, which, though unworthy, we have undertaken by God’s disposition, invites us to measure diverse matters according to the variety of times. For the monastery of Lipari has hitherto been one of the greater monasteries of Sicily and is known to belong by right to the Roman Church. [Col. 0722D] Therefore, as the glory of our glorious son King Roger—bestowed upon him and his sons by the generosity of the Apostolic See—increases, it is sufficiently fitting and just that the government of that church should likewise be enlarged in our times. We therefore decree, with the counsel of our brethren the bishops and cardinals, and establish by this present decree, that the aforesaid monastery of Lipari shall henceforth possess episcopal dignity and shall venerate its own bishop. He shall receive the gifts of consecration through the hands of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Messina; both he and his successors shall be perpetually subject to the church of Messina as to their metropolitan see—yet in all grants and privileges subject only to our glorious son Roger and his heirs, as bestowed by the Roman Church. If any ecclesiastical person, etc. But to all who observe these things, etc. Amen.

Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Crescentius, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Peter and Marcellinus, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Pastor, have subscribed. I, Amatus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Eusebius, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius, have subscribed. I, Silvius, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy, have subscribed. I, Raynaldus, cardinal deacon of Saint Lawrence, have subscribed.

Given at Privernum through the hand of Saxo, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, indiction 11, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Anacletus II. [Col. 0723B]

## XLVII. To Didacus, Archbishop of Compostela  
*(A.D. 1134, April 22)*

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 550.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Blessed James, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because of the exceedingly great affection of love with which we love your person, and by which we likewise believe that we are loved in return, we have already sent you letters from the Apostolic See rather frequently, having such confidence in you that you ought also to visit us often by your letters and messengers. But you, dearest brother in Christ, held back by we know not what torpor, have never deigned to send us any reply. Therefore, although we greatly wonder and are somewhat grieved at this, we nevertheless do not cease both to visit you again by our letters and to inform you concerning matters that have been done or are being done here.

For after the departure of Lothair—whom, as we believe you have already learned, with divine power cooperating on our behalf, we compelled to retreat most disgracefully and shamefully, not without great slaughter of his men—the heresiarch G. [Note: [Col. 0723D] Gregory was formerly called Innocent.], whom he introduced into the houses of our perjurers, in the first nest of his faction, fled by ship to Pisa at night, since, amid the protests of clergy and people against him, he could not remain in the City. There he lurks, somehow surviving in utter misery. By God’s grace, however, we, together with our brethren and sons—the bishops, cardinal priests, and deacons—the whole clergy and people of the City, who cleave to us, as from the beginning they have done, in undivided affection, are safe and prosperous. We have celebrated the Easter solemnities, according to the ancient custom of our predecessors, in the Lateran palace with all the patricians of our city and the other feasts of the year, peacefully and tranquilly, honourably and devoutly. We have recently recovered and retain in our power the basilicas of Saint John and of Saint Paul the Apostle, together with certain other small fortified places that our enemy Lothair’s men had seized at his coming and in which they greatly gloried.

By the assistance of our faithful men, especially of our most beloved son R., king of Sicily, we intend, by God’s grace, utterly to uproot from the midst of the Church those perjurers of ours, Leofraiapane [Col. 0724A] and one brother of his—who, a third man most rashly daring in every crime, together with nearly sixty fighting men, was crushed and killed beneath the collapse of the bell-tower of a certain church which they had undermined at night. For we besiege them so vigorously while they are shut in that either they will shortly surrender themselves into our hands, or, as we have said, they will perish root and branch.

In all these matters, therefore, dearest brother, render worthy thanks with us alike to the Lord, giver of all good things; reject the lies of our enemies through the wisdom given to you; and pray Almighty God that our eyes may see our undertaking brought to completion. Send us frequent letters through the bearer of this present letter and through other messengers, informing us of your condition and of the good will and disposition which you bear toward us, lest, according to the Apostle’s saying, we should seem to love more than to be loved. [Col. 0724B]

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

## XLVIII. He undertakes the protection of the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento and confirms its possessions  
*(A.D. 1130–1136)*

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, 500.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of the Lord, to his beloved son in the Lord, FRANCO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia within the city of Benevento, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever. [Col. 0724C]

We ought indeed to receive the prayers and petitions of all our faithful, but especially of those who are known, and are, more intimately subject to us, as if by a right of their own, to the Apostolic See, whose care and governance, by the Lord’s ordering and favour, we have undertaken. Therefore, most beloved and dearest son in Christ, Abbot Franco, we have judged and considered it proper to consent to your petitions: that we should receive under the protection of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and under our defence, and strengthen by the force of our authority, the venerable monastery of Saint Sophia, over which, by the Lord’s will, you preside and exercise authority, according to the example and pattern of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs of holy memory—Popes Leo IX, Urban, Paschal, and Calixtus.

By this document of our privilege we therefore enact and confirm by apostolic authority that the same monastery, subject to the Roman Church alone and free from the yoke of all churches or persons, shall be held as such; and what our predecessors bestowed upon that shrine, we too bestow by this present decree. That we may deserve to share in the prayers continually offered there to the Lord God, we grant that you, dearest son Abbot Franco, and your successors serving the Lord our God in that monastery [Col. 0725A] may have and possess in perpetuity the mitre and gloves. We likewise grant and bestow, by the liberality of the Apostolic See, the use of the dalmatic and the *semicinctium* on the days only that are named below: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen the protomartyr; Epiphany; Saint Benedict; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Easter and the following Monday; Saint Angelus; the most holy Cross; Ascension; Pentecost; Saint John the Baptist; Saint Peter; all feasts of Saint Mary; Saint Mercurius; the feast of All Saints; the Twelve Thousand Martyrs; the Dedication of the Church; and the Commemoration of All Saints.

Moreover, we confirm for your perpetual possession the cells, estates, and churches which have been justly or canonically acquired for the aforesaid monastery through the efforts of your predecessors or of yourself. These are: the church of Saint Benedict called the Hospice of Saint John; Saint Euphemia; Saint Peter called Rasari; Saint Mary Rotunda within the city of Benevento itself; the churches of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, Saint Nicholas, Saint Erasmus, Saint Marcian, Saint Sophia the Virgin, and Saint Angelus outside that same city of Benevento; in Pantano, the church of Saint Benedict, father and confessor; Saint Vitalis; likewise Saint Mercurius near Olivola; Saint Angelus; Saint Mary of Scolcaturo, with all its appurtenances; at Vado Azanim, Saint Benedict; at Faffone, Saint Valentinianus; near Votum, the church [Col. 0725B] of Saint Felix with all its lands; at Corneto, Saint Silvester; at the Two Streams, Saint Mary at Paritulo; Saint Marcian at Veteteno; Saint Martin at Cocciano; Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, at Pazano; Saint Nicholas the bishop; likewise, in the city of Benevento, Saint Stephen the protomartyr at Palearia; Saint Mary of Lucenaria; and the two estates of Saint Mary at Becellaria; Saint Mary at Templana; in the city called Ariano, Saint Angelus with its cells; Saint Stephen at Fromaria; Saint Gregory at Esde; Saint Angelus at Pesclo Nalibergo; the churches of Saint Mary and Saint John at Calisi; Saint Mary in the territory of Tamari; Saint Marcellus; near Regnum, Saint Mary at Tusculano; Saint Maurus; Saint John at Ascoli; Saint Peter; Saint Desiderius; Saint Archangel at Eliceto; Saint Ephrem at Morteto; Saint Peter near Troia; Saint Mercurius near Bivinum; Saint Martin the Bishop; at Biferno, the monastery of Saint Angelus with all its cells; at Petra, Saint Angelus; Holy Trinity at Petra Findi; Saint Agnellus; Saint Constantine; Saint Elizabeth; Saint Anne; Saint John; Saint Peter at the bath in the valley of Luparia; Holy Cross at Limosana; Saint Martin at Mutale; Saint Marcian at Testonis; Saint Archangel; and Saint Onuphrius with all their appurtenances; at Materia, Saint Agnes; at Alife, Saint Mercurius, Saint Angelus, Saint Mary, Saint Mark, Saint Anne, and Saint Silvester; Saint Mary of Garoinus the Abbot; near Saint Agatha, Saint Adjutor; Saint Adjutor also at Mount Virgin; Saint Adjutor at Trivento; [Col. 0726A] Saint Lawrence near Micerium; Saint Stephen near Matulona; Saint Martin at Palumbe; Saint Abundinus in the district of Stedine; Saint Mercurius; Saint Reparata; Saint Stephen in the district of Noceto; Saint Magnus; Saint Helena; Saint Stephen; Holy Cross; Saint Martin; Saint Simeon; Saint Pollux in the district; Saint Joanna in the territory of Cani; Saint Mary in the district of Alfe; Saint John; Saint Michael the Archangel at Olicino; Saint Mary at Melanica; Saint Mary in the city of Dragonara; Saint Benedict near Cannae; Saint Julian at Avellino; Saint Julian; Saint Germanus; Saint Henry; Saint Theodore; Saint Herman; Saint Lutger; Saint Arostarius; Saint Constantine; Saint Robert; Saint Bartholomew; Saint Mary at Bellula in Caudis; Saint Angelus at Palumbaria; the monastery of Saint Angelus with its cells and all its appurtenances in the city of Naples; Holy Cross at Sessula; Saint Michael the Archangel at Toccula; Saint Raphael the Archangel at the monastery of Foliolano; Saint Benna with its churches and all its appurtenances; at Petra Sturmini, houses, woods, vineyards, and territories; the estate of Lapillo and the church of Saint Bartholomew at Collino; Saint Bartholomew and the estate of Noriano; Saint Peter the Apostle of Great Light; near Roderium, Saint Martin at Alano; Saint Mary at Galdione; and, on Monte Malo, Saint Felix; at Pertore, Saint Vitus; at Balba, near the mountains of Saint Mark, at Fossa Cieca, Saint Stephen; at the Caudine Forks, Saint Fossus in Jerusalem; in the territory of Campilaeti, the church of Saint Lucy the Virgin; Saint Mark; near [Col. 0726C] the city of Florence, the monastery of Saint Saviour with the other churches belonging to that monastery, namely Saint Leo between the aforesaid city and Saint Peter of Vitiano, and Saint Stephen with the estate called Francisca; the monastery of Saint Nicholas the bishop on Mount Filine with the other churches belonging to that monastery; in the territory of Rodi, Saint Barbara the Virgin; in the old city of Sepino, the monastery of Saint Mary with all its cells; near Vaccataria, the monastery of Saint Anthony with its cells and all the appurtenances of the brethren and of Saint Benedict; at Sambuceto, Saint Mary; at the hamlet of Petrifiate, Saint John; at Portula, Saint Vitus; at Caretro, Saint Augustine; at Pontino, Saint Maximinus; at Corteto, Saint Mauritius; at Luceto, Saint [Col. 0726D] Martin; at Causano, Saint Christopher; at Alife, Saint Peter the Apostle at Certia; at Minori, Saint Angelus; at Luniperto, Saint Lawrence; at Luniparia, Saint Lucy; at Ferreria, Saint Herman; at Panno, Saint Bartholomew; likewise the Castle of the Forum, Old Castle of Catalupi, Butticella, Fanetum, Obianum, Ripas Longas, and the estate of Leo Cubans, together with the churches and all their appurtenances.

Furthermore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we decree that all offerings, both of the living and of the dead, which that monastery now possesses or may hereafter lawfully obtain, by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, together with the cells subject to it, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any crafty fraud or violence, except the man whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall see fit to elect according to the fear of God and of the Lord and the Rule of Blessed Benedict; he must always be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and basilicas, and the ordinations of monks to be advanced to holy orders, from the bishops in whose dioceses you are, provided that they possess the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and confer these things freely and without any burden. Otherwise, you may approach whatever bishop you wish and receive consecration and the sacraments from him. [Col. 0727A]

We have therefore decreed that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, remove any of its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass and trouble it with reckless vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the full benefit of the uses for whose maintenance and governance they were granted. But if in the future any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, duke, margrave, prince, count, baron, viscount, *strategos*, judge, *castaldus*, or ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should in any way rashly dare to violate it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him lose the dignity of his power or office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him depart separated from the most holy blood and body of God and of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to stern vengeance. But upon all who justly observe these provisions, may there be the peace and tranquillity of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and there, before the strict Judge, find the reward and recompense of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic faith. I, Gregory, priest and cardinal. I, Aderiscius, cardinal. I, Silvius, cardinal. [Col. 0727D] I, Matthew, cardinal and deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian within the Temple of Romulus. I, Pandulphus, cardinal deacon of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Saxo, in the year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Anacletus II.

## XLIX. To Roscimanus, Archbishop of Benevento  
*(A.D. 1136, October 21)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VIII, 21.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the ARCHBISHOP OF BENEVENTO, and to his successors in perpetuity.

The order of equity demands and the principle of justice persuades that we ought more readily to extend, with the customary generosity of the Apostolic See—over which, though unworthy, we preside by the Lord’s will—a more ample hand of favour to the faithful of Blessed Peter, who dwell continually in his service and whose possessions are known to belong to him. [Col. 0728A] Therefore, venerable brother Roscimanus, archbishop of Benevento, graciously receiving your petitions and those of our brethren, the bishops and cardinals, who have interceded with us on your behalf, we grant and concede to you and your successors in perpetuity the whole undivided paradise and courtyard before the episcopal palace, namely the church of Saint Mary, as it is known hitherto to have belonged to our public domain. This is upon the condition and in the terms that neither you nor your successors shall do or establish anything new there without permission granted by us or our successors, by which our other regalian rights may be impaired or diminished. We remove from the same paradise the market-hall, from which, owing to the crowds and noise of sellers and buyers, no small injury was repeatedly caused to the same holy mother Church.

We also give and grant to you and your successors in perpetuity the *plateaticum* [market due] of the four shops that are in the house of John of the City, and the revenues of those sitting and selling vegetables and fruits in that same paradise, as belongs to our sacred palace of Benevento. We therefore decree and establish by this present authority that no ecclesiastical or secular person whatsoever may violate or alter this enactment of our gift and grant; but that all things, as prescribed, shall remain unimpaired and firm. Upon those who observe these statutes may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ; but upon those who do not observe them, may there be anathema, and eternal fire be prepared. [Col. 0728C]

I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, bishop of Porto. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Crescentius, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Apostles. I, Amatus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Eusebius. I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of Equitius. I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Matthew, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, [Col. 0728D] indiction 15, in the year 1136 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of our Lord Pope Anacletus II.

## L. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento  
*(A.D. 1130–1137, March 10)*

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, 499.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of the Lord, to his dearest son in Christ, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office exhorts us to have compassion upon churches, so that we may accede to the prayers of religious men for their advancement and, as far as we can with the Lord’s help, provide for their tranquillity. [Col. 0729A] Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Franco of the venerable monastery of Saint Sophia the Virgin, we gladly receive your prayers and those of the community entrusted to you in that sacred monastery, with the counsel of our brethren and sons, and we take care to support you insofar as we can in the Lord’s grace.

Accordingly, we remit and grant to you and to your church, for the lighting of lamps, the eighty denarii which you were obliged to pay every year to the Beneventan court from those shops and the stalls established beside them in the public square, at the place called “the Painted Stalls.” We will that those same shops remain free from every payment, whole and inviolate for you, so that in neither our time nor that of our successors shall you pay anything from them to the court or endure any burden from it. [Col. 0729B]

I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Matthew, priest and cardinal. I, Adefisus, cardinal of Saint Agatha. Given at Benevento, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

## LI. From the confiscated property of Potifrid, the faithless count, he restores to the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento two mortgaged mills, after receiving four hundred *romanati* which the count had lent to the monastery  
*(A.D. 1135–1137, March 21)*

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, 502.]

ANACLETUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, FRANCO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia situated within the city of Benevento, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity. [Col. 0729C]

If vengeance is rightly due to persistent wrongdoing, then every precaution must be taken on behalf of the faithful who serve with a pure heart. It is established that Godefridus (Godfrey), formerly the son of Count Rodfrey Pizzica-daemon, through treachery against this our city of Benevento, against his mother the holy Roman Church, and against our person—whose fidelity he had sworn and of whom he had made himself the liege man—had sinned so wickedly and grievously that, by our judgment, that of the magnificent king our son, and that of our judges Jandolphus, Dauferius, and Benedict, many other faithful men of ours, and the whole court, he forfeited to the Apostolic See his person and all his movable and immovable property; and every action and claim that belonged to him in any respect came lawfully to us by settlement.

That same Godefridus (Godfrey) had lent four hundred *romanati* to the monastery of Saint Sophia the Virgin, and held as pledge for them two mills of that monastery at the bridge called Leper Bridge, an island beside the Great Bridge, and a garden outside, near the Golden Gate, together with the charters and title-deeds of those inheritances. Those mills, island, and garden, together with all other movable and immovable appurtenances of the aforesaid Godfrey, came justly and lawfully into our hands because of the perjuries [Col. 0730A] and treachery which he had committed.

Since we did not wish the monastery’s inheritance to be alienated, we graciously summoned, in person and through our other faithful men, our dearest sons Abbot Franco, Provost Azzo, Dean John, and the other brothers of that monastery, requiring them to pay us the four hundred *romanati* that Potiferia had lent them and to recover for the use of the monastery their pledge—that is, the aforesaid mills, island, and garden. Since this seemed to them exceedingly burdensome and difficult, and they sought by every means to evade carrying it out, we brought, and ordered to be brought, a public action against them in full court, and caused distraint to be made according to the custom of the land. At length, being unable to oppose reason and justice, they appeared both before us and before the judges, for the execution of what justice required.

When our claim had been heard—by which we lawfully demanded the four hundred *romanati* from those who, as stated above, had forfeited to us in Gofridus’s (*Gofridi*’s) place all his goods and claims, and which they could in no way deny—and when nearly all the greater men and nobles of the city concurred and consented, the judges adjudged that the abbot and brothers should recover the monastery’s mills, island, and garden that had been pledged, and should pay the four hundred *romanati* without any material uncertainty. This judgment was carried into effect by us and by the monastery. For they paid us the aforementioned money, and we restored to them in full the mills, island, and garden which had been held in pledge, reserving no claim in them either for ourselves, our successors, or any other person. [Col. 0730C]

We therefore decree that neither Godfrey nor his heirs, nor any person sent or in any manner substituted by them, may reclaim that money or the pledge given for it, whether by producing the charters, by presenting witnesses, or in any other way; nor may they bring any suit or harassment concerning it against the monastery. But if anyone should attempt to do anything contrary to this decree of security issued by us, he shall pay one hundred pounds of Pavia denarii of good coinage: one half to our sacred palace and the other half to that monastery. And this decree of our protection shall always remain firm and unimpaired.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we prohibit and establish by perpetual sanction that no abbot, provost, dean, ecclesiastical or secular person whatsoever may presume to place in pledge or mortgage the mills which we restore, or those which the same monastery possesses at Ponticello or near Long Water; and no prince, ruler, count, viscount, citizen, townsman, or peasant may dare in any way to take or pledge the aforesaid mills or anything within them, unless we and our successors command it by our own mouth. [Col. 0731A] Whoever therefore violates this present command shall be anathema, and eternal fire shall be prepared for him. But upon those who preserve it may there be the peace and rest of our Lord Jesus Christ, that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Anacletus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Crescentius, priest and cardinal. I, Benedict, priest and cardinal. I, Amandus, cardinal and priest of the holy church of Sabina. [Col. 0732A] I, Silvius, priest and cardinal. I, Hormannus, cardinal. I, Rochus, cardinal and deacon of Saints Arianus and Marius. I, Pandulphus, cardinal deacon of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian. I, John; Judge Dauferius. I, Quirinus Benedictus, judge.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Matthew, cardinal, priest, and chancellor, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the year … of the pontificate of our Lord Pope Anacletus II.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1143: BENEDICT, CANON OF SAINT PETER’S, ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0731]

# BOOK ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL ORDER OF THE WHOLE YEAR, AND ESPECIALLY ON THE APOSTOLIC DIGNITY AND THE WHOLE CURIA  
### To Guido de Castello, then cardinal of Saint Mark, who afterwards became Celestine II

[Dom MABILLON, *Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 118. Paris, 1724, quarto.]

[Col. 0731B] **1.** To Master GUIDO DE CASTELLO, of clear learning and profound wisdom, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church by divine appointment, of the title of Saint Mark, BENEDICT, unworthy canon of Blessed Peter the Apostle and cantor of the Roman Church, offers the affection of deepest love and an unfading crown among the companies of holy bishops.

Reverend Father, I give immense thanks to the mercy of divine compassion, according to the powers of my slight learning, because I perceive that you take care for your salvation and concern for ecclesiastical order. Therefore I humbly implore the great mercy of God and the abundant goodness of his manifold compassions, that in this most good purpose he may strengthen and establish you, until he himself comes to remove the lampstand from its place.

But concerning your request for the ecclesiastical order of the whole year, and especially the apostolic dignity and the whole curia—on which your illustrious wisdom and distinguished prudence have seen fit to request a little work from me, your servant, explaining, as God grants, how the lord apostolic [the pope], with his curia and the whole Roman Church, may conduct itself in the principal solemnities and daily offices—I shall undertake to elucidate it, although the matter is arduous and not foreign to the duty of my profession. Yet it is very remarkable why you ask me, an unlearned man and one almost devoid of learning, to explain matters which I do not possess in the treasury of my heart to unfold; to investigate matters which I cannot explore; to offer matters which I, a thirsty cupbearer, long to draw from you.

For who can know what the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys does while it crosses mountains and leaps over hills, unless he has been given drink from the torrent of its delight and made drunk with the abundance of its house? Yet, moved, as I have understood it, by your affection and persistent urging, I shall endeavour to record for perpetual remembrance what I have seen over many periods of time concerning the dignity of the Roman pontiff, the cardinal priests and deacons, and the other orders of the curia, as well as concerning [Col. 0733A] the ecclesiastical office of the whole year; what I have heard from learned men of the curia; and what other teachers have left in their writings.

**2.** In the Advent of the Lord, when the annual recapitulation of the office and of the books read in the Church takes place, on Saturday, the vigil of the Lord’s Advent, the antiphon begins at Vespers: “On that day the mountains shall drip.” Under this antiphon all the psalms of that Vespers are sung. When the antiphon has ended, the verse is said: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy.” At the *Magnificat*: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, Mary.” When the antiphon has ended, the prayer [variant: prayers] is said.

[Col. 0733B] **3.** At Matins, the invitatory, “The King who is to come,” with its *Venite*. When this has ended, the first antiphon begins: “The angel Gabriel was sent”; the psalm “Blessed is the man,” as far as “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger”; and the antiphon is said. Then the second antiphon is said: “Hail, Mary, full of grace”; the psalm “O Lord my God, in you have I trusted,” as far as “In the Lord I trust.” When the antiphon has ended, the third antiphon is said: “Do not fear, Mary”; the psalm “Save me, O Lord, for the godly man has failed,” as far as the psalm “O Lord, who shall dwell?” When the antiphon has ended, the verse is said: “Show us, O Lord.” Three lessons are read from the prophet Isaiah.

First lesson: “The vision of Isaiah”; responsory: “Looking from afar.” When this has ended, the verse “All you children of earth” is said in full; then the repetition: “Go out to meet him and say”; the verse “Give ear, you shepherd of Israel” in full; the repetition: “Tell us whether you yourself are he”; the verse “Lift up your gates, O princes” in full; the repetition: “You who are to reign over the people Israel.” “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.” It begins again from the start: “Looking from afar.”

At the second lesson, the second responsory: “They were watching in a vision of the night,” with two verses: “Behold, the Lord, the ruler,” and “His power is an everlasting power,” with their respective repetitions as above; then “Glory be to the Father,” and the responsory again from the beginning. At the third lesson, the responsory: “The angel Gabriel was sent,” with two verses, “Hail, Mary,” and “The Lord God will give him”; the first repetition, “Do not fear, Mary”; the second repetition, “And he shall be called,” and what follows. “Glory be to the Father.” When this is finished, the responsory is sung again from the beginning. [Col. 0733D]

These three responsories ought to be sung in this manner by the congregations. The first and second singers sing the first responsory before the altar with all the verses and repetitions to the end; the third and fourth sing the second responsory in the same way; the fifth and sixth, the third responsory.

In the second nocturn the antiphon begins: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord”; psalm: “Keep me, O Lord.” Another antiphon: “The angel of the Lord”; psalm: “Hear, O Lord, my righteousness.” The third antiphon: “Before they came together”; psalm: “I will love you, O Lord.” When the whole is finished with its antiphon, the verse is said, and three lessons are read from a sermon of Saint Augustine and Saint [Col. 0734A] Leo, and three responsories are sung, as is customary.

In the third nocturn, the antiphons are: “Blessed are you, Mary, who believed the Lord”; “All generations shall call me blessed”; and “The Lord will give him,” with their psalms, “The heavens declare,” “May the Lord hear you,” and “O Lord, in your strength.” The verse is said; two lessons are read from the epistle [Note: [Col. 0733D] Namely, from the epistle of Leo the Great to Flavian, which expounds with great dignity the mystery of the Incarnation against the error of Eutyches; see below, no. 9.], and the third from the homily. When these are finished, *Te Deum laudamus* is sung. When it has ended, Matins Lauds begin, with the antiphon “On that day” and all the other antiphons and psalms. When these are finished, the verse is said. When it has ended, the antiphon “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, Mary” begins, followed by “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel,” etc.

**4.** Then he says Prime and begins the second antiphon of Matins, “Rejoice,” with the psalms. [Col. 0734B] When these are finished, he says the reading from the epistle, the verse, and the prayer of the day. In the morning there is a station at Saint Mary Major, to which the lord pope comes with all the orders; there, honourably and as is customary, he sings Mass with “Glory to God in the highest,” as on the other Sundays until the Nativity of the Lord, and he is crowned. At Terce the third antiphon is sung; at Sext the fourth antiphon; at None the fifth antiphon; at Vespers, with all the antiphons, but “The angel Gabriel was sent” and “Behold, the Lord will come” are not said except during the week; only the prayer is said.

5. During the week, the office is of Advent. At Matins: the invitatory, “The coming King”; the nocturn with the antiphon from the Psalmist; Advent versicles; and readings from the prophet Isaiah. At Matins Lauds [Col. 0734C] one antiphon is sung, “On that day the mountains shall drip,” under which all the psalms are to be sung. Prime is sung with an Advent reading and chapters, as the Church customarily does, with knees bent. Terce, Sext, and None, with Advent antiphons, are said prostrate on the ground, with chapters, psalms, and the prayer, as is customary. At Vespers all the weekday psalms are sung under one antiphon, “On that day the mountains shall drip”; and at the end these antiphons are sung: “The angel Gabriel was sent,” “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee,” with the prayer, “O God, who from the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary,” and the antiphon, “Behold, the Lord will come, and all his saints with him”; versicle: “The saints shall rejoice in glory.” The Mass is of Advent until Thursday [Col. 0734D]. On Friday the Mass of the Cross is sung, which is not suitable in Advent. On Saturday, the office is of Saint Mary, unless there is a feast of nine lessons; and if there is, the entire office is to be that of the feast. If it is a feast of three lessons, at Vespers on the vigil the psalms of the day are sung under one Advent antiphon. When they come to the Magnificat, the versicle of the feast is said with the antiphon and prayer of the saint; and a commemoration of Advent is made: “The angel Gabriel was sent,” etc. Matins is entirely of the saint, though with the nocturn of the day. Matins Lauds, if they have proper antiphons, are sung; otherwise all the psalms are sung under one common antiphon. Prime [Col. 0735A] is sung with one antiphon of the feast and the reading of the day; and the entire office is sung not prostrate, but standing. Terce and Sext are of the feast; None and Vespers, of Advent.

6. On the Second Sunday, three readings are read from the same prophet Isaiah, three readings from a sermon, two readings from an epistle, and the third from a homily; and the office is sung from its proper history. In the morning there is a station Mass at Jerusalem in the Sessorian Palace, where the lord pontiff, with the whole curia, must sing Mass, receive the crown, and celebrate it as customary.

7. On Gaudete Sunday, the station is at Saint Peter’s. When the lord pope comes to Vespers with all the schools, and remains there, then [Col. 0735B] the lord pontiff receives twenty solidi from the confession-shrine, and an allowance for his curia and horses. The cardinals and deacons, the primicerius with the choir, the subdeacons, basilicarii, regional subdeacons, and acolytes receive five Pavia denarii, called the *coenaria* [variant: *cenatica*, “supper-money”]; and the archdeacon receives eighteen denarii for the responsories, which are disbursed through his hands. The canons of the church must receive twelve solidi from the same shrine-fund as their *presbyterium*. The aforesaid orders of the sacred palace lodge in the house of Agulia [variant: Augulia]; and the master of the lodging must provide beds with his own good linen, receive and keep their horses in his stables, and, if it is necessary to provide the dinner of that day, do so nevertheless from the aforesaid [Col. 0735C] denarii called *coenatica*. This applies not only at stations, but throughout the whole year, whenever [variant: wherever] the cardinals come to sing Mass with the primicerius and singers or other Palatine clerics. The master of that lodging must also receive daily, as a benefice, one coin from the offerings [variant: oblations] of the Mass and the drippings of wax remaining from the Mass offering. This aforesaid order is to be observed at all nocturnal stations at Saint Peter’s; at the daytime stations only five solidi are given, while the lord pope at daytime stations receives twenty solidi, as said above.

8. Rising at midnight on hearing the signal, the lord [Col. 0735D] pope, with all the orders, must come to Saint Leo’s. There the *mansionarius* prepares the censer for the bishop, and the bishop for the pontiff, all having put on their vestments. The chamberlains, with two lighted torches, and the camerarii, with two candelabra and lighted torches, must go before the pontiff. The pontiff first incenses the altar of Saint Leo; then, proceeding in procession through the pontifical portico to Saint Gregory’s, he first incenses his altar, the altar of Saint Sebastian, and the altar of Saint Tiburtius; [Col. 0736A] then the two altars in the central aisle by the crucifixes, where, as we have heard from the ancient fathers, the apostles Simon and Jude rest. Afterwards he goes to Christ’s cloth, called the Veronica, and incenses it; likewise the altar of Saint Mary. He then ascends to Saint Pastor beside the triumphal arch and incenses there.
