Descending thereafter to the body [of Saint Peter], he incenses the altar above Saint Peter’s tomb; and thus he sits on the bench with candelabra before him. The paraphonist with the choir begins the Vigils: “Out of Egypt I called my Son”; psalm: “Blessed is the man.” Second antiphon: “Behold, the Lord will appear upon a white cloud”; psalm: “Why have the nations raged?” Third antiphon: “Behold, the Lord will come, whom John proclaimed”; psalm: “Lord, why are they multiplied?” Then two basilicarii subdeacons [Col. 0736B] say the versicle; the acolytes hold the station-book, and the chamberlains the torches; and the basilicarii read the lessons, “I shall rejoice exceedingly in the Lord”; the deacon intones, “But thou.” The primicerius with the choir sings the responsories. When the three lessons are finished, the primicerius says, “We praise thee, O God.” The regional subdeacon hands the sacramentary to the bishop, and the bishop holds it before the pontiff; the basilicarii hold the candelabra, and the pontiff says the prayer. The deacon says, “Let us bless the Lord”; and the lord pope gives the blessing.

9. Then, going out from there—[Note: [Col. 0735D] Here there is a clear distinction between the Vigils and Matins: a double office was said on the Third Sunday of Advent at Saint Peter’s. Something seems to be missing here to indicate the day.]—he ascends to the high altar and incenses it, then descends to the *pectorale* [Note: [Col. 0736D] This is what they call the screen: in the manner in which the Greeks call the orderly array of little columns, joined to an upper entablature, *sēgea* [ςήγεα], as the most learned Cangius observes from Goar on Cedrenus.] before the altar. Around him stand the vested deacons. The bishops stand at the other screen; the cardinals are in choir with the canons [Col. 0736C] of the church. The chamberlains and camerarii place torches before the pontiff. The pontiff begins Matins: “Lord, thou shalt open my lips.” The singers sing the invitatory; when it is finished, the primicerius begins, “Out of Egypt I called my son”; psalm: “Blessed is the man,” and all the psalms of the first nocturn with their antiphons. When the first nocturn is finished, the canons of the church read three lessons, “I shall rejoice exceedingly,” and sing three responsories; the rest are performed by the singers and basilicarii. Then the bishops read the fourth and fifth lessons from the epistle of Pope Saint Leo, sent to Bishop Flavian concerning the Lord’s Incarnation against the heretic Eutyches; the cardinals, the sixth and seventh; the senior basilicarius, the eighth, from the exposition of the epistle, “Rejoice in the Lord always”; [Col. 0736D] and the pontiff himself reads the ninth, where he enters, from the homily, and says, “Lord, give the blessing.” No one blesses him except the Holy Spirit; all merely respond, “Amen.” When the pontiff’s reading is finished, the primicerius says, “We praise thee, O God,” and the others respond; and the antiphon for Matins Lauds begins. When this is finished, the basilicarii sing the versicle before the altar. The primicerius announces to the pontiff the antiphon for “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.” The bishop presents to the pontiff the book handed to him by the regional subdeacon; the pontiff says the prayer; the deacon says, “Let us bless [Col. 0737A] the Lord.” Mass is celebrated by the pontiff, “Glory to God in the highest” is said, acclamations are made by the deacons, subdeacons, and notaries, and he is crowned by Saint Peter through the midst of the city as far as the palace with all the orders, as customary. From the feast of Saint Nicholas until the weekday before the Nativity of the Lord, these antiphons are sung at Matins: “O Wisdom,” at the Benedictus, and all the others in the four seasons [Ember Days].

10. On Wednesday the station is at Saint Mary Major. The gathering is held at Saint Peter in Chains, in Eudoxia. The primicerius with the choir, the regional subdeacons, and the acolytes with the station cross [Note: [Col. 0737D] The station cross, customarily carried to the stations; it was customarily placed upon the altar; below, no. 29.] of Saint Peter take up the cross from there with the processional gathering and sing as they go to Saint Mary Major. There, the lord pope, prepared [Col. 0737B], sings Mass in the Lenten manner; and there he announces the man whom he intends to ordain, in this manner: “With the help of the Lord and our Saviour Jesus Christ, we have chosen this deacon for the priesthood. If anyone has an objection against him for God’s sake, let him come forward confidently and speak. Yet let him remember his own condition.”

11. On Friday the station is at the Holy Apostles, with a procession.

12. On Saturday the station is at Saint Peter’s, where ordination must be performed by the pontiff and Mass celebrated. While the office is being sung most solemnly by the choir, and the hymn of the Three Children, “Bless the Lord, all works of the Lord,” the pontiff descends from the altar and goes to Saint Andrew’s. There he performs the consecration. [Col. 0737C] After the consecration, he returns to the altar, because no consecration may take place at this altar except that of the Roman pontiff. And this is to be done in all the Ember Seasons.

13. On the Sunday of “Sound the trumpet,” there is a reading from the prophet Joel, “Sound the trumpet in Zion,” and from a sermon, an epistle, and a homily. When the weekday antiphons occur, all are sung in order at Matins. At Vespers all the psalms are sung under the first antiphon. At the Magnificat, the proper antiphon is sung.

14. On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, at Matins the invitatory is: “Christ will come to us; come, let us adore.” Antiphon: “The Lord said to me”; psalm: “Why have the nations raged?” Antiphon: “In the sun he placed his tabernacle”; [Col. 0737D] psalm: “The heavens declare.” Antiphon: “Be lifted up, everlasting gates”; psalm: “The earth is the Lord’s.” Versicle: “Today you shall know that the Lord will come,” followed by five lessons and five responsories. The fourth lesson is a sermon of Saint Augustine: “You, I say, I address, O Jews.” During the fourth, the Sibylline verses are sung: “A sign of judgment: the earth is drenched with sweat.” The fifth is from a homily. On that day, “We praise thee, O God” is not said; only “O God, make haste to help me,” with the antiphons of the vigil and [Col. 0738A] the psalm “The Lord reigns,” with the other psalms. Prime is said with the antiphon of the vigil and the lesson, “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ,” with the versicle; without Kyrie; only the prayer of the day is said. Terce, Sext, and None, with their antiphons, are said not prostrate but standing only. On this day the station is at Saint Mary Major, where the lord pope must sing Mass with the schools of clerics and the household of the palace; and the bishop of Albano must provide an excellent dinner for the entire curia, and send to the curia two excellent carcasses of pigs. At Vespers and at the Vigil, the pontiff must remain there throughout the whole night.

15. In the first vigil the canons of the church read three lessons from the prophet Isaiah and sing three responsories: “At the first time the land of Zebulun was lightened,” “Comfort ye,” and “Arise.” The office is thus performed by the cardinals, bishops, and singers, as at the nocturnal stations of Saint Peter’s. In the second vigil are readings from sermons; in the third, readings from the same sermons and from a homily. At the manger he must sing Mass and say “Glory to God in the highest,” only one prayer, and “I believe in one God.” The primicerius with the choir performs the Mass; when it is completed, the primicerius returns to the choir, singing “Behold, Mary has borne us a Saviour,” with psalms and antiphon, as is written in the Antiphonary. When Matins Lauds have been completed in this [manner], with the prayer, the pontiff begins Matins. [Note: [Col. 0737D] Observe here that Vigils are distinguished from Matins, although they are the same office: the former were celebrated at the depth of night, with the nocturns divided as though into so many watches; the latter in the morning [Col. 0738D]. See below, nos. 60 and 63. Amalarius marks this distinction in chapter 15 of the *Antiphonary*: “I found in the Roman Antiphonary two nocturnal offices set in one and the same night, namely at the Nativity.”] The choir says the invitatory, and Matins is performed in the same order as the Vigils.

[Col. 0738C] 16. In the morning he says Mass at Saint Anastasia’s. When it is finished, he descends in procession by the road beside the Portico of the Gallators, before the Temple of the Sibyl, between the Temple of Cicero and the Portico of the Cimii [variant: Crinii]; proceeding between the Basilica of Jupiter and the Flaminian Arch, he then goes beside the Portico of Severinus; passing before the Temple of the Gridiron, before the island of Milicena and of the dragons, and so descends on the left hand to the main road of the Arenula; passing through the Theatre of Antoninus and the Palace of Chromatius, where the *Holomitreum* [variant: *Oloritreum*] stood, and beneath the arch of the emperors Gratian, Theodosius, and Valentinian; entering by Hadrian’s bridge before his temple, beside Nero’s obelisk, before the memorial of Romulus, and ascending through the portico [Col. 0738D] into the Vatican to the Basilica of Saint Peter, where the station is held. There Mass is solemnly sung with all the orders of the palace, as befits; he must receive the crown upon his head there, return in procession through the middle of the city to the palace, and complete the feast of the crown.

17. But because of the shortness of the day and the difficulty of the route, he holds the station at Saint Mary Major and goes to the sacristy. The chamberlains guard the sacristy. [Col. 0739A] The senior bishop serves with the book; the archdeacon with the Gospel; the senior regional subdeacon with the *mappula*; the senior basilicarius with the epistle; the primicerius and choir with the singing. Thus, supported by two deacons, the archdeacon proceeds alone, without an attendant, before the pontiff, and so enters in procession. Every order proceeds in its place, two by two: acolytes with candelabra, and the cross of the lord pontiff before the procession. At the entrance to the church, the chamberlains hold the *mappula* high over the pontiff’s head. When he enters the presbytery, the church’s *mansionarius* hands him a reed with a lighted candle. The pontiff takes it and sets fire to the tow placed upon the capitals of the columns, as a figure of the end of the world by fire. Proceeding into the middle of the presbytery, he halts [Col. 0739B] his course. The primicerius removes the mitre from his own head, kisses the pontiff’s right shoulder, and the pontiff blesses him. When he has come before the altar, the chamberlains offer the *mappula* [Note: [Col. 0739D] Below, no. 40: “with a linen cloth spread over his head.” From this the *mappularii* were named, to whom this function was entrusted; they are discussed in the following booklet of Cencius.] over the pontiff’s head; the pontiff gives the peace to the senior bishop who is to serve him, then to the first and second of the two cardinals.

18. Ascending with the first [bishop] to the altar, he makes confession, kisses the Gospel which the subdeacon holds before him, and enters the altar; with bowed head he says the prayer. When it is completed, he kisses the altar and rises, giving the peace to the archdeacon and all the deacons. The acolyte presents the censer and the box of incense to the archdeacon, who is to read the Gospel. The pontiff [Col. 0739C] takes the box, places incense in the censer, and incenses the altar, while the archdeacon holds back the pontiff’s chasuble lest it impede him. Having put in the incense, he ascends to the seat; the cardinals descend to the choir in their places, and the bishops to their places at the right beside the pontiff. Meanwhile the paraphonist with the choir sings the introit and “Lord, have mercy.” The pontiff begins, “Glory to God in the highest,” and the choir responds, “And on earth peace to men of good will,” to the end. The pontiff says, “Peace be with you”; the choir responds, not in that voice but loudly, “And with thy spirit”; and one prayer is said.

19. Meanwhile the archdeacon, with the deacons and subdeacons standing in a line at the right beside the altar, and the notaries standing below [that is, down below] in the choir [Col. 0739D] clothed in copes, the archdeacon says aloud with them all, “Hear us, O Christ.” The notaries respond: “To our lord Innocent [Note: [Col. 0740D] For this book was written while Pope Innocent II was alive and reigning, to whom these acclamations are addressed.], supreme pontiff and universal pope, appointed by God, life!” Three times the archdeacon says this with his men, and three times the notaries respond. “Holy Mary,” says the archdeacon; the notaries respond, “Help him.” “Holy Mary,” they likewise respond concerning each choir, three times; the saints, twice. At the end, “Lord, have mercy” is said three times by the archdeacon with the deacons and subdeacons; and they receive three solidi for the acclamation.

20. The senior Latin subdeacon and the [Col. 0740A] Greek subdeacon carry books before their breasts, with two subdeacons and one acolyte vested in an alb; before him goes the *oblationarius* [variant: *blacionarius*], making a way with his hand. On this day and on the day of Holy Easter, two singers, the first and second, descend into the ambo, and an acolyte stands before them in the ambo. When the acclamation is finished, the Latin subdeacon reads the Latin Epistle; then the Greek subdeacon reads the Greek Epistle. They return, giving thanks at the altar, and kiss the pontiff’s feet. The singers begin the gradual and Alleluia; the primicerius with the choir, the responsory. The archdeacon and the Greek deacon, carrying the book before their breasts with four subdeacons, and the acolytes bearing candelabra before them, remain with lighted candelabra before the lectern; [Col. 0740B] they read the Gospels. Descending, they carry the Gospels to meet the pontiff; the pontiff kisses them, ascends the pulpit, and proclaims the Gospel. At the end he makes confession, gives the blessing, returns to his seat, and says, “I believe in one God.” The basilicarii respond and sing. The primicerius with the choir sing the Offertory. Then seven cardinals ascend to the altar with books, three on one side and four on the other; and the pontiff, supported by the deacon, enters the altar at the canon in order to sacrifice the host with a cardinal. When the Preface is completed, the basilicarii sing, “Holy, holy, holy,” etc.

21. When Mass is finished, the pontiff, crowned by the archdeacon, mounts his horse and proceeds in procession to the palace in this manner. Behind comes the prefect, clothed [Col. 0740C] in a precious mantle and shod with one golden and one red *zancha*; around him are judges clothed in copes. Before the pontiff go the archdeacon and deacon with the primicerius, two by two; then the subdeacons; before them the cardinals; before the cardinals the notaries, singing before them; before the notaries the bishops; before the bishops the cross of the lord pope; before the cross the dragon-bearer soldiers carrying twelve banners called *bandora*. Then comes the lord pope’s horse, adorned but empty; *dirungarii* surround the procession; two naval prefects, called *dilungarii* [variant: *dirungarii*], wear copes and carry staffs; the *majorentes*, in silk mantles and with staffs, called the *schola stimulata*, guard the procession so that no one may intrude.

[Col. 0740D] 22. When the pontiff comes to the basilica of Pope Zacharias, before he dismounts the cardinals descend to make the acclamations. Then the senior cardinal of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, having removed his mitre, says, “Lord, give the blessing.” The pontiff blesses him. He says aloud: “To the highest, distinguished, and thrice most blessed Pope Innocent, life!” All the cardinals respond: “May God preserve him,” three times. “Saviour of the world”: the cardinals respond, “Help him,” three times. “Holy Mary, help him”; through the entire choir of saints, three saints. At the end: “All saints, help him,” three times. “Lord, have mercy,” three [Col. 0741A] times. And for the acclamation they receive three solidi. The judges then present themselves, and the primicerius says, “Lord, give the blessing.” The pontiff blesses him, and he says aloud: “This day!” The judges respond: “Many years!” three times. “May you have good times!” The judges respond: “May we all have good times!” Then the lord pontiff dismounts. The primicerius of the defenders and the secundicerius take him by the hands and lead him to the chamber. There he gives the *presbyterium* to all the orders. On this day of the Nativity of the Lord and on Holy Easter he gives every senior a “hand” [Note: [Col. 0741D] I think that the common word *mancia*, for a gift made to dependants, derived from this.], that is, a double *presbyterium*: namely, the lord pope gives the prefect twenty solidi and a hand; the primicerius of the judges, four solidi and a hand; each judge, four solidi; the senior bishop, four solidi [Col. 0741B] and a hand; each bishop, [three solidi]; the senior cardinal, four solidi and a hand; each cardinal, three solidi; the archdeacon, three solidi and a hand; each deacon, three solidi; the primicerius of the singers, three solidi and a hand; the secundicerius of the singers, two solidi; the senior basilicarius, two solidi and eight denarii for honor; each singer, two solidi; the senior basilicarius, two solidi and a hand; each subdeacon, two solidi; the senior regional [subdeacon], two solidi and a hand; each of them, two solidi; each acolyte, two solidi; the two *dilungarii*, eight solidi; the scriniarii, ten solidi; the *majorentes*, five solidi; the dragon-bearers, five solidi; and the other orders, as customary.

23. After the *presbyterium* has been given, they enter the prepared dining hall. The bishops and cardinals sit on the right side; [Col. 0741C] the archdeacon, deacon, primicerius, senior basilicarius, and senior regional [subdeacon] on the left; each order in its own place. The doorkeeper places a reading desk with the book of homilies in the middle. About the middle of the meal, by the archdeacon’s command, a deacon rises and reads a lesson; the archdeacon himself determines its end. The pontiff then sends [Note: [Col. 0741D] That is, “dispatches,” in a usage still familiar among Italians today.] an acolyte to summon the singers to rise and sing the Sequence [Note: [Col. 0742D] This Sequence was the one beginning with the word “Laetabundus,” from the Ceremonial of Urban VI.] in modulated voices. Rising, they perform what was commanded. When the Sequence is finished, they go and kiss the pontiff’s feet, receive one Byzantine coin from the sacristan, and the lord pope gives them a cup full of drink from his own mouth [Note: [Col. 0742D] This manner of speaking still adheres among us: *du vin de sa bouche*, “wine from his mouth.”], and they drink. When the meal is over, all return to their homes; the cardinals are customarily sent to their own residences.

[Col. 0741D] 24. On the feast of Saint Stephen, there are three readings from the Acts of the Apostles, “Stephen, full of grace and power,” and three from a sermon on Saint Stephen, with their antiphons and responsories. In the third nocturn, [the office is] of the Nativity of the Lord, with three psalms, versicle, readings, and their antiphons. Matins Lauds are of Saint Stephen. When the prayer of Saint Stephen is finished, the antiphon “The faithful Virgin today” is said with the prayer of the Nativity. Terce, Sext, and None are of Saint Stephen; Vespers, however, of the Nativity of the Lord, with antiphon and prayer of Saint Stephen and Saint John, and similarly of the other [Col. 0742A] feasts. Very early in the morning, the lord pontiff leaves the palace crowned and proceeds solemnly with the procession to Saint Stephen’s, where the station is held. There they sing Mass, as at the Nativity of the Lord, with acclamations. When it is finished, he returns crowned to the palace; after receiving acclamations from the cardinals and judges, giving the *presbyterium* or “hands,” and celebrating the meal as written above, all depart.

25. On the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, there are three readings from the Apocalypse and three from a sermon on Saint John, with their antiphons, psalms, and responsories. Some wish to read his Passion. In the third nocturn are antiphons, three psalms, and three lessons of the Nativity, with their responsories. Matins Lauds are of Saint John, and the commemoration is as above; [Col. 0742B] Prime is of Saint John, the prayer of the Nativity.

26. At the Nativity of the Innocents, at Matins there are three readings from the Apocalypse and three from a sermon. In the third nocturn the office returns to the Nativity of the Lord. “We praise thee, O God” is not sung, but Matins Lauds begin. Prime is sung as above. At Mass, “Glory to God in the highest” and Alleluia are not sung unless the feast falls on Sunday; the entire office is Lenten. On this day Romans do not eat flesh or fat, unless it falls on a Sunday.

27. On the vigil of the Epiphany, the office is of the Nativity of the Lord. At the Epiphany, the station is at Saint Peter’s, where the lord pope with the whole curia sings the versicles, as on Gaudete Sunday, on the day noted above. At midnight he rises, and all the orders with him [Col. 0742C] gather at the altar of Saint Leo. There, in procession, as has been said above, he incenses the altars as far as the body [of Saint Peter], where he performs Vigils of three lessons. When these are completed, he ascends to the high altar and incenses it. He descends to the *pectorale*, and all the orders are in their places. He signals to the primicerius to begin the Vigils. The latter begins the antiphon, “Bring to the Lord, sons of God,” etc. Then three lessons are read from the prophet: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem,” and other lessons from a sermon, except for the ninth lesson from the homily, which is that of the lord pope, in the same order as on Gaudete Sunday. He must solemnly sing Mass with acclamations, receive the crown, return crowned to the palace, and act as at the other crown-feasts. During [Col. 0742D] the octave, at Matins every day there are three psalms and three readings from a sermon, with their antiphons and responsories, except on Sunday, because nine lessons are then performed. After the octave, the Epistles of Paul are read. Some read from an exposition of the Psalter.

28. On the first Sunday after the octave of the Epiphany, the Epistles of Paul are read, and the history from the Psalmist is appointed: “He shall meditate in the law of the Lord,” until Septuagesima. At the first and second nocturns of Matins, antiphons from those same psalms are sung: “Serve the Lord in fear,” etc. In the third nocturn, Alleluia is sung [Col. 0743A] in place of antiphons. At Matins Lauds, Alleluia is sung in the tone: “Light has arisen upon us,” and the remaining antiphons, as contained in the Antiphonary. At Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, Alleluia is sung. Vespers are of the Psalmist. On all the aforesaid Sundays throughout the year, the office at the aforementioned Hours is sung in this manner, except on Sundays from Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost, from the Advent of the Lord until the octave of the Epiphany, and on Sunday feasts. On weekdays, if there is no feast, the following antiphon is sung at Prime: “Blessed art thou, O Lord; teach me thy statutes”; at Terce: “Incline my heart, O God, to thy testimonies”; at Sext: “Lord, give me life according to thy word”; at None: “Look upon [Col. 0743B] me, O Lord, and have mercy on me.”

29. On the Purification of the Blessed Mary, sermons of the same feast are read. In the morning the station is at Saint Mary Major. Eighteen images [Note: [Col. 0743D] Concerning these images, again below, no. 33.] are brought out by the deacons, and they come with clerics and people to Saint Adrian’s, where the gathering is held. But the lord pontiff descends to Saint Martina’s with bishops, cardinals, and the other schools. There he vests with them all. Certain cardinals bless the candles brought by the curia and chamberlains. The pontiff comes out and ascends the seat before the church, distributing them as follows: first he gives to the bishops, then to the cardinals, then to the deacons and the other orders and the people. Then he goes to Saint Adrian’s, where the station cross is. The archdeacon signals for the choir to sing. [Col. 0743C] The primicerius begins and sings: “Arise, O Lord, help us.” When the antiphon is completed, the pontiff says, “Let us pray”; the deacon, “Let us bend the knee”; another [Note: [Col. 0743D] Not another, but the same one who had said “Let us bend the knee” added “Rise” in those earliest times, as we saw above.] deacon says, “Rise”; and the pontiff says the prayer. The deacon says, “Let us proceed in peace.” The choir responds, “In the name of Christ.” Then the regional subdeacon takes up the station cross from the altar, carrying it level in his hands as far as the church. When he comes outside, he raises it aloft and carries it before the pontiff in procession to Saint Mary Major. The primicerius, with his left hand behind him managing the pontiff’s pallium, sings with the singers the antiphon, “Adorn thy bridal chamber, O Zion.” The pontiff says the psalms with the others; proceeding thus barefoot [Col. 0743D] before the Arch of Nerva, he enters through Trajan’s Forum; leaving by the Arch of Gold in the apsed portico, he ascends straight ahead [variant: home] beside Eudoxia; passing over the stone by the house [Note: [Col. 0744D] Added below, no. 52: “where Simon Magus fell.”] of Orpheus, he ascends by the title of Saint Praxedes as far as Saint Mary Major. There, when the choir has finished the antiphon, the regional subdeacon carries the cross to the altar in the customary manner and makes the litany, the choir responding with the acolytes. The lord pope sings Mass, but “Lord, have mercy” is not sung because of the litany.

30. At Vespers on the Saturday before Septuagesima, Alleluia is omitted [Col. 0744A] and “Praise to thee, O Lord” is said. Under the one antiphon, “Call the labourers,” all the psalms are sung. When Vespers is finished, the Pentateuch is read at Saint Peter’s in three lessons until Matins. At Matins, Genesis is appointed, from which six lessons are read: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; the seventh and eighth are from the exposition of the Epistle, the ninth from the homily. Thereafter “We praise thee, O God” and “Glory to God in the highest” are omitted unless there is a feast of nine lessons. At Matins Lauds all the antiphons are sung in order. At Mass “Glory to God in the highest” is not said, but the gradual and tract are sung. During the week Leviticus is read until the Tuesday of Lent. The station on this Sunday of Septuagesima is at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, where the lord [Col. 0744B] pontiff must sing Mass and in the sermon expound the Introits of that Sunday and the coming Sundays. “The sorrows of death surrounded me,” says the sinner, and, set in so great an affliction, he cries: “Arise, why dost thou sleep, O Lord?” And when he can no longer endure so much pain, he says: “Be thou, O Lord, a protector unto me.” But now he, trusting in God’s mercy, says: “Have mercy on me according to thy great mercy.” The Lord, struck by so many lamentations, says: “He called upon me, and I will hear him.” But the sinner, breathing again when he has recognized God’s mercy, says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? My eyes are always toward the Lord, because he will pluck my feet out of the snare.” And he must join this Tract [Col. 0744C] to the Gospel.

31. On Sexagesima Sunday there is a reading about Noah; on Quinquagesima, about Abraham; on Quadragesima, from sermons; on the Third Sunday, about Jacob and Esau; on the Fourth, about Joseph; on the Fifth, about Moses. On the Chair of Saint Peter, the readings are as on the day of his Nativity; yet at Vespers and Matins Lauds, “Behold a great priest” is sung. The station is in his basilica. The lord pope must sit in the chair [Note: [Col. 0744D] That is, in the very chair of Saint Peter, which the Vatican basilica still preserves today.] at Mass.

32. At the Annunciation [of the Blessed Virgin Mary], at Vespers: antiphon, “The angel Gabriel was sent”; psalm, “The Lord said”; antiphon, “Hail, Mary”; psalm, “Praise, O children”; antiphon, “Fear not”; psalm, “I rejoiced”; antiphon, “The Lord will give him”; [Col. 0744D] psalm, “Unless the Lord”; antiphon, “Behold the handmaid”; psalm, “Praise, O Jerusalem”; versicle, “Hail, Mary.” At the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit shall come down upon thee”; psalm, Magnificat. At Matins: “King of virgins,” with its “Come.” In the first nocturn: antiphon, “The angel Gabriel was sent”; psalm, “O Lord, our Lord”; antiphon, “Hail, Mary”; psalm, “The heavens declare”; antiphon, “Fear not, Mary”; psalm, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness”; versicle, “Hail, Mary.” In the second nocturn: antiphon, “The angel of the Lord announced”; psalm, “My heart hath overflowed”; antiphon, [Col. 0745A] “Before they came together”; psalm, “O Lord, our Lord”; antiphon, “The Lord God will give him”; psalm, “The foundations”; versicle, “Blessed art thou among women.” In the third nocturn: antiphon, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord”; psalm, “Sing to the Lord,” first; antiphon, “Blessed art thou, Mary”; psalm, “The Lord reigns”; antiphon, “All generations shall call me blessed”; psalm, “Sing,” second; versicle, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” These are the responsories: “The angel Gabriel was sent,” “Before they came,” “Receive the word,” “Behold a virgin,” “We await the Saviour,” “Let the heavens rejoice,” “A star shall arise,” “All generations shall call me blessed.” Readings are from a sermon and homily of Saint Ambrose.

33. In the morning the gathering is held at Saint Adrian’s, where the lord pope meets with all the orders of the palace. After the blessed candles have been distributed, they go barefoot in procession with the eighteen images [Col. 0745B] of the deacons to Saint Mary Major, as was said for the Purification; and there he sings Mass and Vespers, as was said for the vigil.

34. On the Wednesday at the beginning of Lent, the station is at Saint Sabina’s, and the assembly is at Saint Anastasia’s, whither the lord pope comes with the whole curia. There, vested, he and all the other orders go up to the altar. There the lord pontiff distributes ashes, and the primicerius with the choir sings the antiphon, “Hear us, O Lord.” When the assembly has been made, the pontiff, barefoot, and all the others proceed in procession to Saint Sabina’s. The primicerius with the choir follows behind, singing, “Let us change our garments.” When he has come to the church, the regional subdeacon, having set down the cross, goes to the altar with the litany, the choir and acolytes responding; there the lord pontiff sings Mass without the *Kyrie*, because of the litany.

> [Note: Col. 0745D] That is, because *Kyrie eleison* has been said in the preceding litany, below, no. 35.

Before Communion, however, the regional subdeacon stands beside the altar, saying in a loud voice: “On the coming day the station will be in the church of Saint George the Martyr at the Veil of Gold.” The choir responds, “Thanks be to God.” Then afterward the primicerius sings the Communion. When Mass is finished, the acolyte must take the papyrus wick,

> [Note: Col. 0745D] The ancients so called the wick used in lamps and candles. See Du Cange’s *Glossarium*, under *Papyrus*.

dip it in the oil of the candle, wipe it carefully, and carry it to the palace before the pontiff, saying: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. He then says: “Today the station was at Saint Sabina’s, which greets you.” The pontiff replies, “Thanks be to God.” The acolyte presents him with the papyrus wick; the pontiff kisses it out of devotion to the saint and gives it to the chamberlain. The chamberlain puts it away [Col. 0745D] and carefully preserves it until the pontiff’s death. Thus it is done at all the stations. At his death he makes of them a small pillow and places it beneath his head in the tomb.

35. When the assembly is made, the *Kyrie* is not sung at Mass, because the regional subdeacon has said it in the litany. Throughout the whole of Lent, moreover, the Gradual is repeated on weekdays, unless there is a Tract. The assembly [Col. 0746A] is held on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday throughout Lent; also on the Ember Days of the whole year; and on Thursday at Saint Mary across the Tiber and at Saint Apollinaris.

36. On Laetare Jerusalem Sunday, the station is at Jerusalem, in the Sessorian palace, where the lord pontiff solemnly sings Mass, holding in his hand a rose

> [Note: Col. 0746D] For observances concerning this rose, see Du Cange’s *Glossarium*.

of gold with musk. After the Gospel he ascends the pulpit and preaches concerning the flower, the redness of the rose, and its fragrance, displaying it to the people. Then he treats the Gospel. When the praises have been performed and Mass finished, he receives the crown there and, crowned, returns in procession to the palace, as is customary. Long before the pontiff dismounts, the prefect dismounts, and on foot accompanies him at his right side to the place where [Col. 0746B] the pontiff is to dismount. There he gives him the rose, and the prefect kisses his feet. When the praises have been received and the coronation celebrated, as is customary, all return to their own places.

37. On Passion Sunday Jeremiah the prophet is appointed. There are three readings from the same prophet, three from a sermon; the seventh and eighth are from an exposition of the Epistle,

> [Note: Col. 0746D] Perhaps of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11: “Christ having come as high priest,” etc.

and the ninth from a homily; and the rest of the office in its entirety,

> [Note: Col. 0746D] Namely, Matins Lauds and the other daytime Hours.

as it is written. From this day until Holy Saturday, *Gloria Patri* is sung in no responsory, in no *Venite*, and in no Introit.

38. On Palm Sunday, at Matins, there are three readings from Jeremiah, three from a sermon on the Passion; two from the Epistle, and the ninth is the Gospel of the Passion. Matins [Col. 0746C] Lauds, with their antiphons, are as contained in the Antiphonary; the remaining office is as the Church customarily observes.

In the morning the station is at the Lateran, where palms have been gathered by the acolytes in the basilica of Saint Sylvester. Of these the acolytes give [variant: “are given to the acolytes”] to the basilica of Saint Peter, and receive from the altar eight [variant: two] solidi. The palms of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Sylvester are blessed by one of the cardinals of the basilica of Saint Lawrence in the palace; the doorkeepers carry them to the Leonine basilica to the Pontiff. When all the orders of the palace have been vested, the pontiff distributes the palms. Afterwards he departs thence in procession, the primicerius with the choir singing “The children of the Hebrews” and other antiphons until before the door of the church of Saint Saviour. There, a stool having been placed upon the steps, the pontiff sits. The primicerius with the choir begins, “Glory, praise, and honour.” The chief basilicarius, standing at the closed door with the subdeacons [Col. 0746D], responds and sings the verse, “To whom childlike glory.” After every two verses the choir responds and says, “Glory, praise, and honour.” When these are finished, the door having been opened, they enter the church singing, “As the Lord entered.” In the secretarium the pontiff is vested and enters for Mass without the *mappula*. The primicerius sings the Introit without *Gloria Patri*.

The deacon says the Gospel in this [Col. 0747A] manner: “The Lord be with you.” The choir responds and says, “And with your spirit.” And he says, “The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Matthew.” The choir responds, “Glory to you, O Lord.”

> [Note: Col. 0747D] This is omitted at this time.

Afterwards the Gospel is read, and there is no sermon. On Wednesday and Friday only, the Gospel of the Passion is read with proclamation, without salutation and without response.

39. From the Lord’s Supper until Holy Saturday, “O God, come to my assistance” is not said; neither the Invitatory nor *Gloria Patri* in the psalms is said. Rather, “Zeal for thy house” is begun, as contained in the Antiphonary. Nor does the priest say, “Let us pray”; the reader does not ask for a blessing. When he finishes, he does not say, “But thou, O Lord”; rather, from the words of the reading he is directed to make an end.

[Col. 0747B] Nine readings are read: three from the Lamentation of Jeremiah the prophet, the others from an exposition of the Gospel; nine psalms and eight responsories. Matins follows with its antiphons and psalms. When it is completed, the *Kyrie* is not said, but is sung: “Christ became obedient for us unto death,” and they depart in silence. On Good Friday they extend it: “even death on a cross”; and on Saturday likewise: “Wherefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name.”

40. For Mass the supreme pontiff goes down to the secretarium. The vessels having been prepared full of oil, he mixes balsam with the oil. Then he vests himself with all the others and has seven lit candlesticks before him; and in procession he proceeds to the altar with [Col. 0747C] a linen cloth spread above his head. The primicerius kisses the shoulder of the Pontiff and sings the Introit with *Gloria Patri* and *Kyrie*. The pontiff begins, “Glory be to God in the highest.” The primicerius with the choir responds. When this is finished, the pontiff says only one prayer. The subdeacon reads the Epistle at the ambo. Two singers begin the Gradual, “Christ became obedient for us.” The primicerius with the choir responds, and those two singers repeat the Gradual. The deacon reads the Gospel.

On that day, while the lord pontiff preaches, the cardinals remove the mensa from the altar

> [Note: Col. 0747D] What “to remove the mensa from the altar” means—also mentioned in the following book of Cencius, no. 19—is clear from the preceding Tenth Roman Ordo, no. 7.

and strip the altar, placing it in a secure place. When the sermon has been completed, he grants remission, blesses the people, and goes down to the seat, where he announces, “I believe in one [Col. 0747D] God.” The Offertory is not said; only the pontiff enters the altar for the sacrifice, from which sacrifice he reserves for the following day, Good Friday. He consecrates the chrism and oil, as has been stated in the Episcopal Ordo. The primicerius with the choir sings the *Agnus Dei* three times: “Have mercy upon us,” and says the Communion: “The Lord Jesus, after he had supped with his disciples.”

[Col. 0748A] 41. Mass having ended, the lord pontiff, thus vested, returns to the palace in the basilica of Saint Lawrence. There he removes his vestments down to the dalmatic and, a fur being placed about his neck,

> [Note: Col. 0747D] Thus some placed about the neck an *almutia*, as they call it, against the cold.

he sits. The chamberlains place a basin before him and a clean linen cloth. Twelve subdeacons remain outside the basilica. Two doorkeepers take the first in their arms and carry him before the pontiff. The pontiff washes his feet with warm water, dries them with the linen cloth, kisses them, and gives him five [variant: two] solidi. Thus he does to each of the twelve.

Meanwhile, the primicerius with the singers, cardinals, and deacons sing Vespers. When this is finished, they sing, “The Lord Jesus, after he had supped,” and the lord pope gives four solidi to each bishop, three solidi to each cardinal, three solidi to the primicerius, and two solidi to each [Col. 0748B] singer. When this is finished, they go to supper in the basilica of Theodore, which is the pantry, where continuous reading is done by a subdeacon. Supper completed, he returns to the chamber, where he removes his vestments.

42. On Good Friday the bishop of the week performs the office in the basilica of the Saviour. The lord pope descends from the palace, vests himself there behind the altar with the other orders, and barefoot proceeds with the procession—and all with him—singing the Psalter to the Holy Cross. A certain cardinal solemnly carries the Body of the Lord from the previous day, preserved in the box of the corporals;

> [Note: Col. 0748D] This passage concerning the box of the corporals, in which the Eucharist was reserved from the Lord’s Supper until the following Good Friday, should be noted. Compare the first booklet of the Roman Ordo at its beginning, no. 8.

the regional subdeacon carries upon his breast the veiled stational cross. When the pontiff comes to the church of the aforesaid basilica, having washed his feet, he puts on his shoes and goes up to the altar. First [Col. 0748C] he prays, and afterwards sits. A certain basilicarius goes to the pulpit and begins to read; then follows the whole remaining office, as written in the book. When “Our Father, who art in heaven” has been completed, he receives the Body of the Lord which the cardinal had brought, and receives Communion from wine placed in the chalice.

> [Note: Col. 0748D] It does not say that the wine is consecrated by contact with a particle of the Eucharist placed in the chalice.

When the office is completed, thus vested, they return in the same procession as before, but wearing shoes, to the palace, singing the remaining psalms. In the chamber the lord pope removes his vestments; the others, having removed theirs, depart.

43. On Holy Saturday, in the morning the archdeacon rises and mixes oil and last year’s chrism with clean wax. The acolyte works it and strains it, making from it forms resembling lambs, which the lord pontiff [Col. 0748D] distributes on Low Saturday. At the sixth hour of Holy Saturday a new fire is made and the Paschal candle is blessed. Twelve readings are read in Latin and twelve in Greek, and three canticles are sung: “Let us sing gloriously to the Lord,” “The vineyard was made,” and “Give ear, O heaven.”

When this office has been completed, the lord pontiff descends to the font with the regional deacons and subdeacons, singing the litany. [Col. 0749A] The primicerius with the choir sings “As the deer” as far as the portico of Saint Venantius. There, a faldstool having been prepared, the pontiff sits. The cardinals who remained in the choir depart through the little postern behind the apse, enter through the portico of Saint John, and go into the church of Saint Venantius. Then the archdeacon orders two men to go to the door of Saint Venantius. They obey, take the first of the cardinals by the hands, and lead him at the right hand before the pontiff, all the cardinals following him. The first bows and says, “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. Advancing a little, he does likewise, and the pontiff blesses him. A third time likewise, the pontiff blesses him and says: “Go, baptize

> [Note: Col. 0749D] This is the sending of the cardinals to baptize infants in baptismal churches, of which there were quite a number in Rome; foremost among them was the church of Saint Mary Major, concerning which see below, no. 45. See Cencius below.

all nations in the name of the Father and [Col. 0749B] of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” The cardinals, thus vested, return with horses

> [Note: Col. 0749D] That is, mounted on horses, according to the custom of certain ancients.

to their titles. Then the pontiff enters for the baptism. When it is completed, he returns to the chrismal place, anoints the infants with chrism, and washes his hands. Then he returns to the altar with a litany performed by the regional subdeacon. The primicerius with the singers sings *Kyrie*; the lord pontiff begins, “Glory be to God in the highest.” The primicerius with the choir responds. When it has ended, he says the Prayer; the subdeacon reads the Epistle, and the Pontiff announces *Alleluia*. The primicerius sings it at the pulpit, to which the choir responds. When the chant is ended, the primicerius descends, goes to the pontiff, kisses his feet, and must give him one excellent cope. On that day neither the Creed, nor the Offertory, nor the *Agnus Dei*, nor the Communion is sung; but [Col. 0749C] at Vespers is said: *Alleluia*; Psalm, “Praise the Lord, all nations”; antiphon, “But on the evening of the Sabbath,” *Magnificat*; and the Prayer and “Go, the dismissal is made,” with the blessing, are said.

44. On the day of the holy Resurrection, at Matins, over the *Venite*: *Alleluia*. Some say: “The Lord has truly risen.” Three antiphons and three psalms: “Blessed is the man”; “Why have the nations raged?”; and “O Lord, how greatly are they multiplied?” In place of these three antiphons *Alleluia* is sung, as is written in the Roman Antiphonary. The verse, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” is sung as a Gradual. Three readings from the Gospel with their responsories. When these are completed, *Te Deum laudamus* is sung. Matins Lauds with their [Col. 0749D] antiphons and psalms. When the antiphons have been completed, instead of a verse the Gradual, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” is sung; antiphon, “The Lord rose from the tomb”; psalm, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel”; and only the Prayer of the feast. Prime without an antiphon, with three psalms; when these are completed, the Gradual, “This is the day,” and the Prayer of the day are sung.

45. At Mass only one Prayer is said. On this day the station is at Saint Mary Major. In the morning [Col. 0750A] the lord pontiff rises, goes, and enters the basilica of Saint Lawrence. The chapel and stool having been placed there, he first prays; afterwards he is vested by the regional deacons and subdeacons down to the dalmatic. He rises and enters the Saviour’s church, uncovers the image, and kisses its feet, saying aloud in chant three times: “The Lord rose from the tomb, who for us hung upon the wood, alleluia.” The others respond, and he returns to the stool. First he gives the peace to the archdeacon, who returns to his place; then to the second deacon, who returns and gives the peace to the archdeacon,

> [Note: Col. 0750D] Thus below, in the following number: the Pontiff first gives peace to the first bishop, then to the second, who, having returned to his place, gives peace to his first superior.

and returns in line; thus the other deacons do. Then the primicerius with the singers receive the peace. Likewise they return in line; then the chief basilicarius with the subdeacon receive the peace and return [Col. 0750B] in line; then the acolytes and the other Palatine orders.

When the peace has been completed, the lord pontiff then puts on a white chasuble, and likewise does so from this day until the octave of Easter; and he puts on the pallium and mitre. With all these orders he descends from the palace. The horses having been made ready with white cloths over the saddles, he is crowned and rides in procession to Saint Mary Major. When he arrives at the Merulana, a notary stands there and says aloud: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. The notary says:

> [Note: Col. 0750D] The same rite is described above in the earliest Roman Ordines.

“In the church of Saint Mary, on this night, so many males and so many females were baptized.” The pontiff responds, “Thanks be to God.” The notary receives one Byzantine coin from the sacellarius. On Monday the same is done at Saint Peter’s; on Tuesday, likewise at Saint Paul’s.

[Col. 0750C] 46. When the lord pontiff has come to Saint Mary’s, where the station is held, he dismounts from his horse and removes the crown from his head, giving it to the grooms that they may keep it carefully. The canons of the church receive him in procession with a thurible and incense and holy water, singing; but the pontiff places incense in the thurible and sprinkles water over the people. Then he enters the church, prays, and goes to the secretarium. There, all the orders having been made ready, he first gives the peace to the first bishop who is to serve him, and he returns to his place; then to the second bishop, who, returning, gives peace to his first superior and returns in line; and so with the others. Then similarly with the cardinals; afterwards with the prefect and judges, with the *delungarii*—that is, [Col. 0750D] naval prefects—and the *majorentes*, who are called the School of the Spur-Bearers, and the other lay princes.

Then two basilica subdeacons rise and take the first regional subdeacon by the hands, leading him at the right hand from the entrance of the secretarium before the pontiff. He says aloud: “Command, lord, that I be blessed.” The pontiff blesses him. Then they lead him forward a little, and again he says, “Command, lord, that I be blessed,” and the pontiff blesses him. He advances forward and says, “Command, lord, [Col. 0751A] that I be blessed.” The lord blesses him and says: “Servants of our Lord Jesus Christ; servants of our Lord Jesus Christ; servants of our Lord Jesus Christ: G., archdeacon, shall read the Gospel; Hyacinthus, subdeacon, shall read the Epistle; G., primicerius, and the other singers shall sing.”

47. Then the lord pontiff rises, supported by two men, proceeding in procession as is customary. The chamberlains at the entrance of the church have a cloth spread out, which they carry over his head as far as the altar. When he enters the presbytery of the church, the mansionarius prepares for him a reed with a lighted candle, which he takes and sets fire to the tow upon the tops of the columns standing there. When he comes to the first candle, the primicerius removes [Col. 0751B] the mitre and kisses the pontiff’s right shoulder; the pontiff blesses him. When he comes before the altar, the chamberlains remove the cloth from above his head. Thereafter he performs the office as the Church customarily does. The primicerius with the singers sings the Introit, “I have risen and am still with thee.” The lord pontiff announces, “Glory be to God in the highest”; when it has been completed, the pontiff says the Prayer.

The archdeacon, deacon, and subdeacon stand in order beside the altar, and the notaries below in the choir in copes. The archdeacon with his companions says aloud, “Hear, O Christ.” The notaries respond: “Life to our lord Pope Innocent, supreme pontiff and universal pope, decreed by God.” The archdeacon and deacon again say, “Hear, O Christ.” The notaries respond likewise. Thus it is said [Col. 0751C] three times, and so forth, with the matters that follow in the praise.

The praise having been made, the first basilica subdeacon reads the Latin Epistle; the Greek subdeacon reads the Greek Epistle. Two singers at the pulpit sing the Gradual, “This is the day which the Lord has made.” The primicerius with the choir responds. When the chants have ended, the archdeacon reads the Latin Gospel; the Greek deacon reads the Greek Gospel. At the Secret, two deacons descend before the altar and two subdeacons, standing in order and silence. While the pontiff says, “For ever and ever,” no one responds to him; rather, he begins and says, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” and the other words which follow.

48. Mass having been finished, he is crowned and returns in procession [Col. 0751D] to the palace by the Esquiline Hill. He enters beneath the arch where the Lunan Market [variant: Euman Market] is said to be; proceeds before the temple of Marius, called the Cimbrum; passes through the Merulana; and ascends to the palace beside the Fullery.

> [Note: Col. 0751D] In another manuscript: “which is called the Arch of Gallienus, now Saint Vitus in the Nardini market, passing through the Merulana, [Col. 0752D] ascending to the Cimbrum palace beside the Fullery.”

At the entrance of the basilica of Pope Zacharias, after receiving the praises from the cardinals and judges as in the other coronations, he dismounts from his horse. He is received by the primicerius, and the secondary chief of the judges removes the crown and gives it to the chamberlain, who carefully places it in the chest. On that day the judges lead him into the great Leonine basilica, into the chamber where eleven benches and one stool are prepared around the lord pontiff’s table, [Col. 0752A] and his couch is well prepared in the image of the twelve apostles around Christ’s table, when they ate the Passover. There five cardinals, five deacons, and the primicerius recline for the meal, the presbyterium having first been given in the chamber with handwashing, as on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

He rises from there and comes to the place called the Cubiculum, where the roast lamb is blessed. He blesses it and returns to the prepared couch at the table. The chief basilicarius sits upon the stool before the couch. Then the lord pontiff takes a little of the lamb and first offers it to the chief basilicarius, saying: “What thou doest, do quickly. As that man received it unto condemnation, so receive thou unto remission.” And he puts it into his mouth; he receives and eats it. He gives the remainder of the lamb to the eleven who recline and to such others as he pleases; and thus all [Col. 0752B] eat. At the middle of the feast, by order of the archdeacon, a certain deacon rises and reads a lesson. By command of the lord pontiff, the singers sing a Sequence suitable for Easter, with the organs sounding in measured music. When it is ended, they go and kiss the pontiff’s feet; he gives them a cup full of drink; they drink and receive one Byzantine coin from the sacellarius.

49. When the feast is finished, he descends to the secretarium in the basilica of the Saviour, where he rests briefly. Rising, after None has first been said, he enters Vespers in the order written in the Antiphonary. When the three Vespers have been completed—in the basilica of the Saviour, at the Fonts, and at the Holy Cross—the lord pontiff returns to the prepared portico. A faldstool having been placed there, [Col. 0752C] he sits, with the other orders around him. The chief steward, together with the other young attendants, orderly prepares drink before the lord pontiff; he drinks wine, and all the others drink.

Meanwhile the singers rise and sing this Greek Sequence: **Πάσχα ἱερὸν ἡμῖν σήμερον**, “Today the sacred Pascha is for us.” When the Sequence has ended, they go and kiss the pontiff’s feet, and he gives them a cup of drink to drink. Thus all depart rejoicing.

50. On Monday the station is at Saint Peter’s. At Matins, over the *Venite*: “The Lord has truly risen.” Alleluia. “Come, let us exult.” In place of three antiphons *Alleluia* is sung, and three psalms: “When I called” [variant: “In the Lord”]; “My words”; “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy anger.” Verse: “This is the day which the Lord has made”; three readings from a homily and two responsories of the day; *Te [Col. 0752D] Deum laudamus*. Matins Lauds are sung with their antiphons and psalms and the verses of the preceding day.

When morning has come, all the Palatine orders gather at the palace with the pontiff. They descend from the palace, and the lord pontiff rides. He enters through the field beside Saint Gregory in Martio; descends into the Great Way beneath the arch of the aqueduct; turns right before Saint Clement’s, then turns left beside the Colosseum. Passing through the Arch of Aurea [variant: Nervia] before Trajan’s Forum as far as Saint Basil’s, he ascends the hill near the Tiberian barracks, descends by Saint Abbacyrus, and [Col. 0753A] passes before the Holy Apostles. Descending to the left into the Via Lata, turning through the Quirinal Way, and proceeding to Saint Mary in Aquiro at the Arch of Piety, he thus ascends to the Field of Mars, passing before Saint Tryphon beside the posterns, as far as Hadrian’s Bridge. He enters across the bridge and goes out through the Colline Gate before Hadrian’s temple and castle; proceeding before Nero’s obelisk, he enters through the portico beside the tomb of Romulus; ascends to the Vatican, to the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter; and there sings Mass with all the Roman people.

51. When it is finished, he is crowned before the basilica of Saint Peter in the place where he mounts his horse. Crowned, he returns in procession to the palace by this [Col. 0753B] sacred route, through the portico and across the aforementioned bridge, entering beneath the triumphal arch of the emperors Theodosius, Valentinian, and Gratian. He goes beside the palace of Chromatius,

> [Note: Col. 0753D] Another manuscript has *commentarii*, as I conjecture, instead of “beside the palace of Saint Stephen in the piscina di Bachi.”

where the Jews make their acclamation. He passes through the Parione between the Circus of Alexander and the Theatre of Pompey; descends by the Portico of Agrippa;

> [Note: Col. 0754D] The same manuscript likewise adds, by way of explanation: “Saint Mary of the Round,” the Pantheon.

ascends through the Pinea beside the Palatina; passing before Saint Mark, he ascends beneath the Arch of the Flesh-Hand by the Silver-Smiths’ Slope, between the island of that name and the Capitol; descends before the private place of Mamertinus; enters beneath the triumphal arch between the Temple of Fate and the Temple of Concord; proceeds between Trajan’s Forum and Caesar’s Forum; enters beneath the Arch of Nerva, between the temple of that goddess and the Temple of Janus; ascends before the asylum by [Col. 0753C] the stone where Simon Magus fell, beside the Temple of Romulus; passes beneath the triumphal arch of Titus and Vespasian, called that of the Seven Lamps; descends to the Meta Sudans before Constantine’s triumphal arch; turns left before the amphitheatre; and by the Sacred Way beside the Colosseum [variant: Colliseum], returns to the Lateran. There, received solemnly, the acclamations of the cardinals and judges having been made, he ascends to the palace; gives the presbyterium without handwashing; celebrates a banquet in the same Leonine basilica. The banquet completed, he descends to Vespers and performs the office as written.

52. During Easter week, at Matins: Invitatory, “The Lord has risen,” with its *Venite*. On Tuesday: three psalms, “O Lord my God, in thee I have hoped”; “O Lord, our Lord”; “In the Lord I trust”; verse, “This is the day”; three readings with their responsories; Matins Lauds, as befits the day, and the other office. On Wednesday: psalms, “Save me, O Lord”; “How long, O Lord?”; “The fool has said”; *Alleluia* is sung in place of antiphons, with the verse “This is the day,” and with three readings and responsories; Matins Lauds and the other office as above. On Thursday: psalms, “O Lord, who shall dwell?”; “Preserve me, O Lord”; “Hear, O Lord”; with [read: instead of] three antiphons, *Alleluia*, and with the verse “This is the day,” [Col. 0754A] and with three readings and responsories; Matins Lauds and the other office as above. On Friday: psalms, “The heavens declare”; “May the Lord hear thee”; “O Lord, in thy strength”; verse, “This is the day”; three readings with their responsories of the day; Matins Lauds as above, and the other office.

53. On Low Saturday, at Matins, three psalms: “The Lord shepherds me”; “The earth is the Lord’s”; “Judge me, O God.” In place of the three antiphons *Alleluia* is sung; verse, “This is the day”; three readings with responsories. Matins Lauds and the rest of the office as above. In the morning, for Mass, the station is at the Lateran, where the lord apostolic sings Mass; there the Gradual is changed to *Alleluia*, and two Alleluias are sung with their verses.

While the primicerius with the choir sings the *Agnus [Col. 0754B] Dei*, the lord apostolic distributes lambs among the people for this reason: as the children of Israel, placed in Egypt, by the Lord’s command marked the doorposts of their houses with the blood of an unblemished lamb in the form of the sign T, that they might not be struck by the angel, so we also ought, by faith, to mark the threshold of our houses with this sign from the blood of the Passion of Christ, the unblemished Lamb, lest we be struck by the devil and by vices, and that we may be freed from the devil’s power. Another reason concerns infants newly baptized, who put off their old garment in church and proclaim *Alleluia*, that is, the glory of the blessed heavenly homeland. A third reason is that whoever possesses wax from the aforesaid lambs and has from it a cross in his house, or carries it with him, will not be harmed by any phantom spirit or by thunder.

[Col. 0754C] From Easter until Saturday at Sext, no responsory is said at any verse of the office at Prime, Terce, Sext, None, or Compline, nor is a reading recited in them; but instead of reading, verse, and responsory, the Gradual “This is the day” is sung, and its verse is said, as on the following days.

54. In the morning the station is at Saint Pancras’s. At evening the lord pontiff is to be at Saints Cosmas and Damian’s with all the schools, and there solemnly sing Vespers, as on holy Easter day, and take supper provided by the church, he and all the orders of the palace: namely bread, wine, milk foods, and lettuces.

55. From Easter until the vigil of the Ascension, the [Col. 0754D] three psalms of each nocturn of that weekday and three readings are sung in place of antiphons. Among the Romans there are only three Alleluias, on Sundays as well as on weekdays and feast-days; so that, until the aforesaid limit, the Psalter is completed without bending the knee in any office. No antiphon is sung; rather, *Alleluia* is sung in place of an antiphon, except when Sunday antiphons with *Alleluia*, or the antiphon of some feast likewise with *Alleluia*, are used. On weekdays at Matins the Invitatory is *Alleluia* with its *Venite*. At Lauds, under one *Alleluia*. All [Col. 0755A] psalms are sung to the tone “Weep not, Mary”; likewise at Vespers, except on Sundays and feast-days. At all Matins Lauds and Vesper Hours a commemoration is made of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection: antiphons, “He underwent the holy Cross” and “Weep not, Mary,” with their verses and prayers. On the Monday after the octave of Easter, the Apocalypse is appointed, and the history “I am the vine,” until Modicum Sunday.

56. At the Greater Litanies, all the crosses of the city of Rome proceed solemnly in procession to Saint Mark’s with clergy and people. First they sing the antiphon, “O Lord, our Lord, who with our fathers”; then the psalm “Blessed is the man,” and the rest. When they have come to the church, the responsory “Servant of God, Mark” is sung. When the responsory has ended, [Col. 0755B] they make the Collect: “People of Zion, return to the Lord.” When the chant has ended, they say, “Let us bend the knee”; “Rise”; and the prayer, “Let us proceed in peace.” They respond, “In the name of Jesus Christ.” Leaving the church, they return to the procession, singing antiphons and psalms along the way, and at appointed places the litanies, as is customary, as far as Saint Peter’s. They receive from the curia of the lord pope the presbyterium according to the custom of this day.

57. Meanwhile all the canons of the patriarchal churches assemble with their crosses in the basilica of the Saviour, called the Constantinian basilica, where the lord pontiff vests himself behind the altar of the same church with the bishops, cardinals, and other orders of the sacred palace. Then the primicerius with the singers sings, “People [Col. 0755C] of Zion.” When the chant has ended, the lord pontiff says, “Let us pray”; the archdeacon, “Let us bend the knee”; another responds, “Rise”; and the pontiff says the prayer. The choir responds, “Amen.” The archdeacon announces, “Let us proceed in peace”; the choir responds, “In the name of Christ.”

The regional subdeacon raises from the altar the stational cross, which he carries laid fully along his arm so that it may be kissed by all, in the procession before the pontiff until leaving the church; then he raises it upright. The primicerius with the choir, holding the pallium with his left hand behind the lord pope, first begins the antiphon, “O Lord, our Lord.” Then the Lateran sings the same antiphon; afterwards Saint Mary Major; Saint Peter’s in the fourth place. When the patriarchal churches have finished, [Col. 0755D] the primicerius again begins the same antiphon. In this order the other antiphons are sung throughout the whole route while the pontiff sings the psalms.

When the procession comes before the Colosseum, the regional subdeacon begins the sevenfold litany.

> [Note: Col. 0755D] Note here the sevenfold, fivefold, threefold, and simple litany. Gregory the Great instituted the sevenfold litany, which was divided into seven choirs. Read Menard’s notes on the *Sacramentary*, p. 94. Compare also the first Roman Ordo above, no. 43.

The basilicarii respond to it in the same manner through the seventh. When the procession comes before Saint Mary the New, the lord pontiff rests on a prepared couch with bishops, cardinals, and deacons until the litany is finished. When it is finished, the lord pontiff rises and says, “Let us pray”; the deacon says, “Let us bend the knee”; the response is, “Rise.” The pontiff says the prayer; [Col. 0756A] the deacon says, “Let us proceed in peace”; and all return in procession by the Sacred Way to the aforementioned Silver-Smiths’ Slope.

The subdeacon begins the fivefold litany in the same order as before, as far as the couch before Saint Mark’s, where the lord rests as at the first place. Then they return in procession as far as the triumphal arch of the emperors Theodosius, Valentinian, and Gratian, where he begins the threefold litany as far as the couch on Hadrian’s Bridge. Coming to Saint Lawrence in the Great Portico, he begins the simple litany, to be sung as far as the couch before Saint Mary in Virgarium [variant: *Virgariorum*], at the end of the curtain.

58. When the litany and the other offices have been completed, he ascends to the basilica of Saint Peter, where the station is held; and there the lord [Col. 0756B] pontiff sings Mass. At this station the lord pontiff receives twenty Pavia denarii solidi; the cardinals, deacons, and the *primicerius* together with the singers receive forty Luccan solidi; and the chief *basilicarius* and the scriniaries record all the crosses, and from each receive one Luccan [solidus], of which the acolytes receive one half and the *basilicarii* the other half; the deacons [receive] ten solidi, the regional subdeacons six solidi.

59. On the Sunday of *Modicum* the Catholic Epistles are appointed, as far as the third Sunday, “Father, while I was with them.” On this Sunday the Acts of the Apostles are appointed until the vigil of the Ascension; and from the aforesaid history is sung “If I forget,” and from this book three lessons are read on the Ascension of the Lord, three on Rose Sunday, and two at Pentecost.

[Col. 0756C] 60. On the Ascension of the Lord, the station is at Saint Peter’s, where the lord pontiff, with the bishops, cardinals, deacons, and the other schools, must sing Vespers; and, as at the nocturnal stations, rise at midnight, censing the altars, first celebrate the vigils at the body [of Saint Peter], then begin the same vigils in the choir before the high altar. There are three lessons from the Acts of the Apostles; five from sermons for the feast; the ninth from the homily, in the order stated above. At Mass the praises are performed by the archdeacon, the deacons and subdeacons, and the seven notaries. While the praises are being performed, the pontiff stands; when they are finished, another office of the Mass is sung, and, when it too has ended, he is crowned and thus returns more gloriously to the palace. During the week until the Saturday of Pentecost, on every ferial day [Col. 0756D] three antiphons and three psalms of the aforesaid feast are sung, and three lessons from sermons are read.

61. On Rose Sunday the station is at Saint Mary Rotunda, where the pontiff must sing Mass and, in the sermon, speak of the coming of the Holy Spirit, because roses are thrown down from the height of the temple as a figure of that same Holy Spirit.

62. On the Saturday of Pentecost, at the baptismal office, six Latin lessons and six Greek lessons are read, and the rest of the office is as written in the Sacramentary.

[Col. 0757A] 63. On Sunday the station is at Saint Peter’s, to which the lord pontiff comes at the Vespers of the vigil with all the orders; and in the night at Matins, as at the nocturnal stations. At the body he performs a vigil of three lessons; then Matins at the high altar. The invitatory is “Alleluia,” as on the day of the Resurrection, with its own “Come.” Others sing: “Alleluia. The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world; come, let us adore.” Alleluia. Antiphon: “Alleluia”; psalms: “Blessed is the man,” “Why have the nations raged?” “Lord, how are they multiplied?” Others say: “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven”; “Strengthen this, O God”; “Send forth thy Spirit, and they shall be created,” with their psalms. Three lessons are read. The canons of the church read the first lesson, “When they were being fulfilled,” and sing the first responsory. The cardinals read the second [Col. 0757B] lesson from the sermons; the singers and *basilicarii* sing the responsory. The pontiff reads the third lesson. Moreover, the *primicerius* performs the office with everyone. The pontiff sings Mass with the praises. After Mass, crowned, he returns to the palace, as is customary. During the week sermons are read. On the Saturday of the Ember Days, knees are not bent for the lessons because of Easter; instead of Graduals, Alleluia is sung with its verses. *Kyrie* is not said because of the litany of the procession, where *Kyrie* has been said; but only after the hymn of the three youths has ended, the pontiff begins Mass: “Glory to God in the highest,” and the remainder.

64. It is called the *Pascha annotina*—the “year-old Easter”—because it falls on the anniversary of the preceding Easter.

[Col. 0757C] 65. On the eighth Sunday after Pentecost the book of Kings is appointed, until the Kalends of August; thereafter the nocturn of psalms and the capitula are said with bent knee, as the order requires. At Prime, at all times, the prayer of the day is not changed, except during the days of Easter and on the great feasts of saints, when only the prayer of the feast is said, and during the octave.

66. On the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, at Matins, the invitatory is “The Lord, King of the Forerunner,” with “Come.” There are, moreover, three histories of the feast and three lessons concerning the saint. “We praise thee, O God” is not said; rather, the morning praises begin: “O God, come to my assistance.” One antiphon of Matins is announced, under which all the psalms are sung. At Prime: an antiphon, [Col. 0757D] three psalms, and the lesson of the vigil of the feast, with verse and prayer. He performs Vespers and the night vigils in the basilica of Saint John at the Font; the Greeks, however, [perform them] in the basilica of the Savior. At Matins the Greeks perform the office at the Font, and the curia in the basilica of the Savior. The pontiff sings Mass there where the station is held. On the vigil of Saint Peter, the vigil of Saint Lawrence, the vigil of Saint Mary, the vigil of Saint Andrew, and the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, this office is performed at Matins as we have stated above for the vigil of Saint John the Baptist. At Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, [the office] is sung and read of the saint; at Mass Alleluia is not [Col. 0758A] sung because of the fast, but only the Gradual.

67. On the feast of Saint Peter, the members of the curia assemble in the basilica of that apostle with the lord pope, where Vespers is sung. Antiphons: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” and other antiphons with their psalms. At the Magnificat: “The Lord made known to Peter.” In the first nocturn of the Vigil—

> [Note: [Col. 0757D] Here again, as above at the Nativity, Vigils are distinguished from Matins. Amalarius, in chapter LX of the *Antiphonary*, calls them two Vigils. “From the Roman,” he says, [Col. 0758D] “Antiphonary I have set down two Vigils, namely for the feast of Saint Peter in our Antiphonary.”]

—the *primicerius* begins the antiphon: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth”; psalm: “The heavens declare,” and the other nocturnal antiphons of the apostles with their psalms. The canons read three lessons from the Acts of the Apostles: “Peter and John were going up into the temple,” and sing three responsories. Then the judges read two lessons from sermons on the apostles Peter and Paul; the bishop reads the sixth, [Col. 0758B] a cardinal the seventh, the chief *basilicarius* the eighth; the lord pope reads the ninth from the exposition of the Gospel. The singers and *basilicarii* sing the responsories. When the reading of the lord pope has ended, the *primicerius* says, “We praise thee, O God”; the pope says the prayer and gives the blessing. At Matins the singers sing the invitatory, “The Lord, King of the Apostles,” and “Come.” Antiphon: “If thou lovest me, Simon Peter”; psalm: “Blessed is the man,” and other antiphons with their psalms, as is found written in the Antiphonary. The lessons are read in the order used at the Vigil or on Sundays. Three psalms are sung, as before. The morning praises are sung with the antiphon “Peter and John,” and the remaining antiphons with psalms. In the morning, at the Mass of the lord pope, praises ought to be made and he should be crowned on so great a feast, [Col. 0758C] of which he is the vicar.

68. During the octaves of Saint John, Saint Peter, Saint Lawrence, Saint Mary, the Nativity of the Lord, and Epiphany, this office is performed: three psalms, three lessons, and the whole office of the feast, unless among those days there is a feast of nine lessons.

69. On the feast of Saint Paul the pontiff goes there with all the schools; he performs Vespers and takes supper with all from the church. When supper has been completed, he enters for the Vigils. The monks of the church read three lessons, “Saul, still breathing threats,” and sing three responsories; for each responsory they receive two denarii from the archdeacon, out of the eighteen denarii which the archdeacon had received from them. After the responsory [Col. 0758D] at the fourth lesson, the lord pontiff rises and enters the shrine-altar of Saint Paul, where there is an opening in the bottom of the shrine above the body of the apostle. When this has been uncovered, he puts his hand down and takes hold of a censer, hanging on a hook and full of coals and incense, and draws it out. He gives the incense and coals to the archdeacon; the archdeacon distributes them among the people, for this reason: that anyone suffering from fever who devoutly drinks some of these in faith in the Apostle may be healed. Again he fills the censer with coals, and places upon them a glass lamp full of incense; he kindles the coals, and the lamp begins to boil [*al bollire*, “at boiling”]; and he replaces the censer [Col. 0759A] upon the aforesaid hook, and the opening of the shrine above his body is covered by the pontiff. At the fourth lesson annually, as at the vigils of Saint Paul, the bishops read two lessons, the cardinals two, the subdeacon the eighth, and the Pontiff the ninth; the singers and *basilicarii* sing the remaining five responsories and receive eighteen denarii from the archdeacon. The rest of the office is performed as customary. In the morning the pontiff sings Mass with the greatest solemnity, and the schools receive from the church, as the benefice of the feast, four solidi of coin.

70. On the Kalends of August the book of Solomon is appointed until the Kalends of September. On the feast of Saint Lawrence, the lord pontiff in his basilica in the field of Verano, where he rests, performs Vespers and the office throughout the entire night with all the schools.

> [Note: [Col. 0759D] In the Gregorian Sacramentary, the first Mass of the night is assigned for this feast, p. 120 in Menard.]

In the morning [Col. 0759B] he performs Mass for the Roman people, and the schools receive from the church eight solidi of denarii as the benefice.

71. On the vigil of Saint Mary, in the morning the lord pope, with the cardinals and barefoot, makes seven genuflections, opens the image, kisses the feet of the Lord, and lowers it [*jusum*, that is, *deorsum*, “downward”], while singing “We praise thee, O God.” Pope Leo IV established this.

72. On the Assumption of Saint Mary, the lord pope with the entire curia performs Vespers and a Vigil of nine lessons in the church of Saint Mary Major. When these have ended, he returns to the Lateran. The cardinals and deacons take up the image of Jesus Christ and bring it out from the basilica of Saint Lawrence with all the people, carrying it through the Lateran field beside the basilica of Saint Gregory. A regional subdeacon bears [Col. 0759C] the stational cross after it; after this comes the procession of the curia in ordered advance, singing psalms, while the *primicerius* and the school sing a responsory for the same feast. The prefect, with twelve men, receives twelve torches from the curia; the doorkeepers carry another twelve, burning before the image. While the image passes through the field, the chamberlains stand on the summit of Saint George, holding two burning torches; once the image has passed, they extinguish the torches. And when the image has come to Saint Mary the New, they set it down before the church and wash its feet with basil. Meanwhile the schools perform Matins in the church, namely of three lessons. But the people, praising and blessing the Lord, take it thence and carry it to Saint Adrian; and there [Col. 0759D] they wash its feet. On leaving the church, they return by the way through which they had come and carry it through the arch at Lathone, because in ancient times there was there a great persecution by the devil. Then they pass beside the house of Orpheus because of the basilisk, which at that time lay hidden there in a cave, and by whose stench and hissing persons passing there were made ill and died. Therefore Pope Sergius established this procession on this great feast, so that through the praises of so great a multitude and the intercession before God of the most holy Virgin Mary the Roman people might be delivered from these persecutions. Ascending to Saint [Col. 0760A] Mary’s, the lord pontiff, vested, sings Mass; he blesses the weary people; all depart.

73. On the first Sunday of September the books of Job and Tobit, Judith and Esther are appointed, until the first Sunday of October.
