We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 0913C] take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and applied in every way to the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If anyone, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord [Col. 0913D] Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

**SHOW US, O LORD, THY MERCY.**

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, [lacuna]. I, Peter, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Rainerius, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca, have subscribed. I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of the title of St Cyriacus, have subscribed. I, Hugh, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. [Col. 0914A] I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Ubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Guido, minister of the altar in the Roman Church, [lacuna]. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Rodulf, cardinal deacon of St Lucy in the Septa Solis, have subscribed. I, Astaldus, cardinal deacon of St Eustace, [Col. 0914B] have subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of St Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Berard, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Bruno, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius II.

Copied in the year 1294 by William Marchus and Brancha, notaries of Forlì.

### LXXI. Privilege for the church of St Mary of Ilbenstadt. (1144, 2 December.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, 654.]

[Col. 0914C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANTHONY, provost of Ilbenstadt, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as consonant with reason and propriety, it is fitting for us willingly to grant it and to furnish suitable support for the wishes of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of Ilbenstadt of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, in which you are dedicated to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

[Col. 0914D] We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favor, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state expressly: in the village of Eberbach, the rent of one *mansus* of vineyards; and in Attavilla, the rent of half a *mansus*, which our brother Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, gave you and confirmed by his charter.

We further forbid anyone to usurp the advocacy of that place; rather, as hitherto, it shall henceforth remain free and undisturbed from every advocate. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 0915A] rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and applied in every way to the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amends by satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0915B] Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth Nones of December [2 December], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius II.

### LXXII. Privilege concerning churches subject to the Bishop of Paris and the freedom, granted by the most Christian King Louis, of the furnishings of a deceased bishop. (1144, 5 December.)

[*Cartularies of Notre-Dame of Paris*, vol. I, p. 25.]

[Col. 0915C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEOBALD, Bishop of Paris, and to his successors canonically promoted, in perpetuity.

The more renowned the glorious Church of Paris is because it stands at the seat of the king of the Franks, and the more devoted it is shown by manifest proofs to be, venerable brother Theobald, in love and reverence for blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, the more readily do we grant the desired support in matters known to concern the honor and advantage of both. Therefore, dearest brother Theobald, assenting to your reasonable petitions, we fortify, by the privilege of apostolic protection, for you and your successors—and through you for the Church of Paris—whatever the Parisian Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God favoring, acquire by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just titles.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: namely, the church of Saint Marcellus; the church of Saint Cloud, with its village and all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Germanus of Auxerre; the church of Saint Eligius; likewise the church of Campelles, with its prebends and the three parishes belonging to that church—namely, Saint Merri, La Chapelle, and Karris—saving, however, the annual payment to the Church of Sens of a rent of two solidi in the currency of that land, that is, the currency current in those regions. The aforesaid churches are known to belong by right and ownership to the bishop of Paris.

We also confirm episcopal jurisdiction in the following abbeys and in all their parishes and parishioners: namely, the abbey of Lagny; the abbey of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés; the abbey of Saint-Magloire; the abbey of Saint Victor; the abbey of the Valley of Holy Mary; the abbey of Sarney; the abbey of the nuns of Montmartre; those of Edera and Kala; and the church above Argenteuil.

Furthermore, we likewise confirm the pact and agreement made between you and our dearest son Louis, the king of the Franks of illustrious memory, concerning the place in the Parisian suburb called Campellus: namely, that one third of the entire revenue from the estate of Fossatum in that land—whether arising from rents, purchases, sales, judicial profits, or by whatever other means anything may accrue therefrom—shall be paid to you and your successors without any diminution; but the remaining two thirds shall be paid into the royal treasury. Whoever is the king’s provost shall swear fidelity concerning this to you and your successors, and your provost shall do so to the king and his heirs; and neither shall receive or dispose of anything from that land without the other.

We also decree that, if any canon of the Church of Paris is promoted to the dignity of a bishopric, his prebend shall freely revert to the Church of Paris. By apostolic authority we likewise forbid anyone whatsoever to plunder the household goods of a deceased bishop of Paris; rather, they shall remain untouched for the use of the church and of his successor, as was granted by Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks, and confirmed in your written instrument.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb you or your successors in respect of this our confirmation, or take away the possessions of the Church of Paris, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. Here follow the subscriptions of the cardinals.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Nones of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Lucius II.

LXXIII. He receives the monastery of Savigny under his protection and confirms its possessions. (A.D. 1144, Dec. 5.)

[MARTENE, *Ampl. Collect.*, I, 775.]

[Col. 0917A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SERLO, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Savigny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It befits us gladly to grant with ready mind a desire shown to concern the religious purpose and the salvation of souls, and to afford fitting support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Serlo, we graciously assent to your reasonable petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the monastery of the Holy Trinity, over which, by God’s authorship, you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and reasonably possesses, or may hereafter, God favoring, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: from the gift of Ralph of Fougères and his son Henry, the forest of Savigny with all its appurtenances, and the mill of Romagné. From the gift of Henry, king of the English: near Avranches, the vineyard of Champ-Bodry with its appurtenances; and, in the forest of Passais, the place called Frenusia with the land of Moreth, the place of Saint Alveus with the land of Beau-Champ, and the place of Dom Peter with all that pertains to the aforesaid places; and in the same forest of Passais, pannage and grazing, with the other customary rights; and in his other forests, pannage; and throughout all his land and at the seaports, exemption from tolls and all customary dues. [lacuna]

Furthermore, concerning the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or the sustenance of your animals, we forbid any cleric or layman to exact tithes. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for the use and complete benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[SHOW US YOUR MERCY.] [SAINT PETER. SAINT PAUL. POPE LUCIUS II.]

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Peter, bishop of Albano. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Callixtus. I, Rainerius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Nones of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Lucius II.

LXXIV. Privilege for the abbey of Saint Martin of the Fields. (A.D. 1144, Dec. 5.)

[MARRIER, *Hist. de Saint-Martin des Champs*, p. 76.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ODON, prior of Saint Martin of the Fields, and his brethren, present and future, to be regularly appointed: in perpetuity.

The care of the Catholic Church has been entrusted to us by God, the supreme shepherd, so that we may love God’s servants with paternal affection and endeavor all the more by every means to foster their devotion, as they are known to adhere more fervently to ecclesiastical discipline and to the Rules of the holy Fathers. For then a service acceptable to God is rendered by the Apostolic See, if the salutary institution, rigor, and order of holy places are preserved in purity of religion through our protection.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Theobald, bishop of Paris, who, through God’s grace, is known to have presided usefully over that place, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present document, the church of blessed Martin in which you are bound to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God favoring, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: in the diocese of Exeter, the church of Saint James and the church of Saint Peter of Wertonia, with their chapels, lands, and all appurtenances; the land of Cotheleia and of Raimelia. In the diocese of Amiens, the church of Saint Gervasius of Enchra, with chapels and all appurtenances. In the diocese of Arras, the church of Passu, with chapels and all appurtenances. In the archdiocese of Sens, one prebend in the church of Saint Mary of Étampes. In the diocese of Paris, one prebend in the church of Blessed Mary; one prebend in the church of Saint Geneviève. In the diocese of Beauvais, the church of Prateriis. In the diocese of Châlons, the church of Wale-Mont; the church of Frisivilla with a chapel; the church of Nigro Loco; the church of Espancis; the church of Verreriis; and the chapel beside the castle of Lord Peter at Estanneium, with all their appurtenances.

Moreover, that place itself, with all that belongs to it, shall remain forever in the obedience and subjection of the abbot of Cluny, to whose jurisdiction it is known to belong. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for the complete benefit and use of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve justice for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Conrad, bishop of Sabina. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina. I, Peter, bishop of Albano. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Callixtus. I, Rainerius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus. I, Nicholas, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cyriacus. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Julian Prison. I, Rodolph, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in the Septa Solis. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, G[regory?], cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Astaldus, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Nones of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Lucius II.

LXXV. To Henry of Fougères and Juhel of Mayenne.—He commends the monks of Savigny to them. (A.D. 1144, Dec. 7.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaur.*, I, 396.]

[Col. 0920B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the noble men HENRY of Fougères and JUHEL of Mayenne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It pleases us that you aid and support the religious brethren of the monastery of Savigny within the territory of authority entrusted to you by God, as we have learned from the report of our beloved son Abbot Serlo, and that from the resources entrusted to you by God you provide them with the desired relief. Since virtue consists not in beginning but in completing, by apostolic letters we command you, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that, in accordance with this good beginning, you defend the place and the brethren serving the Lord there from all unjust claims and oppressions, and attend more diligently to the increase of that place. Thus in the future you will be able to merit everlasting reward from the Lord, and in the present to obtain abundance of temporal goods and an increase of honor.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of December.

LXXVI. Privilege for the church of Blessed Mary of Reno. (A.D. 1144, Dec. 27.)

[TROMBELLI, *Memorie Stor. di Reno*, Appendix, p. 363.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIDO, prior of the church of Blessed Mary of Reno, and his brethren, present and future, to be canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

It accords with the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious persons and fortify their places with pious protection. For it is recognized to be fitting and honorable that we, who have been assumed to the government of churches, should both protect them from the wickedness of evil men and cherish them through the patronage of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Innocent II of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are bound to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be kept there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter, God favoring, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. We also forbid any brother, after making profession there, to dare leave that cloister without permission of the prior and the entire community; and let no one whatsoever receive one who has left without letters of authorization from the community. You shall have free authority, without any person’s opposition, to receive into conversion clerics or free laymen living in the secular estate.

Moreover, no cleric or layman whatsoever may presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. You shall receive holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, possesses the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to supply these to you freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of intrusion or by force; rather, by common counsel and equal consent, or by the counsel of the sounder party, you may freely elect a prior according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, without anyone’s opposition. We also grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated; yet the rights of the mother church are preserved.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things be preserved intact for the complete benefit and use of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving nevertheless the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

SHOW US, O LORD, YOUR MERCY.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Rainerius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca, have subscribed. I, Thomas, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, have subscribed. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina, have subscribed. I, Hugh, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Rodolph, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in the Septa Solis, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Astaldus, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Berald, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Lucius II.

LXXVII. To Alvisus, bishop of Arras. (A.D. 1144, Dec. 27.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, II, 167.]

[Col. 0922C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALVISUS, bishop of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received your letter with the kindness due to you, since before your pontifical office we loved your person with true charity in the Lord, and now desire to love you with fuller affection and honor you in whatever ways we can according to God. It therefore concerns you diligently to apply yourself both to establishing peace between our dearest sons Louis, king of the Franks, and Count Theodoric, and to other matters which you recognize to concern the honor of the holy Roman Church, so that God may thereby be honored and your mother, the holy Roman Church, may rejoice in your good actions.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January.

LXXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Magnus of Regensburg. (A.D. 1144, Dec. 28.)

[HUND, *Metropolis Salzburg.*, III, p. 523.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GEBHARD, provost of the church called “at the Banks,” and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

If we graciously receive the petitions of religious men, without doubt we find almighty God kind and merciful toward our own needs. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Gebhard, we gladly assent to your reasonable petitions, and receive under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the church called “at the Banks,” over which, by the Lord’s authorship, you preside; and we fortify it by the text of this present document.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in that place according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the Institution of the brethren of Porto shall be preserved inviolably for future and perpetual times. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God favoring, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors.

Upon the death of you, the present provost of that place, no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the consent of the sounder party, have provided to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. You may also, after deliberation together, elect a suitable defender; and if he appears useless and becomes harmful, presumptuously injuring you and your property in contempt of justice, you shall have free authority to reject him. No one may compel you, against your will, to participate in public processions, or dare in any way to disturb your peace.

We decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated, saving the canonical rights of the Church of Regensburg and the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Theodewin, bishop of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Thomas, cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, have subscribed. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of lord Pope Lucius II.

LXXIX. To Petronilla, abbess of Fontevraud.—He states that he has committed the resolution of her controversy with Ulgerius, bishop of Angers, by agreement or judgment, to delegated bishops. (A.D. 1144.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 419.]

[Col. 0924B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ PETRONILLA, abbess, and the sisters of Fontevraud: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by the Lord, we ought to love and support venerable places, we have for a long time especially loved, and do love, your place of Fontevraud because of its religious character and integrity; and, in whatever ways we can according to the Lord, we desire to provide for you and keep your rights undiminished. We have received your petitions with paternal kindness. Concerning certain matters, during the time of our predecessors, we wrote repeatedly at their command; nevertheless, neither through those letters nor otherwise, as we have learned from your messengers, have you been able to obtain justice.

We have judged it fitting to command orally our legates, whom we intend to send into those regions, that they diligently hear your complaints and cause justice to be rendered to you as justice shall dictate; that they aid and support your house and what belongs to it; and that they diligently admonish the powerful persons of that land to do you good. Moreover, we wish your charity to know that we grieve with paternal affection over the controversy which has for so long been conducted between you and our venerable brother Ulgerius, bishop of Angers, and that we willingly labor, both for you and for our brother, to bring it to its proper conclusion.

For this reason, by apostolic letters we enjoin our venerable brethren G[aufridus], archbishop of Bordeaux; G[aufridus], bishop of Chartres; B[ernard], bishop of Soissons; B[ernard], bishop of Saintes; and G[islebert], bishop of Poitiers, to assemble within forty days after the aforesaid bishop has returned from the Apostolic See and to determine that controversy by agreement or judgment.

> **Note:** [Col. 0923D] The bishop of Soissons at that time was Goslemus; Hugh, archbishop of Tours, took his place, as may be seen in the note appended below.

> **Note:** [Col. 0923D] In the year 1149 this controversy at last reached its conclusion, as is clear from the following instrument:
>
> “I, Engelbaud, by God’s forbearance humble minister of the people of Tours, wish it to be known to those present and future that the controversy which for a long time had been pursued between the Church of Angers and the monastery of Fontevraud with much labor and countless expenses, has at length, by the mercy of God permitting it, been brought by us in the following manner to the harbor of peace.
>
> “Accordingly, the investiture adjudged at Tours by the venerable fathers Hugh, archbishop of Tours, Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux, Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, Bernard, bishop of Saintes, and several other persons—and also granted by our brother Ulgerius, bishop of Angers—we, on behalf of the Church of Angers, have granted and confirmed to the nuns of Fontevraud, so that henceforth they may firmly and undisturbedly have, hold, and possess it.
>
> “The nuns themselves promised and granted us that henceforth they would maintain good peace with the Church of Angers. We decree, moreover, that Basletus shall henceforth have and possess, saving the right of the bishop of Angers, all those things with which we invested him at Calumnam. In compensation for his losses, which he complained were many and serious, we decreed that one thousand solidi in Angevin currency should be paid to him. This was done; and thus, with God’s approval, a good agreement was made between the Church of Angers and the monastery of Fontevraud.
>
> “This agreement was made at Fontevraud through our hand, in the presence of Lady Petronilla, abbess, the prioress of Fontevraud, and Matilda, sister of the count of Brittany, who in the chapter of the nuns approved and confirmed the agreement (*perhaps*: ‘approving and confirming’). Present at this agreement were Bernerius, abbot of Nucariensis; and our clerics Theduinus, master of the schools, William, chaplain, Bricius, chaplain, and Garnerius, notary; the clerics of Angers, Geoffrey of Saint-Saturninus, archdeacon, Jonas, chaplain, and many others. In order that this agreement may remain firm and undisturbed, we took care to commit it to this writing and caused it to be confirmed by the stipulation of a chirograph.
>
> “This was done in the year 1149 from the Lord’s Incarnation, when Pope Eugenius presided in the city and Louis, king of the Franks, was staying on the Jerusalem expedition. Seal of Engelbaud, archbishop of Tours; seal of the monastery of Fontevraud.”
>
> From the *Clypeus* of John de la Mainferme, vol. II, p. 482.

We also earnestly ask that same bishop, and in asking command him, that he love, aid, and support you and your house, and that in this matter and all others he show himself toward you in such a manner as to acquire more abundantly the favor of blessed Peter and ourselves. It therefore concerns you, beloved daughter in the Lord, Abbess Petronilla, when you are summoned by our aforesaid brethren, to go to them and humbly observe what they shall determine in the manner stated above. Furthermore, because we have great confidence in you, we beseech your charity through almighty God that you yourselves make special prayers for me to the Lord, and endeavor that this be done through all the congregations of your order.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends [of January].

LXXX. Bull for the Church of Saint Augustine of Canterbury. (A.D. 1144.)

[*Rer. Anglic. Script.*, III, 1805.]

[Col. 0925B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of Blessed Augustine of Canterbury, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The care of venerable places admonishes us to provide for their perpetual security, and so forth. Accordingly, we confirm by apostolic authority, and decree to remain valid, the agreement made on reasonable terms between you and our venerable brother Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, for the sake of peace, through our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Winchester, and other discerning men, concerning the fifty solidi and seven pence which your monastery was accustomed to pay annually to the Church of Canterbury: namely, that the church of the Holy Trinity of Canterbury shall receive two mills at Dover, which belonged by right to that monastery, and twenty solidi from the prebend which that monastery has in the church of Saint Martin at Dover, upon the condition that it shall no longer exact the aforesaid fifty solidi and seven pence, while in all other respects the dignity of each church remains wholly preserved.

We also decree, as has been provided by us and our brethren for the sake of good peace and the tranquility of both churches, that in exchange for the three solidi which the monks of Blessed Augustine annually paid to the archbishop and Church of Canterbury for bread, drink, and rams, the aforesaid archbishop shall receive three solidi-worth of land belonging to that monastery, which the Church of Canterbury shall henceforth possess peacefully in perpetuity; so that neither the said archbishop nor any of his successors, whether personally or through their officials, may be permitted to exact anything from that monastery or its brethren. If anyone should presume rashly to act against these provisions, unless, when warned for the third time, he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be struck by the sword of anathema.

LXXXI. Fragment of a diploma for the monastery of Saint Augustine of Canterbury. (In the same year.)

[Ibid., p. 1806.]

[Col. 0926B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc. [lacuna]

Furthermore, we confirm to you Estanoris and the entire shore as far as the middle of the water, as it was granted to the monastery by Henry and Stephen, kings of the English, of good memory, etc. [lacuna] (And this bull bears the subscriptions of twenty cardinals.)

LXXXII. He confirms the assignment made by Hugh II, abbot of Saint Augustine of Canterbury, from the sacristy and chamber of the monastery to the church. (A.D. 1144.)

[Ibid., p. 1806.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

[Col. 0926C] Whenever that which follows is requested of us, etc. We therefore confirm by the page of the present writing, and decree to remain valid, the grant of possessions or revenues for maintaining the lights, and for repairing and adorning the monastery itself, reasonably made by you, son Abbot Hugh, with the counsel of the brethren and confirmed by your written instrument: namely, two mills within the city; ten marks from the church of Middleton, three of which are to be for making books and the remaining seven paid to the altar; all money offered on the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian in your chapel at Chistelet; and all money which it was accustomed to receive from the chapel of Saint Mildred in Thanet. Likewise we confirm the arrangement, made by your common counsel and consent, concerning half the candles and wax offered on the aforesaid feast of Cosmas and Damian, for the clothing of the monks. But if anyone knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our confirmation, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the rank of his honour and office, etc.

### LXXXIII. To King Conrad.—Concerning his oppression; and inviting him to the protection of the Roman Church. (Year 1144.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 609.]

[Col. 0927B] LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son CONRAD, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Every good gift” (James 1), etc. For the Roman people, wishing to set no bounds to their madness, added a patrician to the senators whom they had previously established; and, choosing Jordan, son of Peter Leo, to this dignity, they all submit to him as to a prince. And below: Then they approach their pontiff and demand for the right of their patrician all his regalia, both those situated in the City and those outside it; and, saying that he ought to be supported, after the fashion of the ancient priests, solely from tithes and offerings, they did not fear to afflict the soul of the righteous man day by day.

### LXXXIV. He grants certain privileges to William, patriarch of Jerusalem. (Year 1144.)

[ROZIÈRE, *Cartulaire du Saint-Sépulcre*, 6.]

[Col. 0927C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, patriarch of Jerusalem, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The more it is fitting that reverence be shown to the apostolic see and to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by all Churches spread far and wide—since the Lord said to him, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church”—the more diligently ought we to labour, with exact care, for their protection and guardianship. And although we ought especially to honour the other venerable places of the saints, it will not be unfitting if we venerate more particularly the city of the great King, the special place of the Holy of Holies, and the most reverend Church of Jerusalem, and preserve for it its dignity and rights. For it was this city that the same King of kings and Lord of lords deigned to visit in bodily presence, and which he willed to illuminate by his Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit. It ought therefore to be honoured more earnestly by all the faithful and effectively supported in its needs.

Accordingly, dearest brother in Christ, Patriarch William, favourably granting our due assent to your just petitions, we confirm and strengthen by the pages of the present writing for you and your successors—and, through you, for the holy Church of Jerusalem—all cities and provinces which are now subject to you and to the Church of Jerusalem by patriarchal or metropolitan right; likewise whatever, in the times of both Baldwin and Fulk, kings of Jerusalem, has by divine favour been restored to the Church of Jerusalem and confirmed by authentic privileges of the Roman pontiffs; and whatever may hereafter, through the exertion and power of our dearest son Baldwin, illustrious and glorious king of Jerusalem, be restored to the same Church of Jerusalem from beneath the yoke of the pagans, with the Lord’s help, for the honour of God and the salvation of the Eastern Church, or acquired by other just means. [Col. 0928A–B] We confirm to you, by the authority of the apostolic see, patriarchal or metropolitan dignity and reverence in those same cities and provinces, saving the reverence and authority of the holy Roman Church.

### LXXXV. To the Archbishop of Salzburg and the Bishop of Gurk. (Year 1144.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 617.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers CONRAD, archbishop of Salzburg, and ROMANUS, bishop of Gurk: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received with paternal kindness our beloved son Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, who came to the apostolic see; and, honouring his person on account of his religion and integrity, we sent him back to his own place with the favour of the apostolic see. We therefore earnestly commend him to your brotherhood by the present letter and ask that, as hitherto you have done out of regard solely for his religion and integrity, so henceforth, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, you may honour and love him, and give him help and counsel in his necessities.

### LXXXVI. To the Bishop of Burgos in Spain.—That he should entrust the church of Caradigua to the Cluniac brethren for reform. (Year 1144.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 55.]

[Col. 0928D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother . . . , bishop of Burgos.

Your brotherhood ought to remember that, justice so requiring, we restored to you the church called Caradigua. After making that restoration, we earnestly admonished your discretion that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, you should entrust that Church to the Cluniac brethren in order to reform religious life there. Since we have learned that through those brethren much has been reformed in the place and in religious observance, and that it has been increased in temporal goods, we command you by the present letter, as we indicated to you orally, that within forty days after receiving it you entrust the same church to Cluniac monks and grant it as a priory, while preserving the rights of yourself and your Church. [Col. 0929A] But if the abbot who is known to have presided over that place should wish to remain under the obedience of the abbot of Cluny, we have instructed you to treat him charitably; otherwise, according to the prudence granted you by God, provide for him in another place.

### LXXXVII. He commands Otto, bishop of Prague, to protect the monastery of Rajhrad against Vratislav, duke of Brno, and other nobles. (Year 1144.)

[BOCZEK, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae*, I, 232.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother OTTO, bishop of Prague: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The beloved sons . . . , abbot and brethren of the same house of Břevnov, have sent us letters of complaint that not inconsiderable injuries and losses are inflicted upon them by lay persons—namely, Duke Vratislav and certain nobles of that land—who seize and hold the goods of the monastery of Rajhrad, which is known to belong to them. We therefore exhort your brotherhood, etc.

### LXXXVIII. He grants certain privileges to William, patriarch of Jerusalem. (Year 1145.)

[ROZIÈRE, *Cartulaire du Saint-Sépulcre*, 32.]

[Col. 0929C] LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, patriarch of Jerusalem: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is just that one who desires his own commands to be observed by successors should not neglect to observe the enactments of his predecessors. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Patriarch William, we grant favourable assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Innocent, we decree that the agreement made, for the sake of peace, between Warmund, of good memory, your predecessor, and Ebremar, then archbishop of Caesarea, and subsequently confirmed by writings and testimony both by yourself and by our brother Gaudentius, archbishop of Caesarea, shall remain valid and inviolate for all time.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts hereafter rashly to contravene this page of our confirmation, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, recognize himself or herself as guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of January [4 January].

### LXXXIX. To Peter of Cluny.—Concerning the subjection of the abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict above the Po to the abbot of Cluny. (Year 1145, 11 January.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 54.]

[Col. 0930A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having carefully examined the privileges granted by the apostolic see to the monastery of Cluny, we have plainly learned that the monastery of Saint Benedict was entrusted by our predecessor of good memory, Pope Gregory VII, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and his successors, so that they might have it under their government, guardianship, and authority and devote themselves to its administration. [Col. 0930B] Moreover, when the abbot of that place dies, their diligence is always to provide that a suitable person, worthy of this office, be appointed in the place of government according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; and whatever ought to be instituted or corrected in the monastery for the increase and observance of monastic religious life is always to be administered under their direction and dispensation—while in all things preserving the authority of the apostolic see, to whose jurisdiction that place is known to belong.

The same was ordained and confirmed by the successors of that pope, our predecessors, especially Pope Calixtus of happy memory. In his confirmation he added that in the same monastery of Saint Benedict no abbot should under any circumstances be elected without the counsel, provision, and command of the abbot of Cluny; nor should any bishop lay a hand of consecration or ordination upon the elected person without commendatory letters from the abbot of Cluny. Otherwise, both the consecrator, as a transgressor of an apostolic constitution, shall be liable to more serious punishment, and the election or ordination of the consecrated person shall be held void until satisfaction has been made to the apostolic see and to its monastery of Cluny.

But now, in our time, beloved son in the Lord Peter, abbot, you have often complained, both through yourself and through your brethren, to our predecessors and also to us, that they elected an abbot for themselves without consulting you, contrary to the aforesaid tenor, and withdraw from you the obedience and reverence due to you. [Col. 0930C–D] Therefore our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Innocent, ordered them by his letters that Abbot William, who had been elected and ordained without consultation with you, should visit the monastery and brethren of Cluny with honourable and discreet persons among his brethren, and should render to you, Abbot Peter, obedience and reverence with humility and charity, as his predecessor Henry, of good memory, is known to have rendered them.

When they in no way fulfilled this, and you persisted in your complaint, we ordered them by apostolic letters that the aforesaid Abbot William should appear before us during the past octave of Saint Andrew, with honourable and discreet persons among his brethren and with the privileges of his monastery, so that, after hearing the cause of both parties, we might, with the Lord’s help, establish peace between you. But although your brethren appeared before us at that time, he neither came himself nor could peace between you be restored through brethren whom he might have sent to appear before us.

Since therefore we can no longer fail so manifest a right of Cluny, we have commanded and ordered them by apostolic letters that the said Abbot William, as we have stated, without delaying under any pretext, should visit the monastery of Cluny with honourable and discreet persons among his brethren and humbly render to you, Abbot Peter, the obedience and reverence which your predecessors are known to have rendered to your predecessors. [Col. 0931A–B] If, burdened by illness, he cannot do this himself, he is to accomplish the same through the better persons of that monastery. Moreover, lest an election of an abbot take place henceforth in that monastery of Saint Benedict except according to the aforesaid tenor of the privileges of the apostolic see, we prohibit it by apostolic authority. Should such an election occur, it shall be held void and without effect.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Ides of January [11 January].

### XC. Privilege for the church of Saint Blaise at Fridesel. (Year 1145, 16 January.)

[It survives in the royal Hanoverian archive, according to JAFFÉ, *Regesta Romanorum pontificum*, p. 613.]

### XCI. The monastery of Saint Sabas is subjected to Cluny in perpetuity. (Year 1145, 19 January.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 613.]

[Col. 0931C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Although the care of all Churches lies upon us by reason of the administration of the apostolic see, we ought nevertheless to apply ourselves with a more earnest devotion of affection to those places that are specially entrusted to our government, are situated within the City, and are known to belong to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church. The monastery of Saint Sabas is known to have been founded in religious observance and integrity in the time of the most blessed Pope Gregory, and endowed with great and extensive possessions. Now, however, sins demanding it, religious observance has lapsed; and, owing to the excessive wickedness of evil men, its goods and possessions have been dispersed and unjustly alienated from it.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Peter, abbot, since the monastery of Cluny, by the grace of almighty God, has for so long flourished far and wide in exceptional religious observance and has spread its good reputation among many, we entrust to you and your successors in perpetuity the aforesaid monastery of Saint Sabas, with all that belongs to it, in order that religious life may be reformed there and that its affairs may be improved and regulated. [Col. 0931D–0932A] You are to devote care and diligence to its restoration and government and are to have authority over it. We further decree that henceforth no abbot shall under any circumstances be elected there without the provision and counsel of the abbot of Cluny. Rather, your diligence is always to provide that a suitable person, worthy of this office, be appointed to the place of government according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; and whatever ought to be instituted or corrected in the monastery for the increase and observance of monastic religious life is always to be administered under your direction and dispensation, while in all things preserving the authority of the apostolic see, to whose jurisdiction that place is known to belong. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly [contravenes] this page of our constitution, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed, together with eighteen cardinals.

Given at Rome through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February [19 January], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius II.

### XCII. To Peter, abbot of Cluny.—He reports that the Cluniac monks sent to him have been established in the church of Saint Sabas. (Year 1144, 20 January.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 416.]

[Col. 0932C] LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot, and the monks of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received your brethren with due kindness and honourably established them at Saint Sabas. But, hindered by the great disturbance of the City—concerning which you will be able to learn more fully from our beloved sons John the chamberlain and your other brethren—we were unable to ordain an abbot there.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Concerning these disturbances, Godfrey of Viterbo says: “Lucius II, intending to extinguish the senate, climbed the Capitoline at the head of a great force, in order to remove with disgrace the senators then sitting there. But the Roman senate and people, taking up arms, drove the pope and all his party from the Capitoline in an instant. There, as we heard at the time, the pope was struck by great stones and did not sit again in his seat until the day of his death, which followed shortly afterwards.”]

Nevertheless, we granted and confirmed to you by our privilege that place itself with all its appurtenances. As soon as, by God’s grace, we are freed from these troubles, we shall arrange for Master Marius, who has hitherto presided over that place—whom, because of the brethren’s new arrival, we left for a little while as their overseer—to be provided for; and we shall arrange, with the Lord’s help, that the man designated to us by your brethren be ordained there as abbot, for the honour of God, of the holy Roman Church, and of the monastery of Cluny. [Col. 0932D] We ask, moreover, that you offer special prayers to the Lord for us and for the whole condition of the holy Church of God, and that you endeavour to have such prayers offered by the religious communities of your order.

Given at Rome, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January].

### XCIII. Privilege for the monastery of Baumburg. (Year 1144, 23 January.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, II, p. 187.]

[Col. 0933A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GODESCALC, provost of Baumburg, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The care of the Catholic Church has been entrusted to us by God, the supreme shepherd, for this purpose: that we may love the servants of God with paternal affection and may strive all the more by every means to foster their devotion, inasmuch as they are known to adhere more ardently to ecclesiastical discipline and to the rules of the holy Fathers. For then is apostolic service pleasingly offered to God, if the wholesome institution, strictness, and order of holy places are preserved in the purity of religious observance through our protection.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the church of Blessed Margaret, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of the present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, obtain with God’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 0933B–C] Among these we have judged the following to be named expressly: Scirnisca; the estate of Rota and one mill; Homdorf; Windeberc with its appurtenances; and the estates granted to you by Count Berengar and other faithful servants of God for the sake of devotion.

The provost then in office may also, with the counsel of the community or of the sounder part of the brethren, choose before God an advocate whom he judges useful and necessary for that place; and, if the advocate proves useless, remove him, as is known to have been ordained and confirmed in writing by our predecessors of good memory, Paschal, Honorius, and Innocent. Furthermore, no cleric or layperson whatsoever may exact tithes from you on the produce of your labour which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the fodder of your animals.

When you, the present provost of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common counsel or the sounder part of the counsel, foresee as to be elected according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. [Col. 0933D] We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be kept whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted—while preserving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

As a token of this protection received from the apostolic see, you shall pay annually to us and our successors one gold *nisant*. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts hereafter rashly to contravene this page of our constitution and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him recognize himself as guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But to all who preserve what is just for the same place, may there be the peace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0934A–B] Given at Rome through the hand of Baro, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1144 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius II.

### XCIV. To the monks of Saint Pancras.—He declares void the charters through which sons are made successors to their fathers in churches. (Years 1144–1145.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 615.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the prior and monks of Saint Pancras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0934C] Since, by the Lord’s appointment, we have been called to govern the universal Church, we ought both to maintain what nourishes the Church’s integrity and to root out what opposes canonical enactments and appears to introduce a cause of dissolution. We have learned from the tenor of your report that, through the negligence of your predecessors, a corrupt custom was introduced among you: namely, that the sons of those who held your churches, having obtained from our predecessors confirmation concerning the churches to be held as . . . by their fathers, wish, through blameworthy collusion, to possess those churches by hereditary right; and, under the pretext of such confirmations and with some pension retained, fathers appoint their sons as successors.

Since by this both the vigour of canonical discipline is impaired and temporal losses result to you, we judge void the aforesaid grants or confirmations, thus obtained by the prior of those places, or even from the apostolic see, with the truth concealed. By the authority of the present letter we grant you permission, notwithstanding those grants or confirmations, to choose suitable persons for your churches and present those chosen to the bishop, so that, after receiving the care of souls, they may answer to him concerning spiritual matters and to you concerning temporal matters. [Col. 0934D–0935A] Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let that person know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Velletri, Kalends of January [1 January].

### XCV. To *** while he was still a cardinal priest.

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 617.]

Concerning the abuses and acts of abuse that take place at this time in the Church of God, reverend brother, you have recorded much in your letter, and could have recorded more; for, sins demanding it, far more things occur in this perilous age than in the days of our fathers. They are so much the freer and more frequent because there are none, or very few, who climb up against them and stand in battle on the day of the Lord by setting themselves as a wall for the house of Israel.

Therefore we believe that Antichrist has either already come or will come soon; as is read in Job, want goes before his face—want, that is, of virtues and of virtuous persons—so that he may the more freely do his will, because scarcely anyone exists to oppose him. Yet meanwhile, good brother, your religious devotion, instructed from infancy in sacred letters, does not fail to know what you ought to do. But I see that this is what I must do—and would that I do it!—and I advise you, as my dearest brother, to avoid, with the Lord’s help, the abominations that are done and to grieve over those who perform them, so that the man clothed in linen of whom Ezekiel speaks may mark the *Tau* upon our forehead and we may not be slain.

[Col. 0935]

## Eighteen miscellaneous letters to Pope Lucius.

### I. Letter of King Alfonso of Portugal to Pope Lucius II, by which he makes his kingdom tributary to the Roman Church.

(BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, folio edition, vol. III, p. 78.) To LUCIUS II, A., king of Portugal.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Proclaimed king in the year 1139. MARIANA, book X, chapter 17.]

[Col. 0935B]

Recognizing that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were granted by our Lord Jesus Christ to blessed Peter, I have resolved to have him as my patron and advocate before almighty God, so that I may feel his help and counsel in my present needs, and may be able, through the assistance of his merits, to attain the rewards of eternal blessedness. Therefore I, Afonso, by God’s grace king of Portugal, through the hand of Lord G., cardinal deacon and legate of the apostolic see, rendered homage to my lord and father Pope Innocent; and I also offer my land to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church under an annual payment of four ounces of gold, on this condition and understanding: that all who shall hold my land after my death shall annually pay the same tribute to blessed Peter; and that I, as the proper knight of blessed Peter and of the Roman pontiff, may *habeam* (“have”; its object is unstated) both in my own person and in my land, and also in those matters which pertain to the dignity and honour of my land and to the defence and support of the apostolic see; and that I may never receive in my land the authority of any ecclesiastical or secular lordship except that of the apostolic see or of one sent from its side.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] See Innocent III, book I, letters 99, 441, 448, 447; book XIV, letter 59; book XV, letter 24.]

The charter of offering and protection was made on the Ides of December [13 December], in the era 1180 [A.D. 1142]. I, the aforesaid Afonso, king of Portugal, ordered this charter to be made and willingly confirm it with my own hand before suitable witnesses.

[Col. 0935D–0936B]

[Note: [Col. 0936D] For the pope’s reply, see above under no. 26.]

I, John, bishop of Braga, confirm. I, B., bishop of Coimbra, confirm. And I, Peter, bishop of Portugal, confirm.

### II. Ulger, bishop of Angers, to Pope Lucius II.—He commends Odo, dean of Saint Martin at Tours.

(DUCHESNE, *Hist. Franc. script.*, IV, 769.)

To LUCIUS, supreme pontiff by God’s election, his most beloved lord and lord of all, ULGER, by his permission called, though unworthy, bishop of Angers, and his servant: dutiful submission and devoted obedience.

[Col. 0936C] We presume, by prayers and supplication, to entreat the beloved feet of your most sacred majesty that, when the venerable dean of Blessed Martin, Lord Odo, an eminent man, comes into your presence, you may receive him gently and kindly through the mercy of your benevolence; turn his heavy troubles into joy; and send him back to us and to his own place with the fullness of your peace and favour, as befits your serenity.

Before you, to whom it is ruinous to lie, we testify that when we had come to the aforesaid church and entered the chapter, which was then most fully attended, we found among those brethren no one who cried out against the above-named dean or disparaged him in any respect. Rather, they greatly sympathized with him concerning this rebuke of yours; and, unanimously commending him to you with one concordant voice, they promised all their knowledge, all their power, and that they would come, if necessary, to the knees of your mercy and do in his defence whatever the devoted goodwill of good sons ought to do in defending their good patron. [Col. 0936D–0937A] Tested and religious persons pray for him with us—persons whom he himself is accustomed to support with counsel and aid with help. May God preserve you, the desired father and governor of his Church, long living for the whole world. Father, we pray for you and cause prayers to be offered for you both in chapters and in assemblies.

### III. The same writer to the same recipient.—He commends Robert, prior of Saint Cosmas at Tours.

(DUCHESNE, *ibid.*)

[Col. 0937B]

To LUCIUS, supreme pontiff by God’s election, his most reverend father, lord of all, and lord, ULGER, called bishop of Angers, servant of your holiness: devoted submission and dutiful obedience.

Lord Robert, venerable prior of Saint Cosmas at Tours, indeed a man of great religious devotion, has decided to set out for the threshold of your mercy on the affairs and necessities of the poor Church over which, by God’s authorship, he presides and for which he has laboured greatly. Therefore, trusting in the accustomed mercy of your kindness, we presume by entreaty to beg at the feet of your Majesty that, when he comes to your knees, you may receive him kindly, effectively hear the petitions which he may lay before your clemency as worthy of hearing, and send him back to his own place joyful from the serenity of your countenance.

[Col. 0937C] As soon as I can, I shall send to your fatherhood the clerk Peloquin, your servant and my official, with tokens of my service, so that, in my stead, by seeing your desired face and reporting to me your wished-for well-being, he may fulfil my longing. For, hindered by illness and old age, I am unable, dearest lord, to come to you. May the mercy of Christ preserve you long alive upon earth, most gracious father of his Church. Farewell.

### IV. The Church of Liège to Pope Lucius.—Concerning a new heresy and Americ, converted from it, whom it commends to him.

(MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 777.)

[Col. 0937D]

To the reverend lord and father L., by God’s grace supreme pontiff, the Church of Liège: faithful prayers and the obedience of due submission in Christ.

As we suppose, and as the matter itself makes clear, divine providence placed the Roman See in the citadel of the Catholic Church so that, through its foresight, protection might be provided for its members, and those to whom rising wars threaten destruction might have in it a refuge. Therefore we bring to your fatherhood the newly discovered snares of the ancient enemies, since to you has been entrusted the care of all the churches, so that by your diligence the efforts of those may be frustrated who, under the appearance of religion, lead the souls of the simple into error; and so that the holy Church of God may be strengthened in the integrity of the one faith, which has been wounded in many places, as is now known to have happened among us.

From Monte Guimari [Note: [Col. 0938D] Perhaps Monte Limarii, a town in France in the Dauphiné, at the foot of a hill, not far from the Rhône, around which Peter of Bruys, in the time of Lucius II, disseminated his errors, which have great affinity with those described in this letter.], the name of a certain village in France, a heresy is known to have spread through various parts of the world. It is so varied and manifold that it seems impossible to be comprehended under one definite name. Some of its followers among us have been detected, convicted, and have confessed. A disorderly crowd decided to seize them and hand them over to the fire; but, through God’s merciful favor, hoping better things of them, we scarcely rescued almost all of them from immediate punishment. One of these is the man whom we have taken care to send to your fatherhood at his own request.

This heresy is distinguished by different ranks. For it has “hearers,” who are initiated into the error; it has “believers,” who have already been deceived; it has its own “Christians”; it has priests; and it has other prelates, as we too have. The blasphemies of this accursed heresy are these: it denies that sins are remitted in baptism; it regards the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood as empty; it asserts that nothing is conferred by the laying on of a bishop’s hand; it believes that no one receives the Holy Spirit unless preceded by the merits of good works; it condemns marriage; it proclaims that the Catholic Church exists only among themselves; and it judges every oath to be a crime.

Yet those who are followers of this wickedness deceitfully communicate in our sacraments, as a covering for their evil. This Americus was still one of their hearers; and we have therefore sent him to you, so that, by your judgment, he may make satisfaction to God and to His holy Church, and fulfil the vow which he made to the blessed apostles when his life was in danger. For, as he says, he vowed that, if he could escape through their merits and prayers, he would devoutly visit their thresholds, in order to render them thanks for the preservation of his safety [Col. 0938D]. We have distributed the other participants in this error among religious houses, awaiting from you what ought to be done for their correction.

Moreover, we inform your charity that, according to what we have learned from those apprehended by us, all the cities of the kingdom of France and of our own country are, in large measure, infected with the poison of this error. Let the prudence of your fatherhood therefore take care that this poison does not spread more deeply, but is burned away by the cautery of salutary diligence, so that it may perish. Farewell.

## In the Year of the Lord 1143. William of Malmesbury, Monk

[Col. 0939]

## Notice

(From the preface of Dr. Georg Waitz, public professor at Göttingen, to *Excerpts from the Historical Writings of William of Malmesbury*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. X, p. 449.)

Among writers on English affairs who flourished in the twelfth century, the first place belongs to William, monk of Malmesbury: a man distinguished by his love of letters, industry, and learning, who repeatedly undertook to set forth both domestic and foreign events, and thereby earned great praise among posterity. Florentius of Worcester, Henry of Huntingdon, and Symeon of Durham were guided by the same purpose in this century; and writers of a later age, for the most part following in William’s footsteps—Roger of Wendover and others—embellished their books with narratives of events carried out in France, Germany, Italy, and the Holy Land.

William, having devoted himself to letters from boyhood, acquired no ordinary skill in writing; and soon, attracted by a great love of history, he undertook to compose three or four historical books, besides Lives of saints and certain theological and philosophical works. Let us hear him speak on this matter himself [Note: [Col. 0939] *Gesta*, book II, prologue.]:

> “It is a long time since, both through my parents’ care and through my own diligence, I became accustomed to books. This pleasure seized me from childhood; this attraction grew up with me in my equal years. For I had been so instructed by my father that, if I inclined to different pursuits, there would be loss to my soul and danger to my reputation. Therefore, mindful of the saying, ‘Desire whatever is necessary,’ I compelled my youth willingly to desire what I could not honorably refuse to desire.
>
> “I devoted effort indeed to many branches of learning, but differently to different ones. Logic, which arms speech, I merely tasted by hearing alone. Natural science, which treats bodily health, I grasped somewhat more closely. But I explored the parts of ethics to the very marrow; I rise to reverence its majesty, because it lies open to students in itself and forms minds for right living. History above all—because, seasoning character with a certain pleasant knowledge of deeds, it stimulates readers by examples to pursue good things or avoid evil ones.
>
> “And so, after I had assembled at my own expense several historians of foreign peoples, I continued in my familiar leisure to inquire whether anything memorable concerning our own people might be found for posterity. Hence, not content with ancient writings, I myself also began to write—not in order to display my learning, which is almost nonexistent, but in order to draw into the light things hidden beneath a heap of antiquity. Therefore, rejecting flying opinions, I collected chronicles far and wide; but, I confess, I accomplished almost nothing by this industry. For, having gone through everything, I remained poor in knowledge, finding nothing to read before I ceased to have material for reading.”

Three historical works composed by William survive: the *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, the *Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, and the *Modern History*. Besides these, he himself mentions a *Chronicle* arranged in three books, which is now lost [Note: [Col. 0939] Prologue of the *Modern History*, addressed to Robert, son of King Henry and Earl of Gloucester: “I have not neglected to add to my narrative many things concerning the deeds of your father of pre-eminent memory, both in the fifth book of the royal acts and in the three little books to which I gave the title *Chronicle*. Now your Serenity desires that those things which have happened in England in modern times . . . should be committed to posterity.” That chronicle perhaps narrated the history of the years 1120–1128 [Col. 0940]. For in that year the *Deeds of the Kings* ends, while the *Modern History* begins from that point.].

William appears to have completed the greater part of these works before he had fully reached his fortieth year [Note: [Col. 0940] Hardy cites from William’s unpublished commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah (*Preface*, p. I, no. 3) that these works were written in his fortieth year, and that William there professes that he had delighted in writing history in the days of his youth.]. But he did not afterward abandon this concern.
