For, although he wrote the *Deeds of the Kings of the English* between 1119 and 1124, he carried the *Modern History* as far as the year 1142 [Col. 0941], and had intended to continue it further [Note: [Col. 0941] Book III ends with these words: “But these matters will, God willing, be more fully explained in the following volume.” In other manuscripts, in place of these words, after some additions, there occurs the following of the same sense: “Yet I desire to pursue these matters more fully, if ever, by God’s gift, I receive the truth from those who were present.”]. It is probable that death prevented him from doing so.

Besides this, almost nothing is known of William’s life. He seems to have spent his years in the monastery of Malmesbury, where he first held the office of librarian and afterward that of precentor; the dignity of abbot was offered to him but not accepted. Yet he also gathered books and information in other English churches for use in writing history. He frequently associated with men conspicuous in rank, and recorded on slips whatever they told him concerning affairs transacted abroad [Note: [Col. 0941] Compare what is read below in ch. 170: “I shall tell what I remember hearing in childhood from a certain monk of our house, Aquitanian by birth, advanced in age, and a physician by profession”; ch. 263: “I heard it on the serious testimony of one who swore that he had heard these things from the mouth of Hugh, abbot of Cluny”; ch. 290: “I heard a most truthful man relating”; [Col. 0942] ch. 293: “I shall tell what a reverend man related to me as having happened in that same place.”]. And, although he says that he despised “flying reports,” he seems to have trusted them too greatly [Note: [Col. 0942] Thus in ch. 167 he says: “It will not, I think, be absurd if we commit to writing what flies about in everyone’s mouths.” Compare, however, ch. 194: “At this point there occur great miracles reported concerning that man—which I omit because I do not wish to exceed the reader’s judgment”; and the words in which he boasts at the end of the *Deeds*, ch. 445: “For I have followed the true law of history, and have never included anything except what I learned from trustworthy reporters or writers.”].

Although William earned great praise by his elegant and ornate description of his people’s ancient history and by his sufficiently faithful and candid narration of events of his own time, many nevertheless considered him blameworthy because he committed miraculous and fabulous matters to memory with excessive credulity. Nor indeed can it be denied that much is read in Malmesbury which departs far from true history, especially in those portions of the book where he touched upon foreign kingdoms. In these passages he generally employed not written books or other trustworthy monuments, but followed popular rumor and the stories of monks and other persons—perhaps with the intention that, by setting such attractions before them, clergy and laity might be enticed to read books.

This expectation certainly did not deceive him. For these matters especially commended themselves to writers of later times; they were copied by many and more widely disseminated. Nor will they be altogether displeasing to us. For if they contribute little to true history, they serve to make known the traditions and popular narratives circulated among peoples in the Middle Ages.

[Col. 0941]

## Literary Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 152.)

[Col. 0941A] William Somerset of Malmesbury, a monk of the Benedictine order from the house of Maildulf (*Maildulphesbury*), librarian and precentor of Meldunensis or Malmesbury, learned in prose and verse and highly deserving in the history of his country, or of the English. Of his books, Leland says in ch. 166:

> “Whenever I take them in hand—and I do so both very frequently and very willingly—I am compelled again and again to admire the man’s diligence, felicity, and judgment. His diligence, because everywhere he shows that he has read an immense number of good authors; his felicity, because, emulating their elegance and vigor, he beautifully expresses them in his own nocturnal studies; and finally his judgment, because he brings many things rashly written by others back to the anvil, and, having brought them back, restores them to light and truth.”

He was still alive in the year of Christ 1143, having promised more. His published writings are as follows:

*Royal Acts*, or *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*, from the first coming of the Saxons, around the year 449, to the eighteenth year of Henry I, or A.D. 1127 [Col. 0941B], in five books, addressed to Robert, Earl of Gloucester, son of King Henry.

*Modern History*, in three books, from A.D. 1127 to the year 1143, addressed to the same Robert.

*On the Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, to approximately the year 1125, in four books. The first concerns the bishops and monasteries of Canterbury and Rochester. The second concerns the bishops and monasteries of London, of the East Angles, and of the West Saxons. The third concerns those of York, Hexham, Whithorn—Candida Casa—Lindisfarne, and Durham. The fourth concerns those of Worcester, Hereford, Leicester, Dorchester or Lincoln, and Ely [Col. 0942A]. These writings of William appeared in the collection *The Principal Historians of England after Bede*, edited by Henry Savile, London, 1596; and Frankfurt, printed by the Wechel press, 1601, folio.

Henry Wharton first published Book V *On the Bishops of the English* at the beginning of vol. II of *Anglia Sacra*, London, 1691, folio; and Thomas Gale published it at about the same time among the *Fifteen Writers*, Oxford, 1691, folio, p. 337. Besides several charters concerning the antiquities of Malmesbury, it contains the *Life of Aldhelm, Bishop of Sherborne*, of which Bale had seen only an epitome; Mabillon had published it in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century IV, p. 726.

*Life of St Wulfstan, Bishop of Worcester*, addressed to the brethren of Worcester, in three books: in vol. II of *Anglia Sacra*, pp. 241–270; and with notes by Henschenius, vol. VI, 25 May, p. 79.

[Col. 0942B] *Book on the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury*, published by Gale in the aforementioned collection of fifteen writers, p. 289.

Letter to Peter, monk of Meldunensis, prefixed to John Scotus Eriugena’s five books *On the Division of Natures*, and published by Thomas Gale from the manuscript of Thuanus before Scotus’s books, Oxford, 1681, folio.

William composed many other works not yet brought to light, such as those mentioned by Leland, ch. 166, Bale, II.73, and Pits, p. 209:

[Col. 0943A] *On the Sequence of the Evangelists*, in fifteen books, in various kinds of verse.

Commentaries on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, in four books; manuscript in the Cottonian Library.

*On the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, four books. *On the Miracles of St Andrew.*

*On the Miracles of Native Saints.*

Epitome of the history of Haimo, monk of Fleury, from Justinian to Charlemagne; manuscript in the library of Balliol College, Oxford, and in the Bodleian.

Genealogy of Henry II, King of England.

Itinerary of John, abbot of Meldunensis, who journeyed to Rome with Peter, monk of Meldunensis; according to Leland, plainly full of many memorable matters.

*On the Antiquity of Glastonbury Monastery*, addressed to Henry of Blois, bishop of Winchester. Bale calls it *Antiquities of Glastonbury*; manuscripts are in the library of St Benedict’s College, Cambridge.

[Col. 0944A] *Life of Indract, petty king of Ireland*, who was a disciple of St Dunstan.

*Life of St Patrick*, in two books, addressed to the monks of Glastonbury. *Life of St Benignus*; *Life of St Dunstan*, in two books.

*On the People of the Wydeni or Vugdeni.* Three books of *Chronicles*, which he mentions in the preface to the *Modern History*.

Sermons and Letters.

Henry Wharton cites a passage from an abbreviation of Amalarius’s books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, manuscript in the Lambeth Library, at p. 360 of the supplement to Ussher’s work *On Sacred and Vernacular Scriptures*. Peter Allix published the preface, not very fair to Rabanus Maurus, addressed to Robert his friend (whether this was a different person from the Earl of Gloucester, I do not know), for whose favor he undertook this labor, and the epilogue of the first and last book, at the end of the preface to John of Paris’s *Determination on the Mode of Existence of Christ’s Body in the Sacrament of the Altar*. London, 1686, octavo.

[Col. 0943]

## Dedicatory Epistle of the Most Learned Henry Savile

(*Principal Writers of English Annals after Bede*, London, 1596, folio.)

To the Most Serene and Most Mighty Princess Elizabeth, Queen of England, France, and Ireland.

Certain persons have described a part of our history not badly; but that anyone has hitherto existed who has embraced in writing the whole body with that fidelity and dignity which the greatness of the undertaking demanded is plainly not the case. For Polydore, being an Italian, a stranger to our affairs, and—what is the principal point—neither engaged in public affairs nor otherwise a man of great judgment or talent, sampling a few things from many and for the most part accepting falsehoods as truths, left us a history which is both otherwise faulty and written with remarkable thinness and barrenness.

Our native historians, drawn from the dregs of the people, while striving to adorn the majesty of so great a work, contaminated it with the most foul absurdities. Thus it has happened, by I know not what misfortune of this island, that your ancestors, most serene Queen—very great men, who embraced under their dominion a great part of our world and easily surpassed all the kings of their time in the glory of their deeds—lie unknown and concealed, as though deprived of the light of great minds.

While I sought a remedy for this evil, I was neither so free in mind nor equipped with those resources and, as it were, instruments for writing history that I might construct from its foundations a work which would endure and transmit the memory of those times to distant descendants. Yet I willingly did what I could: I resolved to draw from neglect, squalor, and dust, and to bring first into the light, the most ancient authors of our affairs—not indeed eloquent men, but faithful interpreters of deeds—so that others, who possessed both leisure and talent, might have these records of our affairs at hand, as sources from which they might take what was needed for the construction of so great a work.

Among them, since William of Malmesbury holds the foremost place both for trustworthiness of narration and maturity of judgment—a man, learned in letters for those times, who has woven together the history of approximately seven hundred years with such faithfulness and diligence that he seems almost alone among our countrymen to have fulfilled the historian’s office—I took care that he should above all be drawn from obscurity and dedicated to your most august name. Thus he who once dispelled the darkness of several centuries by the light of his talent may now in turn, restored to life, derive light and splendor from Your Most Serene Majesty.

Nearest to him, though perhaps nearest at a long interval, are the historian of Huntingdon and Hoveden, authors especially good and diligent, and most truthful guides to earlier times. To these we added Ingulph, greatly desired by very many who thirst for our antiquities; and Elward, who is related to your ancestors by a close degree of kinship, on account of his nobility no less than his antiquity.

I shall not now undertake, in a longer discourse, to show why I wished this small work of whatever worth to appear particularly under your name; nor shall I adorn with verbal magnificence a matter slight in itself. For if, as we have learned from philosophers, the condition of gifts differs from that of debts—because in gifts great regard must be had for those to whom they are offered, whereas even the smallest debts must be paid to the greatest persons—what was it right for me to do in this matter? Long since carried away by the divine virtues of your Majesty into your service and admiration, you have moreover bound me by your supreme benefits so firmly that I most willingly acknowledge myself and all that is mine to be yours, not only in use and enjoyment, but even in possession and legal bond [Col. 0945].

And indeed, if we reason correctly, to whom ought I rather to offer the deeds of Britons, Saxons, and Normans than to Your Majesty? You have inherited by hereditary right, united in one whole, all the separate dominions which each of them possessed; and you have also embraced in a wholly heroic spirit all the virtues of them all. You alone, through so many years amid the common tempests of all Europe, have poured the most blessed tranquillity upon your most sweet native land. You alone, finally, have taught us by your example what supreme goodness can accomplish in supreme power. But these matters belong to another work and another time.

Meanwhile I most humbly entreat Your Most Serene Majesty that you may deign henceforth to embrace with your royal kindness, and protect with your authority, the man whom until now you have been pleased to adorn with your most ample benefits. May God, best and greatest, preserve Your Majesty safe for us and for the Christian commonwealth for as long as possible.

Most devoted servant of Your Most Serene Majesty,  
Henry Savile.

## The Deeds of the Kings of the English and the Modern History of William of Malmesbury, Monk

Edited from the authority of manuscript codices by Thomas Duffus Hardy.

(London, at the Society’s expense, 1840, octavo, 2 vols.)

[Col. 0945]

## Preface

What we know concerning the life of William, monk of Malmesbury, and the parents from whom he was born [Note: [Col. 0945] Leland, Cave, Tanner, Wharton, and others assert that his family name was Somerset, but their opinion rests on no firm authority.], is known from no other source than what he himself reports here and there. In Book I of the *Deeds of the Kings*, he seems to indicate that his father was Norman by race and his mother Saxon, saying: “Because I draw blood from both peoples”; and near the end of Book II: “Nor, in saying this, do I derogate from the valor of the Normans, to whom I owe loyalty both on account of birth and on account of benefits.”

Nothing is certain concerning the year in which he was born [Note: [Col. 0945] In his Commentary on Jeremiah, Malmesbury observes that “long before, in the days of his youth, he had occupied himself, as if in play, with writing history, and that he had then reached his fortieth year.” Elsewhere he recounts certain events that occurred in the days of King Henry, from which it may be inferred that Henry had already died. Now, assuming that the words “long before” indicate an interval of ten years, and since his histories of kings and bishops were completed in 1125, the matters reported here must have been written around 1135, the time when Henry departed this life. William would thus have to be placed as born around 1095 or 1096. Sharp reasons thus; but there is no sufficiently firm ground for assigning Malmesbury’s birth to either of these years. The hypothesis that King Henry had died very recently, from which the above deduction follows, scarcely appears to be established by the evidence adduced. Yet this much is clear: the author of a history upon which the most eminent critics of the present age have lavished the highest encomia for learning and judgment completed the principal part of his work when scarcely more than twenty-five years old.].

Malmesbury seems to have spent the greater part of his life within the cloisters of the monastery from which he took his name, devoting to letters and learning all the time not spent in religious and monastic duties. Yet he visited the principal monasteries of the kingdom in order to collect books [Note: [Col. 0947] Malmesbury elsewhere states that he enriched his monastery’s library with no small number of books; and he speaks of others that he had seen at Canterbury, Bury St Edmunds, and elsewhere (Gale, III, pp. 298, 376).]. The extraordinary keenness of his intellect and excellence of learning are attested by the titles of no fewer than twenty different works, all of which he composed before his fiftieth year [Note: [Col. 0947] Here is a catalogue of Malmesbury’s works; Tanner ascribes several others to him: 1. *Deeds of the Kings of the English.* 2. *Modern History.* 3. *Deeds of the Bishops.* 4. *Passion of St Indract the Martyr.* 5. *On the Life of St Aldhelm.* 6. *On the Life of St Dunstan, Archbishop.* 7. *Life of St Patrick.* 8. *Miracles of St Benignus.* 9. *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury.* 10. *Life of St Wulfstan, Bishop of Worcester.* 11. *Chronicles.* 12. *Miracles of St Ælfgifu.* 13. *Itinerary of John, Abbot of Meldunensis, toward Rome.* 14. *Exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah.* 15. *On the Miracles of the Virgin Mary.* 16. *On the Sequence of the Evangelists, in every kind of verse.* 17. *On the Miracles of Blessed Andrew.* 18. *Abbreviation of Amalarius on Ecclesiastical Offices.* 19. *Epitome of the History of Haimo, Monk of Fleury, from Justinian to Charlemagne.* 20. *On the Sayings of Philosophers.*].

His fame having spread widely, he was frequently asked—by the monks not of one monastery alone—to undertake the task of writing the history of their patrons or the foundation of their monastery. Yet no one among the men of Malmesbury honored his memory with sufficient veneration to leave a written memorial of the life of so great a man [Note: [Col. 0947] Leland, who seems to have collected everything relating to him, observes indignantly that among the monks of Malmesbury the memory of their most eminent member had almost perished.]. The time of his death, like that of his birth, is uncertain. But because his final work ends abruptly amid the events of the year 1142, a year of the greatest and most serious importance in his age, it is rather generally supposed that he died in that year or the following one.

These few facts contain all that is known of the life of a man who easily surpassed all ancient writers of English history in maturity of judgment and his sure knowledge of events.

The two principal and by far most important works of William of Malmesbury—the *Deeds of the Kings of the English* and the *Modern History*—are published in these volumes. The former comprises five books; the latter occupies three.

The first book of the *Deeds of the Kings of the English* briefly touches the history of Great Britain from the time when the Romans took possession of it until their expulsion; it then continues the contemporary history of the kingdoms of the Saxon rulers, from that people’s first arrival in England to the time of Ecgberht, who “restrained the separate kingdoms by greatness of spirit and, joining them under one dominion, summoned them to a unified sovereignty.”

The second book sets out the history of the kingdom of the West Saxons, following the succession of Anglo-Saxon and Anglo-Danish rulers, as far as Harold’s death and the arrival of the Normans.

The third book is wholly devoted to the reign of William I.

The fourth and fifth books bring the history down to the year 1120. The fourth also contains an important account of the first Christian expedition against the Saracens, together with a vivid portrayal of the leaders marked with the cross.

At what age Malmesbury either began or completed the *Deeds of the Kings of the English* cannot be determined with certainty. It is conjectured, not without some plausibility, that he composed this narrative between 1114 and 1123; that he subsequently reworked it at various times, enlarging it with several important additions, and sometimes changing its style and manner of speech; and that he occasionally deleted what he had previously admitted and substituted other material [Note: [Col. 0947] An opinion has prevailed among some that Malmesbury at first carried this work no further than the third book. The editor has encountered no manuscript codex containing only these three books, and doubts whether the first three books were published by Malmesbury before the whole work had been completed. Sharp, however, holds the opposite view, but has produced no proof for his opinion. What Malmesbury writes in the prologue to the fourth book strongly supports the conclusion drawn by Sharp: “I know,” says Malmesbury, “that it appears foolish to many that I have applied my pen to writing the deeds of kings of our own time, saying that in writings of this kind truth is often shipwrecked and falsehood is supported, since the evils of the present are spoken of dangerously, and its good things flatteringly. Hence, they say, because all things now incline more toward worse rather than better, the writer passes over manifest evils through fear, and, if good things do not exist, invents them for applause. There are others who, measuring us by their own idleness, consider us unequal to so great a task, and pollute this study with malicious disparagement. Therefore, long ago, struck either by the reasoning of the former or by the disdain of the latter, I had withdrawn into leisure, willingly acquiescing in silence. But, when I had for some time rested free from indolence, my customary love of study again pulled my ear and set hand to work. My friends’ urgings were added, that I should carry my work further; and I am now sufficiently disposed to accomplish this.” Another matter also occurs which similarly supports Sharp’s opinion. Sir Thomas Philipps possesses a twelfth-century manuscript (MS Philipps, no. 237), once belonging to the monastery of Camhay in Normandy, which contains, among other things, an epitome of the first three books of the work entitled *Deeds of the Kings of the English*. Jerome Commelin also had a not dissimilar but fuller text (Heidelberg, 1587), which he printed as an unknown author’s continuation of Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*. The manuscript used by Commelin contained much that is absent from Sir Thomas Philipps’s codex; but the additional material is found in none of the surviving manuscripts of the *Deeds of the Kings of the English*. There seems no doubt that Malmesbury composed the fourth and fifth books of this work at the request of Robert, Earl of Gloucester, to whom he addressed the dedicatory epistle. It is no small source of wonder that this dedication, which applies to the whole work, occurs in most manuscripts at the end of the third book. It is clear that the prefaces to each book were written after the work’s completion; words occurring here and there in these prefaces strongly support the opinion of those who hold that the first three books, although evidently written before the others, were not published until the whole work had been completed.], earnestly asking those who knew more fully than he did to communicate it to him, if only to be added in the margin of his work.

The *Modern History* is thought to be William of Malmesbury’s last offspring. At its beginning there is a retrospective, concise account of the final part of the reign of William I; the history then extends to 1142, the year in which the book ends. It is plainly evident that this work was begun after the death of King William I and carried down to the year 1142. Although the portion completed is entire in itself, it was nevertheless left unfinished. The narrative concludes with a brief account of Empress Matilda’s flight from Oxford; but the author had intended to review other matters more fully [Col. 0949], and this was not granted him. It was fortunate, however, that he revised the whole work in the form in which the present edition stands, and illustrated it with several important corrections and additions.

From the time of Bede to the age of Malmesbury—that is, through the space of four centuries—the history of the English consists only of brief and barren annals, in which there is no critical examination of historical documents and no weighing of events in regard to the state of political government. As Malmesbury tells his readers, he was the first after Bede to strive to rise to a reputation higher than that of a mere annalist and to undertake the writing of a continuous history of England:

> “Bede, a man most learned and least proud, set forth the deeds of the English from their arrival in Britain down to his own days in plain and pleasing speech. After him, I think, you will scarcely find anyone who has applied himself to weaving the histories of that people in Latin prose. Let others see whether they have already found, or will hereafter find, anything of those matters; our labor, though it has kept anxious watch in inquiry, has so far spent its effort in vain. There are indeed certain traces of antiquity, arranged year by year from the Lord’s Incarnation in chronicle fashion and in the native tongue. By their means, whatever times passed after that man have deserved to struggle free from the old age of oblivion.
>
> “For Æthelweard, a distinguished and illustrious man, who undertook to arrange those chronicles in Latin, it is better to pass over in silence; were it not tedious, I could set forth what purpose he had in mind. Nor has the work of Lord Eadmer, polished with the sober elegance of his language, escaped our notice: beginning with King Edgar, he rapidly sketched the times down to William I; then, ranging more freely, he supplied students with an extensive and necessary history down to the death of Archbishop Anselm [Note: [Col. 0949] Eadmer had brought his history to the death of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, when Malmesbury published his *Deeds of the Kings of the English*. He afterward continued it to the death of Archbishop Ralph in 1122.].
>
> “Thus, since he has deemed two hundred and twenty-three years from the time of Bede unworthy of any record, the course of time limps in the middle without the support of letters. Therefore, both from love of my country and from the authority of those urging me, I desired to repair the interrupted sequence of times, and to season what was written barbarously with Roman salt. And, in order that the matter may proceed more orderly, I shall cull some things from what Bede, so often to be named, has said; I shall touch upon a few points, and bid farewell to many.”

The principal sources from which Malmesbury drew his history may be divided into three classes:

First: authors and documents still surviving, such as Gildas, Nennius, Bede, the Saxon Chronicles and Laws, Asser, Æthelweard, Eadmer, Osbern, Goscelin, Hariulf, and other ancient writers; original charters, letters, and other documents [Note: [Col. 0949] It should not be inferred from this that Malmesbury always inserted original charters or letters word for word; he merely abridges them, although entire documents are sometimes inserted.].

Second: materials proceeding from authorities now lost, such as metrical compositions, historical traditions, charters, letters, and biographical notices.

Third: his own knowledge of events of which he had been a witness, or which he had learned from trustworthy witnesses.

Since Malmesbury intended to give a faithful and candid account of events, he gathered together whatever he was able to collect. Yet more than once he confesses that the outcome of his labors and studies by no means answered to his intention. Thus he says:

> “If anyone, captivated by affection, reads these things also, let him know that, concerning the past, I affirm nothing as true except the sequence of years; responsibility for the trustworthiness of the statements will rest with the authors. But whatever I have added concerning more recent times I either saw myself or heard from trustworthy men. In either case, however, I do not greatly value the judgment of contemporaries; I shall have, I hope, after the death of affection and envy among posterity, if not the title of eloquence, at least the testimony of industry.”

What he drew from writers older than himself he so intermingled with his own annotations that they can scarcely be separated from the narrative. Whatever seemed necessary to him for elucidating the character and customs of peoples in the different periods of their history—whether concerning the administration and laws of the kingdom, or the arts—he sets forth with the highest credit to his ability. But where material is not abundant, or historical facts are of no importance, he enlivens his work with anecdotes,

> [Note: [Col. 0949] In one place, after introducing various matters, he promises that he will not abuse his readers’ patience any longer; although, unless he sets too high a value on himself, variety in anecdotes should be tedious to no one, unless he be so morose as to emulate Cato’s stern brow.]

often describing in vivid colours the outstanding features of individual character, and with remarkable skill sketching even the smallest actions of those about him.

His History resembles a dramatic play, in which a complete account of events is offered, the tedium of uninterrupted narration being removed. He dedicated his work to his friend and patron Robert, Earl of Gloucester, the illegitimate son of King Henry I. Robert, skilled in law and warfare, burned with an exceptional zeal for letters; he is said to have been most scrupulous in justice. For, when all men were hostile to Matilda and Stephen, had he aspired to the kingdom the way was certainly open; but he judged it better to stand by loyalty and his oath. Near the end of the work entitled *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, Malmesbury addresses him thus:

> “You foster letters in such a manner that, although you are burdened with so great a weight of occupations, you nevertheless steal away for yourselves certain hours in which you can either read yourselves or listen to others reading. Thus you regulate the eminence of your fortune with worthy moderation: you neither put military service behind letters, nor, like some men, spit upon letters for the sake of military service. In this too the wonder of your learning is evident: because, while you love books, you show with what eager marrow you have drunk in their fountain. Many things, indeed, are desired even when they are not possessed; no one will love philosophy unless he has imbibed it to utter satiety.”

Malmesbury asks that it not be held against him that his narrative often passes beyond the bounds of his own country. He himself described it as, so to speak, an epitome of many histories, although, because of the fuller abundance of documents relating to England, he entitled it *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*.

Yet it is greatly to be regretted that in more than one place he inserted legendary tales into history; nevertheless, lest he be accused of invention, he carefully indicates the authorities upon which he relies.

> [Note: [Col. 0949] For example, when speaking of Oswald’s relics, he writes: “Because I am uncertain, from conflicting reports, whether they are preserved to this day in that place, I make no rash assertion. If other historians have recklessly professed anything, let them see to it themselves; let reputation be of less account to me, lest I pronounce anything not worthy of complete belief.”]

Everyone should also remember that, in Malmesbury’s age, miraculous narratives were in everyone’s hands and were intimately bound up with the religious faith of ordinary people. Sharp very rightly observes that it has never occurred to anyone to charge Livy or other historians with fault for recounting the prodigies which they mention in their histories. From certain statements introduced here and there, however, one might infer that William did not wholly credit the miraculous legends which he himself recounts. For when he follows the narrative of the death of Alfred the Great and reports prodigies circulated by tradition—namely, that the soul of the deceased, having resumed its body, wandered by night through the interior of the cathedral church—he writes:

> “The English, through an almost inborn credulity, maintain these foolish tales, like the rest: that they may believe that the corpse of a wicked man runs about after death through the agency of a demon. They plainly borrow this from the pagans, as Virgil says:
>
> ‘After death, such shapes as report says flit about.’”

> [Note: [Col. 0951] *Aeneid*, X.641.]

Yet in one respect these miraculous inventions are not without some usefulness. For frequently, amid so many foolish and absurd things, they contain exquisite and valuable details by which manners and customs are illustrated; and thus a great light is thrown upon the period to which they relate. Moreover, many of these inventions are so distinct from the principal narrative that one may rightly conclude that they were interpolated. In some of the manuscripts which we consulted we found fabricated legends which manuscripts of better quality omit.

That William of Malmesbury was a moderate writer, free from partisan bias, will be plainly evident to all who read his history. He wrote as he thought, praising the good and condemning the bad; while he commends examples of virtue with great esteem, he likewise touches vices with the sharp darts of his satire. Where he speaks of William I, he says:

> “Both Normans and English have written about King William, stirred by different motives. The former have been carried away to excessive praise, proclaiming good and evil alike to the skies; the latter, out of national enmity, have torn their lord to pieces with foul insults. But I, because I derive blood from both peoples, shall preserve this moderation in speaking: deeds well done, so far as I have been able to discover them, I shall openly extol without disguise; deeds wrongly done, so far as my knowledge suffices, I shall touch upon lightly and, as it were, in passing. Thus neither may history be blamed as false, nor may I stamp him with a censor’s mark, since nearly all his acts, if they cannot be praised, can certainly be excused. Therefore I shall willingly and carefully recount such things concerning him as may encourage the inactive, serve as an example to the ready, benefit those now living, and delight those to come . . . . . This is the province that pleases me: to mitigate evils, as far as I can, without injury to truth; and not to praise good things with excessive bombast.”

That Malmesbury was a man of proven integrity and exceptional truthfulness is evident from his works. Where he has uncertain doubts concerning what he writes, even though these things were believed on the common report of his own time, he proceeds cautiously and adduces as guarantors the authors whom he follows for the things he narrates.

His manner of writing, especially in his earlier works, sometimes bears the marks of labour; nevertheless it abounds in elaborate and elegant periods. His work generally flows in a classical manner; and although his style is ordinarily concise, forceful, and vigorous, it must sometimes be judged wordy and obscure. One cannot read through his works without seeing clearly, from his frequent citations and felicitous adaptation of phrases, that he had studied the writings of Roman authors and imbued his own mind with their spirit and graces. More than once he declared that he deliberately varied his style,

> [Note: [Col. 0951] “Moreover, I do not consider it unfitting that discourse should be varied by a many-coloured style.”]

lest the unvarying tenor of one style bring weariness to the reader; and he took the greatest care not to repeat what had once been said.

There is, however, one point in which this eminent author may not undeservedly be censured; but he erred deliberately. Lest his work assume the form of a chronicle, he struck upon the opposite rock, and frequently narrates events without giving their date—whether that in so doing he might imitate Roman writers, or that he might avoid a difficult labour, since there are so many and such great discrepancies concerning chronological dates in the very sources available to Malmesbury. It was not the custom of the Saxons to state in their annals the fixed date of every event. In some manuscripts of those most valuable remains called the Saxon Chronicles, events are presented as though they had occurred in given years, whereas in other manuscripts the same events are assigned to different years. It is now easy to remedy those discrepancies, for they arise because the authors of the chronicles began the year at different times. At Peterborough and in the other monasteries founded by King Æthelwold, they began the year on 25 March; but at Worcester and in monasteries founded by Oswald, on 25 December. Hence, in various manuscripts of the Saxon Chronicles, events occurring between the Feast of the Nativity of the Lord and the Annunciation of his Incarnation are assigned to different years. Asser’s chronology, in the life of Alfred the Great, is more than once erroneous in establishing the beginning of Alfred’s reign. Æthelweard, in the chronology of Saxon princes, is found to differ greatly from the reckoning of the annalists of that same people.

Writers of this kind, taking as the foundation, as it were, of their history the manuscript of the Saxon Chronicle which they had at hand, adhered to it, not having sufficient means for discovering the truth of dates. In every monastery within the respective kingdoms of the Heptarchy, no doubt there was an appointed man who, at the close of the year, committed to writing memorable events which had occurred not only in the kingdom where it was situated but also others which he knew had happened in neighbouring kingdoms. Hence discrepancy in the dates of chronicles necessarily followed, since northerners and southerners are known to have differed as to the beginning of the year. Moreover, in manuscripts of the Saxon Chronicles the dates are represented by Roman numerals; and it could easily happen that, in writing III, IV, or other numbers, one I might be inserted or omitted, by which error the subsequent sequence would be affected. Since this escaped Malmesbury and his contemporaries—or since they cared little for it as a matter of lesser importance—William encountered many obvious discrepancies which he was unable duly to reconcile, and is therefore to be thought to have chosen a narrative method that could easily dispense with chronological dates.

Since he did not wish to be regarded as a mere chronographer, he thought it sufficient for attaining his purpose to establish that something had happened somewhere, and that certain consequences had flowed from it; but whether it happened in the year 800 or 802 he did not care about as a matter of grave importance, since the purpose of his work did not require such minute accuracy. This disregard of dates, however, in certain places where he did state the year of an event, led him into anachronism, and more than once drove him into such error that he placed an effect before its cause. In order that some remedy might be supplied for such a defect, and that what is omitted with respect to the dating of events might be filled in, it was thought proper in the present edition to place an accurate indication of time in the margin whenever it is erroneous or omitted in the author. The foundations upon which we shall generally accomplish this will appear from the notes placed at the foot of the page.

We have already said that Hieronymus Commelinus published at Heidelberg in 1587 a book entitled *Ancient Writers on British Affairs, that is, England, Scotland, and the Neighbouring Islands and Regions*. On page 281 of this work, under the title *Three Books on the Deeds of the English, by an Uncertain Author*, are contained extracts from the first three books of Malmesbury’s work entitled *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*. But it is evident from certain notes, such as “Here not a few things appear to be missing,” “Here too many things appear to be required,” “Some things are lacking,” etc., and especially from the words “by an uncertain author,” that Commelinus was wholly ignorant that the source from which the manuscript compiler had drawn was none other than Malmesbury’s work, *The Deeds of the Kings*.

> [Note: [Col. 0953] The final three chapters, however, of Commelinus’s volume are found in no manuscript of Malmesbury now extant. It therefore seems quite probable that the manuscript compiler from whom Commelinus composed his book had introduced into his work other material drawn from another source. Apart from these three chapters, Sir Thomas Phillipps MS no. 237 agrees exactly with the manuscript from which Commelinus composed his book.]

Nine years after Commelinus’s volume was published, Henry Savile brought out the distinguished collection entitled *The Principal Writers after Bede*, which contains Malmesbury’s *Deeds of the Kings of the English*, *Modern History*, and *Deeds of the Bishops*. In the dedication of his book to Queen Elizabeth, Henry Savile bestows upon Malmesbury this just encomium:

> “Among these, William of Malmesbury holds the foremost place both for truthfulness of narrative and maturity of judgment: a man learned according to the standard of those times, who traced the events of some seven hundred years with such fidelity and diligence that he seems almost alone among our writers to have fulfilled the office of historian.”

> [Note: [Col. 0954] D. Simonds d’Ewes translated Malmesbury’s book from Latin into English, but never published the fruit of his labour. R. John Sharp, however, published a translation of this author in 1815. Sharp’s notes are always full of learning. How much the editor has profited from the knowledge of this skilled translator will appear from the notes placed at the foot of each page.]

The manuscript from which Savile’s volume was produced was either carelessly copied, or the volume was incorrectly printed; it swarms with the gravest errors of the text, for which the list of errata placed at the end of the work provides a most inadequate remedy. From various notes supplied in the margin it is plainly evident that Savile did not establish his edition with the aid of only one manuscript. No manuscript has come to the notice of the editor of the present book which wholly agrees with Savile’s text; Royal MS 13 B. XIX in the British Museum comes nearer, but does not entirely agree. Without relying on any authority, Savile divides his work into chapters, from whose order manuscripts of better quality nevertheless do not depart. The edition commonly called the London edition, having become scarce, was again put to press at Frankfurt in 1601, and is sprinkled with a far greater number of errors than the London edition, although the Frankfurt editor professes to have inserted in his text corrections marked in the London errata list.

The text of this present edition is taken from a manuscript written about the end of the twelfth century, which formerly belonged to Margam Abbey, founded by Robert, Earl of Gloucester, that nobleman to whom Malmesbury dedicated his work. We selected this excellent manuscript, now preserved among the Royal Manuscripts in the British Museum (Royal Library 13 D. II), after mature examination and careful comparison with other manuscripts, both because it is more correct than the rest and because it appeared to display traces of the final revision applied by the author to his work. One other manuscript, which agrees with the Royal manuscript, though many centuries later, is preserved in the collection of Sir Thomas Phillipps, Baronet.

From the variant readings and the many changes of great importance occurring throughout, it is clear that the author reworked his work more than once, and it is believed that there survive traces of at least four distinct classes of manuscripts of the work entitled *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, and of two of the work entitled *Modern History*. No one can inspect the variant readings presented in the notes at the foot of every page of this edition without concluding that the author bestowed persistent care in correcting and enlarging his work. Very many of these changes certainly consist in words alone, but they contribute greatly to elegance of expression. In some places harsher terms are moderated and softened; whole series of clauses are added, and others substituted for those he had previously admitted. It must not, however, be inferred that this entire medley of variant readings is attributable to Malmesbury; very many are the work of copyists.

The text of this volume will appear to differ greatly from Savile’s edition, but the variation in readings is indicated in the notes at the foot of every page under the designation of the letter S. At first sight, some may perhaps think that too many variations exhibited in different manuscripts have been shown; but it is enough to say that account has been taken only of those variations which mark the manuscript in question as belonging, as it were, to a particular class. But where a variation in reading is to be attributed to the carelessness of the person who copied the manuscript, and the manuscript is peculiar to no particular class, we have omitted it. This rule, however, admits one exception. We have reproduced word for word the manuscripts by whose assistance we established our text; if any word seems manifestly to have been intruded through a copyist’s error, we borrow the true reading from other manuscripts, noting the error and indicating the authority. But our manuscript is so excellent and so accurately copied that examples of corrections of this sort are exceedingly rare.

From a careful collation of the various manuscripts it is certainly concluded that there are different editions or classes of manuscripts, to one of which classes every manuscript of this author may be referred.

The principal manuscripts collated are designated in the notes by the letters A, S, C, D, E, F, G, H, K, L, M.

A. Harleian manuscript no. 261; Cottonian manuscript, Claudius C. IX; both in the British Museum; and Sir Thomas Phillipps manuscript no. 2777. S. Savile’s text, in the London and Frankfurt editions. C. Royal manuscript 13 B. XIX; Harleian manuscript no. 447; both in the British Museum. D. Royal manuscript 13 D. V; Royal manuscript 13 B. XVII; both in the British Museum. E. Royal manuscript 13 D. II in the British Museum; Sir Thomas Phillipps manuscript no. 8239. F. Manuscript in the library of All Souls College, Oxford, probably of the same class as E. G. Bodleian manuscript, Laud 548, Oxford, apparently of the same class as L. H. Bodleian manuscript, Hatton 54, probably of the same class as A. K. Bodleian manuscript, Bodley 712, agreeing with class C. L. Arundel manuscript no. 35 in the British Museum; and the manuscript of Trinity College, Cambridge, R. 14. M. Arundel manuscript no. 161, copied verbatim from Royal manuscript 13 D. V.

We examined other manuscripts preserved at Oxford, Cambridge, the British Museum, and the library of Sir Thomas Phillipps [Col. 0955]; but since they appear to have been transcribed from one of the copies mentioned above, it did not seem necessary to enumerate them with the earlier ones.

Perhaps some will think the present edition overburdened with too many notes. But it should be recalled that the particular character of Malmesbury’s *History*, in many places, necessarily requires a sort of commentary or annotation upon the text; and almost nothing has been done which does not either elucidate the author’s meaning or spare the reader the heavy labour of seeking out matters which are not always readily available. Always and everywhere, in our judgment, the matters adduced rest upon arguments drawn either from contemporary sources or from more accessible authority.

The Editor cannot close these preliminary observations without returning due thanks to the friends whose assistance aided him while this work was being put through the press, but especially to Sir Harris Nicolas, G.C.M.G., and to John Holmes, Esq., of the British Museum. Special thanks are due not only from the Editor, but also from the English Historical Society, to Sir Thomas Phillipps, Baronet, because he most generously lent the Editor several Malmesbury manuscripts of the greatest value for the purpose of collation. Nor would the Editor be fair to Samuel Bentley if he did not publicly acknowledge how greatly the skill and diligence prevailing in his printing establishment have served this work. Only those upon whom the burden of putting such a work through the press has fallen can adequately estimate how much an editor may owe to a printer’s vigilance and sagacity.

The Editor cannot bring these observations to an end without mentioning his brother, William Hardy, from whom he received constant and valuable assistance in comparing manuscripts and correcting errors. If he were to acknowledge so great assistance as received from another’s hand, this would certainly not be an adequate acknowledgment.

Record Office, Tower, 22 May 1841.

[Col. 0955]

> [Note: [Col. 0955B] Letter. In manuscripts E and A this dedication occurs at the end of Book III; in codices A and K it is read at the beginning of the work; in others, however (A, G, H, L), it is absent.]

# THE AUTHOR’S LETTER, DEDICATED TO ROBERT, EARL OF GLOUCESTER, SON OF KING HENRY

[Col. 0955A]

To the venerable and renowned lord Count ROBERT,

> [Note: [Col. 0955B] Robert, son of the king. Robert, Earl of Gloucester, illegitimate son of King Henry I. He married Mabel, otherwise called Maud, the elder co-heiress of Robert Fitz-Hamon [Col. 0956B], who possessed the honour of Gloucester in her hereditary right.]

WILLIAM, monk of Malmesbury, sends greetings, and such prayers as he can offer.

The virtue of illustrious men especially commends in itself this quality: that it invites to love of itself even minds far removed. Thus inferiors make the virtues of superiors their own, while they reverence the traces of virtues whose examples they cannot aspire to attain. Moreover, the whole matter redounds to the glory of great men: they both do good and kindle lesser persons to love them. Therefore, O leaders, whatever good we do is yours; whatever worthy thing we write for remembrance is assuredly yours. Your energy is an encouragement to us, so that, because you devote your perils to our peace, you in turn may become renowned in every age through our labours.

For this reason I judged that *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*, which I recently published, should especially be consecrated to you,

> [Note: [Col. 0956B] “To be dedicated,” D, E; “to be followed,” C.]

my lord Earl, venerable and deservedly beloved. For no one is more suited to be a patron of the liberal arts than you, in whom are united the magnanimity of your grandfather, the munificence of your uncle, and the prudence of your father. While you emulate these in the features of your industry, you make this a special part of your glory: that you devote yourself to letters. What need I say of the fact that you honour men of letters with your acquaintance, although envy of their reputation or slenderness of fortune has made them obscure? Since nature allows itself this: what a man approves in himself he does not disapprove in another, men of letters thus find in you dispositions akin to their own. You look upon them kindly, with no perception of any bitterness; you receive them gladly,

> [Note: [Col. 0956B] “Unwillingly,” D, E; “generously,” S; “gift,” C.]

and dismiss them unwillingly. The greatness of your fortune has changed nothing whatever in you, except that you can almost do as much good as you wish. Receive, therefore, most illustrious man, a work in which you may see yourself as in a mirror; for the approval of your serenity will understand that, before you heard their names, you have imitated the deeds of the greatest nobles.

The prologue to the first book sets forth the scope

> [Note: [Col. 0956B] “Of the work,” D, E; “of this work,” S, C.]

of the work; if you are pleased to read it, you will be able to gather the whole subject in summary. I should wish to obtain this from your dignity: that it not be counted a fault against me that the narrative often travels, by way of digression, outside England.

> [Note: [Col. 0956B] “England,” D, E; “our nation,” S, C.]

For I wish this work to be an epitome of many histories, though I have called it, from its larger part, *The Deeds of the Kings of the English*.

[Col. 0957]

# WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY, THE DEEDS OF THE KINGS OF THE ENGLISH, FIVE BOOKS

## PROLOGUE. HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF WILLIAM, MONK OF MALMESBURY, TO THE FIRST BOOK OF *THE DEEDS OF THE KINGS OF THE ENGLISH*

[Col. 0957A]

The Venerable Bede, a man most learned and least proud,

> [Note: [Col. 0957C] Bede. The Venerable Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. London: published at the expense of the Society, 1838.]

related the deeds of the English, from their arrival in Britain to his own day, in a plain and graceful style.

> [Note: [Col. 0957C] “Completed,” C, D, E, M; “described,” A, S, L. For an understanding of the letters by which variant readings in manuscripts are marked, see the Preface.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0957C] “After him . . . expended his labour.” Malmesbury makes the same observation elsewhere.]

After him, I think, you will not easily find anyone who devoted himself to weaving the histories of that people in Latin prose. Others may see whether they have already discovered anything concerning these matters, or will discover it hereafter; our labour, though it has kept anxious vigils in inquiry, has so far spent its efforts in vain. There are indeed certain records of antiquity,

> [Note: [Col. 0957C] He alludes to the Saxon Chronicle.]

arranged in the manner of a chronicle and in the native tongue according to the years of the Lord. By means of these, whatever times passed after that man have deserved to struggle free from the old age of oblivion [Col. 0957B]. For concerning Æthelweard,

> [Note: [Col. 0957C] Æthelweard. Æthelweard, or Ethelward, a noble Saxon, traced his descent from King Æthelred, as he himself indicates [Col. 0957D] in the work of which Malmesbury speaks here. He lived about the end of the tenth century. His *Chronicle*, which begins with the Creation and ends in the year 975, is extant among the *Writers after Bede*. No manuscript of his work is now found; for the manuscript which Savile appears to have had in hand perished in the fire in the Cottonian Library on 23 October 1731.]

an illustrious and eminent man who undertook to arrange those chronicles in Latin, it is better to be silent; I would have been minded to speak of him, were words not wearisome. Nor has the work, polished with the sober elegance of style, of Lord Eadmer escaped our notice.

> [Note: [Col. 0957D] Eadmer’s . . . work. *Historia Novorum*, from A.D. 1066 to 1122. Selden published this work in 1623. [Col. 0958C] Eadmer was a monk of Canterbury and a disciple of Archbishop Anselm. He first carried his History down to Anselm’s death, but later extended it to the death of Archbishop Ralph, that is, A.D. 1122.]

In it, beginning with King Edgar, he rapidly sketched the times down to William I, and then, ranging more freely, offered to students an extensive and necessary history down to the death of Archbishop Anselm.

> [Note: [Col. 0958C] “Anselm,” A, D, E, F, G, H, L, M; “Ralph,” S, C.]
>
> [Note: [Col. 0958C] “To students,” A, S, C, F, L, M; “as a student,” D, E.]

Thus, with two hundred and twenty-three years omitted from the time of Bede—years which this man did not think worthy of any record—

> [Note: [Col. 0958C] “Did not think worthy,” A, S, C, E, F, L; “did not think worthy to support,” D, M.]

the course of time limps in the middle without the protection of letters. Accordingly, both from love of my country [Col. 0957C] and from the authority of those who urged me, I wished to repair the broken sequence of times, season what has been written barbarously with Roman salt, and, that the matter may proceed more methodically, pluck certain flowers from what Bede, who must often be mentioned, has said—touching lightly on a few things and taking leave of more [Col. 0958A].

Let the first little book, then, proceed concisely through the deeds of the English, from their occupation of Britain down to King Ecgbert, who, after the petty kings had been overthrown by varied fortune, attained almost the monarchy of the whole island. But since four very powerful kingdoms sprang up among the English—the Kentish, West-Saxon, Northumbrian, and Mercian kingdoms—which we intend to pursue separately, if leisure permits, we must first speak of that which both grew up more quickly and withered more quickly.

> [Note: [Col. 0958C] “Withered,” A, S, D, E, L, M; “dried up,” C.]

This will certainly be accomplished more readily if I place the kingdoms of the East Angles and East Saxons behind the others, which we judge unworthy both of our attention and of posterity’s remembrance.

> [Note: [Col. 0958C] “We judge unworthy,” D, E, F, L, M; “we judge rather unworthy,” S, C; A, erroneously, has “worthy,” omitting “rather.”]

[Col. 0958B]

The second book will carry the line of royal times down to the arrival of the Normans.

The remaining three will concern the deeds of three kings, with the addition of matters which happened elsewhere in their days

> [Note: [Col. 0958D] “Their,” A, S, D, E, L, M; “those men’s,” C.]

and, through the renown of their deeds, demand notice of themselves. These things I promise if divine favour smiles upon my undertaking and carries me beyond the reefs of a rugged style, upon which Æthelweard struck miserably while hunting for tinkling and borrowed words. But if anyone, as he says,

> [Note: [Col. 0958D] “But if anyone, if anyone too,
>
> Captivated by love, shall read these things also.” Virgil, *Eclogues*, VI.9.]

if anyone captivated by love shall read these things also, let him know that, concerning times long past, I guarantee as true nothing beyond the coherence of the years; the credibility of the statements will rest with the authors. But whatever I have added concerning more recent ages, I either saw myself [Col. 0958C] or heard from trustworthy men.

> [Note: [Col. 0958D] “Trustworthy,” A, S, D, E, L, M; “worthy,” C.]

Moreover, in either case I do not greatly value the judgment of contemporaries; after the passing away of affection and envy, I hope to possess among posterity, if not the title of eloquence, at least the testimony of diligence.

[Col. 0957] End of the Prologue.

## 1–5 HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE

[Col. 0959]

[Col. 0959A] In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 449,

> [Note: [Col. 0959B] “Fortieth,” S, C, E, F; “sixtieth,” A, D, L, M.]

the Angles and Saxons came into Britain. Although the cause of their arrival has been sung everywhere, it will not be irrelevant to weave it in here; and, that my purpose may become clearer, I must begin further back. The Romans, having compelled Britain (55 B.C.) through Julius Caesar to swear allegiance to Latin laws,

> [Note: [Col. 0959B] “Latin,” D, E, M; “Latian,” A, C, F, L; “broad,” S.]

treated it with great favour, as may be read in the annals and seen in the remains of ancient buildings. The emperors themselves, who ruled almost the whole world, were accustomed to sail hither when opportunities were sought,

> [Note: [Col. 0959B] “To sail to it,” E; “willingly to sail to it,” A, S, C, D, F, L, M.]

and to spend their lifetime here. Finally Severus (A.D. 211)

> [Note: [Col. 0959B] Severus. Septimius Severus assumed the purple after the murder of Pertinax, 13 April, A.D. 193.]

and Constantius (A.D. 306),

> [Note: [Col. 0959B] Constantius. Constantius Chlorus assumed the title of Augustus after Diocletian’s abdication in A.D. 305.]

most eminent emperors, both died on the island

> [Note: [Col. 0959B] “Both died on the island.” Severus died at York on 4 February A.D. 211 [Col. 0959C], where Constantius also died on 25 July 306.]

and were buried with the highest honour.

> [Note: [Col. 0959C] “Were buried with the highest honour,” A, D, E, F, L, M; “were buried there with supreme honour,” C; “were buried with supreme honour,” S.]

Severus, in order to fortify the province against barbarian incursions, drew that celebrated and much-discussed ditch from sea to sea.

> [Note: [Col. 0959C] Ditch. That most celebrated monument of Roman rule, commonly called Severus’s Wall, is here described as a ditch, not a wall. Bede speaks similarly: “He judged that it should be divided not by a wall, as some suppose, but by a rampart” (Book I, ch. 5). Where he speaks of the second embassy to the Romans (A.D. 416), Bede again alludes to Severus’s Wall, saying: “They set in place a wall of solid stone, in a straight line from sea to sea, between the towns which had been built there for fear of enemies, where Severus had once also made [Col. 0960B] a rampart” (Book I, ch. 13). Yet nowhere does he refer to the rampart or ditch begun by Hadrian or Antoninus.]

Constantius, a man, as they say, of great civic virtue, left as heir Constantine,

> [Note: [Col. 0960B] Constantine. Constantine the Great.]

a youth of excellent promise whom he had begotten by Helena, an innkeeper (*stabularia*). Proclaimed emperor by the army, Constantine [Col. 0960A], having declared an expedition into the upper regions, led away a great body of British soldiers. Through their exertions, as triumphs flowed according to his wishes, he soon gained possession of power,

> [Note: [Col. 0960B] “Having soon gained possession of affairs,” A, S, D, E, F, L, M; “having soon gained possession of imperial power,” C.]

and settled those who had completed their military service and their labours in a certain part of Gaul, westward along the shore of the Ocean.

> [Note: [Col. 0960B] “Settled.” See note 53 below.]

There their descendants remain to this day, having increased to an immense extent, differing somewhat in customs and language from our Britons.

§ 2. In the years that followed, on the same island, Maximus (A.D. 383), a man fitted for imperial power—had he not, in breach of faith, aspired to tyranny—put on the purple, as though compelled by the army; and immediately, preparing to cross into Gaul, he stripped the province of almost every soldier.

[Note: Maximus. A native of Spain (although Ethelweard, Henry of Huntingdon, and certain others describe him as though native to this island), he was proclaimed emperor in Britain in 383 by the unanimous vote of both soldiers and provincials. Defeated and captured by Theodosius, he was killed by soldiers in A.D. 388. Florence of Worcester places Maximus’s death in the year 386.]

Constantine (A.D. 407), likewise a certain man shortly afterwards in the same place, attracted to imperial power by hope of the name, drained away whatever remained of military strength.

[Note: Constantine. During Honorius’s reign (A.D. 407), an uprising broke out in Britain, and two pseudo-emperors, Marcus and Gratian, were successively elected and murdered. An ordinary soldier named Constantine was afterwards chosen, in honour of the memory of Constantine the Great. After he had reigned about three years, he was captured and killed during the siege of Arles on 28 November 411, and the empire was restored to Honorius.]

But the one was killed by Theodosius and the other by Honorius, and they became a mockery of human affairs. Of the forces that had followed them to the wars, part was killed; part, after flight, withdrew to the northern Britons.

[Note: Thus, when the tyrants . . . she was exposed. According to Gildas and Bede. Britain owes this first diminution of herself to Maximus, who led with him into Gaul a great multitude of inhabitants and soldiers. Archbishop Ussher, who carefully collected the records concerning this island, maintains (*Antiquities of the British Church*, pp. 107–108) that thirty thousand soldiers and one hundred thousand inhabitants migrated and settled in Armorica. Various dates, however, have been assigned to this migration of Britons, and the matter still lies hidden, wrapped in dense darkness.]

Thus, when the tyrants had left in the countryside no one except half-barbarians, and in the towns no one except men enslaved to their bellies, Britain—bereft of every protection of youthful vigour, emptied of every practice of the arts—long lay exposed to the greed of neighbouring peoples.

[Note: “Youthful”: a. d. e. f. l. m.; “military”: s. c.]

§ 3. For immediately many persons were killed in the incursions of Scots and Picts; country houses were set on fire, cities overthrown, and absolutely everything devastated by sword and flame. The alarmed islanders, who thought anything safer than deciding the matter in battle, partly sought safety on foot by fleeing to the mountains; partly, having buried their treasures—most of which are dug up in this age—they intended to go to Rome to seek aid.

[Note: “Set on fire”: e.; “burned”: a. s. c. d. l. m.]

[Note: The Romans rendered their assistance. There is scarcely any doubt that the Romans were more than once successfully summoned to help against the Picts and Scots. Learned men, however, are not agreed about the time. On this matter see Stillingfleet, *Antiquities of the British Churches*, and Ussher’s *Antiquities of the British Churches*.]

The Romans, moved by pity and judging nothing more urgent than to offer help to their exhausted allies, routed the enemy once and twice and gave their assistance. At last, wearied by the long journey abroad, they excused themselves from coming in the future: the Britons themselves should rather learn not to degenerate from the martial ardour of their fathers, but to defend their country with courage and arms.

[Note: “Offer”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “bestow”: c.]

[Note: “Wearied by the long journey abroad”: a. s. c. e. f. l.; “wearied by the labour of a long journey abroad”: d. m.]

[Note: “Excuse themselves”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “accuse”: c.]

They added verbal instructions for constructing a wall for their protection, mounting guard at defensive works, charging against the enemy if necessary, and carrying out the other requirements of military discipline.

[Note: After these instructions . . . they depart. The fixed date of the Romans’ final withdrawal from Britain is still enveloped in the deepest obscurity.]

After their warnings, accompanied by the tears of the wretched, they departed; happy fortune attended their departure and restored them to the fulfilment of their wishes.

[Note: “Happy”: a. s. c. e. f. l.; “unhappy”: d. m.]

[Note: “Their”: e.; “their own”: a. s. c. d. l. m.]

Then the Scots, on hearing the report that all hope of their return had been abandoned, immediately and more fiercely than usual fell upon the Britons, levelled the wall, crushed the few who resisted, and carried home no mean booty. But the remaining common people of the land rushed to the royal court, imploring the loyalty of their king.

[Note: “And immediately”: d. e.; omit *et* (“and”): a. s. c. l. m.]

## Concerning Vortigern

[Col. 0962A]

§ 4. At that time there was a king of Britain named Vortigern, neither prompt in hand nor sound in counsel; indeed, prone to the enticements of the flesh and a slave to almost every vice. For avarice subjected him, pride rode him hard, and lust disturbed him. Finally, as is read in the *Deeds of the Britons*, he violated his own daughter, tempted by the hope of a kingdom, and begot a son by her.

[Note: “Subjected”: s. c. d. e. l. m.; “had subjected”: a.]

[Note: “Rode him hard”: c. d. e. f.; “troubled”: s.; “had troubled”: a.]

[Note: “Disturbed”: s. c. e. f.; “had ridden him hard”: a; “defiled”: d.]

[Note: As is read in the *Deeds of the Britons* . . . “and begot a son by her.” The story that Vortigern violated his own daughter is highly improbable and ought to be rejected as little more than a mere fable.]

In such tumults he made light of the situation; squandering the wealth of the kingdom on revelry, he wasted himself upon the seductions of prostitutes. Yet at length, roused by the clamouring voices, he brought the public condition before a council, seeking the opinions of his magnates.

[Note: “Opinions”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “opinion”: c.]

Therefore, to reduce the matter to its essence, all agreed that Angles and Saxons should be summoned from Germany: men strong in arms but unsettled in dwelling-places. This would provide a double advantage: invincible in arms, they would easily repel the enemy; and, uncertain of a home until then, they would count it an immense favour if they were granted even barren ground and a meagre turf for habitation. Moreover, they would never contrive anything against the country, because the memory of benefits would soften their native savagery of character. The plan being approved, envoys were sent to Germany—men indeed distinguished, and worthy to assume the person of their country.

[Note: “To be summoned.” This appeal of Vortigern to the Saxons, as described by certain ancient writers, may have some foundation in the statements of Gildas and Bede. Pagi conjectures, in his *Critique on Baronius*, that it occurred in 447. From Nennius’s testimony it might be inferred that Horsa and Hengist arrived here uninvited: “Meanwhile three *ciulae* came from Germany, driven out, in which were Horsa and Hengist” (§ 31). Yet it is probable that exile befell them according to the customary pattern and method of migration among the Germans, as related by Malmesbury in § 5.]

[Note: “Because”: a. d. e. l. m.; “since”: s. c.]

## Concerning the Arrival of the Germans in Britain, A.D. 449

[Note: A.D. 449. Bede also assigns this year to the arrival of the Saxons (*Hist. Eccl.* I.15). See notes on Bede, ed. English Historical Society, p. 34.]

§ 5. When the Germans heard that a thing for which they had sought with a thousand prayers was voluntarily requested of them, they obeyed at once, hastening the business with the spur of joy. They bade farewell to their native fields, renounced the affection of their parents, entrusted their sails to fortune, and, under a favourable wind, sailed up to Britain in three long ships, which they call *ceolas*.

[Note: “They call *ceolas*”: e. l.; “they call *cheulas*”: d. m.; “they call *ceolas*”: c.; “they call *ciulas*”: s.; “they call *theolas*”: a.]

At that time and subsequently people came from three peoples of Germany: Angles, Saxons, and Jutes.

[Note: “Jutes.” One manuscript, Cotton Claudius IX, reads “Wights.”]

For almost all the land lying beyond the British Ocean under the northern pole is, not without reason, called Germany, although divided by the boundaries of many provinces, because it produces such a multitude of people.

[Note: “Although divided by the boundaries of many provinces”: s. d. e. f.; a. l. m omit *many*; c omits the entire sentence.]

Therefore, just as those whose task it is to prune luxuriant branches of a tree, so that the life-sap may suffice for the rest, so the inhabitants relieve their mother-country by the expulsion of some, lest she collapse, exhausted by feeding so numerous an offspring. But, in order to lessen the odium of the deed, they draw lots for those to be expelled. Hence the men of that land have found virtue from necessity: driven from their native soil, they claim foreign homes by arms.

[Note: “Have found”: d. e. m.; “found”: a. s. c. l.]

[Note: “Claim”: a. c. d. e. l. m.; “might claim”: s.]

Thus the Vandals once crushed Africa; the Goths possessed Spain; the Lombards still occupy Italy; and the Normans, inhabiting a part of Gaul subdued by arms, called it Normandy. From this Germany there first came to Britain a band, small indeed, but one which supported its small number by courage, under the leadership of Hengist and Horsa, brothers of worthy character and of no obscure stock among their own people. For they were great-grandsons of that most ancient Woden, from whom the royal race of nearly all barbarian peoples traces its line; and the English people, madly believing him to be a god, have in sacrilegious observance consecrated to him the fourth day of the week, and the sixth to his wife Frea, down to the present time.

[Note: “By courage”: s. e. l.; “by virtues”: d. m.]

But Bede does not pass over in silence the places in Britain where Angles, Saxons, or Jutes established their settlements.

[Note: “Jutes.” One manuscript, Cotton Claudius IX, reads “Wights.”]

[Note: Bede does not pass over in silence: Bede, I.25.]

Our purpose is, though material abounds, not to indulge the pen, but to select only what is necessary.

§ 6. When the Angles arrived, people came from every side to meet them. The king bestowed favour, the people poured out goodwill; faith was given and received, and the island of Thanet was handed over for their settlement and support.

[Note: “When the Angles arrived.” Hengist and Horsa were landed at Ypwinesfleot (Ebbsfleet, in the island of Thanet). *Saxon Chronicle*.]

A compact was also made: that they, with shields joined, should expend their labours for the country, receiving the rewards of military service from those for whose safety they professed to keep watch.

[Note: “With shields joined”: a. c. d. f. l. m.; “with shields”: e.; “with invincible shields”: s.]

There was a brief delay, and behold: the Scots were approaching, imagining that the prey would, as before, yield to them easily. The Angles attacked them. The Scots could scarcely form a retreat after joining battle; cavalry pursuing the fugitives struck them down from behind.

[Note: “Pursuing”: c. d. e. m.; “following”: a. s. l.]

Thus they fought more than once; and since victory always favoured the Angles, as commonly happens in human affairs, success inflamed the courage of the one party, while fear nourished the cowardice of the other. The affair came to such a point that the Scots avoided nothing more carefully than joining battle with the Angles.

§ 7. Meanwhile Hengist, no less keen in intellect than vigorous in battle, sent some of his own men back to their homeland, with the king’s consent, to report the king’s and people’s weakness, the island’s wealth, and to offer rich rewards to those willing to come. They carried out their instructions energetically and soon returned with sixteen ships, bringing Hengist’s daughter, a maiden who, as we are told, was both a marvel of nature and a spectacle for men.

[Note: “They carry out energetically”: a. d. e. l. m.; “having carried out energetically”: s; “having carried out generally”: c.]

[Note: Hengist’s daughter. Geoffrey of Monmouth is the first writer known to mention the name of Hengist’s daughter; he calls her Ronwen, a name less usual among the Anglo-Saxons. In chapter 36 of Nennius’s *History*, Hengist’s daughter is called Romwenna, though the name is omitted in the text.]

Upon their return a banquet was prepared. Hengist ordered his daughter to perform the office of cupbearer, in order that she might delight the eyes of the reclining king. Nor was this without result. For he, as one always slavering after women’s beauty, was immediately wounded in spirit by the charm of her appearance and the elegance of her movements. He conceived a hope of possessing the girl and did not delay in seeking marriage, compelling her willing father. Hengist, however, cunningly at first refused, alleging that such a humble marriage was unworthy of a king. Finally, as though reluctant, he consented, taking the whole of Kent as the marriage-gift. There, for a long time, all justice had languished under the rule of a certain *gorong*, who nevertheless, like all the petty kings of the island, was subject to Vortigern’s monarchy.

[Note: Gorong. This word was not used equally often as a proper name. Camden interprets it as *Guorong*, that is, “chief” or “free man.” See Camden, *Britannia*, col. 187, Gibson ed., London, 1695.]

Nor content with this generosity, the barbarian abused the king’s imprudence and persuaded him to summon from Germany his brother and son, men of valour, arranging the scheme so that, since Hengist himself was defending the eastern province, they too might restrain the Scots from the north.

[Note: “Brother and son”: namely Otha and Ebusa.]

Thus, with the king conniving, they sailed around Britain, reached the Orkney Islands, and involved those peoples, together with the Picts and Scots, in equal misery. They settled in the northern part of the island, now called Northumbria, then and afterwards; yet no distinctive royal title or name was used there until Ida, from whom the royal line of the Northumbrians grew.

[Note: “Line”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “stock”: c.]

But more on these matters below; for now I shall continue what I began.

## Concerning Vortimer, Son of Vortigern, and Arthur

§ 8. Vortimer, son of Vortigern, judging that no further concealment was possible when he saw himself and his Britons being ruined by the deceit of the English, directed his mind to their expulsion and at the same time urged his father to undertake it.

[Note: “Urged”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “roused”: c.]

Accordingly, with him as instigator, after seven years from their arrival the treaty was broken; and for twenty years there were frequent minor battles, but four battles fought with all their forces, as the chronicle relates.

[Note: Frequent minor battles. On these battles and the subsequent treachery of the Saxons, see Nennius §§43–45, ed. E.H.S.; compare Matthew of Westminster, under 460 and following, who incorporated British narratives into his *Chronicles*.]

[Note: As the chronicle relates. The *Saxon Chronicle* indicates battles assigned to these years: at Aeglesford (Aeglesford on the Medway), A.D. 455; at Crecanford (Crayford), 457; at Wyppedesfleot (Ebbsfleet, in the island of Thanet, near Stonar), 465; the location of the fourth battle, in 473, is not indicated. Nennius (§44) places these battles on the river Derevent (the Darent in Kent, probably at the very place where it joins the Cray); at Episford, or Rit Hergabail, regarded as identical with Aylesford; and in the field beside the Stone of the Title (Stonar, on the island of Thanet, or, according to some, Folkestone in Kent).]

In the first encounter they parted with equal fortune on either side, while the English lamented Horsa, Hengist’s brother, and the Britons mourned Catigern, the king’s other son, with great public grief.

[Note: Horsa. Horsa was killed in the battle at Aylesford in 455 and is conjectured to have been buried at Horsted in Kent. Bede, I.15, states: “In the eastern parts of Kent he has a monument distinguished by his name.” Nennius calls the battle Epistord.]

[Note: Catigern. Nennius calls him Categirn and represents him as, so to speak, Vortigern’s second son.]

In the remaining engagements the English always had the upper hand. Peace was made when Vortimer, the instigator of the war, was taken away by fate. Greatly unlike his easy-going father, he would have governed the kingdom excellently, had God permitted it. But after his death the strength of the Britons withered, their diminished hopes ebbed backward; and they would certainly then have gone utterly to ruin, had not Ambrosius—the sole surviving Roman, who after Vortigern was monarch of the kingdom—checked the swelling barbarians through the outstanding military service of Arthur.
