[Note: Ambrosius. Nothing is known concerning Ambrosius Aurelianus or the period in which he lived. Bede observes that his parents had worn the purple. According to Gildas: “He was a modest man, the only one who was courteous, faithful, brave, and truthful, perhaps of Roman descent, who survived the shock of that great storm, after his parents, clothed of course in purple, had been killed in it.” Nennius, likewise speaking of him (§48), says: “He was king among all the kings of the British people.” He is distinct from Natanleod, mentioned by the *Saxon Chronicle*, whose wife, together with five thousand of his men, was killed in battle against Cerdic the West Saxon in 508. For fuller treatment see Ussher, *Primordia*, p. 1116, and Carte, *History of England*, vol. I, pp. 197–205.]

This is Arthur, of whom British trifles still rave today: a man plainly worthy to be celebrated not by deceptive fables but by truthful histories, since he long sustained his tottering country and sharpened the shattered spirits of its citizens for war.

[Note: “Tottering”: s. e. f. l.; “falling”: d. m.]

Finally, in the siege of Mount Badon, trusting in an image of the Mother of the Lord, which he had sewn onto his arms, he is said to have attacked nine hundred enemies alone and routed them in an incredible slaughter.

[Note: “Siege”: d. e. l. m.; “siege/blockade”: s. f. Bede, incorrectly interpreting Gildas, wrongly assigns the siege of Mount Badon to 493; according to the *Annales Cambriae*, it should be referred to A.D. 516.]

[Note: Mount Badon. Called Caer-Badon, “the hill of Bannesdon,” near Bath. Gildas places it near the mouth of the river Severn. See note on Gildas, p. 34, ed. E.H.S.]

[Note: “Trusting in an image of the Mother of the Lord.” Gildas §56: “Arthur bore an image of the holy Virgin Mary upon his shoulders,” etc. On this see Ussher, *Primordia*, p. 639. The following statements occur in the *Annales Cambriae*: “The seventy-second year [A.D. 516]: the battle of Badon, in which King Arthur bore the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ on his shoulders for three days and three nights, and was victorious.” Nennius says that this occurred in the battle at the fortress of Guinnion; but he assigns the killing of nine hundred and sixty men on the same day by Arthur’s own hand to the battle at Mount Badon, §56.]

[Note: “Mother”: d reads “with the aid” after “Mother.”]

By contrast, the English, though tossed about by fortune’s changing game, replenished their wavering ranks with the arrival of fellow-countrymen and rushed more boldly upon the sword. Little by little, as the natives yielded, they extended themselves over the whole island, with God’s purpose not opposing—for in His hand lies the change of all empires.

[Note: “Empires”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “kingdoms”: c.]

But this happened in the course of years; for while Vortigern lived, nothing was undertaken against them. Meanwhile Hengist, through a certain vice of human nature—that the more one has, the more one desires—devised a fraud and invited his father-in-law to a banquet with three hundred of his own men. Having encouraged the guests to disorder through repeated draughts, and deliberately stung each man with salty jesting, they first came to quarrels and then to arms. Thus all the Britons, to a man, were cut down and vomited out their lives amid wine; the king himself was captured and redeemed his freedom, casting off servitude by surrendering three provinces.

[Note: “Vomited out”: d. e. l. m.; “spewed out”: s.]

After this, in the thirty-ninth year after his arrival, Hengist died (A.D. 488): a man who pursued his successes no less by fraud than by strength, and who, indulging greatly in native savagery, preferred to conduct everything more bloodily than civilly.

[Note: “Greatly”: e; “and greatly”: a. s. c. d. l. m.]

He left a son, Eisc, who, intent rather on safeguarding than enlarging the kingdom, never exceeded his father’s boundaries.

[Note: Eisc: s. c. d. e. m; a omits Eisc; l reads “his.”]

[Note: “Intent”: s. c. d. e. l. m.; “content”: c.]

After twenty-four years had passed (A.D. 512), he had as successors his son Oth and Oth’s son Yrmenric, more like himself than their grandfather or great-grandfather.

[Note: “More like himself than their grandfather or great-grandfather”: s. c. d. e. m.; “more like their grandfather or great-great-grandfather”: a. l.]

The chronicles assign fifty-three years to the reigns of both; yet whether they reigned separately or jointly is not distinguished.

[Note: In the chronicles. The chronicles now surviving do not contain this.]

## Concerning King Ethelbert and the Arrival of Saint Augustine

§ 9. After them Ethelbert, son of Yrmenric, obtained power. According to the chronicles he spent fifty-three years in rule; according to Bede, fifty-six (A.D. 565). Let the reader see how to reconcile this discrepancy; for we, having sufficiently called attention to it, leave it unresolved.

[Note: “Power”: s. c. d. e. l. m.; “kingdom”: a.]

[Note: Fifty-three years. Although according to the *Saxon Chronicle* (under 565) Æthelberht held power for fifty-three years, he is said to have died in 616 after enjoying the kingdom for fifty-six years. Yet some disagreement remains, for if Æthelberht ascended the throne in 565—as all manuscripts known in these times state—and died in 616, his reign would comprise only fifty-one years. Wheloc and others, however, assign 560, though on what authority is not clearly evident.]

[Note: “Chronicle”: e; “chronicles”: a. s. c. d. l. m.]

[Note: According to Bede: *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, II.5, §§100–101.]

[Note: “Spent”: a. d. e. l. m.; “passed”: s. c.]

In the first years of his youthful kingdom he was so ridiculous in the eyes of neighbouring kings that, beaten in one battle and another, he could scarcely defend his own boundaries. Later, when with riper age there came also more prudent military skill, he brought beneath the yoke all the English nations except the Northumbrians, subdued by continual victories. And, in order to acquire the alliance of foreigners as well, he secured kinship with the king of the Franks by marriage to his daughter.

[Note: “All”: e; a. s. c. d. l. m read *soon* before “all.”]

[Note: His daughter: Bertha, daughter of Charibert, king of Paris, by his wife Ingoberga, and granddaughter of Chlothar I.]

[Note: “By marriage”: s reads “to Bertha” after *nuptiis*; a. c. d. e. l. m omit Bertha.]

Then, through association with the Franks, a people hitherto barbarous, united by common customs, began daily to put off its savage temper and to turn toward gentler ways.

[Note: “Hitherto”: s. c. d. e. m; a. l omit *hitherto*.]

To this was added the notably celibate life of Bishop Liudhard, who had come with the queen; even in silence it invited the king to the knowledge of Christ the Lord. Thus, when the blessed Augustine later preached, the royal mind, already softened, readily yielded; first among the number of his forefathers he renounced profane sacrileges (A.D. 597), so that he who surpassed them in royal power might overshadow them also in the glory of faith.

[Note: Augustine. Augustine and his companions were sent from Rome in 596 and landed on the island of Thanet in 597. For a full account see Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, I.25, §54.]

[Note: “Royal”: d. e. l. m; “of the king”: s.]

[Note: “Surpassed”: c. d. e. l. m; “was pre-eminent over”: s.]

This, indeed, is noble nobility; this is proud virtue: to conquer by honourableness those whom you conquer by rank. Indeed, extending his care to posterity, he promulgated laws in the native tongue, by which he assigned rewards to the good and met the wicked with stricter remedies, leaving nothing concerning any matter ambiguous for the future.

[Note: Laws. The oldest surviving copy of Æthelberht’s laws is the *Textus Roffensis*, compiled by Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, between 1115 and 1124.]

§ 10. In the twenty-first year after receiving the faith (A.D. 616), he died, passing the insignia of the kingdom to his son Eadbald.

[Note: “After receiving the faith.” Æthelberht died on 24 February A.D. 616. These twenty-one years must therefore be counted from the beginning of Augustine’s mission, not from Æthelberht’s conversion. Compare Bede’s testimonies, which do not agree.]

[Note: “Having received the faith”: a. c. d. e. l. m; “having received the faith of Christ”: s.]

As soon as Eadbald had broken the restraints of paternal fear, he cast off Christianity and also violated the chastity of his stepmother. But, lest he should plunge entirely headlong, the sternness of divine mercy set a barrier in his way.

[Note: Stepmother. After Bertha’s death, Æthelberht took another Frankish princess as wife; but her name was not published by historians, probably because of her incest with Eadbald. See Bede, II.5, §102, and the *Saxon Chronicle* under A.D. 616.]

For immediately, when the petty kings whom his father had subjected rebelled, he was diminished by the loss of his kingdom; and, frequently possessed by a demon for hours at a time, he paid the penalties of obstinate unbelief.

[Note: “Torments”: a. d. e. l. m; “punishments”: s. c.]

Augustine’s successor Laurence, offended by these things, was preparing to leave the province after sending his companions ahead. But, moved by a divine scourge, he withdrew his decision.

[Note: Laurence. As to the definite date of Augustine’s death and the election of his successor, we know nothing but what is highly uncertain. Yet, if the first charter printed in the *Codex Diplomaticus of the Anglo-Saxon Age* is accepted as authentic, it would establish that Laurence had assumed the episcopal office before 28 April 604. The genuineness of this charter, however, is disputed. Kemble, whose judgment carries authoritative weight, does not question its authenticity. Dr Smith, the learned editor of Bede, considers Augustine to have died in 603; but Warthon prefers 604. See *Anglia Sacra*, I.89; II.70.]

[Note: “Moved by a divine scourge, he withdrew his decision.” Mellitus and Justus, weary of the insults inflicted upon Christianity, left Britain and returned to the Continent; Laurence himself likewise contemplated departure. It is handed down that Saint Peter appeared to him in a vision and, reproaching his cowardice, struck him with lashes as punishment for his unworthy intention of abandoning his sheep. See Bede, II.6, §104.]

When the king was summoned concerning the matter, the wounds made the bishop’s words credible. He was, as they say, bent without reluctance; he embraced the grace of Christianity and abandoned his incestuous marriage. Yet, so that the stigma of a terrible example in the punishment of unbelief might be impressed upon posterity, he could scarcely retain his ancestral territories and never could aspire to his father’s height.

But for the rest, upright in faith throughout his life, he committed nothing that might injure his reputation. He also enriched with vast estates and most generous gifts the monastery outside the walls of Canterbury, which his father had founded. All English people ought to admire and celebrate their praises and merits, because they allowed the Christian faith to grow strong in England by gentle credulity and credulous gentleness.

[Note: Outside the walls of Canterbury: St Augustine’s.]

For who would not gladly reflect how fully that reply of King Ethelbert, which Bede reports him to have given to Augustine’s first preaching, accords with fairness and harmonizes with gentleness? He said that he could not so quickly give his mind to a new sect, abandoning the practices which he had always observed with the whole English people; nevertheless, they were not to be harassed by any trouble, but rather assisted by permission to preach and by generous maintenance, because they had undertaken so long a journey from their native soil in order to share with the English, in indulgent kindness, what they considered best.

[Note: Bede: Bede, I.25, §55.]

[Note: “Rather”: d. c. l. m; “also”: c.]

The fulfilment was not more lax than the promise, until, gradually discovering the truth of the faith, he himself also was joined with his subjects in the number of believers.

[Note: “More lax”: a. d. e. l. m; s. c omit *remissius*.]

And what of Eadbald? Though at first he had strayed more through fleshly enticement than through obstinacy of mind, did he not nevertheless show great reverence for the life of the bishops whose faith he neglected? Finally, as I have said, readily converted because of the injury done to one man, he was of great consequence for the growth of Christianity.

[Note: “Growth”: s. d. e. l. m; “increase”: a. c.]

Both therefore deserve praise; both earned more abundant commendation, since the good which the former magnanimously began, the latter graciously cherished.

[Note: “Praiseworthy”: a reads “men” after *laudabiles*; s. c. d. e. l. m omit “men.”]

§ 11. When, after twenty-four years of rule, he died (A.D. 640), his son Erconbert succeeded him, born of Emma, daughter of the king of the Franks. He ruled for the same number of years, but under better auspices, distinguished alike by devotion toward God and piety toward his country.

[Note: When he . . . died. Eadbald died on Thursday, 20 January 640.]

[Note: “Twenty-four”: a. s. d. e. l. m; “twenty-five”: c.]

[Note: Of Emma . . . of the Franks. After his first wife had died or been dismissed, Eadbald married Emma, daughter of Theudebert, king of Austrasia (Pagi, A.D. 640). Erconbert was born of this marriage, but Ermenfred of the former. See §13, note.]

[Note: “Indeed”: a. s. d. e. l. m; c omits *quidem*.]

[Note: “Equally distinguished”: s. c. e. l; “distinguished in life”: a. d. m.]

For while grandfather and father had professed our faith without destroying the idols, he considered royal devotion inadequate and beneath his duty if he did not destroy, by a more resolute decision, what they had condemned only in silent judgment. He levelled all the shrines of the gods to the ground, so that no trace of sacrilege might flow down to posterity.

[Note: “Devotion”: a. s. d. e. l. m; “condescension”: c.]

[Note: “Condemned”: c. d. e. l. m; “might condemn”: a. s.]

A splendid act: for the common people might be reminded of their fanatical superstition as long as they did not cease to look upon the sites of their shrines. And in order to teach his people, indulging only their bellies, to accustom themselves to moderation in eating, he commanded the observance throughout the kingdom of the solemn forty-day fast.

[Note: He commanded . . . fast. See Bede, III.8, §172; *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 640; Florence of Worcester, A.D. 640.]

The king then undertook a truly great work: neither the luxury of pleasures could enervate him nor concern for his kingdom divert him from the worship of God. Thus, secure in God’s favour, with affairs at home and abroad turning out as he wished, he grew old in complete tranquillity.

His daughter Ercongota, offspring not unworthy of so great a father and answering her father in corresponding features of virtue, adorned Cala, a monastery in Gaul, with the radiance of her holiness.

[Note: Cala, a monastery in Gaul. In French, Chelles, about four miles from Paris; a monastery founded by Queen Bathild, widow of Clovis II. Bede, however (III, §172), states that Ercongota was a nun in the place called In Brige—Faremoutiers-en-Brie—which was a most celebrated convent of Benedictine nuns.]

[Note: “Holiness”: a. c. s. e. l; “sanctity”: d. m.]

§ 12. But his son Egbert (A.D. 664), having held his father’s throne for nine years, accomplished nothing memorable in the brief span of his reign—unless one counts among the glory of those times the arrival of Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian: learned men who had drunk in every branch of learning to its very marrow. Had the subject not been entirely worn away, I would gladly go on to recount how much light they then shed upon the British world; how Greeks on one side and Latins on the other brought together their schools of letters in a single pursuit; and how they made the island, once the nurse of tyrants, a familiar dwelling-place of philosophy.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] The arrival of Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian. Theodore of Tarsus in Cilicia was ordained Archbishop of Canterbury at Rome on 26 March A.D. 668, and was installed in his episcopal office at Canterbury on 27 May A.D. 669. He was a man wonderfully learned, highly accomplished in Greek and Roman letters, arithmetic, and astronomy. He set out for England on 27 May 668, accompanied by Hadrian and bearing an express mandate from Pope Vitalian, who feared that Theodore might incline toward errors in the Greek Church in which he had been educated. Hadrian was appointed abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury.]

[Note: [Col. 0970D] “Counts.” a. s. c. e. l.; “reckons,” d. m.]

[Note: [Col. 0970D] “Studies.” e.; a. s. c. d. l. m. read “in competing pursuits beforehand.”]

[Note: [Col. 0970D] “Made.” After *made*, s. d. m. read: “But this too, and whatever good may be ascribed to Egbert’s days, is diminished by the crime through which he either killed Elbert and Egelbrict, the sons of his paternal uncle, or calmly allowed them to be killed.” c. omits *calmly*. a. e. l. omit the entire passage.]

[Col. 0971A] § 13. Egbert was succeeded by his brother Lothair (A.D. 673), who entered upon the kingdom under an ill omen. For eleven years, harassed by Edrich, son of Egbert, he was frequently engaged in civil wars, with varying fortune; at last, his body pierced by a spear, he gave up his life while the wound was being treated (A.D. 685). There are those who do not keep silent that both brothers were carried off by a swift death as a deserved punishment for cruelty: Egbert because he killed the innocent sons of his paternal uncle; Lothair because he mocked martyrs who had been publicly proclaimed. Yet the former both lamented the deed and granted to the mother of his cousins a portion of the island of Thanet for the building of a monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Egbert.” Ecgberht died in July A.D. 673.]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Eleven.” a. s. c. d. l. m.; “nine,” e. Bede assigns Hlodhere a reign of eleven years and seven months.]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Do not keep silent.” d. e.; “may not keep silent,” a. s. c. l. m.]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] That Egbert killed the innocent sons of his paternal uncle. Elbert and Aegilbert were sons of Ermenfrid, who was Ecgbert’s kinsman and brother. Malmesbury describes their killing more fully later.]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Innocent.” a. e. l.; after *innocent*, s. c. d. m. read, “as I have said.”]

§ 14. Nor did Edrich long glory in the success of his tyranny; within two years he was stripped of kingdom and life [Col. 0971B] (A.D. 686), and left his country exposed to be ravaged by enemies. Immediately one Cædwalla, together with his brother Mul, otherwise indeed a good and effective man, breathing implacable hatred against the men of Kent, invaded with all the strength he could muster a province once enjoying a long peace, but then divided by civil war, believing that it would yield to him without resistance. Yet he did not find the provincials as unprepared, or as empty of courage, as he had hoped. After receiving many reverses, village by village and town by town, they at last took heart and came to blows; victorious in the encounter, they put Cædwalla to flight and drove his brother into a certain cottage, then set fire to the little house itself. Thus Mul, lacking the courage to break out against the enemy while the fires held sovereign sway round the roof on every side, breathed out his last amid the flames (A.D. 687). Yet Cædwalla did not desist or withdraw his foot from the province, but made good his grief through repeated losses inflicted upon the inhabitants, and handed down the burden of avenging the affair to his successor Ine, as shall be related in its place.

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “And his brother.” a. c. d. e. l. m.; “and his brother Mul,” s.]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] Amid the flames. Cædwalla and his brother Mull devastated Kent in 686; in the following year Mull, together with twelve others, was killed by the punishment of fire. *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 686, 687.]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Breath.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “soul,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0971D] “As shall be related in its place.” See below, § 35.]

§ 15. In these desperate circumstances the royal succession of Kent faltered for about six years. At last, in the seventh year, Wihtred, son of Egbert, having subdued ill-will among his own people by industry and established peace among his enemies with money, was chosen king amid the high hopes of the citizens, which he fulfilled. Peaceable at home and unconquered in war, he cultivated the Christian religion with the greatest holiness, extended its power most widely, and—so that nothing might be lacking to his felicity—after thirty-three years, died at an advanced age, which mortals consider most blessed, leaving alive three children who were also his heirs. Of these, Edbert continued the kingdom for twenty-three years, Edelbert for eleven, and Alric for thirty-four, following their father’s institutions; nor did they bring it to an inglorious end, except that Edelbert, by the accidental burning of a city (A.D. 754), and Alric, by an ill-fated battle against the Mercians (A.D. 774), greatly clouded the glory of their times. Thus, if anything shameful happened, it is not concealed; if anything prosperous occurred, little is recorded in the chronicles—whether because this was done deliberately, or because it was brought about by a defect of human nature. For the reward of good deeds is brief, whereas injuries cause an everlasting grief.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] “In these.” a. s. e. l.; “Meanwhile,” c. d. m.]

[Note: [Col. 0971D] “In the seventh.” If the seven-year period discussed here is counted from Hlohere’s death, Wihtred’s succession must be placed in 692, contrary to authorities of better standing. But if Edrich’s usurpation is included within this number of years, the discrepancy is still greater. It is therefore sufficiently clear that Malmesbury has extended the Kentish interregnum too far, since Wihtred’s accession is most certainly referred to 690.]

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Chosen king. Wihtred began to reign at the end of 690. According to the *Saxon Chronicle*, at this period, A.D. 692, there were two kings in Kent, namely Wihtred and Swaefheard. See also Florence of Worcester, A.D. 691, and Bede, § 375.]

[Note: [Col. 0972C] “Extended.” After *extended*, a. reads: “He is the one who built the monastery of Saint Martin at Dover”; d. m. omit “at Dover”; s. c. e. l. omit the whole passage. In Florence of Worcester’s genealogy of the kings of Kent are these words: “Wihtred, succeeding to the kingdom, built the church of Saint Martin at Dover.”]

[Note: [Col. 0972C] “Thirty-three years.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “thirty,” c. According to the *Saxon Chronicle*, Wihtraed reigned thirty-four years. Bede (*Ecclesiastical History*, V.23) more accurately assigns his reign thirty-four years and six months. He died on 23 April A.D. 725 (*Saxon Chronicle*).]

[Note: [Col. 0972C] Of whom Edbert [reigned] twenty-three years, Edelbert eleven. What Malmesbury relates of Wihtred’s sons is somewhat obscure. He probably means that Æthelbert reigned eleven years after Edbert’s death, having already reigned jointly with him for twenty-three years, and that Alric held the kingdom for thirty-four years after Æthelbert’s death. This agrees very well with other authorities, according to whom, after Wihtred’s death, his sons Edbert and Æthelbert jointly succeeded to the kingdom. The former died in 748, and the latter ruled alone until 761; he was succeeded by Alric, who died in 794.]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] “Twenty-three.” a. s. c. e. l.; “thirty-three,” d. m.]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] Alric. Alric died in 794, and with him Hengist’s line failed. He is commonly regarded as the last king of Kent.]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] “Following.” a. c. d. e. l. m.; “holding,” s., apparently more correctly.]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] “Inglorious.” s.; a. c. d. e. l. m. read “ingloriously.”]

[Note: [Col. 0972D] “The glory of their times.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “the brilliance of their fortune,” c.]

[Col. 0973A] After them the noble stock of kings withered away, the high-born blood grew cold. Then every most shameless man, whom either eloquence had furnished with riches or faction with terror, began to pant after tyranny; then those unworthy of royal distinction abused it. Edelbert, also called Pren, after ruling the men of Kent for two years (A.D. 794), attempted enterprises against the Mercians beyond his strength; captured by them, he gave his hands to chains and his body to captivity. Released not long afterwards by his enemies but not received back by his own people, he died by an uncertain end. Then Cuthred (A.D. 796), heir to the same calamity and faction, reigned for eight years in name alone. Next Baldred (A.D. 805), a miscarriage of royal dignity, after occupying Kent for eighteen years, was defeated in battle by Egbert, king of the West Saxons, and went into exile. Thus the kingdom of Kent, which had stood from the year 444 of the Lord’s Incarnation, passed after 375 years into another’s power.

[Note: [Col. 0973C] Edelbert, also Pren. Eadberht, surnamed Præn, obtained the kingdom of Kent in A.D. 794; he was captured by the Mercians in 796, who put out his eyes and cut off his hands. Elsewhere Malmesbury asserts that Cenwulf, moved by pity, brought him from captivity to the altar at Winchcombe, and that Cuthred, whom Offa had made king of Kent, attached himself to royal clemency.]

[Note: [Col. 0973C] “Attempted.” a. d. f. l. m.; “dared,” s. c.]

[Note: [Col. 0973C] “Occupied.” d. e. l. m.; “will have occupied,” a.; “had besieged rather than ruled,” s.; “occupied rather than ruled,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “Fourth.” c. d. e. l. m.; “sixth,” a.; “ninth,” s., apparently more correctly.]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “Seventy.” a. s. c. e. l.; “sixty,” d. m.]

But because, in briefly tracing the descent of the first kingdom to grow from the English, we have struck, as it were, a spark from the ashes of antiquity, my pen will now examine the kingdom of the West Saxons. Though it began second after the first kingdom, at a long interval, it is the one which, flourishing in unconquered strength through many ages until the coming of the Normans, while the rest decayed, swallowed up the others—if I may so speak—as they were strangled, with its greedy jaws. Therefore, if I carry its account in sequence down to Egbert, I shall weave in some notices concerning the other two kingdoms, avoiding the weariness of excessive length; when these have reached their proper conclusion in the first book, the second will consider the West Saxons alone.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “We have struck a spark from the ashes of antiquity.” a. s. d. l. m.; e. reads “have struck out or elicited”; c. “have elicited the spark of antiquity.”]

## CONCERNING THE KINGDOM OF THE WEST SAXONS

§ 16. The kingdom of the West Saxons, than which Britain saw none either more magnificent or more enduring, first sprang from a certain Cerdic and soon rose to great eminence. German by nation and of illustrious ancestors—being the tenth from Woden—he had nourished great ambitions amid domestic conflicts, and resolved to leave his native country and enlarge his fame by arms. Daring to devise this plan with his son Cynric, and with the young man’s assent—he who pressed his father onward in the nearest steps toward glory—he crossed into Britain with forces in five keels. This occurred in the year 495 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the eighth after Hengist’s death. On the very day he was met in battle by the Britons; but as a man experienced in old warfare, he easily crushed the onrushing multitude and compelled it to flee. By that success he secured for himself a deep and lasting safety, and for the provincials peace; for, believing that they would never again be attacked after that day, they willingly submitted to his authority.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] The kingdom of the West Saxons. From the beginning the kings of that region called themselves kings of the Gewisse, their native tribe; for Cerdic traced his descent in the third degree from Gewis. Later they called themselves kings of the West Saxons, and later still kings both of the West Saxons and of the men of Kent. For the extent of their kingdom, see below, Book I, and Florence of Worcester, Appendix to the *Chronicle*.]

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “Than which.” a. d. e. l. m.; “nor,” c., as immediately below.]

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “With.” a. c. d. e. l. m.; omitted by s.]

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “Into Britain … crossed.” Cerdic and Cynric landed at a place called Cerdices-ora. (*Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 495.)]

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “And on that very day.” s. c. d. e. l. m.; “on that same day also,” a.]

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “Deep.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; omitted by c.]

Yet he did not spend his time in idle leisure, but rather extended frequent victories in every direction. In the twenty-fourth year after his arrival, he gained sovereignty over the western part of the island, which they call Wessex. Having exercised it for fifteen years, he fulfilled his destiny, and the whole kingdom, except the island of Wight, passed to his son. For that island, by the grant of royal generosity, fell under the power of his grandson Wihtgar. Wihtgar, dear to his uncle alike through nearness of blood and military skill, acquired first a renowned principality and afterwards burial in that same island. Cynric, no less valiant than his father, passed on a kingdom somewhat enlarged to his son Ceawlin after twenty-six years (A.D. 560).

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “Wessex.” The beginning of the kingdom of the West Saxons is also assigned to 519, according to the *Saxon Chronicle*.]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] “Having exercised it for fifteen years.” a. d. e. l. m.; “for sixteen,” s.; “who [reigned] sixteen,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] Wihtgar. Cerdic and Cynric took the island of Wight in 530 and gave it to two of their nephews, Stuf and Wihtgar. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] “His grandson.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; omitted by c.]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] “Dear.” d. e. l. m.; “of the flesh,” a.; after *dear*, s. c. add, “for he was his sister’s son.”]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] “Burial.” Wihtgar died in 544 and was buried at Carisbrooke. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] “Twenty-six.” s. c. e.; “twenty-four,” a. d. l. m.]

## CONCERNING CEAWLIN (A.D. 560)

§ 17. The annals exalt to envy his most distinguished strength in battle, since he was a cause of amazement to the English, hatred to the Britons, and destruction to both. I shall set down brief examples. He soundly attacked Æthelberht, king of the men of Kent—otherwise worthy of praise, but then, claiming first place for himself on account of his family’s antiquity and consequently invading others’ territories all the more greedily—and, after routing his forces, drove him back to his own land. He pursued with hostile zeal the Britons who, in the times of his father and grandfather, had escaped destruction at Gloucester, Cirencester, and Bath either by the shield of a pretended submission or by the obstacle of walled enclosures; he stripped them of their cities and thrust them into rugged and wooded places, where they remain even now.

[Note: [Col. 0975C] “Drove [him] back.” Ceawlin repelled Æthelberht, king of the men of Kent, in the battle of Wimbledon, A.D. 568.]

[Note: [Col. 0975C] See the *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 577.]

[Note: [Col. 0975C] “Hostile.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “eagerly,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0975C] “Pursued.” s. c. d. e. m.; “persecuted,” a. l.]

Yet amid these events, because the fatal die deceives mortals with uncertain casts upon the gaming-board of this life, domestic grief clouded such successes in war. In short, when Cutha, his brother, was cut off by an untimely death, and Cutha’s son of the same name was killed in battle before Ceawlin himself—both young men of admirable promise—he sighed more than once that much had been taken away from his good fortune. At last he himself, an exile from his kingdom in his final days, presented to his enemies a pitiable spectacle of himself. For since he had sounded, as it were, a trumpet-call to hatred against himself on both sides, English and Britons alike conspired at Wodnesdic; his army was slaughtered in the thirty-first year, he was stripped of his kingdom and went into exile, and immediately died. Then his nephews, the sons of Cutha, guided the wavering reins of the kingdom: Ceolric for five years (A.D. 593), and Ceolwulf for fourteen. The latter, lower in rank but superior in valour, spent his whole life in wars, never yielding any place to cowardice, but defending and extending what was his.

[Note: [Col. 0975C] Cutha. Cutha and his son fell in a battle fought at Fretherne, in Gloucestershire, A.D. 584. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

[Note: [Col. 0975C] “More than once.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “more than once over,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0975C] Wodnesdic. The site of this battle is uncertain. Some identify it with Wansdyke in Wiltshire, others with Wemborough; according to Florence of Worcester it is called Wodnesbeorh, that is, Woden’s Mount. If the *Saxon Chronicle* is to be trusted, a great slaughter occurred at Woddesbeorge in 591, Ceawlin was expelled from his kingdom, and died in 593.]

[Note: [Col. 0975D] “Thirty-first.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “twenty-first,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Ceolric. He is called Ceol or Ceolus in the *Saxon Chronicle*, but in Florence of Worcester. He succeeded to the kingdom after expelling his uncle Ceawlin in A.D. 591 and reigned five years.]

[Note: [Col. 0975D] “Five.” a. d. e. l. m.; “six,” s. c.]

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Ceolwulf. Ceolwulf began to reign in A.D. 597 and died in 611, having held the kingdom for fourteen years.]

[Note: [Col. 0975D] “Years.” s. c. d. e. l. m.; omitted by a.]

§ 18. After him, Ceolric’s sons Cynegils and Cwichelm [Col. 0976A] put on the royal diadem together in equal measure (A.D. 611). Both were vigorous men, both competing with one another in reciprocal offices of devotion; so that, because of a harmony unusual among kings, they were a wonder to their contemporaries and an example to posterity. They waged very many wars, with a valour or moderation that one could scarcely distinguish, against both the Britons and Penda, king of the Mercians—a man, as shall be said in its place, thoroughly suited to the frenzy of war. When he had crossed his proper boundaries in an attempt to annex Cirencester to his dominion, he could not bear the attack of the united kings and fled with a few men (A.D. 628).

Cwichelm, however, is stained by no small fault, because he sought to attack Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, a man of proven wisdom, through a hired assassin. But if one considers that pagan maxim, “Who would ask whether an enemy uses deceit or valour?”, he may easily be excused for doing nothing beyond customary practice in wishing, by whatever means, to remove from the world one who harassed his power. For Edwin had earlier cut off many portions of the kingdom of the West Saxons; and then, provoked by the injury received, because their hatreds had flared up anew, he inflicted many losses upon the provincials.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] After him, Ceolric’s sons Cynegils and Cwichelm. Compare Malmesbury’s account with Florence of Worcester and the *Saxon Chronicle*.]

[Note: [Col. 0976C] “Frenzy.” s. d. e. l. m.; “theft,” c.; “stealthy,” a.]

[Note: [Col. 0976C] Edwin. On Cwichelm’s design to kill Edwin, who escaped unharmed through the precaution of Lilla, his attendant, see Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, II.9, § 113, ed. English Historical Society, and the *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 626.]

[Note: [Col. 0976C] “Who would ask whether an enemy uses deceit or valour?” Virgil, *Aeneid* II.389.]

[Note: [Col. 0976C] “Since.” s. c. d. e. l. m.; “because,” a.]

The kings, however, survived; and not long afterwards heavenly teaching flowed into them through Bishop Birinus, in the twenty-fifth year of their reign and the fortieth after the coming of blessed Augustine. Cynegils was immediately converted and, softening his royal hauteur, gladly submitted himself to the bishop in baptism. Cwichelm resisted for a while, until bodily illness warned him not to neglect the salvation of his soul; emulating his colleague’s devotion, he too departed from the flesh in the same year (A.D. 636). Cynegils, however, six years later, having enjoyed the benefit of a long peace, ended his life in the thirty-first year of his reign (A.D. 643).

[Note: [Col. 0976C] “Afterwards through Birinus.” a. d. e. l. m.; “afterwards through blessed Birinus,” s.; “after blessed Birinus,” c. Birinus, an Italian by nation, was sent to England by Pope Honorius and made bishop at Dorchester. He died on 3 December A.D. 648; but according to the *Saxon Chronicle*, in A.D. 650.]

[Note: [Col. 0976C] “Heavenly teaching flowed into [them] through the bishop.” a. c. d. e. l. m.; s. reads “heavenly teaching shone upon the holy bishop.”]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] “Augustine.” a. c. d. e. l. m.; “Augustine, apostle of the English,” s.]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] “Immediately converted.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “therefore immediately converted,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] “And.” a. d. e. l. m.; omitted in s. c.]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] “Royal.” a. s. c. d. l. m.; “of the kingdom,” e.]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] In baptism. Cynegils was baptized by Bishop Birinus at Dorchester in Oxfordshire in 635; Oswald, king of Northumbria, was his sponsor. See Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, III.7, § 168, ed. English Historical Society; and the *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 635.]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] Cwichelm. Cwichelm was baptized in the year of the Lord 636 and died in the same year. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] “Thirty-first.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “twentieth,” c.]

§ 19. His son Cenwalh succeeded to the inheritance, a ruler to be ranked with the worst princes at the beginning of his reign and with the best in its middle and end. On first assuming power, as a young man made insolent by royal luxury, he put his father’s achievements in second place and, without hesitation, renounced Christianity and lawful marriage. But Penda, king of the Mercians, whose sister he had repudiated, attacked and defeated him in war, and he fled to the king of the East Angles. There, persuaded to the faith both by his own calamity and by his host’s diligence, after three years he recovered his strength and his kingdom, and gave his citizens the pleasing marvel of his conversion. He became so powerful that he who formerly had not even defended his own borders with impunity now extended his dominion everywhere.

[Note: [Col. 0977C] “Succeeded … Cenwalh.” Cynewalh succeeded his father in A.D. 643. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] “Placed.” a. d. e. l. m.; “was placing,” s. c.]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] But Penda. Cynewalh was expelled from his kingdom by Penda in A.D. 645. (*Saxon Chronicle*; see also Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, III.7.)]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] “Received.” e.; “recovered,” a. s. c. d. l. m.]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] Conversion. Cynewalh was baptized by Felix, bishop of Dunwich, in A.D. 646.]

The Britons, chafing at the consciousness of their ancient liberty and therefore repeatedly plotting rebellion, he thoroughly crushed twice: first at a place called Wirtgernesburg, and secondly beside the hill called Pene. And in Wulfhere, Penda’s son, avenging his father’s injury (A.D. 661), he cut away a great part of that ruler’s kingdom. He was so religious that, the first of his predecessors, he built at Winchester the most beautiful church of that age for God; in establishing an episcopal see there, later generations followed the same tracks, though with more imposing skill.

[Note: [Col. 0977C] “Now everywhere.” a. d. e. l. m.; “nor farther before,” s.; “now somewhat farther,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] First at the place … Pene. s. d. e. m.; c. reads *Pentie*; a. l. omit the whole passage.]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] Wirtgernesburg. The location of this battle remains unknown. In the *Saxon Chronicle*, Cynewalh is said to have fought at Bradford on the river Avon in A.D. 652.]

[Note: [Col. 0977C] “Which is called Pene.” Pen, in Somersetshire; the battle was fought in A.D. 658. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

[Note: [Col. 0977D] “Cut away.” a. d. e. l. m.; “fined,” s. c.]

[Note: [Col. 0977D] At Winchester. [The church] of Saint Peter, Winchester: it was called the Old Church, to distinguish it from the New Monastery (New Minster), which had been erected at the beginning of the tenth century. In A.D. 659 the diocese of Dorchester was divided into two parts. Agilbert remained at Dorchester, and Wini was established at Winchester; but in the following year he obtained authority over the entire province.]

[Note: [Col. 0977D] “Age.” a. d. e. l. m.; “time,” s. c.]

[Note: [Col. 0977D] “Built.” s. c. d. e. l. m.; “will have built,” a.]

[Note: [Col. 0977D] “Same.” a. s. d. e. l.; “these,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 0977D–0978C] But because … “I shall return.” The text from “But because” to “I shall return,” § 29, occurs in d. e. f. m.; a. s. g. h. l. read, “so generous that nothing”; c. k. read, “and he proved generous not only in ecclesiastical matters but also in secular matters, so that nothing,” omitting the whole text from “But because” through “I shall return.”]

But since we have touched upon the times of Cenwalh, and there has presented itself an occasion to speak of the monastery of Glastonbury, I shall set forth from its origin the rise and development of that church, gathering together as much as I can from the heap of records. Annals of sound credibility relate that Lucius, king of the Britons, sent to Pope Eleutherius, the thirteenth in succession after blessed Peter, asking him to illumine the darkness of Britain with the light of Christian preaching. A king of lofty spirit, he undertook a deed altogether worthy of great praise: he freely sought a faith scarcely heard of, though it was then persecuted almost everywhere by kings and peoples. Therefore preachers came to Britain, sent by Eleutherius; their effectiveness will endure for ever, though the great distance of time has consumed their names. By their labour the ancient church of Saint Mary at Glastonbury was established, as faithful antiquity through successive ages has not failed to report.

[Note: [Col. 0978C] Glastonbury. Malmesbury wrote a history of the Church of Glastonbury, from which this passage was extracted. That work was published in Gale’s Collection, vol. III, and by Hearne.]

[Note: [Col. 0978C] Lucius, king of the Britons. Various authors have expended great learning and labour in proving that a king named Lucius once reigned in Britain and was converted to the Christian faith. As many writers—no fewer than twenty-six—as opinions exist concerning the date of his conversion.]

[Note: [Col. 0978C] To Eleutherius. According to Muratori, Eleutherius presided over the Roman Church from 170 to 185.]

[Note: [Col. 0978C–0978D] “Sent.” Elvanus and Meduinus are named as those sent to Rome. The letter supposedly written at that time by King Lucius, and the cause of his mission, are examined by Ussher (*Britannicarum Ecclesiarum Antiquitates*, pp. 24, 27). A copy of this letter is found in Bishop Godwin’s work, p. 22, Canterbury edition, 1743.]

[Note: [Col. 0978D] “Though … consumed their names.” They were Faganus and Duvianus, said to have baptized Lucius and many of his subjects.]

There are also writings of no small authority, found in certain places, to this effect: “The hands of other men did not make the church of Glastonbury; rather, the disciples of Christ themselves built it.” Nor is this far from the truth; for if Philip the apostle preached to the Gauls, as Freculf says in Book II, chapter 4, it may be believed that he also cast seeds of preaching across the Ocean. But lest I seem to disappoint my readers’ expectation with the trifles of conjecture, leaving the disputed matters unresolved, I shall gird myself to recount deeds of solid truth.

[Note: [Col. 0978D] Freculf … says. Freculf, a monk of Fulda and afterwards bishop of Lisieux, lived in the ninth century and wrote a *Chronicle* divided into two parts. The first, from the beginning of the world to Christ’s birth, comprises seven books; the latter, from Christ’s birth to the arrival of the Franks and Lombards, around the year 600, is completed in five books (*Freculphus, Chron.*, vol. II, book II, ch. 4, p. 448, 8vo, Heidelberg, 1597).]

[Note: [Col. 0978D] “Conjectures.” d. m.; “conjecture,” e.]

## CONCERNING THE CHURCH OF GLASTONBURY

§ 20. The church of which we speak, which because of its antiquity is famously called by the English *Ealdechirche*, that is, “Old Church,” at first was made of wattles; from its very beginning it exhaled and breathed forth, I know not what, a divine holiness into the whole country, although great reverence arose from its unsightly appearance. Hence streams of people flowing there along every path; hence gatherings of the wealthy, who laid aside their pomp; hence the frequent lingering of religious persons and men of letters. For, as we have received from our elders, Gildas, a historian neither dull nor witless, to whom the Britons owe whatever knowledge they possess among other nations, spent many years there, captivated by the holiness of the place.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Gildas. According to Malmesbury, in his book *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury*, the historian Gildas died in A.D. 512 and was buried at Glastonbury. This agrees with what is asserted in the *Life of Gildas* by Caradoc of Llancarfan, but not with what may be inferred from this historian’s own words (*On the Ruin of Britain*, § 26), namely that he was born in the very year of the siege of Caer Badon, which cannot now with certainty be assigned earlier than 516. This chronological discrepancy cannot be reconciled unless one assumes that there were two historians writing at approximately the same period. For fuller discussion, see Stevenson’s preface to Gildas, published by the English Historical Society.]

That church, then, is the oldest of all the churches I know in England, and from this received its surname. Within it are preserved the bodily remains of many saints, some of whom we shall mention in due course; no part of the shrine is free from the ashes of the blessed. So thickly is the pavement overlaid with polished stone, so thickly are the sides of the altar, and the altar itself, above and below, piled with relics. One may also observe stones in the pavement, deliberately set opposite each other in triangles or squares and sealed with lead; if I believe that some sacred mystery is contained beneath them, I do no wrong to religion.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] “By.” e.; omitted in d. m.]

[Note: [Col. 0979D] “Beneath which.” e.; “beneath tombs which,” d. m.]

The antiquity and multitude of the saints have inspired such reverence for the place that scarcely anyone dares to keep night-vigils there, and scarcely anyone dares by day to spit out an excess of phlegm, lest, conscious of such mocking foulness, he shudder through his whole body. No one has brought a hunting bird into the adjoining cemetery or led in quadrupeds and departed unharmed in his person or property. All whom present memory embraces, save one, among those who prayed there before being tested by iron or water, have rejoiced in their deliverance. If anyone nearby thought to erect a building that by its shadow would begrudge the church its light, it became liable to ruin. It is sufficiently well known that the inhabitants of that district have no oath more sacred or more commonly used than “by the Old Church,” and that they avoid nothing more, for fear of swift vengeance, than swearing falsely. We shall support with testimonies, in the book which I wrote on the antiquity of that same church, the truth of the statements we have made as the course of years allows.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] “Mocking foulness.” e.; “unfoulness,” d. m.]

[Col. 0979C] [Note: [Col. 0979D] Being tested by iron or water. See Spelman under *Ordalium*.]

§ 21. Meanwhile, it has become plain why it is rightly called a heavenly sanctuary on earth, a repository of so many saints. There are many proofs, which I omit lest they weary the reader, of how venerable this place was even to the foremost men of the country, so that they especially desired to await there, under the protection of the Mother of God, the day of Resurrection. I would gladly set forth one matter almost wholly unknown to all, if I could ascertain the truth: what the pyramids mean which, placed some feet from that church, stand before the cemetery of the monks.

[Col. 0980A] The taller pyramid, and the one nearer the church, has five stages and is twenty-eight feet high. Although it threatens collapse because of its excessive age, it nevertheless preserves certain memorials of antiquity which can plainly be read, though not fully understood. On the uppermost stage is an image made in episcopal dress. On the second is an image displaying royal pomp, and the letters: *Her Sexi et Bliswerh*. On the third likewise are the names *Wencrest, Bantomp Winewegn*. On the fourth, *Bate, Wulfred,* and *Eanfled*. On the fifth, which is also the lowest, there is an image and this inscription: *Logor, Weaslieas, et Bregden, Swelwes, Hiwingendes, Bearn*.

The other pyramid is twenty-six feet high and has four stages, upon which are read: *Centwine*, Bishop *Hedde*, *Bregored*, and *Beorward*. I do not rashly determine what these things signify, but conjecture that the bones of those whose names are read outside are contained inside the hollowed stones.

[Note: [Col. 0980D] “Letters.” e.; “these letters,” d. m.]

[Note: [Col. 0980D] “Wulfred.” d. e. m.; “Wulfled,” f.]

[Note: [Col. 0980D] Centwine. Centwine became king of the West Saxons in A.D. 676 and died in A.D. 685.]

[Note: [Col. 0980D] Bishop Hedde. Bishop of Winchester: he succeeded in 676 and died on 7 July A.D. 705.]

[Note: [Col. 0980D] What these signify. Compare the names of the twelve monks who are said to have established their seat at Glastonbury upon Saint Patrick’s arrival: namely, Wencreth, Bantcommeweng, Loyor, Wellias, Breden, Swelwes, Brumbam, Hyregaam, Brenwal, Adelwared, Hinloernius, and Hin.]

[Note: [Col. 0980D] “In hollowed stones … bones.” The Saxons sometimes used pyramids for burials. See *Anglia Sacra*; Osbern, *On the Life of Saint Dunstan*, part II, p. 110.]

[Note: [Col. 0980D] Logor. e.; Logwor, d. f. m.]

Certainly this Logor is truly asserted to be the man from whose name the place once called *Logweresberh*, now called Sharp Hill, received its designation; Bregden, likewise, gave his name to Brentacnol and Brentemeirs; and Bregored and Beorward were abbots of that same place in the time of the Britons. Concerning them and the others who may occur, the discourse will henceforth range over a freer field. For it will now endeavour to set forth the succession of abbots, and what was assigned to the monastery under each of them and by which king.

§ 22. First, then, we shall draw a little from the history of blessed Patrick, from whom the sequence of our memorials began to shine forth. For when the Saxons were harassing the Britons’ peace, and the Pelagians assaulting their faith, Saint Germanus of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0980D] St Germanus of Auxerre. St Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, came to England with Lupus, bishop of Troyes, to preach the faith in the year 429; his second mission occurred in 449; he died at Ravenna in 449. About forty years after Germanus’s death, Constans, a presbyter of Lyons, wrote his Life, a work from which the accounts given by Bede (Ecclesiastical History, book I, chapters 17–21) of St Germanus’s mission to Britain are drawn almost word for word. Another Life of St Germanus was written in hexameter verse by Heiric, a monk of Auxerre, who died about the year 880.] brought aid against both. The former [Col. 0981A] he routed by the Alleluia chant [Note: [Col. 0981C] He routed them by the Alleluia chant. See Bede, book I, chapter 20, §45.]; the latter he struck down with evangelical and apostolic thunderbolts.

Then, preparing to return to his own country, he admitted Patrick to his familiar companionship; and, after some years, at Pope Celestine’s command, sent him to the Irish as a preacher. Hence it is written in the Chronicles: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation four hundred and twenty-five, Saint Patrick is ordained by Pope Celestine for Ireland [Note: [Col. 0981D] By Celestine, etc. According to the Saxon Chronicle, St Patrick was sent to Ireland by Pope Celestine to preach baptism in the year of the Lord 430.].” Likewise: “In the year four hundred and thirty-three, the island of Ireland is converted to the faith of Christ through the preaching of Saint Patrick, with many miracles.”

He, therefore, diligently carrying out the commission laid upon him, and returning to his homeland in his last days, made landfall in Cornwall upon his altar [Note: [Col. 0981D] Upon his altar … made landfall. It has been handed down that St Patrick sailed from Ireland upon his altar and made landfall at Padstow in Cornwall (Cornouailles). Gough’s *Camden*, I, 19.], which even today is held in great reverence by the inhabitants because [Col. 0981B] of its holiness and usefulness, because it heals the sick. Thus, coming to Glastonbury [Note: [Col. 0981D] Thus coming to Glastonbury. St Patrick is said to have come to Glastonbury in 449, and there to have found twelve monks—the successors of those whom Joseph of Arimathea had first established there—with whom he spent thirty-nine years of his life. When he died and was buried there, the church, which had been dedicated to the Virgin Mary alone, was consecrated jointly to her and St Patrick. Archbishop Ussher demonstrated quite decisively that St Patrick neither lived at Glastonbury nor was buried there. Malmesbury wrote the Life of St Patrick in two books, but no manuscript copy of it is now known. Leland, however, published extracts from it (*Collectanea* III, 273, London, 1770, octavo).], and becoming there a monk and abbot, after some years yielded to nature.

All doubt concerning this assertion was removed by the vision of a certain brother. After the blessed man’s death, when memory had begun to waver as to whether he had been a monk and abbot there, and the question was frequently debated, the brother was confirmed by the following oracle. Falling asleep, he seemed to hear someone reading, after many of Patrick’s miracles, these words: “He was therefore adorned here with the sanctity of the metropolitan pallium; afterwards, indeed, here he became monk and abbot.” Moreover, to one not fully trusting the statement, the reader showed what he had said written in golden letters.

Patrick therefore died [Col. 0981C] in the one hundred and eleventh year of his age, in the four hundred and seventy-second year of the Lord’s incarnation, the forty-seventh year after he had been sent to Ireland. He rests on the right side of the altar of the Old Church, in a stone pyramid which the diligence of later generations clothed in silver. Hence [Col. 0982A] the Irish adopted the custom of frequenting the place to kiss the relics of their patron.

§ 23. It is also a very widely reported tradition that Saint Indract [Note: [Col. 0982C] St Indract. Malmesbury also wrote the Life of St Indract, namely the *Passion of Saint Indract*, which has never been printed. A very fine manuscript copy of this work is preserved in the Bodleian Library. It was abridged in a work by John of Tynemouth entitled *Nova Legenda Angliae*, published under the title *Capgrave’s Legenda Nova Angliae*, fol. 188b, London, 1516.] and blessed Brigid, distinguished natives of Ireland, once came here. Whether Brigid—after leaving certain of her insignia, namely a necklace, a bag, and weaving implements, which are still displayed in remembrance of her holiness and cure various diseases—returned home or found her rest there is uncertain. That the other was martyred near Glastonbury with seven companions, and afterwards translated into the Old Church, will become clear from the course of the narrative.

§ 24. Benignus [Note: [Col. 0982D] Benignus. Malmesbury also wrote a book entitled *Miracles of Saint Benignus*, abridged by John of Tynemouth. See Capgrave’s *Nova Legenda Angliae*, fol. 26. In his *History of Glastonbury* he asserts that this Benignus succeeded St Patrick in the abbacy in A.D. 460, and that his bones were translated to Glastonbury in the year 901 (? 1091).] succeeded Patrick in the office of abbot, though for how many years is uncertain. Who he was, however, and what he was called in his native language, is elegantly expressed by verses written in his epitaph at Ferramere:

> In this stone are laid the bones of Father Beonna,  
> Who in ancient time was father of the monks here.  
> The Irish declare that he was perhaps once Patrick’s attendant,  
> And call him Beonna by name.

How great was, and is, his favour with God is proclaimed by the mighty works of his former life and of his later translation into the greater church.

§ 25. How highly the great David, archbishop of the Menevians [Note: [Col. 0982D] David, archbishop of Menevia. David, archbishop of Caerleon, transferred his see to Menevia; his successors, in veneration of his memory, adopted the title “archbishops of St David’s.” Godwin assigns his death to the year of the Lord 642, but Malmesbury (*Antiquities of the Church of Glastonbury*) assigns it to 546. According to the same authority, David’s body was translated to Glastonbury four hundred and twenty years after his death, in A.D. 936.], esteemed this place is too well known to require illumination by my account. He confirmed the antiquity and holiness of the church by a divine oracle. Intending its dedication, he came to the place with seven bishops, of whom he was chief. When all that the service required had been prepared, on the night preceding what he thought would be the feast, he gave himself to sleep.

His every faculty thus relaxed into rest, he saw the Lord Jesus [Col. 0983A] standing by and gently inquiring why he had come. When David had disclosed the reason without hesitation, the Lord recalled him from his intention, saying: “Since the church has long ago been dedicated by myself in honour of my mother, this sacrament ought not to be profaned by human repetition.” At the same time, he seemed to pierce the palm of his hand with his finger, and added: “Let him have this sign that what I have anticipated doing ought not to be repeated. Yet, because his intention sprang not so much from presumption as from devotion, the punishment shall not be prolonged. In short, on the following morning, when at Mass he is about to say, ‘with him, and through him, and in him,’ the full vigour of health shall be restored to him.”

Awakened from sleep by these terrors, the bishop was at that moment made pale by ulcerous discharge; afterward he found the prophecy true. Yet, lest he should seem to have done nothing, he speedily built and dedicated another church. Whether this eminent and incomparable man died there or ended his life in his own see, I regard as uncertain. For some affirm that he is with blessed Patrick [Note: [Col. 0983D] For some affirm that he is with him. `e`; “for men of religious memory, worthy of remembrance, affirm that he is with him,” `d m`.]; and the Welsh, by frequent acts of prayer and much discourse, certainly maintain and confirm this, producing as evidence that Bishop Bernard [Note: [Col. 0983D] Bernard. In the *Antiquities of the Church of Glastonbury* one reads: “Bernard, bishop of the valley of Rosina.” Sharpe thinks that he is none other than Bernard, bishop of St David’s, A.D. 1115.] sought him once and again and, despite many protests, did not find him. Let this be enough said concerning blessed David.

§ 26. Much time intervened, and Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Into,” `e`; omitted in `d m`.], sent by blessed Gregory, came into Britain in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 596 [Note: [Col. 0983D] A.D. 596.]. The tradition of the elders asserts that Paulinus [Col. 0983C]—his fellow-soldier in preaching, formerly archbishop of York and later bishop of Rochester [Note: [Col. 0983D] Paulinus … bishop of Rochester. Paulinus was sent with others to Augustine bearing letters and the pallium in A.D. 601. He was consecrated bishop of York on 21 July 625. He departed the Northumbrian region with the wife and children of King Edwin to Eadbald, king of Kent, and became bishop of Rochester in 633. He died on 10 October, A.D. 644.]—covered the fabric of the church, as we have said, which had long been made of wattle, with wooden boarding. The skill of that eminently praiseworthy man achieved the remarkable result that nothing was lost of its holiness while much was added to its adornment. Indeed, the more august ornamentation of churches is accustomed to kindle even the most brutish minds to prayer and bend even the stiffest necks to supplication.

§ 27. In the year of the incarnation [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Of the incarnation,” `e`; “of the Lord’s incarnation,” `d m`.] 601—that is, the fifth after the arrival of blessed Augustine—the king [Col. 0984A] of Devon [Note: [Col. 0983D] King of Devon. `e f`; “a king named Dero,” `d m`. —King of Devonshire.] granted to the Old Church, which is situated there, the land called Ineswitrin, at the petition of Abbot Worgrez, comprising five hides. “I, Bishop Maworn, wrote this charter. I, Worgrez, abbot of the same [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Of the same,” `e`; “of it,” `d m`.] place, subscribed.”

§ 28. The antiquity of the document declares that it does not know who this king was. Yet that he was a Briton is beyond doubt, since he called Glastonbury *Ineswitrin* in his own language; for it is established that this is its British name among them. It is also worth observing how ancient is the church which was even then called the Old Church. Its abbots indeed, besides Worgrez, were Lademund and Bregored, bearing names that betray British barbarism. The times of their prelacies are obscure; but their names [Col. 0984B] and offices are plainly visible in the greater church, as a painting beside the altar reveals [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Revealing,” `e`; “extending,” `d m`.]. Happy, then, are the inhabitants of that place, whom the very reverence due to the sanctuary invites to the ordering of their conduct. I would believe that none of these perish from heaven, when, after they have left the body, the praise or advocacy of so many patrons receives them.

§ 29. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 670 [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Seventieth,” `e`; “forty-ninth,” `d m`. [Col. 0984D] See the copy of Cynewalh’s charter, marked A.D. 670, published in Kemble, *Codex Diplomaticus Aevi Saxonici*, p. 10, no. 7. This charter appears to be spurious.], in the twenty-ninth year of his reign, Ceonwalh granted Ferramere, of two hides, to Bertwald, abbot of Glastonbury, through the intervention of Archbishop Theodore. This same Bertwald, renouncing Glastonbury despite the opposition of the king and of the bishop of the diocese, withdrew to govern the monastery of Raculf [Note: [Col. 0984D] Raculf. Reculver in Kent. See Bede, book V, chapter 8, §375.]. Accordingly, Bertwald—most renowned for the fame of his religion, distinguished by nobility of birth [Col. 0984C] (being the son of a brother of King Æthelred of the Mercians), and near Canterbury by the advantageous situation of his place—succeeded Theodore, when the archbishop died, in that see [Note: [Col. 0984D] Theodore, etc. Archbishop Theodore died on 29 September A.D. 690; Bertwald was elected archbishop of Canterbury on 1 July A.D. 692.].

Let this suffice for what I have said concerning the antiquity of the church of Glastonbury [Note: [Col. 0984D] “Let this suffice for what I have said concerning Glastonbury …” What is related here about Glastonbury is drawn in summary from Malmesbury’s own *History of the Antiquities of the Church of Glastonbury*, written no earlier than 1129. It occurs in four of the better manuscripts consulted, namely `d e f m`.]. Now I shall return in order to Kenewalch, who was so generous that he denied no estates to his kinsmen, since with high-minded liberality he shared with his brother’s son almost a third part of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0984D] “Shared with his brother’s son …” According to the Saxon Chronicle, Cynewalh gave his kinsman Cuthred 120,000 jugera of land, equivalent to approximately 300,000 acres.]. The most holy bishops of his province stimulated these royal qualities of mind [Note: [Col. 0984D] “Royal,” `s c d e`; “of a king,” `a l m`.] by the spur of their admonitions [Note: [Col. 0984D] “Admonitions,” `s c d e`; “warnings,” `a l`.]: Angilbert [Col. 0985A] [Note: [Col. 0985C] Angilbert. Ægilbert was consecrated bishop of Dorchester in A.D. 650. Having resigned the episcopal office in 661, he withdrew among the Northumbrians, and later accepted the episcopal see of Paris. See Bede, book III, chapter 28.], of whom you will find much worthy of approval in the deeds of the English [Note: [Col. 0985C] “In the deeds of the English you will find what you may approve,” `d e`; “in the deeds of the bishops of the English you will find what you may approve,” `a`; “you will find [it] in Bede’s deeds of the English,” `s c`. —See Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book III, chapters 25 and 28.], and his nephew Leutherius [Note: [Col. 0985C] Leutherius. Leutherius, nephew of Bishop Ægilbert, obtained episcopal authority over the West Saxons in A.D. 670 (*Saxon Chronicle*). Wini was expelled in A.D. 666; Bede writes of this matter (book III, chapter 7, §170): “And so the province of the West Saxons was for no small time without a bishop.” Leutherius remained bishop for seven years, says Godwin; he died in 676 and had Heddi as successor. See Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum*, book II, “On the Bishops of the West Saxons.”], who after him exercised the episcopal office in West Saxony for seven years [Note: [Col. 0985C] “For seven years in the episcopal office,” `a d e`; “in a seven-year episcopate,” `s c`; “for seven years in a seven-year episcopate,” `l`.].

I have not passed this over because Bede left nothing explicit regarding the years of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0985D] Bede left nothing explicit. Bede, book IV, chapter 12, §286.], and it seemed contrary to conscience to conceal what I learned from the Chronicles [Note: [Col. 0985D] From the Chronicles. See the Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 670.]. At the same time, an opportunity presented itself, which was to be embraced, to mention a praiseworthy man who, by an almost keen and divine insight of mind, raised the monastery of Malmesbury—in which we serve the term of our earthly sojourn—from a humble to a most flourishing state [Note: [Col. 0985D] “Raised,” `a d c l`; “advanced,” `s c`.]. This monastery had been established at exceedingly narrow expense by one Meildulf [Note: [Col. 0985D] “By Meildulf,” `c d e`; “by a certain Meildulf,” `a s l`. Meildulf was an Irish monk who founded a monastery of hermits at Malmesbury about the year 660. See Bede, book V, chapter 18, and Smith’s notes.], a Scot by nationality, as they say [Note: [Col. 0985D] “A Scot by nationality, as they say.” Here a distinction is present between the Scots who inhabit Ireland and the Scots who inhabit Britain.], a philosopher by learning [Note: [Col. 0986C] “A philosopher by learning,” `a s d e l`; “a philosopher by learning, as they say,” `c`.], and a monk by profession. Its inhabitants could scarcely procure their daily [Col. 0985B] sustenance. After long and careful deliberation, he entrusted it to Aldhelm, a monk of the same place, to be governed according to the authority then belonging to bishops. To remove every ground of doubt for later discourse in this matter, I shall insert here some of his words.

§ 30. “I, Leutherius, by the grace of God bishop (A.D. 672), governing the helm of the episcopate in Saxony [Note: [Col. 0986C] “Saxony,” `a s c e l`; “West Saxony,” `d m`.], was asked by the abbots who are known to preside with pastoral solicitude over the monastic body of monks under the jurisdiction of our diocese, that I should deem worthy to grant and bestow upon the priest Aldhelm the land called Meildulfesburh [Note: [Col. 0986C] Meildulfesburh. Malmesbury, so called from Maidulf.] for the regular conduct [Note: [Col. 0986C] “For conducting,” `a s c d l`; `e` reads either *regendam*, “for governing,” or *degendam*, “for living.”] of his life. In that place, indeed, from the first age of infancy and from the very beginning, he was instructed in the liberal studies of elementary letters [Note: [Col. 0986C] “Instructed,” `a s d e l`; omitted in `c`.], and nourished in the bosom of holy Mother Church [Col. 0986A], and led his life. This petition appears to be urged especially by fraternal charity; therefore, assenting to the prayers of the aforesaid abbots, constrained by a brotherly petition, I voluntarily grant that place to him and to his successors who shall follow with diligent devotion the holy Rule. Publicly enacted beside the river Bladon [Note: [Col. 0986C] Beside the river Bladon. This river is conjectured to be the Avon. See the copy of King Æthelbald’s charter (A.D. 718), which contains these words: “Land of six hides, beside the river called Bladaen, near the ford named Daeglesford.” (J. M. Kemble, *Codex Diplomaticus Aevi Anglo-Saxonici*, vol. I, p. 82, no. LXIX.) An ancient British city existed on the site where Malmesbury now stands.], on the seventh [Note: [Col. 0986C] “Seventh,” `a d e l`; “eighth,” `s c`.] day before the Kalends of September, in the six hundred and seventy-second year of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0986C] “Second,” `d e`; “fifth,” `a s c`; “first,” `m`.].”

§ 31. Thus, when the abbot’s enterprise was joined to the bishop’s favour, the resources of the monastery then rose immensely, and monks then gathered there from every quarter. People flocked to Aldhelm from every crossroads: some seeking holiness of life, others learning. For he was a man both simple in religion and manifold in learning [Col. 0986B], one who surpassed reputation by virtue, a drinker deep of the liberal arts, so that he was admirable in every particular and singular among all.

I am mistaken if the manuscripts of his *On Virginity* [Note: [Col. 0986C] Manuscripts of *On Virginity*. Aldhelm also wrote an excellent book *On Virginity*, modelled on Sedulius, in a double form, both hexameter verse and prose. Bede, book V, chapter 18, §410. The prose was published by Henry Wharton, 4°, 1693; and the verses in Canisius’s *Thesaurus Monumentorum*, vol. I, p. 709, Antwerp, 1725, folio; and Paris, 1676, octavo.]—testimonies to his immortal genius—do not bear this out; in my judgment nothing is sweeter or more splendid than they. Yet, such is the indolence of our age, they cause nausea in some, who fail to observe that modes of composition vary according to the customs of nations [Note: [Col. 0986D] “Who,” `e`; “to whom,” `d m`; “because,” `a s c l`.]. In short, the Greeks generally write intricately, the Romans circumspectly, the Gauls splendidly, the English pompously.

And indeed, because it is pleasing [Note: [Col. 0986D] “Because it is pleasing,” `a d e l`; “because it seems pleasing,” `s`; “which seems pleasing,” `c`.] to adhere to the favour of our forefathers and kindle memory from their examples, I would willingly unfold how great were the labours that this saint expended for the privilege of our church, and with how many miracles he marked his life, were it not that [Note: [Col. 0986D] “Because,” `a s d e l`; “that,” `c`.] I am called elsewhere. His deeds appear more clearly even to a bleary eye [Note: [Col. 0986C] [Note: [Col. 0986D] “Than our … brush.” Malmesbury wrote the Life of St Aldhelm, which forms book V of *The Deeds of the Bishops*; it was printed also in Gale’s collection and in *Anglia Sacra*, Wharton, part II, p. 1. Aldhelm died 25 May A.D. 709.] than they can be [Col. 0987A] sketched by our brush [Note: [Col. 0987C] “Brush,” `e`; “little brush,” `a c d l`; “paintbrush,” `s`.]. Countless signs now occurring at his memorial show those present the holiness of his former life. He has, then, his praises and the glory earned by his merits; let our discourse continue the history.

§ 32. Kenwalkius [Note: [Col. 0987C] Kenwalkius. Cynewalh died without offspring in A.D. 673. His widow Sexburh reigned after him for only one year and died at the beginning of 675.] died after thirty-one years and thought the disposal of the kingdom should be entrusted to his wife Sexburga. Nor did the woman lack spirit for undertaking the duties of rule: she herself raised new armies, kept the old ones under discipline, governed her subjects with clemency, and roared threats at her enemies; in every respect she acted so that nothing but her sex distinguished her. Yet life failed one whose aspirations exceeded womanly courage, when she had scarcely completed a year in power.

[Col. 0987B] § 33. Escuinus [Note: [Col. 0987C] Escuinus. Æscwin succeeded Queen Sexburh at the beginning of 675 and died at the end of 676 [Col. 0987D].] spent the following two years [Note: [Col. 0987C] Two-year period. `a s d e l`; “three-year period,” `c`.] in the kingdom, nearest in royal lineage, since he was a great-grandson of Cuthgils, the brother of Cynegils. On his departure—whether by his own death or by another’s violence, for I find neither clearly stated—Chentwinus, son of Cynegils, filled the vacant throne by legitimate succession [Note: [Col. 0987D] Chentwinus. Centwin succeeded to the kingdom in 676 and died in the year of the Lord 685.]. Both had well-known experience in war: the former struck the Mercians [Note: [Col. 0987D] The former struck the Mercians. Æscwin fought at Beadenhead (Bedwin) in 675. (*Saxon Chronicle*).], the latter the Britons [Note: [Col. 0987D] The latter struck the Britons. In the year of the Lord 682, Centwin drove the Britons to the sea. (*Saxon Chronicle*).] with grievous defeat [Note: [Col. 0987D] “Struck,” `d e`; “struck down,” `s`; “will have struck,” `a c l`.]. But they deserve pity because of the brevity of their time: the reign of the latter was extended no more than nine years, while the preceding account has completed that of the former at two years [Note: [Col. 0987D] “Two years,” `a s d l m`; “three years,” `c e`.]. This is according to the authority of the Chronicles; Bede, however, confirms that they did not rule over the undivided kingdom, but divided it between themselves [Note: [Col. 0987D] “Divided,” `a s d e l`; “divided the kingdoms,” `c`.; Note: [Col. 0987D] Bede confirms this. Book IV, chapter 12, §286.].

[Col. 0987C] § 34. Then Caedwalla [Note: [Col. 0987D] Caedwalla. Caedwalla began to reign in A.D. 685. (*Saxon Chronicle*).], a noble shoot of the royal stock, came forth conspicuously: a great-grandson of Cutha, the brother of Ceawlin, a young man of boundless promise, who knew how to let no opportunity for displaying courage pass by. Since he had already long provoked the anger of the rulers of his native land by his more vigorous efforts [Note: [Col. 0987D] “More vigorous,” `a s d e l`; “effective,” `s c`.], he was driven into exile by a conspiracy of factions.

Embracing this injury, he stripped the province of every soldier, carrying off [Col. 0988A] whatever was fit for war [Note: [Col. 0987D] “Carried off,” `a s d e l`; “gathered together,” `c`.]. For, whether their hearts had been softened by pity for his misfortunes or delighted by his courage, the whole youth followed the exile. King Æthelwalh of the South Saxons [Note: [Col. 0987D] King Æthelwalh. See Bede, book IV, chapter 15, §297.] first received the onset of the furious man [Note: [Col. 0987D] “Of the furious man,” `a s d e l`; omitted in `c`.], daring to join battle. But when he and all the people whom he had led were routed, he repented too late of his reckless purpose.

Having raised the spirits of his followers, Cædwalla [Note: [Col. 0988C] Chedwalla. `a s d e`; omitted in `c`.] returned in a carefully prepared yet unexpected move, assailed his rivals for power, and drove them from the kingdom. Thus, having held the kingdom for two years [Note: [Col. 0988C] “The kingdom,” `a s d e l`; “it,” `c`.], he accomplished notable deeds of war. Hostile to the South Saxons with a deadly [Note: [Col. 0988C] “Deadly,” `a s d e l`; “old,” `c`.] hatred, he destroyed Æthelwalh’s successor, Eadric, when he met him in renewed boldness. He came close to annihilating the island of Wight, which was rebelling in reliance on the Mercians. Moreover, attacking the people of Kent [Col. 0988B] [Note: [Col. 0988C] “The people of Kent,” `a d e l`; after “the people of Kent,” `s c` add: “as I have set forth above in treating their affairs.”], he gained repeated victories over them. Finally, as we said above [Note: [Col. 0988C] “As we said above,” `a s d e l`; omitted in `c`. —See §14.], after losing his brother [Note: [Col. 0988C] After losing his brother. See §35, note.], he departed from the region, consoling his loss with the abundant blood of its inhabitants.

Among these events it is difficult to relate how greatly, even before baptism, he served piety: he tithed for God all the spoils which by right of plunder he had transferred to his own use. Though we approve his intention in this, we disapprove the example, according to the saying: “He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who immolates a son in the sight of his father” [Note: [Col. 0988D] “He who offers …” Ecclesiasticus 34:24. For *immolat*, “immolates,” `c` has *victimat*, “offers as a victim.”].

As for his hastening to Rome to be baptized [Note: [Col. 0988D] To be baptized. Cadwalla abdicated and departed for Rome in A.D. 688. He was baptized by Pope Sergius on the vigil of Easter, A.D. 689, and died a few days later, on 20 April. Bede, book V, chapter 7, §372.], being there called Peter by Pope Sergius [Note: [Col. 0988D] “Pope,” `a d e l`; after “pope,” `s c` add “and baptized.”], and, still clothed in his white baptismal garments [Note: [Col. 0988D] “Still,” `a d e l`; “and still,” `s c`.; Note: [Col. 0988D] Still clothed in white. A catechumen was always baptized on Holy Saturday, that is, the vigil of Easter, and wore different garments until the first Sunday after Easter; hence the expression “the Sunday in White.”], happily undergoing the final judgment, this is too well known to require illumination by [Col. 0988C] my account.

§ 35. As he went to Rome, the kingdom was renewed through Ine [Note: [Col. 0988D] Ine. Ine assumed the kingdom in A.D. 688. (Saxon Chronicle.)], who, being the great-grandson of Cynegils through his brother Cuthbald, was admitted to the principate more because of the industry of his acquired virtue than because of descent from a line of succession [Note: [Col. 0988D] Admitted. a. s. c. e. l.; “was adopted,” d. m.]. He was a pattern of courage [Note: [Col. 0988D] A pattern of courage. d. e; “the unique pattern of courage,” a. s. e. l.], an image of prudence, and in religion you would not know his equal; ordering his life by these qualities, he gained favour at home and respect abroad.
