Thus, having exercised power for two years short of forty [Note: [Col. 0989B] “Two years short of forty.” a. c. d. e. l.; “short of sixty,” s.—According to Bede, Ine reigned thirty-seven years. Bede, § 373.], he grew old in security, without fear of any plots, a most holy attractor of public affection.

His first expedition was against the Kentish, against whom his anger had not yet ceased to rage because of the burning of Mul [Note: [Col. 0989B] On the burning of Mul. Mul perished by fire in A.D. 687. (Saxon Chronicle.)]. The provincials dared resist for a little while [Note: [Col. 0989B] “For a little while.” a. d. e. l.; “for a brief while,” s.; “little,” c.], but, after trying every means [Note: [Col. 0989B] “After trying every means.” a. s. c. d. l. m.; e omits *trying*.] and expending their strength to the wind, finding no remedy in their hearts that could avail their cowardice, they took counsel for surrender in view of their losses. They tried the king’s spirit with gifts, pressed him with promises, and bargained for peace with thirty thousand gold mancus-coins [Note: [Col. 0989B] Thirty thousand gold mancus-coins. The *manca* and the ancient mark, as some suppose, are synonymous: namely, a gold or silver coin paid by weight. The value of the gold one is not entirely certain; it seems to be comparable to one eighth of an English pound. In the reign of Henry I, a silver manca was valued at six shillings, while a shilling contained five pence; but in the reign of Edward III, a silver manca amounted to only thirty pence, reckoned in the money of that time. According to the Saxon Chronicle, Ine received from the Kentishmen thirty thousand English pounds because they had earlier killed Mul by punishment of fire [Col. 0989C]. This fine seems excessive, but was probably the legal compensation for Mul’s death. If Æthelweard is to be believed, “30,000 shillings [were reckoned] at the fixed number of sixteen pennies apiece”; but according to Florence of Worcester, it was 3,700 English pounds.], so that, softened by the price [Note: [Col. 0989C] “Softened.” a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.], and dazzled by the metal [Note: [Col. 0989C] “Dazzled.” s. d. e. l.; “restrained,” c.; “prescribed,” a.], he might call a retreat [Col. 0990A]. Having received the money, he forgave the offence and returned to his kingdom (A.D. 694).

Not only the Kentish, but also the East Angles, experienced his inherited hostility: first their whole nobility was driven out, and afterwards they too were defeated in war. Let these remarks concerning the outcome of his battles acknowledge their proper limit [Note: [Col. 0989C] “Acknowledge their proper limit.” a. s. d. e. l.; “recognize,” c.]. But how great he was in the things of God is shown by the laws enacted for the people’s correction of morals [Note: [Col. 0989C] Laws. A new edition of the Anglo-Saxon laws is to appear, under Thorpe’s direction.], in which a living mirror of his purity still shines forth to this day; it is shown by monasteries splendidly raised at royal expense [Note: [Col. 0989C] After *raised*, a. l. g. and other manuscripts, with a few alterations, read as follows, omitting the whole text through *pontiff* at the end of § 36: “Especially Glastonbury, most illustrious even in our own day, which he built in a marshy retreat, so that the more steadfastly the monks might long for things above, the more chastely they should take in earthly things with their eyes. Father Aldhelm assisted his counsel; Ine heard his precepts humbly, received them nobly, and fulfilled them gladly. Finally, he willingly confirmed the privilege which he had obtained from the apostolic Sergius for the liberty of his monasteries; at Aldhelm’s urging he bestowed many gifts on God’s servants; and at last he honoured Aldhelm, though reluctant, with a bishopric. Yet swift death begrudged the world the life of so great a man: for after scarcely four years in the episcopate, he offered up his soul to heaven as incense, in the year 709 of the Lord’s Incarnation. There were those who said that he was the king’s nephew, through his brother Kenten; but we have not thought fit to claim as true what seems more calculated to flatter a flying rumour than suited to historical stability, especially since it is nowhere found written by ancient authority, and the Chronicle plainly declares that Ine had no brother except Ingeld, who died a few years before him. Aldhelm has no need to be supported by lies. So many things concerning him yield undoubted faith; so many are beyond dispute. Ine did indeed have sisters, Cuthburh and Quenburh. Cuthburh was given in marriage to Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians; but, when the marriage was dissolved not long afterward, she first lived a life pleasing to God at Barking under Abbess Hildelith, and soon afterwards herself became mistress of the rule at Wimborne. It is now an undistinguished village, but was then notable, where a numerous choir of virgins, having cut off earthly desires, sighed after heavenly loves. To the pursuit of holy celibacy was added the reading of Aldhelm’s book *On Virginity*, dedicated indeed in name to the women of Barking but beneficial to all who aspired to the same profession. Ine also had a wife, Æthelburh, a woman truly of royal birth and spirit. While she repeatedly impressed upon her husband’s ears that they should bid farewell to worldly affairs, even in their final years, and he put off her exhortation from day to day, she at last prepared to conquer by craft. For once, after they had displayed royal luxuries with great commotion at an estate [Col. 0990C], and had departed on the following day, the steward, with the queen’s knowledge, defiled the palace with every ugliness he could, both with cattle dung and with heaps of refuse. Finally, on the bed where they had slept, he placed a sow newly delivered of young. Meanwhile, when they had gone more than a mile, she approached her husband with wifely caresses and asked that he necessarily return his steps to the place they had left; it would be a matter of great danger if he did not comply. The request was readily granted. The king, seeing the place which the day before had equalled the delights of Sardanapalus now disfigured by foul desolation, marvelled; and his eyes, silently judging and examining the matter, turned back to the woman. Then she, seizing the opportunity and smiling gladly, said: ‘And where, my lord husband, are yesterday’s noises? Where are the hangings drunk with Sidonian dyes? Where the running wantonness of parasites? Where the Daedalian vessels, burdening the very tables with their weight of metal? Where the delicacies sought out on land and sea to entice the palate [Col. 0990D]? Are not all things smoke and wind? And woe to those who cling to them, for they shall pass away together. Are not all things like a swift river running into the sea? And woe to those who cling to them, for they shall be dragged along together. Consider, I beg, how miserably the flesh now nourished in pleasures will waste away. Shall not we, who gorge ourselves more abundantly, rot more miserably? The mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and a stronger punishment awaits the stronger.’ Having said no more, she compelled her husband to adopt by example the judgment which she had vainly whispered to him in many words.” S reads as above, adding after *take in earthly things with their eyes*: “to which that little book will show how much splendour he added, the book which I composed on the antiquity of that same monastery”; and after *709*, also adds: “on the vigil of St Augustine, apostle of the English, 25 May.” C reads: “Especially Glastonbury, to which that little book will show how much splendour he added, the book which I composed on the antiquity of the same monastery. He was present in counsel,” etc.], especially Glastonbury, into which he ordered the bodies of the blessed martyr Indract and his companions to be brought from the place of martyrdom. Indract’s body he placed in a stone pyramid to the left of the altar [Col. 0991A] [Note: [Col. 0991D] Hilda. Abbess of Streaneshalch (Whitby), born in 614 and died 17 November 680. She was the sister of Hereric, son of Eadfrith, himself son of King Edwin. Bede (*Hist. eccl.* IV.23) calls her “the daughter of King Edwin’s nephew Hereric.”], together with which the diligence of later generations placed blessed Hilda [Col. 0991A] [Note: [Col. 0991D] Hilda. Abbess of Streaneshalch (Whitby), born in 614 and died 17 November 680. She was the sister of Hereric, son of Eadfrith, himself son of King Edwin. Bede (*Hist. eccl.* IV.23) calls her “the daughter of King Edwin’s nephew Hereric.”]; the others he placed in the pavement, as chance or deliberate arrangement allowed [Note: [Col. 0991D] “Placed.” e; “dictated,” d. m.]. Here too he built from the foundations a church of the blessed Apostles, an appendage to this ancient church of which we are speaking; he enriched it with great possessions and granted the following privilege:

§ 36. [Note: [Col. 0991D] “In the name … pontiff.” Ine’s charter for West Saxon territory, A.D. 725, is not regarded as genuine. See J. M. Kemble, *Codex Diplomaticus Aevi Saxonici*, vol. I, p. 85, no. LXXIII.]

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Ine, sustained by royal dignity from the Lord, with the counsel of Queen Sexburh, and the permission of Beorhtwald [Note: [Col. 0991D] Berthwald. Berthwald was elected Archbishop of Canterbury on 1 July A.D. 692 and died on 9 January A.D. 731.], pontiff of the church of Canterbury, and of all his suffragans, and also at the urging [Note: [Col. 0991D] “And also at the urging.” e; “and indeed also at the urging,” d. m.] of Baldred and Adelard, under-kings, grant to the ancient church which is in the place called Glastonbury—(which the Great Priest and Highest Pontiff made known to blessed David, by many unheard-of miracles, that he had formerly sanctified it to himself and the perpetual Virgin Mary for his own service and that of the angels [Col. 0991B] [Note: [Col. 0992D] “Made known.” See above, § 25.])—from those things which I possess by paternal inheritance and hold in special lordship, the following adjoining and suitable places for the support of regular life and the use of the monks: ten hides at Brent, ten hides at Sowy, twenty hides at Pilton, twenty hides at Doulting, and one hide at Bleddon, together with all that my predecessors bestowed upon the same church: Cenwalh [Note: [Col. 0992D] Cenwalh. See above, § 29.], who, with Archbishop Theodore intervening, gave Ferremere, Bregereie, Coneneie, Matineseie [Note: [Col. 0992D] Matineseie. Mannesheie, d. m.], and Ederedeseie; Centwine, who used to call Glastonbury ‘the mother of saints,’ exempted it from every secular [Col. 0991C] and ecclesiastical service, and granted it this dignity of privilege, that the brethren of the same place should have power to elect and appoint their own ruler according to the Rule of St Benedict [Note: [Col. 0992D] According to the Rule of St Benedict. Benedict, founder of the Benedictine order, died in 543 according to Mabillon.]; Bishop Hedde [Note: [Col. 0992D] Bishop Hedde. Bishop of Winchester. See § 21, note.], who, with Cædwalla consenting and confirming it by his own hand, though a pagan, gave Lantocai; Baldred, who gave Pennard, six hides; and Adelard, who, with my consent and confirmation, gave Poelt [Note: [Col. 0992D] Poelt. e; Woelt, d. m.], sixty hides.

“I assent to their devotion and kindly petition, and against the snares of malicious men and barking dogs I keep watch with the protection of royal letters, so that the church of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the perpetual Virgin Mary, as it is first in the kingdom of Britain and the fountain and origin of all religion, may itself likewise hold the pre-eminent dignity of privilege and render no servile service whatsoever to any human being on earth, since it rules above the choirs of angels in heaven.

“Therefore, with the consent of the supreme pontiff Gregory [Note: [Col. 0992D] Gregory. Gregory II assumed the supreme pontificate on 19 May A.D. 715 and died 10 February 731.], who receives the Mother of his Lord into the bosom and protection of the Roman Church, and receives me also, though unworthy, together with her, and with the agreement also of all the kings, archbishops, bishops, dukes, and abbots of Britain, I decree and confirm that all the lands, places, and possessions of blessed Mary of Glastonbury shall remain free and undisturbed by all royal exactions and works that are customarily imposed—namely military service and the construction of bridges or fortresses—and by all pronouncements and disturbances of all archbishops and bishops, as is found confirmed in the ancient charters of the same church and known to have been ratified by my predecessors Cenwalh, Centwine, Cædwalla, and Baldred [Col. 0992A–B].

“And whatever causes may arise—in cases of homicide, sacrilege, sorcery, theft, robbery, the arrangement and assessment of churches, the ordination of clerics, synodal assemblies, and all judicial inquiries—shall be concluded by the decision of the abbot and convent, without prejudice to any person. Moreover, upon their honour and my affection, I command all kings, archbishops, bishops, dukes, and princes of my kingdom; and I command all officials, both mine and theirs, upon the safety of their own bodies, that none of them dare enter the island of our Lord Jesus Christ and the perpetual Virgin Mary at Glastonbury, or the possessions of that church, for the purpose of pleading a case, investigating, seizing, or doing anything that could cause scandal to those serving God there [Col. 0992B–C].

“Indeed, under the prohibition of Almighty God, the perpetual Virgin Mary, the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and all the saints, I forbid any bishop, upon any pretext whatsoever, in the church of Glastonbury itself or in churches subject to it—namely Sowy, Brent, Merlinch, Sapwic [Note: [Col. 0992D] Sapwic. e; Sapweie, d. m.], Stret, Budecalech, Pilton [Note: [Col. 0992D] Pilton. e; Wiltune, d. m.]—or in their chapels, or even in the islands, to establish an episcopal see for himself, conduct solemn services, consecrate altars, dedicate churches, confer orders, or make any disposition whatsoever, unless invited by the abbot or the brethren of the same place. If summoned and he comes for this purpose, he shall appropriate nothing for himself from the goods of the church, nor even from the offerings themselves, knowing that two dwellings from the possessions of the church itself have been assigned to him, one at Pilton [Col. 0993A] [Note: [Col. 0993C] Pilton. e; Wiltuna, d. m.], the other in the estate called Poelt [Note: [Col. 0993C] Poelt. e; Wohelt, d. m.], so that he may have somewhere to lodge when arriving or to which he may retire when departing. For he may not stay there overnight, except when detained by the severity of the weather or bodily infirmity, or when asked by the abbot or brethren, nor may he stay with more than three or four clerics.

“The same bishop must also ensure that each year, with his clerics who are at Fontinetum [Note: [Col. 0993C] Fontinetum. Wells, Somerset.], he visits his mother church, Glastonbury, in procession with a litany on the Monday after the Ascension of the Lord. But if, puffed up by pride, he puts this off and violates what has been declared and confirmed above, let him lose the dwellings assigned to him above. The abbot or monks may receive ecclesiastical sacraments in the church of Glastonbury, its dependent churches, and their chapels from whomever they wish, provided that he celebrates canonical Easter.

“Whoever at any later time, on any pretext and whatever his rank, profession, dignity, or degree, attempts to overturn or render void this testament of my generosity and liberality, let him know that, with Judas the traitor, he shall perish in eternal confusion amid the devouring flames of ineffable torments. This charter of donation was written in the year 725 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0993C] “Twenty-fifth.” e; “fifteenth,” d. m.], in the fourth indiction, in the presence of King Ine and Beorhtwald, pontiff of Canterbury.”

§ 37. After the triumphant spoils of wars [Note: [Col. 0993C] “After the triumphant … spoils.” On Glastonbury’s foundations and how Queen Æthelburh induced her husband to undertake a pilgrimage to Rome, see note 23 above. These words are absent in d. e. f. m.; in their place Ine’s charter for Glastonbury Church is inserted.], after the stages of many virtues, contemplating the highest summit of perfection, he went to Rome [Note: [Col. 0993D] He went to Rome. The exact date of Ine’s abdication and pilgrimage to Rome is entirely uncertain. Several manuscripts omit the time reference altogether. Two assign the year 720, but apparently incorrectly. Bede states that Ine had reigned thirty-seven years when he abdicated; on Bede’s calculation, his abdication would have occurred at the end of 725 or the beginning of 726. But according to the Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester, it happened in 728. The year 726 seems to be required.] in the year 720 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0993D] “In the year 720 of the Lord’s Incarnation.” d. m.; e leaves a blank for the date; omitted in a. s. c. l.]. There, lest he make a spectacle of his conversion, he did not expose himself to public gaze but cut off his hair [Note: [Col. 0994C] “Exposed to public gaze, he cut off his hair.” a. s. d. e. l.; “and he removed his hair to the soldiers,” c.]; and, that he might please the eyes of the Lord alone, clothed in common dress, he grew old in secret. Nor was there lacking a woman to guide so great a deed. As she had earlier urged her husband to undertake this course, so then she soothed him when grieving [Col. 0994A] with words, strengthened him when wavering by examples, and omitted absolutely nothing that concerned [Note: [Col. 0994C] “Concerned.” a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.] his salvation. Thus, bound together by mutual love in their own time, they entered upon the way of humankind, not without great miracles, as we have heard [Note: [Col. 0994C] “Often.” a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.], by which divine favour often answers the merits of blessed spouses.

§ 38. Æthelheard [Note: [Col. 0994C] Æthelheard. Æthelheard succeeded to the kingdom after Ine’s abdication in A.D. 726. According to the Saxon Chronicle, he died in A.D. 741.] succeeded to the principate, a kinsman of Ine, although Oswald, a young man of royal blood [Note: [Col. 0994D] Oswald, a young man of royal blood. In the Saxon Chronicle he is called Oswald Ætheling; he was the son of Æthelbald.], frequently disturbed the rising beginnings of his rule. For, having stirred the provincials into rebellion [Note: [Col. 0994D] “For.” a. s. c. e. l.; omitted in d. m.], Oswald attempted to pursue the king in war. But not long afterwards, when he had been removed by fate [Note: [Col. 0994D] “He.” a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.], Æthelheard, after holding the kingdom in the greatest tranquillity for fourteen years, left it to his kinsman Cuthred (A.D. 741) [Note: [Col. 0994D] From the word *Here* through *seventh hundredth*, etc., at the end of § 39, the text is omitted in a. s. c. l. and other manuscripts.]. He bestowed many benefits on Glastonbury Church and granted the following privilege:

§ 39. [Note: [Col. 0994D] “In the name … 745.” Cuthred’s charter, marked as of A.D. 744, has been published in *Codex Diplomaticus Aevi Saxonici*, p. 112, no. XCXIII. Its narrative differs in some respects from that read in the text. Kemble does not regard it as a genuine charter.]

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Cuthred, king of the West Saxons [Note: [Col. 0994D] “West Saxons.” e; “of the West Saxons,” d. m.], decree that this gift, supported by the aid of all former kings—Centwine, Baldred, Cædwalla, Ine, Æthelheard, and Æthelbald, king of the Mercians—in towns and villages, fields and estates, and greater endowments, by which the ancient city of Glastonbury has been strengthened, and confirmed by the subscription of his own hand and the sign of the cross [Note: [Col. 0994D] “Confirmed.” e; “confirmed [feminine],” d. m.], shall endure firm in law, agreeable and ratified, so long as the revolution of the heavens shall roll the lands and seas around beneath the ordered governance of the stars [Note: [Col. 0994D] “By the command of the stars.” e; “by a starry justice,” d. m.].

“But if anyone, relying on tyrannical arrogance, strives upon any pretext to interrupt and annul this testament of my gift [Col. 0994C], let him, separated from fellowship with the former [kings] by the sieve of the last judgment and joined to the company of the rapacious, pay eternally for the presumption of his violence. But whoever, endowed rather with benevolent intention, endeavours to approve, strengthen, and defend these things, may he, having attained his desire, hear the glory of the Most High enthroned, in unfailing eternity, with the blessed companies of angels and all saints. A copy of this grant was promulgated in the aforesaid monastery, in the presence of King Cuthred, who by the generosity of his own hand commended it to the holy altar, in the wooden basilica in which the brethren have the sarcophagus of Abbot Hemgisl by day, in the year 745 from the Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0995C] “By day, in the year from the Incarnation.” e; “on the day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation,” d. m.].”

§ 40. [Note: [Col. 0995C] “Against … left the reins of government.” d. e. m.; “In this [reign], equal in number of years and not unlike in virtue, winning victories against Æthelbald king of the Mercians and the Britons by unceasing exertion, he expended no excessive labour,” a. h. g. l. s.; “This man, winning victories against Æthelbald king of the Mercians and the Britons by unceasing exertion, expended no little labour and, after sixteen years, left the reins of government,” c. k.] The same Cuthred, winning victories against Æthelbald, king of the Mercians [Note: [Col. 0995C] Mercians. In the twelfth year of his reign Cuthred fought a battle at Burford against Æthelbald, king of the Mercians, and put him to flight. (Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 752.)], and the Britons [Note: [Col. 0995D] Britons. In this year Cuthred fought against the Welsh. (Saxon Chronicle.)] through constant campaigning, spent no small labour; and after fourteen years left the reins of government.

§ 41. Sigeberht [Note: [Col. 0995D] Sigeberht. Sigeberht began to reign in A.D. 755.] seized it [Note: [Col. 0995D] “Seized it.” c. d. e. m.; “seized the kingdom,” a. s. l.], a man monstrously cruel among his own people and equally notorious abroad for cowardice. Therefore, when the common hatred of all had conspired against him, he was driven from the throne after one year and made room for a better man. Yet, as often happens in such cases, the magnitude of his disaster [Col. 0995B] [Note: [Col. 0995D] “Magnitude.” a. s. d. e. l.; “greatness of spirit,” c.] recalled some to favour for him; by their valour he retained in obedience the province called Hampshire (A.D. 756). But since even then he did not cease, and by murdering a certain Cumbra, who had adhered to him most faithfully, armed the rest for his own destruction [Note: [Col. 0995D] “His own.” a. s. d. e. l.; “their own,” c.], he withdrew into the hidden caves of wild beasts [Note: [Col. 0995D] “Withdrew.” a. s. d. e. l.; “went,” c.]. There too, as misfortune pursued him [Note: [Col. 0995D] “There.” a. d. e. l.; “thither,” s. c.], he was stabbed to death by a swineherd [Note: [Col. 0995D] He was stabbed to death by a swineherd. Cynewulf drove Sigeberht into the forest of Andred, where he remained until he was stabbed by an assassin at Privett. (Saxon Chronicle, …, A.D. 755.) Compare Florence of Worcester, A.B. 784.]. Thus the king’s cruelty, having ranged through almost the whole nobility, came to rest upon a man of the lowest condition.

§ 42. Cynewulf [Note: [Col. 0996C] Cynewulf. He assumed government in A.D. 756.] took up the reins of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0996C] “Of the kingdom.” a. s. d. e. l.; “of power,” c.], distinguished indeed for uprightness of character and military achievements. But in a single battle against Offa, king of the Mercians, over Bensington [Note: [Col. 0996C] Bensington. A battle was fought at Bensington in Oxfordshire in A.D. 777 (Saxon Chronicle); yet it cannot have occurred in Cynewulf’s twenty-fourth year, as Malmesbury asserts.], in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, he was defeated and afflicted with many corresponding losses; he also met the end of life in a shameful manner. For after ruling for thirty-one years [Note: [Col. 0996C] “For thirty-one years.” Some authorities assign Cynewulf thirty-one years of rule. He began to reign at the end of A.D. 756 and died stabbed in A.D. 785; it follows that he occupied the throne only twenty-nine years. Malmesbury perhaps wrote “one year short of thirty,” since he uses this sort of expression in speaking of Cædwalla’s reign, § 35: “two years short of forty.”], neither timidly nor immoderately, whether elated by the glory of his achievements so as to believe that nothing would oppose him, or fearing for his posterity [Col. 0996A] [Note: [Col. 0996D] “For his descendants.” a. s. d. e. l.; “for his power,” c.], since he saw Cyneheard, Sigeberht’s brother, gaining strength against it [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Beyond measure.” a. s. d. e. l.; “whom,” c.], to leave the borders of the province.

Cyneheard, judging that he must yield to circumstances, concealed his feelings and fled as though willingly. Soon, after gathering a ruined [i.e. desperate] band of wicked men [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Ruined.” a. s. d. e. l.; “of ruined men,” c.] in clandestine assemblies, he watched for the king’s isolation [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Watched for.” a. c. d. e. l.; “hunted for,” s.]. The king had gone to the countryside for pleasure; Cyneheard came there with picked men [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Came.” a. s. d. e. l.; “had come,” c.]. Hearing that the king was devoted to an illicit love, he surrounded the house from outside in ambush. Stirred by the twofold danger, the king took considered counsel with those present, shut the doors, and hoped either to soften the robbers by speech or frighten them by authority. When neither course succeeded, he was roused to anger and rushed upon Cyneheard, and came very near [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Came very near.” a. s. d. e. l.; “harmed,” c.] to depriving him of life. But, surrounded by the multitude, and judging retreat to be a loss of honour, he fell, having exacted worthy vengeance before his death (A.D. 785).

The few of his retainers who were present, seeking not to surrender their hands but to avenge their lord, were slaughtered [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Seeking.” a. s. d. e. l.; “striving,” c.]; [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Were slaughtered.” a. c. d. e. l.; “are slaughtered,” s.]. Immediately the report of so great a disaster reached the ears [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Reached the ears.” a. s. c. e. l.; “reached the ears of,” d. m.] of the nobles, who were keeping watch not far away. Osric, foremost among them in age and prudence, exhorted [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Exhorted.” a. c. d. e. l.; “urged,” s.] the others not to leave their lord’s murder unavenged, to their conspicuous and everlasting shame; drawing their swords, he rushed upon the conspirators. At first Cyneheard pleaded his cause, made great promises, and invoked kinship. When he gained nothing, he encouraged his companions-in-arms [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Companions-in-arms.” a. s. d. e. l.; “soldiers,” c.] to resist. The contest was doubtful, as the one side strove with all their strength for life, the other for glory. At length victory, long delayed, turned to the more just side. Thus that wretched man, acting bravely to no purpose [Note: [Col. 0996D] “To no purpose.” a. s. d. e. l.; “not at all,” c.], lost his life and did not boast long [Note: [Col. 0996D] “Long.” a. s. c. e. l.; “for a long time,” d. m.] of the success of his plot. The king’s body was buried at Winchester, Cyneheard’s at Repton [Note: [Col. 0996D] Repton, Derbyshire.], then a noble monastery [Col. 0997A], now, as I have heard, inhabited by few or none.

§ 43. After him reigned Beorhtric [Note: [Col. 0997C] “After him.” a. s. d. e. l.; “after Cynewulf,” c.] for sixteen years [Note: [Col. 0997C] Beorhtric for sixteen years. Beorhtric obtained the kingdom in A.D. 785 and died in A.D. 802; he therefore reigned seventeen years, which agrees with the time assigned by Symeon of Durham.], more devoted to peace than war; skilled in forming friendships, graciously addressing outsiders, and overlooking the conduct of his subjects, provided only that it did not weaken the vigour of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0997C] “That did not weaken the vigour of the kingdom.” a. s. d. e. l.; “who did not weaken royal vigour,” c.]. To establish greater favour among his neighbours, he took in marriage [Note: [Col. 0997C] “In marriage.” a. s. d. e. l.; “as wife,” c.] the daughter of Offa [Note: [Col. 0997C] Offa’s daughter. Beorhtric married Eadburh, daughter of King Offa, in A.D. 787. See Florence of Worcester, under 787; Asser, *On the Deeds of Alfred*; and the Saxon Chronicle.], then the most powerful king of the Mercians. By her, so far as I know, he had no children.

Supported by this affinity, he procured the exile to Francia of Ecgberht, the sole surviving man of royal stock, whom he feared as the strongest obstacle to his interests. For Beorhtric himself, and the other kings after Ine, although they gloried in the splendour of their lineage because they derived their origin from Cerdic, had nevertheless strayed considerably [Col. 0997B] from the line of the royal house. When Ecgberht had therefore been expelled, Beorhtric began to relax into secure leisure. Then a piratical people of Danes [Note: [Col. 0997C] “Then a … piratical people.” “A.D. 787. This year three ships of Northmen came from the land of pirates.” (Saxon Chronicle; Florence of Worcester, under 787.)], accustomed to live by plunder, secretly arrived in three ships and disturbed the peace of the province. That band had come, in fact, to inspect the fertility of the land and the valour of its inhabitants, as became clear later from the arrival of that multitude which all but inundated Britain. At that time, having secretly landed in the kingdom’s deep peace, they attacked the nearest royal estate [Note: [Col. 0997C] “Nearest.” a. c. d. e. l. m.; “was nearest,” s.], killed the reeve who came to their assistance, and then, frightened by those gathering against them, abandoned their plunder and fled back to their ships.

After Beorhtric [Note: [Col. 0997D] After Beorhtric. According to the Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester, Beorhtric died in A.D. 880; but Symeon of Durham states that he died in A.D. 802, after reigning seventeen years.], who lies at Wareham, Ecgberht ascended the ancestral throne [Note: [Col. 0997D] Ecgberht ascended the throne. According to most authorities, Ecgberht is supposed to have ascended the throne in A.D. 800; but this does not agree with the chronological period assigned by authorities of greater weight to the reigns of his predecessors, as will be plainly evident from what follows. Æthelheard succeeded in 726 and his whole reign comprises nearly fourteen years. Cuthred ascended the throne at the beginning of 741 and ruled fourteen years. Sigeberht succeeded in 755 and was expelled in the following year. Cynewulf began to reign at the end of 756 and, after thirty years of rule, had Beorhtric as successor at the end of 785. The seventeen years assigned to Beorhtric’s reign by Symeon of Durham place the beginning of Ecgberht’s reign in 802. “Therefore Ecgberht,” says Hoveden, “in the year of grace 800, or, as some hold, 802, after Beorhtric’s death, succeeded”; and the latter date seems correct. It is further established that he was still alive in 835, the year assigned to his death by northern chroniclers. In a charter granted in 835 and confirmed in the following year, that year is counted as about the thirty-fourth of his reign. Another of his charters is dated A.D. 838 and was confirmed by his son in 839, which is also counted as the first year of Æthelwulf’s reign. More reliable authority establishes that his reign lasted thirty-seven years; his accession must therefore be assigned to 802 and his death to 839.], deservedly to be preferred to all the kings before him [Note: [Col. 0998C] “Before him.” a. s. e. l.; “before him in Wessex,” c. d. m.]. Since we have extended our narrative to his time [Col. 0998A] [Note: [Col. 0998C] “Time.” a. s. d. e. l.; “times,” c.], let us now turn our attention to the Northumbrians, as we promised.

## HERE BEGINS THE ACCOUNT OF THE KINGDOM OF THE NORTHUMBRIANS.

§ 44. We touched briefly on this above [Note: [Col. 0998C] “We touched briefly on this above.” See § 7.], and must now necessarily repeat that Hengest, once his kingdom in Kent had been secured, sent his brother Ohta and his son Ebusan, men of vigorous and proven ability, to seize the northern parts of Britain. Carrying out the commands laid upon them [Note: [Col. 0998C] *Imperatis*, “commands”: a. s. d. e. l.; *praeceptis*, “instructions”: c.], they achieved an outcome suited to their ambitions. For they repeatedly engaged the inhabitants; having crushed those who thought resistance necessary, they received the rest into allegiance [Note: [Col. 0998C] “Received”: s. c. d. e. l. m.; “received also”: a.] and soothed them for the sake of peaceful tranquillity. Thus, having gathered some power both by their own abilities and through the favour of their subjects, they nevertheless never contemplated rashly assuming the royal title, but marked out the same pattern of moderation for their immediate descendants [Col. 0998B] [Note: [Col. 0998D] “They marked out”: a. d. e. l. m.; “they declined”: s. c. The source of the statement that follows—“they never … conducted themselves”—cannot now be determined.]. For ninety-nine years the Northumbrian leaders, content with their common rank, acted as private persons under the authority of the people of Kent. But thereafter this restraint of ambition did not endure—whether because the human mind always slopes toward worse things, or because that people naturally aspired to more inflated spirits.

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 547, the sixtieth after Hengest’s death, the leadership was transformed into a kingdom, and Ida, unquestionably of the noblest birth, sound in age and strength, was the first to reign there [Note: [Col. 0998D] “Ida.” Before Ida’s accession no notice of Northumbria occurs in the Saxon Chronicles. The *Saxon Chronicle* and Bede (*Ecclesiastical History*, V.24) alike reckon Ida as founder of this kingdom in 547. It is nevertheless doubtful whether Ida was king of both provinces, Bernicia and Deira, or at least of Bernicia alone. Having died in 559, he was succeeded in Bernicia by his sons, who reigned successively until 588, when Æthelric, after the death of Ælla, king of Bernicia, and the expulsion of his son Edwin, obtained the government of both kingdoms. He held it for five years, until his death in 593. Compare Florence of Worcester under 559, and the Genealogies of the Kings of Bernicia and Deira, together with Symeon of Durham.]. Whether he seized power on his own initiative or accepted it when offered by the consent of others, I scarcely determine, because the truth lies hidden. Yet it is sufficiently certain that, descended from a great and ancient stock [Col. 0999A], he added much lustre to noble birth by pure and refined manners. So invincible in war was he that at home he tempered royal severity with an innate gentleness of mind.

At this point I might weave in orderly sequence the lineage of this man, and elsewhere of others, were it not that the very names, harshly hissing with something barbarous, would give readers less pleasure than I should wish. This alone, however, ought not undeservedly to be noted: Woden had three sons—Weldeg, Wiltheg, and Beldeg. From the first descended the kings of Kent; from the second, those of Mercia; from the third, those of the West Saxons and Northumbrians, apart from two whom the following narrative will continue to name. This Ida, therefore, as I find without qualification, was ninth from Beldeg and tenth from Woden; he remained in the kingdom for fourteen years [Col. 0999B] [Note: [Col. 0999C] “For fourteen years”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “for twelve years”: c. Bede (V.24), the *Saxon Chronicle*, and other authorities state that Ida reigned twelve years. Symeon of Durham writes: “King Ida reigned eleven years.”].

§ 45. His successor was Ælla [Note: [Col. 0999C] “His successor was Ælla.” He was king of Deira and ascended the throne in A.D. 560 (*Saxon Chronicle*). No other authority establishes that Ælla ever reigned in Bernicia, although he here appears as successor to Ida, whose sons at this period ruled that province successively [Col. 0999D].], indeed of the same family, but deriving his blood from Woden through a different branch. By the achievements of his exertions he nobly enlarged for thirty years a kingdom effectively advanced by his efforts [Note: [Col. 0999D] “Exertions”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “endeavours”: c.].

In his time boys from Northumbria were offered for sale [Note: [Col. 0999D] “In his time, boys offered for sale.” Compare Bede, II.1, §89, who relates these matters as mere traditions. They are nevertheless inserted in almost the same words by John the Deacon and Paul the Deacon in their respective Lives of St Gregory. Bede omits the pope’s name in connection with this event. Paul the Deacon, or the author of the Life attributed to him, says that the pope was Pelagius; John the Deacon, more correctly, asserts that it was Benedict, his predecessor. On this testimony, therefore, the event must be placed before 578.]—a practice familiar, indeed almost exceedingly common, among that people [Note: [Col. 0999D] “A practice among that people.” This custom of selling children, even close relatives, to foreign merchants was probably peculiar to Northumbria. One provision of law would seem to imply that native slaves could not lawfully be sold: “If anyone buys his fellow-countryman, slave or free, even though he be guilty, beyond the sea, let him pay for him with his wergild.” (*Laws of Ine*, c. 12.)]—so much so that, as our own age also has seen, they did not hesitate, under the pretext of the slightest gain, to break the closest bonds of kinship. Boys from England, then, being brought to Rome for sale, provided the occasion for the salvation of all their countrymen.

For when, by the wonder of their countenances and the grace of their features, they had drawn the eyes of the city, the most blessed Gregory happened to be present with others. He was then archdeacon of the Apostolic See [Col. 0999C]. Marvelling at so great a harmony of beauty in mortal beings, and pitying so abject a condition in captives, he asked those standing by: “What race are they? From what land do they come?” The reply was that they were Angles by race, from the province of Deira [Note: [Col. 1000C] “The province of Deira.” The part of Britain lying north of the River Humber consisted of two great regions, Deira and Bernicia. Deira extended from the Humber to the Tyne; Bernicia from the Tyne to the River Firth or Forth. Each province originally had its own ruler. See Smith’s notes on Bede, III.1.]—for Deira is a province of Northumbria [Col. 1000A]—subjects of King Ælla, devoted to paganism. Sighing deeply at the final word, he made a graceful play upon the rest: that the *Angli*, being like angels, should be rescued from wrath (*ira*) and taught to sing Alleluia [Note: [Col. 1000C] “To sing”: s. e.; “to sing repeatedly”: A. d. c. l. m.].

Without delay, having obtained permission from Pope Benedict [Note: [Col. 1000D] “Pope Benedict.” Benedict governed the Roman Church from 27 May A.D. 574 to 25 July A.D. 578.] to preach, the noble energy of this exceptional man was moved to undertake the journey. Indeed, piety would have fulfilled the work he had conceived, had not the vigorous affection of the citizens recalled him after he had already set out. For the man was eminent in virtues and beloved by his fellow citizens, since by extraordinary excellence he had surpassed the hopes they had cherished concerning him from his boyhood. Thus this good intention, though frustrated at that time, later achieved a praiseworthy end under his pontificate [Note: [Col. 1000D] “Under his pontificate.” Gregory the Great governed the Roman Church from 3 September A.D. 390 to 12 March A.D. 604.], as the reader will find in its proper place.

Meanwhile, I have not thought it burdensome to insert these matters, lest I should cheat readers of knowledge concerning Ælla, whom the Life of Father Gregory mentioned in passing. Although Gregory was the great occasion of Christianity for the English people, he never deserved, whether through God’s counsel or through some misfortune, to hear anything of it [Col. 1000B] [Note: [Col. 1000D] “Of it”: a. s. e. l.; “of it itself”: c.]. The choice, however, certainly passed on to his son.

§ 46. When Ælla died [Note: [Col. 1000D] “When Ælla died.” Ælla died in A.D. 588. (*Saxon Chronicle*).], Æthelric, son of Ida, obtained the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1000D] “Æthelric.” Æthelric ruled both provinces, Bernicia and Deira. He received the former by right of succession in A.D. 586 and gained the latter in 588. He died in 593. See §44, note.]. After a life worn down by want, he had reached extreme old age; but after five years he was quickly removed from the world by death. A pitiable prince, and one whom an altogether obscure reputation would have concealed [Note: [Col. 1000D] “Would have concealed”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “would have hidden away”: c.], had not the conspicuous vigour of his sons raised their father into view.

§ 47. Therefore, when Æthelric had satisfied life’s demands by a long old age, Æthelfrith, the eldest of his sons, ascended the throne [Note: [Col. 1000D] “Æthelfrith ascended the throne.” Æthelfrith succeeded to the kingdom of the Northumbrians in A.D. 593. (*Saxon Chronicle*).] [Col. 1000C]. He compensated for the tenderness of his years by maturity of character. His deeds, brought before the public through the polished writing of historians, await from our style only their place in the sequence. Bede’s genius was so alert in celebrating him and his successors; and Bede’s attention looked all the more affectionately upon the Northumbrians, his neighbours, the closer they were [Col. 1001A]. Our narrative, however, will gather and arrange fragments from his work.

Let no one blame me because a history so diffuse is compressed into narrow compass. Let him know that this has been done deliberately: those who have become nauseated with those banquets may breathe again on these beggarly leftovers. For there is a well-worn saying, venerable for its antiquity: “Foods which suffice less are taken more eagerly” [Note: [Col. 1001C] “Well-worn”: e.; “worn by use”: a. s. c. d. l. m.].

Æthelfrith, then, as I had begun to say, having gained the kingdom, first defended his own possessions fiercely, then wickedly invaded those of others, and created occasions for glory from every quarter. Through him many battles were prudently begun and brilliantly completed, since neither did idleness restrain him from necessity nor boldness hurl him into rashness. Witness to this is Degsa’s Stone [Col. 1001B] [Note: [Col. 1001C] “Degsa’s Stone”: a. s. c. e. l.; “Degla’s Stone”: d. m. The battle at Degsa’s Stone (*Daegsastan*) occurred in 603. See the *Saxon Chronicle*, Bede I.34, and Florence of Worcester. The modern name of this place is unknown; some identify it with Dalston near Carlisle, others with Dawston near Jedburgh.], a place very famous in those regions. There Edan, king of the Scots, envying Æthelfrith’s successes and provoking even one who declined battle into war, was defeated and fled, though not without grave danger to the victor. For Theodbald, Æthelfrith’s brother, exposing his head to danger, and striving all the more earnestly because he wished to show greater service to his brother, left behind a mournful victory, being lamented with all his comrades [Note: [Col. 1001C] “Comrades”: a. s. d. e. l. m.; “soldiers”: c.].

The city of the Legions too bears witness [Note: [Col. 1001C] “The city of the Legions … is called Chester.” Among the Britons this place was called *Caerleon*, “city of the legions,” because a Roman legion always maintained a station there. Bede (II.2, §94) has: “The city of the legions, which is called by the English people *Legacaestir*, but by the Britons more correctly *Carlegion*.”]. It is now simply called Chester, and, up to that time possessed by Britons, nourished the defiant pride of a people hostile to the king. When he turned his mind to besieging it, the townsmen, preferring to suffer anything rather than a siege, and trusting also in their numbers, rushed out en masse to battle. He received them in ambush, routed and put them to flight, after first [Col. 1001C] venting his fury upon the monks, who had assembled in great numbers to pray for the safety of the army.

The evidence that their number was incredible in our own age lies in the numerous half-ruined walls of churches in the neighbouring monastery, the many winding porticoes, and such a mass of ruins [Col. 1002A] as one scarcely sees elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1001D] “Their incredible number in our age.” According to the *Saxon Chronicle*, two hundred priests who had come there to pray for the safety of the Welsh army were slain. The precise date of this slaughter is unknown. Bede assigns no year to the event; Florence dates it to 603, the *Annales Cambriae* to 613, and the *Saxon Chronicle* to 607. Ussher, from the Annals of Ulster, places it in 613.]. That place is called Bangor, then a celebrated refuge of monks, now transformed into a bishopric [Note: [Col. 1001D] “That place, Bangor … now transformed into a bishopric.” Malmesbury here confuses the ancient monastery of Banchor near Chester with the later Bangor, an episcopal see in Caernarvonshire. (Sharpe, p. 47.) See also Tyrrell, vol. I, book IV, p. 164 [Col. 1002C]. There was also a monastery of Bangor in Ulster. See Smith’s note on Bede, II.2.].

Thus Æthelfrith, while matters abroad flowed in accordance with his wishes, desiring to ward off domestic fear and internal danger [Note: [Col. 1002C] “To ward off domestic fear and internal danger”: a. s. e. l.; “to ward off domestic and internal fear”: c.], expelled from kingdom and province Edwin, son of Ælla [Note: [Col. 1002C] “Edwin.” When Ælla, king of Deira, died, his son Edwin, only three years old, was removed from the succession by Æthelric, king of Bernicia, who then united the government of the two provinces. Æthelric died in 593 and was succeeded by his son Æthelfrith. When he continued the persecution, Edwin sought the aid of Rædwald, king of the East Angles [Col. 1002D].]. Edwin, tossed for a long time among uncertain refuges, found many former friends more inclined toward hostility than loyalty, because, as the poet said [Note: [Col. 1002D] “As the poet said”: Ovid, *Tristia*, I.9.5.],

> When you are fortunate, you will count many friends;  
> If times grow cloudy, you will be alone.

At last he came to King Rædwald of the East Angles. Having related his misfortunes, he settled there, protected by royal generosity [Col. 1002B]. Envoys from Æthelfrith arrived, demanding either the surrender of the fugitive or declaring war. Strengthened by the counsel of his wife [Note: [Col. 1002D] “Counsel”: a. d. e. m; “counsel” singular: s. c. l.], Rædwald refused to violate the faith pledged to his friend under anyone’s threats [Note: [Col. 1002D] “Anyone’s”: c. d. e. m.; “his”: a. s. l.]. With forces prepared, he unexpectedly flew against Æthelfrith [Note: [Col. 1002D] “Against Æthelfrith.” Æthelfrith was killed in A.D. 617 while fighting Rædwald near Retford, beside the River Idle in Nottinghamshire. *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 617; Florence of Worcester, 616; and Henry of Huntingdon.], and attacked him, although he expected nothing less than an ambush, in a planned assault.

What courage alone could then discover, with escape cut off, he turned into a remedy at hand. Thus, though almost unarmed and surrounded by danger on both sides, he nevertheless did not fall until he had compensated for his own death by the death of Rædwald’s son Rægenhere. Such was the end of Æthelfrith after twenty-four years of rule [Note: [Col. 1002D] “After twenty-four years of rule.” Symeon of Durham, apparently incorrectly, assigns twenty-eight years to Æthelfrith’s reign.], a man second to none in experience of war [Col. 1002C], but wholly ignorant of divine religion. By Acca, daughter of Ælla and sister of Edwin, he had two sons [Note: [Col. 1002D] “Two sons.” Oswald and Oswi had an elder brother named Eanfrith, who later became king of Bernicia. See below, §49.], Oswald, aged twelve, and Oswi, aged four [Note: [Col. 1002D] “Aged four”: a. d. e. l. m.; “in his fourth year”: s. c.]. When their father was killed, they escaped through the care of their foster-parents and made their way to Scotland.

## Concerning Edwin, King of the Northumbrians

§ 48. Thus Edwin [Note: [Col. 1002D] “Edwin.” He succeeded to the kingdom of the Northumbrians at the beginning of 617, after Æthelfrith had been killed.], with all his rivals defeated [Col. 1003A] or put to flight [Note: [Col. 1003C] “Defeated or put to flight”: a. d. e. l. m.; “slain or expelled”: s. c.], after having earned his reward through many hardships, mounted the summit of kingship no longer inexperienced. When the haughty temper of the Northumbrians had soon risen willingly under his rule, the timely death of Rædwald added to the height of his good fortune. For the provincials, who had formerly tested Edwin’s ready courage and energetic spirit while he was an exile among them, of their own accord joined by a pledged allegiance in submitting to his authority. Edwin granted Rædwald’s son the empty title of king, but administered everything else at his own discretion.

At that time the hopes and resources of the English rested in him. There was no province of Britain that did not await [Note: [Col. 1003C] “Await”: e.; “look toward”: a. s. c. d. l. m.] his command, ready to obey, apart from the people of Kent alone. He had left them free from attack because he had long before fixed his mind upon marrying Æthelburh, sister of their king Eadbald [Note: [Col. 1003C] “For the marriage of Æthelburh.” Edwin’s marriage to Æthelburh—also called Tata or Æthelberta—daughter of the king of Kent occurred in A.D. 625. (Bede, II.9, §111.)] [Col. 1003B]. Having at last won her after seeking her long, he resolved not to despise her when possessed whom he had yearned for while she was delayed. The two kingdoms were united by so great a service of mutual obligation that there was nothing different in their powers or barbarous in their customs.

Moreover, on the same occasion, as Paulinus preached [Note: [Col. 1003D] “Paulinus.” Paulinus was consecrated bishop of York on 21 July A.D. 625.], faith in the Lord Christ, poured into those regions, first penetrated the king himself [Note: [Col. 1003D] “Penetrated the king himself.” Edwin was baptized on the holy day of Easter, 12 April A.D. 627, in the eleventh year of his reign. (Bede, II.14, §132.)]. The queen repeatedly impressed it upon her husband amid their marital affections, and the bishop’s exhortation [Note: [Col. 1003D] “The bishop’s”: a. c. d. e. l. m.; “of Bishop Paulinus”: s.] was not lacking at the proper time. Long wavering and uncertain, once he had accepted the faith he planted it in the depths of his heart. Then he invited neighbouring kings to the faith; then he raised buildings for churches; he neglected nothing suitable for the extension of the faith [Col. 1003C].

Meanwhile, the serene favour of the Godhead smiled upon the king’s devotion. Thus not only the peoples of Britain—the English, Scots, and Picts—but also the islands of Orkney and the Mevanian islands, which are now called Anglesey, that is, “the islands of the Angles” [Note: [Col. 1003D] “They call”: a. c. d. e. l. m.; “we call”: s.], feared his arms and revered his authority. There was then no public robber, no domestic thief; the betrayer of marital chastity was far away, the plunderer of another’s inheritance in exile—a great matter for his praise, and splendid even in our age.

The growth of his dominion was therefore carried to such limits that justice and peace gladly ran into one another’s embraces, exchanging the favour of kisses in grateful reciprocity [Col. 1004A]. The commonwealth of the English might then have prospered happily, had not untimely death—the stepmother of temporal happiness—taken the man from his country in the shameful sport of fortune’s changeableness. In the forty-eighth year of his age and seventeenth of his reign, when Cædwalla of the Britons and Penda of the Mercians, petty kings whom he had put under the yoke, were attacking him [Note: [Col. 1003D] “As they attacked”: e.; “as they resisted”: a. d. l. m.; “as they rebelled”: s. c.], he was killed with his son [Note: [Col. 1003D] “Killed with his son.” Edwin was killed with his son Osfrith at the battle of Hatfield Moor, 12 October A.D. 633. (Bede, II.20, §146; *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 633; and Florence of Worcester, 633.) His feast is celebrated on 4 October in the English Martyrology [Col. 1004C].]. He became a pitiable example of human instability: inferior to no one in prudence, for he would not accept the Christian faith without most carefully examining its rationale [Col. 1004C], nor, once accepted, regard anything as comparable to it [Col. 1004A].

## Concerning Saint Oswald, King

§ 49. Edwin having been killed, the sons of Æthelfrith—also Edwin’s nephews [Note: [Col. 1004C] “Also Edwin’s nephews.” They were sons of Æthelfrith by Acca, Edwin’s sister. See above, §47.]—Oswald and Oswi, now grown men and clothed in the flower of burgeoning youth, returned to their homeland; and with them came Eanfrith, their elder in age, whose mention had slipped my mind above [Col. 1004B]. The kingdom was therefore divided in two. For Northumbria, long separated into twin provinces, had made Ælla ruler from the Deirans and Ida from the Bernicians.

Accordingly, Osric, the son of Edwin’s paternal uncle, received Deira; Eanfrith, son of Æthelfrith, received Bernicia [Note: [Col. 1004D] “Osric received Deira; Eanfrith … Bernicia.” See the *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 634, and Bede, III.1. Osric was son of Ælfric, brother of Ælla and kinsman of Edwin.]. They boasted that they had obtained an hereditary right. Both had been initiated into Christian rites in Scotland; both, scarcely in possession of power, became deserters from the faith. Not long afterwards, when Cædwalla attacked [Note: [Col. 1004D] “When Cædwalla attacked.” Osric and Eanfrith were killed by Cædwalla, king of the Britons: Osric in summer 634, and Eanfrith shortly afterwards. In the meantime both provinces were usurped by Cædwalla.], they paid the penalty for abandoning that faith.

The year spent amid these delays trained Oswald, a young man of great promise, in the art of ruling [Note: [Col. 1004D] “Oswald.” Oswald obtained the kingdom of the Northumbrians in 634. For him see Bede, III.2, 3, and 6.] [Col. 1004C]. Armed more with faith than with steel—for among the Scots, where he had lived in exile with many youths of noble character, he had received the grace of baptism—he first stripped Cædwalla, puffed up by remembrance of his exploits and calling himself a man born for the extermination of the English [Note: [Col. 1004D] “Calling himself”: d. e. l. m.; “calling”: c.; “calling himself”: a.], of his camp in the first attack, and soon destroyed him with all his forces [Note: [Col. 1004D] “Destroyed him with all his forces.” Cædwalla was killed at Dilston, near Hexham, Northumberland. (Bede, III.1, §151.) See also Smith’s Appendix XIII.].

For when he had gathered from every quarter whatever small army he could, he roused them to battle with words that taught his fellow-soldiers they must either conquer or die, thinking nothing of flight. He declared that a matter of shameful reproach was at stake: the English were fighting the Britons at such an unequal hazard that they were struggling for safety against men whom they themselves had customarily provoked for glory. Therefore let them vindicate their liberty with courageous hearts and all their strength [Col. 1005A] [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Let them vindicate”: a. c. d. e. l.; “they vindicate”: s.]; but let there be no thought at all of a rush to flee.

Accordingly the conflict was joined so fiercely and with such force on both sides that it has rightly been said that never had a sadder day fallen upon the Britons, nor a happier upon the English [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Britons”: d. e. m; “British”: a. s. c. l.]. The one party, their strength wholly consumed, did not dare to recover further; the other, with sacred religion in harmony with the king’s greatness of soul, advanced immeasurably. From that time the worship of idols languished into ashes. Oswald himself held his kingdom peacefully for eight years [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Eight”: a. s. c. e. l.; “seven”: d. m. According to Bede, Oswald reigned nine years, including the year of Cædwalla’s usurpation.] [Col. 1005B], within boundaries wider than Edwin’s and without the killing of any human being [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Peacefully”: a. d. e. l.; “with peace”: s. c.].

History celebrates this king’s praises in a panegyrical style [Note: [Col. 1005D] “History”: e.; “Bede’s history”: s. See Bede, III.2–6.]; we shall embrace suitable portions of them in a kind of summary. How great a fervour of faith grew in his breast may easily be seen from this: whenever Bishop Aidan, speaking Scots [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Aidan speaking Scots.” For the Life of Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne, see Bede III.5 and *Acta Sanctorum*, August, vol. VI, p. 688.], proposed to his hearers things that ought to be done and no interpreter was available, the king himself immediately undertook the task with dignity, though clothed in a cloak stiff with gold or glowing with Tyrian purple. He unravelled the covering of the foreign speech into his native tongue [Note: [Col. 1005D] “With dignity”: a. d. l.; “without disdaining it”: s. c.].

It is also widely known that, when food had often been set before him and his guests were sharpening their teeth for eating and directing their minds to the meal, he restrained his own pleasure [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Pleasure”: s. c. d. e.; “will”: a. l. See Bede, III.6.], purchasing the joy of the poor by his own deprivation [Col. 1005C]. Hence I judge that even in temporal matters the truth of the heavenly sentence was fulfilled which the divine oracle once uttered: “He has distributed, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever” [Note: [Col. 1005D] “He has distributed … for ever and ever”: Psalm 112:9.].

What the hearer ought to marvel at, and cannot deny [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Cannot”: a. d. e. l.; “dare not”: s. c.], is that this royal right hand, dispenser of so many alms, still flourishes incorrupt, together with arm, skin, and sinews; while the whole remainder of the body, except the bones, having dissolved into ashes, did not escape the common lot of mortality. Certainly the bodily remains of some saints are untouched by any corruption whatsoever. Let others therefore decide by what test they should weigh their judgment; I pronounce this more pleasing and, by a more evident miracle, more divine [Col. 1006A]. For even precious things deteriorate through use, and whatever seems rarer is praised more abundantly.

Moreover, I should be superfluous if I tried to say how diligent he was in sending prayers upward and burdening heaven with vows. This praise of Oswald is too great to need enlargement by our speech. For when would he neglect a request [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Asked”: s.; “clothed in a toga”: a. c. d. e. l.], he who, when rebellion had been stirred up by Penda, king of the Mercians, and his attendants had been routed, himself too bore an iron forest in his breast [Col. 1006A], yet could not be accused, despite the severity of his wounds and the nearness of death, of failing to beseech the Lord God for the souls of his faithful people? [Note: [Col. 1006D] “When rebellion had been stirred up by Penda.” Oswald was killed by Penda at Maserfelth—now Oswestry—on 5 August A.D. 642, in the thirty-eighth year of his life. (Bede, III.9, and the *Saxon Chronicle*).]

Thus this man, of immense glory in the world and great favour with God, laying aside his gracious soul, poured out his memory to posterity through the abundance of miracles [Col. 1006B], and deservedly. It is no commonplace but something “rarer than a white crow” [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Rarer than a white crow”: Juvenal, *Satires*, VII.202.] for a man to abound in riches and yet refuse to indulge in vices. Therefore the dead man’s arms, with hands and head, were cut off by the insatiable anger of the victor [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Of the victor”: e.; “of victories”: l.] and hung upon a stake.

His body, as I have said, wholly cherished in nature’s gentle bosom, passed into the earthly element [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Earthly”: s. d. e.; “made of earth”: a. c. l.]; but his arms and hands, by God’s agency and on the testimony of the truthful historian [Note: [Col. 1006D] “And”: s. c. d. e; omitted in a. l. “On the testimony of the truthful historian”: Bede, III.6.], remain inviolate. He says that Oswi, his brother, placed them in a shrine at Bebbanburg—the English name for that town [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Bebbanburg”: Bamburgh, Northumberland.]—where they were shown to be miraculous. Because I waver in opinion whether they are preserved there to this day, I make no hasty assertion. Let those other historians see to it if they have rashly affirmed anything; for my part, let rumour carry less weight, and let me assert nothing except what deserves unqualified belief [Col. 1006C].

They say that the head, buried at Lindisfarne by that same brother [Note: [Col. 1006D] “By that same brother”: a. s. d. e. l.; “by blessed Germanus”: c.], is now held at Durham between the arms of the most blessed Cuthbert [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Now at Durham … they say.” St Cuthbert is depicted as holding Oswald’s head between his arms. (Sharpe, p. 53.)]. Queen Osthryth, wife of Æthelred, king of the Mercians, daughter of King Oswi, led by affection for her uncle, wished to convey the remaining bones to her monastery at Bardney, in Mercia, not far from the city of Lincoln. The monks at first resisted for a little while [Note: [Col. 1006D] “For a little while”: a. d. e. l.; omitted in s. c.], begrudging the dead the repose of bones because they had hated him alive, since he had gained dominion over them by right of war. But, instructed in the dead of night by a lamp sent down from heaven upon the relics [Col. 1007A], they softened their foolish swelling [Note: [Col. 1007D] “Swelling”: a. c. d. e. l.; “fear”: s.] and turned to equity, voluntarily asking for what they had previously rejected.

Miracles were frequently performed there by divine power, and every sick person who invoked it felt the help of the most excellent martyr. The turf of the field grew green again from his falling blood [Note: [Col. 1007D] “Grew green again from his falling blood.” See Bede, III.9, §177.], blooming more richly than usual [Note: [Col. 1007D] “Blooming”: c. d. e. m.; “flowery”: a. l.]; by it a horse was healed which, fastened to a post, had escaped the fire by winding turns. The dust produced in washing his relics likewise did not lack miraculous power: a person deprived of reason was restored to soundness of mind. A stake which had absorbed the fresh blood of his head also provided healing: when it was washed, a desperate man received health [Note: [Col. 1007D] “When it was washed”: a. d. e. l. m.; “in the place”: s. c.].

For a long time that monastery, conscious of so great a treasure, flourished through the holiness of its inhabitants and abundance of necessities, especially after King Æthelred there [Note: [Col. 1007D] “There”: e.; “in that place”: a. s. c. d. l. m.] received the crown of monastic tonsure [Col. 1007B]. His tomb too is visited there to this day [Note: [Col. 1007D] “To this day”: e.; “until the present day”: a. l.; “until today”: c. d. m.]. But many years later, when barbarians ravaged those places, the bones of the most blessed Oswald were transferred to Gloucester. This place, possessing canons, is inhabited by no great number of residents [Note: [Col. 1007D] “Canons”: e.; “formerly canons”: a. c. l.; “they read: then monks, now [canons]”: d. m.; “then monks, not …”: text uncertain.].

Oswald, then, was the one who gave his people the first fruits of holiness; for, so far as I know, no Englishman before him was powerful in miracles. Having lived a holy life, giving alms generously, prolonging frequent vigils in God’s service, and finally, from zeal for God, engaging the heathen on behalf of the Church, he breathed out his spirit before he saw what he feared: Christianity’s ruin [Col. 1007C]. Nor shall he indeed be deprived of the glory of martyrs: first applying himself to a good life and afterwards devoting his body to a glorious death, he trod in their footsteps. His praise is almost greater in this respect: whereas they individually consecrated themselves singly to God, he consecrated to God together with himself the whole people of the Northumbrians.

## Concerning Oswi, Brother of Saint Oswald
§ 50. When he had thus been removed from human affairs, his brother Oswiu took possession of the kingdom among the Bernicians (A.D. 642), and Oswine [Note: [Col. 1007D] Oswine. c. d. l. m.; Oswiu, a. e.], son of Osric—of whom I have spoken above [Note: [Col. 1007D] Of whom I have spoken above. §49.]—among the Deirans (A.D. 643). At first they modestly agreed concerning the division of the provinces; with the treaty left in suspense, they departed each peacefully to his own domain. But not long afterward, through men to whom nothing was dearer than sowing discord, peace, often mocked by uncertain agreements, was at last wholly [Col. 1008A] broken and scattered to the winds: a pitiable crime—that there should be persons who begrudged concord to kings [Note: [Col. 1007D] Concord. e; after *concordiam*, a. s. d. l. m. read “of companionship.”], and did not refrain from bringing them, so far as lay in their power, into battle.

Then fortune, which had previously flattered Oswine with many allurements, pursued him with a scorpion’s tail. For, judging that he should abstain from war because of the scarcity of his army, he secretly withdrew to a country estate near the town, and was immediately betrayed by his own men [Note: [Col. 1007D] He was killed by Oswiu. Oswine, king of Deira, was slain by Oswiu, king of Bernicia, on 20 August 651.] and killed by Oswiu: 76 a man remarkably fitted to win the affection of his citizens by lavish expenditure of money, and, as they say, not careless of his own soul in the devotion of his mind. Thus Oswiu, master of the whole kingdom, afterward attempted everything that might clear his reputation and increase his majesty, mitigating the offence of a cruel deed by the excellence of subsequent virtues. The first, and likewise [Col. 1008B] the greatest, sum of his praises is that he nobly avenged his brother and his uncle. [Note: [Col. 1008D] He destroyed Penda, king of the Mercians. Penda, king of the Mercians, was defeated and killed by Oswiu on 15 November 655. (Bede, Book III, ch. 14, §221.)] He destroyed Penda, king of the Mercians, that ruin of neighbouring peoples and nursery of traitors; after that time he either himself presided over the Mercians, as well as over nearly all the English, or commanded those who presided over them.

Thereupon, wholly turning himself to the duties of piety, that he might answer with fitting diligence to God’s benefits flowing in upon him, he strove to raise and animate with royal vigour and full breath the infancy of Christianity [Note: [Col. 1008D] “Christianity.” e; “Christian worship,” a. c. d. l. m.] which, in his kingdom, was gasping after the murder of his brother. That same Christianity, soon mature through the teaching of the Scots [Note: [Col. 1008D] Teaching of the Scots. See Bede, Book III, ch. 25.], yet wavering in many ecclesiastical observances, he first shaped into canonical order through [Note: [Col. 1008D] Angilbert, bishop of Dorchester. See above, note 70, col. 985.] Angilbert and Wilfrid, and finally through Theodore, [Col. 1008C] archbishop. [Note: [Col. 1008D] Concerning his arrival in England. See above, note 43, col. 970.] Prince Oswiu deserves the credit for his coming into England, although Egbert, king of Kent, claims much of that glory by right of his province. He also established numerous dwellings for those serving God, and did not leave his country barren of this benefit.

Their chief monastery, then a convent of women and now of men, lies thirty miles in the northern 77 part from York. Its ancient name was Streaneshalh; now it is called Whitby. Begun by Hilda, a woman of eminent religion [Note: [Col. 1008D] Hilda. See above, note 34, col. 991.], it was enlarged with great accumulations of royal wealth by Ethelfleda, daughter of the same king, who succeeded her in its government. [Note: [Col. 1008D] Ethelfleda. From this passage it might be inferred that Ethelfleda was abbess of Streaneshalch before Hilda’s death, which occurred in 680.] There she also rendered due funeral rites to her father, who died after reigning twenty-eight years. [Note: [Col. 1008D] Having died after twenty-eight years of reign. Oswiu died on 15 February, A.D. 670.]

That monastery, like all those of the same region, was destroyed [Col. 1009A] in the Danish devastation [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Devastation.” a. d. e. l. m; “ravaging,” s. c.], of which we shall speak below, and lost many saints’ bodies. For the bones of blessed Bishop Aidan, Abbot Ceolfrith, most holy Hilda the holy woman [Note: [Col. 1009C] “Holy woman.” a. s. c. e. l; “virgin,” d. m.], and many others, as I have related in the book which I recently published on the antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury, were then transferred to Glastonbury; and likewise certain remains of other saints. [Note: [Col. 1009C] “And the blessed … have related.” This whole passage is omitted in a. s. c. l., except for the following words: “and the bones of the most holy Hilda, the holy woman, and of many others.”] Now, under an altered name and somewhat restored for the present, it scarcely displays a slender trace of its former wealth.

§ 51. Oswiu, who had two sons [Note: [Col. 1009C] Oswiu, who had two sons. Oswiu left a legitimate son, Ecgfrith, and another, illegitimate, named Alhfrith; they ruled the Northumbrians in succession.], was succeeded by the younger, born in lawful wedlock, while the bastard was rejected. He was more commended by the merits of his most holy wife Etheldreda than by his own. Indeed, he is to be praised for precisely two actions [Note: [Col. 1009C] Which indeed I have read in the deeds of the English. What Malmesbury here relates in praise of Oswiu cannot be found in any surviving author to whom the cited work could be referred, unless it is Bede. The Venerable writer alludes to the authority granted by Ecgfrith to his wife to take the sacred veil (Book IV, ch. 19, §310); and Cuthbert’s promotion to the episcopate, while he sat upon the royal throne, is likewise stated among other matters in §340.] which I have read of in the histories of the English: 78 [Col. 1009B] that he serenely permitted his lady, who wished to be free for religious service, to do so; and that, pouring forth tears in pious entreaty, he advanced blessed Cuthbert to the episcopate.

But the mind recoils from recalling the impiety which he vomited forth in persecuting most blessed Wilfrid [Note: [Col. 1009D] Wilfrid. Wilfrid was consecrated bishop of York in A.D. 665 and expelled from his see in 677; he returned to England in 679 and was again expelled in 681. In 687 he was summoned again to Northumbria, and in 692 was once more expelled. He fled to Æthelred, king of the Mercians, and in that same year administered the vacant episcopal see at Lichfield. He was expelled again in 703 and, after his case was decided at Rome in his favour in the following year, returned to England. He died in A.D. 709. His Life was written by Eddius and published in Gale, vol. III; see also Bede, Book V, ch. 19.], when, conceiving a loathing for that goodness, he deprived his country of its most brilliant light. The same man, insolent toward suppliants—a disease from which you will find no tyrants free—brought overwhelming destruction upon the Irish [Note: [Col. 1009D] The Irish. Consult Bede, Book IV, ch. 26, [Col. 1010C] and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 684. On the time and place of the invasion see also *Ogygia*, p. 230.], a people assuredly innocent and, in their native simplicity, never devising any evil.

On the other hand, he was feeble against rebels and, frustrating his father’s triumphs, lost the dominion of the Mercians; indeed, he was put to flight in battle [Note: [Col. 1010C] “In battle.” d. e. m; “in war,” a. s. c; “in flight,” l.] by their king Æthelred, son of Penda, and also lost his brother. [Note: [Col. 1010C] He also lost his brother. In the ninth year of Ecgfrith’s reign, a severe battle was fought between him and Æthelred, king of the Mercians, near the River Trent. Ælfwine, brother of King Ecgfrith, a youth about eighteen years old and much beloved by both provinces, was killed. Bede, Book IV, ch. 21; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 679.] Yet truth requires these latter actions to be attributed to the instability of youth, and those committed against Wilfrid to the counsel of bishops and [Note: [Col. 1010C] By his wife’s counsel. This concerns Irmenburga, Ecgfrith’s second wife; the former had been separated from him by divorce and adopted the religious life.] his wife—especially since Bede, who knew nothing of flattery, [Col. 1010A] calls him “most pious and most beloved by God” 79 [Note: [Col. 1010D] In the book *On the Lives of Abbots*. Published by D. Smith, 1722, folio.] in his book *On the Lives of His Abbots*.

Finally, in the fifteenth year of his reign, while conducting an expedition against the Picts, he stubbornly pressed them as they deliberately withdrew into hidden mountains, and perished with almost all his forces. [Note: [Col. 1010D] He perished with almost all his forces. Ecgfrith was killed on 20 May, A.D. 685. See Bede, Book IV, ch. 26; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 685.] A few escaped by flight and reported the matter at home. Yet divine Cuthbert, through awareness of future events, both tried to restrain him from going and, at the very hour of the slaughter, receiving into himself a spirit flowing down from heaven, did not fail, though absent, to declare that he had been slain.

§ 52. When the conspicuous report of Ecgfrith’s death was spoken everywhere, an “anxious letter, borne by a hurrying pen,” [Note: [Col. 1010D] “An anxious letter had arrived, borne by a hurrying pen.” Juvenal, *Satires*, IV, Book I, verse 149.] reached also the ears of his brother Alhfrith. Since, as we have said [Note: [Col. 1010D] “We have said.” c. d. e. m; “I have said,” a. s. l.], he was illegitimate, he had been judged unworthy of the kingdom by a faction of nobles, although he was the elder, and had withdrawn into Ireland, [Col. 1010B] whether through force or indignation. There, safe from his brother’s hatred and enjoying great leisure, he had furnished his mind with letters and every kind of philosophy.

Accordingly, those who had formerly expelled him now willingly sought him out, judging him better fitted to hold the reins of government; necessity converted its remedy into entreaty. Nor did he disappoint their hope. For nineteen years he governed the province in the greatest peace and joy, admitting nothing that devouring envy could fittingly criticize, except in the persecution of great Wilfrid. [Note: [Col. 1010D] For nineteen years … he governed. Alhfrith died at Driffield on 16 May, A.D. 705. Thus Bede (Book V, ch. 18): “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 705, Alhfrith king of the Northumbrians died, before completing the twentieth year of his reign.”] Yet he did not hold the kingdom within the same boundaries as his father and brother, because the Picts, insolently abusing their recent victory and attacking the English, softened by a long peace, had cut away their northern frontiers.

[Col. 1010C] 80 § 53. He was succeeded (A.D. 705) by his son Osred, a boy of eight years, who for eleven years cast a shadow over the kingdom; defiling the lives of nuns with his adulteries, he was at last slain by the plots of his kinsmen [Col. 1011A] and repaid the same fate upon them. [Note: [Col. 1010D] He had as successor his son Osred. These statements accord with Bede’s narrative, Book V, ch. 18; but according to Eddius, in the *Life of St Wilfrid*, Eadwulf held the royal throne for two months before Osred obtained it. Osred was killed in A.D. 716.]

For Kenred ruled two years (A.D. 716) [Note: [Col. 1011C] Kenred, son of Cuthwine.], and Osric eleven years (A.D. 728) [Note: [Col. 1011C] Osric, eleven years. Osric died on 9 May, A.D. 729 (Bede, Book V, ch. 23). He was the son of Alhfrith.]; and their one memorable distinction was that, paying for the blood of their lord, though they believed him justly slain, they polluted the air by a shameful end. Osric rightly deserved to depart more cheerfully, and, as the pagan says, “more boastful among the other shades,” because while still alive he had adopted Ceolwulf, Kenred’s brother, as his successor. [Note: [Col. 1011C] “He had adopted Ceolwulf …” According to Bede (Book V, ch. 23), Ceolwulf ascended the royal throne in A.D. 729; according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, in A.D. 731; and according to Matthew of Westminster, in A.D. 730.]

Ceolwulf, seventh from Ida, therefore ascended the trembling summit of kingship: adequate in other respects, and not lacking an acquaintance with letters, acquired through a keen mind and eager study. Bede guarantees the truth of my statement; at a time when Britain abounded most in learned men, he offered this man in particular the history of the English [Note: [Col. 1011D] The history of the English. *Ecclesiastical History of the English People.*] for polishing, plainly choosing in him authority to strengthen what had been well said, because of his sovereignty and learning, and capacity to correct what had been wrongly said, because of his intelligence.

## CONCERNING BEDE

§ 54.
