[Note: [Col. 1011D] “In whose fourth year.” A hand contemporary with the manuscript reads, in the manner of a note: “In the fourth year of Ceolwulf, king of the English, seventh from Ida, the venerable priest Bede, after many …” Ceolwulf ascended the throne on 9 May 729, and Bede died on 26 May; whence it is clear that his death occurred in the seventh year of this prince’s reign.] In the fourth year of this king, the same historian, after producing many books in the holy Church, entered the heavenly 81 homeland for which he had long sighed, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 734 [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Seven hundred and thirty-four.” See the preceding note.], in the fifty-ninth year of his age. [Note: [Col. 1011D] “The fifty-ninth year of his age.” Bede was born in 674 and died in 735, consequently in his sixty-first year. He appears to have completed the *Ecclesiastical History* in the fifty-ninth year of his age; for he says: “From the time I received the priestly office until the fiftieth year of my life, I have devoted my labour, for myself and my friends, to gathering these extracts,” etc.] He was a man whom one may more easily admire than adequately praise: born [Col. 1011C] in the farthest corner of the world, he shone so brightly with learning as to illuminate every land.

For Britain—called by some a second world because, being separated by the intervening ocean, it was unknown to many geographers—has, in its remotest district, near Scotland, the place of his birth and education. [Note: [Col. 1011D] “Born in the farthest corner of the world.” The Venerable Bede was born in that part of England which then belonged to the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow of the Order of St Benedict, but which is now included in the county of Durham. (See Stevenson, Introduction to *Ecclesiastical History*, p. vii.)] That district was once sweet with the fragrant flowers of monasteries and gleaming with numerous towns built by the Romans. Now, mournful through the ancient ravaging of the Danes or the recent devastation of the Northmen [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Either the ancient [ravaging] of the Danes or the recent [ravaging] of the Northmen.” Danish devastations began in 793 and spread widely in the following years, during the reigns of Alfred and Æthelred. In 1069 the whole region was laid waste by William I.], it offers nothing greatly attractive to the mind.

There is there the Wear, a river neither scant in breadth nor sluggish in current. Flowing into the sea, it receives in the calm bosom of its mouth ships borne in by a fair wind. [Col. 1012A] A certain Benedict adorned both its banks with churches and 82 built two monasteries there [Note: [Col. 1012D] Benedict. Benedict, surnamed Biscop, came to England with Archbishop Theodore and was appointed by him abbot of the monastery of St Augustine at Canterbury. Soon relinquishing that office, he returned to Rome. Later, having returned to England, he obtained a broad tract of land near the mouth of the River Wear, where he built two monasteries, of which he was abbot. He died on 12 January 690.]: one in the name of Peter and the other in the name of Paul, differing in neither their unity of charity nor their rule. [Note: [Col. 1012D] He built monasteries there: the monasteries of both Wearmouth and Jarrow.]

Whoever reads the book which Bede composed *On the Life of Benedict and of His Other Abbots* [Note: [Col. 1012D] The book which Bede, etc. Bede wrote Lives of Benedict Biscop and his successors, Ceolfrith and Hwaetberht, abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow, in two books; these were published by Sir James Ware in 1664 and by D. Smith in 1722.] will admire his diligence and patience. His diligence: because he brought in an abundance of books; because he was the first of all to introduce into England craftsmen for stone buildings and glass windows; because he spent almost his entire life travelling. [Note: [Col. 1012D] “Life.” e; after *aevum*, a. s. c. d. l. m. read “such things.”] The love of country and delight in refinement deceived the harshness of his labours, since he was eager to bring something unfamiliar to his countrymen. For before Benedict houses [Col. 1012B] constructed with stone stories were seen in Britain only very rarely, nor did the sun’s ray, passing through the transparency of glass, cast its light into dwellings.

His patience: because he willingly yielded the possession of St Augustine’s monastery at Canterbury to Hadrian when he arrived [Note: [Col. 1012D] Hadrian. See above, note 43, col. 970.], not fearing the haughtiness of blessed Archbishop Theodore, but reverencing his authority as teacher; because, while he travelled through foreign lands and remained away for a long time, he bore equably—indeed, magnanimously—the monks of Wearmouth installing, without his consultation, an abbot over him; and when he returned home, he gave that man equal honour in the council and thereafter shared with him all authority.

Indeed, when he had been struck by paralysis so severely that no limb could be moved, he appointed a third, because the other of whom we have spoken was being no less weakened by the same illness. When the growing disease was already 83 shaking his vital powers, he bade farewell to his companion who had been carried to him, by a nod alone. But the latter could not render the office more generously, since he was drawing nearer to death; for he died before Benedict.

Ceolfrith succeeded (A.D. 670), under whom the resources of the monastery increased immensely. When, in prolonged old age, he had renounced the desire of living, he set out for Rome, hoping to pour out his aged soul before the lordly Apostles; [Col. 1013A] but, deprived of the fulfilment of his wish, he paid nature’s debt at the city of Langres [Note: [Col. 1013C] At the city of the Lingones: a city in France, commonly Langres.] (A.D. 716). In later years his bones were returned to his monastery; then, at the time of the Danish devastation [Note: [Col. 1013C] “Devastation.” a. s. d. e. l. m; “ravaging or devastation,” c.], they were carried with the bones of blessed Hilda to Glastonbury.

The renown of these abbots, already sufficiently eminent in itself, is raised to more splendid excellence by their distinguished pupil Bede. For it is written: “A wise son is the glory of his father.” [Note: [Col. 1013C] “A wise son is the glory of his father.” “A wise son makes a father glad” (Prov. 10:1; 15:20).] One made him a monk and the other educated him. [Note: [Col. 1013C] “Educated him.” c. d. e. l. m; “educated him,” with *eum*, a. s.] Since Bede himself appended this account for the sake of brief information, comprehending his entire life in a kind of epitome [Note: [Col. 1013C] “A kind of.” c. d. e. l. m; “brief,” a. s.], the reader may recognize his own words, lest the necessity of casting them into a new form should produce either more or less than my own language. [Note: [Col. 1013C] “May recognize.” d. m; “may recognize,” a. s. c. l; “recognizes,” e.] Thus, at the end of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* [Col. 1013B] [Note: [Col. 1013C] At the end of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book V, ch. 24, §453, edition of the English Historical Society. There is little variation of readings between Malmesbury’s text and Bede’s.], a man praiseworthy both in other respects and in this, that he did not begrudge posterity even so slight a knowledge of himself, says:

§ 55. “With the Lord’s 84 help, I, Bede, servant of Christ and priest of the monastery of the Apostles Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Of the Apostles.” d. e. m; “of the blessed Apostles,” a. s. c. l.] which is at Wearmouth [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Wearmouth.” e; “Wiremudan,” a. s. l; “Wiremundam,” c; “Wirmundisam,” d. m.], have set forth these matters concerning the history of the Britains. Born in the territory of that same monastery, when I was seven years old I was entrusted by the care of my kinsfolk to the most reverend Abbot Benedict for education, and afterward to Ceolfrith. I have spent all the rest [Col. 1013C] of my life in the habitation of that monastery, devoted all my labour to meditation upon Scripture, and, amid observance of regular discipline and the daily duty of singing in church, have always found it sweet either to learn, to teach, or to write.

“In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate, and in my thirtieth the order of priesthood, both through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John [Note: [Col. 1013D] Bishop John: John of Beverley, bishop of Hexham in 686. He became bishop of York in A.D. 705 and died on 7 May 722.], by command of Abbot Ceolfrith. From the time when I received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of my life, I have taken care, for the needs of myself and my brethren, briefly to make these notes from the works of the venerable Fathers, and also to add matters in accordance with the tenor and interpretation of them.”

§ 56. Then, having enumerated the thirty-six volumes which he issued in seventy-eight books, he added: “And I beseech you, good Jesus, that you who in your favour granted me sweetly to draw the words of your knowledge [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Words.” a. s. d. e. l; “gifts,” c.] may also graciously grant that I may one day come to you, the fountain of all knowledge, and always be pleasing [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Be pleasing.” s. c. d. e; “please,” a. l.] before your face.

“Moreover, I humbly ask all persons of our nation to whom this history 85 may come, whether reading or hearing it, [Note: [Col. 1013D] “I ask.” a. s. d. e. l; “I beseech,” c.] that they may remember frequently to intercede before heavenly mercy for my infirmities of mind [Col. 1014B] and body; and that each may repay me in his own region with this return for his reward: that I, who have carefully sought to record from each province and from the more eminent places whatever I believed worthy of memory and pleasing to their inhabitants, may find among all people the fruit of pious intercession.” [Note: [Col. 1013D] “Moreover … may find.” This passage is not inserted at the end of the History, but in the published text of Bede this prologue concludes here.]

§ 57. Here talent fails and eloquence succumbs, not knowing which to praise more: the multitude of his books or the restraint of his language. Divine wisdom had undoubtedly poured itself into him in no unworthy draught, so that in the narrow span of his life he might produce such great volumes. What is more, it is reported that he went to Rome (A.D. 701), in order either to affirm in person that his books agreed with ecclesiastical doctrine [Col. 1014C] or, if they conflicted with it, to correct them by apostolic direction.

[Note: [Col. 1014C] Yet I do not firmly affirm that he was at Rome. From the matters adduced here, it is probable that in Malmesbury’s age there were persons who maintained, as tradition had it, that Bede had gone to Rome, although Malmesbury himself seems not to attach great importance to this tradition. Nevertheless, from the letter of Pope Sergius it is highly likely that Bede was summoned to Rome. The most learned Wilkins provides a probable reason why he refrained from this journey. He conjectures that the letter was written in the last year of Pope Sergius’s pontificate (A.D. 701), and that messengers arrived in England shortly afterward announcing the death of the supreme pontiff; hence Bede was deterred from his intended journey.

[Col. 1015D] Recently, however, the opinion has been put forward that Bede was never summoned to Rome, and that this was a mere fabrication occasioned by Malmesbury’s error. Having found a letter in which Pope Sergius instructed Ceolfrith, or Ceolfrid, abbot of Jarrow, to send one of his monks to Rome, Malmesbury concluded that Bede himself had been sent and inserted his name here with the greatest inconsiderateness. One still extant copy of this letter, older than Malmesbury’s work (Tiberius, A. XV), would expose our author’s carelessness, since it contains no passage mentioning Bede.

It may be answered that Ussher, who had seen that letter and transcribed it from the cited manuscript, drew no such conclusion. Moreover, he had at hand an ancient manuscript containing the complete letter, from which Malmesbury gives only some extracts. In it Bede’s name occurs, although the title “priest” is not attached to him. Ussher infers only this: namely, that the omission of Bede’s title did not occur without reason, especially since at that time he had not yet been raised to priestly rank.

Before it can be admitted as a sound inference that Malmesbury interpolated the passage in question, it must be demonstrated that Tiberius A. XV is the very authentic copy of the letter which he used; but this cannot at all be rightly concluded, since it is utterly incredible that no copies of this letter existed when he was composing his history. On the contrary, it should be maintained more confidently that the copy he had contained the entire disputed passage; for Malmesbury—whose great integrity is acknowledged by all writers—more than once expressly declares that he took diligent care to insert nothing into his history that was not supported by the best authorities. Further, if he were guilty of the interpolation attributed to him, it is altogether improbable that he could have used language so candid.]

Nevertheless, 86 I do not firmly affirm that he was at Rome; but I pronounce without doubt that he was invited there. This letter will make that plain [Col. 1015A] and at the same time show how highly the Roman see [Note: [Col. 1015D] “See.” a. d. e. l; “court,” s.] valued him, since it so earnestly desired him.

§ 58. “Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ceolfrith, religious abbot [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Abbot.” Tiberius A. XV reads after *abbati*, “and priest.”], greeting [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Greeting.” Tiberius A. XV reads after it, “sends.”]. By what words or means can we express the mercy of our God and his ineffable [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Ineffable.” a. s. d. e. l; “memorable,” c.] providence, and render fitting thanksgivings for his immeasurable benefits toward us, who leads those placed in darkness and the shadow of death to the light of knowledge?”

And below: “Meanwhile, know that we have received with willing and joyful mind the gift of blessing which your devout religious community sent us through the present bearer, just as it was sent by it. [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Know.” Several lines occurring in Tiberius A. XV are lacking here.] Therefore, with most earnest devotion favouring the suitable and worthy requests of your praiseworthy concern, [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Therefore” was inserted in Tiberius A. XV by a later hand.] 87 we exhort [Col. 1015B] the God-beloved goodness of your religious devotion [Note: [Col. 1015D] “The goodness of your religious devotion.” Tiberius A. XV reads “the religious devotion of your goodness.”] that, because certain matters of ecclesiastical business have arisen which must be more fully made known not without examination, we need for consultation men trained in the art of letters. [Note: [Col. 1015D] “Without.” s. c. d. m; “of itself,” a. e. l.] As becomes a devoted helper of the holy mother, the universal Church, do not fail to lend obedient devotion to this [Note: [Col. 1016C] “This.” a. d. e. l; “him,” Tiberius A. XV.] exhortation of ours; but, without any delay, send the religious servant of God, Bede [Note: [Col. 1016C] “The servant of God, Bede, etc.” In the Cotton manuscript (Tiberius A. XV, fol. 6), this passage reads: “the servant of God N. of your venerable monastery.” These words, it seems, should rather be read “the servant of our God.” From the occurrence of the letter N in the Cotton manuscript in place of the name of the person summoned to Rome, it might be inferred that in the copy from which the author took his extracts the name had been omitted through a copyist’s negligence, leaving the passage obscure. For some word appears to be lacking to complete the construction of the sentence as it stands in Tiberius A. XV.] [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Bede.” In the margin of Tiberius A. XV, in a comparatively modern hand, is written: “Bede is called to Rome.”], priest of your venerable monastery [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Priest.” In Tiberius A. XV this word has been inserted by a later hand and deleted.], to the thresholds [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Thresholds.” Tiberius A. XV reads “the venerable thresholds.”] of the chief Apostles, my lords Peter and Paul, your patrons and protectors, into the presence of our humble self. Do not delay to direct him thither; and, with the Lord favouring your holy prayers, do not doubt that he will return safely to you after the desired solemn settlement of the aforesaid matters has been completed with God’s help.

“For, as we trust, whatever shall by his excellence be imparted to the universal Church [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Universal.” After *generali*, Tiberius A. XV reads “when its devout assembly has been convened.”] will also benefit all entrusted to you.” [Note: [Col. 1016D] “By his excellence.” Tiberius A. XV reads “most excellently.”]

88 § 59. His reputation was already so celebrated that the Roman high authority required him for resolving questions; nor did Gallican arrogance ever find in the Englishman anything that it could justly censure. [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Already.” a. d. e. l; “so,” c.] Thus all Latinity yielded the palm to his faith and teaching.

For his faith was sound and uncurious, while his eloquence was sweet. In all his explanations of the divine Scriptures he investigated rather those matters by which the reader might preserve love of God and neighbour than those by which he might either sample such subtleties or polish away the rust of language. Moreover, no one is permitted to doubt the holiness of his life by the incontrovertible truth of the saying uttered to the world by the majesty of divine [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Divine.” a. s. c. e. l; “divine,” d. m.] wisdom: [Col. 1016B] “Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins.” [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Into a malicious … sins.” Wisdom 1:4.]

This, surely, is not said of worldly wisdom, which enters human hearts without distinction and is very often seen to flourish in the worst men, who set no limits to their crimes even until their final day, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “The children of this age are wiser in their own generation than the children of light.” [Note: [Col. 1016D] “The children of this age … their own generation.” Luke 16:8.] Rather, it names that wisdom which, as the spirit of discipline, flees deceit and separates itself from thoughts devoid of understanding—understanding, I mean, of living well and speaking well. Thus Seneca, in his book *On Causes* [Note: [Col. 1016D] *On Causes*. Seneca, *Controversies*, Book I.], beautifully recalls that Cato, defining the office of an orator, said: “An orator is a good man skilled in speaking.”

Therefore the ecclesiastical orator first cleansed [Col. 1016C] his conscience, so that he might approach the unfolding [Note: [Col. 1016D] “Unfolding.” a. s. e. l; “expounding,” d. m.] of the meaning of mystical writers. For how could one 89 serve vices who drank in their inmost marrow and consumed all his thoughts in expounding the Scriptures? For, as he himself confesses in the third book of his exposition on Samuel [Note: [Col. 1017D] In the third book on Samuel. This statement is expressed in the prologue to the first book of the *Allegorical Exposition on the Prophet Samuel*, p. 208, vols. III–IV of Bede’s *Works*, Basel, 1563.], even if his expositions brought readers no other profit, they were of no small benefit to himself, because while he pursued these studies with every effort, he put behind him the slipperiness of the world and vain thoughts. Thus, purified from vices, he entered within the veil; and what he had received inwardly in his mind he brought forth outwardly in disciplined speech.

§ 60. Yet the pure holiness and holy purity of his mind shine most brightly at the time [Note: [Col. 1017D] “At the time.” d. e. m; “at a recent time,” a. c. l; “at the first time,” s.] of his death. [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Shine.” c. d. e; “shone,” a. s. l.] For during seven continuous weeks, nauseated by food through an upset stomach and drawing breath with painful and restricted sighing, so that his weakness laid him upon a bed, he nevertheless did not abandon the labour of literary studies. Every day, besides the required task of psalmody, he strove to deceive the heaviness of illness by constant lessons to his disciples and by pondering and resolving difficult questions, his mind being meanwhile fixed upon them.

During those days he also translated into the English tongue the Gospel of John—which exercises the minds of readers by its difficulty—and accommodated himself to persons less instructed in Latin. Again and again he admonished his disciples, saying: “Learn, my little children, while I am with you; for I do not know how long I shall remain, and whether after a little while my Maker may take me away and my spirit return to him who sent [Col. 1017C] it and granted it to come into this life. I have lived long; my Lord has provided well for me in this span of life. I now desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.”

90 § 61. Often, when hope and fear were held in balance and neither outweighed the other, he would say: “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God.” [Note: [Col. 1017D] “It is dreadful . . . living.” Hebrews 10:31.] — “I have not lived among you in such a way that I should be ashamed to live; yet neither do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord”: borrowing the saying of the most holy Ambrose as he was dying. [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Borrowing.” c. d. e.: “imitating,” a. s. l.]

Blessed was he who spoke with so secure a conscience that he neither blushed to live nor feared to die: here unafraid of the sight of men, there calmly awaiting God’s hidden judgment. Often, oppressed by the force of pain, he took breath again through such examples: “The furnace tests gold, and the furnace of temptation tests the righteous man.” [Col. 1017D] “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us.” [Note: [Col. 1017D] “The sufferings . . . in us.” Romans 8:18.] [Col. 1018A]

Tears and the difficulty of sighing accompanied these sayings. At night, moreover, since there were no pupils to teach or to take down his words, he himself kept vigil through the night in thanksgiving and the singing of psalms, fulfilling the saying of that most wise man: that he was never less alone [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Never less alone.” Scipio Africanus used to say “that he was never less at leisure than when at leisure, nor less alone than when he was alone.” CICERO, *On Duties*, book III, ch. 1.] than when alone. If sleep ever crept upon his eyelids—it was slight and heavy—he immediately shook it off, disturbed, and gave utterance to the affection always fixed upon God in these words: “ [Note: [Col. 1017D] “Receive . . . proud.” Psalm 119:122.] Receive, Lord, thy servant for good; [Note: [Col. 1018D] “For good.” d. e.: “in good,” c.; omitted in a. s. l.] let not the proud falsely accuse me” — “ [Note: [Col. 1018D] “Deal . . . thy.” Psalm 119:124.] Deal with thy servant according to thy mercy.” These and other examples from the remnants of his former memory came spontaneously to his lips; he brought them forth at intervals as the distress of his grievous illness was eased.

But on the Tuesday before the Ascension of the Lord, when his sickness was at last growing worse, 91 a slight swelling appeared in his feet: an unmistakable omen and sign of approaching death. Then the community having been summoned, he was anointed and received communion. Having given all the kiss, and entreating each of them to remember him hereafter, he also bestowed upon some, as tokens of a more intimate friendship earned by their services, the little gifts which he kept in private.

On the day of the Ascension, when his soul, weary of the frail use of the body and eager to depart, was fluttering, he lay opposite the oratory in which he was accustomed to pray, with haircloth beneath him. His mind remained unimpaired and his countenance cheerful as he invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, saying: “O King of glory, Lord of hosts, who today as conqueror hast ascended above all [Col. 1018C] the heavens, do not leave us orphans, but send upon us the Spirit of truth, promised by the Father.” When this prayer was ended, [Note: [Col. 1018D] “He breathed his last.” The letter describing Bede’s words at the end of his life, published by one of his disciples who was present at his death, is printed in Stevenson, *Introduction to Beda, Historia ecclesiastica*.] he breathed his last; and there followed, filling the nostrils of all, [Note: [Col. 1018D] “Filling.” d. e. m.: “overwhelming,” a. s. c. l.] a fragrance such as neither cinnamon nor balsam gives forth, but a paradisal scent, like that which the joy of spring exhales wherever it is found. He was then buried in the same monastery; [Note: [Col. 1018D] “But now . . . report confirms.” Ælfrid, a priest, is said to have stolen Bede’s bones from Jarrow and deposited them in Durham Cathedral at about the beginning of the eleventh century.] but report now confirms that he lies at Durham with blessed Cuthbert.

§ 62. With him was buried almost all knowledge of deeds down to our own times. So completely was there no Englishman emulous of his studies, no follower of his glories, to pursue the course of the coinage he had left behind. A few whom just Jesus loved, though not without distinction trained in letters, spent their whole lives in ungrateful [Col. 1018D] silence; others, having scarcely tasted those pursuits with the first touch of their lips, [Note: [Col. 1018D] “Lips.” a. s. c. l.: “books,” d. e. m.] cherished an idle leisure. Thus, as one more slothful always succeeded another, still more slothful, [Col. 1019A] 92 the ardour of learning throughout the whole island grew cold for a long time. The verses of his epitaph—a disgrace utterly unworthy of so great a man’s mausoleum—will bear great witness to this indolence:

> Here rests the priest Bede, buried in the flesh:  
> Christ, grant his soul to rejoice in heaven for ever;  
> And grant that he may be made drunk from the fountain of wisdom, for which already  
> He sighed in exultation, ever with intent love.

[Note: [Col. 1019C] “Him.” c. d. e. m.: “to him,” a. s. l.]

§ 63. Can this disgrace be lessened by any excuse: that even in the monastery where, while he lived, the school of every branch of learning rejoiced, no man could be found to compose his memorial except in a thin and wretched style? But enough has been said of this; I shall now return to what was in hand.

§ 64. Ceolwulf, judging it inconsistent with Christian seriousness [Col. 1019B] to remain occupied with earthly affairs, laid aside kingship after eight years’ reign and received the monastic life in the church of Lindisfarne. [Note: [Col. 1019C] “The monastic life.” d. m.: “a monk,” a. c. e. l.; “the monastic habit,” s. Ceolwulf, having abdicated his kingdom in favour of his kinsman Eadbert, assumed the monastic habit in 737.] How great was the favour of his merits in his conduct in that place is attested by his celebrated burial beside blessed Cuthbert [Note: [Col. 1019C] “Burial.” Ceolwulf was buried at Lindisfarne; but the determined year of his death is unknown.] and by many miracles sent down from above. [Note: [Col. 1019C] “From above,” a. s. c. d. l. m.; “heavenly,” e.]

§ 65. He had provided beforehand against any wavering of the commonwealth by appointing to the kingdom in 737 [Note: [Col. 1019C] “Egbert.” Symeon of Durham and other authors call this king Eadbert. According to Malmesbury, [Col. 1019D] he had a namesake brother, Archbishop of York. Egbert was consecrated bishop of that see in 732. See the immediately following note.] Egbert, the son of his uncle. Egbert, accepting this charge and treading the paths of virtue, ruled for twenty years with excellent moderation. He had a brother of the same name, Archbishop of York, who, 93 both by his own prudence and by his brother’s power, [Note: [Col. 1019D] “That see,” etc. York again became an archiepiscopal see in 735, owing to Ecgbert’s frequent appeals to Rome.] restored that see to its proper rank.

For, as is readily apparent to anyone reading the deeds of the English, [Note: [Col. 1019D] “To one reading the deeds of the English.” Bede, book II, §§ 112, 148, 149.] Paulinus, the first bishop of that city, [Col. 1019C] having been driven from the place by hostile force and dying at Rochester, left there the distinguished pallium which he had received from Pope Honorius. [Note: [Col. 1019D] “Paulinus.” After leaving Northumbria, Paulinus became bishop of Rochester. He died on 10 October, 644. See note 58, col. 983.] After him, several bishops of so great a city, content with the simple title of bishop, had aspired to nothing higher. But Egbert, [Col. 1020A] when enthroned, a man of more spirited character, reflected that, just as it is arrogant to seek what is not due, so it is cowardly to neglect what is due; and by repeated appeals to the Apostolic See he recovered the pallium.

He was, so to speak, an armoury and sanctuary of all the liberal arts, and he established a most noble library at York. I call Alcuin as a fitting witness to this: sent by the kings of England to Charlemagne the emperor on a mission of peace, kindly received and entertained by him, he says in [Note: [Col. 1020C] “Letter,” etc. This letter, written in August 796, must have been sent to Eanbald II, since Eanbald I died on 29 July of that year. Eanbald II was consecrated on 14 August 796 and received the pallium in the following year.] a letter to Eanbald, Egbert’s third successor: [Note: [Col. 1020C] “Praise and glory . . . left.” Alcuin, *Opera*, folio, Regensburg, 1777, vol. I, part I, p. 63, letter 50.] “Praise and glory to God, who has preserved my days in good prosperity, so that I might rejoice at the exaltation of my dearest son, who laboured in my stead in the church where I had been nourished 94 and educated, and who presided over the treasures of wisdom in [Col. 1020B] which [Note: [Col. 1020C] “My master,” etc. A doubt has arisen concerning Alcuin’s master mentioned here. Alcuin heard the teachers Ecgbert and his successor [Col. 1020D] Æthelbert, as the author of his Life relates: “When Ecgbert,” he says, “died in 766, on 19 November, Alcuin by divine gift received Elcbert or Ælbert in the place of his lost master.” Malmesbury here and elsewhere calls him Egbert, and considers him to be identical with the Archbishop of that name who obtained the restoration of the archiepiscopal see in 735. The similarity of names, by which Norman writers were often led into error, probably gave rise to this question.] my beloved master Egbert the archbishop left me as heir.”

Likewise, to Charles Augustus: [Note: [Col. 1020D] “To Charles Augustus.” Alcuin, *Opera*, vol. I, part I, p. 52, letter 38.] “Give me more select books of scholastic learning, such as I had in my homeland through the good and most devoted diligence of my master Egbert the archbishop. And, if it please your wisdom, I shall send back some of our boys, that they may collect from there whatever is necessary and carry back to Francia the flowers of Britain; so that there may not be only a garden enclosed at York, but also streams of paradise at Tours.”

§ 66. This is the Alcuin whom, as I have said, was sent to Francia on a mission of peace and who, captivated there either by the beauty of the land or by the king’s kindness, remained with Charles. Held in high esteem by him, he carefully cultivated the imperial mind, insofar as it was free from courtly cares, through dialectic, [Col. 1020C] rhetoric, and even astronomy. For, of all Englishmen whom I have read, after blessed Aldhelm and Bede he was the most learned, and he displayed the powers of his intellect in many books. [Note: [Col. 1020D] “Displayed.” After *fecit*, s. c. m. read: “He lies in Francia at Saint Paul of Cormery, a monastery which Charlemagne built on his advice; and even today, in that church, the food and drink of four monks are daily offered as alms for the soul of that same Alcuin.” This passage occurs in the margin of d, written in the same hand. Some maintain that Alcuin was buried in the abbey of Saint Martin at Tours, where he died on 18 April 804. Saint Paul of Cormery was a dependency of this monastery (BOUQUET, V, 765).]

§ 67. Indeed, since we have come 95 to the point at which the mention of Charlemagne has introduced itself, I wish to weave truth into the many fables of antiquity concerning the line of the Frankish kings. Nor shall I wander far from my purpose, because I consider ignorance of their descent a loss to learning, since they are both our neighbours and the Christian empire chiefly concerns them. Perhaps it will not seem disagreeable to some to run through this compendium, who have no leisure to turn over great volumes.

## ON THE LINE OF THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS

§ 68. [Note: [Col. 1021B] “Franks,” etc. The author of the work entitled *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks* also contends that the name Franks was imposed upon them by the Emperor Valentinian because they conquered the Alans and drove them into the Maeotian marshes; the name, in the Attic tongue, means “fierce.” To defend this etymology some have thought that we should read “in the Chattic tongue,” which was the language of the Franks. Yet the name Franks is known in history more than one hundred and twenty years before the age of Valentinian. Libanius the sophist, writing in the fourth century, asserts that in that age there existed beside the Rhine, near the ocean, a Celtic people so warlike and vigorous that they were distinguished by the name Φρακτοὶ (*phraktoi*, “protected/fortified”), corrupted into Φραγκοὶ (*phrankoi*, “Franks”). The sounder judgment of critics, however, is that various peoples dwelling between the Rhine, Main, and Elbe joined in a league to defend themselves from the Roman yoke, and assumed the name Franks as a sign of their resolve to defend their liberty. See Bouquet, p. 721. Compare Aimon, *History of the Franks*, in Duchesne, *Writers of Frankish History*.]

The Franks were so called from the fierceness of their customs by a Greek word, because, at the command of the first Emperor Valentinian, they drove out the Alans fleeing into the Maeotian marshes. Formerly a small and insignificant people, they increased to an incredible degree [Col. 1021B] in a short time through a ten-year remission of tribute; for on these terms they had accepted the peril of battle before the war. Since we have reached his time, mindful now of our promise, we shall add a few remarks about the kingdom of the Mercians; for we like economy in speaking, and the abundance of material for much discourse does not please us.

## HERE BEGINS THE ACCOUNT OF THE KINGDOM OF THE MERCIANS

§ 74. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 626, the one hundred and thirty-ninth year after Hengist’s death, [Note: [Col. 1029C–D] Penda, etc. The earliest history of the Mercians is wrapped in dense darkness. Henry of Huntingdon makes Crida the founder of this kingdom, about A.D. 584. Crida died in A.D. 600, and was succeeded by Wibba, who died in A.D. 610. Ceorl was his first successor, and Penda succeeded Ceorl in A.D. 626.] a certain Penda, son of Pibba, tenth in descent from Woden, illustrious by lineage, energetic in war, and likewise pagan and impious, assumed the title of king among the Mercians. Already fifty years old, he had fostered his boldness by frequent raids against neighbouring peoples. Having seized the kingdom, his spirit, ailing for want of rest and ignorant how great a crime it was to conquer by war those bound to him in fellowship, to shake nearby cities, ride through the territories of kings who were his compatriots, and harass them, began to act amid great tumult and terror. [Note: [Col. 1029D] *Inequitare* (“to ride through/harass”). Witnesses e. c. l. read *inquietare*; s. d. read *inequitare*.]

For what would a man not dare who, with wicked rashness, destroyed the lights of Britain, Edwin [Note: [Col. 1029D] Edwin. See note 56, § 48.] and Oswald [Note: [Col. 1029D] Oswald. See note 76, § 49.], kings of the Northumbrians, and Sigebert [Note: [Col. 1029D] Sigebert was killed in A.D. 635.], Egric [Note: [Col. 1029D] *Egricum*. Witnesses s. c. e. read *Egfridum*; a. d. l. m. read *Egricum*. Egric was killed in A.D. 635.], and Anna [Note: [Col. 1029D] Anna was killed in A.D. 654.], kings of the East Angles—in whom nobility of birth and holiness of life were joined? He also drove Chenwalch, king of the West Saxons, into exile after provoking him twice and three times to war, [Note: [Col. 1029D] Drove him into exile. See note 15, § 19.] although Chenwalch deservedly paid the penalty for his faithlessness, through which he had sinned against God by renouncing the faith, and against Penda himself by repudiating his sister. [Note: [Col. 1029D] By repudiating his sister. See above, § 19; Bede, book III, chapter 7, § 169.]

It is tiresome to recount how, ravening for every opportunity of slaughter and flying, like a crow, toward the stench of a corpse, he voluntarily hastened to Chedwalla’s aid [Note: [Col. 1029D–1030C] Chedwalla. Penda, allied with Chedwalla, king of the Britons, defeated Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, at Hatfield on 12 October A.D. 633. See note 56, § 48.] and was of great advantage in recovering his kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1029D] *Ultro* (“voluntarily”). Witnesses s. c. d. e. read it; a. l. omit it.] Thus, for thirty years, he raged against his kinsmen, but accomplished nothing memorable against foreign peoples. At last, however, unbridled ambition [Note: [Col. 1030C] *Cupiditas* (“ambition/desire”). Witnesses a. s. c. d. l. read *cupiditas*; c. also has *temeritas* (“rashness”).] found an end suited to its deserts (A.D. 655); for, defeated by Oswy, who had succeeded his brother Oswald, more through God’s power than through military force, together with his auxiliaries, [Note: [Col. 1030C] He increased the number of infernal souls. See note 97, § 50.] he increased the number of souls in hell. [Col. 1030B]

By Queen Kineswitha [Note: [Col. 1030D] Kineswitha. See Bede, book III, chapter 24, and Smith’s note on Cynuise.] he had sons: Weda, [Note: [Col. 1030D] Weda. Penda’s son and successor is called Penda in Bede, the Saxon Chronicles, and other authorities. He was raised to the kingship of the southern Mercians by his kinsman Oswy in A.D. 656 and was killed the following spring.] Wulfer, Ethelred, Merewald, and Mercelin; and two daughters, Kineburga and Kineswitha, [Note: [Col. 1030D] *Duas* (“two”). Witnesses a. s. c. d. l. read *duas*; e. reads *suas* (“his”).] both eminent in holy continence. Thus a father perpetually rebellious against God produced fruits most holy for heaven.

§ 75. His son Weda succeeded him in part of the kingdom (A.D. 656), being placed by Oswy’s gift over the southern Mercians: a vigorous young man and son-in-law of Oswy even while his father lived, [Note: [Col. 1030D] Son-in-law. Peada married Alchfleda, Oswy’s illegitimate daughter, through whose secret arts he was betrayed in A.D. 657.] for he had received Oswy’s daughter on the condition that, embracing Christianity, he should renounce idols. With his father-in-law’s support, under the favourable calm of the realm, he would have taken care to make his province a participant in that faith, had death—notably hastened, it is said, through the treachery of his wife—not cut down such happy beginnings. [Col. 1030C] [Note: [Col. 1030D] Then Oswy took over the kingdom. After Penda’s defeat, the Mercian kingdom passed into the hands of Oswy the victor. He granted part of it to Penda; when Penda died, that part reverted to Oswy.]

Then Oswy took over the kingdom, which seemed to belong to him both by right of victory over the father and by kinship through the son. But the spirit of the provincials could not endure him as king for more than three years. [Note: [Col. 1030D] Not beyond three years. See Bede, book III, chapter 24, § 224.] Having expelled his commanders and acclaimed Wulfer, Penda’s son, as an omen of kingship, [Note: [Col. 1030D] Wulfer. After Oswy was expelled from Mercia, Wulfher succeeded him in the kingdom in A.D. 657.] they recovered their freedom.

§ 76. Wulfer, lest he disappoint the hopes of the citizens, strove diligently, with great powers both of mind and body, to show himself a useful ruler. In particular, he gave most earnest support to Christianity, which was barely alive in his kingdom and had been introduced through his brother. In his earlier years he was gravely afflicted by the king of the West Saxons; in the following years, repelling the injury by the alertness of his counsel, he even deprived that king of dominion over the island of Wight. [Note: [Col. 1031C] The following events, etc. Wulfer defeated Cynewulf, king of the West Saxons, in A.D. 661, and granted the uncultivated Isle of Wight to Aethelwald, whose sponsor he had been at baptism. (Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 661).] Turning that island, still breathing sacrilegious rites, toward the right path, he soon afterward gave it, as a gift of faith, to Ethelwalk, king of the South Saxons, whose sponsor he had been at baptism.

Yet these deeds, and whatever good things belong to him, are stained and diminished by the grave mark of simony: he was the first of the English kings to sell the holy bishopric of London to a certain ambitious Wina. [Note: [Col. 1031C] To a certain Wina. Wini, or Wina, bishop of Winchester, was torn from his see in A.D. 666; in the same year he purchased the London episcopal see from King Wulfher. See Bede, book III, chapter 7, § 170.]

He married Ermenhilda, daughter of Ercombert, king of Kent, and by her had Kenred and Werburga, a most holy virgin, who lies at Chester. [Col. 1031B] His brother Merewald had as wife Ermenburga, daughter of Ermender, brother of the same Ercombert. By her he had daughters, Milburga, who rests at Wenlock, and Mildritha, who rests in Kent in the monastery of St Augustine, and Mildrith; and a son, Merefinn.

Alfrid, king of the Northumbrians, took Kineburga, Penda’s daughter, as wife. Later, scorning carnal union, she assumed the habit of a nun in the monastery that her brothers Wulfer and Aethelred had built.

§ 77. When Wulfer had died after nineteen years, [Note: [Col. 1031C] *Decem et novem* (“nineteen”). Witnesses a. s. c. e. l. read it; d. m. read *viginti* (“twenty”). According to Bede (book V, chapter 24, § 452), Wulfher died in A.D. 675, after seventeen years of reign.] his brother Ethelred reigned. [Note: [Col. 1031D] Ethelred. Ethelred succeeded his brother in A.D. 675.] He was more distinguished by religious devotion than by practice in fighting. Having shown his valour in one famous expedition into Kent, [Note: [Col. 1031D] Expedition into Kent. Aethilred ravaged Kent in A.D. 676. (Bede, book V, chapter 24, § 452, and Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 676).] he devoted the rest of his life to peace—except that, attacking Egfrid, king of the Northumbrians, who had crossed the bounds of his kingdom, he compelled him to return home after his brother Elwin had been killed in battle (A.D. 679). [Note: [Col. 1031D] King Egfrid of the Northumbrians . . . his brother Elwin having been killed. See note 12, § 51.]

This killing he redeemed from Egfrid by a more generous settlement, with blessed Theodore, archbishop, diligently arranging it and large sums of money being collected. [Note: [Col. 1031D] “This killing . . . he redeemed.” That is, he paid *weregild*, a monetary penalty for a slain man, half of which belonged to the public treasury and the other half to the relatives of the slain. The *weregild* of every person, from prince to servant, was fixed by law. The legal compensation paid to King Ine by the men of Kent for the killing of Mullus or Mollon was, according to the Saxon Chronicle, no less than thirty thousand English pounds. See note 26, § 35.]

After this, in the thirtieth year of his reign, he was tonsured according to rule at Bardney, becoming first a monk and then an abbot. [Note: [Col. 1031D–1032C] “In the thirtieth year of his reign,” etc. Aethilred, having abdicated the kingdom, entered the monastic life at Bardney in A.D. 704; his nephew Coenred, or Chenred, succeeded him.] This is the man who, contemporary with Ine, king of the West Saxons, also confirmed by his own authority the privilege which Saint Aldhelm, as we said above, brought from Rome. [Note: [Col. 1032C] The privilege that Saint Aldhelm brought from Rome, as we said above. See note 33, § 34.] He had Ostgida, sister of Egfrid, the same king of the Northumbrians, as wife, and by her had a son, Ceolred.

§ 78. He appointed as his successor Kenred (A.D. 704), son of his brother Wulfer, distinguished for devotion to God, integrity toward his country, and great purity of conduct. In the fifth year of his reign, setting out for Rome, [Note: [Col. 1032C] “In the fifth year of his reign, setting out for Rome.” Coenred’s abdication and pilgrimage to Rome are assigned to A.D. 709.] he completed the remainder of his time there in religious devotion, especially moved by remorse at the pitiable end of a soldier. As Bede relates, [Note: [Col. 1032C] As Bede relates. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 13.] that man had proudly refused, while sound in health, to confess his crimes; but standing at death’s threshold, he openly saw demons, the instigators leading to the punishments, flattering him toward the sins to which he had yielded his mind.

§ 79. After him reigned Chelred, son of his uncle Ethelred, [Note: [Col. 1032D] Chelred. Ethelred's son succeeded his kinsman in A.D. 709. (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 19, § 412.)] as remarkable for valour against Ine [Note: [Col. 1032D] *Inam* (“against Ine”). Witnesses s. c. e. read *Inam*; a. l. read *viam* (“the way”); d. m. read *vitia* (“vices”).] as pitiable in an untimely death. For, having not completed eight years of kingship, [Note: [Col. 1032D] *Octo* (“eight”). e. reads *octo*; a. s. c. d. l. read *ultra octo* (“more than eight”). Ceolred died in A.D. 716. (Bede, book V, chapter 24, § 452).] he was buried at Lichfield, leaving Ethelbald as heir, Penda’s great-grandson through his brother Alwy. [Note: [Col. 1032D] Ethelbald . . . through his brother Alwy. Ethelbald ascended the throne in A.D. 716. In the Saxon Chronicle he is called Alwy’s son.]

Ethelbald, having conducted affairs in profound peace for a long time—namely, forty-one years—and finally killed by his subjects, turned Fortune’s wheel. [Note: [Col. 1032D] Killed by his subjects. Aethilbald was slain at Seckington in Warwickshire in A.D. 757 by Beornraed, who, after committing this crime, usurped the kingdom.] [Col. 1032C] Bernred, author of his murder, produced nothing memorable except that, soon killed by Offa, he received an end worthy of his treachery. [Note: [Col. 1032D] Bernred. Beornred was driven from the throne and killed by Offa in A.D. 757.]

To this Ethelbald Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, an Englishman by birth, who afterward received the crown of martyrdom, sent a letter. [Note: [Col. 1032D] Boniface, etc. Boniface, whose original name was Winfrith, was archbishop of Mainz and was called the apostle of the Germans. He suffered martyrdom in Frisia on 5 June A.D. 755. He sent his admonitory letter to Aethilbald in A.D. 745.] I shall insert part of it here, [Note: [Col. 1033D] “Of which I shall insert a part here.” This letter survives in full in Wilkins, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 87, and in Spelman, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 232.] so that it may be seen how freely he rebuked the vices already grown prevalent among the English people, whose future arrival Alcuin had feared. At the same time it will be a powerful proof, in the deaths described of certain kings, of how strictly God punishes the guilty whom his wrath, long held in balance, awaits.

§ 80. “To the most beloved lord and, in Christ’s love, to be preferred above the other kings of the English, Ethelbald: Boniface, archbishop, German legate of the Roman Church, eternal greeting of charity in Christ.

“We confess before God that, whenever we hear of your prosperity, faith, and good works, we rejoice; [Note: [Col. 1033D] *Quando* (“when”). Witnesses d. e. m. read *quando autem* (“but when”); a. s. c. l. read *quando*.] but whenever we learn anything adverse concerning you, whether in the outcome of wars or in peril to souls, we are grieved. For we have heard that, devoted to almsgiving, you forbid thefts and robberies, love peace, and are a defender of widows and the poor; and for this we give thanks to God.

“But your contempt for lawful marriage, if it were for chastity’s sake, would be praiseworthy. Yet because you wallow in lust and adultery, even with nuns, it is blameworthy and damnable; for it confounds the renown of your glory before God and men, and places you among idolaters, because you have violated God’s temple. Therefore, dearest son, repent [Note: [Col. 1033D] *Poenite* (“repent”). Witnesses a. c. e. l. read *poenite*; s. reads *poeniteat te* (“may you repent”); d. m. read *poenitere* (“to repent”).] and remember how shameful it is that you, who by God’s gift rule many peoples, should, to his injury, be a slave to lust.

“We have also heard that almost all the nobles of the Mercian people, following your example, desert their lawful wives and ravish adulteresses and nuns. Let the practice of a foreign people teach you how alien this is to honour. For in Old Saxony, where there is no knowledge of Christ, if a virgin in her father’s house or a married woman under her husband is adulterated, they strangle her with their own hands and burn her, and hang her seducer over the pit in which she has been buried. Or, cutting off her garments to the girdle, chaste matrons scourge her and stab her with knives; and new scourgers meet her as she is sent from village to village, until they kill her.

“Moreover, the Wends [Note: [Col. 1033D–1034D] Wends. The Wends lived near the Vistula, close to the Baltic Sea. The Imperial Manuscript likewise reads *Winedi*; Wilkins reads “among the Persians.”], a most foul race of men, have this custom: when her husband dies, a woman throws herself onto the pyre in order to be burned with him.

“If, then, pagans who do not know God have such zeal for chastity, what is fitting for you, dearest son, who are a Christian and a king? Spare, therefore, your own soul; spare the multitude of your people who perish through your example, and for whose souls you will render account.

“Consider this too: if the English people, as we are reproached in Francia and Italy, and even by the pagans themselves, rejecting lawful marriages, flow away into adulteries, then from such mingling there will arise an indolent people, contemptuous of God, who through depraved morals will ruin their country—as happened to the Burgundians, Provençals, and Spaniards, whom the Saracens afflicted for many years because of their former sins.

“Moreover, it has been reported to us that, taking away many privileges of churches and monasteries, you incite your leaders by your example [Note: [Col. 1034D] *Tuo* (“your”). Witnesses d. e. m. read *tuo*; a. s. c. l. read *tuos* (“your leaders”).] to dare the same thing. But consider, I beg you, what terrible vengeance God exercised upon earlier kings who were conscious of the guilt for which we rebuke you. For Chelred, your predecessor [Note: [Col. 1034D] *Praedecessorem* (“predecessor”). Witnesses c. d. e. m. read *praedecessorem*; a. s. l. read *praedecessorem tuum* (“your predecessor”).], a seducer of nuns and violator of ecclesiastical privileges, was seized by an evil spirit while feasting splendidly with his companions; and, without confession or viaticum, conversing with the devil and detesting God’s law, he yielded up his soul.

“Osred likewise, king of the Deirans and Bernicians, guilty of the same offences, was driven to such frenzy that he lost both his kingdom and his youthful life by a contemptible death. Charles also, prince of the Franks, destroyer of many monasteries and converter of ecclesiastical funds to his own uses, was consumed by prolonged torment and a shameful death. [Note: [Col. 1034D] Charles. Charles Martel. e. reads *consumptus est* (“was consumed”); after *est*, a. s. c. d. l. read *et infra* (“and below”).]”

§ 81. “Therefore, dearest son, with paternal and earnest prayers we beseech you not to despise the counsel of your fathers, who strive, for God’s love, to address your highness. For nothing is more salutary for a good king than that such misdeeds, when rebuked, should willingly be corrected; for it is said through Solomon: [Note: [Col. 1034D] “Who loves discipline.” Proverbs 12:1.]

> “Who loves discipline loves wisdom.”

“Therefore, dearest son, in setting forth just counsel, we call upon and implore you by the living God, by his Son Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit, that you remember how fleeting and brief the present life is, how momentary the pleasure of filthy flesh, and how dishonourable it is for a man of brief life to leave evil examples to posterity for ever.

“Begin, therefore, to order your life by better morals and correct the past errors of youth, so that here you may have praise before men and in the future enjoy eternal glory. We pray that your highness may fare well and advance in good conduct.”

§ 82. I have woven into this little book the relevant portions of this letter for the sake of historical information, partly in the author’s own words and partly in mine, abbreviating long passages as seemed appropriate. I shall not unjustly ask pardon for this act, since, in hastening after the course of history, one had to consider the rapidity of expression.

Moreover, the same Boniface sent Archbishop Cuthbert a letter of the same tenor, [Note: [Col. 1035C] Cuthbert, etc. The letter to Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury, is published in Wilkins, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 90, and in Spelman, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 237.] adding that he should rebuke clerics and nuns for the scantiness and splendour of their garments. Further, lest Cuthbert wonder why he concerned himself with another’s business, since it was no concern of his how or in what morals the English people lived, he should know that Pope Gregory III had bound him by oath not to withhold the customs of neighbouring peoples from apostolic knowledge. Therefore, if gentle admonitions did not prevail, he would act so that such vices should not remain hidden from the pope.

Indeed, Alcuin indirectly rebukes Adelard, archbishop and Cuthbert’s successor, concerning the scantiness of clerical dress, [Note: [Col. 1035C] Alcuin. See Alcuin, *Opera*, vol. I, p. 84, epistle 63.] warning him that, when travelling to Rome and visiting the Emperor Charlemagne—the grandson of the Charles of whom Boniface spoke above—he should not bring clerics or monks clothed in variegated and ostentatious garments, since Frankish clerics did not customarily wear anything but religious dress. [Col. 1035B]

§ 83. Nor could the letters of so great a man be without effect—letters which he sent forth with wakeful attention, both because of his legation and from love of his compatriots. [Note: [Col. 1035C–D] *Suae, et* (“of his own, and”). Witnesses s. c. d. e. read this; a. reads *memor* after *suae* and omits *et*; l. omits *et* after *suae*.] Accordingly, Archbishop Cuthbert and King Ethelbald convened a council to correct the excesses which he had rebuked.

I now refrain from inserting the proceedings of that synod, spun out in a great circuit of words, [Note: [Col. 1035D] Proceedings of this synod. See Wilkins, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 94. Malmesbury places this synod in 747; the manuscript of Florence of Worcester (Corpus Christi College, Oxford) in 748. The charter of King Aethilbald, which Malmesbury says was granted in this synod, is dated 749, the thirty-third year of Aethilbald’s reign. If, therefore, the synod of Clofesho was held in 747, as the more trustworthy authorities affirm, Aethilbald’s charter, moreover dated as given at Godmundeslaech, cannot have been granted in this synod. Aethilbald confirmed Wihtraed of Kent’s privilege at the council of Clofesho held in A.D. 752; this may have misled Malmesbury.] because, in my opinion, they will more suitably occupy another part of this work [Note: [Col. 1035D] Another part of our work. See Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum*, book I, “On the Archbishops of Canterbury,” in *Scriptores post Bedam*, London, 1596, p. 112.] [Note: [Col. 1036C] *Occupabit* (“will occupy”). e. reads *occupabit*; a. s. d. l. read *occupabunt*; c. reads *obtinebunt*.] when we come to the account of the bishops. [Note: [Col. 1036C] *Recensionem* (“account/review”). s. c. read *recensionem*; d. e. l. read *recensitionem*.] But since we have in hand the affairs of kings, I shall append Ethelbald’s written declaration, an indication of his devotion, issued at that same council. [Note: [Col. 1036C] “Which was done at the same council.” See above, note 30.]

§ 84. [Note: [Col. 1036C–D] “Let them serve God freely.” Ethelbald’s charter, from which these excerpts are taken, is printed in full in *Codex diplomaticus aevi Saxonici*, vol. I, p. 119, no. XCIX.]

> “It very often happens, owing to the uncertain changes of times, that things confirmed by the testimony and counsel of many faithful persons are dangerously scattered abroad through the deceitful obstinacy of many and the contrivances of pretence, without any consideration of reason—unless they are committed to eternal memory by the authority of letters and the testament of written documents.
>
> “Therefore I, Ethelbald, king of the Mercians, for love of the heavenly fatherland and the salvation of my soul, have judged it necessary to strive by good works to make it free from every bond of sins. [Note: [Col. 1036D] *Providi* (“I judged/provided”). Witnesses d. e. m. read *providi*; a. s. c. l. read *praevidi* (“I foresaw”).] For since almighty God, through the mercy of his clemency and without any prior merit of mine, has granted me the sceptres of rule, I gladly render to him from what he has given.
>
> “For this reason I grant this donation during my lifetime: that all monasteries and churches of my kingdom shall be released from public taxes, works, and burdens, except for the construction of fortresses or bridges, from which no one may ever be exempted. Moreover, let the servants of God have their own liberty in the produce of woods and fields and in the catching of fish; nor are they to offer small dues either to king or to princes, except voluntarily; but let them serve God freely,” and so forth. [Note: [Col. 1036D] *Hanc* (“this [donation]”). s. c. d. e. read it; a. l. omit it. *Dei* (“of God”). s. c. d. e. read it; a. l. omit it. *Peccatorum* (“sins”). s. c. d. e. read *peccatorum*; a. l. read *delictorum* (“offences”).]

§ 85. Boniface was succeeded by Lull, [Note: [Col. 1036D] Lull. Lull was designated by Boniface himself as his successor to the see of Mainz in A.D. 755.] likewise an Englishman by birth. The writer of the Life of blessed Goar speaks of Lull’s holiness and life; [Note: [Col. 1036D] *Et vita* (“and life”). Witnesses c. d. e. m. read *et vita*; a. l. read *in vita* (“in life”). *Goaris*. Witnesses c. d. l. m. read it; after *Goaris*, a. reads *scriptor* (“writer”). See the Life of Saint Goar, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, second age, p. 276.] these verses, which I remember hearing from childhood, also bear witness:

> Bishop Lull—than whom none is holier;
>
> Mighty in healing, granted by God,
>
> He meets diseases, as the whole world proclaims.

§ 86. Yet, to resume the history, Offa succeeded Ethelbald. [Note: [Col. 1036D] Offa. After Beornred was expelled, Offa succeeded to the kingdom by the consent of all in A.D. 757.] He was Penda’s great-great-grandson in the fifth generation, a man of immense spirit; and because he resolved to carry out what he had conceived in his mind, he reigned one year short of forty. [Col. 1036C]

When I consider his deeds, my mind hesitates in doubt whether to approve or condemn him. So in one and the same man did vices at times cloak themselves with virtues, and virtues at times follow vices, that one might wonder:

> By what knot might I hold Proteus, changing his face? [Note: [Col. 1036D] “By what knot might I hold Proteus, changing his face?” Horace, book I, *Epistles*, line 90.]

The account will run through the evidence for each point. In open battle with Kinewulf, king of the West Saxons, [Note: [Col. 1036D] With Kinewulf, king of the West Saxons. See § 42, note 81.] he easily won the victory (A.D. 777), although Kinewulf was no undistinguished warrior.

But, judging that deceit would succeed better for him, he caused King Ethelbert—enticed to him by the allurements of great promises and, within his palace, beguiled by fraudulent flatteries—to be unexpectedly beheaded, [Note: [Col. 1037D] “He caused King Ethelbert . . . to be beheaded.” Aethelberht, king of the East Angles, was killed at Offa’s command in A.D. 793.] and unlawfully seized the kingdom of the East Angles which Ethelbert had held.

§ 87. [Note: [Col. 1037D] The relics of St Alban. In 793 Offa began to build a monastery in honour of St Alban, and arranged for his relics to be placed there, 507 years after his death. See the Life of Offa appended to Matthew Paris’s edition, London, 1640.] He ordered the relics of blessed Alban, until then obscurely concealed, to be reverently raised and placed in a shrine adorned, so far as royal magnificence could achieve it, with jewels and gold; there too he built a basilica of surpassing workmanship and gathered a community of monks. Yet, obstinate against God, [Note: [Col. 1037D] The archiepiscopal see, etc. While Jaenberht—often wrongly called Lambert—archbishop of Canterbury, was not yet dead, in 791 King Offa, on Pope Adrian’s authority, raised Lichfield to an archiepiscopal see. The dispute between Jaenberht and Offa on this matter probably arose in 785, since according to the Saxon Chronicle he was in that year deprived of some part of his see. See also Florence of Worcester under 785, and the Life of Offa, p. 21.] he attempted to transfer to Lichfield the archiepiscopal see founded at Canterbury 119 years earlier [Col. 1037B], plainly begrudging the people of Canterbury the eminence of their archbishopric. Accordingly he deprived Archbishop Lambert, wearied by much exertion and repeatedly producing both recent and ancient decrees of the Apostolic See, of authority over all estates within his boundaries and over the bishoprics.

Through Pope Adrian, therefore, whom he had long wearied with plausible assertions—since, when minds have been preoccupied, many unlawful things may be taken away and stolen—he obtained that there should be an archbishopric of the Mercians at Lichfield (A.D. 790), and that all the bishops of the Mercian province should be subject to it. Their names were these: Denebert, bishop of Worcester; Werenbert of Leicester; [Col. 1037C] Eadwulf of Sidnacester; Wulheard of Hereford; and the bishops of the East Angles, Alheard of Elmham and Tidfrith of Dunwich. The bishop of Lichfield was called Aldulf. Four bishops remained to the archbishop of Canterbury: those of London, Winchester, Rochester, and Selsey. Some of these bishoprics still remain; some have been transferred elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1038D] Some have been transferred elsewhere. A, S, C, D, L, M omit; E has it.]; some, through venal intrigue, have been united to others. For the sees of Leicester, Sidnacester, and Dunwich, by what event is uncertain, do not exist today.

Nor did Offa’s rapacity stop there: the public despoiler stripped the estates of many churches, among them Malmesbury. But this iniquity did not long violate the canonical rules. For soon Offa’s successor Cenwulf, inferior to no king before him in power or religion, sent a letter to Leo, Adrian’s successor, and restored Æthelhard, Lambert’s successor, to his former dignity [Col. 1038A]. Hence Albinus [Note: [Col. 1038D] Albinus. A, D, E, L: Alcuin; S, C. See § 65, note 99.] wrote to that same Æthelhard:

> [Note: [Col. 1038D] “Having heard of the success … deigned.” See Alcuin, Works, vol. I, p. 84, letter 63.] “Having heard of the success of your journey and of your return to your homeland, and how you were received by the Apostolic See, I gave thanks to the Lord our God with all my heart’s affection: he, by the great gift of his mercy, directed your course prosperously, gave you favour in the sight of the pope, granted you to return home with your desire fulfilled, and has deigned through you once more to raise the most sacred see of our first teacher [Note: [Col. 1038D] Our first teacher: St Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury.] to its former dignity.”

I think it worthwhile, therefore, to append part of the royal letter together with the papal one, although I may seem to anticipate the order of events. I do so because interrupted matters are harder to weave together than begun matters to bring to completion [Col. 1038B].

§ 88. [Note: [Col. 1038D] “To the most blessed lord, etc.” This letter was published by Wilkins, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 163, from Malmesbury.] “To the most blessed and truly beloved lord [Note: [Col. 1038D] Leo: Leo III, elected pope 26 December 795; died 11 June 816. See § 68, note 35.] Leo, pontiff of the holy and apostolic Roman See, Cenwulf, by the grace of God king of the Mercians, with the bishops, ealdormen, and every rank of dignity under our rule, sends the greeting of most sincere love in Christ.

“We always give thanks to almighty God, who is accustomed, amid the various storms of this world, continually to draw to the harbour of salvation the Church acquired by his precious blood, appointing new leaders after the former have been taken to life, and to fill her with fresh light, so that she may not be darkened by any error of shadow but may walk with unimpeded foot in the way of truth. Therefore the whole Church throughout the world rightly rejoices, because, when the true Rewarder of all good things had led above the heavens the most glorious shepherd of his flock, Adrian, to receive his everlasting reward, his merciful providence nevertheless raised up for his sheep a guide who knows how to lead the Lord’s fold to the not-lower pastures of life [Col. 1038C].

“We too, though we dwell at the world’s extremity, rightly glory above others in the same fashion, because his exaltation is our salvation and his prosperity our perpetual rejoicing; for from the source from which apostolic dignity came to you, the truth of faith became known to us. I therefore judge it fitting humbly to incline the ear of our obedience to your holy commands; to carry out with all our strength what appears to your piety rightly to be followed by us; and quickly to avoid, and meanwhile wholly [Note: [Col. 1038D] Wholly. A, C, D, L, M: *omnimodis*; S: *omnimodo*; E: *omnimode*.] cut away from ourselves, whatever is found contrary to reason.

“But now I, Cenwulf, by God’s grace king, humbly entreat your eminence [Col. 1039A] that I may be permitted, without offending your mind, to speak to you concerning our advancement, as we desire; that you may receive me in the bosom of your mercy with tranquil peace; and that the abundant richness of your blessing may enrich for governing his people one whom no merit is sufficient to raise up. Thus, together with me, may the Almighty, through your intercession, sustain against assaults from abroad the people whom your apostolic authority has imbued with the rudiments of faith, and may he deign himself to enlarge the kingdom which God himself has given us.

“All who ruled the Mercians before me obtained this blessing from your predecessors. I myself humbly seek it and desire to obtain it from you, O most holy one: first, that you may receive me as your son by the lot of adoption [Col. 1039B], just as I love you in the place of a father and always embrace you with all the powers of my obedience. For holy faith should be preserved among persons so great, and inviolable love maintained; because a father’s affection must be believed to be his children’s happiness in God, according to the saying of Hezekiah [Note: [Col. 1039D] According to the saying of Hezekiah: Isaiah 38:19.], ‘The father shall make known to the children thy truth, O Lord.’ By these words I implore you, beloved father, not to refuse to make the Lord’s truth known to your son, though unworthy, by your most sacred words, so that by your sound instruction, God helping, I may deserve to attain a purpose of better life.

“Moreover, sweetest father, together with all our bishops and persons of every rank among us, I beg you kindly to answer us concerning the many inquiries upon which we have judged it fitting to seek your greatest discernment [Col. 1039C], lest the tradition of the holy fathers and the rule transmitted to us by them should, as though unknown, be corrupted in us in any respect. Rather, let your straightforward word come to us in love and gentleness, so that through God’s mercy it may produce its beneficial fruit in us.

“For first, our bishops and all the most learned among us say that, contrary to the canons and apostolic enactments established for us by our most blessed father Gregory, as you know, the authority of the metropolitan of Canterbury is divided into two dioceses. By command of that same father, twelve bishops ought to be subject to its authority, as is read in our churches in the letter which he directed to his brother and fellow bishop [Col. 1039D] Augustine concerning the two metropolitan bishops of London and York—a letter which we do not doubt is also held among you. But the primatial dignity, originally established at London under the honour and adornment of the pallium, was transferred and granted to Canterbury. For because Augustine of blessed memory, who at Gregory’s command ministered God’s word to the English people and ruled most gloriously over the churches of the Saxons, died in that city [Col. 1040A], and because his body was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which his successor Laurence consecrated, it appeared fitting to all the wise men of our people that the metropolitan honour should be held in the city where he rests in body [Note: [Col. 1039D] “Rests in body.” C, D, E, M: *corpore pausat*; L: *corpus pausat*; A, S: *corpus ejus pausat*, “his body rests.”] who planted the truth of faith in these regions.

“As you know, King Offa first attempted, because of hostility incurred with venerable Lambert and the people of Canterbury, to remove the honour of that dignity and divide it into two dioceses. And your most pious fellow bishop and predecessor Adrian, at the request of the said king, began to do what no one had previously presumed: he raised the Mercian bishop to the pallium. Yet we blame neither of these men, whom, as we believe, Christ crowns with eternal victory. But we humbly entreat your eminence [Col. 1040B], to whom God has deservedly entrusted the key of wisdom, to deliberate concerning this matter with your wise counsellors, and to deign to write back to us what you judge should thereafter be observed by us; lest Christ’s seamless tunic suffer the schism of any dissension among us, but rather, through your sound teaching, be guided, as we desire, to the unity of true peace.

“We have written these things to you, most blessed pope, with great humility and love alike, earnestly beseeching your clemency to answer kindly and justly the matters necessarily set forth by us. And deign in charitable love to examine the letter which Archbishop Æthelhard wrote to you before all the bishops of our province concerning his own affairs [Col. 1040C] and the causes and necessities of all Britain; and remember to make known to us in a document of truth whatever the rule of faith requires concerning the matters written in it.

“Accordingly, last year we also sent our embassy, both mine and that of the bishops, through Abbot Wada; but, having accepted that embassy, he conducted it negligently—indeed, foolishly. But now, beloved father, I send you through the priest Birinus and my servants Fildas and Ceolberht a small gift out of affection: 120 mancuses [Note: [Col. 1039D] Mancuses. It is uncertain whether the value of a mancus was ever the same as an English mark; otherwise it is supposed to have equalled thirty pence of the money of that period, or seven shillings and six pence. (Sharpe, 90).], together with this letter. I beg you to receive it kindly and to deign to bestow your blessing upon us. May Almighty God preserve you unharmed for a long time, to the praise of his holy Church.”

[Col. 1040D] § 89. “To the most excellent lord son Cenwulf, king of the Mercian province of Saxony, Pope Leo. [Note: [Col. 1040D] “To the most excellent lord … we have delivered for observance.” This letter was published by Wilkins, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 165, from Malmesbury.] The most reverend and holy Æthelhard, our brother, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, came to the most sacred thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, faithfully fulfilling the vows of prayer and laying before our Apostolic See the cause of his priesthood. He presented to us letters of your royal excellence; and in the two letters sent by you [Col. 1041A], full of right faith, we found your great humility. We give thanks to Almighty God, who has adorned and endowed your most prudent excellence in every way: with love towards blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and towards us, and with humble agreement in every apostolic judgment.

“Further, in one of those letters we found how kindly you declared that, had you been nearby, you would have laid down your life for us by the grace of our apostolic office; indeed, that you rejoice greatly in the Lord at our prosperity, and that whenever letters of our most sweet admonition reach the ears of your united heart, you confess that you receive the fatherly gift, as sons do, with every sweetness of heart and spiritual joy. You also stated [Col. 1041B] that you had directed a modest blessing from your resources to be offered us—namely 120 mancuses [Note: [Col. 1041D] Mancuses. S, C, E: *mancusas*; A, D, L: *manculas*.]—which we received with great love for the salvation of your soul. And the aforesaid archbishop and his companions were honourably and kindly received by us, and we willingly provided him assistance in his needs.

“Meanwhile, trusting in your most prudent excellence—since it was said in your royal letters themselves that no Christian presumes to oppose our apostolic enactments—we strive with all our strength to issue and proclaim those things that benefit your kingdom. Therefore you must in no way resist in their orthodox teaching the things which our brother Æthelhard, your prelate and archbishop, or the whole synod, sets forth to your royal excellence, to all the rulers of your people, and to the whole people of God, under the canonical censure of evangelical and apostolic teaching, of the holy fathers, and also of our holy predecessor pontiffs [Col. 1041C]. For our Lord and Redeemer says in the Gospel: [Note: [Col. 1041D] “He who receives you … shall receive a prophet’s reward”: Matthew 10:40–41.] ‘He who receives you receives me; and he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward.’

“How much more, then, should this be so concerning the aforesaid archbishop, whom you praised to us very highly and repeatedly—as indeed he is: plainly most distinguished and most learned [Note: [Col. 1041D] “Most distinguished and most learned.” S, C, D, E: *clarissimus atque peritissimus*; A, L: *clarissimus, dignissimus, carissimus, atque peritissimus*, “most distinguished, most worthy, most dear, and most learned.”]—and whom you know to be prudent, adorned with good conduct, worthy before God and men. Behold, sweetest, dearest, and most excellent son [Col. 1041D], good king: in these declarations of yours we praise Almighty God, who has shown you such a bishop. Like a true shepherd, he is able by words, according to the teaching of Holy Scripture, to enjoin worthy repentance and to rescue from the lowest hell the souls of those under his priestly jurisdiction; leading them away from unquenchable fire [Col. 1042A] and bringing them into the harbour of salvation; and to offer for them a worthy and unblemished sacrifice in the sight of the divine majesty of Almighty God.

“And because the aforesaid archbishop has greatly pleased us in all his holiness and manner of life, and because we trust him exceedingly, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we bear, though unworthy, we have granted him such episcopal authority that if anyone among those subject to him—whether kings, rulers, or the whole people—transgresses the Lord’s commandments, he may excommunicate that person until he repents; and if he remains unrepentant, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector.

“Concerning Æthelhard, now made archbishop of the church of Canterbury, as the excellence of your bishops requested us to do him justice [Col. 1042B] with respect to those dioceses—both bishoprics and monasteries—of which, as you learned, he was unlawfully despoiled and which were taken from his venerable see, though it had formerly possessed them: after examining everything more closely, we found in our sacred archives that Saint Gregory, our predecessor [Note: [Col. 1041D] “Our.” S, C, E; after *nostrum*, A and L read *in ipsa sancta sede*, “in that holy see”; D and M read similarly, omitting *nostrum*.], had delivered the whole diocese, numbering twelve [Note: [Col. 1042D] Twelve. A, S, C, E, L: *duodecim*; D, M: *duodecim episcoporum*, “of twelve bishops.”], to blessed Augustine, his *syncellus* and archbishop, and had confirmed his authority to consecrate bishops. Therefore we too, having discovered the truth itself, by our apostolic authority of ordination and confirmation restored and established these for him in their entirety, as they had been in ancient times; and, in accordance with the judgment of the sacred canons, we delivered to his church a privilege of confirmation to be observed.”

[Col. 1042C] § 90. Meanwhile Offa, lest the harsh measures taken against the provincials should harm him, sought friendly kings everywhere and established peace. [Note: [Col. 1042D] He gave his daughter Eadburh in marriage to Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons. See § 43, note 100.] He gave his daughter Eadburh in marriage to Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons (A.D. 787). He secured Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as a friend by frequent embassies, although he did not easily find in Charlemagne’s mind what would serve his own designs. They had previously quarrelled so seriously that, amid great disturbances on both sides, even merchants’ traffic was prohibited. There is a letter of Albinus [Note: [Col. 1042D] Letter of Albinus. This letter was published in full by Ussher, *Sylloge veterum epistolarum Hibernicarum*, quarto, Paris, 1665, letter 18, p. 36; and Alcuin, *Works*, vol. I, p. 6, letter 3.] which attests this matter.
