I shall append part of it here: a great testimony to the magnanimity and courage of Charles, who spent his entire life in wars against pagans rebellious against God.

[Col. 1042D] § 91. “The ancient Saxons,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1042D] Ancient Saxons: that is, Westphalians.] “and all the peoples of the Frisians have been converted to the faith of Christ at King Charles’s urging, as he influenced some by rewards and others by threats. But last year the same king attacked the Slavs with an army and subjected them to his rule. The Avars, whom we call Huns, burst into Italy and, defeated by the Christian commanders of the aforesaid king, [Col. 1043A] returned home in disgrace. Likewise they attacked Bavaria, and were themselves defeated and scattered by the Christian army. Moreover, the dukes and tribunes of that most Christian king took much of Spain from the Saracens—nearly three hundred miles in length along the coast. But alas, grief upon grief, that those same accursed Saracens, who are also called Hagarenes, rule all Africa and the greater part of Asia Minor. I do not know what will become of us; for some discord, inflamed by diabolical kindling, has lately arisen between King Charles and King Offa, so that on both sides navigation for merchants has ceased by prohibition. Some say that we ought to be sent to those parts to arrange peace.”

§ 92. In these words, apart from what I noted above, [Col. 1043B] the curious reader may observe how many years had already passed since the Saracens invaded Africa and Asia Minor. And indeed, had not God’s mercy animated the native vigour of the Frankish emperors, they would long ago have subjugated Europe. So completely had they despised the emperors at Constantinople that they had occupied Sicily, Sardinia, the Balearic Islands, and almost all lands surrounded by the sea, except Rhodes, Crete, and Cyprus. But in our own day they have been compelled to surrender Sicily to the Northmen; Corsica and Sardinia to the Pisans; and to the Franks and Christians of every kind from Europe, a great part of Asia and Jerusalem itself. Since there will be a fuller occasion to speak of these matters later [Note: [Col. 1043D] Later. C, D, E, M: *sequentibus*; A, S, L: *consequentibus*.], I shall now append from Charles’s words the firm treaty concluded between him and Offa [Col. 1043C].

§ 93. [Note: [Col. 1043D] “Charles … silks.” Charlemagne’s letter was published in Wilkins, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 158, and Alcuin, *Works*, vol. II, Appendix, p. 618.] “Charles, by God’s grace [Note: [Col. 1043D] “By God’s grace.” S, C, D, E, M; omitted in A, L.] king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, sends greeting to the venerable man and dearest brother Offa, king of the Mercians.

“First, we give thanks to Almighty God for the purity of Catholic faith which we find commendably set forth in your pages. Concerning pilgrims who desire, for love of God and the salvation of their souls, to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles: let them go in peace and without any disturbance. But if any among them are found not serving religion but pursuing profit, let them pay the established tolls at suitable places. We also wish merchants to have lawful protection in our kingdom by our command; and, if they suffer unjust oppression anywhere [Col. 1044A], let them appeal to us or to our judges, and we shall order full justice to be done.

“Let your affection also know that we have sent, as alms for the lord apostolic Adrian, some generosity from our dalmatics and pallia to every episcopal see in your kingdom and that of [Note: [Col. 1043D] Æthelred: Æthelred, or Æthelberht, king of the Northumbrians, died 19 April 796.] Æthelred, asking that you direct prayers to be made for him. We have no doubt that his blessed [Note: [Col. 1043D] “Soul to be at rest.” Adrian died 25 December 795.] soul is at rest; nevertheless we do so in order to show faith and affection toward a friend most dear to us. From the treasure of worldly goods which the Lord Jesus has granted us in his free mercy, we have also sent something through the metropolitan cities; and to your affection, one belt, one Hunnish sword, and two silk pallia.”

§ 94. I have selected these scattered words from the letter [Col. 1044B] in order that Offa’s and Charles’s friendship may be clear to posterity. Relying on this intimacy, although assailed by many people’s hatred, he nevertheless spent his life in sweet leisure and left as successor his son Ecgfrith, anointed king before his own death [Note: [Col. 1043D] His son Ecgfrith, anointed king before his death. Ecgfrith was anointed king while his father was still alive, A.D. 787.]. [Note: [Col. 1043D] He left him as successor. Offa died on 29 July A.D. 796 and was succeeded by his son Ecgfrith, who died in the same year. Some manuscripts of the Saxon Chronicle, Florence of Worcester, and others wrongly place Offa’s death in 794. Charlemagne’s letter to Offa, written before April 796, mentions Adrian’s death; therefore Offa outlived the supreme pontiff, whose death occurred on 25 December 795.] Ecgfrith, diligently avoiding the traces of his father’s cruelty, restored in humble devotion the privileges of all churches which his father had diminished in his time. He also returned the estate that his father had taken from Malmesbury, placing it in the hands of Cuthbert, then abbot of that place, at the urging of Æthelhard, archbishop of Canterbury, a vigorous man indeed and worthy of God. Constant opinion maintains that he had been abbot there before Cuthbert [Note: [Col. 1044D] “Maintains.” C, E; after *asseverat*, A, S, D, L, M read: “drawing this inference, that he caused himself to be buried there after his death.”].

Thus, when the hope raised by Ecgfrith’s excellent disposition was beginning to grow in his early years [Col. 1044C], savage death harvested the flower of his budding age. Hence Albinus wrote to the patrician Osbert: “I do not think that the most noble young man Ecgfrith died because of his own sins, but because his father shed much blood to secure his kingdom.” [Note: [Col. 1044D] “Hence Albinus to the patrician Albert.” The editor of Alcuin’s *Works* (vol. I, p. 74, note) observes that the letter from which Malmesbury took this passage is unknown.] Therefore, after leaving the kingdom four months later, he made Cenwulf king, a descendant in the fifth generation of Penda through Penda’s brother Cenwealh. [Note: [Col. 1044D] “After four, etc.” Ecgfrith died after only a few months of reign, and Cenwulf was appointed his successor.]

§ 95. Cenwulf, above all a great man whose virtues surpassed his fame, never committed anything that envy could justly attack. Pious at home and victorious in war, he was a man whose praises will deservedly shine on high as long as a fair judge is found in England. He deserves praise both for the sublimity of his kingship and for the humility of mind which he displayed most fully when, as we said above [Note: [Col. 1044D] As we said above: see § 87.], he restored the impaired dignity of Canterbury [Col. 1045A]. [Note: [Col. 1044D] “Canterbury.” E; A, S, C, D, L, M: “of Canterbury.”—The see of Canterbury was restored to its former state in A.D. 798, when Æthelhard returned from Rome for the first time. He held it from 791 to 11 June 805.] Though king, he cared little for worldly arrogance in his own province, so long as he did not violate the course of the canons established long ago.

Inheriting Offa’s enduring hatred against the people of Canterbury, he severely afflicted that region. [Note: [Col. 1045C] “And their king, etc.” See § 15; note 67 wrongly asserts that Cuthred was made king of the people of Canterbury by Offa. Cenwulf, not Offa, made Cuthred king.] He carried off their king, Eadberht surnamed Præn [Note: [Col. 1045D] Præn. S, C, D, E, M: *Pren*; A, L: *Wren*.], in chains, but not long afterwards, softened by human compassion, arranged for his release. At Winchcombe, where he had built for God the church still standing, on the very day of its dedication he released the captive king at the altar and bestowed freedom upon him, displaying a memorable spectacle of clemency. Cuthred was also present, applauding the royal generosity; Cenwulf had appointed him king over the people of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 1045D] Cuthred. Cuthred was made king of the people of Canterbury after Eadberht Præn had been defeated, in 798, not in 796 as stated above in § 15.].

The basilica rang with applause; the open space resounded with people running about, because [Note: [Col. 1045D] “Because.” E; A, S, C, D, L, M: “because there.”] in the assembly of thirteen bishops and ten ealdormen no one was refused generosity; all departed with well-filled purses [Col. 1045B]. Besides the gifts received by the great men, beyond estimate in number and value, in household goods, clothing, and choice horses, he distributed a pound of silver to everyone who held no land, a mancus of gold to priests, one shilling to monks, and finally many gifts to all the people. Having enlarged that same monastery with great revenues, incredible as this may seem in the present age, he honoured it with his burial in the twenty-fourth year of his reign. [Note: [Col. 1045D] “He honoured it with his burial in the twenty-fourth year of his reign.” Cenwulf died A.D. 821, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign.] His son Cynehelm, a mere boy innocently killed by his sister Cwenthryth, obtained the name and glory of martyrdom and rests there. [Note: [Col. 1045D] “His son Cynehelm, etc.” Cynehelm, whom his father Cenwulf left heir to the kingdom, though only seven years old, was soon afterwards murdered at the instigation of his sister Cwenthryth by his guardian Ascebert. See the Life of St Cynehelm.]

§ 96. After him the kingdom of the Mercians was wavering [Col. 1045C] and, so to speak, bloodless; it had nothing which a man of letters would deem worthy to record. [Note: [Col. 1045D] “Had.” A, D, L, M: *habuit*, “had”; S, C: *meruit*, “deserved.”] But lest anyone accuse us of breaking off a half-mutilated history, I shall run through the names of the succeeding kings.

[Note: [Col. 1045D] Ceolwulf. Ceolwulf, Cynehelm’s uncle, succeeded to the kingdom in 821 and was deposed by Beornwulf, a man noble among the Mercians, in A.D. 823.] Ceolwulf, Cenwulf’s brother, reigned one year and in the next was expelled by Beornwulf. [Note: [Col. 1045D] Beornwulf … put to flight. The battle between Beornwulf and Egbert, fought at Ellandun—conjectured to be Wilton near Salisbury—took place A.D. 824. Beornwulf was killed by the East Angles in the same year.] Beornwulf, defeated and put to flight by Egbert, king of the West Saxons, in the third year of his reign, was soon afterwards killed by the East Angles [Col. 1046A], because he had attempted to invade East Anglia as a kingdom due to the Mercians since Offa’s time.

[Note: [Col. 1046C] Ludeca. Ludeca was killed A.D. 825 and was succeeded by Wiglaf.] Ludeca, seeking in spirit to avenge his predecessor, was killed by the same Angles after holding power for two years. [Note: [Col. 1046C] Wiglaf. D, E, M: *Withlacus*; A, L and S: *Withlafius*; C: *Withlavus*. Wiglaf was driven from the Mercian throne by Egbert in A.D. 827 but restored in the following year. He died A.D. 839.] Wiglaf, brought under the yoke by the same Egbert at the beginning of his reign, ruled thirteen years, paying tribute both of persons and money to him and his son. By the same lot [Note: [Col. 1046C] Beorhtwulf. Beorhtwulf ascended the throne when Wiglaf died, A.D. 839. Defeated by the Danes in 851, he died A.D. 852.] Beorhtwulf, reigning thirteen years, was finally driven overseas by Danish pirates.

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Burgred. Burgred ascended the throne A.D. 852. His marriage to Æthelswith, daughter of Æthelwulf, king of the West Saxons, was celebrated at Chippenham after Easter in 854. Defeated and expelled by the Danes in A.D. 874, he fled to Rome, where he died shortly afterwards.] Burgred, having married Æthelswith, daughter of King Æthelwulf, son of Egbert, consoled himself through that kinship with the payment of tribute and the plundering of enemies; but after twenty-two years he was driven from his homeland by those same enemies and fled to Rome, where he was buried among the English School [Col. 1046B] in the church of St Mary. His wife, though then residing in her homeland, afterwards followed her husband and died at Pavia. [Note: [Col. 1046D] “His wife … died at Pavia.” Æthelswith died at Pavia A.D. 889.]

Then that kingdom was handed over by the Danes to a certain Ceolwulf, Burgred’s minister, and secured by an oath that he would not retain it beyond their pleasure. [Note: [Col. 1046D] Ceolwulf. After expelling Burgred, the Danes made Ceolwulf king in A.D. 874; in August 877 Halfdan divided the kingdom of Mercia, of which Ceolwulf held one part.] After a few years Alfred, Egbert’s grandson, acquired it. Thus the Mercian dominion, which had suddenly flourished through the swelling madness of a heathen man, completely withered through the pitiable indolence of a half-man king, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 875. [Note: [Col. 1046D] “Eight hundred and seventy-five.” A, S, D, E, L, M; C: “eight hundred and five.”]

## HERE BEGINS THE KINGDOM OF THE EAST ANGLES.

§ 97. But since the pen has thus far ploughed through the four most powerful kingdoms [Col. 1046C] not superficially, as I think, so far as the reading of the ancients has supplied material, it will now, as I said in the preface, run over in the wake of the others the dominion of the East Angles and East Saxons. [134] For the kingdom of the East Angles sprang up later than that of the Kentish people, but earlier than that of the West Saxons.

[Note: [Col. 1046D] First, etc. Pagi dates the beginning of this kingdom to about the year 526, when the Angles, having landed on the eastern coast of Britain, established settlements there under their twelve leaders. Uffa, one of the twelve [Col. 1047B], who survived the rest, did not assume the title of king of the East Angles before the year 571. He was its head; the line of princes called the Uffings derives its name from him. Uffa died A.D. 578 and was succeeded by his son Titil, who is supposed to have died in 599 and to have been succeeded by his own son Rædwald. See Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, ch. 15.]

The first, and likewise the greatest, king among the East Angles was [Col. 1047A] Rædwald, said to have been the tenth generation from Woden. For all the southern provinces of Angles and Saxons on this side of the river Humber, together with their kings, deferred to his will.

[Note: [Col. 1047C] This is the man whom the preceding account. See above, § 47.]

This is the man whom the preceding account did not fail to mention as having slain Æthelfrith, king of the Northumbrians, in Edwin’s interest. At Edwin’s own urging he was baptized, but afterwards, by his wife’s counsel, fell away from the faith.

[Note: [Col. 1047C] He fell away from the faith. See Bede, book II, ch. 15, § 135.]

But his son Eorpwald, having embraced uncorrupted Christianity, rendered up an undefiled spirit to God, being innocently murdered by the heathen Ricbert.

[Note: [Col. 1047C] Sigebert succeeded him. Eorpwald, who succeeded his father Rædwald about the year 624, was baptized A.D. 627. When he was killed in the same year by Richbert, who, after perpetrating this crime, usurped the throne and held it for three years, the slain man’s brother Sigibert must have ascended the throne in 631.]

Sigebert succeeded him, a man worthy of God, his brother by the same mother, who had shed all barbarism through his upbringing among the Franks. For, driven by Rædwald into exile, and long enjoying fellowship among them, he had received the sacraments of [Col. 1047B] Christianity; and, when he came to power, he worthily poured them forth throughout his whole kingdom, [135] and also established schools of letters in various places. This certainly deserves great praise: through him men formerly rustic and heathen experienced the sweetness of learning.

[Note: [Col. 1047C] Driven into exile . . . established in various places. See [Col. 1047D] Bede, book III, ch. 18.]

Felix, bishop, a Burgundian by origin, who now rests at Ramsey, was religion’s helper and learning’s encourager.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Felix. Felix, first bishop of Dunwich, consecrated in 630, died on 8 March, A.D. 646. He was sent by Honorius, archbishop of Canterbury, to devote himself to the conversion of Sigibert.]

Moreover, Sigebert, renouncing the world and taking the monastic tonsure, left the throne to his kinsman Ecgric. Attacked with him in an allied war by Penda, king of the Mercians, he met death; being himself stronger than his misfortunes and mindful of his profession, he carried only a staff in his hand.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Sigibert, etc. Sigibert, having abdicated the kingdom, became a monk at Bury St Edmund’s in A.D. 634, leaving the throne to his kinsman Ecgric. Both were slain by Penda, king of the Mercians, in the following year.]

Ecgric’s successor was Anna, son of [Col. 1048A] Eni, brother of Rædwald. Involved in the same destruction by the rage of Penda, he yet stood eminent and fortunate in the number of his glorious offspring, as the second book will relate in its proper place.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Successor of Ecgric: Anna. Anna’s accession, as grandson of Rædwald, is said to have occurred in A.D. 635. He was slain by Penda in A.D. 654 and was succeeded by his brother Æthelhere, who was likewise killed in the following year.]

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Eni. a. s. c. d. l. m.; omitted in e.]

[Note: [Col. 1047D] As the second book, etc. In the second book Malmesbury mentions three daughters of King Anna—Æthelthryth, [Col. 1048B] Æthelburh, and Seaxburh—and their descendants [Col. 1048C]. Compare Bede, book III, ch. 7, § 18, and Smith’s note on *Optimae genitor sobolis* (“father of excellent offspring”).]

Anna was succeeded by his brother Æthelhere, who was killed by Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, together with Penda, deservedly because he had come to Penda’s assistance and supported the army that had destroyed his brother and kinsman.

[Note: [Col. 1048C] His successor. On the death of his brother Æthelhere in 655, Æthelwold ascended the throne. He died in 664.]

His successor, his brother Æthelwold, by an unbroken succession left the kingdom to the sons of the same Æthelhere, [136] Aldwulf and Elcwold. Beorna succeeded them, and Æthelred succeeded him. His son was the holy Æthelberht, whom Offa, king of the Mercians, treacherously killed, as has been said and will be said later.

[Note: [Col. 1048C] Aldwulf. Eadwulf, son of Æthelhere, succeeded his uncle upon his death in 664. His mother was Hereswith, daughter of Hild, abbess of Streaneshalch. The year of his death is uncertain; it must have occurred between 680 and 683.]

[Note: [Col. 1048C] Elcwold. Elewold succeeded his brother Eadwulf and, according to Hickes, died in 690. He was succeeded by Selræd, who died in 747 and was succeeded in the same year by Ælfwald, who himself died in 749. After his death Hunbeanna and Albert (called Beorna and Æthelberht by Matthew of Westminster and others) appear to have ruled the East Angles jointly. According to Hickes, Beorna and Æthelred [Col. 1048D] succeeded Elwold in 690, and Beorna died before Æthelred; but the actual year of each man’s death is very obscure. The succession of the kings of East Anglia is wrapped in dense obscurity.]

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Æthelberht. Æthelberht, son of Æthelred, was slain by Offa in A.D. 793. He was regarded as a martyr, and his feast is celebrated in the English Martyrology on 20 May.]

[Note: [Col. 1048D] As has been said. See above, § 86.]

Few powerful men reigned in East Anglia after him until Saint Edmund, who in the sixteenth year of his reign was killed by the heathen Hinguar. From then on, Angles ceased to reign in East Anglia for fifty years. For nine years the province lay subject to heathen devastators without a king; afterwards Guthrum, a Danish king, ruled there and in East Saxony for twelve years in the time of King Alfred.

[Note: [Col. 1048D] St Edmund. Edmund, directly descended from the ancient kings of East Anglia, was crowned on Christmas Day, A.D. 854, and slain by Inguar, leader of the Danes, on 20 November, 870.]

[Col. 1048B]

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Guthrum. Guthorm, or Godrum, assumed the title of king of the East Angles by permission of King Alfred in A.D. 879. Upon his death in 891 he was succeeded by Eohric, who was killed in 905.]

Guthrum had as successor another Dane, named Eohric. After reigning fourteen years, he was slain by the Angles because he had behaved towards them in an uncivil manner. Yet liberty did not rise again for them, since Danish earls either oppressed them or incited them [137] against the kings of the West Saxons, until Edward, Alfred’s son, expelled the Danes, freed the Angles, and added both provinces to his own—that is, West-Saxon—rule, [Col. 1049A] in the fiftieth year after Saint Edmund’s murder, the fifteenth of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 1049B] In the fifteenth year of his reign. According to the Saxon Chronicle, the East Angles submitted to the authority of King Edward in 921, the fifty-first year after the slaughter of King Edmund. If that is accepted, and Edward succeeded his father Alfred in A.D. 901, the Danes must be held to have been expelled in the twelfth year of his reign. In Florence of Worcester, the union of the kingdoms under Edward the Elder is assigned to the year 928.]

## On the Kingdom of the East Saxons

§ 98. At almost the same time as the kingdom of the East Angles began, the kingdom of the East Saxons arose (about A.D. 526). The East Saxons indeed had many kings in succession, but were subject to other kings, especially the Mercians.

[Note: [Col. 1049C] Arose. a. s. c. l.; “succeeded,” d. e. m.]

[Note: [Col. 1049C] First, therefore, etc. According to Henry of Huntingdon, the first king of the East Saxons was Excenwin, whom Florence of Worcester, in his genealogy of kings, calls Æscwin. He was succeeded in 587 by his son Sledd, who himself died in 597.]

The first to reign among them, then, was Sledd, tenth from Woden. His son Sæberht, nephew through his mother Ricula of Æthelberht, king of the Kentish people, received the faith of Christ through the preaching of Mellitus, first bishop of London. For that city belongs to the East Saxons.

[Note: [Col. 1049C] Sæberht. Sæberht, son and successor of Sledd, began to reign in 597 and was converted to Christianity in 604. He died in the year of the Lord 616, leaving as successors his sons Seaxred and Sigeward.]

After Sæberht’s death, his sons [Col. 1049B] Sexred and Seward expelled Mellitus.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] They expelled Mellitus. Mellitus, consecrated bishop of London in A.D. 604, was driven into exile in 617. Later made archbishop of Canterbury, he died on 24 April, A.D. 624. See Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chs. 3–7.]

Not long after, [138] killed by the West Saxons, they paid the penalty for their tyranny against Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Not long after, etc. Seaxred and Sigeward were slain in 623; Sigebert, surnamed the Little, son of Sigeward, succeeded.]

Their successor was Sigebert, surnamed the Little, son of Seward. He left the kingdom to Sigebert, son of Sigebald, who had been Sæberht’s brother.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] He left the kingdom to Sigebert. When Sigebert died in 653, Sigebert surnamed the Good succeeded him, and restored Christianity among the East Saxons. He was slain in the year of the Lord 660. See Bede, book III, ch. 22, § 215.]

This Sigebert, at the urging of King Oswiu, was baptized in Northumbria by Bishop Finan, and through Bishop Cedd brought his people back to the faith which they had rejected together with Mellitus. After administering the kingdom gloriously, he surrendered it still more gloriously: he was murdered by relatives because, in obedience to the evangelical commandment, he calmly spared his enemies and did not, with a wrinkled and stern countenance, hang offenders even if they repented.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Finan. Finan, bishop of Lindisfarne, succeeded Aidan in that see in 651.]

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Cedd. Cedd, consecrated bishop of London about 656, died in A.D. 664. See Bede, book III, § 214.]

After him his brother Swithelm reigned, having been baptized in East Anglia by the same Cedd. Upon his death, Sigheri, son of Sigebert the Little, and Sebbi, son of Seward, held the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Swithelm. Swithelm, son of Sexbald or Sigebald [Col. 1050B], succeeded his brother in 660 and died in [Col. 1050C] 665. At that time Sigheri, son of Sigebert the Little, and Sebbi, son of Sigeweard, held the kingdom. For Sebbi’s parentage compare Dr Smith’s note on Bede, book IV, ch. 30, and the charter of Æthelred of the East Saxons, *Codex Diplomaticus Aevi Saxonici*, no. XXXV, p. 39.]

Yet Sebbi, after his co-ruler had died before him, himself voluntarily departed from the kingdom in the thirtieth year, becoming a monk, as Bede relates. His sons [139] Sigeheard and Sæfrið reigned.

[Note: [Col. 1050C] As Bede relates. Book III, ch. 30, § 250, and book IV, ch. 11, § 283. Sebbi, having resigned the crown, became a monk in A.D. 693 and died the following year. His Life was written by Capgrave from ancient legends found in *Acta Sanctorum*, August, vol. VI, p. 516. He was succeeded by his sons Sigeheard and Swebred.]

After their deaths, Offa, son of Sigheri, governed the kingdom for a short time: a young man of pleasing face and disposition, in the flower of age, greatly loved by his subjects. At the urging of Cyneswith, daughter of Penda, whose marriage he had hoped for, he learned to sigh after heavenly loves; he went to Rome with Coenred, king of the Mercians, and the blessed Egwin, bishop of the Hwicce; and there, tonsured, [Col. 1050B] he entered the heavenly kingdoms in his own time.

[Note: [Col. 1050C] Offa governed the kingdom. Swebred died after 13 June, A.D. 704, and was succeeded by Offa, who went to Rome with Coenred of Mercia in A.D. 709. There both received the tonsure from the hand of Pope Constantine.]

[Note: [Col. 1050C] Egwin. Ecgwin, bishop of Worcester, was consecrated in A.D. 692 and held the see until the year of the Lord 747.]

Selred, son of Sigebert the Good, succeeded him for thirty-eight years. After he was murdered, Swithed ruled the East Saxons. In the same year in which Egbert, king of the West Saxons, defeated the Kentish people, he was expelled by Egbert and left the kingdom vacant. London, however, with the surrounding regions, obeyed the Mercian kings for as long as they themselves held power.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Selred succeeded him. Selræd, or Swebred, succeeded Offa in 709 and died in 738. Selræd, son of Sigebert the Good, was king of the East Angles, not of the East Saxons. He died in 747. See note 2?, p. 136. The texts of Malmesbury and Florence of Worcester are equally obscure concerning the succession of both East-Anglian and East-Saxon kings.]

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Who in the same year . . . left the kingdom vacant. This seems to be a corrupt reading in every manuscript. For if Swithræd succeeded the deceased Swebred in 738, or even followed Selræd, king of the East Angles, killed in 747, it is scarcely likely that he reigned when the Kentish people submitted to King Ecgbert in 824. Florence of Worcester writes thus: “Swithræd held supreme authority for some years; after him few native kings ruled in the East Saxons, for in the same year [Col. 1051C] in which Ecgbert invaded Kent they submitted to his authority.” FLORENCE OF WORCESTER, appendix to the *Chronicle* (East Saxony).]

## On the Division of the Kingdoms, Counties, and Bishoprics of England

§ 99. The kings of the Kentish people ruled properly in Kent, in which are these bishoprics: [Col. 1051A] [140] the archbishopric of Canterbury and the bishopric of Rochester.

§ 100. The kings of the West Saxons ruled in the counties of Wiltshire, Berkshire, and Dorset; these have one bishop, whose seat is now Salisbury, but formerly was either Ramsbury or Sherborne.

[Note: [Col. 1051C] They have one bishop . . . either Ramsbury or Sherborne. Compare this with Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum*, “On the Bishops of the West Saxons.”]

[Note: [Col. 1051C] Seat. a. c. d. l. m.; omitted in e.]

[Note: [Col. 1051C] Was. a. c. d. l. m.; omitted in e.]

And in Sussex, which for some time had its own king, the episcopal see of that county was formerly at Selsey, an island surrounded by the sea, as Bede relates; there also the blessed Wilfrid built a monastery. Now the bishop resides at Chichester.

[Note: [Col. 1051C] In Sussex, etc. The history of this kingdom is not wholly reliable. It is conjectured to have been founded about 490 by Ælle, who entered Britain in 477 with his three sons Cymen, Wlenking, and [Col. 1052C] Cissa, who succeeded his father. The South Saxons were converted to the Christian religion by Wilfrid, bishop of York, during the reign of Æthelwealh, A.D. 681. The kingdom of the South Saxons appears to have been tributary sometimes to Kent and sometimes to Wessex, to which it was finally united by Ecgbert in A.D. 824.]

[Note: [Col. 1052C] As Bede relates. *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, ch. 13, § 289.]

And in the counties of Hampshire and Surrey, which have a bishop whose seat is Winchester.

[Col. 1051B]

And in Somerset, which formerly had a bishop at Wells, but whose bishop is now at Bath.

And in Devon, called Devonshire, and Cornwall, now called Cornu-guallia. There were then two bishoprics, one at Crediton and the other at St German’s; now there is one, whose seat is Exeter.

§ 101. Moreover, the kings of the Mercians ruled in these counties: Gloucestershire, Worcestershire, and Warwickshire. In these there is one bishop, whose seat is Worcester.

[141] And in Cheshire, Derbyshire, and Staffordshire: in these there is one bishop; he possesses part of Warwickshire and Shropshire, and has his seat at the City of the Legions, or Coventry; formerly [Col. 1051C] it was at Lichfield.

And in Herefordshire, where there is a bishop holding half of Shropshire and part of Warwickshire and Gloucestershire, with his seat at Hereford.

And in Oxfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire, half of Huntingdonshire, Bedfordshire, Northamptonshire, [Col. 1052A] Leicestershire, and Lincolnshire; these are governed by a bishop who now has his seat at Lincoln, formerly at Dorchester.

And in Leicestershire and Nottinghamshire, whose Christianity belongs to the archbishop of York; there was formerly a bishop of their own, whose seat was at Leicester.

§ 102. The kings of the East Angles ruled in Cambridgeshire; there is a bishop there whose seat is at Ely.

And in Norfolk and Suffolk; there is a bishop there whose seat is Norwich, but formerly at Elmham or Thetford.

§ 103. The kings of the East Saxons ruled in Essex and half of Hertfordshire; [Col. 1052B] there was, and is, a bishop of London there.

§ 104. The kings of the Northumbrians ruled throughout the whole region beyond the river Humber as far as Scotland. There were there the archbishop of York, the bishops of Hexham and Ripon, of Lindisfarne, and of [the church of] the White House. The sees of Hexham and Ripon disappeared; that of Lindisfarne was transferred to Durham.

[Note: [Col. 1052C] White House. Whithorn, in Galloway.]

[142] § 105. Such were the divisions of the kingdoms, although the kings, as times changed, now these and now those, crossed their boundaries through strength or lost them through weakness. But Egbert, by greatness of spirit, restrained all these shifting kingdoms and, reducing them to a single dominion while preserving each its own laws, called them into a uniform rule. Therefore, since I have completed to my satisfaction the trustworthiness of the chronological survey, and have proceeded beyond his times, I shall set here the boundary of the first volume, so that the manifold track of the kingdoms may end in the single compendium of the West-Saxon realm.

[Note: [Col. 1052C] Survey. s.; “review,” c. d. e. l. m.]

## Prologue to the Second Book

[143]

[Col. 1051]

[Col. 1051D] For a long time, through my parents’ care and my own diligence, I have been accustomed to books. This pleasure took hold of me from childhood; this attraction grew up with me through my advancing years. For I had been so trained by my father that, if I turned aside to different pursuits, there would be loss to my soul and danger to my reputation. Therefore, mindful of the saying, [Col. 1052D] “You must desire whatever is necessary,” I forced my youth to be willing gladly what I could not honourably refuse to will.

I devoted attention to many branches of learning, though differently to different ones. Logic, which arms speech, I merely tasted by hearing; natural philosophy, which ministers to bodily health, I grasped somewhat more closely. But when I had searched the parts of ethics to their inmost marrow, I rise in reverence before its majesty, because it lies open to those who study it for itself and forms minds for right living. History above all, by seasoning character with a pleasant knowledge of deeds, stimulates readers by examples to pursue good things and avoid evil.

Accordingly, after I had gathered, at my own expense, some historians of foreign nations, I continued in my familiar leisure to inquire whether anything memorable concerning our own people could be discovered for posterity. Hence, not content with ancient writings, I too began [144] to write, not in order to display my learning—which is nearly nothing—but to draw into the light matters hidden beneath the heap of antiquity.

[Note: [Col. 1053C] “I too began to write.” s. c. e. l.; “and everything to write,” d.; “I too began to write frequently,” a.]

Therefore, rejecting fleeting opinions, I collected chronicles far and wide; but by this labour, I confess, I achieved almost nothing. For after going through them all, I remained poor in knowledge, since I found nothing to read before I ceased reading. Whatever I clearly learned concerning the four kingdoms I included in the first book. In these, I hope, truth will not be ashamed, even though doubt may perhaps arise in someone.

Now I shall trace the monarchy of the West-Saxon kingdom down to the coming of the Normans, through the successive descent of its kings. If anyone deigns to look upon it favourably, let him observe this rule in brotherly charity: “If he knew only these things beforehand, let him not disdain what I have written; if he has learned more, let him not be angry that I have not said it.” Rather, while I live, let him communicate to me what I ought to know, so that matters which did not occur in their proper order may be added by my pen, at least in the margin.

## Book Two

[145]

[Col. 1053]

[Col. 1053B] § 106. The first volume reached the point at which the four kingdoms of Britain were compressed into one. Its author was Egbert, great-grandson of King Ine’s brother Ingild. Born among his people to high station and nobly educated from childhood, he shone among the West Saxons.

[Note: [Col. 1053C] Egbert. Ecgbert was son of Ealhmund, son of Eafa, son of Eoppa, son of Ingild, brother of Ine, king of the West Saxons. See below, § 116.]

The continuation of his virtues aroused envy; and, since it is almost natural for kings to look with hostile eyes upon those whom they see growing up with hopes of a kingdom, Brihtric, as was said before, regarded the youth of memorable character with suspicion and planned to remove him from the way. Egbert, perceiving this, fled to Offa, king of the Mercians. While Offa gave him careful and diligent protection, Brihtric’s envoys arrived, demanding the fugitive for punishment and carrying in their hands the price of betrayal.

[Note: [Col. 1053C] As has been said. § 43.]

Moreover, Offa’s daughters demanded marriage with their king, so that the bond of a marriage-bed might maintain perpetual friendship between them (A.D. 787).

[Note: [Col. 1053C] His daughters demanded marriage. See § 43, note 100.]

Thus Offa, who would not yield to threats of war, gave way to enticements; and [146] Egbert crossed the sea and came to France (A.D. 798). I understand this to have happened by God’s counsel, so that the man chosen for so great a kingdom might receive from the Franks instruction in ruling. For that people is readily foremost among all western peoples alike in trained strength and in gracious manners.

[Note: [Col. 1053C] He came to France. According to the Saxon Chronicle, before he became king Ecgbert was driven into France by Offa of Mercia and Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons, where he remained for three years. (*Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 836).]

Egbert therefore used this humiliation as a whetstone, by which, rubbing away the rust of idleness, he might sharpen his mind and adopt manners far removed from heathen barbarism.

[Note: [Col. 1053D]

> Therefore I shall serve as a whetstone, able to make iron sharp, though itself incapable of cutting.  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, 304.)

]

When Brihtric died, Egbert returned to Britain at the repeated summons of his people and, immediately ordered to rule, satisfied his longing for his native land in the year of the Lord’s incarnation eight hundred, while Charlemagne was reigning in France in the thirty-fourth year; Charlemagne also survived him by twelve years.

[Note: [Col. 1053D] On Brihtric’s death. See § 43, note 4.]

[Note: [Col. 1053D] In the year, etc. Here Malmesbury falls into an anachronism, following the Saxon Chronicle, which assigns Ecgbert’s accession to 800 instead of 802. By the common method of calculation Charlemagne began to reign on 24 September, A.D. 768, when he succeeded to a part of the Frankish monarchy; thus the thirty-fourth year of his reign was completed in September 802, the year in which Ecgbert unquestionably ascended the throne. Charlemagne died on 28 January 814, having, as Malmesbury observes, survived Ecgbert’s accession by twelve years. See § 43, note 5.]

Meanwhile, having purchased his subjects’ affection by clemency and gentleness, Egbert gave his first proofs of strength against the Britons who inhabited that part of the island called Cornwall. Having [147] subdued them, he made tributary the northern Britons, who are separated from those already mentioned by an arm of the sea.

[Note: [Col. 1054D] First proofs of strength, etc. According to the Saxon Chronicle, Ecgbert devastated the region of the West Welsh from east to west in A.D. 817. Matthew of Westminster states that Cornwall was occupied by Ecgbert as conqueror in 808.]

[Note: [Col. 1054D] Inhabit. d. e. m.; “inhabit,” a. s. l.]

[Note: [Col. 1054D] The northern Britons, etc. According to the Saxon Chronicle, Florence of Worcester, and others, this happened in 828.]

When the fame of these victories frightened the rest, Beornwulf, king of the Mercians, breathing arrogance and thinking it glorious if his boldness removed the fear of the others, declared war upon Egbert. Egbert, considering retreat a loss of honour, met him eagerly. Battle was joined, and Beornwulf fled, miserably defeated. This battle took place at Ellandun in the year of the Lord [Col. 1055A] eight hundred and twenty-six.

[Note: [Col. 1055C] Eight hundred and twenty-six. The battle of Ellandun was fought in A.D. 824, as one of our manuscripts correctly reads. As to the date of this battle, the manuscript from which we established our text departs from better authorities, according to which it would have been fought two years later, after the events which Malmesbury relates as resulting from its successful outcome. For from the matters given in the text, Egbert subjected Kent in 834, the thirty-fourth year of his reign. But according to the more correct computation, by which Egbert’s kingdom began in January 802, the defeat of Beornwulf, king of the Mercians, and the expulsion of Baldred from the Kentish throne must have occurred in the twenty-second year of Egbert’s reign, A.D. 824. Malmesbury, however, taking 800 as if it were the year of Egbert’s accession, wrote incorrectly—though consistently with his own view, and probably—but regarded 824 as the twenty-fourth year of Egbert’s reign.]

Exalted by this outcome, and extending his mind to greater things while victory was still hot, the West Saxon sent his son Æthelwulf, with Ælstan bishop of Sherborne and a picked force, into Kent, that they might add to West-Saxon lordship a province either long numbed by peace or drained of its strength.

§ 107. The men sent diligently carried out their orders, traversed the region everywhere within its boundaries, and with very little effort expelled King Baldred beyond the river [Col. 1055B] Thames. They subjected Kent, Surrey, and [148] the South and East Saxons—who had formerly belonged by right to their forefathers—to their own side, in the twenty-fourth year of Egbert’s reign.

Not long afterwards, the East Angles, encouraged by Egbert’s aid, killed the Mercian kings Beornwulf and Ludeca, caught in successive ambushes. The cause of their deaths was that they continued, with their customary obstinacy, to trouble the outer borders.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Kings of the Mercians. Beornwulf was slain in A.D. 825, and Ludeca in the same year.]

Their successor Wiglaf, at first driven from the kingdom by Egbert and soon received under tributary allegiance, enlarged the West-Saxon dominion.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Wiglaf . . . driven from the kingdom. Wiglaf was expelled by Ecgbert in A.D. 827 and restored to his kingdom the following year, though he held it tributary to the West Saxons.]

In the same year the Northumbrians, seeing that they alone remained and were pointed out by everyone’s finger, feared that he would pour upon them his long-conceived anger. At last, though late, they favoured surrender by giving hostages.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] In the same year, the Northumbrians, etc. Ecgbert led an army to Dore against the Northumbrians, who there offered him obedience and submission in A.D. 827. (*Saxon Chronicle* and FLORENCE OF WORCESTER.)]

Thus, having gained possession of all Britain, he passed the remaining nine years of his life quietly, except that in his last days a piratical Danish force, landing on his shores, disturbed the kingdom’s peace. Such is the hazard of human affairs: ruling first over all the English, he might regard the obedience of his kinsmen as of little account, while a foreign enemy did not [149] cease to attack him and his heirs. When the forces of the English took the field against them, fortune, abandoning its usual flattery of the king, failed him in the very undertaking. For although during the better part of the day he had nearly secured victory, when the sun was already sinking into the ocean he lost the prize; yet, aided by darkness, he escaped the disgrace of defeat.

[Note: [Col. 1056C] A piratical Danish force, etc. “A.D. 833, thirty-five ships of Danish pirates arrived. Ecgbert attacked them at Carrum—Charmouth in Dorsetshire—but after a great slaughter the Danes gained possession of the camp.” (*Saxon Chronicle*).]

[Note: [Col. 1056C] Did not cease. s. c. d. e.; “did not permit,” a. l.]

[Note: [Col. 1056C] Darkness. a. s. d. e. l.; “night or darkness,” c.]

In the following battle, however, with a small force he routed an immense multitude.

[Note: [Col. 1056C] In the following battle, etc. In the battle fought near Hengston in Cornwall in A.D. 835, the Danish fleet, relying on assistance from the inhabitants, was defeated and driven into flight by Ecgbert.]

Finally, after thirty-seven years and seven months, he died and was buried at Winchester, leaving his son great opportunities for renown. He declared that his son would be fortunate if he did not interrupt by the customary indolence of that people the kingdom which he had woven together with such great industry.

[Note: [Col. 1056C] He died after thirty-seven years and seven months. c. e. l.; a. s. d. read “of his reign” after “years.” See King Ecgbert’s charter (*Codex Diplomaticus Aevi Saxonici*, no. CCXL, p. 218), issued in A.D. 838 and confirmed by his son Æthelwulf in A.D. 839, which is described as the first year of Æthelwulf’s reign after his father’s death. If the duration of Ecgbert’s reign is correctly stated here and in the Saxon Chronicles, his death cannot have occurred before August A.D. 839 [Col. 1056D]. Simeon of Durham assigns only thirty-six years to Ecgbert’s reign, and Florence of Worcester asserts that he died in the thirty-seventh year of his reign.]

## On King Æthelwulf
§ 108. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1056D] “Eight hundred and thirty-seven.” a. s. d. e. l.; c. omits “seventh.” — Æthelwulf’s accession should be placed about August A.D. 839. Here, too, Malmesbury, following the Saxon Chronicle, departs by two years from the northern chroniclers.] eight hundred and thirty-seven, Æthelwulf (whom some call Athulf), son of Egbert, reigned [Note: [Col. 1056D] “Twenty years and five months.” In this total Malmesbury probably includes the years during which Æthelwulf reigned while his father was still alive. The Saxon Chronicle assigns eighteen years and six months to his reign; if these are counted from his accession in August 839, it follows correctly that he died in 858. According to Florence of Worcester, on the Ides of January (13 January).] for twenty years and five months. He was mild by nature, and preferred to live in peace rather than to rule many provinces. Finally, content with the ancestral kingdom of the West Saxons, he handed over the other dependencies which his father had subdued to his son [Note: [Col. 1057B] Æthelstan. Æthelstan was made king by his father of Kent, Essex, Surrey, and Sussex in 839.] Æthelstan; when and what end he came to is uncertain.

He assisted [Note: [Col. 1057C] Burhred. Burgred, king of the Mercians, obtained Æthelwulf’s aid against the Welsh in 853; in the following year, after Easter, Æthelwulf gave him his daughter Æthelswith in marriage.] Burhred, king of the Mercians, with an additional [Note: [Col. 1057C] “Additional.” d. e. m.; “and an additional,” a. s. c. l.] army against the Britons, and exalted him enormously [Note: [Col. 1057C] “By the marriage of his daughter,” etc. Asser relates that this marriage was celebrated with great solemnity at Chippenham in Wiltshire.] by the marriage of his daughter. The Danish pirates, ranging throughout the whole island and harassing every shore by unexpected landings, he crushed more than once, both in person and through his commanders; although, as is the lottery of wars, he himself suffered frequent and notable disasters in the same conflicts, with London and almost all Kent devastated. [Note: [Col. 1057C] “Not once,” etc. In 845 the Danes were defeated near the River Parrett in Somersetshire, and again in 851 at Wicganbeorg in Devonshire.] [Note: [Col. 1057C] “London,” etc. This occurred, according to the Saxon Chronicle, in 851; but after the Danes had crossed the Thames and entered Surrey, Æthelwulf met them with his army at Ockley and defeated them.]

Yet the vigorous spirit of the king’s counsellors always stood against these afflictions: they never allowed enemies to commit wrongdoing with impunity, without taking vengeance upon them under the common shield. He had in his time two outstanding bishops: blessed Swithun of Winchester, I mean, and [Note: [Col. 1057D] Alstan of Sherborne. Ealhstan was made bishop of Sherborne in 817 and died in 867.] Alstan of Sherborne. Seeing that the king was of a somewhat dull and sluggish intellect, they spurred him by diligent admonitions toward knowledge of kingship.

[Note: [Col. 1057C] Blessed Swithun. King Ecgbert committed St Swithun as tutor to his son Æthelwulf. Swithun was afterwards made bishop of Winchester in 838 and died on 2 July 862.] Swithun, disdaining earthly things, instructed his lord in heavenly matters; Alstan, considering public affairs likewise not to be neglected, urged him on against the Danes—himself supplying money for the treasury and himself raising the army. Anyone who reads the annals will find much done through him in such matters, both steadfastly begun and successfully completed. [Note: [Col. 1057D] “Whoever reads the annals.” Consult the Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 823–845.]

He lived in the bishopric for fifty years: blessed is he who has been in readiness for good works for so long a time. I would gladly praise him, were it not that, carried away by human greed, [Note: [Col. 1057D] “Carried away.” d. e.; *raptatus*, a. c. l.; *captatus*, s.] he made an unlawful usurpation when he subjected Malmesbury monastery to his own affairs. To this day we feel the reproach of his shamelessness, although, immediately after his death, that place rejoiced at being delivered from all that violence, [Note: [Col. 1057D] “Down to our own time,” etc. Here Malmesbury alludes to the seizure of his monastery by Roger, bishop of Salisbury, in 1118.] down to our own time, when it fell again into the same danger. Thus the accursed hunger of avarice gnaws at mortal hearts; thus it drives into Tartarus men who are great and distinguished in other respects. [Note: [Col. 1057D] “Thus the accursed hunger.” Vergil, *Aeneid* III.56.]

§ 109. Æthelwulf, relying upon these two supporters, and taking good care of external affairs while not neglecting internal ones, after the defeat of his enemies turned to the worship of God. He granted to Christ’s servants a tenth of all the hides [Note: [Col. 1057D] “A tenth of all the hides,” etc. The grant of tithes made by King Æthelwulf became the source of many controversies. See the Wilton charter dated on Holy Easter Day (22 April), indiction II, A.D. 854 (MS Cotton Claudius C. IX). The charter which later appears in § 114 is also found in Matthew of Westminster and Ingulf. Spelman conjectures that the grant was made twice: first in 854 and confirmed by the supreme pontiff when Æthelwulf went to Rome; then afterwards, when he had returned to his country, in a great council of the entire kingdom.] within his kingdom, free from every public obligation and released from every burden.

But how small is this part of his glory! Having put his kingdom in order, he went to Rome, and there offered to St Peter the tribute which England pays even today. [Note: [Col. 1058C] “The tribute … he offered to St Peter.” This plainly concerns Rome-scot, or St Peter’s penny, as a tribute which England still in that age paid to Rome. Both the origin and use of this tribute are uncertain. Spelman states that it was an annual tribute of one penny, paid at Rome on St Peter’s feast by each household. That this grant was made after Æthelwulf returned to England seems supported by the commendatory letter, as Asser calls it, in which the king orders three hundred mancuses to be sent annually to Rome. One third was to go to the Roman pontiff himself, while the rest was to be divided equally between the churches of St Peter and St Paul to provide lights for the Easter vigil. Spelman conjectures that this tribute was granted in a general council of the people.] This he did in the presence of Pope Leo IV, who had formerly honourably received Ælfred, Æthelwulf’s son, when he was sent to him, and had anointed him king. [Note: [Col. 1058D] “Before Pope Leo IV.” Æthelwulf’s pilgrimage to Rome, with his son Ælfred as companion, is assigned to 855. If the name of the pontiff then governing the Roman Church is correctly given here, Æthelwulf departed before 17 July of that year, on which Pope Leo died. This nevertheless raises doubt as to the date assigned to Æthelwulf’s charter of tithes, such as appears in Ingulf, which most authors say was granted before his departure for Rome. See p. 172, note.] [Note: [Col. 1058D] “His son Ælfred.” Ælfred’s first mission to Rome occurred in 853; Pope Leo then anointed him king in succession to his father’s kingdom and adopted him as a son of the Roman Church. Asser maintains that the pope anointed Ælfred as a prophetic sign of his future royal dignity and stood sponsor for him.]

He stayed there for a full year and splendidly restored the English School, [Note: [Col. 1058D] “The English School,” etc. If Matthew of Westminster is to be believed, under A.D. 727, the English School at Rome was founded by Ine, king of the West Saxons, with the consent and approval of Pope Gregory. No ancient authentic account of its foundation is believed to survive. The English School was situated in the vicinity of St Peter’s, where English pilgrims lived at Rome. According to the Saxon Chronicle it was consumed by fire in 816; but the fire meant here is probably no other than that which, according to Anastasius, broke out in Rome on the Via Saxonum shortly after Leo IV’s elevation. Leo reigned from 847 to 17 July 855; the end, rather than the beginning, of his pontificate thus agrees with the assertions of the text. (ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN, *Lives of the Popes*.)] which, as is reported, had originally been founded by King Offa of the Mercians and had burned down in the previous year. Thence, returning home through Gaul, he took in marriage Judith, daughter of Charles, king of the Franks. [Note: [Col. 1059B] “Judith, daughter of Charles,” etc. Æthelwulf’s marriage to Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, was celebrated at the palace of Verberie on 1 October 856.]

[Note: [Col. 1059C] “On the successors of Charlemagne.” Malmesbury appears to have taken a large part of this account from the *Synchronistic Chronicles* (from the book of the monastery of St Wandrille), which extend to 877. Archbishop Ado of Vienne (A.D. 865–875) also used these chronicles, as did Hariulf, if he is the monk of St-Riquier who wrote in 1088. (Fragment from the book of the monastery of St Wandrille, surviving in MS no. 419 of the abbey of St Victor, Paris; Bouquet, VII, 44. — Chronicle of Ado, editions Paris 1522 and 1561; Lyons 1677, in the *Libraries of the Fathers*. — Chronicle of Hariulf, in d’Achery, vol. III of the *Spicilegium*; folio, Paris, 1723.)]

## ON THE SUCCESSORS OF CHARLEMAGNE

§ 110. Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, had four sons: Lothair, Pippin, Louis, and Charles surnamed the Bald. [Note: [Col. 1059C] Louis the Pious. He was associated with his father Charlemagne in the western empire in September 813, and succeeded him as sole emperor and king of the Franks on 28 January 814. He died on 20 June 840.]

Lothair, the eldest, had assumed the title of emperor while his father was still alive and reigned fifteen years in that part of Germany which lies by the Alps and is now called Lotharingia—as it were, “Lothair’s kingdom”—and throughout Italy with Rome. [Note: [Col. 1059D] Lothair. The eldest son of Louis I, he had been declared king of the Franks while his father was still living and was associated with him in the empire in July 817. He became king of Italy in 820 and received the imperial crown from the pope on Holy Easter Day, 5 April 823.] [Note: [Col. 1059D] “He reigned fifteen years.” Lothair reigned fifteen years and three months from his father’s death in 840, when he became sole western emperor. He died in the abbey of Prüm in the Ardennes on 20 September 855, having assumed the monastic habit only six days before.]

At the end of his life, afflicted by ill health, he renounced the world. He was by far the most savage of all men before him, since he repeatedly imprisoned his own father in dungeons. [Note: [Col. 1059D] “His own father,” etc. Emperor Louis I was confined by his sons in the monastery of St Medard at Soissons twice: first in 830, and again in 833.] That father was indeed mild and simple in disposition; but after Ermengard, by whom he had had his elder children, had died, he cherished more closely Charles, born of his wife Judith, and was cruelly harassed by Lothair. [Note: [Col. 1059D] “Charles,” etc. Lothair, Louis, and Pippin were sons of Louis the Pious by his first wife Hermengard, daughter of Count Ingram. After her death, on 3 October 818 [printed “518”], the emperor married Judith, daughter of Guelph, duke of Ravensburg. Charles the Bald was born from this marriage.]

Pippin, Louis’s second son, reigned in Aquitaine and Gascony. [Note: [Col. 1060B] Pippin. Pippin I governed the kingdom of Aquitaine from 814, though he was not acknowledged as king of this region before the assembly at Aachen held in July 817. He died on 13 December 838.] Louis, Louis’s third son, besides Noricum, which he possessed, held the kingdoms which his father had given him: namely, Alemannia, Thuringia, Austrasia, Saxony, and the kingdom of the Avars—that is, the Huns. [Note: [Col. 1060B] Louis. Louis surnamed the German, brother of Emperor Lothair. He was made king of Bavaria in 817 and died at Frankfurt on 28 August 876.] [Note: [Col. 1060B] “Besides Noricum.” The words beginning “Louis, besides Noricum” and ending “was driven into exile” occur in the chronicle from which Malmesbury drew this passage after “they divided the empire of the Franks among themselves,” in place of the words “as we have said above.” (Fragment from the book of the monastery of St Wandrille.)] [Note: [Col. 1060C] “Huns.” Huns or Hungarians, *Fragment of St Wandrille*.]

Charles, however, held the western half of Francia, all Neustria, Brittany, the greater part of Burgundy, Gothia, Gascony, and Aquitaine, after Pippin son of Pippin had been removed and tonsured in the monastery of St Medard. [Note: [Col. 1060C] Charles. a. s. c. e. l.; “Charles IV [the Bald?],” d. III. — Charles the Bald succeeded his father Louis the Pious in the kingdom of the Franks on 20 June 840. His brother Lothair contested the succession with him, but by an agreement in 843 Charles obtained the government of Francia.] [Note: [Col. 1060C] “All Neustria, Aquitaine.” The divisions of Francia were subject to considerable variation. It is enough, however, to observe that Aquitaine lay between the Garonne and the Loire; Gascony stretched from the Garonne to the Pyrenees along the eastern coast; Austrasia, or Eastern Francia, comprised, besides various tracts beyond the Rhine, the land between that river and the Meuse; while Neustria, or Western Francia, extended from the Gallic-British Ocean to the Loire, with Armorica excepted.” (SHARPE, p. 114.) Neustria included the region later called Normandy.] [Note: [Col. 1060D] “After Pippin was removed.” After the death of Pippin I, king of Aquitaine, in December 838, Emperor Louis gave this kingdom to his younger son Charles the Bald. But Pippin, the late king’s last son, then a little boy, contended with him for the crown, retaining the title of king of Aquitaine. In 852 Pippin became a monk in the monastery of St Medard at Soissons; but when he fled thence into Aquitaine in 855, he was betrayed by Rainulf, count of Poitiers, in 864 and led to Charles, who cast him into prison at Senlis, where he died shortly afterwards. See the Chronicle of Ado, Archbishop of Vienne.]

Afterward, having escaped by flight and returned to Aquitaine, he lay hidden there for a long time while fleeing; then, betrayed by the governor Ranulf, he was seized and brought to Charles and thrust into perpetual exile at Senlis. [Note: [Col. 1060D] “Governor.” Malmesbury and the *Fragment of St Wandrille*; “the aforesaid,” Chronicle of Ado.] [Note: [Col. 1060D] “Treach­erously.” s. d. m. and the *Fragment of St Wandrille*; “in good faith,” a. c. e. l. and the Chronicle of Ado.] [Note: [Col. 1060D] “Brought.” a. d. e. l., “led,” s. c.] [Note: [Col. 1061B] “Thrust.” “Condemned,” *Fragment of St Wandrille*.]

After the death of Louis the most pious emperor, Lothair—anointed emperor eighteen years before his father’s death—made war upon his brothers, namely Louis, [Note: [Col. 1061B] “The most pious.” Probably interpolated in the manuscripts. This word does not occur in the chronicle fragment mentioned above, nor is it the surname commonly given to Louis, king of Bavaria. His father, Emperor Louis, bore the surname “the Pious.”] the most pious king of the Bavarians, and Charles. He joined Pippin and the people of Aquitaine to himself in the district of Auxerre, [Note: [Col. 1061C] “Of Auxerre.” Auxerre.] at a place called Fontenoy. There, while the Franks and all the nations subject to them struck each other down in mutual slaughter, Louis and Charles at last put Lothair to flight and gained the victory (A.D. 841). [Note: [Col. 1061C] “They gained the victory.” c. d. e., “they were victorious,” a. s.; “they were conquered,” l.]

[Note: [Col. 1061C] “After the very bloody battle.” The memorable battle of Fontenoy was fought on 23 June 841. Emperor Lothair and his nephew Pippin II, king of Aquitaine, were defeated by Charles the Bald with the assistance and support of his brother Louis of Bavaria. In 843 the possessions of Emperor Louis were divided, by unanimous agreement, among his three brothers. Lothair retained the empire and the kingdoms of Italy, Lotharingia, Provence, and Burgundy; Louis held Bavaria, Germany, Thuringia, Saxony, and Pannonia or Hungary; Charles held the kingdom of Francia, Neustria, Armorica, part of Burgundy, Gothia, Gascony, and Aquitaine. See the Chronicle of Ado, Archbishop of Vienne, and Hariulf’s Chronicle, book III, ch. 6.]

After the very bloody battle, peace having been made between them, they divided the empire of the Franks among themselves, as we have said above. [Note: [Col. 1061D] “As we have said above.” Here the *Fragment of the Chronicle of St Wandrille* reads: “And Lothair indeed received the kingdom of the Romans, all Italy, the eastern part of Francia, and all Provence. Louis, however, besides Noricum,” etc., down to “was thrust into perpetual exile.”]

Lothair, by Ermengard, daughter of Hugh, had three sons: Louis, to whom he gave the kingdom of the Romans and Italy; Lothair, to whom he left the imperial seat; and Charles, to whom he entrusted Provence to govern. [Note: [Col. 1061D] Ermengard. Daughter of Count Hugh; she married Emperor Lothair in October 821 and died on 20 March 851.] [Note: [Col. 1061D] “That is.” a. c. d. e. l.; “first,” s.] [Note: [Col. 1061D] Louis. Louis II, king of Italy, was crowned by Pope Sergius in 844, associated with his father Lothair in the empire after February 849, and received the imperial crown from Pope Leo in 850. He remained sole western emperor in 855 and died without male offspring on 6 August 875; his successor was his uncle Charles the Bald.] [Note: [Col. 1061D] Lothair, to whom he left the imperial seat. That is, Lorraine, Lothair’s kingdom. See Ado’s Chronicle: “Emperor Lothair, seeing himself become ill, divides his kingdom among his sons. He orders Provence and part of Burgundy assigned to Charles, the younger; his own seat to Lothair, the middle son; and Italy to Emperor Louis.” Compare also the Annals of Metz and the Chronicle of Marianus Scotus. A dispute arose as to whether Lotharingia took its name from Emperor Lothair or from his son. King Lothair died at Piacenza on 8 August 869.] [Note: [Col. 1062B] Charles. Charles, the younger son of Emperor Lothair, king of Provence.] [Note: [Col. 1062B] “Entrusted.” a. d. e. l.; “committed,” s. c.]

Lothair also died in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 855, in the thirty-third year of his empire or kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1062C] “Our Lord Jesus Christ.” a. d. e. l.; omitted in s. c.] [Note: [Col. 1062C] “Or kingdom.” a. d. e. l.; omitted in s. c.] [Note: [Col. 1062C] “Thirty-third.” Thirty-two years and six months from the time when he received the imperial crown from Pope Paschal I.] After his death his son Charles, who governed Provence, died in the eighth year. [Note: [Col. 1062C] “He dies in the eighth year.” Charles began to reign in Provence in 855 and died without children in 863.]

Thereupon the brothers Louis, emperor of the Romans, and Lothair divided his kingdom—that is, Provence—between themselves. [Note: [Col. 1062C] “Louis … divide.” Emperor Louis II and King Lothair of Lotharingia divided their brother’s kingdom between themselves. Louis received Provence and that part of Burgundy beyond the Jura; Lothair obtained the remainder. See the Chronicle of Ado, Archbishop of Vienne.]

But Louis, king of the Noricans—that is, the Bavarians—son of Emperor Louis [the Pious], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 865, after the Easter feast, divided his kingdom among his sons. [Note: [Col. 1062C] “Louis.” Louis the Pious.] [Note: [Col. 1062C] “He divided his kingdom among his sons.” No other early historian of Francia mentions this division of 865 except Hariulf, who, as seems probable, derived his account from the same source as Malmesbury, namely the Chronicle of St Wandrille. The three sons of Louis of Bavaria all succeeded jointly to their father’s possessions when he died in 876.]

To Carloman he gave Noricum, that is Bavaria, and the marches against the Slavs and Lombards; to Louis he left Thuringia, the Austrasian Franks, and Saxony; and to Charles he left Alemannia and Curwalia, that is, the county of Cornwall. [Note: [Col. 1062D] Carloman. King of Bavaria; he died on 22 March 880.] [Note: [Col. 1062D] Louis. King of Germany, Saxony, and Austrasia; he succeeded his father Louis the German in 876 and died on 20 January 888.] [Note: [Col. 1062D] Charles. Charles, king of Swabia, surnamed the Fat, afterwards became western emperor and king of the Franks.] [Note: [Col. 1062D] “Cornwall.” a. d. e. l.; “Gaul,” s. c. — “Literally, the horn of Gaul, from the projection of Armorica into the Ocean.” (SHARPE, p. 116.)]

Yet Louis himself happily reigned over his sons in his entire dominion for ten years. [Note: [Col. 1062D] “He reigned,” etc. The *Fragment of St Wandrille* here reads: “He now holds the principate in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 869.” From this one may infer the period in which its author wrote.] [Note: [Col. 1063B] “Ten.” “Eleven,” Hariulf’s Chronicle.] And afterwards King Louis died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 876, after having reigned fifty-four years. [Note: [Col. 1063B] “King Louis.” a. d. e. l. m.; “Louis,” c.; omitted in s.] [Note: [Col. 1063B] “Of the Lord’s Incarnation.” s. c. d. e. m.; “of the Incarnate Word,” a.; omitted in l.] [Note: [Col. 1063B] “Fifty-four.” Louis, king of Bavaria, had nearly completed the fifty-ninth year of his reign from his accession in 817.]

Charles, king of the western Franks, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign went into Italy for prayer and reached the thresholds of the Apostles. There he was chosen emperor by all the Roman people and consecrated emperor by Pope John on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 875. [Note: [Col. 1063C] Charles, etc. Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, succeeded Louis II, his brother’s son, in the western empire and received the imperial crown from Pope John VIII at Rome on Christmas Day 875.] [Note: [Col. 1063C] “For prayer.” a. d. e. l.; “for the sake of prayer,” s. c.] He then entered Gaul prosperously. [Note: [Col. 1063C] “Returned.” a. d. e. l.; “came back,” s. c. and the *Fragment of St Wandrille*.]

In the thirty-eighth year of his reign, and at the beginning of the third of his empire, he again went to Italy. Having conferred with Pope John, he was returning to Gaul when, after crossing Mount Cenis, he lost the sight of this present light on the third day before the Nones of October, in the tenth indiction, in the year of our Lord 877. [Note: [Col. 1063C] “In the thirty-eighth year of his reign.” a. d. e. l.; “but in the year of his reign,” s. c.] [Note: [Col. 1063C] “At the beginning of the third year of his empire.” Charles had not yet completed his second year: crowned 25 December 875, he died 6 October 877.] [Note: [Col. 1063C] “After crossing Mount Cenis.” Charles is said to have died from poison received from the hands of his physician, a Jew named Sedeciah, on 6 October 877 at Brios, a district west of Mount Cenis.] [Note: [Col. 1063C] “The third day before the Nones of October.” Hariulf has the same reading. Some Frankish chronicles read “the Nones of October”; others, better, “the day before the Nones.”] [Note: [Col. 1063D] “Our Lord.” a. e. l.; “Lord,” s.; “our Lord Jesus Christ,” d. m.]

His son Louis succeeded him in the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1063D] “His son Louis.” Louis II as king of the Franks and III as emperor, surnamed the Stammerer, was crowned king at Compiègne on 8 December 877 and emperor in 878.] Then, before the second year of his reign was completed, this same Louis died at the palace of Compiègne on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord 879. [Note: [Col. 1063D] “At Compiègne.” c. d. e. l.; “in Compiègne,” a. s.] [Note: [Col. 1063D] “On the sixth day before the Ides of April.” Hariulf’s Chronicle has the fifth day before the Ides. Authorities of greater reliability state that Louis the Stammerer died at Compiègne on 10 April, the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the year 879.]

Then his sons Louis and Carloman divided his kingdom between themselves. [Note: [Col. 1063D] Louis and Carloman. Louis III and Carloman succeeded their father Louis the Stammerer at his death. The former received Francia and Neustria, the latter Burgundy and Aquitaine. Charles the Fat, son of Louis of Bavaria, obtained the imperial insignia.] The aforesaid King Louis, fighting the Normans in the district of Vimeu, gained the victory and shortly afterward died, on the day before the Nones of August, in the year of the Lord 881, in the fifteenth indiction. [Note: [Col. 1064B] “In the district of Vimeu.” Le Vimeu.] [Note: [Col. 1064B] “Fighting the Normans.” Louis defeated the Normans in 881 at a place called Saulcourt, where their leader Guorm was slain. From the day of this battle, it is reported, Louis suffered an internal injury from which he afterwards died.] [Note: [Col. 1064B] “The day before the Nones of August … the fifteenth.” Malmesbury follows Hariulf in assigning the death of Louis III, king of the Franks, to 4 August 881; from this the duration of the reigns of Louis and Carloman is calculated by both historians. But it should be observed that the fifteenth indiction did not begin before 25 December 881. Louis’s death is commonly assigned to 5 August 881, and Carloman’s coronation to 9 September following. It follows that Louis reigned three years and four months, Carloman—who died on 6 December 884—only two years and three months: together merely five years and eight months from the death of their father Louis.]

He reigned two years, three months, and twenty-four days. [Note: [Col. 1064C] “Three.” a. s. d. e. l.; “four,” c.] His brother Carloman succeeded him in the kingdom. He reigned for three years and six days, and then, in the forest of Yvelines, on Mount Éric, was struck by an extraordinary wild beast. [Note: [Col. 1064C] “Days.” Thus in all manuscripts, but it is probably written incorrectly for “months.” Hariulf writes “three years and a half.”] [Note: [Col. 1064C] “The forest of Yvelines.” The forest of Yvelines near Paris.] [Note: [Col. 1064D] “By a wild beast.” According to certain Frankish annalists, Carloman, while hunting in the forest of Bais, was accidentally wounded by Berthold, one of his counts; and, to save him from punishment, the story of an extraordinary wild beast was circulated (*Annals of Metz* and their Fulda continuation, *Annals of St-Vaast*, and the *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Normans in Francia*). But Malmesbury’s text agrees with the Saxon Chronicle, Asser, and other English writers.]

He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 884, in the second indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of December. Then Charles, king of the Swabians, son of King Louis of the Noricans, assumed the monarchy of the entire empire of the Franks and Romans in the year of the Incarnate Word 885, in the third indiction. [Note: [Col. 1064D] Charles the Fat. Charles the Fat was crowned western emperor on Christmas Day 880 and obtained the kingdom of the Franks upon Carloman’s death on 6 December 884, not without prejudice to Charles the Simple, the posthumous son of Louis the Stammerer. He was acknowledged king of the Franks at the end of January 885.]

Because I consider his vision memorable, I judge it worthy to insert here.

[Note: [Col. 1064D] Vision of Charles. Malmesbury drew the Vision of Charles the Fat verbatim from Hariulf’s *Chronicle*, book III, ch. 21 (*Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 325, folio, Paris, 1723). Alberic of Trois-Fontaines recounts it in substance, referring to Malmesbury: “There follows the wonderful vision which occurred in this year 889 [more correctly, 886] to that same Charles, according to William of Malmesbury.” The annals falsely attributed to Asser likewise recount, under 886, the vision of Charles the Fat: “Charles the third, emperor, son of Hlodwig, king of the Noricans or Bavarians, at this time saw a vision, which, as appears here, he reported in writing, saying: ‘I, Charles,’ etc.” In the Frankish chronicles of St Denis and in certain Latin manuscripts, the vision is incorrectly attributed to Charles the Bald. (BOUQUET, IX, 60).]

## VISION OF CHARLES
§ 111. “In the name of God, the supreme King of kings! I, [Col. 1065A] Charles, emperor, by God’s free gift king of the Germans and patrician of the Romans, and emperor 161 of the Franks, on the holy night of the Lord’s Day, after the divine office of the night hours had been celebrated, when I went to the bed of rest and wished to take the sleep of slumber, a terrifying voice came to me saying: ‘Charles, your spirit will now depart from you for no small span of time.’ Immediately I was caught up in the spirit; and he who bore me up in the spirit was most radiant, and held in his hand [Note: [Col. 1065D] A ball. Thus all the manuscripts. See below, note 67 at the beginning of § 112.] a ball of linen emitting a beam of exceedingly bright [Note: [Col. 1065D] Exceedingly bright. a. s. d. e. m.; ‘most brightly,’ c. l.] light, as comets customarily do when they appear. He began to unwind it and said to me: ‘Take the thread of the gleaming ball, and bind and knot [Note: [Col. 1066D] Knot. a. c. d. e. l.; “mark,” s.] it firmly around the thumb of your right hand, for by it you shall be led through the labyrinthine [Col. 1065B] punishments of hell.’ Having said this, he went before me, swiftly unwinding the thread of the light-bearing ball; and he led me into valleys most deep and fiery, full of wells burning with pitch, sulphur, lead, wax, and fat.

“There I found the bishops of my father and of my uncles. When in fear I asked them why they suffered such grievous torments, they answered me: ‘We were bishops of your father and your uncles, and when we ought to have admonished and preached to them and to their people concerning peace and concord, we sowed discord and were instigators of evils. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1066D] Therefore. s. c. d. e. l.; “thence,” a.] we now burn in these Tartarean punishments, both we and other lovers of murder and plunder. Here too [Col. 1065C] 162 will come your bishops and retainers, who likewise now love to act in this way.’

“And as I heard these things trembling, behold, blackest demons flew upon me with fiery hooks and wished to seize the thread of the ball which I held in my hand and draw it toward themselves. But, beaten back by the rays of that ball, they could not touch the thread. Then, running behind my back, they wished to hook me and hurl me headlong into those sulphurous pits; but my guide, who carried the ball, threw the thread of the ball over my shoulders, doubled it, and pulled strongly behind me [Note: [Col. 1066D] Me. e.; “himself,” a. s. c. d. l.]. Thus we climbed over exceedingly high fiery mountains, from which rose boiling marshes and rivers, and every kind of bubbling metal. There I found innumerable souls of the men and princes [Col. 1065D] of my father and my brothers [Note: [Col. 1066D] Of my brothers. a. s. c. d. e. reads “of mine” after *legit* and “of mine”; in the margin, “of kinsmen,” probably in place of “of uncles.”], plunged in them—some up to their hair, some up to their chin, some up to their navel. And they cried to me [Col. 1066A] with wailing: ‘While we lived, we loved, together with you and with your father, your brothers, and your uncles, to wage battles, murders, and plunder for earthly greed; therefore we endure torments in these boiling rivers and in the various [Note: [Col. 1066D] Various. a. s. c. e. l.; “of various,” d. m.] kinds of metals.’

“As I gazed fearfully upon these things, I heard souls crying behind me: ‘The mighty shall suffer mighty torments.’ I looked back and saw upon the banks of the boiling river furnaces of pitch and sulphur, full of great dragons, scorpions, and serpents of diverse kinds. There too I saw certain princes of my father, and of myself and my brothers, and also of my uncles, saying to me: ‘Alas for us, Charles! You see what grievous torments 163 we endure because of our wickedness and pride and the evil [Col. 1066B] counsels which, through greed, we gave to our kings and to you.’

“When I groaned with them in sorrow at these things [Note: [Col. 1066D] These things. c. d. e. l.; “at these things,” s.; “this,” a.], dragons ran toward me with open jaws full of fire, sulphur, and pitch, wishing to swallow me. But my guide wound the thread threefold around me; by the rays of its brightness their fiery mouths were overcome, and he drew [Note: [Col. 1066D] Drew. s. c. e. l.; “protected,” d. m.; “drew forward,” a.] me onward more forcefully.

“And we descended into a valley which was, on [Note: [Col. 1066D] On. a. s. c. e. l.; “in,” d. m.] one side dark, burning like a fiery furnace, but on the other side so delightful and splendid that I cannot express it in any way. I turned toward the dark, flame-belching side and saw there certain kings of my line in great punishments. Then, pressed by an unbearable [Note: [Col. 1066D] Pressed. a. d. e. l.; “terrified and pressed,” s. c.] anguish, I thought [Col. 1066C] that I would immediately be plunged into those very punishments by blackest giants, who were setting the valley itself aflame with every kind of fire. Trembling greatly, while the thread of the ball illumined my eyes, I saw a light growing somewhat white at the side of the valley, and there two fountains flowing. One was exceedingly hot; the other clear and lukewarm; and there were two vats there.

“As I went there, the thread of the ball directing my steps, I looked over one in which the water was boiling and saw my father Louis [Note: [Col. 1066D] Louis. The Bavarian.] standing in it up to his thighs. Burdened with overwhelming grief and struck by distress, he said to me: ‘My lord Charles, do not fear. I know that your spirit will return again to your body; and God has allowed you to come here so that you might see for what sins I, and all those whom you have seen, endure such [Col. 1066D] punishments. For one day 164 I am in this bath of the boiling vat, and on the next I am transferred into this other, most pleasant vat of water. This happens through the prayers [Col. 1067A] of Saint Peter and Saint [Note: [Col. 1067C] Remigius. Archbishop of Rheims, apostle of the Franks, who is believed to have baptized Clovis. The beginning of his episcopate is commonly assigned to the year 457, and his death to A.D. 530. (Bouquet, IV, 51, note a.)] Remigius, through whose patronage our royal line has hitherto reigned.
