“But if you, my faithful bishops and abbots, and the whole ecclesiastical order quickly come to my aid, by masses, offerings [Note: [Col. 1067C] Offerings. c. d. e. l.; “prayers,” a. s.], psalmody, vigils, and almsgiving, I shall swiftly be released from this vat of boiling water. For my brother Lothair and his son Louis have been delivered from these punishments by the prayers of Saint Peter and Saint Remigius, and have already been led into the joy of God’s paradise.’

“And he said to me: ‘Look to the left.’ When I looked, I saw there two exceedingly high boiling vats. ‘These,’ he said, ‘are prepared for you unless you amend yourself and do penance for your abominable offenses.’ Then I began to shudder deeply. When my companion [Note: [Col. 1067C] Companion. a. c. d. e. l.; “guide,” s.] saw that my [Col. 1067B] spirit was in such terror, he said to me: ‘Follow me to the right-hand side of the most radiant valley of paradise.’

“And as we walked, I beheld my uncle Lothair seated in immense brightness with glorious kings upon a topaz stone of marvelous size, crowned with a precious diadem, and beside him his son Louis, likewise crowned [Note: [Col. 1067C] Crowned. a. s. c. e. l.; “crowned with a crown,” d. m.]. Seeing me, he called me to him [Note: [Col. 1067C] Called. a. d. e. l.; “called me,” s. c.] nearby, saying in a gentle voice: ‘Charles, my successor, now [Note: [Col. 1067C] Third. Emperor Lothair was succeeded by his son Louis II, who was followed by Charles the Bald; he in turn was succeeded by his son Louis III, surnamed the Stammerer [Col. 1067D]. Charles the Fat was therefore fourth from Lothair in the order of succession.] third in the empire of the Romans, 165 come to me. I know that you have come by way of the place of punishment, where your father, my brother, has been placed in the baths appointed for him. But through God’s mercy he will very soon be freed from those punishments, as we too were freed through the merits of Saint Peter and the prayers of Saint Remigius, to whom God gave great apostolic authority [Col. 1067C] over the kings and peoples of the Franks. Unless someone has aided and supported the poor remnants of our line, our genealogy will now fail in its reign and empire. Therefore know that the power of empire will shortly be taken from your hand, and that afterward you will live for a very brief [Col. 1068A] time.’

“Then Louis, turning toward me, said: ‘The empire which you have held until now ought by hereditary right to be received by [Note: [Col. 1067D] Louis, son of my daughter. Louis, surnamed the Blind, was born to Boso, king of Provence, and Ermengard, daughter of Emperor Louis II. Upon the death of Charles the Fat in 888, the kingdom was divided into five parts; Louis was made king of Arles, and in 890 was crowned king of Burgundy. He went to Italy in 899, whence Berengar, the false emperor, drove him out; but when, disregarding the oath by which he was bound, he went again to Rome, he was captured by Berengar and blinded in the year 902. At the end of 900, or the beginning of 901, Pope Benedict IV had crowned him emperor. Louis was still alive after 6 January 923, since on that date he granted a diploma marked in the twenty-third year of his empire. He died about 929.] Louis, the son of my daughter.’ At these words it seemed to me that a little child was present before us.

“Then, looking at him, Lothair, [Note: [Col. 1067D] Grandfather. Emperor Lothair was Louis’s great-grandfather.] his grandfather, said to me: ‘This child appears to be like that boy whom the Lord placed in the midst of the disciples and said [Note: [Col. 1068C] “Of such . . . heaven.” Matthew 18:10.]: “Of such is the kingdom of heaven; I tell you that their angels see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” But you, through that thread of the ball which you hold in your hand, restore to him the power of empire.’

“Accordingly, untying the thread from the thumb of my right hand, I bestowed upon him the whole monarchy of the empire through that thread. Immediately 166 the ball itself [Note: [Col. 1068C] Ball. Except on this occasion, *glomus* is written in the masculine gender throughout the vision. See below, note 67.] shone like a beam of sunlight and was gathered [Col. 1068B] wholly into his hand. Thus, after this marvelous event, my spirit returned to my body, greatly exhausted and terrified.

“Finally, let all know, whether they wish it or not, that according to God’s appointment the whole Roman Empire shall return into his hand. And what I am unable to accomplish for him, because the moment of my summons forestalls me, God, who rules the living and the dead, will accomplish and establish; whose eternal and everlasting kingdom remains without end unto ages of ages. Amen.”

§ 112. [Note: [Col. 1068C] “This vision . . . in the words in which I found it written.” See above, note 42.] This vision, and the division of the kingdoms, I have set down here in the words in which I found it written [Note: [Col. 1068C] Written. s. c. e. l.; “written” [feminine], a. d. m.]. [Note: [Col. 1068C] Set down. s. c. d. e. l. After *apposui*, a adds: “For this reason I also used *glomerem* in the masculine gender, as it appeared corruptly in the exemplar.”] Thus, after Charles had exercised the undiminished power of empire and kingdom for scarcely two years [Note: [Col. 1068C] Scarcely two years. Charles did not survive two years, for he died on 12 or 13 [Col. 1068D] January A.D. 888.], Charles, son of that Louis who died at Compiègne, succeeded [Note: [Col. 1068D] “He was succeeded,” etc. Charles, surnamed the Simple, posthumous son of Louis the Stammerer, was crowned king of the Franks at Rheims on 27 January 893. In A.D. 919 he married Eadgifu, or Eadgyfu, daughter of Edward the Elder, king of the English; by her he had a son, later Louis IV, king of the Franks, surnamed Overseas. In June 923 he was captured by Herbert, count both of Champagne and Vermandois; he died imprisoned at Péronne on 7 October A.D. 929.] to the kingdom. This is the Charles who married the daughter of Edward, king of the English, [Note: [Col. 1068D] And gave Normandy to Rollo. About 912 the Normans settled in Neustria, and Charles gave his daughter Gisela, or Gisella, to Rollo, the first duke of the Normans, on condition that he embrace the Christian religion.] and gave Normandy, with his daughter Gisela, to Rollo, so that she might be a vessel of peace, [Note: [Col. 1068D] Pledge of the treaty. Apparently an allusion to the name of Charles’s daughter Gisela, which has the sense of “pledge.”] a pledge of the treaty.

But in the empire, [Col. 1069A] 167 King Arnulf succeeded [Note: [Col. 1069B] Arnulf, king, succeeded this Charles. Arnulf, illegitimate son of Carloman, king of Bavaria, succeeded Charles the Fat in the empire. Elected king of Germany in November 887, he was consecrated emperor by Pope Formosus before 4 April A.D. 896.] this Charles, being of the imperial line [Note: [Col. 1069B] Guardian of the boy Louis, etc. Boso, whom Charles [Col. 1069C] the Bald had made duke at Pavia in 876, married Ermengard in the same year, when Charles returned to France, and died on 11 January A.D. 887. Their marriage produced Louis, who was therefore about nine years old in the year in which his father died, in which Charles the Fat’s vision is conjectured to have occurred, and in which Arnulf was elected king of Germany. At that age Louis could have been entrusted to Arnulf’s care, but this rests on the authority of no ancient Frankish writer. Ermengard, Boso’s widow, visited Arnulf at Forchheim in 890, apparently, according to Mabillon’s conjecture, in order to persuade him to sanction the inauguration of her son Louis, elected king of Burgundy in the same year at the Council of Valence. (MABILLON, Book III of the *Annals of the Benedictines*, no. 47.) After Boso’s death, Louis, according to the Frankish Annals, approached Emperor Charles the Fat at Kirchheim, who gladly accepted his homage and adopted him as his son. Louis received the imperial crown from the supreme pontiff.], guardian of the boy Louis of whom the preceding vision speaks. After Arnulf’s death fifteen years later, [Note: [Col. 1069D] Fifteen years. It is not apparent from what point these fifteen years should be counted. Emperor Arnulf died on 29 November A.D. 899, in the fifth year of his empire and after the completion of the twelfth year of his reign.] the same Louis succeeded [Note: [Col. 1069D] The same Louis. Louis IV, Arnulf’s son, is here mistakenly understood as Louis, Boso’s son. The former was elected emperor by the German princes after his father’s death in 899. Although he was never regarded as emperor, after his death Conrad was elected, who reigned in Germany until his death on 23 December A.D. 918. Emperor Louis, Boso’s son, outlived Conrad, king of Germany, by many years.]. On his death, [Note: [Col. 1069D] Conrad . . . ruled as emperor. After the death of Louis IV, Conrad, count of Franconia and son-in-law of Emperor Arnulf, was elected emperor of Germany in A.D. 912; but his authority was not recognized in Italy. Some maintain that Conrad and his successor [Col. 1070B] Henry were never emperors, because at that time only those who had received the imperial crown from the supreme pontiff were customarily regarded as emperors. Thus Otto the Great, Henry’s son, was the first, after the extinction of the German branch of Charlemagne’s line, to attain this dignity; he was made emperor in 962 [Col. 1070C].] a certain Conrad, king of the Teutons, ruled as emperor. 168 He was succeeded (A.D. 919) by his son Henry, [Note: [Col. 1070C] Son Henry. Henry, emperor of Germany, surnamed the Fowler, was the son of Otto, duke of Saxony, by Liutgard, daughter of Emperor Arnulf. See above § 68, where a very similar error occurs in calling Otto the Great Conrad’s nephew. Henry died on 2 July A.D. 936 and had his son Otto as successor by election.] who sent to Athelstan, king of the English, for his two sisters Aldgitha and Edgitha. [Note: [Col. 1070C] Of whom, etc. Eadgitha, daughter of Edward the Elder, married Otto, thereafter king and later emperor of Germany, in A.D. 930. She died on 26 January A.D. 947. (*Chronicle of Ethelwerd*).] He married the latter to his son Otto, [Note: [Col. 1070C] The other, etc. The two daughters in question were born to Edward by Ælfflæd, daughter of Earl Æthelhelm, and consequently Athelstan’s half-sisters. Aldgitha, or Ælfgifu—called Adela in Frankish history—had married Eblo or Eble, count of Poitou and duke of Aquitaine. (BOUQUET, IX, 21, note e.) Some modern writers wrongly identify her [Col. 1070D] with Eadgifu, another daughter of Edward—sister of Eadred and Edmund—who married Louis the Blind, son of Boso, king of Arles, because Malmesbury, in § 126, describes him as prince of Aquitaine.] and gave the other in marriage to a certain duke near the Alps.

Thus even today the Roman Empire and the kingdom of the Franks, once united, are divided: emperors possess the one and kings the other. But because I have wandered far from my subject while I have enjoyed tracing in outline the succession of the illustrious [Col. 1069B] Franks, I shall now return to the road upon which I had set out, and go back to Æthelwulf.

§ 113. When, after his year-long pilgrimage, he returned home, having taken in marriage the daughter of Charles the Bald, he offended the feelings of certain persons otherwise than he had expected. For his son Æthelbald, Bishop [Note: [Col. 1070D] Ealhstan and Eanulf. Ealhstan, bishop of Sherborne, and Eanulf died in the same year, A.D. 867. (ETHELWERD, *Chronicle*).] Ealhstan of Sherborne, and Eanulf, earl of Somerset, 169 had conspired to dishonor him [Col. 1070A] and were endeavoring to drive him from the kingdom. But, through the intervention of more mature counsel, the kingdom was divided between father and son.

This division was unjust. Such was the ascendancy of malice that the better western part was given to the son and the inferior eastern part to the father. Nevertheless, Æthelwulf, in extraordinary clemency—fearing more than civil war—yielded patiently to his son, restraining by a gentle address the provincials who had assembled to defend his dignity. Thus, although the whole dispute had arisen over his foreign wife, he held her in such high honor that he even seated her beside himself upon the throne, contrary to the custom of the West Saxons. For the West Saxons do not permit a queen either to sit beside the king or to be distinguished by the title of queen, [Note: [Col. 1070D] Because of the wickedness of Eadburh. Asser asserts that Alfred himself related this story to him.] because of the wickedness of Eadburh, daughter of Offa, king of the Mercians.

[Col. 1070B] She, [Note: [Col. 1070D] As we said before. § 43.] as we said earlier, was married to Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons. She used to incite that gentle man—as they say—by wicked counsels to the destruction of innocent persons; and those whom she could not accuse, she dispatched with poisonous draughts (A.D. 787–802). This became known in the case of a certain young man very dear to the king, whom she killed by poison. Beorhtric immediately took to his bed and died, having tasted beforehand from the drink without, certainly, the queen’s knowledge. The report spread among the people, and compelled the poisoness to leave the kingdom.

She went to Charlemagne and happened to find him standing with one of his sons. When she had offered gifts, the emperor, playfully and full of jest, bade her choose which she preferred, himself or his son. Then Eadburh, choosing the youth because of the sight of his youthful beauty, Charlemagne replied, somewhat moved: “If you had chosen me, you would have had my son; but because you chose my son, you shall have neither me nor him.” 170 Accordingly, he placed her in a monastery, where she could live in abundance, but [Note: [Col. 1071D] Not long afterward he expelled her, etc. After Charlemagne expelled Eadburh, she died most wretchedly at Pavia, where, begging her daily sustenance from many persons with whom Asser had conversed, she was a familiar sight.] not long afterward expelled her when she was convicted of fornication.

Shocked by her wickedness, the Saxons issued the decree I have mentioned; but Æthelwulf nullified it by his own kindness. A few months before his death, [Note: [Col. 1071D] He made a will. See above § 109, note 72.] he made a will in which, after dividing [Col. 1071B] the kingdom between his sons Æthelbald and Æthelberht, he also settled a dowry upon his daughter. He ordained that, until the end of the age, in every [Note: [Col. 1071D] Every. d. e. m.; “all,” a. s. c. l.] tenth hide of his entire inheritance, a poor person should be clothed and fed; and that every year three hundred mancuses of gold should be sent to Rome: one hundred to Saint Peter and one hundred to Saint Paul for lights, and one hundred to the apostolic see for gifts. Having survived for two years after returning from Rome, he died [Note: [Col. 1071D] He dies. Æthelwulf died on 13 January A.D. 858 (*Annals of Bertin*, BOUQUET, VII, 73; SIMEON OF DURHAM and the *Chronicle of Melrose*); in certain manuscripts, June (Florence of Worcester).] and was buried at Winchester in the bishopric. But, to return after this digression to the sequence of events, I shall append the charter of liberty for the churches [Note: [Col. 1071D] Charter of liberty for the churches. Æthelwulf’s grant is likewise found in Ingulf, where it is dated 3 November, indiction III, A.D. 855. The sense seems defective in the two versions occurring in Malmesbury and Ingulf. Compare the charter given on holy Easter Day, A.D. 854. (See § 109 and note to § 114.) Ingulf nevertheless writes that this grant was made after Æthelwulf’s return from Rome [Col. 1072D], whence he did not return before the autumn of 856. It is quite probable that it was only then confirmed. Asser assigns the grant of tithes to 855, before the king went to Rome; Simeon of Durham, the *Chronicle of Melrose*, and other authorities agree.] which he granted to all England.

§ 114. “Our Lord reigning for ever: since in our times we see dangerous times pressing upon us—conflagrations of wars, plundering of our wealth, and also the manifold tribulations inflicted by the most cruel [Col. 1071C] 171 ravages of hostile barbarian and pagan peoples, to the point of utter destruction—we therefore, I Æthelwulf, king of the West Saxons, with the counsel of my bishops and princes, have approved a wholesome counsel and a uniform remedy: that some hereditary portion of lands, formerly possessed by persons of every rank, whether servants and handmaids of God serving God or laypersons, [Note: [Col. 1072D] Laypersons. Ingulf: “poor laypersons.”] should be granted in perpetual freedom to the extent of a tenth dwelling-place at the least, yet a tenth part, so that it may be safe and protected from all secular services, and also from [Col. 1072A] greater and lesser royal tribute or assessments, which we call *Witereden*; and may be free from every burden, to serve God alone for the salvation of our souls and the forgiveness of our sins, without military service, bridge-repair, or fortress-building, so that they may all the more diligently pour out unceasing prayers to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1072D] Lord. e.; “God,” a. s. c. d. l.] for us, inasmuch as we lighten their service in some measure.”

It then pleased Bishops Ealhstan of the church of Sherborne and Swithun of the church of Winchester, together with their abbots and servants of God, to adopt a plan that all our brothers and sisters at every church should, every week on Wednesday—that is, *Wodnesdeg* [Woden’s day]—have the whole congregation sing fifty psalms, and each priest [Col. 1072B] two masses: one for King Æthelwulf and the other for his nobles who consented to this gift, for the reward and relief of their sins. For the living king: “O God who justifiest”; for the living nobles: “Stretch forth, O Lord”; but after 172 they have died, separately for the dead king and collectively for the dead princes. And this shall be established as firmly throughout all the days of Christianity as that liberty is established, so long as faith increases among the English people.

This charter of donation was written in the year of the Lord’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 1072D] Eight hundred and fourteen. d. e. m.; “eight hundred and forty-four,” a. s. c. l. The date appears corrupted in all the manuscripts. In the charter as it occurs in Ingulf, Burgred, king of the Mercians, and Edmund of the East Angles are named as witnesses; the former ascended the throne in A.D. 852, the latter was crowned on Christmas Day 854. See p. 170, note.] eight hundred and fourteen, in the fourth indiction, on the fifth [Note: [Col. 1072D] Fifth. s. c. d. e. m.; “also,” a. l.] day before the Nones of November, at [Note: [Col. 1072D] The city of Winchester.] Winchester, in the church of Saint Peter before the high altar. And they did this in honor of [Col. 1072C] Saint Michael the Archangel; of Saint Mary, glorious queen and Mother of God; likewise of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; of our holy father Pope Gregory; and of all the saints. And then, for greater firmness, King Æthelwulf placed the charter upon the altar of Saint Peter; the bishops received it in pledge of God’s faith, and afterwards sent it through all the churches in their dioceses, as was stated above.

§ 115. [Note: [Col. 1072D] From this man. a. d. e. l. m.; “from this king,” s. c.] From this man the English Chronicles trace upward the line of royal descent as far as Adam, just as we know that Luke the Evangelist did from the Lord Jesus. If I do the same, it perhaps will not be superfluous, although one must fear [Col. 1073A] that the gaps of barbarian names may wound ears unaccustomed to such things.

§ 116. [Note: [Col. 1073B] Æthelwulf was the son of Egbert. This genealogy [Col. 1073C] occurs in the Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 855, and in Asser, Æthelweard, and Florence of Worcester.] Æthelwulf was the son of Egbert; Egbert of Ealhmund; Ealhmund of Eafa; Eafa of Eoppa; 173 Eoppa of Ingild, brother of King Ine, both of whom were sons of Cenred; Cenred of Ceolwald; Ceolwald of Cutha; Cutha of Cuthwine; Cuthwine of Ceawlin; Ceawlin of Cynric; [Note: [Col. 1073C] Cynric. Certain manuscripts, Asser, and Florence of Worcester read: “Cynric of Creoding [Creod], Creoding of Cerdic.”] Cynric of Cerdic, who was the first king of the West Saxons; Cerdic of Elesa; Elesa of Esla; Esla of Gewis; Gewis of Wig; Wig of Freawine; Freawine of Frithogar; Frithogar of Brond; Brond of Beldeg; Beldeg of Woden. From this man, as we have often said, sprang kings of many peoples. Woden was the son of Frithowald; Frithowald of Frealaf; [Note: [Col. 1073C] Frealaf. The Saxon Chronicle reads: “Frealaf son of Frithuwulf, Frithuwulf of Finn.”] Frealaf of Finn; Finn of Godwulf; [Col. 1073B] Godwulf of Geat; Geat of Tætwa; [Note: [Col. 1073C] Tætwa. Saxon Chronicle: *Taetwa*; gloss: “Phillis,” in l.] Tætwa of Beaw; [Note: [Col. 1073C] Beaw. Gloss: “Assaricus,” in l.] Beaw of [Note: [Col. 1073C] Scyld. Gloss: “Ebraucus,” in l.] Scyld; [Note: [Col. 1073C] Scyld, Sceaf. The Saxon Chronicle here reads: “Sceldwea of Heremod, Heremod of Itermon, Itermon of Hathra, Hathra of Hwala, Hwala of Bedwig, Bedwig of Sceaf, that is, son of Noah.”] Scyld of Sceaf.

[Note: [Col. 1073C] This man. e. l.; “this Sceaf,” d. m.—“Scef himself was carried in a single small vessel to an island of the ocean called Scani, surrounded by arms; he was a very young boy and unknown to the inhabitants of that land. [Col. 1073D] Yet they received him and carefully kept him as one of their household; afterwards they chose him as king.” (*Chronicle of Æthelweard*, Book III.)] This man, they say, was cast ashore on a certain island of Germany, Scandza—of which [Note: [Col. 1073D] Jordanes. Or Jornandes, secretary to the Gothic kings who were in Italy and later bishop of Ravenna, wrote two historical works, one entitled *On Gothic Affairs*, the other *On the Succession of Kingdoms and Times*. He lived in the sixth century.] Jordanes, the historian of the Goths, speaks—in a ship without a helmsman, as a little boy, asleep with a sheaf of grain placed at his head. Hence he was called Sceaf [“sheaf”]. The people of that region received him as a miracle and carefully reared him. When grown, he reigned in a town then called Slaswic, but now Haithabu. 174 That region is called Old England, from which the English came into Britain; it lies between the Saxons and the Goths.

[Note: [Col. 1073D] Sceaf was the son of Heremod . . . Strephius. See note 2 to this section.] Sceaf was the son of Heremod; [Col. 1074A] Heremod of [Note: [Col. 1073D] Stermon. Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester: Itermon.] Stermon; Stermon of Hadra; Hadra of Gwala; Gwala of Bedweg; Bedweg of [Note: [Col. 1073D] Strephius. This name does not occur in the Saxon Chronicle, Asser, Æthelweard, or Florence of Worcester.] Strephius. He, as is said, was a son of Noah, born in the ark.

§ 117. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation eight hundred and fifty-seven (858), the two sons of Æthelwulf divided the paternal kingdom: [Note: [Col. 1073D] The paternal kingdom, etc. After their brother died in January 856, Æthelbald reigned in Wessex and Æthelberht in Kent, Surrey, and Sussex. The former died about July A.D. 860, when his brother succeeded to the whole of his father’s kingdom.] Æthelbald reigned in Wessex and Æthelberht in Kent. Æthelbald, cowardly and treacherous toward his father, defiled his father’s bed, [Note: [Col. 1074B] By marrying his stepmother Judith. The Annals of Winchester [Col. 1074C] (*Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 204) state that Æthelbald, admonished by Saint Swithun, repented of his incest and separated from his stepmother. Judith returned to France about 861, though not before Æthelbald’s death. See the *Annals of Bertin*, A.D. 862. (BOUQUET, VII, 77.) She married Baldwin, count of Flanders, surnamed Iron Arm, in 863.] sinking after his parent’s death into marriage with his stepmother Judith. But [Note: [Col. 1074C] After five years. While his father lived, Æthelbald reigned for two and a half years, namely from the time when Æthelwulf went to Rome in 855. The two and a half years from January 858 to July 860, when he died, make the five years assigned to his reign by Malmesbury and the Saxon Chronicle.] after five years he died and was buried at Sherborne, and the whole kingdom passed to the other brother.

[Note: [Col. 1074C] In his time a band of pirates. The Danes ravaged Winchester in 860.] In his time a band of pirates, landing at Southampton, gave the populous city of Winchester to plunder; but [Col. 1074B] soon vigorously routed by the royal commanders, after losing many of their number they sailed beyond the sea. Having circled the ocean, they chose the island of Thanet in Kent as their winter quarters. The people of Canterbury, [Note: [Col. 1074C] Hostages having been given. In 864 (Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 865), the Danes, as Asser relates, after spending the winter on Thanet, made a truce with the people of Canterbury, who promised them money. But scorning their pledged faith and judging that plunder would profit them more than peace kept, they ravaged all eastern Kent.] having given hostages and promised money, would have enjoyed peace had not the pirates, breaking the treaty, ravaged the entire region in nocturnal raids. Therefore, having assembled a force, they expelled the treaty-breakers.

Æthelberht, having governed [Note: [Col. 1074D] “Governed.” e.; “ruled,” a. s. c. d. l.] the kingdom vigorously and gently, paid nature’s debt after five years of his reign, and was buried at Sherborne.

§ 118. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1074D] Eight hundred and sixty-seven. Malmesbury, by assigning Æthelred’s accession to the year 867, is one year later than the Saxon Chronicle, Asser, and Florence of Worcester. Thorne accepts the same chronological indication as Malmesbury. Yet, if the number of years assigned by Malmesbury to the reigns of Æthelred and his predecessor Æthelberht is corrected, it must be concluded that he ascended the throne about February 866 and died on 25 April 871.] eight hundred and sixty-seven, Æthelred, son of Æthelwulf, obtained [Col. 1075A] his paternal kingdom [Note: [Col. 1075C] *Paternal*: c. e. l.; *father’s*, a. s. d. m.] for the same number [Note: [Col. 1075C] *Of years*: s. d. e.; omitted in a. c. l.] of years as his brothers. By a miserable and utterly lamentable fate, all succumbed to an untimely death—except that, amid the clamour of so many evils, these royal sons preferred an honourable end to a bitter sovereignty. So courageously did they commit themselves to the struggle for their country that they should not be blamed if the boldness at which they aimed [176] succeeded less fully than they wished. Indeed, it has been handed down [Note: [Col. 1075C] *Handed down*: a. s. e. l.; *transmitted*, c. d.] to memory that this [Note: [Col. 1075C] *The king fought nine times*, etc. Æthelred fought with the Danes nine times before Easter, A.D. 871. (Saxon Chronicle and ASSER, *On the Deeds of King Alfred*.)] king fought nine times in one year against the enemy, with standards joined and hostile; though fortune varied, he was more often victorious. This was besides the sudden raids in which, skilled in the art of war, he repeatedly harassed the scattered ravagers. On the Danish side there were slain [Note: [Col. 1075C] *Nine earls.* Among the earls who fell on the Norman side was the elder Sidroc, who had committed so many and such great devastations in France under the reign of Charles the Bald. The others, whose names are entered [Col. 1075D] in the Saxon Chronicle, were the younger Sidroc, the earls Osbern, Frana, and Harald, and King Bagsecg. On the English side Æthelwulf, earl of Berkshire, and Heahmund, bishop of Sherborne, were killed.] nine earls, one king, and besides these, people beyond counting.

[Col. 1075B] § 119. Most memorable above the rest was the battle which he fought at [Note: [Col. 1075D] *Escendune*: Aston, in Berkshire.] Ashdown (A.D. 871). For the Danish army had assembled there and divided itself into parties: on one side were two [Note: [Col. 1075D] *Kings*: a. s. c. l.; absent in d. e. m. The kings’ names were Halfdan and Bagsecg—who is conjectured to be the same as Ivar—both of the numerous progeny of Ragnar Lothbrok.] kings, and on the other all the commanders; against them the king came with his brother Alfred. Thus they matched lot against lot, equal against equal: Æthelred was to stand against the kings, Alfred against the commanders. The spirits of both armies were raised, but the falling evening deferred the battle until the next day. Therefore, at the first sudden light of dawn, Alfred was ready; [Note: [Col. 1075D] *His brother occupied with divine service.* See Asser, *Life of Alfred*, A.D. 871.] his brother, occupied with divine service, remained in the tent. Though urged by a messenger that the heathen were rushing on with savage hearts, he refused to go forward anywhere until the office was ended. This faith of the king greatly assisted his brother in his advance, which, owing to the [Note: [Col. 1075D] *Prematurity*: a. s. c. e. l.; *unblemishedness*, d. m.] immaturity [Col. 1075C] of youth, was [Note: [Col. 1075D] *Also*: d. e. m.; *and now*, a. s. c. e. l.] too hasty as well. For already [Note: [Col. 1075D] *For already*: a. s. c. e. l.; *already, already*, d. m.] the English battle-lines were yielding and, pressed by their adversaries from higher ground, were contemplating flight, since the Christians were fighting in an unfavourable position. Then he, signed with the cross of God, flew unexpectedly to the scene, driving back the enemy and calling his countrymen to arms. By his valour and at the same time by God’s miracle, the terrified Danes entrusted their safety to their feet and [Col. 1076A] fled. [Note: [Col. 1075D] *King Osecg was killed there.* In the Saxon Chronicle and Asser this king is called Bagsecg and Bægsceg. [Col. 1076C] In Danish history, however, he is called Ivar. (TYRR., book V, p. 275).] King Osecg was killed there, together with five earls and an innumerable multitude.

§ 120. Meanwhile, let the reader remember that the kings of the Mercians and Northumbrians, taking advantage of the Danes’ arrival—while Æthelred was labouring under their wars—had escaped from subjection to the West Saxons and had almost reasserted their own dominion. Thus all the provinces blazed with savage [Note: [Col. 1076C] *Ravages*: d. e. l.; *of the populace*, s.; *ravaging*, a.; *devastations*, c.] ravages. Each king took care rather to endure enemies in his own territories than to offer help to countrymen in distress; and so, while they preferred avenging injury to preventing it, they reduced their country to weakness by their own indolence. The Danes grew without hindrance, while fear increased among the provincials, and every nearby victory, through the addition of captives, [Col. 1076B] became an instrument of the next. The districts of the East Angles, with cities and villages, were occupied by the raiders. Their king, the saintly Edmund, was killed by these same men; [Note: [Col. 1076C] *King … Edmund.* Edmund, king of the East Angles, was beheaded by Ingwar, son of Ragnar Lothbrok—or, according to some, son of Ivar and grandson of Ragnar—on 20 November 870. Compare the *Acts of the Saints* (vol. VII, pp. 465–472, Cologne edition, 1575), and Matthew of Westminster, *Flowers of History*, p. 314.] [178] [Note: [Col. 1076D] *Killed*: c. d. e. l. m.; *killed in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation eight hundred and seventy, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December*, a. s.] by the brief passage of temporal death he purchased an eternal kingdom. The Mercians, crushed more than once, relieved their miseries by submission. The Northumbrians, long tossed by civil dissensions, corrected their discord when the enemy approached. Thus they restored King Osberht, whom they had expelled, to the throne; made great preparations; and marched out to meet the enemy (A.D. 867). But, easily driven back, they shut themselves within the city of York. Soon, when this had been set ablaze by the victors and the spreading flame drew out its loose tresses as it consumed the whole walls, they too were burned and covered their native land with their bones. [Note: [Col. 1076D] *King Osberht*, etc. In the spring of 867 the Normans set sail to attack King Ælla, who had usurped the throne of Deira after expelling Osberht. The two rival joint kings united their resources against the common enemy; but, when battle was joined at York, the Northumbrians were utterly defeated and Osberht and Ælla were killed. Thereafter Northumbria ceased to be a Saxon kingdom.] Thus Northumbria, acquired by right of war, long afterwards groaned under barbarian dominion, [Col. 1076C] mindful of freedom. But King Æthelred, broken by many toils, died and was buried at Wimborne.

§ 121. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1076D] Eight hundred, etc. Æthelred received a mortal wound in one of the battles fought against the Danes before Easter, 15 April, and died shortly afterward, on 24 April 871. Alfred then succeeded to the throne, upon which he sat for thirty years and six months. From the twenty-eight and a half years assigned to Alfred’s reign by Malmesbury and the Saxon chronicles, even if reckoned from 24 April 872, the year [Col. 1077A] 901 is not completed; yet Malmesbury rightly assigns Alfred’s death and the accession of Edward the Elder to that year.] eight hundred and seventy-two, Alfred, [Col. 1077A] the younger son of Æthelwulf—who, as we have said, had formerly received at Rome the first royal anointing and crown from Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 1077C] *First*: d. e. m.; omitted in a. s. c. l.] the [Note: [Col. 1077C] *The Fourth*: d. e. m.; omitted in a. s. c. l.] Fourth [Note: [Col. 1077C] *Had formerly received at Rome*: A.D. 853. See above, §109, note 73.]—received the kingdom and held it, most laboriously but most courageously, for twenty-eight [Note: [Col. 1077D] *Eight*: s. c. d. e. l.; *nine*, a.] and a half years.

It was not my purpose to unwind one by one the inextricable labyrinths of his labours, because a year-by-year enumeration of his deeds would create a certain confusion for readers. For the hostile [Note: [Col. 1077D] *Hostile army*: Danish or Norman. Whoever wishes to learn its movements should consult the Saxon chronicles.] army, driven by him or his deputies from one part of the country, withdrew into another; driven thence again, it sought other places, filling all with plundering and slaughter. To follow it in writing too, and, so to speak, to travel round the island with it, might perhaps be called the height of madness. I shall therefore set everything forth in summary.

For nine continuous years he fought against the enemy, now deceived by unreliable treaties, now taking vengeance upon those who deceived him; and he was at last reduced to such need that, with scarcely three districts [Col. 1077B] remaining steadfast in allegiance—namely Hampshire, Wiltshire, and Somerset—he took refuge even in a certain island scarcely accessible because of its marshy wetness, called [Note: [Col. 1077D] *Adelingia*: a. e. l.; *Adelingeham*, c.; *Etherelingia*, d. m.—Athelney, in Somersetshire.] Athelney. [Note: [Col. 1077D] *He took refuge.* Alfred was forced to retreat and take refuge in Selwood Forest in A.D. 878. In that year, after Easter, he constructed a fortress at Athelney. To this period seems assignable the story or legend of the herdsman’s wife, related in the annals attributed to Asser—and inserted in certain manuscripts of his *Life of Alfred*—but this tale probably belongs to an anonymous writer of a Life of St Neot. Just as the adversities then endured by the king are said to have been foretold to Alfred by St Neot, his friend and, as is reported, kinsman, as a chastisement, so his deliverance too is attributed to the intervention of that saint, who afterwards manifested himself to the king and sought to raise his spirits. This account and the story of St Cuthbert alike seem mere inventions. The legend of St Cuthbert is found in a fragment concerning the church of Durham, printed in the *Acts of the Saints* (19 March). See also the *Life of St Cuthbert* (MS Cotton Nero A. II).]

In happier times, he would afterwards relate his misfortunes to his intimates with cheerful and pleasant affability, and tell how he had escaped them through the merit of blessed Cuthbert. Such, for the most part, is the way of mortals: the memory of things which they once dreaded having undergone gives them pleasure. For one day, while he was shut up alone at home on the island and his companions were dispersed along the riverbank fishing, he committed his care-worn body to sleep. And behold, Cuthbert, [Col. 1077C] formerly bishop of Lindisfarne, addressed him in sleep as follows:

> “I am Cuthbert, if you have heard of me. The Lord has sent me to announce prosperity to you. For although England has long paid in terrible measure the penalties of its sins, at last now [Note: [Col. 1078D] *At last*: c. d. e. l.; *at last God*, a. s.] he looks upon it with the eyes of his mercy, through the merits of its native saints. You also, though so miserably banished from your kingdom, shall shortly be restored gloriously to the throne. And [Col. 1078A] [Note: [Col. 1078D] *And*: e. d. m.; *so greatly*, a. s. c. l.] I shall give you a remarkable sign of this: today your fishermen will come, carrying in baskets a great quantity of large fish. This will be all the more wonderful because, in these days, with the water frozen, the hardened river promises no such hope; moreover, today the air, dripping with icy dew, defeats every art of fishing. But when you have gained a more favourable fortune, you will act royally if you earn, with fitting devotion, the aid of God and of me, his messenger.”

As he spoke thus, the saint stripped the sleeping king of his anxieties; and he strengthened with the joy of the same message the king’s mother also, who lay near him, inviting thin sleep to her hard bed in order to alleviate her cares. [Note: [Col. 1078D] *Sleeping*: a. s. c. d. k. l. m.; omitted in e.] When both awoke, they repeatedly affirmed, in a recurring exchange of words, that they had dreamed one and the same dream. Then the fishermen [181] [Col. 1078B] came in and produced so great an abundance of fish that it appeared capable of satisfying the gluttony of any great army. [Note: [Col. 1078D] *Satisfying*: e.; *fully satisfying*, a. s. c. d. l.]

Not long afterwards, daring to leave his prison, he risked an act of great cunning. [Note: [Col. 1078D] *For he entered the tents of the king of the Danes*, etc. This is not found in Asser’s *Life of Alfred*. Something very similar is related of Olaf, a Danish prince, entering Æthelstan’s camp in the guise of a minstrel, in §131.] For, entering the tents of the Danish king in the guise of a mime, he shared his secret with only one most faithful man. There, admitted even to the more private parts of the hall as a practitioner of the minstrel’s art, there was no secret which he did not gather with eyes and ears alike. Having remained there several days, and having satisfied his mind from all that he had wished to know, he returned to Athelney. He assembled his followers and explained the enemy’s ease and how light a matter it was to conquer them. All were aroused to daring; [Note: [Col. 1078D] *To daring*: a. d. l. m.; *to hearing*, s. c. e.] and he himself, gathering assistance from every quarter and sending scouts ahead, was informed of the barbarians’ position. Then, attacking them suddenly, [Col. 1078C] he cut them down with incredible slaughter. [Note: [Col. 1078D] *He cut them down with incredible slaughter.* At the place called Ethandun, A.D. 878. (ASSER, *On the Deeds of Alfred*.)] The survivors, with their king, gave hostages that they would accept Christianity and depart from England [Note: [Col. 1078D] *England*, that is, Wessex.]; and this was done. For their king Guthrum, whom our people call Gurmund, was baptized with thirty nobles and almost all his people, and was received as a son by King Alfred. [Note: [Col. 1078D] *Their king Guthrum.* Guthrum was baptized at Aller, near Athelney, in A.D. 878; his baptismal name was Æthelstan.]

The provinces of the East Angles and [182] Northumbrians were granted to him [Col. 1079A] that he might hold by hereditary right, under loyalty to the king, the lands which he had invaded by robbery. [Note: [Col. 1078D] *The provinces were granted to him*, etc. This seems erroneous as regards Northumbria. The Saxon Chronicle has *Notherna*, and Florence of Worcester *the Norman king*, [Col. 1079C] which could at first glance easily be changed into *Northumbria* (SHARPE, 132). See above, §97, note.] But because the Ethiopian does not change his skin, he trampled the lands granted to him with tyrannical arrogance for eleven years, and in the twelfth ended his life, [Note: [Col. 1079C] *In the twelfth he ended his life.* Guthrum died in A.D. 891. “He died, therefore, in the fourteenth year after receiving baptism, and was entombed in the royal vill called Headleaga, among the East Angles.” (*Annals* wrongly attributed to Asser.)] transmitting the inheritance of perfidy also to his descendants. At length, subdued by the grandson of this Alfred, Æthelstan, they consented—though unwillingly—that one king should rule England, as the present day has found it. [Note: [Col. 1079C] *By his grandson*, etc. The Danes were expelled from East Anglia, and their kingdom annexed to Wessex, under Edward the Elder, A.D. 918. Here Malmesbury seems to refer to the time of the death of Sihtric, king of the Northumbrians, A.D. 926, when Æthelstan, having expelled Guthfrith in 927, obtained the kingdom of Northumbria. [Col. 1079D]]

The other Danes who had refused to become Christians crossed the sea with Hasting [A.D. 853], [Note: [Col. 1079D] *They crossed the sea with Hasting.* It is uncertain whether the leader who at that time led the Danes against Alfred was the same Hasting who, during the reign of Charles the Bald, had ravaged France and southern Europe. Some regarded him as the son of the earlier Hasting. The earlier Hasting, it is reported, had converted to Christianity and, as a client of Charles the Simple, joined the royal army when the Normans under Rollo invaded France in 898. Since Hasting was thoroughly defeated by Alfred in 896 and expelled from England, perhaps they should be regarded as one and the same Hasting.] where the inhabitants know what evils they wrought. For, ranging over the entire seacoast as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea, they emptied of inhabitants Paris, Tours, and many other cities situated either on the Seine or the Loire, the noble rivers of Gaul. Then the bodies of many saints were removed from their ancient resting-places and carried to safer locations; their ashes have ennobled foreign churches [Col. 1079B] down to this time.

Then, too, the body of blessed Martin, which Sidonius says is

> Venerable throughout all lands,  
> In which honour lives after life’s span,

was carried by his clergy to Auxerre and placed in the church of blessed Germanus. It stirred the people of the surrounding regions by unheard-of signs. [Note: [Col. 1080C] *The body of blessed Martin.* St Martin, bishop of Tours, died between A.D. 395 and 400. Northern invaders under Hasting entered the Loire in November 853, sailed to Tours, and destroyed the city with the church of St Martin. St Martin’s body was first transferred to Cormery, then to Auxerre. It is reported that, at this time, the sight of the relics of St Martin, patron of the city, stirred the spirits of the citizens in a remarkable fashion. (*Annals of St Bertin*; treatise of ODON, abbot of Cluny; BOUQUET, VII, 69, 371; VIII, 300.)] [Note: [Col. 1080C] *Sidonius.* Gaius Sollius Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of Clermont in Auvergne, was one of the more illustrious prelates of the fifth century. He died on 23 August A.D. 482. His works were already printed in 1473. (His works, ed. Sismondi, Paris, 1652.)]

As many approached to bring gifts in hope of remedies—gifts which, as usually happens, might lighten the burdens of porters—a dispute arose over the division of the money. The people of Tours claimed all of it, because their lord had invited the offerers by miracles; the natives replied that [Note: [Col. 1080C] *Germanus.* Germanus, bishop of Auxerre in the fifth century. See §22, note.] Germanus was not inferior in merit and was equal in office. They said that the power belonged indeed to both, but that the prerogative of the church outweighed the other claim. To untie this knot of doubt, [Col. 1080A] a leper—barely breathing, wasted in every other respect, and already half-dead within a living corpse—was sought out and placed between the bodies of the two saints. All human guardianship was excluded throughout the night; Martin’s glory alone kept watch. For on the following day the man’s skin appeared splendid on Martin’s side, [Note: [Col. 1080C] *On his side, splendid*: a. s. c. d. k. l. m; [Col. 1080D] omitted in e.] but on Germanus’s side it was wan with its usual hideousness. [Note: [Col. 1080D] *But*: a. s. c. d. k. l. m; omitted in e.] Lest they attribute the outcome to chance, they turned the diseased side toward Martin. Then, when the first [Note: [Col. 1080D] *First*: e.; *first [feminine]*, a. s. c. d. l.] dawn crept into daylight, the hurrying attendants found the man wholly sound in his skin, wholly [Note: [Col. 1080D] *Wholly*: c. e. l.; *whole [masculine]*, a. s. d. m.] healthy. He proclaimed the generosity of the local bishop, who had yielded in honour to his most welcome guest.

Thus the people of Tours, from that time onward, safely filled their familiar purse through their patron’s intercession, until a gentler breath of peace brought them back to their own [Col. 1080B] homes. For the marauders, who had troubled Gaul for thirteen years, were finally defeated in many battles by Emperor Arnulf and the Bretons, and hurried to England, as though to a suitable refuge for tyranny. [Note: [Col. 1080D] *By Emperor Arnulf*, etc. The Normans, twice defeated in Brittany, routed the army of Emperor Arnulf near Liège on 26 June A.D. 891; but shortly afterwards they themselves were overthrown by the emperor with great slaughter. (BOUQUET, VIII).]

During this interval Alfred had subjected the whole island to his will, except for what the Danes held. [Note: [Col. 1080D] *He had subjected it to his will.* Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 886.] The English willingly yielded to his authority, rejoicing that they had produced such a man, able to raise them into freedom. He entrusted London, the capital of the Mercian kingdom, together with his daughter Æthelflæd, to the allegiance of a certain leading man, Æthelred. [Note: [Col. 1080D] *London*, etc. Alfred restored the city of London, which the Danes had devastated and ruined in A.D. 886, and entrusted its defence to Æthered or Æthelred, his son-in-law, earl of the Mercians. (ASSER, *On the Deeds of Alfred*.) Æthered died in A.D. 912.] [Note: [Col. 1080D] *Æthelflæd*: a. s. c. d. l.; *Æthelfred*, e.] He acted with great courage and loyalty, diligently safeguarding what had been entrusted to him. He kept the East Angles and Northumbrians—who had long been preparing to desert the king—in submission, compelling them to provide hostages. The following occasion proved how much this achieved.

For when England had enjoyed [Col. 1080C] for fourteen [Note: [Col. 1080D] *Fourteen*: d. e. m; *thirteen*, a. s. c. l.] years the serenity of peace and the fertility of the soil, the northern plague [185] of barbarians returned. [Note: [Col. 1080D] *That northern plague of barbarians returned.* The Danes again landed in England in A.D. 893.] [Col. 1081A] Again there were wars, again slaughter, and again conspiracies of the Northumbrians and East Angles; but neither the foreigners nor the natives met the same fate as in earlier years. The former, diminished by battles overseas, were slower to invade; the latter, encouraged by the experience of war and the king’s exhortations, were readier [Note: [Col. 1081C] *Were*: a. s. c. d. l. m; omitted in e.] not only to resist but also to [Note: [Col. 1081C] *To*: a. s. c. l; omitted in d. e. m.] provoke. The king himself was energetically present in every emergency, terrifying strangers and strengthening his own men by the well-known appearance of his valour. Alone he charged the enemy’s breast; alone he restored a wavering battle-line. The inhabitants point out individual places in which he experienced either an abundance of ill fortune or a scarcity of good. For even when defeated, even when cast down, Alfred had to be fought; so completely did he, when you thought him utterly [Col. 1081B] crushed, “like a slippery serpent escape from the hand that held him,” suddenly emerging from his hiding places and attacking enemies who had assailed him of their own accord. Most often after flight he was unbearable, more cautious in remembrance of repulse, and bolder in the heat of vengeance.

By Ælhswith, daughter of Earl Æthelred, he had children: [Note: [Col. 1081C] *Ægelswith.* Alfred married Ælhswith, daughter of Earl Æthelred and Eadburh, of the Mercian royal house, in A.D. 868; she died in A.D. 903.] Æthelswith and Edward, who reigned after him; Æthelflæd, who married Æthelred, earl of the Mercians; [Note: [Col. 1081C] *Æthelswith.* That is, Æthelflæd. Asser names no daughter of Alfred called Æthelswith. Æthelflæd married Æthered, earl of the Mercians.] Æthelweard, who is said to have been most learned; [Note: [Col. 1081C] *Æthelweard, who is said to have been most learned.* Æthelweard, the youngest of all, was committed, by divine counsel and the king’s admirable foresight, together with nearly all the noble children of the entire kingdom and also many of humble birth, to the diligent care of teachers and to the pursuits of literary learning. In that school books in both languages, Latin and Saxon, were continually read. They also devoted themselves to writing, so that, [Col. 1081D] before they had strength suited to the pursuits of men—hunting, that is, and the other arts fitting for nobles—they appeared diligent and intelligent in the liberal arts.” (ASSER, *On the Deeds of Alfred*.)] [186] Ælfthryth and Ælfgifu, maidens. [Note: [Col. 1081D] *Alfreda.* Ælfthryth married Baldwin the Bald, count of Flanders, though the year of this marriage is not indicated. He died on 2 January 918, leaving by her two adult sons.] [Note: [Col. 1081D] *Ælfgifu.* Ælfgifu, or Æthelgeofu, professed the monastic life and became abbess of Shaftesbury.]

He was of infirm health, [Note: [Col. 1081D] *Was*: a. s. c. d; omitted in e. l.] being a man who was always [Note: [Col. 1081D] *Who always … was afflicted*: a. s. c. d; *which always … were afflicted*, e.] afflicted either by a fig-growth or by some disease of the internal organs. But they say that he obtained this from God by prayer, so that, warned by his afflictions, [Note: [Col. 1081D] *By the warning*: a. s. c. d. l; *warned [feminine]*, e.] he might embrace worldly enticements less eagerly. [Note: [Col. 1081D] *Might embrace*: a. s. c. d. l; *might embrace [plural]*, e.]

[Col. 1081C] § 122. Yet amid these matters, the king’s inner life is remarkable and deserves conspicuous praise. For although, as someone has said, “laws are silent amid arms,” [Note: [Col. 1081D] “Laws are silent amid arms.” Cicero, *Pro Milone*, IV.] he enacted laws amid the clash [Note: [Col. 1081D] “Amid the clash.” d. e., “amid the blaring of trumpets, amid the clash,” a. s. c. l.] of arms, by which his people might be trained both in divine worship and military discipline. And because, taking advantage of the barbarians, even the native population had begun to thirst for plunder, so that no journey was safe without an armed escort, he established the hundreds called *hundrez* and the tithings called *thethingas*, so that every Englishman living lawfully should belong to both a hundred and a tithing. If anyone were accused of some offense, he was immediately to produce from his hundred and tithing persons to stand surety for him; but one who could find no such pledge was to dread the severity of the laws. If an accused person fled, either before or after being placed under surety, all those of his hundred and tithing incurred [Col. 1082B] the king’s fine. By this contrivance he brought peace to the realm; indeed, along the public highways, where paths branch into a crossroads, he ordered golden bracelets to be hung, which might mock the greed of travellers, since there was no one to snatch them away.

Devoted to almsgiving, he confirmed the privileges of the churches, as his father had ordained; and he sent many gifts overseas, to Rome and [Note: [Col. 1082C] To St Thomas in India. The Apostle Thomas is traditionally said to have preached the Gospel among the Indians. On the Christians of St Thomas, see Lacroze, *Histoire du Christianisme dans les Indes*, 2 vols., 12mo, The Hague, 1758. By order of Saint Augustine their history was written and translated into French. (*Histoire orientale des grands progrès de l'Eglise Catholique en la réduction des anciens chrétiens dits de Saint-Thomas*, Brussels, 1609).] to Saint Thomas in India. [Note: [Col. 1082C] The envoy, etc. This mission is assigned to the year 883. The Saxon chronicles call those who then carried the king’s alms to Rome and India Sighelm and Aethelstan, without title. Malmesbury, however, and Florence of Worcester regard Sighelm as the earl who was slain by the Danes in 915; wrongly, they think that he was none other than Sighilm, bishop of Sherborne, whom some suppose to have lived about this period. In the work entitled *Gesta Pontificum*, this bishop is called Sighelmus and is said to have succeeded Asser (in 883); and Florence—who entirely omits him from his catalogue of the bishops of that see—speaking of the mission to Rome and to St Thomas in India in 883, says: “When Asser, bishop of Sherborne, died, Suithelmus succeeded him; he carried King Alfred’s alms to Saint Thomas in India and returned safely thence.” If Suithelmus of Sherborne ever existed as a bishop, he certainly could not have succeeded Asser after the latter’s death (A.D. 909).] Sigelinus, bishop of Sherborne, was sent as envoy on this mission; with great success—something at which anyone in this age might marvel—he penetrated to India. Returning thence, he brought back the exotic brilliance of gems and the juices of spices, with which that land is fertile. Moreover, he brought a gift more precious than all refined gold: a portion of the Lord’s [Col. 1082C] Cross, sent to the king by Pope [Note: [Col. 1082D] Marinus. e: Martinus. d: Marinus, or Martin II, became pope in December 882 and died in 884.] Marinus.

Where he saw it appropriate, he founded monasteries: [Note: [Col. 1082D] One at Athelney. A Benedictine monastery at Athelney in Somersetshire was founded by Alfred in 888 and dedicated to the Saviour, St Peter, and St Paul. Its foundation charter, in Reyner, *Apostolatus Benedictinorum in Anglia*, II, pp. 132–133, is incorrectly dated to 852. This author supposes that the monastery’s foundation occurred before Alfred’s grandfather.] one [Col. 1083A] at Athelney, where, as the preceding account recalls, he had concealed himself; there he appointed as abbot [Note: [Col. 1083B] John. It is uncertain which John is meant here. Asser indicates that he was descended from the stock of the ancient Saxons—that is, of German origin—and Malmesbury applies to John Scotus what Asser relates of his death; [Col. 1083C] but he by no means appears to suggest that they were one and the same man. Mabillon conjectures that John, abbot of Athelney, came from France, probably from the monastery of Corbie, with Grimbald at Alfred’s invitation in 883 (Mabillon, Book XXVIII, *Annales Benedictini*, no. 68). On the other hand, if trust may be placed in the chronicles printed in the work entitled *Scriptores Franciae* (from the Thuan Library), III, p. 359, it may be conjectured that John Scotus, summoned by Alfred from France, where he lived at the court of Charles the Bald, returned in 872. See also the letter of Anastasius the Librarian to Charles the Bald, printed in Ussher, *Sylloge Epistolarum Veterum Hibernicarum*, ep. 24, p. 45.] John, a native of Old Saxony. [Note: [Col. 1083C] “Another at Winchester . . . had come to England.” s. c. d. e. l. But a: “He appointed as abbot the most holy monk Grimbald, his intimate friend, [caniorem, uncertain], and guest-master of the church of Saint Bertin, who had come to England at his summons and by the sending of Fulk, archbishop of Rheims.”] Another was at Winchester, called the New Minster, where he appointed [Note: [Col. 1083C] Grimbald. Grimbald was a monk in the [Col. 1083D] monastery of Sithiu, St Bertin’s, whence he had come to England at Alfred’s invitation. He died on 8 July, A.D. 903.] Grimbald [Note: [Col. 1083D] As abbot. s. c. d. e., “as patron of the church,” l.] abbot. Grimbald had come to England at Alfred’s summons and at the instigation of the [Note: [Col. 1083D] Archbishop of Rheims. See Fulk, archbishop of Rheims’s, letter to Alfred, written on the occasion of Grimbald’s coming to England (*ASSERUS, Annales rerum gestarum Aelfredi*, ed. Fr. Wise, p. 123, 8vo, Oxford, 1722). The archbishop was killed by Baldwin II, surnamed the Bald, on 17 June, A.D. 900.] archbishop of Rheims, because he had once, as is reported, received and cherished Alfred, while still a boy travelling to Rome, with kindly hospitality. [Note: [Col. 1083D] “Had cherished.” s. c. d. e. l.; “had comforted,” a. There follows: “In the famous city of Winchester, so dear to him, he meanwhile established a small monastery and placed him there, so that by visiting and residing there more frequently he might be nourished by Grimbald’s honeyed exhortation, until he should raise him to the higher dignity which he ardently desired.” Tanner maintains that Alfred first founded here a house and chapel for Grimbald, whom he had summoned from Flanders; but that later, in his will, he provided for the construction of a notable house on the [Col. 1084B] north side of the cathedral church of the Old Minster.] The reason for summoning him was [189] that, by his efforts, he might revive the study of letters, which in England had fallen asleep and was almost dead.

[Note: [Col. 1084B] The monastery at Shaftesbury also. A Benedictine convent at Shaftesbury was founded about the year 888. Camden further observes from a manuscript copy of William of Malmesbury then kept in Lord Burleigh’s library that Alfred rebuilt the whole town of Shaftesbury from the ground up.] He also completed the monastery at Shaftesbury for nuns, and there appointed his daughter Ælfgifu abbess. He had [Note: [Col. 1084C] From St David’s, etc. This was Asser, Alfred’s friend and biographer. Taken from the church of St David’s, he was made bishop of Sherborne, apparently about 884, and died in 909. We owe to Asser almost everything authentic transmitted to us concerning Alfred’s private life down to the year 894; yet much reported by Malmesbury concerning this king is absent from Asser.] a certain Asser from St David’s, endowed with no mean learning, whom he made bishop at Sherborne.

[Col. 1083B] [Note: [Col. 1084C] “This man explained,” etc. The assistance which Alfred is here said to have received from Asser has been strangely transferred by the author of a certain *Lecture on the State of Learning under Anglo-Saxon Rule* to Sighelm, whom, with no regard for chronology, he calls Alfred’s particular friend. This would not be worth mentioning, were Malmesbury not cited as an authority.] This man explained in plainer words the meaning of Boethius’s books *On the Consolation [of Philosophy]*, which the king himself translated into English. Moreover, because no one in his kingdom was skilled in letters, he summoned from Mercia [Note: [Col. 1084C] Werefrith, or Wilfrith, bishop of the Hwicce, bishop of Worcester, of whom Asser writes: “well instructed, that is, in Holy Scripture.” He held office from 7 June A.D. 873 until his death in 915.] Werefrith, bishop of the Hwicce, who by the king’s command translated [Note: [Col. 1084D] The books of the *Dialogues*. a. c. d. e. l; “the books of Gregory’s *Dialogues*,” s. (Paris, 4 vols., folio, 1705). Speaking of the author of the Saxon translation, Asser says: “At times rendering sense for sense, he translated it with the utmost care and elegance.” The *Dialogues* had already been printed in 1458.] the books of the *Dialogues* into the English tongue.

At this time there is believed to have been [Col. 1084A] John Scotus, [190] a man of penetrating intellect and great eloquence, who long before, when the din of war resounded everywhere, had gone to France to Charles the Bald. At Charles’s request he translated word for word into Latin from Greek the *Hierarchy* [Note: [Col. 1084D] Of Dionysius the Areopagite. John Scotus departs from the opinion of Hincmar, Anastasius, and other biographers of St Dionysius the Areopagite who sought to make the first bishop of Paris one and the same person as the Athenian martyr.] of Dionysius the Areopagite. He also composed a book which he entitled *Περὶ φύσεων μερισμοῦ*—that is, *On the Division of Nature*—very useful for resolving the perplexity of necessary questions, provided that he is forgiven in some respects in which he departed from the Latin path while gazing intently toward the Greeks.

In later years, attracted by Alfred’s generosity, he came to England; and at our monastery, it is said, he was pierced with writing-styles by the boys whom he taught, and was even considered a martyr. Yet I would not assert this without hesitation, to the injury of his holy [Col. 1084B] soul, since his celebrated memory is attested by a tomb on the left side of the altar and by verses of an epitaph—rough indeed, lacking the polish of the modern age, yet not so misshapen for their antiquity:

> The holy philosopher John lies shut within this tomb,  
> Who, while living, had already been enriched with wondrous teaching;  
> At last, by martyrdom, he ascended Christ’s kingdom,  
> Where all the saints, according to their merit, reign through every age.

§ 123. Supported by these associates, [Note: [Col. 1085C] “Associates,” s. e. l.; “those at his side,” e. d. k. m.] the king devoted himself with all his heart to the liberal arts, so that no Englishman was keener in understanding or more elegant in translating. This was all the more [191] remarkable because [Note: [Col. 1085C] At the age of twelve he was wholly without learning—that is, until the year 887. (ASSER, *De gestis Aelfredi*).] at twelve years old he was wholly without learning. [Note: [Col. 1085C] “But then, invited by his kind mother’s game.” Compare Asser under the year 866.] But when his kind mother offered as a reward the little book which she held in her hands, if he should learn it quickly, he entered upon letters in play and drank them in with thirsty eagerness.

Finally, he gave to English ears the greater part of the Roman library, bringing in for the use of his subjects a rich spoil of foreign wares. His principal books were [Note: [Col. 1085C] Orosius: Paulus Orosius, a presbyter of Tarragona in Spain and friend of St Augustine of Hippo, flourished A.D. 417. His Anglo-Saxon translation of universal history was published by Daines Barrington with an English translation (London, 1773).] Orosius; Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*; Bede’s *Deeds of the English*; [Col. 1085B] Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*; and a work of his own, which in the native language he called [Note: [Col. 1085C] “Encheridion,” a. d. e. l. m.; “Handboc,” that is, [Col. 1085D] “Manual,” s. c. k. See what Asser reports about this book, and Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum* (GALE, III, p. 342).] the *Enchiridion*, that is, the handbook. Indeed, he instilled a great love of learning into the people of the provinces, urging some by rewards and others by injuries, and allowing no unlettered person to aspire to any rank at court. He began translating the Psalter, but had scarcely completed its first portion when he ended his life.

In the [Note: [Col. 1085D] Prologue to the *Pastoral Rule*. Printed in Wise’s edition of Asser, p. 81, Oxford, 1722.] prologue to the *Pastoral Rule*, he says that he was moved to translate books into English because the churches, which from ancient times had contained numerous libraries, had been burnt with their books by the Danes. Consequently, the study of letters had been extinguished throughout the whole island, since each man feared danger to his life more than he pursued the exercise of books. Therefore he was providing for his English people in this matter [Col. 1085C] so that they might now taste in a preliminary and imperfect way what later, should peace perhaps return, [192] they might learn in the Latin tongue. He wished this book, written at his command, to be sent to all the principal sees, together with a golden writing-tablet [Col. 1086A] containing a *manca* of gold. He said that in this and his other translations he had stated nothing from himself, but had drawn everything from distinguished men: Archbishop Plegmund, Bishop Asser, [Note: [Col. 1085D] “Bishop,” s. e. l.; “archbishop,” d. m. Asser had been bishop of St David’s.] and the priests Grimbald and John.

Finally, to describe his entire life briefly: he divided the twenty-four hours which continually revolve between day and night in such a way that he spent eight hours in writing, reading, and prayer; eight in care of his body; and eight in the dispatch of royal business. In his chapel there was a candle marked in twenty-four divisions, and a sacristan was charged with ensuring, by the candle’s burning, that the king was reminded of each of his duties. [Note: [Col. 1085D] “Half the portion,” etc. Asser affirms that he vowed half his revenues to God; thereafter he divided that half again among the poor, two monasteries founded by himself, the school he had established, and other monasteries and churches, whether domestic or foreign (ASSER, *De rebus gestis Aelfredi*).] He assigned half the portion of all revenues, provided they had been justly acquired, to his monasteries; all his remaining revenues he divided into two equal [Col. 1086B] parts. He then divided the first part again into three: the first for the ministers of his court; the second for workmen, whom he continually employed in the construction of new buildings, according to a method wonderful and unknown to the English; and the third for strangers. The second half of the revenues was divided so that the first share was given to the poor of his own country, the second to monasteries, the third to scholars, and the fourth to churches overseas.

[Note: [Col. 1085D] “An investigator of judgments,” etc. In the *Mirror of Justice*, ch. 2, it is asserted that in a single year Alfred condemned no fewer than forty-four inferior judges to hanging because, whether condemning or acquitting, they had wrongly issued judgments without the verdict of jurors [Col. 1086C].] He investigated judgments rendered by his own men and was a most severe corrector of those wrongly rendered. This was strange and unheard of: he always carried in his breast a little book containing the Psalms of the daily office, so that whenever he had leisure he might take it up and run through it with wakeful eye. Thus he lived in great favour with his neighbours; and he gave his daughter Ethelswitha in marriage to Baldwin, count of Flanders, [Note: [Col. 1086C] Ethelswitha. See above, § 122, note, where Alfred’s daughter, married to Baldwin II, count of Flanders, is called Elfreda or Aelfthrytha. In French history she is called Elstruda. Baldwin was called “the Bald” in memory of his maternal grandfather. By this marriage he left two sons, Arnulf and Adulf or Adalolf; from the former—Arnulf the Great, count of Flanders, A.D. 918—was descended Matilda, wife of William I. Adulf died without offspring in A.D. 933.] by whom he begot Arnulf and Adulf. The latter received from his father the county of Boulogne; from the former descend the present counts [Col. 1086C] of [Note: [Col. 1086C] Flanders. s. c. d. e. f. l. After “Flanders,” a. h.: “Commendation and death of King Alfred.—Famous, warlike, victorious; a diligent guardian of widows, wards, orphans, and poor persons; most skilled among Saxon poets; most dear to his people; gracious to all; most generous; endowed with prudence, courage, temperance, and justice; most patient in the illness from which he constantly suffered; most discerning in investigating and carrying out judgments; most watchful and devout in God’s service: Alfred, king of the Anglo-Saxons, son of the most pious King Æthelwulf, after completing twenty-nine years and six months of his reign, died in the fourth indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, a Wednesday; he was buried at Winchester in the New Minster, and awaits with the just the robe of immortality and the glory of resurrection.” These words occur verbatim in Florence of Worcester’s Chronicle under the year 901.] Flanders.

§ 124. Alfred, [Note: [Col. 1086D] “Having fulfilled nature’s office.” Alfred died on 26 October, A.D. 901.] having fulfilled nature’s office, was buried [Col. 1087A] at Winchester in his monastery. [Note: [Col. 1087C] “To equip its workshops,” s. c. d. e. l.; “to equip the workshops of the aforesaid New Minster,” a.] To equip its workshops, [Note: [Col. 1087C] “His son Edward,” a. s. d. m.; omitted in c. e. l.] his son Edward bought from the bishop and canons of that time a sufficient space of land, paying publicly by weight one *manca* of gold for every foot. Truly astonishing was the king’s restraint: he allowed himself to be drained of so much money, unwilling, of course, to offer God a sacrifice taken from the plunder of the poor. The two churches stood so near, their walls adjoining, that the voices of the singers [Note: [Col. 1087D] “Of the singers,” c. d. e. l. m.; “of those singing,” a. s.] drowned one another out. Hence, both for this reason and for others, unhappy envy unearthed many grounds upon which they might inflict not insignificant injuries upon one another. Accordingly, that monastery was recently moved outside the city; it is more healthily inhabited and more freely distinguished.

They say that Alfred was first buried in the bishopric, since his monastery was unfinished; [Note: [Col. 1087D] “Since his monastery was unfinished,” s. c. d. e. l. m.; omitted in a.] then, because of the madness of the canons, who claimed that the royal ghost wandered through houses at night after the corpse had resumed life, his successor son [Note: [Col. 1087D] “Successor,” c. d. e. l. m.; “his successor Edward,” a. s.] removed his father’s remains and placed them in a peaceful resting-place in [Note: [Col. 1087D] The New Minster, later Hyde Abbey. (SHARPE, 140).] the New Minster. Such foolish tales—as also the others, by which they believe that the corpse of a wicked man runs about after death through demonic agency—the English hold with a credulity nearly innate, borrowing it, no doubt, from the pagans. [Note: [Col. 1087D] “The English . . . credulity.” A common belief held that a demon could reanimate corpses and use them to perform various delusions, and that the only remedy was to dig up the body and consume it with fire. See William of Newburgh, V.22 (SHARPE, 140).] As Virgil says: [Note: [Col. 1087D] As Virgil says. *Aeneid*, X.641.]

> “When death is past, such shapes, they say, flit about.”

§ 125. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 901, Edward, son of Alfred, assumed the kingdom and held it for [Note: [Col. 1087D] Twenty-three years. Edward the Elder was not crowned before Pentecost (15 May A.D. 902). Therefore, if the beginning of his reign is to be assigned to that day, he was still in the twenty-third year of his reign when he died; but he had completed twenty-three years on 26 October A.D. 924, if reckoned from his father’s death.] twenty-three years. In learning [195] he was far inferior to his father, [Col. 1087C] but in the power of his kingdom incomparably more glorious. For Alfred had united the two kingdoms of the Mercians and West Saxons, holding the Mercian kingdom only in name, since it had been entrusted to Duke Æthelred. Edward first, [Note: [Col. 1088C] After Æthelred’s death. Æthelred, earl of Mercia, died A.D. 912.] after Æthelred died, entirely subjected the Mercians; then [Note: [Col. 1088D] “Western.” He seems to mean Essex, or the land of the East Saxons.] the West and East Angles, the Northumbrians, who had by then merged into one people with the Danes, the Scots who inhabit the northern part of the island, and all the Britons whom we call Welsh—having defeated them in war, he brought them beneath his authority. Nor did he ever have the worse hand in any [Col. 1088A] battle.

He devised a means of checking Danish raids: he filled numerous suitably situated towns—either restored old ones or newly planned ones—with military forces to protect their inhabitants and drive back enemies. Nor was this without effect. The martial prowess of the people had become so hardened that if they heard enemies were approaching, they rushed into battle even without consulting king or commanders; and they always surpassed their enemies both in numbers and in skill [Note: [Col. 1088D] “In fighting,” a. d. e. l. m.; “of fighting,” s. c.] at warfare. Thus the enemies were objects of contempt to the soldiers and of laughter to the king. Finally, the newcomers, who had arrived under the leadership of a certain [Note: [Col. 1088D] Æthelwold, the son of the king’s paternal uncle. Æthelwold, son of Æthelberht, Alfred’s elder brother, was killed in A.D. 905.] Æthelwold, son of the king’s paternal uncle, were all killed to a man with him; the older settlers were either slain or preserved under the name of Englishmen.

Æthelwold, indeed, in the first days of this king had undertaken many schemes, disdaining Edward’s lordship and asserting that he was inferior neither in birth nor in courage. But the nobles, bound by loyalty, drove him into exile; he brought in pirates, and with them, as I have said, he was slain. He thereby demonstrated that it is foolish to kick against those more powerful. Though Edward deserved praise for these achievements, in my judgment the chief palm belongs to his father, who laid the foundation of so great a power.

Meanwhile, Edward’s sister Æthelflæd, Æthelred’s widow, must not be passed over: [Note: [Col. 1088D] “Meanwhile let not the king’s sister Æthelflæd . . .” On Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, consult the Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 912–919.] she was no small strength to her party, beloved by citizens, feared by enemies, a woman of unbounded spirit. Because of the difficulty she had experienced in her first—or rather her only—[Note: [Col. 1088D] “Or rather her only,” a. c. d. e. l. m.; omitted in s.] childbirth, she permanently recoiled from her husband’s embrace, [Note: [Col. 1088D] “She recoiled,” c. d. e. m.; “she recoiled,” a. s. l.] declaring that it did not suit a king’s daughter to be joined to that pleasure which would afterward bring such distress upon her. A most powerful woman, she was of great assistance to her brother in counsel and no less effective in building towns. One could not determine whether it was more by fortune or by valour that a woman protected her own men and terrified strangers.

She died five years before her brother and was buried in the monastery of St Peter at Gloucester, which she had built with great care together with her husband Æthelred; she had also transferred there the bones of blessed Oswald from Bardney. But after it had been destroyed in the time of the Danes, another monastery, now regarded as the principal one in that city, was restored by [Note: [Col. 1088D] Aldred, archbishop of York, restored it. s. c. d. e. l. m.; omitted in a, where instead one reads: “It then somehow remained; but in the time of the Normans it raised its head through Abbot Serlo.” Aldred, bishop of Worcester, succeeded Archbishop Kinsin in the see of York in A.D. 1061, after Kinsin’s death in 1046, so that he might hold both sees at once; but the supreme pontiff denied him the pallium until he should resign the see of Worcester (MALMESBURY, *Life of St Wulfstan*). He died on 11 September, A.D. 1069.] Aldred, archbishop of York.

[197] **ON THE CHILDREN OF EDWARD THE FIRST**

[Col. 1089A]

§ 126. Since the king had many daughters, he gave Eadgifu [Note: [Col. 1089C] To Charles, king of the Franks: Charles the Simple. See above, § 112.] to Charles, king of the Franks, son of Louis, [Note: [Col. 1089C] “Of Louis,” c. d. e. l; “of Louis the Stammerer,” a. s.] son of Charles the Bald, whose daughter, [Note: [Col. 1089C] “As I have often said.” §§ 109, 113.] as I have often said, King Æthelwulf had taken in marriage when returning from Rome. And since the occasion presents itself, the gracious reader will not think it unworthy that I should set down the names of Edward’s wives and children.

He had his first-born, [Note: [Col. 1089C] Æthelstan by Ecgwynn. Ecgwynn, Æthelstan’s mother, is said to have been Edward’s concubine; but Malmesbury speaks doubtfully of this alleged blemish in Æthelstan’s birth [Col. 1089D]. See below, § 131.] Æthelstan, by the noblewoman Ecgwynn; and a daughter [Note: [Col. 1089D] Her name, etc. The name of Edward’s daughter whom her brother Æthelstan married to Sihtric, king of the Northumbrians, on 30 January 925, occurs nowhere in the ancient English chronicles. Among Scottish historians she is called Beatrix.] whose written name I do not have readily at hand. This daughter her brother gave in marriage to Sihtric, king of the Northumbrians.

Edward’s second son was [Note: [Col. 1089D] Æthelweard. Æthelweard died at Oxford a few days after his father and was buried at Winchester. See below, § 131.] Æthelweard, by Ælfflæd, daughter of Earl Æthelhelm. He was excellently educated in letters and greatly resembled his grandfather Alfred in face and manners, but was taken by an early death shortly after his father. [Col. 1089B] By the same wife Edward had Edwin, concerning whose death I shall later state the tradition, [Note: [Col. 1089D] “I shall later state it.” See below, § 139.] not confidently but hesitantly. By her he also had six daughters: Eadflæd, Eadgifu, Æthelhild, Æthilda, Eadgyth, and Ælfgifu. The first and third, having vowed celibacy to God, disdained the pleasure of earthly marriage: Eadflæd under the consecrated veil and Æthelhild in secular dress. Both lie at Wilton, [198] buried beside their mother. [Note: [Col. 1089D] The father gave Eadgifu to King Charles. See above, § 112. After Charles the Simple’s death, Queen Eadgifu married Herbert, count of Troyes, son of Herbert, count of Vermandois, in A.D. 951 (BOUQUET, IX, 126).] As I have said, their father gave Eadgifu to King Charles. [Note: [Col. 1089D] Æthelhild . . . to Hugh: Count of Paris, surnamed the Great, son of Robert I, king of the Franks, and brother of King Eudes. He died in A.D. 956 but left no offspring by Eadilda.
