He was father of Hugh Capet, king of the Franks [Col. 1090C].] Her brother Æthelstan gave Æthilda to Hugh; he sent [Note: [Col. 1090C] Eadgyth and Ælfgifu . . . near the Alps. See above, § 112.] Eadgyth and Ælfgifu [Note: [Col. 1090C] “Their brother sent,” s. c. d. e. l; “their brother, as I have said, sent,” a.] to Henry, emperor of the Germans. Henry married the second to his son Otto and the other to a certain duke near the Alps.

By a third wife, named Eadgifu, he also had two sons, Edmund and Eadred, who [Col. 1089C] both reigned after Æthelstan; and two daughters, Eadburh and Eadgifu. Eadburh, a virgin consecrated to Christ, rests at [Col. 1090A] Winchester. Her brother Æthelstan married Eadgifu, a woman of exceptional beauty, to Louis, prince of Aquitaine. [Note: [Col. 1090C] Eadgifu . . . to Louis, etc. Eadgifu married Louis the Blind, emperor and king of Arles. By him she had a son named Charles Constantine, count of Vienne (BOUQUET, VIII, 186).]

He brought up his daughters so that all of them should devote themselves especially to letters in childhood and then should become accustomed to working spindle and needle, in order that through these arts they might pass their unmarried virginity modestly. His sons, [Note: [Col. 1090C] “His sons,” d. e. m.; “his sons thus,” a. s. c. l.] he trained so that first a full education in letters might flow into them, and afterward they might come forth, as philosophers, no longer untrained to govern the commonwealth.

**ON THE NORMANS: HOW THEY HARASSED FRANCE; AND HOW ROLLO RECEIVED THE DAUGHTER OF THE KING OF THE FRANKS.**
§ 127. But this Charles, Edward’s son-in-law, compelled by Rollo through many disasters, granted him that part of Gaul which is now called Normandy. It would take too long to pursue for how many years, and with what audacity, the Northmen disturbed everything from the British Ocean—as I mentioned before—all the way to the Tyrrhenian Sea.

[Note: [Col. 1090C] “As I mentioned before.” a. d. e. l.; omitted in c.; “as I mentioned before,” s.—See § 121.]

First Hasting, then Rollo, who, though born of a noble Norwegian lineage obscured by antiquity,

[Note: [Col. 1090C–D] Rollo, etc. Rollo was the son of Rognwald, count of Mære, killed in A.D. 893, who on his mother’s side traced his descent from the famous Sigurd Ring, king of the Danes and Swedes.]

was deprived of his country by the king’s command.

[Note: [Col. 1090D] “By the king’s command,” etc. Rollo, having been discovered while carrying out strandhúgg—that is, collecting provisions—which was then prohibited among the Danes under very severe penalties, was expelled from his native soil by order of King Harald Fairhair in A.D. 895. (Snorre, *Haralds Saga ens Harfagra*, ch. 24, vol. I, p. 100; Copenhagen ed., 1777).]

He drew after him many men whom either debt or consciousness of crimes harassed, enticing them with great hopes. Thus, having taken up piracy, while his unbridled frenzy roamed freely everywhere, he halted before Chartres.

[Note: [Col. 1090D] “He halted at Chartres.” Rollo besieged Chartres in 911.]

For the citizens, trusting neither in arms nor walls, implored the aid of the blessed Lady Mary. They also displayed upon the battlements, like a standard, the shirt of that same Virgin, worn upon the breasts of those guarding it against the winds—a shirt which Charles the Bald had brought from Constantinople with other relics.

[Note: [Col. 1090D] “The shirt also,” etc. Bishop Waltelmus is said to have carried the tunic of the most blessed Virgin in his own hands, after which the besiegers immediately turned to flight.]

[Note: [Col. 1090D] “Charles the Bald,” etc. This is also related in certain anonymous French chronicles of the twelfth century; but there is no evidence whatever that Charles ever visited Constantinople.]

The enemy, seeing it, laughed and shot arrows at it through the empty air; but not without punishment, for presently their eyes were darkened, and they could neither retreat nor advance. When the townsmen saw this with joyful hearts, they satisfied their delight, as far as fortune permitted, by slaughtering many of them.

[Note: [Col. 1091B] “This.” a. c. d. e. l.; “which,” s.] Yet Rollo escaped, for God preserved him for his own faith.

Not long afterward he seized Rouen and the neighbouring towns by force of arms, in the year of the Lord 876, one year before the death of Charles the Bald.

[Note: [Col. 1091B–C] “Eight hundred and seventy-six.” a. s. c. l.; “eight hundred and six,” d. e. m.—French and English chroniclers alike date Rollo’s invasion of Neustria to 876; northern writers say that it occurred twenty years earlier—that is, in the year after Rollo was expelled from Norway. From certain French chronicles we also learn that Neustria was occupied in 896, and not under Rollo’s leadership. Whatever the case, each invasion plainly occurred long before the siege of Chartres and the events narrated above. Rollo’s memorable dream, interpreted as foretelling his settlement in France, is placed in 876. See the *Annals attributed to Asser*, Gale III, 165.]

[Note: [Col. 1091C] “Whose son,” etc. Louis III, son of Louis the Stammerer, whose father was Charles the Bald.]

His son’s son Louis, as has been read above, defeated the Northmen indeed, but did not expel them.

[Note: [Col. 1091C] “As has been read above.” a. c. d. e. l.; “said,” s.—A.D. 881. See above, § 110.]

But Charles,

[Note: [Col. 1091C] Charles the Simple.]

brother of that Louis, grandson of Charles the Bald through his son Louis, as I previously touched upon, had repeatedly experienced adverse warfare and saw that fortune restored to him none of what it had taken away from others. After weighing the matter with his magnates, he judged it good to display royal generosity when he could not repel injury, and summoned Rollo peacefully. Rollo was now already aged, and readily inclined toward agreement.

[Note: [Col. 1091C–D] “Thus the treaty was made.” The terms of this agreement, it is believed, survive nowhere in an authentic form; and it is very doubtful whether it was ever committed to writing. Among the French there became current a certain absurd notion: namely, that the original charter had been taken away by one of the Norman-descended kings of England and deposited in the Tower of London. Even if this were wholly true, every trace of such a document has long since perished.]

Thus the treaty was made: Rollo was to receive baptism and acknowledge that land as held from the king, as from his lord. Here the man’s native and unbridled barbarity might be observed. For when, after the gift had been granted, those standing by urged him to kiss the foot of the giver,

[Note: [Col. 1091D–1092A] “To kiss the foot,” etc. This insolent and arrogant conduct, here attributed to Rollo, is ascribed by William of Jumièges to one of the Norman soldiers accompanying the duke (*Bouquet*, VIII, 257). Robert Wace, however, maintains that the Norman duke himself behaved so arrogantly toward the king of the French (*Roman de Rou*).]

he disdained to bend his knees, seized the king’s foot, and while standing drew it to his mouth. The king fell backward, and the Northmen burst out laughing. When the Franks censured the deed, Rollo excused his impudence by alleging the custom of his country. With matters thus settled, he returned to Rouen and there ended his days.

[Note: [Col. 1091D] “And there he ended his days.” Rollo abdicated in favour of his son William in 927. He died in A.D. 931 (*Bouquet*, IX, 12, note).]

## CONCERNING HUGH CAPET: HOW HE BECAME KING OF FRANCE

§ 128. This Charles’s son was Louis.

[Note: [Col. 1091D] Louis. Louis IV, surnamed “Overseas,” returned from England in 936 with Count William, archbishop of Sens, and was crowned at Rheims on 19 June of that year. He died after falling from his horse at Rheims, on 10 September, A.D. 954.]

This Louis, provoked by a certain Isambard, who had turned to paganism and mocked the faith, consulted his nobles concerning assistance; and when they offered no reply—

[Note: [Col. 1092B–C] “By a certain Isambard.” The matters related in this section are highly confused. What is here reported of Louis IV appears to belong to the reign of his uncle, Louis III. In 881 the Northmen ravaged the Vimeu and Ponthieu, at the instigation, as stated, of Isambard, whose uncle was Louis and who, after incurring his uncle’s hatred and being driven from the kingdom by him, fled to Guormond, or Guorm, leader of the Danes. The notable defeat suffered by the Northmen that year at Saulcourt, where their leader was killed, is related in most French chronicles; and some poems in a German dialect still survive in praise of King Louis (*Bouquet*, VIII, 273; IX, 58, 99–101).]

—a certain Hugh, an inexperienced man of no great name, son of Robert, count of Montdidier, voluntarily sought single combat on behalf of his lord and killed the challenger.

[Note: [Col. 1092C–D] “A certain Hugh,” etc. It is not clear which Hugh is meant here. The author seems to mean either Hugh Capet or his father Hugh the Great, son of Robert I, king of the Franks; but Malmesbury plainly confuses them in what follows. Hugh, son of Conrad, count of Auxerre, and brother of Robert the Strong, grandfather of Hugh the Great, distinguished himself in the battle against the Northmen begun by Louis in 881. Therefore, according to the sequence of time, the events concerning Isambard, if they are not mere inventions, might more plausibly be referred to him than either to his great-grandson or to his great-great-grandson. He died while Paris was under siege, in 886.]

[Note: [Col. 1092D] “He sought single combat for his lord and killed the challenger.” This incident is not mentioned in the *Recueil des Historiens de France*.]

[Note: [Col. 1092D] “Single combat.” a. s. c. d. l.; *duellium*, e.]

Louis followed with his whole army to Ponthieu; and, after all the barbarians whom Isambard had brought had either been killed or escaped, won a rich victory. But not long afterwards, weakened by a fatal illness as a result of the exertion of that campaign, he appointed that Hugh heir to the kingdom—a young man of praiseworthy faith and courage. Thus the line of Charlemagne ended in him, either because his wife was barren or because he died childless through the shortness of his life.

[Note: [Col. 1092D] “Thus the line,” etc. The Carolingian line failed in Louis V, son of Louis the Overseas. Louis IV left by Gerberga, daughter of Emperor Otto, Lothair, who succeeded him on 12 November A.D. 954 and died on 2 March 986, and Charles, duke of Lorraine, who contended with Hugh Capet for the crown of France after the death of Louis V, son of Lothair, and later died in prison in A.D. 994.]

Hugh married another daughter of Edward

[Note: [Col. 1092D–1093C] “Hugh married another daughter of Edward.” Malmesbury here seems to speak of Hugh Capet, whom he mistakenly takes for Hugh the Great, his father, as husband of Aedhild, or Ethild, daughter of Edward the Elder. See § 126. Hugh Capet, king of the Franks, was anointed at Rheims on 3 July A.D. 987 and died on 24 October A.D. 996.]

and begot Robert; Robert, Henry; Henry, Philip; Philip, Louis, who now reigns in France.

[Note: [Col. 1093C] Robert. Robert II was crowned at Orléans on 1 January 988 while his father was still alive; upon his father’s death he succeeded as sole king of the Franks, and died on Tuesday, 20 July A.D. 1031.]

[Note: [Col. 1093C] Henry. Henry I of France was anointed king during his father’s lifetime and succeeded at his death in 1031. He died at Vitry, near Paris, on 4 August A.D. 1060.]

[Note: [Col. 1093C] Philip. Philip I, called Saint Philip, was crowned during his father’s lifetime in his seventh year, on 23 May 1059. He died at Melun on 30 July 1108.]

[Note: [Col. 1093C] Louis. Louis VI, surnamed the Fat, was anointed at Orléans on 3 August 1108 by the archbishop of Sens and died at Paris on 1 August 1137.]

But, to return to our Edward, I think it pleasant to recount what was ordained by Pope Formosus in his time concerning the restoration of bishoprics. Accordingly, I shall insert it in the very words in which I found it written.

[Note: [Col. 1093C–D] “In the very words,” etc. The material reported here is taken from a manuscript codex (Bodley 579) given to Exeter Cathedral by Bishop Leofric, whose death is assigned to 1073. But it teems everywhere with so many and such great anachronisms that it must undoubtedly be considered fictitious. The document is dated 904, whereas Formosus died on Easter Day, 11 April 896, more than five years before Edward began to reign; while Frithestan was not made bishop of Winchester before 910. On the seven vacant episcopal sees, consult *Anglia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 534; Spelman and Wilkins, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 201. See also Ingulf (Gale, vol. I).]

§ 129. In the year 904 from the Lord’s birth, Pope Formosus sent letters into England, in which he pronounced excommunication and a curse upon King Edward and all his subjects, on account of the blessing which Saint Gregory had bestowed upon the English people from the see of Saint Peter. For the whole region of the Gewisse—that is, the West Saxons—had been without bishops for seven full years.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] “Bishops.” a. c. d. e.; “episcopal,” l.]

When this was heard, King Edward assembled a synod of the senators of the English people. Archbishop Plegmund presided,

[Note: [Col. 1093D] “Archbishop.” a. c. d. e. l.; “archbishop of Canterbury,” s.]

explaining the stern words of the apostolic embassy. Then the king and bishops adopted a remedy beneficial to themselves and their people. In accordance with the Lord’s saying, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few,”

[Note: [Col. 1093D] “The harvest … few.” Matthew 9:37.]

they chose and appointed individual bishops for individual provinces of the Gewisse, and divided among five what two had formerly held. When the council had been held, the archbishop went to Rome with honourable gifts, appeased the pope with great humility, and recited the king’s ordinances, which greatly pleased the apostolic see. Returning to his country, in the city of Canterbury he ordained in one day seven bishops for seven churches: Frithestan for the church of Winchester, Athelstan for Cornwall, Werstan for Sherborne, Æthelhelm for Wells, and Eadwulf for Crediton.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] “For Crediton.” a. c. d. e. l.; “for Crediton in Devon,” s.]

He also appointed two bishops for other provinces: Beornheah, a suitable man, for the South Saxons; and Cenwulf for the Mercians, at the city of Dorchester.

[Note: [Col. 1094B] “Dorchester.” a. c. d. e. l.; “Dorchester in Oxfordshire,” s.]

The pope confirmed all this, decreeing that whoever should invalidate this ordinance was to be condemned for ever.

§ 130. Edward, having entered upon the way of all flesh [A.D. 924], rests in the same monastery as his father, which he himself had enlarged with great revenues. There too, four years earlier, he had buried his brother Æthelweard.

[Note: [Col. 1094C] “Four years earlier,” etc. Æthelweard, the youngest son of King Alfred, died on 16 October A.D. 922, two years and somewhat more before the death of his brother Edward.]

## CONCERNING ÆTHELSTAN, SON OF EDWARD

§ 131. In the year 924 of the Lord’s incarnation, Æthelstan, son of Edward, began to reign and held the kingdom for sixteen years.

[Note: [Col. 1094C–D] “In the year 924 of the Lord’s incarnation.” While the national controversy concerning the feudal authority of the kings of England over Scotland was under discussion, Edward I sent orders sealed with the great seal of England to the principal cathedral churches and monasteries of the kingdom, commanding that, after chronicles and ancient documents had been examined, whatever was found in them concerning Scotland should be sent to the king. What was then written and sent from Malmesbury monastery consists of only two rather extensive passages extracted from William of Malmesbury’s history—namely, this entire section and § 148—with a few brief notices concerning Henry I, abridged from the beginning of Book V. In one manuscript (L.) passages headed “Note concerning Scotland,” apparently for the same purpose, are much more numerous than the extracts from Malmesbury’s *History* contained in all reports now extant; hence it must be presumed that the testimony of the house to which this manuscript belonged no longer survives. Extracts from chronicles preserved in monastic libraries concerning the subjugation of Scotland are of the greatest importance. A reader wishing fuller information should consult Palgrave, *Documents and Records Illustrating the History of Scotland*. See also Cotton MS Julius D. VI.]

[Note: [Col. 1094D] “For sixteen years.” William of Malmesbury, Florence of Worcester, and the Saxon Chronicle place Æthelstan’s death in 940; but if, as Florence also states, it must be assigned to Wednesday, 24 October, indiction XIV, it necessarily occurred in A.D. 941, before the seventeenth year of his reign had been completed. See the charter of King Edmund dated A.D. 940, indiction XIII (Cotton MS Augustus II.62).]

His brother Ælfweard, dying a few days after his father, had received burial with him at Winchester. Æthelstan was therefore elected there by the great consent of the magnates and crowned at the royal vill called Kingston. Yet a certain Ælfred, with his faction—for sedition always finds accomplices—had attempted to oppose him; what end he met, we shall later report in the king’s own words.

[Note: [Col. 1095C] “We shall later report in the king’s own words.” See below, §§ 136–137.]

The cause of the opposition, they say, was that Æthelstan had been born of a concubine. But he himself, except for this reproach—if indeed it is true—

[Note: [Col. 1095C] “If indeed it is true.” Here, and again at the end of § 136, Malmesbury appears to indicate that he doubted the alleged lowliness of Æthelstan’s birth.]

had nothing ignoble about him. He surpassed all his predecessors in devotion of mind and eclipsed all their triumphal glories by the splendour of his own victories. It is so much better to possess through oneself the means of distinction than to possess it through one’s ancestors: the former is yours; the latter is accounted another’s.

I refrain from writing how many and how great new monasteries he founded. Yet I shall not pass over this: scarcely any ancient house existed in all England which he did not adorn with buildings, ornaments, books, or estates.

[Note: [Col. 1095C–D] “Or books.” Cotton MS Tiberius A. II is a copy of the Gospels presented by King Æthelstan to the church of Canterbury; Claudius B. V is likewise a volume given by the same king to the church of Bath.]

[Note: [Col. 1095D] “He adorned.” d. e. m.; “he may have adorned,” a. s. c. l.]

Thus he distinguished recent foundations deliberately, and ancient ones as though pursuing another purpose, with an artist’s generosity.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] “Another.” s. c. d. e.; “something,” a. l.]

Having given one of his sisters in marriage to Sihtric, king of the Northumbrians, he concluded an enduring treaty with him.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] “Marriage.” c. d. e. l.; after “marriage,” a. s. read, “as I have said before.” See above, § 126.]

When Sihtric died a year later, Æthelstan subdued that province, expelling a certain Aldulf who was in rebellion.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] “When he died a year later.” Sihtric, king of the Northumbrians, died in A.D. 926. He was succeeded by his son Guthfrith, whom Æthelstan expelled in the following year and whose Northumbria he joined to his kingdom.]

[Note: [Col. 1095D] “Expelling a certain Aldulf.” Ealdred, son of Ealdulf of Bamburgh. (Florence of Worcester; Saxon Chronicle, ann. 926.)]

And because a noble spirit, once stirred, strives for greater things, he compelled Hywel, king of all the Welsh, and Constantine, king of the Scots, to yield their kingdoms.

[Note: [Col. 1095D] “He compelled them to yield their kingdoms.” The kings submitted to Æthelstan at Eamont on 12 July A.D. 926.]

Yet not long afterward, overcome by pity, he restored them to their former position, to reign under him, declaring that it was more glorious to make a king than to be one. Finally he had a war with Anlaf, son of Sihtric, who, hoping to seize the kingdom, had crossed the borders while the aforesaid Constantine again rebelled.

[Note: [Col. 1095D–1096D] “The war with Anlaf,” etc. Several leaders named Anlaf are mentioned in Anglo-Saxon annals of this period: Anlaf son of Sihtric; Anlaf son of Guthfrith; and Anlaf Cuaran, also named in the Annals of Ulster under 944 and 946. The Irish Anlaf, who stirred up allied leaders against Æthelstan at the battle of Brunanburh in A.D. 938, also known as Onlaf or Olaf, traced his descent on his mother’s side from Ragnar Lothbrok and appears to have been a king of the Ostman lineage in Ireland. He married a daughter of Constantine, king of the Scots.]

Æthelstan deliberately gave way so that he might conquer him more gloriously once he was exulting in his success. The most daring young man advanced far into England, breathing unlawful designs in his heart. At Brunefeld he was at last met by the great skill of the commanders and the great strength of the soldiers.

[Note: [Col. 1096D] “Brunefeld.” d. e. m.; “Brunefosd,” a. s. l.; “Breneveld,” c.—Brunanburh among the Northumbrians. It is uncertain what site should be assigned to this town. The battle was fought in 938.]

Seeing that such danger threatened, Anlaf undertook the role of a spy. Putting aside his royal insignia and taking a harp in his hands, he went to the tent of our king.

[Note: [Col. 1096D] “In his hands.” c. d. e.; “in his hand,” a. s. l.]

There, singing before the entrance and occasionally striking the strings with a sweet, resounding rhythm, he was readily admitted, declaring himself a minstrel who earned his daily support by such skill. He charmed the king and his guests for some time with his musical performance, while during his singing he examined everything with his eyes. After the fullness of eating had put an end to their pleasures, and the seriousness of conducting the war had revived in the conversation of the magnates, he was ordered to depart and received payment for his song. Disdaining to carry it away, he buried it beneath him in the ground.

This was observed by someone who had formerly served under him and immediately reported to Æthelstan. The king reproached the man for not betraying an enemy placed before his eyes, but received this answer:

> “I once gave Anlaf the same oath which I recently gave you, O king. If you had seen me violate it in his case, you might likewise have feared a similar example in your own. But deign to hear the counsel of your servant: move your tent from this place, and remain elsewhere until the troops left behind arrive. By prudent delay you will check the enemy who is insolently exulting.”

The advice was approved, and they departed from there. Anlaf came by night, ready for battle,

[Note: [Col. 1096D] “Came.” c. d. e.; omitted in a. s. l.]

and killed a certain bishop, who had arrived at the army in the evening and, unaware of what had happened, had pitched his tent there with all his household on the level of the green field.

[Note: [Col. 1096D] “A certain bishop.” Werstan, bishop of Sherborne.—“They say that Werstan, sent by King Æthelstan into the battle against Anlaf, was slain by the heathen.” (Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum*, “On the Bishops of Sherborne,” p. 248, French edition.)]

[Note: [Col. 1096D] “Level.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; “plain,” c.]

[Note: [Col. 1096D] “Killed.” a. d. e. l.; “fell,” s. c.]

Then, advancing farther, he found the king himself unprepared, since Æthelstan, not imagining that the enemy would dare such a thing, had given himself freely to rest. But when he was roused from his bed by such an uproar and, so far as the night allowed, urged his men to battle, his sword happened to fall from its scabbard. Therefore, amid a scene wholly full of terror and blind confusion, he called upon God and Saint Aldhelm,

[Note: [Col. 1097C] “Aldhelm.” a. s. d. e. l; after “Aldhelm,” s. c. add: “for he was related to him by ancient ancestors.”]

put his hand back to the scabbard, and found a sword which is even today kept among the royal treasures as a miracle.

[Note: [Col. 1097C] “He found a sword,” etc. From the book of letters patent (*Patent Roll*), 9 John, it appears that the king had among his regalia two swords: namely, the sword of Tristan and another sword. It is not improbable that the sword preserved in the royal treasury in Malmesbury’s own time was this other sword mentioned in the letters patent cited above.]

It is, indeed, as they say, capable of being cut on one side, and never able to receive gold or silver. Trusting in this gift of God, and because day was now dawning,

[Note: [Col. 1097C] “Now.” c. d. e. l.; “day,” a. s.]

he attacked the Norwegian and pursued him with his army tirelessly throughout the day until evening.

[Note: [Col. 1097D–1098C] “Constantine, king of the Scots, fell there.” The history attributed to Ingulf, besides the account of the battle at Brunanburh, where Constantine is said to have fallen, contains reports of certain other events occurring about this period which also appear in Malmesbury, whether true or false. There may therefore be some reason to think that Malmesbury followed Ingulf, or some older author common to both historians. If the opinion that the history bearing Ingulf’s name is not genuine is securely grounded—since it is a compilation no older than Edward II—it is especially remarkable and worth noting that in some places the compiler is plainly found to be false. In the poem inserted in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, composed as a memorial of the battle of Brunanburh, Constantine’s son is represented as left slain on the field, pierced with wounds; but there, as also in Florence of Worcester, Constantine and Olaf are said both to have fled to their ships. According to the Chronicle of Melrose, Constantine died in A.D. 943.]

There fell Constantine, king of the Scots, a man of treacherous courage and vigorous old age; five other kings, twelve earls,

[Note: [Col. 1098C] “Twelve earls.” Only five earls are mentioned in the Annals.]

and nearly the whole mass of barbarians.

[Note: [Col. 1098C] “Nearly.” s. c. d. e.; omitted in a. l.]

The few who escaped were preserved in order to receive the faith of Christ.

§ 132. A considerable report is current among the English concerning this king—Æthelstan—that no one administered the commonwealth more lawfully

[Note: [Col. 1098C] “More lawfully.” a. s. d. e. l.; “more effectively,” c.]

or more learnedly. Yet only a very few days ago I learned from a certain very ancient book that he knew letters; its writer was wrestling with the difficulty of his subject and could not express the judgment of his mind as he wished. I would append his words here in summary, were he not carried beyond measure in the prince’s praises, using that manner of speech which Tully, the king of Roman eloquence, calls “supported” in his rhetorical writings. The custom of that age excuses the style; favour for Æthelstan, still living, embellishes the excess of praise.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “Favour.” s. c. d. l.; omitted in e.; “fear,” a.]

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “Therefore a few things,” etc. What Malmesbury here relates of Æthelstan seems to have been drawn from a source now wholly unknown.]

I shall therefore add a few things in a familiar style, which seem to contribute some advantage toward demonstrating his distinction.

§ 133. King Edward, after many noble achievements in war and peace,

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “In war and peace.” s. c. d. e.; omitted in a. l.]

a few days before his death restrained from rebellion the city of the Legions—Chester—which had rebelled in reliance on the Britons.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “The city of the Legions.” Chester.]

Having stationed a military garrison there, he came to the estate of Farndon; struck by illness, he put off this present life [A.D. 924]

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “He put off.” s.; “he went out,” a. c. d. e. l. m.]

and, as I have said, was buried at Winchester.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “Farndon.” a. c.; “Ferdun,” d. e. l. m.]

Then, by his father’s command and testament, Æthelstan was acclaimed king, already recommended by thirty years of age and the maturity of wisdom. For his grandfather Alfred had long ago prayed that his reign might prosper, when he saw and graciously embraced the boy, whose appearance was admirable and whose bearing graceful. Alfred had even made him a knight prematurely, giving him a scarlet cloak, a jewelled belt, and a Saxon sword with a golden scabbard.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “Whom he had even made a knight.” Sharpe considers that this passage implies that knights existed among the Saxons as a distinct order, though perhaps it establishes only that Alfred first received his own arms from his grandfather.]

After this Alfred had arranged for his upbringing at the court of his daughter Æthelflæd and his son-in-law Æthelred. There, through the great care of his aunt and that most illustrious duke, he was reared toward the prospect of kingship; by the glory of his virtues he trod down and suppressed envy; and after his father’s death and his brother’s demise he was crowned king at Kingston. Therefore, because of the glory of such achievements and the joy of that day—not without cause—a poet exclaims:

> Royal offspring brought forth a noble shoot,  
> A brilliant jewel shone upon our darkness:  
> Great Æthelstan, his country’s glory, the track of right,  
> Illustrious virtue, knowing no turning from the true.  
>
> Given at his father’s command to the disciplines of the schools,  
> He feared stern masters and the rattling rod;  
> And drinking the honey of learning with eager inmost parts,  
> He passed through tender years, yet not childishly.  
>
> Soon, clothed in the flower of youthful adolescence,  
> At his father’s command he pursued the study of arms.  
> Nor did the laws of war find him sluggish in this either:  
> The public welfare later learned this too.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “Learned.” c. d. e. k.; “cared for,” a.; “swore,” s. l.]  
>
> His father, eminent beyond all men of his age, had met his fate,

[Note: [Col. 1098D] “Eminent.” s. d. e. l.; *praeduus*, a. c.]  
> Yet would live through every age in undying fame;  
> Then the young man’s name was proclaimed as an omen of the realm,  
> That beneath a fortunate title he might guide his country’s reins.  
>
> The nobles assemble and set the diadem in order;  
> The bishops likewise pronounce anathema upon the faithless;  
> A flame more festive than usual gleams among the people,  
> And they reveal the secrets of their hearts by diverse signs.  
>
> Each burns to show the king his own favour;  
> One fears, another hopes; broad hope drives fear away.

[Note: [Col. 1099D] “Fear.” a. d. e. l.; *timorem* (“fear”), s. c.]  
> The palace boils and overflows with royal splendour;  
> Wine foams everywhere, and the great hall roars with tumult.  
>
> Boys run about; servants hasten to their assigned duties.  
> Bellies are filled with delicacies, minds with song;  
> One rings out on the harp, another vies in applause;  
> All sound together: “To you be praise, to you glory, O Christ!”

[Note: [Col. 1099D] “Glory.” a. s. c. e.; “grace,” d. l. m.]  
>
> The king, not unwilling, drinks in this honour with his eyes,  
> Indulging all, and graciously accepting their personal devotion.

[Note: [Col. 1099D] “Graciously.” a. c. d. e. l.; “deigns,” s.]

§ 134. When the celebration of the consecration was over, Æthelstan, lest he should disappoint the hopes of the citizens or conduct himself beneath expectation, subdued the whole of England by the terror of his name alone, except only the Northumbrians. For a certain Sihtric ruled over them, barbarous in race and spirit, a kinsman of that Gormund [Note: [Col. 1099D] Concerning whom there is an account in the deeds of King Alfred. Guthorm died A.D. 891. See above, § 121.] of whom there is an account in the deeds of King Alfred. Having mocked the power of preceding kings with wrinkled nostrils, he of his own accord sought Æthelstan’s alliance through humble envoys; and then, following swiftly himself, he confirmed the words of the ambassadors. Thus, joined in marriage to his sister [Note: [Col. 1099D] Marriage-union. c. d. e. l.; after *copula*, a. reads “as I have already twice affirmed.”], and enriched with many gifts, he laid the foundations of an everlasting treaty. But, as I have recalled above [Note: [Col. 1099D] “As I have recalled above.” See above, § 131.], when he was removed from life after a year, he furnished Æthelstan with an opportunity to join Northumbria to his own dominion, since it belonged to him both by ancient right and by this new connection.

[Note: [Col. 1099D] “Then Anlaf fled,” etc. The flight to Ireland of Anlaf, son of Sihtric, mentioned here, has led some writers to identify him with the Irish Olaf who fought against Æthelstan in battle in 938. From the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle we learn that two kings, Anlaf son of Sihtric and Ragnald son of Guthferth, were expelled from Northumbria by King Edmund in 944.]

Then Anlaf, Sihtric’s son, fled to Ireland, and Godefrid, his brother, to Scotland. [Note: [Col. 1099D] “Godefrid, his brother, to Scotland.” Guthferth was expelled from the kingdom of Northumbria in A.D. 927.] Royal envoys immediately followed them to Constantine, king of the Scots, and Eugenius, king of the Cumbrians, demanding the surrender of the fugitives under threat of war. The barbarians had no mind to murmur in opposition; rather, without hesitation, they came to the place called Dacor and surrendered themselves and their kingdoms to the king of the English. As confirmation of this treaty, Constantine’s son was ordered to be baptized, and Æthelstan himself received him from the sacred font.

Godefrid nevertheless escaped, slipping away amid the preparations of the travellers with a certain Turfrid, a leader of various factions. Soon he besieged York, soliciting the townsmen to defect, now by entreaties and now by threats; but accomplishing neither as he wished, he departed. Not long afterward, the two were shut up in a certain castle, and by fleeing they made sport of the vigilance of their guards. Turfrid soon met his end, shipwrecked at sea and exposed as prey to fishes. Godefrid, tossed by many miseries on land and sea, at last came as a suppliant to the court. There he was peacefully received by the king and feasted with him most lavishly for four days; then he returned to his ships—an old pirate, accustomed to live in the water like a fish.

Meanwhile Æthelstan razed to the ground the fortress which the Danes had formerly strengthened at York, lest treachery should have any refuge in which to protect itself. The booty found in the fortress, and indeed very great booty, he distributed magnificently, person by person. For that man had resolved in his heart to gather no wealth into money-bags, but generously to spend everything acquired either upon monasteries or upon his faithful men. In this [Note: [Col. 1100D] “In this.” a. c. d. e. l.; s. reads “for in this.”] he exhausted throughout his life his father’s treasures and the trophies of his own victories.

He was kindly and gentle toward those serving God; cheerful and gracious toward laymen; grave toward great men because of the majesty of his appearance; and toward the lowly, because of his condescension to poverty [Note: [Col. 1100D] “Poverty.” a. d. e. l.; “compassion,” s.], with the haughtiness of kingship laid aside, soberly approachable. His stature, as we have learned, did not exceed the proper measure [Note: [Col. 1100D] “Did not exceed.” a. s. c. e. l.; “went beyond,” d. m.]; his body was slender. His hair, as we ourselves saw from his relics [Note: [Col. 1100D] “As we ourselves saw from his relics.” d. e. l.; s. has “from his relics.”], was fair, beautifully twisted into strands like gold. Dearly loved by his subjects for his strength and humility, and terrible to rebels through invincible steadfastness, he compelled the petty kings of North Wales—that is, of the Northern Britons—to meet him near the city of Hereford. After resisting for some time, they submitted; and what no king before him had dared even to contemplate, he brought into effect: annually, as tribute, they were to pay him twenty pounds of gold and three hundred of silver; to number out twenty-five thousand oxen; besides as many dogs as might track the lairs and haunts of wild beasts with scent-following nostrils [Note: [Col. 1100D] “As many as might.” e.; “as many as might please,” a. s. c. d. l.], and birds able to hunt in the air the prey of other birds [Note: [Col. 1100D] “Might know how.” a. c. e. l.; “might recognize,” s.; “are accustomed,” d. m.].

Departing thence, he turned against the Western Britons, called Cornish, who live in the west of Britain and look obliquely toward the horn of Gaul. [Note: [Col. 1100D] “The horn of Gaul … look obliquely toward.” See § 110, note.] He attacked them also vigorously and compelled them to withdraw from Exeter, which until that time they had inhabited on equal legal terms with the English. He fixed the boundary of their territory on this side of the river Tamar, just as he had set the river Wye as the boundary for the Northern Britons.

[Note: [Col. 1101C] “That city therefore.” Æthelstan subjected Howel at Exeter in 926. It is probable that Æthelstan spent Christmas Day here, as he is known to have done, since he established some of his laws in this city: “These are the judgments which the wise men established at Exeter by the counsel of King Æthelstan, etc. I, Æthelstan, etc. Now I have found, with those wise men who were with me at Exeter on the holy Nativity of the Lord, etc.” Compare the description of Exeter given here with that place in *De Gestis Pontificum*, book III.]

That city, therefore, which he had cleansed of the dregs of a polluted race, he fortified with towers and enclosed with a wall of squared stones. Although that soil, barren and desolate, scarcely produces sterile oats and, more often, an empty husk without grain, nevertheless, because of the city’s magnificence, the wealth of its inhabitants, and also the multitude of visitors, every kind of merchandise is there so abundant that one would desire nothing in vain which one might think useful for human needs. Very many monuments of his are seen both in that city and in the neighbouring district, and these are better portrayed by the speech of the natives than by our pen. [Note: [Col. 1101D] “Are portrayed.” c. d. e.; “will be portrayed,” a. s. l.]

§ 135. For these deeds [Note: [Col. 1101D] “These deeds.” c. d. e.; “this deed,” a. s. l.] all Europe proclaimed his praises and exalted his merit to heaven. Foreign kings rightly thought themselves fortunate if they could purchase his friendship either by kinship or by gifts.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] “A certain Harold,” etc. Harold I, surnamed Fairhair, king of Norway. Compare the account of Harold’s embassy to King Æthelstan in 931: Snorri, *Haralds Saga ens Hárfagra*, chs. 41–43, vol. I, pp. 119–121 (*Historia Regum Norvegicorum*, ed. Gerhard Schöning, Copenhagen, 1777).]

A certain Harold, king of the Norwegians, sent him a ship having golden prows and a purple sail, surrounded inside by a dense shell of gilded shields. The names of the envoys were Helgrim and Osfrid. They were received royally in the city of York and had the fatigues of their journey wiped away by fitting rewards. [Note: [Col. 1101D] “The fatigues of their journey.” e.; “the sweats of the journey,” d. m.; “the sweat of the journey,” a. s. c. l.]

Henry the First [Note: [Col. 1101D] Son of Conrad. See above, § 112, note 77.], son of Conrad—for there were many of that name—king of the Germans and emperor of the Romans, asked for Æthelstan’s sister for his son Otto. Passing over so many kings nearby, he had discerned from afar in Æthelstan the nobility of his descent and greatness of spirit. These two qualities had made so harmonious a dwelling in him that none was more illustrious in lineage or more daring and effective in spirit. Therefore, after deliberation, since he had four sisters, among whom there was no difference in beauty except the distinction of age, Æthelstan sent two to the emperor who had asked for them; how he bestowed them in marriage has already been related. [Note: [Col. 1101D] “The narrative has already anticipated this.” See above, §§ 112 and 126.]

The third was joined in lawful marriage to Louis, prince of the Aquitanians, surviving descendant of Charlemagne’s line. [Note: [Col. 1102C] “Louis,” etc. Louis, king of Arles, son of Boso, married Eadgifu, daughter of Edward the Elder.] The fourth, in whom all the concentrated beauty that the others possessed severally had naturally flowed together, was sought from her brother through envoys by Hugh, king of the Franks. [Note: [Col. 1102C] “Hugh, king of the Franks.” Here perhaps one should read “Hugh, duke of the Franks.” For Hugh the Great, count of Paris and son of Robert I, king of the Franks, is so designated in the Frankish chronicles. In A.D. 926 he married Eadhild. (Bouquet, VIII, 289).]

The leader of this embassy was Adulf, son of Baldwin, count of Flanders, by Ethelswith, daughter of King Edward. [Note: [Col. 1102C–D] “By a daughter,” etc. Adulf, or Adalolf, count of Boulogne and Thérouanne and abbot of St Bertin, was the son of Baldwin the Bald, count of Flanders, and Ælfthryth or Elstrude, daughter of King Alfred. He died without issue in November A.D. 933, and was succeeded by his brother Arnulf the Great, count of Flanders.]

When, at an assembly of nobles at Abingdon, he had set out the suitor’s request, he produced gifts truly magnificent, sufficient at once to satisfy the desire of any man, however greedy: aromatic fragrances such as had never before been seen in England; the splendours of gems, especially emeralds, in whose greenness the reflected sun enlivened the eyes of bystanders with delightful light; many swift horses with trappings, “gnawing gold beneath their teeth,” as Maro says [Note: [Col. 1102D] As Virgil says: *Aeneid* VII.279.]; a certain vessel of onyx, carved with such delicate art by the engraver that cornfields seemed truly to wave, vines truly to bud, and human figures truly to move; so bright and polished that it rivalled a mirror in reflecting the faces of those who looked upon it; the sword of Constantine the Great, upon which the name of its ancient possessor was read in golden letters; and on its hilt, above thick plates of gold, one might see an iron nail fastened—one of the four with which the Jewish party had fitted the Lord’s body for execution; the spear of Charlemagne, which that most unconquered emperor, when leading his army against the Saracens, never hurled against an enemy without departing victorious.

It was said to be the same spear which, thrust by the hand of a centurion into the Lord’s side, opened Paradise to wretched mortals through the opening of the precious wound. [Note: [Col. 1102D] “Into the Lord’s side,” etc. “According to the legend of St Longinus, this is the centurion mentioned in the Gospel who pierced the side of our Lord. See Jacobus de Voragine, *Legenda Sanctorum*.” (Sharpe, 156.)] Also there was the banner of Maurice, most blessed martyr and leader of the Theban legion, by which the same king, in the Spanish war [Note: [Col. 1103C] “Spanish.” c. d. e. l.; “Hispanic,” a. s.], was accustomed to break through however hostile and closely packed the enemy’s formations and force them to flee.

[Note: [Col. 1102D] “Maurice,” etc. The history of the martyrdom of St Maurice and the Theban legion in the third century seems apocryphal; it was first issued around the middle of the fifth century by Eucherius, bishop of Lyons. See the discussion of this matter in *Bibliothèque raisonnée*, vol. XXXV, pp. 427–454.]

There was a diadem, of much gold indeed but more precious because of its jewels; their brilliance cast beams of light upon those looking at them, so that the more eagerly anyone strove to fix his gaze upon it, the more he was forced back by the reflected radiance. There was a small piece of the holy and adorable Cross enclosed in crystal, where the eye, penetrating the solidity of the stone, could discern the colour and quantity of the wood; and likewise a small piece of the crown of thorns enclosed in the same manner, which military fury placed upon that most holy head in mockery of kingship.

Delighted by gifts so great and so carefully wrought, the most magnificent king answered with benefits scarcely less great. Indeed, he refreshed the eager mind of the envoy by the marriage of his sister. [Note: [Col. 1103C] “And.” a. s. c. d. l; omitted in e. “And the rest.” Something seems to be missing from the text here. All manuscripts agree.] He enriched his successor kings with the rest. [Note: [Col. 1103D] “Enriched.” d. e. m.; “endowed,” a. s. c. l.] But he assigned the portion of the Cross and Crown to Malmesbury, whose support, I believe, has kept that place alive even now despite so many shipwrecks of liberty and so many wrongs inflicted by persecutors. [Note: [Col. 1103D] “Whose.” s. d. e. l.; “whose [feminine],” a. c. “Place.” d. e. m.; “that place,” a. s. c. l.] There also he ordered the honourable burial of Elwin and Ethelwin, sons of his uncle Æthelweard, whom he had lost in the battle against Anlaf, [Note: [Col. 1103D] In the battle against Anlaf: the battle at Brunanburh, A.D. 938.] declaring that his own body too would rest there.

It is time to set down concerning that battle the judgment of the poet from whom we have extracted all these things:

> He had passed five and three and four years,  
> ruling his subjects by right, subduing tyrants by his valour,  
> when that plague, that ruin destructive to Europe, returned.  
> Now the savage barbarism of the north lies prostrate on the ground;  
> now, pirate no longer at sea, Anlaf lies stretched upon the field,  
> breathing unlawful and grim threats.  
> The northern land gives ready assent  
> to the raging fury, with the king of the Scots willing;  
> and already they swell with great pride, already they terrify the air with words;  
> the natives yield, the whole region yields to the proud.  
> For because our king, confident and buoyant in youth,  
> had long since, as one who had earned it, worn away his sluggish leisure,  
> they were defiling everything with continual plundering,  
> harrying the wretched and setting fire to the fields.  
> The green grass had withered over all the plains;  
> the sickly crop mocked the farmers’ hope.  
> So great was the force of foot-soldiers, so barbarous the mass of horsemen,  
> with the clash of innumerable four-footed beasts.  
> At last the complaint of fame summoned the king,  
> lest he should suffer himself to be branded by such a cautery—  
> that his arms had yielded to barbarian steel.  
> No delay: he unfurls a hundred fierce banners to the wind,  
> leading victorious cohorts.  
> The raw valour of a hundred thousand men  
> accompanies the foremost standards to the field of war.  
> The renowned fame of those coming terrified the robbers.  
> [Note: [Col. 1103D] “Terrified,” etc. d. e. read: “This noise,” etc.; a. s. l. transpose this verse with the following one; c. omits the second.]  
> This noise moved the legions of plunderers  
> so that, laying aside their booty, they sought their own lands.  
> But the remaining multitude, destroyed in pitiable slaughter,  
> infected the moisture-laden air with foul stench.  
> Anlaf fled, one only out of so many thousands,  
> a prize withdrawn from death, a noble gift of Fortune,  
> destined after Æthelstan to give weight to events.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] “Subjects”: a gloss in e., or “English.” “Tyrants”: a gloss in e., or “Britons.” “Not”: d. e.; “nor,” a. s. c. l. “Fame”: a. s. c. d. e.; *turma* (“troop”) written above in l. “Withdrawn”: a. s. c. d. l.; “restored,” e. “Noble”: a. c. d. e. l.; “changeable,” s.]

§ 136. This place seems to require that I set forth, in the king’s own words, the death [Note: [Col. 1104C] “Death.” a. c. d. e. l.; “beginning,” s.] of Elfred, concerning whom above I bound myself by the assurance of a promised account. [Note: [Col. 1104C] “Concerning whom I bound myself above …” See above, § 131.] For since he had ordered the bodies of his kinsmen to be taken to Malmesbury and buried at the head of St Aldhelm’s tomb, he thereafter honoured that place so greatly that he held nothing more sacred. [Note: [Col. 1104C–D] “That he held nothing more sacred.” d. e. m.; after *ut*, a. s. c. l. read “nothing more desirable.”] He granted it many estates and confirmed them by charters, in one of which he added, after the donation:

## ON THE DEATH OF ELFRED, ÆTHELSTAN’S RIVAL

§ 137. “Let the wise men [Note: [Col. 1104D] “Wise men.” a. s. e. l.; “those present,” d. m.; “nations,” c.] of our realm know that we [Note: [Col. 1104D] “We.” c. e. l.; “not,” a. s. d. m.] have not unjustly seized these aforesaid lands [Note: [Col. 1104D] “Lands.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; omitted in c.] or given robbery to God; but I received them as all the nobles of the kingdom of the English, and moreover John, apostolic pope of the Roman church, judged, after the death of Elfred, who proved an enemy to my prosperity and life, consenting to the wickedness of our enemies when, after my father’s death, they wished to blind me in the city of Winchester, unless God in His mercy had rescued me.

[Note: [Col. 1104D] “John.” John XI was consecrated on 20 March A.D. 931 and died in January A.D. 936.]

“But when their plots had been exposed, he was sent to the Roman church in order to defend himself there by oath before John, the apostolic pope. [Note: [Col. 1104D] “Sent.” c. d. e. m.; “sent back,” a. s. l.] And this he did before the altar of St Peter; but after taking the oath he fell before the altar, and was carried in the hands of his servants to the English School. [Note: [Col. 1105C] The school of Saxons living at Rome was situated near the church of St Peter. See above, § 109, note.] There, on the third night, he ended his life.

“Then the pope sent to us and asked our counsel what should be done with him: whether his body should be buried with the other Christians. When these things had been done and reported to us, the nobles of our realm, together with a company of his relatives, most humbly begged that, by our permission, his body might be laid with the bodies of Christians. We, consenting to their entreaty, sent word to Rome, and, with the pope’s consent, he was laid among the other Christians, although unworthy. Thus all his possessions, great and small, were adjudged to me. And we have set down these things in written characters lest they be erased while Christendom endures. Therefore the aforesaid possession, which I have given to God and St Peter, is granted to me; nor do I know anything more just than to give this possession to God and St Peter, who caused my rival to fall in the sight of all and granted me the prosperity of the kingdom.”

§ 138. From these words of the king it is proper to perceive both his wisdom and his piety in matters concerning God: his wisdom, because, especially while still young, he perceived that an offering from plunder is not pleasing to God; his piety, because he gratefully repaid chiefly to God the gift bestowed by divine vengeance. Moreover, it should be observed that the church of St Peter was then pre-eminent over the monastery, though it is now regarded as second; whereas the church of blessed Mary, now frequented by the monks, was built later, in the days of King Edgar, under Abbot Elfric.

[Note: [Col. 1105C–1106D] “Built.” a. s. d. e. l. m.; after “built,” e. reads: “What esteem he enjoyed among the Franks, both amid the toils of war and in Christian devotion, is shown no little by the letter which I append. To the glorious and munificent King Æthelstan, in honour of the supreme and undivided Trinity and through the most excellent intercession of all the saints, I, Rohbod, provost of the supreme pontiff Samson, wish the glory of this world and the blessedness of eternity. Let your goodness understand clearly, most pious King Æthelstan, and most renowned above all earthly kings of this age in the praise of your kindness and exalted rank, that, while our region still stood secure, your father Edward by letter commended himself to the fellowship of the brotherhood of St Samson, chief confessor, and of the venerable Archbishop Leuenan, my cousin, and of his clergy. Therefore, even to this day, we pour forth unwearied prayers to Christ the King for the salvation of his soul and for your salvation; and day and night, seeing your great mercy plainly manifested toward us, I and my twelve canons promise to pray to merciful God for you in our psalms, Masses, and prayers, as though we were prostrate at your knees. And now I send you relics, which we know to be dearer to you than every earthly splendour: namely, the bones of St Senator, St Paternus, and St Scubilion, the master of that same Paternus, who likewise departed to Christ on one and the same day and hour with the aforesaid Paternus. These two saints certainly lay in the tomb with St Paternus, one on his left and one on his right; and their feasts, like that of Paternus, are celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. Therefore, glorious king, exalted patron of the holy Church, humbler of corrupt paganism, mirror of your realm, example of every goodness, scatterer of enemies, father of clerics, helper of the needy, lover of all saints, invoker of angels: we beseech and humbly implore you, as we dwell in France in exile and captivity because of our merits and sins, that the abundant great mercy of your prosperity may not forget us.”

“This is the letter. The king, however, entrusted the relics of blessed Paternus to Malmesbury, and those of the others to Milton, whose monastery he had founded from its foundations. For at that time, as I said above, when the pirates of the Northmen were ravaging the entire sea-coast and also the cities situated upon the Loire, the bodies of saints, transported from Lesser Brittany and from that part of Gaul now called Normandy and brought to safer places, were readily available for sale to anyone because of the scarcity of bearers—especially to Æthelstan, a king of great renown and exceedingly eager for such things.”]

I have written these things concerning the king in full good faith. What follows I have learned rather from songs worn down through the succession of ages than from books laboriously composed for the instruction [Note: [Col. 1106D] “Instruction.” a. c. d. e. l.; “institution,” s.] of posterity. [Note: [Col. 1106D] “Of posterity.” s. e. l.; “of descendants,” a. c. d. m.] I have added them, therefore, not to defend their truth, but lest I cheat readers of knowledge; and first, an account of his birth must be given.

## ON ÆTHELSTAN’S BIRTH AND THE KILLING OF HIS BROTHER EDWIN

§ 139. In a certain village there was a shepherd’s daughter, a girl of elegant appearance who, because birth had bestowed nothing upon her, won favour through the grace of her beauty. In a dream a marvel was shown to her: the moon shone forth from her womb, and by this light all England was illuminated. When in the morning she related this in play to her companions, they did not receive it as a joke but immediately reported it to the ears of the female estate-steward, who used to nurse the king’s children. The woman investigated the matter, received the girl into her household, and treated her as a daughter; she trained the young maiden in finer clothing, more delicate food, and more graceful manners.

Not long afterward Edward, son of King Alfred, passing through the village by chance in the course of a journey, turned aside to the house familiar to him from the beginnings of childhood. For he did not think it consistent with his reputation to disdain greeting his nurse. [Note: [Col. 1106D] “His nurse.” c. d. e. l.; “the nurse,” a. s. “Greeting.” a. s. d. e. m.; “visiting,” c.] There, captivated by love at the sight of the maiden, he asked to spend the night. She conceived in a single embrace; and when she bore a son, Æthelstan, she fulfilled the truth of the dream. For when he passed beyond childhood into adolescence, he gave great hope of royal character, proved by outstanding deeds.

Accordingly, when King Edward died, his son Edward, born of a lawful wife, swiftly followed his father in death. Then, when all hopes had been raised toward Æthelstan, Elfred alone—a man of great arrogance—with his followers secretly resisted as long as he could, disdaining to submit to a lord whom he had not chosen by his own will. [Note: [Col. 1107C] “Elfred.” See above, §§ 136–137. “Resisted.” a. s. c. d. l.; “restored,” e.] When he had been betrayed and put to death, as the king related above, [Note: [Col. 1107C] “Put to death.” a. s. e. l.; “examined,” c. d. m.] there were some who accused the king’s brother Edwin of plotting: a horrid and shameful crime, that they should disturb brotherly devotion by malicious interpretation.

Edwin, appealing personally and through intermediaries to his brother’s loyalty and, though refuting the accusation by an oath, was driven into exile. The whispering of certain men had so much influence upon a mind stretched by many anxieties that, forgetting the tie of blood, he expelled a youth pitied even by strangers. The manner of cruelty was indeed unheard of: Edwin was ordered to board a ship alone with an armour-bearer, empty of rower [Note: [Col. 1107C] “Rower.” c. e. l.; “without a rower,” a. s. d.] and oars, and besides battered by age. [Note: [Col. 1107C] “Battered.” c. d. e. l.; “shattered,” a. s.]

For a long time fortune struggled to restore the innocent man to land. But when at last, in mid-sea, the sails could not withstand the fury of the winds, he—delicate as a youth and weary of life in such circumstances [Note: [Col. 1107C–D] “By voluntary …” Edwin was drowned at sea in A.D. 933. Simeon of Durham adds that this was done by Æthelstan’s command.]—voluntarily sought death by throwing himself into the water. The armour-bearer, by a sounder resolve permitting his life to continue, now evaded the waves, now rowed with his feet, and brought his master’s body to shore: namely, across the narrow sea from Dover to Wissant.

After his anger had cooled, Æthelstan, his mind calmed, recoiled from the deed. Having undertaken seven years of penance, he courageously took revenge upon his brother’s accuser. This man was the king’s cupbearer and thus well placed to persuade the king of whatever he devised. On a feast day, as he was serving wine, he slipped with one foot in the middle of the hall but regained his footing with the other. Then, seizing the occasion, he uttered words fateful to himself: “So does brother help brother.” When the king heard it, he ordered the traitor killed, repeatedly reproaching him with the aid his brother would have given, had he lived, and lamenting his death.

§ 140. Although these things concerning the killing of his brother seem plausible, [Note: [Col. 1107D] “Seem.” c. d. e.; “may seem,” a. s. l.] I am the less inclined to confirm them because he showed remarkable solicitousness in his piety toward his remaining brothers. When their father had left them very young, Æthelstan cherished them tenderly in childhood and, when grown, made them partners in his kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1107D] “Made.” a. s. e. g. l.; “making,” c. k.; after “made,” c. d. k. m. read: “He never took care to marry for their sake.”] It has been read above how greatly he advanced his sisters in dignity, [Note: [Col. 1107D] “His sisters.” c. d. e. m.; “sisters,” a. s. g. l.] whom their father had left both unmarried and without dowries. [Note: [Col. 1107D] “Them.” c. d. e. m.; omitted in a. s. g. l.]

When his life’s term ended—indeed prematurely—Æthelstan died at Gloucester. [Note: [Col. 1107D] “When his life’s term ended … Æthelstan died at Gloucester.” Æthelstan died at Gloucester on Wednesday, 27 October 941.] His triumphant remains were taken to Malmesbury and buried beneath the altar. Many offerings of silver and gold were carried before the body, together with relics of saints bought from Britain across the sea. As is reported, he had been warned in a dream [Note: [Col. 1107D] “Is reported.” e.; “are reported,” a. s. c. d. l.] to spend on such things his father’s treasures, which his father had long amassed and left untouched. [Note: [Col. 1107D] “For on such things he spent his father’s treasures …” See § 138, note 65.] A man who lived little in years, but greatly in glory.

## ON KING EDMUND THE FIRST

§ 141. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 940, Edmund, Æthelstan’s brother, a young man about eighteen years old, held the kingdom for six and a half years.

[Note: [Col. 1107D] “Nine hundred and forty.” Here Malmesbury follows the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle; but it seems more probable that Edmund the First-born succeeded in 941. Yet a charter of Edmund survives dated A.D. 940, indiction XIII (Cott. MSS., Aug. II. LXII).]

In his time the Northumbrians, plotting renewed warfare, broke the treaty which they had made with Æthelstan and established as king Anlaf, recalled from Ireland. [Note: [Col. 1108C] “Anlaf,” etc. In 941 the Northumbrians, breaking the treaty made with Æthelstan, chose as king Anlaf, recalled from Ireland. (*Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* and Florence of Worcester.)] But Edmund, thinking it a disgrace if he did not pursue the remains of his brother’s victory, led forces against the deserters. When they soon gave place, he reduced to his authority all the cities on this side of the river Humber. [Note: [Col. 1108C] “All the cities,” etc. In 942 Edmund recovered the five boroughs after expelling the Danes—Leicester, Lincoln, Nottingham, Stamford, and Derby—and brought all Mercia under his dominion.]

Anlaf, together with a certain petty king, Ragnald, [Note: [Col. 1108D] “Ragnald.” Ragnald was the son of Guthferth, whom Æthelstan expelled from Northumbria in 927. See above, § 131, note 81.] son of that Gormund whom we mentioned in the deeds of Alfred, testing the king’s disposition, offered his submission, professing Christianity as a pledge of his faith. [Note: [Col. 1108D] “His submission.” c. d. e. l.; omitted in a. s. “Christianity … professing.” Anlaf first, and shortly afterward Ragnald, received baptism in 943 while held in the power of King Edmund.] But the barbarian spirit did not remain long in this resolution, but broke its oath and provoked its lord; for that reason, expelled in the following year, he paid the penalty of perpetual exile. [Note: [Col. 1108D] “Expelled in the following year.” In 944 King Edmund expelled both kings, Anlaf son of Sihtric and Ragnald son of Guthferth, from Northumbria. See above, § 134, note 15.] The province called Cumberland was entrusted to Malcolm, king of the Scots, under the obligation of an oath of fidelity. [Note: [Col. 1108D] “To Malcolm, king of the Scots,” etc. In A.D. 945, according to the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*, King Edmund granted the province called Cumberland to Malcolm, king of the Scots, on condition that he adhere faithfully to him by land and sea. Florence of Worcester: “that he might be faithful to him by land and sea.”]

§ 142. [Note: [Col. 1109C] “Meanwhile.” The following two sections, 142 and 143, occur in s. c2 (13 B. XIX), d. e. f. k. m., but are omitted in a, c1 (Harl. 447), h. g. l.] Among the benefits which he conferred upon various churches, he raised the church of Glastonbury with great estates and honours in extraordinary affection, and granted it the following privilege:

[Note: [Col. 1109C] “These.” s. d. e.; “the rest,” f. “He granted in these words.” Malmesbury, *De Antiquitate Glastoniensis Ecclesiae* (Gale, III, 318).]

§ 143. “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Edmund, king of the English and governor and ruler of the other nations dwelling around [Note: [Col. 1109D] *Dwelling around them*, d. e. m.; omitted in s. c 2.], with the counsel and consent of my nobles, for the hope of eternal recompense and the remission of my sins, grant to the church [Note: [Col. 1109D] *Church*, d. e. m.; *holy church*, s. c 2.] of Mary, Mother of God, at Glastonbury, and to the venerable man Dunstan [Note: [Col. 1109D] Whom he appointed abbot there. St Dunstan was appointed abbot of Glastonbury in A.D. 942 (Florence of Worcester), or A.D. 943 (Saxon Chronicle). Compare Bridferth, *Life of St Dunstan*, *Acta Sanctorum*, 19 May.], whom I have appointed abbot there, liberty and authority, rights, customs, and all forfeitures throughout all their lands—that is, *burhgerihta* [borough-rights], and *hundred setena* [hundred-court sittings], oaths, and ordeals, and *infangenetheof* [jurisdiction over a thief caught within the estate], *hamsocn* [penalty for house-breaking], and *friðbryce* [breach of the peace], and *forestall* [forestalling], and toll and team [the right to take toll and to prove title to goods], throughout all my kingdom; and may their lands be free and quit to them from every claim, as my own are held to be free and quit to me.

“But especially may the very township of Glastonbury, in which stands the most renowned ancient church of the holy Mother of God, be freer than all others, together with its boundaries. Authority shall belong solely to its abbot [Note: [Col. 1109D] *Authority shall belong*, s. d. e. m.; omitted in c 2.], alike in known causes and unknown, in small matters and great, and also in those things which are above and beneath the earth, in dry places and streams, in woods and plains; and he shall possess the same authority for punishing and pardoning offences committed there [Note: [Col. 1109D] *There*, s. c 2. d. m.; omitted in e.] as my court possesses, just as my predecessors granted and confirmed by ordinance—namely, Edward [Note: [Col. 1109D] *Edward*, s. d. e. m.; omitted in c 2.], my father; Alfred [Note: [Col. 1109D] *Alfred*, s. d. e. m.; *Ethelfred*, c 2.], his father; Kentwine, Ine, and Cuthred; and many others besides, who, honouring that place, held it glorious.

“And, lest any mortal—whether bishop, ealdorman, prince, or any of their officers—should dare in any way to enter it for the purpose of holding a plea, seizing anything, or doing anything that could be contrary to those serving God there, I forbid it under God’s prohibition. Whoever, therefore, with kindly intent shall endeavour to enlarge my gift, may he in this present age enjoy a prosperous and happy life, and the joys of long life [Note: [Col. 1109D] *Life*, d. e. m.; omitted in s. c 2.]. But if anyone, through his own rashness, should presume violently to invade it, let him know that he will without doubt stand trembling and wavering before the tribunal of the strict Judge to render account, unless he first chooses to make amends through fitting satisfaction.”

This aforesaid grant was made in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 944, in the second indiction [Note: [Col. 1109D] *In the second indiction*, c 2. d. f. m.; omitted in e; *in the first indiction*, s.]; and it was written in letters of gold in the book of the Gospels which he offered to that church, fashioned with considerable elegance.

§ 144. [Note: [Col. 1109D] “But … received.” Present in a. s. c 2. d. e. l. m.; omitted in c 1, but apparently inserted by the same hand that wrote the remainder.] But a pitiable end marred such great and fortunate successes (A.D. 946). A certain robber, Leof [Note: [Col. 1110C] *Leof*, s. c. d. e. m.; *Leva*, a. l.], whom he had banished for robbery, returned after six years. At the feast of St Augustine [Note: [Col. 1110C] *Augustine*, a. c. d. e. l. m.; *Augustine, apostle of the English*, s.], archbishop of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 1110C] *Archbishop*, a. c. d. e. l. m.; *the first archbishop*, s.], he unexpectedly took a seat among the royal guests at Pucklechurch [Note: [Col. 1110D] *Pukelechirche*, e.; *Pugrescerne*, d.; *Puchelecerce*, c.; *Pulchresecerne*, a.; *Pukelecerne*, l.—Pucklechurch, in Gloucestershire.], on the day when the English customarily made festive provision in memory of their preacher. By chance he lay beside an ealdorman whom the king himself had honoured with portions from the supper.

He alone noticed him, while the others were revelling in foaming wine. His anger was thus stirred; and, as fate drove him, he sprang from the table, seized the robber by the hair, and dashed him to the ground. The other secretly drew a dagger from its sheath and, with all the force he could muster, drove it into the breast of the king lying over him. [Note: [Col. 1110D] “From this wound,” etc. Edmund was killed by Leofa on the feast of St Augustine, Wednesday, 26 May, in the fourth indiction, A.D. 946 (Florence of Worcester; the Chronicle of Flodoard; certain manuscripts of the Saxon Chronicle). According to other authorities, however, it was Friday, 26 May, A.D. 948 (the Laud or Peterborough manuscript of the Saxon Chronicle; Symeon of Durham; the Chronicle of Æthelweard; *Life of St Cuthbert*; MS Cotton Nero A. II). A charter of his successor Eadred survives, dated A.D. 947, fifth indiction (MSS Cotton Augustus II, 83).] Slain by that wound, he opened throughout all England the way for the report of his death. The robber too, when the guards immediately rushed together, was cut limb from limb, though first he wounded several men.

Blessed Dunstan, then abbot of Glastonbury, had foreseen so disgraceful an end from the antics and buffoonish clapping of a devil dancing before him. Therefore, as he hastened on a swift horse toward the court, he received news of what had happened in the middle of the journey. [Note: [Col. 1110D] *Received*, s. c. d. e. f. k. m.; after *received*, a. g. h. l. read: “and, taking up the body, he buried it at Glastonbury.”] Thus it was decreed by common counsel that the funeral should be brought to Glastonbury, and there he was magnificently buried on the north side of the tower. That he had desired this, out of his familiar friendship with the abbot, had been made evident by several signs: the estate in which he had died was bestowed as a funeral offering, so that it, having once been conscious of the murder, might thereafter always assist his soul by its benefaction. [Note: [Col. 1111C] “By common counsel … benefaction.” Present in s. c. d. e. f. k. m.; omitted in a. g. h. l.]

§ 145. In his fourth year, that is, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 944 [Note: [Col. 1111C] *Nine hundred and forty-four.* Authorities of better credit assign the murder of William, duke of the Normans, to 17 December, A.D. 943.], William, son of Rollo, duke of the Normans [Note: [Col. 1111C] He was treacherously killed in France. Compare William of Jumièges, Book III, chapters 10, 11, 12; the Chronicle of Saint-Bertin by John of Ypres, chapter 23; and the Chronicle of St Martin of Tours (from the Thuan Library, ed. the brothers du Chesne, vol. III, p. 358).], was killed by treachery in France. The elders relate that this did not happen undeservedly.

For Riulf, one of the nobles of the Norman people [Note: [Col. 1111D] *Of the Norman people*, c. d. e.; *of Normandy*, a. s. l.], having quarrelled with William for some reason unknown to me, harassed him with many attacks. His son Anschetillus was in the count’s service, and, wishing to please his lord, dared to violate nature itself by taking his father prisoner in single combat [Note: [Col. 1111D] *Duello*, s. e. l.; *duellio*, a. c. d.] and delivering him into the count’s power, trusting in the strongest oath that his father would suffer no injury beyond imprisonment. But, as wickedness is always devising causes of evil, after no long time, when an opportunity presented itself, the count sent Anschetillus to Pavia carrying a letter concerning his own death to the duke of Italy.

Having completed the journey and entered the city, he was magnificently received. When the letter was handed over, the duke froze in astonishment at the plot, because a knight of distinguished eminence was ordered to be killed. Yet, because he judged that it would not be prudent for this to recoil upon a count of such great renown, he set an ambush, reportedly of a thousand horsemen, for Anschetillus after he had left the city. There Anschetillus, with the companions whom he had brought from all Normandy as its choicest men, long resisted their violence; but at last, repaying his own death with the slaughter of many, he fell not without courage.

Balzo the Norman alone survived on either side, a man of small body but immense strength. Though some say mockingly that he was called “the Short,” he alone, I say, besieged the city; he alone terrified the citizens with his sword, so long as he thought fit. No one will judge this incredible who reflects how greatly the desperation of a bold man can achieve, and how little those provincials avail in battle.

Returning home, he lodged before the king of France a complaint concerning his lord’s treachery; for rumour also reported that Riulf had been blinded in chains. He was therefore summoned to judgment at Paris, and cut down by Balzo, who met him under the appearance [Note: [Col. 1111D] *Appearance*, s. c. d. e. m.; *hope*, a. l.] of a conference. In the middle of the Seine [Note: [Col. 1111D] Rather, the Somme.], as they say, he paid the price for his treachery and Balzo’s anger. His death produced a long discord between the French and Normans, until it was brought to an end, through the exertions of his son Richard, in a manner worthy of Richard’s valour. [Note: [Col. 1111D] “More truthful writings,” etc. William of Jumièges relates that, after Arnulf, count of Flanders, had invaded the castle of Montreuil, belonging to a certain Count Herluin, Herluin sought the aid of William, duke of the Normans. A conference between the duke and Arnulf was held at Picquigny near the Somme, where Balzo le Court, who was the count’s chamberlain, perpetrated the duke’s murder (Bouquet, IX, 78).]

More truthful writings, however, say that he had incurred hostilities with Arnulf, count of Flanders, and seized one of his castles. Arnulf summoned him to a conference under a pretence of wishing for peace; and, after discussion had begun aboard a ship, he was killed by Balzo. A key found at his belt, which fitted the lock of his private chest, gave proof from the monastic garments wrapped within [Note: [Col. 1111D] *Within*, a. s. c. d. l. m.; omitted in e.] that he had always intended, amid warfare, to become a monk [Note: [Col. 1111D] *Proof*, a. s. c. d. l.; *indititim* [uncertain], e.] at Jumièges. This place, deserted since the time of Hasting, he himself had cleared of thorny undergrowth and raised by princely patronage to its present condition. [Note: [Col. 1111D] *Monk*, a. d. e. m.; *now*, s. c. l.]

## CONCERNING KING EADRED

§ 146. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 946 [Note: [Col. 1112C] *Nine hundred and forty-six.* According to Florence of Worcester, Eadred was anointed at Kingston by Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, on Sunday, 16 August, A.D. 946. Some authors assign his coronation to A.D. 948. See §144, note.], Eadred, the third of Edward’s sons, assumed the kingdom and reigned nine and a half years. His greatness of spirit, not inferior to that of his father and brothers, produced this result: he easily compelled the Northumbrians and Scots to swear allegiance to him; but when they soon broke faith and set a certain King Eric [Note: [Col. 1112D] King Eric. Snorri relates that Erik Bloodaxe, son of Harald, king of Norway, received Northumbria from King Æthelstan (*Saga of Hákon the Good*, ch. 3, p. 127). Nothing certain is known concerning the time when Erik came to the throne or died. Northern historians assign his deposition from Norway to A.D. 938, his acceptance of the Norwegian kingdom to A.D. 939, and his death to A.D. 952. Compare the Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 948–954. From that time Northumbria was governed by earls, whose catalogue is found in Hoveden.] over themselves, he almost annihilated them, devastating the entire province with famine and sword.

Wulstan, archbishop of York, who was said to connive at his countrymen’s defection, he kept long in chains; later, out of regard for clerical dignity, he pardoned and released him. Meanwhile, he devoted his life to God and Dunstan, falling at the feet of the saints; instructed by Dunstan’s counsels, he patiently endured frequent bodily torments [Note: [Col. 1112D] *Torments.* Bridferth, in his *Life of St Dunstan*, portrays Eadred as suffering from an internal disorder, so that at meals he could swallow only the juice of meat, and was compelled to spit out even that, to the great discomfort of his fellow diners (*Acta Sanctorum*, 19 May). From this probably arose the absurd tale, recounted by Wallingford in his *Chronicles*, that King Eadred, being unable in advanced age to chew food because his teeth had failed, and finding the broths prepared to sustain his life inadequate, died of hunger.], persisted in prayer, and made his palace wholly a training-ground of virtues.

[Note: [Col. 1113C] *He died.* Eadred died at Frome on 23 November—A.D. 955 according to Florence of Worcester; A.D. 955–956 according to the Saxon Chronicle; and A.D. 957 according to the calculation in Æthelweard’s chronicle. Tyrrell observes that “this king did not die without issue, as many suppose, and that his two sons, Elfrid and Berefrid, were witnesses in confirming old charters cited by Speed.”] He died amid great mourning of men, but attended by the rejoicing of angels. For Dunstan, hearing that he was ill, spurred his swift horse toward him and heard a voice thundering from above: “King Eadred has now fallen asleep in the Lord.” He rests at Winchester, in the bishopric.

## CONCERNING KING EADWIG

§ 147. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 955 [Note: [Col. 1113D] *Nine hundred*, etc. Eadwig’s accession is assigned to 955 in several manuscripts of the Saxon Chronicle, but to 956 in others.], Eadwig, son of the above-mentioned King Edmund [Note: [Col. 1113D] *Edmund*, c. d. e. l.; *Edmund, brother of Æthelstan*, a. s.], gained the kingdom and held it for four years. He was a wanton young man who abused the beauty [Note: [Col. 1113D] *Beauty*, s. c. e.; *under the guise of beauty*, a. d. l. m.] of his body in lusts. Finally, he took as wife a close kinswoman, whose beauty he passionately desired, and despised the counsels of the wise.

On the very day on which he was consecrated king [Note: [Col. 1113D] *Consecrated*, e.; *had been consecrated*, a. s. c. d. l.], while a very full assembly of nobles was discussing serious matters necessary to the kingdom, he burst from their midst, as if in sport, into the dining-room and collapsed in the embrace of a harlot. [Note: [Col. 1113D] “Into the embrace,” etc. This story is told in all the Lives of St Dunstan. Bridferth alone supplies Ælfgifu’s name; Eadmer and the manuscript *Life of St Dunstan* (MS Cotton Nero E. I) assert that she was “born of a great and lofty family, having an adult daughter with her”; but all agree that there were two women, mother and daughter. Malmesbury retells the same narrative in his *Life of St Dunstan*.] All were indignant at the shameful deed and murmured among themselves.
