Dunstan alone, firm in accordance with his name [Note: [Col. 1113D] *In accordance with the firmness of his name.* A similar expression occurs in Osbern, *Life of St Dunstan*: “but he, according to the etymology of his name, stood immovable as a steadfast mountain.” For in Anglo-Saxon *dun* means “hill,” and *stan*, “stone.”], fearing no royal displeasure, forcibly dragged the lustful youth from the chamber; and Eadwig, compelled through Archbishop Odo to repudiate his concubine [Note: [Col. 1114C] *Through Odo*, etc. According to the Saxon Chronicle, in A.D. 958 Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, separated King Eadwig from Ælfgifu because of their excessively close degree of kinship. Compare Florence of Worcester, A.D. 958.], made Dunstan his permanent enemy.

For Eadwig soon, relying upon wretched attendants, afflicted with unworthy miseries all men of the monastic order throughout England: first stripping them of the aid of their possessions and then driving them into exile. Dunstan himself, the foremost of the monks [Note: [Col. 1114D] He drove him into Flanders. Dunstan, expelled in A.D. 956, was honourably received by Arnulf, count of Flanders. For the location of his exile see Adlard of Blandinium, *Life of St Dunstan*.], he drove into Flanders.

At that time the condition of monasteries was foul and miserable. [Note: [Col. 1114D] “For,” etc. This paragraph occurs almost word for word in Malmesbury, *Life of Aldhelm* (*Anglia Sacra*, Part II, p. 32).] For he made Malmesbury monastery, inhabited by monks for more than 270 years, into a stable for clerics. But you, Lord Jesus, our creator and renewer, good craftsman and greatly able to give form to our deformities through those irregular and wandering men, brought into the light your treasure hidden for so many years: I mean the body of blessed Aldhelm, which they raised from the earth and placed in a shrine. Royal generosity was added to the glory of the clerics, so that it gave the saint an estate well suited in both extent and proximity.

Moreover, my memory shudders deeply at how savage he was toward the other monasteries, both because of the slippery instability of his age and because of the counsel of his concubine, who continually besieged his tender mind. Yet may the soul now long placed in rest forgive my grief, through Dunstan’s intervention. [Note: [Col. 1114D] Through Dunstan’s intercession. The king’s soul is said to have been rescued by St Dunstan’s prayers from demons who were seizing it. See Osbern, *Life of St Dunstan*, in *Anglia Sacra*, Part II, p. 107.] Grief, I say, compels me to condemn him, because private advantage does not take precedence over public injury; indeed, common loss outweighs private benefit.

He paid in this life the penalty of his rash audacity also, being deprived of the greater part of his kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1114D] *The greater part of the kingdom*, etc. The Mercian rebellion occurred in A.D. 957, and Eadgar was elected king by the Mercians.] Struck by this injury, he ended his life [Note: [Col. 1114D] *He ended his life.* Eadwig died on 1 October, A.D. 959.] and was buried at Winchester in the New Minster.

## CONCERNING KING EDGAR

§ 148. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 959, Edgar, the honour and delight of the English, son of Edmund and brother of Eadwig, gained the kingdom as a youth of sixteen and held it for nearly the same number of years. His deeds are celebrated with great splendour even in our own time. During his years the favourable love of the Godhead shone forth, a love which he diligently obtained through devotion of mind and vigour of counsel.

For it is commonly reported that, at Edgar’s birth in A.D. 943 [Note: [Col. 1114D] At his birth, A.D. 943. Compare the *Life of St Dunstan*.], Dunstan received [Note: [Col. 1114D] *Received*, d. e. m.; *did receive*, a. s. c. l.] an angelic voice: “There will be peace in England so long as this boy reigns and our Dunstan lives.” The truth of events answered the heavenly oracle. While they lived, ecclesiastical splendour so flourished and martial tumult so withered that scarcely a year passed in the chronicles in which Edgar did not accomplish some great and necessary thing for his country, or found a new monastery.

He experienced no plots from his subjects and no attack from foreigners. He bound Rinadius, king of the Scots, Malcolm of the Cumbrians, Maccus the arch-pirate [Note: [Col. 1115C] The arch-pirate Maccus. “Maccus, king of very many islands” (Florence of Worcester).], and all the kings of the Welsh—whose names were Dufnal, Giferth, Huual, Jacob, and Judethil—who had been summoned to court, to himself by one perpetual oath. So completely did he do so that, when they met him at the City of the Legions [Note: [Col. 1115C] That is, Chester.], he led them down the River Dee [Note: [Col. 1115C] *He led them down the River Dee*, s. c 2. e. l.; *he led them down the River Deiros*, a. d.; *he led them down the river*, c 1. These events are to be assigned to A.D. 973.] as a display of triumph. Having placed them all in one boat, he himself sat at the prow and compelled them to row; thereby displaying royal magnificence, since he held the power of so many kings subject to himself. It is further said that he declared that only then could his successors glory in being kings of the English, when they enjoyed so great a pre-eminence of honours.

Accordingly, as his fame flew through every mouth, foreigners—Saxons, Flemings, and even Danes themselves—frequently sailed here and became Edgar’s intimates. Their arrival caused great harm to the inhabitants: from the Saxons they learned an uncultivated fierceness of spirit; from the Flemings, enervating softness of body; from the Danes, drinking. Previously men had been uncorrupted in such matters, defended by their native simplicity, and did not admire what belonged to others. For this reason writings deservedly and rightly blame him; the songs merely added colour to the other disgraces which I shall mention later.

## CONCERNING ST DUNSTAN

§ 149. At that time the lights of holy men shone through England, so that one might have believed stars were smiling down from heaven. Among them Dunstan, so often named [Note: [Col. 1115C] Dunstan. The life of St Dunstan seems to have provided monks with a very welcome subject for writing. It was written by Osbern, monk and precentor of Christ Church, Canterbury; Bridferth, monk of Ramsey; Adalard, monk of Blandinium (St Peter’s, Ghent); Eadmer; an anonymous author contemporary with Bridferth; and Malmesbury, in two books not yet published. Dunstan was made abbot of Glastonbury in 942; bishop of Worcester in 957; transferred later that same year to the see of London; designated for the see of Canterbury in 959; and in the following year went to Rome to receive the pallium from Pope John XII (Florence of Worcester).], first abbot of Glastonbury, then bishop of Worcester, and soon archbishop of Canterbury, was mighty in the world and possessed great grace with God: there he displayed Martha, here Mary. He was the remarkable reviver throughout the whole island of liberal studies after King Alfred, and the generous restorer of regular religious houses [Note: [Col. 1115D] *Of regular*, e; *of royal*, a. s. c. d. l. m.]; terrible in rebuking kings and sinful leaders [Note: [Col. 1115D] Toward kings, etc. He imposed a seven-year penance upon King Edgar; among the penalties imposed, he forbade him to wear the crown throughout that period, because he had deflowered Wilfrith, a nun of Wilton. When he found King Eadwig with Ælfgifu, he forcibly dragged him away from his mistress, placed the crown upon his head, and brought him to the archbishop of Canterbury (Osbern, *Life of St Dunstan*).], and just in supporting the poor and those of middling condition.

He was so devoted to peace even in trifling matters that, when his countrymen gathered in taverns and, already drunk, quarrelled about how much they should drink, he ordered silver or gold nails to be fixed into the drinking-vessels, so that, when each knew his limit, shame would prevent him either from desiring more himself or compelling another to desire more. [Note: [Col. 1115D] He himself ordered nails … to be fixed in the vessels, etc. Hence the expression “to drink to the pin.” Yet the custom of drinking to the pin appears to have been brought into England by the Danes, who fixed a pin within the *wassail bowl* (a type of cup); drinking exactly to the pin was an accomplishment attainable only through long practice. Malmesbury elsewhere observes that King Edgar, to curb an excessive appetite for drinking, forbade anyone to drink below the pin in a single draught. He also observes that Archbishop Boniface found drunkenness so common in his day that even bishops, far from resisting it, were addicted to the same appetite. This manner of drunkenness was nevertheless forbidden to clerics at the Council of London in A.D. 1102, where it was decreed that priests should neither attend public drinking-parties nor drink to the pins. See above, §82, note 27.]

Osbern, the cantor of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 1116D] Osbern. The *Life of St Dunstan*, written by Osbern, was published in *Anglia Sacra*, Part II, p. 88, from a manuscript in Lambeth Library; another copy exists in the British Museum (MS Cotton Tiberius D. III, fol. 119), in which almost all of the second book is absent. See also *Acta Sanctorum*, 19 May.], calls me back from saying more, and no contemptible things, about this man. He composed Dunstan’s life with Roman elegance; among writers of our time he is second to none in style, and certainly first of all without dispute in music. At the same time, because, if divine grace accompanies my undertaking, I have resolved after the names of kings at least to run through the names of all the bishops of England in every province, and to set before our contemporaries whatever worthy matter I may succeed in striking from the coinage of antiquity.

Nevertheless, how effective Dunstan was is shown by the holiness and excellence of his disciples. Æthelwold, first a monk of Glastonbury, then abbot of Abingdon, and afterward bishop of Winchester [Note: [Col. 1116D] Æthelwold. Educated under St Dunstan as his master, he was made bishop of Winchester in A.D. 963. He died on 1 August, A.D. 984.], established so many and such great monasteries that it scarcely now appears credible that a bishop of one city could have accomplished things which scarcely the king of all England could have done. I am mistaken, and sin by a rash judgment, if what I say is not manifest. How small are the monasteries of Ely, Peterborough, and Thorney, which he raised from their foundations and completed by his own exertion, and which, though the wickedness of tax-collectors continually harasses them, nevertheless suffice for their inhabitants.

Wulstan, a certain cantor of Winchester, namely his disciple and fosterling, composed Æthelwold’s life in a middling style. [Note: [Col. 1116D] Wulstan wrote his Life. The *Life of Æthelwold* written by Wulstan was published by Mabillon (*Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century V). There is narrated whatever is contained in Ælfric’s *Life of Æthelwold*, often in the same words, though with certain additions not found in the older Life.] He also produced another highly useful work, *On the Harmony of the Tones*, evidence of a learned Englishman, a man of good life and restrained eloquence.

At that time Oswald too [Note: [Col. 1117B] Oswald. Oswald was made bishop of Worcester in A.D. 960 and transferred to the see of York in A.D. 972. He died on 29 February, A.D. 992. His Life, written by Eadmer, was published in *Anglia Sacra*, Part II, p. 191, from a manuscript in Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.], nephew of Archbishop Odo [Note: [Col. 1117B] Odo. Odo was transferred from Worcester to the see of Canterbury in A.D. 934. He died in A.D. 958. Compare *Anglia Sacra*, Part I, p. 101.] (who had preceded Dunstan), first a monk of Fleury, then bishop of Worcester and archbishop of York, earned titles not inferior to the others. For, following the same paths, he enlarged the monastic rule in its rightful domain, and built the monastery of Ramsey in a marshy place. [Note: [Col. 1117B] The monastery of Ramsey. Ælwin, reeve of the town and ealdorman of the East Angles, built Ramsey Abbey at Oswald’s instigation, as appears from Eadmer, *Life of St Oswald*: “The monastery of Ramsey was built from its foundations by his prompting and exertion.”]

He filled the episcopal see at Worcester with regular monks, not by forcibly expelling the clerics but by outmanoeuvring them through holy strategy. [Note: [Col. 1117B] But by holy strategy, etc. When King Edgar had reformed the ecclesiastical communities, Oswald founded a new cathedral church within the enclosure of the old church and installed a prior and monks there. Seeing their own church deserted by the people, the secular canons of the old church soon put on the monastic habit. See Eadmer, *Life of Oswald*, *Anglia Sacra*, Part II, p. 202. Compare Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum*, Book III.] Earlier, by royal command, Æthelwold had expelled the clerics from Winchester. [Note: [Col. 1117C] He had expelled … from Winchester. The secular priests were expelled from the Old Minster at Winchester in A.D. 963 by King Edgar’s command (Thomas Rudborne, *Historia Major Wintoniensis*, *Anglia Sacra*, Part I, p. 218).] Since they had been offered the choice [Note: [Col. 1117C] *The choice having been given them.* Gloss in l.: namely, by the king.] either to live according to rule or to leave the place, they preferred an easy life and then wandered through the whole island with no settled abode.

Thus, while these three men acted, as though a threefold light were making England clear, the thick darkness of vices vanished. [Note: [Col. 1117C] *Vanished.* A. l. omit the entire text from the word *vanished* to §152, “then the monastic order”; c 1 omits all as far as §154, “meanwhile, not unseemly.”] Consequently Edgar enlarged Glastonbury church, which he had always loved above all others, with great possessions; and he watched diligently over everything pertaining to the church’s adornment or advantage, inward as well as outward. The privilege which he granted to that church, moreover, is not inappropriate to insert in this history, as I read it in their ancient schedule. [Note: [Col. 1117C] “Consequently … to insert.” Present in s. c 2. d. e. f. k. m.]

§ 150. “In the name, etc.” [Note: [Col. 1117C] See this charter of King Edgar in Malmesbury, *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury* [Col. 1117D] (GALE, III, 320). The date occurring here is A.D. 971, indiction XIV. Sections 150 and 151 occur in d, e, f, m; they are absent from s, c 2, k, which read in their place: “Edgar, of glorious memory, king of the English, son of King Edmund, whose zeal was especially watchful over divine worship, frequently coming to the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Glastonbury, and striving with the utmost devotion to exalt that place in dignity above all others, granted many and very magnificent privileges, with the common counsel of bishops, abbots, and leading men of the province. The first of these was that no one but a monk of that place should there exercise the name or office of abbot, nor any other than one whom the unanimous assent of the equal community had elected according to the rule. But if necessity should arise for an abbot or monk from another place to be set over it, he decreed that no other should be chosen than one whom the community of that monastery had elected, in the fear of God, to preside over them—provided in every way that this should not occur if anyone there, even the least member of the community, could be found suited to that office. Thus he decreed that the monks’ election of their own abbot should remain perpetual; but he retained for himself and his heirs the power of conferring the pastoral staff upon the brother elected.

“He also enacted that, whenever the abbot of the place or the monks should determine that any of their number were to be distinguished by sacred orders, they should have both monks and clerics whom they judged worthy of the title of Saint Mary ordained by any canonically ordained bishop, either at his see or in the same monastery of Saint Mary at Glastonbury. He also granted that, just as he himself did in his own court, so the abbot or community should settle all causes throughout the whole island, in every ecclesiastical and secular matter, without anyone’s contradiction. Nor should it be lawful for bishop, duke, prince, or any other person of whatever rank to enter that island, conscious of its own birth, in order to do anything that could be contrary [Col. 1118C] to those serving God there; as his predecessors—Cenwines, Ine, Athellard, Cuthred, Alfred, Edward, Athelstan, and Edmund—had enacted and confirmed by privileges, he utterly forbade it.

“Therefore, when he had resolved, as stated, to confer these privileges upon the place with the general consent of his bishops, abbots, and nobles, he placed upon the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, his own crozier, most handsomely fashioned of ivory and adorned with gold; and by its donation he assigned it to the same Mother of God and to her monks for perpetual possession. He immediately caused that same crozier to be cut in half in his presence, lest any subsequent abbot should be able to give or sell it to anyone, commanding that a portion of it be preserved in the place as perpetual testimony to the donation just mentioned.

“Reflecting, however, on the many ways in which the rashness of human levity is accustomed to creep in, and fearing lest someone in future should either take these privileges from that place [Col. 1118D] or attempt to expel the monks from it, he sent this same instrument of royal liberality to the illustrious lord Pope John, who had succeeded Octavian in the honour of government, praying that he also would confirm these provisions by a written decree of apostolic authority. The pope, graciously receiving the embassy sent to him, with the unanimous consent of the Roman council confirmed by writing an ordinance of apostolic authority what they had enacted, fiercely directing against any violators who might arise the punishment of perpetual anathema. Accordingly King Edgar, of pleasing memory, placed likewise upon the altar of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, as a perpetual memorial, the testament sent to that place by the aforesaid apostolic lord, commanding that it be diligently preserved hereafter for the information of all successors. We have thought it fitting to append both documents for this reason, lest we seem to invent such things, against those who seek to break into this sheepfold of Saint Mary not as shepherds through the door, but as thieves and [Col. 1119B] robbers by another way.

“Let all the faithful know that I, John, by the mercy of the pious Creator, though unworthy, pope of the holy Roman see, have been approached by the humble petition of the glorious King Edgar of the English [Col. 1119C] and of Dunstan, archbishop of the holy church of Canterbury, concerning the monastery of Saint Mary, namely Glastonbury. Moved by love for the heavenly King, they had enriched it with many great possessions, multiplied there the rule of monks, and confirmed it by royal ordinance; I too shall not delay to do this. Assenting to their gracious petition, I receive the same place into the bosom of the Roman Church and the protection of the blessed apostles, and establish and strengthen it by privileges: to this end, that it may remain, in the monastic order which it now possesses, and that the monks themselves may appoint from among their own number a pastor for themselves. The ordination both of monks and of clerics shall be at the discretion of the abbot and community.

“We also decree that no person at all may enter that island for the purpose of holding a plea, or of investigating or correcting anything else there. But if anyone should attempt to contravene this, or to take away, retain, diminish, or harass with rash vexations the possessions of that church, by the authority of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of Saint Mary Mother of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints, let him be subjected to perpetual curse, unless he repents. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. And may our undertaking remain unshaken. Done in the time of Ælfweard, abbot of that monastery.”

“Thus the aforesaid King Edgar confirmed by a sacred instrument at London, in the twelfth year of his reign, this charter; and in the same year, the nine hundred and sixty-fifth from the Lord’s Incarnation, Pope John at Rome authorized it in a general synod, and commanded all the men of higher rank who presided over that general council to ratify it. Let those who despise so great a warning, therefore, consider to what sentence of excommunication they are liable; for Christ bestowed upon blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the primacy of binding and loosing and the keys of the kingdom [Col. 1120B] of heaven together. It is plain and evident to all that the president of the Roman Church is the vicar of this apostle and above all the heir of his authority. John, of holy memory, presided over it worthily in his time, and he still flourishes [Col. 1120C] in glorious remembrance, having been raised to it by the election of God and of the whole people.

“If, therefore, the decree of blessed Peter the apostle is valid, then consequently that of Pope John is valid also. But no one, unless mad, denies that the decree of Peter the apostle is valid; therefore no sound-minded person disputes that Pope John’s decree will be otherwise. Accordingly, either these men, acknowledging the authority bestowed by Christ upon blessed Peter and his successors, will cease to violate the authority of so great an interdict; or, despising it, they will acquire for themselves, with the devil and his accomplices, the perpetuity of the curse pronounced above. It is therefore clear that no outsider has seized this monastery for himself without being known to have lost it—nor without disgrace—and that this has befallen each of them not through any contrivance of the monks but through God’s judgment, in vengeance for violation of holy authority. Therefore let no one who reads this despise it; let no one, even in anger, make himself publicly conspicuous. For if he is angry on another’s account, perhaps he will confess that what has been said was spoken of himself.”

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Although the decrees of pontiffs and the words of priests, [Col. 1119A] 241 like the foundations of mountains, are fixed by unshaken bonds, nevertheless the religion of the holy Church of God is often scattered and broken by the storms and tempests of secular affairs, through the stains of the reprobate. Therefore we decree [Note: [Col. 1120D] “We decree”: e; “we have decreed”: d.] that it will be beneficial to succeeding generations for those things determined by sound counsel and common assent to be made firm by confirmation in our little writings. Accordingly, it seems fitting that the church of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, at Glastonbury, as it has from ancient times held the chief dignity in my kingdom, should likewise be honoured by us with a certain special and singular freedom of privilege.

Therefore, at the exhortation of Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and Oswald, archbishop of York, with the consent and approval also of [Note: [Col. 1120D] Brihthelm. At what defined time Brihthelm was promoted to the bishopric of Wells is entirely unknown. He was transferred to the see of Canterbury after the death of Ælfsige—who, travelling to Rome to receive the pallium, was frozen to death by deadly cold among the Alpine ridges—but he held the primacy for only a few days and was removed to the see of Wells. He died 15 May A.D. 973. See *Anglia Sacra*, part I, pp. 101, 556; part II, pp. 109, 682.] [Col. 1119B] Brihthelm, bishop of Wells, and of my other bishops, abbots, and chief men, I, Edgar [Note: [Col. 1120D] “Edgar”: e; “Edgarus”: d.], by divine disposition king of the English and governor and ruler of the other peoples dwelling round about, in the name of the gracious Trinity, for the soul of my father who rests there and of my ancestral forefathers, decree, establish, and confirm by this present privilege that the aforesaid monastery and all its possessions shall remain now and forever free and quit from every tax of fiscal business; and that they shall have sake and soke, on strand, on stream, in wood, in field, and in breach of the peace, in breach of borough-peace, hundred jurisdiction, murders [Note: [Col. 1120D] “Mordas”: e; “murdres”: d.], oaths [Note: [Col. 1120D] “Adas”: e; “hathes”: d.], and ordeals, all treasures [Note: [Col. 1120D] “Above ground and beneath”: e; “above hearth and beneath hearth”: d.] above ground and beneath, the right of taking a thief caught within and a thief caught without, the right concerning fugitives, house-entry, breach of the peace, forsteal, toll, and team, as freely and quietly as I possess them in my kingdom.

I also grant and confirm that the abbot [Note: [Col. 1120D] “Abbot”: e; “abbots”: d.] and monks of the aforesaid monastery shall have in their own court, in every kind of matter, the same liberty and power that I have in my court, both in pardoning and in punishing. If any abbot or monk of that place should meet on the road a thief being led to hanging or to any danger of death, they shall have power to rescue him from the impending danger throughout [Col. 1120B] my entire kingdom.

I also confirm and strengthen that, as has hitherto been diligently observed by all our predecessors, the [Note: [Col. 1120D] Bishop of Wells: Wells in Somersetshire.] bishop of Wells or his officers shall have no authority whatever over this monastery or over its parish churches—namely Street, Meare, Budgellage, Shapwick, and Sowy—or over their chapels, nor even over those situated in the islands, namely Beckery, which is called Little Ireland, Godney, Martinsey, Pathenberge, Edredesey, and Ferrymere, [Col. 1121A] except only when summoned by the abbot for the purpose of dedication or ordination. Nor shall they summon their priests to their synod, chapter, or any court; nor suspend them from divine office; nor presume to exercise any right at all over them.

In accordance with the ancient custom of the church of Glastonbury and with apostolic authority, with the assent of Archbishop Dunstan and all the bishops of my kingdom, the abbot shall cause his monks and the clerics of the aforesaid churches to be ordained by whatever bishop of the province he chooses. We permit, however, their dedications to the bishop of Wells, if he is requested by the abbot. At Easter the abbot shall also receive consecrated chrism and oil, according to custom, from the bishop of Wells and distribute them through his aforesaid churches.

But this especially I forbid, by God’s prohibition and our authority—while preserving, nevertheless, the dignity of the holy Roman Church and of Canterbury—that any person possessing power, whether king, bishop, duke, prince, or any of my officers, shall presume to enter the bounds of Glastonbury or of the aforesaid parishes for purposes of investigation, seizure, litigation, or doing anything else which could be contrary to those serving God there. Authority in known and unknown causes, in small and great matters, and in every matter whatsoever, as we have stated above, shall belong only to the abbot and the community.

But whoever henceforth, under any pretext and whatever his dignity, rank, or profession, should attempt by sacrilegious presumption to subvert or render void [Col. 1121C] the force of this my privilege, let him know beyond doubt that he will stand trembling and wavering before the strict Judge to render account, unless he first strives to amend matters by fitting satisfaction.”

The aforesaid King Edgar confirmed this charter by a sacred instrument at London, with the common counsel of his nobles, in the twelfth year of his reign. In that same year, the nine hundred and sixty-fifth from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth indiction [Note: [Col. 1121D] The nine hundred and sixty-fifth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction fourteen, corresponds to A.D. 971, indiction XIV, as it also does to the twelfth year of Edgar’s reign.], Pope [Note: [Col. 1121D] John: John XIII, Roman pontiff, presided from 965 until 5 September A.D. 972.] John authorized this same charter at Rome in a general synod, and caused all the men of higher [Col. 1121D] dignity who presided over that council to confirm it. Moved by fatherly compassion, he also sent the following letter to Duke Ælfric, who was grievously persecuting the aforesaid church:

§ 151. “John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ælfric, illustrious duke, our most beloved spiritual son: continual greeting and apostolic blessing. [Col. 1122A] From the report of certain faithful persons, we have learned that you are committing very many evils against the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, called Glastonbury, which is the first in all [Note: [Col. 1121D] “Britain”: e; “England,” [lacuna].] Britain and is known from ancient leaders to belong to the possession and protection of the Roman pontiff. We have learned that, in greedy covetousness, you have torn from its jurisdiction estates and villages, and also the churches of Brent and Pilton [Note: [Col. 1121D] “Piltune”: e; “Wiltuna,” [lacuna].], which, through the support given by King Ine, it possesses justly [Note: [Col. 1121D] “Justly”: e; “still justly”: d.] and canonically together with the other churches—namely Sowy, Street, Meare, Budgellage, and Shapwick—and that, because you have a dwelling nearby, you are always harmful to it. [Note: [Col. 1121D] “Because you have a dwelling nearby, etc.” d, e read: “You are always harmful to it, having a dwelling near it.”]

It would have been fitting that, through your support, the holy Church of God, near which you have come to live, should be greatly increased and enriched by the abundance [Col. 1122B] of your assistance; but, what is wicked, it declines through your obstruction and is humbled by your oppression. And because, though unworthy, we do not doubt that we have received from blessed Peter the apostle the care and solicitude of all churches, therefore [Note: [Col. 1121D] “Therefore”: e; “to such a degree”: d.] we exhort your affection that, for love of the apostles Peter and Paul and reverence for us, you cease from plundering that place and invade none of its properties, churches, chapels, villages, or possessions. If you do this [Note: [Col. 1122D] “Do this”: e; “do not do this”: d.], know that you [Note: [Col. 1122D] “You” omitted in d, e.] are, by our authority in the place of the prince of the apostles, excommunicated and removed from the communion of the faithful, subjected to perpetual anathema, and committed forever to eternal fire with Judas the traitor.”

[Col. 1122C] § 152. Then [Note: [Col. 1122D] “Then”: s, c 2, d, e, f, k, m; omitted in a, l.] the monastic order, long fallen, raised its head especially [Note: [Col. 1122D] “Especially”: s, c 2, d, e, f, k, m; “then”: a, l.]; whence it came about that even [Note: [Col. 1122D] “Even”: s, c 2, d, e; omitted in a, l.] our monastery [Note: [Col. 1122D] “Our”: a, s, d, e, l; *nostrum* deleted and “of Malmesbury” inserted in c 2.] again attained its former liberty. I think it more fitting to make this known in the king’s own words.

§ 153. “I, Edgar, emperor of all Albion, and also of the maritime or island kings dwelling around it, raised to such eminence as none of my forefathers had been raised in subjection, by the assistance of God’s abundant grace, often considered most carefully—mindful of so great an honour—what I ought especially to give from my empire to the Lord, King of kings. Therefore heavenly mercy suddenly suggested to the vigilant devotion of my earnest endeavour that I should restore the holy monasteries in my kingdom, which, like structures of moss-covered shingles and decayed boards, had visibly fallen into ruin as far as their beams; and, what is more serious, had within been neglected and left almost empty of the service of God.

Having expelled unlearned clerics [Note: [Col. 1122D] “Having expelled clerics”: interlinear gloss: Edgar says “by me.”], subject to no discipline of regular religion, [Col. 1123A] I set over many places pastors of a holier [Note: [Col. 1123D] “Order”: a, s, c, d, l. A blank was left in e for the insertion of a word.] order, namely of the monastic habit [Note: [Col. 1123D] “I set over”: interlinear gloss: “I, Edgar”; “were set over”: c 2, d.], supplying them with abundant [Note: [Col. 1123D] “Churches”: s, c, e, l; “times”: a, d, m.] resources from royal revenues to restore each ruined church [Note: [Col. 1123D] “Abundant”: d, e, m; “abundant [men]”: a, c 2, l.]. One of these, named Ælfric, a man thoroughly ecclesiastical, I appointed keeper of the most famous monastery which the English call by the twofold name Maldelmesburh [Malmesbury]. For the benefit of [Note: [Col. 1123D] “Soul”: d, e, m; “my soul”: a, c 2, l.] the soul, in honour of our Saviour, his Mother of God [Θεοτόκος], the ever-Virgin Mary, the apostles Peter and Paul, and Aldhelm, the gracious bishop, I restored by generous grant a parcel of land”—and [Note: [Col. 1123D] “Named”: in all manuscripts the sense remains incomplete; but the omission may be supplied from the words of Malmesbury, *On the Life of Aldhelm* (*Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 33): “I restored by munificent liberality a parcel of land of ten hides, called Estotim, with meadows and woods.”] [the transmitted words “non inat terram” are corrupt or uncertain]—“with meadows and woods, by generous liberality.”

“This land, granted on lease by the aforesaid clerics, was unjustly held by Æthelnoð; but when his sophistical and subtle argument [Col. 1123B] [Note: [Col. 1123D] “Heard by my wise men, and his contention”: s, c, d, e, l, m; omitted in a.] had been heard by my wise men and his false contention refuted by them in my presence, it was restored by me to monastic use, in the year 974 from the Lord’s Incarnation, [Note: [Col. 1123D] “But of my reign, etc.” Edgar was not anointed king before 11 May A.D. 973; yet he must have completed the fourteenth year of his reign before 974, since he had ascended the throne in A.D. 959. See below, § 158.] but the fourteenth of my reign and the first of my royal consecration.”

§ 154. Meanwhile, I think it not unfitting to commit to writing something that was divinely shown to him. He had come into a forest rich in game; and, as often happens, when his companions had scattered by byways in pursuit of wild beasts, he was left alone. Thus, continuing his ride until he reached the edge of the wood, he stopped to await his companions. Before long, as sleep weighed down his wavering eyes, [the words *pedes efficitur* are uncertain], so that the pleasure of brief medicinal rest came to ease the labour of the day already passed. [Note: [Col. 1124D] “Medicinal”: e, l; “moderate”: a, s, c, d, e 2.] He lay stretched beneath a wild apple tree, where the hanging branches all round had formed a leafy vault. Weariness prompting him, a brook flowing beneath with babbling springs invited sleep.

Then a pregnant bitch, whose task was to follow the tracks of wild beasts, lying by his feet, startled him as he dozed. For although the mother was silent, the pups enclosed in her womb gave varied and ringing barks, evidently stimulated by some joy in their prison. Astonished by this prodigy, he looked to the top of the tree and saw [Note: [Col. 1124D] “Sees”: a, c, e, l; “saw”: s, d.] one apple and another fall into the stream. As they collided, while the bubbles of the water curled and broke against one another, an articulate voice sounded: “Wel his the!” that is, “It is well [Col. 1124A] with thee!”

Not long afterwards, as the waves rolled on, a little pitcher appeared upon the water, and after the little pitcher a larger pitcher overflowing with water. The former was empty; and although the larger repeatedly pressed upon the smaller through the current’s force, trying to pour its water into it, it could never prevent the empty little pitcher from withdrawing and, as though in proud triumph, again assailing the pitcher. Returning home, therefore, he was, as the psalmist says, exercised and swept his spirit. [Note: [Col. 1124D] “As the psalmist says”: Psalm LXXVII, 6.] But his mother came to him, to restore serenity to his brow and mind. She urged him to seek God [Note: [Col. 1124D] “That he might seek God”: e 2; “that [it might be] from the Lord’s part”: c, e; “the Lord opening [the matter]”: d; “that he might call upon God”: a, s, l.], who could disclose the riddles by his inspiration. At her urging he drove away his sadness and put his cares at rest, conscious of his mother’s holiness, to whom God was accustomed to reveal many things.

[Col. 1124B] Her name was Ælfgifu; she was devoted to good works and endowed with compassion and gentleness, so that she secretly redeemed even criminals whom the grim judgment of the judges had publicly condemned. Clothing of high price, which for most women is an enticement to abandon modesty, was for her a store of generosity: whenever she saw a poor person, she immediately gave away whatever costly garment she had. Even envy would have praised her bodily beauty and skill of hand, since it could find nothing to criticize.

Thus she drank in the prophecy in her inmost marrow, and next morning said to her son: “The barking of the pups, which they gave while their mother was at rest, signifies that after your death, when those now strong and living are at rest, scoundrels not yet born will bark against God’s [Col. 1124C] Church. The fact that one apple followed another, so that at the impact of the second upon the first the voice ‘Wel his the!’ seemed to sound, indicates that from you, who [Note: [Col. 1124D] “Now as a tree shading all England”: c, e, l; “now you are a tree shading all England”: a, s, d.] now shade all England like a tree, two sons will proceed. The supporters [Note: [Col. 1124D] “Supporters”: c, d, e, l; “makers”: a; “makers or supporters”: s.] of the second will destroy the first; then the promoters of opposing parties will say to both boys, ‘Wel his the!’—because the dead man will reign in heaven, the living man in the world.

“Further, the fact that the larger pitcher could not fill the smaller indicates that northern peoples, who are more numerous than the English, will attack England after your death; and although they replenish their losses by the frequent arrival of their countrymen, they will never be able to fill this corner of the world. Rather, our English, when they appear most completely defeated, will expel them; and England will remain under its own and God’s governance until the time appointed by Christ.” [Note: [Col. 1125D] “Christ”: e, l; after “Christ,” a, s read “Amen.” The following is written in the margin of c 2: “The same King Edgar, entering a certain wood to hunt, happened to hear the cry of a wailing infant. He caused the matter to be diligently investigated. At last, at the top of a certain tree, in an eagle’s nest, a little boy of beautiful appearance was found, marked with two bracelets on his arms and with other royal ornaments, as though in token of most noble birth. The king had him carefully reared and most diligently educated, and eventually promoted him to the rank of earl.”]

251 § 155. A later reading will reveal the truth of this prophecy. We should therefore consider the unquestioned holiness of parent and child: the one saw the riddle while awake without obstruction, and the other resolved the problem with the far-reaching eye of prophecy. [Note: [Col. 1125D] “Eye”: c, d, e, l; “oracle”: a, s.] To holiness of life was joined a forceful severity, so that he permitted no person of whatever rank to evade the laws with impunity. [Note: [Col. 1125D] “That he permitted no one … to evade the laws, etc.” Edgar’s laws in punishing offenders were excessively harsh. With eyes gouged out, nostrils cut away, ears torn off, hands and feet amputated, and finally the scalp removed, wretches were exposed to be torn apart by birds and beasts. See *Acta SS.*, 2 July, in the *Life of Swithun* (SHARPE, 183). See certain laws of Edgar, *Decem Scriptores*, vol. I, col. 871.] In his time no private thief or common robber existed, except one who preferred to attack others’ property at the cost of his own life. For how could human boldness [Note: [Col. 1126D] “Human”: a, s, c, d, e 2, l; omitted in e.] have passed unpunished under one who contemplated extirpating from his kingdom even every kind of bloodthirsty beast, and imposed an edict upon Judwal, king of the Welsh, that he should pay him an annual tribute of three hundred wolves? After doing this for three years, in the fourth he ceased, declaring that he could find no more.

§ 156. Moreover, although he is said to have been very slight in stature and build, nature’s favour had enclosed such strength in that little body that he would of his own accord challenge to combat any man he knew to be bold, fearing above all that he might be thought fearful in such a contest. At a certain banquet, indeed, [Col. 1125C] where the wit of fools usually displays itself more freely, Kenneth, king of the Scots, is said jokingly to have remarked that it seemed remarkable that so paltry a little man should have so many provinces subject to him. A certain mimic heard this with his left ear and later flung it in Edgar’s face as a public insult. But Edgar, concealing the matter, summoned Kenneth as though to consult him about a great secret. After leading him far into a forest, he gave him one of the two swords which he had brought with him.

“And now,” he said, “since we are alone, you may test your strength. For I shall make it appear at once which of us ought rightly to be subject to the other. And do not draw back a step from settling the matter with me. It is shameful for a king to be witty at a banquet but not ready in battle.”

Kenneth was confounded and did not dare utter a word. He fell at the king’s feet, begged pardon for a simple joke, and immediately received it. What of this also? Every summer, immediately after the Easter festival had passed, Edgar ordered ships to assemble along all the coasts. With the eastern fleet he was accustomed to sail round to the western part of the island; then, having crossed it, with the western fleet to the north; and thence, with the northern fleet, to the east—an attentive guardian, of course, lest pirates should cause any disturbance. In winter and spring, travelling on horseback through all the provinces, he investigated the judgments of the powerful and sternly punished violations of right. In the former he applied himself to justice, in the latter to courage; in both he provided for the welfare of the commonwealth.

§ 157. There are some who try to place a blemish upon his great glory, saying that in his earlier years he was cruel toward citizens and lustful toward virgins. They offer the following as an example of the former. Æthelwold was a certain distinguished earl of his time and one of the king’s confidants. The king had assigned him the task of examining Ælfthryth, daughter of Orgar, duke of Devon, whose beauty had so charmed the eyes of those who reported it that they commended her to the king’s [Col. 1126B] ears. He had ordered this man, I say, to go and inspect her, intending to arrange a marriage if the truth corresponded with the report.

Æthelwold hastened on his journey and, finding her nothing less than he had heard, concealed the message from her parents and appropriated the girl for his own purposes. On returning to the king, he alleged what served his own interests: that she was a girl of common, everyday appearance and unfit for so great a majesty. When the king’s mind had been diverted from her and directed toward other loves, informers told him how Æthelwold had outwitted him. Edgar drove out one nail by another—that is, countered fraud with fraud. He showed the earl a cheerful face and, as though in jest, set a day when he would visit the woman so highly praised.

The earl, nearly dead with terror at this dreadful game, [Col. 1126C] hurried ahead to his wife, begging her to provide for his safety and make herself as unattractive as possible by her clothing, at last revealing the plan of his own deed. But what will a woman not dare? She dared betray the faith of her unhappy [Note: [Col. 1126D] “Unhappy”: a, s, c, d, e; “unhappy woman”: l; “first”: s.] lover and first husband; she adorned her face before the mirror and omitted nothing that might provoke the loins of a young and powerful man. Nor did the result fail her intention. For Edgar burned with desire upon seeing her and, concealing his hatred, summoned the earl to hunt in the forest of Werewelle [Note: [Col. 1126D] “Werewelle”: c, d, e, l; “Werewelle, called Harewode”: a, s.] and pierced him with a spear.

When the slain man’s illegitimate son came upon him in familiar attendance and the king asked how he liked such hunting, he is said to have answered: “Well, my lord king; what pleases you ought not to displease me.” By these words he so softened Edgar’s swelling anger that afterward [Col. 1126D] nothing was dearer to him in his life [Note: [Col. 1126D] “He had”: s, c, d, e; “the king had”: a, l.] than that young man; he relieved, by royal care for the son, the offence caused by his tyrannical deed against the father. In expiation for that crime, a monastery was founded on the spot by Ælfthryth and is inhabited by a community of nuns.

§ 158. To this example of cruelty they add another of lust. Hearing of the beauty of a virgin consecrated to God, he violently dragged her from the monastery, violated the modesty of the woman he had taken, and placed her in his bed not merely once. When this offended the ears of blessed Dunstan, Edgar was sharply rebuked by him and did not disdain a seven-year penance: the king deigned to afflict himself by fasting and at the same time to go without the diadem for seven years. [Note: [Col. 1127D] “Seven-year … seven years.” This seems sustainable in this particular case because he was crowned with the diadem only two years before his death. (SHARPE, p. 186.) Edgar was crowned A.D. 973. See the end of § 153.]

§ 159. They add a third instance, in which both vices appear. King Edgar, they say, came to Andover, a town not far from Winchester, and ordered that the daughter of a certain duke, whose beauty was widely famed, be brought to him. The girl’s mother, who scorned [Col. 1127B] for her daughter to be a concubine, aided by the darkness of night put a maidservant into the bed—a virgin indeed neither inelegant nor unattractive. When the night had passed and dawn broke into daylight, the woman attempted to rise. Asked why she was hurrying, she answered that she must perform her mistress’s daily work. Though held back with difficulty at the king’s knees, she wept to him over the condition of her miseries, asking that he restore her freedom as the reward for marriage; it befitted his greatness, she said, that one who had known royal pleasure should not henceforward groan beneath the commands of cruel masters.

Then he, with anger stirred and with a terrible smile, while his mind wavered between pity for the maid and indignation against the mistress, relaxed into jesting and remitted both her customary services and her punishment. Straightway he raised her, willing or unwilling, to rule in great honour over her former masters, [Col. 1127C] loved her alone, and kept entire fidelity to her bed until he took as lawful wife Ælfthryth, daughter of Orgar. By her he had Edmund [Note: [Col. 1127D] Edmund died in 971 according to Florence, but in 972 according to the *Saxon Chronicle*.], who died five years before him and lies at Romsey, and Æthelred, who reigned after him. For by Æthelflaed, surnamed the Fair, daughter of the very powerful duke Ordmaer, he begot Edward; and Saint Edith by Wulfthryth, who certainly was not then a nun, but, through fear of the king, a lay girl who had veiled herself, and who was soon afterwards compelled into the imperial bed after her veil had been torn away. Blessed Dunstan, offended because Edgar had desired a woman who had been, if only in outward appearance, a nun, exercised episcopal severity against him.

[Col. 1127D] § 160. But however these matters may stand, this is certain: from the sixteenth year of his age, when he was made king, until his thirtieth he reigned without royal insignia. Then, with princes and men of every rank gathering from all sides, he was crowned at Bath at Pentecost with great glory; nor did he survive more than three years, and he was buried at Glastonbury. [Note: From the sixteenth year of his age . . . he reigned. See § 153, note 88, and § 158, note 9.]

Nor should this be forgotten: when Abbot Eilward opened his tomb in the year 1052 from the Lord’s incarnation, he found the body untouched by any decay. Though this ought to have moved him to reverence, it raised him to audacity. Because the coffin which he had prepared seemed to promise difficult admission owing to the size of the body, he rashly cut into the royal remains with iron; whereupon blood at once burst forth in waves and shook the hearts of those standing by with fear. Thus the royal body was placed in a shrine, which he himself had bestowed on that church, above the altar, together with the head of Saint Apollinaris and the relics of Vincent the martyr, which he had bought at great cost and added for the adornment of God’s house. [Col. 1128B] The violator of the sacred body soon lost his mind; and not long afterwards, having gone out of the church, he was met by death through a broken neck.

[Note: Nor should this be forgotten . . . raging man and blind man. In s. c. d. e.; omitted in a. l., which read: “The body was then covered with earth; but afterwards, placed in a silver and gilded shrine, it is honoured according to the merits of the person.” Compare Malmesbury, *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury* (Gale, III, 324).]

Nor did the manifestation of royal holiness stop at these things, but proceeded further, when there a raging man and a blind man were healed. Therefore, among the English there is deservedly no weak report that no king in England, whether of his own or of an earlier age, was comparable with Edgar in upright and impartial judgement. [Note: “Therefore”: s. c. d. e.; “For indeed”: a. l.] Thus nothing in his life was holier, nothing more commendable than his justice—except for faults which he afterwards obliterated by great virtues. He rendered his country illustrious by conspicuous courage, by the splendour of his achievements, and by the multitude of those serving God. After his death the fortunes and hopes of the English slipped backward. [Note: “After his death”: Edgar died on Wednesday, 8 July 975.]

## Concerning Edward the Second and Martyr

[Col. 1128C] § 161. In the year 975 from the Lord’s incarnation, Edward, son of Edgar, began to reign, and held power for three and a half years. Dunstan and the other bishops who agreed with him raised him to the royal summit, against the will, as they say, of certain nobles and of his stepmother, who was striving to advance her son Æthelred, a boy scarcely seven years old, so that she herself might rule under his name rather than Edward under his own.

From that time, as human wickedness sprouted, the prosperity of the kingdom diminished. Then a comet was seen, which is confidently asserted truly to foretell either a pestilence among the people of the provinces or a change in the kingdom. [Note: “A comet was seen.” Most manuscripts read *visa cometes*; s., *visae cometae*. “In the year 975 a comet-star was seen in the autumn season.” (Florence of Worcester.)] Nor was there delay: barrenness of the fields followed, famine among men, and death among beasts of burden.

At the royal village called Calne an extraordinary event occurred. For, after Edgar’s death, clerics who had once been expelled from churches revived their conflicts. It was, they said, a great and grievous disgrace for a new arrival to compel old settlers to move away; this could be thought pleasing neither to God, who had granted the old habitation, [Col. 1129A] nor to any upright man, who might fear for himself the same thing which he saw happen to others through prejudicial action. [Note: “Great”: a. c. d. e. l.; before “great,” s. reads “saying.”]

On this account there was an uprising into shouting and anger, and they proceeded to Dunstan; the magnates in particular, as is customary with laymen, loudly declaring that the injury which the clerics had unjustly suffered ought to be cut short by a milder policy. [Note: “Clerics”: a. s. c. d. e². l.; omitted in e.] One of them, Ælfer, indeed, had with great insolence destroyed nearly all the monasteries which the most reverend Æthelwold had founded in the province of the Mercians. [Note: “Æthelwold”: a. c. d. e. l.; s., “Æthelwold the monk and bishop of Winchester.”]

Accordingly, a numerous synod having been summoned, they first came to Winchester. [Note: “First to Winchester.” It is certain, according to Florence and Matthew of Westminster, that the council at Winchester was held before Edgar’s death and the anointing of his son Edward in 975; but the Winchester Chronicle, cited by Spelman (*Concilia Angliae*, vol. I, p. 491), places it in 968. See Wharton’s note in *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 112. Osbern incorrectly asserts in the *Life of Dunstan* that the Winchester and Calne councils were held while Edgar was still alive. Yet there seems no doubt that the council of Calne was held in 978, during the lifetime of Edward the Martyr. Florence, however, assigns it to 977.]

Other writings recount what was the conclusion of the conflict there: that an image of the Lord spoke distinctly and confounded the clerics and their supporters. [Note: “Other writings teach.” See Osbern, *Life of Saint Dunstan* (*Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 112).] [Note: “An image of the Lord spoke distinctly.” “Behold, the form of the Lord’s body, fixed to the banner of the cross and placed in the middle part of the building, assuming human speech, restrained every voice, saying: ‘Far be it that this should happen; far be it that this should happen.’” Osbern, *Life of Saint Dunstan* (*Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 112).] But, since tempers had not yet been calmed, a council was convened at Calne. There, while the senators of all England were seated in an upper chamber, the king being absent because of his age, the affair was conducted amid great conflict and dispute. Many insults’ missiles assaulted that mighty wall of the Church—Dunstan, I mean—but did not shake him, each order of men defending its cause with the utmost zeal. Suddenly the whole floor, with its planks and beams, split apart and collapsed. All were dashed to the ground; Dunstan alone, standing upon one beam which remained, escaped safely. The rest were either killed or bound by the fetter of permanent infirmity. This miracle secured peace for the archbishop concerning all the clerics of England, who then and thereafter yielded to his judgement.

§ 162. Meanwhile King Edward treated his little brother and stepmother with fitting affection, retained only the name of king, left them all else, sought out the traces of his father’s piety, and gave ear and mind to good counsels. But the woman, brooding a viperish plot in stepmotherly hatred, so that even the name of king might not be lacking to her son, laid snares for her stepson, which she completed in this manner.

Wearied from hunting, he was returning, panting with thirst because of his exertion. His companions, wherever chance had taken each, were pursuing the dogs. Hearing that they were staying in a neighbouring village, the young man spurred his horse swiftly there alone, fearing nothing because of his innocence, for he measured the minds of others by his own. Then she, enticing his approach by feminine blandishment, caused him to attend to her; and after welcoming kisses, while he eagerly drank the cup offered to him, she had a retainer pierce him with a dagger. Wounded by that blow, he urged his war-horse with the remaining strength of his soul to return to his men; then, slipping from one foot and being dragged by the other through trackless places, he gave those searching for him signs of his death in his streaming blood. [Note: “Trackless places”: a. c. d. e. l.; s., “trackless places and woodland.”]

Then indeed they ordered him buried without honour at Wareham, begrudging the dead, plainly, the turf of the church, when they had begrudged the living royal dignity. [Note: “They ordered him buried without honour at Wareham.” Edward was killed on 18 March 978.] They therefore practised public and festive rejoicing, as though they had buried memory together with his body. [Note: “As though”: c. e.; d., *quas*; s., *quod*; a. l., *quia*.] But divine serenity gave its assent and exalted the innocently slain man with the glory of miracles. [Note: “Exalted”: a. e.; s. c. d. l., “might exalt.”] So greatly do heavenly judgements outweigh human ones: there lights from heaven were shown; there a lame man set his gait in order; there a mute man recovered his organ of speech; there, in short, every infirmity gave place to health. Rumour, spreading through all England, proclaimed the martyr’s merits.

Stirred by this, the murderess began a journey there. Already she was pressing her mounted horse with spurs when she felt the manifest wrath of God. For the familiar animal on which she was accustomed to ride—formerly swifter than the winds, outrunning the very breezes—then, by God’s command, stood motionless. Her servants pressed it, on one side with whips, on the other with shouts, to carry its powerful mistress with its customary [Col. 1130B] liveliness. Their effort was wasted; when the horse was changed, the same outcome followed. Though late, her brutish heart understood what that prodigy signified. Therefore she consented that what she herself did not deserve should be done through another. [Note: “Herself”: c. d. e; “through herself”: a. s. l.]

For that Ælfer whom I above blamed for destroying monasteries, repenting of his rashness and afflicting his mind with much groaning, raised the sacred body from its ignoble place and paid fitting and distinguished funeral rites at Shaftesbury; yet he did not escape, but a year later was consumed by worms which we call lice, in A.D. 979. Since an undisciplined mind is itself its own torment, and an anxious soul suffers its own shades even here, Elfrida, brought low from that royal pride, repented grievously. For many years at Wherwell she wrapped in haircloth flesh nourished in luxury, slept at night stretched upon the ground without a pillow, and devised besides every possible cross for her body. She was a beautiful woman and, towards her husband, commendably sober; but because she committed so great a crime, she deserved punishment. And it was believed and commonly reported that, because of her violence against Edward, the whole country much later groaned under barbarian servitude.

[Col. 1130D] § 163. Certainly at Shaftesbury a splendid mirror of royal holiness shines forth. For to his merits is attributed the fact that in that place a great choir of women devoted to God, illuminating these lands by the splendour of religious life, even touches the stars themselves. There are holy virgins conscious of no corruption at all; there religious women, continent after the losses of a first marriage-bed, knowing no second flame. In the conduct of them all, gracious modesty so agrees with severe elegance that nothing exceeds it. Indeed, one might hesitate uncertainly which quality to praise most: their constancy in God’s service or their affability in human conversation. Thus credence is not unjustly given to those who say that through their prayers the whole world is sustained, though it has long tottered beneath its own sins.

## Concerning King Æthelred

[Col. 1131B] § 164. In the year 979 from the Lord’s incarnation, Æthelred, son of Edgar and Elfrida, obtained the kingdom and for thirty-seven years rather besieged it than ruled it. [Note: “In the year 979 from the Lord’s incarnation.” Æthelred succeeded his brother in 978 and was crowned on 14 September of the following year. (Florence of Worcester.)] The course of his life is said to have been cruel at its beginning, miserable in the middle, and shameful at its end: thus he was savage through the fratricide to which he had given connivance, infamous through flight and softness, and pitiable in death.

Dunstan had foretold his cowardice, warned by a foul sign. For when he was a very little child being immersed in the baptismal font, with bishops standing around, he polluted the sacrament by a discharge from the bowels. Dunstan, disturbed by this, said: “By God and his mother, he will be a cowardly man!” [Note: “By a discharge from the bowels,” etc. Something similar is related of Emperor Constantine V, who acquired the surname Copronymus because he polluted the baptismal font.]

I have seen it written that, when he was a boy of ten and heard the lamentation that his brother had been killed, his weeping so enraged his furious mother that, because she had no whip to hand, she seized candles and beat the innocent child with them, not stopping until she had nearly killed him and then herself bathed him in tears. Therefore throughout his life he afterwards so dreaded candles that he never allowed their light to be brought before him.

By his mother’s support, the nobles having assembled, a day was appointed for Dunstan to come and crown the king by right of the archbishopric. Although hostile, he refrained from resistance, being a pontiff mature in years and retired from secular affairs. [Note: “Refrained”: s. c. d. e., “was silent”; a. l., “kept silent.”] But as he arranged the diadem, he could not restrain himself from pouring forth in full speech the prophetic spirit drawn from the depths of his being:

> “Because,” he said, “you have aspired to the kingdom through your brother’s death, therefore [Note: “Therefore”: a. c. d. e. l.; omitted in s.] hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: the sin of your disgraceful mother, and the sin of the men who attended her wicked counsel, shall not be blotted out except by much blood of miserable inhabitants of the provinces; and evils shall come upon the English people such as it has not suffered from the time when it came to England [Note: “came to England”: c. d. e. l.; a. s., “England was.”] until that time.”

[Note: “Because . . . until that time.” Compare Osbern, *Life of Saint Dunstan*, *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 113.]

Not long afterwards, that is, in the third year of his reign, seven pirate ships came to the harbour of Southampton near Winchester, ravaged the coast, and withdrew into the deep. I have not passed this over because much talk is current among the English concerning these vessels. [Note: Southampton was burned by the Danes in 980, according to the best manuscript of the Saxon Chronicles. Florence and others also assign this disaster to 980.]

## Concerning Æthelred’s Cowardice and the Danish Raids

§ 165. A quarrel had arisen [Note: “Had arisen”: a. s. d. e. l.; c., “arose” (plural).] between the king [Note: “King”: a. c. d. e. l.; s., “the king himself.”] and the bishop of Rochester in A.D. 986, for an uncertain reason. [Note: “A quarrel”: a. s. d. e. l; c., “quarrels.”] Therefore the king led an army against the city. The archbishop ordered him to desist from his rage and not provoke Saint Andrew, in whose protection the bishopric lay—one as ready to forgive as terrible in vengeance. [Note: “Rage”: c. d. e.; s., “by rage”; a. l., “rage” in the accusative.]

Despising the nakedness of words, the king adorned the command with money: he sent one hundred pounds, so that the siege might be raised and he might depart, bought off by a price. Having received it, he sounded the retreat and allowed his soldiers to plunder the district. Dunstan, astonished at the man’s greed, sent back this message through envoys:

> “Since you have preferred silver to God, money to the Apostle, and greed to me, the evils which the Lord has spoken will swiftly come upon you. But these things will not happen while I live, for this also has the Lord spoken.”

[Note: Dunstan died on Saturday, 19 May 988, in the twenty-ninth year of his archbishopric and the sixty-first of his age.]

After the blessed man’s death, which came in the tenth year of Æthelred’s reign, the things foretold hurried to fulfilment and the things predicted hastened to completion. [Note: “For while the Danes …” The Danes ravaged Southampton, the Isle of Thanet, and Cheshire in 980; Cornwall in 981; the Isle of Portland in 982; and Watchet in 988, where they were defeated; finally Ipswich in 991.] For while the Danes infested every harbour and ranged everywhere with pirate swiftness, and while no one knew where they ought to be confronted, Sigeric, the second archbishop after Dunstan, decreed that those who could not be driven back with iron should be repelled by silver. [Note: “Sigeric.” Sigeric, or Siric, succeeded Æthelgar in the see of Canterbury in A.D. 990. After Ipswich had been devastated by the Danes in 991 and the town’s reeve killed, the archbishop arranged for ten thousand English pounds of tribute to be paid to them on condition that they should depart from the country. See the Saxon Chronicle.]

Thus another ten thousand pounds paid out satisfied the greed of the Danes: an infamous example, and unworthy of men, to redeem liberty with money when no violence can tear it from an unconquered spirit. Then indeed there was a brief cessation from raids; but soon, once their strength had returned through rest, they returned to their former course.

Such fear then [Note: “Then”: c. d. e.; a. s. l., “so great.”] seized the English that they thought of no resistance. If any, remembering ancient glory, attempted to oppose them and assemble standards, they were abandoned by the multitude of enemies and by the defection of allies. [Col. 1133A] The standard-bearer of treachery was a certain Ælfric, whom the king had put in command of the assembled ships. When he should have tested fortune in a naval battle, on the night before the day of battle dawned he defected shamefully to the enemy, having first warned them through messengers what they should avoid. Although the king ordered his son blinded for the crime of treachery, he returned again and defected again. [Note: The king ordered his son blinded. Ælfgar, son of Ealdorman Ælfric, was deprived of sight by the king’s command in 993. (Florence of Worcester and the Saxon Chronicle.)]

All Northumbria having been ravaged, the enemy were met in battle and put to flight. London was besieged but stoutly defended by its citizens. [Note: “London besieged.” According to the Saxon Chronicle, Anlaf and Sweyn came to London on the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Mary in A.D. 994 with ninety-four ships and fiercely attacked the city, attempting to consume it with fire, but were vigorously repulsed by the citizens.] Accordingly, the besiegers, exhausted and despairing of taking the city, departed; ravaging the whole eastern province, they compelled the king to pay sixteen thousand pounds. He even had their king Anlaf come to him after hostages had been given; the king received him from the font after baptism, bestowed royal gifts upon him, and bound him by oath never to return to England.

But evil did not rest in this way. For, like the heads of the Hydra, enemies continually sprouted from Denmark, and it was impossible to guard against them anywhere. The western province called Devonshire was overwhelmed; monasteries were destroyed and the city of Exeter burned. [Note: The Danes invaded Devonshire in 997 and again in 1001, the year in which Exeter was ravaged. The Laud and Cotton manuscripts of the Saxon Chronicle differ greatly in this matter from the Cambridge copy of those Chronicles. Exeter was again besieged by Sweyn in 1003.] Kent was given over to plunder; the metropolitan city and seat of the patriarchs was burned. Archbishop Ælfheah himself, a holy and most venerable man, was carried away and held in chains. [Note: Canterbury was besieged by the Danes in 1012, and Archbishop Ælfheah was captured and killed. His life, written by Osbern, was published in *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 122, from a manuscript codex of the Lambeth Library. Cotton MSS Otho A. XII, Vitellius D. XVII, and Tiberius D. III—damaged by fire—also contain Osbern’s *Life of Ælfheah*.]

At last [Note: “At last”: s. c. d. e. l.; a., “finally.”], because he refused to compel his tenants to be stripped of their possessions for his ransom, he was stoned and struck with an axe, and his soul glorified heaven. God exalted the slain man, so that the Danes who had raged to kill him, seeing the miracle in which a dry piece of wood stained with his blood put forth leaves again in a single night, eagerly bowed their necks. [Note: “Eagerly bowed their necks”: c. e. Before this phrase, a. s. l. read “they eagerly rushed to kiss the dead man”; d. reads “they rushed eagerly to kiss him.”] Thus their natural stiff-neckedness was subdued, and they allowed the sacred body to be carried to London. There, gloriously buried, and after ten years raised up free from every stain of decay, it ennobled its own archbishopric. [Note: The body of Ælfheah, or Elphege, was translated from London to Kent in 1023. Osbern also wrote an account of the Translation of the Body of Ælfheah, published in *Anglia Sacra*, part II, p. 143, from Cotton MS Tiberius D. III.] To this day both the fresh blood and unspoiled integrity endure, and it is regarded as miraculous that a corpse can lose life and yet be unable to decay.

And, not to make this too long by enumerating individually the provinces which they devastated, let this suffice as a summary: though there are counted thirty-two districts in England, they had already invaded sixteen, whose names I decline to write because of the barbarity of the language. Meanwhile the king, energetic and finely made for sleeping, yawned while postponing such great affairs. Whenever he recovered his senses enough even to raise himself on one elbow, he immediately fell back into misery, whether through the weight of indolence or the opposition of fortune. His brother’s ghost troubled him, demanding dreadful funeral offerings.

Who could recount how often he gathered an army, how often he ordered ships to be built, [Note: “How often he ordered ships to be built”: s. c. d. e; omitted in a. l.] how often he summoned commanders from every quarter—and yet none of these things ever came to anything? For an army lacking a leader and ignorant of military discipline either melted away before an engagement or readily yielded in the very conflict. Much in war depends upon the presence of a commander, much upon courage proven in such affairs, much upon experience and especially discipline. Lacking these, as I have said, the army was an irrecoverable loss to the provincials and a pitiable plaything to the enemy. Such a kind of men, unless restrained before war, is ready for plunder; unless encouraged in war, it is prone to flight.

A tempest suddenly arising seized the ships constructed to protect the coast while they lay at anchor; it dashed them against one another, scattered their equipment, and rendered them useless. A few ships made from the remnants of many were sunk or burned at the attack of a certain Wulfnoth, whom the king had driven into outlawry; they disappointed the hope of all England. Whenever the commanders met for counsel, one chose this plan and another that; they scarcely or never agreed upon a sound decision. For they deliberated more about domestic rivalries than public necessities. Indeed, if under the pressure of danger they decided upon anything useful and secret, it was immediately carried to the Danes by traitors.

For besides Ælfric, successor to Ælfer, who had killed the preceding king, there was Eadric, especially suited in wickedness for such things, whom the king had appointed over the shire of the Mercians: the dregs of mankind and disgrace of the English, a shameful glutton and crafty rogue, whose nobility had produced wealth for him, and whose tongue and audacity had gained it. [Note: “Whose nobility”: c. e. l; a. s. d, “whose non-nobility.”] [Note: “Tongue”: c. e. l; a. s. d, “but tongue.”] Cautious in concealment and ready in pretence, he hunted out the king’s counsels as a loyal subject and spread them abroad as a traitor. Often, sent to the enemy as mediator of peace, he kindled war. His treachery appeared frequently during the reign of this king, but most especially during that of the next; I shall speak of it later.

Of all men, only Ulfcytel, ealdorman of the East Angles, then resisted the invaders vigorously, so that although the name of victory went to the enemy, those who had conquered were judged much more afflicted than those who had been conquered. [Note: “Ulfcytel.” Ulfcytel defeated the Danes near Thetford in A.D. 1004. See Florence of Worcester and the Saxon Chronicle for 1004.] Nor were the barbarians ashamed to confess the truth, since they often lamented that victory. The ealdorman’s courage especially shone after Æthelred’s death, in the battle that cut down all the flower of the province. There he too, surrounded from behind, deemed it shameful to yield and purchased courage for the king with his own blood. [Note: “In that battle,” etc. Ulfcytel was killed in the battle at Ashingdon in Essex in A.D. 1006.] But these matters belong later.

At that time, lest any misery should be lacking to King Æthelred, famine raged through all England, and the populace that war had left was consumed by starvation. The enemy roamed so freely through the country that they carried booty overland for fifty miles to their ships, fearing no ambush from the provincials. With these evils clamouring on every side, counsel was again considered: that war might be lifted by money. And it was done: first twenty thousand pounds, then thirty thousand pounds, were given. How much that achieved, the following time showed.

Yet, as I reflect on many things, I wonder why a man who, as we have received from our elders, was neither very foolish nor excessively cowardly, spent his life amid so mournful a pallor of calamities. [Note: “Excessively”: c. d. e; a. s. l, “greatly.”] If anyone asks me the cause, I could not easily answer—unless it were the defection of his commanders, arising from the king’s arrogance. Our narrative has already anticipated their treachery; I shall now speak of his own insolence, by which he was so intolerable that he spared not even his own affections.

Besides the English, whom without any existing cause he disinherited or drained of their wealth on fabricated charges; besides the Danes, whom on trivial suspicions he ordered slaughtered throughout all England in a single day—where misery could be seen, when each man was compelled to betray his dearest guests, whom even the closest intimacy had made more beloved, and to drive embraces apart with the sword—[Note: The slaughter of the Danes occurred on 13 November 1002.] besides these things, moreover, he was so insolent toward his wife that he scarcely deemed her worthy of his bed, but, wallowing with concubines, disgraced royal majesty. [Note: “Wife.” Gloss in l.: “Emma, namely.”] [Note: “That he scarcely deemed her worthy of his bed”: a. c. d. e. l; s., “that he deemed her scarcely worthy.”]

She too, conscious of lofty blood, was haughty toward her husband because neither modest nobility nor fertility commended her to him; for she had filled her husband’s household with two sons, Alfred and Edward. [Note: Alfred was later killed through the treachery of Earl Godwine.] She was the daughter of Richard, count of Normandy, son of William, who held that duchy for fifty-two years after his father and ended his life in the eighteenth year of this king’s reign. [Note: Richard died on 20 November A.D. 996.] [Note: “Ended”: c. d. e. l; a. s., “finished.”] He lies at the monastery of Fécamp, which he had enlarged with certain revenues and distinguished with monastic rule through a certain William, abbot of Dijon. He was an outstanding man, who had often assailed Æthelred with injuries.

When this was heard at Rome, the Apostolic See, unwilling that two Christians should fight one another, sent Leo, bishop of Trier, into England to arrange peace. [Note: “That two Christians should fight”: s. c. d. e. l; a., “that two Christian leaders should contend with one another.”] The letter of that embassy is as follows.

## Letter of Pope John

[Note: “Of Pope John.” The rubric in e incorrectly adds: “who was also called Gerbert.” See § 167, note 68.]

[Col. 1136B] § 166. “John the Fifteenth, pope of the holy Roman Church, to all the faithful. [Note: “John”: s. c. d. e. l; a., “John of this name.” The letter is of Pope John XV, sometimes called XVI, who occupied the see from 985 to 996. After the death of John XIV, John, son of Robert, was elected in March 985; but, because he died before consecration, he is not commonly counted among the supreme pontiffs, although his successor is sometimes styled John XVI. He died before July 985.] Let all faithful children of our holy mother Church, and those of both our orders dispersed through the regions of the world, know how we have been informed by many persons of the enmity of Æthelred, king of the West Saxons, and Richard, margrave. Greatly saddened by this, as concerning our spiritual sons, I at last adopted sound counsel and summoned a certain apocrisiary of ours, namely Leo, bishop of the holy church of Trier, and sent him there with our letters of exhortation, that they might come to their senses from this superstition.

“He, crossing the vast intervals of lands, at last crossed the sea-boundaries and, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, came before the presence of the aforesaid king. Immediately, having greeted him on our behalf, he offered the letters which we had sent him. The king summoned all the wiser faithful men of both orders of his kingdom and, for love and fear of almighty God, of Saint Peter prince of the apostles, and through our paternal admonition, granted a most firm peace, without deceit, with all his sons and daughters, present and future, and with all his faithful men. Concerning this, he sent Æthelsige, bishop of the holy church of Sherborne, Leofstan son of Ælfwold, and Wistan son of Æthelnoth. They crossed the sea-boundaries [Col. 1137A] and came to the aforesaid Margrave Richard.

“Richard peacefully received our admonitions and, hearing also the decree of the aforesaid king, willingly confirmed the same peace with his sons and daughters, present and future, and with all his faithful men, on this condition: if any of them, or they themselves, should unjustly commit anything against the other, the matter shall be purged by due amends.
