And peace shall remain perpetually stable and unshaken, guaranteed by the seal of oaths on both sides. On the side of King Æthelred: Bishop Æthelsige of the holy church of Sherborne, Leofstan son of Ælfwold, and Æthelnoth son of Wistan; on Richard’s side: Bishop Roger, Ralph son of Hugh, and Turstenc son of Turgis. Done at Rouen, on the Kalends of March, [Col. 1137B] in the year 991 from the Lord’s incarnation, in the fourth indiction. [Note: “First”: a. s. c. e. l; omitted in d.] And Richard shall receive none of the king’s men or his enemies, nor the king any of Richard’s men or enemies, without their seals.”

## Concerning Gerbert

[Col. 1137C] § 167. [Note: “Concerning Gerbert”: e reads “concerning that same Gerbert.”]

[Note: “Upon the death of this John, Gregory succeeded; and likewise John the Sixteenth. After him, Silvester, who was also Gerbert, concerning whom . . .”: a. d. m. “Concerning this John, who was also called Gerbert”: s. c. e. f. g. k. l. Most ancient witnesses and manuscripts read *scribitur* in the text; but e, that is, the manuscript which the author commonly follows, and certain others wrongly take John XV, called XVI, for Silvester II, whose name was Gerbert and concerning whom Malmesbury’s legends contain much material. Born in Auvergne of obscure parents, Gerbert was educated from boyhood at the abbey of Aurillac. Later appointed abbot of the monastery of Bobbio in Lombardy and head of the school of Rheims, he was made archbishop of that city. He was removed from it by Pope John XV, called XVI, in 995, and in 998, with the favour of Emperor Otto III, whose teacher he had been, was transferred to the see of Ravenna, where he remained until he ascended to the supreme pontificate on 2 July 999.]

Upon the death of this John, Gregory succeeded; then John the Sixteenth; after him Silvester, who was also Gerbert. Concerning him, I think it will not be absurd to commit to writing the things which circulate on everyone’s lips. Born in Gaul, he grew up from childhood as a monk at Fleury; soon, when—[Note: “The Pythagorean fork in the road.” Pythagoras’ fork is represented by the Greek letter *Y* or *υ*.]

> Pythagoras’ forked path spreads out in uncertain branches. (Ausonius, *Idylls*, “On Monosyllabic Letters,” XII.9.) Lactantius, VI.6, says: “They say that the course of human life resembles the letter Y, because each person, when first reaching the threshold of youth and arriving at the place where the road divides in two directions [Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.540], stands wavering in uncertainty.”

Having reached Pythagoras’ fork in the road—whether weary of monastic life or seized by a desire for glory—he fled by night to Spain, chiefly intending to learn astrology and the other arts of that kind from the Saracens. [Col. 1137C]

[Note: Spain … under Gothic rule, etc. The Suevi, Vandals, Alans, and others invaded Spain in 409; and Adolphus, king of the Goths, advanced into Spain in A.D. 414.]

Spain, long possessed by the Romans for many years, had passed under Gothic rule in the time of the emperor Honorius. [Col. 1138A] The Goths, Arians until the time of blessed Gregory, were then united to the Catholic body through Leander, bishop of Seville, and through King Ricared, brother of Hermenegild, whom his father had killed on Easter night because of his confession of the faith.

[Note: Arians. Present in c, d, e, l; omitted in a, s.]

[Note: Ricared. The reading is *Ricaredum* in a, d, e, l; *Recharedum* in c; *Richardum* in s. Recared II, son of Leovigild, was the first Catholic king of Spain. He converted to this faith between 586 and 589, and with him the entire people of the Visigoths in Spain renounced Arianism.]

[Note: Hermenegild, whom his father had killed on Easter night because of his confession of the faith. Hermenegild, the eldest son of Leovigild, was invested by his father with the royal diadem and the government of Baetica, and made an alliance with Ingund, daughter of Sigebert, king of Austrasia. Ingund suffered persecution and was finally killed by her husband’s mother because she professed the Catholic faith. Leander, archbishop of Seville, had little difficulty persuading Hermenegild to avenge the murder of his wife, and assisted him while he attempted to cast his father from the throne. Hermenegild was captured [Col. 1138D] and condemned to death for rebellion. Near death, he utterly rejected Arian communion, which he had renounced at Leander’s urging, not even accepting it to save his life. Accordingly, he has been held in such great honour among us that the Roman Church has numbered him among the saints.]

Isidore, renowned for learning and holiness, succeeded Leander.

[Note: Isidore. Archbishop of Seville in the sixth century.]

In our own age, Alfonso, king of Galicia, transferred his body to Toledo, buying it for its weight in gold. For the Saracens, who had subdued the Goths, were themselves defeated by Charlemagne and lost Galicia and Lusitania, the greatest provinces of Spain. They possess the upper regions to this day. And as Christians have Toledo, so they have Seville—which they commonly call Sibilia [Col. 1138B]—as the capital of their kingdom, devoting themselves to divinations and incantations, practices customary among their people.

Gerbert therefore, as I have said, arrived among them and satisfied his desire. There he surpassed Ptolemy in the astrolabe, Alandraeus in the distances between the stars, and Julius Firmicus in matters of fate.

[Note: Alandraeus. The reading is *Alandraeum* in d, e; *Alhandraeum* in a, e², l; *Alchandraeum* in c; *Alcandraeum* in s.]

[Note: Julius Firmicus. Julius Firmicus Maternus, bishop of Milan, composed eight books on astronomy around the middle of the fourth century.]

There he learned what the song and flight of birds portend; there he learned to summon thin apparitions from the underworld; there, finally, he learned whatever harmful or beneficial thing human curiosity discovers. For there is no need to speak of the lawful arts—arithmetic, music, astronomy, and geometry—which he drank in so deeply that he showed them inferior to his own intellect, and with great industry restored them to Gaul, where they had long since been wholly forgotten.

[Note: The abacus. Sharpe observes that the abacus was a kind of arithmetical table; here it seems to be used for arithmetic itself, since Gerbert composed a treatise on arithmetic under this title. The authors of the work entitled *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VI, interpret this literally, as though he stole a book containing the principles of learning; and they incorrectly identify that supposed book with the book of incantations mentioned below. They also take great offence that Malmesbury wrote such inventions about Gerbert, and attribute them to Cardinal Benno; yet nothing of the kind occurs in Benno’s work, published by Goldast and in Brown’s *Fasciculus*, vol. I. On Gerbert’s *Abacus*, see Chasles, “Explication des traités de l’Abacus et particulièrement du traité de Gerbert” [Col. 1139D], *Comptes-rendus de l’Académie des sciences* (1843), who edited and elucidated this treatise.]

Certainly, having been the first to seize the abacus from the Saracens, he set down rules which sweating abacists can scarcely understand. [Col. 1138C–1139A] He lodged with a philosopher of that sect, whom at first he won over with many gifts, and later with promises. Nor did the Saracen fail to display his learning for sale: he often allowed him to sit beside him, to converse now of serious matters and now of trifles, and to borrow books for copying. There was one volume which contained the secret of the whole art, and which he could obtain by no means. Gerbert burned with longing to acquire the book by whatever servile means he could.

[Note: “We always strive for what is forbidden, and whatever is denied is deemed more precious.” Ovid, *Amores* III.4.17.]

He therefore turned to entreaties: he begged by God and by friendship, offered much, and promised more.

[Note: “Therefore.” Present in a, c, d, e², l; omitted in e.] When this made little progress, he attempted a nocturnal ambush. Taking the man unawares with wine—his daughter also conniving, since frequent association had produced familiarity between them—he seized the volume placed beneath the pillow and fled. [Col. 1139B] The other, shaken awake from sleep, pursued the fugitive by the evidence of the stars, an art in which he was skilled. The fugitive too looked back; perceiving the danger by the same art, he hid beneath a nearby wooden bridge, hanging on and clasping the bridge so that he touched neither water nor earth. Thus the seeker’s eagerness was frustrated, and he returned home.

Then Gerbert hurried on his way and reached the sea. There, having summoned the devil by incantations, he pledged perpetual homage if the devil would carry him beyond the sea, defended from the man who was again pursuing him. And so it came to pass. Yet someone may think these tales popularly invented, since people commonly injure the reputation of learned men, saying [Col. 1139C] that a man speaks with a demon when they see him excel in some work.

Thus Boethius, in the book *The Consolation of Philosophy*, complains that his pursuit of wisdom brought upon him such accusations, as though he had polluted his conscience with sacrilege in pursuit of rank:

> “It was not fitting,” he says, “that I should seek the protection of the basest spirits—I whom you were fashioning to such excellence as to make like unto God. Yet by this very fact we seem related to evil magic, because we have been imbued with your teachings and formed by your moral principles.” [Col. 1140A]

[Note: Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book I, p. 14 (Glasgow, octavo, 1751).]

Such are Boethius’ words.

[Note: “Yet it gives me confidence.” There is, on this passage in the *Recueil des Historiens de la France* (vol. X), a note sharply criticizing Malmesbury as having exercised insufficiently sound judgment. Yet the partisan devotion to Pope Sylvester—the first Frenchman to be raised to the dignity of supreme pontiff—which the editor himself of the work just mentioned acknowledges, can in some measure explain, perhaps even excuse, the severity of this commentary. And if Malmesbury is excessively harsh in his suspicion that Gerbert attained the papal mitre through magical arts, he might have defended his narrative in the same apologetic words used by the most learned editor: “We set down here these fabulous, and, so to speak [Col. 1140C], diabolical reports about Gerbert, not in order to add any weight to them, but so that the reader may lack nothing, whether true or false, concerning so great a man, the first among the Gauls to attain the summit of the supreme pontificate.”]

For my part, the unprecedented design of his death convinces me of this man’s sacrilege. Why, when dying, as we shall say below, would he have torn himself to pieces, acting as the dreadful executioner of his own body, unless he had been conscious of a new crime? Therefore, in an old volume which came into my hands, containing the names and years of all the popes, I saw this written:

> “Sylvester, also called Gerbert: four years, one month, ten days; he ended his life shamefully.”

[Note: “Sylvester, also called Gerbert, four years, one month, ten days.” In a, d, m. “John, also called Gerbert, ten months,” in s, c, e, f, g, k, l. See §167, note 68.]

## On Gerbert’s Pupils

[Col. 1140B] §168. Gerbert, returning home to Gaul and teaching in the public schools, attained the craft of a master. He had fellow philosophers and companions in study: Constantine, abbot of the monastery of Saint Maximin near Orléans, for whom he issued rules on the abacus; Adelbold, bishop, they say, of Wintburg, who too left memorials of his intellect in the letter which he wrote to Gerbert on the question of the diameter in Macrobius, and in several other works.

[Note: Rules on the abacus. See §167, note 77.]

[Note: On the question of the diameter in Macrobius. Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I.20.]

He had pupils of remarkable talent and noble lineage: Robert, son of Hugh surnamed Capet, and Otto, son of Emperor Otto. Robert, later king of France, repaid his teacher and made him archbishop of Rheims. In that church, [Col. 1140C] monuments of his learning remain:

[Note: They remain. Read *extant enim* in a, s, l. The editor of vol. X of the *Recueil des Historiens de la France* accepts the truth of the matters here reported.]

a clock constructed by mechanical skill;

[Note: Clock. It has indeed been conjectured that Gerbert was the inventor of clocks, but Thietmar of Merseburg denied him the claim to the honour of so distinguished an invention. He maintains that the clock set up by Gerbert in the cathedral was merely a kind of sundial.]

and hydraulic organs, in which, wonderfully, wind produced by the force of heated water fills the hollow of the lyre and makes the perforated bronze pipes issue musical cries.

[Note: “Issue cries.” This appears to have been an organ producing sounds by the application of steam. It may perhaps have been a modification of the revolving aeolipile, an instrument described by Vitruvius. An aeolipile ordinarily consists of a spherical metal globe with a tube or small aperture through which a jet of steam can be driven. The globe is filled with water, and fire is applied to its outer surface. As soon as the water boils, steam is driven with the greatest force from the mouth of the tube, and the apparatus thus constructed becomes an excellent replacement for ordinary bellows. Col. 1141D.]

The king himself [Col. 1141A] was no mean scholar in ecclesiastical chant; in this and in other matters he greatly benefited the Church. Finally, he composed the beautiful sequence, “May the grace of the Holy Spirit be present with us,” and the responsory, “O Judah and Jerusalem,” along with many other things which I would not be reluctant to mention if others were not reluctant to hear them.

Otto, emperor of Italy after his father, made Gerbert archbishop of Ravenna and soon afterward pope of Rome. He pressed forward his own fortunes, with the devil’s favour, leaving nothing incomplete that he had once conceived.

[Note: “With the devil’s favour.” Mabillon considers this invention of Cardinal Benno’s, adopted uncritically by later authors.]

Finally, treasures once buried by pagans, discovered through necromancy after massive earthworks had been dug, he made subservient to his desires. Such is the base disposition toward God of wicked men, who abuse his patience—men whom he would rather have return than [Col. 1141B] perish. But in the end he found where his master was vulnerable and, as the saying goes, like a crow gouging out another crow’s eyes, countered his attempts by the same art.

## How Gerbert Found Octavian’s Treasures

§169. Near Rome in the Campus Martius stood a statue—whether bronze or iron I do not know—with the index finger of its right hand extended and with an inscription on its head: “Strike here.” Men of an earlier age, thinking this meant that treasure was to be found there, had mangled the innocent statue with many strokes of axes. But Gerbert exposed their error, resolving the ambiguity in a very different way.

[Note: “Resolving.” The reading is *absoluta* in c, d, e, l; *dissoluta* in s; *obsoluta* in a.]

At noon, when the sun was at its zenith, he observed where the finger’s shadow extended and planted a stake there. [Col. 1141C] Then, when night came, accompanied only by a chamberlain carrying a lantern, he hastened to the spot. There the earth opened by its accustomed arts and revealed a broad entrance to those going in. They beheld a vast palace: golden walls, golden ceilings, everything golden; golden soldiers amusing themselves, as it seemed, with golden dice; a metal king reclining with a queen, dishes set before them, attendants standing by, and vessels of great weight and price, where workmanship surpassed nature.

In the inner part of the house a carbuncle, a most noble precious stone, small to look upon, drove away the darkness of night.

[Note: “To look upon.” The reading is *intuitu* in s; *inventu*, “in finding,” in a, c, d, e, l.]

In the opposite corner stood a boy holding a bow, its string drawn and an arrow aimed. Thus in every respect, while costly art captivated the eyes of the spectators, there was nothing that could be touched, though all could be seen. For as soon as anyone prepared to touch something, [Col. 1141D] all those figures seemed to spring forward and attack the presumptuous person. Overwhelmed by this fear, Gerbert gave up his undertaking. But the chamberlain could not refrain from snatching a knife of marvellous workmanship which he saw lying on the table, thinking, of course, that amid so great a booty a small theft [Col. 1142A] could remain concealed.

[Note: “He saw.” The reading is *videret* in e, l; *viderat*, “had seen,” in a, s, c, d.]

But immediately all the images rose with a roar; the boy too shot his arrow at the carbuncle and brought on darkness. Unless the chamberlain, at his master’s warning, had hurried to throw back the knife, both would have suffered grave penalties. Thus, with the lantern guiding their steps, they departed, their appetite for greed still unsatisfied.

That he contrived such things by hostile arts is the constant opinion of the people.

[Note: The reading is *est*, “is,” in s, c, d, e, l; *ait*, “says,” in a.]

Nevertheless, if anyone carefully investigates the truth, he will see that not even Solomon—whom God himself gave wisdom—was ignorant of this device. For, as Josephus reports, he buried many treasures with his father in chests which, he says, were concealed underground by mechanical means. Nor was Hyrcanus, renowned for prophecy and courage, ignorant of it: to relieve the hardship of a siege, he drew three thousand talents of gold from David’s tomb [Col. 1142B] by mechanical art, in order to pay a portion to the besieger and use another portion to build hostels for strangers. But Herod, who wished to attempt the same thing more through presumption than judgment, lost many of his retainers when fire issued from the inner part.

[Note: Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book VII, chapter 15; book VIII, chapter 2.]

Moreover, when I hear the Lord Jesus saying, “My Father works even now, and I work,” I believe that he who gave Solomon power over demons—as the same historian testifies, even saying that in his own time there were men who expelled them from possessed bodies by placing upon the sufferer’s nostrils a ring bearing a seal shown by Solomon—I believe, I say, that he could have given this man too such knowledge; yet I do not affirm that he did.

[Note: “The Lord.” Read “my Lord” in l.]

## How Certain Men Sought Octavian’s Treasures

[Col. 1142C]

§170. Leaving these matters to those who will read them, I shall tell what I remember hearing in childhood from a monk of our own house, an Aquitanian by birth, advanced in age, and a physician by profession.

“I,” he said, “when seven years old, despising the poverty of my father, a very poor citizen of Barcelona, crossed the snows of the Alps and came to Italy. There, as a little boy of that age, seeking sustenance in the utmost poverty, I cultivated my mind rather than my stomach. When grown up, I took in with my eyes many marvels of that land and committed them to memory.

[Note: “When grown up.” Read *adultus autem* in s.]

[Note: “Took in.” Read *libavi*, “I sampled,” in a.]

Among them, I saw a pierced mountain, beyond which the inhabitants had from ancient times believed Octavian’s treasures to be hidden. It was also reported that many men had entered its windings in order to search, and had perished after losing their way halfway through the journey. [Col. 1142D]

But because almost no fear recalls greedy minds from what they have begun, I and my companions—about twelve men—planned to undertake that journey, whether from eagerness to plunder or merely to see. Thus, following Daedalus’ ingenuity, who led Theseus out of the labyrinth with a guiding thread, we too carried a great ball of thread and fixed a peg at the entrance. Having tied the beginning of the thread there, [Col. 1143A] lighted lanterns lest darkness as well as the winding paths impede us, unrolled the ball, and set a peg at every mile, we somehow directed our journey beneath the hollow mountain.

Everything was dark and full of great terror. Bats emerging from hollows attacked our eyes and mouths. The path was narrow, and on the left was frightening because of a precipice and a river running below. We saw the trail covered with bare bones. We wept over corpses still oozing corruption: people whom the same hope that carried us away had carried beyond the mountain’s entrance, unable to find the exit.

But at last, after many terrors, reaching the farther exit, we saw a calm lake with rippling waters, where the wave played upon the shores, breaking there in sweet laps.

[Note: Read “breaking there in sweet laps” in c, d, e, l; “with those sweet approaches” in s, a.]

A bronze bridge connected the two banks. [Col. 1143B] Beyond the bridge appeared golden horses of marvellous size, with riders equally golden, and the other things said of Gerbert. At midday the brightness of Phoebus shed upon them dulled the eyes of those who looked with doubled radiance. We, seeing these things from afar, delighted in a closer view and hoping, if fortune allowed, to carry off some coating of the shining metal, encouraged one another and prepared to cross the lake—but in vain.

For when one man, more rash than the rest, placed his foot on the nearer end of the bridge, immediately—marvellous to hear—when that end sank, the farther end rose, producing a bronze peasant holding a bronze hammer. Striking the waters with it, he so clouded the air that he veiled day and sky.

[Note: Read *subtexerit*, “has veiled,” in a, e²; *subtexerat*, “had veiled,” in s.]

When the foot was withdrawn, there was peace. Several made the same attempt and had the same experience. Therefore, despairing of crossing, we stayed there for a little while and, so long as we could, at least tasted the gold with our eyes alone. Soon, retracing our path by the thread’s traces, we found a silver bowl. Cutting it into pieces and dividing it into tiny portions merely irritated [Col. 1143C] the itch of our greed; it did not satisfy our hunger.

The next day, after taking counsel, we approached a certain master of that time who was said to know the ineffable name of the Lord.

[Note: “We approached.” The reading is *adivimus* in c, e, l; *audivimus*, “we heard,” in a, s, d.]

Questioned, he did not deny the knowledge, adding that the power of that name was so great that no magic and no *mathesis*—that is, occult astrological art—could withstand it. So, bought for a great price, fasting and confessed, he led us, prepared in the same manner, to the spring.

[Note: “Confessed.” Read *confusus*, “confused,” in l.]

Having drawn water from it into a silver phial, he silently traced letters with his fingers, until we understood with our eyes what we could not utter with our mouths. Then we confidently approached the mountain; but we found the farther exit blocked, I believe, by demons—resentful, no doubt, of the name of the Lord which refuted their devices.

In the morning a Jewish necromancer came to me, summoned by the report of what had happened. [Col. 1144A] Having questioned me about the matter, he learned of our dullness and, shaking with laughter, said: ‘Well then, you shall see how great is the power of my art.’ Without hesitation he entered the mountain and shortly afterward emerged, bringing as proof of his crossing many things I had observed beyond the river: in particular, a most rich powder by which whatever was touched became yellow gold—not because it truly was so, but because it appeared so until washed away with water. For nothing accomplished by necromancy can deceive the sight of onlookers in water. A thing which occurred at the same time confirms the truth of my account.”

## On the Old Women Who Made a Young Man Appear to Be a Donkey

[Col. 1144B] §171. “On the public road leading to Rome were two old women, than whom nothing was more drunken, nothing more shameless.

[Note: “More drunken.” Read *libatius*, “more eagerly,” in a.]

[Note: “More shameless.” Read *pudicitius*, “more modest,” in e; *pudicius* in c¹; *impudicitius* in c²; *putidius*, “more foul,” in a, s, l.]

They lived in a single hut and were trained in a single magical practice. Whenever a guest came alone, they made him appear a horse, a pig, or anything else, offered him for sale to merchants, and swallowed down the money they received.

[Note: “Swallowed down.” Read *abligurientes*, “guzzling away,” in a, s, l.]

One night they happened to receive as a guest a young man who earned his living by theatrical movements. They made him appear a donkey, having a donkey of great profit to them, which held the gaze of passers-by by the marvel of its performances. For however the old woman commanded, the donkey moved. Yet he had not lost his understanding, though he had lost [Col. 1144C] speech.

[Note: “For.” Omitted in a, s.]

[Note: “Although.” Read *etiamsi* in d.]

The old women therefore amassed considerable profit, as crowds of common people flocked from every direction to watch the donkey’s performances. The report brought a wealthy neighbour, who bought the quadruped for no small sum for his own use, being warned that if he wished to retain this performer permanently, he must keep him from water.

[Note: Water. Gloss in l: “namely, from water.”]

Accordingly, a guard was assigned and strictly carried out the instruction. A great deal of time passed. Whenever drink stirred his master to merriment, the donkey delighted the guests with his tricks. But, since all things become tiresome, he thereafter began to be kept more negligently. Having found less watchful custody, he broke his tether, escaped, threw himself into a nearby lake, and, after rolling in the water for a long time, recovered his human form.

[Note: “Less watchful.” Gloss in l: that is, less cautious.]

The guard asked those he met [Col. 1144D] and followed the man’s tracks, then asked whether he had seen the donkey. The man reported that he himself had been a donkey and was now a man, and explained the whole event. The servant, astonished, reported it to his master; the master reported it to Pope Leo—the holiest man, I say, of our age. The convicted old women confessed the same.

Peter Damian, learned in letters, confirmed the hesitant pope: it was no wonder if such things could happen. Giving the example of Simon Magus, who made Faustinianus appear in Simon’s form and be feared by his sons, he made him more fully informed about such matters thereafter.

[Note: Simon Magus. In the fabulous *Itinerary of Saint Peter*, falsely attributed to Clement of Rome, Simon Magus is represented as giving Faustinianus the features of his own face by means of a certain red medicinal ointment. This produced great terror in Faustinianus’ sons, who mistook their father for Simon and fled until Saint Peter recalled them. (Sharpe, p. 208.)]

## On the Speaking Head of a Statue

§172. I have inserted this Aquitanian’s words so that no one may think it strange what rumour spread about Gerbert: that he had cast for himself the head of a statue, by a precise observation of the stars, when all the planets were contemplating the beginnings of their courses; that it spoke only when questioned, yet always declared the truth, affirmatively or negatively.

For example, Gerbert would say:

> “Shall I become pope?”  
> The statue would answer: “Yes.”  
> “Shall I die before I sing Mass in Jerusalem?”  
> “No.” [Col. 1145B]

[Note: “Would say.” Read “when Gerbert said” in a, s, d.]

They say that he was deceived by this ambiguity, so that he devised nothing conducive to repentance, flattering himself that he would live a long time. For when would he resolve to go to Jerusalem in order to hasten death? He did not foresee that at Rome there is a church called Jerusalem—that is, “Vision of Peace”—because whoever flees there, guilty of whatever crime, finds protection. We have learned that it was called the Asylum at the city’s foundation, because Romulus established there a refuge for all accused persons, in order to increase the number of citizens.

There the pope sings Mass on three Sundays entitled “Station at Jerusalem.”

[Note: “At.” Omitted in c, e.]

[Note: “Those.” The reading is *illorum* in c, d, e; *eorum*, “those,” in a, s, l.]

Accordingly, as Gerbert prepared himself for Mass on one of those days, he groaned beneath the stroke of sickness; as it grew worse, he took to his bed. [Col. 1145C] Consulting the statue, he learned of its deception and of his own death. He therefore summoned the cardinals and long lamented his crimes. They were struck with unexpected astonishment and unable to say anything in reply; but he, raving and mentally enfeebled by pain, ordered himself to be torn to pieces bit by bit and his limbs cast outside.

[Note: “Struck.” Read *perculsis* in a, c, d, l.]

“Let him have,” he said, “the service of the limbs whose homage he sought. For my soul never loved that oath—indeed, that sacrilege.”

[Note: Oath. Gloss in l: “namely, that made to the devil.”]

§173. And since I have made a digression, I think it not improper to relate

[Note: “I think.” The reading is *aestimo* in c, d, e, l, m; *opinor*, “I suppose,” in a, s.]

 what occurred in Saxony in the time of this king, and is not very well known, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1012. It is better meanwhile to range over such subjects than to linger over his affairs, which are both idle and sad. This will certainly be more pleasing if I add the writing of the man who suffered it, composed in antiquity; it will also appear nearer to the truth than if I had woven it in my own words. Moreover, I do not think it unsuitable for discourse to be varied by a many-coloured style.

## On Men and Women Leading Dances

[Col. 1146A] §174. “I, Otbert, a sinner—and if I wished to conceal the divine judgment inflicted on me, the trembling of my limbs would betray it—shall tell how it happened, so that everyone may know how great is the punishment of disobedience.

[Note: Otbert. Read *Ethelbertus* in s.]

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, we were in a certain village in Saxony where there was a church of the martyr Magnus. A priest named Robert had begun the first Mass. I, with eighteen companions—fifteen men and three women—was leading dances in the cemetery and noisily singing secular songs, so that I hindered the priest and our very words resounded amid the holy rites of Mass.

Accordingly, when he ordered us to be silent and we disregarded him, he uttered this curse: ‘May it please God [Col. 1146B] and Saint Magnus that you continue singing thus for a year!’ The words carried weight. The priest’s son John seized his sister, who was singing with us, by the arm; immediately that arm was torn from her body, but not a drop of blood came out. She too remained with us throughout the entire year, leading dances and singing.

No rain fell upon us; neither cold nor heat, neither hunger nor thirst, neither weariness affected us. We did not wear out our clothing or our shoes; rather, like mad people, we kept singing.

[Note: “Nor.” Read *nec* in a, s, l.]

First we sank into the earth to the knees, then to the thighs. At times, by God’s will, the frame of a roof rose over us to keep away the rain. At last, when the year had passed, Herbert, bishop of the city of Cologne, released us from the knot by which our hands were bound and reconciled us before the altar of Saint Magnus. The priest’s daughter, together with two others, immediately breathed her last. The rest of us slept continuously for three days and nights. Some later died and shine with miracles; the others reveal their punishment by the trembling of their limbs.” [Col. 1146C]

These letters were given to us by Lord Peregrine, successor of blessed Herbert, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1013.

[Note: “Blessed.” Omitted in a, s, l.]

## On a Most Deformed and Pious Bishop, and an Incestuous Nun

§175. In this city—which was formerly called Agrippina after Agrippa, Augustus’ son-in-law, and was later named Cologne after the emperor Trajan, because, when admitted to imperial power, he brought colonies of Roman citizens there [Col. 1146D]—in this city, I say, there was a certain bishop, distinguished for his piety though grotesque in body. I shall recount one miracle which he foretold when dying, after first explaining how an unusual event raised him to so lofty a rank.

[Note: “Because.” Read “because there” in a, s, c, d, l.]

The emperor of that land, on the Sunday called Quinquagesima, went hunting and, with all his companions scattered, came alone to the edge of a forest. Nearby was a church served by a rustic priest, exceedingly ugly and almost a monstrosity of nature. The emperor, pretending to be a soldier, humbly asked for Mass; the priest immediately prepared it. The other meanwhile considered in his mind why God, from whom all beautiful things proceed, allowed so ugly a man to celebrate his sacraments.

Then, when they reached the verse of the tract, “Know that the Lord himself is God,” the priest, rebuking the negligence of his young attendant, looked back and, in a louder voice, as though answering the emperor’s thought, said: “He made us, and not we ourselves.” At these words the emperor was struck, [Col. 1147A–B] judged him a prophetic man, and raised the unwilling and resistant priest to be archbishop.

[Note: “Struck.” The reading is *repercussus* in e; *reperculsus* in a, c, d, l; *percussus* in s.]

[Note: “Archbishop.” The reading is *archiepiscopum* in a, e; *archiepiscopium* in l; *archiepiscopatum* in d; *episcopum* in c; “archbishop of Cologne” in s.]

Once he had accepted the office, however, he honoured it by conduct worthy of it: gently addressing those who did good; branding the wicked with the mark of excommunication; and showing no respect of persons.

[Note: “Persons.” Read *personae* in a, l.]

The inhabitants constantly recount many of his deeds. Because of the brevity of the work undertaken, the reader shall run through one of them. In the convent of nuns in that city was a certain virgin, who had grown up there more through parental arrangement than through devotion to a good life. By the enticement of her beauty and sweet conversation with everyone, she attracted lovers.

[Note: “Conversation.” Read *alloquio*, “address,” in a, l.]

But although the rest restrained their desires either through fear of God or through fear of worldly disgrace, one man, whom accumulated wealth and lofty birth had inflamed to insolence, broke through the restraints of law and justice, daring to storm the maiden’s virginal [uncertain reading]. [Col. 1147C]

[Note: “Virginal.” The printed reading is *virginal* in e, l; d reads *virginalem aulam*, “virginal chamber”; s reads *virginale*, “virginal thing.”]

He dared to violate her and, having carried her off, kept her in his house as though she were a lawful wife. Much time passed in the abbess’s prayers and the relatives’ warnings that he should not accustom himself to so shameful a crime. But he passed by the warnings with deaf ears and stood unmoved like a cliff in the sea.

At that time the bishop happened to be absent, occupied with the concerns of the court. On his return, the matter was reported to him. He immediately commanded that the sheep be restored to the fold. Thus, after many words exchanged on both sides, the woman was returned to the convent. But not long afterwards, taking advantage of the bishop’s absence, the man carried her off again.

Then excommunication was pronounced against the offender, so that no citizen dared speak or dine with him. Treating the punishment as insignificant, he went far away to estates under his own jurisdiction—not in order to uphold the command, but to escape its enforcement. There he lived with his excommunicated woman, a man of faction and power. [Col. 1147D]

But when God called the bishop above, and he lay on his bed, his limbs consumed by grievous pain, countrymen gathered from every side to share in the final blessing of the holy man. The man alone did not dare come, but sent others to speak for him. At first the pontiff received the hearing of his name with a groan; then he added these words, which I shall repeat:

> “If that wretched man abandons the accursed woman, let him be absolved. If he persists, then in the following year, on this same day and at the same hour at which I die, let him be ready to render an account before God. And you shall see me breathe my last when the bell sounds for the sixth hour.”

[Note: “The woman.” The reading is *mulierem*, “the woman,” in a, d, e, l; *mulierem illam*, “that woman,” in c, s.]

Nor did the event fail to confirm his words: the bishop died at the hour he had foretold; and the other man, when the year had elapsed, was struck dead by lightning with his mistress on the same day and at the same hour.

## How Sweyn Is Invited to Come to England

[Col. 1148B]

§ 176. But King [Note: “King”: a, s, d, e², l; omitted in c, e.] Ethelred, after the martyrdom, as we have said [Note: “As we have said”: see § 165.], of Saint Elphege, gave the bishopric to a certain Bishop Lyfing. [Note: Bishop Lyfing. Lyfing, formerly named Æthelstan, passed from the church of Wells to Canterbury in 1013. He died on 12 June 1020.] Turkill the Dane, who had instigated the stoning of the archbishop, remained in England; and he had the East Angles obedient to his will. For the rest, after a tribute of eight thousand pounds had been paid by the English, dispersed through towns and countryside wherever each could most conveniently go; fifteen of their ships, with their crews, followed the king’s allegiance. Meanwhile Turkill summoned by messengers Swein, king of his own country, to come to England: it was a splendid and wealthy land, he said, but its king was asleep; devoted to Venus and wine, he thought of anything rather than war; consequently he was hated by his own people and laughed at by strangers. The nobles were jealous; the provincials weak, and would abandon battle at the first blare of the trumpets.

§ 177. Swein was inclined to bloodshed, and needed no great encouragement. Therefore, having prepared ships, he hastened the crossing. Sandwich is the harbour where he landed, chiefly intending in his heart vengeance for his sister Gunhild.

[Note: Swein. The slaughter of the Danes on the feast of St Brice, A.D. 1002, and the killing of Gunhild, Swein’s sister, long remained present in their minds as a living fuel of hatred against the Saxon name. The Danish king’s assault upon England in the following year can scarcely be regarded as an ample vengeance for so great an injury; nor did Swein cease to harry the English coast until his death. The Danes landed at Sandwich in July 1013.]

She was a woman of no unattractive appearance, who had come to England with her husband Palling, a powerful earl. Having accepted Christianity, she had made herself a hostage for the Danish peace. Edric’s disastrous frenzy had ordered her beheaded with the other Danes, although she declared that the shedding of her blood would bring great ruin upon all England. She faced death with composure: she neither turned pale as she was dying nor, even after all her blood had been drained, lost her countenance when dead. First, before her eyes, her husband had been killed, and her son—a boy of promising disposition—pierced with four spears.

Then Swein, advancing through East Anglia into Northumbria, subjected it to his rule without a battle. This was not because that native spirit in their hearts, impatient of masters, had grown cold, but because their leader Uhtred first set the example of defection.

[Note: Uhtred first gave the example of defection. Uhtred and the Northumbrians submitted to Swein in 1013.]

When they had been sent beneath the yoke, all the other peoples inhabiting England north of the Humber also gave tribute and hostages. Soon he came into the southern regions. He compelled the men of Oxford and Winchester to submit to his laws. The Londoners alone, protecting the lawful king within their walls, shut their gates.

[Note: The Londoners … shut [their gates]. Ethelred and Turketil repelled Swein from London in 1013.]

The Danes, standing against them with greater ferocity, nourished their courage with hope of glory; the townsmen rushed toward death for liberty, judging that there would be no pardon for them if they deserted the king who had entrusted his life to them. Thus, while each side fought fiercely, the more just cause won the victory. The citizens exerted themselves mightily, each wishing to display his labours to his sovereign and considering it noble to die for him. Part of the enemy was overthrown, part killed in the Thames because, in headlong fury, they had not waited for the bridge.

With his column broken, Swein made for Bath. There Ethelmer, earl of the western region, with all his men submitted to him. Nor would the Londoners yet bend, though all England was now inclining into his clientship, unless Ethelred had deserted them by his own presence. For, a man given to indolence and, through fear arising from his own conduct, believing no one faithful to him, he evaded the necessity of war and siege and left them in the midst of danger by his flight. Therefore, seeking a remedy in extremity, they submitted in imitation of their countrymen.

[Note: “Believing”: c, d, e, l; “fearing”: a.]

They were indeed praiseworthy men, whom Mars himself, had they possessed a leader, would not have disdained to match in a contest of spears. While they were protected even by his shadow alone, they had for not a few months made light of the hazard of the whole battle and even of the siege itself. Meanwhile he, awakened to consciousness of his natural slothfulness, fled from the city; and, having reached Southampton by secret routes, he sailed thence to Wight. There he gathered the abbots and bishops who did not think that, even in such necessity, they ought to abandon their lord, and addressed them thus:

They should see how narrowly confined were his affairs and theirs: through the treachery of nobles, he had been driven from the ancestral throne and was in need of others’ help, though formerly the safety of others had depended upon his hand; once monarch and powerful, now wretched and an exile. This reversal must be lamented, because it is easier to bear not having possessed wealth than to lose what one has possessed; it was all the more shameful to the English because the example of a deserted leader would spread throughout the world. Out of love for him, without payment, they had voluntarily undertaken exile and exposed their homes and property to plunderers; all suffered want of food, and many lacked clothing. He approved their fidelity, certainly, but could find no safety; so completely was the land now subjugated and the coasts guarded that there was nowhere an exit without danger. Therefore they should deliberate together what they judged ought to be done.

If they remained, they must guard themselves more against fellow citizens than enemies. Perhaps by their crosses they might purchase the favour of their new masters; and certainly to be killed by an enemy is attributed to fortune, but to be betrayed by a fellow citizen is assigned to cowardice.

[Note: “Is attributed”: c, d, e; “are attributed”: a, s.]

If they fled to foreign peoples, it would be a loss of honour; if to familiar ones, there was reason to fear that they might alter their disposition with their fortune.

[Note: “Alter”: e, l; “might alter”: a, s, d; “might remove”: c.]

For most upright and distinguished men had been slain on this occasion. Yet they must try fortune and test the heart of Richard, duke of the Normans; if he received his sister and nephews with no ungrateful mind, he too would not disdain to protect them. “For,” he said, “the favour lavishly bestowed upon my wife and children will stand surety for my own safety. But if he sets a hostile foot against me, courage will not fail me—assuredly it will not fail me—so that I would rather fall gloriously here than live dishonourably there. Therefore, meanwhile, in this month of August, while a gentler breeze calms the sea, let Emma sail to her brother, to deposit with him our common pledges. Let the bishop of Durham and the abbot of Peterborough accompany them. I shall remain here until Christmas; if they report good news, I shall follow at once.”

[Note: Bishop of Durham, etc. According to Florence of Worcester, Ælfhun, bishop of London, and Ælfsige, abbot of Peterborough, accompanied Emma and her two sons, Edward and Alfred, into Normandy. See also the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 1013.]

§ 178. When the assembly was dissolved, all made preparations. They sailed to Normandy, while he remained behind, eager to preserve his reputation. Soon word came from overseas that Richard had received his sister with great eagerness and invited the king also to honour his household. Thus Ethelred, arriving in Normandy in January, consoled his misfortunes by the attentions of his host.

[Note: Ethelred, coming to Normandy in January: 1 January, A.D. 1014.]

[Note: Richard, son of Richard I. Richard II, surnamed the Good, succeeded his father in 996. According to most authors he died on 23 August 1027; but William of Jumièges, like a certain earlier author, assigns his death to 1026. (*Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, eleventh century, p. 370.)]

This was Richard, son of Richard I, who equalled his father in good fortune and integrity, and certainly surpassed him in matters concerning God. He brought to completion the monastery of Fécamp, which his father had begun. He was so devoted to prayer and frugality that one would not have missed either monk or hermit in him. He was so lowly in humility that, by patience, he laid beneath himself the arrogance of those who provoked him.

It is said, finally, that at night, evading the watchfulness of his servants, he was accustomed to come unaccompanied to the monks’ matins, remaining in genuflections until daylight.

[Note: “In genuflections”: c, d, e, m; “in acts of genuflection”: a, s, l.]

He practised this especially at Fécamp. One night he came earlier than usual; finding the door barred, he shook the bolt more violently and disturbed the sacristan’s sleep. The latter, astonished at the sound of someone knocking amid the terror of such a night, rose to see who had committed so daring an act. Finding what appeared to be a peasant covered in a common cloak, he could not restrain himself from laying hands upon him. Moved by violent anger, he seized his hair and struck the illustrious man many blows. Richard endured this with incredible patience and did not deign to utter a word.

On the following day he laid a complaint before the chapter. Feigning anger, he ordered the monk to meet him at the village of Argences, threatening to avenge upon the monk’s obstinacy what all Gaul was saying. On the appointed day, when the monk was present and nearly lifeless with fear, he set the matter before the nobles, magnifying the enormity of the act through rhetorical amplification. For some time he held the accused man in suspense as the latter attempted to reply to his clever accusations. At last, so that the occasion for compassion might be more agreeable, he had him mercifully acquitted by the leading men, and assigned to his office [Note: “His office”: a, c, d, e, l; “the office of that same sacristan”: s.] that whole village, said to be productive of excellent wine, with its appurtenances. He declared the monk excellent because, having guarded well the charge laid upon him, he had not, even when provoked to anger, relaxed his silence.

[Note: “Nor when provoked.” The narratives here concerning Richard II, duke of Normandy, are adduced as a singular example of the manners of this age. (Prologue to the *Recueil des Histoires de la France*, vol. X.)]

[Note: After twenty-eight years of his dukedom. Richard II; see note 38 to this paragraph.]

After twenty-eight years of rule, as he entered upon the way of death, he ordered his body buried at the church door, exposed both to the feet of those treading upon it and to raindrops falling from above. But in our time William, the third abbot of that place, judging the arrangement unbecoming, removed a longstanding reproach and placed the body, raised from there, before the high altar.

[Note: To be buried at the church door: at the church of Fécamp. Compare Dudo of St-Quentin, where he reports the death of Richard II.]

He had a brother Robert, whom he made archbishop of Rouen, thereby indeed casting no slight stain upon his glory. For Robert made dreadful abuse of his office, committing first many crimes and many disgraceful acts; but later, as he grew old, he undoubtedly effaced some of them by most lavish almsgiving.

[Note: “He had … at Rouen”: a, s, d, e, l; omitted in c. Robert was the son of Richard I, duke of Normandy, by his second wife Gunnor, who had previously been his concubine. Made earl of Évreux by his father in 989, he was created archbishop of Rouen by him in the same year. He died before Easter, A.D. 1036. Some authors assign his death to 1037. (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. XI.)]

After Richard, his son of the same name obtained the principality, but lived scarcely even one year.

[Note: After Richard, etc. According to Mabillon, Richard III died on 6 August, in the first year of his reign; but Orderic Vitalis asserts that he died in the second year of his reign. Some writers date his death to 3 February 1028.]

An uncertain report certainly circulated that, through the connivance of his brother Robert—whom Richard II had had by Judith, daughter of Conan, count of the Bretons—a poisonous plot had been devised against the young man.

[Note: The opinion, etc. See William of Jumièges, book VI, chapter 2, and the short Chronicle of Saint-Martin of Tours (in Chesne, vol. III, *Scriptors of France*, p. 360).]

[Note: His brother Robert. Robert of Hiémois, count, succeeded his brother in the duchy of Normandy, as also did Robert I, surnamed the Magnificent and the Devil.]

Lamenting the consciousness of this deed, after seven years he departed on pilgrimage to Jerusalem. At that time he undertook a deed deserving great praise, daring with few companions to traverse a journey threatened by barbarian disturbances and alien in its customs through Saracens.

[Note: “Through Saracens”: e; one manuscript reads “through Saracen practices.”]

Yet he pressed on and did not stop, safely completing the whole route. Having purchased entrance with much gold, he venerated barefoot and with tears that glory of Christians—the Lord’s Sepulchre, I mean. Grace, reconciled by this labour before God, as we believe, accompanied him; but, returning home, he ended his days at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, reportedly cut off by poison.

[Note: At Nicaea … he ended his days: 2 July, A.D. 1035; William of Jumièges, book VI, chapter 13.]

His agent was Ralph, surnamed Mowin, who had driven himself to that crime by hope of the duchy; but, on returning to Normandy, he was recognized and driven out by all as a monster, and went into perpetual exile.

[Note: “Reportedly”: a, c, d, e, l; “said”: s.]

Robert was succeeded by his young son William, of whom I shall speak in what follows; now I shall return to the matter at hand.

[Note: Robert was succeeded by his young son William. William the Bastard, later king of England. He was not more than eight years old when his father was taken from life.]

§ 179. Meanwhile Swein oppressed the England he had invaded, in the manner described, with plunder and slaughter. The wealth of the provincials was first stripped away, and then proscriptions were imposed. Entire cities were uncertain what should be done: if rebellion were prepared, they had no champion; if submission were chosen, they would lack a gentle ruler. Thus private and public wealth alike was carried to the ships with hostages, because he was no lawful lord but a most cruel tyrant.

But propitious Divinity did not permit England to fluctuate long in so great a misery; for the invader, at the Purification of Saint Mary, immediately gave up his life, though the manner of his death is uncertain.

[Note: “Gave up his life.” Swein died on 3 February, A.D. 1014.]

It is said that, when he was devastating the land of Saint Edmund, that same martyr appeared to him in a vision. Having gently reproved him for the misery of his own community, and receiving an insolent reply, Edmund struck him on the head. Stricken by that pain, he died shortly afterwards, as has been said.

[Note: “Edmund”: a, c, d, e, l; “Edmund, king and martyr”: s. Compare Herman, *On the Miracles of Saint Edmund*.]

The Danes chose Cnut, son of Swein, as king. The English, on the other hand, declaring that their natural lord was dearer to them—provided he behaved more royally than he had been accustomed to do—summoned Ethelred from Normandy. He first sent his son Edward, to observe in person the loyalty of the nobles and the people’s favour. When he saw all wishes agreeing in a favourable direction, he returned confidently for his father.

[Note: The king returned. Æthelred returned from Normandy in A.D. 1014. The editors of the *Recueil des Histoires de la France*, relying on certain chroniclers, assign both Swein’s death and Æthelred’s return to England to 1015.]

The king returned, soothed by the joyful applause of the English; and, as though he had shaken off his habitual indolence [Note: That he seemed to have shaken off his habitual indolence: see § 177, “for, a man given to indolence,” etc.], he hastened to gather an army against Cnut. Cnut was then in Lindsey, where his father had left him with ships and hostages, demanding recruits and horses in order to pour with united forces upon the unprepared English and exact severe revenge, as he himself declared, upon deserters. But forestalled by the kind of treachery he himself had plotted, he turned his back. Escaping only with difficulty, he put out to sea with his remaining forces; after sailing around the British sea from east to south, he landed at Sandwich.

There, scorning both human and divine law, he mutilated the hostages in his possession—boys of high birth and refinement—by cutting off their noses and ears; he even castrated some of them. Thus he raged against the innocent and boasted that he had done something great; then he sought his native country.

[Note: “Mutilated”: c, d, e, l; “having mutilated”: a, s.]

[Note: He sought his homeland. Cnut returned to Denmark in 1014. See Florence of Worcester and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.]

In the same year the sea-tide which the Greeks call the Euripus and we call the Ledo increased in a remarkable fashion, beyond anything human memory can reach, so that it submerged villages for many miles and killed the inhabitants caught there.

[Note: Sea-tide, etc. *Euripus* seems to denote a sea-tide generally; *ledo* means a lesser tide, not a spring tide, as Malmesbury here indicates. *Malina* means a spring tide. Hoveden, explaining the etymology of Lindisfarne, writes: “Lindis is the name of a river which runs into the sea; when there is a *ledo*, that is, a lesser tide, it is two feet deep and can be seen; but when there is a *malina*, that is, a greater sea-tide, Lindis cannot be seen.”]

[Note: It increased remarkably. “In this year [1014], on the eve of the feast of St Michael [28 September], there came a great sea-tide, which spread widely through this region and rose so high as had never happened before, drowning very many towns and an innumerable multitude of people.” (*Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*.) “The sea overflowed the shore on the third day before the Kalends of October, and submerged in England very many villages and an innumerable multitude of people.” (Florence of Worcester.)]

In the following year a great council of Danes and English was assembled at Oxford.

[Note: “Following”: a, c, e, l; “in the following year”: d, m; “but in the following year”: s.]

[Note: At Oxford. A great council, or council, was held at Oxford in 1015, according to William of Jumièges.]

There the most noble king of the Danes ordered Sigeferth and Morcar to be killed, after the treacherous traitor Edric had accused them before him of disloyalty.

[Note: “Sigeferth and Morcar”: a, s, c, e, l; omitted in d, m. They were sons of Earngrim. (Florence of Worcester.)]

Edric enticed them, deceived by flattering compliments, into a dining hall; and, after making them drink freely, he had them stripped of life by retainers prepared for this purpose. The alleged reason for the killing was that he coveted their property.

[Note: “And after making them drink freely”: a, s, c, d, e², l; omitted in e.]

Their retainers, attempting to avenge their lords’ death, were driven back by arms and forced into the tower of the church of Saint Frideswide. [Note: “Frideswide”: a, c, d, e, l; “Frideswide at Oxford”: s.] When they could not be expelled from it, they were consumed by fire. But soon the king’s repentance removed the defilement, and the sanctuary was repaired. I have read a written record of the deed, contained in the archive of that church.

The wife of Sigeferth, a woman of conspicuous nobility, was brought captive to Malmesbury.

[Note: “Nobility”: a, c, d, e, l; “nobility and beauty”: s.]

Therefore Edmund, the king’s son, concealing his intention, set out for those parts; seeing her, he desired her, and, having desired her, had sexual union with her. In truth he mocked his father’s judgment, who was a laughing-stock to his household as much as to strangers.

This Edmund was not born of Emma, but of another woman whom obscure report conceals.

[Note: From another woman. Florence states that the mother of Edmund Ironside was Ælfgifu, daughter of Earl Æthelberht; but Ailred of Rievaulx says that she was the daughter of Thored, a noble earl.]

[Note: “That”: c, d, e; “this”: a, s, l.]

In all else upright, he was a young man of praiseworthy disposition, great strength of mind and body, and consequently called by the English Ireneside, that is, “Iron Side.” By his courage he properly outweighed his father’s sloth and his mother’s low birth, had the Fates known how to spare him. Without delay, at his wife’s counsel, he sought from his father the earldom of Sigeferth, very extensive among the Northumbrians; when it was not granted, he seized it by his own enterprise, the men of that province readily yielding obedience to him.

§ 180. [Note: In that same summer Cnut … came to England. Cnut came to England in January, A.D. 1016.]

In that same summer, Cnut, having settled affairs in Denmark and made an alliance of friendship with neighbouring kings, came to England, resolved either to conquer or to die.

[Note: “Either to conquer”: a, c, d, e, l; omitted in s.]

Proceeding from Sandwich into Kent and thence into Wessex, he defiled everything with slaughter and fire, while the king lay ill at Cosham. Edmund indeed tried to meet him, but was hindered by Edric and meanwhile kept his forces in a safe place. Edric, however, judging that he should no longer disguise himself instead of exposing his arts openly, defected to Cnut with forty ships. All Wessex likewise, giving hostages and arms, did the same.

[Note: “Likewise”: a, s, d, e, l; “indeed”: c.]

But the Mercians, repeatedly assembled [Note: “Repeatedly”: a, c, d, e, l; “in number and hope”: s.], offered themselves for resistance: let the king only come and direct where they should advance; let him bring with him the nobles of London; they were ready to spend their blood for their country. He, accustomed to entrust his safety to walls rather than sally forth against an enemy, stayed in London on account of traitors, as he said, never going anywhere.

Meanwhile the other man attached cities and villages to his party, never resting: he took counsel by night and fought by day. Edmund, after long deliberation in so great a crisis, judged it best to recover by fighting the towns that had defected. He brought Uhtred, an earl beyond the Humber, to the same view; for they believed that the rest, still hanging in uncertain allegiance, must be confirmed if severe penalties were exacted from the rebels.

But Cnut, endowed with no less cunning, outwitted them by a like contrivance. Entrusting Wessex and the part of Mercia that he had subdued to his commanders, he himself advanced into Northumbria. By ravaging the country he forced Uhtred to return to defend his own lands. Thus, though he had surrendered, he was ordered to be beheaded in barbarous inconstancy. His earldom was given to Iric, whom Cnut later expelled from England when he claimed an equal share for himself.

Thus, after subduing all, Cnut did not stop pursuing Edmund, who fled through byways, until he learned that he had reached his father in London. Then he rested until after Easter, intending to attack the city with all his forces. But Ethelred’s death forestalled his design. At the beginning of Lent, on the feast-day of Saint Gregory—though all manuscripts so read, Saint George is evidently meant—he breathed out a soul born to labours and miseries. He lies at Saint Paul’s in London.

[Note: At the beginning of Lent. According to the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* and Florence of Worcester, Ethelred died in London on Monday, 23 April—the feast of St George—A.D. 1016.]

The townsmen acclaimed Edmund king. He quickly assembled an army and routed the Danes at Pen and Gillingham [Note: “And”: c, e; “near”: a, s, d, l.] during the Rogation Days. After the feast of Saint John, he met them at Seorstan and withdrew with the issue equal, because his English began the flight at the instigation of Edric. Standing among the enemy and holding a sword in his hand, which he had made bloody in battle by vigorously killing a certain peasant, Edric cried: “Flee, wretches, flee! Behold, your king has been killed by this sword!”

[Note: Seorstan. This is supposed to have been the stone that marked the division of the four counties of Oxford, Gloucester, Worcester, and Warwick.]

The English would immediately have fled, had not the king, when he learned the matter, mounted a certain hill and, removing his helmet, displayed his head to his fellow soldiers. Then, hurling an iron-shafted spear with all the force he could muster, he cast it at Edric. But Edric saw and avoided it; it struck a soldier standing nearby, piercing another as well. Night ended the battle, the armies withdrawing as though by mutual agreement; yet the English almost hoped for victory. From this event the Wessex men changed their minds and recognized their lawful lord.

Edmund hastened to London to free its deserving citizens, whom part of the enemy had immediately hemmed in after his departure. They had also surrounded the city on the outside with a ditch wherever the Thames did not wash it, and had inflicted and received many wounds.

[Note: The ditch, etc. A ditch seems to have been dug on the southern bank of the river, and ships brought to the western side of the bridge to besiege the city. See the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*. No trace of this ditch now remains by which its site may be recognized.]

Therefore, upon hearing of the king’s arrival, they took flight down the slopes. He pursued them immediately and, after crossing the ford called Brentford, annihilated them in a victorious slaughter.

[Note: “Flight”: a, c, d, e, l; omitted in s.]

The remaining multitude, which had stayed with Cnut, again besieged London by land and river while Edmund rested briefly and ordered his affairs. But, repelled by the townsmen’s courageous fighting, they poured out their rage upon neighbouring Mercia, ravaging villages and estates with plunder, fire, and slaughter. They carried rich booty to the ships which they had assembled on the river Medway. That river, flowing past the city of Rochester, is violent and threatening in its rapacious current, and washes its handsome walls.

From there too they were routed while the king fought, and, after the ford above mentioned—Brentford—had been seized in advance, they were scattered in notable slaughter. When Edmund tried to press farther in order to pursue the remnants of the plunderers to extermination, that crafty and utterly wicked Edric recalled him. Edric had long since feigned a return to favour; by Cnut’s plan he was with Edmund in order to report Edmund’s counsels.

That day would certainly have been the Danes’ last if the king had judged that he should persevere. But forestalled, as I have said, by the traitor’s whisper that the enemy would dare nothing further, he prepared a premature destruction for himself and for all England. For, given a route of escape, they united again and harried East Anglia by war. They compelled the king himself, coming with assistance, to yield at Assandun. The author of the flight’s beginning was that man whom it is shameful to name so often. The few who had not forgotten their honour and, encouraging one another, had formed a wedge, were killed to the last man.

There Cnut won the kingdom; there all England’s glory fell; there the whole flower of the country withered. Among them was Ulfketel, earl of the East Angles, who had already earned lasting fame in Swein’s time, when he first of all attacked the pirates and gave hope that they could be conquered; and there were also the leading men of that time, abbots and bishops.

[Note: Principal men then. Eadnoth, bishop of Dorchester; Wulfsige, abbot; and the earls Ælfric, Godwine, and Æthelweard are also counted among those slain.]

Edmund, retreating from there almost alone, came to Gloucester, so that, after gathering his strength there, he might attack the enemy, idle after their recent victory, as he supposed. Nor did Cnut lack courage to pursue the fugitive. Thus, when they had drawn up with hostile standards, Edmund challenged him to single combat, lest two little men, through ambition for a kingdom, should be guilty of shedding the blood of so many subjects when they could test fortune without loss to their faithful men. Great glory would accrue to either one who gained so great a kingdom chiefly at his own risk.

When these proposals were reported to Cnut, he wholly refused. He declared that he excelled in courage, certainly, but distrusted his body against a man of such enormous bulk. Yet, because both were not unjustly demanding a kingdom which the fathers of both had held, it was prudent that, laying aside their resentments, they divide England.

[Note: They divide England. According to the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*, the meeting between Cnut and Edmund took place at Olney, an island in the Severn near Deerhurst.]

This proposal was accepted by both armies and ratified with great agreement, since it accorded with fairness and gently provided for the peace of mortals wearied by so many miseries. Thus Edmund, overcome by the unanimous cry of all, yielded to peace and made a treaty with Cnut, granting Wessex to himself and Mercia to Cnut.

Not long afterward, on the feast of Saint Andrew, he died at Glastonbury and was buried beside his grandfather Edgar, though the manner of his death is uncertain. Report accuses Edric of having procured his death through agents in order to please the other man.

[Note: On the feast of St Andrew. The true circumstances of Edmund’s death remain hidden in obscurity; but there seems little doubt that he was killed by treachery in 1017. Florence of Worcester and the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* assign his death to 30 November 1016. Florence, however, adds an indiction-year corresponding to A.D. 1017.]

The king had two chamberlains, to whom he had entrusted his entire life. Edric enticed them with promises; though at first horrified by the enormity of the crime, they soon became his accomplices. At his direction, while Edmund sat to satisfy the necessities of nature, they drove an iron hook into his rear parts.

His brother by the same mother, Eadwig, a young man of integrity not to be despised, left England at Cnut’s command through the traitor Edric. Long tossed on land and sea, his body was afflicted, as commonly happens, by anguish of mind; while he lay concealed among the English after a secret return, he died and was buried at Tavistock.

[Note: His brother, etc. Eadwig, Edmund Ironside’s brother, and Eadwig surnamed *Ceorla cyning* (“king of peasants”) were proscribed in A.D. 1017. The former was later killed at Cnut’s command. (*Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*; Florence of Worcester.)]

His sons, Eadwig and Edward, were sent to the king of the Swedes to be killed; but preserved by that king’s compassion, they went to the king of the Huns. There, after being kindly treated for some time, the elder died; the younger married Agatha, the queen’s sister.

[Note: His sons: [sons] of Edmund Ironside.]

[Note: “Eadwig.” Edmund is probably to be read here. Edmund and Edward, sons of Edmund Ironside, were sent by Cnut to the king of the Swedes. (Florence of Worcester, A.D. 1017.)]

[Note: Edward married Agatha and had by her Edgar Ætheling, Christina, who embraced the religious life, and Margaret, who married Malcolm, king of Scotland.]

His brothers by Emma, Alfred and Edward, maintained secure hiding-places in Normandy throughout Cnut’s lifetime. We find that their uncle Richard did nothing for their restoration to their native country; indeed, he gave his sister Emma in marriage to the enemy and invader. One cannot tell whether greater disgrace belonged to the man who gave her [Note: “His”: s, d, e; omitted in a, c, l.] or to the woman who consented to share the marriage-bed of one who had assailed her husband and driven out her sons.

[Note: Brothers by Emma. “This Edmund was not born of Emma,” etc. See above, § 179.]

Robert, moreover, whom we said above [Note: “Said”: § 178.] had gone to Jerusalem, frequently prepared an expedition, gathering ships and putting soldiers aboard, repeatedly declaring that he would crown his great-nephews. And without doubt he would have fulfilled his word, had not the wind, as we have received from our elders, always blown contrary to him—clearly by the hidden judgment of God, in whose will lie the powers of all kingdoms. The remains of those long-decayed ships could still be seen at Rouen in our own age.

[Col. 1158B] § 181. In the year 1017 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Cnut began to reign, and reigned for twenty years. He entered the kingdom unjustly indeed, but ordered his life with great civility and courage. In the first days of his reign he divided the kingdom into four parts: the West Saxons for himself; the Mercians for Eadric; the East Angles for Thorkell; and the Northumbrians for Eric. At first, he kept concealed with him the murderers of Edmund, who had voluntarily reported the deed in hope of a great reward; then, before a great assembly of the people, he brought them forth into the midst, and, after they openly confessed the nature of their plot, punished them by execution. In the same year Eadric—whom I cannot adequately defame—by the king’s command, was himself caught by the very art through which he had so often [Note: [Col. 1158D] Frequently. a. s. d. e. l.; “before frequently,” c.] entrapped many others, and sent forth his foul spirit to the lower world.

For, when some quarrel had arisen [Col. 1158C] [Note: [Col. 1158D] Arisen. a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.], and they were speaking rather harshly together, he, relying upon his services [Note: [Col. 1158D] Services. s. e. l.; “of the Mercians,” a. c. d.], was reproaching the king in a manner of friendly reproach with his benefits, saying: “I first deserted Edmund for you, and later, out of loyalty to you [Note: [Col. 1158D] To you. d. e. l.; “your,” s. c.; “to you, him,” a.], killed him.” At these words Cnut’s changed expression betrayed anger by a blush; and he at once pronounced sentence: “Deservedly, then,” he said, “you too shall die, since you are guilty of injured majesty against God and against me, you who killed your own lord and my sworn brother. Your blood be upon your own head, because your mouth has spoken against you: you who laid hands upon the Lord’s anointed.” Immediately, lest a disturbance arise, the traitor’s throat was crushed in that same chamber, and he was thrown through a window into the Thames [Note: [Col. 1158D] Thames. a. d. e. l.; “the river Thames,” s. c.—Eadric was killed and cast into the Thames, A.D. 1017.], receiving the reward of his perfidy.

[Col. 1159A] In the course of time [Note: [Col. 1159C] Thorkell. Thurcilus, together with his wife Eadgitha, was expelled from England by Cnut’s order on 11 November, A.D. 1021.] Thorkell and Eric, taking opportunities, were driven from England and sought their native soil. [Note: [Col. 1159C] “The first of whom . . . was destroyed.” Osbern, in the *History of the Translation of the Body of Archbishop Aelfheah or Elfeg*, asserts that Thorkell, after fleeing to Denmark, was put to death by Danish leaders lest he incite the people to revolt.] The former of these, who had instigated the murder of blessed Elfeg, was overpowered by the leaders as soon as he reached the Danish shore.

Thus, when all England obeyed one man, Cnut took great pains to reconcile the English to himself, granting them equal law with his Danes in assembly, in council, and in battle. For this reason, as I said before [Note: [Col. 1159D] As I said before. See § 180.], he summoned from Normandy the widow of the preceding king, so that, while they rendered obedience to their accustomed lady, they might less regret Danish rule; and at the same time, by that act, he sought Richard’s favour, in the hope that Richard would think little of his nephews because he expected that she would bear other children by Cnut.

He restored monasteries throughout England, partly defiled and partly demolished by his and his father’s incursions. [Col. 1159B] He endowed with churches all the places where he had fought, and [Note: [Col. 1159D] Especially Assandun. See the *Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 1020.] especially Assandun; he appointed ministers who, through the succeeding revolutions of the ages, might pray to God for the souls of those killed there. He himself attended the consecration of that basilica, and the nobles of English and Danes offered gifts. Now, as is reported [Note: [Col. 1159D] “Is reported.” s. d. e.; “they report,” a. c. l.], it is a small church assigned to a parish priest.

[Note: [Col. 1159D] “Over the basilica, etc.” This monastery was not founded by Cnut. Sigeberht, king of the East Angles, having abdicated the throne, built the monastery, called in this age Beadarichesworth, and there embraced the monastic life. But when the relics of King Edmund were deposited in this monastery, the name of the place was changed to Eadmundsburh. In 1020 Cnut rebuilt the monastery completely; having expelled the secular clerks, he established in their place a community of Benedictine monks from Hulm in Norfolk.]

Over the body of the most blessed Edmund, whom the earlier Danes had killed, he constructed a basilica with royal zeal, appointed an abbot and monks, and bestowed many and great estates. The abundance of his gifts survives intact even today, for that place sees beneath itself almost all the monasteries of England.

[Col. 1159C] [Note: [Col. 1159D] “The body of blessed Elfeg, etc.” See § 165, note 49.] The body of blessed Elfeg, buried at St Paul’s in London, he himself lifted from there with his own hands; and when it had been sent back to its own place, he venerated it with fitting honour. Thus [Note: [Col. 1159D] Thus. a. s. d. e. l.; “in,” c.] striving to correct all the wrongs committed by himself and his predecessors, he perhaps wiped away before God, and certainly [Col. 1160A] before men, the stain of his earlier injustice.

At Winchester he displayed especially the magnificence of his generosity, where he bestowed such masses of metal as to strike terror into the minds of visitors [Note: [Col. 1159D] Minds. a. c. d. e. l.; omitted in s.], while the brilliance of gems dazzled the eyes of beholders. [Note: [Col. 1159D] At Emma’s prompting. See below, § 196.] This was at Emma’s prompting, for she lavishly expended treasures in such matters with prodigal piety, while he devised hard battles in foreign lands. For his courage did not know how to remain at rest; nor, content with Denmark, which he possessed by hereditary right, and England, which he possessed by right of war, he carried war [Note: [Col. 1160C] “He carried it against the Swedes.” Cnut sailed to Denmark in 1025 and, having hired great forces from Sweden, fought a battle on the plain beside the Holy River against Ulf and Eglaf. (*Saxon Chronicle*).] against the Swedes.

They border upon the Danes and had earned Cnut’s anger by their obstinate designs. But at first, caught in an ambush, he lost many of his men; at last, after restoring his forces, he put the attackers [Note: [Col. 1160C] Attackers. c. d. e.; “resisters,” a. s. l.] to flight, and brought the kings of that people, Ulf and Eglaf, to terms of peace. The English were most eager [Col. 1160B] in [Note: [Col. 1160C] “In.” e.; omitted in a. s. c. d.] that battle, at the urging of Earl Godwine, who exhorted them to prove their strength before the eyes of their new lord, mindful of their former glory: that it had been fortune that they had once been defeated by him, but courage that they were now pressing those who had defeated him. Therefore the English exerted their strength; completing the victory, they won distinction for their leader and glory for themselves.

Returning home from there, he subdued the whole kingdom of the Norwegians, [Note: [Col. 1160C] “King Olaf having been driven out.” King Olaf was defeated and Norway subdued by Cnut in 1028. Olaf returned to Norway in A.D. 1030 and was killed in the same year.] having driven out King Olaf. In the following year, when Olaf returned to the kingdom with a small force to test the disposition of his provincials, he found them faithless to him and was killed with his followers.

308 § 182. [Note: [Col. 1160D] Cnut. According to the *Saxon Chronicle*, Florence of Worcester, and other English writers, Cnut went to Rome in 1031; but this date does not agree with the year in which Emperor Conrad is said to have been crowned at Rome by Pope John XIX, on Easter Day 1027, at which ceremony Cnut is reported to have been present. According to Wipo (*Pistorius, Rerum Germanicarum Scriptores*, III, 472, Regensburg, 1726), the journey to Rome was undertaken in 1027. See below, § 183, note.] In the fifteenth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1160D] Reign. d. e.; “his reign,” a. s. c.], Cnut set out for Rome. Having remained there for some days [Col. 1160C] and redeemed his sins by alms distributed among the churches [Note: [Col. 1160D] Churches. s. c. e. l.; “alms distributed among the churches,” a. d. m.], he returned to England by ship. Soon afterward, leading an expedition into Scotland, he subdued with little difficulty the rebellious country and King Malcolm.
