Nevertheless, it will not seem unprofitable if I append, as an example of reformed life and royal magnificence, the letter which, on leaving Rome, he sent to his English through [Note: [Col. 1160D] Lyfing, etc. Lyfing, abbot of Tavistock, was made bishop in A.D. 1032; after the death of Brihtheah, bishop of Worcester, on 20 December 1038, he was translated to that see. He died in A.D. 1046.] Lyfing, abbot of Tavistock [Col. 1161A] and soon bishop of Crediton. [Note: [Col. 1161C] “I shall append it.” This letter also occurs in Florence of Worcester under A.D. 1031.]

§ 183. “Cnut, king of all England, Denmark, [Note: [Col. 1161C] “And Norway.” If Cnut went to Rome in 1027, as Danish chronographers affirm, he could not properly at this time call himself king of Norway.] and Norway, and of part of the Swedes, to Æthelnoth the metropolitan, [Note: [Col. 1161D] Æthelnoth the metropolitan. Æthelnoth, surnamed the Good, was consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in A.D. 1020 and died in A.D. 1038.] and Ælfric of York, [Note: [Col. 1161D] Ælfric of York. Ælfric was made archbishop of York in A.D. 1023.] and to all bishops and chief men, and to the whole English people, noble and common alike, greeting.

“I make known to you that I have recently gone to Rome to pray for the redemption of my sins and for the safety of the kingdoms and peoples subject to my government. I had long ago vowed this journey to God; but because of the affairs of the kingdom and other hindrances I had not until now been able to accomplish it. But now I give very humble thanks to God Almighty that in my lifetime he granted me to seek out, and, according to my desire, to venerate and adore in person, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and every sanctuary which I could learn of within or outside the city of Rome. And I undertook this especially because I learned from wise men that Saint Peter the Apostle received great power from the Lord to bind and loose, and is the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom; and therefore I considered it most useful especially to seek his protection with God.

“Be it known to you that at that Easter solemnity there was there a great gathering of nobles with the lord [Note: [Col. 1161D] Pope John. John XIX, sometimes called XX, was made supreme pontiff before he had received holy orders; he had been consul, duke, and senator of Rome—‘on one and the same day he was both layman and pontiff.’ He succeeded his brother Benedict VIII in 1024, but his election to the supreme pontificate is believed to have been achieved by corruption. Emperor Conrad II received the imperial crown from his hands on Easter Day 1027, a ceremony at which Cnut is said to have been present, together with Rudolf, king of Burgundy, and other princes. This chronological indication does not agree with the accounts of English chroniclers, who assign Cnut’s journey to Rome to 1031. Cnut’s letter gives neither day nor year, though it speaks of the presence of the emperor with Pope John, and of the immense concourse of noblemen at this Easter solemnity, [Col. 1162C] [Col. 1162D] by whom he was honourably received and loaded with most precious gifts.] Pope John and Emperor [Note: [Col. 1162D] Conrad. Conrad II, surnamed the Salian, after the death of Emperor Henry was elected king by the German assembly and crowned at Mainz on 8 September 1024. He was crowned with the imperial crown, together with his wife, by Pope John XIX, called XX, on Easter Day, 26 March 1027, in the presence, as stated, of Cnut and Rudolf, king of Burgundy.] Conrad: namely, all the princes of the peoples from [Note: [Col. 1162D] Mount Gargano. St Angelo in Calabria.] Mount Gargano [Col. 1161C] as far as this nearest sea. All received me honourably and honoured me with magnificent gifts. Most especially, the emperor honoured me with various gifts and precious presents, both vessels of gold and silver and very costly cloaks and garments.

“Accordingly, I spoke with the emperor himself, the lord pope, and the princes who were there about the needs of all my people, both English and Danish: that a more equitable law and safer peace might be granted them on the road to Rome, and that they might not be hindered by so many barriers on the way or oppressed by unjust tolls. [Col. 1162A] The emperor agreed to my requests, as did King [Note: [Col. 1162D] King Rudolf. Rudolf III, surnamed the Idle (*le Fainéant*), succeeded his father in the kingdom of Arles or Burgundy in A.D. 993. He is said to have been present with Cnut at the coronation of Emperor Conrad at Rome on Easter Day 1027.] Rudolf, who has chief control over those barriers; and all the princes confirmed the decree [Note: [Col. 1162D] Decree. e.; “decrees,” s. c.; “and decrees,” a. d. l.] that my men—merchants and others travelling for prayer alike—may go and return to Rome in secure peace, free from every oppressive barrier and toll.

“I complained again before the lord pope, and told him that I was greatly displeased that my archbishops were so burdened by the immense sums demanded of them when, according to custom, they sought the Apostolic See to receive the pallium. It was decreed that this should not happen in the future. For all that I asked from the lord pope, the emperor, King Rudolf, and the other princes through whose lands we have passage to Rome [Col. 1162B], for the benefit of my people, they willingly granted; and they confirmed the concessions by oath, in the presence of four archbishops, twenty [Note: [Col. 1162D] Twenty. a. s. d. e. l.; “twenty-four,” c.] bishops, and an innumerable multitude of dukes and nobles who were present.

“Therefore I render magnificent thanks to Almighty God, because I have successfully completed all that I desired, according to my resolve, and have satisfied my vows to the full. Let it now be known that I have humbly vowed to God himself henceforth to order my life rightly in all things, to govern justly and piously the kingdoms and peoples subject to me, and to observe equitable judgment throughout [Note: [Col. 1162D] Throughout. c. d. e.; “all things,” a. s. l.]. And if through the intemperance or negligence of my youth anything has hitherto been done by me contrary to what was right, I intend, with God’s help, wholly to amend it.

[Col. 1162C] “Therefore I entreat and command my counsellors, to whom I have entrusted the counsels of the kingdom, that they shall in no way henceforth consent to, or allow to grow up, any injustice anywhere in my kingdom, whether through fear of me or favour toward any powerful person. I also command all sheriffs and reeves throughout my kingdom, if they wish to possess my friendship or their own safety, not to inflict unjust violence upon any person, rich or poor. Rather, all, noble and lowly alike, are to be permitted to obtain what is theirs by just law, [Col. 1163A] from which they are in no way to depart, whether for royal favour, for the sake of any powerful person, or to amass money for me; for I have no need for money to be amassed for me by unrighteous exaction.

“I further wish you to know that, returning by the same route by which I departed, I am going to Denmark, there, with the counsel of all the Danes, to establish peace and a firm agreement with those peoples who wished, if it had been possible for them, to deprive us of life and kingdom. But they could not, since God destroyed their power. May he preserve us by his goodness in kingdom and honour, and annihilate the power of all our enemies.

“Finally, when peace has been made with the peoples around [Col. 1163B] us, and our whole kingdom here in the east has been arranged and pacified [Note: [Col. 1163C] Pacified. a. s. d. e.; “prepared,” c.; “prepared or pacified,” l.] so that we need fear neither war nor hostility from any quarter, I intend to come to England as soon as I can have a fleet ready this summer. I have sent this letter in advance so that all the people of my kingdom may rejoice at my welfare; for, as you yourselves know, I have never spared myself or my labour, nor will I yet spare it, in spending both for the necessary benefit of all my people.

“Now I entreat all my bishops and officers of the kingdom, by the faith which you owe to me and to God, to ensure that, before I come to England, all the dues which by ancient law we owe are paid: namely, [Note: [Col. 1163C] Plough-alms. *Eleemosyna pro aratris*: one penny was paid to the church for each ploughland. ‘For every yoked plough, between Easter and Pentecost, one penny, called *Ploualmes*.’ (*From the Register of Ramsey*, in the Exchequer Archives, fol. 158.)] plough-alms; tithes of animals [Col. 1163C] born in that year; and [Note: [Col. 1163C] “The pennies which you owe to Saint Peter at Rome.” *Romefeoh*, or Saint Peter’s penny. See § 109, note.] the pennies which you owe to Saint Peter at Rome, whether from towns or villages; and, by mid-August, the tithe of crops; and, at the feast of Saint Martin, the firstfruits [Col. 1164A] of seed for the church in whose parish each person lives, which in English is called *Chirchseet* [Note: [Col. 1163C] Chirchseet. e.; *Chirchescot*, d.; *Cyrescet*, c. l.; *Scyrisceat*, a.; *Curescet* or *Chireseth*, s. Kemble, in a most learned dissertation on this word, conclusively shows that *church sceat*, or *church shot*, was not, as some maintain, a certain church tax, but ‘a portion of threshed grain which every person among Britons and English was obliged each year to bring to his church on the feast day of St Martin.’]. If, when I come, these and other dues have not been paid, the person upon whom the fault falls shall strictly pay for it by royal exaction according to the laws, without pardon.”

Nor was the deed worse than the word. For he commanded that all laws enacted by ancient kings, and especially by his predecessor Æthelred, should be observed for ever under threat of the royal penalty. [Note: [Col. 1163D] “For the observance of which, etc.” Sharpe suggests that Malmesbury probably had in mind here the custom followed by the first princes of the Norman line, who swore that they would observe the laws of King Edward. In the margin of manuscript d occur the words: “Here Cnut’s laws are lacking”; and in l: “Here Cnut’s laws are lacking, comprising six and a half folios.”] Even now, in their observance, oaths are taken in the name of King Edward, not because he enacted them, but because he observed them.

§ 184. There were then in England eminent and very wise men, foremost among whom was [Note: [Col. 1163D] Æthelnoth. See § 183, note.] Æthelnoth, archbishop after [Note: [Col. 1163D] Lyfing. See § 176, note.] Lyfing. Having risen from dean to high priest, he performed many works worthy of praiseworthy remembrance. By the authority of his holiness he encouraged the king himself in good deeds and frightened him away from transgression. He exalted the archiepiscopal see first by the presence of the body of St Elfeg, and afterward restored it to its former dignity by his presence at Rome. [Note: [Col. 1163D] “First by the presence, etc.” These two events are reversed: Æthelnoth went to Rome in 1022 and translated the body of Elfeg in 1023. See Osbern, *On the Translation of St Elfeg* (*Anglia Sacra*).]

On his way home, he acquired at Pavia the arm of St Augustine the Doctor [Note: [Col. 1164C] St Augustine the Doctor: Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius in Africa. He died on 28 August A.D. 430, during the siege of Hippo, where he was buried. African bishops, fleeing into exile, took his relics with them to Sardinia in A.D. 500. It was believed that in the eighth century Liutprand, king of the Lombards, transferred them from Sardinia to Pavia, A.D. 721. Tillemont wrote Augustine’s life in volume thirteen of the *Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire ecclésiastique*.] for one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold, and sent it to Coventry.

Moreover [Note: [Col. 1164C] Moreover. a. g. l.; omit the text from “Moreover” to the end of § 125.], Cnut hastened to Glastonbury church in order to visit the spirit of his brother Edmund—for he was accustomed to call him so—and, after praying, placed over the tomb a cloth woven, apparently, with many-coloured figures of peacocks. At the king’s side stood the aforesaid Æthelnoth, the seventh of the monks [Col. 1164C] [Note: [Col. 1164C] “Of the monks.” e.; omitted in s. c. d.] of Glastonbury monastery to hold the see of Canterbury.

The first was [Note: [Col. 1164C] Brihtwald. Berhtwald was elected archbishop of Canterbury on 1 July A.D. 692, but was not consecrated until Sunday, 29 June A.D. 693. The ceremony was performed in Francia by Godwin, metropolitan bishop of Francia; in the same year, on Sunday 31 August, he took his seat in the see of Canterbury. He died on 9 January A.D. 731.] Brihtwald; the second [Note: [Col. 1164D] Æthelhelm. Æthelhelm was the first bishop of the church of Wells, and was translated from that see to Canterbury in 911. It is nevertheless doubtful whether he was a monk of Glastonbury monastery. See Wharton’s note in *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 556.] Æthelhelm, first bishop of Wells; the third, his nephew [Note: [Col. 1164D] Dunstan. See § 149.] Dunstan; the fourth [Note: [Col. 1164D] Æthelgar. Æthelgar, at first a monk of Glastonbury, was elected first abbot of the New Minster at Winchester, founded after secular canons had been expelled. He was consecrated bishop of Chichester (Selsey) in 980, translated to Canterbury in 988, and died on 3 December 989.] Æthelgar, [Col. 1165A] first abbot of the New Minster at Winchester and afterward bishop of Chichester; the fifth [Note: [Col. 1165C] Sigeric. Sigeric was made bishop of Wilton in A.D. 986 from being a Glastonbury monk, translated to Canterbury in A.D. 1000, and died in A.D. 1005.] Sigeric, who, when made archbishop, gave seven cloths to his nurse, with which the whole old church is adorned on her anniversary; the sixth [Note: [Col. 1165C] Elfeg. Ælfheah. From the priory of Glastonbury he became abbot of Bath, and later, in A.D. 984, [Col. 1165D] bishop of Winchester. He was translated to Canterbury in 1005 and killed by the Danes in 1012. See § 165, note.] Elfeg, who from the priory of Glastonbury first became abbot of Bath and then bishop of Winchester; the seventh [Note: [Col. 1165D] Æthelnoth. See § 183, note 14.] Æthelnoth. After showing the king the privileges of his predecessors, he asked—and by asking obtained—that the king confirm them by royal writing [Note: [Col. 1165D] Royal. s. c. d. e, second hand; omitted in e.] in the following words.

315 § 185. “While the Lord reigns [Note: [Col. 1165D] “While the Lord reigns.” This charter occurs in Malmesbury, *Antiquities of Glastonbury Church*, and in Gale, III, p. 323.] for ever—he who by his ineffable power orders and governs all things, wonderfully distinguishes the changes of times and people, and calmly sets an uncertain end as he wills; and who mercifully teaches, through the mysteries hidden in nature, that enduring kingdoms are to be attained by the aid of God from things fleeting and undoubtedly transitory—therefore I, Cnut, king of the English and governor and ruler of the other nations dwelling round about, with the counsel [Note: [Col. 1165D] Counsel. e.; “consent,” s. c. d.] and decree of our chief bishop Æthelnoth, together with all God’s priests and with the counsel of my nobles, for love of the heavenly kingdom, [Note: [Col. 1165D] “And for forgiveness of my crimes and remission.” Omitted in c, first hand.] and for forgiveness of my crimes and remission of the sins of my brother King Edmund [Note: [Col. 1165D] “My brother King Edmund.” ‘For he was accustomed to call him so.’ See § 184.], grant to the church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary at Glastonbury its rights and customs throughout my entire kingdom, and all forfeitures from all its lands. Let its lands be free and exempt [Col. 1165C] from every accusation and disturbance, as my own are held free for me.

“But especially, by the authority of Almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and under the prohibition of the everlasting Virgin, I forbid, and command all the officers and chief men of my kingdom upon peril of their salvation, that no one at all, whatever his rank or dignity, dare enter that island. Rather, in all causes, ecclesiastical as well as secular, they shall wait only upon the judgment of the abbot and the convent, as my predecessors [Col. 1166A] Cenwealh, 316 Ine, Cuthred, Alfred [Note: [Col. 1165D] Alfred. c. e.; Ælred, d.; Ailred or Alfred, s.], Edward [Note: [Col. 1165D] Edward. s. reads Æthelred after “Edward.”], Æthelstan, and the most glorious [Note: [Col. 1165D] “Æthelstan, and the most glorious.” Omitted in c.] Edmund, and the incomparable Edgar established and confirmed by privileges.

“If anyone at any future time, under any pretext, attempts to violate and render void the charter of this privilege, let him be separated from the fellowship of the righteous by the winnowing-fan of the last judgment. But if anyone, with benevolent intention, strives to enact, approve, and defend these provisions, may God, through the intercession of the most blessed Mother of God [Note: [Col. 1165D] Mother. d. e.; “Mother Mary,” s. c.] and of all saints, enlarge his portion in the land of the living.”

This grant of privilege was written and promulgated [Note: [Col. 1165D] Promulgated. c.; “promulgated,” s. c. d.] in the wooden basilica, in the presence of King Cnut, in the year 1032 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second [Col. 1166B] indiction [Note: [Col. 1165D] Second. e.; “first,” d.; omitted in s. c.—A.D. [Col. 1166C] 1032 corresponds to indiction XV.].

§ 186. [Note: [Col. 1166C] “At the prompting also of the same chief bishop, the king.” s. c. d. e.; “at his prompting the king also,” a. g. l.] At the prompting also of the same chief bishop, the king sent money to churches across the sea and especially enriched Chartres, where there then flourished [Note: [Col. 1166C] Fulbert. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, A.D. 1007–1029, had been a pupil of Gerbert, later Pope Sylvester II. Many authors count him among the chancellors of France during Robert’s reign; others, more correctly, question this. He appears to have been only chancellor of the church of Chartres. His works—letters, sermons, canons, hymns, and other poems—were first published in 1608, under the care of Charles V [lacuna] llarensis (*Opera varia*, octavo, Paris, 1608). He died about the year 1029.] Bishop Fulbert, most famous for holiness and philosophy. Among the other proofs of his industry, he brought to a splendid completion the church of our Lady St Mary, whose foundations he had laid; and, eager to honour it as far as he could, he often exalted it in musical compositions.

[Note: [Col. 1166D] “For how greatly he longed in love for the honour of the Virgin . . . sounding.” ‘It is said that he had such particular devotion to the Blessed Virgin that she often honoured him with her special favours.’ (Moreri.)] How greatly he burned with love for the Virgin’s honour may be inferred by anyone who has heard his songs sounding with heavenly prayers. Among his other little works there survives a volume of letters, [Note: [Col. 1166D] “In one of which.” See Fulbert’s letter to King Cnut, A.D. 1020 or 1021, no. XLIV, p. 466, vol. X of the *Recueil des Historiens de la France*. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, *Opera varia*, octavo, Paris, 1608, letter 97, p. 92.] in one of which he gives thanks to Cnut, that most magnificent king, for pouring out the abundance of his generosity upon the expenses of the church of Chartres.

§ 187. In his fifteenth year Robert, king of the French, [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Of whom we have spoken above.” See above, § 168.] of whom we have spoken above, ended his life. He was a man devoted to almsgiving, so much so that on feast days, when he was dressing and taking off his royal insignia, if he had nothing else to hand he would distribute his very garments to the poor, unless the servants of the wardrobe deliberately kept away needy persons who importunately asked for them.

He had two sons, Odo and Henry. [Note: [Col. 1166D] “Odo, the elder by birth, was dull-witted.” Malmesbury, like the *Chronicle of St Martin of Tours* (in [Col. 1167C] Chesne, vol. III, *Scriptors of French History*, p. 360) and certain other French chronicles, here fell into error concerning the sons of Robert, king of France. After the death of his firstborn son Hugh, 17 September A.D. 1025, who had been crowned at Compiègne in 1017, Robert intended to associate his second son Henry, duke of Burgundy, with himself on the throne and in the partnership of rule. But Constance opposed this plan, judging her third son Robert more suited to royal dignity. Henry nevertheless was preferred and ascended the throne at Pentecost, 14 May 1027; at that time his brother Robert was made duke of Burgundy. Odo, the fourth son, who was of dull intellect, lived in affliction. See Rodulfus Glaber, book III, ‘On the Sons of King Robert.’ Alberic of Trois-Fontaines conjectures that Malmesbury meant Robert but carelessly called him Odo. Alberic himself, however, is led into error when he asserts that Henry was younger than Robert and was raised to the royal throne through his mother’s aid, whereas Henry had his mother opposed to him.] Odo, the elder [Col. 1167A] by birth, was dull-witted; the other was shrewd and forceful. Each parent had divided their affection between the two children: the father embraced the firstborn, declaring that he would succeed; the mother favoured the younger, to whom the kingdom was due, if not by age, certainly by prudence. Thus, as women are obstinate in their undertakings, she did not cease until she had drawn all the dukes subject to the kingdom of the Franks into support of her wishes by great rewards and promises.

Henry, therefore, with Robert of Normandy [Note: [Col. 1167D] “Especially striving.” a. c. d. e. l.; “especially consenting,” s.] exerting himself especially, was crowned before his father had wholly expired [Note: [Col. 1167D] “Had expired.” e, first hand; “was expiring,” a. c. d. e, second hand, l.]. Indebted for this benefit, he vigorously helped Robert’s young son William against deserters when Robert, as I said above [Note: [Col. 1167D] As I said above: §§ 178 and 180.], went to Jerusalem.

But Cnut, when he had passed the limit of life, died at Shaftesbury [Note: [Col. 1167D] “Having died.” Cnut died on 12 November A.D. 1035. (*Saxon Chronicle*; Florence of Worcester.)] and was buried at Winchester. [Col. 1167B]

## ON HAROLD, SON OF CNUT
§ 188. In the year 1036 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Harold—whom report called the son of Cnut by the daughter of Earl Ælfhelm—reigned for four years and the same number of months. The Danes and the citizens of London elected him; these had now almost adopted barbarian customs through frequent association. The English resisted for a long time, wishing rather to have as king either one of Æthelred’s sons, who were residing in Normandy, or Harthacnut, Cnut’s son by Emma, who was then in Denmark.

[Note: In the year 1036, after Cnut’s death, the kingdom was at first divided: the northern portion fell under Harold’s rule, while Harthacnut held the southern. In 1037 Harold was elected to rule over all England. (Florence of Worcester.)]

[Note: Harold, etc. “Some said that Harold was the son of Cnut and Ælfgifu, daughter of Ælfhelm, ealdorman, or prefect of a city; but this seemed altogether unbelievable to many.” (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.) If Florence is to be believed, Ælfgifu, unable to bear the king a son, deceitfully presented to him the son of a certain shoemaker.]

[Note: “Were residing”: a, c, d, e, l; omitted in s.]

Godwine, earl, was then the greatest champion of justice. Declaring himself also the protector of orphans, and guarding Queen Emma and the royal treasures, he for a while repelled the opposition under the shield of his own name; but at last, unequal to violence and numbers, he yielded to force.

[Note: “Then”: a, e, l; “however,” d; “but,” c1; “at that time,” c2.]

When Harold’s possession of the sceptre had been confirmed, he banished his stepmother.

[Note: He banished his stepmother: in the year 1037.]

She judged that nothing was safe for her in Normandy, where, after the death of her brother and nephews, resentment against recently abandoned orphans was fiercely aflame; so she crossed into Flanders to Count Baldwin, a man proved in integrity. Later, after the death of King Henry, who had left behind his little son Philip, Baldwin nobly governed the kingdom of the Franks for several years, and faithfully restored it to Philip when grown—for he had married the boy’s aunt.

[Note: Count Baldwin: Baldwin, surnamed “of Lille,” Count of Flanders, succeeded his father Baldwin IV in A.D. 1036—or, as some maintain, in A.D. 1035. Emma was honourably received by the count and by his wife Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the Franks. See the *Encomium Emmae*. Baldwin was appointed guardian by King Henry of his son Philip in 1059.]

[Note: King Henry: King Henry died in 1060, leaving as his successor Philip, then only seven years old. See § 128, note 60.]

[Note: Philip: Philip died in 1108. See § 128, note 64.]

Under Baldwin’s protection Emma spent a secure three years. When these had passed, Harold died at Oxford in April and was buried at Westminster. Then, as English and Danes agreed in one resolution and sent for Harthacnut, he came through Normandy into England in August; for the sons of Æthelred were now held in contempt by almost everyone, more because of the memory of their father’s indolence than because of Danish power.

[Note: Harold died: according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Harold died on 17 March, 1040 (the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April).]

[Note: Into England, etc.: according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Harthacnut landed at Sandwich on 17 June. See the following note.]

Harthacnut, having reigned two years less ten days, lost his life amid drinking at Lambeth near London, and was buried at Winchester beside his father. He was a young man who showed remarkable affectionate devotion toward his brother and sister: for he most indulgently received and retained his full brother Edward, who, weary of a long exile and hopeful of brotherly kinship, was returning to his native land—meeting him, as they say, with open arms.

[Note: Harthacnut … died: Harthacnut died on 8 June, A.D. 1042.]

Yet he was immature in other matters. At the instigation of Ælfric, bishop of York, and others whom it is unpleasant to name, he ordered Harold’s body to be dug up, its head cut off, and—an example pitiable to mortals—cast into the Thames.

[Note: “Bishop”: a, d, e, l; “archbishop,” s, c. Ælfric did not, like his predecessor, hold the two sees of York and Worcester.]

A fisherman drew it out in a net, and it was buried in the cemetery of the Danes in London.

[Note: In the cemetery of the Danes in London: St Clement Danes. “Shortly afterwards it was brought by a certain fisherman to the Danes, and buried in the cemetery which they had in London, beside Saint Clement.” (Ralph de Diceto, *Abbreviatio Chronicorum*.)]

He imposed upon England an inexorable and unbearable tax, so that he was to pay his sailors twenty marks for each ship, as promised. While this was being exacted harshly throughout England, two men who enforced this levy with particular severity were killed by the citizens of Worcester. Consequently, he inflicted an injury both upon his reputation and upon his popularity by having the city burned and devastated through his earls and by stripping away the citizens’ possessions.

[Note: “Twenty”: a, d, e, l; “thirty,” c. In 1040 a tax for sixty-two ships was imposed at the rate of eight marks for each steersman (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). According to Florence of Worcester, “the king ordered eight marks to be paid to each steersman from all England.” In the following year a tax of 21,099 pounds was paid to the army, and later 11,048 pounds to thirty-two ships (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).]

Indeed, lest I suppress in silence what rumour-mongers spread about Alfred, Æthelred’s eldest son: while wavering between Harold’s death and the expectation of Harthacnut, he entered the kingdom, was deprived of his eyes at Gillingham through the treachery of his compatriots, and especially through Godwine; then he was sent to the monastery of Ely, where for a short time he sustained a wretched life on coarse bread. All his companions except one in ten were beheaded, for the lot had exempted every tenth man from death.

[Note: “Between Harold’s death”: according to Florence, Ælfred died in A.D. 1036, and therefore before Harold’s death. We probably ought to read “Cnut’s” in place of “Harold’s.”]

I have not omitted this because rumour reports it; but, because the chronicle is silent, I have not affirmed it as certain.

[Note: Because the chronicle is silent: the published Anglo-Saxon Chronicle makes no mention of this matter, but two manuscripts report it. See Cotton MSS Tiberius B. I and IV.]

[Note: “I have affirmed”: a, s, d, e, l; “I affirm,” c.]

For this reason Harthacnut, hostile to Lyfing, bishop of Crediton, whom report declared the author of the deed, expelled him from his bishopric; but after a year, appeased by money, he restored him. He also regarded Godwine with sidelong eyes and compelled him to take an oath of purgation. Godwine added to his sworn loyalty a gift in order to purchase full favour: a vessel, exceedingly rich and beautiful, with a prow of gold, carrying eighty soldiers. On each arm they wore two arm-rings, each of sixteen ounces of gold; on their heads were gilded helmets; they carried a Danish axe upon the left shoulder and an iron-shafted spear in the right hand. And, not to enumerate every detail, they were equipped with every kind of weapon, in which a brilliance contending with terror concealed the iron beneath gold.

But, to return to what I had begun to say: Harthacnut gave his sister Gunhilda, Cnut’s daughter by Emma, a girl of most distinguished beauty, long desired by many suitors in her father’s lifetime but not obtained by them, in marriage to Henry, emperor of the Germans.

[Note: “Daughter”: a, s, e, l; omitted in c, d.]

[Note: Henry, emperor of the Germans: Henry III, son of Conrad II.]

That wedding procession was famous, and even in our own age was sung in the streets, when a maiden of so great a name was conducted to the ship, attended by all the nobles of England, who contributed to the expense whatever either the public purse or the royal treasury had kept concealed. Thus arriving at her bridegroom, she preserved the marriage bond for a long time. At last, accused of adultery, she set against her accuser, a man of gigantic stature, in single combat a little boy, the foster-child of her starling, whom she had brought with her from England; all her other retainers had withdrawn in cowardly fear.

[Note: “Bridegroom”: a, s, l; “bride,” c, d, e.]

[Note: “Starling”: a, c, d, e, l; “brother,” s.]

[Note: A man of gigantic stature: his name was Rodingar; the little boy set against him is said to have been a dwarf named Mimicon. (Chronicle of John of Brompton.)]

[Note: “Set against”: a, c, d, e; “opposed,” s, l.]

So, when the duel had begun, by God’s miracle the false accuser was disabled when his knee was cut through. Gunhilda, exulting in an unforeseen triumph, repudiated her husband; nor could threats or blandishments thereafter induce her to consent to his bed. Taking the veil of nuns, she grew old peacefully in the service of God.

[Note: “Taking”: a, c, d, e, l; “receiving,” s.]

## CONCERNING EMPEROR HENRY

§ 189. The emperor was endowed with many great virtues and was more warlike than almost all his predecessors. He subdued even the Vindelici and the Leutici, and the other peoples bordering on the Swabians, who to this day alone among all mortals breathe after pagan superstitions. For Saracens and Turks worship God the Creator, considering Mahomet not God but His prophet.

[Note: “His”: e; “God’s,” a, s, c, d, l.]

But the Vindelici worship Fortune. Setting her image in a most famous place, they place at its right hand a horn full of that drink which, made from water and honey, we call by the Greek name *hydromel* [hydromel].

[Note: “Place”: a, c, d, e, l; “put upon,” s.]

[Note: “Which”: a, s; “what,” c, d, e, l.]

Saint Jerome confirms, in his eighteenth book on Isaiah, that the Egyptians and almost all Eastern peoples did the same. Therefore, on the last day of November, sitting round about, they taste it together; and if they find the horn full, they applaud with great noise, because in the coming year a horn full of abundance will, they believe, answer them in all things; but if the contrary is the case, they groan.

[Note: “They applaud”: a, s, d, e, l; “applauding,” c.]

Henry made these peoples so tributary that, at all the solemnities at which he was crowned, their four kings carried on their shoulders to the kitchen, by means of four rings and poles, the cauldron in which meat was cooked.

[Note: “Was crowned”: a, d, e, l; “were crowned,” s.]

## CONCERNING THE EMPEROR’S SISTER AND THE CLERIC WHO LOVED HER

§ 190. Moreover, when he was often free from the disturbances of the realm and gave himself to sociability and cheerfulness, he was full of jesting, as two examples will sufficiently prove.

He loved his sister, a nun, exceptionally dearly, so that he would not allow her to be absent from his side, but always had her dining-hall adjoining his own. Thus, during a certain winter made grim and rough by snow and frost, when he was detained in one place for a long time, a court cleric became more intimate with the girl than was right and frequently prolonged nocturnal vigils in her chamber. Though he veiled his wickedness by all kinds of evasions, someone noticed it—for it is difficult for a crime not to betray itself in face or gesture. Rumour was already circulating the affair everywhere; the emperor alone did not know, and dared believe his sister chaste.

But one night, while they were enjoying their desired embraces and pleasure had stretched itself out too long, morning dawned; and behold, snow covered the whole ground. Then the cleric, afraid that his footprints in the snow would reveal him, persuaded his mistress that she should escape those difficulties by carrying him on her back. She did not reject the shamelessness, provided only that she might avoid disgrace: she lifted her lover upon her back and carried him out beyond the court. By chance, the emperor had then risen to urinate; looking down through the window of the upper chamber, he saw the cleric riding. At first he was stupefied by the sight; but, having examined the matter more closely, he became speechless from shame and indignation.

Meanwhile, as he hesitated whether to leave the sin unpunished or honourably rebuke the sinners, an opportunity arose to give the cleric a vacant bishopric. Whispering these words in his ear, he said: “Take the bishopric, and see that you ride a woman no longer.” Likewise, when he gave the abbey of nuns to his own sister, he said: “Be abbess, and I shall no longer endure a cleric-rider.”

[Note: “His own sister”: a, s, d, e, l; “sister,” e.]

[Note: “Rider”: A nearly similar story about the celebrated Eginhard and Charlemagne’s daughter has been widely circulated. See Du Chesne, *Scriptores Francorum*, vol. II. (Sharpe, 241.)]

Confounded, since they felt themselves struck by so weighty a saying, they ceased from the shameful conduct which they believed had been divinely inspired by the Lord.

## CONCERNING THE CLERIC WHO DID NOT WISH TO READ THE GOSPEL FOR THE EMPEROR

§ 191. He also had at court a cleric who spoiled both his learning and the elegance of his voice by a bodily vice: he was madly inflamed with love for a little prostitute of the town. Having rolled with her on a certain holy night, he stood before the emperor’s Mass in the morning with uncovered face. Feigning ignorance, Caesar ordered him to prepare himself for the Gospel, because he delighted in his melody; for he was a deacon. Because of his consciousness of sin, the man sought by many devices to evade the task; the emperor, on the other hand, pressed him by messengers, in order to test his constancy. At last, when he utterly refused, he said: “Because you will not obey me in such an easy service, I command you to be an exile from my entire land.”

[Note: “To be”: c, e; omitted in a, s, d, l.]

The cleric embraced the sentence and departed immediately. Footmen were sent to pursue him, so that, if they considered him persistent, they might call him back after he had already left the city. Thus, without hesitation, when he had gathered all his possessions and packed them into bundles, and had already set out, they dragged him back with great force and presented him before Henry. Smiling gladly, Henry said: “You have acted well, and I congratulate your integrity, because you valued the fear of God above your homeland, regard for heavenly wrath above my threats. Therefore, have the first bishopric in my empire that falls vacant, provided only that you renounce this unseemly love.”

§ 192. But since nothing in human joys is constant, a certain sad portent occurred in his time which I shall not pass over in silence. The monastery of Fulda is in Saxony, renowned for the body of Saint Gall and enriched with very magnificent estates.

[Note: Saint Gall: Saint Gall, an Irishman and disciple of Saint Columban, followed him into France. His rare merit caused him to be chosen as bishop of Constance; but he had his disciple John elected in his place. In 615 he founded in Switzerland a famous monastery bearing his name, and died in 640, aged ninety-five. (Moréri.)]

The abbot of that place provides the emperor with sixty thousand warriors for war and has an ancient privilege of sitting at his right hand on the most eminent feast days. Henry was therefore celebrating Pentecost at Mainz. Shortly before Mass, while seats were being prepared in church, a dispute arose between the chamberlains of the archbishop and those of the abbot as to which lord should sit beside Caesar: the former alleged the pre-eminence of the bishop, the latter ancient custom.

[Note: “Mainz”: s, l; “Mogontium,” a, c, d, e.]

[Note: “Custom”: a, s, d, e, l; “name,” c.]

When words made little progress toward agreement—since Germans, likewise Teutons, have an untamed spirit—they came to fighting. One party seized stakes, another threw stones, another drew swords; finally, whatever anger first found, that they used as weapons. Thus, while frenzy raged through the church, the pavement was flooded with blood. But bishops immediately hastened together, peace was established between the disputants amid relics, the church was purified, and Mass was celebrated with festive acclamations.

When, however—to add something wonderful—the sequence had been sung, and the choirs had fallen silent at the verse, “You have made this day glorious,” a voice falling from the air sounded loudly everywhere: “I have made this day warlike.” While the rest stood rigid, the emperor, giving more careful attention to the service and understanding the enemy’s joy, said: “You, inventor and inciter of every evil alike, have made this day warlike and mournful for the proud; but through the grace of God, who made it glorious, we shall make it gracious to the poor.” Immediately the sequence was begun again, and with solemn weeping he invited the grace of the Holy Spirit. One might have understood that He had come: these sang, those wept, and all beat their breasts.

[Note: “Sung”: e; “sung,” a, s, c, d, l.]

When Mass was finished, the poor were summoned by heralds; he used up for their benefit every dish prepared for himself and the courtiers. He himself served the food; he himself stood at a distance in accordance with the discipline of servants; he himself wiped away the remnants of food.

§ 193. In the time of his father Conrad, he had taken from a certain cleric a little silver tube with which boys spray water in play, promising him a bishopric when he became emperor. Once he was grown, he promptly gave the petitioner what had been promised. Not long afterwards he was seized by a severe illness and took to bed. As the sickness increased, he lay senseless and mute for three days, while vital breath merely trembled in his chest; there was no other sign of life except that, if a hand was placed to his nostrils, however slight a breathing might be felt.

[Note: “Senseless”: s; all manuscripts read *exsensis*.]

The bishops present proclaimed a three-day fast and besieged heaven with tears and vows for the king’s life. Restored to health, as it is lawful to believe, by these remedies, he deposed by decree of a council the bishop whom he had unjustly made. He declared that throughout the three days he had seen hostile demons shooting flame at him through the tube—a flame so persistent that our fire, compared with it, might be thought a joke and to have no heat at all.

Meanwhile a young man, half-burned, had come carrying a golden cup of immense size full of water. Soothed by its sight and by the sprinkling of the liquid, and his burning extinguished, he recovered his health. That young man had been the blessed Lawrence, whose church roof, decayed by long rot, he had repaired with a framework and, besides other offerings, honoured with a golden cup.

§ 194. At this point occur the great miracles reported of that man: for example, how a hind, while he fled his enemies, carried him on her back across an unfordable river, and certain others. I therefore pass them over, because I do not wish to exceed the reader’s judgment.

[Note: He died, etc.: Henry died at Bodfeld, near the borders of Saxony and Thuringia, in the eighteenth year of his reign and the fifteenth of his empire, on 7 October, A.D. 1056, and was buried at Speyer.]

He died when the eighteenth year of his empire had elapsed and was buried at Speyer, which he himself renewed from a most ancient and ruined *nemetum* [sacred grove] and named accordingly. His epitaph is as follows:

> Caesar, you were as great as the world itself,  
> Yet now you are enclosed in a little tomb.  
> Hereafter let everyone know that he will fall,  
> And that no glory removes the necessity of dying.  
>
> Once flourishing, the glory of the empire,  
> Bereft of its Caesar, now withers;  
> Never again will it have that splendour  
> Which, dying with you, you have concealed.  
>
> The laws enlarged by the fathers of old,  
> Which wearied time had long erased,  
> You yourself restored them all as they had been  
> And strove to return them to Roman causes.  
>
> You cultivated to civic glory  
> Distant kingdoms and lands  
> Which no Caesar could bend,  
> Burdening their limbs with Roman strength.  
>
> Oh, with how great a grief Rome is oppressed,  
> Already bereft by Leo’s death;  
> Now, Augustus, languishing at your funeral,  
> She laments herself widowed of a double light.  
>
> What country did not fear you while you lived?  
> Or what country, Caesar, did not grieve at your death?  
> For you were so gracious to peoples already subdued,  
> And so stern toward unconquered nations,  
> That what did not fear you had reason to mourn,  
> And what did not mourn had reason to fear.  
>
> Mourn, Rome, your name in the shadows;  
> And mourn your two extinguished lights.

[Note: “He will fall”: a, s, c2, d, e, l; “he will die,” c.]

[Note: “Lights”: a, e; “divinities,” s, c, d, l.]

§ 195. This Leo, indeed, of whom the epitaph speaks, had been bishop of Rome; he was called and raised to that office from Bruno, bishop of Speyer.

[Note: “Bishop of Speyer”: read “bishop of Toul.”]

He was of great and wonderful sanctity, and the Romans spread many accounts of his miracles throughout the world. He died before Henry, after five years as pope.

[Note: This Leo: Bruno, bishop of Toul in Lorraine, was elected pope as Leo IX at the end of 1048 by bishops and nobles assembled at Mainz at the command of Emperor Henry III. He took his seat upon the pontifical throne in Rome on 13 February of the following year and died on 19 April 1054.]

[Note: “Henry”: a, c, d, e, l; “Emperor Henry,” s.]

[Note: “Five”: a, s, d, e, l; “fifteen,” c. Leo IX presided over the Church for five years and several weeks.]

## CONCERNING SAINT EDWARD THE THIRD, KING AND CONFESSOR

§ 196. In the year 1042 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Edward, son of Æthelred, assumed the kingdom and remained in it for not quite twenty-four years. He was a man little fitted for rule because of the simplicity of his character, but devoted to God and therefore guided by Him.

[Note: In the year 1042 from the Lord’s Incarnation, etc.: Harthacnut died in 1042, and Edward was elected king in the summer of that same year, but was not crowned until Easter Day—3 April—of the following year.]

[Note: “Edward”: a, c, d, e, l; “Saint Edward,” s.]

[Note: “Guided”: s, c, d, e, l; “beloved,” a.]

Accordingly, while he reigned no domestic disturbance failed to be quickly suppressed, nor was there any foreign war; all was quiet and tranquil at home and abroad. This was all the more remarkable because he behaved so gently that he did not know how to injure even worthless little men by a word. For once, when he had gone hunting and a peasant had scattered the enclosures by which stags are driven into nets, he was stirred by a noble anger of his own and said: “By God and His mother, I shall harm you just as much, if I can.” A splendid disposition: he did not remember himself to be a king in such circumstances, nor did he think he could harm a man of low estate.

Meanwhile, he was held in intense reverence among his household and in great fear among outsiders. God surely cherished his simplicity, so that he who did not know how to be angry might nevertheless be feared. Yet, though he was thought indolent or simple, he had earls to lift him as he strove from lowly things to high:

[Note: “Or indolent”: a, s, c, d, l; omitted in e.]

Siward of the Northumbrians, who at Edward’s command engaged Macbeth, king of the Scots, and stripped him of life and kingdom, establishing there Malcolm, son of the king of the Cumbrians, as king.

[Note: Siward … stripped him: according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, on the day of the Seven Sleepers, 27 July, A.D. 1054, Earl Siward advanced into Scotland with great forces and, engaging the Scots in battle, put Macbeth to flight.]

[Note: Malcolm: Malcolm III; see § 180, note 85, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under A.D. 1067.]

Leofric of the Hereford people, who defended Edward magnificently against the hostilities of Godwine, because Godwine, trusting in his consciousness of services rendered, reverenced the king too little. Leofric, lavish in God’s concerns together with his wife Godgifu, established many monasteries: at Coventry, St Mary Stow, Wenlock, Leominster, and several others. To the rest he assigned ornaments and estates; to Coventry he bequeathed his own body, with a very great display of gold and silver.

[Note: Godwine: concerning Godwine’s rebellion, see the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under A.D. 1051 and 1052.]

Harold, son of Godwine, of the West Saxons—afterwards king of the English—brought about the deaths, by his own cleverness, of two brothers who were kings of the Welsh, Rhys and Gruffydd; and he reduced all that barbarian land to the condition of a province under allegiance to the king.

[Note: Harold: afterwards king of the English.]

[Note: “Reduced”: a, s, d, e, l; “subdued,” c.]

There were nevertheless some things that disfigured the glory of those times: monasteries then deprived of monks; unjust judgments committed by wicked men; and his mother’s possessions entirely swept away at his command. But his admirers attempt to diminish the odium of these matters in this way: the destruction of monasteries and the perversity of judgments were carried out not with Edward’s knowledge but through the violence of Godwine and his sons, who mocked the king’s mildness; once these matters were later reported to him, he punished them severely by their exile.

[Note: Their exile: Earl Godwine was driven into exile together with his sons in 1051. The earl himself, with his wife and three sons—Sweyn, Tostig, and Gyrth—went to Bruges to seek Count Baldwin’s assistance. Harold and Leofwine withdrew to Ireland. (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 1051.) See also Malmesbury, *De Gestis Pontificum*, book I, p. 116, London edition.]

His mother had long since laughed at the restricted means of her sons and had never given anything from her own resources, through an inherited hostility, evidently, of the parent toward her offspring; for she had loved Cnut more while he lived and praised him after his death. Furthermore, having amassed talents from every quarter, she had filled her money-bags, forgetful of the poor; she would not allow even a coin to be given to them, lest the total number be diminished. Thus what had been unjustly heaped up was not dishonourably taken away, so as to serve the advantage of the needy and supply the royal treasury.

[Note: “Dishonourably”: a, c2, d, e, l; “unjustly,” s, c1.]

Although considerable credence ought to be given to those who report these things, I nevertheless find that she was a holy woman and that she perhaps spent her treasures on ornaments for the church of Winchester and other churches.

[Note: “Be given”: a, c, d, e, l; “be applied,” s.]

[Note: Yet that she was a holy woman, etc.: see § 181.]

But to return to the foregoing: when Harthacnut died, Edward, on receiving so sorrowful a report, wavered uncertainly and did not know what to do or where to turn. As he considered many things, the preferable course seemed to be that he should weigh his fortunes by Godwine’s counsel. Godwine had long hesitated and considered whether he should converse under the aforesaid peace through envoys; at last he agreed. When Edward came to him and attempted to fall at his knees, Godwine raised him up. He explained Harthacnut’s death and honoured Edward’s request for aid in returning to Normandy with great promises:

[Note: “Agreed”: c, d, e; “did not refuse,” a, s, l.]

[Note: “Explaining”: a, s, d, e, l; “announcing,” c.]

[Note: “Honoured”: a, d, e, l; “burdened,” s, c.]

“It is better that you should live gloriously in royal power than die shamefully in exile. You are Æthelred’s son and Edgar’s grandson. The kingdom belongs to you by right: your age is mature, your character purified by hardships, and your years enable you to govern sternly and to temper the miseries of provincials in view of your former poverty. Nothing prevents this, if you think me worthy of trust; my authority carries great weight in England. The more readily you incline yourself to this course, the more fortune will incline toward you. If I assist you, no one will dare speak against you—and the contrary will be true if I do not. Therefore make a firm alliance with me: secure undiminished honours for my sons and a marriage for my daughter. In a short time you will see yourself king—you who now, a shipwrecked man as to life and an exile as to hope, beg another’s aid.”

§ 197. There was nothing which Edward would not promise, given the necessities of the time; and so, pledges having been given on both sides, he confirmed by oath whatever was requested. Without delay, a council having been assembled at Gillingham [Note: Gillingham: a. s. d. e. l.; London, c.], and his arguments having been set forth, he made him king, public homage being rendered by all: a man of engaging charm, and one who spoke his native tongue with unaffected eloquence, remarkable in speech, remarkable in persuading the people of what pleased them. Some followed his authority, some were swayed by gifts, and some also embraced Edward’s due claim; a few resisted what was fair and good [Col. 1176C], and were then marked by censure and afterwards expelled from England. [Note: “And”: a. s. c. d. e². l.; omitted in E.]

Edward was crowned with great pomp at Winchester on the solemn day of Easter [Note: Winchester: a. s. d. e. l.; London, c. — “He is raised as king in London (A.D. 1042). He is anointed king at Winchester (A.D. 1043).” (Florence of Worcester)]; and was instructed by Archbishop Eadsige in the sacred precepts of kingship. He gladly stored these in his memory then, and later displayed them holily in his deeds. [Note: “Eadsige … instructed”: Eadsige was transferred from Winchester to Kent in 1038. According to the Saxon Chronicle, Eadsige anointed King Edward at Winchester on the holy day of Easter and instructed him with excellent counsels in the presence of the whole people.]

That same Eadsige, falling in the following year into an incurable illness, appointed as his successor Siward, abbot of Abingdon; having first communicated the plan only to the king and the earl, lest anyone unworthy should aspire to so lofty a dignity, whether by entreaty [Col. 1177A] or by payment. [Note: “Whether by entreaty or by payment”: a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c¹; inserted in the margin of c².]

[Note: “His successor,” etc.: “In this year (1044), Archbishop Eadsige resigned his see on account of illness, and, with the permission and advice of King Edward and Earl Godwine, consecrated Siward, abbot of Abingdon, bishop in his own place. This had become known to only a few persons before it was accomplished; for the archbishop feared that someone else might seek this see or claim it by payment.” (Saxon Chronicle.) See also Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum*, book I, p. 116. Yet Florence and other authorities seem to indicate that Siward was no more than coadjutor of Archbishop Eadsige, or Eadsige: “Siward also died, chorepiscopus of Eadsige, Archbishop of Dorobernia [Canterbury].” (Florence of Worcester, A.D. 1049.) And again, A.D. 1030: “Eadsige, Archbishop of Dorobernia, died; Robert, bishop of London and a Norman by birth, succeeded him.” (Florence of Worcester.)]

Not long afterward, the king took in marriage Edith, daughter of Godwine [Note: “Edith,” etc.: In the same year (1045), King Edward married Edith, daughter of Earl Godwine, ten days before the feast of the Presentation of the Lord (23 January). (Saxon Chronicle.)]; a woman in whose breast was a school of every liberal art, but whose capacity in worldly matters was small. When you saw her, you would admire her learning, but would certainly look in vain for modesty of spirit and beauty of body. [Note: “If you admired her learning”: Ingulf writes of Edith: “A most beautiful girl, highly educated in letters. I saw her very often, when, still a boy, I visited my father, who was staying at the king’s court; and, when I met her on my way back from school, she would often question me about my studies and my verse. Most willingly moving from the firmness of grammar to the subtlety of logic, in which she was skilled, after she had entangled me in the fine chain of an argument, she would always send me to the royal storehouse by a maidservant with three or four coins counted out, and dismiss me refreshed.”]

She did not escape suspicion of disgrace either while her husband lived or after his death; but, dying in William’s time [Note: “William”: c. d. e.; “King William,” a. s. l.], she voluntarily satisfied those standing by, under oath, concerning her perpetual chastity. [Note: “Dying”: Edith died at Winchester seven days before Christmas Day, 19 December, 1075, and by order of King William I was buried with great pomp at Westminster in the same tomb as her husband.] The king treated his wife in such a way that he neither put her away from his bed nor knew her in the manner of a husband. Whether he did this from hatred of her family, which he prudently concealed for the time, or from love of chastity, I have not discovered with certainty. [Note: “Family”: a. s. d. e. l.; “easily,” c.] It is most commonly reported that he never violated his chastity by cohabitation with any woman whatsoever.

But, since I have arrived at this point, I wish to warn the reader that I see here, as it were, a forked path in the narrative, because the truth of the events hangs in doubt. For the king had summoned certain Normans who had once relieved the poverty of the exile with small benefactions; among them Robert [Note: Robert was made Archbishop of Canterbury in 1051 (Saxon Chronicle) and was expelled in the following year.], whom he had made, from a monk of Jumièges, bishop of London and afterwards Archbishop of Canterbury.

Modern Englishmen blame him, together with the others, as the accuser of Godwine and his sons, the sower of discord, and the buyer of the archbishopric. They call Godwine and his sons high-spirited men, energetic founders and protectors of Edward’s kingdom; nor is it surprising if they resented seeing new men [Col. 1177C] and foreigners preferred to themselves. Yet they say that they never spoke even a harsh word against the king whom they had once raised to eminence. The Normans, by contrast, defend themselves by saying that he and his sons behaved with great arrogance and disloyalty toward the king and his household [Note: “In”: a. s. c. l.; omitted in d. e.], claiming equal shares in the realm, often accustomed to mock his simplicity and often to hurl conspicuous jests at him. They say the Normans could not endure this [Note: “Endure”: a. d. e. l.; “suffer,” s. c.] without weakening their power as far as they could.

Finally, they say that God showed with what holy intention Godwine had served him. For when, after the piratical plunderings of which we shall speak below, he had been restored to his former favour and was reclining at table with the king, conversation arose concerning Alfred, the king’s brother [Note: See §188]. “You,” he said, “king [Note: “King”: a. d. e. l.; “O king,” s. c.], I see, whenever you remember your brother, look at me with a furrowed brow. But may God not allow me to swallow this morsel if I was [Note: “I was”: a. s. d. e. l.; “I am,” c.] conscious of any act touching his danger or your injury.” Having said this, he was choked by the morsel which he had put into his mouth and turned his eyes toward death. [Note: “He turned his eyes toward death”: The Saxon Chronicle gives a different account of Earl Godwine’s death. “In this year (1053) the king was at Winchester on the holy day of Easter, and with him were Earl Godwine, his son Earl Harold, and Tostig. On the first day after Easter he sat at table with the king and suddenly fell to the ground against the footstool, deprived alike of speech and strength. They carried him into the king’s chamber, hoping that he would recover; but this did not happen. Thus, deprived of speech and strength, he remained until Wednesday, when he breathed out his life, on 15 April. He was buried at Winchester in the Old Minster.” See also Florence of Worcester, A.D. 1053.] Thereupon he was drawn from beneath the table by his own son Harold, who was standing beside the king, and was buried in the bishopric of Winchester.

§ 198. Because of these disputes, as I have said, my account is endangered, since I do not have the means to determine what is wholly true—whether because of the natural hostility of the two peoples, or because the matter is indeed such that the English arrogantly bear no superior, while the Normans cannot endure an equal. But I shall proceed to speak of their character in the following book, when an opportunity arises from the coming of the Normans into England. For the present I shall sketch, with as much truth as I can, the king’s quarrel with Godwine and his sons. [Note: “With as much truth as I can, I shall sketch”: See the Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 1052 (1050–51).]

§ 199. [Note: Eustace: Eustace II, surnamed *aux Grenons*. He succeeded his father Eustace I in 1049; in 1050 he married Goda, daughter of King Æthelberht and widow of Walter of Mantes, by whom he had no children. By his wife Ida, however, he left three sons: Eustace, who succeeded him; Godfrey, made margrave of Antwerp by Emperor Henry IV in 1076, later duke of Bouillon, and finally elected king of Jerusalem in 1099, on 23 July, where he died on 18 July 1100. His brother Baldwin, count of Edessa, succeeded him.]

Eustace was count of Boulogne, father of Godfrey and Baldwin, who in our time were kings at Jerusalem [Note: “At Jerusalem”: c. d. e.; “of the Jerusalems,” a. s. l.]. He had married the king’s sister Goda in lawful wedlock. By her former husband, Walter of Mantes, she had borne a son, Ralph [Note: See Florence of Worcester, A.D. 1051. Ralph, earl of Hereford, died 21 December 1057. (Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester.)], who was then earl of Hereford: a cowardly and timid man who yielded to the Welsh in battle and left his earldom and its city, together with its bishop, to be consumed by their fires. Harold, arriving promptly, wiped out the disgrace of this affair by his own bravery.

Eustace, therefore, crossed the sea from Wissant to Dover and visited King Edward, for some reason unknown to me. After conversing with him and obtaining what he had requested, he was returning through Canterbury. [Note: “He was returning through Canterbury”: Malmesbury appears to have drawn his account of the fight between Eustace’s men and the people of Canterbury from the Saxon Chronicle, which states that the earl and his men, having eaten at Canterbury, proceeded to Dover, where they intended to lodge. The events here narrated took place there, not at Canterbury, as might seem to follow from Malmesbury.]

One of his forerunners behaved too aggressively toward a citizen and demanded lodging by a wound rather than a request [Note: “Request”: a. c. d. e. l.; “request or payment,” s.], thereby inviting that man to destroy him. [Note: “Destruction”: a. s. d. e. l.; “death,” c.] When this became known, Eustace set out with his whole retinue to avenge the death of his servant. He killed the slayer and eighteen others; but when the citizens ran to arms, he lost twenty of his own men, while countless others were wounded. He himself barely escaped in the very tumult with one companion.

Returning to court, and having found a private audience, he stood forth as advocate of his own cause and inflamed the king’s anger against the English. Godwine, summoned to court by messengers, came. When the case was set forth, and especially as the king was heaping up charges concerning the insolence of the people of Canterbury, this man of keener mind understood that a judgment ought not to be pronounced after hearing allegations from one side only. Therefore, although the king ordered him to proceed immediately with an army into Kent to exact a severe vengeance upon the people of Canterbury, he resisted: both because he begrudged all foreigners their growing influence with the king, and because he wished to preserve friendship with his countrymen.

Moreover, his response seemed more inclined to justice: that the chief men of that town should be gently summoned at the king’s court to answer for the sedition. If they could clear themselves, they should depart unharmed; if they could not, they should make satisfaction, either by money or by the loss of their bodies, to the king whose peace they had broken and to the earl whom they had injured. It seemed unjust that those whom you ought to protect should be condemned by you above all others [Note: “Above all others”: a. s. d. l.; omitted in E.] without being heard.

Thus they then separated, Godwine making little of the king’s anger as though it were momentary. Accordingly, the magnates of the whole kingdom were ordered to assemble at Gloucester, so that the matter might be debated there in a great council. There also came the then most famous earls of Northumbria, Siward and Leofric, and all the English nobility. [Note: “There also”: s. d. e. l.; “also there,” c.; “therefore there also,” a.]

Godwine and his sons alone, knowing themselves to be suspected, thought that they ought not come without an armed safeguard; they held position at Beverstone with a strong force. They spread among the populace the report that they had assembled an army in order to curb the Welsh, who, plotting tyranny against the king, had fortified a town in the district of Hereford, where Sweyn, one of Godwine’s sons, then pretended to be keeping military watch. But the Welsh had already presented their case first and had made those charged with conspiracy hated by the whole court, so that a rumour spread that the royal army would attack them in that very place.

On receiving this news, Godwine sounded the trumpet for his confederates, urging them not actively to resist their lord the king; but, if attacked, not to yield the ground before they had avenged themselves. And indeed the deed would have been dreadful, a war more than civil, had not more prudent counsels intervened. Thus, after some slight reconciliation had meanwhile been made, an order was again issued for a council to be assembled at London. Godwine’s son Sweyn was commanded to mitigate the king’s wrath by his flight.

Godwine and Harold were to come as quickly as possible to the council, under this agreement: unarmed, bringing only twelve men; and they were to surrender to the king the service of the soldiers whom they maintained throughout England. On the other hand, they refused, saying that they could not go to a gathering of factional men without sureties and hostages; that they would obey their lord in surrendering the soldiers, and indeed in all things except at the peril of their honour and safety. If they came unarmed, their lives would be endangered; if they had only a few attendants, it would be a disgrace to their honour.

The king had stubbornly hardened his mind against yielding to the prayers of suppliants; therefore an edict was issued that they should leave England within five days (A.D. 1051). Godwine and Sweyn went to Flanders; Harold withdrew to Ireland. His earldom was assigned to Ælfgar, son of Leofric, an energetic man. He accepted it and then governed it nobly, but willingly restored it when Harold returned. Later, when Godwine was dead and Harold had obtained his father’s earldom, Ælfgar boldly reclaimed it, though he had previously been exiled for some time through the accusations of his enemies. [Note: “Exiled”: Ælfgar was outlawed in 1055; but, joining Gruffydd, prince of the Welsh, he invaded England from exile and won victory. When his father Earl Leofric died on 30 September 1057, he succeeded to the earldom of Mercia; in the following year he was expelled, but shortly returned to his people, aided by Gruffydd of the North Welsh.]

All the queen’s property was squeezed out to the last penny; she herself was placed in custody with the king’s sister at Wherwell, lest, while all her relatives longed for their native land, she alone should snore upon a feather bed. In the following year (A.D. 1052), each of the exiles set out from his own place to cruise around the British Sea, harass the coasts with piratical robberies, and carry off magnificent spoils from the resources of a related people. [Note: “Carry off”: e.; “transport,” a. s. c. d. l.]

Against them, on the king’s side, more than sixty ships remained at anchor. Earls Odo and Ralph, kinsmen of the king [Note: “Kinsmen”: a. s. d. e. l.; “relatives,” c.], commanded the fleet. Nor did that emergency find the king inactive: he himself spent nights aboard ship and watched for the movements of the raiders, diligently making up by counsel, because of his age, for what he could not do by hand. But when they came close and were already almost joining battle, a very dense fog suddenly arose, confused the sight of the furious men, and checked the miserable daring of mortals. Finally, Godwine and his companions, compelled by the wind, were carried back to the place from which they had come.

Not long afterward they returned peacefully to their country and encountered the king at London. [Note: “Encountered”: a. c. d. e. l.; “found,” s.] They were admitted while asking forgiveness. That old man, powerful in speech [Note: “And powerful in speech”: c. d. e. l.; “renowned and powerful in speech,” a; S omits “renowned”], and skilled in bending the minds of his hearers, thoroughly cleared himself of all the accusations brought against him. In a short time he prevailed so greatly that he restored unimpaired honours to himself and his children, drove all the Normans—branded with disgrace—from England, and secured a judgment against Archbishop Robert and his accomplices, on the ground that they disturbed the condition of the kingdom by inciting the king’s mind against the people of the realm.

But Robert, not waiting for violence, had voluntarily fled while the terms of peace were being arranged. He went to Rome and appealed to the Apostolic See concerning his case. On his return by way of Jumièges, he died and was buried there in the church of St Mary, which he himself had built with especially splendid and costly workmanship.

Immediately, while Robert was still alive, Stigand, bishop of Winchester, seized the archbishopric of Canterbury. [Note: Stigand was consecrated bishop of the East Angles in 1046; but because he embraced the cause of the king’s mother, he was deprived of his bishopric in that same year, though he recovered it in the following year. When Ælfwine, bishop of Winchester, died in 1047, Stigand succeeded to that see; hence, when Archbishop Robert was expelled in 1052, he was transferred to Canterbury and received the pallium from Pope Benedict X in 1058.]

He was a bishop notorious for ambition and for desiring honours [Note: “Honours”: c. d. e.; “goods,” a. s. l.] beyond what was due: in hope of a higher throne, he abandoned the bishopric of the South Saxons [Note: “Saxons”: it seems that “East Angles” should be read.] and occupied Winchester, and held that see together with the archbishopric. Therefore he never deserved the pallium from the Apostolic See, except that a certain Benedict, a usurper of the papacy, sent it to him [Note: Benedict: after the death of Stephen IX, the bishop of Velletri usurped the Holy See in 1058 through factional support and held it for nine months and twenty days. Though only a usurper, he is numbered among the supreme pontiffs under the name Benedict X.], having been corrupted by money to grant it [Note: “To grant”: c. e.; “to persuade,” a. s. d. l.], or because evil men favour their like.

But Benedict was soon expelled by Nicholas [Note: Gerard, bishop of Florence, was elected 28 December 1058, crowned on the eighteenth day of the following month, and named Nicholas II. He died at Florence in July 1061.], who had lawfully received the papacy after being bishop of Florence, and, by the zeal of the faithful, laid aside his illegitimate title. Stigand too, in the time of King William [Note: “William”: a. c. d. e. l.; “William the Conqueror,” s.], was deposed by Roman cardinals [Note: “Roman”: a. o. d. e.; “at Rome,” c. l.] and bound in perpetual chains. [Note: “Deposed”: Stigand was reduced from his rank in a great council held at Winchester during the octave of Easter, A.D. 1070, in the presence of the king and three Roman cardinals, for three reasons: namely, because he unjustly held the see of Winchester together with his archbishopric; because, while Archbishop Robert was still alive and had been unjustly expelled, he wore the pallium; and finally, because he had received the pallium from the pseudo-pontiff Benedict. (Simeon of Durham.)]

Even in death he put no end to his insatiable greed. For after he died, a little key was found in private quarters which, when applied to the lock of a chamber cabinet, revealed countless treasures: documents recording both the kind of metals and the quantity by weight which the greedy plunderer had buried throughout all his estates. But of this later; now I shall finish what I began concerning Godwine.

§ 200. In his early years he had Cnut’s sister as his wife, and by her had begotten a boy. When the child had passed his first years of infancy, he proudly displayed with childish boasting the horse which he had received from his grandfather; thrown by it into the Thames [Note: “The Thames”: a. c. d. e. l.; “the River Thames”], he died, drowned in the whirlpool of the water. His mother too, struck dead by lightning, paid the penalty for her cruelty; for it was said that she was accustomed to send to Denmark companies of slaves bought throughout England, especially girls made more valuable by beauty and youth, in order to heap up riches through their shameful trade.

[Note: “After her death,” etc.: The second wife of Earl Godwine was named Gytha. (Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester.)] After her death he married another woman, whose lineage I have not discovered. By her he had children: Harold, Sweyn, Tostig, Wulfnoth, Gyrth, and Leofwine. Harold was king for several months after Edward and, defeated by William at Hastings, lost both life and kingdom with his two younger brothers. [Note: “Younger”: e.; “more junior,” a. s. c. d. l.]

Wulfnoth, whom his father had given to King Edward as a hostage, was sent to Normandy and remained there, entangled in inescapable captivity, throughout Edward’s reign. Under William’s rule he was sent back to England and grew old in confinement at Salisbury. Sweyn, perverse in disposition and repeatedly disloyal to the king, revolted from his father and his brother Harold; becoming a pirate, he stained the virtues of his ancestors with maritime plunder. At last, because of his guilty conscience for the murder of his kinsman, Beorn—and, as some say, his brother—he went to Jerusalem; on his return, he was surrounded by Saracens and slain. [Note: “His kinsman Beorn,” etc.: Sweyn, after violating Eadgyth, abbess of Leominster, fled to Denmark. Anxious to obtain the king’s pardon, he sought Earl Beorn—the son of his maternal uncle, the Danish earl Ulf—that Beorn might be his companion and intercessor. Beorn consented to his kinsman’s request and, fearing no treachery, took only three companions. Yet scarcely had he boarded ship when, by Sweyn’s command, he was handed over to death. (Florence of Worcester and the Saxon Chronicle.)]

Tostig was placed by King Edward over the earldom of Northumbria after Siward’s death, and governed the province for almost ten years. [Note: “Province”: a. s. c. d. e². l; absent in e. — Tostig succeeded Earl Siward in the earldom of Northumbria in A.D. 1055, but was outlawed by his own barons in 1065. See the Saxon Chronicle and Florence of Worcester.] When this period was over, his harshness of character stirred the Northumbrians to rebellion. They drove him out when found alone in the countryside, judging that he ought not be killed in view of his rank as earl. They slaughtered his men, both English and Danes, gathering up horses, arms, and every article of household equipment.

When the report reached the king and the country was disturbed, Harold went to meet them in order to repel the injury. Although the Northumbrians were not inferior in number, they chose peace and excused their action before him. They said that, being men born free and reared free, they could endure the ferocity of no lord; that they had learned from their ancestors either liberty or death. Therefore, if he wished them to be subjects, he should place over them Morcar, son of Ælfgar, and would discover by experience [Note: “Would discover by experience”: a. c. d. e.; “the king [would find] experienced,” s.] how sweetly they knew how to obey if they were treated sweetly.

Hearing this, Harold, who cared more for the peace of the country than for his brother’s advantage, recalled the army; and, having approached the king, established Morcar securely in the earldom. Tostig, hostile to all, went with his wife and children to Flanders and remained there until Edward’s death. The account of that death will meanwhile be deferred in this work, while I say what I learned from older men had happened at Rome in Edward’s time.

§ 201. Pope Gregory VI, formerly called Gratian, was a man of great religious devotion and sternness. [Note: “Gregory VI”: s. c. e. l.; “Gregory, sixth of that name,” a. d. m. — Pagi assigns the beginning of Gregory’s pontificate to May 1044; but Ughelli cites a charter in which August 1046 is stated to be the first year of his pontificate. He was deposed in the council held at Sutri on Christmas Day, A.D. 1046, because he had obtained the Holy See by simony. Sharpe observes that what Malmesbury relates here about this pontiff is considered apocryphal. Compare Rodulfus Glaber, book V, chapter 5.]

He found the condition of the Roman apostolate so diminished through the negligence of his predecessors that, apart from a few towns near the city and the offerings of the faithful, it had almost nothing by which to support itself. Cities and distant possessions belonging by right to the Church had been seized by robbers; public routes and paved roads throughout Italy were crowded with bandits, so that no pilgrim could pass safely except with a large company. Swarms of ambushers teemed on every road, and the traveller could find no contrivance by which to escape them. They robbed the poor man as readily as the rich; neither submission could obtain favour nor resistance endure violence.

People ceased from every region to undertake the journey to Rome, since anyone preferred to distribute his money among local churches rather than feed brigands by his own labours. What of the city, once the unique dwelling-place of holiness? There assassins wandered in the middle of the forum, a faithless and cunning race of men. If anyone, desiring at the peril of his life to see the church of the Apostle, had passed the watchers of the roads by some device, he fell among assassins and could by no means return home without loss of property or life.

Over the very bodies of the holy apostles and martyrs, over the sacred altars, swords were drawn. The offerings of those who approached were scarcely laid down before they were snatched from their hands; once snatched, they were squandered on revels and the abuse of prostitutes. Such a whirlwind of evils confronted Gregory’s papacy.

At first he acted gently, as befitted a pontiff, dealing with his subjects more by love than by fear and correcting offenders more by words than by blows. Let the citizens cease from harassing pilgrims and plundering sacred things. It was contrary to nature that one who breathed the common air should not enjoy the common peace. A Christian ought to be free to go wherever he pleased among Christians, since all belong to one service, all are joined by the clot of one blood, and all redeemed at one price. It was contrary to God’s commands, since He had commanded that those who serve at the altar should live by the altar.

Moreover, the house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of robbers, not a gathering-place of gladiators. Let them allow the offerings to be applied to the needs of priests or the expenses of the poor. He would provide for those whom poverty compelled to robbery, so that they might have support through some honourable occupation; those driven by greed should set limits upon themselves, out of fear of God and regard for worldly honour.

He invited by commands and letters those who had seized ecclesiastical property either to restore what was unlawfully held or to prove before the Roman senate that they possessed it by right. If they did neither, they were to recognize that they were not members of the Church, since they resisted the head of the Church, blessed Peter, and his vicar.
