Having often preached such things and profited little or nothing, he tried to meet the inveterate disease with harsher remedies. Accordingly, by the cautery of excommunication, he cut off from the body of the Church all who did such things and all who shared in a feast or even conversation with those who did them.

He did enough in this matter for his office; but his diligence almost turned to destruction. For, as he says, “He who reproves a scoffer brings injury upon himself,” those wicked men, lightly touched by admonition, began to rage against him, terrify the air with threats, and make the city walls ring with arms, so that they nearly killed the pope. Therefore, judging that the sword of excision must be used, he gathered arms and horses from every quarter and equipped soldiers and cavalry. First occupying the basilica of St Peter, he either killed or drove out the robbers of the offerings. Then, seeing fortune favour him, he advanced farther; and, after killing any who resisted, restored to their ancient right all the estates and towns which had been lost for many years.

Thus peace, exiled through the sloth of many, returned to its country through one man. Pilgrims in safety trod the unfamiliar tracks of the roads; rejoicing, they feasted their eyes in the city upon ancient marvels, and returned home singing after making their offerings. Meanwhile the Romans, accustomed to live by plunder, called him bloodthirsty and said that one conscious of so many killings was unworthy to offer sacrifice to God. And, as often happens when the disease of slander spreads from one to all, even the cardinals approved the people’s arguments. Thus, when that holy man lay ill with the sickness of which he died, they first took counsel among themselves and, in reckless boldness, warned him not to order that he be buried in the church of St Peter with the other apostolic pontiffs, since he had stained his office with the deaths of so many men. Then he, gathering his spirit and threatening with grim eyes, delivered this speech:

§ 202. “If there were in you even a spark of human reason or knowledge of divine authority, you would not have confronted your pontiff with such headlong persuasion—I who, [Col. 1185B] for as long as I have lived, have poured out my patrimony for your benefit, and at last disregarded worldly reputation for your deliverance. And if others were weaving together the charges which you tear apart, it was fitting that you should oppose them, softening fools’ opinions by sounder interpretations. For whom, I ask, did I amass treasure? Perhaps for myself? Yet I possessed the treasures of my predecessors, sufficient for any man’s greed. To whom did I restore safety, to whom liberty? You will reply: to myself. Yet I was adored by the people, and freely did whatever I wished; all prayers applauded me, all days resounded with acclamations in my praise. The sight of your poverty took from me these praises and these applauses; I turned my mind toward you and judged that sterner action was necessary. An impious robber was devouring the titles to your estates; you lived a destitute life on daily bread. He bought precious silks for himself from your offerings, while you moved my eyes to pity by your common and tattered clothing. Therefore, since I could not endure this, I declared war upon others, that at the cost of citizens I might purchase the favour [Note: [Col. 1185D] *Favour.* a. c. d. e. l: *glory*, s.] of the clergy. But, as I now learn, I have squandered benefits bestowed upon the ungrateful: what others mutter in corners, you vomit forth in public.

“And indeed I approve liberty, but I demand filial devotion. Do sons assail their dying father over his burial-place? Will you deny me the common dwelling of mortals? No little prostitute, no usurer, no thief is barred from entering the church; and do you forbid the pope to enter? What difference does it make whether a dead man or a living man enters the sanctuary, except that the living man is tempted by many [Col. 1185D] allurements, so that even in church he does not remain free from stains, often finding there matter for sin where he had come to wash away guilt? The dead man does not know how to sin—indeed, cannot sin—being without his final provision. How monstrous, then, is the barbarity that excludes from God’s house one who lacks both the will and the power to sin! Therefore, my sons, repent of such precipitous boldness, if perhaps God may forgive you this offence. For up to this hour you have spoken foolishly and bitterly.

“But lest you suppose that I rely upon authority alone, receive the argument: ‘Every human act ought to be [Col. 1186A] examined according to the intention of the heart, so that judgment upon the deed may tend toward that from which the purpose of acting proceeded.’ I am mistaken if Truth itself does not say the same: ‘If your eye be single, your whole body shall be full of light; but if it be evil, your whole body shall be full of darkness.’ Often [Note: [Col. 1185D] *Often.* a. s. d. e. l: *certainly often*, s.] a pitiable needy man came to me, asking that I relieve his want. I, ignorant of what was to come, did not refuse, but sent him away laden with coins of various kinds. Departing, he encountered a robber upon the public road; unwary, he entered into conversation with him, preaching the indulgence of the Apostolic See and, to prove the truth of his words, produced his purse. Meanwhile, as they went along and the road was beguiled by much talk, that treacherous man, delaying for a moment and striking the pilgrim’s head with the club which he carried, [Col. 1186B] killed him without delay. Having stolen the money, he gloried in the murder which greed for money had induced him to commit. [Note: [Col. 1185D] *Will you therefore rightly judge me on that account, because I had given the pilgrim that by which he incurred the cause of death?* [Col. 1186D] Omitted in c 1.] Will you therefore rightly judge me on that account, because I had given the pilgrim that by which he incurred the cause of death? For the robber, however cruel, would not have crushed a man unless he hoped to stuff his greedy bosom with coins.

“What shall I say of civil and ecclesiastical laws? Is not one and the same deed, viewed differently, both punished and praised in them? A robber is punished because he has killed a man in secret; a soldier is approved if he has slain an enemy in war. Thus homicide is judged blameworthy in the one and praiseworthy in the other, because the latter killed for his country’s safety, [Col. 1186C] while the former killed for the gluttony of greed. Our predecessor Adrian I, of memorable renown, was once praised because he granted Charlemagne the investitures of churches, such that no elected man was consecrated 349 by a bishop unless he had first been invested by the king with ring and staff. Conversely, the pontiffs of our age are praised because they have taken these grants away from princes. What could then reasonably be granted must now reasonably [Note: [Col. 1186D] *Reasonably.* c. d. e: *praiseworthily*, a. s. l.] be removed. Why is this so? Because the spirit of the Great Charles was unconquered by greed, and no one could easily find entrance unless he entered through the door. Moreover, across so great distances of land the Apostolic See could not be consulted so as to give its assent to every person elected, while a king was nearby who arranged nothing through avarice but, according to the sacred decrees [Col. 1186D] of the canons, religiously installed suitable persons in churches. Now luxury and ambition have occupied all royal palaces; therefore the bride of Christ rightly asserts her liberty, lest a tyrant prostitute her to an ambitious usurper. Thus my case can be attacked or defended on either side.

“It is not a bishop’s office to command that battle be undertaken; [Note: [Col. 1186D] *Command that battle be undertaken.* c. d. e: *command, or command that battle be undertaken*, a. s. l.] nevertheless, it belongs to a bishop’s duty, if he sees innocence suffering shipwreck, to come to its aid both by hand and by speech. Ezekiel accuses the priests because they did not stand [Col. 1187A] against the enemy, nor set up [Note: [Col. 1187D] *Set up.* s. l: *placed*, a. c. d. e.] a shield for the house of Israel on the day of the Lord. There are, of course, two offices established in God’s Church for cutting away vices: one sharpens speech; the other bears the sword. I, as you can bear witness for me, have not neglected my part. So long as I hoped to achieve something, I armed my tongue. I informed by messenger him whose business it was to act with the sword. He wrote back that he was occupied with the war of the Vindelici, asking that I would not shrink, at the expense of my labours, from overthrowing the assemblies of robbers. If I had refused, what excuse could I have offered God, when the emperor had transferred his own responsibility to me? Would I see the slaughter of citizens and the loss of pilgrims, and sleep? Indeed, he who spares a robber kills an innocent man.

“But it will be objected that it is not for a priest [Col. 1187B] to stain himself with anyone’s bloodshed; and I grant it. Yet he does not defile himself [Note: [Col. 1187D] *Yet he does not defile himself.* d. e: *if he defiles himself*, a. s. c. l.] who restrains the guilty and frees the innocent. Indeed—indeed—blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times. Priests of the highest renown, Phinehas and Mattathias, both had their foreheads marked by the sacred tiara, both wore priestly robes, yet both took vengeance by hand upon sinners. [Note: [Col. 1187D] *The one … mingled.* See Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book IV, ch. 6, §12; book XII, ch. 6, §2.] One pierced illicit embraces with a dagger; the other mingled one who was sacrificing with sacrificial blood. If they, as though feeling their way through the thick darkness of the Law, were inflamed by divine zeal for the sake of those shadowy mysteries, shall we, beholding truth with unveiled face, permit our sacred things to be profaned? The priest Azariah [Note: [Col. 1187D] *The priest Azariah.* a. s. d. e. l: *but the priest Zachariah*, c 2; *but the priests Zachariah*, c 1. (See 2 Chronicles, ch. XXVI, 16–21.)] [Col. 1187C] expelled King Uzziah as he burned incense; and without doubt would not have hesitated to kill him, had Uzziah not hastened to withdraw. The divine stroke anticipated the episcopal hand, so that leprosy consumed the body of him whose mind had panted after unlawful things. Was the king’s devotion thrust out, and shall not a robber’s ambition be thrust out? It is too little that I excuse my deed, unless I also praise it. For I conferred a benefit upon those to whom I seem to have brought destruction; I diminished punishment for those whose death I hastened. For the more long a criminal lives, the more he will sin—unless perhaps there be someone [Note: [Col. 1188D] *Someone.* c. d. e: omitted in a. s. l.] whom God has regarded as a singular exception. Death is commonly good for all: through it the just man is placed among heavenly things; the unjust ceases from crimes; the evil man gives an end to wickedness; the good man presses on toward the prize; the saint [Col. 1187D] approaches the palm, the sinner looks toward pardon, because death fixes a limit to sins. Therefore thanks ought to be given me in the stead of those who have been delivered from such great miseries by my service.

“This I have had to say for myself, in order to refute your assertions. But since both my reasoning and yours may be mistaken, let us commit everything to divine judgment. Place my body, prepared according to the custom of my predecessors, before the doors of the church; let the doors be shut with bars and bolts. If God wishes me to enter, you will applaud the miracle; if not, do with my corpse whatever may best please your minds.”

§ 203. Moved by this speech, when he had breathed his last [Note: [Col. 1188D] *Had breathed his last.* c. e. l: *had breathed his last breath*, a. s. d.], they bore the lifeless remains of the bishop before the doors, which were closed with bars. But immediately a divinely sent whirlwind, breaking through every obstruction of the fastenings, violently threw open the very doors and drove them against the wall. The people standing by cried out with joy; the pontiff’s body was placed with the fathers [Note: [Col. 1188D] *Fathers.* c. d. e: *priests*, s. l; *predecessors*, a.] in solemn veneration.

## CONCERNING A WITCH WOMAN DRAGGED FROM A CHURCH BY DEMONS

[Col. 1188B] § 204. In those same days something similar occurred in England—not by a heavenly miracle, but by infernal deception. When I relate it, confidence in the story need not waver, though the minds of hearers may be unbelieving. I heard it from such a man as swore that he had seen it, and whom I should be ashamed not to believe.

There lived at Berkeley a woman, devoted, as afterwards became clear, to sorceries; not ignorant of ancient divinations; a patroness of gluttony, an arbiter of wantonness, setting no limit to her wickedness, although she was not yet old, though old age was knocking at the threshold with a neighbouring foot. One day, as she feasted, a little crow which she kept as a pet cawed something more loudly than usual. Hearing this, her mistress’s knife fell from her hand [Note: [Col. 1188D] *From her hand.* c. d. e: omitted in a. s. l.], and her face at once grew pale. [Col. 1188C] Then, with a drawn-out groan, she said: “Today my plough has reached its final furrow; today I shall hear and receive great misfortune.”

No sooner had she spoken than a messenger of calamity entered. Asked why he came looking so troubled, he said, “I bring you news from that estate”—and he named the place—“of the death of your son and the destruction of the whole household in a sudden collapse.” Wounded in heart by this grief [Note: [Col. 1188D] *By this grief.* a. c. d. e: *by this word and grief*, s. l.], the woman immediately took to her bed. Feeling the illness creeping into her vital parts, she urgently summoned by letters her surviving children, a monk and a nun. When they came, she addressed them in a sobbing voice:

“My children, by some wretched fate of my own I have always served demonic arts; I have been a cesspool of every vice, a mistress of seductions. Yet amid these evils there was the hope of your religious life, which soothed my wretched [Col. 1188D] soul. Despairing of myself, I rested upon you; I set you before me as champions against demons, protectors against most savage enemies. Now therefore, because I have approached life’s end, and shall have as exactors in punishment those whom I had as counsellors in sin, I beg you by a mother’s breasts—if there is any faith, any filial devotion—that you at least try to relieve my torments. You will not indeed revoke the sentence pronounced upon my soul, [Col. 1189A] but perhaps you will save my body in this way. Sew me [Note: [Col. 1189D] *Me.* c. d. e: omitted in a. s. l.] into a deer-hide; then lay me on my back in a stone sarcophagus; bind the lid with lead and iron. Over these things place a stone, encircled with three iron chains, of great weight, of course. Let there be psalm-singers for fifty nights and an equal number of masses by day, to soften the fierce assaults of my adversaries. Thus, if I lie safely for three nights, bury your mother in the earth on the fourth day—although I fear that the earth may refuse to receive and cherish me in its bosom, burdened as it has so often been by my evils.”

It was done as she commanded, they applying themselves with great care. But, alas for the crime! Neither pious tears, nor vows, nor prayers availed anything: so great was the woman’s wickedness, so great the devil’s [Col. 1189B] violence. For on each of the first two nights, while choirs of clerics chanted psalms around the body, individual demons easily broke through the church door, closed with a massive bar, and snapped the outermost chains. The middle chain, which had been made with greater effort, remained untouched [Note: [Col. 1189D] *Remained untouched.* c. d. e: omitted in a. and l 1; *remained whole*, s. and in l 2, written above the line in another hand.].

On the third night, about cockcrow, the whole monastery seemed to be shaken from its foundations by the din of the enemies’ arrival [Note: [Col. 1189D] *Seemed to be shaken.* c. d. e: *seemed to be overthrown*, s; *seemed*, a l 1; *was overthrown*, written above the line in l 1 by another hand.]. One, more terrible in face and more towering in stature than the rest, struck the doors with greater force and dashed them to pieces. The clerics froze with fear: “Their hair stood on end and their voices stuck in their throats.” [Note: [Col. 1190D] “*Their hair stood on end,* etc.” Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 48.]

He approached the sarcophagus with an arrogant gesture, as it seemed, and, calling her by name, ordered her to rise. When she answered that she could not because of the bonds, [Col. 1189C] he said, “You shall be loosed—and to your misery!” Immediately he broke, without effort, as though it were a rope of tow, the chain that had defied the ferocity of all the rest. He also kicked off the lid of the tomb; seized her by the hand; and, in sight of all, dragged her from the church. Outside the doors there appeared a black and proud horse, neighing, with iron hooks projecting along its whole back. The wretched woman was set upon these, and immediately disappeared from the eyes of the spectators with the whole company. Yet for nearly four miles pitiable cries could be heard, begging for help.

No one who has read blessed Gregory’s *Dialogues* will judge these things incredible. [Note: [Col. 1190D] *Gregory’s Dialogues … in the fourth book.* Many legends of this sort occur in Gregory’s *Dialogues*.] In the fourth book he relates that a wicked man, buried in a church, was cast outside by demons. Among the Franks also, more than once, what I am about to say has been heard: Charles Martel, a man of distinguished courage, who forced the Saracens who had entered Gaul to return to Spain, was buried, after the completion of his days, in the church of Saint Denis. Yet because he had diminished the estates of almost all the monasteries of Gaul to pay his fellow-soldiers, he was visibly snatched from his tomb by evil spirits and has never been seen anywhere to this day. [Col. 1190A] Finally, this was related to the bishop of Orléans and through him spread abroad among the people.

## CONCERNING A RING ENTRUSTED TO A STATUE

§ 205. But, to return to Rome: a citizen of that city, an ephebe [Note: [Col. 1190D] *Ephebe.* Gloss in a. 1: Lucian.], young in years, wealthy in possessions, and exalted by senatorial birth, had recently married a wife [Note: [Col. 1190D] *Wife.* Gloss in a. 1: Eugenia.]. Having summoned his companions, he prepared a large feast. After the meal, when they had invited merriment with smaller cups, they went out onto a field, that by leaping, 355 throwing, or some exercise they might lighten stomachs burdened with food. The host himself, leader of the game, called for a ball. Meanwhile he placed his wedding ring upon the outstretched finger of a bronze statue standing nearby.

But when nearly everyone was making for the ground, he, sighing and with his insides inflamed, [Col. 1190B] first withdrew from the game. Seeking his ring again, he found the statue’s finger bent down to the palm. He struggled there for a long time; unable either to remove the ring or break the finger, he departed silently, concealing the matter from his companions, lest they laugh at him in his presence or rob him of the ring in his absence. Thus, as he returned with his servants in the depth of night, he was amazed to find the finger once more outstretched and the ring stolen. He concealed the loss and was soothed by the caresses of his new bride.

When the hour for going to bed [Note: [Col. 1190D] *For going to bed.* a. s. c. d. e: *for lying down*, l.] came, and he had placed himself beside his wife, he felt something misty and dense rolling between himself and her—something that could be felt but could not be seen. Prevented by this obstacle from embracing her, he also heard a voice: “Lie with me, for today you betrothed me. I am Venus, upon whose finger you placed [Col. 1190C] the ring. I possess it and shall not return it.” Terrified by so great a marvel, he dared not and could not tell anyone. He passed that night sleepless, silently examining the affair in his mind.

Much time passed in this manner: whenever he wished at any hour to lie in his wife’s embrace, he felt and heard the same thing. In other respects he was well, competent both at home and in military service. At last, prompted by his wife’s complaints, he disclosed the affair to his parents. They consulted and revealed the matter to a certain suburban priest named Palumbus. He was skilled in necromantic [*nigromanticis*] practices, able to raise magical figures, terrify demons, and compel them to any service. He therefore bargained for a great payment: if he joined the lovers, his purse would be supported by much money. He roused himself to every device known to his arts and gave the young man a composed letter:

“Go,” he said, “at that hour of night to the crossroads where the way divides into four roads, and stand silently watching. Figures of men and women of every age, rank, and condition will pass there: some mounted, some on foot; some with faces cast down to the ground, others [Col. 1191A] lifted up in haughty pride. In short, whatever belongs to joy or grief, you will see in their faces and gestures. Address none of them, even if they speak with you. Behind that crowd one will follow, taller and more massive than the rest, seated in a chariot. Silently give him the letter to read. What you wish will be done immediately; only make sure that you are fully composed.”

He undertook the prescribed journey; standing under the open sky by night, he tested by sight the truth of the priest’s words. There was nothing that fell short of the promises [Note: [Col. 1191D] *Fell short.* e: *you should find lacking*, a. s. c. d. l.]. Among the others passing by, he also saw a woman in harlot’s dress riding a mule. Her loose hair fluttered about her shoulders, though a golden band fastened it above. In her hands was a golden rod with which she directed her mount. She herself, nearly naked because of the thinness [Col. 1191B] of her clothing, made obscene gestures.

Why say more? Last of all, the one who seemed to be the lord, fixing terrible eyes upon the young man, asked from a proud chariot adorned with emeralds and pearls the reason for his arrival. The young man said nothing in reply, but stretched out his hand and offered the letter. The demon, not daring to despise the familiar seal, read the writing. Then, lifting his arms to heaven, he said: “Almighty God [Note: [Col. 1191D] *Almighty.* a. c. d. e: *in whose sight every sin is like a stench*, s. l 2; this was written in the interlinear space in l 1 by a later hand.], how long will you endure the wickedness of the priest Palumbus?” Without delay he sent attendants from his side to wrench the ring from Venus. She, after much evasion [Note: [Col. 1191D] *After much evasion.* a. c. d. e. l: *having turned away her face*, s.], at last scarcely gave it back. Thus the young man, attaining his desire, enjoyed his long-sought love without obstacle.

But when Palumbus heard the demon’s cry to God concerning him, he understood that the end of his days was being foretold. [Col. 1191C] Therefore, having voluntarily mutilated all his limbs, he died in miserable repentance, confessing before the pope and the Roman people unheard-of crimes. [[Note: [Col. 1191D] This is added by Pertz’s copy. See *Monumenta Germaniae*, X, 471, where he transcribed this legend from a Cambridge manuscript. Patristic Edition.] All the Roman region recounts this to the present day, and mothers teach it to their children, so that the memory may be transmitted to posterity.]

## CONCERNING THE BODY OF PALLAS, SON OF EVANDER

§ 206. Then the body of Pallas, son of Evander—of whom Virgil tells [Note: [Col. 1192D] *The body of Pallas, son of Evander, of whom Virgil tells.* *Aeneid* X, 474–487.]—was found at Rome intact, to the immense amazement of all that it had survived so many ages without corruption. Such, it is said, is the nature of buried bodies: when the flesh decays, the outer skin contains the sinews, and the sinews the bones. The opening of the wound which Turnus had made in the middle of his breast measured four and a half feet. [Col. 1191D] The following epitaph was found:

> Pallas, Evander’s son, whom Turnus’ spear—  
> A soldier, in his usual manner—slew, lies here.

I would not believe that this was composed at that time, although Carmentis, Evander’s mother, is said to have invented Latin letters; rather, it was composed by Ennius or some other ancient poet. [Note: [Col. 1192D] *Poet.* a. c. d. e. l: omitted in s.]

[Col. 1192A] A burning lamp was found at its head, contrived by mechanical art so that no force of wind and no sprinkling of liquid could extinguish it. While many marvelled at it, one man—since there are always some whose ingenuity is keener in evil—made a hole beneath the flame with a stylus. Thus air was introduced, and the fire vanished. The body, set against a wall, exceeded the wall’s height by its size; but as days passed, soaked by dripping moisture, it underwent the common corruption of mortals: its skin dissolved and its sinews melted away.

## CONCERNING A WOMAN WITH TWO BODIES

§ 207. At the same time, on the border between Brittany and Normandy, a prodigy was seen in one woman—or rather [Col. 1192B] two women. There were two heads, four arms, and all the other parts doubled as far as the navel; below that, two legs, two feet, and all the other parts single. One laughed, ate, and spoke; the other wept, hungered, and was silent. Food was eaten with two mouths, but digested through one passage. At last one died and the other survived. The living woman carried the dead one for nearly three years, until she too succumbed, both to the weight of the burden and to the stench of the corpse.

Some thought—and even committed it to writing—that these women signified England and Normandy. Though separated by spaces of land, they are nevertheless united under one dominion. Whatever wealth they swallow with greedy jaws flows into a single pool, whether that be the avarice of princes or the violence of surrounding [Col. 1192C] peoples. England, flourishing in wealth, sustains Normandy, dead and almost exhausted, until perhaps England too succumbs to the violence of tax-collectors. Happy would she be if she could ever breathe freedom, whose empty shadow she has long pursued. Now she groans, oppressed with calamities and bound to payments. I shall describe the cause of this misfortune, if I first say certain things pertinent to the matter.

For, since I have thus far woven together the civil affairs and military enterprises of the kings of England, I wish for a little while to range through the holiness of certain persons. At the same time, we must consider how far the radiance of divine mercy has surrounded that people from the beginning of the faith; for nowhere among nations, I think, will you find so many bodies of saints, intact after death, displaying an image of that final incorruption [Col. 1192D]. I believe this happens by heaven’s will, so that a nation situated almost outside the world might be more confidently encouraged, by considering the saints’ incorruptibility, toward hope of the resurrection.

There are indeed altogether five whom I know—though their countrymen proclaim more—Saint Etheldritha [Note: [Col. 1192D] *Etheldritha.* She was the daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles, and wife of Eclrith. In 673 she founded the monastery of Ely, of which she became the first abbess. She was buried at Ely, where her body remained incorrupt. Bede celebrated this nun (*Book* IV, chs. 9 and 20).] and [Note: [Col. 1192D] *Wiburga.* Another daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles. Her “body (A.D. 797) was found at Dereham entirely whole and incorrupt, fifty-five years after she had departed this life.” (*Saxon Chronicle.*) But Florence assigns the following year: “A.D. 798. The body of Saint Wihtburga, virgin, daughter of Anna king of the East Angles and sister of the holy virgins Sexburga, Aethelburga, and Aetheldritha, was found without corruption, nearly fifty-five years after she had been buried at the village called Dereham.” (*Florence of Worcester.*) Compare the *Life of the Blessed Virgin Wihtburga*, MSS Trinity College, Cambridge, Gall. O. 2.] Wiburga, [Col. 1193A] virgins; King Edmund; [Note: [Col. 1193C] *King Edmund.* King of East Anglia; he suffered martyrdom on 20 November 870. See §97, note.] Archbishop Elfegus; [Note: [Col. 1193C] *Archbishop Elfegus.* See §165, note.] and the ancient father Cuthbert [Note: [Col. 1193D] *Cuthbert.* Sixth bishop of Lindisfarne and its patron saint. When his tomb was opened eleven years after his burial, his body was found incorrupt and whole and was transferred elsewhere. In 1104, more than four centuries after he had first been exhumed, his coffin was opened again, and his body, still whole and incorrupt, was brought to Durham. Finally, in 1827, Cuthbert’s tomb was opened a third time. A complete and worthy account of the vestments and relics found there was published by Raine of Durham (Durham, quarto, 1828).]—all with skin and flesh uninjured, joints flexible, and with their extremities retaining a certain life-like warmth, suggesting the appearance of sleepers.

Who could enumerate the other saints, of every kind [Note: [Col. 1193D] *And profession.* a. s. c. d. e 2. l: omitted in e 1.] and vocation? To recount individually their names and lives [Note: [Col. 1193D] *Their names and lives.* a. s. c. e: l reads *everything* for *names*; d: *to set forth now their names and life*.] is neither my purpose nor within my leisure—though, ah, if only there should someday be time left over! [Note: [Col. 1193D] *Though, ah, if only there should someday be time left over!* a. s. c. e. k. l: *though, if someday there should be leisure time left over*, s.] But I shall be silent, lest I seem to promise more than my powers can perform.

Nor is it necessary to name anyone of common birth, but only boys or girls of royal stock, that I may carry forward the course of the subject begun: most of them innocently slain, whom not human conjecture but divine judgment consecrated as martyrs. From this it may be understood how sparingly they allowed themselves the pleasures of licence, [Col. 1193B] since, by the easy shortcut of death, they attained heavenly glory.

§ 208. [Note: [Col. 1194C] In the praises of the most blessed Oswald, king and martyr, the discourse dwelt for some time in the preceding book: §49.] In the preceding book the discourse dwelt for some time upon the praises of the most blessed Oswald, king and martyr. Among the evidences of his holiness were other things, [Note: [Col. 1194C] *And also that which, according to certain copies, is asserted in the history of the English.* Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book IV, ch. 14. In certain manuscript copies of Bede this chapter is lacking; it occurs in the Moore manuscript, followed by Smith. Thus the most learned editor explains the reason for the omission of this passage: “There is great variation among manuscripts here in numbering the chapters. Neither this title nor the next following appears in the table of chapters of the Moore codex, although chapter 14 is to be marked in Cottonian manuscript II; but in Cottonian manuscript I this chapter 14 concerning Oswald is absent, and in the margin, in a very ancient hand, is written: ‘Here a leaf is missing.’ Hence later manuscripts also omit either the summaries of chapters 14 and 15 or chapter 14 itself, according as they were copied from this or that ancient manuscript. But since the chapter summaries and arrangement agree well with the matter in the common manuscripts, and one of the old manuscripts admits that a leaf is missing, while an alteration of the received order would create some confusion for readers, I have followed the common arrangement amid the disagreement of the ancient codices.”] including this, which according to certain copies is asserted in the history of the English.

At the monastery of Selsey, which Wilfrid [Note: [Col. 1194D] *Wilfrid.* See §51, note.] had filled with Northumbrian monks of holy religious life, a deadly sickness arose and killed many. The survivors, having proclaimed a three-day fast, tried to drive away the plague. On the second day of the fast, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul appeared to a boy lying ill with the same disease and encouraged him with these words: he ought not fear the death [Col. 1193C] threatening him, since it would be both the end of his present sickness and the entrance to everlasting life. Moreover, no one in [Col. 1194A] that monastery would die of this plague, because God had granted this through the merits of the illustrious King Oswald, who on that same day interceded for his countrymen. For this was the day on which that king, slain by the faithless, ascended in a moment to his starry tribunal. They should therefore look in the register in which the names of the dead were written; and if they found it so, then, ending the fast, they should give themselves to confidence and joy and sing the solemn offices of the Mass to God and the holy king.

The boy’s death immediately followed this vision; the martyr’s day was found in the martyrology; and the expulsion of the disease was confirmed by the testimony of the whole district. Thus from that time Oswald’s name was entered among the martyrs, though before then, because of the recentness of his death, it had been joined merely to the number of the faithful. Rightly, therefore—rightly, I say—was he praised: divine approval raised up his glory by a confirmed sign, commanding him to be celebrated in the proclamation of Masses—an example, I think, unprecedented among mortals. But that these things may not appear trivial, the unquestioned authority of the historian forbids it, together with blessed Bishop Acca, [Note: [Col. 1194D] *Bishop Acca.* Acca, priest of Wilfrid, was raised to the episcopal see of Hexham in 710. (See Bede, book V, ch. 20, and Smith’s note on this passage).] the narrator’s fellow-initiated associate.

§ 209. Egbert, king of Kent, son of Erconbert, [Note: [Col. 1194D] *Egbert, king of Kent, son of Erconbert,* concerning whom I have spoken above, §12.] of whom I spoke above, had young kinsmen closely related by blood to the royal line, [Note: [Col. 1194D] *Ethelred and Egelbert,* namely the sons of his paternal uncle Ermenred. See §§12 and 13.] Ethelred and Egelbert, sons, that is, of his paternal uncle Ermenred. Fearing that they were growing up with a claim to the kingdom, and fearing for his own safety, he kept them for some time near him on a wretched and pitiable subsistence. At last, begrudging them his sight, he removed them from the company of the court; and shortly afterwards, through an agent named Thunre—whose name means “thunder”—he secretly [Col. 1194C] had them killed. [Col. 1195A] He plunged them into a deep heap of shavings, thinking that a murder concealed from human sight could remain hidden.

But that divine eye, which is not deceived by the secrets of hearts, brought the innocents into the light, granting many graces of healing there. At length the neighbours, stirred by this, dug up the ruins, upon which a rough turf had been heaped over the bodies [Note: [Col. 1195D] *Heaped.* c. d. e: *thrown upon*, a. s. l.], levelled the pit into the form of a grave, and built a little church above it. They lay there until the time of King Edgar. Then Saint Oswald, bishop of Worcester [Note: [Col. 1195D] *Bishop.* a. s. c. e. l: *archbishop*, d.—Oswald was archbishop of York and at the same time bishop of Worcester.], raised them up and carried them to the monastery of Ramsey. From that day they made themselves known by many miracles, answering the vows of suppliants.

§ 210. Offa, king of Mercia, in order, as he thought, to secure his kingdom, slaughtered many powerful men without distinguishing friend from foe. Among them was King Egelbert, [Note: [Col. 1195D] *King Egelbert.* See §§86 and 97, note 10.] committing a wicked deed against a suitor for his daughter’s hand. Yet his blameless death is believed, as I said above, to have been avenged by the brief reign of Offa’s son. Indeed, God revealed his holiness by signs so evident that, even today, the episcopal see at Hereford is consecrated under his name. Nor should it seem foolish or incongruous that our predecessors, upright and religious men, either tolerated this in silence or confirmed it by their authority.

§ 211. What worthy thing can this pen devise concerning Saint Kenelm, a boy of very tender age? His father, Cenwulf, king of the Mercians, left him, at seven years old, to be brought up under the guardianship of his sister Quendryth; but she, falsely foretelling the kingdom for herself, entrusted her little brother—who was to be removed from the way—to a retainer who had been his fosterling. He, taking the innocent child out hunting, as though to restore his spirits, slew him among the thickets and concealed him.

And, wonderful to relate, a treachery committed so secretly in England was divinely made known at Rome. For a parchment, borne by a dove, descended from above upon the altar of Saint Peter, reporting in order the murder and the place of burial. Since it was written in English characters, the Romans and men of other nations who were present tried in vain to read it. But an Englishman providentially arrived in time; unfolding to the Roman citizens in Latin the covering of the language, he brought it about that the apostolic letter informed the English kings of their compatriot martyr. Therefore the body of the innocent was raised and carried to Winchcombe by a great gathering.

Thus, stirred by the sung chant of the clergy and the joyful applause of the laity, the parricidal woman put her head out of the window of the upper room in which she stood. By chance she had a psalter in her hands, and in the course of her reading had come to the psalm, “O God of my praise” [Ps. 109:1]. From the end, by some strange trick, she recited it backwards, striving to weaken the joy of those singing. Then indeed, by divine power, the sorceress’s eyes, torn from their hollow sockets, stained the verse with blood: “This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord, and who speak evil against my soul” [Ps. 109:20]. Traces of the blood remain to this day, proclaiming the woman’s monstrous wickedness and God’s vengeance. The saint’s little body is solemnly venerated; scarcely any place in England is revered by a greater multitude of arrivals at its feast. Both the conviction of its ancient sanctity and the frequent manifestation of miracles demand this.

[Note: Col. 1195D. Kenelm. See § 95, note.]

[Note: Col. 1195D. “Of very tender age.” a. s. c. d. e: “for tender age,” l.]

[Note: Col. 1195D. “Spirits.” a. c. d. e. l.; after *animum*, s. reads perhaps “or to refresh.”]

§ 212. Nor shall our pages lack your praise, blessed boy Wistan, son of Wigmund, son of Wiglaf, king of the Mercians, and of Æthelflæd, daughter of Ceolwulf, who was Kenelm’s paternal uncle. You, I say, I shall not pass over in silence: you whom your kinsman Berhfrith wickedly killed.

Let posterity, if any judge these writings worthy of their knowledge, know that nothing in the world was more glorious than the nobility of your character, by which the hostile butcher was provoked to murder you; nothing in God more innocent than your purity, by which the inward Judge was moved to honour you. For a bright pillar sent down from heaven, rending the veils of dense night, revealed the crime of the deep pit and exposed the murderer’s wickedness. Therefore your venerable relics, raised by the devoted care of your parents, were placed at Repton, then a famous monastery; it is now an estate of the Earl of Chester, whose glory has, owing to the place’s antiquity, faded away. Now you dwell at Evesham, worthy to grant serene favour to the prayers of those devoted to you.

[Note: Col. 1196D. “Hostile butcher.” a. d. e. l: “hostile robber,” s.; “unlucky robber,” c.]

[Note: Col. 1196D. “Pillar.” d. e. l: “dove,” a. s. c.]

[Note: Col. 1196D. “Famous.” s. c. d. e. l; after *famoso*, a. reads as he said in the first book.]

[Note: Col. 1195D. Wistan. For Saint Wistan see MSS Harley 2253, “On the Martyrdom of Saint Wistan.”]

§ 213. Bede related much concerning the sanctity of the kings of the East Saxons and East Angles. I briefly set out the genealogy of those kingdoms in the first book of this work, because nowhere could I find full accounts of their kings’ deeds. Yet a fuller discourse shall be forged concerning Saint Edmund, whom Bede’s age did not reach, and who held the sovereignty in East Anglia.

That province is bounded on the south and east by the ocean; on the north by the marshy moisture and devouring gulf of fens and pools, which stretch to a breadth of three or two miles and an immeasurable length, supplying their inhabitants with an abundance of fish; on the west it is joined to the rest of the island, but is strongly defended by an embankment cut out of the ground like a wall. The land is excellent for the pasturage of cattle and the taking of wild beasts; it abounds in monasteries, with very numerous communities of monks established even upon the islands of the fens. Its people are cheerful and agreeable, readily inclined to a witty festiveness of jokes that borders on wantonness.

[Note: Col. 1197D. “Here he reigned.” What is added from these words to the end of § 213 occurs in Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum*, p. 136.]

Here Edmund reigned, a man devoted to God and distinguished by his ancestral line of kings. Though he had governed the province peacefully for some years, he was not induced by any softness of the times to unman himself of virtue. The Danish leaders Ingwar and Hubba came to ravage the provinces of the Northumbrians and East Angles. The former captured the king—not resisting, but having cast away his weapons, lying prostrate upon the ground and praying—and, after some tortures, beheaded him.

After the death of the blessed man, the purity of his past life shone out in unheard-of miracles. The head, severed from the body by the executioner’s cruelty, the Danes had hidden by throwing it into thickets. When the citizens sought it, following the departing enemy’s tracks and intending to pay due funeral rites to their king, they received God’s joyful gifts: the voice of the lifeless head, calling all searchers to itself. They found a wolf, a beast accustomed to the corpse, embracing it with its forelegs and providing harmless protection. Like a domestic animal it followed the bearers modestly behind to the tomb; it injured no one and was injured by no one.

Then, for the time, the venerable body was committed to the earth, covered with a clod of soil, and a wooden chapel of little value was built over it. But the martyr’s power was present to the negligent people of the province, awakening their half-sleeping minds to reverence for him by signs. The first example of his miracles which I shall offer, though slight and commonplace, is this. Some thieves, attempting by night to strip the sacred building, were entangled by invisible cords in the very course of their undertaking: a remarkably pleasing spectacle, in which the booty held the robbers fast, so that they could neither abandon what they had begun nor complete what they had started.

Therefore Theodred, bishop of London, who lies at Saint Paul’s, removed the long-standing disgrace of the humble structure, devising a more stately building over the venerable remains. These proclaimed the glory of the holy soul both by their remarkable incorruption and by a kind of milky whiteness. The head, once torn from the neck, was now joined to the rest of the body, yet displayed the mark of martyrdom in a scarlet scar.

Moreover, this exceeds human miracles: the hair and nails of the dead man gradually sprouted. Oswen, a certain holy woman, used each year to cut the former and pare the latter, preserving them for posterity’s sacred veneration—a woman of holy boldness, who beheld and touched limbs before which all this lower world stands in awe. But Lefstan, a youth of reckless and unbridled audacity, was not such a person. He insolently demanded that the martyr’s body be shown to him, intending, as he said, to weigh the uncertainty of report against the testimony of his eyes. Accordingly, he paid the penalty for his headlong daring: he became mad, and shortly afterwards, swarming with worms, died.

Edmund surely knows now how to do what he once was accustomed to do:

> To spare the submissive and to subdue the proud.

By these powers he so bound to himself all the inhabitants of Britain that each considers himself especially blessed if he enriches Edmund’s monastery with even a coin or something of value. Kings themselves, lords of others, glory in calling themselves his servants, and send him a royal crown, redeeming it at a great price if they wish to use it. Tax-collectors, who elsewhere rage, measuring right and wrong alike, there humbly bring their disputes to a halt before the ditch of Saint Edmund, having learned by the punishment of many that they ought not persist.

[Note: Col. 1196D. “Kingdoms.” Omitted in a. s. c. d. e2. l. m.; present in e1.]

[Note: Col. 1196D. “I briefly set out in the first book of this work.” §§ 97–98.]

[Note: Col. 1196D. “Find.” a. c. d. e. l: “discover,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1196D. On Saint Edmund. See § 97, note.]

[Note: Col. 1197D. “Ravage.” a. c. d. e: “to ravage,” s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1197D. After several tortures he was tied to a tree and pierced to death with arrows. See Abbo, *On the Passion of Saint Edmund, King of the East Angles*; MS St John Baptist, Oxford, no. 199.]

[Note: Col. 1197D. “Embracing.” a. c. d. e. l: “having embraced,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1197D. “Miracles.” a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.]

[Note: Col. 1197D. “Removed the disgrace.” c. d. e: “removed the opprobrium,” a. s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1197D. “Intending.” c. d. e: “desiring,” a. s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1198D. “They thought.” Much fuller material on this subject occurs in Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum*, book II, p. 136b, London edition.]

§ 214. The praise of my voice shall also touch upon the names of certain girls of royal birth—subject, as stated above, to the pardon due to brevity, which arises not from weariness or disgust but from ignorance of their miracles.

Anna, king of the East Angles, had three daughters: Æthelthryth, Æthelburh, and Seaxburh. Æthelthryth, married to two husbands, nevertheless—as Bede attests—won for heaven the laurel of perpetual virginity by blessed continence, without any loss of chastity or any sting of desire. Æthelburh, first a nun and then an abbess in the monastery in Gaul called Brie, flourished with the seal of unblemished integrity. It is certainly a splendid thing that both sisters, just as while alive they subdued within themselves the desire of the flesh, so when dead they display it incorrupt: the one in England, the other in Gaul, so that their holiness, abundantly radiant, may “suffice to illuminate the twin poles.”

Seaxburh, given in marriage to Erconbert, king of Kent, was veiled after his death in the same monastery as her sister Æthelthryth and is proclaimed holy. By that king she had daughters, Eorcongota and Ermenilda. Bede’s account will inform those who wish to know about Eorcongota. Ermenilda, married to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, had a daughter, Werburh, a most holy virgin. Both are saints: the mother rests at Ely, where she was abbess after her mother Seaxburh; the daughter rests in the city of the legions, in that city’s monastery, newly built by Hugh, Earl of Chester, after the expulsion of the few clerics who had there been living a shameful and poor life. Their merits, and especially those of the younger, are praised there, and their miracles extolled. While they are immediately favourable to the petitions of all, they particularly reach the prayers of women and children with the near and ready foot of aid.

[Note: Col. 1198D. As Bede is the authority: *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapters 19–20.]

[Note: Col. 1198D. Brie: Faremoutiers-en-Brie, the celebrated convent of Benedictine nuns.]

[Note: Col. 1198D. Those wishing to know about Eorcongota will be informed by Bede’s account: *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 8, § 172. See also Malmesbury, *Gesta regum Anglorum*, § 11, note.]

[Note: Col. 1198D. Ermenilda, married to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, had a daughter, Werburh, a most holy virgin. See above, end of § 76.]

[Note: Col. 1198D. “Was.” After *fuit*, s. l. also read “and.”]

[Note: Col. 1199D. “Then.” c. d. e: “then,” a. s. l.]

§ 215. Merewald, Wulfhere’s brother, by Ermenburh, daughter of Eormenred, brother of Erconbert, had daughters, Mildrith and Milburh. Mildrith, on the Kentish island of Thanet—which King Ecgberht had given to her mother in compensation for the murder of her brothers Æthelred and Æthelberht—devoted herself to celibacy and there reached life’s end. Later she was translated to Saint Augustine’s monastery at Canterbury, where she is honoured by the exceptional devotion of the monks, her fame for piety and sweetness being everywhere worthy of her very name. Although almost every recess of that monastery is full of saints’ bodies, neither obscure in name nor in merit, but such that each one by itself could make England illustrious, yet she is venerated no less than any of them; indeed, she is loved and commemorated with greater sweetness. She is present to those who love her, passing none by with a deaf ear and caring for the salvation of the soul.

[Note: Col. 1199D. Merewald. See end of § 76.]

[Note: Col. 1199D. “Daughters.” a. c. d. e: “two daughters,” s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1199D. On the island of Thanet in Kent. Having been granted the right to determine the compensation (that is, their *weregild*), she asked for as much land as a stag could encircle in one run on the island of Thanet, where she founded a monastery. See W. Thorn, col. 1910, and *Natale S. Mildrithae* (in Saxon), MS Cotton Caligula A. XIV, 4; Sharpe, 278.]

§ 216. Milburh rests at Wenlock. Once known to the local people, she was for some time forgotten after the coming of the Normans, because the location of her tomb was unknown. But recently, after a community of Cluniac monks had assembled there, when work had begun upon a new church and a certain boy was running rather hastily over the pavement, the broken hollow of a mausoleum openly revealed the virgin’s body.

Then, as a breath of balsamic fragrance spread through the church, the body was raised higher and produced so many miracles that the broad open fields could scarcely contain the throngs of travellers streaming together from all those peoples. Rich and poor alike pressed forward shoulder to shoulder, faith impelling all together. Nor was the result empty: so much so that no one departed except with illness either extinguished or alleviated; and the royal disease, indeed incurable by physicians, left some through the virgin’s merits.

[Note: Col. 1199D. Milburh. See § 76.]

[Note: Col. 1199D. “Spreading.” c. d. e: “breathing,” a. s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1199D. “Of those.” e: “by that,” a. s. c. d. l.]

§ 217. Edward the Elder, of whom I have related much above, had many daughters by his wife Eadgifu, among them Eadburh. When she was scarcely three years old, she gave a striking proof of her future holiness. Her father wished to test whether the little girl would incline toward God or toward the world. In the hall he had placed ornaments belonging to different callings: on one side a chalice and Gospels, on the other bracelets and necklaces.

The little virgin was brought there in the coaxing arms of her nurse and sat at her father’s knees. Commanded to choose which she wanted, she contemptuously looked down upon worldly things and, quickly crawling with her hands, adored the Gospels and chalice in childlike innocence. The company seated around cried out that in the girl there was an omen of future holiness. Her father kissed her and honoured his child with closer embraces: “Go,” he said, “where Divinity calls you; with fortunate step follow the Bridegroom whom you have chosen. Truly both I and my wife shall be happy if we are overcome in religion by our daughter.”

Thus, clothed in the habit of nuns, she drew all her companions in the city of Winchester to love her by the diligence of her service. Nor did the high greatness of her lineage make her proud, for she considered it noble to bend down to Christ’s service. Holiness grew with her age; as she became an adult, humility matured, so much so that by night she secretly took each woman’s shoes and, having carefully washed and anointed them, placed them again beside their beds. Therefore, although God distinguished her while alive by many miracles, I particularly recount this example because charity began all her actions and humility completed them. Finally, very many miracles during her life and after her death commend both the devotion of her heart and the integrity of her body—miracles which the custodians of her churches at Winchester and Pershore recount orally to those who do not know them.

[Note: Col. 1199D–1200D. On Edward, see above § 125, note.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. Eadgifu. e: Ælfgifu, a. s. l.; Eadelswith, c. d.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Scarcely.” a. d. e. l; s. c omit *vix* (“scarcely”).]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Callings.” a. c. d. e. l: “possessions,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Nurse.” a. c. d. e. l: “of the nurse,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Looking down upon.” e: “spurning,” a. c. d. l. m; “rejecting,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Crawling.” a. c. d. e. l: “snatching,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “We shall be.” a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Again.” d. e: “again,” a. s. c. l.]

§ 218. Blessed Edith, daughter of King Edgar, adorns with her sweet remains and cherishes Wilton monastery, the resting place of her bones. There, entrusted from infancy to the Lord’s school, she deserved God’s grace through perpetual intact virginity and frequent vigils, suppressing the pride of birth by nobility of mind.

I received one thing from my elders that not moderately offended people’s judgment, deceiving their eyes by the display of gilded clothing: she regularly appeared adorned in finer garments than the holiness of her profession required. Hence, when Saint Æthelwold publicly reproved her, she is said to have answered, neither foolishly nor without wit: “The true and unanswerable judgment of God is covered only by the conscience of mortals; for even under mourning rags there may be pride. Therefore I think that a mind equally incorrupt may exist beneath these garments as beneath your torn skins.”

The bishop, struck by this saying and approving its truth by his silence, was silent, blushing with pleasure that he had been branded by the girl’s sparkling sentence. Saint Dunstan had seen her, at the consecration of the basilica of blessed Dionysius—which she had built out of love for the martyr—frequently extend her right thumb and make the sign of the cross directly upon her forehead. Greatly pleased, he said, “May this finger never decay.”

Immediately, during the celebration of Mass, he burst into tears—tears so copious that, with sobbing voice, he shook a disciple standing near. Asked the reason, he said: “Soon this flowering rose will wither; soon the bird beloved by God will fly away, six weeks from this day.” The event immediately fulfilled the bishop’s prophecy. For, faithful to her noble purpose, she breathed her last on the foretold day, before reaching the limit of youth, at the age of twenty-three.

Not long afterward the same blessed man saw in a dream Saint Dionysius holding the virgin’s hand affectionately and, by a divine oracle, firmly ordering that she be honoured on earth by her servants, just as she was venerated in heaven by her Bridegroom and Lord. Thus, as miracles multiplied at her tomb, an order was issued that the virgin’s body should be raised and elevated. It was found entirely dissolved into ashes except for the finger, the belly, and what lay beneath the belly. When some disputed this, the virgin herself appeared in sleep to one of those who had seen it and said that it was no wonder if those parts of the body had decayed, since dead bodies have a natural tendency to flow into certain secret recesses of nature, and since she, being a girl, had sinned with those members. But the belly, she said, was rightly uncorrupted by any decay, because it had never been pricked by any desire: she had been free from gluttony and carnal intercourse.

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Sweet.” a. s. c. d. e2. l: “leaders,” e1.]

[Note: Col. 1200D. “Profession.” a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.]

[Note: Col. 1201D. “Blessed.” c. d. e: “saint,” a. s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1201D. “Martyr.” a. c. d. e. l: “mother,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1201D. “Before reaching the limit of youth she breathed her last.” c. e. f. l; “before the approaching end, having breathed out, that…,” d. m; “before the approaching end she breathed her last,” a. s.]

[Note: Col. 1201D. “Has.” a. c. d. e. l: “had,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1201D. “Nature.” a. c. d. e; l reads “of that woman” after *naturae*.]

[Note: Col. 1201D. “Ever.” Omitted in e1.]

§ 219. Certainly both these virgins sustain their respective monasteries by their merits, communities of many nuns having gathered in each place; these nuns, when their ladies and teachers call them to grace, answer through obedience. Blessed is one who has a share in virgins’ prayers, for the Lord Jesus grants ready assent to their devotion.

For, as I have said of the nuns of Shaftesbury, all virtues have long ago left the earth and sought heaven; only in the minds of nuns, if they exist anywhere upon earth, will you find them—if I may say so without offence to holy men. For greatly to be praised are women who, putting aside the weakness of their sex, preserve continence with striving zeal and carry up to heaven a rich victory.

[Note: Col. 1202D. “I have said.” See § 163.]

§ 220. I think it relevant to have known several members of the royal family of both sexes, so that it may be known that King Edward, of whom I was speaking before this digression, did not at all fall short of his ancestors’ virtues. For he was distinguished by miracles and by the spirit of prophecy, as I shall say below.

He was sparing in the exaction of taxes, since he detested tax-collectors; free from royal luxury in food and drink. On the chief feasts, though he wore garments interwoven with gold which the queen had made at great expense, he was so restrained that he neither failed in royal dignity nor raised his brow in arrogance, pondering in his mind God’s generosity in these things rather than worldly glory.

There was one thing in which he delighted his mind in this world: the racing of swift hounds, whose barking about the hunting-grounds he used gladly to applaud; and the flights of birds whose nature it is to make prey of kindred birds. He devoted himself to these exercises every day after hearing the divine offices in the morning. In all else, a man voluntarily given to God, he lived like an angel amid the affairs of the kingdom: kind in his manner of address to poor people and guests, especially those from overseas and religious persons; generous in giving; and encouraging the monks of his own country to emulate their holiness.

He was of well-proportioned stature, white as a swan in beard and hair, rosy in face, milky-white over his entire body, and admirably well formed in the proportions of his limbs.

[Note: Col. 1202D. “God’s.” a. s. l; omitted in c. d. e.]

[Note: Col. 1202D. “In the world.” c. e: “in this world,” a. s. d. l.]

[Note: Col. 1202D. “From overseas.” s. c. e. l; after *transmarinis*, a. d add “monks.”]

§ 221. Brihtwold, bishop of Wilton, once saw the prosperity of that age in a dream-revelation; he saw it and proclaimed it. For during Cnut’s reign, as he kept nightly heavenly vigils at Glastonbury, a thought came upon him—one which often troubled him—concerning the royal line of the English, almost wiped out. As he meditated, sleep stole over him; and behold, caught up on high, he saw Peter, chief of the apostles, consecrate as king Edward himself, then an exile in Normandy. Peter marked out for him a celibate life and assigned his reign a fixed term of twenty-four years. When Edward complained about succession, Peter replied: “The kingdom of the English belongs to God; after you He has provided a king according to His pleasure.”

[Note: Col. 1202D. “Of the English.” d. e. l; omitted in s.]

§ 222. Now to speak of miracles: a young woman, whose husband was equal to her in nobility of birth but who lacked the fruit of marriage, contracted a foul illness, horrible with swollen glands, from excessive humours around her neck. Ordered in a dream to seek the water from the king’s handwashing, she entered the court. The king himself, personally performing the work of mercy, dipped his fingers in water and handled the woman’s neck. Swift health followed the healing right hand; the deadly crust dissolved, so that worms and pus flowed out and the entire harmful swelling subsided.

But because the gaping ulcers were ugly and open, he ordered that she be maintained at court expense until complete recovery. Yet before a week had elapsed, the scars had so covered over that lovely skin returned and you could perceive nothing of the former disease. After a year she also bore twins, thereby increasing the miracle of Edward’s holiness. Those who knew his inner life report that he often cured this disease in Normandy. Hence, in our own time, some falsely advance the claim that the cure of this disease flowed not from holiness but from inheritance in the royal lineage.

[Note: Col. 1202D. “Hands.” a. c. d. e; omitted in s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1202D. “Subsided.” a. c. d. e. l: “receded,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1203D. “But.” c. d. e: “but nevertheless,” a. s. l.]

[Note: Col. 1203D. “Put forward.” a. c. d. e. l: “introduce,” s.]

[Note: Col. 1203D. “Inheritance.” “flowed.” See Peter of Blois, Letter 150.]

§ 223. A certain blind man, from what ailment is uncertain, spread a common report at court that he would recover his sight if water from the washing of the king’s hands touched his eyes. When this was reported to the king by several messengers, he laughed, looking upon the reporters with a furrowed brow; he said that he was a sinner and that the works of holy men did not suit him.

But the attendants judged that the matter should not be neglected. While the king did not know, and while the man was praying in church, they gave him confidence by a dream. For as soon as he had been washed with the water, the long-lasting darkness fled and timely light filled his eyes, while joyful applause arose with a loud sound. The king asked about the matter and learned the cause. Then, once the certainty of his sight had been established—when the king, directing his fingers toward the healed man’s eyes, saw him avoid them by drawing back his head—he lifted his hands toward heaven and gave thanks to God. In the same way he cured a certain blind man at Lincoln, who survived for many years as a witness to the royal miracle.

[Note: Col. 1203D. “Touched his eyes.” c. e. l: “touched his eyes,” a. s. d.]

[Note: Col. 1203D. “Church.” c. d. e. l: “church of God,” a. s.]

[Note: Col. 1203D. “By a dream.” a. d. e. l; omitted in s. c.]

[Note: Col. 1203D. “As soon as he had been washed with the water.” s. e. c. l; “as soon as he had been washed otherwise,” a. d.]

§ 224. And that you may recognize the man’s perfect virtue, especially in this sphere of power, I shall relate something at which you may marvel.

A certain Wulfwine, surnamed Spillecorn, son of Wulmar of Nuthanger’s Hall, was one day cutting wood in Brill Wood. After prolonged labour he gave himself to sleep, and, I think, because blood congealed about his eyes, lost his sight for seventeen years. When these had passed, instructed in a dream, he visited eighty-seven churches, demanding from the saints a cure for blindness. At last he came to the king’s court and, though the chamberlains opposed him, wore out the threshold of the royal chamber for a long time in vain. Yet the importunate knocker persisted until, with the king himself very reluctantly giving the order, he was admitted.

On hearing the dream, the king answered innocently: “By my lady Saint Mary, I shall take it most gladly if God chooses through me to have mercy on a miserable man.” Therefore, though he did not dare claim anything concerning miracles, compelled by his attendants he laid his hand upon the blind man with water. Immediately, as blood streamed abundantly from the man’s eyes, the healed man uttered a joyful cry: “I see you, king! I see you, king!”

Having received sight, he presided for many years over the royal palace at Windsor, for there he had been cured, outliving his healer’s years by the length of his life. On that same day, three blind men and one man blind in one eye, maintained by royal alms, were healed from the same water, the attendants distributing the health-giving liquid in full faith.

[Note: Col. 1203D. “The king himself.” a. s. c. d. e2. l; *ipso* omitted in e1.]

[Note: Col. 1204D. “He was admitted.” a. s. d. e. l: “he himself was admitted,” c.]

[Note: Col. 1204D. “Immediately.” c. d. e: “immediately,” a. s. l.]

§ 225. On the holy day of Easter he sat down at table at Westminster, adorned with the diadem and surrounded by a company of nobles. While the others, making up for the long abstinence of Lent with fresh foods, ate eagerly, he, his mind withdrawn from earthly things and contemplating something divine, moved the minds of the guests by breaking into a fuller laugh. [Note: [Col. 1204D] “Breaking into a fuller laugh.” c. d. e.; “drenched,” a. s. l.] No one ventured to inquire into the cause of his joy; and he indeed remained silent until satiety in eating put an end to the dishes. But when the tables had been removed and he was taking off his royal garments in the dining-hall, three nobles who had followed him—one of whom was Harold, [Note: [Col. 1204D] “Harold.” c. e.; “Earl Harold,” a. s. l.] the second an abbot, the third a bishop—boldly questioned him, under cover of their familiarity, why he had laughed. It seemed strange to all, and not without reason, that amid the great solemnity [Note: [Col. 1204D] “Solemnity.” c. e. l.; “serenity,” a. s. d.] of the day and occasion, while the rest were silent, he should have uttered a buffoonish burst of laughter.

“I saw wonderful things,” he said, “and therefore I did not laugh without cause.”

Then they, as is the habit of human nature, began more eagerly to ask and investigate the cause, [Col. 1204C] [Note: [Col. 1204D] “That he may graciously communicate the matter to his suppliants.” a. s. d. e. l.; “that he may communicate the matter more carefully to his suppliants,” c.] that he might graciously impart the matter to his petitioners. After much hesitation, at last, pressed by their insistence, he gave this extraordinary reply: the Seven Sleepers were resting on Mount Caelius, having lain on their right sides for two hundred years; but then, at the very hour of his laughter, they had turned over onto their left side. They would lie thus for seventy-four years: certainly a dreadful omen for wretched mortals. For in those seventy-four years would occur all the things which the Lord foretold to His disciples concerning the end of the world: “nation rising against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; earthquakes in various places; pestilence and famine; terrors from heaven and great signs; changes of kingdoms; wars of gentiles against Christians; and likewise victories of Christ-worshippers over pagans.”

As they marvelled, he impressed upon them the story of the Seven Sleepers and the position of each body—matters which no written account records—expounding them as readily as though he had lived with them in daily fellowship. On hearing this, the earl sent a knight, the bishop a cleric, and the abbot a monk to Manichetus, emperor of Constantinople, in order to ascertain the truth of the words; they carried letters and gifts from their king. The emperor received them kindly and sent them on to the bishop of Ephesus, with the document also called sacred, so that the martyrial remains of the Seven Sleepers [Note: [Col. 1205C] “The Seven Sleepers,” etc. The Seven Sleepers were inhabitants of Ephesus: six of them were of no ignoble birth, while the seventh was their servant. When the Decian persecution raged, they fled into a wine-cellar, from which they repeatedly sent their servant to buy food. Decius, upon hearing this, ordered the entrance to the cellar to be sealed. After some centuries had passed, part of the masonry by which the entrance had been blocked collapsed; light entering there awakened the sleepers. Thinking themselves refreshed by the rest of a quiet night, they sent their servant to purchase food. The servant was astonished at everything in Ephesus, and an exceedingly strange dialogue began: the citizens accused him of having discovered a hidden treasure, while he steadfastly declared that he was offering lawful imperial money. When this was learned, the emperor hurried with the bishop and count to the place. After relating what had happened to them, they shortly afterwards breathed their last. Because of this miracle they were regarded as martyrs. See Capgrave, *Legenda nova* (SHARPE, 287).] might be shown to the envoys of the king of England.

And it came about that King Edward’s prophecy was confirmed by all the Greeks, who swore that they had received from their fathers the tradition that the sleepers rested upon their right side; but, after the English entered the cave, they proclaimed to their companions the truth of the foreign prophecy. Nor did the onset of evils delay: the Hagarenes, Arabs, and Turks—peoples alien from Christ—ravaged Syria, Lycia, all Asia Minor, and many cities of Greater Asia, among them Ephesus and even Jerusalem itself, and attacked the Christians.

Then too, after the death of Manichetus, emperor of Constantinople, Diogenes, Michael, Bucianus, and Alexius successively hurled one another from the imperial power. The last of these, whose rule has endured to our own times, left his son John as heir: a man more notorious for cunning and fraud than for integrity, who devised many harmful schemes against pilgrims on the holy journey. Yet he accepted the allegiance of the English and attached them to his closest circle, transmitting his affection for them to his son. [Note: [Col. 1205D] “Yet he accepted the allegiance of the English,” etc. When the Normans invaded England, many Englishmen fled to Constantinople, where Alexius received them most graciously and set them against the Normans who followed Duke Robert Guiscard (ORDERIC VITALIS, p. 508).]

In these last seven years three popes—Victor, [Note: [Col. 1206C] Victor II, successor to Leo IX in 1056, died in 1057.] Stephen, [Note: [Col. 1206D] Frederick, brother of Duke Godfrey, succeeded Victor II on 2 August 1057.] and Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1206D] He was elevated to the Apostolic See in 1059.]—weakened the vigour of the papacy by their successive deaths. Immediately thereafter Henry, the pious emperor of the Romans, died and had as successor his son Henry, who by his folly and wickedness brought many oppressions upon the Roman world [Note: [Col. 1206D] “Upon the Roman world,” c. e. l.; “upon the Roman city,” a. s. d.] [Note: [Col. 1206D] Henry III died at Botfeld, on the borders of Saxony, in the autumn of 1056.]. In the same year Henry, king of the Franks, a valiant and good soldier, died after drinking a potion. [Note: [Col. 1206D] “Henry king of the Franks … died from a draught of a potion.” Henry died on 4 August 1060. “For the sake of bodily health he received a potion from John, most skilful of physicians; but when the poison produced excessive thirst, he disregarded the order of his chief physician and, receiving drink from a chamberlain while the doctor was absent, drank before the purgation. Thus made gravely ill, he died on the same day after receiving the sacred Eucharist.” (WILLIAM OF JUMIÈGES, *History*, ch. 38. Compare ORDERIC VITALIS, p. 480.)]

Not long afterward a comet-star appeared, as they say portending changes of kingdoms, trailing long flaming hair through the void [Note: [Col. 1206D] “Through the void,” a. c. d. e. l.; “in the morning,” s.]. Quailing at the terrifying sight of the flashing star, a monk of our monastery, named Eilmer, said:

“You have come—you have come, lamented by many mothers. Long ago I saw you, but now I behold you far more terrible, brandishing the ruin of this land.”

For his time he was well instructed in letters, and was advanced in years. In his early youth he had attempted an act of monstrous daring: he had attached wings to his hands and feet by some device or other, so that he might fly in the manner of Daedalus, accepting fable as truth. Catching the breeze from the summit of a tower, he flew a distance of a stadium and more; but the violence of wind and whirlwind, together with consciousness of his rash act, made him tremble and fall. Thereafter he was permanently crippled, with his legs broken. He himself maintained that the cause of his fall was that he had forgotten a tail at the rear.

§ 226. Edward, when dying, displayed a prophecy similar to this, which I shall here relate in anticipation. For after he had lain speechless for two days, on the third day, after sleep, he sighed heavily and deeply and said:

“Almighty God, if what I have seen is not a phantasmal illusion but a true vision, grant me the power to explain it to those standing by—or the contrary.”

His speech immediately became clear:

“I have just seen standing beside me two monks, whom in my youth I had seen long ago in Normandy living most religiously and dying most Christianly.”

They declared themselves messengers of God and brought him this message:

“Since the leading men of England—dukes, bishops, and abbots—are not ministers of God but of the devil, God has, one year and one day after your death, delivered this kingdom into the hand of an enemy; and demons shall roam throughout this whole land.”

When I said that I would reveal these things to the people and promised that, if they repented, they would be delivered—setting before them the example of the Ninevites—they replied: “Neither shall occur: for they will not repent, nor will God have mercy upon them.”

“And when,” I asked, “may the remission of such great calamities be hoped for?”

Then they said: “As though a green tree were cut down in the middle and the severed part carried away from the trunk for the space of three acres, when, without any assistance whatsoever, it is again joined to its own trunk and begins, through the former love of the coalescing sap, both to become covered with flowers and to bear fruit—then at last the remission of such evils may be hoped for.”

[Col. 1207A] § 227. Although the rest feared the truth of this prophecy, Stigand the archbishop then received it with laughter, saying that the old man, under the advance of illness, was raving nonsense. Yet we experience the truth of this prophecy: England has indeed become the dwelling-place of foreigners and the dominion of aliens. Today there is no Englishman who is duke, bishop, or abbot; newcomers consume England’s wealth and vitals, and there is no hope that misery will end. It is time for our narrative, as I promised long ago, to attempt briefly to explain the cause of this evil.

§ 228. King Edward, inclined toward old age, because he himself had begotten no children and saw the sons of Godwine growing powerful, sent to the king of the Huns, asking him to send Edward, the son of his brother Edmund, with all his family. Either he or his sons, he said, would succeed by hereditary right to the kingdom of England; his childlessness ought to be supported by the aid of his kinsmen.

Thus Edward came, but immediately died by fate at St Paul’s in London, leaving three children alive. [Note: [Col. 1207D] “Thus Edward came.” Edward returned to England in 1057 and died in the same year.] He was a man neither active in hand nor honourable in character: Edgar, who, after Harold’s death, was elected king by some and, tossed by the varying sport of fortune, now lives out an almost decrepit old age in obscure rural retirement; Christina, who grew old in the religious habit at Romsey; and Margaret, whom Malcolm, king of the Scots, married in lawful wedlock.

She, fruitful in a numerous offspring, had sons Edgar and Alexander, who ruled in Scotland after their father in unbroken succession. For the elder, Edward, fell in battle with his father; [Note: [Col. 1207D] “Edward in battle,” etc. King Malcolm and his son Edward were killed in A.D. 1093.] while the younger, David, celebrated for gentleness and wisdom, is now reckoned king of Scotland. She also had daughters: Matilda, whom King Henry married in our own age, and Mary, whom Eustace the younger, count of Boulogne, took as wife.

Accordingly, when his kinsman had died, and the hope of his earlier support was dissolved, the king granted William, count of Normandy, the succession to England. [Note: [Col. 1207D] “He granted William, count of Normandy, the succession to England.” Edward, now weighed down with old age, turned his mind to his kinsman William, count of Normandy, and by a fixed declaration ordained that he should succeed him in the kingdom of England. (INGULF, p. 899.) William’s elevation to royal dignity is enveloped in dense obscurity among the annalists.] William was worthy of this favour: an outstanding young man of spirit, who had risen through energetic labour to the highest eminence. Moreover, he was his nearest blood-relative, the son of Robert, son of Richard II, whom we have often said was brother to Emma, Edward’s mother.

Some report that Harold himself was sent by the king to Normandy for this purpose. [Note: [Col. 1207D] “Some report that Harold himself was sent by the king to Normandy for this purpose.” “Edward, king of the English, lacking offspring to succeed him, had formerly sent Robert, archbishop of Canterbury, to Duke William, appointing him heir to the kingdom granted him by God. Then he sent Harold, foremost among all the counts of his dominion in riches, honour, and power, to the duke, that he might do him fealty for his crown and confirm it by oaths in Christian fashion.” (WILLIAM OF JUMIÈGES, *History*, ch. 31.) See also WILLIAM OF POITIERS, year 1065, among the Norman writers.]

Others, privy to a more secret counsel, say that he was unwillingly driven there by the violence of the wind, and that he devised a stratagem to preserve himself there. Since this seems nearer the truth, I shall set it forth. [Note: [Col. 1208D] “Since this seems nearer the truth, I shall set it forth.” e omits *vero* (“truth/indeed”).
