Compare these matters with the Chronicle of Robert of Mont, appended to Sigebert, in Acherius, p. 721.]

Harold had come to his estate at Bosham [Note: [Col. 1208D] Bosham, near Chichester.]. There, to amuse himself, he boarded a fishing vessel; and at first they proceeded farther out to sea in a somewhat extended pleasure-trip. But when a sudden adverse storm arose, he and his companions were forced into the district of Ponthieu. The people of that region, according to a deeply rooted custom of their race, rushed together suddenly from every side. The unarmed were overcome by armed men, the few by the many—which was easy—and offered their hands to manacles and their feet to fetters.

Harold, turning over in his crafty mind a remedy for his plight, sent a man, won over by immense promises, to William. He reported that Harold had been sent to Normandy by the king, so that he might chiefly confirm by his own presence what lesser messengers had stammered out; that he was detained in chains by Guy, count of Ponthieu, and thus prevented from carrying out his instructions; that it was the barbarous and unbridled custom of the region that those who escaped shipwreck at sea should find danger on land; that it befitted a man of so great a name not to leave unpunished the fact that chains had been laid upon one who appealed to his good faith, thereby somewhat diminishing his majesty; and that if ransom were required to free him from captivity, he would gladly pay Count William, but not Guy, who was scarcely a man.

Thus Harold was released at William’s command and was led by Guy himself into Normandy. The count treated him with great distinction, honouring him with the customary elegance of food and clothing. In order both to make him better known and to test his valour, he took him with him on the Breton expedition which he had then happened to undertake. There Harold proved himself in character and in arms, and won the Norman’s affection. To commend himself more highly, he then voluntarily confirmed by oath to William the castle of Dover, which belonged to his own right, and the English kingdom after Edward’s death. Therefore he was honoured with betrothal to William’s daughter, still under age, and with the extent of the whole patrimony, and was regarded as one of the family.

Not much time passed before, after Harold had returned home, the king [Note: [Col. 1208D] “The king,” s. c. e. l.; “King Edward,” a. d. m.] was crowned at London on Christmas Day. [Note: [Col. 1208D] “He was crowned.” It was customary for the king to wear the crown on the solemn feasts—namely Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord—and the archbishop of Canterbury placed it upon his head in the customary manner. (See AELRED OF RIEVAULX, *On the Life of St Edward*.)] There he was struck by illness; and, knowing that he was about to die, he ordered Westminster church to be consecrated on the day of the Holy Innocents. [Note: [Col. 1209D] “Westminster church,” etc. Westminster Abbey was dedicated on 28 December 1065. Aelred of Rievaulx states that the church had been begun some years earlier in fulfilment of a vow made by the king to go to Rome. When he was dissuaded from that pilgrimage, he sent to the pope to obtain a dispensation, which the supreme pontiff granted on condition that, from the sum of money intended for fulfilment of the vow, he should build a monastery in honour of St Peter.]

Thus, full of years and glory, he rendered up his simple spirit to the heavenly kingdom, [Note: [Col. 1209D] “His simple spirit.” The editor of the *Saxon Chronicle* (Rev. John Ingram) suggests that Malmesbury adopted the very mode of lamentation concerning the death of Edward the Confessor: “Here King Edward, lord of the English, sent forth his steadfast soul to Christ, his holy spirit into the kingdom of God.” (*Saxon Chronicle*, year 1065.) King Edward died on Thursday, 5 January 1066, after a reign of twenty-three years, six months, and twenty-seven days.] and was buried in the same church on the day of the Epiphany. He had been the first in England to build it in that style of construction which now almost all emulate at lavish expense.

The lineage of the West Saxons, which had ruled in Britain from Cerdic for five hundred and seventy-one years and from Egbert for two hundred and sixty-one, wholly failed in him as regards kingship. For while the grief for the royal funeral was still fresh, Harold, on the very day of the Epiphany, seized the diadem, having extorted the allegiance of the magnates—although the English say that it had been granted by the king. I think this is asserted more from affection than judgment: that he might transfer his inheritance to the man whose power he had always regarded with suspicion. Yet, lest the truth be concealed, in view of the character he bore, he would have governed the kingdom with prudence and courage had he received it lawfully.

For while Edward lived, he crushed by his own valour whatever wars were raised against him, wishing to display himself before the provincials, panting with a hope that itched for the kingdom. As I said above, he first defeated Griffin, king of the Welsh, in war; then, when Griffin repeatedly attempted to rise again, he deprived him of his head, and appointed as successors two of his own retainers, Griffin’s brothers Blegent and Riwallon, who had earned his favour by their service.

In the same year Tostig sailed from Flanders into the Humber with sixty ships and harassed the districts along the riverbank by piratical raids. But he was vigorously driven out of the province by Edwin and Morcar, brothers of united power, and turned his sails toward Scotland. There he joined forces with Harold Hardrada, king of the Norwegians, [Note: [Col. 1210D] “Harold Harvagre.” Harold, called Fair-Haired (or “of the blond hair”), is often called Hardrada (“the Stern”) in order to distinguish him from Harald Fairhair, who was contemporary with Alfred the Great.] who was planning to attack England with three hundred ships.

Thus both, with shields locked, ravaged Northumbria. Falling upon the brothers, still idle after their recent victory and fearing nothing less than such brigandage, they defeated them and shut them up within York. Harold, upon receiving the news, hastened there with all the forces of the kingdom. A great battle was joined, with both peoples striving with their utmost strength. The English gained the upper hand and drove the Norwegians into flight. But the victory over so great and so many men was delayed for many hours—something perhaps posterity will find difficult to believe—by a single Norwegian. For he stood at the entrance of the bridge called Stamford Bridge [Note: [Col. 1210D] “Stamford Bridge.” The battle at Stamford Bridge began on 25 September 1066.], killed one, then another, then many of our side, and barred them all from crossing.

He was invited to surrender, so that a man of such strength might experience the Englishmen’s abundant clemency; but he laughed at those inviting him, repeatedly rebuking them with a grim expression and calling them men of feeble spirit because they could not resist one man. Therefore, since no one ventured nearer—for they judged it unwise to engage hand-to-hand with one who, despairing of life, had expended every means of saving it—one of the king’s retainers hurled an iron javelin at him from afar. While he swaggered and sported in triumph, less cautious because of that very confidence, he was pierced by it [Note: [Col. 1210D] “By it,” a. c. d. e.; “which,” s. l.] and yielded the victory to the English.

The army immediately crossed freely and struck the scattered Norwegians from behind. King Hardrada and Tostig were killed; the king’s son, [Note: [Col. 1210D] “The king’s son.” Apparently named Edmund. (*Saxon Chronicle*).] together with all the ships, was mercifully sent home. Harold, proud of his triumphal success, did not deem his fellow-soldiers worthy of any share of the booty. Consequently many slipped away wherever they could and deserted the king when he set out for the battle of Hastings. Apart from paid and mercenary soldiers, he had very few men from the provinces.

Thus, after nine months and some days of a kingdom obtained by craft, he was outmanoeuvred and defeated by William on 14 October 1066. This was an easy matter of war, indeed, but accomplished by God’s hidden and wondrous counsel: afterwards the English never breathed freely in liberty through a common battle, as though all England’s strength had fallen with Harold. He certainly could—and ought—to have paid the penalty for his perfidy, even by the most inactive of men.

Nor in saying this do I detract from the valour of the Normans, toward whom I have loyalty both by race and by benefits received. But those who inflate the number of the English and diminish their courage seem to me mistaken; while intending to praise the Normans, they bespatter them with disgrace. For it is plainly a distinguished praise of a most unconquered people to have defeated men whom numbers encumbered and cowardice made afraid. On the contrary, the English were few and most ready of hand: renouncing love of their bodies, they laid down their lives for their homeland. But since these matters call for a more careful account, I shall now end the second book, so that both my zeal for dictating and the zeal of others for reading may recover strength.

## Prologue to the Third Book

[Col. 1211A] Both Normans and English have written about King William, prompted by different causes. The former have been driven to excessive praises, extolling good and evil alike to the heavens; the latter, because of national hostilities, have torn their lord to pieces with foul reproaches. But since I draw blood from both peoples, I shall preserve this balance in my treatment: deeds well done, so far as I have been able to know them, I shall openly set forth without disguise; [Note: [Col. 1211C] “Set forth,” a. s. d. e. l.; “bring forth,” c.] deeds wrongly done, so far as knowledge suffices, I shall touch upon lightly [Note: [Col. 1211D] “Lightly,” a. s. d. e. l.; “gently,” c.] and, as it were, in passing; [Note: [Col. 1211D] “As it were,” a. s. c. d. e2. l. m.; omitted in e1.] so that history may not be condemned as false, nor may I stamp with censorious reproach one whose deeds almost all can, if not be praised, at least certainly be excused.

Accordingly, I shall willingly and deliberately narrate such matters concerning him as may encourage the sluggish, serve as an example to the energetic, be useful to those now living, and afford pleasure to those who come after. Yet I shall not spend much time prolonging matters which bring profit to no one—rather, disgust to the reader and hatred to the writer. There are more than enough men who tear apart the deeds of the good with their native molar teeth. My chosen field is to minimize evils, as far as I can do so without loss to truth, and not to praise good deeds with too windy a voice. [Note: [Col. 1211D] “Too,” a. s. c. e. l.; “less,” d.] Those who are fair judges of this moderation, I think, will pronounce me neither timid nor inelegant.

My pen will observe this rule not only with William, but also with his two sons: nothing shall be said excessively, nothing except truthfully. The first did little worthy of praise except during the first days of his reign; throughout his life he purchased the favour of soldiers at the cost of his subjects. The second, more obedient to his father than to his brother, maintained an unconquered spirit amid adversity and prosperity. If you consider his campaigns, you will not know whether he was more cautious or more daring; if you consider his fortunes, you will hesitate whether he was more fortunate or more in need of good fortune. But there will be time for such questions when [Note: [Col. 1211D] “When,” a. c. d. e. l.; “so that,” s.] the reader judges. Now, as I am about to begin the third volume, I think I have done enough to make him attentive and receptive; he himself will kindly persuade himself to be well disposed.

# Book Three: On the Coming of the Normans into England

[Col. 1211C] § 229. Robert, [Note: [Col. 1211D] Robert, the second son of Richard II. Robert I. See § 178, notes 46 and 48.] the second son of Richard II, after he had held the duchy of Normandy gloriously for seven years, resolved to go to Jerusalem. At that time he had a seven-year-old son by a concubine. He had happened to see her dancing in the choruses, and could not refrain from joining her in bed that night; thereafter he loved her alone and for some time kept her in the place of a lawful wife. The boy was born to her in A.D. 1028 and called William after the name of his great-grandfather.

His mother’s dream portended his future greatness: she had seen her entrails stretched and spread throughout all Normandy and England. At the very moment when, the confinement having opened, the little boy was brought forth into life and touched the ground, he filled both hands with the rushes used to keep the dust of the floor in place, gripping tightly what he had seized. This sight was shown to the women, who shrieked with joyful applause; the midwife too cried out under a favourable omen that the boy would become king.

[Col. 1212B] § 230. When therefore everything had been made ready to provide the supplies for the journey to Jerusalem, [Note: [Col. 1211D] “For the journey to Jerusalem.” Robert set out for Jerusalem in 1035. (BOUQ. XI, 120.)] a council of nobles was summoned at Fécamp. There, by his father’s command, all swore fealty and allegiance to William. [Note: [Col. 1211D] “Count Gilbert was appointed guardian of the boy.” This too is related by Orderic Vitalis: “He left his duchy, which he would not return to, to William, a boy of eight years; and entrusted him to his kinsman Alan, count of the Bretons.” And again: “The nobles of Normandy rebelled against the infant William, who, when his father set out on the journey to Jerusalem with Count Drogo, was only eight years old and had been entrusted by his father to the guardianship of his kinsman Alan, count of the Bretons.”] Count Gilbert was appointed guardian of the boy; the oversight of the guardian was assigned to Henry, king of the Franks. [Note: [Col. 1212D] Henry I.]

Once Robert had advanced upon the journey he had undertaken, all the Normans, with a united shield-wall, protected their homeland each through his own fortifications and revered their little lord out of affection. This loyalty lasted until the report of Robert’s death; when it spread everywhere among the nations, their affection changed with fate. At once each began fortifying his own towns, raising towers, gathering grain, and seeking pretexts for planning as quickly as possible a rupture with the boy.

Meanwhile he grew up in safety—not, I think, without the help of God, who foresaw that he would rule over so great an empire—while almost Gilbert alone defended justice and right by his arms. The rest were driven by partisan ambitions. But after Gilbert was murdered by his cousin Ralph, [Note: [Col. 1213C] “After Gilbert was murdered by his cousin Ralph.” “Count Gilbert of Eu, son of Count Geoffrey, the shrewd and strong guardian of the boy William, yet his lord, was killed one morning while riding and talking with his godfather Wacelin of Pont-Erchenfrid, suspecting no evil, together with Fulcoius son of Geroius. This evil was done through the treacherous instigations of Ralph of Wacy, son of Archbishop Robert, by the cruel hands of Odo the Fat and the bold Robert son of Geroius.” (WILLIAM OF JUMIÈGES, *History*, book VII, ch. 2.)] there was slaughter everywhere and fire everywhere. The country, once most illustrious, ulcerated by internal dissensions, was divided at the whim of brigands, so that it might justly utter the complaint: [Note: [Col. 1213D] “Woe to the land whose king is a child!” (Ecclesiastes 10:16).] “Woe to the land whose king is a child!”

But as soon as he was old enough, he received the insignia of knighthood from the king of the Franks and raised his countrymen’s hopes for peace. The sower of discord was a certain Guy, Burgundian on his father’s side and grandson of Richard II through a daughter. He had run about in childhood with William, and they were then likewise pressing upon the threshold of adolescence together. Shared upbringing had produced familiarity, and familiarity friendships. [Note: [Col. 1213D] “Friendships,” a. c. d. e. l.; “friendship,” s.] Moreover, William had given him the castles of Brionne and Vernon, judging that nothing should be withheld on account of kinship. [Note: [Col. 1213D] “Kinship,” a. c. d. e. l.; “blood-relationship,” s.]

Forgetting these things, the Burgundian, inventing accusations to make it seem that he acted with justification, withdrew his allegiance from the count. It would be lengthy and unnecessary to pursue the deeds done on both sides and the castles taken. For treachery had found him allies in Nigel, viscount of the Cotentin; Ranulf, viscount of Bayeux; [Note: [Col. 1213D] “Of Bayeux,” a. c. d. e. l.; “of Tembayeux,” s.] and Haimo Dentatus, [Note: [Col. 1213D] “Haimo Dentatus.” A lord of Thorigny in Normandy, from whom the house of Duredent or Duerden, which settled in England, probably derives.] grandfather of Robert, who in our time proved to be an occupier of many estates in England. With them this most lawless robber ranged throughout Normandy, drawn on by a vain hope of the county.

Necessity summoned forth the king, the guardian, to help the boy when his cause had become desperate. Recalling his father's goodwill, because Robert had raised him to royal power by his favour, he fell upon the rebels at Val-des-Dunes. [Note: [Col. 1213D] “Val-des-Dunes.” “This place, now seemingly unknown, differed from Val-le-Dun, a place in the district of Caux and the diocese of Rouen, situated upon the Tala or Dune river, commonly Le Val-Dun. It was located on the river Olin in the county or district of Hiémois and in the diocese of Sées.” (BOUQ. XI, 178, note.) The battle at Val-des-Dunes is assigned to 1047.] Many thousands of them were killed there; many were swallowed up by the greed of the river Orne [Note: [Col. 1214C] “Of the river Olne”: the Orne.], because, hemmed into a narrow place, they spurred their horses to cross its whirlpools.

Guy barely escaped and withdrew to Brionne. Driven thence by William, unable to bear the disgrace, he went of his own accord to Burgundy, his native soil. Yet his restless mind found no rest even there: driven out by the count of that province, his brother William [Note: [Col. 1214C] William, duke of Burgundy, surnamed the Great.], whom he had attacked by plots, he met an unknown end. Nigel and Ralph were received into allegiance. Haimo was slain in battle; his remarkable ferocity is praised because he unhorsed the king himself. For this he was killed by the bodyguards rushing upon him; by the king’s command, in recognition of this extraordinary feat of courage, he was splendidly buried.

King Henry received the recompense of this service from his Norman lord when, against Geoffrey Martel at Moulin-Herle, a castle in the Angevin region, he was aided with the greatest force. William had now grown to manly strength; alone he was feared by men older and more numerous than himself, alone he would expose himself to dangers, alone—or with a few men—he would leap upon the densest ranks of the opposing side. Therefore from that expedition he carried away a proof of praised courage and the height of favour with the king, so that Henry, as if with a father’s counsel, often warned him not to despise his life by rushing into dangers: it was an honour to the Franks, a safeguard to Normandy, and an example to both peoples.

§ 231. At that time Geoffrey, surnamed Martel (“the Hammer”), was count of Anjou. [p. 395] [Note: [Col. 1214C] Geoffrey surnamed Martel. Geoffrey II, son of Fulk III, count of Anjou, whom he succeeded in A.D. 1040.] He had appropriated this surname for himself [Note: [Col. 1214C] “He had appropriated.” a. s. c. e. l.; “had appropriated the name,” d.] because he seemed, by a certain good fortune, to crush all who opposed him. Indeed, he took his own lord, [Note: [Col. 1214D] The count of Poitou: William IV, 1029–1038.] the count of Poitou, [Note: [Col. 1214D] “He captured him in open war.” “In the year 1033 Geoffrey Martel captured William, count of Poitou, whose wife—his [stepmother] Agnes—he had previously married.” (From the Chronicle of St Michael-in-Peril-of-the-Sea; in Labbe, vol. I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 350.) The Chronicle of St Albinus of Anjou likewise assigns the year 1033 to this battle, but it seems more correctly to be assigned to 1034. (*L’art de vérifier les dates*, II, p. 355.)] in open war (A.D. 1034), bound him in iron chains, and brought him to accept disgraceful terms of peace: he was to surrender Bordeaux and its neighbouring towns, and pay an annual tribute for the rest. [Col. 1214C] But he, it is believed, owing to the injury of his irons and the scarcity of food, was released by the boon of a timely death, after three days, from everlasting disgrace. [Note: [Col. 1214D] “But he … was released.” The count of Poitou endured captivity for about three and a half years, was ransomed by his wife Eustachia, but survived his release by only three days. The authors of *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, in confirmation of the latter opinion, adduce Malmesbury, whom they cite under the name of the Continuator of Bede.]

Then Martel, so that no element of shamelessness might be lacking, married the dead man’s stepmother, receiving his brothers into guardianship until they should be capable of governing the principality. Soon, having entered the territory of Theobald, count of Blois, [Note: [Col. 1215D] “He besieged Theobald of Blois.” “In the year 1044 Geoffrey Martel captured Count Theobald of Tours and extorted from him the city of Tours.” (From the Chronicle of St Michael-in-Peril-of-the-Sea.) See also the Chronicle of Anjou in Labbe, vol. I, *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 257.] he besieged the city of Tours. He involved Theobald himself, when attempting to bring aid to his citizens, in a share of his misfortune; for Theobald, once captured [Note: [Col. 1215D] “Theobald,” c. d. e.; omitted in a. s. l.], shut up in prison, renounced the city for himself and all his heirs for the future. [p. 396]

Who can describe the shameful misery of the man? For the ambition of however brief a life, he deprived his successors forever of the lordship of so great a city. Yet we are for the most part harsher judges of others than we know how to counsel ourselves, should we perhaps be caught in such circumstances. Thus Martel, swollen by the increase of such great strength, [Col. 1215B] also harassed the Norman count through possession of the castle of Alençon, [Note: [Col. 1215D] Alençon.] whose inhabitants were inclined to treachery. Angered by this injury, the Norman repaid like with like; and he surrounded Domfront, [Note: [Col. 1215D] Domfront. See note c, Bouquet XI, p. 178.] then belonging to the count of Anjou, with a siege. Without delay Geoffrey, warned by the complaints of the besieged, flew to the scene, attended by an innumerable host of soldiers.

When news of his arrival was received, William sent Roger of Montgomery [Note: [Col. 1215D] Roger of Montgomery. He was the son of Hugh of Montgomery and his wife Joceline, daughter of Thorold of Pont-Audemer by Weva, sister of Gunnora, who was the Conqueror’s great-grandmother. He later commanded the centre division at the battle of Hastings and became governor of Normandy. William the Conqueror gave him the earldoms of Arundel and Shrewsbury. For fuller information, see Sir Henry Ellis’s Introduction to *Domesday*, vol. I, p. 479.] and William son of Osbern [Note: [Col. 1216D] William son of Osbern. William FitzOsbern of Crépon, steward of Normandy, was kinsman of the Conqueror, by whom, after England was subdued, he was created earl of Hereford. In Domesday Book this nobleman is described as Count William. For accounts of his death abroad in 1071, see Orderic Vitalis, p. 536, and Malmesbury, below, § 256.] to scout. In the eagerness of youth they covered many miles in a short time; and, seeing Martel riding, they reported their lord’s boldness to him. Martel, on the other hand, raged and uttered monstrous threats: on the following day [Note: [Col. 1216D] “On the following day,” s. c. e. l.; “after three days,” a. d.] he would come there, he said, and show the world [Col. 1215C] how much the Angevin surpassed the Norman in arms. With extraordinary arrogance, he also described the colour of his horse and the insignia of the armour which he would wear.

The scouts, [p. 397] declaring no less proudly the same things concerning William, returned and inflamed their countrymen for the contest. I have recounted this in sequence in order that Martel’s arrogance might be made plain to readers. Yet at that time, attempting nothing of his customary boldness, before they came to blows he turned his back. When this was heard, the men of Alençon surrendered, having stipulated safety of limb; afterwards the men of Domfront followed the more fortunate standard.

§ 232. In later years William, count of Arques, [Note: [Col. 1216D] William, count of Arques. He was the son of Richard II, duke of Normandy, by his third wife Papia. Compare William of Jumièges, book VII, chapter 20, concerning the rebellion of which Malmesbury speaks.] William’s uncle but illegitimate, rebelled. From the very beginning of the duchy he had been unfaithful and deceitful; for during the siege of Domfront he had slipped away secretly, and had often disclosed the hidden purposes of his heart. Therefore William had entrusted the security of the castle [Col. 1216A] to certain men whom he falsely believed faithful. But the count, by the craft in which he was skilled, giving much and promising more, drew these same men to his side. Having thus gained the fortress, he declared war upon his lord.

William, in his usual fashion, besieged Arques with the greatest vigour, though his friends advised against it; he openly declared that robbers would dare nothing if they came within his sight. Nor did the promise lack fulfilment. For more than three hundred soldiers, who had gone out to forage and plunder, at almost the sight of him alone took refuge within the fortifications.

The duke, wishing to settle the matter without bloodshed, strengthened the castle opposite Arques [Col. 1216B] and turned to other wars which pressed more urgently. He also knew that the king of the French, long hostile to him through some quarrel I know not what, was coming to assist the besieged. For reasons of prudent restraint, [p. 398] though he seemed to have the more just cause, [Note: [Col. 1216D] “He avoided deciding the matter with him by the sword.” On this point the editors of the *Recueil des Historiens de la France* say: “For before he could join battle with King Henry, William ought to renounce his homage and fealty, which could indeed be done because of the king’s wrongdoing.”] he avoided deciding the matter with the sword against one to whom he was bound both by oath and by obligation of aid.

He nevertheless left some leading men to delay the royal attack. Caught in an ambush by their craft, he bitterly lamented to see Isembard, count of Ponthieu, struck down before his eyes, and Hugh Pardulf captured. Not long afterwards, when the king had returned to beloved France because affairs had gone badly, the count of Arques, wasted by hunger and scarcely clinging to his bones, agreed to surrender. [Col. 1216C] His life and limbs were spared—as an example of clemency and a proof of skill.

During this siege, the people of the castle called Moulins, in youthful recklessness, went over to the king’s side at the instigation of one Walter. A considerable force of soldiers was stationed there, under Guy, brother of the count of Poitou. For some days Guy diligently performed the duties of war; but as the report of the victory at Arques spread, he escaped into France, and no slight increase thereby accrued to the duke’s glory.

§ 233. Nor did King Henry yield himself to idleness without grumbling that his armies had been made a mockery by William. Having therefore gathered all his strength and divided his forces in two, he flooded all Normandy. He himself led whatever troops there were from the part of Celtic Gaul [Col. 1217A] [Note: [Col. 1217C] “Gaul,” c. d. e. l. 1; “Galicia,” a. s. l. 2.] lying between the rivers Garonne and Seine; and he placed his brother Odo [Note: [Col. 1217C] Odo his brother. See § 187, note.] over the people of [p. 399] Belgic Gaul, [Note: [Col. 1217C] Belgic Gaul. Pomponius Mela says: “From the Garonne to the Seine are the Celts; from there to the Rhine, the Belgians”; Pliny, however, says: “From the Seine to the Scheldt.” Ptolemy, Orosius, and others describe the boundaries of Belgic Gaul as follows: “On the north, the British Ocean; on the east, the River Rhine, or the Adula and Jura mountains; on the southeast, the Pennine Alps; on the south, part of the province of Narbonensis; on the west, the River Seine and Lyonnaise Gaul.”] which lies between the Rhine and the Seine.

William in the same fashion divided his own men with all the spirit he could, walking gradually about near the king’s camp, which was already being pitched in the district of Évreux. Thus he neither gave the king an opportunity to fight at close quarters [Note: [Col. 1217D] “Of fighting,” a. s. c. d. e. 2. l.; “by fighting,” e. 1.] nor allowed the province to be ravaged before his face. His commanders—Robert, count of Eu; Hugh of Gournay; Hugh of Montfort; and William Crispin—took their stand under hostile standards against Odo at the castle called Mortemer. [Note: [Col. 1217D] Mortemer. The interpolator of William of Jumièges assigns the celebrated battle at Mortemer to the year 1054.]

Odo, swollen with confidence in the number of his soldiers, did not delay battle. He dared resist for a while, but soon, unable to withstand the Norman attack, [Col. 1217B] he exposed his back in flight, the first to inaugurate the omen of rout. There Guy, count of Ponthieu, while too eagerly pursuing vengeance for his brother, was captured and shuddered at the fatal hand which seemed to pursue his family. Many others too were taken: men eminent in deeds [Note: [Col. 1217D] “In deeds,” d. e. 1; “in wealth,” s. e. 2. l. 2.] and proud of their ancestors’ birth.

William learned of this success from those arriving [Note: [Col. 1217D] “Those arriving,” c. d. e.; “those coming,” a. s. l.] and had it proclaimed around the king’s tents in the depth of night. On hearing it, the king, after spending a few days in Normandy, fled back to France. Not long afterwards, messengers passing to and fro, peace was agreed: the royal captives were to be released, and the count was to claim by lawful right what had been taken, or was to be taken, from Martel.

§ 234. It would be long and unnecessary to recount [Col. 1217C] how great were the disputes between them and how William always gained the upper hand. Why mention that, with an inestimable presumption of courage, he never deigned to attack his opponent suddenly or except on a day announced beforehand, [p. 400] scorning by greatness of spirit the custom of our age?

I pass over, too, the fact that, when friendship was again broken, [Note: [Col. 1217D] King Henry, etc. King Henry entered Normandy for the third time in the year 1058.] King Henry entered Normandy and advanced through the district of Hiesmois [Note: [Col. 1217D] “Hiesmois,” a. d. e.; “Exmes,” s. l.; “Exmes,” c.] as far as the River Dives, boasting that only the ocean hindered [Col. 1218A] his onward advance. But William, seeing himself oppressively pressed because of the king’s breach of faith, at last shook the weapons of a courage conscious of itself. He cut down the royal forces around the river—for a party had crossed the ford shortly before, on hearing of his arrival—with such slaughter that France thereafter feared nothing more than to provoke Norman ferocity. [Note: [Col. 1217D] “Had feared,” s. d. e. 1; “might fear,” a. c. l. e. 2.]

The hastened death of Henry [Note: [Col. 1217D] Death of Henry: 4 August, A.D. 1060.] ended their quarrels, and not long afterwards that of Martel. [Note: [Col. 1217D] Martel. Geoffrey Martel died on 14 November 1060. “In the same year, moreover, 1060, King Henry died on the Nativity of St John; and my uncle Geoffrey, on the third day after the feast of St Martin, rested in a good end.” (From a fragment of the *History of Anjou*, by Fulk, count of Anjou; in Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 233.)]

As he died, the king entrusted the guardianship of his very young son Philip to Baldwin, count of Flanders. Baldwin was equally admirable for faithfulness and wisdom: grey-haired though his limbs were still in their early vigour; moreover exalted by marriage to the king’s sister. His daughter Matilda had long since married William: a woman in our time, [Col. 1218B] a singular model of prudence [Note: [Col. 1218C] “Of prudence,” a. s. c. d. e. 2. l.; omitted in e. 1.] and summit of modesty. Thus, as mediator between ward and son-in-law, he restrained by sound policy the disturbances of dukes and provincial lords.

§ 235. But since the occasion of Martel has presented itself so often, [p. 401] I shall briefly run through the genealogy [Note: [Col. 1218C] Counts of Anjou. On the counts of Anjou consult the *Deeds of the Consuls of Anjou*, by a Benedictine monk of the Greater Monastery. (In Achery, vol. III.)] of the counts of Anjou, insofar as [Note: [Col. 1218D] “Insofar as,” c. e; “the genealogy which,” a. s. d. l.] our narrator’s memory reached, with the aforesaid excuse for this digression. [Note: [Col. 1218D] “With the aforesaid excuse for this digression,” a. c. d. e. l.; omitted in s.]

The elder Fulk [Note: [Col. 1218D] The elder Fulk: Fulk III, surnamed Nerra or Niger, “of Jerusalem” and “of the Palm.” He succeeded his father Geoffrey I in 987.] governed that county for many years, until old age; he did many things ably and many nobly. There is only one act for which I have heard him blamed: he caused Count Herbert of Maine, enticed by a promise of the city of Saintes, to be seized by officers in the midst of a conference and ensnared by such terms as pleased him.

In other respects holy and upright, he yielded the principality during his lifetime, in his very last years, to his often-mentioned son Geoffrey [Note: [Col. 1218D] Geoffrey: Geoffrey II, surnamed Martel.] [Col. 1218C]. Geoffrey behaved—monstrously!—with such cruelty toward the provincials and with such arrogance toward the very man who had conferred honour upon him, that, when ordered to lay down office and authority, he arrogated so much to himself that he took arms against his father.

Then the old man’s blood, now cold and exhausted, grew hot with anger; and within a few days he so crushed his son, who attacked him with youthful insolence, by maturer counsel that Geoffrey, carrying a saddle on his back [Note: [Col. 1218D] “Carrying a saddle on his back.” “To carry a saddle on one’s back was a punishment than which none was more disgraceful. See another example in William of Jumièges, Du Chesne, p. 259. Du Cange, under *Sella*, most justly supposes that the insult arises from the offender’s acknowledging himself to be a beast and wholly delivering himself into the offended party’s power.” (Sharpe, 306.)] [Note: [Col. 1218D] “Carrying,” c. e; “carrying forth,” a. s. d. l.] for several miles, prostrated himself with the burden at his father’s feet. [Col. 1219A]

The old man, in whom the ancient spirit still throbbed, rose up and struck the prostrate man with his foot, repeating [p. 402] three or four times: “You are conquered—at last conquered.” Yet the defeated man retained courage, and noble courage too, enough to answer: “Conquered by you alone, father, because you are my father [Note: [Col. 1219C] “Father,” a. s. c. e. l.; “my father,” d.]; by all others I am unconquered.”

This reply softened the swelling heart of the father; and, soothing the shame of his offspring with paternal affection, he restored him to the principality. He admonished him to conduct himself more maturely, saying that the fortunes and peace of his subjects were his honour before foreigners and his advantage among his own people.

That same year the veteran, discharged from worldly service, now thinking of provision for his soul, went to Jerusalem. There, by two servants compelled under oath to do what he commanded, he was dragged naked in public to [Col. 1219B] the Lord’s sepulchre, while Turks watched. One had twisted a wooden rope [Note: [Col. 1219D] “Rope,” a. s. d. e; “beam,” c; “rake,” l.] about his neck; the other drove his stripped back with whips. [Note: [Col. 1219D] “With whips,” a. c. d. e. l.; “with scourges,” s.] Amid this he cried: “Receive, Lord, wretched Fulk, your perjurer, your fugitive. Deign, Lord Jesus Christ, to receive this confessing soul.”

Yet he did not then obtain what he desired. Rather, returning home peacefully, he died after some years. [Note: [Col. 1219D] “He died.” Fulk III died at Metz, 21 June 1040.] The preceding narrative has shown the headlong boldness of his son Geoffrey. As he died, [Note: [Col. 1219D] “As he died.” Geoffrey Martel died leaving no offspring by any of his three wives.] he entrusted his inheritance to Geoffrey, his sister’s son; [Note: [Col. 1219D] Geoffrey, son of his sister. Geoffrey III, surnamed the Bearded, was son of Geoffrey Ferreol, count of Château-Landon, and Ermengarde, daughter of Fulk Nerra.] but he could not transfer to him the resourcefulness of the age.

For Geoffrey was a young man of simple character, accustomed rather to pray in churches than to handle arms. He provoked the contempt of the men [Col. 1219C] of that region, who did not know how to live quietly. Therefore, with the whole land exposed to brigands, [p. 403] his brother Fulk voluntarily seized the duchy. Fulk, called Rechin, [Note: [Col. 1219D] Fulk called Rechin: Fulk IV, also called “the Quarrelsome.”] because, often raging against his brother’s simplicity, he finally deprived him of his honour and confined him under perpetual guard, [Note: [Col. 1219D] “Simplicity,” a. s. c. d. e. 2. l.; “supplication,” e. 1.] had a wife [Note: [Col. 1219D] “He had a wife.” Her name was Bertrada. Fulk married her in 1089, while his second and third wives, whom he had repudiated, were still alive.] who, attracted by the itch for a loftier title, left him and married Philip, king of the French.

Forgetful of the saying,

> Majesty and love do not agree well, nor do they dwell in one abode,

Philip burned with so great a passion for her that, although he desired to command everyone else, he bore with equanimity her commanding him. In short, he endured for several years being pointed out by everyone as if a fool, [Col. 1220A] and being excommunicated by the whole Christian world because of his lust for her.

Fulk’s sons were Geoffrey and Fulk. Geoffrey, inheriting the surname Martel, enlarged its renown by his own labours. He established such peace and tranquillity throughout those lands as no one had seen [Note: [Col. 1220C] “No one had seen,” a. s. d. l.; omitted in c. e.] and no one will see. Therefore he was killed by the plots of his own people, and paid the price for the distinction of outstanding integrity.

Fulk, succeeding to the government, is still among the living; [Note: [Col. 1220D] “Fulk in government,” etc. Therefore Fulk IV was at that time still governing the county of Anjou. From this it consequently follows that Malmesbury completed this work before 1129, the year in which Geoffrey le Bel, better known as Geoffrey Plantagenet, son of Fulk, became count of Anjou.] perhaps I shall speak of him in connection with the time of King Henry. Now I shall explain what remains concerning William.

§ 236. When he had settled the civil dissension through much campaigning, William, pursuing in his mind a matter of greater glory, intended to recover [p. 404] lands once appendages of Normandy, [Note: [Col. 1220D] Appendages of Normandy. “In the year 931, the Bretons, situated at the extremity of Gaul, rose against the Normans to whom they were subject and were repressed by William Longsword.” (From the little book of Hugh, monk of Fleury.) Bouquet XI, 181, note a.] which had grown unruly through long-established practice: I mean the county of Maine [Col. 1220B] and Brittany.

Maine, long ago burned by Martel and deprived of its lord Hugh, [Note: [Col. 1220D] “Long ago,” a. s. d. e. l.; “formerly,” c.] had recently recovered somewhat under Herbert, Hugh’s son. [Note: [Col. 1220D] “Hugh,” a. s. c. d. e. 2. l.; omitted in e. 1.] To make himself safer against the Angevin, Herbert had committed himself to William’s hands, swearing an oath of fealty to him. He had also sought and betrothed William’s daughter; but before she was old enough for marriage, Herbert died of illness. He named William as his heir, having bound the citizens by oath not to receive another; they would have, if they wished, a gentle and worthy lord, but, if they did not, an uncompromising exactor of his right.

After Herbert’s death the men of Maine inclined rather toward Walter of Mantes, to whom Hugh’s sister [Col. 1220C] was married. At last, though late, they came to their senses and received William (A.D. 1065), repeatedly instructed by grievous losses.

This was when Harold, driven unwillingly to Normandy by an adverse wind, arrived. As said above, [Note: [Col. 1220D] As stated above, § 228.] William took him on the Breton expedition, wishing to test his hand; and also, with a more calculated purpose, to display his own equipment, so that Harold might see how greatly a Norman sword surpassed English battle-axes.

Alan was then count there, a man in the bloom of youth and outstanding in strength. He had bound his uncle Eudo [Note: [Col. 1220D] “He had bound,” a. c. d. e. l.; “had conquered,” s.] and performed many noble deeds. He not only did not fear William but even provoked him. William, however, claiming Brittany as hereditary soil, because Charles had given it to Rollo with his daughter Gisla, [p. 405] [Col. 1221A] [Note: [Col. 1221D] “With his daughter,” c. d. e.; “with his own daughter,” a. s. l.] quickly brought matters about so that Alan came of his own accord and humbly surrendered himself and his possessions.

But because I shall say little else of Brittany, I shall insert here briefly a certain miracle which occurred about those days in the city of Nantes.

## CONCERNING TWO CLERICAL COMPANIONS

§ 237. In that city were two clerics, priests though not yet of age to bear the weight of years. They had obtained that office from the local bishop more by entreaty than by merit of good life. In the end, the pitiable death of one taught the survivor how both of them had previously rushed headlong toward hell.

Yet in literary learning they were so instructed that they owed little or nothing to the arts. From the earliest rudiments of childhood they had rivalled one another in the delightful duties of friendship, so that, according to the comic poet’s saying, [Note: [Col. 1221D] Saying of the comic poet: Terence, *Andria*, IV.1.] “with hands and feet striving, they would even, if need were, risk their lives for each other.”

One day, then, having gained a mind freer [Note: [Col. 1221D] “Mind,” a. s. c. d. e. 2; omitted in e. 1.] from outward cares, they uttered in a private room reflections of this kind. They had exercised their minds for many years, now in letters and now in worldly gains [Note: [Col. 1221D] “Gains,” a. c. d. l.; “cares,” s.], but had not satisfied them; their efforts had tended more toward crookedness than rectitude. Meanwhile, that bitter day was gradually approaching which would break the inextricable bond of their fellowship in life. They must therefore provide in good time that the loyalty which had bound them together while living might accompany the first to die to the shades below.

They agreed that whichever of them died first should, without doubt, appear to the survivor, whether asleep or awake, within thirty [p. 406] [Col. 1221C] days. If this happened, he would teach him that, according to the Platonists, death does not extinguish the spirit but sends it forth from prison to God, its source; if not, they must yield to the Epicurean school, who think that the soul, released from the body, vanishes into the air and dissipates into the breezes.

Thus having pledged and received their promise, they constantly renewed the compact in daily conversations. Not much time passed, and behold: death, suddenly threatening, violently drew an unwilling breath from one of them. The other remained and, seriously considering his companion’s promise, awaited his imminent arrival. For thirty days he fed the winds with vain expectation. When these had elapsed, despairing, he had turned his leisure to other affairs when suddenly, while awake [Col. 1221D] and engaged in some task, his companion stood before him, bloodless in face, as those dying commonly are when the soul departs.

Then the one who had died first addressed the living man, who was silent: “Do you recognize me?” he said.

“I recognize you,” he replied, “and I am disturbed not so much by your unfamiliar presence as I wonder at your long absence.”

When the other had excused the delay of his coming, he finally said: “At last, released from the bonds of delay, I have come. But this visit will be useful to you, if you choose, my friend, and wholly fruitless to me; for after the sentence has been pronounced and proclaimed, I have been assigned to everlasting punishments.” [Col. 1222A]

The living man promised, for the rescue of the dead, to spend all he possessed on monasteries and the poor, and to continue day and night in fasts and prayers. But the dead man said: “What I have said is fixed, because God’s judgments are without repentance. I have been plunged into the sulphurous abyss of hell. There, while the firmament turns the stars, while the sea beats the shores, I shall be rolled in punishment for my sins. The severity of an inflexible sentence remains, [p. 407] [Note: [Col. 1221D] “Severity,” a. c. d. e. l.; “eternal severity,” s.] devising eternal and innumerable kinds of torments, even if the whole world should now seek remedies strong enough to prevail.

“And that you may experience some part of my innumerable punishments”—he stretched out a hand dripping with a festering sore—“behold,” he said, “one of the least of them. Does it seem light to you?” [Col. 1222B]

When the living man said that it seemed light, the dead man bent his fingers into his palm and cast three drops of the flowing corruption upon him. Two touched his temples and one his forehead, penetrating skin and flesh like a burning cautery and making a hole large enough to hold a nut. As he testified to the greatness of his pain with a cry, the dead man said: “This shall remain in you [Note: [Col. 1222D] “In you,” e. 1; “for you,” a. s. c. d. e. 2. l.] as long as you live: a grave proof of my torments and, unless you neglect it, a singular reminder of your salvation.

“Therefore, while it is permitted, while wrath wavers, while God’s mercy waits in suspense, [Note: [Col. 1222D] “God’s mercy waits,” c. e; “God waits for you,” a. d. l.; “God awaits you,” s.] change your clothing, change your disposition: become a monk at Redon, under Saint Melaine.”

When the living man did not wish to answer these words, the other fixed him with a piercing gaze. “If you hesitate, wretch,” he said, “to convert, read these letters.” [Col. 1222C] As he spoke, he opened his hand, inscribed with grim characters. In them Satan and all the retinue of hell sent thanks from Tartarus to the whole clerical body, because, while the clerics lacked nothing for their own pleasures, they permitted through neglect of preaching so great a number of subject souls to descend to hell as no former age had ever seen.

With these words, the sight of the speaker disappeared. The listener distributed all his possessions among churches and the poor, went to Saint Melaine, and by his sudden conversion [Note: [Col. 1222D] “Conversion,” c. d. e.; “conversion and distinguished manner of life,” a. s. l.] admonished all who heard and saw him to say: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.”

408 §238. I have not regretted inserting these matters for the benefit of readers; now I shall speak of William. For since I have briefly, and, as I think, not uselessly, reviewed his deeds during the thirty years in which he acted merely as count in Normandy, the order of time now demands a different beginning to my narrative: that, concerning his kingship, so far as our inquiry has been able to penetrate, I may expose falsehood and declare truth.

King Edward had died by fate. England wavered in uncertain favour, undecided to which ruler she should commit herself—Harold, William, or Edgar. For the king had also commended Edgar to the nobles as nearest to the throne by birth, doubtless by a silent judgment of his mind, though with an inclination to mercy. Therefore, as I said before, the English were carried in different directions by their wishes, although all openly prayed for Harold’s success. He, indeed, raised to the diadem, gave no thought to the agreements between himself and William; he maintained that he had been released from his oath because the daughter to whom he had been betrothed had died before reaching marriageable age.

For that man, endowed with not a few virtues, is said to have taken insufficient precautions against treachery, provided only that by whatever tricks he could suspend men’s judgment. Moreover, thinking that William’s threats would never issue in action, since William was entangled in wars with neighbouring dukes, he gave his whole mind to ease with his subjects. Indeed, had he not learned that the king of Norway was approaching, he would not have thought fit either to summon troops or draw up a battle-line.

Meanwhile the other approached him gently through envoys, complained of the broken compact, and wove threats into his entreaties. Let Harold know that, before the year had passed, he would exact with the sword what was owed, and would go wherever Harold thought his footing safest. In reply, Harold repeated what I have said concerning the girl’s marriage, and added concerning the kingdom that it had been presumptuous for him to swear away another man’s inheritance without a general assembly and decree of senate and people; therefore the foolish oath must be broken.

[Note: Col. 1223D. “What I have said”: See §228.]

[Note: Col. 1223D. “Without a general …”: From these words it seems to follow that the great council of the kingdom had never consented to any transfer of the crown to a duke; and, lacking such authorization, no oath given by Harold in William’s favour could have had binding force.]

For if an oath or vow which a girl, without her parents’ knowledge, voluntarily makes concerning her own body while in her father’s house is judged void, how much more should that which he, being under the king’s authority, made concerning the whole kingdom, without the knowledge of all England and under pressure of circumstances, be considered invalid.

[Note: Col. 1223D. “Be considered”: s. d. e. l.; “is judged,” a. c.]

Moreover, he said, William unjustly demanded that he resign the sovereignty which he had undertaken to govern with so great a measure of citizens’ favour; this would be welcome neither to the inhabitants of the country nor safe for the soldiers. Thus the envoys returned empty-handed, refuted by arguments either true or plausible.

But throughout that year the count made ready all necessities of war. At lavish expense he kept his own soldiers and invited foreign ones. He organized ranks and battle-lines so that the soldiers were tall in body and outstanding in strength; the commanders and standard-bearers, besides military knowledge, possessed maturity of judgment and age. If you had seen any of them singly, whether in battle array or elsewhere, you would have thought them not nobles but kings.

Thus the bishops and abbots of that age vied in religious devotion, and the magnates in high-minded liberality, so that it is astonishing that, after very few years had elapsed, you should see most things—indeed almost everything—changed in both orders: the former duller in some respects but more generous; the latter wiser in all respects but more grasping. Yet both were strong of hand in defending their country, provident in counsel, ready to advance their own fortunes and crush those of their enemies.

[Note: Col. 1223D. “Magnates”: a. s. d. e. l.; “chief men,” c.]

[Note: Col. 1223D. “After very few years … ready to crush”: c. e. f. k. read this shorter passage; a. s. g. h. l. read: “before sixty years had yet elapsed, both groups, having become miscarriages of goodness, undertook sworn wars against justice: the former, from ambition for sacred offices, embracing what was more crooked than just and good; the latter, having cast off shame, begging for gains of money like daily alms, snatching opportunities from every side.” d. m contain both passages, but omit “after very few years” and the words after “daily alms.” From the words in the passage cited above, “before sixty years had elapsed,” we are permitted to approach closely the time when the first version of the work entitled *Deeds of the Kings* was completed; but it must be thought that a less definite manner of expression was used, as the text shows, since probably after some years he returned his work to the anvil.]

But then William’s industry, agreeing with the providence of God, was already hoping to invade England; and, lest rashness should tarnish a just cause, he sent to the apostolic pope, who, having formerly been Anselm, bishop of Lucca, was called Alexander, pleading the justice of the war he had undertaken with all the force of eloquence he could command.

[Note: Col. 1224D. Alexander II, invested with the papal crown on 20 September 1061, died on 21 April 1073.]

Harold abstained from doing this, whether because he was naturally overbearing, or because he distrusted his case, or because he feared that his envoys would be obstructed by William and his accomplices, who held all the ports. Therefore, after weighing both sides within himself, the pope granted William a banner as an omen of kingship. On receiving it, William held an assembly of magnates at Lillebonne and asked every man’s opinion on the affair. When all had welcomed his wish with applause and encouraged him with splendid promises, he imposed a contribution of ships upon everyone according to the extent of his possessions.

[Note: Col. 1224D. “Magnates”: a. c. d. e. l; “great [assembly],” s.]

[Note: Col. 1224D. “Had encouraged”: s.; “had encouraged [plural],” a. c. d. e. l.]

Then they dispersed; and in August they assembled together at Saint-Valery, the harbour being so called by metonymy.

[Note: Col. 1224D. “Thus”: a. s. d. e. l.; “that harbour,” c.]

[Note: Col. 1224D. “By metonymy”: There are two towns called Saint-Valery. One is in Picardy, at the mouth of the Somme, formerly called Leuconaus; the other is a notable harbour in Normandy, in the diocese of Rouen, formerly called Saint-Valery-les-Plains and now Saint-Valery-en-Caux. The former seems to be the one meant here by William of Malmesbury. “In Ponthieu he caused [the fleet] to lie suitably at anchor at Saint-Valery,” says William of Jumièges.]

When ships had been gathered from every quarter, they awaited a favourable breeze to carry them to their appointed place.

[Note: Col. 1224D. “Place”: d. e.; omitted in a. s. c. l.]

As this was delayed for many days, the common soldiers, as usually happens, muttered through the tents: that the man was mad who wished to bring another’s land under his own right; that God was opposing him by holding back the wind; that his father had wished the same thing and had been restrained in the same way; that it was fated for that family, when aspiring beyond its strength, to experience God as an adversary. These reports were spread publicly and could have weakened the resolution of the brave.

The duke therefore, after taking counsel with the elders, ordered the body of Saint Valery to be brought outside and exposed in the open air, so that a wind might be prayed for. No delay intervened before a favourable breeze filled the sails. Then joyful shouting arose and summoned all to the ships. The count himself, first to put out from the mainland into deep water, waited for the rest, having cast anchor almost in mid-sea.

[Note: Col. 1225C. “To”: c. d. e.; “in,” a. s. l.] When all had flown to the embroidered sail of the flagship’s stern, they took food and reached Hastings under a gentle course.

As he disembarked from the ship on 28 September 1066, he slipped with his foot, but turned the omen to good when a soldier nearby cried to him: “You hold England, Count, who are to become king!”

[Note: Col. 1225C. “You hold England”: “These words were said in allusion to feudal investiture, or the formal taking possession of a lordship by displaying certain symbols.” (Sharpe, 315.) Yet this story gives some reason to suspect that the words are exactly like those uttered by Caesar when, landing in Africa, he stumbled because his footing failed and exclaimed: “I hold you, Africa.” Its credibility is also impaired by the complete silence on the subject of William of Poitiers, who was the duke’s chaplain and was present at his landing.]

He restrained the whole army from plunder, declaring in advance that things which were theirs should be spared; and for fifteen continuous days he behaved so peacefully that he seemed to think of anything rather than war.

[Note: Col. 1225D. “Things which were theirs”: Whatever the Conqueror’s orders may have been by which his forces were restrained from plundering, it must nevertheless be concluded from Domesday Surrey that they achieved nothing. The whole region around Hastings seems to have been devastated. In his latest edition of the work entitled *General Introduction to Domesday*, Henry Ellis states that the devastations committed by the Conqueror’s forces in the first invasion are plainly evident, especially near Hollington, Bexhill, and elsewhere. The value of each holding is given as it stood in King Edward the Confessor’s reign; then there appears the note, “It was devastated”; afterwards follows its value when Domesday Surrey, or the survey, was made. As these estates now stand, it is still plainly evident that they were devastated by an advancing army. It follows clearly that, in the invasion, William did not land his forces at only one part of the coast, namely Bulverhythe or Hastings, as is supposed, but at different places suitable for landing along the seacoast, from Bexhill to Winchelsea.]

[Col. 1225B] §239. Meanwhile Harold was returning from battle with the Norwegians, happy in his own estimation because he had conquered; in my judgment, on the contrary, because he had purchased victory by parricide. When news of the Norman arrival was brought to him, he pressed on to Hastings just as he was, bloodstained and in arms, attended by very few soldiers. Fate was plainly driving him headlong, so that he neither wished to summon auxiliaries nor, if he had wished it, would have found many prepared to obey. For, as I said before, all were hostile to him because he alone had seized the northern spoils.

He nevertheless sent men ahead to reconnoitre the enemy’s numbers and strength. William caught them within his camp, ordered them led around the tents, then immediately fed them lavishly and sent them back unharmed to their lord. On their return Harold asked what news they brought. After describing in the most expansive terms the splendid confidence of the leader, they added seriously that almost everyone in that army appeared to be priests, because they had their whole face shaved, including both lips. The English leave their upper lip unshaven, its hair growing continually into a thicket; Julius Caesar also asserts in his *Gallic War* that this was a national custom of the ancient Britons.

[Note: Col. 1226C–D. In the *Gallic War*: “Their hair is long, and they shave every part of their body except the head and upper lip.” (Book V, ch. 14 of Caius Julius Caesar, *On the Gallic War*, ed. Oudendorp, Leiden, 1737.)]

The king smiled at the folly of the reporters and followed it with a witty laugh: they were not priests, he said, but soldiers strong in arms and unconquered in spirit. Then his brother Gyrth seized the words from his mouth—a man more mature than his age, and of great courage and intelligence beyond his years.

[Note: Col. 1226D. “Brother Gyrth”: Gyrth, Harold’s brother, certainly fell in the battle at Hastings; but Harleian manuscript 3776, fol. 21b, states that Gyrth escaped unharmed and was seen in extreme old age by King Henry II.]

“If,” he said, “you proclaim such courage among the Normans, I judge it unwise to fight with a man in comparison with whom you are thought inferior in strength and in right. For you will not deny that you made him an oath, whether unwillingly or willingly. You will therefore act more prudently if, withdrawing yourself from the present necessity, you allow us to try the hazard of battle. We, released from every oath, shall justly draw the sword for our country. You must fear that, if you yourself decide the contest, you may meet either flight or death. But if we alone fight, your cause will sail into harbour whichever way the event turns; for you will be able both to restore those who flee and avenge those who die.”

[Note: Col. 1226D. “With whom”: a. s. d. e. l; “who,” c.]

§240. Unbridled rashness refused to lend a calm ear to this warning. Harold thought it inglorious and a disgrace to his past life to expose his back to any danger. With the same impudence—or, to speak more indulgently, imprudence—he did not even deem the monk, William’s envoy, worthy of a kind look, but drove him away harshly, praying only that God might judge between himself and William.

The envoy offered three alternatives: either Harold should descend from the kingdom according to the agreement; or he should hold it under William’s authority; or else, with both armies looking on, they should settle the matter by the sword. For William laid claim to the kingdom which King Edward, on the counsel of Archbishop Stigand and the earls Godwin and Siward, had granted him; and Edward had sent Godwin’s son and grandson to Normandy as hostages for that gift. If Harold wished to deny this, he should submit himself either to the judgment of the apostolic see or to battle. Frustrated in all these matters by the single answer I have mentioned, the envoy departed and gave his own side more vigorous spirits for fighting.

[Note: Col. 1226D–1227D. “On the counsel of Stigand, etc.”: “These claims come from William of Poitiers, who represents the Conqueror as making the speech; but they are plainly false. Godwin died in 1053 and Siward in 1054; in 1054 we have seen Edward the Confessor recall his brother’s son from Hungary in order to establish him as successor to the kingdom, and he accordingly returned in 1057 and died soon afterwards. It clearly follows that the things here asserted could by no means have been done by Edward.” (Sharpe, 316.)—“Stigand never obtained a pallium from Rome, although venality operates much there also. The king refused to receive the crown of the kingdom from his hand, having by his customary cunning procured agents, on the apostolic side, to forbid it. Not long afterwards, sailing to Normandy under a pretence of honour, he dragged Stigand there against his will, lest any treachery should arise in England by Stigand’s influence during his absence. It is difficult to say how many honours he showed him: rising courteously everywhere in his presence, and causing a long procession of pomp to be made before him in every bishopric and abbey of Normandy. But what these wrappings concealed came to clear light—namely, when Stigand was deposed, he appealed to William’s good faith.” (*Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, p. 116b.)]

§241. Thus the courageous leaders on both sides drew up their battle-lines on 14 October, each in his national manner. The English, as we have learned, spent the entire preceding night without sleep in singing and drinking; in the morning they advanced without hesitation against the enemy. All were infantrymen with double-headed axes; placing before themselves a close-packed tortoise-shell of shields, they formed an impenetrable wedge. This would certainly have saved them that day, had not the Normans, by their customary feigned flight, drawn apart their compact companies.

[Note: Col. 1227D. “That”: a. s. e. l; “that [other],” c. d.]

The king himself stood on foot by the standard with his brothers, so that, with danger equally shared, no one might think of flight. After the victory William sent that standard to the pope. It represented a fighting man, woven with costly workmanship in gold and precious stones.

[Note: Col. 1227D. “Woven”: c. d. e; “interwoven,” a. s. l.]

§242. The Normans, on the other hand, spent the entire night in confession of sins and in the morning received communion in the Lord’s body. Infantry armed with bows and arrows secured the first line; the cavalry stood behind, divided into wings. The count, serene in expression and loudly declaring that God would support his party as the more just, called for his arms. Presently, when the bustle of his attendants put a coat of mail upon him inside out, he corrected the omen with a laugh: “The strength of my county,” he said, “will be turned into a kingdom.”

[Note: Col. 1228D. “Inside-out coat of mail”: Since coats of mail in those times were made of linked rings, this could easily happen.]

[Note: Col. 1228D. “County”: It is evident that historians of that period used the words *comitatus* (“county”) and *ducatus* (“duchy”) interchangeably.]

Then, after the Song of Roland had been begun in order to inflame those who were about to fight by the example of a warrior, and after God’s aid had been invoked, battle was joined. The fighting was fierce, and neither side gave way for much of the day.

[Note: Col. 1228D. “Song of Roland”: A metrical song is supposed, commemorating the heroic deeds of Roland and the other nobles of Charlemagne who fell at Roncesvalles. From this passage Rivet (*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VII, p. 72) concludes that the Romance language was then in use.]

[Note: Col. 1228D. “Those who were about to fight”: a. s. c. d. e². l; “fighters,” e¹.]

[Note: Col. 1228D. “Battle was joined”: c. d. e. l; “battle was joined on both sides,” a. s.]

When William perceived this, he signalled his men to withdraw from the field in feigned flight. By this stratagem the English wedge was broken up; thinking to cut down the scattered enemy from behind, it hastened its own destruction. For the Normans turned their ranks back again, attacked the dispersed English, and drove them into flight. Thus outwitted, they earned a noble death in avenging their country. Yet they did not fail in their vengeance: frequently making a stand, they made great heaps of slaughter among their pursuers. Having seized a hill, they hurled down into the valley the Normans, fiercely striving upward in the heat of battle; throwing missiles and rolling stones downward upon those below, they cut down every one.

Likewise, after escaping a certain steep ditch by a short and familiar passage, they trampled down so many enemies there that the heap of corpses made the plain of the field level. This alternation, now one side and now the other gaining the victory, lasted as long as Harold’s life delayed the outcome. But when he fell, his brain pierced by an arrow-shot, the English flight continued through the night.

[Note: Col. 1228D. “Harold’s”: a. s. d. e. l; “Harold,” c.]

There the courage of both leaders shone forth.

§243. Harold, not content with the commander’s duty of exhorting others, diligently performed a soldier’s office. Often he struck down an enemy approaching hand-to-hand, so that none came near unpunished: immediately, with one blow, horse and rider fell. Therefore, as I have said, struck from afar by a fatal shaft, he met his death. One of the soldiers cut through the thigh of his fallen body with a sword. William marked him with disgrace for having committed a cowardly and shameful act, and expelled him from military service.

§244. William likewise exhorted his men by voice and presence; he himself ran forward first and attacked the massed enemy. Therefore, while he raged everywhere and gnashed his teeth everywhere, he lost beneath him that day three excellent horses, pierced through. Yet both body and spirit of the high-minded duke remained steadfast, although his bodyguards tried to draw him back with familiar whispers. He remained steadfast, I say, until the coming night poured upon him a complete victory. And without doubt the divine hand protected him, so that no enemy drew blood from his body, although they assailed him with so many missiles.

[Note: Col. 1228D. “Enemy”: a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.]

§245. That was the fatal day for England, the grievous ruin of a sweet fatherland, in exchange for new lords.

[Note: Col. 1228D. “For England”: d. e. l.; “for the English,” s.] Long before this the manners of the English had become such as they were, though they had changed greatly with the times. In the first years after their arrival they lived in barbarous appearance and bearing, military practice, and heathen rite; but afterwards, when they had accepted the Christian faith, little by little and through the passage of time, because of the peace they enjoyed, they put military exercise in second place and devoted all their effort to religion.

I say nothing of the poor, whose lack of resources commonly restrains them from crossing the barriers of justice. I pass over men of ecclesiastical rank, whom regard for their profession, and also fear of disgrace, sometimes prevents from straying from the truth. I speak of kings, who, because of the extent of their power, could freely indulge their pleasures. Some of them, in their own country and some at Rome, changed their manner of life and gained the heavenly kingdom, making a blessed exchange. Many, outwardly, embraced the world all their life, in order that they might lavish treasures on the needy and distribute them to monasteries.

What shall I say of so many bishops, hermits, and abbots? Does not the whole island shine with so many relics of its native people that you scarcely pass any distinguished village in which you do not hear the name of some new saint? And how many persons’ memory has perished for want of writers! Yet the studies of letters and religion fell into decay as time advanced, not many years before the Norman arrival.

[Note: Col. 1229C–D. “The learning of the clergy”: See §123. King Alfred, in his preface to Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, declares that knowledge of letters had so failed in England that on this side of the Humber very few priests could understand the ordinary Church office; and that he knew no one south of the Thames who could translate the common text of Latin discourse into English.]

The clergy, content with a haphazard education, could scarcely stammer out the words of the sacraments. It was a matter of astonishment and wonder to others if a man knew grammar. Monks mocked their rule by refined clothing and indiscriminate kinds of food. The nobles, devoted to gluttony and lust, did not visit church in the morning in the Christian manner; rather, in their bedchambers, amid their wives’ embraces, they merely listened to the offices of matins and masses hurriedly performed by a priest.

The common people, exposed in the middle, were prey to the more powerful, who, having exhausted their property or even sold their bodies away into distant lands, amassed heaps of treasures—although it is more innate in that people to hunger after feasting than riches.

[Note: Col. 1229D. “Riches”: a. c. d. e. l; “works,” s.]

This was unnatural: many men, after satisfying their lust with their own maidservants whom they had made pregnant, sold them either into public prostitution or foreign servitude.

[Note: Col. 1229D. “Sold into foreign servitude”: c. d. e. l; “claimed [them] for eternal servitude,” a. s. See §45, note 20.]

All drank together, pursuing this occupation by turning nights into days. They spent all their resources on small and mean houses, unlike the French and Normans, who incurred moderate expenses upon spacious and splendid buildings.

[Note: Col. 1229D. “Spent”: s. c. d. e; “guzzled away,” l.]

The vices that accompany drunkenness followed, effeminizing men’s minds. Hence it happened that, meeting William with rashness and headlong fury rather than military knowledge, they cast themselves and their country into servitude in one battle—and that a very easy one. Nothing is more fleeting than rashness: whatever it begins in a rush, it quickly ends or is checked.

In short, the English then wore garments reaching to the middle of the knee; their hair was cut, their beards shaved; they loaded their arms with gold bracelets and marked their skin with painted tattoos. In food they pressed themselves to gluttony; in drink they provoked vomiting.

[Note: Col. 1229D–1230D. “The English then were …”: This description of the English is to be referred to the ancient Britons, not to the Saxons. It agrees completely with what Caesar, Diodorus, Pomponius Mela, and Dio Cassius—and especially Herodian (*History of Herodian*, ed. Irmisch, Leipzig, 1789)—relate concerning them. As this historian writes, the Britons go naked over the greater part of their body; for they do not know the use of clothing. They wear iron bands around their loins and necks, considering these an ornament and a mark of wealth; they tattoo their bodies with figures of animals of every kind, and for this reason wear no clothing, lest they cover the figures painted on their bodies.]

[Note: Col. 1230D. “In drink”: a. s. d. e. l; “in cups,” c.]

They had already shared these worst practices with their conquerors, passing in other respects into their customs.

[Note: Col. 1230D. “Already”: d. e. l.; omitted in a. s. c.] Yet I do not wish these evils to be understood as said indiscriminately of all Englishmen. I know that many clergy at that time trod the path of holiness by a simple way; I know that many laypeople of every sort and condition in that nation pleased God. Let envy depart from this account: this reproach does not enfold all alike. But just as, in tranquillity, God’s calmness commonly cherishes evil people together with good, so in captivity his severity sometimes binds good with evil alike.

## ON THE CUSTOMS OF THE NORMANS

§246. Furthermore, the Normans—to speak of them also—were then, and still are, dressed with an elegance that provokes envy and delicate in their food without any excess. They are a nation accustomed to warfare and almost incapable of living without war: eager to rush against the enemy and, when strength has failed them, no less ready to overcome by trickery and money. At home they undertake, as I have said, enormous buildings at moderate expense; they envy equals, wish to surpass superiors, harass those subject to themselves while protecting them against outsiders; faithful to their lords, and soon unfaithful for a slight offence. They weigh treachery against fate and change their purpose for money.

Yet, of all nations, they are most kindly toward foreigners, whom they honour on equal terms with themselves. They also contract marriages with their subjects. By their arrival they restored the standard of religion, which had everywhere died out in England. You may see churches rising in villages, monasteries in hamlets and cities, in a new style of building; the country flourishing in a fresh fashion, so that every wealthy man thinks the day lost unless he distinguishes it by some notable magnificence.

[Note: Col. 1230D. “Themselves”: e¹; “himself,” a. s. c. d. e². l.]

[Note: Col. 1230D. “New”: a. s. c. d. e². l; “new [feminine],” e¹.]

[Note: Col. 1230D. “Notable”: a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.]

But since enough has been said about these matters, let us continue William’s deeds.

## HOW WILLIAM WAS RECEIVED BY THE ENGLISH

§247. Once he had gained a complete victory, he took extraordinary care that his own men should be buried; he also gave the same permission to the enemy, if any wished to perform that duty. He sent Harold’s body without payment to his mother when she demanded it, although she had offered much through envoys. She received it and buried it at Waltham, a church which Harold himself had built from his own resources in honour of the Holy Cross and filled with canons.

[Note: Col. 1230D–1231C. “Harold’s body”: In the twelfth century there was a report that Harold had escaped from the battle at Hastings. Gerald of Wales states that many were persuaded that Harold fled from the battle, pierced with innumerable wounds and deprived of his left eye, and ended his days piously and religiously, after the manner of anchorites, at Chester. Knighton and Brompton mention this story. William of Poitiers says that William denied the dead king’s body to Harold’s mother, who offered its weight in gold for it, and that, by William’s command, it was buried on the seashore. In Harleian manuscript 3776, mentioned above, Gyrth, Harold’s brother, is reported to have escaped unharmed; and, when he came into Henry II’s presence and conversation and could speak more safely of Harold because of the passage of time, he is said to have declared that Harold’s body was not buried at Waltham. Henry Ellis, citing this manuscript, rightly observes that all these things were fabricated by the secular canons who were expelled when Waltham Abbey was rebuilt in 1177.]

Then William gradually advanced with his army, as became a conqueror, not in a hostile but in a royal manner, towards London, the greatest city of the kingdom. Immediately all the citizens poured forth to meet him with congratulations. A flood of greeters burst from every gate, led by the magnates, especially Stigand, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Aldred of York.

For on the preceding days Edwin and Morcar, brothers of great promise, had, at London after hearing news of Harold’s death, urged the city-dwellers to raise one or the other to the kingship. Having attempted this in vain, they departed for Northumbria, judging from their own dispositions that William would never come there. The other nobles would have chosen Edgar if they had had bishops as supporters; but, with immediate danger pressing and domestic dissension dividing them, not even this was accomplished. Thus the English, who, by uniting in one resolve, could have restored their country’s ruin, introduced a foreigner because they would have none of their own.

Then William, undoubtedly proclaimed king, was crowned by Archbishop Aldred on Christmas Day, 25 December 1066. He took care not to receive that office from Stigand, because Stigand was not a legitimate archbishop.
