[Note: Col. 1231C. “Was crowned”: A full account of William’s coronation is found in the chronicle of William of Poitiers, who was the Conqueror’s chaplain.]

## SUMMARY OF WILLIAM’S WARS IN ENGLAND

§248. The sum of all the wars which he waged is as follows. He easily subdued the rebellious city of Exeter, aided, that is, by divine help, because a section of its wall collapsed of its own accord and opened an entrance for him. For he himself had attacked it more boldly, declaring that men irreverent toward God should be deprived of his aid; because one of them, standing above the wall with his buttocks bare, had disturbed the air with a noise from his lower part, in contempt, of course, for the Normans.

[Note: Col. 1231C–1232C. “Exeter”: a. c. d. e; “Oxford,” s.—It should be observed that all manuscripts, except the one used by Savile, agree in reading *Exoniam* (Exeter); but Matthew Paris, following Malmesbury, seems to have written *Oxoniam* (Oxford) in place of *Exoniae*, the best manuscripts of Matthew Paris (Royal MS 14 C VII and Cotton MS Nero D V) reading *Oxoniam*. From a passage in the Domesday Survey, where Oxford is described as containing 468 houses so devastated that they were unable to pay geld, a kind of tax, Henry Ellis says: “We must ask why so many houses are found devastated at Oxford. If the passage under discussion is credible, Matthew Paris probably reveals the reason under the year 1067, when the Conqueror subdued Oxford while advancing towards York: ‘At the same time King William besieged the city of Oxford, which was rebelling against him. Upon its wall a certain man, standing with his groin bare, disturbed the air with the sound of his lower part, plainly in contempt of the Normans; whereupon William, turned to anger, subdued the city with little difficulty.’” (Matthew Paris, ed. Watts, under 1067, p. 4.) The siege of Exeter in 1067 is also mentioned by Symeon of Durham, col. 197; Hoveden, col. 258; Ralph de Diceto, col. 482; Florence of Worcester, Frankfurt edition, 1601, p. 635; and Orderic Vitalis, p. 510.]

He almost destroyed York, the sole refuge of rebellions, killing its citizens by famine and sword. There Malcolm, king of the Scots, with his people; there Edgar, Morcar, and Waltheof with English and Danes, repeatedly fostered the nest of tyranny. They frequently killed William’s commanders; and if I were to recount their individual ends, perhaps I should not be superfluous, although weariness threatens, since it is difficult for a narrator to return to pardon if he should happen to lie in accordance with his informants.

[Note: Col. 1232C. “York”: e; “the city of York,” a. s. c. d. l.—The year 1068 is assigned to the destruction of York.]

## HOW HE TOOK YORK AND LAID WASTE THE WHOLE PROVINCE
§ 249. Malcolm gladly received all English exiles, extending to each whatever protection he could; Edgar especially, whose sister, in remembrance of her ancient nobility, he had made his wife. On Edgar’s account he harassed the English provinces adjoining his realm with plunder and fire; not because he believed this would advance Edgar’s claim to the kingdom, but in order to vex William’s mind, since he resented his lands’ being exposed to Scottish raids. Therefore William, having assembled a force of infantry and soldiers [Note: [Col. 1232C] “Soldiers,” d. e. l.; “horsemen,” s.], marched to the northern parts of the island. First he received into surrender the metropolitan city, which the English together with the Danes and Scots held obstinately, its citizens worn down by a long famine; and he routed, in a vast and fierce battle, a very large number of enemies who had come to aid the besieged, losing many of his own men in a victory not won without bloodshed.

[Note: [Col. 1232C] “Then he ordered the villages of the whole region,” etc. What is stated here and immediately following is amply confirmed by the Domesday Book: namely, that the resources of this province, once most flourishing [Col. 1232D], were destroyed by fire, slaughter, and devastation; and that the land itself has remained wholly uncultivated and unproductive even to the present day over a stretch of more than sixty English miles. Land which had belonged to Edwin and Morcar in the Yorkshire region is represented almost everywhere in the Domesday Book as waste; and in Amounderness, after no fewer than sixty-two places are listed, where the holdings amounted to one hundred and seventy ploughlands, it is written: “All these villages lie in Preston and three churches. Of these, sixteen are inhabited by a few people, but how many inhabitants there are is unknown. The rest are waste.” Moreover, the term *wasta* is added in countless places to lands belonging to the Archbishop of York, to St John of Beverley, to the Bishop of Durham, and likewise to lands which had formerly belonged to Waltheof, Gospatrick, Siward, and Merleswein.]

Then he ordered the villages and fields of the entire region to be ruined, and its fruits and crops to be destroyed by fire or water—especially the coastal districts, both because of his fresh anger and because a report had spread that Cnut, king of the Danes and son of Sweyn, was approaching. The reason for this command was that a pirate raider might find nothing along the coast to carry away if he had to return quickly, or to sustain himself with food if he judged that he should remain longer. Thus the sinews of a province once fertile and a nurse of tyrants were cut by fire, plunder, and bloodshed; the ground lay altogether uncultivated for sixty miles and more; and all its soil remained bare even to this time. Whoever now sees its cities once renowned, their towers threatening heaven by their height, their fields happy with pasture and watered by rivers, groans if he is a stranger; if any old inhabitant survives, he does not recognize it.

## CONCERNING MALCOLM, KING OF THE SCOTS

§ 250. Before battle was joined, Malcolm submitted himself; and throughout William’s lifetime he passed his years under uncertain treaties, often broken. But when William’s son William was king, Malcolm was attacked in the same manner and drove off his pursuer by a false oath. Not long afterward, while forgetful of his pledged faith he was riding arrogantly through the province, he was slain, together with his son, by Robert de Mowbray, Earl of Northumbria.

[Note: [Col. 1233D] “He was slain with his son.” Malcolm was killed with his son Edward on 13 November 1093 by Morel of Bamburgh, steward to the Earl of Northumbria. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

After many years’ burial at Tynemouth, he was recently transferred by Alexander, his son, to Dunfermline in Scotland.

## CONCERNING EDGAR

§ 251. Edgar, having surrendered to the king along with the archbishops Stigand and Aldred [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Having surrendered,” s. l.; “having submitted,” e.], fled in the following year to the Scot [Note: [Col. 1233D] “To the Scot,” a. s. e. l.; “to Scotland,” c. d.] and thereby stained his oath. But after living there for some years, and finding neither any present advantage nor any hope for the future, except a daily allowance, he set out to test Norman generosity and sailed to William, who was then living overseas. This, they say, was most welcome to the king, so that England might be free of an instigator of wars. For William was accustomed voluntarily to take to Normandy, ostensibly as an honour, whatever Englishmen he regarded as suspect, lest they disturb anything in the kingdom during his absence.

Edgar was therefore received and given a great gift; and after remaining at court for many years, he gradually began to be held in contempt because of his sloth—or, to put it more gently, his simplicity. For how extreme a simplicity it was to give the king a pound of silver, which he received each day as an allowance, in exchange for a single horse! Later he set out for Jerusalem with Robert, son of Godwin, a most daring knight. This was the time [Col. 1233D] (A.D. 1103) when the Turks besieged King Baldwin at Ramla. Baldwin, unable to endure the hardship of the siege [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Of the siege,” a. s. c. d. e². l.; omitted in e¹.], escaped through the midst of the enemy’s battle-lines, delivered solely through the exertions of Robert, who went before him and, sword drawn, struck down Turks on his right and left. But when Robert, made fiercer by success itself, rushed forward with excessive eagerness, his sword fell from his hand. As he bent down to recover it, he was overwhelmed by the attack of all and gave up his hands to chains. Thence he was led, as they say, to Babylon; because he would not renounce Christ, he was set up as a mark in the middle of the marketplace, pierced with arrows, and consummated his martyrdom.

Edgar, having lost his knight, returned; and although he obtained many benefits from the emperors of the Greeks and the Germans—for they had even attempted to retain him because of the distinction of his birth—he despised everything out of longing for his native soil. Indeed, love of country so deceives some men that nothing seems pleasant to them except the familiar sky they have breathed. Thus Edgar, deluded by a foolish desire, returned to England, whence [Note: [Col. 1233D] “Whence,” c. e.; “where,” a. s. d. l.]—as I said above—after being tossed about by Fortune’s varied sport, he now spends his grey hairs withdrawn and silent upon an estate.

[Note: [Col. 1233D] “He now spends his grey hairs withdrawn and silent,” etc. It is probable that Edgar lived in the Herefordshire region, since he occurs in the Domesday Survey as a tenant-in-chief in Herefordshire. Fordun (Book V, chapters 27–34) relates that Edgar was accused by a certain Godwin of treason against William Rufus, and cleared himself of the charge by single combat. This Godwin’s son Robert is afterward described as one of those who adhered to Edgar in Scotland; and the *Saxon Chronicle* states that he was one of those captured in the battle fought at Tinchebray in Normandy in 1106. Dr Sayers, in his *Disquisitions*, octavo, 1808, p. 296, relying on the authority of the Spelman manuscript codices, maintains that Edgar again invaded Scotland in old age and died in that kingdom in 1120. If this date must be accepted, it would clearly follow from the passage cited above that Malmesbury wrote this part of his history before that year had elapsed.]

## CONCERNING THE BROTHERS EDWIN AND MORCAR

§ 252. Edwin and Morcar were brothers, sons of Ælfgar, son of Leofric. They had received the earldom of the Northumbrians and guarded it peacefully under their shared shield. For, as I have said [Note: [Col. 1234D] As I said before, § 228.], a few days before the death of King Edward, the northern provincials had risen in rebellion, expelled their earl Tostig, and sought and received one of the brothers as their lord, through Harold’s support. These things happened, as we have learned from those who knew them, against the king’s will, because he loved Tostig. But weakened by illness, burdened by old age, and already beginning to be held in almost universal contempt [Note: [Col. 1234D] “Universal,” a. s. d.; omitted in c. e. l.], he could not help the man he loved. Therefore, from grief of mind he contracted a more serious bodily illness and died not long afterward.

Harold persisted in his purpose of outlawing his brother. Accordingly Tostig first polluted his ancestral triumphs by piratical raids, and soon afterward, as I wrote above, was slain together with the king of the Norwegians. His corpse, recognized by a wart between his shoulder-blades, deserved burial at York. Then Edwin and Morcar, at Harold’s command, brought hand-carried plunder to London; for he himself was hurrying to the battle of Hastings, from which [Note: [Col. 1234D] “From which,” c. d. e.; “and thence,” a; “thence,” l; “where,” s.] he falsely dreamed, as an ominous foreknowledge, of victory already gained. But after he had been killed, the brothers fled [Col. 1234D] to the lands under their power and disturbed William’s peace for some years, harassing the forests by secret brigandage, yet never thereafter waging war openly. Though often captured, they generally surrendered, but were released unpunished through pity for their youthful beauty and favour toward their nobility. At last they were killed neither by the force nor by the stratagems of their enemies, but by the treachery of their own men.

[Note: [Col. 1235D] “Killed by the treachery of their own men.” According to the *Saxon Chronicle*, Earl Edwin was treacherously killed by his own men in 1071; in the same year Earl Morcar submitted himself to the king.]

They moved the king to tears. He would long before have granted them marriages with his kinswomen and the honour of friendship, if they had been willing to rest content in peace.

## CONCERNING EARL WALTHEOF

§ 253. Waltheof, an earl of distinguished lineage, had gained much familiarity with the new king, because William, forgetful of previous offences, ascribed them rather to bravery than to disloyalty. For Waltheof [Col. 1235B] had alone cut down many Normans in the battle at York, beheading them one by one as they emerged from a gate. Strong in his arms, broad-chested, mighty and tall in his whole body, he was the son of the most magnificent Earl Siward, whom they called *Digera*, a Danish word meaning “the strong.” Later, when his party had been defeated, he voluntarily submitted, was granted marriage with Judith, the king’s niece [Note: [Col. 1235D] “Judith, the king’s niece.” Judith was daughter of Count Enguerrand and Adeliza, sister of the Conqueror. William appears to have been especially lavish in gifts to her.], and received into private friendship. Yet he did not remain faithful, being unable to restrain his depraved disposition. For when all his compatriots who had thought resistance necessary had been killed or subdued, he too involved himself in the treachery of Ralph de Gael.

[Note: [Col. 1235D] “But when the conspiracy was discovered.” Earl Waltheof, or Wallefus, as he is always called in the Domesday Survey, was beheaded at Winchester on 31 May 1076, according to the *Saxon Chronicle*. Yet the Chronicle of Melrose and Florence of Worcester assign this to the preceding year.]

But when the conspiracy was discovered, he was seized and held for a long time in chains (A.D. 1074–1075); finally he was beheaded [Col. 1235C] and buried at Crowland. Some nevertheless say that he took the oath of disloyalty under compulsion, not by voluntary commitment. This is the English defence; the Normans assert the rest [Note: [Col. 1236D] “Assert,” a. s.; “adduce,” c. d. e. l.], the Normans who are far superior. The Deity seems to support their attestation, displaying many and very great miracles at his tomb. For they say that, cast into chains, he washed away his wrongful deeds with daily sobs.

§ 254. Hence the king’s policy may perhaps deservedly be excused if he was at times harsher toward the English, since he found almost none of them faithful. These circumstances so exasperated his fierce spirit that he first stripped the more powerful men of money, then of lands, and some even of life. Indeed, following Caesar’s character, he acted as Caesar had acted toward the Germans concealed in the great forest of Ardennes, who repeatedly issued from it and harassed his army: Caesar expelled them not through his own Romans but through allied Gauls, so that, while foreigners pierced one another, he might celebrate a bloodless triumph.

William, I say, did the same with the English (A.D. 1068). Against certain men who, after the first battle of ill omen, had fled to Denmark and Ireland and had returned in the third year with a strong force gathered together, he set an English army and commander against them, allowing the Normans to be struck. He prudently arranged a great advantage for himself, whichever side should win. Nor did his calculation fail him: after the two English forces had fought each other for some time, they yielded their unearned victory to the king. The newcomers were driven to Ireland; the royal party, after a very great loss of its men, purchased an empty title of victory at the cost of its commander.

[Note: [Col. 1236D] “This was Ednoth,” c. d. e. l.; “This was Isednoth,” a. s.—Ednoth was Harold’s master of horse. He was killed in 1068 while resisting Harold’s sons as they returned from their expedition to Ireland.]

His name was Ednoth, in peace and war alike almost distinguished among the Englishmen of his time, father of Harding, who still survives and is more accustomed to whetting his tongue for lawsuits than to brandishing arms in war. Thus, after breaking the power of the laity, William further established by a fixed edict that he would allow no monk or cleric of that race to aspire to any dignity. He differed violently from the indulgence once shown by King Cnut, who granted undiminished honours to the conquered; hence it came about that, after Cnut’s death, the native people easily expelled the newcomers and reclaimed their ancient right. But William, for definite reasons, canonically deposed certain living men (A.D. 1070), and in the places of those who died installed an industrious man of whatever nation [Note: [Col. 1236D] “*industrium*” (‘industrious’), c. e.; “*industrium hominem*” (‘an industrious man’), a. s. d. l.], except an Englishman. This, unless I am mistaken, was required by their hardened obstinacy toward the king; for the Normans, as I said before [Note: [Col. 1236D] As I said above, § 246.], are naturally inclined to kindness toward resident foreigners.

[Col. 1236C] § 255. Ralph, whom I mentioned earlier, was Earl of Norfolk and Suffolk by the king’s gift.

[Note: [Col. 1236D] “A Breton on his father’s side.” But his father was an Englishman, native to Norfolk. (*Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 1075.)]

A Breton on his father’s side, he possessed a character warped away from every good thing. Because he had betrothed a kinswoman of the king, daughter of William fitz Osbern, he measured out ambitions greater than was right and planned to seize sovereign power. Thus, on the very day of the wedding, a feast was held with great display—for Norman gluttony had now absorbed English extravagance. When the guests were drunk and swollen with wine, he disclosed his plan in a long speech. Since every faculty of judgment in their minds was clouded by drink, they shouted their assent to his words with enormous applause. There were Earl Roger of Hereford, brother of Ralph’s wife; Waltheof; and very many others besides, conspiring to kill the king. But on the next day, when the heat of the wine had subsided and a more temperate breeze had breathed upon the hearts of some, most, repenting of their act, slipped away from the gathering.

One of them, Waltheof, it is said, on the advice of Archbishop Lanfranc, voluntarily sailed to Normandy [Note: [Col. 1236D] “Sailing voluntarily to Normandy,” etc. Ingram, editor of the *Saxon Chronicle*, has been accused of William of Malmesbury’s twisting the words of the *Saxon Chronicle* here. [Col. 1237D] He further rebukes Latin historians for generally interpreting these words incorrectly, and maintains that “some have omitted the entire passage because they did not understand it.” Yet the arguments Ingram employs in reaching this conclusion are far from conclusive.] and reported the matter to the king, concealing only his own involvement.

[Col. 1237A] [Note: [Col. 1237D] “Sailing,” e¹; “having sailed,” a. s. c. d. e². l.]

But the earls persisted in their undertaking, each stirring his own provincials into rebellion. God, however, opposed them, bringing all their efforts to nothing. For when the matter was soon discovered, the king’s commanders, who were maintaining the guard, brought Ralph to such extremity that he seized a ship at Norwich and committed himself to the sea. His wife, after securing safety for her limbs and surrendering the castle, followed her husband. Roger, entangled in chains by the king, frequented—or rather inhabited—a prison throughout his life: a youth of detestable treachery and unlike his father in character.

§ 256. Indeed his father [Note: [Col. 1237D] “His father.” William fitz Osbern was only Ralph de Gael’s father-in-law.], William fitz Osbern, may be compared with the best princes; I do not know whether he ought even to be preferred to them.

[Col. 1237B] By his counsel King William was first encouraged to invade England, and afterward, aided by his courage, to retain it. He possessed a boldness of spirit commended by a hand almost prodigal in generosity. Thus, by the multitude of soldiers to whom he gave liberal pay, he checked the greed of enemies and gained the devoted service of citizens. Consequently, for his lavish expenses he incurred the king’s very severe displeasure, because he squandered his treasures imprudently. To this day, in his earldom around Hereford, the laws which he established retain unshaken force: no knight pays more than seven shillings for any offence whatever, whereas in other provinces, for a very slight occasion of transgressing a lord’s command, they pay twenty [Col. 1237C] or twenty-five.

But Fortune concluded such success with a shameful end, when the supporter of so great a kingdom, the counsellor of England and Normandy, went to Flanders from desire for a woman and perished in an ambush. For that Baldwin the Elder, whom I mentioned above, father of Matilda, had two sons: Robert, who while his father was alive took as his wife the Countess of Frisia and acquired the surname “the Frisian”; and Baldwin, who ruled Flanders for several years after his father and died by an untimely fate. Two children of his wife Richilde survived him, Arnulf and Baldwin. He had commended their guardianship to Philip, king of the French, [Note: [Col. 1237D] “Whose aunt’s son he was.” Robert, king of France, begot Henry, who reigned twenty-nine years; Henry begot Philip, who was left a boy when Henry, his father and king of France, died. Baldwin, Count of Flanders, was Philip’s guardian, for he had married Philip’s aunt, sister of King Henry.—*Book concerning the Castle of Amboise*, in Achery, vol. III, p. 272. (Bouquet XI, 186.)] whose aunt’s son he was, and to William fitz Osbern.

William gladly undertook this charge in order to establish his own name more highly by marriage allied with Richilde. But she, aspiring to greater things in feminine arrogance [Note: [Col. 1238D] “Greater things,” c. d.; “higher or greater things,” e.; “higher things,” a. s. l.], and demanding new taxes from the provincials, stirred them into treachery. For, having sent a messenger to Robert the Frisian to ask him to take the reins of his suppliant country, they all renounced their fidelity to Arnulf, who was now called count [Note: [Col. 1238D] “They renounced,” a. s. d. e. l.; “he renounced,” c.]. Yet there were not lacking men to support the orphan’s cause; thus Flanders was disturbed for many days by internal dissensions. The son of Osbern, wholly given over to love of the woman, could not endure this without gathering a military force and entering Flanders. At first he was received by those whom he had come to protect; but a few days later he rode securely from one castle to another, unencumbered and with few men. The Frisian, on the other hand, to whom such folly was not hidden, laid concealed ambushes, caught him unprepared, and slew both him, despite his vainly valiant resistance, and his own nephew Arnulf (A.D. 1071).

[Col. 1238B] § 257. Having thus gained Flanders, Robert often provoked King William by Norman raids. His daughter married Cnut, king of the Danes, and by her was born Charles, who now rules in Flanders.

[Note: [Col. 1238D] “Charles, who now,” etc. Charles surnamed the Good. He was the son of Cnut IV, King of the Danes, and Adela, daughter of Robert the Frisian. He succeeded Baldwin VII as Count of Flanders on 17 June 1119, and died on 27 March 1127.]

He made peace with King Philip, receiving Philip’s stepdaughter in marriage; by her Philip had Louis, who now reigns in France. But not long afterward, weary of the marriage because she was excessively corpulent, he removed her from his bed and unlawfully and unjustly married the wife of the Count of Anjou. Secure in this alliance, Robert saw nothing in his time that he had cause to lament, although Baldwin, Arnulf’s brother, who possessed the county in Hainaut and the castle of Valenciennes, made several attacks with the help of King William.

Three years before his death, his head already sprinkled with grey, he set out for Jerusalem for relief from his sins. Upon returning, he renounced worldly entanglements and awaited the end of his life, free from affairs and under Christian concern. His son was that Robert who became renowned for his admirable conduct in the Asian expedition which Europe in our own time undertook against the Turks. But by some misfortune, after returning home, he stained that noble labour when he was mortally wounded in a certain tournament, as they call it.

[Note: [Col. 1238D] “Mortally wounded.” He died in A.D. 1111.]

Nor did happier Fortune receive his son Baldwin, who, of his own accord challenging in Normandy the forces of Henry, king of the English, paid the price for the rashness of youthful daring. Struck on the head by a lance and deceived by the promises of many physicians, he ended his life [Col. 1238D] (A.D. 1119), handing over the principality to that Charles of whom we spoke above.

§ 258. But King William, acting gently toward his subjects [Col. 1239A] and harshly toward rebels, held all England in happy possession, having all the Welsh tributary to him. Moreover, never idle beyond the sea, he nearly pronounced extermination upon the territory of Le Mans (A.D. 1073), leading there an expedition of Englishmen, who, as they could easily be subdued upon their own soil, so always appeared unconquered upon foreign ground.

[Note: [Col. 1239C] “The territory of Le Mans . . . Englishmen.” A.D. 1073. In this year William, king of the English, led an army of Frenchmen and Englishmen across the sea and occupied the region of Le Mans. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

At Dol, a castle in Brittany across the sea, because he had been provoked by some quarrel of which I know nothing, he lost countless men when he led a military force there (A.D. 1075).

[Note: [Col. 1239C] “At Dol,” etc. King William then crossed the sea and, leading an army into Brittany, encircled the castle of Dol with a siege. But the Bretons stoutly repelled the besiegers until the king was summoned from France and arrived; upon hearing of his arrival, William departed, many of his men having been killed and his treasure diminished. (*Saxon Chronicle*, A.D. 1076.) These events are more correctly assigned by Florence and others to the preceding year.]

He always found Philip, king of the French, whose aunt’s daughter he had married, disloyal, because Philip envied so great a glory in a man whom he knew to be the man both of Philip’s father and of Philip himself [Note: [Col. 1239D] “Man,” a. s. d. e. l; omitted in c.]. Yet William no less vigorously opposed Philip’s efforts [Note: [Col. 1239D] “No less vigorously opposed his efforts,” a. s. c. e. l.; “more slowly,” d.], although his eldest son Robert supported those efforts with foolish counsel [Note: [Col. 1239D] “Supported his efforts,” c. d. e. l.; “supported him against his father,” a. s.]. Thus it came about that in a certain assault at Gerberoy [Note: [Col. 1239D] “At Gerberoy,” etc. A.D. 1079. In this year Robert fought with his father outside Normandy, near a castle called Gerberoy; his father was wounded by his hand, and the horse on which he rode was killed. (*Saxon Chronicle*.)], the son, striking back at his father, wounded him and pierced his horse. William left wounded, caught between his sons, while many of the royal party fell.

Nevertheless, throughout his life he was so fortunate that foreign and distant peoples feared nothing more than his name. He had made the provincials so subject to his will that, without any opposition, he was the first to conduct a census of every head, to add to his written knowledge the revenues of every estate throughout England, and to compel every free man, of whatever condition, by oath to his loyalty.

[Note: [Col. 1239D] “First to conduct a census . . . compel.” Malmesbury here alludes to that outstanding and most important record, the Domesday Book, which was printed at public expense in 1783 and afterward explained and illustrated with commentary so learnedly and expertly by Henry Ellis, first librarian of the British Museum. Two octavo volumes, 1833.]

Cnut [Note: [Col. 1240C] “Cnut,” a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.—Cnut IV, A.D. 1080–1086.], king of the Danes, alone shook his majesty [Col. 1239C]. He was exalted beyond measure both by his relationship to Robert the Frisian and by his own power. He spread among the peoples a rumour that he would invade England, the land owed to him by his kinship with the earlier Cnut; and indeed he would have done so, had not God weakened his boldness by an adverse wind. This fact reminds me to give a brief genealogical account, in succession, of the Danish kings after our Cnut, adding a few things also about the Norwegians.

§ 259. As was said before, he was succeeded by his sons: Harold in England and Harthacnut in Denmark [Note: [Col. 1240D] “Him.” According to Sweyn, the Danish historian, Cnut died on 12 November 1036; see p. 318, note 4.]. Magnus, son of Olaf—whom I said in my account of Cnut [Note: [Col. 1240D] “Olaf, whom I said in my account of Cnut,” § 181.] had been killed by his own subjects [Note: [Col. 1240D] “Of Cnut,” a. c. d. e. l; “of our Cnut,” s.]—recovered Norway, which Cnut had subdued. When Harold died in England, Harthacnut held both kingdoms for a short time.

[Note: [Col. 1240D] “Harthacnut held both kingdoms for a short time,” § 188.]

At Harthacnut’s death, the simple Edward succeeded. Content with his ancestral kingdom, he despised the overseas dominion as laborious and barbarous. A certain Sweyn, undoubtedly of very noble birth, was then elevated as king of the Danes. After his kingdom had prospered for some years, Magnus, king of the Norwegians, with the support of certain Danes, expelled him by force of arms and subjected the land to his own rule.

[Note: [Col. 1240D] “Then the king of the Danes,” etc. Magnus succeeded Harthacnut as king of Norway in 1042; in the following year Sweyn attempted to dislodge him from the kingdom of Denmark. On Magnus’s death in 1047, Sweyn obtained the kingdom.]

Sweyn, expelled, went to the king of the Swedes; and, gathering Swedes, Wends, and Goths with that king’s help, he returned to recover his realm. But the Danes conspired [Col. 1240B], loving the authority of Magnus, and he experienced the calamity of his former fortune. This was a great and memorable battle among those barbarian peoples, in which [Note: [Col. 1240D] “In which,” s.; “which,” a. c. d. e. l.] the Danes had never seen either a more fearful danger or a happier omen. To this day, therefore, they preserve inviolate the vow which they bound themselves to make before the battle: that in all future ages they would consecrate the vigil of St Lawrence by fasting and almsgiving [Note: [Col. 1240D] “Consecrate,” a. s. d. e. l.; “hallow,” c.]. The battle was fought on that day, and Sweyn then fled; but not long afterwards, when Magnus died, he recovered his kingdom whole (A.D. 1047).

§ 260. Magnus was succeeded in Norway by a certain Sweyn surnamed Herdhand, not of royal descent but elevated by his hand and ardour; he by Olaf [Col. 1240C], Magnus’s uncle, whom they call a saint; Olaf by Harald Hardrada, Olaf’s brother, who had also served in his youth long before under the emperor at Constantinople. By the emperor’s command, because of the rape of a distinguished woman, Harald was thrown to a lion; he strangled the savage beast by the bare strength of his arms. This Harald was killed in England by Harold son of Godwin [Note: [Col. 1240D] “Of Godwin,” a. s. d. e. l; omitted in c.] (A.D. 1066).

[Note: [Col. 1240D] “Was killed,” c. e; “was killed,” a. s. d. l. See § 228.]

His sons Olaf and Magnus divided their paternal kingdom; but when Magnus died prematurely, Olaf occupied the whole. He was succeeded by his son Magnus, who was recently killed miserably in Ireland after rashly landing there. They relate that the earlier Magnus, Harald’s son, after his father’s death was mercifully sent home by Harold, king of England; and that, remembering this benefit, Magnus treated Harold son of Harold kindly when he came to him after William’s victory. He also had him as a companion in the expedition (A.D. 1098) which he led into England during the reign of William the younger. In that expedition he subjected both Orkney and the islands of Man and Anglesey [Note: [Col. 1241D] “The Mevanian islands”: Man and Anglesey.] to himself; and when the earls Hugh of Chester and Hugh of Shrewsbury came against him, he put the former to flight [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Put to flight,” c. e. l.; “drove away,” a. s. d.] and killed the latter.

The sons of the last Magnus, Hasten and Siward, still rule while the kingdom is divided between them. The latter, a handsome and bold young man, not long ago sailed to Jerusalem by way of England, accomplishing innumerable and brilliant exploits against the Saracens, especially at the siege [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Siege,” c. d. e. l; “siege,” a. s.] of Sidon, which, with the Turks’ complicity, raged with monstrous fury against the Christians.

§ 261. But after Sweyn had been restored to the Danish kingdom, as I have narrated, he could scarcely endure peace and twice sent his son Cnut to England: first with three hundred ships, then with two hundred. Osbern, Sweyn’s brother, accompanied the first fleet (A.D. 1069); Hakon accompanied the second (A.D. 1075) [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Hakon,” a. c. d. e. l¹; “Bakon,” s. l².]. Both, having taken money, frustrated the young man’s attempts and returned home without result. For this reason King Sweyn branded them with grave disgrace, because they had violated their faith for money, and sent them into exile.

As he approached death, Sweyn bound all his subjects by oath that, since he had fourteen sons [Col. 1241C], they should assign the kingdom to all of them in order, for as long as that offspring [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Offspring,” a. s. d. e. l; “progeny,” c.] might endure. Therefore, after his death (A.D. 1076), his son Harold succeeded for three years (A.D. 1077) [Note: [Col. 1241D] “His son,” a. s. c. e. l; “his son,” d.]; Cnut succeeded him (A.D. 1080–1086), the son whom his father had sent to England. Mindful of the previous repulse, Cnut prepared, as we have heard, a fleet of a thousand ships and more for England.

[Note: [Col. 1241D] “A fleet,” a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.—These matters may be assigned to the year 1085.]

His father-in-law Robert the Frisian, master of six hundred vessels [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Vessels,” a. s. d. e. l; “ships,” s.], was to assist him. But after he had been restrained for almost two years by adverse winds, he changed his purpose, declaring that it was not without God’s will that he could not cross the sea. Soon afterward [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Soon afterward,” c. d. e; “afterward,” a. s. l.], however, he was corrupted by the conversations of certain persons who attributed the difficulty of the crossing to the evil arts of old women. He imposed unbearable levies upon the nobles whose women were accused of this. He also put his brother Olaf in chains, accused as leader of the same faction, and sent him into exile to his father-in-law. Therefore the barbarians, unable to bear the injury to their liberty, slaughtered Cnut within a certain church as he clung to the altar and promised amendment for his conduct [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Conduct,” a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.].

[Note: [Col. 1241D] “They slaughtered him.” Cnut was killed in the church at Odense on 10 July 1086. See *Antiquities Celto-Scandinavian*, p. 228.]

They say that many miracles were shown from heaven at that place, because he was a man devoted to fasts and almsgiving, and one who punished in transgressors of the law injuries against God rather than insults to himself. Accordingly, the honour of martyr was bestowed upon him by the Roman pope. After him, the murderers, to compensate for the odium of their deed by some good action, redeemed Olaf from his chains for ten thousand marks of silver (A.D. 1086). He ruled weakly for eight years and left the kingdom to his brother Henry (A.D. 1095). This man, living temperately for twenty-nine years, went to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Went,” a. c. d. e. l; “came,” s.] and breathed out his spirit in mid-sea.

[Note: [Col. 1241D] “Nicholas is now fifth,” etc. Nicholas succeeded his brother in the kingdom after an interregnum of two years in A.D. 1105; he was killed on 25 June 1135.]

Nicholas, the fifth, now remains upon the throne (A.D. 1103).

§ 262. The king of the Danes, therefore (as I have said), was the sole obstacle to William’s enjoying uninterrupted happiness (A.D. 1085). In view of him, William hired so great a multitude of mercenary soldiers from every province on this side of the mountains that their number burdened the kingdom; yet, in his greatness of spirit, he felt no loss from the expense, and had even brought Hugh the Great, brother of the king of the French, with his military following, into his service. He also encouraged and stirred up his own courage by recalling Robert Guiscard (A.D. 1020–1085), declaring it shameful to yield to him in bravery whom he surpassed in nobility. For Robert,

> [Note: Col. 1242D. Robert Guiscard. His origin, character, and early achievements were described by Geoffrey Malaterra (book I, chapters 3, 4, 11, 16, 17, 18, 38, 39, 40); William of Apulia (book II, pp. 260–262); William of Jumièges (book XI, chapter 30, pp. 663–664, Camden edition); and Anna Comnena (*Alexiad*, book I, pp. 23–27; book VI, p. 165), together with the annotations of Du Cange, notes on the *Alexiad*, pp. 230–232, 320), who investigated all the French and Latin chronicles for fuller understanding. (GIBBON, *Decline of the Roman Empire*, VII, 217.)]

> [Note: Col. 1242D. Of modest lineage. Robert Guiscard’s lineage is variously derived by different writers from noble and ignoble stock. His true origin may be assigned to the second, or middle, rank of lesser nobility. He sprang from a family of *valvassors*, or bannerets, from the diocese of Coutances in Lower Normandy (ibid.).]

born in Normandy of modest lineage, which neither grovelled on the ground nor swelled with any lofty pride, had gone to Apulia with fifteen knights a few years before William’s arrival in England, intending to remedy the want of necessities among that indolent people by military service. Nor had many years passed before, by the wondrous gift of God, he brought the whole land into his power.

> [Note: Col. 1242D. “Land,” a. s. d. e. l.; “that land,” c.]

For where he lacked strength, he excelled in ingenuity, first adding towns and then cities to his dominion. Thus he advanced so far as to make himself duke of Apulia and Calabria, his brother Richard prince of Capua, and another brother, Roger, count of Sicily (A.D. 1060). At last, having given Apulia to his son Roger, he crossed the Adriatic Sea with his other son, Bohemond; and, having immediately captured Dyrrhachium,

> [Note: Col. 1243D. Dyrrhachium captured. Dyrrhachium was taken on 8 February 1082.]

he was advancing farther against Alexius, emperor of Constantinople. A message from the apostolic Hildebrand restrained his fury. For Henry, emperor of the Germans,

> [Note: Col. 1243D. Henry, son of Henry: Henry IV.]

son of Henry,

> [Note: Col. 1243D. Concerning whom we have spoken above: § 189.]

whom we have mentioned above, angry with the pope because he had pronounced excommunication against him on account of the investitures of churches, came with an army,

> [Note: Col. 1243D. He besieged Rome. Henry besieged Rome in 1081 and 1084.]

besieged Rome, expelled Hildebrand, and introduced Guibert of Ravenna. When Guiscard, by a letter from the expelled pope, heard this, he left his son Bohemond with soldiers to carry forward his father’s undertaking and returned to Apulia. Quickly gathering a force of Apulians and Normans, he marched toward Rome. Henry did not await the messenger of his approach, but, terrified merely by the report, fled with the false pope.

> [Note: Col. 1243D. “Fled,” s. d.; “condemned,” a. c. e. l.]

Rome, emptied of its besiegers, received its lawful bishop; but not long afterward it lost him by the same violence as before. At the same time Alexius, hearing that Robert had been recalled to his own urgent affairs and hoping to bring the war to its conclusion, attacked Bohemond, who was defending the territories left to him.

> [Note: Col. 1243D. “Attacked,” a. s. d. e. l.; “came,” c.]

But the Norman youth, tenacious of his native vigor, put to flight the Greeks who charged against him and the other peoples who had assembled, though he was far inferior in numbers, through his military experience. At the same time the Venetians, a people accustomed to the sea, attacked Guiscard as he wished to cross over after settling the matters for which he had come, and suffered a worse disaster: some were drowned or slain, others put to flight. Continuing his intended voyage, he brought many of Alexius’ cities under his own control. The emperor removed by treachery the man whom he could not overcome by courage,

> [Note: Col. 1243D. “Could not,” a. s. d. e. l.; “was not able to,” c.]

deceiving Robert’s wife with a promise of an imperial marriage. Robert, exhausted by those plots, drank poison and died,

> [Note: Col. 1243D. “He died after drinking poison.” Writers of greater credibility—William of Apulia (book V, p. 277), Geoffrey Malaterra (book III, chapter 41, p. 589), and Romuald of Salerno (*Chronicle*, in Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, vol. VII)—are wholly ignorant of this accusation. Hoveden furthermore (p. 710, in *Writers after Bede*), who follows Malmesbury, adds that Alexius married the woman himself, made her a participant in his crown, and afterward burned her alive as an accomplice in the crime. (See Gibbon, *Decline of the Roman Empire*, VII, 247.)]

deserving, had God willed it, a better end: invincible by an enemy’s sword, yet vulnerable to poison from his own household.

> [Note: Col. 1244D. He was buried at Venosa. He died on 17 July 1085, under his tent, on the island of Cephalonia. The ship carrying Guiscard’s remains was wrecked off the Italian coast; but his body was recovered from the sea and laid in a tomb at Venosa in Apulia, made famous by the birth of Horace. (Ibid.)]

He was buried at Venosa in Apulia, with this epitaph:

> Here lies Guiscard, terror of the world; here he drove from the city  
> Him whom the Ligurians, Rome, and the Germans hold as king.  
> Neither Parthian nor Arab nor Macedonian phalanx protected Alexius,  
> But flight; and against the Venetians neither flight nor sea availed.

> [Note: Col. 1244D. On Pope Hildebrand. The accounts to be read of Gregory VII’s life are either reproaches (SAINT-MARC, *Abrégé*, vol. III, p. 235, etc.), and his miracles or magical operations are equally incredible to a modern reader.]

# ON POPE HILDEBRAND

[Col. 1244A]

§ 263. But since mention of Hildebrand has presented itself, I shall tell of him things which I did not absorb from frivolous hearsay, but heard in a serious account from one who swore that he had heard them from the mouth of Hugh, abbot of Cluny. I admire and celebrate him for this reason: he declared the thoughts of others by the prophetic insight of his mind.

> [Note: Col. 1244D. “Whom,” e¹; “which,” a. s. c. d. e². l.]

Pope Alexander, an energetic man, observing his zeal, had placed him over the chancery of the Apostles.

> [Note: Col. 1244D. “Him,” e.; omitted in a. s. d. l.; “indeed,” c.]

He therefore travelled through the provinces in the discharge of his office, to correct what had been wrongly done. Men of every rank came running to him, seeking decisions in various cases.

> [Note: Col. 1244D. “Of every,” c. d. e.; “by all,” a. s. l.]

All secular power submitted to him,

> [Note: Col. 1244D. “Secular power submitted to him,” a. s. c. d. e. l¹; “they submitted to secular persons,” l².]

both out of reverence for his holiness and for his office. Thus one day, when an unusually great company of riders attended him,

> [Note: Col. 1244D. “Of riders,” d. e.; “to ride alongside,” a. s. c. l.]

the aforesaid abbot was slowly advancing at the rear of the procession with his monks. Seeing from afar the great honour paid to the man—so many worldly powers waiting upon his nod—he turned such thoughts over in his mind: “By what judgment of God is a little man, of slight stature and contemptible lineage, attended by the service of so many rich men?” Undoubtedly he is puffed up and measures himself worthy of higher things because of the attendance of so many who walk around him.”

He had scarcely, as I said, revolved these matters in his mind when the archdeacon turned his horse, spurred it on, and from afar cried out, rebuking the abbot: “You—yes, you—have thought wickedly, falsely defaming one who is innocent in this matter alone. For I neither attribute this glory to myself, if glory it may be called which quickly passes away, nor wish it to be attributed to me by others; rather, it belongs to the blessed apostles, by whose privilege it is displayed.”

> [Note: Col. 1244D. “Rebuking,” d. e.; “rebuking / accusing,” a. s. c. l.]

The other, covered with shame and daring to deny nothing, replied only: “I beg you, lord, how did you know my thought, which I communicated to no one?” “From your mouth,” he said, “as though through pipes, that entire thought was conveyed to my ears.”

§ 264. Likewise, having entered a town church in the same province, they prostrated themselves before the altar, their sides stretched out and joined together. After their prayer had been prolonged for a long time, the archdeacon looked at the abbot, gnashing with a troubled mouth. When they had prayed longer, he left the doors and, asking the cause of his agitation, received this answer: “If you wish to love me,

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Erase,” a. c. d. e. l.; “assail,” s.]

take care not to strike me again with this injury. My Lord Jesus,

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Jesus,” a. c. d. e. l.; “Jesus Christ,” s.]

that one beautiful beyond the sons of men, visibly stood present at my petitions, giving heed to my words and favouring me with serene eyes. But compelled by the violence of your prayer, he left me and turned to you. I think that you yourself will not deny that it is a kind of injury if you rob a friend of the author of his salvation. Moreover, know beforehand that a great mortality of men and the destruction of this place are imminent. I have as a sign supporting this inference that I saw the angel of the Lord standing above the altar, draw a naked sword and whirl it here and there. I have a more striking indication of the coming disaster: already the thick and cloudy air, as you see, is circling this province. Let us therefore hasten our flight, unless we wish to undergo destruction with the others.”

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Mortality,” a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.]

Having said this, they entered their lodging and sat down to attend to their bodies. As soon as food had been set before them, mourning arose in the house and checked the hunger of the hungry; for one and another, and soon more members of the household, struck down by some uncertain calamity,

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Struck down,” a. c. d. e. l.; “killed,” s.]

suddenly lost their lives. Then, as the same plague spread through the neighbouring houses, they fled on mules, hastening their journey through the spurs of fear.

# ON A BISHOP INSTALLED THROUGH SIMONY

§ 265. In Gaul, the deputy pope

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Deputy pope,” c. e.; “in the place of the pope,” a. s. d. l.]

presided over a council. There several bishops, formerly introduced into churches through simony, were deposed and gave place to better men. One man was under suspicion of this apostasy, but he could be accused by no witnesses and refuted by no arguments. When you thought him most tightly bound, you marvelled to see him slip away like a smooth snake; so skilled was he in speech that he eluded everyone.

Then the archdeacon said: “Let human eloquence cease; let a divine oracle be brought forth into the midst. We know certainly that episcopal grace is a gift of the Holy Spirit; and whoever gains a bishopric thinks that the gift of the Holy Spirit can be purchased with money. Let this man therefore say before us, who are gathered by the judgment of the Holy Spirit: ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’ If he says it plainly and without hesitation, I shall be convinced that he has exercised the episcopal office not for payment but lawfully.”

The man gladly accepted this condition, supposing nothing less than that these words contained any difficulty. Indeed, he pronounced “Glory to the Father, and to the Son” without fault, but stumbled at “and to the Holy Spirit.” When all raised an outcry, he could not, by any effort, either then or throughout the rest of his life, name the Holy Spirit. The often-mentioned abbot was witness of this miracle; taking the deposed bishop about with him from place to place, he often laughed at the proof of that occurrence. All Europe refutes anyone who doubts the truth of his words, for it knows that through him the number of those in the Cluniac religious order was increased.

§ 266. Alexander having died, Hildebrand succeeded him,

> [Note: Col. 1245D. Called Gregory VII. He was elected on 20 April 1073 and died on 25 May 1085.]

called Gregory VII. What others had muttered,

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Had muttered,” a. c. d. e. l.; “had made unusual,” s.]

he openly proclaimed: he excommunicated elect bishops who received the investitures of churches from the hand of a layman by ring and staff. Thus Henry, emperor of the Germans, furious that a man elected without his knowledge

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Elected,” c. d. e. l.; omitted in a. s.]

should presume such actions, expelled him from Rome after eleven years, as I have said, and introduced Guibert. Not long afterward the pope was struck by a mortal illness, by which he did not doubt that he would die. The cardinals asked him to appoint a pope, citing the example of blessed Peter, who, while the Church was still in its infancy, appointed Clement during his own lifetime. He denied that he would follow that example, because it had been forbidden by councils from ancient times. But he said that he would give advice: if they wished for a man powerful in the secular sphere, they should choose Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino,

> [Note: Col. 1245D. “Of Monte Cassino,” a. s. d. e. l.; “of Cassiore,” c.]

who could beneficially and at the proper moment break Guibert’s violence with a military force; but if they wanted a churchman and an eloquent man, they should choose Odo, bishop of Ostia. Thus died a man of blessed favour with God and, perhaps, of excessive severity among men.

Finally, it is reported that, at the beginning of the first disturbances between him and the emperor,

> [Note: Col. 1246D. “That man barefoot, etc.” Sharp observes that these signs indicated complete submission and readiness to undergo every kind of penance. The excommunicated sometimes wore a rope around the neck; at other times they were even shorn or beaten with rods before receiving absolution. See Basnage, preface to Canisius, pp. 69–70.]

he did not even admit the latter when barefoot and carrying tongs and a broom, detesting him as a sacrilegious man

> [Note: Col. 1246D. “Sacrilegious,” a. s. c. e. l.; “sacrilegious, as was reported,” d.]

and guilty of incest with his sister-in-law. The emperor departed excluded, declaring that this rebuff would cause the death of many. At once, inflicting every injury he could upon the Roman see, he stirred up the pope’s supporters, conversely, to tyranny. For when one Rudolph rebelled, at the command of that apostolic man, who had sent him a crown on behalf of the Apostles, Henry was assailed on every side by the din of wars; but always superior to adversity, he finally crushed both Rudolph and the others who rose wickedly against him. At last, expelled from the empire not by the assault of others but by the domestic hatred of his son,

> [Note: Col. 1246D. “Son,” a. c. d. e. l.; “sons,” s.]

he met a miserable end to his life.

Desiderius succeeded Hildebrand (A.D. 1085), called Victor; but at his first Mass he fell lifeless, through some uncertain mischance, the chalice having been poisoned, if this is worthy of belief. Then the election turned toward Odo. A Frenchman by nation, first archdeacon of Rheims, then prior of Cluny,

> [Note: Col. 1246D. “Of Cluny,” a. s. c. d. e¹. l; “of Duny,” e².]

then bishop of Ostia, and finally pope at Rome, he was called Urban (A.D. 1088).

§ 267. Let this wandering digression suffice, while, on the occasion of William’s deeds, certain matters occurred to me which I did not think should be omitted. Now the reader who wishes may hear of his domestic life and inward character. First, he was humble toward the servants of God,

> [Note: Col. 1247D. “Of God,” a. s. d. e. l; omitted in c.]

kind to those subject to him, and inexorable toward rebels. He practised the Christian religion as much as secular power allowed,

> [Note: Col. 1247D. “Allowed,” a. s. d. e. l; “of power,” c.]

so that every day he attended Mass and every day heard evening and morning hymns.

> [Note: Col. 1247D. “Every day,” c. d. e. l; omitted in a. s.]

He built two monasteries, one in England and the other in Normandy. The first, at Caen,

> [Note: Col. 1247D. Caen, commonly *Caen*. Therefore the Breton and certain others absurdly suppose that Cadomus, “the house of Gaius,” was named from Gaius Julius Caesar. William the Conqueror granted the people of Caen a three-day fair—that is, a market lasting three days—as will appear below from his own charter. (BOUQUET, XI, p. 188, note.) The abbey of St Stephen at Caen is known to have been completed in 1064; but the time of its dedication is uncertain. Some assign the dedication to 1076, others to 1081, while Orderic Vitalis assigns it to 1077. The foundation charter was nevertheless granted after 1066, since in it William claims the title of king for himself.]

which he consecrated to St Stephen, he distinguished with suitable estates and most magnificent gifts. There he established Lanfranc as abbot, and afterward as archbishop of Canterbury: a man comparable with the ancients in learning and religion, of whom one may truly say, “A third Cato fell from heaven.” So thoroughly had heavenly savour imbued his breast and palate; so eagerly did all Latinity, through his teaching, apply itself to knowledge of the liberal arts; so earnestly did the monastic profession labour in religion, whether through his example or through fear of him. At that time bishops’ ambition and abbots’ venality did not prosper. The man of greater glory and greater favour with the king and archbishop was he who enjoyed the reputation of more steadfast holiness.

He built the other monastery at Hastings,

> [Note: Col. 1247D. “Built,” a. s. d. e. l; “constructed,” c. Although William the Conqueror founded and endowed Battle Abbey, its church, according to Florence, was not dedicated before 1094; William Rufus halted at Hastings there while travelling to Normandy.]

for St Martin, and it is called Battle, because there is seen on that spot the principal church where Harold is remembered to have been found amid piled heaps of corpses. Though almost a boy, yet wise beyond his years,

> [Note: Col. 1248D. “Beyond his years,” a. c. e. l; “mature,” d.; “with greater maturity,” s.]

he removed his uncle Malgerius from the archbishopric of Rouen. This man was indeed by no means uneducated; but, forgetful of his profession through consciousness of his birth, he devoted himself too often and too intently to huntsmen and contests of birds,

> [Note: Col. 1248D. “Devoted himself,” a. s. d. e. l; “applied himself,” c.]

and spent ecclesiastical treasures on excessively lavish banquets. As the report of this conduct spread, he was deprived throughout his life of the use of the pallium, since the apostolic see denied that privilege of honour to a man who neglected his sacred office. He was therefore often summoned; but although his nephew reproached him with paternal offences, he behaved no more reverently. At last, compelled by necessity, he was deposed.

Some report that there was a hidden reason for his deposition: Matilda, whom William had married, was related to him by blood. Malgerius, out of zeal for the Christian faith, could not endure that they should share a consanguineous bed; he had directed the weapon of excommunication against his nephew and fellow-relative. Thus, when his young nephew’s anger was joined by his wife’s complaints, grounds were devised for driving the persecutor of sin from his see. But afterward, in more mature years, William built for him the monastery of St Stephen at Caen as expiation for the offence, while Matilda did the same for the Blessed Trinity in the same town,

> [Note: Col. 1248D. “She [built] it for the Blessed Trinity.” The monastery of the Holy Trinity was founded by Matilda in 1066, and its church was dedicated on 18 June of the same year. On that same day Duke William brought his infant daughter Cecilia to the altar and dedicated her to God’s service in this monastery, in which she later became the second abbess in succession.]

each choosing inhabitants suited to their respective sex.

§ 268. Maurilius, a monk of Fécamp, succeeded Malgerius. He was praised for many virtues, but especially for abstinence. After a good and holy life, when he came to the end at God’s call, deprived of the breath of life,

> [Note: Col. 1248D. “Breath,” a. s. c. e. l; “panting breath,” d.]

he lay apparently dead for nearly half a day. Yet when he was already being prepared for conveyance to the church, his soul returned, and he bathed the bystanders in tearful joy. Confirming them by these words, he said: “Attend carefully, receiving the last words of your shepherd. I was released by natural death; but I have been returned so that I might disclose to you what I saw. Nor shall I remain much longer, because it delights me to sleep in the Lord. The guides of my spirit were adorned in face and clothing with every elegance. The gentleness of their speech corresponded to the brightness of their garments, so that I desired nothing except the service of such men. Delighted by their flattering attentions, I went, as it truly seemed to me, toward the east. A seat in paradise, to be entered not long afterward, was promised me.

“In a moment Europe was passed; entering Asia, we came to Jerusalem. There, after venerating the saints, we proceeded to the Jordan. The inhabitants of the nearer bank, mingled with the company of my guides, made a joyful assembly. I, eager to see the regions beyond, hastened my crossing. Then my companions reported that God had commanded that I should first be terrified by the sight of demons, so that the venial faults which I had not washed away by confession might be purged by fear of dreadful forms. No sooner had they spoken than so great a host of demons stood on the other side, brandishing sharp spears and breathing fire, that the ground seemed iron and the air flame. I was so affected by their terror

> [Note: Col. 1248D. “By their terror,” s. c. d. e; “by the terrors,” a. l.]

that, if the earth had opened or heaven stood open, I should not have thought that I could safely flee to either. Thus fearful, while I doubted where to escape, I suddenly recovered my breath,

> [Note: Col. 1248D. “Breath,” a. s. c. e. l; “panting breath,” d.]

only to breathe it out again at once—as I say these things in order to counsel your salvation, unless you neglect it.”

He spoke, and almost breathed out his spirit with the word. His body, then buried in the ground in the church of St Mary, was, as they say, by divine miracle raised three feet above the earth.

> [Note: Col. 1249D. “Then,” a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.]

§ 269. (A.D. 1070.) Moreover William, steadfast in the purpose he had begun in Normandy, allowed Stigand, an improperly and falsely appointed archbishop, to be deposed by Roman cardinals and Ermenfrid, bishop of Sion. Walkelin succeeded him at Winchester.

> [Note: Col. 1249D. Walkelin. A gloss in l¹: “Walkelin, of whom elsewhere it is written that he took from the monks three hundred pounds’ worth of land and applied it, to his own and his successors’ uses, in a blameworthy fashion.”]

His good works, surpassing his fame, will repel the antiquity of oblivion from themselves as long as an episcopal see endures there. At Canterbury came Lanfranc, of whom I have spoken above, who shone forth in England by God’s gift,

> [Note: Col. 1249D. “Shone forth,” a. s. d. e. l; “appeared,” c.]

as Lucifer, scattering the fleeing stars, brings forth the bright day with rosy face.

So by his industry the monastic shoot flowered; so while he lived episcopal vigour grew firm. The king made himself so compliant with Lanfranc’s counsel that he thought nothing ought to be refused which Lanfranc said should be done. At his instigation also he broke the traffic of scoundrels who, in their customary manner, sold their slaves into Ireland. To whom I should more properly ascribe the praise for this act—to Lanfranc or to Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester—I cannot truly decide. They scarcely compelled the king to do this, though he resisted because of the profit from the trade which was paid to him; except that Lanfranc commended what Wulfstan commanded, Wulfstan being more than sufficiently endowed, by episcopal authority, with the moral force of holiness. No man ever appeared more just than he, nor any man in our age equal to him in the power of miracles and prophetic grace. I intend to relate some of these later, if it shall please his most holy spirit.

§ 270. Yet because fortune’s die rolls with uncertain casts, many adversities occurred at that time.

> [Note: Col. 1249D. “At that time,” a. c. d. e. l; “of the time,” s.]

A foul quarrel arose between the abbot of Glastonbury and his monks, so that after verbal disputes they came to arms.

> [Note: Col. 1249D. “Foul … quarrel.” This disgraceful conflict occurred in 1083. It seems to have been caused by the abbot, Thurstan, attempting to introduce a new chant brought from Fécamp in place of the Gregorian chant customary among the monks.]

The monks, therefore, shut up within the church, groaned out their miseries to the holy altar.

> [Note: Col. 1249D. “Groaned,” c. d. e; “wept aloud,” a. s. l.]

But soldiers broke in: two of them were killed, fourteen wounded, and the rest driven back; indeed, the soldiers’ fury even made the crucifix bristle with arrows. The abbot, disgraced by the charge of this crime, was banished for the whole of the king’s lifetime; after the king’s death, however, he was restored to honour when money had been reckoned among the payments assisting the redemption of his sin.

[Col. 1250A] § 271. Miserable and unspeakable was the slaughter of Walcher, bishop of Durham,

> [Note: Col. 1249D. Walcher, bishop of Durham. He was killed on 1 May 1089.]

whom the people of Northumbria, ever given to rebellion, attacked with many insults and killed, casting aside respect for holy orders. No small number of Lotharingians were slain there, because the bishop himself was of that nation. The cause of the murder was this. Besides his episcopal office, the bishop was guardian of the entire county.

> [Note: Col. 1250D. Guardian of the entire county. The bishops of Durham were palatine princes, and in the county of Durham possessed “royal power in all things,” no less than the king in his own palace. (BRACTON, book III, chapter 8, § 4.)]

He had appointed his kinsman Gilbert over external affairs and the clerk Leobwin over internal matters. Both were energetic in the tasks entrusted to them, but uncontrolled. The bishop tolerated their excesses, induced by their effectiveness; and because he had raised them up, he increased the measure of his favour. For nature indulges itself and smiles with gentle favour on its own gifts.

This Leobwin caused Liulf, servant of the most blessed Cuthbert—so beloved that the saint himself, appearing before him while awake, would direct the pleas—to be murdered by Gilbert. He was struck by envy because Liulf held a place of greater friendship with the bishop through the integrity and fairness of his judgments. Stricken by the news, Walcher offered the enraged relatives of the dead man the judgment of a lawful court,

> [Note: Col. 1250D. He offered the judgment of a lawful plea. Walcher proposed to clear himself by oath of every share in the killing. (FLORENCE OF WORCESTER, A.D. 1080.)]

declaring Leobwin the author of his own death and that of his followers. When they came to the hearing, the savage people could by no arguments be softened from laying the blame upon the bishop, since they had seen both murderers living familiarly in his household after Liulf’s murder.

They therefore rose to shouting and anger. Gilbert voluntarily left the church in which he had been sitting with the bishop, to purchase his lord’s life at the cost of his own danger, and was wickedly killed. Then the bishop, standing before the doors and offering peace with an outstretched branch, satisfied the fury of the mob by being killed. Leobwin too, the kindling-material of the evil, half-burned because he refused to leave until the church was burned, leapt out and was received by a thousand spears.

This had been predicted by Edith, widow of King Edward. For when she had once seen Walcher at Winchester being led to consecration—fair-haired, rosy-faced, and very tall—she said: “Here we have a fine martyr,” evidently led by her judgment of that unruly nation to foresee the event. William, abbot of St Carilef, succeeded him,

> [Note: Col. 1250D. William, abbot of St Carilef. William de Carilef was consecrated bishop of Durham on 3 January 1082 and had held the office of chief minister of justice under William the Conqueror. Driven from his episcopal see for a long time by William Rufus, he died on 6 January 1095.]

and placed monks at Durham.

§ 272. Furthermore, in the year immediately before his death there was a mortality of men and beasts, frequent violence of storms, and a force of lightning such as no one had seen or heard of. In the year in which he died, too, a widespread fever consumed more than half the people, so that disease carried off the greater number; then, owing to the unwholesomeness of the air, famine followed and spread among the population, carrying off what the fevers had left.

§ 273. Among his other virtues, he especially cherished chastity in early youth, so much so that it was publicly reported that he was incapable with a woman. Yet, compelled by the judgment of the nobles to marry, he conducted himself so that for many years he was marked by no suspicion of disgrace. He had many children by Matilda, who, obedient to her husband and fruitful in offspring, drove a spur of love for herself into the mind of the noble man. Although there are not lacking people who mutter that, when royal power had increased, he renounced his former celibacy and had intercourse with the daughter of a certain priest, whom he carried off from Matilda by means of an attendant after cutting the woman’s hamstring; and that for this reason he disinherited the man and had the woman beaten to death with a horse’s bridle.

> [Note: Col. 1251C. “But I ascribe these things …” “Therefore the Norman chronicle is foolish and wholly fabulous in this respect, while it reports this monstrous tale and, contrary to the authority of contemporary writers, presents it as the reason for the construction of the two abbeys at Caen. See the *Apology of William*, published there in octavo by our lord Matthew de la Dangie de Rauchie, cellarer of the abbey of St Stephen at Caen.” BOUQUET, XI, p. 188, note.]

But I account it madness to believe these things of so great a king. I assert confidently only that in their final years some slight hostility arose between them over their son Robert, to whom his mother was said to supply a military force from the revenues of the treasury. Yet he showed that no marital affection was diminished on this account, when she died four years before him (A.D. 1083): he honoured her with most magnificent funeral rites, followed her death with abundant tears for many days, and mourned his lost beloved. Indeed, from that time onward, if we may believe it, he renounced every pleasure.

> [Note: Col. 1251D. The queen was buried at Caen. Matilda died on 2 November 1083. By her will she left this monastery her crown, sceptre, and ornaments of rank. A transcript of her will may be seen in *Essais historiques*, by Abbé de la Rue, vol. II, p. 437.]

The queen was buried at Caen in the monastery of the Holy Trinity. No less was the evidence of his piety in arranging the funeral of Queen Edith,

> [Note: Col. 1251D. Queen Edith, who had been the wife of Edward the Confessor. “In this year [1075] Edith, the widowed relict of King Edward, died at Winchester seven nights before Christmas Day; the king arranged for her to be carried to Westminster with great ceremony and laid in the tomb with Edward.” (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

who, through his care, was laid near her husband at Westminster and has a tomb laboriously wrought at the expense of silver and gold.

§ 274. He had sons: Robert, Richard, William, and Henry. The latter two reigned in England in uninterrupted succession after him.

> [Note: Col. 1251D. “In England,” s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.]

Robert, while his father was still alive, bitterly resented that Normandy was withheld from him. He stubbornly went to Italy in order, after marrying the daughter of Marquis Boniface, to oppose his father with assistance from those regions. But disappointed of this request, he incited Philip, king of the French, against his father. He was therefore deprived both of his father’s blessing and of his inheritance, and after William’s death did not receive England, retaining only the duchy of Normandy with difficulty.

Afterward, having mortgaged Normandy to his brother William for money nine years later,

> [Note: Col. 1251D. Mortgaged for money. Robert pledged Normandy to his brother for the sum of ten thousand marks in 1096.]

he undertook the Asian expedition with the other Christians. Four years later, illustrious for his martial exploits, he returned and entered Normandy without difficulty.

> [Note: Col. 1251D. He entered Normandy without difficulty. “In this year [1100], at harvest time, Count Robert returned to Normandy, and all his people there received him with great joy.” (*Saxon Chronicle*.)]

For, since his brother William had recently died, King Henry, insecure in his new position, had enough to do to retain England’s allegiance. But because I must speak of this elsewhere, I shall now end the narrative I began concerning the sons of William the Great.

§ 275. Richard, a delicate boy, nourished in his high-spirited father hopes of glory, breathing lofty thoughts despite his tender age. But bitter death quickly consumed and blighted the promise of his early bloom. [Note: [Col. 1252C] They relate that he was hunting stags, etc. Certain chroniclers report that he died, pierced by a stag’s antlers, about three years before his father’s death. William of Malmesbury’s account, however, is more credible. Richard was buried at Winchester, and his epitaph hails him as duke of Bernay. (SAND., *Genealogical History*, fol. 1707).] They relate that, while piercing stags in the New Forest, he contracted an illness from a mist of unhealthy air. This was a place which his father William had turned into forest haunts for wild beasts over thirty miles and more, after demolishing churches [Note: [Col. 1252D] “After demolishing churches,” etc.: omitted in c. e. k.] and abandoning villages. [Note: [Col. 1252D] “There gladly . . . for afterwards,” c. d. e. k.: “a spectacle altogether unspeakable: where previously either human intercourse or divine worship had flourished, stags, roe deer, and other beasts of that kind now run about there wantonly; nor are even these commonly exposed for the use of mortals. Hence it is truly asserted that,” a. s. g. h. l.] There he gladly spent his life; there, passing over the fact that he delighted to pursue hunting for many days—indeed, for months. There many misfortunes befell the royal family, which the present memory suggests to those willing to hear of the inhabitants: for afterwards, in that same forest, his son William and his grandson Richard, son of Robert count of Normandy, met their deaths—the former, by God’s severe judgment, pierced in the breast by an arrow; the latter in the neck, or, as some say, caught by the throat on a branch as his horse passed beneath it.

§ 276. He had five daughters: [Note: [Col. 1252D] Cecilia, c. d. e. l.; Cecilia first, a. s.—“Baldric of Bourgueil, in verses addressed to Cecilia, daughter of the king of the English, recalls a sister whom Cecilia had drawn with her into the monastery; for he says:

> I heard that you had retained a certain sister,  
> Whose renown at one time struck my ears.  
> Her name has escaped me, yet I remember having seen her.”

(BOUQ. XI, 189, note).] Cecilia, abbess of Caen, is still living; [Note: [Col. 1252D] “Is still living,” c. e. l.; “who is still living,” a. s. d.] the second, Constance, given in marriage to Alan Fergant, count of Brittany, sharpened the provincials’ hostility against herself into a deadly draught by the severity of her justice; the third, Adela, wife of Stephen count of Blois, a woman of power renowned in the world, has lately taken the religious habit at Marcigny. The names of the other two [Note: [Col. 1253D] “Of the two,” a. c. d. e. l.; “of the other two,” s.] [Note: [Col. 1253D] The names have dropped out. The five daughters of William the Conqueror named by Orderic Vitalis (book IV, p. 512) are: Agatha, Constance, Adeliza, Adela, and Cecilia. William of Jumièges asserts that Adeliza was betrothed to Harold: “Then the duke, after Harold had confirmed his fidelity to him concerning the kingdom by many oaths, promised that he would give him Adeliza, his daughter, together with half of the English kingdom.” (book VI, ch. 31.) More recent historians speak of Margaret and Eleanor as though they were betrothed: the former to Harold, the latter to Alfonso VI, king of León. See Hayward’s *Lives*, p. 128; Tyrrel, *History of England*, II, 61; and Lytt., *Henry II*, vol. I, p. 356.] have been lost: one, who had been promised to Harold (as we have said), [Note: [Col. 1253D] As we have said, § 228.] died before she had reached marriageable years; the other, who had been pledged by envoys to Alfonso, king of Galicia, obtained from God a virgin’s death. A callus found on the dead woman’s knees was evidence of her frequent prayers.

§ 277. Extolling his father’s memory upon every possible occasion, he was having the bones, once buried at Nicaea, transferred through a legate toward the end of his life; [Col. 1253B] but the latter, returning safely, heard of William’s death and settled in Apulia, where the remains of the distinguished man were buried. He honoured his mother with remarkable devotion as long as she lived. Before his father’s death, she had married a certain Herluin of Conteville, a man of middling means. By him William had brothers: Robert, [Note: [Col. 1254D] Robert. Shortly after William’s occupation of England, Robert was raised to the earldom of Cornwall, and extensive estates in nearly the whole county were granted him by his half-brother. He died in 1091.] whom he made count of Mortain, a man of gross and dull intellect; and Odo, [Note: [Col. 1254D] Odo. Odo was made bishop of Bayeux in 1049 and earl of Kent in 1067. He died at Palermo, while travelling to the Holy Land, in 1097.] whom the count advanced to the bishopric of Bayeux and the king made earl of Kent. This latter, a man of subtler mind, was the king’s viceroy over all England after the killing of William fitz Osbern. Thus, marvellously skilled in heaping up treasures, and of marvellous cunning in evasion, [Note: [Col. 1254D] “Cunning,” c. d. e.; “self-restraint,” a. s. l.] he had almost purchased the Roman papacy, though absent from the citizens, [Col. 1253C] stuffing pilgrims’ wallets with letters and coins. When, because of the expectation of his intended journey, soldiers flocked to him competitively from the whole kingdom, the king took offence and put him in chains, declaring that he was seizing not the bishop of Bayeux but the earl of Kent. His retainers, compelled by threats, disclosed so great a quantity of gold that the heap of yellow metal surpassed the estimate of our own age. Indeed, several bags were also drawn out of rivers, where he had buried them in particular places after removing those who knew of them, full of coined gold. Released after his brother’s death, he opposed his nephew William and supported Robert’s cause. But when fortune again went against him, he was exiled from England, while pressing the claims of his Norman nephew and of his bishopric. Afterwards he set out upon the road to Jerusalem with the same nephew and died at Antioch, during the Christians’ siege.

§ 278. He graciously admitted men of foreign nations to friendship and raised them impartially to honours. He attended to almsgiving, granting many estates in England to churches beyond the sea. Hardly any monastery, especially in Normandy, escaped either his generosity or that of the dukes, so that their poverty might be sustained from England’s abundance. Thus in his time the monastic flock increased in both directions across the sea: monasteries rose, ancient in religious observance but new in buildings. Yet here I notice the muttering of those who say: it would have been better for the old foundations to be preserved in their condition than for new ones to be built from plunder after the old had been half mutilated.

[Col. 1254B] § 279. He was of moderate height and enormous bulk, fierce of countenance, bald upon the forehead, and of immense strength in his arms. It was often a great spectacle that no one could draw his bow, which he himself would bend by stretching the string with his feet while mounted on horseback. Majestic seated and standing, although the excessive protrusion of his paunch disfigured his royal body; he enjoyed sound health, for he never lay dangerously ill except at the end. He was so devoted to woodland pursuits that, as I said before, he ordered many thousands of inhabitants to be expelled and their lands made wild, so that there, withdrawn from other affairs, he might relax his mind. On the principal festivals he held costly and magnificent feasts: Christmas at Gloucester, [Col. 1254C] Easter at Winchester, Pentecost at Westminster, every year in which he was able to remain in England. By royal edict he summoned all magnates of every rank, so that ambassadors of foreign nations might marvel at the spectacle of the multitude and the display of luxuries.
