At no time was he more courteous or readier to show generosity, so that all peoples everywhere who came might boast that his generosity rivalled his wealth. His first successor stubbornly retained this custom of feasting; [Note: [Col. 1254D] The second abandoned it. See below, § 407.] the second abandoned it.

§ 280. The accumulation of money is the only point for which he is somewhat blamed, [Note: [Col. 1254D] “Somewhat,” c. d. e.; “deservedly,” a. s. l.] [Note: [Col. 1254D] “Accumulation,” c. d. e.; “avarice,” a. s. l.] which, seizing opportunities from every quarter, he amassed by whatever means he could call not inferior to honour and royal dignity. [Note: [Col. 1254D] “Honourable . . . could govern,” c. d. e. k.; “he never thought anything of any consequence, provided that he might scrape together, do, or say certain things—and almost everything—unworthy of so great a majesty, whenever the hope of money gleamed forth,” a. s. g. h. l.] But he will easily be excused, [Col. 1255A] because he could not govern a new kingdom without great wealth. I can offer no other excuse here [Note: [Col. 1255D] “Other,” c. d. e.; omitted in a. s. l.] except what someone said: “He whom many fear must necessarily fear many.” For, through fear of enemies, he squeezed money from his provinces, by which he might either delay or even repel their attacks, often—as happens in human affairs—when strength had failed, securing hostile loyalty by a reward. The calamity of this disgrace still reigns and increases daily: villages and churches too are subjected to payments; and this not even under the lasting fidelity of tax-farmers, but whoever offers more immediately obtains the prize, previous agreements being annulled.

§ 281. Toward the end of his life, while dwelling in Normandy and involved in hostilities with the king of France, [Col. 1255B] he held himself quiet for a time. Philip, abusing his patience, is said to have remarked: “The king of England lies at Rouen, warming his bed like women recently delivered of children,” mocking his belly, which he had relieved by a draught. Stung by the insult, he answered: “When I go to Mass after childbirth, [Note: [Col. 1255D] One hundred thousand candles. This alludes to the custom of women in those times to offer lighted candles when first entering a church after childbirth. Sharpe observes: “According to the Roman Ritual, a woman, kneeling and holding a lighted taper in her hand, is sprinkled with holy water at the church door and introduced into the church. This practice seems connected with the feast of the Purification. See DURAND, book VII, ch. 7.”] I shall offer him one hundred thousand candles.” He pronounced such words “by the Resurrection and Splendour of God,” for he deliberately used oaths which, by the very opening [Note: [Col. 1255D] “Opening,” c. d. e.; “dress,” s.; “breath,” l.; “mouth,” a.] of his mouth, sounded something terrifying in his hearers’ minds.

§ 282. Not long afterwards, as August was declining, when crops in the fields, clusters in the vineyards, and fruit in orchards offer their abundance to those who desire it, he raised an army and entered France as an enemy. He trampled everything down and ravaged all; nothing could soften his raging mind, as he sought to avenge an insult arrogantly received by the ruin of many. At last he burned the town of Mantes, setting it on fire; the church of St Mary was burned there, together with one enclosed woman who thought her cell not to be abandoned even in such necessity; all the citizens’ fortunes were ruined. Elated by this success, while he urged his men more boldly to add fuel to the fire, he approached the flames too closely and contracted illness through the heat of the blaze and the unevenness of the autumn weather. Some say that his war-horse, leaping a steep ditch, ruptured his entrails, [Note: [Col. 1256D] “Ruptured,” e¹; “burst,” a. s. c. d. e² l.] because his belly protruded over the front of the saddle. [Col. 1255D] Afflicted by this pain, he sounded the retreat for his men and returned to Rouen, where, as his discomfort increased daily, he took to his bed. The physicians, having examined his urine, predicted certain death. When this was heard, lamentation filled the house because death was overtaking him just as he had long been contemplating amendment of his life. Recovering his composure, he performed those acts belonging to a Christian in confession and reception of the viaticum. Reluctantly and under compulsion he assigned Normandy to Robert, England to William, and his maternal possessions to Henry. He commanded all his prisoners to be brought out and freed, his treasures to be carried forth and distributed among the churches. He himself fixed a definite sum of money for rebuilding the church recently burned. Having thus arranged his affairs well, he died on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the twenty-first year of his reign, [Note: [Col. 1256D] “Twenty-first,” c. d. e.; “twenty-second,” s. l².] the fifty-second of his duchy, the fifty-ninth of his life, and the year 1087 of the Lord’s Incarnation. This was the year in which Cnut, [Note: [Col. 1256D] As we said above, § 261. Malmesbury here follows the *Saxon Chronicle*, which assigns Cnut’s death to 1087, whereas it should instead be assigned to the preceding year (*Art de vérifier les Dates*, II, 85).] king of the Danes, was slain, as we said above; and in which the Saracens of Spain, having raged against the Christians, were soon compelled by Alfonso, king of Galicia, [Col. 1256B] to return to their own lands and even unwillingly surrendered towns which they had formerly held.

§ 283. His body, prepared with royal solemnity, was conveyed by the Seine to Caen and there committed to the earth amid a great gathering of clergy but few laymen. It was then possible to see the misery of human vicissitude: that man, once the glory of all Europe and more powerful than all his predecessors, could not obtain without dispute a resting-place of eternal repose. For a certain knight, [Note: [Col. 1256D] A certain knight. His name is reported to have been Asselin Fitz-Arthur.] whose inheritance that place had been, publicly denounced the robbery and forbade the burial, saying that the ground was his by ancestral right and that William ought not to rest in a place which he had violently seized. Therefore, at the wish of his son Henry, the only one of his children present, one hundred pounds of silver paid to the claimant [Col. 1256C] restrained the bold challenge. For Robert, the firstborn, was then waging war in France against his native land; William, before his father had fully breathed his last, had sailed for England, judging it more useful to provide for his future advantage than to attend at his father’s obsequies. Moreover, neither slow nor sparing in distributing money, Henry brought from the secret royal treasuries into the light all the treasure accumulated at Winchester throughout his father’s reign. He bestowed gold upon monasteries; upon country churches, five silver shillings; and upon every village one hundred pounds to be divided individually among the poor. He also conspicuously honoured his father’s memory with a vast accumulation of silver and gold, together with the brilliance of gems.

## Concerning Berengar

[Col. 1256D]

§ 284. At this time there was Berengar, the heresiarch of Tours, who denied that the bread and wine placed upon the altar, after the priest’s consecration, are the true and substantial body of the Lord, as the holy Church teaches. [Col. 1257A] All Gaul was already teeming with his teaching, disseminated through poor scholars whom he himself encouraged with daily gifts. Therefore Pope Leo, of holy memory, fearing for the soundness of Catholic faith, convened a council against him at Vercelli and drove away the darkness of the cloudy error with the brightness of Gospel testimonies. But after Leo’s death, when the poison of the heresy, long cherished in the bosoms of certain worthless persons, burst forth again, Hildebrand—then archdeacon at Tours and soon pope at Rome—convened councils and compelled Berengar, having been convicted, to anathematize his doctrine. Those who wish may find the writings on these matters in their proper places. Lanfranc the archbishop answered him in books, [Note: [Col. 1257D] Lanfranc in books. “He wrote,” says Sigebert, “polemical letters against Berengar of Tours, refuting his writings concerning the body and blood of the Lord.” According to the same bibliographer, Lanfranc also wrote praises, triumphs, and the deeds of William, count of the Normans. BOUQ. XI, 191, note.] but above all, powerfully, did Guitmund, formerly monk of Saint-Leufroy in Normandy and later bishop of Aversa in Apulia, the most eloquent man of our age. Yet although Berengar had brought disrepute upon the first heat of youth by defending certain heresies, in riper age he so returned to sound judgment that some consider him a saint without retraction, approved by countless good qualities, especially humility and almsgiving. He was master of great possessions in distributing them, not a servant in hoarding and worshipping them; so sparing of female beauty that he allowed no woman to be admitted to his sight, lest his eye appear to have sampled a form for which his mind did not itch. He did not despise the poor or flatter the rich; he lived according to nature; having food and clothing, he was content with these, according to the Apostle. Hence Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, himself pre-eminent among versifiers, praises him. I have inserted his words in order to show the praiseworthy bishop’s affection for his master; and at the same time his teaching will furnish posterity with an example of how one ought to live, although perhaps, stirred by affection, he has overstepped the bounds of true praise.

> He whom the world now marvels at, the world will always marvel at:  
> Berengar, not destined to perish, dies.  
> Him who held the highest heights of sacred faith  
> The fifth day has already taken away—an act of wicked daring.  
> That day was a ruinous day, faithless to the world,  
> On which there was sorrow and the utter ruin of things;  
> On which the Church’s state, its hope, the clergy’s glory,  
> And the champion of law fell, while law itself fell.  
> Whatever philosophers said, whatever poets sang,  
> Yielded to his intellect and eloquence.  
> A holier and greater wisdom, undertaking greater things,  
> Filled his sacred breast and lips with God.  
> His heart willed it, his voice uttered it, his action made it ready;  
> Thus each faculty devoted itself to its Creator.  
> A holy and wise man, whose name grows hour by hour;  
> He, than whom every other man is lesser, is the greatest of men.  
> His judgment won and preserved the honours it had acquired;  
> To him the poor man was greater than the rich, and justice than gain.  
> Neither idleness nor luxury did abundant wealth give him,  
> Nor did abundant and lofty honour make him proud.  
> He turned his eyes neither to silver nor to gold;  
> But grieved whenever someone to whom he might give these was absent.  
> He never ceased to shore up the ruin of the needy,  
> Until, impoverished by giving, he himself became poor.  
> His concern was to follow nature, to employ the laws,  
> And to deny vice to his mind and deceit to his lips;  
> To set virtues above riches, truth above falsehood,  
> To say or do nothing devoid of sense;  
> To harm no one, to benefit all; to drive from mind and hand  
> Popular favour and profit.  
> His garment was of rough weave; he never drank before thirst  
> Nor ate before hunger.  
> Modesty made him its dwelling-place; and as Lust surpasses  
> The unchaste, so he surpassed Lust.  
> When mother Nature brought him forth into the world, she said:  
> “Others degenerate; this man is born for me.”  
> And Justice, which had wandered and almost abandoned the world,  
> He enclosed within his sacred breast.  
> A holy man from boyhood, who surpasses the world in renown  
> As much as he himself surpasses his renown.  
> Though fame, less than his merits, should fly through the whole world  
> And should grow forever, it would still not equal them.  
> A devout and grave man; in both respects so moderate  
> That Envy could gnaw at him in neither.  
> For Envy now laments the man whom it previously reviled;  
> It did not revile and hate him as much as it now praises and loves him.  
> As it formerly groaned at his life, so now it groans at his death,  
> And complains that his days departed so swiftly.  
> A man truly wise and blessed in every respect,  
> Who enriches heaven with his soul and earth with his body.  
> After death may I live with him, rest with him;  
> May my lot not become better than his lot.

§ 285. In these verses you see that the bishop exceeded the measure of praise. But such is the display of eloquence, such the gait of golden wit; in this manner

> Rich eloquence pours forth purple flowers.

Berengar, however, although he himself corrected his opinion, [Col. 1258C] could not convert all those whom he had corrupted from every land. So evil a thing it is to weaken others in goodness by example or word, because perhaps another’s sin will weigh upon you when your own has been blotted out. They say that Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, [Note: [Col. 1258D] Fulbert, whom the mother of the Lord, Mary, was once seen to heal while sick with milk from her breasts. See § 186.] whom the mother of the Lord Mary had once been seen to heal while sick with milk from her breasts, foretold this. For when many were visiting him as he lay at the point of death and the capacity of the house scarcely sufficed for the crowd, he scanned with his eye across the opposing groups and judged that Berengar must be expelled with whatever effort was possible, declaring that a monstrous demon stood there because of him and was corrupting many, enticing them to follow Berengar with a flattering hand and alluring breath. Indeed, when Berengar himself was dying on the day of Epiphany and, with a prolonged groan, remembered how many wretches he had infected with his sect in youth through the first heat of error, he said: “Today, on the day of His manifestation, my Lord Jesus Christ will appear to me—because of my repentance, I hope, for glory; or, because of others, I fear, for punishment.”

§ 286. We assuredly believe that, after the Church’s blessing, those mysteries are the true body and blood of the Saviour, persuaded both by the authority of the ancient Church [Col. 1259A] and by many miracles recently shown. Such was that which blessed Gregory displayed at Rome. Such was that which Paschasius relates to have occurred in Germany: the priest Plegildus visibly handled upon the altar the form of a boy, and, after devoutly bestowing kisses, received it in the likeness of bread according to the Church’s rite. Berengar, they say, used to censure this with arrogant mockery and say: “Surely a fine peace for a scoundrel: he gave the kiss of his mouth to one upon whom he inflicted the destruction of his teeth.” Such also was the story of the Jewish boy, who happened to enter a church with a Christian companion of his own age, in play and jest, and saw a boy being cut limb from limb upon the altar and distributed piece by piece among the people. When in childish innocence he told his parents that this was true, they thrust him into a furnace where, with the door closed, the fire raged. [Col. 1259B] Many hours later Christians drew him out without injury to body, clothing, or even hair; and when asked how he had escaped the devouring masses of fire, he replied: “That beautiful woman whom I saw sitting in the chair, whose son was divided among the people, always stood at my right in the furnace, driving away the threats of flame and the clouds of smoke with her veil.”

§ 287. Then in the Welsh district called Ros, the grave of Gawain was discovered. He was a nephew of Arthur through his sister and not unworthy of his lineage. He ruled in that part of Britain which is still called Gawain’s Land. A knight renowned for valour, he was expelled from his kingdom by Hengist’s brother and nephew, of whom I spoke in the first book; but before then he compensated for his exile at their great cost. He shared deservedly in the praise of his uncle because they delayed for many years the downfall of their collapsing country. But Arthur’s grave is nowhere to be seen; therefore the antiquity of tales still fables that he will return. The tomb of the other, however, as I have said, was discovered in King William’s time upon the seashore, fourteen feet long. Some maintain that he was wounded by enemies and cast ashore in a shipwreck; others say that citizens killed him at a public feast. Knowledge of the truth therefore wavers in uncertainty, though neither account lacks the support of tradition.

§ 288. This was the storm under which Germany groaned for fifty years at the wretched and [Col. 1259D] almost fatal empire of Henry, of whom I have spoken among William’s deeds. He was neither unlearned nor cowardly, but was attacked by all men through a kind of fate, so that whoever took up arms against him seemed to be dealing with the cause of religion. He had two sons, Conrad and Henry. The former, having attempted nothing impious against his father, subdued Italy and ended his days at Arezzo, a city of Tuscany. The latter, [Col. 1260A] attacking his father in the first trial of life when he had some respite from foreign enemies, compelled him to yield the empire; and not long afterward, when he was dead, celebrated his imperial funeral rites. He still lives, stubbornly following the very opinion for which he had thought his father should be persecuted: he grants the investiture of churches by staff and ring, and does not consider legitimate a pope elected without his approval, although Calixtus, who now presides over the apostolic see, [Note: [Col. 1259D] “Who now presides over the apostolic see,” etc. Pope Calixtus was made pope on 1 February 1119 and died on 12 or 13 December 1124.] has excellently restrained the man’s excessive greed. But let the reader wait for me to say more of these matters when the sequence of the narrative requires it.

§ 289. Further, after Pope Hildebrand died, and Urban was elected by the cardinals, the emperor persisted in his purpose of preferring Wibert, calling him pope, [Col. 1260B] and installing him at Rome after expelling the other. But the armed forces of Countess Matilda supported the fairer cause, as it seemed: [Note: [Col. 1259D] Countess Matilda. She was the daughter of Boniface, duke of Tuscany, and at her death bequeathed her immense possessions to the Holy See.] a woman who forgot her sex and, no less than the ancient Amazons, led armoured ranks of men into war. By her assistance Urban later obtained the apostolic throne and enjoyed secure tranquillity for eleven years. After him Paschal was appointed by the Romans, Henry’s authority being scorned. Wibert, the sole sower of schism, still burdened the upper air by living; as long as he lived he never laid aside his obstinacy so as to submit to the hand of justice, declaring that the emperor’s judgment must be followed, not that of Roman gladiator-trainers [Note: [Col. 1259D] “Gladiator-trainers,” etc. Sharpe suggests that by these words the author intended to ridicule the bloodthirsty habits of the Romans and papal bulls. In the dispute concerning the credibility of the arguments adduced, it is certainly established that the oral testimony of three bishops ought to be preferred to sheep-skins stained with ink and burdened with a lead seal. (EADMER, *Historia Novorum*, p. 65.)] or parchment-makers. Therefore both men, excommunicated by Urban at subsequent [Col. 1260C] [Note: [Col. 1260D] “Subsequent,” c. e.; “frequent,” a. s. d. l.] councils, suspended the sentence in witty mockery. Yet there was much in the emperor that one might approve: he was eloquent in speech, sharp in intellect, learned through extensive reading, diligent in almsgiving; in him one could perceive every excellence of mind and body. [Note: [Col. 1260D] “In him,” a. s. d. l.; “in it,” c. e.] He ran readily to arms, having fought in pitched battle sixty-two times; he settled disputes justly; and when affairs did not prosper, he turned his complaints toward heaven and expected help from there. Several of his enemies ended their lives by miserable deaths.

## Concerning the Man Torn Apart by Mice

§ 290. I heard a most truthful man relate that one of Henry’s adversaries, a powerless and factious man, while reclining at a feast with his neck thrown back, was suddenly surrounded by mice so that there was no escape anywhere. Their number was so great that no one would have thought so many existed in any province, however vast. Thus they were beaten for a long time with sticks and fragments of benches that came to hand, but to no effect; and although all were driven back, they inflicted retaliatory injury upon no one, pursuing that man alone [Col. 1261A] with their teeth and with a certain dreadful clamour. Therefore his servants carried him farther than an arrow’s flight into the sea; yet even so he did not escape the assault, for at once so great a multitude of mice flooded the sea that you would have sworn the water was paved with straw. But when they began to gnaw through the ship’s planks and the water entering through the cracks threatened an unquestionable shipwreck, the servants turned the stern back toward the shore. Then the animals, swimming alongside the keel, arrived on land before them. Thus the miserable man was set upon dry ground and immediately torn entirely to pieces, satisfying the dreadful hunger of the mice.

## That Mice Urinate upon Anyone Whom a Leopard Has Bitten

§ 291. I judge this less wonderful because it is certain that in Asiatic regions, if a leopard bites someone, a multitude of mice immediately comes to urinate upon the wounded man, so that an unclean deluge of urine accompanies the person’s death. But if, through the diligent activity of servants who ward them off, the danger has been avoided for nine days, the skill of physicians may surely be summoned with effect. My informant saw a man wounded in this way who, despairing of safety on land, put out to sea after casting anchor. Without delay more than [Note: [Col. 1261D] “More than,” c. d. e.; “more than a thousand,” s.; “over a thousand,” a. l.] a thousand mice swam there, enclosed in the rinds of pomegranates whose pith they had eaten out—marvellous to say—but they were drowned despite the sailors’ outcry. For that Parent of all things has left nothing created devoid of its natural faculty, and nothing harmful [Col. 1261C] without a remedy.

## Concerning Marianus Scotus

§ 292. Under the reign of this emperor flourished Marianus Scotus, [Note: [Col. 1261D] Marianus Scotus was born in Ireland in A.D. 1028. He was the compiler of a chronicle, first published in 1569, from the beginning of the world to his own time (A.D. 1082), which furnished the foundation for the work of Florence of Worcester. He seems to have died in 1086.] first a monk of Fulda, then [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Then,” c. d. e. l.; “immediately,” s.] a recluse at Mainz, who by contempt for the present life earned the grace of the future. After examining chronographers in the long leisure of his life, he detected a discrepancy between the cycles of Dionysius Exiguus [Note: [Col. 1262D] The discrepancy of the cycles of Dionysius Exiguus. Sharpe observes that this supposed correction of Dionysius rests upon an entirely erroneous foundation.] and evangelical truth. Accordingly, recounting each year from the beginning of the age, he added twenty-two years missing from the aforesaid cycles; but he had few or no adherents to his opinion. I often wonder why this misfortune afflicts the learned men of our age: among so great a number of students, amid so much pale nocturnal study, scarcely anyone attains the full praise of learning. So pleasing is inveterate custom; so nearly no one grants the clear light of assent according to their merit to new discoveries, even probable ones. With all their efforts men creep after the judgments of the ancients; everything recent is despised. Thus, because favour alone nourishes talents, when favour ceases all things have grown numb. [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Have grown numb,” a. s. d. e. l; “are numb,” c.]

## Concerning the Miracle That Occurred in the Monastery of Fulda

[Col. 1262A]

§ 293. But since I have named [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Named,” a. s. d. e. l; “named once,” e.] the monastery of Fulda, I shall tell what the reverend man Walkerius, prior of Malvern, related to me as having occurred there. Whoever does not believe his words does religion an injury.

> “It is not more than fifteen years,” he said, “since a deadly plague raged in that place. It first seized the abbot and soon killed many of the monks. At first the survivors each feared for himself and offered more abundant prayers and alms. But in the course of time, as is human nature everywhere, as fear diminished they gradually ceased these practices. The cellarer especially shouted publicly and ridiculously that the stores could not suffice for such expenses; he had lately hoped for some relief through so many funeral processions, but no further hope remained if the dead consumed what the living could not.  
>
> “One night, having long delayed sleep because of necessary business, he was at last proceeding to the dormitory, freed from the snares of delay. And behold—you will hear a marvellous thing—he saw in the chapter-house the abbot and all who had died that year sitting in the order in which they had departed. Terrified and eager to flee, he was forcibly drawn back, rebuked, and chastised with lashes according to monastic custom. He heard the abbot speak entirely to this effect: that it was foolish to long for profit from another’s death, since each person’s fate hangs under the same destiny; that it was impious for a monk, who had spent his whole life in the Church’s service, to lack even the allowance of a single year after death; that he himself would die very soon, but whatever might be done for him would be repaid for the benefit of the others from whom he had taken it; and that he should now go and correct by his example those whom he had corrupted by his speech.”  
>
> He went away; and by the still-fresh blows, as by his own imminent death, he showed that he had seen nothing unreal.

§ 294. Meanwhile, while we are engaged with other matters, the subject has crept in and the desire has arisen to set down what was decided in King William’s time concerning the dispute still being debated between the archbishops of Canterbury and York. So that posterity may know clearly what the ancient fathers thought concerning this matter, I shall append it.

## That All Bishops of the Whole of Britain Are Subject to the Archbishop of Canterbury

[Col. 1262D]

Pope Gregory to Augustine, first archbishop of Canterbury.

§ 295. “Your Fraternity shall have subject to it, by the authority of God our Lord Jesus Christ, not only those bishops whom you ordain, nor only those ordained through the bishop of York, [Note: [Col. 1262D] “Of York,” a. s. d. e.; “York,” c.] but also all the clergy of Britain.”

[Col. 1263A]

Boniface to Justus, archbishop of Canterbury.

§ 296. “Far be it from every Christian that anything should be diminished from, or altered in, that city of Dorobernia [Canterbury], now or in times to come, from what was established by our predecessor, Lord Pope Gregory, whatever upheavals human affairs may suffer. Rather, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we confirm and strengthen by this very command that the metropolitan see of all Britain shall forever hereafter be held in the city of Dorobernia; and we decree, with unimpaired and perpetual stability, that all the provinces of the kingdom of the English shall be subject to the metropolitan church of the aforesaid place. And if anyone should attempt to diminish this church, which stands in a special manner under the power and protection of the holy Roman Church, and should take anything from it of the right of authority granted to it, may God remove him from the book of life, and let him know that he is bound in the chains of anathema.”

473 Alexander to William, king of the English.

§ 297. “We have entrusted to our brother Bishop Lanfranc the careful reconsideration and determination of the case of Ælric, who was formerly called bishop of the church of Chichester. [Col. 1264A] Likewise, we have firmly enjoined and committed to him the business of deciding the dispute between the archbishop of York and the bishop of Dorchester concerning the extent [Note: [Col. 1263B] *Pertinacia*: c. e., *pertinentia*; s. d. l., *obtinientia*; a.] of their dioceses, that he may investigate this case with the most diligent inquiry and settle it by a just decision. In investigating and determining cases, moreover, we have so granted him the exercise of our own and apostolic authority that whatever he shall determine in them at justice’s prompting shall thereafter be held firm and inviolable, as though determined in our presence.” [Note: [Col. 1263B] *Teneatur* (“shall be held”). s. c. d. e. l. 2; in the margin of l. 1: “Here ends the section on William the Great. His laws, occupying nearly one folio, are missing.” A contains the laws of the Conqueror as follows:

“HERE ENDS THE SECTION ON WILLIAM THE GREAT, COUNT OF NORMANDY AND KING OF THE ENGLISH.

[Col. 1263C] “THE LAWS OF THE SAME BEGIN.

“William, king of the English, to all throughout England to whom this writing shall come: greeting and friendship. I command and order that the following be observed throughout the English nation: If an Englishman challenges a Frenchman to trial by combat concerning theft, homicide, or any matter for which combat ought to be undertaken, or concerning a judgment between two men, he shall have full permission to do so. And if the Englishman does not wish for combat, the challenged Frenchman shall clear himself against him by oath with his witnesses according to the law of Normandy.

“Likewise: if a Frenchman challenges an Englishman to combat over the same matters, the Englishman may freely defend himself by combat, or by judicial process if that pleases him more. And if he is alone—that is, infirm—and does not wish, or is unable, to fight, he shall seek a lawful defender for himself. If the Frenchman is defeated, he shall pay the king sixty shillings. And if the Englishman does not wish to defend himself [Col. 1263D] by combat or by testimony, he shall clear himself by God’s judgment [ordeal].

“Concerning all matters of outlawry, the king ordained that an Englishman should clear himself by judgment. And if an Englishman accuses a Frenchman of outlawry and wishes to prove this against him, the Frenchman shall defend himself by combat. If the Englishman does not dare to prove it against him by combat, the Frenchman shall defend himself by a straightforward oath, not by observance of verbal formulae.

“Likewise: the clear perception of truth and, finally, the experience of every individual have recognized that the king of England, by singular majesty, is lord of his realm. Since this results from the king’s renowned benevolence and justice and from the due fidelity of his subjects, the situation of the country also confidently assists it: enclosed by nature’s gifts and the proximity of the sea, it allows no one an exit or entrance without the gracious permission of its rulers. Hence such security and such abundance of every good has come to this people that, if it were governed by the honor of true reason, it would match [Col. 1264B] the former times of the Golden Age. But what calls it forth to such great advances is that, though free from every external disturbance and raised to such delights of joy, it nevertheless—as is the pitiable condition of mortals, namely, inclined to evil and prone to falling—always rages with internal rebellions of the mind and a blind striving after novelty.

“Thus, from the earliest beginning of the world’s birth, those whom God, the Maker of things, had enriched with equal [Col. 1264C] freedom, the stirring of inflamed disobedience cast out. And those who could not endure the Lord of heaven serve, distinguished by human wickedness, and, through continual persecutions of evils, are hurled into ever worse conditions. Yet divine mercy follows even the undeserving so greatly, and orders rulers by such instruction, that slavery may neither destroy some utterly nor unchecked security cast down those puffed up by it. It also continually visits kings, who outstrip others in the transitory splendor of pomp, with bodily weakness and very human necessities, through an entirely salutary care, lest they grow insolent in their power.

“For a king is not made by the fabulous inventions of the mob concerning rods of office, nor by the madness of frenzy or limitless acres, nor by ingenious feasting friendly to decay, nor by money wrenched from the laments of the poor. A king is not made by Tyrian garments, by beams shining with gold, by the color of his brow, or by royal vows. Rather, he is king who has set aside fears and the dreadful evils of his heart, whom powerless ambition and the never-stable favor of a headlong populace do not move. [Col. 1264D] He is king who empties himself of the foulness of a dreadful heart and watches diligently to benefit each individual—such men as were lately raised to the height of this eminence not by popular ambition but by moderation proven among the good. For gentleness is necessary for those set over others, and discipline for those subject to them. After men’s shrewd intention had penetrated every object, and nothing seemed disadvantageous in relation to money, wealth grew, envy grew, from envy hatred, from hatred war; faithfulness existed for no one, and almsgiving benefited no one. Yet if any traces of innate goodness remained, they enacted laws and rules of life; they established cities and trustworthy refuges so that innocence might be safe among the wicked. And those whom the very exhortations of uprightness do not stir should at least rest under fear of punishment. One law is natural, the same among all peoples; another is customary, in which every country possesses something of its own.”]

.”

474 THAT THE ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, AND ALL SUBJECT TO HIM, SHALL BE SUBJECT TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF DOROBERNIA.

[Col. 1264B] General council of the kingdom of the English concerning the right and primacy of the church of Dorobernia, or Canterbury.

§ 298. “In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1072, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander, and in the sixth year of the reign of William, glorious king of the English and duke of the Normans, by command of that same [Col. 1265A] Pope Alexander, with the assent of the same king, and in his presence and that of the bishops and abbots, the case concerning the primacy which Lanfranc, archbishop of Dorobernia, claimed over the church of York by right of his church was discussed; as were also the ordinations of certain bishops, concerning whom it was by no means certain to whom they especially belonged. At length it was proved and shown by various authorities of various writings that the church of York ought to be subject to Canterbury and that its archbishops ought in all things concerning the Christian religion to obey the directions of that church’s archbishop, as primate of all Britain.

“But the metropolitan of Canterbury granted to the archbishop of York and his successors possession of the subjection of the bishop of Durham—that is, Lindisfarne—and [Col. 1265B] of all the regions from the boundaries of the bishopric of Lichfield and the great river Humber to the furthest limits of Scotland, as well as whatever on this side of the aforesaid river rightfully belongs to the parish of the church of York. Thus, whenever the archbishop of Canterbury wishes to summon a council, wherever he thinks fit, the archbishop of York shall attend at his pleasure with all those subject to him and shall obey his canonical ordinances.

“Lanfranc, archbishop of Dorobernia, showed from the ancient custom of his predecessors that the archbishop of York ought also to make a profession to the archbishop of Canterbury under oath; [Note: [Col. 1265D] “Also under oath”: a. s. c. d. e. 2. l.; omitted in e. l.] but, out of love for the king, he released Thomas, archbishop of York, from the oath and received only a written profession, without prejudicing his successors should they wish to demand from Thomas’s successors an oath together with the profession. If the archbishop of Canterbury dies, the archbishop of York shall come to Dorobernia and, with the other bishops of the aforesaid church, shall duly consecrate as his own primate the man who has been elected. But if the archbishop of York dies, the man elected to succeed him, having received from the king the grant of the archbishopric, shall come to Canterbury, or wherever the archbishop of Canterbury pleases, and shall receive ordination from him according to canonical custom.

“To this constitution consented the aforesaid king; Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury; Thomas, archbishop of York; Hubert, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church and legate of the aforesaid Pope Alexander; and the other bishops and abbots who were present. This case had first been discussed at the city of Winchester during the Easter solemnity [Note: [Col. 1265D] *Solennitate* (“solemnity”): a. s. d. e. l.; *festivitate* (“festival”), e.], in the royal chapel situated in the castle; afterwards at the royal estate called Windsor, where it was brought to its conclusion in the presence of the king, bishops, and abbots of different orders, assembled at court for the feast of Pentecost.

[Col. 1266A] “The mark of King William.” “The mark of Queen Matilda.” “I, Hubert, reader of the holy Roman Church and legate of Lord Pope Alexander, have subscribed.” “I, Lanfranc, archbishop of Dorobernia, have subscribed.” [Note: [Col. 1266D] “I, Lanfranc, archbishop of Dorobernia, have subscribed”: a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.] “I, Thomas, archbishop of York, [477] have subscribed.” “I, William, bishop of London, have consented.” “I, Hermann, bishop of Sherborne, have subscribed.” “I, Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, have subscribed.” [Col. 1266B] “I, Walter, bishop of Hereford, have subscribed.” [Note: [Col. 1266D] *Subscripsi* (“I have subscribed”): e i; *consensi* (“I have consented”), s. e. 2. l.] “I, Giso, bishop of Wells, have consented.” “I, Remigius, bishop of Dorchester, have subscribed.” “I, Walkelin, bishop of Winchester, have subscribed.” “I, Herfast, bishop of Elmham, have subscribed.” “I, Stigand, bishop of Chichester, have consented.” “I, Siward, bishop of Rochester, have consented.” “I, Osbern, bishop of Exeter, have consented.” “I, Odo, bishop of Bayeux and earl of Kent, have consented.” “I, Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances and one of the chief men of the English, have consented.” [Col. 1266C] “I, Scotland, abbot of the monastery of Saint Augustine, have consented.” “I, Ælfwine, abbot of the monastery called Ramsey, have consented.” “I, Elnoth, abbot of Glastonbury, have consented.” “I, Thurstan, abbot of the monastery situated on the island called Ely, have consented.” “I, Wlnoth, abbot of the monastery called Chertsey, have consented.” “I, Ælfwine, abbot of the monastery of Evesham, have consented.” “I, Frederick, abbot of Saint Alban’s, have consented.” “I, Gosfrid, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, situated not far from London, have consented.” “I, Baldwin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Edmund, [Col. 1266D] have consented.” “I, Turold, abbot of Burgh, have consented.” “I, Adelelm, abbot of Abingdon, have consented.” “I, Ruald, abbot of the New Minster at Winchester, have consented.”

Profession of Thomas, archbishop of York.

§ 299. “It befits every Christian to be subject to Christian laws and not, on any grounds, to oppose the measures beneficially instituted by the holy fathers. For from this arise wrath, dissensions, envies, contentions, and the other things that plunge their lovers into punishments. [Note: [Col. 1267D] *Poenas* (“punishments”): c. d. e.; *poenas aeternas* (“eternal punishments”), a. s. l.] And the higher each person’s rank, the more earnestly ought he to obey commands. Therefore I, Thomas, now ordained metropolitan bishop of the church of York, having heard and understood the reasons, make to you, Lanfranc, archbishop of Dorobernia, and to your successors, an unqualified profession of canonical obedience; and I promise that I shall observe whatever is justly and canonically enjoined upon me by you or by them. While I still had to be ordained by you, I was uncertain about this matter; and therefore I promised that I would obey you without condition, but your successors conditionally.”

§ 300. In ancient times, moreover, as I remember having said in the first book, [Col. 1267B] [Note: [Col. 1267D] “As I remember having said in the first book”: §§ 99 ff.] the archbishop of Canterbury had these bishops: those of London, Winchester, Rochester, Sherborne, Worcester, Hereford, Lichfield, Selsey, Leicester, Elmham, Sidnacester, and Dunwich. In the time of King Edward the Elder there were added those of Cornwall, Crediton, Wells in Wessex, and Dorchester in Mercia, as I said in the second book. [Note: [Col. 1267D] “As I said in the second book”: §129.] The archbishop of York, however, had under his jurisdiction all bishops beyond the Humber: those of Ripon, Hexham, Lindisfarne, and Whithorn, which is now called Witerne, together with all bishops of Scotland and Orkney; just as Canterbury has the bishops of Ireland and Wales.

But the bishoprics of Ripon and Hexham had long since perished through hostile force; and those of Leicester, Sidnacester, and Dunwich, I do not know in what manner. Further, in the time of King Edward the Simple, Cornwall and Crediton were united and the bishopric was transferred to Exeter. Under King William, in this very council it was decreed, in accordance with the canons, that bishops moving from villages should establish [Note: [Col. 1268D] *Constituerent* (“should establish”): a. s. d. e. l.; *construerent* (“should build”), c.] their sees in the cities of their dioceses. The bishop of Lichfield therefore moved [Note: [Col. 1268D] *Migravit* (“moved”): a. s. d. e. l.; *transiit* (“transferred”), c.] to Chester, once called the City of the Legions; the bishop of Selsey to Chichester; the bishop of Elmham first to Thetford, and now, under Bishop Herbert, to Norwich; the bishop of Sherborne to Salisbury; and the bishop of Dorchester to Lincoln. The bishop of Lindisfarne had indeed long before moved to Durham, and recently the bishop of Wells to [Col. 1267D] Bath.

§ 301. At this assembly Lanfranc, still inexperienced in England, asked the senior bishops what was the order of seating in council established by ancient custom. Excusing the difficulty of an answer, they postponed it until the next day. Then, having summoned their memories with the utmost care, they declared that they had seen this custom: the archbishop of Canterbury, presiding over the council, should have at his right the archbishop of York, and beside him the bishop of Winchester; at his left, the bishop of London. But if, as happens, the primate of Canterbury has excused [Note: [Col. 1268D] *Negaverit* (“has refused”): c. d. e.; *excusaverit* (“has excused”), a. s. l.] his attendance for some necessity, or is absent through death, the archbishop of York, presiding over the council, should have the bishop of London at his right and the bishop of Winchester at his left; the others should recognize their seats according to the times of their ordinations.

480 § 302. Then too the complaint of the archbishop of York concerning his claim against the bishops of Worcester and Dorchester was decided and laid to rest. He said that they ought to be subject to his jurisdiction; and, after having long brooded on this in mute silence, when he went to Rome with Lanfranc to receive their pallia from the apostolic see, he publicly advanced it before the Roman senate. Lanfranc, though he was unshaken in firmness against every [Col. 1268B] injury, was nevertheless somewhat disturbed by so impudent and previously unheard-of a demand; he showed the movement of his anger in his face, after swallowing words for some time in his throat. But Pope Alexander, who was reluctant to grieve Lanfranc—for when Lanfranc arrived, he had honorably risen to meet him, declaring that this remarkable mark of reverence was paid not to the honor of the archbishopric but to love for his master—then likewise rejected from himself the odium of judging, [Note: [Col. 1268D] *Rejecit* (“rejected”): a. s. d. e. l.; *removit* (“removed”), c.] transferring arbitration of the dispute to a council of the English. Therefore, as I have said, when the matter had been much and long debated in this council, it reached this conclusion: because these bishops were on this side of the Humber, they should belong to Canterbury; but the archbishop of York should possess all those beyond the Humber.

[Col. 1268C] § 303. Here the holy simplicity—indeed, the great-hearted confidence in God—of blessed Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, merits praise and applause. Challenged both about this matter and about his slight knowledge of letters, he went out in order to seek his answer from more stringent counsel, with his mind removed from the turmoil. “Believe me,” he said, “we have not yet sung the sixth hour; let us therefore sing.” When his companions replied that they should first dispatch the business for which they had come, since there would be time more than sufficient for singing; and that the king and nobles, if they heard this, would think them objects of ridicule, he said, “Believe me, first [481] we shall perform God’s service, and afterwards deal with men’s litigation.”

When the hour had thus been sung, without any contrived evasion of falsehood or fabricated embellishment of truth, he immediately made to enter the council chamber. Though his men tried to hold him back, they could not persuade him, fearing as they did for the case. “Know certainly,” he said, “that I visibly see here the blessed archbishops Dunstan of Canterbury and Oswald of York, who today, protecting me by their prayers, will blunt the edge of false speakers.” Thus, after giving a blessing to a monk, a man of very little eloquence but acquainted with the Norman language, he pleaded the case and prevailed, so that he who had previously been thought unworthy to govern his own diocese was humbly asked by the archbishop [Col. 1269A] of York to deign to visit his territories, [Note: [Col. 1269D] *Partes* (“territories”): s.; omitted in a. c. d. e. l.] which the latter himself was wary of approaching for fear of enemies or through ignorance of the language.

§ 304. But I shall not further wear out the expectation of readers who perhaps do not look gladly upon these matters because they await the deeds of William’s successors. Yet, unless excessive self-regard deceives me, I think that no one will dislike this variety of narratives, unless he is so gloomy as to emulate Cato’s sternness. Those who wish will find other matters in the fourth and fifth books; for the third recognizes its due limit. [Note: [Col. 1269D] *Modum* (“limit”). In d. e., after *modum* follows the author’s dedicatory letter to Robert, earl of Gloucester, which we placed at the beginning of the work.]

483 PROLOGUE TO THE FOURTH BOOK.

[Col. 1269]

I know that it seems foolish to many that I have applied my pen to recording the deeds of the kings of our own time. They say that in writings of this kind truth is often shipwrecked [Col. 1269B] and falsehood assisted, since the evils of the present are spoken of perilously and its good things flatteringly. Thus, they say, because now everything [Note: [Col. 1269D] *Omnia* (“everything”), d. c.; *pene omnia* (“almost everything”), l.] tends more toward worse than better, the writer passes over evident evils out of fear [Note: [Col. 1270D] *Propter metum* (“out of fear”): a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.], and, if there are no good things, invents them for applause.

Others, measuring us by their own indolence, think us unequal to so great a task and pollute this pursuit with malicious disparagement. Therefore, long ago, struck either by their reasoning or by these men’s scorn, I had withdrawn into leisure, gladly acquiescing in silence. But after I had spent some time free from exertion in idleness, my accustomed love of study again pulled my ear and laid hold of my hand, because I could neither do nothing nor knew how to devote myself to these worldly concerns unworthy of [Col. 1269C] a man of letters. The encouragements of my friends were added; I ought not to have failed even their unspoken prompting. They modestly spurred me, already eager, to continue what I had begun. Thus encouraged by the exhortations of those whom I love with affection laid wholly aside, I rise up, that they may hold from the storehouse of my heart a pledge of friendship [484] that will live among them. [Note: [Col. 1270D] *Amicitiae* (“of friendship”): a. s. d. e. l.; *amicitiarum* (“of friendships”), c.]

Accordingly, grateful for the goodwill of those who fear for me lest I either be hated or tell lies, I shall, with Christ’s help, satisfy them in such a way that I shall be found neither a falsifier nor hateful. For I shall touch upon things well done and otherwise done in such a fashion that, as though a ship sailed unharmed between Scylla and Charybdis, nothing will be lacking in judgment, [Col. 1270B] even if something is thought lacking in the history. To those, moreover, who weigh down another’s labor by their own judgment, I answer what Saint [Note: [Col. 1270D] “Saint”: a. c. d. e. l.; omitted in s.] Jerome once threw at his dogs: “If it pleases them, let them read; if it does not please them, let them cast it aside.” For I do not force these things upon the weary, but dedicate them to students, if any deign to receive them. These men too will declare this to accord with justice [Note: [Col. 1270D] *Juri concinere* (“to accord with justice”): a. e. l.; *viri concinere* (“to accord with a man”), c. l.], unless they are among those of whom it is said: “Fools can easily be convicted, but are difficult to restrain.”

Therefore, in this book, the fourth of this work, I shall say whatever can be said of William, son of William the Great, so that neither the truth of events may falter nor princely majesty be discolored. Into these pages will also go certain things which occurred under him—sorrowful in this land, glorious elsewhere—[Col. 1270C] [Note: [Col. 1270D] *Acciderunt* (“occurred”): a. s. d. e. l.; *contigere* (“happened”), c.] insofar as our knowledge can reach. Especially, it will not be improper to insert here the pilgrimage of Christians to Jerusalem, because it is worth the effort to hear of so renowned an expedition in these days and because it is an incitement to courage. I do not indeed trust that these matters will be told more suitably by me than by others who have written them, but rather that what is written by many may be read by many. But lest such a long preface produce nausea in the reader, I shall now begin what I intend.

485 BOOK FOUR. CONCERNING WILLIAM RUFUS, KING, SON OF KING WILLIAM THE FIRST.

[Col. 1269]

[Col. 1269D] (A.D. 1087.) William, son of William, was born in Normandy many years before his father came to England. Brought up with great care by his parents, and possessing by nature a spirit that produced great things, he attained the summit [Col. 1270D] of the highest dignity. He was without doubt an incomparable prince in our age, had he not been overshadowed by his father’s greatness and had fate not cut short his youth, preventing him from erasing in more mature age [Col. 1271A] the errors contracted through license of power and youthful impetuosity. When childhood was past, he spent his youth in military exercise: riding, throwing the javelin, competing with his elders in obedience and with his equals in duty. He counted it a loss of courage if, in a military tumult, another happened to seize arms before him, or if he did not first challenge an opponent or unhorse one who challenged him. In all things he rendered obedience to his father, displaying himself before his eyes in war and walking at his side in peace.

As hope gradually welled up, he was already longing for the succession, especially after the renunciation [Note: [Col. 1271D] *Abdicationem* (“renunciation”). It can scarcely be believed that Robert abdicated voluntarily.] of his elder brother, since he was somewhat suspicious of his younger brother’s apprenticeship [Note: [Col. 1271D] *Nonnihil* (“something”): a. c. d. e. l.; *nihil* (“nothing”), s.]. Thus, when his father lay sick in his final illness, he was adopted as successor; before his father breathed his last, he hastened to occupy the kingdom. Soon he was received with willing hearts by the people of the provinces [Col. 1271B] and obtained the keys of the treasuries; relying on these, he brought all England beneath his sway.

There also contributed to his favor the archbishop Lanfranc, a factor of the greatest importance, because he had brought him up and made him a knight. [Note: [Col. 1271D] “Made him a knight.” According to the custom still prevailing in this age, bishops and abbots admitted knights into the equestrian order. A law was enacted by Henry I forbidding abbots to presume to make a knight.] With Lanfranc as adviser and supporter, he was crowned on the feast day of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Note: [Col. 1271D] “On the day of SS. Cosmas and Damian.” Their feast is celebrated on 27 September. Florence of Worcester and other authors maintain that William was crowned on Sunday, 26 September. According to the Saxon Chronicle, this occurred “three days before the feast of St Michael.”] (27 September), and lived through the remainder of winter quietly and favorably.

HOW KING RUFUS OVERCAME HIS OPPONENTS.

§ 306. When that winter had passed, his first conflict came at the beginning of spring [Note: [Col. 1271D] “At the beginning of spring.” The conspiracy was formed during Lent, and as soon as Easter came the conspirators went forth, etc. (Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 1088.)] against his uncle Odo, bishop of Bayeux. For Odo, as I have said, released from imprisonment, had confirmed his nephew Robert in the county of Normandy. He then came to England and received [Note: [Col. 1272D] *Recepitque* (“and received”): a. s. c. d. l.; *recepit* (“received”), e.—Odo was created earl of Kent in A.D. 1067.] [Col. 1271C] from the king the earldom of Kent. But when he saw that not everything in the kingdom was being arranged at his own will, as formerly—for the administration of public affairs had been entrusted to William, bishop of Durham [Note: [Col. 1272D] “William, bishop of Durham”: William of St-Calais.]—he was struck with envy and himself rebelled against the king.

He infected many with the same whisper: that the kingdom belonged to Robert, who was both of gentler disposition and had already worked off youthful follies through many labors; that this king, delicately reared, was swollen with arrogance of spirit, as his very face displayed, and would dare everything against divine and human law; that before long they would lose the honors gained long ago through many labors; that nothing had been achieved by the father’s death if the man whom he had bound should slay them. Odo said these things, as did Roger of Montgomery and Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, [Note: [Col. 1272D] “Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances.” Geoffrey de Montbray was made bishop of Coutances in 1048. He was the great justiciar of England and presided over the celebrated lawsuit between Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and Odo, bishop of Bayeux, in the county court held at Penenden Heath in Kent. He died 4 February 1093. In Domesday Book he is styled “bishop of Coutances”; elsewhere (fol. 165) he is called bishop of Saint-Lô, a city of Lower Normandy; and among the witnesses of the charter granted by the Conqueror to the monastery of St Augustine, Canterbury, appears “Bishop Golfryd of Seynt Loth.”] together with his nephew Robert, earl of Northumbria, and [Col. 1272A] the rest. At first they murmured secretly; afterwards they stirred openly, sending letters by mounted messengers.

William, bishop of Durham, whom the king had kept in his confidence, had even joined their treachery. The king is said to have borne this heavily, because, along with the loss of an affection, he was deprived of the advantage of remote provinces. Odo accordingly conveyed all plunder to Rochester, devastating the royal revenues in Kent, especially the lands of the archbishop. He breathed an undying hatred against Lanfranc because he asserted that he had been thrown into prison by his brother on Lanfranc’s counsel. Nor did the truth of his words waver. For when William the elder had once complained to Lanfranc that he was being deserted by his brother, Lanfranc said: “You, seize him and put him in chains.” “But what,” William replied, “because he is a cleric?” Then the [Col. 1272B] archbishop, with witty humor—as Persius says, [Note: [Col. 1272D] “As Persius says”: *Satires* I.85.] “balancing crimes of the shaven-headed in antitheses”—said: “You shall not seize the bishop of Bayeux, but keep the earl of Kent in custody.”

Bishop Geoffrey, with his nephew, devastated Bath, Berkeley, and part of Wiltshire, depositing his booty at Bristol. Roger of Montgomery, sending his army from Shrewsbury with Welshmen, plundered the settlement of Worcester; and he had already arrived threateningly at Worcester when the king’s soldiers, who were stationed in advance, relying on the blessing of Bishop Wulfstan, to whom the custody of the castle had been entrusted, put many to flight though few in number. Having wounded and killed many, they carried some away. Moreover, Roger Bigod at Norwich [Col. 1272C] and Hugh of Grandmesnil at Leicester pressed on with plundering, each in his own region.

Thus all the forces of rebellion raged in vain against one who lacked neither prudence nor good fortune. Seeing that nearly all the Normans had conspired in one frenzy, the king summoned by inviting letters the upright and brave Englishmen who still remained. Lamenting to them over his injuries, and promising good laws, relief from taxes, and free hunting, he bound them to his allegiance. With no less cunning he also outwitted Roger of Montgomery, who rode with him while concealing his treachery. Drawing him aside, he inspired great resentment, saying that he would gladly resign the sovereignty if that seemed good to him and to the others whom his father had left as guardians. He did not understand why they were so unrestrained: if they wished, let them take money as they pleased; if an increase of estates, likewise; in short, let them have whatever they wanted. Only let them see that their father’s judgment was not imperiled; if they considered him contemptible, [Col. 1273A] let them beware of his example in their own case, for he was the same king who had made them earls.

Inflamed by these words and promises, the earl, who had been the first standard-bearer of the faction after Odo, was the first to defect. He immediately marched against the deserters and broke into the castles of his uncle at Tonbridge and Pevensey, capturing Odo himself in the latter. He compelled him, when captured, to swear whatever oath he pleased: to leave England and surrender Rochester. [Note: [Col. 1273D] “And surrender Rochester”: a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.] He sent him ahead with his followers to perform this, following after at a slow pace.

[Col. 1273B] At Rochester there was then nearly all the noble youth of England and Normandy: [Note: [Col. 1273D] “And Normandy”: a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.] the three sons of Earl Roger, the younger Eustace of Boulogne, and many others whom I think below my concern. The king’s men, few and unarmed along with the bishop—for who would have feared treachery in his presence?—jumped down by the walls, calling to those in the town to open the gates: the bishop present wished this, the king absent commanded it. But the townsmen, seeing from the wall that the bishop’s expression did not accord with the envoys’ words, rushed out when the gates were hastily opened, mounted their horses, and led away everyone, bishop included, in chains.

News of this soon reached the king. More severe in adversity and swallowing his anger within himself, he called upon his Englishmen and ordered them to summon their countrymen to come to the siege, unless any wished to remain under the name *Nithing*, [Note: [Col. 1273D] *Nithing*. Matthew Paris writes of this word: “*Nithing*, which in Latin may be rendered *nequam* [worthless]. The English, who consider nothing more insulting or contemptible than this disgraceful term,” etc. Spelman conjectures that it may perhaps derive from *nidus* [nest] and *pullus* [young], and believes it to mean the same as *culvertagium*. Somner (*Gavelkind*, 56) supposes that *Nidering* denotes those so infamous that they plundered the dead.] which means “worthless.” The English, who considered nothing more miserable than to be branded [490] with the disgrace of this word, [Note: [Col. 1274D] *Aduri* (“to be burned/branded”): a. s. d. e. l.; *notari* (“to be marked”), c.] flocked to the king in bands and formed an invincible army. The townsmen could not endure longer without surrendering, having learned that however noble or however closely packed a force might be, it could accomplish nothing against the king of England.

Odo, captured a second time, renounced England forever. The bishop of Durham voluntarily crossed the sea; out of regard for their former friendship, the king allowed him to escape unharmed. All the rest were received back into allegiance. During these delays of the siege, the king’s men guarding the sea overwhelmed, partly by slaughter and partly by shipwreck, certain men whom the count of Normandy had sent to aid the traitors. The rest fled and tried to spread their sails; then, immediately abandoned by a failing wind, they became a mockery to our men and destruction to themselves. For, lest [Col. 1273D] they be captured alive, [Note: [Col. 1274D] *Ne* (“lest”): a. s. d. e. l.; *eum* (“him”), c.] they threw themselves from the benches into the sea.

ON THE PEACE BETWEEN WILLIAM AND ROBERT.

§ 307. In the following year (A.D. 1090), since grief always grows bitter through repeated recollection, the king began to consider very carefully how he might avenge his injuries and repay his brother’s insult in kind [Col. 1274A]. Accordingly, by his ingenuity—bribing the guards with money—he acquired the castle of Saint-Valery [Note: [Col. 1274D] Castle of Saint-Valery. See the Saxon Chronicle, A.D. 1090.], the neighbouring harbour, and the town called Aumale. The count had no intention of resisting; rather, through envoys he set before his lord, the king of France, the violence of his brother and asked for aid. That king, indeed, sluggish and reeking of his daily drunkenness, came belching and gasping from gluttony to the war; but the English king’s money, with its great promises, met him. Broken by it, he unfastened his belt and returned to the banquet.

Thus Normandy long suffered from civil war, now one side and now the other prevailing. The great men stirred up the fury of both: utterly fickle persons, faithful to neither side. A few, of sounder counsel, considering their own interests because they held possessions on both sides [Col. 1274B], acted as mediators of peace: the king was to obtain the county of Maine for the count, while the count was to yield to the king the castles which he held and the abbey of Fécamp. This agreement was sworn, and confirmed by the oath of the retainers of both parties (A.D. 1091).

## HOW WILLIAM AND ROBERT BESIEGED THEIR BROTHER HENRY AT MONT SAINT-MICHEL

§ 308. Not long afterwards the king crossed the sea in order to fulfil his pledged promises. Both leaders therefore made great preparations to invade Maine; but, when all was ready and they were on the point of departure, they were checked by the spirited action of their younger brother Henry. He was enraged [Col. 1274C] at his brothers’ greed: each was dividing the paternal possessions, while they were not ashamed to leave him almost entirely without a share. Accordingly, he occupied Mont Saint-Michel under arms, and by frequent sorties harassed the besieging forces of his brothers.

In that siege an outstanding example of character appeared in both king and count: gentleness in the one, greatness of spirit in the other. For the reader’s information I shall set down the marks of both examples. [Note: [Col. 1274D] Set down. a. s. d. e. l.; “imprint,” c.]

## OF WILLIAM’S GREATNESS OF SPIRIT

§ 309. The king left his tent and, seeing enemies proudly riding about at a distance, charged alone against many, impatient in the ardour of his courage and at the same time confident that none would dare withstand him. Soon, however, his horse—the one which he had bought that day for [Col. 1274D] fifteen marks of silver—was killed beneath him, and he was thrown down; he was even dragged for some distance by the foot. But the strength of his mail prevented him from being hurt.

The knight who had unhorsed him was already putting his hand to his sword-hilt to strike, when William, terrified by his extreme danger, cried: “Hold, rascal! I am the king of England!” At the familiar voice of the fallen man the crowd of soldiers trembled, and immediately, having respectfully raised him from the ground, they brought another horse. Without waiting for mounting assistance, he leapt upon the charger [Col. 1275A], swept all who stood around him with a keen glance, and said, “Who unhorsed me?” While all murmured, the knight conscious of his bold deed did not fail to speak in his own defence: “I did, for I did not think you a king, but a knight.”

Then the king, calm and serene of countenance, said: “By the Holy Face of Lucca”—for this was his oath—“from this moment you shall be mine; enrolled in my household, you shall obtain the rewards of honourable knighthood.”

Hail to your courage, most noble king! What praise could I offer you adequate to this saying? Your glory does not fall short of that of the great Alexander, who preserved unharmed, in admiration of his bravery, a Persian soldier who had attempted to strike him from behind, though the man’s treacherous sword had failed of its hoped-for effect.

[Note: [Col. 1275D] “By the face … of Lucca.” These words have often, but incorrectly, been translated: “By the face of Saint Luke!” The contrary is the meaning: “By the Face at Lucca!” As Lord Lyttelton says: “At Lucca in Tuscany there is an ancient image of Christ, said by its advocates to have been brought there miraculously. They call it *Il santo volto de Lucca* [the Holy Face of Lucca], and it is stamped on their coins with this legend: *Sanctus vultus de Lucca* [the Holy Face of Lucca]. In an Italian book entitled *Il Forestiere informato delle cose di Lucca* [The Visitor Informed about the Things of Lucca], this legend is explained in very great detail. The author maintains that it is the work of Nicodemus mentioned in the Gospel.” See a fuller treatment of this question in the Rev. J. E. Tyler’s highly worthwhile volume, *Oaths, their Origin, Nature, and History*. London, 8vo, pp. 289–296.]

## OF COUNT ROBERT’S GENTLENESS

[Col. 1275B] § 310. Now to speak of the count’s gentleness. When the siege had advanced so far that the besieged lacked water, Henry sent envoys to the count [493] to remonstrate with him about his thirst. It was wicked, they said, to bar him from water, which was common to mortals; otherwise, if he wished, let him test their valour, and let him fight not with the violence of the elements but with the courage of soldiers.

Then Robert, moved by his native softness of heart, ordered his men to keep looser guard where they were stationed, lest his thirsty brother should lack drink. When this was reported to the king, who was always prone to heat, he said to the count: “You certainly know how to wage war finely, supplying your enemies with an abundance of water! And how shall we subdue them if we indulge them in food and drink?” But Robert, smiling, uttered that gracious [Col. 1275C] and deservedly famous saying: “What? Should I let our brother die of thirst? And whom else shall we have if we lose him?”

Thus the king, mocking the disposition of the gentle man, abandoned the campaign. Since the Welsh and Scottish disturbances summoned him, he returned to his kingdom with both brothers, leaving unfinished the enterprise which he had intended.

§ 311. Immediately undertaking an expedition first against the Welsh and then against the Scots (A.D. 1091), he achieved nothing worthy of his magnificence: many soldiers were lost and pack-animals captured. Nor on that occasion only, but often, did he have little success against the Welsh. This may seem surprising to anyone, since in other matters the chances of war had always smiled most favourably upon him. But I understand that, just as their rebellion was aided by the unevenness of the ground and the harshness of the climate [Col. 1275D], so his military excellence was impeded.

King Henry, however, the man of outstanding ability who now reigns, discovered by what contrivance he might undermine their strength: he settled Flemings in their country, to serve as a barrier against them and restrain them continually. But at that time Count Robert, who had long enjoyed favour with the Scot, was active in bringing about peace between Malcolm and William [Col. 1276A]. Nevertheless, after many disputes on both sides and while justice wavered because of the fierceness of each party, Malcolm came of his own accord to Gloucester, asking only equitable terms and earnestly pleading for peace. [Note: [Col. 1276D] Pleading. a. d. e. l; “sinner,” s. c.] He gained nothing except permission to return unharmed to his kingdom [Note: [Col. 1276D] Return. a. d. e. l; “depart,” s. c.], for the king disdained to take by deceit one whom he had subdued by force (A.D. 1093).

The following winter Malcolm was killed by the men of Count Robert of Northumbria, more through treachery than strength. When news of his death arrived, his wife Margaret, distinguished for almsgiving and chastity, weary of the delay imposed by this life, begged God to grant her death. Both were eminent for their pious practice, but especially she. Throughout her life [Col. 1276B], wherever she was, she maintained twenty-four poor persons, whom she refreshed with food and clothing.

Moreover, anticipating the priests’ chant in Lent, she kept vigil by night in the church, herself attending three Matins—of the Trinity, of the Cross, and of Saint Mary—and then the Psalter, with tears flowing down upon her garment and with beatings of her breast. On leaving church she fed the poor: first three, then nine, then twenty-four, and finally three hundred, standing beside the king herself and pouring water over their hands. William restored her son Edgar, who had been expelled by his uncle, to the throne—an act of piety truly noble and worthy of so great a man: forgetting his father’s wrongs, he restored the suppliant son [Col. 1276C] to his kingdom.

§ 312. He excelled in greatness of spirit, which in the course of time he obscured by excessive severity. Thus vices crept secretly into his heart in the guise of virtues, so that he could not distinguish them. For a long time the world doubted to what outcome, to what direction, his character would finally incline. At the beginning, while Archbishop Lanfranc lived, he shrank from every crime, so that he was hoped to become the sole mirror of kings. After Lanfranc’s death, for a while he showed himself variable, with virtues and vices held in an equal balance. But in his final years, while zeal for good things froze, a growing crop of evils [Note: [Col. 1276D] “While zeal for virtues froze, the heat of vices boiled over in him,” s. c. d. e.; “while zeal for good things froze, a growing crop of evils grew hot,” a. l.] sprang up and burned fiercely. [Note: [Col. 1276D] Crop. s. c. e.; “crop or sluggishness,” d.]

He was so generous as to be wasteful, so high-minded as to be proud, so severe as to be cruel. Let it be permitted me, with due reverence for royal majesty, [Col. 1276D] not to conceal the truth: he revered God little and men not at all. Whoever calls this immoderate will not be wrong, for moderation ought to be observed by the wise: God is to be feared at all times, man according to circumstance.

In public and in gatherings he stood with haughty face, fixing upon the person before him a threatening eye and rebuffing one who spoke to him with a savage voice and affected sternness [Col. 1277A]. So far as one may infer, fear of poverty and of others’ treachery made him more devoted than was fitting to gain and severity. Indoors, however, and at table among his intimates, he was suited to every gentleness [Note: [Col. 1277D] Gentleness, d. e. l; “frivolity,” s.; “kindness,” a. c.]; he spent much time in jest. He was also a very witty mocker of any mistake he himself had made, so that he might dilute resentment at the deed and turn it into laughter.

But there will be a longer discussion of his generosity, by which he deceived himself, and afterwards of his other qualities, in order to show how many vices sprouted in him beneath the pretext of virtues.

§ 313. There are, indeed, two kinds of generous persons: some are called spendthrifts, others liberal. Spendthrifts are those who pour out their money on things which [496] will leave them either brief memory in the world or none at all, and no almsgiving before God. Liberal persons are those who ransom captives from robbers, relieve the needy, or assume the debts of friends. One should therefore give, but carefully and moderately. Many have squandered their patrimonies by giving without judgement. What, indeed, is more foolish than to take care, by doing gladly what you do, that you will be unable to do it for long? [Note: [Col. 1277D] “What indeed … for long?” Cicero, *On Duties*, II.15.]

Accordingly, some, when they have nothing to give, turn to plunder; and they acquire greater hatred from those from whom they take than gratitude from those upon whom they have bestowed. We regret that this happened to this king. At the very beginning of his reign, because fear of disturbances had led him to gather soldiers, he thought nothing should be denied them, promising still greater things in the future [Col. 1277C]. Having energetically exhausted his father’s treasures [Note: [Col. 1277D] Energetically, a. s. d. l; omitted in c. e.], and receiving only small revenues, he now lacked resources; yet his willingness to give did not fail, since through the habit of giving it had almost become his nature.

He was a man who did not know how to establish the price of anything or appraise a transaction: the seller disposed of goods as he pleased, and the soldier stipulated his own pay. He wished the price of his clothes to be raised without limit, taking offence if anyone lowered it. Thus one morning, as he was putting on [Note: [Col. 1277D] “As he was putting on,” s. c. e. l; “as he was putting on according to his pleasure,” a. d.] new stockings, he asked his chamberlain what they had cost. When the man replied, “Three shillings,” William exclaimed angrily and fiercely: “Son of a whore! Since when does a king have stockings of so paltry a price? [Col. 1277D] Go and bring me ones bought for a mark of silver.” The chamberlain went and brought much cheaper ones, falsely claiming that they had been bought for the price commanded. “Indeed,” said the king, “these are suitable to royal [497] majesty.” Thereafter the chamberlain charged whatever price he pleased for William’s garments [Col. 1278A], trafficking extensively for his own advantage.

§ 314. The fame of his generosity stirred the whole West and extended even to the East. Soldiers came to him from every province on this side of the mountains, and he rewarded them with the most lavish expenditure. Therefore, when he lacked anything to give, poor and exhausted, he turned his mind to revenues [Note: [Col. 1277D] Revenues, c. d. e; “plunder,” a. s. l.].

To the royal mind came Ranulf the clerk [Note: [Col. 1277D] Ranulf the clerk: Ralph Flambard, or Passeflabere. Raised to the dignity of bishop of Durham, he was consecrated on 5 June 1099. See *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 705.], a fuel for its greed, a man risen from the lowest rank through eloquence and cunning [Note: [Col. 1277D] Cunning, a. d. e. l; “assiduity,” s. c.] to the highest. Whenever a royal edict was issued requiring England to pay a specified tax, he added a second amount: a despoiler of the rich, a destroyer of the poor, a confiscator of other persons’ inheritances [Col. 1278B]. An unconquerable advocate, excessive alike in word and deed, he raged as much against suppliants as against rebels. Some repeatedly laughed and said [Note: [Col. 1277D–1280D] “Some laughing and saying,” s. c. d. e; “the king laughing and saying,” a. l.] that he alone knew how to exercise his talents in this way and cared nothing for others’ hatred provided he pleased his lord.

At his instigation the sacred benefices of churches, whenever their pastors died, were put up for sale. For as soon as the death of any bishop or abbot was heard, the king’s clerk was immediately sent there to record in writing everything found, and to transfer all future revenues into the royal treasury. Meanwhile an inquiry was made as to who might suitably replace the deceased—not by a test of character but by a test of money. At last the benefice, naked as it were, was given, though purchased at a high price [498]. These things seemed all the more outrageous because in his father’s time, after the death of a bishop or abbot, all revenues had been kept intact for surrender to the successor-pastor, and persons commendable for religious merit had been chosen. Yet in the span of a few years everything was changed.

No one was rich unless a moneylender; no cleric unless an advocate; no priest unless, to use a scarcely Latin word, a *firmarius*, a revenue-farmer. Any little man of whatever rank, guilty of whatever crime, was heard immediately if he made an appeal based on the king’s profit. A noose was untied from the very throat of a robber if he promised royal advantage. With military discipline dissolved [Note: [Col. 1278D] Military discipline dissolved. Compare Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, p. 94.], courtiers devoured the possessions of peasants, consumed their fortunes, and snatched food from the mouths of the wretched [Col. 1278D].
