Then appeared flowing hair, luxurious garments, and shoes [Note: [Col. 1278D] Shoes, etc. “Footwear of this kind, which provided occasion for so many and such varied edicts, is said to have had as its inventor the count of Anjou, to conceal his misshapen feet.” (*Orderic Vitalis*, p. 682), who also observes that they first received their final feature—the long curved point with which they ended—from a certain rogue in William Rufus’s court, named Robert (Sharpe, p. 386).] with curved points. To compete with women in softness of body, to mince one’s walk, and to proceed with loose bearing and one side [Col. 1279A] exposed, was the badge of young men. Enervated and effeminate, they remained unwillingly what they had been born; conquerors of others’ chastity, prodigal of their own. [Note: [Col. 1279C] “Conquerors … their own.” Orderic Vitalis censures nearly similar vices among the French, and especially among the Normans under Duke Robert.]

Bands of effeminates and troops of brothel-haunters followed the court, so that it was not without reason that a certain wise man said England would be fortunate if Henry reigned. He inferred this because Henry had detested obscenities from his youth. [Note: [Col. 1279D] “England would be fortunate … detested obscenities,” s. c. d. e; “the court of the king of England is not a lodging-place of majesty but a brothel of catamites,” a. l. L2 has “the court … brothel,” with the gloss: “Therefore England would be fortunate … detested obscenities.”]

§ 315. I would add to these things, if it were necessary [Note: [Col. 1279D] “I would add … necessary,” s. c. d. e; “it pertains to the disgrace of those times,” a. l.], that Archbishop Anselm attempted to correct them but, deserted by the support of his suffragans [Note: [Col. 1279D] “His,” a. s. c. d. e2. l; omitted in e1.], voluntarily departed, yielding to the hardness [Note: [Col. 1279D] Hardness, c. d. e; “wickedness,” a. s. l.] of the times.

Anselm—than whom no one was ever more steadfast in justice, no one in this age more anxiously learned, no one more profoundly spiritual—was the father of his country, the mirror of the world [Col. 1279B]. [Note: [Col. 1279D] Mirror, a. s. c. d. e2. l; “was a mirror,” e1.] As he waited in harbour for winds, on the very point of sailing, he was despoiled like a public robber [Note: [Col. 1279D] “Was despoiled,” d. e; “was despoiled by the king’s order,” l.]: all his bags and wallets were brought out and searched. I would say more about the wrongs done to him if the sun had seen anything more shameful than this alone; but I must also refrain in a history whose subject has already been pre-empted by the eloquence of the most reverend Eadmer. [Note: [Col. 1279D] Eadmer also wrote the *Life of Saint Anselm*.]

§ 316. You see how great a source of evils [Note: [Col. 1279D] Source of evils, s. c. d. e; “whirlpool of vices,” a. l.] sprang from what he considered generosity. Because, in correcting them, he displayed not so much diligence as negligence, he incurred great and scarcely erasable infamy. I believe this undeservedly, because one who remembered himself set over so great an empire would never submit himself to such disgrace.

Therefore I run through these matters in a hasty and unelaborated style [Col. 1279C], because I blush to speak ill of so great a king, striving to lessen and mitigate his evils. [Note: [Col. 1279D] Evils, d. e; “crimes,” l.]

§ 317. In his time the Jews gave evidence of insolence toward God. On one occasion at Rouen, trying to induce certain persons who had abandoned their error to return to Judaism by gifts; on another occasion in London, emboldened to enter into a contest against our bishops, because, I think in jest, he had said that if they defeated the Christians by open argument and refuted them, he would enter their sect. [Note: [Col. 1279D–1280D] “Their insolence … enter their sect,” s. c. d. e; “This was a sign of their insolence—or rather ignorance—against God. The Jews living in London, whom his father had brought there from Rouen, approached him at a certain festival bearing gifts; won over by them, he even dared to encourage them to a contest against Christians. ‘By the Face of Lucca!’ he said, declaring that, if they prevailed, he would enter their sect,” a. l. Compare Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, p. 47.]

The matter was thus conducted amid great fear among bishops and clergy [Col. 1280A], who feared for the Christian faith with pious concern. In this contest, however, the Jews gained nothing except disgrace, though they often claimed that they had been overcome not by argument but by faction.

§ 318. At a later time, that is, about the ninth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1280D] “At a later time … ninth,” s. c. d. e; “On another occasion he gave evidence of equal arrogance, for …,” a. l.], when Count Robert of Normandy had resolved to go to Jerusalem at Pope Urban’s urging—as will be related later—he mortgaged Normandy to his brother for ten thousand marks (A.D. 1096). Consequently, an edict imposing an unbearable levy ran throughout England.

Then many bishops and abbots approached the court [Note: [Col. 1280D] Court, s. c. d. e; “the king,” a. l.], complaining of this exaction and saying that they could not meet so great a tax unless they drove away the wretched peasants altogether. [Note: [Col. 1280D] Drive away: *effugarent*, s. d; *effugerent*, c1, l2; *effugent*, c2, e1, l1; *effugaret*, a; *effugient*, e2.] The courtiers [501], with the harsh expression customary to them [Note: [Col. 1280D] Courtiers, s. c. d. e; “he,” a. l. “Were accustomed,” s. c. d. e; “was accustomed,” a. l.], replied: “Do you not have coffers made of gold and silver, full of dead men’s bones?” [Note: [Col. 1280D] “They reply,” s. c. d. e; “he replies,” a. l.] They deigned no other answer to those who begged them. [Note: [Col. 1280D] “Deigned,” s. c. d. e; “deigned,” singular, a. l.]

Thus they, understanding where the answer tended, stripped the shrines of saints, despoiled crucifixes, and melted chalices—not for the use of the poor but for the royal treasury. For almost everything preserved by the frugality of holy forefathers [Note: [Col. 1280D] Forefathers, a. s. c. d. e2. l; “others,” e1.] was consumed by the greed of those plunderers. [Note: [Col. 1280D] “Those plunderers,” s. c. d. e; “one man,” a. l.]

§ 319. They nevertheless continued to prey upon men [Note: [Col. 1280D] “They preyed upon,” s. c. d. e; singular, a. l.], first taking money and then lands. Poverty protected no poor person, nor wealth the rich. Hunting, which the king had initially permitted, he prohibited so strictly [Col. 1280C] that to catch a deer was a capital offence.

Accordingly, by much severity, which no sweetness tempered, it came about [Note: [Col. 1280D] “Accordingly … it came about,” d. e; “By these practices he had so driven provincial affection from himself,” l.] that plots were often formed by magnates against his life. One of these was Robert de Mowbray, earl of Northumbria. After a substantial quarrel of words had arisen between him and the king, he returned to the province under his jurisdiction, intending great enterprises against his lord. But the king pursued him; he was captured and bound in perpetual chains.

Another, William of Eu, accused before the king of treason, challenged his accuser to judicial combat. While he cleared himself only sluggishly, he was blinded and castrated. [Col. 1281A] That accusation implicated many others—entirely innocent [Note: [Col. 1281D] Entirely, a. d. e. l; omitted in s. c.] and upright men. Among them was William of Aldrie, a man of handsome appearance and the king’s *compater* (spiritual kinsman). Ordered to be put on the gallows, he confessed to Bishop Osmund of Salisbury and was scourged through all the churches of the town. Then, after his clothes had been distributed to the poor, he went naked to the hanging, bloodying his delicate flesh by frequent kneelings on stones.

With bishop and people following to the place of punishment, he made this declaration: “So may God help my soul and free it from evils [Note: [Col. 1281D] Free, a. d. e. l; “rescue,” s. c.] as I am innocent of the charge for which [Note: [Col. 1281D] “Of the charge for which,” d. e1; *de re qua*, a. c. e2. l; *de hac re qua*, s.] I am accused. The sentence pronounced against me will indeed not be recalled, but I wish all men to know my innocence.” Then, after he had spoken this commendation of his soul and been sprinkled with holy water, the bishop departed [Col. 1281B]. He was hanged, displaying astonishing courage: neither about to die did he groan, nor in dying did he draw out a sigh.

§ 320. Yet there are certain examples of the king’s splendid greatness of spirit which I shall not begrudge to posterity. While he was intent on hunting in a certain forest, a messenger detained him with news from overseas that the city of Le Mans was besieged—a city which, after his brother’s departure, he had recently added to his own authority. As soon as he was ready, therefore, he turned his horse and set out for the sea (A.D. 1099).

When magnates advised him to summon, equip, and marshal an army, he said: “I shall see who follows me. Do you suppose that I shall lack men? If I know my young men, they will be willing to come to me even through shipwreck.” [Col. 1281C] Thus he reached the sea almost alone. The sky was then cloudy and the wind contrary; the violence of the blast swept the sea’s surface. When he wished immediately to cross, the sailors begged him to await a calm sea and gentler winds. “But,” said the king, “I have never heard that a king perished by shipwreck. Rather, cast off the ships’ moorings; you will see that the elements, now united, obey me.”

When he had crossed the sea, the besiegers scattered upon hearing of his arrival. The author of the disturbances, a certain Elias, was captured. When he was brought before the king, William said mockingly: “I have you, master!” [Note: [Col. 1281D] “Said,” a. c. d. e. l; “says,” s.] But Elias’s lofty nobility did not know how, even in so great danger, to think humbly [Note: [Col. 1281D] “But his lofty nobility did not know,” a. d. e. l; “but he, whose lofty nobility did not know,” s. c. “Humbly,” a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.] or speak humbly: “You captured me by chance,” he said, “but if I could escape, I know what [Col. 1281D] I would do.”

Then William, almost beside himself with anger and goading Elias, said: “You rascal! You—what would you do? Go on, depart, flee! I grant you leave to do whatever you can; and, by the Face of Lucca [Col. 1282A], if you conquer me, I shall demand no payment from you for this favour.” His act fell no short of his word: he immediately allowed him to escape, admiring rather than pursuing the fugitive. [Note: [Col. 1281D] Elias, count of Le Mans, captured by Robert of Bellême in 1098 and delivered into the king’s hands, redeemed his freedom only by surrendering Le Mans, as Orderic Vitalis testifies.]

Who would believe such things of an unlettered man? Perhaps someone reading Lucan [Note: [Col. 1282D] Lucan, *Pharsalia*, II.515, v. 580.] will wrongly suppose that William borrowed these examples from Julius Caesar. But he had neither inclination nor leisure enough ever to attend to letters. Rather, innate ardour of mind [Note: [Col. 1282D] Mind, a. s. c. d. e2. l; omitted in e1.] and conscious courage compelled him to perform such deeds. And certainly, if our Christianity permitted it, just as the soul of Euphorbus was once said to have passed into Pythagoras of Samos, so it might be said that the soul of Julius Caesar passed into King William.

§ 321. He began [Col. 1282B] and completed one building, itself a very great one: a residence in London. [Note: [Col. 1282D] “He began a residence in London.” From this passage it has been inferred that Malmesbury meant to say that the Tower of London was built by William Rufus. Yet it is sufficiently clear that the principal structure, now called the White Tower, was begun by the Conqueror and completed by William Rufus under the supervision of Gundulf, bishop of Rochester.] He spared no expense, so long as he displayed the magnificence of his generosity.

From what we have said the reader may observe his character. If anyone wishes to know his physical appearance, let him know that he was squarely built, ruddy in complexion, with yellowish-red hair, a broad-open forehead, and eyes of different colour, marked by certain glinting specks. He possessed exceptional strength, though he was not tall, and had a somewhat protruding belly. He had no eloquence, but a noticeable stammer, especially when anger rose. Under him many sudden and grievous events occurred, which we shall arrange individually according to his years, serving truth especially according to the authority of the chronicles.

[Col. 1282C] § 322. In the second year of his reign, a great earthquake terrified all England on the third Ides of August (11 August, A.D. 1089), with the dreadful marvel that all buildings seemed to leap away from one another and soon settled again in their former manner. A scarcity of every kind of produce followed. The crops ripened so late that harvests were scarcely stored by the feast of Saint Andrew. [Note: [Col. 1282D] “Every,” a. s. c. d. e2. l; omitted in e1.]

§ 323. In the fourth year there were storms of lightning and movements of whirlwinds. Finally, on the Ides of October (15 October, A.D. 1091), at Winchcombe a stroke sent from heaven struck the side of a church tower with such force that, after the wall at the edge of the roof had been weakened, it opened a great hole as large as a human body. Entering there, it struck a very large beam [505], so that fragments were scattered throughout the church. [Note: [Col. 1282D] “Were scattered throughout the church,” a. d. e. l; “were scattered through the whole church,” s. c.] It also threw down the head of the crucifix with its right shin, and the image of Saint Mary. A most foul odour followed, unbearable to human nostrils. At last the monks, boldly breaking in [Col. 1283A], drove away the enemy’s deceptions by sprinkling holy water.

§ 324. What event unknown to all ages was that? A conflict of winds at variance with one another, coming from the east-southeast, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November (17 October), broke down more than six hundred houses in London. [Note: [Col. 1283D] Six hundred, a. s. c. d. e. l; “hundreds,” s., variant reading.] Churches fell upon houses, walls upon walls. The fury of the winds dared an even greater outrage: it lifted the roof of the church of Saint Mary called “at the Arches,” and buried two people there. Beams and timbers were carried through the air—a spectacle to those watching from afar, terror to those standing near, lest they be crushed.

Four beams, twenty-six feet long, were driven into the ground with such force that scarcely four feet remained above it. It was a remarkable sight how they had broken through the hardness of the public roadway [Col. 1283B], standing there in the same arrangement in which an artisan’s hand had placed them in the roof, until, because they impeded passers-by, they were cut down level with the ground, since they could not otherwise be extracted.

§ 325. In the fifth year (A.D. 1092), the same violence of lightning at Salisbury completely shattered the roof of a church tower and greatly damaged the masonry—on the fifth day after Osmund, bishop of illustrious memory, had dedicated it.

§ 326. In the sixth year (A.D. 1093), there was such a flood of rain and such a storm of downpours as no one remembered. Soon, as winter arrived, rivers froze so solidly that riders and carts could pass over them. Before long, when the ice thawed, the force of the ice-crusts broke the bridges [Col. 1283C].

§ 327. In the seventh year (A.D. 1094), agriculture failed because of the taxes which the king, while in Normandy, had ordered. Famine immediately followed its failure; and as famine also grew severe, a mortality of men followed, so frequent that care for the dying and burial for the dead were lacking. At that time the Welsh, raging against the Normans, laid waste the county of Chester and part of Shropshire, and took Anglesey by force of arms.

§ 328. In the tenth year, on the Kalends of October (1 October, A.D. 1097), a comet appeared, for fifteen days sending out a greater tail toward the east and a lesser one toward the east-southeast. Other stars also appeared, as though shooting darts at one another. That was the year in which Anselm, the light of England, voluntarily fleeing the darkness of the erring [Col. 1283D], went to Rome.

§ 329. In the eleventh year (A.D. 1098), Magnus, king of the Norwegians, together with Harold, son of Harold, formerly king of England, subdued by arms the Orkney Islands, the Mevanian Islands, and whatever other islands lie in the ocean. He was already obstinately seeking to attack England through Anglesey, but the earls Hugh of Chester and Hugh of Shrewsbury met him and drove him away by force before he landed on the mainland [Col. 1284A]. Hugh of Shrewsbury fell there, pierced from afar by an iron spear.

§ 330. In the twelfth year (A.D. 1099), a tidal wave ascended the river Thames and drowned many villages with their inhabitants.

§ 331. In the thirteenth year (A.D. 1100), which was also the last of his life, many calamities occurred. Most terrible was this: the devil visibly appeared to people in woods and lonely places, speaking to travellers. Moreover, in Berkshire, at the village of Hampstead [Note: [Col. 1283D] Hampstead, a. s. c. d. e. l; “Finghamsted,” s., variant reading.], for fifteen continuous days a spring poured forth blood so abundantly that it stained the neighbouring ford. He heard these things and laughed [Note: [Col. 1283D] Laughed, s. c. d. e; “chattered,” a. l.], paying heed neither to dreams about himself nor to the visions of others.

§ 332. People tell many things both foreseen and foretold about his death [Note: [Col. 1283D] Death, s. c. d. e; “demise,” a. l.]. Of these I shall communicate to readers three, on the testimony of credible reporters.

Eadmer, a historian of our times commendable for the truthfulness of his integrity, says that the noble exile Anselm—together with whom all religion, as it were, was in exile—came to Marcigny in order to lay the complaints of his cares before the conscience of Hugh, abbot of Cluny. There, when conversation turned upon King William, the said abbot declared that on the preceding night that king had been brought before God and, after a judgement weighed in the balance, had undergone the sorrowful sentence of condemnation. [Note: [Col. 1284D] Condemnation, a. s. c. d. e2. l; omitted in e1.]

How Hugh knew this he did not then explain, nor did any hearer ask. Yet, because of the dignity of his religious life, no one present had any doubt as to the credibility of his words [Col. 1284C]. Hugh’s life and reputation were such that all revered [Note: [Col. 1284D] Revered, a. s. c. d. e. l; “received,” s., variant reading.] his utterance and admired his judgement, as though an oracle had sounded forth from a heavenly entrance. Not long after the king was killed, as we shall relate, a messenger came requesting that the archbishop would deign to return to his see.

§ 333. On the day before he departed this life [Note: [Col. 1284D] *Departed this life.* d. e.; *perished*, l.], he saw in a dream that blood was being let from him by the stroke of a phlebotomist; that the stream of gore, stretched as far as heaven, darkened the light and interrupted the day. Therefore, calling aloud upon Saint Mary, he started from sleep, ordered a light brought in, and forbade the chamberlains to leave him. 508 Then for several hours before dawn [Note: [Col. 1284D] *Before dawn.* a. s. c. d. e 2. l.; *before-dawn*, e 1.] he kept some watch. A little later, when dawn was already preparing to bring in the day, a monk from beyond the sea reported to Robert [Col. 1284D] fitz Haimo, a man foremost among the magnates, a wondrous and dreadful dream which he had seen that same night concerning the king: that he had entered a certain church and, with proud and insolent bearing, as was his custom, looked scornfully upon those standing about him. Then, seizing the crucifix with his teeth, he had gnawed away its arms and almost cut off its legs. The crucifix had endured this for a long time, but at last had thrust the king away so forcefully with its foot that he fell backward; from the mouth of the prostrate man [Col. 1285A] such an outpouring of flame issued that the whorls of smoky clouds even licked the stars [Note: [Col. 1285C] *That the whorls of smoky … licked [the stars].* s. c. d. e. l.; *that the vastness of the smoke darkened even the stars*, a.].

Robert judged that this dream was not to be disregarded and immediately conveyed it to the king, since he was one of his intimates. But the king, doubling his bursts of laughter, said: “He is a monk, and, for the sake of money, dreams in monkish fashion; give him one hundred shillings.” Yet, greatly disturbed, he long hesitated whether to go into the forest as he had intended, his friends advising him not to test the truth of dreams at his own cost. Accordingly, before eating he abstained from hunting, venting in serious business the rawness [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Rawness.* a. d. e. l.; *cruelty*, s. c.] of his untamed mind. It is said that on that day he feasted lavishly and brightened his brow with cups more frequent than usual.

Immediately after the meal, therefore, he hastened into the woodland, attended by few men. The closest of them was [Col. 1285B] Walter, surnamed Tirel [Note: [Col. 1285D] *Walter surnamed Tirel.* The widespread received tradition is that William Rufus was killed by the hand of Walter Tyrell while hunting in the New Forest. But Suger, a contemporary historian and apparently a friend of Tyrell, alluding in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, king of France, to the death of William Rufus, observes: “Certain persons laid upon a nobleman, Walter Tyrell, the charge that he had pierced him with an arrow. Since he neither feared nor hoped for anything, we have often heard him affirm under oath, as something almost sacred, that on that day he had neither come into that part of the forest in which the king was hunting nor seen him anywhere at all in the forest.” See also Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, p. 54, and Orderic Vitalis, *Historia Ecclesiastica*, book X, p. 783.], 509 who had come from France, attracted by the king’s generosity. When the others had scattered during the delay of the hunt, wherever chance had carried each, he alone remained with the king.

And now [Note: [Col. 1285D] *And now.* a. s. c. d. e 2. l.; *And therefore*, e 1.], as Phoebus was declining toward Ocean, the king drew his bow and shot an arrow at a stag passing before him, but did not inflict a sufficiently savage wound. For a long while he pursued the still fleeing animal with the vigour of his eyes, holding up his hand against the violence of the sun’s rays. Then Walter, conceiving in his mind a noble exploit—so that, while the king was meanwhile looking elsewhere, he might bring down another stag which happened to pass close by—unaware and unable to restrain himself, pierced the royal breast (good God!) with a fatal shaft. The wounded king uttered no word; [Col. 1285C] but after breaking off the wooden arrow where it projected from his body, he at once fell upon the wound and hastened death (2 August, A.D. 1100).

Walter ran up; but, since the king drew neither breath nor voice, he swiftly mounted his horse and escaped successfully by the aid of his spurs. Nor indeed was there anyone to pursue him: some connived, others pitied, and all at last busied themselves with other designs. One party secured its refuges; another drove off stolen plunder; another already looked about for a new king. A few countrymen placed the corpse in a horse-drawn cart and carried it down to Winchester, to the bishopric, blood dripping in waves along the whole [Col. 1286A] road. There, within the enclosure of the tower, amid the gathering of many nobles and the lamentation of few, it was committed to the earth.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] *There followed … had been buried.* s. c. d. e.: Nor were there lacking opinions of certain persons who said that the collapse [Col. 1286C] of the tower, which occurred in later years, had happened because of his sins: since it was an outrage that one who throughout his life had been grasping and dissolute, and who even in dying lacked Christian viaticum, should be buried in a consecrated [Col. 1286D] place, a. l.—The tower fell on 7 October 1107. *Annals of Winchester*, *Anglia Sacra*, part I, p. 297.]

In the following year 510 the tower collapsed. What opinions there were about this matter I spare myself from reporting, lest I seem to believe trifles [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Believe trifles.* c. d. e.; *believe bare trifles the more*, s.], especially since, owing to instability of construction, the fabric might have fallen even if he had never been buried there. He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, in the thirteenth year of his reign, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, more than forty years old: a man aspiring to great things, and destined to accomplish great things, had he been able to unwind the threads of the Fates or break and struggle free from Fortune’s violence. So great was his force of spirit that he dared promise himself any kingdom whatsoever [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Any kingdom whatsoever.* a. c. d. e. l.; *any kingdom*, s.].

Finally, asked on the day before his death where he would celebrate his Christmas feast [Col. 1286B] [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Celebrate.* s. d. e.; *keep*, l.], he replied, “At Poitiers,” because the Count of Poitou, eager to go to Jerusalem, was said to be about to pledge his land to him for money. [Translator’s note: the supplied text reads *invadaturus*, apparently a corruption of *invadiaturus*, “about to pledge”; this contextual emendation fits *ei terram suam pro pecunia*, “his own land to him for money.”] Thus, not content with his paternal possessions and carried away by hope of greater glory [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Carried away.* a. c. d. e. l.; *sought after*, s.], he pursued honours not rightly his own. To men of sacred order he was a man most to be pitied, because of the harm to his soul, whose salvation they labour to restore [Note: [Col. 1286D] *They labour to restore.* c. e.; *they cannot restore*, a. s. d. l.]; to hired soldiers, wonderful for the abundance of his gifts; to provincials, not to be regretted, because he allowed their substance to be stripped away [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Allowed … to be stripped away.* s. c. d. e.; *stripped away*, a. l.].

I do not recall that in his time any council was held [Note: [Col. 1286D] *I recall.* s. c. d. e.; *he permitted*, a. l.] in which, after offences had been weakened, ecclesiastical vigour might be strengthened. He deliberated for a long time before granting ecclesiastical dignities, whether for profit or for weighing [Col. 1286C] merit [Note: [Col. 1286D] *He deliberated … merit.* s. c. d. e.: but, because he was borne headlong by greed for money, he kept declaring that sacred offices belonged to his own jurisdiction, a. l.], so that on the day on which he died 511 he held in his own hand three bishoprics and twelve [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Twelve.* s. c. d. e. l.; *fourteen*, a.] abbeys vacant of pastors. Moreover, taking advantage of the occasion on which Urban at Rome and Guibert at Ravenna were at odds with one another, he refused tribute to the Roman see; yet he was more inclined to Guibert’s favour, because the fact that that man, beloved by God, pronounced Urban the apostolic pope and the other an apostate was the tinder and incentive of the discord between him and Anselm.

## CONCERNING THE CISTERCIANS

§ 334. In his days the Cistercian religion [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Cistellensis.* s. c. d. e. l.; *Cisterciensis*, a.] began, [Col. 1287A] which is both believed and called the best road of the highest ascent to heaven [Note: [Col. 1287D]

*Now is the best path of the highest ascent into heaven.*

*Now the best path of supreme ascent bears them to heaven.*  
(Juvenal, *Satires* I.38.)

A similar allusion to the Cistercian order, as though it were the safest road to heaven, may be seen in the prologue to Richard of Devizes: “How much higher the cell of the Carthusians is, and nearer to heaven, than the cloister of Winchester.” (*Chronicle of Richard of Devizes*, ed. Joseph Stevenson.)].

It does not seem inconsistent with the work I have undertaken [Note: [Col. 1287D] *Of the work undertaken.* s. d. e.; *with the undertaking work*, l.] to speak here of it, since it pertains to England’s glory that she produced such a man, who was both author and mediator of this religious order. He was ours, and as a boy began the apprenticeship of his earliest years in our school. Therefore, if we are not envious, we embrace his virtues more graciously in proportion as we acknowledge him more nearly our own; and at the same time I intend to raise his praises, because a mind is noble if it approves in another a good which it sighs to find absent in itself.

He was named Harding among the English, born of no very obscure parentage. As a boy he was a monk at Sherborne [Note: [Col. 1288D] *At Sherborne.* a. s. c. d. e. l.; *at Cineburn*, s., variant reading.]; but when, as a young man, the nettle of the world stung him, he detested those garments 512 and made first for Scotland, then for France. There, after several years’ training in the liberal arts, he received the impulses of divine love. For, when a stronger age had put away boyish follies, he set out for Rome with a cleric who was his companion in study; and neither the length and difficulty of the journey nor lack of resources could ever prevent them, going and returning alike, from singing the whole Psalter every day.

Surely the spirit of the man already breathed forth what, not long afterward, through God’s grace, he undertook. Returning to Burgundy, he cut off his hair at Molesme, a new and great monastery; and at first he readily recognized the elementary principles of the Rule which he had once seen. But when other observances were set before him, which he had neither read in the Rule [Col. 1287C] nor seen anywhere, he began to demand their reason—modestly, indeed, and as becomes a monk:

“By reason the supreme Author of things made all things; by reason He governs all things. By reason the fabric of the heavens revolves; by reason even those stars which are called wandering pursue their courses; by reason the elements move; and by reason and equilibrium [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Equilibrium.* a. c. d. e. l.; *uniformity*, s.] our nature ought to subsist. But because through negligence it often falls away from [Note: [Col. 1288D] *From.* a. s. c. d. e 2. l.; omitted in e 1.] reason, many laws were formerly enacted; and most recently, through blessed Benedict, a Rule came forth by divine agency to recall the flux of nature to reason. Though that Rule contains some things whose rationale I am unable to penetrate [Note: [Col. 1288D] *I am unable.* a. d. e. l.; *I am not able*, s. c.], I nevertheless judge that we must rest content with authority.

“For reason and the authority of the divine writings, though they appear discordant, are one and the same. [Col. 1287D] For since God created and renewed nothing without reason, how can I believe 513 that the holy Fathers, who are God’s followers, prescribed anything contrary to reason, as though we owed faith to authority alone? Therefore produce either reason or authority for the things which you forge. Although not much credit should be given if anything from human reason can be alleged which may be overthrown by arguments of equal force. Therefore give examples from the Rule, which rests upon reason and authority, being, as it is, dictated by the spirit of all the righteous. If you cannot, you profess in vain the prerogative of one whose teaching you disdain to follow.”

§ 335. This opinion, spreading, as often happens, from one person to others, rightly stirred the hearts of those who feared God, lest perhaps they were running or had run in vain. After the question had been debated at frequent chapters, it came to this conclusion: that the abbot himself approved the opinion that superfluities should be set aside and that the marrow of the Rule alone should be pursued. Accordingly two brothers were chosen, in whom knowledge of letters [Col. 1288B] corresponded with religious devotion, to investigate by reciprocal discussion the intention of the author of the Rule and set what they had discovered before the others.

The abbot worked diligently to win the assent of the whole community. But because what has long taken root is difficult to tear from human minds, because men unwillingly spit out what they have drunk in with their first saliva, almost all refused to accept [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Accept.* a. d. e. l.; *receive*, s. c.] the new measures because they loved the old [Note: [Col. 1288D] *They loved.* s. l.; omitted in a. c. d. e.]. Only eighteen, among whom was Harding, also called Stephen, persevered in holy obstinacy and, with their abbot, left the monastery. They declared that the Rule’s purity could not be preserved in a place where both heaps of wealth and abundance of food would stifle even a reluctant mind.

They therefore came to Cîteaux, a place formerly 514 [Col. 1288C] wooded, but now so conspicuous for the thronging religious life of monks [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Conspicuous.* a. c. d. e. l.; *visible*, s.] that it may deservedly be judged conscious of the Divinity Himself. There, with the support of the Archbishop of Vienne, who is now pope [Note: [Col. 1288D] *Who is now pope:* Calixtus II, A.D. 1119–1124.], they began a work memorable and venerable in every age.

§ 336. Many of their practices certainly seem harsh, but especially these. They wear nothing of fur or linen, nor that finely woven woollen material which we call *staminium*; they never wear drawers except when travelling, and on their return restore them washed. Having two tunics with cowls, they take no additional clothing in winter; but in summer, if they wish, they receive some relief. They sleep clothed and girded, and at no [Note: [Col. 1288D] *And at no.* a. c. d. e 2. l.; *not at any*, s.; *at no*, e 1.] time return to bed after Matins. Rather, they regulate the hour of Matins so that it is daylight before Lauds; [Col. 1288D] they devote themselves so closely to the Rule that they judge not one iota or stroke to be passed over.

Immediately after Lauds they sing Prime; after Prime they go out to work at the appointed hours. Whatever is to be done or sung during the day they complete without an external lamp. No one is ever absent from the daytime Hours or from Compline, except the sick. After hearing Compline, the cellarer and guest-master serve guests, while observing silence with the utmost care. The abbot permits himself nothing which is not permitted to others; he is everywhere present, everywhere carrying concern for his flock. Only when they are eating is he absent, because his table is always with pilgrims and the poor.

Nevertheless, wherever he may be, he abstains from words and from delicacies; for never are more than two dishes set before either himself or others, and fat and meat are never served except to the sick. From the Ides of September until Easter, with no regard to any feast except Sundays, they break their fast only once a day. They never leave the cloister except for work; nor do they converse with one another there or anywhere else except with the abbot or prior. They continue the canonical Hours without weariness, adding no external supplement [Note: [Col. 1289D] *Supplement.* a. e. l.; *appendage*, s. c. d.] except the vigil for the dead. In the divine offices they regularly use the Ambrosian chants and hymns, as far as they have been able to learn them from Milan. Caring for guests and the sick, they devise crosses unbearable to their bodies for the remedy of souls.

§ 337. At first that abbot himself did these things with great zeal and compelled others to do them [Note: [Col. 1289D] *Compelled.* s. d. e.; *compelled [them] to do [them]*, l.]; but as time passed, the man, delicately reared and finding such prolonged sparing of food hard to endure, repented. The monks who remained at Molesme, learning his wish, drew him back to the monastery—whether by certain words or also by letters is uncertain—by a stratagem under obedience to the pope [Col. 1289C] [Note: [Col. 1289D] *Draw back.* d. e.; *draw him back*, a. s. l.], compelling him though willing. Thus, as though wearied by the importunity of petitioners, he left the narrow walls of the poor and returned to a more august throne.

All who had come with him from Cîteaux followed him, except eight. Few in number but great in merit, these appointed from among themselves an abbot named Alberic and Stephen as prior. Alberic did not remain alive for more than eight years, and happily met his final destiny. Then Stephen, though absent, was chosen abbot also, doubtless by divine nod: the former leader of the entire enterprise, a special and eminent glory of our times. His merit is attested by the sixteen abbeys already established through him and seven begun. 516 Thus he, God’s resounding trumpet, directs those around him toward heaven both by word [Col. 1289D] and by example, doing nothing beneath the commandment. He is gracious in speech, cheerful in countenance, and ever joyful in soul in the Lord.

Hence the manifest joy of his distinguished face; hence, secretly, that refreshing dew which comes from above, because, disdaining this sojourn, he longs continuously and lovingly for his homeland. By these qualities he is held dear by all, because God has graciously poured the affection for the man whom He loves into human hearts. Therefore whoever sends his money through that man’s hand to [Col. 1290A] God counts himself blessed as a native of that land [Note: [Col. 1289D] *To God.* a. s. e 2. l.; *to him*, c. d. e. l.]. He indeed receives much, but, after spending little upon his own and his household’s needs, immediately distributes the rest among the needy and for the building of monasteries. Stephen’s purse is the public treasury of all the needy.

The evidence of his abstinence is that there one sees nothing, as in other monasteries, gleaming with gold, shining with gems, or flashing with silver. For, as Gentilis says, “What is gold doing in a holy place?” We judge that too little has been done with sacred vessels unless the honour of stones overshadows the crust of heavy metal, whether with the flame of topazes, the violet of amethysts, or the grass-green radiance of emeralds; unless priests’ vestments play with gold; unless walls shine with many-coloured paintings and summon the sun to their ceilings. But they, regarding what mortals falsely prize first as secondary [Col. 1290B] things, place all their care in adorning their character and love shining minds more than gilded garments, knowing that the best recompense of benefactors is to enjoy a clean conscience.

Indeed, even when the mercy of their praiseworthy abbot either wishes, or pretends to wish, to relax something of the Rule’s yoke, they strive against it, 517 saying that not much of their life remains, that they will not live as long as they have lived; that they hope to persevere in their purpose and to be an example to successors, who will sin if they are relaxed. And in truth this will come to pass because of human weakness, whose perpetual law is that nothing won by the greatest labours can endure for long. But, to gather into one sum all that has been said or can be said concerning them: the Cistercian monks today are the training-ground of all monks, the mirror of the diligent, the gadfly of the idle.

## CONCERNING THE TRANSLATION OF THE THREE BISHOPRICS OF WELLS, CHESTER, AND THETFORD

§ 338. In these times three bishoprics in England were transferred from their ancient seats to others: Wells, by John, to Bath; Chester, by Robert, to Coventry; and Thetford, by Herbert, to Norwich—all with more ambition than ought to have concerned men of such distinction [Note: [Col. 1289D] *All with more ambition … distinction.* s. c. d. e: all through the wickedness of money, all through the ambition [Col. 1290D] and sacrilege of venality, l.].

Finally, to begin with the last: Herbert, surnamed Losinga because the art of flattery had fastened that name upon him, bought the bishopric of Thetford while abbot of Ramsey; and his father Robert, of the same surname, was also intruded into the abbacy of Winchester [Col. 1290D]. Thus that man was a great source of simony in England, hunting after abbey and bishopric with money; that is, ensnaring royal attention with money and whispering no small promises into the favour of princes. Hence a distinguished versifier of that time wrote:

> A monster rises in the Church, Losinga its father,  
> Of the sect of Simoniacs, cut off from the virtue of the canons.  
> 518 Peter, you delay too long: Simon attempts lofty things;  
> Had you been present, Simon would not have flown on high.  
> [Note: [Col. 1290D] *Would not have flown on high.* This alludes to the legend of Saint Peter and Simon Magus, who attempted to fly by magical arts, but was cast down to earth at Peter’s adjuration and killed. See Fabricius, *Codex Apocryphus*. (Sharp, 402.)]  
> Alas! Churches are sold for coins and bronze.

[Col. 1291A]

> And below:  
> The son is bishop, the father abbot; both are Simon.  
> What may we not hope, if we possess money?  
> Money has everything; it does what it wishes, adds, and removes.  
> A thing most unjust: by money a bishop and an abbot are made.

## CONCERNING HERBERT LOSINGA

§ 339. Yet repentance effaced the wandering impulse of youth. In more mature years he went to Rome, where, laying down simony, staff, and ring, he deserved to be received again by the pardon of the most merciful see. For the Romans judge it more holy and orderly that the revenues of all churches should serve their own purses rather than minister to the needs of whatever kings.

Thus Herbert, returning home, transferred the episcopal seat, formerly at [Col. 1291B] Elmham and then at Thetford, to a notable town distinguished for commerce and the multitude of its people, called Norwich. There he established a congregation of monks celebrated for both its numbers and its religious observance, purchasing for them from domestic funds all necessities. He was, that is, providing against the complaints of successors: he granted the monks none of the episcopal lands, lest, if they found any gift which they judged belonged to their own possessions, they should deprive God’s servants of provisions.

Moreover, at Thetford he established Cluniac monks, because the professed members of that monastery, scattered almost throughout the whole world, are wealthy in secular things and most splendid in devotion to God. Thus, by a great and abundant grace of virtues, he overshadowed the mass of his former offences. He was worthy of regard even by Roman eminence for eloquence and abundance of learning, no less than for practical knowledge [Col. 1291C] of secular affairs.

And Herbert was changed—“the turning-point and change of affairs,” as Lucan said of Curio. As he had been an advocate of simony in the time of this king, so later he was its invincible repeller; nor did he wish others to do what he had once rashly undertaken in youthful ardour and afterward regretted. He always had before him, as they say, Jerome’s dictum: “We erred when young; let us amend when old.” Finally, who can fittingly proceed to praise that deed of his, by which a bishop not very rich made so noble a monastery? In it one vainly seeks nothing—whether in the appearance of lofty buildings, the beauty of ornaments, the monks’ religious devotion, or their diligent charity toward all. These things caressed him in life with happy hope; and after death, if faith in repentance is not vain, bore him above the heavens [Col. 1291D].

## CONCERNING JOHN, FIRST BISHOP OF BATH

§ 340. John was bishop of Wells, a native of Tours; a physician approved by practice rather than by letters. Upon the death of the abbot of Bath, he obtained the abbey from [Col. 1292A] the king without difficulty [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Without difficulty.* a. s. c. d. e 2. l.; *oppressing*, e 1.], because everything at court was conducted for sale, and because a rationale seemed to cloak greed: that so notable a city should receive a more celebrated name from a bishopric.

Accordingly, at first he exercised severity toward the monks, because they were dull and barbarous in their own estimation. He withdrew all the lands that supplied their food 520 [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Withdrawing.* s. d. e.; *taking away*, l.] and had a scanty subsistence brought in meagrely by laymen [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Laymen.* d. e.; *his laymen*, a. s. l.]. But as the years went on, once new monks had been made, he behaved more mildly, allowing the prior a small amount of land [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Land by which.* l.; *land through which*, s. d. e.] by which he and his guests might somehow support themselves.

Although at first he had begun somewhat harshly [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Although at first he had begun somewhat harshly.* s. d. e.: and although he was almost wholly of a foolish and little steadfast disposition, l.], many things were nobly begun and completed there through him, in ornaments and books, and especially in the community of monks, who are praiseworthy for knowledge of letters and diligence in [Col. 1292B] office [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Office.* c. d. e.; *offices*, a. s. l.] [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Praiseworthy.* c. d. e.; *comparatively praiseworthy*, a. s. l.]. Yet he never, not even at death, wished to amend [Note: [Col. 1292D] *Wished to amend.* d. e.; *could be softened*, a. s. l.; *could be amended*, c.] matters by liberating with a full hand the service due from the lands; he left [Note: [Col. 1292D] *Leaving.* c. d. e.; *bequeathing*, a. s. l.] his successors an example not to be imitated.

## CONCERNING ROBERT, BISHOP OF CHESTER

§ 341. [Note: [Col. 1292D] *There was in the diocese of Chester … vindicating.* a. s. c. e. l.; the whole section is omitted in d. m.]

In the diocese of Chester there was a monastery called Coventry, which the most magnificent earl Leofric, as I said above, had founded with his wife Godiva. Its display of gold and silver was so great that even the walls of the church seemed too narrow to contain the treasures [Note: [Col. 1292D] *To contain the treasures.* a. s. e. l.; *for displays*, c.], a marvel indeed to the eyes of those who saw it. Robert, bishop of that same province, coveting it, swooped upon it in a manner unbefitting a bishop [Note: [Col. 1292D] *In a manner unbefitting a bishop.* s. d. e.; *in the manner of a robber*, l.]. From the very treasures of the church [Col. 1292C] he stole what would fill the hand of the donor [Note: [Col. 1292D] *Of the donor.* s. d. e.; *of the king*, l.], what would elude the pope’s demands, and what would worm its way into Roman greed. He stayed there for many years and showed no virtue whatever.

He never removed the danger from roofs that threatened collapse; he dissipated the sacred wealth so thoroughly that he incurred the crime of embezzlement, a bishop liable for extortion—if only there had been an accuser ready. He fed the monks on miserable rations and cared neither to kindle in them love of the regular order [Note: [Col. 1292D] *To kindle.* a. c. e. l.; *attenaere* [uncertain or corrupt reading].], nor allowed them to aspire beyond elementary learning [Note: [Col. 1292D] *To aspire.* a. c. e. l.; *to ascend*, s.], lest either abundance of food make them pampered or the strictness of the Rule and strength of learning make them proud against him. Content, then, with rustic fare and commonplace learning, they had enough if only they could live in peace.

Indeed, when about to die, making little of the canons which prescribe that bishops ought to be buried in their own sees, he ordered that he be buried not at Chester but at Coventry [Col. 1292D], leaving to successors, in his own view, not an improper ground for complaint, but something like a lawful right to claim.

[Col. 1293A] § 342. Here the opportunity of the times would encourage William to set forth the translation of Augustine, the pre-eminent apostle of the English, with his companions, had not the skill of the highly learned Goscelin [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Goscelin.* Goscelin’s *Life and Translation of St Augustine* was published in the *Acta Sanctorum*, Antwerp, 26 May.] preceded him. Goscelin, a monk of Saint-Bertin, had once come to England with Herman, bishop of Salisbury, and was distinguished by his knowledge of letters and chant. Travelling for a long time through many bishoprics and abbeys, he left monuments of excellent learning in many [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Many.* s. d. e.; *more numerous*, l.] places; in praises of the saints of England he was second to none after Bede [Note: [Col. 1293D] *To none.* a. c. d. e.; omitted in s. l.]. In music he attained the palm after Osbern.

Finally, he set forth in modern style innumerable 522 lives of saints; he refined and renewed those of the ancients, whether lost through hostile violence or published in an unformed manner. He likewise polished the account of this translation so that he seems [Col. 1293B] to have pointed it out with a finger to those present and set it before the eyes of those to come. Happy the tongue that served so many saints; happy the breast that sent forth so many vocal melodies, especially since integrity vied with learning in his manner of life!

Yet, because I have thus far composed matter concerning some bishops that is little praiseworthy, I shall introduce certain bishops of another kind and contrasting life, though contemporaries, lest our age seem to have grown so dull as not to have produced some saint. But whoever wishes may test this promise in the following book, after the deeds of King Henry have been narrated.

## A CERTAIN PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING NARRATIVE

§ 343. Now I shall set forth in writing the journey to Jerusalem, presenting in my own words the things others have seen and thought. Accordingly [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Accordingly.* a. c. d. e.; *Moreover, thence*, s. l.], as occasion offers, I shall weave in extracts culled from the writings of earlier authors concerning the situation and riches of Constantinople, Antioch, and Jerusalem, so that one who does not know them, but perhaps finds these matters, may have at hand what he himself may set before others for their knowledge. But to narrate these matters a more fervent spirit is needed, so that I may effectively complete what I begin so gladly. Therefore, having invoked the Divinity for help [Note: [Col. 2193D] *For help.* a. d. e. l.; omitted in s. c.], as is customary, I shall seek such an opening.

## CONCERNING THE JOURNEY OF THE CHRISTIANS TO JERUSALEM

§ 344. In the year 1095 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Pope Urban II, who presided over the apostolic summit, crossed the Alps and came into Gaul. The evident reason given for his coming was [Col. 1293D] that, expelled from Rome by Guibert’s violence, he might summon the churches on this side of the mountains to reverence for himself. A more secret purpose was not so widely publicized: by Bohemond’s counsel he would stir almost the whole of Europe to an Asiatic expedition, so that, amid so great a disturbance of all the provinces, with auxiliaries easily burdened by debt, Urban might seize Rome and Bohemond Illyricum and Macedonia. For Bohemond claimed that those lands, and whatever besides stretches from Dyrrhachium to Thessalonica, belonged by right to him, because his father Guiscard had acquired them from Alexius; while he himself lacked the Apulian inheritance which his father had assigned to his younger son, Count Roger [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Count.* c. d. e.; *younger*, a. s. l.].

Whatever the occasion of the crossing may have been, his coming was of great and conspicuous benefit to Christians. A council was therefore convened at Clermont, the most celebrated city of the Auvergnats. The number of bishops [Note: [Col. 1293D] *The number of bishops.* s. d. e.; *the number of bishops assembled was*, l.] and abbots was three hundred and ten. There, for several days, prolonged discussions were first held concerning the Catholic faith and peace among those [Col. 1294B] at variance with one another [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Among those at variance with one another.* s. d. e.; *of those who were at variance with one another*, l.].

For, besides the offences to which individuals freely devoted themselves, all the peoples on this side of the Alps had reached such a pitch of calamity that, on no cause at all or the slightest pretext, each would seize another and would not permit him to depart except after a great ransom. Moreover, the serpentine evil of simony had raised its slippery head so high and steamed forth the eggs of a poisonous brood of deadly seed so copiously that it infected the whole world with its deadly hissing and corrupted ecclesiastical offices. For then, I do not say that bishops aspired to churches, but no one at all aspired to any order except through money.

Then, lawful wives having been put aside, many divorced, assailing another’s marriage. Therefore, because in these matters and in others there was a confused [Col. 1294C] forest of crimes, the names of certain more powerful men were singled out for punishment. To avoid prolixity, I shall append the proceedings of the whole council, abbreviating some things in my own words for brevity.

## CONCERNING THE COUNCIL OF CLERMONT
§ 345. At the council held at Clermont, in the presence of Pope Urban, the following chapters were concluded.

[Note: [Col. 1294D] Clermont. The Council of Clermont in Auvergne continued from 18 to 28 November, A.D. 1095. At it the decrees of the councils held by Pope Urban at Melfi, Benevento, Troia, and Piacenza were confirmed, and new canons were enacted. The account given by Malmesbury is perhaps the better account of this most celebrated council. See *Acts of the Council of Clermont*; *Councils*, vol. XII, p. 829, etc.]

That the Catholic Church be sound in faith, chaste, and free from every servitude.

[Note: [Col. 1294D] “That . . . servitude.” s. d. e.: “That the Church be Catholic in faith, chaste in purity, free from every secular servitude,” l.]

That bishops, abbots, or any member of the clergy shall not receive any ecclesiastical dignity from the hand of princes or of any laymen. That clerics shall not hold prebends in two churches or cities. That no one may at the same time be bishop and abbot. That ecclesiastical dignities shall neither be bought nor sold by anyone.

[Col. 1294D] That no one in any sacred order shall engage in carnal intercourse. That those who, unaware of the canonical prohibition, have bought canonries be forgiven. That those who knowingly possessed offices bought by themselves or by their parents [Col. 1295A] shall be deprived of them.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] “Possessed.” s. d. e.: “held,” l.]

That no layman from the beginning of the fast, and no cleric from Lent until Easter, shall eat meat. That at all times the first fast of the Ember seasons shall be observed in the first week of Lent. That ordinations shall at all times be celebrated either on Saturday evening or, with the fast continuing, on Sunday; that on Easter Saturday the office shall not be celebrated before the ninth hour; and that the second fast shall be observed in the week of Pentecost.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] “Be observed in the week of Pentecost.” s. d. e.: “be held at Pentecost,” l.]

That from Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany, from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, from the first day of the Rogations until the octave of Pentecost, and at all times from sunset on Wednesday until sunrise on Monday, the Truce of God shall be observed.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] The Truce of God. The Truce of God arose in Aquitaine. Its name derives from the eagerness with which it was initially received by all. While it was in force, no one dared, on the appointed days, to violate it by attacking an enemy. It fell under censure from certain bishops as an occasion for perjury, and was rejected by the Normans as contrary to their privileges. (DUCANGE, *Glossary*, vol. VI, pp. 682–685. Compare also ROBERTSON’S *Charles V*, vol. 1.)]

[Col. 1295B] That whoever seizes a bishop shall altogether be held an outlaw. That whoever seizes men in sacred orders or their servants shall be anathematized. That whoever seizes the goods of bishops or clerics at their death shall be anathematized. That whoever contracts a union within the seventh degree of consanguinity shall be anathematized.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] “Seventh.” d. e. l.: “sixth,” s.]

That no one shall be elected bishop unless he is a priest, deacon, or subdeacon, and is supported by the dignity of birth—unless there be the utmost necessity and papal permission. That sons of priests or concubines shall not be promoted to the priesthood unless they have first lived a religious life. That those who have fled to a church or to a cross shall, once immunity from mutilation has been granted, be handed over to justice, or, if innocent, released.

[Col. 1295C] That every church shall possess its own tithes, and that they shall not pass to another. That no layman shall either buy or sell a tithe.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] “A tithe.” c. d. e.: “tithes,” a. s. l.]

[Note: [Col. 1295D] “Neither buy nor sell.” s. d. e.: “neither sell nor retain,” l.]

That no payment shall be received for the burial of the dead.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] “Received.” c. d. e.: “exacted,” a. s. l.]

At that council the lord pope excommunicated Philip, king of the Franks, and all who should call him either king or lord, obey him, or speak with him, except in matters concerning his correction. Likewise, he excommunicated that accursed wife of his and all who should call her queen or lady, until they should amend matters so that each departed from the other.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] “At that council he excommunicated . . . departed from the other.” It is beyond doubt that King Philip, together with his concubine Bertrada, was struck with anathema by Urban at the Council of Clermont; but no French writer known to us before Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines and a thirteenth-century author, asserted that Urban also forbade anyone to obey him or to address him as lord and king. Indeed, the trustworthiness of this assertion is refuted by the course of history itself: among those Frenchmen who believed Philip lawfully excluded from the communion of the faithful, we read of none who on this account renounced obedience to him. (Note in BOUQUET, XIII, 6.)]

Likewise, he excommunicated Guibert of Ravenna, who calls himself pope, and Henry, emperor of the Germans, who supports him.

[Col. 1296A] § 346. In the days following, a notably eloquent and effective address was delivered to the people, such as befits a priest—

[Note: [Col. 1296D] “A priest.” s. d. e.: “a pontiff,” l.]

—concerning the expedition of Christians against the Turks. Since I received it from hearers, I have thought fit to transmit it to posterity, preserving the full sense of its words.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] “Transmit.” Other speeches are said to have been delivered by Urban at this council and have come down to us. Labbe published one of them in *Councils*, vol. X, from a Vatican manuscript. (SHARPE, 410.)]

For who could preserve the force of that eloquence? We shall proceed successfully if, while treading the nearby course, we return by some bypath to the subject.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] “Return.” s. d. e.: “run back,” l.]

527

## ADDRESS OF POPE URBAN

§ 347. “You recall, dearest brothers,” he says, “the many things that have been said to you these days: some commanded in our council, some forbidden. The unformed and confused chaos of crimes required an interval of many days; the inveterate disease called for cautery.

[Col. 1296B] For while with the indulgent cord of mercy we let down the line, many things now offend the office of our apostolate—things which it should cut off, none to which it should spare itself. But let what you have sinned hitherto be attributed to human frailty: that, lulled by the entanglements of pleasures, you have provoked heavenly mercy, lightly esteeming wrath held in suspense. Let it be attributed to worldly drunkenness that, disregarding lawful marriages, you have not weighed the wrong done to another’s bed. Let it be attributed to excessive greed that, ensnaring your brothers—purchased at that great and identical price—as each was able, you shamefully squeezed money from them.

Now, though you stand amid these shipwrecks of sins, a harbour of tranquil peace is opened to you, if you do not neglect it. In exchange for a small labour [Col. 1296C] against the Turks, a permanent station of everlasting salvation will be rendered to you. Compare now the labours which you have had in the practice of wickedness with those you will have on the journey which I command. The contemplation of adultery or murder brings many fears—for nothing is more fearful than wickedness, as Solomon says—

[Note: [Col. 1296D] “Solomon.” s. d. e.: “Wisdom through Solomon,” l.]

—and many labours; for nothing is more cowardly than wickedness, and what is more laborious than injustice? But he who walks uprightly walks confidently. The end of those labours and fears was sin; but the wages of sin are death, and the death of sinners is most wretched. Now a comparable labour and fear are demanded of you for a better reward. The cause of these labours will be charity: that, admonished by the Lord’s command, you may lay down your lives for your brothers. The wage of 528 charity will be the grace of God, and the grace of God will be followed by eternal life.

[Col. 1297A] Go therefore happily; go confidently, to pursue the enemies of God. For they have long since—alas, what shame for Christians!—occupied Syria, Armenia, and finally all Asia Minor, whose provinces are Bithynia, Phrygia, Galatia, Lydia, Caria, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycia, and Cilicia. Now they ride insolently through Illyricum and all the lower lands as far as the sea called the Arm of Saint George.

[Note: [Col. 1297D] “George.” a. s. c. d. e² l.: “Gregory,” e¹.]

What of the fact that they claim for their dominion the Lord’s tomb, the unique pledge of faith, and sell admission to that city to our pilgrims—a city which ought to stand open to Christians alone, if any trace of their customary courage remained in them? This alone, were it all, would be enough to burden our brows. But who, unless he is wholly sluggish and envious of Christian glory, can endure that we have not divided the world equally? They inhabit Asia, a third part of the world, as an hereditary nest; and it was not without reason considered by our ancestors equal to the other two remaining parts both in the length of its regions and the size of its provinces.

[Col. 1297B] There the branches of our devotion once put forth shoots; there all but two of the apostles consecrated their deaths; there, if any worshippers of Christ survive, they pass their hunger in poor farming, pay tribute to those abominable men, or in silent sighs long for an awareness of our freedom because they have lost their own. They have held Africa, another part of the world, by arms for two hundred years and more. I declare this a danger to Christian honour, [Col. 1297C] because that land was once the nurse of illustrious minds, and so shall repel from itself all the mould of antiquity by means of divine writings as long as there remains anyone to read Latin letters. The learned know what I mean.

Europe, the third region of the world, remains; and what a small part of it do we Christians inhabit! For who would call Christian all that barbarism which frequents the icy ocean on remote islands, since it lives according to beastly custom? Thus the Turks and Saracens press upon this small portion of our world with war; and, having already subdued Spain and the Balearic Islands for three hundred years, they swallow in hope what remains—men most cowardly, who, having no confidence for close fighting, delight in a fugitive warfare. For the Turk never dares to join battle foot to foot; but when driven back, [Col. 1297D] he stretches his bowstrings from a distance and lets wounds fly upon the winds. And because he has missiles drunk with deadly juice, in the man whom he strikes it is not courage but poison that causes death. Whatever, therefore, he accomplishes I should attribute to fortune, not courage: he fights by flight and poison.

It is certainly established that every nation born in that region, dried by excessive heat of the sun, is indeed more intelligent but has less blood; and therefore they flee close combat because they know they have little blood. By contrast, the people who arise amid Arctic frosts and are distant from the heat of the sun are indeed less prudent, but, proud in their abundant and luxuriant [Col. 1298A] blood, fight most readily. You are a people born in the more temperate provinces of the world, lavish of blood in contempt of death and wounds, and not lacking in prudence. For you preserve discipline in camp and use counsel in battle. Therefore, endowed with knowledge and strength, undertake a memorable journey.

I command those present in God’s name, and enjoin those absent, that if you free your brothers from danger, you shall be proclaimed through all ages. Let those who are going forth and defending Christianity mark their garments with the sign of the cross, so that outwardly they may display love for the faith within. Through God’s grant and blessed Peter’s privilege, let them possess absolution for all crimes, and in this present joy lighten the labour of the journey, being thereafter to receive the reward of a blessed [Col. 1298B] martyrdom after death.

Therefore, setting a holiday for your crimes, so that Christians may at least be allowed to live peacefully in these regions, go forth; expend in a more just war that courage and prudence which you have been accustomed to show in civil conflict. Go, soldiers renowned throughout the world! Go and overthrow the cowardly nations! Let the famous valour of the Franks go forth, together with the peoples attached to it, to move the whole world by the terror of its name alone.

But why should I delay you longer, to diminish the courage of the Gentiles by words? Rather, set before your minds the divine saying: ‘Narrow is the way that leads to life.’ Let the travellers’ path therefore be narrow, full of deaths, beset by dangers; yet this same path will lead you to the country that has been lost, for [Col. 1298C] through many tribulations you must enter the kingdom of God.

[Note: [Col. 1297D] “Enter.” a. c. d. e. l.: “go in,” s.]

Consider in your mind the crosses, should you be taken; consider chains, and whatever torments, finally—

[Note: [Col. 1298D] “Finally.” a. c. d. e. l.: “at last,” s.]

—may be inflicted. Arm yourselves against dreadful punishments by the strength of your faith, so that, if need be, by the loss of your bodies you may secure the healing of your souls. Do you fear death, most valiant men, eminent in courage and boldness? Certainly human wickedness can threaten you with nothing for which heavenly glory will not make recompense; for the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us.

Do you not know that for human beings life is misery and death happiness? This teaching, if you remember, was poured into you with your mothers’ milk by the word of priests; your forefathers the martyrs displayed it as an [Col. 1298D] example. For death frees souls from the foul prison, that they may fly to their proper place according to their merits. Death hastens the country of the good; death cuts short the wickedness of the guilty. Through death, therefore, free souls either delight in joys, anticipating better things in hope, or enjoy punishments, fearing nothing worse.

But while souls are entangled in the bonds of bodies, they draw from them fearful contagions and—if one may speak truthfully—are dead. For the muddy does not fittingly cohere with the heavenly, nor the divine with the mortal. The soul indeed has great power even now, joined to the body: it gives life to its instrument, moving it secretly and carrying it by its deeds beyond mortal [Col. 1299A] nature. Yet, when the burden that drags it down to earth has been loosed and it has received its proper place, it shares in blessed strength, free on every side, in some manner participating in the invisibility of the divine nature.

Having therefore a double office, it supplies life to the body when present, but causes its transformation when it departs. You see how pleasantly the soul keeps watch in the sleeping body and, led away from the senses, foresees many future things by reason of its divine kinship. Why then do you fear death, when you love the repose of sleep, which is like death? Surely it is madness, for desire of a brief life, to grudge oneself life everlasting.

Rather, dearest brothers, if it so happens, lay down your lives for your brothers; empty God’s sanctuary of the impious; drive out the robbers; [Col. 1299B] bring in the devout. Let no affection of family hold you back, because the first duty of a human being is toward God. Let no love of native soil delay you, because in different respects the whole world is exile to a Christian, and the whole world is homeland: thus exile is homeland and homeland exile. Let no greatness of estates detain you, because greater things are promised.

Nor let those things which flatter the wretched with empty hope, or soothe a cowardly mind with the sluggish remedy of possessions, hold you back; rather, they have been displayed by frequent examples and proved by frequent use. These things indeed are sweet, but perishable; and they bring to those who despise them a hundredfold reward.

[Note: [Col. 1299D] “Those who despise them.” a. c. d. e. l.; “with times,” s.]

This I declare; this I command; and I set the limit at next spring. God will be with those who go, so that [Col. 1299C] a good year may smile upon them, with abundance of crops and fair weather. Those who die will enter the banquet hall of heaven; those who survive will see the Lord’s tomb. And what greater happiness is there than that a human being, living on earth, should see those places in which the Lord of heaven lived as a man? Happy are those called to these offices, that they may obtain those gifts! Fortunate are those who undertake these battles, that they may gain those rewards!”

§ 348. I have written down the tenor of this speech, presenting a few things in unpolished language for the truth of what was said, and passing over more. Therefore the people of the hearers, inflamed, declared the judgment of their minds with a shout, approving the speech and approving the pilgrimage. Immediately at the council certain nobles, prostrate at the pope’s knees—

[Note: [Col. 1299D] “Prostrate.” s. c.: “bowed down,” a. d. l.; “prostrate or bowed down,” e.]

—consecrated themselves and their possessions to God’s warfare. Among them was Aimar, bishop of Le Puy, a man of notable power, who afterwards directed that army by prudence and increased it by eloquence.

[Col. 1300A]

[Note: [Col. 1299D] “Directed by prudence, increased by eloquence.” a. d. e. l.: “increased by prudence, directed by eloquence,” s. c.]

Thus, in November, the month in which the council was held, each departed for his own home. At once the fame of this good news, spreading throughout the world—

[Note: [Col. 1299D] “Spreading.” a. d. e. l.: “scattering,” s. c.]

—infected the minds of Christians with a sweet breath. As it blew everywhere, there was no people so remote or so hidden that it did not send some part of itself. For this love moved not only the inland provinces, but also all who had heard Christ’s name on the most distant islands or among barbarian nations.

[Note: [Col. 1299D] “Most distant.” e.; “or most distant,” a. s. c. l.; “or next-to-last,” d.]

Then the Welshman abandoned hunting in the woods; then the Scot, intimacy with fleas; then the Dane, continual drinking; then the Norwegian, raw fish. Fields were deserted by their cultivators, houses by their inhabitants; indeed, whole cities emigrated.

[Col. 1300B] No love of kinship, no attachment to homeland, counted for anything; God alone was before their eyes. Whatever had been stored in barns, whatever in dining rooms, and would have answered either the greedy farmer’s wishes or those of the hoarder of treasures, was abandoned; hunger existed only for the journey to Jerusalem. There was joy among those going, grief among those remaining. What do I say of those remaining?

[Note: [Col. 1299D] “I say of.” a. c. d. e² l.: “I say,” s.; “shall I say of,” e¹.]

You might see a husband going with his wife, and indeed with his whole household; you might laugh to see all their household gods loaded into carts and carried off upon the journey. The track was narrow for those passing, the road constricted for those travelling, so the columns rushed onward, stretching out in a long succession.

[Note: [Col. 1300D] “Stretching out.” a. d. e. l.: “drawing along,” s. c.]

[Note: [Col. 1299D] “You might see . . . household gods.” “The peasant,” as Guibert observes, “shod his oxen as though they were horses and put his whole family into a cart. Hence it was very amusing to hear children, whenever they came to some notable city or castle, asking whether it was Jerusalem.” GUIBERT OF NOGENT, *Works*, p. 482. (SHARPE, 416.)]

Their number surpassed human estimation, although those travelling were reckoned at six million.

[Note: [Col. 1300D] “Six million.” Fulcher of Chartres reckons the number of pilgrims fit to bear arms at six hundred thousand, excluding priests, monks, women, and children. “Those who took the cross,” he says, “are reckoned at six million,” but many returned home without crossing the sea. (*Gesta Dei per Francos*, pp. 387–389.) Guibert criticizes Fulcher’s credulity in this matter. Urban II puts the number of pilgrims at only three hundred thousand. (*Epistle* 16; *Councils*, vol. XII, p. 731.)]

[Col. 1300C] Never, certainly, had so many peoples united in one resolve; never had such great barbarism subjected its stubbornness to a single authority—and almost to no authority at all. For it was an especially striking miracle to see so infinite a multitude proceeding gradually through Christian lands without plundering and without anyone restraining it. Mutual love burned in all, so that if anyone found something which he knew was not his own, he would set it out for recognition everywhere over many days. Meanwhile the finder’s greed was suspended, lest perhaps the need of the person who had lost it should be relieved.

[Note: [Col. 1300D] “Need.” “Although this description conflicts with opinions however generally received, it is offered by an eyewitness when he recounts the army assembled at Constantinople. FULCHER OF CHARTRES, p. 389.” (SHARPE, 417.) See the note in Bouquet, XIII, 7.]

## ON THE LEADERS OF THE CHRISTIANS’ JOURNEY TO JERUSALEM

§ 349. And now March, the month desired by them, had come (A.D. 1096), when the world, putting aside winter’s old age and clothed in springtime youth, invited those who were to go toward the [Col. 1301A] East. Nor did they make delays; so great an ardour had seized their minds.

Godfrey, duke of the Lotharingians, set out through Pannonia, second in valour to no soldier ever born. He drew his line from the ancient stock of Charlemagne, and truly had much of Charles in him, both in blood and in mind. The Frisians, Lotharingians, Saxons, and every people dwelling between the Rhine and the Garonne followed him.

[Note: [Col. 1301D] “Peoples.” a. s. c. d. e² l.; omitted in e¹.]

[Note: [Col. 1301D] “The Garonne.” Perhaps the Elbe should be read.]

Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, and Aimar, bishop of Le Puy, began their journey through Dalmatia—

[Note: [Col. 1301D] Raymond. See below, § 388.]

—a distinguished pair in courage, men illustrious in arms against enemies and in piety toward God. Under their standards served the Goths and Gascons, and every people spread out across the Pyrenees and the Alps.

Bohemond had preceded them by a shorter route, Apulian by place and Norman by nation. At Brundisium he embarked upon ships, landed at Dyrrhachium, and from there hastened overland to Constantinople by routes known to him. Under his leadership Italy waged war, together with every adjacent province stretching from the Tyrrhenian Sea to the Adriatic.

[Col. 1301B] All these, meeting together at Constantinople, shared somewhat in mutual rejoicing. There they found Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the Franks. He had imprudently entered the emperor’s territories with few soldiers, had been captured by the emperor’s men, and was held in lenient custody.

Alexius, emperor of that city—

[Note: [Col. 1301D] “Emperor of that city.” c. e: “emperor of this city,” s. d; omitted in a. l.]

—frightened by the arrival of these nobles, willingly, but as though compelled by entreaties, granted him release from captivity. He was a man notorious for evasion, who never devised anything great except by deceit.

[Col. 1301C] He himself, as I said above—

[Note: [Col. 1301D] “As I said above.” See above, § 262; and Bouquet, XIII, note c, p. 7.]

—had corrupted Guiscard by poison and his wife by gold, having falsely pledged marital fidelity through messengers. Finally, he allowed Count William of Poitou, led into an ambush of the Turks and deprived of sixty thousand armed men, to escape almost alone (A.D. 1101).

[Note: [Col. 1301D] “Sixty thousand armed men.” See also below, § 383. Orderic Vitalis writes: “Three hundred thousand armed men adhered to the count of Poitou.”]

He was angered by William’s response, in which the latter denied homage to a Greek. In later times he attacked Bohemond himself two or three times by ambush when Bohemond came against him to avenge injuries done to the pilgrims. But when he made little progress, he stripped him of his brother Guy and almost his entire army, pouring poisons by his customary arts into rivers or garments. But of this later.

Then, however, keeping the army outside the city, [Col. 1301D] and speaking smoothly to the nobles, Greek eloquence prevailed so far that he demanded from each a homage and oath that they would devise no treachery against him; [Col. 1302A] that, if they could acquire cities dependent upon his empire, they would restore them to him—purchasing another’s advantage at the risk of their own blood.

Raymond alone thought that the cause of preserving ancient liberty should prevail: he would neither submit his homage to Alexius nor profess the oath. Therefore, gathering all their forces, they attack the city of Nicaea in Bithynia (A.D. 1097). They had first chosen to assault it because it obstructed travellers and because they intended to avenge the death of pilgrims recently killed there.
