For a certain Walter, a proven but rash knight—for in one person you will scarcely behold wisdom and boldness, since the one delays and the other precipitates—had been killed, with a great company, while recklessly riding around its walls. Peter the Hermit had drawn that company from their homeland by his [Col. 1302B] preaching.

## ON ROBERT THE NORMAN

§ 350. Now in September (A.D. 1096), Robert, count of the Normans and brother of King William, whose title this book bears, eager to undertake that journey, had as companions Robert of Flanders and Stephen of Blois, husband of his sister. All were counts of eminent lineage, in whom valour did not fall short of birth. The English, Normans, western Franks, and Flemings obeyed them, as did the companies of all peoples lying from the British Ocean to the Alps along the Mediterranean region.

Thus setting out, they found Pope Urban at Lucca.

[Note: [Col. 1301D] “They found.” e: “they found again,” d; “they find,” s. c; “they discovered,” a. l.]

Hostile to Guibert, as I said, he was, with Matilda’s aid, filling Italy [Col. 1302C] and the city with the noise of arms. Thus—

[Note: [Col. 1301D] “Thus.” e: “and now,” a. s. c. d. l.]

—he had made such progress that the Romans, turned to his favour, assailed Guibert’s supporters with words and blows alike. Neither side was inclined to spare the other, either in churches or crossroads, until Guibert, unequal in strength, left his see vacant for Urban and escaped to Germany.

## ON THE CITY OF ROME

§ 351. Of Rome, once mistress of the world, now seeming a small town compared with its antiquity; and of the Romans, once masters of affairs and the toga-clad people—

[Note: [Col. 1302D] “The Romans, masters of affairs and the toga-clad people.” VIRGIL, *Aeneid* I.286.]

—who are now the most indolent of men—

[Note: [Col. 1302D] “Are now the most indolent of men.” d. e: “are said to be the most indolent of men,” s. c; “are said to be most indolent men,” a. l. Sharpe cites a manuscript reading *incertissimi*, “most uncertain.”]

—weighing justice against gold and selling the rule of the canons for a price: of the city, I say, and its citizens, whatever I might try to say has been anticipated by verses of Hildebert of Le Mans, first [Col. 1302D] bishop and afterwards archbishop of Tours.

[Note: [Col. 1302D] “First.” s. c. d. e; omitted in a. l.]

[Note: [Col. 1302D] “Afterwards archbishop of Tours.” Absent from a. l. Hildebert was translated to Tours in A.D. 1125, after the death of Giselbert, who died at Rome around the middle of December 1124, in the same week as Pope Callixtus. (ORDERIC VITALIS, book XII, p. 882.)]

When I have inserted them here, I shall do so not in order to transfer to myself glory won by another’s labour, but it will be a mark of a candid mind if, not envying his glory, I add testimony to his graceful [Col. 1303A] eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Graceful.” a. s. c. d. e. l¹; “ancient,” l².]

## VERSES OF HILDEBERT ON ROME

Nothing, Rome, is equal to you, though you are almost wholly a ruin;  
Broken, you show how great you were when whole.

Long time has destroyed your magnificence; the citadels  
Of Caesar and the temples of the gods lie in marshland.

That labour, that labour has fallen, at which dread Araxes  
Trembled while it stood, and grieves that it has fallen;

Which the swords of kings, the prudent laws of the senate,  
And the gods established as head of the world;

Which Caesar, alone, desired more to possess criminally  
Than to be a partner and a dutiful father-in-law;

Which, growing, by three pursuits subdued  
Enemies by force, crime by laws, friends by generosity;

For whose creation the care of earlier generations kept watch;  
Piety aided the work, and a host’s water aided the site;

Both ends of the earth sent materials, workmen, and expenditure;  
[Col. 1303B] the very place offered itself for walls.

Leaders spent treasures, fate its favour,  
Artisans their zeal, and the whole world its wealth.

The city has fallen. If I undertake to say anything worthy  
Of it, I shall be able to say this: “Rome was!”

Yet neither the succession of years, nor fire, nor sword  
Has been able wholly to efface this splendour.

Human care was able to construct a Rome so great  
As the care of the gods was not able to destroy.

Bring together wealth, new marble, and the gods’ favour;  
let craftsmen’s hands keep watch over new works:

yet neither can a structure equal to the standing wall be made,  
nor can a ruin be restored by ruin alone.

Here the gods themselves admire forms of gods,  
and desire to be equal to their fashioned faces.

Nature could not create gods with that countenance  
with which humankind created the wondrous images of gods.

A face is present to these divinities, and they are worshipped  
more because of the craftsman’s art than their own divinity.

[Col. 1303C] Happy city, if that city either lacked rulers,  
or if it were shameful for its rulers to lack faith.

539

## ON THE NUMBER OF THE GATES AND THE SAINTS OF ROME

§ 352. Are these things slight for showing, in the ancient city, the dignity of its former goods or the grandeur of its present evils? But, lest anything be lacking to its honour, I shall add both the number of its gates and the multitude of its sacred ashes. And lest anyone—

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Anyone.” a. c. d. l: “someone,” s; omitted in e.]

—plead obscurity of language as an excuse for being excluded from knowledge of these matters, my speech shall be ordinary and plain.

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Plain.” A description of the walls and gates of Rome occurs in Andrew Lumisden, *Remarks on the Antiquities of Rome and Its Environs*, London, quarto, 1797.]

## FIRST GATE

The first gate is the Cornelian Gate, now called the Gate of Saint Peter, and the Cornelian Way. Beside it stands the church of blessed Peter, in which his body lies, adorned with gold—

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Gold.” c. d. e: “gold and silver,” a. s. l.]

—and jewels; nor does any human being know the [Col. 1303D] number of martyrs—

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Martyrs.” d. e: “holy martyrs,” a. s. c. l.]

—who rest in that church. On the same road is another church, in which the holy virgins Rufina and Secunda rest. In a third [Col. 1304A] church—

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Church.” s. c. d. e: “basilica,” a. l.]

—are Marius and Martha, and also their sons Audifax and Abacuc.

## SECOND GATE

The second gate is the Flaminian Gate, now called that of Saint Valentine—

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Saint Valentine.” Now the Porta del Popolo.]

—and the Flaminian Way. When it reaches the bridge of Molbium—

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Molbium.” a. s. c. d. e. l; “Milvium,” s. (variant reading).]

—it is called the Ravennan Way because it leads to Ravenna. There, one mile outside the city, Saint Valentine rests in his church.

540

## THIRD GATE

The third gate is the Porcinian Gate—

[Note: [Col. 1303D] “Porcinian.” a. d. e. l: “Portitian,” s. c. Porta Pinciana.]

—and the road is called by the same name, but when it reaches the Salarian Way it loses its name. Near there, at the place called Cucumeris, rest the martyrs Festus, John, Liberalis, Diogenes, Blastus, and Lucina; in one tomb, two hundred and sixty—

[Note: [Col. 1304D] “Two hundred and sixty.” s. c. d. e: “two hundred and forty,” a. l. Two hundred and sixty martyrs are said to have been pierced with arrows in the amphitheatre by command of the Emperor Claudius. Thirty, however, suffered under Diocletian.]

—and in another thirty.

[Col. 1304B]

## FOURTH GATE

The fourth gate and road are the Salarian Gate and Way, now called that of Saint Sylvester.

[Note: [Col. 1304D] “Now called that of Saint Sylvester.” Now the Porta Salaria.]

Beside the road rest Saint Hermes, Saint Vasella, Protus, Hyacinthus, Maxilianus, Herculanus, and Crispus. Nearby in another place rest the holy martyrs Pamphilus and Quirinus, seventy steps beneath the surface of the earth. Then comes the basilica of Saint Felicitas, where she rests, along with her son Silanus and, not far away, the martyr Boniface. In another church there are Chrysanthus, Daria, Saturninus, Maurus, Jason, their mother Hilaria, and countless others. In another basilica are Saint Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis, sons of Saint Felicitas; and seven holy virgins: Saturnina, [Col. 1304C] Hilarina, Dominanda—

[Note: [Col. 1304D] “Dominanda.” a. c. d. e. l: “Dunanda.”]

—Rogantina, Serantina—

[Note: [Col. 1304D] “Serantina.” d. e: “Serotina,” a. s. c.]

—Paulina, and Donata. Then comes the basilica of Saint Sylvester, where he lies covered in a marble tomb; and the martyrs Celestinus, Philip, and Felix. There too, in one tomb, three hundred and sixty-five martyrs rest; [541] and nearby rest Paul, Crescentianus, Prisca, Semetrius, Praxedis—

[Note: [Col. 1304D] “Praxedis.” a. c. d. e. l: “Praxides,” s.]

—and Potentiana.

## FIFTH GATE

The fifth gate is the Nomentan Gate.

[Note: [Col. 1304D] Nomentan. Now the Porta Pia.]

There—

[Note: [Col. 1304D] “There.” d. e: “in that place,” a. s. c. l.]

—is Saint Nicomedes, priest and martyr; and the road likewise is called by the same name. Beside the road is the church and body of Saint Agnes; in another church—

[Note: [Col. 1304D] “Another.” c. d. e: “another church,” a. s. l.]

—are Saint Emerentiana and the martyrs Alexander, Felix, and Papias. At the seventh mile of the same road rests Pope Saint Alexander with Eventius and Theodolus.

[Col. 1305A]

## SIXTH GATE

The sixth gate and road are the Tiburtine Gate and Way—

[Note: [Col. 1305D] Tiburtine. Now the Porta di San Lorenzo.]

—now called the Gate of Saint Lawrence. Beside this road lie Saint Lawrence in his church and the martyr Abundius. Nearby, in another church, rest these martyrs: Cyriaca, Romanus, Justinus, and Crescentianus. Not far away is the basilica of Saint Hippolytus, where he rests with his household, that is, eighteen persons. There also rest blessed Tryphena—

[Note: [Col. 1305D] “Tryphena.” d. e: “Tryphonia,” s. c; “Tryphona,” a. l.]

—the wife of Decius, and her daughter Cyrilla, and her nurse Concordia.

[Note: [Col. 1305D] “Her.” s. c. d. e: “Hippolytus’s,” a. l.]

On the other side of that road is the church of the martyr Agapitus.

[Note: [Col. 1305D] “Agapitus.” a. s. c. d. e. l¹: “Saint Agapitus,” l².]

## SEVENTH GATE
The seventh gate is now called the Major Gate; formerly it was called Sircurana [Note: [Col. 1305D] Sircurana, e. l.; Siracusana, a. c. d.; Seracusana, s. It is now the Porta Maggiore.], and the Lavican Way, which leads to blessed [Col. 1305B] 542 Helena. Nearby are Peter, Marcellinus, Tiburtius, Genuinus, Gorgonius, and forty soldiers [Note: [Col. 1305D] Forty soldiers. Forty soldiers suffered martyrdom under Licinius at Sebaste in Armenia.], and countless others; and not far away are the holy Four Crowned Ones [Note: [Col. 1305D] Four Crowned Ones. They are so called because, although they had long been crowned by martyrdom, their names remained unknown; and although their true names were later revealed to a certain priest, they nevertheless still retain their original designation. (SHARPE.)].

## EIGHTH GATE

The eighth gate is that of Saint John [Note: [Col. 1305D] Gate of Saint John. Porta di San Giovanni.], which among the ancients is called Assenarica.

## NINTH GATE

The ninth gate is called Metrosa [Note: [Col. 1305D] Metrosa, s. c. d. e.; Metrosi, a. l. No mention of this gate occurs in Lumisden.], and before both of these lies the Latin Way.

## TENTH GATE

The tenth gate and the Latin Way [Note: [Col. 1305D] Latina. Porta Latina.] are so called. Beside it, in one church, rest the martyrs Gordian, Epimachus, Sulpicius, Valerian [Note: [Col. 1305D] Valerianus, d. e.; Servilianus, a. s. l.; Seasserianus, c.], Quintus, [Col. 1305C] Quartus, Sophia, and Triphenus [Note: [Col. 1306D] Triphenus, s. c. d. e.; Triphonius, a. l.]. There nearby, in another place, is Tertullinus; and not far away is the church of blessed Eugenia, in which she lies, together with Claudia her mother; and Pope Stephen with his clergy, nineteen in number, and Nemesius the deacon.

## ELEVENTH GATE

The eleventh gate and way are called Appian [Note: [Col. 1306D] Appia. Porta di San Sebastiano.]. There rest Saint Sebastian and Quirinus; and formerly the bodies of the Apostles rested there. And [543] somewhat nearer Rome are the martyrs Januarius, Urbanus, Xenon, Quintinus [Note: [Col. 1306D] Quintinus, d. e.; Quirinus, a. s. c. l.], Agapitus, and Felicissimus. In another church are Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus. Not far away is the church of the martyr Cecilia, and there are laid up Stephen, Sixtus, Zepherinus, [Col. 1306A] Eusebius, Melchiades, Marcellus, Eutychianus, Dionysius, Anteros, Pontianus, Pope Lucius [Note: [Col. 1306D] Pope: the manuscripts read “popes.”], Optacius, Julianus, Colocerus, Parthenius, Tarsicius, Policamus [Note: [Col. 1306D] Policamus, a. d. e. l.; Politanus, s. c.], martyrs. In the same place is the church of Saint Cornelius, together with his body. In another church [Note: [Col. 1306D] Church, a. s. d. l.; omitted in c. e.] is Saint [Note: [Col. 1306D] Saint, a. s. c. l.; “of Saint,” d. e.] Soteris; and not far away rest the martyrs Hippolytus, Adrian, Eusebius, Maria, Martha, Paulina, Valeria, and Marcellus; and nearby Pope Mark, in his own church.

## ON THE ARDEATINE WAY

Between the Appian and Ostian Ways [Note: [Col. 1306D] Ostensam, e. l.; “the Ostian Way,” a. s. c. d.] lies the Ardeatine Way, where are Mark and Marcellianus. Pope Damasus lies there in his own church; and not far away are Saint Petronilla, Nereus, and Achilleus [Note: [Col. 1306D] Anchilleus, e.; Achilleus, a. s. c. d. l.], and many others.

[Col. 1306B] ## TWELFTH GATE

The twelfth gate and way are called Ostian [Note: [Col. 1306D] Ostensa, c. e. l.; Ostiensis, a. s. d. It is now Porta di San Paolo.]; it is now called the Gate of Saint Paul, because he rests beside it in his own church. There likewise is Timothy the martyr; and not far away, in the church of Saint Thecla, are the martyrs Felix, Adauctus [Note: [Col. 1306D] Adauctus, a. c. e. l.; Audactus, s. d.], and Nemesius. At Aqua Salina [Note: [Col. 1306D] Aqua Salina. Now Trefontane.] is the head of Anastasius the martyr.

[544] ## THIRTEENTH GATE

The thirteenth gate and way are called Portuensian [Note: [Col. 1306D] Portuensis. Porta Portese.]. Nearby, in one church, are the martyrs Felix, Alexander, Abdon, Sennes, Symeon, Anastasius, Polion, Vincentius, Milex, Candida, and Annocentia [Note: [Col. 1306D] Annocentia, e.; Innocentia, a. s. c. d. l.].

## FOURTEENTH GATE

[Col. 1306C] The fourteenth gate and way are called Golden [Note: [Col. 1306D] Aurea, e.; Aurelia, a. s. c. d. l. It is now Porta di San Pancrazio.], now called the Gate of Saint Pancras, because he rests beside it in his own church; and there are other martyrs: Paulinus, Artemius, Saint Wisdom, with her three daughters Faith, Hope, and Charity. In another basilica [Note: [Col. 1306D] Basilica, c. d. e.; church, s.; “basilica [and] martyrs,” a. l.] are Processus and Martinianus; in a third, the two Felixes; in a fourth, Saint Callixtus and Calepodius; in a fifth, Saint Basilides. At the twelfth mile within the city, on the Caelian Hill, are the martyrs John and Paul, in their own house, which was made into a church after their martyrdom; and Crispinus and Crispinianus, and Saint Benedicta. On the same hill is the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and there are laid up the martyrs Primus and Felicianus. On the Aventine Hill [Col. 1307A] Saint Boniface, and on Mount Nola Saint Tatiana, rest.

## ON THE JOURNEY OF THE COUNTS FROM ROME TO CONSTANTINOPLE

§ 353. These are the Roman sanctuaries; these are the divine pledges upon earth. Yet within this, as it were, heavenly storehouse, a drunken people, in mad frenzy, at the time when the pilgrims came there, disturbed everything by disgraceful sedition, and above the very bodies of the saints poured out civil blood, unable to satisfy their lust for money. Therefore, relying upon Urban’s blessing, the counts, after passing through Tuscany and Campania, came through Apulia into Calabria; and they would immediately have crossed the sea, had knowledgeable sailors [Note: [Col. 1307D] Sailors, a. c. d. e. l.; “natures,” s.] not forbidden it because of the violence of the south winds. Accordingly, the Norman and Blois counts wintered wherever each was able, staying with friends. The Count of Flanders alone entrusted his sails to the winds, making fortunate use of a rash decision; and therefore the mass of common followers—some because of want—returned home, while others perished from illness caused by the unhealthiness of the soil. The remaining leaders too, when they saw the sea calmed for fleets by the return of the spring sun, tested the sea’s trustworthiness and, unharmed by Christ’s help, made landfall at two ports. From there they came through Thessaly, whose metropolis is Thessalonica, through Thrace, and thence to Constantinople. Many of the poor died on that road from disease and hunger; many were caught in a ford called “the Devil’s” because of its swiftness [Note: [Col. 1307D] Caught, s. c. d. e.; “drowned,” l.; “about to be drowned,” a.]; and many more would certainly have died had horses sent in, set against the current [Note: [Col. 1307D] Against the current, e.; “against the stream,” d.; “into the opposing stream,” a. s. l.; “against the current,” c.], not broken the whirlpools of the violent [Col. 1307C] torrent. Thus life was secured for some; the rest were carried across on horses [Note: [Col. 1307D] Horses, a. s. c. d. e. l.; “waters,” s. (variant reading)]. The entire multitude therefore took relief from its earlier hardships for fifteen days, having pitched camp in the suburbs of the city. Since the occasion has arisen, a few words must be said about it.

## CONSTANTINE’S VISION

§ 354. Constantinople was first called Byzantium; imperial coins called Byzantine retain the form of the ancient name. Saint Aldhelm, in his book *On Virginity* [Note: [Col. 1307D] In the book *On Virginity*, chap. 25, Wharton edition. See § 31, note 87.], states that its name was changed by divine intervention, in the following account. While Constantine was asleep in that city, an old woman appeared standing by him, her forehead furrowed with the wrinkles of age. Soon, clad in an imperial cloak, [Col. 1308A] she blossomed again into a young woman and, by the beauty of her fresh complexion, so charmed Constantine’s eye that he could not refrain from offering her a kiss. Then his mother Helena, who was present, said: “She shall always be yours, and shall never die, except at the end of the world.” When he awoke, the Emperor sought the interpretation of this dream from heaven by fasts and almsgiving. And behold: after eight days, when again asleep, he seemed to see Pope Sylvester, recently dead, who, fixing his disciple with a sweet smile of his eyes [Note: [Col. 1307D] Disciple. The legend that Constantine was baptized at Rome thirteen years before his death was fabricated in the eighth century. He seems to have received baptism and the laying on of hands for the first time in his final illness. (EUSEBIUS, *Life of Constantine*, IV.61.)], said: “You have acted with your customary prudence, in expecting God to untie the knot of an enigma whose meaning escaped human understanding. The old woman whom you saw is this city, decrepit through the passage of time; its walls, already shattered by age and threatening imminent collapse, need a restorer. But you shall renew it with walls and wealth, shall honor it also with your own name, and an imperial line shall reign in it forever. Yet you shall lay the foundations at your own direction. Mount the spirited horse upon which, when you were still an untrained follower of Christ, you rode around the churches of the Apostles at Rome; loosen the reins and allow it freedom to go wherever it wishes. You shall hold in your hand a royal spear; by drawing its point along the ground, the traces of the walls shall be marked out. Therefore, observe upon the ground the spear’s direction, according to which the foundations of the walls ought to be laid.”

## ON THE CITY OF CONSTANTINOPLE

§ 355. The Emperor nobly obeyed the vision and founded a city equal to Rome, declaring by law [Note: [Col. 1307D] Declaring by law, c. d. e.; “confessing by law,” s. (variant reading); “declaring,” a. s. l.] [Col. 1308C] that an emperor ought not to rule in Rome, where the Apostles crowned by Christ held sovereignty. In it he built two churches, one called that of Irene, the other that of the Apostles, bringing there numerous bodies of saints, who might obtain heavenly protection against hostile assaults. He also placed in the Circus statues of triumphant men brought from Rome, images of gods to mock those who saw them, and Delphic tripods, both for spectacle and for the city’s adornment. They report that it was especially pleasing to the imperial mind to found a city there by divine command [Note: [Col. 1307D] “To found a city there …” In law 7, title XV, he took care to teach posterity that, obedient to God’s command, he had laid the foundations of Constantinople, which was to endure forever. The words are: “For the benefit [Col. 1308D] of the city which, by God’s command, we have endowed with an eternal name.” (*Codex Theodosianus*, XIII.v.7.)], where both the fertility of the soil and the mildness of the climate suited human health. For, because he had been born in Britain [Note: [Col. 1308D] “He had been born in Britain.” A gloss on law I: “Note concerning Constantine, that he was born in Britain, which is now called England.” The place of Constantine’s birth, no less than the status of his mother Helena, furnished occasion for disputes not only among scholars but also among national partisans. There are three opinions concerning his birth. English antiquaries claim this distinction for Britain from the words of his panegyrist: “By being born there, you made the Britains renowned”; but these words apply no less properly to his accession than to Constantine’s birth. Greek writers of more recent times assign the honor of his birth to Drepanum, a city in the gulf of Nicomedia, where his maternal grandfather kept an inn; but Naissus in Dacia is the place where he most probably first saw the light. The claims of this city rest upon contemporary authorities.], he hated the heat of the sun. [Col. 1309A] Thrace is one [Note: [Col. 1309D] One, s. c. e. l.; “third,” a. d.] of the provinces of Europe, frozen, as the poets also sing, by the ice of the Hebrus River and the Bistonian north wind; neighboring fertile [Note: [Col. 1309D] Fertile: *foecunda*, d.; *foecundas*, e. l.; omitted in a. s. c.] Moesia, whose crops, as Virgil says [Note: [Col. 1309D] As Virgil says, *Georgics* I.103.], “the harvests of Gargara marvel at.” But Constantinople, surrounded by the Pontus, draws a balanced mildness from both Europe and Asia, because the Asiatic east wind, coming near at hand, softens the northern openings. The city accordingly extends with enormous walls, but the countless population of immigrants constricts it. Therefore, masses of rock and heaps of sand having been cast into the deep, people go far out into the sea, and by a new contrivance land is created that confines the ancient waves. Thus the sea marvels at foreign fields amid its glassy waters, and surrounds and feeds its city with all the earth’s resources. The city is [Col. 1309B] indeed surrounded on every side except the north by the great sea, angular in the circuit of its walls in accordance with the configuration of the sea, and enclosed by a wall twenty [Note: [Col. 1309D] Twenty, s. c. e.; twelve, a. d. l.] thousand paces in circumference. The Danube, also called the Ister [Note: [Col. 1309D] Danube, also called the Ister. See Pomponius Mela, II.1; Ptolemy, III.8.], flows into the city through hidden channels [Note: [Col. 1309D] Through hidden channels. The Danube flows through six mouths into the Euxine Pontus. But the Lycus, formed by the confluence of two streams, continually pours an abundance of cold water into the harbor of Constantinople, washing the inner part of the gulf and attracting periodic shoals of fish to seek refuge in Constantinople’s capacious harbor.] beneath the earth; and on appointed days, when a sluice is opened, it carries the filth of the streets into the sea. Individual men competed in zeal for the Emperor to add adornment, each thinking that he owed something to the work he had undertaken: one offered saints’ relics, another riches; Constantine offered all things.

[549] ## ON THE EMPERORS OF CONSTANTINOPLE

§ 356. After Constantine the Great, the following emperors ruled there: his son Constantine; Julian the Apostate; Jovinian; [Col. 1309C] Valens; Theodosius the Elder; Arcadius; Theodosius the Younger; Marcian; Leo the First; Leo the Younger; Zeno; Anastasius; Justin the Elder; Justinian (renowned for letters and wars, he built at Constantinople the church of Divine Wisdom—that is, of the Lord Christ—which he called Hagia Sophia; a work said to be more magnificent than all buildings throughout the world, and one whose visible reality surpasses the inflated words of those who describe it); Justin the Younger; Tiberius; Maurice, the first Greek; Phocas; Heraclius; Constantine, son of Heraclius; Heracleonas; Constans (coming to Rome and stripping away what remained of its ancient adornment, he even denuded the roofs of churches of their bronze tiles, desiring, forsooth, a triumph at Constantinople from these spoils; but this greed ended unhappily [Col. 1309D] for him, because, killed soon afterward at Syracuse, he left behind all these trophies when the Saracens carried them off to Alexandria); Constantine; Justinian; Leontius; Tiberius; Justinian again; Philippicus; [Col. 1310A] Anastasius; Theodosius; Leo the Third. All these [Note: [Col. 1310D] All these. The final division of the two empires, namely East and West, had taken place much earlier, under the sons of Theodosius the Great, A.D. 395.] ruled both in Constantinople and Rome; the following only in Constantinople: Constantine; Leo; Constantine; Nicephorus; Stauracius; Michael; Leo; Michael; Theophilus; Michael; Basil; Leo; Alexander; Constantine; two Romanuses; Nicephorus Phocas; John; Basil and Constantine; Romanus; Michael; Michael; Constantine; the Empress Theodora; Michael; Sachius [Note: [Col. 1310D] Sachius: Isaac Comnenus.]; Constantine; Romanus Diogenes; [550] Nicephorus Butanius; Michael [Note: [Col. 1310D] Michael VII preceded Nicephorus Botaniates, who was expelled by Alexius.]. This man, driven from the empire by Alexius, secretly fled to Guiscard in Apulia; and, by transferring authority to him, imagined that he had done something that [Note: [Col. 1310D] “Done something that,” s. c. d. e.; “accomplished by which,” a. l.] would harm Alexius. Hence Guiscard’s desire to attack greatly increased, so that he falsely imagined [Note: [Col. 1310D] Imagined, a. c. d. e. l.; “strove,” s.] that through industry he could acquire what another had lost through indolence [Note: [Col. 1310D] Indolence, a. s. c. d. e. l.; “disgrace,” s. (variant reading)]; but how much these things profited them the preceding book has shown. In that city is the wood of the Lord, brought by Helena from Jerusalem. There rest the Apostles Andrew, James the brother of the Lord, and Matthias; the prophets Elisha, Samuel, Daniel, and many others; Luke the Evangelist; innumerable martyrs; confessors John Chrysostom, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, and Spyridon; virgins Agatha and Lucy; and, finally, all the saints whose bodies emperors could bring there from every region.

§ 357. The Norman and Blois counts therefore tendered their homage to the Greek [emperor] [Note: [Col. 1310D] Tendered, s. c. d. e.; “prostitute,” a. l.]; for the Fleming had already crossed over and had disdained to do this, remembering that he had been born and brought up free. The others, having given and received pledges of faith, pressed on to Nicaea in the first week of June [Note: [Col. 1310D] June, a. d. e.; “fasting,” s. c. l.] (A.D. 1097), which the rest had already besieged from the middle of May. Thus, when forces were joined, many deaths occurred on both sides: since every kind of missile was easily hurled by the townsmen upon those below, and not even the hand of the most sluggish man could fail among such densely packed targets. The Turks even dragged the corpses of the slain onto the wall with iron hooks, to mutilate them in mockery of our men or strip them naked after removing their clothes [Note: [Col. 1310D] Strip naked, d. e.; “cast down,” a. s. c. l.]. The Franks were grieved by this, and did not cease to express their grief by the sword until the Turks, exhausted by extreme misfortunes, surrendered to the Emperor through secret envoys on the day of the summer solstice. He, who knew how to consider nothing but his own advantage, ordered the Franks to depart, preferring that the city be preserved for the Turks’ open treachery rather than for the Franks’ suspected power. Yet he ordered silver and gold distributed to the nobles, [Col. 1311A] bronze coins to the lower ranks, lest they complain that they had gone unrewarded. Thus the Turks, who for fifty years had possessed Bithynia—part of Asia Minor, which they call Romania—after crossing the Euphrates, withdrew in flight into the upper regions. Nevertheless, when the siege had been raised, they dared to attack the army as it advanced farther, instigated by a certain Solimannus [Note: [Col. 1311D] Solimannus. Among the Turks his name was Kilij Arslan; his kingdom extended from the Hellespont to the borders of Syria and blocked the road to Jerusalem. See de Guignes, vol. III, part II, pp. 10–30.], to whom dominion over all Romania had fallen [Note: [Col. 1311D] Had fallen, a. d. e. l.; “had befallen,” s. c.]. Gathering, by estimate, three hundred and sixty thousand archers, he attacked our men, who were thinking of anything but war, with such force that, terrified by an overwhelming iron rain of arrows, all immediately turned their backs. At that moment Duke [Note: [Col. 1311D] Duke, a. s. c. d. l.; omitted in e.] Godfrey, Hugh the Great, and Raymond had taken another road, both to ravage enemy territory [Col. 1311B] more widely and to obtain fodder for their own men more easily. But the Norman, alarmed by this double danger, sent swift riders by safe routes to inform Godfrey and the others of the Turks’ arrival. They, strangers to delay, turned their standards against the enemy and rescued their comrades from danger. For these men were already being slaughtered indiscriminately in their tents, intent upon nothing warlike, but filling the air only with tears and prayers. The enemy did not seek an opening for a wound, but, casting fortune among the ill-born [*nothos*: perhaps “the unknown/unprotected”], never drew back an empty hand because of the density of the formations. The sole delay of death came from the fact that fighting took place near a certain reed-bed, where the Turkish horses, impeded, could not range freely. But at last, seeing the standard-bearers of the approaching nobles, [Col. 1311C] our men emerged from the reed-bed and, raising the military cry, “God wills it [Note: [Col. 1311D] The military cry, “God wills it.” “When Urban II addressed the multitude from a high platform in the marketplace at Clermont, urging the people to take up the cross, he was repeatedly interrupted by the cry of those present, shouting: *Deus lo volt! Deus vult!*—‘God wills it! God wills it!’ ‘Indeed, it is God’s will!’ the pope added; ‘and let these words, most certainly inspired by the Holy Spirit, be adopted forever as your military cry.’]!” attacked the enemy’s scattered ranks, signaling to their allies to strike them from the other side. Thus, pressed from both sides, the Turks, uttering I know not what dreadful cries and sending up howls to heaven, fled. They did not employ their customary fleeing mode of combat; rather, throwing down their bows, by a continuous flight of three days they showed a fear greater than human. There was no one to pursue them, because our horses, barely sustaining life on barren grass, could not undertake a vigorous pursuit, showing their exhaustion as soon as the weary spur struck their flanks [Note: [Col. 1311D] Their exhaustion, s. d. e.; “his exhaustion,” l.]. Asia, once a land most fertile in crops, had been so stripped by the ravages of Turks in recent and earlier times that it could scarcely supply food even to a small army, much less to so great a multitude, which seemed likely to consume whole harvests and drink whole rivers [Note: [Col. 1311D] “To drink whole rivers,” d. e. l.; “to drink themselves rivers,” c.; “to drink rivers,” a.; “to drink rivers away,” s.]. When they left Nicaea [Note: [Col. 1311D] “From Nicaea,” a. s. d. e. l.; “beforehand,” c.], they were reckoned at [553] seven hundred thousand; the remainder had either been killed by the sword or diminished by disease, while the greater part had scattered homeward.

§ 358. From there, then [Note: [Col. 1312D] Then, a. s. c. d. l.; omitted in e.], they came through the cities of Pisidian Antioch and Iconium to Heraclea. There they saw in the sky a sign formed like a flashing sword, its point extended toward the east. From the Kalends of July (1 July) [Note: [Col. 1312D] July, a. e. l.; June, s. c. d.], when they had left Nicaea, until the ninth of October (7 October) [Note: [Col. 1312D] “The ninth [day] passed,” a. s. c. d. l.; “did not pass,” e 1.], time passed before they came to Antioch in Syria. I would describe its site, did not Ambrosian eloquence in Hegesippus forestall [Col. 1312B] my desire [Note: [Col. 1312D] “Ambrosian eloquence in Hegesippus.” Hegesippus, a Greek writer of the second century, composed an *Ecclesiastical History* in five books, of which only a fragment survives. The work *On the Jewish War and the Destruction of Jerusalem*, said to have been translated into Latin by Saint Ambrose, has also been attributed to him.], and did I not fear that my narrative, so frequently wandering into digressions, might be blamed. Nevertheless, I shall say as much as the account of the undertaking requires [Note: [Col. 1312D] Account, s. c. d. e.; “necessity,” a. l.].

## ON THE CITY OF ANTIOCH

§ 359. The city is enclosed by a very great wall, which also embraces a mountain [Note: [Col. 1312D] Embracing, s. c. d. e.; “encircling,” a. l.]. It was named after Antiochus, father of Seleucus, king of Asia. After Rome, Constantinople, and Alexandria, it is ranked fourth among all the cities of the world; secure in its walls and formidable in its mountains, it can, if ever captured, be won more by ingenuity than force. The river nearest it, which I understand is now called Fernus and was formerly called the Orontes, is received by the sea twelve miles from the city; its swift currents, colder through their very movement, temper the healthful air for the well-being [Note: [Col. 1312D] Well-being, s. d. e.; “health,” l.] of the citizens [Note: [Col. 1312D] Citizens, s. d. e.; “civic,” a. c. l.]. It also brings supplies by ship to the townspeople and mocks the persistence of besiegers, however long they may remain. There the venerable name “Christianity” [Note: [Col. 1312D] Christianity, d. e.; “of the Christian name of old,” a. s. l.; “of Christianity’s ancient name,” c. See Acts 11:26.] was first devised. From there Paul, the instigator and kindling-force of this religion, went forth to preach. There blessed Peter occupied the chair of the first episcopate; and the church founded there in his honor remained inviolate throughout the entire Turkish period. No less did another church, consecrated in honor of Saint Mary, [Col. 1313A] hold the eyes of spectators by the beauty of its appearance—wonderfully so, that those who persecuted her faith nevertheless reverenced her shrine.

## ON THE SIEGE OF ANTIOCH

§ 360. The Franks therefore besieged this city from October to June [Note: [Col. 1313D] From October to June: 21 October 1097–3 June 1098.], pitching their tents around the walls after crossing the river. Having recognized the difficulty of taking it by storm [Note: [Col. 1313D] Of taking by storm, a. d. e. l.; “of capturing,” s. c.], and thinking that they must counter the timidity of some, all the leaders together swore an oath not to abandon the siege until the city had been taken either by force or ingenuity. To carry out their purpose more easily, they established many camps on this side of the river, assigning soldiers to them to extend the line of camps [Note: [Col. 1313D] Camps, c. e.; “watches,” a. s. d. l.]. Aoxianus, governor of the city, likewise, seeing that the Franks were acting neither in sport nor half-heartedly but were seriously attacking [Col. 1313B] the city, sent his son Sansadoles to the Sultan, the emperor [Note: [Col. 1313D] Emperor, c. d. e.; “emperor of Persia,” a. s. l.], to lay before him the Franks’ audacity and seek aid [Note: [Col. 1313D] Seek, s. c. d. e.; “entreat,” a. l.]. The Sultan is among the Persians what Augustus is among the Romans: ruler of the whole East and of all the Saracens. This empire, I think, endures and extends for so long because that people, little warlike, as I have said, and deficient in vigorous blood, once it has accepted servitude, does not know how to unlearn it; and they do not know, as Lucan says [Note: [Col. 1313D] As Lucan says, *Pharsalia* IV.579.],

> For this purpose were swords given, that no one might be a slave.

But the western people, bold and fierce, scorns the long domination of a single people [Note: [Col. 1313D] People, s. d. e.; “nation,” l.]; often casting off servitude and transferring itself from one ruler to another. [Col. 1313C] Thus the Roman Empire first passed to the Franks, then to the Germans; the eastern empire endures always among the Persians.

## WHY THE TURKS KILLED THE CHRISTIAN INHABITANTS OF THE CITY

§ 361. Sansadoles, then, sent to the head of this empire, hurried on his journey with youthful eagerness. Meanwhile his father was not lacking in his imperial duty of guarding the city. The courage of those shut within was not content merely to defend their own position, but provoked our men on its own initiative, frequently and suddenly attacking them while they foraged and traded. For, having made a bridge out of ships they had found, they had established a market beyond the river [Note: [Col. 1313D] Had established, d. e.; “had instituted,” a. s. c. l.]. With Christ’s help, our men resolutely took up arms and boldly drove the persistent enemy back, [Col. 1313D] never allowing them to carry off the glory of superiority. The Turks repaid the vengeance for this humiliation upon the Syrians and Armenians, native inhabitants of the city [Note: [Col. 1313D] Repaid, a. d. e. l.; “inflicted,” s. c.], hurling the heads of those killed by crossbows and stone-throwers [Col. 1314A] [556] into the Franks’ camp, in order to inflame them to grief in this manner.

## ON THE HUNGER OF THE BESIEGERS

§ 362. By now everything around the city that could be procured for food had been laid waste, and reckless hunger—which often captures even what is secure—began to assail the army. The stalks had not yet risen into full grain, yet some embraced pods of beans not yet [Note: [Col. 1314D] Not yet, a. s. c. d. l.; omitted in e.] mature as the greatest delicacies. Some swallowed the flesh of beasts of burden; others hides softened in water; some, barely cooked thistles, down scraped throats into their stomachs. Some even sold mice or delicacies of that sort to others who desired them, while the seller remained hungry, enduring fasting in exchange for the gold offered. Nor were there lacking those who stuffed corpses with corpses [Col. 1314B] and fed upon human flesh—though far off and in the mountains, lest the others be offended by the stench of roasted meat. Many wandered on unfamiliar paths in hope of finding food and were slaughtered by brigands familiar with the roads. But not long afterward the city consented to surrender.

## HOW BOHEMOND INDUCED A CERTAIN TURK TO BETRAY THE CITY

§ 363. Bohemond, a man of ingenious intelligence, had by intermediaries solicited, with enormous promises, a certain Turkish leader who guarded a very large tower in the section of the city under Bohemond’s watch, to betray it [Note: [Col. 1314D] A certain Turkish leader … by intermediaries had solicited. Phirouz, a Syrian apostate, contriver of this treachery.]. To cloak the shame of betrayal with an outstanding pretext, that man in turn gave Bohemond his son as a hostage [Col. 1314C] and declared that he did so at Christ’s command, which he had learned in a dream. Bohemond therefore moved his men toward the tower, having first secretly obtained from the nobles of the city a perpetual gift [Note: [Col. 1314D] Gift, a. c. d. e. l.; “lordship,” s.] if he could acquire it. Thus the Franks, climbing the wall by rope ladders in the dead of night, displayed Bohemond’s embroidered banner to the winds on the summit of the tower and, with joyful shouts, repeated the Christian signal: “God wills it! God wills it!” The Turks, awakened and rendered inactive by lack of sleep, fled through the narrow streets. Our men, pursuing with drawn swords, heaped up great slaughter among the enemy. In that flight Aoxianus, governor of the city, was killed [Note: [Col. 1314D] Was killed, a. c. d. e. l 2; “fell,” s.; “is killed,” l 1.] by a certain Syrian peasant and beheaded. His head, brought to the Franks, was a cause of mockery and joy.

## ON THE ARRIVAL OF THE TURKS

[Col. 1314D]

§ 364. They did not long rejoice in their rich victory: on the next day they groaned under a Turkish siege outside the walls. The Turks had come at Sansadoles’ invitation, [Note: [Col. 1314D] “Under the leader Corbaguath … three hundred thousand,” etc. In describing Kerbogha’s army, most Latin historians—the author of the work entitled *Gesta* (p. 17), Robert the Monk (p. 56), Baldric (p. 111), Fulcher of Chartres (p. 392), Guibert (p. 512), William of Tyre (VI.3, p. 714), Bernard the Treasurer (ch. 39, p. 695)—use no expressions other than these: “an infinite multitude,” “an immense host,” “innumerable forces,” “innumerable peoples.” Albert of Aachen says that the Turks numbered two hundred thousand (IV.10, p. 242); Ralph of Caen, four hundred thousand horsemen (ch. 72, p. 30). (GIBBON, *Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire*, VII, pp. 364–5.)] under the eastern satrap Corbaguath [Col. 1315A], who had received from the emperor of Persia three hundred thousand men with twenty-seven admirals. Sixty of these [Note: [Col. 1315D] Sixty, d. e.; “sixty thousand,” a. s. c. l.] climbed by rocky paths into the city’s citadel, summoned by the Turks who had remained there. Thus they wore out the Christians especially by frequent sorties, and there was no hope except in God’s help, [558] while hunger increased among men harassed by war—hunger, always the first companion of great evils [Note: [Col. 1315D] Great, a. s. c. d. l.; omitted in e.]. Therefore, after a three-day fast had first been observed with litanies, the envoy Peter the Hermit was sent to the Turks. In speech familiar to himself, he set forth the following [Note: [Col. 1315D] Peter the Hermit … set forth the following. William of Tyre (I.11) describes him thus: “Small of stature, contemptible in appearance, of lively intelligence, possessing a keen and pleasing eye; nor did fluent speech fail him of its own accord.”]: that the Turks should now voluntarily evacuate the Christians’ lands, which they had formerly invaded unjustly. It was just that, as Christians did not harass [Note: [Col. 1316D] Harass, c. d. e.; “press hard upon,” a. s. l.] Persia, so the Turks should not press upon [Col. 1315B] [Note: [Col. 1316D] Press upon, c. d. e.; “harass,” a. s. l.] Asia. Accordingly, they should either return willingly to their native soil or expect battle on the following morning; let them test their fortune by twos, fours, or eights, lest the peril extend to the entire army.

## HOW THE CHRISTIANS DEFEATED THE TURKS
§ 365. Corbaguath was not of such a disposition as to deem the envoy worthy of an answer; but, playing at chess and grinding his teeth, he dismissed him empty-handed, saying only that the pride of the Franks was now utterly undone. The envoy too, returning swiftly, informed the army of the Turk’s insolence. Then all encouraged one another, and had proclamation made that each man should, that night, furnish his horse with fodder to the best of his ability, lest, exhausted by manifold wheeling movements on the following day, it should fail. And dawn had already broken when, drawn up in battle-lines, they advanced against the enemy with hostile banners. The first division was led by the two Roberts, the Norman and the Fleming, and Hugh the Great; the second by Duke Godfrey; the third by the Bishop of Le Puy. Bohemond marched in the rearmost division [Note: [Col. 1316D] Marched. a. d. e. l.; omitted in s. c.], intending to support the others. Raymond remained in the city, to provide our men with a refuge should it prove necessary. Seeing this from afar, the Turks at first hesitated as to what it might mean. But, once they recognized the bishop’s banner—which they especially feared, because they kept calling him the Christians’ pope and the instigator of wars [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Kept calling.” a. d. e. l.; “said,” s. c.]—before they themselves were struck, observing how courageously and without delay our men advanced [Col. 1316A], they turned their backs. The others too, springing out in unexpected exultation, fell while retreating, as far as infantry legs and cavalry spurs could carry them. They persuaded themselves that they saw the ancient martyrs, once soldiers, who had purchased the rewards of life at the price of death—I mean George and Demetrius—rushing down from the mountainous regions with banners raised, wielding weapons against the enemy and aid for themselves. Nor should it be denied that the martyrs were present with the Christians, just as angels once were with the Maccabees fighting for a similar cause. Returning then to the plunder, they found in the enemy camp such abundance as might satisfy, or even check, the greed of any army, however avaricious [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Of any army, however greedy,” c. d. e.; “of any army, however avaricious,” a. s. l.].

This battle was fought in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July (June 28) [Col. 1316B]; for the city had been taken on the day before the Nones of July [Note: [Col. 1316D] “July,” c.; corrected in a later hand to “July” from “June,” e.; “June,” a. s. d. l.] (July 6). Soon afterward, on the following Kalends of August (August 1), the Bishop of Le Puy, standard-bearer of the Christians and chief author of that good deed, happily yielded to the common condition of mortals. Hugh the Great, meanwhile, returned to France by the leave, as they say, of the heroes, alleging continual torment of his bowels.

560 § 366. (A.D. 1099.) But when, after remaining six [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Six,” a. c. e. l.; “seven,” s. d.] months at Antioch, they had effaced their former labours by so long a rest, they began to plan to resume the journey long since undertaken. First Raymond, never conscious of sloth, and ever concerned to be foremost in military readiness; then after him [Col. 1316C] the Roberts and Godfrey, set out upon the journey [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Set out upon the journey,” d. e.; “made their way,” a. s. c. l.]. Bohemond alone was held back for the time by the sight of the flourishing city and by hunger for money. Yet beneath this greed lay a plausible argument: he could say that Antioch ought not to be exposed without a prince to the Turks, who would immediately swoop down upon it. He therefore remained in the city; and the men of Raymond, who held one district, that wicked exactor drove out beyond the walls [Note: [Col. 1316D] “Drove out,” a. d. e. l.; “expelled,” s. c.].

But the rest, passing through Tripoli, Beirut, Tyre, Sidon, Accaron, Caipha, and Caesarea of Palestine, leaving the coastlands on their right, came to Ramla. They were graciously received by some cities, while by the subjection of others they made their strength conspicuous. For they had no intention of prolonging delay, since it was the month of April [Col. 1317A] and the crops of the plains had ripened into harvest. Ramla is a small town lacking a wall, known, if report is to be believed, as the place of the martyrdom of blessed George. The Turks had somewhat defaced a church founded there long ago in his honour; but then, in fear of the Franks, they stole away into the mountains, carrying off all their possessions.

The following morning, while the boundary between day and night was still uncertain, Tancred, Bohemond’s nephew, a soldier of outstanding courage, took up arms with certain others and hastened to Bethlehem, 561 wishing to reconnoitre the neighbouring places. The Syrians living there came forth to meet them, revealing their joy with tears born of longing, while fearing for their safety because of their small number; for scarcely more than a hundred soldiers had come. But they, having reverently worshipped the holy shrine with suppliant vows [Note: [Col. 1317D] “They, having reverently worshipped . . .” The Church of St Mary at Bethlehem contained within its walls a certain cave in which Christ was said to have been born. See Bede, *On the Holy Places*.], immediately advanced upon Jerusalem [Col. 1317B] with resolute hearts. The Turks too, their spirits emboldened by confidence in their strength, sprang out and for a while charged our men; for the whole army had now arrived. But soon, as the Franks pressed on, the repulsed enemy secured their safety behind the barrier of the city walls.

## CONCERNING THE CITY OF JERUSALEM

§ 367. The abundance of writers warns me to say nothing about the site and position of Jerusalem; nor need our discourse [Note: [Col. 1317D] “Our,” a. d. e. l.; “my,” s. c.] exult in this field. For what Josephus, Eucherius, and Bede wrote is known to almost everyone. Who does not know that it was called Salem by Melchizedek, Jebus by the Jebusites, and Jerusalem by Solomon? Who has not heard [Col. 1317C] how often, falling in adverse war, it buried its citizens beneath its own ruins—whether Nebuchadnezzar, Titus, or Hadrian were the agents?

That Hadrian built Jerusalem, named Aelia after his own surname, with a circular and larger circuit of walls, so as to enclose the place of the Lord’s Sepulchre, which had formerly been outside; for Mount Zion too was received within the city and rises above it like a citadel. There is no spring within [Note: [Col. 1317D] “No spring within.” Jerusalem had only the torrent Cedron, dry in summer, and the stream called the spring of Siloam (RELAND, vol. I, pp. 294, 300). Tacitus mentions a perennial spring, an aqueduct, and cisterns for rainwater. The aqueduct began at the stream of Tekoa, or Etham, of which Bohadin also speaks (*Life of Saladin*, p. 238).]; but waters useful for the citizens’ thirst are collected in cisterns prepared for the purpose. The site of the city itself begins on the northern brow of Mount Zion and is so arranged on a gentle slope that rain falling there never makes mud, but is either received in cisterns like rivers or, flowing out through the gates, increases the torrent Cedron.

There stood the Temple of the Lord and the temple [Col. 1317D] called Solomon’s, whose builders were unknown [Col. 1318A], and frequented in great numbers by the Turks; especially the Temple of the Lord, which they honoured with daily watches and from which they barred Christians, having placed there an image of Mohammed. There also stood the spacious church of the Holy Sepulchre, constructed with fine workmanship [Note: [Col. 1317D] “Fine,” s. c. e.; “smoothly finished,” a. d. l.] and built by Constantine the Great. It never suffered injury from the enemies of the faith, because, I suppose, they were struck with fear of the heavenly fire which every year, on the vigil of Easter, shines serenely upon the lamps. When this miracle began, or whether it existed before the time of the Saracens [Note: [Col. 1317D] “Saracens,” s. d. e.; “pagans,” l.], cannot be determined from the knowledge preserved in any history.

I read in the writing of the monk Bernard [Note: [Col. 1317D] “I read in the writing of the monk Bernard.” Bernard, with two companions, sailed from Italy to Alexandria, whence he travelled by land to Jerusalem in the year 870. Their journeys were published by Mabillon in the *Acts of the Benedictines*. The account is brief, but contains much of great importance. There is also a manuscript copy of this work of good standing in the British Museum (Cotton MS, Faust. B. I), where, through the copyist’s error, it is dated A.D. 970. This is plainly erroneous, since Bernard names Louis, king of Italy, as still living; he died in A.D. 875. (SHARPE, 438.)], that 250 years ago—that is, in the year of the Incarnation 870—he himself, having gone to Jerusalem [Col. 1318B], saw that fire and lodged in the hospice which the most glorious Charlemagne had ordered to be built there [Note: [Col. 1318D] “There,” a. d. e. l.; “the same,” s. c.], where he had also assembled a library at vast expense. Bernard further records such peace as Christians enjoyed under Turkish rule in Egypt and throughout those regions, that if a traveller’s beast, by chance, died at a crossroads while carrying his necessities, he could leave his baggage [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Hoes,” e.; “baggage,” a. s. c. d. l.] and go unencumbered to the nearest city for assistance, undoubtedly to find everything he had left untouched. Yet no foreign Christian could live there safely because of suspicion of espionage unless protected by the seal of the Emperor of Babylon; native Christians purchased peace from the Turks with three annual talents or Byzantine coins.

Nevertheless, because Bernard does not omit the name of Theodosius, then patriarch [Col. 1318C], the occasion itself prompts me to set forth the names of all the patriarchs.

## NAMES OF THE PATRIARCHS OF JERUSALEM

§ 368. James, brother of the Lord, son of Alphaeus [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Alphaeus,” c. d. e.; “Joseph,” a. s. l.]; Symeon, son of Cleophas, Christ’s cousin (for Cleophas was Joseph’s brother); Justus, Zacchaeus, Tobias, Benjamin, John, Maccabeus, Philip, Seneca, Justus, Levi, Ephrem, Justus [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Justus,” c. d. e.; “Jesse,” a. s. l.], Judas (these fifteen were circumcised); Mark, Cassian, Publius [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Publius,” a. s. c. e. l.; “Publicus,” d.], Maximus, Julian [Note: [Col. 1318D] “Julian,” a. s. d. e. l.; omitted in c.], Gaius (he was the first to celebrate Easter and Lent according to Roman usage); Symmachus, Gaius, 564 Julian, Capito, Maximus, Antony, Valens, Docilianus, Narcissus, Dius, Germanio, Gordius, Alexander, Mazabanus, Irenaeus [Col. 1319A], Zabdas, Hermon, Macarius (in whose time the Holy Cross was discovered by Helena) [Note: [Col. 1319D] “By Helena,” c. d. e.; “by blessed Helena,” a. s. l.]; Cyriacus, Maximus, Cyril (he built the churches of the Holy Sepulchre, Mount Calvary, Bethlehem, and the Valley of Jehoshaphat). All these were called bishops.

After them patriarchs arose: Cyril, the first patriarch; John; Prailius [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Prailius,” a. s. c. e. l. 1; “Julius,” d.]; Juvenal; John [Note: [Col. 1319D] “John,” a. c. d. e. l.; “Julius,” d.; absent in s. l. 2. No patriarch of this name is known at this period. Anastasius succeeded Juvenal in A.D. 458. Malmesbury omits the names of the eleven successive patriarchs down to Zacharias, A.D. 458–609.]; Zacharias (in whose time, A.D. 614, Chosroes [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Chosroes,” d. e.; “Cosdroe,” a. c. l.; “Cosrel,” s. Chosroes II, king of the Persians.] king of the Persians came to Jerusalem, destroyed the churches of Judaea and Jerusalem, and thirty-six thousand Christians were killed by his army); Modestus (he was appointed patriarch by Emperor Heraclius after the latter returned victorious from Persia); Sophronius (in whose time the Saracens came and expelled all Christians [Col. 1319B] from Jerusalem, except the patriarch, whom they left there out of reverence for his holiness. This was the time when the Saracens overran all Egypt, Africa, Judaea, Spain, and the Balearic Islands. Charlemagne took part of Spain from them; they possess the rest [Note: [Col. 1319D] “The rest,” d. e.; “the remainder,” a. s. c. l.] and all the lands I have named to this day, for about five hundred years); Theodore [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Theodore.” After Sophronius died (A.D. 644), the Church of Jerusalem remained vacant until 705, when John V succeeded; Theodore followed him in A.D. 754.], Elias, George, Thomas, Basilides [Note: [Col. 1319D] “Basilides,” d. e.; “Basil,” a. s. c. l.], Sergius, Salomontos, Theodosius.

Bernard relates that this Theodosius had been an abbot, was seized from his monastery fifteen miles from Jerusalem, and was made patriarch of Jerusalem. He says that Michael [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Michael,” d. e.; “also Patriarch Michael,” s.; “also Michael,” a. c. l.] was then [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Says,” a. d. e.; “say,” s. c.; “day,” l.] patriarch of Babylon over Egypt [Col. 1319C], the patriarchate having been transferred from Alexandria to Babylon: Elias, Sergius, Leonthos, Athanasius, Christodulus, Thomas, Joseph, Orestes (in whose time, A.D. 1009, Achim, Sultan of Babylon, nephew of Patriarch Orestes, came, sent his army to Jerusalem, destroyed all the churches—namely four thousand—and had his uncle the patriarch brought to Babylon and killed there); Theophilus; Nicephorus (he, in A.D. 1048, built the present church [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Church,” d. e.; “hut,” a. s. c. l.] of the Holy Sepulchre with the favour of Sultan Achim); Sophronius (in whose time the Turks came to Jerusalem, A.D. 1059, fought the Saracens, killed them all, and took the city; Christians remained there under Turkish rule); Euthymius [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Euthymius,” a. c. e. l.; “Eubinnus,” d.; “Cuthimus,” s.]; Symeon. In his time the Franks came and captured [Col. 1320A] Jerusalem (A.D. 1099), freeing it from the hands of the Turks and the king of Babylon.

§ 369. Therefore, in the fourth year of the Jerusalem pilgrimage, the third after the capture of Nicaea, the second after Antioch, Jerusalem was besieged by the Franks (A.D. 1099): the greatest prize of wars, the solace of labours, the provision of their highest hope. It was then the seventh day of June. The besieging army feared no lack of food or drink, since harvest had ripened in the fields and grapes in the vineyards; their concern was solely, and pitifully, for their beasts of burden [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Pitiful,” a. s. c. d. e. l.; “for the wretched,” s. (variant reading).], which, owing to the nature of place and season, had no watered pasture. For the sun’s heat had drunk up the recess of the spring of Siloam, which at uncertain hours bubbles with sweet waters.

That spring, whenever fed by rainwater, increases the torrent Cedron [Col. 1320B], and thence runs with wave-pouring force into the Valley of Jehoshaphat. But this occurs very rarely, because there is no fixed [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Fixed,” a. c. e. l.; “certain,” s. d.] limit to its increase or decline. Thus enemies emerging from caves unexpectedly slaughtered our men as they repeatedly dispersed to water their animals. Meanwhile, each leader attended to his own duty, while Raymond diligently held his position by David’s Tower [Note: [Col. 1320D] “David’s Tower.” David’s Tower was the ancient Tower Psephina, or Nebulosa; it was also called the Pisan Castle after Patriarch Daimbert (D’ANVILLE, pp. 19–23).]. This tower, guarding the city from the west, was constructed nearly halfway up of squared stones joined with poured lead and, with few defenders inside, repelled all fear of the besiegers.

Accordingly, seeing that the city was difficult to capture because of the steepness of the mountains, the strength of its walls, and the fierceness of its defenders, they ordered engines to be made. First, indeed, on the seventh day of the siege [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Siege,” s. d. e; “blockade,” l.], they tested fortune by setting up ladders and directing winged arrows against the resisting defenders. But because the ladders were few and disastrous to those climbing them, who, exposed to wounds from every side, were protected in no quarter, they changed their plan.

One engine was what our men call a “sow” (*suem*) and the ancients a *vinea*: an engine made of light timbers, roofed with boards and interwoven hurdles, and fortified with shields of raw hides [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Fortified,” a. d. e. l.; “reinforced,” s. c.], protecting those crouching beneath it [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Crouching,” s. c. d. e.; “standing beneath,” a. l.], who penetrate, as in their customary manner, to undermine the foundations of the walls. Another was, because of the scarcity of timber, a not-large tower built like a structure; they call it a *berfreid*, because it matched the height of the walls. Construction of this engine delayed the siege because of the workmen’s inexperience and the scarcity of timber [Note: [Col. 1320D] “Scarcity,” c. d. e.; “shortage,” a. s. l.].

And now the fourteenth [Col. 1321A] day of July was passing when some began to undermine the wall with the *vineae*, while others began to advance the tower. To make this more effective, they carried it to the walls in separate pieces and there assembled it, as close as they could safely bring it from arrow-shot; then, by the turning of wheels, they brought it almost into contact with the wall. Meanwhile the slingers with stones, the archers with arrows, and the crossbowmen with bolts, each performing [Note: [Col. 1321D] “Performing,” a. s. c. d. e. l.; “perform,” s. (variant reading).] his own office, pressed on and drove the defenders from the wall. Soldiers of incomparable valour also climbed the tower, now dealing missiles and stones to the enemy in almost equal combat.

Nor were the defenders idle: entrusting all hope of safety to courage, they hurled molten fat and burning oil with slings onto the tower and the soldiers, boasting that, by the deaths of many, they had achieved their desire. Thus the whole day [Col. 1321B] was fought out, so that neither side thought itself defeated. On the following day, the fifteenth of July, matters came to a climax. The Franks, made wiser by the outcome of the previous day’s battle, threw into the tower close to the wall bundles of branches green with olive sap, together with their guards. The flame, driven upward into its tresses by the wind, first seized the wood, then [Note: [Col. 1321D] “Then,” a. d. e. l.; “afterward,” s. c.] the stones, and drove away the guards.

Indeed, the Franks cut the ropes and drew toward themselves the beams which the Turks had hung from the wall, intending, if the tower were brought nearer, to smash it by ramming with a backward pull of their arms. Throwing the beams from the engine onto the wall and laying hurdles across them, they made a bridge joining the tower to the fortifications. Thus what the faithless had prepared for [Col. 1321C] relief was turned to their destruction. Then, shattered by the smoky globes of flame and by the boldness of our men, the enemy took to flight. Others, advancing onto the wall and thence into the city, wrought with their hands as greatly as the joy in their hearts demanded. This victory occurred in the sector of Godfrey and the two Roberts.

Raymond did not know of it until the cry of fugitives and the fear of those voluntarily hurling themselves from the wall—who, fleeing death, rushed into death—revealed that the city had been taken. Seeing this, he drew his sword and rushed upon the fugitives [Note: [Col. 1321D] “Fugitives,” c. d. e.; “those fleeing,” a. s. l.], hastening, insofar as he judged sufficient for his courage, to avenge the wrongs done to God. He also sent unharmed to Ascalon five hundred Ethiopians who had taken refuge in David’s citadel and surrendered the keys of the gates upon being promised immunity for their limbs, having witnessed the present advantage of peace [Col. 1321D]. The Turks had no refuge anywhere: the insatiable anger of the victors consumed both suppliants and rebels alike. Ten thousand were killed in Solomon’s Temple; more were hurled down from the roofs of the temples and the citadel. Afterwards the accumulated corpses were set on fire and dissolved into the airy [Col. 1322A] element, lest, decomposing in the open air, they infect the inert world with contagion.

Thus, once the city had been purified by the slaughter of the unbelievers, they sought with suppliant hearts and bodies the Lord’s Sepulchre, for which they had longed so long and endured so many labours. How many times they kindled heaven with the incense of prayers there, how many tears recalled God to favour, no one, I confess, could ever unfold—not even if the ornate eloquence of the ancients came forth, nor if Orpheus, who, they say, bent listening rocks with his singing lyre, should rise again. Let it therefore be imagined rather than spoken.

§ 370. This was a notable example of self-restraint among all the nobles: neither on that day nor on those following did anyone, through concern for plunder, divert his mind from pursuing the triumph begun. Tancred alone, seized by untimely greed, carried off certain most precious objects from Solomon’s Temple; but afterward, through his own conscience and the collective discussion of others, he restored either the same things or their assessed value to the place. Then whoever was poor and seized either a house or some wealth never thereafter endured the reproach of one richer than himself, but adopted what he had once possessed into hereditary right.

Without delay, that radiant mirror of Christian nobility, in which, as in a splendid coffered ceiling, the brightness of every virtue was reflected—Godfrey—was elected king [Note: [Col. 1321D] “Godfrey is elected king.” This devoted servant of the Cross refused the insignia of royal dignity in the city where the Saviour had been crowned with thorns; he wished to be distinguished by no title other than Defender and Baron of the Holy Sepulchre.]. All of us, placing our hopes upon him, held that the interests of the Church could in no way be more fittingly provided for; the decision about a patriarch, to be appointed by the judgment of the Roman pope, was meanwhile postponed [Note: [Col. 1321D] “The decision about a patriarch was meanwhile postponed,” etc. Pope Urban died before he could rejoice in this memorable event: he died on 29 July 1099, fourteen days after Jerusalem had been taken and occupied. Daimbert, Archbishop of Pisa, was appointed Patriarch of Jerusalem without a competitor. See William of Tyre, IX.15–18; X.4, 7, 9.].

[Col. 1322C] § 371. But the emperor of Babylon—not that Babylon which is asserted to have been founded by Nimrod and enlarged by Semiramis [Note: [Col. 1322D] “Is asserted to have been.” d. e.; “is now asserted to be deserted,” a. s. c. l.], but that which Cambyses, son of Cyrus, built in Egypt, on the site where Thaphnis had formerly stood—the emperor of Babylon, then, bringing to birth the anger he had long conceived against the Franks, sent a military commander to drive them from what he called his kingdom [Note: [Col. 1322D] “Drive them out,” s. d. e.; “disturb them,” l.]. The commander hastened to carry out his appointed duties; and when he heard that Jerusalem had been taken, he pursued the undertaking with greater urgency, although he had earlier shown no slackness. The barbarian intended to besiege the Christians in Jerusalem and, after the victory which he already dreamed of in falsely prophetic imagination, to tear up the Lord’s Sepulchre from its foundations and scatter its stones.

Our men, who wished for nothing less [Col. 1322D] than to endure anew the miseries of a siege [Note: [Col. 1322D] “Endure,” s. c. d. e.; “experience,” a. l.], drew courage from God and marched from the city toward Ascalon, bringing their breasts to meet the enemy. They carried with them a portion of the Lord’s wood, which a certain Syrian citizen of Jerusalem had disclosed as being kept in his home through hereditary succession. A happy indeed and faithful theft, that the mystery should have remained hidden from the Turks all that time!

Having found a great herd of cattle and beasts near [Note: [Col. 1323D] “Near,” c. d. e.; “beside,” a. s. l.] Ascalon, they issued a general decree that all should leave their animals in the open fields, lest they impede those who were to fight the next morning. They would have plunder enough and more if victorious, provided that, unencumbered, they avenged the divine wrongs. So, when the army was now marching out in the morning [Note: [Col. 1323D] “Marching out,” s. c. d. e.; “advancing,” a. l.], one might see, I believe by heavenly prompting, cattle walking beside the soldiers with horns raised, unable to be driven away by any force. The enemy beheld this at a distance, and, their sight weakened by the sun’s rays, lost heart before battle because they believed the opposing host to be innumerable, though they themselves possessed no lack of troops prepared for combat by much training.

They advanced more slowly [Col. 1323B] and tried to enclose the Franks with a force divided in two and with curved wings. But the commanders—and especially Robert the Norman, who bore the standard in front—met stratagem with stratagem, or rather frustrated cunning by valour. Leading forward the archers and infantry, they broke through the centre of the heathen ranks. The Lotharingian horseman also, who was in the rearmost division with his lord, swooped upon their flanks and cut off every route and open field for escape. Thus the Turks, [Note: [Col. 1323D] “Thus the Turks . . . were slain.” s. c. d. e. l.; omitted in a. The battle near Ascalon was fought on 12 August A.D. 1099.] pierced from the front and enclosed from the outside, were slaughtered at the will [Note: [Col. 1323D] “At the will,” s. c. d. e.; “to the satisfaction,” l.] of the victors; the rest were saved by the benefit of the approaching night. Much golden plate was found in their camp, and many gems, whose rarity is unknown in our lands but there shines with native beauty [Col. 1323C]. No victory was more joyful to the Christians, because they carried off rich spoils unbloodied.

§ 372. Returning to Jerusalem, and having restored their strength through the settled rest of many days, some, longing for their native soil, prepared a return by sea. Godfrey and Tancred alone remained—princes worthy of praise indeed, to whose titles no future age, if it judges rightly, will ever set bounds. They were men who plunged themselves from Europe’s farthest cold into the unbearable heats of the East, prodigal of their lives so long as they might hasten to the aid of suffering Christendom [Note: [Col. 1323D] “Hasten to its aid,” a. c. d. e. l.; “bring aid,” s.]. Beyond fear of barbarian incursions, always exposed to danger because of the unhealthiness of an unknown climate [Note: [Col. 1323D] “Unknown climate,” c. d. e.; “burning climate,” a. l.; “unknown people,” s.], they despised the security of rest and health in their homeland. Few in number, they oppressed so many enemy cities by the fame and actual achievement of their virtues: a memorable example of trust in God, in that they did not hesitate to remain where they might be assailed by pestilential air or killed by Saracen fury.

Let therefore the praises of poets yield, and let ancient fable no longer exalt the heroes of old [Col. 1324A]. No age has ever produced anything comparable to the glory of these men. For whatever virtue those others possessed vanished after death into sepulchral ashes, having been spent rather upon the smoke of worldly display than upon the solid reality of any good. But the usefulness of these men’s courage will be felt, and its worth made manifest, so long as the world continues its turning and holy Christendom flourishes.

What, indeed, should I say of the discipline and self-restraint of the whole army? There was no gluttony of the belly, no filthiness of the sexual organ, that was not immediately corrected either by the authority [Note: [Col. 1324D] “Authority,” s. d. e.; “austerity,” l.] of the commanders or by the bishops’ discourse. There was no desire to plunder in Christian lands; no dispute among themselves that was not readily cut short after examination by the judgment of mediators. [Col. 1324B] Therefore, since the glory of so well-ordered an army redounds to the honour of its leaders, I shall mark with writing the deeds and ends of the individual nobles; and, according to the credibility of my informants, I shall withhold nothing from the truth. Yet let no one to whom fuller knowledge of these deeds has come accuse me of carelessness, because, hidden away beyond the British Ocean, we are scarcely illuminated by even the faint murmur of reports concerning Asian affairs.

## CONCERNING GODFREY
### § 373. Concerning Godfrey

King Godfrey therefore takes the first place in praise [Note: [Col. 1324D] *Occupat*: a. c. d. e. l.; omitted in s.], the son of Eustace, count of Boulogne, of whom I spoke in the time of King Edward. On his mother’s side, which was the more distinguished lineage, he traced his descent to the line of Charlemagne [Col. 1324C]. For his mother, named Ida, daughter of the elder Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, had a brother, also named Godfrey after his father, surnamed Bocard.

This was when Robert the Frisian, of whom I have spoken above, upon the death of Florence, duke of Frisia, married his wife Gertrude and advanced his stepson Theodoric to succeed to the duchy. Bocard would not endure this; driving out the Frisian, he subjected the region to his own will [Note: [Col. 1324D] *Voluntatibus*: a. c. d. e. l.; *voluptatibus*, s.]. Robert avenged himself by treachery, since he could not do so in battle, and had him killed through his Flemings while he sat attending to the calls of nature [Note: [Col. 1324D] *Requisita naturae*: d. e.; *secreta naturae*, s. c.; *necessaria*, a. l.], a sword being thrust through his genitals. Thus the stepson succeeded to the victorious duchy by his benefactor’s favour.

The wife of this Godfrey was Matilda the Marchioness, whom the preceding book praises. After her husband’s death, she energetically tried to retain the duchy against the emperor, especially in Italy; for the emperor held Lorraine and the Lower Lands. Ida, however [Note: [Col. 1324D] *Vero*: d. e1; *ergo*, a. s. c. e2. l.], as I had begun to say, raised her son Godfrey in great hopes of seeking the county of Lorraine [Note: [Col. 1324D] *Lotharingorum*: a. s. c. d. e2. l.; omitted in e1]. The paternal inheritance had fallen to the elder son Eustace [Col. 1325A], while the younger, Baldwin, was still passing his boyish years.

When Godfrey attained an age suitable for arms, he devoted his military service to Emperor Henry, of whom the next book speaks. By his immense exertions he won Henry’s friendship, and, through the emperor’s exceptional generosity, received all Lorraine as his reward. Hence, when hostility arose between the pope and Henry, he went with him to attack Rome, and was the first to break through that portion of the wall assigned to his watch [Note: [Col. 1325D] *Muri*: a. d. e. l.; omitted in s. c.], opening a broad entrance for those about to rush in.

Thus, sweating especially hard, short of breath from overheated veins, he entered an underground chamber, which by chance presented itself as he moved about [Note: [Col. 1325D] *Discursanti*: s. d. e.; *discurrenti*, l.]. There, after he had allayed the immoderate violence of his thirst with a great draught of wine [Col. 1325B], he contracted quartan fever. Others say that poisonous Falernian wine had been administered to him, since Romans and people of that land are accustomed to pour poisons into whole casks. Others say that by lot he had received that part of the walls where the entering Tiber exhales cruel mists in the morning, by whose destructive force all his soldiers except ten died; while he himself, having lost his hair and nails, recovered doubtfully.

Whatever the case may have been, it is agreed that he was never free from the affliction of a continuous, though slow, fever, until, having heard of the road to Jerusalem, he vowed that he would go there if God graciously granted him health [Note: [Col. 1325D] *Salutem*: s. d. e.; *sanitatem*, l.]. When he had made this vow, the duke’s strength so flourished again that, sound in his knotty limbs and standing erect with broad chest, as though stripped of his wasted years, he shone forth in fresh youth [Col. 1325C].

Accordingly, wishing to answer the divine benefits flowing upon him, he went to Jerusalem either first or among the first, leading great bands to war. Though he had soldiers hardened by difficult service and training, no one was regarded as either earlier in joining battle or readier in action than he. It is well known that, at the siege of Antioch, he cut in two at the waist, with a Lorrainer sword, a Turk demanding single combat; one half of the man was already throbbing upon the ground when his swift-running horse carried off the other, so firmly had the wretch been seated. Another, whom he encountered on horseback [Note: [Col. 1325D] *Aeque*: a. c. d. e. l.; *equo*, s.], he split with a sword-stroke aimed at the head from crown to groin; nor did the terrible blow stop there, but cut entirely through saddle and the horse’s spine [Col. 1325D; Note: “Nor did the blow … cut through”: a. s. c. d. e2. l.; omitted in e1].

I heard a truthful man report that he had seen what I shall relate. During that very siege, one of the duke’s soldiers, gone out to gather forage, was attacked by a lion and for some time deferred death by presenting his shield [Col. 1326A; Note: [Col. 1325D] *Distulisse*: s. d. e.; *propulsasse*, l.]. Godfrey grieved at the sight and pierced the beast with his spear. Wounded and made fiercer by pain, it rushed upon the prince, so that the iron protruding from its wound injured his leg [Note: [Col. 1325D] *Laederet*: s. d. e.; *sauciaret*, l.]. Unless he had hastened to disembowel the beast with his sword, that proof of courage might have perished by a wild beast’s tooth.

Famous for these successes, he was raised to the kingship of Jerusalem because he was conspicuous both in birth and courage, yet not proud. The kingdom was very small and narrow in territory, possessing scarcely any cities besides a few surrounding villages. For the king’s unhealthy condition, which he had contracted immediately after the Babylonian war, brought a pause in warfare, so that nothing was acquired; and divine providence thoroughly checked barbarian greed throughout that whole year [Col. 1326B], so that nothing was lost.

It is said that the king contracted his old fever from being unaccustomed to rest. But I conjecture that God wished to transfer promptly to a better kingdom a soul pleasing to Him and deserving through so many labours, lest wickedness should change his soul [Note: [Col. 1325D] *Ejus*: c. d. e.; *ipsius*, a. s. l.] or deceit deceive his understanding.
