Therefore, when the wheel of time had completed the yearly span of his reign, he died peacefully on 18 July, A.D. 1100, and was buried beneath the rock of Golgotha [Note: [Col. 1325D] The church of Golgotha enclosed within its walls the rock in which the cross was fixed for the Crucifixion. Bede, *On the Holy Places*, [Col. 1326D] p. 315.].

He was a king unconquered in spirit alike toward iron and toward death, who often kindly restrained the tears of those standing by. Asked about a successor, he named no one specifically, but declared that the person worthy of it should succeed [Note: [Col. 1326D] *Sed eum*: c. d. e.; *sed tantummodo eum*, a. s. l.]. He never consented to wear the royal insignia [Col. 1326C], professing that it would be unparalleled arrogance if he were crowned for glory in the city where God had been crowned for humiliation [Note: [Col. 1326D] *Unicam*: a. c. d. e. l.; *nimiam*, s.]. He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July; Note: this sentence is omitted in c. d.].

### Concerning Baldwin

#### § 374

After his death, Tancred and the other magnates proclaimed his brother Baldwin, who was then staying in Mesopotamia, to be the future king. For the elder Eustace, who had come to Jerusalem with Godfrey, had long since returned to his hereditary soil.

Baldwin’s deeds shall be set down with complete and concise truth, in accordance with the reliable statements of Fulcher of Chartres [Note: [Col. 1326D] Fulcher’s account, *History of Jerusalem* from A.D. 1095 to 1127, was published in *Gesta Dei per Francos* and in Duchesne, *Hist. Franc. Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 816. Malmesbury appears to have drawn much from this source.]. Fulcher, Baldwin’s chaplain, wrote some things about him in a style not uncultivated, indeed, but, as the saying goes, without polish or training, though capable of admonishing others to write more carefully [Col. 1326D].

Baldwin, therefore, having undertaken the holy journey with the rest, had many soldiers who shared his disposition. Relying on them, he himself began to devise new armies and to seek brilliant opportunities [Col. 1327A] in which courage might shine. Finally, not content with the common praise of all, he separated from the others three days’ journey from Antioch and received, at the citizens’ wish, Tarsus, a noble city of Cilicia [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Suscepit*: c. d. e.; *recepit*, a. s. l.]: Tarsus, once the foster-city of the apostle Paul, in whose honour an episcopal church is seen there.

The people of Tarsus voluntarily submitted themselves to his protection because they were Christians and hoped to be defended from the Turks by his patronage. Thus the Cilicians eagerly passed under his authority, especially after Turbexel surrendered [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Deditum*: d. e.; *flexum*, a. s. c. l.], a naturally fortified town [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Munitum*: a. d. e. l.; *invictum*, s. c.] upon whose decision the lower castles depended. Once it had surrendered, the rest followed its judgment.

Not only Cilicia, but Armenia and Mesopotamia also sought his friendship [Col. 1327B; Note: [Col. 1327D] *Ejus*: d. e.; *viri*, s. l.]. Those lands were nearly free from Turkish domination but were harassed by raiding. Therefore the ruler of Edessa, oppressed both by the hatred of his citizens and by the sword of enemies, sent Baldwin a letter explaining his need. He was to come as quickly as possible; the ruler would compensate the labour of coming by the reward of adoption, since he himself lacked children of either sex.

This is a city in Syrian Mesopotamia, famous for the yield of its fertile soil and the merchandise of its traders, twenty miles from the Euphrates and a hundred from Antioch. The Greeks call it Edessa, the Syrians Rotasia. Baldwin therefore, after exacting an oath of fidelity from the envoys, crossed the Euphrates with only eighty soldiers [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Octoginta*: a. c. d. e. l.; *sexaginta novem*, s.]. It was a remarkable spectacle—whether one calls it courage or rashness—that among barbarian peoples surrounding him, whom another might suspect either on national or religious grounds, he did not hesitate to advance with so tiny a force.

He was welcomed by Armenians and Syrians with grateful joy [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Grato*: a. s. c. d. e2. l.; *gratato*, e1] and entertained with generous hospitality, crosses and candelabra meeting him on the roads. But when the Turks attempted to attack the rear division, Baldwin’s skill frustrated every ambush; the people of Samosata set the example by fleeing.

Samosata is a city beyond the Euphrates [578], from which came Paul of Samosata [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Fuit*: a. s. c. d. e2; omitted in e1], whose heresy anyone wishing to do so may read refuted in the history of Eusebius [Note: [Col. 1328D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII.30.]. Josephus also says, if my memory serves, that Antony besieged it when Herod came to him.

[Note: [Col. 1327D] Paul of Samosata was bishop of Antioch in A.D. 260. The title of financial procurator pleased him more than that of bishop. His followers, like the Noetians and Sabellians, refused at the same period to admit the mysterious distinction of the divine persons. He was expelled from his see and deprived of his rank in 270 by the judgment of eighty bishops, and in addition deprived of his office by Aurelian in 274. Mosheim, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. I, p. 702, etc.]

The Turkish inhabitants of this city, who had first encouraged one another to boldness against the Franks, first gave the signal for defection [Col. 1328A]. Baldwin therefore arrived safely at Edessa and found matters no worse than he had hoped [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Nihil inferius quam sperabat invenit*: s. d. e; l reads, “he found nothing less than what had been promised”]. Welcomed by the lavish favour of the man who had invited him [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Invitatoris*: a. c. d. e. l.; *invitatoriis*, s.], and shortly afterwards, when that man had been torn to pieces by treacherous citizens, he obtained the lawful rule of the city. Throughout the time when the Franks struggled at Antioch and Jerusalem, he was not free from wars, constantly distressing his enemies by attacks.

But in November, warned by Bohemond, prince of Antioch, that they should at last attempt the journey to Jerusalem, he made preparations to depart. Having driven back by the mere sight of his white banner—the emblem he bore in battle—the Turks who, hoping for his departure, had violated the peace, he left Antioch on his right and came to Laodicea [Col. 1328B]. There, through the generosity of Count Raymond, who ruled that city, he bought a sufficient stock of provisions at a low price. Passing Gibellum, he followed Bohemond’s fresh tracks; Bohemond was awaiting him with his tents pitched.

Daimbert, archbishop of Pisa, joined them as a companion on the road. He had arrived at Laodicea by ship with many fellow citizens; moreover, two other bishops joined them. Their united forces were estimated at twenty-five thousand. Many, after entering Saracen lands, were shut in by hunger because of the dearness of provisions; many horsemen became foot-soldiers after their horses had died of hunger. Their misery was increased by abundant rain, because in those lands rain floods like a rushing torrent only in the winter months [Col. 1328C]. The poorer men [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Pauperes*: s. d. e; *pauperiores*, l.], lacking changes of clothing, died from the freezing cold, for many days finding no shelter.

There was no remedy for this calamity, since both tents and timber were lacking. Yet they somewhat relieved their condition by constantly chewing sweet reeds, called *cannamellae*, “sugar-canes,” a compound name from *canna*, “reed,” and *mel*, “honey” [Note: [Col. 1328D] Sugar-bearing reed. For its cultivation and the ancient manufacture of sugar, see Albert of Aachen, in *Gesta Dei*, p. 270.]. Thus, having twice [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Bis*: e. l.; *his*, c1 d.; *hii*, a. s. c2] obtained necessities at vast expense [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Immenso*: s. d. e; *infinito*, l.] from the Tripolitans and Caesareans, they came to Jerusalem on the day of the winter solstice.

At the gates King Godfrey met them with his brother Eustace, whom he had retained until this time, omitting no act of generosity or favour [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Gratiae*: c. d. e; *gratiarum*, a. s. l.] in serving them. After they had performed at Bethlehem, according to custom, the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity, they made Daimbert patriarch [Col. 1328D]. [Note: I do not doubt that Pope Urban’s consent was secured in this action; see §370, note 31.] I do not doubt that Pope Urban’s consent was secured in this action [Col. 1329A], because Daimbert was venerable in age, powerful in speech, and well supplied with money.

Accordingly, after the Circumcision of the Lord, having taken palms at Jericho [Note: [Col. 1329D] Hence the English word *palmer*, or pilgrim. See Albert of Aachen, *Gesta Dei*, p. 290. At this point l reads *caesis*, “having cut,” for *sumptis*, “having taken.”], the emblem that antiquity had instituted for pilgrims, everyone hastened to return quickly to his own abode. The cause of their haste was the stench of unburied corpses, whose filth exhaled so strongly that it polluted heaven itself. Accordingly, a wasting plague, spreading into the air, brought death to many of the recent arrivals. The rest hastened their journey through the coastal cities—Tiberias, I mean, and Caesarea Philippi—pressed by scarcity of food and fear of the enemy.

But they met famine, as I have said, with swift feet; and they provided for the fury of three hundred soldiers from the fortress of Baldac who harassed them by skill in military art [Col. 1329B]. They feigned flight briefly in order to draw the Turks, as they escaped the narrow places, out into the open; they deliberately yielded, but then wheeled about and scattered the dispersed enemy as they pleased [Note: [Col. 1329D] *Fudere*: s. d. e; *cecidere*, l.]. The Turks had thought our men unfit for battle because their shields and bows had been slackened by the abundance of rain. They did not know that victory for men lies not in confidence in weapons or coverings, but in outstanding strength of spirit and the raw power of their arms.

#### § 375

Baldwin then returned safely to Edessa and Bohemond to Antioch. At the beginning of July, rumour brought to Baldwin’s ears the news that the brilliant pearl of our leaders had been dimmed: Bohemond had been captured [Col. 1329C] and cast into chains by a pagan named Danishmend, powerful in those lands. Baldwin therefore hoped to avenge this signal insult to Christians by gathering together the forces of the Edessans and Antiochenes.

The Turk, who had captured the prince more through fraud and opportunity than through courage and military service [Note: [Col. 1330D] *Bellica militia*: d. e; *militia*, s. c; *bellica justitia*, a. l.], when Bohemond had come with few men to recover the city of Melitene, knew that the Franks would expend their utmost strength upon him out of shame at the event. He withdrew to his own territory, arranging his ranks not as though intending flight, but as though conducting a triumph.

Then Baldwin, having advanced two days’ journey beyond Melitene and seeing that the enemy avoided the necessity of battle, thought that he should return. Yet he entered the city first for his own purposes, not against the will of its governor Gabriel.

#### § 376

Meanwhile, when news of his brother’s death and the consent of the provincial leaders and magnates to his election reached him, he entrusted Edessa to Baldwin, his kinsman, connected to him by very close family ties and, besides, neither imprudent nor inactive. He then turned his mind toward the kingdom of Jerusalem.

Gathering two hundred horsemen and seven hundred foot-soldiers, he entered upon a journey full of death and dangers. At the sight of such great boldness, many whom he mistakenly believed faithful [Col. 1330A] slipped away in secret flight. He himself went with the rest to Antioch, destined to be of great support to those left desolate, and with the counsel of his shrewd mind advised them to seek Tancred as their ruler.

From there he came through Gibellum and Laodicea to Tripoli. The governor of that city, a Turk by nation but naturally lavish in compassionate kindness, sent him necessities of life outside the walls. He added a kindly warning that Baldwin should proceed cautiously, because King Ducah of Damascus had occupied the narrow pass through which he had heard that Baldwin would come.

Baldwin, ashamed to be moved by Saracen threats, proceeded with steadfast mind toward his purpose; but, arriving at the spot, he found their report true. About five miles short of the city of Beirut [Col. 1330B] is an altogether narrow place beside the sea, so confined by steep cliffs and narrow hills [Note: [Col. 1330D] *Collium*: s. c; *callium*, a. d. e. l.] that a hundred men, once holding those defiles, can prevent any number of travellers from passing. It is an unavoidable place for those going from Tripoli to Jerusalem.

When Baldwin arrived there, he sent scouts to report the character of the place and the enemy’s strength. The returning envoys, scarcely intelligible through fear, gasped out the difficulty of the pass and the confidence of the opponents occupying it. But Baldwin, who fell little short of the finest soldier who had ever lived, was not at all frightened and resolutely formed his battle-line against them.

Ducah then sent some men to provoke the first skirmishes and draw out the unwary, while he kept his greater strength in suitable places [Col. 1330C]. Thus they came at first with great force, then repeatedly slipped away, in order to draw our men into the narrow ground. This stratagem did not escape Baldwin. Trained in the practices of ancient warfare, he signalled his men to feign flight. At the same time, to intensify the appearance of fear, he ordered the baggage and impedimenta which they had set down to be taken up again [Note: [Col. 1330D] *Posuerant resumit*: d. e; a. s. c. l read, “what they had already put down, to be taken up”], the pack animals to be driven with goads, and even the ranks to be loosened, so that the enemy might charge.

At the sight, the Turks rejoiced and, gnashing horribly, pursued our men—as though one might believe the Eumenides were howling. Some boarded ships to seize the shore in advance; others rode ahead and killed pilgrims walking unsuspectingly near the sea. Nor did the Franks abandon their feigned flight until they reached the plain they had selected [Col. 1330D]. No tumult shook the men’s resolve; indeed, the necessity by which they were hemmed in nourished and supplied their courage. Few withstood innumerable forces by land and sea.

Once they thought they had feigned fear sufficiently, they closed their ranks, turned their standards, and enclosed the enemies who were now charging upon them. Thus the face of events was reversed: those who had been victorious were defeated, and those defeated became victors. The Turks were struck down in ruinous slaughter. The survivors fled headlong to the ships; once they had gone more than an arrow-shot into the deep [Col. 1331A], they drove their vessels away with oars and all the force of their chests as though the hands of their opponents could drag them back to land.

And so that you may not doubt the marvel as something merely plausible, but may in some sense touch it as visible: only four Christian soldiers were killed; by their blood they won victory for the rest. Therefore I affirm that worshippers of Christ would never be defeated by pagans if before battle they strengthened their courage with heavenly protection, and in battle joined the friendly powers of those above to their arms. But because in peace they gorge themselves with every vice and in combat rely on boldness alone, their courage often, and not without cause, strays from good fortune.

The count, rejoicing in his splendid triumph, returned to strip the slain [Col. 1331B] and found quite a few Turks alive. He released them unharmed in body, though deprived of money. He himself withdrew with his men lest some ambush should remain, and rested that night beneath olive bushes. But at first light he came with lightly equipped men to the pass, intending to see its nature with his own eyes. Seeing that everything was safe—for the Turks who on the preceding day had ranged about the mountain had all fled in the middle of the night when they saw their countrymen’s slaughter—he made the agreed signal with smoke, informing his companions that the enemy had departed.

Freed from the chains of delay, they immediately followed the leader. Then the governor of Beirut sent provisions to the passing men [Note: [Col. 1331D] *Praetereuntibus*: a. d. e. l; *praeeuntibus*, s. c.], astonished at the courage of so small an army [Note: [Col. 1331D] *Tam pauci*: d. e. l; *tanti*, s. c; *tam parvi*, a.]. The Tyrians, Sidonians, and Acharonites—who are also Ptolemais people—did likewise [Col. 1331C], accepting the Franks’ courage in silent fear. The men of Tancred who were at Chaipha were no less generous, though he himself was absent.

I cannot discover the ancient name of that fortress, because all inland cities which Josephus records as having once existed [Note: [Col. 1331D] “which … are read as having once existed”: a. c. d. e. l; s reads, “which … we read as having once existed”] either no longer exist or, reduced to villages, have lost their names; the maritime cities remain intact. Thus they came through Caesarea of Palestine and Azotus to Joppa, where he received the first congratulations of his kingdom, the citizens opening their gates with immense joy.

#### § 377

Brought from Joppa to Jerusalem and welcomed there with favour, he gave himself six days’ rest [Note: [Col. 1331D] *Sex*: a. c. e. l; *septem*, s. d.]. Then, lest the Turks doubt that the character of his kingdom was growing to their great harm, he moved an expedition toward Ascalon [Col. 1331D]. Displaying his forces not far from the city, he easily repelled the attacking Ascalonites, waiting for a suitable opportunity to accomplish his intention.

Finally, thinking that their repulse was for the moment sufficient for his glory, he sounded a retreat toward the hills, so that the enemy might pursue. He also sought to acquire necessities for his men from the enemy’s loss. His men were sobbing from hunger through the land’s scarcity, because that year a sickly harvest had denied food [Col. 1332A], frustrating the province’s hopes with sterile yield.

He therefore climbed into the hills, to which the Turkish inhabitants of the land had withdrawn after abandoning their villages, carrying Syrians with them down into utterly hidden caves. But the Franks found a means to defeat the fugitives’ contrivance: they sent smoke into the mouths of the caverns. By this means [Note: [Col. 1331D] Here a new section begins in d. e.] the routed brigands lost their obstinacy, coming out one by one. Thus all the Turks were killed to a man; the Syrians were spared.

The army then departed, intending to go toward Arabia, and passed the tombs of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of the three matrons Sarah, Rebecca, and Leah. The place is in Hebron, thirteen miles from Jerusalem. Joseph’s body lies at Neapolis, formerly called Shechem, covered with white marble and visible to all passers-by [Col. 1332B]. There also the mausoleums of his brothers may be seen [Note: [Col. 1332D] “There also the mausoleums of his brothers may be seen”: c. d. e; a. s. l read, “and there the mausoleums of his brothers may be seen”], though with lesser distinction.

The army then came into the valley where God once overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, hurling heavenly fire upon the wicked. There a lake spreads for eighteen miles, capable of sustaining no living thing. Its nature is moreover so horrible that it twists the mouths of those who drink and, by its bitter taste, stretches their jaws. A mountain rises over the valley, belching salty pits in places and wholly translucent, like frozen glass; from it is collected what some call natron and others a gem of salt.

Having escaped the lake, they came to a very wealthy village, fruitful in sweet fruits called dates [Note: [Col. 1332D] *Dicunt*: s. d. e; *vocant*, l.]. Stuffing themselves with these, they could scarcely fill the hollows of their bellies [Col. 1332C], scarcely restrain the gluttony of their throats because of their sweetness. Everything else had been stripped bare by the inhabitants through fear, except a few Ethiopians, displaying the sooty darkness of their skin beneath the rusty down of their hair. Thinking their slaughter beneath their own courage, our men deemed them worthy not of anger but of laughter.

Below that village lies a valley in which the stone may still be seen that Moses struck when he poured waters out for the murmuring people [586]. The spring still flows in so abundant and rapid a stream that it turns mill-wheels by its force. Then on the slope of the mountain stands a church built in honour of Aaron the lawgiver, where he himself, through the mediation and assistance of his brother, held conversations with God.

There, learning from guides familiar with the roads—Saracens who were Christians—that from that point to Babylon there was nothing but barren ground lacking every good thing [Col. 1332D], they returned to Jerusalem, intending to consecrate to God the first-fruits of the kingdom through the subjection of so many hostile regions.

#### § 378

The royal insignia having therefore been prepared [Note: [Col. 1332D] *Regiis insignibus*: a. d. e; *regalibus insigniis*, s; *regis insignibus*, l; *regalibus insignibus*, c.], Baldwin was crowned at Bethlehem with great glory by Patriarch Daimbert on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, 25 December A.D. 1100, amid the favourable acclamations of all. For from then onward he both deserved through his own labour, and obtained through the favour of others [Col. 1333A], every mark of royal reverence—although lord of a very small kingdom, indeed almost, I may say, a shamefully small one.

We ought therefore to behold the mercy of Christ the Lord and dwell upon the sight of His power [Note: [Col. 1333D] “to dwell upon the sight of His power”: a. s. d. e. l; c, “to dwell upon His sight”]. By His aid Christians could be feared even though they could not inflict harm. There were scarcely four hundred knights in the whole force, and as many foot-soldiers, to guard Jerusalem, Ramla, Haifa, and Joppa. Those who arrived by ship, despite sailing boldly among so many enemy ports, would worship the holy places and immediately judge that they ought to return home; the land route was wholly blocked.

The difficulty was increased because in March Tancred had departed to rule Antioch. Neither he could bring aid to the king nor the king to him because of the distance of the journey [Note: [Col. 1333D] *Ferre valebat*: d. e; *conferre valebat*, a. l; *conferre valebant*, s; *ferre valebant*, c.]. Add that, should need demand it, the king could not transfer his people from one castle to another without fear of irreparable disaster [Col. 1333B]. I therefore declare it an evident miracle that so great a nation of barbarians stood in dread of people protected only by God’s aid.

#### § 379

In that year, which was 1101 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the sacred fire which was accustomed to illuminate the vigil of Easter was delayed beyond its usual time. For on Saturday, after the lessons had been read alternately in Greek and Latin, after *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—had been repeated three times, and while the clear melody of the Syrians resounded, the fire had not yet appeared. The setting sun was already pressing on evening and bringing night; all departed sadly to their houses.

After deliberate consultation it had been decided that on that night the church of the Holy Sepulchre should be empty of every person, lest anyone whose conscience was foul with ulcers [Col. 1333C] should further provoke God by the boldness of intruding. At dawn, as daylight was gradually creeping forth, a procession of Latins was ordered to the Temple of Solomon, to invite God’s mercy there by prayer. The Syrians did the same around the Lord’s sepulchre, plucking at their beards and hair in the violence of grief.

The divine compassion could not endure this long. At once fire was placed in one lamp of the sepulchre. When a Syrian saw it sparkling through the windows, he showed his joy by clapping his hands and hurried to the patriarch. The patriarch opened, with the keys he carried, the inner sanctuary of the sepulchral shrine and brought forth the heavenly gift by lighting a candle from it [Note: [Col. 1333D] See Fulcher, *Gesta Dei*, p. 407.], distributing it to all who ran there.

Soon the other lamps throughout the church were lit by divine agency. Wonderfully, the lamp nearest to the one to be lit would first emit smoke, thereby announcing the lighting of its neighbour [Col. 1333D; Note: *Illuminanda*: a. s. c. d. e2. l; omitted in e1]. Thus Christ’s ancient practice knows how to frighten those whom He loves in order to comfort them; the threatening of power becomes material for praise [Col. 1334A]. Since God’s gifts, when familiar, become cheap to people through their very constancy, He often commends the favour of His mercy by rarity [Note: [Col. 1333D] *Caritate*: e1; *ratitate*, a. c. d. l; *veritate*, e2; probably *raritate*, “rarity”], so that what had been desired more ardently may be loved more gratefully.

#### § 380. A.D. 1102

Then a fleet of Genoese and Pisan ships had arrived at Laodicea and sailed thence with favourable passage to Joppa. The sailors drew their vessels ashore and spent Easter at Jerusalem with the king. He secured their valour by payment and contracted for one third of all the money from every city which they might acquire together [Note: [Col. 1333D] *Pariter*: d. e; omitted in a. s. c. l.], and one district of whichever city they chose.

Thus he drove them, headlong and blinded by greed for gold rather than moved by love of God, to sell their blood and immediately besiege Azotus [Col. 1334B], which they compelled to surrender after three days. The townsmen did not surrender with difficulty, fearing the king’s wrath if they were taken by force. In the preceding year they had fiercely repelled Godfrey when he attacked them, aided by the evil chance of fortune. For when he was raising his men by ladders onto the wall [Note: [Col. 1333D] c. d. e, “was raising by ladders onto the wall”; s. l, “had advanced by climbing ladders onto the walls”; a, “had advanced by the erection of ladders onto the wall”], already victorious and already holding the tops of the ramparts, the sudden collapse of a wooden tower added outside the wall robbed the men of victory and killed many. More were captured and torn apart by Saracen cruelty.

Then Baldwin besieged Caesarea of Palestine with all his forces and unwavering resolution. Seeing the citizens’ obstinacy and the difficulty of storming it, he ordered engines to be constructed. Thus stone-throwers were made and an enormous tower was made, twenty cubits higher than the wall [589; Col. 1334C].

But our men, impatient of delay and unable to endure such long expectation, set up ladders and attempted to overcome the wall. Through determined effort they reached the heights, raging in consciousness of their courage that, already engaged for fifteen days in Saracen warfare, they had wasted so great a length of time. Although the Caesareans fought with their utmost strength, rolling millstones down upon those ascending, our men disregarded the danger and broke through the opposing wedges, fighting with bared arms and drawn swords.

The Turks could endure no longer and took to flight; they either hurled themselves down or fell by the enemy’s hand. Many were kept for slavery, few for ransom, among them the governor of the city and the bishop called Arcadius [Col. 1334D]. It was a spectacle to make an onlooker laugh aloud when a Turk, struck on the neck with a Christian’s fist, vomited up Byzantine coins.

[Note: [Col. 1333D–1334D] Fulcher calmly reports seeing the bodies of Turks slain at Caesarea heaped together and burned in order to recover the Byzantine coins they had swallowed (*History of Jerusalem*, in Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 845). Pope Urban speaks of the practice of swallowing money; and from his words it follows that the custom of burning corpses to recover coins derived from Saracen usage. Before the crusading expeditions, Saracens used to give pilgrims bound for Jerusalem scammony carefully infused in water, to induce vomiting; if the expected effect did not follow, they used incisions. Guibert, Abbot, *Works*, p. 379. (Sharpe, p. 461.)]

For the wretches, out of fear of extreme poverty, men had hidden coins within their gums [Col. 1335A], women within parts not to be named. You see that the narrative is ashamed to speak openly; yet the reader surely understands what I wish—or rather do not wish—to say.

§ 381. Nor had the emperor of Babylon yet ceased from repeatedly sending a commander and an army to overcome the Franks. They landed by ship at Ascalon and soon ranged about near Ramla, taking advantage of the king’s preoccupations, 590 for he was then engaged in the war of Caesarea. By ravaging the countryside, therefore, they repeatedly provoked him to battle. But he, with no less cunning, allowed them, though pressing for battle, to grow slack through prohibition, so that their ungovernable heat might cool: by this delay he brought it about that most dispersed.

> [Note: “Dispersed.” c. d. e.: “dispersed, weary of delays,” a. s. l.]

The remainder—eleven thousand cavalry and twenty-one thousand [Col. 1335B] infantry—he attacked with his own two hundred and fifty horsemen and somewhat fewer than seven hundred foot soldiers.

> [Note: “Twenty-one.” s. c, d. e 2. l: “twenty”; e 1; a omits “of cavalry, twenty-one.”]

After saying a few words to his soldiers—promising them victory if they held firm, glory if they died, and reminding them that France lay far away if they fled—he was the first to rush upon the enemy. When the engagement had continued for some time and he saw his ranks beginning to waver, he met the desperate situation head-on. Thus, driving back the Turks by the familiar sight of himself, he struck down their commander with his lance; when he was killed, all the squadrons fled. Our men, who at the beginning of the battle had been so surrounded that no one could see another, then displayed such courage, with the banner of the Lord’s Cross going before them, that they slew five thousand; of the Franks, eighty knights and somewhat more infantry were lost.

[Col. 1335C] Moreover, the ensuing success was a consolation: they killed five hundred Arab horsemen. These had ridden to Joppa two days earlier, but, having accomplished little, were returning to Ascalon. Seeing our army from afar and hoping that it was their own, they went out to meet it as though to congratulate victors in triumph. But at last, when missiles had been discharged among them and they understood that these were Franks, they grew pale just as he who has trodden on a snake with bare heel—as I may use the poet’s phrase.

> [Note: “As the poet.” Juvenal, *Satires* I.43.]

Thus, dulled by sheer stupefaction, they exposed their backs to those striking them down. The king, arriving at Joppa, corrected by a truer letter the false report of a letter which the people of Joppa had sent to Tancred, announcing that the king and his army had been destroyed. Tancred had already prepared to set out for Jerusalem when a messenger arrived; displaying the [Col. 1335D] royal seal, he dispelled grief and restored joy.

§ 382. It would be lengthy were I to explain all his battles: how he subdued Tiberias, Sidon, Accaron—that is, Ptolemais—and finally all the maritime cities; how he marked almost every day by the deaths of Turks, whether by secret assault or open war. Such great deeds demand the discourse [Col. 1336A] of a man abounding in grandiloquent language and leisurely exactness; we lack both, and, what is most harmful, ready knowledge of the facts. Yet to believe everything upon indulgent hearsay and to deceive the credulity of one’s hearers is not the part of a truthful historian.

> [Note: “Discourse.” c. d. e: “account,” a. s. l.]  
> [Note: “Historian.” a. s. c. d. e. l: “history,” s. (variant reading).]

Accordingly, I shall add only those things which I have learned in writing, by which the man’s glorious devotion and enduring grace may be proved to the letter. And I shall steadfastly affirm this: that with a small force he very often played at great battles, and never fled the field except at Ramla and Accaron.

> [Note: “In writing.” a. s. c. d. e. l: “written things,” s. (variant reading).]  
> [Note: “I shall affirm.” a. c. d. e. l: “I shall assert emphatically,” s.]  
> [Note: “Small.” s. d. e: “few,” l.]

Indeed, memorable victories followed both flights, because they resulted more from unconsidered courage than fear, as the reader will recognize from the few matters inserted below.

[Col. 1336B] § 383. In that September, on the seventh day before the Ides—that is, 7 September, A.D. 1101—a battle took place.

> [Note: “A battle took place.” c. d. e: “the aforesaid battle took place,” a. s. l.]

William, count of Poitou, went to Jerusalem, leading with him great forces, so that he was reckoned to have sixty thousand soldiers and many more infantrymen.

> [Note: “Sixty thousand soldiers.” See § 349, note 76.]

With him went Stephen, count of Burgundy; Hugh of Lusignan, brother of Count Raymond; Hugh the Great; and Stephen of Blois, wishing by fresh and contrived courage to repair the reproach of their former departure. Having proceeded through Constantinople, he offended Alexius by an insolent reply, as I said above; Alexius, taking no concern—or rather, taking deliberate care—he fell into the ambushes of Soliman. Soliman, knowing that the army suffered from hunger and thirst because for several days it had wandered through marshy and inhospitable places, met it with three hundred thousand archers.

[Col. 1336C] Never did the Franks see a battle more mournful, for neither flight could rescue the timid nor courage the bold from danger: they fought in a confined place, and clouds of arrows did not fail against a packed mass. Thus more than one hundred thousand were killed and all the booty carried away. Soliman, having obtained splendid funeral offerings for the shades of his own men from the spoils of the Franks, avenged the loss of Nicaea.

But because the army had traveled by many routes, not all were killed nor all plundered. For, apart from the Poitevin, who was almost stripped naked to his genitals, the other counts had promptly defended their property. Therefore all, having gathered again the soldiers scattered in flight—except Hugh the Great, whose corpse was received by the tomb of the city of Tarsus—hastened to Antioch. [Col. 1336D] Among them Tancred, a knight of outstanding piety, showed the great favor of his generosity by supporting all with money as far as he could, but especially William, whom Fortune’s reversal had afflicted the more grievously because she had previously advanced him more serenely. Besides his treasures, whose loss did not trouble him so greatly because they are fleeting and recoverable, he alone had remained almost the sole survivor of so many 593 excellent soldiers.

[Col. 1337A] Thus, their spirits refreshed, they planned their journey and sought occasions for war wherever they could. The city of Tortosa first felt the thirst of these raging men; after it had been stormed and plundered, they relieved their previous hardships considerably. From there they came to the narrow passes of which I have spoken above, where the king had long been awaiting them, prepared to bring help against the Turks if they wished to prevent them. Protected by his valor and received with kindly hospitality at Joppa, they hastened to Jerusalem for the following Easter; there they took in with joyful eyes the most holy fire and adored it with devout hearts. After this they returned to Joppa, boarded ships, and each planned to return to his own country. The Poitevin, carried forward by a continuously favorable wind, reached his homeland; the others were violently driven back.

[Col. 1337B] § 384. Now, at the beginning of May, A.D. 1102, the Turks and Arabs besieged Ramla, repairing the loss of the preceding year by the reinforcement of a new army, equal in number.

> [Note: “At the beginning.” s. c. d. e: “in the middle,” a. l.]

The bishop of the city, wisely judging the opportunity, secured his own safety by secretly departing for Joppa. The king had already set out, believing those who falsely asserted that the enemy numbered no more than five hundred. Therefore he took no care either to form a battle line or summon infantry; the trumpeters merely instructed the soldiers to follow the king, although his friends strongly urged him to beware Turkish stratagems.

The two Stephens, of Blois and Burgundy, followed the king on horseback, lest they should return to their lands idle and inglorious rather than conscious of triumphal splendor.

> [Note: “Conscious.” a. s. c. d. e. l 1: “companions,” l 2.]

But the Fates were preparing for the men a glory other than they expected, [Col. 1337C] and another kind of victory. For when the king saw the multitude of the enemy and realized that his expectation had deceived him, wounded in mind by anger and raging with consciousness of his own high spirit, he hesitated what to do: if he yielded, he considered the disgrace to his former glory; if he fought, he revolved in his mind the deaths of his men. Yet his inborn ardor prevailed, and fear was already making him turn his back, when, encouraged by his comrades’ exhortations to direct his flight through the midst of the enemy toward the fortress, he consented.

The rest followed with a shout and broke through the densest ranks, consecrating their lives to God and zealously avenging their deaths. The counts too, worn out by striking until their hands stiffened upon their swords, succumbed to slaughter. The king, having slipped into the citadel, had only a few companions left out of the two hundred whom he had led forth. When they begged [Col. 1337D] him to deem it right to preserve his life by flight—saying that his own dangers were of little weight to the world, whereas his life availed the benefit of many, since he was in every age a spectacle of valor—he judged himself worthy of life, though his fortunes were shattered, because of his great steadfastness of spirit. Thus, accompanied by five knights, he made his way through the mountain country and eluded those lying in wait.

One of the knights was Robert the Englishman, as I said above; the fame of so remote a time has hidden the others from our knowledge. He was captured with [Col. 1338A] three others.

> [Note: “Three.” c. d. e: “three others,” a. s. l.]  
> [Note: “One.” c. d. e: “the fifth,” a. s. l.]

One escaped with the king. The Turks vented the final violence of their fury upon those who had escaped into the citadel, including Hugh of Lusignan and Geoffrey of Vendôme.

> [Note: “Had escaped.” s. d. e: “had taken refuge,” l.]

Only three survivors were messengers of their miseries to the people of Jerusalem. The king, hiding by day, spurring on his horse exhausted by running, reached Azotus.

> [Note: “Hiding.” c. d. e: “hiding by day, [and traveling] by night through trackless places,” a. s. l.]

It was a fortunate outcome, beautiful and inclined toward the miracle of God, because the Turks who had been driving off plunder around the city for two days had departed shortly before. From there he came by ship to Joppa and sent the Jerusalemites a letter assuring them of his survival. 595 The bearer of the letter was a little Syrian man who, if he were discovered, could deceive those lying in wait by the poverty of his dress and by conversing in the familiar local language. Knowing short cuts through byways, he avoided the dangers posed by traitors and [Col. 1338B] reached Jerusalem on the third day.

Then the knights who guarded the city, joined by companies of auxiliary infantry, set out for Joppa and directed their route close to the sea, avoiding the inland districts. Yet men at the rear of the column were killed as the Turks pressed them, because they lacked either horses or infantry.

> [Note: “Yet.” a. s. c. d. e 2. l; omitted in e 1.]

Thus ninety knights were assembled from Jerusalem and eighty from Tiberias, whom Duke Hugh, a most valiant man, had brought as reinforcements; owing to the shortage, squires too were enrolled in the place of knights. On the next day the delay before battle ended, since the Turks had now grown so fierce that, having prepared siege engines, they were planning to attack the wall of Joppa.

> [Note: “Were planning.” s. d. e: “were deliberating,” l.]

This was forestalled by Baldwin’s diligence and by the Cross of the Lord going before them, which the earlier battle had lacked. [Col. 1338C] They advanced eagerly against the enemy with all their strength and fought fiercely.

> [Note: “Strength.” c. d. e: “the strength of the kingdom,” s. l; “governments,” a.]

But the enemy, circling our men in their customary fashion, thought the Christians finished and shouted with joyful howling. Yet the Lord Jesus was present and at last looked down from heaven; instilling courage into the Franks, he drove the enemies, deprived of the field, into flight. This had happened also in the earlier battle: although they had been driven from their tents more than once, they afterwards prevailed by their multitude. But then, while infantry struck from afar with arrows and cavalry at close range with lances, they continued to flee, placing all hope in their feet.

§ 385. Another battle occurred for him in later years, A.D. 1113. Our knights, pressed by the multitude of Turks and driven into flight, even lost the saving banner; 596 but, after fleeing some distance, they returned.

[Col. 1338D] Shame for their reputation gave courage to the terrified so that they might repel disgrace. A great battle of men took place there, fighting foot to foot and breast to breast. Our men recovered the Cross, claiming the field after routing their opponents. Many fell there whom I too had known, among them Geoffrey, his illegitimate great-nephew, who from boyhood gave the appearance of courage in his face and breathed its reality in his soul.

Both flights, therefore, were at first like a fomentation of disgrace, but in the end [Col. 1339A] a true nourishment of glory: the former more famous, but the latter more fruitful.

> [Note: “Finally.” a. c. d. e. l: “Then,” s.]

Finally, to replenish the resources he had lost and also for a lawful marriage, the countess of Sicily came to Jerusalem not long afterwards, bringing such treasures into the king’s chamber that anyone might wonder from where a woman had gathered such infinite heaps of precious furnishings.

> [Note: “Had gathered.” Albert of Aachen provides various examples of Countess Adela’s wealth and asserts that the mast of the ship in which she crossed to Palestine was covered with gold. (*Gesta Dei*, p. 373.)]

At that time he received her into his marriage-bed, but not long afterward dismissed her. They say that she suffered from an affliction by which cancer, an incurable disease, consumed her genitals.

> [Note: “Consumed.” Some authors assign a different reason for the divorce. His second wife—Taplanuz, daughter of the prince of Armenia—whom he had repudiated about the year 1105 and confined in the monastery of St Anne at Jerusalem, was still alive. Therefore his marriage with the countess of Sicily, his third wife, was annulled by the supreme pontiff. Accordingly, Adela returned to Sicily in 1117, where she died shortly after Baldwin’s death. (Albert of Aachen, book XII, chapter 24; William of Tyre, book II, chapters 1 and 15.) His first wife, who had accompanied him in the holy war, died before reaching Antioch; she was the daughter of Ralph II, co-lord of Tosny, and had been separated from her former husband, Robert, count of Meulan.]

It is certain that the king lacked offspring. Nor is it surprising that a man whose leisure was to suffer illness should have shrunk from wifely embraces, spending his whole lifetime in wars. 597 By these labors he made his admirable, almost divine valor an incentive to those present and a marvel to posterity. [Col. 1339B] He died on an Arabian expedition in April, A.D. 1118, and was buried at Jerusalem beside his brother in a public funeral, when the fourth month of the seventeenth year of his reign was beginning.

> [Note: “When the fourth month of the seventeenth year of his reign was beginning.” s. c. d. e 2. l; “of his reign” omitted in e 1; “when seventeen years of reign…” a.]

A man tried by many labors, whose glory no envious malice casts into shadow, except that he was more grasping of money than was right. Yet there is an easy and true excuse for this fault, if one considers that his necessary expenditure of gifts upon those who remained prevented him from purchasing less of the favor of those who departed.

§ 386. He was succeeded by his kinsman Baldwin, duke of Edessa, whom the dying king had named king, already commended by his former services. This man, having vigorously defended the kingdom for many years, enlarged it also by the principality of Antioch, [Col. 1339C] which he acquired after Roger, son of Richard, had been killed.

> [Note: “For many years.” s. c. d. e: “up to this time,” a. l.]  
> [Note: “Acquired.” Roger, prince of Antioch, son of Richard, seneschal of Apulia, married Hodierna, sister of Baldwin II. He was killed in 1119.]

He governed both regions with excellent moderation, with less boastful presumption indeed, but with greater and more prudent foresight. Yet there are some who attack his reputation, accusing him of excessive stinginess. Thus, when in the previous year the Turks captured him while he was riding not far from [Col. 1340A] Jerusalem, his own people mourned him little or not at all.

> [Note: “Mourned.” s. d. e: “mourned, as they say,” l.]

For almost a year it remained unknown both to the inhabitants and to rumor-mongers to what lands he had been taken, or whether he still breathed the upper air. The Jerusalemites, however, refused either to make a king or to interrupt the order and command of the knights until the truth of the matter should be known, being in no respect weakened by his absence.

Afterward, when the place where he had been bound was known, very daring knights, pretending to be merchants and concealing weapons beneath their clothing, entered the town and rescued the king from danger. They declared that they did this not in return for his avarice but for the favor of Joscelin of Turbessel,

> [Note: “But for the favor of Joscelin of Turbessel.” This account seems, in at least some respect, inaccurate: [Col. 1340C] Joscelin and the king were confined in the same castle. When it was captured, Joscelin escaped and gathered forces to liberate the friends who were then themselves surrounded by siege; but before he could reach the place, the Turks took possession of the castle and removed the king, who, deprived of liberty for some time, finally regained it only after an enormous sum of money had been paid. Fulcher of Chartres and William of Tyre, in *Gesta Dei*. (Sharpe, p. 469.)]

who had never considered anything important except to distribute to the knights everything he could. He lived long,

> [Note: “Lived long.” s. d. e: “is still alive,” l.—Baldwin died 21 August, A.D. 1131.]

a frugal man and [Col. 1340B] subject to no reproach save this. The principality of Antioch belongs to the son of Bohemond,

> [Note: “Bohemond.” a. c. d. e: “Bohemond,” accusative, s. l.—Bohemond II, son of Bohemond I and Constance, daughter of Philip I, king of France.]

of whom I shall now speak.

## On Bohemond

§ 387. Bohemond was the son of Robert Guiscard by a Norman woman.

> [Note: “Bohemond.” Bohemond, son of Guiscard by his first wife Alberada, had been called Marcus at baptism; but his father, having heard the tale of a certain giant named Buamund, gave him this name. (Orderic Vitalis, p. 817.)]  
> [Note: “Norman woman.” e. 1: “Normandy,” a. s. c. d. e. 2. l.]

The other son, Roger,

> [Note: “Roger.” Roger, later king of Sicily, was Guiscard’s son by his second wife Sikelgaita, daughter of Gaimar IV, prince of Salerno.]

was born in Apulia. He earned from his father the surname “Purse” (*Marsupius*), because his father, observing him with paternal and careful attention, discovered that even in tender childhood he delighted in counting coins. Bohemond, though already somewhat older, retained nothing but distributed even his childish gifts. Thus Roger received Apulia, which seemed to belong to him through his mother’s family; Bohemond set out with his father for the war at Dyrrhachium.

When the townspeople, trusting in their walls, boasted [Col. 1340C] that the city was named Dyrrhachium because it endured unshaken against every siege, he said: “I too am called Durandus, and I shall endure in the siege until I take the city’s name away, so that henceforth it shall be called not Dyrrhachium but Mollichium.”

> [Note: “He said.” c. d. e: “Guiscard said,” a. s. l.]  
> [Note: “Dyrrhachium.” The Romans changed the ill-omened name Epidamnum to Dyrrhachium (Pliny, III.26); and the popular corruption *Durachium* bore a certain resemblance to *duritia*, “hardness.” One of Robert’s names was Durandus, from *durando*, “enduring.” (Alberic the monk, in the *Chronicle*, in Muratori, *Annali d’Italia*, [Col. 1341D] vol. IX, p. 137.) The wordplay concerns *Durachium* and *Mollicium*, whose intended senses are “hard” and “soft.”]

[Col. 1341A] The firmness of this reply caused the terrified men immediately to open the gates. Thus secure in his rear, he subdued the remaining cities as far as Thessalonica with less effort. He had already reached that place and thought that Alexius could be conquered both by himself and by his son, when, deceived by his wife’s treachery, he died and left behind a great undertaking unfinished.

> [Note: “Left behind.” e 1. l 2: “arranged,” s. c. d. e 2. l 1.]

Then Bohemond returned to Apulia, held several castles through his brother’s indulgence, and acquired many through his own courage and prudence. For the duchy had come to his brother only in appearance; the better men followed the other in war.

> [Note: “The better men followed.” e: “the better men followed,” a. d. l; “followed the better man,” s. c.]

Nor was it of small consequence that, following his father’s policy, he repelled Guibert, gave Urban very strong support, and urged him, though hesitating, to go into Gaul for the council of Clermont, to which letters from Raymond, count of Provence, [Col. 1341B] and the bishop of Cahors invited him.

After the council had been held, he gladly seized the opportunity and transported forces into Greece. As he then advanced his army, he waited with restraint for Raymond and Godfrey.

> [Note: “Waited.” s. d. e: “waited for them to come,” l.]

When they arrived and joined him, he was a great encouragement to the rest, second to none in knowledge of military discipline and in valor. But because Fortune assigns the deeds he did with others to common praise, and the preceding account has made known how he was captured, it must now be said how he freed himself from bondage.

For Danishmend, seeing that no benefit accrued to him from holding so great a man, changed his mind

> [Note: “Mind.” s. d. e: “through softness of spirit,” l.]

and began to negotiate terms of peace. He wished neither to kill him, lest he provoke against himself the outpouring of Christian hatred, nor to release him without hope of a peace [Col. 1341C] that would last forever. Bohemond therefore promised perpetual peace with the heathen and returned to Antioch, carrying with him the silver fetters by which he had been bound.

> [Note: “Bound.” a. d. e: “fettered,” s. c. l.]

Received with applause by his people, he took possession of Laodicea and the other cities which Tancred had acquired, lest he seem to be drowsing in leisure while his uncle sighed in prison. Not long afterward he came to Gaul and offered the chains, which had been a burden to him, in honor of St Leonard. For that saint is said above all to have had power to loose chains, so that a captive could carry away his own burdens free, while his opponents looked on and did not dare utter a word.

> [Note: That saint, etc. Leonard was a nephew of Clovis, king of the Franks. By this monarch’s favor he obtained that, wherever he saw anyone in chains, that person should be immediately set free. Finally, God was pleased to honor him so greatly that, if anyone imprisoned invoked his name, the chains would suddenly fall, so that he could escape, the guards themselves being rendered [Col. 1342D] unable to hold him any longer. See Surius, *Lives of the Saints*, 6 November. (Sharpe, p. 471.)]

Thus, having married a daughter of the king of France and sent another woman to Tancred, he returned to Apulia. Frankish nobles followed him, leaving their homeland in hope of greater profit and also wishing to see at close hand [Col. 1342A] what the living image of valor could accomplish, of which such remarkable fame spoke everywhere.

Accordingly, after settling his affairs in Apulia, he again became fierce against Alexius, alleging as the cause of war the injury done to pilgrims, for which Alexius was notoriously infamous. But he accomplished little, indeed almost nothing, successfully, deceived by the cunning of the resourceful emperor, who either alienated all Bohemond’s commanders from him by money-induced debts or removed them by poison, as I have said.

> [Note: “As I have said.” a. s. c. d. e 2. l; omitted in e 1.]

Therefore, dejected in spirit, he returned to Apulia. There, a few days later, while planning a journey to Antioch, he died in February A.D. 1111, before old age, inferior to none in prudence, leaving behind a son of tender age.

> [Note: “While planning.” d. e: “while he was planning,” a. s. l.]

[Col. 1342B] A man steadfast in adversity and circumspect in prosperity. For, suspecting a harmful drink, he had devised a ready remedy: a knife which, fixed before the eater’s mouth, would, wonderfully to relate, betray by sweat upon its handle if any concealed poison had been introduced.

After him Tancred held the principality of Antioch, A.D. 1111, a nephew not unworthy of his uncle. When he too had trodden the common path of mortals by a premature death, 6 December A.D. 1112, Roger, son of Richard, succeeded. He was not inferior in war to the glory of his predecessors, but nevertheless incurred the disgrace of avarice. Therefore, when the knights avoided him, he met the Turks with almost no paid soldier and few natives, and was killed in A.D. 1119, having not cowardly avenged his own death.

For when he had been captured and mangled by them and was ordered to surrender his sword, he refused, saying that he would give it to no one except the commander,

> [Note: “By them.” c. d. e: “by the Turks,” a. s. l.]  
> [Note: “Would give.” a. d. e. l: “would surrender,” s. c.]

because he regarded everyone else as beneath a surrender commensurate with his rank. [Col. 1342C] The unfortunate Turk believed him, marveling at his feigned words; and, after removing his helmet so that his head was bare, stretched out his hand to receive Roger’s sword. Then Roger, grinding his teeth and summoning all that remained of his strength into the blow, struck off the Turk’s head. Immediately pierced through, he escaped the disgrace of slavery by an ingeniously conceived act of courage.

Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem, splendidly avenged his death and faithfully reserved the principality of the city and his own daughter for Bohemond, Bohemond’s son.

> [Note: “And his own daughter … faithfully.” s. d. e: “faithfully reserves [it] for Bohemond’s son,” l.—The advancement of Bohemond II and his marriage to Alice, daughter of Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem, belong to the later year 1126. (*Art de vérifier les dates*, I, p. 442.)]

## On Raymond
§ 388. Raymond was the son of William [Note: [Col. 1342D] William. More correctly, Pons. Raymond was the brother of William and the son of Pons, count of Toulouse. Everything here related by Malmesbury concerning William must therefore be referred to Pons. Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles and Toulouse, took his title of Saint-Gilles from his birthplace or first appanage. It lay in Lower Occitania, between Nîmes and the Rhône. [Col. 1343D] Moreover, he was duke of Narbonne and margrave of Provence.]—the most ancient count of Toulouse—who, a vigorous and capable man, rendered his country, made obscure by the slothfulness of his predecessors, illustrious through his titles. His wife Almodis [Note: [Col. 1343D] Almodis. She was the daughter of Bernard, count of La Marche and Limousin. Her first husband was Hugh V, lord of Lusignan; separated from him by divorce, she afterwards married Pons, count of Toulouse.], successively married to many men, bore many children by them all. For with a mad and unrestrained itch, the little woman, whenever a husband displeased her through long familiarity, migrated elsewhere to fill a new household. Thus, having first married the count of Arles [Note: [Col. 1343D] The count of Arles. More correctly, Hugh of Lusignan.], she soon grew weary of him and joined herself to this William; and, after bearing him two sons, she enticed the count of Barcelona into marriage [Note: [Col. 1343D] The count of Barcelona. Raymond Berengar I, count of Barcelona.].

Now William, standing at death’s threshold, gave the county of Toulouse to his namesake son, though one unlike him in character, because he was of duller intellect [Note: [Col. 1343D] Intellect. s. d. e.: “spirit,” l.], so that the people of Toulouse might attempt no innovation against him, being accustomed to that family’s rule. Raymond, however, being of a livelier spirit, received Quercy [Note: [Col. 1343D] Quercy.] 603 and enlarged it not moderately [Note: [Col. 1343D] Not moderately. c. d. e.: “by an immense amount,” s. l.; “without limit,” a.], adding Arles, Narbonne, Provence, [Col. 1343B] and Limousin. He also bought Toulouse from his brother, many years before he set out for Jerusalem on the expedition of the great commotion. But these achievements had cost much time and the labour of a lifetime.

Accordingly, ever engaged in fighting, he did not seek a lawful wife, but pursued pleasure in repeatedly renewed concubinage. Finally, he acknowledged as kin and heir a son, Bertrand, born of one of his concubines, because in some respects he resembled his father; and he united him in marriage with the niece of the marchioness Matilda [Note: [Col. 1343D] The niece of the marchioness Matilda. Elvira, or Helena, sister of Otto I, duke of Burgundy.], born of a Lombard woman, so that through that alliance he might protect those parts [Note: [Col. 1344D] Those. a. d. e. l: “that,” s. c.] of the province. He himself, too, in his very last years took a wife, the daughter of the king of Tarragona, having stipulated a splendid dowry—namely, perpetual peace among the neighbouring provinces. [Col. 1343C]

Not long afterwards, reflecting upon the snow of his head, he vowed the journey to Jerusalem, so that the strength of his weary and exhausted body might at last serve God. He was especially prompted by the bishop of Cahors, by whose chief exertions he himself had always been opposed. In a certain duel he had also lost one eye; displaying this conspicuous mark of misfortune, he not only did not conceal it, but even voluntarily gloried in it, exhibiting it as evidence of noble soldiery. Then, bound by mutual friendship, so that they might spend their old age in divine worship, they added incentives to Urban—already inclined toward preaching—to convene a council, after crossing the Alps, especially at Clermont, since that city was both near their own country and convenient for those coming from all France. Yet on the very journey [Col. 1343D] to the council the pope died.

The bishop [Note: [Col. 1344D] Bishop. c. d. e: “pope,” a. s. l.] of Le Puy, of whom we have spoken above, succeeded to his concern. Encouraged by his exhortations and shielded by his protection, Raymond was the first of all laymen to take the cross (A.D. 1096). He added to his vow that he would never return to his native country, but would rather, by labour enduring against the Turks, diminish the ruin [Note: [Col. 1344D] *Arvinum*. c. e 1, l: “ruin,” a. s.; “from ruin,” d. e 2.] of his former iniquities. On the journey he gave many proofs of courage: first in hardship and last in rest; and many proofs also of patience, since he willingly yielded the citadel [Note: [Col. 1344D] Citadel. e: “part,” a. s. c. d. l.] of Antioch, which he had occupied [Note: [Col. 1344D] Had occupied. a. d. e. l: “had preoccupied,” s. c.], to Bohemond, and the Tower of David to Godfrey.

But at last, his patience broken by the excessive demands of certain persons, he consented to the surrender of the city of Ascalon (A.D. 1099). For when the Franks first arrived, the townsmen, having examined the characters of all our leaders, chose him as their protector, because many men who had previously come from Montpellier [Note: [Col. 1344D] Montpellier. s. c. d. e: “Pislerio,” a. l.] [Col. 1344B] by ship for trade had extolled his good faith to the skies. Accordingly, after handing over the keys, they bound the duke by oath not to deliver the city’s control to any Christian, if he himself should either refuse or be unable to hold it.

Then the nobles murmured, demanding the city for the king’s dominion, because his kingdom would be of little value if he did not possess Ascalon, which was a refuge for enemies and an obstacle to our own people. The king indeed put the case mildly [Note: [Col. 1344D] Mildly. c. d. e: “gently,” a. s. l.], as he did everything, his tranquil expression suited to his character; the others more obstinately. This old campaigner made little of all this, refuting their statements with arguments that were not weak [Note: [Col. 1344D] Refuting. a. d. e. l: “rendering void,” s; “they are void,” c 1; “refuted,” c 2.]. All his companions, he said, had already made provision for their return: some had been carried back to their native land, while others were inhabiting the province they had acquired. He alone, having renounced his native [Note: [Col. 1344D] Native. d. e: “birth,” a. s. c. l.] land, could neither return there nor find a place here. He had yielded in other matters; let them allow him at least to hold Ascalon in fealty for the Holy Sepulchre. Besides, he had done so as not to violate his oath by surrendering it.

Hearing this, all raised an outcry, called him faithless and greedy, and could scarcely restrain their hands. Blushing with shame at this insult, the count abandoned the conduct proper to a fair and honourable man: he handed over the keys of the city [Note: [Col. 1344D] Of the city. d. e; omitted in a. s. c. l.] to the enemies of God, and compensated for fear of perjury with the blood of many thereafter. For to this day that city has been unable to be taken either by force or by strategy. Indeed [Note: [Col. 1344D] Indeed. a. c. d. e. l: “because,” s.], many of his own men, delighted by the city’s abundant wealth, earned the affection of its citizens by deserting the faith.

Thus that man, having left Jerusalem, came to Laodicea. After subduing it, he lingered there for some time; and when he went to Constantinople, Tancred gained possession of Laodicea, whether by force or affection is uncertain. Meanwhile, while remaining at Byzantium, Raymond’s vigorous prudence won him Alexius’s favour. Consequently, being conducted safely through the emperor’s kindness, he was not involved in the fellowship of the hardships which, as we said above, befell William of Poitiers and the others [Note: [Col. 1345D] Above. a. s. c. d. e 2. l; omitted in e 1.]. With them he captured the city of Tortosa [Note: [Col. 1345D] Tortosa. s: “Tortuous,” a. c. d. e. l.], but when they went farther on, he held it alone.

To spread his power more widely, he fortified the town opposite Tripoli called the Castle of the Pilgrims, and there appointed Herbert, previously an abbot, as bishop. And so that the shattered strength of his men might recover through some rest, he concluded a seven-year truce with the people of Tripoli. Yet before the appointed term the peace was broken, when a certain townsman was caught [Col. 1345B] inside the castle with a poisoned dagger concealed beneath his thigh. Then he would surely have put the finishing touch to the conquest of Tripoli, had death, arriving shortly afterwards, not taken away the breath of his present life while he was planning great things (28 February, A.D. 1105).

When news of his death was received, William of Montpellier [Note: [Col. 1345D] Montpellier. s. c. d. e: “Pislerio,” a. l.], and the other leaders of the province, arranged for William the Pilgrim, whom he had begotten during the siege by a Spanish woman and who was four years old [Note: [Col. 1345D] Four years old. d. e: “scarcely four years old,” a. s. c. l.], to be taken to his native land and brought up, amid the anxious hopes of all, for the succession. Bertrand did not unwillingly hear of this action [Note: [Col. 1345D] Action. a. s. c. d. e. l: “brother,” s, variant reading], although taken without consulting him, in order that he might restore his father’s glory. Accordingly, supported by countless soldiers—and especially by the Genoese and [Col. 1345C] Pisans, who were allied through his wife’s family—he attacked Tripoli by land and sea, and after a long siege reduced it, weakened by hardship, under his power (A.D. 1109).

His son Pons, born of the Lombard woman, succeeded him (A.D. 1112), a young man emulous of his ancestors’ glory. He married the wife of Tancred, formerly prince of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1345D] Wife. a. s. c. e. l: “marital,” d.]. For Tancred, when dying, had commanded this, declaring that in the youth lay both the advantage of the Christians and the utter ruin of the Turks [Note: [Col. 1345D] “In the youth.” c. d. e: “to grow up in the youth,” a. s. l.]. Pons therefore rules Tripoli, professing himself servant of the Holy Sepulchre, following, that is, the example of his grandfather and father.

## CONCERNING ROBERT CURTHOSE

§ 389. Robert, son of William, the first king of the English, was born in Normandy. He was already regarded as a young man of proven valour [Col. 1345D] 607 when his father came to England: of tested courage, although slight in body and stout in belly. He grew up beneath his father’s warlike wings in his earliest training, obeying his parent in all things. Yet, putting on the ardour of youth [Note: [Col. 1345D] “Putting on the ardour of youth.” c. e; “having put on the ardour of youth,” d; “putting on the green ardour of youth,” a. s. l.], [Col. 1346A] he hoped, at the urging of foolish companions, that he could obtain Normandy from his father while the latter was still alive.

When his father refused, driving the young man away with the roar of a voice that shook the earth, Robert departed angrily and harassed his homeland with many assaults. At first his father burst into laughter and repeatedly said, “By God’s resurrection! Robelin Curthose will prove a worthy man.” For that was his nickname because he was short. Otherwise, there was nothing in him to provoke displeasure: he was neither unattractive in appearance, nor inelegant in speech, nor weak in courage, nor feeble in counsel.

Later, however, the king became so inflamed with savage anger that he deprived him both of his final blessing and of the English inheritance—though Robert retained the duchy of Normandy, reluctantly granted and improperly held. After nine years he tested his courage amid the hardships of the journey to Jerusalem. In many respects he appeared wonderful, so that no Christian or pagan could ever make him dismount from his horse [Note: [Col. 1346D] Make. a. d. e. l: “be made,” s. c.].

Most notably he distinguished himself in the battle of Antioch, whose victory he ennobled by a fine exploit. For when the Turks, as we have said, suddenly terrified, had taken themselves to flight [Note: [Col. 1346D] Had taken themselves. s. d. e: “had committed themselves,” l.], and our men, scattered about, pressed them with increasing vigour, their commander Corbaguath, mindful of his native courage, reined in his horse and shouted to his men [Note: [Col. 1346D] Shouted. c. d. e: “shouted,” a. s. l.], calling them cowardly servants who had forgotten victories won over many years: were they, once conquerors of the East, to allow themselves to be driven from its territories by a foreign and almost unarmed people? At that cry many recovered their courage, turned back against the Franks, pressed them, and those nearest began to give way. Corbaguath heartened his own men and struck down enemies, properly performing the duty both of commander and soldier. [Col. 1346C]

Then the Norman count, Philip the cleric—son of Count Roger of Montgomery—and Warin of the castle of Tannières in Maine [Note: [Col. 1346D] Tannières. c. d. e: “Tanneo,” a. s. l.], encouraging one another with mutual spiritedness, turned their chargers; they had previously been retreating in feigned flight, and each attacked and unhorsed his opponent. There Corbaguath, although he recognized the count, was brought down by sheer bodily force. Judging flight shameful, he paid the price of his bold encounter with approaching death, immediately deprived of life’s breath (A.D. 1097). When his death was seen, the Turks, who had been exultantly howling, emptied of their newfound hope, resumed their flight.

In this confusion Warin fell; Robert and Philip gained the victory [Col. 1346D]. Philip was distinguished by this exploit [Note: [Col. 1346D] Distinguished. a. s. c. d. e. l 1: “shut out,” l 2.], but, it is said, died a good death at Jerusalem; apart from equestrian exercise, he was eminent in letters. Thus Robert, arriving at Jerusalem, stained his nobility with an indelible blot by refusing the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1346D] Kingdom … refused. The original histories of the crusading expedition mention no Robert by name as having refused the crown. It occurs, however, in Henry of Huntingdon. The honour of having refused the crown is also attributed to Raymond of Toulouse (VILLEHARDOUIN, no. 136). It appears that the crown was offered and successively refused by all the princes; but Godfrey of Bouillon, designated by the unanimous voice of the entire army, was compelled to accept it. (ALBERT OF AIX, book VI, ch. 33.)], offered to him with the consent of all [Col. 1347A], as being a king’s son [Note: [Col. 1347D] As being a king’s son. By the same reasoning the crown could also have been offered to Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the French; but he had availed himself of the uncertain opportunity to return home. Guibert attempts to exculpate Hugh the Great (pp. 518, 523).]—not, as is said, from reverence, but from fear of inextricable hardships.

Yet when he returned home, where he thought he would freely devote himself to refined pleasures, God, I believe [Note: [Col. 1347D] I believe. c. d. e: “as I believe,” a. s. l.], mercifully raging everywhere on account of this fault, attended him; and darkened all his delights with the bitterest afflictions, as the following narrative will plainly show. His wife, daughter of William of Conversano, whom he had married in Apulia on his return (A.D. 1100)—whose extraordinarily beautiful appearance could scarcely be expressed by any eloquence—he lost to illness after a few years [Note: [Col. 1347D] Lost to illness. Sibylla, duchess of Normandy, died by poison, according to Orderic Vitalis and the continuator of William of Jumièges. What Malmesbury reports appears to rest on no contemporary testimony.] (A.D. 1103). She was, they say, misled by the advice of a midwife [Note: [Col. 1347D] Midwife. s. d. e: “concubine,” l.], who, to secure an abundant supply of milk, had ordered the mother’s breasts to be tightly bound with a bandage.

But there came a great consolation amid such grievous evils: a son born of his wife [Note: [Col. 1347D] Born. s. c: “raised up,” a. d. e. l.]. Named William by prophetic reference to his grandfather’s name, he was to nourish hopes for the future of outstanding piety [Note: [Col. 1347D] Piety. d. e: “natural ability,” s. c; “uprightness,” a. l.]. The immense sum which his father-in-law had paid him as a dowry, in return for which he was to release Normandy from pledge [Note: [Col. 1347D] Pledge. Normandy had been mortgaged for only ten thousand marks, that is, approximately one hundredth part of its then value.], he squandered so completely [Note: [Col. 1347D] Squandered so completely. c. d. e: “so poured into the bosoms of mimes and vagabonds,” [Col. 1348C] a. s. l.] that within a few days not a coin remained.

His ill-considered arrival in England to wrest the kingdom from his brother Henry (A.D. 1106) also hastened his disgrace. But deserted by the assistance of those exiles who had invited him, he readily accepted peace with his brother, through the aid [Note: [Col. 1348C] Aid. c. d. e: “arbitration,” a. s. l.] of the leaders of both [Note: [Col. 1348C] Both. a. s. c. d. e 2. l: “each,” e 1.] parties, being nominally to receive from England an annual gift of three thousand marks. For the king had promised this without intending to pay it; but, knowing his brother’s pliability, he had played upon his easy credulity until the heat of war should cool. [Col. 1347C]

Robert, as though competing with fortune as to whether she might give more or he squander more, upon merely learning of the queen’s silent request, generously remitted this great mass of silver forever; he kissed as a great favour the suppliant prayers of feminine pride. For she was his goddaughter. He was therefore forgetful of injuries, forgiving of faults beyond the proper measure, responding according to their wishes to all who approached him lest he dismiss them sadly, and promising again what he could not give [Note: [Col. 1348D] Promising again. d. e: “pledging,” a. s. c. l.]. By this sweetness of character, through which he ought to have won praise and [Col. 1348A] the affection of his subjects, he provoked the Normans to such contempt for himself that they reckoned him of no consequence [Note: [Col. 1348D] Reckoned. a. s. c. d. e 2. l: “had reckoned,” e 1.].

Then each of the powerful men began to oppose him; then plunder was carried on throughout the region; then the common people were stripped. When the inhabitants of the province reported these troubles to the count, they obtained no assistance. At first stirred, he was soon appeased, either by trifling gifts or by anger subsiding with the lapse of time. Therefore, warned by their extreme hardships, they decided to implore King Henry’s help, that he might come to the aid of their distressed country.

Henry, adhering to Caesar’s maxim [Note: [Col. 1348D] Caesar’s maxim. Compare Cicero, *On Duties*, book III, ch. 21.], “If justice must be violated, violate it for the sake of citizens; in all other matters practise piety,” crossed forces into Normandy more than once, to lend a hand to suffering justice. At last he prevailed so far as to subdue the entire land except Rouen, Falaise, and Caen. Robert had now come to such a pass that he wandered almost like a beggar in those towns, obtaining a precarious 611–612 livelihood by sale from the burgesses [Note: [Col. 1348D] Obtaining by sale. a. d. e. l: “being about to obtain by sale,” s; “having obtained by sale,” c.].

The people of Caen, offended, did not remain long in their allegiance. Having warned the king through messengers, they shut the gates, set barriers in place, and closed the city. When Robert learned this and anxiously sought to escape, he was permitted to do so only with difficulty, while his armour-bearer was detained along with the hangings of his chamber. Then he hastened to Rouen and sought aid from his lord, the king of France, and from his kinsman, the count of Flanders. Receiving nothing, he came to open war, prepared to try his last fortune.

As fortune pursued him with an unlucky foot, he was captured (A.D. 1106) and kept until the day of his death [Note: [Col. 1348D] Until the day of his death. s. d. e: “to this day,” a. l.] in free custody, through the praiseworthy affection of his brother. He suffered no evil except solitude [Note: [Col. 1348D] Suffered. s. d. e: “suffers,” a. l.], if solitude can be called such where neither the attentiveness of guards nor an abundance of entertainments and provisions was lacking. He was thus held [Note: [Col. 1348D] Was held. s. d. e: “is held,” a. l.], the survivor of all the companions of the journey [Note: [Col. 1348D] Journey. a. c. d. e. l: “life,” s.], and was never released until his death (February, A.D. 1134) [Note: [Col. 1348D] “And was never released until his death.” s. d. e: “and whether he will ever leave, truth wavering, remains uncertain,” a. l. The variant readings exhibited here by the manuscripts appear to indicate the various periods in which the author composed and revised his history.].

He was eloquent in his native tongue, so that none could be more agreeable; judicious in other matters, so that nothing could be more excellent; skilled in war as any man might be. Yet because of softness of character he was never judged fit to govern a commonwealth. [Col. 1349A] But since above [Note: [Col. 1349A] Above. c. d. e: “already above,” a. s. l.] I have said everything I knew about Hugh the Great and the counts of Blois and Flanders [Col. 1350A], I shall, not inappropriately, I think, bring the fourth book to an end with this boundary.

**HERE ENDS THE FOURTH BOOK OF MASTER WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY’S *DEEDS OF THE KINGS OF THE ENGLISH*.**

613 **PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTH BOOK**

[Col. 1349]

[Col. 1349A] The order of events calls us to enter upon the time of King Henry. To hand down his deeds to posterity through the service of the pen is a task greater than should be required of us [Note: [Col. 1349D] Required. d. e; omitted in a. s. c. l.]. For even if only those things which have reached our ears were committed to writing, they could exhaust the powers of any most eloquent man and fill vast libraries. Who, then, would attempt to unfold in detail all those weighty counsels, [Col. 1349B] all those great royal undertakings? These belong to a loftier enterprise and a more leisured mind. Cicero himself would scarcely dare them in prose, though all Latin literature worships his wit; nor would anyone who challenges the Mantuan poet by the favour of verse.

Moreover, while I distrust uncertain informants—being a man remote from courtly mysteries, living apart, and ignorant of greater deeds—I set my hand to only a few matters. Therefore it is to be feared that, because the written word falls short of my mind’s intention, he whose many deeds I omit may appear the lesser.
