[Col. 1350A] Yet for this fault, if it is to be called a fault, I shall have a good excuse before one who remembers that I could neither know all his deeds nor ought to have written all that I knew. The insignificance of my position made the former necessary; the weariness of readers will compel the latter.

This fifth book, therefore, will claim in its bosom a few of his deeds; the rest assuredly fame will sow abroad, and memory, surviving into posterity, will preserve. Nor will it depart from the purpose of the previous four books; rather, it will set forth some things which occurred in his time here and elsewhere, perhaps either unwritten or unknown to many. These, then, will occupy a great part of the volume; pardon having been requested beforehand for such long digressions, both here and elsewhere.

615 **BOOK FIVE**

[Col. 1349]

[Col. 1349C] Henry, the younger son of William the Great, was born [Note: [Col. 1349D] Was born. Henry was born in 1068, not 1070, as Orderic Vitalis states. (*Annals of Burton*, in Fell, among the *Writers of English Affairs*, V, p. 246.)] in England in the third year after his father came there. Even as an infant he was brought up excellently, amid the united wishes of all, because he alone among William’s sons had been born as a king’s son and the kingdom seemed to belong to him.

Accordingly, he underwent his elementary training in literary schools [Note: [Col. 1349D] Literary. a. c. d. e. l: “liberal,” s.], and implanted the honey of books [Note: [Col. 1349D] Of books. d. e: “of letters,” a. s; “letter,” c 1, l; “literary,” c 2.] so eagerly in his marrow that no later tumults of war and no disturbances of care could dislodge it from his noble mind. Although he himself neither read much openly nor sang except in a subdued voice, learning—though sampled in a desultory manner—was, as I truly affirm, a great resource for the knowledge of ruling [Note: [Col. 1350D] For the knowledge of ruling. s: “knowledge for ruling,” a. c. d. e. l.], in accordance with that saying [Note: [Col. 1350D] That saying. a. s. c. d. e 2. l; omitted in e 1.] of Plato, in which he says: “A state is happy if either philosophers rule [Col. 1349D] 616 or kings practise philosophy.”

Thus instructed in philosophy not too scantily, he gradually learned to govern the inhabitants of his provinces more mildly, and not to permit soldiers to be committed except after the necessity had been examined with utmost care. Accordingly, as a boy, he fortified his hope of the kingdom through letters; and from time to time, even while his father heard him, he was accustomed to repeat the proverb: “An unlettered king is a crowned ass.” They even relate that his father, observing the composition of his character by which he fostered a lively prudence, did not pass by when Henry, injured by one of his brothers, was weeping, but encouraged him with these words: “Do not weep, my son, for you too shall rule.”

§ 391. Therefore, in the twenty-first year of his father’s reign [Note: [Col. 1350D] “Therefore, in the twenty-first … year.” William the Conqueror was outside England about Pentecost in the twenty-first year of his reign, A.D. 1087. It is certain that Henry was admitted to knighthood in 1086, that is, in the twentieth year of his father’s reign.], at nineteen years of age, at Pentecost (24 May, A.D. 1086), at Westminster, he received arms from his father. Sailing with him then to Normandy, he was present not long afterward at his father’s funeral, [Col. 1350D] while his other brothers had dispersed wherever hope carried each, as the preceding narrative has not concealed.

Accordingly, supported by his father’s blessing, his mother’s inheritance, and abundant treasures [Note: [Col. 1351D] Supported. a. s. c. d. e 2. l: “bound,” e 1.], he made little of his brothers’ arrogance, supporting or opposing either according to his deserts. Yet he was more inclined toward Robert because of Robert’s gentleness, and endeavoured to sharpen that brother’s mildness with his own severity. Robert, on the contrary, through harmful indulgence credulous toward informers, harassed his undeserving brother with injuries, which it will not be inappropriate briefly to recount.

§ 392. At the time (A.D. 1088) when, as the nobles of England raged against William II, Robert was waiting in Normandy for a favourable wind [Note: [Col. 1351D] Favourable. a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.] in order to sail, Henry had departed for Brittany by his command. Robert then, seizing the opportunity, spent on his mercenaries the whole sum of money—three thousand marks—which his father had bequeathed to the young man [Col. 1351B] by will.

When Henry returned, though he perhaps bore it with difficulty, he passed it over in silent prudence. But when the conclusion of peace in England was announced, they laid down their military service and gave arms a holiday. The count departed to his own territory; the younger brother, to that which his brother had given or promised him. For he counted promises as possessions received, while guarding the tower of Rouen in Robert’s fealty. Yet, through the accusation of most wicked men, his loyalty turned to the contrary, and through no fault of his own Henry was freely confined in that very place, lest he deceive his guards’ vigilance by escape.

Released after half a year, he offered himself to serve his brother William when invited; but William, rewarding the young man no more generously, deferred him for more than a year in needy dependence upon empty promises. Therefore, when Robert promised through messengers to amend what he had done, Henry came to Normandy and experienced the snares of both brothers. For the king, angry at having been rebuffed, had fruitlessly ordered that he be detained; while the count, changed by the seductions of his accusers, had altered his purpose, so as not easily to release one whom he had beguiled with flatteries.

But Henry, by God’s providence and his own shrewd diligence escaping all dangers, compelled his brother gladly to make peace by occupying Avranches and certain castles. Not long after, when William came to Normandy to take vengeance upon his brother Robert, Henry gave the count his service, being stationed at Rouen [Note: [Col. 1351D] Stationed. a. c. d. e. l: “having arisen,” s.]. In short, he soundly expelled the king’s men who came there by day and had long since occupied the whole city through the citizens’ treachery. [Col. 1351D] He warned the count by messengers to drive from the front those whom he himself pressed from behind.

As a result, a certain Conan, accused of treachery before the count (A.D. 1090), whom Robert wished to bind in chains, was entrusted to Henry’s care. Robert thought that nothing more calamitous could be inflicted on the wretch than to drag out his hated life in a prison. [Col. 1352A] Henry therefore requested that this Conan be reserved for his own charge. Once this was granted, he led him to the upper part of the tower of Rouen [Note: [Col. 1351D] Led. a. c. d. e. l: “led him,” s.]. Ordering him to look attentively in all directions from the height of the fortress, while ironically predicting all that would come to pass, he suddenly cast him down from the battlement into the Seine below, his companions present with him joining in the push. He declared that no delay of life was owed to a traitor: injuries done by any other person could be endured in some fashion, but punishment of the man who, having sworn homage to you, had been proved faithless could in no way be delayed [Note: [Col. 1351D] Could. a. s. c. d. l; omitted in e.].

This service was of little use with Robert, a man of changeable disposition [Note: [Col. 1351D] Changeable. a. c. d. e. l: “noble,” s.], who immediately turned to ingratitude and compelled one who had deserved well to leave the city. This was the time (A.D. 1091) when, as has been read above [Note: [Col. 1351D] As has been read above. § 308.], Henry resisted both brothers at Mont-Saint-Michel, for his own safety and likewise for glory. Thus, although he had been loyal and effective to each brother, they, judging the young man worthy of no possessions, trained him through want of provisions to greater prudence as he advanced in age [Note: [Col. 1351D] Trained. a. s. c. d. e 2. l: “reformed,” e 1.].

§ 393. After King William was killed, as has been said above [Note: [Col. 1351D] As has been said above. § 333.], and after the proper rites had been rendered for the royal funeral, Henry was chosen king (A.D. 1100), though certain disputes among the nobles had first been discussed and settled. Count Henry of Warwick, a man upright and holy, was especially active in this, having long enjoyed Henry’s familiar companionship.

Accordingly, after immediately issuing an edict throughout England [Note: [Col. 1351D] “After issuing an edict …” King Henry’s charter is found in Matthew Paris and in the *Textus Roffensis*, p. 51.], he prohibited the injustices instituted by his brother and Ranulf; he remitted payments and bonds; he expelled effeminate persons from the court; and he restored the use of lamps at night in the court, which had been discontinued in his brother’s time. He fully restored the moderation of the ancient [Note: [Col. 1352D] Ancient. a. c. d. e. l: “certain,” s.] laws [Note: [Col. 1352D] Fully. a. c. d. e. l: “customarily,” s.], confirming this by his own oath and that of all the nobles, lest these measures should be made a mockery.

Thus the day seemed joyful and renewed for the peoples, since, after so many clouds of anxiety, the lights of serene promises shone forth. And lest anything should be lacking from their accumulated joy, after Ranulf had been imprisoned in the darkness of a dungeon because of the dregs of his wickedness [Note: [Col. 1352D] Imprisoned in a dungeon. Ranulf Flambard, bishop of Durham, was confined in the Tower of London on 14 September, A.D. 1100, and escaped on 4 February, 1100.], swift messengers were sent for Anselm. Accordingly, amid the competing cheers of the common people, Henry was crowned king at London on the Nones of August (5 August), the fourth day after his brother’s death.

These events were celebrated the more earnestly lest the minds of the nobles should be shaken by regret at the election, because a report circulated that Robert, count of Normandy, was coming from Apulia and was on the point of arriving. Not long afterwards, persuaded by friends, and especially by bishops, to put aside the pleasure of concubines and embrace lawful marriage, on Saint Martin’s Day (11 November, A.D. 1100) [Note: [Col. 1352D] He married Matilda, daughter of Malcolm, king of the Scots. At the suggestion of certain persons Matilda had received the sacred veil. Religious scruples therefore arose concerning her impending marriage. A synod was convened at Lambeth by Archbishop Anselm, in which it was decreed that Matilda, who had not become a nun voluntarily, could marry according to God’s law. See Eadmer, pp. 56–57.] [Col. 1353A] he married Matilda, daughter of Malcolm, king of the Scots. Long before, he had set his heart on her love, caring little for dowry wealth, provided that he might possess the embraces he had long desired. For though high-born—being the great-granddaughter through Edmund, brother of King Edward—she possessed only modest household goods, being then orphaned of both parents. Of her there will later be fuller matter for narration.

§ 394. Meanwhile Robert, coming to Normandy, recovered his county without resistance. When this was heard, almost all the magnates of this land deserted the allegiance they had sworn to the king: some for no existing reason, others with slight pretexts begged up, because Henry would not freely assign them whatever lands they wished, according to their own pleasure. Only Robert son of Haimo, [Col. 1353B] Richard de Redvers, Roger Bigod, and Robert count of Meulan supported the just cause with brother Henry.

All the rest either secretly sent messages for Robert to become king, or openly branded their lord with insults, calling him Godric and his consort Godgifu [Note: [Col. 1353D] “Godric and his consort Godgifu.” “These appellations appear to ridicule Henry’s and the queen’s regular manner of life. Godric signifies ‘God’s kingdom.’” (SHARPE, 486.)]. He heard these things and, postponing anger, gave forth terrible laughter. He dissolved the mad folly of fools by calculated silence, a gentle dissembler of hatred but, in due time, an excessive requiter.

Ranulf’s cunning added to the storm of the times. Having induced his steward by messengers, he obtained a rope to be brought to him. The servant, a carrier of water, brought it immersed in a jar (alas for the trick! [Note: [Col. 1354D] “Alas for the trick!” a. d. e. l: “alas for the grief!” s. c.]); by it he was lowered from the wall of the tower [Note: [Col. 1354D] Tower. a. c. d. e. l: “lands,” s. — On the bishop’s escape, see Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 787.]. [Col. 1353C] Whether it injured his arms or scraped the skin from his hands, the people cared little. Escaping thence to Normandy, he gave spurs to the count, already panting and inclined toward the heat of battle, so that he should come without delay.

§ 395. In the second year of Henry, therefore, in the month of August (A.D. 1101), he landed [Note: [Col. 1354D] *Allitans*: c. d. e. l, *applicans* (“putting in; landing”), a. s.] at Portsmouth and deployed, poured out, and exposed his forces over the whole region. Nor indeed was the king given up to indolence, but drew together an innumerable force from the opposite side [Note: [Col. 1354D] *Traxit*: e., *contraxit* (“drew together”), a. s. c. d. l.], ready, if necessary, to defend his rank. For although the magnates were failing him, his party remained firm, protected by the support of Archbishop Anselm, together with his fellow bishops [Note: [Col. 1354D] *Episcopis*: c. d. e., *coepiscopis* (“fellow bishops”), a. s. l.], and of all the English. Therefore, welcomed for his loyalty to the people of the province and solicitous for their safety, he himself commonly went around the formations, teaching them how, while evading the fierceness of the soldiers, they should present their shields and return the blows. He thus brought it about that they demanded battle of their own accord, fearing the Normans in no respect.

But when men of sounder counsel urged that the law of piety would be violated if brotherly kinship met in battle, they inclined their minds toward peace, [Col. 1354A] reflecting that, if either should fall, the other would remain weaker, since no brother besides themselves survived. Moreover, the promise of three thousand marks deceived the count’s easy credulity, so that, his military array disbanded, he flattered himself with the prospect of so great a sum of money. In the following year Henry readily bestowed it, at the queen’s wish, granting whatever she asked.

§ 396. In the following year (A.D. 1102), Robert of Bellême, the eldest son of Roger of Montgomery, rebelled, fortifying against the king the castles of Bridgnorth and Arundel. Grain from every part of Shropshire was collected there, together with everything that protracted warfare demands [Note: [Col. 1354D] *Diuturnum*: a. c. d. e. l, *devectum* (“transported”), s.]. Nor was Shrewsbury Castle less ready to join the rebellion, the Welsh being, owing to the mutability of fortune, inclined toward evil.

The king therefore, great in spirit [Note: [Col. 1354D] *Ingens*: a. c. d. e. l, *rigens* (“rigid; stern”), s.] and crushing every adversity by courage, assembled an army and besieged Bridgnorth. Robert had already crossed from there to Arundel, trusting that the place was abundantly secured by a supply of provisions and the fierceness of its soldiers. Yet after a few days the townsmen, bent both by fear of their guilt and by the strength of the royal army, surrendered. On hearing this, Robert abandoned Arundel and his swelling enterprise, committing himself to royal service—on the excellent condition, indeed, that he should be permitted to depart for Normandy with every limb unharmed.

The people of Shrewsbury, through Ralph, then abbot of Sées and later archbishop of Canterbury, sent the king the keys of the castle: tokens of their present surrender and pledges of their future devotion. Thus the fire of dissension, which had been thought likely to become great, grew old into ashes within very few days and checked the appetite of deserters, ever greedy for novelties. Robert, with his brothers Ernulf, who had inherited his father’s surname, and Roger of Poitou—so called because he had taken a wife from that region—abjured England forever. Yet the force of the oath was qualified by the addition: unless he should at some time satisfy the king by service acceptable to him.

§ 397. Then the torch of wars, cast into Normandy and nourished by the accession of traitors as though by fuel for a pyre, grew strong, catching hold everywhere it was placed. For Normandy is a convenient and patient nurse of evils, although it is not spread over a great extent of territory; hence it long endures internal seditions well, and, when peace is restored, quickly rises again into a more fruitful condition, sending its disturbers, when it pleases, by free windings into France, once they despair of that province. England, on the contrary, does not long endure hostile persons; but those once admitted into her bosom she either renders submissive or destroys. Nor, worn down by ravaging, does she quickly raise again [Col. 1355A] a reviving head.

Accordingly, when the man of Bellême came to Normandy, he then and thereafter had accomplices in his malice, and, lest that should seem too little, instigators as well. Among them was William, Count of Mortain, son of Robert, the king’s uncle. From boyhood he had always envied Henry’s glory; and especially upon the Norman’s arrival he gave expression to his perverse spirit. For, not content with two counties—Mortain in Normandy and Cornwall in England—he demanded from the king the county of Kent, which his uncle Odo had held. So hostile and lawless was he that, with infamous arrogance, he vowed that he would not put on a cloak unless he obtained from his uncle, as he kept saying, the inheritance denied him.

For the moment, however, the most prudent king frustrated the man by the craft of a suspended answer. But after the storms had been dispersed and the calm of peace restored [Note: [Col. 1355D] “and the calm of peace restored”: c. d. e. l; s. reads “and peace having been restored in calm weather”], he not only refused what William requested, but also began to reclaim what had been improperly retained—yet moderately and by judicial process, so that nothing he did might seem to conflict with law or kick against equity. Then William, struck down by the judgment of the court, departed for Normandy in anger and fury (A.D. 1104). There, besides the attacks which he had vainly made on the royal castles, he also raged against Richard, Count of Chester, son of Hugh, invading, cutting away, and stripping off certain appurtenances of his lands. Richard was then a small child by reason of his age and had been entrusted to the king’s faith and guardianship.

§ 398. (A.D. 1106) These two, then, leaders of factions and inciters of rebellions, together with others whom it is shameful to name, grievously afflicted the country far and wide with ravaging. Frequent but fruitless complaints of provincials crying out against violence were carried to the count. He was moved by them; but fearing for his own affairs, lest the exasperated men should disturb his repose, he dissembled. King Henry, however, could not endure a passing grief for his brother’s disgrace, aggravated by the misery of the country. He judged it cruel and far removed from the duty of a good prince that impious men should glut their greed upon the fortunes of the poor [Note: [Col. 1355D] *Urgebant* (“pressed; pursued”). Compare Malmesbury, *De gestis pontificum*, book I, p. 227, Frankfurt ed., 1601.].

Accordingly, he admonished his brother, once when summoned to him in England with gentle words, and later, when he came to Normandy, more than once with harsh wars, to act as a count rather than as a monk. He deprived William the instigator of everything he possessed in England and razed his castles to the ground. But when this advanced nothing toward peace, royal majesty long exercised its anxious heart in deliberation: whether, forgetting brotherly kinship, it should rescue the country from danger, or permit it to waver through undiscriminating [Col. 1356A] [Note: [Col. 1355D] *Indiscreta*: c. d. e. l; s. has *indiscretam*.] affection. And indeed the common good and public duty would, in view of private kinship, have yielded ground, unless, as they say [Note: [Col. 1355D] “As they say.” No trace of this exhortation survives in the letters of Pope Paschal to King Henry. Paschal, writing to Archbishop Anselm, does order him to make peace between the king and his brother. He writes: “We inform your belovedness that the Count of the Normans has complained to us against the King of the English, because, having broken the oath which he had made to him for the acquisition of that same kingdom [Col. 1356D], he has invaded the kingdom. And you know that we owe assistance to the same count, on account of the labours which he undertook for the liberation of the Asian Church,” etc. (*Anselmi Opera*, new edition, p. 382, col. 2).], Pope Paschal had urged the hesitating king to this undertaking by letters, affirming, with the eloquence in which he excelled, that it would not be civil war but an advantage gloriously to be proclaimed for the country.

Accordingly, coming into Normandy, he quickly took the whole land—or rather recovered it—with all flocking to his lordship, so that he might provide for the exhausted province by the strength he possessed. Yet he did not complete so great a victory without bloodshed, losing many of his dearest men. Among them were Roger of Gloucester, a proven soldier, struck in the head by a crossbow-shot at the siege of Falaise; and Robert, son of Hamo [Note: [Col. 1356D] Robert, son of Hamo. His daughter Mabel became the wife of Robert, Count of Gloucester, to whom Malmesbury dedicated this work.], whose temple was struck by a lance and whose mind was dulled, so that for no short [Note: [Col. 1356D] *Pauco*: s. c. d. e². l, *parvo* (“small”), e¹.] time he survived as though bereft of reason.

They say that he was deservedly punished because, to secure his release, King Henry burned the city of Bayeux together with its principal church. Yet, as we hope, this was purgable for both: the king wonderfully repaired the Church’s losses, and Robert raised the monastery of Tewkesbury by his patronage to an extent not easily recalled. There the beauty of the buildings and the charity of the monks seize visitors’ eyes and attract their hearts. To make good these losses, Fortune put forth her utmost hand as war approached; and he brought under his dominion with ease [Col. 1356C] his brother, who came against him with no contemptible force, together with William, Count of Mortain, and Robert of Bellême.

This battle was fought at Tinchebray, a castle of the Count of Mortain, on the Saturday [Note: [Col. 1356D] Saturday. The vigil of St Michael’s feast fell on Friday in A.D. 1106.] of Saint Michael’s vigil. It was the same day, about forty years earlier, on which William had first landed at Hastings; perhaps by God’s provident judgment, so that Normandy should be subjected to England on the day on which the Norman host had once come to subdue England.

There the Count of Mortain was captured. He had come promising the townsmen his eager assistance and hoping at the same time to avenge his own injuries; but, as I have said, having been taken [Note: [Col. 1356D] *Prensus*: a. e. l, *pressus* (“pressed”), s. c. d.], he wore the necklace of prison-filth for the rest of his life. He deserves some praise for vigour of mind and youthful energy, but earned a harsh end for treachery. Bellême, indeed, at the very beginning of the war [Note: [Col. 1356D] *Belli*: a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.] avoided death by flight. But afterward, when he had provoked the king by secret factions, he too was captured and involved in the danger of the others, shut up for life in a prison-house [Note: [Col. 1356D] “He too was captured … prison-house.” Robert of Bellême was arrested by Henry’s command in A.D. 1112, when an envoy of the king of the French had come to him in Normandy to negotiate peace. In the following year Robert was transferred to England and kept prisoner in Wareham Castle until his death.] (A.D. 1112).

A man intolerable for his disordered habits [Note: [Col. 1357D] *Intolerabilis*: a. s. l; omitted in c. d. e.], [Col. 1357A] inexorable toward the faults of others, and notable for cruelty—among other things, in this: he blinded a little boy, his godson, whom he had received as a hostage, for a slight fault of the boy’s father, tearing out the poor child’s eyes with accursed nails. He was full of pretence and cunning; by a serene countenance and affability of speech he deceived the credulous, while terrifying those who knew his malice, so that no greater sign of coming disaster existed than the expression of his feigned friendliness.

§ 399. Thus the illustrious king, exulting in his successes, returned to the kingdom (A.D. 1107), having established in Normandy such peace as no age remembered and such as not even his father, despite that great pomp of deeds and words [Note: [Col. 1357D] *Fastu*: s. c. d. e, *roncho* (“boastful bombast”), a. l.], had ever been able to achieve. Emulating his father in other respects too, he restrained by edict the robberies, thefts, and sexual violations of courtiers [Note: [Col. 1357D] Edict. The laws of Henry I have recently been published by the most learned Mr Thorpe in the book *On the Ancient Laws and Institutions of England*.], ordering that the eyes and testicles [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Testibus*: c. d. e, *testiculis* (“testicles”), a. s. l.] of those convicted be torn out.

Against the money-changers, whom people commonly call minters, he showed especial diligence, allowing no counterfeiter to go unpunished by the loss of his fist if he had been discovered, through his fraudulent trade, to have mocked unsuspecting people.

§ 400. He won over the kings of the Scots by gentleness, emulating his brother’s practice. For that brother had both made Duncan, Malcolm’s illegitimate son, a knight and established him as king of the Scots after his father’s death (A.D. 1093). But when Duncan was slain through the treachery of his uncle Donald (A.D. 1094), he advanced Edgar to the throne, after the aforesaid Donald had been put to death [Col. 1357C] by the cunning of the younger David and the strength of William (A.D. 1099).

When Edgar fell by fate (A.D. 1107), Henry held his successor Alexander by a marriage alliance, giving him an illegitimate daughter as wife. By her, while she lived, he had, so far as I know, no offspring; nor did he grieve greatly when she died before him. For the woman was, it is said, lacking in what might be desired, whether in modesty of conduct or elegance of person. When Alexander was gathered to his forefathers (A.D. 1124), the younger David [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Minor*: c. d. e, *junior* (“younger”), a. s. l.], one of Malcolm’s younger sons, whom the king had made an earl and honoured with marriage to a distinguished woman, ascended the Scottish throne. He was more courtly than his brothers; polished from childhood by association and familiarity with our people, he had wiped away every trace of Scottish barbarism.

Finally, when he had gained the kingdom, he immediately relieved all his countrymen [Col. 1357D] of the payment of triennial tributes [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Tributorum*: a. s. d. e. l; *cubitorum* (“of cubits”), c.]—those who wished to dwell more civilly, dress more elegantly, and eat more carefully. Nor has it ever been recorded in the annals of history that three kings and brothers of such great holiness existed together, breathing the nectar of maternal piety. For, besides moderation in food, abundance of alms, and constancy in prayer, they so overcame the vice customary among kings that no woman but their lawful wives is ever said to have entered their bedchambers, nor is any one of them reported to have wounded chastity by any concubinage.

Edmund alone, a son of Margaret, degenerated from goodness. Sharing the wickedness of his uncle Donald, he was not ignorant of his brother’s murder, having stipulated, of course, for half the kingdom. But, captured and held in perpetual fetters, he repented frankly; and when he came to die, he ordered that he be buried in those very chains, confessing that he had deservedly been bound for the crime of fratricide.

§ 401. King Henry kept the Welsh, always rising in rebellion, under his power by frequent expeditions. Relying on sound counsel, in order to lessen their insolence, he transferred there all the Flemish settlers in England [Col. 1358B]. For England sheltered many who had flocked in during his father’s time because of maternal kinship, so that by their multitude they seemed burdensome to the kingdom itself. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Quapropter*: c. d. e; *quapropter omnes* (“therefore all”), a. s. l.] he gathered them, with their goods and families, at Rhos, a district of Wales, as into a cesspool, in order both to clear the kingdom of sediment and to blunt the blind rashness of its enemies.

Yet he did not for that reason refrain from directing expeditions there when circumstances required. In one of them (A.D. 1121), attacked by an arrow from an ambusher at a distance—whose boldness it is uncertain—he escaped soundly and splendidly, aided faithfully by the protection of his hooked mail-shirt and at the same time by God’s counsel frustrating treachery. Neither then did the shooter become known, nor could he ever afterward be discovered, although [Col. 1358C] Henry did not hesitate immediately to say that the arrow had been fired not by any ordinary Welshman but by a native of the district, declaring, “By the death of our Lord!” This was a manner of swearing drawn from the prince’s mouth either by excess of anger or by the gravity of the matter. For even at that moment the army was advancing slowly and cautiously on its own soil, not in hostile territory, so that no one could have expected anything less than an ambush. Nevertheless, through fear of internal danger, he did not withdraw a step from his purpose until the Welsh, by giving as hostages the sons of their nobles, together with some money and much livestock, calmed the movement of royal magnanimity.

§ 402. He brought the Bretons across the sea—whom, when young, he had had as neighbours of his castles [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Castellis*: c. d. e, *castellis suis* (“his castles”), a. s. l.] of Domfront and Saint Michael [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Sancti Michaelis*: c. d. e, *monti Sancti Michaelis* (“Mount Saint-Michel”), a. s. l.]—into obedience by money. [Col. 1358D] For that race of men is poor in its homeland and otherwise earns wages for a laborious life with foreign pay. Give them money, and they do not shrink even from civil wars, without regard for right or kinship; but according to the amount of gifts [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Munerum*: a. c. d. e. l, *nummorum* (“coins”), s.] they are bound to whatever party you choose. Not ignorant of this habit, whenever he needed mercenary soldiers, Henry spent much [Col. 1359A] upon the Bretons, borrowing the loyalty of a faithless people with his own money [Note: [Col. 1359C] *Mutuatus* (“having borrowed”): a. s. c. d. e². l; *mutuans* (“lending”), e¹.].

§ 403. In the early years of his reign he offended Robert, Count of Flanders, for this reason. Baldwin the Elder, this Robert’s grandfather, had energetically assisted William when he came to England, with the shrewd counsel he possessed and with an addition of soldiers. William had repeatedly repaid these distinguished services, counting out, as they say, three hundred silver marks every year to his father-in-law for loyalty and kinship [Note: [Col. 1359C] “Three hundred silver marks.” From two charters printed in Rymer’s *Foedera*, vol. I, pp. 6–7, it appears that Henry paid Robert, Count of Flanders, an annual pension of four hundred marks, agreed in return for a contracted force of one thousand armed horsemen.]. That generosity, not diminished in Baldwin the son, stuck in the malice of Robert the Frisian, which the preceding account [Note: [Col. 1359C] See § 257.] did not pass over.

This Robert, son of the Frisian, had not found it difficult to obtain from William II the payment that had been omitted, both because he advanced their kinship and because William had an unconquerable spirit in scattering money. But Henry, weighing matters more carefully, so as neither improperly to amass [Note: [Col. 1359C] *Adunaret*: a. c. d. e. l; *adamaret* (“should love”), s.] money nor to squander what he had except as was due, replied as follows when Robert returned from Jerusalem and demanded three hundred silver marks as though by right of command:

“The kings of England are not accustomed to pay tribute to Flemings; nor do I wish to stain the liberty of my ancestors by the mark of my own timidity. Therefore, if he leaves the matter to my judgment, I shall gladly give my kinsman and friend whatever circumstances permit; but if he judges that he must persist in exaction, I shall refuse altogether.”

Defeated by this reasoning, Robert remained angry with the king for a long time; but receiving little or no assistance from his enmities, he turned his mind toward gentleness, having learned that the king could be bent by entreaty [Col. 1359C], not by tyrannical arrogance.

But the vicissitudes of the times gave Baldwin, Robert’s son, grounds for anger against the king. Seeking to impose William, son of Robert of Normandy [Note: [Col. 1359C] William, son of Robert of Normandy. William, surnamed Clito, son of Robert, duke of Normandy, and Sibyl of Conversano, assumed the rule of the county of Flanders after the death of Charles the Good, A.D. 1127.], upon his inheritance, Baldwin voluntarily involved himself in another man’s affairs and repeatedly harassed the king’s castles in Normandy by unexpected attacks (A.D. 1118), threatening great injury to the land if fate had allowed it. But near Arques [Note: [Col. 1359D] Arques. Historians dispute both the place where Baldwin was wounded and where he died; indeed, they do not even agree about the time of his death. Whatever the case, he seems to have spent the final ten months of his life in the monastery of Saint-Bertin, where he died and was buried (*Annals of Flanders*, book IV, under the year 1119), as noted in Bouquet XIII, 14. There the following is read concerning the same count: “At that time Henry, king of the English, threw his brother Robert, duke of Normandy, into chains when he returned from the Holy Land, because Robert, as the eldest of the stock, claimed the kingdom of England, which Henry had occupied. Robert’s disinherited son William fled to this Count Baldwin, his kinsman. The count supported him and trained him in military arms; and, when William reached his eighteenth year, he urged him to rebel against his uncle Henry, king of England, and often, with him, harassed Normandy by severe incursions. Thus this young Baldwin, accustomed to wars and adorned with frequent victories, shone with such great praises that the fame of his valour was spread through every region. But just as his courage shone beyond the measure of his age by sudden advances, so, through God’s hidden ordering opposing his enterprises, it could not endure long. For, while he endeavours to restore the said young William to his paternal inheritance and repeatedly harasses Normandy, he is grievously wounded, it is said, when the shield of a certain soldier strikes against his forehead; and from that wound he at length lost his life and his principality, leaving no surviving offspring, in the eighth year of his rule.”] he met with a larger force of soldiers than he feared and hastened his death, his helmet being shattered by repeated blows and his brain injured.

They assign as the cause of the aggravated illness that on that day he had rashly eaten garlic with goose and had not abstained from sexual intercourse at night. Here posterity may observe an outstanding example of royal compassion: Henry sent a most skilled physician to the sick man and, if we may believe it, wept that illness should destroy one whom, in admiration of his courage, he would rather have saved. His successor Charles (A.D. 1119) did not trouble the king’s strength by any disturbance; after first entering into a treaty and then completing it [Note: [Col. 1360D] *Consummato*: c. d. e, *confirmato* (“confirmed”), a. s. l.], he embraced Henry’s friendship.

§ 404. Philip, king of the French, was neither useful [Note: [Col. 1360D] *Utilis*: a. s. c. d. e². l; *inutilis* (“useless”), e¹.] nor hostile to our king, because he was more devoted to his belly than to affairs and was not, moreover, a bordering neighbour in respect of Henry’s castles. For the few places then held by Henry in Normandy were nearer Brittany than France. Add that, as I said above [Note: [Col. 1360D] See § 235.], Philip, advancing in age and burdened with lust, was enslaved by unlawful passion for the beauty of the Countess of Anjou [Note: [Col. 1360D] The Countess of Anjou: Bertrada, fourth wife of Fulk IV, Count of Anjou.].

Therefore, excommunicated by the pope, when no divine service was performed in the town where he stayed, but, upon his departure, the ringing of bells resounded everywhere, he expressed his foolish stupidity with laughter: “Do you hear,” he said, “how the bells drive us away!” So great was the mockery in which he was held by all the bishops of his province that none would marry them except William, Archbishop of Rouen [Note: [Col. 1360D] “Except William, Archbishop of Rouen.” Orderic Vitalis ascribes this crime to Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Pope Urban II, in a letter to Raynald, Archbishop of Rheims, ascribes it to Ursio, bishop of Senlis.]. He paid for the rashness of this act [Col. 1360C] by being under interdict for many years, and was at last, only with difficulty and through Archbishop Anselm, restored to communion with the Apostolic See.

Meanwhile, no delay put an end to Philip’s satiation with mad drunkenness, except that, struck by illness at the end of his life, he received the monastic habit at Fleury [Note: [Col. 1360D] “He received the monastic habit at Fleury.” Although King Philip seems, from a letter written to him by Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to have intended some years before his death [Col. 1361D] to put on the monastic habit, what he proposed to himself concerning adoption of the religious habit never took effect.]. Bertrada acted more beautifully and fortunately in seeking the veil among the nuns at Fontevraud while her age and health were intact and her beauty not wrinkled. Not long afterward she took leave of this present life, perhaps because God had provided that the body of a delicate woman could not serve the labours of religion.

§ 405. But Louis, Philip’s son, showed himself changeable, steadfast in neither direction. At first he was a chief inciter of Henry’s anger against his brother, urging Henry to take Normandy, being corrupted, indeed, by English spoils and much royal gold. This was not because Henry had offered them, but because Louis had himself invited him, freely exhorting him not to allow the sinews of a land once most glorious to be cut away by his own inaction.

Afterward, however, enmity arose between them over Count Theobald of Blois, son of Stephen who fell at Ramla, because Theobald had been born to Stephen [Col. 1361B] by Adela, daughter of William the Great. Thus, for a long time envoys on our king’s behalf wore out the roads, seeking that Louis might deign to grant satisfaction to Theobald. But Louis, making little of these entreaties, caused Theobald to be anathematized by the pope [Note: [Col. 1361D] *Devotari* (“be anathematized”): a. c. e. l; *denotari* (“be denounced”), s. d.] as arrogant and rebellious against God. Theobald, besides an austerity of manners that seemed intolerable to everyone, was accused of depriving [Note: [Col. 1361D] *Privare*: a. c. d. e. l; *fraudare* (“defrauding”), s.] his lord of ancestral possessions.

Therefore, after enmities had been prolonged for a long time [Note: [Col. 1361D] *Diu*: a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.], while each swelled with anger and neither would yield to the other on the personal issue [Note: [Col. 1361D] *Pro*: a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.], Louis came into Normandy, greedily exhausting everything far and wide with an ever more inflated breath. These things were reported to the king, who remained at Rouen, so much so that [Note: [Col. 1361D] *Adeo ut*: a. d. e¹; *adeo*, e². l; *quoad*, s.; *qui*, c.] the common soldiery besieged his ears, urging him to allow Louis to be repelled: a man who had formerly cherished his bed because of the weight of his belly [Col. 1361C], but now, because of Henry’s inaction, burdened the air with threats.

Remembering his father’s example, Henry preferred to blunt the Frenchman’s folly by patience rather than repel it by force. Indeed, he gently addressed his soldiers and soothed them with this reasoning:

“They should not wonder if he took care not to be prodigal of their blood, since they had proved their loyalty to him by no slight tests. It would be impious that, in procuring a kingdom for himself, he should glory in the deaths of men who voluntarily devote their lives to contests for his safety. They were the foster-children of his realm, pupils of affection; therefore he wished to follow the example of a good prince, so that by his moderation he might restrain the attack of men whom he saw so prepared to die for him.”

At last, when he saw that his prudence was being disturbed by hostile interpretation and called cowardice [Col. 1361D], to such a degree that Louis was making fires and driving off plunder within four miles of Rouen, he stirred up the greater strength of his spirit; and, after preparing his battle-line, he won a splendid victory, punishing former dissimulation by a fierce victory [Col. 1362A].

Nevertheless, peace was made some time afterward, because all things undergo change and money lightens whatever injuries powerful men wish to overcome by persuasion. Therefore William, our king’s son, did homage to the king of France for Normandy, receiving that province from him by lawful right [Note: [Col. 1362D] “Receiving that province from him”: a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.]. This was the time (A.D. 1119) when the same boy was betrothed to and married the daughter of Fulk, Count of Anjou; his father prudently strove that, through money on one side and kinship on the other, nothing should be stirred up against his son.

§ 406. In these days Pope Calixtus, of whom I shall say more later, made his presence known near Normandy (A.D. 1119). [Note: [Col. 1362D] Having obtained an interview with Henry, Pope Calixtus met the king at Gisors after the Council of Rheims had been held, in October A.D. 1119.] By obtaining an interview with him, the king of England compelled the Romans to admire [Col. 1362B] and praise the prudence of the Normans. For Calixtus, as is said, had come in a hostile spirit, intending sharply to ask why Henry held his brother—a pilgrim of the Holy Sepulchre—in captivity. But, constrained by the prince’s answer, which resembled the truth, and by plausible arguments, he made little reply in opposition.

For commonplace arguments can be bent to either side according to the eloquence of the speaker [Note: [Col. 1362D] *Loci*: a. c. d. e. l; omitted in s.], especially when the eloquence is not despised that costly gifts season [Note: [Col. 1362D] *Oratoris*: a. c. d. e. l; *orationis* (“of the speech”), s.]. And, so that nothing might be lacking to the accumulated display, Henry put forward young men of most distinguished birth, sons of the Count of Meulan, to debate dialectic against the cardinals. Since their twisting sophisms could not be resisted by the vigour [Note: [Col. 1362D] *Vivacitate*: c. d. e, *pro vivacitate* (“for the vigour”), a. s. l.] of arguments, the cardinals were not ashamed to confess [Col. 1362C] that the western regions flourished in greater literary learning than they had heard or thought existed in their own country. Thus this conference earned the result that the pope declared nothing more just than the cause of the king of the English, nothing more eminent than his prudence, nothing more copious than his eloquence.

§ 407. The father of these boys was Robert, Count of Meulan, as I have said: son of Roger of Beaumont, who founded the monastery of Préaux in Normandy. He was a man of ancient simplicity and loyalty. Often invited by William I to come to England, where he would be rewarded with abundant possessions according to his desire, he declined, declaring that he wished to foster the inheritance of his fathers, not seek or seize overseas and undeserved possessions.

He had two sons: this Robert and Henry. Henry, Count of Warwick, a man of sweet and peaceful disposition, lived and ended his life in pursuits suited to his character. The other, more cunning and with a heart more prone [Note: [Col. 1362D] *Pronioris*: a. e. d. e. l; *pro moribus* (“according to his habits”), s.] to craft, possessed, besides his paternal inheritance in Normandy [Col. 1363A] and extensive estates in England, the castle named Meulan, which had been held by his mother’s brother Hugh, son of Waleran; he purchased it from the king of France for money.

While under the preceding kings he had advanced into eminence as hope gradually grew, in Henry’s age he flowered with the highest success. His counsel was held [Note: [Col. 1363D] *Habebaturque*: a. c. d. e. l; *habebatque* (“and he had”), s.] as though one had consulted an oracle of God. And not without reason he was thought to have attained this reputation: mature in age for counsel, an advocate of concord, a dissuader from discord, and, whatever he undertook, a most rapid persuader to the full extent of his eloquence. He carried such weight in England that by his example he altered the established custom of dress and food.

Finally, through him the practice of dining once a day became frequent in the courts of all the great men [Note: [Col. 1363D] “The practice of dining once a day.” Henry of Huntingdon mentions this custom (*History*, book VI, p. 209), speaking of Harthacnut, who sat down at table four times a day: “Whereas the custom in our time is, either through avarice or, as they themselves say, through disgust, for princes to set food before their households only once a day.”]. He had adopted it for the sake of good health and, by his example, transmitted it to others, having received it, as I said, from envoys [Note: [Col. 1363D] *Nunciis*: a. s. c. d. e². l; omitted in e¹.] of the Emperor Alexius of Constantinople.

Yet he is unjustly blamed for having done and taught this more through frugality in lavish entertainment than through fear of indigestion and want, because no one, it is said, was more lavish toward others at table or more restrained toward himself. In judicial proceedings he was a champion of justice; in wars, a provider of victory. He urged his lord the king to preserve the severity of the laws, while not following them himself but setting them before others. Free from treachery against the king [Note: [Col. 1363D] *Regem*: e¹, *rege*, d., *reges*, a. s. c. e². l.], he was its persecutor in others [Note: [Col. 1363D] “Persecutor.” Henry of Huntingdon, in his letter to Walter (*Anglia Sacra*, part II, [Col. 1364D] p. 695), attributes an outstanding character to Robert. Orderic Vitalis relates that he died on the first day of June, A.D. 1118.].

§ 408. King Henry also had Roger, bishop of Salisbury, as his confidential adviser, upon whose counsel he relied most heavily; for even before he became king he had set him over all his household. [Note: “He had set him over.” See William of Newburgh, I.6.] He first appointed him chancellor, then bishop, having tested the man’s prudence. His skillful administration of the episcopal office gave hope that he was worthy of a greater charge; accordingly, Henry delegated to his justice the government of the whole kingdom, whether he himself were present in England or staying in Normandy. The bishop shrank from involving himself in such heavy concerns, unless three archbishops of Canterbury—Anselm, Ralph, and William—and finally the pope, had imposed this duty of obedience upon him. Henry worked to bring this about, knowing well that Roger would faithfully manage his interests; nor did Roger disappoint the king’s hope. Rather, he conducted himself with such integrity and diligence that no envy was stirred up against him.

Finally, when the king, having commonly remained three years, sometimes four, and even longer in Normandy, returned to his kingdom, he ascribed it to the restraint of the justiciar that he found no trouble, or very little. [Note: “When he returned … trouble.” a. c. d. e. g. k. l.; omitted in s.] Meanwhile, he did not neglect ecclesiastical duties, but every morning duly discharged them all, so that he might attend to his other affairs more readily, swiftly, and safely. A high-minded bishop, sparing no expense whatever when he had proposed works to be done—especially buildings—he brought them to completion; as may be seen elsewhere, but above all at Salisbury and Malmesbury. [Note: “And Malmesbury.” s. d. e.; omitted in 12.] For there he made buildings extensive in area, costly in expenditure, and most beautiful in appearance; their stones are arranged in such well-proportioned order that the joining deceives the eye, and the whole wall seems to the mind to be a single stone. He both built anew Salisbury church and adorned it with ornaments, so that it yields to none in England and surpasses many; and he himself might without falsehood say to God: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house.”

§ 409. Henry kept Murchad, king of the Irish, and his successors, whose names fame has not brought forward, so devoted to himself that they wrote nothing except what flattered him and did nothing except what he ordered. Yet Murchad is said, for some reason unknown to me, to have behaved rather arrogantly toward the English for a few days; but he soon calmed the swelling of his heart when navigation and the commerce of seafarers were prohibited. For what value would Ireland have if merchandise did not sail there from England? Thus, owing to the poverty—or rather the ignorance—of its cultivators, it produces beyond the towns a soil barren of every good and an uncultivated, squalid population of Irishmen; while Englishmen and Frenchmen, with their more cultivated manner of life, inhabit the towns through the commerce of markets.

Paul, earl of Orkney, although subject by hereditary right to the king of Norway, held the king’s friendship in such reverence that he frequently sent him small gifts. For Henry, with eager delight, coveted the marvels of foreign lands: lions, leopards, lynxes, and camels—whose young England lacks—demanding them from foreign kings with great pleasure, as I have said. He had an enclosure called Woodstock, in which he maintained the delights of such creatures. He had placed there an animal called a *hystrix*, sent to him by William of Monte Pislerio. [Note: *Hystrix*. The manuscripts: read *strix*.] Of this animal Pliny the Second, in the eighth book of his *Natural History*, and Isidore, in the *Etymologies*, relate that it is an African animal which the Africans call a kind of hedgehog, covered with bristling quills, which it naturally shoots at pursuing dogs. For the quills are [Note: “For the quills are.” e1: “But those quills are”; e2: “But the quills are”; a. c. d. l.: “But they are”; s.: “But they are”]—as I have seen them—a palm’s length and more, sharp at both ends, like the feathers of geese where the down ceases, but somewhat thicker; black and white, as though variegated.

§ 410. This especially distinguished Henry among other things: although because of disturbances in Normandy he was often and long absent from his kingdom, he restrained rebels by fear of himself so completely that you would have found nothing lacking to peace in England. Therefore foreign peoples also gladly made for that place as for the one harbor of secure repose.

Finally, Siward, king of the Norwegians, a man comparable in the first vigor of life to the bravest, having undertaken a journey to Jerusalem and requested the king’s peace, spent the whole winter in England. Having lavishly expended gold among the churches, as soon as the west wind opened the vernal gates to a calm sea, he returned to his ships. Sailing out upon the deep, he left the Balearic islands, called Majorca and Minorca, terrified by his arms and made easier to subdue for the aforesaid William of Monte Pislerio. [Note: “The Balearic.” a. s. c. d. e2. l.; e1: “of the Balearics.”] From there he pressed on to Jerusalem, all his ships safe except one. That vessel, while slow to cast off its moorings from the harbor, was swallowed by a monstrous whirlpool—which Paul, historian of the Lombards, declares to lie between the coasts of the Seine region and Aquitaine—so violent in the rush of its waters that their roar can be heard for thirty miles. [Note: “Paul, historian of the Lombards.” Paul the Deacon, also called Winfrid, was secretary to Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards. Paul wrote his *History of the Lombards* in six books before Charlemagne established his empire. Sharpe says: “Malmesbury seems here to narrate that a ship was consumed in the Mediterranean Sea, but incorrectly; for Paul the Deacon certainly speaks here of the gulf of Alderney.” See Paul the Deacon, I.6, in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, I.]

Coming to Jerusalem, he besieged, broke into, and subdued Tyre and Sidon, cities lapped by the sea, for the benefit of Christendom. Changing his route, he entered Constantinople and affixed, as a trophy upon the summit of Hagia Sophia, a ship adorned with golden dragon-prows. When his men were dying in groups in that city, [Note: “In that city.” a. s. c. d. e2. l; omitted in e1.] he devised a remedy: the survivors were to drink sparingly, and wine mixed with water. By sharpness of intellect [Note: “By sharpness of intellect.” c. d. e: “by great sharpness of intellect,” a. s. l.], he first conjectured that the same would happen in men when a pig’s liver was thrown into unmixed wine and immediately dissolved by the harshness of the liquor; afterward, when someone had died and been disembowelled, he learned it by sight.

Accordingly, when the emperor, struck by the prince’s prudence and courage—which promised something great—tried to retain him, he cleverly frustrated the emperor’s hope, which was already swallowing up Norwegian gold. [Note: “He cleverly frustrated.” a. c. d. e2. l; e1: “with beauty he frustrated”; s.: “he nobly ceased.”] Having obtained leave to go to the next city, he deposited with him chests of treasure, filled with lead and sealed, as pledges of his very swift return. Thus the emperor was deceived; the other hastened home on foot.

§ 411. But to return to Henry: in managing his affairs he was effective in foresight and persistent in defence. He restrained wars as far as he could with honor; but when he had resolved not to endure something, he was an unbearable exactor of vengeance for wrongs, beating aside dangers that stood in his way with the shield-boss of valor. He was steadfast in hatred and friendship toward everyone, satisfying, in the one case, an excessive heat of anger, and in the other, royal magnanimity: that is, he cast down enemies into misery and raised friends and dependants to the point of envy. For philosophy presents this as among the first, or the greatest, duties of a good ruler: that he should spare the subjected and crush the proud. [Note: “That he should spare,” etc.: “To spare the subjected, and subdue the proud” (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.853).]

Inflexible in the rigor of justice, he kept common people in peace and nobles under honorable restraint; he sought out hidden thieves and counterfeiters with the greatest diligence and punished them when found; nor did he neglect small matters. When he heard that broken coins, although of good silver, were not accepted by sellers, he ordered all coins to be either broken or cut. [Note: “When [he heard of] broken coins … he ordered all to be broken or cut.” “Since genuine coinage could not be distinguished from doubtful, silver coins were frequently broken and therefore more often rejected. Henry accordingly decreed that all coins should be broken, so that everyone could distinguish whether the coinage was sound or not, and that even broken coin should be accepted everywhere. See Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, p. 94.” (Sharpe, 507).] He corrected the false ell-measure of merchants, using the measure of his own arm and publishing it throughout England.

As for his courtiers, [Note: “As for his courtiers.” With these words book I ends abruptly, mutilated.] wherever they were in villages, he prescribed how much they might receive from peasants without payment, and how much, and at what price, they were to buy. Transgressors he punished either with a heavy monetary fine or with loss of life. At the beginning of his reign, in order to brand offenders through the terror of an example, he was inclined to mutilation of limbs; later, to monetary payment. Because of his prudence in conduct, as mortal nature commonly brings it about, he was held venerable by nobles and beloved by country people.

If any of the greater men, forgetful of their sworn oath, strayed from the path of loyalty, he immediately recalled the erring to the line, both by effectiveness of counsel and by persistence in labor; bringing those who resisted through the severity of wounds back to health of mind. I could not easily enumerate how long and exhausting were the toils he expended in such cases, since he allowed nothing to go unpunished that offenders had committed contrary to his dignity. Normandy, as I said before, was the chief cause of warfare. While he himself lived there for many years, he also watched over England; no one dared raise his head, while he beheld their boldness and they looked up to his prudence.

Nor was he ever attacked by plots because of the rebellion of any of his nobles, except once. Their author was a certain chamberlain, born of a father of common rank but himself a man of notable name because of his custody of the royal treasures. Once detected [Note: “Once detected.” Suger relates that Henry was so terrified when the conspiracy of his chamberlains was revealed that he frequently changed his sleeping place, increased the number of guards, and constantly kept shield and sword at hand throughout the night. The man mentioned here, convicted of conspiracy, although formerly singularly cherished and promoted by the king, deservedly might have been hanged, but lost only his eyes and his sexual member. *De Vita Ludovici Grossi*, Duchesne IV.308 (Sharpe, 508).] and readily confessing, he paid harshly the penalty of treachery. Apart from this, throughout his life Henry was secure, holding all men’s minds bound by fear and their speech by affection.

§ 412. In height he exceeded the shortest men but was surpassed by the tallest; his hair was black and receding near the forehead, [Note: “Receding.” a. c. d. e. l2; s: “flowing.”] his eyes gently clear, his chest broad, his body fleshy. He was full of wit when the occasion allowed, nor, despite the weight of affairs, less agreeable when he gave himself to company. Less famed for fighting, he represented Scipio Africanus’ saying: “My mother bore me a commander, not a warrior.” Therefore, inferior in wisdom to none of modern kings, [Note: “To none ever.” s. c. d. e2; e1: “never”; a: “to none”; l2: “not to none.”] and, I might almost say, plainly first among all his predecessors in England, he preferred to wage war by counsel rather than the sword. He conquered, if possible, without bloodshed; if otherwise impossible, with little bloodshed.

Throughout his entire life he was wholly free from the desire for every kind of lustful obscenity, [Note: “Free from lustful obscenities.” Compare Malmesbury on Henry’s character in this particular case with Henry of Huntingdon on the same.] because, as we have learned from those privy to him, he entered women’s embraces not from unrestrained pleasure but from desire to beget offspring. [Note: “Desire.” a. s. c. d. l2; e: “of desire.”] Nor did he deign to assent to a passing pleasure unless royal seed could issue in result; he spent his natural power as a master, not obeying lust as a slave. He used food without discrimination, satisfying hunger rather than driving greed by many delicacies; he never yielded to drink beyond thirst. He detested the slightest excess in temperance, both among his own people and among all others. His sleep was heavy and interrupted by frequent snoring. His faculty in speaking was more natural than cultivated, not hasty but deliberate.

§ 413. To make known his devotion to God, he founded monasteries in England and Normandy. Since he had not yet put the finishing hand to them, I too would for the present suspend my judgment, unless the affection of the brothers of Reading would not permit me to be silent. He established this monastery between two rivers, the Kennet and the Thames, in a place where it could be almost a lodging-place for all travellers going to England’s more populous cities. He placed there Cluniac monks, who today furnish a brilliant example of holiness and a proof of untiring and gracious hospitality: there you may see what you see nowhere else, namely that guests arriving throughout every hour consume more than the residents.

Perhaps someone will call me hasty and a flatterer because I praise so highly a religious house now only beginning to grow, not knowing what a coming day may bring forth. Yet they themselves, as I hope, will strive with God’s grace to persevere in goodness. I do not blush to speak favorably of holy men, nor to admire in others a good which I do not possess myself. He surrendered to God and Saint Peter the investitures of churches, after many disputes between himself and Archbishop Anselm; at last, scarcely bent to agreement by the great grace of God and by an inglorious victory over his brother. But Master Eadmer has treated the course of these matters in a long circuit of words. [Note: “Eadmer.” See Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, ed. Selden, London, 1623.] For fuller knowledge, we shall append writings of the oft-mentioned pope Paschal relating to this matter.

§ 414. “Paschal, bishop, to King Henry, greeting. In the letter which you recently sent us through your clerk William, son of our affection and your familiar attendant, we learned both that your person is well and of the prosperous successes which divine goodness has granted you, after the enemies of your kingdom were overcome. We further heard that you have received a desired male child from a freeborn and religious wife. Since this has indeed given us joy, we judged it fitting now to impress more forcibly upon you the commands and will of God, when you see yourself indebted to his goodness for more abundant benefits.

“We too desire to join our goodwill toward you to the divine benefits; but it grieves us that you seem to demand from us what we cannot grant. [Note: “What.” c. d. e: “what entirely”; a. s. l2.] For if we consent to or permit investitures to be made by your Highness, both yours and ours will undoubtedly face enormous peril. In this matter we wish you to consider what you lose by not doing it, or gain by doing it. For in this prohibition we obtain through the churches nothing more of obedience or liberality; nor do we endeavor to subtract anything from your due power or right, except so that God’s anger toward you may be lessened and consequently every prosperity may come to you. For the Lord says: ‘Those who honor me I will honor; but those who despise me shall be held of no account.’

“You will therefore say, ‘This belongs to my right.’ Certainly not: it is not imperial, not royal, but divine; it belongs to him alone who said, ‘I am the door.’ Therefore, for the sake of him whose office this is, I beg you to restore it to him; to leave it to him, to whose love you owe even what is yours. Why should we oppose your will, why resist your favor, unless we knew that, by consenting in this affair, we should oppose God’s will and lose his favor? Why should we deny you anything that ought to be granted to any mortal, when we have received greater benefits from you?

“Consider, dearest son, whether it is honor or dishonor to you that Anselm, the wisest and most religious of the Gallican bishops, fears on this account to remain at your side or to remain in your kingdom. What will those who have hitherto heard such good things about you think and say of you when this is spread abroad in the regions? Those very persons who in your presence extol your faults will, when they lack your presence, certainly defame this matter still more vigorously. Return therefore, dearest son, to your heart; we beseech you for God’s mercy and for love of the Only-Begotten. Recall your shepherd; recall your father. And if, as we do not suppose, he has acted more harshly against you should you reject investitures, we shall moderate matters according to your will, as far as we can with God. Yet remove from your person and kingdom the disgrace of such a repulse.

“If you do this, then, should you request from us any grave matters which it is possible to grant with God, you shall certainly obtain them. With his help, we shall take care to beseech the Lord for you; and, through the merits of the holy apostles, we shall grant indulgence and absolution from sins both to you and to your wife. As for your son, whom you have received from your distinguished and glorious wife and whom, as we hear, you have named William after your excellent father, we shall protect with you by such powerful support that whoever injures either you or him shall be thought to have injured the Roman Church. Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.” [Note: “December.” See the letter in Eadmer, p. 74.]

§ 415. “Paschal to Anselm. We have received your most sweet letter of affection, written with the pen of charity. In it we embrace the reverence of your devotion; considering the firmness of your faith and the persistence of your pious concern, we rejoice because, with God’s grace granting you help, neither promises lift you up nor threats shake you.

“But we grieve because, although we kindly received our brother bishops, the envoys of the king of the English, on their return home they reported things which we neither said to them nor thought. For we have heard that they said that, if the king acted well in other matters, we neither forbade ecclesiastical investitures nor excommunicated those already made; and that we did not wish to commit this to writing lest other princes use the occasion to cry out against us. Therefore we call Jesus, who searches hearts and reins, as witness upon our soul that, since we undertook the care of this holy see, such an enormous crime has not even entered our mind.”

And below: “If a lay hand gives the pastoral staff, the sign of pastoral office, and the ring, the seal of faith, what are bishops doing in the Church? As for bishops who have changed truth into falsehood, with Truth itself—who is God—brought into the midst, we separate them from the favor of blessed Peter and from our communion until they make satisfaction to the Roman Church. Whoever, however, within the aforesaid interval has received investitures of consecrations, [Note: “Investitures or consecrations.” All manuscripts read thus. The letter printed in Eadmer, p. 72, correctly reads “investiture or consecration.”] we hold alien from our fellowship and from the Church.” [Note: “We hold.” See this letter in Eadmer, pp. 71 ff.]

§ 416. “Paschal to Anselm. We give thanks to the Lord of mercies, almighty God, in whose hand the hearts of kings are moved, that he has deigned to incline the heart of the king of the English to obedience toward the Apostolic See. We believe that this has been done through the grace of your charity and the urgency of your prayers, so that heavenly mercy might look upon that people over which your care presides.

“You should know that our great concession both to the king and to those who seem liable was made out of such affection and compassion that we might be able to raise those who had fallen. But we absolve you, venerable and dearest brother in Christ, from that prohibition—or, as you believe, excommunication—which you understand to have been made by our predecessor Pope Urban of holy memory against investitures and homages. [Note: “And.” a. c. d. e. l2; s: “or.”] You, however, shall receive those who have either received investitures, blessed persons invested, or made homages, with the satisfaction which we communicate to you through our common envoys William and Baldwin, trustworthy and truthful men; and, God cooperating, absolve them in exercise of our authority. Either bless them yourself or order them to be blessed by whomsoever you wish, [Note: “You may order.” a. c. d. e. l2; s: “you may receive.”] unless perhaps you find in them some other reason why they should be excluded from holy offices.

“But if anyone henceforth assumes ecclesiastical preferments apart from the investitures, even if he has made homage to the king, he is by no means to be excluded on that account from the gift of blessing, until the grace of almighty God [Note: “The grace of almighty God.” c. d. e; a. s. l2: “through the grace of almighty God.”] softens the royal heart, by the rains of your preaching, to abandon this practice. Moreover, regarding the bishops who, as you know, reported a false rumor as coming from us, our heart has been strongly stirred, because they have not only injured us but deceived the souls of many simple people and incited the king against affection for the Apostolic See. Therefore, with the Lord’s aid, we do not permit their offence to go unpunished. Yet because our son the king urgently intercedes with us for them, you shall not deny even to them a share in your communion.

“Certainly, you shall absolve from sins and penances, according to our promise, the king and his wife, and those nobles who labored in this affair with the king by our command; you shall learn their names from the report of the above-mentioned William. We entrust the case of the bishop of Rouen to your judgment, and whatever you grant him we grant.” [Note: “We grant.” See this letter in Eadmer, p. 87.]

§ 417. Pope Paschal, supreme pontiff, was diligently conducting these affairs for the liberty of God’s churches. The bishops whom he accused of falsehood were Gerard, archbishop of York, and Herbert of Norwich. Their errors were reproved by more truthful envoys: William, afterward bishop of Exeter, and Baldwin, monk of Bec.

At that time Archbishop Anselm was again an exile at Lyons during the reign of this king, with Hugh, archbishop of that city, when the first letter which I have appended was sent. [Note: “Again … an exile at Lyons.” Anselm had been recalled when the king returned, but afterward departed again.] For neither was Anselm held by any desire to come, nor did the king allow his obstinacy to be calmed by the abundance of whisperers. Thus he long delayed both recalling Anselm and complying with apostolic admonitions, not from the pursuit of arrogance but at the prompting of the nobles, especially the count of Meulan. In this matter the count, arguing more from ancient custom than from the proper rule of right, alleged that royal majesty would be greatly diminished if, abandoning the custom of his predecessors, the king did not invest the elect with staff and ring.

Nevertheless, after considering more carefully what the vigorous argument of the letters and the abundant bestowal of divine gifts flowing upon him admonished, the king permanently surrendered the investiture of ring and staff, retaining only the privilege of election and of royal rights. [Note: “Only.” a. c. d. e. l2; s: “nevertheless.”] Accordingly, a great council of bishops, nobles, and abbots having been assembled at London, many matters both ecclesiastical and secular were ordered and disputes decided. Not long afterward, on one day, five bishops were ordained in Kent by Archbishop Anselm: William for Winchester, Roger for Salisbury, William for Exeter, Rainald for Hereford, and Urban for Glamorgan. Thus the controversy, pursued through frequent dissensions and debated through Anselm’s many journeys to and returns from Rome, received a praiseworthy end.

§ 418. The king’s wife was Matilda, descended from an ancient and illustrious line of kings, daughter, as I have said, of the king of the Scots. [Note: “The king’s.” a. s. c. e2; d: “his”; e1 l2: “to the king.”] From her tender years she had been brought up among nuns at Wilton and Romsey, and she also exercised her womanly mind in letters. Hence, in order to reject lowly marriages offered more than once by her father, she wore a veil indicating consecrated profession. [Note: “Consecrated.” a. c. d. e. l2; s: “holy.”] Therefore, when the king wished to take her to his bed, [Note: “Wished to take.” a. d. e. l2; s. c: “was taking.”] the matter came into dispute. [Note: “The matter came into dispute.” See Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, pp. 56–57.] The archbishop could not be brought to consent except when lawful witnesses were produced who swore that she had worn the veil without profession, because of suitors.

Content with two births, one of each sex, she thereafter ceased both to conceive and to bear children. She bore with equanimity that, while the king was occupied elsewhere, she herself should take leave of court, residing for many years at Westminster. Yet she lacked nothing of royal magnificence: by unwearied crowds, waves of those paying respects and bringing gifts at every season, the splendid buildings received and disgorged their visitors. This was commanded by the king’s generosity; this was drawn by her own grace and sweet kindness. Of outstanding holiness and not altogether contemptible beauty, an imitator of her mother’s piety, she admitted nothing blameworthy into her conduct, so far as concerned herself. Apart from the royal bedchamber she was whole in modesty, injured not even by suspicion.

Beneath royal dress she was wrapped in haircloth; during the days of Lent she wore out the thresholds of churches barefoot. Nor did she shrink from washing the feet of the sick, touching ulcers dripping with pus, or finally prolonging kisses upon their hands and setting food before them. She found her sole delight in hearing the service of God, and therefore was heedlessly generous toward sweetly singing clerics. [Note: “Therefore.” a. s. c. d. e2. l2; e1: “therefore.”] [Note: “Generous.” c. d. e: “generous”; a. l2: “lavish.”] She would address everyone kindly, give much, and promise more.

Thus, because her generosity was sown abroad through the world, scholars famous both in song and verse came here in crowds; and he counted himself fortunate who could delight the lady’s ears with the novelty of a poem. Nor did she bestow expense only upon these, but on every kind of person, especially strangers, who, having received gifts, sold her fame far and wide through the lands. For the desire of glory is so innate in human minds that scarcely anyone, content with the precious fruits of a good conscience, does not find it sweet, if he has done something well, to be celebrated among the people.

Consequently, as they say—and it is established—the lady was led astray into soothing with rewards whatever foreigners she could, and holding others in suspense with promises, sometimes effective but sometimes, and more often, empty. It came about that she did not escape the fault of lavish givers: she brought manifold lawsuits against her tenants, inflicted injuries, and took away possessions. Having thereby acquired the reputation of a good giver, she counted the affront suffered by her own people as little. But anyone wishing to judge these matters rightly will impute them to the counsels of her servants, who, in the manner of harpies, either buried in their purses whatever they could seize with their claws or spent it in feasts. Her ears filled with their foul whisperings, she contracted a blemish upon a most honorable mind. In all her other deeds she is to be approved and deemed holy.

Meanwhile she was taken from her country, to the great loss of the provincials but to no loss of her own. Her funeral was honorably conducted at Westminster, where she received rest; and her spirit showed by no trifling signs that it dwells in heaven. She died [Note: “She died.” 1 May, A.D. 1118.] after a reign of seventeen years and six months, [Note: “Six.” a. c. d. e. l2; s: “seven.”] gladly leaving it behind, having experienced the fate of her parents, who almost all departed from the world especially in the vigor of their age. Adela, daughter of the duke of Louvain—Louvain being the principal castle of Lotharingia—succeeded her in the king’s bed, though not so quickly, in A.D. 1121. [Note: “Adela.” Henry married Adela, daughter of Geoffrey, count of Louvain, in February A.D. 1121.]

§ 419. King Henry had by Matilda a son named William, brought up and advanced toward the succession with sweet hope and great care. [Note: “Brought up toward the succession.” Bromton (col. 1013, *X Scriptores*) ascribes to Malmesbury words found nowhere in our text: “William of Malmesbury says that this William, the king’s firstborn, had openly threatened the English that, if he ever reigned over them, he would make them pull the plough like oxen; but God’s vengeance destroyed his glittering hope along with the others.”] For when he was scarcely twelve years old, all the free men of England and Normandy, of whatever rank and dignity and faithful to whatever lord, were compelled to give themselves to him by hand and oath.

Though still under age, he also betrothed and married the barely marriageable daughter of Fulk, count of Anjou, [Note: “He betrothed.” The marriage of Prince William to Matilda, daughter of the count of Anjou, was celebrated in June A.D. 1119 before the Fathers of the Council of Reims.] receiving from his father-in-law the county of Maine as a wedding gift. Indeed, when Fulk was preparing to go to Jerusalem, he entrusted his county to the king while he lived, certainly to belong to his son-in-law if he did not return. [Note: “If he lived.” a. c. d. e: “if he should come”; s. l2.] Thus several provinces awaited the boy’s nod. It was thought that King Edward’s prophecy would be fulfilled in him; and hope for England, like a tree that had been cut down, was said to be growing green again with blossoms and to be putting forth fruit in that young man, so that an end of evils might be hoped for. [Note: “Like a tree cut down.” See §226.]
