God saw otherwise: for such opinions were carried away on the winds, because the next day pressed him to satisfy fate. For indeed, then, at the urging of his father-in-law, and likewise of Theobald, son of Stephen, and of his aunt Adela, King Louis of France granted Normandy to the boy, so that, after doing homage to him, he might possess it by lawful right, in A.D. 1119. The wisdom of his most prudent father arranged and accomplished these things, so that the son—delicate and thought to have entered upon the way of the world—would not refuse the homage which Henry himself, because of the pinnacle of empire, disdained to render.

The king spent four years in conducting these affairs and settling the agreed peace, remaining in Normandy throughout that time. Yet the changing lot of human fortune confounded the serenity of so splendid and carefully contrived a peace, and the hopes of all men raised upon the watchtower. For, when a return to England had been proclaimed, the king set sail from Barfleur at twilight on the seventh day before the Kalends of December—25 November A.D. 1120. [Note: “At twilight.” c. d. e. l2: “at the twilight of night,” a. s.] The wind, which filled his sails, happily carried him into his kingdom and broad prosperity.

But the young man, now seventeen years old and a little more, to whom, through his father’s indulgence, nothing of luxury was lacking except the title of king, ordered another ship to be prepared for himself. Nearly all the young sons of the nobles ran to it as though to a sport of youthful age. The rowers too, immoderately drenched in unmixed wine, cried out that, through the pleasure of sailing supplied by drink, they must quickly leave behind those who had gone ahead. For it was an excellent ship, newly decked and recently fastened with nails.

Thus, now in blind night, the youth lacking wisdom and overwhelmed with drink pushed the ship from shore. It flew swifter than a winged arrow; skimming the crisping ridges of the sea, it struck, through the folly of the drunken men, a rock rising above the water not far from the shore. The wretches rose up and with great shouting brought forth their iron-shod poles, struggling for a long time to thrust the ship off the rock; but fortune resisted, bringing all their efforts to nothing. Thus the oars, braced against the rock, cracked, and the shaken prow hung fast. [Note: “Braced,” etc.: “The oars, pressed hard, cracked, and the battered prow hung fast” (Virgil, *Aeneid* V.206).]

*...straining, they creaked, and the battered prow hung fast.* (Vergil, *Aeneid* V.206.)

Already the waves were exposing some; water entering through the cracks was drowning others, when the king’s son was taken up into a launched boat. He could have been saved by returning to shore, had not his illegitimate sister, the Countess of Perche, struggling with death in the larger vessel, called upon her brother for help with a woman’s cry, begging him not so cruelly to leave her. Overcome by pity, he ordered the skiff to be brought alongside the hull [654] so that it might take his sister aboard; the poor youth thus gained death as the reward of tender compassion. For immediately the boat, overwhelmed by the multitude leaping into it, sank, and engulfed all alike in the depths.

One man escaped, a peasant; floating all night upon the mast, he recounted in the morning the whole course of the tragedy. Never was there a ship of England so great a misery, nor one of such widespread fame throughout the world [Col. 1374B]. There perished with William another son of the king, Richard, whom he had begotten before he became king by a woman of the provinces: a high-spirited youth, dear to his father for his obedience; Richard, Earl of Chester, and his brother Otuel, fosterer and tutor of the king’s son; the king’s daughter, Countess of Perche; and her niece, sister of Theobald, Countess of Chester. Besides these, there perished every most distinguished knight or chaplain at court, and the sons of magnates who were to be advanced to knighthood. For they had flocked together from every quarter, as I have said, judging it no small addition to their glory if they either brought some amusement to the king’s son or rendered him service.

[Note: Col. 1374D. *Accurrerant*: a. s. c. d. e2. l2.; *accurrerunt*, e1.]

The calamity was increased by the difficulty of finding the bodies; for, though searchers were scattered along the shores, scarcely one body was easily found. Those bodies, so delicately nurtured [Col. 1374C], became cruel food for the monsters of the sea.

When the young man’s death became known, affairs changed in a remarkable manner. His father renounced the celibacy to which he had devoted himself after Matilda’s death, now expecting heirs from a new wife. His father-in-law, returned home from Jerusalem, wickedly supported the cause of William, son of Robert, Count of Normandy, giving him his other daughter in marriage and the county of Maine (A.D. 1123).

[Note: “Giving him his other daughter in marriage.” The marriage of William, son of the Duke of Normandy, with Sibyl, contracted in 1123, was dissolved in the following year at the insistence of King Henry by the papal legate.]

The dowry of his daughter sharpened his incentives to anger against the king: it was retained in England after his son’s death.

§ 420. King Henry gave his daughter Matilda, born of Matilda, to Henry, emperor of the Germans, son of the Henry mentioned in the third book.

[Note: “His daughter Matilda ... to Henry, emperor of Germany.” Matilda was betrothed to Emperor Henry V in 1109; the marriage was not celebrated before 7 January 1114.]

This Henry was the fifth German emperor of that name [Col. 1374D]. Although he had been fiercely angered with his father because of insults to the Apostolic See, he nevertheless followed the same policy and was, in his own time, its hostile champion. For when Paschal succeeded Pope Urban, a man lacking in no kind of virtue, the question of the investiture of churches, wars, and disputes were again set in motion [Col. 1375A], neither side yielding ground.

The emperor had as supporters all the bishops and abbots of his kingdom lying on this side of the mountains. For Charlemagne, in order to subdue the ferocity of those peoples, had granted almost all lands to churches. He had most shrewdly considered that men of the sacred order would not cast off loyalty to their lord as easily as laymen; moreover, if laymen rebelled, they could be restrained both by the authority of excommunication and by the severity of power. The pope had brought the churches beyond the mountains under his policy; and the cities of Italy had little regard for Henry’s dominion, considering themselves freed from servitude after the death of his brother Conrad, whom his father had left as king in Lombardy and who died at Arezzo.

But Henry, inferior to the ancient Caesars in no respect of courage [Col. 1375B], after pacifying the German kingdom, confidently intended to subdue the rebellion of the Italian cities and to settle the question of investiture according to his own will.

[Note: Col. 1375D. *Recisurus*: a. c. d. e. l2.; *decisurus*, s.]

This expedition to Rome [656], accomplished amid great exertions of mind and great bodily sufferings, was described by David the Scot, Bishop of Bangor; he was more deferential to the king’s favour than is fitting for a historian.

[Note: Col. 1375D. *Acclinis*: a. c. d. l2.; *acclivus*, s.]

Indeed, he even treats as praiseworthy the unheard-of violence by which Henry seized the pope, although he held him in free custody, drawing an analogy from Jacob, who forcibly held the angel and extorted a blessing from him. Further, he labours to maintain that the Apostle’s saying, “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” [Col. 1375C], does not oppose the desires of pontiffs invested by laymen, because it is not a secular affair if a cleric performs homage to a layman. Anyone of sound judgment will decide how frivolous these claims are. Yet, lest I seem to press too hard upon a good man with a word, I judge that indulgence is due him, because he wrote not history but a panegyric. I shall now insert truthfully the privilege and agreement (A.D. 1111) extorted from the pope by a violent captivity of three weeks, and shall add how they were soon afterwards invalidated by a more religious deliberation.

[Note: Col. 1375D. “No one ... secular affairs”: 2 Timothy 2:4.]

§ 421. “Pope Paschal shall not trouble the lord king, nor his empire or kingdom, concerning the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys, nor concerning injury inflicted upon himself and his followers in person or property [Col. 1375D]; nor shall he inflict any harm upon him or upon any person on this account. He shall never place an anathema upon the person of King Henry; nor shall there be any failure on the pope’s part to crown him, as is contained in the order; and he shall assist him, to the extent of his ability, by the aid of his office, to hold the kingdom and empire. And the lord pope shall fulfil these things without fraud or evil intent.”

These are the names [657] of those bishops and cardinals who, by order of Pope Paschal [Col. 1376A], confirmed by oath the privilege and friendship granted to Lord Henry the emperor: Peter, Bishop of Porto; Cencius, Bishop of Sabina; Robert, Cardinal of St Eusebius; Boniface, Cardinal of St Mark; Anastasius, Cardinal of St Clement; Gregory, Cardinal of the Apostles Peter and Paul; likewise Gregory, Cardinal of St Chrysogonus; John, Cardinal of St Pudentiana; Riso, Cardinal of St Lawrence; Rainier, Cardinal of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; Vitalis, Cardinal of St Balbina; Teuzo, Cardinal of St Mark; Theobald, Cardinal of Saints John and Paul; John, dean in the Greek School; Leo, dean of St Vitalis; Albo, dean of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

[Note: Col. 1375D. *Illorum*: a. s. c. d. e2. l2.; omitted in e1.]

[Note: Col. 1375D. “In the Greek School.” The Church of St Mary is so called “in the Greek School,” because St Augustine is said to have taught rhetoric there before his conversion to the faith.]

[Col. 1376B] § 422. The king himself also made this oath:

“I, King Henry, shall release, on the next Wednesday or Thursday, the lord pope, the bishops and cardinals, and all captives and hostages who have been captured on his account or with him; and I shall cause them to be conducted safely within the gates of the city of Trastevere. Nor shall I thereafter seize, or allow to be seized, those who remain faithful to Pope Paschal. I shall preserve peace and security, both through myself and through my men, for the Roman people [Col. 1376D] and the city of Trastevere, in respect of those persons who keep peace with me. I shall faithfully help the lord pope to hold his papacy peacefully and securely. I shall restore the patrimonies and possessions of the Roman Church which I have taken away, and shall in good faith assist it to recover and hold all that it ought to possess according to the custom of its predecessors [658], without fraud or evil intent. And I shall obey Pope Paschal, with the honour of kingdom and empire preserved, as Catholic emperors obey Catholic Roman pontiffs.”

[Note: Col. 1376D. “Nor thereafter ... city”: s. c. d. e.; omitted in a. l2.]

[Note: Col. 1376D. “Roman people”: s.; *populi Romani* (“of the Roman people”), c. d. e.]

The following were oath-takers on the king’s behalf: Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne; Godehard, Bishop of Trent; Bruno, Bishop of Speyer; Count Berengar; Albert the chancellor; Count Hermann; Frederick, Count Palatine; Boniface the margrave; Albert, Count of Blandriac; Count Frederick; Count Godfrey; and Warner the margrave.

§ 423. When this agreement had been completed and confirmed by the oaths of the bishops and cardinals mentioned above, and the kiss had been exchanged on both sides, the lord pope celebrated Mass on 13 April 1111, the fourth day before the Ides of April, the Sunday *Quasi modo geniti* [Col. 1376D]. In it, after receiving communion himself and administering it to the ministers of the altar, he gave the emperor the body and blood of the Lord in these words:

“This body of the Lord, which the most holy Church holds, born of the Virgin Mary and raised upon the cross for the redemption of humankind, we give to you, most beloved son, for the remission of your sins and for the preservation of the peace [Col. 1377A] and true friendship to be confirmed between me and you, and between kingdom and priesthood.”

[Note: Col. 1376D. *Domini*: a. s. c. d. e2. l2.; omitted in e1.]

On the following day the pope and king met at the columns in the Forum.

[Note: Col. 1377D. “At the columns.” They are regarded as remains of the Temple of Jupiter Stator.]

Guards in armour were stationed wherever they seemed necessary, lest the king’s consecration be impeded. At the Silver Gate the king was received by the bishops, cardinals, and the whole Roman clergy. When the Bishop of Ostia, because the Bishop of Albano was absent, had begun the prayer contained in the order—which the Bishop of Albano ought to have said had he been present—the king was led to the middle wheel; there he received the second prayer from the Bishop of Porto, as the Roman order directs. Then they led him, with litanies, to the confession of the Apostles; there the Bishop of Ostia anointed him between the shoulders and upon the right arm. Thereafter [Col. 1377B] he was led by the lord pope to the altar of the same Apostles; and there, after the pope himself had placed the crown upon him, he was consecrated emperor.

[Note: Col. 1377D. “And there he anointed him ... led.” Present in a. d. e. g. k. l2.; omitted in s. c.]

After the crown had been placed upon him, the Mass of the Resurrection of the Lord was celebrated. Before communion in this Mass, the lord pope [Col. 1377D] gave the emperor the privilege in his own hand, granting him and his kingdom what is written here and confirming it under anathema in that place.

[Note: Col. 1377D. *Apostolicus*: a. c. e.; *papa*, s. d. l2.]

§ 424. “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry, most beloved son in Christ and, by the grace of almighty God, august emperor of the Romans: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Divine ordinance has established that your kingdom should be joined to the holy Roman Church [Col. 1377C]. Your predecessors, by the greater grace of their uprightness and prudence, obtained the crown and empire of the Roman city; and to the dignity of that crown and empire divine majesty has likewise advanced your person, most beloved son Henry, through the ministry of our priesthood.

“Therefore, the prerogative of dignity which [660] our predecessors granted to your predecessors, the Catholic emperors, and confirmed in pages of privileges, we also grant to your beloved person and confirm by the page of this present privilege: namely, that you may confer investiture by staff and ring upon the bishops or abbots of your kingdom when they have been freely elected without violence or simony; after investiture they shall receive canonical consecration from the bishop to whom this belongs. But if anyone is elected by clergy or people without your assent, no one shall consecrate him unless he is invested by you—except, of course, those who ordinarily fall under the disposition of archbishops or of the Roman pontiff.

[Note: Col. 1377D. “Therefore, the prerogative of dignity which”: a. d. e. l2.; “therefore, the privilege of dignity which,” s. c.]

“Archbishops and bishops shall indeed have liberty canonically to consecrate bishops [Col. 1378A] or abbots invested by you. For your predecessors enlarged the churches of their kingdom with such great grants from their royal resources that the kingdom itself must especially be fortified by the support of bishops and abbots; and popular dissensions, which often occur in all elections, must be restrained by royal majesty.

[Note: Col. 1378D. *Maxime*: a. s. c. d. e2. l2.; omitted in e1.]

“Accordingly, the care of your prudence and power ought the more diligently to be directed to preserving, by the benefits and services which you render—God granting it—the greatness of the Roman Church and the welfare of the others. Therefore, if any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the page of our concession, attempts through rash presumption to act against it, let him, unless he repents, be bound by the bond of anathema and suffer the loss of his honour and dignity [Col. 1378B]. But may divine mercy preserve those who observe these things, and grant that your person and power may rule happily for His honour and glory.”

[Note: Col. 1378D. *Ergo*: e1; *igitur*, a. s. d. e2. l2.]

§ 425. When the whole rite of his consecration had thus been completed, the pope and emperor, clasping one another’s right hands, went in solemn procession to the chamber before the confession of St Gregory [661], so that there the pope might lay aside his priestly vestments and the emperor his imperial regalia. As the emperor came out of the chamber and had put off his regalia, the Roman patricians met him with a golden circlet, which they placed upon the emperor’s head. By this they conferred upon him the supreme patriciate of the city of Rome, with the common consent and willing mind of all.

[Col. 1378C] § 426. I have translated word for word from the writings of the aforesaid David this whole ambitious business of privilege and consecration, which he, as I have said, bends more favourably than he should toward the king’s interest. In the following year a council was assembled at Rome, not so much by the pope’s command as with his connivance, and that privilege was made void. The authors of this change were the Archbishop of Vienne, who afterwards governed the Apostolic See, and the Bishop of Angoulême, named Gerard, who urged his fellow bishops to invalidate these acts.

[Note: Col. 1378D. “Of Vienne”: a. s. c. d. e. l2.; “of Angoulême,” s. variant reading. Afterwards Pope Calixtus II.]

The proceedings of that council are as follows.

§ 427. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1112, in the fifth indiction, the thirteenth year of the pontificate [Col. 1378D] of Pope Paschal II, in March, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April (18 March), a council was held at Rome in the Lateran, in the Constantinian basilica.

[Note: Col. 1378D. *Pontificatus*: a. c. d. e. l2.; omitted in s.]

[Note: Col. 1378D. “Constantinian basilica.” A church built by Constantine the Great.]

There Pope Paschal sat with archbishops, bishops, cardinals, and a varied multitude of clergy and laity. On the final day of the council, after publicly professing the Catholic faith so that no one might doubt his faith, he said [662]:

[Col. 1379A] “I embrace all divine Scripture of the Old and New Testament: the Law written by Moses and by the holy prophets. I embrace the four Gospels, the seven catholic epistles, and the epistles of the glorious teacher, the blessed Apostle Paul; the holy canons of the Apostles; the four universal councils as the four Gospels—the Nicene, Ephesian, Constantinopolitan, and Chalcedonian; further, the Council of Antioch; and the decrees of the holy fathers, Roman pontiffs, especially the decrees of my lord Pope Gregory VII and of Pope Urban of blessed memory.

[Note: Col. 1379D. *Papae*: a. s. c. d. e2. l2.; omitted in e1.]

“What they approved, I approve; what they held, I hold; what they confirmed, I confirm; what they condemned, I condemn; what they rejected, I reject; what they forbade, I forbid; what they prohibited [Col. 1379B], I prohibit. In all things and through all things I shall always persevere in these.”

When this was completed, Gerard, Bishop of Angoulême and legate in Aquitaine, rose on behalf of all and, with the common assent of Pope Paschal and of the entire council, read this document.

§ 428. “That privilege, which is no privilege but ought truly [Col. 1379D] to be called a *pravilegium*—that is, a wicked privilege—extorted from Pope Paschal by the violence of King Henry for the release of captives and of the Church: all of us assembled with the lord pope in this holy council condemn it, by canonical censure and ecclesiastical authority, through the judgment of the Holy Spirit. We judge it void, wholly overthrow it, and, lest it possess any authority or force, utterly excommunicate it.

[Note: Col. 1379D. *Vere*: a. s. c. d. e.; *jure* (“rightly”), l2.]

[Note: Col. 1379D. *Pravilegium*: c. d. e. l2.; *privilegium*, a. s.]

“And it is condemned for this reason: because that *pravilegium* contains the provision that one canonically elected by clergy and people shall be consecrated by no one [663] unless he has first been invested by the king. This is contrary to the Holy Spirit and to canonical institution.”

[Note: Col. 1379D. *Pravilegio*: c. e. l2.; *privilegio*, a. s. d.]

When this document had been read through, all and the entire council cried out: “Amen, amen! Let it be done, let it be done!”

§ 429. The archbishops present with their suffragans were these: John, Patriarch of Venice; Semies of Capua; Landulf of Benevento; the Archbishop of Amalfi; of Reggio; of Otranto; of Brindisi; of Capua; of Girgenti; and the Greeks, the Archbishop of Rossano and [Col. 1379D] the Archbishop of Santa Severina.

[Note: Col. 1379D. *Semies*: c. d. e.; *Sennes*, a. s. l2.]

[Note: Col. 1379D. “And”: a. c. e. l2.; omitted in s. d.]

The bishops were: Cencius of Sabina; Peter of Porto; Leo of Ostia; Cono of Palestrina; Gerard of Angoulême; Galo of Lyons, legate for the Archbishop of Bourges and the Archbishop of Vienne; Roger of Volturno; Geoffrey of Siena; Roland of Populonia; Gregory of Terracina; William of Troy [Col. 1379D]; William of Syracuse [Col. 1380A], legate for all Sicily; and nearly a hundred other bishops.

[Note: Col. 1379D. “William of Troy”: a. l2.; *Turianus*, s.; omitted in c. d. e.]

Siwinus and John, Bishop of Tusculum, though they were in Rome, were not present at the council on that day. Afterwards, when the condemnation of the privilege had been read, they agreed to and approved it.

§ 430. These matters were reported throughout the world, and all Gaul openly showed that it execrated the emperor, its ecclesiastical zeal being directed against him.

[Note: Col. 1379D. *Vigore*: a. s. c. d. e2. l2.; omitted in e1, which has *rigore* (“severity”) in the margin.]

Moved by this, in the seventeenth year of Pope Paschal’s pontificate he hastened to Rome (A.D. 1117), intending to take harsher vengeance upon him.

[Note: Col. 1379D. “Seventeenth”: more correctly eighteenth, since the emperor went to Exonium before Easter, A.D. 1117.]

But Paschal had escaped worldly troubles through a happy passing and, resting in peace, laughed from on high at the threats of the defiant Caesar.

[Note: Col. 1379D. *Is*: a. c. d. e. l2.; *hic*, s. Paschal died in January 1118.]

When he heard of Paschal’s death, the emperor pursued his course more eagerly, so that, after expelling John Gaetano [Col. 1380B], chancellor of the preceding pope, who had now been elected and called Gelasius, he might intrude Maurice, Bishop of Braga, surnamed Burdinus.

[Note: Col. 1380D. *Gaitano*: a. c. d. e. l2.; *Gritano*, s.]

[Note: Col. 1380D. “Maurice, Bishop of Braga.” Maurice Burdinus, Archbishop of Braga, was elected pope with the support of Emperor Henry V on 9 March 1118, under the name Gregory VIII.]

But Gelasius’s following letter will set this forth more certainly.

§ 431. “Gelasius, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, clergy, princes, and other faithful throughout Gaul: greetings. Since you are members of the Roman Church, we are concerned to communicate to your affection the things recently done in it.

“For after our election the lord emperor came secretly to Rome with unexpected speed and forced us to leave. Afterwards he demanded peace by threats and terrors, asking what he could do unless we gave him assurance of peace by oath. To this we replied: ‘Concerning the controversy [Col. 1380C] between Church and kingdom, we willingly submit either to agreement or to justice at a suitable place and time—namely at Milan or Cremona on the coming feast of St Luke—by the judgment of our brethren, who have been appointed judges in the Church by God and without whom this cause cannot be treated. Since the lord emperor asks us for security, we promise it to him in word and writing, unless he himself meanwhile prevents it. For otherwise to provide security is neither in accordance with the honour of the Church nor with custom.’

“On the forty-fourth day after our election, he at once installed as an invader of the mother Church [665] the Bishop of Braga—whom Pope Paschal, our predecessor [Col. 1380D], had excommunicated in the Council of Benevento in the preceding year.

[Note: Col. 1380D. *Quadragesimo quarto*: a. s. c. d. e.; *quadragesimo tertio*, l2.]

[Note: Col. 1380D. *Praedecessore*: a. s. c. d. e2.; *praecessore*, e1. l2.]

[Note: Col. 1380D. *Invasionem*: a. d. e. l2.; *gremium* (“bosom”), s.; omitted in c.]

“He too had formerly received the pallium through our hands and sworn fealty to the same lord, our predecessor, and to his Catholic successors, of whom I am the first. In this enormous crime the lord emperor had no Roman accomplice—thanks be to God!—but only the adherents of Wibert: Romanus of St Marcellus, Cencius called ‘of St Chrysogonus,’ and Teuzo, who raged through Dacia for a long time, celebrated so shameful a glory [Col. 1381A].

“Therefore, by your receipt of this letter, we command your experience that, after considering these matters in common deliberation by God’s grace, you arm yourselves, with God supplying common assistance, for the vengeance of the mother Church, as you recognize to be fitting. Given at Gaeta, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [16 January 1119].”

§ 432. Gelasius, having been expelled, embarked on ships at Salerno and came thence to Genoa. From there, travelling on foot to Cluny, he died there.

[Note: Col. 1381D. *Obiit*: a. s. c. d. e2. l2.; *obiit diem* (“died his day”), e1. Gelasius II died at Cluny, 29 January 1119.]

Then, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 1381B], the cardinals who had come with Gelasius, together with the entire Church of Cisalpine Italy, raised Guido, Archbishop of Vienne, to the papacy with great ceremony and called him Calixtus, in view of his religion and effectiveness.

[Note: Col. 1381D. *Contuitu*: c. d. e.; *intuitu*, a. s. l2.]

They hoped that through his power, since he possessed the greatest means of providing help, they could withstand the emperor’s forces. Nor did he disappoint their hopeful expectation. As soon as he had celebrated a council at Reims, he removed from churches those invested or to be invested by laymen, likewise involving the emperor in the sentence unless he repented [666]. Having remained for some time in the lower regions in order to strengthen his party, he came to Rome after settling affairs in Gaul, and was willingly received by the citizens, for the emperor had already departed [Col. 1381C]. Then Burdinus, left in the middle, fled to Sutri, intending to support his papacy through many calamities inflicted upon pilgrims; but how he was expelled from there you will learn from the following letter.

§ 433. “Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to beloved brothers and sons—archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and all others, clergy and laity alike, faithful of St Peter established throughout Gaul—greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Because the people have abandoned the law of the Lord and do not walk in His judgments, the Lord visits their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; nevertheless, preserving the tender heart of fatherly mercy, He does not abandon those who trust in His mercy. For a long time, as sins required, the faithful of the Church were troubled by that idol of the German king [Col. 1381D], namely Burdinus. Some were captured; others were afflicted unto death by the wasting of prison.

“But recently, after the feast of Easter had been celebrated, since we could no longer bear at all the cries of pilgrims and poor people, we departed from the city with the faithful of the Church and besieged Sutri until divine power [Col. 1382A] wholly delivered into our control both the aforesaid enemy of the Church, Burdinus—who had made there a nest for the devil—and the place itself.

“Therefore we ask your charity to give thanks with us to the King of kings for such great benefits, and to remain most steadfastly in obedience and service to the Catholic Church, about to receive through His grace from almighty God the recompense due in the present life and in the future [667]. We also ask that, removing all negligence, you arrange for these letters to be presented to one another. Given at Sutri, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.”

§ 434. It was an entirely urbane and calculated witticism to call the man whom he hated “the idol of the German king,” because that king held Maurice’s skill—in letters and civil affairs alike—in high esteem. He was, as I have said [Col. 1382B], Archbishop of Braga, a city of Spain.

[Note: Col. 1381D. *Is*: a. c. d. e. l2.; *hic*, s.]

[Note: Col. 1381D. *Archiepiscopus*: a. c. d. e. l2.; *episcopus*, s.]

Anyone ought to have held him in great reverence, almost worshipping him for the vivid appearance of great ability, had he not preferred to win distinction by so notorious a crime. Indeed, he would not have hesitated to make merchandise of the most holy see for money if a seller as desperate as he himself was ready to buy had been found.

Having then been captured and made a monk, he was sent to Cava—“for that is what they call the monastery.”

[Note: Col. 1381D. “For that is what they call the monastery”: e1; “a monastery so called,” d; “for they call the monastery thus,” a. s. c. e2. l2. A certain monastery near Salerno was called “the hiding-place.” All who seemed to be feared because of their manner of life were confined there. See Orderic, p. 870.]

§ 435. The praiseworthy magnificence of the pope proceeded further in increasing good, in order to restrain that unbridled and inborn greed of the Romans. In his time there were no attacks on travellers around Rome, no injuries to those entering the city. Calixtus restored to the common fund—that is, to the public use of the ruler of the Apostolic See—the offerings at St Peter’s [Col. 1382C], which powerful men had seized according to their insolence and pleasure, subjecting earlier popes who dared even to protest to unworthy insults.

Nor could either the ambition to acquire money or love of money already possessed work anything alien to good in his heart. So much was this so that, because of the length of the journey, he advised English pilgrims to go rather to St David’s [668] than to Rome: those who went twice to that place were to receive the same benefit of blessing as those who went once to Rome.

[Note: Col. 1382D. *David*: a. c. d. e. l2.; *dictum*, s.]

What of the long-standing controversy over investiture between kingdom and priesthood? For more than fifty years it had caused disorders, so that whenever some supporter of the heresy was cut off by illness or death, more heads immediately sprang up like those of the Hydra [Col. 1382D]. Calixtus by his own skill scraped it away, cut it down, and destroyed it, striking off the necks of German obstinacy with the force of the apostolic axe.

[Note: Col. 1382D. *Delevit*: c. d. o.; *delevit, evellit* (“destroyed, uprooted”), a; *delevit vel evellit* (“destroyed or uprooted”), s. l2.]

The professions of faith made by him and by the emperor will show the world this in the following words.

[Note: Col. 1382D. “This ... will show”: a. s. c. d. e. l2.; e reads, “This, of him and the emperor ... burns in God’s service,” omitting all intervening paragraphs down to “For besides the abandonment of other allurements,” § 44[...].]

§ 436. “I, Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God [Col. 1383A], grant to you, beloved son Henry, by God’s grace emperor of the Romans, that the elections of bishops and abbots of the German kingdom which pertain to the kingdom shall take place in your presence, without simony and without any violence. If any disagreement should arise between the parties, you shall give assent and assistance to the sounder side in accordance with the counsel or judgment of the metropolitan or provincial bishops.

[Note: Col. 1383D. *Imperatori*: c. d. e.; *imperatori augusto* (“august emperor”), a. s. l2.]

“The elected man shall receive the regalian rights from you and shall perform from them what is owed to you by right. In the other parts of the empire, the consecrated person shall within six months receive the regalian rights from you by the sceptre and shall perform from them what is owed to you by right, with the exception of all things known to belong to the Roman Church. Concerning matters of which you make complaint to me and ask help, I shall give you help according to the obligation of my office. I grant you [Col. 1383B] true peace, and likewise to all who are or have been on your side during this conflict. Farewell!”

[669] § 437. “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Henry, august emperor of the Romans by God’s grace, for love of God, of the holy Roman Church, and of Pope Calixtus, and for the remedy of my soul, relinquish to God, to the holy apostles of God Peter and Paul, and to the holy Catholic Church, all investiture by ring and staff. I grant that in all churches which are in my kingdom or empire canonical election and free consecration shall take place.

“I restore to the same holy Roman Church the possessions and regalian rights of St Peter which, from the beginning of this conflict until the present day, whether in my father’s time or [Col. 1383C] my own, have been taken away and which I hold. Those which I do not hold, I shall faithfully help to have restored. I shall also restore, according to the counsel of the princes or justice, the possessions of all other churches, princes, and all others, lay and clerical alike, which have been lost in this war: those which I hold, I shall return; those which I do not hold, I shall faithfully help to have returned.

“And I grant true peace to Pope Calixtus, to the holy Roman Church, and to all who are or have been on its side. In matters in which the holy Roman Church asks help, I shall faithfully help; and in matters of which it makes complaint to me, I shall provide the justice due to it.”

All these things were done with the consent and counsel of the princes whose names are subscribed: Albert, Archbishop of Mainz [Col. 1383D]; Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne; the Bishop of Regensburg; the Bishop of Bamberg; Bruno of Speyer; the Bishop of Augsburg; the Bishop of Utrecht; the Bishop of Constance; the Abbot of Fulda; Duke Hermann; Duke Frederick; Margrave Boniface; Margrave Theobald; Count Palatine Ernulf; Count Palatine Otbert; and Count Berengar.

§ 438. When that lethargic disease which had disturbed the condition of the Church was calmed, everyone of Christian understanding [Col. 1384A] received great joy that the emperor who, in glory of courage second only to Charlemagne the Great, vigorously pressed his footsteps had not fallen away from his devotion to God. Besides nobly suppressing the rebellions of the German kingdom, he so subjugated Italy that no one had done so to that extent. For three times in a decade he entered Italy and restrained the arrogance of its cities. On his first arrival he destroyed Novara, Piacenza, and Arezzo by fire; on his second and third arrivals, Cremona and Mantua. He also subdued an uprising at Ravenna by a siege of a few days. For the Pisans and Pavians, together with the Milanese, preferred his friendship to experiencing his force.

To him, as I have said above [Note: Col. 1383D. “As I said above.” See §420.], the daughter of the king of England was married; she displayed her father in courage [Col. 1384B] and her mother in piety. In her devotion rivalled her energy, and one could not easily determine which was more worthy of praise.

§ 439. At that time William, count of Poitou, was foolish and unstable. After he returned from Jerusalem (as was related in the preceding book) [Note: [Col. 1383D] Postquam. a, c, d, e, l1: “after”; s: “before.”], he wallowed so completely in every cesspool of vice as though he believed that all things happened by chance and were not governed by providence. He dressed up his jests with a certain false charm and passed them off as wit, stretching his hearers’ mouths in loud laughter. Finally, near a certain castle, Niort [Note: [Col. 1383D] Niort. l2: “Niorth”; a: “Ivor”; s: “Nior”; c, d, e: “Mort”; s (variant reading): “Mort.”], he built some dwellings like little monasteries and madly declared that he would establish there an abbey of harlots. He continually sang that he would appoint this woman and that woman—whichever was more notorious as a prostitute—as abbess or prioress, and the others [Note: [Col. 1383D] Caeterasve. c, d, e: “and the others”; a, l2: “but the others”; s: “but the rest.”] as officers.

Having put aside his lawful wife, he seized the wife of a certain viscount [Note: [Col. 1384D] Vicecomitis cujusdam. Maubergeon, wife of Viscount Gerald of the castle.]. He burned so fiercely for her that he placed an image of the little woman on his shield, declaring that he wished to bear her in battle just as she bore him in the dining hall. Rebuked and excommunicated on this account by Girard, bishop of Angoulême, and ordered [Note: [Col. 1384D] Jussusque. a, s, c, d, e2, l2: “and ordered”; e1: “ordered.”] to renounce his illicit passion, he jeered at the man: “You will sooner comb back from your brow the hair that flees before the comb than I shall declare a divorce to the viscountess.” His mockery concerned a man whose exceedingly thin hair did not need a comb.

Nor was he less violent when Peter [Note: [Col. 1384D] Peter. Peter II, bishop of Poitiers, died at Cluny on 4 April 1115. (*Gallia Christiana*, II, col. 1120).], bishop of Poitiers and a man of outstanding holiness, rebuked him more freely and began openly to excommunicate the reluctant count. Roused to headlong fury, William rushed at the bishop’s hair and, brandishing a drawn sword, said: “You will die at once unless you absolve me.” Then the bishop, feigning fear and requesting a delay in order to speak, confidently completed what remained of the excommunication. Thus he suspended the count from Christian communion [Note: [Col. 1384D] A Christianitate. a, s, c, d, e2, l2: “from Christian communion”; omitted in e1.], so that he dared neither dine nor even speak with anyone unless he promptly came to his senses.

Having, as it seemed to him, discharged his duty, and thirsting for the trophy of martyrdom, he stretched out his neck: “Strike!” he cried. “Strike!” But William, more obstinate still, resorted to his customary jest: “Certainly I hate you so much that I do not even deem you worthy of my hatred; nor shall you ever enter heaven through the ministry of my hand.” Yet shortly afterward, poisoned by the serpent-like hiss of the harlot [Note: [Col. 1385D] Meretriculae. s, c, d, e: “of the harlot”; a, l2: “of the little woman.”], he drove the opponent of his incest into exile. There Peter ended his life with a blessed death and, by frequent and great miracles, showed the world how gloriously he lives in heaven.

On hearing this, the count did not abstain from insolent sarcasm. He publicly professed regret that he had not hastened Peter’s death long before, so that the holy soul might chiefly have owed him thanks, since through his fury it had gained the advantage of heaven.

The following verses commend Peter’s life and death. Of him while living it was said:

### VERSES ON PETER, BISHOP OF POITIERS

[Col. 1385B]

His body—wealth—study—manners: harsh food—poverty—  
Reading—rebukes, subdues—cuts off—nourishes—they flee.

Virtues—faults—fruit: he cultivates—prunes—augments.  
Right—litigation—peace: he protects—hates—loves.

He bears aid to the wretched—grants pardon to the sinner—keeps for his friend  
Help—forgiveness—and unbroken faith.

In mind he is free for Mary, but in action Martha labours;  
Martha attends to the flock, Mary to God.  
Thus in this man God reigns within, his neighbour without;  
He serves God by longing, his neighbour by service.

He loves Rachel, nor does he refuse to bear Leah,  
And, a new Jacob, has taken each as wife.  
He loves the beauty of the one; he delights to gather the fruit of the other:  
Rachel is beautiful, Leah more fruitful.

[Col. 1385C] Of him after death it was said:

### VERSES ON THE SAME PETER, DEAD

Stripped of possessions, intent, driven from the city,  
The bishop endured poverty, chains, and exile.

Now rich—free—secure, this Peter receives—follows—possesses  
His rewards—Christ—the stars.

Religion adorned his life, discernment his mind,  
The radiance of deeds his reputation, study his reading, restraint his speech;

Judgment his law, severity his justice, beauty his countenance,  
Compassion his heart, the pastoral staff his hand.

The pope advanced him—the count deprived him—Christ received him as an exile,  
In rank—in see—in heaven.

## ON THE FOUNDERS OF THE MONASTERIES OF FONTEVRAULT AND TIRON

§ 440. Peter’s contemporaries and companions in religion were Robert of Arbrissel [Note: [Col. 1385D] Robert of Arbrissel. He founded the monastery of Fontevrault in 1099 and died in 1117.] and Bernard [Note: [Col. 1385D] Bernard. He founded the abbey of Tiron in 1109 and died in 1116.], abbot of Tiron. The former was the most famous and copious preacher of all the speakers of that age. His eloquence flourished with a force not merely frothing but honeyed, so that people competed in heaping up wealth for him and he built that distinguished monastery of nuns at Fontevrault. There, with every pleasure of the world cut off, such a multitude of women devoted to God as exists nowhere else burns with zeal in God’s service. For, besides renouncing all other allurements, how slight a matter is this: nowhere do they speak except in chapter, a rule of perpetual silence having been laid down by their master, because, once silence has been relaxed, women are inclined to whisper frivolities.

The other, a renowned lover of poverty, left a monastery of very great wealth and withdrew with a few companions to a wooded and deserted place. There, because a lamp could not remain hidden beneath a bushel, crowds flocked to him in waves, and he founded a monastery more remarkable for the religious life and number of its monks than for the brilliance and accumulation of money.

## ON SERLO, ABBOT OF GLOUCESTER

§ 441. And, lest England be thought devoid of good men, who could pass over Serlo, abbot of Gloucester, who raised that place from lowliness and near-nothingness to glorious prosperity? All Englishmen know the discerning religious observance of Gloucester [Col. 1386B], which the weak may admire and the strong cannot despise. Serlo, their standard-bearer, brought them this principle: nothing in excess. Though, as he was humble toward the good, so he was threatening and terrible toward the proud. To confirm this, I shall bring forward verses on him by Prior Geoffrey:

### VERSES ON THE SAME MAN, DEAD

With Serlo’s fall, the wall of the Church has fallen:  
The sword of virtue, the trumpet of justice,

Speaking truth and not employing empty words,  
And pleasing the great men whom he rebuked.

Rash judgment, error opposed to order,  
And levity of conduct did not please him.

The third month from January, the third day of the month,  
Life raised him up, subdued by death.

## ON LANZON, PRIOR OF ST PANCRAS

§ 442. Who could be silent about Lanzon, who flourished in holiness inferior to no one of that age—a Cluniac monk and prior of St Pancras in England [Note: [Col. 1386D] St Pancras in England: at Lewes in Sussex.]? By his integrity he so ennobled that place with the grace of monastic reverence that it was affirmed to be the one true dwelling-place of goodness. Since whatever I might say about his life I declare to fall below his merits, I shall set down only his death, in the words in which I found it written, so that it may plainly appear how gloriously he lived who died so graciously.

## ON THE DEATH OF THE SAME LANZON

§ 443. “The merciful Lord, who chastens every son whom he receives, and who promises that the just will share alike in his passion and consolation, permitted Lord Lanzon, through three days of so bitter an illness, to anticipate His Passion [Col. 1386D], that, if any dust from earthly intercourse had clung to his most pure mind, there can be no doubt that it was shaken off by that tribulation. For since that great apostle who reclined on the Lord’s breast says: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’ [Note: [Col. 1386D] “If we say … the truth is not in us.” 1 John 1:8–9.]; and since Christ judges every sin either more lightly here or more severely in the future, he did not wish any offence to meet after death one whom he knew loved him with his whole heart. Therefore, if he judged that anything in him needed examination, he wished to purge it away while he was alive [Note: [Col. 1387D] In vivente. a, e, l2: “while living”; s, c: “in youth”; omitted in d.].

“The confidence of the dying man bore witness to this assertion. On Thursday before the Lord’s Passion, he was well. Having recited the psalter according to the daily Lenten custom, he had put on his chasuble and was about to celebrate Mass at the third hour; he had even said in advance all that was to be said until the Mass began. Suddenly he was seized by a sickness so distressing that, taking off the vestments which he had put on, he left them unfolded. Leaving the oratory, he suffered without interruption for two days, that is, until Saturday. He had no rest whatever by sitting, walking, lying down, standing, or sleeping.

“Yet he never spoke at night. When asked [Note: [Col. 1387D] Rogantibus. c, d, e: “when they asked”; a, s, l2: “when the brethren asked.”] to break silence, he did not consent, begging them not to violate the chastity of his monastic profession, since, from the time he had assumed the monastic habit, he had never spoken after leaving Compline until Prime on the following day. On the following Saturday, believing himself so shaken that he was about to die immediately, he ordered the brethren rising for the morning synaxis to come and anoint him. After being anointed, he wished to kiss them according to custom; overcome by his great love for them, he kissed them not lying down or sitting, but standing, though in agony near death and supported in their arms.

“At daybreak he was brought into chapter. When he had sat down, he asked all the brethren to come before him. Giving them his fatherly blessing and absolution, he wished them to give the same to him [Col. 1387C]. Afterwards he instructed them what they should do if he died. Thus he returned whence he had come and spent the remainder of the day and the following Sunday somewhat more quietly. But after this—that is, after Sunday—the signs of approaching death appeared. Having washed his hands and combed his hair, he entered the oratory to hear Mass; after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, he returned to bed.

“Shortly afterwards he became speechless. As the brethren came before him one by one, he blessed them, and likewise the entire convent. But with eyes raised to heaven, he strove with both hands to bless the lord abbot and all entrusted to him. Asked by the brethren to remember them before God, to whom he was going, he most kindly assented by inclining his head [Note: [Col. 1387D] Caput. a, c, d, e, l2: “his head”; s: “with his head.”].

“After doing these things and others like them, he indicated that a cross should be brought to him. Bowing his head—indeed his whole body—he adored it. Embracing it with his hands, he seemed to greet it with a joyful countenance and kissed it with glad affection [Note: [Col. 1387D] Affectu. a, s, l2: “with affection”; omitted in c, d, e.]. Immediately, by dying, he struck the bystanders with grief; still alive, he was carried in their hands into the presbytery before the altar of St Pancras [Col. 1388A]. There he lived for a while longer, sweet with the rosy flush of his face; at the very hour on which he had fallen ill to be purged, he departed pure to Christ, destined to be forever free from every evil.

“See how wonderfully [Note: [Col. 1387D] Mirabiliter. a, s, d, l2: “wonderfully”; c, e: “changeably.”] all things converged in him: the servant’s passion with the Lord’s Passion; the hour of his beginning sickness with the hour of the beginning of eternal salvation; the five days of sickness which he endured, with the cleansing of the five bodily senses through which no one avoids sin. Further, because he died before the fifth day had fully elapsed, it indicates, as we suppose [Note: [Col. 1387D] Remur. c, d, e: “we suppose”; a, s, l2: “I suppose.”], that in the final sense, called touch, he had not brought sin to completion. The third hour of the day, at which he both fell ill and through dying entered eternal life, indicates what else but that the same grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1388B], by which we know that his whole life was governed, was manifestly present both when he fell ill and when he died?

“Moreover, that we may not doubt that he was equal both in merit and reward to our fathers, Odo and Odilo [Note: [Col. 1387D] Odo and Odilo. Odo, the second abbot of Cluny, was the founder of the Cluniac rule in the tenth century. Odilo was the fifth abbot of Cluny; he succeeded in 994.], a distinctive favour granted to them was also conferred upon him. The Lord granted them to die on the octave day of the solemnities which they loved above all others: blessed Odo especially loved the feast of St Martin, and holy Odilo the Nativity of the Lord, and each died on its octave day. To Lord Lanzon, who observed the Rule of St Benedict more than other men of his age and venerated the blessed Mother of God and her feasts with singular devotion, he granted that, according to his customary practice, he should celebrate the greater Mass in the convent both on the feast of St Benedict’s departure [Col. 1388C] and on the feast of St Mary called the Annunciation of the Lord; then, struck by sickness on the octave day from the aforesaid departure of St Benedict [Note: [Col. 1388D] “And struck by sickness on the octave day from the aforesaid departure of St Benedict.” a, s, l2; omitted in c, d, e.], he should nevertheless depart to Christ on the octave day from the Lord’s Annunciation.

“Therefore, whoever does not know Lord Lanzon’s life may infer from his end how pleasing he was to God. Nor should he suppose with us that these things happened to him by the ordinary lot of the dying, since he knows that no man of that age was endowed more richly with the gifts of the Holy Spirit.”

## ON GEOFFREY, PRIOR OF WINCHESTER

§ 444. Nor should the memory of Geoffrey, prior of Winchester [Note: [Col. 1388D] Geoffrey was prior of Winchester from 1082 to 1107.], perish. In these times he was distinguished for learning and religion [Col. 1388D]. His learning is attested by many books and by letters composed in a familiar and pleasing style; above all, by epigrams which he completed in satirical fashion, and besides these, verses on the praises of England’s primacy. What more? He made the entire divine office, grown obsolete through a certain rustic antiquity, shine forth in native elegance, refined by his industry [Col. 1389A].

He traced a beautifully begun pattern of religion and hospitality for the monks, who even today tread in both respects the footsteps of their prior so closely that little or nothing is lacking to complete their praise. Finally, that house has a lodging-place, an inn for those arriving by land and sea in whatever numbers they please, with expenditure that does not fail and charity that does not tire. Alongside these things, the holy man possessed such humility of character that nothing issued from that singular storehouse of philosophy except what was humble, nothing except what was sweet.

Yet how slight may this praise of him appear? For how many there are who, even slightly imbued with letters, do not consider others beneath their dignity, displaying their consciousness of learning by swelling gesture and pompous gait? Nevertheless [Col. 1389B], lest anything should be lacking to his holy soul’s perfection, for many years he cherished a sickbed, his marrow and sins being purified in the furnace of prolonged wasting sickness [Note: [Col. 1389D] Excoctus. a, c, d, e, l2: “purified”; s: “purifying.”].

## ON THE TRANSLATION OF ST CUTHBERT AND ON ST ETHELDREDA, WHOSE BODIES WERE FOUND INTACT

§ 445. But why say more of such men? At that time England indeed had many men illustrious in knowledge and celebrated in religion. Their virtue was more commendable because, as the world grew old, it remained more steadfast and vigorous. By living praiseworthily, therefore, they confirmed the credibility of earlier histories, lest ancient accounts be accused of falsehood when the examples of later times prove that such things could occur.

Indeed, if there were any prelates of churches who seemed to have fallen away from the holiness of the ancients—effective, that is, in worldly matters but sluggish in spiritual ones—such men, if any existed, tried to cloak their faults through lavish adornment of places. Each raised new churches and clothed the bodies of his saints in silver and gold, omitting nothing in the charity of his expenditure that could draw the eyes of beholders by its attractiveness.

Of this kind was the Ranulf previously mentioned. Made bishop at Durham, he sought some glory for his name in new monastic buildings and in the veneration of blessed Cuthbert. The translation of that sacred body [Note: [Col. 1389D] Sacrati. a, c, d, e, l2: “sacred”; s: “saintly.”] enhanced his fame. In 1104, when it was raised from its tomb, he made it visible to all who wished to see it. Ralph, then abbot of Sées and later archbishop of Canterbury, handled it with fortunate boldness [Col. 1389D] and openly displayed it uncorrupted, when some had begun to doubt whether the miracle long reported—the preservation of its bodily frame—still endured [Note: [Col. 1389D] Miraculum. See above, § 207, note 4.].

At nearly the same time, in the monastery of Ely, under Abbot Richard, the virgin remains of blessed Etheldreda were seen intact [Col. 1390A], causing astonishment and applause among those who saw them. That monastery, recently transformed by King Henry into a bishopric, first received Hervey as bishop in 1109. Because of a shortage of provisions, he had abandoned Bangor, where he had been enthroned. So that the bishop of Lincoln might not complain that his diocese had been mutilated, the king made good the loss from the possessions of Ely monastery and settled the complaint.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] “Settled the complaint.” Here manuscript f ends. The following verses, which appear to conclude the work, indicate the author’s name as Ivo:

“Perhaps, reader, you will ask who wrote this book.  
Sharpen your mind and read the verses; you will quickly learn.  
Three elements compose his name;  
The first of these numbers sufficiently indicates one;  
The laws of numbers set the second as five;  
If a Greek writes it, infer the final letter.”]

Certainly, what was either taken from justice by stealth or presumed by force in his time concerning the primacy of the two metropolitans, Canterbury and York, I shall say when I come to the proper place. For, the series of kings now ended, I see that I must speak of the succession of all England’s bishops. Would that a rich abundance of eloquence flowed to me [Col. 1390B], lest such brilliant lights of our country lie any longer buried in oblivion.

There will perhaps be many in different regions of England who say that they have heard or read certain things otherwise than I have stated [Note: [Col. 1390D] Dixi. a, s, c, d, e2, l2: “I have stated”; omitted in e1.]. Yet if they are guided by sound judgment, they will not on that account erase me with the censor’s pen. For I have followed the true law of history and have never recorded anything except what I learned from trustworthy narrators or writers. Whatever the case may be, privately, with Christ’s help, I congratulate myself that I have arranged a continuous history of the English after Bede, either alone or first. [Note: [Col. 1390D] “If anyone … subject matter.” Sharpe says that William of Malmesbury may here be alluding to Henry of Huntingdon, who shortly afterward wrote a *History of England*.] Therefore, if anyone, as I now hear whispered, attempts after me the task of writing about such matters [Note: [Col. 1390D] De talibus. a, s, c, d, e2, l2: “about such matters”; omitted in e1.], let him owe me thanks for the collection, while retaining for himself the material for selection [Col. 1390C].

§ 446. These, venerable lord Count, are what I had to say concerning the deeds of the English, from their arrival in England until the twenty-eighth year [Note: [Col. 1390D] Vicesimum octavum. c, d, e, k: “twenty-eighth”; a, s, l2: “twentieth.”] of your father’s most fortunate reign. The remainder will occupy a separate little book, if you do not refuse these pages a gracious countenance.

After completing this work and considering very many men, I judged that it should be dedicated especially to you. For when I consider others, I find nobility in one, military prowess in another, learning in this man, justice in that, generosity in few. Thus I admire certain qualities in others, individual qualities in individuals, but all of them in you. If ever anyone was noble, you excel in that respect: your lineage derives its line from the most excellent kings and counts, while your mind takes its pattern from their conduct.

You have, therefore, from the Normans skill in war, from the Flemings [Note: [Col. 1390D] “From the Flemings.” a, s, d, e, l2. Manuscript a3 originally ended at this word; what now follows was added by a much later hand.] gracefulness of features, and from the French distinction of birth. Who could doubt the competence of your military service, when your most excellent father admires it in you [Col. 1391A]? When disturbances in Normandy are reported, he sends you ahead, so that they may be crushed by your courage and harmony restored by your discernment. When he returns to the kingdom, he brings you back, so that you may be his protection abroad, his joy at home, and his ornament everywhere.

§ 447. You foster letters so faithfully that, although burdened by the weight of so many occupations, you still steal for yourself some hours in which either you yourself may read or may hear others reading. Thus, by worthy governance, you regulate the height of your fortune: you neither set military service aside for letters nor, like some, scorn letters for military service. In this too the wonder of your learning becomes evident: while you love books, you give proof [Note: [Col. 1391C] Indicium. a, c, d, e, l2: “proof”; s: “judgment.”] how eagerly [Col. 1391B] you have drunk their fountain to the marrow. Many things, indeed, are desired even when they are not possessed; but no one will love philosophy unless he has drunk it in to utter satiety.

§ 448. The fame of your justice has reached even our regions. Neither the eminence of a person nor the lowliness of fortune has ever forced from you a perverse judgment. He who attempts to undermine justice, whether by the offer of a gift or the allurements of favour, finds nothing in your breast that serves his arts.

§ 449. [Note: [Col. 1391C] “Your generosity … judgment.” a, s, c, d, e2, l2. This whole paragraph is omitted in e1.] Tewkesbury monastery displays your generosity and contempt for money. Of it, as I hear, you not only do not consume the gifts of hospitality, but even return presents sent voluntarily [Note: [Col. 1392C] Remittitis. a, s, l2: “you return”; d, e2: “you send.”]. How great this is, especially in the present age—how great its glory in the world and its favour with God—you surely understand. Blessed, therefore, according to Plato’s maxim, is the commonwealth whose ruler is a philosopher, whose prince takes no delight in gifts.

I would say more on such matters, were I not restrained as I begin to speak by the suspicion of flattery and by the praiseworthy modesty of your reserve. Yet I have purposely not omitted what I have said, so that through the service of my tongue your excellence may not remain unknown to posterity, and may itself strive to advance from virtue to virtue. Indeed, long ago, at the persuasion of some, I had almost resolved to add to this work, year by passing year, the matters which I did not think should be passed over. But it seems wiser to forge another book upon such matters than often to sew new material into a work already finished.

Nor should anyone say that I expend superfluous labour if I set forth the deeds of the most illustrious of all kings in his age. My humility owes much to his greatness and will owe still more; if for no other reason, because he rejoices in possessing such a son. For after your birth under a fortunate destiny, he ordered you to be educated in letters not perfunctorily—as is now evident; afterwards he made you lord of very extensive possessions; and now, finally, he inclines his paternal [Note: [Col. 1392C] Patrium. a, d, e2, l2: “paternal”; s, c: “fatherly.”] affection toward you.

Let this book, then, as it is, be wholly consecrated to your glory. In the other, there will be the same limit to life as to writing. For the rest, receive my gift graciously, so that I may rejoice in the grateful judgment of its recipient, since I did not err in my choice [Note: [Col. 1392C] Judicio. a, s, c, d; c1 adds: “These, venerable lord Count, are what I had to say concerning the deeds …”].

[Col. 1391]

# THREE BOOKS OF THE *HISTORIA NOVELLA* OF WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY, MONK

## PROLOGUE TO THE BOOKS OF THE *HISTORIA NOVELLA*, ADDRESSED TO ROBERT, COUNT OF GLOUCESTER

[Col. 1391D] 684–687. To his most beloved lord Robert, son of King Henry and earl of Gloucester: William, librarian of Malmesbury—after earned triumphs on earth, may you triumph in heaven.

[Col. 1392D] I did not neglect to commit to writing many deeds of your father, of most distinguished memory: both in the fifth book of the royal deeds [Note: [Col. 1391] Actuum. e, l2: “deeds”; omitted in s, c, d.] and in three little books to which I gave the title *Chronicles* [Note: [Col. 1391] “In three little books to which I gave the title *Chronicles*.” They are now lost.]. Now your serenity desires that those things which, in the present age, have occurred in England by the great miracle of God should be entrusted to posterity [Col. 1393A]. A most beautiful desire indeed [Note: [Col. 1393D] Plane. s, e, l2: “indeed”; c, d: “fully.”], and one like that of all your family.

For what is more conducive to the benefit of honour, or more useful to equity [Note: [Col. 1393D] Conducibilius. e: “more useful”; s, c, d, l2: “contributes more.”], than to recognize God’s mercy toward the good and his vengeance against the wicked? What, moreover, is more delightful than to commit the deeds of brave men to the records of letters, so that others [Col. 1394A] may cast off cowardice by their example and arm themselves in defence of their country? Since I have been enjoined to do this by the office of my pen, I think the history can be conducted more systematically if, returning a little farther back, I weave together the sequence of years from the empress’s return to England after the death of her husband [Note: [Col. 1393D] Sui. e: “her”; omitted in s, c, d, l2.]. Therefore, having first called upon the Divinity, as is fitting, for aid, and intending to write the truth of events while giving offence neither from hostility nor favour, I shall begin thus.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1393]

## FOR WHAT REASONS KING HENRY RECALLED THE EMPRESS FROM GERMANY

[Col. 1393B]

§ 1. In the twenty-sixth year of Henry, king of the English, which was the year 1126 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Henry, emperor of the Germans, to whom Matilda, daughter of the aforesaid king, had been married, died in the very flower of life and victories [Note: [Col. 1393D] Obiit. l2 reads either *obierat* (“had died”) or *obiit* (“died”). Emperor Henry V died on 23 May 1125; in September 1120 King Henry returned from Normandy with his daughter, the empress.].

At that time our king was staying in Normandy to quiet any disturbances which might arise in those regions [Note: [Col. 1393D] Ob. e: “on account of”; s, c, d, l2: “for.”]. As soon as he learned of his son-in-law’s death, he soon afterward sent honourable men to recall his daughter. The empress returned unwillingly, it is said, because she was accustomed to her dower lands and possessed many estates there. Certainly, in the years that followed, some princes of Lorraine and Lombardy came to England more than once to seek her as their mistress [Col. 1393C]. Yet they gained no fruit from their labours, because the king intended to establish peace between himself and the count of Anjou by marrying his daughter to the count.

For that man—greatest of all kings held in the memory of our own and even our fathers’ age—nevertheless always regarded the power of the Angevins with suspicion. This is why he dissolved and annulled the betrothal [Note: [Col. 1393D] Sponsalitia … cassavit. See § 419.] which his grandson William, afterward count of Flanders, seemed about to contract with the daughter of Fulk, count of Anjou and later king of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1393D] Videbatur. e: “seemed”; s, c, d, l2: “was said.”]. This is why he joined another daughter of the same man to his own son William, still under age and scarcely an adolescent [Note: [Col. 1393D] Conjunxit. See § 419.]. This is why he gave this daughter of his—the one of whom we have begun to speak—in marriage, after her imperial bed, to the son of that same Fulk [Col. 1394B], as the ensuing narrative will continue to relate.

## ON THE COUNCIL HELD AT LONDON

§ 2. In the twenty-seventh year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1393D] Regni sui. s, c, d, e2, l2: “of his reign”; omitted in e1.], King Henry came to England in September 1126, bringing his daughter with him. At the following Christmas, having summoned a great number of clergy and magnates at London, he gave his wife, daughter of the duke of Louvain, whom he had married after Matilda’s death, the earldom of Shrewsbury. Grieving that this woman did not conceive and fearing that she would remain permanently barren, he was rightly anxious about the succession to the kingdom.

Having previously deliberated much and long concerning this matter [Note: [Col. 1393D] Considerato. e, l2: “having considered”; s, c: “having deliberated”; d: “having desired.”], he then compelled and bound by oath all the great men of the whole of England, including bishops [Col. 1394C] and abbots, that, if he should die without a male heir, they would receive without delay and without any reservation Matilda, his daughter and former empress, as their lady. He declared how great a loss the fortune of the realm had inflicted upon the country by taking from him his son William [Note: [Col. 1394D] Suum. s, c, d, e2: “his”; omitted in e1, l2.], to whom the kingdom belonged by right; that there now remained his daughter, to whom alone legitimate succession was due—from grandfather, uncle, and father, all kings; and from the maternal line, for many preceding ages.

Indeed, from King Egbert [Note: [Col. 1394D] Rege. s, e, l2: “king”; omitted in c, d.] of the West Saxons, who was the first either to expel or to subdue the other kings of the island, in the year 800 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1394D] “In the year 800 of the Lord’s Incarnation.” The union of the kingdoms was accomplished only over several years during Ecgbert’s reign, after he became king in 802; see §§ 106–107.], through fourteen kings until the year 1043 of that Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1394D] Tertium. See § 196, note 7.], when King Edward [Note: [Col. 1394D] Edwardus. e: “Edward”; s, c, d, l2: “Edward, who lies at Westminster.”] was elevated to the throne [Col. 1394D], the line of that royal blood had never failed or faltered in succession to the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1394D] “Nor ever … faltered.” Malmesbury has here passed over the reigns of Cnut and his sons.].

Edward, the last and also the most illustrious of that lineage, gave his great-grandniece Margaret, descended through his brother Edmund Ironside, in marriage to Malcolm, king of the Scots [Note: [Col. 1395C] “Edward … gave … in marriage.” Margaret married after Edward the Confessor’s death. Her brother Edgar Ætheling, then an exile in Scotland, consented to her marriage with King Malcolm. (*Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*, annal 1067).]. That Matilda, the mother of this empress, was their daughter is certain [Note: [Col. 1395C] Filiam … constat. e: “Matilda, a daughter, became the mother of this empress”; s, c, d, l2: “Matilda, mother of this empress, was their daughter.”].

## ON THE OATH WHICH THE PRIMATES OF ENGLAND TOOK TO THE EMPRESS
§ 3. Therefore all those who were regarded as of any consequence in that same council swore: first William, archbishop of Canterbury; then the other bishops; and no less the abbots. Of the laymen, David king of Scotland, the empress’s uncle, swore first; then Stephen, count of Mortain and Boulogne, nephew of King Henry through his sister Adela; then Robert, the king’s son, whom he had acknowledged before he became king and had made earl of Gloucester. He had given him in marriage Mabel, a woman distinguished and eminent, dutiful to her husband and blessed with the fertility of numerous and very beautiful offspring.

[Note: [Col. 1395C] “Were regarded.” c. d. e. l 2: “were being regarded,” s.]

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “Earl of Gloucester.” Robert was made earl of Gloucester in A.D. 1119. In the Pipe Roll of 31 Henry I one reads: “Gloucestershire.” “And to the earl of Gloucester, £20 by reckoning, for his share of the earldom.”]

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “Given … blessed.” e; omitted in s. c. d. g. k. l 2.]

Notable, as is said, was the contest between Robert and Stephen, as they vied with one another in the rival glory of their virtues over which of them should swear first: the former looking to the privilege of being a son, the latter to the rank of being a nephew. Thus, when all the magnates had been bound by faith and oath, each then departed to his own home.

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “As is said.” e: “as is reported,” s. c. d. l 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “Magnates.” e; omitted in s. c. d. l 2.]

After Pentecost, in A.D. 1127, the king sent his daughter into Normandy, ordering that she be betrothed by the archbishop of Rouen to the son of the aforesaid Fulk, a young man of great nobility and renowned strength; nor did he delay in sailing to Normandy himself and joining them in marriage.

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “King.” s. c. d. e 2. l 2; omitted in e 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “Daughter.” e: “his daughter,” s. c. d. l 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “And joining them in marriage.” Matilda’s marriage with Geoffrey Plantagenet, later count of Anjou, was celebrated in the presence of his father in September 1127.]

Once this had been done, everyone, as though by some prophecy, declared that after his death they would abandon their oath. I often heard Roger, bishop of Salisbury, say: “I am released from the oath which I made to the empress; for I swore on the understanding that the king would not marry his daughter to anyone outside the realm without the counsel of myself and the other magnates. No one was the author of that marriage or privy to it, except Robert, earl of Gloucester, Brian the son of the count, and the bishop of Lisieux.”

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “Oath.” e: “from the oath,” s. c. d. l 2.]

Nor do I say this because I believe the words of a man who knew how to adapt himself to every occasion according to the changing course of fortune; rather, as a truthful historian, I record in writing the opinion of the provincials.

## ON THE DEATH OF POPE HONORIUS AND THE CONTEST OVER ELECTING THE APOSTOLIC

§ 4. I should like briefly to recount the remaining years of the life and reign of King Henry, so that posterity may not be deprived of knowledge of events, while I may not seem to linger too long over matters less relevant to this history.

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “King.” e; omitted in s. c. d. l 2.]

In the twenty-eighth year, A.D. 1129, the king returned to England from Normandy.

[Note: [Col. 1395D] “In the twenty-eighth year.” The twenty-eighth year of Henry’s reign was completed on 4 August 1128; the Saxon Chronicle, however, places his return from Normandy in the autumn of 1129.]

In the twenty-ninth year something occurred in England which may seem strange to our long-haired contemporaries, who, forgetting what they were born to be, gladly transform themselves into the appearance of the female sex.

[Note: [Col. 1396C] “Gladly transform themselves into the appearance of the female sex.” e: “by the length of their hair transform themselves into the appearance of the female sex,” s. c. d. l 2. Orderic Vitalis (BOUQ. XII, 696) testifies how much men throughout England and Gaul attended to their hair in this age. This custom, which prevailed not only among laymen, was held in honour in England at various times; decrees of councils and royal edicts were issued to restrain it. At the Council of London held in 1102, over which Anselm presided, it was ordered: “Let the long-haired be so shorn that part of the ears is visible and the eyes are not covered.” For more on this, see Eadmer, p. 81. In the twenty-first year of Henry II’s reign, the king ordered: “King [sends] greeting to William de Percut. Know that we have granted and given you full authority to cut the hair of our clerks, who belong to our household and family, who wear long hair and nourish their locks, and to make them lay aside the curls of their hair. And therefore we command you diligently to attend to this in the proper manner; exercising the authority granted you in such a way in cutting the aforesaid hair and removing the curls that we need not apply shears to cut your own hair. Witnessed by myself at Clyve, on the second day of September.” (Patent Roll, 21 Henry III, membrane 3.)]

One of the provincial knights, proud of a great luxuriance of hair and terrified by the prompting of his conscience, dreamed that someone was strangling him with the little locks of his own hair. Therefore, shaken awake from sleep, he quickly cut away whatever superfluity of hair he had. The example spread through England and, as a recent punishment is accustomed to move the mind, almost all knights calmly accepted having their hair cut to a proper length. But this holiness did not last long. For scarcely a year had passed when all who seemed to themselves to be courtly men fell back into their former vice: they competed with women in the length of their hair and, where their own hair failed, tied on certain attachments; forgetting, or rather ignorant of, the apostolic saying: “If a man wears long hair, it is a disgrace to him.” [Col. 1397A]

[Note: [Col. 1397D] “If a man wears long hair, it is a disgrace to him.” 1 Corinthians 11:14.]

In the thirtieth year, A.D. 1130, King Henry crossed into Normandy. In that year Pope Honorius died, on 14 February, and the Roman Church was shaken by a great contest over the election of the Apostolic. At that time there were in the same city two most famous cardinals: Gregory, deacon of Saint Angelo, and Peter, cardinal priest, son of Leo, prince of the Romans. Both were distinguished for learning and ability, and it was not easy for the people to discern which of them ought more justly to be chosen by the clergy.

Yet the party favouring Gregory moved first, so that, once ordained pontiff, he was called Innocent. A rumour was also spread among the common people that Honorius was still alive and had ordered this to be done. The authors of this ordination were William, bishop of Palestrina; Matthew of Albano; Conrad of Sabina; John of Ostia; Peter of Cremona, of the title of Saint Chrysogonus; and Haimeric the chancellor. But the other party, after Honorius had already been buried, with the support of Peter’s brothers, the wealthiest and most powerful Romans, declared him elected and consecrated as Anacletus. The foremost instigator and author of this ordination was Peter, bishop of Porto. If I set down his letter, it will disclose the entire controversy, though it is more inclined toward Anacletus.

## LETTER OF PETER OF PORTO CONCERNING THE SAME CONTEST

§ 5. “Peter, bishop of Porto, to the four bishops William of Palestrina, Matthew of Albano, Conrad of Sabina, and John of Ostia.

[Col. 1397C]

“How great is the distress of my heart on your account, he alone knows who knows all things. You too would at least now have learned it in part from my letters, had not the judgement of the Church and common authority forbidden it. This is not the time to judge the praise or blame of the persons about whom differing reports are now circulated: there is one who will investigate and judge. Yet if anyone is ready to accuse, there will be one ready to answer; especially since, in your sight and mine—indeed, in the sight of the whole Church—each has lived wisely and honourably, and has hitherto exercised with full freedom those duties which belonged to his office.

“You ought rather to abstain from idle talk and rash words. If the matter concerns rumours, the facts are far otherwise than your letters to me declare. Moreover, if you attend to the words which you have set down and to the requirements of order—if I may speak without prejudice to your reverence—with what confidence, with what face, do you presume to call that faction of yours an election? Why do you say that your man was ordained, when there was no order whatsoever in his cause? Is this how you have learned to elect a pope—in a corner, in concealment, in darkness and the shadow of death? If you wished a living man to succeed the dead pope, why did you proclaim the dead man to be alive?

[Note: [Col. 1397D] “Wished.” s. c. e: “wished” or “were wishing,” l. 2.]

“It would have been far better to pay the dead man the offices due to humanity, and then to consider the consolation of the living. But behold: while you seek consolation for the living from the dead, you have suffocated both the living and the dead together. Finally, it belonged neither to you nor to me to elect, but rather to reject or approve the man elected by the brethren. Therefore, what you presumed to do—disregarding order, despising canon law, and even spurning the anathema enacted by yourselves; without consulting me, your prior; without consulting the senior brethren and priors; indeed, without even calling or waiting for them; while you were novices and only a very few in number—must be held void, and you may perceive from your own judgement that it is altogether nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1397D] “While.” s. c. d. e 2. l 2; omitted in e 1.]

“But the Lord quickly came to our aid and showed us the way by which we might oppose your error.
