For your brother cardinals, whose power in the election is paramount, together with the clergy, at the request of the whole people and with the assent of the eminent men, in the light and openly, by unanimous vote and desire elected Lord Peter the cardinal as Anacletus, Roman pontiff. I witnessed this election, canonically celebrated, and confirmed it by God’s authority. The Church receives and venerates him; through God’s grace bishops, abbots, princes, captains, and barons come to him before our eyes—some in person, some through their envoys. We do not see the plundering and cruelty which you allege. Whoever come to him for answers or their business are received kindly and return more kindly treated.

“Return, return now to your senses. Do not make a schism in the Church; do not labour any longer for the ruin of souls. Let the fear of God hold you, not worldly shame.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] “God.” e. l 2: “the Lord,” s. c. d.]

“Will not one who sleeps add that he may rise again? Cease now from lies, in which the wicked have been accustomed to place their hope. Lord Tiburtius testified in writing under oath, saying that I judged the deacon of Saint Angelo alone fit for the rank of pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] “Under oath.” e: “under a sacred oath,” s. c. d. l 2.]

“Let him see what he has said. I have spoken nothing in secret; there is no one who has ever heard this statement from my mouth. My judgement has always been that no mention should be made of a successor until the pope had been buried. I have maintained and shall maintain the unity of the Church. I shall strive to adhere to truth and justice, confidently hoping that justice and truth will deliver me.” [Col. 1398D]

Thus the aforesaid Peter of Porto, more favourably disposed toward Peter Leo, wrote.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] “Of Porto, more favourably disposed toward Peter Leo.” e: “Peter, bishop of Porto, against Peter the son of Leo,” s. c. d. l 2.]

Nor indeed did the other party cease to call Peter himself “the lion’s whelp” and to name his supporters accomplices in a faction. And they conducted various negotiations among themselves concerning doubtful matters. Innocent, however, excluded from Rome, crossed the Alps and made for Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 1398D] “Gaul.” s. c. d. l 2: “Galba,” e.]

There he was received without hesitation by the whole Church on this side of the Alps. King Henry also, who did not readily abandon an opinion once formed, voluntarily gave him his hand at Chartres; and at Rouen he honoured him with gifts, not only his own but also those of the magnates and even of the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 1399C] “Honoured him.” s. c. d. e 1. l 2: “deigned to receive him,” e 2.]

Yet Innocent, although he was greatly assisted by the kings of England and France, together with the emperor of the Germans, could never enjoy peace so long as Anacletus held the see of the Roman Church. But when Anacletus himself died in the eighth year of his assumed, as it was said, episcopate, on 25 January A.D. 1138, Lord Innocent enjoyed the dignity of the Apostolic See in peace undisturbed to this time.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “Himself.” s. c. d. e 2. l 2; omitted in e 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “Innocent … dignity.” Pope Innocent died on 24 September 1143.]

§ 6. In the thirty-first year of his reign, A.D. 1131, the king returned to England.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “King.” e: “King Henry,” s. c. d. l 2.]

The empress too made her appearance in her native land in that same year; and, a considerable assembly of magnates having been held at Northampton, she renewed the former pledge among those who had given it and received it from those who had not.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “Native land.” s. c. d. e 1. l 2: “her native English land,” e 2.]

In the same year Louis, king of the French, advancing in age and weighed down by excessive corpulence, ordered his son to be crowned as successor to the kingdom. When that son died shortly afterwards from a fall from a horse, he adorned another son with the crown by the hand of the Roman pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “In the same year.” Philip, the elder son of Louis VI, was consecrated at his father’s command on 14 April 1129. Having died as a result of this accident on 13 October 1131, King Louis arranged for his second son Louis to be crowned at Rheims by Pope Innocent II.]

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “Roman.” s. c. d. l 2: “of Rheims,” e.]

This man, as they report, not degenerating from the ancient valour of the French, acquired Aquitaine also for his lawful possession through his wife’s dowry settlement; after Louis, son of Charlemagne, the kings of the French are known not to have held it in their own dominion.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “They report.” s. c. d. e 1. l 2: “they say,” e 2.]

## ON A MURRAIN AMONG LIVESTOCK

[Col. 1399C]

§ 7. In the thirty-first year of Henry’s reign, more correctly the thirty-second, A.D. 1132, a destructive plague of domestic animals spread throughout all England. Full pigsties were suddenly emptied; entire stalls of cattle were abruptly deserted. The same pestilence lasted in the following years, so that no village in the whole kingdom, exempt from this misery, could laugh at another’s misfortunes.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “In the thirty-first year.” More correctly, the thirty-second. See Henry of Huntingdon.]

At that time also the contention between Bernard, bishop of St Davids, and Urban, bishop of Llandaff, concerning the rights of parishes unlawfully usurped by Urban, was settled by a final end. After being debated for many years in so many appeals to the Roman court, with so many expenses of journeys and so many clashes of advocates, it was at last dissolved—or rather decided—by Urban’s death at Rome. For the Apostolic, after weighing the equity of the matter, gave satisfaction by a fitting judgement to the piety and justice of the bishop of St Davids. In the same year William, archbishop of Canterbury, personally obtained from the indulgence of the Roman See the legateship in England.

## ON KING HENRY’S CROSSING AND HIS DEATH

§ 8. When the thirty-second year of his reign had passed on the preceding day, Henry sailed for Normandy on the Nones of August, A.D. 1133—the day on which he had once received the summit of the crown at Westminster. That was the king’s last and fateful crossing.

[Note: [Col. 1399D] “When the thirty-second year … received.” Although all manuscripts read “thirty-second,” it is clear from the events that “thirty-third” is required here, Henry completing the thirtieth year of his reign on 4 August 1133. From this place and others it is evident that Malmesbury reckons Henry’s reign from 5 August, the day of his coronation, not from the third of the same month, the day of his brother’s death.]

A truly remarkable providence of God then played upon human affairs: that on the day on which he had long before been crowned, to reign so long and so prosperously, he should board a ship never to return again alive.

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “On that.” s. c. d. e 1. l 2: “on that same,” e 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “Again.” e: “alive,” s. c. d. l 2.]

As I have said, it was the Nones of August; and on the following Wednesday the elements attended with their grief the last passage of so great a prince. For on that very day, at the sixth hour, the sun covered its shining head with gloomy rust, as poets are accustomed to say, terrifying human minds by its eclipse; and on the following Friday, early in the morning, there was so great an earthquake that the earth seemed wholly to sink, with a dreadful sound heard beneath the ground such as had never been heard before.

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “Wednesday.” On Wednesday, 2 August A.D. 1133.]

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “The sun … at the sixth hour.” The sun suffered an eclipse on 2 August, after midday.]

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “Terrifying … by its eclipse.” e: “shaking [men] by its eclipse,” s. c. d. l 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “Earth.” e: “lands,” s. c. d. l 2.]

I myself saw stars around the sun during the eclipse; and during the earthquake I saw the wall of the house in which I sat lifted by two impulses and settle back at the third. The king was therefore in Normandy continuously for three years—more correctly, two—and so much longer as the interval between the Nones of August, on which day, as stated, he crossed the sea, and the Kalends of December, 1 December A.D. 1135, on the night of which he died.

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “Three years.” More correctly, two.]

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “It has been stated.” e: “as has been stated,” s. c. d. l 2.]

There is no doubt that he did many things in Normandy which deserved to be recorded; but it was my decision to pass over matters that have not come fully to our knowledge. Many were the expectations of his return to England; whether by some fate or by divine will, all were frustrated. He therefore reigned for thirty-five years and from the Nones of August to the Kalends of December—that is, four months less four days.

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “And.” s. c. d. e 2. l 2; omitted in e 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1400D] “Less four days.” s. c. d. l 2: “less days,” e 1; “five days more,” e 2. Calculation by lunar or calendar months suitably reconciles the various readings.]

At Lyons, while occupied with hunting, he was struck down by illness.

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “Lyons.” e: “Leonas,” s. d. l 2; “Leonibus,” c.]

As it grew worse, he summoned Hugh, surnamed of Amiens, whom he had first made abbot of Reading from prior of Lewes, and afterwards archbishop of Rouen, and who was bound to him and his heirs for such great benefits. The report of his illness swiftly gathered the magnates. His son Robert, earl of Gloucester, was also present; through integrity of faith and eminence of virtue, he deserved an enduring and particular memory in every age.

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “Growing worse.” s. c. d. e 1. l 2: “more plainly,” e 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “Hugh.” Surnamed of Amiens.]

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “His.” e; omitted in s. c. d. l 2.]

When they asked him concerning a successor, he adjudged all his land on both sides of the sea to his daughter by lawful and perpetual succession, being angry with her husband because he had provoked him with certain threats and injuries. On the seventh day after the onset of his sickness, deep in the night, he yielded to nature. I refrain here from recounting his high-minded character, because in the fifth book of the *Deeds of the Kings* I have set it forth most fully; but the following letter of the aforesaid archbishop of Rouen will show how Christianly he died.

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “In the fifth book.” § 411.]

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “But.” e; omitted in s. c. d. l 2.]

## LETTER OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN ON THE DEATH OF KING HENRY

§ 9. “To his lord and father Pope Innocent: Hugh, servant and priest of Rouen, the duty of obedience.

“Concerning my lord the king, whom it cannot be remembered without grief, we judged it right to inform your pious fatherhood. Overtaken by a sudden illness, he summoned us by his envoys with all speed and desired us to be present with the consolations appropriate to his sickness.

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “His sickness.” e: “his own sickness,” s. c. d. l 2.]

We came to him and spent three days with him, full of sorrow. As we spoke to him, he confessed his sins with his own mouth, struck his breast with his own hand, and renounced evil will. By the counsel of God, of ourselves, and of the bishops, he promised that he would observe an amendment of his life. Under this promise, to which he firmly assented, we absolved him for the third time and over three days, as our office required.

[Note: [Col. 1401D–1402D] “Under this promise, to which he firmly assented.” e: “with his firm assent to this,” d; “under this promise,” s; “with his firm assent to this very promise,” c. l 2.]

He adored the cross of the Lord and devoutly received the body and blood of the Lord. He arranged his almsgiving, saying: ‘Let my debts be paid; let the allowances and fixed payments which I owe be rendered; let the remainder be distributed to the needy.’

[Note: [Col. 1402D] “Which.” e: “which things,” s. c. d. l 2.]

Would that those who held and hold his treasures had acted thus! At last we carefully explained to him the authority for anointing the sick, which the Church received from the blessed apostle James; and at his own pious request we anointed him with holy oil. Thus he rested in peace. May God grant him peace, because he loved peace!”

## HOW KING HENRY’S BODY WAS EVISCERATED

§ 10. The aforesaid archbishop of Rouen truly attested these things concerning the faith of the dying King Henry. His funeral was royally prepared, and his body was carried in turn by the magnates as far as Rouen. There, in a certain secluded part of the principal church, it was eviscerated, lest, corrupted by delay, it should offend the nostrils of those seated or standing nearby. The remains of his entrails were buried in the monastery of Saint Mary of Pré near the city, which, as I hear, he had honoured with considerable endowments after its foundation by his mother. His body was kept at Caen until a somewhat gentler winter, then harshly raging, should bring more tranquil weather.

## ON THE ADVANCEMENT OF KING STEPHEN TO THE KINGDOM

§ 11. Meanwhile Stephen, count of Mortain and Boulogne, King Henry’s nephew, as I have said above, who after the king of Scotland had been the first layman to bind his faith to the empress, hastened to England by way of Wissant. The empress, for definite reasons, and likewise her brother Robert, earl of Gloucester, together with nearly all the magnates, delayed their return to the realm. Some castles in Normandy, however, among them especially Domfront, attached themselves to the cause of the heiress.

It is certainly established that, on the day Stephen landed in England, early in the morning, there was, contrary to the nature of winter in our regions, a thunderous crash with dreadful lightning, so that the world was thought almost to be dissolving. Once he had been received as king by the Londoners and the men of Winchester, he also won over Roger, bishop of Salisbury, and William de Pont de l’Arche, keepers of the royal treasures. Yet, lest the truth be concealed from posterity, all his efforts would have been futile if his brother Henry, bishop of Winchester—now legate of the Apostolic See in England—had not lent him his ready assent.

[Note: [Col. 1402D] “Now.” s. e. l 2; omitted in c. d.]

He was doubtless drawn by the very great hope that Stephen would preserve, in governing the kingdom, the practices of his grandfather William, especially in the discipline of ecclesiastical rigour. Accordingly, when William, archbishop of Canterbury, exacted from Stephen a solemn oath to restore and preserve the liberty of the Church, the bishop of Winchester made himself mediator and guarantor. I shall not omit in its proper place the text of that oath, afterwards put into writing.

## ON THE CORONATION OF KING STEPHEN AND HIS CHARACTER

§ 12. Stephen was therefore crowned king of England on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, a Sunday, 22 December A.D. 1135, in the presence of three bishops—the archbishop, the bishop of Winchester, and the bishop of Salisbury—of no abbots and very few magnates, on the twenty-second day after his uncle’s death, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1135.

[Note: [Col. 1402D] “On the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.” Most contemporary writers state that Stephen was crowned on 26 December.]

He was indeed energetic but not very prudent; brave in arms; of unrestrained spirit in beginning every arduous enterprise; gentle and merciful to enemies; affable to all. Yet, although one admired the sweetness of his promises, one desired truthfulness in his words and effectiveness in his pledges. Thus, after not much time had elapsed, he set aside his brother’s advice, though it was by that brother’s aid, as I have said, that he had both removed opponents and ascended the throne.

[Note: [Col. 1403D] “Not very prudent.” e: “prudent,” l. 2; “imprudent,” s. c. d.]

## ON THE BURIAL OF KING HENRY

§ 13. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1136, after Christmas, King Henry’s body, borne by gentle winds, was placed on a ship and brought to England; and at the monastery of Reading—which he had adorned outwardly by the magnitude of its estates and inwardly by its community of religious monks—it was buried in the presence of the successor to the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1403D] “In the year … 1136, after.” e. l 2: “in the year … 1135,” s. c. d.]

Afterwards, shortly before Lent, King Stephen went into Northumbria to meet David king of Scotland, who was said to hold different views. Nor did he obtain with difficulty what he wished from him, because David, softened both by gentleness of disposition and by advancing age, readily granted the benefit of either true or feigned peace.

[Note: [Col. 1403D] “Nor did he obtain with difficulty.” e: “nor was it difficult,” s. c. d. l 2.]

## ON THE ARRIVAL OF ROBERT, EARL OF GLOUCESTER, IN ENGLAND

§ 14. In the same year, after Easter, Robert, earl of Gloucester, whose prudence King Stephen greatly feared, came to England. While he was in Normandy, he had troubled his mind with much reflection as to what decision he should make in this affair. If he submitted to King Stephen, he saw that he would act against the oath which he had made to his sister. If he resisted, he understood that he would be of no benefit to his sister or nephews and certainly would cause himself immense harm.

For the king possessed, as I touched upon above, an immense quantity of treasures which his uncle King Henry had accumulated over many years. The coinage, all of the finest kind, was reckoned at almost one hundred thousand pounds; there were also vessels of gold and silver, of great weight and inestimable value, collected through the prudence of ancient kings and especially of Henry.

[Note: [Col. 1403D] “Which his uncle King Henry had accumulated.” e: “which his uncle had accumulated,” s. c. d. l 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1403D–1404D] “Coinage, all of the finest kind.” The author of the *Dialogue concerning the Exchequer* relates that for some time after the Norman arrival money was extremely scarce in England, and that until Henry I’s reign all revenues owed to the king were paid in grain and other provisions for the use of his household. Henry I, however, ordered all to be paid in money. Payments were therefore made by scale and by weight; by number or counting; by burning or melting. These methods of payment ensured that sellers and buyers used only tested money. Perhaps for this reason coins struck during Henry’s reign were considered exceptional.]

One who possessed such a store of riches could not lack supporters, especially since he was lavish in giving and—what least befits a prince—prodigal. Knights of every kind and lightly armed men flocked to him, especially from Flanders and Brittany. They were a most rapacious and violent race of men, who thought nothing of breaking into cemeteries or despoiling churches; indeed, of not only driving men of religious orders from their horses but also carrying them off into captivity. Nor were they merely foreigners, but native knights too, who hated King Henry’s peace because under it they had lived on scanty fare.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] “Despoiling.” e: “plundering,” s. c. d. l 2.]

All these readily assented to a prince whom they could easily bend to their own advantage, advancing their fortunes at the cost of the provincials. Moreover, while he was count, Stephen had won such affection through his affability and by sharing jesting, sitting, and meals even with the lowliest that scarcely anyone could conceive it in his mind.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] “Sharing meals.” e. l 2: “associating,” s; omitted in c. d.]

And now all the magnates of England had passed to his side with ready minds. The most prudent count was therefore anxious to convict them of their fault and by a personal conference recall them to a sounder judgement; for, owing to the reasons stated above, he had no power to resist them by force. Indeed, he was not even free to come to England unless, as though a party to their defection, he concealed for a time the secret of his mind. He therefore did homage to the king on a certain condition: namely, so long as Stephen preserved his own dignity unimpaired and kept the agreements made with him. For, having long observed the king’s character, he foresaw the instability of his good faith.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] “Therefore.” e: “indeed,” s. c. d. l 2.]

## ON THE OATH WHICH KING STEPHEN MADE TO PRESERVE JUSTICE, THE PRIVILEGES, AND THE LAWS OF THE REALM

§ 15. In the same year, not long after the count’s arrival, the bishops swore fidelity to the king so long as he should preserve the liberty of the Church and the vigour of discipline. He too swore according to the text of a document, which reads as follows:

“I Stephen, by the grace of God, elected king of England by the assent of clergy and people, consecrated by Lord William, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the holy Roman Church, and afterwards confirmed by Innocent, pontiff of the holy Roman See, out of reverence and love for God grant that the holy Church shall be free, and confirm to it the reverence due to it. I promise that I shall do or permit nothing simoniacal in the Church or in ecclesiastical affairs. I acknowledge and confirm that the jurisdiction and authority of ecclesiastical persons and of all clerics, and the distribution of ecclesiastical goods, are to remain in the hands of the bishops. I ordain and confirm that the dignities of churches confirmed by their privileges, and their customs held according to ancient practice, shall remain inviolate.

[Note: [Col. 1405D] “I ordain and confirm.” e: “I grant and ordain,” s. c. d. l 2.]

“I grant that all possessions and tenures of churches which they held on the day when King William, my grandfather, was alive and dead shall be free and unencumbered to them, without objection by any claimant. But if a church hereafter seeks to recover anything held or possessed before the king’s death, of which it is now deprived, I reserve it for consideration or restoration by my favour and dispensation. Whatever has been conferred after the king’s death, by the generosity of kings, the gifts of princes, offering, purchase, or any transfer whatsoever by the faithful, I confirm. I promise that I shall establish and preserve peace and justice in all things to the best of my ability.

“I reserve for myself the forests which King William, my grandfather, and William II, my uncle, established and held; all the rest, which King Henry added, I render and grant free from claim to the churches and the kingdom. If any bishop, abbot, or other ecclesiastical person before his death has reasonably distributed his own goods, or prescribed their distribution, I grant that it shall stand firm; but if he is overtaken by death, the same distribution shall be made for the salvation of his soul by the counsel of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1405D] “Other ecclesiastical person.” e: “another ecclesiastical person,” s. c. d. l 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1405D–1406D] “Before his death.” It had been customary to seize for the king’s use everything which ecclesiastics left at death. Henry of Huntingdon relates that, when Gilbert Universalis, bishop of London, a man notorious for avarice, died, all his goods—including chests full of gold and silver—were carried to the treasury. *Anglia Sacra*, II, 698. Sometimes even property distributed at a dying man’s bedside was reclaimed in the king’s name. See 3 Newburgh III.5 (SHARPE, 563). The practice of seizing the goods of deceased ecclesiastics seems to have passed into the custom of claiming for the king the cup and riding-horse of a deceased bishop, prior, or abbot. See Close Roll, 39 Henry III, membrane 17, dorse.]

“While sees are vacant of their proper pastors, they and all their possessions shall be entrusted to the hand and custody of the clerics and worthy men of the same church until a pastor is canonically appointed.

[Note: [Col. 1406D] “And custody.” s. c. d. e 2. l 2; omitted in e 1.]

“I utterly abolish all exactions, *meschenningas* [an uncertain technical term], and injustices improperly introduced, whether by sheriffs or by any others whatsoever. I shall observe, and command and ordain to be observed, good laws and ancient and just customs in cases of murder, pleas, and other causes. At Oxford, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1136, the first of my reign.”

## THAT KING STEPHEN WRONGFULLY ALTERED ALL THESE THINGS WHICH HE HAD SWORN
### §16

I am weary of adding the names of the witnesses, who were many, because he altered almost everything so perversely, as though he had sworn solely to show the whole kingdom that he was a violator of his oath. Yet let it be permitted me, without offence to this most mild-tempered man, not to conceal the truth [Col. 1405D]. For had he entered the kingdom lawfully, and had he not, in administering it, lent credulous ears to the whisperings of ill-wishers, he would indeed have lacked little of the dignity proper to a royal person [Col. 1406A].

Accordingly, under him the treasures of certain churches were plundered, landed possessions bestowed upon laymen; churches belonging to clerks were sold to strangers; bishops were arrested and [Note: [Col. 1406D] “And.” e, l 2; “or,” s, c, d.] compelled to alienate their property; abbeys were granted to unworthy men, either for the sake of friends or in remission of debts. Yet I think these things should be attributed not so much to him as to his advisers, who persuaded him that he ought never to lack money while monasteries were full of treasures.

### 710. Of the Passage of King Stephen and Earl Robert into Normandy, and of the Plot Laid by the King against the Earl

#### §17

In the year 1137 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1406D] “One thousand one hundred and thirty-seven”: s, c, d, l 2; “one thousand one hundred and thirty-six,” e.], the king crossed the sea in the first part of Lent [Col. 1406B]. The earl likewise, having tested and learned the dispositions of those whom he knew to be more steadfast in the faith they had pledged, and having decided what course he should thereafter adopt, embarked upon the sea on Easter Day itself [Note: [Col. 1406D] “On that very day”: e, l 2; “he himself,” s, c, d.], and was carried safely to land.

Not long afterward he came very near to experiencing the malignity of adverse fortune. For the king, at the instigation of a certain William of Ypres, attempted to seize him by a plot. But the earl, forewarned of it by one acquainted with the conspiracy, escaped the snares prepared for him; and for several days he kept away from the court, to which he was often invited. The king, dismayed that his plot had achieved little, judged that he must proceed by cunning. By serenity of countenance and a gratuitous confession, he endeavoured to diminish the magnitude of his fault. He nevertheless swore [Col. 1406C], in words framed as the earl desired, that he would never again take part in so great a crime; and, that he might be more fully restored to favour, he confirmed the oath by placing his hand, through Archbishop Hugh of Rouen, into Robert’s hand.

These things he did; but he never showed him complete friendship, since he always regarded his power with suspicion. Thus, before the earl [Note: [Col. 1406D] “Before the earl”: s, c, d, l 2; omitted in e.], he called him “earl” pleasantly and cheerfully [Note: [Col. 1406D] “Him”: s, c, d, l 2; omitted in e.], but behind his back he bit him with malicious words and harassed him in whatever possessions he could. Robert likewise, matching craft with craft, concealed his mind behind his countenance; and, letting the king return peacefully to his kingdom, remained in Normandy and attended to his own interests.

Thus, while Stephen was hindered by many disturbances in England [Col. 1406D], attacking now these men [Note: [Col. 1406D] “These”: e; “some,” s, c, d, l 2.] and now others, so that what was said of Ishmael might fittingly be applied to him—“because every man’s hand is against him [Col. 1407A], and his hand against every man”—Robert enjoyed secure leisure in Normandy throughout that year. The king was accustomed frequently, when confronted with resistance, to say, as was reported: “Since they chose me as king, why do they abandon me? By God’s birth, I shall never be called a deposed king!” Robert, as though posted on a watchtower [Note: [Col. 1407D] “Watchtower”: s, c, d, e 1, l 2; “mirror,” e 2.], foresaw the outcome of events; and he diligently considered how he might avoid being branded before God and men as faithless to the oath he had made to his sister.

### How and for What Reasons Earl Robert Renounced Homage to the King

#### §18

In the year 1138 of the Lord’s Incarnation, England was shaken by internal dissensions. Many men, driven to unlawful acts by nobility of birth [Col. 1407B], greatness of spirit, or rather by the boldness of more vigorous youth [Note: [Col. 1407D] “Of age”: s, c, d, e 1, l 2; “of spirit or age,” e 2.], did not hesitate to demand from the king—some estates, some castles, and finally whatever each happened to desire. When he delayed granting these things, pleading the impaired state of the kingdom or alleging that others claimed or even possessed them, they were immediately stirred to anger: they fortified castles against him and carried off immense plunder from his lands.

Nor was he disheartened by the defection of any persons. Rather, he appeared suddenly now here, now there, and always brought the matter to an end more at his own loss than at that of those resisting him. For, after many great labours had been spent in vain, he obtained from them a feigned peace for a time by granting either honours or castles. [Col. 1407C] At last he even created many earls who had not been earls before, attaching to them lands and revenues which belonged to the king by his own right. They were greedier in asking, and he more lavish in giving, because a report flew through England that Robert, Earl of Gloucester [Col. 1408A], who was in Normandy, would shortly assist his sister’s cause, once he had first renounced his allegiance to the king.

Nor did the reality of events fail the lightness of rumour [Note: [Col. 1407D] “Reality”: e; “truth,” s, c, d, l 2.]. For soon after Pentecost, having sent his men from Normandy to the king, Robert, in the manner of his ancestors, renounced friendship and fealty, and also repudiated his homage. He set forth his reason for doing so justly: the king had unlawfully aspired to the kingdom and had neglected, not to say falsified, every pledge sworn to him; indeed, the king had himself acted against the law, since, after swearing to Robert’s sister, he had not been ashamed, while she was alive, to give his hand to another.

The responses of many religious men whom he had consulted on the matter undoubtedly strengthened his resolve: that he could in no way pass through the present life without disgrace, nor deserve the blessedness of the life to come, if he treated as void the oath arising from his paternal relationship [Col. 1408B]. In addition, he produced the tenor of an apostolic decree commanding him to obey the oath which he had made in his father’s presence; I shall have care to insert the text of that decree in a later book. This man, who had drunk deeply of learning to complete satiety, knew that these matters would be of great benefit to him thereafter.

The king, however, grievously offended by the earl’s high-mindedness, deprived him of all the possessions in England that he could [Note: [Col. 1407D–1408D] e: “deprived him of the possessions in England”; s, c, d, l 2: “deprived him, so far as lay in his power, of possessions in England.”], and razed some of his castles. Bristol alone remained, so that it might not only drive out enemies but also wear down the king by frequent incursions. But since it has sufficed to carry the first book of the *New History* from the return of the empress—after her husband’s death—to her father down to this point [Col. 1408C], I shall now begin the second, from the year in which that heroic woman came to England to assert her right against Stephen.

## 714–715. Book Two

[Col. 1407]

#### §19

In the year 1139 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the poison of malice, long nourished in King Stephen’s mind, at last burst forth openly. Rumours were spread in England that Earl Robert would very soon [Col. 1407D] come from Normandy with his sister. Since many, in expectation of this, were deserting the king not only in intention but in action, he made good his own losses by injuries inflicted upon many persons [Note: [Col. 1408D] e: “he repaired his losses by injuries to many”; s, d, l 2: “he repaired his injuries by the losses of many.”].

He also arrested many at his court, contrary to royal dignity, merely on suspicion that they held different allegiances against him; and he compelled them to surrender their castles and to accept whatever terms he pleased. At that time there were two exceedingly powerful bishops in England: Roger of Salisbury, and his nephew through his brother [Col. 1408C], Alexander of Lincoln. Alexander had built the castle of Newark, as he said, for the protection and dignity of his bishopric. Roger, wishing to seem great-minded through the construction of buildings, had raised towered structures at Sherborne and at Devizes, embracing much land with buildings [Col. 1408D].

At Malmesbury, in the very cemetery, scarcely a stone’s throw from the principal church, he had surrounded with a wall and drawn into his own custody the castle of Salisbury, which belonged properly to the royal jurisdiction and which he had obtained from King Henry. Certain powerful laymen, moved by this, resented the prospect of being surpassed by clerks both in the accumulation of wealth and in the size of their strongholds, and nourished in their breasts [Note: [Col. 1409D] “Breasts”: e; “breast,” s, d, l 2.] the hidden wound of envy. Therefore they poured out their complaints to the king: the bishops, forgetful of their order, were raging in building castles. There ought, they said, to be no doubt that all this was being done for the king’s destruction, since, as soon as the empress arrived, they would go over to their lady along with the surrender of their castles, prompted, of course, by remembrance of paternal benefactions. They should therefore be forestalled promptly and compelled to surrender their fortifications; otherwise the king would repent too late when he saw in the power of his enemies [Note: [Col. 1409D] “To be”: e; omitted in s, d, l 2.] what, had he been wise, he might have secured for himself.

The magnates frequently urged these arguments. Though he was excessively obliged to them by favour, for some time he pretended not to hear their flattering words, softening the bitterness of delay either out of respect for the bishops’ religious office [Col. 1409B], or, as I think more likely, through fear of reproach to himself. At last, as soon as opportunity presented itself, he did not delay to carry out what the nobles had advised. The occasion was as follows.

### Of the Arrest of the Bishops

#### §20

At Oxford, when an assembly of magnates had been held about the eighth day before the Kalends of July (24 June), the aforesaid bishops also arrived. The bishop of Salisbury began this expedition with great reluctance. For I heard him say words to this effect [Note: [Col. 1409D] “For”: e; omitted in s, d, l 2.]:

> “By my lady Saint Mary, I do not know how, but my mind recoils from this journey! I know this: I shall be of as much use at court as a colt is in battle.”

Thus his mind foreboded the evils to come. Then, as though fortune seemed to favour [Note: [Col. 1409D] “Favour”: e; “serve,” s, d, l 2.] the king’s will, a disturbance arose between the men of the bishops and those of Alan, Earl of Brittany, over the claiming of lodgings. The outcome was wretched: the men of the bishop of Salisbury’s church [Note: [Col. 1409D] “Church”: e; omitted in s, d, l 2.], sitting at table, sprang up to fight before their meal was half eaten. At first the matter was conducted with curses, then with swords. Alan’s retainers were put to flight [Note: [Col. 1409D] “Alan’s retainers put to flight”: see below, §24.], and his nephew was nearly killed. Victory fell to the episcopal party, though not without bloodshed: many were wounded and one knight was killed [Note: [Col. 1409D] “Killed”: e; “slain,” s, d, l 2.].

The king, seizing the occasion [Note: [Col. 1409D] e: “having seized the opportunity”; s, d, l 2: “having hunted for an opportunity.”], ordered the bishops to be summoned by his longstanding instigators, so that they might make satisfaction to his court [Note: [Col. 1409D] “His”: s, d, e 2, l 2; omitted in e 1.] because their men had disturbed his peace. The manner of satisfaction was to be that they should hand over the keys of their castles as pledges of loyalty. They were prepared to make satisfaction, but hesitated about surrendering the castles; he ordered them to be kept under closer guard lest they depart.

Thus he led Bishop Roger without chains, and the chancellor [Col. 1410A; Note: [Col. 1409D] “Chancellor” has been written over “Alexander” in d after deletion of that word, but incorrectly. Roger, chancellor of England, was the son of Roger, bishop of Salisbury, and of Matilda of Ramsbury, his concubine.], who was said to be his nephew—or more than his nephew—in fetters, to Devizes, that he might, if possible, obtain the castle, built at vast and almost uncountable expense—not, as the bishop himself maintained, for ornament, but, as the truth of the matter shows, to the injury of the church. [Note: [Col. 1410D] e 1: “that he might, if possible, obtain the castle, by many…”; s, l 2: “namely, the castle, by many…”; d, e 2: “the second castle, by many…”; s reads *si* (“if”) for *sive* (“or whether”).]

During this siege the castles of Salisbury, Sherborne, and Malmesbury were delivered to the king. Devizes itself was surrendered after three days, when the bishop imposed a voluntary fast upon himself in order that by this hardship he might bend the mind [Note: [Col. 1410D] e: “mind”; s, d, l 2: “spirit” or “resolution.” The author of the *Gesta Stephani* relates that both bishops were, by the king’s order, deprived of food: one was confined in a stable and the other in a miserable cell. (*Florence of Worcester, Continuation*, A.D. 1138).] of the bishop of Ely, who held it. Nor did Alexander, bishop of Lincoln [Note: [Col. 1410D] “Alexander”: e; omitted in s, d, l 2.], act more obstinately: he bought his release by surrendering the castles of Newark and Sleaford [Note: [Col. 1410D] e: “the castles of Newark and Sleaford”; s, d, l 2: “the castle.”].

#### §21

This act of the king gave many people occasion to speak in divergent judgments [Col. 1410B]. Some said that the bishops appeared to have been lawfully deprived of castles which they had built contrary to the prescriptions of the canons: they ought to be heralds of peace, not builders of houses that would serve their authors as refuges for wrongdoing. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, the king’s greatest defender so far as his eloquence could achieve it, developed this argument with fuller reasons and speeches.

Others, by contrast—among whom stood Henry, bishop of Winchester, papal legate in England and brother of King Stephen, as I said above—took the other side. Neither brotherly relationship nor fear of danger compelled him then [Note: [Col. 1410D] “Then”: e; omitted in s, d, l 2.] to depart from the truth. He spoke thus:

> “If bishops transgressed the path of justice in any matter, judgment belonged not to the king but to the canons. They should not have been deprived of any possession without a public ecclesiastical council [Col. 1410C]. The king did this not from zeal for rectitude [Note: [Col. 1410D] e, l 2: “from zeal for rectitude”; s, d: “out of zeal for rectitude.”], but for the advantage of his own profit; for he did not restore the castles to the churches from whose resources and on whose lands they had been built, but handed them over to laymen, and to men little given to religion.”

Affirming these things both privately and publicly before the king, and appealing to him to release and restore the bishops, that man exhausted every effort, but was heard in nothing. Therefore, judging that the force of the canons must be tried, he ordered his brother without delay to be present at the council which he was to hold at Winchester on the fourth day before the Kalends of September (29 August).

### Of the Council Held concerning the Arrest of the Bishops

[Col. 1410D]

#### §22

On the appointed day nearly all the bishops of England came to Winchester, together with Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, who had succeeded William. Thurstan, archbishop of York, excused his absence because of the illness that oppressed him—for he could scarcely govern his body with the strength of his spirit [Col. 1411A]—while the others excused their absence by letters because of the war.

First there was read in the council a decree of Pope Innocent, by which, from the Kalends of March, if I remember correctly, the same pope had entrusted to the lord bishop of Winchester, by right of legation, a share of his pastoral charge in England. This was received with the greatest favour, because the bishop, showing restraint through long delay, had not abruptly proclaimed himself legate with boastful display.

There followed in the council a Latin speech, directed to learned hearers, concerning the outrage of the bishops’ arrest: the bishop of Salisbury had been seized in the court chamber, the bishop of Lincoln in his lodging; and the bishop of Ely, fearing similar treatment, had escaped the calamity by swift flight to Devizes [Col. 1411B].

> “It was a pitiable outrage that the king had been so misled by instigators as to order hands laid upon his own men, especially bishops, within the peace of his court. To royal disgrace had been added an offence against heaven: under the pretext of the bishops’ fault, churches were stripped of their possessions. The king’s transgression against God’s law caused him such grief that he would rather suffer great loss both in body and property than see episcopal dignity cast down by so great an indignity. Indeed, the king had often been warned to amend his sin [Note: [Col. 1411D] e, l 2: “warned”; s, d: “admonished.”], and at last he had not refused [Note: [Col. 1411D] e: “at last”; s, d, l 2: “at last then.”] the summoning of the council. Therefore let the archbishop and the others deliberate together on what ought to be done. As for himself, he would not fail in carrying out their decision, whether through friendship for the king, who was his brother [Col. 1411C], through loss of possessions, or even through danger to his life.”

#### §23

While he gradually set these matters forth with rhetorical enlargement, the king, not despairing of his cause, sent earls to the council to ask why he had been summoned. The legate gave a brief answer:

> “He who remembers that he is subject to Christ’s faith ought not to be angered if he is summoned to make satisfaction by Christ’s ministers, being conscious of so great a crime as our age has nowhere seen. For it belongs to pagan ages to imprison bishops and strip them of their possessions. Let them therefore tell their brother that, if he deigned to lend a peaceable assent to their counsel, he would grant him, with God’s help, such a settlement as neither the Roman Church, nor the court of the king of France, nor Earl Theobald, brother of them both—a man indeed wise and religious—could reasonably oppose [Col. 1411D], but which they ought rather to embrace favourably. At present the king would act prudently if he either gave an account of his deed or submitted to canonical judgment. It is also his duty to favour the Church, from whose bosom he was received into the kingdom, rather than advanced to it by the hand of soldiers.”

With this the earls departed [Note: [Col. 1411D] e: “With this”; s, d, l 2: “Thus, with this.”], and not long afterwards returned with an answer [Note: [Col. 1411D] e: “with an answer”; s, d, l 2: “with a considered answer.”]. They were accompanied by a certain Aubrey de Vere, a man practised in the varieties of litigation [Col. 1412A]. He delivered the king’s reply and, so far as he could, pressed the case against Bishop Roger—for Bishop Alexander was absent [Note: [Col. 1411D] e: “was absent”; s, d, l 2: “had departed.”], though he supported him [Note: [Col. 1412D] “Whom he supported”: e; omitted in s, d, l 2.]—yet he did so moderately, without any insult in words, although certain earls standing nearby repeatedly interrupted his speech, casting reproaches upon the bishop.

#### §24

This, then, was the substance of Aubrey’s statement:

> “King Stephen had suffered many injuries from Bishop Roger. He had scarcely ever come to court [Note: [Col. 1412D] e: “court”; s, d, l 2: “the king’s court.”] without Roger’s men, presumptuous because of his power, raising disturbances. They had often done so at other times [Note: [Col. 1412D] “Often”: s, d, e 2, l 2; omitted in e 1.], and recently at Oxford had attacked [Col. 1412B] the men and even the nephew of Earl Alan; they had also attacked the men of Hervey of Léon, a man of such nobility and such haughtiness that he had never yielded to King Henry’s request to come into England. The infliction of so great violence upon that man [Note: [Col. 1412D] e: “that man”; s, d, l 2: “him.”], who had come out of affection for King Stephen, therefore reflected upon the king’s injury.

> “The bishop of Lincoln, from an old hatred of Alan, had been the author of the disturbance through his men. The bishop of Salisbury secretly favoured the king’s enemies, while for the present concealing this by craft. The king had learned this beyond doubt from many indications, and especially because, when Roger de Mortemer, leading the royal knights [Note: [Col. 1412D] e: “led”; s, d, l 2: “was leading.”], was in the greatest fear of the men of Bristol, the same bishop would not permit him to remain at Malmesbury even for one night. Everyone was saying that, as soon as the empress came [Col. 1412C], he would join her with his nephews and castles.

> “Roger was therefore arrested not as a bishop but as a servant of the king, because he administered the king’s procurations and received his fixed payments. The king did not seize the castles by force: both bishops surrendered them willingly in order to escape the accusation arising from the disturbance they had caused at court. The king found some money in the castles, which was lawfully his, because Bishop Roger had collected it from the revenues of the royal treasury during the reign of King Henry, the king’s uncle and predecessor. Yet the same bishop willingly yielded this money, as he did the castles, through fear of his offences against the king. Witnesses to this are not lacking for the king. He therefore desires that the agreements between himself and the bishops remain valid.” [Col. 1412D]

#### §25

Bishop Roger protested against Aubrey’s statements that he had never been King Stephen’s servant and had never received his fixed payments. This resolute man, who was ashamed to be broken by misfortunes, even uttered threats: if he did not find justice in that council concerning the things taken from him, he would seek it before the hearing of a greater court.

The legate replied gently, as in other matters:

> “Everything alleged against bishops ought first to have been charged and examined in an ecclesiastical council to determine whether it were true, before a judgment contrary to the decrees of the canons was pronounced against men still uncondemned [Col. 1413A]. Let the king therefore do what is lawful even in secular courts: restore the bishops to possession of their property; otherwise, being dispossessed contrary to the law of nations, they will not plead.”

#### §26

After many things had been said on both sides in this fashion, the case was deferred at the king’s request until the following day; and then it was prolonged again until the day after, in expectation of the arrival of the archbishop of Rouen. When he came, while all minds were held in suspense concerning what he would bring, he said that he agreed that the bishops should have castles if they could prove by the canons that they ought lawfully to have them. Since they could not do so, it was the height of perversity to wish to maintain a claim contrary to the canons.

> “And grant,” he said, “that it is just [Col. 1413B] for them to possess them. Yet, because the time is dangerous, according to the custom of other peoples all magnates ought to surrender the keys of their fortifications to the king’s will, since he must fight for the peace of all. Thus the whole controversy of the bishops will be defeated [Note: [Col. 1413D] e: “will be defeated”; s, d, l 2: “was defeated.”]. For either it is unjust according to the prescriptions of the canons for them to have castles; or, if this is tolerated by princely indulgence [Note: [Col. 1413D] e 1: “by”; s, d, e 2, l 2: “instead of,” i.e. “in place of.”], they ought to yield by handing over the keys to the necessity of the times.”

#### §27

To these arguments the aforesaid advocate Aubrey added [Note: [Col. 1413D] e: “added”; s, d, l 2: “subjoined.”] that the king had been informed that the bishops were murmuring [Note: [Col. 1413D] e: “were murmuring”; s, d: “were threatening”; l 2: “were making threats.”] among themselves and preparing to send some of their number against him to Rome.

> “And the king commands you,” he said, “that none of you presume to do this [Col. 1413C]; for if anyone should go anywhere from England against his will and the dignity of the kingdom, perhaps his return would be difficult. The king himself, moreover, because he sees that he is being burdened, voluntarily appeals against you to Rome.””

#### §28

After the king had sent this message, partly in what seemed praise and partly as a threat, it was understood to what end he aimed. The meeting therefore broke up with the result that he was unwilling to undergo the censure of the canons, and the bishops did not judge it advisable to exercise their accustomed decision against him [Note: [Col. 1413D–1414D] e: “to exercise a decision against him”; d: “to curse him according to custom”; s: “to exercise him according to custom”; l 2: “to exercise a decision against him.”]. This was for two reasons: either because it would have been rash to excommunicate a prince without apostolic knowledge, or because they heard—and some even saw—swords being drawn about them. The words were no longer playful: men were almost contending for life and blood.

Nevertheless, the legate and the archbishop did not fail to carry out the tenor of their office [Col. 1413D]. Prostrate at the king’s feet in his chamber, they begged him to have mercy upon the Church, mercy upon his own soul and reputation, and not to allow discord between kingship and priesthood. He rose graciously; and although he tried to shift from himself the odium of their action, being forestalled by evil counsels he gave no effect to his good promises.

### Of the Arrival of the Empress and Earl Robert in England

[Col. 1414A]

#### §29

The council was dissolved on the Kalends of September (1 September). On the day before the Kalends of October (30 September), Earl Robert, having at last struggled free from the bonds of delay, landed in England with his sister the empress, trusting in God’s mercy and in the faith of a lawful oath. Yet he came with a far smaller military force than anyone else would have undertaken so dangerous a war with: he then brought with him no more than one hundred and forty knights. My account rests on the testimony of truthful informants.

I would say, did it not seem flattery, that in courage alone he was not unequal to Julius Caesar, of whom Livy records that he had only five cohorts when he began the civil war; with them, he says [Note: [Col. 1414D] This word, *inquiens* (“he says”), seems superfluous.], he assailed the whole world [Col. 1414B]. Yet Julius and Robert are compared unequally. Julius, a stranger to the true faith, rested his hope, as he said, upon his fortune and the valour of his legions. Robert, distinguished by Christian piety, depended wholly upon the protection of the Holy Spirit and of his lady Saint Mary. Julius had supporters throughout Gaul and partly in Germany and Britain, and had also bound all the Roman populace, except the senate, to himself by gifts. Robert, apart from a very few in England who did not forget the faith once sworn, found the magnates either hostile or offering no assistance.

He therefore put in at Arundel; and there he placed his sister for the time being in what he believed to be safe custody with his stepmother. After the empress’s mother had died, as I said above, King Henry had formerly joined this woman to himself in marriage [Col. 1414C]. Robert himself made for Bristol through such dense wilderness, accompanied, as I heard, by scarcely twelve knights; and on the road Brian, son of the earl of Wallingford, met him. Not long afterwards he learned that his sister had left Arundel, for his stepmother, with feminine fickleness, had broken the faith she had promised, even though she had sent messengers into Normandy many times.

The king, however, granted the empress a safe-conduct under Henry, bishop of Winchester, and Waleran, count of Meulan—a protection which the custom of honourable knights does not permit them to deny to anyone, even a most hostile enemy. Waleran indeed stopped short of proceeding beyond Calne, while the bishop continued the escort [Col. 1414D]. The earl therefore quickly gathered forces, arrived at the limits fixed by the king, and led his sister more safely to Bristol [Note: [Col. 1414D] e: “to Bristol more safely”; s, d, l 2: “to safer places, to Bristol.”]. Later Milo, who had held the castle of that city under the earl in King Henry’s time, received her into Gloucester after doing homage and swearing fealty to her; for that city is the head of its own county.

### 726. How the King Took Malmesbury, and of the Siege of Trowbridge

[Col. 1415A]

#### §30

[Note: [Col. 1415D] “On the Nones of October … departed”: e; the entire chapter is omitted in s, c, d, g, k, l 2, m.]

On the Nones of October (7 October), a certain Robert son of Hubert, a savage and barbarous man, secretly entered by night the castle of Malmesbury, which Bishop Roger had begun under unlucky auspices. Having burned the town, he gloried as though in a great triumph. Yet before fifteen days had passed, his joy vanished: he was driven out by the king. Meanwhile the king ordered the castle to be guarded until, once peace had been made, it could be destroyed.

Before coming to Malmesbury, the king had occupied a small fortification of the aforesaid Milo, called Cerney, and had stationed his knights there. Therefore, believing that success would attend him elsewhere as well [Note: [Col. 1415D] e 1: “also there”; e 2: “for himself.”] as at Malmesbury, he attacked the castle of Humphrey de Bohun, called Trowbridge [Col. 1415B], who favoured the empress’s party, but departed unsuccessfully.

### How Hereford Yielded to the Empress

#### §31

Thus the whole region around Gloucester as far as the depths of Wales gradually attached itself to the lady empress during the remaining months of that year, partly by force and partly through goodwill. Some castellans, sheltering within their fortifications, watched for the outcome of events. The city of Hereford was received without difficulty; a few knights, shutting themselves up stubbornly in the castle, were besieged from outside [Note: [Col. 1415D] “From outside”: s, d, e 1, l 2; “at the gates,” e 2.].

The king approached in case he might devise some help for those under pressure; but disappointed in his hope, he withdrew ingloriously. He also rode near Bristol and, pressing onward, burned the villages around Dunstor [Col. 1415C], leaving absolutely nothing, so far as he was able, that could serve his enemies for food or any other use.

### Of the Death and Character of Roger, Bishop of Salisbury

#### §32

On the third day before the Ides of December (11 December), Roger, bishop of Salisbury, escaped by the benefit [Note: [Col. 1415D] s, d, l 2: “by the benefit”; e: “from the benefit.”] of death from the quartan fever by which he had long been shaken. They say that he contracted the illness through grief of mind, having been assailed by such great and frequent misfortunes at the hands of King Stephen.

God seems to me to have set him forth as an example to the rich of the instability of worldly affairs, lest they place their hopes in the uncertainty of riches—riches which, as the apostle says [Note: [Col. 1415D] Apostle: 1 Timothy 1:19.], some, desiring them, have suffered shipwreck in the faith. He first became attached to Count Henry, who later became king [Col. 1415D], because of his prudence in managing household affairs and restraining the extravagance of the household. Before becoming king, Henry was sparing and frugal in expenditure, constrained, that is, by the poverty of his estate, while his brothers William and Robert treated him arrogantly.

Having learned his character, Roger so won Henry’s favour during the time of his need that, when Henry ascended the royal throne, he denied him nothing, or scarcely anything, which Roger thought fit to ask: he granted him estates, churches, clerks’ prebends, entire abbeys of monks; finally, he entrusted the kingdom itself to his fidelity. At the beginning of the reign he made him chancellor and, not long after, bishop of Salisbury.

Roger therefore managed lawsuits, regulated expenditure, and guarded the treasure. He did this when the king was in England; he did it without colleague or witness when the king was staying in Normandy—as frequently and for long periods happened. And not only from the king, but also from the magnates—even those whom envy of his prosperity secretly gnawed—and especially from the king’s servants and debtors, he received whatever he almost could have conceived [Col. 1416A; Note: [Col. 1416D] “Then”: e; omitted in s, d, l 2.]. If anything adjoining his lands would serve his interests, he immediately extorted it by request or price, and, if those failed, by force.

He was singularly illustrious, so far as our age can remember, in the building of houses. Throughout all his possessions he constructed splendid residences [Col. 1416B], whose successors will labour in vain merely to maintain them. He raised one see to immeasurable magnificence through wondrous ornaments and buildings, with no restraint whatsoever in expenditure.

It was altogether marvellous to see how great an abundance of riches attended that man in every kind of dignity and flowed, as it were, to his hand. How small was that glory—what greater thing could happen?—that, through the labour of his upbringing, he made two nephews, men of honourable learning and diligence, bishops; and not bishops of obscure sees, but of Lincoln and Ely, whether England possesses wealthier bishoprics I do not know. He knew how great his power was, and sometimes, more harshly than became such a man, abused the indulgence of the Godhead [Col. 1416C].

Finally, as a certain poet says of a certain rich man [Note: [Col. 1416D] “A certain”: e; “any,” s, d, l 2.],
He demolishes, builds, and changes squares into circles. [Note: [Col. 1416D] “He demolishes . . . circles”: Horace, *Epistles* I.1.100.] Thus Roger tried to transform abbeys into a bishopric, and the possessions of a bishopric into an abbey. Malmesbury and Abingdon, most ancient monasteries, he assigned—as far as lay in his power—to the bishopric; he transformed the priory of Sherborne, which properly belonged to the bishop of Salisbury, into an abbey, after destroying and annexing to it the abbey of Horton. These things occurred in the time of King Henry, under whom his affairs, as I have said, flourished with great success; but under King Stephen [Note: [Col. 1416D] e reads “king”; s, d, and l2 omit it.] they slipped backward, as I foretold—except that, at the beginning of his reign, he obtained for his nephews, for one the chancellorship, [Col. 1416D] for the other the treasury, and for himself the borough of Malmesbury, while the king repeatedly said to his intimates: “By God’s nativity! I would give him half England, if he asked for it, until the time passes: he himself will fail in asking before I fail in giving.”

In his later years Fortune, which had excessively and long smiled upon him, at last cruelly struck the man with a scorpion’s tail. What was it like for him to see before his eyes men who had deserved well of him wounded, and his most intimate knight cut down? [Note: [Col. 1416D] “Knight”: s, d, e2, and l2 read *militem*, “knight”; e1 reads *militum*, “of knights.”] [Col. 1417A] Then, on the next day, as I said above, to see himself and his nephews—most powerful bishops—one put to flight, another held captive, and a third, a young man most dear to him, bound in fetters; after the surrender of the castles, to see his treasures plundered; and afterwards to be torn to pieces by foul insults in a council; finally, when he was almost drawing his last breath at Salisbury, to have carried away against his will whatever money and vessels remained, namely those which he had set upon the altar for completing the church. I think the climax of his misery—one that moves even me to pity—was that, though he seemed wretched to many, he was pitiable to very few. Such envy and hatred had he incurred through excessive power, and undeservedly among some whom he had even raised to honours.

## ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF ABBEYS

[Col. 1417B]

§ 33. In the year 1140 of the Incarnate Word, the monks of the abbeys which Bishop Roger had held contrary to right, having approached the king, succeeded in recovering their ancient privileges and abbots. The monks elected as abbot of Malmesbury, according to the tenor of the privilege which Saint Aldhelm had obtained from Pope Sergius four hundred and sixty-six years earlier, and had caused to be confirmed by King Ine of the West Saxons and Æthelred of the Mercians, John, a monk of that house, a man especially distinguished for gentleness of character and generosity of spirit.

The legate approved the cause but disapproved the person; for his mind could by no means be persuaded that the king had consented to the election except in return for payment of money. [Col. 1417C] And indeed some money had been promised, for the sake of the church’s liberty, not for the election of the individual. Therefore John, although he was carried off by an untimely death in the same year, nevertheless left to all succeeding ages an enduring and praiseworthy remembrance of himself. For no monk of that place, I truly confess, would have ventured upon so magnanimous a deed had John not begun it. Therefore let his successors have the praise if they have guarded the liberty of the church; he, beyond doubt, reclaimed it from servitude.

## ON THE CONFUSION OF WAR THROUGHOUT ENGLAND

§ 34. That whole year bristled with the harshness of war. Castles were numerous throughout all England, each defending its own side—or rather, to speak more truly, despoiling the country. The soldiers of the castles drove off cattle and sheep from the fields, sparing neither churches nor cemeteries. Seizing vavassors, peasants, and all who were thought wealthy, they compelled them, by the severity of tortures, to promise anything whatever. [Note: “Vavassors . . . compelled”: omitted in s, c, d, g, k, and l2.] Having plundered the homes of miserable country-dwellers down to the straw, [Note: “Straw”: e reads *stratum*, “bedding”; s, d, and l2 read *stramen*, “straw.”] they imprisoned the inhabitants in chains and did not release them unless everything they possessed, and whatever they could acquire by any means, [Note: e reads *quocunque modo*, “by any means”; s, d, and l2 read *quaecunque quocunque modo*, “whatever, by any means.”] [Col. 1418A] had been spent upon their ransom. Many, amid the very tortures by which they were constrained to ransom themselves, breathed out their sweet lives, bewailing to God their miseries—the only thing they could do.

Indeed, at the earl’s wish, the legate, with the bishops, repeatedly excommunicated all breakers-open of cemeteries, violators of churches, and those who had laid hands upon persons of sacred or religious order, or upon their servants; yet this effort achieved almost nothing. Thus one could see the calamity: England, once the splendid nurse of peace, the special dwelling-place of tranquillity, reduced to such misery that not even bishops or monks could travel safely from village to village.

Under King Henry, many foreigners, harassed by disturbances in their native soil, [Note: e and l2 read *inquietationibus*, “disturbances”; s and d read *turbellis*, “storms/tumults.”] [Col. 1418B] sailed to England and lived in peaceful repose beneath his wings. Under Stephen, many from Flanders and Brittany, accustomed to live by plunder, flew into England in hope of great spoils.

Meanwhile Robert, earl of Gloucester, behaved with restraint, taking greater care of nothing than not to conquer even with slight loss to his own men. [Note: “Robert, earl of Gloucester”: omitted in s, d, and l2.] He was content to keep in check the English magnates whom he could not bend to observe the sanctity of their oath, so that those unwilling to help might do less harm—according to the comic poet: “Willing what he could, since he could not do what he wished.” Yet whenever he saw it could conveniently be done, he admirably fulfilled the duty both of soldier and commander. In short, he vigorously subdued the strongholds especially injurious to the cause he had undertaken: namely Harpetreu, which King Stephen had taken from certain soldiers of the earl before he came into England; many others at Sudeley and Cerney, which the king, as I said, had filled with his own soldiers; and the castle which that same king had fortified against Wallingford he levelled to the ground. [Note: “Namely Harpetreu . . . levelled”: omitted in s, c, d, g, k, and l2.]

He also made his brother Reginald earl of Cornwall in so difficult a time. Nor was the king less resolute in undertaking the duties incumbent upon him; he missed no opportunity of frequently repelling his opponents and defending his own interests. But success failed him, and everything turned for the worse through the lack of justice. Already the dearness [Note: s, e, and l2 read *caritas*, “dearness”; d reads *raritas*, “scarcity.”] of provisions was gradually increasing; and because of the falseness and difficulty, indeed, [Note: e reads *enim*, “indeed”; omitted in s, d, and l2.] of the coinage, it sometimes happened that scarcely twelve pence were received in exchange for ten shillings or more. [Col. 1418D] It was reported that the king himself had ordered the weight of the pennies, which it had had in King Henry’s time, to be reduced, because, after exhausting that immense treasury of his predecessor, he could not meet the expense of so many soldiers. Therefore everything in England was for sale; and churches and abbeys were now openly, not secretly, sold like merchandise.

## ON THE ECLIPSE OF THE SUN

[Col. 1419A]

§ 35. In that year, A.D. 1140, during Lent, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April (20 March), at the ninth hour, on Wednesday, there was, as I have heard, an eclipse throughout all England. Certainly among us and all our neighbours the failure of the sun was so striking that people—since it was Lent, and they were sitting at table, as happened almost everywhere at that time—[Note: “For it was Lent”: omitted in s, d, and l2.] first [Note: d reads *primo*, “first”; s and l2 read *primum*, “at first”; e omits it.] feared the ancient chaos; then, when they understood what it was, went outside and saw stars around the sun. It was thought and said by many, not without reason, that the king would not complete the year in his kingdom without loss. [Note: “Without loss”: omitted in s, d, and l2.]

## ON THE CAPTURE OF ROBERT, SON OF HUBERT

§ 36. In the following week, at the very time of the Passion, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April (26 March), the aforesaid barbarian Robert, son of Hubert—[Note: e reads “the aforesaid barbarian Robert, son of Hubert”; s, d, and l2 read “a certain Robert, son of Hubert, savage and barbarous.”] [Col. 1419B] very skilful at the thefts of war—secretly seized the castle of Devizes. He was the most savage man of all whom the memory of our age embraces, and a blasphemer even against God. For he used openly to boast that he had been present where four times twenty monks had been burned together with their church. [Note: d, e, and l2 read “four times twenty”; s reads “twenty-four.”] He declared that he would do the same in England, and would grieve God by plundering the church of Wilton and even [Note: e1 reads *etiam*, “even”; e2, *jam*, “already”; s, d, and l2, *et*, “and.”] by destroying Malmesbury, with the slaughter of all that place’s monks; this, he said, he would repay them as a service because they had admitted the king to his harm. For this he laid to their charge, though falsely.

With these ears I heard that, if he ever released captives unharmed and without tortures—which was indeed very rare—and thanks were offered him on God’s behalf, [Col. 1419C] I heard him, I say, reply: “May God never thank me!” He exposed captives, smeared with honey, naked beneath the blazing sun in the open air, [Note: s, d, and l2 read “under the open sky”; e2, “under the air”; e1, “under the open sky or under the air.”] provoking flies and animals of that kind to sting them.

Once he had obtained Devizes, he did not hesitate to boast that through that castle he would occupy the whole region from Winchester to London, and would send soldiers into Flanders for his own protection. As he planned these actions, heavenly vengeance thwarted him through John, son of Gilbert, [Note: e reads “John, son of Gilbert”; s, d, and l2 read “a certain John.”] a man of great cunning, who held Marlborough Castle. Bound in chains by him because he refused to restore Devizes to his lady, the empress, [Col. 1420A] he was hanged from the gallows and put to death. [Note: e reads “hanged from the gallows and put to death”; s, d, and l2 read “hanged in the manner of robbers.”] By a remarkable judgment of God aroused against a sacrilegious man, he deserved so shameful an end, not at the hands of the king whom he opposed, but from those whose cause he seemed to favour. The authors of his death deserve to be raised by worthy praise, since they freed their country from so great a pest and justly condemned such an internal enemy.

## ON THE MEETING OF THE LEGATE, THE ARCHBISHOP, THE QUEEN, AND ROBERT EARL OF GLOUCESTER, TO NEGOTIATE A TREATY OF PEACE BETWEEN THE KING AND THE EMPRESS

§ 37. In the same year, at Pentecost (26 May), the king remained in the Tower at London, with only the bishop of Séez present; the rest either disdained or feared to come. A little later, through the mediation of the legate, a conference [Col. 1420B] was appointed between the empress and the king, to see whether, by God’s inspiration, peace might be restored. They met near Bath: on the empress’s side her brother Robert and the rest of her adherents were sent; on the king’s side, the legate and the archbishop, together with the queen. But vainly [Note: d, e, and l2 read *inaniter*, “vainly”; s omits it.]—vainly, I say—they spent both words and time; peace remained unmade, and they departed.

Nor was the dispute between the two sides an equitable one. The empress, being more inclined to what was good, had declared that she did not fear ecclesiastical judgment; whereas the king’s party were especially unwilling to submit to it, because they could maintain dominion for their own advantage. [Note: e reads: “and the king especially avoided it, too ready to trust the counsels of those who desired nothing less than peace, because they could maintain dominion over him for their own advantage”; s, d, and l2 read: “and the king’s party were especially unwilling to submit to it, because they could maintain dominion for their own advantage.”]

In the following September [Note: e reads “the following”; s, d, and l2 read “finally.”] the legate, knowing that it especially concerned his office that peace should be reached, undertook the labour of a sea journey in order to restore it and hastened to sail to France. There, after extensive and anxious negotiation concerning peace in England with the king of France, Count Theobald, and many persons of religious order, he returned near the end [Col. 1420C] of November, [Note: “Near”: omitted in e1; retained in s, d, e2, and l2.] bringing salutary instructions for his country, if there were anyone to match words with deeds. And indeed the empress and the earl immediately agreed; [Note: e1 reads “agreed”; s, d, e2, and l2 read “assented.”] but the king delayed from day to day, and in the end utterly disappointed them. Then at last the legate kept himself within bounds, waiting, like the rest, to see the outcome of events. For what is the point of stretching one’s arms against a torrent, when it is the height of madness, as someone says, to gain only hatred from one’s labours?

[Note: “Prologue”: e and l2 place it after the end of §37 in Book II; but l2 begins Book III with the chapter which e calls the “Prologue.” S and some manuscripts continue Book II to the end of the work.]

## PROLOGUE TO BOOK THREE

[Col. 1421]

[Col. 1421A] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1141, [Note: e1 reads 1141; s, d, e2, and l2 read 1142.] I undertake to unravel the inextricable labyrinth of the events and affairs that occurred in England, lest through our negligence they remain unknown to posterity. For it is worth while to know the fickleness of Fortune and the mutability of the human condition [Note: e reads *humani*, “human”; s, d, and l2 omit it.], permitted—or commanded—by God alone. [Col. 1422A] Therefore, since modern people rightly and not moderately reproach our predecessors because after Bede they left no record either of themselves or of their own times, [Note: s, d, e2, and l2 read “any”; e1 omits it.] I, because I have proposed to remove this disgrace from us, ought to secure from readers a favourable grace, if they judge rightly. [Note: s, d, e1, and l2 read *gratiam*, “grace/favour”; e2 reads *gloriam*, “glory.”]

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1421]

## HOW THE KING CAME TO THE SIEGE OF LINCOLN

[Col. 1421B]

§ 38. Before Christmas (A.D. 1140, 25 December), King Stephen had peacefully withdrawn from the district of Lincoln, and had increased the honours of the earl of Chester and his brother. [Note: “Increased their honours”: Ranulf, earl of Chester, and his uterine brother William de Roumare, were sons of Lucy, countess of Lincoln.] This earl had long before, in King Henry’s time, married the daughter of the earl of Gloucester.

Meanwhile the burgesses [Note: e reads “burgesses”; s, d, and l2 read “citizens.”] of the city of Lincoln, wishing to secure great favour with the king, informed him through messengers, while he was staying in London, that both brothers were remaining unsuspecting in the castle of that city; that, expecting nothing less than the king’s arrival, they could easily be entrapped; and that they themselves would take care that the king acquired the castle as secretly as possible. He, gladly wishing to omit no opportunity of enlarging his power, hastened there. Thus the brothers were surrounded [Col. 1421C] and besieged during the very feast-days of the Lord’s Nativity.

This seemed unjust to many, because, as I have said, he had departed from them before the feast without any suspicion of ill will, nor had he, according to the custom of their ancestors, formally renounced his friendship with them—what they call *diffidiare*. The earl of Chester, however, although involved in double danger, nevertheless cleverly escaped the straits of the castle. I do not determine by what contrivance: whether by agreement with some of the besiegers, or because courage, once detected, is accustomed to seek—and often to find—counsel in many ways.

Accordingly, not content merely with his own liberation, but anxious for the safety of his brother and wife, whom he had left in the castle, [Col. 1422B] he turned his thoughts in every direction. The sounder course seemed to be to demand help from his father-in-law, although he had long offended his feelings for certain reasons, especially because he appeared faithful to neither side. He therefore sent messengers, pledging perpetual loyalty to the empress if, through regard for mercy rather than for any merit of his own, she would rescue from injury those who stood in the very jaws of capture.

## HOW ROBERT, EARL OF GLOUCESTER, WENT TO RELIEVE THE BESIEGED

§ 39. The earl of Gloucester did not turn a deaf ear, unable to endure the indignity of the affair. At the same time, weary of delay because a most illustrious national cause was being ravaged by the internecine plundering and slaughter of two men, he preferred, if God permitted, to bring the matter to its utmost [Col. 1422C] issue. He also hoped for divine favour in the undertaking, because the king had wronged his son-in-law though he was guilty of no fault, was besieging his daughter, and had made a fortress of the church of the Blessed Mother of God at Lincoln. How important ought these things to be in the mind of a prince? Would it not be better to die and fall gloriously than to endure such a signal affront?

Therefore, to avenge God and his sister, and at the same time to free his relatives, he exposed himself to danger. The supporters of his party eagerly accompanied him; most of them were disinherited men, whom grief for their lost possessions and conscious courage inflamed for war. [Col. 1423A] Yet throughout the whole route that stretches from Gloucester to Lincoln, he cleverly concealed his intention, keeping the entire army, save a very few, in suspense by various evasions.

## ON THE BATTLE OF THE EARL OF GLOUCESTER AND THE CAPTURE OF THE KING

§ 40. The decisive moment came on the very day of the Purification of the most blessed Mary (A.D. 1141, 2 February), at the river flowing between the two armies, called the Trent. Both from its source and from the inundation of rain it had become so great that it offered no fordable crossing whatsoever. Then, at last revealing his purpose to his son-in-law, who had met him with a strong force, and to the others whom he had led, he added that he had long set before himself this resolve: never, under any necessity whatever, to turn his back; if he did not conquer, he must either die or be taken captive.

Therefore, when all had filled him with good hope—marvellous to hear—he immediately crossed by swimming, with all his men, the swift river mentioned above, as he was about to enter the hazard of battle. So great was the earl’s zeal to put an end to evils [Note: “Evils”: omitted in e; retained in s, d, and l2.] that he preferred to try the utmost rather than see the kingdom’s calamity prolonged further.
