For the king too, with a great many earls and no feeble number of soldiers, had courageously offered battle after abandoning the siege.

At first the royalists attempted a preliminary exercise of battle, which they call a *justa* [joust], because they were skilled in that art. But when they saw that the men of the earl’s party, so to speak, fought not at a distance with lances but hand-to-hand with swords, and with hostile force and standards broke through the royal battle-line, all the earls, to a man, [Col. 1423C] resolved upon flight. Six earls had entered the battle with the king; [Note: c reads: “Six earls entered battle with the king; many barons”; s, d, and l2 read: “a few barons.”] many barons, of praiseworthy loyalty and courage, who judged that the king ought not to be abandoned even in this emergency, were captured.

The king himself, though courage did not fail him in defending himself, was at last attacked on every side by the soldiers of the earl of Gloucester and fell to the ground from the blow of a certain stone; but who dealt it is unknown. Thus, with all about him either captured or fled, he yielded for the time and submitted to captivity. The praiseworthy earl of Gloucester ordered the king to be kept alive and uninjured, [Note: e reads “preserved”; s and d read “kept”; l2 reads “reserved.”] and did not permit him even to be assailed with any insulting reproach. [Note: e1 reads “assailed”; e2 reads “provoked”; s, d, and l2 read “torn to pieces.”] The man whom he had angrily attacked when exalted on the throne, he now, calm—behold!—protected after his defeat; so that, moderating the impulses of anger and joy, he showed humanity to a kinsman and, in a captive, respected the dignity of the crown. But a great part of the common people of the burgesses of Lincoln [Note: e reads “the common people of the burgesses of Lincoln”; s, d, and l2 read “the common people of the citizens of Lincoln.”] was cut down, by the just wrath of the victors and with no regret from the defeated, because they themselves had been the origin and tinder of this evil.

## HOW THE KING WAS PRESENTED TO THE EMPRESS

§ 41. The king, according to the custom of that class [Col. 1424A] of men whom they call captives, was presented to the empress by her brother, the earl of Gloucester; afterwards he was taken to Bristol and at first kept there honourably, except for the freedom to go where he pleased. Later, however, because certain men openly and shamefully kept saying that it was not expedient for the earl to keep the king otherwise than they wished, and also because it was reported that he himself, more than once, either having deceived or softened his guards, had been found outside his prescribed custody, especially at night, he was bound with iron rings. [Note: “Indeed”: e reads *enim*; s, d, and l2 read *vero*, “however.”]

## HOW THE EMPRESS, THROUGH THE EFFORT OF THE EARL OF GLOUCESTER, WAS RECEIVED AT WINCHESTER BY THE LEGATE AND CERTAIN BISHOPS AND MAGNATES

§ 42. Meanwhile the empress and the earl sent messengers to the legate, her brother, asking him to receive her without delay into the Church and kingdom, as the daughter of King Henry and the one to whom all England and Normandy had sworn. The fourteenth day before the Kalends of March (16 February) of that year was the first Sunday of Lent. Thus, messengers mediating on both sides, the arrangement was made that they should meet for conference on the open plain of the fields outside Winchester.

They came together, therefore, on the third Sunday of Lent (2 March), a rainy and cloudy day, as though the fates portended the mournful uncertainty of the cause. The empress swore and pledged to the bishop that, if he received her as lady in [Note: s and d read “in”; e and l2 read “with.”] holy Church and maintained perpetual fidelity to her, all the greater affairs in England, especially grants of bishoprics and abbeys, would depend upon his will. [Col. 1424C] Robert, her brother, earl of Gloucester, and Brian Fitz-Count, lord of Wallingford, and Miles of Gloucester, later earl of Hereford, and certain others, swore and gave pledge with her and on her behalf.

Nor did the bishop hesitate to receive the empress as lady of England and to pledge with certain of his men that, so long as she did not break the agreement, he too would keep faith with her. On the following day, the fifth day before the Nones of March (3 March), she was received with an honourable procession in the cathedral church of Winchester, the bishop, who was also legate, leading her at his right hand, and Bernard, bishop of St Davids, at his left. Present also were Alexander, bishop of Lincoln; Robert, bishop of Hereford; Nigel, bishop of Ely; Robert, bishop of Bath; and the abbots Ingulf of Abingdon, Edward of Reading, Peter of Malmesbury, Gilbert of Gloucester, Roger of Tewkesbury, and some others.

A few days later Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, came to the empress at Wilton, [Note: e reads “Wilton”; some manuscripts wrongly read “Winchester.”] having been invited by the legate. He delayed making his oath of loyalty to his lady, judging it unworthy of his reputation and person to turn elsewhere without consulting the king. [Col. 1425A] Therefore he himself and most of the prelates, with some laymen, having been permitted to go and speak with the king and having honourably obtained leave to yield to the necessity of the time, accepted the legate’s judgment. [Note: e1 reads “accepted”; s, d, e2, and l2 read “yielded.”] The empress spent Easter, which that year fell on the third day before the Kalends of April (30 March), at Oxford; the others departed to their own places.

## HOW THEY CONFIRMED THE EMPRESS AS LADY OF ENGLAND IN A SOLEMN COUNCIL

§ 43. On Monday after the octave of Easter (7 April), a council of Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, all the bishops of England, and many abbots, with the legate presiding, began at Winchester with great ceremony. Those absent sent representatives and letters stating why they had not come. [Note: In e2, from “Of this council” through “obstacles to his legation,” §70, the text is defective.] Since I attended the proceedings of this council, [Col. 1425B] I shall not deny posterity the whole truth of the matter.

For I distinctly remember that on that day, after letters of excuse had been read by which some justified their absence, the legate called the bishops aside and held a private consultation with them; then [Note: “Then”: omitted in s, d, and l2.] immediately summoned the abbots; finally, the archdeacons. Nothing from the deliberation came out into public; nevertheless, what was to be done was turning over in everyone’s thoughts and upon everyone’s lips.

## HOW THE LEGATE COMMENDED THE EMPRESS’S DUE AND LAWFUL SUCCESSION TO THE KINGDOM

§ 44. On Tuesday (8 April), the legate’s speech ran approximately as follows:

“By the favour of the pope, I hold his place in England; and therefore, by his authority, I have assembled the clergy [Col. 1425C] of England to this council, in order that counsel might publicly be taken concerning the peace of the country, which was being shipwrecked in great danger. In the time of King Henry, my uncle, England was a singular dwelling-place of peace. Through the vigour, courage, and diligence of that most excellent man, not only did natives, of whatever power or rank, dare to disturb nothing, but even all neighbouring kings and princes, following his example, themselves embraced tranquillity and either invited or compelled [Note: e reads “compelled”; s, d, and l2 read “urged.”] their subjects to do so.

“That king, a few years before his death, caused all bishops and barons alike to swear the whole kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy to his daughter, once an empress—his only surviving child by a wife once betrothed to him—if he should lack a male successor by the wife whom he had taken from Lorraine. And cruel Fortune, he says, begrudged my most excellent uncle such that he died in Normandy without a male heir. Therefore, because it seemed too long to wait for the lady, who contrived delays in coming to England—for she remained in Normandy—provision was made for the peace of the country, and [Col. 1426A] my brother was permitted to reign.

“Yet although I gave myself as surety between him and God that he would honour and exalt holy Church, maintain good laws, and abolish bad ones, I am ashamed to remember, embarrassed to tell, what manner of man he showed himself in the kingdom: how no justice was exercised against offenders; [Note: e reads “exercised”; s, d, and l2 read “administered.”] how all peace was almost immediately abolished in that very year; bishops captured and compelled to surrender their possessions; abbeys sold; churches stripped of their treasures; the counsels of wicked men heard, those of good men either deferred or wholly despised. You know how often I have approached him, both personally and through the bishops, especially in the council convened for this purpose in the aforesaid year, [Note: e reads “aforesaid”; s, d, and l2 read “previous.”] and have gained nothing but hatred.

“Nor is it hidden from anyone who wishes to weigh the matter rightly that I ought to love my mortal brother, but must esteem the cause of the immortal Father far more highly. Therefore, since God has exercised His judgment upon my brother, permitting him, without my knowledge, to fall into the power of powerful men, I have invited all of you to meet here by right of my legation, lest the kingdom, deprived of a ruler, should totter. Yesterday the case was examined in secret before the greater part of the clergy of England, to whose right [Note: s and d omit “right”; e has “and examination” in the margin.] it chiefly belongs both to choose and to ordain a ruler. Therefore, having first, as is fitting, invoked the Godhead for help, we choose as lady of England and Normandy the daughter of a peaceful king, a glorious king, a rich king, a good king, and in our time an incomparable king; and we promise her faith and support.”

## HOW THE LONDONERS APPEARED IN THE COUNCIL

[Col. 1426C]

§ 45. When all present had either moderately acclaimed the decision or had not objected in silence, the legate added: [Note: “The legate”: omitted in s, d, and l2.]

“We have summoned by our messengers the Londoners, who, because of the greatness of their city, are as it were the leading men in England; we have sent them safe-conduct to come securely, and I trust that they will not delay beyond this day. With your kind permission, let us wait until tomorrow.”

§ 46. On Wednesday (9 April), the Londoners came and, having been introduced into the council, made their case thus far: they said that they had been sent by the commune, as they call it, of the Londoners, not to offer conflicts but prayers, [Note: e reads “offer”; s, d, and l2 read “bring.”] that their lord the king might be released from captivity. This, they said, all the barons who had long been admitted into their commune earnestly demanded from the lord legate, the archbishop, and all the clergy present.

The legate gave them a copious and splendid reply, and repeated the same speech delivered the previous day to explain why their request should not be granted. He added also: “It is not fitting that the Londoners, who are regarded in England as pre-eminent like magnates, should support the party of those who abandoned their lord [Col. 1427A] in battle, by whose counsel he had dishonoured holy Church, and who, finally, appeared to favour the Londoners themselves for no other reason than to squeeze money from them.”

## ON THE QUEEN’S CLERK

§ 47. Meanwhile a certain man arose, named, if I remember rightly, Christian, a clerk of the queen, as I heard. He handed a document to the legate. After reading it silently, the legate said in as loud a voice as he could that it was not lawful, nor [Note: e reads “nor”; s, d, and l2 read *ne quae*, “nor that it.”] ought it to be read in so great an assembly, especially of persons eminent and religious. For among other matters written there which were blameworthy and notable, there was introduced as a witness one who, in the preceding year, in the very chapter-house where they were then sitting, had inflicted the gravest insult of words upon the venerable bishops. [Col. 1427B]

Thus, while he equivocated, the clerk did not fail in his legation but confidently read the letter aloud; its substance was this: “The queen earnestly begged all the assembled clergy, and particularly the bishop of Winchester, brother of her lord, to restore that same lord to the kingdom—the lord whom wicked men, though they too were his own men, had cast into chains.” To this submission the legate replied in the same terms as he had answered the Londoners.

After consulting together, they said that they would report the council’s decree to their fellow citizens and would extend their support as far as they could. On Thursday (10 April), the council was dissolved, after many who supported the royal party had first been excommunicated—especially William Martel, formerly butler of King Henry and then steward of Stephen. This man had grievously embittered the legate’s mind by intercepting and carrying off many of his possessions.

## HOW THE EMPRESS WAS RECEIVED BY THE LONDONERS

§ 48. Thus it was a very difficult task to win over the minds of the Londoners, so that, although these things had been done immediately [Col. 1427C] after Easter, as I have said, they scarcely received the empress until a few days before the Nativity of Saint John. At that time the greater part of England looked expectantly to her rule. [Note: e1 reads “accepted her rule”; s and d read “graciously accepted her rule”; l2 reads the same, with *dignanter* repeated.] Her brother Robert was constantly at her side, raising her glory in every fitting way: kindly addressing the magnates, making many promises, intimidating various factions, or through intermediaries urging them to peace; and now, with all regions favouring the empress, restoring justice, the laws of the country, and peace.

It is sufficiently clear that if her followers had trusted her moderation and wisdom, they would not afterwards have experienced so adverse a turn of Fortune’s dice. The lord legate too was at hand, as it seemed, diligently and faithfully attending to the empress’s interests. But behold: while she was thought immediately able to take possession of all England, everything changed. The Londoners, always suspect and inwardly raging, then burst into open expressions of hatred; they even, it is said, laid plots against their lady and her companions. [Col. 1428A] When these had been discovered beforehand and avoided, the empress and her party gradually withdrew from the city without disturbance, in a certain military order.

The legate accompanied the empress, as did David, king of Scots, uncle of that same woman of masculine spirit, and her brother Robert—always, as then, the companion of his sister’s fortunes—and, to speak briefly, every one of her supporters; all escaped unharmed. Once the Londoners learned of their departure, they rushed into the lodgings, stripping away whatever property had been left behind in the haste.

## ON THE DISCORD BETWEEN THE EMPRESS AND THE LEGATE
§ 49. Not many days later, a quarrel arose between the legate and the empress—a development which I can truly call the seed-bed of all the evils that again befell England. How it came about, I shall explain. King Stephen had a son, named Eustace, born of the daughter of Eustace, Count of Boulogne. For King Henry, the empress’s father—to go back further, lest the truth of events be hidden from posterity—had given in marriage to the aforesaid count his wife’s sister, the mother of this lady, named Mary, because he was of illustrious ancestry and likewise distinguished for prudence and courage. By Mary, Eustace had no children except a daughter called Matilda. When her father had died, the same most magnificent king gave this marriageable woman in lawful marriage to his nephew Stephen, and at the same time industriously acquired for him the county of Boulogne; for previously he had given him Mortain in Normandy from his own holdings.

The legate had intended that these counties should be granted by right to his nephew Eustace, whom I have named, while his father was held captive; but the empress utterly refused, perhaps also promising them to others. Offended by this wrong, he kept away from her court for many days; and although he was often recalled, he persisted in refusing. Meanwhile, at Guildford he held a private conference with the queen, his brother’s wife; overcome by her tears and satisfaction, he turned his mind toward freeing his brother. He also absolved, without consulting the bishops, all those of that party whom he had excommunicated in the council. Complaints against him concerning the empress were circulated throughout England: that she had wished to seize him; that she had regarded as nothing whatever she had sworn to him; that all the barons of England had fulfilled their pledged faith toward her, but that she had broken hers, since she did not know how to use her acquisitions with moderation.

### How the Count of Gloucester Met the Legate with the Empress and Her Supporters

§ 50. To settle these disturbances, if possible, the Count of Gloucester made for Winchester with a not especially large retinue; but, accomplishing nothing, he returned to Oxford, where his sister had for some time remained in fixed residence. She therefore, from what she continually heard and what she then learned from her brother, understood that the legate was contemplating nothing conciliatory toward her party, and came to Winchester with as great an array as she could muster.

There she was immediately received within the royal castle. Perhaps with good intentions, she approached the bishop through messengers, asking that, since she herself was present, he would not be reluctant to come to her. He, thinking that it would not be safe for him to come, evaded the messengers with an ambiguous answer, saying only: “I shall make myself ready”; and at once he sent for everyone whom he knew would support the king. Almost all the earls of England accordingly came. They were young and frivolous men, preferring the excursions of riding to peace. Moreover, many of them, ashamed because they had deserted the king in battle, as was said above, tried in that gathering to soften the reproach of their flight.

Few had come with the empress: David, King of Scots; Robert, Count of Gloucester; Miles of Hereford; and a few barons. Ranulf, Count of Chester, arrived late and to no purpose. To state the long course of events in brief: the queen and the earls who had come kept watch over all the roads outside the walls of Winchester, lest provisions be brought to the empress’s faithful followers; and the village of Andover was also burned. Thus necessities were brought in scantily and by narrow routes from the west, some travellers being intercepted, killed, or mutilated in part of their limbs. From the east, however, every path toward London was crowded with a multitude of supplies to be brought in for the bishop and his followers—by Geoffrey de Mandeville, who had again turned to their aid, though after the king’s capture he had previously sworn fidelity to the empress; and with the energetic support of the Londoners, who omitted absolutely nothing within their power by which they might distress the empress.

The people of Winchester, however, favoured her in their silent judgment, remembering the faith they had pledged to her when they had been driven to it almost against their will by the bishop. Meanwhile, fire shot from the bishop’s tower caught the houses of the burgesses—who, as I have said, were more inclined toward the empress’s success than the bishop’s—and burned the entire abbey of nuns within the city, together with the monastery called Hyde outside it. There was there an image of the crucified Lord, large in its mass of gold, silver, and gems, fashioned with painstaking devotion from the gift of Cnut, once king. This image, caught by the fire and cast to the ground, was afterward stripped of its covering by order of the legate. More than five hundred marks of silver and thirty of gold were found; they served as a bounty for the soldiers. The abbey of nuns at Wherwell was also burned by one William of Ypres, an impious man, who observed reverence neither toward God nor toward men, because supporters of the empress had taken refuge there.

### On the Departure of the Count of Gloucester from Winchester and His Capture

§ 51. Meanwhile the Count of Gloucester, although he and his men were harassed daily by the royalists’ fighting, and matters turned out less as he had hoped, nevertheless always thought that churches ought to be spared from burning, although he was lodged near St Swithun’s. Yet, unable to bear the indignity any longer—seeing himself and his followers nearly besieged and fortune inclining to the other side—he judged that he must yield to circumstances and prepared his departure with his ranks drawn up.

Accordingly, he sent his sister ahead in the first division with the rest, so that she might depart freely; he himself proceeded slowly with a few men who had the courage not to fear many. Therefore, when the royal earls immediately pursued him, he was captured, since he judged both flight shameful and beneath his dignity, and was especially attacked by all, being alone. The others continued their begun journey—especially the nobles—and reached Devizes with the greatest haste.

Thus they departed from Winchester on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, 14 September, which that year fell on a Sunday, having arrived there a few days before the Assumption of the Blessed Mother of God. It became an example of something like a miracle and the subject of much talk in England that, just as the king on a Sunday at the Purification of Our Lady, so the count on a Sunday at the Exaltation of the life-giving Cross, experienced one and the same fate.

It was indeed especially celebrated and splendid that no one, because of this event, saw the Count of Gloucester broken in spirit or even sad in expression. So strongly did he breathe the consciousness of lofty nobility, lest he subject himself to fortune’s mockery. Although he was first invited by blandishments and afterward assailed with threats, he was never induced to allow negotiations for his release apart from his sister’s consent. At last the matter was arranged so that both the king and he were released on equal terms, with no other agreement intervening except that each should defend his own party to the best of his ability, as before.

These matters were repeatedly discussed at great length from the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until the feast of All Saints, and were then finally brought to their proper conclusion; for on that day the king escaped captivity. At Bristol he left his queen and son with two magnates as hostages for the count’s release, and immediately the king came by hurried journey to Winchester, where the count was held, having been brought back from Rochester, to which he had first been taken. On the third day, as soon as the king came to Winchester, the count departed, leaving there his son William as hostage until the queen should be released. Having quickly traversed the road, he came to Bristol and released the queen; upon her return, William, the count’s son, was released from hostage status.

It is sufficiently well known that throughout the time of his captivity, and in the months following until Christmas, he was solicited by many great promises to desert his sister, but always valued the duty of kinship above any promises whatsoever. For, leaving his own estates and castles, from which he could comfortably have profited, he remained assiduously with his sister at Oxford, where, as I said before, she had established her seat and held her court.

### On the Council in Which the Legate Tried to Mitigate the Matter of Receiving the Empress as Lady

§ 52. Meanwhile the legate, a bishop of immoderate spirit, who wished never to leave unaccomplished what he had once undertaken, convened by the authority of his legateship a council at Westminster on the octave of St Andrew, 7 December. I do not report the proceedings of this council with the same exact reliability as those of the earlier council, because I was not present.

It was heard that letters from the apostolic lord were read there, in which he gently rebuked the legate for having neglected to free his brother. Nevertheless, he granted forgiveness for the earlier offence and earnestly urged him to devote himself, by whatever means he could, ecclesiastical or secular, to his brother’s release. The king himself entered the council and laid before the holy assembly his complaint that his own men had both seized him and almost destroyed him through humiliating afflictions, although he had never denied them justice.

The legate himself tried, with great powers of eloquence, to lessen the odium of his actions:

> “He had received the empress not by choice but by necessity, since, while the disaster of his brother was still recent—all the earls either scattered in flight or awaiting the outcome with anxious minds—she and her followers had surrounded the walls of Winchester with their clamour. She had obstinately violated everything that she had promised concerning the rights of churches. Indeed, trustworthy authorities had reported to him that she and her followers had laid plots not only against his dignity but also against his life. But God, in His mercy, had turned events otherwise than she had hoped, so that he himself might avoid destruction and free his brother from chains. Therefore, on God’s behalf and that of the Apostolic See, he commanded them to assist with all their strength King Stephen, anointed by the will of the people and the assent of the Apostolic See; while disturbers of the peace who favoured the Countess of Anjou were to be called to excommunication—except her who was lady of the Angevins.”

### How a Supporter of the Empress Spoke for the Empress

§ 53. I do not say that all received these words with goodwill; certainly no one challenged them. All the clergy restrained their tongues either from fear or from reverence. There was one layman, the empress’s messenger, who publicly forbade the legate, by the faith he had pledged her, to decree anything in that council that would be contrary to her honour. The legate had pledged the empress that he would give no aid whatever to his brother, except perhaps that he might send him twenty soldiers, and no more. Her coming into England had occurred at his repeated invitation by letters; her capture of the king and his continued captivity had been accomplished above all with his connivance.

The messenger said these things and many others with great severity of speech, offering the legate no flattery whatever. Nor could the legate be moved by any force of words to reveal anger, being, as I said before, no sluggish executor of what he had once undertaken. Thus this year, whose tragedies I have summarized, was fateful and almost ruinous for England. When England thought that it had somehow been allowed to breathe toward freedom, it fell again into misery; and unless God’s mercy speedily intervenes, it will remain there long.

### Recapitulation Concerning the Count of Gloucester

§ 54. I have resolved to repair in mind the beginnings of the events of this year, 1143 from the Lord’s Incarnation, which followed from the remainder of the preceding year; and at the same time to submit to the reader’s judgment, by way of recapitulation, a summary gathered, as it were, into one bundle, of the matters said here and there concerning Robert, son of King Henry and Count of Gloucester.

For just as he first undertook the task of justly defending his sister’s cause, so he always persevered in that undertaking with unconquered spirit, freely. I say “freely” because some of her supporters either follow fortune and change with its instability, or, having already obtained many advantages, fight for justice in hope of still greater rewards. Robert alone, or almost alone, was never bent to either side, neither by hope of gain nor by fear of loss, as will become clear from what follows. Therefore, if I write these things fully, let no suspicion of flattery steal into anyone’s mind; for I shall grant no favour, but will set forth to posterity only the truth of history, without any colouring of falsehood.

§ 55. It has been said concerning the count how, first of all after David, King of Scots, in the presence of his father Henry, he confirmed by oath his loyalty to his sister the empress concerning the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy. There was, as I said, some dispute between him and Stephen, then Count of Boulogne and afterward King of England, as to which should swear first: Robert asserting the precedence of a son, Stephen the dignity of a nephew.

[Note: The manuscript reading is “first of all primates”; nevertheless Malmesbury previously reported that Stephen swore allegiance to Matilda before Robert did.]

§ 56. It has also been said how reasonable causes kept him in Normandy from December, when his father died, until after the following Easter, so that he did not immediately come into England to avenge his sister’s wrongs. Finally, when he came, it has been said with what prudent deliberation and on what terms he submitted to homage to the king, and how justly he rejected that allegiance in the following year and thereafter.

§ 57. Nor has his second arrival in England from Normandy with his sister after his father’s death been omitted: he plunged into England as into a kind of forest of roaring beasts, relying indeed on God’s grace and on confidence of spirit, but accompanied by scarcely one hundred and forty knights. Nor has it been left unsaid that, amid so great a disturbance of wars, when anxious watches were displayed everywhere, he came boldly to Bristol with only twelve knights, while his sister was meanwhile entrusted, as she thought, to faithful protection at Arundel.

With what prudence he then received his sister from the midst of her enemies and afterward advanced her cause by every means in his power; always remaining about her, procuring her interests and postponing his own, while certain men, abusing his absence, harassed his lands on every side. Finally, constrained by necessity to rescue from danger his son-in-law, whom the king had shut in, he entered upon a serious war and captured the king. But his own capture at Winchester, as I briefly related among the events of the preceding year, almost ruined that happy outcome. Yet by that captivity, through God’s grace, he showed himself not so much pitiable as praiseworthy. For when he saw the royal earls so determined to pursue that the matter could not be managed without loss to his own followers, he sent ahead all those for whom he feared, and especially the empress. When they had passed beyond and could now escape safely, he rode slowly himself, lest the departure seem like flight, and allowed himself to fall into the hands of his pursuers, purchasing his friends’ freedom at the cost of his own hindrance.

In captivity itself, moreover, no one, as I said before, perceived him cast down in spirit or heard him humble in speech. He seemed so far above fortune that he inspired his pursuers—for I do not wish to call them enemies—to respect him. Thus the queen, although she remembered that her husband had been put in chains by his order, never allowed any bonds to be imposed upon him, nor presumed anything dishonourable against his dignity. In short, at Rochester, whither he was taken, he freely went, as he wished, to the churches within the castle and spoke with whomever he wished, provided only that the queen herself was present. After her departure, however, he was taken to the tower under free custody, with a mind so present and secure that, using money received from his men in Kent, he bought horses of no small value, which later proved both useful and advantageous to him.

### On the Release of the King

§ 58. At first the earls, and those whose business it was to speak of such matters, tried to see whether he would allow the king and himself to be released on equal terms. Although Countess Mabel, out of longing for her beloved husband, immediately embraced this proposal when messengers brought it to her, being inclined by marital affection toward his release, he opposed it with more profound counsel, asserting that the king and the count were not of equal weight. But if they allowed all those who had been captured either with him or on his account to be released, he could accept it.

The earls and the others of the royal party would not agree. They wanted the king released, but without losses to themselves in money. For Gilbert, the earl, had captured William of Salisbury; William of Ypres, Humphrey de Bohun; and several others whom they could seize at Winchester, greedily desiring many marks for their ransom.

### How It Was Attempted to Bend the Count of Gloucester to the King’s Party

§ 59. They therefore approached the count by another route, wishing, if possible, to entice him with enormous promises. Let him abandon his sister and join the king’s party: in return, he would possess dominion over the whole land, so that everything would depend upon his decision; he would rank below the king only in the crown, while ruling all others according to his will.

The count rejected these immense promises with a memorable reply which I want posterity to hear and admire:

> “I am not my own master, but subject to another’s authority. When I see myself to be in my own power, I answer that I shall do whatever reason dictates concerning the matter you put forward.”

§ 60. Then they became more excited and somewhat angered. Since they made no progress through blandishments, they began to threaten that they would send him overseas to Boulogne, to be bound in perpetual chains until death. But he calmly dismissed their threats, steadfastly and truthfully declaring that he feared nothing less. For he trusted in the greatness of spirit of the countess, namely his wife, and in the courage of his followers, who would immediately send the king to Ireland if they heard that anything improper had been done to the count.

§ 61. A month passed amid these matters, so difficult was it to free princes whom fortune had bound in its chain. At length, after consultation, all who favoured the empress repeatedly sent envoys to the count, saying that, since he could not do what he wished, he should, in the comic poet’s phrase, “wish what he can.” Therefore he should allow the king and himself to be released on reciprocal terms.

> “Otherwise,” they said, “we fear that the earls, emboldened by the consciousness of their greatest and most glorious deed—capturing you—will attack us one by one, storm castles, and besiege your very sister.”

§ 62. At last Robert relented and agreed to the legate and the archbishop, but on the condition that no castles or lands should be restored which, after the king’s capture, had passed into the right of the empress or of any of her faithful followers. He could by no means obtain that his own men should be released with him, since the others were offended that he had rejected, with a kind of proud disdain, their great promises of supremacy over the whole realm.

Because they were especially striving that, owing to royal dignity, the king should be released first and the count afterward, and because he hesitated to grant this, the legate and archbishop confirmed by oath that, if the king after his own release refused to release the count, they themselves would without delay place themselves in the count’s captivity, to be taken wherever he pleased.

§ 63. Nor did he rest even then, but his shrewd mind found a further means of providing for himself. It might happen that the king, led astray by evil counsel—as often occurs—would count his brother’s and the archbishop’s captivity as little, provided he himself lay free upon a feather bed. Therefore he required from each separately letters and seals addressed to the apostolic lord, to this effect:

> “Let the apostolic lord know that, for the king’s release and the peace of the kingdom, they have bound themselves to the count by this agreement: if the king, after his own release, neglected to release him, they would voluntarily submit themselves to his captivity. Therefore, should this misfortune occur, they earnestly request—as apostolic humanity would spontaneously do—that he free both those who were his suffragans and the count as well from unlawful bonds.”

And other such matters.

§ 64. Robert received these writings from both bishops and deposited them in a safe place. He came to Winchester with them and with a great multitude of barons. The king likewise, as was said above, came there not long afterward and held a private conference with the count. Yet although the king himself and all the princes present strove with great effort to bring the count over to their wishes, he resisted like an unmoved rock in the sea, rendering all their efforts either fruitless or restraining them by reason:

> “It was neither reasonable nor humane,” he said, “to abandon his sister, whose cause he had undertaken to defend justly; not for the sake of any advantage, nor so much from hatred of the king as from regard for his oath, which they too ought to recognize as unlawful to violate—especially since he remembered that the apostolic lord had instructed him to render obedience to the oath which he had made to his sister in his father’s presence.”

Thus both departed without peace.

§ 65. I did not insert these things in this manner among the events of the preceding year because they had been unknown to me. For I have always considered it dreadful to commit to writing for transmission to posterity anything which I did not know rested on solid truth. What must be said concerning the present year will have this beginning.

### Negotiations for Sending for the Count of Anjou

§ 66. Both parties, that of the empress and that of the king, conducted themselves with peaceful restraint from Christmas until Lent, studying more to preserve their own positions than to attack those of others. The king went away into the upper regions, to arrange I know not what. Lent arrived and proclaimed a cessation of all wars. In its midst the empress came with her followers to Devizes, intending there to hold a secret council with her own men. Yet this much became public: all her supporters agreed that messengers should be sent for the Count of Anjou, who ought lawfully to defend in England the inheritance of his wife and sons. Distinguished men were therefore sent, men worthy of undertaking the care of so great a matter.

### On the King’s Illness

§ 67. Not long afterward, during the Easter festival, the king, contemplating, as they say, certain harsh measures, was detained at Northampton by a grave illness, so that through almost all England he was proclaimed as though dead. His unfavourable condition lasted until after Pentecost; then strength gradually restored by health raised him to his feet.

§ 68. Meanwhile the envoys returned from Anjou. At a council again assembled at Devizes during the octave of Pentecost, they reported what they had heard to the empress and the nobles:

> “The Count of Anjou is in some measure favourable to the embassies of the magnates; but of all men he knows only the Count of Gloucester, whose prudence, loyalty, greatness of spirit, and energy he has long since found tried and tested. If this man crosses the sea and comes to him, he will not fail to do what he can in accordance with his wishes. Otherwise, the others will consume their labour uselessly in going and returning.”

### How the Count of Gloucester Went to the Count of Anjou

§ 69. Thus the hopes of all who heard were raised, and their entreaties turned toward the count, that he would deem this labour worthy for the inheritance of his sister and nephews. At first he evaded the request, representing the difficulty of the undertaking: the journey across and beyond the sea was dangerous amid swarming enemies; and it endangered his sister, whom others would scarcely protect in his absence—men who had nearly abandoned her during his captivity because they despaired of their own affairs.

Finally yielding to everyone’s unanimous wish, he required separately from those who appeared to be the chief men hostages to be taken with him to Normandy, who would guarantee both to the Count of Anjou and to the empress that all would, with shields joined, ward off injuries from her while he was absent, remaining in turn at Oxford. The proposal was acclaimed, and hostages were given to be taken to Normandy.

### How the Count of Anjou, with the Count of Gloucester’s Aid, Took Ten Castles in Normandy

§ 70. Robert therefore bade farewell to his sister and, taking the hostages with him, set out with picked soldiers by safe quarters for Ware, a town and castle which he had long before entrusted to his eldest son William. There, some time after the feast of St John, entrusting himself boldly to God’s grace, he set sail in the ships which he then had.

When they had been carried almost into the middle of the sea, a storm arose and scattered all but two in different directions: some turned back, others were driven beyond their destination. Only two, one of them carrying the count with his most faithful followers, held their proper course and reached a suitable harbour. Arriving at Caen, he summoned the Count of Anjou by messengers. The latter came without disdain, but raised numerous obstacles to the matter proposed in the embassy. Among them was the fact that rebellion by many castles in Normandy prevented him from coming to England.

This delayed the Count of Gloucester’s return beyond what had been intended. In order to deprive the Angevin of every excuse, he captured ten castles in Normandy with him: Tenerchebrai, Serthilaret, Brichesart, Alani (variant: Alnai), Bastonborg, Triveres, Castel de Vira, Plaiseiz, Vilers, and Moretoin. Yet this exertion advanced the embassy almost not at all. The Count of Anjou, when the earlier pretexts had been removed, supplied other excuses for excusing his arrival in England.

As a great favour, however, he permitted his eldest son by the empress to be taken by his uncle into England, so that, at the sight of him, the magnates might be encouraged to champion the cause of the rightful heir. The boy is called Henry, bearing his grandfather’s name; would that he may someday bear also his happiness and power.

### How the King Took Ware during the Count’s Absence

§ 71. Meanwhile the king in England, seizing the opportunity of the count’s absence, suddenly came to Ware and, finding it not well defended by defenders, burned and plundered the town and at once gained possession of the castle. Not content with this—for he saw fortune favouring him—three days before the feast of St Michael he unexpectedly burned the city of Oxford and besieged the castle, in which the empress was with her household knights. His resolve was so firm that he declared he would not withdraw for hope of any advantage or fear of any loss unless the castle were surrendered and the empress brought under his control.

Therefore all the empress’s chief men, ashamed because they had been away from their lady contrary to the arrangement, gathered in close formations at Wallingford, intending to attack the king in battle if he wished to try the fortunes of war in open country. But they did not plan to attack him within the city, which the Count of Gloucester had fortified so with ditches that it appeared impregnable except by fire.

### On the Count of Gloucester’s Return to England

§ 72. When these reports were spread abroad in England, Robert, Count of Gloucester, hastened his return. He embarked three hundred and somewhat more soldiers in fifty-two ships, though their total number did not reach four hundred; to these he added two ships which he captured while returning at sea. God notably favoured his pious intention through His grace: none of so great a number of ships wandered far away, but all, either sailing alongside one another or proceeding gently one before another, furrowed calm seas. Nor did the violence of the waves assail the vessels; rather, the sea seemed to attend them in service, as the sight of the sea is most delightful when the wave, breaking in gentle movements, plays upon the shores.

Carried therefore into the harbour of Ware, the ships restored the count and all his companions, happy in the longings of their own people.

### How the Count of Gloucester, on His Return, Took Ware

§ 73. At first he had intended to land at Southampton, in order to avenge his wrongs at the cost both of the burgesses and of their lord. But the men called Vituli turned his purpose aside with many prayers, fearing that their relatives, bound to them by the closest ties, who lived at Southampton, would be involved in the sufferings of the others. The Vituli are a class of seafaring people. Since they were the count’s faithful retainers, he judged that their prayers should not be disregarded and abandoned his undertaking. At the same time, it seemed more honourable to return to the place from which he had departed and recover by force what he had lost through force.

As soon as he had brought the harbour and town under his power, he besieged the castle. The protection of the select knights whom the king had placed there had strengthened their courage—rather, I should say, their obstinacy. But soon the soldiers, weakened and terrified by the count’s siege-engines, requested a truce so that, as is the custom of such men, they might demand aid from the king, appointing a day on which, if he refused to come, they would surrender the castle.

This was most welcome to the count, in the hope of drawing the king away from the siege of his sister, although he was held by an impatient desire to possess the castle. With what confidence of spirit, we may suppose, did he boldly await the king with only three hundred and somewhat more knights, still supported by no aid from England, though the king was said to have a thousand knights and more! For many had flocked to the siege not so much from hatred for the empress as from greed for plunder.

### How the Count of Gloucester, Having Gathered an Army, Marched to Free the Empress

§ 74. Nevertheless, when it was reported that aid was being denied by the king to those besieged at Ware [Col. 1440A], he captured that castle with the same obstinacy of which I have spoken before; and with the same onset he subdued the island of Portland, which they had fortified with a castle; and likewise a third place, named Lulworth, which had belonged to William of Glastonbury, a certain chamberlain, who had recently defected from allegiance to the empress. [Note: [Col. 1439B] “Which … had defected.” e.: “he subdued [it] by arms,” s. c. d. k. l 2.] He then summoned all supporters of the empress to Cirencester, with Advent now begun. [Note: [Col. 1439B] “Advent.” e.: “the Lord’s Advent,” s. d. l 2.] There, united with all their strength to aid their lady, [Note: [Col. 1439B] “Their.” Omitted in s. d.] they planned an expedition to Oxford, intending, unless the king withdrew, to fight him with hostile purpose. [Note: [Col. 1439B] “To fight.” s. d. l 2: “that he would fight,” e.] But when they had already set out, welcome news was brought that the empress had escaped from the besieged castle of Oxford and was safely staying at 769 Wallingford [Col. 1440B]. Turning aside thither, therefore, by the counsel of that same lady of theirs, [Note: [Col. 1439B] “Their.” Omitted in s. d. l 2.] and judging that they should abstain from war, because the soldiers who had remained when she departed had surrendered the castle and gone away unharmed, and because the holy days urged them to rest, if only a little, each returned to his own home. [Note: [Col. 1439B] “Returned.” The third book ends here in e.; the other manuscripts carry the work through to its end without interruption.]

§ 75. I would gladly set down the manner of the empress’s deliverance, if I had ascertained it with certainty. For it is plainly a miracle of God. This at least is certain: out of fear of the approaching count, [Note: [Col. 1439B] “Approaching.” e.: “arriving,” s. d. l 2.] when very many of the besiegers at Oxford had scattered wherever each could, those remaining kept less strict guards and more relaxed watches, being more concerned for their own safety, should battle come, than eager for the destruction of others.

[Note: [Col. 1439B] “But these matters will, God willing, be explained more fully in the following volume.” e 1, e 2. Here the paragraph seems first to have ended with “if ever … I receive”; in that manuscript the words now following, “eager for the destruction of others,” are written partly over an erasure in a later hand; and the sentence “But these matters … will be explained” has been attached after “I receive.” s. c. d. g. k. 12 read: “When this had been noticed by the townspeople, the empress, leaving by a postern with only four knights, crossed the river. Soon afterwards—as necessity sometimes, indeed almost always, both devises a remedy and supplies courage—she set out on foot for Abingdon, and from there was conveyed on horseback to Wallingford. Yet I am minded to pursue these matters more fully, if ever, by God’s gift, I receive the truth from those who were present.”]

But these matters will, God willing, be explained more fully in the following volume.

[Col. 1441]

# WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY’S FIVE BOOKS ON THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

(The first four books were edited by Savile, *Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores post Bedam praecipui*, London, 1596, folio, p. 111; the fifth, or *Life of Aldhelm, Bishop of Sherborne*, by Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, II, 1.)

## PROLOGUE TO THE FIRST BOOK

[Col. 1441A] The first episcopal see after the conversion of the English was, and remains, at Canterbury. This is a city of England neither especially large nor meanly small; by its situation—for it lies beside a most fertile soil—and by the unbroken circuit of its walls, though it has often experienced the fortunes of Mars, it shelters its citizens. Rich in the ashes of many saints and glorious in their patronage, it lacks neither the watering of a river nor the convenience of woods; moreover, being twelve miles from the sea, it abounds in fish. Its urban and rural people, more than the other English, still breathe an awareness of ancient nobility; they are readier both to show honour and hospitality to every person, and keener to repel injuries. There is the first see of the archbishop, who is primate and patriarch of all England.

[Col. 1441B] But where the archbishopric stood in the time of the Britons is uncertain, because antiquity has consumed the memory of our age. I have resolved to speak, so far as it has come to my knowledge, of the archbishops of this city and its suffragans. Nor do I think it inconsistent with reason that, having once briefly treated the deeds of the kings of the English, I should now run through the names of the English bishops, so that at last, with the Lord’s help, I may complete the work promised long ago. When I have done this, I shall seem to myself to have completed a task attempted by no one else—not trusting in my own talent, but drawn by zeal for worthy knowledge. For what is sweeter than to recount the favour of one’s ancestors, so that you may know the deeds of those from whom you have received both the first elements of faith [Col. 1442A] and incentives to live well? Certainly it would be full of sloth and disgrace not even to know the names of the leading men of our own province, while our knowledge extends elsewhere even to the regions of India and to whatever lies beyond, spread out over the boundless Ocean.

Moved by these considerations, here and elsewhere I have carried my pen through histories full of obscurity; although I do not here possess the same abundance of information as in the deeds of the kings. There, indeed, borrowing something from the chronicles before me, I was guided—as from a lofty watchtower by a shining torch—so that I might direct my course without error. Here, deprived of almost every aid, I grope amid the thick darkness of ignorance and, with no lamp of history leading the way, make out my path. Yet, as I hope, the light of minds will be present, [Col. 1442B] so that truth may not falter in its integrity and the intended brevity may be preserved. Whoever does not neglect these two things will be neither inept nor tedious.

Accordingly, I shall maintain the order of exposition proposed in my other volumes: just as in the first book of the royal deeds I distinguished the succession of kingdoms, so here, in individual volumes, I shall distinguish the episcopal sees of the provinces. If anything is found below the promise, the reader who sees that it was done for a reason will grant pardon. This first book, therefore, will contain the deeds of the archbishops of Canterbury and the bishops of Rochester, among whom the kingdom first grew; all the rest will follow in their proper order.

# BOOK I. ON THE ARCHBISHOPS OF CANTERBURY

[Col. 1441]

[Col. 1441B] The first to sit at Canterbury was Augustine (A.D. 598), the disciple of Gregory the Great, as is commonly known. [Col. 1442B] That same Gregory, however, granted Augustine the pallium and the privilege of an archbishopric at London, as we showed in the first book of the *Royal Deeds* through the letter of Cenwulf; for until that time knowledge of any other obscure city had not reached the Romans. Yet because the first teacher, won by the diligence of the king and by the affection of his host and of the citizens, during his life occupied the throne at Canterbury for fifteen [elsewhere, sixteen] years and, in death (A.D. 613), rested there in the tomb, all honour was thereafter transferred to that place. How highly his merits are valued before the Lord is proclaimed by the splendid signs which He has not disdained to repeat even through so many centuries, refusing to let his Kent—indeed all England—grow sluggish in reverence for him.

Laurence succeeded him for five years. The virtues of Laurence and of the others—for Bede, when narrating their lives, touches briefly upon all things, doubtless fearing the offence of tedium [Col. 1443B]—their virtues, then, so far as he could learn them from the reports of the ancients, Goscelin [Note: [Col. 1443D] “We have collected his writings at the beginning of volume CLV of the *Patrology*.” Editor.] (of whom I have spoken elsewhere) described as altogether marvellous and worthy of praise, adding fresh accounts which he had himself seen with eyewitness faith. Their names are these:

Mellitus, likewise five years. Justus, three years. Honorius, twenty-six. Deusdedit, ten. Theodore, twenty-two.

Bede records that, having been sent from the Apostolic See, Theodore was the first of all the bishops of Canterbury to exercise episcopal authority throughout Britain. In short, on either side of the Humber he removed some bishops and appointed others as he pleased; at York itself he consecrated bishops for other cities and, as is read in the *Life of St Wilfrid*, expelled the bishops of that city, Ceadda [Col. 1443C] and Wilfrid himself, whether by argument or by force. Here one may see and lament human misery: however great a person’s holiness, he does not wholly put off obstinate habits; for those two eyes of Britain carried on controversies against one another.

For Theodore unjustly expelled Wilfrid, so far as our conjecture goes; and Wilfrid, after being buffeted by many previous dangers, brought his complaint before Pope Agatho of Rome. He did so modestly: he neither pressed accusations against one sent from the Apostolic See, nor yet allowed his own innocence to remain in doubt. For these are his words in the petition which he presented to the pope:

> “As for what happened—namely, that Theodore, most holy archbishop, while I was still alive in the see which, though unworthy, I administered, ordained three bishops by his own authority, without the consent of any bishop and without the acquiescence of my humility—it is more fitting, out of reverence for that man, to pass it over than to press it; for I do not dare accuse one sent from this supreme authority of the Apostolic See.”

Thus, although Wilfrid was then judged innocent by the decision of the Roman council and was sent back to his see, he did not obtain his case because of the violence of King Ecgfrith, especially since Theodore either opposed him deliberately or allowed it by connivance. I have not abstained from saying this in order to show how highly Theodore was held at Rome: although his enactments had been made wrongly, that see was unwilling entirely to invalidate them.

For the letter which the same Agatho sent to the sixth synod gathered at Constantinople supports this account and confirms my point. Among other things it says:

> “We had also hoped that Theodore, our fellow-servant and fellow-bishop, archbishop and philosopher of the great island of Britain, would join us from Britain with others who still dwell there; and for this reason we have delayed our deliberation until now.”

You see how highly he valued him, since he delayed an ecumenical council in expectation of him.

Berhtwald succeeded him for thirty-seven years; then Tatwine. Their miracles—as I had begun to say—and no less those of St Liudhard, whom antiquity relates to have come with Queen Bertha, the aforesaid writer [Note: [Col. 1444D] Goscelin.] proclaims and exalts. He recounts that Liudhard, powerful in other respects and swift in obtaining rain, provided a pleasing spectacle not many years ago. For when in mid-summer the sun scorched Cancer, the fields were dusty and parched, and raging Sirius scorched the thirsty lands, the saint’s body, carried out in procession, first sharpened the expectation of those waiting by the delay of the miracle. Then, after its return, an angered singer cried out with a great open mouth: “Do you not see how great the drought and affliction are throughout the whole world, and yet you act negligently?” The saint, thus reproached in this festive manner, satisfied beyond measure the eager desire of those who sought rain by a great deluge.

He next recounts the succession of kings, with all their kinship ties, resting in Augustine’s church; [Col. 1444C] he rightly calls them the lights of England and the senators of the English court. To this choir of saints, like jewels of priceless glory added to the wrought diadem of the eternal King, he adds those who flash forth ruin against the insolent and aid for suppliants: I mean Abbot Hadrian and the virgin Mildrith, conspicuous in equal praise.

Tatwine, who held the archbishopric for three years and died in the same year as Bede, was succeeded by Nothelm. He is said to be the man whom the same historian, in the prologue to his *History of the English*, calls a priest of the church of London who greatly assisted him in compiling the work by bringing letters from the Roman archive which were necessary for it.

[Col. 1444D] When Nothelm died five years later, Cuthbert, bishop of the Mercians at Hereford, renewed the apostolic office. He was a contemporary of Boniface and, to restrain vices, assembled a great council of England at Boniface’s admonition and with the support of King Æthelbald, as I have said in the deeds of the kings. The beginning and proceedings of this synod will here be set down chapter by chapter, sometimes in my own words but always according to the sense of the ancients; pardon for the resulting tedium is requested, because we possess little concerning episcopal deeds, and it is worth hearing the zeal of the Fathers who went before us in matters of God.

> While our Lord Jesus Christ reigns for ever, He who orders all things by the command of the Father and likewise by the life-giving grace of the Holy Spirit, these synodal proceedings set out below were carried out on the eleventh [elsewhere, at the beginning] of September near the place called Clovesho. Present were these bishops, beloved of God, of the churches of Christ: the honourable Archbishop Cuthbert; Dunn, venerable bishop of the church of Rochester; and the most reverend bishops of the Mercians, Totta, Hwita, and Podda; also the most approved bishops of the West Saxons, Humphred and Herewald; and the venerable priests Heardulf of the East Angles, Egiulf of the East Saxons, and Mildred of the Wiccii; likewise the honourable bishops Ælwhine of the province of Lindsey and Sige of the South Saxons. This was in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 747, in the fifteenth indiction, and in the thirty-third year of the reign of Æthelbald, king of the Mercians, who was then present with his princes and leaders.

[Col. 1445B] When, therefore, the aforesaid bishops of sacred rank, together with dignitaries of lesser rank, had gathered from the different provinces of Britain, and writings in two documents of the venerable Pope Zacharias had been read, in which he admonished the English to live more chastely and threatened excommunication against the disobedient:

> “In the first chapter they decreed that bishops should henceforth live more diligently and admonish their subjects more diligently. Second, that they should live in a spirit of peace, although they dwelt in separate places. Third, that each should go round his own parishes every year. Fourth, that each in his own diocese should admonish abbots and monks to live according to rule, and that superiors should not oppress but love those subject to them. Fifth, that monasteries already seized by laymen, and which could not then be taken from them, should be taught to live [elsewhere, conduct themselves] according to rule. Sixth, that no one should be ordained unless his life had first been examined. Seventh, that the reading of the holy Scriptures should be frequent in monasteries. Eighth, that priests should not be managers of secular business. Ninth, that priests themselves should not receive payment for baptizing children. Tenth, that they should learn and teach the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed in English. Eleventh, that all should perform their ministries in one and the same manner. Twelfth, that they should sing sacred things in churches in a restrained voice. Thirteenth, that everywhere the feasts of the Lord and the birthdays of the saints should be celebrated at one and the same time. [Col. 1445D] Fourteenth, that the Lord’s Day should be honourably observed. Fifteenth, that the seven canonical hours should be observed every day. Sixteenth, that the days of the lesser and greater Rogations should not be omitted. Seventeenth, that the feast of St Gregory and Augustine our Father should be observed. Eighteenth, that the fasts of the Four Seasons should be observed. Nineteenth, that monks and nuns should be clothed according to rule. Twentieth, that bishops should see that these decrees are not neglected. Twenty-first, that the ecclesiastical order should not become drunk. Twenty-second, that communion should not be neglected by clerics. Twenty-third, that it should likewise be observed by laypeople at the appropriate times. Twenty-fourth, that laypeople should first be tested before becoming monks. Twenty-fifth, that almsgiving should not be neglected. [Col. 1446A] Twenty-sixth, that each bishop should make these commands known to those subject to him. Twenty-seventh, discussion was held on the usefulness of almsgiving. Twenty-eighth, on the usefulness of psalmody. Twenty-ninth, that a community should be established according to the measure of its resources. Thirtieth, that monks should not live among laypeople. Thirty-first, that public prayer should be offered for kings and princes.”

Cuthbert the archbishop immediately sent the proceedings of this synod—for we have touched only its chapters—to Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, through his deacon Cynebert. Boniface himself replied in an elegant letter of congratulation, as the reader will find in its place.

But since mention has so often intruded itself of Boniface, this man who was formerly called Winfrid, I shall commit to writing something concerning his disciple Frederic which has reached my ears, is not widely known, and deserves remembrance. For the master’s holiness may be inferred from the disciple’s virtue: Boniface had at home a source from which he could learn not to fear the powerful and to despise death.

Willibrord, the first bishop of Utrecht, whom Bede mentions, had ended his days, distinguished by holiness and old age. Boniface had succeeded him in the care and preaching in Frisia, after Conabo [elsewhere, Cobano; elsewhere, Banco] had been ordained bishop at Utrecht. A considerable time passed before both men, weary of their mortal habitation, were summoned to heaven; when, behold, the Frisians, driven, it is believed, by infernal furies, slaughtered them both and made them martyrs. Lull succeeded Boniface in the see of Mainz, as I have said [elsewhere, “he said”]; but because of the savagery of the people, Frederic was not so quickly made the successor of Eubano [Col. 1446C] [elsewhere, Banco] at Utrecht.

Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, advanced Frederic—who breathed the nectar of Boniface’s holiness, being his kinsman and disciple—to that office, though many exerted themselves both for their own sake and for their associates. On the first day of his ordination, the emperor honoured the new bishop by seating him at his right hand at dinner. When a large part of the meal had been consumed, the man in purple addressed Frederic, urging him, mindful of his recent profession and following his predecessors’ steadfastness, to set forth the truth without respect of persons and pronounce anathema against those who despised it.

Frederic, with modest eyes and bowed head, said: “You act rightly, lord emperor, in encouraging the tender beginning of my profession with holy exhortations. But I beg your majesty not to find it burdensome to resolve something which the recesses of my mind have long pondered. And, lest we seek examples far away: is it more proper to begin eating this fish placed upon the table from its head or its tail?” The emperor, hastily and unaware how he would be caught, answered, “From the head.”

Without delay Frederic seized upon the answer, saying: “So let it be, lord Augustus, so let it be: let Christian faith and piety rebuke you securely for your errors, so that your subjects may not dare despise what they see you have tolerated. Renounce, therefore, the incestuous marriage which you have contracted; for this Judith, whom you have joined to your side, is near to you in blood, and it is not fitting that a royal marriage-bed should be dishonoured by lust.”

Although Louis took this saying ill, he dismissed it with restrained silence and promptly permitted the bishop to depart for his see. Yet speech uttered in the presence of so great a multitude of courtiers could not be concealed; it disturbed the ears and wounded the hearts of all the bishops of the region. With no trifling grief they discussed how a new bishop had proclaimed with open freedom such things as the old bishops themselves would not have condemned even by a whispered murmur. They therefore listened attentively and held frequent councils until the emperor put away the marriage and lived celibately.

Accordingly they confined the emperor himself in prison and the woman in a monastery. Lothair, Louis’s eldest son, exerted himself to the utmost in this, as I said above, alleging the prompting of Christianity but in truth using it as a pretext for envy. Later, however, through the mercy of the Apostolic See, a gentler council decreed that, after a penance had been imposed, they should thereafter rejoice in a lawful marriage. The emperor willingly yielded to the judgment, banishing resentment against all by the generosity of his mind.

[Col. 1447B] But Judith, exhaling feminine venom, complained among her followers of the injuries inflicted by Frederic, bishop of Utrecht; and, having suffered these evils chiefly through his agency, found two men who promised their service for his murder. These things did not escape the bishop, who was a sanctuary of the Godhead itself; but fearless, he awaited the executioners who were to come, and, impatient in his desire for martyrdom, reproached the delay of the scoundrels.

Thus, on the very morning when he knew that they would come, he prepared himself for Mass. He had already put on the alb when a boy entered—the boy whose duty it was to admit those wishing to meet his master—and announced that the empress’s agents were standing at the doors. Excusing himself on account of his impediment, [Col. 1447C] Frederic ordered them meanwhile to wait in the dining-room. When Mass had been sung, he entered the sacristy still dressed in his sacred vestments, and ordered that the officers be brought in there after all bystanders had been removed.

The sight of his splendour and the awe inspired by his vestments struck them so deeply as they entered that their courage failed and daggers fell even from their hands. Perceiving this, he who had cast aside present life in hope of the future encouraged the murderers of his own accord to carry out that for which they had come, exhorting them to take courage and recover their strength. Thus—for wickedness is easily persuaded—they attacked him as he sat: one drove his dagger from breast to groin, the other through the middle of his loins.

Then he, grasping and holding fast with both hands his flowing vitals, said: “Go, miserable men, go, [Col. 1447D] while the matter is still hidden from my faithful servants, lest, if they catch you, it is all over with you.”

The assassins, adding the spurs of fear to the speed of their feet, ran down to the Rhine and, by the strength of their arms, drove a boat across it. Meanwhile, when his chamberlain came in and asked why he sat so bloodless, Frederic harshly drove him away, ordering him swiftly to look out from the wall and see whether the empress’s messengers had crossed the Rhine. When he learned that the distance of their flight had made their capture difficult, he ordered the clergy to be summoned at once. He set forth the whole tragedy to them, complete both in words and in understanding.

Then, having himself begun the antiphon, “Open to me the gates of righteousness,” and the rest, while still alive he arranged himself in his mausoleum and attained heaven by a noble and venerable death. I judged it not useless to bring this account before readers, though it lies outside my subject, so that it might be reckoned to the glory of the English that they illuminated foreign lands, holiness itself being in pilgrimage.

[Col. 1448A] After seventeen years in the episcopate, Cuthbert was struck by sickness and, as he approached death, ordered his people to bury him at the archiepiscopal church. Since the monks of Augustine, according to an ancient custom, stubbornly seized the bodies of deceased archbishops with a kind of violence, he ordered the mournful wailing throughout the court and city to cease and forbade public funeral rites. Thus, while the disturbance was stilled within and outsiders were kept from access, the bishop’s corpse was brought into the bosom of the chief church and was not reclaimed by the others, who saw that they had been outwitted.

Bregwine succeeded him for three years and vacated his see for Lambert, formerly abbot of St Augustine’s. We have spoken of this man in the first book of the *Royal Deeds*, and do not now pass over the fact that Offa, king of the Mercians, after contracting hostilities with the people of Canterbury, tried to deprive him of the primacy. At the same time, desiring to adorn the Mercian kingdom with an archbishopric, Offa procured by letters to Pope Hadrian, and perhaps by gifts, that the bishop of Lichfield should be elevated with the pallium contrary to ancient custom, and that all the bishops of the Mercians should be subjected to him. Their names were: Deneberht of Worcester, Weremberht of Leicester, Eadwulf of Sidnacester, and Wulfheard of Hereford; and two bishops of the East Angles, Ealhheard [elsewhere, Aliterd] of Elmham and Lifred of Dunwich. The bishop of Lichfield was called Aldwulf.

[Col. 1448C] For Offa, in accordance with his power, had made several bishoprics in Mercia and had invaded the East Angles after killing their king Æthelberht. Some of these bishoprics were transferred elsewhere, as Elmham to Norwich; some were united to others, as Dunwich to the same see; and some no longer exist at all, as Leicester and Sidnacester. Four bishops remained under the bishop of Canterbury: those of London, Winchester, Rochester, and Selsey.

This perversion lasted throughout Lambert’s episcopate, although he omitted neither expenditure nor labour by which he might defend the dignity of his see and crush the greed of its usurpers.

But after Lambert died twenty-seven years later and was buried in the chapter-house at St Augustine’s, Æthelhard [elsewhere, Athelard], bishop of Winchester, succeeded for thirteen years (A.D. 803), [Col. 1448D] a man of outstanding energy and powerful influence among the nobles. By his counsels Ecgfrith [elsewhere, Egfrid], Offa’s son, had been persuaded to restore to Canterbury the honour of the archbishopric, had fate not hastened to remove him from the world. But King Cenwulf of the Mercians, instructed by Æthelhard’s and Eanbald, archbishop of York’s, admonitions how great an impiety his predecessor had committed, completely restored the ancient order. He sent his own letters and those of all the bishops of England to Leo, Hadrian’s successor, while the archbishop himself earnestly conducted the embassy. To demonstrate this more clearly, I shall append suitable small extracts from Alcuin’s letters.

> To the most holy father and greatly venerable member of Christ, ÆTHELHARD, archbishop, ALCUIN, deacon, sends greeting in the love of Christ.
>
> “Hearing of your health and prosperity, and of your meeting with Eanbald, archbishop of York, my son, I was greatly pleased, hoping that through the conference of your holiness the honour of the holy Church might be exalted and the life of those who serve God therein corrected. Therefore, in other letters of mine I urged your holiness to remain in your native land, unwilling that the light of Britain should be extinguished. But let what pleases God be done, so that it may advance the churches of Christ. May God make your journey prosperous, and, with His angel accompanying you, happily lead you forth and bring you back, sweetest and most loving Father. Above all, I pray that you will remember me at the holy apostles, just as we gladly remember you at St Martin’s.”  

> To the lord ÆTHELHARD, most holy and most worthy of all honour, archbishop.
>
> “Having read your letters concerning your prosperity, the success of your journey and return to your country, and how you were received by apostolic kindness, with all the affection of my heart and with a most joyful mind I gave thanks to the eternal Lord God. By His great gift of mercy He directed the path of your pilgrimage in a successful journey, gave you favour in the sight of the Father of the Apostolic See, and permitted you to return having attained the effect of your mission and the fulfilment of your desire [elsewhere: “in the sight of the Apostolic Father, and having attained the effect of your mission and the fulfilment of your desire”]. [Col. 1449C] Through you He has deigned once more to raise to its former height of dignity the most holy see of our first teacher—a see which seemed for a time to have been torn apart by the breach of a certain dissension and the jealous rivalry of certain persons.
>
> “Blessed is the man who strives to preserve the unity of peace by brotherly love; but far more blessed is he who strives by pious labour to restore to the cohesion of one body the members of charity torn apart by others. Therefore now, through divine grace at work, the unity of the members cleaves to its proper head; priestly dignity rejoices in its ancient honour; true peace shines between the chief bishops of Britain; and under the two metropolitan cities one purpose of devotion and concord flourishes, as I understood from reading the letters of your blessedness.”

Likewise, in another letter, he intercedes for the Mercian bishop, that he should not be stripped of the pallium while alive, in these words:

> “May the reading of the holy Scriptures be renewed through your most holy care, ecclesiastical dignity everywhere exalted, and the holy see which was first in faith be first in holiness and honour. It has been partly divided, not by reasonable consideration but by a certain zeal for piety. But if it can be peacefully united and the division repaired, it seems good that this should be done with the counsel of all Christ’s priests and of your fellow bishop of the church of York—yet so that the pious Father should not in his lifetime be stripped of the pallium, although the ordination of bishops returns to the holy and first see.”

Æthelhard, therefore, was one man who restored the matter for us, not through delay but through vigorous effort—although we might borrow Ennius’s saying about Fabius. Not only does Kent owe him an immense benefit, because by his labours he raised it to its former dignity [Col. 1450A]; all England does as well, because he did not allow it to be subjected to a degenerate see. He was a man to be compared with, and I would almost say preferred to, the greatest bishops after the first teachers. Nor do I know whether I sin by saying so: surely it seems more excellent to restore dignity once lost than to preserve dignity once acquired, though the latter too is held to deserve some praise.

If anyone should question how great were his holiness and reverence, let him read Pope Leo’s letter to King Cenwulf, found in the first book of the *Royal Deeds*, where Leo calls him most holy, most worthy, dearest, and most learned. That supreme and holy pope would certainly not repeat such terms unless he knew them to be true.

After him came Wulfred for twenty-eight years; Ægeld [elsewhere, Theogild] for three months; Ceolnoth for forty-one years; and Æthered [elsewhere, Æthelred] for eighteen years. In uninterrupted succession the archbishops performed many things worthy, as we believe, of God and of the world; but antiquity has silenced and erased all of them, and nothing of theirs remains among us except a faint report.

After Æthered came Plegmund, for thirty-three years. He was master of King Alfred and, as I said in the second book of the *Royal Deeds*, ordained seven bishops at Canterbury in one day; whoever wishes may read their names and sees there.

His successor was Athelm, one of those whom he had ordained for the church of Wells.

[Col. 1450C] Wulfhelm succeeded Athelm: for thirteen years at Wells, and after Athelm’s death at Canterbury.

Then St Odo, bishop of Wilton, shone forth as archbishop for twenty years.
