Besides those five bishops of Wessex whom, in the time of Edward the Elder, I have said more than once that Plegmund consecrated, a sixth was added not long afterwards. He had his see at Ramsbury and his diocese in the district of Wilton, while a bishop remained at Sherborne and the parishes of Dorset and Berkshire were preserved.

It is fitting to taste, so far as renown has descended to us by succession, no slight portion of Odo’s glory in holiness and miracles. I am minded to do this not only for him but also for other saints of England when occasion offers, especially where their deeds are not everywhere celebrated; for to rehearse in detailed fashion the deeds of those whom other writers’ talents have extolled would be madness.

Odo, so that the character of his holiness might be more clearly attested, was, like a rose overcoming the roughness of thorns by its birth, raised above the barbarity of the Danes from whom he was descended, and grew into a great example of goodness. His parents had harried England in King Alfred’s time. Odo himself served Edward for some time after the others had either departed or perished; not long afterwards he cut his hair and professed the clerical life. As his merits became increasingly known, he was placed over the church of Wilton and drew King Æthelstan into friendship with himself. Thus, when the king marched against Anlaf, the bishop was at his side, to encourage him in prosperity and correct him in adversity.

Accordingly, on that mournful night when, as I said in the second book of the *Royal Deeds*, made less cautious by security itself, Æthelstan was nearly surprised by his enemies and even lost his sword, Odo came when called. While all things were full of blind confusion, he was the first, with prayers raised to heaven, to see the sword—a gift from heaven, indeed—fall divinely into the royal scabbard. When this occurrence was immediately reported to Æthelstan by Odo’s cry, it had such effect that the king both then did not hesitate to call Odo the guardian of his life and, after Wulfhelm’s death, raised him to the primacy of Kent.

[Col. 1451A] Odo, who had not yet assumed the monastic habit, [Note: [Col. 1451D] That is, “put on.”] resisted more firmly, lest he appear by his ambition to disturb the custom of his ancestors; for until that time no archbishop had existed who was not clothed in the monastic habit. But when the consent of all the bishops was added to the king’s will, at last, though scarcely, the most reverend man, his steadfast resolution overcome, yielded to the general judgment, recalling the proverb: “The voice of the people is the voice of God.”

Thus he crossed the sea and received monastic observance at Fleury, a prudent and temperate man, so as neither to mock the favour of the citizens nor to tarnish ancient custom. During all the lifetime of Æthelstan, the uncorrupted friendship of king and bishop flourished: one exercised eloquence in matters of God by mutual services, the other, if need arose, wielded the sword.

But after envious fate carried off the flourishing young man, Odo, mature in age and ennobling his grey hairs by holiness, held equally friendly favour with Edmund and Eadred, because they displayed no conduct against which episcopal strictness ought to be directed. Indeed, he went with them into Northumbria, not to wage battles, but to bring forth the sacred ashes of saints, of whom that soil had once been fertile.

Thus, when he sorrowfully saw that the church at Ripon of the most eminent Father Wilfrid had been destroyed by the Danes, he cleared away the ruins above the mausoleum, reverently transferred the relics to Canterbury, and, to bring that most brilliant light of his homeland into view, ordered Wilfrid’s life to be composed in heroic metre. One Fridegodus performed this office in verses not altogether to be condemned, except that, hating Latinity, he loves Greekness and constantly employs little Greek words—so that Plautus’s saying may rightly be applied to his compositions: “No one but the Sibyl will read these.”

Odo himself also gave no slight proof of his learning in the letter which, after the synodal council held in King Edmund’s time, he issued to his suffragans [Col. 1451D]. Its form is as follows:

> “With the wondrous mercy of the almighty Ruler of the heavens assisting, I, ODO, archbishop of the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour, metropolitan of the city of Canterbury, to my fellow bishops, fellow-builders in the Catholic faith, my brethren, accompanied by spiritual charity and also by firmness, wish prosperity in the present life and the blessedness of heavenly glory.
>
> “If it could in any way come about that all the riches of the whole world were set before our eyes, so that they might universally serve us by an imperial gift, I would gladly distribute them all, and moreover expend myself for the salvation of your souls [Col. 1452A]. For I desire and hope to be strengthened by the zeal of your holiness in that work in which the Lord God has appointed us labourers.”

He added many further matters setting out the burden of the episcopate:

> “Therefore I humbly pray and exhort your holiness, as one unworthy yet devoted, that you may not conduct yourselves lukewarmly and negligently in the governance of souls, lest at the time of dreadful vengeance the Lord complain of you, saying: ‘The shepherds did not feed my flock, but themselves’ (Ezek. XXXIV). And again: ‘Princes arose, and I did not know it’ (Hosea VIII). Rather, let us take care to give the household of the Lord, over which He has appointed us rulers, food in its season: a measure of wheat, that is, approved doctrine.
>
> “And although, because of the quality of my merits, I do not presume to console or exhort anyone—for I alone am unworthy and guilty of countless faults, and rejoice and need to be faithfully strengthened by brotherly admonitions—yet, because of the ancient authority of my predecessors, Augustine of blessed memory and the other saints, through whose efforts the rule of Christianity first became known from this archiepiscopal see to all the regions of the English, I have determined to inscribe these divine letters for the benefit of you all. Thus may the most august king, Edmund by his eminent name, together with all his people, joyfully imitate what he hears in us and from us; and may all the nations subjected on every side to his royal power love and delight in eagerly following the examples of our transparent manner of life.”

But Edwin, Edmund’s son and successor to his uncle Edred in the kingdom, notorious for rash audacity and bodily licentiousness, provoked the bishop’s indignation. Odo both suspended him from Christian communion and broke off his adulterous liaison with a prostitute—first by expulsion, then by cutting the sinews behind his knee. Edwin retaliated by raging like a Bacchant against the monks throughout Britain, while no one except Odo and Dunstan, then an abbot, dared oppose him even in speech. For, as Seneca says, “A cock is strongest on his own dung-heap.”

Meanwhile the bishop directed his mind toward God, performed miracles in no scant measure, and restored to lawful possession many estates appurtenant to his see which had been taken away during Danish incursions. So much so that it is agreed that no archbishop of that age equalled Odo in such matters. Yet how slight is the testimony Osbern bears him, when he says that, for his holiness and diligence, he should always be mourned by the whole realm of the English, had Dunstan not succeeded him. By some negligence the church of the archbishopric stood roofless; Odo covered it so effectively by his prayers while the roof was being prepared that throughout the entire period—unless what I say seems unbelievable—not even a drop of rain wetted the circuit of the place [Col. 1452D].

This is held all the more remarkable because a vast fall of rain and frequent violent storms shook the whole world in those days. It also strengthened many who doubted the reality of the Lord’s body, so that he openly showed the bread of the altar changed into flesh and the wine of the chalice into blood, and then restored them, turned back into their natural appearance, for human use [Col. 1453A].

When he blessed the most blessed Dunstan, elected bishop of Worcester, at Canterbury, he performed the whole order of consecration in such a manner that he seemed to be blessing not a bishop of the Wiccii, but an archbishop of Canterbury. When the clergy murmured discreetly, he uttered a prophecy: he knew what he was doing, for after his own death Dunstan would be ruler of the primatial church. Therefore, if they judged rightly, what the divine will had brought about through his ministry ought to be free from reproach.

Nor did mature fulfilment fail the prediction, although Elfinus, bishop of Winchester, had attempted to interfere with it. For when Odo had long since gladdened the expectant heavenly powers by his presence, Elfinus, having prepared advocates whose hands he had bribed and having surreptitiously obtained an edict of King Edgar, intruded himself into Kent [Col. 1453B]. On the first day of his office he did not refrain from vomiting forth the furies nourished in his mind. Striking the holy man’s tomb with his foot, he assailed his soul aloud:

> “At last, most wretched old man, you have poured out your tenacious life; too late you have departed, making room for a better man. Thus I hold, against your will, what I have long desired; for this I offer you and render you evil thanks.”

But when that day had passed and the exhaler of madness had gone to his bed, he saw the holy man’s figure standing beside him, reproaching his insult and swiftly threatening destruction. Thinking that he was being mocked by a fleeting phantom, he nonetheless hastened over the Alps toward Rome to receive the pallium. There, frozen by snowy cold, he could devise no remedy except to immerse his feet—the feet with which he had violated the saint’s tomb—in the still breathing entrails of disembowelled horses [Col. 1453C]. Yet even thus the cold did not abate; as his soul fled toward death, he stiffened and died.

Therefore, after Elfinus’s death, Dunstan, already marked out by a divine oracle as archbishop, was in A.D. 987 urged by the prayers of King Edgar to honour the primatial see with the service of his holiness. He repeatedly deferred the petitioner with deaf ears; at last, pressed by the unanimous agreement of all the bishops, he yielded.

He was the nephew, through a brother, of Æthelhelm, archbishop; first abbot of Glastonbury, afterwards bishop of the Wiccii and of London, and finally archbishop of Canterbury. He adorned every stage of his advancement with untiring virtues. Truly, the king’s heart had been inspired by a divine influence, so that he accepted Dunstan’s counsel in everything without hesitation, doing whatever the bishop judged should be commanded [Col. 1453D]. Dunstan likewise omitted nothing which he understood to accord with the king’s reputation and salvation. He pressed him all the more sharply when he delayed, first fashioning the king’s character into a mirror for his subjects and, when he transgressed, punishing him more sternly without respect of persons.

I have recorded an example of this in the deeds of the kings: Dunstan imposed upon him seven years’ penance for unlawful desire for a woman who had, at least in outward appearance, been a nun. Thus the nobles, shaped according to the example and standard of their king, dared little or nothing contrary to law and equity, knowing their lord to be so answerable to Dunstan.

Nor should you doubt how greatly the mixed multitude restrained itself from wrongdoing [Col. 1454A], whether desiring to win the favour of their lords or seeking to avoid the stern sentence of the laws. To this were added military discipline, effective restraint of the rapacity of thieves, and punishment of the fraud of money-changers by capital penalties. Nothing at all was omitted which might offend the inward Judge.

The monastic order did not neglect, in every place, a life corresponding to the profession it emulated. For it had rulers religious in life and distinguished in learning, whom neither sloth rendered slow nor rashness headlong. Such men, after long and very carefully weighed examination and keen, competing discernment of minds, the king and archbishop alike promoted wherever they were found. Thus the clergy of many churches, being given the choice either to change their dress or to leave their places, yielded to better men [Col. 1454B], leaving their dwellings vacant.

Religious monasteries consequently arose throughout the whole island; the altars of the saints were heaped with masses of precious metal; nor did the morals of those who built them fall below the beauty of the buildings. Thus, while persons of every rank burned with zeal for God’s service, the very land seemed to rejoice in tranquillity. The fields answered their cultivators with abundant produce; plenty of every good overflowed from full horns; and scarcely ever in Dunstan’s time did a poor harvest disappoint the hope of the country people.

The elements shone with cheerful countenances; no mists and no clouds gathered their contagion beneath an idle sky. Fear of enemies from across the sea was far away; all things were quiet and peaceful. In the cities there was no injury to the poor, no discord among the living, and no cessation of justice because of the dead [Col. 1454C]. By the Lord’s grace, the root of these blessings looked to Dunstan; from Dunstan it passed into Edgar, and from Edgar it sprouted among the people.

Happy indeed were those times, possessing a bishop who did nothing beneath what has been described, and a king who diligently attended to the bishops’ commands. These things won and preserved for the man immortal glory far more than his miracles, although, with the Lord’s aid, he was not lacking even in these. Reason demands that I set down here, if only briefly, a list of them, so that, if anyone unfamiliar with his deeds should perhaps come upon this account, he may know how greatly this saint, still an inhabitant of this earthly pilgrimage, anticipated in his mind the joys above; and how God, both author and foreknower of his future holiness, preceded his birth with a delightful portent [Col. 1454D].

For when his mother, pregnant and with the child already mature for birth in her womb, was standing in church at the Purification of Saint Mary among a great gathering of citizens, all the lights were suddenly extinguished, whether by chance or by God’s will. While all were astonished, the woman’s candle received light from heaven; sharing its fire with the others, it drove away fear and brought reassurance.

When the boy was given to learning, he mastered all the books of instruction with power; but he embraced more gladly and dearly those which, by shaping the character, directed the mind toward things above. While still a little child, he drove away with a rod the devil who met him by night, attended by a troop of raging dogs. Carried gently down to the ground with the aid of angels standing in his way, he entered a locked church. As he entered [Col. 1455A], his harp, hung on a peg, sounded a vocal melody without a human finger:

> “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven,”

and what follows. When he heard this, he understood that he was being warned to endure tribulations; he shuddered, and not long afterwards experienced them.

As a young man, while performing the office for one who had died, he received an oracle concerning how great an advance he was to make in the Lord and in the world. Lest he suppose himself mocked by the mist of an empty phantom, he received a sign: a place was shown where, three days later, a priest was to be buried, though he was not yet infirm or ill. By calling out his own name beforehand, though absent, Dunstan saved a king being carried by the course of an unbridled horse toward a precipice, checking the animal’s run. At the very mouth of the steep chasm he restored to its place a massive beam which, through the carelessness of workmen, had been falling downward [Col. 1455B], extending from afar the sign of the cross.

Now bishop and primate of Britain, when water was needed for divine service, he brought forth a flow of water from the native hollow of a rock; it sends out perennial streams to this day. Whatever snares of the devil he foresaw, he perceived them clearly and evaded them powerfully. Once, when the devil whispered filthy suggestions of women, he burned him with red-hot tongs; and when the same enemy troubled him in prayer, clothed in the form either of a fox or of a bear, he drove him away with a staff. When the devil repeatedly burst into laughter over the joy of Dunstan’s exile, Dunstan rebuked him with threats—and fulfilled those threats when, on returning from exile, he inflicted a great loss on the devil by winning souls for the Lord.

Taught by the demons’ joy of the death shortly to come for King Edmund and of the death already past for Edwin [Col. 1455C], he buried the former’s body at Glastonbury and rescued the latter’s soul from the violence of its enemies. What of this? Is it not something to be spoken of with great reverence and awe: that, looking with bodily eyes, he saw the Holy Spirit present in the form of a dove to a woman in travail and to himself as he celebrated Mass, and from there settle in gracious flight upon the memorial of the most blessed Odo? Henceforth, whenever occasion offered, he called Odo “the Good,” in the customary and indeed proper name, *Ode the good*.

And besides, how familiarly, good God, did heavenly spirits appear to him! How closely did they serve with him, encouraging with holy exhortations one who still sighed for his homeland and was wearied by this present life. By an angelic harmony he learned the birth and future happiness of King Edgar; by a more violent assault of clouds, Edred’s death [Col. 1455D]. For the dreadful crash was proved to signify death by the immediate death of the animal on which he was riding.

Though absent, he saw and announced a disciple’s blessed passing to heaven, clear in prophecy and never once repulsed by the event as false. He foretold to King Æthelred the misery to come, and to the virgin Edith and Bishop Æthelwold death near at hand; he appointed holy Ælfheah in Æthelwold’s place, having received the Apostle Andrew as his adviser. For he especially enjoyed Andrew’s consolation, whether to avoid adversities or to moderate prosperity.

But surpassing all and presiding over all was this: he beheld with a waking eye and in a present miracle the Lady, the Lord’s Mother, inviting companions in chastity—among them the mother of this same bishop—to the praise of Christ, and singing and repeating in modulated song the following lines of Sedulius [Col. 1456A]:

> Let us sing to the Lord, companions; let us sing honour:
>
> Let the sweet love of Christ sound forth from a devout mouth.

It is altogether wonderful, wholly wonderful, what is related, yet not remote from the firmness of truth: namely, that what by God’s great gift is to be granted to saints in the future life now tenderly stirs them by blessed hope and happily caresses them, he himself, enclosed in a frame of clay, should receive with his eyes and drink in with his ears. Indeed I believe—and the belief is not vain—that he also heard the song of angels chanting *Kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy,” which the churches of the English now gladly learn and teach.

Glorious in these triumphs and victorious in these honours, he was translated to the heavenly world in the twenty-seventh year of his patriarchate, to his own great glory and his country’s immense affliction [Col. 1456B]. For immediately the joyful aspect of the elements withered; the peace secured through his wisdom vanished with the arrival of the Danes, although he alleviated his children’s calamities by very great signs.

I have not seen the written account of the following; I recently heard it related by a certain monk of Christ Church. A thief condemned to be thrown from a height called upon the aid of Saint Dunstan. Blindfolded and forced backward by the executioners, he leapt into the precipice unharmed. There blessed Dunstan spoke with him bodily and loosened the bonds over his eyes. Encouraged by this consolation, the wretched man escaped upward over rough paths, a hand which he could not see supporting his hanging back as he climbed, lest he slip backwards [Col. 1456C]. But since the succession of the times is recorded in our writings, and that of the saint’s miracles in others’ writings, I shall return to the succession of bishops.

Æthelgar succeeded Dunstan for one year. He had first been made abbot in the new monastery at Winchester by blessed Æthelwold, and afterwards received the bishopric of the South Saxons, whose see was then at Selsey and is now at Chichester. After his removal, Ælfric, previously bishop of Wilton, sat for eleven years; earlier he had also been abbot of Abingdon. What some say of him—that he placed monks at Canterbury after driving out the clerics—does not seem probable. For it is certain that monks had been in the church of the Holy Saviour from the time of Archbishop Laurence, the first successor to the most blessed Augustine, as will appear from Pope Boniface’s letter to King Æthelberht, to be set out below [Col. 1456D].

After him came Sigeric, likewise bishop of Winchester, for five years. In the Deeds of the Kings I said that by his counsel King Æthelred redeemed his freedom of mind from the Danes by payment, buying their peace with silver when he could have driven them away by the sword, had he not lacked courage. Consequently an unbearable payment of tribute was imposed upon England and reduced the fortunes of the country people to the ground.

When his successor Ælfheah—formerly bishop of Winchester, archbishop for six years and seven months—

> [Note: [Col. 1455] He omits Ælfric, who held the see for eleven years, A.D. 995–1005.]

—refused to do this, lest he purchase the softness of his own ease at the loss of the wretched, he was captured, put in fetters, and at last stoned by the Danes themselves, yielding up his soul to heaven [Col. 1457A].

Osbern wrote his life, full of virtues and miracles. Chief among these was that, while in Rome, Ælfheah announced to his companions with manifest truth the death of Cenwulf, who had succeeded him at Winchester. Further, when the day of his glory dawned and he was about to satisfy the rage of his enemies by his death, he saw Dunstan foretelling a passing punishment and promising future glory. For I have already said that his body, even while bearing traces of fresh blood, has remained free from the corruption of decay to this day; and the fact is so commonly repeated that it need not be urged again.

The martyr Ælfheah was succeeded by Lyfing, also called Æthelstan, for seven years. He was promoted from bishop of Wells to archbishop through the support of King Æthelred [Col. 1457B]. That king still breathed, having experienced too fully in his calamities the true prophecy of the most blessed Dunstan which we mentioned above: a man who saw his provinces overthrown before his eyes, himself at last driven into exile, and could devise no remedy.

Some attribute this to an imbalance of body, others to sluggishness of mind. Yet however posterity may take my words, I state without qualification that it was a great mark of wretchedness that, when the primate of the country had been imprisoned for seven months, the king brought no aid and roused himself to no vengeance, moved neither by the majesty of the bishop nor by the indignity of his plight. Therefore I can apply to Æthelred that ancient proverb: from the conspicuous lightning-flash of virtue there had been born inert darkness [Col. 1457C]. For what did England ever have comparable to Edgar the father in goodness, or to this son in lethargy? Lyfing, as I said, filled the place of the dead Ælfheah.

After him came Æthelnoth for eighteen years, concerning whom I have mentioned certain matters in the Deeds of Cnut.

Edsius succeeded him for eleven years. After the death of Harthacnut, he advanced King Edward to the kingdom, supporting Edward’s efforts by his authority and blessing, while the designs of Earl Godwine and the opposing wishes of the Danes came to nothing. Not long afterwards, afflicted by an incurable illness, he resigned power while still living and willing [Col. 1457D], after first arranging in more private counsel with the king and the earl that Siward, abbot of Abingdon, should succeed him.

But because Siward was ungrateful toward the man who had bestowed the honour upon him, even depriving the sick man of necessary food, the designated successor was expelled, and the bishopric of Rochester was given him to alleviate his shame and console his loss.

Then the king made Robert archbishop for two years. He had made him bishop of London from being a monk of Jumièges, recompensing with a very great reward the benefits which Robert himself had once bestowed upon him during his exile in Normandy. Thus Robert, by both old affection and recent honour, claimed the leading part in royal counsels: whom he wished he deposed, freed, or elevated. I speak of matters known to the English and repeat what I have said elsewhere [Col. 1458A].

The English therefore envied the Norman and diminished the king’s goodwill toward him. Robert, in turn, persisted more obstinately, until he drove Godwine and his sons, the leading nobles accused before the king of treason, out of England. There were other causes and other instigators of their expulsion also, as I have not elsewhere concealed. But Robert sounded the trumpet more loudly and pressed the accusation more insistently.

At that time the outcome gratified his judgment; but in the following year, when the case was brought before the popular assembly, the exiles were restored. Since the archbishop did not doubt that their reconciliation would harm him, he forestalled the deliberation of judgment by going to Rome. Returning from there with letters pleading his innocence and restoration, he met the end of his life at Jumièges.

Then a certain Stigand, who had once abandoned the bishopric of the East Angles and, contemplating a higher rank, had seized Winchester, grasped the desired opportunity. By circumventing the simplicity of the innocent king, he joined the archbishopric to such high honours for seventeen years [Col. 1458B]. In other respects he was neither unwise nor ineffective. Yet, in the face of ambition, he took no care for his own dignity: whatever he could seize from others, he stored away for himself; he never restrained his avarice. He acquired sacred offices in the churches for himself by money and asserted them for others by speech. In short, he made a public market of bishoprics and abbeys, admitting moderation in desire only where what he desired was unavailable.

Would you not call it bestial rapacity that he alone possessed the bishopric of Winchester and the archbishopric of Canterbury, besides many abbeys, each of which would have been more than sufficient for one worthy man? Yet I suppose that he sinned through error rather than judgment, because, being unlearned—as were most, indeed almost all, bishops of England at that time—he did not know how greatly he offended, imagining that ecclesiastical affairs were to be conducted like secular business [Col. 1458C].

Therefore he never deserved a pallium from Rome, though venality has much power there also, except that one Benedict, an intruder into the Apostolic See, sent one to him in congratulation because Stigand had called him pope when other archbishops treated him as a mockery. But not long afterwards Benedict was deposed; all his acts were annulled, and it was decreed, by sound counsel, that he could not lawfully give a pallium who had not justly possessed the papacy.

Stigand did not come to his senses over these matters, but persisted, thinking little of the salvation of souls so long as he enjoyed earthly honour. Meanwhile William, count of Normandy, came to England and subdued the land by arms, with God’s permission aiding him and with certain causes at hand which he himself judged not weak. Having spread terror of his name through victory at Hastings and the surrender of Dover Castle, he came to London. Stigand, together with the most powerful Englishmen, met him with procession and favour; after exchanging words of agreement, William received him as father and archbishop, and Stigand received William as king and son [Col. 1458D].

Nevertheless, the king refused to receive the crown of the kingdom from Stigand’s hand, using his customary craftiness to suborn opponents on the Apostolic party. Not long afterward, when sailing to Normandy, William drew the reluctant Stigand with him under the pretext of honour, lest any treachery spring up in England through Stigand’s authority while William was absent.

Meanwhile it is difficult to say with what great honours William received him, rising respectfully to him wherever he was, and causing a long ceremonial procession to be made for him in every bishopric and abbey of Normandy. But whatever was concealed under these coverings came openly to light when Ermenfrid, bishop of Sion, legate of Pope Alexander, arrived in England. At the king’s pleasure, he convened a council and deposed Stigand, who appealed to William’s faithfulness and protested violence [Col. 1459A].

Although William gently excused himself and cited the pope’s command, he did not dispel the suspicion that the deposition had been sought, since he held Stigand in chains at Winchester for the rest of his life. There Stigand sustained life on scant food, because little was supplied to him from the treasury and because, through his inborn hardness of mind, he permitted none of his own resources to be brought in.

Indeed, when friends—and especially Queen Edith, widow of King Edward—urged him to dress and feed himself more comfortably, he swore by every holy thing that he possessed not a penny nor anything of value. But the absence of truth from this oath was proved by the vast quantity of wealth found after his death in underground hiding-places. A small key hanging from the dead man’s neck helped lead to this discovery. As keeper of a private chest, when inserted in its lock it revealed, through documents found there [Col. 1459C], both the kinds of metals and the amounts of their weights.

Stigand had not yet breathed his last when King William chose Lanfranc, abbot of Caen, for the archbishopric. Lanfranc was by nation a Lombard, born of a family neither wholly low nor obscure. Eminently learned, he summoned from Italy into Gaul the liberal arts which had long been neglected and refined them by his acuteness. Having spent his younger years in secular studies, he matured both in mind and age in the divine Scriptures.

Instructed by these, he despised the smoke of the world and the inflated eloquence of the pagans, and conceived a desire for monastic life. Having long surveyed many places, he chose in preference to all the abundance of abbeys Bec in Normandy [Col. 1459D], captivated by the poverty of the place and the religious devotion of its monks. For, happening to arrive there, he saw the abbot himself, named Herluin, girded for baking bread and with his hands smeared with dung.

Thus, once made a monk there, although he did not know how to seek his livelihood by rustic labour, Lanfranc publicly taught schools of dialectic, so as to relieve the monastery’s poverty by the generosity of scholars. His reputation reached the most distant regions of the Latin world, and Bec became a great and famous academy of learning.

The glory of praise stirred envy against him among wicked men. Chaplains who saw themselves to be below his learning disturbed Count William’s mind against him, because Lanfranc had openly mocked one of them for ignorance of letters. Lanfranc therefore received an edict ordering him to free Normandy from his troublesome presence [Col. 1460A]. He came to court and quickly obtained the count’s pardon, because William immediately understood, from Lanfranc’s impressive appearance and the wit of his reply, what great prudence he possessed, inferring the inner qualities from the outward signs.

Not long afterwards William made him abbot at Caen, where he had raised from its foundations the monastery of Saint Stephen. Then, elevated to the throne of the kingdom, he appointed him archbishop, as I have said. Lanfranc himself will explain this better in his own writing. Concerning his appointment, and the controversy stirred up and settled between himself and Thomas of York, he wrote as follows.

> In the year 1070 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Lanfranc, abbot of the monastery of Caen, entered the land of England, at the urging and command of William, the glorious king of the English, and Alexander, of happy memory, supreme pontiff of the whole holy Church [Col. 1460B]. A few days after his arrival, he undertook the governance of the Church of Canterbury.
>
> He was consecrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the metropolitan see, by the suffragans of that see: William, bishop of London; Siward of Rochester; Walchelin of Winchester; Remigius of Dorchester, or Lincoln; Herfast of Elmham, or Thetford; Stigand of Selsey; Herman of Sherborne; and Giso of Wells. The others who were absent made known the causes of their absence both through legates and through letters.
>
> In the same year Thomas, bishop-elect of the Church of York, came to Canterbury, according to ancient custom, to be consecrated by Lanfranc. When Lanfranc demanded from him a written profession of obedience, with the addition of an oath, preserving the custom of his predecessors, Thomas answered that he would never do this unless he first read written authorities on the matter, saw witnesses affirming this ancient custom, and finally heard suitable reasons why he ought justly and reasonably to do this without prejudice to his own church [Col. 1460C].
>
> He did this more through ignorance than through the stubbornness of an exalted spirit. For he was a new man, wholly unfamiliar with English custom, and gave more credence than was proper and good to the words of flatterers. Nevertheless, in the presence of the few bishops who had come to Lanfranc for this consecration, Lanfranc showed him what he demanded. But Thomas rejected everything and departed unconsecrated.
>
> When the king heard this, he took it seriously, believing that Lanfranc was demanding unjust things and relying more upon literary learning than upon truth and reason—although Thomas himself was not lacking in learning, acquired by great talent and great application. After a few days had passed, Lanfranc came to court and asked for a hearing from the king. Having given his reasons, he calmed the king’s mind; and he convinced the overseas men who were present that justice was on his side. The English, who knew the matter, bore fully steadfast testimony to his assertions [Col. 1460D].
>
> Accordingly, by royal edict and the common decree of all, it was established that Thomas must for the present return to the mother church of the whole kingdom, write a profession, read what he had written, and, after it had been read, present it to Lanfranc in the presence of the bishops while under examination. In it he was to promise without qualification, and without any condition being interposed, that he would obey Lanfranc’s commands in all matters pertaining to the observance of the Christian religion. But he was not to make the same unconditional promise to Lanfranc’s successors unless first, either in their presence or in an episcopal council, a sufficient reason were given him, demonstrating most clearly that his predecessors had done this and ought to have done it for the primates of the Church of Canterbury.
>
> Therefore he returned, fulfilled what had been ordered, and departed consecrated. Not many days later Lanfranc sought and received professions from all the bishops of the English kingdom who, at different times and in different places, had been consecrated by other archbishops or by the pope in Stigand’s time. In the following year he went to Rome with the aforesaid archbishop [Col. 1461A]. Received honourably by the Apostolic See, he received one pallium from the altar according to Roman custom; Pope Alexander himself gave him with his own hand another, in token of his affection, namely the one in which Pope Alexander was accustomed to celebrate Mass.
>
> In Alexander’s presence Thomas raised a complaint concerning the primacy of the Church of Canterbury and the subjection of three bishops: those of Dorchester or Lincoln, Worcester, and Lichfield, now Chester. He said that the churches of Canterbury and York possessed equal honour in relation to one another, and that neither ought in any way to be subject to the other under the ordinance of Saint Gregory, except that one of the two archbishops must be prior and more dignified than the one known to have been consecrated later. He further said that the aforesaid three bishops had from ancient times been subject to his see and his predecessors [Col. 1461B].
>
> Lanfranc, on hearing this, though he took it badly, answered with moderate discernment that Thomas’s words were wholly devoid of truth. He maintained that the Gregorian ordinance had been issued not concerning the churches of Canterbury and York, but concerning those of London and York. After many arguments on both sides concerning this matter and the three bishops, Pope Alexander decreed that the case ought to be heard in England and settled there by the testimony and judgment of the bishops and abbots of the whole kingdom.
>
> Although Lanfranc held Thomas bound during his own lifetime by the profession Thomas had made, he nevertheless preferred to labour on behalf of his successors rather than leave them so great a disputed claim to be adjudicated in the future [Col. 1461D]. Therefore both came to the king at the Easter solemnity, and there, after the arguments of the parties had been set forth, the royal court gave judgment on the matter.
>
> It was ordered that a record be made containing the whole case and its conclusion. Lanfranc sent Pope Alexander a letter in which he briefly and truthfully related the entire course of the affair. Both documents are written below, appended after the profession previously given, which Thomas presented hand to hand to Lanfranc in the presence of the king and his court.

> “It is fitting that every Christian be subject to Christian laws and not oppose, on any grounds whatsoever, those things which have been beneficially instituted by the holy Fathers. For from this arise wrath, dissensions, envies, quarrels, [Col. 1462A] and the other things that plunge their devotees into eternal punishments; and the higher a person’s rank, the more earnestly he ought to obey the divine commands. Therefore I, Thomas, now ordained metropolitan bishop of the Church of York, having heard and learned the arguments, make to you, Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, and to your successors, an unqualified profession of canonical obedience; and I promise that I shall observe whatever shall be justly and canonically enjoined upon me by you or by them. But in this matter, while I was to be ordained by you, I was uncertain. And therefore I promised that I would obey you without condition, but your successors conditionally. In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1072, [Col. 1462B] in the sixth year of the reign of William, glorious King of the English and Duke of the Normans, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander, the case concerning primacy was discussed and debated in the presence of the king, bishops, and abbots. Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, asserted over the Church of York the right belonging to his Church, and also concerning the ordinations of certain bishops, regarding whom it was by no means certainly established to which see they particularly belonged. At length it was proved and shown, by the authorities for the several causes, that the Church of York ought to be subject to the Church of Canterbury, and that its archbishops ought in all matters pertaining to Christian religion to obey the ordinances of the Primate of all Britain.  
>
> “Moreover, the metropolitan of Canterbury granted that the Archbishop of York and his successors should hold in perpetuity the subjection [Col. 1462C] of the Bishop of Durham—that is, Lindisfarne—and of all regions from the boundaries of the Bishop of Lichfield and the great river Humber to the uttermost limits of Scotland, together with whatever on this side of the aforesaid river rightfully belongs to the diocese of the Church of York. Thus, if the Archbishop of Canterbury wishes to convene a council, wherever he sees fit, the Archbishop of York shall, at his command, present himself with all bishops subject to him and shall obey his canonical ordinances.  
>
> “Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, showed from the ancient custom of his predecessors that the Archbishop of York ought to make his profession to the Archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 1462D] even under oath. But, out of love for the king, he released Thomas, Archbishop of York, from the oath and received only a written profession, without prejudicing his successors who might wish to require from Thomas’s successors an oath together with the profession. If the Archbishop of Canterbury dies, the Archbishop of York shall come to Canterbury and, with the other bishops of the aforesaid Church, shall lawfully consecrate as his own primate the person who has been elected. But if the Archbishop of York dies, the person elected to succeed him, after receiving from the king the grant of the archbishopric, shall come to Canterbury, or wherever the Archbishop of Canterbury sees fit, [Col. 1463A] and shall receive ordination from him according to canonical custom.”

If I were to set out here Lanfranc’s entire letter to Pope Alexander, it would certainly be burdensome. I shall therefore insert only what pertains to the matter, adding also the privileges of the Apostolic See, which he himself declares were of great assistance in establishing his case. Thus no one should justly accuse me of transferring another’s glory to myself by filling my volume with writings of this sort; rather, if he judges fairly, he should excuse the necessity undertaken by this history. Indeed, the diligent reader should thank the writer, because he will find gathered here everything which it would be laborious to search out through many volumes and doubtful whether it could ever perhaps be found. Moreover, since the controversy between the two metropolitans [Col. 1463B] has not even yet subsided, but is still the subject of great litigation, when I come in due order to those who now disagree, I shall not need to show which side rests upon truth, since I shall already have anticipated the matter in the time of this Lanfranc.

> “To the lord Alexander, supreme overseer of the whole Christian religion, pope, Lanfranc, bishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, offers due obedience with all service.
>
> “At the council convened in England by your authority, where the complaints of Archbishop Thomas were presented and debated, there was produced the Ecclesiastical History of the English people, composed by Bede, priest of the Church of York and teacher of the English. [Col. 1463C] Passages were read which, with the assent of all, demonstrated that from the time of blessed Augustine, first Archbishop of Canterbury, down to Bede’s own last age—a period extending over nearly one hundred and forty years—my predecessors exercised primacy over the Church of York, over the whole island called Britain, and also over Ireland; they bestowed pastoral care upon all; they frequently celebrated episcopal ordinations and councils in the city of York itself and in neighboring places, wherever they saw fit; they summoned the bishops of York to these councils and, when circumstances required, compelled them to give an account of their actions.
>
> “It was also shown that the bishops whose subjection Thomas had called into question [Col. 1463D] had, within that period of one hundred and forty years, been consecrated by the Archbishops of Canterbury, summoned by them to councils, and in some cases, when their faults required it, deposed by them with the authority of the Roman See; and there were many other matters of this kind which the modest limits of a letter cannot explain individually. Various councils were produced for reading, which my predecessors had held at different times and for different causes. Although they did not have the same subject in their enactments, they nevertheless maintained the same judgment concerning primacy and the subjection of bishops. There were also recited the elections, made before my predecessors, of those bishops concerning whom the dispute was being conducted, and their ordinations by my predecessors; these bishops had left written professions to the Church of Canterbury concerning their obedience.
>
> “For the city now [Col. 1464A] called Canterbury was in ancient times called Dorobernia by the inhabitants of the land itself. Nor were records lacking that disclosed how, when England was divided among several petty kings, the king of the Northumbrians, in whose territory the city of York lies, sold a bishopric to a certain simoniac for a price; for this fault he was summoned by the Archbishop of Canterbury to a council, and, refusing to come, incurred a sentence of excommunication for his disobedience. The whole Church of those regions abstained from his communion and fellowship until he appeared at the council and corrected what had been wrongly done.
>
> “Finally, as the last support and foundation of the entire case, there were produced the privileges and writings of your predecessors Gregory, Boniface, Honorius, Vitalian, Sergius, and likewise Gregory, Leo, and John, which were given and sent, at different times and for different reasons, to the bishops of Canterbury and the kings of the English. For the remaining originals and copies, as authoritative as these, were utterly consumed in the burning and destruction suffered by our Church four years ago. After these and other matters, which cannot be explained separately and briefly, had been argued on behalf of our Church, Thomas advanced, against evidence of so many and such great authorities, only the fewest objections. Chiefly, he produced the letter in which blessed Gregory established that the Churches of London and York were equal and that neither [Col. 1464C] was subject to the other. Since all immediately agreed that this document was irrelevant, because I was not Bishop of London and the question did not concern the Church of London, he turned to other feeble and inadequate arguments, which, after a short delay and through Christ’s revelation, were overthrown by a few objections, etc.”

> “To the most excellent and most distinguished lord son Æthelberht, King of the English, Boniface, bishop, servant of the servants of God.
>
> “Since the soundness of your Christianity has so grown in devotion to the worship of its Creator that it shines far and wide, and reports throughout the whole world the increase of your God-worthy works, we render immense thanks to God, the giver of all good things, [Col. 1464D] who has looked down upon you from on high and raised you to so lofty a summit of virtues. Therefore, glorious son, we willingly grant what you requested from the Apostolic See through our fellow bishop Mellitus: namely, that your generosity may establish without restriction a dwelling-place for monks living according to rule in the monastery situated in the city of Canterbury, which your holy teacher Augustine, disciple of Gregory of blessed memory, consecrated to the name of the Holy Saviour, and over which our most beloved brother Laurence is now known to preside. By apostolic authority we decree that your preachers, being monks, may join to themselves a community of monks and adorn their life with the practices of holiness.
>
> “If any of your successors—whether kings, [Col. 1465A] bishops, clerics, or laypersons—should attempt to invalidate these our decrees, let him be bound by the bond of anathema under the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, and all his successors, until he repents of what he has rashly done by satisfaction pleasing to the Lord and makes true amends for this disturbance. Farewell in Christ, lord son. Sent by the hand of Mellitus, Bishop of London, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 615.”

> “To the most beloved brother Justus, Boniface, bishop, servant of the servants of God.
>
> “Having received the letters of your affection, in which we found, among other things, that very many gentiles dwelling there have, by the aid of Almighty God and our Lord Jesus Christ, been converted, and especially that in the regions of Kent they have been brought through your labors [Col. 1465B] to faith in our true God, we rejoiced greatly. We also praise Almighty God because the mind of King Eadbald has been corrected toward the way of true knowledge: he has not abandoned the sacrament of his name or the fruit of your labor, as he himself truly promised to the preachers of the Gospel: ‘Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age’ (Matt. 28). For much mercy has been shown in us before the Lord, as the hearts of barbarian peoples are opened to receive the unique mystery of your preaching. Their salvation has been procured through your merits, that they might advance; for the Lord says: ‘He who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved’ (Matt. [Col. 1465C] 10).
>
> “I have learned from your writing that, as our predecessor Gregory of holy memory established, Augustine and all his successors were henceforth to possess the metropolitan and primary see in the city of Canterbury, where the head of the whole English people has been located since pagan days. But now, through the revelation of Jesus Christ, who is the origin and head of Christianity, that same city is exalted, and the orthodox faith, which is the most noble root, is established there, so that all islanders may reap from that field the most abundant fruit of good work as sustenance for the heavenly homeland. O how happy is that city which deserved to have Christ dwelling within it! Happy is that city, and happy the whole people, since heavenly mercy did not disdain to visit those whom, before the creation of the world, it had predestined to join to itself.
>
> “Therefore let it be far from every Christian that anything established by our predecessor, Lord Pope Gregory, for the city of Canterbury should be diminished or changed now or in future times, whatever disturbances may shake human affairs. [Col. 1465D] Rather, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command and confirm to that effect: that in the city of Canterbury there shall always hereafter be a metropolitan see for all Britain, and we decree with undiminished and perpetual stability that all provinces of the kingdom of the English shall be subject to the metropolitan Church of that place. If anyone should attempt to diminish this Church—which is special and stands under the power and protection of the holy Roman Church—or remove anything from the right of the authority granted to it, [Col. 1466A] may Almighty God remove him from the book of life; and let him know that he is bound under the bonds of anathema. May God keep you safe, reverend brother.”

> “To the most beloved brother Honorius, Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God.
>
> “Having received the letter of your affection, we found in it the concern of your labor for the flock entrusted to you, occupied amid much weariness. As evils and worldly practices increase, your mind often endures the burden of difficulties through much labor and distress. We therefore urge your affection to maintain the work of the Gospel which you have begun, a work in which you must labor and persevere rather than abandon it. Remember the Gospel command which says: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers’ (Luke [Col. 1466B] 22). And again in the Apostle: ‘Be steadfast and immovable, knowing that your labor is not in vain before the Lord’ (1 Cor. 5).
>
> “Therefore we earnestly admonish your affection that the acquisition of you and your predecessors, which has sprung up from the beginnings of Lord Gregory, may through faith and works in the fear and love of God grow stronger and spread more widely; so that the promise of the Lord’s word may summon you to the eternal feast, which says: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matt. 11). And again: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many’ (Matt. [Col. 1466C] 25).
>
> “Meanwhile, you requested that the authority of your see be confirmed by the privilege of our authority. Without any delay, and with a gracious disposition, we assent to what is right: that what we know was once established and ordered by our predecessors should be confirmed also by us. Following in their footsteps, according to the rite of ancient custom which your Church has possessed until now from the time of Augustine, your predecessor of holy memory, we grant by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that you, Honorius, and your successors shall possess forever the primacy of all the churches of Britain. We therefore command that all the churches and regions of England be subject to your jurisdiction, and that in the city of Canterbury the metropolitan see, the honor of the archbishopric, [Col. 1466D] and the headship of all the churches of England be preserved forever hereafter; and that it not be transferred to another place by any person through evil counsel. But if anyone, prompted by the swelling of pride, acts otherwise, disobeys our command, and strives to resist the dignity granted to the aforesaid Church, let him know that he is separated from participation in the body and blood of Jesus Christ the Redeemer. May God keep you safe, reverend brother.”

> “To the most beloved brother Theodore, Vitalian, bishop, servant of the servants of God.
>
> “Among the many matters which you directed to be made known to us in your letter, we have also learned of your desire for confirmation of the diocese subject to your authority, because you desire that in all things it should shine by the privilege of apostolic authority granted through you. We therefore assent to your petition, since, in pastoral concern for the churches of God, we understand that they were established from ancient times by this See; and by irrefragable reasoning we wish them to be fortified with perpetual stability both by us and by our successors. [Col. 1467A] We have therefore thought fit to exhort you and presently to entrust to your most discerning holiness all the churches situated in the island of Britain.
>
> “Accordingly, we grant to you forever everything that was established and confirmed by our predecessor Saint Gregory for Augustine, his *syncellus* [confidential clerical assistant], or granted through the sacred use of the pallium; and hold the city of Canterbury, where the Catholic faith was first received, through the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in accordance with the institution of the sacred canons. By the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord God gave power to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, we—though unworthy, yet holding the office of the same blessed Peter, key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven—grant to you, Theodore, and to your successors in perpetuity, [Col. 1467B] to possess without diminution in your metropolitan see situated at Canterbury those things which were bestowed from ancient times.
>
> “But if anyone—which we do not desire—should attempt to contravene the authority of this privilege of our apostolic decree: if he is a bishop, priest, or deacon, we decree by this apostolic authority that the bishop shall lose the rank of his episcopate, and that the priest or deacon shall know himself deposed from his grade. But if he is numbered among the laity, whether king or prince, or person great or small, let him know himself excluded from participation in our Lord Jesus Christ. We entrust this document of privilege, supported by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose ministry we exercise, to you, Theodore, and your successors for perpetual possession. [Col. 1467C] May God keep you safe, most beloved brother.”

> “Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Æthelred, Alfred, and Aldulf, kings of the English.
>
> “The gift of spiritual grace kindles the faithful hearts through the illumination of the Holy Spirit; it restores them by renewing them; it strengthens them by the constancy of wondrous virtue; it establishes them to deserve perpetually the aid of heavenly gifts and benefits; and likewise to forestall the downfall of transient things. By using this gift of God’s mercy, the holy Fathers, shining gloriously across the whole circuit of the world like certain radiant luminaries of the heavenly stars, deserved, after the happy joys of this present life, to be enrolled among the number of the elect.
>
> “But you, holy nation, chosen race, people for God’s possession, children of light, royal stock, offspring of faith: rejoice in the Lord and exult in the increase of virtues, because the excellent and chief of the apostles, Peter—the most steadfast rock of faith—is not forgetful of your zeal. Delighting in the disposition of your minds and consciences, he remembers and acknowledges your names. For we trust that [Col. 1468A] he opens the entrance to the heavenly kingdom for those upon whom, conspicuous among the nations by God’s favor, he has bestowed so great a favor of dignity.
>
> “Therefore, most Christian and most beloved sons, receive with eager heart and devout mind Bishop Brithwald, prelate of the see of Kent and first bishop of all Britain, appointed over you by his authority. Know that whoever receives him as a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; but if anyone, which God forbid, should rise up to despise him in arrogant pride, he despises not him but the one by whom he was sent. According to the Lord’s word, such a person shall be condemned without any defense. Therefore let such unspeakable presumption be far from you and far away, lest the ancient enemy find in you the dreadful countenance of disobedience—you whom the holy Church of God has deemed worthy to join to her bosom as adopted children. [Col. 1468B] We pray that our Lord Jesus Christ, in his accustomed mercy, may exalt you beyond expression in the honor of your ministry and royal eminence, and preserve you at the examination of the future judgment.”

> “To all most beloved brothers, bishops established throughout Britain, Sergius.
>
> “As the heavenly condescension of mercy, which has granted us the care and governance of the pastoral office of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, brought us the venerable presence of an unknown brother, so also the welcome news of your most religious company of bishops brought us a double gift of rejoicing. For we rendered immense thanks to the Lord our God, author of all good things, on finding among faithful brothers in the bosom of holy mother Church the devout constancy of unanimity, fervent love, [Col. 1468C] and fellowship of mutual affection. For in this way they are known to propitiate God with discerning diligence, offering him pure offerings while nourishing in the ark of their hearts the brightness of the true light: so that no allurements deceive their minds, no provocations of brothers strike their hearts, and they do not stir their neighbors to harm by malicious intentions; but, as ministers of God, may they present themselves to those subject to them as a mirror of life and conduct through the excellence of their character. Thus they shall find the Lord favorable to them in adversity, nor shall the snares of the enemy be able to harmfully steal anything from them; for where the Lord’s help is at hand, every hostility of evil spirits is driven away.
>
> “Since this is so, rejoicing in paternal utterances with the unanimous devotion of your brotherly love, we make known [Col. 1468D] to you that our most beloved brother Brithwald [otherwise Bertwald], prelate of the province of Canterbury, who has succeeded to the see of Theodore, former archbishop of venerable memory, has, according to the rite of ancient custom which his Church has possessed from the time of our predecessor Gregory, bishop of Rome, of holy and venerable memory, obtained from us—or rather from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—the primacy of all the churches of Britain, and has there been entrusted with the sacred use of the pallium and the venerable dalmatic. He deservedly obtained this office, dearest brothers, since he gained so great a gift not by arrogance or boastful inflation, but by a lowly disposition and humble heart.
>
> “Therefore we exhort your company, consecrated to God, brethren, and advise you with salutary counsel that, for love of God and hope of future recompense, you should render to that brother, Archbishop of your region, the honor of ministry due as though to ourselves, and should know how to obey effectively a prelate who holds primacy. You are not ignorant of what the vessel of election teaches: ‘Obey your rulers’ (Heb. 13); and again: ‘Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance’ (Rom. 13). [Col. 1469A] Therefore, brethren, we admonish you and command every rank by this apostolic authority that no one presume, either now or in time to come, to oppose these matters which were long ago established by this Apostolic See; rather, let the powers granted to the aforesaid Church always be kept unimpaired forever. And since we confidently trust that, by divine clemency, you will carry out what we have determined to urge upon you, we pray the ineffable power of our holy Saviour that he may grant you, ever flourishing in devout religion, to rejoice in everlasting gladness and, rejoicing in brotherly affections, to be joined through the merits of the saints in eternal blessedness. May God keep you safe, most beloved brothers.”

> “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, greeting to the bishops of England.
>
> “We praise together the greatness of the boundless mercy of Almighty God, who has deigned so to spread the glory of his majesty that now the sound of his preachers has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. By the grace of his ineffable mercy, [Col. 1469C] as we are known to have been begotten, so we have also been adopted, bearing the mystery of holy regeneration in hope of the glory of the children of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Rejoicing with the consecrated college of your reverences, we exhort you to be found steadfast in faith and effective in works, outdoing one another in honor and bearing one another’s burdens. Thus you will fulfill the law of Christ, maintaining constant charity in the love of God and neighbor, without which it is impossible to please God.
>
> “The arrival of our brother Tatwine, who has succeeded to the chair of Augustine of blessed memory, your preacher, greatly delighted us, because while he stayed with us we recognized him as a man of religion and great integrity. Accordingly, having heard his petitions, [Col. 1469D] we caused the rights of dignity belonging to his predecessors to be sought in the sacred archive; and, finding that he had made a just request, we delivered to him by apostolic authority the sacred pallium together with the venerable use of the dalmatic, likewise granting all the rights of dignity which his predecessors are known to have held from the time of Augustine of blessed memory.
>
> “Therefore, just as the decree of our predecessor Gregory, bishop of Rome, subjected all bishops of England to Augustine, his *syncellus* and your aforesaid preacher, so we, with God as author and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, though unworthy holders of his office, subject to you, Tatwine, Archbishop of the city of Canterbury, and to your lawful successors all churches of Britain and their rulers. By apostolic authority we command [Col. 1470A] that every person throughout England obey your canonical commands and recognize you as primate and overseer of the whole island, to whom we have entrusted in every respect the exercise of our authority in that region. We hold your Church, established at Canterbury, as the special and first offspring of your Christian religion, particularly under the protection of our hand in Christ. We desire it to flourish in the tranquility of peace and that its rights and privileges of dignity be forever preserved undiminished, since it is the first and mother of all the others, first founded in your region in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ the Holy Saviour. For it is written: ‘There is none holy as the Lord’ (2 Sam. 2); and where the head is vigorous, the remaining members thrive more strongly.
>
> “Therefore, brothers, hear and receive these commands of apostolic authority with eagerness and the reverence of subjection, and labor with your aforesaid brother, your archbishop, in God’s harvest. But if anyone wishes to disturb these things and strives to tear down and violate the provisions of our decree, let him know that he is opposing the Saviour of the world himself and the authority of blessed Peter, and consequently, unless he comes to his senses, [Col. 1470B] will incur the sentence of eternal damnation. May God keep you safe, most beloved brothers.”

> “Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Edhelard [otherwise Athelard], Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, in perpetuity.
>
> “It particularly befits episcopal discernment to grant a hearing to prelates of churches according to their irreproachable faith and to grant effect to those things which they desire to conduct through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through us, provided they do not conflict with canonical enactments; so that, once they have obtained what they desire, they may become more fervent in love for religion. We must therefore exhort and commend your brotherly graciousness concerning the dioceses of England entrusted to you, namely those of bishops and of monasteries of monks, clerics, and nuns. As your Church has held these from ancient times, as we have learned on inquiry in our sacred archive, so we confirm them to be held by you and your successors.
>
> “The holy and excellent preacher Gregory ordained and Catholicly confirmed that all the churches of the English should be subject forever to blessed Augustine, archbishop and his *syncellus*, [Col. 1470D] through the sacred use of the pallium. Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord God granted power to bind and loose, saying, ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 16)—and indeed according to the decrees of the sacred canons—we, though unworthy, holding the office of that same Peter, key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, grant to you, Adelard, and to your successors, that all the churches of the English, as they have been from ancient times, shall be possessed in perpetuity in your metropolitan see by an irrefragable right of acknowledged subjection.
>
> “But if anyone—which we do not desire—should attempt to contravene the authority of this decree of ours or apostolic privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that, if he is an archbishop or bishop, he shall be deposed from episcopal rank; likewise, if he is a priest, deacon, or any other minister of sacred ministry, he shall be deposed from his order. But if he belongs to the laity, whether king, prince, or any person great or small, let him know himself excluded from participation in holy communion. [Col. 1471B] We grant this document of privilege, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose ministry we exercise, to you, Edhelard, and your successors for perpetual possession. For its confirmation we have signed it with our own hands and commanded it to be marked with our name. We also ordered it to be written by Sergius, our archivist, in the month of January; issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January], by the hand of Eustathius, *primicerius* of the holy Apostolic See, in the reign of the most pious lord Charles, consul Augustus, God-crowned, great and peaceable emperor, in the second year after the consulship of that same lord, in the tenth indiction.”

> “To all the bishops of England, brothers and sons in Christ, Formosus.
>
> “Having heard that the abominable rites of pagans had sprung up again in your regions, and that you had kept silence like [Col. 1471C] dogs unable to bark, we had determined to strike you with the sword of separation from the body of God’s Church. But because, as our beloved brother Plegmund informed us, you have at last awakened and have begun to renew the seeds of God’s word once reverently sown in the land of the English, we draw back the sword of zeal and send you the blessing of Almighty God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, praying that you may persevere in what you have well begun.
>
> “For you are the brothers of whom the Lord says among other things: ‘You are the salt of the earth; but if salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted?’ (Matt. 5). And again: ‘You are the light of the world,’ intending to signify that human minds ought to be seasoned by you through the word of wisdom, and that the zeal of good action should appear in your conduct and life as a light of faith. By this light, those who walk may see how cautiously they ought to proceed toward life, so that, running without stumbling toward the promise of eternal blessedness, they may be able to arrive there.
>
> “Now therefore gird yourselves and keep watch against the lion that goes about seeking whom he may devour. Do not allow the Christian faith any longer to be harmed in your land by a shortage of shepherds, nor God’s flock to wander, be scattered, and be dispersed. But when one dies, let another qualified person be appointed in his place without delay according to canon law. For under the Law ‘many were made priests, because they were prevented by death from remaining.’ David, considering this and foreseeing in the Spirit of Christ that the Church would endure until the end of the age, says: ‘In place of your fathers sons shall be born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth’ (Ps. 44).
>
> “Therefore let there be no delay in appointing another [Col. 1472A] when any priest departs this life; rather, as soon as the death of a brother is reported to the one who holds the primacy of the first see among you and is known to preside over the other bishops, let a canonical election be made and another be consecrated to succeed him. But who among you ought to hold primacy, and which episcopal see ought to surpass the others and possess primacy, has been most well known since ancient times. For, as we maintain from the writings of blessed Gregory and his successors, the metropolitan and first episcopal see of the kingdom of the English is certainly in the city of Canterbury, over which our venerable brother Plegmund now presides. We in no way permit the honor of his dignity to be diminished, but command him to exercise apostolic authority in every respect.
>
> “And just as blessed Pope Gregory established that all bishops of the English should be subject to Augustine, the first bishop of your people, so we confirm the same dignity to the aforesaid brother, Archbishop of Canterbury—or Cantorbury—and to his lawful successors. We command, and by the authority of God and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, direct [Col. 1472B] that all obey his canonical ordinances and that none shall violate the things granted to him and his successors by apostolic authority. But if any person should ever strive against these matters or attempt to diminish them, let him know beyond doubt that he shall be punished with a grave anathema and, unless he comes to his senses, shall be perpetually separated from the body of the holy Church which he seeks to disturb.”

> “John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his fellow bishop [Col. 1472C] Dunstan, Archbishop of the Church of Canterbury: abiding salvation in Christ unto eternal life.”

> “If shepherds of sheep are content to endure sun and frost by day and night for the protection of their flock, keeping watch with vigilant eyes lest any sheep perish by straying or be carried off, torn by the bites of wild beasts, how great must be our care and labour in keeping vigil for the salvation of souls, whose shepherds we are said to be. Let us therefore attend to the duty laid upon us of guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest, terrified when the wolf comes, we take flight; lest, on the day of divine judgment, we be tormented before the supreme Shepherd for our own sloth and your negligence—though now, through the reverence owed to our office, we are judged in a higher station than others. [Col. 1472D]

“Accordingly, we fully confirm to you your primacy, in which, according to the custom of your predecessors, it is fitting that you exercise the functions of the Apostolic See, just as Saint Augustine and his successors, bishops of the aforesaid church, are known to have possessed it. We likewise entrust to your brotherhood the pallium, according to custom, for celebrating the solemnities of Mass. We permit you to use it only in the manner handed down by our predecessors, while the privileges of your church remain unimpaired. Nor is it unknown to your prudence how formidable the honour of this garment will be, unless your conduct is kept within due bounds. These ornaments befit the uprightness of your morals, so that, with God as author, you may be conspicuous, and your life may be a rule for your sons. Whatever strength is in them [Col. 1473A] may be directed thereby, while they behold in it what they should imitate.

“And at the end of the letter: May the Holy Trinity surround your brotherhood with the protection of its grace, and so guide you in the path of its fear that, after the bitterness of this life, we may together deserve to attain eternal sweetness. And this was written by the hand of Leo, notary of the Apostolic See, in the month of October, on the first day before the Kalends of October, in the fourth indiction, in the twelfth year of the supreme pontiff John.”

These sacred privileges of the holy Apostolic pontiffs, read in a council of all England, then brought great weight [alternatively, support] to the primacy of the Church of Canterbury. Inserted here as well, they will occupy no unsuitable place, if they can avoid wearying readers.

Against these Thomas, Archbishop of York, [Col. 1473B] had little force; nor was a wider field for accusations open to him, though he enlisted battalions of supporters. Yet he maintained that Saint Gregory had granted to Augustine alone that he should have subject to him—not only the bishops whom he ordained, nor merely those ordained by the bishop of York, but all priests of Britain, by the authority of our Lord God Jesus Christ. After Augustine’s death, however, there was to be a reciprocal interchange of favour between the bishops of London and York; and precedence in honour was to belong to the prior ordination. Gregory, he said, had wished Augustine to establish his see in London, but Augustine, softened by the affection of King Æthelberht, had settled in Kent. It would not have been difficult for Gregory, had he seen it to be appropriate, to remove the ambiguity of the controversy with a few words, [Col. 1473C] saying, “I grant these things to you, Augustine, and to all your successors.” But, he claimed, Gregory saw that this conflicted with reason and therefore chose to scatter his words to the winds.

As Thomas continued to say these and many similar things—supplied with weapons for his speech alike by the necessity of defence and by his ignorance of antiquity—Lanfranc entered the disputation, meeting him with the following most vigilant reply:

“The opinion upon which you rely—that subjection of all the bishops of Britain, including those ordained by the bishop of York, was granted to Augustine alone—is devoid of truth. It would have been a paltry and altogether narrow gift for an apostolic man to bestow upon one who had long been his intimate, a newly converted Englishman; especially since, while Augustine lived, no bishop of York was ordained whose subjects Augustine might have had, indeed no bishop existed there at all. For Saint Paulinus, the first bishop of that city, was sent there not in Augustine’s time but in the time of Justus, who was the fourth bishop of Kent. [Col. 1473D]

“The deeds of the English will teach one ignorant of them that what I say is true. Understanding this, the most holy bishops of the Apostolic See confirmed to Augustine’s successors the subjection of all the bishops of England, as the privileges just recited testify. They adorned and most liberally advanced, as they say, the Gregorian constitution, being arbiters of the same see and defenders of the same judgment. They deem it equitable that all the churches of the English should draw their rule of life from that place [Col. 1474A] from whose spring they drew the flame of faith. For who does not know that belief in Christ flowed from Kent into York and the other churches of England?

“Further, what you say—that Saint Gregory could, had he wished, have confirmed to Augustine’s successors in words what he granted Augustine—is entirely true and cannot be doubted. But what injury, I ask, does this bring to the see of Canterbury? I shall propose a similar case. When our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ said to Saint Peter, ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. 16), he could, had he wished, have added, ‘I grant the same power to your successors.’ Yet the omission of those words diminishes nothing of the reverence due to Peter’s successors. [Col. 1474B] Will you oppose these words? Will you make an objection? Indeed, it is renowned in the consciences of all Christians that, no less than before Saint Peter himself, they tremble before his successors when they threaten and joyfully applaud their serene dignity when they grant indulgence. And the administration of all ecclesiastical affairs is valid only when it has been approved by the judgment of the successors of Saint Peter. What accomplishes this except the force of divine liberality, diffused by the Lord Jesus from Saint Peter into his vicars? Therefore, if you know dialectic, you will pronounce the same judgment concerning like cases.

“Moreover, what holds in the whole holds in the part; what holds in the greater holds in the lesser.
