The Roman Church is, as it were, the whole of all churches, [Col. 1474C] and the other churches, as it were, its parts. For just as, in a certain respect, a human being is the genus of individual human beings, and yet in every individual the entire property of humanity is present, so, in a certain respect, the Roman see is the genus and whole of all churches; and yet in every church the entire integrity of the Christian faith reigns. It is the greatest of all churches, and what holds in it ought also to hold in lesser ones: namely, that the authority of the first ruler of any church passes down to his successors, unless something is excepted personally and by name. Therefore, just as Christ said to all Roman bishops what he said to Saint Peter, so Gregory said in Augustine what he said to all Augustine’s successors. From this it follows that, just as Kent is subject to Rome, [Col. 1474D] because it received the faith from Rome, so York is subject to Kent, because Kent sent preachers there.

“Now, what you allege—that Gregory wished Augustine to reside in London—is plainly uncertain. For how could it be established that Augustine, opposing his master’s will, acted contrary to his decrees? Yet I refuse to detract from the credibility of a report confirmed by the agreement of so many. Grant, then, that he might have moved elsewhere: what is that to me, who am not bishop of London? It does not concern me, except that ancient custom does not permit you to share the honour of the primacy with the bishop of London. If you wish this matter to be examined in peaceful negotiation, the dispute being set aside, I shall not fail, as my office requires, to assist a right judgment.”

Thomas yielded to arguments so great and, referring the settlement to a compromise, willingly accepted the condition that the farther bank of the River Humber should be the beginning of his diocese, and the nearer bank the boundary of the parish of Canterbury. [Col. 1475A] Lanfranc, exulting and confident in his victorious cause, recorded the proceedings in writing, lest they pass away and, still recent, slip from memory, and lest posterity be deprived of knowledge of matters necessary to know. He did this modestly indeed: neither omitting what should be known nor overflowing in speech—for to embellish one’s own praises is odious boasting.

Yet I judge that no other man, however great his industry and even if justice herself, which supported Lanfranc, had aided him, could have resolved so great an uncertainty so plainly. For at that time he was most renowned in learning and worldly wisdom, and was reverently admired by Alexander, the Apostolic pontiff. [Col. 1475B] The highest token of honour was that, when Lanfranc came to Rome, Alexander laid aside the aloof pride of Roman hauteur and graciously rose to meet him, declaring that he rendered this reverence not to Lanfranc’s archiepiscopal office but to his mastery of letters. Therefore, Alexander had done what honour required; Lanfranc ought to do what justice required: namely, according to the custom of all archbishops, to cast himself at the feet of Saint Peter’s vicar. Lanfranc repaid the marks of so great affection which he had experienced, so that he would undoubtedly obtain whatever he considered worth asking.

Finally, he restored to office, by his intercessions, both companions of his journey—Thomas, Archbishop of York, and Remigius, Bishop of Lincoln—who had been stripped of staffs and rings: the first because he was the son of a priest; the second because he had been made [Col. 1475C] bishop in return for aid furnished to William when he came to England, thus trading a divine office for military services. The pope, transferring consideration of the matter from himself to Lanfranc, said that Lanfranc himself should return their investitures if he wished and judged it right; if not, he should do whatever he thought expedient. Thus they received staffs and rings from Lanfranc’s hand and joyfully arranged their return home with him.

Nor did Gregory, Alexander’s successor, take less care to court him with affection, transacting many matters by Lanfranc’s advice and sharing with him many matters unknown even to Gregory’s own household. A letter sent to England at the beginning of Gregory’s papacy, found among Lanfranc’s letters, attests the truth of this account. [Col. 1475D] Moreover King William deferred to Lanfranc in all things, rejoiced in him and in others whom he heard to be zealous for good, and permitted him to assemble councils, one proceeding of which is as follows:

> “In the year of the Lord 1075. In the ninth year of King William’s reign, a council was assembled in London, Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, presiding, with Thomas, Archbishop of York, and the other bishops seated with him. The church of Rochester was at that time without a pastor. The bishop of Lindisfarne, who is also bishop of Durham, having a canonical excuse, could not attend the council. Since the practice of councils had fallen into disuse in the English kingdom for many years, certain matters were renewed which had also been defined by ancient canons.
>
> “Accordingly, from the Fourth Council of Toledo, the Council of Milevis, [Col. 1476A] and the Council of Braga, it was decreed that each should sit according to the time of his ordination, except those who by ancient custom or by the privileges of their churches hold more distinguished seats. Concerning this matter, elders and men advanced in age were asked what they themselves had seen, or had truthfully and reliably heard from their elders and predecessors. A delay was requested on the basis of their answer and granted until the next day. On the following day they unanimously declared that the Archbishop of York ought to sit at the right hand of the Archbishop of Canterbury; the Bishop of London at his left; and Wenlanus beside the Archbishop of York. But if the Archbishop of York is absent, the Bishop of London is to be at the right hand and Wenlanus at the left.
>
> “From the Rule of Saint Benedict and from the ancient custom of regular houses: [Col. 1476B] monks are to keep their proper order and possess no property. But if anyone dies unconfessed while possessing property, he is not to be buried in the cemetery.
>
> “From the decrees of the supreme pontiffs Damasus and Leo, and also from the Councils of Sardica and Laodicea, in which an episcopal see is prohibited from being situated in villages: by royal munificence and synodal authority, bishops were permitted to transfer from villages to cities—Hermann from Sherborne to Salisbury; Stigand from Selsey to Chichester; Peter from Lichfield to Chester.
>
> “From many decrees of Roman pontiffs and various authorities of sacred canons: no one is to ordain or retain another’s cleric or monk without letters of recommendation. To restrain the insolence of certain indiscreet persons, it was decreed by common resolution [Col. 1476C] that no one may speak in council without leave granted by the metropolitan, except bishops and abbots. From the decrees of Gregory the Greater and Gregory the Lesser: no one may take as wife a woman of his own kin, or of his deceased wife’s kin, or a woman whom a kinsman has had as wife, where the kinship on either side reaches to the seventh degree. No one may buy or sell sacred orders or an ecclesiastical office. No one may practise lots or divination. From the Councils of Elvira and the Tenth Council of Toledo: no bishop, abbot, or anyone of the clergy may judge a person to be mutilated or put to death, or support those who so judge.”

[Col. 1476D] Meanwhile, while Father Lanfranc strengthened his intellect and ordered his soul with every virtue, his particular maxim, they say, was especially almsgiving: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). When this saying was joyfully accepted by those acclaiming him, he turned with cheerful countenance to the Lord: “Let us compete, then, in reciprocal exchange: you by giving, I by distributing.” Heavenly mercy answered the wish of this praiseworthy man; such abundance flowed to him as could satisfy and surpass any conceivable extent.

Nor was he slow in giving, driving away and shaking off from himself avarice, the vice familiar to Lombards. He was not an unreflecting giver; nor did his generosity go to waste, since discretion and cheerful spirit seasoned it. The radiance of his face [Col. 1477A] did not fall to the ground, but was most welcome to the recipient, like the newly rising sun in the morning, which, scattering clouds, calms the winds and clears the air. Bread, shoes, and indeed everything belonging to food and clothing were distributed to the poor. Money was not given without more mature consideration and deeper counsel, because the common people of that time, even with a stuffed purse, consumed hunger with a dry mouth. As though it were something sacred, he avoided giving money for food, lest the sum be diminished. To needy clerics and monasteries he heaped up an immense quantity of money, often inviting those too bashful to ask.

The archbishop was not ashamed to serve food to the poor, girded high, or to set scholars of slenderer means against one another in contests of disputation. [Col. 1477B] After the debate both went away happy: the victor received the prize of learning, and the defeated received consolation for his modesty. A ravening fire had not long before consumed the buildings of the church over which he presided, while heaps of walls and collapsed roofs increased its ruin. Removing the old foundations, he raised everything to a grander condition; one cannot tell whether by greater beauty or by speed. For the industry of speed increased the glory of his good will. First, indeed, he enclosed the monks in temporary and cramped buildings; afterwards he provided finished and magnificent structures.

It would be excessive to recount how many ornaments he assembled there: in palls and sacred vestments, where the work of goldsmiths surpassed the cost of the material itself; in paintings of diverse colours; [Col. 1477C] or in the enticing brilliance of pigments, where a splendid art seized the mind and the grace of beauty drew the eyes upward to the ceilings. All landed possessions which, through the negligence of predecessors or the violence of officials, groaned under alien control, he restored to domestic right, with the king’s favour and support. He even wrested by legal action from Odo, Bishop of Bayeux and Earl of Kent, the king’s own brother, what that man unjustly held. For that crafty and deceitful spirit had coveted the goods of the Church of Canterbury and would indeed have ruined them, had Lanfranc not stood in his way.

Lanfranc’s soul possessed great vigour, and the favour of the most blessed Dunstan was poured out upon him. Whenever Lanfranc, hesitating in such matters lest affairs turn badly, deferred an unresolved judgment, [Col. 1477D] Dunstan appeared to him in sleep, exposing his opponents’ stratagems and showing paths of escape. Indeed, on one occasion, in a vision, he rescued Lanfranc when ill and weary of his protracted life, seeming to wrestle with him; he delivered him from danger and restored him to health.

The monks of Canterbury, like all monks in England at that time, differed little from secular men except that they did not readily betray chastity. They were diverted by hunting dogs, followed through the air the prey of birds snatched by other birds, pressed the backs of foaming horses, shook dice, indulged in drink, delicate food, and refined dress; they did not know frailty, rejected frugality, and did other such things. Because of the multitude of attendants, you would call them consuls rather than monks. [Col. 1478A] Seeing this, Lanfranc held his peace for some time and did not terrify men already afraid with the bitterness of severity. For, most skilled in the art of arts—that is, the governance of souls—he knew that habit is a second nature and that tender minds are exasperated by a sudden conversion of morals.

Accordingly, by gentle admonitions and at intervals of time, removing now one thing and now another, he sharpened their unformed minds for good on the whetstone of virtues and polished away the rust of vices. Wherever he uprooted seedlings of evil, he immediately planted seeds of good. Nor did he cease until, after repudiating bastard offspring, they freely adopted the fruitful progeny of virtues. Today they are more numerous than anywhere in England, as is fitting, and are not inferior in religious observance to the Cluniacs.

[Col. 1478B] Lanfranc is still greatly present among them: much remembrance of the man, great devotion to God, and gracious kindness toward visitors remain; nor shall his universal charity toward all and singular care for each individual ever be erased. He never allowed anyone to remain sad; but if he saw anyone downcast, he immediately asked the cause and, once he knew it, promptly sought a remedy. Of his own accord he offered money to young men with which they might meet the wants of their own dependents. If, however, what he gave were accidentally lost, he doubled it and ordered that this be kept hidden from others. He further provided for monks throughout England, so that they should neither lack necessities nor fall short of the Rule.

By this time the envy of bishops had increased; they wished to drive monks from episcopal sees by introducing clerics. [Col. 1478C] The author of this faction was Walchelm of Winchester, otherwise a good man, but in this matter bent to an evil purpose by the counsels of whisperers. He had arrayed more than forty canons in copes and surplices. He had drawn the king to his view, and the measure had advanced so far that he sought the archbishop’s consent. That this consent should not be obtained was beyond doubt. Lanfranc shuddered when he heard of the deed and dissolved, at a mere glance, the contrived devices of so many powerful men as if they were spiderwebs. Moreover, lest their successors should dare the same thing, he secured a written prohibition from Pope Alexander. This was a great and praiseworthy act: what the diligent benevolence of holy men had begun in the time of King Edgar, Lanfranc did not permit to be shaken.

[Col. 1478D] Yet his deed should never be measured by comparison with theirs. They, teachers of all England and favoured also by the king, easily accomplished whatever they wished. Lanfranc alone, however, opposed so many adversaries, brought the undertaking through, and prevailed. Through Abbot Paul, whom he installed there, he raised the abbey of Saint Albans to its present condition. In the bishopric of Rochester, the serving clerics could scarcely rise to the number of four, and they themselves lacked daily bread. Supporting them at his own expense through Bishop Gundulf, he introduced fifty monks and procured for them a splendid estate, so that they might not only suffer no want but even enjoy abundance of provisions.

Outside the city of Canterbury, on the northern side, he established stone houses for all the needy; on the western side, wooden ones for persons afflicted with royal sickness. [Col. 1479A] He also established regular canons at Saint Gregory’s to perform the divine offices for them. With dwellings divided according to sex, expenses supplied, and attendants assigned, he pursued works of this kind during the reign of William the Elder. He suffered few refusals from William in matters he thought should be sought. For although the king was less courteous toward others, toward Lanfranc he was affectionate and gentle. Thus he extended his hand to justice when it struggled, lest it fall headlong.

Yet Lanfranc often lamented to his friends that he was weary of life. A man of penetrating mind and mature age, he conjectured and foretold from present circumstances the calamity to come. Nor did his judgment deceive him. For when his father died and the younger [Col. 1479B] William succeeded to the kingdom, finding Lanfranc little disposed to connive at his purposes, he won him over to support his cause by enormous promises to preserve right and justice. But after obtaining power and being beset by many anxieties arising from the rebellion of nearly all the magnates, he neglected his promises. Therefore, reminded by the archbishop of his pledge, he answered stormily, “Who can do everything that he promises?”

Wearied by this, Lanfranc did not prolong his time in the light much longer. After nineteen years in the episcopate, he contracted a fever. When the consulted physicians prescribed a necessary drink, he first fortified himself by confession and the viaticum. Then, having taken the cup, he breathed his last when its effect turned contrary, receiving the kind of death he had always wished for. [Col. 1479C] For he confessed to those of his household that he prayed to the Lord to die while dysentery or fever pressed upon him, because such illnesses neither disturb the memory nor impede speech.

Canterbury will praise his industry, and Latin letters will marvel at his learning in his pupils, for as long as all years endure. He himself left few monuments of his intellect: decretal letters, and especially his work against Berengar.

After him the archiepiscopal see stood vacant for more than four years. The king, too credulous of the counsels of wicked whisperers, counted all its revenues as his own. But I have elsewhere spoken much of such matters, giving, as is fitting, great deference to royal majesty. At present another task presses upon us: to continue the sequence of events concerning Lanfranc’s successor. Although I shall relate words in order but deeds in summary, [Col. 1479D] yielding with ready favour to Lord Eadmer, who set everything forth so clearly that he seems in some manner to have placed it before our eyes.

The subject is Anselm. Born in the city of Aosta, which presents itself as the first city beyond the Alps, he raised the modest rank of his birth to the highest renown by the torch of his virtues. As a boy he applied himself to letters; after passing beyond childhood, he never disturbed his chastity even by a wanton glance. His father’s anger gave the young man occasion to leave his native land. Since he could not soften that anger by any resource, he escaped through departure, lest domestic hostility pass into a violation of nature. Having crossed the Alps, he anxiously pondered where to turn; divine favour calmed his uncertainty, directing him to go to Lanfranc in Normandy, [Col. 1480A] with whom, if he remained, he might ease his exile both through the bond of homeland and through the stimulus of learning.

When, therefore, he came to Bec, Lanfranc received him graciously, and he became a great assistance to him in directing the schools. Meanwhile virtue grew with age and diligence with talent. The springtime of his life was already preparing to advance into the strength of youth. He was twenty-seven years old when he was inspired with the desire for monastic religion.

For even long before, while still a small child, he had desired this same thing, entertaining great aspirations within a little body. He had asked for and received an illness so severe that both parents, terrified, vowed their son to God. But then he reasoned extensively with himself whether it were better to live as a hermit or as a monk. [Col. 1480B] If as a monk, whether a rich or a poor house better benefited the soul. A rich house would offer abundance of revenues but take away the burden of penitence through the abundance of necessities. A poor one, on the contrary, would drive out luxury through labour, but might multiply grumbling through weakness of resources. Again, whether it were better to become a monk at Bec or elsewhere. If at Bec, he had worn out his intellect in letters to no purpose, because there would be no one there to teach; for however great his learning, Lanfranc’s fame would eclipse it. If elsewhere, where few were distinguished in letters, pride might arise from the isolation and singularity of his learning.

After long maturing these reflections within himself, he poured them out at a suitable moment into the breast of Lanfranc, who loved him. [Col. 1480C] Lanfranc judged that the matter should be referred to Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, because Maurilius was a monk and, by reason of his long religious experience, a discerning judge of every form of religious life. Why delay? When the arguments had been presented and considered, monastic life was preferred to all religious vocations, because monks alone live under another’s judgment, submit to obedience, and renounce their own will. Bec was chosen as the place: there a measured way of life between poverty and excess would neither crush him with labour nor enervate him with softness; there comparison with Lanfranc would suppress rising pride in Anselm. A monk was not to trade teaching for fame or sell learning for the desire of glory.

Thus he became a monk there; and after three years, when Lanfranc was transferred to Caen, Abbot Herluin appointed him prior. In this office he cultivated his life for fifteen years with every virtue, attending especially to the young, whom, because of the tenderness of their age, either diligence might shape toward good or negligence toward evil. [Col. 1480D] He accustomed himself to such frugality that his vital organs, then constricted, even later, had they wished, refused an entrance to more ample food. He rooted out the vice of private possession in himself by determination and in others by preaching, declaring that this alone had expelled the devil from heaven and humanity from paradise: namely, that they who had deserted God’s command had indulged their own will.

Thus, removing indulgence from the independent judgment of his mind, he accumulated nothing external at all, avoiding every kind of sin so strictly that he said he would rather be without sin in hell than with sin in heaven. A saying received then with applause, [Col. 1481A] it now requires an interpreter; but another expositor must be sought elsewhere. The intensity of his prayers and meditations is shown by the book written on these matters, as we believe, at the dictation of the Holy Spirit; from its abundance he had drunk deeply to the marrow. So also do the books of his soliloquies with himself and addresses to God show it: in them he surpassed the thoughts of all predecessors—or, to speak more mildly, gathered them into a single heap.

For whereas they wish to compel our belief by authority, he strengthens it by reason, proving with invincible arguments that what we believe is so and cannot be otherwise. By discernment and patience he won the hearts of those rivals who grieved that he had been placed over them. By his diligent care for a dead youth, he kindled all the others’ indolence toward good and encouraged their diligence.

Nor meanwhile did religion live silently in his breast without miracles; rather, God showed the man’s grace through not a few signs. [Col. 1481B] Once, while he pondered at night how God could in a single moment show prophets things past, present, and future, the same gift was bestowed upon him. For, with all the intervening walls from dormitory to church opened to him, he saw the monk whose duty it was rise from bed and hold the bell-rope by which he was to warn the monks to rise.

The discharge of shameful parts, by his sight alone, returned to health; a leper who drank water in which his hands had been washed cast off his sallow skin. A sick man near death saw himself surrounded by savage wolves and about to be devoured by their bestial jaws; for this reason he uttered dreadful cries. At Anselm’s arrival the enemies fled, and the man was granted peaceful rest. [Col. 1481C] Another recovered from a hopeless illness through an application of holy water; a third escaped the enticements of the flesh through Anselm’s blessing. This was Boso, then a young man and later Abbot of Bec, who speaks with Anselm in the book *Why God Became Man*.

He, while still a young man and a monk under him, was suffering the weariness of his recent profession, recognizing and lamenting the traces of an old and long-disused flame. Therefore, having confessed his inner agitations to the Father, he received only this reply: “God have mercy on you, my son.” At these words a calm light flowed into the suffering soul, thinning and driving away the clot of vices.

Then, after the death of Abbot Herluin, Anselm received a greater office, having been elected abbot by all the monks of Bec, though he strove to decline it with many excuses. He joined this office [Col. 1481D] to his great virtues, of which it might seem fitting to touch upon a few; for he exercised this office for fifteen years. But because my purpose is rather to describe those things which concern his archbishopric, I shall pass over this place. The necessity of the work undertaken rebukes and hastens the delays of speech, lest I seem to retrace matters already anticipated by a most distinguished talent. Nevertheless, as I have said of others, it will not seem absurd if I weave together a register of his virtues and deeds, so that one who has not consulted those extensive volumes may be informed by this brief compendium.

Accordingly, when Lanfranc had entered the other life, the plundering of churches and confiscation of goods was carried on everywhere in England. The mother church at Canterbury was added to the royal fisc and harassed by annual, and often even monthly, tax-gatherers. [Col. 1482A] Indeed, it would almost have seemed more tolerable to groan under the permanent rule of one master, to whom it had become accustomed, than to lie subject to new masters continually succeeding one another.

Meanwhile there was great silence among the bishops; there were no dogs able to bark. No utterance was entrusted with expressing grief; judgment was strangled within the conscience through fear of one man. For what use is there in speaking where by speaking one provokes hatred and gains no advantage? Yet there was some hope that an end might be put to these evils whenever they should see an Archbishop of Canterbury, who would be the mouth of all, the standard-bearer in the van, the public shield. And a rumour was spread abroad among the people—not, I think, without the purpose and providence of God—that Anselm would become archbishop: a man wholly [Col. 1482B] holy, anxiously learned, and that England would be made fortunate by this man’s blessings.

Words of this sort, brought to his ears, kept him in Normandy for the full five years, although he was often summoned across the sea by pressing causes. Thus the needs of many invited him, but fear held him back, lest, forgetful of his better reputation, he should be thought to be carried away by ambition for the archbishopric. At last, since he could no longer delay without harm to souls, he sailed for England, sacrificing to the Lord the purity of his conscience. What people might say, however, they could see for themselves, since he had long avoided their dishonourable slanders by an upright manner of life, knowing how much was at stake for him. At the same time, the rumour that had formerly threatened him with the archbishopric had cooled through the length of time.

There were several sound causes for his arrival, but these were the chief: that he might establish an abbey near Chester, which Hugh, earl of that city, wished especially to fill with monks from Bec; that he might visit the same Hugh, who had long been ill; and that, should Hugh die, Anselm might receive the pledge of their old friendship and, by interceding with a softened king, obtain relief for the revenues of Hugh’s estates. Though at the point of death, Hugh rejected all arrogance in confession and sought Anselm. Having immediately accomplished the first matter, and intending to settle the third, he hastened to court.

Without seeking gentle approaches, as others did, he was admitted to the inner chambers as soon as he arrived, out of reverence for his holiness. Given an opportunity for private speech, he unhesitatingly [Col. 1482D] disclosed all the charges against the king that rumour made, and modestly set forth his own needs as well. The king settled all the affairs of the church of Bec according to its ruler’s judgment, but dismissed with laughter the bitterness of the other matters, repeatedly saying that he could not prevent the licence of rumour. Yet, he said, a holy man ought not to believe such things. For at that time he did not wish to dismiss Anselm with a more insolent answer, knowing how highly his father and mother had been accustomed to esteem him while they lived.

For this also should be considered a noble quality in the king: although he could do everything by sheer power, he rather evaded certain matters in jest, transferring many things to wit beyond the serious purpose of his mind. Thus, when bishops suggested that he permit prayers to be made throughout the kingdom, that God might deign to inspire him to provide the mother of churches with a shepherd, he replied mockingly, disguising anger with a laugh:

> “Pray for what you please; I shall do what pleases me. No one’s prayer will ever weaken my will.”

Likewise, when Anselm was discussed in an assembly of magnates, one man remarked that he alone in their time was desirous of no honour. Then the king jeeringly said: “Not even of the Archbishopric of Canterbury?” When his interlocutor denied this as firmly as before, the king asserted that Anselm would exert himself with feet and hands if only he perceived the slightest hope of attaining that dignity. “But by the holy face of Lucca,” he said, “both he and all competitors for the archbishopric shall yield to me at this time, for I shall be archbishop.”

Repeating such things frequently, he soon felt the violence of a grave illness; as it increased, after a few [Col. 1483B] hours he took to his bed. By chance Anselm had then withdrawn from the tumults of court, but, summoned urgently by a messenger sent from the king, he presented himself to the king, who desired his presence. Having received his confession with the consent of the bishops, Anselm instructed him, sorrowing for his sins, to place upon the altar, through the bishops then gathered in large numbers, the rod of amendment as a pledge: that he should supply pastors to widowed churches, restore exiles, and release prisoners.

The king did all these things with devotion no less wholehearted than if God had commanded them. His illness pressed him more bitterly, and he was thought to be paying the penalties of his offenses. Then the sick man aptly introduced to those around him the subject of comforting the church of Canterbury, referring consideration of the matter to the bishops. The word was received with applause, [Col. 1483C] and a cry went up to heaven from those wishing good things and health for the king. Yet the honour of making the decision was transferred to him, and with minds inclined toward royal assent they awaited the king’s declaration, so that whomever he pronounced worthy all would certainly receive.

Thus, raising himself upon his elbow, he said: “I choose this holy man Anselm,” and an immense acclamation of approval followed.

At this, fear swallowed up the security of Anselm’s heart, and his face at once grew pale. As he attempted to frame excuses on these grounds, the bishops took him aside. At first they soothed him with these words: he should rejoice in the time, which God himself had undoubtedly ordered, so that through his archbishopric so many evils throughout England might be cut off and a right measure imposed upon every disturbance; he should declare what he wished done in God’s affairs, and they would not fail to support him; he should pray to the Lord for them, and they would undertake for him whatever secular matters there might be; therefore he should graciously accept what seemed divinely inspired in the fierce king, lest he be responsible for all the perversities that would subsequently arise in the kingdom. [Col. 1483D]

They urged such arguments. But he, foreknowing what was to come, dismissed all their reasoning with a brief reply. He was not equal to so great a burden because of the weakness of his age; it would be presumptuous for any young man to undertake so great a labour, much less for one whose blood had grown sluggish and whose strength hostile old age had worn away. He did not know secular business because he had not wished to know it, having always recoiled after becoming a monk from its occupations, desiring to devote a free mind to the delight of Holy Scripture.

They wished, he said, to make things discordant: the plough of holy Church, which in England ought to be drawn by two strong oxen striving with equal strength toward the good—that is, the king and the Archbishop of Canterbury—would now be pulled from a straight course by an old ewe yoked with an untamed bull.

> “And I,” he said, “am the old ewe. If I were left in peace, perhaps I might be of some not unwelcome use to certain persons through the milk of God’s word and the covering of wool. But if you yoke me with this bull, you will see that, because those drawing are unequal, the plough will not proceed straight. You will therefore gain no benefit from this action; indeed, while fear stops your mouths, you will see the Church, for which you wish to provide so unwisely, deprived of a shepherd while he yet lives. Moreover, since I am abbot in another realm, you see how improper and ambition-filled it would be for me to defraud the monks to whom I owe protection, and dishonour the archbishop to whom I owe profession.” [Col. 1484B]

They pressed him more insistently and promised prompt remedies for every objection he had raised. The king too, informed of his obstinate refusal, begged him by the friendship of his father and mother not to persist in a resolution harmful to his soul. Indeed, when all had thrown themselves at Anselm’s feet, the king too fell upon his face. Yet the hero was bent by no tears and softened by no promises. So anxious was he then, as he later declared under solemn appeal to the Godhead, that, if it were God’s will, he would rather lose his life than be tossed by such a storm of cares. He even appealed tearfully for assistance to his own monks who were present, until [Col. 1484C] the bishops, mutually encouraging one another, conspired in a rush as though against an enemy.

Thus, some from behind and some from in front forced him toward the sick king’s bed. Seizing his hand, they tried to straighten the fingers which he had tightly bent into his palm. Their effort was long frustrated by the anger and pain that had aroused strength in the man. At last, when scarcely his index finger had been lifted and he uttered cries of pain at the violence, they placed the pastoral staff in it. Immediately gripping his hand so that he could not cast it aside, they dragged him rather than led him into the church and performed the customary solemn rites. And although the joyful voices of all singing *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God”—resounded through the air, he cried out with all the effort he could:

> “What you are doing is nothing; I do not wish it; I do not consent.”

Returning to the king, [Col. 1484D] he said that when the king was soon better he had not consented to the violence, and therefore everything that had been done concerning this matter could and ought to be annulled as far as he was concerned.

Having said this, he left the court in the company of the magnates and went to his lodging, shedding abundant tears and weighed down with great grief. His manner thus interpreting his inward will, it stirred [variant: “kindled”] the feelings of the sick king all the more, so that he immediately ordered Anselm to be proclaimed publicly archbishop and invested with all the revenues belonging to the church of Canterbury. Moreover, he granted him outright the city of Canterbury, which Archbishop Lanfranc had held by royal favour.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, on the day before the Nones of March, the first Sunday of Lent.

Anselm therefore entered upon the estates belonging to ecclesiastical right, [Col. 1485A] and the king, his illness shaken off, recovered. For he zealously pressed forward with what he had begun, in order to establish Anselm in the archbishopric. Messengers were sent to Normandy with the king’s letters to the Archbishop of Rouen and the monks of Bec, seeking their free release of him. They too, carefully weighing the grounds of the request, raised and examined several objections, but finally consented.

Yet his consecration was delayed by a quarrel arising between him and the king for the following reason. The king had approached him with flattering persuasions, asking him voluntarily to transfer into the perpetual right of his retainers those possessions of the Church of Christ which the king himself had alienated, and which they had occupied after Lanfranc’s death through his grant. Anselm refused [Col. 1485B] to inflict loss upon a church to which he himself had contributed nothing.

At this the prince’s anger was aroused, and what he had previously celebrated with the greatest eagerness concerning Anselm’s elevation to the see was postponed and nearly abandoned. From this Anselm’s noble mind rose in joy, hoping that he was released from every duty of pre-eminence and would be transferred to a solitary life. For he had already resigned the abbey by handing over the staff, having been released by William, Archbishop of Rouen. At that time he used often to profess that he was fit for no position of pre-eminence except the priorate of a cloister, because he delighted in leisure, was unequal to other labours, and had a tongue ready to bless.

Nevertheless, after much time had passed, the king, troubled by everyone’s complaints that the churches were going to ruin because they lacked a ruler, scarcely persuaded him to accept the archbishopric and strengthen by his consent the desire of all. After enormous promises had been poured forth—promises that, as it were, burdened the very air, intended to entice and impel the reluctant man—he performed homage to the king, according to the custom of that time, and was enthroned at Canterbury on the seventh day before the Kalends of October. But on the day before the Nones of December he received the episcopal solemnities from all the bishops of England.

His prophetic text was: “He called many and sent his servant at supper-time to say to those invited, ‘Come, because all things are now ready’; and they all began at once to make excuses” (Luke 14). Soon afterward the king crossed the sea.

At that time there were two claimants to the Roman see, Wibert and Urban, both eminent and distinguished men, and neither yielded to the other in personal qualities. [Col. 1485D] England wavered in uncertain allegiance, though it inclined more toward Wibert out of fear of the king. Anselm had long since accepted Urban as pope, and this had been accepted without the king’s opposition when he was elected to the archbishopric. Nevertheless, when the king had returned to the realm, unsuccessful in the scheme by which he had intended to deprive his brother of a province, Anselm approached him and sought permission to go to Rome in order to receive the pallium from Pope Urban.

At this the king, as always prone to anger, found fresh reasons for wrath. Stirred to malice, he declared that Anselm could not preserve faithfully the allegiance he had promised him if, without royal permission, he recognized Urban or any other pope. Anselm replied that this should be deferred to a fuller assembly [Col. 1486A] and seriously examined: whether he would thereby weaken the allegiance owed to his earthly lord if he appealed to the vicar of Saint Peter.

Thus there were great stirrings on both sides and great deliberations. The king’s argument was as follows:

> “It is a custom of my realm, established by my father, that no pope be appealed to without the king’s permission. Whoever abolishes the customs of the realm violates also its power and crown. Whoever takes away my crown acts toward me with hostility and disloyalty.”

Anselm replied:

> “The Lord judges otherwise; by two commandments he settles and makes this question clear. For he himself teaches what allegiance we owe to the vicar of blessed Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’; and, ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind [Col. 1486B] upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 16). And he says to all in common: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me’ (Luke 10). And again: ‘Whoever touches you is as one who touches the pupil of my eye’ (Zechariah 2). Further, he declares elsewhere what we owe the king: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matthew 22). Therefore, without offense, in matters that belong to God I shall render obedience to the vicar of blessed Peter; and in matters that pertain to the earthly dignity of my lord, I shall not withhold faithful aid and counsel according to my ability.”

In carrying out these matters, all the bishops of England denied support to their primate, playing the part of hirelings and fugitives from liberty. As though this were too little, [Col. 1486C] they renounced all obedience and subjection to him. The instigator and standard-bearer of the faction was William, bishop of Durham, a man of importunate eloquence and hostile ambition. He hoped to be thrust into the archbishopric after Anselm had been removed; therefore he pressed the business more shamelessly and had promised the king that by his skill Anselm would yield the dignity, voluntarily surrendering ring and staff.

But he displayed his ingenuity against God in vain, for Anselm crushed all his counsels and those of the others—after they had been spun out through long windings—with one answer:

> “If anyone presumes to prove that I deny allegiance to my earthly king because I appeal to the vicar of blessed Peter, I am ready to answer him, to whom and where I ought.”

All the more shaken in mind, they recognized that there was greater prudence in the man than they had imagined: he knew that the Archbishop of Canterbury ought not to be judged except in the consistory of the pope. Thus all the ingenuity of men refined in counsel was vainly exerted against one with whom God stood. For whatever they thought ought to be said, he at once found a reason that tore it apart like cobwebs in a violent blast. So unmoved in mind and free from anxiety was he that, when they withdrew into groups and weighed their arguments back and forth, he himself, leaning against a wall, gave himself to sleep. With the same expression and an unshaken mind, neither disturbed by anger nor troubled by fear, he both professed inner tranquillity and displayed it in the cheerfulness of his face.

Then they rose to shouting and fury, and the Bishop of Durham openly declared: [Col. 1487A] “He whom reason cannot restrain ought to be restrained by force.” The magnates protested; far more than the bishops, they judged that one should refrain from injuries against the archbishop. Finally, when ordered to renounce subjection to him, they refused altogether, saying that they were Christians and did not wish in any respect to oppose the will of their archbishop. Though the king took this badly, fear of a greater disturbance made him suppress his anger.

Then, because the bishops’ undertaking had not succeeded, he fell back upon their counsel, wishing Anselm to be expelled from the realm after being deprived of staff and ring. But since he could not obtain this by force, and Anselm declared that he would indeed leave England but would not surrender his insignia and title, all matters were postponed peacefully from the Ides of March then approaching until the Octave of Pentecost. When the magnates reported this to him as he was already contemplating a period of release, he replied with a drawn-out, grieving sigh:

> “Although I am not ignorant of the future from the past, yet lest I seem to press everything according to my own judgment, I embrace peace; as far as depends on me, I shall not depart from it. Whoever proves to be its violator must answer for it, so far as God is concerned.”

Nor did this utterance of the man fall short of truth. Before the appointed time many adversities were inflicted upon him: his chamberlain was seized for punishment before his eyes; some men upon whose counsel he especially relied fled beyond the sea; clever schemes of malice, devised to harm his dignity, were put into effect. Two messengers, singular masters of deceit, were sent to Rome without his knowledge, when he suspected nothing of the kind, [Col. 1487C] to ascertain the condition of the city and negotiate with the pope that he should send the pallium to the king, to be bestowed upon whomever he wished.

They diligently and energetically carried out their orders, bringing Walter, Bishop of Albano, to England by Pope Urban’s command. Having landed at Dover, he came secretly to court without Anselm’s knowledge and satisfied William’s greedy mind with immense promises. If Urban were received in England as pope, then whatever the king might judge worth requesting, Urban would confirm by the privilege of the Apostolic See. But regarding the archbishop’s case, he offered no support except this: when asked to expel Anselm, he replied that it was impossible to remove a man of the most celebrated holiness and learning, legitimately admitted to the episcopal office and guilty of no offense.

Accordingly, an edict was immediately promulgated throughout the province that Urban was to be called and believed to be pope. When Anselm heard this he was astonished. Then a large number of bishops sent to him came; gradually sounding out whether he had become more pliant in order to regain the king’s friendship, they found him unchanged and disclosed what had been concealed. The lord king, they said, had earned the pallium from Rome through his own work and expense, [Col. 1487D] having completed the business by his own effort at a cost of many marks. It was fitting that Anselm should answer so great a benefit from the prince by a worthy service.

He groaned that the device of deceit had been brought to effect. Receiving the bishops’ words with deep sighs, he denied that he would give anything on this account, because he judged slight a benefit whose greatness they themselves valued so highly. By this the king learned that Anselm’s firmness of mind could in no way be weakened so that he would yield to royal friendship. With the greatness of spirit appropriate to his dignity, the king himself sought and obtained reconciliation. Public authority was granted Anselm freely to exercise the right of his primacy throughout the realm.

On the appointed day, when the Bishop of Albano came to Canterbury with the pallium, the people applauded his arrival and the holy insignia borne in a silver vessel. The archbishop met him barefoot, but clothed in priestly vestments. Then, taking the pallium from the altar of the Lord the Saviour, the consecrated bishop placed it upon his blessed shoulders and proceeded to celebrate the divine offices. It was Sunday, the fourth day before the Ides of June. To some it seemed a great miracle that the Gospel occurring that day was the same as that which had previously been his prophetic text: [Col. 1488B] “A certain man made a great supper and invited many, and sent his servants at supper-time, etc.” (Luke 14).

Thus peace having been made and the king having gone beyond the sea, the serene calm of peace drove cares from Anselm’s mind throughout that year and relieved the anxieties of good men. But after William’s return, the storm again thundered, and the tempest of hatreds again rose violently. For, delighted by his fortunate success, he immediately marched against the Welsh. Since God’s greatest favour attended all his undertakings, he experienced fortune’s gentle aid in everything, so that God seemed to contend with him in benefits. If he entered battle, he brought back rich spoils; if he wished to sail upon an unruly sea, [Col. 1488C] the winds immediately laid aside their fury.

Anselm saw this and rejoiced with him, hoping that because of such abundant favour he would at some time make the Church free. Therefore he intended gently to approach the king when he returned from the Welsh expedition. But the king forestalled him by assailing the archbishop with insults through a messenger, alleging the small number and ineffectiveness of the soldiers whom Anselm had sent against the enemy.

When this was reported, every hope of reform grew numb in Anselm. He therefore dismissed the messenger without a response, lest an arena for quarrels be opened by exchanges of messages. Fortune, I think, raged against the bishop through the devil’s prompting; and schemes were prepared against him for the next court. All these he shattered and repelled by requesting permission to go to Rome, after he had first tried the king’s disposition regarding the state of the churches by many efforts.

Accordingly, wishing to communicate these things to the pope, he asked, as I have said, permission to go to Rome—twice and three times in vain. “For,” said the king, “I understand that permission must be refused. I know that no grave sin burdens him for which he should seek absolution from Rome, nor does he need the counsel of that place, since he lacks no abundance of learning. Indeed, I would rather say that Urban must yield to Anselm’s wisdom than that Anselm needs Urban. But if he persists more stubbornly in what he has begun, I shall reduce the whole archbishopric to my fisc. For he transgresses the promises by which he bound his allegiance to observe all the customs of my realm. [Col. 1489A] It is foreign to my practice for any of my magnates to go to Rome unless chiefly on my own mission. Therefore, either let him swear to me that henceforth, under any oppression [variant: “imposition”], he will never appeal to the Apostolic See, or let him leave the kingdom. Say these things to him, my faithful men; and if you see that he wishes to desist from his journey, let him then experience the force of the court’s judgment, since he has not feared to trouble me so often about a matter which he does not wish to bring to conclusion.”

Anselm judged that this should not be dealt with through messengers. He himself entered before the king, sat at his right hand according to custom, and spoke to this effect:

> “You say that I ought not to go to Rome because I am free of grave sin and abound in learning. Although I do not arrogate either claim to myself as true, I commit them to God’s scales for examination. You say that I promised to observe your customs. I accept this, but I require the conditions: I said that I would observe only those customs which had been established honourably and were consistent with God’s laws. You say that I go beyond my allegiance because, disregarding your customs, I appeal to the Apostolic See. With due reverence for your sovereignty, this would not be true if another were to say it [variant: ‘it would not be true, another would say’]. For the allegiance which I owe you, O king, I hold from allegiance to God, whose vicar is Saint Peter, whose see I appeal to. You say that I must swear never again to appeal to Rome for any cause. I publicly declare that a Christian prince unjustly requires such an oath from his archbishop. For if by an oath I were to renounce Saint Peter, I would deny Christ. [Col. 1489C] When I have denied Christ in any matter, then I shall not delay to make satisfaction to you for the fault of seeking this permission. Yet perhaps, after my departure, God will provide that the affairs of the Church will not for long, as you threaten, serve your profits.”

The king and magnates interrupted him as he spoke, especially reproaching him that in the undertaking to observe the customs there had never been any mention of God or of honourable right.

Then, with a gracious expression, almost breaking into laughter, he spoke these same words:

> “Good heavens! If, as you say, no mention was made either of God or of rectitude, whose mention was made then? Far be it from any Christian to maintain and defend laws or customs known to be contrary to God and rectitude.”

At these words they were struck as though by a hammer upon their shameless foreheads. By lowering their heads and keeping silence, they acknowledged their injustice. [Col. 1489D] He himself was not disturbed in the least; whenever they shouted against him, he would fall silent and then return, unmoved, to the central point of his argument.

Yet the king could not restrain himself from hurling cruel threats, saying that Anselm would carry nothing out of his kingdom. But he fearlessly answered: “I shall go on foot and naked, if anyone asserts that my horses and garments are yours.” The prince was ashamed of this remark, and his face was covered with blushes. “That is not what I wish,” he said, “but eleven days from now, when you reach the port, you shall obey my messenger concerning what is to be carried away or left behind.”

Another might have been angered, but Anselm remained undisturbed. He offered his blessing to the king, who did not refuse it, saying beforehand that he bore the king’s anger painfully and with grief; but if the king would deign to understand, he would see that the course he had begun concerned the welfare of the king’s soul.

The bishops evaded this issue, as they had before. When he sought their support, they replied that he was both devout and wise. Because of his wisdom, he did not need their counsel, but knew best what should be done; because of his holiness, he both wished and could without hesitation do what was good. But they could not rise against their lord, whose favour they did not wish to lose for the sake of their honours and their parents, whom they loved. He, free from every stain of worldly desire and greed, should pursue God’s cause as he had begun. He would have the bishops’ silent approval, but no assistance from their voices. [Col. 1490B] Yet, if there were any trust or access to better counsel, it would be preferable to cherish sweet leisure at home than to devote himself to so great a labour, exiled from country and honours.

Thus all departed. Only two, asking forgiveness before he crossed the sea, received his gracious pardon. Their names were Osmer, bishop of Salisbury [variant: Sherborne], and Robert, bishop of Hereford.

Having stayed one day at Canterbury, he took up, according to custom, his satchel and staff—the consolations and signs of his journey. Arriving at Dover, he was held there against his wish for fifteen days because of adverse winds. During this interval, a messenger sent by the king, as was said, constantly enjoyed his companionship and table-fellowship, while concealing the secret purpose of his coming. But when favourable winds summoned the ships into the deep, [Col. 1490C] the messenger, by the king’s order, commanded all bags and wallets to be brought out before him and plundered.

It was a cruel and pitiable spectacle: the primate of England, the head of all religion and learning, treated like a robber. But since only necessary equipment was found and no money at all, the man who had come regretted the deed he had done unwillingly and allowed him to depart unharmed.

When the ships were loosed, the south wind carried them out to sea, at first slowly, so that with the wind turned back they seemed to be sailing again toward England. The father could not see this, because of the grief of his heart, with dry eyes. Raising his hands on high, he drew help down from heaven. The winds, their anger calmed, made the waters smooth and turned the sails toward Flanders. Thus, with a favourable wind ploughing the sea, the ships reached Wissant not long afterward. [Col. 1490D]

His first lodging, with his monks, was at Saint-Bertin’s. Thereafter favour provided for him, as all bishops and abbots competed in inviting him, even drawing him away against his will. Report of the man went before him and breathed upon the hearts of those who heard it with a sweet breeze. Therefore speech fails, and the narrative collapses, when one tries to say with how much love he was received by all and with what services he was cherished: such was the marvellous reversal of circumstances that he was more honoured in a foreign province than he had been as a citizen in his own homeland, as archbishop in his own Church.

Hugh himself, Archbishop of Lyons, apostolic legate in Gaul, a man of great name and power and not lacking in religious devotion, heard that Anselm was directing his journey to Lyons. He eagerly came to meet him and served him devoutly. [Col. 1491A] By Hugh’s counsel, Anselm stayed there, sending to Urban, the pope at Rome, persons acquainted with the whole case. A sudden illness demanded both rest and counsel.

Meanwhile he seemed to yield to the robber bands of Wibert’s party. For a report was carried through every mouth that the Archbishop of Canterbury had come from England and was travelling to Rome to Urban laden with money; great, they said, must be what the Archbishop of England carried with him, since England was the most fertile of all provinces. Inflamed by these reports, they had already blocked every route and occupied the narrow places, lest anything escape. It would be a great advantage to their lord if he were captured, since he was a champion of Urban’s party.

Therefore Anselm allowed their ardour to cool for a time by withholding the prey, so that, believing themselves deceived in their expectation, they might return home. By this plan he deprived those lying in wait of their gain. Then a messenger had already returned with the pope’s command that, setting aside every excuse, he should come to Rome under obedience. Unknowing how to resist obedience, and made bolder by hope in God’s mercy, he undertook the journey. For renewed health supplied courage, and his old age, still green and unspent, endured labour well.

Having crossed the Alps, he came safely to Rome, lacking neither a single man of his party nor a beast of burden. He encountered only one danger during the entire journey; yet it proved an occasion and nourishment of glory. For the Duke of Burgundy, seized by the same hope as Wibert’s adherents, [Col. 1491C] had resolved in a more inflated spirit to plunder him. But softened by merely seeing him, he breathed out all pride and recovered humility. His sweet gaze, gentle face, and tranquil grey hair so captivated anyone looking upon him that, upon whomever he cast the favour of his eyes, he immediately drew that person into love for himself.

Thus, when the duke saw him, the swelling of heart conceived through the words of scoundrels subsided. He was immediately received with the pontiff’s kiss and spontaneously sought his blessing. Calling one of his magnates—for he had arrived attended by many amid a great commotion—he commanded him to conduct Anselm safely through his territory and to ensure that he was served everywhere no less than the duke himself. Having thus formed an alliance of friendship, the duke departed, often gnashing against slanderers and repeating that God’s hatred was upon them for having persuaded him [Col. 1491D] to persecute an angel of God.

Anselm, therefore secure, came to Cluny, then, as I have said, to Lyons, and from there to Rome.

Whom the pope received with great honour and extolled before the senate with the highest praises. He declared that throughout the Latin world none could be found his equal in the liberal disciplines or in religion; that he had suffered many insults for his fidelity to Rome; that at last, by paths full of dangers and deaths, he had come to him, seeking aid from one who himself had greater need of his counsel. Such were Urban’s boasts; but Anselm, lowering his head in modesty, kept silence. When, however, the supreme pontiff had ended his praises, Anselm, being given the opportunity, truthfully set forth his entire case. The pontiff, together with the senate, promised assistance. Letters were written [Col. 1492A] to William, king of England; and it was ordered that Anselm be restored to all his possessions. For as soon as he had crossed the sea, William had ordered the whole archbishopric to be brought under his own control and everything previously established to be annulled. The archbishop was ordered to await the reply to the letters near the pope.

But he had no wish to remain there long, since the air of that city was unhealthy for foreigners. Accordingly, he yielded to the request of a certain John, formerly his monk at Bec, but then, by Urban’s appointment, abbot of the monastery of Saint Saviour near the city of Telesina [variant: Teselnia], and went to his estate called Sclavia to avoid the heat of summer. This estate stood on the summit of a very high mountain and, being cooled by breezes coming from every side, was almost at every moment free from unhealthy air. Thus his captivity proved a delight to Anselm, [Col. 1492B] since he saw restored to him the leisure he had long desired. Therefore, raising to God a mind that had long been inactive, he there completed the excellent book entitled and concerned with *Why God Became Man*. He was loved and honoured by all, so much so that Roger, duke of Apulia—at whose court the king of England had arranged by letter that charges should be laid against him—despised those trifles and changed his opinion altogether in honour of the man, offering him estates, castles, and finally whatever he pleased, provided only that his remaining in that land would bless it.

While he was with the pope, he ranked next to him in everything—in processions and at stations. Greetings and, after the pope, gifts came to him. Everyone willingly heard him, and what he commanded was done when he thundered forth divine discourses. His greatest delight was to declare [Col. 1492C] that the fruit of learning was this: when one speaks well, another should receive from one’s teaching an advance in living well. He was therefore eagerly desirous, once the burden of the archbishopric had been laid down, to devote himself to God. When he earnestly requested this from the pope, Urban refused altogether: “Rather,” he said, “I command you under obedience that, wherever you may be, you do not lay aside the name and honour of archbishop of Canterbury. It is the part of a soft soldier to flee before battle; nor is it the part of a religious and steadfast mind to yield without any injury, merely to threats and terrors.”

Then Anselm said: “Father, [Col. 1492D] I do not refuse obedience, nor blows, since I do not fear even death itself for God—unless perhaps my own mind deceives me. But what,” he said, “am I to do there, where justice not only totters, but is now wholly oppressed? Where my suffragans not only fail, through fear, to support the cause of good, but even attack it through favour?”

“Concerning these and similar matters,” the pope replied, “my purpose is to deliberate at the council at Bari, where I desire both your presence and your assistance.”

When they came to the council, the pope, having spread carpets and coverings before the body of Saint Nicholas, himself clothed in a chasuble with the pallium, mounted the tribunal. The others sat in copes. While all claimed their places by ancient right, Anselm, supreme in humility, sat wherever he could. Amid the press of business the supreme pontiff had forgotten to assign him a place. But he was reminded of this error by a question necessarily raised by the Greeks, who wished to prove that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. As the pope attempted to resolve this question, he entangled it more deeply; and the Greeks opposed him with arguments not lacking plausibility. Remembering Anselm, he cried aloud. The thunder of his vigorous voice was repeated by the capacity of the building and the multitude of the crowd: “Father and master Anselm, archbishop of the English, where are you?”

When Anselm heard himself called, he stood up. [Col. 1493A] Addressing him, the pope said: “Now, master, there is need of your learning and the service of your eloquence. Come, ascend here, and defend your mother, the Church, whom the Greeks are attempting to shake. Come to her aid, as one sent here by God.”

Immediately all standing and sitting there [Col. 1493B] turned their eyes and faces towards him and asked who he was. Assisted by those near him, he was raised up at the pope’s command and ordered to sit beside the Roman archdeacon, whose custom it is to sit before the pope. “Let us enclose him,” said the pope, “within our circle, as though he were the pope of another world.” Without delay he publicly explained his lineage, homeland, learning, eloquence, religious life, and the great sufferings he had endured for fidelity to the Roman see. Discussion of the question was postponed until the next day, although Anselm did not hesitate to answer it at once.

But on the following day, when the assembly had gathered earlier than usual, he was brought forward to an elevated place. He so examined the sides of the question, so penetrated and illumined its inner depths, that the Latins testified [Col. 1493C] to their joy with shouts, while the Greeks were pained that they had made themselves ridiculous. No one departed poor and empty of learning. In later time he set forth the meaning of that discourse clearly in his book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. When he had finished speaking, all turned their eyes and faces upon him: one praised his faith, another his learning, all his eloquence. When the uproar raised by his praise had subsided, the supreme pontiff, looking intently at him, said: “Blessed be your heart and your spirit, and blessed be your mouth and the speech of your mouth.”

Without delay, when strengthened by the consent of all, he had hurled the thunderbolt of excommunication against those who held contrary views, discussion began concerning the king of England. Crimes horrible to recount were brought forward; [Col. 1493D] to contempt for human authority was added injury against heaven, namely that, though warned twice and three times, he had shown no correction. Therefore, when the pope, supported by the voices and clamour of all, was already prepared to excommunicate him, Anselm threw himself at his knees, prayed for delay, and obtained it only with difficulty. This won him no small favour among all who saw it, because by the manifestation of true holiness he had surpassed the glory of his reputation. How beautiful it was that he should pray forgiveness for one from whom he had received such great insult!

When the pope had returned to Rome and Anselm was accompanying his retinue, a messenger sent by the king arrived to weaken Anselm’s charges and clear away the accusations brought against him. Although the king had cast off all shame and had risen to excessive arrogance, he cared little what was said about him. The envoy spoke thus to the pope in the archbishop’s presence:

“My lord wonders why it should even have entered [Col. 1494A] your mind to order that Anselm be restored, when he had unequivocally foretold this to him: if he left England without his permission—”

“Does he accuse him of anything else?” asked the pope.

“No,” he replied.

“And for this,” said the pope, “you undertook the great labour of coming here, to say that the primate was stripped of all his possessions because he appealed to the apostolic judgment? Therefore, if you love your lord, hasten back and tell him that, unless he wishes to be excommunicated, he must quickly restore him to all his possessions. And lest I leave you uncertain about the deadline: bring his answer to the council to be held in this city in the third week after Easter. Indeed, the complainant would already have been excommunicated, had not the defendant intervened.”

Stunned by so unexpected a reply, [Col. 1494B] the envoy answered that he would privately disclose to him his lord’s secret. He was eager to accomplish something by which he might secure greater favour with the king. Thus, conducting the affair with the skill in which he was practised, courting individuals with gifts and promises, he obtained for the king a postponement until the feast of Saint Michael. Urban long hesitated to grant this, for Anselm’s piety and the offer of gifts struggled within his mind; but money prevailed at last. Does money thus overcome and crush everything? It was shameful that concern for reputation should become worthless in the breast of so great a man—I mean Urban—that regard for God should yield and money pervert justice.

Anselm therefore thought it best not to waste expectation [Col. 1494C] on such a venal man, but to return to Lyons. Yet he could not obtain leave, since the pope detained him in order to soften the odium of his conduct with some consolation. He therefore made him remain with him until the council in the patriarchal palace, and gave him a house with the perpetual right of hospitality. Often coming to him, he spent both serious and light moments with him, so that you would have said there was one court, not two. The time for the council was now at hand; and while all the Gallic bishops acknowledged their seats, and no one remembered that any archbishop of Canterbury had attended a Roman council, a seat was assigned him within the circle, as I said before, and a right to it was permanently entered for him and his successors.

The council was held in the church of Saint Peter. [Col. 1494D] There was great noise among those standing about and a large gathering of arrivals. Since the decrees were therefore heard with difficulty, the pope ordered Reinger, bishop of Lucca, to announce everything aloud to the people. He rose to the duty imposed upon him, and the cry he began did not fail the open-mouthed crowd, but struck and penetrated even the hearing of those far away. After he had expounded a great part of the decrees, he suddenly, as though his mind had been diverted, introduced words foreign to and apparently disconnected from the business:

“But alas! What are we to do? We burden subjects with commands, yet give no help to those who seek it from us. The whole world grieves and complains that the head of all does not grieve with its members. Behold, there sits among us modestly and silently one whose silence is a great cry before God. He has now been waiting for the vigour of the apostolic see for a second year: [Col. 1495A] of all that has been unjustly taken from him, what help, I ask, has he received? It is Anselm, archbishop of England, of whom I speak.”

As he said this, he seemed to magnify the indignity of the matter by striking the pavement heavily with the staff he held. The pope, turning towards him, said: “Cease to be disturbed, brother Reinger; a remedy will be provided for this matter.” But Reinger, moved by fervour of spirit, said: “So it must be; otherwise the matter will not escape the just Judge,” and then resumed the interrupted sequence of decrees.

These words astonished Anselm, since he knew that Reinger had been induced to mention these matters neither by any of his own people nor by complaints on his behalf. At this council the pope, together with all, pronounced the sentence of excommunication [Col. 1495B] against lay investers of churches; against those invested by laymen; against those who consecrated persons so invested; and against those who become the men of laymen for ecclesiastical honours.

On the day after the council, the archbishop arranged his return journey. Having been tossed by very many perils of labour, he made for Lyons through mountainous and wooded places. He could not take the direct route, because it was said that Wibert had sent a painter to Rome to paint his likeness on a panel, so that, whatever disguise he adopted, he could not remain concealed. On reaching Lyons, he experienced Hugh’s customary kindness, being treated as the true lord of the place rather than as a stranger. The bishop offered him all rights, within and without, without waiting to be asked, and compelled him to accept what he wished: precedence in the assembly, affection in private, reverence in public, service in all things. He consoled his cares, [Col. 1495C] shared honours with him—or rather yielded them entirely—so completely that he served him in the place of a suffragan when he celebrated Mass, and sat at his feet wherever he preached: a great-souled and steadfast man who dared despise wealth and challenge fortune.

Father Anselm remained there throughout the time that Urban and William survived. Not long afterwards fate carried off both. On hearing of the king’s death, Anselm shed tears—the signs of affection and interpreters of pity. Immediately invited by the new king Henry, he honoured England with his arrival. There, in assemblies often convened at the king’s wish, he frequently invited many great men who had fallen away from loyalty to the right course. The others, conscious of guilt, feared him; yet, gazing at him with open countenance and eager eyes, they even applauded as he spoke.

Finally, when Robert [Col. 1495D], the king’s brother, had already landed and many were contemplating withdrawal, Anselm ascended an elevated place with the whole army standing around and addressed the people. As though the ranks had been roused by a trumpet-call, they promised the king, with raised voices, their goodwill and loyalty, if he would abolish the evil institutions established under William Rufus and enact good laws. The king offered Anselm as surety for the performance of these things to all and gave his pledge into his hand. Thus all were encouraged with greater zeal to be faithful to the king, so that, if necessary, with united hearts and devoted hands they would rush to arms for him. When this became known, Robert, who had come relying more on the treachery of others than on his own vigorous action, abandoned battle and withdrew from the enterprise. He who had presumed upon the kingdom in hope readily embraced peace, accepting the offered hands and hastening gladly into the affection of brotherly relationship.

Nevertheless, when the king, following the practice of his predecessors, demanded homage [Col. 1496A] from the archbishop, and Anselm delayed because of the excommunication pronounced at Rome, messengers were sent to Rome by both parties. It was ordered that he should in the meantime do homage to the king, or, the bonds of delay being released, leave the kingdom. “Rather,” he answered, “let the apostolic letters be examined, and let what their tenor contains be done.” For the messengers had already returned from Rome and had worn out the road in vain, since Pope Paschal upheld his predecessor’s ruling with invincible strength.

“What are the pope’s letters to me?” said the king. “I do not wish to lose the rights of my kingdom.”

As the dispute continued, Anselm declared [Col. 1496B] that he would not leave the land, but would go to his church and consider who was doing violence to himself or his people. Thus they parted; but in the following days gentler letters came from the king, asking him to appear before the court in a peaceful spirit. After they had spoken together, all contention, it was promised, would be quieted. He did not refuse to come, if perhaps God had touched the royal mind by His prompting.

Again, therefore, by common decree envoys were sent to Rome to attempt either to soften or repeal these harsh commands: on the archbishop’s side Baldwin and Alexander, monks; on the king’s side Gerard, archbishop of York, Herbert, bishop of Norwich, and Robert, bishop of Chester. But the earlier envoys also had private concerns pressing upon them: Gerard, concerning the obtaining of the pallium; Herbert, concerning the repeal of the privilege of the abbey of Saint Edmund, which Baldwin, abbot of that monastery, had acquired for it through Pope Alexander with much effort. The privilege was that the abbot of that place should be subject neither to the bishop of Norwich, in whose diocese it was known to lie, nor to anyone else except the primate of England.

Herbert, intending to remove this privilege, set out [Col. 1496C] and—by some misfortune of which I am ignorant—left his companions, took by-roads, and fell into the hands of bandits. But after giving forty marks, he freed himself from bondage and recovered liberty of travel. He was first compelled to swear by every saint, as the saying goes, to Guido—this being the name of the man who was leader of the robbers—that he would do nothing at Rome to the disadvantage of his lord Anselm, archbishop. Having paid the money, he hurried after his companions with freer leisure because of a lighter purse. Once reunited, they took the road and, appearing before the pope, [Col. 1496D] used all their powers in promises and gifts to bring the king’s will to effect; but in vain. The pope stood inflexible, unwilling, as he said, to weaken the decrees of the holy Fathers for the will of one man.

This labour therefore accomplished nothing except to sow disputes in the kingdom, since the envoys disagreed with one another. The king thought that the letter brought to him by the bishops, because he saw it opposed to his will, should be concealed. Instead, he published bare words [Col. 1497A] outside it, by which they asserted, on episcopal authority, that the pope was willing to tolerate the king’s investitures if he performed the other duties of a good prince. He had been unwilling for this to be seen in writing lest, given the opportunity, other princes should cry out against him. The monks, by contrast, publicly complained that fraud was being woven around the apostolic commands. Indeed, the letter which they had brought to Anselm was now being read everywhere, and it proved that Paschal not only did not permit investitures, but also insistently enforced Urban’s decrees and urged their observance.

The whole court therefore buzzed with the murmur that monks should not be heeded, since they gladly obscure truth by deceptions provided that they please the archbishop; that episcopal rank and testimony carried great weight; and that monks had lost the right to testify in secular affairs.

“But this,” said Baldwin, “is not a secular matter.”

Then the magnates replied: “We know you to be an honourable and prudent man, not one of those whom a great multitude dishonours in your order by bad living. Yet both human and divine reason require that greater trust be placed in the testimony of three bishops than of two monks.”

Thus Anselm’s judgment long wavered [Col. 1497B] as to which side it should incline. To refute the bishops’ testimony openly seemed proud; yet not to believe a letter bearing the apostolic seal seemed foolish. Strengthening his resolve, he replied that he would send to Rome to discover the certainty of the matter. Meanwhile, those who had been invested were neither to be denied his communion nor granted his blessing. The elect were Roger, the king’s chancellor, for Salisbury; Reynold, the queen’s chancellor, for Hereford; and William, who, under Henry’s still recent authority, had been violently elected to the bishopric of Winchester.
