He did not consent to the election; indeed, he assailed the electors with harsh insults and threats. But when Anselm returned, William received the pastoral staff from him [Col. 1497C] and was admitted into the Church. Therefore he willingly gave his consent to Anselm’s blessing.

The king, somewhat more angered, charged Gerard of York with the consecration of them all. Nor would Gerard have refused, had not the elect resisted on a higher ground. Reynold, after at once returning ring and staff to the king, relinquished the bishopric. William did likewise, except that he did not return the ring. Roger, with commendable prudence, so moderated the affair that he neither angered the king nor injured the archbishop. Since Anselm in no way relented, saying that he would not act against the definitions of the apostolic see even at the cost of his life unless a remedy of absolution proceeded from that same see, the whole storm of trouble fell upon him.

He was approached by the king, bishops, and magnates [Col. 1497D] and asked to go to Rome himself, to supply by his presence what others had done inadequately. Whatever he wished, they said, would not lack effect, since the apostolic see valued him so highly. Let him only undertake this labour for his country, so that he might restore peace to the Church and dignity to the realm. Knowing that he could be moved by prayers, and lest he seem to presume everything upon his own judgment alone, he agreed. He would go, lest he fail the will of all, although the scarcity of envoys had reduced them to sending one old man, burdened with years and weak in body. Yet they should know that he would suggest nothing to the pope which would abrogate his predecessor’s glory or break his decrees.

“You,” they said, “only go, and in the pope’s presence, if the envoy speaks truth, support his testimony with the authority of your own.”

Having received agreement, they separated. [Col. 1498A] Anselm immediately crossed very great dangers under favourable winds and, with equally good fortune, completed the land journey to Rome. There, received with papal favour and a crowd of senators, he devoted a few days to silence and rest at the pope’s command. When leisure had restored his strength, he entered the Lateran palace on the appointed day. The messenger who had preceded his arrival by a few days was also present: William de Warlewast, already known in Rome, elect of the church of Exeter. He devoted all his eloquence to pleading the king’s cause: that all his father’s and brother’s customs should be restored to him; that England was a special province of the Roman Church and paid it annual tribute; that the king was as generous as he was high-minded. It would be disgraceful for him both to seem and to be deprived of the rights of his predecessors, whom he far surpassed and eclipsed both in greatness of spirit and abundance of wealth. The pope should therefore protect the king’s honour and consider his own interest, since he could no doubt extract a great profit of money from him, unless he thought canonical severity must be maintained.

By these and other arguments useful to the cause, [Col. 1498B] the Roman court was won over, under the king’s strenuous patronage, and declared that his wishes ought to be fulfilled. Meanwhile the two pontiffs kept silence, prudently observing and secretly ridiculing the bombast of the speaker and the vapours of his flatterers. Then the envoy, thinking their silence agreement, confidently burst out: “Many words may be debated on both sides, but this is the sum: my lord will not suffer the investitures of churches to be taken from him, even for the loss of his kingdom.”

“Nor,” said the pope, “will I permit him to retain investitures with impunity, even for the redemption of my head.”

At the tenor of such a statement, the tongues of the king’s supporters turned [Col. 1498C] and changed in another direction: “Blessed,” they said, “be the constancy of your heart; blessed be the speech of your mouth.” The envoy, confused, fell silent. Yet he obtained that some of the father’s customs should be relaxed for the king; and that, in the meantime, the king should be exempt from excommunication for having invested certain persons, while those invested should remain subject to the authority of the canons, their satisfaction being entrusted to Anselm’s judgment.

When Anselm had received leave to return, the other excused his own return, [Col. 1498D] saying that he was bound by a vow to go to Saint Nicholas. His intention was at variance with his words. For he was striving by every means to turn the pope from his ruling. When he saw that this was leading nowhere, he took a shorter route and arrived at Piacenza ahead of the archbishop. They then travelled together for several days. But when the roads separated them, he disclosed what he had previously concealed:

“My lord commands you that, if you show yourself to him as your predecessor showed himself to his father, he will gladly welcome your arrival in England; but if not—I speak to a prudent man—you know what follows.”

Thus William hastened to England, while Anselm made for Lyons. From there he sent letters to the king to establish the truth of William’s words. It has not seemed good here to weave in the sequence of letters [Col. 1499A]—stretching to an immense length—from the pope to the king, from Anselm to the king, and from the king to Anselm. Those wishing to read them will find them in Eadmer’s book. That man included them so that no one might accuse him of falsehood and so that he himself might derive invincible support for his statements; for he overflowed with leisure, being intent solely upon carefully explaining Anselm’s deeds. I undertake a greater work and attempt the deeds of many; therefore, selecting only what is necessary, I intend to relieve my readers’ weariness.

The king therefore took possession of the archbishopric, though with greater moderation than his brother, entrusting the administration of ecclesiastical matters not to outsiders but to men of the archbishopric itself. Anselm, however, remained at Lyons for a full year and four months. Throughout that time he obtained from the pope nothing but letters of persuasion, [Col. 1499B] and from the king nothing but reasons for delay. Royal envoys frequently went to Rome and returned without effect, except that they obtained certain postponements which prolonged the good man’s exile and hindered reform.

Therefore, seeing the condition in which fortune had placed his affairs, he at last stirred his breast, fruitful in compassion, toward punishment and contemplated excommunicating the king. When the king learned of this from a letter of his sister Adela, countess of Blois, he asked Anselm to come with the countess into Normandy, where the king was expected to be. He came, and the king, showing him much favour, restored him to all his possessions. But his crossing into England was delayed because he would not communicate with those who had been invested. The king went to England; Anselm turned aside to Bec.

Envoys were sent to Rome: William de Warlewast [variant: Warelwast] and the monk Baldwin. [Col. 1499C] They settled with singular excellence the controversy that had been conducted for so many years. For the pope allowed the king to receive homages from the elect, but not to invest anyone by staff and ring. While the envoys delayed, frequent complaints were brought to Anselm from England concerning crimes excessively multiplying everywhere. He was asked to hasten his return, especially by bishops whom the crimes themselves had now made weary. For the king was contemplating punishing by a pecuniary fine those priests who violated the council of Lyons, which had been held before Anselm’s departure: priests, I say, who after the council had either introduced new little women into their houses or recalled the old ones. Anselm, judging this intolerable, wrote to the king that he should refrain from this exaction, because the vices of ecclesiastical ministers ought to be corrected through the agency of bishops, not laymen.

The king, whose judgment, under the counsel of Robert, count of Meulan, [Col. 1499D] had now in every respect been clarified and matured by his own prudence, graciously accepted this salutary advice. He replied mildly that he would soon come to Normandy and, if he had offended in these matters or others, would make correction through obedience to Anselm. When the envoys had returned from Rome, the king sought Anselm at Bec without seeking many delays. Thus everything which had hitherto drawn them in different directions was then, through God’s grace, brought forward and settled. The churches which his brother William had subjected to fiscal revenue, [Col. 1500A] he restored freely into Anselm’s hands; and he promised that he himself would receive nothing from them so long as they lacked pastors. He compensated the loss of those priests who had paid money by exempting them from all dues for a full three years; those who had refrained from paying were to pay nothing further. He gave a pledge that, when Anselm returned to England, he would restore everything taken from the archbishopric.

Thus Anselm, carried to England by favourable winds, did not disappoint the good hope which the inhabitants of the province had placed in him. For immediately the farmers of churches were expelled, simoniacs condemned, priests’ concubinage prohibited, and unions of relatives broken up; and many other unlawful practices which had previously ranged with impunity were punished in like fashion. To the tranquillity of the times was added the king’s good fortune: [Col. 1500B] at that time in Normandy his brother Robert was captured and thrown into chains, together with many others whom he either already hated because of their troublesome conduct or feared because of rebellion. He seemed to repay his brother the due retaliation because Robert had troubled him when the kingdom was at peace; and at the same time he alleged that Robert was less fit to govern the commonwealth because of his mild temperament, since he saw his Normandy—the native land of both brothers—being ravaged by utterly wicked marauders and did not know how to defend it.

The king immediately announced the joy of this victory to Anselm in his own letter, which it does not seem out of place to include here because of this singular mark of royal devotion.

> HENRY, king of the English, to ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and friendship.
>
> We inform your fatherhood and holiness that Count Robert of Normandy, [Col. 1500C] with all the forces of knights and foot-soldiers whom he was able to gather by entreaty and payment, fought fiercely against me on the named and appointed day before Tinchebray; but at last, under God’s mercy, we conquered, and without great slaughter among our own men. What more need be said? By the mercy of God, the duke of Normandy, the count of Mortain, William Crispin, William de Ferrers, old Robert de Stuteville, and as many as four hundred other knights and ten foot-soldiers, together with Normandy, were delivered into our hands. There is no number of those whom the sword killed. But I attribute this not to self-exaltation or arrogance, [Col. 1500D] nor to my own strength, but to the gift of divine providence. Therefore, venerable Father, throwing myself in supplication and devotion at the knees of your holiness, I beg you to entreat the heavenly Judge, by whose will and decision this glorious and useful triumph has befallen me, that it may not be to my loss and harm, but to the beginning of good works and God’s service, and to maintaining and strengthening the state of God’s holy Church in tranquil peace, so that henceforth it may live free and be shaken by no storm of wars.

From this one may perceive how much material for good lay in the king’s breast, if anyone had encouraged the sparks of such noble faith with the fostering warmth of words and stirred them to greater strength by good admonitions. The king therefore came to England, resplendent with a lofty trophy and triumphal glory, [Col. 1501A] and permanently surrendered into Anselm’s hand the investitures of churches. Anselm consented that no one should be excluded from blessing on account of the homage rendered to the king.

Accordingly, five bishops were consecrated at Canterbury by Anselm on the fourth day before the Ides of August: William for Winchester, Roger for Salisbury, Reynold for Hereford, William de Warlewast for Exeter, and Urban for Glamorgan. Also present and assisting were the suffragans of the first see: Gerard of York, Richard of Lincoln, John of Bath, Herbert of Norwich, Robert of Chester, Ralph of Chichester, and Ranulf of Durham. Thus, through the venerable Anselm, the liberty of the churches returned and clear peace shone forth.

But it is unnecessary to speak of the decrees of the councils held by him, [Col. 1501B] since all are known to have perished in oblivion. Therefore it is thought to have happened not by chance but by divine intention that both at his consecration and at his reception of the pallium there was read: “He sent his servant at supper-time, etc.” (Luke 14). For in nothing was he effectively obeyed; almost everyone offered an excuse for what he taught by preaching or forbade by threats. Yet, after the example of the Gospel servant who, by two departures, filled the wedding banquet-hall with those not invited, Anselm himself, by twice leaving England, raised many gains of souls to heaven through preaching. Nevertheless, lest I seem to deprive students of historical matters, I shall think it no small labour wasted to set down the text of the council.

[Col. 1501C] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102, the fourth of the pontificate of Paschal, supreme pontiff, and the third of the reign of the glorious king Henry of the English, with his assent and by the common consent of the bishops, abbots, and magnates of the whole kingdom, a council was assembled in the church of St Peter, situated in the western part near London. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all Britain, presided; seated with him were the venerable men Gerard, archbishop of York, Maurice, bishop of London, William, bishop-elect of Winchester, and other bishops and abbots. At Anselm’s request to the king, the leading men of the kingdom attended this assembly, so that whatever should be decreed by the authority of the same council might be maintained as valid by the united care and concern of both orders. [Col. 1501D] This was necessary, since, for many years past, synodal discipline having ceased and brambles of vice having sprung up, the fervour of the Christian religion in England had grown exceedingly cold.

“First, therefore, by the authority of the holy Fathers, the intrusion of the Simoniacal heresy was condemned in that council. Those found guilty of this offence were deposed: Guy of Pershore, Wymund of Tavistock, and Aldwin of Ramsey. Others, not yet consecrated, were removed from their abbeys: namely Godric of Burgh, Haimo of Cerne, and Ælfric of Middleton. Others, however, were removed from their abbeys without simony, each for his own cause: Richard of [Col. 1502A] Ely, Robert of St Edmund’s, and the man who was at Michelney.

“It was also decreed that bishops should not undertake the office of secular courts; that they should wear appointed garments befitting religious persons, rather than dress as laymen; and that they should always and everywhere have reputable persons as witnesses to their conduct. That archdeaconries should not be farmed out; that archdeacons should be deacons; that no archdeacon, priest, deacon, or canon should marry or retain a wife. Any subdeacon who is not a canon, if after professing chastity he takes a wife, shall be bound by the same rule. That a priest, so long as he maintains an unlawful relationship with a woman, shall not be in good standing, shall not celebrate Mass, and, if he does celebrate it, his Mass shall not be heard. That no one should be ordained subdeacon or above without a profession of chastity; that priests’ sons should not inherit their fathers’ churches; and that no clerics should be secular stewards, administrators, or judges in cases involving bloodshed. That priests should not attend drinking bouts, nor drink ad pinnas (“at the pinnas”) [Note: [Col. 1501D] See *Gesta regum*, above, §149, note.]; that clerics’ garments should be of one colour and their footwear proper; that monks or clerics who have cast off their order should either return to it or be excommunicated; that clerics should wear open tonsures; that tithes should be given only to churches; that churches or prebends should not be purchased; that new chapels should not be made without the bishop’s consent; that a church should not be consecrated until the necessities of priest and church have been provided; that abbots should not make knights; and that they should sleep and eat in the same house with [Col. 1502C] their monks, unless prevented by some necessity. That monks should not impose penance upon anyone without their abbot’s consent, and that their abbots cannot give them permission for this except in the case of persons whose souls are in their care. That monks should not become godfathers, nor nuns godmothers; that monks should not hold villages at farm; that monks should not receive churches except through bishops, nor strip churches given to them so thoroughly of their revenues that the priests serving there suffer want in those things necessary for themselves and their churches. That a pledge of marriage given secretly and without witnesses between a man and a woman should, if denied by either party, be held void. That men with long hair should be so shorn that part of their ears is visible and their [Col. 1502D] eyes are not covered. That relatives within the seventh degree should not marry, nor, if married, remain together; and that anyone aware of such incest who does not report it should know himself to be a participant in the same crime. That the bodies of the dead should not be carried outside their own parish for burial, so that the parish priest loses what is justly due to him therefrom. That no one should, through reckless innovation, render the reverence of holiness to dead bodies, springs, or other things—as we have learned has occurred—without episcopal authority. That no one should henceforth presume to engage in that wicked traffic by which men hitherto used to be sold in England like brute animals.

“Those committing the Sodomitical [Col. 1503A] offence, and those voluntarily living in it [variant: assisting them], were condemned in the same council by a severe anathema, until through confession and penance they merit absolution. It was decreed that any person publicly known to be guilty of this crime, if a religious, should never thereafter be promoted to any rank and, if he already possesses one, should be deposed from it; but if a layman, he should be deprived throughout the whole kingdom of England of the dignity of his lawful status. Further, no one except a bishop should henceforth presume to grant absolution for this crime to those who have not bound themselves by a rule. It was also decreed that throughout England this aforesaid excommunication should be renewed in all churches and on every Sunday.”

[Col. 1503B] Thus there persisted in Anselm, to the end of his life, an unconquered strength and a fervour of piety. He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1109 [variant: 1110], the ninth of Henry’s reign, the sixty-sixth of his age, and the sixteenth of his pontificate. He was first buried at the head of his predecessor Lanfranc, but later received a worthier tomb in the eastern portico: a man surpassing, in wisdom and religion, all whom we have seen.

He was so free from sin that he told a most truthful man, well known to me, that since becoming a monk he had never been so driven by the goads of anger as to hurl an insult at anyone, except that he had fallen into this only once. Nor had he ever uttered more than a single saying whose memory wounded his conscience. Once, at supper, he recalled [Col. 1503C] that he had eaten raw herring; striking his breast, he groaned over his sin in having consumed raw flesh contrary to the law. When Eadmer, who sat beside him, said that salt had removed the rawness of the herring, he replied: “You have cured me, so that I am no longer tormented by the memory of sin.”

A steadfast guardian of obedience, though as archbishop he possessed free authority, he asked Pope Urban to appoint someone whose commands should govern his life. The pope presented Eadmer, and Anselm so highly valued Eadmer’s orders that, once he had put him to bed, he would not only not rise without his command, but would not even turn on his side. In ordinary conversation also he was a flowing torrent of eloquence, and even during meals did not cease from divine discourse. He was especially delighted [Col. 1503D] when questions were proposed and he could test the sharpness of objectors, resolving or eluding almost everything by analogies of his own devising or objections drawn from others.

Indeed, deliberately he displayed himself as dull in secular matters, so that, harassed by the stormy turmoil of such business, his bodily strength too would fail. When his household companions observed this, they removed the crowds and arranged for someone to sharpen his resting mind upon the whetstone of little questions. Immediately his mind was aroused, and, fixing his sparkling gaze upon his questioners, he recovered strength in both kinds of subject matter. How deeply he penetrated the hidden recesses of human and divine meanings is attested by his books, to which, envy having long since died away, the favour of the Latin world has succeeded.

[Col. 1504A] “Nor did the burden of the episcopate or the mass of such great affairs interrupt his customary miracles. Material fires and fires from lightning, already devouring neighbouring buildings, he checked and reduced to ashes by extending the saving sign. Champagne marvelled that a new spring bubbled forth from a rock when, at his blessing, the hollowed stone vomited water. A little hare, surrounded by hunters, sought refuge beneath the feet of the animal on which the saint sat and escaped unharmed; he gave the command, and the hunters’ eager hounds ceased their barking and their running pursuit failed them. Behold: by applying spittle he filled a woman’s empty eye-sockets with clear light; bread given by him restrained the shivering of one sick with fever.

“When, after sixteen years of episcopate, he had breathed his last, Ralph, [Col. 1504B] bishop of Rochester, who was present, asked Baldwin whether he had balm, or at least a few drops of it, with which the head, once anointed, might thereafter avoid the stain of decay. He brought out a vial, at the bottom of which a very small amount remained. Thus the fragrant liquid poured into Eadmer’s hand, such as it was, scarcely moistened half his palm. When it had quickly been spent, he marvelled that the same quantity flowed out again; and, an avaricious exacter, he did not cease to press the miracle with repeated attempts, until he had anointed the entire body in every part, and not perfunctorily, with balsamic unguent. And, that you may applaud the deed still more, although the vial was emptied so often—now held upright, now tipped sideways—when the solemn office of anointing was finished, it was found more than half full.

“On the following day, when the body was being prepared for burial, they discovered [Col. 1504C] that the stone receptacle of the body had heedlessly been cut less than a palm’s breadth too short. While all murmured that another stone could not easily be found, and that they did not wish, by bending the body, to injure the instrument of the Holy Spirit, suddenly they saw the stone made suitable and the body decently sink into the tomb without assistance. Joy arose among the bystanders and their cry struck the stars; a cry earned less by the worthiness of the miracle—though it deserves proclamation—than by the swiftness of aid not sought.

“On the eleventh day before the Kalends of May he passed into the next age. Yet he did not leave those who loved him in the world deprived of help. He still serves those who invoke him, and scarcely anyone approaches his tomb in ready hope without receiving the full effect of his prayers.

“That remarkable event [Col. 1504D] which happened recently at Lyons: there were there two aged anchoresses, than whom nothing was holier or more harmonious. While Anselm was staying there, he graciously visited them and instilled frequent exhortations to virtue. But after his departure, discord quickly boiled up between them—as is women’s way—broke the peace, and tore apart their concord. Gradually it came to blows: crooked envy and bitter spurs of reproach drove them day and night; fury armed their tongues and anger supplied insults. Both were entangled by their shared folly, but guilt weighed more heavily upon the one who had begun the quarrel.

“To her Anselm appeared by night, his countenance much changed from the gentleness she had seen in him while he lived. His sternness gave authority to his words, [Col. 1505A] and his severity seemed summoned from afar and from another world. ‘You have finely kept my counsels,’ he said, ‘which the religion of your profession and the affection of my diligent care ought to have commended to your observance. Now you sow quarrels and provoke hatreds, forgetful of your reputation, of my reverence, and of the advancement of you both. Why have you wearied me to come to you across such great distances? If you cease, I shall restore peace; if you persist, I shall threaten punishment.’

“This vision tamed the minds of the quarrelling women and softened their swelling anger. On the following night, when continual tears had exhausted them and sleep had laid them down, she prolonged her heavenly vigil. For, the clouds of earthly perception removed, she clearly saw him standing by our holy Lady Mary; at her command he sat at her feet. When the Lady’s graciousness gave her freedom to ask what she wished, emboldened by happy daring [Col. 1505B] she asked what might be hoped concerning Hugh, the recently deceased archbishop of that place. ‘It will be well, daughter,’ he said; ‘through God’s mercy remission is near and already at the doors.’ ‘And what ought be known concerning my lord Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury?’ ‘Concerning him,’ he said, ‘do not doubt in any way that he is in the great glory of God.’”

Let no one, I pray, receive these words as inventions of old women’s dreams with laughter or pursue them with mockery. For it is well established that those women were inferior to no saints whatever, both in the full rigour of abstinence and in the health-giving compunction of their minds.

Therefore, after Anselm of venerable memory, escaping the bonds of his earthen body, had taken leave of this life, the archbishopric remained vacant for a full five years. Throughout this entire [Col. 1505C] period, when the king was urged to provide for the widowhood of his mother Church, he postponed the matter with a mild answer: the archbishops appointed by his father and brother had been excellent, and he did not wish to fall away from the good fortune of his parents. Therefore, he said, the counsel must be considered with great scrutiny, so that he might appoint as archbishop one who either followed his predecessors in virtue with equal step or rivalled those nearest to them.

Such answers seemed full of justice and equity, and indeed they were. So, after long and careful deliberation, he convened a council at Windsor, intending to put the finishing hand to the business. His purpose was that Faricius, abbot of Abingdon, a man of great penetration and remarkable industry in bringing to completion what he had begun, should be chosen. Nevertheless, in the election of an archbishop alone he yielded nothing to his own wish, but referred the election to common judgment. That he did both then and on other occasions with notable self-restraint is clear; it concerns those very persons, at the divine judgment, with what intention they exercised the judgment delegated to them.

When, therefore, they wished to choose someone from the clerical order, there was an outcry: no cleric had ever been archbishop of Canterbury save Stigand alone, who had entered presumptuously and been deservedly expelled. A custom of such antiquity, they said, need not be made foolish, especially since it could not be proved contrary to the faith. Their plan thus defeated, and suspicious of Faricius’s severity, they said this: “If that Lombard becomes archbishop, there will again be lawsuits, again dissensions. [Col. 1506A] He will spare none of us, especially since the king will receive him as though he had descended from heaven. But this must not be said openly; let something be said that wounds no one’s conscience. There have been more than enough archbishops from foreign nations. The country abounds in men of our own tongue who may match Lanfranc in learning, display Anselm in religion, and surpass both in dress.

“There is Ralph, bishop of Rochester, whose reputation equals the ancients and whose humble affability surpasses both old and new. If you examine his birth, he springs from a distinguished Norman family; if you investigate his life, it is touched by no stain of infamy. He alone is such that not even envy can attack the discrimination of his religious life. If you search out learning in letters, he has drained all Athens dry; if you require eloquence, speech flows from his mouth in a kind of honeyed stream. Added to this is the polished and, as it were, carefully combed speech native to his soil, that is, Maine.”

These commendations prevailed, and the king immediately changed his decision in accordance with their will. This was done on the fifth day after the completion of five years from Anselm’s death.

Ralph had devoted himself as a monk in the first bloom of youth at Sées, an abbey in Normandy. As his virtues increased, he first became subprior, then prior, and finally abbot. This place, exceedingly poor and narrow, he had thoroughly raised up, outwardly and inwardly. At first Robert of Bellême, lord of that region, favoured him and allowed the man freely to keep watch over religion. But when Robert, as we have said elsewhere, had been expelled from England by King Henry and withdrew into [Col. 1506C] Normandy, he began to press the abbot for an oath and homage with ever greater persistence. Ralph, who had heard at Rome the pope’s prohibition, utterly refused. Therefore, leaving the abbey, he came to England and spent and wasted much time in visiting abbeys, where he was graciously received for the merit of his life and conversation.

For he judged it unworthy to return to Robert in Normandy, since Robert was the deepest abyss of every foulness and wickedness. Nor did he think it honourable to maintain hospitality for long anywhere in England, lest his importunity seem to provoke the disgust of the natives. A multitude of Norman abbots had then flooded the province, bringing to the English discourses rehearsed and polished in their homeland and consuming idle leisure now here, now there, at others’ expense. Accustomed to peddling their tongues and hunting the breezes of favour, Ralph avoided these grounds for distaste as modestly as he could. Instead, he spent more time with the archbishop, with whom he had been joined in holy and familiar companionship from youth.

Hence, when Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, died, Anselm appointed Ralph in his place, first receiving from him homage and an oath that he would be faithful to the holy Church of Canterbury. As the day of consecration approached, we have heard that Anselm earnestly prayed God that, since he had chosen Ralph as bishop, God would bring forth such an omen for him that he might rejoice that his judgment agreed with the divine will. Holy divinity answered this simple prayer and presented this verse: “They shall be like [Col. 1507A] the angels of God.” Thus made bishop, he did not disappoint the high expectation men had formed of him; rather, he brought it to fulfilment and made it publicly evident.

Accordingly, when the question of an archbishop arose, all concurred in his election, not only with ready will but with a united voice. Having been led to the see, he soon received the pallium through the favour of the Roman see, brought by Anselm the legate, nephew through the sister of Archbishop Anselm. For at the beginning of Henry’s reign Guy, archbishop of Vienne, who later became pope, had come to England to exercise the legation; then came Anselm, and not long afterward a certain Peter. All returned with no result, having made great gain for themselves—Peter especially, because everyone was careful not to provoke him, since he was the son of Peter Leo, [Col. 1507B] chief prince of the Romans.

Roman legates, plotting against Ralph’s weakness, therefore travelled frequently to England. Yet all were driven off by Henry’s caution. For he would not, contrary to ancient custom, receive a legate in England other than the archbishop of Canterbury; and, because of their violent monetary exactions, their advance was readily checked. But Cono, legate in Gaul, was not so easily turned: he involved all the bishops and abbots of Normandy in the stigma of suspension because, though summoned three times to his councils, they had not come. After consultation on this matter, Archbishop Ralph and Herbert of Norwich were sent to Rome to settle by their own efforts so great a confusion caused by legates.

But when he came to the castle called La Ferté, a most foul ulcer attacked and swelled his face, a sure sign of the paralysis to come. Pliny the Second calls it a carbuncle, a particular disease of the face which either eats away the skin to the bone or, if forestalled by physicians’ diligence, leaves an ugly scar. Thus he lay ill for many days. But afterward, when his sickness had been quieted—or rather his death deferred—he reached Rome. Paschal the pope was then absent and staying at Benevento. The emperor’s soldiers, who at that time were terrifying Rome with arms for the second time, had beset the roads between; and the archbishop could not obtain an interview with the pope except through envoys. What they accomplished with the pope will be shown by the letter.

“PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of England, and to his most dear [Col. 1507D] son HENRY, illustrious king, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“When our most dear and most reverend brother Archbishop Ralph came to us, we learned of the embassy sent to us by you through the venerable Bishop Herbert of Norwich. Indeed, hindered by serious and troublesome illnesses, these same brothers and fellow bishops were quite unable to come into our presence. But when honourable and venerable persons of the messengers arrived, we received their letters, in which we perceived both the wishes of their petition and those of your embassy. For this was desired and requested: that the Church of Canterbury should not in our times be deprived of its dignity; that we should not diminish, or permit to be diminished, that dignity which it has possessed from the time when it was founded by St Gregory through St Augustine. Besides these attestations of the letters, the legates sent to us, being wise and vigorous men, prudently, persistently, and effectively advanced their assertions.

“We certainly received kindly and gladly, as those of most dear brothers, both the persons of the legates, their assertions, and the embassy of you all; and we desire that this may please you in the Lord for the Lord’s sake. Therefore we wish your charity to know that we neither diminish nor desire to diminish [Col. 1508A] the dignity of the Church of Canterbury [variant: nor deliberate upon diminishing it]. We venerate St Gregory, pontiff of the apostolic see, in all things as a foremost member of Christ the Lord, as shepherd and teacher of the Christian people, and as minister of eternal salvation; and we wish those things to remain binding which proceeded from his institutions. Therefore, the dignity which the Church of Canterbury received from him through St Augustine, and which our brother Anselm of holy memory is known to have held by right and lawful possession, we by no means diminish. Rather, we wish the Church of Canterbury to remain in the same condition, so that its authentic privileges, in accordance with canonical decrees, may be violated by no disturbances. Given at Benevento, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.”

If the pope had expressly said, “The Church of Canterbury possessed these and these dignities, and I confirm those same dignities to it,” he would have resolved the lawsuit and set a limit to the controversies. But by saying, “Whatever authentic [Col. 1508C] privileges it possesses, we in no way diminish,” he left the matter, as it was, undetermined in the middle. Thus Roman cunning knows how to turn itself to the artifices of advocates and suspends what it wishes in empty ambiguity, sparing not others’ labour, so long as it serves its own advantage.

Ralph accordingly remained for several days near Rome, sometimes waiting for an interview with the pope in the emperor’s camp, but only with papal permission, sometimes at Sutri, where rumour had spread that the pope was just about to arrive. Suspended in that expectation, he lost his expenditure. Since the pope did not come, Ralph returned to Normandy and remained more than a year with the king, planning to meet Paschal’s successor Gelasius as he came this side of the mountains, so that, present as champion of his own cause, he might dispel the objections of his adversaries. For Thurstan, archbishop-elect of York, unwilling to make a profession to the archbishop of Canterbury, was energetically soliciting the minds of the Romans in his own favour.

Moreover, after Gelasius had been removed from the scene, when Guy, archbishop of Vienne, who was called Calixtus in the papacy, succeeded him and held a council at Reims, Ralph sent him envoys to support his cause. Calixtus received them openly with greater favour, but secretly deceived them more cunningly than befitted so great a man, by consecrating the archbishop-elect of York in contempt of every rule of antiquity. But by what means Thurstan defended his claims, even against the king, will not be omitted when the account reaches the bishops of York.

[Col. 1509A] But when Ralph returned to England, he was afflicted by the old infirmity of paralysis, which increased day by day, though not so greatly that he neglected ceremonial duties. Although his speech was more impeded, he was no feeble authority in counsel; indeed, he was sharper in anger, as is customary with that illness, which drives the mind toward irritability. Whenever anything was done against the right of his church, he bore it with difficulty and avenged it severely. Nor did he remain long alive, as the disease, daily growing fiercer, hastened his end. He died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the ninth year of his patriarchate, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1122.

Such was the end of Ralph [Col. 1510A], inferior to none in religion, magnificently powerful in literary learning, and certainly foremost of all in easy affability. He sought nothing more from the abundance of his fortunes than the ability to do greater good to those whom he wished. Yet, in the estimation of the common people, his glory was thought fitting only in proportion as his fortune increased. No suspicion of any fault, however slight, could attach to him, except that he was more inclined to laughter and jesting than appeared appropriate to his dignity or rank. But whatever he did, that man undoubtedly did with good intent; to suspect anything sinister concerning him is to act against religion.

## CONCERNING THE BISHOPS OF ROCHESTER

[Col. 1509]

[Col. 1509B] Next after the church of Canterbury comes that of Rochester: nearest by situation, though not by the authority of privilege. In former times it drank in the faith while the former was still nursing it, and now strives to imitate its mother in a following line of virtues. Rochester is a town exceedingly narrow in site, but placed on a height and washed by a very swift river, inaccessible to enemies without danger.

I have learned very few, indeed almost no, deeds of the bishops of that city which I consider worthy of record. Therefore, if I set down bare names, no one should be angry with me. For the lack of material will remove envy from one who says little.

Justus, first appointed bishop there by St Augustine, ascended the throne of Canterbury upon the death of Archbishop Mellitus.

Romanus was appointed at Rochester by Justus and, sent to Pope Honorius on ecclesiastical business, lost his life, drowned by the fury of the sea’s waves.

Paulinus succeeded to the vacant see. Antiquity has always held forth his praise and exalted it without measure. He was a Roman by nation, sent by St Gregory to England with the others for the ministry of the Word; appointed bishop to the Northumbrian people by Archbishop Justus; and he called the reluctant apostate king to the faith by declaring a heavenly oracle: that the divine mercy had once revealed itself to Edwin, and now had poured the spirit of prophecy into Paulinus. He himself received the pallium from Pope Honorius and consecrated Honorius as archbishop of Canterbury after Justus. After taking many spoils from the devil among the northern people, lest a veteran soldier should lack the trial of persecutions, he was driven in disturbance from his see by hostile violence and went to Kent. There, as I said above, he undertook the governance of the church of Rochester, Archbishop Honorius and King Eadbald eagerly seeking the favour of this most holy priest. He accepted what [variant: so that] brotherly charity urged from their minds, and, content for a time with the throne of an inferior place, entered upon the path of the flesh after nineteen years, two months, and twenty-one days from his consecration to York. He was buried in the church which King Æthelberht had raised from its foundations and [Col. 1510B] dedicated to St Andrew the Apostle, whose honour adorns that see: a saint famous in that province and reverently loved by all because he swiftly and eagerly comes to prayers.

Ithamar filled Paulinus’s place at Rochester, appointed and consecrated by Archbishop Honorius. He was English by birth, but in him one could desire nothing lacking in perfect holiness as regards life, nor in Roman elegance as regards learning. Thus, as the first Englishman to bear in England the grace of episcopal office in his native land, he added no small dignity to his countrymen. After Honorius, he ordained Deusdedit archbishop at Canterbury. This ought by custom to have belonged to the archbishop of York, but, Paulinus having been expelled, as I have said, no successor had arisen. For the Scots, who had filled that province through the favour of the Northumbrian kings, were more accustomed to hide obscurely in marshes than to dwell in lofty cities. Moreover, since they erred in many matters, and especially in the observance of Catholic Easter, the Roman remnant in Kent took care not to receive the ordinations of those in error.

After Ithamar’s death, Damian succeeded, appointed by Archbishop Deusdedit.

Theodore ordered Putta to succeed Damian: as suitable for ecclesiastical leisure as he was dull and sluggish in public affairs. Finally, though he often intended, while affairs were still in profound peace, to resign the episcopate, he willingly took up the cause of hostile injury. For King Æthelred of Mercia, angered by some insolent response of the king of Kent, was oppressing all Kent with sword and fire and had consigned every estate of the bishopric of Rochester to destruction. Putta embraced this misfortune with patient spirit and withdrew to Sexwulf, bishop of the Mercians. By the gift of his generosity he obtained a church in the countryside and a small field, and spent the remainder of his life in peace, conducting a public school of ecclesiastical chant wherever he was asked to go.

Then Quichelm was appointed to the see, but shortly afterward, confounded by lack of necessities, he too departed.

[Col. 1511A] Gebmund, appointed in his place, endured to remain.

He had as successor Tobias, filled to the utmost fullness with literary learning, as Bede says; for he possessed not only Latin but also Greek so familiarly that he could express in either language whatever he wished, as if it were his own, no less elegantly than readily.

He died, leaving Aldwulf as successor, who is indeed the last bishop of Rochester found in Bede’s list; for Bede goes only this far. I shall add the names of the rest as they are recorded in little documents: Dun, Erdulfus, Deora, Weremundus, Berumodus, Burthricus, Alstanus, Godwinus, Siwardus. The latter was bishop at the time when the Normans came to England and, surviving only a few days, fulfilled his fate. He left the [Col. 1511B] church wretched and empty, in want of everything both within and without; there were scarcely four canons, who sustained life on scant food, itself procured for the moment either by entreaty or payment, and in common clothing.

Proceeding to remedy these miseries, the most wise Archbishop Lanfranc appointed a certain monk, Arnost, as bishop of the place.

But when Arnost was snatched away by swift death, Lanfranc introduced Gundulf, likewise a monk. Under him the resources of the church increased magnificently. The monks became more than fifty; they cherish the rule, and all necessities abound. This is attributed to Gundulf’s glory and especially to Lanfranc’s industry, for from his own resources he also conveyed in perpetual right to the needs of the monks serving the holy Apostle the purchased village of Heddraam. Gundulf was full of religion, not unlearned in letters, keen and polished in secular affairs, and was thought to have deserved this honour above all by divine election.

For while he was still studying Holy Scripture at Caen, he happened to be sitting near his master, holding the Gospel, with two others. One was named Walter; the name of the other has escaped me. While their master was meanwhile occupied elsewhere, they engaged in some playful exchange and said to each other, “Let us test, by turning the leaves, which of us will become an abbot and which a bishop.” At once, upon turning the page, Gundulf, who went first, found: “The faithful and prudent servant, whom the Lord has appointed over his household” (Matthew 24). Walter found: [Col. 1511D] “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25). The third found something harsh, which troubled him. Though I heard it, I have gladly [Col. 1512A] forgotten it, since it is not the part of a noble mind to insult the misfortunes of others.

As they burst into laughter at the outcome, Lanfranc asked the cause of their joy; and when he learned it, he declared without hesitation that Gundulf would be a bishop, Walter an abbot, and the third one destined to be tossed about in the slippery affairs of the world. The event proved the truth of his saying. Gundulf became bishop at Rochester and Walter abbot at Evesham; the third came to nothing. And the miracle appeared all the greater afterward because Lanfranc had not yet conceived any hope of becoming archbishop, or even of crossing into England.

Thus Gundulf, having completed a holy end, had as successor Ralph, abbot of Sées, as I said before.

When Ralph was raised to the archbishopric, Ernulf succeeded him. [Col. 1512B] A Frenchman by birth, Ernulf spent no small time as a monk at the monastery of St Lucian at Beauvais. But when he saw some things full of insolence which he could neither correct nor wished to endure, he resolved to leave. First he sought Lanfranc’s counsel, intending without hesitation to do whatever Lanfranc judged should be commanded. Lanfranc, who well knew the man’s industry—for Ernulf had also studied for a long time at Bec under him—persuaded him to come to him, because he could not save his soul there. He came, and was a monk at Canterbury throughout Lanfranc’s lifetime; then prior there under Anselm; soon afterward abbot at Burgh; and was appointed bishop at Rochester by Ralph.

It would be difficult indeed to recount how great was his integrity and prudence in every office. At Canterbury he restored so splendidly the ruined earlier part of the church that Lanfranc had built that nothing like it could be seen in England: in the light of its glass windows, the brightness of its marble pavement, and the many-coloured paintings which draw admiring eyes to the heights of the ceiling. At Burgh the number of monks increased; religious life was fostered by good instruction; the ruins of old buildings were thrown down, new foundations laid, and roofs raised. When ravenous fire had consumed all these things, as he planned their rebuilding, episcopal honour was imposed upon him. At Rochester, though everything already seemed complete—for Gundulf’s energy had anticipated the diligence of all successors—he nevertheless always devised something in which his virtue might shine: strengthening ancient works and undertaking new ones. He lived as bishop a few days beyond nine years, and died at the age of eighty-four, leaving many monuments of his integrity.

## PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 1511]

[Col. 1511D] With Christ’s comfort I have brought the first book thus far, in which I seem to have done nothing short of my promise, by relating whatever memorable matter concerning the bishops of Canterbury or Rochester our knowledge could attain. Now, therefore, the order of my plan for the *Deeds of the Kings* would require that I proceed at once to the West Saxons, were I not prompted by the proximity of places to set first the bishops of the East Saxons [Col. 1512D] and East Angles. Let the reader understand that I followed another sequence of kingdoms from necessity: having first enumerated the greatest kingdoms, whose years and deeds remained extant, I then placed beneath them those in which almost everything had grown obsolete through the oblivion of years and the slightness of their power. Here, however, it might be reckoned an injustice if I deprived the bishoprics of their proper places; for their succession is neither [Col. 1513A] broken nor their renown so obscure. In this second book, therefore, I shall list the names of the bishops of the East Saxons and East Angles, and beneath them I shall place all the bishoprics of Wessex. Nor shall my care pass over any abbeys known to me within the dioceses of these bishoprics, nor the saints resting in them; and, arranging everything briefly, I shall, as far as I can, serve both the information of the diligent and the distaste [*nausca*] of the fastidious.

I ask, moreover, that no one blame me because I have transferred here, in the same words and sense, certain matters which I had set down elsewhere. I did this so that the sequence of matters not to be sought from another source might stand more elegantly together in one place; and, if I spoke suitably elsewhere, I did not think that I could speak more suitably here.

## Book II. On the Bishops of London

[Col. 1513]

[Col. 1513B] Not far from Rochester, about twenty-five miles away, is the noble city of London, wealthy in the riches of its citizens and thronged with the trade of merchants coming from every land, especially Germany. Hence it happens that, although throughout England provisions are dear [variant: scarce] because of the poor yield of the harvests, necessities are sold and bought there more cheaply than elsewhere, whether to the sellers’ profit or the buyers’ loss. The famous river Thames carries foreign merchandise into the city’s precincts. Rising from a small spring less than eighty miles before the city, it bears its name for more than seventy miles beyond it; for it enters the sea at Dover.

Here Mellitus first occupied the episcopal chair, Augustine the blessed having established him. Mellitus, an abbot at Rome, had not come to England with Augustine, but had later been sent [Col. 1513C] as reinforcement for the preachers. When ordained bishop, he had his see in the church of the apostle Paul, which Æthelberht, king of Kent, had built in London. For Sebert, king of the East Saxons, to whom London belonged, was subject to Æthelberht’s authority; he was Æthelberht’s nephew through his sister Ricula. In ancient times the East and South Saxons and the East Angles obeyed the king of the Kentish people, because Hengist, the first king in Kent, had obtained those provinces from Vortigern, king of the Britons, not by war but by guile. After Æthelberht, however, the South Saxons were subjected to the dominion of the West Saxons. Kings of the Mercians ruled the others, until the power of the West Saxons seized and subjected both these and those. But of this later.

At that time Mellitus, with God’s help and Æthelberht’s support, splendidly spread the Christian faith in the province. He also founded a monastery for blessed Peter in the western part of the city, warned, it is said, by a message from the apostle himself. Peter was seen there and is said to have dedicated in person the newly built church; and, through a rustic, he sent the bishop a most welcome gift, namely a large fish. Nor did Mellitus choose to doubt the man’s word, when he saw that this person, simple through rustic ignorance and not even a Christian, brought a message from Peter and accurately described, from a painting, the features of the apostle’s body which Mellitus knew. Thus the account was believed; and the rite of consecration was not repeated, since candles burning throughout the church, crosses made, water sprinkled, and the unmistakable traces of holy oil in their proper places showed it complete. Human diligence gave way to divine service, and Peter declared prophetically that the monastery would become very great, since the Apostle had performed episcopal service within it.

Little by little the truth of the prophecy came to light, especially in the time of King Edward the last, who, having gathered there a larger community of monks, rebuilt the church in a new style. King William likewise—and much more—raised the place with great revenues from estates, because he had received there the insignia of the kingdom. Thus the custom prevailed among later generations that kings about to reign should receive the royal crown there, because of the memory of Edward, buried [Col. 1514C] in that place.

After the death of Æthelberht and Sebert, Mellitus was driven from his see by their successor-kings and came to Canterbury. There, overwhelmed by the great anxiety that was consuming his companions’ hearts, he joined Justus and withdrew into Gaul, waiting in the hope that the storm of the times might perhaps grow calm. Yet a divine prompting was present: it softened King Eadbald’s heart to faith and quickly recalled them both. Justus indeed re-entered his own see without difficulty; but Eadbald could not restore Mellitus because he lacked the power to do so. Thus Mellitus remained for some time deprived of honour. Later, upon the death of Laurence, he became archbishop of Canterbury.

The stain of unbelief remained among the East Saxons [Col. 1514D] until the time of their King Sigeberht. At the urging of King Oswiu of the Northumbrians, he was baptized by Bishop Finan and restored his people, through Bishop Cedd, to the faith from which they had expelled it together with Mellitus. Cedd was the second bishop of London, but was buried in Northumbria at his monastery of Lastingham. You will find these matters more fully in Bede, who also records that Ceadda, brother of this Cedd, had an episcopal see and burial-place at Lichfield.

After Sigeberht, his brother Swithelm reigned. When he died, Sighere and Sebbi held the kingdom under the rule of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians. Sebbi attained a fine end of unblemished faith. In the time of pestilence Sighere broke the seal of faith, but through Wulfhere’s persistence he received it again by means of Bishop Jaruman.

When Cedd died, this Wulfhere, corrupted by money, installed upon the vacant throne a certain Wine, formerly bishop of the West Saxons.

In the following years Theodore, sent by Pope Vitalian as archbishop to Canterbury, gave the Londoners the venerable Erkenwald as bishop. Both recent report and ancient remembrance confirm that he was distinguished for miracles. The more notable of them was this: while ill, he was visiting parishes in a litter and happened to arrive at the bank of a very swift river. His companions hesitated, because the infirm man could cross neither on horseback nor on foot, and they feared [Col. 1515B] that the violence of the waters would sink the vehicle. Suddenly the whirlpool disappeared and the river wholly fled away at that point. As soon as the bishop crossed with his companions, the stream—which had stood apart, gathering itself into a mass with rippling waves—was restored to its channel. Bede attests that many weak persons were healed by touching the same litter.

He founded two monasteries, one for himself and another for his sister. His own is called Chertsey; with the support of a certain Frithwold, who acted as a sub-king under Wulfhere, Erkenwald filled it with wealth and monks. Religion flourished there, and no necessary provision was lacking until the Danes overwhelmed that place as they did others, burning the church together with its monks and abbot. But King Edgar, an incomparable prince, was not content with the new monasteries which he was then building everywhere, both personally and through bishops, unless he also restored the old ones. He wholly rebuilt this monastery, diligently gathering old charters on every side, by whose testimony he might restore to the place estates which certain great men had occupied as their own, either by force or by the authority of long possession.

His sister’s convent is called Barking, situated eight miles from London. There his sister, called Æthelburh, had companions joined to her in holiness and piety [variant: power]: Hildelith, her immediate successor, to whom the extant book of the most blessed Aldhelm *In Praise of Virgins* was sent; and Wulfhild, almost of modern times, who preceded the age of King Edgar by only a few years, and who by the grace of her holiness compensated for—and, I might almost say, anticipated—the antiquity of the others. For nothing which one who prays asks is denied, provided faith is not lacking. By their prayers, I truly confess, that place was never wholly destroyed; even now, in the time of the Normans, like many other places it has been raised to the highest point in number of nuns and beauty of buildings.

Erkenwald, then, is held to be especially holy at London, and has deserved no small favour from the canons through the speed with which prayers are answered. Others lie beneath so great a cloud of obscurity that even their tombs are unknown. This same misfortune has infected all bishoprics: among their inhabitants, it is counted a great glory if anyone can even give the names of the bishops of the place. But of their deeds or tombs—not a word. These, therefore, are the names of Erkenwald’s successors: Waldhere, Ingnald, Egulf, Wigeth, [Col. 1516A] Edbriht, Eadgar, Kenwalk, Eadbald, Hecbert, Osmund, Æthelnoth, Celbert, Cernulf, Swithulf, Etstan, Wlsius, Æthelward, Elstan, Theodred.

The citizens preserve a memory of this last man that has not entirely faded, saying that he lived in the time of King Æthelstan. They say that, when he went with him to war against Anlaf, he was, together with Odo of Wiltshire, an intercessor and announcer of that heavenly gift of which we spoke above. He gained the popular surname “the Good” because of the pre-eminence of his virtues, though he fell once through error rather than crime, in that he had thieves caught at St Edmund’s—whom the martyr had bound with an invisible knot when their attempts came to nothing—sentenced to the gallows under the severity of the laws. But, reflecting upon the deed, he repented, and for the whole remainder of his life practised penance, his conscience stung by guilt. His body lies beside the crypt window, elevated and visible to passers-by. After Theodred, the following held an unbroken succession:

Wulfstan, Brihthelm, Dunstan—later archbishop of Canterbury—Ælfstan, Wulfstan, Ælfhun, Ælfwig, Ælfword, and Robert, formerly a monk of Jumièges, made bishop by King Edward, first bishop of London and then archbishop of Canterbury. The preceding account has already related what his end was.

William, appointed by the same king, was his successor.

Moreover, William, king of England and formerly count of Normandy, made a certain Hugh, surnamed de Orival, [Col. 1516C] bishop. After a few years of his ordination, he fell into an incurable illness. A royal disease, covering his whole body with festering ulcers, led him to a shameful remedy. Believing those who asserted that the sole cure would be to cut away the shameful parts that receive the humours—that is, the genitals—he did not refuse. Thus the bishop bore the disgrace of being a eunuch, yet found no remedy; he lived as a leper until his death.

Hugh was succeeded by Maurice, the king’s chancellor. Though his reputation was in some respects less than favourable, he was nevertheless praiseworthy in effectiveness. The basilica of St Paul, which he began in London, is certainly evidence of his greatness of spirit: its magnificence of adornment is so great that it is rightly counted among splendid buildings; the crypt is so spacious and the upper church so capacious that they seem able to suffice for any multitude of people. Since Maurice was excessive in his ambitions, he left the expense of this laborious work to posterity.

Finally, when his successor Richard assigned all revenues belonging to the bishopric to the building of the basilica, supporting himself and his household from other sources, he seemed to accomplish almost nothing. He lavishly—and commendably—exhausted all the income on this, and little came to completion. Therefore the impetus toward good which he had at the beginning of his episcopate, weakening through despair as the years passed, gradually languished.

There is a place in the diocese of London among the East Saxons called Chich [variant: Cic] in the native tongue, where rests the blessed virgin Osgyth, famous for miracles. This man endowed it with some lands and with regular canons. There were, and are, clerics there eminent in learning; and through their example so great a crop of men, if I may put it so, clothed the whole country in joy. He himself planned one day, after laying aside the wrappings of the world, to withdraw there, especially when warned by the wasting effects of prolonged paralysis—had not the habit of power drawn his sick mind back by its allurements. [Col. 1518A]

The first prior of this place was William of Corbeil, who, upon the death of Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, was raised to that dignity. Though the monks had feared to receive him because he was a clerk, he gave them no cause for regret. For he was very religious, somewhat affable, and moreover neither idle nor imprudent.

## On the Bishops of the East Angles and Their Monasteries

[Col. 1517]

[Col. 1517A] The first bishop of the East Angles was Felix, a Burgundian by birth. Having become a friend of Sigeberht during the latter’s exile in Gaul, he came to England with him after the death of Eorpwald. When Sigeberht obtained the kingdom of the province, Felix was ordained bishop and did not fail the king’s zeal, but with great devotion and vigilant labour instilled Christian belief throughout the whole region. He also founded schools of letters in suitable places, gradually shaping the barbarism of the people by Latin refinement. Having completed the course of life after seventeen years as bishop, he was buried at his see of Dunwich; from there he was translated to Soham, a settlement beside the mere. This was once dangerous to boats travelling toward Ely, but now, a way having been made through the marshy reed-bed, it is crossed on foot. There still remain signs of the ruined church, burned by the Danes, whose ruins buried its inhabitants, burned with it. The saint’s body, sought and found much later, was buried at Ramsey monastery, of which there will be later mention.

Thomas, his deacon, a native of the province of the Gyrwe, was appointed in his place.

After Thomas died five years later, Boniface, a man of Kent, filled his see and held office for the same number of years as his predecessor Felix.

Then Bisi, a venerable man, was made bishop by Archbishop Theodore; as long as health permitted, he lived without reproach. But struck by a disabling illness, he made room for two men. Thus two bishops always ruled that province until the time of Egbert, king of the West Saxons: one sat at Dunwich, the other at Elmham.

[Col. 1517D] Baldwin and Hetha; Northbert and Astulf; Nethlac and Eadred; Edelfrith and Cuthwine; Lamferd and Albrith; Æthelwulf and Eglaf; Hufred and Eadred; Sigge and Alliun; Alherd and Titfrid—these were the two bishops of the East Angles. Ælheard was bishop of Elmham and Titfrith bishop of Dunwich when Offa, king of the Mercians, created an archbishopric at Lichfield.

Humbrith and Weremund, and after him Wilred: in the time of Ludeca, king of the Mercians, and Egbert, king of the West Saxons, Humbrith and Wilred were bishops of the East Angles. But when Ludeca and his predecessor Burhred invaded the province, the bishops too were deprived of necessary supplies. Both kings indeed perished within the region in attacks by the people of the province; nevertheless [Col. 1518A] the two bishoprics ceased, and from two there was made one, whose see was established in the not very large village of Elmham. These, therefore, were its bishops:

Æthelwulf, Ælfric, two Theodreds, Æthelstan, [Col. 1518B] Algar. The writer of the Life of the venerable St Dunstan gives no slight indication of this man’s holiness; I shall place it here in his own words:

> The feast-day of Christ’s Ascension preceded by three days the day of the glorification of blessed Dunstan. Therefore, at dawn on so great a day, a certain priest named Algar, pre-eminent in learning and conduct—whom we later learned had shone as illustrious bishop at Elmham—while he was keeping vigil and rendering the holy honours due to the Lord’s Ascension in the church of the Saviour, and stretching his mind toward contemplation of heavenly things, having gone beyond himself and all things of this world, saw Dunstan seated upon a pontifical throne and giving canonical precepts to the clergy. And behold: through all the doors of the church entered countless bands of angels rushing in. When, drawn up in ordered ranks, they stood before the seated bishop, they addressed to him this greeting: “Hail, our Dunstan. If you are ready, come and enjoy our gracious companionship.” Dunstan answered: “You know, O holy spirits, that Christ ascended today, and that it is our duty to refresh the people of God both by word and sacrament; therefore I cannot come today.” They said: “Be ready on Saturday to pass hence with us to Rome and dwell eternally before the supreme pontiff as a saint [variant: with the saints].” The angels departed. But the priest, who had been so clear a spectator of these events, silently and in amazement awaited their outcome.

And below:

> The priest also, who had seen so wonderful an ecstasy in the church, when he learned that he had experienced it not in an image but in the reality of events, openly recounted to all, with great groans, what he had seen.

I have borrowed this from another writer, that readers may be shown how venerable Algar was: he was worthy not only to behold such hidden things with mystical eyes, but also to reveal them publicly. Nor would I think it credible that, after taking up a higher rank, he devoted less watchfulness to holiness. Rather, one must believe that he was made bishop because of reverence for his virtues, and that on his own day he was received into heaven among the bands of angels which he had seen.

After him came Ælfwine, two Ælfrics, and Stigand, or “the Expelled.”

Grimketel, elected for gold, held the dioceses [Col. 1519A] of the East Angles and South Saxons. But as time passed Stigand so recovered his position that he restored to himself the bishopric of the South Saxons and obtained that of the East Angles for his brother Æthelmer. Thinking this too little for his ambition, he ascended the thrones of Winchester and Canterbury, scarcely and reluctantly persuaded to have a bishop specially ordained for the South Saxons.

After Æthelmer, Herfast was bishop of Elmham, as is found in the record of the council held in the sixth year of King William concerning the primacy of the two metropolitans. So that he might not appear to have done nothing—as Normans are exceedingly eager for future fame—he transferred the bishopric from Elmham to Thetford. He was, as they say, a man of narrow mind and not inconsiderably learned; yet before Lanfranc became a monk at Bec, he was esteemed in Normandy for respectable learning. But after Lanfranc had become a monk at Bec, when scholars everywhere were belching dialectic with puffed cheeks, Herfast—then chaplain to Count William, later king—arrived at that famous school with a great display of companions and horses. Lanfranc, understanding from their first conversation how nearly Herfast knew nothing, set before him an alphabet to work through, mocking the man’s arrogance with Italian wit. Enraged by this, Herfast procured through the count that Lanfranc be expelled from Bec and from all Normandy. But through God’s grace William’s anger was calmed and Lanfranc was retained, chiefly through the efforts of William, son of Osbern. A great occasion for recovering favour [Col. 1519C] arose when Lanfranc came to court seeking leave to travel, and his horse happened to limp, causing the count to burst into laughter.

After him, in the days of William Rufus, Herbert, surnamed Losinga—so called because he was skilled in flattery—bought the bishopric of Thetford. He had been prior of Fécamp and abbot of Ramsey, and his father Robert, bearing the same surname, had been intruded into the abbacy of Winchester. This man, then, was a great source of simony in England, having hunted both abbey and bishopric with money, ensnaring royal attention with cash and whistling no slight promises into the favour of princes. Yet in more mature years, after going to Rome, he erased the erroneous impulse of youth by repentance. There, laying aside the simoniacal staff and ring of the see, he deserved to receive them again through the indulgence of the most merciful See, because the Romans judged it holier and more orderly that the revenues of all churches should serve their own purses rather than be employed for the uses of any kings.

Thus, returning home, Herbert transferred the episcopal see to the town called Norwich, distinguished for commerce and populousness. There he founded a community of monks illustrious in number and religion, purchasing at his own domestic expense everything necessary for them. Foreseeing complaints from successors, he granted the monks no lands from the bishopric, lest they might deprive God’s servants of provisions, should they take offence at anything touching their own [Col. 1520A] property. Moreover, at Thetford he established Cluniac monks, for the professed members of that order are scattered almost everywhere among all peoples, wealthy in the world and splendid in their devotion to God.

Thus, by an immense and abundant grace of virtues, he overshadowed the mass of his former offences, especially warned away from evil and lifted toward good by both his predecessor’s prediction and his own. Herfast’s saying was, “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John 18); Herbert’s was, “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matthew 26). On hearing this, he could scarcely refrain from tears and words to this effect: “I confess that I entered badly; but, through the working of God’s grace, I shall leave well.” He possessed eloquence and learning in abundance, no less than expertise in secular affairs, and was worthy of the regard of Roman greatness. Herbert was changed—as Lucan says of Curio—“the turning-point and change of affairs”: as he had been an advocate of simony in King William’s time, so under King Henry he was its unconquered opponent. He would not allow others to do what he had once rashly undertaken in youthful ardour. As they report, he always carried before him Jerome’s saying: “We erred when young; let us amend when old.”

Finally, who could worthily add to the praise of that deed: that a bishop not very wealthy made so noble a monastery, in which you would desire nothing in vain, whether in the appearance of lofty buildings, the beauty of ornaments, the monks’ religious life, or their diligent charity toward all? These things both sustained him while living with a happy hope and bore him, when dead—if trust in repentance is not vain—above the heavens.

The monastery of St Edmund is known to belong to the diocese of the bishop of Norwich. Although I have spoken of it elsewhere, it is not without reason if I now mention it briefly. Thus my arrangement will proceed in the order I have devised: after mentioning bishops, I shall not pass over saints resting in their dioceses. It has also happened fittingly, I confess, that St Edmund appears first, so that, as king and prince of the country, he might claim first the palm of praise among his fellow-countrymen, the saints.

He reigned in East Anglia, a man devoted to God and distinguished by the ancestral lineage of kings. After governing the province peacefully for some years, he was compelled to forswear his valour amid the softness of those times: the Danish leaders Ivar and Ubba came to lay waste the provinces of Northumbria and East Anglia. The former captured the king, who did not resist but had cast down his arms, lay prostrate upon the ground, and prayed; after several tortures, Ivar beheaded him. Then too the episcopal see at Soham, as I have said above, and the monastery of Ely, its nuns having fled, were burned and levelled to the ground. But after the blessed man’s death, the purity of his past life shone forth in worthy miracles.

The executioner’s cruelty had severed the head from the body, and the Danes had hidden it by throwing it into thickets. When the citizens sought it, following the tracks of the departing enemy in order to perform the due rites for the royal funeral, they received joyful gifts from God: all heard the voice issued by the lifeless head, calling everyone to it; a wolf, a beast accustomed to flesh, held the head harmlessly in the embrace of its forelegs as its guard. [Col. 1521A] Like a domestic animal, it followed the bearers modestly behind to the tomb, harming none and harmed by none.

For the time being, the venerable body was committed to the ground: a hastily heaped turf was thrown over it, and a wooden chapel of little value was built above. In the following period, thorns covered even the small structure, and the people of the province abandoned the martyr’s memory in their hearts. He came to the aid of the negligent, awakening their half-sleeping minds to reverence for himself by signs. The first proof of his powers which I shall add is slight and unremarkable, yet still the first: a blind man, feeling his way with a staff, entered the chapel by a nocturnal mistake, and heavenly light met him and filled his eye-sockets. Soon after, when thieves attempted by night to plunder the same shrine, invisible cords entangled them in the very act, a most beautiful spectacle: the prey held the plunderers, so that they could neither abandon their undertaking nor complete what they had begun.

For this reason the bishop of London removed the long-standing reproach of the common structure, building a more confined edifice over the venerable limbs. They proclaimed the glory of the holy soul both by their marvellous incorruption and by a certain milky whiteness. The head had been joined to the rest of the body, yet it bore the sign of martyrdom in a crimson scar. But this surpasses human miracles: the hair and nails of a dead man grew, and a certain holy woman, Oswen, each year cut the former and trimmed the latter, to be preserved for posterity with great reverence. She was a woman of holy boldness, touching limbs beneath which all the lower world lies.

Not so Leofstan, a youth of unrestrained audacity. In swollen threats he demanded that the martyr’s body be shown to him, intending, as he said, to weigh the uncertain report by the testimony of his eyes. For this rash act he paid the penalty: he became mad, and soon afterward swarmed with worms and died. Edmund surely knew how to do what he had once been accustomed to do:

> To spare the subject and to subdue the proud.

By these two qualities he so bound to himself all the inhabitants of Britain that a man counts himself blessed above all if he enriches the place of Edmund’s repose even with a coin or some payment. Kings themselves, lords of others, glory in being his servants and send him a royal crown, redeeming it at a great price if they wish to use it. Tax collectors, [Col. 1521D] who elsewhere rage, measuring right and wrong alike, humbly halt their litigations before the ditch of St Edmund, having learned the punishment of many who thought they ought to persist.

King Cnut ordered the ditch to be made, taught by the miserable end of his father Swein to turn toward good. For when Swein, in King Æthelred’s time, was devastating all England and breathed no less fierce threats against the land of St Edmund, the martyr, they say, lightly warned him in a dream. But Swein, answering more harshly in barbarous folly, was struck by a spear and killed. There was only this delay in between: awakening from sleep, he revealed to those standing by both the author and manner of his death. For the guardians of the body had heard in a remarkable manner the conversation of disputants and the sound of the blow. Cnut knew these things and therefore did everything possible to win the saint’s favour. Besides the ditch already mentioned, which protected the saint’s lands from all disturbance, he finally built over the venerable body a basilica with royal zeal, as the practice of that age required; he appointed an abbot and monks and bestowed many great estates. The magnitude of his gifts remains whole even today, for that place looks down upon certain monasteries of England.

In the succession of abbots there was Leofstan in the time of King Edward. Giving bad counsel to certain people who badly disbelieved in the saint’s incorruption, he safeguarded others’ faith at his own risk. He brought the body into the open for inspection, himself pulling at the head while his monk pulled at the feet. Then he openly prayed:

> Lord St Edmund, you know that I have done this not with an unbelieving mind, but for the salvation of others, lest the divine miracle in you should be hidden from the world.
