Yet because I am guilty of many sins, and the instrument of the Holy Spirit ought not to have been touched by me, if this action displeases you, punish me in this life. For it is better, evil though it be, that I suffer some notable bodily injury than be enveloped in eternal vengeance.

He had scarcely finished the prayer when, behold, the fingers of both hands were either miserably bent backward or stubbornly pressed into the palms; the punishment which he had requested afflicted the man. Later, struck by other infirmities as well, he approached King Edward by messengers to ask him to send a doctor. The king arranged to send Baldwin, a monk of St Denis skilled in that art. Though he did well in other matters, he made no progress in treating the fingers. The man, who had had great success in healing, began to wonder. But once those who knew informed him of the cause of the illness, he remained in that place, embracing with all his heart love for the martyr. Thus, after gaining full acquaintance with the leading men over many years, Baldwin did not so much succeed Leofstan as join him as abbot—Leofstan losing office, with the king’s consent.

Under Baldwin and through him, Pope Alexander granted freedom to the monastery: that the place should in no respect be subject to any bishop, looking only to the archbishop’s direction in lawful matters. Everything within and without was renewed. Nowhere in England were the splendour of the buildings and the weight of offerings such as there. Two saints, Germanus and Botulf, lie in the church. I do not recall finding their deeds either there or elsewhere, except that the former is said to have been brother of St Æthelthryth, the latter a bishop.

## On the Bishops of the West Saxons, and First on the Bishop of Winchester

[Col. 1521]

[Col. 1521D] Come now: since we have run through the names of the bishops of Canterbury and Rochester, of the East Saxons and East Angles, let us commemorate the sees and deeds of the rest, insofar as they are known either by report or writing. [Col. 1522D] First, according to the logic of our plan, the West Saxons present themselves. They first had one bishop at Dorchester; then two, one at Winchester and the other at Sherborne. In the time of King Edward, three were added to the two: the bishop of Wells, of Crediton, and of Cornwall. Not long afterward a sixth was established at Ramsbury. Since the discourse intends to treat all these in order, first, because of the city’s rank, we must speak of the bishop of Winchester.

In the time when Cynegils and Cwichelm ruled among the West Saxons, Birinus—whose origin is uncertain—undertook the office of preaching in Britain at the urging of Pope Honorius. Ordained bishop by Asterius, bishop of Genoa, he made for the sea in order to cross into Britain. As he was packing his belongings, the sailors urgently pressing him because the wind was favourable, he forgot the corporals, as they are called. But once he had put out to sea and the happy ship was ploughing the calm deep, he remembered his loss and was troubled in mind: if he called to the sailors to return, he would undoubtedly be laughed at for a second voyage; if he kept silent, he would suffer loss in his apostolic office.

> Therefore, arming himself with all the force of faith, he descended on foot into the sea and, running swiftly, returned to the shore he had left. There, having found and taken up the corporals, he returned to his companions with a twofold venture of blessed confidence, scattering by faith the heaps of waves and a thousand deaths confronting him.

They too, softened by so great a miracle, cast off the anchors and held the ship’s course. Thus, received with the eager service of all, not long afterward he reached the mainland in the territory of the West Saxons. This was the fortieth year after Augustine’s arrival, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of the aforesaid kings. Birinus had promised Pope Honorius that he would penetrate the furthest provinces of the English, scattering the seeds of faith where even the name of the Gospel had not been heard. Yet as soon as he landed, he found everyone there most stubbornly devoted to sacrilegious rites. It therefore seemed foolish to press farther on and, finding no one sound there, to seek out sick people to heal. He stayed, and, both by God’s direction and his own effort, first gave King Cynegils himself and then the whole province the saving washing.

A most praiseworthy coincidence occurred: the day appointed for the king’s baptism fell upon the day on which he had resolved to give his daughter in marriage to Oswald, the most holy king of the Northumbrians. Thus, by a generous exchange, Cynegils’ future son-in-law according to the flesh first became his spiritual father in baptism. The two kings therefore gave their preacher the episcopal see of Dorchester—then a city, now a village. The kings of the West Saxons possessed it at that time; later the bishops of the Mercians did so. Indeed, down to our own age the episcopal see of the Mercians remained there, but now it is at the city of Lincoln.

Thus Birinus, his holy labours completed and his life ended, was buried at Dorchester in the church which he had built. In later years, when the bishopric of the West Saxons had been established at Winchester, Bishop Hedda translated him there; he is held, after God, to be the city’s patron.

After him Angilbert, a Gaul by nation, held the episcopal office of the province. You will read more fully in Bede concerning his arrival and departure; here you shall learn the matter briefly. When Wine—an Englishman, but ordained among the Gauls—had been introduced into the bishopric of Winchester, Angilbert departed in anger. Nor did the intruder enjoy his leisure long: driven out by the tyranny of the same king, he fled for refuge to Wulfhere, king of the Mercians; and, having bought from him the bishopric of London, he spent the remainder of his life there—a harsh example to posterity, so that one can scarcely decide whether the greater sin and disgrace belonged to him who put a sacred office up for sale, or to him who bought it.

Then Angilbert, asked through the king’s messengers to return, excused his coming on the ground that he was bound by the obligations of the bishopric of Paris. Yet, lest he disappoint the petitioner’s hope, he sent his nephew Leutherius. Received with the ready consent of the provincials and consecrated by Theodore, archbishop, Leutherius governed the church of the West Saxons for seven years. [Col. 1524A–B] I have not passed this over in silence because Bede left no explicit statement concerning the years of his episcopate; and, having learned them from the Chronicles, I thought it contrary to due conscientiousness to conceal them.

His successor for more than thirty years was Hedda, formerly a monk and abbot. Bede says that he performed his office more through an inborn love of virtues than through any training in letters. Hence I am troubled by no small perplexity, since I have read his formal letters, composed with no great lack of learning, and Aldhelm’s writings to him, which breathe the greatest force of eloquence and learning. The number of miracles sent from heaven made the reverence due to his holiness known to men; for the present I suppress them, content with the glory acquired immediately after his death. [Col. 1524B–C]

When he died, because his diocese could not suitably be governed by one man owing to the vastness of its extent, it was divided into two: one portion was given to Daniel, the other to Aldhelm. With God’s help, there will be an occasion, when the discourse reaches Aldhelm and his successors, to speak of him as far as may suffice for the profit of listeners; now I shall address the men of Winchester, as I promised.

Daniel outlived Aldhelm by a long time and held the episcopate for forty-three years. Afterwards, in order to bring his vigorous old age to its holy completion in leisure, he relinquished his living office, practising the monastic life at Malmesbury for as long as he lived, as report, sincerely transmitted to us through successive generations, relates. He is also said to have been buried there, although the people of Winchester claim that they possess him among themselves, while unable to show his tomb either truly or even plausibly. [Col. 1524C–D]

Humfred succeeded him, whose memory occurs in the council of Archbishop Cuthbert. Then came Cyneberht; after him Æthelard, formerly abbot of Malmesbury and soon afterwards archbishop; then Egbald, Dudd, Cyneberht, Almund, Wighten, Herefrith, Eadmund, and Helmstan. This last was bishop in the time of Egbert, king of the West Saxons.

When Helmstan had entered upon the way of his fathers, Swithun succeeded him, a priest of the same church, long before ordained by Helmstan. In him, since religious life accorded with unassuming prudence, his natural and cultivated merit did not escape the king’s notice. Accordingly, the king so cultivated his acquaintance that he both conducted many of his affairs by Swithun’s counsel and placed his son Adulf under his instruction. [Col. 1525A] By this act the young man’s future good fortune foreshadowed its own prosperity: under a most holy teacher he learned how he might later proceed, not untrained, to govern the commonwealth.

For there is Plato’s old and celebrated maxim: “A state will then be happy, if either philosophers rule or kings practise philosophy.” The truth of this saying came to fulfilment in this Adulf. When his father died, because no other lawful heir existed, he was transferred from the rank of subdeacon of Winchester to kingship, with the consent of Pope Leo III. Then it was evident what spiritual philosophy had taught him: he looked more to the servants of God than to his own interests, tithed the whole kingdom to God, did nothing unless it was right, and commanded nothing unless it was pious. But we have treated these matters elsewhere. Now we unfold the deeds of Swithun, which are in hand.

Regarding him as his foster-father and teacher—for so he called him—the king did not desist until he had honoured him with the bishopric of Winchester, with the clergy consenting and Ceolnoth, archbishop of Canterbury, ordaining him. Thus, while the king joyfully laid the foundations of good things in the kingdom, they sprang up through the bishop: the latter pressed forward the good which the former had begun, especially by his admonitions. Swithun was indeed a storehouse of every virtue, but he particularly delighted in two: mercy and humility. The pen shall set forth examples of both.

He happened to be sitting beside workmen building a bridge in the eastern part of the city, so that his pressing presence might spur the negligence of the idle. [Col. 1525B–C] And behold, a woman passed over the bridge into the city, carrying eggs for trade [variant: “for commercial purposes”]. Men leapt out from every side—as is the custom of people of that sort—and, with wanton jostling, broke every egg, down to the last. This did not seem a slight matter to people of sounder mind, but was immediately reported to the lord bishop. He listened to the complaint of the poor little woman, worn down by age and rags, sighed over her loss, and compassion stirred his hesitating mind to a miracle [variant: “stirred his mind into a miracle”]. At once, extending the sign of the cross, he restored the brokenness of all the eggs. Is this a slight proof of holiness and mercy?

What of his humility? Whenever he had to dedicate a new building for God’s Church, however long the journey might be, he made his way energetically not on horseback or in a vehicle but on foot. And lest he be made a laughing-stock by the ignorant or be marked out by the proud with a boastful encomium, concealed from human sight, he travelled the whole route by night. A lover of solitary holiness, he displayed none of his good works with pomp. I suppose this is why, having enjoyed heaven alone as witness, he deprived posterity of knowledge of all his miracles.

Now, when about to bid farewell to the present life, the bishop commanded those standing by, under pontifical authority, to bury his body outside the church, where it would be exposed to the feet of passers-by and to raindrops falling from above. He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 863, six years after the death of Adulf. Many years passed, and God’s pearl lay hidden without glory for nearly a hundred years. [Col. 1525C–1526A]

During this course of years, eight bishops completed their days: Alfrith, Duubert, Denewulf, Frithestan, Byrnstan, Ælfheah, Ælfsige, and Brihthelm. Our diligence will not omit some of these, whose lives were made more famous.

Denewulf, if report is to be believed, was not only without learning until advanced age but was also a swineherd. King Alfred, driven from his kingdom by the violence of enemies and fleeing into the woods, happened upon him tending swine. To avoid a lengthy digression: having discovered Denewulf’s aptitude for good, Alfred handed him over for instruction in letters. Nor did Alfred abandon this task until he made Denewulf, more fully trained, a bishop, devising an undertaking worthy of a miracle.

Frithestan was one of the seven bishops whom Archbishop Plegmund consecrated at Canterbury in a single day during the reign of Edward, son of Alfred. An abundance of books still reveals his many good qualities; his holiness of life, however, lies hidden in an obscure burial, unlike that of others. [Col. 1526A–B]

Byrnstan governed the bishopric for only four years. We have received that he was of most pure holiness: every day, without interruption, he sang Mass for the repose of the dead; at night, overcoming fear, he was accustomed to walk about alone, frequently reciting psalms for the salvation of souls. On one occasion, when he was doing this and, after completing all else, added, “May they rest in peace,” he heard voices, as though of an innumerable army, answering from the graves: “Amen.” This is all the more remarkable because it is uncommon for the dead to hold converse with the living, lest he grow weary in a service which he heard to be welcome to so many souls.

The same man, a most ardent fulfiller of the Lord’s example, daily washed the feet of the needy with all witnesses removed, set out table and food, and no less, as part of the discipline of service, wiped away the leftovers. When the service was complete and the poor had been dismissed, he remained there for many hours, occupied, as is believed, in prayer. [Col. 1526B–C] One day, then, having entered as usual and having previously been troubled by no sickness, he suddenly, with no one aware, lost the breath of life. His attendants, knowing his custom, believed on this occasion too that he was engaged in prayer, and allowed him to lie there the entire day. But at dawn on the following day, bursting in, they found a senseless corpse. Thus he was mourned and given burial.

But the citizens, seeing that his life had been cut short by death, erased every memory of him by silence, not knowing what is written: “He cannot die badly who has lived well. And the righteous man, whatever death may overtake him, shall be in refreshment.” [Col. 1526C–D] Divine justice corrected this long afterwards, when Æthelwold succeeded. At the beginning of the night, while Æthelwold was accustomed to keep vigil before the relics of the saints, three figures appeared standing before him—not in ecstasy, but while he was plainly awake. The middle one was heard to utter these words:

> “I am Byrnstan, once bishop of this city. This man”—pointing to his right—“is Birinus, its first preacher; and this one”—pointing to his left—“is Swithun, the special patron of this church and city. Know that, just as you see me here with them in the present, so I enjoy with them in heaven a glory not unequal. Why, then, am I deprived of the honour of mortals, when I am exalted by fellowship with heavenly spirits?”

He had finished; and, vanishing into the air with his companions, he added the precious memory of himself to the people of the province, thereafter earning every mark of veneration. [Col. 1526D–1527A]

Ælfheah, in addition to the accumulation of other virtues in which he excelled as abundantly as he did praiseworthily, was also renowned for prophecy. Two sayings of this sort served as examples.

It was Ash Wednesday [variant: “the day was Ash Wednesday”], and the bishop, as customary, was excluding penitents from the thresholds of the church. He urged the rest, while devoted to fasting and chastity, to reject even the pleasures of marriage: in those days it was a fruit worthy of repentance if one who had committed many unlawful acts abstained even from lawful ones. While the others listened reverently to his teaching, one man uttered a jesting remark that provoked laughter in the rest. He said that he could not restrain himself from both feasting and marriage, so as to abstain alike from food and Venus. Indeed, he would soon recall to nocturnal use the wife whom he had kept from his bed for some time; and with a wanton, vulgar phrase he intensified his own folly. [Col. 1527A–B]

Then those present heard and understood the bishop murmuring: “You grieve me, wretch, not knowing what the coming day will bring forth.” The nearby death of the scoundrel fulfilled the grim prophecy. For on the following morning he was found lifeless in his chamber, apparently dashed to death by a devil.  

At another time he ordained three monks together to the rank of priest: Dunstan, Æthelwold, and a certain Æthelstan. The latter afterwards apostasized from the monastic habit and, scorning celibacy, spent his life in the embraces of prostitutes. When the rites had been completed, the bishop of holy memory addressed those who remained near him:

> “Today, before God, I laid hands upon three men. Two of them shall attain the grace of pontifical rank: one in the city of Worcester, then in Kent; the other shall one day fill my see by lawful succession. The third, plunging himself into the mire of pleasures, shall meet a wretched end.”

Æthelstan, present because of a close family relationship, assailed the priest with an insolent question: “Shall I be one of the two to be raised to episcopal dignity?”

“No,” he replied. “You shall have neither part nor lot in the rank of which I have spoken; nor shall you remain in the garment by which you now entice the eyes of men.” [Col. 1527B–C]

How great was the dignity of that most holy mind, to disclose the secrets of heaven openly and without disguise! For these words did not fall to the ground, but all were confirmed by their consequences: Dunstan and Æthelwold, treading the narrow way which leads to life, shone conspicuously in the bishoprics foretold; the third ran along the broad paths of the world. [Col. 1527C–D] The preceding book has related Ælfsige’s headlong madness in buying the archbishopric and his wretched death.

I now judge it fitting to say something, however briefly, concerning the father Æthelwold, who succeeded Brihthelm, the successor of Ælfsige, at Winchester. Both his parents, neither poor in means nor lowly in lineage, were citizens of Winchester. In childhood he studied letters; in youth, frequenting the court, he was very dear to Æthelstan. On that king’s advice he was tonsured into the clerical state by the aforementioned Ælfheah [Col. 1528A], and not long afterwards Dunstan, abbot of Glastonbury, clothed him in the monastic cowl and appointed him dean of the monastery. He won the affection of some by learning, of others by religious devotion, and of all by love.

At that time the abbot had a dream about him, certainly memorable. He saw a tree growing within the enclosure of the same monastery, which, spreading its branches through the four quarters of the world, shaded all England. It was covered throughout its foliage with cowls; and a very great cowl placed at its summit protected the smaller ones beneath, as though by the shelter of sleeves. Astonished by the marvel of so great a vision, he asked its meaning of a venerable old canon standing nearby. “That tree,” he said, “is this island; the greater cowl is the life of your monk Æthelwold; the others are the lives of countless men whom he will draw to the Lord by word and example.” [Col. 1528A–B]

A vision of his mother agrees with this portent. It was shown to her when he was already growing large in her womb and she was expecting childbirth. A golden eagle flew from her mouth, surveyed the city for a long time with the beating of its wings, and finally, rising to the height of the clouds, entered heaven.

His approaching fortunes were already bringing the true fulfilment of these visions before the people, when, desiring exile in Gaul out of longing for a stricter life, he was kept back by King Eadred. This was done through the influence and urging of the king’s mother, Eadgifu, known throughout the British world for every praise of religious devotion. He was therefore given the very small monastery called Abingdon, where he might test the powers of his prudence. Nor did he fail the hopes of those who gave it to him through lack of energy; rather, he raised it to a praiseworthy height, as can be seen today. [Col. 1528B–C]

A few years passed. Dunstan had now become archbishop, and Æthelwold himself was elected by King Edgar to the bishopric of Winchester and consecrated by the same archbishop. Then he rose with great efforts for the benefit of the churches: to uproot vices and plant virtues. One could not tell what to praise in him more: zeal for holiness or exercise of learning; persistence in preaching or industry in construction.

The clerics of the bishopric and of the other church nearby, which they called the New Monastery, were given a choice: either change their manner of life or yield the place. Choosing the easier alternative, they were expelled, and monks were brought in. Several estates from the bishopric, nearer in situation and more ample in revenue, were assigned to them. In the same city a monastery of nuns was founded and established. [Col. 1528C–D] The other foundations which he instituted in various regions will be discussed when we come to their bishops.

Indeed, it seems remarkable that he accomplished so much, were it not that King Edgar was wholly devoted to his will. The king loved him above all men except Dunstan; and the most blessed Swithun, revealed at the same time, greatly and commendably advanced his works. Retaining the humility of his former life, Swithun appeared in a vision to no eminent person, but to a poor little man who supported himself by manual skill, and seemed to utter the following:

> “Go to Winchester, to the Old Monastery. Seek out the keeper of the place and command that Bishop Æthelwold be told to open the tomb of Swithun, once bishop, and raise up his relics; there he will find pearls more precious than every treasure. Merciful divinity has looked upon his times, that through me they may be illumined by heavenly miracles. And, lest you hesitate, take this as a sign: you shall be able, whenever you wish, with slight effort to pull out and replace the iron rings forcibly fixed with lead to the stone of the tomb. If others attempt the same, it will be in vain.”

[Col. 1528D–1529A] The man went; and, having obtained fulfilment of the promise in the presence of the custodian, he was admitted to the bishop’s presence. There he fearlessly presented the matter and gained belief for his words. On the appointed day, therefore, the bones were raised from the tomb and placed in a shrine. A huge multitude gathered, to offer vows and heap up vows. No one complained of being defrauded: all was done, all was granted.

Finally, such an abundance of miracles was displayed for every kind of illness as no human memory can attest to have occurred elsewhere. Thus that saint bears the surname *Pius*, “the Compassionate,” swift to aid every person who calls upon him, unless faith be lacking. His goodness, long since begun, has not grown stale even in our own age. I myself saw—marvellous though it is—a man whose eyes robbers had gouged out by violence receive clear daylight through the merits of Swithun, his eyes being restored, whether the same eyes or others, for the original eyes had been thrown far away. The evidence of his former calamity remained: the scars of pointed wounds disfigured his eyelids. [Col. 1529A–B]

Meanwhile the saint wishes God to be glorified in all things and does not allow anyone healed through him to wallow wantonly in fleshly vice, if that person does not wish to be entangled in the former sickness. Indeed, when the monks had once become weary of the frequency of miracles and, because some marvel occurred in the middle of the night, delayed [variant: “were summoned”], being deprived as they were of sleep, their dullness did not escape the eye of the saint, who watched from afar. Immediately he appeared to Æthelwold while the latter was asleep at the royal court, threatening to withdraw the calling of healings if the monks thought that they ought any longer to cease from the praise of God. For why should they sleep during God’s praise, when he himself kept watch for their salvation? [Col. 1529B–C]

Nor was Æthelwold himself idle in miracles. The compassion of the living and dead saints seemed to vie with one another: as the miracles of the saints grew frequent on either side, the faith of one was strengthened and health was restored to the other. He dispersed by faith a deadly poison drunk through the treachery of servants, when it had already crept through his limbs and was consuming his vital organs. He repaired a lost vessel for olive oil and, having found it, filled it full. By a word he bound the arms of a thieving monk with invisible snares, and by his blessing alone loosed the bonds when that same monk confessed. A fall cast down another man standing on a precipice, but Æthelwold’s prayer put a hand beneath the falling man and restored him to his former function. [Col. 1529C–D]

A famine of food had seized the province because of the barrenness of the soil. He ordered sacred vessels to be broken up and distributed, declaring that it was better for their metal to serve the need of the wretched than the ostentation of priests. When the New Church, long desired, had been built, he was taken from the world, to the great distress of the monks but none to himself. For he exults on high in glory; the monasteries which he had made, many ruined and all diminished after his death. [Col. 1529D–1530A]

Ælfheah succeeded Æthelwold, good after one who was good. I have said something concerning him above, but now I should like to speak at greater length. As a boy he embraced books and schools; as a young man he changed his habit at Deerhurst [variant: Duhest], then a small monastery, now an empty image of antiquity. There, having received the rule of monastic life, he aspired to something higher and made for Bath, where, shutting himself within the walls of a more secluded cell, he inwardly tasted heavenly things.

Many good monks gathered to the place through him, but, as happens in a great body, they also contracted the corruption of disease. Certain of them, without the father’s knowledge, prolonged their banquets into the night and likewise persisted in drinking until daylight. [Col. 1530A–B] God did not endure this longer, but struck the ringleader of the faction with death in the very building that knew of their gatherings, at dead of night.

Meanwhile the saint, while interrupting his prayers, heard a sound coming from the same house, like men attacking and resisting one another. Wondering at this novelty, he approached the door slowly, holding his breath. Through the cracks of the windows he then saw two huge demons tormenting a lifeless corpse with repeated blows of hammers, while the man sought help with miserable cries. The enemies answered: “Neither did you obey God, nor do we obey you.” When he related this to the others in the morning, it was no wonder that the accomplices in the revelries became abstinent.

When Wentanus, bishop of Winchester, died, Dunstan the archbishop—moved by an oracle of the apostle Andrew, who named Ælfheah as the one to be chosen—placed him on the throne. [Col. 1530B–C] He was prudent in worldly matters and simple in relation to God, providing for outward things without neglecting inward ones. He raised up his predecessor’s bones in the twelfth year after the latter’s deposition, persuaded to dare this by certain signs, and not insignificant ones.

In order worthily to adorn the see of so great a father, he followed the footprints of that father’s holiness. When he sat at table, he neither crammed the hollow of his belly nor fell into the display of one who practises abstinence. He never indulged in meat unless ill; he always merely touched cups with the tip of his lips. The thinness of his body, which scarcely clung to its bones, revealed the abstinence of his eating. At night, deceiving his guards, he went alone to the river. There, immersed up to the waist and keeping vigil in God’s praises, he returned to his chamber at the whitening of dawn, unknown to his attendants. [Col. 1530C–D]

After completing twenty-two years in the episcopate, he was transferred to Kent, unwillingly, they say, because he was deprived of a familiar honour in order to be burdened with a greater charge. For Cenwulf, abbot of Burgh, had purchased the bishopric of Winchester with money; but he did not long rejoice in his sacrilegious daring, dying within two years. Ælfheah, meanwhile, set out for Rome to receive the pallium from the Apostolic See, and crossed the Alps.

There, when he had lodged in a certain village, a rustic mob attacked him and stripped him of all that he possessed. Immediately a fire, arising from an unknown source, seized the houses and, strengthened by a gust of wind, threatened destruction to the whole village. Then these people of brutish mind, though only with difficulty perceiving their offense, pursued him as he had already departed and was now well on his way. They bowed before him, begged forgiveness, and restored what they had taken. [Col. 1530D–1531A] Ælfheah, easily moved to mercy, set the sign of the cross opposite the fire; immediately it recoiled upon itself and died away, and the entire blaze cooled into ashes.

While he was at Rome, he saw and announced the death of his successor, though no one had brought him news of it, as was said elsewhere. Returning from there to his see, he happily held the patriarchate for seven years. When these had passed, he was thrown into chains by the Danes and lived in prison for seven months. Seek elsewhere the causes of his imprisonment.

Meanwhile a deadly pestilence raged among the Danes and cast down the enemies in heaps, so that the swiftness of death forestalled the sensation of pain. The stench of unburied corpses infected the air; the more corrupted atmosphere produced plague among others who seemed healthy. They fell, therefore, without measure and without number, until, at his entreaty, Ælfheah shared with them bread blessed by himself and drove away the plague, restoring health. Yet those ungrateful recipients of his benefits nonetheless stoned their healer to death. [Col. 1531A–B]

Others, however, who had sounder judgment, contended for the burial of the bishop’s remains and for some time had the murderers as opponents. But when the dispute was brought to judgment, it was agreed that, if a dry piece of wood which chance had supplied, once smeared with his blood, should grow green again on the next day, the Christians might bury the body according to their judgment. And so it happened: the wood, which at that time even lacked bark, was found green in the morning, budding with flowers and swelling with fruit. Therefore the body was then allowed to be buried peacefully at St Paul’s in London; thence, in the tenth year, at the command and in the presence of King Cnut, it was raised and glorified the seat of the patriarchate without any corruption in itself. [Col. 1531B–C] The freshness of the blood and the integrity of the body still endure and were seen very recently.

Nor indeed did any one of the murderers escape without paying the penalties, which I could recount truthfully if I were not reluctant to relate the sufferings of the wretched. The persecutor’s misery is sufficiently impressed upon us when the martyr’s glory shines forth.

After Ælfheah, Æthelwold sat at Winchester; Ælfsige [variant: Ægelsige] succeeded Æthelwold; Ælfwine succeeded Ælfsige; and Stigand succeeded Ælfwine.

When Stigand was deposed, as has often been said, Walkelin, appointed by King William, succeeded him. His good works, surpassing fame, will repel the old age of oblivion for as long as the episcopal see endures there. [Col. 1531C–1532A] Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, when contemplating the approach of death, had commended him as a pledge of faith, because there was hope in him of praiseworthy character if he should obtain material in which virtue might shine.

Walkelin made the archbishop’s promise true, accomplishing things in religious life, in the number of monks, and in the construction of buildings beyond what could have been hoped. At first, indeed, as a newly arrived stranger, he had hated the monks; but he was easily corrected and often lamented that cloistered hatred. Thereafter he cherished them as sons, loved them as brothers, and honoured them as masters, withholding from them neither assistance nor intimacy because of their different dress. He insulted no one with abuse, declaring that episcopal dignity stained its own glory with an unworthy blot if it descended to insult those who were poorer. [Col. 1532A–B]

There is one very great matter in which he sinned: he took from the monks lands worth nearly three hundred pounds and assigned them to his own use and that of his successors. He appointed as prior of the place a certain Godfrey, born at Cambrai, a man distinguished by religious devotion and learning. His learning is attested by his letters, published in that familiar and pleasing style, and especially by his epigrams, composed in a satirical manner; further, by verses in praise of England’s primacy. What more? He made the whole divine office, obsolete through a certain antiquity, shine with native elegance.

He beautifully set forth for the monks a pattern of religious devotion and hospitality, so that today they follow Godfrey’s model in both respects so closely that nothing, or little, is lacking to complete their praise. Finally, in that house there is a lodging for those arriving by land and sea: for as long as they please, an inn with expenditure unfailing and charity untiring. [Col. 1532B–C] The holy man also possessed such humility of character that nothing proceeded from that single storehouse of philosophy except what was humble, nothing except what was sweet.

Yet how slight may this praise of him seem? How many are there who, though only slightly steeped in letters, do not consider others beneath their dignity, displaying consciousness of their learning by swollen bearing and pompous gait? Nevertheless, lest anything be wanting to his holy soul’s perfection, for many years he endured a sickbed, his sins purged in the furnace of prolonged wasting illness.

## On the Monasteries

[Col. 1531]

[Col. 1531D] There is also in the same city a monastery which King Alfred had once conceived in mind, which his son Edward had built, and in which he had placed canons, at the persuasion of Grimbald, formerly a Fleming [variant: “a certain Flemish monk and priest, etc.”]. Grimbald was buried there with great honour and is proclaimed and believed to be a saint. But Æthelwold of blessed memory expelled the canons and installed monks, appointing over them an abbot named Edgar, of whom I have spoken above.

For establishing the facilities of this monastery, the aforesaid king bought a sufficient tract of land from Bishop Denewulf and the canons of that time, paying a gold *mancus*, weighed by public standard, for every foot of land. [Col. 1532D] The two churches were so close together, with adjoining walls, that the voices of the singers interfered with one another. Hence, both because of this and for other reasons, unhappy envy unearthed many grounds upon which they might inflict no small injuries upon each other.

For this reason, that monastery was recently transferred outside the city, where it is inhabited more wholesomely and endowed more freely. Moreover, the aforesaid king built in the same city a convent of nuns; but in later years that place was enlarged by blessed Æthelwold. He set over them the aged virgin Æthelthryth, who, drawing an inference from the dream that his mother had seen about a golden eagle, prophesied much concerning him.

Before her there had been a small monastery there, in which Eadburh, daughter of King Edward the Elder, had lived as a religious and died; but by that time it was almost destroyed. [Col. 1533A] When Eadburh was scarcely three years old, she gave remarkable proof of her future holiness. Her father wished to test whether the little girl would incline toward God or toward the world. In a hall he placed ornaments of different callings: on one side a chalice and Gospels, on the other bracelets and necklaces.

The little girl, carried there by her nurse, sat at her father’s knees. Ordered to choose which she wished, she scorned the worldly things with a stern look; crawling quickly with her hands toward the Gospels and the chalice, she adorned them with her childish innocence. The assembly of those sitting by cried out, acclaiming in the girl the omens of her future holiness. Her father himself honoured his child with closer kisses: “Go,” he said, “where divinity calls you; follow with blessed step the bridegroom whom you have chosen.”

Thus, clothed in the habit of nuns, she invited all her sisters to love of herself by assiduous service. [Col. 1533B–1534A] Nor did the loftiness of her lineage make her proud, as though she thought it noble to bow down in Christ’s service. Her holiness grew with age, and her humility matured with adulthood, to such a degree that she secretly took away each sister’s shoes at night and, after carefully washing and oiling them, put them back by their beds.

Many miracles, in life and after death, commend both the devotion of her heart and the integrity of her body; the custodians of the churches recount these better by word of mouth.

In the diocese of this bishopric are three monasteries: Chertsey, Romsey, and Wherwell. Chertsey has already been discussed. Of Wherwell it is known that Ælfthryth, wife of King Edgar, built it in honour of the Holy Cross, struck by remorse over the undeserved murder of her stepson Edward, of whose death she herself was aware and the instigator. [Col. 1534A–B] At Romsey, a monastery founded by the most excellent King Edgar, I know that the bodies of two virgins, Merewenna and Ælfthryth, lie buried. I do not know their deeds; I do not so much pass them over as reserve them for more diligent writing, should I perhaps learn them.

## On the Bishops of Sherborne, Salisbury, and Wilton

[Col. 1533]

[Col. 1533C] In the division of the West Saxon bishopric, this arrangement is plainly observed: he who sat at Winchester held the two districts of Hampshire and Surrey; the other, who sat at Sherborne, held Wiltshire, Dorset, Berkshire, Somerset, Devon, and Cornwall. Sherborne is a village, attractive neither by the number of its inhabitants nor by its situation; it is astonishing, and almost shameful, that an episcopal see should have endured there for so many centuries. Now its bishopric has been turned into an abbacy, by a transaction not unfamiliar in our age, when all things are corrupted by faction and greed and virtue is held in mockery and reproach.

The first to sit there was Father Aldhelm, whom I name here only for the sake of order. Since I have nowhere found his life fully arranged, and since very many matters pertain to it—matters which I should wrongfully conceal from posterity [variant: “which, if I conceal from posterity, etc.”]—I have determined, with God’s assent, to deal with material of this kind more freely and at greater leisure in the final book of this little work.

After him sat at Sherborne Forthere, Herewald, Æthelmod, Denefrith, Wibert, and Alstan. [Col. 1533C–D]

Alstan lived in the time of Egbert, king of the West Saxons, and of his son Adulf, and beyond it. He had great worldly power and enormous authority in counsel. By military exertions he subdued the people of Kent and the East Angles for King Egbert. Seeing that Aldulf was of a gentler disposition, he urged him by constant admonitions toward knowledge of kingship; he roused him from lethargy against the Danes, who were then first ravaging the island; he himself supplied enough money from the treasury and himself assembled an army. Whoever reads the annals will find that through him many undertakings of this sort were both begun steadfastly and completed successfully.

He lived fifty years in the episcopate—happy, if for so long he remained within the bounds of good works! I would gladly praise him, except that, carried away by human greed, he usurped what was not due when he subjected our monastery to his own business. [Col. 1534C] We feel to this day the grievance arising from his shamelessness, although that place, immediately after his death, struggled free from all violence of bishops until our own time, when it fell again into the same danger.

> “So presumptuous is the beginning of evils that, though their author dies, the example does not pass away. A stubborn mind delights to recall what evil another has done, and to hear what it may itself do.”

The monks of that time lamented the liberty taken from them with less disgrace than we, who have lost ours, especially because theirs was immediately restored through those same men. Yet he was, as we have heard from writings, as burning in greed as he was exceptional in generosity. Our plunderers both ravage and oppress, so that not even a free voice is granted to grief. [Col. 1534C–D]

Anyone may perceive his power from the fact that he kept the king himself, returning from Rome, out of the kingdom. Having set the king’s son up to rule in his father’s shadow, he did not allow the old man to return to his own realm until peace had been arranged according to Alstan’s judgment. He left his church exceedingly rich in estates acquired from every side; if you heard how great they were, you would wonder at either the man’s greed or his good fortune.

Those who followed him were Eadmund, Æthelweg, Ælfsige, Asser, and Sighelm, the last two of whom are known to have lived under King Alfred, the fourth son of Adulf. Asser, summoned from St Davids, was a man of learning not wholly contemptible: he elucidated Boethius’s *On the Consolation of Philosophy* in plainer words—a necessary labour in those days, ridiculous in ours. But it was done at the king’s command, so that it might more easily be translated by him into the English language. [Col. 1535A]

Sighelm, sent across the sea on behalf of the king’s alms and also to Saint Thomas in India, penetrated India with remarkable success—something which anyone in this age may regard with wonder. Returning from there, he brought back gems of exotic kinds, in which that land is fertile. Some of them may still be seen among the church’s treasures.

Sighelm was succeeded by Ethelweard. On his death the bishopric of the West Saxons lapsed for seven years, compelled, that is, by the force of hostilities. Afterwards Plegmund the archbishop and King Edward, son of Alfred, constrained by the threats and decrees of Pope Formosus, made five bishops in place of two, as we have often said and now repeat—somewhat inopportunely, for the sake of maintaining the sequence of events. [Col. 1535B] They appointed Athelm to the church of Wells, Eadwulf to that of Crediton, Werstan to Sherborne, Athelstan to Cornwall, and Fidestan to Winchester. Thus Ethelmus had Somerset, Eadwulf Devon, and Athelstan Cornwall; I find nowhere the names of the latter’s successors. Three districts were left to Werstan: Dorset, Berkshire, and Wiltshire. Yet not long afterwards, while the same king was still alive, a separate bishop, also named Athelstan, was made for Wiltshire and had his seat at Ramsbury. Werstan, they say, whom King Athelstan had taken with him in the battle against Anlaf, was slaughtered by pagans. For when, as was said elsewhere, the king had deliberately withdrawn, the bishop came with his men to the battle and, unaware of the ambush, [Col. 1535C] pitched his tent on the level of the green field from which the king had departed. Anlaf, who had reconnoitred the place on the preceding day, arrived prepared by night and promptly destroyed whatever he found.

After him these were bishops: Ethelbald, Alfred, and Wilffinus. Dunstan, when he was bishop of London, had made this man abbot at Westminster, furnishing the little monastery with twelve monks, on the site where Mellitus had once built a church for St Peter. Since he administered the office entrusted to him piously and wisely, episcopal rank was conferred upon him at Sherborne. At once he established monks in the episcopal seat, having expelled the clerics, lest he should seem to sleep amid the great diligence of the bishops of his own time. He granted the monks nothing from the bishopric for [Col. 1535D] the necessities of life, but bought provisions elsewhere; he also conceived the plan of appointing an abbot. When they objected that, while he lived, they could not bear to be deprived of his sweet lordship, he yielded unwillingly, openly declaring that this would be the beginning of great calamities for their successors.

The proof of his holiness was shown often in life, but especially in death. For, when he was already pressing close upon the gates of death, he cried out with the eyes of his mind opened, in song: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” [Acts 7]. Having uttered this chant without faltering, he died while singing: a holy and venerable soul, able to borrow the words of the first and most blessed martyr; blessed because it saw heaven opened [Col. 1536A] and deserved to enter it. His staff is still preserved there, together with certain other episcopal insignia, presenting, so to speak, a living likeness of his moderation and humility.

He was succeeded by Alfwold, Ethelric, Ethelsius, Brithwin, Elmer, Brinwin, and his brother Alfwold, formerly a monk of Winchester and later bishop. At Sherborne he installed an image of the most holy Swithun and kindled the flame of his veneration. It is agreed that he lived a most reverent life. Amid the lavish preparations for banquets then displayed in England in the Danish period, he always used a wooden bowl without any richer food, and a small cup into which water had been poured so that every flavour of ale might be diluted. I myself heard a trustworthy priest, already sprinkled with grey hairs, [Col. 1536B] recounting his virtues with tearful joy.

Of these things one has not escaped me: no one, either before or after his death, could without punishment press upon his seat by sleeping there, without at once springing back in terror at dreadful apparitions rebuking him for usurping, though unworthy, the bishop’s seat. This was a spectacle to many.

A troubled enmity had arisen between him and Earl Godwin, for what reason I do not know. On the day appointed for a hearing, when the matter was proceeding not toward peace but toward litigation, the bishop departed after an altercation, hurling this threat at the earl: “By my lady St Mary, it shall go badly with you because you have grieved me.” Having returned home, he had scarcely set foot on the ground, changing from riding to walking, [Col. 1536C] when, behold, an attendant of the earl arrived, having spurred his horse and showing by the beating of his pace the speed of his course. Throwing himself miserably at the bishop’s knees, he begged him to return. His lord, he said, had begun to burn in heart immediately after the bishop’s departure and could scarcely move his tongue.

Then the bishop said: “My anger has not yet been appeased. By my lady St Mary, woe shall be his.” But moved by the united prayer of the petitioners, he granted reconciliation to his beloved friend, gave his blessing, and restored the sick man.

The priest also related that the bishop had been devoted to St Cuthbert with humble obedience, gladly weeping at every remembrance of him. He almost always held in his heart that antiphon concerning the saint; he pondered it with his mouth and practised it in deed:

> St Cuthbert, the holy bishop,  
> a man perfect in all things,  
> was among crowds a monk  
> worthily revered by all. [Col. 1536D]

As his daily love took sweet increase in his breast and the good flame did not consume itself there, he went to St Cuthbert at Durham. There, in what seems great boldness, he removed the lid of the tomb, spoke faithfully with him as with a friend, deposited a small gift as a pledge of perpetual love, and departed. When the destined moment was now at hand, he kept singing the antiphon as long as his voice held out; when speech failed, he signalled with his hand for the others to continue. Thus, with his final breath, he gave evidence of the love he bore for the saint. After his death the bishopric of Wiltshire was again joined to that of Salisbury. How this occurred I shall tell, if I first set down the names of the bishops.

[Col. 1537A] The first bishop of Wiltshire was Ethelstan; the second, Odo, afterwards archbishop; the third, Osulf; the fourth, Algar; the fifth, Elstan. He was first a monk of St Ethelwold at Abingdon. The narrator of that saint’s life thus relates a miracle of his obedience:

There was in the community a certain brother named Elstan, a simple man of great obedience. The abbot ordered him to oversee the food supplies for the monastery’s workmen. Devoting himself most faithfully to this service, he himself cooked meat every day and diligently attended the labourers, bringing water and cleaning the vessels again; while the abbot supposed that he did this with the assistance and help of another servant. It happened one day, when the abbot was making his customary round of the monastery, that he unexpectedly encountered [Col. 1537B] the brother standing beside a boiling cauldron, and saw that all the vessels were clean and the floor swept. Delighted with this work, he said to him: “Brother Elstan, you have stolen this obedience from me. But if you are the kind of soldier you show yourself to be, put your hand into the boiling water and briskly draw up for me a piece from the bottom.” He obeyed; the untamable heat yielded to his bold faith, and the monk suffered no injury. We afterwards saw this same brother as abbot; later elevated also to episcopal rank, he rested in the Lord with a holy end.

The sixth was Siricius; the seventh, Aelfric—both, as was mentioned above, afterwards archbishops of Canterbury. The eighth was Brithwold, formerly a monk of Glastonbury, who administered the bishopric for many years from the time of King Ethelred [Col. 1537C] until Edward the last king. In King Cnut’s time, while one night at Glastonbury he was occupied, as he often was, in heavenly vigils, he experienced a divine vision. A thought frequently troubling him had arisen: that the royal line of the English was almost destroyed. As he pondered this, sleep came over him; and behold, caught up to the heights, he saw Peter, prince of the apostles, holding by the hand Edward, son of King Ethelred, then an exile in Normandy, and consecrating him king. Peter designated for him a celibate life and fixed the definite number of twenty-four years as the limit of his reign. When Edward lamented to him concerning his descendants, Peter answered: “The kingdom of the English belongs to God; after you He will provide a king according to His pleasure.” [Col. 1537D]

When his life was completed Brithwold was buried at Glastonbury, whose possessions he had enlarged with many estates and revenues; he was also very generous to our monastery. Edward was now reigning. He thought it right immediately to confer the bishopric upon his chaplain Herman, a Fleming by birth. The narrowness of his resources did not suffice for Herman’s greatness of spirit—or rather, his greed—since at Ramsbury there was neither a body of clerics nor any means by which he might support himself. He therefore asked the king not to permit one whom he had deemed worthy of honour to live without honour. His predecessors, he said, had been natives; he was a foreigner and possessed no support from his family by which to maintain his life. Therefore, the king should grant him the monastery of Malmesbury as the place for his seat, since its abbot had recently died by a convenient chance.

The king, because of a simplicity to which he was always more inclined than to prudence, judged that this should lawfully be granted, but rescinded it three days later. Before Herman had become involved in the property or [Col. 1538A] seisin, monks of outstanding prudence, having heard what had been done at court and what had been stolen from justice, hastened with utmost speed to Earl Godwin and his son. Disturbed by the scandalous novelty of the matter, they approached the king and turned him from his decision. This was easy for men of the highest rank and greatest authority, aided both by the justice of the cause and by the king’s pliability. Thus Herman was expelled before he had been fully installed. Confounded by this disgrace, he left England in indignation.

Not long afterwards, warned both by illness and by the poor success of secular affairs, angry with Fortune he renounced the world and became a monk at Saint-Bertin. But, as commonly happens when that sudden impulse toward religion cools, he began each day to contemplate returning to England. It troubled a man accustomed to attendance and bred amid luxuries to lack the comforts he had known from early youth. Moreover, favourable news had reached his ears: Alwold, bishop of Sherborne, had died, and Herman hoped to join that bishopric to his own under the old promises of Queen Edith. Arriving all the more eagerly, he found an outcome suited to his hope. Godwin, whom he had greatly feared, had now died; and Godwin’s son had yielded to the king’s will in this and other matters, being eager for adoption.

Herman therefore received the entire bishopric of Sherborne with its three districts, King Edward granting it to him. Outliving the years of his benefactor, he endured into the time of William. [Col. 1538C] Under William, when it had been decreed by canonical ordinance that episcopal seats should be moved from villages to cities, he transferred his throne from Sherborne to Salisbury: a castle standing in place of a city on an eminence, enclosed by a substantial wall, reasonably supplied with other necessities, but suffering from lack of water, so that water is sold there at a pitiable price. A church of new construction was begun there, but old age brought death before its dedication.

Nevertheless, when Osmund, a most excellent man, succeeded him, the church was brought to completion and all that was fitting was increased. Clerics distinguished in learning came from every quarter; they were not merely willingly retained, but liberally induced to remain. Indeed, there shone there, more than elsewhere, the distinction of the canons in chants and learning, comparable to that of nobles. A great collection of books was acquired, since the bishop himself did not disdain either to write or to bind books already written. He excelled in chastity; the ever-changing voice of rumour would blush to lie about his virtue. Hence he seemed harsher than fairness allowed toward penitents, since he punished more severely in others what he did not find in himself. Free from ambition, he did not foolishly squander his own possessions or seek those of others, nor did he oppress with any heavy payment the abbeys situated within his diocese. Nevertheless, whatever worldly stain he is believed to have contracted, he expiated by his patience, being worn down by a long illness before death. [Col. 1538D]

## On the Monasteries

[Col. 1539]

[Col. 1539A] In Dorset are the abbeys of Cerne and Milton, for men, and Shaftesbury, for women, besides certain others that have either been entirely destroyed or greatly diminished.

We have received the following account of Cerne’s beginning. Augustine, the first teacher of the English, after Kent had been subjected to Christ, travelled through the remaining English provinces as far as King Ethelbert’s authority extended. For, as we said elsewhere, all the English who inhabit Britain were subject to him, except the Northumbrians alone. Augustine therefore entered the district named above and increased the number of Christians, rescuing them repeatedly from the Devil’s destruction. But in that place the Devil’s power, forged by envy, held firm, grieved at such great gain of souls. The inhabitants, their minds maddened, attacked the man and his companions. [Col. 1539B] Having dishonoured him with great insults—even fastening the tails of rays to his garments—they drove him, pushed him away, and expelled him. Patiently and modestly, rejoicing to suffer insult for Jesus’ name, and not wishing further to provoke the madness of the wretches, he shook their dust from his feet and withdrew about three miles away.

Then, the storm of persecution removed and his mind returned to calm, he saw with the eye of his mind the divine presence near. With joyful countenance he said to his companions: “I see God, who will both repay us with grace and pour a more amendable spirit into those furious men.” No sooner had he spoken than they came with hurried steps, now converted, seeking pardon and pledging their faith. The event—or rather, the saying—gave the place its name: it was called *Cernel* from two words, Hebrew and Latin, because *Hel* is said to mean “God” in Hebrew, while *cerno* is Latin for “I see”; Augustine said that he saw the Lord. Nor did the truth fail his word, since the people, formerly deranged, believed so swiftly after changing their minds. For when water was lacking there for baptism, a spring burst forth from hidden channels at the bishop’s command; even today it is famous among the inhabitants both for Augustine’s merit and for its practical usefulness. [Col. 1539C]

In later years Edwold, brother of King and Martyr Edmund, wore out an eremitical life there on bread alone for food and water, weary, as report has it, of worldly delights because a harsher fortune had received both himself and his brother. For it often happens that a noble spirit, admonished by the adversities of the age, turns itself more earnestly to the Lord, who neither knows how to be deceived nor to deceive. “The first virtue indeed is to will well of one’s own accord; the second is to be capable of being compelled.” Paul, I think, who was compelled to goodness by a harsh scourge, is counted of no less merit than Peter, who willingly and immediately ran to the Lord’s call.

Edwold, after living religiously, was buried there in great repute for holiness. In a later age he gave Egelwald, a very wealthy man, occasion to build a monastery on that site for St Peter—not meanly, as is supposed, but abundantly, if those concerned would distribute its goods not to their parasites but to God’s servants. Yet in our time ambition has so changed and perverted everything in England [Col. 1539D] that possessions liberally given by ancient men to monasteries are scattered more for the gluttony of their holders than they serve the life of monks, guests, and needy people. Certainly the donors will not be deprived of their reward; let these men see how their intentions will one day be weighed in the divine balance.

King Ethelstan built the church of Milton for the soul of his brother Edwin, whom, corrupted by wicked counsel, he drove from England. I have not elsewhere kept silent about what became of him. There he deposited many relics of saints purchased from overseas Brittany. Among them the bones of most blessed Samson stand out especially: once archbishop of Dol, a most holy man and plainly worthy of God. I would relate some of his virtues here, were they not well known and were not my hands occupied with writing the miracles of native saints. [Col. 1540A]

Shaftesbury is now a village, once a city, a place situated upon a steep mountain ridge. A stone inscribed in the chapter-house of the nuns gives evidence of its antiquity, having been brought there from the ruins of a most ancient wall:

> In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 880, King Alfred built this city, in the eighth year of his reign.

There Elgiva, wife of Edmund, who was the great-grandson of this Alfred, founded a monastery of nuns and there deposited her bodily remains after death. She was a woman always intent on good works, endowed with piety and sweetness. Those accused persons whom the stern judgement of judges had publicly condemned, she herself secretly redeemed. Costly clothing—which for some women is an enticement to the surrender of modesty—was for her an equipment of generosity: whenever she saw a poor person, she at once gave away any garment, however expensive. Envy itself would praise in her beauty of body and skill of hands, since it could find nothing to censure. [Col. 1540B]

Of the prophetic grace that God had poured upon her, something has been said elsewhere. Living, she worked deeds of virtue; after death her miracles shone forth, as I once sang in verse:

> For after she had endured for some years the distress of illness,  
> she gave to God a soul refined and purified.  
> When therefore her blessed remains had fulfilled life’s destiny,  
> the merciful God adorned them with countless signs.  
> Those deprived of sight and hearing, if they worship at her tomb,  
> prove by their restoration to health the holy woman’s merit.  
> The lame man who approached returns home with a straight step;  
> the madman returns sound, rich in good sense.

In that place lies—or rather, lay—St Edward, grandson of this holy woman through her son Edgar. Innocently slain through his stepmother’s treachery, he was received into heaven. His first burial was at Wareham, which stands above the sea not far from the place called Corfe where he was killed. For three years he lay there, while his enemies begrudged the dead man the turf of the church, as they had begrudged the living man royal dignity. But divine power was present, raising the innocent man to the glory of signs:

> There lights were shown from heaven; there the lame man set his step in order; there the mute recovered speech; there every sickness entirely yielded to health. [Col. 1541A] Rumour spread through England, proclaiming the martyr’s merits, and stirred up his murderess to set out for that place. But the familiar animal on which she was accustomed to ride—formerly swifter than winds, outrunning, as the saying goes, the very breezes—then stood motionless at God’s command. Though the servants applied their whips, their labour was wasted; and when the mount was changed, the same result followed. Though late, her brutish heart understood what that portent meant. Therefore, what she could not accomplish herself, she allowed another to do: the sacred relics were raised from their ignoble grave and carried to Shaftesbury with great glory.

In a later time one part of the body was taken to Leominster and another to Abingdon. Everywhere he is powerful; but especially at Shaftesbury he shines both by the grace of his miracles and by the most holy choir of virgins. The place received a surname from him and, by metonymy, is commonly called St Edward’s.

> Indeed, as a miracle, the lung is displayed, still throbbing with unimpaired freshness though the whole body was long ago consumed.

But because almost every miracle is open to criticism, some twist this by a hostile interpretation: they say that the lung is incorrupt for good reason, since, as Suetonius testifies, if it has been steeped in poison, it cannot be consumed either by decay or by fire. For it is agreed that he was pierced with a dagger while drinking; they maintain that poison was given to him while thirsty and that the power of the poison was forestalled by the blade. But, on a more careful consideration of the matter, I perceive this to be false: poison could not have penetrated the vital organs so quickly, especially since Suetonius said this not about the lung but about the heart. Let it therefore be a heavenly miracle, [Col. 1541C] not liable to any human evasion.

In Wiltshire are these monasteries: Malmesbury, for men; and Wilton and Amesbury, for women. I have resolved to speak elsewhere about Malmesbury. Nothing else has reached my knowledge concerning Amesbury except that both it and Warewell were founded by Elfrida, murderer of St Edward, as acts of penitence. St Melor lies there; of his lineage and holiness I am uncertain. The convent of Wilton is adorned and cherished as the resting-place of the sweet remains of blessed Edith, daughter of King Edgar.

Wilton is a considerable village situated on the River Wyle, so renowned that the whole district takes its name from it. There Edith, consecrated to God from childhood and preserving inviolate virginity for the Lord, won human affection through her diligent services, suppressing the pride of her birth by nobility of mind. I have received one thing from my elders that offended human judgement not a little: namely, that she deceived their eyes by the splendour of gilded garments. If she appeared dressed in finer clothing than the holiness of her profession seemed to require, St Ethelwold publicly reproved her. She is said to have answered neither stupidly nor without wit: “The true and indisputable judgement of God is concealed only by the conscience of mortals; for, as Augustine says, there can be boasting even in mournful rags. Therefore I think that a mind as uncorrupted may exist beneath these gilded garments as beneath your torn skins.” [Col. 1541D]

At the consecration of the basilica of St Dionysius, which she had built out of love for the martyr, St Dunstan saw her frequently stretch out her right thumb and make the sign of the cross on her forehead. Greatly delighted, he said: “May this finger never decay.” Immediately during the Mass he burst into tears—tears so profuse that his sobbing voice nearly shook the deacon standing beside him. Asked the reason, he said: “Soon this flourishing rose will wither; soon the bird beloved by God will fly away, six weeks from this day.” The truth of events immediately followed the bishop’s prophecy. For she, steadfast in her noble purpose, breathed her last on the day foretold, before the term of youth, when she was twenty-three years old.

Not long afterwards, the same blessed man saw in a dream St Dionysius holding the virgin’s hand affectionately and commanding by divine oracle that she should be honoured by servants on earth, just as she was venerated in heaven by her Spouse and Lord. [Col. 1542A]

> Thus, as miracles became frequent at the tomb, an order was given that the virgin’s body should be raised. It was found wholly dissolved into ashes, except for the finger, the belly, and what lay beneath the belly. The virgin herself then appeared in a vision to the doubting saint and said that it was no wonder if those parts of the body had decayed, because it is the nature of lifeless bodies to flow away into certain hidden channels of nature, and because she too, being a girl, had sinned with those members. But that the belly was rightly not corrupted by any decay, because it had never been goaded by lust; she had been free from gluttony and from carnal intercourse.

Her brother was King Ethelred, born almost for the destruction of England because of his indolence. Cnut, a Dane by birth, succeeded him: an energetic man, but one who, because of ancestral hostilities, did not love the English saints. More stubborn through this habit, when he was at Wilton one Pentecost, he poured out solemn laughter upon the virgin herself. He said that he would never believe the daughter of King Edgar to be a saint, since Edgar, given over to vices and a most extreme slave of lust, had been more like a tyrant toward his subjects.

While he belched out these barbarous cruelties in service to his anger, Archbishop Ednoth, who was present, contradicted him. More enraged, Cnut ordered the tomb opened, wishing to see what a dead virgin could show as evidence of holiness. When the mausoleum had been broken open, the dead woman was seen to rise as far as her waist, with a veil drawn before her face, and to rush upon the insulting [Col. 1542C] king. Terrified by this sight, he drew back his head far away; the strength left his knees and he fell to the ground. The fall bruised his body so severely that, his breathing stopped for a considerable time, he was thought dead. But when strength gradually returned, he rejoiced with shame that, though sternly chastised, he had been spared for repentance. Her venerable feast is therefore observed in many places in England, and no one should presume to profane it with impunity.

In the same church lies her mother Wilfrith. Contrary to the common opinion, which errs [variant: “raves”], she was not a nun; it is certain that, terrified suddenly by the king, she was veiled only on her own advice, then snatched from the veil and forced into the royal bed. For this reason he, because he had touched a woman who was, even if only nominally, a nun, was rebuked by St Dunstan and performed seven years’ penance. After giving birth, she did not cling to repeated pleasure; rather, she grieved and despised it. She is therefore asserted and venerated as truly holy. [Col. 1542D–1543A]

In Berkshire there are two monasteries, Abingdon and Reading, both for men. The monastery at Abingdon was founded by Cissa, father of Ine; soon afterward by Ine himself, king of the West Saxons; and by many kings from the beginning. But in the time of King Alfred, when the barbarous Danes ranged everywhere with insolent violence, the buildings of the place were levelled to the ground. Then the king, occupied with plans against his misfortunes, converted all its lands and appurtenances to his own uses and those of his household.

But King Eadred, Alfred’s grandson, pitying the site’s desolation and at the same time providing for his grandfather’s soul, restored everything that had been taken away, through the hand of Ethelwold, whom he had made abbot there. He conceived so great a love for the church that he personally marked out the sites of its buildings and laid its foundations, intending to construct there a monastery of the greatest renown. He would have fulfilled his wish had not fate quickly removed him. Ethelwold nevertheless persisted in what had been begun; but before he could put the finishing touch to the work, King Edgar of praiseworthy memory drew him away to the bishopric of Winchester. Ordgar, whom he appointed in his place as abbot, completed his master’s undertakings. The place was enriched and raised to an immense degree, each successor always devising something new, lest he should be judged inferior to his predecessors. [Col. 1543B]

Especially eminent in our own time in improving its affairs was Abbot Faricius, Tuscan by origin, a physician by profession, an Aretine [variant: a citizen of Arezzo], and indeed a monk of ours. Since I have resolved to portray his praises, I shall append verses not of my own invention but by my companion Peter the monk. In them the virtue of this praiseworthy abbot will shine forth, and anyone who deigns to read them will especially observe the charm of their most excellent versifier. This will be merely a small sample of his eloquence; elsewhere he has gained the fame of a higher glory in many works.

[Col. 1544A]

> A worthy and wise man, truly a man of counsel,  
> he enriched outward things and cultivated the inner life of character.  
> Equipped with every fruit which learning imparts,  
> he turned the monuments of wisdom to the Church’s glory.  
> Steeped in all the laws that natural science teaches,  
> he won over kings themselves by the service of healing.  
> You would see kings and nobles, suddenly [variant: submissively], obeying  
> his nod, believing that safety lay in life under his care.  
> Hence English favour so strengthened his spirit  
> that he dared to contend in defence of his rights against the powerful.  
> He so broke them, so reduced them to such smallness,  
> that, as ruler, he pressed down lords made subject to himself.  
> I lie if Giffard did not bend his neck to the cowl—  
> among free-born men he was equalled by none.  
> Hence he recalled under his rule possessions long lost;  
> hence he drove back ambition snarling against him.  
> Why should I recount the crowd of nobles and the common people?  
> All whom he challenged concerning his rights he overcame.
>
> From these things the man gained renown; from renown his glory grew.  
> From these things the Church’s estate quickly flourished.  
> Mindful that the flowing abundance of good things is God’s gift,  
> he turned all splendour toward inward things.  
> Added estates, royal cloths, gifts, garments,  
> rich vessels, and woven tapestries are witnesses for me.  
> Through the golden panels of the ceilings flashes the splendour  
> of metal plating, gem-studded workmanship full of wonder.  
> Yet life did not suffice for the blessed man’s desire;  
> a fate rarely so lamentable broke both at once.

At Reading there was once a convent of nuns, but it has now for many years been destroyed. King Henry, intending to restore it as a penance imposed upon him, joined to it the two monasteries long ago ruined, Leominster and Cholsey. He established it between the two rivers, the Kennet and the Thames, in honour of the Mother of the Lord and John the Evangelist, in a place where it might be a lodging for almost all travellers to the more populous cities of England. [Col. 1544B] He placed there Cluniac monks, a brilliant example of holiness and an unfailing evidence of hospitality. There is no need to speak of the bodies of saints resting in the two monasteries, since, brought thither from elsewhere, they draw pilgrims to the place, and the praises proclaimed long ago by writers do not need to sigh for silence from us.

## On the Bishops of Wells

[Col. 1543]

[Col. 1543D] The third bishopric of the West Saxons was at Wells, a village in Somerset named from the abundance of little springs bubbling up there. From the time of King Edward the Elder until that of William the Younger, these were its bishops:

Athelm; Wlfhelm—both afterwards archbishops of Canterbury; Elfeh; Wlfhelm; Brithhelm; Kineward; Sigar; Elwin.

Living, also called Elstan, afterwards archbishop of Canterbury in King Ethelred’s time, after the most holy Elphege.

Ethelwin [variant: Elwin], abbot of Evesham, afterwards expelled.

Brithwin. Elwin returned again, and Brithwin was expelled; then Elwin in turn having been expelled, Brithwin returned.

Meruith [variant: Merewitt], also called Brithwi, a Lotharingian by birth, in the time of Kings Edward and William [Col. 1544D] the Great. All these had their seats at Wells, in the church of St Andrew.

When John succeeded them, a man of Tours by birth and a physician by profession, who had amassed no small profit by that craft, he thought it less glorious to reside obscurely in a village and resolved to transfer his throne to Bath. Although he had considered this plan unsuccessfully while William the elder, the father, was alive, he carried it out in the time of William the son. Nor was he content with this: he transferred the whole city also to the use of himself and his household, having bought the city from King Henry for five hundred pounds of silver. There a stream of hot baths rises, whose founder is believed to have been Julius Caesar. The waters are healthful for those bathing, but their sulphurous smell is burdensome to first arrivals, until habit restrains the senses’ horror.

King Offa had founded a monastery there, and Edgar, as was his custom with many other places, had enlarged it, delighted by the site’s magnificence and because he had received the royal crown there. John therefore obtained this abbey from the king without difficulty. At first he dealt rather harshly with the monks, because they were dull and, in his estimation, barbarous. He took away all lands supplying food, providing only scanty provisions through his lay servants. But as the years advanced he became a new man and treated the monks more gently, granting their prior some land by which he and his guests might somehow be supported. Much was nobly begun and completed there through him in ornaments and books, especially in the community of monks, who are equally praiseworthy for literary learning and diligent observance. [Col. 1545A]

He was an excellent physician not by learning but by practice, as report—though I do not know whether it is true—spread abroad. He delighted in the company of learned men, in order to acquire some credit for himself from their association. Yet he was more sharply witty toward those who spoke against him than his rank ought to have permitted. He enjoyed good health and was generous both toward himself and others. He died in old age, but even in dying could not be softened enough to restore the monks’ lands with a full hand, furnishing his successors an example not to imitate. He was buried in the church of St Peter, which he had raised from its foundations with a great and elaborate circuit of walls. For Andrew yielded to his brother Simon, the elder brother to the younger.

The entire extent of his bishopric lies in Somerset alone, and it has three abbeys for men: Glastonbury, Athelney, and Muchelney. [Col. 1545B]

Glastonbury is a village set in a marshy recess, yet accessible by horse and on foot; it is pleasing neither in situation nor in charm. There King Ine first, on the advice of the most blessed Aldhelm, built a monastery, granting it many estates that are still named today. Through varied changes of time, but with never-failing successions of monastic communities, the place flourished until the arrival of the Danes under King Alfred. Then, like other places, it was desolated and for some years lacked its familiar inhabitants.

But Dunstan splendidly restored everything that the storm of war had destroyed. He had first lived there as a monk in solitude. Later, having acquired through the generosity of King Edmund all its former appurtenances and many more besides, he established the abbey: such as nowhere else in England exists or has existed. So extensive and well-situated are its estates; so abundant are the beauty and antiquity of its books. Yet, through some misfortune—I know not what—after the arrival of the Normans it has always been crushed by the worst hardships and has prospered neither in new buildings nor in benefits for its inhabitants. Its abbots, puffed up by the glory of wealth, behave not as religious men but as tyrants: proud but powerless abroad; cruel and oppressive within. Turstin’s deed alone will suffice to prove this. [Col. 1545C]
