Made abbot of the monastery by the gift of King William, his father, he squandered its lands and money upon the excesses of his flatterers [or: parasites]. He exacted strict observance of the rule from the monks, yet meanwhile treated them wretchedly in provisions. Hence came quarrels of words and discord of minds; for, as Lucan says, “A hungry populace does not know fear.” When disputes had proceeded to arms, the monks, driven into the church by soldiers, bewailed their miseries before the holy altar. But as the soldiers burst in, two of them were slain there, fourteen wounded, and the rest driven back. Indeed, while the frenzy of the madmen attacked the monks from a distance, it made the Crucified bristle with arrows. Branded all his life by the guilt of this crime, the abbot was banished to Caen; after the king’s death, however, money being reckoned among the aids supplied for the redemption of sin, he was restored to honour. Shameless and infamous was the man who, conscious of so great a sacrilege, dared again to be thrust into the place he had violated.

Patrick lies there—if the report deserves belief—a Briton by birth, disciple of blessed Germanus of Auxerre. Pope Celestine ordained him bishop and sent him as apostle to the Irish. After, through his own labour in converting that people, and with the co-operation of God’s grace, he had made no small progress over many years, at length wearied alike by his long pilgrimage and by advancing age, he judged that he must return to his native land, and there ended his days. His master was followed by Hindrachus [or Indrahtus], son of an Irish king—than whose character nothing was gentler or holier—and seven distinguished nobles of that country. When robbers rushed upon them and killed them there, credulous antiquity consecrated them as martyrs.

What feeble discourse could devise anything worthy of the majesty of the facts concerning the other saints resting there? King Edmund brought many persons thither whom he had discovered in his northern expedition and raised from the earth; among them Hilda, abbess of the monastery once called Streoneshalh, now Whitby, then a house of nuns but now of monks. How highly her merits were valued will be made clear by the truthful historian Bede’s account of Ceolfrith, abbot of the monastery of Wearmouth, of whom the same Bede composed a separate book. Ceolfrith, overtaken by death and buried among the Lingones while travelling to Rome in extreme old age, was later, it is established, brought back. There too is a portion of the bones of Aidan, first bishop of Lindisfarne. For that Colman carried a portion to Scotland, as the same historian testifies, is too well known to admit doubt. Benignus the confessor is celebrated there; not far from this place he had been an anchorite, and by distinguished miracles stirred the neighbouring monks to venerate him and translate his relics.

Kings were buried in that monastery: Edmund, of whom I have spoken above, the restorer of the place, and his son Edgar, who, not ungrateful to his father’s memory, added to his father’s gifts a mass of very extensive possessions.

Adelingea is not an island of the sea, but is so inaccessible through the overflow of pools and marshes that it can in no way be approached except by boat. It contains a very large alder-grove, deer, roe-deer, and many beasts of that sort. Its firm ground, scarcely two acres broad, contains a small monastery and the workshops of monks. Its founder was King Alfred, who, once driven from the country by the Danes, had for some time cherished safe hiding-places there. Soon, after receiving in a dream holy Cuthbert as a guarantor of his restoration, he vowed to God that he would build a monastery there. He made a church modest in size because of the narrowness of the site, but constructed by a novel method of building. For four posts fixed in the ground support the whole structure, with four screens carried around in spherical work. There are few monks there, and poor; yet they either highly value their poverty for love of peace and solitude, or find consolation in it. They carry the praises of their patron, Saint Egelwin, to the stars in their proclamations, and experience his holiness in continuous benefits lavishly bestowed.

A constant tradition holds that he was brother of Cenwealh, king of the West Saxons, and heightened the greatness of his lineage by the quality of his holiness; though held throughout his life in the fetter of sickness, he served God none the less zealously, attained a good end, and is ready to bring remedies to all who invoke him. He was founder of the monastery of Michelney [or Micelney], as also of that at Milton, where, drawn by the same motive, he bestowed similar gifts of estates and relics; and all the more because monks can keep freer watch upon heavenly mysteries in proportion as gatherings of people visit them less frequently. For the place is difficult of access: in summer it is generally passable on foot or horseback, but in winter not at all. But enough of this; the narrative must turn, because the remaining matters of this province call for it.

## ON THE BISHOPS OF CREDITON, EXETER, AND CORNWALL

[Col. 1547]

[Col. 1547B] This account, then, will set forth the succession of the bishops of Crediton. Crediton is a small village of Devonshire, commonly called Devenescira, twelve miles from Exeter. These bishops sat there in order: Edulf, Edelgar, Elfwod, Sideman, Alfric, Elfwold, Ednod, also called Wine.

Livingus, formerly a monk of Winchester, then abbot of Tavistock and bishop of Crediton, was held in the greatest intimacy and influence with King Cnut. Having spent much time with him in Denmark, he attached himself to the royal retinue on the journey to Rome. When affairs at Rome had been completed, and the king set out for Denmark by land, Livingus came to England by ship, intending to be bearer of royal letters and executor of commands. Having wisely and admirably completed, before the king’s arrival, everything that had been entrusted to him, he advanced so far in the king’s favour that, when his uncle Brithwold, bishop of Cornwall, died, Cnut united both bishoprics under Livingus’s authority.

He was, so report says, an ambitious and insolent tyrant over ecclesiastical laws, invincible in the pursuit of whatever served his own will. Finally, we have received from our elders that when he breathed his last, such a dreadful crash was heard throughout all England that people thought the entire world was collapsing and ending. He was buried at Tavistock, a place to which he had brought many splendid benefactions and where he had established such favour among the monks that, even today, by a custom continued by their successors, they sing the fifteen Gradual Psalms for the repose of his soul.

In King Edward’s time Lefric succeeded him, a man of Lotharingian birth and learning. He transferred the episcopal see to the city which, because the river Exe washes its walls in its course, is called Exeter. King Æthelstan first reduced this city to English authority after driving out the Britons; he distinguished it with towers and enclosed it in a wall of squared stone. Every sort of merchandise is so abundant there that one seeks in vain nothing which one judges useful for human needs. Yet its soil is barren and desolate, scarcely producing sterile oats and, for the most part, an empty husk without grain.

Here Lefric expelled the nuns from the monastery of Saint Peter and established the bishopric and canons, who, contrary to English custom, after the Lotharingian manner ate in one refectory and slept in one dormitory. A rule of this kind was passed down to their successors, although through the luxury of the times it has now in some respects fallen away. The clerics have a steward appointed by the bishop, who supplies them daily with necessities of food and annually with suitable clothing.

Osbern succeeded Lefric in the time of King William. He was a Norman by birth and brother of William, a most eminent count; under King Edward he had lived freely and familiarly [or: modestly] in England, since he was connected with the royal family by a close degree of kinship. Accordingly, in food and other matters he was more inclined to English usages and held Norman pomp in little esteem. He extolled the customs of his lord King Edward; and, when such customs were displayed by others, he rejoiced with those seated by gesture and hand. Thus, after the manner of the ancient bishops, content with old buildings, generous in spirit, and chaste in body, he lived until the fourth year of King Henry, deprived of sight for no few years as old age approached.

There is in Devonshire, near the river Tavy, a monastery of monks called Tavistock. It received its first beginning of growth through Ordgar, earl of Devonshire and father of Elfrida, who was King Edgar’s wife; through Bishop Livingus it received the auspices of enlargement. The place is pleasant, with the advantages of woodland, an abundant catch of fish, a church suitably built, and streams of the river running through the monks’ workshops; pouring forth by their own force, they carry away whatever surplus they encounter.

Saint Rumon is said to be honoured and to lie there, a bishop adorned by the beauty of his shrine. No trustworthiness of writers supports the belief, for throughout that place, and in many parts of England, one finds that the violence of warfare has obliterated all record of deeds: bare names of saints remain, together with whatever miracles are now claimed to be known. In the same monastery may be seen the tomb of Ordgar, and the enormous size of his son’s mausoleum is displayed as a spectacle. He was called Edulf, a man of giant stature and enormous strength, as the following incident briefly suggests.

He was travelling toward Exeter with King Edward, to whom he was related. When, near a gate, they had dismounted from their horses, they found the entrance barred externally by crossbars and internally by bolts. By chance the gatekeeper, unaware of their arrival—for they had ridden out in private leisure—had gone far away. Then Edulf, seizing the crossbars with both hands, broke them into pieces with what seemed little effort, tearing away part of the wall as well. Once heated and inwardly raging, he gave a second proof of his strength. With a thrust of his foot he smashed the doors, forced open their double hinge, and even splintered the timber. While the others praised him, the king jestingly discounted the deed, attributing it to diabolical strength rather than human courage.

There is also in Dorset a wood near Horton, which is now destroyed but was then, through his generosity, counted among the abbeys. There he displayed his astonishing strength whenever, with cares laid aside, he came for leisure. A stream runs beside a hunting-wood rich in game, ten feet from one bank to the other. Standing with his legs apart, he spanned both banks; with a small knife he struck off into the stream the heads of animals driven toward him, with light and almost idle blows. Yet a man so great and such as he, still burning with the heat of youth, yielded to death and ordered himself buried at Horton. Nevertheless, because he had entrusted certain gifts to be given to the church with him, Abbot Sictritius’s violence anticipated the giver, transferring both donor and gifts into his own possession. Sithtricius afterward, under King William, embraced piracy, polluted religious life, and disgraced the church.

As for the successive order of the bishops of Cornwall, I neither know it nor record it, except that the episcopal see was at Saint Petroc the Confessor. The place is among the northern Britons, above the sea near the river called Hegelmithe; some say it was at Saint German, near the river Liner above the sea, in the southern region.

## ON THE BISHOPS OF SELSEY

[Col. 1549]

[Col. 1549B] Having enumerated all the bishoprics of the West Saxons, the order of the narrative now turns to the bishops of the South Saxons. That province borders the West Saxons on one side and the people of Kent on the other. It was always subject, together with its petty kings, to the authority of the western kings after Cædwalla defeated their king Æthelwealh in war. Æthelwealh, at King Wulfhere’s urging, was baptized in Mercia. He received with kindly hospitality the most blessed Wilfrid, exiled from his see, and raised him to an episcopal seat at a place called Selsey, which can be approached by only one entrance, being surrounded everywhere by the sea.

Yet, as I have said, after the king’s death and Wilfrid’s return home when peace had been restored—he had built a monastery there—the bishopric remained vacant for many years, and its administration meanwhile belonged to the bishop of Winchester.

Later Edbrith was made bishop by Archbishop Nochelm. Ella succeeded him. After his death the succession continued: Sigelin, who attended the council of Archbishop Cuthbert; Alubrith, Bosa, Gislhere, Totta, Pentum, Ehelnulf, Bernegus, whom his consecrator Archbishop Plegmund declared worthy; Cenred, Gutheard, Elfred, Eallhelm, Æthelgar, first abbot of Winchester and later archbishop of Canterbury; Ordbrich, Elmar, Æthelric, Grimketel, who, driven from the see of the East Angles which he had purchased, also purchased this one with money and occupied it; Hetta; and Stigand—not the man who later became bishop of Winchester and archbishop of Canterbury.

This Stigand, made bishop there by King William, transferred the see to Chichester, a city of his diocese near the sea, where in ancient times there had also been a monastery of Saint Peter and a community of nuns. William succeeded him. Ralph succeeded William, remarkable for his bodily height but also famous for strength of character. Mindful of the priestly office, he openly opposed William Rufus on behalf of Archbishop Anselm, whom the king unjustly harassed. When William, inflated by consciousness of power, repeated his threats, Ralph, fearing nothing, held out his staff and removed his ring for the king to take if he wished. Neither then nor afterward would he bend his severity, had he possessed an advocate; but Anselm, by his departure, weakened Ralph’s hope and that of all others, if any were good. Thus the cause failed then and afterward succumbed to loss.

In succeeding years he also offered religious resistance to the commands of King Henry, who wished to exact money from priests throughout England. While others either yielded or kept silence through fear, episcopal firmness could not be softened in Ralph alone. Throughout his diocese he ordered divine services to cease and church doors to be blocked with thorns, not forbidding the monks’ chanting, yet barring laypeople from entering. The severity of the action persuaded the king to remit to Ralph alone, as though he were a man of unsound judgment, the priests’ tax. Yet the man’s religious integrity and courage won him great praise in the royal mind. The king remitted everything to him, repeatedly saying that the bishopric was poor, that the church had been ruined, and that it ought not to be plundered by taxes but enriched by offerings. Thus his steadfast innocence made him so notable that the king, who took from others, willingly and humbly gave to him. Finally, when accidental fire—as I have said—had destroyed his church, which he had built anew, he soon restored it chiefly through the king’s generosity.

He died most Christianly, having disposed of all his possessions for the use of the poor; and, as he lay dying, he ordered even his little garments, down to his bedding, to be distributed before him. He was a man deservedly granted an everlasting memory for good, who raised his see from a low and miserable condition to the summit of glory. He gathered as many clerics as the revenues of the bishopric could support, and added ornaments of every kind, whose previous shameful scarcity I am reluctant to reckon. [Col. 1551A] Three times each year he travelled around his diocese to preach, demanding nothing from his provincials by episcopal authority, but gratefully accepting what was offered. He spared no rebuke of offenders; and if rebuke was insufficiently effective, he removed their fault by frank jesting.

## ON MONASTERIES

[Col. 1151]

[Col. 1551A] In his diocese there are only two monasteries newly established: Saint Martin’s of Battle, founded and endowed by King William on the place where he had conquered England, leaving it many costly gifts both in life and at death. The church altar stands at the place where the lifeless body of Harold, slain for love of his country, was found.

Saint Pancras’s of Lewes was raised to the highest summit of religious life by Lanzo, a monk of Cluny, under the patronage of William, earl of Warenne. The eminence of the place demonstrates the man’s effectiveness, so that it is truly asserted that no monastery whatever can surpass it in religious discipline toward monks, affability toward guests, and charity toward all. The reality of its excellence surpasses the splendour of its reputation, though the verbosity of those relating it may weary listeners. Certainly, I would say more of Lanzo, if I had not elsewhere said things not to be despised, and if every manner of speech did not at once fall short of his merit.

## PROLOGUE TO THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 1551]

[Col. 1551B] York is second in dignity after Canterbury, a large city and metropolitan see, displaying evidence of Roman elegance. Built on both sides of the river Ouse, it encloses in the hollow between them ships arriving from Germany and Ireland. Always especially exposed to the fury of northern peoples, it received and groaned beneath the barbarian commotions of the Danes throughout the time in which they ruled England. Therefore, shaken by many disasters, it fell in the final devastation under King William. Angry with the citizens because, at the Danes’ approach, they had been a refuge and a source of counsel, he first consumed the city by famine and then by fire. He ordered the villages and fields of the entire region likewise to be ruined and crops and grain destroyed by fire or water. Thus the sinews of a province once fertile were cut down by plunder, conflagration, and bloodshed.

[Col. 1551C] For sixty miles and more the ground lies everywhere uncultivated, stripped of all things even to the present time. Whoever now sees as a stranger cities once illustrious, towers threatening heaven by their height, fields rich in pasture, and rivers plentifully watering them, groans; any old inhabitant does not recognize them. Yet amid some ruins of walls, half-collapsed remnants, one may see the marvellous workmanship of the Romans. Such is the vaulted hall in the city of Lugabalia, roofed with arches of stone; no violence of weather has ever been able to damage it, nor even timber deliberately piled against it and set aflame. The region is called Cumberland and its people Cumbri; on the front of the hall is written: “MARIUS’S VICTORY.” What this means I hesitate to say, unless perhaps some portion of the Cimbri settled long ago in these places after being driven out of Italy by Marius.

Indeed, the whole speech of the Northumbrians, especially at York, crackles so uncouthly that we southerners can understand nothing of it. This has happened through their proximity to barbarous peoples and through the remoteness of the kings—formerly English, now Norman—who are known to reside more often in the south than in the north. The king himself, content in those regions with his household troop of soldiers, never goes there, whenever he visits those parts of his realm, except with a great escort of auxiliaries.

Albinus [or Alquinus] had once foreseen that this calamity would come upon the region, from a prodigy that had occurred at York. He saw it, I say, and announced it in these words in a letter to King Æthelred:

> “What does the rain of blood signify, which we saw during Lent, in the city of York, the head of the whole kingdom, falling ominously in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, from the northern side of the building, in clear weather, from the top of the roof? May it not be thought that blood will come upon the people from the northern regions?”

Alcuin indeed conjectured in his own time that these things would occur; posterity has plainly learned that they came either through the violence of northerners or because of northerners’ guilt. For in the time that followed, the Danes ravaged the province; then the Normans, made savage by the Danes’ arrival, destroyed what remained.

Therefore in this third book of the Deeds of Bishops I shall recount whatever concerning the bishops of York has come to our knowledge by report of elders or by the examination of books. As it seems to me, Wilfrid the First was their chief figure, tossed undeservedly through almost his whole life by so many perils. I think it fitting to incorporate his life and all his deeds in this compendium, because they are not so well known, and much is lacking from Bede’s history. Although, therefore, an immense work opens before one considering this task, I shall nevertheless try, as far as I can, to proceed briefly—always bearing in mind this excuse for my bold undertaking: that one who cannot read the lives of all the saints may here find their more useful features selected. Thus, omitting the windings of long narratives, I shall follow truth and compress into a summary what Stephen the priest has treated concerning Wilfrid in a great host of words.

# BOOK THREE: ON THE ARCHBISHOPS OF YORK, THE BISHOPS OF HEXHAM, AND OF WHITHORN

[Col. 1553]

[Col. 1553A] Paulinus was the first archbishop of York; as is known, he received the pallium from Pope Honorius.

After he had been driven out, the Scots—Aidan, Finan, and Colman—were unwilling to be exalted either by a pallium or by the city’s rank, remaining concealed on the island of Lindisfarne.

After Wilfrid had convicted Colman regarding the erroneous Easter, that same Wilfrid was elected to the bishopric of York and was ordered by King Alhfrith, son of King Oswiu, to go to Gaul for consecration.

While he prolonged his delays overseas, King Oswiu, forestalled by the counsels of the Quartodecimans—so called because they celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon—intruded Cedd, a most holy man but contrary to the rules, into the see of York. But this injustice was corrected when Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, was sent from the Apostolic See; Cedd was expelled and Wilfrid enthroned.

To return, then, to Wilfrid: born of not undistinguished parents among the Northumbrians, he made up by nobility of character whatever favour might have been lacking to his birth.

> “When his mother, in labour, brought him forth into the light, retainers standing outside saw, as they thought, the house privy to the childbirth blaze on every side with fire, so that the flame already sent long locks upward. As they shouted and threw water to quench the blaze, servant-girls, roused by their cries, ran out; and when they ordered them not to disturb their mistress in labour, they wondered that these men loudly declared they had seen what was not before their eyes [or: that they had seen it]. For the harmless fire had already vanished, and the servants had no means of excusing their embarrassment, while the house stood unharmed. It was therefore understood that the boy possessed fiery vigour, since at his birth so great a blaze had been breathed forth.”

He spent his childhood without letters. But when his advancing years had added four to ten, loathing the arrogance of a stepmother—for his mother had died—he left his father’s house. At the urging of courtiers, to whom he had rendered service in his paternal home, he was brought to the notice of Queen Eansfled [or Eanfled]. By frequent questioning she drew out the youth’s private thoughts: he preferred to serve God rather than the world. She therefore entrusted him to a certain Cudda, who, after being a senator and a royal chamberlain, was contemplating a religious life at Lindisfarne. Cudda kindly kept him with himself for some years and returned him to the queen, retaining by memory the Psalms and some ecclesiastical learning, but now seized by the desire to go to Rome in pursuit of more outstanding progress.

The queen embraced the young man’s desire, which was beyond his years, and sent him to King Erconbert of Kent, the son of her uncle, to be assisted by his particular care. Thus Wilfrid came to Kent and learned thoroughly Roman observances, which surpassed the knowledge of the Scots. Finally, the Psalter which he had received from the Scots according to the translation of blessed Jerome, he read and retained in the Roman manner according to the Fifth Edition. After a year the king gave him to accompany the energetic young Benedict, later abbot of Wearmouth, who was preparing for the Roman journey.

On reaching Lyons, Wilfrid invited Archbishop Dalfinus of that city to love him through the beauty of his face and the composure of his manners. The archbishop tried to retain him either by ordaining him a cleric or by marriage to his niece, but achieved neither: Wilfrid excused himself from marriage through zeal for celibacy and postponed ordination until he returned from Rome. Therefore, supported by the archbishop’s advice and aided by his purse, he set out upon his intended route and shortly caught up with his companion, who in anger at his delay had gone ahead.

He came, then, to Rome and, through blessed Andrew’s help, prosperously obtained all that he desired. Prostrate at the victorious thresholds of the saint, he had prayed for assistance and aptitude in letters. Having gained personal acquaintance with the most blessed Boniface, then archdeacon, he obtained through him the favour of the pontiff of the supreme see. Enjoying their companionship and instructed in the calculation of the Paschal cycle, after staying for a considerable time in the city he returned to Lyons, to Archbishop Dalfinus. The latter welcomed him with no less generosity and they made this agreement: the foreigner was adopted as a son and made a cleric; the archbishop was chosen as a father. Through his kindly devotion he had removed from Wilfrid’s mind all thought of returning to his native country.

But the devil begrudged Wilfrid Gaul and Dalfinus a longer life, instilling infernal furies in Queen Balthild so that, after murdering nine bishops, she might add him as the tenth. She commanded through agents that he come. Stronger than misfortunes, though he knew well a woman’s wickedness, he hurried to come. When executioners immediately met him with drawn swords, the English youth, with marvellous constancy, almost throwing himself upon the very blades, desired to share in his father’s death. Yet, although already stripped and with the noose [or: throat] stretched out, he was spared for his England through the pity of the executioners.

When report spread the news of his arrival, he was honourably summoned by King Alhfrith, son of King Oswiu. As he described the hardships and stages of his journey, Gallic refinement, Roman splendour, and moreover the rule of the canons, he was gladly and gratefully heard. The king therefore kept him carefully about himself for many days, cultivating the friendship recently formed through Wilfrid’s honourable conduct, diligence, preaching, knowledge of affairs, and eloquence. He gave him a dwelling at Ripon in which to build a monastery, and the nobles bestowed offerings of many gifts.

There Wilfrid was ordained priest by the Gallic bishop Agilbert, coming from Scotland; and, having refuted the Scots’ error concerning the false Easter, he became abbot not many days later, banished that error and restored knowledge of the truth. Kings and nobles rejoiced; the province gloried that it possessed a native preacher, now weary of Scottish crudeness. Many gifts were bestowed on Wilfrid, with which he could maintain his life and relieve the poverty of the needy. Nor was his heart narrow in giving to poor people and strangers what flowed to him from the world; by a kind of emulous delight, the more he spent upon the poor, the more abundantly God provided things to be spent.

Moreover, he was more restrained in eating, more ready for vigils and prayers, preserving his virgin purity unbroken from his mother, and incurring no fault even in youth. Until old age he observed the custom of pouring cold water over his whole body at night when going to bed. But at Pope John’s command he eventually, though late, ceased, lest old age’s chill, increased by the application of the cold element, should bring on an incurable illness. For this he was chosen by all with favourable applause as worthy to sanctify the chair of the Church of York.

Yet he continued to refuse consecration from Scottish bishops or from those ordained by Scots, whose communion the Apostolic See rejected. Since it was no concern of theirs to name anyone as his own bishop, and because it was proper to provide for his reputation and safety, the royal dignity permitted—and popular devotion granted—that he be marked with the sacred office by Gallic bishops. Thus, once lawfully enthroned, his authority would be greatly increased. Having been tested in counsel, he was sent to Gaul for consecration with a great escort of those travelling outward and with great expectation among those awaiting his return. There twelve bishops—among whom Agilbert was eminent—acclaimed his election, raised him while he sat on a golden seat [or: supported him from beneath], and finally led him before the altar and consecrated him.

But when the work was complete and he was returning, contrary winds swept him to the opposite shore of the South Saxons. The returning tide of Ocean, having driven the ship ashore, left it as prey for hostile men gaping for it. The barbarians, still ignorant of the true God and living in Bacchic frenzy, stirred to rage, joined their forces for war and sounded the trumpet. Then, although the bishop thought it necessary to yield to the occasion, offered peace, and heaped up promises, the pagans, no less unyielding, rushed to arms. Indeed, a priest of sacrilegious rites, standing on a higher place, strove by frenzied incantations to break the Christians’ strength.

Then one of the bishop’s companions hurled a stone from a sling and struck the pagan’s forehead with such force that, piercing the bone, it injured his brain. All the more fiercely, the barbarian people renewed war against the Christians. But they, prepared for either result to which fortune might turn—either to fall in a noble death or obtain victory—formed in a dense company of one hundred and twenty and charged, repulsing the enemy twice and three times. Meanwhile the eminent bishop, together with the clergy, prayed and bent the knee upon the shore. Before the hour of Ascension, at their prayer, the returning tide of the sea, its hollow accommodating them, received the sailors. Not long afterward they reached Sandwich, singing a joyful sea-chant, because, though countless enemies had been slain, they missed scarcely five of their own number.

Thus the victor over every danger returned home and found matters in disorder, with Cedd installed in his own see—something which may easily deceive even most devout minds, especially where their own honour is concerned. Therefore Wilfrid lived at Ripon for three years, exercising priestly office wherever he was asked to go, always attended by a great company of men who did not think he should be left. He was very frequently invited by Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, who gave him a place called Lichfield for the construction of whatever he might wish, whether bishopric or monastery.

Nor was King Egbert of Kent less diligent in honouring him. At Egbert’s summons Wilfrid advanced many in Kent through ecclesiastical orders. One of these was Putta, promoted by Wilfrid to the priesthood and later by Theodore to the bishopric of Rochester. For after the death of Archbishop Deusdedit, Theodore was awaited from overseas. When Theodore arrived and learned that the affair had wrongly been done contrary to the canons, he deposed Cedd, who bore the injury with a calm and unshaken spirit. The patience of this most holy man moved Wilfrid’s heart, so that, through Wilfrid’s support, Cedd was again raised through all the grades and installed bishop at Lichfield, where he survived for some years and found an end fitting his holiness.

Meanwhile Wilfrid did not indulge in delights, but first of all increased Christianity and formed Christian manners; secondly, he raised new buildings and repaired old ones. The basilica at York, formerly built by King Edwin at Saint Paulinus’s instruction, lacked a roof. Its walls were half-ruined and threatening complete collapse; they served only as nests for birds. Moved by inward grief at this unworthy state, the bishop strengthened its fabric, raised its roof, and secured the raised roof with sheets of lead against the assaults of storms. The windows admitted light either through thin linen cloths or through latticed wooden screens pierced with many holes; he made them of glass. Age and the varied weather had obscured the beauty of the materials; he whitened them with white lime.

Ripon too experienced the bishop’s industry: there he built a church from its foundations, remarkable for the curving of its vaults [or: remarkable in its vaulted curves], its pavement of stone, and the winding plan of its porticoes. Kings Egfrid and Ælwin—Oswiu their father having meanwhile died—were invited to its consecration. They endowed the place with immense estates and repaid the reward [or: price] of its renown, being praised before the people in most lavish words. For three days they continued the joy of what seemed worldly splendour by an exceedingly sumptuous provision of foods; a divine miracle of the resurrection of a dead child followed. The event occurred as follows:

> “As the bishop entered the village of Tiddanefræ, a great crowd of women met him, offering little children for confirmation. A little woman mingled herself with the streaming throng and, acting cunningly, presented her lifeless son for catechizing, concealing his death and swallowing back her tears. She fully believed that by this contrivance he could recover life. But when the bishop uncovered the boy’s veiled face in order to perform the office, he perceived that he was deprived of soul. Then the woman, disappointed in the success of her deceit, turned to entreaties, praying by God, by his mother, by whatever faith and whatever pity there might be, that he would raise the lifeless child. At the same time, throwing herself at his feet, she applied a kind of force, refusing altogether to move from the place. Meanwhile the judgment of the most holy man wavered: should he rashly attempt an unfamiliar miracle, or disregard the harsh tears of the bereaved woman? But pity conquered the breast of power. Muttering quietly to himself a few verses of the divine Psalms, he then laid his right hand upon the corpse and restored the soul to the little body. Immediately the child yawned and, by a lively motion of his eyelids and by the effort of his whole little body, testified that he had come back to life. His mother cried out in joy, but, restrained by the bishop, was silent. The boy was called Æthelwald, and afterward became a monk at Ripon; he was regarded as no slight confirmation [variant: increase] of Wilfrid’s miracles.”

A similar miracle he displayed at Henglesteld [otherwise Hengsteldeheim] at about the same time. “There, at his expense, a church was rising to a great height; from the summit of its construction a monk fell and was shattered in every bone. Carried thence into the oratory, he left onlookers uncertain whether he were wholly dead, since he had neither voice nor sensation. But the bishop, his eyes filled with tears, summoned the monks to prayer [Col. 1557C] and urged them to cast off the sluggishness of unbelief: nothing, he said, would be difficult for those who believed. Thus prayer was sent upward with one voice, mercy was drawn down from heaven, the monk breathed again, and those who saw him began to hope for signs of recovery. The fracture of his bones was bound up, and the sick man recovered through grace.”

Nor was King Egfrid lacking in his own duty, extending his realm over the Picts and defending it against the Mercians. For after King Oswi’s death, the Picts, making light of the tender age of the young prince, broke forth of their own accord and conspired against the Northumbrians. The royal youth, meeting them with the under-king Bernego, destroyed their countless army of Picts with so few soldiers of his own that the plains, strewn with corpses, lost their level surface and the rivers, their current obstructed, came to a standstill. Wlfelius, king of the Mercians, [Col. 1557D] likewise, enraged against the same people, led an army against them, remembering that his father had been killed by them. Thus the king came with a confident purpose, either to repair the loss or to win a kingdom. Yet fortune did not attend him well, nor was it much more favorable than it had been to his father: except that, shamefully turning his back, he escaped ingloriously; and, surviving only a few days thereafter, he yielded part of the Northumbrian provinces to the king.

As a result of these victories Wilfrid’s estates were enlarged and churches established with monks. For he was loved by all because of his praiseworthy reverence for virtue; and, besides the qualities enumerated above, he was commended for abstinence. It is very well known that at his most restrained meal he rarely consumed more than one dish, and that he never [Col. 1558A] drained even one cup. Moreover, gentle and affable toward all, he drew them into friendship. Accordingly abbots and abbesses, while still living, made him lord of their possessions, or, when dying, their heir. Nobles entrusted their sons to him for education, to serve, once grown, either God or the world. From this the unhappy envy of Queen Ermenburga and of certain retainers was breathed into their hearts, so that they begrudged Wilfrid such great riches.

For while the most blessed Etheldritha outwardly served in the royal marriage-bed, she reconciled the king with the most blessed bishop whenever anything was whispered against him, soothing it by the soundness of her counsel. He himself, too, while supported by the favor of the bishop, enjoyed affairs proceeding as he wished, in war and at home. But after the new bride entered [Col. 1558B] the royal hall, the bishop’s peace was broken and vanished; the king’s household changed little by little, and at last declined entirely. The queen therefore stirred up envy against the bishop: because he possessed so many abbots and so many abbeys; because he had himself served in vessels of gold and silver; because a throng of clients, proud in the splendor of their clothing, walked about at his side.

This report, so full of envy, ran to Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. He did not delay; but, under the pretext of gifts, weakening his firmness of mind, he introduced into Wilfrid’s diocese, without consulting Wilfrid, three bishops from another region. They nevertheless alleged [otherwise, alleged] the cause of justice: that three bishops ought to be maintained from the revenues from which one then luxuriated; that the expenses were sufficient, and the circuit of so great a diocese, for four bishops. These things might indeed [Col. 1558C] seem rightly said, had he cast down a man who had acquired everything through his own industry without stripping him entirely, or at least acted with his consent. Nor could the most manifest violence be concealed when Wilfrid himself appeared before the tribunal of the king, demanding an explanation for the wrongs done him.

“For,” they said, “we bring no charge of guilt against you; but we wish what we have established to stand ratified.”

What could be more absurd than this? It was as though they said that line of Juvenal:

> Thus I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.

But when the bishop appealed to the apostolic see, the scoffers standing by because of the king burst into laughter, and he answered them with this saying: “This mockery which you now make concerning my departure will turn for you into great sorrow next year [Col. 1558D] on this very day.” The true event fulfilled the bishop’s saying. For Ethelred, king of the Mercians and brother of Wlferius, shortly after Wilfrid’s departure began a war, wishing to avenge his brother’s injuries. Bold Egfrid met him, thinking that he would act with his customary terror; but the Mercian routed his forces and slew his brother Edwin. Northumbria, therefore, was turned to mourning and now bewailed the absence of the counsellor whom it had once possessed.

And it happened that, when a year had gone round, on the very day on which he had suffered this adverse judgment at York, the corpse of the royal youth was brought into the city and proclaimed a long public mourning. Thus Ethelred, having enjoyed his triumph and recovered the integrity of his kingdom, expelled Bishop Winfrid, who had succeeded Cedd at Lichfield, because he had belonged to Egfrid’s party. [Col. 1559A] By chance Winfrid landed on the Gallic shore and fell in with King Theodoric and Ebroin, duke of the Franks; they had received orders from Britain to seize and despoil Bishop Wilfrid. Misled by the similarity of names, they killed his companions, took his possessions, and allowed him to depart. Thus he paid the price of an ambiguous name, redeeming another man’s danger with his own, and fled naked from the robbers.

But Wilfrid, whose prudence was not unaware of the devices of hostile counsels, carried out to sea by a light west wind, turned his prows toward the east in order to sail to Frisia. Received honorably by king and people, he passed there the winter which was approaching. A pitiable exchange: safer among barbarians than among his own people; driven from his homeland, beloved in Frisia. Immediately, therefore, King Adalgisus, yielding his pagan arrogance to Wilfrid’s preaching, opened an easier path for preaching to the rest. [Col. 1559B] Ebroin attempted, by letters and by the promise of an immense sum of gold, to induce him to kill or expel the man of God; but the attempt failed. For while Wilfrid listened and dined in the hall, Adalgisus had the letter read and threw it into the fire, saying: “So may he burn who breaks an agreement made with a friend out of greed for gold.”

Now spring weather was opening into flowers, and Wilfrid, resuming his journey, came to Dagobert, king of the Franks beyond the Rhine. Dagobert had not forgotten that, when he himself had once been driven out by a faction of nobles and had come to him from Ireland, Wilfrid had received him as a guest and sent him back to his homeland with horses and companions. He treated him kindly and wearied him with many entreaties that he would [Col. 1559C] honor the province by remaining there and accept the bishopric of Strasbourg. When Wilfrid deferred the petitioner until his return from Rome, Dagobert relaxed his anger toward his bishop Deodatus [otherwise, “go”].

Relying, then, upon this friendly favor, he traveled through Champagne, intending thereafter to enter Rome, and turned aside to Bertharius, duke of Provence. Bertharius had already learned Wilfrid’s case through the embassies of his enemies and had been enticed by promises to harm him. Although at first he had raised himself in pride, after hearing the true account he swallowed his anger. Thus he not only refrained from harming him, but by his support brought the affair to a favorable end. He said that he was reminded by this of the humanity of a certain king of the Huns, with whom he had once lived in exile: though a pagan, that king could nevertheless be corrupted by no bargain to harm one to whom he had sworn an oath. [Col. 1559D]

At last, coming to Rome, he found the city astonished by expectation of him. For Theodore had sent ahead a monk of modest religious profession, Kenewald, bearing written accusations and expressing the bitterness of his denunciation in harsh words. Moved by this, the most holy Pope Agatho convened a council of fifty bishops and abbots in the basilica of the Savior called the Constantinian. The record of this council is as follows:

> “Agatho, most holy and most blessed bishop of the Catholic and Apostolic Church of the city of Rome, said to those sitting with him: I do not believe that your holy brotherhood is unaware why I have summoned it to this venerable assembly. For I desire [Col. 1560A] to learn your reverence’s judgment and to deliberate with you what dissension has recently arisen in the Church of the island of Britain, where through God’s grace a multitude of believers has grown. It has been reported to us both by the account of those arriving here and by a series of writings.”

The most reverend Andrew, bishop of Ostia, and John, bishop of Porto, said:

> “The ordering of all Churches depends upon the decision of your Apostolic authority, since you bear the office of the blessed Apostle Peter. Yet we also, recently sitting with our fellow bishops and fellow servants, by your command reread all the writings which those sent from the island of Britain brought before your apostolic presence: both those sent from the person of the most reverend archbishop, formerly dispatched hence thither from the Apostolic See, [Col. 1560B] and other reports against a certain bishop who, as they say, fled; as well as those presented by Wilfrid, beloved of God, bishop of the holy Church of York. Expelled from his see by the aforesaid most holy man, he has come hither. Although the documents introduced many questions, we have found neither that he was convicted by the subtlety of the holy canons of any crimes, nor that he was therefore canonically deposed; nor have his accusers shown in their own words that he had committed any offences for which he ought to have been degraded. Rather, we have learned that he maintained moderation: he did not involve himself in certain seditious disputes, but, driven from his see, made known to his fellow bishops the nature of the act, and the aforementioned Wilfrid, bishop beloved of God, hastened here to the Apostolic See.”

Agatho, most holy and thrice most blessed bishop of the Catholic and Apostolic Church of the city of Rome, said to those sitting with him:

> “Let Wilfrid, bishop beloved of God of the holy Church of York, whom we are told is outside the doors of our venerable secretarium, be admitted to our secretarium according to his request, together with the petition which he is said to bring.”

As Wilfrid, bishop beloved of God, entered the venerable secretarium, he said:

> “I beseech your pontifical blessedness that you command the petition of my humility to be received and read aloud in your presence.”

“Agatho, most holy bishop, said: ‘Let the petition of Wilfrid, bishop beloved of God, be received and read aloud before all.’ And John the notary took it and read it before [Col. 1560D] the holy and apostolic council.

> “Wilfrid, humble and unworthy bishop of the Saxons, have, with God going before me, directed my steps to this apostolic eminence as to a fortified place and a tower of strength; for I know that from it the norm of the sacred canons flows forth to all Churches of Christ. From it I confidently ask that justice be done to my humility. For I do not doubt that your pontifical eminence has learned, both from the representation of my humility and from what I personally presented in spoken words before your apostolic eyes at the very beginning of my arrival, that certain invaders of my bishopric, although no fault had been proved against me, contrary to the enactments of the sacred canons, in an assembly of the most holy Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 1561A] and other bishops gathered with him, attempted to usurp my see, which I had held for more than ten years; and that three bishops have been promoted in my bishopric, although their promotion is not canonical.

> “What occasioned the most holy Archbishop Theodore, while I was still alive, to ordain by his authority, without the consent of any bishop and against the acquiescence of my humility, three bishops in the see which, though unworthy, I administered—I ought rather to pass over than demand an account of, out of reverence for that man. Because he was sent from this See of Apostolic supremacy, I do not dare accuse him. Nevertheless, if it shall become clear that, contrary to the law of regular enactments and without any guilt deserving the penalty inflicted by canonical severity, [Col. 1561B] I was driven from my former see, I did not appear as a disturber of the peace before anyone; but merely having called my fellow servants and fellow priests, the bishops of that province, to witness, I departed. If, indeed, your apostolic supremacy judges me to be deprived of it, I willingly embrace in humble devotion whatever is decreed. But if it decrees that I should recover my former bishopric, I follow and with all my strength reverence the judgment issued by the Apostolic See, provided only that the invaders be expelled from the former parishes of the Church over which I, your unworthy servant, presided. And if it should further decide that bishops are to be appointed in the same diocese over which I presided, let it at least command the promotion of such men as those with whom I may, God granting, serve in peaceful and tranquil concord with one mind,” etc.

Agatho, most holy and thrice most blessed bishop of the holy [Col. 1561C] Catholic and Apostolic Church of the city of Rome, said:

> “The course of the petition offered by Wilfrid, bishop beloved of God, gives no small satisfaction to those who hear it. Although he knew himself to have been unworthily expelled from the episcopal see, he did not resist contumaciously by secular force; but, humbly recognizing the canonical aid of our author, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he sought it. In suppliant expectation he declares himself willing to accept whatever may be judged concerning him, as the blessed Apostle Peter our author, by whose ministry we act, shall see fit to establish through our mouth.”

The entire holy synod then sitting, defining among other things, said:

> “We establish and decree that Wilfrid, bishop beloved of God, shall recover the bishopric which he formerly held; and that those whom he shall choose as assistants, with the consent of a council to be gathered there, shall be ordained and promoted bishops by the most holy archbishop. Those who were irregularly placed in his bishopric during his absence are to be expelled far away; and the rest follows, imposing penalties upon those who do not accept these decrees.”

Exulting in these decrees, the bishop was also, by the pope’s command, ordered to sit among the number of the one hundred and fifty holy bishops who were conducting a council against those who preached one operation in the two natures of our Lord Jesus Christ. Then, beginning his return, protected by God and unharmed by every danger, he reached his homeland. Although he obtained access to the king only with difficulty, he presented the sealed decrees of the Apostolic See. When the king had them read [Col. 1562A] to the bishops, his companions in faction, he was so far from reverence for the Roman See that, after stripping the blessed bishop of everything and taking his companions away in different directions, he committed him to a certain prefect, a man of notorious cruelty, to be thrown into prison. He believed those who asserted that the decrees had been bought with money, since Romans, they said, were seduced by gifts.

The whole court burned with desire for episcopal injury, so much so that the queen did not hesitate—horrible to relate—to carry about on her neck or in her carriage the bishop’s chrismarium, forcibly torn from him, together with the relics. The priest endured everything with unshaken mind and countenance, exhorting by holy admonitions those whom he feared might lose courage to bear it bravely, until God’s mercy and invincible good fortune should bring an end to their calamities.

But the prefect, barbarous and savage toward others, was English and gentle toward this man. He inflicted on him no punishment except darkness, not daring entirely to disobey the royal commands. Yet the divine majesty would not suffer the light of Britain to be oppressed by the indignity of darkness—a light which the heavenly torch had marked when his mother was still relieved of the burden of childbirth. A lamp sent from above pierced the density of the prison, and a light rivaling the absent day performed the office of daylight. Its radiance struck the eyes of the executioners peering through the cracks and compelled them to flee to their master. He indeed shuddered at the report, but through fear of Egfrid changed nothing from his usual conduct. The illness of his wife urged him on as he hesitated. Suddenly seized by it, she terrified her husband with gaping jaws and foaming vomit; soon shaken also by a greater demon, she grew bloodless and speechless and stiffened. He leapt up and, prostrate at the bishop’s feet, [Col. 1562C] readily obtained pardon from the merciful bishop. For Wilfrid immediately prayed, poured blessed water down the throat of the woman as she gaped, and she was freed from her illness and recovered sound health.

Egfrid heard this from the report of the grieving prefect, who begged that he should not be offered undeservedly to the devil as guilty of the punishment of an innocent bishop. But in no way changed, he commanded that Wilfrid be taken away from Offrith—for that was the man’s name—as from a man of cowardly spirit, and handed over to a retainer of more cruel daring named Tumber.

> “As the king’s cruelty increased, so did the miracle. When he ordered Wilfrid to be bound and the fierce servant took out iron fetters with which to fasten the saint’s shins, the treacherous fetter continually slipped away as if by stealth from between the hands attempting to apply it. Either the narrower fetter could not encompass the larger shins, [Col. 1562D] or the looser chain did not touch the slender shins. And if at any time nothing was lacking to the painstakingly worked device, the bonds unwound themselves with such swiftness that the eyes of those watching could not follow them. Wickedness gave place to religion: the saint was unbound and held under free custody.”

Egfrid took no notice of any of these things; whenever he heard of them, he either dismissed them as a joke or defamed them with insults. Yet messengers frequently went from him to the bishop with commands that Wilfrid should of his own accord invalidate the terms of the decrees he had brought, declaring that they had been extorted for money, not obtained by judgment. If he did so, then by the king’s indulgence he would receive back part of his bishopric and all his possessions; if not, the loss would be his own, since he [Col. 1563A] was the cause of the dissension. These threats did little to move the bishop’s mind to consent. Rather, he replied that he would not, even at the risk of his life, defame the authority of the Apostolic See.

Meanwhile, what did Queen Ermenburga—the fuel and instigator of all this evil—do? Day and night she continued with banquets, and in triumphal procession carried the bishop’s chrismarium, rejoicing in the rich spoils. But one night, when she had lodged with Abbess Ebba, her husband’s aunt, the devil entered into her in all her inmost being; she began to think alien thoughts and to speak madly. Awakened by her cries, the abbess hurried to her and gently asked what illness she had. The queen answered nothing, for the distress of sickness had already stopped her voice. Then the handmaid of God, understanding the cause, advised her nephew to [Col. 1563B] restore the chrismarium of the most blessed man; that he himself should be reclothed with all his possessions in accordance with the apostolic commands. He was to do this if he wished his wife to be safe; but if royal boldness thought it must persist in evil, he should restore what he had taken and permit Wilfrid himself to depart free. This was done. The queen then indeed recovered completely; and, after her husband’s death, changing her manner of life, she religiously repented of what she had done.

Wilfrid, then, driven from his native soil, made for Wessex. There he was received by a certain nobleman, Berethwald, and for very few days found a hiding-place. For Ethelred, king of the Mercians, to whom this man was subject—he was Ethelred’s nephew—sharply commanded through messengers that he should not retain Wilfrid even for one day. This was done to flatter Egfrid, [Col. 1563C] whose sister Osdrida had married Ethelred in consolation for her slain brother Elwin, reconciling her husband and brother.

Thereupon, leaving his monks in a small monastery already built there, Wilfrid fled to the South Saxons, still pagans; among Christians no place remained for him to hide. Their king was called Edelwalk [otherwise Edelwalch]. When he heard the reasons for Wilfrid’s wandering, he eagerly set his mind to aiding the bishop. He made a most firm covenant [otherwise, “made”]: that he would betray him to his enemies neither through entreaty nor for a price. Secure under this protection, Wilfrid first preached Christianity to the king and queen and afterward to the people of the province. Nor was there difficulty in persuading them: as soon as the king had been baptized, he encouraged the rest to do the same by his example. He gave the bishop his own residence, called Selescy, in which Wilfrid lived more familiarly; filling it with monks, he transmitted it to posterity as an episcopal see. [Col. 1563D]

At that time Cedwalla had been expelled from Wessex by a faction of nobles. The saint readily assisted him whenever he came to him for counsel, providing both horses and money for him and his followers. Cedwalla, raging against all and snarling at all, put King Edelwalk to death when he encountered him through some misfortune. Having gained possession of all Wessex, he appointed Wilfrid as master and lord over the whole province, believing that nothing should be done in the entire province without Wilfrid’s consent. Finally, he gave him very extensive estates on the island of Wight and willingly confirmed by edict those which Wilfrid had previously held. [Col. 1564A]

Several years passed in these circumstances. Egfrid had now fallen in the war against the Picts. Theodore was now approaching death, his conscience wounded by the sin he had committed against Wilfrid. He summoned Wilfrid and Bishop Erkenwald to London. Confessing all his sins to them, he said that he was especially troubled by the scruple that he had sinned against the saint, allowing him, contrary to the rules, to be despoiled either by open pressure or hidden acquiescence.

> “And because,” he said, “my end is near next year, as I have learned through God’s foretelling and as frequent illness warns me, I beg you, most holy bishop, kindly to forgive me what was committed against you, and to assume the see of my archbishopric. For you are the most expert of all the English in Roman law; [Col. 1564B] and I, God granting, shall endeavor to erase former offences by recent diligence in service, making the kings your friends by both authority and entreaties.”

Wilfrid answered these words gently and as befitted a holy man; but he did not consent [otherwise, consented] to assume the archbishopric without the decision of a greater council. Theodore therefore exerted all his strength that Wilfrid should recover his bishopric. He sent envoys and letters to Alfrid, king of the Northumbrians, who had succeeded Egfrid, and to his sister Elfleda, abbess of Strenelhath, urging them, with their former hostilities put aside, without delay to embrace Wilfrid’s friendship.

To show the ardor of this effort, I shall set down here the letter which he sent to Ethelred, king of the Mercians:

> “Theodore, by God’s grace archbishop, in the Lord sends everlasting salvation to the most glorious and excellent king [Col. 1564C] of the Mercians. Let your admirable holiness know, most beloved son, that I am at peace with the venerable Bishop Wilfrid; and therefore, dearest one, I admonish you and command you in the charity of Christ to grant protection to his holy devotion, so far as your resources allow, as you have always done, for as long as you live. For, deprived for a long time of his own possessions, he has labored much in the Lord among pagans. And therefore I, Theodore, a humble bishop in decrepit old age, make this known to your blessedness, because apostolic authority, as you know, commends this course; and that most holy man, in his patience, possessed his soul and, meek and humble, following his Head, endured the injury brought upon him and awaited healing. And if I have found favor in your sight, although the length of the journey may seem burdensome to you, let my eyes see your delightful face and let my soul bless you before I die. [Col. 1564D] Act then, my son, toward that aforesaid most holy man as I have asked you. If you obey your father, who is not far from departing this world, it will greatly profit your salvation. Farewell.”

Thus when Wilfrid came to the kings with the archbishop’s letters, he was greeted and granted favor. Alfrith, who had once known him well, first freely granted him, when he came at his invitation, the monastery of Deugstoldeim; then, by a decision of a council, the bishopric of York and the monastery at Ripon. This friendship [Col. 1565A] stood between them scarcely five years, until poisonous counsels, fostered in the bosoms of certain men, burst into the open. Influenced by them, King Alfrith planned to mutilate Ripon monastery by taking away its own possessions and to establish a bishopric there. He asserted that the decrees of Archbishop Theodore were to be obeyed—not those issued at the beginning and end of his time, but those which are known to have been enacted during the intervening days of discord.

Angered by this, Wilfrid departed to his friend Ethelred, king of the Mercians. He remained under him for a considerable time and, after the death of Sexwlf, bishop of Lichfield, ruled that bishopric, beloved and revered alike by all the provincials. Meanwhile King Alfrid and Archbishop Berthwald, Theodore’s successor, constructed many devices against Wilfrid and wore him down [the text reads *deterentibus*]. [Col. 1565B] At last they settled upon this: under a show of hope for peace, they would summon him to a council and there either bend him by blandishments to their will, or, if he did not consent, crush him.

Unaware of their trickery and measuring others by the uprightness of his own heart, he went to the council. But he experienced something far other than he had hoped. After they had long wearied him with insults and false accusations of crimes, they finally asked whether he would obey the decrees of Archbishop Theodore. Perceiving their wickedness, he frustrated them by a shrewd response, saying that he would gladly obey those determinations of Theodore which agreed with the holy canons. Then, in a long argument attacking them, he sharply and truthfully declared that for twenty-two years they had cherished decrees enacted in dissension, contrary to the commands of the three apostolic men—Agatho, Benedict, and Sergius Incredulus [“the Unbelieving,” possibly uncertain]—and to the decrees of Archbishop Theodore. He then ceased. Alfrid’s arrogance rose so high that he said to the archbishop: [Col. 1565C] “If you command it, Father, I will crush him by force.”

But even his enemies disliked the prospect that a man of such renown, who had come to the council trusting in their good faith, should suffer the prejudice of oppression. They thought another course necessary. Therefore, as if giving peaceful counsel, they urged him that, since most frequent dissensions in God’s Church were springing up because of him, he should voluntarily give up his possessions and bishopric and confirm this renunciation in writing. This, they said, would commend his reputation and increase his glory, if as a private man he preferred to remain concealed in quiet [Col. 1565D] rather than stir up storms of sedition, whether himself or through others, on behalf of his bishopric.”

The Father perceived the business involved in these threats [otherwise, “excessively”], and replied:

> “Nothing contributes so much to the full measure of a man’s disgrace as condemning himself by his own voice. I was the first to teach the true Easter in Northumbria after the Scots had been expelled; the first to establish antiphonal church chants; the first to command monks to observe the Rule of the most holy Benedict. And now, for all this, I—a bishop, an old man of nearly seventy years—am to receive this reward: that I should be compelled to condemn myself in writing. Let them know, then, that I shall not do what would be disgrace to myself, calamity to those subject to me, and harm to all. Rather, I appeal to the Apostolic See, and I summon thither anyone among them who may presume to undertake an ecclesiastical contest.”

Now a man of seventy, he again prepared himself for labors, again for Rome. Without long delay he crossed the sea, completed the journey, and entered the city. He waited some days for the accusers to come. When they had come, they set out their case in letters; he pleaded what concerned himself in this manner:

> “To the lord, most blessed universal Pope JOHN, WILFRID, a suppliant and humble servant of the servants of God, bishop.

> “Let your holiness know that, because disturbances recently arose in Britain at the hands of those who, contrary to the decrees of the most blessed Pope Agatho and his venerable successors, usurped for themselves my bishopric, monasteries, lands, and all my possessions, [Col. 1566B] I was compelled to appeal to this most holy Apostolic See. I called them to witness through the almighty Lord and the blessed Apostle Peter that, if anyone had an accusation against me, he should come into your presence, as the writings of your most blessed predecessor Sergius decreed. Therefore I have taken care to present the petition of my humility to your glorious presence, that you may deign, out of the overflowing benevolence of your mercy, to confirm what your most blessed predecessors decreed concerning my lowliness. And if any accuser comes against me, let him be brought forward by your command and state whatever he wishes to charge. If I do not reasonably refute any charge whatsoever, even the least, I am ready to undergo the severity of the canons.

> “Next I ask that I may obtain letters of recommendation from your eminence to Ethelred, king of the Mercians, so that all my monasteries within his province may enjoy peace; and that I may have a letter to Alfrid [otherwise Alfrith], king of the Northumbrians, that he may restore everything to me. If it should perhaps seem burdensome to him that I possess the bishopric of York, let the Apostolic See decide who is to be bishop there. Yet I shall not lose the two monasteries situated in that province, Ripon and Hexham, which I founded. Finally, I promise to obey all the decrees of Archbishop Brethwald [otherwise Berthwald] which are not contrary to the most firmly established decrees of your predecessors concerning my lowliness.”

When the accusers sent by Archbishop Berthwald were ordered to respond, [Col. 1566D] they first said this: that it was a capital offence that Wilfrid had contumaciously declared, in a council assembled in Britain, that he would not obey the decrees of Archbishop Brithwald. Standing in the midst, the bishop cleared himself of this charge by saying that he had not answered in such an unqualified manner, but had declared only that he would obey those decrees which were not contrary to the decrees of the canons; and that it was contrary to the rules for him to condemn himself when no accusation of crime had been brought against him.

This response, so convincing and straightforward, elicited joyful applause among the Romans. The accusers were ordered to return home. The bishops said that, although the canons had provided that an accuser who failed in the first article of accusation should not afterward rise to attempt others, nevertheless, out of reverence for Archbishop Brithwald, they would not fail to examine all matters in order. Thus it came about that during four months seventy councils were convened, either for this purpose alone or principally for this purpose. They had a glorious outcome for Wilfrid and an ignominious one for the accusers. The Romans, at great expense, marveled at the accusers’ shamelessness and Wilfrid’s eloquence: whatever charges they put forward, he refuted and overthrew them, supported by God’s help and truth, not with a contrived answer but as if dispersing spiders’ webs at the first movement of his lips. The bishops marvelled still more at the audacity of advocates who, exempt from ecclesiastical orders—except that one of them was a deacon—presumed to accuse a venerable bishop of seventy years, a torrent of eloquence. After much and prolonged discussion in Greek among themselves, they finally turned to our language, condemned the envoys as deserving imprisonment, rebuked those who had sent them for folly, and pronounced Wilfrid free from every charge.

Here I would insert how much benefit to his cause was brought by the council of Pope Agatho when it was read aloud, and also how, in the city of Meaux in France, east of Paris, as he was returning home oppressed by illness, he was healed by an angelic vision—were it not that the venerable historian Bede, worthy of belief for the restraint of his language, had anticipated the account. We briefly insert what he omitted from the narrative. Although the bishop had obtained his case, he nevertheless sought to remain at Rome, to pour out his aged spirit at the feet of the apostolic lords [Col. 1567C]. Pope John opposed this pious wish, saying that he was needed by England; and therefore he ordered that what remained of his life should not be spent among foreign ears, but devoted to the interests of his native country.

He therefore returned and brought apostolic letters to Æthelred, king of the Mercians, now a monk. Æthelred humbly and on bended knee received the honour of the apostolic greeting; and, after the letters had been read, he readily secured from Cenred, son of Wilfhere, whom he had appointed king in his place, the fulfilment of what their tenor commanded. For Cenred too was full of the fear of God, as was proved to the world four years later by his voluntary renunciation of the kingdom. Nor was Archbishop Brithwald slower in eagerly seeking peace [Col. 1567D] and hastening into the unity of brotherly concord. They say that he was terrified by the threats of the apostolic see, the legates piling up grave complaints concerning his condemnation, although Wilfrid had already released them from judgment. King Aldfrith of the Northumbrians alone, treading the path [variant: “decision”] of a more obstinate mind, persisted in stubbornness.

For when messengers had been sent to him on Wilfrid’s behalf, he at first returned a favourable answer; but, corrupted, as is believed, by the counsels of ill-wishers, to whom he indulged too much beyond their station, he distressed the returning messengers on the appointed day with this declaration: that he indeed paid honour, as to parents, to the persons of the legates, because they were grave in life and venerable in appearance; but that he wholly refused assent to their embassy, because it was contrary to reason to communicate, whatever apostolic letters might say, with a man who had already twice been condemned by the whole council of the English [Col. 1568A].

Nor did he himself remain long thereafter alive. For immediately after their departure he was seized by a grievous illness and was being driven toward death. The bitterness of his torment brought forth a consideration long dormant in his royal mind, and, according to the prophet, “Vexation gave understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28). Understanding that he was deservedly entangled in the snare of disobedience, he promised Wilfrid every amendment of his conduct. If Wilfrid could be brought to him while he still lived, he did not cease, so far as he could speak with a voice already closing, to make the same promises; and, if he himself should be deprived of fulfilling his vow, to adjure his heir to perform it. He died soon afterward, and too late regretted that he had despised the apostolic letters, whose threats [Col. 1568B] he did not deserve to escape. Since I have repeatedly mentioned those letters, I am inclined to set them down here in abbreviated form, so that it may be clear what great misery it brings upon mortals that those men whom antiquity celebrates as most holy—Theodore, Bertwald, John, Bosa, and also Hilda the abbess—should have pursued with bitter hatred Wilfrid, who, as the foregoing has shown, was most acceptable to God.

> “To the most eminent lords, ÆTHELRED, king of the Mercians, and ALDFRITH, king of the Deirans and Bernicians: Pope JOHN.
>
> “We rejoice, by the cooperation of God’s grace, at the progress of your religion, seeing in you the fervour of the faith which, through the preaching of the prince of the apostles and God’s illumination of your minds, you have received and effectively maintain. May the increase of better things enlarge our joy [Col. 1568C]. Yet the inextricable dissension of certain persons grieves our minds, and it ought to be corrected, lest you be found transgressors rather than guardians of apostolic commands.
>
> “For formerly, under Pope Agatho of apostolic memory, when Bishop Wilfrid appealed to this see concerning his case, and accusers sent hither and thither by Theodore, archbishop of the holy church of Canterbury, and by Hilda, abbess of religious memory, had arrived, the bishops then assembled here from various regions investigated the matter canonically and pronounced judgment. The successors of that pontiff, our predecessors, maintained the same decision. Nor is Archbishop Theodore known to have opposed it [Col. 1568D], for afterward he never forwarded any accusation here. Now likewise we have caused the accusations of those who came here from Britain against Bishop Wilfrid, and his defences, to be presented before the assembly of the most reverend bishops found here over several days, both concerning earlier and recent letters and concerning what the parties submitted orally. But since the principal persons from whom the entire controversy arose are not present here, they must come, if the dispute is to receive an end.
>
> “Therefore we exhort our brother Archbishop Berthwald to summon a synod together with Bishop Wilfrid, to cause Bosa and John to attend the synod, to hear the arguments of the parties, and to consider what the parties can establish against one another [Col. 1569A]. If he can settle the matter in that synod, it will be pleasing to us. But if not, let him admonish them to hasten to the apostolic see, so that what has not hitherto been capable of settlement may be decided by a larger council. Let him know that whoever refuses to come submits himself to deposition and is no longer to be received as a bishop, either here or there. Let your royal eminence therefore bring about the assembly, so that what we have discerned, with Christ’s inspiration, may take effect. But whoever, with rash audacity, despises this, whatever his rank, shall not go unpunished by God, nor escape without loss, bound by a heavenly judgment.”

Aldfrith having died, a certain Eadwulf, plotting tyranny, also vomited forth the frenzy of his diseased mind [Col. 1569B] against Wilfrid, as though he had sworn to emulate Aldfrith’s madness. When Wilfrid, remembering that he had formerly been a friend, judged it not unadvisable to approach him, Eadwulf boiled over with such folly that he immediately ordered him to leave his kingdom, unless he wished to be stripped of all that he possessed and shamefully expelled. Yet two months later, deprived both of life and kingdom, he struck the ground with his captive diadem as he died; and the nobles of the realm restored Alfred’s son Osred to the throne.

Berfrith, greatest among those nobles in faith and authority, at Archbishop Berthwald’s urging consented to a council being held in Northumbria, so that Wilfrid’s just cause might at last receive a conciliatory settlement. There, in accordance with apostolic commands, the bishops were given the choice either to yield Wilfrid his episcopal see or to go to Rome to defend their cause; whoever thought these commands to be resisted was to become excluded from communion [Col. 1569C]. When the bishops resisted in their customary manner, the most blessed virgin Ælfflæd, Aldfrith’s sister, abbess after Hilda at Streaneshalh, fixed the issue by saying:

> “Putting evasions aside, I produce the testament of my brother, at which I was present: if he recovered, he promised that he would without delay do what the apostolic see commanded; and, should death intervene so that he could not do it, he is known to have enjoined its performance upon his heir.”

Then Berfrith [variant: Berthfrith], joining his own words to those of the virgin, said:

> “I judge that the pope’s commands must be obeyed, especially since their authority is supported both by the command of our king and by the pledge of our necessity. For when, after his death, pressed by enemies, we were shut up in Bamburgh, in the straits of siege and danger of life, we vowed to God that we would fulfil the pope’s command if we could escape. We had scarcely finished our vow when, I confess, most holy archbishop, acts of obedience at once vied with one another; the entire province rallied to our agreement [Col. 1569D]. The royal boy was raised as king, the enemy driven out, the tyrant destroyed. It is therefore the royal will that Bishop Wilfrid be restored.”

When these words were spoken, the clouds of dissension were dispersed and the calm of peace was poured forth. The episcopal body hastened into an embrace, and with harmonious minds they passed the remainder of their lives. Two monasteries, at Ripon and Hexham, were left to Wilfrid. Having obtained unshaken peace, four years after his return, as the archangel Michael had foretold, he was attacked by the same illness as formerly at Meaux [Col. 1570A], so violently that he suddenly lost consciousness and speech.

But when his followers prayed that he might at least recover speech in order to divide his possessions, he recovered naturally, so that he immediately spoke; and after some days, his strength restored by health, he went around [variant: “went about”] all his places. Then, being in no doubt because of his frequent illnesses that death was near, he supplied whatever good works he seemed formerly to have performed too lukewarmly. He appointed superiors over all his monasteries and divided his treasures into four parts: one portion—the best—was to be given to the Roman Church, by whose authority he had always been exempted from all injuries and restored to honours.
