Though burdened with years, he intended to fulfil this himself, had iron rest not overtaken him while planning it. The second portion [Col. 1570B] he assigned to the poor; the third to the heads of the monasteries, so that they might purchase the friendship of the powerful and restrain the attacks of opponents; the fourth to those who had been inseparable companions in his labours but had not yet received lands on which to support themselves.

Thus, having received leave from the people of Ripon, whom he had always cherished with special affection, and from the other Northumbrians, he set out for an interview with King Ceolred of the Mercians, who had invited him, in order also to secure the peace of his monasteries, many of which he had established in that region through the favour of kings. There, after visiting and enlarging everything, a year and a half after he had been warned for the second time of his approaching death, he was seized by illness at Oundle and sensed that his last day was at hand [Col. 1570C]. He addressed his sons briefly, as far as his strength allowed, imparted the sacred blessing, and, as it seemed, wholly free from anguish, came to his end. The monks had already recited the Psalter as far as the verse, “Send forth thy Spirit, and they shall be created,” etc.; he died in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the forty-sixth of his episcopate.

He was a man shaken by many dangers for the sake of righteousness; even in exile he did not give himself to leisure, but laboured in founding monasteries and bishoprics. He was outstanding in winning the favour of princes among whom he lived in exile, and equally odious to the kings of his homeland for the severity of his justice. He left more monasteries than any other man, which he alone had assembled and divided among many heirs. His body was carried to Ripon and buried with great reverence. At the hour in which he breathed his last, sweet birdsong and the clapping of wings flying heavenward were heard but not seen [Col. 1570D]. When this often occurred during the funeral procession, those present who understood it wished it to be taken as the gathering of angels, come to receive the dead man.

A paralytic woman, touched by the washing-water of the garment upon which his body had lain, recovered the use of her limbs. When certain men entered the building in which he had died intending to burn it, the fire drew back; indeed, a handsome young man was seen removing the flame. Many years later, when the monastery at Ripon had been destroyed, Wilfrid was carried to Kent; there he is reckoned among the foremost and honoured among the chief ones.

Yet, to return to the enumeration of bishops, as though returning to the road after a long digression: when Wilfrid, bishop of the entire Northumbrian region, had first been expelled, as stated above [Col. 1571A], two were appointed in his place: Bosa at York, and Eata at Hexham.

When Eata died, John was ordained in his place. In the time of King Aldfrith, Wilfrid returned to the whole bishopric for five years, John being expelled from Hexham and Bosa from York. After five years Wilfrid was again expelled by Aldfrith, and they were restored to their sees. But when Aldfrith died, Wilfrid was received into concord and held the see at Hexham, while John moved to York, because Bosa had by then died.

John, a man of outstanding virtues, has Bede as his most famous herald in the *History of the English*. Nor is he now inferior to his renown, nor, though dead, in miracles. The following is especially famous, which the inhabitants of Beverley, where he lies, commonly display as a spectacle [Col. 1571B]:

> “The fiercest bulls, bound with very knotted chains and brought with the great exertion of strong men, as soon as they enter the cemetery become so quiet, all their ferocity being subdued, that you would think them sheep in their gentleness. The knots are then loosened and they are allowed to play about the courtyard—though before this they were accustomed to attack with horns and hooves whatever stood in their way.”

He was succeeded at York by his priest Wilfrid, who outlived Bede’s time; for Bede affirms that he was bishop at York in the year in which Bede died. Hence arises an inextricable dispute between the men of Canterbury and those of York: the Canterbury men say that they possess the elder Wilfrid, whereas the York men contend that this younger one was transferred to Kent by Archbishop Odo.

[Col. 1571C] After his death Egbert, brother of Egbert king of the same province, shone forth as a model bishop. By his own prudence and his brother’s power he restored that see to its proper condition. For, as is readily known to anyone reading the deeds of the English, Paulinus, its first bishop, was driven from the place by hostile force; dying at Rochester, he left there the distinguished pallium which he had received from Pope Honorius. The bishops after him of so great a city, content with the simple title of bishop, aspired to nothing higher.

But Egbert, when enthroned, a man of more spirited disposition, considered: “Just as it is proud to seek what is not due, so it is cowardly to neglect what is due.” By frequent appeals to the apostolic throne, he recovered the pallium. He was, so to speak, an arsenal of all the liberal arts [Col. 1571D], and established a most noble library at York. I call Alcuin as a fitting witness to this, for he said in a letter to Charles Augustus:

> “Give me more choice books of scholarly learning, such as I had in my native land through the good and most devoted diligence of my master, Archbishop Egbert. And, if it please your Excellence, I shall send some of our boys to collect from there whatever is necessary and carry back to France the flowers of Britain.”

He was buried with his brother in one [variant: lowest] porch at York, after thirty-six years as bishop.

His successor was the aged Eanbald, the industrious disciple of the aforementioned Alcuin. Hence Alcuin said in a letter to him:

> “Praise and glory be to God, who preserved [Col. 1572A] my days in good prosperity, so that I might rejoice in the exaltation of my dearest son, who would labour in my place in the church where I had been nourished and educated, and preside over the treasures of wisdom in which my beloved master Archbishop Egbert left me his heir.”

This is the Eanbald who, together with Archbishop Æthelheard of Canterbury, by reciprocal offices of integrity reduced to nothing the encroachment which King Offa of the Mercians had made upon the church of Canterbury. Alcuin seems to indicate this in a letter to the same Æthelheard:

> “Hearing of your health and prosperity, and of your conference with my son Eanbald, bishop of York, pleased me greatly, since I hope that, through the conversation of your holiness, the unity of the holy Church may be restored [Col. 1572B], which has been partially rent apart—not by rational consideration, but by a certain desire for power.”

After him these were archbishops: Wilfrid, Wymund, Wulfhere, Æthelbald, Rædwald, and Wulfstan. In the time of King Edmund, brother of Æthelstan, Wulfstan earned the king’s anger by persistent efforts on behalf of the Danes who had rebelled against him; he so roused that otherwise calm and kindly spirit that the king cast him into chains. But not long afterwards, moved by repentance and respect for clerical dignity, the king permitted him to depart unharmed. Yet Wulfstan, indignant at the pardon granted him, immediately gave up his life [variant: “departed”].

After him Oskytel received the rank of honour and flourished in the reigns of Kings Eadred, Eadwig, and Edgar; he had as successors Oswald, Eadwulf, and Wulfstan [Col. 1572C]. All these were bishops of Worcester as well, for the following reason. Oswald, born of no low lineage, being the nephew of Archbishop Odo, became a monk at Fleury in France, in accordance with a custom then familiar among the English: that those inspired by a desire for goodness should assume the monastic habit in the monastery of most blessed Benedict, from whom this form of religious life took its origin.

There he broke the licentiousness of youth, serving religion and letters for many years. Although invited by the archbishop, he resisted repeated letters, alleging the novelty of his dress and his immaturity in religion; he did not come until late, moved by the message that his uncle, now sick, was lying at the point of death. Having already landed at Dover [Col. 1572D], when he heard that his uncle was dead, he was scarcely prevented from immediately returning to Fleury. But at his companions’ admonition not to neglect the obligations of kinship, after rendering the due rites to the holy archbishop, he came to Oskytel, archbishop of York, whom he touched by the nearest degree of relationship. Captivated by Oskytel’s sweetness, he enjoyed [variant: “made use of”] his religious companionship for many years.

Meanwhile Dunstan, leaving the bishoprics of Worcester and London, went to Kent. Knowing Oswald’s holiness and effectiveness, he obtained for him from the king the bishopric of Worcester. Oswald gradually perceived that in the minds of the clergy established there was material for good, if someone knew how to animate and form it by exhortation. He did not drive them out tumultuously, but surrounded them with a most holy stratagem [Col. 1573A]. Since the episcopal see served the honour of St Peter, he built another church in the same cemetery in the name of the Mother of God; and, having placed monks there, he preferred to associate with them and celebrate the divine offices more familiarly.

When the people saw this, thinking it a great impiety to be deprived of the blessings of so religious a bishop, all flocked there. Thus the clergy, left in the middle, preferred to assume the habit of monks rather than suffer loss themselves and be a laughing-stock to the people. From that time the key-bearer of paradise gave way to the gatekeeper of heaven [variant: “Mother of God”], in a fine exchange among the heavenly inhabitants. By holy zeal the breath of this report won Oswald much friendship with the king and the nobles.

The king filled the see of York, made vacant by Dunstan’s counsel, with a man who, from long familiarity, knew well how to moderate the barbarism of the nation [Col. 1573B]. Yet Oswald was not permitted to renounce the see of Worcester, lest the recent community of monks should be deprived of the encouragement of its altar. The nobles submitted themselves to the man and eagerly offered possessions for founding monasteries where none existed and restoring those that had declined. Of these, when the occasion arises, I shall say as much as appears appropriate.

Moreover, he generously supported learned men summoned into England, lest the country be deprived of that good without which all other goods seem to me nearly empty. One of these was Abbo, monk of Fleury, who brought much fruit of learning into England and, at Archbishop Dunstan’s command, gave literary fullness to the Passion of Edmund the Martyr. Afterward he returned home and was made abbot there; he proved diligent in the severity of religious observance. When he sought to enforce this discipline in a certain cell of the monastery of Fleury, situated in Gascony and still called *ad Regulam* (“at the Rule”), Gascony would not endure it, but sent him, slain by a spear, to heaven [Col. 1573C].

Oswald, sufficient for both bishoprics during many years, spent more time at Worcester. He outlived Dunstan by five years and Æthelwold by ten, and inspired such admiration in England that he alone seemed to display both men—Dunstan in authority, Æthelwold in effectiveness, and both in holiness. On the day before he died, standing outside the gates at Worcester, he gazed long at heaven, weeping joyfully [Col. 1573D]. When those present asked why he looked upon the unclouded light in this way, he replied:

> “Allow me, brothers, to look toward the place to which I intend to go. The putting off of my body is swift, and the time of my dissolution is at hand.”

They were astonished, because he had previously given no indication of illness, but rather had taken more generous care of his body. Yet on the next day, while, as was his custom, he was washing the feet of the poor and saying the hymn, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” he was deprived of the vital spirit in the very act of kneeling. He was then buried in the church of Blessed Mary; after twelve years, divine signs having been shown, he was raised from the earth.

What miracle it may be that, though his whole body has been reduced to dust, the priestly stole in which he was clothed has suffered no injury from decay up to this day, must be left to the Lord’s judgment [Col. 1574A]. He was succeeded in both sees by Aldwulf, formerly abbot of Peterborough, a holy and venerable man, as they report. For his holiness he is forgiven for holding two sees contrary to the rules of the canons—namely, because he did it not through ambition but necessity. Wulfstan is not thus excused, for he differed both in holiness and habit. Aldwulf lies at Worcester and deserves praise also for the abundance of gifts with which he strove to rival Oswald’s generosity toward the monastery of Fleury.

After Wulfstan, Ælfric held the see of York and Leofwine that of Worcester. Ælfric lived in the time of Cnut and Harthacnut and is held detestable in this respect: on his advice Harthacnut ordered the corpse of his brother Harold to be dug up, its head cut off, and, as an infamous example to mortals, thrown into the Thames [Col. 1574B]. Indeed, hostile to the Worcester men because they had rejected his episcopate, he advised Harthacnut to burn their city and confiscate the citizens’ property because they had resisted royal tax-collectors too obstinately.

Kynesige succeeded Ælfric. Aldred was in turn appointed as successor, formerly a monk of Winchester and bishop of Worcester. Mocking Edward’s simplicity, and appealing to the custom of his predecessors more through money than reason, he assumed the archbishopric of York without relinquishing his former see. Having arranged the matter with the king, he proceeded to Rome accompanied by two bishops-elect, Giso of Wells and Walter of Hereford, and also by Tostig, earl of Northumbria [Col. 1574C].

Pope Nicholas received the earl graciously and made him sit at his side in the synod which he had assembled against the Simoniacs. He granted Giso and Walter the object of their desire, since they possessed learning by no means contemptible and were marked by no disgrace of simony. But, finding Aldred culpable on both counts by his own answer, he sternly stripped him of every honour. As they returned with differing outcomes, one hardship alike enveloped them all: when robbers attacked, they were stripped of everything except plain clothing, down to the smallest coin [variant: “the least”], though their bodies were unharmed, and they fled back to Rome.

This calamity gave Aldred an opportunity to recover his honours. Tostig too, assailing the apostolic see with grave verbal insults [Col. 1574D], brought it round to the decision he desired. He said that the pope’s excommunication was little to be feared by distant peoples when it was mocked by nearby brigands; that the pope raged against suppliants but had little power against rebels; and that either his possessions must be restored to him by the pope’s authority, since it was established that they had been lost through the pope’s deceit, or the king of England, when he heard this, would deservedly withhold St Peter’s tribute from Nicholas. Tostig would not fail to amplify the true account of events.

Terrified by this thunderbolt of threats, the Romans bent the pope so that he restored Aldred’s archbishopric and pallium. It would be impious, they said, if he returned to his country both dishonoured and despoiled. The pope did what reason advised, adding this balancing condition: that a proper bishop should be installed in the see of Worcester. Thus they went home unharmed, all consoled for their former loss by the great and lavish generosity of the apostolic see [Col. 1575A].

Roman legates followed the departing party and, with Aldred’s consent, ordained the most holy Wulfstan bishop of Worcester. For at that time no good man would receive the pontifical office from Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury in name only, since he had not entered the sheepfold through the door. Although he was often summoned by the apostolic see, he evaded everything, now by delays and now by gifts, until King William came, whom no cunning of evasion could corrupt. William publicly marked Stigand as notorious, refusing to receive from him the sacrament of royal blessing.

Aldred, having first exacted before all the people an oath that William would behave moderately toward those subject to him and treat English and Frenchmen with equal justice, performed the consecration [Col. 1575B]. Accordingly, so long as William maintained moderation toward his people, Aldred loved him as a child and revered him as a king. But when William demanded an unbearable assessment of tribute from the provincials, the bishop approached him through envoys. When William had scarcely admitted them and sent them away with a turbulent reply, Aldred without delay launched the weapon of a curse against him and all his offspring, declaring that he could deservedly give a curse, since he had undeservedly given a blessing.

When this was reported to the king, softened by his friends’ advice, he sent men to appease the bishop. Yet the bishop’s death forestalled the messengers: from distress of mind, as often happens, he had fallen ill and died. The freedom of his spirit shone most brilliantly in one saying, which I shall give in English, since Latin words do not correspond in the same elegance [variant: “elegance”] as the English.

Urse had been made sheriff of Worcester by the king. He built a castle almost in the very jaws of the monks, so that its ditch cut away part of the cemetery. A complaint was brought to the archbishop, who was guardian of the bishopric. Seeing it, he addressed Urse in these words:

> “Hatest thou Urse, have thou God’s curse.”

The play upon the euphony of the names is elegant in these words, though harsh: “You are called Urse,” he said, “have God’s curse”; and, what I have not supplied in English, “mine, and that of all consecrated heads, unless you remove the castle from here. Know assuredly that [Col. 1575D] your offspring shall not long inherit the land of St Mary.”

He spoke what was to be fulfilled, as we see fulfilled. For not many years later his son Roger, in possession of his father’s estates, was driven out by the grave indignation of King Henry because in reckless fury he had ordered one of the royal officers to be put to death. Aldred having died and been buried at York, the calamity mentioned above immediately followed, inflicted by King William’s command. Then all the popular nobility withered, cut down by the sickle of war.

For long before, in the time of the Danes, monasteries throughout the province, shining like stars, had fallen into ruin. Their half-ruined walls still stand, not as a delight to the eye but as monuments of sorrow. There was once at Wearmouth a monastery, a noble school of Bede and many learned men [Col. 1576A]. There was Streaneshalh, distinguished by its choir of holy virgins and by the mausoleums of blessed bishops and illustrious kings; it is now called Whitby, and the zeal of certain persons is striving to restore its half-sleeping ashes to life. Recently discovered and raised into prominence are the holy bodies of Bishop Trumwine, King Oswiu, and his daughter Ælfflæd, who governed the same monastery after Hilda; likewise that monk to whom, Bede relates, knowledge of song was given by divine gift.

That his merit with God was not ordinary is indicated, they say, by many miracles now sent down from above. Therefore I do not survey the monasteries of that province, because the ancient ones have been wholly destroyed, and, if there are new ones, they are still unknown—although in this work I have undertaken to enumerate not all things throughout England [Col. 1576B], but only those of greater renown and higher glory because of the bodies of native saints. In addition, the antiquity of memory hides some from our knowledge; the newness of their construction hides others; in some cases the remoteness of the province, in others the obscurity of the saints resting in them because of the rarity of miracles. Although the service of my pen is necessarily lacking to all these, they will lament our silence little, since once they were made known either by God’s will or their own activity.

Meanwhile, while we are lingering in this province, it occurs to me not to leave unmentioned the names of the bishops of Hexham and of Candida Casa, called in English Whithorn. Because they were formerly subject to the archbishopric of York and did not extend beyond our period for long, they do not rightly occupy a separate place in the account; let them therefore secretly insert themselves among the archbishops, so that, joined to their company, they may not lack commemoration.

Hexham is a place fifty miles distant from York. It belonged to the royal fisc when Wilfrid of blessed memory exchanged it with the most blessed Queen Æthelthryth for other estates [Col. 1576C]. There he splendidly adorned buildings raised to a formidable height in their walls and carried around through diverse windings by spiral stairways—largely by his own design, but also through the skill of masons whom the hope of generosity had drawn from Rome. At that time it was commonly said among the people, and even put in writing, that nowhere this side of the Alps was there such a building. Those who now come from Rome say the same, so that those who see the structure of Hexham swear that they imagine Roman magnificence; so little have the injuries of so many ages and wars taken away the beauty of its buildings [Col. 1576D].

Wilfrid was the first bishop there. When he was violently expelled, Eata, Tumbert, and John were appointed in succession.

But when Wilfrid returned and, after recovering the see, died, Acca succeeded him, a man exceedingly industrious and holy. Bede is an adequate witness for both qualities; by Bede’s inspiration and support, as is known, Acca produced many volumes through diligent work. Yet, as I learn from the chronicles, he did not enjoy better fortune than his master: three years after Bede’s death he was driven from his see, and it is uncertain whether he returned.

[Col. 1577A] Fredebert succeeded Acca; Tilbert succeeded him; Æthelberht succeeded Tilbert. To him and his community there is a letter of Alcuin, in which, among other things, he says:

> “O most noble offspring of holy fathers, successors to their honour and venerable life, and inhabitants of most beautiful places: follow the footsteps of your fathers, that from these most beautiful dwellings you may deserve to attain to the fellowship [Col. 1578A] of eternal blessedness of those who begot us.”

After Æthelberht there were only three bishops of Hexham: Heardred, Eanberht, and Thiffriddid. For the Danish army, already feared in Alcuin’s time, as we have said and shall say elsewhere, came; after the inhabitants had been killed or put to flight, it set fire to the roofs of the dwellings and exposed their inner parts to the sky [Col. 1578A]. Hexham is now an estate of the archbishop of York.

## On the Bishops of Candida Casa

[Col. 1577]

[Col. 1577A] Candida Casa is the name of a place on the furthest borders of England, near Scotland, where the blessed confessor Nima rests. A Briton by birth, he was the first there to preach Christ’s Gospel. The place took its name from the construction, because he built there, to the Britons’ amazement, a church of polished stone [Col. 1577B]. Antiquity found this holy Ninian illustrious in virtues. Alcuin writes in a letter to the brethren of that place:

> “I beseech the united charity of your piety to keep our name in memory in the church of your most holy father, Bishop Nima, who shone with many virtues, as was recently reported to me in poems in metrical form sent to us through our faithful disciples, the scholars of the church of York. In them I recognized both the learning of their author and the holiness of the worker of miracles.”

There, toward the end of Bede’s time, Pecthelm was first made bishop. Long before, while dwelling in Wessex, he had been worthy to attend the instruction of the most holy Aldhelm. He was followed by Frethewald, Pecwine, Æthelberht, and Bealdulf; nor do I find any more anywhere, because the bishopric, lying on the outer edge of the English and exposed to the ravaging of Scots or Picts, soon failed [Col. 1577C].

Having run through these matters, which it was not advisable to omit, the narrative will return to York.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1070, Thomas, canon of Bayeux, was made archbishop of York by King William. He remained in office thirty years, blameless throughout his life; nothing in his deeds or words deserves displeasure, except that, in the early period of his archiepiscopate, he contended over the primacy of Canterbury more through error than obstinacy. The first book of the *Deeds of the Bishops* has completed the account of this matter [Col. 1577D].

In elegance of bearing he was a striking young man, pleasing to behold, well-proportioned in strength and symmetry of limb; as an old man, he had a lively flush of face and swan-white hair. By his generosity he saddened his successors: being, as they say, excessively prodigal, he alienated much of the episcopal lands for the use of clerics. Yet he assembled a clergy sufficient in wealth and learning, completed the church begun from its foundations, and no adverse rumour ever stained his celibacy. He was a philosopher comparable in learning to the ancients, not elevated in speech, gracious in expression, and gentle in character. Nor was he inferior in singing or voice; he composed many ecclesiastical songs.

If anyone sang some vocal piece before him in the minstrel’s art, he immediately shaped it into divine praise. Above all he worked among the clergy to ensure that they had manly music in church, and that they should not, in an effeminate manner, draw out anything in a delicate manner, as Persius says [Col. 1578A–B]:
. . . . . “… words might displace the palate.” Therefore, full to overflowing in years, in the honour of the world, and in the grace of God, he died in the first year of Henry, in November, having previously crowned him king in August, because the Archbishop of Canterbury was absent.

Without delay Gerard, nephew of Walkelin, bishop of Winchester, who was bishop of Hereford, was elected and installed as archbishop. When he hesitated to submit to the primacy of Canterbury, Pope Paschal sent him this letter:

> “PASCHAL, pope, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GIRARD, Archbishop of York: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> [Col. 1578C] “Although we know that you have acted perversely against us—indeed, against your mother, the holy Roman Church—nevertheless by this present letter we command you not to neglect making your profession to our venerable brother Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. For we have heard that Thomas, formerly your predecessor, raised a dispute on this very matter; and when it was debated in the presence of Lord Pope Alexander II, a decision having been reached by his command after various inquiries, Thomas made that same profession to Lanfranc, his predecessor, and to his successors. Therefore we too will, God being the author, that what was then decided be kept firm and inviolate.”

Girard did not read this letter addressed to him, [Col. 1578D] because there was no need. He himself had anticipated the apostolic command and, at the king’s urging, had given Anselm his hand that he would observe towards him, in the archbishopric of York, the same profession which he had made in the bishopric of Hereford. The misconduct for which the pope reproaches him was this: returning from Rome with the pallium, he tainted the Apostolic See by his lie, telling the king that, if he behaved properly in other ecclesiastical matters, the pope would calmly tolerate the investitures of churches.

He was not ignorant of letters and was expansive in eloquence. He died unexpectedly, having indeed previously been touched by a mild illness. For, when somewhat unwell, he lay in a certain garden adjoining his house, so that he might enjoy outdoors a healthier air, enlivened by the sweet-breathing flowers of the grasses, [Col. 1579A] he ordered those standing by to withdraw indoors, intending meanwhile to attend to the body’s needs. They went away; and when they returned after their meal, they mourned their lifeless lord. Would that rumour had invented this, and that a man endowed with pontifical grace had not died thus! Certainly the canons of York most stubbornly opposed his burial in the church, scarcely permitting a mean turf to be cast over the corpse outside the doors.

Yet after some years his successor Thomas, softening the indignity of the deed, gave him most honourable burial in the church beside his predecessors. He was the son of Samson, bishop of Worcester. When, elected to the archbishopric, he was invited by Anselm to come to Canterbury, as was customary, to receive his consecration, he first replied graciously, saying that he gave thanks [Col. 1579B] for the summons, but asked a delay, since such great preparation required excessive expense. Summoned a second time, he declared that he was restrained by force and by the arguments of his clergy. When approached a third time through the bishops of London and Rochester, he refused outright.

Accordingly Anselm, after informing Pope Paschal of Thomas’s conduct, and himself hastening toward the heavenly journey through failing bodily strength, wrote Thomas a letter, which he sent under his own seal to every bishop of England, one copy to each, so that they might know how they ought to act toward Thomas.

> “ANSELM, minister of the Church of Canterbury, to THOMAS, elected Archbishop of York.
>
> “Thomas, in the sight of almighty God, I, Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury and Primate of all Britain, [Col. 1579C] speak to you, speaking on God’s behalf. I forbid you the priestly office which, at my command, you received in my diocese through my suffragan; and I command you in no way to presume to involve yourself in any pastoral care until you withdraw from the rebellion which you have begun against the Church of Canterbury and make to it the submission which your predecessors—namely, the archbishops Thomas and Girard—professed according to the ancient custom of their predecessors.
>
> “But if, in what you have begun, you choose rather to persist than to desist, I forbid, under perpetual anathema, all the bishops of the whole of Britain to lay hands on you for promotion to the episcopate; or, if you should be ordained by foreigners, [Col. 1579D] to receive you as bishop in any Christian communion. And I forbid you, Thomas, under that same anathema and on God’s behalf, ever to receive the blessing of the bishopric of York unless you first make the profession which your predecessors, Thomas and Girard, made to the Church of Canterbury. If you wholly relinquish the bishopric of York, I permit you to exercise the priestly office which you have already received.”

For the king was in Normandy; when he had returned to the kingdom, he began to examine the case. Anselm’s letter of prohibition was read before him and accepted and approved by all the bishops, although Count of Meulan seemed to construe their acceptance of it as contempt for royal power. Yet so great [Col. 1580A] was the agreement of the bishops, with not even Thomas’s father, the bishop of Worcester, dissenting, that they preferred to be stripped of every honour rather than transgress the commands of their father Anselm. The king’s approval confirmed their religious resolve when he added:

> “Whatever judgment others may give, I by no means wish to be subject, even for an hour, to Father Anselm’s excommunication. Therefore, since besides Anselm’s letter there are privileges of the Apostolic See, and decrees established before my father and mother with the counsel of the whole kingdom, upon which the authority of the Church of Canterbury rests: let Thomas choose either to make submission to the Church of Canterbury or to bid farewell to his bishopric.”

He yielded, not to reason but to power; and, having made his profession of submission to the Church of Canterbury, he received from the minister—namely Richard, bishop of London—[Col. 1580B] what he had refused to receive from his master. Thus he came late to regret his ready credulity toward clerics, carrying throughout his life a wounded conscience because he had been deprived of Anselm’s blessing.

At that time there was in England a certain cardinal, Odolric, who had brought the pallium for the Church of York, to be given on Anselm’s advice. But finding that Anselm had already died, he hesitated, uncertain what to do. Once all the controversy had been settled through the king’s authority, it was decreed that the cardinal himself should convey the pallium to York. This was done; Thomas, crowned with the pallium, shone forth as archbishop—free, as was believed, from women since youth and from every obscenity; lavishly beneficent to all; [Col. 1580C] exemplary in the piety and favour toward clerics that should be proclaimed. He died young, having held the rank scarcely fourteen years.

Thurstan, a cleric of commendable steadfastness, succeeded. When, some years after his election, he refused to make his profession to Ralph, Archbishop of Canterbury, he voluntarily surrendered the archbishopric at the king’s wish. But later, at his clergy’s urging, he went to Rome and obtained this letter:

> “PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “With God as author, we hold not merely good but better expectations of your uprightness. Therefore we urge Your Highness always to remember divine grace, [Col. 1580D] which has granted you both peace in your kingdom and knowledge of justice. Diligently preserve, then, the honour of God and of His churches in your kingdom, and effectually administer justice; for through God’s honour your own will surely be increased.
>
> “We have heard that the elected Archbishop of York, a wise and vigorous man, has been removed from the Church of York without judgment; this plainly conflicts with divine justice and the ordinances of the holy Fathers. We indeed wish neither that the Church of Canterbury be diminished nor that the Church of York suffer injury; but we judge that the constitution established between these churches by blessed Gregory, apostle of the English people, must be kept firm and inviolate. Therefore let that same elect be restored by every means to his church, as justice requires. But if any dispute [Col. 1581A] should arise between the churches, let it be handled in our presence, with both parties present.”

Relying on this letter, Thurstan gladly reclaimed his see. The disagreement between him and Archbishop Ralph increased daily, because no inducements and no threats could bring Ralph to lay hands upon him unless he made a profession, while Thurstan did not promise that he would do so even at the peril of his head. Both therefore resolved to meet Pope Gelasius, Paschal’s successor, when he came this side of the Alps, to plead their causes. But the pope’s death, not long delayed, checked their efforts, until Calixtus, his successor, came to Rheims to hold a council.

Thurstan [Col. 1581B] pressed on there vigorously, having promised the king that he would attempt nothing against the honour of the Church of Canterbury. As soon as he judged the moment favourable, he broke that promise in forgetfulness: from the pope, contrary to all the customs of his forefathers, he received episcopal consecration. Indeed, before Thurstan, the king’s envoy—and also Ralph’s brother, Seffrid, later bishop of Chichester—had gone to the pope, to declare that he must in no way either consecrate Thurstan himself or allow him to be consecrated by anyone other than the bishop of Canterbury, according to ancient custom. And if the pope wished to rely on the right of his apostolic office against this, he should be certain that the king would not alter his resolve in this matter even for the loss of his crown.

The pope replied to this:

> “Let not the king suppose that I shall act otherwise in the affair in question than he himself wishes. [Col. 1581C] For my will has never led me to humble in any way the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, over which so many distinguished [Col. 1582A] Fathers have presided, as is known to almost the whole world.”

Persuaded by these soothing words, the envoy hastened home. After his departure, however, the pope, subject to the commands of the Romans, who had entered into Thurstan’s friendship, consecrated him. John, Archdeacon of Canterbury, publicly forbade this; and the pope replied to him: “We wish to do no injustice to the Church of Canterbury, but, with its justice and dignity preserved, let us carry out what we have proposed.” Those who heard this judged it frivolous, since the deed differed from the word.

When the king heard of it, he prohibited Thurstan from entering any land under his dominion. He would not mitigate this severity even when the pope personally appealed to him at Gisors, asserting that by the authority of blessed Peter he would release Thurstan from the pledge by which the king said he was bound. When this proved fruitless, the king remained unreconciled for the time. But in the following year, when the aforesaid pope had become more firmly established in the Apostolic See and could arrange more freely what he wished, he sent a letter which appeared to mean that either Thurstan should possess his bishopric, or the king should be punished with anathema and the bishop of Canterbury with suspension from priestly office. [Col. 1582B] This fear compelled the king to abandon his undertaking: Thurstan was restored to his see.

Thus, although Ralph and his successor William made many attempts and expended many efforts, Thurstan dissolved and rendered futile all their allegations by his persistence. He died most piously, four years after the death of King Henry, having first renounced his bishopric and become a monk at Pontefract, a cell of Cluny.

## ON THE BISHOPS OF LINDISFARNE AND DURHAM

[Col. 1581]

[Col. 1581C] Of all those who had once been established in bishoprics in Northumbria and looked up to the primacy of York, only the bishop who was at Lindisfarne remained. Lindisfarne is a small island, now called by the local people Holy Island, which the most holy Aidan, a lover of solitude and holy poverty, chose as the seat of a bishopric, despising the pomp of York’s crowded population. His successors followed the man’s frugality and moderation: Finan, Colman, Tuda, and Eata.

Most celebrated is the outstanding Cuthbert, still resting with his body uncorrupted, who alone obtained this favour: that his incorruption never even came into question.

[Col. 1581D] Eadbert, because of his pre-eminent holiness, deserved to be buried in the same tomb—a tomb which his predecessor, of most blessed memory, had consecrated eleven years earlier for the intact body. He himself foretold the event of his impending death and burial when the most sacred vestments were brought to him: though buried for so many years, they had escaped the stain of decay. Bede recounts this at greatest length in his *Life of Cuthbert*.

Eadfrith, at whose command and request that same historian [Col. 1582C] extolled blessed Cuthbert both in rhetorical prose and in the sweetness of verse; Ethelwold, Cinewulf, and Higbald. In Higbald’s time the Danes devastated the island, sparing not even the most holy altars, as Alcuin’s letter to him clearly shows, in these words:

> “ALCUIN, deacon, greeting to HINGBALD, bishop, and to the whole community of the Church of Lindisfarne, sons in Christ of the most blessed Father Cuthbert, bishop.
>
> “The familiar affection of your charity used greatly to gladden me; but, in exchange, the calamity of your tribulation has greatly saddened me though absent: the heathen have defiled God’s sanctuaries, shed the blood of saints around the altar, and trampled the bodies [Col. 1582D] of saints in the temple as dung in the street. What confidence remains for the churches of Britain, if Saint Cuthbert, together with so great a number of saints, did not defend his own church? And so forth.”

By this he urges them not to degenerate from the ways of their predecessors, nor to stain the reverence due to their profession by luxurious dress and intemperance in eating; such things had befallen them through transgression of the divine law, and worse would follow if they thought to persist in forbidden practices. He adds also at the end [Col. 1583A] of the letter:

> “When our lord King Charles returns home, his enemies having been subdued through God’s mercy, we intend, God helping, to go to him; and we shall take diligent care to bring about, as far as we can, whatever may then be of benefit concerning the boys carried off into captivity by the heathen or concerning our other necessities.”

Likewise, to King Ethelred:

> “Behold, the church of Saint Cuthbert, priest of God, sprinkled with blood, stripped of all its ornaments—the place most venerable in all Britain—is handed over to heathen peoples for devastation. And where, first after the departure of Saint Paulinus from York, the Christian religion took its beginning among the Northumbrian [variant: *Northanimbrorum*] people, there began the onset of misery and calamity.”

Accordingly, after deliberation, it was decreed that the bodies of the saints should be transferred from that island, which lay exposed to the incursions of sea-raiders, onto the mainland. Then, when certain persons attempted, as they supposed piously, to carry the blessed body of great Cuthbert secretly to Ireland, they lost the fruit of their labour: either they waited on the shore for wind during many days, or, after being carried some distance out to sea by a rather stronger blast, they were immediately driven back.

Therefore they laid the sacred body, with due honour, at Bulbeford [variant: Bubedford], perhaps the episcopal seat, beside the River Tweed. It lay there for many years until the coming of King Ethelred. Yet meanwhile it did not cease to aid the people of the province, but ranged throughout England in miracles. If I recount one of them, I think I shall not do so without reason—especially because, shown in a most illustrious person, it restored freedom to all England and cast off servitude.

King Alfred had been reduced by the attacks of barbarians to such destitution that he lay hidden, without glory, on a very small island called Athelney. I have spoken above of this island in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Wells*. There, then, one day, while he lay asleep in his dwelling—for grief of mind had brought on sleep—and his companions were scattered along the riverbank, behold, blessed Cuthbert addressed him as he slept:

> “I am Cuthbert, formerly bishop of Lindisfarne. God has sent me to announce good news to you. For although England has long paid an overwhelming penalty for its sins, at last He has looked upon it with the eye of His mercy through the merits of its native saints. You also, though so miserably banished from your kingdom, shall within a short time be gloriously restored to the throne.
>
> “And I shall give you a remarkable sign: today your fishermen will come, carrying away in baskets a great quantity of large fish. This will be all the more wonderful because in these days the water is frozen and the roughened pool allows no expectation of such a thing. Besides, the air dripping with cold dew defeats every fisherman’s skill. But you will truly become master of good fortune and act as a king if you merit, by fitting devotion, God as your helper and me as His messenger.”

With these words the saint freed the sleeping king from his anxieties and strengthened his mother, who lay nearby, with the joy of the same message. Awakened, both repeatedly said that they had dreamed one and the same dream, repeating its words; [Col. 1584A] and the fishermen came in with an innumerable abundance of fish, confirming the dream. Not long afterward he regained the kingdom and its glory, as we have related more fully in the *Deeds*.

Hingbald was succeeded by Egbert, Eardwulf, Cutheard, Milred, Witred, Sexhelm, Aldred, Ælfsige, Aldhun, and Eadmund, who was made bishop by a most remarkable chance. For in the time of the English, the election of bishops and abbots belonged to clerics and monks. Monks did not serve at Saint Cuthbert’s body, although the bishops were customarily monks, following the example of the most holy Father, who had been a monk set over clerics.

When Bishop Aldhun died, the clerics sat in consultation about electing their future ruler; but, as happens in such cases, they decided nothing certain because of the division of parties. [Col. 1584B] Then Eadmund, whom no one had thought should be summoned, came upon them while they hesitated, and, using his customary wit, said: “Take me and make me bishop.” All of them, as though their spirits had been kindled by God, caught the words from his mouth as though they were a divine miracle. Though astonished and regretting what he had said—for he preferred playing ball to wearing the monk’s hood—they made him a monk and petitioned King Ethelred [variant: *Egelred*], then reigning, to appoint him bishop. This jest, as the natives of the place relate, proved a happy omen: the king’s graciousness granted what was asked, and God’s own power fulfilled what was hoped for.

Under this bishop the Church’s prosperity advanced exceedingly. The holy body was carried to Durham; the basilica there was completed from its foundations; and many further things were accomplished which no false oblivion will ever consume among the citizens. Durham is a hill swelling gradually, with a gentle slope, from the flat ground of a valley into a mound; and although its high position and steep rocks bar every approach to enemies, the people of the present day have nevertheless set a castle upon the hill. At the foot of the castle flows a fish-filled river, like most—indeed almost all—the rivers of Northumbria. For the Isis so overflows in the western and northern regions of England that peasants feed their swine with fish thrown aside.

After Eadmund came Edred, Ægelwine, and Ægelric. The last, under King William, was accused of rebellion because he had disturbed the king’s peace by undertaking piracy; he was carried into perpetual exile at Westminster. There, as long as he lived, he lessened and washed away his former offences by voluntary fasting and an abundance of tears, acquiring among men the reputation of holiness. Finally, as those who saw him handed down his memory to posterity, his tomb even today lacks neither vows nor crowds of petitioners.

While he was still alive, Walcher was placed over him, to be both earl of the province and bishop, to restrain the rebellion of the people by the sword and reform their morals by speech. While diligently carrying this out, he was shamefully slain, giving the king an occasion utterly to destroy the districts [variant: remnants] of that province, which had somewhat recovered their breath.

The cause of the killing was this. The bishop had put his kinsman Gilbert [Col. 1585A] in charge of external affairs and the cleric Leobwin of internal matters: both vigorous in their commissions, but unbridled. Won over by their efficiency, the bishop tolerated their excesses; and, because he had elevated them, he increased the fullness of his favour. “For nature indulges itself, and with gentle favour assents to its own gifts.”

This Leobwin caused Liulf, minister of the most blessed Cuthbert—so beloved that the saint himself, standing before him while he kept vigil, was said to dictate legal judgments—to be killed by Gilbert. Leobwin, I say, had been struck by envy because Liulf, through his knowledge and fairness in judgments, held a place of greater friendship with the bishop. Struck by this report, Walcher offered the deceased man’s enraged kindred a lawful hearing, protesting that Leobwin was the author of his own and his followers’ death.

When [Col. 1585B] they came to the hearing, no arguments could soften the savage people so that they would not lay blame upon the bishop, because they had seen both murderers moving familiarly about his court after Liulf’s killing. Thereupon they rose in shouting and anger. Gilbert left the church, where he had been sitting with the bishop, of his own accord, to purchase his lord’s life at the cost of his own danger; and he was wickedly killed. The bishop too, holding before him the branch displayed outside the doors, was given over to death. Leobwin, the fomenter of the evil, was half-burned; because he would not leave the burning church, he leapt out and was received by a thousand spears.

This had been foretold by Queen Edith, widow of King Edward. When she saw Walcher being led at Winchester for consecration—fair-haired, rosy-faced, [Col. 1585C] very tall, and handsome—she said: “Here we have a martyr,” doubtless led by her knowledge of that ungovernable people to make the prediction.

Walcher met this end of life, a man neither immoderate nor unlearned. He restored to the condition of clerics the canons accustomed to monastic service, because they had always had a monk as bishop.

He was succeeded by William, formerly abbot of Saint-Carilef, who installed monks at Durham. Powerful in worldly affairs and ready in fluent speech, he was very great [variant: most great, or in the highest degree] under King William Rufus; consequently, though admitted to the king’s circle of friends and set over England, he did not remain in favour. For, although no word or deed of the prince had been directed against him, he withdrew from friendship, involving himself in the treason of Odo of Bayeux and the others. Therefore, after the party was defeated, he was expelled from England; two years later he returned through the prince’s indulgence.

Having resumed his bishopric, he worked diligently to recover his former favour. Observing the king’s disposition, whichever way he thought the king inclined, he himself inclined the same way. Thus it happened that, in the storm which arose between Anselm and William, this man as standard-bearer stirred up the greatest disturbances against the archbishop, hoping, as they say, either to win the king’s favour or that he himself would become archbishop in Anselm’s place. But he failed everywhere. For, not long afterward, a disagreement arising between him and the king, he fell ill at Gloucester, where the court then was, and the bishop was ordered to appear to defend his cause. When the answer was made that illness kept him from coming, [Col. 1586A] “By the face of God, he is feigning it,” he said. Yet in truth he was seized by real sickness and nearing death.

When the bishops sitting with him suggested that he be buried in the church of Durham, which he himself had magnificently begun, he regained strength and breathed these words:

> “May it not please God that the reverence due to my lord Saint Cuthbert should be altered or diminished, for whose honour none of my predecessors was ever buried in the church. Put me instead in the chapter-house.”

Thus, after his death and conveyance to Durham, he has among the monks a fine monument to his industry: he gathered them together and adorned the church both with books and with other ornaments; moreover, he raised the prior of the place to this distinction, that throughout the bishopric he should be dean and steward.

[Col. 1586B] When Turgot, appointed prior by him, enforced this arrangement too strictly, he so embittered Ranulf, William’s successor, that, once Turgot had been transferred to the bishopric of Saint Andrews in Scotland, Ranulf thought that no other prior should be appointed.

This was Ranulf, once chaplain to King William, who, obscure in origin, speech, and cunning, rose to the highest rank and became administrator of the whole kingdom. Whenever a royal edict went forth ordering England to pay a stated tax, he doubled it. The king repeatedly laughed and said that he alone was a man who knew how to exercise his talent in this manner and did not care for others’ hatred, provided he pleased his lord. Relying on such arts, he obtained the bishopric of Durham.

He came to Durham and at first bore himself rather arrogantly, fearing to offend the saint, who is said to be an especially severe corrector of sinners. But after one or two offences had been committed without punishment, he went so far that, whenever a culprit fled to the saint’s church, he did not hesitate to drag him away—daring a crime unheard of in all preceding years.

[Col. 1586C] Yet by new buildings for the monks and by the translation of most blessed Cuthbert he gained some glory for his name. The lifting of the sacred body therefore enhanced his fame, because, once raised from the mausoleum, he made it visible to all who wished. Ralph, then abbot of Séez and later Archbishop of Canterbury, handled it with fortunate boldness and openly displayed it uncorrupted. For some had come to doubt whether the miracle once reported, of the body’s members remaining whole, still endured. He also displayed all the garments shining with fresh brightness; the chalice upon Cuthbert’s breast, whose upper part was of gold and lower part of onyx; his face so tightly wrapped in a cloth that it could not be uncovered by any effort of the abbot; the head of King and Martyr Oswald found between his arms; and the bones of the saints Bede and Ceolwulf—who had been a monk at Lindisfarne and a saint—found in separate linen bags.

[Col. 1586D] It was a great spectacle in the cemetery, beneath a clear sky with no thickness of clouds hanging overhead: all the monks dressed in ceremonial vestments, a long procession of those going and returning, and a great crowd pressing in, since it delights one to see again and again what has once been seen [variant: “again”].

But it seemed, as is thought, unworthy of the saint that he should thus be exposed as a spectacle; and an immense rainfall, unexpectedly arising, forced everyone into the church. Nor was the matter without miracle: despite so great a storm, the monks’ vestments were not merely undamaged but not even wet.

Hail, most holy bishop, for your power: a miracle altogether splendid and befitting your holiness. For not many days before, you had also displayed another. Everything was ready in the new church for the translation of the body: the choir of monks, the altar, and the tomb. They waited only for the timber supporting the newly made vault of the presbytery to be gently removed. But, most blessed one, you did not permit the holy desire of your people to be prolonged, [Col. 1588A] and in the dead of night you brought everything down. For who else was author of so great a deed? The prior ran up, roused by the sound, fearing for the altar and pavement, with less concern for the timbers; but you had preserved intact not only the things feared for, but also the timbers, just as they had been placed.

Rightly are you feared by your monks, so that no one guilty either of rebellion against the prior or of some grave sin in himself dares spend the night without confession. Therefore I shall beseech you that you may deign to remember me for good: I, who, whenever occasion offered, did not wish to omit your praise, however slight it might be—holy Lord and Father, deservedly beloved.

## PROLOGUE TO BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1587]

[Col. 1587B] The books are unequal in what they have to say, because an equal abundance of material for speaking does not flow to us everywhere. Certainly I am ready and willing to praise the saints of my native land; but knowledge and ability fail one who attempts it. For I cannot know all the saints: either those separated from us by regions most remote, or those of whose lives no accounts survive, through the negligence of writers, that we might have seen. Nor can barren talent and slender eloquence clothe with worthy titles of praise, or equal to the triumphs of their victories, even those whom the gift of God, the nearness of their lands, and some knowledge of letters has granted me to know.

Yet, as I consider this, faith comes to meet me, dispels the clouds of doubt, and brings confidence; since I know that good will alone in a human being, if perhaps hostile fortune begrudges its accomplishment, suffices for eternal reward. I should be lying if the angels had not announced peace to men of good will. Therefore, if nothing else is in me, let the devotion of a willing mind serve the saints; and, if it can, let the tongue of one speaking serve them—one whom they have often preserved until now and recently rescued, by a brilliant miracle, from a notable danger.

Accordingly, following the course I have begun, in this fourth book I shall survey the bishoprics of the Mercians, just as I formerly ranged through their kingdom in the fourth order. That kingdom was always, for its time, exceedingly extensive and therefore divided into several bishoprics, especially through the ambition of King Offa, who established an archbishopric at Lichfield, not guided by authority but by the inner core of all religion. Such an opening to the discourse therefore presents itself as I undertake my proposed course.

# BOOK FOUR: ON THE BISHOPS OF WORCESTER

[Col. 1587]

[Col. 1587C] The province of the Mercians now has five bishoprics, perhaps more in former times. And at Worcester these were bishops:

Bosel, Oftfor, Ecgwine, Wilfrith, Mildred, Weremund, Tilhere, Ethelred, Deneberht, Hereberht, Alwin, Hemferth, Ecelin [variant: Ethelin], Wilferth, Cynwold, Dunstan, Oswald, Aldulf, Wulfstan.

These were archbishops: Leofwine, Brihtheah [variant: Britegus], Living, and Ælfric.

Wulfstan was the most renowned in holiness in our age; and if the account of him should extend rather far, I ask that no one be wearied. Wulfstan was honourably educated from boyhood and grew up among disciplined men and with such attention to letters as England then possessed. When he reached the age for it, he received the priesthood and did not fall from the standard of moral character into vices.

For he did not, as some then and now do, chant mass hurriedly in the morning [Col. 1588C] and thereafter devote the entire day to gluttony or gain. Rather, with more serious care he completed the office due, added daily and prolonged prayers, and was content with the offerings of the faithful. By these he supported his life. After a virgin life, he offered heaven the unbroken seal of exceptional chastity.

While still in the world, he was considered greater than any monk. Abstaining from superfluous drink, he nevertheless indulged in eating meat; but as soon as he could seize an opportunity, he rejected it. The cause was that he had to attend a certain legal assembly on an appointed day, and the necessity of the business barred every excuse. Yet he decided that before singing mass he should provide against hunger. His attendants hurried him, lest their lord depart without breakfast; a goose was put on the fire. The priest stood at the altar and conducted the service with his customary devotion, when, during the secret prayers of the mass—because the church [Col. 1589A] stood near the house—the smell of roasting meat filled his nostrils.

The scent summoned his mind, so that he was caught by the enticement of pleasure. Immediately, recovering his mind and recognizing the fault, he struggled strongly to turn his thought elsewhere; but when that was in vain, angry with himself, he swore an oath upon the sacraments which he touched that he would never again under any circumstances eat that kind of food. When mass had been sung, he left without food for his business, saying that the now-late hour pressed him. That occasion brought it about that, following an arduous example completely, he abstained forever from every kind of flesh and even from richer food. Yet he did not look sternly down upon those who ate; he declared that he was held by no desire for such foods, though, if there were any delightful meat, he supposed that larks gave greater pleasure to those who ate them.

As his devotion to the monastic purpose increased, he became a monk at Worcester and rose through every office to the priorate. There, while he shone with the highest praise for his virtues, he experienced a temptation from the devil, who, I believe, envied his good qualities. One night, as he was praying before the altar, the devil attacked him in order to wrestle with him. Stronger than his assailant, he seized the challenger without fear and crushed him in the grim knots of his arms. He did the same a second and a third time, except that on the third occasion, sighing and with his inward parts growing hot, the adversary all but indicated by his struggle that he was exhausted; but merciful divinity came to his aid and drove away the raging monster. When it vanished into thin air, Wulstan understood that it had been the devil, though he had previously supposed it to be a certain servant whose appearance the devil had assumed. [Col. 1589C]

A sure indication of this, not a deceptive one, was given: whenever he happened to see that servant, he at once grew wholly pale, a tremor running through all his limbs. In all other matters he was free of fear, so that he declared that he did not know what terror was. He never dismounted from his horse because a bridge was broken; he walked safely on the highest parts of buildings over the narrowest beams. Thus it may rightly be said of him: “The righteous is as confident as a lion.”

Meanwhile, the occasion arose which I mentioned above: Archbishop Aldred, returning from Rome with cardinals immediately following him, was being pressed to consecrate a bishop for the city of Worcester. Having brought the matter under deliberation, and looking to his own future interests, he chose Wulstan, judging him to be ineffective—one under whose simplicity and holiness he could cloak his own plundering, taking from the possessions of the bishopric whatever he pleased. Wulstan, therefore, approved by the favor of the cardinals and examined with severity, received the divine gift; and a beautiful and venerable prophetic utterance befell him: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile!” Nothing could have been truer. For there was in him no counterfeit holiness, nor, on the other hand, any crafty deceit. Yet Aldred did not find him so sluggish as he had imagined. For Wulstan coaxed from him, by persuasion, the greater part of the possessions which he was unjustly retaining, pleading his own poverty as occasion demanded. Thus, relying more upon an innate love of virtue than upon learning, he exercised the office laid upon him, though weakened [or “in a state of frailty”]. [Col. 1589D]

Yet he was not so dull in letters as he was thought to be. He understood all other matters except poets’ fables and the twisted syllogisms of dialecticians—things which he neither knew nor considered worthy of knowing. Moreover, he was well taught how to make a speech, however elegant, extemporaneously; he knew the art of moving his hearers’ tears by setting before them the joys of heaven and the punishments of hell, and of persuading them of whatever point he wished, provided that his life matched his teaching and that he did not live otherwise than he taught others to live. Therefore God supplied him with eloquence, both for the increase of His praise and for the profit of his hearers.

As I said before, he abstained from food and drink, although in his household, according to English custom, drinking continued for whole hours after dinner. Sitting among them, he meditated upon the psalms, though he pretended to drink in his turn according to the prescribed order. The others drained foaming bowls; he, holding a very small cup, urged them toward cheerfulness, satisfying the custom of his country more than the judgment of his own mind. [Col. 1590A]

Nor did he omit Norman customs: he kept a display of soldiers about him, who consumed an enormous amount through annual stipends and daily provisions. Concerning his religious observances, we have received this account: every day, after singing Mass, he added the Psalter and the commemorations of all the saints whose individual feasts occur throughout the year; divided into seven portions, he did not omit them during the seven canonical hours. Whenever he was at Worcester, he diligently sang the principal Mass, saying that he thereby discharged the duty of the weekly officiant, from which he would not allow himself to be excused on account of being bishop. He also frequently attended the chapter meeting; going with the others into church, after confession had been made and the blessing given, he withdrew to the refectory.

Wherever he went on horseback, he recited the Psalter, repeatedly singing the prayer-verses which occurred to him, until his companion grew weary. Out of regard for no person—not even when he was at the royal court and sat at the king’s table—did he omit the blessings which the English pronounced over their drink. If necessity compelled him to attend the county court, he first invoked a curse upon unjust judges and a blessing upon upright ones. Then, sitting down, if something divine were being discussed, he directed the sharpness of his mind toward it attentively; if it was secular business, as more often happened, he fell asleep sluggishly from boredom. Yet anyone who thought something should be said against him would discover that he was not dull in replying. [Col. 1590B]

A priest named Ælfric, drawn to him by the fame of his religious life, came to him. From the shining example of this man Wulstan had drawn into himself a great fuel of holiness. For Ælfric devoted himself continually to prayer, even amid crowds, to the wonder of those who saw him: every day after Mass he recited the Psalter together with prayers no fewer in number. He was so sharp in rebuking that, if the bishop himself were at any time, as happens in conversation, somewhat too relaxed, he immediately either reproved him with words or struck him with his eyes.

For the bishop corrected the transgressions of his pupils from the right path, though he more often tolerated them as far as decency allowed. But he would in no way endure slackness in divine service. If any minister, overcome by drunkenness or sleepiness, were absent from Matins, he punished him with a sharp blow of the rod. Finally, he himself awakened the more respectable persons individually and sang Matins for them. [Col. 1590C]

He wore rather plain clothing indiscriminately, driving away the cold more with lambskins than with furs of another kind. If anyone told him that he ought at least to put on cat-skins, he answered with playful good humor: “Believe me”—for this manner of swearing had become habitual with the bishop—“I have never heard sung ‘Cat of God,’ but ‘Lamb of God’; therefore I wish to be warmed not by a cat but by a lamb.” Thus deeply had the fear of God taken possession of his mind: what others turned into display, he transformed into matter for compunction.

When the work on the greater church, which he himself had begun from the foundations, had advanced so far that the monks were now to move into it, orders were given that the old church, which Saint Oswald too had built, should be uncovered and demolished. Wulstan, standing in the open air to watch this sight, could not restrain his tears. [Col. 1591A] His household gently reproved him, saying that he ought rather to rejoice that, while he still lived, such honor had come to the church: the enlarged number of monks required more spacious dwellings. He replied: “I understand it very differently: we miserable men destroy the works of saints in order to win praise for ourselves. That age of blessed men did not know how to build ostentatious houses, but how, beneath whatever roof they had, to offer themselves to God and draw those subject to them by example. We, on the contrary, strive—neglecting the care of souls—to heap up stones.” He said much more in this manner, refuting the arguments advanced against his own reasoning.

Now the following account will show that he was not without miracles; for what has been said concerning his character will end at this point. [Col. 1591C] At the dedication of a certain church he delivered a sermon to the people, in which, among other matters, he spoke at length about peace. Moved by this, several persons who were divided by murderous hatred mutually forgave their offences. There was one man, however, whom no admonitions and no persuasions could bring to pardon the enemy who had killed his brother. This man having been brought forward, and after much discussion still refusing most obstinately, the bishop spoke these words which I shall report:

“The Lord said in the Gospel: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God’ (Matt. 5). It follows, therefore, that if peacemakers are blessed and sons of God, those who are at discord are wretched and sons of the devil. I therefore commend you to him whose son you are, and I hand you over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, in accordance with the Apostle’s command: ‘that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord’ (1 Cor. 5).” [Col. 1591D]

The saint had scarcely finished speaking when the wretched man, made a slave of the enemy, began before all the people to gnash his teeth, foam at the mouth, and toss his hair. Finally, flung to the ground, he rolled about in a frenzy. Wulstan was asked to have pity on him, but he delayed. At last, pressed and overcome by tears, he ordered the enemy to depart. The man went away, restored to his senses as easily as he had been possessed; but when urged to grant pardon for the offence, with astonishing folly he refused peace. He was therefore tormented again; and, ordered again to be healed, he persisted in his refusal. The third time, now wholly shaken in his limbs by the devil’s violence and almost breathing out his soul in full sobs, he made peace; thereafter, until death, he remained sound and unharmed.

[Col. 1592A] Under William the Elder, Lanfranc accused Wulstan of ignorance of letters; Thomas, Archbishop of York, alleged that he ought, by ancient right, to be subject to him. When he was ordered to answer both objections in council, he withdrew in order to prepare his answer with more exact deliberation. Then, while the monks with him were stunned in spirit by the gravity of the affair, he said: “Believe me, we have not yet sung None. Let us therefore sing it.” His companions replied that they should first dispatch the business for which they had come, since there would be more than enough time for the chants; and that the king and nobles, if they heard of it, would quite reasonably think themselves mocked. “First,” he said, “believe me, we shall perform God’s service; afterwards we shall deal with men’s lawsuit.”

When the hour had been sung, he went to enter the council chamber without devising any evasive falsehood or inventing any embellishment of truth. Though his people tried to hold him back, he could not be persuaded. Rather, when they feared for the case, he said confidently: “Know that I see here visibly the blessed archbishops Dunstan and Oswald, who today, defending me with their prayers, will blunt the sharpness of the false speakers.” [Col. 1592B]

Thus, having given his blessing to a monk of very little eloquence but somewhat acquainted with the Norman language, he prevailed. He who had previously been thought unworthy to govern the diocese was humbly begged by the Archbishop of York to deign to visit York’s own territories—where that archbishop himself had feared to go because of enemies or because he did not know the language. Nor was this all: he recovered all but one of the remaining estates of the bishopric which Archbishop Aldred had retained, while Archbishop Lanfranc steadfastly supported his cause, pressing, of course, the rival of his primacy and power. [Col. 1592C]

Under William the Younger, Earl Roger of Montgomery, plotting treachery against the prince, took up arms in hostility with accomplices of the same faction. Having devastated everything from Shrewsbury as far as the settlement of Worcester, he was already approaching the city itself when the royal soldiers stationed in advance reported the danger to the bishop. Wulstan hurled the thunderbolt of a curse against the traitors who had not kept faith with their lord, and ordered the soldiers to hurry to avenge the wrongs done to God and the Church.

What I shall relate might seem wonderful; yet the authority of truthful narrators must be believed. Some of the enemy, struck by cowardly fear at the sight of the royal forces; others even blinded, yielded a complete victory—one which the townsmen could not have hoped for. For many were put to flight by a few; some were slain and others carried off wounded. [Col. 1592D]

Nor was he without prophecy. A certain Aldwin had become a monk through him, and in that very extensive wood called Malvern was pursuing an eremitical life with his companion Guy. After long struggles, Guy thought there was a shorter path to glory: that he should go to Jerusalem, where, through the toil of travel, he might either see the Lord’s sepulchre or happily anticipate death by the hand of the Saracens. Aldwin was persuaded to the same view, but sought counsel from his father Wulstan. The bishop dissuaded him, cooling his ardor: “Please, Aldwin, do not go anywhere, but remain in this place. Believe me: if you knew what I know, you would wonder how much God will work through you in that place.”

Hearing this, the monk departed, now firm in his purpose, and the hope of the prophecy lightened every sort of hardship. Not long afterward the prophecy hastened to fulfilment: men came to Aldwin: a second after the first, a third after the second, and so on until they numbered thirty. At first provisions flowed abundantly to them, the neighbors considering themselves blessed if they could bestow anything upon God’s servants. What they lacked they supplied by faith, thinking little of the absence of bodily food because they were fattened on spiritual joy. [Col. 1593A]

A merchant named Sewlf had been accustomed to come to Wulstan every year, in order to heal the diseases of his soul by his counsel. Once, after he had received absolution, Wulstan said to him: “You often repeat the sins which you have confessed, because, as the saying goes, ‘Opportunity makes the thief.’ Therefore I advise you to become a monk; if you do so, you will lack the opportunity for these sins.” The man replied that, owing to the strictness of the calling, he could not become a monk. The bishop, somewhat angered, said: “Go; you will become a monk whether you wish it or not, but only when the instruments of vice have grown old within you.”

We ourselves later saw this fulfilled, because in our monastery, broken by old age and admonished by illness, he converted. Yet although he often repented, whenever anyone brought the bishop’s saying to his mind, he checked his impulse and softened his resolve. [Col. 1593B]

Nicholas, his special pupil, who afterward became prior of the Church of Worcester, was sitting at his feet. The bishop, meanwhile, overflowing with cheerfulness, gently stroked the young man’s head; his hair was falling out, a reproach approaching baldness. “And I think,” he said, “you will become bald.” But the youth, distressed that already in adolescence he was growing old in that respect, complained of the fate of his falling hair: “Why,” he asked, “do you not keep it?” The bishop, smiling, replied: “Believe me, as long as I live, the hairs that remain to me will never fail.”

What he said came to pass. But in the same week in which he renounced this life, they all vanished, I know not where, leaving his scalp bare. He often made his own death known by signs not obscure, but here more clearly. When word was brought him of the death of his sister, his only sister, he replied: “Now the plough has reached my furrow; brother will follow sister, not many days hence.” [Col. 1593C]

He therefore took to his bed with fevers, being now half a year from his death, and prepared himself for entry into heavenly life. He bore his suffering nobly and consoled his own people, weeping before him and fearing the tyranny of the future bishop: “Let groaning cease; let tears be idle. This is not a loss of life but an exchange of life. Nor shall I ever fail you; rather, the more present I am to God when this muddy framework is dissolved, the more swift I shall be in helping you. By my intercession prosperity will come to you; by my driving it back adversity will depart from you.”

Happy tongue, which dared to pour such confident words into human ears from the overflowing storehouse of conscience. Others use sighs and sobs to obtain prayers for themselves; he promised that he would pray for others. What miracle is this? Was he conscious of no sin? No indeed: holy simplicity was speaking, a simplicity ignorant of despairing of God’s mercy. [Col. 1593D]

Thus he was taken away amid the great lamentation of laypeople and monks present, and carried into the church, where he remained above ground for three days. For the very appearance and form of his lifeless body seemed to display the grace of the living bishop, soothing the eyes and easing grief. The body lay in state before the altar, adorned with pontifical insignia and without a covering; people streamed in from every direction, offered gifts, venerated the body, and departed sorrowfully.

On the fourth day he was committed to the earth by Robert, Bishop of Hereford, who had long been joined to him in holy friendship. He lies between two pyramids, with a stone arch beautifully vaulted over them. From the upper part projects a piece of timber, fitted with iron latticework called “spiders.” I have mentioned this because it is connected with the subject of the miracle which follows. [Col. 1594A]

Not many years after his death, a fire arising through carelessness in the city utterly consumed the roof of the church. The lead melted; the boards, while the fire raged, were turned into charcoal; beams as huge as whole trees, burned through, fell to the ground. Whatever could escape the fire within the church was shattered and cracked by the collapse of so great a mass.

“Yet amid this, the saint’s tomb was not merely untouched by the fury of the flames: it was neither stained with soot nor covered with ash. And, to increase the miracle, the mat on which people customarily reclined in prayer before the mausoleum was found unharmed. The timber which I said projected above was found intact so far as it stood outside the stones; but the stone which had enclosed it had itself been reduced to ashes.” [Col. 1594B]
