This was not his first miracle, but it was more celebrated than others because it was public. For who could enumerate those daily miracles which people experience in private necessities, when no one who approaches his tomb with faith departs without obtaining what he asked for? Such things exceed the power of the most eloquent speech: they can neither be counted nor recorded in writing. And indeed, if the receptive disposition of ancient people had aided him, the saint would long ago have been raised on high and publicly proclaimed. But the unbelief of our people, which adorns itself under the guise of caution, refuses to put faith in miracles, though it sees with its eye and touches with its finger. I feared that I should be guilty of silence if I consigned to silence matters known from reliable authorities and deprived diligent readers of knowledge. For whom should I take upon myself to write, if the indolent may read neither for love of the saint nor for our sake—those who disdain the holy Gospels? [Col. 1594C]

Samson, a canon of Bayeux, succeeded Wulstan: a man of no small learning and not contemptible eloquence; a man of old-fashioned habits, himself eating generously and giving liberally to others. He was harmless toward the monks, except that he took from them Westbury, where Wulstan had placed monks and fortified them with the privilege of his holiness. Samson broke that arrangement, and not many years later died in the same village where he had committed the offence.

After Samson’s death, he who had received the bishopric as a gift from William the Younger was succeeded in the same see, by King Henry, by Theulf of Bayeux, likewise a canon. In character he was not unlike his predecessor, and he died while the same king still reigned. Both were buried in the nave of the church before the crucifix. [Col. 1594D]

The bishopric was then granted by the king to Simon, chaplain of Queen Adeliza, whom Henry had married after the death of his former wife. Simon, therefore, was distinguished for affability, gentleness of character, and generosity—as far as the limited resources of the bishopric permitted.

After him succeeded Alfred, chaplain of King Henry the Younger. The diocese of Worcester comprises the districts of Gloucester, Worcester, and half of Warwickshire. Gloucester is a city situated on the River Severn, and is thought to have been named from Claudius, the second Roman emperor after Julius Caesar to enter Britain. In British it was called Airchalu. Seneca too mentions, in his book *On the Death of Claudius*, that “the barbarians in Britain worship him as a god and build a city in his honor.” From that city the whole region is called the Vale of Gloucester. [Col. 1595A]

The whole land is rich in grain and fertile in fruits—here through nature’s favor alone, there through the skill of cultivation—so that, although indolence makes labor seem tiresome, it invites one toward its attractions, where abundance will repay one with a hundredfold return. You may see public roads clothed in fruit trees, not planted by the industrious hand, but growing by the nature of the soil itself. The earth of its own accord rises into fruit, and produces fruits far surpassing others in taste and appearance. Many do not know decay before the year has passed, so that all provide their service until their new successors arrive.

The region is denser than other English provinces in the abundance of vineyards, richer in yield, and more pleasing in flavor. Its wines do not twist drinkers’ mouths with grim harshness, for in sweetness they yield little to French wines. There are innumerable estates, distinguished abbeys, and populous villages. To the glory of them all is added the River Severn, than which no riverbed in this land is broader, no current more rapacious, no river more abundantly supplied with fish through skill. [Col. 1595B]

In it there is a daily fury of waters—whether I should call it a gulf or a whirlpool of waves I do not know—which sweeps sand from the deepest bottom and heaps it into a mass as it comes with force. It extends no farther than the bridge, though sometimes it even overflows the banks and, having encompassed a great portion of land by violence, returns victorious. Woe to any ship it strikes on the side! Experienced sailors, when they see it coming—they call it in English the *Digram*—turn their ship toward it and, cutting through its middle, break its violence.

In the same vale is a very famous town named Bristol, possessing a harbor that receives ships coming from Ireland, Norway, and other lands beyond the sea, lest this region, fortunate in its native riches, should be deprived of commerce in foreign wealth.

## Concerning Monasteries

[Col. 1595]

[Col. 1595C] In the city of Gloucester itself, then, is the monastery of Saint Peter, which, as I have more than once said, Archbishop Aldred began there. Abbot Serlo, having received a small grant from King William the Elder, found only a few monks there—not more than three. But who could adequately explain in fitting eloquence how greatly the grace of God, working in harmony with his industry, raised up the place?

The moderation of Gloucester’s religious observance is well known: the weak can undertake it [alternative: “can admire it”], and the strong cannot despise it. Serlo brought them this guiding principle: “Nothing in excess.” Yet, humble as he was toward the good, he was threatening and formidable toward the proud.

The canons of Saint Oswald rage against him because Archbishop Thomas gave the monks lands which ought to serve their church. For in the same city, in the time of King Alfred, his daughter Æthelflæd and her husband Æthelred had built a monastery, sparing no expense and lacking no provisions. They had transferred there from Bardney the relics of King Oswald, to whom all Mercia had obeyed. [Col. 1595D] That monastery flourished until the time of the Danes and was joined in the closest kinship with ours—that is, Malmesbury—as is found in the archives of both churches.

But when the monks had been scattered by hostile force, and the Archbishop of York had obtained that monastery through the opportunity afforded by the bishopric of Worcester, he admitted canons there. Archbishop Thurstan displayed especial care there, both in restoring the shrine of the saint and in enlarging the church. When the old foundations had been removed and new ones were being laid, the tombs of both spouses were found in the south porch, together with bodies showing signs of their ancient veneration. [Col. 1596C]

I have said more about the most blessed Oswald in the book *Deeds of the Kings*, declaring that I was uncertain whether his arms were preserved at Bamburgh, as I remembered Bede to have said. Nevertheless, when I come to the proper place, I shall not keep silent concerning what further knowledge of these matters has afterward come to me.

In the same district is Winchcombe monastery, which King Cenwulf of the Mercians built with immense munificence, incredible in our own times. He had the church dedicated by thirteen bishops, the chief among them Wilfrid, Archbishop of Canterbury. In the splendor of that dedication, in an assembly of ten dukes, he freed at the altar the king of Kent, whom he had recently captured as a prisoner by right of war. Besides the gifts received by the great men—beyond estimation in number and value—he gave a pound of silver to all who possessed no land, a mark of gold to priests, one solidus to monks, and many further gifts to the entire people. [Col. 1596D]

This monastery, as all mortal things always decline in their course, stood in the time of King Edgar almost in name alone; through the blessed Archbishop Oswald it was somewhat revived. Germanus was made abbot there; Oswald had brought him with him from Fleury, and he was of great assistance both to religious life and to the restoration of the church.

There rests Father Cenwulf with his son Cenhelm, whom his father had left, at seven years old, to be brought up by his sister Cwoenthryth. But she, falsely promising the kingdom to her own greed, entrusted her little brother’s removal to a retainer who was his tutor. He led the innocent boy out as though hunting, murdered him among the thickets, and concealed him.

“And, wonderful to relate, a crime committed so secretly in England was divinely made known at Rome. A parchment, borne down from above by a dove, fell upon the altar of Saint Peter and indicated in order the place of the murder and burial. Because it was written in English characters, Romans and men of other peoples who were present tried in vain to read it. But an Englishman came forward providentially and at the right moment; unfolding the covering of its language into Latin, he caused the letter of the Apostolic See to inform the English kings of their compatriot martyr. [Col. 1597A]

“Accordingly, amid a great gathering, the boy’s washed body was carried to Winchcombe. As the clerics sang aloud and the laypeople applauded joyfully, the parricidal woman, moved by this, put her head out of the window of the upper chamber in which she stood, and happened to be singing the psalm, ‘O God, my praise’ [Ps. 108/109]. By some trick, beginning from an unknown point near its end and singing backward, she tried to weaken the singers’ joy. Then, by divine power, the eyes of the sorceress were torn from their hollow sockets, and the blood defiled the verse: ‘This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord, and who speak evil against my soul’ [ibid.]. To this day, traces of the blood remain, breathing forth the woman’s monstrous wickedness and God’s vengeance.” [Col. 1597B]

There is also the monastery of Tewkesbury, which Robert, son of Hamo, has recently advanced through his patronage, raising it to a degree not easily recorded. There the beauty of the buildings and the charity of the monks toward visitors seize the eyes and attract the mind. Originally it had been at Cranborne; but through the foresight of Abbot Gerald, because of the convenience of the neighboring river and the adjoining demesne lands, Tewkesbury seemed a more suitable site.

At the same time, the name seemed to favor a religious intention, because Tewkesbury is called as it were *Theotocosbiria*, that is, “the dwelling of the Mother of God,” a word composed from Greek and English. In our times Malvern monastery has also grown in the same province; it seems to me to have received its name by antiphrasis. For religious life does not flourish badly there, but well and most beautifully: I recall this in hope of immortality, while scarcity of earthly things draws and animates the monks. [Col. 1597C]

The Worcester province also possesses the abbeys of Evesham and Pershore. Evesham was founded by the blessed Bishop Ecgwine. I have not yet been able, either by myself to discover or from others to learn, what miracle it was that Bede omitted—especially since Ecgwine went to Rome with King Cenred of Mercia and King Offa of the East Angles, whose journey the historian did not pass over in silence. Yet whatever caused this silence, it is established that Ecgwine was the third bishop of Worcester. He especially loved the place where the monastery is now seen, formerly uncultivated and bristling with thornbushes, though possessing from ancient times a small church, perhaps the work of Britons. [Col. 1597D]

In that place, while the most holy man kept vigils frequently, invited by the solitude, he deserved to be comforted by a vision and address of the Mother of God, who plainly and without ambiguity commanded him to establish there a monastery that would be pleasing to her and laborious for him. He set himself to the commands, completed the work, and strengthened it with apostolic and royal privileges.

“What then? Is the traditional account to be believed? Once conscious of youthful sins, he bound his feet in fetters, threw the keys of the fetters into a river, and publicly declared that only when the fetters should be opened either by divine power or by the very keys would he at last be secure concerning his sins. Thus he set out for Rome and returned safely. Then, while he was sailing upon that sea by which England is crossed by ship from the Gallic mainland, a monstrous fish leapt into the stern in which the bishop was riding and was held fast despite the sailors’ competing efforts. In the liver of the fish, once it had been cut open, the key was found; applied to the lock of the fetters, it released the saint and gave him the fullest assurance of safety.” [Col. 1598A]

He is indeed a most renowned father and ready to grant petitions, if the faith of those who ask does not waver.

“You too shall fill a part of this little page with your praise—you who honor the same monastery: Felix, boy, son of Wulstan, son of Wymund, son of Wiglaf, king of the Mercians, and of Æthelflæd, daughter of Ceolwulf, who was Cenhelm’s paternal uncle. You, I say, I shall not pass over—whom your kinsman Berferth wickedly killed. Let posterity, if anyone considers these writings worth knowing, know this: nothing in the world was more glorious than your natural character, which enraged your murderer and gave you over to death; nothing in God was more innocent than your purity, by which the inward Judge, moved to favor, glorified you. For a pillar sent down from heaven, bright with light and piercing the veils of thick night, disclosed the crime in the deep pit and exposed the executioner’s wickedness.” [Col. 1598B]

Accordingly, his venerable relics were raised up by his parents’ devotion and placed at Repton, then a famous monastery. It is now an estate of the Earl of Chester, its glory worn away by the passage of time. Now, as I have said, you dwell at Evesham, worthy to grant graciously the vows of those who seek your favor.

Æthelweard, ealdorman of Dorset, founded and completed the monastery of Pershore in the time of King Edgar. His spirit was by no means sparing, but poured itself out in the zeal of generosity. Yet it too, like the others, has suffered a lamentable loss, diminished by more than half. Ambition seized one portion of its riches, forgetfulness buried another, and Kings Edward and William bestowed the larger share upon Westminster. Some bones of blessed Eadburh are kept here and are honored with persistent reverence, because there she has been granted a more frequent glory of miracles than elsewhere. [Col. 1598C]

## Concerning the Bishops of Hereford

[Col. 1599]

[Col. 1599A] Across the Severn, almost bordering on the Welsh, lies the city of Hereford. It is not large, yet the ruins of its steep ditches show that it was once something great. From the beginning its bishops were these: Putta, Tyrhtel, Torhtheah, Walstod, and Cuthbert, afterwards Archbishop of Canterbury. I have described Cuthbert’s outstanding diligence in ecclesiastical matters when the discussion concerned the archbishops. But these verses, recently seen by me, will indicate both how greatly he honored the antiquity of his predecessors and how he completed by his own zeal anything which they had begun for the adornment of God’s house:

> This venerable cross of Christ, venerable and consecrated,  
> the venerable bishop Walstod had begun  
> to fashion with great ornaments of silver and gold.  
>
> But because all mortal things fall at their appointed time,  
> he died in the midst of the work and departed from the flesh.  
>
> But I, successor of the aforesaid bishop,  
> who, by God’s gift, perform the office of bishop,  
> and who bear the sure name Cuthbert, called from the light,  
> completed in fitting order what he had beautifully begun.

Likewise, upon the tomb of the predecessors:

> This marble, casting its shade, contains the bodies  
> of six men who were once famous and exalted throughout the world.  
> The tomb now made with wondrous beauty  
> encloses them above, covered by its lofty summit.  
>
> I, Cuthbert, successor to their sacred honor,  
> enclosed them with inscriptions and adorned their tombs.  
> The holy mitre crowned three of them as bishops:  
> their names are Walstod, Torhere, and Tyrhtel.  
>
> The fourth is the petty king Milfrith, with his beautiful wife  
> Cwenburh; she stood fifth in the sequence from the elder.  
> The sixth besides is Offrith, son of Oselin.

After Cuthbert came Podda, Ecca, Cedda, Æthelberht, Esne [alternative: Elne], Ceolmund, Utel, Wulfheard, Benna, Eadwulf, Cutwulf, Mucel [alternative: Mutel], Deorlaf, Cuemund, Edgar, Tidhelm, Wulfhelm, Ælfric, Æthelwulf, Æthelstan, and Leofgar. In the time of King Edward, Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, after burning the city, drove Leofgar from both see and life. [Col. 1599B]

Walter succeeded him. Consecrated at Rome by Pope Nicholas, he survived until the fifth year of King William; he died with an unseemly end, if report does not lie. There was in the town a little woman whom he saw, through some mischance, when she happened to pass him, and for whom he burned for a long time. She did not know the bishop’s flames, and, if she had known them, would have despised them. Meanwhile the bishop often reflected that nothing was more wretched than an old man in love, and struggled, out of respect for his age and rank, to drive away the disease. [Col. 1599C]

He had recovered well, and the defeated madness had retreated, when, on an occasion supplied by the devil’s deceit, he summoned her into his chamber. A pretext was put forward [alternative: “there was a pretext”]: that she might cut garments for the chamberlains, for she was said to be skilled in this work. Once she had entered and was intent upon the work for which she had come, his attendants, aware of his secret intentions, departed in a body. Then, not to delay with many words: as the bishop, after obscene speech, was preparing to use force, the woman wounded his groin with the shears which she held.

The report of the crime and the retaliation spread throughout all England and reached even the king’s ears. He, concealing his belief out of royal dignity lest others spread the story further, suppressed it by a most severe edict. [Col. 1599D]

[Col. 1600A] Not long afterwards Robert the Lorrainer received that see. There he built a church on a circular plan, modelling its proportions upon the basilica at Aachen. He was most skilled in all the liberal arts, especially in the abacus; he investigated the lunar computation and the course of the heavenly stars. At that time the monk Marianus [variant: Marinianus] was living enclosed at Mainz. In the long leisure of his solitude, having examined chronographers, he was the first—or perhaps the only one—to observe that the discrepancy in Dionysius’ cycles ran contrary to Gospel truth. Therefore, reckoning every year from the beginning of the age, he added the twenty-two years missing from the cycle and began to compose a great and very extensive chronicle. Robert, greatly admiring that book, took extraordinary pains to have it brought into England. Indeed, captivated by Marianus’ genius, he excerpted and condensed whatever the latter had said at greater length. [Col. 1600B] He did so so brilliantly that the abridgment appears more valuable than the vast diffusion of that enormous volume.

Above all his contemporary bishops, he devoted himself to the friendship of the most holy Wulstan, whom he also touched by the proximity of their episcopal sees. Therefore, very often putting aside public business, he kept him close domestic company, delighted by the purity and innocence of his life. Although he exalted him above himself, his death, though delayed, did not break the bond of their affectionate companionship. Wulstan lay ill at Worcester, now close to his blessed end. Robert was reluctantly attending to royal pleas at court when Wulstan stood before him in a vision and said with complete intelligibility: “If you wish to see me alive, hurry to come [Col. 1600C] to Worcester before I die.”

When he had seen this vision and obtained leave from the king, he hurried eagerly to come, allowing himself no rest by day or night. For a devout fear had instilled a presentiment—which the event confirmed—that he would not find him alive. The court was, indeed, rather far away. And already, when lodging near Worcester and given over to sleep, he again saw Wulstan saying:

“You have done nothing less than devout affection requires; but you have been disappointed in your desire. For I have now departed. But you, my friend and companion, look to your life; provide for your salvation, because you will not remain long after me in this light. And lest you think yourself deceived by a phantom vision, receive this sign: after you have tomorrow committed to the earth the body which has now awaited your arrival for three days, [Col. 1600D] there will be given to you a gift from me, which you will recognize as mine.”

Thus the bishop, awakening, completed his journey, came to Worcester, and performed the burial office, recounting everything. Then, having taken leave of the monks, he was considering departure; his horse awaited him as he put on his spurs, when the prior of the place reverently fell at his knees and offered him a gift, saying: “Receive, my lord, if it please you, the cloak lined with lambskins of your friend, in which he was accustomed to ride. May it bear witness both to your long affection and to your deserving the protection of our lord through his holiness.”

On hearing this and recognizing the gift, he grew pale, and an icy shudder ran through his bones. Immediately [Col. 1601A] postponing his departure, he summoned the assembly of monks to the chapter-house and, with tears and sighs befitting the matter, related how exactly the dream and the event corresponded. So, having commended all to his care at his death, he departed, glad indeed at the warning but always troubled by holy fear. In the middle of January Wulstan died, and Robert did not outlast June.

His successor, Gerard, was translated to York.

A certain Roger Lardarius was ordered by the king to be appointed in his place. But, having received no episcopal office, he died within eight days of his election at London, where the court then was. Beforehand he had enjoined upon Archbishop Anselm—good God, what astonishing folly!—that [Col. 1601B] he should consecrate him bishop before he died; and although he demanded this anxiously and most insistently, the holy prelate refuted the man’s foolishness, without giving any answer, merely by the restraint of his laughter.

Then Rainald, the queen’s chancellor, was immediately elected to hold the dead man’s place. According to the custom which the king at that time considered lawful, he was invested by the prince with ring and staff. But when the archbishop refused to bless him and the others thus invested, he understood that he had acted wrongly and, of his own accord—neither asked nor commanded—returned the ring and staff to the king. For this reason, banished from royal favour, he was ordered also to be excluded from court. He bore this silently and patiently, until a gentler breeze calmed the royal heart and he was lawfully [Col. 1601C] admitted and honourably consecrated.

He remained in the bishopric with great humility, distinguished both by other virtues and by compunction born of the fear of God; everywhere, but especially during the celebration of Mass, he was drenched in tears. No reputation for any evil attached to him, except that he was said to be less generous than befitted him and than his means allowed.

After a few years he died of gout. Geoffrey, surnamed de Diva, succeeded him for no more than five years, confirming the now widely repeated misfortune that no bishop at Hereford survives long. He too was good and very self-controlled, using food and clothing of no greater cost than the cheaper kind. Devoted to agriculture, [Col. 1602A] he restored and improved the lands of the bishopric, which had previously suffered severely from exactions of revenue. Consequently, though well supplied with grain and the other things that furnish sustenance, he was rather hard-hearted toward the poor. He therefore justly exposed his reputation to reproach, because, moved by no pity for the needy, he left a great store of provisions to no heir.

King Henry therefore gave the bishopric to Richard, clerk of the seal, who survived only a few years.

At last, under a good omen—if God so wills—Robert, prior of the canons of Lantony, was elected and made bishop. He survives to this day; posterity will judge his deeds. At present fame has plainly [Col. 1602B] prepared a kindly path for him: he is said to be exceedingly religious and abstemious in food and dress. He is so well known to the Apostolic See that, after the legate and the archbishop, it entrusts all its arrangements in England to him.

King and martyr Ethelbert, born among and ruler of the East Angles, adorns the episcopal see with his relics. Offa, king of the Mercians, killed him, without any causes being evident, for the confirmation—as he thought—and advancement of his kingdom, having wickedly plotted the deed under the pretext that he was a suitor for his daughter. Immediately after his death he invaded the East Anglian kingdom, transmitting the inheritance of that invasion to his successors. But Ethelbert’s death was avenged, it is believed, by the guiltless death of Offa not long afterwards and by the brief reign of Offa’s son. Moreover, God made his holiness known to the citizens by signs so evident [Col. 1602C] that a bishopric of such dignity is consecrated in his name. He is therefore a martyr, believed to be so not on human reasoning but through divine miracles. Nor should it seem foolish or incongruous that our predecessors—especially upright and religious men—either endured this in silence or confirmed it by their authority. For would not blessed Dunstan, to omit others, into whom literary learning and the grace of God had poured themselves in full measure, have prevented Kenelm, Ethelbert, or Wulstan from being honoured as martyrs, unless he knew that this was pleasing among the citizens of heaven? Let mortal judgment therefore yield where God’s favour is shown through miracles.

## ON MONASTERIES

[Col. 1601]

[Col. 1601D] In the diocese of this bishopric are two monasteries: at Shrewsbury and Wenlock. The monastery of the Shrewsbury monks is recent, founded by Roger, earl of Montgomery. There he installed monks from Sées, strict in food and clothing, but men who count these hardships as little, with joyful hearts, in hope of their future reward.

At Wenlock there was a very ancient habitation of nuns. There the most blessed Milburga, sister of St Mildred [variant: Mildrith], niece through a son of Penda, king of the Mercians, lived and is buried. But the aforesaid earl filled the place, which was utterly deserted, with Cluniac monks, where now beautiful shoots of virtues strive [Col. 1602D] toward heaven. Indeed, the virgin’s tomb was unknown to the new arrivals, since all memorials of antiquity had been destroyed by the violence of enemies and of time:

> “But recently, while the fabric of the new church was being begun, a certain boy ran rather hastily across the pavement; breaking open the hollow of the tomb, he openly revealed the virgin’s body. Then, as a breath of balsamic fragrance wafted through the church and rose high, it produced so many miracles that waves of people flocked there in crowds. The open plain could scarcely contain the throngs, while rich and poor alike pressed together shoulder to shoulder, faith impelling all indiscriminately. Nor was the outcome without effect, [Col. 1603A] for no one departed thence without illness being removed or alleviated; indeed, the royal disease, utterly incurable to physicians, left some people through the virgin’s merits.”

## ON THE BISHOPS OF LICHFIELD AND CHESTER

[Col. 1603]

[Col. 1603A] Lichfield is a small town in the district of Stafford, far from the bustle of cities. The surrounding region is wooded; a little stream flows beside it; the church stood in a confined site, displaying the moderation and austerity of ancient men. It is a place shameful to the bishops of our age, a place in which episcopal dignity ought to lodge. There, as was said above, the most holy Chad both sat and died.

For, apart from the two Mercian bishoprics which I have enumerated above, the whole remaining province of the Mercians and Lindisfaras had, in the first years of Christianity, one bishop, each succeeding the previous one. Their names are these: Diuma and Ceollach, both from Scotland; after these, Dumhere, an Englishman by nation; Jaruman; and Chad, whose see was, as has often been said, at Lichfield. [Col. 1603B] Archbishop Theodore appointed Wilfrid in Chad’s place; Wilfrid had been his predecessor’s deacon. Theodore appointed Sexwulf after him.

Two bishops succeeded Sexwulf: Headda at Lichfield and Wilfrid at Leicester. When Wilfrid was driven out by hostile force, Headda held both dioceses, and Aldwin succeeded him. Upon Aldwin’s death, three [Col. 1604A] bishops were made in that diocese: Wita at Lichfield, Totta at Leicester, and Eadheard at Dorchester.

These were the bishops of Lichfield: after Wita, Hemel, Guthfrith, Berthun, Aldwulf, who received the pallium in the time of King Offa; Herewine, Herewald, Humbert, Cyneberht, Tumfrith, Ælle in the time of King Athelstan; Ælfgār, Cynsige, Winsige, Ælfwēah, Godwine, Leofgar, Brihtmær, Wulfsy, Leofwine. Peter, in the time of King William the Elder, abandoned Lichfield and moved to Chester, which is twenty-five miles from that place. Chester is called the City of the Legions because discharged soldiers of the military legions settled there. It borders the North Britons. The region is poor and barren in grain, especially wheat, as are most northern regions, but rich in livestock and fish. [Col. 1604B] Its inhabitants consider milk and butter luxuries; those who are wealthier live on meat, while they value barley bread and rye as a great thing. Goods are sent from Chester to Ireland, and necessities are brought back into the city, so that what the nature of the soil has in lesser measure, the labour of merchants may supply.

## ON MONASTERIES

[Col. 1603]

[Col. 1603B] From ancient times there was in the city a monastery of nuns, now filled with monks by Hugh, earl of Chester. There is celebrated the virgin Werburga, daughter of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, and of Ermenhild, daughter of Sexburga, who was daughter of Anna, king of the East [Col. 1603C] Angles, and wife of Eorconbert, king of Kent.

> “Werburga, having professed celibacy, shone with excellent virtues in that city through a very long course of years. I shall relate one miracle of hers, which earned fame and remembrance among the inhabitants through its renown. She had an estate outside the walls, whose crops were being devoured by wild geese. The steward, whose office required him to drive them off with every care, made little progress. Therefore, while attending his mistress, he included a complaint about this matter among the other tales of the day. ‘Go,’ she said, ‘and shut them all up in the house.’ Astonished at the novelty of the command, the rustic thought his lady was joking; but she gave the order firmly and seriously. Returning to the cornfield, where he first caught sight of those previously mentioned offenders, he cried aloud that they should follow him at their mistress’s command. Then all, moving in a flock with bowed necks, followed their mistress and were enclosed under a roof. The peasant took one of them for supper, presuming that he had no accuser to fear. At dawn the virgin came; rebuking the birds for their plundering of another’s goods, she ordered them to take flight. Nor did the birds lack understanding, knowing that they were not whole: circling around their mistress’s feet and going nowhere, they sought, by the complaint they could make, to awaken the virgin’s pity. Understanding through God’s revelation that such a complaint from the birds was not without cause, she carefully questioned the steward and discovered the theft. [Col. 1604B] She ordered the bones to be gathered. Without delay, at the healing sign of the virgin’s hand, skin and flesh were drawn over the bones; the skin began to grow feathers, until the bird was restored to life. First with a lively leap, then in flight, it poised itself in the air. The others followed without hesitation, their number now complete, [Col. 1604C] after first rendering the homage of reverence to their liberator.”

The merits of this virgin are celebrated at Chester and her miracles exalted. Though she is unfailingly favourable to the petition of everyone, she most especially brings swift and immediate aid to the prayers of women and children.

In that same city, as I have said, Bishop Peter established his seat in the church of St Peter, having installed a few canons.

But his successor Robert again moved the see to Coventry. In the diocese of Chester there was at Coventry a monastery built by the most magnificent Earl Leofric and his wife Godiva, with so great a display of gold and silver that the very church walls seemed too narrow to contain the treasures, a marvel to visitors’ eyes. Coveting this, Robert seized the church’s treasures themselves in such a way as to evade the king’s demands and to elude Roman greed. From one beam alone he scraped together five hundred marks of silver; it supported chests. Having remained there many years, he displayed no integrity toward the place. Thus he never removed the danger from roofs threatening collapse; thus, by squandering sacred riches, he incurred the crime of embezzlement and would have been liable to an action for extortion [variant: *repetundarum*] had an accuser been ready. Feeding the monks on miserable provisions, he took no care to kindle in them love of the regular order [Col. 1605A] and allowed them to aspire only to elementary learning, lest either an abundance of food make them self-indulgent or the strictness of the rule and vigour of learning make them proud against him. Content, then, with rustic fare and rudimentary learning, they thought it enough if they could merely live in peace.

Indeed, when dying, he ordered that he should be buried not at Chester but at Coventry, leaving his successors, in his view, not an unjust right to challenge this but what seemed a lawful right to claim it.

Another Robert, surnamed Peccam, succeeded him, raised from Henry’s chapel to the bishopric. He lived only a few years and was buried in the same place, having diligently imitated the footsteps of his predecessor as long as he lived.

Now Roger is bishop there, through the gift of the same king; he is the nephew of a certain Geoffrey de Clinton, once a name of great [Col. 1605B] importance in England. At Coventry is kept an arm of the great Augustine, enclosed in a silver reliquary. [Col. 1606A] The following words are seen engraved upon it: “This arm of St Augustine was bought at Pavia by Archbishop Æthelnoth, returning from Rome, for one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.”

There Bishop Robert lies, not wholly infamous in every respect; for he is called pleasant and generous, and he proved the initiator of great building works at Lichfield. In the two porticoes at Coventry lie the most eminent married founders of the place, of whom the woman is especially celebrated. While living, she had amassed there all its treasures, and when close to death she ordered a circlet of jewels, which she had sewn upon a thread so that, beginning individual prayers at the touch of each one, she might not omit their number, to be hung round the neck of the image of St Mary. But how precious do you think the jewels were? [Col. 1606B] Those who know estimate them at one hundred marks of silver.

## ON THE BISHOPS OF LEICESTER

[Col. 1605]

[Col. 1605B] Leicester is an ancient city in the interior of England, so called from the River Leire which flows past it. I shall merely list its bishops’ names, since nothing else concerning them has come down to us:

[Col. 1606B] Totta, Eadberht, Unwona, Werenberht, Beorhthelm, Aldred, Ceolred, Leofwine. In the time of King Edgar, this Leofwine united the bishoprics of the Lindisfaras, now called Lincoln, and of Leicester.

## ON THE BISHOPS OF DORCHESTER, OR LINCOLN

[Col. 1605]

[Col. 1605B] Dorchester is a small and thinly populated town in the district of Oxford. Yet the magnificence of its churches is great, whether from ancient workmanship or new diligence.

[Col. 1605C] After Headda, these were bishops there: Æthelwine [variant: Eadwine], Edgar, Cyneberht, Ælfeah [variant: Ælfwīh], Aldwulf, Ceolwulf, Eadwulf, Brihtred, Leofwine. This is the man who united both bishoprics. Ælfnoth, Esopi [variant: Escwi], Ælfhelm, Eadnoth, Æthelweard, Eadnoth, Wulfwine, Remigius, formerly a monk of Fécamp. When William, count of the Normans, came into England, Remigius gave him much assistance, on the agreement that, if William won, he would receive a bishopric. Nor was William slower in giving than Remigius in receiving. When Pope Alexander, as I have already said, convicted and condemned him for this, he was nevertheless restored to honour at the request of Archbishop Lanfranc.

In his first years Remigius planned great things at Dorchester and began some works; at last he transferred all care and the see to Lincoln, one of the [Col. 1605D] more populous cities of England, a market-town for people coming by land and sea. There Remigius filled the church founded in honour of the Lady Mother with many canons, themselves distinguished by learning and by the abundance of wealth that he had assembled from his own resources. He newly founded a monastery of monks at St Mary’s of Stow, and renewed another at Bardney out of his earlier favour toward it. This was all the more pleasing because, owing to the smallness of his body, he himself seemed almost a human prodigy; his spirit strove to excel and stand out in public, and he was:

> “More pleasing, the virtue that comes from a small body.”

Nature seems for this reason to have formed him compactly, so that it might be known that a most blessed intellect can dwell in a most wretched body. Thus, after a life successfully conducted, amid the very preparations for Lincoln’s consecration, on the day before its intended dedication, envious death took him away from such great rejoicings. [Col. 1606B] For, at the urging of this high-spirited man, a royal edict had summoned bishops from every quarter. Bishop Robert of Hereford alone refused to come; by a sure observation of the stars he had foreseen that the dedication would not take place in Remigius’ lifetime, and he had not kept silent about it.

Then his successor, Robert Bloet by name, completed the delayed matter without great difficulty, as one who, delicately nurtured, had entered into another’s labours. He lived in the bishopric a little less than thirty years and died far from his see at Doodffocke [uncertain place-name], where, while riding beside the king with another bishop, he was suddenly overtaken by fate. In other matters cheerful enough and not very serious; in knowledge of secular affairs second to none, but not so in ecclesiastical matters; he adorned the church over which he presided with exceedingly precious ornaments. The dead man’s body was [Col. 1606D] disembowelled, lest foul odours taint the air; the entrails were buried at Eynsham, the remainder at Lincoln. During his lifetime he had transferred the monks who were at Stow to Eynsham.

It is known, moreover, that the Eynsham monks are devoted to Our Lady and beloved by her. Last year one of their young men lay sick and saw her coming to his aid and driving away crowds of demons who had assembled. Pointing them out to those present with his finger, he begged that they might be driven away by sprinkling holy water. Driven back from one side, they immediately appeared elsewhere. Yet when the mighty Empress arrived, all vanished. Then the sick man, entirely as though sound, began in a melodious voice the responsory: “Rejoice, Virgin Mary.” When he had [Col. 1607A] reached the middle, he faltered through the power of illness, or rather through failure of memory; but, reminded by a monk standing beside him, he recovered the words, and, with the final word, breathed out his last spirit. Having thus spoken beforehand of this monastery on this occasion, we shall survey in writing the others situated in the diocese of Lincoln.

In ancient times there was in the city of Oxford a monastery of nuns, in which rests the most holy virgin Frideswide [variant: Fritheswide], a king’s daughter. She despised a king’s marriage-bed, having vowed her virginity to the Lord Christ. But when he had turned his intention toward marriage with the virgin, and had wasted prayers and entreaties in vain, he intended to use force. When Frideswide learned this, she sought escape into the forest. Neither could her hiding-place conceal her from her lover, nor did any slackness of heart prevent him from pursuing the fugitive. [Col. 1607B] Therefore, when the virgin again learned of the young man’s fury, she entered Oxford by secret paths under God’s guidance in the dead of night. When the inquisitive lover flew there in the morning [variant: “hastened there”], the girl, now despairing of escape and also unable through weariness to proceed anywhere, prayed for God’s protection for herself and punishment for her pursuer. He was already entering the gates of the city with his companions when a heavenly stroke came upon him and he was blinded. When he understood the sin of his obstinacy, and Frideswide had been entreated through messengers, he received [variant: recovered] his sight with the same speed with which he had lost it.

From this there arose among the kings of England a fear of entering that city or lodging there, since it is said to be deadly: each avoids testing, at the cost of his own danger, the truth of a matter whose [Col. 1607C] peril is known. There, then, the woman who had won her virginal triumph established a monastery, and in her days, when her bridegroom called, she underwent death.

In the time of Æthelred, when the Danes condemned to death had taken refuge in that monastery, they were consumed with the buildings in flames by the insatiable anger of the English. But soon the king’s repentance purified the sanctuary; the monastery was restored, its old lands returned, and new possessions added. In our own time, when only very few clerks remained there, living as they pleased, Roger, bishop of Salisbury, gave the place to Guimund, a canon of outstanding learning and respectable religious observance. Labouring diligently at the charge entrusted to him, Guimund furnished God there with many canons who would live under a rule.

[Col. 1607D] The district of Bedford contains the abbey of St Alban. This martyr—not a mercenary nor insignificant one—has Bede and Fortunatus as the chief extollers and witnesses of his martyrdom. If I wished to add anything to their abundance, it would be as though I wished to pour waters into the sea. King Offa raised the most holy body, which had long lain in the dust of the earth, from its shrine into the light, and honoured it with a basilica of most beautiful workmanship and a multitude of monks. Nor is the matter doubtful: while Offa was staying at Bath, he was warned in a dream; as he travelled there, a man nearby was moved by the sign of a light like a huge torch descending above the burial-place by night and by day [the syntax is uncertain]. That monastery was never altogether exposed to ruin; but in our age, under Abbot Paul and through the action of Archbishop Lanfranc, [Col. 1608A] it rose to the highest auspices of religious life.

In the district of Huntingdon are Peterborough, Ramsey, and Crowland. Peterborough was once called Medeshamstede; but after Abbot Kenulf enclosed the place with a wall, it was called *Burch*, from its resemblance to a town. Here the most blessed Æthelwold built a monastery with expenditure so painstaking and possessions so enlarged that almost the whole surrounding region is subject to it. There the distinguished virgins Kynedreda and Kyneswitha, daughters of King Penda, are honoured and cherished by their relics. Both, dedicated to God from infancy, maintained their noble purpose into old age. But the younger, not content with her own salvation alone, also consecrated her betrothed Offa to celibacy. He was king of the East Angles for a few years, a youth of pleasing countenance [Col. 1608B] and character, in the flower of age and greatly beloved by his people, taught by Kyneswitha—whose marriage he had expected—to change his love for the better. He went to Rome with King Coenred of the Mercians and Egwin, bishop of the Hwicce; there, tonsured as a monk, he bade farewell in his own time to earthly things.

The community of virgins is adorned, as they proclaim, by holy King Oswald, whose arm, they say, is kept there, whole in sinews, skin, and flesh, secretly removed from its ancient resting-place. A large reliquary, the container of that treasure, is displayed; yet faith in the report wavers where the hearer verifies nothing by sight. I say this not because I doubt the integrity of the saint, but because I do not wish to make a hasty assertion whether it is kept in that place.

The builder of Ramsey Abbey was St Oswald, bishop [variant: archbishop] of York, with the cooperation of a certain Æthelwine, earl of the East Angles. Both deserve praise for commendable generosity, but especially the layman. For at this place, seeing the bishop celebrating the funeral rites of a certain prince and shedding sincere tears with his gaze fixed upon the ground, he was so captivated by the bishop’s piety that he made all his possessions available to him. Thus, inclined by holy favour, he built that monastery most richly in a marshy fen. Felix, the first bishop of the East Angles, was brought from Soham at Earl Æthelwine’s command and lies there. So too do the two brothers Æthelred and Æthelberht. Their uncle, King Ecgberht of Kent, fearing that the boys might grow toward the hope of the kingdom, [Col. 1608D] after keeping them for some time near himself, finally removed them from the court crowd, begrudging them his own sight.

A baleful servant joined the king’s malice, named Thunre, which means “thunder.” Having deceived them with daily kisses, he stabbed them with a dagger in the very midst of his embraces; after killing them, he threw them into a deep pit—so it is said—beneath the king’s own seat, so that no one might think to look for the boys there. For who would look for them there? But that divine eye, which is not deceived by the secrets of hearts, brought the innocent ones into the light, granting there many acts of healing and, in addition, striking the king with a terrible miracle: fire blew upon him as he sat above them. Their neighbours, disturbed by this, excavated those ruins, where the bodies had been hastily covered with turf, and built a basilica in honour of their martyrdom. The king himself, repentant [Col. 1609A] of the murder, assigned a very large part of the Isle of Thanet to the boys’ sister for building a monastery, as an expiation for the slayer and the slain. When Thunre, with his customary impudence, perverted this to evil, he was suddenly swallowed up by a fissure in the earth: seeing and alive, he entered hell.

The saints’ burial-place was in East Anglia, in a place called Eastrey. Therefore Æthelwine, earl of the province, raised them from their obscure church and brought them to Ramsey in solemn procession. But the one who lies there, Ivo, Persian bishop, precedes both him and them in miracles and surpasses them in signs. Once weary of the pleasures administered to him by a very wealthy bishopric, he secretly left everything behind, undertaking a most lengthy pilgrimage with only three companions. [Col. 1609B] Thus, after travelling through many years and passing himself off to observers as a rustic in ragged clothing, he finally sailed to England. Greatly pleased by the barbarity of an unknown language, because he was mocked by everyone as though a fool, he remained in a muddy district and spent there whatever life was allotted to him. His companions followed in the order foreseen by God, but the people of the region knew neither his burial-place nor the saint’s name.

Many stretches of time passed, and the heavenly pearl lay under the darkness of oblivion. Blessed Oswald had already left the earth; Æthelwine had already ended his life. But when it pleased Him who, ordering times by measure, number, and weight, disposes all things, St Ivo appeared in a vision to a man of innocent simplicity. He explained to him in order his name, rank, and the site of his grave. [Col. 1609C] He was therefore to go to the abbot of Ramsey, explain the sequence of the vision, and add that, when he had transported Ivo to Ramsey, he should leave his companions there; that Ivo’s body was not to be placed in a shrine, but in a place next to the altar convenient for those approaching.

Thus far the vision prevailed, so as to draw forth the credence of the abbot of Ramsey. Slow to believe, but once faith had been conceived swift and diligent in performing what he had seen, he went there. The tomb was sought, found, and opened; and immediately, when the holy body had been laid out in linen, a stream most abundant in fleeting bubbles broke out from the winding recesses of the tomb itself. To this day a spring flows, sweet to drink and suitable for every sickness. The multitude healed through that blessed man cannot be counted, much less comprehended in writing, [Col. 1609D] so that there is no saint in England more readily entreated or more effective in result than St Ivo.

I have seen what I say. A certain monk was languishing with dropsy. His swollen skin had risen high; his heavy breath drove away those standing near; he seemed ready to drink whole rivers himself and drain full casks. Warned in a dream, he went to St Ivo, and there, having drunk the water three times, he vomited from his mouth a wave of superfluous fluid. His belly subsided, his legs shrank, and, not to say more, the whole man grew green again into health. At last, glorying in so salutary a vomit, he said that he was at last able to satisfy himself with drink.

Crowland is one of the islands lying in that region [Col. 1610A] of eastern fens; the waters there rise in the heart of the land and, flowing for a hundred miles and more to the sea, rush onward with many great rivers. Here Guthlac, a young man born of no low stock, despised the practice of arms in which he excelled. At twenty-five years of age he entered the solitary life and lived in it for fifteen years. By God’s grace assisting him, he was approved by the rank of priesthood, the honour of miracles, and the truth of prophecies. But the grace of his virtues shone more brightly after death, especially through the incorruption of his most sacred body after a year and the display of many miracles. It is also attributed to his merits that, after a monastery was built beside his body, amid so many storms of war and so many turns of time, [Col. 1610B] that place has experienced no hardship or loss.

A new guest also came, but an old patron with the Lord: St Neot, who had once been a disciple of the most blessed Erkenwald and was always held in the greatest reverence at Cinultelberi [place-name uncertain]. But removed from there because of Danish incursions and carried to Crowland, he now, joined under one shield with Guthlac, protects the inhabitants and is also responsive to the prayers of visitors. Although the place can be reached nowhere except by water, a public passage, as it were, exists before the monastery gate for those sailing past. Hence guests passing to and fro almost never fail to be present there.

Our time too has found someone to honour as a martyr, since report declares that he was killed innocently—would that it did not differ from the truth. This was Earl Waltheof, of noble lineage, son of Siward, the most magnificent earl of the Northumbrians. King William the Elder arrested him on suspicion of a conspiracy made against him, held him long in chains, and at last deprived him of his head; he was buried at Crowland. I have set down the Norman accounts of the evil deeds of kings; here I shall not keep silent about the contrary claims of the English. The English, who excel greatly in truthfulness, assert that the earl was caught unexpectedly at a feast and compelled by necessity to swear an oath of disloyal conspiracy with his lips alone, not his will [variant: “induced”]; and that this was manifest because he freely confessed it both to Archbishop Lanfranc and to the king himself, and did penance for his pretended consent for the moment. [Col. 1610D] Divinity appears to assent to the English testimony, displaying many and very great miracles at his tomb. They say that, bound in chains, he washed away his wrongful deeds with daily sobs. The prior of the place told me that, moved by the miracles, he had touched the noble body, untouched by all corruption, and had seen the head joined to the rest of the body, with only a red line, as it were, displaying the mark of the killing. For this reason, he said, he did not hesitate to call him a saint in every discourse, and to grant in his name prayers and the benefits of the place to those who requested them.

## ON THE BISHOPS OF ELY

[Col. 1611]

[Col. 1611A] It remains for us to survey the bishopric of Ely; once this is completed, our labour will take its rest from so many circuits. Ely, the greatest of the islands in the fens, is so called from the abundance of eels, as Bede, agreeing with common knowledge, attests. Indeed, there is such abundance of these and of almost every kind of river fish that it is a wonder to strangers and, because of their astonishment, an object of mockery to the inhabitants. Nor are waterfowl less cheap, so that for a single penny five persons or more may, from both kinds of food, not merely drive away hunger but satisfy themselves fully.

There the most blessed lady Æthelthryth [variant: Etheldritha] first established a monastery of handmaids of God; after her came her sister Seaxburh, wife of Erconbert, king of Kent, and mother of the most holy virgin Ercongota. In the same place she grew old under the religious rule and title of abbess. She was succeeded in government by her other daughter, Ermenilda, who had been wife of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, and mother of the virgin Werburh, whose truth the preceding discussion touched upon. These three were abbesses in unbroken succession; and in successive times they had many imitators both of their rule and their religious life, down to the time of the Danes. The Danes, breaking even into the marshes, drove out the inhabitants and demolished their dwellings.

“One of them, whose savage heart breathed fury, stole the precious pall that covered the tomb of the virgin Æthelthryth, and struck the marble of the mausoleum with a double-headed axe. When the marble crust split from the blow, the fragment, rebounding from the ground, flew into the striker’s [Col. 1611C] eye; he himself also fell senseless to the ground. The others, casting him out [variant: raising him up], left untouched the tombs of the other holy women which they had intended to violate, and rushed headlong into flight.”

But the desolation of that most sacred place did not last long, through the efforts both of the king of England and of the people of the region. “Clerics were therefore installed for a time to conduct the divine offices. One of them, more impudent than the rest—or perhaps sincerely seeking more certain proof of the virgin’s incorruptibility—tried to spur his companions on. While they represented to him the danger of the undertaking, he himself approached; first, through the opening made by the Danes, he inserted a candle fastened to a rod and, following as far as he could with the curiosity of his eyes, examined everything. Then [Col. 1611D] he tried with the split end of the rod to draw towards himself the wrappings in which the sacred body was enclosed. He had already pulled away part of them when the virgin, angered that her naked body should be seen by a scoundrel, violently drew the cloth back inside, so that she threw him, struggling against her, flat onto the ground. From that fall he was permanently disabled, and afterwards was not free from madness.”

Later Saint Bishop Æthelwold sealed up that opening with cement and stone; he expelled the clerics and introduced monks. He granted the place large and astonishing estates, buying all of them from his own resources. Infer the extent of its ancient possessions from this: although many have been taken away and many seized, the man who now administers the property counts into his own purse 1,040 pounds each year; [Col. 1612A] he has granted scarcely 300 to the monks, apart from what he spends on the needs of his own household, servants, and guests.

Æthelwold appointed Brihtnoth abbot there, and he transferred to the monastery the body of Withburh, sister of Saint Æthelthryth. “At that time she lay in an obscure rural place, where she herself had passed many years unmarried and abstinent from food. A tame doe, accustomed to her hand, supplied her daily drink from its udders. When someone attacked and killed it, whether with an arrow or a spear, the region soon afterwards wasted away, seized by illness. Brihtnoth therefore was carrying her uncorrupted body on board a ship, and, when the townspeople sprang to arms upon learning of the matter, he would certainly have paid the penalty unless he had hurried to launch the stern into the waves. For then the island could be approached only by ship. [Col. 1612B] But our more ingenious age overcame nature: embankments thrown into the fen provided a land route and made the island accessible on foot. While the sailors were endangered amid the heaving waters—for through fear of danger they had committed themselves to an unknown marsh—a fiery column stretching from heaven to the ship swiftly guided the vessel to shore.”

But because Withburh’s incorruptibility had come into doubt for some, the doubt was resolved in the time of Abbot Richard, when the bodies of the holy women were transferred. No one at all ventured to touch blessed Æthelthryth, in reverence for the ancient belief; Withburh herself, however, was uncovered down to the breasts and was seen wholly intact in body, more like one asleep than dead: a silken pillow was placed beneath her head; her veil and all her clothes retained a fresh newness; her face was serene and sweet with rosy colour; her teeth white, her lips slightly drawn back, and her nipples very small.

This monastery accordingly had abbots until the ninth year of King Henry. Then, because the diocese of the bishopric of Lincoln was extended too widely, it was decided that a bishop should be established at Ely, with the district of Cambridge; and, lest the bishop of Lincoln complain that his revenues had been diminished, royal generosity gave him, from another’s holdings, the Ely estate called Spalding, to compensate the bishop’s loss and silence his complaint.

A certain Hervey was therefore enthroned there. He had been bishop of Bangor, but had abandoned that see in hope [Col. 1612D] of greater riches, alleging that he and the Welsh could not agree. Bangor, indeed, is a monastery in Wales itself, once noble and filled with so many inhabitants that, as Bede relates, if divided into seven parts, no portion would contain fewer than three hundred persons. Certainly even now there are there so many half-ruined church walls, such crowds of ruins, as scarcely exist elsewhere.

Within the diocese of that bishop—that is, of Ely—is the monastery of Thorney. Thorney comes later in the text and is smaller in extent, but foremost in the title of praise: an image of paradise, which by its beauty now seems to portray heaven itself. In the midst of the fens it is rich in trees, which, with knotless height, struggle towards the stars. A level expanse, with the green foliage of its grasses, invites the eyes; for those running through the fields, nowhere is there anything to impede them. No, not even the smallest portion of ground lies unused: here the soil subjects itself to fruit-bearing trees; here the field is clothed with vines which either creep along the ground or rise high upon supporting poles. Nature and cultivation engage in mutual contest, so that what the one neglects, the other produces. What may be said of the beauty of its buildings, which the ground—marvellous to say—supports amid those fens upon firm, unshaken foundations? Vast solitude is granted to the monks for quiet, so that they may cling the more steadfastly to heavenly things as they behold mortal matters more chastely. If a woman is seen there, she is regarded as a prodigy; male visitors are welcomed as though they were angels. Moreover, no one stays there except briefly; even the monks’ servants are absent on feast days. Truly I would call that island a refuge of chastity, a fellowship of honour, a training-ground of divine philosophers. Thorney is so called because of the thickness of its thorn-bushes.

[Col. 1613B] But Æthelwold ordered the brambles uprooted and the thorns cleared away [variant: repaired?; *sarriri*]. From the beginning of his episcopate he had intended, abandoning every worldly concern, to practise there the eremitic life. And as far as he could, he took beforehand the first fruits of his future quiet, spending forty days in the most remote church, which he himself had built, alone and devoted to God. Therefore he did not assemble there as much land as elsewhere, but only as much as would suffice for himself and twelve monks. Whatever he bestowed on the place he made, by royal decree confirmed with the assent of all bishops and nobles, free in perpetuity from every public burden.

He brought there so many bodies of saints who had formerly dwelt in that wilderness, as well as others from throughout England, that nearly every corner of the church is full of them. I deliberately refrain from writing their names, because they sound somewhat barbarous—not because I would disbelieve or deny that they are saints: for what authority have I, to call into question what antiquity has consecrated by its actions? But, as I said, their names sound uncouth and smell of harshness; I do not wish to expose saints to ridicule by foolish people—of whom our age produces many. This is especially so since even the inhabitants do not read their lives, and it seems frivolous to proclaim the merits of those whose miracles one can find nowhere. Therefore, preserving every reverence, I venture to make known only Benedict, who was Bede’s foster-father and abbot.

[Col. 1614A] He lined both banks of the river Wear—of no obscure fame among the Northumbrians—with monasteries named for the Apostles Peter and Paul, not differing in their union of charity and rule. Whoever reads the book which Bede himself composed about his life and those of his other abbots will admire this man’s enterprise: that he brought in an abundance of books; that he was the first of all to summon to England craftsmen for stone buildings and glass windows. He spent almost his entire life travelling in pursuit of such things. For love of country and delight in refinement softened the harshness of his labours, as he strove to bring something unusual to his own people. Before Benedict, stone-built structures were seen in England only very rarely, nor did a ray of sunlight cast its light through the transparency of glass.

One may admire his patience, because he yielded possession of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury to Hadrian when Hadrian willingly arrived, neither fearing the hauteur of Archbishop Theodore nor failing to venerate his authority as teacher. Benedict had been appointed abbot of that monastery by King Egbert; but, as I have said, he yielded in deference to Theodore. Pope Vitalian had ordered Theodore to keep Hadrian beside him, to watch lest Theodore introduce into the Church any novelty in the Greek manner. While Benedict travelled through foreign lands, and was absent for a long time, his monks at Wearmouth installed an abbot without consulting him. He bore it with equanimity—or rather magnanimity; on returning home he shared with that man equal honour in their meetings and equal authority in all matters. Indeed, when he was struck so severely by paralysis that no limb could move, he appointed a third man, because the other of whom we have spoken was wasting away from the same illness no less severely than he himself. As the advancing illness was already shaking his vital powers, he summoned his companion and bade him farewell by a mere gesture. Yet the latter was unable to perform the office more effectively, since he was drawing nearer to death himself: for he died before Benedict.

Æthelwold therefore bought Benedict’s body at great cost and brought it to Thorney, introducing a radiant light among more obscure saints.

# BOOK FIVE, OR THE LIFE OF ALDHELM, BISHOP OF SHERBORNE

(Henry Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, II, p. 1.)

[Col. 1613]

# NOTICE

[Col. 1613]

Among other works, William of Malmesbury composed a history, *On the Bishops of England*, from the first acceptance of the faith down to approximately the year 1125, and divided the work into five books. Of these, the first four are found in many manuscript codices in our possession, but copies of the fifth are exceedingly rare. Today scarcely any other is found besides that which we have used; and John Joscelyn, after listing many copies of the first four books which he had seen, testifies that he had seen only one copy of the fifth, in the possession of John Foxe (*Tractatus de historia Anglica*, ch. 16). It therefore appears that William wrote it long after the earlier books had been published, and consequently it became separated from the rest.

William had promised it in Book II of *On the Bishops of England*, in the chapter “On the Bishops of Sherborne”: “The first to sit there was Father Aldhelm, whom here I mention only in his place in the order. For I have never found his Life fully arranged, and very many matters pertain to it; if I conceal them from posterity, I am at fault. With God’s assent, I have thought, in the final book of this little work, when I have freer leisure for matter of this kind, to undertake it.” The fifth book, therefore, to use Joscelyn’s words, treats only of the Life and miracles of Saint Aldhelm and of the condition of the monastery of Malmesbury. William says that he was bound by an obligation of gratitude to write it, for Aldhelm founded the monastery of Malmesbury.

The first four books were published in London in 1596 by that most learned man Sir Henry Savile; the fifth now appears for the first time. The distinguished John Mabillon thought that he had published it in the *Acts of the Benedictines*, century IV, part I, p. 726, transcribed from a Cottonian codex; but in truth he published only a slight epitome of it. The epitome certainly has no negligible antiquity—for that Cottonian manuscript (Claudius A. 51) seems to have been written nearly five hundred years ago—but it has extracted scarcely an eighth part of William’s genuine history.

In his preface Mabillon writes that Egwin of Worcester, Osmund of Salisbury, and Eadmer composed accounts of Aldhelm’s Life before William. Bale and Pits ascribe such a work to Egwin; I fear, however, upon very uncertain authority. Nor is the matter established concerning the others. In his prologue William acknowledges that Faricius, abbot of Abingdon, had collected some material concerning Aldhelm’s Life before him. Bale had never seen William’s genuine book on Aldhelm’s Life. For he gives this opening (*Centuries*, II, ch. 73): “Blessed Aldhelm, in Saxon ...,” with which words the epitome published by Mabillon begins. Bale made another error about the same book, treating William’s *On the Antiquities of Malmesbury* as distinct from his book *On the Life of Saint Aldhelm* (ch. 201). Pits, as usual, copied both of Bale’s errors into his compilation.

I transcribed William’s genuine book from a manuscript codex of Trinity College, Cambridge. The codex was written in a very poor hand about two hundred years ago, and besides the copyist’s frequent blunders it suffered more serious damage from a bookbinder, who often cut off whole lines at the tops of the folios.

William wove into this book several ancient charters of Malmesbury monastery. It will not be useless to make some observations about them, especially because I have often rejected the authenticity of charters in the first part, and have done so still more frequently in the third. It has long been the case that learned men have exposed the frauds of monastic charters. I pass over what Launoy and other foreign writers have discussed on this subject. Whoever wishes to learn more certain things about the charters of our nation should consult Sir John Marsham’s preface to the *Monasticon Anglicanum* and the vernacular work *On the Origins of the British Church* by the most learned prelate Edward, bishop of Worcester (p. 14 ff.).

Before either of them Sir Henry Spelman, in his notes on the English councils, had observed (p. 125) that the authenticity of charters is generally suspect. Producing an ancient fragment from the archives of the Church of Canterbury, he showed that charters first began to be written in England toward the close of the seventh century, and that the first of all was the charter granted by King Wihtred to the Church of Canterbury in 694. Whatever therefore claims an earlier date is certainly fabricated. Moreover, among those that follow down to the time of King Edgar, though written in Latin, the greater part may rightly be judged spurious. I have learned this from the frequent comparison of the appended dates and of the subscribing bishops. After Edgar’s time I have been able to detect comparatively few false charters. But fraud occurs in very few charters written in Saxon, whether before or after Edgar’s time.

For almost all fabricated charters seem to have been forged after the coming of the Normans, when the conquering Normans, seeking by fair means or foul to take lands and possessions from the English, demanded that the English give an account of what right or title they possessed their lands and privileges under. The monks then had either to produce charters from their archives or invent them, unless they preferred to be driven from their monasteries and reduced to poverty. But it would have done little good to forge charters written in Saxon characters: the Normans would have held them in contempt and would not have thought them worthy even of a cursory glance.

Ingulf thus described Norman arrogance in the early years of King William’s reign (fol. 512): “They so abhorred even the language of the English that the laws of the land and enactments of the English kings were handled in the French language; the English method of writing was abandoned, and the French manner was admitted into charters and into all books.” It would therefore have been pointless to produce Saxon charters to Normans who neither knew nor liked the English language; hence they had to be fabricated in Latin.

William the Norman also gave the monks another reason for fabricating charters. He, who disposed of ecclesiastical affairs at pleasure and cultivated neither the ancient discipline of the Church nor the laws of justice more than he chose, completely exempted from episcopal jurisdiction the monastery of Saint Martin at Battle, which he had founded. From this time an insane ambition seized the monks of more important monasteries to obtain a like exemption (Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, p. 62). Before 1073 Baldwin, abbot of Saint Edmund’s, obtained such an exemption from Pope Alexander. Yet the pope, since he had ventured upon a thing hitherto unheard of and untried, used such moderation that he decreed it should occur without prejudice to obedience owed to the primate. Archbishop Lanfranc, however, stripped the abbot of the privilege upon his return to England.

Later, when archbishops of milder temper—Ralph, William, and Theobald—presided over the English Church, and its liberty had been broken by the Roman pontiffs, the monks, imagining that nothing was unlawful to them, sought exemption from both archiepiscopal and episcopal jurisdiction. First they denied obedience to their bishops by fabricating charters of ancient popes and kings; then, litigating in the Roman curia, they secured confirmation of their charters by the power of money. Any monastic charters before the Norman period that claim exemption from ordinary episcopal jurisdiction must therefore rightly be judged false. For if it had previously been customary for Roman pontiffs to grant monks such very extensive charters of exemption as were later produced, Pope Alexander would surely not have withheld a complete exemption from Abbot Baldwin, a man of great power and ample wealth.

Certainly, with regard to the charters of exemption granted to Malmesbury monastery—which occur in this book of William—the letter of Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, to Pope Alexander, written in the hand of Peter of Blois in 1180 (Epistle 68), proves them fraudulent. The monks of Malmesbury had recently elected an abbot. When the bishop of Salisbury forbade the elect, even after an appeal had been lodged, to receive his blessing from anyone other than himself, the elect secretly went to Wales and secured consecration from the bishop of Llandaff. The archbishop therefore suspended the abbot until he should produce, to excuse his disobedience, a privilege of liberty or exemption.

The abbot displayed before the archbishop certain letters asserting his exemption, which appeared defective in their cord and seal and did not at all resemble the style of the Roman curia. The bishop accused them of falsity and produced many professions of obedience made by the abbots of Malmesbury to himself and his predecessors. The abbot withdrew obstinately, saying that he was bound to answer no bishop or archbishop except the supreme pontiff alone. “Wretched and miserable,” he said, “are abbots who do not utterly cast off the authority [Col. 1617] of bishops, since for an annual ounce of gold they can obtain full liberty from the Roman see.”

The archbishop therefore begs the pope not to favour him, and at the same time bitterly laments the injury inflicted upon bishops and upon the whole Church through exemptions granted to abbots by the Roman see. For monasteries which have obtained this benefit of most reprehensible liberty, whether by apostolic authority or, as more often happens, by forged bulls, have incurred more disturbance and more poverty. The deceptive malice of forgers has armed itself so strongly to the dishonour of bishops that falsity prevails in the exemption of nearly all monasteries.

A notable proof of this matter is preserved in the archives of Christ Church, Canterbury, concerning the forged bulls of the monks of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury. For almost the whole twelfth century they caused the archbishops of Canterbury much trouble, in order to shake off archiepiscopal authority; and they achieved this again by producing, for that purpose, ancient privileges of Archbishop Saint Augustine, King Æthelberht, and others. Concerning these and other similar privileges, Giles, bishop of Évreux, sent a letter to Pope Alexander. It is preserved in the archive of the said church, authenticated by his seal, around whose edge is inscribed: “Of Giles, by the grace of God bishop of Évreux.” On its back is written: “Against the false privileges of Saint Augustine’s: how they fortified themselves through the forged privileges of Saint Médard by means of a single monk, a forger.” See this letter among the various letters to Alexander III in the volumes of the *Patrologia* shortly to be published, under the year 1181.

# PROLOGUE TO BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1617]

[Col. 1617A] Having travelled through the bishoprics of all England, wherever they extend, I return, as after a long pilgrimage, to my home, in order to fulfil my promise concerning the most blessed Father Aldhelm. [Note: [Col. 1617C] Book II of *On the Bishops of England*, chapter “On the Bishops of Sherborne.”] What moves me to accomplish this according to my ability is not an unusually rich subject for writing, but a fuller devotion toward the saint which he himself has deserved. Would it be fitting for me to deny the proclamation of my voice to him who, after God, bestowed upon me whatever small measure of ability I have? Should I not devote my tongue to him—to whom, if necessary, I would devote my life? Surely he is excessively miserly who clings tightly to his words.

Therefore, since it would be a monstrous departure from justice if, in this brief account of the saints, our sole lord and patron were obscured by silence, I have undertaken to say at least a little about his life. Yet [Col. 1617B] through ignorance of the facts I am by no means able to satisfy my desire. Apart from what Bede touches upon concerning him in the *Deeds of the English*, Aldhelm has always lain below his merits, always remained obscure and unhonoured through his countrymen’s neglect. Great indeed in renown for learning and eminent in miracles, he has been illuminated by no surviving written account.

Someone may rejoice that he has thus read more of Aldhelm’s miracles than he performed while alive. Certainly nothing has come down to me, nothing has been reached even by my most painstaking inquiry, except that an artisan’s hand engraved them upon a silver and very ancient shrine. Faricius, abbot of Abingdon, assembled these matters in a little book, relying on his own authority and adducing no external testimony to confirm his statements. [Note: [Col. 1617C] This Faricius was made abbot of Abingdon from being a monk of Malmesbury in 1100. He died in 1117, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. Additions of the monk of Abingdon to Florence of Worcester in an ancient manuscript codex of Lambeth Library, [Col. 1618C].]

I preferred a different manner of writing: through those deeds absent from Faricius’s writings I would proceed inwardly, and surround every assertion with suitable witnesses, as with supporting posts. For who would otherwise believe deeds so remote from our memory, and, because of the scarcity of written records, buried as though they had never been spoken? There also remain many things awaiting my service as a monk of Malmesbury, which that man either did not know or refrained from recounting. For although his eloquence was not altogether contemptible, in these matters alone he lacked diligent knowledge because of his ignorance of the language, being born, as it were, under a Tuscan sky. [Note: [Col. 1618C] “Tuscan” should be read. For the aforesaid monk of Abingdon reports that he was Italian by origin.]

Therefore, my fair and kindly reader, do not let the obscurity of my person suffer prejudice in comparison with an abbot’s rank. Yet if you attend to honours, we too have borne some name and distinction. This narrative will therefore proceed in four divisions.

First, I shall show the lineage and learning of the most holy man.
