Second, I shall set out which monasteries he made, and by what privileges [Col. 1618B] and endowments he distinguished this monastery of ours. Here, from the outset, I ask my hearer’s patience, lest he escape burdened by other people’s writings. This little book promises not a display of eloquence but a gathering of knowledge, so that it may be called not so much the life of a saint as evidence for his life, an instrument of knowledge.

Third, I shall not omit the very few miracles he performed in youth—not because he performed no more, but because only these have been able to escape the scruple of doubt.

Fourth, I shall trace, with as much truth as I can, the course of events after the blessed man’s death: how many shipwrecks of liberty our Church endured, and how, although it seemed most oppressed, it nevertheless always raised its head prosperously against fortune through the saint’s patronage. I know that I am unequal to recounting these things; but, guided by the Holy Spirit, who now seems to have filled my sails not sluggishly, I shall willingly sail secure over the immensity of this sea.

# BOOK FIVE, PART ONE

[Col. 1619]

[Col. 1619A] Aldhelm, then, sprang from a Saxon lineage and a family undoubtedly most noble; by the nobility of his character he surpassed the nobility of his descent. Faricius played upon the name in saying that Aldhelm meant “nourishing old man”; but I, if it were permitted to steal the reader’s attention from serious occupations by inserting a jest, would say that the interpretation is very differently distorted: that *Aldhelm* means “old helmet.” For the saint himself clearly indicates in the prologue to his *Riddles* that his name ought to be written with an H inserted.

The man’s life corresponds to this interpretation: protected in his head by the helmet of salvation, trained in Christ’s warfare so as to have completed his service and never to yield to an enemy, he bore a rich laurel of victory over the devil up to heaven. Some assert—though it is uncertain whence they derived it—that he was the nephew of Ine, king of the West Saxons, through the latter’s brother Centor. We have not wished to claim this as true, because it seems more suited to a flying rumour than to historical truth. The chronicles make clear that Ine had no brother except Ingild, who died a few years before Ine himself.

I might also object that Aldhelm, dying not less than seventy years old, left Ine surviving him by more than eighteen years; and that the king himself went to Rome after so many years while still in vigorous age. Is it plausible that a young uncle should have had a nephew of seventy, born from a younger brother? Yet let what is disputed remain unresolved; let what is free from ambiguity be stated. Whoever reads the handbook of King Alfred will find that Centor, Saint Aldhelm’s father, was not the full brother of King Ine, but related to him by a very close bond of kinship.

That Aldhelm himself was of Saxon stock he teaches in a letter sent to a certain Cellanus, in these words: “I wonder that the industry of your fraternity, from the famous and flower-bearing land of the Franks, should address me, so insignificant a little man, born of Saxon stock and beneath the northern pole in the tender cradles of infancy.” [The transmitted *franite* is perhaps to be read *Francicae*, “Frankish”.]

[Col. 1619C] Therefore his father, who because of the awareness of his nobility entertained no lowly ambition, entrusted his son for instruction in the first elements not to the school of an undistinguished teacher but to Hadrian, abbot of Saint Augustine’s. Whoever has read the *Deeds of the English* knows that Hadrian stood at the summit [variant: “in the summit”] of learning. When Aldhelm had grown older and returned from Kent to the West Saxons, he received the religious habit in the monastery of Malmesbury. It had been founded by a man called by some Meildulf, a Scot by nation, a philosopher in learning, and a monk by profession.

There the boy, trained in Greek and Latin letters, soon shone forth, admired even by his teachers. Deprived voluntarily of his native soil, Meildulf had come there and, charmed by the beauty of the wood—which at that time had grown enormously in that place—practised the eremitic life. When necessities failed, he accepted pupils as disciples, so that their generosity might remedy the scantiness of his livelihood. In time the pupils who followed their master became monks and grew into a considerable community. Formed by their example and companionship in the pursuit of study, Aldhelm added the liberal arts to the fullness of learning. To drink them in deeply, he again studied in Kent at Hadrian’s feet—Hadrian being the fountain of letters and stream of the arts—until compelled by illness to return home.

Let testimonies support the thread of this account, lest the hearers’ faith be uncertain. That Hadrian educated him in infancy, Aldhelm himself says in a letter to Hadrian: “To the most reverend father and venerable instructor of my unformed infancy, Hadrian: Aldhelm, a native servant of Christ’s household and a suppliant foster-child of your kindness, greetings, etc.” That he was both reared and taught from boyhood in the monastery of Malmesbury is indicated by Bishop Leutherius in the privilege by which he granted Aldhelm the abbey:

“I, Leutherius, by the grace of God bishop, have been asked by the abbots to deem worthy the granting and bestowal upon Aldhelm the priest of that land which bears by established usage the name Maldulfesberg, so that he may live there according to the Rule. In that place, from the first flowering of infancy and from the very beginning of elementary training, he was educated in the liberal studies of letters and nourished in the bosom of holy Mother Church, and there he lived.”

That Meildulf founded that monastery, Pope Sergius attests in the privilege granted to Aldhelm: “At your religious request that we strengthen with apostolic privileges the monastery of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul which Meildulf of religious memory founded, which is now also called Meldumesberge, situated in the province of Wessex, and which we have learned your religious devotion administers wisely, we grant favour to your pious petition.”

That he studied again in Kent but left because of illness, he says in the same letter to Hadrian: “I confess, my dearest one, whom I embrace with the grace of pure affection, that since I departed from your social fellowship about three years ago and was separated from Kent, my littleness has until now burned with ardent desire for fellowship with you. I had long considered how I might fulfil what I desired, if circumstances and changes of time permitted and if the various obstacles of hindrances did not delay me—above all, if the health of my bodily frailty did not prevent me, as it wastes my limbs to the marrow. For formerly, when I was again with you after my first elementary instruction, I was compelled by this illness to return home.”

[Col. 1621A] These testimonies have, I think, made it plain that he possessed the liberal arts, since he enjoyed the companionship of so great a colleague. Nor, indeed, did he fail to offer testimony in praise of himself when he said that he had been the first man of his nation to venture his talent and direct his mind towards knowledge of metres. These are his words at the end of the book which he wrote on metrical figures:

“These things concerning the kinds and figures of metres you have, collected for the benefit of my own intellect, very wordily—I do not know whether fruitfully—although I am conscious that I can boast that Virgilian saying:

> I first, if life remains to me, returning to my native land,  
> will lead down the Muses from the Aonian summit.”

Thus fully equipped with letters, he did not neglect poetry in his native tongue either. So much so that, according to the book of Alfred mentioned above, [Note: [Col. 1621D] He seems to mean some book published by the most learned King Alfred. For in Book II of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, chapter 4, he mentioned several books either written by Alfred or composed under his auspices.] there had never at any time been anyone equal to him in the ability to make English poetry, compose so much of it, and sing or recite it aptly.

Finally, Alfred recalls a popular song, still commonly sung, which Aldhelm composed. He adds a reason demonstrating why so great a man reasonably devoted himself to what seem trifling matters: the people at that time were half-barbarous and gave little attention to divine discourse; as soon as Mass had been sung, they customarily hurried home. Therefore the holy man placed himself like a barrier on the bridge joining countryside and town, presenting himself to those leaving as though he were a professional singer. Having done this more than once, he won the people’s favour and assembled a crowd. By this device, gradually inserting words of Scripture amid amusements, he restored the citizens to soundness. Had he thought that he should act sternly and with excommunication, he would certainly have achieved nothing.

The high esteem in which his distinguished learning was held is shown by the letters sent to him by his friends. I say nothing of his countrymen, who eagerly sent him their writings to undergo the judgment of his criticism. I pass over the Irish, then especially learned, who are known to have done the same; among whom I could name several men of no obscure scholarship, especially Arcivil, son of the king of Scotland. Whatever roughness there was in his literary art—and it was by no means slight—he submitted to Aldhelm’s judgment, that the Scottish roughness might be erased by the file of a perfected talent. From the very heart of Francia men came to him for learning, as this letter will plainly show:

“To Aldhelm, Archimandrite of the Saxons, a lord enriched with studies of reading and adorned with honey-sweet nocturnal compositions, marvellously finding upon his own shores what some scarcely gain, with labour and sweat, in a foreign field: Cellanus, born on the island of Hibernia, an exile hiding in a remote corner at the furthest border of the Franks, the lowest and most worthless servant of Christ’s renowned colony, sends greeting in the whole and secure Trinity.” [Col. 1622A]

And a little later:

“Like a winged flight, the panegyrical report of your Latin eloquence has reached the ears of our poverty—a report which the ears of quick-witted readers do not receive with scorn or with the dregs of deceit, renowned through the glory of the nourishing guide of Roman speech [the reading should, I think, be *almae ductricis*, ‘the kindly guide’]. Although we have not deserved to hear you in person, we have nevertheless read your annals, constructed with a fine balance and painted with the delights of diverse flowers. But if you refresh the sad little heart of an exile, send a few small words from those most beautiful lips of yours, from whose most pure fountain sweetness may refresh the minds of many, to the place where the Lord Furseus rests in a holy and incorrupt body.”

How generously he replied to this letter is attested by the one of which a portion was recently appended here [Col. 1622B]: it gave proof that Aldhelm was born of Saxon stock.

Moreover, it is not easy to relate how effective he was in exhorting friends and disciples: the former, that they should show unbroken faithfulness to their friends; the latter, that they should shape their tender years exactly according to the rule of divine instruction. Brief notices of individual admonitions shall nevertheless be set down here. When Bishop Wilfrid, of whom I said not a little in the third book, was driven into exile, many of his followers, following the wheel of their abbot’s fortune, were considering turning aside to the favour of his enemies. Distrusting their loyalty and fearing for his venerable friend, Aldhelm attempted to raise their wavering spirits with these words. After an appropriate preface, he says:

“Recently, as you have learned by experience, the disturbance of a raging storm [Col. 1622C] shook the foundations of the Church as though by some immense earthquake; its noise resounded through various regions of the earth, far and wide, like the crash of thunder. Therefore, my beloved fellow-countrymen, with the knees of my legs bent, I earnestly beg you: do not let yourselves be scandalized in any way by the turn of this disturbance; let none of you grow numb in faith through slothfulness of mind, even though necessity requires you to be driven from your native land together with your own bishop, deprived of the summit of his pontifical office, and though any of you must enter regions beyond the sea of broad kingdoms. For who, I ask, however harsh or cruel the labour may be, can forbid you to remain with that bishop who, from the very first training in the rudiments and from the earliest infancy of tender age until the flower of mature youth, advanced you by nourishing, teaching, and correcting you with affection; and who, as a nurse carrying her beloved children refreshes them with the outstretched bounds of her arms, so gently embraced you, warmed in the bosom of charity? Consider, I ask, the order of created things and the nature divinely implanted in them, so that, by comparing the smallest things, you may, with Christ’s help, receive a pliant pattern for conduct: how swarms of bees, when the heat sent from heaven grows warm, eagerly emerge from hives fragrant with nectar; and, their leader departing, the companies of dense caverns leave their winter dwellings and, gathering in swift flight, rise into the air, except only the guardians of their ancient seats, left behind for the future propagation of offspring. Their king, I say—more wonderful to tell—surrounded by dense ranks of companions, goes out with the whole troop from its winter camp and searches the hollow strength of tree-trunks. If he has been impeded by the dusty sprinkling of sand, or delayed by sudden rains dripping down from the sluices of Olympus, and returns to his welcome lattice and former seat, the whole army at once breaks through its accustomed entrances and joyfully enters the ancient enclosures of its cells.” [Col. 1623A]

And after other matters:

“If therefore a creature without reason, governed by the life and nature implanted in it without written laws, obeys its leader’s command according to the recurring succession of seasons, answer me, I beg: should not those be reproached with the disgrace of a dreadful abomination [Col. 1623B] who, endowed with the granted grace of the sevenfold Spirit, break the reins of devoted submission in a frenzied fashion? But hear why, gathering together arguments from diverse things, I run through them with a shrill pen in order to stir the inmost feelings of your hearts. Behold: if secular men, strangers to divine knowledge, should desert the devoted lord whom they loved in prosperity when the abundance of good fortune has ceased and the adversity of calamity presses in, and should prefer the secure, sweet leisure of their native country to the distress of their exiled lord, would they not be regarded by all with the ridiculous mockery of detestable laughter and the noise of sneering? What, then, will be said of you if you leave alone in exile the bishop who nourished and raised you?” And so forth.

Having set forth an example of most steadfast loyalty to a friend, there follows an excellent admonition to a disciple:

[Col. 1623C]

“To my most beloved son and at the same time disciple ADILWALD, ALDHELM, the least of the servants of God, greeting.

“As I have taken care on several occasions to admonish you orally concerning certain matters, so now, though absent, relying upon paternal authority according to God, I do not hesitate to exhort you by letter. For we do this because, as the Apostle says, the charity of Christ constrains us (2 Cor. 5:14). Therefore, my dearest son, although you are young in age, do not subject yourself too greatly to the most vain pleasures of this world: whether to shamefully excessive daily drinking and banquets of too frequent and prolonged a kind; or to the blameworthy wandering involved in riding; or to the pursuit of any pleasures of bodily delight. Always remember what is written: ‘Youth and pleasure are vain’ (Eccl. 11:10). Nor should you serve beyond measure an excessively vehement love of money and every boastfulness of secular glory, always hateful to God, remembering that saying: ‘What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but suffer loss of his soul?’ (Mark 8:36)—‘For the Son of Man will come in his glory and that of the holy angels, and will render to each according to his works’ (Matt. 16:27). But much more, my beloved, be ever watchful in divine reading and holy prayers. If, moreover, you labour to know any secular literature, do this only for the reason that, since all, or almost all, the texture of words in the divine law rests entirely upon the system of grammatical art, you may more easily understand by reading the most profound and most sacred senses of that same divine utterance, in proportion as you have more fully learned the many rules of the system by which it is composed. But do not fail to keep this letter continually before you among the other books that you read, so that by reading it very frequently you may be reminded in my stead to fulfil the things written in it. Farewell.” [Col. 1624A]

And would that this reading might bring benefit and advantage to the monks who profess themselves Aldhelm’s disciples, so that at last, despising enticements, [Col. 1624B] they may rely upon the footsteps of his holiness and learning. For undoubtedly his institutions would never have been uprooted unless we had transgressed his commands. But because we sinned against him, we are justly punished. Meanwhile he is silent as though he did not know, and overlooks matters as though he did not see, while we are tossed about amid dangers; while his privileges are mocked by rebels and trampled under foot by tyrants. But let us return, even late, to our right mind, that he may look upon his servants, already battered by many dangers, with an eye of compassion and gather them back into the bosom of mercy.

Yet, to resume the narrative: Bede placed the highest crown upon the praises of his scholarship. Because of the nearness of the time, he knew the matter as it was; and because of his devotion to truth, he would not lie. After enumerating some of his books, he added:

“He wrote,” he says, “several other works also, as a man most learned in every respect. For he was polished in speech and remarkable for his learning in both ecclesiastical and secular writings.”  
[Note: [Col. 1623D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 19.]

Can anything more exalted than this praise be said? Finally, I shall cite that same witness concerning the arts to which, although he never refused attention to any of them, he nevertheless applied his mind especially while studying during his repeated stay in Kent. Thus, in a letter to Hedda, his predecessor, he describes his labour and commends his own exercise:

“I confess, most blessed bishop, that I had long determined, if the changing course of times permitted, to celebrate there in the company of the brethren, rejoicing, the approaching and desired feast of the Lord’s Nativity, [Col. 1624D] and afterwards, life accompanying me, to enjoy the presence of your charity. But since we were delayed by diverse obstacles of hindrances, as the bearer of this letter will declare orally, and were unable to accomplish this, I ask that you grant pardon for the difficulty. For no short intervals of time are required for this study of reading by one who, fired with the eagerness of reading, searches out to the marrow the laws of Roman jurisprudence and examines all the secrets of jurists in the depths of his heart; and, what is much more intricate than these matters, distinguishes a hundred kinds of metre by the rule of prose and surveys the modulations of musical song by the correct course of syllables. [Col. 1625A] For students of this subject the obscurity becomes so much more inextricable as the number of learned teachers to be found is rarer. But the narrowness of a letter does not at all permit a lengthy discussion of how the hidden instruments of the metrical art are combined from letters, syllables, feet, poetic figures, verses, tones, and times; nor how the discipline of poetry’s sevenfold division—that is, acephalic verses, *procilos* [a metrical term; uncertain], and the rest—varies; which verses called *monostichs*, *pentastichs*, and *decastichs* are bounded by a fixed measure of feet; and by what method catalectic, brachycatalectic, or hypercatalectic verses are determined by acute reasoning. These matters, I think, and similar things cannot at all be grasped in a brief interval of time.

[Col. 1625B] “And what need is there to mention the method of calculation, when the threatening despair of so great a reckoning oppressed my mind so greatly that I counted as nothing all my former labour in reading, though I had once believed that I knew its secret chambers? And, to use the saying of blessed Jerome when opportunity has presented itself: ‘I who formerly seemed to myself a little learned man began again to be a disciple.’ Thus, relying at last upon heavenly grace, by persistent study I discovered the most difficult arguments of things and the calculations of reckoning, which they call the parts of number. But concerning the zodiac and the twelve signs which revolve in the turning of heaven, I judge that I ought to remain silent, lest an obscure and profound art, requiring a long explanation of matters, should be disgraced and cheapened if exposed in a cheap series of interpretation; especially since expertise in the art of astrology and the intricate computation of the horoscope require the painstaking investigation of a learned teacher.” [Col. 1625C]

Filled with delight in such arts, he too issued little books containing good fruit from the most sacred storehouse of his heart, lest he should never open the treasures accumulated for so long, lest he should never set down anything from what he had heard. His first trial of talent he gave in the book which he made for the Britons, that they might return to the true Easter; some misfortune, I know not what, has begrudged its teaching to our use and removed it from our enjoyment. There is also his book *On the Praise of Virgins*, composed with rhetorical charm, in which he first praises the glory of virginity and then shows by the examples of saints that celibacy is not difficult. He made another work on the same subject in heroic verse, to which he added a third, likewise in verse, *On the Conflict of the Eight Principal Virtues*. There also survives his notable book *On Riddles*, emulating the poet Symphosius, divided into a hundred titles and a thousand verses.

He ingeniously wove the prefaces of both works with recurrent verses. Thus, in *On the Praise of Virgins*, the letters of this verse, *Metrica tirones nunc promant carmina castos* (“Now let beginners in metre bring forth chaste poems”),

began each successive verse of the preface from beginning to end; and, repeated backwards according to the number of verses, they formed the same verse. In *On Riddles* it is arranged differently, so that this verse, *Aldhelmus cecinit millenis versibus odas* (“Aldhelm sang odes in a thousand verses”),

both begins and ends with the first and last letters respectively of the individual verses in the prologue, making both extremes identical. [Col. 1626B] In these things he displayed both the sport and craftsmanship of ancient learning, while accompanying uncurious subjects with an eloquence that was copious and vigorous.

Moreover, for a certain Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians, learned in letters, as Bede relates, he produced a book containing the following chapters:

- On the dignity of the number seven, collected from the flowers of the Old and New Testaments and from the disciplines of philosophers.
- On the exhortation to brotherly charity.
- On the nature of insensible things, which are represented as speaking according to metaphor.
- On the rules of feet.
- On metaplasm.
- On synaloepha.
- On the scanning and elision of verses.
- On metre: question and answer in alternation.

He also composed many letters, most of which do not survive; the carelessness of our predecessors has mutilated part of some that we possess. His discourses impart less cheerfulness than those persons would wish who, indifferent to matters, weigh words—importunate judges who do not know that styles of composition vary according to the customs of nations. For the Greeks customarily write in an involved manner, the Romans splendidly, and the English pompously. One may observe this in all ancient charters: how greatly they delight in certain obscure words borrowed from Greek. Aldhelm, however, conducts himself more moderately and uses exotic words only very rarely and when necessary. His eloquent discourse presents catholic meanings, and rhetorical colouring adorns his most forceful assertions. If you read him thoroughly, [Col. 1626D] you will take him for a Greek because of his keenness, swear that he is a Roman because of his polish, and recognize him as an Englishman because of his magnificence.

## PART II

[Col. 1625]

[Col. 1625D] Having, in whatever fashion, patched together the first part of my undertaking, I approach the second, which promises to show what monasteries Saint Aldhelm founded, with what privileges he distinguished them, and with what estates he enriched them. Its completion will be easy, because the substance of the task will be accomplished by another’s labour. It pleases me, therefore, to taste beforehand in my own words the necessary matters [Col. 1626D], to seize an opportunity to hasten the work, and then to range with freer care through the writings of others.

From what has been said above, then, it may be understood that Meldulf built—or rather began—the monastery of Meldun, which a more corrupt age now calls Malmesbury. For there was such a shortage of necessities there that its inhabitants could scarcely procure their daily sustenance; but Aldhelm’s nobility remedied the lack of provisions, as the narrative proceeding will show. A very small basilica was visible there a few years before this time, which antiquity reports—though it is uncertain whether it fabricates the story—that Meldulf built; and there was a more spacious church in honour of the Lord Saviour and of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. That in this church there had from ancient times been the head of the place and a congregation of monks is confirmed by the authority of the charters which I shall set forth: they establish belief and refute disbelief. And because it was then customary, at the dedication of new churches, to set up some honourable epigram in honour of the heavenly Bridegroom and Mother Church, the holy man composed this wedding-song in honour of the apostles:

> Here flourishes the glory to be celebrated of a newly founded temple,  
> Which marks the bright banners of sacred triumph.  
> Here are Peter and Paul, lights of the shadowed world,  
> The chief fathers who govern the reins of the people,  
> Celebrated with frequent songs in the kindly hall.  
> O key-bearer, you who open heaven’s gate in the heights,  
> You who by your merits unclose the bright [perhaps add: “thresholds of heaven”].  
> Mercifully hear the vows of the praying peoples [reading: *praecantum*, “those praying/singing”],  
> Who moisten their withered faces with streaming rains.  
> Receive the sobs and confessed sins of those who groan,  
> Who with ardent prayer melt away the sins of their conduct.  
> Once fierce Saul, now Paul, Lamb of God made gentle  
> By the laying aside of savagery and change of name,  
> Now kindly open your ears to the voices of those praying;  
> [Col. 1627C] And, together with Peter, as guardian extend your right hand to the trembling.  
> Those who frequent the sacred [lacuna] lights [perhaps the reading should be *sanctorum limina*, “the thresholds of the saints”] behold them,  
> So that swift forgiveness of sins [these words seem to need insertion here] may be given,  
> Flowing abundantly from mercy and from the heavenly fountain,  
> Which never dries up for worthy peoples through the ages.

He also founded another monastery beside the river called Frome, as is read in the privilege which Pope Sergius granted to both monasteries. There still stands there the church which he built in honour of Saint John the Baptist, and it has overcome so many ages by its endurance. A persistent tradition also asserts that he established a third monastery at Bradford. This seems to be confirmed by the name of the estate appended in the series of the privilege which, now a bishop, he gave to his monasteries and which is depicted in the ancient strokes of the document. To this day there is a little church in that place, which he is said to have built in the name of most blessed Lawrence. But both monasteries, Frome and Bradford, imitating the lot of mortals, have fallen into nothingness; only an empty name remains. Yet whether the destruction of such great buildings should be attributed to the mad wars of the Danes or the rapacious bands of the English, I could not easily determine. Meldun alone, the same as Malmesbury, still flourishes in the number of its inhabitants and the beauty of its dwellings. I think that this has been arranged by the pity of the saint, who devoted himself and his body there, so that it might escape so many afflictions, endure so many calamities, and sigh for the faint shadow of liberty lost long ago. [Col. 1628A] Consequently, what estates he granted there to repair the broad ruin caused by the destruction of the others has entirely escaped our knowledge.

But, as I am about to tell how much land he added to this monastery, there first presents itself for insertion the privilege which Leutherius, bishop of the West Saxons, granted to Aldhelm. Seeing him there striving upward through the advancing success of his virtues, Leutherius raised him first to the priesthood and afterwards to the abbacy; and by this document transferred into the abbot’s jurisdiction possession of that place, which was under his own authority.

[Col. 1628B]

“It often happens that, when the scorching heat of autumn has departed, the winter blasts of raging winds succeed one another in alternating courses; by these the stormy blue waters of the sea and the immense gulfs of ocean are battered hither and thither, so that no one sailing on a wandering ship crosses without dangers while the furious wind tears the sails. Thus indeed, now that the swelling glory of the world has been cast down and its end is approaching, the waves of the age appear manifestly to be pressing upon us; so that truly and without any doubtful hesitation those predictions of the Lord seem at last to be fulfilled in our times, concerning which he spoke in the heavenly oracle: ‘See the fig tree and all the trees,’ etc. (Luke 21:29). But amid these turbulent storms of the world, the rudders of Scripture must be turned, and the equipment and instruments of the whole vessel must be prepared, so that, scorning the chattering song of the Sirens, it may be brought prosperously by a straight course to the harbour of its native land. [Col. 1628C]

“Therefore I, Lutherius, by the grace of God bishop, steering the rudders of the Saxon episcopate, have been asked by the abbots who are known to preside, with pastoral care, over monastic companies of monks under the jurisdiction of our diocese, to deign to confer and grant to the priest Aldhelm the land named Maldumesburge for the regular ordering of life. In that place, from the first stage of infancy and the very beginning of elementary training, he was educated in the liberal studies of letters and led his life nourished in the bosom of Holy Mother Church. And especially for this reason brotherly charity seems to urge this petition. Therefore, acceding to the prayers of the aforesaid abbots, compelled by brotherly petition, I freely grant the place mentioned above to him and to his successors who diligently follow the rule of the holy Rule with devoted zeal, so that in future generations, once all conflicts of arising disputes have been removed, they may be able to serve the Lord without hindrance in continual quiet and perpetual peace.

“But lest an occasion for contention should perhaps arise hereafter, I confirm this with the following condition: that none of the bishops or kings who shall hereafter succeed may, relying upon tyrannical power, violently invade this charter of our gift, persistently claiming that something has been removed and separated from the right of episcopal authority. Indeed, it must be known, and proclaimed against opponents, that I have added benefit and increase to the pontifical Church far more than I have withdrawn anything by force. Finally, that the gift of the aforesaid grant may remain ever more firmly established, we have ordered the aforesaid abbots to subscribe with their own hands. If anyone attempts to make void these our writings, decisions, and decrees, let him know that he will render an account before Christ’s judgment seat. Done publicly beside the river Glaston, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Incarnation of Christ 675.”

Having thus been made abbot, he led the monks according to their profession, urged their reputation toward goodness, and desired God’s glory above all things. And when the bishop’s favour joined with the abbot’s industry, the resources of the monastery then increased beyond measure. Men hastened to Aldhelm by every path: some seeking holiness of life, others knowledge of letters. For although, as we have said, he was manifold in learning, he was nevertheless gracious and simple in religion. He overwhelmed opponents with a flood of speech, while he soothed learners with the nectar-like [lacuna] stream of teaching, so that from his mouth there flowed toward both parties a discourse of salted wit; he was admirable in each respect and singular in all. Thus it came about that kings and earls of the Mercians and West Saxons, drawn by the man’s religion, which his nobility commended, bestowed many things upon the place.

The first of these, as we have learned, was Kenfrith, earl of the Mercians, a kinsman of royal blood: a man serving God in body, in the world, and in mind. He gave ten cassati at Wodecim to Abbot Aldhelm in these words:

[Col. 1629B]

“The forward Fortune of the deceptive world is not lovely with the milky whiteness of unfading lilies, but hateful with the bitter gall of corruption to be avoided. [Col. 1629C] She cruelly tears her children with the venomous jaws of foul flesh in the valley of tears. Though by smiling she may seem attractive to the unhappy, yet she slopes shamelessly toward the depths of Acherontic Cocytus, lest the deep abyss come to the aid of those who roar [perhaps read: *ne situs alti subveniat boantibus*]. Therefore, because she herself falls away carnally into ruin, we must hasten with all urgency toward the pleasant fields of unutterable joy. There, the instruments of angelic hymn-like rejoicing and the honey-sweet scents of roses are perceived as inestimably sweet by good and blessed nostrils, and are drunk in without end by the ears of the happy. Drawn by the love of this blessedness, I, Kenfrith, earl of the Mercians, have granted in perpetual right a certain portion of land, estimated at ten cassati, in the place called Wodecim, to the venerable Abbot Aldhelm, for the service of God and Saint Peter, with the consent of my lord King Ethelred, in the year 680 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction eight.” [Col. 1629D]

The gift of this most eminent earl stirred up and advanced the king’s generosity, so that in the following year he himself granted two estates and confirmed them in a single document, as follows:

“In the name of the Lord our God Jesus Christ the Saviour. ‘We brought nothing into this world,’ as the apostolic oracle confirms, ‘and we can take nothing away’ (1 Tim. 6:7). Therefore eternal and enduring things must be purchased with earthly and perishable things. Accordingly, I, Etheldred, king of the Mercians, at the request of my patrician and kinsman Kenfrith, for the salvation of my soul and for the prayer of the brethren serving God at Meldulfesburge, have willingly granted in perpetual freedom from earthly services to Abbot Aldhelm and his successors thirty cassati on the western side of the public road, and, at another place not far distant, fifteen near Tettan monastery. I have confirmed this my gift with the sign of the sacred cross in my own hand, and have strengthened it by the illustrious consent of favourable men, so that after your death no royal audacity or secular dignity may attempt to break our decree. If anyone wishes to increase and enlarge this gift, may the Lord increase his portion in the book of life. But if anyone, relying on tyrannical power, strives to diminish it, let him know that [Col. 1630B] he will render an account before Christ and the nine orders of angels. This charter of conveyance was written in the year 681 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction nine.”

A nephew of that king through his brother Wulfhere was named Brithwald, of whom I spoke above in the deeds of Bishop Wilfrid. He was not indeed a king in authority, but a sub-king in a certain part of the kingdom. Led by love of God, he gave this noble gift to blessed Aldhelm:

“Things which are determined by the devotion of religious generosity according to the fear and love of the Lord, although speech alone might suffice to proclaim them, must nevertheless, because of the uncertain condition of times to come, be confirmed by public writings and documentary records. Therefore I, Berthwald, king under the rule of the Lord, have decreed, for the salvation of my soul [Col. 1630C] and forgiveness of the sins I have committed, to confer and grant to Abbot Aldhelm a certain land: namely, the land on the eastern side of the river called Thames, beside the ford named Summerford, comprising forty cassati. It is granted upon this condition: that this portion of land may be perpetually free from every service owed to secular powers, for the needs of the monks serving God in the monastery named Maldumesburge. And in order that this gift may be strengthened more firmly and securely, we have also called the most eminent monarch, King Ethelred, as witness; by his consent and confirmation this generosity was enacted. If anyone attempts to act against this gift or, relying on tyrannical power, invades it, let him know that in the terrible judgment of all he will render an account before Christ. Done publicly in synod beside Bregford ford, in the month of July, on the thirtieth day of that month, indiction thirteen, in the year 685 from the Incarnation of the Lord.”

The subscribers to these three documents were Theodore, archbishop; Ethelred, king of the Mercians; Berthwald, sub-king; Kenfrith, patrician; and Sexwulf, bishop of Lichfield, and Bosel, bishop of Worcester.

At the same time Kentwin, king of the West Saxons, weighed down by illness and old age, had appointed as his successor Cædwalla, a young man of royal stock. Though not yet king or Christian, he nevertheless anticipated the kingdom in hope and sought baptism in faith. Therefore he rejoiced to be called king; and, while generously granting many things to monasteries around him, he liberally provided for this monastery, as is made clear by this document. [Col. 1631A] . . . .

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: all things which are seen are temporal, and those which are not seen are eternal (2 Cor. 4:18). Again, the slippery frailty of this age is shown, for the same Apostle says: ‘We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing away’ (1 Tim. 6:7). Therefore the eternal crown of the heavenly diadem must be acquired with perishable and earthly things. Wherefore I, Cædwalla, king under the rule of the Lord, had decreed to confer and grant a certain land to Abbot Aldhelm for the salvation of my soul and the forgiveness of my sins: namely, on both sides of the wood named Cemele; on the eastern side, from the boundary of the roads as far as the famous [Col. 1631B] river called Thames, one hundred and forty manentes; and, in another place, where the two rivers Avon and Wylye meet, especially for the enjoyment of fishing. Thus may this grant remain firm and immovable for future generations, so that no one may presume to break the privilege of this donation. But if anyone, puffed up by tyrannical power, attempts to act against this generosity, let him know that he incurs the obstacle of God’s wrath and will render an account at the last judgment before Christ and his angels. This grant was written in the year 688 from the Incarnation, in the month of August, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the indiction [number omitted].”

In the same year he exchanged part of these lands with a certain Baldred for others which appeared both richer in revenue and more convenient of access. Yet by some event, although Cædwalla’s gift remained valid during his lifetime, the exchange was annulled after several years. This, then, is the charter of exchange:

“In the name of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, I, Baldred, have decreed to grant a certain land to Abbot Aldhelm: namely, a hundred manentes beside the river Avon and around the wood called Stercanley and Cnebbanburge; and in exchange I received from him a hundred cassati, namely, on the eastern side of the wood called Bradon. This was strengthened by the counsel and confirmation of King Kentwin and all his princes and senators. If anyone attempts to act against these provisions, let him know that he will render an account before the judgment seat of Christ the Judge and before the holy angels. This grant—or rather reciprocal exchange—was written in the month of August, indiction one, in the year 1188 from the Incarnation of Christ.” [The date is evidently problematic as printed.]

Hedda, bishop of Winchester, King Kentwin, Cessa, and Cenred—the father of Ina, afterwards king—subscribed to these two charters.

In King Cædwalla, after Kentwin, I see energy in worldly affairs and piety toward God. Bede has related more fully how, after defeating his enemies and gaining the kingdom, he went to Rome and was baptized there, happily meeting his final destiny; we have touched upon it in our *History of the Kings*. When he went to Rome, the kingdom was renewed through Ina. Ina was a unique example of courage, an image of prudence, and one could not find his equal in religion. His wars which he brought to an end are evidence; the monasteries which he built are testimony. These royal qualities of mind were encouraged by the exhortations [Col. 1632A] of Father Aldhelm, whose precepts Ina heard humbly, esteemed highly, and fulfilled effectively. At Aldhelm’s urging he founded for Christ the monastery of Glastonbury, as I said in the *Deeds of the Kings*; nor did he bring lands of small value to Meldun, following up his gifts with liberal written charters, of which this is one.

“In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, I, Ina, king of the Saxons under the Lord’s rule, considering the reward of eternal life and fearing the everlasting punishments of hell, have decreed, for the remedy of my soul and the remission of my sins, to give some portion of land [Col. 1632B] to the venerable Abbot Aldhelm, for the enlargement of his monastery called Malmesbury: namely, forty-five hides in the places named below by the inhabitants; that is, five holdings in the place called Iserdum; and there rises the stream called Consuburtia; twenty hides there, and ten in another place beside the same stream, and ten beside the watercourse called Redburna. And this was done in the year 701 from the Incarnation of Christ, in the fourteenth indiction.” Bishop Hedda subscribed, as did Winberht, the king’s clerk, who had drawn up both this charter and Cædwalla’s other grants; Aldhelm had formerly invited him by this letter, in order to secure him as his patron with Cædwalla:

“To Winberht, lord most dearly beloved in the Lord of lords, Aldhelm, servant of the servants of God, sends everlasting salvation in the corner-stone [Col. 1632C] of the two Testaments, cut from the lofty mountain peaks (Dan. 2): he who crushed to its legs the statue fashioned from four kinds of metal, signifying four kingdoms of peoples, though it had a golden head.”

“We have sent a bearer of letters into the presence of your piety, who will explain to you more fully in person the matter of our pressing necessity: namely, the land which the venerable elder Baldred offered us for possession on receipt of payment, especially because it is a suitable and convenient place for the catching of fish. And therefore, since it appears to have been granted and conveyed within the power of our king, we earnestly ask that, through the patronage of your charity, we may be able securely to obtain and hold that same portion of land, lest, deprived of that possession by force, we be defrauded—because [Col. 1632D] the claims of justice often waver—and so forth.”

These are the estates which the blessed abbot, through his own exertions, added to the monastery: pleasant in situation, agreeable in extent, convenient in proximity. Thus anyone leaving the monastery at dawn may easily go round them all in one day and still return home while daylight is full. After his death, indeed, some persons gave some things; but robbers took everything except these, though they also snatched away part of these. Thus through Aldhelm the place grew to four hundred hides and more, though it had scarcely sixty before. For the estate now called Brockenborough, adjoining the place containing the monastery, is reckoned at that many hides by the customary designation of country people.

## Part III

[Col. 1633]

[Col. 1633A] Now that, having fulfilled my second promise, we have made no small progress and seem already to hold the middle sea, greater strength is needed, so that, aided not by the winds of talent but by those of the Holy Spirit, we may drive the ship to the shore of silence. Here certainly I shall disappoint the reader’s expectation, if anyone supposes that I shall prove by ancient written testimony the miracles I am about to insert. Yet, though I lack that support, I bind myself to the truth by a confident assurance. For I shall relate only those things which the favor of the whole community recounts, drawn down from ancient times. I shall relate what the common assent of the people of the province maintains, transmitted to posterity through uninterrupted succession. Divinity implanted them in human minds in place of written records, lest the deeds wonderfully performed through the saint should perish uselessly [Col. 1633B]. They ought not, therefore, to appear to come from nothing, since through successive generations they are proclaimed by all the people.

But if anyone thinks I deserve censure because I write what I have heard rather than seen, let him summon to judgment, and call into the same accusation, the illustrious Fathers and eminent heroes who did the same: Luke in the Gospel and Gregory in the Dialogues. If such conduct is judged presumptuous, why, I ask, should I not be permitted in a small matter what was permitted to them in a great one? Nor are these accounts wholly without eyewitness authority, since we saw them impressed in the silver of an ancient shrine by the kind of workmanship called relief carving (*anaglyphum*). Trusting, then, in this excuse, I shall carry through what I have begun, even in rustic speech. Love for the saint will lessen the charge of presumption: so that he who dislikes the eloquence may be pleased by the subject.

After he became a monk, we learn that he lived thus. He applied himself frequently to reading and earnestly to prayer, so that, as he himself said in a certain letter, by reading he might hear God speaking, and by praying might speak with God. Feeding his mind through voluntary spareness of food, never leaving the monastery except of necessity, and by no means greedy for money, he immediately assigned to suitable uses whatever was given. Moreover, in order to break the force of his rebellious body, he immersed himself to the shoulders in the spring nearest the monastery. There, caring neither for the freezing severity of winter nor for the vapors exhaled in summer from marshy places, he passed the nights unharmed. Only the completion of the Psalm-book he was chanting [Col. 1633D] set a limit to his labor. That spring, named after the saint, flows in gentle bubbling streams in the valley of the monastery and is delightful to see and sweet to drink.

In another part of the town is the spring called Daniel’s, because Daniel kept heavenly vigils there by night; he received episcopal insignia together with Aldhelm. In the midst of these matters, language would almost shrink from describing the man’s outstanding purity of conscience, unless there were occasion for a glorious victory in the deed itself. For whenever he was stirred by the stimulus of the flesh, he not only denied the enticement its effect, but won an otherwise unprecedented triumph. Yet he did not then reject the company of women, as others do who fear an occasion of falling. Rather, whether sitting or lying down, he kept some woman beside him until, with the slippery impulse of the flesh cooled, he departed with a calm and unmoved mind. The devil seems to be mocked when he sees a woman clinging to the man while the man, with his mind turned elsewhere, persists in chanting the Psalter. He bade the woman farewell with modesty intact, she with chastity unharmed. The bodily discomfort subsided; the wicked spirit grieved that he had been made a laughing-stock.

How greatly he fostered the love of celibacy is attested by the distinguished books *On Virginity*, in which he defines its honor, adorns its beauty, and crowns its perseverance. It is not permissible to believe that the holy man acted otherwise than he taught, or lived otherwise than he said. And, that this assertion may remove every offense of doubt, hear how he warned a disciple not to read the wanton poems of poets, not to attach himself to the company of little prostitutes, and not to let the seductive charm of delicate garments effeminize the vigor of his mind.

“To the lord Wilefrid, venerably beloved and delightfully revered, Aldhelm, your humble countryman in Christ, sends everlasting salvation. Rumor-bearers have reported to me of the zeal of your charity that, with the Lord directing you and with eagerness for reading kindled, you have resolved to undertake an overseas journey. Therefore, when—with life as your companion—you attain the desired harbor of Ireland, read above all the most sacred oracles, [Col. 1634C] rejecting the fabricated doctrines of philosophers. For I judge it absurd, after despising the inextricable rule of the New and Old Testament, to pursue one’s way through the slippery bypaths of a thorny field, or rather through the harsh winding paths of philosophers; or, after the clear waters of glassy springs have been covered over, to drink thirstily from muddy pools and stagnant waters, in which a black troop of toads swarms in crowds and the chattering croak of frogs resounds.

“What advantage, I ask, does it bring to the sacrament of orthodox faith to labor diligently by reading and investigation into the violation of foul Proserpina, which it is abhorrent even to mention? Or to revere, with the praise bestowed by reading, Hermione—the wanton offspring of Menelaus and Helen—who, as ancient works report, was formerly betrothed to Orestes by right of dowry, but afterward, when the decision was changed, married Neoptolemus? Or to inscribe in heroic style the history of the priestly leaders of the bacchant Luperci, parasites who sacrifice to Priapus? All these vanished utterly when the serpent was raised upon the summit of the sceptre and set before the gaze of the Hebrew congregation—that is, when, by the blessed death of death, fastened to the wood of the cross, they were destroyed even to the ground.

“Compelled by your richly productive reputation, I ask for your discipleship, kneeling as it were with bowed knees and bent hams: do not in any way visit the brothel-stews, [Col. 1635A] those trifles in which painted prostitutes lurk amidst seductive luxury, adorned like richly caparisoned chariots with gleaming gold anklets and smooth armlets; but rather, despising the lofty magnificence of the palace which patricians and governors enjoy, let your brotherhood happily be content with the humble shelter of a cottage. Likewise, neglecting dyed purple, let your brotherhood, as Christ’s teaching directs, use against the cold blasts of winter that arise from the northern region rather the covering of a slender cloak and the rough, unadorned garment of a *mastruca*.”

Thus holiness of conduct issued in the fruit of miracles. And, to come to their manifestations, he first appeared for the compassion and correction of the Britons [Col. 1635B]. For the Britons, who had once possessed the whole land now called England, were then subjects of the English. They had rendered this service to those who invited them in: seizing opportunities, they drove from their ancient seats those whom they had come to protect and forced them into rugged and wooded places, where they lived obscurely and half-wild.

Those among them called the North Welsh—that is, the northern Britons—had fallen to the share of the kings of the West Saxons. Formerly diligent in their customary services, they long gave no harsh response. But when they were then plotting rebellion, King Kentwine subdued them with such grievous slaughter that they could hope for nothing further. Therefore the final evil was added to their captivity: the performance of tribute, so that those who had previously grasped even the mere shadow of liberty now openly groaned beneath the yoke of subjection.

The unhappy people were also burdened by an error in sacred belief: living, as it were, outside the world, they obeyed their own traditions rather than Roman ones. They accepted many other Catholic doctrines, but especially rejected this: the celebration of the Paschal feast on the lawful day. Neither drawn by the harmonious custom of the universal Church nor corrected by the admonitions of the most blessed Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury, they fostered an obstinate controversy. Hence frequent assemblies of West Saxons and repeated councils were convened to determine what ought to be done so that the Britons, now converted anew, might enter the right path of ecclesiastical observances. The question was debated for many days amid a great array of words [Col. 1635D], and came to this conclusion: schismatics were not to be compelled by force but led by arguments. Therefore everything capable of overturning their errors or meeting their stubbornness was to be committed to writing, so that, persuaded by the arguments of those letters, they might amend their minds. Nothing, they thought, could prevent this if Abbot Aldhelm would deem the erring worthy of his admonition. It suited his life to be willing, and his learning to be able, to remove from anyone whatever long-standing disease of unbelief.

Thus the most blessed man was besought by the prayers of all to devote this labor to the conversion of schismatics, the honor of his country, and the common salvation of all. He undertook the charge prompted by charity from brotherly hearts, and his effectiveness in accomplishing it was no less than his obedience in undertaking it [Col. 1636A]. Thus he refuted the false Easter; thus he taught the true one. His discourse was seasoned with the special testimonies of the Gospel, and a shower of patristic assertions followed the thunderbolt of unanswerable reason. Having completed the work with the highest praise, he sent it to the Britons, adding prayers to God, so that for those to whom he gave words he might also multiply petitions. For this is the twofold diligence of an ecclesiastical steward: correction must not be absent from his mouth in order to amend those who wander, nor prayer sleep in his heart. Nor could the labor of this most holy man be deprived of its effect; rather, reaching a praiseworthy conclusion, it converted those in error to true religion. To this day the Britons owe their correction to Aldhelm, although, through their inborn perversity, they neither acknowledge the man nor have preserved the book, but have destroyed it [Col. 1636B].

As I have said, the chief church of the monastery was Saint Peter’s; nevertheless, since a mind of noble industry does not know how to impose holidays upon its work, he intended to build another church within the precinct of the same monastery in honor of Mary, Mother of God. Accordingly he built the church, and beside it another adjoining church in honor of Saint Michael, traces of which we have seen. For the entire structure of the larger church, renowned and unimpaired, endured even into our age, surpassing in beauty and size everything which antiquity was seen to have made anywhere in England.

For the more elaborate construction of this temple, after the stone flooring had been laid, a supply of timber was gathered without any sparing of expense [Col. 1636C], the saint urging it more earnestly, that he might please the Lord through ready service. They had now come to the framing of the beams. These had been bought at great cost, and the difficulty of transport over so long a journey had increased their price. All had been cut to one measure except one, which, by its shortness, had defeated the skill of the workmen—whether through their carelessness, or, as I would rather believe, through the will of God, so that the holiness of the distinguished man might shine forth.

Too late, then, the laborers noticed the loss caused by the felled tree. At first they muttered among themselves, then reported the matter to Aldhelm. He bore their fault calmly, though he was somewhat troubled by the difficulty of replacing the material. For he had provided no surplus remedy, and to bring timber again seemed an immense task. Therefore, despairing of human help, he placed his hope in God and resolved to correct the matter quickly. He was moved to perform a miracle, since he had already begun to give many proofs of miraculous power, though secretly, lest the breath of popular favor should shake down the most holy flowers of his conscience. So, praying only by the movement of his lips and exerting a slight effort with his arms, he made the shortened beam equal in length to the others. Then, in order to conceal the miracle, he modestly reproached the workmen for joking with him about damage to the beams, when the beam lacked nothing in length compared with the others. They applied a measuring line and found the sign and its correction; they blushed joyfully [the transmitted reading *crubuere* is uncertain] and, bearing the sharpness of his words without resentment, rejoiced while concealing that they had been overcome by the saint’s power [Col. 1637A]. Raised with the others to the roof by a rope machine, it completed the framing.

Our elders gave a truthful account of this beam: that even in the two fires which consumed the whole monastery in the times of Kings Alfred and Edward, it suffered no injury, until at last it gave way, overcome by years and decay.

The monastery had now risen; the adjoining basilica of Blessed Mary shone more brightly; and Aldhelm could be seen and called happy—the patron of so many monks and lord of so many possessions. But with the far-reaching gaze of prudence, he thought that provision must be made against events to come. He resolved in his mind to go to Rome. The reason for going was to obtain apostolic privileges for his monasteries, especially for Malmesbury, which, having arisen through the generosity of Bishop Leutherius, might fall into the calumnies of successors [Col. 1637B]. As I have said, foreseeing these with prophetic eye, he considered how either to repel or weaken them.

Having therefore consulted King Ina of the West Saxons and Æthelred of the Mercians, whose friendship he enjoyed and whose generosity was eminent, and since they did not dissent from the plan, he entered upon the Roman road. Yet, in order to arrange necessary matters more freely, he went to estates under his jurisdiction in the district of Dorset. There, while awaiting favorable weather, he built a church in which, while his companions were occupied with necessities, he might commend his journey out and return to God. The materials of this building still remain, open to the sky and without a roof [Col. 1637C], except that something projects above the altar to protect the sacred stone from the filth of birds. Yet however great the force of rains raging outside all around, not a drop falls within the bounds of the church. The shepherds who tend livestock in the nearby fields regard this no longer as a miracle but as customary fact. Whenever a storm threatens downfall with the fleece of clouds thickening, the whole crowd of country folk gathers there in flight; standing within the church’s enclosure under the open sky, they feel no rain.

Moved by this miracle, the leading men of the district more than once attempted to put a roof on the building, wishing to render their service to the saint. But, having found their efforts futile, they stopped, understanding that the saint was pleased by the rainwater—read *proluvium*, not “prelude”—through which he repeatedly displayed a miracle [Col. 1637D]. The abundance of signs there draws the people yearly to his feast; and there are frequent offerings of gifts and manifestations of cures, as many as even in the place where his most sacred bones are venerated. I believe that by this God indicates that the glory of his body ought to suffice more than enough for the people of Malmesbury, provided only that they do not begrudge others the presence of his miracles.

But, as I had begun to say, after overcoming the dangers of the sea and conquering the difficulties of the long journey, he came to Rome. At that time Sergius was bishop of the supreme see. He received the arrival of this distinguished man with fitting courtesy and fostered his pilgrimage in episcopal fashion. What stirred the bishop’s reverence for the abbot was that his learning seemed not to differ from the devotion of his life, nor his teaching to disagree with his conduct. Favorable divinity nourished the fragrance of his good reputation, exalting its servant in so great a city by the renown of his virtues.

There is in Rome an assembly hall called the Lateran, where the Emperor Constantine made, from his own palace, a patriarchal residence for the apostolic bishops. There Aldhelm, staying with the pope, enjoyed his kindly companionship, and allowed no day to pass without singing Mass, by whose solemnities he might alleviate the weariness of pilgrimage and commend himself and his people to God. One day, after he had done this as usual and Mass had been said, he threw behind his back the vestment called a chasuble, mistakenly thinking that someone was standing ready to receive it—his mind, of course, cast elsewhere, and still full of divine ecstasy [Col. 1638B]. The inattentive attendant was searching for something at another side of the altar. But “he who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps” (Ps. 120:4), and, when human service failed, he displayed his own wonders. Immediately a bright ray of sun flashed through the transparency of the glass window; slipping beneath the chasuble, it carried it through the air, suspended some distance above the ground.

Who can recount how great the cry of the people was there, when they saw nature serving the servant of Christ contrary to nature? Rightly so: since he always weighed his mind in the heavens, his garment was suspended in the air; and the void became solid at his service, because, scorning all earthly things as transient and perishable, he longed only for heavenly things. This garment—whether brought with him from England, or lent there for the occasion, is uncertain—is still kept among us [Col. 1638C]. The vestment conscious of so great a miracle is guarded most diligently, the custodians omitting no care so that it may delight the eyes of succeeding generations without blemish. It is of very delicate fabric, having taken on a crimson color saturated with dyes from shellfish; and black roundels contain pictured figures of peacocks. Its great length teaches us that the saint was of tall stature. The bones of his arms and the other remains which we have been permitted to see likewise attest that Aldhelm once grew to such a build as we may define not as bulk, but as worthy height of body.

He stayed in Rome, and the Lord continued the grace of miracles in his servant, repeatedly bringing forward occasions by which he might exalt one beloved to himself [Col. 1638D]. In due course there occurred an affair which gave occasion for a second miracle. A child had just been born in the house of one of the pope’s chamberlains; and a rumor spread noisily among the people that a woman who had professed religion, changed her clothing, and veiled her head, had given birth, while no father was known. The bishop was accused of the crime, no longer on doubtful suspicion but by public outcry, because it was said that the woman used to visit and converse privately with him. Such is the familiar misery of mortals: anyone wounded by any misfortune is at once made the object of everyone’s hatred. Then he is called guilty of every crime and deserving of every cross.

Thus the madness of the crowd pressed the praiseworthy bishop with suspicions and defamed him with cries—a man than whom none was ever keener or readier in letters, more upright and sound in faith, or holier and more perfect in life [Col. 1639A]: a man who did all that he called holy and Catholic, and whom fear of no earthly power oppressed. Indeed, he openly condemned by a pronounced judgment the emperor of Constantinople when he spoke against the Catholic faith, and involved in the same peril the consenting magnates unless they repented. Other writings will teach anyone wishing to know how many letters he wrote and how many labors he suffered on this account.

I return to Aldhelm. Deeply grieved in spirit by the bishop’s injury, he pleaded the unsettled case before the people with all the strength of eloquence he could command. It was shameful and pitiable, he said, that they should assail their own bishop with suspicion of crimes. What authority would the bishop of Rome have among the Britons or any nation lying beyond the Ocean, if he were attacked by his own citizens? Finally, it did not seem true that a man who remembered himself set over the whole world would entangle himself in the mire of such a sin.

While he poured these words into the air—for a popular disturbance once raised could not readily be calmed—the bishop, somewhat stirred by consciousness of his holiness, said: “Bring the infant, that by its own mouth it may repel the injury done to the bishop. Let them therefore abandon their foolish suspicions and return to the favor of their bishop; for my own part, I shall not fail the cause of peace insofar as it concerns me.” Some received the statement with laughter, since the foreigner seemed to promise unusual things and presume unwarranted ones. Nevertheless, when the infant had been brought, scarcely nine days from its mother, he first renewed it in the washing of baptism [Col. 1639C]. He then publicly asked whether the common report concerning the father accorded with truth. Then, so that you might see God’s grace present, the little child made an effort toward perfectly articulate speech and broke the knot of doubt: Sergius was holy and undefiled, and had never had intercourse with the woman.

The people applauded the miracle. The innocent bishop celebrated a triumphant victory. Rome exalted Aldhelm’s merit; and the reflected and repeated shout of those rejoicing shook the very stars. Yet when asked, since he had cleared the falsely accused father from infamy, also to identify the real father for public knowledge, he refused. He declared that it was his office, insofar as he could, to free the innocent from harm, not to crush the guilty with death.

Greatly delighted by such proofs of miraculous power, the bishop did not make himself difficult to entreat, but granted to the monasteries for which he was asked a privilege of carefully wrought authority. I shall set it down here in full, so that all doubt may be removed concerning how many curses bind, and how many punishments await, those who now suppose they may violate and transgress it with impunity [Col. 1639D].

“Sergius, servant of the servants of God, to Abbot Aldhelm and his successors, and through you to your venerable monastery. Those things which, in view of religious life, are bestowed upon monks, servants of God, for the freedom to live freely, are granted by the bishops and guardians of the Christian religion decreed by God—not for license to indulge pleasures, but for the diligence of good conduct and, without doubt, for dedicating themselves to divine service. Thus, released from the bond of human condition and made immune from every burden of secular duties, as the rule of their profession declares, they may devote themselves wholly to God and attend only to his service. For reverence toward his majesty they are free not only from the burdens of temporal jurisdictions, but are also worthy of the highest honor through love of religion.

“Therefore, since your religious community has asked us, in the place of our author, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—to whom our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, deigned to grant the keys of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, and whose ministry we, though unworthy, perform, and whose Church we govern by God’s favor—to strengthen by apostolic privileges the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, founded by Meldum of religious memory, now called Malmesbury [Col. 1640B], situated in the province of Saxony, and the other monastery in the same province, dedicated in honor of Saint John the Baptist and situated beside the river called Frome. By the truthful report of many, we have learned that you prudently govern these establishments with God’s aid; and we grant the request of your devout petition.

“We exhort you to be diligent and watchful in the praises of God and in prayers; to cling firmly to abstinence, chastity, and purity; to be devoted to the offices of hospitality and kindness; to show yourselves loving adherents of Christ’s obedience and humility; to be united among yourselves in devout charity; to preserve unimpaired the rectitude of apostolic faith by serving spiritual commands and the rules of the holy Fathers; to apply yourselves to good pursuits; to offer kindness to strangers and the needy; to render due reverence to bishops and priests of the churches of God; to devote yourselves to God, fleeing worldly cares and gains; to love moderation and poverty; to enter into converse with God by psalms, spiritual hymns, and constant prayers; to practice abstinence as the purification of the body in every pursuit of life; to encourage one another in all God’s commandments; to be solicitous for your own salvation and to emulate those advancing toward better things; to trust in God’s protection; and to keep yourselves unstained not only from carnal pollution but also from harmful words and thoughts, so that the chastity and sobriety of both your body and your spirit may shine before God’s eyes [Col. 1640D], and so that the inward person may be illumined by the grace of virtue while the outward person obtains the praise and reputation of good conduct.

“Since the benefit of episcopal indulgence is due to such persons, we decree that the aforesaid venerable monasteries be protected by these present apostolic privileges: so that they may now be, and remain forever, under the jurisdiction and protection of the same blessed Peter the Apostle, our author, whom we also serve, and of the Church which we administer, as your religious community has requested; and that they be subject to no other jurisdiction. Let no bishop, priest, or cleric of any ecclesiastical rank presume at any time to claim any jurisdiction over them, or extort or demand receptions or any gifts from the religious community [Col. 1641A]; nor let anyone establish an episcopal chair in their oratory or celebrate the solemnities of Mass there, except when invited by the religious abbot and congregation.

“If they need to have a priest ordained for the solemnities of Mass, or a deacon, let them ask the most reverend neighboring bishop to consecrate him, provided only that he examines under divine judgment those matters which belong to the sacred rule and ordains without payment of a fee. If the religious abbot should die and the election of another become necessary, let the person whom the religious congregation of God’s servants chooses by common counsel be promoted immediately, so that the discipline of monastic life may suffer no loss and the possessions of the monastery may not perish through lack of an abbot. The neighboring bishop likewise shall, by authority of the apostolic bishop, confer upon him the prayer of abbacy.

“If any bishop, priest, cleric of any ecclesiastical order, or even layperson of whatever rank, should attempt to transgress or rashly violate these decrees established by us under divine judgment, let him know himself guilty before the sight of God and excluded from participation in the saving body and blood of the Lord. Let him incur the condemnation which Judas Iscariot received, and let him be struck down by the prince of the apostles as Ananias and Sapphira were, unless he repents of the rash presumption he has begun. But life, salvation, and eternal blessedness be to those who preserve these things and command their preservation. Fare well, most beloved brothers [Col. 1641C].”

Exulting in the privilege of this document, and at the same time supported by the bishop’s blessing and the pledges of holy relics, Aldhelm vigorously undertook the homeward journey. He carried with him many valuable foreign wares, which he brought as a new and wonderful abundance to his homeland. Among them was an altar of shining marble, white in color, a foot and a half thick, four feet long, and three palms broad, beautifully enclosed all round by a projecting rim of the same stone. A camel, it is said—for what animal of our country could bear so great a weight?—carried it as far as the Alps, and bore it unharmed. There the camel, or whatever four-footed animal it was—for it makes no difference which beast carried it—collapsed, either through injury from the unjust load [Col. 1641D] or because of the steep descents of the road. The fall crushed the beast and broke the marble into two parts. While his companions groaned over the loss of both, the saint repaired it by the secret murmur of his heart and the outstretched blessing of his right hand. Strength of health was restored to the animal, which at once shook itself with lively movement and stood on its feet. The fracture of the stone, which had cracked not in a straight line but in a winding break, immediately united again into solidity. Yet, lest the memory of the marvelous sign should fade, the scar of the split remains visible to this day: healed indeed by miracle, but discernible to the attentive eye.

Sorrow fell away and the journey was resumed. Thus, with all his company safe, he came to the sea separating Gaul and England. There, received into the calm bosom of a ship, he crossed the sea successfully and favorable fortune restored him to the longing of his compatriots [Col. 1642A]. Everywhere a great company came out to meet him, with a long procession of greeting. Some of the religious made the air sweet with harmonious song; others bore before them the divine wood; others filled the roads with fragrant incense. Some of the laity beat out dances with their feet; others revealed inward joy by diverse movements of their bodies. All together praised God, who had brought back the light of Britain, which had long since sent its wandering rays across other lands.

Nor did royal grandeur exclude Ina and Æthelred—one prince of the West Saxons, the other of the Mercians—from this rejoicing. For to their old love for the man had now been added reverence for apostolic salutations. Received, therefore, with great joy and a display of humble veneration, he showed the privileges of his monasteries to both kings. Reason required this: what stood by the gifts of both ought to be confirmed by the consent of both. Royal devotion immediately responded to the bishop’s words, and did not delay to carry out his commands with the ready step of obedience [Col. 1642B].

Although the princes worthy of remembrance would not have found this difficult to do because of their natural graciousness, Aldhelm nevertheless, to make assurance doubly sure, elicited their voluntary consent through offerings of great gifts. He gave different things to each, but gave the altar to Ina. Ina placed it in service of the most holy Mother of God in a village then called Briwecane. There it remains to this day, offering, as it were, living proof of Aldhelm’s holiness [Col. 1642C]. There too is another, larger church in Saint Peter’s name, which tradition confidently maintains was built and consecrated by the blessed man. The eastern front of this church was lately extended further by the ambition of a new construction. In this manner, as I have said, the praiseworthy undertaking assumed for the honor of holy Church advanced. And he himself was by then advancing day by day toward old age.

Editorial and textual readings: at Iserdum, *ibi* (“there”) is corrected to *ubi* (“where”); *Hic* (“this”) to *haec* (“these”) in the introduction to the estates; corrupt *vavor* to *favor* (“favor, approval”) of the whole community; *villa* (“estate”) to *villa quae* (“the estate which”); *tunc* (“then”) to *tamen* (“nevertheless”); corrupt *rintugerulis* to *rumigerulis* (“rumor-bearers”); *rudis* (“rough”) is glossed *i. e. Novi* (“that is, [of the] New [Testament]”); *gurgitii* to *gurgustii* (“cottage”); masculine *falerati* (“caparisoned”) to feminine *faleratae*, agreeing with the women; *Northwallos* to *Northwalli* (“North Welsh”); *Hic* (“here”) to *hinc* (“hence”); *ducit* (“leads”) to *desit* (“be absent”); *in* (“in”) to *et* (“and”); *videbatur* (“seemed”) to *videbat* (“saw”); *curia* (“court”) to *incuria* (“carelessness”); *animadvertis* (“you notice”) to *animadvertentes* (“noticing”); and *proludium* (“prelude”) to *proluvium* (“rainwater, runoff”). In the papal privilege, *pro* (“for”) is editorially supplied in “for which [*pro quibus*] he was asked.”

Indeed, after some intervening span of years, Hedda, bishop of all Wessex, whose see was at Winchester, departed this world.
