His death was most welcome to the heavenly beings, because by the holiness of his past life he increased their number; mournful to mortals, because they could scarcely find his equal willing to govern the extent of so great a diocese. For what four bishops now govern, that one man then controlled, repressing the rebellious by authority and soothing the suppliant by gentleness. Therefore, by synodal counsel, the diocese, extended beyond measure, was divided into two sees: one at Sherborne, the other at Winchester. That division was unfair and unequal: one was to govern only two districts, the other all that the vast extent of Wessex contains. Bishops were appointed to the individual sees according to their merit in learning and the region of their birth. Daniel, a native of that country and not lacking in letters, was placed over Winchester. Aldhelm received Sherborne: the preeminence of his wisdom and the maturity of his age raised him toward a higher summit, while affection for his native land also supported him, since he was a native of that province. Thus, as is believed, a universal election proceeded under God’s guidance; and the most blessed old man was pressed to deign to accept the bishopric. The judgment of every age and rank agreed that he seemed worthy of the episcopate: mature through advanced age, rich in learning, and inferior to none in religion. But if you think noble birth should be considered—though the blessed Apostle does not introduce it in such matters—who was nobler than one closely connected by lineage with the royal house? His reputation and his life had always been such that no even slightly adverse report had ever been circulated concerning him.

He resisted as far as he could, diligently raising whatever objections might support his refusal or weaken their unanimity. But he laboured in vain, since he was refuted by the very argument he had prepared for himself. This was his weight of years: as one looking toward the nearby finishing-line, old age, he ought to rest in gentle leisure rather than engage in perilous business. But those who heard him at once turned this into another argument: the more mature he was in years, the more purified from vices and the readier in counsel he was. He therefore observed moderation and resisted as long as reason seemed to require. But when he saw their unanimous and lasting agreement aflame, he loosened the reins of his own life to fraternal obedience, fearing to resist the divine oracle which had united all their hearts and filled all their mouths. Thus the bishops received a colleague, the clergy a father, and the laity a patron.

[Col. 1643C] Then, amid universal acclamation and no objection, he was led to be consecrated in the customary manner by B[.....]rthwald, archbishop of the primary see. The latter, embracing graciously the election of his companion from their former fellowship—for they had studied letters together and together trodden the path of religion—increased his favour. Thus he not only granted consecration, but kept him with himself for many days, lightening the burden of his archbishopric by Aldhelm’s counsel and examining the reasoning of cases.

It happened that in these days he went to Dover [now called Devoram], a shore twelve miles from Canterbury, having heard that ships had put in there. The harbour, like most maritime places, was dangerous because narrow. From there the sea-crossing is very swift, a passage of very few miles. [Col. 1643D] Hence, in the narrowness of that space, waves running against and colliding with one another make the sea rough on the slightest occasion; and danger is greatest where escape from dangers was hoped for. But once ships have been received into harbour, there is rest secure against any storm. I have mentioned this because it pertains to the matter I shall relate.

The saint was walking by the sea and fixed his eyes attentively upon the merchandise, to see whether the sailors, who had come from the Gallic gulf into England and brought a supply of books, had brought anything perhaps useful for ecclesiastical purposes. Seeing a book containing the whole course of the Old and New Testaments, he turned his attention away from everything else in order to buy it. As, knowledgeable in such matters, he turned the leaves and pressed about the price, barbarian sailors assailed him with insults in their nautical wantonness. [Col. 1644A] Why did he disparage another’s wares and diminish the value of things that were not his? Let him examine his own goods if he wished; let him leave others’ goods at their own price. Against the insolence of these words he returned nothing but laughter. Finally, while he was still asking the price of the book, they drove him from the place with disgrace and, stretching their ropes, moved farther from shore.

But divine vengeance, which did not delay long, more sharply avenged the injury done to the saint. A storm rose, a whirlwind raged, cloud thickened, daylight was withdrawn, and the gloom of sea and terror of air brought on night. The fury of the winds and the creaking of the ropes redoubled the terror. The yard could not withstand the violence of the storm; the ship’s side was battered here by pounding waves. The skill of the rowers failed; the sailors’ expertise collapsed. And now they were going to the bottom [*pessum*, for printed *pessimum*]; all the elements seemed to have conspired for the death of the wretches. Then understanding came even upon their brutish minds: they were paying the penalty for insulting the saint whom they had reviled. [Col. 1644B] They cried out in lamentation and stretched suppliant hands toward the shore. They begged for help and promised amendment.

It was easy for the blessed bishop to remit their fault, since he had not been hurt by their insult. First, by extending the sign of the cross against the raging blasts, he somewhat diminished and calmed the storm. Soon, after he had boarded a small boat and, by the strength of its rowers, approached those in peril, all things changed for the better: the entire storm fell calm, the whirlwind subsided, the force of the winds turned and drove the ship toward shore; the waves which had threatened destruction now gently gliding in promised [Col. 1644C] obedience. Having therefore gained the desired sand of the anchorage, the sailors freely offered the book: let him receive it without payment; let him deign to accept the gift of servants whom he had brought from the very jaws of death onto dry land. He placed the price in the middle, weighing it fairly, so that he might neither strip poor men through great loss nor reject the prayers of suppliants. That volume is still seen at Malmesbury, displaying a venerable token of antiquity.

Thus newly possessed of his office, he returned to his province; and, while matching his title with its duties in all things, he devoted himself especially to the liberties of monasteries. His seat was at Sherborne, where he splendidly constructed a church which I too have seen. At first, fearing the uncertainty of human life, when he wished to place abbots over his monasteries, the monks opposed this intention by the barrier of their accustomed Father’s sweetness. He committed the tenor of this affair to writing, lest it should lapse and lest successors should turn necessity into tyranny, threatening destruction under divine obligation upon those who would not obey. The text of that document is as follows:

> “Nothing in this world enjoys lasting happiness; nothing possesses enduring dominion; nothing is not stretched forward by the course of place toward the fated end of life. Therefore we must enjoy the possessions of worldly things in such a way that we are never defrauded of the benefits of the eternal homeland. Accordingly I, Aldhelm, after divine grace had raised me to the seat of the episcopal office, though undeserving and proved worthy by scarcely any merits, resolved in the secret affection of my mind that I should appoint over my monasteries—over which, long established in the rank of abbot, I had regularly presided with the Lord’s support—a religious abbot, chosen by the unanimous voice of the voluntary election of my communities, according to canonical rule and regular observance. Against these voluntary proposals of mine the pious obstinacy of my monks resists.
>
> “And although I had diligently and repeatedly declared this confidently in the assembly of my brethren, none gives a most willing assent to these wishes of mine, saying: ‘So long as you are quickened by the breath of life and are assigned with us to the course of this present life, we do not disdain always to submit our most humble necks to the yoke of your rule. But we beg and entreat this with humble prayer and common petition: that under the solemn testimony of the Scriptures and the manifest agreement of favourable men you confirm that, after your death, neither royal boldness nor episcopal authority, nor any man of ecclesiastical or secular rank, may claim lordship over us without the decision of our own will.’
>
> [Col. 1645B] “To this fitting petition of my monks, and especially of the servants of God, I most willingly consented. In the monastery situated beside the river called Winburna, over which Cuthburh, sister of our venerable king, presides, I confirmed by the sign of the holy cross the most proper devotion of the profession presented and the petition of the Lord’s household servants, with the desirable consent of the most famous King Ine and the approval of my most reverend brother and fellow bishop Daniel. Likewise, the venerable king and the aforementioned bishop subscribed with equal hand of devotion. Not long afterward, in the most sacred council assembled, as is known, beside the river called Noodr [read *esse*, ‘to have been’], the authority of all the archimandrites of the Saxon people also consented, with the assent of royal power and the approval of episcopal precedence.
>
> “[Col. 1645C] If anyone should devise any plot against these decrees of such illustrious persons and presume to violate the sacred enactments of this present charter, let him know that before the dreadful throne of the divine Majesty he will be struck, together with the transgressors of the Lord’s commands, by the mournful judgment of condemnation. The names of the monasteries are Malmesbury, Frome, and Bradford. The charter of this confirmation was written in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 705, in the third indiction.”

King Ine, Bishop Daniel, and Æthelfrith the patrician subscribed.

Although, therefore, he seemed by this charter to have provided for his monasteries and warded off the tyranny of successors, his noble mind was not satisfied unless he also made provision for all the churches in Wessex. Accordingly, by pressing the king’s receptive mind with gentle exhortations, he obtained the following edict:

> “In the name of the Lord God our Saviour. I, Ine, king by the Lord’s reign, with the counsel and decree of our bishop Aldhelm, together with the recommendation of all God’s priests and the petition of the monks dwelling in the parish of the Saxons, bestow this abundance upon the churches and confer this dignity of privilege upon the monasteries: that, without hindrance from secular affairs and free from the tribute of fiscal obligations, they may serve God alone with free minds; that, Christ granting aid, they may regularly practise the monastic discipline of the community; and that they may deign to pour out prayers before the presence of the divine Majesty for the stability and prosperity of our kingdom and forgiveness of sins committed, and, diligently performing the offices of prayer in the churches, may strive to intercede for our frailty.
>
> “[Col. 1646A] But if anyone attempts to act against the document of this decree, let him know that he will render an account before Christ and the nine orders of angels at the dreadful judgment. We decree that this decree, willingly granted by us, be observed and confirmed in such manner that, both while we, with life accompanying us and propitious Divinity, govern the helm of the kingdom, and while future successors possess the monarchy by hereditary right of reigning, it may be firmly strengthened by an indissoluble law. For a testimony of greater firmness, we caused princes and senators, judges and patricians, to subscribe. Publicly enacted and confirmed in the place called Eburleagere, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May], in the second indiction, happily in the year 704 from Christ’s Incarnation.”

King Ine subscribed. “I, Aldhelm, servant of the servants of God, have ratified this decree with my own hand.” Abbots and nine nobles also subscribed.

This indefatigable divine bishop was doing these things, not unaware that his end was near. Earthly things had now grown loathsome to him, and he longed for heavenly ones. Therefore he judged it best to complete the course of life by deeds that would bring honour to his memory and benefit and favour to those subject to him. And although his flesh, now exceedingly worn out, refused to bear labour, yet his steadfast mind, now already projecting beyond the world and pressing upon the very gates of heaven, conquered the condition of time. [Col. 1646C] He therefore subjected the frail service of his body, not long afterward to desert his spirit, to spiritual exercises. Continuing preaching by night as by day, diligently travelling through the dioceses, and himself observing fasts and other goods of that kind entirely and no less than in vigorous youth, he led a life pleasing to men and pleasing to God. After four years of episcopacy:

> The worshipper and companion of the Most High withdrew to those above;  
> He exchanges earth for stars, and fields for heaven.  
>
> [Col. 1646D] His breath rises on high; the hospitable earth cherishes his limbs;  
> Each place claims its own deposit.  
>
> Phoebus had twice driven Latona through five days,  
> When, loosed from the coverings of the world, he departed.

There is, in the district of Somerset, an estate called Doulting, where he put off the human being; he had long before given it to the monks of Glastonbury, having stipulated its usufruct. The dwelling that witnessed his death was a wooden church, into which, breathing his last, he ordered himself to be carried, so that there above all he might expire, as the inhabitants today affirm through successive generations. When a monk of Glastonbury had rebuilt this church in stone and caused it to be consecrated in the name of God [printed *die*, perhaps for *Dei*], a little woman, long deprived of both eyes, mingled with the dense crowd. In the sign of faith she broke through the press of people, [Col. 1647A] crying that she should be brought without delay to the altar. She believed that the saint whose basilica was being consecrated would remove a widow’s blindness, since throughout his life he had customarily bestowed solemn alms upon widows. The boldness of her faith drew help from heaven: clear light filled her empty eye-sockets. The miracle performed before the people could not remain hidden, especially because both the person and her calamity were widely known throughout the district. It is established that in the same church there is a stone upon which the saint sat as he was dying; by washing with it, many sick people are known to have entered into health.

Then a heavenly vision shining upon the blessed Egwin, bishop of Worcester, made known to him the death of his companion and commanded him to go to the place. Grieving, and then hastened by the spur of love, he quickly reached Doulting. [Col. 1647B] After offering a prayer for the repose of his soul, he ordered that the body be carried to Malmesbury, in accordance with the saint’s desire and command. He restrained the tears of the mourners by confidence of faith; he hastened the work, himself standing by as the work’s promoter. Thus the blessed remains were borne forth amid a great company going before and following, while each considered himself happier the nearer he was; and it was immense consolation to the companions at least to see the bier, if they could not touch it. For the very appearance and form of the lifeless body greatly relieved grief; the grace that remained and the enduring countenance soothed the eyes.

That funeral procession was celebrated; because of the frequency of miracles, stone crosses were continually set up at intervals of seven miles. [Col. 1647C] At these, many disabled by long-standing diseases approached in faith and, by the force of their prayers, seized swift healing; the signs of miracles remaining down to the present day. Nor should it exceed the faith of hearers that there are nearly as many witnesses of miracles as there are inhabitants of the district. I promptly call the blessed Egwin as the most certain witness, who in a certain writing says, after some other matters:

> “After two years Aldhelm, the religious bishop, passed to Christ. Learning this by revelation, I summoned the brethren and disclosed to my attendants the death of the venerable Father. At swift pace I came to the place where his sacred body lay, situated nearly fifty miles beyond the monastery of Malmesbury, and I brought it to burial and honourably buried it. And I commanded that, in every place where the sacred body had rested during its conveyance, sacred memorials should be erected to God.”

[Col. 1647D] All the crosses remain, and none has suffered injury from age; they are called *Bisceps-tune*, that is, “the bishop’s stones.” One of them may readily be seen in the monks’ cloister.

This matter has reminded me not to pass over what report tells concerning Biscepstune. It is an estate in a valley, to which he is said to have come to fulfil the duty of preaching. While he was sowing discourse among the people, he happened to fix in the ground the ash staff on which he leaned. Meanwhile, by God’s wondrous power, it grew to a remarkable size, quickened with sap, clothed with bark, and put forth [Col. 1648A] the down of leaves and the beauty of branches. The bishop, intent upon his words, was alerted by the people’s cry and looked back. Having worshipped God’s miracle, he left the gift there. From offshoots of the first tree many ash trees sprang up, so that, as I have said, that estate is popularly called “the bishop’s trees.” I have not indeed affirmed these things as certain, but, lest I be accused of having omitted anything, I have not omitted them. I confirm the rest from writings or ancient carvings; and, God being witness, I have added nothing of my own, except perhaps if some word has slipped in for the sake of making the reading more polished. Aldhelm does not need to be supported by falsehoods: so many things concerning him are put forward that invite uncertain belief; so many do not admit dispute. The countless signs now performed at his memorial show those present the holiness of his past life.

Meanwhile the men of Malmesbury received their patron with immense weeping and reverent affection. Veneration was joined to love, and faith contended with devotion. One would not know which to choose: feeling for a parent or joy for an advocate. They rejoiced for their patron sent ahead to God, yet were compelled to grieve for the consolation of life they had lost. After several days had passed amid these conflicting emotions, they at last allowed him to be buried in the church of Saint Michael, where the most holy man had long before provided for his own burial.

> [Note: [Col. 1647D] He died, having exercised the episcopate scarcely four years, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 709, on the vigil of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May]. WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY, book I, *De gestis regum Anglorum*, fol. 7.]

He died in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 709, eighteen years before Ine, twenty-five before Bede, thirty-four after he was made abbot by Leutherius, and in the fifth year after he was made bishop by Berthwald. [Col. 1648C] No writing has recorded his age in calculation; but there is a reliable conjecture that he had become old, since he remained in ecclesiastical office for somewhat less than thirty-four years and, especially in that age, could not have assumed the dignity except at lawful age.

That year was grievous for Britain, as one which either extinguished or removed many lights. In the same year Bishop Wilfrid died—of whom the preceding account plainly showed that no one in England was more vigorous or more steadfast for justice. Moreover, Cenred, king of the Mercians and successor of Æthelred, together with Offa, king of the East Angles, went to Rome and completed the course of life. Their company, as I said above, was joined by the fortunate Bishop Egwin; after paying the last rites to blessed Aldhelm, he undertook, entered upon, and traversed that arduous journey, bound in voluntary fetters. [Col. 1648D] But other reading, both mine and that of others, will inform one who wishes to know these matters more fully.

The body of the blessed man lay in the aforementioned church for 246 years. Throughout that whole time, whatever miracles it displayed—neither small nor few, I believe—rival oblivion buried and suppressed them all. In truth, the monks transferred themselves to the church of Saint Mary, so that they might attend more closely and conveniently to their needs at the saint’s mausoleum, although, as we proved by charters, Saint Peter retained precedence throughout all the years down to King Edgar.

## PART IV

[Col. 1649]

[Col. 1649A] Now, with the Lord’s help, I shall proceed to fulfil my fourth promise: to show with what fluctuations of fortune the monastery of Malmesbury grew, and how often it also would have gone to ruin unless the saint had extended help. I shall therefore pursue my purpose through the succession of kings and the presentation of charters.

Æthelheard succeeded Ine for fourteen years; Cuthred succeeded him for the same period. We have his gift written thus:

> “I, Cuthred, king of the Gewisse, compelled by the bond of Christ’s charity and the indivisible affection of love, have, with the consent and knowledge of the eminent Bishop Daniel and of my nobles and dignitaries, for remembrance of their prayers and redemption of my soul, so that I may be placed in the fullness of the Lord’s elect, bestowed with lavish liberality and gladly upon the monastery of Malmesbury a portion of land at the place called Wdecim, assessed at ten hides, to be possessed by an inalienable possession, under the attestation of the Holy Trinity, for Aldhelm the abbot and the community living under the love of his rule.”

And after some further matter:

> “The copy of this grant was promulgated in the year from Christ’s Incarnation 745, in the aforesaid monastery, in the presence of King Cuthred.”

It is clear, therefore, that this was done in the last year of King Cuthred’s life, while Bishop Daniel was still alive; thirty-six years after the death of the same Father, with whom he had been made bishop. Hence it is established that this Abbot Aldhelm, to whom King Cuthred gave Wdecim, was someone other than the great Aldhelm. It is indeed reported that the second Aldhelm was nephew of the first.

Sigebriht succeeded King Cuthred for one year [printed *anno primo*, read *uno*]. Cynewulf, Sigebriht’s successor, ruled for thirty-one years. In the third year of his reign he enriched the monastery with a notable gift:

> “In Christ’s name. I, King Cynewulf, with the consent of the princes, have given in perpetual possession to the community of Christ established in the monastery of Malmesbury a portion of land amounting to about thirty hides, for the remedy of my soul: namely, where the two streams of the Marden and the Rochburn join, and around them, according as the inhabitants themselves are known well to know the boundaries and limits of those places; and also the estate to which belong pastures, dry and watered meadows, and woodland places. These things were done in the year 758 from Christ’s Incarnation, in the eleventh indiction, in the forty-ninth year after the passing of Lord Aldhelm the bishop.”

Cyneard, bishop-elect of Winchester, and Herewald, bishop of Sherborne, subscribed. Against this same King Cynewulf, now in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, Offa, king of the Mercians, waged war over the estate of Bensington and, victorious, usurped both it and a large part of the regions [Col. 1650A] of Wessex. Finally, the hostile robber took away both the estates of the monastery—Ettamunster, which King Æthelred of Mercia had given, and Piritune, which King Cædwalla of Wessex had given. The first he gave to the bishop of Worcester; the second his son Ecgfrith restored by this document:

> “In the name of the Lord. I, Ecgfrith, king of the Mercians, in the first year of the reign granted us by God, at the request of Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons, and Archbishop Æthelheard, have restored to Abbot Cuthbert and the brethren of the monastery of Malmesbury thirty-six hides of land at the place called Ecpirigeam, on the eastern side of the wood called Braden, for forgiveness of my sins and for the repose of the soul of my father Offa, from whom he had taken it from them by poison. And [read *ea*, ‘for that’] [Col. 1650B] I grant the aforesaid land on the condition that it be free from the secular services of kings, to serve the needs of the brethren serving God in the aforesaid monastery, so that our memory may remain forever in that holy place among their holy prayers. But the abbot and brethren of that monastery gave me, in exchange for that land, two thousand solidi of pure silver. I did this with the counsel of my bishops and nobles, whose names are written below. And this was done in the year 796 from Christ’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, in the eighty-seventh year after the passing of Father Aldhelm. May the Lord preserve and bless this my growing alms-gift. But the name of one who diminishes or breaks it—something we do not wish—shall be rooted out from the land of the living and he shall be deprived of the fellowship of the saints, unless he make worthy amendment.”

Æthelheard, archbishop, subscribed. Having first been abbot of Malmesbury and afterward bishop of Winchester, he attained the highest dignity and appointed this Cuthbert abbot at Malmesbury. [lacuna] Beorhtric, king of the West Saxons, subscribed, sixteen years after Cynewulf. Cineberht of Winchester, Benefrith of Sherborne, Hedered of Worcester, and Edulf, bishop-elect of Hereford, subscribed.

Egbert succeeded Beorhtric for thirty-seven years; he subjected all the kingdoms of the English to West Saxon authority, down to the present day. His son Æthelwulf succeeded him for eighteen years; he is indeed called Athulf. A man who, through liberty granted to churches, surpassed all his predecessors and, by a new liberality, even surpassed himself. [lacuna] He also made a shrine in which to place the bones of the holy confessor, with images cast in solid silver on its front. On the back he represented in raised metal the miracles which the narrative has already related. Hence it was thought that this was the book of life in which he had read those things; but it was later lost in the time of the Danes. [Col. 1651A] King Æthelwulf added a crystal canopy to the shrine, upon which his name may be read in letters of gold. Some say that the venerable relics were raised by him; but when we come to that point, we shall follow the more familiar account. Now let us set down the king’s gifts to the monastery:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, the supreme and ineffable Creator of all things: I, Æthelwulf, king of the West Saxons by God’s grace, at the holy and most celebrated Paschal solemnity, for the remedy of my soul and for the prosperity of the kingdom and people entrusted to me by God, completed a salutary plan with bishops, ealdormen, and all my nobles: that I should give a tenth part of the lands throughout my kingdom not only to [Col. 1651B] holy churches but also permit my ministers to possess it in perpetual freedom, so that such a gift might remain fixed and unchangeable, free from every royal service and released from all secular servitude. It pleased Alhstan, bishop of the Church of Sherborne, and Swithun, bishop of the Church of Winchester, that every Saturday the whole community should sing fifty psalms and each priest two masses every week for King Æthelwulf and for the ealdormen consenting to this, etc. This charter was written in the year 854 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second indiction, on Easter Day, in our palace called Wilton. The land pertaining to the church of Malmesbury which we place in freedom is as follows: Piretune, thirty-five hides; Lacot, fifteen; Sutton, five; Corsaburn, five; Cridanville, ten; Kemble, ten; Dantsey, eleven.”

He had, however, made a charter of liberty for the churches alone, which I have omitted here because I included it in the *Deeds of the Kings*.

In the first year of his reign, 844 from the Incarnation, 135 years from the passing of blessed Aldhelm, when he had named these lands pertaining to Malmesbury: Ellendune, thirty hides; Elmhamstede, fifteen; Undecune, ten; Cerlatune, twenty; Toccanham, five; Minti, five; Reodbirnam, ten:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever, I, King Æthelwulf, have given a portion of the land of the Gewisse, namely five holdings, to God, Saint Peter, and the community of Malmesbury at the place called Toccanham, on condition that they continually pray to Almighty God for us, that he may grant us prosperous times for preserving our faith and the government of our kingdom through all the ages of the English people. Let no one dare to alter this gift from that monastery, on pain of the wrath and vengeance of Almighty God. This gift was enacted in the year 854 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and let it be kept in peace.”

Bishops Swithun and Alhstan subscribed.

> “Our Lord God, our Saviour Jesus Christ, reigning and governing us forever—he who saved all ages, redeemed the human race by his blood, and delivered it from the eternal destruction of diabolical condemnation through the true faith and the sacrament of baptism—I, King Æthelwulf, not by my merits but by the bounty of God’s grace, king of the West Saxons, and also, by God’s gift and by God’s grace coming upon me, ruler of the people of Kent and of the whole southern race of the English, have granted in perpetual possession to Almighty God, for the monastery of Malmesbury, a small portion of land, namely five small holdings in the place called Minti, on this condition: that whoever attempts to take this land from that church shall be condemned forever. This was enacted in the year 855 of the Lord’s Incarnation.”

Cenwulf, archbishop of Canterbury, Alhstan, bishop of Sherborne, and Æthelstan, son of the same king and king of Kent, subscribed.

Three sons succeeded him in continuous succession and reigned for fifteen years. The fourth, also named Alfred, reigned thirty years less six months. In his time John the Scot came to England, a man of penetrating intellect and great eloquence. Long before, as though an exile from his country, he had crossed into France to Charles the Bald. Received by Charles with great favour, he was counted among his intimate circle and spent with him both serious business and jest; he was an inseparable companion at table and in the bedchamber. He possessed much wit and natural charm, examples of which remain even today, such as these.

He was sitting at table opposite the king, at the other side of the board. After the cups had been passed and the dishes consumed, Charles, with a more cheerful expression, saw John do something that offended Gallic politeness. He rebuked him wittily and said: “What is the difference between a sot and a Scot?” John turned the usual insult back upon its author and replied: “Only the table.” [Col. 1652C] The king had asked, in a spirit of inquiry, about a difference of character; John had answered about the distance of position. Yet the king was not angered, for, captivated by the wonder of his learning, he did not wish to rise even verbally against his master—for that was what he habitually called him.

Again, when a servant presented to the king at dinner a dish containing two very large fish and one small one, he gave it to his master to divide among two clerics reclining beside him. They were of gigantic stature, while he himself was extremely slight of body. Then John, who always found some clever means to excite the diners’ amusement, kept the two larger fish for himself and distributed the one smaller fish to the two others. When the king reproached him with the unfairness of the division, he said: “On the contrary, I have done well and fairly. For here is one small person,” speaking of himself. Touching the two [Col. 1652D] large fish and turning likewise toward the clerics, he said: “Here are two large persons,” indicating the clerics, “and one small one,” nonetheless touching the fish.

At Charles’s request he translated Dionysius the Areopagite’s *Celestial Hierarchy* from Greek into Latin, word for word. Consequently the Latin wording is scarcely intelligible, since it is constructed more by Greek flow than by our own arrangement. He also composed the book which he entitled *Periphyseon*, περὶ φύσεως μερισμοῦ, that is, “On the Division of Nature.” It is very useful because of the intricacy of certain questions to be solved, provided he is forgiven in certain respects in which he departed from the path of the Latin writers while fixing his eyes too keenly upon the Greeks. For this reason he was also thought a heretic, and a certain Florus wrote against him. There are indeed very many things in the book *Periphysion* which, unless carefully examined, seem to diverge from the faith of Catholics.

Pope Nicholas is known to have shared this opinion. In a letter to Charles he says:

> “It has been reported to our apostolic office that a certain man, John, a Scot by birth, has recently translated into Latin the work of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he wrote in the Greek tongue concerning the divine names or the celestial orders. According to custom, it ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment, especially since the same John, although he is said to possess much learning, is commonly reported formerly not to have held sound views in certain matters.”

Because of this ill repute, I believe, France wearied him, and he came to King Alfred. Attracted by that king’s generosity and by his teaching office—sublime, as I have understood from the king’s writings—he settled at Malmesbury. There, after some years, he was pierced with writing-styles by the boys whom he taught, according to John of Paris in his history, under the year 877:

> “John the Scot, among other things, wrote a book on the Eucharist, which was afterward read and condemned at the Synod of Vercelli, held by Pope Leo in the same year in which Lanfranc cleared himself of Berengar’s error. Hence, as Lanfranc said, he himself became unsound in the faith. At last he went to England to King Alfred, and at the monastery of Malmesbury was pierced with writing-styles by boys.”

Pierced through, he gave up his soul amid severe and bitter torture; for, as violent wrongdoing and weak hands repeatedly failed and repeatedly struck, he suffered a cruel death. For some time he lay in an unhonoured grave in the church of Saint Lawrence, which had witnessed the dreadful slaughter. But when divine favour granted fiery light above him for many nights, the monks, admonished thereby, transferred him to the greater church. Setting him at the left of the altar, they proclaimed his martyrdom in these verses:

> Holy John the Philosopher is buried in this tomb,  
> Who, while still living, had been enriched with wondrous doctrine.  
> At last, through martyrdom, he deserved to ascend Christ’s kingdom,  
> Where all the saints reign through everlasting ages.

King Alfred and his son Edward conferred nothing upon this monastery, except where an exchange appears more like a gift. Yet I shall set down here the documents indicating that this church was formerly consecrated in the name of the Holy Saviour and Saint Peter; [Col. 1653D] and thus it is worthwhile to hear and review the writings of the ancients.

> “In the name of the Lord, I, Alfred, by the grace of God king of the Anglo-Saxons, with the consent of the venerable community of the church of Malmesbury, grant to my faithful man named Dudi a small portion of land—namely, four cassates—belonging to that same church, at the place called Callanthurd. But after the third generation of heirs, the aforesaid land shall return, without any opposition, to the church of the Holy Saviour and Saint Peter at Malmesbury. This document was drawn up in the same place which by its ancient name is called Maildubery, but by ours Maldumesburg.”

In the course of time, under Edward, Alfred’s son, the very powerful ealdorman Ordlaf restored to the monastery, in exchange for another estate, land belonging to Dudi; [Col. 1654A] and, being a man of peaceable and good disposition, when he entered upon the way of death he commanded that both properties be restored without objection. Accordingly, he was honoured there with a noble burial and enduring remembrance. The documents are as follows:

> “With the consent of Edward, most glorious king of the Anglo-Saxons, and also of his nobles who were then present with him, the community of God’s servants at the ancient place called Maildubery, in the church of the Holy Saviour—there seen to be most beautifully constructed in masonry—grants and bestows upon the venerable earl Ordlaf a small tract of land, namely five hides of his own property, at the place called Mehandim, in exchange for another estate, namely four hides, at the place which the country people call Cellewarde. When [Col. 1654B] the four generations of heirs have ended, the aforesaid land shall be restored to the brethren of the church without any opposition. I, Ordlaf, grant and bestow upon the community of the Holy Saviour at Maildubery a small parcel of land of my own right, which I bought with money from the venerable man Dudi by leave of my lord, the most glorious King Edward, at the place which the country people call Cellanwirdan, in exchange for another land called Mebandim, etc. This document was drawn up in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 901, the one hundred and ninety-second after the death of the most holy grantor.”

> “In the name of the Lord. I, Edward, by the grace of God king of the Anglo-Saxons, gave to the venerable community of the church of Malmesbury a small tract of land at the place called [Col. 1654C] Hanecintun, in exchange for another land of equal extent—namely, ten cassates—at the place which the country people call Frenberg. The aforesaid lands are free from all secular obligations. I made this exchange, at the brethren’s request, for their convenience; for the land which I gave those brethren lies only two miles from their monastery, whereas that which I received lies nearly twenty miles from the said monastery. This charter was written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 901, the first year of my reign.”

Ealhswith, the king’s mother, and Ælfflæd, his wife, subscribed.

Edward, who reigned twenty-four years, was succeeded by his son Æthelstan for sixteen years. To his most blessed kinsman Aldhelm—as he said, and as was in fact the case—he rendered such service [Col. 1654D] that he devoted to him both soul and body. The saint himself too henceforth gradually displayed a clearer and more frequent character in miracles, as though indicating that he disdained his unworthy burial in the ground. Nor did he cease until, after a few years, he was raised and placed in a shrine.

Meanwhile Æthelstan arranged for Elwin and Æthelwin, sons of his uncle Æthelward, whom he had cherished with especial affection and who had fallen in battle against Anlaf, to be brought to Malmesbury and buried on the right and left of the altar in the church of the Mother of God. The oft-repeated reason was that, endowed with a heavenly sword at the invocation of Aldhelm’s name, he had been rescued from his enemies. From that day he bestowed upon the monastery many estates, many cloths, a golden cross, likewise golden reliquaries, together with a portion of the Lord’s wood—that is, the True Cross—which King Hugh of France had sent him. [Col. 1655A]

It would take too long to recount how zealous he was in building and repairing monasteries [variant: “was”]; how he routed barbarism with a very small army; how he set a boundary to his dominion in Scotland. For I might seem to be indulging a compliant subject and repeating what has elsewhere been said for rhetorical display; and it might appear an ostentation of praise for our church to extol so often the man who honoured it by many benefits in life and, finally, in death, with the relics of his venerable body. Nevertheless, I dare say this: although he either surpassed all his predecessors by himself, or, to speak more modestly, equalled them, what he accomplished was nothing in comparison with what he was to accomplish, because a hurrying day cut short such great deeds sufficiently abruptly. Thus, carried off from the world at Gloucester by an untimely death—one which, had the Lord wished, did not suit that bold spirit—[Col. 1655B] … [lacuna] … he was conveyed to Malmesbury and buried beneath the altar of Saint Mary in the tower. Therefore those are mistaken who say that Abbot Ælfric built that tower; for it is certain that he became abbot more than thirty years after Æthelstan’s death.

> Here lies the honour of the world, his country’s grief, the loss of justice,  
> The thunderbolt of righteousness, the mirror of purity.  
> His breath enters heaven, the body’s frame dissolved;  
> The urn receives his triumphant remains.  
> The sun had shone through twice six risings of Scorpio,  
> When that creature struck [reading: *perculit*, “struck”] the king with its tail.

The relics of many saints which he brought in augment his merits toward the monastery. In purchasing them he splendidly and lavishly expended his father’s treasures, having been instructed by a heavenly [Col. 1655C] dream. Thus, from transmarine Brittany and Normandy—for he was bound in friendship with Count Rollo—he bought many relics of saints, including those of Saint Paternus, bishop of Avranches.

Paternus was Aquitanian by origin [reading: *genere*], a monk from youth and in later age a hermit. Having amassed no small wealth of virtues through the pursuits of a more secluded philosophy, he came forth into public life, worthy to be a ruler of souls because he knew how to rule himself. Accordingly, first abbot in the district of Coutances and then bishop among the people of Avranches, he was not without miracles. Thirsting, he struck a flint lightly with his staff and drew forth water. It was altogether astounding that, nature refusing, the man’s holiness should force the marble veins into watery [Col. 1655D] bubbles. He poured oil into the mouth of a girl deprived of the use of her tongue and restored the organ. A contraction which had long fixed a woman’s fingers into her palm was released at the saint’s touch. He raised unharmed a boy swelling toward death, into whom the poisonous fangs of a serpent had fastened; the swelling of the skin was calmed and subdued to its proper condition. Evil spirits, foreseeing the saint’s coming, left their familiar dependants, excusing the cowardice of their flight on the ground that they could not stand against Paternus’s force. Birds fed with grain seasoned by his blessing followed him as he departed for many miles on the oarage of their wings, and could never be torn from affection for him while they lived. Besides these, there are other things which Fortunatus has conveyed to our knowledge with that graceful salt of eloquence.

King Æthelstan associated him [Col. 1656A] with Saint Aldhelm as a companion, and he never failed to show himself a saint through the frequency of his miracles. What I shall relate our elders remembered notably well and especially recounted. A thief had taken a gold plate from the shrine, left the church, and spent it for whatever purposes he pleased. The saint, though patient on other occasions, did not silently tolerate this. For when the culprit, conscious of his guilt, thought he would enter the church again with impunity, he stuck at the door, caught in invisible straps. If he attempted to go further, then a great force of unseen fire scorched the wretch and forced from him a pitiful cry. If he tried to retreat, he was dragged back by a noose twisted about his throat. The bystanders saw none of these things, but marvelled at the robber’s shouting and struggling. Yet, when he confessed both guilt and punishment, they learned the cause and made intercessions to the saint. Once restitution for the damage had been made, he was released from punishment.

The following inscription is read on this shrine:

> “King Æthelstan, emperor of all Britain and of many surrounding peoples, ordered this work to be made in honour of Saint Paternus, because he had obtained these relics from regions beyond the sea.”

I shall append the letter:

> “To the glorious and munificent King Adelstan, in honour of the supreme and undivided Trinity and through the most excellent intercession of all the saints: I, Radhodus, provost, wish the glory of this world and the blessedness of eternity from Samson, supreme pontiff. Let your piety know, best King [Col. 1656C] Adelstan, that while our country still retained its stability, your father Edgvard, by letters, commended himself to the fellowship of the brotherhood of Saint Samson, supreme confessor, and of the elder Archbishop Jovenian, my cousin, and his clergy. Therefore, to this day we pour out unwearied prayers to Christ the King for his soul and for your welfare. Seeing day and night your great mercy manifested over us, we promise—in our psalms, masses, and prayers, as though I and my twelve canons had prostrated ourselves at your knees—to pray to the merciful God for you.
>
> “And now I send you relics which, we know, are dearer to you than all earthly wealth: namely, the bones of Saint Senator, Saint Paternus, [Col. 1656D] and Saint Soubilion, the master of that same Saint Paternus, who likewise departed to Christ on one and the same day and at the same hour as the aforementioned Paternus. These two saints most certainly lay in the tomb with Saint Paternus, on his right and left; and their feast-days, like that of Paternus, are celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of October [23 September].
>
> “Therefore, glorious king, exaltor of the holy Church, humbler of perverse paganism, mirror of your kingdom, example of every goodness, scatterer of enemies, father of clerics, helper of the needy, lover of all saints, invoker of angels: we beseech and humbly entreat you—we who dwell in France in exile and captivity because of our deserts and sins—not to let the great mercy of your most fortunate generosity forget us; and from this time forward you can obtain without any delay whatever you deign to entrust to me.” [Col. 1657A]

This letter was found in a shrine at the monastery of Nedeleton, which the same king built from the foundations in order to place there the relics of Saint Samson.

But now I see that I should append the evidences for the estates which the king granted to the monastery. Though these occurred in many charters, they bear one and the same text, woven together in this fashion:

> “The insolent fortune of this deceitful world, lovable not with the milky whiteness of lilies but hateful for the bitter corruption of its gall, tears asunder with venomous jaws the sons of fetid flesh as they revel in the valley of tears. Though by its smiles it is alluring to the unfortunate, yet it slopes shamelessly down to the depths of Acherontic Cocytus, unless the salvation of the high God comes to aid those crying out [perhaps *boantibus*, ‘those who cry aloud’]. [Col. 1657B] And therefore, because it itself, ruinous in its failure, falls away carnally, we must hasten with all urgency to the delightful fields of inexpressible joy, where the hymn-singing instruments of angelic jubilation and the honey-sweet fragrances of blooming roses are received as beyond measure sweet by good and blessed nostrils, and where the pleasing sounds are heard without weariness by the ears of the happy.
>
> “Drawn by love of this happiness, I, Æthelstan, king of the English, raised through the Almighty’s right hand to the kingdom of all Britain, have granted in perpetual right to the venerable community of Malmesbury, for the souls of my paternal cousins, the sons of Æthelred the ætheling—namely Ælfswine and Æthelwin—to God and Saint Peter, parcels of land: sixty cassates at the place called Wdetun; sixty cassates [Col. 1657C] at the place called Breomet; five cassates at the place called Sumerford; likewise five at the place called Nortun; likewise five at the place called Ewulm. I command that none of our successors, so long as Christianity flourishes, attempt even in the least to interrupt this our gift. If anyone should attempt it, let him know that he is to be condemned by God.
>
> “Let the wise men of our realm know that we did not unjustly seize these aforesaid lands and give God plunder; rather, I received them in the manner shown by all the nobles of the kingdom of the English, and also by John, apostolic pope of the Roman Church. When Alfred had died—he who had been an enemy to my prosperity and life, assenting to the malice of my enemies [Col. 1657D] when they wished, after my father’s death, to blind me in the city of Winchester—unless the Lord in His mercy had delivered me. But when their machinations had been exposed, he was sent back to the Roman Church, that he might defend himself there before the apostolic John by oath. He did this before the altar of Saint Peter; but, after taking the oath, he fell before the altar and was carried in his servants’ hands to the English school, and on the third night he ended his life. And now the apostolic lord has sent to us and asked what should be done concerning him. At the request of our nobles we granted that he should be placed with the other Christians, though unworthy. And thus possession of all his property, great and small, was assigned to me, etc.
>
> “This charter of a will found and inspired by God and the Lord Jesus [Col. 1658A] Christ was written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 938, in the eleventh year of the kingdom freely entrusted to me, in the eighth indiction, with epact fourteen, concurrent third; on the third day before the Kalends of January [30 December], the tenth lunar day of the changing month, in the very celebrated city called Dorchester, while the entire assembly of nobles rejoiced beneath the wings of royal generosity.”

The sub-kings Eugenius, Howell, Morcant, and Indual subscribed; the archbishops Willfelmus of Canterbury and Wulstan of York; the bishops Burgrice of Rochester, Tedred of London, Æthelgar of the East Angles, Ælfric of Winchester, Alfred of Sherborne, Wulfermus of Wells, Æthelgar of Crediton, Oda of Wilton [reading: *Wiltunensis*], Eadhelm of Selsey, Sephelm of Saint Cuthbert’s, Tidelm of Hereford, [Col. 1658B] Elwine of Worcester, Kinsi of Lichfield, and Winsi of Leicester.

Æthelstan was succeeded by the brothers Edmund for six years, Eldred for six, and Edred for nine. Edred was succeeded by Edwin for four years, Edmund’s son, who, as we have explained more fully elsewhere, seduced by the charms of a certain little harlot, expelled Dunstan, the most vehement reprover of his folly, from his native land. Thereafter, once infected by evil, he subjected throughout all England every man of the monastic order to undeserved calamities, first stripping them of the support of their resources and then driving them into exile, to Dunstan’s grief.

Indeed, in the 246th year after the passing of Father Aldhelm, he made the monastery of Malmesbury a community of clerics, after it had been entrusted by Leutherius to monks in the 276th year. But You, Lord Jesus, our Creator and Restorer, good craftsman and most powerful to refashion [Col. 1658C] our deformities, through those irregular and wandering men brought Your treasure, hidden for so many centuries, into the light: I mean the body of the most holy Aldhelm, which they raised from the ground and placed in the shrine mentioned above.

Royal generosity added to the glory of the clerics, so that it gave the saint an estate highly suitable in nearness and extent. I would name it, except that it is known and earlier kings had given many portions of it, lest this king alone claim, or diminish, all or any part of a common glory. But all the iniquity of those times soon passed away when Edgar, brother of all those predecessors, succeeded. He would readily bear the palm before all, unless Æthelstan had pre-empted it. At first, indeed, you would not know whom to prefer, except that this man maintained what the other began; the one was stronger, the other more fortunate; the former relied upon God’s aid and his own, the latter trusted the counsel of prudent men. Edgar therefore, having abolished the edicts of his brother, which royal luxury and youthful impulse [had produced], will better disclose in his own words [Col. 1658D] what he gave to our church and what he took away.

> “Since a certain boundary awaits the totality of the common mass, and since, as the Apostle says, visible things are temporal but invisible things eternal (2 Cor. 4), it remains for each person to receive there the recompense for deeds done here. Therefore I, Edgar, basileus of all Albion and also of the maritime or island kings dwelling round about it—so exalted by the abundant subjection granted through God’s grace as none of my forefathers had been—have often considered with special care, mindful of so great an honour, what I should most fittingly give from my empire to the King of kings, the Lord.
>
> “Accordingly, divine mercy, favouring pious devotion, suddenly revealed to my vigilant zeal that I should restore the holy monasteries in my realm. They had visibly fallen, as it were, down to their beams through moss-covered shingles and decayed boards; and, what was worse, within they had been almost empty of God’s service through neglect. Having expelled ignorant clerics, subject to no regular discipline, I appointed in many places shepherds of a holier succession—that is, of monastic profession—and furnished them lavish means from royal revenues for restoring the ruined churches. Of these I appointed one named Ælfric, a man highly experienced in ecclesiastical conduct and offices, guardian of the most celebrated monastery [Col. 1659B] which the English call by the double name Malmesbury.
>
> “For the benefit of my little soul, in honour of our Saviour, His Mother Mary ever-virgin, the *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, ‘God-bearer’), of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of Aldhelm, blessed bishop, I restored by munificent generosity a parcel of land—namely ten hides—called Estotim, together with meadows and woods. This land, once lent to the aforesaid clerics, had long been possessed unjustly, first by many persons and finally by a contentious man named Athelind. But after his superstitious and subtle allegation had been heard by my wise men, and its false argument had been refuted by them in my presence, the land was restored by me for the monastery’s use in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 974, the fourteenth of my reign, [Col. 1659C] the first of my royal consecration, after the passing of the precious confessor Aldhelm. At the request of the aforesaid abbot, I ordered this charter of restoration to be inscribed for the firm remembrance of future posterity, so that, while the Christian faith flourishes among our people, the aforesaid estate may not, God forbid, be forcibly alienated from that holy place by anyone wielding tyrannical power.”

There follow the subscriptions of the archbishops Dunstan of Canterbury and Oswald of York, and of the bishops Æthelwold of Winchester, the three Ælfstans of London, Rochester, and Wilton, etc.

This is Ælfric, who, transferring all care to Blessed Mary, assigned the possessions and name of the monastery to her dominion, so that Saint Peter’s most blessed name being meanwhile suppressed, she alone appears to rule the place. [Col. 1659D] Nor did the glorious Lady disdain the gift of that distinguished and praiseworthy man; indeed, she presides over the church to this day, embracing in her power fellowship with the most holy Aldhelm.

Unless deceptive antiquity misleads us, he was learned in letters, a most elegant interpreter, and skilled in building. He founded and completed all the monastic workshops, then outstanding and not even now altogether contemptible. Abbo of Fleury refers to him without naming him in the preface to the Passion of Saint Edmund, addressed to the blessed Archbishop Dunstan, in these words:

> “Your Holiness, in my presence, related historically to the lord bishop of the church of Rochester and the abbot of the monastery [Col. 1660A] called Malmesbury, and to other brethren standing round—as is your custom—the Passion of Saint Edmund, written by no one and unknown to many, gathered from the memory of antiquity.”

Ælfric, indeed, when already very old, was raised to the bishopric of Crediton and survived scarcely four years. He left several books, no slight memorials of his talent: the Life of Saint Æthelwold, before Wulstan composed it more elaborately; an abridgment of the Passion of Saint Edmund; and many books translated from Latin into the native tongue.

In King Edgar’s time, the most holy Archbishop Dunstan devoted exceptional care to the restoration and adornment of our monastery. He was drawn by love of Saint Aldhelm and by kinship with the West Saxon race; for he was born in this province and rejoiced that, as miracles became more frequent, the saint of his own region should above all in his own time be raised to eminence. [Col. 1660B] Therefore he was generous to the place in many respects, frequently offering things which then would have been considered a great wonder in England and which displayed both the splendour and the ingenuity of the donor: among them bells, outstanding in sound and size; and organs, in which an anxious bellows expels air long gathered through bronze pipes fashioned to musical measures. There he inscribed this distich upon bronze plates:

> Bishop Dunstan, for Saint Aldhelm, made these organs;  
> May he lose the eternal kingdom who wishes to remove them hence.

The following verses may likewise support the truth of the account. We saw them stamped upon a vessel which served the ministers of the altar in the service of water:

> Archbishop Dunstan had this ewer cast,  
> That it might serve Saint Aldhelm in the holy temple.

[Col. 1660C] In these verses, by poetic licence, the first letter *l* had been omitted from the saint’s name so that the verse might scan. For in neither inscription was *Aldhelmo* engraved, but *Adelmo*.

Meanwhile, foreknowing by prophetic spirit his future calamity in England and the Danish devastation—as one who predicted them to the king himself, not in enigmatic obscurity but in plain speech—he feared for the bones of the most holy confessor. Turning over in his mind the Danes’ avaricious cruelty and cruel avarice, he imagined that the monastery would be plundered through greed for money. He feared greatly lest someone, drawn by the gleam of metal, should seize the shrine, greedily gather its precious covering plates into his robe, and throw away somewhere the stripped wood along with the bones. Therefore, after long and careful deliberation, he removed the most reverend relics from the stone shrine and placed them in a tomb raised high up to the right of the altar, at a place visible to all who looked about the church. [Col. 1660D]

Beside the bones he placed first a shining, delicate linen cloth, then a flask of the purest glass filled with most precious balsam, wrapped in costly scarlet fabric: fragrances surely fitting for a bishop who had always offered to heaven the incense of the holocausts of virtues and prayers. He also placed part of the boards from the most ancient sarcophagus in which all the flesh had passed into its mortal condition. Nor did he refrain from verses, with which he adorned the outer circumference of the tomb; their substance was this: that the saint might deem him, his lover, worthy of pardon for sins, and might not charge him with fault [Col. 1661A] because he had placed him in a higher position; he should know that this had been done for protection, not insult.

The event did not deceive the prophet, nor did anything of his words fall to the ground. I shall briefly explain this if I continue the succession of kings which I had interrupted.

Edgar, after sixteen years of reign, was succeeded by his son Edward for three and a half years. Edward was replaced by his brother Æthelred, who for thirty-seven years besieged, undermined, and utterly ruined his wretched kingdom. I judge it superfluous to insert his deeds here, especially since elsewhere I have unfolded the labyrinths of his miseries. Yet I shall not pass over this: when Edgar died—he who boasted that he ruled over more peoples than any of his ancestors, not because he ruled more extensively, but because he ruled more securely—the matter turned to the contrary; the highest happiness of the kingdom stood on a precipice. For, as someone says, great things are denied a long continuance.

Thus the Danish race, accustomed to live by plunder, boiled up along all England’s coasts. To speak briefly, once every shore had been devastated, it fed upon the very marrow of the inland land; and it was the more insolent toward the natives because it was farther from knowledge of the man [reading uncertain: *vivi* or *veri*, “living” or “true”] of God. [Col. 1661B] One party, led by its commander, came to Malmesbury. Expecting to act there with its customary terror, it burst furiously into the church. Looking about on both sides, they saw nothing to satisfy their greedy rapacity except the saint’s shrine. The monks’ cautious provision had removed everything else from the searching fury. This alone they had exposed to fortune—or, more truly, to the saint’s protection: let him protect it if he wished; otherwise let him allow himself to be mocked.

The invaders, gaping at it with enormous mouths, rushed upon it with frenzied steps. One of them, made bolder by a wicked hunger for silver, seized a knife and tried to remove the precious stones from their settings. He had already put forth his hand when the saint’s prompt power checked the advancing pestilence of avarice. He paid for his rash attempt by losing his mind and being hurled backward onto the pavement, as though he gasped because a penetrating weapon had been driven into his heart. The punishment of one restored the others to sanity: they ceased raging and making noise; they left the holy place undefiled and fled. [Col. 1661C]

They hastened their flight through level country and trackless places, rejoicing that they had escaped danger with their bodies alone. For after an uninterrupted run of many miles, they reported that they had endured something greater than human terror, though no one pressed them from behind and no one barred their way in front. When this report spread through the host of enemies, it made them slower to plunder and more timid in their reverence toward the saints. Thus it happened that, though all the monasteries round about were devastated or stripped, this one alone never lamented so grave a calamity.

This king gave to the monastery of Saint Aldhelm an estate of ten hides [Col. 1662A] under Abbot Æthelwold, who had succeeded Ælfric. While he was still young in the kingdom, the most distinguished nobles who survived spurred him on; after their deaths he wholly withered away into self-indulgence in life and injury to the kingdom. For the abundance of possessions which his father left him incited him to wantonness; offence against God earned wrath; God’s wrath brought the nation to destruction. The document is as follows:

> “To all who search intently and repeatedly after the study of wisdom, it clearly appears that the end of this present life, varied by the distress of diverse calamity, is imminent and already recognized as threatening with excessive terror. Therefore I, Æthelred, basileus of all Albion, with Christ’s grace assisting me and instructed by the counsel of my nobles, desiring to purchase eternal things with perishable ones, have granted in perpetual inheritance a certain portion of land—namely ten hides—at a celebrated place which those skilled in the language of this country call by the familiar name Redburne, to our Lord Jesus Christ and His Mother Mary ever-virgin, in veneration of the blessed bishop Aldhelm, who made the place itself called by the customary name Malmesbury, for the use of the monks dwelling there under the rule of Abbot Æthelward, etc.”

> **[Note: Col. 1661D]** An error is concealed in the dates. The charter of King Edgar, who preceded Æthelred, quoted above was issued in 974, and Æthelred did not enter upon the kingdom before 978. I therefore think that 982 should be read. This charter was written 273 years after the passing of that same Father. It must, moreover, have been issued at the beginning of King Æthelred’s reign, because it has Bishop Ælfric as a witness; as was said above, he had been raised to the episcopate before Æthelred assumed the kingdom and survived scarcely four years.

“This charter was written in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 962, 263 years after the passing of that same Father.” Those who subscribed the preceding charter subscribed this one also, along with Ælfric, now a bishop, and also Escewin, bishop of Dorchester.

After Æthelred died, having reigned thirty-seven years, Cnut succeeded for twenty years; Cnut was succeeded by his son Harold for [Col. 1662C] four years; he by Harthacnut for one year; and he by Edward for twenty-four years. In these eighty-six years, after Æthelward there were Kineward, Brichtwold, Ederic, and Wulsin.

Brichtwold, as we observe from English writings, inflicted many injuries upon the monastery by either disposing of its lands altogether or seizing them at a small price. Yet he is excused on the ground that, oppressed by the great tax then paid to the Danes, he found this the sole remedy for evils, unaware of the future and not seeing how it could later do harm. Wulsin restored to its former vigour the monastic observance, much weakened by the arrival of the Danes. In our own time there were monks who had seen him in the flesh and who delighted to ponder and recount to others the memory of the man. From their account, hanging upon their words, I stored many of his notable deeds in my mind; but I decline to relate them, because they do not fit the work I have undertaken.

Ægelward succeeded him for ten years; then Elwin for a year and a half. Brichtwold followed him for seven years. Tradition says that he was sluggish in good and energetic in evil, and that he died a miserable death, extinguished in a village amid preparations for drinking; he was buried among his predecessors in the church of Saint Andrew, which adjoined the great [Col. 1663A] church. It is also well established that the guardians of the place were troubled by phantasmal apparitions until they dug up the corpse and plunged it deep into a marsh far from the monastery. From there a foul smell sometimes rises and breathes out a cruel stench upon the neighbours. But leaving these unpleasant matters, let us turn to the miracles which Divinity displayed at the tomb of the blessed confessor in this course of time.

When the Danes had firmly resolved to come to England, they took the Norwegians into an alliance for victory. The barbarity of both peoples was monstrous, but the Norwegians’ greed was more rapacious and their lust more violent. While one of their counts was laying everything waste, a certain girl named Elfildis fell to him as part of the booty. She had been born among the English in an honourable station, with a free-born body and face. She [Col. 1663B] became an incentive to desire for the barbarian, so that he repudiated his lawful marriage and bent all his powers toward marrying his captive—whose chastity he ought to have protected and whose captivity he ought to have pitied, had he not been a barbarian. Thus, when his blandishments had first been exhausted, the nocturnal plunderer attacked and violated the modesty of the resisting girl, though she begged him earnestly and repeatedly.

Yet he did not long survive, nor did he rejoice either in the hope of the child conceived or in a long life after the injury done to the woman. When he had died, the report of beautiful Elfildis reached the ears of the king of the land. He immediately, according to his nation’s custom, greedily desired to possess the woman. Thus the king became a lover, the powerful man a suppliant. Through intermediaries he paid homage to the majesty of the captive, asking that she might deign to receive him as a friend. He promised mountains of gold and perpetual love, and finally everything [Col. 1663C] that might either deceive a woman or entice a captive—while concealing his wife, whom he greatly feared she might offend.

Elfildis answered that she had devoted herself to serving God, intent upon other loves; that he had carried away with him her affections, who had both tasted her first fruits in union and, dying, had been buried with them. Hearing this, the king, grieved that he had been despised by a mere woman, attacked her against her will; and one night, when she feared no such thing, he violently entered her embrace. From this one union a child was conceived and a boy born, against the wishes of them both. For the king, fearing the danger to his reputation, wished indeed to practise his pleasure but did not wish to possess its fruit. Elfildis, moreover, first feared God because of the man’s incestuous union, and secondly guarded against the queen’s jealousy.

Nevertheless, once the child was born, he won the eyes of both with his charms [Col. 1663D], so as to reconcile them to himself: the man, lest he cast off the woman whom he had made a mother by himself—especially as she was beautiful in body, free-born in descent, captive in condition, and, apart from him alone with whom she had dealings, consistently chaste; the woman, that through habitual intercourse and the sweetness of her son she might receive the man into love. Thus she willingly cherished the sin which she had entered into reluctantly, being drawn on by pleasure. And, to escape the queen’s awareness [read *reginae*, “of the queen,” for *regni*, “of the kingdom”], she had a hiding-place with a certain bishop of the land, whence she was brought away whenever desired for nocturnal use. But the king’s approaching death abruptly ended these delights of lust, and she remained in the midst of affairs with her orphaned son.

Accordingly, well aware how far women’s anger may dare against concubines, she fled to the remotest provinces of Norway [Col. 1664A], aided faithfully and supplied with necessities by the bishop. To him alone the king, at his death, had entrusted in his last words the guardianship of the orphan.

Consequently, when the nobles rejected the rule of a woman, he did not conceal the whole matter as it stood. Thus, by common decree, the little boy was placed, under a shadow, upon the summit of the kingdom, while guardians disposed of all affairs at their own discretion. But after no more than a year and a half had passed, that little boy, called Magnus, was taken from life by a bitter death and unwound the distaff of the Fates. It is said that this happened through the plots of the great men; but I do not agree that they would have devised a violent death for an innocent child whom they had made king.

Then, not to spin out a long tale, Elfildis, bereft of every counsellor, sounded the retreat for her homeland. And, that God might favour so perilous a voyage, she vowed that, if she reached England safely by sea, [Col. 1664B] she would never eat the flesh of a land animal and would never take richer food except on feast-days. Having, by God’s will, obtained a fortunate outcome, she conscientiously kept her vow. From the money which she had acquired through the generosity of her husband and son, she bought three estates, from whose income she supported herself and her household.

After several years, at a more lavish feast, she gave herself up to merriment and urged her guests to be cheerful. In turn they begged her to take at least a very small quantity of meat, wasting many words to no effect. Yet, pressed by the entreaties of the priests present, who promised prayers and Masses and said that even the guilt of great indulgence could be erased by the celebration of Masses, she touched with the tips of her fingers [Col. 1664C] some meat—I know not what kind—and, though her senses recoiled, put it to her mouth. Immediately the merciful correction of divine severity followed: while she was chewing, she was struck so violently by the illness which in Greek they call *paralysis*, that is, “a loosening of the limbs,” that no member could perform its function. Her tongue alone fluttered within her jaws, so that it might confess the offence and beg pardon.

Her innocent lapse was admirably chastised by a temporal stroke. But if she had committed a punishable guilt, she would not have received a pardonable punishment. For a full three years, worn down by this affliction, she travelled in a litter about the shrines of the saints, soliciting the aid of those whom fame had made most renowned for miracles. Every earlier holy patron yielded and gave place to the glory of most blessed Aldhelm, so that, when so illustrious a person had been healed, his renown might fly more magnificently [Col. 1664D] through their mouths.

After three years she came to the saint’s Nativity feast, celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May] by a great gathering from the province. The master’s power did not delay: on the very vigil of the solemnity it touched her as she prayed at the tomb. Health blossomed again; the slack structure of her limbs became firm; the paralysed woman rose whole. Her acquaintances marvelled and gave praise; the monks made an excited noise and inquired into the matter; all rejoiced. Elfildis, not ungrateful to her healer, gave her soul to the place, professing herself a nun. While alive she served the Church; when dead she received a celebrated burial in the cloister. This miracle, transmitted to us through successive generations because of the distinction of the person, as I have said, and the nearness in time, proves that many things have existed which the neglect [read: injury] of years has obscured and the neglect of writers has concealed.

At the same time [Col. 1665A] a certain Greek monk named Constantine came to the place; but whence he sprang is uncertain, and whether necessity or choice had driven him from home and country. He was the first cultivator of the vineyard situated on the hill near the monastery to the north, which endured for many years. He was of suitable stature, gentle in manners, agreeable in conversation, moderate in food, sparing—indeed nearly abstinent—in drink. He spent the leisure of feast-days in prayer, and consumed all the hours of other days in labour in the vineyard.

Now, as he was dying, with his voice cut off and apparently about to breathe out his soul with only the smallest remnants of life, he revived and, with slow effort, rose. Feeling for the bag which always hung at his side, [Col. 1665B] he drew from it a *pallium*, the insignia of archbishops. So far as his recumbent position allowed, he put it on in the manner he knew; immediately afterwards, relapsing under the violence of death, he breathed his last and died. It was thereby perceived that he had been an archbishop; but knowledge still wavers as to why he had long ago bade farewell to his homeland. We may turn the uncertainty to a favourable interpretation: love of the religious life may have compelled the bishop to become a pilgrim.

He was therefore reverently buried among the tombs of the abbots in what was then the church of St Andrew. But when, in the course of years, the need for new buildings displaced him and the others from their ancient resting places, his bones, found to be of unusual whiteness and sweetest fragrance, gave evidence that Constantine had not been of common holiness.

[Col. 1665C] A certain peasant in the neighbourhood of Malmesbury, known to the monks and the town, was tormented by a most evil demon. At those standing near whom he could not reach, he gnashed his teeth; those closer at hand he struck with foot or fist. At those farther away he hurled foam; whatever came to hand he whirled about as an instrument of torment. Frenzy supplied weapons, so that no one could approach with impunity without departing injured. Moreover, uttering mad words, he hurled insults at the very stars. From one mouth diverse and confused voices were heard, so that now from barking you would suppose a dog, from lowing an ox, now from shrieking an owl. He plunged into the gulf of his belly foods neither fit for human consumption nor prepared by cooking. Madness had sharpened his molars so greatly that he could demolish, as it seemed, any object of bone, wood, or iron with ease.

Then, dissolving that voracity and raw indigestion in a single opening of his jaws, he expelled in a light vapour everything he had consumed. Moved by the misery of such a man, his neighbours formed the plan of leading him about to the places of saints. Madness prevented this, and he had to be bound. The matter was therefore difficult on both sides: because, owing to his ferocity, he could not be bound; and no one, however tested his strength, tried to fasten chains upon him without having his brains dashed out by his mere struggle. Necessity therefore found a remedy: ropes were stretched out so that his feet might be entangled wherever the force of his motion carried him. Thus, caught by a stratagem, he yielded to ingenuity, though he surpassed others in strength. Yet even so, though his body was ensnared, the spirit in his mind could not be restrained, until [Col. 1666A] all necessary preparations had been made and they began to lead him, patient as he was, to the saints.

As they travelled, Malmesbury offered itself to them on the very sacred vigil of the Ascension of our Lord and Saviour. There, having heard and believed that St Aldhelm had once been ready to heal illnesses of this kind, they stopped. They approached the monks and explained the journey and its cause. The monks promised the saint’s intercession and gave counsel freely: the day was at hand on which the Lord’s flesh had been borne in triumphal joy into heaven; hope had been given to all the members that they might follow the head—provided, of course, that their works had not fallen away from faith. Aldhelm, an eminent member of God, had surely attained the presence of his head by the merit of his deeds.
