Nothing, therefore, was difficult for him to obtain; this had been proved by many experiences. Let them consequently pour out humble prayers to the merciful [Col. 1666B] saint, because he was undoubtedly at hand for all who prayed with unfeigned faith.

Encouraged by this pronouncement, the strangers did not fail in their exhortations, so far as men of that sort and knowledge were able. That the prayers of these rustics were not fruitless was shown by the sick man’s health, which followed immediately. For when he was laid before the altar, he at once lost the savage disorder of face and eyes; he gave over those turbulent neck-muscles to a light sleep. Thus freed from the slavery of the devil and restored to freedom of mind, when he was shown by the gentleness of his words to be of sound understanding, he lifted the hearts of those present into praise of God and the saint and loosened their tongues.

A man of the same condition had been reduced to this misery by contracted hamstrings behind his knees, so that every use of walking rested upon his knees alone. [Col. 1666C] With these he swept dusty paths whenever he went anywhere; with these he made his way across muddy ground. Since his legs adhered to his buttocks, he presented the appearance of a quadruped rather than a human being. He looked like a shapeless monstrosity, or, if I may say so, a lump of flesh which nature had cast out as an immature birth. He scarcely ever raised himself toward the sky; so condemned was he always to look downward at the ground. Thus he struggled with all things [read: with all his soul], and he had no other victory than the endurance of misery.

Yet he continually considered from which saint he might seek help: that one was powerful, this one powerful; some could drive out demons, some were effective in curing manners [read: “diseases”]; but Christ, the author of all, excelled in all things. For at that time report especially proclaimed—and it was true—that great miracles occurred at a certain place called by the solitary name *Christistecerce*, that is, “Christ’s Church.” There was no human affliction so troublesome that Christ did not remove it there. The cripple then planned to go there in a hired conveyance [“journey”].

On his way, Malmesbury offered him accessible lodging. By chance, it was then the fourth day of the feast, while the report of the saint’s miracles was still fresh and fervent. For that festival had gathered there more sufferers than usual through necessity and had sent them away healed through the compassion of the most blessed Father. Having taken this in, the cripple meanwhile withdrew into the church, intending to resume his journey the next morning if his prayer did not succeed. [Col. 1667A] It was then Saturday, and the Sunday dawn was awaited. The saint’s power was altogether wondrous: as soon as he came beneath the church roof, he felt some portion of his bodily weakness shaken off, and he sensed an indescribable healing running through all his limbs. Made more confident by this and more eager for what remained, he prolonged a sleepless vigil there through the night.

Now the day had arrived, bringing to the wretch aid beyond what he could have hoped. As the monks proceeded through the cloister according to custom, he saw the choir from a distance empty, moved his hams with the assistance of the footstools, and crawled into it. Thus, rolling himself before the altar with all his body’s ruin, he rested, as though in ecstasy, with sleep-heavy eyes. But awakened from sleep by the commotion and chant of the returning monks, he recovered into an active leap. He looked at [Col. 1667B] those looking at him, and himself marvelled at so unexpected a recovery. He explained openly why he had come, but did not know how he had so quickly been raised. The matter was believed and praises were returned to God, especially because the host who had received him the previous day as a cripple now saw him standing upright.

This was the time when the relics of the most blessed Audoen, archbishop of Rouen, were brought to our monastery. The reason for their removal was this. Queen Emma, after the death of King Æthelred, had gone over to Normandy to her brother, believing that nothing was safe for her among the Danes who had occupied England. Living a long time at Rouen, she had won into friendship, by gifts, both certain monks of St Audoen’s and the secretary of the place, [Col. 1667C] directing her efforts especially to purchasing for herself the body of the blessed bishop. Christianity had fallen so low, greed had increased so much, that we made merchandise of saints’ bodies and offered blessed remains for sale.

At first the monk shuddered at the monstrous crime. Afterwards, however, compelled by the need of his nephew, who had been captured in France and sought ransom, he put up for sale the commodity that was requested. Having obtained this rich spoil, the woman returned to England when more settled weather came, brought the remaining body to Canterbury, and kept the head in her private chamber.

But many years later, when her son Edward had assumed the kingdom, memory of past events stirred the king’s heart against his mother. Because she had been insufficiently generous toward her offspring while he was spending his youthful years, he ordered all his mother’s furnishings to be stripped to the smallest item. This was done; and a certain goldsmith, who had been one of her confidential servants, stole the saint’s shrine with the head, while the others were meanwhile greedily seeking treasures. He deposited it [with] a brother who was a monk at Malmesbury, judging that sacred things could be entrusted to no one more suitably than to a monk. Not long afterwards, satisfying his fate, he left an enduring memorial of himself to the place, which he enriched with such great treasures.

I have received these accounts, widely circulated, from authorities not doubtful: men who had seen the events and greatly surpassed others in age, trustworthiness, and knowledge. But that it is not our office to write about Audoen’s miracles will be judged by anyone who has read the substantial books on his deeds, published through the care of earlier writers and deservedly very well known. [Col. 1668A] The healed man repaid grace to his healer, binding his whole future life by oath to his service.

Meanwhile, after the death of Abbot Brithwold, as we said above, Bishop Hermann considered filling the vacant abbacy from among his own household. But the monks, supported by Earls Godwine and Harold, forestalled his attempt. Their leading candidate, Brithric, made abbot from being provost, ruled the monastery most gloriously for seven years. But when William, count of Normandy, became king of England, he imposed upon the still-living Brithric a certain Turold, a monk of Fécamp, who had earned William’s favour by great services. Yet later, understanding that the act had been wrongly done and grieving that he had been deceived by the ambition of one in haste, William consoled the exile’s loss by the gift of the abbey of Burton.

[Col. 1668B] This same Turold, while exercising tyranny over his subjects, was transferred by the king to the wealthy abbey at Burgh, which at that time was harassed by robbers under a certain leader, Hereward, because it stood among marshes. “By the splendour of God,” he said, “since he behaves more as a soldier than as an abbot, I shall find him an equal to receive his attacks. There let him test his courage and his soldiery; there let him rehearse battles.”

He was succeeded by Warin, a monk of Lyra, an effective man chiefly in this respect: he had been trained as a monk under the Rule. Otherwise he was not very useful to the Church, since he was rashly seized by hope of higher honour. Accordingly, he was well suited to emptying the monks’ purses and snatching money from every source; yet not so greedily did he conceal what he gained, but rather squandered the Church’s possessions both on this side of and beyond [Col. 1668C] the sea, so as to purchase greater favour among the powerful and acquire an ostentatious reputation among those who had formerly seen him poor.

When he first came to the abbey, despising the deeds of his predecessors, he was possessed by a certain haughtiness and disgust toward the bodies of saints. The bones, therefore, of Meildulf of holy memory and of the others who had formerly been abbots there and afterwards bishops in many places—who, out of reverence for their patron Aldhelm, had ordered that they should be buried in that place—the bones which venerable antiquity had reverently placed in two stone receptacles set on either side of the altar, with wooden partitions between each person’s bones: all these, I say, he gathered together indiscriminately and cast out beyond the church doors as though they were a heap of rubble or the remains of worthless slaves.

And, lest anything should be lacking to his shamelessness, he also removed St John the Scot, whom the monks revered with almost equal devotion to St Aldhelm. All these, therefore, he ordered to be buried heedlessly in the farthest corner of the basilica of St Michael, which he himself had ordered enlarged and raised, and to be shut in with stones. He aggravated the outrage of the deed with a jesting taunt: “Let whoever can now help better assist the others.” O the times! O the manners! Who could pursue such audacity with reproach worthy of it? What shamelessness in the man! Shall we, frivolous men born for mockery, destroy what most blessed Dunstan and other men most wise and most devout either did themselves or permitted to be done?

But I shall restrain my pen and curb my spirit, because by his great devotion to St Aldhelm he either softened or erased the offence against the others. Yet at first he was doubtful and uncertain of [Col. 1669A] Aldhelm’s holiness, because the saint did not serve his wishes by displaying miracles. Nevertheless, the saint’s compassion came to the aid of his wavering and, [read: “so that”] he might lay aside the cloud of doubt and receive the light of certainty, accomplished this by the following deed.

A native of the Isle of Wight earned his living by fishing. Among his countrymen engaged in the same craft he was not undistinguished, and he had amassed respectable household goods at home. One day, as he was already labouring at his customary work, a wind blowing against him raised a very thick fog, which filled the rower’s mouth and eyes. Thus deprived of sight, at first he laughed, thinking that the sudden darkness of day would soon depart. But, as the darkness thickened more and more [Col. 1669B], he understood that it was true blindness and proclaimed his misery by cries to his companions engaged in the same work along the shore.

His calamity accordingly proclaimed a holiday from fishing for the others. Abandoning the catch they had begun, all laboured with one effort to restore him to land. Brought ashore and led by the hand, he was taken home. The event supplied matter for rustic conversation. They conferred together and debated what that chance or diabolical blast had been which had stolen daylight from an innocent fisherman and brought on night. With his sight obscured, he wept over each detail and tirelessly asked after a remedy for his misfortune. The reply was that human assistance was hopeless; he must flee to the protection of God and the saints.

This, they said, could be accomplished very suitably in Christ Church [Col. 1669C], of which I spoke above, which lies a very short sea-crossing from that island to the mainland. Approving the advice, the blind man boarded a small boat with his companions. By the equal assistance of rowing effort and favourable winds, it immediately bore him to the opposite shore. There the blind man spent a full three years in service, desiring recovery. The Lord Jesus delayed the cure so that he might stir up fervour, and that the remedy, received at last, might be the more welcome because it had been deferred longer and more painfully desired.

When the three years had elapsed, a heavenly vision warned him plainly in a dream that, if he wished to recover his sight, he should not be reluctant to go to Malmesbury. Full of joyful hope, when day broke he pursued his fortunate course; with a guide to direct his unsteady steps, [Col. 1669D] he came to the place. There he remained seven days, awaiting the divine promise, and meanwhile supported his poverty on the begged food of monastic alms. Sunday had come, the eighth day, when, lying prostrate in the church before the crucified Christ, he perceived that he had not dreamed vainly. His sight was restored clear, while blood burst forth and trickled from his eyes, just as a copious stream of milk is wont to flow from the udders of livestock when milked by women. The man released a cry of joy. Requesting a vessel, lest the holy pavement suffer the injury of blood, he caught what flowed out.

That occurrence, openly performed before a similar crowd and all the monks, greatly increased their honour among the Normans. The islander, scorning the staff with which he had risked the hazardous journey, returned home unencumbered along the clear road and regained his accustomed dwelling.

When the abbot saw this, nothing excused any further delay. He roused his mind’s diligence to cultivate the honour due to the most precious confessor. Since, with the storm of the times calmed, no hostile danger [Col. 1670A] was feared, it seemed reasonable that the saint should leave the stone enclosure in which he had been shut away for fear of the Danes. It was unworthy that stone should press his bones down into the earth when the glory of miracles raised them [into] heaven. Warin therefore intended that the bones be removed from the mausoleum and placed in a shrine. To ensure that this religious matter might proceed more orderly, he proclaimed a three-day fast for the people of the province.

Then, on the day of Pentecost itself, accompanied by Serlo, abbot of Gloucester, [Col. 1670B] he approached the tomb, removed the obstructions, and shifted the stone. Seeing within both that the bones remained whole and that the facts supported the monks’ report, he closed it again until the eighth day, when the saint’s Nativity feast was expected. For the varying Paschal moon causes the feast to be celebrated sometimes before and sometimes after Pentecost.

A monk named Hubert, an assistant in the work and sharer in carrying the burden, was present at the spectacle, suffering from an old internal complaint. On this occasion it had attacked him more severely than usual; but as he looked more closely, the fragrance of the relics striking his face drove it back. Healing ran from the smell through his bones and permeated his marrow. Until the day of his death the monk felt nothing more that shook his vital parts or disturbed his inward organs. This became widely known both by his frequent testimony and especially through the testimony of others who had often previously seen him almost at the point of death from the severity of his illness.

Accordingly, on the following Sunday, with the venerable Osmund, bishop of Salisbury, summoned, the finishing touch was put to the work begun: the bones were suitably placed in a shrine, and joy was poured out among the people. From that day so many miracles were performed there that no capacity of speech could suffice to record them: some accomplished before witnesses’ eyes, others experienced in private necessities. With Christ’s help, we shall set down here some of them, insofar as we judge suitable to the work undertaken. This second translation took place ninety-two years after the saint had been reinterred by blessed Dunstan; three hundred and sixty-nine years after his death; in the year 1078 from the Incarnation of the Lord, [Col. 1670D] and the thirteenth after the arrival of the Normans.

Cologne is a very great city, the metropolis of all Germany, crowded with commerce and filled with the patronage of saints. A citizen of this city, guilty of fratricide through misfortune rather than deliberate purpose, concealed for many years the deed that was hidden from men. But, as Augustine says, the mind conscious of evil is itself a torment to itself and, while alive, anticipates the punishments of the dead. Thus the stain of guilt consumed his wretched soul, and he imagined hell already present.

At last, therefore, he disclosed the wounds of his ulcerated conscience to Anno, archbishop of the same city, a man especially stern. Having inveighed against the guilty man as the atrocity of the deed required, [Col. 1671A] he added gentle counsels. Admirably, and following the Gospel example, he first poured wine into the wounded man, in order to wash his festering recesses, and then added oil, in order to soothe the sinner with hope of forgiveness.

He imposed, therefore, a seven-year penance: the man was to visit the churches of saints and clothe in iron the arms which, in parricidal violence, had drawn a kinsman’s blood—so that what had been the instrument of guilt might become the instrument of punishment. He was to accustom himself to fasting and silence, and deceive his heavy labours with hope of good. Thus he was to endure, since what he was then undertaking for pardon would one day lead to glory. The penitent carried out the commands, adding several crosses besides and imposing on his own body a kind of hostile war against wine. He went to Rome and [Col. 1671B] reached Jerusalem—an undertaking great and notable at that time, because the valour of our Christians had not yet made those routes passable.

There, while he prayed, scarcely admitted before the tomb, his coat of mail burst into fragments by God’s power. On his return he travelled throughout all Europe, battered by many dangers on land and sea. The goal of his labours was our monastery, which he sought. There, as he lay prostrate before the mausoleum of the blessed confessor, he obtained pardon. The force of his prayer struck heaven, entered the stars, and drew help down from above. The bonds on his arms were uncoiled; the iron was flung away with greater force and cast fifteen feet farther off; the penitent, with his soul fainting, burned with heat. But when he recovered after being sprinkled with cool water, he gave praises and thanks to God, while all those present sang in harmony. Nor [Col. 1671C] indeed could they doubt the miracle, since they had known him earlier to have been fed for many days by the monks’ alms and to have been bound most severely.

Meanwhile, the patience of readers should not be disturbed if I add a miracle of the same kind, displayed in a different person, in a different style of narration. I have described a recent cure in a lame man of advanced age; now I shall add the same concerning a boy. Folkwin was the name of the little child, whom his mother’s womb had brought forth incomplete. From his upper part to the waist he was a human being; in the rest he was either a quadruped or—I know not how else to describe him. His calves, denying the natural flexibility of the legs, adhered so stubbornly to his buttocks that they could not be pulled apart. Some men, prompted either by malice or unbelief, put their hands upon him to separate them, [Col. 1671D] causing the poor child immense suffering. He uttered dreadful shrieks and called down cruel curses upon those who tormented him.

They saw that he was innocent and free from cares, eager for laughter and the company of games; yet they hesitated, uncertain whether he had learned from an instructor to feign the contraction so that by this device he might extract a larger alms from compassionate people. But, as I said, when the attempt proved fruitless, they came over to the belief and pity of others. He had added three or four years to two five-year periods. The older he became, the more incapable he was of walking, as his tendons stiffened more obstinately. He especially moved the compassion of townspeople, for at Malmesbury he was maintained by the monks. Whenever he tried to crawl anywhere [Col. 1672A], his legs, impeded by the mud of the roads, stuck fast in place; he writhed in the mire and filled the air with cries until someone, overcome by pity, lifted the wretch in his arms.

After two years, Aldhelm dissolved this hateful rigidity in a second revelation. The boy lay at the saint’s Nativity feast, which had fallen on the first day of Pentecost; but the postponed observance was held on the second day. He lay, I say, behind the choir, taking a light sleep through his limbs. The monks, having finished the night offices, had begun morning lauds. A verse was frequently sung at his sacred tomb: “In l. m. s. q. m. f. g. are restored.” During this, he saw a person sitting kindly beside him, neither exceeding normal stature nor towering over the smallest men: with grey chin and hair [Col. 1672B], a face threatening nothing harsh but promising benefit, and dress and staff suggesting a bishop. This woman [read: “this man”], as I have said, seemed gently to stroke the little legs and gradually draw them straight, restoring them to nature. Those standing by saw the sleeping boy beautifully extend his legs; the tendons were heard to crack, as the joints of fingers crack when someone tries to stretch out his hands rather forcefully.

Awakened from sleep by the monks’ voices sounding together at the miracle, Folkwin stood upon his feet with easy effort and marvellous exertion. Immediately, in childlike joy and manly firmness, he began to run and fell before the altar. Then the people, applauding the miracle, eagerly rushed together, brought offerings to the healed boy, and heaped them upon the saint. This [Col. 1672C] sign possessed such miraculous force that the monks sent swift letters about it to the abbot, who was absent at the king’s court. When he thought these should be shown to Archbishop Lanfranc, that man illustrious for learning, measuring the merits of the confessor from the prodigy, promulgated a law throughout all England commanding that Aldhelm be held and venerated without hesitation as a saint. At once annual fairs were established for his feast, so that those whom the confessor’s holiness did not invite might at least be drawn by desire for merchandise.

This was the time when Osmund, bishop of the same diocese, a man of most reverend life, requested a relic of the saint. He judged and declared it fitting that he should share in the remains of his most approved predecessor; that it would be profitable for himself and pleasing to the saint, who, at a small loss of his bodily [Col. 1672D] wholeness, would purchase new honours and great favours. Nor was Abbot Warin difficult to persuade, since he saw himself led to agreement by reason. There was accordingly given to the bishop a bone from the left arm, which he always held in the greatest affection and honour. At great expense and with careful artistry he made a silver reliquary in which to enclose it.

The feast-day of All Saints, assigned for the work, had arrived, when, during the commemoration of the bishop, the illness of his archdeacon Everard came to mind: he lay prostrate, worn away to the marrow. It was therefore ordered that the man have himself conveyed to the church by whatever means possible. The sick man obeyed and came to the place, his servants carrying him on their backs as though he were a lifeless body. For he could not by himself naturally move, in service, either [Col. 1673A] a foot or any member except his tongue. Observing the pallor of his face and the weakness of his whole body, the bishop somewhat lost hope of his recovery. But quickly returning to himself, he kindled the flame of faith from the tinder of former miracles. Indeed, by his exhortations he struck sparks of belief into the sick man’s breast, that he might not doubt that he could be healed by the saint’s power.

The result strengthened faith; and both obtained an outcome corresponding to their efforts: the one, by offering water consecrated through immersion of the sacred bone; the other, by swallowing healing together with the drink. To make the cure more certain and free from doubt, during that same Mass, as they sang the Alleluia, the sick man’s voice, in which he excelled by skill, sounded forth. He was not unlike Peter’s mother-in-law, who rendered diligent service to the Lord who healed her—except that she obtained health through the prayers of others, whereas he claimed it through his own faith.

The other archdeacon of the same bishop was Hubald, a man who had acquired no slight experience in the liberal arts, though, because of the hesitation of his speech, he could impart them only poorly to his hearers. He had devoted himself as a familiar client to the saint, because once, when he was at Malmesbury for a feast, he had been healed by the saint’s power from a serious illness. For when he was oppressed by a painful affliction of the neck and shoulders, which denied him sleep and deprived him of food, he stole—if I may so speak—health by the mere touch of the shrine, beneath which he had crept in a bowed posture. For the guardians regularly observe this custom: after the procession they arrange the chest across the doorway [Col. 1673C] in such a way that no one can enter through the open entrance unless he lowers his body. There whoever approaches full of faith carries off whatever he desires; scarcely ever does anyone depart without obtaining his vow. The bold faith of those who make offerings strives so that, for one penny or halfpenny, a great sum of petitions may be lent at interest by the saint.

This same Archdeacon Hubald, while living at Salisbury, groaned under the same affliction mentioned above; and the pain had passed its former bounds, so that it pressed not only his neck and shoulders but also his arm, right to the tips of his nails, so stubbornly that he was unable either to bring his hand to his mouth or to use it for any purpose. It was then Ascension Day, when throughout Christendom a solemn procession is carefully prepared. Relics are brought out from their repositories; the arm of the most blessed Aldhelm was appointed to be carried with the others. The sight of the arm strengthened the archdeacon’s drowsy faith and recalled his slumbering memory: he trusted that by the merit of the same saint he would be freed from the same trouble from which he had once before been delivered. He therefore besought the bishop with earnest prayers to let him carry the arm in the procession, although this office scarcely belonged to him. He declared that carrying that pious burden would greatly help to advance his recovery. The bishop, rejoicing at such faith and earnestly desiring his health—for Hubald was both his close associate and, as I have said, no superficial scholar—took it from the altar with his own hand and entrusted it to him to bear.

What I am about to say may perhaps seem incredible, were it not to us who are accustomed to such works of Aldhelm. [Col. 1674A] For as soon as the archdeacon had placed the fingers of his weak hand so as to touch the relics, the pain in his arm fled, the heaviness of his shoulders vanished, and the morbid swelling of his neck subsided. And before he could speak, before he could burst into utterance, the bishop anticipated him with a question: why did his face shine so brightly? Hubald replied with words of good omen, so far as that joy allowed him. For a long time he poured forth praises; for a long time he dwelt upon the saint’s glory.

These are Aldhelm’s daily works; these are the first fruits of his miracles. If anyone calls them small, even so the mercy of our praiseworthy Father will appear, since we see that he does not disdain the least things, while we know him powerful in the greatest. Yet I do not know whether it is a lesser miracle to grant easy things daily than to display very great things once.

When Abbot Guarin died, Geoffrey succeeded him immediately, within fifteen days; he had been a monk of Jumièges. In his time, and through his industry, the honour of the Church grew greatly, religion was increased, and very many ornaments were made, insofar as a man of such limited resources could accomplish amid such pressing demands. Several books were written—or rather, the first offerings of a library were made. If I praise this devotion to books, I seem to do so by a certain special right of my own; for in this matter especially I have yielded to no predecessors in this place, indeed, unless what I say be boastful, I have easily surpassed them all. Let there be someone now to preserve what has been acquired; I have amassed much for reading, emulating only in this respect the worthy man’s zeal for preaching. [Col. 1674C] I therefore did not fail, according to my ability, to assist his praiseworthy undertaking. Would that there be someone to foster our labours!

Monks who had merely stammered out ordinary letters were thoroughly trained. The service of God was established generously and performed diligently, so that no monastery in England surpassed Malmesbury, and many yielded place to it. He himself arrived among the first and departed with the last; he soothed the good with courtesy and frightened offenders by severity; he was quick to anger, but he who had stirred it up could immediately restrain or break it with a sweet reply. He was temperate in frugality and, as was said, excessive in it: often content, so far as he himself was concerned, with one dish, he would ordinarily drink no more than once between dinner and supper. He was exceedingly fond of sumptuous fare, allowing nothing to be brought to his table unless it had been prepared with the most exquisite care. [Col. 1674D] He was of entirely unimpeachable celibacy after becoming abbot; before that he had been touched by some disgrace, infamous for one—and that a dreadful—deed.

For when King William Rufus had imposed an unbearable tax upon England, intending by it to buy Normandy from his brother Robert, Geoffrey, in order to settle his own share easily, shamefully sold the Church’s treasures, amassed by the care of earlier generations, following the advice of the worst men. I could name them, if participation in sin could lighten the master’s guilt. Indeed, a crime makes equal those whom it stains. In one day, twelve Gospel books, eight crosses, and eight chests were stripped and despoiled of silver and gold. But it happened fittingly that scarcity, frustrated by greed, did not satisfy his desire. For no more than seventy-two marks were found.

On the following night he dreamed that he saw a man of terrifying face and bearing rush upon him and throw boiling water from a pitcher into his face. Shaken awake by that terror, he shortly experienced in punishment the truth of the dream. First his face, then his whole body, wasted away, seized by a loathsome disease, the “king’s evil”: not the milder kind, but that which is more hideous than the others, with pustules protruding over the whole body from the most corrupt melancholic humours. It was a disease familiar and common to everyone, accustomed indeed to endure insults for a long time, but, once it has determined no longer to endure its assailant, to display him as a spectacle to the whole world. [Col. 1675A] We have laughed at this happening in many cases; in many others we confidently hope, with eager expectation, that it will happen.

In the dead man’s body a bronze band was found, which had encircled his whole belly and, with skin already grown over it, had penetrated even into his vital parts. When this was exhibited as a miracle, a monk who had been his confidant came before the people and said that not long before, an iron band similarly fixed on him had been broken by divine power; therefore a bronze one had been put in its place, so that, if his belly stretched beyond its accustomed measure, it might be not a pleasure but a punishment. He declared himself bound by oath not to reveal this while Geoffrey still enjoyed the breath of life. But because nothing is done so well that it cannot be distorted by words, someone attacked the matter in malicious verses as follows:

> It is fitting to mortify the fleshly members by vices.  
> It is not fitting that they be mortified by iron.  
>  
> This man ought to have been released by a natural death;  
> Since he forestalled it, he is his own murderer.

One may answer in as many verses:

> Rather, it is fitting to restrain the body in whatever way.  
> Examples teach this; kindly faith maintains it.  
> Nor did he wish to devise his own death by iron,  
> But by iron to put a brake upon his vices.

In the days of this abbot the precious confessor did not cease [perhaps *cessavit*] from miracles; indeed, he seemed to shine all the more brightly, as the energetic man smiled favourably upon their joy. Two of these miracles, which I shall set down, occurred before my time; the rest I both saw and delight to have seen.

In the neighbourhood there lived a woman whom birth had not so debased that she was wholly common, nor so exalted that she entertained lofty notions; but the fortune of middling stock supplied her with a middling household provision. [Col. 1675D] After reaching the years of puberty, she obtained a husband of equal station; by equality of character, a not unattractive appearance, and fruitfulness of womb, she diligently secured her husband’s affection. They delighted in their modest condition; there was nothing [read *quidquam*] that they desired more, for they had harmony of mind, bodily health, and moreover abundance of provisions.

But, as almost always happens in mortal affairs, the woman’s illness interrupted those joys. Her sinews contracted throughout her whole body: at first she crawled through the house with the pace of a tortoise, then lay stretched out upon a bed. Worn down by this illness for five years, she spent whatever necessities her household appeared to have gathered, either on alms or on physicians. And since no new addition supplied the continual drain, the once well-appointed house failed even of daily bread. [Col. 1676A] Accordingly hunger, a newcomer, drove out the old inhabitants and brought in new ones. Her faithless husband, a deserter of marital affection, repudiated the woman; he held loyalty cheap and thought little of the accustomed bonds of love. Thus, after he had gone away and had shamefully mortgaged their home for food, the sick woman was sustained by another’s mercy.

But at last the Lord looked upon her with a merciful eye and strengthened her in a vision with this oracle: “If you wish to recover health, go to the monastery at Malmesbury; there, through the merits of Saint Aldhelm, you will obtain whatever you ask.” Interpreting the voice she had heard, whose author she had not seen, as a favourable omen, she shook off sleep and rejoiced that much of her former heaviness had departed with the active movement of her limbs. After testing her steps around the house, but making little progress, she was placed in a cart and drawn to the abbey. There, a few days before the feast, she came with heart raised to good hope; soon, breaking through however dense a crowd, she lay before the altar and demanded complete healing from the saint, from whom she had received both a promise in the dream and a pledge in the movement of her limbs. Neither the force of her prayers nor her unpolished cry harmed her; rather, it brought her praise among men and prompt, complete healing from God and the saint. [Col. 1676B] Having received it, she had as many witnesses of an unfeigned miracle as there were townspeople nearby or country people from afar. Afterwards, living happily and for a long time, she brought the deserter from their marriage back into her embrace by judgment of a lawful court. He too willingly accepted the law, since it was known that his wife had never betrayed her chastity through any scarcity or through the pressure of any wanton man.

A girl native to the village called Pukelicorce suffered the misery of the same, indeed a more severe, contraction before she reached marriageable years. Her spine was so bent that her cheeks were almost upon her knees. Moreover, her knees were bent as if into a cone; she could neither crawl on little stools, as many cripples of this kind do, nor move except when supported by another’s hands. She was in the sixth year of her illness and the twelfth of her age. Her disability had increased with her age, and the girl’s days were divided equally between health and infirmity. Her uterine brother, pitying his sister’s misfortune, to which a lack of necessities added the weight of poverty, brought her in a vehicle to Malmesbury. [Col. 1676D] He did this once, and a second time, as the yearly cycle returned to the feast. He did so in vain: both on the first and the second occasion she returned without health, deprived of the gift she sought. This was not because the saint’s compassion was sluggish, for it readily comes to all who call upon it with faith; rather, I think, either because the belief of those who carried her wavered and their faith grew cold—for what could that age know of believing or disbelieving?—or because the miracle performed on the little girl might become more widely attested, since the town could not fail to know one so often brought and so often returned.

In the third year, therefore, when she had been brought again, she also spent a third earnest round of prayers in vain. Thus, when weariness and disbelief caused her brother to leave, she remained until the Lord’s Ascension, which on the third day was to receive our feast. [Col. 1677A] The day solemn for the triumph of the Lord Jesus arrived, a day on which the distinguished patron often—or always—does not refuse to perform something remarkable. For then the shrine is carried out among the people; and the doors are shut, as I have said, so that no one may enter the church unless he bows the spine of his back beneath it. Thus, according to custom, the body had gone out of the church in the service of its bearers; but the wondrous Spirit, the giver of healing, remained with the infirm girl. She lay level with the ground before the crucifix; she drank in with her ears the joyful sounds of those leaving, and this [read *id*] shook her breast the more with tears. Another’s joy doubled her own pain.

Immediately, therefore, touched by the divine remedy, she rose; the rigidity of her knees was undone and the curvature of her back straightened. She sprang forward to meet the returning saint and give thanks. [Col. 1677B] Who could tell how many were the applauses of the joyful, how many the voices of those bearing witness? I saw her; I knew her: this is that crippled girl; now she is healed.

But it is little to recount what has been heard unless one’s pen also strives to record what God granted us to see. When I have done this, the reader, if he is a fair judge and is not driven by party zeal, ought no less to believe than he would wish to be believed if he related in writing or speech something remarkable done in his own days. Nor, I think, will anyone say that I ought not to have believed my own eyes, or that I ought not to have written what I saw for God’s glory. The former would be foolish and unbelieving; the latter proud and ungrateful. I seem indeed to have rendered no small service to the saints of my own country, and not to have left my lord and patron without honour; he has deigned to grant me until now both life, that I might be able, and learning, that I might know how, to praise him. [Col. 1677C] He is plainly to be praised for the notable signs of many virtues, a man whom ancient philosophy could not equal in its aspirations. In short, what philosophy taught ought to be done was less than what he accomplished; and the simple faith of truth is greater than the ambitious falsehood of eloquence. The miracles performed after his death bear witness to the devotion he had toward God while alive; and the things I myself saw compelled me to believe their truth. Deeds of the past deserve credit from present deeds, and recent signs confirm the accounts of the ancients.

Let Ernulf of Hesdinge be brought forward: a man of outstanding reputation among England’s nobles, remarkable for his skill in husbandry and so scrupulous in paying tithes to relieve the poverty of the poor generously that, if a barn not yet tithed remained untouched, he ordered everything thrown out and tithed without delay. He had repeatedly discovered by divine grace that his rural produce increased in proportion as he took care that no fraud should occur in tithing. [Col. 1677D] His hands were afflicted by a most grievous disease: besides ulcers dripping black pus, their sinews twitched in trembling contortions. He could therefore bring them to no task; nor—something shameful even to say—could he use them to wipe away the remnants of food. His own need fed him; his own shame was washed away by another’s hand.

He therefore determined to go to Malmesbury and there try the skill of a certain Gregory, a most approved physician. Gregory applied in vain every device of his art, both under Abbot Geoffrey’s instruction and out of goodwill toward the man; finally he pronounced the incurable illness to be left to fate. He acted as a good man should, lest he vainly drain an invalid yearning for health through gifts and empty him of money. But the abbot, thinking that something should be attempted through the saint’s miracles, ordered balm found in the tomb to be brought and his hands anointed. What a beautiful sight! As soon as a drop of the precious liquid touched his hand, the trembling of the sinews ceased, the flowing corruption dried up, and, not to make a long story of it, within very few days he was wholly restored. [Col. 1678A] It is sufficiently well known that this miracle increased the distinguished man’s devotion so greatly that, despising attachment to his relatives and casting aside his heap of riches, he set out for Jerusalem with no hope of return.

Among the crowd of religious persons coming to the feast [read *venientium*], a multitude of rogues too mingles itself: they procure their food by easy gain while provoking their hearers’ laughter with invented witticisms. One of them had come there when I was a boy, more sharply witty in his biting jesting than the others, and skilled as well in imitating obscene gestures whenever acting mimes [perhaps *mimos*] failed him in words. When the blessed saint’s shrine was carried outside, this man impudently stood against it and did something offensive even to recount: first he exposed his groin and polluted the air, then disturbed the atmosphere by releasing the noise of his belly. Though this might have compelled laughter from fools, it caused terrible grief to the monks, who lamented that the rogue uttered his insolence with impunity. [Col. 1678C] But as they called down vengeance, the confessor’s nearby ear was not lacking. He had scarcely lowered his clothes when, behold, in sight of the people he was violently seized by a demon and paid the penalty of his shamelessness. He spun in circles; he foamed like a pig pursued by the barking of dogs; he ground his molars with a rattling noise, so that it became plain that he had passed into the dominion of him at whose prompting he had begun so great a crime. His companions, in pious violence, seized him and dragged him home by force, whether he wished it or not.

There, tied to a post while he was thought to be quietly meditating, he suddenly burst upon guests at table. He overturned the table, battered some with his fists, struck others senseless with missiles, and drove all away, using the vessels that had been set out as weapons. But his companions, judging that the wretched man should not be abandoned, drew him, tightly enclosed in a wedge, to the tomb. [Col. 1678D] There, after three nights of vigil and an equal number of days of fasting, while the monks prayed and purchased another’s healing with their groans, he was healed not only of the demon but also—more remarkably—of his talkativeness. Thereafter he was always modest and mild; except that his eyes remained deceptive and threatening, and by their bloodshot glare he always frightened us boys, recalling how before his healing he sat at the tomb and rushed at us with fixed face, or, if he could do nothing else, spat out filthy spittle.

A woman born at Kiligeham was spinning on Saturday evening, when the day was already declining toward sunset. Those sitting beside her warned her, out of reverence for the Lord’s Day, to keep the holiday. [Col. 1679A] Not only did she refuse, but she also charged them with arrogance for criticizing her as she attended to necessities, and with foolish idleness for not doing the same themselves. Punishment followed the word: immediately she was thrown to the ground, with one half of her body rendered dead, and she came very near to dying. But when frequent dashing of water restored her breath, she acknowledged her fault, bewailed her misery, and prayed for forgiveness.

Yet we do not obtain pardon as easily as we commit guilt: pleasure flies and passes away, but sin drives down a stubborn root. Therefore, supporting her steps on both sides with crutches, in a living corpse now almost buried, the woman visited the patronage of many saints over very many years. [Col. 1679B] But when she seemed to herself to have worn out useless toil everywhere, she at last hurried to Malmesbury after hearing of the miracles of Blessed Aldhelm. Her arrival preceded the days of Lent; throughout them she remained in church, going out nowhere except once a day, and lessened the weight of her sins by fasting. The favour of Easter joy had now made mortal hearts glad; we were now observing the second day of the feast. That verse was being sung in which Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, had confronted the Jews with a most beautiful alternative [the text has *disjuncta*, apparently for *dilemmate*]: either let them restore Christ, whom they had buried, or adore him risen.

As she stood leaning upon crutches before the crucifix, she struck the pavement in a fall more violent than usual. Many ran up, wishing to raise the fallen woman, fearing [Col. 1679C] that the severe fall had broken the paralytic’s limbs. Others, whose counsel was sounder, restrained them, saying that the outcome should be entrusted to God, who knew how to order it rightly. Therefore, with hearts lifted upward, all stood attentive and silent, when she rose uninjured, her eyes flashing, her fingers moving, and her whole body restored. The certainty of the miracle made the townspeople—who knew her fully because of their long familiarity—open their mouths in praise of God and the confessor.

Calne is a village ten miles from Malmesbury, its lands adjoining those of the abbey and of the village. A man native to it, deprived of speech, came in the same year, if I remember correctly, to the feast. He was well known throughout the district because of the notable nature of his affliction, and had been tested repeatedly [Col. 1679D] as truly mute. For the governor of the province had more than once subjected him to tortures in an effort to force from him a confession that the condition was feigned and thereby bring the supposed pretence to light. The governor was cruel, certainly; but the feigning of certain wretches demanded severity, for, making a mockery of God and men, they counterfeit any illness in order to fill the emptiness of their belly with coins begged under this fiction.

Thus amid his torments the man uttered pitiable roars; and, with a contrite spirit such as the Lord loves, he longed for the end of his miseries. Though his tongue was powerless, his understanding was clear; he joined the crowd of people hurrying to the feast. At first he alone was granted the sight of the bishop walking near the base of the high altar, and with the joy of his smiling countenance gently regarding the singing monks. [Col. 1680A] Seeing this, he tried, by the motion of his fingers and a great opening of his mouth, to show it to the others, whose sight had been overwhelmed by the burden of sins. But since the power of speech failed him as he wished to speak, and since the others were not divine so as to understand him, he rushed indignantly into the crypt, then under new construction. There, when he saw the same thing and strove with great effort to speak, a monk who was present, foreseeing something divine, placed the fingers of Blessed Aldhelm’s arm in the mouth of the shouting man. Then, out of reverence for the holy fingers, he drew his teeth far apart, uttered deep sighs from below, and with great exertion cast out a morsel of meat together with blood, crying: “Lord Saint Aldhelm, help me.”

That voice, freed from obstruction, gave from then onward a happy beginning to speech; for some years thereafter he spoke without impairment, except that, because of the narrow passage of his throat, he modulated his voice with a rather hoarse sound. [Col. 1680B]

A woman, not native but a resident of the same village, deprived of sight, recovered at the following year’s feast of Father Aldhelm the light she had lost for eighteen years. I do not know the cause of her blindness and do not wish to recount it, lest by talkativeness I deceive the trust of my readers. This is certain: as she stood before the crucifix, conspicuous for her yellow hair flowing loose down her back but disfigured by the darkness of her eyes, the orbs deprived of light began to move with frequent prickings. Irritated by these, the woman first drew blood by light rubbing; but when she satisfied the greater itching by a harsher injury of her nails, blood flowed more copiously, and a bowl was requested to receive it. Thus, when the obstructions had been removed, the brightness of light illuminated the hollows of her windows. [Col. 1680C] Then her utterly truthful relatives who were present both applauded the miracle and support her to this day from a pension.

Having professed the veil of a holier religious habit, she suffers no loss of sight, except insofar as advancing age approaches old age. She is alive in this year in which we write these things: the year 1125 from the Incarnation of the Lord; the four hundred and sixteenth from the death of the most holy confessor; the twenty-fifth of King Henry’s reign. It is notable for the mutilation throughout England of counterfeiters who had debased the coinage; infamous likewise, through that same falsification, for the dearness of grain and devouring famine; and further notorious for indiscriminate devastation among the people. It is made mournful by the deaths of very eminent men, especially Pope Calixtus and Henry V, emperor of Germany, than whom none had ever been more outstanding in their respective offices; it has been troubled by thunder and lightning in every month, by a continuance of rain with scarcely a day’s interruption, rainy and muddy even in the summer months. [Col. 1680D]

[Col. 1681]

# WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY’S BOOK ON THE ANTIQUITY OF THE CHURCH OF GLASTONBURY

(Edited from a manuscript of Trinity College, Cambridge, by Gale, *Historiae Britannicae, Saxonicae Anglo-Danicae Scriptores XV*, Oxford, 1691, folio.)

# WILLIAM’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 1681A] To the lord Henry, bishop of Lincoln, greatly beloved and honoured in the bowels of Christ, William, son of your dignity, wishes whatever happiness may be desired.

If there is anything that holds a person firm in this life and persuades him to remain even-minded amid the adversities and storms of the world, I believe it to be, above all, meditation upon the holy Scriptures. The writings of the pagans, indeed, claim such usefulness for themselves as to flatter the reader’s intellect with brilliance of language and to impress him with eloquence. But the fruit of books inspired from heaven far outweighs theirs, because they both pour into the mind food of pleasant sweetness here and acquire for it the reward of eternal blessedness elsewhere.

Moreover, in the holy Scriptures there are many things—indeed, in my judgment, countless things—by which divine condescension trains mortal minds in the practice of a good life: both precepts and examples. By the former we are instructed how to live; by the latter we are shown, with God’s help, how easy to accomplish are the things commanded. [Col. 1681B] Nature has implanted in some souls this disposition: although they know both to be necessary, they are nevertheless more drawn by hearing examples than exhortations. They rise in reverence before the deeds of foreigners because of their holiness, but are seized by a livelier delight if the life of some saint who was their fellow-countryman is brought forward, in which, as in a mirror, there appears—so to speak—a visible living image of religion. For a pleasing account gains force from nearness, lest anyone despair that, through God’s grace, what he hears to have been done by another close at hand can be done by himself.

Therefore, I think I have devoted my pen to a task not to be despised: I have consigned to eternal remembrance by my labour the life of Blessed Dunstan, first abbot of Glastonbury and afterward archbishop of Canterbury. At the wish of the brothers of Glastonbury, your sons, my lords and companions, I long ago completed two books on him, preserving the full truth of events. Yet, lest anything be lacking to the duty of my diligence, I shall in the opening of this book set forth from its origin the beginning and development of this church of yours. [Col. 1682A] Nor should this be thought far removed from my purpose, since the Church’s honour redounds to Dunstan and Dunstan’s praise to the Church. For she nurtured Dunstan in her maternal bosom into manhood, and he added very great splendour to his mother. Thus my mind rises somewhat in hope that this holy writing may perhaps procure this: that, through the occasion of the foster-child, the dignity of his nurse may be set in order.

Those little books, and also the *Life of Saint Patrick*, the miracles of the venerable Benignus, and the Passion of the martyr Indract, which I had composed with like care, I had long ago permitted to circulate in their hands, so that anything said without due reason might be corrected in time. They, weighing the writings for a long time with more favourable judgment, freed me from every stain of fault, neither yielding anything to offence from regard for religion nor granting anything to favour. I therefore dedicate this modest work, whatever it may be, to your wisdom for examination, venerable lord and deservedly beloved Father. The reason for my undertaking is obvious: that your excellency may know what men, and how great, founded and advanced the church which now relies, under God and his saints, especially upon your protection.

Know also that you have imitated—and, I nearly say, surpassed—the deeds of ancient heroes before you had heard their names. For, to engage more boldly with anyone who might wish to criticize: in what may the former possessors be preferred to you? In enlarging estates? You restore what was long ago alienated and, through diligent industry, add to what is held. In erecting buildings? How far you surpass all predecessors in that matter, the finger of an astonished observer will show better than the title of a praiser. [Col. 1682C] In maintaining the peace of the inhabitants? With the shield of your name, you cast down all robbers; by the brightness of your face you drive away clouds of sadness; by the wisdom of your speech you unravel the accusations of litigants. In the religious life of the monks? Under your times, by God’s favour, it has always flourished in such a way that unhappy envy blushes to invent any slander against it.

There is also your open-hearted love for them: you frighten them with no harsh growl, but pleasantly receive them when they come, treat them affably, and bid them a fatherly farewell when they depart. For certainly it is not said of us what the poet fittingly sings of certain powerful men:

> “He drives far away from himself the whole common crowd  
> and rules as a basilisk over empty sands.”  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* IX.725)

[Col. 1684A] All eloquence, therefore, falls short of your merit. Your praises excel so greatly that nothing lies beyond them. Since this is so, receive, I pray, this gift of my devotion, this pledge of diligence, and take care that I do not lose the fruit of my labour. Be present, then, if it please you, and attend while I attempt, through the succession of generations, to rescue the Church’s antiquity from suspicions, gathering together as much as I could from the heap of your records.

# ON THE ANTIQUITY OF THE CHURCH OF GLASTONBURY

[Col. 1683]

## Here begins the account of how twelve disciples of the holy apostles Philip and James first founded the church of Glastonbury.

[Col. 1683B]

After the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, the triumph of his ascension, and the sending down from heaven of the Paraclete Spirit, who filled the hearts of the disciples—still trembling with fear of temporal punishment—by granting them knowledge of all languages: “All who believed were together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus,” as Luke the Evangelist recounts; and the word of God was spread abroad, the number of believers grew daily, and all had one heart and one soul.

The Jewish priests, inflamed by the torches of envy, together with the Pharisees and scribes stirred up persecution against the Church, killing Stephen the first martyr [Col. 1683C] and driving almost all far away beyond their borders. Therefore, while this storm of persecution raged, the scattered believers made for various kingdoms of the earth assigned to them by the Lord, offering the word of salvation to the nations.

Saint Philip, however, as Freculf testifies in book II, chapter 4, went to the region of the Franks for the sake of preaching and converted and baptized many. Wishing, therefore, that Christ’s word might be spread, he chose twelve of his disciples to preach the incarnation of Jesus Christ; devoutly stretched out his right hand over each one; and sent them to Britain to evangelize the word of life. Over them, as they relate, he set his dearest friend Joseph of Arimathea, who had also buried the Lord.

They came into Britain in the sixty-third year from the Lord’s Incarnation and the fifteenth after the Assumption of Blessed Mary, and confidently preached the faith of Christ. But the barbarian king and his people, hearing doctrines so new and unfamiliar, refused utterly to agree to their preaching and would not change the traditions of their fathers. Yet, because they had come from afar and the modesty of their life commended them, he granted them at their request, for habitation, a certain island on the edge of his territory, encircled by woods, brambles, and marshes, called by its inhabitants Yniswitris. Later two other kings, though pagans, in succession learned the holiness of their life and granted each of them one portion of land, confirming it at their request according to custom. [Col. 1683D] Thus the twelve hides, as is believed, still derive their name from them.

The aforesaid saints, living in this same wilderness, were shortly afterward instructed by a vision of the archangel Gabriel to build, in honour of Holy Mary, Virgin and Mother of God, a church in a place shown to them from heaven. They did not sluggishly obey the divine command. According to what had been shown them, they completed a small chapel, making the walls all around below from twisted withies, in the thirty-first year after the Lord’s Passion and the fifteenth after the Assumption of the glorious Virgin: an unsightly structure indeed, but one abundantly adorned by God’s power. Since it was the first church in that region, the Son of God marked it with a greater dignity, namely by dedicating it himself in honour of his mother.

The twelve often-mentioned saints, rendering devoted services to God and the Blessed Virgin in the same place, giving themselves to vigils, fasts, and prayers, were refreshed in all their needs by the aid and vision of that Virgin, as piety bids us believe. [Col. 1684B] We know this to be so both from the charter of Saint Patrick and from the writings of the elders. One of these, a historian of the Britons—as we saw at Saint Edmund’s and likewise at Saint Augustine’s, apostle of the English—began as follows:

> “On the border of western Britain lies a royal island, called Glastonbury by an ancient name, broad in the extent of its territory, surrounded by fish-filled waters and rivers forming pools, furnished with many things useful for human need, and, what is greatest, dedicated to sacred gifts. There the first neophytes of the English Catholic law found an ancient church, constructed, certainly as they say, by no human hand—indeed prepared by God for human salvation. Later the builder of heaven itself showed, through many miraculous deeds and many mysteries of virtues, that he had consecrated it to himself and to Holy Mary, Mother of God.”

But of these matters later; now let us return to our beginning. The saints mentioned above, dwelling thus in the same wilderness, after the passing of many years were led out from the prison of the flesh. The same place, which had formerly been the habitation of saints, began to be a haunt of wild beasts, until it pleased the Blessed Virgin that her oratory should return to the memory of the faithful. How this happened, we shall now relate.

## How Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus converted the Britons to the faith and came to the island of Avalon.

The annals of sound credibility relate that a king of the Britons, named Lucius, sent to Eleutherius, the thirteenth pope after blessed Peter, begging him to illuminate Britain’s darkness with the light of Christian preaching. This high-minded king undertook a deed wholly worthy of great praise: he voluntarily sought the faith which, at that time, nearly all kings and peoples persecuted when it was offered, and scarcely knew even by report. To say something by way of comparison, King Æthelberht of Kent, many years after Lucius, concurred in praise of equal merit: he did not drive away with a harsh reply the preachers sent to him from Rome, but received them with kindly hospitality. [Col. 1685B] His kindness was accompanied by shrewd pleasantness of speech; for although he would not give his own assent to their words, nevertheless, since they had come from far away in order to communicate to him what they believed best, it might seem unreasonable were he to inflict any inconvenience upon them. These, therefore, are men worthy of the fullest remembrance: the one wisely invited Christianity; the other willingly received it.

Accordingly, when Eleutherius sent them, two most holy men, namely Phaganus and Deruvianus, came to Britain, as the charter of Saint Patrick and the deeds of the Britons attest. Preaching here the word of life, they washed the king and his people in the sacred font in the year of the Lord 166. Then, travelling through the regions of Britain by preaching and baptizing, [Col. 1685C] they entered the island of Avallonia, penetrating the depths of the wilderness in the manner of Moses the lawgiver. There they found an ancient church, established at God’s command, constructed, as is said, by the hands of Christ’s disciples, and prepared by God for human salvation. Later the very Maker of the heavens would demonstrate, through many miraculous acts and mysteries of many virtues, that he had consecrated it to himself and to Mary, the holy Mother of God. One hundred and three years had elapsed from the arrival in Britain of the disciples of Saint Philip to the arrival of the saints just mentioned.

Therefore the aforesaid holy Phaganus and Deruvianus, having found the oratory in this condition, were filled with ineffable joy. Remaining there long in the praises of God—for nine years, that is—and carefully investigating the place, [Col. 1685D] they found a figure of our redemption and other manifest signs, by which they clearly recognized that Christians had formerly inhabited the place. Afterwards, considering a heavenly oracle, they understood that the Lord had specially chosen this place above the rest of Britain, so that the name of his glorious Mother might be invoked there.

They also found in ancient writings the entire account of how, when the holy apostles had been scattered throughout the world, Saint Philip the apostle came into France with a multitude of disciples and sent twelve of them to Britain to preach. Instructed by an angelic revelation, these built the aforesaid chapel, which afterwards the Son of the Most High dedicated in honour of his Mother. Three kings, though pagans, gave those twelve twelve portions of land for [Col. 1686A] their support. They also found written accounts of their deeds. Accordingly, they loved this place above all others; and, in remembrance of the first twelve, selected twelve of their own number and caused them to dwell on the aforesaid island, with King Lucius’s consent.

Afterwards they remained there in different places as anchorites, namely in the same places in which the first twelve had originally dwelt. Yet they came together daily and frequently in the ancient church, to perform divine offices with greater devotion. And just as the three pagan kings had formerly granted the said island with its appurtenances to Christ’s first twelve disciples, so the aforesaid Phaganus and Deruvianus obtained from King Lucius confirmation that it should remain free from secular claims for these twelve companions and for others thereafter. Thus [Col. 1686B] many succeeded others, always nevertheless in the number of twelve, and remained on the aforesaid island through many courses of years, until the coming of Saint Patrick, apostle of the Irish.

To this church, thus found, the holy neophytes added another stone-built oratory, which they dedicated to Christ and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Thus the ancient church of Saint Mary at Glastonbury was restored through their work, as faithful antiquity has not failed to report through successive ages. There are also records of no slight authority found at Saint Edmund’s, stating that this most holy church of Glastonbury was not made by the hands of other men, but that Christ’s own disciples built it, Saint Philip the apostle having sent them, as has been stated. Nor is this at variance [Col. 1686C] with truth, as has been said; for if Philip the apostle preached to the Gauls, as Freculf says in book II, chapter 4, it may be believed that he also cast the seeds of the word beyond the ocean.

### How a monk of Saint-Denis spoke concerning Glastonbury

To confirm the antiquity of the church of which we have spoken, let us digress a little. A certain monk of Glastonbury, named Godfrey, from whose letter we have taken both this chapter and that which follows, was staying, in the time of Blesensis, abbot of Glastonbury, at Saint-Denis in the district of Paris. An elderly monk asked him: “Of what race are you, and from what home?” He replied, [Col. 1686D] “A Norman, a monk of the monastery in Britain called Glastonbury.” “Tell me,” said the elder, “does that ancient church of the perpetual Virgin and Mother of Mercy still stand?” “It does,” he replied.

Then, touching Godfrey of Glastonbury’s head with a graceful gesture, the old man held him long in suspenseful silence; at last he opened his lips and said: “The church of my most glorious martyr and that church of which you speak possess the same rank of privilege: this one in Gaul, that one in Britain, both arising at one and the same time and consecrated by the supreme and great pontiff. Yet that one surpasses this by one degree, for it is called a second Rome.” While Godfrey hung upon the man’s words, the monk charged with receiving the brethren separated them, reluctant as they were to part and never see one another again. But enough on this matter.

### How a multitude of people first inhabited Glastonbury

[Col. 1687A]

Having described the foundation, dedication, and later discovery of this oratory, it remains to add how this island came to be inhabited by a multitude. We read in the ancient deeds of the Britons that twelve brothers came from the northern part of Britain into the West and occupied many regions—Venedocia, Demetia, Buthir, and Kedweli—which their forefather Cuneda had held. The names of those brothers are noted below: Ludnerth, Morgen, Catgur, Cathmor, Merguid, Morvined, Morehel, Morcant, Boten, Morgen, Mortineil, and Glasteing.

This is that Glasteing who, travelling through the inland country of the Angles, beside the village called Escebtiorne, followed his sow with her piglets as far as Wells; and from [Col. 1687B] Wells, along a pathless and watery way called Sugewege, that is, “the sow’s way,” he found her suckling beneath an apple tree beside the church of which we speak. Hence the name has descended to us that the apples of that tree are called *Ealdcyrcenes epple*, that is, “apples of the old church.” The sow too was for that reason called *ealdcyre suge*, “old-church sow.” While other sows have four feet, this one, marvellous to say, had eight.

Therefore Glasteing, after he had entered that island and seen it abounding in every kind of good thing, came with all his household to live there and spent the course of his life there. The place is said to have been first peopled by his descendants and household who succeeded him. These matters are drawn from the ancient books of the Britons.

### The different names of the same island

[Col. 1687C]

This island was first called *Yniswgtrin* by the Britons; later, when the English had subdued the land, translating the earlier name, they called it in their own language *Glastynburg*, or after the Glasteing of whom we have spoken. It is also famously called the island of Avallonia, and this was the origin of that name. As stated above, Glasteing found his sow beneath a fruit-bearing tree beside the ancient church. Since, on first arriving, he found apples—very rare in those parts—the island was called in his language Avallonia, that is, “island of apples”; for *avalla* in British means “apples” in Latin. Or it is named after a certain Avalloc, who is said to have lived there with his daughters because of the [Col. 1687D] seclusion of the place.

### With what devotion various saints came there

The church of which we are speaking, which because of its antiquity is commonly called “the Old Church” by the English, from its first beginning gave forth and breathed throughout the whole country, I know not what fragrance of divine holiness. This was evident despite the coarse form of its cult, in the great reverence shown it: on the one hand, the throng of people converging there by every road; on another, the gatherings of the wealthy, laying aside their pomp; and again, the frequent sojourn of religious and learned persons.

### On Saint Gildas

For, as we have received from our elders, Gildas, a historian neither dull nor inelegant—whom the Britons owe for whatever knowledge they possess among other peoples—spent many years there, captured by the holiness of the place. There, having departed this life in the year of the Lord 512, he was buried in the Old Church before the altar.

### On Saint Patrick

At about that time—though earlier—when the English were troubling the Britons’ peace and the Pelagians attacking their faith, Saint Germanus of Auxerre, as is read elsewhere, brought aid against both. He routed the former with an *Alleluia* chant and struck the latter down with evangelical and apostolic thunderbolts. Intending then to return home, he took Patrick into his familiar companionship and, after several years, sent him as preacher to the Irish at the command of Pope Celestine.

Patrick, having vigorously carried out the task laid upon him, returned to Britain in his final days. Rejecting former rank and the greetings of the public square, [Col. 1688B] he put in at Cornwall above his own altar, which remains to this day in great veneration among the inhabitants, both on account of its holiness and efficacy and because of the healing of the sick. From there he came to Glastonbury. Finding twelve brothers living there as anchorites, he gathered them together; accepting the office of abbot, he taught them to live the cenobitic life, as the following document, which he himself wrote in his own time, more clearly declares.

### Charter of Saint Patrick, bishop

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Patrick, humble little servant of God, in the year of his Incarnation 430, sent as legate into Ireland by the most holy Pope Celestine, by God’s grace converted the Irish [Col. 1688C] to the way of truth. When I had established them firmly in the Catholic faith, I at length returned to Britain. And, as I believe, with God as my guide—he who is life and way—I came upon the island of *Yniswgtrin*. There I found a holy and ancient place, chosen and sanctified by God in honour of Mary, the undefiled Virgin and Mother of God.

“There I found certain brothers instructed in the rudiments of the Catholic faith and of pious conduct, successors of the disciples of Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus. I truly believe that their names, by reason of the merits of their life, are written in heaven; and since the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance, when I had come to love these brothers with constancy, I wished to record their names in my own writing. They are Brumbam, Hyregaam, Brenwal, Wencreth, Bantcommeweng, Adelward, Loyor, Wellias, Breden, [Col. 1688D] Swelwes, Hinloernius, and another Hin.

“Though born of noble lineage, they desired to adorn their nobility by works of faith, and chose to lead the eremitic life. Since I found them humble and peaceable, I chose rather to be lowly with them than to dwell in royal courts. But because we all had one heart and one soul, we chose to live together, eat and drink together, and sleep in the same house. Thus, although unwilling, I was placed over them; for I was not worthy to untie the laces of their sandals.

“When we had thus adopted the monastic life according to the rule of approved Fathers, the aforesaid brothers showed me the writings of Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus. These stated that twelve disciples of Saints Philip and James built that very ancient [Col. 1689A] church in honour of our aforesaid advocate, through the instruction of the blessed archangel Gabriel; moreover, that the Lord had dedicated that same church from heaven in honour of his Mother; and that three pagan kings had given the same twelve twelve portions of land for their support. In more recent writings I also found that Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus had obtained from Pope Eleutherius, who had sent them, ten years’ indulgence. And I, Brother Patrick, obtained twelve years in my own time from Pope Celestine of pious memory.

“After a considerable time, taking with me my fellow brother Wellia, with great difficulty we climbed through the thick forest to the summit of the mountain which rises on that island. When we reached it, we found an ancient oratory, almost ruined, yet suitable for Christian devotion and, as it seemed to me, chosen by God. When we entered it, [Col. 1689B] we were so refreshed by the sweetness of its fragrance that we believed ourselves set amid the delights of paradise. Going out, then entering again, and investigating the place more carefully, we found a book in which the Acts of the Apostles were written together with the acts and deeds of Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus. It had been consumed to a great extent. At the end of that book, however, we found writing stating that the aforesaid Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus, by revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, built this same oratory in honour of Saint Michael the Archangel, so that he who, at God’s command, is to bring human beings into everlasting honours might receive honour there from human beings.

“As this writing delighted us, we strove to read it through to the end. The writing further stated that the venerable Phaganus and Deruvianus remained there for nine years, and that they also obtained thirty years’ indulgence for all Christians who should devoutly visit the place in honour of blessed Michael. Having therefore discovered so great a treasure of divine goodness, Brother Wellias and I fasted for three months, devoting ourselves to prayer and vigils and commanding demons and beasts that appeared in manifold forms.

“One night, when I had given myself to sleep, the Lord Jesus appeared to me in a vision and said: ‘Patrick, my servant, [Col. 1689D] know that I have chosen this place for the honour of my name, and that here they may honourably invoke the aid of my archangel Michael. This shall be your sign, and that of your brothers, that they too may believe: your left arm shall wither until you announce to your brothers, who are in the lower cell, what you have seen, and return here again.’ And so it happened.

“From that day we appointed two brothers there in perpetuity, unless future pastors should decide otherwise for a just cause. To Arnulf and Ogmar, Irish brothers who had come with me from Ireland and who began, at my exhortation, to remain humbly in the said oratory, I entrusted this present document, retaining another like it in the chest of Saint Mary as a memorial for posterity. And I, Patrick, with the counsel [Col. 1690A] of my brothers, grant one hundred days of pardon to all who, with pious intent, shall cut down with axe and hatchet the forest on every side of the aforesaid mountain, so that easier access may be made for Christians who will devoutly visit the church of the blessed and perpetual Virgin and the aforesaid oratory.”

We have established that these matters are true by the testimony of a very ancient similar writing and by the reports of elders. This holy man mentioned above, apostle of the Irish and first abbot on the island of Avallonia, after suitably instructing the aforesaid brothers in regular discipline and adequately enriching the same place with lands and possessions from the gifts of kings and other princes, after several years yielded to nature. He was granted burial in the Old Church at the right of the altar, an angel showing the place, while a great flame burst forth from the same spot before all present. [Col. 1690B]

### On the death of Saint Patrick

Patrick died in the one hundred and eleventh year of his age, in the year 472 of the Lord’s Incarnation; this was the forty-seventh year since he had been sent to Ireland. For he was born in the year of the Lord 361, and in 425 was sent to Ireland by Pope Celestine; this was the sixty-fourth year of his age. In the year of the Lord 433 he converted the Irish to faith in Christ. Returning at last to Britain, he remained for thirty-nine years in the island of Avallonia in the best manner of life. He rested in the Old Church on the right side of the altar for many years, [Col. 1690C] namely seven hundred and ten years, until that church was burned.

His body was placed in a stone pyramid beside the altar, toward the south; in reverence for the saint, the devotion of his household later nobly clad it in gold and silver.

### Vision concerning Saint Patrick

Long after blessed Patrick’s death, the frequent question arose whether he had been a monk and abbot there. A vision of a certain brother resolved every doubt.
