After the blessed man’s death, while his memory was uncertain whether he had been monk and abbot there and the question was often debated, the brother received this confirming oracle. Falling asleep, he seemed to hear someone reading, after recounting many of Patrick’s miracles, these [Col. 1690D] words: “This man was adorned with the sanctity of the metropolitan pallium. Afterwards he was made a monk and abbot here.” In addition, lest he should believe unwillingly, the reader showed him the words just spoken written in letters of gold.

### On Saint Indract and Saint Brigid

Hence the Irish adopted the custom of frequently visiting the place to kiss the relics of their patron. It is therefore a most widely known tradition that Saint Indract and blessed Brigid, notable inhabitants of that land, formerly travelled there. Brigid, indeed, came there in the year of the Lord 488; after spending some time on the island called Beokery, she eventually returned, leaving there certain [Col. 1691A] tokens of hers—namely her bag, necklace, bell, and woven implements—which are preserved there in memory of her. Indract, however, was martyred and buried there with his companions, as our writing has elsewhere not failed to state. Afterwards King Ine translated him from the place of martyrdom to the church of Glastonbury.

### On Saint Benignus

In the year of the Lord 460 Saint Benignus came to Glastonbury. He was a disciple of Saint Patrick and the third successor to Patrick in the Irish episcopate, as their deeds testify. Warned by an angel, he abandoned by vow his homeland and episcopal dignity; having embraced voluntary pilgrimage, he arrived at Glastonbury under God’s guidance, where he found Saint Patrick also. How great was his grace with God is evident from many signs of miracles. His tokens at Fernigemere likewise attest it: water supplied in greatest abundance at his prayers, and from his dry staff a huge tree, vigorous and leafy. [Col. 1691B] After countless years in the said island, he rested in a blessed end; and after many courses of years, that is, in the year of the Lord 901, he was honourably translated to Glastonbury.

### On Saint Columkille

In the year of the Lord 504 Saint Columkille came to Glastonbury. Some affirm that this saint completed the course of his life there; but whether this was so, or whether he returned home from there, I do not determine.

### On Saint David, archbishop

How highly the great David, archbishop of Menevia, revealed that place is more famous than need be made illustrious by our account. He proved the antiquity and holiness of the church by a divine oracle. Intending to dedicate it, he came to the place with seven bishops, of whom he was the first. When all things required for the rite had been prepared, on the night preceding, as he supposed, the festival, he gave himself to sleep. His senses wholly relaxed in rest, he saw the Lord Jesus standing by and gently asking the cause of his coming. When David had explained it without hesitation, the Lord recalled him from his purpose by saying that the Church had long ago been dedicated by himself in honour of his Mother, and that it was not right for the sacrament to be rashly violated by a human repetition. At the same moment [Col. 1691D] he seemed to pierce David’s palm with his finger, adding: “You shall have this as a sign that what I have done beforehand ought not to be repeated. But since your purpose has proceeded not so much from presumption as from devotion, the punishment shall not be prolonged. For tomorrow morning, when you are about to say Mass through me, with me, and in me, your full vigour of health shall be restored.”

The bishop, shaken from sleep by these terrors, became pale with festering discharge, as he was then afflicted; but afterwards he assented to the truth of the teaching. Yet, lest he should seem to have accomplished nothing, he quickly built and dedicated another church.

### On the relics of Saint David

This saint, worthy of God, died in the year of the Lord 546. Some indeed affirm that the relics of this holy and incomparable man were placed with blessed Patrick in [Col. 1692A] the Old Church; and the Welsh, by frequent prayers and much testimony, undoubtedly maintain and confirm this, adducing the fact that Bernard, bishop of the valley of Rosina, sought there once and a second time the relics of Saint Pergeus, and, despite many objections, did not find them.

But we shall relate below how the said relics were translated from the valley of Rosina to Glastonbury. A certain matron named Alswitha, in the time of King Edgar, acquired the aforesaid relics through a kinsman of hers, who was then bishop at the valley of Rosina. At that time the whole land there had been so devastated that scarcely any man was to be found there, except a few women, and even they in scattered places. She conveyed the relics to Glastonbury.

### On relics translated from Wales to Glastonbury

[Col. 1692B]

The religious Welshmen of that land testify that, at that time, carrying with them many bodies and relics of saints, they brought them to Glastonbury on their way to Rome and, as they continued their journey, left them there. This translation occurred in the four hundred and twentieth year after his death, in the year 966 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

### On the holiness and dignity of the church of Glastonbury

The church of Glastonbury, therefore, is the most ancient in England of all those known to me. Hence it has received its surname. Within it, besides blessed Patrick and the others of whom I have spoken above, are preserved the bodily remains of many saints; no part of the sanctuary is free from the ashes of the blessed. So densely are relics heaped beneath the stone-paved floor, at the sides of the altar, and above and beneath the altar itself, [Col. 1692C] that it is rightly called a heavenly sanctuary upon earth, a repository of so many saints.

How happy, good God, are its inhabitants, whom the very reverence of the place invites to the ordering of their conduct. I should believe that none of those whose bodies have departed is lost to heaven, when the praise or intercession of so many patrons receives them. Wherever one can observe stones set with deliberate design in the pavement, either in a triangle or a square, and sealed with lead, beneath them some holy secret is contained; if I believe this, I do no injury to religion.

The antiquity and multitude of saints have stirred such reverence for the place that scarcely anyone presumes to keep vigil there at night; scarcely anyone, during the day, casts out superfluous phlegm without shuddering in every limb, conscious of mockery and foulness. No one who has brought hunting birds or driven quadrupeds among the adjoining cemetery has departed unharmed in person or property. All those subjected to trial by iron or water who have offered a prayer there—as far as present memory reaches—have rejoiced in their safety, without exception. If anyone nearby thought to erect a building whose shadow might deprive the church of light, he became exposed to ruin. It is well known that no man of that district has any oath holier or more frequent than “by the Old Church,” and that nothing do they avoid more, for fear of its famous vengeance, than perjury. [Col. 1693A] The truth, threatened with decay through the lapse of years, of the assertions we have set forth is sustained by the testimony of very many most truthful persons.

### On Saint Paulinus, bishop

But to return to our subject: the birth of Saint Patrick, which was in the year 361 of the Lord’s Incarnation, preceded blessed Augustine’s arrival in Britain by two hundred and thirty-six years. Tradition of the Fathers asserts that Paulinus, fellow-soldier of Augustine’s preaching and formerly archbishop of York, later bishop of Rochester, clad the framework of the church—long ago, as we said, built of wattle—with wooden panelling, and covered it from top to bottom with lead. The diligence of this praiseworthy man thus ensured that nothing was diminished from its holiness while much was added to its ornament. Certainly, more stately adornment of churches often draws even brutish minds to prayer and bends even the most stiff-necked to supplication. [Col. 1693B]

### On the translation of Indract and his companions

After several years had elapsed, King Ine of the West Saxons, recipient of a divine vision, translated the bodies of the martyr Indract and his companions from the place of martyrdom and buried them in the same church. Indract himself was placed in a stone pyramid at the left of the altar; the others in the pavement, as either circumstance allowed or skill arranged.

### On relics translated from Northumbria to Glastonbury

Again, much later, when the Danes were harrying Northumbria, Tica, abbot of those regions, migrated from the north into the west under the pretext of peace, came to Glastonbury, and governed the same church by right of abbacy in the year 754 of the Lord’s Incarnation. For many years the northern region had lain open to plunder by pirates, while the other parts of England suspected no hostility. He brought with him the precious hostages of his former settlement: namely, the relics of Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne; the bodies of Saints Ceolfrid, Benedict, Estrepin, Hæthberht, and Selgfrid, abbots of Wearmouth; of Bede the priest; of Hæbba, Bega, and Borsil; and also the body of Hilda, abbess of the monastery once called Streoneshalh and now called Whitby. [Col. 1693C] These relics, placed above the altar, added no little reverence to the place.

When Tica died, he received a notable burial in the right-hand corner of the greater church, beside the entrance to the Old Church. Its structure is not undistinguished either by the mass of its construction or by the art of its carving.

### On various relics deposited at Glastonbury

Since the island of Glastonbury is made illustrious by the ashes of many saints, it is pleasing to note the names of a few out of many whose bodily remains, for the most part, we do not doubt rest there. To enumerate the individual relics of saints bestowed there by kings and magnates would extend the volume beyond measure; they are also noted in Gospel-books.

Leaving aside those previously mentioned—namely, the twelve disciples of Saint Philip; Phaganus and Deruvianus [Col. 1694A] and their many disciples; Patrick; Indract; Benignus with his companions; learned Gildas; Saint David of Menevia; and others whom venerable Tica is reported to have brought there—it should be known that the following are truly said to rest there: Saint Paulinus, archbishop of the Northumbrians; two Innocents translated there from Bethlehem by the pious King Edgar; Saint Dunstan, the magnificent Father, whose translation from Canterbury to Glastonbury we shall relate below; Saint Idanus, bishop; and Saint Ultanus, bishop and brother of blessed Fursa, whose wonderful deeds are read.

There too are Saint Iltuit, most famous among the Welsh, and Saint Besilius, martyred in tender age; likewise relics of Saint Urban, pope and martyr; the bones of Saint Anastasius, martyr; the bones [Col. 1694B] of Saint Caesarius, martyr; the bones of Saint Benignus, martyr; and the bones of Saint Melanus, bishop and martyr. There too rest holy Queen Ealfleda and Saint Celrgitha, virgin, wholly intact in flesh and bone, as those who saw her testify, with her hair-shirt and sacred veil uncorrupted. There also are the bones of Saint Bathildis, queen, and of Saint Mamilla, virgin; moreover the bodies of Saints Ursula, Daria, Crisanta, Udilia, Mary, Martha, Lucy, Lucei, Walburga, Gertrude, and Cecilia.

Besides the saints enumerated, there are innumerable relics of saints there, gifts of kings, princes, bishops, and other nobles. Some names are recorded in the ancient books of the church; many relics also came from Northumbria during the war inflicted upon it by the Danes. Moreover, during its persecution, relics were brought from Wales to Glastonbury, as to a repository of saints. Though we do not possess full knowledge of them, [Col. 1694C] they enjoy more fully divine knowledge and contemplation.

### On the translation of Saint Dunstan from Canterbury to Glastonbury

Since we have mentioned the other saints, we shall set forth the manner of Saint Dunstan’s translation. In the year 1012 from the Lord’s Incarnation, while the illustrious King Edmund, called *Yreneside* in the language of his country, was reigning, the Danes arrived in the eastern regions of England and brought the whole territory of Kent under their power. Many were deprived of their proper rank, many driven from their homeland, and many slaughtered by a most cruel death. Thus, even as far as the city of London, sparing neither rank, age, nor sex, they destroyed divine and human things by murder, robbery, and fire.

Accordingly, to say nothing of others, the venerable Archbishop Ælfheah was driven from the seat of his dignity; estates were laid waste, possessions plundered—who could recount the rest without tears? Alas for sorrow! Those most wicked men entered the metropolitan church of the English, rushing upon Christ’s religious servants; and—horrible to relate!—expelling each one from the house of God, while fire consumed all things. At the same time the aforesaid King Edmund came to Glastonbury and, having stayed there for some time, [Col. 1695A] related in order to Abbot Brichred and the brothers of that place the history of so great a captivity. He told them that the church of Canterbury had been burned and stripped utterly of inhabitants and religious life.

Hearing this, the abbot and the entire community were so grieved as though a sword had pierced each of their souls. Among other matters they recalled the exalted virtues of their eminent Father Dunstan, who, while he lived, had wonderfully adorned Glastonbury with broad possessions, gifts, splendid liberties, and, more importantly, regular observances. Considering it contrary to religion to remain silent about these things, they earnestly implored the king for aid and counsel, that the relics of the glorious man might be transferred to a religious place where he had once been nourished with the milk of religious life and had grown [Col. 1695B] to such virtues that he could illuminate not only the flock of Glastonbury but the provinces of all England by his teaching.

When the king heard this, meeting their desires with devout affection, he decreed that their request should swiftly be put into effect. Without delay, the aforesaid abbot, now possessing the object of his desire, imposed the duty of this mission upon four of his fellow-brethren: with the help of companions added to them, they were to hurry to Canterbury and bring Saint Dunstan’s bones to Glastonbury. The sons accepted their father’s command with the greatest devotion. Having prepared what was necessary for so great a journey and received a blessing, they eagerly pursued the task assigned to them, greatly trusting in God’s mercy and in the aid of the saint.

These monks had long attended blessed Dunstan while he lived in the flesh, performing the office of his chapel. They had also committed his body to burial when his soul was transferred to the seats of rest; afterwards they had remained with his holy successor, Archbishop Ælfheah, until that man’s martyrdom. Those bishops had indeed been pleased to have inseparable companions from Glastonbury’s monastic community, both because of the special love with which they embraced their nursing mother and, especially, so that, inflamed by the example of their familiar companionship, they might not depart from the earlier life which they had been accustomed to lead with them in the monastery. [Col. 1695C] The brothers’ names were Sebirchtus, Ethelbuthtus, Bursius, and Adelwardus surnamed Quadrans.

Thus the aforesaid brothers, arriving at Canterbury, found the place, as they had heard from the king, stripped of every inhabitant. Immediately they approached the tomb of the most holy man, which was very well known to them, since they themselves had placed him in the mausoleum. Opening it, they found Saint Dunstan’s bones more precious than gold and topaz. His flesh had dissolved over so long a time; they gathered up the bones that they found with fitting reverence and not without tears. They also recognized the ring placed on the saint’s finger when he had been committed to burial, which he himself is said to have made in his younger years.

Having accomplished all for which they had come, they returned immense thanks to the one who made their journey prosper and went back to Glastonbury, bearing with them in joy the most precious relics. How greatly they were received on their return, [Col. 1696A] to the joy of all and especially of the monks, the charity of the reader can better appreciate than the capacity of the writer can unfold. This translation occurred in the year of the Lord 1012: namely, the second year after the killing of Saint Ælfheah, archbishop, and the twenty-fourth year after Saint Dunstan’s falling asleep.

### How Saint Dunstan’s relics were hidden beneath the ground
Once these things had been done, the brethren, refreshed by God’s immense benefits, frequently conferred together, considering how they might commit the aforesaid treasure to safer custody. Not without reason they feared that, once the hostile fury had been calmed and the Church of Canterbury restored to its former condition, pre-eminent through the authority and power of its archbishops, it might reclaim for itself those relics which had been taken away. [Col. 1696B] Thus, the happier they had been in acquiring them, the more miserable they would become through their subsequent loss.

Having at last taken counsel together, they resolved that two of the elder brethren, more trustworthy in secrets entrusted to them, should hide the most holy bones in a more secluded place, and should communicate knowledge of so great a secret to no one while they lived. Yet, when labouring at the end of life, they were to point out the place to some more mature and wiser brother, who likewise, at the moment of death, should reveal the matter to someone else, as had been done for himself. Thus, as time passed and circumstances changed, the place itself might remain unknown to all, with only one person aware of the truth, until it should please the Most High that the light should not lie hidden under a bushel, but, set upon a candlestick, should shine upon all who were in the house of God. [Col. 1696C]

Accordingly, the two brethren chosen for this purpose carried the plan into effect. They prepared a small wooden chest, suitably fashioned for the purpose and painted inside. On the right side of the chest they inscribed an **S.** with its title, and on the left likewise a **D.** with its title; by these letters they wished to signify the name of St Dunstan. They then placed the aforesaid relics in the chest and concealed them beneath a stone cut out for this purpose in the greater and ancient church, beside the holy-water vessel, on the right-hand side of the entrance, while all the other monks remained wholly ignorant of the place. There, therefore, he lay hidden for one hundred and seventy-two years, entrusted successively, in the manner described, to the knowledge of one person alone.

### How the same relics were found again

[Col. 1696D]

As time went on, while the saint still lay hidden in that subterranean place, there was there a monk named John Canan, mature in years and very shrewd in mind, thoroughly acquainted with the ancient observances of the monastery. The brethren commonly and not falsely believed that knowledge of this secret had been entrusted to him by successive transmission. A certain brother, John of Watelege by name, was assigned to his care, called “young” both in age and in religious profession; the elder embraced him with an exceedingly great affection of heart because of the flower of his good disposition.

Urged on by his companions, this young man pressed his master—though he resisted for a long time—with abundant entreaties, intermingling flatteries, [Col. 1697A] to show him the place that held so great a treasure. At last softened by the repeated blandishments of his prayers, one day, when the youth questioned him as usual, the elder spoke in these words:

> “My most beloved son, you do not enter the church to sprinkle yourself with holy water without touching with your garments the stone beneath which those things are hidden for which you inquire. But do not press me further concerning them; rather, ponder in silence and shrewdly what you have heard.”

These words did not become veiled in forgetfulness for the youth. After the elder had completed his days, he passed to his fate. After his death, what had been spoken by him in darkness was proclaimed upon the housetops and became generally known. Yet, while all wavered because of the ambiguity of the saying and remained chilled by excessive sluggishness, no one put his hand to the test that might untie the knot of so great an uncertainty.

After a short passage of time, fire seized the monastery of Glastonbury. It consumed not only the church and the other buildings, but also, for the greater part, its ornaments, treasures, and—what was more valuable—its relics.

We need not here describe the grief caused by such a fire, since that is not our present purpose. The monks, however, seeking consolation in their sorrow, gathered together the few things which the flame had left, especially relics. At last, anxious about St Dunstan, they brought before the community, having recalled them to memory, the things which John Canan and later John of Watelege, as we have noted, [Col. 1697C] had said concerning him.

After a few days had passed, two brethren bolder than the rest in this matter—Richard of Canton and Ralph Foc—went with equal eagerness to the place formerly indicated by John. Searching it more carefully, they found the stone, as they had heard long before. When they rolled it away, they saw beneath it the wooden chest, reinforced on every side with iron fittings. They therefore summoned the prior and the whole convent; opening the shrine, they found the most sacred bones of blessed Dunstan, together with his ring upon a bone of one of his fingers. To remove every knot of uncertainty, they saw inside the painted marks: an **S.** with its title on the right side of the chest, and a **D.** with its title on the left, expressing the name of St Dunstan placed there. [Col. 1697D]

Thus the truth of John Canan’s report having been plainly established, the monks, refreshed after their former misery by the discovery of the relics for which they had so greatly longed, received them joyfully and placed them in a shrine suitably clad in gold and silver. With the reverence and devotion which were fitting, they associated with them the shoulder and arm of St Oswald, king and martyr.

Let the church of Glastonbury therefore rejoice, fortified by the presence of so great a patron, through whose intercessions and merits God does not cease there to work His mighty deeds: most frequently restoring life to the dead and complete health to the sick, and often also assisting dumb animals in many dangers.

### Concerning the venerable cross which once spoke

[Col. 1698A]

In the church of Glastonbury is a certain cross, deservedly venerable, covered with gold and silver, which once spoke. Or rather, the Holy Spirit spoke in it to a certain monk of that place, named Aylsi, in this manner. As this monk passed by the same cross, as also by the altars, without bowing himself with the reverence due according to regular discipline, at length, on one occasion as he was passing by it, he bowed himself. The cross then burst forth into a voice, as though formed by the proper organs, and said:

> “I nod too late, Aylsi; I nod too late, Aylsi.”

Struck by the divine voice, he immediately expired.

### Concerning another cross, from which a diadem fell

There is also there another most ancient cross, [Col. 1698B] which formerly used to stand in the refectory. Of it they relate that, when King Edgar and Archbishop Dunstan were seated at table one day, thoughts contrary to the divine will arose in the king’s heart in the refectory. Marvellous to relate! The image of the Lord affixed to the wood of the cross shook its whole body, so that the king’s diadem fell by the force of the movement between the king and the archbishop.

The king’s confession revealed what this portended. For when St Dunstan asked the king what he had then been thinking, or what he intended to do, he confessed what he had conceived at that very hour: namely, that, after transferring the monks to another place, he would gather nuns there. Rebuked reverently by the archbishop, who said that this was contrary to the divine will, [Col. 1698C] the king abandoned that purpose as void.

### Concerning the wounded cross

There is there a third cross, smaller than the others but more famous among the people, anciently clad in gold and silver. Long ago, through the blow of an arrow, a great quantity of blood flowed from it by divine power. How this occurred will be related elsewhere in writing.

### Concerning a certain image of Blessed Mary

There is also there an image of Blessed Mary. When a great fire once consumed the hangings and all the ornaments of the altar around it, it did not touch the image itself, nor even the veil suspended from her head. Yet on her face, because of the heat of the fire, blisters arose as though upon a living human being; they bore witness to divine power and were visible to beholders for a long time.

### Concerning the altar of St David, commonly called the Sapphire

[Col. 1698D]

It is read in the Life of St David, archbishop of Menevia, that, while this saint was serving many brethren in the office of abbot in the monastery which he himself had built in the Valley of Bosina, an angel came to him one night and said:

> “Tomorrow, girding yourself and putting on your shoes, set out as far as Jerusalem. You shall also have as companions on this journey two of your household, known for uprightness, namely Eliud and Paternus, who tomorrow will meet you at the appointed place which I now show you.”

The saint, delaying nothing, put the affairs of his cell in order, received the brethren’s blessing, and, setting out at first light, came to the appointed place. [Col. 1699A] There he found the promised brethren.

Thus they entered upon the road together, not surrounded by the pomp of attendants but enriched by unity of spirit: such was their lord, and such his servant. When they came into foreign provinces, St David was so endowed with the gift of languages that they had no need of an interpreter among barbarians. At last, as they drew near to the place they desired, on the night before their arrival an angel appeared to the patriarch of Jerusalem and said:

> “Three Catholic men are arriving from the confines of the west. Receive them joyfully and hospitably, and consecrate them bishops for me.”

The patriarch, recipient of the divine vision, joyfully carried out the command when the saints arrived. Having consecrated them, the patriarch said:

> “The power of the Jews is growing strong against the Christians, and they assail us and reject the faith. Go, therefore, and preach every day, so that their violence, being refuted, may cease when they learn that the Christian faith has been spread to the western bounds and proclaimed at the uttermost ends of the earth.” [Col. 1699B]

They obeyed the command, persisted in preaching, and converted unbelievers through their preaching. They strengthened the sick; and, when all things had been completed, they prepared to return home. Then the patriarch enriched the venerable Father Dewy with four gifts: a consecrated altar, on which he consecrated the Lord’s body, an altar which is powerful in innumerable miracles; also a notable bell, a staff, and a tunic woven with gold—all of which are proclaimed as resplendent with glorious miracles.

“But,” said the patriarch, “because these would burden you while travelling, when you have returned to your own country, I shall send them to you.”

Having taken leave of the patriarch, they finally returned home, the holy men awaiting what had been promised. At last they received the gifts sent to them by angels: Dewy in the monastery called Langemelech, and Paternus and Eliud in their respective monasteries. Therefore the common people call them “things coming from heaven.”

St David, desiring in his lifetime to secure so precious a treasure after his death, assigned this most worthy stone to the church of Glastonbury. For, because of the venerable antiquity of the place and especially because of the relics of St Patrick and of other saints laid up there, he loved it with wonderful affection, as many proofs make clear to those who read his deeds. [Col. 1699D] The aforesaid altar is still shown in the church of Glastonbury in memory of the said saint, preserved not by human contrivance but by divine providence, which amid countless upheavals, amid changes of kings and kingdoms, amid the most grievous storms of wars—when almost everything else was removed—continually restrained the greedy hands of enemies from stealing it. The little chest, however, in which blessed David received the same stone is still preserved with fitting honour in his episcopal see.

When the oft-mentioned stone had formerly lain hidden for a long time through fear of war, unknown to everyone in that place, Henry, bishop of Winchester and abbot of Glastonbury, of pious memory, found it in a certain doorway of the Church of Blessed Mary and magnificently decorated it with gold, silver, and [Col. 1700A] precious stones, as may still be seen.

### Concerning nobles buried at Glastonbury

How venerable the church of Glastonbury was even to the leading men of the country, and how desirable as a place of burial—so that they might especially await there, under the protection of the Mother of God, the day of Resurrection—many facts show, which I pass over to avoid weariness.

I pass over the renowned Arthur, king of the Britons, buried with his wife in the monks’ cemetery between two pyramids; and I pass over many princes of the Britons. I pass over also Kenwin, placed in one pyramid. Moreover, I pass over the tombs of Kings Edmund the Elder, in the tower to the right; Edmund the Younger, before the great altar; and Edgar, formerly in the chapter-house before [Col. 1700B] the entrance of the church, now in the shrine which boasts also of the martyr Vincent. If opportunity is afforded, posterity will not accuse me of having undertaken these matters in vain.

I say nothing either of the tombs of the bishops Brithuvius and Brithuwold, which adorn the wealthy northern portico dedicated to St John the Baptist; nor of the bishops Siving and Seifrid; nor of the ealdormen Ælfhere, Æthelstan, Æthelwine, and Delnot. Each of these ealdormen, indeed, bestowed upon Glastonbury one hundred hides of land together with many other goods.

### Concerning the two pyramids

I would gladly declare that which is hidden from almost everyone, if I could establish the truth: namely, what those pyramids signify, which stand a few feet from [Col. 1700C] the ancient church and mark the monks’ cemetery. The taller, and nearer to the church, has five stages and a height of twenty-six feet. Although, through excessive age, it threatens to fall, it nevertheless possesses certain signs of antiquity [perhaps *specimina*, “specimens”], which can plainly be read, though not fully understood.

On its upper stage is an image made in pontifical dress. On the second is an image displaying royal splendour, and the letters: **Her, Sexi, and Blisger**. On the third likewise the names: **Wemereste, Bantomp, Pinepegn**. On the fourth: **Hats, Pulfred, and Eanfled**. On the fifth, which is also the lowest, is an image and this inscription: **Sogpor, Peslicas, and Bregden; Spelpes, Hgin, Gendes, Bern**.

The other pyramid is eighteen feet high and has four stages, upon which are read: **Bishop Hedde, and Bregored, and Bearward**. What these things signify I do not rashly define, but infer conjecturally that the bones of those whose names are read outside are contained within hollowed stones. Certainly, Sogpor is confidently asserted to be the man after whose name Sogperesbeorh was called, now called Mons Acutus [“Sharp Hill”]. Bregden is he from whom Brentacnolle derives its name, now called Brentamerse. Likewise Beorwald was abbot after Hemgisel. Concerning these and the others whom we may encounter, our discourse will henceforth range over a freer field. Now it will endeavour to set forth the succession of abbots, and what was assigned to each for the uses of the monastery by what king.

### Concerning the kings, abbots, and other founders of the church of Glastonbury, set forth in order

[Col. 1701A]

First it should be remembered that, when twelve disciples of the holy Apostles Philip and James came to Britain in the year 63 of the Lord’s Incarnation, three kings, though pagans, granted them twelve portions of land, from which the name “the Twelve Hides” still remains.

Then Saints Phaganus and Deruvianus came to Britain and illuminated it with the grace of faith. From King Lucius, reborn in Christ through them, they obtained confirmation of the island of Avallonia with its adjacent lands for the twelve brethren established there and for others to be established after them.

After a long time blessed Patrick succeeded. Finding still twelve brethren leading a quasi-eremitical life, he trained them in the cenobitic life [Col. 1701B] and enriched them, as it is lawful to believe, with many possessions unknown to us.

St Benignus succeeded him. Who this man was, and what he was called in his native language, is expressed rather neatly by verses written on the epitaph of his tomb at Ferremere:

> Within this stone are laid the bones of Beonna, the father,  
> Who in ancient time was father of the monks here.  
> Him perhaps long ago the minister of Patrick,  
> The Irishmen say, and by name they call him Beonna.

There succeeded there many abbots of the British nation, whose names, deeds, and memory antiquity, covering them with the cloud of forgetfulness, has effaced. Yet that the church itself was held in the greatest veneration among the magnates of the Britons is shown by their remains resting there. A painting, mindful of things past, reveals the names of only three of these abbots: Worgret, Lademund, and Bregored. But of these later.

### Concerning the illustrious Arthur

It is read in the deeds of the most illustrious King Arthur that, at a certain feast of the Nativity of the Lord at Karlium, after he had adorned with military insignia a most valiant young man—the son of King Nuth, named Ider—and had led him, in order to test him, to the Mountain of Frogs, now called Brentenol, where he had learned that three giants notorious for their wicked deeds were living, so that he might fight against them: this young knight, going ahead without Arthur and his companions knowing it, [Col. 1701D] courageously attacked the said giants and slaughtered them in a remarkable carnage.

When they had been killed, Arthur arrived and found Ider exhausted by excessive labour and wholly powerless, collapsed in a swoon. He mourned him with his companions as though he were dead. Returning home in inexpressible grief, he left there the body which he thought lifeless, until he could send a vehicle there to carry it back. He also considered himself the cause of Ider’s death because he had come too late to his aid. Therefore, when he eventually came to Glastonbury, he established there twenty-four monks for Ider’s soul, abundantly granting possessions and lands for their support, together with gold, silver, chalices, and other ecclesiastical ornaments.

### Concerning the land of Yneswitrin granted to Glastonbury in the time when the English were converted to the faith

[Col. 1702A]

In the year 601 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the king of Domnonia granted to the ancient church situated there the land called Yneswitrin, at the request of Abbot Worgret, in five cassates.

> “I, Bishop Mawron, wrote this charter; I, Worgret, abbot of the same place, subscribed.”

The antiquity of the document declares that it does not know who this king was. Nevertheless, that he was a Briton may be presumed from this: he called Glastonbury Yneswitrin in his own language, for it is established that this is how it is called in British among them.

Abbot Worgret, whose name has the flavour of British barbarism, was succeeded by Lademund, and he by Bregoretd. The times of their prelacy lie in obscurity; but their names and ranks are openly displayed in the greater church by a painting beside the altar. Berthwald succeeded Bregored.

### Concerning King Kenwalch and Abbot Berthwald

In the year 670 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Kenwald, also called Kenwalch, seventh from Cerdic among the West Saxons, who came to faith in Christ through blessed Birinus, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign gave Abbot Berchwald two hides at Ferremere, Archbishop Theodoret intervening.

> “I, Theodoret, subscribed.”

The same king also gave Beokerie, Godenie, Martynesie, and Andregesie. This Beorwald, after spending ten years in the governance of Glastonbury, became archbishop of Canterbury. Why he renounced the rule of Glastonbury, though the king and the bishop of that diocese opposed it, [Col. 1702C] will be made clear in what follows.

### Concerning King Kenwin, who endowed Glastonbury with liberty

Hemgesel succeeded Berthwald and presided over Glastonbury for twenty-five years. In the year 678 from the Lord’s Incarnation, King Kenwin granted to Glastingoi six hides free from every service. On account of his faithful manner of life, and at the request of Bishop Hedde and the monks, he appointed him abbot there, on this condition: that the brethren of that place should have the right to elect and appoint a ruler, according to the Rule of St Benedict, **MUNECATONE** [an unclear vernacular term].

> “And beside the wood,” he says, “which is called Contuedun, I have humbly bestowed twenty-three hides; in Caric, twenty hides; and in Crucan, three hides, under the prompting of divine fear, for the support of the regular life in the monastery of Glastingabiri,”

and so forth. The remains of this king rest in the monks’ cemetery, in a pyramid once nobly sculpted.

### Concerning King Baldred, who gave Pennard and Muntagu

In the year 681 of the Lord’s Incarnation, King Baldred gave Abbot Hemgillo Penward, one hide; Penger, six hides; Logporez Beorh, sixteen hides; and a fishery in Pedride, for the support of the venerable church of Blessed Mary and blessed Patrick situated at Glastingabari, with the consent and permission of our bishop Hedde, and with Kenwin also consenting.

And shortly afterward:

> “I, Bishop Hedde, drew up this little charter. I, Abbot Aldelinus, consented and subscribed in the same year; Bishop Hedde.”

### Concerning Leghe

[Col. 1703A]

He gave Lanctocacy, six hides, to Glastonbury, with Kenwin and Baldred likewise consenting. Cedwalla confirmed this gift and, though a pagan, made the sign of the cross with his own hand.

### Concerning the glorious King Ina, who honoured Glastonbury in many ways through gifts and privileges

Now, since the succession of years has brought us to Ina, king of the West Saxons, it is pleasing to enumerate separately the lands which this eminent man bestowed in pious liberality upon the ancient church at Glastonbury.

### Concerning Brente, given by Ina

In the year 620 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Ina gave Abbot Hemgisel ten hides at Brente. Abbot Berthwald voluntarily abandoned this land and, without our [Col. 1703B] violence and without expulsion, left the place of his own monastery and departed contrary to the prohibition and will of our bishop. The same king granted the same abbot the following privilege.

### The lesser privilege of King Ina

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Ina, king, by the decree and counsel of our bishop Aldhelm, and at the suggestion of all God’s priests and the petition of the monks who dwell in the parish of the West Saxons, grant this liberty to the monks who serve almighty God under Abbot Hemgisel in the church of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of blessed Patrick, in the ancient city called Glastingai. I lay this dignity of privilege upon the altar, so that, without hindrance from secular affairs and free from the tribute of fiscal obligations, they may serve God alone with free minds, regularly observe monastic discipline through Christ’s granting of aid, and deign to pour forth prayers before the sight of the divine majesty for the stability and prosperity of our kingdom and for pardon of the sins we have committed.”

And below:

> “For a fuller testimony of firmness, we caused princes and senators, judges and patricians to subscribe. This was done publicly and confirmed in the wooden basilica in the year 704 from the Lord’s Incarnation. I, Aldhelm, subscribed,”

and so forth.

This Hemgisel, that is, Cinis, having met his fate, received bodily rest in the ancient church.

### Bouelt

[Col. 1703D] Bervald succeeded in the year 705 from the Lord’s Incarnation. Ina gave Abbot Bervald twenty hides near the Tamar and twenty hides in the place called Bouelt.

### Sowy

Soeg: twelve hides. Corregs: six hides.

### Exford

Exford: half a hide with a fishery.

### Dulting

Dulting: twenty hides.

> “I, Aldhelm, wrote this document.”

### Pilton

King Ina also gave Pilton, twenty hides, to the same abbot.

### Cliwere

Bishop Wilfrid gave the island of Wethmor, [Col. 1704A] seventy hides, granted to him by King Kenwin, and the estate of Cliwere, one hide.

### Bledehit

Albert succeeded him in the year 712 of the Lord’s Incarnation. Bishop Forthere, successor of St Aldhelm, gave him Bledahit, one hide.

Echfrid succeeded. In the year 719 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Ina gave him one hide with the fishery of Axe. Abbot Bugu gave the same man Ora, three hides.

Moreover, Ina founded the greater church of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Since there were several churches there, it is fitting to insert the truth concerning the location of Glastonbury’s various churches and their founders.

The first and most ancient was made by the twelve disciples of the Apostles Philip and James, as has been stated above. [Col. 1704B] It stood to the west of the others. The second was made by St David, bishop of Menevia, east of the older church, in honour of Blessed Mary, when he intended to dedicate the ancient church and was prevented by the Lord because He Himself had dedicated it. The third was made by the twelve men who came from the northern part of Britain, namely Morgen, Catgur, Badimor, and the others mentioned above; this too was situated east of the ancient church. The fourth and greatest was built by King Ina, in honour of the Lord Saviour and the Apostles Peter and Paul, east of the others, for the soul of his brother Mules, whom they had burned at Canterbury within Canterbury. On its uppermost level he caused these verses to be inscribed:

> Starry mountains, fair peaks of Zion,  
> Two cedars from Lebanon, flourishing with leafy bloom,  
> Gates of heaven, two broad lights of the world:  
> Paul thunders with his speech; Peter flashes from the height.  
>
> Among the apostolic crowns shining with radiant light,  
> The one is higher in rank, the other more learned in counsels.  
> Through this one the hearts of men are opened; through that one, the stars.  
> Those whom this one teaches by his pen, the other receives into heaven.  
>
> This one opens the path of heaven by doctrine; the other by keys.  
> Paul is the way; Peter the faithful gate.  
> This one remains the firm rock; that one is held to be the architect:  
> In them rises the temple whose altar pleases God.  
>
> England, gladly rejoice: Rome sends you greeting;  
> Apostolic brightness shines upon Glastonbury.  
> Two bulwarks rise against the hostile face,  
> Whom the city that is head of the world possesses as towers of faith.  
>
> This devout and eminent King Ina, filled with love,  
> [Col. 1704D] bestowed upon his people benefits that shall not die.  
> Entirely devoted to the affection of holy piety,  
> He enlarged the Church’s continual resources.  
>
> Our Melchizedek, deservedly king and priest,  
> Completed the work of true religion.  
> Governing public laws and maintaining lofty palaces,  
> He was the unique glory and model of pontiffs.  
>
> Departing hence, there he lives in the honour of his merits;  
> Here too he shall endure in the praise of his deeds.

### Concerning the silver chapel which King Ina made there, with its vessels

The same king also caused a certain chapel of gold and silver to be built, with ornaments and vessels likewise of gold and silver, and placed it within the greater church. For the construction of this chapel he gave two thousand six hundred and forty pounds of silver. [Col. 1705A] Its altar was of two hundred and sixty-four pounds of gold; its chalice with paten, of ten pounds of gold; its censer, of eight pounds and twenty mancuses of gold; its candlesticks, of twelve and a half pounds of silver; the covers of the books of the Gospels, of twenty pounds and sixty mancuses of gold; ewers and other altar vessels, of seventeen pounds of gold; basins, of eight pounds of gold; a vessel for holy water, of twenty pounds of silver; images of the Lord, Blessed Mary, and the twelve Apostles, of one hundred and seventy-five pounds of silver and thirty-eight pounds of gold; and an altar-cloth and priestly ornaments, skilfully woven throughout with gold and precious stones.

The said king most devoutly bestowed this treasure upon the monastery of Glastonbury through love of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary. Moreover, by a royal document he confirmed the lands, possessions, and liberties of the same church in the following words.

### The greater privilege of King Ina

> “Help us, O God our Saviour. Whatever is determined by sound counsel according to the decrees of the canons and ecclesiastical institutions, although mere speech without written text might suffice, nevertheless, because in our times the storms and whirlwinds of secular affairs very often beat even upon the gates of the Church, we have judged it worthwhile, for the protection of the future, to attach to written pages those things which have been determined, lest they be handed over to oblivion and become unknown to posterity.
>
> “Therefore I, Ina, strengthened by royal dignity from the Lord, with the counsel of Queen Sexburga, and the permission of Beorchwald, bishop of the church of Canterbury, and [Col. 1705C] of all his suffragans, and likewise at the exhortation of Baltdred and Athelard, under-rulers of the ancient church which is in the place called Glastein—a church which the great priest and supreme pontiff, by the ministry of angels, made known that he had formerly sanctified for himself, for the perpetual Virgin Mary, and for blessed David, by many unheard-of miracles—from those things which I possess by paternal inheritance and hold as my own special domain, grant contiguous and suitable places for the support of regular life and the use of the monks: Brente, ten hides; Sowi, twelve hides; Pilton, twenty hides; Dulting, ten hides; Bledein, one hide; together with all those things which my predecessors bestowed upon the same Church.
>
> “Benewalchius, with St Theodore the archbishop intervening, [gave] Ferlinguere, Beokerie, [Col. 1705D] Godenie, Martinesie.
>
> “King Kenwin, who used to call Glastingeia ‘the mother of saints,’ made it immune from every secular and ecclesiastical service and granted this dignity of privilege: that the brethren of the same place should have power to elect and appoint their ruler according to the Rule of St Benedict.
>
> “Bishop Hedde—when Cedwalla consented and confirmed it with his own hand, though a pagan—[gave] Lantokay; Baltdrec, Pennard, six hides; Adthelard, Preld, sixty hides, Ina consenting and confirming.
>
> “I assent to their devotion and kindly petition, and keep vigilant guard through the protection of royal letters against the snares of malicious men and barking dogs, so that the church of our Lord [Col. 1706A] Jesus Christ and of the perpetual Virgin Mary, as it is first in the kingdom of Britain and the fountain and origin of all religion, may likewise possess in itself the pre-eminent dignity of privilege, and may render no servile service whatsoever to any human being upon earth, since in heaven it rules above the choirs of angels.
>
> “Therefore, with the consent of the supreme pontiff Gregory, and since, though unworthy, I too have received with myself into the bosom and protection of the holy Roman Church the Mother of my Lord; with the consent also of all the kings, archbishops, bishops, dukes, and abbots of Britain, I decree and confirm that all lands, places, and possessions of Blessed Mary of Glasteia shall remain undisturbed and unimpaired, free from all royal exactions and works which are customarily imposed, namely military service and the building of bridge or fortress; and free from the ordinances and molestations of all archbishops and bishops. This is found to be established in the ancient charters of the same church, and is known to have been confirmed by my predecessors Kenewalch, Kenwin, Cedwalla, and Baldred.
>
> “And whatever cases may arise concerning homicide, sacrilege, poisoning, theft, robbery, the ordering and assessment of churches, the ordination of clerics, synodal assemblies, and all judicial examinations, shall be determined, without prejudice to any person, by the disposition of the abbot and convent. [Col. 1706C] Moreover, I command all the kings, archbishops, bishops, dukes, and princes of my kingdom, upon their honour and their love for me; and I command all their officials and mine upon the salvation of their bodies: that none of them dare enter the island of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the perpetual Virgin Mary of Glasteia, nor the possessions of the same church, for the purpose of pleading a cause, persecuting, seizing, commanding, prohibiting, or doing anything that may become a scandal to those who serve God there.
>
> “By the intercession of almighty God, of the perpetual Virgin Mary, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints, I forbid under prohibition that, upon any pretext whatever, a bishop presume either to establish an episcopal seat for himself, celebrate solemn masses, consecrate altars, dedicate churches, confer orders, or make any disposition whatsoever in the church of Glastonbury itself, in the churches subject to it—namely Sowy, Brente, Merlinge, Sapewic, Stret, Sbudecaleth, and Pilton—or in their chapels or islands, [Col. 1706D] unless he has been invited by the abbot or brethren. If he is invited to do these things, he shall appropriate nothing for himself from the goods of the church, nor even from the offerings themselves.
>
> “From the possessions of this church we assign him two residences in two places: one at Poert and the other in the estate called Pilton, so that he may have a place to lodge when arriving or to which he may withdraw when coming from there. Yet he may not stay there overnight, except when delayed by the severity of the weather or bodily infirmity, or when requested by the abbot or brethren; nor may he stay longer than one night with more than three or four clerics.
>
> “The same bishop shall also ensure that every year, with his clerics who are at Fontanetum, he visits his mother, namely the church of Glastonbury, with a litany on the Monday after the Ascension of the Lord. If, swollen with pride, he should defer this and violate what has been said and confirmed above, he shall lose the residences assigned to him above. The abbot or monks may direct whomever they wish to celebrate the canonical Easter rites in the church of Glastonbury, in the churches subject to it, or in their chapels.
>
> “But whoever, at any future time and upon any pretext of whatsoever rank, profession, or degree, shall attempt to overturn or render void this testament of my bounty and liberality, let him know that with Judas the traitor he shall perish in eternal confusion in the devouring flames of unspeakable torments.” [Col. 1707B]
>
> “The document of this gift and privilege was written in the year 725 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, in the presence of King Ina, Beortwald bishop of Canterbury, the venerable bishops Daniel and Fordred, and others whose names are noted below.”

> “I, King Ine, decree by the subscription of my own hand that this donation and freedom be made valid under the seal of the holy Cross. I, Queen Æthelburh, have consented. I, King Baldred, have confirmed. I, Adelard, the queen’s brother, have consented. I, Borthwald, archbishop of the church of Canterbury, [Col. 1707C] have strengthened King Ine’s donation and freedom under the seal of the holy Cross, together with very many other magnates.”

### On the end of King Ine

Thereafter the aforesaid King Ine sent to the supreme pontiff letters sealed with the royal seal, containing all the matters set forth above, together with a certain golden cup and other royal gifts, beseeching him to receive the church of Glastonbury, with its appurtenances and liberties, into the protection of the holy Roman Church, and to confirm it forever by apostolic authority. In the same year in which the king himself went personally to Rome, he brought back to Glastonbury, on his return, a privilege strengthened by the apostolic seal. Afterwards he went again to Rome with his wife Queen Æthelburh, [Col. 1707D] at her prompting, that is. There, lest he make a display of his conversion, and so might please the eyes of God alone, clothed in humble dress he secretly grew old; at length he entered upon the way of all flesh, not without great miracles, as we have heard.

### On Abbot Cengille

Cengille succeeded Abbot Æthfrith in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 729. Edelard, Ine’s successor, granted to the household serving almighty God in the monastery of Glastonbury under the religious Abbot Cengille, as a permanent possession, sixty hides at Polonholt and ten at Torric. His wife Fredogipa gave five hides at Brunantun.

### Privilege of King Cuthred

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 744, Cuthred, king [Col. 1708A] of the West Saxons, granted Glastonbury the following privilege:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Cuthred, king of the Saxons, decree that this grant, strengthened as the ancient city of Glastonbury has been by all the supports of earlier kings—Kentwine, Baldrad, Cædwalla, Ine, Æthelard, and Æthelbald king of the Mercians—in towns and villages, fields, estates, and great dwellings, and confirmed by the subscription of my own hand and the sign of the Cross, shall remain firm, pleasing, and valid by rightful title, while the turning of the heavens rolls lands and seas beneath the circling sky of the stars according to its ordained governance. But if anyone should be seen to break the testament of this my donation, or to take away, beyond the prescribed boundaries, determined limits, or established bounds, the fertile land and the footing of ground delivered to us at Hengissing, let him be punished more severely, plunged into the punishment of the infernal prison, and pay forever for the violence of his presumption. Amen.
>
> “I, Cuthred, king of the West Saxons, by the subscription of my own hand marking the image of the holy Cross, decree that no one who knows himself regenerated in Christ presume to alter this donation. I, Bishop Kerewald, have subscribed and confirmed. The sign of the hand of Cumbran, the aforesaid king, and of many other nobles. A copy of this grant and privilege was promulgated in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 744, in [Col. 1708C] the aforesaid monastery, in the presence of King Cuthred, who, by the munificence of his own hand and with votive devotion, committed it to the holy altar in the honourable wooden basilica in which the brethren have the sarcophagus of Hemgille of blessed memory. I, Daniel, have subscribed.”

### On Ure and Baltenesbeorge

In the following year, that is, 745 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the same Cuthred gave Abbot Cumbert three hides at Ure; and to Lull, ten hides at Baltenesbeorghe and Scrobbamuth. In the following year, that is, in 746 of the Lord’s Incarnation, I, Æthelbald, for the redemption of my soul, while Tumbert had presided for nine years, granted to the household faithfully serving God in [Col. 1708D] the monastery of Glastonbury, for the price of four hundred shillings, four hides in two places, Jetelig and Bradanlegh.

### On Abbot Tica

In 754 Sigebert granted to Abbot Tica, for one gold shilling, and to the monks dwelling in the city of the Glastonians, twenty-two hides at Polilt. The same Tica also bought from that king, at the royal price of fifty gold shillings, the six hides which remained in its western part, so that they might be the perpetual inheritance of Glastonbury monastery. I have already anticipated speaking above of this man, who also governed Glastonbury for six years: namely, what relics he brought to the church, and where he received burial with his companions. The following epitaph, which I have not neglected to read, bears witness:

[Col. 1709A]

> This tomb shines, fashioned with wondrous splendour;  
> Beneath its carved summit it encloses Tica.

Of this tomb the following miracle has been related through succeeding ages: when a certain man attempted to tear it down, he was immediately punished with blindness; he recognized his fault, but I do not know whether he obtained pardon.

### On Abbot Guban under King Cynewulf

In 760 King Cynewulf gave Abbot Guban, who also governed Glastonbury for two years, five hides at Sudeton. On the eastern bank of the Parrett, his minister Æthelard gave three hides at Cedern in Huneresburg. Sulca, a handmaid of Christ, gave eleven hides at Culum and three hides at Cumba.

In 712 Cinewlt gave Abbot Waldun five hides at Cunctum; he governed Glastonbury for thirty-two years.

[Col. 1709B] In 724 Offa, king of the Mercians, gave Abbot Beadewulf ten hides at Espirht for the support of the venerable church; he governed for six years. With the assent of King Offa, Æthelmund gave one hide at Huneswelle.

### On the liberty granted to Kinelm in the church of Glastonbury

In 726 Leo III, of that name, became pope. At that time Charlemagne was reigning in Francia; Brihtric was king of the West Saxons; and Kenwulf, after Ecgfrith, who had succeeded his father Offa for scarcely four months, was king of the Mercians in England. But anyone who deigns to read may find concerning that pope and those kings in Book I of the *Deeds of the Kings of the English*; for the present it is enough to have mentioned their names, since this bears greatly upon the matter we are trying to explain. Pope Leo confirmed for Kinelm the liberty of the donation of [Col. 1709C] Glastonbury monastery, consisting of eight hundred hides, for him and his successors in their religious observance and stability forever—provided, however, that the monastery should persevere in its religious observance and stability through all ages. This liberty was granted to Kinelm through the support and confirmation of King Kenwulf of the Mercians. Perhaps too, as may be inferred from what follows, the condition of kingdoms having changed—as often happens—although Glastonbury lies in Wessex, the Mercian kings either protected it out of affection or exercised authority over it by right. Since I have found the privileges of pope and king nowhere except written in English, I shall translate them into Latin in this work, insofar as I understand, rendering sense for sense.

### Privilege of Pope Leo

[Col. 1709D]

> “LEO, pope of the apostolic see, servant of the servants of God, wishes and sends perpetual peace and salvation to KING KINELM, his ministers, kinsmen, and successors.
>
> A purpose of good will and praiseworthy desire ought then to be confirmed and strengthened by apostolic writings, so that what has been well done and confirmed by reasonable precedents may thereafter be neither disturbed nor broken by any corruption, but rather ought to remain unshaken in inviolable rectitude and by divine authority. Therefore the apostolic judgment excellently commands that what is known to have been rightly begun ought without delay to be confirmed. Accordingly, since it is known that your illustrious faith has asked us to confirm for you in writing the monastery of our Lord Jesus Christ at Glastonbury in the kingdom of the West Saxons, in which monastery there is a congregation of servants [Col. 1710A] of God, whose lands, located in many provinces and places, amount to eight hundred hides, just as King Ecgfrith recorded all that land, with the judgment and permission of King Brihtric, and with the permission and testimony of the bishops and princes of the Mercians, and just as afterwards all those lands were confirmed in writing to King Kenwulf of the Mercians: therefore we confirm for you, Kinelm, and your successors, with apostolic force and authority, that grant of kings, bishops, and princes, together with the ratification of Kenwulf, king of the Mercians: namely, that you may hold the monastery freely forever, with all its villages and fields distributed through many regions, with all things belonging to it—woods, meadows, pastures, and fisheries—on the condition that lights before God, spiritual chants, psalms, and Masses be maintained there, together with concord without pretence. For it is written in the Gospel: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’ [Matt. 21]. Therefore the servants of God who labour in this life ought continually to perform the whole spiritual office in the fear of God, that they may please our Lord Jesus Christ.
>
> “Furthermore, by apostolic command, under fear of divine judgment and threat of excommunication, we ordain that no king, archbishop, bishop, prince, or man exalted in any authority, whether in a greater or lesser rank, shall violently violate or diminish these our apostolic decrees. Rather, we decree that the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1710C] shall remain firm and stable for all time. Therefore, if anyone—which we do not desire—should weaken these our commands, let him know that, by the authority of the Lord Peter, prince of the apostles, he has bound himself in the bond of excommunication and excluded himself from the kingdom of God. But whoever maintains and observes these our apostolic decrees, let him know that he has deserved the apostolic blessing and eternal life from our merciful Creator. Given through the hand of Eustachius, chief of the notaries, in March, in the third indiction, on the eighth day of March; confirmed through the hand of Paschal the elder, counsellor of the apostolic see; while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns with God the Father through endless ages; in the third year, by the mercy of God, of the papacy of our lord Leo, in the holy and apostolic see of Saint Peter; and likewise by permission of Lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign.”

### Privilege of King Cenwulf

> “While our Lord Jesus Christ, Lord of all kingdoms, reigns forever, I, Cenwulf, king of the Mercians, after I was chosen king by almighty God, who is the giver and rewarder of all good things, obtained from Lord Leo, the apostolic pope, the liberty written below for Kinelm and his successors. And just as King Ecgfrith, my predecessor, firmly bestowed the same liberty upon him, so I also confirm it to him in writing, with the counsel and permission of the earthly princes whose names are written below; and I grant it to him to hold firmly, without any falsehood or [Col. 1711A] deceit. This confirmation of Cenwulf, his bishops, and princes was established and written in the venerable place called Glastonbury, in the year 712 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of my reign, which God granted me.
>
> “Subscriptions.—I, Abbess Kenedrip, together with my dearest kinsfolk Ethelbard and Celfled, subscribe in granting to Kinelm the liberty here written, on this condition: that even if it should happen in future that a man of another lineage should receive possession and authority over the venerable place of Glastonbury, Kinelm and his successors shall nevertheless remain securely, without any disturbance, in their liberty and perpetual peace.
>
> “To confirm this power of liberty, [Col. 1711B] I, King Cenwulf, have impressed the sign of the holy Cross.
>
> “Æthelard of Canterbury and Higbert of York, archbishops, subscribed; and nine bishops, thirteen abbots, among whom Beadulf, abbot of that place, and six princes.” I am uncertain who this Kinelm was, to whom King Cenwulf granted so great a liberty. For although his son was called Kenelm and, when scarcely seven years old, was treacherously slain after his father’s death through the plot of his sister, this cannot be the same man—especially since this liberty was granted in the second year of Cenwulf’s reign, whereas he himself reigned twenty-four years. But let us leave these matters and continue our undertaking.

### On Abbot Cuman and King Egbert

[Col. 1711C] In 800 Abbot Cuman succeeded; he also governed Glastonbury for two years.

In the year of the Incarnation 802, Egbert, king of the West Saxons, gave to the church of Glastonbury, for the use of the monks, an estate of five manentes beside the river called Toric, at the request of Abbot Muca. Edgisilius gave twenty hides at Budecleg, with King Egbert’s assent.

In the year of the Incarnation 824, Abbot Guthlac gave Canulf a portion of one cassate at Brumham for the price of five hundred shillings—two hundred to the abbot and three hundred to the monks.

### On Abbot Elmund and King Æthelwulf, who gave a tenth part of his lands to the Church

In 851 Abbot Elmund, with King Æthelwulf’s approval, [Col. 1711D] transferred Dulting into the right of the monastery. The aforesaid king also added twenty hides to it, with the consent of Bishop Alhstan, for the support of regular life. The same king is said to have piously bestowed a tenth part of his lands upon the churches of his kingdom. At that time he gave Glastonbury twenty-four hides at Offaculum, five hides at Bocland, nine hides at Pennard, Occenefeld, six hides at Scearamton, ten hides at Powg, Pyrinton, Logderesbeorgum, Occemund and Bedul, Branuc, and Duneald. Earl Æthelstan gave ten hides at Clutton, with the assent of the same King Æthelwulf. The aforesaid earl, along with his own body, committed the charter of this his aforesaid inheritance to Glastonbury monastery, beseeching in the name of Jesus Christ that the brethren of that monastery should never abandon it. Earl Ænulf gave Dichespite and thirty hides at Lotteshan, with the assent of King [Col. 1712A] Æthelwulf, and also Honblaperton and Beangean Hangran. King Æthelred, son of Æthelwulf, gave twenty-five hides at Winterburn to Earl Wlfera, who afterwards bestowed them upon Glastonbury.

In 867 Æthelbald, son of King Æthelwulf, gave to Abbot Hereferth, who had presided for fourteen years, ten hides at Branucmunster, with the fishing-right at Isic, to the old church of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and for the use of the monks in Glastonbury monastery. At that time King Alfred, Æthelbald’s brother and son of Æthelwulf, gave Glastonbury the wood of the Lord, which Pope Martin had given him.

### On King Æthelstan

In 916 King Æthelstan gave ten hides at Mertefburg to Duke Althelm, who afterwards bestowed them upon Glastonbury.

[Col. 1712B] Archbishop Wlhelm gave twenty hides at Devereb, with the assent of the same king. Offric gave ten hides at Werdeverel, that is, Munecaton.

### On Winterburn and Wrington

Ælfleda, queen of King Edward, gave ten hides at Wintburn.

Duke Æthelstan gave twenty hides at Wrington, which King Æthelstan had granted him. The same duke, converted and made a monk, offered this estate with himself to Glastonbury monastery. He further gave Weston, now called Foxcote, namely five hides. He also gave six hides at Lim. Uffa, a widow, gave five hides at Stoka. At that time Abbot Elfric governed Glastonbury for fourteen years. Therefore all the aforesaid properties, bestowed upon Glastonbury through the ministers of King Æthelstan, are credited to the munificence of that king; and the liberality of servants, whose devotion is often directed wherever they see the mind of their lords burn, attests his pious affection for Glastonbury. The same king, devoutly confirming to the old church at Glastonbury eighty-six hides [Col. 1712C] and adding many outstanding and innumerable relics, as is recorded in the text of Saint Dunstan, bestowed them on Glastonbury.

### On Styward

In 991 Styward succeeded. Pictures testify that his character did not depart from his name, always representing him in every image with a whip or a broom.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 922, Edward restored Cumton to Abbot Aldhun.

### On Saint Dunstan, Abbot

[Col. 1712D]

I think it plain how far from the truth that man was who absurdly maintained that blessed Dunstan was the first abbot of Glastonbury. But since we have filtered knowledge of events from the gulf of antiquity and, as it were, escaped from the darkness of ignorance into brighter times, we shall now, with freer leisure, range through those things known to have been bestowed on the monastery in the time of the blessed man who governed Glastonbury for twenty-two years. Thus Edmund, Æthelstan’s brother, carried off the first palm of generosity in his days; he too, as was said above, had appointed Dunstan abbot there by the counsel of a godly mind. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 940 he gave Dunstan twenty hides at Cristemulefard, eight hides at Hingestan, five hides at Wudetun, four hides at Watelca; he restored twenty hides at Wrigton; he also gave thirty hides at Pakelescirke, Escford with [Col. 1713A] its fishery, and half a hide. At his command his wife Epelfled gave Domham with Mertone and Pendrigton, one hundred hides, and thirteen hides at Stane. “These,” he says, “for the wiping away of my sins and those of my grandfather Alfred and my father Edward, I bestow upon the old church of the blessed Mother of God on the hill of Glastonbury.”

### On Acford, Bocland, Plis, and Hamedone

Alfleda, widow of King Edward, gave Acford, Bocland, and Plis, twenty-seven hides; and Hamedeine, fifteen hides, with King Edmund’s assent. Wilfrid, minister of the said king, with his assent, gave thirty hides at Hington, ten hides at Girlingeton, and five hides at Furnanwrthe. The same Wilfrid, after the death of his wife, gave thirty hides at Gretelington and twenty hides at Netelington. His successor Ælwin, however, having given charters and assumed the regular habit, fulfilled the gift. Likewise the aforesaid King Edmund had given to the same Wilfric five hides at Tintanhulle, which Wilfric afterwards committed to Glastonbury along with his body. Sigewulf gave five hides at Abbedesburgh, with King Edmund’s assent; Welfeh gave two hides at Langeford. All these lands—namely, three hundred and fifty-eight and a half hides—bestowed by King Edmund and his ministers, [Col. 1713B] bear witness to the remarkable devotion of that king and his servants towards Glastonbury monastery and its most glorious protector, Dunstan. The same king also, in order to distinguish the said place with greater gifts, piously bestowed upon Glastonbury many relics which he had sought out through the land of the Northumbrians and also overseas; you will find them recorded in old books. Drawn by the holiness of the place, he also devoted his own body to it after his death; there he rests to this day. He also granted the following privilege:

### Privilege of King Edmund

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I, Edmund, king of the English and governor and ruler of the other nations dwelling round about, with the counsel and consent of my nobles, in hope of eternal recompense and remission of my sins, grant to the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, at Glastonbury, and to the venerable man Dunstan, whom I have appointed abbot there, liberty and authority, [Col. 1713D] rights and customs, and all forfeitures from all their lands: borough-breach (Burgebrice), hundred-court jurisdiction (Humdred), soke or jurisdiction (Socna), oaths (Athas), ordeals (Ordelas), infangenetheof—the right to try a thief caught within the jurisdiction (Infangenetheosas), hamsocn or violent entry into a house (Hamsocre), breach of the peace (Trithbrice), foresteal or unlawful interception (Foresteall), toll, and team or warranty (Feam), throughout all my kingdom. Let their lands be free and discharged from every claim, as my own lands are held by me. But above all, let Glastonbury itself, in which the most celebrated old church stands, be freer than the rest with its boundaries. Let the abbot of that place alone have authority in known as well as unknown cases, in small matters and great, and in all things above and below ground, in dry places and streams, woods and plains; and let him have, for offences committed there, the same authority to punish or pardon as my court possesses, as my predecessors granted and established by ordinance: namely [Col. 1714A] my father Edward, his father Alfred, Centwine, Ine, Cuthred, and many others who held that place glorious in honour and strengthened it by apostolic authority, with all of whose acts I cheerfully concur.
>
> “By God’s prohibition, I forbid any mortal—bishop, duke, or any of their officers—to dare rashly enter it for the purpose of holding a plea, seizing anything, or doing anything which could be contrary to those serving God there. Therefore whoever, with a benevolent mind, strives to enlarge my donation and preserve the dignity of this privilege, may his life in this present age prosper and may he possess the joys of long life. But if anyone, by his own rashness, attempts violently to invade it, let him know beyond doubt that he will stand trembling and shaking before the tribunal of the strict Judge to give account, unless he first chooses to make amends by fitting satisfaction. This charter of privilege was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 944, in the second indiction.”

It was written in golden letters in the Book of the Gospels which he presented to the same church, a work composed with sufficient elegance. Thus far concerning Edmund, who, as I have said more than once in this little work, lies at Glastonbury on the left, in the tower of the greater church.

### On Eadred, King of the English

In 954 Eadred, brother of Edmund, gave for the price of fifty gold shillings twenty-six hides at Baddebari, and beside the town of Twinam—that is, [Col. 1714C] Christchurch—one hide and a fishery. He also gave Ternuc and Stapelwilt, part of Dennuni, and Elenberwe. Moreover, he restored Pukelescirke and Dulting, formerly alienated either through some tyranny or through the negligence of prelates. The same king also gave ten hides of gardens to his minister Wilfric; with his lord’s consent Wilfric assigned them to Glastonbury after his death. But Elwin, successor to the inheritance, having assumed the regular habit there, carried another’s vow into effect. Alfred gave five hides at Camelarton, with King Eadred’s assent.

### On King Eadwig

In 956 Eadwig, son of Edmund, after Dunstan had been driven into exile, gave one hide at Pagenebeorth, free from every service, to the false abbot Elsius whom he had intruded upon Glastonbury. The same king gave three [Col. 1714D] hides at Blakeford. Elsegus, his minister, with his assent, gave twelve hides at Cranmere. Ezericus, with the assent of the same king, gave six hides at Widecumbe. Ælwin, a knight, gave one part of Sturton. Brihtric gave five hides at Giffelton, with the assent of the same king. Buhtric committed the charter of this aforesaid inheritance, together with his body, to Glastonbury monastery, beseeching in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ that the brethren of that monastery should never abandon it. Buthcere gave Widangere with the assent of his lord King Eadwig.

### On King Edgar

After the enumeration of the earlier abbots and the gifts of kings, we have at last come to Edgar’s most fortunate times. I call them most fortunate because they flourished alike through the rejoicing announced by angels and through the elevation of blessed Father Dunstan to the archiepiscopate, [Col. 1715A] and therefore in the abundance of every good. Let us treat these matters somewhat more fully. Blessed Dunstan himself, while applying himself to heavenly studies in the church of Blessed Mary at Glastonbury, heard at the hour of Edgar’s birth a voice resounding from heaven: “Peace to the Church of the English in the time of the child now born and of our Dunstan.” As has been set forth elsewhere, the outcome of events proved the truth of this oracle. When Edgar assumed rule of the kingdom, he gloriously recalled Dunstan, whom Eadwig had condemned to exile; amid the great eagerness of the nobles, he advanced him first to the bishopric of Worcester, second to that of Sherborne, and third to the primacy of Canterbury. While the king governed the affairs of the realm exceedingly well, he did not neglect the peace of the Church. No king of the English can compete in praises with [Col. 1715B] Edgar, who surpassed them all in tranquillity during peace, abundance of wealth, and devotion toward God.

Yet he did not abuse the quiet of the times like some who, seizing the occasion of peace granted them for their private use, either lie slack in pleasures or devote themselves to piling up mountains of gold and wealth. Rather, stirred by the frequent admonitions of his teacher and patron, he responded to God’s grace with an office of devotion, as though in emulous rivalry; both personally and through his agents he provided for the welfare of monasteries. He honoured Glastonbury, which he deemed worthy of greater love than the rest, with such a privilege, by counsel of the nobles of the realm, that no abbot should ever be appointed there except a monk of that place, if one at all suitable—even the lowest member of the community—could be found. But if the extreme lack of native candidates required a monk from another place, that man should be promoted in whom the unanimous agreement of the Glastonbury community [Col. 1715C] should concur. Moreover, the abbot himself was to receive blessing from any bishop whatsoever, and cause his monks or clerics to be blessed; and, without prejudice to the bishop or the king’s officers, he was promptly to restrain the offences of those serving under him. Absolutely no one—whether bishop, duke, prince, or person of any other rank—was to enter the island that knew his birth, for the purpose of holding pleas or doing anything [and below], as his predecessors likewise had enacted: namely, Kenwine, Ine, Æthelard, Cuthred, Alfred, Edward, Æthelstan, and Edmund.

So that this grant should not be unstable or inglorious, he confirmed it upon the altar with an ivory horn (lituus) interwoven with strands of gold.
