In his presence he ordered the staff to be cut through the middle and preserved under trustworthy custody, so that it might serve as testimony in the future and that the loss caused by its division might restrain the greed of plunderers. He also gave another privilege in these words:

### Privilege of King Edgar

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Although the decrees of pontiffs and the words of priests, like the foundations of mountains, are fixed with unshaken bonds, nevertheless the religion of holy Church is often scattered and broken by the storms and whirlwinds of worldly affairs through the stains of the reprobate. Therefore we have decreed that it will benefit succeeding generations for those things decided by wholesome counsel and common assent to be established firmly by the strengthening of our writings. [Col. 1716A] Accordingly, it seems fitting that the church of the most blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary at Glastonbury, just as from ancient times it holds the principal dignity in my kingdom, should likewise be honoured by us with a special and singular liberty of privilege.
>
> “Therefore, at the exhortation of Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and Oswald, archbishop of York, with the consent and approval also of Brithalm, bishop of Wells, and of the other bishops, abbots, and chief men, I, Edgar, by divine dispensation king of the English and governor and ruler of the other nations dwelling round about, in the name of the gracious Trinity, for the soul of my father, who rests there, and of my predecessors, decree, establish, and confirm by this present privilege that the aforesaid monastery and all its possessions shall now and forever remain free and quit from every tribute of fiscal obligations; and that they shall have jurisdiction and legal claim (Socam et Sacam) on shore, stream, wave, and field; breach of the king’s peace (Grithbrice), borough-breach (Burgbrice), hundred-court jurisdiction (Hundred), Setena [uncertain legal term], oaths (Adas), ordeals (Ordelas), Calle, Hardas, Bufam, Corderam, and Beneorderam [all uncertain legal terms], the right to try a thief caught within the jurisdiction (Infangenepeof), the right to try a thief caught outside it (Outfangenetheof), [Col. 1716B] Flemene and Ferdere [uncertain legal terms], hamsocn or violent entry into a house (Hamsocne), breach of the peace (Friderbrice), foresteal or unlawful interception (Forteal), toll, and team or warranty, as freely and quitly as I hold them throughout my whole kingdom. The abbot and monks of the aforesaid monastery shall also possess in their court the same liberty and authority that I possess in mine, both in pardoning and punishing and in every kind of business whatsoever.
>
> “If the abbot or any monk of that place should meet upon the road a thief being led to hanging or to any peril of death, they shall have authority to rescue him from the imminent danger throughout my whole kingdom. I also confirm and strengthen that, as has hitherto been diligently observed by all our predecessors, the bishop of Wells and his officers shall have no authority at all over this monastery or its parish churches—namely Stret, Miricling, Budeclega, Sapenix, and Sowy—or over their chapels, nor yet over those situated in the islands, namely Bekeria, called Little Ireland, Gadeneia, Martenseia, Ferramere, Papeneberga, and Adredesera, except when summoned by the abbot for the purpose of consecrating or ordaining. Nor shall they summon their priests to their synod, chapter, or any court; suspend them from divine office; or presume to exercise any right whatsoever over them.
>
> “In accordance with the ancient custom of the Church of Glastonbury and apostolic authority, with the consent of Archbishop Dunstan and all bishops of my kingdom, the abbot shall have his monks and the clerics of the aforesaid churches ordained by whichever bishop of the province he chooses. But we permit the consecration of churches to the bishop of Wells if requested by the abbot. At Easter the abbot shall also receive the chrism of sanctification and oil from the bishop of Wells according to custom and distribute them among his aforesaid churches.
>
> “Above all, by God’s prohibition and our authority—while preserving, however, the dignity of the holy Roman Church and of Canterbury—[Col. 1717A] I forbid any person of authority, whether king, bishop, duke, prince, or any of their officers, to presume to enter Glastonbury’s boundaries or those of the aforesaid parishes for the purpose of investigation, seizure, litigation, or doing anything else which may be contrary to those serving God there. Authority shall belong only to the abbot and convent, in known as well as unknown cases, in small matters and great, and in every business whatsoever, as we have said above. Whoever henceforth, by sacrilegious presumption, attempts on any pretext of whatever rank, order, or profession to overturn or render void the dignity of this my privilege, let him know beyond doubt that he shall give account trembling and shaking before the strict Judge, unless he first strives to make amends by fitting satisfaction. This charter of privilege was executed and confirmed at London, by the common counsel of all my chief men, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 971, indiction XIV.”

The following were the sureties of this grant, whose names appear to be inscribed below:

> “I, Edgar, king of all Britain, have confirmed the aforesaid liberty with the seal of the holy Cross. I, Ælfgifu, mother of the same king, have joyfully consented. I, Prince Edward, have impressed my father’s gift with the triumph of the holy Cross. I, Cináed, king of Alba, have assented. [Col. 1717C] I, Maccus, high pirate, have strengthened it. Likewise I, Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury; Oswald, primate of York; Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester; Burithtelin, bishop of Wells; and this man and many others, whose names are recorded elsewhere, consented and confirmed, and impressed the sign of the Cross.”

Moreover, to provide additional security so that so great a generosity might not waver, he persuaded John, then the eighth pope of that name, and supported his gift with an apostolic decree, whose text follows.

### Privilege of Pope John

> “Let all the faithful know that I, John, by the mercy of the gracious Creator the unworthy pope of the Holy Roman [Col. 1717D] See, have been earnestly petitioned by the glorious King Edgar of the English and also by Dunstan, archbishop of the holy Church of Canterbury, on behalf of the monastery of Saint Mary at Glastonbury. Moved by love for the supreme King, they restored it to a better condition, gathered there a greater number of monks, established a stricter rule, and strengthened this arrangement by royal command; they have asked that I should not delay in doing the same.
>
> “Assenting to their gracious request, I receive that place into the bosom of the Roman Church and into the protection of the blessed Apostles, and establish and strengthen it with privileges, so that it may remain to the end in the monastic order which it now possesses; and so that the monks themselves may choose for themselves their shepherd from among their own number and may send themselves and those whom they judge suitable, wherever they please in the diocese of Canterbury, [Col. 1718A] for ordination. We also decree that no person whatsoever may enter the same island to hold a plea or to investigate or correct anything else there. If anyone attempts to oppose this, or to take away, retain, diminish, or harass with rash vexations the possessions of that church, by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of holy Mary, Mother of God, of Saint Peter the Apostle, and of all the saints, let him be subject to perpetual curse unless he repents. But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve what is right for that place, and may our ratification remain unshaken. This apostolic decree was enacted in the time of Egelward, abbot of the same monastery, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 965.”

[Col. 1718B] The same pope proclaimed it ratified in a general council at Rome and sent it to the king there to be joined to his authority. Royal consent approved the pontiff’s act; and, in a full court at London in the twelfth year of his reign, by the consent of all the nobles, with great devotion he committed the matter to everlasting stability against transgressors. So long as he lived, he made himself the fulfiller of his vow; following the steps of his father and forefathers, he did not fail either their honour or his own glory, and he encouraged others to do the same, as the ensuing account will show.

### On estates bestowed upon Glastonbury by Edgar: Dundene, Hamme, and Wethul

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 963, I, Edgar, king strengthened solely by the merciful clemency of God, for the reward of a greater recompense, gave to the Church [Col. 1718C] of the Blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary, in the celebrated place called Glastonbury, for the use of monks serving God according to the Rule under Abbot Egelward, thirty hides at Sture; I restored ten hides at Merkesbiry; I gave two hides at Midelton and six hides at Blakeford.

In the year 965, I, Edgar, grant to Abbot Sigegar, in perpetual right, for the old venerable church, for the remedy of my soul and of the soul of my father, Hamme, seventeen hides; Dundene, ten hides; and Petehulle, three hides.

### Concerning Westbury and Othley

In his time Duke Alfara also gave Westbury, forty hides, and Othley, five hides. I, Duke Alfara, committed this charter of the aforesaid inheritance to Glastonbury monastery, for the remedy of my soul [Col. 1718D] and that of King Edgar, beseeching in the name of Jesus Christ that the brethren of that monastery may never abandon it. Alwine gave Gritelington, twenty-five hides; Netelcumbe, twenty hides, and thus fulfilled the vow of Wilfric, the first donor. Ealdorman Aelfare gave Batamcumbe, twenty hides; Ealdred gave Clifan, eleven hides. This rural estate and the aforesaid Clifan Ealdred committed to the church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, and to Saint Patrick, under the witness of King Edgar and his nobles. Aelthelm gave Dureberge, two hides; Alfeah gave Cranemere, ten hides; Aedelfleda gave Hanandon, fifteen hides. Queen Alswit gave Winescumbe, fifteen hides; Feimeston, ten; Strettun, six; Tintanhusse, five; Aeweredesie, half a hide; and ornaments: a stole with maniple, and an incomparable chasuble. Hedred [Col. 1719A] gave Mildenhele, fifteen hides, and Essebur, forty hides. Brinsige gave Healtone, five hides. King Edgar confirmed all these lands—namely, 215 hides—to the venerable church at Glastonbury by royal authority.

Moreover, he made a cross above the high altar, woven throughout with gold and silver, and larger images; he also bestowed the most precious royal garment in which he had been crowned, to serve as an adornment of the altar. He gave a great shrine covered with silver and gold, suitably inlaid with ivory images, containing relics of Saint Vincent and the head of Saint Apollinaris, in which he himself now rests. He further entrusted to Glastonbury monastery, with the reverence proper to them, many relics which he had acquired throughout all the lands he had travelled, together with relics of the two Innocents brought from Bethlehem to Glastonbury monastery. [Col. 1719B]

So much concerning the times of Edgar, whose merits no age will ever leave unspoken; for he surpassed fame by his virtues, and compressed the deeds of ages into the scarcely thirty-two years that he lived. As we have said, he was buried in the chapter-house at the church door; but how he was translated thence will become clear below.

### Concerning King Ethelred

His son Ethelred gave to Abbot Figegar, who presided for twenty-eight years, Austanctif, six hides; and Siteberge, one hide. He restored Pukelescirce, thirty [units unspecified]; at Pilton, one estate bought for forty mancuses of gold, in the year 884. He also gave Hanandune. In the year 1000 of the Incarnation, King Ethelred gave to Abbot Berred, who also presided for sixteen years, [Col. 1719C] Fiscwere, Alwine, and Estun, twenty hides.

### Concerning Abbot Brithwius

In the year 1017 Abbot Brithwius was appointed. He made a panel before the altar, embellished with gold, silver, and ivory, and a cross. After ten years of governance he was elected bishop of Wells.

### Concerning Cnut

At about the same time Cnut, king of the Danes, was ravaging England in hostile fashion. Although Edmund, son of Ethelred, had checked him in several battles, they finally made a treaty and agreed upon a brotherly peace: Mercia was to remain to Cnut, Wessex to Edmund. Not long afterwards, however, Edmund was struck by a fatal illness and came to his end. At his death he bequeathed to Glastonbury monastery Newton Kastel, seventeen hides, [Col. 1719D] together with his body, and was buried there before the high altar. When Cnut came there on the feast of Saint Andrew, on the occasion of a journey, honouring his brother’s shade with pious lamentation, he laid upon Edmund’s tomb a cloth apparently woven with multicoloured peacock feathers; and he granted the following privilege:

### Privilege of Cnut

> “While the Lord reigns for ever—he who by his ineffable power orders and governs all things, wonderfully distinguishes the vicissitudes of times and men, and, as he wills, calmly imposes an uncertain end—he also mercifully instructs us through the mysteries hidden in nature that enduring kingdoms are to be obtained through God’s aid out of things fleeting and undoubtedly transitory.
>
> “Therefore I, Cnut, king of the English and governor and ruler of the other nations dwelling round about, [Col. 1720A] with the counsel and decree of Aethelvot, together with all the priests of God, and with the consent of my nobles, for love of the heavenly kingdom, for remission of my sins, and for the soul of my brother King Edmund, grant to the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, at Glastonbury, its rights and customs throughout my whole kingdom, and all the forfeitures arising from all its lands. Let its lands be free and discharged from every claim and disturbance, as my own are held for me.
>
> “But above all, by the authority of the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by the prohibition of the perpetual Virgin, I forbid, and I command all the officers and chief men of my kingdom, upon peril of their salvation, that no one whatsoever, of whatever order or dignity, dare enter that island. Rather, in all matters, ecclesiastical as well as secular, let them await only the judgment of the abbot and convent, as my predecessors Cenwealh, Ine, Cuthred, Alfred, Edward, Edmund, and incomparable Edgar ordained and confirmed by privileges. [Col. 1720B]
>
> “If anyone hereafter, at any time and under any pretext, attempts to interrupt or invalidate the testimony of this privilege, let him be separated from the fellowship of the righteous by the winnowing-fan of the Last Judgment. But if anyone with benevolent purpose strives to perform, approve, and defend these things, may God, through the intercession of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of all the saints, increase his portion in the land of the living. This grant of privilege was written and promulgated in the wooden basilica, in the presence of King Cnut, in the year 1032 from the Incarnation of the Lord.” [Col. 1720C]

### Concerning Abbot Egelward

In the year 1027 Egelward succeeded, holding Glastonbury for twenty-six years. Hardecnut gave him the shrine in which the body of blessed Benignus now rests.

### Concerning Abbot Egelnoth and the Translation of King Edgar

In the year 1053: Egelnoth [entry incomplete]. The rule of both men was harmful to the Church: one alienated lands outwardly, the other disposed of ornaments inwardly. From that time Glastonbury’s affairs began to decline and to worsen. [Col. 1720D] Finally, it was believed that some vengeance had fallen upon the place because of Egelward’s audacity against King Edgar. For, perhaps with a good intention, forty years after Edgar’s death he opened his tomb and found the body untouched by any corruption, but held together in complete integrity. This should have inclined him to reverence, but instead it emboldened him to presumption. Since the casket he had prepared threatened to be difficult to enter because of the body’s size, he profaned the royal remains with iron—an act terrible even to hear of, much less to perform. Immediately blood flowed forth in streams, shaking the hearts of those standing by with fear and whitening their faces with pallor.

Thus the king’s bones were placed in a shrine above the altar, together with the head of Saint Apollinaris and the relics of blessed Vincent the martyr, which Edgar had bought at great cost and added for the adornment of God’s house. [Col. 1721A] The violator’s spirit then left his body; and not long after he had departed from the church, death found him with his neck broken. Egelward, the first successor of Saint Dunstan in the government of Glastonbury, was buried in the king’s tomb.

Nor did this manifestation of royal sanctity stop here, but proceeded to greater things. A madman and a blind man were healed there. The madman, a German by birth, gave many signs that he was not sound in mind. He had armed the hands of the townspeople against himself, so that they did not hesitate to bind him with iron; pitiable as he was, he carried about his own punishments, himself both judge and author of his penalties. One could not tell whether he was more wretched or more pitiable: enslaved in mind and burdened in body. Thus, wandering for many years through many provinces, he wasted his time to no purpose, except that the continuance of travel was an increase of toil. At last, visited by the regard of divine mercy, he received an oracle by night directing him to go to Glastonbury, where through the merits of King Edgar he would be relieved of both afflictions. He came, therefore, and obtained an outcome corresponding to the answer. While he was praying in the same church, though at some distance from the tomb, every iron fastening burst apart, and, as though driven by a whirlwind, he fell upon the mausoleum. Moreover, a blind man well known throughout the district, who had persistently kept vigil at the tomb for his healing, found sight. [Col. 1721B]

### Concerning Archbishops and Bishops Chosen from the Convent of Glastonbury

Since we have now come to Norman times, and since the deeds and names of the abbots after that period are known, leaving them aside for a little I shall set down the names of those who were elsewhere chosen bishops and archbishops from that church. [Col. 1721C] These many distinguished persons are plainly a splendid example both of Glastonbury’s authority and of the grace which sufficed not only for itself but also for other churches. Yet I do not promise that I can set out the sees of them all, except insofar as I have found in chronicles that this or that bishop died as a monk of this place. So greatly have the courses of the longer ages flowed away that no human memory can trace them.

First, concerning archbishops: Berthwald, formerly abbot of Glastonbury, was archbishop of Canterbury. Adthelmus was first bishop of Wells, then archbishop [Col. 1721D] of Canterbury.

Dunstan, through whose exertions the church flourished again, made organs, two principal images, one pallium, and a bell in the refectory, where these verses are found:

> Dunstan commanded this bell to be cast for himself, etc.

On the altar ewer:

> Archbishop Dunstan had this water-vessel cast—  
> May the Almighty release him unto eternity.

From monk and abbot of Glastonbury he became bishop of Worcester, afterwards bishop of London, and finally archbishop of Canterbury.

Egelgar, formerly a monk of Glastonbury, became the first abbot of the new monastery at Winchester, namely Hyde; then bishop of Chichester; and finally archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 1722A] Sigeric, formerly a monk of Glastonbury, was bishop of Wells and afterwards archbishop of Canterbury, third after Dunstan. He gave Glastonbury seven pallia with white lions, with which the old church is entirely adorned on his anniversary.

Alphege, formerly monk and prior of Glastonbury, was abbot of Bath, then bishop of Winchester, and then archbishop of Canterbury.

Elnoth, formerly monk of Glastonbury, became archbishop of Canterbury; he has been mentioned above. When Dunstan was baptizing him, he held his raised hand in the manner of a bishop blessing the people. Dunstan therefore, as though aware of his divine destiny, foretold that he would be an archbishop. He was archbishop in the time of Cnut, by whose assistance [Col. 1722B] and command he translated the martyr Alphege to Kent from his resting-place near London. He gave Rabanus’ *On the Praise of the Cross* and a prayer-book painted with gold.

### Concerning Bishops

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 782, Bishop Canfrid died, a monk of Glastonbury.

In the year 782, Bishop Ethelwmus died, a monk of Glastonbury.

In the year 800, Bishop Wibert died, a monk of Glastonbury.

In the year 836, Bishop Wigthegn died, a monk of Glastonbury.

In the year 842, Bishop Alhstan died, a monk [Col. 1722C] of Glastonbury.

In the year 876, Tumbert, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died.

In the year 956, Daniel, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died.

In the year 988, Elfric, bishop and abbot of Glastonbury, died.

Those who follow were bishops in various places during the time of King Edgar. In the fourth year of Pope Julius, Sigegar, bishop of Wells and abbot of Glastonbury, died.

He is said to lie beneath Saint Benignus. On the Ides of May, Britelm, bishop of Wells and monk of Glastonbury, died. On the Ides of February, Alfuold, bishop of Crediton and monk of Glastonbury, died. On the Nones of April, Sigefrid, bishop of Norway and monk of Glastonbury, died. He sent four copes, two with lions and two saffron-coloured. On the Kalends of August, Athelwold, bishop of Winchester, monk and prior of Glastonbury, and abbot of Abingdon, died. [Col. 1722D] On the Ides of January, Wilmus, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died. On the Ides of February, Aelfstan, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died. On 8 May, Aegelric, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died. On 28 June, Kenewald, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died. On 3 April, Almer, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died. On 19 March, Livingus, bishop and monk of Glastonbury, died.

In the year of the Incarnation 1034, Brihwius, bishop of Wells and abbot of Glastonbury, died. We have touched above on certain matters concerning him. He lies in the northern aisle by Saint John the Baptist.

### Concerning Bishop Brithwold

In the year 1045 Brithwold, bishop of Salisbury and monk of Glastonbury, died. He sent a most precious silk alb, [Col. 1723A] and also ten copes of rich cloth suitably adorned with gold and gems. He also sent an amice, stole, maniple, chasuble, two chalices—one of twenty marks of silver and four of gold, the other of lighter weight but greater value—two Gospel books, a thurible of remarkable size made of gold and silver, an altar valued at twenty marks, a processional cross, and twenty-five other crosses. When Abbot Aegelnot had stripped them, together with other ornaments, of their gold and silver, he received twenty-two marks of gold from two of them. One may therefore infer how great a quantity of money there was in all. Brithwold also gave a collectar illuminated in gold, a pallium woven with gold, and nine others; two candlesticks; and he redeemed all the land of Wiltshire. He gave three shrines of Saints Guthlac, George, and Oswald, upon which are these verses:

[Col. 1723B]

> Brithwold, a humble bishop so named,  
> Devoutly offers this humble gift  
> To the Lord Ruler and also to Mother Mary,  
> Sending it to the old church of Glastonbury,  
> That he may receive the sweet joys of everlasting life.

A cope with white birds. He lies with Brihtwius in the northern part, a man to be praised throughout his life, who gave the Church such great things as not even plunderers have yet been able to tear away. Though there are some who attempt to charge his glory with fault, saying that he gave the property of his bishopric to Glastonbury, they vainly set their teeth against him. He neither seeks praises nor fears reproaches—especially since it is fitting that doubtful acts of saints be interpreted in the better sense. Indeed, if the holy man had known himself to be at fault, he would never have done those things. Finally, there is a well-established report that all those lands had of old belonged to Glastonbury. But in the Danish period, when unbearable exactions burdened the kingdom, they were pledged either to the royal fisc or elsewhere, and were redeemed and restored by the bishop. [Col. 1723C] And, as they say, when a penny was lacking for the redemption, that splendid man threw his ring to the creditors, testifying by the performance of the act to the devotion which he bore toward Glastonbury.

### Concerning the Possessions Given to Glastonbury by English Converts to the Faith

Since the hands of those who bestowed possessions have now been withdrawn, it is pleasing to insert briefly what was granted to Glastonbury by whom, or confirmed by royal authority. [Col. 1723D]

First, King Arthur, in the time of the Britons, gave Brentemaris and Poweldon, with many other lands situated on the boundary, for the soul of Ider, as mentioned above. These lands, taken away by the English when they arrived as pagans, were restored after their conversion to the faith together with many others. Thus the king of Dumnonia gave the land called Yneswitherin, five hides.

King Cenwealh, or Cedwald, gave Ferremere, two hides; Beokeri; Godenia; Martenesie; and Andrewesye.

King Cenwine gave Munekaton, twenty-three hides; at Caru, twenty hides; and at Crucam, three hides.

King Baldred gave Pennard, six hides; Loggaresbeorg, sixteen hides; and Westwere, with the fishery at Peret.

[Col. 1724A] Bishop Hedda gave Lantokai (read: I), six hides, with Cedwalla confirming it, though he was a pagan king.

King Ine gave Brentemareis, twenty hides; Sowi, twelve hides; Pilton, twenty hides; Dulting, twenty hides; and near Famer, namely Linig, twenty hides and Roualt, twenty hides; and elsewhere one hide with a fishery.

Bishop Wilfrid gave Wethrnon, seventy hides; Eliwawerre, one hide. Bishop Forthere gave Bledanhid, one hide. Abbess Buggu gave Ora, three hides, with King Ine consenting and confirming.

King Athelard gave Poholt, sixty hides, and at Torric, ten hides. His queen Kedeswita gave Brumanton, five hides.

King Cuthred gave Ure, three hides; Lady Lulla gave Baltenesbeorge and Scrobammurth, or Sabewrtha, ten [Col. 1724B] hides.

King Athelbald gave Jeksig [gassie?], five hides, and Bradelegh, four hides.

King Sigebert gave at Polhoc, twenty-one hides.

King Binewlf gave and confirmed Wodeton, five hides; Cumpton, five hides; and Huneresburg.

His minister Adthelard gave three hides at Ceddren [Eleanbearo?] and Cumbe, three hides.

Sulca, handmaid of Christ, gave Culum, eleven hides.

King Offa gave Ineswurth, ten hides. Ethelmund gave Hinespulle, almost five hides, with Offa confirming.

King Egbert gave five hides beside the river Torric. With his confirmation, Edgisilus gave Budeclege, twenty hides.

King Aethelwulf gave twenty-five hides and restored Dulting. [Col. 1724C] He also gave Offaculum, twenty-four hides; Bocland, five hides; Pennard, nine hides; Occenefeld and Suaromton, six hides; Sowy, ten hides; Periston, Legderesbeorgune, Ocemund, Bedul, and Branuc Duneafd. He also confirmed Clutton, ten hides, from the gift of Aethelstan; Dicheswita and Lottesham, thirty hides, from the gift of Aenulf; Hornblawerton; and Beanganhangran.

King Edthelbald gave Bramnucmiister, ten hides. His brother Alfred gave a cross made from the wood of the Lord.

King Athelstan granted and confirmed: Merkesburi, ten hides, from the gift of Duke Athelm; Deverel, twenty hides, from the gift of Wulfelm; Werdeverel [read: Mimecaton?], ten hides, from the gift of the office; Winterbarne, ten hides, from the gift of Queen Alfleda, wife of Edward; Wrington, twenty hides, Weston or Foxate, ten hides, [Col. 1724D] and Lim, six hides, from the gift of Duke Aethelstan; and Stoka, five hides, from the gift of the widow Uffa.

King Edmund gave Cristemaleford, twenty hides; Kingeston, eight hides; Wodeton, five hides; Wathelego, ten hides; Pukeleschurice, thirty hides; Escford, half a hide with its fishery; Domerhom, Mertun, and Pendrith, one hundred hides; and Stane, eight hides. He also confirmed Acford, Bocland, and Plis, twenty-seven hides, and Hommedone, fifteen hides, from the gift of Queen Aelfleda, wife of Edward; Kington, nineteen hides; Girdlingeton, ten hides; at Turnanwrthe, five hides; and Tintamhulle, five hides, from the gift of Wilfrid; Batecumbe, twenty hides, from the gift of Alsy; Melnes, twenty hides, from the gift of Earl Ethelstan; Abbedesbari, five hides, from the gift of Sigewlf; Langefore, two hides, from the gift of Wlfec. He also restored Wrington, twenty hides.

King Eddred gave Baddeburi, thirty hides, and at Cristeschurche, two hides; Ternuc and Stapelwilt; [Col. 1725A] also a part of Nuni S., two hides, and of Elenberwe, one hide; and restored Bulting. Aelfred gave Camelarton, five hides, with Eddred confirming; and Aelfgita, a religious woman, gave Pengeardmunster, ten hides.

King Edwi gave Padenebeorge, two hides; Blakeford, six hides; and confirmed Cranemere, twelve hides, from the gift of Alphege; Widecumbe, six hides, from the gift of Eseric; one part of Sturton S., eight hides, from the gift of Alwin; Giffelton, five hides, from the gift of Brithric; and Widingate, from the gift of Brithere.

King Edgar gave Sture, thirty hides; Midelton, two hides; Lucum, two hides; Blakeford, five hides; Hamme, twelve hides; Dandene, five hides; Wetehulle, three hides; and restored Merkesbury. He confirmed Westbury, forty hides, and Otherlee, five hides, from the gift of Duke Aelfere. From the gift of Alwine: [Col. 1725B] Gritilingtone, twenty-five hides; Netelton, twenty hides; Horton, ten hides. From the gift of Ealdorman Aelfere: Badecumbe, twenty hides. From the gift of Caldred: Clifan, eleven hides. From the gift of Aelfhelm: Dirambeorg, two hides. From the gift of Aelfeah: Cranemere, ten hides. From the gift of Adelfled: Hanandon, fifteen hides. From the gift of Queen Aelswith: Winescumbe, fifteen hides; Idemeston, ten; Stretton, six; Adredesie, half a hide. From the gift of Edred: Middelhale, fifteen hides; and Essebury, forty hides. From the gift of Brinsige: Healton, five hides.

King Ethelred gave Austanclif, six hides; Streberge, one hide; Fiscwere; one manor at Wilton; and Hanandon; and restored Pukeleschun. He confirmed Estun, twenty hides, from the gift of Wlfwine. Edmund Ironside gave Ninneton; Kastel, eighteen hides.

### Likewise, Concerning Other Gifts to Glastonbury

[Col. 1725C]

Memorandum concerning Aldamton and others: Cinemereffordi, Lemucerine, Pillesdune, Portbrig, Litlanton, Eatumberg, Siwiamhame, Brentefordlande, Pendesclive, Halbanleghe. Likewise: Elonsanige, Ocemund, Ceolumwrthe, Korstone, Camel, Ruthanbeorg, Peasacmere. Likewise: Lidenige, Lamageate, Hengestesteshriege, Dilwisce, Orcirleage, Pidelan, Birtwlfintone, Betocer, Huppavene, Easaetenatone. These manors, granted by different kings to their household men, came to the church of Glastonbury, as appears from old charters. Although we have here set down an incredible number and quantity of lands belonging to one place, we nevertheless do not doubt that all these, and many more [Col. 1725D] which we do not wish to enumerate because of uncertainty, were given to Glastonbury monastery. Nor should it be wondered if certain manors are said to have been granted by different persons, whether in fact or merely in name: some names are identical; many things once given were later taken away and restored; and one person gave part of a manor and another another part of the same, while perhaps the whole was recorded for each.

### Boundaries of the Twelve Hides

Since the twelve hides of Glastonbury are privileged with greater liberty than its other lands, it is fitting not to be ignorant of their boundaries. It must therefore be known that the boundary begins first at Brutascha by Stretebrugge, at the southern end of the same bridge, and runs eastward, along the southern side of the marsh, as far as the southern end [Col. 1726D] of the bridge of Baltenesberge; on the northern side, from the house of Wlgar with Barba, who was the builder of that bridge in the time of Saint Dunstan the abbot. It then goes above Caucetum, beyond Pinueslake, through the middle of the marsh, to the house of Norman by the mill of Baltenesberg; then thence upward along the road to the path coming from that church; then upward into Jeholt, as far as Lupwite, on the eastern side of the house of Hosgar and Attaholt. Thence it goes to the path leading straight through the middle extremity of that Holt, to the bridge of Kineward, at the ditch of Saint Dunstan the abbot. Then to the brook which comes from Colebari, and so upstream against the current, to the house of Osward de la Barne. Thence upward along the Burne to the court of Ailmer, steward at la Brodelee. Then upward from that burn to [Col. 1727A] the road lying before his court; then on the southern side of that church eastward to Stoke on the broad road; then from that road up the hill of Withelee, to the path lying on the southern side of Chulebury. Next, to a certain path as far as la Windeiete; then to the boundaries of Bikenhan and Ferlege; then, descending through the middle of Pilton park beyond the road extending above the stone bridge, to the path leading to Woltun; then along a certain path to Falebroc; thence on the southern side of that church beyond the brook to Loffellegethe; then descending into the moor as far as Hochge; thence through the middle of the moor beyond la Sowere, to the boundary ditch on the northern side of Bachinwere; thence to the bank, and then along the length of the old watercourse [Col. 1727B] to the bridge of Bledesne; then descending through the middle of that bridge to Lithlenie, which is the boundary of Martenesie. Then around the same island to the ditch between the moor of Stoke and Withtrichelham; then to la Wynerdlake; then through the boundaries of the island of Andredesie and of Draicote, ascending up the hill to la Horestone. Next to Wiarepath; then descending to Upper Badecumbe; then through the boundaries of Ceddre to la Grene Balle, and so to Littelakewepe. Thence to la Ymerwivel; thence directly through the middle of the alder-grove (Alneti) to la Hore Wgthege, and so to Mune Keneleghe. Thus all covered ground belongs to Ceddre, [Col. 1727C] and all uncovered ground to Glastonbury. Thence to a certain trench called Bitwynenorde; then to la Scearpeorde. Thus all covered ground there eastward belongs to Glastonbury, and the uncovered ground westward to Ceddre. Thence to Nottepulle. Thus all covered ground remains to Glastonbury; all level land outside the covered ground remains to Ceddre. Thence to Glake; then following Glake downstream to Ywere; then following Gwere upstream from Abbedesdith to Sangeby. Thence to the course of the great water; then following that water upstream eastward to the boundaries of Wethmore and Northilade, as far as Tunsingwere. Thence to Kimpingmere; thence to Middelmede; thence over the hill to Cumessam; thence to la Likhlake. Then through the middle of the moor to the boundaries of Mere and Poldane. Then along those boundaries eastward, on the southern side of that moor, to below Scerpham; thence below Hundewode; thence eastward to la Brittafebe, which we set down as the first boundary of the twelve hides. [Col. 1727D]

### Principal Places within the Twelve Hides

We shall now add the places lying within these limits and enjoying the same privilege. First, the island of Glastonbury itself, with the fields, woods, meadows, and hill belonging to it. Then the island of Hurty, with its beautiful and extensive alder-grove and with very fertile meadows and pastures; after this, a great part of Pilton pasture. Then Bikenham with Stikaling; after these, Witebgh and Colebari with all West Pennard, [Col. 1728A] and the fields, meadows, and pastures belonging to them. Finally, la Burne and Kineard with their fields and meadows; afterwards, a certain part of Baltenesberghe, with fields, meadows, abundant pastures, the entire alder-grove, and all the moors westward, on the northern side, from Bodeclee to la Britasca at the southern end of Strete bridge. Finally, Edgarlegsi, with its fields and meadows; then the island of Beokeri with its appurtenances. From the aforesaid Brutaschda, all the marsh westward which lies north of Hundeswode and Scerpham, as far as the boundaries of Poldon and Demere, to la Liklake. Finally, the islands of Mere and Westie, with fields, meadows, woods, and moors. Lastly, the island of Godenie, with its lands and extensive moors; then the island of Martenesie with its adjoining lands. Finally, the island of Badenebeorge and Northilade, with the lands, meadows, pastures, moors, and broad woods belonging to them; after these, the island of Andrewesie, surpassing the others in situation and pleasantness of site, with lands, woods, meadows, and extensive moors. [Col. 1728B] It is so named from Saint Andrew, whose chapel is there; just as Godenie is named for the chapel of the Holy Trinity, and Martenesie for Saint Martin, whose chapel is there. After the aforesaid places comes Badecumbe, near Mount Munidop, with all the lands and pastures belonging to it upon that same hill. All these places contained within the boundaries of the twelve hides and belonging to Glastonbury enjoy every immunity of royal dignity from ancient times; and this has been confirmed to Glastonbury church by the kings of Britons, English, and Normans. [Col. 1728C]

### Concerning Turstin, the First Norman Abbot

Having disposed of certain matters for the sake of which we made a slight digression, we must return to the order of the history. The first abbot from among the Normans was Turstin. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1082, William—formerly duke of Normandy and now king of England—appointed him abbot there, though he had been a monk of Caen. After William had subjected the kingdom to his rule, he enfeoffed very many of his own comrades with possessions taken from Glastonbury. From this and the foregoing one may infer how and through whom the monastery of Glastonbury, once exceedingly wealthy, was almost stripped of its lands: namely, through the wastefulness of Aegelward and Agelnot, and through the hostile incursions or violent oppression of Danes and Normans. [Col. 1728D] Yet the same King William, in order to redress the wrong formerly inflicted upon Glastonbury, confirmed by royal authority certain lands which they claimed had been taken away, in the following words:

### Charter of King William I

> “Let it be known to those present and to those to come that I, William, by the grace of God king of England, having seen and examined the charters of the church of Glastonbury, grant and confirm to that church in perpetuity, for the sustenance of the monks there serving God and for the salvation of my soul, certain lands which it claimed belonged to the aforesaid church by hereditary right.” [Col. 1729A]

The names of the lands are appended: Midelton, Fulebroc, Berges, Burmington, Lim, Blakeford, and Witon; with Bishop W. of Durham, Archbishop Lanfranc, Archbishop Thomas, Wakelino, Robert count of Mauric, and many others as witnesses.

### Concerning the Abbots of Muchelney and Athelney

After these matters had been accomplished at Abbot Turstin’s instance, let us also relate how effectively he asserted the neighbouring abbots of Muchelney and Athelney to be subject to his jurisdiction. When Lanfranc, archbishop, bitterly attacked them in a general council of England on the false accusation of Giso, bishop of Wells, the abbot of Muchelney, being more practiced in secular affairs, replied that he would answer in the chapter-house of Glastonbury at the command of the abbot of that place and his own; but that he did not fear extraordinary accusations. The abbot of Athelney, however, playfully evaded the question. When the archbishop threatened to take away his staff, he said: “I do not care, because I have a better one; yet I shall not hand this one over to you.”

Then Abbot Turstin was commanded to plead the case if he knew it belonged to him. Rising to deliver his judgment, he spoke at length with firm eloquence, reciting from memory the privileges of the kings from Cenwine and Ine to Edward. By these he maintained that the abbots owed no jurisdiction to anyone except the abbot of Glastonbury, so that no abbot ought to enter the aforesaid churches unless elected by the Glastonbury convent. [Col. 1729B] Then, when the archbishop turned to the king and said, “I do not wish to diminish the nurse [Col. 1729C] of Saint Dunstan,” and the king replied, “Nor do I wish to grieve the Mother of the Lord; but, for security in the future, the bishop of Wells ought to settle the matter in Glastonbury chapter,” the abbot resumed his speech. He said that the privileges of his church were authentic; that no person of any dignity ought to come to Glastonbury for judicial proceedings; that all jurisdiction there, in ecclesiastical as well as secular matters, belonged to Glastonbury; and that it would be easy for the unconquered prince and the holy archbishop to incur perpetual odium by establishing a novelty. Yet he would by no means abandon what his predecessors had possessed entire, since he watched with the same spirit over the defence of the Church’s dignity. Therefore, if the bishop of Wells believed he had anything to allege, he should come to Glastonbury by his own authority, not at the king’s or archbishop’s command. In short, the abbot won the case. A certain bishop did come into the chapter-house; but when the abbots defended themselves, he lost his case and departed without honour. [Col. 1729D]

### Concerning the Translation of Saint Benignus

The translation of most blessed Benignus also belongs to the glory of Turstin’s times. Our pen has elsewhere treated it, notable for miracles. He made two pallia, two thuribles, and two candlesticks.

### Concerning the Discords between Turstin and His Convent, and the Wounded Cross
At this same time an unfortunate event occurred which reason advises should by no means be passed over in silence—not so that the recollection of a bitter affair may seem a reproach, but so that the miracle which followed may be brought forward [Col. 1730A] for the edification of the hearers.

For it is reported that the tares of discord were sown between this abbot and his convent, and that the cause of the dissension was attributed to the abbot’s negligence—or rather, imprudence. While he withdrew from the convent many ancient and approved customs, and altered certain others according to the usage of his own country, he was frequently remonstrated with privately and reproved publicly concerning these matters; nevertheless, he neglected to correct his errors and did not in any way put off his presumptuous obstinacy. Among other things, he also rejected Gregorian chant and began to compel the monks, abandoning it, to learn and sing the chant of a certain William of Fécamp. They received this with difficulty, since they had already grown old in conformity with the practice of the Roman [Col. 1730B] Church, both in this matter and in the rest of the ecclesiastical office; moreover, they perhaps bore more grievously with the habits of a man who was a foreigner and had not been canonically trained in the bosom of the Church.

Accordingly, when one day he left chapter in a disturbed state of mind and addressed the monks more tumultuously on these and other affairs, and could not bend them to his will, he was immediately blinded by anger and ordered his armed knights and retainers to be summoned. At the sight of this the monks, seized by overwhelming fear, took flight as best they could and entered the church as a sanctuary, securing its doors with bolts. But the ministers of Belial burst into the temple and perpetrated an outrageous example of wickedness. They pursued even the monks who fled as far as the altar and, with copious tears, [Col. 1730C] implored divine help; they shot arrows at them. Some even climbed the galleries erected between the columns, that they might more freely glut their malevolent minds with the blood of innocents. Neither reverence for the place nor for the saints could restrain them, until they had killed one monk, who was embracing the sacred altar, by piercing him with a spear; killed another at the step of the altar, riddling him with arrows; and severely wounded fourteen others.

Therefore the monks, compelled by the extremity of so great a crisis, at last defended themselves as best they could, driving their opponents from the choir. But one member of the abbot’s household, more obstinate than the rest in wickedness, saw a monk holding in his hands a cross covered with silver, to serve him as a shield of defence. In indignation he aimed an arrow at him; but, by God’s providence, the arrow wounded beneath the knees the image of the Lord affixed to the cross, and caused from it a little stream of blood. Flowing from the altar down the steps and from the steps to the ground, it struck the ill-fated men with terror at divine vengeance. [Col. 1730D] On seeing this, the perpetrator of this crime, unable to endure his own shame, immediately became mad; leaving the threshold of the church, he fell, broke his neck, and breathed out his soul. The others, seeing this and fearing that they might undergo like punishments, hastened to leave the monastery. Yet the rod of divine justice did not permit those whom it knew to have been accomplices in perpetrating wickedness to escape punishment. Some within, some without, being rendered helpless in mind and body, paid penalties [Col. 1731A] which they had not undeservedly incurred.

At length a complaint concerning this affair was brought before King William I. Since the abbot’s fault was plainly very great, the king compelled him to return in disgrace to Normandy, to the monastery from which he had come. Many of the monks, however, were dispersed by the king’s command, to be maintained in bishoprics and abbeys. After the king’s death, the same Turstin, aided by his relatives, is said to have redeemed the abbey of Glastonbury from his son William, called Rufus, for five hundred pounds of silver. Having occupied the monastery for some years and ranged through its possessions, he ended his life miserably, far from it, as he deserved.

Let us rather admire Turstin’s other deeds than censure this one, in which he stumbled more by mischance than sinned through deliberate purpose. Let us imitate in him his zeal for religion, [Col. 1731B] some measure of piety toward God, and much foresight in worldly affairs. The cross mentioned above, clad in silver from ancient times, is held venerable by the convent and renowned among the people because of so great a miracle; it still plainly displays the marks of its wound to those who look upon it. These things occurred in the year of the Lord 1081; Orosius, historian of the English, is also a witness to this event.

### On Abbot Herlwin

Herlwin succeeded in the year of the Incarnation 1101. Like Turstin, he was a monk of Caen, distinguished by due clemency and liberality. Henry I, with the consent of the convent, appointed him abbot there, and he presided for nineteen years. At the beginning of his arrival, he was reproached throughout the kingdom of England for meanness in the provision of food. In truth, he lived more strictly than befitted the rank of his estate, not from narrowness of spirit but according to the national custom of the country from which he came. Yet, as I have said, marked by the shame of this bad repute, he tore out from their foundations the gates of the court by which the entrance of visitors was barred, so that access was open by night no less than by day, and no one encountered difficulty in entering. [Col. 1731C]

To show how greatly he hated the reputation of stinginess, he summoned all the officials and asked from them, as a favour freely granted, that they would assist him in recovering a reputation for lavish hospitality. He threatened the porter, if he excluded anyone, not only with loss of property but also with the cutting off of an ear. Thus it came about that the man who had formerly been called miserly was said to be profuse; for in mortal affairs it commonly happens that the provident man is called avaricious, while he who is generous is termed prodigal.

Because the church begun by his predecessor did not correspond to the extent of his possessions, he razed it to the ground and began a new one, upon which he spent 480 pounds. He bought an image and a cross for seventy marks, in exchange for lands seized since the time of the Normans. When he had offered the king a thousand marks and suffered refusal, he turned his mind to the saying of Terence: “Let us do what we can, if we cannot do what we wish.” Accordingly, by giving one hundred marks of silver and two of gold, he repaired the loss of his manors. For he recovered six hides in Pucklechurch and increased their value to forty pounds, whereas previously they had scarcely been worth sixteen; [Col. 1732A] for sixty marks he redeemed the land which Geoffrey de Mandeville held at Wilton; and, with King Henry’s consent, he recovered the land of Cranemere, holding it defensively for three hides. He wrested Milne and Sim from the hands of Harding, son of Eadnoth, then a very powerful advocate. From Ulric, brother of the bishop of Durham, who had been deprived of ecclesiastical communion because worldly wisdom had profited him too little, he recovered Blackford. He caused one hide at Compton and another at Soei to return, as it were from exile, to the Church. In Wales he acquired land worth ten pounds.

He made a cross of marvellous and incomparable workmanship; nine altar-cloths, nine copes, one carpet, five hangings, three albs, and an altar. When this altar was shown to John of Crema, at first its enormous price stunned him; but he soon said that, if it were at Rome, it would be valued at one hundred marks of gold. [Col. 1732B] He enlarged the monks’ workshops; he freely received clerics who were bringing forth a vow of religion, not, as some do, trafficking for a price in their conversion.

On the day before he died, while singing Mass, he made himself a victim to God through contrition of heart and a flood of tears. Soon afterwards, in chapter, he asked and obtained from all the monks forgiveness for any offence he had committed against them. To their astonishment, he foretold that he had reached the goal of life. At twilight, on the physicians’ advice, he took pills. But before midnight, when these turned to torment, the monks came running; he was anointed with holy oil and, at the midpoint of the night, closed his day. He was buried beside Turstin at Saint Andrew’s.

### Customs

[Col. 1732C]

The customs observed in the times of the abbots Turstin and Herlwin were these. On ordinary days—namely Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday—the brethren had three general dishes at the meal and two *pitantiae* [special portions]; on the other three days, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, two general dishes and three *pitantiae*. On solemn days, when the brethren wore copes, they had mead in measure-cups, fine wheaten bread upon the table, wine for the charity-cup, three general dishes, and four or five *pitantiae*. On days when they wore albs, they likewise had mead in measure-cups, fine wheaten bread on the tables, three general dishes, and three or four *pitantiae*.

On the principal feasts—namely the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, [Col. 1732D] the Assumption and Nativity of Saint Mary, and the Dedication of the Church—the quantity of everything was greater in accordance with the dignity of the feasts. On the anniversaries of kings, bishops, abbots, and dukes who built the church of Glastonbury, the brethren must celebrate Masses for their souls at the several altars, and especially honourably in the common convent before the ornaments placed out which they gave to this church. Meanwhile thirteen poor persons are to be fed for them; afterwards the brethren are to be served in the refectory as on feast days.

The custom concerning their clothing is this: each brother ought to have two cowls, two frocks, two undergarments, two pairs of breeches, four pairs of hose, and one new fur-lined garment each year. On Maundy Thursday each is to have [Col. 1733A] day shoes, and in winter night shoes, and two bed-coverings; moreover, they are to have ten foot-coverings, namely eight at the feast of Blessed Saint Martin, and the remaining two when they need them. And this is the allowance when they ought to have wine instead of ale: each should have two charity-cups a day. For the smaller portions, consult the text.

### On Abbot Sigfrid

Sigfrid, a monk of Sées and brother of Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, succeeded in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1120. He too was appointed by Henry I, and governed Glastonbury for six years. He gave one altar-cloth, a white chasuble, and the following privilege.

### Privilege of Pope Calixtus

“Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son [Col. 1733B] Sigfrid Pelochin, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“It is fitting readily to grant favourable consent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore we, most beloved son in Christ, more graciously assenting to the desires of your petition, receive into the guardianship and protection of the Roman Church the monastery of the blessed Mother of God and glorious ever-virgin Mary, over which, by God’s permission, you preside; and we strengthen it by the privilege of that Church against the molestations of perverse men. By the authority of the present decree we establish that whatever has been bestowed upon our monastery by lawful gift from popes, archbishops, kings and princes, and other faithful persons, shall be preserved to it peacefully and intact. Whatever, moreover, you may be able justly and canonically to acquire in future times, by the Lord’s gift, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

“We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may in any way disturb the said monastery, or take away its possessions, or retain what has been taken, or diminish them, or harass it with rash vexations. Rather, let all be preserved intact for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and preservation they were bestowed. But if any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall hereafter rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, and let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, and from the most sacred body of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus may those who do what is right receive the fruit of good action and find, at the strict judgment, the rewards of eternal [Col. 1734B] recompense.

“Given at the Lateran by the hand of Anneric, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of May, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.”

### On Henry of Blois, Abbot of Glastonbury

When Sigfrid became bishop of Chichester, he had at Glastonbury as his successor in 1126 Henry, brother of Theobald, count of Blois, nephew through his sister Adela of King Henry. Not long afterward he too became bishop of Winchester. Besides the splendour of his birth, he was distinguished by literary learning, gracious in speech, and liberal in kindness of heart. You know how much advantage his beginnings and subsequent course [Col. 1734C] brought you, and thereby how much favour he won among men. I would neither weary you by saying more of him, nor would you be weary of hearing it, were it not fitting to spare his remarkable modesty; for he has this characteristic: although he does praiseworthy things, he blushes to be praised.

[Col. 1733]

## William of Malmesbury’s Three Books on the Life of Saint Wulfstan, Bishop of Worcester

(H. Wharton, *Anglia Sacra*, London, 1691, folio, vol. II, col. 241.)

### Notice

I transcribed the Life of Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, from the ancient Cottonian manuscript, Claudius A. 5. This manuscript bears the name of Senatus Bravonius, written in a later hand. Senatus administered the priory of Worcester from 1189 to 1196. Bale reports that he committed Wulfstan’s Life to writing; from the ancient name of the city of Worcester, *Bravonium*, Bale gave him the surname Bravonius.

But the Life of Wulfstan which we publish was written not by Senatus but by a certain William, at the request of the monks of Worcester, though he himself was a monk of another monastery, as is entirely clear from the dedicatory epistle and the prologue. That he was none other than William of Malmesbury, the outstanding historian of this age, is evident from Book I, chapter 12, and still more clearly from Book III, [Col. 1735] chapter 16, in which the author refers the reader to his books *On the Deeds of the Bishops* and *On the Deeds of the Kings of the English*, written by himself long before.

William had previously related Wulfstan’s deeds at length in Book IV of *On the Deeds of the Bishops*, where certain matters are found which are sought in vain in this fuller account. In transcribing this work of William, I have here and there omitted many idle passages, and have generally passed over whole chapters, though for the most part indicating the subjects with which each deals. To have included them would have brought much weariness to readers and useless bulk to the present volume, while contributing nothing to ecclesiastical history or learning. Besides this Life of Wulfstan and the preceding Life of Aldhelm, William wrote, in two books, a Life of Saint Dunstan, and Lives of Saints Patrick, Benignus, and Indract, as he himself declares in the prologue to his *Antiquities of Glastonbury*.

### Epistle of William to the Brethren of Worcester, for the Life of the Venerable Wulfstan, Bishop of Worcester

[Col. 1735]

[Col. 1735A] To the venerable lord Guarin, prior, and to the whole most reverend convent of Worcester: William, the affection of a son and the service of a dependent.

Long ago, commanded by you to set my hand to the Life of our holy father Wulfstan, I for some time evaded the task. The reasons for evasion were many, but first, or at least greatest, was this: conscious of unequal merit, I arrogate a burden beyond my powers if I praise a saint. For “praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15). There was added to this a fear which not a little weakened your command: lest the envy of certain persons should assail my obedience, if I undertook a work hitherto unattempted and thus best left to someone better qualified.

Terrified by these reasons, I would have restrained my tongue in obstinate silence, [Col. 1735B] had not hope conceived from the mercy of the blessed bishop healed my fear and come to my aid with consolation. For Blessed Wulfstan was accustomed, even to those who loved him merely in words, both to grant remission of offences and to defend them with the shield of his protection. Much more, therefore, will he favour with pardon one who meditates a lasting work concerning him, and will not withhold the aid of eloquence. The Lord Christ also will deign to remove from this work all envy, because it has been undertaken not from the arrogance of learning but in the service of sincere devotion.

Therefore, trusting in his help, I shall do what you have commanded. No longer shall dangerous hesitation obscure my undertaking; rather, I shall compensate for delay in the past by speed in execution. And you, while you still enjoy the breath of life, will know well that I say nothing which is not supported by solid truth, nothing which has not been ascertained by the testimony of trustworthy [Col. 1736A] men. So deeply have what they saw remained fixed in the minds of the old; so wholeheartedly do the younger embrace what they have heard. But when the memory of deeds grows cold among posterity, doubt may arise unless I produce a suitable witness. Therefore, since the deeds of saints ought to be recounted only with scrupulous fidelity, I shall provide a witness not unworthy for my statements. He will be Coleman,

> **[Note: Col. 1735B]** William relates below, Book III, chapter 10, that Wulfstan later made him prior of Westbury. He died in 1113, on 4 October, if Florence is to be believed. He received many accounts of Wulfstan’s deeds from Hamming, subprior [Col. 1736B] of Worcester. This Hamming, at Wulfstan’s command, wrote a book *On the Possessions of the Church of Worcester*, which survives in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 128.

your monk: a man neither unskilled in learning nor inelegant in his native speech. To prevent the memory of the deeds from vanishing, he wrote in English a Life of this same Father—graceful in a serious fashion if one attends to its sense, though rude in simplicity if one attends to its wording. He deserves that his credibility should in no respect be questioned, for he knew his master’s character intimately as a disciple, and his religious life as his chaplain for fifteen years. Following his writings, as you wished, I have disturbed nothing in the order of events and corrupted nothing in the truth of the deeds.

Certainly, I have refrained from elaborating speeches which were either spoken or might have been spoken at the time, consulting truth in all things lest it seem endangered. For it belongs to an idle man, indulgent toward his own eloquence, to traffic in speeches when deeds suffice—unless perhaps there are certain matters which, because of their exceptional brilliance, demand brief mention. Since this is so, I ask you to render me this favour: deign to keep detractors away from this little work, and commend my service to the regard of most pious Wulfstan, you venerable and deservedly beloved Fathers, who are nearer to him.

### Prologue

[Col. 1735]

[Col. 1735B] There are many things in Holy Scripture—indeed, as our judgment holds, innumerable things—by which divine condescension trains the minds of mortals in the cultivation of a good life: both precepts and examples. By the former we are taught how we ought to live; by the latter we are shown how easy, with God’s help, the things commanded are to accomplish. Yet nature has implanted in certain people this disposition: although they know both to be necessary, the hearing of examples delights them more than that of exhortations.

The deeds of the ancients indeed inspire reverence because of their antiquity; but people are seized with livelier delight if the life of a saint who lived very recently is brought before them, a life in which, as in a mirror, they behold, if I may so speak, a living image of religious devotion. The pleasing account is further enhanced by novelty, lest anyone despair that, through God’s grace, he may do what he hears was recently done by another. Hence, I think, a concern arose in the mind of Blessed Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, which should not be despised: not to begrudge his life to posterity, but to commit it by some manner of writing to eternal remembrance. For he was a man both close to our own times and not unlike the earlier Fathers in virtue.

Accordingly, I promise the kindly reader a great benefit: though he may welcome Wulfstan as familiarly as the saints of old because of the glory of his miracles, he should nevertheless strive, because of Wulfstan’s recent age, to follow the pattern of his conduct with the foot of emulous practice. [Col. 1737B] I do not say this because I attribute such blessedness to many, that, just as he was an imitator of Christ, so they may be able to imitate him. Few—or rather, few whom the righteous Jesus shall love—will be able, as they look toward him across a great interval, to follow in the footsteps of his virtues rather than to imprint that very perfection upon themselves.

So true is it that, with reverence for the elders preserved, I would say that he was inferior to none in freedom from the excesses of vices; so true that he continued from a happy beginning in youth to old age in a purpose of virtue. Therefore it would have been fitting for the writer of his deeds to be polished in language and proven in learning, so that lofty acts might not be expressed in humble speech, and that the man who praised might follow by example what he praised. But I have neither rhetorical ability nor a mind that applauds itself for integrity of life. Obedience alone encourages and presses me, lest I obstinately refuse a task which fraternal obligation imposes, especially one promised and fruitful for the soul.

May the mercy of the Holy Spirit be present with me, so that, by the same Spirit’s inspiration, our pen may be directed by him through whose agency Wulfstan acted well. Those who rely on rhetorical training arrange their speech so that they first make the hearer well disposed, then attentive, and finally teachable. I too do not neglect this when the matter requires it. But here such rhetorical procedure is outside my purpose. It is superfluous to seek arguments where faith itself prompts belief and the subject invites reading. For this reason, I judge that readers will not be lacking for this holy Father while the heavens turn the stars and any letter remains in the world. By God’s mercy he established this favour for himself among people during life and retains it after death. But it is enough to have prolonged the preface thus far. Now, trusting in heavenly assistance, let us begin the intended work with the following opening.

## Book I

### Chapter I

[Col. 1737C]

There is a well-known district in the region of the Mercians called Warwickshire. It contains a village named Icentun, of which the parents of the venerable Wulfstan had been inhabitants since the time of their forefathers. His father was named Æthelstan and his mother Wulfgeva; they were neither poor in resources nor low-born. Joined by marital affection rather than by lust, they deserved to have a son who would become a conspicuous glory of England. The name Wulfstan was given to the boy, formed from the earlier part of his mother’s name and the latter part of his father’s.

He was initiated into the first elements of letters at Evesham, and soon afterwards at Burgh his tender mind was shaped by more advanced learning.

> **[Note: Col. 1737D]** Ingulf and John, abbot of Burgh, state in their manuscript chronicle that Wulfstan was once a monk in the monastery of Saint Peter at Burgh. Yet it is clear from William that he did not assume, or wear, the monastic habit at Burgh, but was instructed there only in the first elements of learning during childhood.

It is pleasant to tell how many indications he already gave, even then, of the disposition of the virtues that were to come, though he had scarcely crossed the first threshold [Col. 1737D] of childhood. So much maturity, sanctity, and praiseworthy modesty breathed and spoke through the boy. He did not refuse to devote himself to fasting, insofar as a person of that age could bear it; he raised humble prayers on high. He rejected childish chatter—the source of enticements—first in himself and then in others. He followed the traces of mature life, so that he earnestly begged his contemporaries and even older persons that, by living well themselves, they might fashion for him an image of good living; that they might rebuke him if he did anything wrongly; and that he himself might willingly submit to correction.

Devotion brought him to this practice: he saw nothing worthy of imitation without forming it into an example for himself. By these deeds he plainly showed that he was wise and would be wise, according to the saying which divine wisdom joined to Solomon’s writings: “Reprove a wise man,” it says, “and he will love you” (Proverbs 19). No less naturally did he seize upon the maxim formerly issued from philosophy’s inner chambers: one should always set before the eyes of the mind some good man by whose regard one’s conduct may be ordered. For one does not readily depart from justice who always thinks either of God or of a human being [Col. 1738D] through fear of whom he restrains sins.

At that time he had as teacher a man named Ervenius, skilled in writing and in depicting whatever he pleased in colours. This man arranged for written books—a Sacramentary and a Psalter, whose principal letters he had illuminated in gold—to be entrusted to the boy Wulfstan. Captivated by the marvel of the precious lettering, Wulfstan scrutinized their beauty with fixed [Col. 1739A] eyes and drank in the knowledge of letters with the depths of his heart. But the teacher, looking to worldly advantage and hoping for a greater reward, gave the Sacramentary to King Cnut, then reigning, and the Psalter to Queen Emma. The loss grieved the boy’s heart, and he drew deep sighs from his inmost breast. Sorrow invited sleep; and behold, while he slept, a man with an angelic countenance stood beside him, banished his sadness, and promised the restoration of the books. The event followed the promise, not immediately but much later, as the course of the narrative will relate.

Thus his flourishing age, childhood having passed, had brought him into adolescence; and Wulfstan was as much more advanced in learning as he was older in years. In short, he never, as that age often does, lost chastity through any stain; [Col. 1739B] rather, he bore the palm of unblemished modesty to heaven. In all things the generosity of divine grace was present with him, lest freedom of choice should falter. He had formerly felt that the gift of chastity had been infused into him from heaven, and he did not allow himself to conceal this through ungrateful silence. Yet the heavenly nectar which he had drunk he shared with others without envy.

How this happened I shall tell, so that posterity may know how great was the grace of God which both went before and followed the young man. When he had returned from Delvith [reading uncertain], a girl born in the neighbourhood troubled him, threatening the wreck of his chastity and enticing him to pleasure. She would take hold of his hand, beckon with her eyes, and make even wanton gestures of immodesty—other signs of virginity that is about to perish. But, since his impulse toward chastity frustrated the desires of the shameless girl, she almost ensnared him in this way.

A great crowd of youths had gathered in a field, cheerfully engaged in some game which I cannot identify. They ran, as is usual on such occasions, across the expanse of green grass; the shrill air answered the applause and encouragement of those urging them on. Wulfstan sprang out among the rest and, in the common judgment of all, won the victory in that contest. A crowd of country people shouted praise; and, to gratify his ears, repeated and redoubled it. Another might have been delighted by such trifles and, stirred by the breath of flatterers, might have formed puffed-up bubbles in his heart. But Wulfstan did not yield to those praising him, either by bodily gesture or movement of mind.

Therefore, so that the devil, defeated in this matter, might triumph in another way, he inspired the mind of the aforementioned girl, who was standing nearby, to run forward. [Col. 1739D] She was not slow to act the plausible female harp-player with shameless gestures and immodest movements, in order to serve the eyes of her lover. And he who had not yielded to words or touch was no less wholly dissolved, with a more unguarded expression, panting for love. Yet immediately recalling his mind to goodness, he shed tears and directed his flight to places rough with thickets and brambles. He lay at some distance, while the others nevertheless continued their game. There, as he turned over many things and accused himself repeatedly, sleep stole upon him; and then a prodigy was seen.

For a clear cloud, playing upon the eyes of the beholders with gentle brightness, descended from above. Shrouding the sleeping youth for a while, it astonished those who watched. Immediately the brightness of the cloud dispersed the mist of vanity and breathed an air of seriousness upon the frivolous minds of the young people. They therefore ran hastily to the spot and, addressing Wulfstan with anxious words, asked what this sign had been. He judged that nothing should be denied, so that the flame of heavenly love which had shone upon him might kindle sparks in his companions; and he disclosed the whole matter in order. Recently, he said, he had been inflamed without measure by the pricks of the flesh; now, watered by heavenly dew, he was cold in his belly and in all his vital parts. He hoped that henceforth he would lack the incitement of the flesh and, aided by God’s mercy, would be troubled by no temptation.

The truth of events accompanied the prophetic saying. Never afterward did the beauty of any person trouble either his mind or eyes; never did a turbulent discharge interrupt the peace of his sleep. Coleman affirms that he learned this from Hamming the subprior, who remembered that he had heard it from the holy man himself after he became bishop. [Col. 1740B] For the most reverend Father was accustomed to adapt his speech to the age and capacity of his hearers, and sometimes to introduce his own deeds, so that they would not despair of being able to do those things which they had heard him, through God’s grace, accomplish.

### Chapter II

Meanwhile, both parents of the young man, weary of secular life, burned with a devout desire and frequently spoke of adopting other clothing and other manners. For advanced age and declining fortune were already pressing upon them. Nor did they delay long before satisfying their desire. His father assumed the monastic habit at Worcester, and his mother received the veil of a religious woman in the same city. [Col. 1740C] Thus, with simple devotion and effective zeal, they carried out their intention; when their days were completed, they yielded to nature.

Meanwhile Wulfstan remained in the world in appearance, not in mind; not in spirit, but in body. Yet, to trace in himself the pattern of virtues proper to a higher rank and gradually unlearn worldly ways, he entrusted himself to the care of Brihtheah, bishop of Worcester. The bishop gladly received him and, through the support of his kinsmen and his own kindness, favourably embraced the grace of God in the young man. Nor did Wulfstan fail to answer that favour; instead, by uprightness of conduct, he compelled it even from people of the most disreputable and harsh disposition. In him no insolent mind, abrupt speech, or affected gait was found. He fled arrogance, was free from wantonness, and—what is the greatest ornament of youth—was the most diligent guardian of modesty.

The beauty of his body increased the grace of his heart. Though I do not count this among the virtues, neither do I exclude it wholly, because, just as an artist’s skill shines more clearly in more suitable material, so virtue stands out more splendidly in physical beauty. [Col. 1740D]

By these qualities he had so won the bishop’s affection that the latter of his own accord promoted him to the priesthood, although Wulfstan could scarcely and reluctantly be brought to consent. It is noteworthy in the young man that he considered himself unworthy of that rank, and equally noteworthy that he adorned the rank he received by conduct worthy of it. Thus he did not seek to receive it from arrogance, nor, having received it once, did he tarnish it through idleness. So greatly did he strive to weaken his body through fasting and every form of abstinence, and to enlarge the powers of his spirit; [Col. 1741A] so sober was his mind, grave his speech, venerable his appearance, and kindly his disposition: in clothes he acted as a layman, in manners as a monk. If he saw fault in anyone, he so moderated his speech that the rigour of sharp rebuke became material for praise. For nothing could seem harsh which, though it sounded rather severe, breathed charity within.

### Chapter III

More than once the bishop offered him a church in the suburbs, whose rich revenues would have been more than enough for his daily support. Wulfstan often put off the offerer by deferring his decision; but at last, when the bishop pressed more strongly, he disclosed his purpose. The unstable state of the world had become worthless to his mind; he wished to become a monk and to offer his whole life to God, not merely [Col. 1741B] parts of it. When he received this answer, the venerable bishop leaped up with great joy and stirred Wulfstan’s youthful ardour to greater intensity with the trumpet-call of his exhortations. Thus, their desires agreeing—while one desired what the other urged—Wulfstan put on the monk’s habit at Worcester, Brihtheah consenting and granting both favour and habit.

If any hearer, desiring to range about in the manner of rhetoricians, were to set before his audience how many blessings that happy day brought to Worcester—the day which first saw Wulfstan as a monk—he would certainly fail of his wish and be unable to accomplish his purpose. Therefore let the mind at least strive to meditate what the tongue cannot express. This must not be passed over in silence: in our age there was never a monk either further removed from vices or more perfect in virtues. Therefore, once the brethren of that church had tested the sincerity of his life, they shortly made him guardian of the boys, then cantor, and finally sacristan, so that he might have freer opportunity for prayer and more abundant material for rising from virtue to virtue.

Gratefully embracing this opportunity, he spent his days in fasts and his whole nights in vigils. He reckoned a delight what we weak people regard as a great punishment. Every day he bent his knees at each verse of the seven Psalms; at night he did the same during Psalm 118. In the western porch of the church, where there was an altar of All Saints with the trophy of the Lord’s standard, after locking the entrance, he called upon Christ, struck heaven with his tears, and burdened the air with lamentations. [Col. 1741D] He had neither feather-bed nor any bed at all; he did not give himself to sleep, but stole it. Laying his head on the steps before the altar, he exposed himself to the ground; or, placing some book beneath his head, he invited a slight sleep upon wood. Before each of the eighteen altars in the old church he prostrated himself seven times daily. He did not regard these things as hard, but rather what others would have thought hard to imitate.
