And though he was pre-eminent above all in virtues, [Col. 1742A] he was nevertheless most inclined to humility toward every individual, so that he promptly performed certain lowly tasks which another disdained to do.

### Chapter IV
The blessed man had acquired the habit of visiting by night the churches situated nearby, keeping vigil with the Psalms, and in each presenting the vows of his prayers before God. He went through the midst of the cemetery with no faltering step, his mind dulled by no fear. Thus it came about that one night he reached the church of the Prince of the Apostles. This had formerly been the episcopal seat, but St Oswald had emptied it of irreligious clerics, having, by a sure and reasonable exchange, borrowed the Apostle’s authority for the Mother of the Lord.

[Col. 1742B] He stood therefore before the altar, now poured out in prayer, now wholly yearning toward God.

There follows an account of his struggle with the devil, who, taking the form of a rustic, attacked Wlstan while he was praying. See William, Book IV of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*, fol. 159, and Capgrave, *Nova Legenda*, fol. 332.

## Chapter V

As time passed, every shoot of virtue grew in Wlstan, especially obedience and submission to his superiors. However hard or harsh a command seemed, he at once brought forth willingness, although ability might not be at hand. Then too, from the fountain of divine grace, love for humankind flowed into him, so that he judged that everyone whom he knew to have been accepted by heavenly favour ought to be won over by every service.

The bishop especially was so disposed toward Wlstan [Col. 1742C] that he considered him worthy of any honour. For the diligent energy with which he had performed his office had inspired the salutary hope that he would discharge a higher dignity well, if it were conferred upon him. On this occasion he was appointed provost—what is now called prior—of the monks, and immediately seized upon material through which his virtue might shine, repelling many difficulties within and without. For he completely restored, by the liveliness of his intelligence, the outward affairs which his predecessors’ negligence had brought low, and restrained the inward ones by the bridle of the Rule.

To make this more effective, he offered those subject to him religious examples from his own life, ashamed, that is, to preach what he disdained to do. Nor did he devise his teaching from his own invention, or set it forth in lofty and [Col. 1742D] applause-winning eloquence. Rather, keeping watch over the writings of our forefathers, he drank with a thirsty breast the streams of doctrine which he afterwards poured forth in a honeyed flood. For I may borrow what was said in the Life of Blessed Gregory, which, having been translated by Colemann into the native tongue like many other things, I have myself translated anew into Latin. Thus, while he kept diligent watches over all the books of divine Scripture, he did so especially over those [Col. 1743A] that commend chastity: eagerly carrying out its integrity in himself and sternly pursuing its corruption in others, as one example will make plain.

> [Note: [Col. 1741D] Aldred, bishop, substituted Wlstan for Agelwin, the deceased prior of Worcester, according to Florence. The same Aldred, having restored the monastery of Gloucester, appointed in 1058 a certain Wlstan, a Worcester monk, as abbot. Thus the Worcester manuscript Chronicle; Thomas Stubbs, *On the Archbishops of York*, p. 1701; the Gloucester Chronicle in the *Monasticon*, vol. I, p. 110; and Florence. This Wlstan set out for Jerusalem and died on the journey in 1072, according to the Gloucester Chronicle. Therefore Ingulph (p. 511), and Bollandus, who followed him (*Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. II, p. 240), are mistaken in maintaining that this Wlstan had become abbot of Gloucester from being prior of Worcester, and bishop of Worcester from being abbot of Gloucester. Col. 1742D]

## Chapter VI

There was in the same city a married woman, rich in household resources beyond what was sufficient for sustenance, and endowed with features of beauty that enticed the gaze of curious onlookers.

There follows an account of how Wlstan rejected a woman inviting him to fornication. See Capgrave, fol. 332.

## Chapter VII

Nor did he scatter the seeds of his mercy only upon monks, but upon the common people also. For, often early in the morning, once he had completed the daily offices, he made himself visible before the doors of the church, so that those wishing to meet him might have easier [Col. 1743B] access. There, a diligent and compassionate investigator, he commonly spent the day until the sixth hour, and often until evening, provided that he might aid those who had suffered violence by whatever help he could offer, or baptize the children of the poorer people.

For venality had already emerged from the infernal shadows, so that priests did not administer even that sacrament freely to infants unless their parents filled the purse. Wlstan, therefore, taking pity on the poverty of the one party and on the souls of the other, and by deed piercing avarice, devoted the service of voluntary condescension to baptizing the poor. People ran to him from cities and fields, especially those to whom it mattered nothing to pay a coin in order to purchase the washing for their children. The custom passed from [Col. 1743C] people of narrower means to the rich, so that scarcely anyone in that region considered a member of his own household lawfully baptized unless Wlstan had baptized him. This belief was fostered by no false opinion of the holy man’s sanctity, nor by any rash presumption concerning his religious devotion.

The proclamation of his fame was thus carried throughout England, so that the most powerful English nobles of that time both eagerly desired and steadfastly retained his friendship. They promised themselves from it security in prosperity, deliverance in adversity, and protection in every circumstance. Among them Harold, breathing a power still greater through consciousness of his resources and already aspiring to the kingdom through greatness of spirit, loved the man singularly. Thus, while travelling, he did not hesitate to turn thirty miles aside from the straight road, so that in Wlstan’s conversation he might remove the burden of his cares [Col. 1743D]. So entirely was he devoted to Wlstan’s wishes and patronage that Wlstan was only as reluctant to command as Harold was unhesitating to perform.

Nor did the saint return lesser favour to the earl, receiving his confessions kindly and acting as a faithful interpreter of his prayers before God. Aldred, bishop of Worcester after Brihteg, followed the same path of affection: a man very shrewd in worldly matters and not a little religious. He rendered great service to the Lord Prior out of reverence for his holiness, humbly obeyed him, and in every respect deferred to him as to a most welcome father.

## Chapter VIII

Nor shall I withhold from readers an event no less worthy than those already recounted of an illustrious title. Observing that the people, through lack of preaching, were falling away from good morals, he poured out counsels of salvation to them in church every Sunday and on the greater feast-days. One might have thought that the words which he proclaimed to the people from his elevated station thundered forth from the inner sanctuaries of the Gospels and the prophets: so did thunderbolts strike the wicked, so did showers water the elect.

[Col. 1744A] He did this with the utmost modesty and, as far as he himself was concerned, under the cover of humility. Yet envy found and assailed him though he wished to remain hidden; nor did heavenly vengeance pass by the assailant, as will become clear from what follows.

There was in the same church a monk of a nation beyond the sea, named Winrich: most learned, if one considered scholarship; powerful in speaking, if eloquence; most prudent, if worldly cunning; elegant in conduct and [Col. 1744B] therefore acceptable and dear to men. Yet he was at other times fiercely hot-tempered, and, under the goad of envy, readily disposed to anger at whatever displeased him. He habitually mocked the saint’s preaching greatly, arguing to this effect: that it was contrary to the rules for him to usurp the office of a bishop; that preaching to the people belonged to the bishop alone, since he alone, by the authority entrusted and granted to him, could absolve sins; that silence and enclosure suited a monk, not insolently attacking the people with pompous bearing and speech.

Thus, he said, it appeared rather to be an ambition for some dignity than the performance of piety. These reproaches he uttered against Wlstan not only behind his back, but one day, inflamed with a bitterer gall, to his face. Wlstan, armed with the shield of patience, [Col. 1744C] answered briefly: nothing was more pleasing to God than to call back a people rushing to ruin onto the path of truth; therefore he would not desist. But if he could learn anything else more pleasing to Christ, he would do it without hesitation.

So they parted and went to sleep. But God, to show how highly he esteemed the holy man’s action, shook the slanderer with a dreadful vision. For when he had laid his limbs to rest in bed, in spirit he was carried to the tribunal of an unknown judge. Rebuked there with grave severity for having the day before reproached God’s servant on account of the good work of preaching, and insufficiently clearing himself, he was ordered to be stretched upon the floor and beaten. Then, as executioners succeeded one another, he was sharply scourged, crying amid the [Col. 1744D] torments nothing but: “Have mercy, Lord; Lord, have mercy!”

At last, when released, he was asked whether he would any longer prevent the herald from summoning people to that court. He, from whom the necessity of that moment would have extorted anything, swore by all that is holy that he would not merely cease to prevent him, but would himself urge both him and others to preach—provided only that the judge’s mercy should prolong his life for the future, so that he might escape this extremity of anguish. Having pledged his faith not to violate his promise, he was dismissed.

Therefore, as soon as he could—and he could as soon as day dawned—he threw himself at the prior’s feet, kissed his knees, confessed his offence, and begged forgiveness. Asked the cause of his sudden change, he recounted the sequence of the vision under oath. Tears, drawn forth by sincere prayers, guaranteed the truth [Col. 1745A] of his account. The swollen welts on his shoulders bore witness that he had seen nothing unreal and suffered nothing mild. Nor did he find it difficult to obtain pardon from the saint; at whose blessing his health returned and every pain vanished.

Let the present examples, therefore, win belief, and let antiquity be freed from every doubt, antiquity which presents to us a similar event in Blessed Jerome. For there is little difference between his being beaten because of pagan books and this man’s being beaten because of the office of preaching which he had forbidden. It is nearly the same thing to neglect divine Scripture because of pagan trifles and to refuse that it be preached.

It was at this time that he was constructing over the roof of the church a structure from which bells might hang. Yet I do not readily have at hand the proper name by which I may most nearly [Col. 1745B] call that structure. For raising it, therefore, he was making a series of ladder-rungs upon which the workmen might stand. One of them fell headlong from these in Wlstan’s presence, and he rescued the man from danger by making the sign of the cross. Capgrave briefly tells the matter in the *Nova Legenda*, fol. 332.

## Chapter IX

Meanwhile King Edward sent Aldred, bishop, to Cologne, to the elder Emperor Henry, to settle certain affairs whose particulars the occasion does not require us to know. Having found favour in the eyes of the imperial majesty, he took there a respite of several days from his labours. Out of regard either for himself or because he was the envoy of so great a king, many people gave him many things; one gave him as a gift a Sacramentary [Col. 1745C] and the Psalter of which I have spoken above. For Cnut had formerly sent both books to Cologne, in order to place the favour of his memory among those peoples.

Aldred, then, ignorant of the prophecy once spoken to Wlstan, when he had sailed back to his homeland, judged that the books belonged to Wlstan alone by merit of his life, and restored them to him. Wlstan received the heavenly deposit with great rejoicing and gave thanks to God because he was not deprived of his religious desire.

## Chapter X

At the same time, when Kynegisus, [Col. 1745D] archbishop of York, had ended his days, Aldred, bishop of Worcester, was acclaimed as his successor. This seemed good to King Edward, a man of simple soul. Aldred went to Rome according to custom and found Pope Nicholas, then reigning, at first opposed to his wishes. For Aldred was unwilling to renounce the bishopric of Worcester, and the pope was unwilling to invest him with the pallium of York unless he relinquished it. So deeply had love for Worcester bound him that he set its name above the price of higher honour.

After a long and strenuous dispute, Aldred turned back and came to Sutri, while Earl Tostig, who had accompanied him, [Col. 1746A] uttered great threats: that the money which England paid every year to the Roman pope would on this account no longer be delivered. Nevertheless, having been stripped by robbers, to the grief and pity of those who saw them, they hastened to return to Rome. This event bent the severity of the Apostolic See so far that Aldred was granted the pallium of York, on condition that he should leave the church of Worcester and substitute in it the best person that could be found in his diocese.

The archbishop therefore presented to the king the cardinals who had been brought as arbiters of this arrangement and to settle certain other ecclesiastical matters in England. The prince, most devoted to God, received them in that manner of his, imitated by few, by which he was accustomed to conform in every respect to the customs of the Roman Church. [Col. 1746B] Having kept them with the highest reverence and honour for some time, he again entrusted them to the protection of their guide, to be brought back to court at Easter. For they would associate more familiarly with one whose customs they had learned during a long companionship and whose language they did not fail to understand.

Aldred, following the tenor of the apostolic command and travelling with them through almost all England, turned back toward Worcester as Lent approached. From there he went to estates under his authority and placed them in a settled lodging with Wlstan the prior. Not rejecting the advice, they gladly withdrew into repose, resting after the labours of the journey. Their host’s kindness was present, omitting nothing by which they might experience the generous liberality and liberal generosity of the English.

He meanwhile, not forgetting his customary diligence in prayer and abstinence from food, persistently pursued his resolution. Passing whole nights in psalm-singing, prolonging vigils, frequently bending his knees, and utterly mocking sleep, [Col. 1746C] on three days of the week he abstained from every kind of food and continued the night’s fast as he did the day’s. On those very days, lest he might slip even in a word, he restrained his tongue in perpetual silence. On the other three days he supported himself with cooked or boiled leeks or cabbages, adding bread for nourishment. On Sundays, out of reverence for the feast, he relaxed the frugality of his abstinence with fish and wine, more in order to sustain nature than to indulge his appetite. Moreover, every day he lovingly cared for three poor people, fulfilling the command of the Lord by providing [Col. 1746D] both their daily food and the washing of their feet.

> [Note: Kynsinus, archbishop of York, died in 1060, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January [22 December]; Aldred was elected his successor at Christmas. He went to Rome in 1061, obtained the pallium, and in 1062 consecrated Wlstan bishop of Worcester on the sixth day before the Ides of September [8 September], in the fifteenth indiction, when Wlstan was more than fifty years of age. Florence reports these matters and adds that Aldred performed this office in place of Stigand, archbishop [Col. 1746D] of Canterbury, to whom the pope had then forbidden episcopal functions; and that Wlstan made his profession of subjection not to Aldred, who ordained him, but to Stigand, his metropolitan. Thomas Stubbs therefore misled the reader in the *Acts of the Archbishops of York*, p. 1702, where he says that Aldred consecrated Wlstan as bishop for himself, as though Wlstan were his suffragan.]

## Chapter XI

These things prompted the cardinals to admire his life and praise his learning; and it made that learning more venerable that he anticipated by example what he preached in words. Finally, after returning to court, when the election of the bishop of Worcester was being discussed, they put forward his name: he was worthy of the episcopate, [Col. 1747A] because he would add more reverence to the priesthood than he himself would receive dignity from it; because his nature answered to his diligence; because his life corresponded to his wisdom.

By these praises they stirred up the greater spirit of King Edward, a man in whose breast no trafficker in churches, no greedy person, ever found anything that might serve his own devices. The archbishops of Canterbury and York supported the wishes of the cardinals: the former by favour, the latter by testimony, both by judgment. The earls Harold and Elgar also added their praise, an eminent pair in courage, though not equally in religion. This gave the cause great weight, so that riders were sent in haste and competition for Wlstan. The messengers traversed many miles in a short time, speeding their errand with the spurs of diligence.

When the saint [Col. 1747B] had been brought to court, he was ordered to receive the gift of the bishopric. But he resisted, crying out against all who urged him that he was unequal to so great an honour. The cardinals and archbishops would have laboured in vain unless they had held before the reluctant man obedience to the pope. Confounded by this objection, he yielded and consented to the election, grieving, unwilling, compelled. Rightly and deservedly, the obstinacy of one man here gave way to the will of God and the people.

Nor shall I omit that there was then at Evesham an abbot named Ailwius, possessed of the greatest prudence in worldly matters and by no means slight religious devotion. Therefore the aforesaid Aldred, because of the agreement he had made with the Apostolic See, had for some time [Col. 1747C] wavered in mind whether to choose for the bishopric Ethelwius’s shrewd worldly ability or Wlstan’s simple piety in God. For, in different respects, these men were pre-eminent in the diocese of Worcester. Yet, after reasons had been weighed long and on both sides, although Ethelwius exerted himself anxiously on behalf of his own cause, the careful contrivances of human artifices yielded to divine providence.

> [Note: Ethelwin, abbot of Evesham, succeeded Abbot Mannio near the end of the year 105—[the final figure is uncertain]—or at the beginning of the following year. At last exceedingly pleasing to King William, he died in 1077, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March [16 February], according to the History of Evesham in the *Monasticon*, vol. I, p. 151. Col. 1747D]

## Chapter XII

King Edward therefore fully invested Wlstan with the bishopric of Worcester, though Aldred, through the power by which he was strong among many and almost all men, stripped him of many estates, as will later become clear. Although the saint bore this with pain, as he afterwards showed, he nevertheless suppressed his grief in silence, judging that he must yield to the times.

[Col. 1747D] Not long afterwards he was consecrated at York by the same archbishop, since the Roman pope had forbidden Stigand of Canterbury to exercise his office. It is not the time to set forth the reason for the prohibition. Our other writings will instruct anyone who wishes to know.

> [Note: William of Malmesbury gives the reasons for the prohibition laid upon Stigand’s office, both repeatedly elsewhere and especially in Book I of *On the Deeds of the Bishops of England*. From this it is clear that the author of this Life, William, is none other than that historian of great renown, William of Malmesbury. Col. 1748D. Malmesbury seems once, indeed, to disagree with our William in *On the Bishops of England*, where he writes that Wlstan was ordained bishop of Worcester by cardinal legates, whereas our author more correctly asserts that he was consecrated at York by Aldred. But that passage of Malmesbury may quite properly be judged to mean only that Wlstan was appointed to the see of Worcester through the efforts of the legates—a sense wholly consistent with the History before us.]

Nor may it be believed that this prophecy was spoken of him without divine prompting: “Behold truly an Israelite, in whom is no deceit” (John 1:47). For no one who has seen, heard, or read of his conduct will find anything truer.

[Col. 1748A] Yet he received the imposition of the bishopric so unwillingly that, as those present testify, he said that he would rather be beheaded than bear that burden. Indeed, he would have prepared flight into any remote region of the world, had certain friends not kept a watchful and suspicious diligence over him. Some cheered his mind, cast down by grief, with persuasions; others with admonitions. With persuasions: reverently throwing themselves at his knees and feet, and sometimes even kissing them. With admonitions: lest he disfigure by impatience a heavenly gift freely bestowed, which he ought rather to distinguish by endurance. Obedience, they said, was the seal of all virtues; whoever judged that it should be resisted would be held worthy neither as a cloistered monk nor as a bishop of the people. Therefore he ought not only to bear it modestly but also to give thanks to God, who had raised him to a rank through which He willed to provide for those beneath him.

This they said to him. Nor should it be doubted that the holy breast sweated in a mighty struggle, while love on one side and fear on the other held equal sway and dragged him this way and that: the latter lest he should collapse under an unfamiliar burden; the former lest he seem to resist the commanding authority of so many worthy men and the devout attachment of the people. Indeed, the more unworthy he considered himself, the more insistent was the acclamation; for the very fact that he approached the administration with fear gave assurance that he would administer the office prudently. For it is foolish to thrust oneself unthinkingly into a task without knowing how great [Col. 1748C] the labour is to carry it out.

## Chapter XIII

Thus ordained, as I had begun to say, and left at York by Aldred under the pretext of honour, he saddened Worcester by his absence for no short time. Meanwhile the archbishop applied the revenues of that church to his own uses. Afterwards, when Wlstan returned, he granted him scarcely seven estates, stubbornly usurping all the rest. But Wlstan, knowing that he could accomplish nothing by force against him, gradually crushed his grasping spirit’s greed by prayers, so that he restored to the church’s right all but twelve estates. The following account will teach at what time and with what labour our Father recovered these.

## Chapter XIV

[Col. 1748D]

But, to return to the point from which I had begun: when Wlstan was raised to the episcopate, he immediately directed his mind toward works of piety. There was no delay. For on the second day after his ordination he dedicated a church to Blessed Bede, fittingly giving the first beginning of his dedications [Col. 1749A] to the man who had been the foremost scholar among the English people. On that day he watered the people with such an abundant outpouring of preaching that there was no doubt that Wlstan, through the Holy Spirit, exerted the same eloquence which had once moved Bede’s tongue.

Nor only then, but throughout his life, did the fame of his preaching delight the common people so much that one might see crowds flocking in companies wherever it was heard that he was dedicating a church. He himself eagerly seized every occasion, that he might always proclaim Christ, always set Christ before his hearers, and finally, so to speak, draw even a resistant Christ to his cause. For he persisted so resolutely in fasts and vigils, so forcefully cast his prayers upon heaven, that the Lord might rightly have said of him and his followers: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

He ordered his life with such balance that he retained both callings and lost neither: a bishop in such a way that he did not renounce the monk in religious devotion; a monk in such a way that he represented the bishop in authority. Most remote from the manners of men which our age produces, he was, if consulted, most wise in counsel; if asked, most approachable. When something had to be obtained, he deliberated decisively and pronounced swiftly; when judgment had to be made, he inclined more to justice. He did not flatter a rich man for money, nor strike at a poor man for poverty. He was devoted to no flattery, nor pleased by those who flattered him. He never departed from justice through fear of princes; he never rose in honour to meet their favour with any honour except what was due.

[Col. 1749C] When praised for good conduct, he attributed it to God’s grace, not to his own pride. When blamed, he forgave the error of those who blamed him, while rejoicing in his conscience. This, however, occurred very rarely, because, as he cherished every person in the love of charity as a child, so all in return loved him as a father. In the gladness of his heart and the cheerfulness of his face, he tasted beforehand the joys above; already by hope he anticipated the fountain of heavenly happiness, which he now drinks and imbibes in unending reality.

Although he always adhered inwardly to God, those who experienced him did not find him sluggish or dull in the Lord’s outward affairs. Many churches throughout the diocese were boldly begun and splendidly completed by him, especially the church of the episcopal see, which, having been begun from the foundations, he brought to completion; [Col. 1749D] there too the number of monks was enlarged and arranged according to the standard of regular observance. But these works, accomplished later and daily set before our eyes, require only a brief account. Therefore, that our discourse may move more freely in a field of ampler material, let us continue in orderly leisure through the remaining matters.

## Chapter XV

Besides the other things by which he adorned his episcopacy, he had this practice also: he diligently travelled through the diocese, supplied to infants whatever remained of the sacraments, and sharpened the people’s faith toward what was good. Whatever chapel [Col. 1750A] presented itself to him on his journey, no pressing or hasty necessity compelled him to pass it without greeting. Rather, entering it, he offered incense to God and to the saint whose temple it was, with prayers and tears always ready at the place of worship, as someone has said.

Following this custom, one day, when summoned to a royal assembly and travelling by way of Evesham, he ignored his companions’ objections that he should not turn aside to the church. Having entered, he prostrated himself before the relics of St Egwin and prayed there earnestly for his own salvation and that of his people. When his prayer was completed, he honoured all the monks with his greeting and kiss and also delighted them with salutary preaching.

There was in that community a monk named Egelricus, whom a long-standing fever, having penetrated his inner marrow, had confined to his bed as one near death—*morti*, “death,” is printed for *mori*, “to die,” as it seems. Summoning Wlstan, [Col. 1750B] he was freed from his illness through the benefit of Wlstan’s prayers.

## Chapter XVI

In the fifth year after Wlstan’s receipt of the bishopric, King Edward died and left England a vast seedbed of discord, with Harold on one side and William, count of Normandy, on the other claiming it by lawful right. Then Harold, having obtained the crown either by favour or by force, possessed nearly the entire kingdom. The Northumbrians alone, swelling with great national pride, delayed to obey; they did not deem it worthy to subject northern stiff-neckedness to southern softness, as they called it.

Tostig, brother of that same [Col. 1750C] king, encouraged them toward tyranny, and his insolence fed their great spirits. He was not deficient in courage, had he preferred to apply his passionate disposition to peaceful pursuits. Afterwards, in the same province, he was slain with Harald, king of the Norwegians, whom he had enlisted as an ally, and paid the penalty for his unconsidered boldness. But this came later.

At that time, however, Harold, intending to go there in order to cure their obstinacy by gentler remedies, since there was no plan to break it by the sword, brought the holy man with him. For the fame of his holiness had penetrated even the remotest peoples, so that he was believed capable of softening every arrogance. Nor did the outcome fall short of expectation. Those peoples, untamable by the sword and always breathing something great from their ancestors, readily yielded to Harold’s authority out of reverence for him. And indeed they would have persevered, [Col. 1750D] had Tostig not, as I have said, turned them away.

Although he was a good, gentle, and mild bishop, he did not indulge the wicked with blandishments. Rather, rebuking their vices, he gnashed threatening words at them. If this made little progress, he openly proclaimed to them by prophecy how great a punishment awaited them. Nor did the conjecture of the prudent man or the prophecy of the seer easily ever deceive. Many things were foreknown and foretold, both on that journey and frequently on other occasions.

Finally, he testified openly to Harold how ruinous it would be both for Harold and for England unless he resolved to amend the wickedness of his conduct. For at that time life throughout almost all England was marked by corrupt morals, and, amid the abundance of peace and luxuries, excess burned fiercely. He attacked immoral men, especially those who wore long hair; and if any such person bowed his head to him, he himself cut off the wanton locks with his own hands. He had for this a small knife which he was accustomed to use to clean nail-growths or the dirt from books. With it he took the first cut from the hair and enjoined under obedience that all the rest of the hair should be cut level with it. If any thought resistance proper, he publicly reproached them for effeminacy and publicly threatened them with evils. It would come to pass, he said, that those who were ashamed to be what they had been born, who rivalled women in flowing hair, would be no stronger than women in defending their homeland against peoples from beyond the sea. Who can deny that this became clear at the arrival of the Normans in that same year?

> [Note: King Edward died rather in the fourth year of Wlstan’s episcopate. For he was elected bishop in 1062 after Easter and consecrated in September [Col. 1750D]; Edward, however, departed this life on the Nones of January [5 January] in 1066.]

Since we have touched upon the times [Col. 1752A] of the Normans, let the first little book end here. For I think it can be done more harmoniously if I set out distinctly what the most holy man did in the time of the English and what in the time of the Normans. Colemann, indeed, made the first division at the election to his episcopate.

Yet I shall not conceal from your consciences, lord brethren, that I have suppressed the names of nearly all the witnesses, lest the barbarism of their names should wound the ears of the refined reader. I have likewise omitted lofty language and certain rhetorical flourishes which he, with ready devotion, inserted from the lives of other saints. For, as I said above, whoever tries to exalt by words a deed already sufficiently eminent in itself wastes his labour. Indeed, while he wishes to praise, he rather discredits and diminishes it, because he seems unable to rely on the subject’s own merit if he is supported by another’s advocacy.

# Book Two

[Col. 1751]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1751B]

Meanwhile William, Count of Normandy, came into England and, having met Harold in battle, secured the kingdom under his own dominion by Harold’s death and the slaughter of the English. There, as I have said before, the truth of the prophecy became clear: so great was the weakness of the wretched natives of the land that, after the first battle, they never attempted to rise for liberty beneath a common shield—as though with Harold all the strength of the country had fallen.

King William, however, never inflicted any hardship upon the holy man.

> [Note: [Col. 1751C] Once King William had learned of the outstanding holiness of Wlstan, he received him with the greatest reverence. Earlier, however, both he and Archbishop Lanfranc had sought to remove him from his bishopric, and at the council of Westminster had ordered him to surrender the insignia of his pontificate—the ring and pastoral staff—into the royal hands, although Wlstan, if historians are to be believed, evaded the order by performing a miracle. The matter is recounted by Ailred of Rievaulx, *Life of St Edward*, book II, p. 450; Capgrave, *New Legend*, fol. 332; and the Florilegus, who reports that it occurred in 1074. [Col. 1752C]]

Indeed, he held him in great honour and reverence, calling him “Father” and according him that name with affection. Thus Wlstan, having obtained the favour of the times, restored to their proper uses many possessions of the Church of Worcester which either the insolence of the Danes long ago or the power of Archbishop Aldred more recently had taken away. So greatly did the king’s favour assist him; so does holiness invite the possessors of goods to love it. So does religion bend those who are to be feared by others to reverence for itself.

Aldred was succeeded at York by Thomas, canon of Bayeux: distinguished for learning, not undistinguished in secular prudence, superior to many in the balance of his character, and certainly at that time by far the foremost of all in music. Against him Wlstan, the man of God, brought a suit concerning the estates of his Church. Aldred, as has been stated, had seized them and never restored them; Thomas defended their retention as though by legitimate right. Thomas, on the other hand, thought not merely that the estates need not be restored, but also—whether because he was newly come to England or because he had been persuaded by the whisperings of some people—claimed that the Church of Worcester was subject to his jurisdiction: that lordship over it belonged to him by lawful succession and had belonged to his predecessors.

> [Note: [Col. 1752C] The archbishops of York Oswald, Aldulph, and Wlstan II had simultaneously held the bishopric of Worcester from 972 to 1023.]

He pursued the case with great energy, first in England and then, in the presence of Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, before Pope Alexander at Rome. Lanfranc, knowing that the privilege of his own Church was endangered if he remained silent, would not tolerate this; he replied as justice rather than resentment dictated. Then the pope, unwilling to offend Lanfranc, his former master, yet not wishing to burden Thomas, removed from himself the odium of judgment and referred the hearing of the cause to a council in England.

Accordingly the case was conducted amid a great contest and an assembly of the nobles of England.

> [Note: [Col. 1752C] Wlstan initiated the suit at the Council of Winchester in 1070. But since the see of York was then vacant, it seemed unfair to pass sentence concerning its possessions. At last, after Thomas had obtained the archbishopric of York, these matters were determined at the Council of Pedred, held shortly afterwards. See Florence under the year 1070.]

Thomas was supported by Odo, immensely wealthy and competing with the king in riches, to whom he was related by blood: for Odo was his uterine brother, Earl of Kent, and Bishop of Bayeux. The whole body of magnates accompanied him—some bought with money, others corrupted by flattery. Lanfranc alone upheld the cause of justice. The king too leaned readily in favour of his brother, though Lanfranc had some weight in his mind.

What more need be said? The parties took their places and the case was argued. Thomas went out with his supporters to compose what he should object and how he should answer the objections. Meanwhile Wlstan gave himself to sleep, his limbs refreshed by sweet repose. When the other returned, with much sharpness of mind and a great flow of words, he said: “The man, awakened by his companions, redoubles psalms with his mouth and prayers in his heart.” At last, ordered to withdraw so that he might refine his reply by more concentrated deliberation, he went out with a few others, began the ninth hour, and chanted it through.

When they urged him to attend to matters other than psalms and settle the affair for which he had come, he replied: “Fools, do you not know what the Lord said: ‘When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you are to speak. For in that hour there shall be given you what you are to speak’ [Mark 13:9]. The same Lord Jesus Christ, the Creator, who said this, can grant me today a speech by which I may defend the justice of my cause and overthrow their strength.”

A truly admirable saying from the man.

> [Note: [Col. 1753D] See William, book IV, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*.]

He then had in his hands the Lives of the blessed bishops Dunstan and Oswald, both of whom had at different times formerly presided at Worcester. As he imitated their lives, so he defended their judgment. And how marvellous was the clear-sightedness of his eyes of faith! He declared that he saw before him those whose support of his cause he did not doubt.

Thus entering, he won the case without difficulty. For when the king asked what he had found in his counsel, and he replied, “My counsel is in you,” the king at once—for the king’s heart is in God’s hand—issued, at Lanfranc’s urging, an edict that the Bishop of Worcester ought to be subject to the Archbishop of Canterbury and that the Archbishop of York had no jurisdiction over him. Moreover, he granted to the Church of Worcester twelve estates which Aldred had assigned for his own benefit until the day of his death, providing the archbishop, in royal generosity, with compensatory lands.

The miracle was completed by this: at the same council, held at Pedred, Lanfranc the archbishop entrusted to him the visitation of the bishopric of Chester. That province, containing the three districts of Chester, Crowland, and Theford, was still inaccessible to the Normans because of its remoteness and unrestful because of its barbarism. This affair was for a long time a subject of discussion among men, who marvelled at the abundance of God’s grace in him. For he came to the council as though about to lose one bishopric, and departed bearing two.

In this narrative Coleman cites as his witness Walkelin, Bishop of Winchester, at that time second only to Lanfranc in virtues, though at a long interval. For I myself heard him more than once recounting how the holy man, almost alone, went away victorious against so many magnates, men themselves of great sharpness of mind, who opposed him.

## Chapter II

> [Note: [Col. 1754D] William has almost the same account in book IV of *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*.]

But enough of this. Now, with the Holy Spirit filling our sails, let us launch out into the deep to recount certain miracles which Christ displayed through Wlstan. There were many signs of his prophetic holiness, of which it will suffice to touch upon two.

Aldwyn, a monk by habit but unlearned, had attempted to establish a religious community at Malvern. After some years, frightened by the immensity of the labour, he was thinking of abandoning what he had begun. Yet, because it would have been rash to leave his diocese without the bishop’s knowledge, he approached Wlstan and tearfully laid before his holiness the difficulty of the undertaking and his lack of money. He wished to set out for Jerusalem, so that, if he could not serve God along with others, he might at least devote himself alone to God’s service.

“No,” said the bishop; “believe me”—for this was the oath he customarily used—“if you knew how great a religious house God foresaw in that place, you would rejoice greatly.”

Supported by this oracle, Aldwyn persevered and fulfilled the truth of the prophecy, as may still be seen today, by his own labour.

## Chapter III

The following is similar. Having obtained, as I said, the opportunity to visit the bishopric of Chester, and frequently passing through Shrewsbury, he would prolong frequent vigils of prayer in the then very small oratory of St Peter in that town. When the townspeople wondered and diligently asked why, passing over the church they called St Mary’s, he honoured that oratory with his prayers, the bishop is reported to have replied:

“Believe me: this oratory, which you now despise, will hereafter be the most glorious place in all Shropshire and the joy of the whole province; you will love it while living and lie there when dead.”

He spoke thus then; but it is now more widely known than need be pressed by our pen that the event was fulfilled not below the level of the promise.

## Chapter IV

The miracle of the woman of Evesham whom Wlstan freed from madness.—See Capgrave, fol. 332.

## Chapter V

The miracle of the demon expelled from a Gloucestershire peasant.—See Capgrave, ibid.

## Chapter VI

The miracle of his servant, possessed by a demon, restored to sanity.

## Chapter VII

The miracle of the poor man of Kent whose king’s evil he cured at Kemoseya.—See Capgrave, ibid.

## Chapter VIII

The miracle of escaping the danger of a fire at Wycombe.

## Chapter IX

How he dedicated, with the permission of Remigius, Bishop of Lincoln, the church at Wycombe built by a townsman named Spurt Lunser, and freed the man’s maidservant from a grievous disease.

## Chapter X

Concerning a blind man of Worcester who was given sight.

## Chapter XI

How he healed the diseased eyes of Gunhild, a nun of Wilton and daughter of King Harold. Capgrave recounts the matter at fol. 332.

## Chapter XII

King William had introduced a custom which his successors observed for some time and then allowed to grow obsolete. It was that three times a year all the magnates should assemble at court, to discuss the kingdom’s necessities and at the same time to see the royal splendour, as the king went crowned with his jewel-studded diadem. It is not relevant here to state the places and times of the court.

Bound, then, by the necessity of this custom, the holy man was hastening to Winchester before Easter. On the road lay a man, French by birth, tormented by internal pains, etc. There follows the account of the cure bestowed by Wlstan.

## Chapter XIII

The miracle of Segild, a matron freed from gout through Wlstan’s letter.

## Chapter XIV

Throughout his life he placed concern for the body beneath practices that fostered contempt for earthly things and drew in desire for heavenly things. Whenever he travelled through his diocese, he never dismissed the people without Mass and a sermon; he did this frequently and diligently. He never gave himself food during the day until he had confirmed however many children had been brought from every direction. From the first rising of the sun until the evening light he performed this work, not only on winter days but also in summer heat. Reliable witnesses attest that he often confirmed two thousand as though it were a small number, and often more than three thousand, in one day.

This he did not merely in youth, when both manly vigour and the very pleasure of doing good called him to labour, but even when gemlike grey hair was already sprinkling his head with snow, and, in frail health, he could scarcely follow his spirit with his bodily strength. All were astonished that, while usually eight clerics carrying the chrism-vessel succumbed in turn to fatigue, he himself remained untiring. Love of God, undoubtedly, made him insensible to such great labours.

There follows the story of Wlstan’s slanderer, seized by a demon and healed through Wlstan’s prayer.

## Chapter XV

How, summoned by Abbot Serlo to Gloucester to dedicate a church, he dissolved many enmities, displaying upon those who resisted a terrible example of divine punishment.—William recounts the matter in book IV of *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, fol. 160.

## Chapter XVI

How Wlstan entrusted to Coleman the office of preaching peace, valuing highly in him purity of life, distinction of person, abundant eloquence, and knowledge of letters; and concerning one who despised Coleman’s sermons and was punished from heaven.

## Chapter XVII

Concerning a tree cursed by Wlstan which withered.—See Capgrave, fol. 333.

## Chapter XVIII

Concerning an insult inflicted upon Wlstan and the vengeance which followed by divine action.

## Chapter XIX

Concerning the aid Wlstan brought to sailors in peril.—See Capgrave, fol. 333.

## Chapter XX

There is a coastal town called Bristol, from which one crosses directly to Ireland, and it is therefore adapted to the barbarity of that land. Its inhabitants, together with others from England, frequently sail to Ireland for trade. Wlstan abolished among them an ancient custom, so hardened into their minds that neither love of God nor King William’s authority had hitherto been able to eradicate it. They bought men throughout England and sold them in Ireland in hope of greater profit; and female slaves, first used for the sport of the bed and now pregnant, they put up for sale.

One might see, and grieve, ranks of wretches chained by ropes, and young persons of both sexes, who by their noble appearance and unspoiled age might have moved barbarians to pity, daily exposed and daily sold. An abominable crime, a pitiable disgrace: human beings, unmindful even of brute feeling, consigning their own relatives, and finally their own blood, to slavery.

As I said, Wlstan gradually eliminated this deeply rooted custom, handed down from ancestors to descendants. Knowing that their stubbornness was not easily bent, he often stayed among them for two months, often three, coming there every Sunday and scattering the seeds of divine preaching. In time these took such force among them that they not only renounced the vice but became an example to others throughout England in doing the same. Finally, they expelled from the town one of their number who more obstinately opposed the bishop’s commands, and soon deprived him of his sight. In this I praise their devotion but condemn their action; though, once the minds of rustics have been corrupted, no force of reason can resist them.

## Chapter XXI

Once, proceeding to York before Easter on an embassy from King William and Archbishop Thomas in order to bless chrism there, he came to Nottingham. There his holiness was proved by a miracle to the sheriff’s doubting wife.

## Chapter XXII

A certain Sewius, a man of no small wealth, had built a church in his village of Radclive. Eager in religious devotion to have it dedicated by the saint, he sought and obtained permission from the archbishop whose diocese it was. There Wlstan vainly urged a wealthy priest to make peace with a poor man, and foretold the man’s fatal end, which followed shortly afterward.

# Book Three

## Chapter I

Thus far I have spoken—and gladly spoken—of miracles: few indeed, but sufficient to demonstrate Wlstan’s holiness. I shall now undertake to describe his inward life and character. First, his bodily appearance must be described.

He was of medium height, yielding to the very tall and exceeding the short, proportionately formed in all his limbs. Serenity of mind suited the constitution of his body, so that it drew anyone to reverence for him. His health was excellent, aided both by moderation in food and by no indulgence in sleep. His clothing, bedding, and footwear were moderate: neither of ostentatious cost nor of contemptible shabbiness. Affectation was avoided in both extremes, because even in mournful garb there can be self-display. Yet he inclined more readily toward what was humble: so that all pomp was absent and no grace was lacking.

Always fleeing every kind of display, amid all riches he clothed himself only in lambskins. On one occasion Geoffrey, Bishop of Coutances, gently reproved him for this, and he sprinkled the man with exceedingly witty jests.

> [Note: [Col. 1757D] See William, book IV, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, fol. 160.]

For when Geoffrey asked why he wore lambskins when he could—and ought—to have sable, beaver, or fox furs, Wlstan replied neatly: “A man, and men skilled in worldly prudence, ought to use the skins of crafty animals; I, conscious of no evasiveness, am content with lambskins.” When Geoffrey persisted and suggested that he should at least wear cat-fur, Wlstan replied: “Believe me, the *Lamb of God* is sung more often than the *cat of God*.”

Geoffrey received these words with laughter, much delighted that he himself could be mocked and the other could not be swayed.

## Chapter II

Except when he took refreshment with monks, he always dined openly in the royal hall, with knights seated around him. For he declared it indecent and ungenerous to dine in secret while the household murmured outside. Yet after taking the religious habit—and for several years before it—he never nourished his body with richer foods, but always abstained from fat and from meat other than fish. It will not be irrelevant to relate more fully the occasion on which he imposed this practice upon himself.

As stated above, Bishop Brihteg advanced him from the first orders to the priesthood, and after advancing him entrusted to him the church of the village called Hawkesbury. He was then a youth in his first down of beard; yet he did not, as a man of unformed age, spend his time in the dissipations of the world. Nevertheless, still not abhorring rich food, he ordered a goose to be cooked one day. The bird, fixed upon a spit, was carefully roasted by the exquisite skill of a young household servant. Melted fat dripped out under the force of the fire; for it had been selected from the choicest fattened geese. Some servants added coals, others ground seasoning; all were eager for the savour and could not conceal their pleasure in words.

Drawn in by these things, the priest too gave his mind over to delight, tasting the goose in advance by hope. The table was almost laid when an unwelcome but necessary business arose, driving both him and the overseer of the food from home. Thus departing hungry, he rebuked in his mind the fault of momentary pleasure: miserable flesh stirred to such things; the pleasure passes away, the sin remains. “The flesh not . . .”

[An entire leaf appears to be missing in the manuscript. William recounts the matter in book IV of *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, fol. 159.]

## Chapter III

“. . . having found him more wakeful.”

> [Note: [Col. 1758D] See Capgrave, fol. 333.]

One of them, named Eadric, whom I too knew, sat down beside him one night while he was singing. But because Wlstan wished to omit nothing of his solitary psalmody, the monk, weary of the delay, presumed even to signal with his hand to the bishop that he should stop. At Wlstan’s nod reproving his drowsiness, he unwillingly resumed his seat and persevered, though sleepy. Soon afterward, when he had lain down in bed, he was violently shaken in a vision and even beaten with whips; thus he paid the penalty for his rash presumption. Finally, after pledging his word that he would never again deter or hinder the good man from a good work, he was released from the danger of that terrifying vision.

## Chapter IV

He always sang Matins in church, however far the church might be from his lodging. He went there whether it snowed or rained, whatever inconvenience the weather caused. If the road was foul with mud, that mattered no more. If dense darkness covered the sky, he no less patiently endured every difficulty of the journey, provided he might reach the church and truthfully say to God: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house” [Psalm 25:8].

In keeping with this custom, once when travelling to court before Christmas he lodged at the village of Merlave and said that in the morning he would go to church. It was far away, and the muddy road would deter anyone even walking by day. Moreover, a snowy rain—or wet snow, for the weather raged in both fashions—would be an obstacle. Though the clerics set these things before him, he held firm to his decision and could not be dissuaded: he wished to go to church with only one companion, or even none, if only the way were shown him so that he might not lose the path in uncertainty.

Thus, yielding against their wishes, the clerics’ perversity gave way and restrained its anger in silence. Frewin, more reckless in mind than the others, seized his lord’s hand and doubled his offence by leading him where the marsh was more waterlogged and the road steeper. Wlstan, immersed in mud to the knees and deprived of one shoe, for the time concealed the insult. For the cleric’s intention was that the bishop should regret what he had undertaken then, and afterward accept his advice.

When, after much of the day had passed and the freezing cold had numbed his limbs, he returned to his lodging, then he disclosed both his own discomfort and the cleric’s offence. He ordered the shoe to be sought, yet brought no abuse against the insolent man, softening the cruelty of the act by cheerfulness of expression. For the bishop possessed great forbearance, and had armed his mind so that no mockery disturbed him and no inconvenience shook him into sin. Some often openly pricked him with words or secretly teased him with ridicule. Yet against such things, coming upon him outwardly from the world, he stood so fearless that he was affected in mind but did not fall in speech.

Yet I do not wish to claim for him a praise I cannot prove: that he was not moved even in his mind. No religion ever has or ever will wholly erase the emotions of the soul. It can perhaps restrain them for a time, but cannot remove them forever.

## Chapter V

Every day he heard at least two Masses, neglecting his offering at neither, and himself sang a third. If he had to ride anywhere, as soon as he mounted he began the Psalter and made no pause except at its end. Litanies with many collects were added, and Vigils with Vespers for the dead. Then, if the road were extended, the Psalter was repeated until the canonical hours were sufficiently supplied. Clerics and monks rode alongside, either to take up the sequence of verses or to assist his memory if he seemed to falter. This was done so that they might unlearn idle tales, which especially press themselves upon travellers.

His chamberlain kept at hand a purse that was the treasury of all the needy. No one who begged alms from Wlstan ever groaned at being turned away. When the journey had been completed and he came to his lodging, he did not enter his chamber for rest, as I have said above, until he had greeted the church with prayers. He also ordered the houses throughout the lodging to be sprinkled by a priest with holy water and the banner of the cross. Thus adverse things were driven away; thus favourable things were brought in.

## Chapter VI

He was always praying or preaching in words when he had leisure. If not, his mind fixed on heaven, he thirsted for God. Whether lying down, standing, walking, or sitting, a psalm was always on his lips and Christ always in his heart. What is more, even while his body slept, he kept vigil in prayer. Whenever exhausted by excessive labour in prayer he had composed his limbs for rest, he yielded to nature in sleeping; but, whether awakening on his own or roused by another, he began a psalm: “Preserve me, O Lord” [Psalm 15:2]; or “I will love thee, O Lord” [Psalm 17:2]; or other such verses that gave voice to prayer.

On summer days he generally allowed himself bed after dinner; yet—something one may rightly call astonishing—he could not fall asleep unless someone was reading aloud before him. If the reader performed his duty, he seemed to sleep; when the other stopped, he immediately broke off sleep. Before him were read Lives of the Saints and edifying writings. You would rightly declare that the man’s life was like a heavenly mirror, from which the image of every form of holiness was reflected together; like a watchtower of divine delight, containing what advanced religion, what answered to salvation, and what finally accorded with beauty.

## Chapter VII

He received with pleasure those who came to confess their sins and comforted them kindly; he listened to confessors with most welcome humanity, not disdaining them with arrogant gesture. He compassionately condescended to their offences, rather than recoiling as though they were unheard-of. This resulted in people coming from all England and not being ashamed to confess to him what they would trust to no one else. They were therefore not ashamed to tell him only what they were ashamed to have done.

He in turn bestowed equal kindness upon those confessing, diligently warning them not to despair and instructing them how to avoid sins and how to wash away those committed. Nor was this less worthy of preaching—indeed, I do not know whether it was more worthy—that he thereafter held as more intimate those whose sins and penances he knew.

## Chapter VIII

With the greatest diligence arranging care for the needy, he placed them in groups on seats before him and generously distributed every necessity. Sons of noblemen, bound to service at his court, brought the dishes before him as he ate, according to custom. He diligently poured salutary admonitions into them: not to be arrogant, but to put on humility; above all, not to injure the purity of the flesh, lest under the slippery impulse of youth they stain their bodies in the mire of pleasures.

He compelled these same young men, kneeling, to lay table and food before the poor and, as part of their instruction in serving, to pour water over their hands. If any of them, conscious of lofty birth, showed pride even by his expression, he rebuked the disobedient youth. There were other matters in which he would rather be offended than that a poor person should be grieved even by a gesture. The Lord’s command must be observed: the needy are to be served, etc.

By these and such means the pious teacher boiled away the insolence of however uncultivated minds, so that they might become ready to show reverence to the poor. Indeed, gently caressing handsome boys with the touch and kisses of his holy hands, he embraced in them the grace of divine design; and from the beauty of their features he drew material for good, repeatedly saying: “How beautiful is the Creator who makes such beautiful creatures!”

## Chapter IX

In each of his estates he had a small cell, where after Mass in the morning he shut himself in behind closed barriers. There, having gained solitude, he set the free gaze of his mind upon contempt for the world and contemplation of God. No one interrupted him while he meditated, except when a cleric knocked at the door to announce the time for dinner or the canonical hours. This enclosure lay between his chamber and the private house, known only to his household, lest he seem to make a display of religion.

He restrained himself with this care among men at all times, but especially during Lent, so that in this way he might steal away from the body which he fled with all his mind. For, as Nicholas, venerable prior of Worcester, told me, he was not merely frequent in prayer but diligent in it. Thus, when he came to a verse of a psalm by which he might kindle affection for God, such as: “Incline thine ear, O Lord, and hear me; for I am needy and poor” [Psalm 85:1], he would repeat this, I say, and others like it twice or three times, redoubling it with his eyes raised to heaven.

Moreover, as the same prior attests, he carefully observed diligence in prayer not only in himself but also in his household. He tolerated the transgressions of his men when appropriate and rebuked them at the proper time. Thus, if he saw a monk absent from the gathering for Matins, although he might conceal the matter at the time, afterward, when the others had yielded to sleep after the office, he gently roused the negligent man and compelled him to fulfil his duty, himself answering the singer in the place of a minister: “What is more wonderful than this man,” etc.

I should gladly say more concerning the most reverend Nicholas, if I can first set forth what I have in hand concerning Wlstan’s character.

## Chapter X

As I have noted above, he diligently travelled through his diocese, omitting nothing belonging to the duty entrusted to him. To make this more manageable, he set a limit once a year, considering both his own health and the fatigue of those who came to meet him. For throughout the bishopric, after advance notice from the archdeacons, such a crowd of people poured forth to meet him that it could not be counted. While he was obliged to minister to their infirmities, the burden and difficulty were indeed great, but his spirit shone forth as one lifting the burden and conquering the labour.

Throughout his parish he built churches on estates under his own control; on others’ estates he urged that churches be built. At Westbury there had been a church from ancient times, but it was then half-ruined and half-roofed and needed repair.

> [Note: [Col. 1761D] Oswald, Bishop of Worcester, restored in 983 the house of Westbury, which had for many centuries been dedicated to religious life, and filled it with monks. Wlstan restored it when it had fallen into ruin and gave it to the Church of Worcester in 1093, on the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The charter of donation survives in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 126. Bishop Samson later took it away from the monks of Worcester.]

Wlstan restored it entirely, raised it to its full height, repaired the walls with mortar and the roof with lead; and, assigning revenues from estates and tithes and service-books, he presented it as a solemn gift to the Church of Worcester. Having installed monks there, he appointed as their head the often-mentioned Coleman.

Yet although, as I have said, he was skilful and diligent in equipping divine houses, he appeared almost dull and negligent in secular buildings. For nowhere on his estates did he build halls or dining rooms. Undoubtedly he was troubled not only by laborious architecture in these worldly buildings but even in churches. He regarded such things as belonging more to human pomp and display than to divine will and grace.

Nicholas said that this could have been seen on the day when Wlstan caused the old church of Worcester to be uncovered.

> [Note: [Col. 1761D] After the old church of Worcester had been demolished, construction of the new one began in 1084, according to the manuscript Worcester Annals. See William, book IV, *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*.]

He stood silently in the cemetery and from time to time groaned. For a thought welled up in his mind, bringing a great shower of tears, and at last broke forth: “We miserable people,” he said, “destroy the works of saints, thinking in our pomp that we make better things. How far superior to us was St Oswald, who built this church! How many holy and religious men served God in it!”

Though those standing by said that he ought not to be sad but rather rejoice, since God had preserved him for the grace of seeing the church so magnificently enlarged, he held fast to his purpose of tears. Nor are there lacking people who say that he foretold the burning of the new church, which was consumed by fire in later years.

> [Note: [Col. 1761D] The city of Worcester, with its principal church, all the other churches, and the castle, was burned by fire on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June], a Thursday, in 1113. Thus Florence of Worcester. But from William of Malmesbury, who recounts the same fire in book IV of *De gestis pontificum Anglorum*, it is clear that not the entire church but only the roof was burned. [Col. 1762D]]

But it did not seem right to accept as true what is inconsistent. At that time he also completed the new church, and you would scarcely find an ornament which did not adorn it. Thus he was admirable in each thing and singular in all. Therefore, that nothing might be lacking to its magnificence, he affixed seventy-two marks of silver to a shrine, in which he placed the remains of his most blessed predecessor Oswald together with those of many saints. This was done on the eighth day before the Ides of October [8 October], in the presence of a great gathering of people, Bishop Robert, and abbots; and it was ordered that on that day the translation of the aforesaid saint, together with the octave of all the relics of the place, should be commemorated annually.

> [Note: [Col. 1762D] Aldulph, Archbishop of York, had earlier raised Oswald’s bones from the tomb and honourably placed them in a shrine which he had prepared, in 1002, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May [15 April], a Wednesday, according to Florence. Oswald had died on the last day of February in the leap year 992.]

This was devised because the saint’s deposition, which falls in Lent, cannot be celebrated as conveniently. Let the reader further know that the shrine had formerly been made by Blessed Oswald but was enlarged by Wlstan.

## Chapter XI

He was held by such great compassion for the aid of the souls of the faithful that he continually restrained by edict the rashness of those who rode through cemeteries. Many bodies of saints lie there, he said; reverence is owed to their souls, which are with God. Yet this effort profited little, since even today reverence for the saints is trampled underfoot.

Whenever and wherever, as I said above, he heard of anyone’s death, he immediately directed those present to say the *Our Father*, while he himself said three psalms—“Praise the Lord, all nations” [Psalm 116:1], “Out of the depths” [Psalm 129:1], and “Praise the Lord in his saints” [Psalm 150:1]—with prayers. In prayer for the departed soul, he gave a sermon for the dead person, if time permitted: brief and unelaborate, or lengthy and necessary. He had Mass for the dead sung every day without exception, save Sundays and major feasts. He yielded to festivity what he owed to piety, so that he might increase forgiveness the more by pressing the case less. Thus there was abundant tenderness in his praying on other days, and abundant hope in his refraining on Sundays. Yet the Lord deprived him of neither, because the Lord’s mercy smiled where the servant’s confidence rejoiced.

## Chapter XII
He hated the stain of unchastity and favoured integrity in all persons, especially those of the sacred order. Whenever he discovered any one of them devoted to chastity, he made him a member of his household and loved him as a son. By a single edict he compelled all married priests to renounce either lust or their churches. [Note: [Col. 1762D] I suspect that William has made a mistake. The Council of Winchester in 1076 had indeed forbidden wives to priest-canons. But marriage was not yet unlawful to the remaining priests. This was first done at the Council of London in 1102. Wulfstan’s concern, therefore, was not with married priests generally, but with canons alone.] If they loved chastity, they were to remain with favour; if they served pleasure, they were to depart with disgrace. Some preferred to lose their churches rather than their little wives. Of these, hunger consumed some in wandering; others were not abandoned in the end by household resources acquired elsewhere. A few, governed by sounder judgment, renounced their unlawful attachments and grew old honourably in the leisure of their churches. Therefore, taking precautions for the future, the bishop thereafter promoted no one to the priesthood who did not swear to preserve chastity.

## CHAPTER XIII

There were many signs, everywhere among the monks, of his profound humility. When he was at Worcester, he celebrated the principal Mass almost every day, more often undertaking the duty voluntarily than being asked by the one whose week it was. [Col. 1763B] For he is said to have been accustomed to say—though I report this on Nicholas’s authority—that he was a monk of that place and, like the rest, owed his week’s service to the church; and therefore, what he could not fulfil in his own appointed order, he supplied during Advent. He always attended the conference; then, after making confession and giving the blessing in church, he returned to his own affairs.

At the first light of dawn, while the others were resting, he went early to church. There, if one of the brethren—as commonly happened—wished to say Mass but lacked the assistance of a server, he himself without hesitation undertook the minister’s office. When he saw boys or others improperly vested, he himself graciously adjusted the hanging folds of the acolytes’ garments and set their disordered creases in order.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 1763C]

When some maintained that such beloved [perhaps: lowly] humility was beneath episcopal dignity, he replied: “He that is greatest among you shall be your minister” (Matt. 20:26). “I am your bishop and teacher, and therefore, according to the Lord’s command, I ought to be the servant of you all.” Nor did he ever yield himself to the easy discretion of his own will, obeying God’s commands in all things. Most agreeable in manner, he offended those living with him by no harshness and embarrassed those serving him by no ingratitude. Often withdrawing things prepared for his own use, provided that he might look after the convenience of his people, he did and said everything belonging to his office.

He displayed this not only at Worcester, but wherever in his diocese he was asked to come to monasteries. [Col. 1763D] He was not accustomed to hold petitioners off with a stern countenance or excuse his arrival by evasions and delays. Whenever children to be confirmed were announced to him, as I said before, he at once rose to meet the requests of those bringing the news—if awake, setting aside what he held in his hands; if asleep, instantly shaken free from sleep.

At that time wooden altars, surviving from ancient days, still existed in England. He demolished these throughout his diocese and constructed others of stone. Thus it happened that sometimes he dedicated two altars in one village in a single day, and, setting out on the second and third days for other places, dedicated the same number there. So tirelessly was he present wherever he was called that one would have thought him flying rather than travelling. I shall not allow the miracle [Col. 1764A] which he performed on that occasion to be buried in silence.

## CHAPTER XV. A miracle concerning mead multiplied through Wulfstan’s merits at a feast after the dedication of a church built by Egelric the archdeacon

## CHAPTER XVI

The subject seems to require that, since the discussion has turned to drink, I should tell what portent happened to a certain man who drank contrary to his prohibition. He had many knights in his household, not because he delighted in it or because the frequent multitude of retainers flattered his mind. For he conceived no boasting in his heart because he possessed the service of many; rather, King William had ordered this arrangement because a report was spreading among the people that the Danes were coming and would shortly be present. [Col. 1764B] Nor was this belief far from the truth: they would doubtless have come had other events not intervened. I set out the cause of their threats and the obstacle to their undertaking in my *Deeds of the Kings of the English* (book III); there, if he wishes, the friendly reader will find it.

Accordingly, to return to what I had begun to say, the king, alarmed by fear, summoned a council and consulted it publicly about what ought to be done. The unanimous opinion, prompted by Lanfranc, was that the households of magnates should be fortified with knights, so that, if circumstances required, they might defend the commonwealth and all private property against the barbarians under a common shield. Therefore the bishop retained a larger number, soothing them with abundant pay and filling them with luxurious provisions. The narrative follows of how Nicholas, disregarding Wulfstan’s command and drinking, was attacked by a demon at night.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 1764C]

Indeed, so that the memory of a venerable master’s disciple may also enter our pages on this occasion, Nicholas was, as English lineage went, of very distinguished birth. His parents honoured the holy man with great reverence and secured his friendship by many services. He himself baptized the boy; and, after he had been nobly trained in letters, kept him always at his side as soon as his age allowed. When the full completion of his education had come to him, he sent him to Kent to serve for some time under Lanfranc’s instruction.

Later, when Tiulf was bishop, Nicholas became prior and in a short time gave many proofs of his ability. More importantly, as I judge, he either instilled learning among the inhabitants of that place by teaching [Col. 1764D] or impressed it upon them by example, so that they yield to the foremost churches of England in number, perhaps, but are not surpassed by them in zeal. Nicholas moreover took pleasure in recounting Wulfstan’s words and deeds; perhaps he is blameworthy in this, that he did not commit his life to writing. For no one could have consigned it to memory more truthfully than the person who knew him more immediately.

Finally, he said that even Wulfstan’s words casually uttered were almost never devoid of weight, as in this instance. The bishop was gently stroking his head with paternal kindness; a troublesome mass of hair was already abandoning Nicholas’s forehead. Then the young man, joking with the bishop, said: “You take fine care of my hair, which is all escaping.” “No,” Wulfstan replied, “believe me: so long as I live, you will be bald.” Nor was the saying less true than it was spoken. [Col. 1765A] In the very week in which Wulfstan’s spirit left the earth, whatever hair remained on Nicholas’s forehead drifted away on the air. [Note: [Col. 1765] See William, book IX of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, and Capgrave, fol. 333.]

## CHAPTER XVIII

Every day in Lent, as the reader recalls was said earlier, after washing feet and hands he gave the poor an allowance of food. He did this more willingly by night than by day, evidently avoiding human judgments, which incline in either direction through affection or hatred. If, among the others sitting there, someone afflicted by the royal disease were present, he would press that person’s feet more insistently, kiss them more tenderly, and fix his eyes upon the sores themselves.

Moreover, on the Lord’s Supper he devoted the whole day and likewise the night, as they succeeded one another, to works of active charity. Though he was always intent upon God’s worship, on that day especially he took care that nothing secular should creep into his actions. After singing Matins with the monks in the greater church, he returned to his chamber, where the officials whose duty it was had prepared warm water and towels. [Col. 1765B] There, after washing many poor persons, as I have said, he even gave each of them a complete outfit of clothing, personally dispensing charity with his own hand.

Then, after briefly resting his body, the attendants filled the whole hall with as many poor people as could sit there in dense crowds and packed rows. When the Father had given shoes and food with his own hand to them all, if someone said to him, “Lord, rest now; you have done well,” he replied: [Col. 1765C] “I have done little; but I have the desire to perform the command of my Lord.” Then he withdrew to church; and throughout the day until None, shunning worldly matters, he longed for heaven. There followed the reconciliation of penitents, the celebration of Mass, and the blessing of chrism.

Although Coleman has treated all these matters in a great circumlocution of words, I resolved to pass them over, because I have undertaken not to describe episcopal office but to portray his life. For what is the point of describing things which others also do and can do only as the books prescribe? Yet I do not think this should be omitted: his appearance was so gracious to penitents that, when they looked upon him with their eyes, they imagined God’s angel in their minds.

On that day, we are told, he customarily ate with those reconciled; after supper washed the feet of all the monks; and served cups with kisses. Thus from midnight until the deep twilight of the following night he habitually withdrew himself from the world.

## CHAPTER XIX

In the year immediately before his death, he performed this office on Maundy Thursday with such energy that the diligence of previous years seemed to have been nothing. He surely foresaw that he would do it for the last time, and he struck all the attendants with the wonder of his solicitude. He had ordered each reeve that, from each village, he should provide a complete outfit of clothing for one person, shoes for ten persons, and food for one hundred persons. [Col. 1766A] He had also ordered the chamberlains to procure the same, so that the household might supply what the estates lacked.

That day the hall was filled three times with needy persons pressed together so closely that anyone could scarcely move forward with difficulty, so completely had their long and confusedly clustering ranks blocked every entrance. The house roared with a great tumult, while monks and clerics washed the feet of those sitting there. He sat in the middle, supported by an episcopal seat. The immense labour had exhausted his strength, so that he could be a singer of psalms but could not be a washer.

Yet his compassionate mind wished that all should be satisfied, lest anyone depart empty-handed. And indeed, the first and second time, all left clothed, delighted with coins and shoes, their bellies fully laden.
