But when the line of poor people was arranged for a third time, a monk whispered to the bishop that money and clothes had failed, food too was scarce, and that the steward and chamberlains, consulted, denied that there were funds available. What use then was it to wash feet when there would be nothing to give those whose feet had been washed?

“No,” said the bishop, “let the Lord’s command be done. His bounty will not fail, so that the servants may somehow be fed. My attendants will not act for me; they will wish to do so when they no longer have me.” He had scarcely spoken when, behold, three messengers entered, one almost treading on another’s heels in their haste. The first announced money brought; the second, a horse led in; the third, oxen given to the bishop. Raising eyes and hands to heaven, he rejoiced at the miracle—not so much for his own sake as for the benefit of the poor. [Col. 1766C] The monks wept for joy and congratulated the Lord on such a gift. God was blessed by all, because he did not disappoint the hopes of those trusting in him or allow Wulfstan to grieve even for an hour. Thus the horse was turned into money, the oxen converted into coins, and together with the money newly brought, they benefited the needy.

## CHAPTER XX

He had warned his attendants that at that Easter he wished to dine with good men on carefully prepared dishes. They misunderstood this, and had invited many wealthy people. Easter Day had now dawned; but after bringing into the hall as many poor people as it could hold, he ordered a seat to be placed among them and food to be served to him there.

The steward received this with enormous indignation. Grumbling with much angry muttering, he attacked [Col. 1766D] the man’s gentleness, saying that it was more fitting for a bishop to dine with a few rich people than with many poor ones. He replied that those were rich who knew and were able to do God’s will; that those should be served who had nothing with which to repay; and that God, in recompense, would repay what the needy could not return in reciprocal exchange. He said that he saw this gathering more gladly than if, as often happened, he had sat with the king of the English.

For, as I have said, the king held him in great honour, and so did the nobles, who often invited him to their feasts and rose at his counsel. Those especially who pursued justice often honoured him, since some are born with such a disposition that they cultivate in others what they themselves cannot attain. Why speak of England’s magnates? The kings of Ireland venerated him with great favour. Malcolm, king of Scotland, together with his venerable wife Margaret, committed himself to his prayers. The fame of his holiness penetrated the inmost parts of lands and the furthest reaches of kingdoms. The Roman pope, the archbishop of Bari, and the patriarch of Jerusalem, in letters still surviving, sought his intercession with God.

In short, scarcely any worldly glory existed that did not follow him against his will and resistance. There was a contest between the man and glory: the more sharply he fled it, the more insistently it pressed upon him. But let us so far have ranged abroad concerning such matters, while my discourse hesitates to approach his passing—lamentable indeed to earth, but exultant to heaven. Now, as I am about to speak beyond the measure of my knowledge, I beseech thee, Lord Christ, etc.

## CHAPTER XXI

On the Pentecost immediately following the events I have just related, he was struck by severe illness throughout all his limbs and took to his bed. He immediately ordered that horses be spurred and that Robert, his friend and bishop of Hereford, be asked to come. Robert, hearing the report, came at once. Wulfstan made confession of his human failings and also received discipline. Thus monks call the strokes of rods which the severity of the striker inflicts upon the bare back. What a great man, who, weakened by age, broken by sickness, and yet serene in conscience, did not abstain even from bodily scourges, so that he might shake out whatever stain of the soul remained!

From that time [Col. 1767C] until the Circumcision of the Lord, he seemed sometimes to be somewhat better and at other times fell back into bed. Thus a sluggish but continual fever carried him toward his end. The decay of his body increased the strength of his soul, so that, if anything in him were unripe for eternal glory, the heat of illness might bring it to maturity. After the Circumcision, the aforementioned bishop and the venerable abbots of his diocese—Serlo of Gloucester and Gerald of Tewkesbury—visited him as he lay ill. He first accused himself, according to his custom, then duly absolved them by his own authority, and finally bade them farewell.

The force of his illness swelled day by day, and Christ hastened the departure of the man whom he was calling to heaven. Yet he did not take a holiday from God’s service; instead, remembering his former pursuits, he generally prayed aloud and always in mind. More often sitting than lying, he turned his ears to the psalms and his eyes to the altar, arranging his chair so that he could freely see whatever was done in the chapel. [Col. 1768A] Eight days before his death he received from Thomas, prior of the place, the office of holy anointing; thereafter he safeguarded his departure by the daily provision of the Eucharist.

He breathed his last on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, a little after midnight on Saturday. It was the year 1087 from the Lord’s Incarnation, the tenth of the reign of William the Younger, after thirty-four years, four months, and thirteen days of his episcopate, in about the eighty-seventh year of his age. [Note: [Col. 1767C] Many errors can be detected in these figures. First, Wulfstan died not in 1087 but at the beginning of 1095. Next, in 1087 King William Rufus began his reign, so that his tenth year coincides with the year of Christ 1097. Finally, Wulfstan sat from consecration until death for thirty-two years, four months, and twelve days. William has wrongly given thirty-four years.

Florence defined Wulfstan’s death by very many chronological eras: “He departed from the world,” he says, “on the eighteenth day of January, at the middle of the seventh hour of the night on Saturday, in the 5299th year from the first day of the world, in the year 1095 from the Lord’s Incarnation, etc.; 745 years from the coming of the English [read 645], 498 from the coming of St Augustine, 103 from the death of St Oswald, etc.; in the third year of the leap-year cycle, the third of the indictional cycle, etc.; in the eighteenth five-year period of his life, and in the third year of the seventh five-year period of his pontificate.”

The year is correctly assigned, but the day does not agree. For in that year 18 January fell on a Thursday. Therefore, on the authority of William and others, 19 January must be substituted, on whose evening Saturday began, or what Florence calls the seventh day of the Sabbath—that is, of the Christian week. Moreover, Wulfstan could not have died in the eighteenth five-year period of his life. For he was ordained priest by Brithego, bishop of Worcester, who died in 1038; indeed Florence himself, reporting under the year 1062 that Wulfstan was consecrated bishop, declares that this occurred after the fiftieth year of his age. Therefore William’s opinion should be accepted: namely, that Wulfstan died at approximately eighty-seven years of age. Florilegus and Capgrave erred still more grossly. The latter placed Wulfstan’s death in 1067; the former assigned it to 25 March.]

Who, moreover, can wonder that during his life he was not ignorant of his future longevity? On many occasions, and once especially in chapter, he expressed this most sweetly. As the brethren sat around and, as happens, held much mutual conversation, he suddenly bowed his head and yielded to sleep. [Col. 1768B] Amid the sobbing tears of all, he was mournfully declared to be about to leave them by a swift death. Not long afterward, when he had shaken off sleep and learned the cause of their weeping, he replied in words nearly these: “Believe me: as long as an aged body can endure, I shall not die; and this frame shall not be dissolved except by great old age. But when I have departed, then I shall be more present with you; and none of those whom you fear will be able to harm you, if you are willing faithfully to serve God.”

## CHAPTER XXII

[Note: [Col. 1768C] See William, book IV of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*.] They washed the body, which already shone with the perpetual brightness of hope in the resurrection and was an object of astonishment and reverence to those who saw it. It was so translucent in brightness that it seemed jewel-like, so milky in marvellous purity. Finally, the nose, [Col. 1768C] which had projected excessively while he lived, sank back and shone so beautifully in death that those who saw it marvelled.

What I am about to say seemed a miracle to many present. The ring which he had received at his episcopal consecration had sometimes slipped off of its own accord before this hour. But then it could not even be drawn off, and so was buried with the body, as he himself had long ago foretold. Concerning this miracle see Florence under the year 1094, and Capgrave, fol. 333.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Meanwhile the body was borne forth, and the procession proceeded to the church which he had made new from old. It was placed before the altar in its bier, with the clergy seated around. There, through that night and the following day and night, a festival of prayers and funeral rites of tears were offered to God as incense.

At that time Robert, the aforementioned bishop of Hereford, was at the king’s court. [Note: [Col. 1769D] William recounts the same history of the vision in book IV of *The Deeds of the Bishops of the English*, fol. 163, and adds that Wulfstan appeared again to Robert on the night before the burial and foretold that Robert’s own death would soon follow. Robert certainly died in the same year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, according to Florence of Worcester, who writes that the first vision occurred in the village of Cricklade.] He was a man endowed indeed with worldly prudence, but free from no allurements. At the very hour when the saint departed this life, Wulfstan appeared to him, much changed from the man Robert had seen in recent years. He was clearly visible in star-like radiance, rosy with a flourishing complexion; clad in episcopal vestments and holding a staff in his hands, he seemed to address the sleeping man in these words: “Come now, beloved brother Robert, to Worcester. I wish you to perform my funeral rites and commit my body to the earth and my soul to God.”

Robert was thought to answer him thus: “Lord and beloved friend, you command me to bury you, though I have not seen you in such vigour for five years.” “Let it be,” Wulfstan said, “such is the will of God, which must be fulfilled. [Col. 1769B] Go quickly now, and do not receive my words negligently.” The bishop, moved by the oracle of so manifest a vision, immediately woke from sleep and reported the vision to the king. Having received his permission, he urged on his horsemen and sped over the delaying fields, continuing his journey to Worcester. The strength of holy friendship, which had bound him to the man from the beginning of his episcopate, relieved his immense labour; and divinity favoured his kindly wishes, so that he arrived before the time for burial.

Thus, on the first night, Wulfstan’s spirit summoned his episcopal friend, though far away, to the duty of funeral rites. But on the following night, as though returning home from travel, he showed many wonders to those present. Some monks, wearied by long labour, had withdrawn wherever they could into corners, in order to seek sleep more freely in private leisure without observers. He at once appeared to all of them, striking the snoring and rousing those half asleep. They were to rise immediately, renounce drowsiness, begin the Psalter from the beginning, and finish it with the commendation of the soul. They did as he commanded, gaining strength from necessity: since they could not do what they wished, they somehow submitted to what was permitted.

One of them had indeed entertained in his mind an enormous crime, though he had not yet brought it into action. The Saint appeared in anger, reproaching his thought of wickedness, emphasizing its enormity, and threatening punishment if he carried it out. It was more than enough that he had thought it; therefore he should refrain from fulfilling it. [Col. 1769D] If he wished to provide for himself, he should restrain the deed. For he would shortly pay the penalty and die in that same year if he did not desist from that sin. Terrified alike by the thunderbolt of the threats and by the torment of conscience, the monk gave his pledge: renouncing what he was accused of, he would henceforth devote himself to the Rule.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Sunday, the day of burial, had arrived; and the aforesaid bishop had now come, scarcely able for haste to breathe out the proof of his vision as true. After the customary Masses had been celebrated, he arranged the burial of the blessed body. [Col. 1770A] Then, as though there had been no weeping before, they broke into lamentation and prolonged groaning. The crowd cried aloud in mourning, multiplied by the echoing vaults of the roof. Nor was the weeping simple or feigned; tears flowed in genuine sobs, testifying in one man to the ruin of religion and the misery of the country.

It was difficult to distinguish who alleged the more just causes for their tears: clergy or people—the latter crying out for a shepherd as protector, the former for a teacher of discipline; old men or boys—the former longing for his maturity, the latter for his gentleness; rich or poor—the former praising his abstinence from wealth, the latter the lavishness of his expenditures. At last they committed the bones of their most loving Father to the tomb, but his memory was never buried in their minds.

For you will scarcely find a community or city where reverence for the dead bishop is observed with care not merely greater, but even equal. This is done every week, when the day is free; and whenever the annual cycle returns to the anniversary of his death. Monks multiply psalters and Masses; citizens, almsgiving at most lavish expense. He himself also runs unbidden to the vows of those praying; nor is there anyone who asks in faith and does not obtain his aid.

## CHAPTER XXV. A miracle concerning the epistolary book of Worcester church, which Wulfstan caused to be restored after it was stolen

## CHAPTER XXVI. A similar miracle

## CHAPTER XXVII. A miracle concerning a certain recluse who, after putting on Wulfstan’s tunic, was freed from the devil’s temptations

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How Wulfstan appeared after death to the same recluse and bestowed benefits

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 1770C]

The monks persisted faithfully; letters, interpreters of grief and tokens of love, were sent throughout England. It was requested that, if God should make anything known to anyone concerning his salvation, that person would fulfil the eager wishes of those longing for good news.

At that time there was at Brompton a priest of good life named Dunstan, whose holiness’ sweet fragrance I remember hearing of from my childhood onward. A recluse of the same village, a woman inferior to no man in holiness, kept watch with a like zeal for virtue. One would not know which to prefer: so closely did they contend in rival virtues—the priest by his doctrine of instruction, the woman by her discipline of obedience. They were persons of outstanding religious devotion, whom God judged worthy of contemplative visions [Col. 1770D] while they had not yet left this life.

They informed the people of Worcester that they ought not to doubt anything concerning Wulfstan’s salvation. They had seen him among the choirs of saints, possessing no less glory than the others and somewhat more grace than certain persons of lower rank. Whoever does not believe their words wrongs religious devotion, which, as I said, they cultivated with such earnestness that nothing in our age, especially, was greater. Finally, whatever they said was received as though it had sounded from heavenly temples, as though it had poured forth from divine sanctuaries.

## EPILOGUE

[Col. 1771]

[Col. 1771A] I seem to have fulfilled your commands, Fathers and lords, that I should portray in whatever style I could the Life of this most holy man. I have therefore rendered obedience, though I have not fulfilled your wish. Whether I have done both will be for your judgment. Intention excuses inability: for though I could not do what I ought, I did what I could.

I ask, therefore, to make with you an everlasting bargain [Col. 1772A] over this small labour: because I have kept nightly vigils, somewhat less than six weeks, for the sake of your zeal and wish. It will be fair, then, that after the separation of this soul and body, you offer sacrifices to God for me during as many days as I devoted nights of vigil to Wulfstan. Farewell.

[Col. 1771] Here ends the *Life of St Wulfstan, Bishop and Confessor*, whose holy deposition is celebrated on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February.

[Col. 1771]

# WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY’S LETTER TO PETER THE MONK CONCERNING THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF JOHN SCOTUS (ERIGENA)

[Col. 1771]

(See *Patrology*, vol. CXXII, col. 92, among the Prolegomena to the Works of John Scotus.)

[Col. 1771]

# EXCERPTS FROM WILLIAM OF MALMESBURY’S ABRIDGMENT OF AMALARIUS

(P. Alixius, preface to John of Paris’s *Determination concerning the Mode in Which Christ’s Body Exists in the Eucharist*; London, 1686, octavo, p. 82, from Lambeth Library manuscript no. 39, quarto.)

[Col. 1771B] **WILLIAM’S PREFACE TO HIS ABRIDGMENT OF AMALARIUS BEGINS**

Your wish, my friend Robert, diverted me from the purpose on which I was engaged, historical narrative. For recently, while we were sitting in our library and each turning over books according to his own interest, you came upon Amalarius’s *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. Recognizing its subject matter from the very face of its title, you embraced the opportunity of encouraging the beginnings of a new vocation. But because the complexity of its testimonies and the harshness of its language immediately disturbed your eagerness of mind, you asked me to abridge it.

I, having once resolved to comply with you as a most beloved man, accepted the task imposed upon me without reluctance. In this work it will be possible to discover how much labour I spent, for easier understanding, in reducing the language, although perhaps I could have spoken more elegantly. For the subject under discussion is most necessary, and ignorance of it is shameful to all priests.

Meanwhile, I want you to be warned that you should know to avoid one of those who have discussed such matters, named Rabanus. In his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* he says that the sacraments of the altar contribute to the nourishment of the body and are consequently subject to corruption, disease, age, excretion, and finally death. You see how perilous it is to say, believe, or write such things about the Lord’s body.

Moreover, his books by themselves add little to knowledge and contribute least of all to teaching, since they are wholly appropriated from the labours of others, either word for word or in sense. Indeed, two books of that volume which I mentioned above are transcribed from Isidore, and the third word for word from Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine* and Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*. Further, in the book *On the Nature [Col. 1772C] of Things*, what does he say other than Isidore’s *Etymologies*? Or in his book *On Computation*, what does he say other than what Bede says in *On Times*, apart from certain allegorical inventions? [Col. 1773A] For that man was especially prone to this vice, as though he entirely despaired that his readers had any memory by which they could detect his thefts.

Indeed, just as it is considered creditable prudence to borrow a few words discreetly from one’s elders, so it is reckoned audacity to steal whole arguments with open shamelessness. Therefore, rejecting him, turn your mind to Amalarius, who wrote soundly on these matters.

(At the end of the first book of the Abridgment, he addresses the reader thus.)

Up to this point, with as much brevity and understanding as I could manage, I have selected the best parts of Amalarius’s first book, adding to the first book certain chapters of the second and third, so that the whole first book might be completed concerning the variations of the Mass throughout the entire year. Therefore I thought it fitting [Col. 1773B] to make Amalarius’s third book the second here, so that after the variations of the offices throughout the year, the meanings of daily observance might immediately follow. [Col. 1774A] I have placed as the third book what he himself placed second, so that after the explanation of ministries there might be discussion of the ranks and vestments of ministers.

(At the end of the work he again addresses his friend.)

I seem to myself, my friend, to have satisfied your command by abridging Amalarius. If, through lack of skill, I have fallen short of your wish, you will grant pardon. If I have said anything suitably and appropriately, give thanks to the Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift. I further advise that, if you wish to know briefly the meanings of the Mass, you should read the verses of Hildebert, first bishop of Le Mans and afterward archbishop of Tours; and, if you wish to know the meanings of sacred vestments and other matters of that kind, the sermons of Ivo, bishop of Chartres. For these men seem to have understood such matters more clearly and expressed them more beautifully. But concerning the variations of the offices, you will seek in vain for anyone other than Amalarius: perhaps someone has written more eloquently, but certainly no one more knowledgeably.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1143: HUGH FARSIT

[Col. 1773]

## NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine Religious, XII, 294)

Hugh Farsit was a regular canon of the abbey of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes at Soissons before 1128. [Note: [Col. 1773] Dom Michel Germain, *History of the Abbey of Notre-Dame of Soissons*, Proofs, p. 481.] In that year several sick persons afflicted with the burning sickness, having gone on pilgrimage to the church of Notre-Dame at Soissons, obtained healing there through the intercession of the august patroness of that church. Hugh, a witness of these miracles, composed their account. He did not publish it, however, until several years later, since he mentions Abbess Matilda I as already dead; this corresponds to 13 December 1143.

We have few accounts more authentic or more worthy of belief than this one, since the author reports only recent and public events, which he attests either to have seen himself or to have received from eyewitnesses. What, for example, can unbelief set against the miracle of that woman of Oignoncourt, named Gundrade, whose nose and lips had been destroyed by the pestilential carbuncle, and whose entire face was found perfectly restored in a single night? “We ourselves saw her,” says Hugh, “and in the restoration granted to her she suffered absolutely no defect in any respect; rather, the newly formed flesh was like the rest of her flesh, except that to careful observers it seemed brighter.”

Dom Michel Germain, not content to give this work in the original among the documentary proofs of his *History of Notre-Dame of Soissons*, translated it almost entirely in the body of the work. Before him, Vincent of Beauvais had inserted various extracts from it in his *Historical Mirror* (book XXVIII, chapters 2–4). Fragments of it are even found in certain contemporary authors. But the person who made the greatest use of this account was Gautier de Coinci, prior of Vic-sur-Aisne in the Soissonnais, a writer of the late twelfth century. It is wholly incorporated into his three French verse books *On the Miracles of the Holy Virgin*—if only he had had the discretion to confine himself to this text, instead of adding, as he did, a quantity of fables that affront common sense, wound modesty, and dishonour religion. [Note: [Col. 1773] *Memoirs of the Academy of Belles-Lettres*, vol. XVIII, pp. 357–365.]

A celebrated academician who took the trouble to point out these faults himself fell into another: he transferred the vices of the copy to the original and attributed Gautier’s extravagances to Hugh. This judgment is all the more surprising because the critic had both works in his hands and professed to have compared them. Without claiming to fail in the respect due to him, one may venture to challenge him to show in the first work the scandalous examples that he cites from the second. That challenge certainly will not be met. It is indeed true that Gautier de Coinci did not invent these episodes; but he drew them from Gautier of Compiègne, of whom we shall speak later, not from Hugh of Soissons. [Note: [Col. 1773] *Mar. Aug.*, book IV, chapter 76, p. 438.]

[Col. 1775] If Ferreolus Locrius is to be believed, there must also be credited to our author—whom he wrongly makes a canon of Laon—an anonymous account of miracles performed in the church of Our Lady of Rocamadour in Quercy in the year 1140. This work is preserved in manuscript in the library of Saint-Martin at Tournai. It begins with these words: “Being about to write the miracles of Mary, Mother of God and perpetual virgin, of Rocamadour.” [Note: [Col. 1775] Sander, *Bibl. Mss. Belg.*, part I, p. 137.] But since Locrius’s conjecture rests on no proof, we shall refrain from adopting it.

Here are two other manuscript works which may with greater certainty be attributed to Hugh of Soissons. The first is a letter entitled, in copy no. 2842 of the King’s Library: “Letter of Brother Hugh of Soissons to the Fathers assembled at Confluence [Koblenz].” This assembly of the Fathers of Koblenz was, as will be seen, a general chapter of the Premonstratensians. The salutation reads: “To the venerable Fathers and lords assembled at Confluence, Brother Hugh of Soissons, servant of your holiness.” The author begins with declarations of attachment and respect for all those who compose the Premonstratensian order. “That I have loved you equally,” he says, “both those of you whom I know by sight and those whom I have learned of only by report, many among you can remember.”

He next praises Saint Norbert, whom, he says, he had always regarded as an angel whom the Lord had filled with His Spirit. Among his virtues he commends his ardent love for the unity of the Church, and on this occasion he discusses the different ways of remaining in the same communion. “The first,” he says, “consists in belief in the truths of salvation; the second, in the practice of the virtues without which the kingdom of heaven is not attained; the third, in observances established by men in order to bind the ties of unity more closely. These observances,” he continues, “would not be at all necessary if divine love were equally rooted in every heart. For, according to the Apostle, the law is not made for the righteous; but the weak need it. In order to secure for these observances the respect which they deserve, care must be taken to shield them from every innovation. This is what Moses himself commanded when he said: ‘Do not pass beyond the boundaries which your fathers have set.’” All this is merely a preamble to the new practices which the Premonstratensians had introduced. “These principles being established,” he continues, “I ask you what advantage you have found in abandoning the black copes which the entire order of regular canons has until now used. Are you ignorant of the maxim of our father Saint Augustine, who says that a custom not contrary to law ought itself to have the force of law? It is therefore a ridiculous and unreasonable affectation in you to have preferred white copes. But do you not even transgress the divine law by wearing woollen tunics instead of the linen ones which Moses recommended to priests—wearing them, I say, not only in choir but even at the altar?” Hugh attacks with the same vehemence several other new practices which the Premonstratensians had substituted for the ancient usages of the order.

The second manuscript work of our author, preserved in the same library under no. 2484, is a letter to his sister Helvide. Its heading is expressed in these terms: “To his most reverend sister Helvide, whom those who see may count among the Lord’s own: Hugh of Soissons.” The author tells her that he intends to dedicate to her a work to which he has resolved to devote all his leisure for the whole remainder of his life; that he will entitle this work: *Hugh’s Leisure to His Sister Helvide*; that he will divide it into annual books: “I have wished to distinguish the whole of the little work by yearly books”; and that, if a year should pass in which he is unable or not permitted to write anything, he will take care to mention this in the following book: “But if perhaps some year should pass in which I am not permitted or am unable to write anything, this too will be recorded in the following little book—if indeed one follows, life accompanying me.” For, he adds, “we have not yet brought forth the whole book and the whole writing, since the Lord will still give [more] in the future.” If, he continues, the Lord should call you to Himself before me, I shall continue writing while retaining the same title for my work, for your memory, dearest sister, will always be pleasing to me: “But if the Lord calls you first, I shall write, and the title affixed above will remain: HUGH’S LEISURE TO HIS SISTER HELVIDE. For your memory is pleasing to me, my sister.” He then speaks to her of death and of the uncertainty of that dreadful hour, of the miseries of this life, and of eternal blessedness. What was the object of this great work which our author was preparing, and whether he brought it to completion, is unknown. What is certain is that no trace or remembrance of it remains in history.

Dormay [Note: [Col. 1775] *Hist. de Soiss.*, book V, p. 47.] also ascribes to him a treatise *On the Sacraments*, a work which, he says, formed part of the books which Arculf or Ansculf of Pierrefonds, bishop of Soissons, bequeathed to his church in 1158. But he appears to be relying only on an ambiguity of name in assigning this work to the regular canon of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes. It is all the more probable that it should be credited to Hugh of Saint-Victor and identified with his great treatise *On the Sacraments*, since it does not bear our author’s surname.

The year of his death is uncertain. The day is marked as 4 August in the necrologies of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes and of Soissons Cathedral. The latter records it in these terms: “Hugh Farsitus died, who gave us books both of sacred Scripture and of secular learning.” This date, imperfect though it is, would suffice, in the absence of any other, to distinguish him from Abbot Hugh, who governed Saint-Jean-des-Vignes from 1177 until 1186. [Note: [Col. 1775] *Gall. Chr. nov.*, vol. IX, p. 337.] For the latter’s death is recorded under 28 October in the house’s obituary.

[Col. 1777]

# HUGH FARSITUS’S LITTLE BOOK ON THE MIRACLES OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY IN THE CITY OF SOISSONS

(Dom Michel Germain, *History of Our Lady of Soissons*, p. 481, from the Corbie manuscript.)

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 1777]

[Col. 1777A] To the praise and honour of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, God has deigned in our times to show His people the power of His wonders, so that He may give to believers the inheritance of the nations, and to those who love Him the good things He promised to Israel. Therefore, to those who, once enlightened and made partakers of the Holy Spirit, already tasted the powers of the age to come, tasting likewise the good word of God, and who therefore treat these present things with disdain and negligence, it has been granted as a gift of consolation to taste, by the desired vision, the power of the invisible kingdom, and to drink in with their eyes fear and love in relation to divine severity and mercy. For this is the great strength of God, by which He restrains evils and bestows upon those who love Him the invisible goods and the riches of His glory. This, I say, is the great strength of God and the surpassing power of His kingdom: an invisible and hidden power for checking evils, which would overflow like a disease in His kingdom unless restrained; and, on the other hand, a power of grace and mercy exercising its works ineffably, through which, fear having been cast out, it rejoices with the elect, while superabounding love supplies confidence. But of these matters elsewhere.

## THE MIRACLES OF SAINT MARY OF SOISSONS BEGIN

[Col. 1777]

### I. On the initial sequence of the miracles

[Col. 1777B] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1128—by what judgment of God and for what reasons, let him who can understand—power was granted to the adverse force to strike, by an invisible scourge, persons of different ages and both sexes in the district of Soissons. Once their bodies had been set aflame, they burned with intolerable agony until the soul departed, unless God’s medicine alone came to their aid. This disease is a wasting one: beneath stretched, livid skin it separates and consumes flesh from the bones; as time passes, it increases pain and burning at every moment; it compels the wretched to die, yet denies this sole remedy to those who desire death. Until its earlier prey, the limbs, has been devoured, the swift fire invades the vital members; and, what is remarkable, this fire, though powerful to consume without heat, bathes the miserable in a cold as icy as it is intense, so that by no remedy can they be warmed. Again, and no less remarkable: once it has been extinguished by divine grace, and the deadly cold driven away, so great a heat pervades the same parts in the sufferers that the disease of cancer very often joins itself to that burning, unless remedies are applied. It is dreadful to look upon those afflicted and those recently healed, and to trace in their bodies and disfigured faces, with one’s eyes, the marks of death escaped. [Col. 1778B]

But the greater the misery, the more gracious is the mercy. Thus, while such necessity pressed hard, the scourge was already raging, and general danger threatened—when human aid could not even be imagined—those upon whom the fire had already spent its fury took refuge in the compassionate and propitious Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary; and at last they were not disappointed in their hope. For six days in September they remained in the church of the Blessed Virgin situated in the city of Soissons. As the pains did not cease and the number of sufferers increased each day, those who could not be still, with continual and dreadful cries such as that death is accustomed to produce, allowed no hearer to rest. The city was struck with a new terror; and even the hardest [Col. 1778C] hearts were shaken by fear of the imminent danger, of the fire attacking so near at hand, and of the scourge devastating them unawares.

All the people flocked to the same church. Communities from the other churches as well as from the principal church went forth barefoot, armed with the humility of the Ninevites and accompanied by the forces of penitence, to contend with the merciful and compassionate God—to contend, I say, and to prevail. For He is compassionate and cannot long endure the assaults of heartfelt grief and boundless misery; He immediately yields and is overcome, because He is compassionate. These are the heavenly weapons that protect; these are the heavenly weapons that teach us to stand firmly, to contend confidently, and to yield. Thus the church of the Blessed Virgin and Mother of the Lord was made the field of this battle, so that they might bring her also to their aid in such necessity.

When the priest gave the signal that they should meet and rush upon the devastating sword with prayers—“Now is the hour,” he said—then indeed they gave free rein to their tears. Holding out the shield of faith, they pressed on with mighty fervour, and their cry rose to heaven. And behold, the sovereign Queen and Lady of the angels was present to aid them, bringing with her mighty hosts of heavenly spirits. At her presence hell would tremble and the gates of death would quake; no hostile and mighty power, nor any power inflicting the scourge, could stand. [Col. 1779A]

Lest this seem remarkable to anyone, so great a trembling filled the church as the herald of her coming that everyone fled, thinking an earthquake had occurred or that the church had been shaken from its foundations; and to each person the doors and exits seemed too slow to open. For the elements and human minds had to feel reverence for such power, and mortal hearts to be struck by the presence of divine might. But when they perceived that no danger was present, they returned to themselves and found every burning of the sick extinguished, every pain lulled, with an exceedingly swift sweetness bestowed. Those whose groans of pain had just been unbearable now, because of their sudden deliverance, sent up innumerable cries of joy to heaven; and, as all the people rejoiced with them, praises, tears, and thanksgivings seemed unable to end for the remainder of the day. Bells and drums gave forth their sound, loudly proclaiming the glory of God’s victory; competing in song, they urged the faithful more and more to conceive a new spirit and to let Christ resound in their hearts. Who then ceased from Christ’s praises? And how often, glorious Virgin, was your name repeated, how often was it cried aloud? “Merciful Lady” was said a thousand times; “kind and propitious and blessed Virgin” was shouted ten thousand times. [Col. 1779B–C]

### II. On the lights seen on the preceding day

They say that some of the sick saw, on the day before this heavenly benefit was granted, abundant brightnesses descending from heaven through the glazed windows of the church—like certain heralds of the gift that was to follow. [Col. 1779D]

### III. On the girl healed through the shoe

A few days before, the kindness of that same glorious Virgin had also encouraged people generally to dare to ask for this gift: a certain girl had been signed and healed through the shoe of the same Mother of the Lord, which is preserved in that church. For Abbess Matilda, who then presided over that place, wearied by the importunity and shrillness of the girl’s continual crying, took up the Blessed Virgin’s shoe and proceeded with her attendants. As soon as the aforementioned girl was signed with it, her pain fled without delay; restored to ease, she recovered. Thereafter, in overflowing kindness, the most blessed Virgin, Mother of mercy, extinguished and healed all who came each day, and they returned home with their pain driven away. Nor was there now any difficulty in granting relief.

By night and by day, again and again, drums rang out and praises of almighty God, sung with modulated sweetness by those dwelling in the church, sounded very frequently; and those who had already withdrawn to their homes and supper could not restrain either tears or proclamations of praise. In short, within fifteen days one hundred and three persons, summoned by name, were extinguished from this fire; and three girls who had arrived with distorted limbs were restored to the grace of health. [Col. 1780A]

### IV. On the stars driving away darkness

At the same time, many firmly assert that they saw, during the night, a dark gloom, and stars of wonderful size pursuing and driving that same gloom beyond the church. [Col. 1780B]

### V. On the woman who bit the shoe

It was customary for the sick, once health had been recovered, to remain there for nine days; during these days they were blessed, one by one, with the shoe being carried around, and they kissed it. One of those who had received health, while pressing her kisses upon it, seized it with her teeth, inflamed by excessive ardour of faith. Stirred to indignation, the bearer and guardian of the shoe began angrily to assail her as guilty of so great an offence, sharply blaming her for daring this and saying that she would no longer bring it out for them after such an excess. But the woman, conscious of charity yet fearing her accuser—or rather, praiseworthily silent in such frenzied love—said nothing; and concerning the multitude of those whose fire had been extinguished, we confess ourselves wholly defeated: for I do not think that anyone could recount anything except this alone, that report of such abundant grace stirred everyone as far as the shores of the Ocean and the banks of the Rhine, and all who came were healed. [Col. 1780B–C]

### VI. How great was the people’s devotion

But who would dare even to begin a narrative of the people’s devotion, their gathering, and the innumerable reverence of men and women, rich and poor, old people, young people, and children? Who could describe tender and delicate persons—not only men but even young women—whose feet were hardened, who endured cold and roads, overcame winter’s severity and the harshness of the journey, and offered to God in this same devoted sacrifice their tender flesh, preserved for the world, to be cut by the cold and made bloody? [Col. 1780D] What was in their hearts, Lord? What fervour, what charity, what frenzy of love for You? Who knows the tears, prayers, groans wrung from the deepest heart, and cries of penitence, except You alone, Lord, who knew them through Your Holy Spirit and mercifully received them?

Let those who wish admire bodily miracles, as indeed it is right to do; but we admire Your grace more, Lord, in sinners crushed by fear of You, turned to devoted penitence, as though raised from the tomb, and, not ungrateful for the remembrance of grace, burning in Your love through tears and humility. These are our miracles, which are especially dear to us; for these we glorify You, Lord Jesus, praise and adore You, because this whole fruit endures unto eternal life: piety and humility burning within us in You. [Col. 1781A]

### VII. On the woman who recovered her nose

I relate one miracle, the like of which I do not know whether I have read, heard, or seen in past ages. A woman named Gundrada, wife of a man named Theodoric, dwelling on the bank beyond the river Aisne, which flows past the city of Soissons, came from a village called Audiguncurtis (Oignoncourt), among the others whose limbs that judicial fire was devouring, to the church of the Blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. She sought the help of healing grace through that same Mother of mercy. [Col. 1781B]

For this same fire had attacked the face and mouth of the said woman; and, to the horror of onlookers, the wasting fire had ravaged and disfigured whatever fleshy cartilage projected in her nose, and the upper lip lying beneath the nose, as far as the jaws and molar gums. Why say more? She sought mercy and obtained it, and the ravaging fire was extinguished from her face. But since this was general and public, it was counted almost a lesser miracle; for greater things followed, and an unprecedented power was displayed in the same person.

Meanwhile, although through the benefit of grace she had been spared so great a pain, she did not escape the honour of being seen—a bearer, Lord, of Your mercy and judgment. [Col. 1781C] Thus she became already burdensome and hateful to everyone she met and was compelled to return to her own people, so that the grace of kinship might make her intolerable company bearable. Yet even this did little good: she was grievous for all to see. She was therefore compelled to cover her entire face, except the eyes, with a moist cloth; and even with such an aid she scarcely gained anything by which to excuse the aversion and nausea people felt, even through the kindness of humanity and kinship. What could she do? Where could she go, if she was not to be rejected from people’s company—she who was now showered with hatred and curses even by the members of her own household?

Thus hemmed in by every necessity and despairing of all human help, a better plan entered her mind and more abundant help came to her. Recalling her faith, which had begun to grow cold, she reproached herself as though forgetful of the former benefit, because she had through forgetfulness set aside the Mother of mercy, rich in mercy—that is, Mary, Mother of Christ. [Col. 1781D] Therefore, girded as with weapons by renewed faith and hope, she prepared on the following day to make her way again to the shrine of the Blessed and glorious Virgin in the city of Soissons. Having made, according to her poverty, a candle to offer, she returned to sleep.

Waking early that same night and anxiously awaiting the first light, mindful of her vow and intention, she complained that the nights were excessively long, as was natural before the spring equinox. Then she felt the cloth that she had placed over her mouth loosen and hang loose. When she tried to tighten and draw it upward again, she made little progress; she was forced to call for the help of those around her. While they delayed, sluggish with sleep or cold, she nevertheless asked for a lamp to be lit and help brought to her. Meanwhile she felt flesh grow under her fingers and the pressure of the cloth, but did not know that it was the flesh of a re-formed nose and lip. As she repeatedly drew back the cloth and repeatedly touched by it the newly fashioned creature, she cried: “God and Saint Mary, help! God, Saint Mary, help!” At this cry, those around her, alarmed and awakened, quickly brought in a light. Then they marvelled at the new formation and pledge of renewed resurrection wrought in her disfigured nose and lip, and joy arose as though life had returned from the dead. [Col. 1782A]

The next day she went to the city, as she had intended in her other vows, to offer the candle in thanksgiving. What wonder if she then worked a miracle for those who newly recognized her, since throughout the rest of her life she bore about so great a mercy of God and publicly displayed testimony to divine grace? We too saw her; and in the restoration granted her, she suffered absolutely no defect. Her new flesh resembled the rest of her flesh, except that to careful observers it seemed brighter. Thus the people’s ardour and burning faith did not shrink from kissing her nose and mouth, as though they had been newly made by God’s own hands. [Col. 1782B]

### VIII. On the faithless but corrected smith

An iron-smith from the district of Laon had made an annual agreement to remain at Soissons, repairing the implements of the *materones* [term uncertain] and performing throughout the year whatever belonged to his trade and whatever was commanded him. Later, however, led by regret and considering himself cheated in the bargain over his wage, he returned home on the pretext of visiting and arranging his household and family. Yet he did not conceal the complaint that troubled him concerning his pay. He went back as though intending to return at once and to fulfil, whether it proved easy or difficult, what he had contracted to do. He is said to have obtained leave on this condition: because he had no surety to give for himself, he gave the holy Lady Mary as surety for his very speedy return and for the fulfilment of his agreement. Thus, with this surety pledged, he was dismissed.

But then, little mindful of what a surety he had left for himself, he delayed beyond expectation and returned when he pleased, intending to announce that he did not wish to serve for such a wage—namely, sixty solidi—for the entire year. The man in charge of the work, with whom he had made the agreement, accused him of falsehood and reminded him of the punishment that might justly befall him: for he had lied not to men but to God and Saint Mary. The smith promised to work there without pay for fifteen days, as though, by rendering this service, he ought deservedly to be free from the annual service which he did not wish to continue. [Col. 1782C–D]

When these fifteen days had elapsed, he was leaving, despite the protests of the overseer of the work. The latter angrily reproached him with the vows of faith and agreement he had broken and reminded him of the surety he had given. But the smith, no less fixed in his purpose, went away. After he had passed the village called Crovicus (Croug), beyond Saint-Médard, and was climbing a hill, striving to reach its summit, his hands and feet suddenly became useless and his limbs began to contract. All ability to continue the journey home was denied him, and he was forced in tears to return to the city of Soissons, to the shrine of the Blessed Virgin Mary whom, as a liar, he had left as his surety, and to implore her aid.

For stubborn and faithless as he was, he had tried more than once to shake off what he regarded as accidental and chance numbness; but the more he exerted himself, the more he was hindered, until affliction alone gave understanding and instruction: he could more easily return to the monastery, whereas every capacity to proceed to his own home was denied. At last, bound by the chains of his own faithlessness—or rather brought back by the power of the avenger of his faithlessness—to the shrine of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, he embraced her altar in tears. Recognized by the overseer of the work, he was asked: “Then are you our runaway and lying smith?” [Col. 1783A–B]

“I am he,” he said, “unhappy and wretched, and guilty before the Blessed Virgin, who is now exacting from me the just penalties which, as you see, I deservedly endure at present. For God has done this and this to me. But now I promise God and the Blessed Virgin, and I am ready with all my heart to serve her for my whole life, if only the kindly and merciful Lady will deign to look upon me and have mercy on so great a sinner.” While, embracing the altar, he begged in this way with tears and lamentation, he was freed from that contraction of the sinews. Remaining steadfast in service, he did not dare to lie a second time. [Col. 1783B–C]

### IX. On the boy carried away in a vision

At the beginning of this blessing poured out from heaven, a certain boy of eleven years, a keeper of livestock, whose feet were burning, was brought by his mother. He remained there for a few days; having received relief from his pain, he was carried back home. He was from Vaux, a village beyond the Aisne, lower down beside the bank of the same river. But the same boy, by divine prompting, did not forget so great a benefit. Desiring to see the house of the Blessed Virgin, he pressed his mother daily and urgently that they ought to return to Soissons, as though in thanksgiving. She refused altogether, saying: “Since abundance is not given to one who is well, at least the necessity of renewed illness compels what is denied to one who desires it greatly; let Him who beholds the hearts and desires of sinners hear me.” At these words the boy immediately began to be tormented by his former sufferings, the wasting fire already devouring his flesh. [Col. 1783C–D]

His mother was terrified and, setting aside every other concern, they returned together to the city and to the house of the Blessed Virgin. Owing to the former affliction and its present renewal, his limbs were now becoming useless. Yet he received a second time the grace of deliverance, enjoyed sweet sleep, and, at the entrance of the procession of the mother church, as a great crowd accompanied it, he was roused from rest. In thanksgiving he burst forth with cries that pierced the sky; he testified to and recounted the benefits newly performed in him; and he told everyone that he had been carried away before God and had seen Our Lady, the Mother of God, supplicating for the people, that God might deign to remove this disease from the people and take away this spark that had fallen upon them. From her Son she graciously received this answer: “Mother, you are the star of the sea; let all your will be done.” [Col. 1784A]

When the same blessed Virgin likewise complained concerning her house, which was lowly and despised in comparison with the others, she again heard from her Son that money should be brought from beyond the sea and beyond the Rhine, from which her house would be built; and that He would adorn it before the eyes of all beholders with great brightness and glory. He also foretold that evils would befall the people of Soissons from God’s side because they did not repair the church of His Mother. Indeed, many from that same city were attacked by the fire; what things, and of what kind, remain [to befall them], we do not know.

The witnesses to this vision are as numerous as those alive today who wish to see: both in the splendour with which it is honoured by every age, sex, and rank, and in the abundance of gifts and offerings. For the boy testified that he would die shortly thereafter, and so it happened: he did not survive a month. But a very remarkable thing about this boy was that, recounting all ancient history from the beginning of the world, he delivered his entire narrative rapidly in verse. He also rehearsed, in such order, the text of the Gospel and the acts of the Lord under the New Law, as though he had read everything in a book and were reciting words dictated by others. [Col. 1784B]

Concerning the holiness and virginity of Joseph, who was guardian and spouse of the sacred Virgin, he said among other things: “He who holds the sceptre of the flowering rod was guardian of the glorious maiden.” It is remarkable where we read that Joseph preserved the flower of virginity, by which the virginity of blessed Mary might likewise receive confirmation. Here too the ancient gifts of the Holy Spirit are renewed: filling a boy who was a shepherd, He makes him a harpist and a prophet. As he told these things so copiously, like a rushing torrent driven by the Spirit of the Lord, with his eyes closed as though hating transitory light, he scarcely deigned to speak to laypeople and the unlettered, as though wearied by their ignorance—he who within heard great and profound things and beheld a light not of this age. Yet He who makes the tongues of infants eloquent and chooses the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong deigned to make even this boy a witness to His glorification. [Col. 1784C–D]

When his time of testimony had been completed, as we said, he died shortly afterward. Such grace had also suffused his face that the whiteness and brightness of his countenance displayed something, I know not what, angelic and divine.

### X. On the mute man healed through a vision

Three mute men came to the same shrine of the Blessed Virgin Mary. As they lay asleep in the church at night, one of them, disturbed by a vision, was awakened from sleep. Running to the altar, he began with a tongue hitherto unknown to speak fully and to give thanks to the Blessed Virgin, and to relate the manner of his deliverance. While he was oppressed by heavy sleep, two doves, as it seemed to him, began by scratching to pluck at his ears. Awakened by this impulse of terror, he bore witness while awake to the gifts which, rejoicing, he had received while asleep and unaware. [Col. 1785A]

By this sign the brutish heresy is refuted which tries to maintain that the grace of the Holy Spirit accomplishes nothing in infancy because children do not yet understand the baptism which they receive. Behold: it worked in this man while he slept and did not know it. The other two mute men departed without the office of their tongues being opened. Why this happened is better known to Him who says that Naaman the Syrian alone was healed, though many lepers were in Israel under the prophet Elisha.

### XI. Likewise, on another mute and deaf man healed through a vision

We also saw another man from the district of Laon, from above the little river Serre, who had been deaf and mute from infancy. His name was Christian; he was about eighteen years old. He too came with the others to seek the aid of the blessed and glorious Mary, Mother of God. Amid the most densely crowded throngs of people, he kept watch in the church, crying to God solely in mind and gestures, for his tongue could not do so. [Col. 1785B]

Thus he was always present, awaiting the time and hour when divine grace might look upon him. When the sacristans drove him from the sanctuary because they could not bear such importunate crowds of people, he lingered and waited, departing unwillingly. But behold: God regarded his unfailing faith, though it had been delayed for a time of testing. Two crowned persons, like a bridegroom and bride, appeared to him descending from above, and a flashing light filled the entire church. The appearance of the glorious Virgin, both in garments and face, was of marvellous brightness, such as it is fitting for the inhabitants of heaven and eternal light to appear. [Col. 1785C]

Then, touching the sick man’s throat and mouth with her sweet hand, she loosed the bond of his tongue and ears. A flow of blood which burst forth through his nostrils, ears, and mouth bore witness to the power of the sovereign Lady. Having received so great a benefit, he departed silently, rejoicing in silence. Returning to his people, he testified in stammering speech that he had received the gift of speaking, since he was only then learning to speak. The report quickly spread among his contemporaries and fellow-countrymen that God and Saint Mary had shown mercy to Christian.

The priest of the same village, called Mortaria, would not at all believe the report that had preceded him. He denied that Christian could speak or hear until the young man was brought into his presence. Thereupon the priest, moved by repentance and condemning his own unbelief, went in fear to the shrine of the Blessed Virgin. Prostrating himself before the altar and clinging to the pavement, he poured forth such grief, tears, and renewed groans—adding to his sins that he had dared to doubt the power of the Lord and His Mother—that onlookers might have supposed he himself was being tortured by fire or afflicted by some kind of suffering. [Col. 1785D]

At length, when questioned, he related everything in order and promised that he would bring the same Christian on the appointed day; and this was done. As Christian himself spoke concerning and on behalf of himself, all the facts were established by the testimony of the neighbours present: that he had been deaf and mute from infancy. The very result bore witness to the grace of God, because he plainly heard and spoke. Then praises were sung to God Most High; then the din of drums and the sounds of bronze instruments imitating trumpet-blasts; then prayers, tears, thanksgiving from every age, sex, and rank; and the glory of God was proclaimed by all together. [Col. 1786A]

### XII. On the punished rashness of a certain peasant
A servant of a certain knight of Soissons, assigned to agricultural labor, used on several occasions, when free on feast days, to come with his companions from the village to the shrine of the blessed Mary, Mother of God. But while the others, according to their means, made offerings and honored the slipper of the blessed Virgin Mary, he offered nothing. Once, as they were returning and, among other things, speaking of the wonders of God in connection with the aforesaid slipper, Boso—for that was the servant’s name—added: “Truly, you are fools if you think that this is Saint Mary’s very slipper; surely it may long ago have rotted away.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when, behold, his blasphemous mouth was twisted toward his ear with such force and torment that, from the severity of the anguish, his eyes seemed almost to be forced from his head; under the pressure of the pains his whole face was distorted, swollen, and rendered unrecognizable in human appearance, striking horror into those who looked on by his labored breathing. As though handed over to his tormentor, he barely managed to utter these words: that he be taken back to the church of the holy Mother of God. And so it was done.

Cast down before the altar, he for some time displayed the spectacle of his madness and of the avenging power to which he had been delivered. His body, turned into a swelling, was constricted; his breath, within his entrails, polluted the surrounding air with a smoke-like exhalation. His voice was like a roar; his tongue and mouth refused their office. Then Mathilda the abbess and the others present, moved by compassion, brought him to the altar. Having embraced it, he was signed with the relics and with the slipper, and began to improve and to be released from the oppressive swelling. What more need be said? Both his face and body were restored in complete health.

Boso, not unmindful of this benefit—as one rescued from the jaws of death—asked and obtained from his own lord release from servitude. Henceforth he no longer wished to serve a human being, but to devote himself to her through whom he had obtained health; and he subjected himself to the service of the church.

### XIII. A Blind Woman Given Sight

A certain woman had pain in one eye and applied celandine or other herbs to prevent its hurting. Not only did she gain nothing, but through the violence of the herbs the eye, swollen, was thrust from the socket and from the whole head; sewn into the membranous sac, it hung upon her face and cheeks like a little bladder, so that she had lost every hope of seeing.

Thus wholly deprived of human help, she gathered the powers of faith and hope and turned to divine aid. With her relatives she went to the church of the aforementioned Mary, Mother of God; there, with others ardently seeking her help, she kept vigil. On a certain night [Col. 1787A], during which this woman too received sight, a seven-year-old boy, crippled in his feet, was being watched there by his mother. A great crowd likewise kept vigil: some from devotion, others attending their sick.

The mother of the aforesaid boy, worn out by both vigil and grief, fell asleep. Suddenly the boy rose upright and healthy and began to walk toward the altar. Then, as the surrounding people shouted aloud, he was lifted up; then the name of the blessed Virgin was repeated a thousand times, so that by the cries of the people and the clangor of drums the still fragile walls of the church seemed about to be overthrown from their foundations.

Good Jesus, had you not foreseen this spectacle, which you yourself greatly love, when burning faith and the passionate zeal of those who love you competed to seize you, and the sacrifice of a contrite spirit was seasoned with the offering of sweet tears? Awakened by these voices, the mother, shut off from her son and pressed in by the crowd, joined their joyful and tumultuous cries with her own.

The woman who grieved over her lost eye, however, heard these cries of joy rising to heaven without rejoicing; and she broke out in these words: “O glorious and merciful Lady, now others rejoice, and your church rings full of praise; but to me, wretched woman that I am, participation in so great a joy has been denied.” While she continued these and other words dictated by her sorrow, suddenly, thinking that the eye hanging upon her face—which she had believed wholly lost—was falling into dust, she cried to those around her: “For God’s sake, bring a light here quickly, for now my eye is running down into the dust.”

For she had seemed to herself to see someone standing by and, by inserting a finger, bursting the sac which was like a little bladder. When a light was brought, they found the membrane torn, and a stream of pus and accumulated corruption flowing down over her cheeks and face to the ground, soaking the dust in a broad splash; but they found her eye bright and shining, seated wholly sound in its socket. Then they cried out to her, repeated it to her while she still did not believe, and assured her, by God and the blessed Virgin, that she had recovered health and her eye. When she discovered this and verified it by the result, she was filled with joy; and with renewed praises, the church was filled.

### XIV. A Deaf and Mute Man Healed

A certain deaf and mute man from the district of Arras [Col. 1787D], learning that some people from those regions were coming to Soissons for prayer and to seek the aid of the blessed and glorious Mary, Mother of God, joined their company and, through their daily association, had become known to them all.

On arriving, he entered the church with those entering; after remaining there briefly, he indicated to some companions standing about him that he had recovered his hearing, though the power of speech was still denied him. His companions rejoiced, and after making an offering they began, as arranged, to return; the mute man went with them.

Clerics from Arras, who had come with that company, were among them. But while they were at Soissons, intent upon seeing and hearing other things, they had not yet learned anything of the miracle begun in the mute man through his hearing. Once they were on the road, however, when the companions told them and the man himself indicated that he had recovered hearing, they were amazed and rejoiced, and blamed themselves because, with this miracle kept silent, they had offered no praises of thanksgiving to God.

At once, since they were on horseback, they returned, bringing back with them the man in whom the miracle of hearing had been manifested. They related what had occurred, presented the man as hearing keenly but not yet speaking, and gave thanks to God and the blessed Virgin, through whose merits these benefits were bestowed. Then the good and gracious Lord, and the blessed Mother of mercy, would no longer allow the faith and devotion of those who had not begrudged delaying their journey already begun, so as not to prove ungrateful in the duty of piety, to remain empty and barren.

While they waited and delayed, and while in mind they looked toward God and [Col. 1788B] the Mother of mercy, the man standing in their midst, the bond of his tongue was suddenly loosed, and he spoke properly. At this sight those clerics, now enjoying the fruit of their faith, eagerly strove to raise praises to heaven. As the bells rang out and the choir of God’s handmaids lifted *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, O God”—on high, the shout of the devout multitude mingled with confused voices, yet all sounding together in praise of God.

### XV. A Mute Boy from Cologne Healed

There was also a boy of Cologne by birth, being reared in the district of Beauvais, at a castle named Clermont. His poor mother had brought him with her from the Rhineland while he was still an infant; but since the gift of speech had not been granted him by God, he had remained mute from early childhood, now for twelve years.

It seemed good to the boy’s patrons—the boy’s name was Vasselinus—on whose alms he had been supported for five years or more, that they should bring him with them to Soissons, to the shrine of holy Mary, Mother of God. And so it was done.

On the night of the Purification of the blessed Virgin, although he was overwhelmed by the deep sleep customary in children, they compelled him nevertheless to join them in keeping vigil, for the entire church was full of watchers. After part of Matins had passed, when the responsory was begun, “Behold the miracle of the Mother of the Lord,” the boy was suddenly disturbed by the terror of a dream. For he had seemed to see a dove flying about his head and then, as if angrily and threateningly, pinching his lips and tongue.

Moved by this vision and by fear of the dove’s anger, he cried out in a very fine and piercing voice, one that seemed more that of a spirit than of a human being, so that it surpassed both the singing of girls and the noise of the whole crowd: “Holy Mary, Holy Mary!” Who was not terrified and amazed at that angelic voice, newly created, distinguishing itself entirely amid persons of every age and both sexes, and surpassing the high and still higher melodies of the virgins?

Immediately those nearest at hand—his patrons, who were watching over him for God’s sake—were the first to cry out. The entire people cried out; the multitude of the sick also raised a united cry, asking similar aid for themselves. The crash of the whole church and the sound of trumpets [Col. 1789A], now ringing through the air, and the ardor of those who love you, O God, broke through heaven itself. He was led to the altar amid the joy of the exulting Church.

Lord Jesus, who then restrained tears? Whose breast, even if stony, was not torn apart when they saw you walking once more among human beings? These are the solemn feasts which you commanded your people to offer to you; these are the celebrated days on which true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and truth.

Thus the whole Church rejoiced and together offered prayers also for those who still required healing. The boy’s patrons triumphed, their faith and works made manifest; and they brought him to the abbess and to others to whom he had been known the day before.

### XVI. A Woman Freed from a Demon

And behold, before the praises for this miracle had yet ended [Col. 1789B], a certain woman, possessed by a demon while she had scarcely recovered from childbirth, was lying in that church of the Blessed Virgin in a most dreadful frenzy; this had continued for several days, so that through her ceaseless agitation and innumerable cries she had become known to, and burdensome for, everyone.

Thus, through the working grace of God and the cooperation of the blessed Mother of mercy, she was freed from the demon. She went to the altar without needing another’s help, blaming herself and confessing herself guilty because in her ignorance, with a frenzied mouth, she had said and done many things against God and his glorious Mother. Her friends rejoiced with her and wept compassionately with her.

Then, while the strength of faith and charity had not yet grown cold, a repeated blessing of divine grace, poured out, gave permanence to their joys; and through the vigils of that entire holy night there came to be, as it were, one commonwealth of angels and human beings assembled together.

### XVII. A Mad Wealthy Man from Douai

Moreover, from the castle called Doacus (Douai), toward the district of Arras, a madman named Guarinus was brought, his hands bound behind his back, his neck fastened with iron and a huge chain. Five men could scarcely drag him, even though they drove him with whips and blows. For he was a man full of physical strength and vigorous age, and wealthy too; hence this miracle could not remain concealed from public knowledge.

By what occasion the devil had obtained power over him—whether through anger or through grief over money fraudulently taken from him, as some said—we did not sufficiently discover. But his madness, and the health later granted through God’s grace, were held to be very widely known. God allowed him, while raving, to lie in the church for several days as a spectacle to all: either that, after health was restored, he might be confounded by shame; or that, handed over to Satan for his sins, he might pay the penalty, so that while the adversary tortured him to his heart’s desire, satisfaction having been made, he might more readily release him; or that, while the bitterness of the hateful sight was prolonged before everyone’s eyes, the delayed grace of liberation might be sweeter and better known, and God more gloriously praised.

Thus he was fastened by his chain to the larger benches of the church and bound with ropes, as has been said; nevertheless he often dragged the benches and almost overpowered his guards. But what need is there to recount the madness of his words and the savagery of his deeds?

After it had seemed sufficient to you, Lord Jesus, and to your holy Mother, the hostile power was restrained from him, his understanding was restored, and he raised his eyes to heaven and glorified him who lives for ever and ever, who is able to humble the proud, bring down the arrogant from their haughtiness, and set them again before his face.

He too then went to the altar, as was customary. How devoutly and humbly he honored the image of his liberation with whatever vows and prayers he could; and what joy he gave his friends, those present, and those whom he had left at home, need not be told. Thereafter, conducting himself as a man of composed and sound mind, he mounted a horse and returned with those who had brought him back to his homeland. Once and wholly restored to sanity, he was returned to his wife, household, and friends, who had grieved and mourned for him. And not only at Soissons, where the light of joy first dawned for him, but also in those parts, praises were given to God; his healing was celebrated with such joy as though life had returned from the dead, for the love and glory of God and for the reverence and honor of the blessed and glorious Mother of God and of our Lord, the perpetual Virgin Mary.

### XVIII. Those Who Wandered Were Restored to the Road by Blessed Mary

Because report spread abroad of these and other most famous miracles of God, Christ, and the Virgin Mother, people of every age, both sexes, and diverse conditions came and gathered from far and wide to the city of Soissons out of love and devotion for the holy Virgin.

Then men and women from the mountains of Hainaut, as many as twenty-five, set out upon the road leading to Saint-Quentin. As night was already approaching, they hurried because fear of robbers compelled them to hasten on that road, for the region was exposed to marauders. They entered a certain forest, where, because of the now very dense darkness of night and their ignorance of the routes, they lost the right way. Wandering, they retained not only no hope of reaching the lodging they had expected to attain earlier, but not even certainty of their situation or progress.

All were dismayed, particularly because, exhausted by a long day’s journey extended into the night—and the women especially—their spirits were worn down within them by fatigue and weariness. They sat down, tired, in a thicket. Some feared everything that might happen; others, stronger and more active, searched here and there for the lost road.

Then, not far from the place where they had halted, they saw a whiteness of immense brightness, made far more conspicuous by the darkness of the night, yet promising far more gentleness than terror. In the midst of that splendor they saw what seemed to be the image of a woman of virginal appearance, whose snowy garment and the radiance of her divine and heavenly face, distinctly set apart and shaded by their own vision, seemed to have all brightness surrounding her in dutiful attendance.

[Col. 1791A] This vision was so certain and so clear that those who beheld it retained it most effectively in mind, and later recounted from memory her gesture, appearance, and the linen of her sleeves fluttering in the moving air. All saw it, and in wonder all cried out. All agreed upon one decision: to go where God was calling them.

They rose, made better by good hope; whoever could follow more swiftly did not wait for the slower. In their desire to grasp sooner the vision that had appeared, they hastened through rough places and thickets, however forbidding, as though at the very same moment when they had reached the definite place of that brightness set there. Yet they most certainly found the public road, and, gathered into one body, rejoiced that they had been restored to the road they had lost.

Walking upon it and coming to a house of hermits situated nearby beside the road, they received the answer that this was the public and surest route leading to Saint-Quentin. This miracle is confirmed by as many witnesses as there were persons present—no fewer than twenty-five, as we have said. All of them came joyfully to the shrine of the blessed and glorious Virgin; after fulfilling what they had vowed, they returned joyfully to their homes. No less remarkable is what follows.

### XIX. A Woman Who Gave Birth to Stones

At a village called Kala (Chelle), in the territory of Soissons, itself a possession of the mother church of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius [Col. 1791C], a certain woman was in labor and, because of the difficulty of the birth, began to be in danger. Worn down by continuous pains for three weeks, she was very near death.

Persuaded therefore by neighboring women, she vowed that, if she were freed from the imminent danger of death, she would go barefoot to the church of the blessed and glorious Mary, Mother of God. She vowed, and was delivered—but in a wondrous manner.

First she expelled three stones from her womb. The first was the size of a goose’s egg; the second nearly the size of a hen’s egg; the third no smaller than a French walnut. Once these stones had been discharged, the birth of an infant immediately followed; the child received the grace of baptism and survived for a few days.

As soon as she could after recovering from this illness, barefoot and clothed in wool, as she had promised, she went to the church of our Lady—indeed, the Lady of the entire human race and Queen of the angels—carrying with her the stones, witnesses of her ordeal and proofs of the divine work. Neighboring women who had been present through the entire event accompanied her.

She also offered at the altar a candle whose wick and length she had extended to the measure of her body while she was still in danger in childbirth, and which she had kept until then. She herself gave a most truthful account of her danger and of the deliverance granted through the blessed Virgin: “These stones,” she said—producing the stones—“bear witness even if I am silent.” Therefore, after praise had been given to God Most High, as was customary, those stones were pierced and hung up for those who came to see the miracles; and for some time they furnished a visible memorial of this event.

### XX. A Paralytic Healed

A certain paralytic lay for a very long time in the portico of the same church. With the strength of his whole body dissolved, he had also lost the power of speech. Every hour was grievous to him, but especially in winter, when the cold was doubled by the severity of the season and his illness. As his limbs stiffened from the violence of the disease, he seemed to feel piercing pains, like spears, boring through his bones and marrow.

Then he began to send pitiable cries toward heaven and, because he could not speak, to repeat terrifying roars. Moved by compassion for his sufferings, many stopped and offered vows, prayers, and compassion for him, that God and the blessed Virgin might help him. At last, when it pleased her, divine grace regarded their devotion and the wretched man’s distress, and perfectly healed the sick man: every pain vanished, and he received both bodily strength and full power of speech.
