Those who had sympathized with him in sickness rejoiced with him in health. Since so evident a miracle had been performed here and could not remain hidden, praises and thanksgiving for it also were offered to God and the Mother of the Lord.

### XXI. A Blind Woman Given Sight

A certain married woman from Blericurt (Blérencourt), a village near Cociacum (Coucy) [Col. 1792C], was struck with blindness. She too was brought to seek the aid of the blessed Virgin, and for several days sat there, both waiting for and requesting divine help.

She would likewise have sat in vain before the presence of Truth, so long as she wished to conceal the truth. It happened on one of those days that a priest from Austrechia (Autresche), accompanied by crosses and a large company of parishioners, entered the church of the Virgin Mother of the Lord with praises. After the prayers and vows had been completed, the leading man of that village—that is, Autresche—recognized there his kinswoman, the aforesaid woman, embracing the altar. Asking the cause of her presence, he learned the misfortune that had happened to her.

Then, with the abbess Mathilde present, he said: “Deservedly, my kinswoman, have you been struck with such blindness, because, although you are a servant of our Lady Saint Mary, you renounced her lordship and denied that you belonged to her and to her household. Therefore confess the truth, if you wish to obtain any help from the Mother of Truth.”

Admonished by the word of one who loved her and by the scourge of divine punishment, she accepted the counsel. Once she acknowledged and confessed the truth regarding the lordship which she had denied, immediately her eyes and face were flooded with brightness. Having made this declaration of fidelity, needing no guide, she joyfully returned home.

### XXII. A Woman Who Could Not Enter the Church

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1131, on the feast day of Luke the Evangelist, God did not disdain again to glorify his name also by an unusual miracle. Pope Innocent, driven from Rome by his rival, had been honorably received by the churches on this side of the Alps and by the kings and princes of the earth. He had recently dedicated the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons, situated across the river.

For that solemnity so great a multitude of people had assembled as can scarcely be described, both on account of the Dedication and in order to pay their vows and prayers to Mary, the blessed Virgin and Mother of God, in her church. Among the others was a woman from the district of Laon, namely from the castle called Ruminiacus (Rumigny). Not forgetful of her sins, she entered the monastery of the blessed Virgin with others and proceeded forward; when, behold, she was barred from entering by an invisible force. Twice and three times she attempted it and was driven back more forcibly. Mingling with the crowd and rashly forcing herself in, she accomplished no more.

Then, as divine judgment pressed upon her, because the present affliction gave understanding to the hearing, her accusing conscience at last—though late—moved by the greatness of her guilt, she began to tremble throughout her whole body and to be tormented in all her limbs by excessive fear. Falling face down and feeling the hand of divine judgment upon herself, she urgently begged with loud cries for the help of those around her and for their prayers to God on her behalf.

A summoned priest appeared, already prepared to celebrate Mass. Trusting in his office and in the priestly vestment with which he was clothed, he raised the wretched woman as she lay and, giving her his hand, tried to lead her into the church while crowds pressed forward. But, as she later related, her feet were weighted with so great a burden that she thought masses of lead were tied to them.

She accomplished nothing, whether by her own effort, the priest’s assistance, or the forceful pressure of the people. She could be led right or left and could move freely like the others; but when she prepared to enter the church, a secret force opposed her more violently.

Then the people’s cry rose, and there were the sorrow and tears of the crowd, lamenting their sins and their judgment in that woman. What then? What else remained but to appease the divine countenance through confession, and thus more securely implore his mercy? She wished to confess to that priest; but by what judgment this happened we do not know: as she herself said, she was in no way able to do so. Pressed by pain and fear, she wished to proclaim her sins publicly, but was prevented.

Another priest having been summoned, she confessed, with groaning and sorrow, as truly and sincerely as she could—indeed, as was necessary for one being reconciled through truth to Truth. She begged the priest to declare it publicly, so that God might spare her in proportion as she was covered with confession and shame out of fear of him. But he, judging more moderately, suppressed it and said what was then prescribed.

Having received absolution, reborn and renewed, she began, drenched in tears, to stretch out suppliant hands to the surrounding crowd, so that she who distrusted her own merits might be helped by theirs. She begged the abbess of the place to come; she came, and when she gave her hand and began to lead her, then there was a great cry; then the thickly gathered multitude gave tears and groans; then the passion of burning charity and the passion of frenzied pity followed her as she went, broke through the air, penetrated heaven itself, and offered God the violence that he chose to endure, wresting from him the mercy that he was not unwilling to grant.

Once she had been brought into the church, how great were the praises and thanksgivings offered to God and to Mary, the glorious Mother of God, cannot be expressed, since it is unspeakable.

### XXIII. A Woman’s Swollen Womb Healed during the Easter Feast

At the castle called Nigella (Nesle), situated in the district of Vermandois, a certain woman suffered anxiously from an excessive swelling that distended her womb and limbs. While her husband hurried to bring her medical help [Col. 1794B], she said she could not endure such a long delay. Pressed by the violence of the illness, she urgently demanded that a horse be prepared for her as quickly as possible, already trusting in faith that she would obtain health from the Mother of God, if she should merit to touch the threshold.

She therefore departed for the city of Soissons with her husband. Led to the altar of the Blessed Virgin, she laid heavy hands upon it in fear and, trusting in faith, asked that a ring be drawn from her finger, though no force could remove it, saying: “Sweet Lady, draw this ring from my finger, and it shall be yours.”

This was immediately done. From Thursday before Easter, she endured the swelling of her womb, by which she was almost bursting, until, after that feast-day had passed and the following night had come, she fell asleep and was perfectly healed. Awakening and feeling no heaviness at all, she rushed swiftly to the altar. Her husband, awakened and alarmed, said: “Where are you rushing, wretched woman, now about to die?” She replied: “No; for through God’s grace and the mercy of the blessed Virgin I am now wholly delivered, and I suffer no pain or remaining effect of my former illness.”

Her illness, previously very well known, soon gave way to a healing celebrated by all, and the news spread everywhere of what the Lord had just done. For this, praises were given to God and to the blessed Virgin, Mother of his Christ; and joy was enlarged during the Easter feast.

### XXIV. A Sick Man Healed by Bread That Had Touched the Slipper

“Say to the righteous that it is well, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds” [Col. 1794D]. Now the righteous person is righteous by faith, and “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1); and the fruit of faith is righteousness. There is no fruit of righteousness except from the root of faith. Therefore faith is resourceful in finding means by which it may bear fruit.

Thus it did not suffice for faithful people seeking remedies to go to the place dedicated to the blessed Virgin, where she customarily bestowed benefits. Those from distant regions who despaired of having easy access there used, even after receiving remedies, to take away with them some memorial from that church—wood, earth, or bread that had touched the blessed Virgin’s slipper—so that, protected more securely by this aid, they might not fear adverse illness.

There is a place, a castle called Batpalmas (Bapaume); and a place called Latgniacurtis (Lagnicourt) [Col. 1795A], where a certain young man, already of advanced age, was tormented by epilepsy to such an extent that almost every day, as many as ten times, his wretched limbs were dashed against the ground, to the horror of those watching.

What was his unhappy mother to do, compelled daily to behold death within her household? What feelings did she bear, as she warmed in her lap her son’s foaming mouth and limbs stiffened by deathly cold, reviving them, as it were, with her native warmth, and was compelled to give birth to him anew? One day she remembered that one of her neighbors had returned a few days earlier from the shrine of the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and had brought with him bread that had touched her slipper. He frequently distributed it to sick persons who asked for it, and they recovered.

Hurrying to that man’s house, burning with a faith sharpened by the inward pains of a mother’s womb, she pleaded with maternal affection that she might be worthy to receive some of that bread sanctified by God for her son’s need, as a remedy for her own pain—she who was a mother seeking to call back to life the dying man who suffered so grievously.

But he tried to dismiss the importunity of her plea, alleging that scarcely a small amount remained to him, since he had distributed the greater part of that health-giving bread to people suffering from similar illnesses. At last, overcome by the sorrow and insistence of the frantic woman, he took a little from that little and gave it to the wretched mother.

She considered herself blessed by so great a gift and thought that in the tiny fragment she had received her son’s life. Already made better by the eagerness of faith and hope, she hurried to her son, carrying with her food of life and health. When the young man received and swallowed it, he suddenly recovered perfectly from so great an illness. For it belongs to God to give without measure, and thereafter no trace of his former affliction, nor any mark, seemed to remain.

These are the fruits of resourceful faith. “He who tends his fig tree shall eat its fruit.” Through these transitory fruits we are invited to those that minister eternal life, provided that we have faith proportionate to them; for to each is given according to the measure of faith. Hence one kind of faith merits these temporal things, and quite another merits eternal things.

### XXV. Two Young Squires Released from Captivity

Two young squires from the district of Laon were captured and taken beyond the forest called Tereschia (Thiérache), to the castle called Avesnia, and both were put in stocks. While they were kept there, the elder remembered that, for the building of the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Soissons, some people carried and offered, among other needed things, iron nails.

He therefore vowed that he would bring one hundred nails there if the blessed and glorious Mother of God would help him and free him from captivity. Immediately, before his very eyes, the biting timbers opened, and he drew out his foot free. Yet something still remained to be said; sitting there, he began to await the night more suitable for escape.

Then he said to his companion: “I indeed am free through the grace of God and the help of holy Mary, Mother of God, and could go away if what remains of the day did not hinder me. For I have vowed to the blessed Virgin that I shall bring one hundred iron nails for building her church. And behold, you see me free. If you did the same, and placed faith in her, she would free you also.”

“Certainly,” replied the younger, “I would bring not only one hundred, but a thousand nails, if she had mercy on me so that I might be freed.”

That same night the man who had first been released crossed the barriers and guards and escaped to safety without anyone opposing him. The one left behind, after learning by experience how great and what kind of good faith was, abandoned by his companion and stirred to better things by an evident benefit, then began from his anxious heart to call upon our Lady Saint Mary, that she too might bring help to him, a sinner.

A little later the man holding him captive, alarmed and fearing that he might be taken away from him there, decided to transfer him to safer custody. While he did so, that captive escaped safe and unharmed by the grace of God. He was a nephew of Milo of Asceacum. As soon as he could, he came barefoot to the church of his liberator; not ungrateful for so great a benefit, he joyfully and eagerly related the entire sequence of events.

There are many things whose order we cannot set forth, because they are many and exceed the poverty of our ability; nevertheless, that we may speak at least briefly, we wish to pass some over in silence.

### XXVI. A Mother Who Recovered Her Son

[Col. 1796C]

At Saint-Riquier in Ponthieu, a town in the district of Amiens, a certain noblewoman, though herself short of money, had given her son as a pledge to a moneylender and excessively harsh creditor for many marks of silver. As days multiplied, the sum of the interest increased; consequently, unless they sold their land, the boy could not be redeemed by his parents.

Then the mother, in whose heart a deeper sense of grief had fixed itself, wholly deprived of and despairing of human help, turned to divine aid and to the gracious Mother of mercy, who is accustomed to hear those contrite in spirit. One day, compelled by maternal sorrow that pressed on without any relief, she went to the place where her son was held under guard and in chains, that she might at least refresh her miserable eyes by seeing her son, who was paying the penalty for his father’s necessity.

Arriving at Saint-Riquier, a town inhabited by a great multitude of people, she suddenly found her son in the middle of the street, fastened merely with iron bands fitted to his body for security. She took him up before the people’s eyes and, with no one forbidding or resisting, lifted him onto her horse and carried him back. How much joy and happiness she showed, and what thanks she offered to her glorious Virgin benefactress when she came to her home in distress of spirit and humiliated body, is not easy to say.

### XXVII. A Blind Woman Given Sight

A certain blind woman from the territory of Le Mans heard [Col. 1797A] of the fame of the miracles that the Lord performed at Soissons through the favor of his blessed Virgin Mother. She therefore vowed that she would go barefoot to seek her aid. She vowed from a contrite and faithful heart, and immediately received sight.

### XXVIII. Ralph Cantellus
Thomas, lord of the castle called Coucy, situated in the district of Laon, was about to go to the king of England. He wished to take with him one of his retainers, Ralph, surnamed Cantellus, because he considered him more faithful to himself. He therefore ordered him to make ready. When all things for this journey had been prepared, that Ralph was suddenly seized by an adverse illness: all his sinews began to contract, and he became nearly useless in all his limbs, while sharp pains, as though boring into them, pierced his bones and marrow. Because of this affliction, [Col. 1797B] he was excused from the duty of the journey. For the disease was very like a fiery plague: it ranged through his limbs, feeding beneath his stretched skin and tearing the flesh away from his bones. Thus he endured the most acute pains for the time being, but escaped an outwardly visible deformity because help came quickly. For as soon as he could, he sought the house of the blessed Mother of God, Mary, begging aid for himself in his misery. It was the day before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.

He sat before the altar, clothed and shod in his customary dress, distressed as the sharp pains came upon him, and dripping with sweat over his whole body. Now brought to awareness of himself, he was compelled, in place of an offering, to confess his unrighteousness and sins, saying: “And deservedly do you suffer these things, wretched man, [Col. 1797C] and eat the fruit of your ungodliness. For you sowed pains, and you reap them; and, as is fitting, you receive them. What crime indeed have you ever omitted? What evil have you not perpetrated? By what adulteries have you not been defiled? Or to what woman have you ever shown honour? By how many murders are your hands full of blood, whether by deed or counsel? How many burnings or violations of churches have you procured? How many thefts and robberies have you stirred up; how many wars and lawsuits have you aroused by your counsel and your tongue? How many acts of gluttony, how many drunken excesses, have you swallowed down? What frauds have you not practised?

“Now therefore these things are deservedly turned back upon your head, wretched man; now you pay the punishments you have earned. [Col. 1797D] You are righteous, O Lord, and you exercise righteous judgment upon me. For I have always stood forth as the standard-bearer of every evil; and, forsaking you, my Creator and Redeemer, I have always carried out the will of the enemy. And you, blessed Virgin, pious Lady, Mother also of my Lord: although I am the greatest of sinners, you now exact just punishments from my body—a body unclean, a body foul-smelling, a body worthy of sulphur and the fire of hell. You now exact just punishments from a deceitful soul, a faithless soul, a soul which bore the image of the devil through unbridled pride, and the likeness of horse and mule through filthy and unclean lust.

“Come then, Lord; come then, Lady: double and triple punishments and torments upon me, because no human body has more justly deserved already to endure the pains of hell. For the earth ought neither to have borne nor carried so great a sinner; and deservedly it is long since it should have swallowed up such a sinner. [Col. 1798A] Wretched tears, why have you ceased? Why do you not attend this funeral body, now almost dead, to burial? Perform the funeral service while it is permitted, which deservedly no one will perform for one criminal and hateful to all. Come, unhappy soul! Behold: where you see your miserable body placed in such dreadful death—a body which always obeyed your desires, always served your impieties. And this body, breathed upon by the heat of hell, is now being burned; but you, after a little while, will endure dreadful fires and flaming balls. Alas for miserable me! Both what I suffer will endure, and the death which I await is eternal. Woe, woe, woe, to the wretched sinner most justly condemned!”

While he uttered these and similar things publicly before all, [Col. 1798B] sweat flowing from every limb, he compelled those seeing and hearing him to grief and tears. But behold: suddenly the gracious Lady and the gracious Lord, who does not will the death of a sinner but rather that he be converted and live, brought relief when the pains ceased. He began to recover, and to utter other voices—voices of joy and exultation; thanksgiving and a voice of praise were heard from his mouth. It was the evening hour of the day, and, springing to his feet, sound and whole, he ran and embraced the altar. Not unmindful of so great a benefit, not long afterward, when his journey had been prepared, he set out for Jerusalem.

### XXIX. Concerning Two Women Burning and Extinguished

Two women from the monastery of Nider [Col. 1798C] came to Soissons. One of them displayed the horrifying spectacle of a cheek consumed by fire; the other carried before her a hand and arm consumed by wasting fire, with putrid and pallid flesh, offensive to all. Having fulfilled their vows, they were perfectly healed in the house of the blessed Virgin. Only a rosy colour remained on the surface of the skin, as though inscriptions of former praise, in remembrance of their virtues. The commanding Virgin, most worthy of every praise, did not wish these to be erased or to fall from memory; they remained like the marks of life and death.

### XXX. Concerning the New Fire

The year of the Lord, reckoned from the Incarnation, 1131, was beginning—the twenty-third year of Louis [Col. 1798D] and the second of his son Philip. On the day of Saint Vincent the Martyr, while Mass was being celebrated and the priest was seated after the prayer of the Mass introit, one of the two candles which by custom were always kept at the altar every day until the end had burned entirely away, while the other still retained its usual condition. But the sister serving at the altar, frightened and hurrying, zealously tried to replace the candle. Snatching one of those hidden in the chest so that she might promptly remedy the situation, she sought a light; yet, while bringing it to the burning candle, she did not impart flame, and, through careless mishap, extinguished even the candle that was burning, having knocked it down upon the altar.

Then, troubled and considering herself dead, she was compelled to seek fire from the kitchen. But the deacon, alarmed during the office of Mass that the fire had failed, quickly seized the candle lying devoid of flame. As he handed it to the subdeacon so that he might quickly fetch fire, suddenly, between the hand of the one giving it and that of the one [Col. 1799A] preparing to receive it, the candle was kindled with a new fire. Seeing this miracle in his own hands, the deacon was struck with astonishment and deprived of his strength; he was compelled to lean upon the chest which then stood nearby. This became so celebrated and well known because it occurred in a place which lacked no multitude of people at any hour of the day. They therefore give praise to God Most High; and, with sounding drums, melodious sweetness, chanted far and wide, rises to heaven, and the whole city resounds with praises of Christ. With this new fire all the lamps of the church were also lit, and many of the faithful hastened to carry it into their homes.

### XXXI. Concerning a Certain Man Wonderfully Freed from an Illness of the Foot

[Col. 1799B]

But in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102, while a certain man named Robert, from the village called Joüy—which village belongs to the same church—was keeping vigil in the church of the Blessed Virgin among the others, he obtained healing of his foot in the following manner. The illness was beyond remedy: his entire foot had swollen, and was wounded with many pustules, so that continual discharge of pus corrupted the surrounding air with such a stench that it became intolerable to everyone. Therefore the guardians were compelled to tell him to leave, because they could endure him no longer. He had already remained there for a very long time, and, wholly despaired of by physicians, his entire foot was dissolving into decay.

He left the church unwillingly, intending to return to his own people, from whom he hoped [Col. 1799C], because of kinship, that service and compassion would be provided him. Yet as he departed he called the blessed Mary to witness in this manner: “O glorious Lady, although I have awaited your help in this place for many days and have not yet received it, nevertheless, though my limbs rot and waste away, the faith of my soul neither wastes away nor fails. I depart unwillingly, but I am compelled to go out. Yet you, pious, merciful, and commanding Lady, wherever I may be, can obtain health for me from your Son. For I am yours—yours, *caesus capite a* [perhaps *servus a*], from my forebears. [Col. 1799D] Therefore I do not merely ask grace, but also demand the due which you are accustomed to render to those who are yours. My flame burns. Lord Jesus, look upon the servant of your Mother. Behold, I withdraw and die because I am torn away from you. Most high God, remember your servant and the servant of your Mother. My heart is afflicted with renewed pains because I depart from you. At this sight, my bodily pain is soothed and almost passes into forgetfulness.”

Having said this, he went away. When he returned home, at first, as usual, he was patiently borne by his household; but as time passed, he began to become an object of weariness and disgust. For the stench was so great that at night, when he put his foot out into the air because of the heat, neither his wife nor his children could endure it. Yet he did not cease from prayer, but with unremitting cries called upon the help of the blessed Virgin.

When it seemed sufficient, and when the gracious Lady was pleased—not by the sufferer’s pain, but by the persevering faith [Col. 1800A] of the believer and lover—she appeared to him one night as he slept, in such splendour as mortal eyes could not endure. Starry light struck back against the gaze of the one looking, and he could bear its brightness no longer. Then it seemed to him that with one hand she supported his neck, setting him upright to sit upon the bed, while with the other hand she held and stretched out his foot. Awakened by the novelty of the vision, the man then tested his ability to walk and learned by experience that he was perfectly healed.

How great was his gladness, how much joy he caused his little household, how great were the thanks he gave to God and the glorious Virgin, is not easy to say. Unable to contain himself, he prepared to return to the church of his Lady and healer; in his excessive exultation, nothing could be done quickly enough, and every delay seemed long to him. Entering the church, he approached the altar. [Col. 1800B] When he came to it crying aloud, how many tears he poured out there with joy and thanksgiving, because through the persevering and unwavering faith of his heart he had obtained health of body as well, God himself knows better—he who forms words of devotion and holds them within himself by living understanding.

Torn away from the altar like one possessed by Bacchic frenzy, he began to run about within the Holy of Holies, striking the ground with his healthy foot. When people asked the cause of so great a joy, he answered nothing else, saying: “This is the foot of my Lady Saint Mary; this is the foot of my Lady Saint Mary.” Again and again striking the ground with his foot, he explained, to those who insisted, the manner and cause of such exultation: [Col. 1800C] “Am I not,” he said, “the man from Joüy, belonging to my Lady Saint Mary, whom you expelled from the church because of the intolerable stench of my foot? Has not the pious Virgin, my Lady, Mother of my Lord Jesus Christ, healed me in this and this manner?”

By relating these things he easily established the truth of his words: the person was known, since he was a dependent of the church; and the fact itself was displayed, since the foot which they had seen as a putrid and foul-smelling corpse was now shown whole and strong. The person was known, and the miracle evident. At once the drums gave forth their sound, and the praise of the Lord and the glorious Virgin for power and mercy was celebrated publicly.

[Col. 1800D] Times of affliction and misery will come, in which devout minds will recall these days that we are now spending in peace and in abundance of temporal goods, when the Church is venerated and honoured by every people and religion is more widespread than in former times. When the faithful recall these things and compare their persecutions with these prosperous circumstances, they will grieve more deeply. Therefore we believe that in these very days so great and so many miracles are performed in the churches of the Holy Mother of God, God himself bearing witness by signs, wonders, and diverse mighty works to the incarnation of his Son, so that, because we hope the hostile time of Antichrist is near, the faithful may die all the more steadfastly for this truth in proportion as it is celebrated with the more certain testimony and praise of all nations.

## After the Year 1131: Frowin, Abbot of the Monastery of Mount of the Angels among the Helvetians

[Col. 1801]

## Notice

(D. Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. VI, Appendix, p. 657)

In the celebrated monastery of Einsiedeln, among other things, we found two codices containing the works of Frowin: first a monk of Einsiedeln, then abbot at Mount of the Angels among the Upper Woodland Helvetians, after Saint Aldhelm, who was the first to preside over that place from the foundation of the monastery by blessed Conrad, about the year 1125.

The first codex, in quarto, as it is called, contains an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer. The second, in folio, contains seven books *On the Praise of Free Choice*, as the author himself entitles his work—or rather, concerning the principal questions of theology—which Frowin treats learnedly, solidly, and, for his age, elegantly, against the errors of certain innovators, perhaps against Peter Abelard. For at the same time Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg in Bavaria, is reported to have written a little work against the disciples of Peter Abelard. It is therefore less surprising if the report of this sect reached the Helvetians and prompted Frowin to write.

It would be desirable that our Einsiedeln monks, whose interest in this matter is greatest and who already have this latter work copied out and prepared for the press, should bring it to light in their own printing. Meanwhile, as a foretaste of the future edition, we publish here Frowin’s prologue to the exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, and likewise the preface to the seven books *On Free Choice*, together with their chapter headings. At the beginning the author places the following verses:

> Live, I pray, Berhtold; I ask that the Lord be *filholt* to you.  
>   
> [Note: [Col. 1801A] That is, “very friendly” in German.]  
>   
> This book teaches that I am free through you.  
>   
> I vowed this book; now I discharge my promise to you.  
>   
> It is right, if you are wise, that you receive it gratefully.

[Col. 1801]

## Here Begins the Prologue of Frowin, Abbot at Mount of the Angels, to the Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer

[Col. 1801A] Although my memory is frail, yet I remember firmly that your most sweet affection, O venerable priest Berhtold, required of my littleness that I should display the capacity of my small talent in an explanation of the Lord’s Prayer. I hesitated long and much within myself about this matter. For I considered whether it would be better to obey the charity of one who asks and thereby expose myself to the bites of the envious, or to refuse what charity has commanded and thereby perhaps offend God, who is charity. But my mind at last settled upon the judgment that I considered it safer to have God propitious than to be exposed to the envy of detractors.

Accordingly, immediately knowing that I was putting my hands into flames, I resolved to undertake the task you imposed upon me: [Col. 1802A] not to set forth new things, but to gather together certain matters which the Fathers have said, though scatteredly, concerning the Lord’s Prayer. It is therefore your responsibility to pray that the propitious Divinity may help me complete what it inspired me to will. I shall therefore endeavour, according to my ability, to explain how sufficient and fitting is that prayer which is called the Lord’s Prayer.

“No man fails to know that God created man with free choice,” etc.

(At the end: Here ends the book of explanation by Abbot Frowin.

> This I pray, this I urge: say, reader, in devout prayer,  
>   
> May the Lord make Frowin blessed.  
>   
> May the heavenly divine power give him true light,  
>   
> For he laboured that the writings of this book might come to be.)

[Col. 1801]

## Eight Books by the Same Frowin, on Free Choice, Addressed to the Monk Adelbert

> Frowin caused these pages, full of choice doctrine,  
> To be written: Christ, do good to him.

## Here Begins the Short Preface to the Following Work

[Col. 1801B]

I have taken care to comply with your desire, brother Adelbert, especially because I have perceived that you are vigorous both in the keen sharpness [Col. 1802B] of an agile intellect and in reliance upon the light of assisting grace, and that you are watchful in the pursuits of investigating truth. I have therefore assembled this little work, excerpted [Col. 1803A] from the writings of those teachers who have shone either in our own age or in an earlier one. In it I have endeavoured to insert judgments concerning free choice and other questions which I believed would be most acceptable to your judgment and most powerful against the errors of certain persons who glory in the inventions of their novelties.

I wished to give this codex the title *On the Praise of Free Choice*, because it is wholly directed to the end of commending how greatly free choice is divinely endowed with glory above the other powers which rational nature has received from God, its maker. Yet because this common intention of praise has separate subjects, I have thought it good to divide the little book into parts, both that weariness might be lessened for the reader and that understanding might emerge more easily, as the mind breathes [Col. 1803B] through the individual distinctions and, refreshed by breathing, is renewed for what remains.

The first part contains what free choice is; and, if it speaks anywhere concerning its corruption, it does not thereby forget its purpose. For where vice is censured, integrity and virtue are, by contrast, exalted. The second shows that God is perceived, though faintly, by free choice even in the present life, and that in the future he is happily known only by free choice. The third extols free choice in that it shows it able to judge all other things and judged by none, and that within it is found all knowledge of the disciplines. The fourth compares the two powers of free choice with Jacob’s two wives, and his sons with the powers of reason and will, and treats many other matters on the same subject. The fifth attributes to it the image of God [Col. 1803C] and the mirror through which its Creator must be investigated. The sixth instructs it to contemplate the substance of God. The seventh directs it onto the way of faith by which it returns to the homeland of vision.

Since, therefore, this codex demonstrates that all knowledge and wisdom, justice and blessedness, consist and are founded in free choice, I have accordingly entitled it *On the Praise of Free Choice*. For it attributes many things to free choice by which it appears praiseworthy. But because divine help must be invoked even in the smallest matters, and without it no beginning is rightly founded, I pray before all else that the truth of him whose divine charity made me willing to write may be present with me as I write.

## Index of the Chapters of Book I

[Col. 1803D]

Chapter I. What free choice is, and that will is understood in three ways.

Chapter II. That will as instrument is simple, will as disposition is twofold, and will as use is manifold.

Chapter III. How those three wills may be distinguished.

Chapter IV. That although the will as instrument is said to perform all human works, God is more truly said to work all things in three ways.

Chapter V. How the two wills which are dispositions differ.

Chapter VI. That every good or bad merit proceeds from the two wills which are dispositions.

Chapter VII. Why the will is so prone to evil, [Col. 1804A] though it was not created so; and what in man is the honour of God.

Chapter VIII. That the will, having abandoned justice, cannot return to justice by itself.

Chapter IX. Which will is free choice.

Chapter X. Various definitions of free choice, with the reasons for them appended.

Chapter XI. That no substance, action, or any essence is just except justice, nor unjust except injustice; and that nothing but the will is punished or delighted.

Chapter XII. What God or man has in good or evil works.

Chapter XIII. Why rational nature is praised for its justice.

Chapter XIV. That injustice is nothing and does nothing, although it is the cause why evil works are done.

Chapter XV. What evil is, and that there are two evils.

Chapter XVI. That God does not punish man for nothing.

Chapter XVII. That evils arise only from goods [Col. 1804B] and can exist only in goods.

Chapter XVIII. Definitions of dispositions and authorities on the same matter, to prove that will is not evil in itself; that the same motion, though not in the same form, is virtue and vice; and certain matters concerning the causes and disturbances of the mind; what confession accomplishes; and that virtue is injured only by its contrary vice.

Chapter XIX. That by the mercy or wrath of God the human will is inclined toward evils or goods.

Chapter XX. That it is good not only that goods exist, but also that evils exist; and that even what occurs without God’s will is not contrary to God’s will.

Chapter XXI. Enumeration of the goods which are from God.

Chapter XXII. How God is known through his works, and how useful this knowledge is.

Chapter XXIII. That original sin is sin absolutely speaking.

Chapter XXIV. On what grounds infants are subject to Adam’s sin and evil, [Col. 1804C] and by what justice Christ is exempted from it.

Chapter XXV. Why it is called original sin, and what it is.

Chapter XXVI. How infants are said to have sin immediately upon conception, although sin is in no part of a human being except the rational will, which they do not yet possess.

Chapter XXVII. How one should understand that man has lost free choice, although it is natural to man.

Chapter XXVIII. How the first man lost freedom from sin and from misery, although they cannot be lost after they have been possessed; whence comes the defect that we do not do what we will; and that perfection of will suffices for every good.

Chapter XXIX. That the image and likeness of God are contained in three freedoms; that freedom of choice is always equal, while the other two freedoms are possessed unequally in different places. [Col. 1804D]

Chapter XXX. That the will is compelled entirely by no one, unless perhaps by itself; and in what respect that which is called free choice is said to be free.

Chapter XXXI. That grace establishes, rather than nullifies, free choice; that God works human salvation in three ways; and where human merit lies.

Chapter XXXII. That some receive true love of God but do not receive perseverance in it.

Chapter XXXIII. The question: if the first man did not possess perseverance, how was he without vice?

Chapter XXXIV. What grace the first man received; and that there are different helps, different freedoms of will, and different powers of perseverance.

Chapter XXXV. Why some who are truly righteous do not receive the gift of perseverance.

Chapter XXXVI. A necessary argument that good [Col. 1805A] will is from the grace of God; that without good will we receive or possess nothing salutary from God; and why good works are our merits, although they are only from God’s gift.

Chapter XXXVII. On the harmony of free choice and God’s foreknowledge.

Chapter XXXVIII. On the harmony of free choice and God’s predestination.

Chapter XXXIX. The question whether faith is in our power, and what it is for something to be in our power.

Chapter XL. The question whether a human being can be without sin in this life, although no example of this exists.

## Book II

Chapter I. An inquiry into how we know justice and blessedness, since no one can love what he does not know merely from faith.

Chapter II. Many authorities of the holy Fathers that God is seen even in this life. [Col. 1805B]

Chapter III. The difference between believing and seeing.

Chapter IV. A definition of knowing, and a careful inquiry whether God is now merely believed or also known.

Chapter V. What we love in saints whom we do not see.

Chapter VI. That one who loves a brother must love love itself, and thereby God, because God is love; and therefore knows and sees God because he knows and sees love.

Chapter VII. That God and neighbour are loved through the love which is God; and that faith does not make us love God as wholly unknown and unloved, but makes us know and love more fully him whom we have known and loved.

Chapter VIII. That in the good which is God we see that nothing could have been except what ought to have been.

Chapter IX. That even the ungodly see eternity and rightly judge many things by the rules of truth, which is God.

Chapter X. Why we are not blessed when we see God, which is blessedness. [Col. 1805C]

Chapter XI. That all know blessedness, but not all know where it is or who is blessed.

Chapter XII. What the image of God in man is, and that its perfection is eternal life.

Chapter XIII. What the good of man is; that it is threefold; and how man’s true honour is lost.

Chapter XIV. On human intellectual capacity.

Chapter XV. That some foolishly promise themselves a blessedness greater than God’s own.

Chapter XVI. On the words of Saint Augustine by which some carelessly affirm that the righteous in the future kingdom of God will see God with bodily eyes.

Chapter XVII. Saint Augustine is introduced, setting forth and explaining Saint Ambrose’s statements on the same question.

Chapter XVIII. Saint Augustine’s arguments against those who think that God will be seen with bodily eyes.

[Col. 1805D] Chapter XIX. Against those who say that the statements of Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine adduced to prove the future vision of God should be understood of the vision of God in the present life.

Chapter XX. Statements of Cassiodorus and Jerome concerning the future vision of God.

Chapter XXI. On the question, and matters predicated in themselves which are also predicated conjunctively, and conversely.

Chapter XXII. Division of the question.

Chapter XXIII. Division of the answer.

Chapter XXIV. What determination is and where it should be placed.

Chapter XXV. What confirmation and controversy are, and what an argument properly is.

Chapter XXVI. Division of the argument, and what discourse is argumentation.

Chapter XXVII. Division of argumentation.

Chapter XXVIII. A division of logic, and which affirmation and negation are properly opposed.

[Col. 1806A] Chapter XXIX. Division of topics, with an explanation of some of them.

Chapter XXX. The opinion of those who say that genera and species are not merely words but also things.

Chapter XXXI. Definition of opposites, and explanation of certain topics.

Chapter XXXII. On sophisms.

Chapter XXXIII. On proposition, truth, and falsehood.

Chapter XXXIV. Division and exposition of proposition.

Chapter XXXV. On modal propositions, and also on others.

Chapter XXXVI. On the rules of inference.

Chapter XXXVII. On the arrangement and resolution of syllogisms.

Chapter XXXVIII. On the confirmation and refutation of syllogisms, and on manifold truth, justice, and freedom of choice.

Chapter XXXIX. A description of things, together with certain [Col. 1806B] natures of propositions.

## Book III

Chapter I. The opinion of the most learned Boethius on the four powers of apprehension that are in man.

Chapter II. Saint Augustine’s teaching on the three kinds of visions signified by the three heavens.

Chapter III. Distinction of these same visions by appropriate terms.

Chapter IV. That God moves every creature by hidden power.

Chapter V. On animal and natural motion, and sensation.

Chapter VI. That the five bodily senses are distinguished according to the four elements.

Chapter VII. That bodily vision is referred to spiritual vision, and spiritual to intellectual vision.

Chapter VIII. On distinguishing bodily from spiritual vision.

Chapter IX. That images of bodies in the spirit sometimes [Col. 1806C] signify and sometimes do not; that the spirit of a human being and that of a demon are sometimes so mingled as though they were one spirit; and that it is sometimes difficult to discern whether a good or evil spirit has taken possession of the human spirit.

Chapter X. That unclean spirits deceive by bodily and spiritual, not intellectual, vision.

Chapter XI. On the consent of those dreaming.

Chapter XII. That the things which are sensed are immediately made in the spirit, which is superior to every body—not a body, however, but a spirit forming them within itself.

Chapter XIII. That memory preserves images of bodies, both generally and distinctly, received through any sense.

Chapter XIV. Whence it happens to the soul to see things not brought or reported to it through the senses.

Chapter XV. That bodily vision does not occur without spiritual vision, though spiritual vision can occur without bodily vision; but intellectual vision judges both.

Chapter XVI. That the soul is deceived through its own fault by the likeness of things, and that it is a gift of God when they are distinguished from the bodies themselves.

Chapter XVII. That transparent truth is perceived by intellectual vision; [Col. 1806D] that blessed life is drunk at its fountain; that there we speak with God mouth to mouth; that God himself is the light of the soul; and that there is the paradise of paradises.

Chapter XVIII. That these three kinds of things seen remain even in the world to come, and that blessed creatures are aided inwardly alone so that they may be wise and blessed.

Chapter XIX. On the glory of free choice, and certain descriptions of wisdom.

Chapter XX. Another definition of wisdom.

Chapter XXI. Division of philosophy, with certain observations on its parts.

Chapter XXII. For what purpose logic is necessary, how subtly it considers things, and certain matters concerning rhetoric.

[Col. 1807A] Chapter XXIII. That the eye of free choice must be illuminated by the disciplines of wisdom; certain matters concerning calculation are also added.

Chapter XXIV. Saint Augustine’s assertion that the disciplines of disputation, calculation, and eloquence are very necessary; that they were not instituted by human beings but merely observed and noted; that memory holds not their images but the things themselves; and many other matters, including knowledge of immutable truth itself.

Chapter XXV. On the eight vices, the target and the arrow, and the examination of thoughts.

Chapter XXVI. On the twice-seven parts of blessedness.

Chapter XXVII. On the disturbances of the mind.

## Book IV

Chapter I. On reason and will, and their functions.

Chapter II. What Jacob’s two wives, two concubines, and their children signify.

Chapter III. That Joseph signifies knowledge of ourselves, and Benjamin knowledge of God. [Col. 1807B]

## THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1147: ARNULF

[Col. 1811]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, XII, 292)

Arnulf was a remarkable Flemish preacher, says the Chronicle of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 1811] *Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 625.], distinguished by the austerity of his life, the singularity of his clothing, his learning, and, still more, the success of his preaching. At the proclamation of the Second Crusade, he felt inspired to follow in the footsteps of Saint Bernard and exhort the peoples of France and Germany to enroll in this pious militia. But, being equally ignorant of the Romance and German languages, he took with him Lambert, abbot of Gembloux, who explained to the people in the language of the country what Arnulf said in Latin or Flemish.

The crusaders divided: some went to Palestine, others to Spain to fight the Moors. Arnulf followed the latter, commanded by Arnulf, count of Aarschot. The principal result of their expedition was the capture of Lisbon, which they took on 21 October 1147. Our preacher sent an account of this siege to Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, in a letter published by Dom Martène in the first volume of his great Collection (pp. 800–802), from two manuscripts, one from Anchin and the other from Gembloux.

There one sees that the Christian army, composed of Lorrainers, Flemings, and Englishmen, assembled in England. It departed on the Friday of the Rogation Days—that is, 23 May—in a fleet of two hundred sail; after a few days at sea, it was scattered by a violent storm. About fifty vessels, on one of which our author was embarked, arrived on 31 May in a Spanish harbour called Gozzem. Having rested there for three days, the crusaders embarked again and came to another harbour called Viver. They set sail again on the Friday before Pentecost and landed at the harbour of Fambré, only eight miles from Saint James in Galicia. They immediately went thence to that place, so famous, to spend the time of the feast there.

Eight days later, having re-embarked, they went to await the remainder of the fleet at Portugal, a town at the mouth of the Douro. During the eleven days they stayed there, the bishop of the place had provisions and the other things which he knew they needed supplied to them abundantly. [Col. 1813] Finally, when the whole fleet had reunited, they sailed toward Lisbon, before which they arrived on 28 June, the eve of Saints Peter and Paul. On that same day Alfonso Henriques, king of Spain, appeared in sight of the city with his land army. They immediately disembarked, and on 1 July the suburbs were taken.

Thereafter, throughout the month, various assaults were made upon the city with rather little success. The advantage of its position, the strength of its fortifications, and the courage of the besieged threatened the crusaders with a long resistance and did not even promise them a certain victory. Far from discouraging them, these signs redoubled their efforts and ingenuity. They devised the construction of two great wooden towers on the riverbank: one east of the city, where the Flemings were quartered; the other west of it, occupied by the English. In addition, four bridges were made, each supported by six ships, by which they could pass onto the city walls. In various sorties the besieged destroyed part of these works; fortunately, they were promptly repaired.

Finally, after four months of siege, a mine had thrown down two hundred feet of wall. Encouraged by the king of Spain, the crusaders made an effort to enter through the breach. The battle remained obstinate; but the besieged, exhausted by hardship and seeing no further recourse, requested terms on Saint Ursula’s Day, 21 October. The proposal was accepted. The conditions were that the city should remain to the king of Spain and the booty to the crusaders.

Such is the substance of Arnulf’s account, differing from that of Robert of Mont [Note: [Col. 1813] Under the year 1147.], adopted by M. Fleury [Note: [Col. 1813] *Histoire ecclésiastique*, vol. XIV, book LXIX, no. 21.]. The latter represents the crusaders as attacking the city from their ships while the king besieged it by land; whereas our author, an eyewitness, attests that the former disembarked immediately after arriving, pitched their tents in the open country, and conducted with the Spaniards nearly all the operations of the siege on land.

[Col. 1813]

## LETTER OF ARNULF TO MILO, BISHOP OF THÉROUANNE, ON HOW LISBON WAS TAKEN

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, col. 800, from the manuscripts of Anchin and Gembloux.)

[Col. 1813A] To MILO, venerable bishop of Thérouanne, ARNULF, by the grace of God what he is, wishes that he may provide the spirit of wisdom for his subjects.

We know that the tower of humility has so fortified the wall of your virtues that that ancient enemy is kept farther off. We learned this by experience when Your Holiness condescended to us and, by the most sacred blessing of your right hand, enclosed our motions at sea, so that we were disturbed neither by the movement of storms nor by that of winds.

Therefore, placed in the valley of tears, we briefly set down for your fatherhood what condition the King of kings has made for his recruits. In the English port called Tredemunde [otherwise, Tredemude], a naval army, driven together from every region by the divine breath, assembled. On the sixth day [Friday] before the Rogation Days [Col. 1813B] we sailed with nearly two hundred ships. For seven continuous days and nights we laboured on the high sea; on the vigil of the Ascension and on the solemn day itself we were battered by a most savage tempest; and at last, on the eighth day, with nearly fifty ships—the rest having been scattered in every direction—we reached a Spanish harbour called Gollim [otherwise, Gozzem]. There, restoring our weary bodies for three days, we again came to the harbour called Viver.

Leaving there on the sixth day before Pentecost, we reached a Galician harbour called Fambre, which lies eight [Col. 1814A] miles from Saint James. Coming to his venerable tomb on the vigil of Pentecost, we celebrated the holy solemnity with great joy. Returning from there to the harbour, we sailed during the octave of Pentecost. On Monday we came by the channel of the river called the Douro to Portugal, where we found the bishop of that city awaiting our arrival with great joy, in accordance with the king’s command.

There, while for eleven days we awaited the arrival of Count Arnold of Aarschot [otherwise, Arnulf of Aarschot] and also of the constable Christian, who had been separated from us by the aforesaid storm, we enjoyed, through the king’s goodwill, a fair market both for wine and for other provisions. Thereafter, having received Count Arnold and the constable, we sailed and [Col. 1814B] entered the channel of the river called the Tagus. On the following day, at Lisbon, on the eve of the apostles Peter and Paul, we arrived.

That city, as the histories of the Saracens relate, was founded by Ulysses after the destruction of Troy. It stands upon a mountain, unassailable by human powers, with a marvellous construction of walls and towers. Having pitched our tents around it on the first of July, aided by divine power, we took its suburbs. After this, making various assaults upon the walls, not without great loss on both our side and theirs, we prolonged the time until the first of August in constructing [Col. 1815A] engines of war.

For we built, at great expense, two towers beside the shore: one on the eastern side, where the Flemings were stationed, and another on the western side, where the English had placed their camp. We also constructed four bridges upon ships, six [ships] for each bridge, by which access over the city walls might be opened to us. When we brought these forward on the feast of the Finding of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, they were driven back by an adverse wind and in some measure damaged by mangonels [otherwise, *maganellis*]. We withdrew the ships.

Then, while we on our side were fighting the Saracens, the English, guarding their tower less cautiously, could not extinguish it when it was unexpectedly set on fire. Meanwhile, with a certain engine we began to undermine the wall. Seeing this, the Saracens reduced that engine to ashes with fire mixed with oil, and stoned to death the master of the engine at the breach in the wall. Moreover, while they inflicted countless deaths upon us by mangonels and arrows, they too were punished by our men. Our people, somewhat disheartened by the destruction of their engines and the slaughter of their companions, nevertheless trusting in God’s mercy, began to repair the devices and engines.

[Col. 1815B] Meanwhile the Saracens of the city, though themselves abundant in food, withheld provisions so severely from their needy fellow citizens that very many of them died of hunger, while some did not shrink from devouring dogs and cats. The greater part of these offered themselves to the Christians and received the sacraments of baptism. Others, with their hands cut off, were sent back to the wall and [Col. 1815C] stoned by their own fellow citizens.

Many adverse and favourable events, according to the variable course of war, befell us; to avoid prolixity, we have passed them over in silence. If there are any, perhaps, who may set them forth more fully, we leave this to them.

At last, near the Nativity of Saint Mary, a certain Pisan by birth, a man of great ingenuity, fitted up a wooden tower of marvellous height in the place where the English tower had earlier been destroyed. By the middle of October he completed this praiseworthy work, both through royal expenditure and through the labour of the entire army. Likewise, beneath the city wall, a certain man made great excavations by his skill and with the assistance of many persons. The Saracens, vexed by this, secretly came out about the third hour on the feast of Saint Michael and continued fighting with us over the trench until evening. But, setting archers against them, we so barricaded the ways by which they hoped to return that either none, or scarcely any, escaped without a wound.

Accordingly, our men labouring day and night completed the underground work, filled with smoothed timbers, on the same day when the king, with the English, brought his tower up to the walls. [Col. 1816A] Indeed, on that very night, the feast of Saint Gall the abbot, fire having been set in the trench and the timbers burning, a stretch of wall two hundred feet long fell. Awakened from sleep by so great a collapse, our men took up their arms and attacked with a great shout, hoping that the watchmen guarding the walls had fled.

But when they came to the ruin, a mountain difficult of access rose above it, and a body of Saracens stood ready in defence. Nevertheless our men attacked, and they did not cease from the battle, begun at midnight, until the ninth hour of the day. At last, worn down by various blows, they withdrew from the fight until the connecting structure of the tower should be brought up [otherwise, removed], and thus the Saracen people might be harassed on both sides.

And behold: the tower, filled with fighting men, rose above the wall. At that same hour the troops on our side, with the Lorrainers fighting at the breach of the walls as a signal, attacked the Saracens in a remarkable assault. Meanwhile the king’s knights, who were fighting in the tower’s citadel, terrified by the Saracens’ mangonels, fought less bravely; so much so that the Saracens, coming out, would have burned the tower, had not some of our men, who happened to come upon them, resisted. When the report of this [otherwise, of that] danger reached our ears, we sent the best men of our army to defend the tower, lest our hope in it be brought to nothing.

But when the Saracens saw the Lorrainers and Flemings climbing with such ardour into the tower’s citadel, they were struck with such terror that they laid down their arms and asked that hands be given them as a sign of peace. [Col. 1816C] Thus it came about that their leader Alchaida agreed with us on this condition: our army should receive all their property, with gold and silver, while the king should possess the city, with the stripped Saracens and the whole land.

This divine, not human, victory was completed with two hundred thousand and five hundred Saracen men on the feast of the Eleven Thousand Virgins. Therefore we glorify his name, in whom and through whom are all things, who is blessed for ever.

You should know that the bodies of certain of our brothers, slain in various killings, are buried at Lisbon. Witnesses of this peace are certain persons whom divine mercy caused to speak though mute from birth: one on the feast of Saint Gereon and his companions; another whom it awakened from sleep and led, as he himself thought, by the hand of a most splendid man to the tomb of the martyrs; there it cast him down in ecstasy and loosed the bond of his tongue. Likewise, on the feast of All Saints, we heard another speak there by the grace of the same mercy and praise him who is wonderful in his saints. Farewell.
