Ælwin, son of Æthelweard, whose father was Alfred the Great, 218. Æsc, son of Hengest, king of the people of Kent, 16. Æscwine of Wessex, 45. Æthelard, archbishop of Canterbury, recovers his jurisdiction, 124, 125. Æthelbald of Wessex: his incest, 174. Buried at Sherborne, 174. Æthelberht, king of the people of Kent, embraces Christianity, 17. His memorable reply to Saint Augustine the monk, 19. The character of his laws, 17. His death, 18. Æthelberht, son of Wihtred: his reign in Kent, 24. Æthelberht of Northumbria, expelled, 104. Restored to his former dignity, 105. Slain, 105. Charlemagne’s indignation against his murderers, 106. Æthelberht of East Anglia, slain by Offa, 118, 136, 362. Æthelberht of Wessex first reigns in Kent, 174. After his brother’s death he obtains Wessex, 174. He repels Danish pirates, 175. Buried in a tomb at Sherborne, 175. Æthelflaed, daughter of Ceolwulf, king of Mercia, 364. Æthelflaed, daughter of King Alfred and wife of Æthelred, 184, 210. Together with her husband she builds the church of Saint Peter at Gloucester, 196. Her heroic spirit, 196. She assists her royal brother in governing the kingdom, 196. Æthelflaed, daughter of Edward the Elder, 197. Æthelfrith of Northumbria, 64. His victories, 65. He expels Edwin, 66. He demands him back from Rædwald, 67. Suddenly attacked and slain by him, 67. The flight of his children into Scotland, 67. Æthelgar, archbishop of Canterbury, 314. Æthelgeofu, also called Elgiva, daughter of Alfred the Great, 186, 189. Æthelheard, archbishop of Canterbury: allusion to his anti-churchly garments, 115, 116. Alcuin’s letter to him, 120. He is said to have been abbot of Malmesbury, 130. Æthelheard of Wessex: rebellion against him, 55. The subsequent tranquillity of his reign, 55. Æthelhilda, daughter of Edward the Elder, 197. Ætheling: interpretation of this word, 97. Æthelred of East Anglia, father of Saint Æthelberht, 136. Æthelred, king: he fights nine battles with the Danes in the same year, 176. His piety and martial courage in the battle at Aston, 176. The attempts of Mercia and Northumbria to throw off his yoke, 177. His death, 178.

[Col. 1819] Æthelred II, 261. Crowned by Dunstan, 262. He besieges the bishop of Rochester and does not withdraw from the siege except upon receiving payment, 262. His cruelty toward his wife and his quarrels with his father-in-law, 268. His kingdom ravaged by the Danes, 263. He buys an interruption of hostilities with money, 268. Again compelled to pay tribute, 264. His indolence and irresolution, 266. He pays a third tribute to the Danes, 267. His general injustice, 268. He flees to London from Sweyn’s power, 290. From there he escapes to the Isle of Wight, 291. His address to the assembly of bishops, 291. He sends his family to Normandy and shortly afterward follows them himself, 292. After Sweyn’s death he returns to England and drives Cnut out of it, 296. He orders Sigeferth and Morcar to be put to death, 297. When Cnut returns, he flees to London, 299. There he dies and is buried in Saint Paul’s church, 300. Æthelric of Northumbria: the wretched condition of his reign, 64. Æthelstan, 204. Chosen and crowned king, 205. Poetic account of his consecration, 210. Trained from childhood in the use of arms, 210. Brought up by his aunt Æthelflaed and her husband, 210. His succession to the kingdom opposed because of his illegitimate birth, 205. Account of his popular birth, 222. He erects new monasteries and enriches old ones with gifts, 206. He gives his sister in marriage to Sihtric of Northumbria, 206. He annexes that kingdom to his own, 206. His victories in Wales and Scotland, and restoration of the conquered kings to their lost thrones, 206. Victorious at the battle of Brunanburh, 208. He destroys the Danish fortress at York, 213. His appearance and character, 213. Annual tribute from the Welsh, 214. He expels the Cornish from Exeter and fortifies the city by his own labour, 214. His treaties with foreign kings, 215. Poetic description of his battle with Anlaf, 218. His charter to Malmesbury monastery, 220. At last his death and the procession of his funeral, 225. Æthelswitha, daughter of Earl Æthelred and wife of Alfred the Great, 185. Æthelswitha, daughter of Alfred the Great, 185, 193, and note. Æthelwulf, also called Athulf, king: his character, 149. Having preserved Wessex, he entrusts the remainder of his kingdom to his son Æthelstan, 150. He assists Burgred with troops and joins his daughter to him in marriage, 150. His conflicts with the Danes, 150. His officials, 151. His generosity to the clergy, 151, 170. His pilgrimage to Rome, 152. He rebuilds there the English school that had collapsed after being consumed by fire, 152. He marries Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, 153. His subjects, resenting this, oppose his return to his native land, 168. His will, 170. Charter, 170. Æthelweard, son of Alfred the Great, 185, 204. Æthelweard, son of Edward the Elder, 197, 205. Æthelwold, son of Æthelberht the Firstborn, who was Alfred’s brother, 195. Æthelwold, intimate adviser of King Edgar, 252. Killed because of his duplicity, 253. Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester: his generosity in founding monasteries, 258. Æthelred, earl of Mercia, marries the daughter of King Alfred and is appointed governor of London, 184. Together with his wife, founder of the church of Saint Peter at Gloucester, 196. His death, 197. Æthelbald, king of Mercia: his long and peaceful reign, 112. Rebuked by Archbishop Boniface for his evil example, 112. His general charter to monasteries, 116. Slain by Beornræd, 112. Æthelred, king of Mercia, 73. His military expedition into Kent, 110. He repels Ecgfrith of Northumbria and kills his brother, 110, 78. He pays the latter’s wergild, 110; and, having abdicated the kingdom, embraces the monastic life, 74, 111. Æthelred, son of Penda, king of Mercia, 108. Æthelwealh, king of Sussex, conquered by Cædwalla, king of Wessex, 46. Agatha, married to Edward, son of Edmund Ironside, 303. Aidan, bishop of Lindisfarne, 71, 77. Ailward, abbot of Glastonbury, profanes the body of King Edgar where it was discovered, and shortly afterwards breaks his own neck, 236. Aimar, bishop of Le Puy, takes the cross against the unbelievers at the Council of Clermont, 532. He proceeds through Dalmatia with Count Raymond, 534. Their arrival at Constantinople, 535. He professes fealty to the Greek emperor, 536. He leads the third squadron of cavalry in the Christian sortie from Antioch, 558. The Turks flee when they see his military standard, 559. Alan, count of French Brittany, 404. Alcuin, educated at York, 93. He goes to the court of the king of the Franks, 94. His great learning, 94. Extracts from his letters, 93, 102, 105, 106, 127, 130.

[Col. 1820] Alderia (William of), godfather of William Rufus, accused of treason, 501. After confessing to the bishop of Salisbury, he is scourged through all the churches of the city, 501. He gives all his clothes to the poor and goes naked to prison, 501. Dying, he declares himself innocent, 501. Aldgitha, also called Elfgiva or Adela, daughter of Edward the Elder, wife of Ebles, son of Rainulf, count of Poitou, 168, 197, 198. Saint Aldhelm, account of, 43. His works, 44, 49, variant reading. Made bishop, 49, variant reading. His body found in Malmesbury abbey and deposited there in a shrine, 234. See *Virginity*. Aldred, archbishop of York, crowns William the Conqueror, 421. Aldwulf, bishop of Lichfield, 119. Aldwulf, also called Ealdulf, of Northumbria, 206. Alexander, king of the Scots, 382. He marries an illegitimate daughter of Henry, king of the English, 627. He translates his father’s remains from Tynemouth to Dunfermline, 424. Alexius I, emperor of Constantinople: Robert Guiscard invades his country, 440. Alexius attacks Bohemond during his father’s absence, but is put to flight, 440. With the help of his wife he poisons Robert to death, 441. On his arrival, he seizes Hugh the Great, attended by a small body of soldiers, 535. He releases him from custody when the other crusaders arrive, 535. Proofs of his bad faith, 555. He flatters the Christian leaders and induces them to profess fealty to him, 536. He secretly receives the surrender of Nicaea while it is besieged by the Christians and orders them to move on, 531. He allows William of Poitiers and his army to fall into the hands of Solyman, 592. His dominions again occupied by Bohemond because of his evil treatment of pilgrims, 601. He frustrates the expedition’s purpose by deceiving or poisoning its leaders to death, 601. Alfleta, see Æthelflaed. Alfred, see Ælfred, Alhfrith. Alhfrith, king of Northumbria, recalled from Ireland and raised to the royal throne, 79. Invasions of his kingdom by the Picts, 79. Alhhred of Northumbria expelled from the kingdom, 104. Ælla of Northumbria: the conversion of the English during his reign, 63. Almodis, countess of Toulouse: her character and manners, 602. Alphege, see Ælfheah. Alphonso, king of Galicia, 456, 461. Alric, king of Kent, conquered by the Mercians, 24. Alric, bishop of Chichester, 473. Alstan, see Ealhstan. Ambrisil (Robert of), see Arbricellensis. Ambrosius, the sole survivor of the Romans, struggles against the Saxons, 14. Anacletus: his election as supreme pontiff opposed by the party of Innocent II, 695. Letter of Peter, bishop of Porto, who favoured his party, 695. His rival is acknowledged by the kings of France and England, and likewise by the emperor of Germany, 697. He occupies the papal see until his death, 698. Angles and Saxons summoned from Germany, 9. Their arrival in England, 10, 11. History of the English, with Bede as author, 77, 80. Anglesey, the island of the Angles, 69. Girard, bishop of Angoulême, reads at the Second Lateran Council the decree by which Paschal’s concession to Emperor Henry V is revoked, 662; and excommunicates William of Poitiers because of his scandalous conduct, 671. Fulk, count of Anjou, marries one of his daughters to William, English prince, 634; and grants Maine as her dowry, 652. He presses the prince to profess fealty to Louis VI for Normandy, 652. He sets out for the Holy Land, 652. On returning, he takes the part of William, duke of Normandy, against his uncle King Henry, and gives him Maine and another daughter in marriage, 654. At last he becomes king of Jerusalem, 690. Genealogy of the counts of Anjou, 400. Anlaf, son of Sihtric, rebels against Æthelstan, 206. Disguised in a foreign guise, he enters the king’s camp, 207. He suddenly attacks the king, but is defeated and put to flight, 208, 212. Poetic account of his battle with Æthelstan, 218. Recalled from Ireland and chosen king by the Northumbrians, 225. He submits to King Edmund and receives baptism, 226. He rebels and is sent into exile, 226. Anlaf, king of Norway, is baptized and promises to desist from attacking England, 264. Anna, king of the East Angles, slain by Penda, 107, 135. Anschetil, a certain noble Norman: account of him, 230. Anselm, archbishop, 2. His ineffective attempts [Col. 1821] to restrain the licence prevalent during Rufus’s reign, 499. For this reason he leaves England, 499. Before his departure his baggage is opened and plundered insultingly, 499. Recalled by Henry I, 619. Paschal’s letter to him concerning investitures; he is recalled from his second exile after this question has been settled, 654. He consecrates five bishops on one and the same day, 649. Anselm, bishop of Lucca, later Pope Alexander II, 410. Antioch: why it is designated by this name, 553. Its power and fame, 554. Besieged by the Franks, 554. And captured, 556. The battle of Antioch, 559. Aoxianus, prefect of Antioch, implores help from the Sultan, 554. Slain by a Syrian peasant during the assault upon the city, 557. His head displayed for the Franks’ mockery, 557. Robert of Arbrissel: his great eloquence, 673. He establishes the convent of nuns at Fontevraud, 673. William, count of Arques, rebels against William, duke of Normandy, the son of his brother, 397. But shut up in Arques, he is compelled by hunger to submit, 397. A new style of architecture at Westminster, 385. In various places, 420. At Salisbury and Malmesbury, 687. Golden bracelets displayed by Ælfred on public roads, 187. Arnulf, son of Baldwin II, count of Flanders, by Ælfthryth, daughter of Alfred the Great, 193. Arnulf, count of Flanders, slain with his guardian in an ambush prepared by Robert the Frisian, 432. Arthur, king: his illustrious deeds, 14. It was commonly reported in the Conqueror’s time, because his tomb was still concealed, that he would appear again, 466. Ascalon: battle near this town, 570. Ashdown, battle at, 301. Its church built by Cnut, who was present at its consecration, 306. Ancient Asia: its fertility, 552. Its barren state under Turkish rule, 552. Assandun, see Ashdown. Asser of St David’s, made bishop of Sherborne by King Ælfred, 189. He renders Boethius’s Latin diction simpler before the king translates the work into the Saxon language, 189. Aston, battle at, 176. Athelmus, archbishop of Canterbury, 314. Athelstan, see Æthelstan. Saint Augustine: his arrival in Britain, 17. See Goscelin. The licence of William Rufus’s court, 498, 500–501. Aylnoth, see Ægelnoth. Siege of Azotus, 588.

## B

Babylon in Egypt, built by Cambyses on the site where Tahpanhes formerly stood, 569. Badon, see Bannesdon. The city of Bayeux burned by fire, 625. Baldred, king of the people of Kent, driven from his kingdom by Ecgberht, 25, 147. Baldwin I, king of Jerusalem, brother of Godfrey of Bouillon, takes the cross, 576. Leaving the main army behind, he receives the surrender of Tarsus, 576. He is favourably received in Armenia and Mesopotamia, 577. He assists the ruler of Edessa on the condition that he be made his heir, 577. He succeeds to the power of the murdered ruler, 578. He celebrates Christmas at Jerusalem, 579. Returning to Edessa, he hears of Bohemond’s captivity, 580. He sets out to free him, but is disappointed by the Turks’ withdrawal, 581. He receives news of his brother’s death and of his own election as king, 581. He entrusts Edessa to his kinsman Baldwin and recommends that Tancred be chosen in Bohemond’s place, 581. Having acquired provisions at Tripoli, he is warned by the Turkish governor of a plot, 581. When he reaches the place, he overcomes the enemy by a feigned flight, 582. Throughout the journey he receives food and all necessities by way of contributions, 584. Proclaimed king at Joppa, he is escorted by the inhabitants of that town as far as Jerusalem, 584. He advances against Ascalon and pursues its inhabitants into the mountains, 584. He puts the Turks to death but spares the Syrians, 585. He turns his steps toward Arabia, but when he reaches the edge of the desert he retraces his route, 585. He is crowned at Bethlehem on Christmas Day, 586. He employs against Azotus certain Pisans and Genoese who had very recently arrived, having hired them as soldiers, 588. He takes Caesarea by assault, 589. He routs an army coming from Babylon and kills its leader, 590. He destroys five hundred marauding Arabs who, deceived by an error, had come to him, 590. He arrives at Joppa, where he dispels a false rumour of his death, 591. His victories along the seacoast, 591. His defeat at Ramla, or Rama, 425. His swift flight to Azotus, 594. From there he makes for Joppa by ship and sends a messenger to Jerusalem, 594. Reinforced by a small body of soldiers from that city, he drives the Turks from the neighbourhood of Joppa, [Col. 1822] 595. The other occasion on which he was compelled to seek safety in flight, 595. He marries the countess of Sicily, whom he later neglects, 596. His death and public funeral, 597. His qualities of mind and body, 597. Baldwin II receives the governorship of Edessa from his kinsman Baldwin I, 581. He is appointed by him as his successor, 597. He adds Antioch to his kingdom, 597. He is accused of avarice, 597. He is carried off by the Turks, and for almost a whole year no news of him is received, 597. He is freed by some of his own knights disguised as merchants, 598. He gives Antioch and his daughter to Bohemond, son of Bohemond, 602. Baldwin II, count of Flanders, marries the daughter of King Ælfred, 193. Baldwin V, count of Flanders, 319, 400. Baldwin, nephew of Robert the Frisian, assists William of Mortain against his kinsman King Henry I, 630. He is severely wounded in the head, 433, 631. Cause of his hastened death, 631. Ballad, an ancient kind of history, concerning which see 222, 236, 466. Balso, surnamed the Short: his history, 230. Great ruins of Bangor, 66. Slaughter there of British monks, 66. Bannesdon: siege of this town. Bardulf, Hugh, 398. Battle Abbey, founded by William I, 447. Roger of Beaumont, founder of the monastery at the place called Préaux, 635. He refuses the Conqueror’s invitation to cross into England, content with his paternal inheritance, 635. Bede, 2, 80. His education, 83. Invited to Rome, 86. His learning and holy life, 88. His last illness, 89. Buried at Wearmouth, 91. His body translated to Durham, 91. His epitaph, deservedly given below, 92. Alcuin’s eulogy of him, 102. Robert of Bellême, eldest son of Roger of Montgomery, fortifies Bridgnorth and Arundel against King Henry I, 621. On hearing of the surrender of Bridgnorth, he gives up Arundel and is permitted to go into exile in Normandy, 622. His companions are his brothers Arnulf and Roger, surnamed of Poitou, 622. He joins William, count of Mortain, and again makes war against the king, 623. He takes flight in the battle at Tinchebray, 626. Afterwards captured by the king, he is thrust into prison until his death, 626. His rude and deceitful nature, and cruelty toward his spiritual son, 626. Benedict Biscop builds two monasteries at Wearmouth, 81. He imports books, craftsmen, and very precious objects, 84. His great patience, 81. Benedict X, 341. Benignus, abbot: his epitaph, 38. Bensington, battle at, 57. Beorhtric, king of Wessex: his political administration, 59. He marries a daughter of Offa, 59, 127, 169. He expels Ecgberht, 59, 145. Descent of Danish pirates upon his kingdom, 145. Killed by poison administered by his wife, 169. Beorn, earl, son of a brother of Earl Godwin, 342. Beorna, king of East Anglia, 136. Beornræd, king of Mercia, kills his predecessor Æthelbald, 112. He himself is also slain by Offa, 112. Beornwulf, king of Mercia, expelled by Ecgberht and killed by the East Angles, 132, 148. Beorhtwulf, king of Mercia, expelled from his kingdom by the Danes, 133. Beregored, abbot of Glastonbury, 40. Berengar, heresiarch of Tours: his opinions condemned in councils and refuted in writings by Lanfranc and others, 462. He is compelled to recant, 462. His later sanctity, 462. Poems published in his praise, 463. His death, 465. Berfreid—French *beffroi*—a movable wooden tower used to raise assailants to the level of those defending their walls, 567. It was successfully used by the crusaders at Jerusalem, 567. Berhtwald, abbot, elected archbishop of Canterbury, 41, 314. Bernard, bishop, 39. Bernard, founder and abbot of Tiron monastery, 673. Bernard, monk who visited the Holy Land in the year 870, 562. The kingdom of Bernicia, 70, 75. Bernulf, see Beornwulf. Bertha, daughter of the king of the Franks and wife of Æthelberht, king of the people of Kent, 17. Bertrada, wife of Fulk IV of Anjou, taken from her husband by seduction by King Philip, 403. She is joined in marriage to her abductor by the archbishop of Rouen, 631. She takes the veil [Col. 1823] at Fontevraud and dies shortly afterward, 631. Bertram, illegitimate son of Raymond surnamed *le Croisé*, to whom his father gives in marriage Matilda “the Margravine,” daughter of his brother, 603. After his father’s death, attended by a great host of troops, he advances to occupy the regions which his father had subdued in Syria, 606. He besieges and captures Tripoli, 606. Bezants, a coin so called, 546. Drinking by means of a brooch: what it means, 237. Roger Bigot, one of those rebelling against William Rufus, ravages the neighbourhood of Norwich, 488. He remains loyal to Henry I when other noblemen abandon him, 620. Blegent, brother of Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, 385. The count of Blois, Theobald, on the denunciation of Louis VI, is declared by the supreme pontiff to be a rebel against God, 633. He presses William, the English prince, to profess fealty to the king of the Franks for Normandy, 652. His sister is drowned at sea with the prince, 654. Of Blois, see Henry Stephen. Bohemond I, son of Robert Guiscard: his nobility even as a boy, 598. He accompanies his father on the expedition against Alexius, 598. Left by his father as commander of the army, 440. Pursued by the emperor, he puts him to flight, 440. After his father’s death he returns to Apulia, supports Pope Urban, and urges him to convene the Council of Clermont, 599. The motive secretly assigned by some for this conduct, 523. He proceeds to the Holy Land as leader of the Italians, 535. He reaches Constantinople before the other crusaders, 535. He induces a certain Turkish commander to allow Antioch to come into his power, 556. He assaults a great tower with ladders and attacks the city, 557. He leads the supporting line in the famous Christian sortie from the town, 559. He is left behind as prince of Antioch, 560. He proposes to Baldwin, ruler of Edessa, that they celebrate Christmas at Jerusalem, 578. He goes ahead of him on the journey and awaits his arrival, 578. Their forces are joined by a band of soldiers led by Archbishop Daimbert, 578. What they suffer on the journey; they are received with great joy by King Godfrey, 579. Bohemond returns to Antioch, 580. He is captured by Danishmend, 580. He is restored to liberty on condition that he keep perpetual peace with the Turks, 600. He goes to France and offers his silver fetters to Saint Leonard, 600. Having married the daughter of the king of France, he returns to Apulia, 600. He leads an army against Alexius because of Alexius’s evil treatment of pilgrims, 601. His commanders are either corrupted and led astray or poisoned to death by the Greek emperor, 601. He dies in Apulia, 601. His bodily and mental qualities, 601. Bohemond II, son of the preceding, receives Antioch from Baldwin II, whose daughter he marries, 602. Humphrey of Bohun, one of those who adhered to the Empress Matilda, repels King Stephen from Trowbridge, 726. He becomes the captive of William of Ypres, 760. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz: his admonitory letter to Æthelbald, 11. His letter to Archbishop Cuthbert, 115. Bologna and Bouillon, see Baldwin, Godfrey, and Eustace. Bordinus, Maurice, bishop of Braga, excommunicated by Pope Paschal at the Council of Benevento, 665. He is placed by Emperor Henry V upon the papal throne, 660. He flees Rome at Pope Calixtus II’s approach, is captured at Sutri, and detained, 660. He is banished to a penal monastery called La Cava, 667. Britons: their great poverty; they willingly allow themselves to be hired as mercenaries, 629. Henry I, king of England, sometimes made use of them in this way. Brian, son of Robert, count of Gloucester, joins his father when he arrives to uphold the empress’s rights, 725. He was one of her hostages when she was acknowledged by the Legate, 744. Saint Brigid is said to have visited Glastonbury, 37. Brihtwold, bishop of Wilton: his dream concerning Edward the Confessor, 374. Britain under Roman rule, 5. Abandoned by them, 7. Occupied by Scots and Picts, 7. The Romans bring aid, 8. Brithric, see Beorhtric. The avarice and rapacity of the Britons, 103. Western Britons, or Cornishmen, 214. Brittany is granted by Charles to Rollo, along with his daughter Gisela, 404. Alan, count of Brittany: a quarrel between his retainers and the servants of the bishops of Salisbury and Lincoln, in which his nephew is nearly killed, 717. See also Alan. Battle of Brunanburh, 207. Metrical description of it, 218.

[Col. 1824] Bruno, later Pope Leo IX, 329. Burgred, king of Mercia, marries Æthelswitha of Wessex, 133, 150. Expelled by the Danes, 150.

## C
Caedwalla, king of Wessex; his power, 46. He defeats Æthelwealh, king of Sussex, 46. He lays waste the Isle of Wight, 46. He gains many victories in Kent and avenges the death of his brother Mul, 22, 46. He abdicates and goes to Rome, 17. His baptism and death, 17. Caer Badon, see Bannesdon. Caesar, Julius, subdues Britain, 5. The siege of Caesarea, 588. Shoes with curved points, 498. Calixtus II: while he was archbishop of Vienne, he was one of those through whose care Paschal’s concession to Emperor Henry V was revoked, 661. He is elected supreme pontiff by the cisalpine Church, 665. He convenes a council at Rheims and deposes all who had received investitures from a secular hand, 665. He comes to a meeting and conference with Henry I and is induced to change his judgment concerning the king’s conduct toward his brother Robert, 634. The flight of the antipope Burdinus upon his arrival at Rome, 666. The pope’s letter to the French nation, in which he explains how Burdinus had been captured, 666. His reforms at Rome and his indulgence toward English pilgrims, 667. His letter to the emperor concerning the settlement of the investiture controversy, 668. At Calne, the collapse of a building upon the council sitting there, 258. Secular canons expelled from Winchester, 239, 240. Their attempts to recover their monasteries, 257. Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury: while abbot of Séez, he brought the keys of Bridgnorth to King Henry, 622. He displays to the people, for a second time after it had been dug from the earth, the body of St Cuthbert, 680. Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, is present at the council held at Winchester concerning King Stephen’s treatment of bishops, 719. He asks the king for mercy toward the Church, 724. He considers it a religious duty to profess allegiance to the Empress while the king is captive, 744. He is permitted by the king to yield to the necessities of the time, 744. William, archbishop of Canterbury, is the first to bind himself by oath to admit the succession of the Empress Matilda, 692. He is appointed legate to England, 699. He attends King Stephen’s coronation and receives his oath concerning the restoration and preservation of the Church’s liberties, 704. The see of Canterbury: attempts to remove it to Lichfield, 119. Controversy with the see of York, 471. The monastery of Canterbury founded, 19. The city of Canterbury consumed by fire, 24, 265. A most grievous injury done to it, 337 and note. Canute: see Cnut. Capet, Hugh: how he became king of France, 201. In the reign of Henry I, the English had a custom of wearing their hair long, 693. A magical head made by Gerbert, 283. Ceadwalla, king of the Britons, kills Eanfrith, king of Bernicia, and Osric, king of Deira, 70. Penda, king of Mercia, joins him, 108. He is killed by St Oswald, 70. Ceawlin, king of Wessex, defeats Æthelberht and the Britons, 27. His domestic troubles, 27. He is expelled from the kingdom, 28. Cecilia, the younger daughter of the Conqueror, abbess of Caen when the book entitled *Gesta* was being written, 455. Cedwallus, see Caedwalla. Celwulphus, see Ceolwulf. Cenelm, king of Mercia, killed by his sister, 132, 363. Centwine, king of Wessex: his victories over the Britons, 45. Ceol, king of Wessex, 28. Ceolfrith, abbot, 77, 83. Pope Sergius’s letter to him, 86. He dies on his journey to Rome, 83. Ceolred, king of Mercia: his military prowess and premature death, 111. *Ceols*, vessels so called, described, 10, 26. Ceolwulf, king of Mercia, expelled by Beornwulf, 132. Ceolwulf, Burgred’s minister, made king of Mercia by the Danes on conditions, 137. Ceolwulf of Northumbria: his learning, 80. He revises Bede’s history, 80. He abdicates and embraces monastic life, 92. Ceolwulf of Wessex, 28.

[Col. 1825] Cerdic: his arrival in Britain with his son Cynric, 26. He subdues the inhabitants and establishes the kingdom of Wessex, 26. He gives the Isle of Wight to his brother’s son, Wihtgar, 26. Charlemagne: the fortunate outcomes of his wars, 127. His letter to Offa, 126. His spear, 217. Charles the Bald, king of France, 158. Charles the Fat: his astonishing vision, 160. Charles the Simple, king of France, whose wife was Eadgyfu, daughter of Edward the Elder, 166. Charles, son of Cnut IV, count ruling Flanders at the time when the Malmesbury historian wrote his *Gesta*, 432. Ethelfleda, daughter of Oswin and abbess of Streaneshalch, 77. Ethelfleda, see Æthelflæd. Ethelfrida, see Æthelfrith. Ethelhere, king of the East Angles, killed with Penda by Oswiu, 135. Ethelred, see Æthelred. Ethelric, see Æthelric. Ethelsinus, bishop of Sherborne, 270. Ethelstan, see Æthelstan. Ethelswitha, daughter of King Alfred, married to Baldwin, count of Flanders, 193.

[Col. 1832] Ethelwold, or Elward, translates the Saxon Chronicle into Latin, 1, 2. Ethelwold, see Æthelwold. Ethelwulf, see Æthelwulf. Eugenius, king of the Cumbrians, 212. Euripus, or a sea-flood, destroys several villages, 297. Eustace of Boulogne, father of Godfrey of Bouillon and Baldwin I, kings of Jerusalem, visits Edward the Confessor, 336. A quarrel between his servants and the people of Dover, 337. What followed from this as far as Godwin was concerned, 337. Eustace, son of King Stephen: the Empress refuses him Mortain and Boulogne as long as his father remains captive, 750. He is one of the hostages for the liberation of the earl of Gloucester, 754. Exeter, fortified with walls and ditches by Æthelstan, 214. Its situation and wealth, 214. Consumed by fire, 260. Subdued by William I, 421.

## F

Famine devastates England, 267. John Fitz-Gilbert, keeper of Marlborough castle, hangs Robert Fitz-Hubert, who seemed to favour the Empress, after arresting him, because he refused to surrender Devizes to his lady, 734. Robert Fitz-Hamon remains faithful to Henry I when he is deserted by the other nobles, 620. Struck by a wound in the forehead in Normandy, he survives long while out of his senses, 625. He splendidly adorns Tewkesbury monastery, 625. His daughter Mabel is given in marriage by the king to Robert, earl of Gloucester, his illegitimate son, 625, note, and 692. Robert Fitz-Hubert, after seizing the unfinished castle of Malmesbury, burns the town, 726. Expelled from it by King Stephen, 726. He occupies Devizes castle, which he refuses to surrender to the Empress, 733. Captured and held in prison, he is at last hanged, 734. His blasphemies and cruelty, 733. William Fitz-Osbern, sent by William, duke of Normandy, to inspect the disturbances caused by Geoffrey Martel, 396. He advises William to invade England, 431. He is rebuked by him for prodigality towards his soldiers, 431. His leniency towards offending soldiers, 431. With King Philip, he is appointed guardian of the children of Baldwin, count of Flanders, 431. He goes there to suppress the insurrection, 432. Unexpectedly overwhelmed by Robert the Frisian together with his royal ward, he is killed, 432. Baldwin, count of Flanders, father-in-law of the Conqueror, 432. He assists William in invading England with counsel and troops, 629. He is said to have received an annual pension of three hundred marks as payment, 629. The same payment, made also to his son Baldwin, is withdrawn from Robert the Frisian, 630. Robert the Frisian, count of Flanders, see Friso. Robert, count of Flanders, son of Robert the Frisian, obtains from William Rufus an annual pension of three hundred marks which William the Conqueror had ceased to pay to his father, 630. Henry I refuses it to him upon his return from the Holy War, 630. Flanders, see Baldwin. Formosus, pope, in a letter attributed to him, excommunicates Edward the Elder because he permitted many episcopal sees to remain vacant, 203. Fulk III of Anjou: his treachery towards the count of Maine, 401. He compels his rebellious son to humiliating service, 401. He undertakes a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, 402. The severity of the penance he imposes upon himself, 402. Succession of the kings of France down to Hugh Capet, 95, 101; from Louis I to Henry I, 153, 168. Origin of the Franks, 95. Their distinguished physical and intellectual qualities, 146. Frea, wife of Woden, 11. History of the Franks, 95–101, 153–168, 201. The church of St Frideswide at Oxford burned, 297. Robert the Frisian marries Gertrude, widow of Florent, duke of Frisia, 431, 573. He upholds the succession of his stepson Theodoric, 573. Expelled by Godfrey the Hunchback, who seizes the duchy, 573. After the Hunchback is killed, he restores his stepson to his former rank, 573. He frees the Flemings from the oppression of Arnulf, his nephew, and Arnulf’s mother, 432. He unexpectedly captures and kills Arnulf and his guardian William Fitz-Osbern, 432. He becomes count of Flanders, 432. He provokes William by his raids in Normandy, 432. He marries his daughter to Cnut IV, king of the Danes, and gives his stepdaughter in marriage to Philip I, king of the Franks, 432. In old age he goes to Jerusalem, 433. On returning, he departs this world, 433. The fate of his sons, 433. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres: his qualities and works, 316, 465. Fulcher of Chartres, chaplain of Baldwin I, king of Jerusalem, 576. Fulda monastery, 325–26. A strange and wonderful occurrence there, 326. A contagious disease there, 471.

## G

The Gauls: their manner of speech, 44. Gelasius II, pope: his letter to the Frankish people, in which he speaks of his disputes with Emperor Henry V, 664. Expelled from Rome by him, he dies at Cluny, 665. Geoffrey, see Martel. Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, takes part in Odo’s conspiracy against William Rufus, 487. With his nephew Robert Mowbray, he ravages Bath, Berkeley, and part of Wiltshire, 488. He returns to the king’s favour, 490. Gerbert (Pope Sylvester II), see *Legends*. St Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, 36. His miracles, 183. Germany: why it is called by this name, 10. Various migrations from this region, 10. Gildas is said to have lived many years at Glastonbury, 33. Gerald, archbishop of York, excommunicated by Pope Paschal for falsifying his words in the question of investitures, 646. At King Henry’s intercession he is absolved, 648. Gyrth, or Curthose, son of Godwin, 342. His prudence, 417. Gisla, or Gisella, daughter of Charles, king of the Franks, given in marriage to Rollo, duke of the Normans, 166, 405. Count Gilbert, guardian of William, duke of Normandy, 392. The fidelity with which he discharges the charge entrusted to him, 392. He is killed by his kinsman Ralph, 392. The sword of Constantine the Great, 217. History of Glastonbury monastery, 31, 54. The history of this monastery by the historian of Malmesbury, 50, variant reading, 77. Charters granted for the benefit of that monastery, 227, 240, 315. Dissension between the abbot and his monks, 450. Two monks killed and several wounded, 451. The abbot expelled by the Conqueror, 451. But after the Conqueror’s death, he is restored to his rank upon payment of a sum of money, 451. Robert, earl of Gloucester, illegitimate son of Henry I and born before his father ascended the throne, 692. He is married by Henry to Mabel, daughter of Robert Fitz-Hamon, 625, note. By his father’s favour he receives the earldom of Gloucester, 692. He swears that he will consent to his sister, the Empress Matilda, succeeding their father, 692. He is present at his father’s death, 701. His perplexity when Stephen seizes the kingdom, 705. He comes to England and, subject to a condition, acknowledges Stephen as lord, 707. When Stephen leaves for Normandy, he follows him there shortly afterwards, 710. Warned of the snares prepared for him by the king, he refuses to come to court, 710. Ashamed that the affair has been uncovered, the king swears, in the manner proposed by Robert, never to pursue such a course, 710. The earl remains in Normandy to observe the course of public affairs, 711. At the counsel of many religious men, and by the pope’s command, he openly undertakes his sister’s cause and sends envoys to Stephen to renounce the homage he had rendered him, 712. All his English possessions, except Bristol, are confiscated by the king, 713. The earl arrives at Arundel with his sister and one hundred and forty followers, 725. Leaving her there and entrusting her to the care of his stepmother Adela, he himself proceeds to Bristol with twelve knights, 727, 758. Halfway along the journey he meets his son Brian, and, learning that his sister had left Arundel with provisions supplied by the king, 725, waits for her at the boundary specified in the grant of safe-conduct; having received her from the bishop of Winchester, 725, he brings her with him to Bristol and afterward entrusts her to the care of Miles of Gloucester, 725. He strives to keep neutral those whom he cannot win to his sister’s cause, 731. Having taken many castles from the king, he makes his brother Reginald earl of Cornwall, 732. He advances to rescue his daughter in Lincoln Castle, besieged by the king, 741. He defeats the besiegers and captures the king, 741. His kindness toward the captive king and severity toward the treacherous townsmen, 741. He confirms the Empress’s oath to preserve the liberties of the Church, 743. When she departs in resentment from the legate, he accompanies her to a conference with this bishop at Worcester, 751. With the roads cut off by men loyal to the king and the citizens’ houses burned, he resolves to withdraw from the town, 758. Having sent the Empress forward with the chief body of troops, he himself follows slowly with a small force so that the enemy might not pursue them, 758. But he is captured by men loyal to the king and made prisoner, 758. The honourable manner of his captivity at Rochester, 759. He resists alike blandishments and threats aimed at inducing him to agree to an exchange on equal terms with the king; nevertheless, he finally yields to his friends’ entreaties, 760. Precautions taken by him that the pledged faith should not be violated, 761. In a meeting and conference with the king, he declares that he opposed the king for no reason other than the oath, 762. Given leave to depart, he releases the queen from custody at Bristol, 754. He goes to Caen to seek help from the Empress’s husband, who pleads the distracted condition of his realm, 765. He remains with him briefly and assists him in recovering ten castles, 765. But he again pleads an excuse; nevertheless, Robert receives his son Henry from him to bring to England, 765. He hastens his return on hearing that Wareham has been captured and that his sister is in danger in Oxford Castle, 776. He arrives at Wareham, 767. He recovers the castle, 768. He regains the island of Portland and occupies Lulworth Castle, 768. He gathers his adherents at Cirencester and proceeds to Oxford, 768. Hearing that his sister has fled to Wallingford, he turns his march thither, 769. At the Empress’s advice the army is disbanded and the soldiers return home, 769. An enumeration of the earl’s merits and eminent qualities, 682. The *New History* is written by the historian of Malmesbury at his request, 687; he also dedicates the *Deeds of the Kings of the English* to him. See the dedication. Roger of Gloucester, killed by a crossbow-shot at the siege of Falaise, 625. Serlo, abbot of Gloucester, modifies the rule of his house so that, though an infirm man could observe it, a robust man could not despise it, 674. Verses of Prior Godfrey in his praise, 674. Goda, daughter of King Æthelberht, 336. Godfrey the Hunchback, husband of Matilda, or the Margravine, expels Robert the Frisian and Theodoric from Frisia and seizes the duchy, 573. He is treacherously killed by the Flemings, 573. Godfrey of Bouillon, son of Eustace II of Boulogne, 572. Through his mother Ida, he traced his lineage from Charlemagne, 534, 572. Urged by his mother to seek the acquisition of Lotharingia, 573. He offers military service to the emperor and obtains that reward, 573. He accompanies him on the expedition against Rome, 573. He opens an entrance for his followers through a broad window in the city walls, 573. Stricken with a quartan fever because, burning with excessive heat, he drank wine, 574. He vows to go to the Holy Land; recovering his strength, 574, he sets out to fulfil the vow, leading on the expedition Frisians, Lotharingians, Saxons, and neighbouring peoples, 534. He reaches Constantinople, 535. He is induced to render homage to the emperor, 536. He is present at the siege of Nicaea, 536. During the siege of Antioch he undertakes two single combats with Turks and kills his adversaries, 574. He also kills a lion attacking one of his soldiers, 575. He leads the second troop of cavalry in the sortie from the city, 558. He is chosen by the Christians as king of Jerusalem, 569. His eulogy, 571. He is repulsed from Azotus, 588. Return of his former illness, 575. His death and burial beneath the rock of Golgotha, 575. The pious reason for his refusal of coronation, 576. Godfrey, Prior, see Winchester. Godiva, wife of Leofric, earl of Hereford, 330. Godwin, earl: his conduct in the expedition to Sussex, 307. On Cnut’s death he protects Emma, 319. Accused of complicity in Alfred’s blinding, 321. Compelled to deny it on oath, 321. His splendid offering to regain favour, 321. After Harthacnut’s death he raises Edward to the throne, 332. His daughter is married to the king, 333. His quarrel with him, 336. He is expelled with his sons, 339. He plunders maritime towns, 339. Fog prevents him from engaging the royal fleet, 340. He returns to the king’s favour, 340. He secures the expulsion of his Norman rivals, 340. His wives and children, 342. The Norman account of his death, 335. Hugh of Gournay, 339. Goscelin, monk of St Bertin, visits many episcopal sees and abbeys and leaves memorials of his learning, 521. His great fame as a musician and writer of saints’ lives, 521. His vivid description of the Translation of St Augustine, 522. The Goths, 10. Succession of the Greek emperors, 549. The manner of speech of the Greeks, 44. St Gregory resolves upon the conversion of England, 63. The affection of his fellow citizens prevents him from going to England himself, 64. Pope Gregory VI: his methods for restraining assassins at Rome, 344. His own vindication of his conduct, 346. The miracle at his death, 351. Gregory VII (Hildebrand): legendary narrative concerning him, 441. Raised to the papal see, 444. He excommunicates bishops who receive investiture from lay hands, 444. Deposed by Emperor Henry IV, 445. Restored by Robert Guiscard, 440. Again expelled from Rome, 440. His death and warning concerning his successor, 445. Anecdotes concerning him and the emperor, 445. Hugh of Grantmesnil, one of Odo’s conspirators against William Rufus, ravages the neighbourhood of Leicester, 488. Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, defeated and put to death, 230, 385. Grimbald, invited into England by Alfred and made abbot of his new monastery at Winchester, 188, 192. Ralph of Gael, or Wader, made earl of Norfolk and Suffolk by the Conqueror, 429. He marries William Fitz-Osbern’s daughter, 429. At the very celebration of the wedding, he induces many nobles to conspire against William, 430. Expelled from the realm by the king’s officers, 430. His wife follows him after surrendering her castle, 430. Guimond, bishop of Aversa: his eloquence, 462. Robert Guiscard of Normandy, surnamed Durandus, 599. His origin, 439. With fifteen followers he goes to Apulia, 439. He occupies the region and is made duke of Apulia and Calabria, 439. He establishes his brothers Richard as prince of Capua and Roger as count of Sicily, 439. Having entrusted Apulia to his son Roger, he crosses the Adriatic with another son, Bohemond, 439. He obtains the surrender of Dyrrachium, ingeniously playing upon his surname and the city’s name, 599. He advances against the Greek emperor Alexius, 440. But, hearing of Gregory VII’s deposition, he entrusts the army to Bohemond and returns to Apulia, 440. Having gathered forces, he restores the pope, 440. Attacked by the Venetian fleet while returning to Greece, 440. He sinks part of their ships and puts the remainder to flight, 440. He takes several cities from Alexius, 440. At last, at the Greek’s instigation, he is killed by poison administered by his own wife, 441. His epitaph, 441. Gunhild, Sweyn’s sister, killed with her husband and son in the great slaughter of the Danes, 289. Gunhild, daughter of Cnut, married to Emperor Henry III, 321. The splendid magnificence of her departure from England, 322. Accused of adultery, 322. Defended by the emperor’s page, who kills her accuser, 322. Refusing reconciliation with her husband, she takes the veil, 322. Guthferth, son of Sihtric, flees to Scotland from King Æthelstan, 212. He escapes thence with Turfrith, 213. He vainly besieges York, 213. He returns to the king’s favour, 213. He again becomes a pirate, 213. Guthrum, a Dane, defeated by Alfred, 181. Baptized and appointed to the government of East Anglia and Northumbria, 181, 136. His tyranny and death, 182. Guy, son of Renaud I of Burgundy, brought up from childhood with the Conqueror, 193. He receives from him the castles of Brionne and Vernon, 193. He quarrels with him and ravages Normandy, 193. Pursued by the king of the Franks, he is defeated, 193. He flees to Brionne, 394. Expelled thence by William, he withdraws into Burgundy, 394. He is expelled by his brother the duke for conspiring against him, 394. Guy, count of Ponthieu, 384.

## H
## H

Hampstead-Finch; a spring of blood there, 506.

Harald Fairhair, king of Norway, enters as a young man into Greek military service, 436. Having violated a noble matron, he is thrown to a lion, which he strangles with his immense strength, 436. He is killed by Harold, king of the English, in the battle at Stamford Bridge, 386, 436. Harthacnut is elected king by the unanimous consent of all, 319. He receives his brother Edward kindly, 320. He imposes upon the country a burdensome tribute, 320. He burns and plunders Worcester because two of his tax-collectors had been killed there, 320. His anger against those who had blinded Ælfred, his wife’s brother, 321. He joins his sister Gunhilda in marriage to Emperor Henry III, 321. His death, 320. His body is treated shamefully and cruelly, 320.

[Col. 1836] Harding, an Englishman (also called Stephen), 513. Brought up from childhood as though a monk at Sherborne, 511. Having travelled in Scotland and France, he goes to Rome, 512. Returning to Burgundy, he enters the monastery of Molesme, 512. He inveighs against certain additions made to the old monastic Rule, 512. After these had been discussed at several assemblies, the matter is referred for examination to the judgment of two learned monks, 517. But since most of the monks refuse to abandon the innovations, he departs with the abbot and seventeen others, 517. They arrive at Cîteaux, where they establish this most celebrated monastery, 514. The severity of their Rule, 514. When the abbot had departed and returned to Molesme, Harding is elected prior, 515. Afterwards raised to the dignity of abbot, 515. The immense growth of the Order, owing to his industry, 515. His great charity and personal influence, 515. The conspicuous character of the Cistercians, 517.

Harold, king of Norway, sends gifts to Æthelstan, 215.

Harold I is chosen king by the Danes and the citizens of London, 315. The English resist him, 315. He expels Queen Emma, 319. His death, 319.

Harold, son of Godwine, after killing Rhys and Gruffydd, takes possession of the country, 330. Expelled by Edward, 339. He returns to favour, 339. Thrown about at sea by a storm and laden with chains, 383. Restored to liberty by Duke William, 384. He joins William in the expedition to Britain, 384. He takes William’s daughter in marriage and promises on oath to assist him in mounting the English throne, 384. After the Confessor’s death, he assumes the royal crown for himself, 385. The excuse he uses for violating his oath, 408. He wins a victory over the enemy in the battle at Stamford Bridge, 386. But, on hearing of William’s landing in England, he sends scouts into the Norman camp, 412. His brother Gyrth’s warning, 413. He rejects William’s proposals, 413. His conduct in the battle at Hastings, 416. His death, 416. His body buried at Waltham, 420.

Harold, son of Harold II, king of England, accompanies Magnus, king of Norway, on his expedition to invade England, 506.

Hasting, a Danish leader, defeated by Alfred, plunders the coast of France, 182.

Hastings (battle at), 387, 414.

Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, 6, 546.

Helgrim, envoy of Harold, king of Norway, to Æthelstan, 215.

Elias of La Flèche stirs up disturbances in Normandy, 503. How he is dealt with by Rufus, 503.

Hengist, his origin, 11. He arrives in Britain, 11. He obtains Kent, 12. His and his brother’s sons arrive in Orkney, 12. And establishes settlements in Northumbria, 13. Slaughter of British nobles perpetrated by him, 15. His death, 16.

Henry I, born in England in the third year after England’s occupation by the Normans, 615. Since he was the only son born in the purple, he is educated with greater care than the others, 615. The enduring and useful nature of the endowments granted him, 615. Made a knight by his father at Westminster, 616. He proceeds with him to Normandy and is present at his death, 616. He receives his blessing, his mother’s inheritance, and a legacy of three thousand marks, 616. He satisfies a knight who claims as his own the place in which Henry’s father was to be buried, 461. Through the contrivance of slanderers, his effort on behalf of his brother Robert is harshly answered by that brother, 616. He is sent by him to Britain and, while absent, is despoiled by his deputy, 617. On returning, he makes no complaints, 617. He is treated badly by both his brothers, 617. He takes Avranches and several castles and compels Robert to come to an agreement, 617. He aids him against Rufus when Rufus invades Normandy, 617. He gains custody of a certain Conan, a traitor to Robert, and throws him from the top of the tower at Rouen into the Seine, 618. His reason for acting thus, 618. He again experiences Robert’s ungrateful disposition, being expelled by him from this city, 618. He resists Robert and Rufus when they attempt to invade Maine, and is besieged by them on Mont-Saint-Michel, 491. He sends Robert a message asking that he might be allowed to obtain water, 493. Peace having been restored, he proceeds to England with his brothers; and, after William Rufus’s death, is chosen king, 618. He restrains the abuses introduced by Rufus and Ralph Flambard, 619. He casts Flambard into prison, but recalls Archbishop Anselm, 618. He is crowned in London on the fourth day after his brother’s death, 618. The reason for this haste, 618. He marries Matilda, the orphan daughter of King Malcolm, 618. He joins Mary, his wife’s sister, in marriage to Eustace of Boulogne, 750. When Robert returns from the holy war, Henry is deserted by most noblemen, 620. Insulting epithets uttered against him and his queen by these men, 620. He collects a very large army to repel Robert’s invasion, [Col. 1837] 621. Anselm, all the clergy, and all his Saxons support him, 621. He passes through the ranks of the army and teaches them how the Normans must be opposed, 621. Hostilities are prevented by more prudent men, and the king promises the duke three thousand marks, 621. Henry refuses Robert, count of Flanders, the annual pension which William Rufus had granted him, 630. He suppresses the rebellion of Robert of Bellême and permits him to cross into Normandy as an exile, 622. He denies the county of Kent to William, count of Mortain, his kinsman, and brings suit against him to recover certain usurpations, 623. He is attacked in Normandy by William himself and by Robert of Bellême, 623. He orders his brother Robert to cross to England and rebukes him for permitting these things, 624. At the complaint of the Normans, with Pope Paschal urging and Louis VI inciting, 632. He sails to Normandy to restore peace, 625. He wins a victory at Tinchebray over Duke Robert, the count of Mortain, and Robert of Bellême, in the fortieth anniversary year of England’s occupation, 625. He casts the count of Mortain into perpetual imprisonment, 626. But commits his own brother to honourable custody, 611. His severe laws, 625. He gives his illegitimate daughter in marriage to Alexander, king of Scotland, 617. He makes David—Malcolm’s younger son and Alexander’s successor—an earl, and gives him a noble maiden in marriage, 617. He places a colony of Flemings between himself and the Welsh, 493, 628. He is struck by an arrow while advancing against the Welsh, 628. He suppresses their uprising and takes as hostages the children of noble men among them, 629. His practice of hiring Britons as mercenaries for pay, 629. He quarrels with Louis VI on behalf of Theobald of Blois, 633. When Louis invades Normandy, he restrains the ardour of his soldiers, 633. He defeats Louis in battle and makes peace, 634. He joins his son William to the daughter of the count of Anjou in marriage, and permits him to render homage to Louis for Normandy, 634. In a conference with Pope Calixtus, he induces the supreme pontiff to change his judgment concerning the manner in which Henry had treated his brother Robert, 634. He is the reason why the younger sons of Robert of Meulan contend with the cardinals, 635. His great confidence in Roger, bishop of Salisbury, whom he appoints administrator of public affairs, 637. The devotion of the kings of Ireland to Henry, 638. He receives gifts from Paul, count of Orkney, 637. His livestock-rich palace at Woodstock, 637. Foreigners flee into his kingdom as into a haven of safety, 639. He is visited by Siward, king of Norway, travelling to the Holy Land, 639. His abbey at Reading of Cluniac monks, 643. Pope Paschal’s letter to him concerning investitures, 644. He recalls Archbishop Anselm from his second exile and agrees to surrender the disputed right, 648. The death of his wife Matilda, 651. He loses his son William in a shipwreck, 653. After the death of his heir, he marries Adela, daughter of the duke of Louvain, 651, 654. The marriage of his daughter Matilda to Emperor Henry V, 655. He converts Ely monastery into an episcopal see and compensates the bishop of Lincoln for the injury done him, 680. While staying in Normandy, on hearing of the emperor’s death, he sends an embassy to bring back his daughter, 689. He refuses to give her in marriage to certain princes of Lorraine and Lombardy, 689. He returns with her to England, 690. He assembles a great council in London, where he grants the county of Shrewsbury to the empress and compels bishops and nobles to accept his daughter in succession to the kingdom, 690. He sends the empress to Normandy to marry Geoffrey, son of Fulk of Anjou, and shortly afterwards follows in person to attend the marriage, 692. He supports Pope Innocent’s cause against Anacletus, 698. Returning to England, and his daughter also having returned, he compels the nobles at a great council held at Northampton to renew their oath, 698. A great slaughter of livestock in the thirty-first year of his reign, 699. His final journey to Normandy is followed by an eclipse and an earthquake, 700. His final illness and death there, after he had spent three years there, 701. He leaves all his possessions to his daughter, 701. Letter of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, describing his religious end, 701. His funeral rites, 702. His body is conveyed to England and buried in his monastery at Reading, 705. His immense treasures, 705. Summary of his history, 640. An attempt on his life only once throughout the course of his reign, 642. His person and character, 642.

Henry, afterwards Henry II, son of Geoffrey Plantagenet and the Empress Matilda, sent into England by his father under the guardianship of his uncle, the count of Gloucester, 765.

Henry I, king of the Franks, appointed inspector of the guardian of William, duke of Normandy, 392. He confers knighthood upon the young duke, 393. After Duke Robert’s death, he restores order in Normandy, [Col. 1838] 393. Aided by William against Geoffrey Martel, 394. He advises the duke not to be too careless of his own safety, 394. Becoming less favourably disposed towards William, he aids William’s rebellious uncle, 397. He invades Normandy and, defeated in the battle at Mortemer, 398, makes peace, 399. He again invades the country and suffers a severe defeat, 400. His death, 400.

Henry I, emperor, 168, 215.

Henry III, emperor, marries Cnut’s daughter, 321. His warlike character, 322. Legendary anecdotes concerning him, 323 ff. His epitaph, 328.

Henry IV, emperor, excommunicated by Gregory VII because he persisted in granting investitures, 440. He deposes the pope and puts Guibert in his place, 440. When Robert Guiscard approaches, he saves himself by flight with the antipope, 440. He again deposes Gregory, 440. Excommunicated by Pope Urban, 468. Compelled by his son to resign the empire, 467. Favourable traits of his character, 468.

Henry V, reigning emperor of Germany at the time when Malmesbury was writing his *Deeds*, 101, 467. He deposes his father Henry IV, 467. He marries Matilda, daughter of Henry I, king of England, 655. He contests with Pope Paschal concerning investitures, 655. His cause is embraced by the bishops on this side of the mountains, 655. He proceeds to Rome and seizes the supreme pontiff, 656. He extorts from him the surrender of the disputed privilege, 656. His oath to the pope, 657. He receives from him an oath to confirm their mutual friendship, 658. Description of his solemn coronation, 658. Paschal’s pardon granted to him, 659. He receives the Roman crown from the Patricians, 661. Paschal’s pardon is revoked by the Second Lateran Council, 662. He leads another army against Rome, 663. On hearing of the pope’s death, he hastens his journey so that he may establish Maurice Burdinus in the papal see, 664. Names of Romans devoted to the emperor, 665. Gelasius having been driven from Rome, he leaves Burdinus there as pope, 666. In his letter to Calixtus II, he yields the disputed right, 669. His three expeditions into Italy, 670. His death, 689.

Herbert, count of Maine, 401.

Herbert Losinga, abbot of Ramsey, buys the episcopal see at Thetford for money, 517. His corrupt morals, 517. Epigrams on his simony, 517. Penitent, he goes to Rome, 518. Iricus expelled from the kingdom by Cnut, 299.

Jerusalem, the various names by which it has been called, 561. Its boundaries enlarged by Hadrian, 561. Water is not abundant, 361, 566. John Scotus; his literary studies in France, 190. His arrival in England, 190. His death and epitaph in Malmesbury monastery, 190.

Kategis, or Categirnus, son of Vortigern; his death, 13.

Kenelm, see Cenelm.

Perpetual lamp, 357.

Leofa expelled by Edmund because of his robberies, 228. He intrudes himself into the royal feast, 228. Pursued by the king himself, whom he mortally wounds, 229. Torn to pieces by the king’s earls, 229.

Leofwine, son of Godwine, 342.

Exemplary life of Bishop Liudhard, 17.

Books, or library, at York, 93. At Jerusalem, 563. Books, or libraries, formerly attached to churches, 191. Burned by the Danes, 191.

Lichfield made an archiepiscopal see, 119, 123.

Louis VII, crowned by Innocent II while his father was still alive, 698. He receives Aquitaine with his wife and reunites it to the crown of France, 699.

Mabila (daughter of Robert Fitz-Hamon), given in marriage by Henry I to his illegitimate son Robert, earl of Gloucester, 692. She became the mother of a numerous and very beautiful offspring, 692. Macbeoth, king of the Scots, 330. Maccus, pirate, 286. Magnus restores Norway to its former liberty, 435. He invades Denmark and expels Sweyn II, 435. When Sweyn returns with foreign forces, Magnus defeats him again, 436. Magnus, king of Norway, with Harold, son of Harold II king of England, occupies Orkney and other islands, 506. He attempts to invade England by way of the island of Anglesey, 506. He is repelled by Hugh of Chester and Hugh of Shrewsbury, 506. Malcolm, king of the Scots; Wales assigned to him, 226. Malcolm, king of Wales, 236, 330. Malcolm II, king of Scotland, 308. Malcolm III, son of the king of Wales, raised to the throne of Scotland by Earl Siward, 330. He receives his wife’s brother Edgar Aetheling and the other English exiles, and espouses his cause, 422. He submits himself to the Conqueror, 424. He makes peace with Rufus through Robert, duke of Normandy, 424, 494. He is treacherously killed, together with one of his sons, 424, by men devoted to Robert Mowbray, earl of Northumbria, 494. He is buried at Tynemouth, 424. His body is transferred to Dunfermline by his son Alexander, 424. Malger, archbishop of Rouen (the Conqueror’s uncle), an ardent lover of hunting and the pleasures of the table, 447. The pallium is denied him by the supreme pontiff because of his unbecoming conduct, 447. He is condemned and deposed by William while still young, 447. The reasons assigned by the prelate’s adherents for the duke’s conduct, 448. William of Malmesbury drew his origin equally from Saxon and Norman stock, 389. Under his father’s care, he was devoted to books from a tender age, 143. He is taught logic orally and studies medicine and ethics, 143. He purchases several foreign histories at his own expense and begins to investigate the history of his own nation, 143. He begins to write, 144. His reasons for writing history, 1. He scorns common reports and asserts nothing not wholly worthy of belief, 73. He despises popular traditions and adheres to chronicles, 144. He complains that they are devoid of events, 144. He solicits correction and communication of facts, 144. Giving ear to those suggestions of persons who think it impossible for anyone to write a true history of contemporaries without either suffering persecution or being stained by the base charge of flattery, he breaks off his work at the close of the third book; but some time later resumes it, intending to show the futility of that opinion, 483. His distinction between extravagance and liberality, 496. His censures of splendid ornaments and magnificent garments, the use of which had prevailed in churches, 516. Why he dedicated his *Gesta* to Robert, earl of Gloucester, 681. At the earl’s request he writes the work entitled *Historia novella*, 687. He was present at the council held at Winchester, 745. He refers to his history of Glastonbury, 50, variant reading. Malmesbury monastery founded, 43. Occupied by Offa, 117. By Ealhstan, 151. Its possessions restored, 130. The monks expelled by Eadwy, 234. Edgar’s charter to the aforesaid monastery, 247. Occupied by Roger, bishop of Salisbury, 728. Singular report of one of its monks, 380. Cuthbert, abbot of Malmesbury, 130. John, abbot of Malmesbury; his character, 730. Geoffrey de Mandeville, attached by turns to King Stephen and the empress, 752. Walter of Mantala, 404. The city of Mantala destroyed, 400. Margaret, sister of Edgar Aetheling and wife of Malcolm king of the Scots; her great piety and charity, 382, 494. The sanctity of three of her sons, 628. Mary, daughter of Malcolm king of Scotland and wife of Eustace the Younger, count of Boulogne, 382. Marianus Scotus; his chronological works scorned by contemporaries, 471. A great tide of the sea, 29. Charles Martel, see Tudites. Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou; he casts off obedience to his enraged father, 401. He compels the counts of Poitou and Blois to surrender part of their possessions, 395. He occupies the Norman castle of Alençon, 396. His arrogance, 396. He escapes Duke William, into whose power Domfront will fall, 397. His death, 400. William Martel, steward of King Stephen’s household, excommunicated with the other adherents of the king at the council held at Winchester, 748. Saint Martin of Tours; his body transferred to the church of Saint Germanus at Auxerre, 183. Controversy concerning the reciprocal merits of these saints, 183. His relics cure a leper, 183. Matilda, the Marchioness; her Amazonian spirit, 467. She supports Urban against Henry IV and the antipope, 468. Matilda, wife of the Conqueror, founds the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity at Caen, 448. Estrangement between her and William because of their son Robert, 453. She is buried in her monastery at Caen, 453. Matilda, queen, daughter of King Malcolm, 382. Her noble birth but comparative poverty, 620. Educated from childhood in convents of nuns, 649. She wishes to put on the sacred veil in order to escape the attentions of her low-born lovers, 649. The resulting obstacle to her marriage with Henry I, 649. After her husband’s death her father sends envoys to bring her back to Normandy, 689. She is said not to have returned without reluctance, 689. She is sought in marriage by several princes of Lorraine and Lombardy, 689. She returns to England with her father, 690. Her long line of royal ancestors, 691. She receives the oath of fealty from prelates and nobles, 692. She is sent to Normandy to marry Geoffrey, son of Fulk of Anjou, 692. Returning again to England, she again receives the oath of fealty, 698. After her father’s death she remains for a time in Normandy, 703. She arrives at Arundel with her brother, the earl of Gloucester, by whom she is entrusted to the custody of her stepmother Adela, [Col. 1843] 725. She departs thence, having been granted leave by the king to return to her brother, 725. By him she is placed at Gloucester under the protection of Milo, 725. Hereford is captured by her supporters, 726. When peace is being negotiated, she declares that she will obey the judgment of the Church, 735. The king is captured by her brother, 742. Her husband is approached by the earl, who seeks his assistance, 765. In his absence she is besieged by the king in Oxford castle, 766. She escapes thence to Wallingford, 768. There her brother meets her and, at her request, orders the army to be disbanded, 769. Matilda, queen, only child of Eustace of Boulogne, married to Stephen, count of Mortain and afterwards king of England, 750. When her husband is captured, she sends a cleric to the council assembled at Winchester to procure his release, 748. She is visited at Guildford by the legate, whom she induces to embrace her husband’s cause, 750. She is one of the hostages given for the earl of Gloucester when he is exchanged for her husband, 754. ### O

Odo, archbishop of Canterbury, separates Eadwy from Aelfgyfa, 234. Odo, archdeacon of Rheims, later bishop of Ostia, and finally Pope Urban II, 446; see Urban. Odo, brother of the Conqueror, made bishop of Bayeux and earl of Kent by William, 456. After the death of William Fitz-Osbern, he becomes deputy administrator of the English kingdom, 457. He keeps immense treasures and attempts, through corruption, to obtain the papal see, 457. A great multitude of soldiers gathers around him, awaiting his departure, 457. For this reason William casts him into prison as earl of Kent and despoils him of his treasures, 477. At his brother’s death he is restored to liberty, 457. He confirms Robert in possession of Normandy and returns to England, 457, 486. The earldom of Kent is restored to him, 486. He is aggrieved that he has not been put in charge of public affairs, 486. He forms a faction in Robert’s interest, 457, 486. He plunders the royal treasures in Kent, ravages the estates of the archbishopric, and transfers his spoil to Rochester, 487. He is held captive in Pevensey castle, 489. He is sent with some of the king’s supporters to obtain Rochester’s surrender, 489. He is rescued by his own men after his companions are captured, 489. Seized again, he renounces his ambition to rule, 490. He goes with Robert to the Holy Land and dies during the siege of Antioch, 457. Osbern, precentor of Canterbury, writer of the *Life of Saint Dunstan*, 238. His skill in music, 238. Oseg, king of the Danes, killed in battle at Aston, 177. Olfrid, envoy of Harold, king of Norway, to Aethelstan, 215. Osred, king of Northumbria; his sensuality, 80, 114. Slain by his kinsmen, 80. Osred, king of the Northumbrians, expelled from his kingdom, 105. Osric, king of Deira; his apostasy, 70. Killed by Ceadwalla, 70. Osric, king of the Northumbrians, 80. Osthryth, or Ostgitha, daughter of Ecgfrith, king of Northumbria, and widow of Aethelred, 111. Saint Oswald: his flight into Scotland, 67. His return thence and accession to the throne of Northumbria, 70. He kills the defeated Ceadwalla, 70. He acts as interpreter for Aidan, 71. His piety, 72. He is killed by Penda, 71. His relics and miracles, 73, 360. Oswulf, king of Northumbria, killed, 104. Oswald, chosen as successor to Aethelberht, king of the Northumbrians, 106, note; and deposed, 106, note. Oswald, archbishop of York, is hostile to the secular clergy but favours the regular clergy, 239. Oswin, king of Deira, betrayed to Oswiu and killed, 75. His liberality and piety, 76. Oswiu, king of Bernicia, kills Oswin, 75, and acquires Deira, 76. His compunction, 76. He kills Penda and brings Mercia under his dominion, 76. Oswy, see Oswiu. Othus, son of Aesc, king of Kent, 16. William of Eu: unable to clear himself of the charge of treason by trial in combat, he is mutilated and deprived of his eyes by order of William Rufus, 501. Councils held at Oxford, 297, 716.

Pallas; his body discovered at Rome, 357. Palling, a noble Dane, killed, 289. The palm branch, badge of pilgrims, 580. Palumbus, a Roman priest; his skill in necromancy, 355. His remarkable death, 357. Lanzo, prior of Saint Pancras at Lewes, improves the condition of his monastery, 674. Detailed description of his final illness and death, 675. Pope Paschal II: his letter to Henry I concerning investitures, 644. Letter to Archbishop Anselm, 646. His controversy with Emperor Henry V on the same subject, 655. Delivered into prison by him and compelled to concede the disputed right, 656. He receives the emperor’s oath, 657, and administers the Eucharist to him as a testimony of reconciliation, 658. Saint Patrick is said to have been buried at Glastonbury, 37. Paulinus, archbishop, 39. He converts the Northumbrians to the Christian faith, 68. Peter the Hermit sent by the Christians at Antioch to conclude peace with Kerbogha, 558. The fierce and arrogant conduct of this Turkish commander, 558. Peter’s pence: what it is, 152. Philip I, king of the Franks, 203, 219. He makes peace with Robert the Frisian, marrying the sister of Robert’s wife, 432. Having repudiated her, he takes the wife of the count of Anjou, 432. He is excommunicated by the supreme pontiff, 632. Divine offices are suspended in the city where he resides, 632. His shameless remark upon hearing the ringing bells while leaving it, 632. He is joined in marriage to his mistress by the archbishop of Rouen, 632. His continual quarrels with the Conqueror, 434. Summoned by Robert, duke of Normandy, to assist against William Rufus, 491. His opposition to William purchased with gold, 491. Near the end of his life he assumes the monastic habit at Fleury, 632. History of Philip surnamed the Clerk, 608. Geoffrey Plantagenet, son of Fulk of Anjou, marries the Empress Maud, 692. Visited by the earl of Gloucester, who implores his assistance on behalf of the empress, 764. He offers an excuse but sends his son Henry instead to assist, 765. Plegmund, archbishop of Canterbury, 192. William IV, count of Poitou, compelled by Geoffrey Martel to surrender Bordeaux and the neighbouring cities, and to pay tribute for his remaining possessions, 395. William VII, count of Poitou, takes the cross and sets out for the Holy Land, 591. He reaches Constantinople with a great army, 592. He refuses allegiance to Alexius, 535, 592. He is defeated by Solyman with great slaughter, 592. He flees to Antioch, where Tancred receives him hospitably, 592. Having celebrated holy Easter day at Jerusalem, he returns home, 593. He gives himself wholly to every kind of disgraceful conduct and lust, 670. Having repudiated his wife, he takes the wife of a certain viscount, 671, and note. He is excommunicated by the bishops of Angoulême and Poitiers, 671, note. His shameless answers to the bishops, 671, note. He removes the bishop of Poitiers from his diocese, 471, note.
