Pons, successor to his father Bertrand in the rule of Tripoli, marries Tancred’s widow, 606. William of Pont-de-l’Arche, one of the custodians of the royal treasures, transfers his allegiance to King Stephen after the death of Henry I, 703. The practice of precedence among the West Saxons, 169. Battles: Antioch, 559; Ascalon, 570; Ashdown, 301; Aston, 176; Bannesdon, 15; Bensington, 57; Brentford, 301; Brunanburh, 207, 218; Cirencester, 29; Daegsastan, 65; Dol, 433; Ellandun, 147; York, 434; Hastings, 387, 414; Pen, 30; Penn and Gillingham, 300; Sceorstan, 300; Stamford Bridge, 386; Tinchebray, 625; Walsdun, 393; Wirtgernesburg (Vortigern’s fortress), 30; Wodnesdic, 28. Primacy of England: council assembled to settle the dispute concerning it, 474. Extracts from ancient documents on this matter, 472. Marvel of a double woman, 358. Pyramids, ancient tombs in the cemetery at Glastonbury, 35. Pythagoras: his twofold path, 271.

### Q

Quenburga, sister of Ine, king of the West Saxons, 49, variant reading. Quendrida kills her brother Cenelm, king of Mercia, 132. Quicelm, see Cynegils.

### R

Raegenald, son of Guthferth, 226. Ralph Flambard, see Flambard. Ralph, earl of Hereford; his cowardly conduct against the Welsh, 336. Description of Ramla, 560. It is surrounded by siege, 593. Ranulf, viscount of Bayeux, one of the confederates against William, duke of Normandy, [Col. 1847] 393. His defeat and surrender, 394. Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles and Toulouse: having received Cahors from his father, he enlarges his inheritance, 602. He buys Toulouse from his brother, 603. His intemperate manner of life, 603. He marries his illegitimate son Bertrand to the daughter of Matilda, or the Marchioness, 603. He marries the daughter of the king of Tarascon, 603. Together with the bishop of Cahors he urges Pope Urban to convene the council at Clermont, 603. He is the first layman to take the cross and devotes the remainder of his life to the holy cause, 604. With Bishop Aimar he leads the company of Goths, Gascons, and mountaineers of the Pyrenees and Alps, 524. He reaches Constantinople, 535. He refuses to profess allegiance to Alexius, 536. Antioch is left in his custody during the great sortie made thence by the Franks, 559. He stands opposite the Tower of David during the siege of Jerusalem, 566. He intercepts those fleeing from the city and pierces them with the sword, 568. He accepts the surrender of five hundred Ethiopians, whom he allows to depart safely for Ascalon, 568. He receives the keys of Ascalon, swearing that he will never hand them over to any of the other leaders, 604. He refuses them to the king of Jerusalem, 604, and restores them to the citizens, 605. Leaving Jerusalem, he occupies Laodicea, 605. While staying there, he comes to the aid of Baldwin’s army as it advances toward Jerusalem, 578. Returning to Constantinople, he cultivates the emperor’s favour, 605. By means of that friendship he escapes the danger posed by the count of Poitou, 605. He obtains the city of Tortosa and concludes a seven-year peace with the citizens of Tripoli, 605. As he was preparing to advance against them after the truce had been broken, he died, 606. His little son is sent home by the other leaders, 606. The Cluniac monastery at Reading founded by Henry I, 643. Great hospitality of its monks, 643. Henry’s body buried there, 705. Recula, sister of Aethelberht, king of Kent, 137. Richard de Redvers, Henry I’s support when deserted by the other noblemen, 620. Redwald, see Reodwald. Queens: the consort of a king of the West Saxons is not permitted to sit with him on the throne or to take the title of queen, 169. Reginald, made earl of Cornwall by his brother Robert, earl of Gloucester, 732. Reiner, son of Redwald, king of the East Angles, killed by Aethelfrith, king of Northumbria, 67. Noteworthy events occurring under the reign of the Conqueror, 452; likewise under the reign of William Rufus, 504. Redwald, king of the East Angles; extent of his dominion, 134. He kills Aethelfrith, king of the Northumbrians, 134. His baptism and apostasy, 134. Archbishop of Rheims, 188. Richard, the Conqueror’s second son; his premature death, 455. Richard, illegitimate son of Henry I, drowned at sea with Prince William while returning from Normandy to England, 654. Richard I, duke of Normandy, 269. Richard II, duke of Normandy; his great piety, 292. What happened to him with the sacristan of Fécamp, 293. His successors, 294. Richelda, wife of Baldwin VI, count of Flanders, 432. Riwal, brother of Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, 385. Robert, king of the Franks, pupil of Gerbert, 275. His great charity toward the poor, 317. Robert I, duke of Normandy, father of the Conqueror, 304, 391. He is said to have been implicated in the killing of his brother, 294. He goes on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, entrusting his son William to the care of Count Gilbert, 392. Overtaken by death on his return, he is buried at Nicaea in Bithynia, 295. His body removed thence by William’s command, 460. Robert II, duke of Normandy, surnamed Curthose from his short stature, eldest son of the Conqueror, 607. Normandy denied him by his father, 454, 607. He attempts to obtain in marriage the daughter of an Italian marchioness, 454. He incites Philip, king of the Franks, against his father, 454. He wounds his father in the battle at Gerberoi, 434. At his father’s death he loses England but obtains Normandy, 454. He treats Henry, stripped of his paternal legacy, badly in other respects, 617. He assists the rebels against William Rufus, 490. His duchy is invaded by William, 490. He seeks aid from the king of the Franks, 490. He makes peace with his brother on the condition that the county of Maine be granted him, 491. They advance together on that account, but are resisted by their brother Henry, 491. They besiege Henry on Mont-Saint-Michel, 491. Robert’s humanity toward Henry when he is pressed by the extreme hardships of the siege, 492. Peace restored, he crosses to England with both his brothers, [Col. 1848] 493. He exerts himself to make peace between Malcolm and his brother William, 494. Normandy mortgaged to William for ten thousand marks, 454, 500. He proceeds to the Holy Land with Robert, count of Flanders, and Stephen of Blois, 536. The mixed character of those who follow them, 536. They meet Pope Urban at Lucca in Italy, 536, and receive his blessing, 545. They reach Calabria, where Robert, count of Flanders, leaves his companions, 545. In spring they cross the sea and proceed to Constantinople, 545. They lose many of their men on the journey, 545. They profess allegiance to Alexius and join the army before Nicaea, 550. Robert’s division, attacked by Solyman on the march, is rescued by Godfrey and his companions, 551. He is one of the leaders in the sortie from Antioch, 558. He kills Kerbogha, leader of the Turks, 608. He is present at the assault on Jerusalem, 568. In the battle of Ascalon he breaks through the centre of the Turkish line, 571. He declines the crown of Jerusalem, 608. Returning home, he takes a wife in Apulia, 609. He enters into possession of his duchy, 454, 620. He loses his wife while she is giving birth to his son William, 609. He squanders the sum of money given in lieu of a dowry, with which he was to redeem Normandy, 609. He crosses to England in order to take the kingdom from Henry, 609, 621. He returns to his brother’s favour, Henry promising him an annual pension of three thousand marks, 609, 621. The next year he resigns his pension to the queen, 610, 621. He becomes despised by the Normans because of excessive indulgence, 610. Through fear, he neglects to restrain the unbridled licence of the count of Mortain and Robert of Bellême, 624. Summoned to England by Henry, he is rejected for his own indolence, 624. Henry despoils him of the greater part of Normandy, 610. Aid is denied him by the king of France and the count of Flanders, 611. Having committed his fortune to the issue of one battle, he is defeated and captured in the battle at Tinchebray, 611, 625. His brother Henry commits him to honourable custody until his death, 611. Robert of Jumièges invited to England by the Confessor, 334. He is made archbishop of Canterbury, 334. His conduct described differently by various historians, 385. Anticipating his expulsion, he appeals to Rome, 340. Returning to Jumièges, he dies, 340. Robert, bishop of Chester, occupies the wealthy monastery at Coventry, 520. He transfers his see there, 517. He plunders Chester church and allows its roof to collapse in ruin, 521. He relaxes the monks’ abstinence, permits them to depart from the rule, and confines their learning to secular literature, 521. He violates the canons when he orders his body to be buried at Coventry rather than in his own see, 521. Robert, count of Eu, 399. Robert, count of Mortain, brother of the Conqueror; his stupidity, 456. Robert, count of Flanders, son of Robert the Frisian, proceeds to the Holy Land with Robert, duke of Normandy, and Stephen of Blois, 536. He leaves his companions in Calabria, 545. He refuses to profess allegiance to Alexius, 550. He is one of the leaders in the great sortie from Antioch, 558. He is present at the assault on Jerusalem, 568. On his return he is killed in a mock cavalry combat, 433. Robert, son of Godwin, proceeds to the Holy Land with Edgar Aetheling, 425. He arrives when Ramla is under siege, 425. He opens a way for himself through the besiegers and frees King Baldwin, 425. Defeated in battle, he is led away in chains to Babylon, 425. Refusing to renounce the faith, he dies pierced by arrows in the marketplace, 425. Roger, bishop of Salisbury, see Salisbury. Roger, son of Richard, succeeds Tancred as prince of Antioch, 601. Captured by the Turks, 601. As he approaches their leader to recover his sword, he cuts off his head, 601. He is killed by those standing by, 601. Roger, son of Robert Guiscard, surnamed “Purse” by his father because of his love of money, 598. He receives Apulia from his father, 439, 598. The Song of Roland sung by William the Conqueror at the battle of Hastings, 415. Rollo the Norman, 166. His defeat at Chartres, 199. He occupies Rouen and neighbouring cities, 200. Baptized, he obtains a settlement in Normandy, 200. His unbecoming conduct toward the king of France, 201. The Romans bring aid to the Britons and finally withdraw from the island, 7, 8. Their manner of speech, 44. English school at Rome, 152. Embassy sent there, 187. Description of that city, 537. The narrow bounds of the modern city and the miserable condition of its inhabitants, 537. Verses by Bishop Hildebert in its praise, 537. Enumeration of its gates, churches, [Col. 1849] and the saints whose bodies lie near each of them, 539, 544. Ross among the Welsh, where the Flemings settled, 628. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, raised to this dignity by Henry I, 701. He attends the dying king’s bed, 701. His letter to Pope Innocent describing the king’s religious end, 701. He gives his hand to the earl of Gloucester as a pledge of King Stephen’s good faith, 710. He excuses the king’s conduct in seizing bishops’ castles, 718. He crosses into England and defends him before the council assembled at Winchester, 723. William, archbishop of Rouen, joins Philip, king of France, in marriage to his mistress, the countess of Anjou, 632. For this reason he remains suspended for many years, 632. Through Archbishop Anselm’s intervention he is restored to sacred office, 632.

### S
Saeberht, king of the East Saxons, embraces the Christian faith, 137. Sacred fire, a miracle wrought at Jerusalem, 562, 587. Berkeley Saga, 351. Two sagas at Rome, 282. Anglo-Saxon saints; particular notices of Wihtburh, Ælfheah, and Cuthbert, 359; of Oswald, king and martyr, 70, 74, 360; of Æthelred, Ælberht, and Ægelberht, 361; of Æthelberht, 362; Cenelm, 363; Wistan, 364; Edmund, king and martyr, 359, 364; Æthelthryth, 359, 368; Ethelburh, Sexburh, Eorcongota, Ermenhild, and Werburh, 368; Mildrith and Milburh, 369; Eadburh, 370; Edith, 371. Enumeration of saints whose bodies lie at Rome, 529, 544; and of those buried at Constantinople, 550. Rain of blood, 103. Spring, 506–7. Physical effects, 529.

Roger, bishop of Salisbury, the intimate counsellor of King Henry I, was administrator of the king’s affairs before Henry ascended the throne, 636. Because of his diligence in administering his diocese, he is appointed administrator of the kingdom, 636. He refuses to accept this office until compelled by the command of the archbishop and supreme pontiff, 636. He performs the office honourably while the king, detained in the duchy of Normandy, is absent from the realm, 636. His munificence and acute judgment in constructing ecclesiastical buildings, 636. He promises on oath that he will accept the Empress Matilda as successor to the king, 692. William of Malmesbury frequently heard him say that he was released from this oath because its conditions had been broken by the king, 692. He transfers his allegiance and service to King Stephen, 703. He is present at Stephen’s coronation, 704. He builds and fortifies castles, 715. The envy of nobles who complain of him to the king, 716. The fatal quarrel at Oxford between his servants and those of his nephew, and the retainers of Alan, count of Brittany, 717. Stephen compels him to surrender his castles as punishment for breaking his peace, 717. Charges brought against him by Aubrey de Vere at the council of Winchester, 721. His reply, 722. His death, 727. Recapitulation of his principal deeds, especially of the monastic possessions seized by him, 727.

A terrible storm at Salisbury, 505. The church rebuilt from the ground up, 637. Dancers and profane singers punished, 285. Learning and divination of the Saracens, 271, 273. Their defeat at Ascalon, 589.

Saxons summoned from Germany, 9. Their arrival in Britain, 10. They establish themselves on the island of Thanet, 11. They repel the Scots, 11. Their arrival in Northumbria, 60. Kingdom of the East Saxons, 137, 139; its boundaries, 140. Kingdom of the West Saxons, 25, 60; its boundaries, 140.

English School at Rome, 220. Said to have been founded by Offa, king of the Mercians, 153. Burned down, 152. Restored by Æthelwulf, 152. A school established in East Anglia, 135.

Scotland subdued by Cnut, 308. Scots defeated by the English, 11. Their character and customs, 533. Their ferocity softened by King David, 627.

Scottus, see John. Marianus Scotus: notice concerning him, 470.

Seaxred and Sigiweard, kings of the East Saxons, expel Mellitus, 147. They are killed by the West Saxons, 138.

Sebbi, see Sigheri. Sebert, see Saeberht. Selraed, or Suaebriht, king of the East Saxons [read: of East Anglia], 139. Selsey monastery, formerly an episcopal see, 140. A remarkable occurrence there, 361.

[Col. 1850]

Legend of the Seven Sleepers, 378. Pope Sergius baptizes Cædwalla, king of the West Saxons, 47. His letter to Abbot Ceolfrith, 86. Serlo, abbot, see Gloucester. Severus dies in Britain, 5. His wall, 6.

Sexburh, queen of the West Saxons: the firmness and vigour of her rule, 45. Sexburh, daughter of Anna, king of East Anglia, and wife of Earconberht, king of Kent, 368. Sanctity and affability of the nuns of Shaftesbury, 261. Sidonius, bishop of Clermont in Auvergne, 183.

Sigebert, see Sigiberht. Sigeferth, a noble Dane, put to death by King Æthelred, 297. His widow marries Edmund Ironside, 298. Sigehard and Suaebræd rule jointly among the East Saxons, 139. Sigeric, or Siric, archbishop of Canterbury, induces the Danes to make amends, 263. Sigiweard, see Seaxred.

Sighelm, envoy sent to Rome and to Saint Thomas in India, 187. Sigheri and Sebbi rule jointly among the East Saxons, 138. Sebbi, after the death of his associate, abdicates and enters the monastic life, 138.

Sigiberht, king of East Anglia: his exile and education in France, 134. He establishes schools, 135. He abdicates and becomes a monk, 135. He is killed by Penda, 107, 135. Sigiberht the Little, king of the East Saxons, 138. Sigiberht II the Good restores Christianity among the East Saxons, 138. He is killed by his neighbours, 138.

Sigiberht, king of the West Saxons: his cruelty and sloth, 56. Driven from the kingdom, he perishes when stabbed with a dagger by a swineherd, 56.

Sihtric, king of the Northumbrians, takes in marriage the daughter of King Æthelstan, 197, 206, 212. His death, 206. New Forest, see Forest, New. Simony widely prevalent, 523.

Siward, abbot of Abingdon, 333. Siward, earl, kills Macbeth, king of Scotland, 330. He raises Malcolm of Cumbria to the throne in his place, 330. He is present at the council held at Gloucester, 338.

Siward, one of the kings reigning in Norway when William of Malmesbury wrote his *Deeds*, 437. He winters in England while travelling to the Holy Land and is lavish in gifts to churches, 639. Passing the Balearic Islands, he inspires fear, 639. He loses one ship in the passage, 639. He reaches Jerusalem and subdues Tyre and Sidon, 639. He proceeds to Constantinople and places an ornamented small ship as a trophy on the summit of the church of Saint Sophia, 640. When a severe pestilence ravages his men, he orders that wine be drunk sparingly and diluted with water, 640. He employs this precaution on the basis of experiments made with it in a pig’s gall-bladder and confirmed by a dissected human corpse, 640. The ingenuity by which he eludes the emperor, who wished to detain him, 640.

Female slaves prostituted and sent to Denmark, 342. The practice of selling them, 418. Sledda, king of the East Saxons, 137. Solyman, governor of Romania, defeats and routs the Christian army led by Robert, duke of Normandy, 551. He destroys the army of William of Poitiers and kills Hugh the Great, 592.

The “Sow” (formerly *Vinea*), a machine used to protect excavators; its description, 566. Introduction of glass-making into England, 82. A fragment of the Crown of Thorns offered to King Æthelstan, 217. Battle of Stamford Bridge, 386. Humane conduct by one of the invaders, 386. Statue in the Campus Martius, 277. Bronze statue at Rome, 354.

King Stephen, count of Mortain and Boulogne and nephew of Henry I, joined in marriage to Matilda, only daughter of Eustace of Boulogne, 750. He binds himself by oath to allegiance to the Empress Matilda, 692. Shortly after Henry’s death he comes to England, 703. He is received as king by the citizens of London and Winchester, 703. With the aid of his brother Henry, bishop of Winchester, he secures the keepers of the royal treasury, 703. He is crowned with only three bishops and a small body of nobles present, 704. A great number of soldiers flock to him because of his liberality, 706. He receives the conditional allegiance of the count of Gloucester and the clergy, 707. By oath he promises to restore and preserve the liberties of the Church, 707. The bishop of Winchester becomes his surety, 704. He breaks his oath in almost every particular, 709.

At the beginning of Lent he crosses to Normandy,

[Col. 1851]

and on Easter Day is followed there by the count of Gloucester, 710. William of Ypres induces him to lay an ambush for the count, 710. But when the count flees the court, the king, overcome by shame, swears that he will never again be guilty of such a crime, 710. In the count’s presence he dissembles; in his absence he reviles him insultingly, 710. Returning to England, he encounters many disturbances, 711. He purchases peace by grants of possessions and the creation of dignities, 712. He receives a message from the count of Gloucester withdrawing his allegiance, 712. His violence toward those who are suspected, 715. He receives complaints from nobles against the bishops of Salisbury and Lincoln because they were fortifying their castles, 716. Cleverly exploiting a quarrel between their servants and the retainers of Alan, count of Brittany, he compels them to surrender the keys of their castles, 717. Conflicting opinions concerning his conduct in these circumstances, 718. He is summoned to defend himself before an ecclesiastical council at Winchester, 719. He sends envoys there to inquire into the reason for the summons, 729. His defence is conducted by Aubrey de Vere, 721. He obtains a postponement of the council until the arrival of the archbishop of Rouen, 722. He threatens any prelates who appeal to Rome and intimidates the council, 723. At the request of his brother and the archbishop of Canterbury, he promises to be merciful to the Church, 724.

But when the empress comes to assert her rights, he grants her permission to travel in order to join her husband, 725. He occupies Malmesbury Castle and the small fortress of Cerne, but fails in besieging Trowbridge, 725. He vainly attempts to bring help to Hereford, ranges through the neighbourhood of Bristol, and ravages the region around Dunster, 725. He restores their privileges to those monasteries despoiled by the bishop of Salisbury, 730. Terrible devastations committed throughout the country by his troops, 730. Distress caused by a severe scarcity and the depreciation of money, 732. He comes to a conference with the empress, but refuses to submit his cause to the judgment of the Church, 735. Invited by the citizens, he enters Lincoln and besieges in the castle the wife and brother of the earl of Chester, 739. The count of Gloucester arrives to aid them; having routed the besiegers, he takes the king captive, 741. Stephen is brought before the empress, 742. He is then taken to Bristol and at first held in honourable custody, but later cast into chains, 742. He permits the archbishop of Canterbury and other prelates to submit themselves to the authority of the empress, 744. He is exchanged for the count of Gloucester, captured by the king’s adherents, 754. Entering the council of Westminster, he complains to the assembled prelates of the injury previously done him, 755. The excuses of his envoys, who order everyone to obey the king, 755. The king burns Wareham and occupies its castle, 766. He also commits Oxford to the flames and besieges the empress in the castle, 766. But after she escapes from the town, he receives the surrender of the garrison and permits the soldiers to return home, 769.

Stephen, count of Blois, marries a daughter of the Conqueror, 456. He proceeds to the Holy Land with Robert, duke of Normandy, 356. He returns home, 571. He sets out again with the count of Poitou, 592. He dies in battle near Ramla, 593, 633.

Stephen, count of Burgundy, accompanies the count of Poitou on the expedition to the Holy Land, 592. He dies in the disastrous battle near Ramla, 593. Stephen, Cistercian abbot, see Harding. Stigand occupies the see of Canterbury by unjust intrusion, while at the same time retaining his see at Winchester, 360. By bribes he induces Benedict, a false pope, to send him the pallium, 341. Deposed from office, he is cast into perpetual imprisonment, 341, 449. His insatiable avarice, 449. He mocks the prophecy of the Confessor, 381.

Streaneshalch, or Streneshalh (Whitby): the abbesses Hilda and Æthelflæd, 77. Suaebræd, see Sigehard. Sugar-bearing cane, which Christian soldiers on their way to Jerusalem suck to quench thirst, 579. Sultan: meaning of the word, 555. Sussex, formerly a kingdom, 140. Swithhelm, king of the East Saxons, baptized by Cedd, 138. Swithræd, king of the East Saxons, expelled by Ecgberht, 139.

Sweyn, king of the Danes, lands at Sandwich, 289. His successful progress, 289. Repulsed from London, 290. He ravages the whole country, 295. His death, 295.

Sweyn II, king of the Danes, expelled by Magnus, king of Norway, 435. He returns with foreign forces, 435. He suffers a great defeat, 436. After Magnus’s death he recovers his kingdom, 436. He twice sends fleets to invade England, 437. He expels his commanders because they had been corrupted by William I, 437.

[Col. 1852]

Sweyn, son of Godwine, banished to Flanders, 339. He becomes a sea-raider, 342. Tancred, nephew of Bohemond I, leaves the army with several companions to visit Bethlehem, 560. While they travel to Jerusalem, pursued by enemies, they put their pursuers to flight, 561. Division of time by means of a candle, 192. Terrible earthquakes, 504, 700. Tewkesbury monastery, 625. Island of Thanet, allotted to the arriving English, 11. A portion of that island granted for the building of a monastery, 22.

Theobald, count of Blois, compelled by Geoffrey Martel to cede Tours in perpetuity, 395. Theodore, archbishop, arrives in England, 21. His learning and labours, 21. His death, 41. Walter Tirel, one of the companions of William Rufus in his final hunt, 508, accidentally kills the king with an arrow aimed at a passing stag, 508. Mounting his horse, he secures his escape by flight, 509.

Tostig, son of Godwine, appointed earl of Northumbria, 343. Expelled by the inhabitants, 343. He crosses to Flanders, 343. Returning to the Humber, he ravages the seacoast, 386. Truce of God, 525. Tudites, or Charles Martel, 98. His body carried off by evil spirits, 354. Turcil, or Turkill, a Dane, invites Sweyn, king of the Danes, into England, 288. His expulsion and death, 205. Turfrith escapes from the hands of Æthelstan, 213. He is drowned in the sea, 213.

Waherus, or Guader, see Guader. The Welsh pay tribute to Æthelstan, 214. Their land reduced to a province, 330, note 1. The Welsh subdued by Edward the Elder, 195. Walkelin succeeds Stigand in the bishopric of Winchester, 449. His goodness, 450. Walcher, bishop of Durham and guardian of the county, 451. Earl Waltheof, son of Siward, one of those allied at York against the Conqueror, 422. He kills many Normans with his own hand in the battle fought there, 427. Because of his extraordinary strength, he is surnamed Digera, 427. After those who upheld his cause are dispersed, he submits to William, 427. He marries Judith, the king’s niece, and enjoys private friendship with him, 427. But he becomes an accomplice in the conspiracy of Ralph de Guader, 428. He is said to have gone to Normandy and disclosed the matter to the king, 430. After long imprisonment, he is finally beheaded, 428.

Walwen, nephew of King Arthur, expelled by Hengist and Horsa after a severe contest, 466. His tomb discovered in the age of the Conqueror, 466.

Henry, count of Eu, chief promoter of Henry I’s election as king, 619. When Henry is deserted by his other nobles, he adheres to him steadfastly, 620. His gentle and peaceful disposition, 635.

The Isle of Wight granted to Wihtgar, 26. Converted to Christianity, 109. Wells—that is, the bishopric of the Church of Wells—transferred to Bath, 517. Saint Werburh, daughter of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, 110, 368.

Whitby monastery, formerly called Streneshalh, 77. Wibba, father of Penda, king of the Mercians, 107.

Wihtred, king of Kent, restores peace to the kingdom, 23. His qualities and death, 23. Wiglaf, king of the Mercians, defeated by Ecgberht and paying him tribute, 132, 148. Rising at Worcester, 310. Wihtburh, daughter of Anna, king of East Anglia, 359. Wihtgar: his honourable rule on the Isle of Wight, 27.

Wilfrith, bishop of Hexham, 76. Expelled from his see, 78. Wilfrith, see Werefrith.

William, duke of Normandy, son of Rollo: an attempted assassination against him is recounted, 229.

William, duke of Normandy and later king of England, surnamed the Conqueror: his mental and bodily qualities are variously represented by Norman and Saxon writers, 389. His birth, 391. He is entrusted by his father to the care of Count Gilbert, under the supervision of Henry I, king of France, 392. On hearing of his father’s death, disturbances arise in Normandy, 392. He is admitted to knighthood by the king of France, who restores this order in the duchy, 393. He repays the favour by giving the king aid against Geoffrey Martel, 394. After Geoffrey captures Alençon Castle, he retaliates by occupying Domfront, 396. He recovers Alençon, 397. He suppresses the rebellion of his uncle, the count of Arques, 397. When friendship with the king of France is broken, he wins victory at the battle of Mortemer and obtains peace, 399. He is appointed by the Confessor as successor to the throne of England,

[Col. 1854]

382. He orders Harold to be released from captivity and receives him honourably, 384. He takes him with him on his successful expedition against Brittany, 384. Having received Harold’s promise, confirmed by oath, that he will aid William’s accession to the throne of England, he receives him as his son-in-law, 384. At Edward’s death he asserts his right and protests vainly with Harold, 408. He prepares an invasion, 409. He refers his cause to the supreme pontiff, from whom he receives a consecrated banner, 410. He crosses into England, 411. His fall when he disembarks is turned into a favourable omen, 410. His noble treatment of Harold’s spies, 412. His proposals rejected by Harold, 413. He gains victory in the battle at Hastings, 415. His conduct in that battle, 415. He sends Harold’s body to Harold’s mother, 420. He enters London in triumph and is crowned by the archbishop of York, 221. He subdues Exeter, 421. He destroys York and lays waste the surrounding region, 422. His liberality toward Edgar Ætheling, 425. His political treatment of Englishmen not devoted to him, 425. His frequent pardons of Edwin and Morcar, and his grief on hearing of their deaths, 427. He is reconciled with Earl Waltheof and gives him his niece Judith in marriage, 427. He orders the earl to be punished with death for treason, 428. He becomes harsher toward the English, 428. He repels an invasion by exiled Englishmen with an English army, 428. He deposes many native clergy and thereafter forbids the promotion of Englishmen, 429. He reproaches William Fitz-Osbern for his military frenzy, 431. His duchy ravaged by Robert the Frisian, 432. He retaliates by aiding Baldwin against his uncle Robert, 433. He makes the Welsh tributary, 433. He sends an English expedition into the territory of Maine, 433. He suffers a great loss in Brittany, 434. He refuses Normandy to his son Robert, 454, 607. His sarcasm against Robelin, 607. His disputes with King Philip, to whom Robert gives aid, 434. He is wounded by Robert in battle, 434. He exacts a great tax from the people, 434. He prevents two Danish invasions by corrupting their leaders, 435. He counts Hugh the Great among his mercenaries, 439. His private life and domestic habits, 446. The abbeys of Saint Stephen at Caen and Battle founded by him, 446. The reason given for the earlier foundation, 448. He consents to the deposition of Stigand, 449. His reverence for Lanfranc and Bishop Wulfstan, 450. His chastity assailed by slanders, 453. Coolness between him and the queen because of her attachment to Robert’s party, 453. His intense grief at the queen’s death, 453. He ensures that the relics of the Confessor are buried with magnificent funeral rites, 454. His sons, 454. His daughters, 455. He orders the body of his father to be brought to Nicaea, 456. He marries his mother to Herluin of Conteville, 456. His brothers by that marriage, 456. He casts Bishop Odo, as earl of Kent, into prison and acquires his immense treasures, 457. His liberality toward foreigners, 457. He strips and impoverishes England by granting lands to Norman monasteries, 457. Description of his person, 458. His magnificent display at the principal solemnities, 458. His love of money, 458. King Philip’s foolish jest about his corpulence, 459. His bitter reply and swift vengeance, 459. His last illness, 460. His testament and death, 460. His burial at Caen obstructed by a man claiming the ground where they were burying him, 461. Satisfaction given by his son Henry to the claimant, 461. Great alms distributed by Rufus because of his death, 461.

William II, Rufus, born in Normandy before England was occupied, 485. His education, 485. His military ardour, 485. He receives the kingdom from his dying father and quickly sets out to occupy it, 486. Auspiciously received, he is crowned by Lanfranc, 486. He restores his uncle Odo, once released to freedom, to the earldom of Kent, 183. Rebellion of the nobles against him, stirred up by Odo, 487. He summons the English to his aid and promises satisfaction for their complaints, 488. He draws Roger of Montgomery away from the conspiracy by a subtle argument, 488. He seizes Odo’s castles of Tonbridge and Pevensey and takes him captive in Pevensey Castle, 489. He sends an armed force with Odo to obtain the surrender of Rochester, 489. Odo is led from prison by the garrison soldiers, and the king’s supporters are seized, 489. William besieges the town with English troops, 489. Having captured it, he suppresses the rebellion, 490. The king’s officers intercept and destroy aid sent from Normandy to the rebels, 490. He invades Normandy and acquires some towns by bribery, 490. Peace between the brothers is restored on the condition that William obtain Maine from Robert, 491. They proceed together for that purpose, 491. They are opposed by their brother Henry, whom they besiege on Mont-Saint-Michel, 491. Examples of the king’s magnanimity, 491, 502. He reproves Robert for his ill-timed compassion, 493. Peace having been arranged, he returns to England with his brothers, 493. He is unsuccessful in his expeditions against the Welsh and Scots,

[Col. 1855]

493. His defeat is attributed to the harshness of the climate and the nature of the soil, 493. Peace with Malcolm restored through Robert’s mediation, 494. He makes Duncan, Malcolm’s illegitimate son, a knight and establishes him as king after his father’s death, 627. After Duncan is killed by his uncle Donald, he establishes Edgar as king, 627. The close union of William’s virtues and vices, 495. His fierceness in public and affability in private life, 495. An amusing example of his prodigality, 496. Extortions of Ralph Flambard to satisfy William’s mad prodigality, 497. Hence the prevalence of simony, the impunity of wealthy offenders, and the corruption of public morals, 497. He incites the Jews of London to dispute with bishops, 500. Robert mortgages Normandy to him for ten thousand marks, which William exacts by a very heavy tax imposed on England, 500. His reply to the clergy’s complaint, 500. Severity of his forest laws, 500. Severe punishment of certain rebellious nobles, 500. He builds a vast and costly palace in London, 504. Detailed description of his person, 504. Notice of notable events of his reign, 504. Portents preceding his death, 505. His friends attempt to dissuade him from going to the forest, 508. Having changed his intention, he is accidentally pierced by an arrow shot by Walter Tirel, 509. His body is carried in a cart to Winchester and buried in the cathedral church, 509. Recapitulation of his bodily and mental qualities, 510.

William, prince, son of King Henry I by Matilda, 651. Barely twelve years old, he receives promises of allegiance from all the free men of England and Normandy, 652. He marries the daughter of Fulk of Anjou, 634, and receives Maine as her dowry, 652. It is commonly believed that the prophecy of the Confessor (381) would be fulfilled in him, 652. He does homage to Louis VI for the duchy of Normandy, 634, 652. Detailed description of the shipwreck in which he loses his life, 653.

William, son of Robert II, duke of Normandy: his birth, 609. He is assisted against his uncle Henry I by Baldwin, count of Flanders, 623. He marries the daughter of Fulk of Anjou, 654. The marriage is dissolved through the influence of King Henry, 690. He becomes count of Flanders, 690.

William, eldest son of Robert, count of Gloucester, is given as a hostage for King Stephen’s wife when his father is released from captivity, 754. He is put in command of his father’s castle at Wareham, 765. The town is burned and the castle captured by the king, 766. The town recovered by the count of Gloucester, 768. A terrible storm at Winchcombe, 504. Wine, bishop: his simony in purchasing the see of London, 109.

Henry, bishop of Winchester, brother of King Stephen, supports his brother’s cause and becomes surety that Stephen will restore and preserve the liberties of the Church, 703. He is present at Stephen’s coronation, 704; appointed legate by the supreme pontiff, 709. He reproaches the king for arresting the bishops of Salisbury and Lincoln and occupying their castles, and compels him to defend his conduct at the council held at Winchester, 719. The legate’s speech at the opening of the council, 719. His reply to the nobles sent to inquire why the king was being summoned to judgment, 720. He declares his view that the bishops’ possessions must be restored before they can plead or conduct a case according to the laws, 722. When the council is dissolved because of the king’s threats, he strives to bring Stephen back to goodwill toward the Church, 724. He sends the empress to the count of Gloucester after she obtains permission from the king to travel, 725. He vainly attempts to make peace between his brother and the empress, 734. He receives the empress as supreme lady on the condition that she swear to preserve the liberties of the Church, 743. In solemn procession he conducts her into Winchester Cathedral, 744. He convenes a great council of clergy at Winchester to confirm acceptance of the empress, 744. His speech in these circumstances,

745. He asks the council to await the arrival of the Londoners, 747. His reply to the Londoners demanding the king’s release, 747. He refuses to allow a writing sent by Stephen’s wife to be read publicly, 748. His reply when this writing is insistently read by the queen’s messenger, 748. Excommunication of many supporters of the king, especially William Martel, who had greatly angered the legate, 748. The legate breaks friendship with the empress because she refuses to grant Mortain and Boulogne to Eustace while his father the king is held captive, 750. He visits Stephen’s wife at Guildford and absolves the excommunicated supporters of the king, 750. Surrounded by a large retinue, he proceeds to a conference with the empress at Winchester, 751. Andover, Hyde Monastery, and Wherwell Abbey burned by adherents of his party, 752. He swears that he will voluntarily make himself the empress’s captive if the king refuses to grant freedom to the count of Gloucester, 761. Once the king is freed, he convenes the council of Westminster, in which he excuses his former conduct toward the king and orders all to obey him, 755. His great indignation when insulted by a supporter of the empress, 756.

Godfrey, prior of Winchester: his learning and piety, 678. He is the author of many books and familiar letters, 678. He arranges for the divine office to be performed in better order and offers an example of hospitality and humility, 678. He lies bedridden for many years before dying, 679.

Council at Winchester concerning secular clergy, 257. Another, to settle the dispute arising between King Stephen and the bishops of Salisbury and Lincoln, 719. Saint Wistan, son of Wimund, whose father was Wiglaf, king of the Mercians, 364. Withlaf, see Wiglaf. Wulfheard, bishop of Hereford, 119. Mention of Woden, 11. His sons, 62. Woodstock: King Henry’s well-stocked palace there, 638. Worgret, abbot of Glastonbury, 40.

Wulfhere, king of the Mercians: his labours for the cause of Christianity, 109. He grants the Isle of Wight, taken from the West Saxons, to Æthelwealh, king of Sussex, 109. He sells the episcopal see of London to Wine, 109. His family, 110. Wulpher, see Wulfhere.

Wulfstan, archbishop of York, cast into prison by Eadred, 232. Wulfstan, precentor of Winchester, writes the life of Bishop Æthelwold, 239, and a book on the harmony of sounds, 239. Wulfstan, bishop of Worcester, attends the council concerning primacy, 477. He prevents the council from postponing the performance of the religious office, 480. EPISTLE LXIX.—To Guilencus, Bishop of Langres.—That he not permit Herbert, Abbot of St. Stephen at Dijon, to be harassed by Humbert, a priest. 114  

EPISTLE LXX.—At the request of Heloise, prioress, he receives under protection the convent of the Holy Trinity [the Paraclete] and confirms its goods, on condition that six coins be paid annually by the nuns to the Lateran palace. 114  

[Col. 1860]

EPISTLE LXXI.—To John, Bishop of Glasgow.—That he obey Thomas [Thurstan], Archbishop of York. 115  

EPISTLE LXXII.—To all the bishops of Scotland.—Concerning the obedience to be rendered to their metropolitan, the Archbishop of York. 115  

EPISTLE LXXIII.—To Stephen, Abbot of Reigny.—He exempts the abbots of Reigny from the obedience which they had rendered to the Bishop of Autun for the place of Fontem. 116  

EPISTLE LXXIV.—To Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours.—Privilege of Fontevraud. 116  

EPISTLE LXXV.—To Hebert, Abbot of St. Stephen at Dijon. 117  

EPISTLE LXXVI.—To the Abbot of Fontenelle.—That he receive blessing from his prelate and obey him. 117  

EPISTLE LXXVII.—To William, Bishop of Langres. 118  

EPISTLE LXXVIII.—To the archbishops and bishops of France, etc.—He orders that the nuns of Fontevraud, unwilling to defend their property by the ordeal of red-hot iron or by judicial combat, be defended in their possessions by two or three suitable witnesses. 118  

EPISTLE LXXIX.—To Louis VI, King of the Franks.—He writes that he has arrived safely at Cluny. 119  

EPISTLE LXXX.—Privilege for the Church of St. Stephen at Die. 119  

EPISTLE LXXXI.—To Briccius, Bishop of Nantes.—That he not subject the monastery of Trénores to injuries. 121  

EPISTLE LXXXII.—To Peter, abbot, and the monks of St. Benignus at Dijon.—By apostolic authority he confirms to them the revenues from the toll of the town of Dijon, concerning which there had been a dispute. 121  

EPISTLE LXXXIII.—He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Cîteaux. 122  

EPISTLE LXXXIV.—He assigns to Henry, Bishop of Toul, the estate of Berchem, adjudicated to the monastery of Moyenmoutier. 123  

EPISTLE LXXXV.—At the request of Bishop Henry, he confirms the goods of the Church of Toul. 125  

EPISTLE LXXXVI.—To Herbert, Abbot of St. Stephen at Dijon. 125  

EPISTLE LXXXVII.—At the request of Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of St. Mary of Clairvaux. 126  

EPISTLE LXXXVIII.—Bull for the establishment of regular canons in the convent of St. Laudus at Coutances. 126  

EPISTLE LXXXIX.—To those who visit the monastery of Cluny on the day of the dedication of the high altar, he remits forty days of the penance undertaken. 127  

EPISTLE XC.—To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—The dispute between Cluny and the abbey of St. Giles is settled. 128  

EPISTLE XCI.—To all archbishops and bishops.—Cluniac privileges. 129  

EPISTLE XCII.—He informs the abbots, clergy, princes, and people of Trier that Albero, whom they had elected, had been consecrated by him and granted the pallium. He warns them to obey him. 131  

EPISTLE XCIII.—Privilege for the monastery of Trénores. 131  

EPISTLE XCIV.—Bull for the monastery of Tiron. 132  

EPISTLE XCV.—To William, lord of Montpellier.—He receives his person and all goods belonging to him under the guardianship and protection of the Roman Church, so that no one may dare to take them away, diminish them, or harass them with any molestations. 133  

EPISTLE XCVI.—To Peter the Venerable.—Privilege concerning the monastery of Blessed Mary of La Charité-sur-Loire: it is always to be a priory of the Cluniac Order, and an abbot is never to be established there. 134  

EPISTLE XCVII.—To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—He newly invests him with the abbey of St. Bertin, commanding its monks to obey him. 135  

EPISTLE XCVIII.—To William, lord of Montpellier.—He commends his devotion toward himself and the Roman Church and urges him to persevere in his good resolve. 136  

EPISTLE XCIX.—He confirms the possessions and rights of the Church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca. 136  

EPISTLE C.—He communicates this to [Walter, Archbishop of Ravenna]: “We have crossed the Alps; at Asti we celebrated the Resurrection of the Lord; then, at the request of the people of Novara, we went to their city and consecrated their principal church.” He instructs him to come to meet him at Pavia. 136  

[Col. 1861]

EPISTLE CI.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Blessed Alexander at Bergamo. 136  

EPISTLE CII.—He receives the monastery of St. Savior at Pavia under the protection of the holy Roman Church and confirms its goods. 138  

EPISTLE CIII.—He receives the Church of Novara under his protection and confirms the possessions of Bishop Litifred and his successors. 139  

EPISTLE CIV.—He confirms the goods of the canons of the Church of Novara. 141  

EPISTLE CV.—He grants to the canons of St. Alexander at Bergamo certain churches belonging to the Apostolic See. 143  

EPISTLE CVI.—He confirms the Church of Aquileia as metropolitan of sixteen bishoprics, and grants Patriarch Peregrinus the use of the pallium, rationale, mitre, and cross. 144  

EPISTLE CVII.—To Atto, prior of the Church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca. 145  

EPISTLE CVIII.—He confirms all the goods and privileges of the monastery of St. Sixtus in the diocese of Piacenza. 146  

EPISTLE CIX.—He confirms all the goods, rights, and privileges of St. Antoninus the martyr in the city of Piacenza. 148  

EPISTLE CX.—He informs Henry, King of the English, that he has directed Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, to satisfy the king’s wishes concerning certain abbots. But he urges him not to allow abbots to be without a head. He commends Archbishop Hugh. 150  

EPISTLE CXI.—To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen.—He urges him to yield somewhat of ecclesiastical right to the king. 150  

EPISTLE CXII.—Privilege for the monastery of Tilley. 151  

EPISTLE CXIII.—He receives the Lenensis monastery under protection and confirms its privileges and possessions. 152  

EPISTLE CXIV.—Privilege for the canons of the Church of St. Mary at Piacenza. 153  

EPISTLE CXV.—Privilege for the monastery of SS. Faustinus and Jovita, in the diocese of Brescia, of the Cassinese Order. 154  

EPISTLE CXVI.—Privilege for the convent of St. Julia, in the diocese of Brescia, of the Cassinese Order. 156  

EPISTLE CXVII.—Privilege for the Church of St. Peter at Guastalla. 159  

EPISTLE CXVIII.—He confirms to the Church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca the Church of St. Savior, granted by Landulf, Bishop of Ferrara. 160  

EPISTLE CXIX.—He decrees that the monks of the monastery of St. George Major, received under the protection of the Apostolic See, shall henceforth elect as abbot whomever they themselves consider suitable. 160  

EPISTLE CXX.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Nonantola. 161  

EPISTLE CXXI.—To Berthold, Abbot of St. Blasien.—He approves the separation of the Church of Bürgeln from the Church of Eggenheim. 164  

EPISTLE CXXII.—To Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, and Stephen, Bishop of Paris.—That they strive to restore to the subdean of Orléans and his associates the honors and goods taken away from them. 165  

EPISTLE CXXIII.—Privilege for the Church of St. Ursus at Aosta (province of Tarentaise). 165  

EPISTLE CXXIV.—To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—The monastery of SS. Facundus and Primitivus in Spain is granted. 166  

EPISTLE CXXV.—He confirms, both generally and specifically, their possessions and goods to Norbert and his successors, the Archbishops of Magdeburg. 167  

EPISTLE CXXVI.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Mary of Morrona. 168  

EPISTLE CXXVII.—Privilege for the convent of St. Mary of Fontaines. 170  

EPISTLE CXXVIII.—He confirms the Premonstratensian discipline and possessions of the Church of Upper Celle. 170  

EPISTLE CXXIX.—To Diego, Archbishop of Compostela, Aria, Bishop of León, and Peter, Bishop of Lugo. 171  

EPISTLE CXXX.—He informs the archbishops, bishops, and abbots established throughout the provinces of Toledo, Braga, and Compostela that A., invader of the Church of Oviedo, has been excommunicated by him. 172  

EPISTLE CXXXI.—At the request of Bishop Landulf, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Ferrara. 172  

EPISTLE CXXXII.—He adorns Syrus of Genoa, made archbishop from bishop, with the pallium and subjects to him as suffragans the bishops of Mariana, Nebbio, and Accia. 174  

EPISTLE CXXXIII.—To Hugh, Duke of Burgundy.—He warns him to protect Herbert, Abbot of Dijon, against the monks of Saint-Seine, whom he declares excommunicated. 176  

[Col. 1862]

EPISTLE CXXXIV.—He receives the Church of St. Stephen at Prats under his protection and confirms its rights. 177  

EPISTLE CXXXV.—To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—Having been rescued from various dangers, he requests votive prayers. 178  

EPISTLE CXXXVI.—He establishes the monastery of Brugnato as an episcopal see, suffragan to the Church of Genoa. 178  

EPISTLE CXXXVII.—To Adalbero, Archbishop of Hamburg.—That all the bishops of Denmark, Sweden, Norway, etc., be subject to him. 180  

EPISTLE CXXXVIII.—To Nicholas, King of the Danes.—On the same subject. 181  

EPISTLE CXXXIX.—To . . . . . King of the Swedes.—On the same subject. 181  

EPISTLE CXL.—He commands Ascer, Bishop of Lund, to obey Archbishop Adalbero as metropolitan. 182  

EPISTLE CXLI.—He commands the bishops of Sweden to obey [Adalbero], Archbishop of Hamburg, as metropolitan. 182  

EPISTLE CXLII.—Bull concerning certain bishoprics in Poland and those subject to the Archbishop of Magdeburg on this side [of Poland]. 183  

EPISTLE CXLIII.—He grants Bernard, Bishop of Paderborn, and his successors the use of the *rationale*. 186  

EPISTLE CXLIV.—At the request of Abbot Bertoo, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of the Savior and St. Boniface at Fulda. 187  

EPISTLE CXLV.—To Lothair and Richiza.—He grants the allodial lands of Countess Matilda. 188  

EPISTLE CXLVI.—Privilege by which the monastery of Prüm, in the diocese of Trier, together with all its possessions, is received under the protection of the Apostolic See. 189  

EPISTLE CXLVII.—Privilege for the Vallombrosan monastery. 190  

EPISTLE CXLVIII.—He rebukes [Rainald], Archbishop of Reims, and [B., read Henry], Archbishop of Sens, because they had not more swiftly pronounced sentence of excommunication against those who killed the prior of St. Victor. 191  

EPISTLE CXLIX.—To Atto, Bishop of Pistoia.—Concerning the immunity granted to the Church of Pistoia. 192  

EPISTLE CL.—To Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, and Stephen, Bishop of Paris.—What penance the killers of Archembald, subdeacon of Orléans, must perform in order to make satisfaction and be absolved from excommunication. 193  

EPISTLE CLI.—Privilege for the monastery of Reesbach. 194  

EPISTLE CLII.—Bull by which the convent of Frankenthal is established and at the same time received under the protection of the Holy See. 197  

EPISTLE CLIII.—He confirms the possessions of the monastery of St. Flora at Arezzo. 199  

EPISTLE CLIV.—To Briccius, Bishop of Nantes. 201  

EPISTLE CLV.—He informs Diego, Archbishop of Compostela, that after the departure of Emperor Lothair he remained for some time in the city with his household; then, “so that a safer and easier access to us might lie open to our brethren,” he went to Pisa. He commends Astaldus. 203  

EPISTLE CLVI.—Privilege for the abbey of Prémontré. 204  

EPISTLE CLVII.—Privilege for the monastery of Sesto. 206  

EPISTLE CLVIII.—He grants Henry, Abbot of Padilirone, and his successors the Church of St. Caesarius (of Vilzacara), on condition that they pay three bezants each year. 208  

EPISTLE CLIX.—Bull confirming the estates and other property of the monks of Quincy. 209  

EPISTLE CLX.—To Archbishop Geoffrey and the suffragan bishops and abbots of the Church of Dol established throughout the same province.—He invites them to the Council of Pisa. 210  

EPISTLE CLXI.—At the request of Bishop John, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Fiesole. 211  

EPISTLE CLXII.—He informs Gregory, Bishop of Bergamo, that he has summoned the canons of St. Alexander, who had rejected judges appointed by himself, and the canons of St. Vincent, for the next Ascension of the Lord (16 May 1135). 213  

EPISTLE CLXIII.—He gives thanks to Diego, Archbishop of Compostela, for the gifts sent. 213  

EPISTLE CLXIV.—To Rainald, Archbishop of Reims; Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen; Hugh, Archbishop of Tours; and their suffragans.—Concerning the murder of Thomas, prior of St. Victor. 214  

[Col. 1863]

EPISTLE CLXV.—He confirms the possessions and rights of the Church of Mortara, consecrated by himself. 215  

EPISTLE CLXVI.—He receives the monastery of Huysburg under protection. 215  

EPISTLE CLXVII.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the abbey of St. Peter of the Golden Valley. 215  

EPISTLE CLXVIII.—Bull confirming the privileges of the monastery of Scheningen. 217  

EPISTLE CLXIX.—He confirms the privilege of the Church in the town of Roncaglia, built by the Bishop of Piacenza and given to the canons of St. Antoninus. 218  

EPISTLE CLXX.—He grants the Church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca a hospice and the Church of St. John. 220  

EPISTLE CLXXI.—He confirms the possessions of the abbey of Heilissem, to be built by Rainer. 220  

EPISTLE CLXXII.—He confirms the Order of St. Augustine for the Premonstratensian church, on 3 May. 221  

EPISTLE CLXXIII.—He restores to the Church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca a parish seized by the monks of St. George. 221  

EPISTLE CLXXIV.—To Bishop Hubert and the canons of Lucca. 221  

EPISTLE CLXXV.—He confirms certain possessions of the Church of Bonn. 222  

EPISTLE CLXXVI.—Privilege for the abbey of Vendôme. 223  

EPISTLE CLXXVII.—Privilege for the Church of Selva Munda. 225  

EPISTLE CLXXVIII.—He exhorts the archbishops and bishops established throughout the German kingdom to observe the privilege of the Roman Church: that major cases be referred for examination to the Apostolic See and that all oppressed persons appeal to it without fear. 226  

EPISTLE CLXXIX.—Privilege for the monastery of Nobiliac. 227  

EPISTLE CLXXX.—The privileges and liberties of the Abbey of St. Peter on Mont Blandin, of the Order of St. Benedict, are confirmed. 227  

EPISTLE CLXXXI.—To Henry, Bishop of Toul.—He confirms the agreement made between him and Count Frederick of Toul. 228  

EPISTLE CLXXXII.—He adjudicates the Church of St. John at Vico to the canons of Blessed Mary at Piacenza, under an annual payment to be made to the Apostolic See. 230  

EPISTLE CLXXXIII.—Bull for the Abbey of Juncelles. 231  

EPISTLE CLXXXIV.—Privilege for the Abbey of Mailly. 233  

EPISTLE CLXXXV.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Michael at Hugthoven. 234  

EPISTLE CLXXXVI.—Bull by which he raises the priory of St. Peter of Nantes to the rank of an abbey, uniting several churches to it. 237  

EPISTLE CLXXXVII.—At the request of Goslenus, Bishop of Soissons, he confirms to Marmoutier the Church of SS. Rufinus and Valerius at Basel. 238  

EPISTLE CLXXXVIII.—To Heloise and the others dedicated to the divine service in the oratory of the Holy Trinity. 239  

EPISTLE CLXXXIX.—He informs the clerics of the Church of Milan that Tetaldus of Medolacus has been excommunicated because of his hostile conduct toward the Church of Virgis. 240  

EPISTLE CXC.—He informs Gregory, bishop, clergy, and people of Bergamo that he has settled the controversy between the canons of St. Vincent and St. Alexander. 240  

EPISTLE CXCI.—Privilege for the monastery of the Holy Cross at Donauwörth. 240  

EPISTLE CXCII.—He confirms by letter the judgment rendered concerning the controversy of the canons of St. Alexander and St. Vincent at Bergamo. 242  

EPISTLE CXCIII.—Privilege for the monastery of Blessed Mary at Cagia. 244  

EPISTLE CXCIV.—Privilege for the Church of St. John at Monza. 246  

EPISTLE CXCV.—Bull confirming the possessions of the monastery of Quadraginta. 247  

EPISTLE CXCVI.—He grants Albero, Bishop-elect of Liège, the use of the *rationale*. 247  

EPISTLE CXCVII.—Privilege for the canonry of SS. Peter and Ursus at Aosta. 248  

EPISTLE CXCVIII.—To Diego, Archbishop of Compostela. 249  

EPISTLE CXCIX.—He confirms to William, Archbishop of Canterbury, and to the Church of Canterbury the Church of St. Martin at Dover, given by Henry, King of the English. 250  

EPISTLE CC.—To Albero, Archbishop of Trier.—Against the Abbot of St. Maximin, whom, if the accusations made against him are true, he judges should be deposed. 251  

EPISTLE CC *bis*.—Privilege for the monastery of Liesborn.  

[Col. 1864]

EPISTLE CCI.—To Gerard, Abbot of St. Maximin.—He charges him with simony and dissipation of property. 252  

EPISTLE CCII.—To certain abbots.—He praises their congregations for strengthening the discipline of the order. 253  

EPISTLE CCIII.—He forbids Bernard, Bishop of Hildesheim, and his successors to alienate Vincenburg Castle. 254  

EPISTLE CCIV.—He informs [Leopold], margrave, that, having learned from Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg, of his devotion, he has undertaken the protection of the Church of Blessed Augustine. He addresses greetings to [Agnes], his wife, [Adalbert], margrave, and his other sons. 254  

EPISTLE CCV.—To Albero, Archbishop of Trier.—He entrusts to him for settlement the delayed case of the Abbot of St. Maximin. 255  

EPISTLE CCVI.—To the clergy and chapter of St. Deodatus in the valley of Galilee. 255  

EPISTLE CCVII.—To Guigo, Prior of the Carthusians.—He informs him that St. Hugh of Grenoble has been enrolled among the saints and urges him to write his life. 256  

EPISTLE CCVIII.—He receives the monastery of Ahausen under protection. 256  

EPISTLE CCIX.—He commands [Albero], Archbishop of Trier, to compel Brunicus and his sons to restore the estate of Filestanges to the monastery of Remiremont. 256  

EPISTLE CCX.—Privilege for the monastery of Ripoll. 256  

EPISTLE CCXI.—To John, prior, and the brethren of St. Mary in Porto. 257  

EPISTLE CCXII.—To the clerics of Modena.—He states that the consuls of Modena have been excommunicated for attacking the monastery of Nonantola. 257  

EPISTLE CCXIII.—To the abbot and monks of Le Bec. 258  

EPISTLE CCIV.—To Berthold, Abbot of St. Blasien.—Concerning maintaining peace with the monks of Schaffhausen. 258  

EPISTLE CCXV.—Privilege for the monastery of Hilsenburg. 259  

EPISTLE CCXVI.—To Fromundus, Abbot of Vendôme.—Concerning the agreement made between Ulgerius, Bishop of Angers, and the monks of Vendôme. 261  

EPISTLE CCXVII.—He orders Henry, Archbishop of Sens, to abstain from episcopal office. 264  

EPISTLE CCXVIII.—To Robert, Abbot of St. Mary de la Rote, in the diocese of Angers. 265  

EPISTLE CCXIX.—Privilege for the monastery of Fosses. 266  

EPISTLE CCXX.—To Gregory, Bishop of Bergamo. 268  

EPISTLE CCXXI.—To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—Confirmation of the Church of Rochabo at Vecurti. 268  

EPISTLE CCXXII.—To the same.—Confirmation of Mont-Dieu. 269  

EPISTLE CCXXIII.—Privilege for the Church of Nice. 270  

EPISTLE CCXXIV.—To Alvisus, Bishop of Arras. 271  

EPISTLE CCXXV.—Privilege for the Camaldolese congregation. 272  

EPISTLE CCXXVI.—He congratulates Lothair, Emperor of the Romans, after Frederick, Duke of Swabia, had been defeated. He urges him to act so that he may “obtain David’s empire and Solomon’s kingdom.” (For *Papia*, one must read *Pisis* [Pisa].) 275  

EPISTLE CCXXVII.—Privilege, or confirming bull, for the Church of Rora. 275  

EPISTLE CCXXVIII.—Privilege for the monastery of Lorch. 276  

EPISTLE CCXXIX.—He confirms the discipline and goods of the monastery of St. Paul at Verdun. 277  

EPISTLE CCXXX.—He confirms the cemetery of the monastery of Celta Paulina. 278  

EPISTLE CCXXXI.—To Raynald, Archbishop of Reims.—That he grant his archdeacon, elected Archbishop of Bourges, to the people requesting him. 278  

EPISTLE CCXXXII.—To Master A., Archdeacon of Reims.—That he obey God, who calls him to the archbishopric of Bourges. 279  

EPISTLE CCXXXIII.—Privilege for the Church of St. Aubert at Cambrai. 280  

EPISTLE CCXXXIV.—To Alvisus, Bishop of Arras. 283  

EPISTLE CCXXXV.—Privilege for the Abbey of Balne. 283  

[Col. 1865]

EPISTLE CCXXXVI.—He grants Henry, Patriarch of Grado, the use of the pallium and of the cross to be borne before him, and confirms the goods of the Church. 286  

EPISTLE CCXXXVII.—He confirms the possessions of the Church of St. Victor at Marseilles. 287  

EPISTLE CCXXXVIII.—At the request of Archbishop James, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Guesnes. 287  

EPISTLE CCXXXIX.—To Gregory, Bishop of Bergamo. 287  

EPISTLE CCXL.—Privilege for the Church of Blessed Mary of Reno. 288  

EPISTLE CCXLI.—Privilege for the monastery of St. George at Prüfening. 289  

EPISTLE CCXLII.—To Henry, Bishop of Regensburg. 291  

EPISTLE CCXLIII.—Privilege for the Church of Polling. 291  

EPISTLE CCXLIV.—Privilege for the Abbey of Schuttern. 293  

EPISTLE CCXLV.—General privilege for the monastery of St. Nicasius at Reims. 294  

EPISTLE CCXLVI.—He confirms the foundation of the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu in the diocese of Reims. 296  

EPISTLE CCXLVII.—He confirms the immunities of the Church of Marsna near Maastricht, belonging to the monastery of Blessed Remigius, in which monks are substituted for canons. 298  

EPISTLE CCXLVIII.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the canons of the Church of St. Lawrence at Genoa. 299  

EPISTLE CCXLIX.—He confirms the Order of the regular canons of St. Augustine, recently introduced into the monastery of Steinfeld in the diocese of Cologne. 299  

EPISTLE CCL.—To Stephen, King of the English.—He receives him, unanimously elected and consecrated king, as a special son of Blessed Peter and the Roman Church. 301  

EPISTLE CCLI.—Bull in favor of the regular canons of St. John in the suburb of Sens. 302  

EPISTLE CCLII.—To the canons of St. Frigdianus at Lucca. 303  

EPISTLE CCLIII.—He commends Atto, prior, and the brethren of the Church of St. Frigdianus to all clerics and laymen established throughout the diocese of Lucca. 303  

EPISTLE CCLIV.—To Petronilla, Abbess of Fontevraud. 304  

EPISTLE CCLV.—To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen: severe in correcting faults, he exhorts him to gentleness, promising that, if the Abbot of St. Wandrille “should disdain to obey him until the approaching solemnity of Pentecost, we shall hold valid the sentence which he may reasonably pronounce against him.” He sends a stole as a gift. 304  

EPISTLES CCLVI–CCLVII.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Peter at Melk. 305  

EPISTLE CCLVIII.—He consoles Agnes, widow of the late Margrave Leopold, and her sons upon Leopold’s death. He commends the monks of Melk. He adds: “In accordance with your requests, when we have occasion to see our dearest son Emperor Lothair, we shall willingly and affectionately ask him to preserve your rights for you.” 306  

EPISTLE CCLIX.—He receives the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Sacargia under protection and confirms its privileges. 307  

EPISTLE CCLX.—Privilege for the Church of Good Hope. 307  

EPISTLE CCLXI.—Bull confirming the transfer of the abbey from St. Firminus to St. John beside the Sélune, as well as the possessions of that abbey. 308  

EPISTLE CCLXII.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Peter at Selincourt. 310  

EPISTLE CCLXIII.—At the request of Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, he confirms the possessions of the monastery of St. Mary of La Colombe. 311  

EPISTLE CCLXIV.—He receives the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem under protection, confirms its possessions, and increases its privileges. 312  

EPISTLE CCLXV.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Peter at Perugia. 314  

EPISTLE CCLXVI.—Bull for the monastery of La Charité. 316  

EPISTLE CCLXVII.—Privilege for the Church of Orange. 318  

EPISTLE CCLXVIII.—To Petronilla, Abbess of Fontevraud. 320  

EPISTLE CCLXIX.—At the request of Archbishop Hubert, he confirms the goods of the Church of St. Mary at Pisa. 321  

EPISTLE CCLXX.—To Diego, Bishop of Compostela. 323  

EPISTLE CCLXXI.—He commands Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz, to protect the household of the monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg against the knight Sigebot. 323  

[Col. 1866]

EPISTLE CCLXXII.—Privilege for the Church of London. 323  

EPISTLE CCLXXIII.—Privilege for the Hospital of Roncesvalles. 325  

EPISTLE CCLXXIV.—He sends letters “to all monasteries dependent on the Church of Monte Cassino” ordering that they obey neither Rainald, abbot-elect of Monte Cassino, nor the brethren. 325  

EPISTLE CCLXXV.—To the monks of Murbach. 325  

EPISTLE CCLXXVI.—To Walter, Bishop of Augsburg.—He commands him to refrain from inflicting injuries upon the monastery of Buron, since it is a royal monastery. 326  

EPISTLE CCLXXVII.—To the monks of Benediktbeuern, commanding them, since Abbot Engelschalk has been absolved from the bond of excommunication, to render him reverence and obedience as their prelate and master. 326  

EPISTLE CCLXXVIII.—At the request of Abbot Conrad, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of the Savior and St. Boniface at Fulda. 327  

EPISTLE CCLXXIX.—Concerning the reverence due to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre. 329  

EPISTLE CCLXXX.—To Peter, Abbot of Cluny. 329  

EPISTLE CCLXXXI.—Bull for Aldo, first abbot of Châtillon. 330  

EPISTLE CCLXXXII.—To William, lord of Montpellier.—He asks him to work effectively, as the Roman Church’s special son, for its honor and advantage; when time and circumstance require, he will receive recompense from him. 331  

EPISTLE CCLXXXIII.—He confirms to Albero, Archbishop of Trier, and his successors the primacy of Belgic Gaul. 331  

EPISTLE CCLXXXIV.—He appoints Adalbero, Archbishop of Trier, legate of the Apostolic See throughout the archdioceses of Trier, Mainz, Cologne, Salzburg, Bremen, and Magdeburg. 333  

EPISTLE CCLXXXV.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Mary at Salzburg. 334  

EPISTLE CCLXXXVI.—At the request of Archbishop Conrad, he confirms the boundary between the Archbishopric of Magdeburg and the Bishopric of Meissen. 335  

EPISTLE CCLXXXVII.—At the request of Margrave Conrad, he receives the convent of St. John at Gerbstedt under protection and confirms its privileges. 335  

EPISTLE CCLXXXVIII.—He entrusts the Church of St. Pantaleon to the Church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca, and confirms its tithes from the estate of Moveti in the county of Ferrara. 335  

EPISTLE.

CCLXXXIX.—He informs A., archpriest, and the brethren of the church of St Martin of Lucca that he has entrusted the church of St Pantaleon to the brethren of the church of St Frigdian. 335  
EPIST. CCXC.—To B., chaplain of the church of St Julian. 336  
EPIST. CCXCI.—He confirms to the monastery of St Blaise in the Black Forest the cell of Wishilkon. 336  
EPIST. CCXCII.—Privilege for the monastery of St Blaise. 338  
EPIST. CCXCIII.—He confirms the foundation of the canonry of Klosterneuburg, made by St Leopold, Margrave of Austria, receives that canonry under the protection of the Apostolic See, etc. 339  
EPIST. CCXCIV.—To Albero, bishop of Liège.—He states that he has promoted Arnulf to be abbot of Gembloux and has bestowed on him the blessing of office, etc. 341  
EPIST. CCXCV.—To the archbishops of Rheims, Sens, and Tours, whom he admonishes to be merciful and to leave those unjustly oppressed free to appeal to the Apostolic See. 342  
EPIST. CCXCVI.—Privilege for the monastery of Le Port, of the Cistercian Order.—No person is to hunt within the district of the monastery. 343  
EPIST. CCXCVII.—To A., archdeacon, and A., priest, of the Church of Lucca. 344

EPIST. CCC.—To certain priests and canons of St Martin of Lucca. 345

EPIST. CCCII.—On the obedience owed to the Patriarch of Jerusalem. 347

EPIST. CCCIV.—Privilege for the monastery of St Martin of Laon. [Col. 1867] 349  
EPIST. CCCV.—To Hugh, abbot of Prémontré. 350  
EPIST. CCCVI.—He confirms the possessions of the canons of the church of St Marianus at Gubbio. 351  
EPIST. CCCVII.—Privilege concerning churches subject to the bishop of Paris, etc. 352  
EPIST. CCCVIII.—Privilege for the abbey of Alba-Ripa. 353  
EPIST. CCCIX.—To all the faithful dwelling in the kingdom of Constantinople. 354  
EPIST. CCCX.—He transfers the episcopal see of the Church of Roselle to Grosseto. 355  
EPIST. CCCXI.—Privilege for the monastery of St Martin-des-Champs. 357  
EPIST. CCCXII.—Privilege for the convent of St Alexander at Parma. 357  
EPIST. CCCXIII.—He confirms the order of Premonstratensian canons at the monastery of Viltina and its goods, and grants various privileges. 359  
EPIST. CCCXIV.—To Conrad, archbishop of the Church of Salzburg. 561

EPIST. CCCXXI.—To William, Patriarch of Jerusalem.—Concerning the diocese of Tyre. 370  
EPIST. CCCXXII.—He receives the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem under his protection and confirms its possessions. 370  
EPIST. CCCXXIII.—On the subjection owed by the Church of Tyre to the Church of Jerusalem. 372  
EPIST. CCCXXIV.—Privilege for the abbey of Sept-Fontaines. 372  
EPIST. CCCXXV.—He confirms the discipline and rules of the regular canons established throughout the bishopric of Halberstadt. 373  
EPIST. CCCXXVI.—He receives the convent of St Mary at Lamspringe under protection and confirms its privileges and possessions. 373  
EPIST. CCCXXVII.—Privilege for the Church of Hamersleben. 373  
EPIST. CCCXXVIII.—He confirms the discipline, privileges, and possessions of the monastery of St John at Halberstadt. 376  
EPIST. CCCXXIX.—He confirms Bishop Atto’s sentence by which the consuls of Pistoia, plunderers of church property, had been excommunicated. 376  
EPIST. CCCXXX.—He admonishes the clergy of Pisa, Pistoia, Florence, Fiesole, Lucca, Volterra, and Siena to publish and ensure observance of the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the consuls of Pistoia. 376  
EPIST. CCCXXXI.—Privilege for the church of Grace of God. 377  
EPIST. CCCXXXII.—Privilege for the canons of the Church of Porto. 378  
EPIST. CCCXXXIII.—Privilege for the abbey of Floreffe, of the Premonstratensian Order. 381  
EPIST. CCCXXXIV.—He confirms the foundation and privileges of the abbey of Vicoigne, of religious of the Premonstratensian Order near Valenciennes. 382  
EPIST. CCCXXXV.—He receives the Church of Prémontré under the protection of St Peter. 384  
EPIST. CCCXXXVI.—He grants Premonstratensian monasteries immunity from tithes. 386  
EPIST. CCCXXXVII.—Privilege for the Premonstratensian Order. 387  
[Col. 1868] EPIST. CCCXXXVIII.—He confirms the goods of the Church of Belleval. 387  
EPIST. CCCXXXIX.—Privilege for the monastery of St Nicholas of Clairfontaine. 389  
EPIST. CCCXL.—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of St Nicholas of Seven Fountains, in the diocese of Langres. 391  
EPIST. CCCXLI.—To Manasses, bishop of Meaux. 393

EPIST. CCCXLII bis.—Privilege for the Premonstratensian Order. 393  
EPIST. CCCXLIII.—To Stephen, bishop of Autun.—He appoints Al. abbot of Vézelay. 394  
EPIST. CCCXLIV.—To Gregory, bishop of Bergamo. 394

EPIST. CCCXLVI.—Privilege for the church of St John at Madalhorstorf. 395

EPIST. CCCLVI.—Privilege for the monastery of Ringstadt. 405  
EPIST. CCCLVII.—To Bernard, bishop of Sagunto. 407

EPIST. CCCLXIII.—Privilege for the abbey of Walburg. 416

EPIST. CCCLXXII.—Privilege for the monastery of Castellence. 427

EPIST. CCCLXXIV.—Privileges for the abbey of St Saviour at Carraceto. 429

EPIST. CCCLXXVIII.—Privilege for the monastery of Admont. 433  
EPIST. CCCLXXIX.—Privilege for the monastery of Blessed Martin at Muri. 434  
EPIST. CCCLXXX.—At the request of Bishop Ortlieb, he receives the Church of Basel under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 435

EPIST. CCCLXXXII.—Privilege for the abbey of St Stephen at Dijon. 439  
EPIST. CCCLXXXIII.—Privilege for the monastery of St Nicholas and St Medard at Tournai. 441

EPIST. CCCLXXXV.—To Manfred, bishop of Mantua, and Lothair, bishop of Vicenza. 443  
EPIST. CCCLXXXVI.—To Theobald, bishop of Verona. 443  
EPIST. CCCLXXXVII.—Privilege for the monastery of Kamp. 444  
EPIST. CCCLXXXVIII.—Confirmation of the foundation of the abbey of Averbode; certain decrees are laid down concerning its government and immunity. 445  
EPIST. CCCLXXXIX.—Privilege for the monastery of Nonantola. 446

EPIST. CDLXXXVI.—Privilege for the church of Freising. 557

EPIST. DXXIII.—Confirmation of the possessions of Grand-Selve. 588  
EPIST. DXXIV.—Privilege for the church of St Lawrence at Viterbo. 590  
EPIST. DXXV.—Privilege for the church of St Stephen at Toulouse. 591

VARIOUS LETTERS ADDRESSED TO INNOCENT. 657.

LETTER I.—The replies and apologetic writings of Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz, for the Synod of Mainz, which excommunicated Gebehard after he had been examined and convicted of proven crimes, and refuted the allegations that Gebehard’s friends had advanced to Innocent II by stealthy and insinuating approaches. 657.

LETTER II.—From Guigo, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse, to Innocent.—He consoles the supreme pontiff amid the troubles of the schism. 658.

LETTER III.—From the clergy of Trier to Innocent II, Supreme Pontiff, reporting that they have elected Albero as their archbishop. 660.

LETTER IV.—From Lord Olegarius, Bishop of Tarragona, to Innocent. 663.

LETTER V.—From the abbots and clergy of Paris to Innocent.—They report the obstinacy of Theobald, Archdeacon of Paris, toward his bishop. 664.

LETTER VI.—From Stephen, Bishop of Paris, to Innocent.—Concerning the wicked murder of Thomas, prior of St Victor’s. 665.

LETTER VII.—From Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, and A. S. L., to Pope Innocent.—Concerning their proceedings concerning the church of Beciano. 665.

[Col. 1876] LETTER VIII.—From Erbo, Dean of Halberstadt, to Pope Innocent II.—Concerning the election of Gerard, provost of St John’s, as Bishop of Halberstadt. 666.

LETTER IX.—From Emperor Lothair to Pope Innocent II.—Concerning the disputed election of the Bishop of Halberstadt. 668.

LETTER X.—From Henry I, King of England, to Innocent.—He complains that Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, demands obedience from abbots. 669.

LETTER XI.—Letter of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, to Pope Innocent II.—Concerning the death of Henry, King of England. 670.

LETTER XII.—From the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order to Innocent.—It writes on behalf of Humbert, Bishop of Autun, whose jurisdiction the monks of Virzilly did not acknowledge. 671.

LETTER XIII.—From the bishops of the province of Reims to Innocent.—Concerning the condemnation of Abelard at the Council of Sens. 671.

LETTER XIV.—Letter of Albero, Bishop of Verdun, to Pope Innocent.—Concerning the church of St Paul granted to the Premonstratensians. 672.

## ANTIPOPE ANACLETUS

Historical notice. 688 Diplomatic notice. 689 **LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF ANACLETUS.** 689

I.—To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, and all other clergy and laity established throughout Germany and Saxony. 689

II.—To Lothair, King of the Romans, and Queen Richiza. 691

III.—He grants Simon, abbot of Rastede, the use of the mitre, gloves, and sandals, at the request of Adalbero, archbishop of Hamburg. 692

IV.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Paul of the City [Rome]. 692

V.—He exhorts Diego, archbishop of Compostela, to persevere in devotion and faith toward Blessed Peter and to send envoys to him. He recalls his former friendship with the archbishop’s father, Peter Leo, of blessed memory. 696

VI.—He writes to the Cluniacs concerning his devotion to their monastery, where, he recalls, he took the monastic habit. He states that, after Honorius’s death, he was elected in the church of St. Mark and consecrated in the basilica of St. Peter. 696

VII.—[To Girard, bishop of Angoulême] he grants a legation from the apostolic see in the regions of Aquitaine. He commends Cardinal Gregory and commissions him to convene a council. 698

VIII.—He commends Gregory, cardinal deacon, sent by him into the regions of Aquitaine, to certain bishops. He exhorts them to show reverence to Girard of Angoulême, to whom, he writes, he has entrusted the holding of a council. 699

IX.—He calls to mind the “noble prudence” of a certain person, on account of friendship with his father of blessed memory. He sets forth the matter of the pontificate conferred upon him, etc. 699

X.—[To Louis, king of the Franks] he commends his legate Otto, bishop of Todi. 700

XI.—[To Philip, son of Louis king of the Franks] he commends his legate Otto. He asks him not to lend his ears to the lies of his enemies. 701

XII.—He commends his legate Otto to certain bishops. 702

XIII.—He commends Otto, bishop of Todi, his legate, to certain bishops. He exhorts them to faithfulness. 703

XIV.—He commends Otto, his legate, to a certain bishop. 703

XV.—To a certain bishop.—He excuses himself for sending letters to him too late. 704

XVI.—He endeavors to bring a certain French prince over to his cause. 705

XVII.—He informs the bishop of Drivasto that he has been made pontiff. He announces that he has sent a legate to the emperor of Constantinople. 706

[Col. 1877]

XVIII.—He laments that King Lothair neither replied to his letters sent through Adalbert, archbishop of Bremen, nor dispatched envoys. 706

XIX.—To Queen Richenza.—He extols her virtue with praises and exhorts her to strengthen King Lothair’s devotion to the Roman Church. 707

XIX *bis*.—To a certain bishop.—He states that he has received homage from the Romans, and complains of the abbot of Farfa as an adversary. 708

XX.—He commands Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, to restore what he has unjustly taken from the archdeacon, and to appear before him on “the next octave of Blessed Martin [18 November].” 709

XXI.—To certain friends. Concerning his promotion. 710

XXII.—He declares that he has resolved to exalt and honor the city of Jerusalem. 711

XXIII.—To a certain friend.—He wonders that he has sent him neither letters nor a messenger, and exhorts him to visit him by letter. 711

XXXII.—To a certain bishop.—He commends to him Marmaldus, a priest whom he has permitted to celebrate Mass. 713
